text:
The Japhug language (local name kɯrɯskɤt ) is spoken by several thousand speakers in Mbarkhams county (in Chinese Maerkang 马尔康 ), Rngaba prefecture, Sichuan province, China, in the 乡 xiāngtownships of ʁdɯrɟɤt ( གདོང་བརྒྱད་ gdoŋ.brgʲad, 龙尔甲 lóng'ěrjiǎ ), sarndzu ( གསར་རྫོང་ gsar.rdzoŋ, 沙尔宗 shāěrzōng ) and tatsʰi ( ད་ཚང་ da.tsʰaŋ, 大藏 dàzàng ), collectively called tɕɤpʰɯ or tɕʰɤpʰɯ (from which the name Japhug is taken). The township of Gdongrbyad is however not traditionally included under the name tɕɤpʰɯ, and is referred instead by the term sɤŋu. All speakers of Japhug are classified as ethnic Tibetans ( 藏族 zàngzú ). The language can be referred to as 茶堡话 chápùhuà in Chinese, reading the character 堡 as pù rather than the more usual bǎo. In Western languages, the `ph' should be pronounced as a stop rather than labiodental fricative, and the `g' read as a voiceless stop. In French for instance, I call the language dʒapuk.

This work focuses almost exclusively on the dialect of kɤmɲɯ village ( 干木鸟 gānmùniǎo, 32° 12′ 43″ N, 101° 57′ 42″ E ), henceforth written as Kamnyu.

Japhug is one of the four Core Gyalrong languages, Tshobdun, Zbu and Situ, represented in fig:map.rgyalrong. It is particularly closely related to the West Gyalrongic languages: Khroskyabs, Stau and Tangut.
Gyalrong languages

Core Gyalrong and West Gyalrongic form the Gyalrongic group, itself a subbranch of Burmo-Gyalrongic  and possibly the larger Tibeto-Gyalrongic group.

Japhug is in contact with both Standard Mandarin and a local variety of Sichuanese. Since no study has focused on the Sichuan Mandarin as spoken by Gyalrong speakers in Mbarkham, the present work represents all Chinese words in Standard Mandarin and pinyin (between chevrons), except for highly nativized Chinese words, presented in IPA.

Situ Gyalrong and Amdo Tibetan used to be the two dominant languages in the area, and many speakers of Japhug also have a passive understanding of Situ, and sometimes also of Tshobdun and Zbu. There is no immediate intercomprehensibility between Gyalrong languages, and speakers of Japhug reportedly need several months to acquire basic conversational skills in Tshobdun. See for example ( ex:nW.mACtsxa ) (§ sec:terminative ), ( ex:nWlWz.thWkWGe.tsa ) (§ sec:relative.postverbal ) and ( ex:mAkABzu.mWjkHW ) (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ), where Tshendzin recounts her experience as a teacher in Tshobdun village, where she had to learn Tshobdun to make herself understood by the pupils' parents.
summary:
Japhug (kɯrɯskɤt) is spoken by several thousand people in Mbarkhams county, Sichuan, in the townships collectively called tɕɤpʰɯ, though Gdongrbyad is traditionally excluded from that name. The language is an ethnic Tibetan language, known in Chinese as 茶堡话, and the work described here focuses mainly on the Kamnyu village dialect.

Japhug is one of the four Core Gyalrong languages and is especially closely related to the West Gyalrongic languages; together these form the Gyalrongic group within Burmo-Gyalrongic, possibly within a larger Tibeto-Gyalrongic family. It is in contact with Standard Mandarin and local Sichuanese, but there is no immediate mutual intelligibility among Gyalrong languages, and Japhug speakers reportedly need months to learn basic Tshobdun conversation.

text:
corpus
With the exception of a chapter in on phonology and a few articles by Lin Youjing  (all on the Tatshi dialect), the available data on Japhug
are essentially from my own fieldwork, based on nine trips (July-August 2002, April-July 2003, July-August 2005, July 2010, July-August 2012, April-May 2014, July-August 2015, July-August 2016, May 2018) and constant contact by phone with my main language consultants. Some texts have been recorded with the help of my former PhD students Gong Xun and Lai Yunfan.

A short grammar, some texts and a dictionary have previously been made available, to which a corpus of transcribed stories on the Pangloss archive can be added, available on https://pangloss.cnrs.fr/corpus/Japhug.

My main consultant is Tshendzin (Chenzhen 陈珍, female, born 1950), a retired schoolteacher (a native speaker of Japhug, bilingual in Sichuan Mandarin since childhood), whose speech and grammaticality judgements are taken as the norm of this grammar.

Stories have also been collected from her husband χpɤltɕin Dpalcan 柏尔青, her maternal uncle Andzin, her nephew (sister's child) Ayang/ Kunbzang Mtsho, and other Kamnyu people, in particular Tshering Skyid. Most traditional stories are typical of Tibetan folklore and not specific to Japhug-speaking areas, but some procedural texts, descriptions of local plants and animals, as well as accounts of local topography, include unique insight into local culture. In addition, a few conversations have been recorded.

The majority of examples in this grammar (except in the grammar sketch in chapter chap:sketch ) are taken from texts or conversations rather than elicited. Most of the texts cited are already available on Pangloss.
Temporal synchronization between transcription and audio was automatically accomplished using forced alignment, and whenever available, a hyperlink to the doi of the segment is provided for each example sentence in the grammar. The doi were semi-automatically added using the program DOI-Mercy written by Alexander Delaporte. Only the informative part of the URL is indicated. To obtain the complete URL, the string https://doi.org/10.24397/pangloss- has to be prefixed to it.

In addition, I indicate for all examples a title in ASCII characters: reports that this citation format is sufficient to find the relevant data.

Conversations are not included in the archive at the moment of writing, but individual sound files of the sentences quoted in this grammar are preserved in a private database. In addition, a certain number of sentences have been noted down during participant observation, and lack recordings.

Since speakers I have worked with only recount a limited number of traditional stories (some of which in any case are from written sources; in particular, the story `The fox' 0004087 told by Kunbzang Mtsho is clearly adapted from the Grimm fairy tale `Der goldene Vogel'), I have resorted to translation from Chinese to collect a larger corpus. Tshendzin provided surprisingly idiomatic renderings of various storybooks for children (including Grimm tales, Andersen tales, Liaozhai zhiyi 聊斋志异, Arabian nights and Xiyouji 西游记 ). These documents are not given the same value as more spontaneous texts, and are systematically indicated by adding the extension ``-zh" to the document name. Systematic comparison with the original text is offered whenever any suspicion of calque from Chinese exists. However, the immense morphosyntactic difference between Chinese and Japhug makes it necessary to completely rework the structure of the sentences in most cases (see for instance ex:CWmaqʰua, § sec:apprehensive.function ), so that even if there is undoubtedly influence from Chinese, even the way Chinese is adapted into Japhug is itself an interesting topic of research.
summary:
The Japhug data in this grammar come mainly from the author’s own fieldwork over nine research trips, plus ongoing phone contact with consultants, with additional recordings made by former students and some published materials, texts, and Pangloss corpus data. The main consultant is Tshendzin, whose speech and judgments serve as the norm, while other speakers contributed stories, procedural texts, local descriptions, and conversations.

Most examples in the grammar are drawn from texts or conversations rather than elicitation, and many are linked to recordings through forced alignment and DOI references. Because spontaneous traditional stories were limited, the author also used Chinese-to-Japhug translations to expand the corpus, marking these texts separately and comparing them with the originals when Chinese influence is suspected.

text:
Rather than being intended as the final word on Japhug grammar, this book is conceived as a tool for exploring the Japhug corpus and learning the language.

The reader is invited to start with the grammar sketch (chapter chap:sketch ). The rest of the grammar contains two chapters on phonology ( chap:phono, § sec:clusters.redp ), five on nouns and noun phrases ( chap:nominal.morphology to chap:noun.phrase ), eleven on verbal morphology ( chap:verb.template to chap:tame ), five on syntax (§ sec:basic.syntax to chap:degree ), as well as a chapter chap:ideophones.sfp on expressives and another one chap:kinship on kinship.

In writing this grammar I have always preferred to abstain from definite judgement rather than provide incorrect data, and the description remains thus incomplete in many aspects, in particular in accounting for minute semantic differences between similar constructions, or on the grammaticality of borderline sentences (about which speakers sometimes change their mind). There are many points of uncertainty in many aspects of the morphosyntax (and even in some topics of phonology), and further research on finer points of phonology, morphosyntax and historical linguistics are much needed, with additional data from different speakers.
summary: The book is presented not as the final word on Japhug grammar, but as a tool for exploring the Japhug corpus and learning the language, beginning with a grammar sketch and then covering phonology, nominal morphology, verbal morphology, syntax, expressives, and kinship. The author emphasizes that the description is deliberately cautious and incomplete in many areas, especially regarding subtle semantic distinctions and borderline grammaticality judgments, and calls for further research based on more data from different speakers.

text:
This work focuses on the grammar of the language, and only contains a single chapter ( chap:kinship, on the kinship system) dedicated to ethnology. However, the corpus that has been collected contains many traditional stories, as well as procedural texts describing the traditional life before massive sinicization. Examples from these texts are found on nearly all the pages of this grammar, and their interest is not purely linguistic. Thus, the section on place names presents a mythological story explaining the origin of a name ( ex:qaprANar.kW, § sec:place.names ), the chapter on orientation preverbs contains an account of the traditional living-room/kitchen (§ sec:orientation.kitchen ) and an introduction to weaving (§ sec:orientation.loom ), and the section on antipassive derivations includes a passage on rain-calling and mountain tutelary spirits (see example ex:znArGAma, § sec:antipassive.avoidance ). In this sense, traditional culture permeates this grammar from beginning till end.

Further ethnographical work is necessary, in particular on kinship, traditional houses, weaving and ethnobotany, and it is hoped that this grammar (together with the dictionary) will make it possible to properly describe local culture through the medium of Japhug rather than Chinese.
summary: The grammar is primarily a study of the language, with only one chapter devoted specifically to ethnology, but its corpus includes many traditional stories and procedural texts about life before major sinicization. As a result, ethnographic material appears throughout the grammar, including mythological explanations of place names, descriptions of traditional houses and weaving, and accounts of rain-calling and mountain spirits. The author concludes that further ethnographic work is needed, especially on kinship, houses, weaving, and ethnobotany, and hopes the grammar and dictionary will help describe local culture through Japhug rather than Chinese.

text:
This chapter offers a short introduction to the phonology and morphosyntax of the Japhug language. It is written for typologists and comparative linguists wanting to get a quick general picture of this language, before delving into the core of the grammar.

Morphosyntactic phenomena are illustrated mainly using simplified elicited examples rather than examples gleaned from texts and conversations as in the rest of the grammar.
summary: This chapter provides a brief introduction to the phonology and morphosyntax of Japhug for typologists and comparative linguists who want an overview before studying the full grammar. It presents morphosyntactic phenomena mainly through simplified elicited examples, rather than through examples taken from texts and conversations.

text:
vowel consonant
Japhug has 8 vowels (§ sec:vowels ) and 50 consonant phonemes (§ sec:consonant.phonemes ), which can be combined into more than 400 biconsonantal or triconsonantal clusters in the onset (§ sec:inventory.clusters ). Additional clusters are attested across syllable boundaries (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ). In coda position, only 12 consonants are found, and no clusters are possible: several phonological contrasts are neutralized (§ sec:codas.inventory ).

The IPA-based transcription in this grammar is a spelling system that is not strictly phonological: it uses different symbols to represent the allophones of some phonemes (in particular w, § sec:consonant.phonemes, § sec:wC.clusters ). An alternative Tibetan-based orthography for use by native speakers (§ sec:tibetan.script ) is also provided.

Japhug is very far removed from the isolating, tonal and ``monosyllabic'' type once considered to be typical of Sino-Tibetan languages. Japhug lacks tonal contrasts (§ sec:stress ), and monosyllabic and monomorphemic words are a minority (§ sec:wordhood.verb ). Words of six syllables or more are not rare in the corpus, as shown by the verb form ( ex:akAtWnWrAZinW ) below.

exe

a-kɤ-tɯ-nɯ-rɤʑí-nɯ \\
irr - pfv -2- auto -stay- pl \\
`May you stay (here).'
exe

Non-final syllables have strong phonotactic constraints at least in the native vocabulary (§ sec:non.final.syllable ). The last syllable of verbal and nominal stems generally receives stress (as the syllable -ʑi- in ex:akAtWnWrAZinW, § sec:stress ) and allows the maximal number of vowel and consonant contrasts.
summary:
Japhug has 8 vowels and 50 consonant phonemes, with extensive onset clustering and some clusters across syllable boundaries, but codas are highly restricted: only 12 consonants occur there and no clusters are possible. The grammar’s IPA transcription is not strictly phonological, since it distinguishes some allophones, and an additional Tibetan-based orthography is provided for native speakers.

The language differs sharply from the stereotypical isolating, tonal, monosyllabic Sino-Tibetan type: it has no tonal contrasts, monosyllabic and monomorphemic words are a minority, and words of six or more syllables are not uncommon. Non-final syllables have strong phonotactic restrictions, while the final syllable of verbal and nominal stems usually bears stress and allows the greatest number of vowel and consonant contrasts.

text:
parts of speech
Unlike other Trans-Himalayan languages such as Sinitic, where the identification of word classes requires extensive syntactic analysis, most parts of speech in Japhug can be straightforwardly defined on the basis of morphology.

Japhug has open and closed parts of speech. The three main open parts of speech are nouns, verbs and ideophones.

noun
Nouns can in their turn be subdivided into four classes with different morphological properties. First, inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ) require the presence of a possessive prefix (§ sec:possessive.paradigm ). Second, alienably possessed nouns allow a possessive prefix, but do not require it. Third, counted noun (§ sec:counted.nouns ) take numeral prefixes (§ sec:numeral.prefixes ). Fourth, unpossessible nouns cannot be prefixed (§ sec:unpossessible.nouns ).

verb
Verbs are at the core of Japhug grammar, and have the richest morphology of all parts of speech -- no less than nine chapters (from chap:verb.template to chap:tame ), about half of the grammar, is devoted to verbal morphology. Unlike other Trans-Himalayan languages such as Khaling,
whose verbs are a closed class, Japhug has a productive system of denominal and deideophonic morphology (§ chap:denominal ), allowing a constant creation of new verbs. Apart from a handful of defective verbs (§ sec:intr.person.irregular, § sec:irregular.transitive ), all verbs require orientation preverbs (§ sec:orientation.preverbs ) in most finite forms, and are the only part of speech compatible with these preverbs. Person indexation morphology (§ sec:intransitive.paradigm ) is also a criterion for identifying verbs, but it is not always applicable since some verbs only occur in 3sg with no indexation affixes (§ sec:intransitive.invariable ), and since a few predicative words have adopted number indexation suffixes by analogy with verbs (§ sec:non.finite.indexation ).

ideophone
Ideophones (§ sec:idph ) can also be distinguished from other parts of speech by specific morphological patterns (§ sec:ideo.regular ).

adjective
There is no specific class of ``adjective'' in Japhug. Words describing properties belong to three different parts of speech: adjectival stative verbs, which can be distinguished from other stative verbs by their ability to undergo the tropative derivation (§ sec:tropative ), ideophones, and also property nouns, a subclass of inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:property.nouns ).

Closed parts of speech comprise numerals (§ sec:plain.numerals ) and pronouns (chapter chap:pronouns ), which also have specific morphology, and invariable words including postpositions (§ ex:postpositions ), determiners (§ sec:determiners ), adverbs (§ sec:sentential.adverbs, § sec:degree.adverbs ), linkers (§ sec:coordination, § sec:tCe.topic ), interjections and calling sounds (§ sec:other.expressive ) and sentence final particles (§ sec:sfp ).
summary:
Japhug word classes can mostly be identified directly through morphology, unlike in some other Trans-Himalayan languages that require extensive syntactic analysis. Its main open classes are nouns, verbs, and ideophones, while closed classes include numerals, pronouns, and several invariable word types.

Nouns fall into four morphological types: inalienably possessed, alienably possessed, counted, and unpossessible. There is no separate adjective class; property words are expressed through adjectival stative verbs, ideophones, and property nouns. Verbs are especially central and highly inflected, with productive denominal and deideophonic morphology, and they are the only class that combines with orientation preverbs in most finite forms.

text:
noun
This section presents nominal inflection, derivation as well as grammatical categories expressed by syntactic rather than morphological means within noun phrases and postpositional phrases.
summary: This section covers noun morphology, including nominal inflection and derivation. It also discusses grammatical categories that are expressed syntactically rather than through morphology within noun phrases and postpositional phrases.

text:
There is no gender, definiteness, obviation, negation and tense-aspect-modality-evidential inflection or derivation on nouns in Japhug.

The whole category of gender is completely absent from Japhug grammar; there are only suffixes for male and female animals, and even these are borrowed from Tibetan (§ sec:gender ).
gender

There is no dedicated marker of definiteness (§ sec:definiteness ), but the aforementioned topic marker iɕqʰa only occurs on definite referents (§ sec:iCqha ). Indefiniteness can be marked by the indefinite article ci (§ sec:indef.article ) derived from the numeral `one' (§ sec:one.to.ten ).
definite

While an obviative/proximative contrast is reflected by some uses of the inverse prefix in the inflection of transitive verbs (§ sec:obviation.possessor ), Japhug lacks obviative morphology on nouns (§ sec:possessive.prefix.obv.def ), unlike Algonquian languages (for instance ).
obviative proximate

Polarity and Tense-aspect-modality-evidentiality, which are prominently encoded by verbal morphology (§ sec:negation, chapter chap:tame ), even on nominalized verb forms (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes ), are completely absent from nominal morphology, and various types of participial clauses have to be used instead (§ sec:non.existing.derivation ).
summary:
Japhug has no gender system, no nominal definiteness marking, and no obviative morphology on nouns. Indefiniteness may be expressed with the article *ci*, and the topic marker *iɕqʰa* occurs only with definite referents.  

Nominal morphology also lacks negation and tense-aspect-modality-evidential marking, which are instead expressed through verbal morphology or by using participial clauses.

text:
number dual
Number can be indicated by the dual ni (§ sec:dual.determiners ) and plural ra (§ sec:plural.determiners ) determiners. These determiners are not mutually incompatible with numerals, as shown by ( ex:jla.RnWz.ni ), where the redundant ʁnɯztwo can be added (these redundant forms, though grammatical, are not very common). The fact that numerals (and other postnominal modifiers, including relative clauses) can be inserted between nouns and number determiners show that they are not analyzable as number suffixes.

exe

jla (ʁnɯz) ni \\
male.hybrid.yak two du \\
`The two male hybrid yaks' 0003660#S7
exe

Some nouns however do have an inflectional number category, expressed by a prefixal paradigm partially illustrated in Table tab:num.prefixes.introduction (§ sec:numeral.prefixes ).

This type of nouns corresponds to the category called `classifiers' (, ) ( 量词 <liàngcí> in Chinese) in works on the grammar of Chinese, Japanese and other languages of East Asia. However, this terminology is particularly clumsy in the case of Japhug. Unlike in languages such as Chinese or Thai, nouns in Japhug do not require a `classifier' to be used with a numeral, as shown by ( ex:tCheme.ci ) The numeral cione is grammaticalized as an indefinite marker (§ sec:indef.article ). and ( ex:tCheme.XsWm ).

exe

tɕʰeme ci \\
girl one/ indef \\
`A/one girl'

tɕʰeme χsɯm \\
girl three \\
`Three girls'
exe

When occurring as postnominal modifiers ( ex:tCheme.tWrdoR ), the two main functions of nouns with numerals prefixes are partitive (`one of the $X$') and distributive (`each $X$') depending on the constructions where they appear (§ sec:CN.quantifier ).

exe

tɕʰeme tɯ-rdoʁ \\
girl one-piece \\
`One of the girls'; `Each girl...'; `One girl' 0004053#S36
exe

In addition, although a handful of `classifiers' are indeed specific to a particular semantic category of nouns (§ sec:CN.classification ), the generic `classifier' tɯ-rdoʁone piece can be used as modifier with nearly all referents.

For these reasons, this grammar favours the term counted noun based on morphology, rather than ``classifier'' (an extremely marginal function of these words) or ``quantifier'' (not specific enough, since there are many quantifiers that are not counted nouns, § sec:quantifiers.determiners ) to refer to nouns with numeral prefixes such as tɯ-sŋione day or tɯ-rdoʁone piece.
summary: The passage explains that Japhug number can be marked by dual and plural determiners, which can co-occur with numerals and other postnominal modifiers, showing that they are not number suffixes. It also notes that some nouns have prefixal number morphology; although these have sometimes been called “classifiers,” Japhug nouns do not require such forms with numerals, and their main functions are partitive or distributive in certain constructions. For this reason, the grammar prefers the term *counted noun* for these prefixed forms rather than “classifier” or “quantifier.”

text:
Japhug lacks case inflection, but has a few regular adverbializing derivations (§ sec:denominal.adverb ), whose functions resemble that of oblique cases: the comitative kɤ́- (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) and the perlative (§ sec:perlative ).

Grammatical relations on noun phrases are encoded by postpositions such as the ergative kɯ (§ sec:erg.kW ), the genitive ɣɯ (§ sec:genitive ) and the comitative cʰo (§ sec:comitative ), as well as relator nouns (§ sec:relator.nouns ) such as the dative ɯ-ɕki or ɯ-pʰe (§ sec:dative ). With the sole exception of the genitive forms of a few pronouns such as aʑɯɣ 1sg: gen (from aʑo 1sg and ɣɯ, § sec:pronouns.gen ), the postpositions do not merge phonologically with the previous word. As shown by ( ex:Wpi.ni.kW ) and ( ex:ra.GW.nWfsapaR ), they are located at the end of the noun phrase, further away from the head noun than all determiners, including number markers.

exe

[[ɯ-pi ni] kɯ ] pɣa nɯ pa-mto-ndʑi\\
3sg. poss -elder.sibling du erg bird dem 3: aor -see- du \\
`His two elder siblings saw the bird.'
exe

exe

[[tɯrme ra] ɣɯ ] nɯ-fsapaʁ \\
person pl gen 3pl. poss -cattle \\
`People's cattle'
exe

genitive
In addition, it is possible to make a pause between the noun and the postposition kɯ or ɣɯ that follows: the postposition can be procliticized to the following word. A considerable number of examples can be found in the corpus (§ ex:word.vs.clitic.postp ).

locative
While Situ Gyalrong does have locative suffixes, Japhug only uses postpositions (§ sec:core.locative ) and/or relator nouns (§ sec:relator.postposition.location ) to express location, goal and source of motion. The only traces of the proto-Gyalrong suffixes are the locative postposition zɯ, which was degrammaticalized from a suffix *-s (§ sec:core.locative ), and a few isolated lexicalized forms (§ sec:locative.j, § sec:relator.postposition.location ).
summary:
Japhug lacks case inflection, but uses a small set of adverbial derivations and postpositions to express relations that resemble oblique cases. Grammatical relations on noun phrases are marked by postpositions such as the ergative, genitive, and comitative, plus relator nouns for functions like dative, and these elements normally occur at the end of the noun phrase; they usually do not fuse with the preceding word, though the genitive can form some fused pronoun forms and may also cliticize to the following word after a pause.  

For spatial relations, Japhug uses postpositions and relator nouns to express location, goal, and source, rather than locative suffixes. The only remnants of the older suffix system are the locative postposition zɯ and a few isolated lexicalized forms.

text: The main nominal morphosyntactic category expressed by an inflectional paradigm in Japhug is possession, encoded by a series of possessive prefixes (§ sec:possessive.paradigm ).
summary: In Japhug, the main nominal morphosyntactic category expressed through an inflectional paradigm is possession. This is encoded by a series of possessive prefixes.

text:
prefix!possessive possession!prefix

The possessive paradigm is nearly the same for all nouns ( tab:possessive.paradigms.intro ), but some nouns such as tɯ-kuhead require a indefinite possessor prefix tɯ, tɤ- or ta- when no definite possessor is present, while other nouns like kʰahouse can occur in bare stem form. The former are inalienably possessed nouns, comprising in particular body parts (§ sec:body.part ) and kinship terms (§ sec:kinship ), while the latter are alienably possessed nouns. Some inalienably possessed nouns have been grammaticalized as relator nouns (§ sec:relator.nouns ) marking the syntactic function of noun phrases. Furthermore, a handful of nouns have become TAME markers (§ sec:WmdoR.TAME ).

Possessors are obligatorily indicated by possessive prefixes. An overt possessor can be optionally added. For instance, the meaning `my cow' can be expressed by the noun form a-nɯŋa with a simple possessive prefix, but this noun can be additionally preceded by the genitive pronoun aʑɯɣ ( ex:aZWG.anWNa ) or even by the absolutive aʑo.

exe

(aʑɯɣ) a-nɯŋa \\
1sg 1sg. poss -cow \\
`My cow'
exe

The possessive prefix cannot be elided, even in the case of alienably possessed nouns like nɯŋacow. In ( ex:aZWG.anWNa ), removing the a- prefix would result in an agrammatical form ($ $ aʑɯɣ nɯŋa ).

The phrase expressing the possessor always precedes the possessum. Genitive marking on the possessor is optional: in ( ex:ni.GW.ndZinWNa ), the genitive postposition ɣɯ (§ sec:gen.possession ) can be elided.

exe

[a-mu a-wa ni] (ɣɯ) ndʑi-nɯŋa \\
1sg. poss -mother 1sg. poss -father du gen 3du. poss -cow \\
`My parents' cow'
exe

The person and number of the possessive prefix on the possessum is the same as that of the noun phrase or pronoun marking the possessor: in ( ex:ni.GW.ndZinWNa ) for instance, the third dual possessive prefix ndʑi- agrees in number with the dual possessor phrase a-mu a-wa ni. Number agreement mismatch is only attested in very restricted contexts (§ ex:prefix.expression.of.possession ).
summary:
The passage explains that nouns fall into two possessive classes: inalienably possessed nouns, which require an indefinite possessor prefix when no definite possessor is present, and alienably possessed nouns, which may occur as bare stems. Possessors are always marked by a possessive prefix on the noun, and an overt possessor phrase may optionally be added before the possessum, with genitive marking on the possessor also optional.  

It also notes that the possessive prefix cannot be omitted, and that the person and number of the prefix normally agree with the possessor phrase or pronoun. Some inalienably possessed nouns have been reanalyzed as relator nouns or as TAME markers.

text:
alienabilization
Nouns can only take one single possessive prefix, except when inalienably possessed nouns are turned into alienably possessed nouns (§ sec:alienabilization ), by stacking a definite possessor prefix (any of the prefixes in tab:possessive.paradigms.intro except the indefinite ones) on the indefinite possessive form. For instance, the possessed form ɯ-lu ( ex:nWNa.Wlu ) of tɤ-lumilk without prefix stacking is used when the possessor is the cow producing the milk, but the alienabilized possessive forms ɯ-tɤ-lu `his/her/its milk, the milk for him/her/it' ( ex:lWlu.WtAlu ) or a-tɤ-lu `my milk' ( ex:atAlu ), expressing the person or animal drinking the milk as possessor, have a combination of two prefixes.

exe

xlist

nɯŋa (ɣɯ) ɯ-lu \\
cow gen 3sg. poss -milk \\
`(The/a) cow's milk'

lɯlu (ɣɯ) ɯ-tɤ-lu \\
cat gen 3sg. poss - indef. poss -milk \\
`The milk for the cat (i.e. given to the cat to drink)'

(aʑo) a-tɤ-lu \\
1sg 1sg. poss - indef. poss -milk \\
`My milk (i.e. for me to drink)'
xlist
exe

Stacking of two definite possessor prefixes, or of a numeral prefix with a definite possessor prefix, are not grammatical.
summary:
Nouns normally take only one possessive prefix, but inalienably possessed nouns can be “alienabilized” by adding a definite possessor prefix to the indefinite possessive form, resulting in two prefixes. This construction is used when the possessor is interpreted as the recipient or user of the possessed item, as in forms meaning “the milk for the cat” or “my milk.”  

However, stacking two definite possessor prefixes, or combining a numeral prefix with a definite possessor prefix, is ungrammatical.

text:
generic
The indefinite possessor prefix has three allomorphs tɯ- (as in tɯ-kuhead), tɤ- (as in tɤ-seblood) or ta- (as in ta-mawork). It has to be distinguished from the generic possessor prefix tɯ- (§ sec:indef.genr.poss ). Generic possessors are identical with indefinite possessors in the case of inalienably possessed nouns selecting the tɯ- prefix, for instance tɯ-ku can either mean `head' or `one's head'. With inalienably possessed nouns selecting the tɤ- or ta- allomorphs, a contrast is found between tɤ-se `blood' and tɯ-se `one's blood' ( ex:tWse.kutshi ) for instance.

exe

qajɯsmɤnba kɯ tɯ-se ku-tsʰi ŋu \\
leech erg genr. poss -blood ipfv -drink be: fact \\
`The leech drinks people's (i.e. one's) blood.'
exe

The generic possessor prefix can also occur on alienably possessed nouns, as in tɯ-kʰa `one's house'.

No more than one generic referent is possible per clause, so that if a noun with generic possessor prefix is found in the same clause as a verb with generic indexation, there is obligatory co-reference (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ), as in ( ex:tWrpW.WrZaB ) between the possessor of tɯ-rpɯ `one's mother's brother' (indefinite form tɤ-rpɯ, § sec:kinship ) and the transitive subject of the verb tu-kɯ-ti `one says' (§ sec:irregular.transitive ).

exe

tɯ -rpɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rʑaβ ɯ-ɕki tɕe ``a-ɬaʁ" tu- kɯ -ti ŋu \\
genr. poss -mother's.brother gen 3sg. poss -wife 3sg. poss - dat loc 1sg. poss -aunt ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
` One $_i$ calls one $_i$'s mother's brother's wife `my aunt' (i.e. one says `my aunt' to one's mother's brother's wife).'
exe
summary:
The indefinite possessor prefix has three allomorphs, tɯ-, tɤ-, and ta-, and must be distinguished from the generic possessor prefix tɯ-. With inalienably possessed nouns, the generic and indefinite possessors are sometimes identical when the noun takes tɯ-, but they contrast when the noun selects tɤ- or ta-; the generic possessor can also occur on alienably possessed nouns.  

Only one generic referent may appear per clause, so if a noun with generic possessor marking co-occurs with a verb marked for generic indexation, they must refer to the same participant.

text:
predicative possession
Predicative possession can be expressed by the verb aroown (§ sec:semi.transitive, § sec:possessive.constructions ), encoding the possessor as subject, but the most frequent construction involves an existential verb (§ sec:existential.basic ) with the possessum as subject and the possessor marked by a possessive prefix on the possessum, optionally with a genitive phrase (§ sec:possessive.mihi.est ). The construction is the same for alienably ( ex:nWnWNa.XsWm.pjAtu ) and inalienably ( ex:nWtCW.XsWm.pjAtu ) possessed nouns.

exe

xlist

kɯβʁa ra ɣɯ nɯ-nɯŋa kɯ-dɤn pjɤ-tu \\
noble pl gen 3pl. poss -cow sbj: pcp -be.many ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`The nobles had many cows.'

kɯβʁa ra ɣɯ nɯ-tɕɯ χsɯm pjɤ-tu \\
noble pl gen 3pl. poss -son three ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`The nobles had three sons.'
xlist
exe

In this construction, the existential verbs rarely agree in number with the possessum: in both ( ex:nWnWNa.XsWm.pjAtu ) and ( ex:nWtCW.XsWm.pjAtu ), the singular verb form pjɤ-tu is by far more commonly used than its plural counterpart (§ sec:optional.indexation ).
summary: Predicative possession may be expressed with the verb *aroown*, which encodes the possessor as subject, but the most common pattern uses an existential verb with the possessum as subject and the possessor marked by a possessive prefix on the possessum, optionally followed by a genitive phrase. This construction is used for both alienably and inalienably possessed nouns. The existential verb usually does not agree in number with the possessum, and the singular form is much more common than the plural.

text:
compounding
Compounding can be realized by the simple concatenation of noun (or verb) stems.

In compounds comprising two noun stems (§ sec.n.n.compounds ), whose order is modifier-modified, no possessive prefixes occur between the nominal stems, even if the second noun is inalienably possessed. For instance, the compound built from kɯrɯTibetan and the inalienably possessed tɯ-ŋgaclothes is kɯrɯ-ŋga `Tibetan clothes', rather than $ $ kɯrɯ-tɯŋga.

In many cases, the non-final elements of the compound appear in a bound form, the bound state (§ sec:status.constructus ), which is characterized by a vocalic change to either -ɤ or -ɯ (§ sec:vowel.alternations.compounds ) For instance, compounding tɯ-kuhead with tɤ-rmehair yields tɤ-kɤ-rme `head hair' with the bound state kɤ- from -ku. The compound inherits the allomorph tɤ- of the indefinite possessor prefix of the head of the compound tɤ-rmehair.
summary: Compounding is formed by simple concatenation of noun or verb stems. In noun–noun compounds with modifier–modified order, no possessive prefix appears between the stems even when the second noun is inalienably possessed, and non-final elements often take a bound form with vocalic change to -ɤ or -ɯ. The compound also inherits the allomorph of the indefinite possessor prefix from the head noun, as in tɤ-kɤ-rme ‘head hair.’

text:
Some suffixal nominal derivations come from compounds with a grammaticalized noun as second element, in particular the diminutive suffixes (§ sec:diminutive ). The recent origin of these suffixes can be shown by the fact that a free form still co-exists with the corresponding compound in some cases. For instance, the compound χpɯn-pɯ `little monk' from χpɯnmonk with the diminutive -pɯ occurs in free variation with the phrase ( ex:XpWn.WpW ), in which the main noun is followed by the alienably possessed property noun ɯ-pɯlittle one (§ sec:property.nouns ) derived from tɤ-pɯoffspring, young.

exe

χpɯn ɯ-pɯ \\
monk 3sg. poss -little.one \\
`(The/a) little monk'
exe

Not all suffixal derivations have transparent origins. For instance, the privative -lu suffix (§ sec:privative ) is not related to any independently attested nominal or verbal root. It turns an inalienably possessed noun into a non-possessible one mainly used as postnominal modifier (§ ex:attributive.postnominal ), removing possessive prefixes and subjecting the nominal stem to bound state alternation ( tɯ-kuhead kɤ-lu `headless').

Prefixal nominal derivations, however, do not originate from elements of compounds, but rather from participial forms of denominal verbs (§ sec:denom.aGW, § sec:denom.andZi ).

The social relation collective kɤndʑi- prefix (§ sec:social.collective ) occurs on the bare stem of kinship terms and a few other terms of social relationship to indicate a group of people. When the group members are related to each other by a symmetrical relationship ( tɤ-xtɤɣbrother (of a male) kɤndʑi-xtɤɣ `group of brothers'), the social relation collective is based on only one nominal stem, but when the relationship is asymmetrical, kɤndʑi- can be prefixed to two compounded noun stems, as in kɤndʑi-wɤmɯ-snom `group of siblings' from tɤ-wɤmɯbrother (of a female) and tɤ-snomsister (of a male).

The comitative derivation (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) is built by adding the prefixes kɤ́- or kɤɣɯ- to reduplicated noun stems. It derives an adverb meaning `together with $X$' which can have scope over the whole clause, or be restricted to a noun phrase. It can apply to both inalienably possessed nouns ( tɯ-ŋgaclothes kɤ́-ŋgɯ ŋga `together with his/her clothes') or alienably possessed ones ( jlamale hybrid yak kɤ́-jlɯ jla `together with the/his/her hybrid yak'). Comitative derivation can preserve the indefinite possessor prefix of inalienably possessed nouns, causing alienabilization (§ sec:alienabilization.intro, § sec:alienabilization ). For instance, tɤ-rtehat has two comitative forms: kɤ́-rtɯ rte `together with his/her hat' (wearing it) and kɤ́-tɤ-rtɯ rte `together with a/the hat' (not wearing it).
summary:
Some suffixal nominal derivations come from compounds with a grammaticalized noun as second element, as shown by diminutive suffixes such as -pɯ, whose recent origin is supported by the coexistence of a free form and a corresponding compound. By contrast, the privative suffix -lu has no independently attested root and derives inalienably possessed nouns into non-possessible postnominal modifiers, removing possessive prefixes and triggering bound state alternation.

Prefixal nominal derivations do not come from compounds but from participial forms of denominal verbs. The passage also describes the social relation collective kɤndʑi-, which marks groups of kin or social relations, and the comitative derivation, which uses kɤ́- or kɤɣɯ- with reduplicated noun stems to mean “together with X” and can affect possessive marking, including alienabilization.

text:
Verbs have a considerably more elaborate morphology than all other parts of speech (§ sec:verb.intro ). Verbal morphology is strongly prefixal (§ sec:prefixal.chain ), with some vowel contractions (§ sec:contraction ). Non-concatenative morphology includes stem alternations (§ sec:stem.alternation ) as well as infixation (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain, § sec:intr.person.irregular, § sec:autoben.position ).

Japhug verbal morphology is considerably more regular than that of other Gyalrong languages, in particular Zbu  and Situ. Most alternations are productive and predictable, and irregular verbs are limited in number (§ sec:intr.person.irregular, § sec:irregular.transitive ).

As illustrated by ( ex:amAGWnWtWwGznAre ), a verb form can comprise six inflectional prefixes (in blue) arranged in a rigid template (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) and several derivational prefixes (in red).

exe

a$^-6$-mɤ$^-5$-ɣɯ$^-4$-nɯ$^-3$-tɯ́$^-2$-wɣ$^-1$- z-nɤ-re \\
irr $^-6$- neg $^-5$- cisl $^-4$- pfv $^-3$-2$^-2$- inv $^-1$- caus - denom -laughter \\
`Don't let him come and make you laugh.'
exe

The suffixal chain (§ sec:suffixes ) only includes inflectional suffixes, with a maximal number of four slots ( ex:WmApWkWmtoandZici.intro ).

exe

ɯmɤ$^-6$-pɯ$^-3$-kɯ$^-2$-mto- t$^+1$-a$^+2$-ndʑi$^+3$-ci$^+4$ \\
prob $^-6$- aor $^-3$- peg $^-2$-see- pst: tr $^+1$- 1sg $^+2$- du $^+3$- peg $^+4$ \\
`It looks like I have seen the two of them.'
exe

Numerous non-adjacent dependencies (§ sec:templatic.verb ) are observed across the prefixal and the suffixal chains.

Inflectional verbal morphology encodes person and number of one or two core arguments (chapter chap:indexation, § sec:indexation.tr.intro ), orientation (§ sec:orientation.preverbs ), associated motion (§ sec:associated.motion ), negation (§ sec:negation ) and Tense-Aspect-Modality-Evidentiality (chapter chap:tame ).
summary:
Japhug verbs have much richer morphology than other parts of speech, and this morphology is mainly prefixal, though it also includes vowel contractions, stem alternations, and infixation. Compared with other Gyalrong languages such as Zbu and Situ, Japhug verbal morphology is more regular, with most alternations being productive and predictable and only a limited set of irregular verbs.

Verb forms can contain up to six inflectional prefixes in a fixed order, plus several derivational prefixes, while the suffixal chain contains only inflectional suffixes and can have up to four slots. The system also shows many non-adjacent dependencies, and inflectional morphology marks person and number, orientation, associated motion, negation, and TAM-evidential meanings.

text:
indexation
All finite verb forms in Japhug have obligatory person indexation. Since the 3sg has zero marking as in many languages of the world, indexation is not conspicuous on intransitive verbs requiring a 3sg subject (§ sec:intransitive.invariable ), but indirectly observable even on transitive dummy verbs (§ sec:transitive.dummy ) due to the presence of stem alternation (§ sec:stem3 ).

Transitive and intransitive verbs are clearly distinguished by a series of seven morphological parameters (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ). Intransitive verbs only index one argument (the intransitive subject, S), and transitive verbs index two arguments (the transitive subject A and the object O). Semi-transitive verbs have intransitive indexation (§ sec:semi.transitive ), but select a second core argument (§ sec:semi.object ). Only a handful of verbs are labile, and can be conjugated either transitively or intransitively (§ sec:lability ).
summary: All finite Japhug verb forms require person indexation, though 3sg is marked by zero and may therefore be less visible, especially on intransitive verbs; even some transitive dummy verbs show it indirectly through stem alternation. The language distinguishes transitive and intransitive verbs morphologically: intransitives index only the subject (S), transitives index both subject (A) and object (O), semi-transitives use intransitive indexing while taking a second core argument, and only a few verbs are labile and can be used either transitively or intransitively.

text:
verb!intransitive
Person indexation in Japhug is best introduced with the intransitive paradigm (§ sec:intransitive.paradigm ), since it is considerably smaller than the transitive one. The regular paradigm is illustrated in tab:intransitive.indexation.intro with the verb mbɣombe in a hurry in the Factual Non-Past, the only TAME without orientation preverb (§ sec:factual ).

The intransitive paradigm has different forms for singular, dual and plural. First persons have dedicated suffixes encoding both person and number; there is no inclusive/exclusive contrast. Second and third person forms are distinguished by the second person tɯ- prefix (on the historical significance of this prefix, see and ). There is no overt third person marker on intransitive verbs. Number markers are shared by second and third person forms: absence of suffix for the singular, -ndʑi for the dual and -nɯ for the plural. Slightly different forms are found in dialects of Japhug other than Kamnyu (§ sec:indexation.suffixes.history ). In addition to the paradigm in tab:intransitive.indexation.intro, a generic person kɯ- prefix also occurs on intransitive verbs (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ).

A handful of intransitive verbs infix rather than prefix the second person (§ sec:intr.person.irregular ). It is the only irregularity related to person indexation in intransitive verbs in Japhug.
summary: Japhug intransitive verbs have a smaller person-indexation paradigm than transitive verbs, with distinct singular, dual, and plural forms. First person forms use dedicated suffixes, while second and third persons are distinguished by the second-person tɯ- prefix; third person has no overt marker, and dual/plural number is marked by shared suffixes (-ndʑi and -nɯ), with no inclusive/exclusive contrast. A generic kɯ- prefix can also occur, and only a few intransitive verbs are irregular in that they infix rather than prefix second person.

text:
verb!transitive
The transitive paradigm is too large to be described in this introductory chapter in its entirety (§ sec:polypersonal ). tab:transitive.paradigm.singular presents the singular forms of the paradigm of the transitive verb satkill (a verb lacking stem alternations) in the Factual Non-Past, which are sufficient to illustrate its basic structure. In this table, the columns represent the objects (O), and the rows the subjects (A). The shaded cells indicate configurations with coreferent subject and object, which are expressed by the reflexive derivation (§ sec:reflexive ) and do not belong to the transitive paradigm.

The comparison of Tables tab:intransitive.indexation.intro and tab:transitive.paradigm.singular shows that the 1sg -a suffix and the second person tɯ- prefix have neutral alignment: they can index intransitive subject, transitive subject or object. In the following, the person configurations are referred to by $X Y$, where $X$ represents the subject and $Y$ the object (for instance 1 3 means `first person subject, third person object'). The eight non-shaded cells of the paradigm in tab:transitive.paradigm.singular can be divided into three groups.

First, 1 3, 2 3 and 3 are the direct configurations with a third person object, whose forms resemble the 1, 2 and 3 forms of the intransitive paradigm (at least in the Factual Non-Past).

Second, 3 1, 3 2 and 3$'$ 3 are the inverse configurations, which have the same prefixes or suffixes as the corresponding intransitive and direct forms (at least in this paradigm), but take in addition the inverse prefix ɣɯ- / wɣ- (the allomorphy of this prefix is explained in § sec:allomorphy.inv ).

Third, 1 2 and 2 1 (without third person) are the local configurations (§ sec:indexation.local ). They are characterized by the presence of the portmanteau ta- and kɯ- prefixes (§ sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history ) not found in the intransitive paradigm.

The reasons for using the terms ``direct'' and ``inverse'' to describe the transitive paradigm are discussed in § sec:direct-inverse.

When both arguments are third person (§ sec:indexation.non.local ), there is a contrast between direct 3 and inverse 3$'$ 3 configurations, whose meaning is not entirely straightforward (§ sec:inverse.3.3.saliency ). The subject of the direct configuration, and object of the inverse one is called proximate (3), and the other argument obviative (3$'$). The direct 3 configuration is by far the most common one in narratives and conversation. The inverse 3$'$ 3 is more restricted; it occurs in particular to index a generic subject with a third person object (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ), and also when the subject is inanimate and the object animate (§ sec:obviation.animacy ).

The majority of transitive verbs (all verbs ending in closed syllables or with front vowels) are non-alternating like satkill. However, about a third of all transitive verbs (those ending in -a, -u, -o and -ɯ ) have stem alternation in the direct configurations with a singular subject in the Factual Non-Past and a few other tenses (§ sec:stem3 ).

tab:transitive.paradigm.singular.alternating illustrates the singular forms of the alternating verb ʁndɯhit, which has additional stem -ʁndi in the 1sg 3, 2sg 3 and 3sg configurations (with blue colouring), which are thus different from the corresponding intransitive forms.

In the Aorist (§ sec:aor.morphology ), a slightly different paradigm is found, illustrated in tab:transitive.paradigm.singular.aorist with the ʁndɯhit. Unlike the Factual Non-Past shown in the previous tables, the Aorist requires an orientation preverb (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), here the upwards tɤ-. There is no stem alternation marking the direct forms, but all verbs have a different series of preverbs (here ta- ) in the direct 3 forms (§ sec:aor.morphology, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). In addition, the 1sg 3 and 2sg 3 forms require a -t suffix which redundantly encodes both person and tense-aspect (§ sec:suffixes ).

There is no ambiguity in person indexation in Japhug (unlike for instance in Khaling where 2 1 and 3 1 configurations are identical, ), but there are strong restrictions on number indexation: unless the 1sg suffix is present, only one of the two arguments can be indexed for both person and number, the subject in direct configurations, and the object in inverse and local configurations. Double number indexation only occurs in forms with the 1sg -a suffix, to which additional number suffixes can be added (§ sec:double.number.indexation ), for instance ɣɯ́-ʁndɯ-a-nɯ `they will hit me' ( 3pl 1sg ) where the plural morpheme -nɯ, indexing the number of the subject, follows the 1sg.
summary:
The passage explains the structure of the Japhug transitive verb paradigm using singular forms of a non-alternating verb, distinguishing direct, inverse, and local configurations, while noting that subject–object coreference is handled by a reflexive derivation rather than the transitive paradigm. It also describes person and number indexing patterns: 1sg and second-person markers have neutral alignment, inverse forms add an inverse prefix, local forms use portmanteau prefixes, and number is generally indexed on only one argument unless the 1sg suffix is present.

It further notes that many transitive verbs show stem alternation in direct configurations with singular subjects in the Factual Non-Past, and that the Aorist has a different system with an orientation preverb and no stem alternation marking direct forms. Finally, the text states that person indexation is unambiguous, but number indexation is restricted, with double number marking occurring only when the 1sg suffix is used.

text:
indexation
Person indexation markers (including person-indexing stem alternation and orientation preverbs) are not found on participles, infinitives and other non-finite verb forms (chapter chap:non-finite ). A handful of phatic and exclamative words of nominal origin have however developed the ability to take number suffixes (§ sec:inflectionalization.intro, § sec:non.finite.indexation ). Apart from these, words belonging to parts of speech other than verbs are incompatible with the indexation affixes described in this section.
summary: Person indexation markers, including person-indexing stem alternation and orientation preverbs, do not occur on participles, infinitives, or other non-finite verb forms. A few phatic and exclamative words of nominal origin can take number suffixes, but otherwise parts of speech other than verbs are incompatible with the indexation affixes discussed here.

text: This section focuses on morphology. Since the use of the TAME categories involve sometimes subtle semantic nuances, and have to be explained on the basis of examples with a clear context, the discussion of the semantic function of each category is deferred to chapter chap:tame.
summary: This section is devoted to morphology. Because the semantic nuances of the TAME categories are subtle and need to be illustrated with contextual examples, their semantic functions are discussed later in the chapter on TAME.

text:
orientation!preverb
The main morphological exponents of tense, aspect, modality and evidentiality (henceforth TAME) in Japhug are the orientation preverbs (§ sec:orientation.preverbs ). All regular finite verb forms require one and only one preverb (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ), except the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ) which does not take any preverb. The stacking of two or more preverbs is ungrammatical. Only a handful of irregular defective verbs are incompatible with orientation preverbs (§ sec:intr.person.irregular, § sec:irregular.transitive ).

Preverbs encode one out of seven orientations ( tab:orientation.preverbs.intro ), divided into three dimensions: vertical (§ sec:vertical.dimension ), riverine (§ sec:riverine.dimension ) and solar (§ sec:solar.dimension ), to which an unspecified orientation is added. This tridimensional system is not restricted to verbal morphology: locative relator nouns (§ sec:relator.nouns.3d ), egressive postpositions (§ sec:egressive ) and locative adverbs (§ sec:preverbs.adverbs ) have similar systems with six orientations, built from morphemes that are historically related to the preverbs.

There are four series of preverbs ( tab:orientation.preverbs.intro includes two of them, the series A and B) in the Kamnyu dialect, used in different TAME categories (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). Some dialects of Japhug have a slightly different system scriptsize footnotesize footnotesize scriptsize (§ sec:xtokavian.preverbs ).

Orientable verbs (§ sec:orientable.verbs ) are compatible with all orientations; this includes in particular motion verbs like ɣicome and ɬoʁcome out (§ sec:motion.verbs ). With this type of verbs, the preverbs indicate either the absolute direction of the motion (§ sec:tridimensional.preverb ), for instance upwards in ( ex:tANe.tAlhoR ) or have extended meanings (§ sec:orientation.extended ), such as the illative function (§ sec:illative.elative ) of the upstream preverb in ( ex:WNgW.lAGi ).

exe

tɤŋe tɤ-ɬoʁ \\
sun aor: up -come.up \\
`The sun rose.'
exe

exe

ɯ-ŋgɯ lɤ-ɣi \\
3sg. poss -in imp: upstream -come \\
`Come in! (for instance, inside a house)' 0003884#S90
exe

Non-orientable verbs only select a restricted number of lexically determined orientations, sometimes only one (§ sec:lexicalized.orientation ). For instance, the verb ndzaeat and mtosee require the upwards (§ sec:preverb.ingestion ) and downwards (§ sec:preverb.perception ) preverbs, respectively.
summary:
In Japhug, orientation preverbs are the main markers of tense, aspect, modality, and evidentiality, and regular finite verbs require exactly one such preverb, except for the Factual Non-Past, which takes none. These preverbs express one of seven orientations organized into vertical, riverine, and solar dimensions plus an unspecified orientation, and similar orientation systems also appear in some other word classes.

Orientable verbs can combine with all orientations, especially motion verbs, where the preverb may indicate literal direction or extended meanings. Non-orientable verbs, by contrast, allow only a limited set of lexically fixed orientations, sometimes just one.

text:
There are eleven primary TAME categories, which can be divided into four main groups: Non-Past (Factual Non-Past, Egophoric Present, Sensory, § sec:TAME.npst ), Imperfective (§ sec:imperfective ), Past (Aorist, Inferential, Past Imperfective, and Inferential Imperfective, § sec:TAME.pst ) and Modal (Irrealis, Imperative, Prohibitive, Dubitative, § sec:TAME.modal ) categories.

In the finite TAME categories, the B-type preverbs are found in the Imperfective (§ sec:imperfective ) and the A-type preverbs in the Imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ), the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.morphology ) and the Aorist (§ sec:aor ), though with slightly different vowel contraction rules (§ sec:contraction ). In the Aorist paradigm of transitive verbs, another series of preverbs (C) is found in the direct 3 forms (§ sec:indexation.tr.intro ), based on the A-type preverbs but with -a vocalism instead of -ɯ and -ɤ (originating from fusion with another prefix, § sec:xtokavian.preverbs ). For instance, the 2pl 3 Aorist of ndzaeat is tɤ-tɯ-ndza-nɯ ( aor: up -2-eat- pl `you$_pl$ ate it') with the upwards A-type tɤ- preverb, but the corresponding 3pl form is ta -ndza-nɯ ( aor:3: up -eat- pl `they ate it') with the C-type preverb ta-. It is the only case when an orientation preverb encodes person in addition to TAME.

The Inferential (§ sec:ifr ) has a series of preverbs (series D) based on series B, but with -o and -ɤ vocalism instead of -u and -ɯ, respectively (§ sec:xtokavian.preverbs ). For instance, the upwards and downwards D-type preverbs are to- and pjɤ, corresponding to the B-type tu- and pjɯ, respectively (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ).

Five TAME categories neutralize the orientation contrast, and require the same marker for all verbs: the Sensory evidential ɲɯ- (§ sec:sensory ), from the B-type westwards preverb ( tab:orientation.preverbs.intro ), the Egophoric Present ku- (§ sec:egophoric ), the Dubitative ku- (§ sec:dubitative ), from the B-type eastwards preverb, the Past Imperfective pɯ- from the A-type downwards preverb (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology, ), and the Inferential Imperfective pjɤ- from the D-type downwards preverb (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ).

In addition to orientation preverbs, TAME categories are marked by several morphological exponents, including stem alternations (§ sec:stem.alternation ), allomorphy of negative prefixes (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ) and additional affixes: the Irrealis a- prefix (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) and the Past transitive -t suffix (§ sec:suffixes ).

In the Non-Past, Imperfective and Modal categories (all except Past), transitive alternating verbs have a specific stem in direct configurations with a singular subject (see tab:transitive.paradigm.singular.alternating above and § sec:stem3 ). Another stem is found in the Aorist of a handful of verbs (§ sec:stem2 ).

Some of the primary categories can be combined with the copula ŋube to form periphrastic TAME categories (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ), for instance the Periphrastic Past Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic ) illustrated in ( ex:tundzea.pWNu2 ), built from the Imperfective ( tu-ndze-a, with the B-type upwards preverb tu, the alternating stem ndze from ndzaeat and the 1sg suffix) and the Past Imperfective of the copula pɯ-ŋu.

exe

tɤ-mtʰɯm tu-ndze-a pɯ-ŋu \\
indef. poss -meat ipfv -eat[III]- 1sg pst. ipfv -be \\
`I was eating meat/I used to eat meat.'
exe

In addition, primary TAME categories can be combined with prefixes expressing secondary aspectual (§ sec:second.aspect ) or modal (§ sec:second.modal ) meanings.

There is a robust contrast between Past and Non-Past tenses in Japhug, but no grammaticalized future tense. Future events in main clauses are mainly expressed by the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:fact.main.clauses ) or the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.main ).

The tripartite evidential system between Egophoric Present, Sensory (or Testimonial) and Factual observed in the non-past is structurally very similar to that found in some Tibetic languages.
summary: Japhug has eleven primary TAME categories grouped into Non-Past, Imperfective, Past, and Modal sets, and these categories are marked by orientation preverbs, stem alternations, prefix and suffix morphology, and in some cases periphrastic constructions with the copula ŋube. The system shows a strong Past vs. Non-Past contrast but no grammaticalized future tense, with future events usually expressed by the Factual Non-Past or the Irrealis. It also has a tripartite non-past evidential system, structurally similar to that of some Tibetic languages.

text:
verb!stative verb!dynamic
TAME morphology presents a contrast between stative and dynamic verbs. In the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.inchoative ), the Aorist (§ sec:aor.inchoative ) and the Inferential (§ sec:ifr.inchoative ), stative verbs have an inchoative meaning, different from their meaning in Non-Past tenses.

For example, the verb zribe long means `become long(er)' in the Imperfective ( tu-zri ipfv: up -be.long `it becomes longer') or the Aorist ( tɤ-zri aor: up -be.long `(when) it became longer'). By contrast, in the Sensory ( ɲɯ-zri sens -be.long `it is long') and the other Non-Past tenses, it retains its basic stative meaning.

Stative verbs also differ from most dynamic verbs in being compatible with Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective in all contexts ( pɯ-zri pst. ipfv -be.long `it was/used to be long'), while dynamic verbs generally require the periphrastic Past Imperfective instead (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic ), except in some limited contexts (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.apodosis ). This criterion is however not absolute, since a few atelic dynamic verbs can occurs in the non-periphrastic Past Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ).

The stative/dynamic contrast is not completely independent from transitivity (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ). Only intransitive stative verbs have a distinctive morphological marking: the kɯ- infinitive appears in some contexts (§ sec:infinitives.participles ). Transitive stative verbs include in particular verbs derived from adjectival stative verbs by the tropative derivation (§ sec:tropative.pst.ipfv ).
summary:
The passage explains that TAME morphology distinguishes stative from dynamic verbs. Stative verbs take an inchoative meaning in the Imperfective, Aorist, and Inferential, but keep their ordinary stative meaning in the Sensory and other Non-Past tenses; they also more freely occur in Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective forms than most dynamic verbs.

It also notes that this distinction is linked to transitivity: only intransitive stative verbs have a special morphological marker, the kɯ- infinitive in some contexts, while transitive stative verbs include those derived from adjectival statives by tropative derivation.

text:
verb!finite
Finiteness can be defined in Japhug by the ability of a given verb form to occur in the person indexation paradigms (§ sec:indexation.intro ). Non-finite verbs forms cannot take indexation affixes, though some of them can mark the person and number of at most one argument by means of possessive prefixes like nouns (§ sec:possessive.paradigm.intro ). The distinction between finite and non-finite verbal forms is categorical: there are no intermediate semi-finite forms, unlike in Situ where some participles take person indexation in specific contexts.

The main verb of a complete sentence has to be in a finite form, and non-finite verbs are restricted to subordinate clauses (including relative and complement clauses).
summary: In Japhug, finiteness is defined by whether a verb form can occur in the person indexation paradigms: finite forms can take indexation affixes, while non-finite forms cannot, though some may mark one argument with possessive prefixes. This distinction is categorical, with no intermediate semi-finite forms. In complete sentences, the main verb must be finite, whereas non-finite verbs are limited to subordinate clauses such as relative and complement clauses.

text:
participle
There are three types of participle in Japhug: subject, object and oblique, respectively marked by the prefixes kɯ- ( ex:nAkWqur ), kɤ- ( ex:nAkAqur ) and sɤ/z- ( ex:WsAthu ). They are fully productive, and only a handful of defective verbs lack participles (§ sec:intr.person.irregular, § sec:irregular.transitive ).

exe

xlist

nɤ-kɯ-qur \\
2sg. poss - sbj: pcp -help \\
`The one/someone who helps you'

nɤ-kɤ-qur \\
2sg. poss - obj: pcp -help \\
`The one/someone that you help'

a-sɤ-tʰu \\
1sg. poss - obl: pcp -ask \\
`The one whom I ask'
xlist
exe

Participles can take a possessive prefix (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive, § sec:object.participle.possessive, § sec:oblique.participle.possessive ), marking either the subject ( ex:nAkAqur and ex:WsAthu ) or the object ( ex:nAkWqur ).

Participles can in addition be combined with negative, orientation and associated motion prefixes (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:object.participle.other.prefixes ), as shown by ( ex:WmApjWkWnWfkAB2 ).

exe

ɯ-mɤ-pjɯ-kɯ-nɯ-fkaβ \\
3sg. poss - neg - ipfv: down - sbj: pcp - auto -cover \\
`The one/those who do(es) not cover it' (from example ex:WmApjWkWnWfkAB, § sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes )
0003604#S20
exe

One of the main function of participles is to build participial relative clauses (§ sec:participial.relatives ). Participial clauses can relativize core arguments (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative, § sec:object.participle.relatives ) and various oblique arguments and adjuncts (§ sec:subject.participle.other.relative, § sec:object.participle.relatives, § sec:locative.participle.relatives, § sec:instrumental.participle.relatives, § sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ).

In particular, the Japhug equivalent of attributive adjectives are adjectival stative verbs in subject participle form (§ ex:attributive.participles.stative.verbs, § sec:intr.subject.relativization ), occurring in generally head-internal (§ sec:head-internal.relative.postnominal ) relative clauses as in ( ex:tCheme.kWmpCAr ).

exe

tɕʰeme kɯ-mpɕɤr \\
girl sbj: pcp -be.beautiful \\
`A/the beautiful girl'
0006312#S89
exe

The subjects of both intransitive (§ sec:intr.subject.relativization ) and transitive (§ sec:tr.subject.relativization ) verbs are relativized by means of a participial relative clause in kɯ-. Subject participles of transitive verbs take an obligatory possessive prefix coreferent with the object (unless another prefix is present) as in ( ex:nAkWqur ) and ( ex:WkWrAt.part ), while those of intransitive verbs lack possessive prefixes as in ( ex:kWrArAt.part ), The verb rɤ-rɤt in ( ex:kWrArAt.part ) is the antipassive derivation (§ sec:antipassive.rA ) from rɤtwrite, draw ( ex:WkWrAt.part ). except in very restricted cases (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ).

exe

xlist

ɯ-kɯ-rɤt \\
3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -write \\
`The one/someone who writes it'

kɯ-rɤ-rɤt \\
sbj: pcp - apass -write \\
`The one/someone who writes things, a writer.'
xlist
exe

Another important function of participles is to build the purposive complements of motion verbs (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation, § sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs, § sec:am.vs.mvc ), as in ( ex:akWtoR.jAGe ) (see also ex:WkWXtW.jaria in § sec:am.intro below).

exe

a-kɯ-rtoʁ jɤ-ɣe \\
1sg. poss - sbj: pcp -look aor -come[II] \\
`S/he came to see me.'
exe

Participles have several additional morphosyntactic functions, presented in § sec:participial.clause.complementation strategies.
summary: Japhug has three fully productive participle types: subject, object, and oblique, marked by the prefixes kɯ-, kɤ-, and sɤ-/z-, with only a few defective verbs lacking participles. Participles can take possessive prefixes, combine with other prefixes such as negation, orientation, and associated motion, and are used chiefly to form participial relative clauses that can relativize core, oblique, and adjunct arguments. They also serve to express adjectival meanings, purposive complements of motion verbs, and several other morphosyntactic functions.

text:
infinitive converb
The infinitives in kɯ- and kɤ, called ``velar infinitives'' in this grammar, serve as the citation forms of verbs (§ sec:inf.citation ). They occur in some complement clauses as in ( ex:kAtaR.rgaa ) (§ sec:inf.complementation, § sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ) and also serve as converbs (§ sec:inf.converb, § sec:manner.converbs ). They are easily confused with subject or object participles (§ sec:infinitives.participles ).

exe

kɤ-taʁ rga-a \\
inf -weave like: fact - 1sg \\
`I like to weave.'
exe

In addition to velar infinitives, two other types of infinitives are attested: the bare (§ sec:bare.inf ) and the dental (§ sec:dental.inf ) infinitives. These forms are only used in the complement clauses of a handful of verbs such as ʑabegin (§ sec:bare.dental.inf, § sec:aspectual.complement, § sec:bare.dental.inf.sWpa ). Bare and dental infinitives are in complementary distribution (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ): the former is found with transitive verbs ( ex:Wndza.toZa2 ), and the latter with intransitive ones ( ex:tWrJaR.pjAZa ).

exe

xlist

ɯ-ndza to-ʑa \\
3sg. poss - bare. inf:eat ifr: up -start \\
`S/he/it started eating it.'

tɯ-rɟaʁ pjɤ-ʑa \\
inf:II-dance ifr: down -start \\
`S/he started dancing.'
xlist
exe

In this construction (and a few other ones), the complement-taking verb takes the orientation that is lexically selected by the verb in the complement clause (§ sec:orientation.raising ), for instance upwards like ndzaeat in ( ex:Wndza.toZa2 ) and downwards like rɟaʁdance in ( ex:tWrJaR.pjAZa ).
gerund
In addition to the infinitives, three converbs are attested: the reduplicated gerund sɤ- (§ sec:gerund ) expressing temporal simultaneity (§ sec:simultaneity ), the purposive converb (§ sec:purposive.converb, § sec:purposive.clauses ) and the converb of immediate subsequence (§ sec:immediate.converb, § sec:immediate.subsequence ), which stands out in having a perfective meaning `as soon as...' (for instance pjɯ-tɯ-mto `as soon as $X$ saw $Y$') while selecting the B-type preverbs which usually mark Imperfective and Non-Past tenses. Despite the existence of these converbs, temporal (§ sec:temporal.clauses ), manner (§ sec:manner.clauses ) and causal (§ sec:causality ) subordinate clauses mainly select finite verb forms in Japhug narratives and conversations.
summary:
The passage explains that Japhug has velar infinitives in kɯ- and kɤ, which function as citation forms, occur in some complement clauses, and also serve as converbs, though they can be confused with participles. It also notes two further infinitive types, bare and dental, which appear only in the complement clauses of a few verbs and are in complementary distribution: bare infinitives occur with transitive verbs, while dental infinitives occur with intransitive ones.  

In addition, three converbs are described: a reduplicated gerund expressing simultaneity, a purposive converb, and an immediate-subsequence converb meaning ‘as soon as,’ which uniquely combines a perfective meaning with B-type preverbs. Despite these nonfinite forms, temporal, manner, and causal subordinate clauses in narratives and conversations mainly use finite verb forms.

text:
Several productive abstract nominalizations are found in Japhug. The degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominals ), combining a tɯ- with a possessive prefix coreferent with the subject (for example a-tɯ-mtsɯr 1sg - nmlz: deg -be.hungry `my degree of hunger'), are highly common and occur in degree and equative constructions (§ sec:degree.nominal.subject ).

Action nominals (§ sec:tW.action.nominal ) and abstract nouns (§ sec:tA.abstract.nouns ) can be formed by prefixation of tɯ- and tɤ, for instance the noun tɯ-rɟaʁ `dance' from the intransitive verb rɟaʁdance, and tɤ-mtsɯr `hunger' from mtsɯrbe hungry. These derivations are not rare, but not fully productive either. The tɯ- and tɤ- prefixes here are not analyzable as indefinite possessor prefixes with which they are homophonous (§ sec:possessive.paradigm ), as they cannot be replaced by definite possessor prefixes.
summary: Japhug has several productive abstract nominalizations, including degree nominals formed with tɯ- plus a possessive prefix coreferent with the subject; these are common and used in degree and equative constructions. It also forms action nominals and abstract nouns with tɯ- and tɤ-, such as tɯ-rɟaʁ ‘dance’ and tɤ-mtsɯr ‘hunger’, though these derivations are not fully productive. The prefixes in these forms are not indefinite possessor prefixes, since they cannot be replaced by definite possessor prefixes.

text:
associated motion
Japhug and other Gyalrong languages stand out in Trans-Himalayan by having a system of associated motion clearly different from orientation markers. Unlike Arandic or Tacanan, the category of associated motion in Japhug only comprises two different prefixes (§ sec:am.prefixes ) marking either cislocative or translocative motion of the subject (§ sec:AM.argument.motion ) prior to the action expressed by the verb root.

Although associated motion prefixes ( ex:CtAXtWta ) seems at first glance semantically similar to motion verbs with a purposive clause ( ex:WkWXtW.jaria ), there are systematic differences between these two constructions (§ sec:am.vs.mvc ), both in terms of presuppositions (§ sec:am.concessive ) and in syntactic constraints of relativization (§ sec:AM.mvc.relativizability ).

exe

xlist

ɕ-tɤ-χtɯ-t-a \\
tral - aor -buy- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I went and bought it.'

ɯ-kɯ-χtɯ jɤ-ari-a \\
3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -buy aor -go[II]- 1sg \\
`I went to buy it.'
xlist
exe
summary: Japhug and other Gyalrong languages have an associated motion system that is distinct from orientation markers and, unlike in Arandic or Tacanan, consists of only two prefixes marking cislocative or translocative motion of the subject before the event expressed by the verb. Although these prefixes may resemble motion verbs used with purposive clauses, the two constructions differ systematically in presuppositions and in relativization constraints.

text:
The rich and redundant morphological expression of transitivity (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ) and the rarity of labile verbs (§ sec:lability ) in Japhug are correlated with a highly productive system of voice derivations, treated in chapters chap:valency.increasing.derivation, chap:valency.decreasing.derivation and chap:other.derivations. There are eleven fully productive valency-changing prefixes, These derivations are not fully productive in the sense that they can be applied to any verb (since there are transitivity and semantic restrictions on their uses), but in the sense that some recent loanwords can be subjected to them. summarized in tab:voice.overview, to which a certain number of non-productive derivations such as the applicative nɯ- (§ sec:applicative ) and the anticausative (§ sec:anticausative ) can be added.

All productive voice derivations are marked by prefixes (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ). Only fossil traces of derivational suffixes are found (in particular the applicative -t, § sec:applicative.t ). The anticausative is marked not by a prefix, but by an alternation whereby unvoiced obstruents are converted into their voiced prenasalized counterparts (see § sec:anticausative.morphology ).

There are, in addition, productive verbal derivations that do not change valency, such as the autive nɯ- (§ sec:autobenefactive ) and the distributed action derivation (§ sec:distributed.action ).

The following sections present a representative sample of voice derivations and their main morphosyntactic functions.
summary: Japhug has a highly productive system of voice derivations that correlates with its rich morphological marking of transitivity and the rarity of labile verbs. There are eleven fully productive valency-changing prefixes, though their use is limited by transitivity and semantic restrictions; some non-productive derivations such as the applicative and anticausative are also mentioned. Productive voice derivations are marked mainly by prefixes, with only fossil suffix traces, while the anticausative uses a consonant alternation, and there are also productive derivations that do not change valency, such as the autive and distributed action forms.

text:
causative
There are two productive causative derivations, the sigmatic causative (which has four productive allomorphs sɯ, sɯɣ, s- and z- depending on the phonological and morphological context, § sec:sig.caus.allomorphs ) and the velar causative ɣɤ- (from wɤ, a form still found in some Japhug dialects).

The latter is restricted to a subset of stative verbs. Some stative verbs are compatible with both causative derivations: for instance zbaʁbe dry can be causativized as both ɣɤ-zbaʁ or sɯ-zbaʁ. The semantic contrast between the two causatives in this context remains unclear (§ sec:velar.causative.vs.sigmatic.causative ).

The sigmatic causative is the most productive derivation in Japhug. It is compatible with intransitive, transitive and even ditransitive verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.causative ), and has a wide range of meanings (§ sec:sig.caus.function ), from coercion (§ sec:sig.caus.coercitive ) as in ( ex:kW.tuznAme ) to indirect causation (§ sec:sig.caus.indirect ).

exe

rɟɤlpu kɯ ɯ-ma nɯ mkʰɤrmaŋ ra tu- z -nɤme pjɤ-ŋu \\
king erg 3sg. poss -work dem people pl ipfv - caus -do[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The king used to make the people do work for him.'
0006248#S5
exe

The sigmatic causative is also used to mark instruments (§ sec:sig.caus.instrumental ), for example in ( ex:kW.chAsWtsxWB ), where the instrument taqaβneedle receives ergative marking (§ sec:instr.kW ) like a causee (§ sec:causee.kW ): the construction literally means `s/he made the needle sew the clothes'.

exe

ki taqaβ ki kɯ tɯ-ŋga cʰɤ- sɯ -tʂɯβ \\
dem. prox needle dem. prox erg indef. poss -clothes ifr - caus -sew \\
`S/he sewed the clothes with this needle.'
exe

In addition to the productive causatives, there are irregular causative forms (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular, § sec:causative.m ), some of which co-exist with their regular counterparts, but with a more lexicalized meaning. For instance, the verb tsʰidrink has the irregular causative jtsʰigive to drink (§ sec:caus.j ) as opposed to the regular one sɯ-tsʰi `make drink, drink with'.

The sigmatic causative prefix can be combined with nearly all other derivational prefixes (§ sec:sig.caus.other.derivations ). It can precede the velar causative, as in z-ɣɤ-mpja `heat up $X$ with $Y$, make/let $Y$ heat up $X$' from ɣɤ-mpja `heat up', causative of mpjabe warm.

It is also the only prefix that can occur more than once in a single verb form, A double reciprocal form is attested (§ sec:sAmW ), but not with the same reciprocal prefixes. as shown by examples such as sɯ-sɯ-spoʁ `make a hole with' from sɯ-spoʁ `make a hole', causative of the intransitive verb spoʁhave a hole (§ sec:sig.caus.other.recursion ).
summary:
Japhug has two productive causative derivations: a sigmatic causative with four allomorphs and a velar causative ɣɤ-, the latter being limited to certain stative verbs. The sigmatic causative is the most productive and can apply to intransitive, transitive, and ditransitive verbs, with meanings ranging from coercive and indirect causation to instrumental uses.
