The passage also notes that some verbs have irregular causative forms that may coexist with regular ones but are more lexicalized in meaning, and that the sigmatic causative can combine with other derivational prefixes and even recur within the same verb form.

text:
tropative
The tropative nɤ- prefix (§ sec:tropative ), like a causative derivation, turns an intransitive verb into a transitive, but its meaning differs: the added argument is not a causer, but an experiencer feeling/perceiving the state expressed by the base verb. For instance, the tropative of mpɕɤrbe beautiful is nɤ-mpɕɤr `find beautiful', with the experiencer encoded as subject and the stimulus (corresponding to the intransitive subject of the base verb) as object, as shown by ( ex:YWtanAmpCAr ).

exe

ɲɯ-ta-nɤ-mpɕɤr \\
sens -1 2- trop -be.beautiful \\
`I find you very beautiful.'
exe

The tropative can be used to define adjectives as a sub-class of stative verbs: only adjectival stative verbs can undergo this derivation, unlike for example existential verbs and copulas (§ sec:copula.existential ).
summary: The tropative prefix **nɤ-** converts an intransitive verb into a transitive one, but unlike a causative it adds an **experiencer** rather than a causer. In tropative constructions, the experiencer functions as the subject and the original intransitive subject becomes the object, as in **nɤ-mpɕɤr** ‘find beautiful’ from **mpɕɤr** ‘be beautiful’. The tropative also shows that **adjectives form a subclass of stative verbs**, since only adjectival stative verbs can undergo this derivation.

text:
antipassive
When the object of a morphologically transitive verb (thus excluding labile verbs in intransitive conjugation, § sec:lability ) is non-overt, it is necessarily interpreted as definite (§ sec:nonovert.core.arguments ). For instance, example ( ex:kW.chAtsxWB ) can only be used if the referent that has been sewn has been previously mentioned or is retrievable from the context, and cannot be understood as `sewed something' with an indefinite object. To express this meaning, several strategies are possible, including the antipassive rɤ- derivation (§ sec:antipassive.rA ).

exe

xlist

tɕʰeme nɯ kɯ cʰɤ-tʂɯβ \\
girl dem erg ifr -sew \\
`The girl sewed it.'

tɕʰeme nɯ cʰɤ-rɤ-tʂɯβ \\
girl dem ifr - apass -sew \\
`The girl sewed / did sewing.'
xlist
exe

The rɤ- turns a transitive verb into an intransitive one, whose only argument is semantically the agent, but does not take ergative marking ( ex:chArAtsxWB ).
summary: When a morphologically transitive verb has a non-overt object, that object must be interpreted as definite and contextually recoverable, not indefinite. To express an indefinite-object meaning like “sewed something,” the language can use the antipassive rɤ- derivation, which turns the transitive verb into an intransitive one whose sole argument is the agent and does not receive ergative marking.

text:
reflexive
Japhug has a dedicated reflexive prefix ʑɣɤ- (§ sec:reflexive ), different from other valency-decreasing derivations. The reflexive verb is conjugated intransitively, as shown by ( ex:thWZGArkua ) If the verb in ( ex:thWZGArkua ) were transitive, a past transitive -t suffix would be inserted (§ sec:suffixes, § sec:indexation.mixed ) and the expected form would be $ $ tʰɯ-ʑɣɤ-rku-t-a.

exe

tʰɯ-ʑɣɤ-rku-a \\
aor: downstream - refl -put.in- 1sg \\
`I put myself (in the bag).'
exe

The reflexive is frequently combined with the sigmatic causative (§ sec:refl.caus ) to express an unintentional indirect causation affecting oneself ( ex:tAZGAsWmpCaa ).

exe

tɤ-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-mpɕa-a \\
aor - refl - caus -scold- 1sg \\
`I got myself scolded.'
exe

reciprocal
The reciprocal derivation (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ), entirely different from the reflexive, is built by prefixing a- and reduplicating the verb stem (§ sec:partial.redp ). For instance the transitive verb rqoʁhug yields a-rqɯ rqoʁ `hug each other'. Reciprocal verbs generally require a non-singular intransitive subject, and can also select a comitative postpositional phrase (§ sec:comitative ).
summary:
Japhug has a dedicated reflexive prefix ʑɣɤ-, and reflexive verbs are conjugated intransitively; if they were transitive, a past transitive -t suffix would be expected. The reflexive can combine with the sigmatic causative to express unintentional indirect causation affecting oneself, as in “I got myself scolded.”  

The reciprocal derivation is distinct from the reflexive and is formed by prefixing a- and reduplicating the verb stem. Reciprocal verbs typically take a non-singular intransitive subject and may also take a comitative postpositional phrase.

text:
autive
The autive nɯ- (§ sec:autobenefactive ) is a highly productive derivation, which
does not affect verbal transitivity unlike the previous ones (§ sec:autoben.transitivity ).

autobenefactive
Its most basic function is self-affectedness or autobenefactive (§ sec:autoben.proper ). In particular, the autive on transitive verbs taking a inalienably possessed object can be used to specify that the subject and the possessor of the object are coreferent ( ex:WsroR.konWri ), whereas the absence of the autive is generally interpreted as indicating the absence of coreference ( ex:WsroR.kori ). This is not an absolute syntactic rule, however, since the Autive has additional unrelated uses (see below and § sec:autoben.spontaneous, § sec:autoben.permansive ) which can interfere with this particular function.

exe

xlist

ɯʑo kɯ ɯ-sroʁ ko-nɯ-ri \\
3sg erg 3sg. poss -life ifr - auto -save \\
`S/he$_i$ saved his/her$_i$ own life.'

ɯʑo kɯ ɯ-sroʁ ko-ri \\
3sg erg 3sg. poss -life ifr -save \\
`S/he$_i$ saved his/her$_j$ life.'
xlist
exe

volitionality spontaneous
Another function of the Autive is to indicate spontaneous or non-volitional actions (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ), occurring for example by mistake, as illustrated by the minimal pair between ( ex:pWnWprata ) and ( ex:pWprata ).

exe

xlist

tɤ-rɣe pɯ-nɯ-prat-a \\
indef. poss -necklace aor - auto -break- 1sg \\
`I broke the pearl necklace (by mistake).'

tɤ-rɣe pɯ-prat-a \\
indef. poss -necklace aor -break- 1sg \\
`I broke the pearl necklace (on purpose).'
xlist
exe

The third main function of the Autive is to express permansive aspect (§ sec:autoben.permansive ).
summary: The autive nɯ- is a highly productive derivation that does not change verbal transitivity. Its main uses are to mark self-affectedness or autobenefactive meaning, especially on transitive verbs with inalienably possessed objects where it can signal that the subject and possessor are coreferential, and it is also used for spontaneous or non-volitional actions such as mistakes. A third major function is to express permansive aspect.

text:
denominal derivation
Verbalizing denominal (chapter chap:denominal ) and deideophonic (§ sec:voice.deideophonic ) derivations are rich and productive in Japhug.

A considerable number of denominal prefixes can be identified. Some of them have a well-identifiable meaning, for instance the proprietive aɣɯ- (§ sec:denom.aGW ) deriving verbs meaning `having a lot of $X$' or `producing a lot of $X$' (such as aɣɯluproducing a lot of milk (of a cow) from tɤ-lumilk) or the similative arɯ- (§ sec:denom.arW ). For the prefixes rɯ/ɤ- (§ sec:denom.rA ), nɯ/ɤ- (§ sec:denom.nW ) and ɣɯ/ɤ- (§ sec:denom.GW ), several different functions have to be postulated, since these prefixes can derive both intransitive (§ sec:denom.intr.rA, § sec:denom.intr.nW, § sec:denom.intr.GA ) and transitive (§ sec:denom.tr.rA, § sec:denom.tr.nW, § sec:denom.tr.GA ) verbs.

Some denominal derivations occur in pairs (§ sec:denom.nW.pairing, § sec:denom.rA.pairing ). For instance, when a noun has both rɯ/ɤ- and nɯ/ɤ- denominal verbs, the former is usually dynamic intransitive, and the latter transitive, as illustrated by the pair comprising the intransitive verb rɤ-ma `do (some) work' and its transitive counterpart nɤ-ma `do (a work)', both from the noun ta-mawork.

Denominal derivations compete with light verb constructions to turn nouns into predicates (§ sec:denominal.vs.light.verb, § sec:light.verb ). For instance, the meaning `tell lies, cheat' from the noun kʰrambalie can be expressed either by a collocation with the light verb βzumake (§ sec:Bzu.lv ) or by the denominal verbs rɯkʰrambatell lies (§ sec:denom.intr.rA, intransitive) and nɯkʰrambacheat (§ sec:denom.tr.nW, transitive).

reanalysis
An important proportion of voice prefixes originate from the reanalysis of denominal derivations from bare nominalized forms (§ sec:voice.denominal ), most clearly in the case of the rɤ- antipassive (§ sec:antipassive.history, ).

When applied to noun-verb compounds (§ sec.n.v.compounds, § sec:action.nominal.compounds ), denominal derivations can serve to build incorporating verbs (§ sec:incorp.denom ). For instance, the intransitive verb ɣɯsɯpʰɯtcut firewood is derived by the prefix ɣɯ- (§ sec:denom.intr.GA ) from the compound sɯpʰɯtfirewood cutting, itself made from the bound state sɯ- of the noun siwood compounded with the transitive verb pʰɯttake out, cut, `cut'. A tripartite contrast exists between the basic transitive construction ( si+pʰɯt ), a light verb construction combining βzumake with the corresponding action nominal compound ( sɯpʰɯt+βzu ) and the denominal incorporating verb ɣɯ-sɯpʰɯt, all three meaning `cut firewood' (§ sec:incorp.vs.other ).
summary:
Japhug has rich and productive denominal and deideophonic verbal derivation, with many prefixes that can turn nouns into verbs. Some prefixes have specific meanings such as proprietive aɣɯ- and similative arɯ-, while others like rɯ/ɤ-, nɯ/ɤ-, and ɣɯ/ɤ- have multiple functions, often forming intransitive and transitive pairs, and these derivations may compete with light verb constructions for expressing the same predicate meaning.

The passage also notes that many voice prefixes, especially rɤ- antipassive, come from reanalysis of denominal derivations. When applied to noun-verb compounds, denominal derivation can create incorporating verbs, yielding contrasts among a basic transitive construction, a light verb construction, and a denominal incorporating verb with the same meaning.

text:
The morphosyntactic properties of arguments can be studied from the point of view of flagging (§ chap:postpositions.relators, § ex:postpositions, § sec:relator.nouns ) and indexation (§ sec:intr.indexation, § sec:polypersonal ), but also relativization (§ sec:function.relativization ) and coreference restrictions between complement and matrix clauses (§ sec:complement.types ).

argument!core
Core arguments are defined as those that are indexed by the verb morphology. In the case of intransitive verbs (§ sec:intr.indexation ), the only argument indexed on the verb is the intransitive subject, but the argument structure of intransitive verbs can contain up to two additional oblique arguments (§ sec:semi.transitive.dative ). Morphologically transitive verbs index two arguments (including in some cases a dummy one, § sec:transitive.dummy ). Although there are no different morphological slots for transitive subjects and objects (§ sec:indexation.tr.intro, § sec:direct-inverse ), the transitive paradigm contains no ambiguity in person configurations (§ sec:polypersonal ), and the person of the agentive and patientive core arguments can always be clearly identified in finite verb forms. The core argument indexed like the agentive argument of verbs of action such as satkill or ʁndɯhit (as in § sec:indexation.tr.intro ) is called transitive subject, and the other one is the object. The term object in this grammar is restricted to this particular core argument, to the exclusion of all object-like patientive arguments.

Outside of verb indexation, the three basic core arguments (intransitive subject, transitive subject and object) are encoded in various ways, and present different types of alignments.
summary: Core arguments are defined as those indexed by verb morphology: for intransitive verbs, only the intransitive subject is indexed, while morphologically transitive verbs index two arguments, whose person features are always unambiguous in finite forms. The grammar distinguishes the transitive subject from the object by their alignment with agentive and patientive roles, and restricts the term “object” to this specific core argument. Outside verbal indexation, these three core arguments are encoded in different ways and show different alignment patterns.

text:
alignment!neutral
Person indexation affixes in general have neutral alignment: for instance the 1sg suffix -a indexes the subject of intransitive verbs, and is also found in 1sg 3, 3 1sg and 2 1sg configurations (§ sec:indexation.tr.intro, § sec:direct-inverse ).

The absence of strict coreference restrictions between matrix and subordinate clauses in some categories of complement clauses (§ sec:velar.inf.coreference, § sec:rYo.complements, § sec:finite.complement.coref ) and in manner (§ sec:manner.converbs ) and temporal clauses (§ sec:temporal.clauses ) could be interpreted as a type of neutral alignment, but it appears that the neutralization in those cases is not limited to the three core arguments: there can also be complete absence of coreference, or coreference with an oblique or a possessor of an argument.
summary: Person indexation affixes generally show neutral alignment: the 1sg suffix -a marks intransitive subjects and also appears in 1sg 3, 3 1sg, and 2 1sg configurations. Some complement, manner, and temporal clauses lack strict coreference restrictions between matrix and subordinate clauses, which might seem like neutral alignment, but this neutralization is not confined to the three core arguments since coreference may also be absent or may involve an oblique or possessor.

text: alignment!nominative-accusative
summary: The passage indicates a nominative-accusative alignment system. In this type of alignment, the subject of a transitive verb and the subject of an intransitive verb are treated alike, while the object of a transitive verb is marked differently.

text:
subject!intransitive subject!transitive
Nominative-accusative alignment appears in several unrelated constructions in Japhug.

participle!subject
The first piece of evidence for this type of alignment in Gyalrong languages to have been proposed is the fact that the kɯ- (subject) participle (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ) is the only form that can be used to relativize both intransitive (§ sec:intr.subject.relativization ) and transitive subjects (§ sec:tr.subject.relativization ). However, the kɯ- participles are not exclusively used to relativize intransitive and transitive subjects: they can also relativize possessors of intransitive subjects (§ sec:possessor.relativization ), and are the only option to do so, resulting in ambiguities (see examples ex:WlaXtCha.pWkWtu and ex:jla.nWRrW.kWtu in § sec:possessive.mihi.est ).

lability
The fact that nearly all labile verbs are subject-preserving (§ sec:lability.apass ) could also be adduced as evidence of nominative-accusative alignment, but the existence of a handful of object-preserving labile verbs (§ sec:lability.pass ) makes it less compelling.

Clearer cases of constructions where strict nominative-accusative alignment is observed include associated motion and complementation.

First, the argument performing the motion encoded by the associated prefixes (§ sec:am.prefixes ) is always the intransitive subject in the case of intransitive verbs, and the transitive subject in the case of transitive ones (§ sec:AM.argument.motion ), and can never be the object, a possessor of the subject or any oblique argument (but it can be the causee of a causative verb).

Second, several subtypes of complement clauses require coreference between the (intransitive or transitive) subjects of the complement clause and that of the main clause, in particular bare and dental infinitives (§ sec:bare.inf.coreference ).
summary:
Japhug shows nominative-accusative alignment in several unrelated constructions. The kɯ- participle can relativize both intransitive and transitive subjects, and most labile verbs are subject-preserving, though these facts are not fully decisive because of some exceptions and other possible relativizations.

Clearer evidence comes from associated motion and complementation: in associated motion, the motion argument is always the subject whether the verb is intransitive or transitive, and in certain complement clauses the subject of the complement must corefer with the main-clause subject.

text:
object
While evidence for subjects independent from person indexation can be identified, evidence for objects (as opposed to other non-subject arguments in absolutive form, § sec:semi.object, § sec:theme.ditransitive, § absolutive.goal ) is more elusive.

In subject participles of transitive verbs, the object is marked by a possessive prefix (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ), obligatorily if no other prefix (of orientation, negation or associated motion) is present, as in ( ex:WkWndza2 ).

exe

xlist

spjaŋkɯ nɯ kɯ ɕa ɲɯ-ndze \\
wolf dem erg meat sens -eat[III] \\
`The wolf eats meat.'

ɯ-kɯ-ndza \\
3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -eat \\
`The one/someone who eats it'
xlist
exe

However, possessive prefixes on subject participles cannot be used as evidence for objects outside of finite indexation, as they can mark other grammatical functions. For example the verb rgalike is conjugated intransitively as shown by ( ex:WkWrga ): its subject spjaŋkɯ has no ergative marking, and no stem alternation is observed on the verb (a form like $ $ ɲɯ-rge would be expected if this verb were transitive as in ex:Ca.YWndze, § sec:stem3.form, § sec:transitivity.morphology ). However, in addition to its subject, this verb takes an absolutive argument ( ɕameat in ex:Ca.YWrga ) that cannot be indexed: the semi-object. This argument is also marked as a possessive prefix on the subject participle like a real object, as in ( ex:WkWrga ).

exe

xlist

spjaŋkɯ nɯ ɕa ɲɯ-rga \\
wolf dem meat sens -like \\
`The wolf likes meat.'

ɯ-kɯ-rga \\
3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -like \\
`The one/someone who likes him/her/it.'
xlist
exe

Moreover, objects do not have any relativization construction that is specific to them. They can be relativized by object participial relatives (§ sec:object.participle.relatives ) and finite relatives (§ sec:finite.relatives ), but these categories of clauses can also be used to relativize semi-objects (§ sec:semi.tr.relativization, § sec:object.participle.other.relative ) and other participants such as goals (§ sec:locative.relativization.object, § sec:locative.relativization.finite ) and possessors of objects (§ sec:possessor.relativization ). For instance, headless participial clauses relativizing the object of ndzaeat ( ex:akAndza ) or the semi-object of rgalike ( ex:akArga ) have the same structure.

exe

xlist

a-kɤ-ndza \\
1sg. poss - obj: pcp -eat \\
`[The things] that I eat.'

a-kɤ-rga \\
1sg. poss - sbj: pcp -like \\
`[The things] that I like.'
xlist
exe
summary:
The passage argues that evidence for objects is harder to identify than evidence for subjects. In subject participles of transitive verbs, an object is often marked by a possessive prefix, but this is not diagnostic because the same marking can also appear on semi-objects and other absolutive arguments.

It also notes that objects do not have a relativization construction unique to them. Object participial and finite relatives can relativize objects, but the same constructions are also used for semi-objects, goals, and possessors, so they do not distinguish true objects from other arguments.

text:
alignment!ergative-absolutive

Although the terms ``absolutive'' (§ sec:absolutive ) and ``ergative'' (§ sec:erg.kW ) are used in this grammar to refer to flagging, Japhug does not display perfect absolutive-ergative alignment in case marking.

absolutive
Absolutive form (absence of postposition or relator noun) does indeed serve to mark intransitive subjects (§ sec:absolutive.S ) and objects (§ sec:absolutive.P ) by default, and transitive subjects normally take the ergative kɯ postposition (§ sec:A.kW ). However, both absolutive (§ sec:semi.object, § sec:essive.abs, § absolutive.goal ) and ergative forms (§ sec:instr.kW, § sec:comparee.kW ) have many functions other than marking core arguments. In addition, there is some fluidity in the use of the ergative postposition: some intransitive subjects can also be marked by it (§ sec:S.kW ), in particular due to anticipation of a transitive verb in the following clauses (§ sec:long.distance.kW ).

The clearest evidence of absolutive-ergative alignment in Japhug is found in generic person indexation (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ): generic intransitive subjects and objects are both indexed by kɯ, while generic transitive subjects are marked by the inverse wɣ- (§ sec:direct-inverse ).
alignment!ergative-absolutive

In addition, in local configurations (§ sec:indexation.local ), the fact that the suffix closest to the verb stem indexes the object (like an intransitive subject) can also be analyzed as ergative alignment in this sub-part of the indexation system.

There are no cases of syntactic pivot with exclusive neutralization of intransitive subject and object in complementation or relativization.
summary: Japhug does not show a perfect absolutive-ergative case-marking system: the absolutive form normally marks intransitive subjects and objects, while transitive subjects usually take the ergative postposition kɯ, but both forms have several other functions and the ergative can also mark some intransitive subjects. The clearest ergative-absolutive pattern appears in generic person indexation, where generic intransitive subjects and objects are both indexed by kɯ, while generic transitive subjects take the inverse wɣ-; local configurations may also be analyzed as ergative in the indexation system. There is no syntactic pivot that uniquely groups intransitive subjects and objects in complementation or relativization.

text:
Most ditransitive verbs have indirective alignment (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ): the theme is indexed (treated as the object of a monotransitive verb), and the recipient marked with the genitive (§ sec:genitive ) or the dative (§ sec:dative ). There are however a few highly common verbs such as mbigive which have secundative alignment (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ) and index the recipient.

Causativized transitive verbs have a different indexation pattern: either the causee or the patientive argument is indexed as object, depending on factors such as person hierarchy (§ sec:ditransitive.causative ).
summary:
Most ditransitive verbs show indirective alignment, where the theme is indexed like the object of a monotransitive verb and the recipient is marked with the genitive or dative. However, a few frequent verbs such as **mbigive** use secundative alignment and index the recipient instead.

Causativized transitive verbs follow a different pattern: either the causee or the patientive argument is indexed as the object, depending on factors such as person hierarchy.

text:
word order
Japhug has a strict verb-final order, with only a limited number of exceptions: right dislocated constituents (§ sec:right.dislocation ), only a few adverbs, particles (§ sec:sfp ) and ideophones (§ sec:idph.syntax ) can occur postverbally (§ sec:postverbal.adv ).

When both the subject and the object of a monotransitive verb are overt as in ( ex:lWlu.nW.kW.tondza ), the former is placed by default before the latter (§ sec:monotransitive.word.order ). For ditransitive verbs, the order between theme and recipient is not rigid (§ sec:secundative.word.order, § sec:indirective.word.order ).

exe

lɯlu nɯ kɯ pɣa nɯ to-ndza \\
cat dem erg bird dem ifr -eat \\
`The cat ate the bird.'
exe

Noun phrases have by default (Demonstrative)-Noun-Adjective-Numeral-Demonstrative order (§ sec:noun.phrases.word.order ) as illustrated by ( ex:tCheme.kWmpCAr.XsWm ).

exe

(kɯki) tɕʰeme kɯ-mpɕɤr χsɯm kɯra \\
dem. prox girl sbj: pcp -be.beautiful three dem: pl \\
`These three beautiful girls'
exe
summary: Japhug has a strict verb-final word order, with only a few exceptions such as right-dislocated constituents, certain adverbs, particles, and ideophones appearing after the verb. In monotransitive clauses, the subject normally precedes the object, while in ditransitive clauses the order of theme and recipient is not fixed. Within noun phrases, the default order is (Demonstrative)-Noun-Adjective-Numeral-Demonstrative.

text:
relative clause
Japhug lacks relative pronouns, and most relative clauses are participial (§ sec:participial.relatives ). Finite relative clauses are also attested (§ sec:finite.relatives ).

Most arguments and adjuncts are relativizable, though there are constraints on relativizability (§ sec:accessibility.relativization ).

In the text corpus, an important proportion of relative clauses are headless (§ sec:headless.relative ). When the head noun is overt, it is either internal to the relative clause (§ sec:head-internal.relative ) or follows it (§ sec:prenominal.relative ), depending in part on the syntactic function of the relativized element and on the type of relative clause.

Example ( ex:lWlu.nW.kW.tAkAndza ) illustrates a head-internal finite relative: the relativized object pɣabird is located between the transitive subject lɯlu nɯ kɯ and the finite verb (an object participle tɤ-kɤ-ndza ( aor - obj: pcp -eat) would also be possible to express the same meaning), at the position it would normally occupy in the corresponding independent sentence (see ex:lWlu.nW.kW.tondza above).

exe

[lɯlu nɯ kɯ pɣa ta-ndza] nɯ \\
cat dem erg bird aor:3 -eat dem \\
`The bird that the cat ate'
exe

In ( ex:pGA.WkWndza ) on the other hand, the relative clause precedes the relativized transitive subject lɯlucat.

exe

[pɣa ɯ-tɤ-kɯ-ndza] lɯlu nɯ \\
bird 3sg. poss - aor - sbj: pcp -eat cat dem \\
`The cat that ate the bird'
exe
summary:
Japhug lacks relative pronouns, and most relative clauses are participial, though finite relative clauses also occur. Most arguments and adjuncts can be relativized within certain constraints, and many relative clauses in the corpus are headless.  

When an overt head noun is present, it may occur inside the relative clause or after it, depending partly on the syntactic role of the relativized element and the clause type. The examples show both a head-internal relative, with the relativized object in its usual position, and a prenominal relative where the relative clause precedes the head noun.

text:
complement clause
Complement clauses in Japhug (chapter chap:complement.clauses ) occur in intransitive subject ( ex:kABzu.mApe, § sec:adjective.complement ), object ( ex:kABzu.mAspe, § sec:spa.verb ) and semi-object ( ex:kABzu.mAnAz, § sec:nAz.verb ) functions. There are also complement-taking nouns ( ex:kABzu.WRjiz, § sec:complement.taking.nouns ).

exe

xlist

[kʰramba kɤ-βzu] mɤ-pe \\
lie inf -make neg -be.good: fact \\
`Telling lies is bad.'

ɯʑo kɯ [kʰramba kɤ-βzu] mɤ-spe \\
3sg erg lie inf -make neg -be.able[III] \\
`S/he is not able to tell lies.'

[ɯʑo kɯ kʰramba kɤ-βzu] mɤ-nɤz \\
3sg erg lie inf -make neg -dare \\
`S/he does not dare to tell lies.'

[kʰramba kɤ-βzu] a-ʁjiz mɤ-ɣi \\
lie inf -make 1sg. poss -wish neg -come: fact \\
`I do not want to tell lies.'
xlist
exe

As shown by ( ex:kABzu.mAnAz ), when the complement-taking verb is semi-transitive (and thus morphologically intransitive, § sec:semi.transitive ), the verb in the complement clause is transitive and they share their subjects, the subject can take ergative case following the verb in the complement clause rather than absolutive (§ sec:case.infinitive ).

Not all complements are infinitive clauses as in ( ex:kABzu.complements ) (§ sec:inf.intro, § sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ). Some verbs are also compatible with finite complements (§ sec:finite.complement ) as in ( ex:pjWtasWXCAt.YWspea ), with subject coreference.

exe

[pjɯ-ta-sɯxɕɤt] ɲɯ-spe-a \\
ipfv -1 2-teach sens -be.able[III]- 1sg \\
`I am able to teach you.'
exe

Verbs of speech also take reported speech clauses (§ sec:reported.speech ), which present morphosyntactic properties different from regular finite complements (§ sec:hybrid indirect ).

Aside from complement clauses proper, various complementation strategies are also found, including relative clauses in core argument function (which resemble, and can even be ambiguous with, complement clauses, § sec:relative.core.arg ), participial clauses (§ sec:participial.clause.complementation strategies ), action nominals (§ sec:complementation.strategy.action.nominals ) and simple coordination (§ sec:coordination.comp.str ).
summary:
In Japhug, complement clauses can function as intransitive subjects, objects, or semi-objects, and some nouns also take complements. Most complement clauses are infinitival, but some verbs can also take finite complements with subject coreference, and speech verbs take reported-speech clauses with distinct morphosyntactic properties.

The passage also notes that other complementation strategies exist besides true complement clauses, including relative clauses in core argument position, participial clauses, action nominals, and coordination.

text:
Subordinate clauses other than relative and complement clauses (treated in chapter chap:temporal.conditional ) tend to be expressed by finite clauses headed by a relator noun or a postposition. For instance, clauses of temporal precedence (§ sec:precedence.CWNgW ) require a finite verb in the Imperfective regardless of the TAME category of the verb in the main clause (§ sec:ipfv.temporal ) followed the postposition ɕɯŋgɯbefore (§ sec:temporal.postpositions ) as in ( ex:chWstanW.CWNgW ).

exe

[cʰɯ-sta-nɯ ɕɯŋgɯ] tɕe, ɯʑo cʰɤ-rɤru \\
ipfv -wake.up- pl before lnk 3sg ifr -get.up \\
`S/he got up before they had woken up.'
0006065#S35
exe

Converbial clauses do exist (§ sec:converbs ), but are all in competition with a finite clause type. For instance, the immediate converb (§ sec:immediate.converb ) illustrated in ( ex:tutWlhoR ) has a corresponding construction ( ex:tAlhoR.CimWma2 ) with a finite verb in the Aorist (§ sec:immediate.subsequence ).

exe

xlist

tu-tɯ-ɬoʁ \\
ipfv: up - imm: conv -come.out \\

tɤ-ɬoʁ ɕimɯma \\
aor: up -come.out immediately.after \\
`As soon as it comes out / immediately after it has come out'
xlist
exe

Some finite clauses not followed by postpositions or relator nouns still have clues of a subordinate status. In particular, periphrastic TAME constructions involving an Imperfective verb (§ sec:imperfective ) and a copula (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ), when they occur in chains, tend to elide the auxiliary in the non-final clauses (§ sec:periphrastic.subordination ), resulting in constructions like ( ex:turAma.kunWrNgW ), where the first clause ɕɤr tɕe tu-rɤma `it is active during the night' is incomplete (lacking the auxiliary ɲɯ-ŋu ), and the copula ɲɯ-ŋu has scope over the two clauses preceding it (see also ex:chain.pjANu, § sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME, for a example of the same type with more than ten clauses sharing a single auxiliary).

exe

lɯlu nɯ, [ɕɤr tɕe tu-rɤma], sŋi tɕe ku-nɯ-rŋgɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
cat dem night loc ipfv -work day loc ipfv - auto -lie.down sens -be \\
`The cat, active during the during the night, sleeps during the day.'
0003576#S33
exe

We also find a special type of serial verb construction expressing manner (§ sec:svc.manner ), in which the verb in the manner clause (with a similative verb § sec:svc.similative.verb or a deideophonic verb § sec:svc.deideophonic ) shares the same TAME, subject (and often object) as the verb in the other clause. In ( ex:ki.tAstuta.nWXtCita ) for example, studo like and the χtɕiwash are in Aorist 1sg 3sg form (§ sec:aor.morphology ) and share a-ŋga `my clothes' as object (the demonstrative ki is semi-object, § sec:ditransitive.secundative ).

exe

a-ŋga nɯ ki tɤ-stu-t-a tɕe nɯ-χtɕi-t-a \\
1sg. poss -clothes dem dem. prox aor -do.like- pst: tr - 1sg lnk aor -wash- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I washed my clothes like this.'
exe
summary: Subordinate clauses other than relatives and complements are usually finite and marked by a relator noun or postposition; for example, temporal precedence clauses use an imperfective verb plus the postposition ɕɯŋgɯ “before.” Converb clauses also occur, but they compete with finite clause constructions, and some finite clauses still show subordinate behavior through ellipsis of auxiliaries in chained periphrastic TAME constructions. The passage also describes a special manner serial verb construction in which the two verbs share TAME, subject, and often object.

text: After this overview of the core features of Japhug grammar, this section presents a selection of topics of particular interest to linguistic typology and comparative grammar in Japhug.
summary: This section moves beyond the overview of Japhug’s core grammar to present selected topics of special interest for linguistic typology and comparative grammar. It highlights features of Japhug that are particularly relevant for broader cross-linguistic comparison.

text:
consonant!cluster
The Kamnyu dialect of Japhug has over four hundred consonant clusters in onset position (§ sec:inventory.clusters, ), whose internal structure can be studied through alternations in reduplication patterns (§ sec:partial.redp, ).

In addition to the size of the inventory, which in itself is significant, because Japhug is one of the languages with the greatest number of clusters in the Trans-Himalayan family. Only Khroskyabs boasts more clusters,. The system of clusters presents two main points of interest.

First, syllable onsets in Japhug are rich in clusters violating the sonority sequencing principle ( ssp, § sec:ssp, ), and in particular present cases of ssp -infringing clusters without corresponding ssp -compliant equivalents. For instance, the ssp -infringing clusters rm- and rt- are relatively common, while $ $ mr- and $ $ tr- are unattested (except across syllables, § sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ) due to a series of sound changes (§ sec:NC.clusters, § sec:Cr.clusters ).

Second, some of these clusters are of considerable antiquity, as they appear to be preservations from proto-Trans-Himalayan, and thus of considerable importance for the reconstruction of syllable structure in this family in general  and in Old Chinese in particular.
summary: The Kamnyu dialect of Japhug has over 400 onset consonant clusters, making it one of the richest cluster systems in the Trans-Himalayan family, surpassed only by Khroskyabs. These clusters are notable for including many sonority sequencing principle violations, such as common rm- and rt- clusters without corresponding mr- or tr- forms, and some are ancient retentions from Proto-Trans-Himalayan that are important for reconstructing syllable structure in the family and Old Chinese.

text:
direct-inverse inverse
Direct-inverse systems, while relatively well-attested in languages of the Americas, are very rare in the Old World. Japhug and the other Gyalrong languages  are in fact the only languages in Eurasia to have a near-canonical direct-inverse indexation system (§ sec:direct-inverse, ), in particular with a direct-inverse contrast in both mixed (§ sec:indexation.mixed ) and non-local domains (§ sec:inverse.3.3.saliency ). Inverse-like phenomena are observed in Japanese, Circassian and some Trans-Himalayan languages, especially Kuki-Chin and Northern Naga, but the inverse morphemes in these languages are in the process of being grammaticalized, and still retain a cislocative meaning, whereas the inverse wɣ- in Japhug is dedicated to the expression of person indexation. Kiranti languages also have direct-inverse systems (in particular Bantawa and Puma, see and ), but the distribution of inverse and direct markers in these languages is much less transparent than in Gyalrong.

Moreover, Japhug is unique among Gyalrong languages in lacking inverse marking in the local 2 1 configuration (§ sec:indexation.local, § sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history, ), and possibly the only known language to use the inverse marker as the sole marker of generic transitive subject (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ).
summary: Direct-inverse systems are common in the Americas but very rare in Eurasia, where Japhug and the other Gyalrong languages are described as the only languages with a near-canonical direct-inverse indexation system. The passage notes that while some other languages show inverse-like phenomena, these are still grammaticalizing and retain cislocative meanings, unlike Japhug’s dedicated inverse marker. It also states that Japhug is unique among Gyalrong languages in lacking inverse marking in the local 2→1 configuration and may be the only language to use the inverse marker as the sole marker of a generic transitive subject.

text:
inflectionalization
While person indexation is one of the defining properties of verbs in Japhug (§ sec:indexation.intro ), a handful of expressions of nominal origin have acquired the ability to take dual -ndʑi and plural -nɯ indexation suffixes by analogy with imperative verb forms (§ sec:non.finite.indexation ).

For instance, the phatic expression sɤrmagood night (§ sec:phatic.inflectionalization ) has the dual sɤrma-ndʑi `good night (to both of you)' when addressing two people. This unusual phenomenon has parallels in Indo-European.
summary: In Japhug, although person indexation is generally a property of verbs, a few expressions of nominal origin have analogically acquired dual **-ndʑi** and plural **-nɯ** indexation suffixes, like imperative verb forms. One example is the phatic expression **sɤrma** ‘good night,’ which can take the dual form **sɤrma-ndʑi** when addressing two people. The text notes that this unusual development has parallels in Indo-European.

text:
prefix!prefixing preference
Japhug, like other Gyalrong languages, has a large prefixal template (§ sec:prefixal.chain ), allowing more than seven or eight prefixes in a row (example ex:amAGWnWtWwGznAre, § sec:verb.overview.intro ), while the suffixal chain is much more restricted (§ sec:suffixes ). It is among the rare strongly prefixal languages with strict verb-final order, alongside Ket and Athabaskan.

While the verb-final word order is relatively ancient, Reconstructing word-order is a notoriously difficult task, but there is no positive reason to assume any other order at least for the common ancestor of Tibeto-Gyalrongic languages.
there is evidence that the part of the prefixal chains in Gyalrongic languages have been recently innovated, either through grammaticalization and integration of verb roots from serial-verb constructions, or the absorption of adverbs or clause-final particles occurring immediately before the verb into the verbal word (§ sec:khWti, § sec:apprehensive.history; see also on Khroskyabs).

Japhug also has a few bipartite verbs, made from two verb stems with identical TAME and person indexation cliticized to each other and with elision of either the suffixal chain of the first verb as in ( ex:atAtWstunatAtWmbatW ), the prefixal chain of the second verb, or both (§ sec:bipartite, ).

exe

a-tɤ-tɯ-stu= a-tɤ-tɯ-mbat- nɯ \\
irr - pfv - 2 -try.hard(1)= irr - pfv - 2 -try.hard(2)- pl \\
`Do your best/try hard.'
exe
summary: Japhug, like other Gyalrong languages, has an unusually large prefixal template that can stack more than seven or eight prefixes, while its suffixal chain is much more limited. It is a strongly prefixal language with strict verb-final order, and the text suggests that some parts of the prefixal chains in Gyalrongic languages were recently innovated through grammaticalization or incorporation of earlier adverbs, particles, or verb roots. Japhug also has a small set of bipartite verbs consisting of two verb stems with matching TAME and person marking, with some verbal material omitted from one stem or the other.

text:
indirect speech!hybrid
Reported speech in Japhug frequently presents mismatches in person indexation, with the main verb representing the point of view of the subject of the complement-taking verb, and the nouns and possessive prefixes that of the current speaker.

For instance, in ( ex:CWrtoRi.hybrid ), the verb rtoʁ has 1pl indexation, reflecting the point of view of the transitive subject of the complement-taking verb tɯ-nɯ-sɯso-nɯ `you think, you want' (the daughters-in-law, the addressee). On the other hand, the 2pl possessive prefixes on nɯ-pʰama `your parents' and the other nouns correspond to the point of view of the father-in-law (the current speaker) -- a 1pl possessor would be expected in the reported speech clause if no shift of point of reference had taken place, as in ( ex:CWrtoRi.hybrid2 ).

Three different translations of the Japhug sentence are proposed in ( ex:CWrtoRi.hybrid ), the first in direct speech, the second in indirect speech (with shift toward the current speaker) and the third as a merger of the two (agrammatical in English), directly reflecting the original hybrid indirect speech (§ sec:hybrid indirect ).
