Hybrid indirect speech is also found in Tibetic languages (, ), where it has contributed to confusion around the notion of ``conjunct/disjunct'' marking. The presence of person indexation makes this phenomenon more easily identifiable in Japhug than in Tibetan.
summary: Reported speech in Japhug often shows hybrid person indexation: the main verb reflects the point of view of the complement-taking subject, while nouns and possessive prefixes reflect the current speaker’s perspective. The passage illustrates this with a sentence where the verb is indexed for 1pl but the possessive prefixes are 2pl, and it notes that the result combines direct- and indirect-speech features. It also states that similar hybrid indirect speech occurs in Tibetic languages, where it has complicated analyses of conjunct/disjunct marking, though it is easier to identify in Japhug because of person indexation.

subsection: The expression of degree and comparison
text:
Japhug lacks comparative and superlative derivations, but has a rich array of constructions expressing degree and comparison (chapter chap:degree ), some of which are rather uncommon at least in this part of the world.

superlative
High degree can be marked by combining a finite adjectival stative verb with a degree adverb (§ sec:degree.adverbs ) as in ( ex:wuma.YWCqraR ) as in most languages. However, the most common construction conveying this meaning, illustrated in ( ex:WtWCqraR.YWsaXaR ), comprises a degree nominal (§ sec:degree.nominal.subject, § sec:degree.nominals ) serving as the intransitive subject of a verb of degree `be extremely'. Thus the neutral way in Japhug to say `$X$ is very intelligent' is literally `$X$'s degree of intelligence (of being intelligent) is extreme.'

exe

xlist

wuma ʑo ɲɯ-ɕqraʁ \\
really emph sens -be.intelligent \\
`S/he is very intelligent.' 0006380#S72

ɯ-tɯ-ɕqraʁ ɲɯ-saχaʁ \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.intelligent sens -be.extremely \\
`S/he is extremely intelligent.' 0006380#S13
xlist
exe

The main comparative construction in Japhug is unusual for a different reason. In many languages including Tibetic (, ), the ergative or the ablative are used to mark the standard of comparison. In Japhug, as illustrated in ( ex:sAz.mpCAr ), the standard has a dedicated postposition (§ sec:comparative ), whereas the ergative marker kɯ is used to mark the comparee instead (§ sec:comparee.kW, § sec:sAz.kW ).

exe

[ɯ-ʁi sɤz] [ɯ-pi nɯ kɯ] mpɕɤr \\
3sg. poss -younger.sibling comp 3sg. poss -elder.sibling dem erg be.beautiful: fact \\
`The elder sibling is more beautiful than the younger sibling.'
exe

This observation is all the more surprising given that kɯ is most likely borrowed from Tibetan.
summary:
Japhug lacks dedicated comparative and superlative derivational morphology, but it uses several degree constructions, including some that are unusual regionally. High degree is often expressed with a finite adjectival stative verb plus a degree adverb, but the most common superlative-like construction uses a degree nominal as the intransitive subject of a verb meaning “be extremely,” yielding a literal sense like “X’s degree of intelligence is extreme.”  

Its comparative construction is also atypical: the standard of comparison is marked by a dedicated postposition, while the comparee is marked by the ergative marker kɯ. This is notable because kɯ is likely borrowed from Tibetan.

subsection: Japhug morphology and Trans-Himalayan comparative linguistics
text:
morphology!Trans-Himalayan comparison
The rich verbal and nominal morphology of Japhug and other Gyalrongic languages comprises both archaisms and innovative features illustrating interesting grammaticalization pathways.

Among innovations, many voice prefixes (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ) have been created through reanalysis of denominal derivation (§ sec:voice.denominal ). The clearest case of an innovating voice marker is the antipassive rɤ- (§ sec:antipassive.rA ): irregular forms provide direct evidence that it originated from the intransitive denominal rɤ- (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ) applied to deverbal nouns (§ sec:antipassive.irr.form, ). Other representative innovations include the reflexive ʑɣɤ- from an incorporated pronoun (§ sec:reflexive.origin, ), the associated motion prefixes grammaticalized from motion verbs (§ sec:am.prefixes, ), the orientation preverbs from locational adverbs or nouns (§ sec:preverbs.adverbs ) and the comitative adverbs (§ sec:comitative.adverb, ).
comitative adverb
While Japhug did innovate many affixes, it also preserves morphological archaisms which go further back than proto-Gyalrongic, some potentially even up to proto-Trans-Himalayan.

indexation!antiquity
The antiquity of person indexation in Gyalrongic (§ sec:indexation.suffixes.history ) and the rest of Trans-Himalayan is a notoriously controversial topic, but in any case, a paradigm comprising a second person prefix with suffixes for first person and number of third and second person should at least be reconstructed back to the common ancestor of Gyalrongic, Kiranti and probably Jinghpo.

In a few cases, archaic morphology only remains as lexicalized traces in Japhug, in particular the applicative -t suffix, very prominent in Kiranti  for instance, which is only attested in two verbs (§ sec:applicative.t ), or the nominalization -z (§ sec:z.nmlz ) suffix, which has cognates in Tibetan and Chinese.

In other cases, derivational processes that only exist as traces in most of the family are still productive in Japhug and other core Gyalrong languages, in particular the sigmatic denominal and causative prefixes (§ sec:sigmatic.denominal, § sec:sig.causative, ), velar (§ sec:velar.nmlz.history ) and sigmatic (§ sec:sigmatic.nmlz.history ) nominalization prefixes, and the dental indefinite possessor prefix of inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:indef.genr.poss, § sec:inalienably.possessed ).

Gyalrong data is particularly relevant to the debate regarding the voicing alternation in Old Chinese and other Trans-Himalayan languages. Old Chinese and many other languages have pairs of verbs with a voicing contrast correlated with transitivity, in which the unvoiced verb is transitive and the voiced one intransitive. It is not obvious which one is the derived form, and the direction of derivation is still being debated.

Japhug and other Northern Gyalrong languages (, ) however provide a crucial piece of evidence showing that the directionality was from the transitive verb to the intransitive one (§ sec:anticausative.direction ), confirming evidence from unrelated sources: the Tibetan borrowing χtɤrscatter (from གཏོར་gtorscatter) has an intransitive counterpart ʁndɤrbe scattered (§ sec:anticausative.morphology ) with prenasalized onset without equivalent in Tibetan. This intransitivizing derivation can be described as anticausative (§ sec:anticausative.function ). There is further evidence that the prenasalization alternation comes from a nasal prefix, very probably a lexicalization of the autive nɯ- prefix (§ sec:autoben.historical ), whose spontaneous function (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ) is very close to that of anticausative verbs. Evidence for autive derivation only exists in Gyalrongic (, ). However, the presence of traces of the anticausative derivation as voicing alternations in various branches of Trans-Himalayan, for instance in Kiranti, Old Chinese or Tibetan, implies that the autive derivation by extension must also be of proto-Trans-Himalayan age, and thus represents a unique archaism of Gyalrongic.

The richness and high productivity of morphology in Japhug and other Gyalrong languages, comparable with that of Sanskrit in Indo-European or Meskwaki in Algonquian, offer a framework to explore the fossil morphology of other Trans-Himalayan languages, in particular those belonging to the Burmo-Gyalrongic and Tibeto-Gyalrongic branches, but also potentially for the family as a whole.

morphology!irregular
Commenting on the irregularity of correspondences between Tibetan, Old Chinese and Burmese, concludes that ``the phonetic influence of defunct morphology will one day explain these complicated correspondences, but this possibility will manifest only when more languages, particularly archaic languages such as those of the Rgyalrong and Kiranti branches, are brought within purview.'' One of the aims of this grammar is precisely to provide comparativists with sufficient data on this language to make it systematically usable in Trans-Himalayan etymological research, in the hope that this field can one day reach the degree of sophistication of Indo-European.
summary:
The passage argues that Japhug and other Gyalrongic languages preserve both many innovative morphological developments and important archaisms, some possibly inherited from proto-Trans-Himalayan. Innovations include voice prefixes, reflexive and motion markers, and other affixes created through grammaticalization, while archaic features include person indexation, old nominalizing and derivational suffixes, and traces of older processes such as anticausative derivation and voicing alternations.

It also emphasizes that Japhug data are crucial for reconstructing the history of Trans-Himalayan morphology, especially in debates over the direction of transitive/intransitive alternations and the explanation of irregular correspondences across languages. The grammar aims to provide the evidence needed for broader comparative work on the family.

text:
Japhug syllables follow the template (C)(C)(C)V(C) with initial clusters containing at most three consonants, and at most one consonant in the coda. Given the complexity of possible onsets, it is not practical to provide an exhaustive list of possible syllables in the language (unlike Naish languages for instance, see ). However, onsets and rhymes can be listed exhaustively.

This chapter, partly based on previous publications (in particular and ), presents the inventory of consonants and vowels, offers a focused discussion on syllabic structure and quasi-neutralization, and describes suprasegmental phenomena and speech errors. The complete inventory of consonant clusters is listed and analyzed in § sec:inventory.clusters in the following chapter.

This chapter does not treat the phonology of loanwords from Chinese (except highly nativized ones). Non-nativized Chinese loanwords are represented in this grammar in pinyin (even though this system is an imperfect way of rendering Sichuanese Mandarin) between angled brackets.
summary: Japhug syllables have the template (C)(C)(C)V(C), allowing up to three consonants in the onset and only one consonant in the coda, so an exhaustive list of all possible syllables is not practical, though onsets and rhymes can be listed completely. The chapter presents the consonant and vowel inventories, discusses syllabic structure, quasi-neutralization, suprasegmental phenomena, and speech errors, while the full inventory of consonant clusters is treated in the following chapter. It excludes the phonology of non-nativized Chinese loanwords, which are written in pinyin between angled brackets.

text: consonant syllable!structure
summary: The passage appears to be only a fragment, “consonant syllable!structure,” without enough context to summarize the linguistic content meaningfully. It suggests a topic related to consonant syllable structure, but no argument or factual details are provided.

text:
There are fifty consonantal phonemes in Japhug ( tab:consonants ). All can occur as simple onsets. Stops and affricates have a four-way contrast between voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced and prenasalized series.

The voiced fricatives ɣ and ʁ should be classified as non-nasal sonorants (§ sec:medials ), alongside the glides j and w, the lateral l and the rhotic r.

tab:consonants2 provides examples of each of these phonemes, followed whenever possible by the vowel ɯ. Among these consonants, four are only attested in borrowings from Tibetan and/or ideophones: ʂ, dʐ, dʑ and g.

The phoneme w is realized as a fricative f or ɸ before voiceless obstruents and as v or β before voiced ones, and can also be fricativized when it occurs as coda. In the orthography used in this work, it is transcribed as < f > when followed by an voiceless stop, affricate or fricative, and as < β > when followed by a voiced one (§ sec:wC.clusters ), or in coda position (§ sec:codas.inventory ).

As in many languages of the Tibetan area, the r is a trilled retroflex voiced fricative ɽ͡ʐ in onset position, sometimes realized as a simple voiced fricative ʐ. It is devoiced to ʂ (with neutralization of the contrast with ʂ) when followed by a voiceless consonant in clusters (§ sec:rC.clusters ).

The prenasalized voiced stops and affricates mb, nd, ndz, ndʑ, ndʐ, ɲɟ, ŋg and ɴɢ all have voiceless and voiceless aspirated counterparts such as mp(ʰ), nt(ʰ), nts(ʰ), ntɕ(ʰ), ntʂ(ʰ), ɲc(ʰ), ŋk(ʰ) and ɴq(ʰ) (§ sec:NC.clusters ). Yet, there are several pieces of evidence showing that the prenasalized voiced stops and affricates are of a different nature from the prenasalized voiceless ones.

First, the former can appear in clusters preceded by fricatives or non-nasal sonorants, as in ʑmbr, jndʐ or rɴɢl, while the latter cannot. Clusters such as * ʑmp(ʰ)r, * jntʂ(ʰ) or * rɴq(ʰ)l are not permitted in Japhug. Clusters of this type may have existed, but have been removed by voicing the stop/affricate (§ sec:voicing.alternation.non.anticausative ).

Second, the uvular voiced prenasalized ɴɢ has no simple voiced counterpart * ɢ, a fact which therefore precludes analyzing ɴɢ as a cluster n+ɢ.

There is a three-way contrast between tɕ, c and k before the front vowel i, as shown by the triplet comprising the correlative additive focus marker tɕialso (§ sec:ri.additive ), the highly polyfunctional cione (§ sec:ci.someone, § sec:other.pro, § sec:partitive.pronouns, § sec:identity.modifier, § sec:one.to.ten, § sec:indef.article and § sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ) and the demonstrative kithis (§ sec:demonstrative.pronouns ).

The palatal stops c, cʰ, ɟ and ɲɟ cannot be analyzed as velar+ j clusters, as a clear contrast exists between the palatal series and velar stops followed by j (§ sec:Cj.clusters ), in minimal pairs such as ɲɟohave damages and ŋgioslip, `glide'. The grapheme <i> represents an allophone of j in medial position with dental and dorsal initials (§ sec:Cj.clusters ). That the onsets ɲɟ- and ŋgj- have a different syllabic structure is confirmed by their reduplication patterns (§ sec:partial.redp ): while in the former the palatalization is present on the reduplicant pɯ-nɤ-ɲɟɯ ɲɟo `have damages everywhere' (in the distributed action derivation, § sec:distributed.action ), in the latter the j is not reduplicated as pɯ-nɤ-ŋgɯ ŋgio `he slipped everywhere'.

The alveolo-palatal affricates tɕ, tɕʰ, dʑ and ndʑ are also contrastive with dental affricates+ j clusters, as shown by the minimal pair ndziaʁbe tight (of knot) vs. ndʑaʁswim (§ sec:Cj.clusters ). There is also a contrast with dental stops+ j, though no good minimal pairs can be found due to the rarity of these clusters.

The attested contrasts between coronal affricates and dorsal stops with and without the j medial are illustrated in tab:coronal.dorsal in combination with the vowel o.

The voiceless lateral ɬ (realized by some speakers as a postaspirated lateral lʰ ), is a marginal phoneme in Japhug, which does not appear in clusters (except heterosyllabic ones, as in cɯɣɬaj `symptom in which the oral cavity becomes white') and is very rare in the native vocabulary. Yet, its phonemic status is justified by the fact that it contrasts with lx. There are no minimal pairs contrasting the two, but the contrast can be indirectly illustrated by examples such as alxajnot properly put (of clothes) and lxɯlxithick and cumbersome on the one hand, and ɬɤtbecome old and ɬɤndʐighost on the other hand.
summary: Japhug has fifty consonantal phonemes, all of which can occur as simple onsets, and its stops and affricates show a four-way contrast among voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced, and prenasalized series. The passage also explains several phonological patterns and contrasts, including special behavior of w and r in different contexts, the distinct status of prenasalized voiced vs. voiceless stops, and clear contrasts between palatal/alveolo-palatal consonants and velar or dental consonants plus j. It ends by noting that ɬ is a marginal but phonemically contrastive voiceless lateral.

text:
consonant!coda syllable!closed
The inventory of consonants in coda position in Japhug is more restricted than in initial position. In particular, the voicing and aspiration contrasts are neutralized in codas.

Only twelve consonants out of fifty appear as codas: -p, -w, -m, -t, -z, -n, -l, -r, -j, -ɣ, -ŋ, -ʁ. The stop -p is restricted to a few ideophones (§ sec:coda.idph ), and is found neither in the inherited non-ideophonic vocabulary nor in Tibetan loanwords, except as the first element of the heterosyllabic cluster pt in the word sqap.tɯɣ `eleven' (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ). The codas -n, -l and -ŋ are extremely rare (but not entirely absent) in the non-ideophonic native vocabulary.

A list of possible combinations between codas and vowels in Japhug is described in § sec:rhyme.inventory.

In word-final position, codas are voiced when followed by a word beginning with a voiced consonant or a vowel, but are devoiced in phrase-final position, before a pause or before a voiceless segment (even across word boundaries, § sec:sandhi.word ). In isolation, word-final -z, -r, -j, -ɣ and -ʁ in particular are realized as s, r̥, j̥, x and χ, respectively. The coda -ʁ can also be realized alternatively as pharyngealization of the preceding vowel.

Since the voicing contrast between the voiceless fricatives s, x, χ and the voiced ones z, ɣ, ʁ is neutralized in coda position, it could seem better to argue that the fricative codas, whatever their phonetic realization, are archiphonemes s,z, x,ɣ and χ,ʁ, and that any discussion of their underlying voicing is futile. However, in the case of Japhug at least, some morphophonological rules are easier to describe if one assumes that fricative codas are underlyingly voiced. I owe the idea that final -z is voiced to, where a similar analysis is implicitly proposed about Tshobdun.

First, when the 1sg -a suffix is added to a verb stem ending in a fricative coda, that coda is resyllabified, becoming the onset of the syllable with a as rhyme. In these cases, the voiced allophone always surfaces (§ sec:intr.1 ): for instance the 1sg 3sg Imperfective of ntɕʰozuse is tu-ntɕʰóz-a, syllabified as tu.ntɕʰo.za. If one were to assume that the fricative coda -z were voiceless or underspecified for voicing, a context-specific voicing rule would have to be assumed to have taken place, since V́sa is a permissible sequence in Japhug, as in pjɤ́-wɣ-sat ifr - inv -kill (see for instance example ex:pjArwGrzWrzWG in § sec:denom.tr.rA ). It is more economical to assume that -z and the other fricative codas are underlying voiced, and become devoiced in the same contexts as the sonorants.

Second, the locative postposition zɯ (§ sec:core.locative ) is the result of the degrammaticalization of the locative *-s suffix still attested in Situ (§ ex:word.vs.clitic.postp ). The fact that it has a voiced, rather than an voiceless onset, suggests that the fricative was voiced when it was a suffix.
summary:
Japhug has a much smaller set of consonants in coda position than in onset position, and voicing and aspiration contrasts are neutralized there. Only twelve consonants occur as codas, with some being rare or highly restricted, and word-final codas are devoiced in phrase-final position but voiced before voiced segments or vowels.

Although the fricative codas could be analyzed as underlyingly voiceless/archiphonemic, the passage argues that it is better to treat them as underlyingly voiced, because this makes the language’s morphophonological patterns easier to explain. Evidence comes from resyllabification with the 1sg -a suffix, where voiced allophones surface, and from the locative postposition zɯ, which reflects a historically voiced suffix.

text:
vowel
Japhug has eight vowel phonemes, listed in tab:vowels. The mid-open unrounded vowels ɤ and e are only marginally contrastive: ɤ does not occur in word-final open syllables except in unaccented clitics (like the additive nɤ, § sec:additive.nA ), and e only occurs in the last (accented) syllable of a word. They are clearly contrastive only with the coda -t (§ sec:rhyme.inventory ).

Not all speakers of Kamnyu Japhug have a phoneme y in the native vocabulary. Even for those speakers, it is only attested in the word `fish' and the verbs derived from it. It nevertheless contrasts with ɯ and u, as shown by the quasi-minimal pairs qaɟy `fish', waɟɯ `earthquake' and ɟuli `flute'. Other speakers pronounce `fish' with a medial w as qaɟwi. However, y is found in the speech of all Japhug speakers in Chinese loanwords such as 洋芋 yángyùpotato.
summary: Japhug has eight vowel phonemes, but the mid-open unrounded vowels ɤ and e are only weakly contrasted: ɤ is restricted from word-final open syllables except in certain clitics, and e occurs only in the final accented syllable, so both are mainly contrasted by their behavior with coda -t. The phoneme y is not present in the native vocabulary of all Kamnyu Japhug speakers, though it appears in the word for “fish” and related verbs, contrasts with ɯ and u, and is used by all speakers in Chinese loanwords.

text:
vowel!assimilation assimilation!vowel
When followed by a syllable containing a rounded vowel ( u or o), the back unrounded vowels ɯ and ɤ optionally undergo rounding harmony to u and o, respectively. For instance, ɣɤʑu `exist (sensory)' (§ sec:existential.basic ) is generally pronounced as ɣoʑu, and the reduplicated form tɯ tu-dɤn `more and more' (§ sec:redp.gradual.increase ) is realized as tutudɛn.

The phoneme ɤ in prefixes tends to be pronounced more open as ɐ when followed by a syllable whose main vowel is a, making it sometimes difficult to perceive the contrast, for instance between ta-mawork and tɤ-mamother (honorific). In the verbal system, the 1sg -a suffix triggers obligatory regressive assimilation ɤ a on the preceding syllable (see tab:verb.stem.1sg, § sec:intr.1 ).
summary: When a following syllable contains a rounded vowel /u/ or /o/, the back unrounded vowels /ɯ/ and /ɤ/ may optionally undergo rounding harmony, becoming /u/ and /o/ respectively. The phoneme /ɤ/ in prefixes is also often realized as a more open [ɐ] before /a/, and in the verbal system the 1sg suffix -a causes obligatory regressive assimilation of /ɤ a/ in the preceding syllable.

text:
vowel!synizesis
While no true diphthongs exist in Japhug, when the 1sg -a suffix is added to a verb stem ending in an open syllable, the two syllables undergo synizesis (§ sec:intr.1 ). When the verb stem contains the mid vowels -e and -o, they become the corresponding high vowels -i and -u due to merging with a, and the contrasts between e and i on the one hand, and o and u on the other hand, are neutralized. For instance, tso-a tsua `I understand' and βze-a βzia `I (will) do it' are homophonous with tsu-a `I have time' and βzi-a `I (will) be drunk', respectively. Three pseudo-diphthongs are thus attested: ia (from e-a and i-a ), ua (from o-a and u-a ) and ɯa (from ɯ-a ).

Synizesis results in syllables homophonous to the rhymes -wa and -ja in clusters ending in -w- (§ sec:Cw.clusters ) or -j- (§ sec:Cj.clusters ) followed by the vowel -a. For instance, aro-a `I own' (§ sec:semi.transitive ) is homophonous with a-rwa `my tent' (§ sec:Cw.clusters ).

Apart from synizesis, two other types of vowel contraction are found in Japhug. First, verb stems with initial a- have specific conjugation patterns, where initial a- merges with the immediately preceding prefix following rules that are not completely trivial (§ sec:contraction ). Second, the 1sg -a suffix merges with -a stems as a, without vowel lengthening in Kamnyu Japhug (§ sec:intr.1 ). However, vowel lengthening is found in some dialects, such as that of Sarndzu.
summary:
Japhug has no true diphthongs, but when the 1sg suffix -a is added to a verb stem ending in an open syllable, the two syllables merge by synizesis. In this process, mid vowels -e and -o raise to -i and -u, creating three pseudo-diphthongs (ia, ua, ɯa) and neutralizing contrasts such as e/i and o/u.

The resulting forms can be homophonous with sequences involving -w- or -j- followed by -a. The passage also notes two other kinds of vowel contraction: stems beginning with a- have special conjugation patterns with prefix merging, and the 1sg -a suffix merges with -a stems as a in Kamnyu Japhug, though some dialects show vowel lengthening.

text:
There are strong phonotactic restrictions on vowel-initial stems and words in Japhug.

In word-initial position, only a- and ɯ- are found. These vowels can merge with previous open syllables (§ sec:sandhi.word ), and no glottal stop appears, unlike in many Trans-Himalayan languages such as Khaling. Phonetic u, o, i- do appear in word-initial position, but are preferably analyzed as wu, wo- and ji- with a glide.

The only possible stem-initial vowel in verbal stems is a- (§ sec:contraction ). It is relatively common due to the fact that it appears in many derivational prefixes (§ sec:denom.contracting, § sec:passive, § sec:reciprocal, § sec:distributed.amW ). Stem-initial a- undergoes vowel contraction with all preceding prefixes. By contrast, stem-initial wu- or ji- (for instance, wumgather and jiplant) never merge with preceding prefixes.

In noun stems, initial a- also exists and interacts with prefixes (§ sec:a.nouns ), but is considerably rarer.

Comparison with other Gyalrongic languages indicates that word-initial a- and ɯ- (in the native vocabulary, excluding loanwords and interjections) are secondary. Word-initial ɯ- is only attested in a few interjections (such as ɯtɕʰɯtɕʰɯ, § sec:interjections ) and in the third possessive prefix (§ sec:possessive.paradigm ). The form $ $ ɣɯ- (homophonous with the inverse prefix, § sec:allomorphy.inv ) would be expected, and the unexpected form ɯ- in Japhug might be due to false segmentation in sandhi (§ sec:3sg.possessive.form ). Word-initial a- originates mainly from *ŋa-, due to loss of the simple initial *ŋ- in non-stressed syllables (including wumareal, really from ངོ་མ་ŋo.mareal, true, but excluding monosyllabic verb stems such as ŋube and ŋabuy on credit, owe).
summary:
Japhug shows strong restrictions on vowel-initial stems and words: in word-initial position, only a- and ɯ- occur, while apparent initial u, o, and i are better analyzed as sequences with glides. In verbal stems, only initial a- is possible, and it commonly contracts with preceding prefixes, whereas initial wu- and ji- do not merge.

The passage also notes that word-initial a- and ɯ- in the native vocabulary are secondary developments in comparison with other Gyalrongic languages. Word-initial ɯ- is rare and may reflect segmentation issues, while word-initial a- mainly comes from *ŋa- after loss of initial *ŋ- in non-stressed syllables.

text:
rhyme syllable!structure
There are strong phonotactic constraints on possible rhymes in Japhug. tab:rhymes lists all attested rhymes; the coda -w is transcribed as -β in the orthography used in this grammar.

The only coda attested with all vowels is -t ( tab:t.rhymes ). Among these rhymes, -et and -yt are only attested in verb forms with the past transitive -t suffix (§ sec:suffixes, § sec:other.TAME, § sec:indexation.mixed ), which occurs in word-final position only in 2sg 3 forms.

In closed syllables with an alveolo-palatal or a palatal consonant preceding the vowel, ɯ is fronted and its contrast with i is neutralized (§ sec:W.i.closed.syllables ). It is only maintained before -t in forms with the past transitive -t suffix. For instance, we find the minimal pair tɤ-tɯ-cɯ-t `you opened it' ( aor -2-open- pst ) and lɤ-tɯ-cit `you moved' ( aor -2-move).

With the coda -j, the contrasts between ɯ and i on the one hand, and ɤ and e on the other hand, are neutralized. The rhyme -aj is realized as ɛj or æj.
summary: Japhug has strong phonotactic restrictions on allowable rhymes, and the coda -w is written -β in the grammar’s orthography. The only coda found with all vowels is -t, and some rhymes like -et and -yt occur only in verb forms with the past transitive -t suffix. In closed syllables, ɯ is fronted after alveolo-palatal or palatal consonants and merges with i except before -t, while with coda -j the contrasts ɯ/i and ɤ/e are neutralized and -aj is realized as ɛj or æj.

text:
rhyme!historical phonology
Some notions of Japhug historical phonology are useful to account for the gaps in the distribution of rhymes (§ sec:rhyme.inventory ) as well as some vowel alternations (§ sec:stem3.form ).

Comparison of inherited vocabulary between Japhug and extra-Gyalrongic languages shows that the codas *-l, *-n and *-ŋ have been lost in the native vocabulary ( tab:lnN.coda ). Words with these codas are either borrowed from Tibetan or have an ideophonic origin.

The proto-Gyalrong rhyme *-aŋ corresponds to Japhug -o (Situ -o, Tshobdun -i, Zbu -æ, ); this correspondence is also found in some early loanwords. A secondary -aŋ rhyme has been created from several sources (§ sec:aN.oN.free ), most importantly Tibetan borrowings postdating the sound change *-aŋ -o.

A chain shift has taken place, as Proto-Gyalrong *-o has regularly changed to -u and *-u to -ɯ.

In closed syllables, rounded vowels have become unrounded in the native vocabulary. In the earliest layer of Tibetan loanwords, -od, -or, -ob, -ol and -os correspond to -ɤt, -ɤr, -ɤβ, -ɤl and -ɤz, respectively, but are unchanged in the later layers ( tab:unrounding.loanwords ).

This sound change did not affect rhymes with uvular codas: proto-Gyalrong *-oq remained -oʁ.

The rhymes *-aj, *-oj and *-uj on the other hand have merged as -e, -e and -i, respectively. These vowel fusions occurred before *-o -u, as shown by the -u / -e alternation in Stem III (§ sec:stem3.form,, ), which is cognate to the ``transitivity marker'' -jə in Tshobdun, as illustrated in sec:stem3.sound.change.

After this sound change had removed all -j codas, secondary -oj and -uj rhymes were later analogically created by the addition of the locative *-j suffix to stems in -o and -u. A handful of examples remain in Japhug (§ sec:locative.j ). The origin of the rhyme -aj in Japhug is an unsolved problem, and may be due to contextual vowel breaking (Gong Xun, p.c.).

The only other closed rhymes with o in the native vocabulary are -oz, which originates from *-aŋs, as in sozmorning, and -ot (in the case of verb stems in -o with the past transitive -t suffix, § sec:suffixes ).
summary: Japhug historical phonology explains several gaps in rhyme distribution and vowel alternations through a series of sound changes. In inherited vocabulary, the codas *-l, *-n, and *-ŋ were lost, Proto-Gyalrong *-aŋ became Japhug -o, and later *-o shifted to -u and *-u to -ɯ, with rounded vowels in closed syllables generally becoming unrounded except before uvular codas. The passage also notes mergers of *-aj, *-oj, and *-uj, later analogical re-creation of secondary -oj and -uj forms, and a few special remaining rhymes such as -oz and -ot.

text:
dissimilation!rhotic
The rhotic coda -r cannot co-occur with a rhotic or a retroflex consonant in the onset: syllables of the type $ $ CrVr, $ $ rCVr or $ $ tʂVr are not attested. However, a -r preinitial can be preceded by a syllable containing a r or a retroflex fricative or affricate in its onset, in reduplicated forms such as rdardɯldust, dirt (§ sec:redp.coll ), or a compound like qrornired ant (§ sec:second.member.alternation ). Since the r sounds in rda.rdɯl and qro.rni are heterosyllabic, they do not violate the rhotic dissimilation constraint (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ).
summary: The rhotic coda **-r** cannot co-occur in the same syllable with a rhotic or retroflex onset consonant, so syllable patterns like **CrVr**, **rCVr**, and **tʂVr** are unattested. However, a **-r** preinitial may follow a syllable whose onset contains **r** or a retroflex fricative/affricate in reduplicated forms or compounds, because the relevant consonants are heterosyllabic and therefore do not violate the rhotic dissimilation constraint.

text:
assimilation!uvular consonant!uvular consonant!velar
Velars and uvulars do not coexist well within the same syllable in Japhug. There are no syllables of the type $ $ QCVɣ or $ $ KCVʁ (where K and Q represent any velar and uvular initial consonant, respectively): the onset and the coda have to be both velars, or both uvulars. Thus, syllables such as qraʁploughshare and krɤɣshear, mow are possible, but not $ $ kraʁ or $ $ qrɤɣ.

With preinitials and medial consonants, the constraint depends on the context. Several cases have to be distinguished.

First, the uvular coda -ʁ is compatible with the velar medial -ɣ, as shown by examples such as pɣaʁturn over (§ sec:CG.clusters ); the opposite case is not attested, but given the relative rarity of medial -ʁ, this may be accidental.

Second, the uvular preinitial ʁ- is attested before velar initials in some Tibetan loanwords, such as ʁgraenemy (§ sec:Cr.clusters, from Tibetan དགྲ་dgraenemy). The Tibetan preinitial d- normally corresponds to r- before velars, but the expected $ $ rgra would have violated the rhotic dissimilation rule (§ sec:rhotic.dissimilation ).

Third, a uvular preinitial with the velar medial -ɣ- is only found in the dialectal word tɯ-χpɣithigh (§ sec:CG.clusters ).

These constraints do not apply across syllables, as shown by words such as kóʁmɯzonly after, in which the ʁ is the preinitial of the second syllable.

The discrimination of uvulars and velars is due to a recent sound change that occurred in Japhug and affected both native words and Tibetan loanwords, viz. the uvularization of velar initial consonants in syllables with uvular -ʁ. This sound change explains for instance why Japhug words such as tɯ-qʰoχpaorgans, state of mind (phonologically qʰoʁ.pa with internal sandhi) from Tibetan ཁོག་པ་kʰog.painsides See § sec:body.part for an account of the prefix tɯ-. has a uvular qʰ- corresponding to a velar kʰ- in Tibetan: dorsal codas (transcribed as -g ) are realized as uvulars after a and o in most Tibetan varieties, so that a correspondence of Tibetan -ag and -og to Japhug -aʁ and -oʁ is expected. At an earlier stage, tɯ-qʰoχpa has probably been borrowed as * tɯ-kʰoʁpa and the sound law * velar uvular /_V ʁ applied to it like in the rest of the vocabulary. In Tshobdun, there is a doublet of loanwords corresponding to the same Tibetan etymon: o-kʰoχpe `its abdominal cavity' without uvularization and o-qʰɔ́χpe `her heart' with uvularization.

An older example of uvular harmony is found in the noun qʰaqʰubehind the house from kʰahouse and ɯ-qʰuafter, behind: this word has a Tshobdun exact cognate qʰɐqʰu, showing that the assimilation occurred in the common ancestor of the two languages.
summary:
In Japhug, velar and uvular consonants generally cannot co-occur within the same syllable: the onset and coda must both be velar or both be uvular, though some mixed cases occur in larger consonant clusters depending on the specific segmental context. These patterns are explained by a recent sound change in which velar initial consonants became uvularized before syllabic -ʁ, affecting both native words and Tibetan loanwords.

The passage also notes that this harmony does not apply across syllable boundaries, and gives examples of loanwords and dialectal forms showing partial compatibility between uvular and velar preinitials and medials. An older case of uvular assimilation is also cited, with cognates in Tshobdun showing that the change predates the split of the two languages.

text:
vowel!neutralization vowel!free variation
The present section discusses four particularly thorny problems of synchronic Kamnyu Japhug phonology, which are the source of uncertainty in some transcriptions. They involve quasi-neutralization and interdialectal contact, which constitute challenging problems for phonologists (see ).

The contrast between -oŋ and -aŋ
Inherited Japhug words never have final -ŋ (in particular, proto-Gyalrong *-aŋ shifts to -o, see § sec:historical.phono ). Words with this coda belong to four groups: Tibetan loanwords, ideophones, borrowings from other Gyalrong varieties (in the case of rkaŋbe strong, the corresponding inherited Japhug etymon is rkobe hard) or function words with irregular syllable fusion ( koŋlareally from kɯŋula, see § sec:intensifier.adverbs ).

Despite some minimal pairs ( caŋdammed wall vs. coŋdamage, loss from གྱང་gʲaŋdammed wall and གྱོང་gʲoŋloss, respectively), the contrast between -oŋ and -aŋ in Kamnyu Japhug has some degree of instability: some words in -oŋ and -aŋ, but not all, allow free variation between the two pronunciations. This free variation is presumably due to influence from neighbouring dialects of Japhug such as that of Rqakyo, where words with -oŋ and -oʁ in Kamnyu are pronounced with a more open vowel.

Words with stable -aŋ in final syllable include rkaŋbe strong, fsaŋfumigation, kʰɯrtʰaŋadministrative position, mkʰɤrmaŋpeople, praʁkʰaŋcave, rɲaŋbe ancient. In non-final position, stable -aŋ is found in particular in words whose final syllable contains a, as in fsraŋmaprotecting deity (as opposed to unstable fsroŋ / fsraŋ `protect', see tab:aN.oN.free ).

Words with stable -oŋ in the final syllable include ɕoŋtɕatimber (as opposed to ɕaŋβzu / ɕoŋβzu `carpentry' with unstable rhyme), koŋlareally, pʰoŋbottle, qɯmdroŋwild goose, ʁmbroŋwild yak or tɯ-phoŋbubody.

tab:aN.oN.free presents a list of words with unstable -oŋ / -aŋ, mostly loanwords from Tibetan, coming either from rhymes in a+nasal or from rhymes in rounded vowel+nasal. It also includes the egressive postpositions with ɕaŋ- as first element such as ɕoŋtaʁ / ɕaŋtaʁup from (see § sec:egressive ).

For all these words, the orthography used in this work and in the corpus generalizes the -aŋ variant, which is considered by Tshendzin to be more ``correct''.

The contrast between ɯ and i after palatal and alveolo-palatal consonants
The contrast between ɯ and i is partially or completely neutralized after palatals ( c, cʰ, ɟ, ɲɟ, ɲ and j) and alveolo-palatal ( tɕ, tɕʰ, dʑ, ndʑ, ɕ, ʑ) consonants in some contexts.

In stressed open syllables, in particular in word-final position, the contrast between ɯ and i is nevertheless very clear after all consonants. The existence of minimal pairs such as cɯstone and cione or the stem alternations between ndʑɯ (stem I) and ndʑi (stem III) in the paradigm of the verb ndʑɯaccuse (§ sec:stem3 ), show that this contrast is not neutralized after palatal and alveolo-palatal consonants in this context.

The contrast between ɯ and i is completely neutralized in most closed syllables and near-neutralized in unstressed syllables, including verbal suffixes, prefixes, and non-final elements of compounds. Each of these contexts is extensively discussed below.
summary: The passage describes two major synchronic phonological problems in Kamnyu Japhug: instability in the contrast between final -oŋ and -aŋ, and partial neutralization of the contrast between ɯ and i after palatal and alveolo-palatal consonants. The -oŋ/-aŋ variation affects some words, especially loans and certain function forms, and the author standardizes these as -aŋ in the orthography, while the ɯ/i contrast remains clear in stressed open syllables but is neutralized in most closed and unstressed syllables.

text:
vowel!neutralization syllable!closed
In closed syllables, the contrast between ɯ and i is almost completely neutralized after palatals ( c, cʰ, ɟ, ɲɟ, ɲ and j) and alveolo-palatal ( tɕ, tɕʰ, dʑ, ndʑ, ɕ, ʑ) consonants. The archiphoneme ɯ,i is realized as ɯ before -ɣ, -β (and the rare -p ), and as i before -m, -r, -n and -l, as shown by tab:palatal.WC.iC. In the orthography adopted in the present work, the archiphoneme ɯ,i is transcribed as ɯ in all these contexts.

The proof that the underlying phoneme is ɯ rather than i is provided by the rhyme reduplication of mtɕɯrturn in the distributed action form nɤmtɕɯrlɯrturn in all directions (§ sec.distributed.action.l ): if i had been the underlying vowel, a form such as $ $ nɤmtɕirlir would have been expected.

The contrast between ɯ and i used to be neutralized before the codas -z and -t, with the archiphoneme ɯ,i realized as i. However, new rhymes -ɯt and -ɯz contrasting with -it and -iz have been reintroduced by the transitive 1/2 sg 3 past suffix -t or -z (depending on the dialect of Japhug, see § sec:suffixes, § sec:other.TAME ).

Minimal pairs between open syllable -ɯ stem verbs taking the -t suffix (such as tɤ-tɯ-cɯ-t `you opened it' aor -2-open- pst ) and -it stem verbs ( lɤ-tɯ-cit `you moved' aor -2-move) can easily be found (§ sec:rhyme.inventory ). Even if this contrast is extremely marginal and restricted to this morphological context, ɯ and i cannot be considered to be neutralized before -z or -t (depending on the dialect of Japhug).
summary:
In closed syllables after palatal and alveolo-palatal consonants, the contrast between ɯ and i is largely neutralized, with the archiphoneme pronounced as ɯ before -ɣ, -β, and rare -p, and as i before -m, -r, -n, and -l; the orthography nevertheless writes this archiphoneme as ɯ in all these contexts. The text argues that the underlying vowel is ɯ, not i, based on rhyme reduplication evidence.

It also notes that the earlier neutralization of ɯ and i before -z and -t has been disrupted by the reintroduction of contrasting rhymes -ɯt/-ɯz and -it/-iz through a transitive past suffix. As a result, ɯ and i can no longer be said to be neutralized before -z or -t, even though the contrast is very limited and morph

text:
In compounds and other polysyllabic stems, the contrast between ɯ and i is very difficult to perceive in non-final open syllables with palatal or alveolo-palatal consonant onsets, and my main consultant Tshendzin has, during our decade-long collaboration, expressed conflicting views about whether a contrast does or does not exist in this context.

While there are no minimal pairs only distinguished by the ɯ vs. i contrast in non-final syllables after palatal or alveolo-palatal consonants, it now seems clear that some words are consistently pronounced with ɯ rather than i in this context. This unstable contrast, which does not carry much information load, is likely to differ at the idiolectal level. The orthography used in this work reflects a normalization based on Tshendzin 's judgements (rechecked several times).

paragraph tɕʰi° vs. tɕʰɯ°
Many nouns in Japhug have tɕʰi° or tɕʰɯ° as first element, in particular due to words of Tibetan origin containing ཆུ་tɕʰuwater or མཆུ་mtɕʰulip. The variant tɕʰi° is found in the great majority of these words. In some cases like tɕʰirawater jar (from ཆུ་ར་tɕʰu.rawater container), I have used an etymologizing transcription with ɯ ( tɕʰɯra ) in previous works (in particular ), but changed my mind after careful rechecking (using for instance the stems I and III of the verb tɕʰɯgore, stab for comparison).

The variant tɕʰɯ° is essentially restricted to words with a cluster with a uvular or a labial fricative as first element (such as rtɕʰɯʁjɯcaterpillar, tɕʰɯχprisalamander, tɕʰɯβroʁtype of tsampa), but also found in tɕʰɯmɲɯɣwater hole (from ཆུ་མིག་tɕʰu.migwater hole) and tɕʰɯzɯtype of weaving tool.

The noun tɯ-mtɕʰimouth (from མཆུ་mtɕʰulip) has an unexpected i (the expected form would be $ $ mtɕʰɯ ). It is possible that it was extracted from a compound (like tɯ-mtɕʰirmemoustaches) where ɯ and i are neutralized as i, and that this phonetic variant was then reinterpreted as an independent root.
paragraph
paragraph ndʑi° vs. ndʑɯ°
Compounds with ndʑi° or ndʑɯ° as non-final element are not common, but social relation collective nouns (§ § sec:social.collective ) containing the prefix kɤndʑi, are particularly numerous. Words with the variant ndʑɯ° are very rare: the two verbs ndʑɯrpɯtbe numb and andʑɯβriprotect each other (with the rare reciprocal prefix andʑɯ- / andʑi- of denominal origin, see § sec:denom.andZi ), and the nouns ndʑɯrwɯzSonchus sp and ndʑɯnɯAngelica (minimal pair with ndʑi-nɯ `their breast', see § § sec:verbal.suffixes.possessive.prefixes.i.W ).
paragraph
paragraph ci° vs. cɯ°
Compounds comprising cɯstone or the root of tɯ-ciwater as non-final element are common, and the majority of these words have the variant ci°, even when the noun comes from cɯstone (for instance ciχɕizstony earth). Exceptions include cɯrmbɯstone heap, scɯʁzɯɣappearance (from སྐྱེ་གཟུགས་skʲe.gzugsphysical appearance) and ɣɤcɯqʰlɯβmaking noise (of water when agitated). This verb is a denominal verbalization from a noun-ideophone compound (§ sec.n.idph.compounds ).
paragraph
paragraph cʰi° vs. cʰɯ°
Nouns with cʰi° or cʰɯ° include in particular Tibetan loanwords in ཁྱི་kʰʲidog. The form cʰi° occurs in most cases (for instance cʰisɲurabies from ཁྱི་སྨྱོ་kʰʲi.smʲorabies), but exceptions include cʰɯmufemale dog, cʰɯrdomroaming dog and nɯcʰɯrakeep guard (rechecked using the minimal pair cʰibe sweet vs. tɤ-cʰɯwedge).
paragraph
paragraph ɟi° vs. ɟɯ°
Words containing the status contructus of ɟubamboo can have either the vowel i (as ɟispjɤtperson making bamboo baskets) or ɯ ( ɟɯmɢombamboo tweezers). Other words in ɟi° include ɟigatortuous path and its derived forms.

The root of tɯ-rɟɯfortune commonly occur as first element of compounds, and have the vowel ɯ, as in rɟɯrŋomcoveting other people's fortune. The syllable -rɟɯ- also occurs as the status constructus of tɤ-rɟitchild in the word tɤrɟɯstionly child.

paragraph
paragraph ji° vs. jɯ°
Compounds with non-final jɯ° are extremely rare, limited to the two Tibetan loanwords jɯɣiwriting (from ཡི་གེ་ji.geletter) and pjɯrɯcoral (from བྱུ་རུ་bʲu.rucoral).
paragraph
summary: The passage notes that the contrast between ɯ and i is hard to perceive in non-final open syllables after palatal or alveolo-palatal consonants, and that the consultant’s judgments have been inconsistent, suggesting an unstable and likely idiolect-specific contrast with low functional load. It then surveys several non-final elements in compounds, showing that i is usually the default variant in forms such as tɕʰi°, ndʑi°, ci°, cʰi°, and ji°, while ɯ is restricted to a smaller set of words and a few exceptions, often influenced by etymology or particular lexical items.

text:
reduplication!vowel contrasts prefix!vowel contrasts
The vowels ɯ and ɤ are by far the most common ones in prefixes in Japhug. In the case of verbal prefixes with palatal and alveolo-palatal onsets, the same phonological problem as in compounds (§ § sec:W.i.compounds ) is observed, namely the question whether the contrast between ɯ and i has been neutralized or not, and whether the vowel should be transcribed as i rather than as ɯ.

The prefixes in which this problem arises are few, and are exhaustively listed in tab:pref.palatal. For prefixes in ɕV- and cʰV, testing the vowel is possible using minimal pairs ( ɕɯwho vs. ɕipolar interrogative and cʰibe sweet vs. tɤ-cʰɯwedge as in § § sec:compounds.chi.chW ). For pjV- and jV prefixes, comparison is possible with the first syllable of the nouns jɯɣiwriting and pjɯrɯcoral (§ § sec:compounds.ji.jW ).

The main consultants on the basis of whose expertise this work has been written have presented conflicting judgments regarding the nature of the vowel in these prefixes. After some hesitation, Tshendzin considers it to be i for all of these prefixes (for instance, she considers the vowel of pjɯrɯcoral to be different from that of pjɯ-ɣi `he comes down'). I nevertheless keep here the orthographic `etymological' transcription with the vowel ɯ for three reasons.

First, the contrast is marginal, if existent at all, for most speakers, and given the limited number of prefixes affected, it is possible to automatically change the transcription from ɯ to i only in these prefixes without loss of information (this can be necessary for instance as a pre-treatment for the purposes of automatic transcription training).

Second, the prefixes in tab:pref.palatal are affected by vowel fusion (§ sec:contraction ) and coalescence with the inverse prefix -wɣ (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ) like other prefixes in Cɯ, and these morphophonological phenomena are easier to state by assuming the underlying vowel ɯ for all prefixes.

Third, the assimilation from ɯ to i following palatal and alveolo-palatal consonants appears to be general in the morphology of the language, including partially reduplicated forms, whose rhyme is replaced by -ɯ (§ sec:partial.redp ). For instance, Tshendzin judges that the reduplicant here transcribed as -ɕɯ- of the reduplicated form nɤɕɯɕego around (from ɕego) to be phonetically closer to ɕipolar interrogative than to ɕɯwho. Adopting a transcription with i in the prefixes in tab:pref.palatal would therefore only make sense if reduplicated forms of syllables with palatal and alveolo-palatal consonants are also transcribed with i (thus nɤɕiɕe instead of nɤɕɯɕe ). However, such an orthography would cause unnecessary problems when automatically researching for reduplicated forms in the corpus. Since also in this case the pronunciation of the grapheme ɯ as i is completely predictable, and could be corrected automatically without difficulty, I choose to keep an etymological transcription.

In other words, in the transcription adopted in this work I transcribe the contrast between ɯ and i before palatal and alveolo-palatals when non-predictable (in noun and verb stems), but neglect it and use ɯ throughout in verbal prefixes and reduplicated syllables.
summary: The passage explains that in Japhug, vowels in verbal prefixes with palatal or alveolo-palatal onsets often raise the question of whether underlying ɯ has been neutralized to i, since speakers give conflicting judgments and the distinction is marginal. The author nonetheless keeps an etymological transcription with ɯ in these prefixes and in reduplicated syllables, because the alternation is predictable, helps state morphophonological rules more clearly, and avoids problems for automatic corpus searching.

text:
prefix!vowel contrasts suffix!vowel contrasts
A few unstressed verb suffixes have alveolo-palatal onsets and high unrounded vowels: the dual indexation suffixes 1du -tɕi and 2/3du -ndʑi (§ sec:intr.1, § sec:indexation.mixed ) and the suffix -ci (§ sec:peg.circumfix ). It is clear that these suffixes originally had a schwa-like vowel rather than a front vowel as in most Gyalrong languages (see § sec:indexation.suffixes.history ), but here too Tshendzin considers the vowel of these suffixes to be i rather than ɯ (the suffix -ci, for instance, according to her resembles cione more than cɯstone), and since no vowel fusion or other phenomena takes place with these suffixes (unlike verbal prefixes), using an etymological notation would have been an unnecessary complication.

In the prefixal possessive paradigm (§ § sec:possessive.paradigm ), we also find a series of prefixes with palatal and alveolo-palatal onsets and high unrounded vowels: 1du tɕi, 1pl ji- and 2/3du ndʑi-. Unlike verbal prefixes, but like the verbal indexation suffixes, possessive prefixes in the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug never undergo vowel fusion and remain invariable. The vowel is phonologically i, as shown by the minimal pair between ndʑɯnɯAngelica and the dual possessive ndʑi-nɯ `their$_du$ breast' (§ § sec:compounds.ndZi.ndZW ). For these reasons, I prefer a phonological (with -i ) rather than etymological (with -ɯ ) transcription for these prefixes.

The contrast between ɤ and e after palatal and alveolo-palatal consonants
The vowels ɤ and e in Kamnyu Japhug contrast in very few contexts. In word-final stressed open syllables, only e is found, ɤ being attested only in clitics and unstressed final syllables in words such as kɯnɤalso, even. In closed syllables, e is only found with the coda -t in the past 2sg 3 of transitive -e stem verbs (§ sec:rhyme.inventory ); the word-final -et vs. -ɤt are the only cases where ɤ and e are clearly contrastive.

In non-final open syllables, there are no examples of minimal pairs involving a contrast between ɤ and e. Phonetic e is clearly heard after palatal and alveolo-palatal consonants when the vowel of the following syllable is e, for instance in words such as tɕʰemegirl or sɤrɲɟeleextend (limbs), but in other contexts I generally transcribe ɤ throughout, except when the word is an obvious compound whose elements are recognized by the speakers (for instance tɕetʰalater, `soon' from tɕethen and tʰalater).

The contrast between ɤ and a
The contrast between ɤ and a, while clear in most contexts, is difficult to perceive in unstressed syllables when followed by a uvular (in particular when followed by a cluster with a uvular preinitial) and in syllables containing a (due to regressive assimilation of height, § sec:vowel.harmony ).

In slow syllable-by-syllable pronunciation, Tshendzin makes it clear that some unstressed syllables preceding a uvular have a rather than ɤ. This concerns the indefinite possessor prefix in words such as ta-ʁiyounger sibling, ta-ʁrɯhorn, ta-ʁridirt, ta-ʁjɯβshadow, ta-ʁrɯmlight, shadow, ta-χpishape, model, ta-ʁrɤtcharcoal, ta-ʁɟazsoot and ta-ʁafree time (§ § sec:inalienably.possessed ), and the fossilized prefix in nouns such as taqaβneedle. The noun tɤ-ʁarwing, however, has tɤ- rather ta-.

Another context where the variant ta- is found is with the m- initial nouns ta-mawork and ta-marbutter. Note that a contrast exists with the honorific noun tɤ-mamother (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ), showing that the two allomorphs tɤ- and ta- are synchronically contrastive in the Kamnyu variety at least for some speakers.

With some verbal prefixes, in particular the antipassive prefixes rɤ-/ra- and sɤ-/sa- (§ sec:antipassive ), the proprietive sɤ-/sa- (§ sec:proprietive ) and the tropative nɤ(ɣ)-/na- (§ sec:tropative.allomorphy ) and several denominal prefixes), the a allomorph is found where followed by a stem with a uvular preinitial. For instance, the antipassive of χtɯbuy is raχtɯdo shopping with the variant ra- rather than rɤ-. Not all prefixes in ɤ present this alternation: for instance, the causative, facilitative and denominal prefixes ɣɤ- never have a variant $ $ ɣa-.

However, in the case of orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) and other inflectional prefixes, no such phonologically determined alternation is found. For instance, the A-type preverb tɤ- upwards remains unchanged when preceding stems with a uvular preinitial as in tɤ-χtɯ-t-a ( aor -buy- pst: tr - 1sg ) `I bought it', where the prefix tɤ- is different from the corresponding C-type preverb ta- in ta-χtɯ ( aor:3 -buy) `he bought it'.
summary: The passage notes that several unstressed verbal suffixes and possessive prefixes have palatal or alveolo-palatal onsets with phonological high front vowels, and the author prefers an i transcription rather than an etymological ɯ because these forms do not undergo vowel fusion. It then explains that ɤ and e contrast only in a few restricted contexts, while the contrast between ɤ and a is sometimes weakened by uvulars and height assimilation, producing alternations such as ta-/tɤ- in some nouns and prefixes. However, this a~ɤ alternation is not found in orientation preverbs and some other inflectional prefixes, which remain unchanged before uvular stems.

text:
speech error!consonant
The Japhug corpus, being exclusively an oral one, contains many speech errors, and immediate self corrections by the speakers, which have been systematically transcribed. tab:self.corrections presents examples of phonological errors that are followed by self-corrections in the corpus.

Phonological errors can result in the replacement of a word by a similar-sounding one (as in the case of sqiten for sqʰitripod), but more often by a non-sense form. Errors generally involve one phonological feature at a time, including aspiration, nasality and place of articulation, especially the contrast between dental and alveolo-palatal affricates, and that between uvular and velars. A more puzzling replacement is that of χ by r ( saχaʁ sara ) despite the absence of any common phonological feature between these two phonemes.

The phoneme j is particularly prone to metathesis, either within initial clusters ( ɯjmŋo ɯmɲo, with fusion of j and ŋ as ɲ, see § sec:NC.clusters ), or across vowels ( pɤjka pjɤka ).
summary: The Japhug oral corpus contains many systematically transcribed speech errors and immediate self-corrections. Phonological errors may replace a word with a similar-sounding form or, more often, with a nonsensical form, usually changing only one feature at a time such as aspiration, nasality, or place of articulation, though some replacements are less predictable. The phoneme /j/ is especially prone to metathesis, both within initial clusters and across vowels.

text:
stress tone suffix!indexation circumfix!peg
Unlike all other Gyalrong languages, including Tshobdun, Situ and Zbu, Japhug has no tonal contrasts. However, there is morphologically determined stress. Phonological words only have one stress, which is located by default on the final syllable of the word (§ sec:wordhood, § sec:wordhood.criteria.verb ).

The personal agreement suffixes (§ sec:intransitive.paradigm, § sec:suffixes ) and the peg suffix -ci (§ sec:peg.circumfix ) never receive stress, and their vowels are optionally devoiced. For instance, tɤ-ndza-t-a `I ate it' ( aor -eat- pst - 1sg ) is realized as tɤndzátḁ or tɤndzáta. Stress can be antepenultimate in the case of verb forms with two suffixes as in to-k-ɤmɯ-rpú-ndʑi-ci `they bumped into each other' ( ifr - peg - recip -bump- du - peg ).

There are only three verbal prefixes which can attract stress: the inverse -wɣ- (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ), the negative Sensory mɯ́j- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs, § sec:sensory.morphology ), and the interrogative ɯ- (§ sec:interrogative.W.morpho ). Outside of verbal morphology, the only other process that affects stress is the comitative adverb derivation (§ sec:comitative.adverb ).
comitative adverb
Some ideophones have emphatic stress on the first syllable (§ sec:emphatic.idph ), but it is not phonologically distinctive.

A few function words have penultimate stress: kɯ́nɤ `also' (§ sec:kWnA ), cínɤ `not even one' (§ sec:cinA ), nóʁmɯz and kóʁmɯzonly after (§ sec:temporal.postpositions ).
summary:
Japhug, unlike other Gyalrong languages, has no tonal contrasts but does have morphologically determined stress, with phonological words normally bearing a single stress on the final syllable by default. Certain elements do not receive stress, including personal agreement suffixes and the peg suffix -ci, while stress can shift to earlier syllables in some verb forms with multiple suffixes or with certain prefixes such as the inverse, negative sensory, and interrogative markers.

Outside verbal morphology, stress is affected only by comitative adverb formation, and some ideophones may show emphatic first-syllable stress without a phonological contrast. A few function words also have penultimate stress.

text:
Although no native expression exists to designate `words' in Japhug (as in the immense majority of the world's languages, ), speakers have an intuitive notion of a minimal unit which can be the object of metalinguistic discourse, as opposed to prefixes and suffixes.

The intuitive notion of `word' can be correlated with some phonological and morphological criteria.

The clearest phonological criterion for wordhood is stress. Stress is by default word-final, and words have at most one stress. Most function words, including linkers (§ sec:coordination ), determiners (§ sec:determiners ), postpositions (§ ex:postpositions ) and even relator nouns (§ sec:relator.nouns ) lack stress (unless they receive special emphasis). In example ( ex:clitics.words ), the stressed syllables are indicated by an acute accent, and the unstressed function words by a grave accent.

There are only three groups of exceptions to word-final stress placement (for instance the unstressed suffix -ndʑi in ex:clitics.words ), as seen in the previous section (§ sec:stress ). Given its predictability, stress is not noted in the transcription employed in this grammar, except on stress-attracting prefixes.

Among the morphological criteria for wordhood (§ sec:wordhood.verb ), the scope of partial reduplication can be employed, at least for the word classes that allow it. Initial reduplication, almost exclusively restricted to verb forms (§ sec:verb.initial.redp ), applies to the first syllable of the word almost without exception. The only exception is the reduplicated subject participle kɯ kɯ-tu of the existential verb tuexist, which can take (non-reduplicated) possessive prefixes, but this may be a lexicalized form (§ sec:totalitative.redp ). In the case of verbs, several additional morphological tests converge to indicate the same left boundary. For the right boundary of the words, partial reduplication is less useful, as it only applies to stems (§ sec:verb.stem.redp ): inflectional suffixes are never reduplicated.

Inflectional suffixes (§ sec:suffixes ), in particular person indexation suffixes (§ sec:intr.1, § sec:intr.23 ), do present clitic-like properties, since they are not stressed, and are outside the scope of reduplication. However, these morphemes cannot be isolated, follow a rigid order, have non-adjacent dependencies with verbal prefixes (§ sec:peg.circumfix ), and no external element can be inserted between them. Moreover, the 1sg marker -a, despite being unstressed when following consonant-final verb stems, undergoes fusion with vowel-final stems (§ sec:synizesis ), causing vowel mergers. The verbal word in Japhug is thus slightly larger than the prosodic domains of stress and partial reduplication.

There are, however, three problems challenging the notion of `word' in Japhug: clitized sentence final particles (§ sec:verb.enclitics ), bipartite verbs (§ sec:bipartite ) and prenominal attributes (§ ex:attributive.prenominal ) when they receive no stress. These issues are discussed in more detail in the relevant sections.
summary: Japhug has no native term for “word,” but speakers still recognize a minimal unit distinct from prefixes and suffixes, and this unit can be identified by phonological and morphological criteria. The clearest phonological sign is word-final stress, with most function words unstressed; morphological evidence comes from the scope of partial reduplication, which usually applies to the first syllable of a word and helps locate the left boundary. Inflectional suffixes behave somewhat like clitics because they are unstressed and outside reduplication, but their fixed order and fusion with stems show that the verbal word is larger than these prosodic domains, though some cases such as sentence-final particles and bipartite verbs complicate the notion of wordhood.

text:
Putting aside function words, monosyllables are considerably less common than polysyllables in Japhug; in particular, verbs can be monosyllabic only in one form of their paradigm ( 3sg Factual Non-past, § sec:fact.morphology ), and inalienably possessed nouns are always at least disyllabic (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ).

The stem-final syllable (excluding inflectional suffixes), in addition to having stress by default, is also generally the part of the word with the maximum of phonological contrasts. Since polysyllabic roots are rare, non-final syllables are in the immense majority of cases either prefixes or compound roots.

Prefixes have strong phonotactic constraints: with the sole exception of some orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). Their main vowels are always ɯ (including i in contexts where the contrast is neutralized or quasi-neutralized § sec:W.i.contrast ), ɤ and a, and they cannot have aspirated or plain voiced consonants. Specific classes of prefixes have even stricter constraints: productive nominalization prefixes can only be obstruents (§ chap:non-finite ) and verbal derivation prefixes (Chapters chap:valency.increasing.derivation, chap:valency.decreasing.derivation, chap:other.derivations and chap:denominal ) can only contain nine consonants: m, n, s, z, ɕ, ʑ, r, j and ɣ (a subset of the consonants that occur as preinitials, § sec:inventory.clusters ).

Roots occurring as non-final elements of compounds do not have such stringent constraints on consonants, but due to a process of rhyme reduction (bound state, § sec:vowel.alternations.compounds ), most vowels are converted to either ɯ or ɤ.

Hence, in non-final syllables, the vowels are mostly restricted to a, ɯ, or ɤ, the latter two being subject to rounding by vowel harmony (§ sec:vowel.harmony ) or assimilation with w (§ sec:wC.clusters, § sec:Cr.clusters, § sec:allomorphy.inv ). An example of a typical Japhug word is the verb form atɤtɯʑɣɤɣɤ ʑó ( ex:atAtWZGAGAZo.vowels ), which has a vowel other than a, ɯ, or ɤ only in the last syllable.

`Make yourself light.' (from ex:atAtWGAZo.AtAZGAGAmbjom, § sec:refl.caus.volitional )
exe

Vowels other than a, ɯ, or ɤ in non-final syllables of verb and noun stems are only found in four cases. First, there is a handful of synchronically unanalyzable polysyllabic nominal and verbal stems with o, u or i in non-final syllables, for instance ɴɢoɕnaspider, ɟuliflute or nɯpodɯditickle. Second, compounds whose first element does not undergo bound state can preserve any vowel (for instance qrormbɯanthill from qroant and rmbɯheap up). Third, Tibetan loanwords, especially in the most recent layers (§ sec:historical.phono ), are not subject to the phonotactic constraints of native nouns and allow any combination of vowels (for instance loŋbutɕʰielephant from གླང་པོ་ཆེ་glaŋ.po.tɕʰeelephant).
summary:
In Japhug, monosyllabic words are uncommon outside function words, and verbs can be monosyllabic only in one paradigm form; inalienably possessed nouns are always at least disyllabic. Non-final syllables are usually prefixes or compound roots, and they show strong phonological restrictions, especially on prefixes, whose vowel and consonant inventories are highly limited.

As a result, vowels in non-final syllables are generally restricted to a, ɯ, and ɤ, with ɯ and ɤ often affected by harmony or assimilation. Exceptions are limited to a few unanalyzable native stems, compounds whose first element is not reduced, and Tibetan loanwords, which can preserve more diverse vowel patterns.

text:
reduplication!partial consonant!cluster syllable!structure
A useful test to analyse and classify clusters is partial reduplication, a very productive process which can be applied to both verb and noun stems and has a variety of morphosyntactic functions depending on the position of the syllable affected by reduplication.

Partial reduplication of the first syllable of the verbal complex can mark the protasis of a conditional construction (§ sec:redp.protasis ), iterative coincidence (§ sec:iterative.coincidence ), degree incrementation (§ sec:redp.gradual.increase ) and totalitative relativization (§ sec:totalitative.redp ).
comitative adverb
When the target of partial reduplication is the last syllable of the verb, it can indicate emphasis (§ sec:emphatic.autive, § sec:emph.redp ), and also serve as a secondary exponent (§ sec:verb.stem.redp ) of several derivational processes, such as reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ), distributed action (§ sec:distributed.action ), auto-evaluative (§ sec:autoevaluative ), attenuative (§ sec:attenuative ), as well as some non-finite verb forms (gerund § sec:gerund and purposive converb § sec:purposive.converb ). Outside of verbal morphology, we find partial reduplication in comitative adverbs (§ sec:comitative.adverb ), perlative (§ sec:perlative ) and collectives (§ sec:redp.coll ). There are in addition a few sporadic cases of full reduplication (§ sec:redp.voice, § sec:antipassive.redp ).

When partial reduplication is applied to a syllable, the rhyme of the reduplicated syllable is changed to ɯ in the reduplicant (other types of partial reduplication are treated in § sec:irregular.reduplication ). This vowel can undergo rounded assimilation to u when the base syllable has the main vowel u or o (§ sec:vowel.harmony ).

Some clusters are only partially copied: when the last consonant of a cluster is one of the non-nasal sonorants ( r, l, j, w, ɣ or ʁ), and the preceding consonant is neither a non-nasal sonorant nor a sibilant or alveolo-palatal fricative, the sonorant is deleted, as in the gerund of mbɣombe in a hurry, which yields sɤ- mbɯ mbɣom (example ex:sAmbWmbGom.YABdenW, § sec:gerund.clauses ) instead of $ $ sɤ-mbɣɯ mbɣom, or the emphatic form kʰɯ kʰro from kʰromuch (§ sec:khro ), instead of $ $ kʰrɯ kʰro.

However, in some of the clusters ending in a non-nasal sonorant, but whose penultimate consonant is either a non-nasal sonorant, a sibilant ( s, z) or an alveolo-palatal fricative ( ɕ, ʑ), the final sonorant is not deleted in partial reduplication. For instance, the emphatic reduplication of the infinitive of aɕɤrɣibe quick is kɯ-ɤɕɤrɣɯ rɣi ( ex:kACArGWrGi ), not $ $ kɯ-ɤɕɤ rɯ rɣi, and the perlative (§ sec:perlative ) of tɤ-jroʁtrace is ɯ- jrɯ jroʁ `following X's trace', not $ $ ɯ-jɯ jroʁ.
