However, in the cluster rj- for instance, the glide j is deleted, as in the negative gerund masɤrɯrjuquietly, in secret from arjuspeak (§ sec:gerund.neg ). A precise inventory of the clusters with sonorant deletion is provided in § sec:medials and § sec:summary.clusters.

Partial reduplication is crucial in analyzing and classifying consonant clusters. Sonorants that undergo deletion when partial reduplication is applied are henceforth designated as medial consonants (corresponding to the terms 介音 jièyīnmedial in the Chinese phonological tradition and འདོགས་ཅན་ⁿdogs.tɕanattached letter in the Tibetan one) and do not belong to the same phonological constituent as the rest of the onset.
summary: Partial reduplication is a productive process used with both verb and noun stems, and its function depends on which syllable is copied: initial-syllable reduplication marks meanings such as conditional protasis, iteration, degree increase, and totalitative relativization, while final-syllable reduplication can express emphasis and various derivational or non-finite forms. In the reduplicant, the rhyme is typically changed to ɯ, with possible rounding to u, and the behavior of consonant clusters shows that some final sonorants are deleted during reduplication while others are retained depending on the cluster type. This pattern is used to classify clusters, with deleted sonorants treated as medial consonants rather than part of the same phonological onset constituent.

text:
consonant!cluster
Japhug counts at least 423 clusters in syllable onset position: 319 clusters with two consonants and 104 with three consonants. A few new clusters have been discovered since the article was written. In addition, there are additional types of consonant clusters across syllable boundaries (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ) and secondary clusters due to vowel fusion (§ sec:synizesis ), which are too numerous to be systematically surveyed. While the number of clusters in Japhug is considerably smaller than that of Khroskyabs, which counts as many as 757, it is still much richer than most languages in the Trans-Himalayan family.

In the following discussion, phonemes or clusters found exclusively in ideophones (§ sec:idph ) or Tibetan loanwords are systematically indicated, in order to bring out the phonotactics of inherited Japhug vocabulary. For each cluster, an example is provided; in the case of verb roots, the base stem is indicated, rather than a conjugated form (unlike what was done in ).

2clusters
3clusters
summary: Japhug has at least 423 consonant clusters in syllable onset position, including 319 two-consonant clusters and 104 three-consonant clusters, with a few more discovered later. It also has many additional clusters across syllable boundaries and from vowel fusion, making its phonotactics rich by Trans-Himalayan standards, though less complex than Khroskyabs. The discussion that follows marks clusters found only in ideophones or Tibetan loanwords to highlight inherited Japhug patterns.

text:
consonant!cluster consonant!preinitial
This section deals with consonant clusters whose last consonant is not one of the six non-nasal sonorants ( r, l, j, w, ɣ or ʁ) and thus cannot contain a medial consonant.

Clusters of this type have a limited number of possible consonants in first position: w, s- z, ɕ- ʑ, l, ʂ- r, j, x- ɣ, χ- ʁ, n, m and the homorganic nasal, to which must be added a few clusters in stop+ ɕ. These consonants, which correspond to both སྔོན་འཇུག་sŋon.ⁿdʑugprefixed letter and མགོ་ཅན་mgo.tɕansuperscript letter in Tibetan traditional grammar, are referred to as preinitial. The last consonant of these clusters is called the initial ( མིང་གཞི་miŋ.gʑiradical letter in Tibetan). The following sections list clusters by preinitial, and in each table present them by place and mode of articulation of the initial. Clusters with three consonants are dealt with separately.

It is striking that (except in the stop+ ɕ- clusters, which are secondary, § sec:kC.pC.clusters ), all preinitials are either sonorants or fricatives. There are no stop preinitials in Japhug, unlike in Situ, which allows labial and velar stops. The preinitial stops p- and k- in Situ regularly correspond to Japhug w- and x/ɣ- or χ/ʁ, suggesting that a general rule of preinitial fricativization took place in Japhug.

w+C clusters
consonant!cluster consonant!labial
prein.w lists all consonant clusters in Japhug with w as first element not ending in a non-nasal sonorant.

2wC3wC

The phoneme w has fricativized allophones when occurring as first member of a consonant cluster (§ sec:consonant.phonemes ), transcribed here as f- before unvoiced obstruents, and β- before all voiced consonants. It does not appear before nasal or prenasalized segments, due to a nasalization rule *wN- mN, attested notably in the irregular m- allomorph of the ɣɤ- causative (§ sec:causative.m ). It cannot be followed by any of the labial consonants: for instance $ $ fp- and $ $ βb- are not acceptable onsets. Some clusters with w + voiced obstruents ( βz- and βg- ) are only attested in Tibetan loanwords.

Clusters with three consonants whose first element is w and the last one is not a sonorant are all restricted to Tibetan borrowings (verb forms with the past tense b- prefix, for example βzɟɯr from བསྒྱུར་bsgʲurchange) except for wxt, which is realized as xʷt with a labiovelarized fricative, rounding the preceding unrounded vowels ɯ and ɤ: the participle kɯ-wxti `the big one' is realized as kuxʷti. Not all speakers maintain the contrast between wxt and xt; the verb wxtibe big is the only item with this cluster.

Non-segmental realizations of w, limited to vowel rounding, are also found in the group wɣr- (treated in § sec:Cr.clusters ) and the inverse prefix wɣ- (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ).
summary:
The passage describes Japhug consonant clusters whose final consonant is not one of the six non-nasal sonorants, so they cannot contain a medial consonant. Such clusters have a restricted set of first consonants, called preinitials, which correspond to Tibetan prefixed or superscript letters; unlike Tibetan, Japhug has no stop preinitials, and the text suggests these were generally fricativized historically.

It then focuses on clusters beginning with **w-**, noting that **w** has fricative allophones before obstruents and cannot occur before nasals or labial consonants. Many three-consonant **w**-clusters are limited to Tibetan borrowings, while **wxt** is exceptional in being realized with labiovelarization and vowel rounding.

text:
consonant!cluster consonant!sibilant
prein.sz lists all consonant clusters with a sibilant fricative s or z as first element not ending in a non-nasal sonorant.

2szC3szC

The contrast between s and z is neutralized before obstruents: we find s- before unvoiced stops, fricatives and affricates and z- before voiced ones (including prenasalized stops). With nasals, a contrast is found between sm- and sn- on the one hand, and their voiced counterparts zm- and zn- on the other hand. The latter are only found in morphologically complex nouns or verbs, as several sibilant prefixes. These include the causative (§ sec:caus.z ), the oblique participle (§ sec:oblique.participle.allomorphy ), the gerund (§ sec:gerund.allomorphs ) and the abilitative (§ sec:abilitative ) prefixes, all of which have z- allomorphs when prefixed to polysyllabic stems whose first syllable has a single sonorant followed by a vowel. In particular, zmaqʰucause to be late and znɤjafind $X$ a shame in prein.sz are the causative derivations of maqʰube after, `be late' (§ sec:denom.mA ) and nɤjabe a shame (§ sec:sig.caus.tropative ), respectively.

Before non-nasal sonorants, a voicing contrast is attested between sj- vs. zj- (§ sec:Cj.clusters ), sl- vs. zl- (§ sec:Cl.clusters ), sr- vs. zr- (§ sec:Cr.clusters ) and sɣ- vs. zɣ- (§ sec:CG.clusters ).

The sibilant preinitials are compatible with all stops, but do not occur with affricates, whether dental, alveolo-palatal or retroflex, except in heterosyllabic clusters (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ). The loanword koxtɕɯnbrocade from གོས་ཆེན་gos.tɕʰenbrocade suggests that a sound change *stɕ- xtɕ- has removed all instances of sibilant+alveolo-palatal clusters.

The aspiration contrast in unvoiced stops and affricates is not neutralized after the s- preinitial, as shown, for instance, by the minimal pair stʰoʁpush, `press' vs. stoʁbroad bean.

l+C clusters
consonant!lateral consonant!cluster

There are considerably fewer clusters with an l preinitial
than with other preinitials. These clusters are listed in prein.l. They contain a high proportion of ideophones and Tibetan loanwords, as the genuine proto-Gyalrong *l- preinitial has changed to j- in most contexts (§ sec:jC.clusters ).

2lC3lC

A possible example of an additional cluster lŋ- is found in the verb nɯndzɯlŋɯzdoze off, but both nɯ.ndzɯl.ŋɯz and nɯ.ndzɯ.lŋɯz are possible syllabifications.

The cluster lpɕ, only attested in qalpɕaopen (of fern leaf), is discussed further in § sec:kC.pC.clusters.

r+C clusters
consonant!rhotic consonant!cluster
prein.r lists all consonant clusters not ending in a non-nasal sonorant with the rhotic r or its unvoiced counterpart, the retroflex fricative ʂ, as first element.

2rC3rC

The contrast between r and ʂ is almost completely neutralized in preinitial position, the former occurring with voiced obstruents, and the latter with unvoiced ones. The symbol r is used in the orthography employed in this grammar for the archiphoneme r,ʂ preceding obstruents, except in the group ʂχ-.

However, a contrast between r and ʂ is found before sonorant initials, in particular with the palatal nasal ( ʂɲ- vs. rɲ-), the velar nasal ( ʂŋ- vs. rŋ-) and the velar fricative ( ʂɣ- vs. rɣ- see § sec:CG.clusters ).

When preceding sonorants, r is initial when occurring before w and j (§ sec:Cw.clusters, § sec:Cj.clusters ), but preinitial in rl, rɣ- and rʁ- (§ sec:Cl.clusters, § sec:CG.clusters, § sec:CRR.clusters ).

There is one case of a preinitial r apparently originating from a rhotacized sibilant, in the verb form arɴɢlɯmbe caved in (§ sec:Cl.clusters, § sec:fossil.prenasalization ).
summary:
The passage describes the distribution of sibilant, lateral, and rhotic preinitial consonant clusters in the language. It notes that s/z are largely neutralized before obstruents, with voicing contrasts appearing before nasals and sonorants in certain morphological contexts, while sibilant preinitials do not occur with affricates and seem to have undergone a sound change eliminating sibilant + alveolo-palatal clusters.  

It also states that l-initial clusters are relatively rare and often occur in ideophones or Tibetan loanwords because the inherited proto-Gyalrong *l- mostly changed to j-, and that r/ʂ contrasts are nearly neutralized before obstruents but remain contrastive before some sonorant initials.

text:
consonant!cluster consonant!alveolo-palatal
prein.C.Z lists all consonant clusters with an alveolo-palatal fricative ɕ or ʑ as preinitial and not ending in a non-nasal sonorant.

2CZC3CZC

As in the case of the sibilant preinitials s- and z, the voicing contrast between ɕ and ʑ is neutralized in preinitial position before obstruents, the former occurring when followed by unvoiced stops, fricatives and affricates, and the latter when followed by voiced ones.

A voicing contrast is attested between ɕn- and ʑn, but the latter only occurs when the ʑ- allomorph of the translocative prefix (§ sec:translocative.morpho ) precedes the A-type nɯ- or C-type na- `westward' orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), as in examples ( ex:iCqha.ZnWzmWnmuta ) (§ sec:iCqha ) and ( ex:ZnasAmWmtshWmtshAmnW2 ) (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ).

Before non-nasal sonorants, the voiced contrast is attested between ɕl- vs. ʑl- (§ sec:Cl.clusters, also only with the translocative prefix), ɕr- vs. ʑr- (§ sec:Cr.clusters ) and ɕɣ- vs. ʑɣ- (§ sec:CG.clusters ).

Unlike sibilant preinitials, alveolo-palatal preinitials are compatible with affricates of all places of articulation, even alveolo-palatal affricates in the cluster ɕtɕ- found in the noun sɤɕtɕɯɣstrap (to carry children). There is evidence, however, that *ɕtsʰ- dissimilated to jtsʰ- in the irregular causative jtsʰigive to drink (§ sec:jC.clusters, § sec:caus.j ).

There are two examples of alveolo-palatal preinitials followed by a palatal segment: ʑɲ- and ɕcʰ, but they are not stable and hence not included in prein.C.Z. They only occur when the ʑ- and ɕ- allomorphs of the translocative prefix are found before the B-type ɲɯ- and cʰɯ- or the D-type ɲɤ- and cʰɤ- `westward' and downstream orientation preverbs. These clusters are always in free variation with zɲ- and scʰ, respectively, which are considerably more common ( tab:transloc.allomorphs.counts, § sec:translocative.morpho ), since the translocative prefix generally undergoes a palatal dissimilation rule to a dental fricative s- or z- when it precedes a palatal consonant. The non-dissimilated clusters ɕcʰ- and ʑɲ- are extremely rare: the former is only attested in one single example in the corpus ( ex:CchWZGABdea ), and the second in a handful of verb forms (see for instance ex:ZYWlata, § sec:translocative.morpho ). These non-dissimilated forms are undoubtedly due to analogical levelling, which generalized the alveolo-palatal allomorphs of the translocative.

Secondary clusters with alveolo-palatal preinitials are created by prefixes with the shape ɕ- or ʑ, including allomorphs of the translocative as mentioned above (§ sec:translocative.morpho ), but also irregular causatives (§ sec:caus.C, § sec:caus.Z ) and perhaps lexicalized oblique participles (§ sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle ).

j+C clusters
consonant!cluster consonant!palatal
prein.j lists all consonant clusters with the semi-vowel j as first element not ending in a non-nasal sonorant. It cannot precede alveolo-palatal obstruents and palatal stops.

2jC3jC

Most of these clusters violate the sonority sequencing principle (§ sec:ssp ), but those that are attested in verb roots (such as jpumbe thick) can occur in word-initial position in the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ).

Comparison with Zbu reveals that one of the sources of the Japhug j- preinitial is proto-Gyalrong *l-: for instance jmɯtforget, tɤ-jtsipillar, tɤ-jmetail and tɯ-jmŋodream correspond to Zbu lmɑ̂t, tɐltsíʔ, -lméʔ and -lmɑ́ʔ, respectively. In other cases, j- comes from a dissimilated coronal fricative, as in jtsʰigive to drink (§ sec:caus.j ) and perhaps jqube able to lift (§ sec:abilitative.lexicalized ).

The group jmŋ- in tɯ-jmŋodream has two preinitials j and m. The labial nasal is the ancient initial (as shown by the Zbu cognate -lmɑ́ʔ ), and the nasal velar arose as a trace of proto-Gyalrong vowel velarization *-lmaˠŋ *-jmɣo -jmŋo (; on velarized vowels in proto-Gyalrong, see § sec:CG.clusters ).

When preceding sonorants, j is preinitial in all cases: jw, jl, jr, jɣ, jʁ- and rʁ- (§ sec:Cw.clusters, § sec:Cl.clusters, § sec:Cr.clusters, § sec:CG.clusters, § sec:CRR.clusters ).
summary:
The passage describes Japhug consonant clusters with alveolo-palatal preinitials ɕ/ʑ and shows that their voicing contrast is neutralized before obstruents but retained before sonorants in some clusters, especially with the translocative prefix. It also notes that these preinitials can combine with affricates of all places of articulation, though some rare palatal combinations like ɕcʰ- and ʑɲ- are unstable and usually alternate with more common dissimilated forms.

It then turns to clusters with j-, explaining that j- cannot precede alveolo-palatal obstruents or palatal stops, that many j-clusters violate sonority sequencing but occur in certain verb roots, and that j- has historical sources in proto-Gyalrong *l- or in dissimilated coronal fricatives. The passage also notes that when j precedes sonorants, it consistently functions as

text:
consonant!cluster consonant!velar
prein.x lists all consonant clusters with the velar fricatives x and ɣ as preinitial and not ending in a non-nasal sonorant.

2xGC3xGC

Velar preinitials are not compatible with dorsal (velar and velar) initial consonants, but are attested with all other places of articulations. The complementary distribution between x (before unvoiced segments) and ɣ (before voiced segments, including obstruents and nasals) is complete, and the voicing contrast can be considered to be completely neutralized in preinitial position.

Comparison with Situ shows that some of these velar fricative preinitials originate from velar presyllables *kə-. Two non-productive prefixes are sources of velar+C clusters: the animal velar prefix (§ sec:velar.class.prefix ) and the lexicalized participle x/ɣ- prefix (§ sec:G.nmlz ). Another source of secondary velar preinitials is the intrusive ɣ found as element of some derivation prefixes, including the sɯɣ- (§ sec:caus.sWG ) and ɕɯɣ- (§ sec:caus.CWG ) allomorphs of the causative, the nɯɣ- allomorph of the applicative (§ sec:allomorphy.applicative ), the nɤɣ- allomorph of the tropative (§ sec:tropative.allomorphy ) and the sɤɣ- allomorph of the proprietive (§ sec:proprietive.allomorphy ).

In addition, the velar preinitial in some counted nouns like tɯ-xpaone year is due to a fausse coupe (§ sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history ).
summary:
The passage says that velar fricative preinitials x and ɣ occur in consonant clusters only when they are not followed by a non-nasal sonorant, and that they are incompatible with initial dorsal consonants but otherwise occur with all places of articulation. It also notes that x and ɣ are in complementary distribution by voicing, with this contrast fully neutralized in preinitial position.

It further explains that some of these preinitials come from older velar presyllables *kə-, from two non-productive prefixes, from intrusive ɣ in several derivational prefixes, and in some counted nouns from a false segmentation.

text:
consonant!uvular consonant!cluster
prein.X.R lists all consonant clusters with the uvular fricatives χ and ʁ as first element and not ending in a non-nasal sonorant. They cannot precede velars except in heterosyllabic clusters (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ).

2XRC3XRC

The voicing contrast between χ and ʁ is only attested before sonorants: a handful of ideophones have the cluster χɲ contrasting with ʁɲ. Uvular preinitials are particularly common in Tibetan loanwords, where they correspond to the g- and d- sŋon.ⁿdʑug. The voiced fricative ʁ is more often realized as an epiglottal ʕ in this context.

Some uvular preinitials come from the reduced allomorphs χ- and ʁ- of the uvular animal prefix qa- (§ sec:uvular.animal ).
summary: The passage describes consonant clusters in which the uvular fricatives χ and ʁ occur as the first element, noting that they do not occur before velars except in heterosyllabic clusters and do not end in a non-nasal sonorant. It also says that the voicing contrast between χ and ʁ is only found before sonorants, especially in a few ideophones, and that uvular preinitials are common in Tibetan loanwords, where ʁ is often realized as epiglottal ʕ. Some uvular preinitials also derive from reduced forms of the uvular animal prefix qa-.

text:
consonant!cluster consonant!nasal
The Tables prein.nasal and prein.nh.nasal list all consonant clusters with a nasal consonant as preinitial and without medial consonant.

Unlike the previous preinitials, nasals can never be directly followed by any non-nasal sonorant: groups such as *mj, *mw, *mr, *ml, *mɣ- and *mʁ- are not attested in onset position (they are, however, found as heterosyllabic clusters, § sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ). This gap is due to a combination of two sound changes.

First, the medials *j and *ɣ were nasalized when preceded by a nasal, so that pre-Japhug *mj- and *mɣ- became mɲ- (in tɯ-mɲaarrow, compare མདའ་mdaarrow from *mla, ) and mŋ- (in tɯ-jmŋodream, see § sec:jC.clusters ), respectively.

Second, pre-Japhug *mr- became mbr- by epenthesis, as shown by mbrohorse, mbrobe high and mbricry, sing (in Burmese mraṅḥ, mraṅʔ and mraññ, ).

Additionally, nasal preinitials cannot be followed by any fricative. As in Tibetan, this absence is due to the conversion of post-nasal fricatives to the corresponding affricates, as in tɯ-mtsʰiliver (from *m-si, Burmese asaññḥ, ).

2NC3NC

While voiced stops and affricates with homorganic prenasalization are monophonemic (§ sec:consonant.phonemes ), unaspirated and aspirated ones ( prein.nasal ) are better analyzed as clusters. All places of articulation are possible, from labial ( mp(ʰ)- ) to uvular ( ɴq(ʰ)- ). The special case of mpɕ- is discussed in § sec:kC.pC.clusters.

Two non-homorganic prenasalized preinitials are also attested, m- before all places of articulation except labials (where m- corresponds to the homorganic nasal preinitial), and n- before (voiced) labials and velars ( prein.nh.nasal ). When preceded by m or n, the contrast between plain voiced and prenasalized voiced stops and affricates is neutralized; for instance the b in nb- stands for the archiphoneme b,mb. In the case of the cluster mɢ, since the prenasalized phoneme ɴɢ lacks a plain voiced counterpart (§ sec:consonant.phonemes ), the only analysis possible is mɴɢ-. In the orthography used in this grammar, the simplified (but non-ambiguous) transcription mɢ- is used.

The other nasal phonemes ɲ and ŋ are not attested as preinitials: for instance, clusters such as $ $ ŋp- or $ $ ɲt- are prohibited.

2mnC3mnC

Some m- preinitials come from the nasalization of *w- before nasal or prenasalized stops (as in the irregular causative mɲoprepare from ɲobe prepared, see § sec:causative.m ), a sound law accounting for the absence of preinitial w in this context (§ sec:wC.clusters ). This sound law does not operate across syllables (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ), and heterosyllabic clusters with a non-nasalized coda -β followed by a nasal do exist.

Some n- preinitials originate from former *t- before nasal or prenasalized stops, as in tɯ-nŋadebt (§ sec:NC.clusters; see also ). Another source is a reduced n- allomorph of denominal nɯ- (as in ngobe ill from the noun tɯ-ŋgodisease, § sec:denom.intr.nW ).

Stop+ ɕ clusters
consonant!cluster consonant!stop
A handful of onsets have an unvoiced stop followed by ɕ, including kɕ- (as in kɕiluyear of the dog from ཁྱི་ལོ་kʰʲi.loyear of the dog, pɕ, ( tɯpɕiflax) as well as lpɕ- (§ sec:lC.clusters ) and mpɕ- (§ sec:NC.clusters ). These clusters, found in both native vocabulary and borrowings from Tibetan, mainly originate from the combination of aspirated stops pʰ and kʰ with the medial -j-.

Evidence that these groups should not be synchronically analyzed as kʰj- and pʰj underlyingly comes from two facts. First, the groups pʰj- and kʰj- are otherwise attested (§ sec:Cj.clusters ). Second, the clusters (C)(p|k)ɕ- are not affected by partial reduplication; for instance mpɕɤrbe beautiful is reduplicated as mpɕɯ mpɕɤr (see for instance ex:anWtABzu.smWlAm, § sec:smWlAm.TAME ), not $ $ mpʰɯ mpɕɤr as would have been expected if mpɕɤr were really $ $ mpʰjɤr. In addition, mpɕɤrbe beautiful is probably borrowed from མཆོར་པོ་mtɕʰor.pohandsome, so that the analysis as mpʰj is wrong even historically.
summary:
The passage describes several types of consonant clusters involving nasal preinitials and stop+ɕ onsets in Japhug. It notes that nasal preinitials cannot occur before non-nasal sonorants or fricatives because of earlier sound changes such as nasalization, epenthesis, and conversion of fricatives to affricates, and it explains that prenasalized voiced stops and affricates are usually clusters rather than single phonemes.

It also traces the origins and distribution of m- and n- preinitials, including cases derived from earlier *w- and *t-. Finally, it argues that clusters like kɕ- and mpɕ- should not be synchronically analyzed as kʰj- or pʰj-, because their behavior and historical development show they are distinct cluster types.

text:
consonant!cluster consonant!medial consonant!rhotic consonant!lateral consonant!semi-vowel
This section deals with consonant clusters whose last consonant is one of the six non-nasal sonorants ( r, l, j, w, ɣ or ʁ). These sonorants can either be medials (§ sec:partial.redp ) or initials, depending on whether they are deleted when the cluster is partially reduplicated. They are always medials when the preceding consonant is not one of the possible preinitials (§ sec:preinitials ). Clusters ending in a non-nasal sonorant whose penultimate element is a possible preinitial (sibilant/alveolo-palatal fricative or non-nasal sonorant) Nasal sonorants cannot directly precede non-nasal sonorants in syllable onset position, due to a series of sound changes (§ sec:NC.clusters ), so they are not possible preinitials when the initial is a non-nasal sonorant. are referred to as ambiguous clusters, as they need to be systematically tested with partial reduplication to determine the phonological status of the final sonorant (initial or medial).

The secondary clusters with medial glides created by the effect of synizesis (§ sec:synizesis ) with the 1sg suffix -a (§ sec:intr.1 ) are not included in the listing below, even though what is transcribed as Ce|i-a and Co|u-a in the orthography is homophonous with Cja and Cwa, respectively. Including them would have the effect of introducing an enormous number of secondary and predictable clusters. In addition, synizesis of Cɯ-a generates the ɰ allomorph of ɯ, constituting a seventh glide not found in the vocabulary.

C+ w clusters
consonant!cluster consonant!labial
med.w lists all clusters ending in w. Clusters of this type are very rare, as a combination of two sound changes have removed all instances of proto-Gyalrong *Cw. First, the labiovelars, still preserved in Zbu, have merged with plain velars (for instance nɯŋacow, Zbu ŋwéʔ, ), and the remaining instances of *w have become ɣ (as in tɯ-ɕɣatooth from *-ɕwa, § sec:CG.clusters ).

2Cw3Cw

There are no clusters with labial consonants followed by w, but there is a triple contrast between hw, χw- and xw-: it is the only context where minimal pairs between the glottal h, the uvular χ and the velar x unvoiced fricatives can be found.

The combination of cluster-final w with the rhyme -a is homophonous with the result of synizesis of the 1sg -a with verb stems in -o and -u; for instance, the 1sg possessive a-rwa `my tent' is not distinguishable from aro-a `I own' (§ sec:synizesis ). Both are phonetically realized as arwa.

Clusters in w are mainly found in ideophones and Chinese loanwords (including nativized ones such as kwitsɯtcupboard from 柜子 guìzǐcupboard with a mysterious coda -t ). The only native clusters with w as final element are jw- (as in tɤ-jwaʁleaf) and zw- ( zwɤrmugwort), where the w comes from the lenition of a voiced labial stop.

In ambiguous clusters, cluster-final -w- is a medial consonant in zw and lw, as shown by the distributed action derivation (§ sec:distributed.action ) nɤ-zɯ zwɤr `burn everywhere' and nɤ-lɯ lwoʁ `spill everywhere' from zwɤrburn and lwoʁspill (not $ $ nɤ-zwɯ zwɤr or $ $ nɤ-lwɯ lwoʁ).

In jw, the labial glide is initial, as it is not deleted in reduplication, for example in the comitative adverb kɤ́-jwɯ jwaʁ `together with (its) leaves' (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) from tɤ-jwaʁleaf.
comitative adverb
The cluster rw is intriguing, as it presents two alternative reduplication patterns. The labial glide is treated as initial in the distributed action derivation nɤ-rwɯ rwɤt `dig everywhere' from rwɤtdig (not $ $ nɤ-rɯ rwɤt), but in the comitative derivation, rwayak felt tent can either be reduplicated as kɤ́-rɯ rwa or kɤ́-rwɯ rwa `together with the felt tent'.

C+ j clusters
consonant!cluster consonant!palatal
Tables med.j and med.j.3 list all clusters ending in j. This glide can follow consonants of all places of articulation except palatals, alveolo-palatals and retroflex consonants (other than r). In the orthographical system used in this grammar and previous publications on Japhug, j is transcribed as < j > after ʁ, ɣ, labial consonants and dental fricatives, and as < i > after velar and uvular stops, as well as dental stops and affricates and l.

In ambiguous clusters, cluster-final j is medial when following r, l and s ( rj, lj- and sj-), and initial when preceded by w, ɣ and ʁ ( wj, ɣj- and ʁj-).

There is in addition a highly unstable cluster ʑj- when the alveolo-palatal allomorph of the translocative prefix (§ sec:translocative.morpho ) precedes the `unspecified' orientation preverbs. As in the case of the other palatal preverbs, the dissimilated dental allomorph z- is more commonly found (§ sec:shC.clusters, § sec:translocative.morpho ). There is no example with ʑj- in the corpus, and all instances of this cluster come from elicitation of verb forms with the translocative.

Clusters with velar stops+ j and dental affricates+ j are clearly distinctive with palatal stops ( kiocause to glide vs. covalley, cf. sec:consonant.phonemes, § tab:coronal.dorsal ) and alveolo-palatal affricates ( ndziaʁbe tight (of knot), `be deep' (of colour), `be completed' vs. ndʑaʁswim). There are no perfect minimal pairs between alveolo-palatal affricates and dental stop+ j clusters, as they are very rare and restricted to a handful of ideophones, but quasi-minimal pairs such as ndiɤndiɤtgracious and ndʑɤβbe burned(§ sec:anticausative.morphology ) suffice to establish the reality of this phonological contrast.

Aspirated velar and labial stops followed by j are rare, since pre-Japhug *kʰj- and *pʰj- have changed to kɕ- and pɕ, respectively (§ sec:kC.pC.clusters ). This sound change, however, did not affect the cluster spʰj- ( med.j.3 ), and new instances of kʰj- have been created from interjections.

The combination of cluster-final j with the rhyme -a is homophonous with the result of synizesis of the 1sg -a with verb stems in -e and -i.

2Cj3Cj

In triconsonantal groups, j can co-occur with all preinitials except velar and alveolo-palatal fricatives and itself ( med.j.3 ).
summary: The passage describes Japhug consonant clusters ending in non-nasal sonorants, especially clusters ending in **w** and **j**, and explains how their phonological status is determined by whether the final sonorant is deleted in partial reduplication. It notes that many **w** clusters are rare or confined to ideophones and loanwords, while **j** clusters occur with a wide range of preceding consonants but are restricted or unstable in some environments; several contrasts are established through reduplication patterns and minimal or quasi-minimal pairs.

text:
A group ɕpj- with alveolo-palatal preinitial does exist, but it is not completely stable. It only occurs when the ɕ- allomorph of the translocative prefix (§ sec:translocative.morpho ) precedes the B-type pjɯ- or the D-type pjɤ- downwards preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), as in examples such as ( ex:tWmWchW ) (§ sec:approximate.locative ). It is in free variation with spj- in this context, as the translocative has another s- allomorph when preceding pj- and cʰ- (§ sec:translocative.morpho ). For instance in ( ex:spjWlAtnW ) we find s-pjɯ-lɤt-nɯ instead of ɕ-pjɯ-lɤt-nɯ (the more common form).

Tables med.l and med.l.3 list all clusters ending in l. The lateral sonorant cannot follow retroflex affricates, dental stops and alveolo-palatal affricates.

The cluster ʑl- is only attested when the translocative prefix occurs before upstream preverbs (§ sec:translocative.morpho ).
comitative adverb
In the clusters with the fricative s or a sonorant as first element ( sl, wl, jl, rl, ɣl and ʁl), l is initial. For instance, the distributed action derivation (§ sec:distributed.action ) of sloʁdig and ɣleknead, rub are nɤ-slɯ sloʁ `dig everywhere with snout' nɤ-ɣlɯ ɣle `rub again and again' (not $ $ nɤ-sɯ sloʁ and $ $ nɤ-ɣɯ ɣle), and the comitative adverb (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) from jlamale hybrid yak is kɤ́-jlɯ jla `together with his/her/their hybrid yak(s)' (not $ $ kɤ́-jɯ jla).

On the other hand, l is medial in ɕl, as shown by the fact that the verb ɕluplough has the distributed action derivation nɤ-ɕɯ ɕlu `plough everywhere' (not $ $ nɤ-ɕlɯ ɕlu as would have been expected is l were initial). In, I claimed that ɕl could be reduplicated either with or without deletion of l, but I have not been able to confirm my earlier data and it may have been an error. The groups zl and ʑl are not found in words that can be subjected to partial reduplication, and their status is undecidable at the present moment.

2Cl3Cl

In triconsonantal clusters ( med.l.3 ), the medial l co-occurs with dental, alveolo-palatal and uvular fricatives, as well as r and m. The only word with a preinitial r and a medial l, arɴɢlɯmbe caved in, derives from sqlɯmcollapse by prenasalization alternation (§ sec:fossil.prenasalization ): the r- originates here from rhotacism of s- (through *z ).

C+ r clusters
consonant!rhotic consonant!cluster
The Tables med.r2, med.r3 and med.r3.n list all clusters ending in r. The rhotic sonorant can follow all places of articulations except retroflex fricatives and affricates.

In the ambiguous clusters with a sonorant as first element ( wr, jr, ɣr and ʁr), r is initial, as shown by the perlative ɯ-jrɯ jroʁ `following X's trace' (§ sec:perlative ), the emphatic participle kɯ-wɣrɯ wɣrum `very white (one)' ( ex:khWlu, § sec:possessive.n.n ) and the reciprocal a-zɣɤʁrɯ ʁre `respect each other' from zɣɤʁrerespect.

By contrast, in ambiguous clusters with a coronal fricative as first element ( sr, zr, ɕr, ʑr), r is medial, as illustrated by the emphatic participles kɯ-zɯ zri `very long (one)' (in ex:Wmi.kWzWzri, § sec:S.possessor.relativization ), kɯ-ʑɯ ʑru `very strong (one)' and kɯ-ɣɤχsɯ χsrɯ `very handsome (one)' ( ex:kWZWZru.kWGAXsWXsrW ). Reduplication of the simple sr cluster in the comitative adverb kɤ́-sɯ srɯn `together with (its) cotton wool' (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) confirms that r is medial in sr, not only in χsr. Tshendzin rejects reduplication of these clusters without deletion: $ $ kɯ-zrɯ zri and $ $ kɯ-ʑrɯ ʑru are not grammatical.

The w preinitial in the group wɣr- is not realized as a separate segment (§ sec:wC.clusters ). It is an orthographic device used to indicate that the preceding back unrounded vowels ɯ and ɤ turn into their rounded counterparts when adjacent. For instance, reduplicated participle kɯ-wɣrɯ wɣrum `very white (one)' is phonetically realized as kuɣruɣrum.

An extra-short svarabhakti vowel can be heard in some clusters with -r- medial, in particular after coronal affricates and dorsal stops. For instance, cʰɤ-kro `s/he distributed it' can be realized as cʰɤkə̌ro.

The retroflex affricates originate at least in part from clusters of dental stops followed by r; direct evidence for the sound change *tr- tʂ- comes from alternations between tʂ and r, as that between the numeral kɯtʂɤɣsix and sqaprɤɣsixteen (§ sec:teens ) and between tʂuroad and ftɕɤrupath in the middle of the fields is a compound of ftɕarsummer and tʂuroad
(§ sec:second.member.alternation ). The gap in the system caused by this sound change has been filled by some ideophones in dr- (§ sec:idph.onsets ); the only non-ideophone with a cluster of this type is qɯmdroŋcrane, whose onset can either be analyzed as dr or as ndr, as the contrast between d and nd is neutralized due to assimilation with the m coda of the preceding syllable.

In triconsonantal clusters (Tables med.r3 and med.r3.n ), the medial r is compatible with all preinitials except itself.

It shows that some forms are restricted or in free variation, especially with the translocative prefix, and that the status of certain clusters remains uncertain because of limited or conflicting evidence. It also notes that retroflex affricates partly derive from earlier stop+**r** clusters, and that some pronunciations include extra-short epenthetic vowels in **-r-** clusters.

text:
In ambiguous clusters, the ɣ is initial in zɣ and when preceded by a non-nasal sonorant ( wɣ, jɣ, lɣ and rɣ, as illustrated by the distributed action derivation (§ sec:distributed.action ) nɤ-lɣɯ lɣa `dig everywhere' from lɣadig (not $ $ nɤ-lɯ lɣa).
comitative adverb
The velar sonorant is medial in ɕɣ, as shown by the comitative adverb (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) kɤ́-ɕɯ ɕɣa `together with its teeth' (not $ $ kɤ́-ɕɣɯ ɕɣa) from tɯ-ɕɣatooth. In, I claimed that ɕɣ could be reduplicated either with or without deletion of ɣ, but in my more recent data only the variant with deletion is attested. The group ʑɣ cannot be tested with partial reduplication.

2CG3CG

Cluster-final ɣ is secondary, and has at least three proto-Gyalrong origins.

First, it comes from proto-Gyalrong medial *-w, as in lɣadig (Situ rwâ, ) or tɯ-tɣaone span (Situ tə-təwá; the Tibetan cognate མཐོ་mtʰospan underwent Laufer's law, ). Most *-w- medials in the inherited vocabulary have undergone this sound change (except after dorsals, where they have disappeared), and the present w medials are secondary (§ sec:Cw.clusters ).

Second, it originates from the lenition of velar stops in clusters with two stops in proto-Gyalrong, as in pɣabird (from *pk, see Cogtse Situ pká, ).

Third, it is a secondary trace of velarized vowels, as in tɤjpɣomice (from *tɐ-lpaˠŋ, see Zbu tɑlvɑ́mʔ, ).

In triconsonantal clusters ( med.G3 ), medial ɣ can occur with all preinitials except velar fricatives and the labial w- and m, a further clue of its diachronic origin from *w. Combinations -w.Cɣ- are possible, however, in heterosyllabic clusters (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ), as in the noun laβzɣisteamed turnip.

C+ ʁ clusters
consonant!uvular consonant!cluster
Clusters with ʁ as last element are listed in med.R. The uvular fricative is medial only in a handful of clusters with dental or alveolo-palatal affricates, where it contrasts with ɣ, as shown by the minimal pair tɯ-ndzʁicollar bone vs. tɯ-ndzɣifang.

2CR3CR

In ambiguous clusters, with the dental fricative zʁ and non-nasal sonorants ( wʁ, lʁ, rʁ and jʁ), ʁ is always initial, as illustrated by rɤβʁɯ βʁa from rɤβʁaroar, kɯ-ʁrɯ rʁom `very rough (one)' from rʁombe rough and kɯ-ɤjʁɯ jʁu `very bent (one)' from ajʁube bent.

One of the origins of cluster-final ʁ is the result of the lenition of the uvular stop *q in double stop clusters, as in βʁaprevail, win (from *pq,, as shown by the Situ cognate pkâ, ).
summary: The passage explains that in ambiguous clusters, ɣ and ʁ are initial after certain consonants, while their cluster-final positions are secondary and reflect earlier historical developments. For ɣ, the main proto-Gyalrong sources are medial *-w, lenition of velar stops in stop clusters, and traces of velarized vowels; for ʁ, one origin is the lenition of proto-Gyalrong *q in double-stop clusters. It also notes that ɣ occurs in triconsonantal clusters with most preinitials except velar fricatives and labial w- and m-, and that ʁ is only medial in a few clusters, where it contrasts with ɣ.

tab:clusters.tot summarizes the numbers of clusters identified in § sec:preinitials and § sec:medials. Since in ambiguous clusters (§ sec:medials ) partial reduplication is not always available to determine whether the final non-nasal sonorant is medial or initial, no attempt is made at distinguishing between [initial+medial] and [preinitial+initial] clusters in this table.

Clusters with four elements can appear at least at the phonetic level if the last syllable of a verb stem with a triconsonantal onset undergoes synizesis with the 1sg -a suffix (§ sec:synizesis ). The denominal verb ɣɤjmŋodream of (§ sec:denom.tr.GA ) from the noun tɯ-jmŋodream (§ sec:jC.clusters ) provides examples like pjɤ́-wɣ-ɣɤ-jmŋo-a ( ifr - inv - denom -dream- 1sg ) `s/he dreamed of me' realized as pjó.ɣe.jmŋwa with a complex onset jmŋw comprising four segments.

Attested ambiguous clusters are listed in tab:ambiguous.clusters. Grey shading indicates phonotactically impossible combinations, due in particular to the constraints against the combination of velars and uvulars (§ sec:CG.clusters, § sec:CRR.clusters ), and against the combination of alveolo-palatals with j (§ sec:jC.clusters, § sec:Cj.clusters ). Orange colour indicates [initial+medial] clusters, whose final sonorant is removed in partial reduplication. Blue colour marks [preinitial+initial] clusters, whose final sonorant is unaffected by reduplication. Clusters left in white are those for which partial reduplication cannot be tested. The cluster rw has two possible reduplication patterns (§ sec:Cw.clusters ) and is thus left unmarked.

Even though some of the clusters cannot be subjected to testing with partial reduplication, the data in tab:ambiguous.clusters suggest the following rules:

itemize
If the first element of the ambiguous cluster is an alveolo-palatal fricative ( ɕ, ʑ), the following sonorant is medial.
If the first element of the ambiguous cluster is a glide ( w, j) or a dorsal sonorant ( ɣ, ʁ), the following sonorant is initial.
If the first element of the ambiguous cluster is a dental fricative ( s, z), the rhotic r or the lateral l, the following sonorant is medial if it is a glide or l, and it is initial if it is the rhotic or a dorsal sonorant.
itemize

From the attested data, it proposes that alveolo-palatal fricatives are followed by medial sonorants, glides and dorsal sonorants are followed by initial sonorants, and dental fricatives, r, and l show a split pattern depending on the type of sonor

text:
consonant!cluster syllable!heterosyllabic cluster
In addition to the clusters attested in onset position described in this chapter, another type of consonant clusters is found whenever a closed syllable is in non-final position in the word. These heterosyllabic clusters, whose first element is the coda of the first syllable, present considerably fewer phonotactic constraints than onset clusters.

The most obvious difference is the fact that, while a strict prohibition against having the same segment as preinitial and a medial is observed in onset clusters, this constraint does not apply in heterosyllabic ones. For instance, the noun tɕʰɤrprɯrain shelter, a compound from Tibetan ཆར་tɕʰarrain and the native word tɤprɯrain shelter, has the sequence -r.pr, which would be completely impossible as syllable onset (§ sec:rhotic.dissimilation ).

The phoneme w, realized as -β in coda position (§ sec:codas.inventory ), does not become an unvoiced fricative when followed by an unvoiced obstruent in the next syllable, as in the noun slɤβkʰaŋschool, which is not realized as $ $ slɤfkʰaŋ as would have been expected if the w were in preinitial position (§ sec:wC.clusters ). The coda -β is generally deleted when it precedes labial stops, especially the voiced b in ideophones. For instance, the pattern II ideophone (§ sec:ideo.II ) from the root bɤβ is bɤbɤβ `stubborn, bulky'; the alternative realization bɤβbɤβ is also possible.

Unlike w in preinitial position (§ sec:NC.clusters ), the coda -β does not assimilate with nasals or prenasalized onsets that follow it. For instance, the coda -β in the last syllable of verb stems is not nasalized by the dual -ndʑi or plural -nɯ indexation suffixes (§ sec:intr.23 ): pjɯ-fkaβ-nɯ ( ipfv -cover- pl ) `they cover it' (example ex:WtaR.kutanW, § sec:preverb.cover ) cannot be realized as $ $ pjifkámnɯ. The same is true in noun compounds; for example jlɤβndʑuweft stick from tɯ-jlɤβweft and ndʑustick.

A puzzling cluster -p.t- is observed in the numeral sqaptɯɣeleven (§ sec:teens ). The -p- is a linking element between the bound form sqa- `ten' and the following numeral, also found in other Gyalrongic languages, but its expected form would be the preinitial f- (from w) in this position. It is better analyzed as the coda of the first syllable.

The dental t, which exists as coda (§ sec:codas.inventory ), but not as preinitial (§ sec:preinitials ), is attested in heterosyllabic clusters followed by unvoiced labial or velar stops, mainly in Tibetan loanwords such as rgɤtpuold man (from རྒད་པོ་rgad.poold man) or mtɕʰɤtkʰohouse shrine (on which see § sec:historical.phono ). In compounds, the coda t is either lost in non-final syllables (§ sec:loss.codas.compounds ), or nasalizes to n if the following segment is a nasal sonorant or a prenasalized obstruent (§ sec:internal.sandhi.compounds ), in particular with the dual -ndʑi and plural -nɯ indexation suffixes (§ sec:intr.23 ), so that even heterosyllabic clusters with t a first element are infrequent.

Exceptions to the loss of -t before coronal stops and affricates do exist, however, for instance tɤɕphɤtta, the name of a type of sewing method, compound of tɤ-ɕpʰɤtpatch (n) (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ) with the verb taput (§ sec:ta.lv ). In this noun, a geminated -t.t- occurs across syllable boundaries.

While dental fricative preinitials cannot precede affricates (§ sec:sC.clusters ), the coda z does occurs before the dental affricate tsʰ- in the cluster -s.tsʰ- in mbrɤstsʰirice gruel (from mbrɤzrice and tɯtsʰirice gruel), assimilating in voice (§ sec:internal.sandhi.compounds ).

The preinitial j is not compatible with palatal and alveolo-palatal initials (§ sec:jC.clusters ), but the coda j can precede those segments across syllable boundary, as in qajʑmbraʁear of wheat from qajwheat and ʑmbraʁear (of corn).

The velar coda ɣ is generally deleted before velar stops, even in reduplicated ideophones. For instance, the pattern II ideophone (§ sec:ideo.II ) from the root gɤɣ `curved; moving with difficulty' is gɤgɤɣ, though gɤɣgɤɣ is also possible. There is only one example of ɣ preceding a uvular segment even across syllable boundaries: the sigmatic causative sɯɣʁaʁcause to hatch from ʁaʁhatch (§ sec:caus.sWG ). The Tibetan form འབྲུག་གློག་ⁿbrug.glogthunder and lightning would have been expected to yield $ $ mbrɯɣ.ʁloʁ in Japhug, but we find instead mbrɯɣloʁ (in dialects other than Kamnyu) or mbɣɯrloʁthunderstorm in Kamnyu with irregular metathesis of ɣ and r.

The uvular ʁ can surface before velar and uvular stops in heterosyllabic clusters (unlike when it occurs as preinitial, § sec:XC.clusters ), as in taʁkiup and down (§ sec.v.v.compounds.degree; realized as taχki ) and qʰoʁqʰoʁingot. The uvular coda is deleted, however, in the compound paskɤɣpig to be fattened from paʁpig and skɤɣfatten (pig), avoiding the non-attested cluster -ʁ.sk-.

When preceding unvoiced obstruents, the fricative codas z, ɣ and ʁ assimilate in voice and are converted to s, x and ʁ, respectively (§ sec:internal.sandhi.compounds ).

Onset clusters with nasal preinitials followed by non-nasal sonorants have been completely eliminated by a series of sound changes detailed in § sec:NC.clusters. However, the nasal codas m, n and ŋ can occur before syllables with l, r, j, w, ɣ- or ʁ- as onset. For instance, we find n.l in srɯnloʁring, m.ɣ (instead of mbr ) in nɤtsɯmɣɯttake away and bring back (from tsɯmtake away and ɣɯtbring, § sec:denom.compound.verbs ), n.r- in smɤnrɯɣmedicinal plants (from སྨན་རིགས་sman.rigstype of materia medica) or m.j (instead of mɲ ) in zɯmjɯbarrel handle (compound of zɯmbucket and ɯ-jɯits handle, from ཟོམ་zombucket and ཡུ་བ་ju.bahandle, respectively).
comitative adverb
These clusters, although heterosyllabic, are reduplicated as a whole when partial reduplication is applied, as in the comitative adverb (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) kɤ́-srɯnlɯ nloʁ `together with his/her ring' from srɯnloʁring (instead of $ $ kɤ́-srɯnlɯ loʁ, an incorrect form).

More complex clusters with a nasal as first element are found when the second member of the compound has a complex onset, for instance -n.rʑ- in χɕɯnrʑiYama (from གཤིན་རྗེ་gɕin.rdʑeYama, the Buddhist god of the underworld) and -m.xtsʰ- in jpumxtsʰɯmthickness (a compound noun derived from jpumbe thick and xtsʰɯmbe thin, § sec.v.v.compounds.degree ).
summary: The passage describes heterosyllabic consonant clusters, where the first consonant is the coda of a non-final syllable, and notes that they are subject to fewer phonotactic restrictions than onset clusters. It gives many examples showing that codas such as -β, -t, -z, -j, -ɣ, -ʁ, and nasal codas can occur before a following syllable’s onset in ways that would be impossible word-initially, though some codas are often deleted or assimilate in specific environments. It also notes that these clusters can be treated as a unit in partial reduplication and may become more complex when the second syllable has a complex onset.

text:
Some heterosyllabic clusters are avoided by insertion of an anaptyctic vowel ɯ, in particular in Tibetan loanwords. For instance, སེམས་སྡུག་sems.sdugsadness, worry is borrowed as sɯmɯzdɯɣworry instead of expected $ $ sɯmzdɯɣ, with the ɯ breaking the cluster -m.-zd-.

The anaptyctic vowel can be i if the cluster in the second syllable has a palatal or alveolo-palatal preinitial. For instance, ɕomiron and tɤ-jŋoʁhook are compounded as ɕɤmiŋoʁiron hook, in which the preinitial j is converted to i.
summary: Some heterosyllabic clusters are avoided by inserting an anaptyctic vowel ɯ, especially in Tibetan loanwords, where it breaks up clusters that would otherwise occur across syllable boundaries. In some cases the inserted vowel is i instead, particularly when the second syllable contains a palatal or alveolo-palatal preinitial, which is realized as i in the compound.

subsubsection: The sonority sequencing principle in Japhug
text:
syllable!sonority sequencing principle
hierarchy!sonority sequencing principle
A considerable amount of work in phonology supports the idea that the segments of the world's languages follow a universal scale of sonority (for instance; see for an opposing view). Several versions of this sonority hierarchy have been proposed, for instance (§ sec:sonority.hierarchy ).

exe

low vowels > mid vowels > high vowels > ə > glides > laterals > flaps
> trills > nasals > h > voiced fricatives > voiced stops > voiceless
fricatives > voiceless stops and affricates
exe

The notion of sonority is invoked in particular to account for observed generalizations in the structure of consonant clusters: in many languages, clusters follow the so-called sonority sequencing principle ( ssp, ):

exe

`Between any member of a syllable and the syllable peak, a sonority
rise or plateau must occur.'
exe

According to this hierarchy, in onset clusters, sonorants are expected to be closer the syllable nucleus than obstruents ( krV is favoured over rkV ), and glides to be closer to the nucleus than any other consonant ( mjV is preferred over jmV ).

Japhug, like other Gyalrongic languages (see in particular and ), is rich in ssp -infringing clusters.

For instance, the 17 biconsonantal clusters with j as first element ( 2jC in § sec:jC.clusters and 5 in § sec:medials ) all contravene the ssp except for jw. Moreover, some of these clusters, such as jtʂʰ, jm and jŋ, have no ssp -compliant counterpart: $ $ tʂʰj, $ $ mj, and $ $ ŋj are not attested as syllable onsets (though the last two can occur across syllables, § sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ).

A certain number of ssp -compliant clusters have been removed by specific sound changes, in particular *mj- mɲ, *mr- mbr- (§ sec:NC.clusters ) and *tr- tʂ- (§ sec:Cr.clusters ).
summary: The passage explains that phonological research often assumes a universal sonority hierarchy and uses the sonority sequencing principle to describe consonant-cluster structure: sonority should rise or plateau toward the syllable peak, so sonorants and especially glides are expected closer to the nucleus than obstruents. It then notes that Japhug, like other Gyalrongic languages, frequently violates this principle, with many j-initial clusters and some clusters lacking any sonority-compliant counterpart, although some compliant clusters were later lost through sound changes.

text:
assimilation!external sandhi sandhi!external word
Word boundaries in Japhug can be defined by a combination of criteria, including stress (§ sec:stress ) and also morphology in the case of verbs (§ sec:wordhood.criteria.verb ), but they are not completely impenetrable from a phonological point of view: some sandhi phenomena, including assimilation and resyllabification, do occur across word boundaries.

First, the codas -z, -r, -ɣ, -ʁ can assimilate in voicing to the following consonant (§ sec:codas.inventory ), as in heterosyllabic clusters (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ).

Second, the coda -t is nasalized when directly followed by a nasal or prenasalized segment, and tends to drop when followed by a dental, alveolo-palatal and retroflex segment. In (§ sec:rWmtChAt.cthWwGlAt ) for example, the -t coda of rɯmtɕʰɤtoffering to the mountain drops before the translocative prefix and that of lɤt merges with the following affricate tɕ.

exe

rɯmtɕʰɤt s-cʰɯ́-wɣ-lɤt tɕe ɲɯ-pʰɤn \\
mountain.offering tral - ipfv: downstream - inv -release lnk sens -be.efficient \\
`If you go and make offerings to the mountain (god), it will solve (your problem).' (Lobzang) 0003370S#S27
exe

These rules are optional, and it is possible to find examples in the corpus where they do not take place. For instance, in (§ sec:tolAt.ri ), the coda -t of to-lɤt is clearly audible even before r-.

exe

tɯrpa ci to-lɤt ri \\
axe once ifr -release lnk \\
`He wielded his axe, but...' (140430 jin e-zh)
0003893#S37

Third, when a [preinitial+initial] cluster is preceded by an open syllable, the preinitial can be resyllabified as coda of the previous syllable. In (§ sec:Wrna.XchoRe ) for instance, the preinitial χ- of χcʰoʁeright and left becomes the coda of -rna and voices to ʁ, and yields a sequence -rnaʁ.cʰo-. This type of phenomenon is considerably rarer than the previous ones.

exe

ɯ-rna χcʰoʁe ʑo ko-sti. \\
3sg. poss -ear left.and.right emph ifr -plug \\
`He plugged both hid left and his right ears.' (140514 huishuohua de niao-zh)
0003992#S183
exe

Fourth, when a word ending in open syllable precedes a vowel-initial word (§ sec:zero.onset ), the initial vowel a- and ɯ- of the latter very commonly merge with the final vowel of the former. For instance, the sentence in (§ sec:amu.Wxtsa ) is realized as amuxtsaːpɯŋu: the ɯ- prefix is elided by merging with the preceding u, and the -a rhyme of ɯ-xtsa merges with the a- prefix of the following word, yielding a phonetically long aː.

exe

a-mu ɯ-xtsa a-pɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ra \\
1sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss -shoe irr - ipfv -be sens -be.needed \\
`Let (me take this) shoe (as a present) for my mother.' (tWxtsa 2003)
exe

External sandhi is not represented in the transcription used in this grammar.
summary: Word boundaries in Japhug are identifiable by stress and, for verbs, morphology, but they are not fully impermeable phonologically because several kinds of external sandhi can apply across them. These include voicing assimilation of certain codas, optional nasalization or deletion of final -t before particular following consonants, rarer resyllabification of preinitials as the coda of a preceding syllable, and frequent vowel merging across word boundaries before vowel-initial words. These sandhi effects are not marked in the grammar’s transcription.

text:
script Tibetan
The IPA orthography chosen to write Japhug in this grammar is probably not viable for use by native speakers, and an alternative writing system based on Tibetan script is preferable. Fortunately, it is relatively easy to transcribe Japhug into Tibetan script.

Concerning the vowels (§ sec:vowels ), i, u, e and o can be represented using the གི་གུ་ gi.gu, ཞབས་ཀྱུ་ ʑabs.kʲu, འགྲེང་བུ་ ⁿgreŋ.bu and ན་རོ་ na.ro symbols, respectively. The vowel ɤ, being very common word-internally, can be taken as base vowel of the aksharas. As for ɯ, the Old Tibetan གི་གུ་ལོག་ gi.gu.log can be employed. Finally, the a can be represented by the long vowel symbol འ་ཆུང་ ɦa.tɕʰuŋ.

A few consonants found in Japhug do not have Tibetan equivalents. The letter ཝ w can be reserved for the velar fricative ɣ. The uvulars can be differentiated from the velars by the ཚ་རྟགས་ tsʰa.rtags, for instance ཀ༹ q, འག༹ ɴɢ and ཝ༹ ʁ. In coda position however, the contrast between ɣ and ʁ does not need to be transcribed, since these two codas are in complementary distribution with the preceding vowels (§ sec:rhyme.inventory ). The unvoiced velar fricative can be written as ཧ x and the uvular one as ཧ༹ χ in initial position (for the rare phoneme h an additional diacritic symbol such as ཧ྇ can be employed). In preinitial position, however (§ sec:xC.clusters, § sec:XC.clusters ), the voiced stop symbols should be preferred, since there is no contrast between fricatives and stops in this context.

The retroflex affricates can be represented by the Sanskrit symbols for retroflex stops ( ཊ tʂ, ཋ tʂʰ and ཌ dʐ) and the retroflex fricative by the corresponding Sankrit consonant ( ཥ ʂ ).

The glide w in initial position can be written as བ༹ w with ཚ་རྟགས་ tsʰa.rtags, but as medial (§ sec:Cw.clusters ) the ཝ་ཟུར་ wa.zur can be employed. Medial -ɣ- and -ʁ- can be represented by underscript ཝ and འ, for instance in པྺཱག pɣaʁ `turn over' and ཏྀ་འཛྰི་ tɯ-ndzʁi `collar bone'.

The clusters with fricatives preceding prenasalized obstruents can be transcribed by combining a prefixed འ marking prenasalization with a superfixed letter marking the fricative, as in འཤྦྲྀ་ ʑmbrɯ `boat', འཤྒྲི་ ʑŋgri `star' or འསྡེznde `wall'. Since the voicing contrast is neutralized in this position (§ sec:sC.clusters, § sec:shC.clusters ), the unvoiced fricative symbols ས s and ཤ ɕ can be used.

The following examples illustrate how this script can be used to write complete sentences.

exe

ɕ-tɤ-χtɯ-t-a \\
tral - aor -buy- pst: tr - 1sg \\
ཤྟ་ག༹ཏྀ་ཏཱ།
`I went and bought it.'
exe

exe

tɤ-rʑaβ nɯ pjɤ-rɤ-ɕpʰɤt \\
indef. poss -wide dem ifr. ipfv - apass -patch \\
ཏ་རྮཱབ་ནྀ་པྱ་ར་ཤྥད།
`The wife was patching clothes.'
0003366#S20
exe

exe

ɯ-me nɯ kɯ andi paχɕi ɲɯ-ntsɣe ŋu\\
3sg. poss -daughter dem erg west apple ipfv -sell be: fact \\
འྀ་མེ་ནྀ་ཀྀ་འ་འདི་པཱག་ཤི་ཉི་འཙྺེ་ངུ།
`Her daughter is selling apples over there.'
exe
summary: The passage argues that the IPA-based orthography used in the grammar is unlikely to be practical for native speakers and that a Tibetan-script writing system would be preferable, since Japhug can be transcribed into Tibetan fairly easily. It then outlines how Japhug vowels, consonants, glides, and consonant clusters can be represented using Tibetan letters and diacritics, and gives example sentences showing the system in use.

text:
This chapter focuses on possessive prefixes, compounding and noun derivations.

It does not discuss flagging, number and quantification, as these grammatical categories are expressed by independent words or clitics, such as postpositions and noun modifiers, and are treated in chapters chap:postpositions.relators and chap:noun.phrase.

Nominalization (including lexicalized deverbal nouns) and denominal verbalization are treated in chapters chap:non-finite and chap:denominal, respectively.

The morphology of counted nouns (quantifiers, time nominals) is discussed in § sec:counted.nouns, and that of nouns of location in § sec:relator.location.
summary: This chapter covers possessive prefixes, compounding, and noun derivation. It does not address flagging, number, or quantification because these are expressed by independent words or clitics and are treated elsewhere, and it likewise refers nominalization, denominal verbalization, counted nouns, and nouns of location to other chapters or sections.

text:
prefix!possessive possession!prefix
Nouns in Japhug can be divided into four main subclasses, inalienably possessed nouns, alienably possessed nouns, unpossessible nouns and counted nouns, depending on the type of prefixes they can take. The present section focuses on the first two, the ones that are compatible with possessive prefixes. Unpossessible nouns are treated in § sec:unpossessible.nouns, and counted nouns in § sec:counted.nouns in another chapter.
summary: Japhug nouns are divided into four main subclasses based on the kinds of prefixes they can take: inalienably possessed, alienably possessed, unpossessible, and counted nouns. This section deals only with the first two classes, since they can occur with possessive prefixes, while the other two are discussed elsewhere.

text:
The paradigm of possessive prefixes in Japhug is shown in tab:possessive.prefixes. It presents obvious commonalities with the personal pronouns (§ sec:pers.pronouns ) and the indexation suffixes (§ sec:indexation.suffixes.history ). tab:possessive.prefixes includes comparative data on the dialect of Tatshi (from, and personal communication), which differs from Kamnyu in having non-palatalized forms in the dual prefixes.

In this paradigm, the contrast between second and third person is neutralized in the dual and plural, while it is preserved in pronouns and person indexation.

Xtokavian

The indefinite possessor prefixes tɯ-/tɤ-/ta- only occur on inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:inalienably.possessed.morpho ). The syntactic function of these prefixes corresponds to that of the ``absolutive'' suffix in Nahuatl (``suffixe absolu'' in ). The indefinite possessor prefixes saturate the possessive prefixal slot, just like antipassive prefixes (§ sec:antipassive ) saturate the object function of transitive verbs. They do not mark that the noun is indefinite, On the various strategies to express definiteness in Japhug, see § sec:indefinite.markers and § sec:definiteness. but rather indicate that it lacks a definite possessor, when the possessor is unknown or irrelevant. A reviewer suggests the term ``neutral'' instead, but I find it not specific enough, and ``absolutive'' is to be avoided for obvious reasons, in a language with numerous constructions following ergative-absolutive alignment (§ sec:ergativity ).
alignment!ergative-absolutive

Possessive prefixes other than the indefinite possessor prefixes are collectively referred to as ``definite possessor prefixes''. The semantic difference between indefinite and generic possessors is discussed in § sec:indef.genr.poss.

The vowel contrast ɯ vs. ɤ vs. a on the indefinite possessor prefixes is lexically determined (§ sec:inalienably.possessed.morpho ). This contrast is neutralized on definite possessor prefixes, which all have the same form regardless of the noun. This neutralization is an innovation: in Situ, the vowel contrast is present on all possessive prefixes, analyzes the vowel as part of the nominal root.

Stacking of possessive prefixes is not allowed in Japhug, with the exception of the combination of a definite possessor prefix with an indefinite possessor prefix tɯ- or tɤ- to turn an inalienably possessed noun into an alienably possessed one (see § sec:alienabilization ).

The only irregularities in possessive morphology are found with a- initial nouns (§ sec:a.nouns ).

a- initial nouns

Unlike verbs (see § sec:contraction ), nouns whose stem begins with a a- are extremely rare in Japhug. Nevertheless, as is the case with verbs, the vowel a- merges with any prefixed element, so that nouns of this type do not have regular possessive forms. The only noun in a- to commonly receive possessive prefixes is araʁliquor (a loanword from ཨ་རག་ʔa.ragliquor). Its possessive forms are highly anomalous: 1sg aʑɤ-raʁ, 2sg nɤʑɤ-nɤ-raʁ and 2pl nɯʑɤ-nɯ-raʁ (as in ex:nWZAnWraR ), combining the pronoun in bound state (§ sec:status.constructus ) followed by the possessive prefix, which takes over the initial a-.

exe

nɯʑɤ-nɯ-raʁ ɯ́-ra \\
2pl - 2pl. poss -liquor qu -be.needed: fact \\
`Do you need liquor?' (elicited)
exe

To account for these forms, it is necessary to assume that the initial a- was reanalyzed as a 1sg possessive prefix. However, this analysis did not occur directly. The expected 1sg possessive form *a-araʁ ( 1sg. poss -liquor) would automatically yield *a-raʁ by vowel fusion (following the rule described in § sec:contraction ). The resulting 1sg *a-raʁ then became the pivot for the analogical reshaping of the rest of the paradigm, from which for instance *nɤ-raʁ ( 2sg. poss -liquor) was generated (replacing putative earlier forms such as *nɤ-araʁ * naraʁ). Due to homophony with the base noun araʁ, the 1sg pronoun aʑo was systematically added and *aʑo a-raʁ underwent morphological fusion to the attested aʑɤ-raʁ, followed by the rest of the possessive paradigm.
summary:
Japhug possessive prefixes show clear parallels with personal pronouns and person indexation, but second- and third-person contrasts are neutralized in the dual and plural. The language distinguishes indefinite possessor prefixes, used only on inalienably possessed nouns to mark the absence of a definite possessor, from definite possessor prefixes; stacking of possessive prefixes is generally impossible except when an indefinite prefix is added to make an inalienably possessed noun alienable. 

Irregular possessive morphology is found mainly with rare noun stems beginning in *a-*, whose initial vowel merges with prefixes and yields anomalous possessive forms, especially in the noun *araʁ* ‘liquor’. These forms are explained as the result of reanalysis and analogical reshaping of the paradigm, with the original initial *a-* being treated as a possessive prefix.

text:
prefix!possessive possession!prefix possessor
Possession cannot be expressed without a possessive prefix on the possessee, except for a handful of constructions where a pronoun occurs instead (§ sec:pronouns.possessive.markers ).

Possessive prefixes can be used on nearly any noun (except the unpossessed nouns, see § sec:unpossessible.nouns ), including recent borrowings from Chinese (or quasi-code switching), as 老家 lǎojiā `native place' in ( ex:aZo.GW.alaojia ). They also occur on several non-finite verbal forms, including participles (see § sec:subject.participle.possessive and § sec:object.participle.possessive ), bare infinitives (§ sec:bare.inf ) and degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominals ).

exe

aʑo ɣɯ a-<laojia> ɣɯ ɯ-lɤcu nɯre ri ku-rɤʑi-nɯ ŋu \\
1sg gen 1sg. poss -old.house gen 3sg. poss -upstream there loc ipfv -stay- pl be: fact \\
`They live in a place upstream from my old house.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S215
exe

In the case of first or second person possessors, it is possible to have simply a possessive prefix on the noun, ( a-ɣɲi `my friend', a-mbro `my horse' and a-ʁgra `my enemy' in ex:ambro ), a personal pronoun and a possessive prefix (same person and number, as in ex:aZo.ambro ) or even a pronoun, the genitive clitic ɣɯ and a possessive prefix as in ( ex:aZo.GW.alaojia ) (§ sec:gen.possession ).

exe

a-ɣɲi ci tɯ tɯ-ŋu nɤ, a-mbro ɯ-lwa ɯ-taʁ kɤ-zo, a-ʁgra ci tɯ tɯ-ŋu nɤ, a-mbro ɯ-jme ɯ-taʁ kɤ-zo \\
1sg. poss -friend indef cond 2-be: fact lnk 1sg. poss -horse 3sg. poss -mane 3sg -on imp -land 1sg. poss -enemy indef cond 2-be: fact lnk 1sg. poss -horse 3sg. poss -tail 3sg -on imp -land \\
`If you are my friend, land on my horse's mane, if you are my enemy, land on my horse's tail.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

exe

aʑo a-mbro nɤrwɯrɯnbotɕʰi ŋu, tɯ-sŋi χpaχtsʰɤt ci ɲɯ́-wɣ-tsɯm-a cʰa \\
1sg 1sg. poss -horse anthr be: fact one-day yojana indef ipfv: west - inv -take.away- 1sg can: fact \\
`My horse is Norbu Rinpoche, he can make me cross one yojana per day.' (2003 smanmi2)
exe

It is possible to have a first singular possessive preceded by a first plural pronoun, as in ( ex:iZo.amu ) (see § sec:agreement.mismatch for other examples of person mismatch involving 1pl pronouns).

exe

iʑo a-mu nɯ tʰamtʰam kɯrcɤsqaptɯɣ tʰɯ-azɣɯt ŋu. \\
1pl 1sg. poss -mother dem now 81 aor -reach be: fact \\
`My mother is now 81.' (2010-histoire09-2)
exe

In the case of a possessee shared by the speaker and the addressee, the 1sg possessive is the preferred form. For instance, a couple of parents or grandparents talking to each other about their son or their grandchild more often use a-tɕɯ `my son' or a-ɣe `my grandchild' than a 1du or a 2sg possessor such as tɕi-ɣe `our grandchild' or nɤ-ɣe `your grandchild', as I have noticed by participant observation. Nevertheless, the use of other possessive prefixes than 1sg in such contexts is not agrammatical, and systematically occurs in texts translated from Chinese (by calquing), as in ( ex:tCitCW.YWsAzdWxpa ).

exe

tɕi-tɕɯ ɲɯ-sɤzdɯxpa, \\
1du. poss -son sens -be.pitiful \\
`Our poor son!' (150831 renshen wawa-zh) 0006418#S15
exe
summary:
Possession in this language normally requires a possessive prefix on the possessed noun, with only a few cases using a pronoun instead. These prefixes occur on most nouns, including some recent Chinese borrowings, and also on several non-finite verbal forms such as participles, bare infinitives, and degree nominals.  

The passage also notes that first- and second-person possession allows some variation in expression, including possessive prefix alone, pronoun plus prefix, or even pronoun plus genitive clitic plus prefix; in shared possession contexts, the 1sg possessive is often preferred, though other forms are grammatical and appear especially in translations from Chinese.

text:
definite obviative
Nouns with a definite possessor in Japhug can be indefinite, unlike in most languages of Europe. They can occur with an indefinite determiner (example ex:ambro above). With a quantifier such as tɯ-rdoʁone piece as in ( ex:Wzda.tWrdoR ), a noun with a definite possessor is interpreted as referring to a certain number of persons out of a group (`one of his X').

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ ɯ-zda tɯ-rdoʁ ɯ-pʰe to-ti, tɯ-rdoʁ nɯ kɯ li ci ɯ-pʰe tɕe ɲɤ-k-ɤ-sɯ-ɤmɯ-mtsʰɯ mtsʰɤm-nɯ \\
indef. poss -son dem erg 3sg. poss -companion one- cl 3sg - dat ifr -say one- cl dem erg again indef 3sg - dat lnk ifr - peg - recip - caus - recip -hear- pl \\
`The boy told one of his companions, and that one another one, and [in this way] they informed each other.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S70
exe

Unlike in Algonquian languages, but like in Mapudungun, inverse marking on the verb (§ sec:indexation.non.local ) is not required if the subject is a possessed noun whose possessor is also object of the same sentence, as shown by example ( ex:prox.naBde ) where the direct form na-βde appears. In other words, nouns with a third person possessor are not automatically obviative (see and § sec:obviation.possessor for additional discussion).

exe

ɯ-rʑaβ nɯ kɯ na-βde \\
3sg. poss -wife dem erg aor:3 -throw.away \\
`His$_i$ wife left him$_i$.' (14-siblings)
exe

The inverse form nɯ́-wɣ-βde is also possible in exactly the same context -- example ( ex:obv.nWwGBde ) comes from the same text and refers to the same event.

exe

ɯ-rʑaβ cʰo ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ ʁnaʁna kɯ nɯ́-wɣ-βde\\
3sg. poss -wife comit 3sg. poss -son dem both erg aor - inv -throw.away\\
`His$_i$ wife and his$_i$ son left him$_i$.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S266
exe

Although not obligatory, the inverse on the verb (like in example ex:obv.nWwGBde ) is more common than a direct form (example ex:prox.naBde ) in this type of configuration (§ sec:indexation.non.local ).
summary: In Japhug, a noun with a definite possessor can still be interpreted as indefinite, even appearing with an indefinite determiner, and with a quantifier it can mean “one of his X.” Unlike in Algonquian languages, a possessed third-person noun whose possessor is also the object of the same sentence does not automatically require inverse marking on the verb; both direct and inverse forms are possible, though the inverse is more common in this configuration.

text:
prefix!possessive possession!prefix
Possessive prefixes are also used to express beneficiaries, recipients and other oblique arguments, such as the `person needing' in the construction with the verb rabe needed, as in ( ex:ambro.tARndo.kWtso ). See § sec:gen.beneficiary for a more detailed account of the expression of beneficiaries in Japhug.

exe

a-mbro taʁndo kɯ-tso ci tɕi ra \\
1sg. poss -horse speech sbj: pcp -understand one also be.needed: fact \\
`I also need a horse who understands speech.' (2003kAndzwsqhaj2)
exe

In the case of beneficiaries and recipients, if a genitive pronoun or genitive phrase is present, the presence of a possessive prefix is possible ( ex:aZWG.akWra ) but not obligatory ( ex:aZWG.kWra ), in particular in the case of possessed nouns that already have a definite possessor ( ex:aZWG.Wlu ).

exe

aʑɯɣ a-kɯ-ra ci tu tɕe nɯ `ɣa' tɤ-ti ra \\
1sg: gen 1sg. poss - sbj: pcp -be.needed indef exist: fact lnk dem yes imp -say be.needed: fact \\
`There is one thing I need, and you have to say `yes' to it.' (140429 qingwa wangzi-zh)
0003890#S47
exe

exe

aʑɯɣ kɯ-ra me \\
1sg: gen sbj: pcp -be.needed not.exist: fact \\
`I don't need anything.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

exe

aʑɯɣ ɯ-lu ra \\
1sg: gen 3sg. poss -milk be.needed: fact \\
`I want its milk.' (02-deluge2012) 0003376#S12
exe

We also find 3sg possessive prefixes ɯ- indexing not a possessor or a beneficiary/recipient, but anaphorically referring to a whole clause, as in ( ex:Wcha.mWm ), where ɯ-cʰa does not mean `its/his alcohol', but `the alcohol made in the fashion described in the previous clause'. As pointed out by a reviewer, this type of construction reminds of the diachronic evolution from third person possessive suffix to definite article in Amharic.

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe iɕqʰa ʑmbrɯβɟaj nɯ kɯ nɯnɯ cʰa nɯ tú-wɣ-sɯ-ɕmi tɕe
ɯ-cʰa mɯm tu-ti-nɯ pɯ-ŋgrɤl \\
in.former.times lnk the.aforementioned boat.oar dem erg dem alcohol dem ipfv - inv - caus -mix lnk 3sg. poss -alcohol be.tasty: fact ipfv -say- pl pst. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`In former times, people used to mix the alcohol with boat oars, the alcohol [made this way] is tasty, they used to say.' (cha-31)
0003764#S38
exe

The form of the 3sg possessive prefix
Japhug differs from other Gyalrong languages ( tab:3sg.inv, data from, ) in that the third person possessive prefix is not homophonous with the inverse prefix (§ sec:allomorphy.inv, § sec:direct-inverse ).

Independently of the question of whether these two prefixes could be historically related, it is probable that Japhug is innovative here.

In the same way as the inverse prefix ɣɯ- has an allomorph transcribed as wɣ when preceded by another prefix, realized as vowel rounding in most cases (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ), there is a possible trace of a vowel rounding allomorph of the possessive prefix in the linker núndʐafor this reason (§ sec:consequence ).

This linker originates from a phrase combining the demonstrative nɯthat (on which see § sec:anaphoric.demonstrative.pro, § sec:demonstrative.determiners and § sec:nW.topic ) with the 3sg possessed form of the noun ɯ-ndʐacause (§ sec:causal.clauses ). The form núndʐa possibly reflects earlier *nɯ-w-ndʐa, *-w- being a frozen allomorph of the 3sg possessive prefix in non-initial position.

There is a possible trace of the expected allomorph $ $ ɣɯ- (from proto-Gyalrong *wə- ) in the noun ɣɯfsufriend, etymologically `his equal'; the inalienably possessed noun ɯ-fsuof the same size, which shares the same root, has a regular possessive prefix that is coreferent with the standard of comparison (as in ex:nWfsu with the 3pl; see § sec:Wfsu.equative on this construction). The alienably possessed noun ɣɯfsufriend is thus possibly a lexicalized equivalent of ɯ-fsuof the same size (used in one of the equative constructions, § sec:Wfsu.equative ), whose 3sg prefix was frozen before the change from *ɣɯ- to ɯ- occurred.

exe

tɯrme kɯ-mbro ra nɯ-fsu jamar tu-zɣɯt ma mɤ-cʰa \\
person sbj: pcp -be.high pl 3pl. poss -equal about ipfv -reach apart.from neg -can: fact \\
`It can only grow about as high as a tall human.' (15-babW)
0003512#S4
exe

Furthermore, additional evidence for the idea that the third person prefix contained *w- comes from the etymology of the reflexive prefix ʑɣɤ-, which is argued to originate from the third person pronoun (§ sec:reflexive.origin ).

It remains unclear why the regular allomorph of the third person possessive is ɯ- rather than expected $ $ ɣɯ-. A possible explanation could be false segmentation, due to reanalysis with the genitive marker ɣɯ, since the genitive can optionally occur between the possessor and the possessee, as in ( ex:qaCpa.GW.WpW ). A pre-Japhug form such as *qaɕpa ɣɯ-pɯ could have been misanalyzed as qaɕpa ɣɯ ɯ-pɯ due to vowel fusion sandhi (§ sec:sandhi.word ), and a new allomorph ɯ- extracted from such constructions. The weakness of this hypothesis is that some Japhug dialects have kɯ rather than ɣɯ as their genitive marker.

exe

nɯnɯ qaɕpa ɣɯ ɯ-pɯ ŋu tɕe, \\
dem frog gen 3sg. poss -young be: fact lnk \\
`It (the tadpole) is the young of the frog.' (hist-28-kWpAz)
0003714#S203
exe
summary: Possessive prefixes in Japhug are used not only for possession, but also to mark beneficiaries, recipients, and other oblique arguments, and they can appear optionally alongside genitive pronouns or genitive phrases. The 3sg possessive prefix ɯ- is also used anaphorically to refer to an entire preceding clause, and the passage argues that Japhug’s 3sg possessive prefix is innovative, possibly reflecting an earlier form with *w- whose remnants survive in a few lexical and grammatical forms.

text: noun!inalienably possessed
summary: The passage identifies **inalienably possessed nouns**, meaning nouns that are obligatorily associated with a possessor. Such nouns typically refer to entities like body parts, kinship terms, or other closely related items that cannot normally be discussed without indicating whose they are.

text:
Inalienably possessed nouns differ from alienably possessed ones in that they require the presence of a possessive prefix. Unless when used with the indefinite possessor prefixes, inalienably possessed nouns are not formally distinguishable from alienably possessed ones; for instance, a-pi `my elder sibling' and a-mbro `my horse' both take the 1 a- prefix and no direct clue indicates that the first noun is inalienably possessed and that the second one is alienably possessed.

The citation form however differs between inalienably and alienably possessed nouns: the former must take an indefinite possessor prefix (or in some cases a 3 ɯ- ), while the latter can occur without possessive prefix, as for instance tɤ-pielder sibling (with the indefinite tɤ-; the bare root $ $ pi is not a correct form) vs. mbrohorse (without prefix).

Inalienably possessed nouns are divided into four classes depending on their citation form. The indefinite possessor prefix has three allomorphs ( tɯ, tɤ, ta- ) whose distribution is not completely predictable on the basis of phonology or semantics (though some generalizations are provided below). In addition, some inalienably possessed nouns only take definite possessor prefixes. The contrast between these four classes is neutralized when the noun takes a definite possessor prefix (unlike in Situ, see and ).

The most common allomorph of the indefinite possessor prefix is tɯ-. Inalienably possessed nouns selecting this allomorph, such as tɯ-jaʁhand, arm, have identical indefinite and generic possessor forms (see § sec:indef.genr.poss ).

The allomorph tɤ- is also very common, in particular with kinship terms and some body parts (see § sec:body.part and § sec:kinship ). The form ta- is a phonological variant of tɤ, occurring mainly with nouns whose stem begins with a uvular such as ta-ʁrɯhorn or ta-ʁiyounger sibling. The contrast between ɤ and a in this prefix is very difficult to perceive before uvulars with some speakers (see § sec:A.vs.a.prefixes ), and the transcription adopted in this grammar (and the online corpus and dictionary) is based on the slow syllable-by-syllable pronunciation of these words by Tshendzin.
