Two inalienably possessed nouns, however, ta-mawork and ta-marbutter, have the ta- allomorph with an initial m, probably originally due to vowel assimilation (§ sec:vowel.harmony, § sec:A.vs.a.prefixes ).

The minimal pair between tɤ-mamother and ta-mawork shows that this vowel contrast, however marginal, is distinctive, and that even if the two allomorphs tɤ- and ta- were originally phonologically conditioned, it is no longer the case in Kamnyu Japhug.

Some inalienably possessed nouns never occur with indefinite possessor prefixes, for instance ɯ-tʰoʁground is only attested with the 3 ɯ- prefix (see § sec:earth.IPN ). In some cases, the indefinite possessor form is difficult to elicit and in case of doubt the third singular form is given in the dictionary (for instance ɯ-mdoʁcolour). Future reasearch may reveal an indefinite possessor form for some of these nouns.

When denominal verbs are derived from inalienably possessed nouns, the vocalism of the denominal prefix tends to be the same as that of the indefinite possessor prefix (for instance tɤ-βɟumattress nɤβɟuuse as a mattress, not $ $ nɯβɟu ), though there are exceptions ( tɯ-rpaʁshoulder mɤrpaʁcarry on the shoulder), as discussed in § sec:denom.mA.

By analogy with several non-finite verb forms, in particular the subject participle of transitive verbs and the bare infinitive, which index one argument (the object) by a possessive prefix (§ sec:bare.inf ), the possessors of inalienably possessed nouns are considered to be core arguments, while those of alienably possessed nouns are treated as adjuncts. In other words, inalienably possessed nouns have a valency of 1 like intransitive verbs, while alienably possessed nouns have a valency of 0. On nominal valency and inalienability, see also. The indefinite possessor prefix can be viewed as a valency-decreasing device, the nominal equivalent of passive and antipassive derivations, especially given its use in the alienabilization of inalienably possessed nouns (see § sec:alienabilization ). Wider implications of the assumption that possessors of inalienably possessed nouns are core arguments are explored in § sec:complement.taking.nouns.
summary:
Inalienably possessed nouns in Kamnyu Japhug require a possessive prefix and differ from alienably possessed nouns mainly in their citation form: inalienable nouns must take an indefinite possessor prefix (or sometimes 3rd singular ɯ-), while alienable nouns can appear without any possessive prefix. The indefinite possessor prefix has three allomorphs, tɯ-, tɤ-, and ta-, whose distribution is only partly predictable, and some nouns occur only with definite possessor prefixes.

The passage also classifies inalienably possessed nouns into four citation-form classes and notes that the contrast among these classes is neutralized with definite possessors. Finally, it argues that possessors of inalienably possessed nouns behave like core arguments, giving these nouns a valency of 1, whereas alienably possessed nouns have valency 0, with the indefinite possessor prefix functioning as a valency-decreasing device.

text:
inalienabilization
Derivation from alienably possessed to inalienably possessed nouns is not common in Japhug. An interesting case is that of ɯ-ʁlereputation, which originates from the alienably possessed qalewind with a reduced form ʁ- of the class prefix qa, as some second members of compounds (see § sec:second.member.alternation and § sec:class.prefixes ).

Conversion of counted nouns (§ sec:counted.nouns ) to inalienably possessed nouns is a regular process (§ sec:CN.IPN ).
summary: In Japhug, derivation from alienably possessed nouns to inalienably possessed nouns is uncommon, with ɯ-ʁle ‘reputation’ given as an example derived from the alienably possessed qale ‘wind,’ using the reduced ʁ- form of the class prefix qa- as seen in some compounds. By contrast, conversion from counted nouns to inalienably possessed nouns is described as a regular process.

text:
body part
The great majority of body parts are inalienably possessed nouns with the indefinite possessor tɯ-. These include native words, but also borrowings from Tibetan such as tɯ-qʰoχpaorgans, state of mind from Tibetan ཁོག་པ་kʰog.painnards (see § sec:uvular.harmony on the phonology of this word).

Among body parts, inalienably possessed nouns selecting the prefix tɤ- are mainly liquids from the body such as tɤ-seblood, tɤ-spɯpus and tɤ-lumilk (though some liquids also take the prefix tɯ, for instance tɯ-ɕtʂisweat), hair ( tɤ-rmehair, tɤ-kɤrmehead hair and some animal body parts ( tɤ-jmetail, tɤ-ŋkɯpig skin, tɤ-rkʰomfeather rachis).

Parts of plants on the other hand mainly have the prefix tɤ, as tɤ-jwaʁleaf, tɤ-tsrɯsprout, tɤ-zrɤmroot etc.

Alienably possessed nouns are rare among body parts. Some nouns with the qa- class prefix (see § sec:class.prefixes ) such as qamemole and qambɣoearwax referring to physical defects or excretions from the body are alienably possessed nouns. A similar situation is observed in Koyukon Athabaskan, where nouns `denoting certain temporary or abnormal parts of the body' are also alienably possessed noun, though in Koyukon this subclass is considerably larger than in Japhug.

The compound tɯcisteamniotic sac from tɯ-ciwater and tɤ-stebladder has a tɯ- which is originally an indefinite possessor prefix (see § sec:earth.IPN ), but which has become frozen after being integrated into a compound (§ sec:frozen.indef ), as can be shown by ( ex:WtWciste ).

exe

ɯ-tɯciste cʰɤ-ndʑɣaʁ \\
3sg. poss -amniotic.sac ifr - acaus:squeeze.out \\
`Her waters have broken.' (elicited)
exe
summary: Most body-part nouns are inalienably possessed with the indefinite possessor prefix tɯ-, including many native terms and some Tibetan borrowings. Nouns with tɤ- are mainly body liquids, hair, and some animal parts, while plant parts also mostly take tɤ-; alienably possessed body-part nouns are rare and tend to denote defects or excretions. The compound tɯciste ‘amniotic sac’ contains a frozen historical tɯ- prefix that no longer functions as a regular indefinite possessor.

text:
kinship
The great majority of kinship terms select the indefinite possessor prefix tɤ- or ta- (see chapter chap:kinship for a description of the kinship system). The only kinship terms in tɯ- are tɯ-medaughter (but this form is not attested in the text corpus) and tɯlɤtsecond sibling; however, the tɯ- prefix in the latter word has become non-analyzable and this word has become an unpossessible noun (see § sec:unpossessible.nouns ).

There are other unpossessible nouns among kinship terms, including woɬaʁ(bad) stepmother, which derives from tɤ-ɬaʁmother's sister by replacing the possessive prefix with an unidentified element wo, and the social relation collectives (§ sec:social.collective ). Being a unpossessible noun, woɬaʁ(bad) stepmother cannot take possessive prefixes, and the forms of tɤ-ɬaʁmother's sister are used instead ( a-ɬaʁ can mean `my (bad) stepmother').

Kinship terms do not commonly occur with the indefinite possessor prefix. For those denoting spouses, forms with the indefinite prefix are found in the expression `look for a wife/husband', as in ( ex:tArZaB.WkWCar ).

exe

`ŋoj tɯ-ɕe?' to-ti, `aʑo tɤ-rʑaβ ɯ-kɯ-ɕar ɕe-a' to-ti. tɕe `ndʑiʑo ŋoj tɯ-ɕe-ndʑi?' to-ti ri, `tɕiʑo tɤ-nmaʁ ɯ-kɯ-ɕar ɕe-tɕi' to-ti. \\
where 2-go: fact ifr -say 1sg indef. poss -wife 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -search go: fact - 1sg ifr -say lnk 2du where 2-go: fact - du ifr -say lnk 1du indef. poss -husband 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -search go: fact - 1du ifr -say \\
`She said: `Where are you going?'; He said: `I am looking for a wife. Where are you going?'; She said `We are looking for a husband.'' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

Kinship terms The glosses used to described kinship terms are explained in chapter chap:kinship (Table tab:kinship.abb ). also occur with the indefinite possessor prefix to talk about family relationships in abstract terms, as in ( ex:tArpW.tAftsa ) (see also ex:tArpW below). Note that in this example the verb is in the generic transitive subject form (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ). The kinship terms in this sentence cannot take the generic possessor prefix tɯ, since only one argument in a given sentence can be generic (§ sec:genr.3pl ). If the generic possessor forms ( tɯ-rpɯ `one's maternal uncle' and tɯ-ftsa `one's sister's child') were used instead, the meaning would be different (`One's uncle cannot marry one's nephew'), as it would include the speaker as a potential possessor.

exe

tɤ-rpɯ cʰo tɤ-ftsa ni ci kú-wɣ-pa mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
indef. poss -MB comit indef. poss -ZC du one ipfv - inv -make neg - inf: stat -be.possible sens -be \\
`Maternal uncles and sister's children cannot marry each other.' (140427 kWmdza stWnmW)
0003844#S14
exe

Some kinship terms have an extended meaning when they take the indefinite possessor prefix: they can alternatively be used to denote a class of humans based on gender and age. The noun tɤ-tɕɯson also commonly means `boy' or even `male human' (regardless of age). The nouns tɤ-wafather and tɤ-mumother can denote older people without reference to their children; translations such as `old man' and `old lady' are more appropriate in these cases, for instance in ( ex:tAmu.ci ). The same applies to tɤ-wɯgrandfather and tɤ-wigrandmother.

exe

praʁkʰaŋ zɯ tɤ-mu ci ɯ-ku tɤ-kɯ-wɣrum ci zɯŋzɯŋ pjɤ-rɤʑi tɕe, \\
cave loc indef. poss -mother indef 3sg. poss -head aor - sbj: pcp -be.white indef idph (II):white ifr. ipfv -stay lnk \\
`In the cave, there was an old woman whose hair was completely white.' (2003 sras)
exe
summary:
Most kinship terms take the indefinite possessor prefix tɤ- or ta-, though a few occur with tɯ-; in tɯlɤt ‘second sibling,’ the prefix has become non-analyzable and the noun is now unpossessible. Other unpossessible kinship-related nouns include woɬaʁ ‘(bad) stepmother’ and social relation collectives, and these cannot take possessive prefixes.

Kinship terms do not usually appear with the indefinite possessor prefix except in special contexts, such as expressions for ‘look for a wife/husband’ or abstract statements about family relations. With tɤ-, some kinship nouns also broaden in meaning to refer to classes of people by gender or age, for example tɤ-tɕɯ ‘son’ can mean ‘boy’ or ‘male human,’ and tɤ-wa, tɤ-mu, tɤ-wɯ

text: Relator nouns are a subset of inalienably possessed nouns which have been grammaticalized as quasi-adpositions and compensate for the relative dearth of postpositions in Japhug (§ ex:postpositions ). Some are used to express basic grammatical relations (such as the dative, § sec:dative ), as well as most locative and temporal relations with noun phrases and subordinate clauses (§ sec:relator.location, § sec:temporal.reference ). A list of relator nouns and a detailed account of their functions is presented in § sec:relator.nouns.
summary: Relator nouns are a type of inalienably possessed noun that have been grammaticalized into quasi-adpositions in Japhug, helping make up for the language’s limited use of postpositions. They express basic grammatical relations such as the dative, along with most locative and temporal relations involving noun phrases and subordinate clauses.

text:
Inalienably possessed nouns can take nominalized or finite clauses as prenominal modifiers. When the head inalienably possessed noun is at the same time an argument or an adjunct inside its modifiying clause, that clause is considered to be a prenominal relative (§ sec:prenominal.relative ). The generic inalienably possessed noun ɯ-spamaterial is in the process of becoming a relativizer when occurring with a prenominal relative (§ sec:Wspa.relative ). In other Gyalrongic languages, such as Khroskyabs, former generic nouns have become fully grammaticalized as relativizers (see § sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle, § sec:Wspa.relative ).

When the head noun is not a participant of the clause, the modifying clause is a complement clause (§ sec:complement.taking.nouns, see ). Inalienably possessed nouns selecting complement clauses include for instance ɯ-skɤtlanguage, noise or ɯ-ʁjizwish (§ sec:complement.taking.noun.list ).

The inalienably possessed noun ɯ-mdoʁcolour (from Tibetan མདོག་mdogcolour) has been further grammaticalized from a complement-taking noun to a sentence-final particle marker of epistemic modality `it looks like...' (§ sec:WmdoR.TAME ).
summary:
Inalienably possessed nouns may be modified by nominalized or finite clauses placed before them; if the noun is also an argument or adjunct within that clause, the construction is analyzed as a prenominal relative clause. The generic noun ɯ-spa ‘material’ is developing into a relativizer in this use, while in related Gyalrongic languages such as Khroskyabs similar former generic nouns are already fully grammaticalized as relativizers.

If the head noun is not a participant in the clause, the clause is a complement clause, as with nouns like ɯ-skɤt ‘language, noise’ and ɯ-ʁjiz ‘wish.’ The noun ɯ-mdoʁ ‘colour’ has advanced further, being grammaticalized from a complement-taking noun into a sentence-final epistemic particle meaning roughly ‘it looks like…’.

text:
noun!property adjective!property noun
Property nouns are a subclass of inalienably possessed nouns that designate (mainly in a derogatory fashion) an entity that possesses a particular characteristic. They generally follow another noun as in ( ex:penzi.WpW ) and ( ex:kha.WNqra ), but not exclusively ( ex:Wxso.tWrme ). In the /noun+property noun/ phrase, the latter is the syntactic head but semantically modifies the former (see § sec:attributes on the various attributes found in the noun phrase).

exe

<penzi> ɯ-pɯ, sɤlaŋpʰɤn ɯ-pɯ jamar ɲɯ-wxti cʰa \\
basin 3sg. poss -little.one basin 3sg. poss -little.one about ipfv -be.big can: fact \\
`It can grow about as big as a little basin.' (18-NGolo)
0003530#S45
exe

exe

kʰa ɯ-ɴqra tɕe znde ɯ-mbe ma tʰam kɯ-tu me. \\
house 3sg. poss -broken.one lnk wall 3sg. poss -old.one apart.from now sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact \\
`Now there is nothing [there], apart from some ruins and old walls. (140522 tshupa)
0004053#S58
exe

These phrases can be turned into compounds made of the first noun and a quasi-suffix corresponding to the property noun. All diminutive and derogatory suffixes described in § sec:diminutive and § sec:derogatory ( tab:property.nouns ) have corresponding property nouns. In the case of sɤlaŋpʰɤn ɯ-pɯ from example ( ex:penzi.WpW ) for instance, it is possible to say sɤlaŋpʰɤn-pɯlittle basin as one word. In some cases the non-final element is in bound state, as in kʰɤɴqraruin from kʰahouse and ɯ-ɴqrabroken one, a form which occurs in ( ex:khANqra ), in the same text as ( ex:kha.WNqra ) (referring to the same house). The opposite however is not always possible; for instance, lexicalized diminutives like staχpɯpea from stoʁbroad bean cannot be turned into a phrase with ɯ-pɯlittle one as second element.

exe

tɕe nɯ tɤtsoʁsta nɯnɯ kʰɤɴqra ɕti tʰam tɕe kɯ-rɤʑi me \\
lnk dem place.name dem ruins be: aff: fact now lnk sbj: pcp -stay not.exist: fact \\
`Now Tatsogsta (`the place of silverweed') is a house in ruins, nobody lives there.' (140522 tshupa)
0004053#S56
exe

Property nouns are not necessarily always contiguous to the noun that they follow. In ( ex:GzW.ci.WpW.ci ), the indefinite determiner ci (§ sec:indef.article ) redundantly occurs both after the constituent ɣzɯ kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi (a relative clause, § ex:attributive.participles.stative.verbs ) and the property noun ɯ-pɯ `the little one'. The nouns ɣzɯ and ɯ-pɯ are thus separated by the participle kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi and the determiner ci.

exe

wo nɯnɯ, ɣzɯ kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ci ɯ-pɯ ci ɲɯ-ɕti \\
interj dem monkey sbj: pcp -emph be.small indef 3sg. poss -little.one indef sens -be. aff \\
`Oh, this is [just] a little monkey.' (18-04-28 xiyouji01-zh)
0006111
exe

The property nouns ɯ-doold one and tɤ-mbeold thing differ in that the former one is used for living things (including animals and plants), while the second occurs with inanimate objects. The quasi-suffix -rqɯ is mainly used in tɯ-cirqɯcold water.

The noun ɯ-jluuncooked (used in particular with stoʁbroad bean) has become grammaticalized as a restrictive focus marker (§ sec:restrictive.focus ).

Property nouns are not commonly used with an indefinite possessor prefix; in attested examples, it is always tɤ-. Their origins are diverse: ɯ-pɯlittle one derives from tɤ-pɯoffspring, young (see § sec:diminutive ), while tɤ-mbeold thing, ɯ-kʰesomething nasty and ɯ-doold one originate from mbebe old, kʰebe stupid and dobe old (of plants) by deverbal derivation (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ). The property noun ɯ-maŋin big groups derives from maŋbe many, itself from Tibetan མང་maŋmany. Some tɤ- prefixed nouns of verbal origin like tɤkʰeidiot, fool (from kʰebe stupid) may come from former property nouns.

The property noun ɯ-xsoempty, normal is related to the verb sobe empty; it originally comes from its subject participle (the regular form kɯ-soempty is still attested) with loss of vowel and fricativization of the velar participle prefix (see § sec:G.nmlz ). It had no corresponding quasi-suffix, but does appear as second element in some compounds (see for instance § sec:collective ).

The most common meaning of ɯ-xso is `normal, usual, common', a meaning already very different from the base verb. It occurs both before and after the noun with which it is linked (compare ex:Wxso.tWrme and ex:tWrme.Wxso ). It is also used adverbially, meaning `usually' or `without doing anything' ( ex:Wxso.kurAZi ).

exe

ɯ-pa ɲɯ-kɯ-ɕe nɯ tɕe kɯmaʁ tɯrme, ɯ-xso tɯrme ra nɯ-tɕʰaʁra pjɤ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -down ipfv: west - sbj: pcp -go dem lnk other people 3sg. poss -normal people pl 3pl. poss -toilet ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The toilet for other people, for normal people (i.e., not lamas), were on the [balcony] facing west under it.' (08-kWqhi) 0003454#S8
exe

exe

nɤʑo tɯrme ɯ-xso tɯ-maʁ \\
2sg people 3sg. poss -normal 2-not.be: fact \\
`You are not a normal human.' (150829 taishan zhi zhu-zh) 0006350#S39
exe

exe

ɯ-xso ku-rɤʑi tɕe, ɯ-βri nɯnɯ scoʁ-pɯ pɯ-kɤ-βʁum ʑo fse \\
3sg. poss -normal ipfv -stay lnk 3sg. poss -body dem ladle- dim aor: down - obj: pcp -cover emph be.like: fact \\
`When [the ladybug] is resting (staying like that, without doing anything), its body looks like a little laddle put upside down.' (26-kWlAGpopo) 0003670#S3
exe

The meaning `empty' is however also attested; in ( ex:nWxso.chAnWlhoRnW ) it is used adverbially, and note that the possessive prefix is coreferent with the plural intransitive subject.

exe

toʁde tɕe tɕendɤre, nɯ-xso cʰɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ-nɯ. \\
a.moment lnk lnk 3pl. poss -empty ifr: downstream - auto -come.out- pl \\
`A moment later, they came out empty-handed.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S34
exe

The obsolete property nouns *ɯ-te `big' is not productive, but traces of it are still attested in some compounds (§ sec:augmentative ).
summary:
Property nouns are a subclass of inalienably possessed nouns that designate an entity characterized by a particular property, often with derogatory or diminutive force. They usually follow the noun they modify, with the property noun as syntactic head but the earlier noun as the semantic target; these phrases can also be lexicalized into compounds, and the order is not always fully fixed.  

The passage also notes several lexical and grammatical developments: some property nouns are restricted by animacy, some have become grammaticalized or obsolete, and others derive historically from verbs or other nouns. In attested data, property nouns are not commonly used with an indefinite possessor other than tɤ-, and some can appear separated from the noun by intervening material.

text:
exclamative
A small class of inalienably possessed nouns in Japhug occur as exclamative verbless nominal predicates (§ sec:non.verbal.predicates ), sometimes with the sentence final particle nɯ (§ sec:fsp.attitude ). This class includes degree nominals (§ sec:degree.monoclausal ), as well as the non-derived tɯ-scawapoor $X$ and tɯ-kʰilucky $X$.

The inalienably possessed noun tɯ-scawapoor $X$ only occurs in the exclamative constructions, as in ( ex:nWscawa ) and ( ex:ascawa ). In example ( ex:nWscawa ), the possessive prefix is coreferent with the entities that experience suffering (the pigs).

exe

tsuku kɯ paʁndza ɲɯ-nɯ-pʰɯt-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu ri, paʁ ra nɯ-scawa ma mɤ-mɯm ma ɯ-tɯ-qiaβ saχaʁ ʑo. \\
some erg hogwash ipfv - auto -pluck- pl sens -be lnk pig pl 3pl. poss -poor lnk neg -be.tasty: fact lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.bitter be.extremely: fact emph \\
`Some people cut [ Sambucus ] as hogwash, poor pigs, it is so bitter.' (12-ndZiNgri)
0003488#S28
exe

The possessive prefix on this noun can also be coreferent not with the person suffering, but rather with another person who caused it, and expresses his apologies in this manner, as in ( ex:ascawa ).

exe

wo a-tɤɕime a-scawa, wo a-tɤɕime a-scawa \\
interj 1sg. poss -lady 1sg. poss -poor interj 1sg. poss -lady 1sg. poss -poor \\
`My lady, sorry [for what] I [have done to you].' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

Alternatively, the indefinite possessive form tɯ-scawa can occur, even if the person/entity experiencing misfortune is definite and known, as in ( ex:tWscawa ).

exe

wo tɯ-scawa, ku-tɯ-tso mɯ-pɯ-ra \\
interj indef. poss -poor ipfv -2-understand neg - pst. ipfv -be.needed \\
`Alas and woe, you should not have known that.' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S142
exe

The inalienably possessed noun tɯ-kʰilucky $X$ is another example of the nominal exclamative construction, as in ( ex:nWkhi.Ge ), with the possessive prefix coreferent with the person experiencing good luck. This noun can also occur in the idiom tɯ-kʰi+ŋgɯbe lucky, as in ( ex:akhi.YWNgW ).

exe

ɕɯ ɣɯ ŋu kɯ, nɯ-kʰi ɣe! \\
who gen be: fact sfp 3pl. poss -how.lucky sfp \\
`Whose are these, how lucky they are!' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

exe

a-kʰi ɲɯ-ŋgɯ \\
1sg. poss -lucky(1) sens -be.lucky(2) \\
`I am lucky.' (140425 shizi puluomixiusi he daxiang-zh) 0003798#S40
exe
summary:
Japhug has a small class of inalienably possessed nouns that are used as exclamative verbless nominal predicates, sometimes with the sentence-final particle *nɯ*. This class includes degree nominals and the non-derived nouns *tɯ-scawa* ‘poor X’ and *tɯ-kʰi* ‘lucky X’.

The noun *tɯ-scawa* occurs only in these exclamative constructions, and its possessive prefix can refer either to the person suffering or to the person responsible, as in an apology. The noun *tɯ-kʰi* ‘lucky X’ is another exclamative noun, with the possessive prefix coreferent with the person experiencing good luck, and it also appears in the idiom *tɯ-kʰi+ŋgɯ* ‘be lucky’.

text:
inalienabilization
It is possible to turn an inalienably possessed noun into an alienably possessed one by adding a definite possessor prefix before the indefinite one; this is the only case of possessive prefix stacking in Japhug. This process is very productive, and better illustrated by minimal pairs; the following examples involve the inalienably possessed nouns tɯ-ciwater, tɤ-lumilk and tɤ-mujfeather.

The noun tɯ-ciwater with a definite possessor ( ɯ-ciits juice/water) refers either to the juice of a plant, or to water in which a plant has been soaked as in ( ex:Wci )

exe

ɯʑo tɯ-ci kɯ-sɤ-ɕke ɯ-ŋgɯ pjɯ́-wɣ-ɣɤ-la, tɕe nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-ci ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu tɯ-mi pjɯ́-wɣ-ɣɤ-la tɕe nɯnɯ, χtɕoŋ nɯ ɲɯ-pʰɤn ɲɯ-ti-nɯ ri, \\
3sg indef. poss -water sbj: pcp - prop -burn 3sg -in ipfv - inv - caus -soak lnk dem gen 3sg. poss -water 3sg -in dem: loc genr. poss -foot ipfv - inv - caus -soak lnk dem, rheumatism dem sens -be.efficient sens -say- pl lnk \\
`One puts it in hot water, and then one puts one's feet in that water, and it is efficient against rheumatism, they say.' (20-sWrna)
0003564#S133
exe

The alienabilized form ɯ-tɯ-ciits water, as in ( ex:WtWci ), is used to talk about water given to an animal to drink, or water absorbed by a plant.

exe

tɕeri ɯ-tɯ-ci wuma ʑo na-ʁzi tɕe, ɯ-tɯ-ci nɯ mɯ-pjɯ-mbrɤt ɲɯ-ra. \\
but 3sg. poss - indef. poss -water really emph trop -be.necessary: fact lnk 3sg. poss - indef. poss -water dem neg - ipfv - acaus:break sens -be.needed \\
`But it needs water a lot, it needs to have water continuously.' (07-Zmbri)
0003438#S10
exe

When a definite possessor is present on the noun tɤ-lumilk in a form such as ɯ-luher milk, that prefix refers to the animal producing the milk, as in ( ex:Wlu ).

exe

tɤ-pi kɯ-wxti nɯ kɯ nɯŋa ɣɯ ɯ-lu nɯ cʰondɤre ɯ-ɕa nɯ to-nɯ-ndo. \\
indef. poss -elder.sibling sbj: pcp -be.big dem erg cow gen 3sg. poss -milk dem comit 3sg. poss -meat dem ifr - auto -take \\
`The elder brother took the cow's milk and meat.' (02-deluge2012)
0003376#S18
exe

The form ɯ-tɤ-luhis/its milk with alienabilization is used on the other hand when indicating the person or animal drinking the milk, as in ( ex:WtAlu ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-tɤ-lu pjɯ́-wɣ-rku tɕe nɯnɯ pjɯ-tsʰi qʰe,\\
lnk 3sg. poss - indef. poss -milk ipfv: down - inv -put.in lnk dem ipfv: down -drink lnk \\ \\
`People pour milk for it (i.e., the cat) to drink, and it drinks it.' (21-lWLU)
0003576#S43
exe

The inalienably possessed noun tɤ-mujfeather takes as its possessor a bird (or a bird body part such as `wings'), as in ( ex:Wmuj ).

exe

jinde tɕe ɯ-kɯ-sat koŋla maŋe tɕe, nɯ qarma ɯ-muj kɯnɤ tɯ-jaʁ mɯ́j-ɣi wo \\
nowadays lnk 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -kill completely not.exist:C lnk dem crossoptilon 3sg. poss -feather also genr. poss -hand neg: sens -come sfp \\
`Nowadays, nobody kills them, and one cannot get crossoptilon feathers.' (23-qapGAmtWmtW)
0003608#S152
exe

Its alienabilized form, such as ɯ-tɤ-mujhis feather in ( ex:WtAmuj ), is used when the feather is detached from the body of the bird, and belongs to a human.

exe

tɤtɕɯpɯ kɯ-xtɕi nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-tɤ-muj nɯ li ɯ-tʰoʁ nɯtɕu pjɤ-nɯ-jɣɤt \\
boy: dim sbj: pcp -be.small dem gen 3sg. poss - indef. poss -feather dem again 3sg. poss -ground dem: loc ifr: down - auto -go.back \\
`The younger boy's feather fell back on the ground again.' (140510 sanpian yumao)
0003947#S65
exe

As the examples above show, alienabilized inalienably possessed nouns occur to refer to disconnected or severed body parts, for instance body parts removed from an animal that are used or owned by a human or another animal on which they do not grow. They are also used for bodily fluids that have left the body, or also clothes that are not worn but held in the hand. Similar phenomena are observed in other Gyalrong languages (see on Tshobdun).

The referent marked by the possessive prefix can be beneficiary as in ( ex:WtAlu ) or possessor as in ( ex:WtAmuj ).
comitative adverb
Alienabilization is also observed with prenominal modifiers (§ sec:possessive.prefixes.prenominal ), in compounding, when the indefinite possessor prefix of an inalienably possessed noun is preserved in the final member of the compound (see § sec:possessive.prefix.second.compounds ), in comitative adverbs derived from inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) and in conversion from inalienably possessed noun to counted noun (§ sec:CN.IPN ). A related phenomenon is also the optional neutralization of possessive prefixes in relative clauses (§ sec:relative.possessor.neutralization ).

A lexicalized way of alienabilizing nouns is by compounding with a generic possessor. For instance, pɣɤmujfeather is an alienably possessed noun built from the bound state of pɣabird with the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-mujfeather. Here the first element of the compound pɣɤ- saturates the inalienable possessor without need to use the prefix tɤ-.
summary: The passage explains that in Japhug an inalienably possessed noun can be turned into an alienably possessed one by adding a definite possessor prefix before the indefinite one, and this is the only case of possessive prefix stacking in the language. This productive process changes interpretation: for nouns like “water,” “milk,” and “feather,” the alienabilized forms refer to things such as water given to animals or absorbed by plants, milk for drinking, and feathers detached from birds and owned by humans. It notes that such forms are used for severed body parts, bodily fluids outside the body, and unworn clothes, and that a related lexicalized strategy is compounding with a generic possessor.

text:
morphology!frozen
Alienably possessed nouns with a disyllabic root whose first element is tɯ- or tɤ, with the exception of loanwords such as tɯrsagrave (from དུར་ས་dur.sagrave), are mainly ancient inalienably possessed nouns whose indefinite possessor prefix tɯ- has become frozen and reanalyzed as part of the root. Comparison with other Gyalrong languages can demonstrate that such reanalysis took place in Japhug.

For instance, the noun tɯrmeperson is alienably possessed in Japhug (as shown by examples such as ex:atWrme ), but in the Situ language the 3 form of tə-rmî `man' is wǝ-rmî, showing that tə- is the indefinite possessor prefix, cognate of Japhug tɯ-.

exe

ci nɯ tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ χawo, nɯnɯ aʑo a-tɯrme nɯ a-pɯ-ŋu ndɤre, nɯ ɯ-tɯ-pe nɯ\\
one dem indef. poss -boy dem interj dem 1sg 1sg. poss -man dem irr - ipfv -be lnk dem 3sg - nmlz: deg -be.good fsp \\
`That boy, if only he could be my man, it would be so nice.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

This shift may be due to the fact that the 3 form is used in Situ in constructions where the non-possessed form is preferred in Japhug, such as in prenominal relatives, and was therefore less prone to lexicalization. The stem -rme of tɯrmeperson is still attested as second element of compounds like tɯ-pɤrmeone year of life (whose first element pɤ- is related to the stem of tɯ-xpaone year, § sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history ).

The noun tɤjmɤɣmushroom is alienably possessed, but the stem jmɤɣ- appears as first element of compounds such as jmɤɣnirussula, suggesting that it was formerly inalienably possessed and occurred without its indefinite possessor prefix in this compound (see § sec:loss.possessive.prefix.compounds ). The status of tɤjmɤɣmushroom as a former inalienably possessed noun is less surprising if one takes into account the likely etymological relationship with Chinese 帽 mawH `hat' (from *mˤuk-s; etymology suggested by L. Sagart; see also the Tibetan cognate རྨོག་rmoghelmet, ). If the noun for `mushroom' in Japhug and other Gyalrongic languages comes from `hat' (cf Breton tog touseg `toad hat' for `mushroom'), it is expected that it would become an inalienably possessed noun (like tɤ-rtehat), and for the indefinite possessor tɤ- to become frozen after the noun ceases to be a term for head covers.
summary: The passage argues that many alienably possessed disyllabic nouns beginning with tɯ- or tɤ are actually ancient inalienably possessed nouns whose indefinite possessor prefix has become frozen and reanalyzed as part of the root. Evidence comes from comparison with other Gyalrong languages, especially Situ, where forms like tə-rmî ‘man’ preserve the possessor prefix more transparently, and from compound forms showing that stems such as -rme and jmɤɣ once occurred without the prefix.

subsubsection: Unusual inalienably possessed nouns in Japhug
text:
While it is crosslinguistic expected that nouns of body parts or kinship terms are inalienably possessed, we also find in Japhug inalienably possessed nouns denoting natural entities such as tɯ-ciwater, tɯ-mɯsky, weather or ɯ-tʰoʁground, a highly unusual fact. There is no grand insight about Gyalrong Weltanschauung to be gained from this observation however; explanations should be sought in the etymology of these words, and solved on an item per item basis.

The noun tɯ-ciwater also means `juice' or `water in which $X$ has been soaked' with a definite possessor, as was seen in § sec:alienabilization. Cognates are found in Core Gyalrong languages, but not in West Gyalrongic (Stau ɣrə and Wobzi Khroskyabs jdə̂, ) or elsewhere in the family, and it is therefore a good candidate for a Core Gyalrong lexical innovation.

Japhug has a transitive verb cipour completely (of grains or liquids), from which a bare action nominal *ɯ-ci `(liquid/grain) that has been poured out' could have been regularly derived (see § sec:bare.action.nominals; similar to ɯ-ndzɯinstruction, advice from ndzɯeducate in example ex:WmW.mbWt below). The meaning `water' would then be trivial narrowing of the meaning of this noun `water poured out', then replacing the older term for `water' still preserved in West Gyalrongic. Bare action nominals being inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ), the form of tɯ-ciwater accounted for by this etymology.

The stative verb acibe wet is then derived, after the semantic narrowing, from the noun tɯ-ciwater by denominal derivation (§ sec:denom.a ) -- despite superficially looking like a passive of cipour completely (of grains or liquids) (§ sec:passive ), it is only indirectly derived from it.

Concerning tɯ-mɯsky, weather, it superficially resembles a noun with non-analyzable tɯ- prefixal element, but the status of this element as an indefinite possessor prefix can be ascertained with rare examples such as ( ex:WmW.mbWt ). In addition, note the compound kɯndzarmɯtype of rain contains the root -mɯ as its last syllable (see a precise definition of this noun and a discussion of its etymology in ex:kWndzarmW, § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ).

exe

ɯ-ndzɯ mɤ-kɯ-sɤŋo ɯ-mɯ mbɯt \\
3sg. poss -instruction neg - nmlz -S/A-listen 3sg. poss -sky acaus:take.off: fact \\
`Those who do not listen to advice from other people do not end well.' (`their sky falls') (elicited)
exe

There is no clear explanation of how this noun come have become inalienably possessed, but I propose here a tentative etymology. Cognates of tɯ-mɯsky, weather are attested elsewhere in the Trans-Himalayan family, but mainly in languages that poorly preserve presyllables (for instance Yongning Na mv̩˥°, ). Yet, in Rawang, among the conservative languages, has a word dvmø̀ `celestial being', with the same vowel correspondence to Japhug -ɯ as sharø `bone' with ɕɤrɯbone. Moreover, the name དམུ་ dmu, attested in Tibetan texts to refer to a type of divinity, is probably related to the Gyalrong etymon for `sky'  and provides additional support for the antiquity of a dental presyllables in this etymon.

If dvmø̀ and དམུ་ dmu are indeed cognate with Japhug tɯ-mɯsky, weather, Another potential cognate could be Rawang muq `sky, thunder', but the final glottal stop transcribed -q is from a former *-k, and this word is better compared to Situ ta-rmōk `thunder'  this noun may originally have been disyllabic, and its first syllable reinterpreted as indefinite possessive; the form ɯ-mɯhis sky in ( ex:WmW.mbWt ) would then be a backformation, an idea compatible with its very marginal character.

The Japhug noun ɯ-tʰoʁground cannot take any possessive prefix other than 3 ɯ, not even the indefinite possessor prefix. It has no known cognates in other Gyalrongic languages, but it is a perfect match for a Tibetan word with the shape tʰog (compare the other borrowed noun tʰoʁthunder from Tibetan ཐོག་tʰogthunder). Two etymologies accounting for the possessive prefix on ɯ-tʰoʁ can be proposed. On the one hand, it could be a bare action nominal (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ) from the transitive verb tʰoʁstamp on. On the other hand, it could alternatively be a borrowing from Tibetan, a hypothesis requiring a four step scenario.

First, Japhug borrowed the Tibetan relator noun ཐོག་ཏུ་tʰog(tu)on as ɯ-tʰoʁ *`on' (not attested), adding a third person possessive prefix like all relator nouns (see § sec:relator.nouns ). This relator noun was in competition with the existing native equivalent ɯ-taʁon, above. It is not surprising in Japhug to have several competing relator nouns for the same functional slot; the same is true of the dative ɯ-ɕki and ɯ-pʰe, see § sec:dative.

Second, it became restricted to the collocation *sɤtɕʰa ɯ-tʰoʁ zɯ `on the ground' (not attested), with the native locative zɯ and the noun of Tibetan origin sɤtɕʰaearth.

Third, the tautological collocation *sɤtɕʰa ɯ-tʰoʁ zɯ `on the ground' was reduced to ɯ-tʰoʁ zɯon the ground (attested).

Fourth, the noun ɯ-tʰoʁground was created by backformation from the locative phrase ɯ-tʰoʁ zɯ `on the ground'. The fact that the locative postposition zɯ is always optional (§ sec:core.locative ) made this step less unlikely. Thus, Japhug possibly attests an example of degrammation (see ) from a relator noun meaning `on' (with or without motion) to a common noun meaning `ground'.

The etymologies discussed above suggest that inalienably possessed nouns referring to natural phenomena in Japhug were created by unrelated pathways.
summary: The passage notes that, unusually, Japhug has inalienably possessed nouns for natural entities such as “water,” “sky/weather,” and “ground,” and argues that this should be explained separately for each word rather than by a general cultural principle. For *tɯ-ci* ‘water,’ an etymology from a bare action nominal related to the verb ‘pour’ is proposed, while *tɯ-mɯ* ‘sky/weather’ may be historically connected to cognates in other languages and possibly reanalyzed from a longer form. For *ɯ-tʰoʁ* ‘ground,’ the author offers two possible origins, including a borrowing from Tibetan and subsequent backformation, concluding that these possessed nouns arose through different historical pathways.

text:
Some inalienably possessed nouns can be used adverbially (§ sec:sentential.adverbs ). In this function, the possessive prefix can be neutralized to indefinite possessor or third singular possessor, as ɯ-stutruth, truly in ( ex:Wstu.Zo ), but in some cases it can also be coreferent with an argument, and different inalienably possessed nouns display different alignment patterns.

exe

koŋla ɯ-stu ʑo a-pɯ-tɯ-rɤ-βzjoz, <zuoye> a-pɯ-tɯ-βze, \\
really 3sg. poss -truth emph irr - pfv -2- antip -study homework irr - pfv -2-do[III] \\
`Study seriously, do your homework.' (conversation 140501)
exe

The prefix of the inalienably possessed noun ɯ-stutruth, truly can be coreferent with the singular or the transitive subject (like the 2sg prefix nɤ- in ex:nAstu.Zo.WYWkWnWrgaa ), but never with the object, thus displaying an accusative alignment.

exe

nɤʑo nɤ-stu ʑo ɯ-ɲɯ-kɯ-nɯ-rga-a nɤ, \\
2sg 2sg. poss -really emph qu - ipfv -2 1- appl -like- 1sg lnk \\
`If you really love me,...' (150907 yingning-zh) 0006264#S136
exe

On the other hand, ɯ-βrait is X's turn to... presents a neutral alignment pattern: the possessive prefix can be coreferent with the intransitive subject, the object (as in ex:nAZo.nABra ), or the transitive subject ( ex:nAZo.nABra.tAndze ).

exe

iɕqʰa nɤ-zda nɯ pɯ-sat-a ŋu tɕe, tʰam tɕe nɤʑo nɤ-βra pjɯ-ta-sat ra \\
just.before 2sg. poss -companion dem aor -kill- 1sg be: fact lnk now lnk 2sg 2sg. poss -turn ipfv -1 2-kill be.needed: fact \\
`I just killed your companion, now it's your turn.' (elicited)
exe

exe

nɤj nɤ-βra tɤ-ndze \\
2sg 2sg. poss -turn imp -eat[III] \\
`It is your turn to eat.' (elicited)
exe

Thus, the alignment pattern of each adverbial inalienably possessed noun must be specified.
summary:
Some inalienably possessed nouns can be used adverbially, with their possessive prefix sometimes neutralized to an indefinite or third-singular possessor. However, different nouns show different alignment patterns: ɯ-stutruth, truly has accusative alignment, since its prefix can refer to the singular or transitive subject but not the object.

By contrast, ɯ-βrait “X’s turn to…” shows a neutral alignment pattern, since its prefix can be coreferent with the intransitive subject, object, or transitive subject. Therefore, the alignment of each adverbial inalienably possessed noun must be specified individually.

text:
noun!biactantial
A few inalienably possessed nouns, such as words designating speech or presents, select more than one argument, and can be considered to be the nominal equivalent of ditransitive verbs (if alienably and inalienably possessed nouns are compared to intransitive and transitive verbs, respectively, § sec:inalienably.possessed.morpho ). Since only one argument however is marked by a possessive prefix on the noun (possessive prefix stacking is not possible except for alienabilization, see § sec:alienabilization ) a choice has to be made as to which of the two arguments, the speaker/giver or the addressee/recipient, is marked on the noun.

The possessive prefix of inalienably possessed noun tɤ-pɤropresent always marks the giver; the recipient of the present (which is optional) receives genitive case.

For instance, in ( ex:apAro ) the genitive pronoun nɤʑɯɣ encodes the recipient, and the 1sg possessive prefix on the noun is coreferent with the subject of the main verb. In ( ex:nApAro ), the recipient is not overt, and the 2sg prefix on the noun is again coreferent with the transitive subject of ɣɯtbring.

exe

nɤʑɯɣ a-pɤro tɕʰi ju-ɣɯt-a ra? \\
2sg: gen 1sg. poss -present what ipfv -bring- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`What present should I bring for you?' (140504 huiguniang-zh)
0003909#S27
exe

exe

nɤʑo dɯxpa pɯ-tɯ-tu ma li nɤ-pɤro jɤ-tɯ-ɣɯt! \\
2sg hardship pst. ipfv -2-exist lnk again 2sg. poss -present aor -2-bring \\
`Thank you, you brought another present [for me].' (elicited)
exe

Other biactantial nouns use possessive prefixes to indicate the recipient rather than the agent. For instance, the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-rkuzparting present (a rare example of -z nominalization suffix in Japhug, see § sec:z.nmlz ) always marks the recipient, as in ( ex:nArkuz ), never the agent -- the form nɤ-rkuz `your parting present' with 2sg possessive prefix can only mean `a parting present for you', not `the parting present you give to me/him'.

exe

kɯki nɤ-rkuz ŋu \\
dem: prox 2sg. poss -parting.present be: fact \\
`This is a parting present for you.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S248
exe

In other cases, the alignment of possessive prefixes on an inalienably possessed noun depends on the particular construction where it appears. For instance, the inalienably possessed noun tɯ-tɕʰainformation, news (about someone) marks the recipient when used with the verbs kʰogive or tuexist, but has neutral alignment in other contexts. In ( ex:atCha.mWnakho ), the indirective verb kʰogive (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) does not index the recipient, whose only mark is the possessive prefix on a-tɕʰa `news for me'. Changing the prefix to the third singular ɯ- to refer to the subject here would be agrammatical (see however § sec:hybrid.intro and § sec:hybrid indirect on hybrid indirect speech).

exe

a-tɕɯ kɯ a-tɕʰa mɯ-na-kʰo. \\
1sg. poss -son erg 1sg. poss -news neg - aor:3 -give \\
`I have not heard from my son.' (`My son did not give me any response.') (elicited)
exe

However, in other constructions, there are no such constraints on the use of possessive prefixes on tɯ-tɕʰainformation, news(about someone): for instance, with the verb ɣɯtbring (§ sec:nouns.speech.complement ) in ( ex:WtCha.pjWGWta ), although the recipient is second person dual, ɯ-tɕʰa takes the 3sg prefix, coreferent with the preceding complement clause (using second person singular nɤ-tɕʰa here would be agrammatical).

exe

`ma-nɯ-tɯ-ɣɤwu-ndʑi tɕe aʑo tu-ɕe-a tɕe atu ɕ-tu-tʰe-a tɕe,
ndʑi-pa ndʑi-ma ni ɯ-ɲɯ-nɯjʁo-ndʑi kɯ' ɯ-tɕʰa pjɯ-ɣɯt-a \\
neg - imp -2-cry- du lnk 1sg ipfv: up -go- 1sg lnk up tral - ipfv -ask[III]- 1sg lnk 2du. poss -father 2du. poss -mother du qu - ipfv -scold- du qu 3sg. poss -information ipfv: down -bring- 1sg \\
`Don't cry, I will go up there, ask whether your parents will scold you and come back to tell you.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

Alignment effects are also found with alienably possessed nouns. For instance, the alienably possessed skɯrmapresent can also optionally take a possessive prefix, which is always coreferent with the recipient, not with the agent, as shown by ( ex:askWrma ), where nɤ-mu ɣɯ ɯ-skɯrma means `a present (sent) to your mother' and a-skɯrma can only mean `a present sent to me' (from a text explaining the meaning difference between skɯrma, tɤ-pɤro and tɤ-rkuz ). Japhug has three words that can be translated as `present': tɤ-pɤro is used for presents one give to the recipient in person, tɤ-rkuz is a parting present one gives before a person leaves a place, and skɯrma is a present given with the help of a third party.

exe

nɤ-mu ɣɯ tʰɯci tu-rke-a tɕe ju-tɯ-tsɯm tɕe nɯnɯ nɤ-mu ɣɯ ɯ-skɯrma ju-sɯ-ɣɯt-a ŋu nɤ-mu kɯ a-tɤ-rke tɕe, a-jɤ-tɯ-ɣɯt tɕe, tɕe nɯnɯ li a-skɯrma jɤ-kɤ-sɯ-ɣɯt ŋu \\
2sg. poss -mother gen something ipfv -put.in[III]- 1sg lnk ipfv -2-take.away lnk dem 2sg. poss -mother gen 3sg. poss -present ipfv - caus -bring- 1sg be: fact 2sg. poss -mother erg irr - pfv -put.in[III] lnk irr - pfv -2-bring lnk lnk dem again 1sg. poss -present aor - obj: pcp - caus -bring be: fact \\
`When I prepare something for your mother and you take it to her, [I can say] `I sent a present to you mother', if your mother prepares something and you bring it [to me], it is `a present sent to me.'' (def-skWrma)
exe

Other inalienably possessed nouns of this type include tɯ-nŋadebt (§ sec:bare.action.nominals, used with the verbs tʂopay, ɬoʁcome out and stiblock), which select as possessor the person owing money (rather than the one to whom one owes money), and ɯ-pʰɯpʰɯalms, whose possessor is the person receiving alms (example ex:nAphWphW.kAGWt, § sec:distributed.action.lexicalized ).
summary:
Some inalienably possessed nouns in Japhug are biactantial, meaning they take more than one argument and can be compared to ditransitive verbs, but only one argument can be indexed by the possessive prefix. Depending on the noun, the prefix may mark either the giver/agent, as with *tɤ-pɤro* ‘present’, or the recipient, as with *tɤ-rkuz* ‘parting present’; for some nouns like *tɯ-tɕʰa* ‘news’, the alignment depends on the construction and verb used.

The passage also notes that similar alignment effects occur with alienably possessed nouns such as *skɯrma* ‘present’, whose possessive prefix always refers to the recipient, not the giver. Other nouns of this type include forms for debt and alms, where the possessor is likewise determined by the semantics of the construction.

text:
The generic possessive prefix tɯ- is formally identical to the indefinite possessor prefix of some inalienably possessed nouns, but must be strictly distinguished from it. Five criteria can be used to determine if a tɯ- prefix is generic, rather than indefinite.

First, generic possessors are coreferent with the generic argument indexed on the verb, by the prefix kɯ- for intransitive subject and object and the inverse prefix wɣɯ- for transitive subject (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ): there can only be one generic argument in a given clause (see also ex:tWZo.kW.tWZo, § sec:genr.pro ).

For instance, in ( ex:genr.tWmtChi ), we know that the tɯ- prefixes in tɯ-mtɕʰi `one's mouth' and tɯ-ɕɣa `one's teeth' are generic and not indefinite possessors because they refer to the same generic human as the transitive subject of the verbs pʰɯttake out, cut and ndzaeat in the previous clause, marked by the inverse prefix (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ).

exe

tɕe ɲɯ́-wɣ-pʰɯt tɕe tú-wɣ-ndza ŋgrɤl ri, wuma ʑo tɯ-mtɕʰi cʰo tɯ-ɕɣa ra ɲɯ-sɯɣ-ɲaʁ ŋu. \\
lnk ipfv - inv -take.out lnk ipfv - inv -eat be.usually.the.case: fact but really emph genr. poss -mouth comit genr. poss -tooth pl ipfv - caus -be.black be: fact \\
`One can pluck it and eat it, but it causes one's mouth and teeth to become black.' (11-qarGW)
0003480#S58
exe

Second, the generic possessor prefix appears on alienably possessed nouns, as in example ( ex:tWlaXtCha ) with tɯ-kʰa `one's house' and tɯ-laχtɕʰa `one's things', the generic forms of kʰahouse and laχtɕʰathing.

exe

tɕe aʁɤndɯndɤt ʑo ku-zo qʰe ɯ-qe ku-lɤt qʰe wuma ʑo tɯ-kʰa cʰo tɯ-laχtɕʰa ra sɯ-ɴqʰi. \\
lnk everywhere emph ipfv -land lnk 3sg. poss -feces ipfv -throw lnk really emph genr. poss -house comit genr. poss -thing pl caus -be.dirty: fact \\
`(Flies) land everywhere, shit and make one's houses and things dirty.' (25 akWzgumba)
0003632#S56
exe

Third, the generic tɯ- occurs on inalienably possessed nouns that normally select the tɤ- indefinite possessor prefix, such as tɯ-rɟit `one's child' and tɯ-rpɯ `one's maternal uncle' in examples ( ex:tWrJit ) and ( ex:tWrpW ), by contrast with the citation forms tɤ-rɟitchild and tɤ-rpɯmother's brother.

exe

nɯ kɯ-fse tɕe tɯʑo tɯ-rɟit kɯnɤ ʑa mɤ-sci tu-ti-nɯ \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.like lnk genr genr. poss -child also early neg - fact:be.born ipfv -say- pl \\
`People say that in this way, one's child will be born late.' (27 qartshaz)
0003702#S109
exe

exe

tɯ-rpɯ ɯ-rɟit ɯ-ɕki tɕe tɕe ``a-rpɯ a-ɬaʁ" tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
genr. poss -MB 3sg. poss -offspring 3sg - dat lnk lnk 1sg. poss -MB 1sg. poss -MZ ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`One has to say `my maternal uncle, my maternal aunt to one's maternal uncle's sons and daughters.' (140425 kWmdza01) 0003785
exe

The use of the generic possessive tɯ-rpɯ `one's maternal uncle' in ( ex:tWrpW ) can be contrasted with the indefinite possessed form with tɤ- in example ( ex:tArpW ).

exe

nɤʑo tɤ-rpɯ ɯ-rɟit a-pɯ-tɯ-ŋu, tɕe tɕe aʑo kɯ `a-rpɯ' tu-ti-a kɯ-ra. \\
2sg indef. poss -uncle 3sg. poss -offspring irr - ipfv -2-be lnk lnk 1sg erg 1sg. poss -uncle ipfv -say- 1sg sbj: pcp -be.needed \\
`If you are the maternal uncle's son, (and I am the nephew) I have to address [you] as `my uncle'.' (140425 kWmdza)
exe

Fourth, in the case of inalienably possessed nouns whose indefinite possessive is tɯ, such as tɯ-mtɕʰimouth, the indefinite and generic forms are homophonous, but are nevertheless distinguishable. In the case of a generic form the generic pronoun tɯʑoone (§ sec:genr.pro ) can always be added as in ( ex:tWZo.tWmtChi ).

exe

tɯʑo sɤz kɯ-mna, kɯ-ɤʑɯχtso ra a-pɯ-ŋu nɤ, tɯʑo tɯ-mtɕʰi maŋtaʁ nɯtɕu ɲɯ-ɬoʁ ŋu. \\
genr comp sbj: pcp -be.better sbj: pcp -be.clean pl irr - ipfv -be lnk genr genr. poss -mouth upper.side dem: pl ipfv -come.out be: fact \\
`If [one gets this disease after using the bowl of] someone who is cleaner than oneself, the [pimple] will appear on one's upper lip.' (25-khArWm)
0003644#S9
exe

Additionally, a generic noun such as tɯrmeperson can occur as possessor of a noun with a generic possessive prefix as in ( ex:tWrme.tWCa ). This usage is similar to that found in other generic constructions.

exe

tɯrme ɣɯ tɯ-ɕa ɯ-mdoʁ tsa asɯ-ndo kɯ-fse \\
people gen genr. poss -flesh 3sg. poss -colour a.little prog -take: fact sbj: pcp -be.like \\
`It has a little the colour of human flesh.' (14-sWNgWJu)
0003506#S91
exe

Fifth, possessed case markers such as the dative ɯ-ɕki (§ sec:dative ) do not have indefinite possessive forms, and therefore if prefixed in tɯ, it will always mark a generic possessor, as in ( ex:tWCki ) -- such forms are often preceded by the generic pronoun tɯʑoone anyway.

exe

ma tɯ-ɕki wuma ʑo ʑɣɤ-sɯ-ɤrmbat tɕe núndʐa kʰe tu-ti-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk genr - dat really emph refl - caus -be.near: fact lnk for.this.reason stupid: fact ipfv -say- pl sens -be \\
`It comes near humans a lot, so people call it `stupid'.' (23-scuz)
0003612#S59
exe
summary: The passage distinguishes the generic possessive prefix **tɯ-** from the homophonous indefinite possessor prefix and gives five criteria for identifying generic uses. Generic **tɯ-** refers to the clause’s generic argument, can appear with alienably and inalienably possessed nouns, can occur where the usual indefinite possessor is **tɤ-**, and is especially clear when it can co-occur with the generic pronoun **tɯʑo** or with nouns/case markers that have no indefinite possessive form.

subsubsection: The generic possessor as a first person marker
text:
prefix!possessive possession!prefix generic possessor
As in the generic verbal forms (§ sec:1.genr, § sec:genr.3pl ), the generic possessive prefixes can be used as an indirect way to express first person singular or plural. In example ( ex:tWrkW.mWjrAZinW ) the generic as first person and the first person are used in two contiguous clauses, both referring to the narrator. On the phrase tɯ-mu tɯ-wa in ( ex:tWrkW.mWjrAZinW ), see § sec:dyads.

exe

tɕe tɯ-mu tɯ-wa ra tɯ-rkɯ mɯ́j-rɤʑi-nɯ tɕe, aʑo a-wi ci pɯ-tu. \\
lnk genr. poss -mother genr. poss -father ra neg: sens -stay- pl lnk 1sg 1sg. poss -grandmother indef pst. ipfv -exist \\
`My parents were not by my side, but I had a grandmother [to take care of me].' (2010-09)
exe
summary: The passage explains that generic possessive prefixes, like generic verbal forms, can indirectly express first person singular or plural. In the example, both generic and explicit first-person forms appear in adjacent clauses referring to the narrator, illustrating this usage.

text:
morphology!Trans-Himalayan comparison
Indefinite and generic possessive dental stop prefixes are found in all Gyalrong languages, but only indirect traces thereof exist in Khroskyabs.

Outside of Gyalrongic, potential cognates of these prefixes include the `relational prefix' tə- in Ao (, as first noticed by ) and some d- or g- prefixes in body parts in Tibetan (see ).
summary: Indefinite and generic possessive dental stop prefixes occur in all Gyalrong languages, but in Khroskyabs they survive only as indirect traces. Outside Gyalrongic, possible cognates include the relational prefix tə- in Ao and some dental prefixes (d- or g-) used with body-part terms in Tibetan.

text:
noun!modifier
When prenominal modifiers occur with inalienably possessed noun, this head noun can either take a 3sg possessive prefix, or undergo alienabilization (§ sec:alienabilization ).

Thus in ( ex:XsAr.tAsno ) we find χsɤr tɤ-sno `golden saddle' with the indefinite possessor prefix tɤ-; χsɤr ɯ-sno with the 3sg possessive prefix is also attested in the same text. Neutralization of possessors of alienably possessed nouns is also attested in relative clauses (§ sec:relative.possessor.neutralization ).

exe

χsɤr tɤ-sno tʰa-nɯ-ta ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
gold indef. poss -saddle aor:3 -put sens -be \\
`He harnessed the golden saddle (on the horse).' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S50
exe

However, when the whole modifier+head noun complex is possessed, the possessor is rarely marked by a possessive prefix on the head noun; rather, the prefix occurs on the leftmost noun of the phrase, as in ( ex:aXsAr.tArte ), where the 1sg prefix a- occurs on the modifier χsɤrgold, and alienabilization of the head noun tɤ-rtehat (compare with the form a-rte `my hat' when no prenominal modifier is present).

exe

a-rte, a-χsɤr tɤ-rte ra kɯnɤ nɤʑɯɣ ɲɯ-kʰam-a jɤɣ \\
1sg. poss -hat 1sg. poss -gold indef. poss -hat pl also 2sg: gen ipfv -give[III]- 1sg be.possible: fact \\
`I will even give you my hat, my golden hat.' (140429 qingwa wangzi-zh)
0003890#S53
exe

When the head noun is an alienably possessed noun, it is not usual either to strand the modifier and the following noun by putting a possessive prefix on the latter. The possessor is normally indicated by a possessive prefix on the leftmost word. For instance in ( ex:nAXsAr.khWtsa ) the 2sg prefix nɤ- occurs on the modifier χsɤrgold.

exe

nɤ-χsɤr kʰɯtsa nɯra ku-kɯ-sɯ-ntɕʰoz-a \\
2sg. poss -gold bowl dem: pl ipfv -2 1- caus -use- 1sg \\
`Let me use your golden bowl.' (140429 qingwa wangzi-zh) 0003890#S132
exe

However, we do find cases with a stranded NP modifier when the possessor on the head noun is first or second person, as in ( ex:XsAr.akWmtChW ), where the prenominal modifier χsɤrgold does appear before the possessive prefix a-. The alternative form a-χsɤr kɯmtɕʰɯ is possible to express the same meaning, and does occur in the same text. This construction, though rarer, is considered to be acceptable by native speakers. Other examples are found with unpossessible modifiers (§ sec:place.names ).

exe

nɯnɯ a-kɯmtɕʰɯ, χsɤr a-kɯmtɕʰɯ nɯnɯ kɤ-ɣɯt a-pɯ-tɯ-cʰa qʰe, \\
dem 1sg. poss -toy gold 1sg. poss -toy dem inf -bring irr - ipfv -2-can lnk \\
`If you can bring my toy, my golden toy back...' (140429 qingwa wangzi-zh)
0003890#S51
exe

Note that unlike the inalienably and alienably possessed noun modifiers discussed above, pronominal prenominal modifiers (§ sec:other.pro ) do not take possessive prefixes that have scope over the head noun. For instance, with the modifier kɯmaʁother, the possessive prefix must appear on the following noun, as second person nɤ- on slamastudent in ( ex:kWmaR.nAslama ).

exe

kɯmaʁ nɤ-slama ci tu-tɯ-ndɤm ju-tɯ-ɣɯt ɯ́-ŋu \\
other 2sg. poss -student indef ipfv -2-take[III] ipfv -2-bring qu -be: fact \\
`So you are bringing other students of yours?' (conversation)
exe
summary: When prenominal modifiers occur with inalienably or alienably possessed nouns, the possessor prefix may appear either on the head noun or, more often, on the leftmost word of the modifier+noun phrase. In alienably possessed nouns, the possessive prefix is normally placed on the leftmost word, though stranded modifier constructions with the prefix on the head noun are possible and acceptable, especially with first- or second-person possessors. Pronominal prenominal modifiers, however, do not take prefixes that scope over the head noun; the possessive prefix instead attaches to the following noun.

text:
noun!unpossessible
In addition to inalienably and alienably possessed nouns seen in the previous sections, Japhug also has a category of unpossessible nouns, which includes names of places and ethnic groups (as in Koyukon Athabaskan, ), colour terms of Tibetan origin and some derived nouns like the `social relation collectives' (§ sec:social.collective ). With the exception of colour terms (§ sec:tibetan.colours ), these nouns can modify other nouns and are one of the three classes of `property words' (corresponding to the adjectives of Standard Average European), alongside adjectival stative verbs (§ sec:parts.speech.introduction ) and property nouns (§ sec:property.nouns ).
summary: Japhug has a third class of nouns, called unpossessible nouns, in addition to inalienably and alienably possessed nouns. This class includes place names, ethnic group names, Tibetan-origin colour terms, and some derived nouns such as social relation collectives; except for colour terms, these nouns can modify other nouns and belong to one of the three classes of property words.

text:
noun!place name
Place names ( mbarkʰomMbarkham, kɤmɲɯKamnyu etc) and names of ethnic groups (such as kɯrɯTibetan or kupaChinese), like personal names, cannot take possessive prefixes when used independently. They can only be used with independent pronouns as in ( ex:jiphe.kAmYW ) or ( ex:iZo.KamnYW ) below.

exe

iʑora ji-pʰe kɤmɲɯ nɯtɕu <xiaoxue> <yinianji> <ernianji> pɯ-ndɯn-a. \\
1pl 1pl. poss - dat topo dem: loc primary.school first.grade second.grade aor -read- 1sg \\
`I studied the first and second grade of primary school at our place in Kamnyu.' (140501 tshering skyid) 0003902#S12
exe

These types of nouns can serve as strictly prenominal modifiers (as in kɯrɯ sɤtɕʰaTibetan areas) and commonly occur as first member of nominal compounds (as in kɯrɯɕɤmɯɣdɯtraditional gun, with ɕɤmɯɣdɯgun as second element, see § sec:determinative.n.n ). Although these nouns are unpossessible by themselves, when used as first members of a compound, or even as prenominal modifiers (on which see § sec:possessive.prefixes.prenominal ), they can take a possessive prefix which has scope over the head noun, as in examples ( ex:jikWrWlAsAr ) and ( ex:jikAmYWskAt ), where the 1pl possessive prefix ji- occurs prefixed on the name kɯrɯTibetan and on the place name kɤmɲɯKamnyu.

exe

nɯtɕu tɕe iʑora ji-kɯrɯ-lɤsɤr ŋu \\
dem: loc lnk 1pl 1pl. poss -Tibetan-new.year be: fact \\
`At that time, it is our Tibetan new year.' (conversation)
exe

exe

nɤʑo ji-kɤmɲɯ-skɤt nɯnɯ <quanshijie> ʑo ju-tɯ-sɯ-ɤzɣɯt ŋu \\
2sg 1pl. poss -pl.n.-language dem whole.world emph ipfv -2- caus -reach be: fact \\
`You are spreading our Kamnyu language to the whole world.' (conversation)
exe

The pair of examples in ( ex:nAkWrWrmi ) and ( ex:faguo.nArmi ) illustrates the different behaviour of unpossessible nouns as first elements of compounds on the one hand, and as noun modifiers on the other. In ( ex:nAkWrWrmi ), kɯrɯ-rmiTibetan name constitutes a single compound noun (from kɯrɯTibetan and tɤ-rminame; the phrase kɯrɯ ɯ-rmi is also possible).

exe

nɤ-kɯrɯ-rmi \\
2sg: poss -Tibetan-name \\
`Your Tibetan name.'

$ $kɯrɯ nɤ-rmi \\
Tibetan 2sg: poss -name \\
exe

The possessive prefix occurs before kɯrɯ. Stranding the modifier as in ( ex:nAkWrWrmi2 ) is considered to be agrammatical by native speakers.

exe

nɤʑɯɣ <faguo> nɤ-rmi \\
2sg: gen France 2sg. poss -name \\
`Your French name.'
exe

In ( ex:faguo.nArmi ) however, the modifier faguo `France, French' (from Chinese) cannot be compounded with tɤ-rminame and cannot take possessive prefixes. This is a rare example where a noun modifier can be stranded from the stem of the head noun by a definite possessor prefix (§ sec:possessive.prefixes.prenominal ).

Place names followed by the plural ra designate the people living in the place ( ex:iZo.KamnYW ), even without -pɯ suffixation (§ ex:gentilic.pW ). Example ( ex:iZo.KamnYW ) also shows that in this usage, it is possible to use a personal pronoun in apposition as in iʑo kɤmɲɯ ra `we Kamnyu people'.

exe

iʑo kɤmɲɯ ra kɯ tɕʰɯχpri tu-ti-j ŋu. rcaqo ra cʰo mɤŋi ra kɯ tɕʰɯχpɯχpri tu-ti-nɯ ŋu \\
1pl topo pl erg salamander ipfv -say- 1pl be: fact topo pl comit topo pl erg salamander ipfv -say- pl be: fact \\
`We Kamnyu people call it tɕʰɯχpri, and people from Rqakyo and Mangi call it tɕʰɯχpɯχpri.' (25-tChWXpri)
0003662#S20
exe

Place names can take some prenominal modifiers such as pʰawhole as in ( ex:pha.RdWrJAt ), but no example of bare place names with prenominal demonstratives have been found.

exe

pʰa ʁdɯrɟɤt nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕe rqaco cʰo katɕa nɯ stu ɣɤndʐo \\
whole topo dem 3sg. poss -inside lnk topo comit topo dem most cold: fact \\
`In the whole of Gdongbrgyad, Rqakyo and Kacha are the coldest.' (140522 RdWrJAt)
0004061#S11
exe

Place names and ethnic names can be used as core arguments, or nominal predicates with a copula, as in ( ex:kupa.Nu ) and ( ex:taRdo.Nu ).

exe

a-wa nɯnɯ kupa ŋu \\
1sg. poss -father dem Chinese be: fact \\
`My father is Chinese.' (140501 tshering skyid) 0003902#S4
exe

exe

tɕe ʁnɯ-tɯpɯ nɯnɯ taʁrdo ŋu \\
lnk two-household dem topo be: fact \\
`These two households are Taqrdo.'
0004053#S20
exe

Like locative relator nouns (§ sec:relator.location ), bare place names can be used without postposition to express motion ( ex:mbarkhOm.thWwGGWta ) or static location ( ex:kAmYW.GJW ), but are also found with locative postpositions, most often ri as in ( ex:tshuBdWn.ri ) but also tɕu or zɯ (as in ex:jiphe.kAmYW above).

exe

a-pi kɯ tɤ́-wɣ-ndo-a tɕe tɕe, mbarkʰom tʰɯ́-wɣ-ɣɯt-a, \\
1sg. poss -elder.sibling erg aor - inv -take- 1sg lnk lnk topo aor: downstream - inv -bring- 1sg \\
`My elder brother brought me to Mbarkham.' (140501 tshering skyid) 0003902#S27
exe

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe kɤmɲɯ ɣɟɯ kɯɕnɯz pjɤ-tu. \\
former.days lnk topo watchtower seven ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`In former times, there were seven watchtowers in Kamnyu.' (140522 GJW)
0004051#S1
exe

exe

tɕe alo tsʰuβdɯn ri pɯ-rɤʑi-j tɕe \\
lnk upstream topo loc pst. ipfv -stay- 1sg lnk \\
`We were living up there in Tshobdun.' (28-kWpAz) 0003714#S164
exe

Toponyms hardly ever occur as transitive subjects with the ergative postposition (§ sec:A.kW ). The only example in the corpus is ( ex:qaprANar.kW ), in the context of a mythological story associated with a cliff called qaprɤŋar in Kamnyu village.

exe

tɕe tɯ-mɯ lɤt tɤkʰa tɕe, qaprɤŋar ɯ-stu ri ɲɯ-kɯ-ru tɕe zdɯm ci tu-nɯ-ɬoʁ ŋu. tʰam kɯnɤ zdɯm tu-nɯ-ɬoʁ ŋu tɕe, nɯ maka qaprɤŋar kɯ zdɯm to-tɕɤt ra tu-ti-nɯ \\
lnk indef. poss -weather release: fact at.the.time lnk placename 3sg. poss -direction loc ipfv: west - genr:S/O-look lnk cloud indef ipfv: up - auto -come.out be: fact now also cloud ipfv: up - auto -come.out be: fact lnk dem at.all placename erg cloud ifr -take.out pl ipfv -say- pl \\
`And when it is about to rain, when one looks towards Qaprangar, a cloud comes out from it. Even now a cloud comes out, and [the elders] say `Qaprangar released a cloud.'' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S317
exe
summary:
Place names and ethnic-group names cannot take possessive prefixes when used independently, but they may appear with independent pronouns. They can function as prenominal modifiers or as the first member of nominal compounds, and in those positions they may bear possessive prefixes whose scope is over the head noun; however, some modifiers cannot be stranded from the compound stem, and such stranding is usually ungrammatical.  

Place names with the plural suffix *ra* can denote the people living there, and place names and ethnic names may also serve as core arguments or nominal predicates. Bare place names can express motion or location, sometimes with locative postpositions, though toponyms rarely appear as ergative transitive subjects.

text:
colour
Colour names of Tibetan origin, such as ldʑaŋkɯgreen from ལྗང་གུ་ldʑaŋ.gugreen, ʁmɤrsmɯɣdark red from དམར་སྨུག་dmar.smugdark red or kʰatoʁvariegated from ཁ་དོག་kʰa.dogcolour, multicolour designate objects or animals with a particular colour. To serve as predicates, they need an existential verb ( ex:khatoR.Zo.tu ), like participles of adjectival stative verbs of colour ( ex:ldZaNkW ).

exe

ɯ-muj nɯra wuma ʑo mpɕɤr, kʰatoʁ ʑo tu. \\
3sg. poss -feather dem: pl really emph be.beautiful variegated emph exist: fact \\
`Its feathers are very beautiful and variegated.' (24-kWmu)
0003618#S64
exe

exe

qambalɯla rcanɯ ɯ-mdoʁ ʑakastaka ʑo kɯ-ŋu tu..... kɯ-qarŋe tu, ldʑaŋkɯ tu, kɯ-ɤrŋi tu, kɯ-ɲaʁ tu. \\
butterfly unexp: deg 3sg. poss -colour each emph sbj: pcp -be exist: fact.... sbj: pcp -be.yellow exist: fact blue/green exist: fact sbj: pcp -be.green exist: fact sbj: pcp -be.black exist: fact \\
`There are butterflies with all kinds of colours, yellow, green, blue/green, black. (26-qambalWla)
0003680#S2
exe

These nouns are only very rarely used as postnominal modifiers (§ ex:attributive.postnominal ); ( ex:tAri.khatoR ) is such an example.

exe

tɤ-ri kʰatoʁ nɯ kɯ tʰɯ-kɤ-sɯ-βzu nɯ snalŋaɕtʰɤβ tu-kɯ-ti \\
indef. poss -thread variegated dem erg aor - obj: pcp - caus -make dem multicolour.lace ipfv - genr -say \\
`[The laces] that are made of multicoloured thread are called snalŋaɕtʰɤβ.' (30-rkAsnom) 0003754#S32
exe

The adjectival stative verbs in arɯ- derived from them (for instance arɯldʑaŋkɯbe green, see § sec:denom.arW ) are as common as the colour nouns, and their participles are generally used as noun modifiers instead of the colour nouns.
summary: Tibetan-origin colour nouns such as *ldʑaŋkɯ* ‘green,’ *ʁmɤrsmɯɣ* ‘dark red,’ and *kʰatoʁ* ‘variegated’ denote objects or animals characterized by a colour, but when used predicatively they require an existential verb. These nouns are only rarely used as postnominal modifiers. In contrast, the corresponding *arɯ-* derived adjectival stative verbs are equally common, and their participles are generally preferred as noun modifiers instead of the colour nouns.

text:
Unpossessible nouns other than proper names and colour terms include nouns occurring as postnominal modifiers like tɯlɤtsecond sibling In tɯlɤtsecond sibling the tɯ- element in this word is originally an indefinite possessor prefix, but has become lexicalized. as in ( ex:tWlAt ), and privative nouns in -lu described in (§ sec:privative ).

exe

nɯ-me tɯlɤt nɯ ɲɤ-mbi-nɯ \\
3pl. poss -daughter second.sibling dem ifr -give- pl \\
`They gave him their second daughter.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

Numerals under 99 are also unable to take possessive prefixes and serve as postnominal modifiers (§ sec:one.to.ten ), and can be considered to be a subclass of unpossible nouns.
summary: Besides proper names and colour terms, unpossessible nouns include certain postnominal modifiers such as *tɯlɤt* ‘second sibling,’ where the *tɯ-* element was originally an indefinite possessor prefix but has become lexicalized, and privative nouns in *-lu*. Numerals under 99 also cannot take possessive prefixes and function as postnominal modifiers, so they may be treated as a subclass of unpossessible nouns.

text:
noun!place name
This section focuses on three topics: the absence of vocative forms, the Tibetan origin of personal names, and their use with pronouns and possessive prefixes.
summary: The passage states that this section addresses three issues concerning personal names: the lack of vocative forms, their Tibetan origin, and how they are used with pronouns and possessive prefixes. It indicates that these are the main topics for discussion in the section.

text:
vocative
Unlike other Gyalrong languages, Japhug does not have specific vocative forms for personal names and kinship terms. In Tshobdun, and reports that personal names in the vocative have stress retraction. The same is found in Khroskyabs. In Situ, inalienably possessed nouns have their possessive prefixes replaced by a- in vocative forms (, ).

In Japhug, due to the almost complete loss of contrastive stress (§ sec:stress ) and the fact that the 1sg possessive prefix has the form a- (§ sec:possessive.paradigm ) unlike in Tshobdun and Situ (where it is ŋa-/ŋə- ), there is no specific vocative form for either personal names or kinship terms.

A prefix a- does occur in the familiar form of personal names (reminding of Lin's linxr93jiarong description of this prefix as a 爱称 `pet name' marker), but not exclusively in vocative use as in example ( ex:kWlAGacAB.nW.kW ) where we see the name acɤβ as transitive subject, familiar form of a Tibetan name with scɤβ as second element (see § sec:names.tibet below).

exe

kɯ-lɤɣ acɤβ nɯ kɯ, ɯ-pʰɯŋgɯ nɯtɕu qapɯtɯm ci na-rku ɲɯ-ŋu, \\

Since similar a- prefixes exist in Tibetan and Chinese, and since personal names are exclusively borrowed from one of these languages (there are no clear remnants of native personal names in Japhug), it is likely that the familiar form of the names was also borrowed.
summary: Japhug lacks special vocative forms for personal names and kinship terms, unlike some other Gyalrong languages. Although an a- prefix appears in familiar forms of personal names, it is not restricted to vocative use, and the author suggests this familiar naming pattern was likely borrowed from Tibetan or Chinese.

text:
Tibetan
Speakers of Japhug generally have Tibetan names ( kɯrɯ ɯ-rmi or kɯrɯ-rmi, § sec:place.names ), and in addition a Chinese official name which may or may not be related to the Tibetan one (see ex:nAkWrWrmi § sec:place.names on the use of ethnic or countries names as prenominal modifiers with the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-rminame). Buddhist or Bonpo monks are also given religious names (in Japhug χpɯn ɯ-rmi, see ex:XpWn.Wrmi ).

exe

tɕe χpɯn ɯ-rmi nɯ, aʑo a-rmi nɯ stɤnbiɲima tɤ́-wɣ-sɤrmi-a-nɯ. \\
lnk monk 3sg. poss -name dem 1sg 1sg. poss -name dem anthr aor - inv -give.name- 1sg - pl \\
`They gave me the name Bstanpa'i nyima as my monk name.' (160721 XpWN)
0006181#S36
exe

In one traditional story, we find an example of person names based on Japhug words as in ( ex:zrAntCW ), but it looks so strange that the narrator felt it necessary to specify that these are people's names.

exe

zrɤntɕɯ tɯrme ci pjɤ-tu, tɯpɕi kɯ-rmi ci pjɤ-tu, tɯrme nɯ-rmi ɲɯ-ŋu nɤ \\
mung.bean person indef ifr. ipfv -exist flax sbj: pcp -call indef ifr. ipfv -exist people 3pl. poss -name sens -be sfp \\
`There was [a lady] was was called `Mung bean', and [another one] called `Flax', these are names of people.' (zrAntCW)
exe

Names used by Japhug speakers are not markedly different from those found in other Tibetan areas. Lady names often include the suffixes ltɕɤm, rcit or mtsʰu, (from ལྕམ་ltɕamlady, sister, སྐྱིད་skʲidhappy and མཚོ་mtsʰolake), and there are also non-gender specific suffixes like scɤβ (from སྐྱབས་skʲabsprotector, for instance tsʰɯraŋ scɤβ from ཚེ་རིང་སྐྱབས་tsʰe.riŋ.skʲabsp.n.).).

Many Tibetan names have alternative readings reflecting different reading traditions belonging to more than two layers (see § sec:historical.phono and on the layers of Tibetan borrowings in Japhug). For instance, some people with the Tibetan name འཕྲིན་ལས་ⁿpʰrin.lasKarma are called mpʰrɯlɤz (with preservation of the coda), other mpʰrɯli (with Amdo-type change to -i ). The names however tend to have non-Amdo phonological features even for people of the younger generation. For instance, the name ཀུན་དགའ་kun.dgaÂnanda is pronounced kɯnga without assimilation of the dental nasal to a velar nasal, and ཀུན་བཟང་kun.bzaŋSarvabhadra is kɯnɯβzaŋ with an anaptyctic vowel (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ).
summary: Japhug speakers typically have Tibetan names, along with a Chinese official name that may or may not be related, and Buddhist or Bonpo monks receive additional religious names. Japhug naming is broadly similar to other Tibetan areas, with common feminine suffixes such as ltɕɤm, rcit, and mtsʰu, as well as non-gender-specific suffixes like scɤβ. Many Tibetan names have multiple readings from different historical traditions, and Japhug pronunciations often preserve non-Amdo phonological features even among younger speakers.

text:
Personal names superficially look like unpossessible nouns, as they do not usually occur with possessive prefixes, even when taking placenames as modifiers, as in taʁrdo χpɤltɕin ` Dpalcan from Taqrdo' (see ex:taRrdo.dpalcan in § sec:personal.names.modifiers )

Personal names commonly occur preceded by kinship terms which, being inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:kinship ), have a possessive prefix as in ( ex:anmaR.dpalcan ).

exe

a-nmaʁ χpɤltɕin \\
1sg. poss -husband anthr \\
`My husband Dpalcan.' (heard in context)
exe

It is considered impolite to address someone from an older generation than oneself without adding a kinship term -- for instance, the author of this grammar, being much younger, has to address the aforementioned Dpalcan as a-βɣo χpɤltɕin with the 1sg form of tɤ-βɣofather's brother.

Although personal names rarely occur with possessive prefixes, there is no grammatical constraint against it. There is one such example in the whole corpus, in a conversation where a clarification was needed. Tshendzin asks about Dpalcan, younger brother of Tshering Sgrolma, but she does not understand at once, because Tshendzin 's husband is also called Dpalcan; thus Tshendzin says ( ex:nWχpAltCin ) with the possessed form nɯ-χpɤltɕin `your$_pl$ Dpalcan ' to disambiguate between the two.

\\

Given the existence of such forms, personal names are treated as a subclass of alienably possessed nouns rather than as unpossessible nouns. Only plural forms ( ji-χpɤltɕin `our Dpalcan ', ʑara nɯ-χpɤltɕin `their Dpalcan ' etc) are attested.
summary: Personal names usually appear without possessive prefixes, but they can occur with kinship terms, which are obligatorily possessed, and speakers often use such kinship terms as a polite way to address older people. Although possessive marking on personal names is rare, it is grammatically possible and attested in a clarifying context, so the grammar treats personal names as a subclass of alienably possessed nouns rather than as unpossessible nouns. Only plural possessed forms of personal names are attested.

Proper nouns are more often than not used without demonstratives and determiners (see § sec:non.overt.definite ). However, examples of person or place names taking the postnominal distal determiners nɯ or nɯnɯ (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners ) are not rare ( ex:Yimawodzer.NW and ex:XpAltCin.nWnW ).

To distinguish between persons with the same name (a common occurrence among speakers of Japhug, given the relatively limited inventory of Tibetan names available), house names ( kʰa ɯ-rmi ) are generally added as prenominal modifiers, as in ( ex:taRrdo.dpalcan ).
