summary: Proper nouns in Japhug are usually used without demonstratives or determiners, but person and place names can also take distal demonstratives such as *nɯ* and *nɯnɯ*. Personal names may take dual or plural markers to refer to several people with the same name, and ambiguity is often resolved by adding a house name as a prenominal modifier or, if needed, a locational modifier. Personal names can also serve as heads of non-restrictive relatives, though this is uncommon, and no examples of personal names as heads of head-internal relatives are reported.

text:
bound state
The term bound state refers to the non-autonomous form of (mainly nominal, but also verbal and adverbial) roots occurring as non-final element of compounds. The term status constructus or construct state is also used in Gyalrongic linguistics (,, ) to describe to the same phenomenon, but I decided to follow the advice of a reviewer and to change it to avoid confusion with works such as, or in which `construct form' refers to a specific form that is obligatory on the head noun in specific noun-modifier constructions (including with a possessive marker).

In Gyalrongic languages including Japhug, nominal compounds generally exhibit modifier-head order. Thus, the form undergoing bound state alternation in Japhug is often the modifier noun, In addition, in Japhug the possessed forms of nouns do not show morphological alternations (§ sec:possessive.paradigm ) with the only exception of qalewind (§ sec:apn.to.ipn ). except in Noun-Verb compounds where the second element is an adjectival stative verb.

This section presents the various types of alternations attested for first or other non-final members of compounds, in particular vowel alternation (the most common type). Additionally, exceptional changes to the final members of compounds are discussed in § sec:final.compounds.
summary:
The term **bound state** refers to the non-autonomous form of mainly nominal, but also verbal and adverbial roots when they occur as a non-final element in compounds. In Japhug and related Gyalrongic languages, compounds usually have modifier-head order, so the element showing bound state alternation is often the modifier noun; possessed nouns generally do not alternate morphologically, except for a noted exception, and noun-verb compounds can show alternation on the second element when it is an adjectival stative verb.

The section goes on to describe the different alternations found in non-final members of compounds, especially vowel alternation, and notes that exceptional changes in final compound members are treated separately.

subsection: Vowel alternations in non-final members of compounds
text:
bound state vowel!alternation alternation!vowel
Regular bound state is Japhug applies to open syllables, following the correspondences in tab:sc.regular.

tab:sc.regular shows that vowels other than i shift to ɤ, and i to ɯ.

In a few cases, u can also alternate with ɯ, as in ŋɤtɕɯ- which occurs in the expression ŋɤtɕɯkɤti+kʰɯbe obedient (more details on this form are provided in § sec:interrogative.indef ), the bound state of ŋotɕuwhere.

The vowel i also alternates with ɤ in bound state, as in qaprɤftsacentipede from qaprisnake and tɤ-ftsasister's child or
tɯ-mɤmɲaʁastragalus from tɯ-mifoot, leg and tɯ-mɲaʁeye.

Nouns ending in -ɯ never have a bound state form that is different from the base form, as for instance tɯmɯpaʁslug from tɯ-mɯsky, weather and paʁpig.

Vowel alternation in closed syllables is very rare, and affects only a few stems with o as the main vowel ( tab:sc.irregular ). The bound state ɕɤm- of ɕomiron occurs in a few other nouns, but the form staʁ- (with internal sandhi to staχ, cf. § sec:internal.sandhi.compounds ) from stoʁbroad bean is unique.
summary:
In Japhug, regular bound-state vowel alternation applies to open syllables: vowels other than *i* shift to *ɤ*, while *i* shifts to *ɯ*. There are a few irregular cases, including *u* alternating with *ɯ* and *i* alternating with *ɤ*, but nouns ending in *-ɯ* do not change in bound state.

Vowel alternation in closed syllables is very rare and is limited to a few stems with *o* as the main vowel. The passage notes forms such as *ɕɤm-* from *ɕom* “iron” and the unique bound form *staʁ-* from *stoʁ* “broad bean.”

text: Apart from the regular vowel changes described above, four types of alternations are observed in non-final member of compounds: internal sandhi, coda loss, reduced forms and loss of the possessive prefix.
summary: In non-final members of compounds, four additional alternation types occur besides the regular vowel changes: internal sandhi, coda loss, reduced forms, and loss of the possessive prefix. These alternations affect the form of the non-final compound element.

text:
sandhi!internal assimilation!compound
First, the first element of a cluster undergoes internal sandhi (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters, § sec:sandhi.word ), with voicing and nasal assimilation as in tab:sandhi.compounds.

There are cases of irregular internal sandhi attested only in lexicalized compounds. For instance jaŋntsɤrpaone-handed axe from tɯ-jaʁhand, arm, ɯ-ntsione of a pair and tɯ-rpaaxe, showing a rule ʁ ŋ /_[+nasal] which is not productive in the language (as shown by words such tɯ-jaʁndzufinger, also with tɯ-jaʁhand, arm as first element).
summary: In compounds, the first element undergoes internal sandhi, including voicing and nasal assimilation. Some compounds also show irregular internal sandhi found only in lexicalized forms, such as *jaŋntsɤrpa* ‘one-handed axe’, which reflects a non-productive rule changing /ʁ/ to [ŋ] before a nasal.

text:
Coda loss is not a regular process in first elements of compounds. The following is a list of some of the most representative examples. Further examples can be found in numerals (see § sec:approx.numerals and § sec:numeral.prefixes ).

itemize
Loss of -β:

ɴqiaβdark side of the mountain + zwɤrmugwort ɴqiazwɤr Artemisia sp.
Loss of -t:

xtɯtbe short + rɲɟibe long xtɯrɲɟilength (n)

tsʰɤtgoat + ta-ʁrɯhorn tsʰɤʁrɯgoat horn
Loss of -z:

qartsʰazdeer + tɯ-ndʐiskin qartsʰɤndʐideer hide
Loss of -r:

zwɤrmugwort + wɣrumbe white zwɤɣrum Artemisia sp.

ɕɤrnight + ɯ-χcɤlcenter ɕɤχcɤlmiddle of the night
Loss of -ɣ:

tɤjmɤɣmushroom + --stialone jmɤtɤstispecies of mushroom

tɯ-mtʰɤɣwaist + rŋgɤβattach tɯ-mtʰɤrɴɢɤβwaistline of the trousers (where one can tuck things in)
Loss of -ʁ:

ɕoʁbuckwheat + wɣrumbe white ɕɤɣrumtype of buckwheat

paʁpig + tɤ-qapaw, root pɤqastuffed pig feet
itemize

With the exception of the loss of -t, which is relatively common, the other cases are rare and cannot be predicted by any rule based on phonology (the presence of a cluster in the following element is irrelevant, for instance). Some of them occur with other alternations in the second syllable (cf § sec:second.member.alternation ).
summary: Coda loss in the first element of compounds is not a regular process, though the passage lists representative examples of loss of final consonants such as -β, -t, -z, -r, -ɣ, and -ʁ. Of these, loss of -t is relatively common, while the others are rare and cannot be predicted by any phonological rule, since factors like clusters in the following element do not matter. Some examples also involve additional alternations in the second syllable.

text:
A handful of nouns have reduced bound state forms when occurring as the first member of a compounds.

The noun nɯŋacow corresponds to the syllable ŋɤ- in the compounds ŋɤnɯudder (with tɯ-nɯteat as second element), ŋɤqecow dung (with tɯ-qeshit, dung) and ŋɤlitɕaʁmbɯmdung beetle (on which see § sec:second.member.alternation ), which would be the regular bound state from a stem ŋa-. The apparent `loss' of a nɯ- element is due to the fact that the noun nɯŋacow is itself an ancient compound comprising tɯ-nɯteat as first element (`bovid with udders').

In the case of kʰɯnadog, we find the bound state kʰɯ- in the compounds kʰɯndʐidog skin (with tɯ-ndʐiskin as second element), kʰɯdoold dog (see § sec:derogatory ), kʰɯtsʰoʁhunting with dogs (probably a noun-verb compound with tsʰoʁattach, see also the related incorporating verb in § sec:incorp.denom ) and a few plant names such as kʰɯluEuphorbia helioscopia (a possessive compound meaning `(the plant) having dog milk' -- referring to its toxic juice, see § sec:possessive.n.n ) and kʰɯrtsʰɤzPolygonum sp. (`dog lung'; the second element is tɯ-rtsʰɤzlung). Unlike nɯŋacow, whose reduced bound state corresponds to the second syllable, the syllable kʰɯ- corresponds to the first syllable of kʰɯnadog, which must also be an obscured compound. The etymology of the element -na is unclear.
summary: A few nouns have reduced bound forms when they occur as the first element in compounds. The passage notes that nɯŋacow appears as ŋɤ- in several compounds because it is actually an old compound itself, while kʰɯnadog appears as kʰɯ- in compounds such as words for “skin,” “dog,” and several plant names, suggesting that it too is an obscured compound. The source of the -na element in kʰɯnadog is unknown.

text:
possessive prefixes!loss
Some inalienably possessed or alienabilized nouns lose their possessive prefix (or frozen indefinite possessive tɯ-/tɤ, see § sec:frozen.indef ), as for instance the noun jmɤrtaʁweevil, which comes from tɤ-jmetail and artaʁbe forked (`forked tail'). The verb artaʁbe forked itself is denominal from tɤ-rtaʁbranch (§ sec:denom.a ). Its first element tɤ-jmetail loses the prefix tɤ- and undergoes regular vowel alternation.

Similar examples are particularly common with tɯ-xtsashoe, as mainly parts of the shoes are referred to by alienably possessed noun compounds with xtsɤ- as first element ( xtsɤɕnatip of the shoe, xtsɤrkɯsides of the shoe etc).

In some derivations that originate from compounds, such as the privative (§ sec:privative ) or the derogatory (§ sec:derogatory ), the indefinite possessor prefix is also removed.
summary: Some inalienably possessed or alienabilized nouns can lose their possessive prefix, including the frozen indefinite prefix tɯ-/tɤ, as illustrated by forms such as jmɤrtaʁ “weevil” from tɤ-jmetaʁ “tail” plus artaʁ “be forked.” The passage notes that such loss is common in compounds like tɯ-xtsa “shoe,” especially in references to parts of the shoe, and that some derivations from compounds, such as privative and derogatory forms, also delete the indefinite possessor prefix.

text: Morphological changes affecting the last members of compounds are less common than those on the first members. The only productive morphological alternation in this context is the loss of possessive prefix when the last member is an inalienably possessed noun.
summary: Morphological changes on the last member of compounds are less common than changes on the first member. The only productive alternation in this position is that an inalienably possessed noun loses its possessive prefix when it appears as the final member of a compound.

text:
possessive prefixes!loss
In compounds with an inalienably possessed noun as final element, the indefinite possessor prefix is lost as a rule, as in for example in the plant name kʰɯnajmeSetaria viridis from kʰɯnadog and tɤ-jmetail. The absence of the bound state kʰɯ- is indicative in this case of a later loanword, perhaps calqued from Chinese 狗尾草 gǒuwěicǎo Setaria viridis.

Exceptions are very few. They include compounds whose second element is itself a compound, such as lɤndʐitɤlɤtsʰaʁ Delphinium sp. from lɤndʐighost and tɤlɤtsʰaʁmilk filter; the second element is from tɤ-lumilk in bound state and tsʰaʁsieve. In lɤndʐi-tɤ-lɤ-tsʰaʁ (ghost- indef.poss -milk-sieve), the indefinite possessor prefix tɤ- has become frozen when the compound tɤlɤtsʰaʁmilk filter was formed, and is therefore not subject to deletion.

Another exceptional example is ɯ-qataʁrɯhoof from tɤ-qapaw, root, `root', `bottom' and ta-ʁrɯhorn, perhaps because the second element was perceived as being alienabilized, meaning `the horn-like thing on the foot'; in alienabilized possessive forms, definite possessor prefixes are stacked onto the indefinite possessive instead of replacing it, see § sec:alienabilization ).
summary:
In compounds whose final element is an inalienably possessed noun, the indefinite possessor prefix is usually deleted, as shown by the plant name kʰɯnaj ‘Setaria viridis’ from words meaning ‘dog’ and ‘tail.’ The text notes that the lack of the bound form kʰɯ- suggests this compound may be a later loan, possibly calqued from Chinese.

Only a few exceptions occur. In some cases the second element is itself a compound, so the indefinite possessor prefix has become frozen and is not deleted, and in another example the form may reflect alienabilization, where the possessor prefix is stacked rather than replaced.

text:
consonant!alternation alternation!consonant
Morphophonological alternations affecting last members of compounds are very rare in Japhug.

Internal sandhi influencing the second member of a compound rather than the first occur when a root ending in -ʁ is followed by a cluster with a velar fricative as first element. Thus, the incorporating verb amɲaχtsʰɯmbe petty is the denominal of a lost compound *mɲaχtsʰɯm comprising tɯ-mɲaʁeye as first element and xtsʰɯmbe thin: the combination of -ʁ+xtsʰ- yields -χtsʰ-.

Several cases of alternations in the last member are found with animal nouns with the uvular class prefix qa, which has a variant χ-/ʁ- in this context in some compounds (see § sec:uvular.animal and § sec:uvular.other ).

Other alternations are restricted to specific lexical items, which are discussed below one by one ( rŋgɤβattach, ɣɯrnibe red, tʂuroad and tɯ-ɣliexcrement, dung).

The inalienably possessed noun tɯ-mtʰɤrɴɢɤβwaistline of the trousers (a noun whose meaning is better explained by an example sentence like ex:WmthArNGAB ) is a compound of the noun tɯ-mtʰɤɣwaist with the transitive verb rŋgɤβattach, which appears as a uvularized allomorph -rɴɢɤβ not attested elsewhere: it is unclear why uvularization took place in this word (dissimilation with the coda -ɣ of the previous root is unlikely).

The noun ftɕɤrupath in the middle of the fields is a compound of ftɕarsummer and tʂuroad (such paths are made during summer to allow workers to work in the field without damaging the crops, see a definition in ex:tusANke.Wspa in § sec:instrumental.participle.relatives ). The first element ftɕɤ- is the bound state of ftɕar (with loss of final consonant) and the form -ru for the second member of the compound is a clue that tʂu comes from earlier *t-ro with a dental stop+ r cluster changing to a retroflex affricate (see § sec:Cr.clusters and § sec:teens ) -- the *t- element being prefixal (perhaps a fossilized indefinite possessor prefix).

The noun jmɤɣnirussula clearly derives from tɤjmɤɣmushroom and ɣɯrnibe red, but while the loss of the tɤ- prefix can be explained (see § sec:frozen.indef ), the form of the second element (without r- preinitial) is a mystery. The form -rni (without ɣɯ, a prefix possibly of denominal origin, § sec:denom.intr.GA ) is found in qrornired ant with qroant as first element (a late innovation specific to the Kamnyu dialect).

The compound ŋɤlitɕaʁmbɯmdung beetle, with the irregular bound state ŋɤ- (see § sec:reduced.forms.compounds ) of the noun nɯŋacow, contains a syllable -li clearly derived from the inalienably possessed noun tɯ-ɣliexcrement, dung. The second part of the noun -tɕaʁmbɯm contains aʁmbɯmbe concave.

The examples above show that most of the forms with an irregular second member also present some irregularity in the first member of the compound.
summary: Morphophonological alternations affecting the last member of compounds are very rare in Japhug, though some internal sandhi and a few lexicalized cases do occur. The passage gives examples involving uvularized or otherwise irregular second members in compounds such as *tɯ-mtʰɤrɴɢɤβ*, *ftɕɤru*, *jmɤɣni*, and *ŋɤlitɕaʁmbɯm*, and notes that most compounds with an irregular second member also show irregularity in the first member.

text:
noun!compound
Nominal compounds in Japhug can be build by compounding nouns, but also verbs, adverbs and ideophones. In this section, compounds are first classified by the part of speech of their elements, and then by the semantic relationship between these elements.
summary: Nominal compounds in Japhug can be formed not only from nouns, but also from verbs, adverbs, and ideophones. The section classifies these compounds first by the parts of speech of their elements and then by the semantic relation between the elements.

text:
compound!noun-noun
Noun-Noun compounds can be divided in three classes: Determinative, possessive and coordinative compounds.
summary: Noun-noun compounds are divided into three classes: determinative, possessive, and coordinative compounds. The passage states this classification without further elaboration.

text:
compound!determinative
In determinative (or endocentric) compounds, the two elements either have a genitival or an attributive relationship. I use this term to encompass both the traditional notions of karmadhāraya- and tatpuruṣa-: since pre-nominal modifiers are not easily distinguishable from possessors, this distinction would not be practical. Modifier-Head order is by far the most common, but Head-Modifier is found in some compounds based on postnominal modifiers.

While genitive phrases are followed by a noun with a third person possessive prefix (§ sec:gen.possession ), in the corresponding compounds the possessive prefix is deleted (except the indefinite possessor prefix in exceptional examples, see § sec:possessive.prefix.second.compounds ).

In this type of compounds, the first element is most commonly in bound state if derived from a word ending in open syllable, both for highly lexicalized compounds qaɕpɤrnoʁwild strawberry (`frog's brain', from qaɕpafrog and tɯ-rnoʁbrain) and more transparent ones ( jlɤndʐihybrid yak hide from jlamale hybrid yak and tɯ-ndʐiskin).

Among determinative compounds, we commonly find nouns denoting locations and places or ethnic names such as kɯrɯTibetan and kupaChinese (as in kupaŋgaChinese-style clothes or kupastaχpɯsoja(with staχpɯpea, on which see § sec:vowel.alternations.compounds ).

Some compounds comprise elements that are themselves compounds. For instance, the first element sɯŋgɯforest in sɯŋgɯrmɤβjalophophorus (with rmɤβjapeacock) and sɯŋgɯpɤjkatype wild squash (with pɤjkasquash)
is a compound from sitree and ɯ-ŋgɯinside, and its original meaning was presumably `among the trees'. The noun sɯŋgɯforest is better translated as `wild' when occurring as prenominal modifier or first member of compounds.

Compounds also exist with specific placenames such as tɕʰitɕɯnChuchen, for instance in tɕʰitɕɯn paχɕipear (with paχɕiapple as second element), a noun which can undergo denominal derivation to nɯtɕʰitɕɯnpaχɕicollect pears (§ sec:denominal.vs.light.verb ), showing that the place name modifier has been integrated. I am indebted to Gong Xun for this observation.

In addition to nouns, participles also occur in determinative compounds. They are found both as first or second element of the compound, and both subject participles in kɯ- (§ sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ) and oblique participles in sɤ- (§ sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle ) are attested.

For instance, the compound tʂɤsɤɴɢɤtcrossroad combines the bound state of tʂuroad and the oblique participle ɯ-sɤ-ɴɢɤtplace where X part ways from nɯɴɢɤtpart ways. This intransitive verb itself is the anticausative of qɤtseparate, with an additional nɯ- prefix, § sec:anticausative.direction. The obsolete noun sɤqrɤcʰaalcohol offered to one's guests, comprises the oblique participle ɯ-sɤ-qru of the verb qrugreet, welcome, receive and the noun cʰaalcohol (see other examples in § sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle ).

Compounds with the participle of a transitive verb as their second element do not necessarily derive from a genitival construction, though they might be superficially similar to compounds of this type. For instance qalekɯtsʰispecies of kite comes from qalewind and the participle ɯ-kɯ-tsʰiblocking (it) (§ sec:subject.participles ) of the transitive verb tsʰiblock; the phrase qale ɯ-kɯ-tsʰi (wind 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -block) `blocking the wind' is more properly a headless participial relative (§ sec:headless.relative, § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ), and is more similar to Object-Verb compounds (§ sec:object.verb.compounds ).

Only a handful of Head-Modifier determinative compounds are attested. Most of these are the lexicalized versions of nouns followed by post-nominal modifiers (§ sec:unpossessible.nouns ). A good example of such compounds is provided by ʑmbrɯkɤluwillow that does not grow high from ʑmbriwillow and the privative form kɤluheadless (§ sec:privative ) of tɯ-kuhead), a name explained in ( ex:kAlu ).

The counted noun tɯ-pɤrmeone year of life attests a different type of Head-Modifier determinative compound. It comes from tɯ-xpaone year and tɯrmeperson (see § sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history on the alternation between -xpa and -pɤ-, and § sec:frozen.indef on the tɯ- prefix in `man'), and originally meant `man's year (of life)'. Despite this meaning, the modifier `man' appears as the second element. Unlike `headless willows' ( ex:kAlu ), in this case the modifier would not be postnominal in the corresponding noun phrase.
summary:
Determinative (endocentric) compounds express either a genitival or attributive relation, and the author uses this term broadly because distinguishing pre-nominal modifiers from possessors is not practical. The most common pattern is Modifier-Head order, with the possessive prefix deleted relative to corresponding genitive phrases, though some compounds show Head-Modifier order from postnominal modifiers.

These compounds often use the first element in bound state and frequently involve nouns for places, ethnic names, or even other compounds; participles may also occur as either element. A few Head-Modifier compounds are attested, typically lexicalized forms of nouns with postnominal modifiers, such as “headless willow” and “man’s year,” where the modifier appears second even though it would not be postnominal in the corresponding noun phrase.

compound!possessive
Possessive (or exocentric) compounds ( bahuvrīhi- ) are uncommon in Japhug, and tend to be synchronically obscure. All known examples appear to have Modifier-Head order, and are plant names.

The name kʰɯluEuphorbia helioscopia combines the reduced bound state of kʰɯnadog (§ sec:reduced.forms.compounds ) with tɤ-lumilk. It presumably means `(having) dog milk', a reference to a whitish toxic liquid that comes from it ( ex:khWlu ).

The compound kɯngɯttɤrtsɤɣLeonurus, from the numeral kɯngɯtnine and the noun tɤ-rtsɤɣstairs, can be analyzed as meaning `(plant having) nine stairs', referring to the nodes on the stalk of this plant. The Numeral-Noun order in this compound is remarkable, since numeral normally follow the noun (see § sec:uses.numerals, § sec:noun.phrases.word.order ) but similar to some quantifiers (§ sec:quantifiers.determiners ). The same Numeral-Noun order is found in the more complex compound kɯngɯttɤrqʰɤɴɢaʁLonicera sp. discussed in § sec.n.v.compounds.
summary: Possessive compounds (bahuvrīhi) are uncommon in Japhug, often synchronically obscure, and all known examples are Modifier-Head compounds used as plant names. The passage gives examples such as *kʰɯlu* ‘Euphorbia helioscopia,’ interpreted as “having dog milk,” and *qaprimdʑu* ‘Cicerbita roborowskii,’ interpreted as “having a snake’s tongue,” both referring to plant features. It also notes *kɯngɯttɤrtsɤɣ* ‘Leonurus,’ analyzed as “(plant having) nine stairs,” with the unusual fact that the numeral precedes the noun.

text:
compound!coordinative
Coordinative compounds are uncommon in Japhug, and are formally indistinguishable from the previous classes. In this type of compounds, both elements are heads.

This class includes the traditional traditional dvandva-, which are semantically intrinsically collectives, for instance cʰɤmtʰɯmfood and drinks from cʰaalcohol and tɤ-mtʰɯmmeat, sŋiɕɤrnight and day from tɯ-sŋione day and ɕɤrnight and χcʰoʁeright and left from χcʰaright and ʁeleft, the latter two being mainly used as adverbs.

An even rarer type of coordinative compound are the appositive compounds, the only clear example of which is kɯrŋukɯɣndʑɯrharvestman, a noun built from two subject participles, from the transitive verbs rŋuparch and ɣndʑɯrgrind. The two elements of the compound refer to the actions supposedly performed by that type of chelicerate (`the parcher-grinder') like the participial form of a bipartite verb (§ sec:bipartite ).

The compound qajɯsmɤnbaleech, from qajɯworm and smɤnbadoctor, is possibly interpretable as an appositive compound `bug acting as a doctor' or `doctor who is a bug', since its meaning is clearly not `doctor treating bugs'.
summary: Coordinative compounds are uncommon in Japhug and are formally indistinguishable from other compound types, but in them both elements function as heads. They include dvandva-like collectives such as “food and drinks,” “night and day,” and “right and left,” as well as a very rare appositive type exemplified by *kɯrŋukɯɣndʑɯr* ‘harvestman,’ formed from two participial verbs. The compound *qajɯsmɤn* ‘leech’ may also be appositive, though its interpretation is uncertain.

text:
compound!verb-verb
There are two types of Verb-Verb nominal compounds in Japhug, action nominals (involving transitive action verbs) and degree nouns (with adjectival stative verbs).
summary: Japhug has two types of verb-verb nominal compounds. These are action nominals formed from transitive action verbs and degree nouns formed from adjectival stative verbs.

text:
noun!action nominal
Action nominals built from two verb roots are not common in Japhug. Some of these action nominals are made from verbs with complementary or near-identical meanings, for instance joʁβzɯrtidying up from joʁraise and βzɯrmove. This noun occurs in a light verb construction as in ( ex:joRBzWr ). The denominal compound verb rɤjoʁβzɯrtidy up has a meaning verb close to this construction (§ sec:denom.compound.verbs ).

exe

joʁβzɯr tɤ-βzu-t-a \\
tidying.up aor -do- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I did some tidying up.' (elicited)
exe

Another type of verb-verb action nominals are made from verbs with opposite meanings, for instance βʁɤnŋowinning and losing from βʁaprevail, win and nŋolose, which is used with existential verbs as in ( ex:BRAnNo.maNEndZi ). A similar compound
fqɐ́-nŋət with identical meaning is found in Tshobdun.

exe

βʁɤnŋo maŋe-ndʑi \\
winning.and.losing not.exist: sens - du \\
`One cannot decide who [of the two of them] is winning and who is losing.'
exe

At an earlier stage, such compound action nominals may have been common, as is suggested by the existence of denominal compound verbs without a corresponding noun, such as raχtɯtsɣedo business (from χtɯbuy and ntsɣesell, § sec:denom.tr.nW on the -n- element).
summary: Action nominals made from two verb roots are uncommon in Japhug, but the passage notes two main types: compounds formed from verbs with complementary or similar meanings, such as “tidying up,” and compounds formed from verbs with opposite meanings, such as “winning and losing.” These nominals are used in constructions with light or existential verbs, and some related denominal compound verbs suggest that such verb-verb nominal compounds may have been more common in an earlier stage of the language.

text:
noun!dimension
The productive way of building degree nouns in Japhug is by adding the prefix tɯ- to an adjectival stative verb (§ sec:degree.nominals ), but an alternative formation involves the compounding of two antonymic verbs or location adverbs, such as jpumxtsʰɯmthickness from jpumbe thick and xtsʰɯmbe thin. All known examples are listed in tab:degree.comp (note that whenever possible, the first member of these compounds is in bound state).

In the case of xtɕɯxtesize, the second element xte is a variant also found in the derived verb mɯxtebe the majority, probably the relic of a former *i/e alternation still observed in the verb ɣicome (§ sec:stem2.form ).

Locational adverbs/nouns can also be compounded to express the three spatial dimensions encoded by verbal morphology and locative markers (§ sec:tridimensional.preverb, § sec:locative.adv ): taʁkiup and down from taʁup and akidown, lotʰiupstream and downstream from loupstream and tʰidownstream and kundieast and west from kɯeast and ndiwest. An example of the use of these nouns can be found in ( ex:maNlo.dpalcan ), § sec:personal.names.modifiers above.

Nouns of dimension can further derive denominal verbs in a- meaning `of unequal $X$' (§ sec:denom.a ).
summary: Japhug commonly forms degree nouns with the prefix tɯ- added to adjectival stative verbs, but an alternative pattern compounds two antonymic verbs or location adverbs, such as *jpumxtsʰɯm* ‘thickness’ from ‘thick’ and ‘thin’. Locational adverbs or nouns are also compounded to express spatial dimensions like ‘up and down,’ ‘upstream and downstream,’ and ‘east and west,’ and some dimension nouns can further derive denominal verbs in *a-* meaning ‘of unequal X’.

text:
compound!noun-ideophone
Nominal compounds comprising an ideophone (§ sec:ideo:morpho ) are rare. Three examples are attested.

First, the noun mcirɯβrɯβperson whose saliva drips continuously is built from the inalienably possessed tɯ-mcisaliva (§ ex:body.part.prefix ) and the reduplicated ideophonic root rɯβ, found in the pattern III form (§ sec:ideo.III ) rɯβnɤrɯβ meaning `dripping (drop by drop) continuously' (§ sec:ideo.irregular ) and the deideophonic verb ɣɤrɯβrɯβdrip continuously. The collocation of tɯ-mci with both the ideophone and its derived verb is commonly attested (see example ex:nWrqo.YWmNAm, § sec:sensory.endopathic ).

Second, the bird name jaʁmɤzdoʁzdoʁ contains the bound state form of tɯ-jaʁmuthumb and the pattern II ideophone zdoʁzdoʁ meaning `small and active'.

Third, the name of the mushroom salaboŋboŋpuffball contains the pattern II ideophone boŋboŋ `ovoid'. The first part of this word is obscure.
summary: Nominal compounds containing ideophones are rare, with only three attested examples. These include a noun for a person whose saliva drips continuously, formed from the possessed noun for “saliva” plus a reduplicated ideophone; a bird name combining a bound noun form with an ideophone meaning “small and active”; and a mushroom name containing the ideophone “ovoid,” though its first element is obscure.

compound!adverb-verb
Adverb-Verb compounds are relative marginal. Compounds with kɯzɣaa long time in bound state kɯzɣɤ- followed by a verb are however attested, as kɯzɣɤ-ɕarsearching for a long time from the verb ɕarsearch in ( ex:kWZGACar ). These compounds are studied in more detail in § sec:action.nominal.compounds (see also ).

text:
compound!noun-verb
Noun-Verb compounds include three main types, Subject-Verb, Object-Verb and Adjunct-Verb compounds. Participles or other nominalized verbs forms are treated in sections sec.n.n.compounds, but criteria to distinguish between ambiguous forms in cases of homophony between noun and verb are provided in § sec:object.verb.compounds.
summary: Noun-verb compounds are divided into three main types: Subject-Verb, Object-Verb, and Adjunct-Verb compounds. Participles and other nominalized verb forms are discussed elsewhere, while criteria for distinguishing ambiguous forms where noun and verb forms are homophonous are given in the section on object-verb compounds.

text:
Subject-Verb compounds occur exclusively with intransitive verbs, mainly adjectival stative verbs. The noun is generally in bound state (see tab:subj.v.compounds ). Based on their semantics, three types of subject-verb compounds can be distinguished: attributive, possessive and action nominals.

Attributive Subject-verb compounds are equivalent to a relative clause comprising a stative verb and its subject (§ ex:attributive.participles.stative.verbs, § sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ). If the nominal and verbal elements are represented as $N$ and $V$, an attributive $NV$ compound means `$N$ which is $V$'. They are common with stative verbs of colour such as ɲaʁbe black or wɣrumbe white as in tab:subj.v.compounds.

The compounds in tab:subj.v.compounds are highly lexicalized; in the case for instance of pɣɤɲaʁPucrasia macrolopha, this bird is not even black as the speakers themselves point out ( ex:pGAYaR ).

`The Pucrasia macrolopha is of course also a bird (like the previous ones we talked about), but it is not black, it is beautiful, its feathers are very beautiful and those that are there (visible) are iridescent.' (23-pGAYaR) 0003626#S80

More complex $NV$ compounds of this type are found, such as tɯ-jaʁndzumɤpaχcɤlmiddle finger from tɯ-jaʁndzufinger and mɤpaχcɤlbe in the middle (itself a denominal verb from ɯ-χcɤlcenter).

In such compounds, some stative verbs occur with a -x- element in individual forms. This is the case of tɤlɤxcʰifresh milk from tɤ-lumilk and cʰibe sweet. It is possible that this velar fricative represents the remnant of a participle prefix kɯ-. This -x- is however present in the causative (§ sec:caus.sWG ) and the tropative ( nɤxcʰifind sweet, § sec:tropative.allomorphy ) derivations.

Possessive $NV$ compounds are equivalent to a participial relative with the possessor of the subject as the relativized element (§ sec:possessor.relativization ): In other words, a possessive $NV$ means `(person/animal/entity) whose $N$ is $V$'. Examples are considerably fewer than the previous ones.

tab:compounds.Xa illustrates a few Noun-Verb compounds based on the verb aχalacking a piece, `have a hole', which surfaces as -χa with elision of the a- prefix. It is however alternatively possible that the verb aχa is denominal from an unattested inalienably possessed noun *-χa `hole, chip, notch', and that the compounds in tab:compounds.Xa are also from that lost noun. Among these examples, ɕɣɤχaperson lacking a tooth and rnɤftɕɯχawhose ear has ten holes The compound rnɤftɕɯχa occurs exclusively as postnominal modifier (§ ex:attributive.postnominal ) in the fixed expression qala rnɤftɕɯχa `the rabbit with ten holes in his ear', a trickster character found in traditional stories. are possessive compounds, while tʂɤχachuckhole and tɯ-jaʁmɤχa ( 虎口 hǔkǒuspace between thumb and index are possessive compounds.

A particularly interesting Noun-Verb possessive compound is the plant name kɯngɯttɤrqʰɤɴɢaʁLonicera sp., which comprises three elements: the numeral kɯngɯtnine, the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-rqʰuhull, skin and the intransitive verb ɴɢaʁpeel, shed skin (anticausative of qaʁpeel, see § sec:anticausative.morphology ). This compound is to be parsed [ kɯngɯt-tɤrqʰɤ- ][ ɴɢaʁ ] from a morphological point of view, as its meaning is `(plant) whose nine skins shed off' as is explained in the text excerpt in ( ex:kWngWttArqhANGaR ): the first element kɯngɯt-tɤrqʰɤ- Note that this compound has Numeral-Noun order as in other examples (see § sec:possessive.n.n ). corresponds to the intransitive subject of ɴɢaʁpeel, shed skin.

summary:
Subject-verb compounds occur only with intransitive verbs, especially adjectival stative verbs, and the noun is usually in bound state. On semantic grounds, three types are distinguished: attributive compounds, which mean “N which is V,” possessive compounds, which mean “(person/animal/entity) whose N is V,” and rare action nominals.  

The passage notes that attributive compounds are common with colour statives and often highly lexicalized, while possessive compounds are fewer and can involve more complex morphological analyses. Action nominal compounds are described as rare, with only a few examples such as compounds meaning “bird song” or “harming people.”

Object-Verb nominal compounds in Japhug are very productive, and can be classified into two main types: actor $OV$ compounds, and action $OV$ compounds.

Actor $OV$ compounds are common in names of trades, animals and even plants, such as rŋɯlfɕisilversmith, βɣɤrumiller, zrɯɣndzapraying mantis and tɤtɕɯβraʁburdock. The first of these examples, from the Tibetan loanword rŋɯlsilver and the labile verb fɕiforge, requires little explanation. Some compounds present significant morphological alterations, as βɣɤrumiller, which comes from the bound state of βɣamill and the non-reduplicated form of the verb rɯruguard (§ sec:redp.voice ). In addition, some compounds of this type do not make much sense without some cultural background; as an illustration of how the Japhug corpus can be used to better understand the origin of these compounds, I discuss below the latter two nouns.

The compound zrɯɣndzapraying mantis derives from zrɯɣlouse and ndzaeat, and literally means `louse eater', a descriptive term based on the feeding habits of that insect, as described in ( ex:zrWGndza ).

Like actor $OV$ compounds, action nominal compounds comprise a nominal root and a transitive verbal root. The nominal root in bound state corresponds to the object of the verb, as in the compound cʰɤtsʰialcohol drinking from cʰaalcohol and tsʰidrink. This class of nouns, which occur in light verb constructions and serve as bases for incorporating denominal verbs (§ sec:incorp.denom ), is discussed in § sec:action.nominal.compounds and § sec:compound.action.nominal.Bzu.

Not all compounds whose second element originates from a transitive verb are Object-Verb (or Adjunct-Verb) compounds. Two potentially ambiguous cases must be pointed out.

First, there are Noun-Noun compounds whose second element is a bare action nominal, deriving from a transitive verb (see § sec:bare.action.nominals ), but which loses its possessive prefix as is usual in compounding (§ sec:possessive.prefix.second.compounds ). In such cases the resulting Noun-Noun compound is not formally distinguishable from a Noun-Verb compound, and only the meaning can be used to differentiate between the two classes. For instance, the plant name tʂɤɕpʰɤtplantain has the bound state of tʂuroad as a first element, while its second part -ɕpʰɤt can be interpreted as either directly from the verb ɕpʰɤtpatch (`road patcher') or from the derived noun tɤ-ɕpʰɤtpatch (n) (a piece of fabric used to patch worn clothes) (`road patch'). In this particular case, the second interpretation is more likely, and hence tʂɤɕpʰɤtplantain is better analyzed as a Noun-Noun compound.
summary: Japhug has highly productive object-verb nominal compounds, which fall into two main types: actor OV compounds and action OV compounds. Actor OV compounds often name trades, animals, or plants and can be morphologically altered or culturally opaque, as shown by examples like “praying mantis” meaning “louse eater” and burdock names meaning “attaching boys/girls”; one rare compound even overtly expresses both subject and object. Action nominal compounds also combine a nominal root with a transitive verb, but the nominal element corresponds to the object and these forms are used in light verb constructions and as bases for denominal verbs.

text:
Second, when the second element of a Noun-Verb compound is a a- passive verb (see § sec:passive ), the a-/ɤ- prefix is absorbed by the first element of the compound and becomes invisible. In the resulting form, the second element superficially looks similar to the transitive verb. For instance, the noun ɕnɤstiperson with a stuffy nose appears to derive from tɯ-ɕnanose and the transitive verb stiblock. However, semantics rules out such a derivation: it is a possessive compound whose literal meaning is `whose nose is blocked' (see § sec:subject.verb.compounds ), and cannot be interpreted as `(person) blocking noses', the expected meaning of an Object-Verb compound. Since the passive astibe blocked of stiblock is well-attested, as shown by ( ex:pjAkAstici ), it is better to analyze ɕnɤstiperson with a stuffy nose as a Subject-Verb possessive compound (§ sec:subject.verb.compounds ) derived from that passive form.

The passage explains that when a Noun-Verb compound has an a-passive verb as its second element, the a-/ɤ- prefix is absorbed by the first element and no longer appears overtly. As a result, the compound can superficially resemble one built from a transitive verb, but semantics may show this is not correct.

The example ɕnɤsti ‘person with a stuffy nose’ is not analyzed as ‘(person) blocking noses,’ but as a possessive Subject-Verb compound meaning literally ‘whose nose is blocked.’ This analysis is supported by the well-attested passive form asti ‘be blocked’ of the verb sti ‘block.’

Adjunct-Verb compounds are action nominals (§ sec:action.nominal.compounds ). Like other action nominal compounds, they can undergo denominal derivation to become incorporating verbs (§ sec:incorp.denom ).

Adjunct-Verb compounds typically take body parts or locative nouns as first element, as zgrɯtɕʰɯnudge and kɤtɕʰɯheadbutt, which combine the body parts tɯ-zgrɯelbow and tɯ-kuhead with with the verb tɕʰɯgore, stab as second element. Here the body parts cannot be analyzed as objects: the object of tɕʰɯgore, stab is the person being gored/hit, not the part of the body one uses, as shown by the 1sg indexation on the verb in ( ex:tAwGtChWa ).

exe

mbala kɯ tɤ́-wɣ-tɕʰɯ-a \\
bull erg aor - inv -stab- 1sg \\
`The bull gored me.' (elicited)
exe

These compounds are used with the light verb lɤtrelease as in ( ex:zgrWtChW ). Additional examples are discussed in § sec:action.nominal.compounds and § sec:incorp.denom and § sec:incorp.vs.other.

The incorporating denominal verbs sɯzgrɯtɕʰɯgive a nudge or nɤkɤtɕʰɯgive a headbutt, `gore' are considerably more common that light verb constructions with compound action nouns such as ( ex:zgrWtChW ).

The compound mɲaʁmtsaʁgrasshoper from tɯ-mɲaʁeye and mtsaʁjump is obscure, but unlikely to be a possessive compound `whose eyes jump', and should rather be analyzed as an adjunct compound (maybe `jumping with (big) eyes', as if from a comitative adverb like kɤ́mɲɯmɲaʁwith eyes § sec:comitative.adverb ). If this analysis is correct, mɲaʁmtsaʁ is the only example of actor Adjunct-Verb compound.
summary:
Adjunct-Verb compounds are action nominal compounds that can also undergo denominal derivation to form incorporating verbs. They often begin with body-part or locative nouns, but these are not analyzed as objects; rather, the verb’s object is the affected person, as shown by examples like “gore” and “headbutt,” with such compounds sometimes used in light-verb constructions.

The derived incorporating verbs are more common than the corresponding light-verb constructions. One obscure form, mɲaʁmtsaʁ ‘grasshopper,’ is probably an adjunct compound rather than a possessive compound, and it may be the only example of an actor Adjunct-Verb compound.

text:
compound!verb-noun
Verb-Noun compounds are extremely rare in Japhug, as they are in general in Trans-Himalayan languages other than Chinese.

Adjectival stative verbs nearly always occur as second element in compounds with a noun (§ sec:subject.verb.compounds ), but the opposite order is attested in sɤŋaβdiunpleasant smell from tɤ-dismell and sɤŋaβbe unpleasant (on which see § sec:denom.sA.proprietive ) a noun which can occur with the intransitive verb mnɤmsmell as in ( ex:sANABdi ).

exe

sɤŋaβ-di ʑo ɲɯ-mnɤm \\
be.unpleasant-smell emph sens -smell \\
`There is an unpleasant smell.' (elicited)
exe

A possible example of Verb-Noun compound with a transitive verb is ndzɤpribrown bear, comprising pribear and ndzaeat -- as shown by ( ex:ndzApri ) from a text about bears, it is considered by some native speakers of Japhug as a man eater, though this explanation could be folk-etymology. Note that this compound is also anomalous in that when transitive verbs are used in compounds with a noun, that noun is either an object (§ sec:object.verb.compounds ) or adjunct (§ sec:adjunct.verb.compounds ), never the subject.

We find several examples of nominal compounds whose structure is tɤ- +Verb +Noun, where the verb is an adjectival stative verb. This category includes tɤqiaβjmɤɣLactarius sp., literally `bitter mushroom', from the noun tɤjmɤɣmushroom (see § sec:frozen.indef concerning the lost of tɤ- ) and the verb qiaβbe bitter, or tɤmbextsatype of shoes from tɯ-xtsashoe and mbebe old. These should not be analyzed as Verb-Noun compounds however, as the first element originates from a nominalized form of the verb (either a property noun deriving from a verb (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ) in indefinite possessor tɤ- form (§ sec:property.nouns ) or a tɤ- abstract noun, § sec:tA.abstract.nouns ): they are rather a subtype of Noun-Noun compounds.

The same applies to compounds whose first element comes from a participle, such as kɤrŋijmɤɣtype of mushroom from tɤjmɤɣmushroom with the subject participle kɯ-ɤrŋigreen one kɤrŋi from the verb arŋibe green (see additional examples in § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ). Note that the compounding order is unexpected, as participles of adjectival stative verbs generally follow the noun (§ ex:attributive.participles.stative.verbs ).
summary: Verb-Noun compounds are very rare in Japhug, as in other Trans-Himalayan languages except Chinese. The passage notes a few possible examples, but most apparent cases are better analyzed as Noun-Noun compounds because the verb element is actually nominalized or participial rather than a true verb.

text:
noun!class prefix!class
Noun class prefixes are prefixal elements that occur in some nouns, whose root cannot occur on its own, except for a few rare exceptions (such as qapɣɤmtɯmtɯhoopoe discussed in § sec:uvular.animal ). Uvular qa-/χ-/ʁ- and velar kɯ-/x-/ɣ- prefixes are attested, and occur on animal names, plant names and nouns referring to traditional objects. Additional body part class prefixes, in particular m- are also present in Japhug.

Dental prefixal elements such as tɤ- or tɯ- are very common, but are better interpreted as frozen indefinite possessor prefixes (see § sec:frozen.indef ), rather as noun class prefixes.
summary: Noun class prefixes are prefixal elements found on some nouns whose roots generally cannot stand alone, with only a few rare exceptions. In Japhug, uvular qa-/χ-/ʁ- and velar kɯ-/x-/ɣ- prefixes occur on animal, plant, and traditional-object nouns, and additional body-part class prefixes such as m- are also attested. By contrast, common dental prefixes like tɤ- and tɯ- are analyzed not as noun class prefixes but as frozen indefinite possessor prefixes.

text:
The uvular animal prefix has a basic form qa- ( tab:animal.qa ) and a reduced allomorph χ-/ʁ, attested in a few names like ʁmbroŋwild yak, rtɕʰɯʁjɯcaterpillar and tɕʰɯχprisalamander.

Note that ʁmbroŋwild yak is a borrowing from Tibetan འབྲོང་ⁿbroŋwild yak, a fact that possibly suggests that the χ-/ʁ- prefix has some degree of productivity (see ).

The noun qapɣɤmtɯmtɯhoopoe is clearly a compound containing the bound state of pɣabird and the reduplicated form of the noun ɯ-mtɯcrest, to which the class prefix qa- has been added. The origin of this compound is still transparent to native speakers (see ex:qapGAmtWmtW, § sec:causal.clauses ).

The allomorph qa- is reduced to its non-syllabic variants χ-/ʁ- when the prefixed noun occurs as the second member of a compound. The nouns tɕʰɯχprisalamander and rtɕʰɯʁjɯcaterpillar are examples of this reduction. The former is a compound of tɕʰɯ- (a syllable borrowed from Tibetan ཆུ་tɕʰuwater) and -χpri, a variant of qaprisnake. The latter comprises the syllable rtɕʰɯ, bound state of the unprefixed root of tɯrtɕʰitype of vegetable ( 酸酸菜 ), and the second -ʁjɯ is the reduced variant of qajɯworm.
summary:
The animal prefix has a basic form **qa-** and reduced allomorphs **χ-/ʁ-**, which appear in a few animal names and when the prefixed noun is the second member of a compound. The passage notes that one example, **ʁmbroŋ** ‘wild yak,’ is borrowed from Tibetan, and this may suggest that the reduced prefix is at least somewhat productive.  

It also explains that **qapɣɤmtɯmtɯ** ‘hoopoe’ is transparently analyzable as a compound, with the **qa-** prefix added to a combination of **pɣa** ‘bird’ and a reduplicated form of **ɯ-mtɯ** ‘crest.’

text:
While most nouns beginning in kɯ- are frozen participles (see § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ), there is a residue of forms which cannot be analyzed as deverbal nouns: no corresponding verb root is attested, and moreover some of them have cognates elsewhere in the family. tab:animal.kW presents animal names that are not derivable from any verb root, and appear to bear a kɯ- class prefix, which is to be distinguished from the uvular one. Among these words, kɯrtsɤɣsnow leopard has a Tibetan cognate གཟིག་gzigleopard with a g- preinitial, which is possibly related to the kɯ- prefix in Japhug.

There is a handful of nouns with reduced allomorphs ɣ, x- or even metathesized as βɣ- in some words, corresponding to kə- in Situ (see the phonological discussion in ), including xɕiriweasel, xtɯtwild cat, ɣzɯmonkey, ɣniflying squirrel, βɣɯzbadger and βɣɤzafly. The same allomorphy is observed between the subject participle kɯ- (§ sec:subject.participles ) and the nominalization prefixes x- / ɣ- (§ sec:G.nmlz ).
summary:
Most nouns beginning with kɯ- are frozen participles, but some cannot be derived from verbs because no corresponding verb root is attested, and some have cognates elsewhere in the family. These include animal names that appear to take a kɯ- class prefix, distinct from the uvular prefix, such as kɯrtsɤɣ ‘snow leopard,’ which may be related to Tibetan gzig ‘leopard.’

The passage also notes a small set of nouns with reduced allomorphs ɣ-, x-, or metathesized βɣ-, corresponding to kə- in Situ, as in forms meaning ‘weasel,’ ‘wild cat,’ ‘monkey,’ ‘flying squirrel,’ ‘badger,’ and ‘fly.’ This same alternation is found between the subject participle kɯ- and the nominalization prefixes x- / ɣ-.

text: Some plant names have a uvular class prefix qa, including both cultivated and wild plants (and even plant parts), such as qaɕtipeach, qaɟɤɣioat, qampʰoʁoak leaves, qandzitype of fir, qaʑmbrivine, qawɯzedelweiss and many others.
summary: Some plant names take a uvular class prefix **qa-**, and this applies to both cultivated and wild plants, as well as to some plant parts. Examples include words for peach, oat, oak leaves, fir, vine, and edelweiss.

subsection: Other uses of the uvular class prefix
text:
In addition to animal and plants names, the class prefix qa- appears on some tools ( qajoearthen pot, qaseleather rope, qarɤtrake,
qapiwhite stone), names of periods of the year ( qartsɯwinter, qartsɤβharvest), materials ( qandʑitin, qambɯtsand) or natural forces like qalewind.

The reduced form ʁ- of the class prefix occurs with the noun qalewind in some compounds such as akɯcʰoʁleeast wind and the abstract inalienably possessed noun ɯ-ʁlereputation (and the verbs derived from it, such as raʁlebe polite).
summary: The class prefix **qa-** occurs not only with animal and plant names, but also with some tools, seasons or periods of the year, materials, and natural forces such as “wind.” A reduced form, **ʁ-**, appears in the noun *qalewind* in compounds like “east wind,” and also in the inalienably possessed abstract noun *ɯ-ʁlereputation* and related verbs such as *raʁle* “be polite.”

text:
body part
The identification of class prefixes in body parts mainly rests on comparative evidence. Other Trans-Himalayan languages that preserve clusters such as Tibetan have in some names for body parts cluster that do not match those found in Japhug, for instance མཁྲིས་པ་mkʰris.pabile and སྐེ་skeneck corresponding to the Japhug inalienably possessed nouns tɯ-ɕkrɯtbile and tɯ-mkeneck (see § sec:body.part ), suggesting that body part class prefixes such as ɕ- and m- have been added to these words in Gyalrongic and Tibetan independently.

Apart from the m- and ɕ-/ʑ- class prefixes, some alienably possessed body parts such as qambɣoearwax have a qa- prefix (§ sec:body.part ).
summary: The identification of body-part class prefixes is based mainly on comparative evidence. In some cases, forms in Tibetan and Japhug show different consonant clusters, suggesting that prefixes such as ɕ-/ʑ- and m- were added independently in Gyalrongic and Tibetan. In addition, some alienably possessed body-part nouns, such as the word for ‘earwax,’ have a qa- prefix.

text: Nominal derivations pale compared to the rich verbal (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ) and even ideophonic (§ sec:ideo:morpho ) derivations in Japhug. There is little derivational prefixation in nouns (aside from the collective kɤndʑi- prefix and derivational uses of class prefixes, as seen in § sec:class.prefixes above), and nearly all of the suffixes or quasi-suffixes involved in these derivations are traceable to inalienably possessed nouns that are still attested in the language, and have thus nearly no antiquity.
summary: Nominal derivation in Japhug is relatively limited compared with the language’s rich verbal and ideophonic derivational systems. Aside from the collective prefix kɤndʑi- and some derivational uses of class prefixes, nouns show little prefixation, and most noun suffixes or quasi-suffixes can be traced to still-attested inalienably possessed nouns, indicating that they are not very old.

text:
privative
The suffix -lu can be combined with the bound state form of body part nouns, without possessive prefix, to derive a noun meaning `...less', `without...' that can be used as a modifier (§ sec:unpossessible.nouns ). Examples attested in the corpus are indicated in tab:privative.lu, but this derivation appears to be productive.

These privative forms can modify other nouns, and are placed after the nouns and before determiners such as demonstratives or numerals, as in ( ex:RrWlu ) and ( ex:jmAlu ).

`They gave them a hornless female yak (to take with them back to the husband's home.' (2005-stod)

Privative nouns are systematically glossed in Japhug with possessor participial relatives in kɯ-me `not having' (§ sec:S.possessor.relativization ), as in ( ex:jmAlu ) (see also example ex:kAlu from § sec:determinative.n.n ).

exe

tɕe kɯju jmɤlu nɯnɯ tɯrme ɲɯ-ŋu, ɯ-jme kɯ-me nɯ tɕe, tɕe kɯju jmɤlu nɯnɯ ɲɯ-sɲu ɕti tɕe nɯ nɯ-sɲu tɕe tɕe iɕqʰa tɯ-rɣi cʰɯ-kɯ-χtɤr nɯ nɯ-kɯ-sɲu tu-sɤrmi-nɯ. \\
lnk animal tailless dem man sens -be 3sg. poss -tail sbj: pcp -not.exist dem lnk lnk animal tailless dem ipfv -be.crazy be: aff: fact lnk dem aor -be.crazy lnk lnk the.aforementioned indef. poss -seed ipfv - sbj: pcp -spread dem aor - sbj: pcp -be.crazy ipfv -call- pl \\
`The `tailless animal' is the man, and `he becomes crazy', [when the crow says] that [people] became crazy, it means that they are sowing seeds.' (22-qajdo)
0003596#S46

The noun ʁejluleft-handed is not a privative noun deriving from ʁeleft, but rather a compound comprising the property noun ɯ-jlu (§ sec:property.nouns ) as second element, in its grammaticalized meaning as a restrictive focus marker (§ sec:restrictive.focus ), literally meaning `only (with) left (hand)'.
summary:
The suffix **-lu** can attach to the bound-state form of body-part nouns, without a possessive prefix, to form productive privative nouns meaning “without X” or “X-less,” which can function as modifiers. These privative forms follow the noun they modify and come before determiners such as demonstratives or numerals, and in Japhug they are systematically glossed with possessor participial relatives meaning “not having.”  

The passage also notes that **ʁejlu** ‘left-handed’ is not a privative derivation from ‘left’ but a compound with the property noun **ɯ-jlu** in its grammaticalized restrictive-focus meaning, literally “only (with) left (hand).”

text:
The prefix maŋ- can be used to derive nouns referring to the position of the referent on either the vertical, the riverine or the solar dimensions (§ sec:tridimensional.preverb ), which are encoded in verbal morphology, postpositions, relator nouns and locative adverbs (§ sec:egressive, § sec:relator.nouns.3d, § sec:locative.adv ). These nouns are homophonous with corresponding verbs of relative location (§ sec:verbs.relative.location ).

The nouns of relative location can either occur as postnominal attributes, but can also (less commonly) be used their own as illustrated by ( ex:Cnat.maNthi ).

exe

iɕqʰa nɯ, tʰi nɯ, kɯki ɕnat maŋtʰi ki tɤ-joʁ-a pɯ-ŋu tɕe, tʰam tɕe maŋlo nɯra tú-wɣ-joʁ ra \\
just.before dem downstream de dem. prox heddle downstream.one dem. prox aor -lift- 1sg pst. ipfv -be lnk now lnk upstream.one dem. pl ipfv - inv -lift be.needed: fact \\
`Just before, I had lifted the heddle on the lower (downstream) side [of the loom], now we have to lift the ones on the upper (upstream) side.' (video 20140429090403) 0003776#S68
exe
summary: The prefix **maŋ-** derives nouns that refer to a referent’s position along the **vertical, riverine, or solar dimensions**, and these nouns are homophonous with verbs of relative location. Such nouns can function as **postnominal attributes**, though they may also appear **independently** in some cases.

text:
diminutive
There are four diminutive formations in Japhug, with the quasi-suffixes -pɯ, -tsa, -tɕɯ and -li.

The most productive is the -pɯ suffixation. This transparent suffix comes from the noun tɤ-pɯoffspring, young (from Tibetan བུ་buson). A diminutive formation based on the same noun also exists in Tibetan (, ); whether the diminutive formation was independently innovated, or was borrowed from Tibetan is a question that needs to be further investigated. It is also attested in Situ (, ).

Earlier diminutives are formed with the bound state of the noun, for instance tɕʰemɤpɯlittle girl from tɕʰemegirl, staχpɯpea from stoʁbroad bean, or kʰɯzɤpɯpuppy from a non-attested form *kʰɯza, propably itself the -tsa diminutive of kʰɯnadog, borrowed from a Situ dialect.

More recent diminutives are directly formed with the base form, such as qapripɯlittle serpent. This formation is extremely productive, and applies to plants, animals and even objects as in ( ex:srWnloR ).

exe

tɕe srɯnloʁ-pɯ ci ɲɤ-kʰo tɕe \\
lnk ring- dim indef ifr -give lnk \\
`He handed him a little ring.' (2011-4-smanmi)
exe

The suffix -pɯ is recursive: examples of doubly suffixed nouns are found in the corpus, as in ( ex:lhAndzxipWpW ) for instance.

exe

ɬɤndʐi-pɯ-pɯ nɯra kɯ, ɯ-pʰoŋbu nɯra ko-sɤlɤɣɯ-nɯ ri, \\
demon- dim - dim dem: pl erg 3sg. poss -body dem: pl ifr -link- pl lnk \\
`The little demonlings put back his body together, but...' (150909 xifangping-zh) 0006408#S89
exe

Suffixation with -pɯ is the fused variant of the property noun construction with ɯ-pɯlittle one described in § sec:property.nouns.

A diminutive that is common to all Gyalrongic languages is the suffix -tsa / -za (Situ -tsa or -za, Khroskyabs -ze / -zə / -zɑ, -tsi, Stau -zə ), found in fossilized forms in nouns such as kʰɯtsabowl and βɣɤzafly, The noun βɣɤzafly is cognate to Brag-dbar kəvɐ̂s, Khroskyabs jvɑzɑ́ (, ) and originates from proto-Gyalrong *kpɔs-tsa. but still visible in diminutive forms like paʁtsapiglet (from paʁpig). It originates from the noun `son' that is lost in Japhug but still attested in Situ and Khroskyabs (Wobzi zî `young man').

In Japhug the -tsa diminutive is not very productive; it applies to some nouns that already have a -pɯ diminutive such as stoʁtsaname of plant from stoʁbroad bean (besides staχpɯpea).

The third diminutive suffix -tɕɯ, like the two preceding ones, originates from a noun meaning `offspring', tɤ-tɕɯson, and requires bound state.

It is used for animals ( kumpɣɤtɕɯsparrow from kumpɣafowl) or inanimate objects ( kʰɤtɕɯlittle house from kʰahouse or lʁɤtɕɯlittle gunny bag from lʁagunny bag). It occurs in some lexicalized forms such as mbrɯtɕɯknife. The root of this noun is metathesized from *mbɯr; its cognates have a -tsa diminutive in Situ (Brag-dbar mbərtsiɛ̄, ) and Khroskyabs (Wobzi (bərzé, ).

The suffix -li is the least productive of all diminutive formations, and the only one that cannot be traced to an existing noun. It appears is tɕʰemɤlilittle girl (a synonym of tɕʰemɤpɯlittle girl) and in rgaliyoung cow.
summary: Japhug has four diminutive formations: the productive quasi-suffix **-pɯ**, the less productive **-tsa**, the **-tɕɯ** suffix, and the least productive **-li**. The first three derive historically from nouns meaning ‘offspring/son,’ with **-pɯ** especially productive and able to be recursive, while **-tsa** is common across Gyalrongic languages but limited in Japhug and **-tɕɯ** requires bound state and is used for animals, objects, and some lexicalized forms. The suffix **-li** cannot be traced to an existing noun and appears only in a few forms such as *tɕʰemɤli* ‘little girl’ and *rgali* ‘young cow.’

text:
augmentative
A handful of nouns, some of Tibetan origin, have an augmentative form in -te, originally from a property noun *ɯ-te `big' (related to the verb wxtibe big).

Augmentatives include tɕɣomtecultivated xanthoxylum (from tɕɣomxanthoxylum), tɯjitebig field (from tɯ-jifield, name of several fields in Kamnyu), tɕʰɯtebig river (from ཆུ་tɕʰuwater, river) and the possessive compound ŋguteperson with a big head (with ŋgu- from Tibetan འགོ་ⁿgohead, top; this stem is not attested in Japhug as an independent word).
summary: A small number of nouns, including some of Tibetan origin, form augmentatives with the suffix -te, which originally came from a property noun meaning “big.” This pattern appears in forms such as tɕɣomte ‘cultivated xanthoxylum,’ tɯji-te ‘big field,’ tɕʰɯte ‘big river,’ and the compound ŋgute ‘person with a big head.’

text:
derogatory
There are three derogatory quasi-suffixes in Japhug, deriving designations of old or broken things: -do and -mbe `old X' and -ɴqra `broken X'. These suffixes are the fused variants of the property nouns ɯ-ɴqrabroken one, ɯ-doold one and tɤ-mbeold thing (see § sec:property.nouns ).

The suffixes -do and -mbe, like their corresponding property nouns, differ in that the former occurs with animals and plants ( nɯŋa-doold cow, rɟɤlpu-doold king), while the latter is used for inanimate objects.

In a few cases, the suffixed noun is in bound state (as kʰɤɴqraruin from kʰahouse and -ɴqra, or kʰɯdoold dog (from kʰɯnadog and -do, see § sec:reduced.forms.compounds ). When the suffixed noun is inalienably possessed, addition of a derogatory suffix does not turn it into an alienably possessed noun, as in tɯ-rcɤmbeold jacket from tɯ-rcujacket and -mbe.
summary: Japhug has three derogatory quasi-suffixes used to form terms for old or broken things: -do and -mbe meaning “old X,” and -ɴqra meaning “broken X.” These are fused forms of earlier property nouns, and -do is used with animals and plants while -mbe is used with inanimate objects. In some cases the derived noun appears in bound form, and if the base noun is inalienably possessed, adding a derogatory suffix does not change it into an alienably possessed noun.

text:
gentilic
The gentilic suffix -pɯ derives from the same noun tɤ-pɯoffspring, young from which the diminutive -pɯ ultimately originates (see § sec:diminutive ). It is used to derive nouns referring to inhabitants of a certain place, and occurs without bound state. For instance, from the village names of kɤmɲɯ (the village whose speech is described in this grammar) and snarndi (a village in Tshobdun), one derives kɤmɲɯpɯperson from Kamnyu and snarndipɯperson from Snarndi (see the text 26-tshubdWnpW in the corpus). Given the high productivity of this derivation, these nouns are not indicated in the dictionary, as it would unnecessarily inflate the number of entries.

An alternative way to refer to the inhabitants of a place is by adding the plural ra to it (§ sec:place.names ).
summary: The gentilic suffix -pɯ, historically related to the noun tɤ-pɯ ‘offspring, young’ and ultimately to the diminutive -pɯ, is used productively to form nouns meaning ‘inhabitant of X’ from place names, and it appears without bound state. Examples include kɤmɲɯpɯ ‘person from Kamnyu’ and snarndipɯ ‘person from Snarndi’; because this formation is so productive, such nouns are not listed individually in the dictionary. Another way to refer to inhabitants of a place is by adding the plural ra to the place name.

text:
gender
There is no morphological expression of gender in Japhug. For animals, the nouns pʰumale and mufemale (from Tibetan ཕོ་pʰomale and མོ་mofemale) can be used on their own (as in ex:phu.mu ) or occur as second member of compounds, as kumpɣapʰurooster and kumpɣamuhen from kumpɣafowl, or lɯlɤmufemale cat from lɯlucat, with bound state of the first noun.

exe

tɤkʰe pɣɤtɕɯ ndɤre pʰu mu saχsɤl \\
stupid bird: dim on.the.other.hand male female be.clear: fact \\
`The male and the female of the `stupid bird', as opposed [to the birds previously discussed], are easy to distinguish.' (23-scuz)
0003612#S42
exe

The suffixes -pa and -mɯ (from Tibetan -pa and -mo, respectively) also occur for a handful of nouns, some of Tibetan origin ( srɯnmɯrâkshasî from སྲིན་མོ་srin.morâkshasî) but also some local names such as ɴɢarpamale one quarter yak hybrid vs. ɴɢarmɯfemale one quarter yak hybrid.

The noun paʁɟuboar from paʁpig has a suffix -ɟu that is not found in any other word.

For some farm animals, a lexical distinction is made between male and female animals (see tab:lexical.gender ).
summary: Japhug has no morphological gender marking in general, but the nouns pʰu ‘male’ and mu ‘female’ can be used independently or as the second element in compounds to mark the sex of animals. A few nouns also use the suffixes -pa and -mɯ for gender, including some Tibetan loanwords and local animal names, and one noun, paʁɟu ‘boar,’ has a unique suffix -ɟu. For some farm animals, male and female forms are distinguished lexically rather than by morphology.

text:
collective
While Japhug lacks number inflection, there are several collective derivations: the social relation collective, reduplicated collectives and the dvandva collective.
summary: Japhug does not mark number by inflection, but it does have several collective derivations. These include the social relation collective, reduplicated collectives, and the dvandva collective.

text:
The first type of collective is a noun prefixed in kɤndʑi- and built either from kinship or social relation terms (which can be either inalienably or alienably possessed nouns), designating a group of people linked to one another by a specific relation. There is some doubt about whether this prefix should be transcribed as kɤndʑɯ- or kɤndʑi-. See § sec:W.i.compounds on the question of the contrast between i and ɯ following palatals and alveolo-palatals in non-final syllables.

Two types of social relation collectives should be distinguished: reciprocal and non-reciprocal collectives.

Reciprocal collectives ( tab:reciprocal.collectives ) are derived from nouns designating a relationship in which all members of the group call each other by the same term: these can be non-kinship terms like `companion' or `friend' or kinship terms like tɤ-sqʰajsister (of a female) (§ sec:siblings.gender ).

Non-reciprocal collectives ( tab:non.reciprocal.collectives ) are based on nouns designating unequal relationships, in which the members designate each other by different terms, in particular kinship terms involving relatives from different generations or different gender. Aside from kinship terms, groups comprising farm animals and their owners can also be formed by the same process from the name of the animal, as kɤndʑimbrohorseman and his horse and kɤndʑiftsoʁfemale hybrid yak and its owners (see example ex:kAndZWftsWftsoR below).

Non-reciprocal collectives are either formed from one of the two nouns, which can be either from the lower ( kɤndʑiɣegrandparents and grandchildren) or the higher generation ( kɤndʑiɲipaternal aunt and her nephews), or by a combination of two kinship terms, the first of which, in some cases, undergoes changes to the point of being barely recognizable ( kɤndʑipɤmdɯpaternal uncle and his nephews). In the case of kɤndʑiwɤɬaʁmaternal aunt and her nephews, the origin of the element -wɤ- is not identifiable.

The collective nouns can be used as normal nouns and take flagging, numerals and other modifiers, as in ( ex:kAndZWxtAG.XsWm ).

exe

kɤndʑi-xtɤɣ χsɯm pjɤ-tu-nɯ \\
coll -brother three ifr. ipfv -exist- pl \\
`There were three brothers.' (07-deluge) 0003426#S2
exe

Social relation collectives are also found in Situ and Tshobdun, where they have optional reduplication; in Japhug, partial reduplication (as in § sec:redp.coll ) is used by some speakers, as kɤndʑiftsɯftsoʁfemale hybrid yak and its owners in example ( ex:kAndZWftsWftsoR ), from a story by Kunbzang Mtsho.

exe

kɤndʑi-ftsɯ ftsoʁ χsɯm nɯ, tsʰɯntsʰɯn kɯ-pa kɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
coll -female.yak.hybrid three dem idph (II):in.order inf: stat - aux aor: east - auto -come.out- pl sens -be \\
`[The girl, her husband] and their female hybrid yak crossed [the large river] without damage.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

The lists in Tables tab:reciprocal.collectives and tab:non.reciprocal.collectives comprise most common social relation collectives, but are by no means complete lists. For instance, next to kɤndʑirpɯftsamaternal uncle and his nephews from tɤ-rpɯmother's brother and tɤ-ftsasister's child, the terms kɤndʑirpɯmaternal uncle and his nephews and kɤndʑiftsanephew with his maternal uncles and aunts are also possible though less common. However, some combinations are considered incorrect. For instance, Tshendzin considers that $ $ kɤndʑirʑaβ (from tɤ-rʑaβwife) is only found in children's language ( nɯ tɤ-pɤtso ra kɯ tu-ti-nɯ ŋgrɤl `children talk like that'), as the correct term is ʁzɤmihusband and wife from Tibetan བཟའ་མི་bza.mihusband and wife.

There is in addition an irregular collective kɤtsaparents and children, with the same element -tsa found in some diminutives (see § sec:diminutive ), from an earlier word for `child'.

It can be used without any preceding noun as in ( ex:kAtsa.ra ), but more commonly serves as the modifier of a kinship term, as in ( ex:tAmu.kAtsa ) (note also tɤ-tɕɯ kɤtsa `father and son' and tɕʰeme kɤtsa `mother and daughter' from tɤ-tɕɯson, boy and tɕʰemegirl).

exe

tɕe tɤ-mu nɯ kɯ ɯ-pɯ nɯnɯ ju-ɕpʰɣɤm tɕe, ʑara kɤtsa ra stɯsti ʁɟa ʑo ɕe-nɯ ɲɯ-ra. \\
lnk indef. poss -mother dem erg 3sg. poss -young dem ipfv -flee.with[III] lnk 3pl parents.and.children pl alone completely emph go: fact - pl sens -be.needed \\
`And the mother (i.e. lioness) flees with her cubs, and they (i.e. mother and children) have to go alone (without the father).' (20-sWNgi)
0003562#S71
exe

exe

tɤ-mu kɤtsa ci pjɤ-tu-ndʑi tɕe \\
indef. poss -mother parents.and.children indef ifr. ipfv -exist- du lnk \\
`There was a mother and her son.' (tWJo 2012)
0004089#S4
exe
comitative adverb
Like comitative adverbs (§ sec:comitative.adverb ), it is clear that social relation collectives originate from participles of denominal verbs. The only example of the verbal denominal andʑɯ- derivation from which they originate is andʑirɣabe neighbours from the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-rɣaneighbour (§ sec:denom.andZi ). The social relation collective kɤndʑirɣaneighbours can thus be analyzed as the participle of this verb kɯ-ɤndʑirɣa.

However, since the andʑi- denominal derivation attested only in this single example, from a synchronic point of view it is better to consider this collective formation as a strictly nominal derivation.
summary:
The passage describes social-relation collective nouns in Japhug, especially those prefixed with kɤndʑi-, which denote groups of people linked by kinship or other social relations. These collectives are divided into reciprocal types, where all members use the same term for each other, and non-reciprocal types, where relations are unequal and may involve different generations, genders, or even animals and their owners.

It also notes that these collective nouns can function like ordinary nouns and may take modifiers, and that the catalog of forms is not exhaustive because some less common combinations exist while others are judged incorrect. Finally, an irregular collective kɤtsa ‘parents and children’ is mentioned, along with the observation that although these formations may historically come from denominal verb participles, synchronically they are better analyzed as nominal derivations.

text:
reduplication
The reduplicated collectives are built using partial reduplication. There are three different patterns.

First, some nouns allow standard partial reduplication with -ɯ in the reduplicated syllable (§ sec:partial.redp ) expressing a vague collective. This reduplication can apply to loanwords from Tibetan, such as χsɯ χsɤrthings in gold and rŋɯ rŋɯlthings in silver from χsɤrgold and rŋɯlsilver (Tibetan གསེར་gsergold and དངུལ་dŋulsilver).

exe

a-χsɯ χsɤr ra, a-rŋɯ rŋɯl ra mɤ-ra kɯ ɕom rɟɤskɤt ɯ-taʁ tu-ɕe-a ŋu \\
1sg. poss - coll gold pl 1sg. poss - coll silver pl neg -be.needed: fact erg iron stairs 3sg. poss -on ipfv: up -go- 1sg be: fact \\
`I don't need things in gold or silver, I will go up the iron stairs.' (not the golden or silver stairs, 2005-Kunbzang)
exe

Some nouns, which only appear in a reduplicated form are presumably ancient collectives, like kʰrambaχtɯχtɤmlies from a possible non-reduplicated form *kʰrambaχtɤm (from ཁྲམ་པ་གཏམ་kʰram.pa.gtamdeceiving words).

Second, we find some reduplicated collectives with the vowel a, not ɯ, in the replicated syllable. There are only a few examples, as shown in tab:coll.n, but several of them are borrowings from Tibetan. In one case, fɕafɕɤtwords, the base word is a transitive verb ( fɕɤttell).

Reduplicated collective nouns in a- can be used without a number clitic, as in ( ex:WntChantChWr ), but they often appear with the raplural as in ( ex:rdardWl ).

exe

znɤrɣama nɯ mtʰa ɯ-kɤcu ŋu. tɕe nɯnɯtɕu tɯ-ji ɯ-ntɕʰantɕʰɯr pɯ-dɤn, jinde kʰro ɲɤ-s-qapɯ-nɯ,\\
anthr dem anthr 3sg. poss -east be: fact lnk dem: pl indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -fragment: coll pst. ipfv -be:many now much ifr - caus -be.fallow- pl \\
`Znargama (`The place where one calls the rain') is on the east of Mtha, there used to be many little fragments of fields, but now people have left them become fallow.' (150903 kAmYW tWji3)
0006288#S20
exe

exe

tɕe tɤɕi nɯ tú-wɣ-χtɕi tɕʰɣaʁtɕʰɣaʁ ʑo tɕe, rdardɯl nɯra ɲɯ́-wɣ-ɣɤ-me tɕe \\
lnk barley dem ipfv - inv -wash idph (II):completely.clean emph lnk dush: coll dem: pl ipfv - inv - caus -not.exist lnk \\
`Then one washes the barley very thoroughly, one removes all the dirt.' (2002 tWsqar)
exe

The noun rgargɯnold person has the form of a collective noun as those in tab:coll.n, but it is commonly used with singular or dual referents (as in ex:rgargWn ). It could be analyzed as the collective form of a loanword from Tibetan རྒན་པོ་rgan.poold person, though the expected form would have been $ $ rga-rgɤn.

exe

rgargɯn ni kɤ-fstɯn pɯ-ra \\
old.person du inf -serve pst. ipfv -be.needed \\
`She had to take care of two old people.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S33
exe

A third reduplicated collective derivation is only attested by one example, the form qajɯqajaall kinds of worms (see ex:qajWqaja ) which derives from qajɯworm by reduplicating the whole word and changing the last rhyme to -a, a reduplication template reminiscent of that found in Khroskyabs (see, ).

exe

tɯ-ci ɯ-ŋgɯ qajɯqaja tʰamtɕɤt, sɯŋgɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rɯdaʁ kɯ-xtɕi kɯ-wxti, mɤʑɯ pɣa nɯnɯra lonba ʑo kɤ-fsraŋ kɯ-ra ɲɯ-ɕti ma \\
indef. poss -water 3sg -inside worm: coll all forest gen animal sbj: pcp -be.small sbj: pcp -be.big yet bird dem: pl all emph inf -protect inf: stat -be.needed sens -be: aff lnk \\
`All the creatures in the water, the small and big animals of the forest, and also the birds have to be protected.' (160703 jingyu)
0006169#S43
exe

A fourth type of collective has the vowel -e in the reduplicated syllable. It is attested in the noun ɯ-ʁɟoʁɟeall kinds of diluted drinks from ɯ-ʁɟodiluted drink (derived from the verb ʁɟorinse).
summary: The passage describes several patterns of partial reduplication used to form collective nouns. The most common type uses -ɯ in the reduplicated syllable and can apply to loanwords, while a smaller set uses -a; there is also an isolated whole-word reduplication with final -a, plus a rare type with -e. Some of these collectives are lexicalized or historically opaque, and a few are used with singular or dual referents despite their collective shape.

text:
The dvandva collective is derived from two nouns, the first one in bound state followed by the element -lɤ- and then by the second noun stem without a possessive prefix. All known forms, some of which have Tshobdun cognates, The nouns tɯ-mɤlɤjaʁlimbs and ɯ-kɤlɤjmehead upside down correspond to o-kolɐjmɐ `head and tail' and o-melɐ́ja `limbs', respectively. are listed in tab:dvandva.coll.n.

Among the examples in tab:dvandva.coll.n, ɯ-kɤlɤjmehead upside down and kɯmɤlɤxsouseless, `in vain' are mainly used adverbially. The first one mostly occurs with verbs such as ɕtʰɯzturn towards and rulook at at, as in ( ex:WkAlAjme ). See a definition of this noun in ( ex:WkAlAjme.pjWkACthWz ), § sec:inf.citation.

exe

The -lɤ-/-la- element found in collective dvandva -s is also attested in approximate numerals (§ sec:approx.numerals ) and in adverbs such tɯxpalɤskɤrthe whole year (from tɯ-xpaone year and fskɤrturn around) and rtsɯɕaŋlaŋmtɕɤtall the plants (from rtsɯɕaŋplant and tʰamtɕɤtall, respectively from Tibetan རྩི་ཤིང༌rtsi.ɕiŋplant and ཐམས་ཅད་tʰams.tɕadall).
