Another linking morpheme -mɤ- instead of -lɤ- is found in the possessed noun ɯ-ŋgɯmɤpɕithe inside and the outside from the locative relator nouns ɯ-ŋgɯinside and ɯ-pɕioutside (the latter from Tibetan ཕྱི་pʰʲioutside, § sec:other.locative.relator ).
summary:
The passage explains that collective dvandva nouns are formed from two nouns, with the first in bound state, the linker -lɤ-, and the second stem appearing without a possessive prefix. It gives examples such as words meaning “head upside down” and “souseless/superfluous,” noting that some are used mainly as adverbs, often with meanings like “in vain” or “for nothing.”

It also states that the linker -lɤ-/-la- occurs in other constructions, including approximate numerals and certain adverbs, and may be seen in forms like “the whole year” and “several mountain ranges.” A different linker, -mɤ-, is mentioned in the possessed noun meaning “the inside and the outside.”

text:
superlative
While there is no adjectival superlative derivation in Japhug (the available constructions to express this meaning are described in § sec:superlative ), we find nevertheless a derivation applied to locative nouns (§ sec:relator.location ), expressing the furthest location. As shown in tab:superlative.n, it is built by adding an element -ɕɯ- followed by a complete copy of the root of the noun without bound state alternation or partial replication; the resulting noun is still an inalienably possessed locative noun. Example ( ex:WqaCWqa ) illustrates the use of one of these forms.

exe

rɟɤmtsʰu ɯ-qaɕɯqa pjɯ-ɕe tɕe, nɯnɯ ɯ-kɤ-nɤ-mɯm nɯra ɕ-tu-nɯ-tɕɤt ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
ocean 3sg. poss -bottom: super ipfv: down -go lnk dem 3sg. poss - obj: pcp - trop -be.tasty dem: pl tral - ipfv - auto -take.out sens -be \\
`[The sperm whale] goes to the lowest depths of the ocean and catches the things it likes to eat.' (160703 jingyu) 0006169#S24
exe
summary: Japhug has no adjectival superlative derivation, but it does have a derivation on locative nouns that expresses the furthest location. This form is built by adding -ɕɯ- plus a full copy of the noun root, without bound-state alternation or partial replication, and the resulting noun remains an inalienably possessed locative noun.

text:
noun!negation
The only negative morphology possible on Japhug nouns is the privative derivation (§ sec:privative ). Negative prefixes only occur verbs (§ sec:negation ), and the only way to express non-privative negation on nouns is by using a relative clause (§ sec:negation.noun ).
noun!tense tense!nominal
There is no nominal tense derivation corresponding to the English prefix ex -. This meaning can only be expressed by participial relatives with the past imperfective participle of the copula pɯ-kɯ-ŋu ( ex:WnmaR.pWkWNu2 ) (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes ).

exe

ɯ-nmaʁ pɯ-kɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -husband pst. ipfv - sbj: pcp -be \\
`Her ex-husband (the one who used to be her husband).' (several attestations)
exe

nominalization!abstract
In addition, although it is possible to derive abstract nouns from verbs (§ sec:degree.nominals, § sec:tA.abstract.nouns, § sec:action.nominal.compounds ), there is no direct way of deriving an abstract noun from a noun. There is however an indirect way of doing it by building a denominal verb, and then to subjecting it to a nominalizing derivation. For instance, from the inalienably possessed tɤ-mdzuthorn, the proprietive verb aɣɯ-mdzu `be thorny, have a lot of thorns' can be derived (§ sec:denom.aGW ) and its (productive) degree noun ɯ-tɯ-ɤɣɯ-mdzu `its degree of thornity' is well attested in the degree construction (§ sec:degree.monoclausal ) as shown in ( ex:WtAGWmdzu ).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-ɤɣɯ-mdzu saχaʁ \\
3sg. poss - prop: denom -thorn be.extremely: fact \\
`It is very thorny (its degree of having thorns is extreme).' (18-NGolo) 0003530#S70
exe
summary: Japhug nouns do not take negative prefixes; the only negative noun morphology is privative derivation, and other kinds of noun negation must be expressed through a relative clause. Likewise, there is no nominal tense affix equivalent to English *ex-*, so meanings like “ex-husband” are conveyed by participial relatives. Although abstract nouns can be derived from verbs, they cannot be formed directly from nouns; instead, a denominal verb must first be created and then nominalized, as in the derivation meaning “degree of thorniness.”

text:
comitative adverb
Comitative adverbs are productively derived from nouns. Their meaning is `having $X$', `together with $X$', `including $X$' or in the case of clothes or covers `wearing $X$'.

Comitative adverbs are built by partially reduplicating the last syllable of the noun stem (following the morphophonological rules in § sec:partial.redp ) and prefixing either kɤ́- or kɤɣɯ-. This derivation applies to native words and loanwords from Tibetan. From instance, χɕɤlmɯɣglasses (from Tibetan ཤེལ་མིག་ɕel.migglasses) yields kɤ́-χɕɤlmɯ lmɯɣ or kɤɣɯ-χɕɤlmɯ lmɯɣ `together with glasses; wearing glasses'. Note that reduplication applies accross morpheme boundaries, as the coda of χɕɤlglass (from ཤེལ་ɕelglass) is reduplicated with the following syllable.

No semantic difference between the comitative adverbs in kɤ́- and those in kɤɣɯ- has been detected: Both are fully productive and can be built from the same nouns. As argued in, the kɤɣɯ- form is inherited (from proto-Gyalrong *kɐwə- ), while kɤ́- is borrowed from Tshobdun ko, the exact cognate of kɤɣɯ-. The prefix kɤɣɯ- and its Tshobdun cognate ko- both originate from the participle kɯ- (§ sec:subject.participles ) of the proprietive aɣɯ- denominal derivation (§ sec:denom.aGW.comitative ), attesting a proprietive $ $ comitative grammaticalization pathway.
comitative adverb
When the base noun is inalienably possessed, it is possible to build a comitative adverb with the indefinite possessor prefix or with the bare stem. For instance, from tɤ-rtehat one can derive both kɤ́-rtɯ rte / kɤɣɯ-rtɯ rte `with his/her hat' and kɤ́-tɤ-rtɯ rte / kɤɣɯ-tɤ-rtɯ rte `with a/the hat' with the indefinite possessor prefix tɤ-. These two sets of forms have different meanings: the former kɤ́-rtɯ rte / kɤɣɯ-rtɯ rte mean `wearing one's hat' (example ex:kAGWrtWrte ), while the latter kɤ́-tɤ-rtɯ rte / kɤɣɯ-tɤ-rtɯ rte imply that the subject is not wearing the hat ( ex:kAGWtArtWrte ); preserving the indefinite possessor in the derived form alienabilizes the inalienably possessed noun (see § sec:alienabilization ).

Comitative adverbs can be used as sentential adverbs, with scope over the whole sentence (examples ex:kAGWrtWrte, ex:kAGWtArtWrte ).

They also occur as noun modifiers (as in ex:tsxha.kAtAlWlu above), and either follow ( ex:tsxha.kAtAlWlu, ex:kAjWjaR ) or precede ( ex:kArnWrna, ex:kAthAlwWlwa ) the noun that they modify.

summary:
Comitative adverbs are productively formed from nouns by partial reduplication of the final syllable and the prefix kɤ́- or kɤɣɯ-, with the same pattern applying to native words and Tibetan loanwords. The two prefixes have no semantic difference; both are productive, though kɤɣɯ- is inherited and kɤ́- is borrowed, and the construction reflects a proprietive-to-comitative grammaticalization pathway.

With inalienably possessed nouns, either the bare stem or the indefinite possessor prefix tɤ- can be used, yielding different meanings: the bare-stem form means the subject is wearing or otherwise accompanied by the item, while the tɤ- form implies the item is merely taken along and not being worn. Comitative adverbs can function as sentential adverbs or noun modifiers, can modify nouns serving as subjects or objects, and in some contexts have specialized meanings such as describing resemblance in

comitative adverb
Nouns incorporated into comitative adverbs lose their nominal status and cannot be determined by relative clauses (including attributive adjectives), numerals or demonstratives. In a sentence such as ex:kAGWNkhWNkhor for instance, the attributive participial relative [ kɯ kɯ-ŋɤn] `all the ones who are evil' does not determine kɤɣɯ-ŋkʰɯ ŋkʰor `with his subjects', a syntactic structure which would correspond to the translation `with all his evil subjects'. Rather, it determines the head noun together with the comitative adverb rɟɤlpu kɤɣɯ-ŋkʰɯ ŋkʰor `the king with his subjects', which implies the translation given below.

Other denominal adverb formations are also attested in Japhug, but are described in the sections on time nominals (§ sec:time.ordinals ) and locational nouns (§ sec:relator.location ) in other chapters.
summary: Nouns incorporated into comitative adverbs lose their nominal properties, so they cannot be modified by relative clauses, adjectives, numerals, or demonstratives. The passage illustrates this with Japhug examples showing that a relative clause modifies the whole phrase “the king with his subjects,” not just “his subjects,” and notes that other denominal adverb formations are discussed elsewhere in the grammar.

text:
perlative reduplication
Partial reduplication of nouns, in addition to the reduplicated collectives (§ sec:redp.coll ), can also derive location adverbs such as tʂɯtʂualong the road from tʂuroad with a perlative meaning, as in ( ex:tsxWtsxu ). A similar use of the reduplication appears in Zbu, but with an additional kə- prefix.

exe

cʰa ra tʂɯ tʂu kú-wɣ-nɯ-tsʰi tɕe \\
alcohol pl path perlative ipfv - inv - auto -drink lnk \\
`One drinks alcohol along the way [back home].' (2010-histoire10)
exe

Other examples of perlative include ɯ-jrɯ jroʁ `following X's trace' from tɤ-jroʁtrace (see example ex:lunAkhWkhrWta, § sec:distributed.action.lexicalized ).

-z suffix
The postposition ʁazwhile... still, which is mainly used in a particular type of temporal clause (§ sec:RaznA ), probably originates from the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-ʁafree time with the fossil locative suffix -z (related to the locative postposition zɯ, § sec:core.locative ) cognate to Situ -s.

s- prefix
The adverbs stʰɯciso much (§ sec:sthWci.equative ) and stʰamtɕɤtso much are derived from the indefinite pronoun tʰɯcisomething (§ sec:thWci ) and the universal quantifier tʰamtɕɤtall (§ sec:universal.quant ) by what appears to be an s- prefix.

They are attested in derived forms such as kɯstʰɯcithis much and nɯstʰɯcithat much (§ sec:nWtshWci ) with the prefixed demonstrative stems kɯ- and nɯ- (§ sec:demonstrative.pronouns ).

The standard marker staʁcompared with and its variant sɯstaʁ (§ sec:comparative ) are clearly related to the locative relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:WtaR ). The prefix s- is doubled as sɯ-s- in the form sɯstaʁ.

The ultimate origin of the prefix s- in the adverbs and postpositions above is unclear, but it could be the result of the degrammaticalization of the locative -z suffix (§ sec:denominal.postposition.s; this suffix eventually became the locative postposition zɯ, § sec:core.locative) and subsequent procliticization to the following host. For instance, in the case of staʁ, the hypothesized process would be: The symbol $X$ represents a noun phrase. The forms are presented in their Japhug orthography for convenience, but at the stage when this reanalysis happened, the actual pronunciation of the forms in question was probably different.
reanalysis
enumerate
*$X$ -z (ɯ)-taʁ (Suffix)
*$X$ zə=taʁ (Procliticization)
$X$ staʁ (monosyllabicization and reanalysis as a postposition)
enumerate
summary:
The passage describes several derived adverbs and postpositions in Japhug. Partial noun reduplication can form perlative location adverbs like *tʂɯ* “along the road” from *tʂu* “road,” and other markers such as the *-z* suffix and an *s-* prefix appear in forms meaning “while,” “so much,” and “compared with.”

It suggests that the *s-* prefix may ultimately come from a former locative suffix *-z*, through reanalysis and procliticization, though its exact origin is uncertain. The development of *staʁ* is illustrated as a likely historical pathway from a noun phrase plus suffix to a monosyllabic postposition.

text:
pronoun prefix!possessive possession!prefix
The pronominal system of Japhug distinguishes singular, dual and plural. Alongside free pronouns, a system of pronominal prefixes is used not only to express possession on nouns (§ sec:gen.possession ), but also appears in various non-finite verb forms (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive, § sec:object.participle.possessive, § sec:oblique.participle.possessive, § sec:bare.inf, § sec:bare.action.nominals ). These prefixes do not distinguish the second and the third person in the dual and plural forms; their use is described in § sec:possessive.paradigm.

Free pronouns and possessive prefixes are remarkably similar in Kamnyu Japhug. In this dialect, all the pronouns except the third person dual and plural are formed by adding the root -ʑo to the corresponding possessive prefix. In the eastern Japhug dialects (represented by Tatshi in tab:pronoun ), the 1sg ŋa and 3sg mi pronouns differ from the corresponding possessive prefixes (the former is possibly borrowed from Situ ŋā ).

The first and second person singular pronouns aʑo and nɤʑo also have the shorter monosyllabic forms aj and nɤj, respectively. These short forms are considerably less common in stories (in the reported speech of the characters), but appear frequently in free conversations.

Japhug lacks any inclusive/exclusive distinction, unlike other Gyalrongic languages such as Tshobdun, Situ or Khroskyabs (see,,, ). Example ( ex:tCiZo.CetCi ) shows the dual pronoun tɕiʑowe (dual) in inclusive use (it is clear from the context that the son tells his mother to come with him), and ( ex:tCiZo.tCitAYi ) illustrates the same pronoun in exclusive use. Similar pairs of examples can be found with the first plural pronoun iʑowe (plural) and its variants.

Personal pronouns are not used as head of relative clauses (as in Chinese ……的你... de nǐ you who are...), though there are case of relativization of first or second person possessor, as in ( ex:amu.kWme ) (§ sec:S.possessor.relativization ).

`Who will give you a wife, you frog.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

The relationship between the pronouns and the following noun is not necessarily appositional; for instance, in ( ex:iZora.tuhanzu ), despite the absence of possessive prefix on the borrowing 土汉族 tǔhànzúlocal Chinese, the meaning of iʑora <tuhanzu> is `the local Chinese living among us' rather than `We local Chinese'.

exe

iʑora <tuhanzu> ra kɯ, <qingyang> tu-ti-nɯ ŋu. \\
1pl local.Chinese pl erg bharal ipfv -say- pl be: fact \\
`The local Chinese among us call it ``qingyang''.' (20-xsar)
0003568#S41
exe

As in most languages with polypersonal indexation, pronouns (especially first and second person pronouns) are never obligatory, and a finite verb form without overt argument NPs is a perfectly well-formed sentence (§ sec:word.order ). Overt pronouns are obligatorily overt as core arguments only when focalized (§ sec:focalization.overt ).

Japhug presents a very common subtype of split ergativity: the ergative kɯ being obligatory on transitive subject third person pronouns (except in the case of the emphatic use of pronouns, § sec:pronouns.emph ) but optional on first and second person pronouns (§ sec:absolutive.A and § sec:A.kW ).
summary:
Japhug distinguishes singular, dual, and plural in its pronominal system, and it uses both free pronouns and pronominal prefixes: the prefixes mark possession on nouns and also occur in several non-finite verb forms. Free pronouns in Kamnyu Japhug are very similar to possessive prefixes, with most being formed by adding -ʑo to the corresponding prefix, and Japhug has no inclusive/exclusive distinction.  

The language also has shorter forms of some first- and second-person singular pronouns, though these are more common in conversation than in stories. Pronouns are not obligatorily expressed, can take determiners or appositive nouns, and Japhug shows split ergativity in which ergative kɯ is obligatory on third-person transitive subjects but optional on first- and second-person ones.

text:
plural!honorific
The second plural pronoun nɯʑo can be used as honorific pronoun, as in ( ex:nWZo.tChi.WrWG ), where the addressee is unambiguously singular.

exe

ɯtɤz nɯʑo tɕʰi ɯ-rɯɣ tɯ-ŋu-nɯ? \\
actually 2pl what 3sg. poss -race 2-be: fact - pl \\
`Actually, which type of being are you?' (2003 smanmi)
exe

This pronoun correlates with plural honorific indexation -nɯ (§ sec:honorific.indexation ). Note that the plural ra also occurs as a honorific marker on nouns (§ sec:ra.honorific ).
summary: The second plural pronoun **nɯʑo** can also be used as an honorific pronoun, even when the addressee is clearly singular. This use corresponds to plural honorific indexation **-nɯ**, and the plural marker **ra** likewise appears as an honorific marker on nouns.

text:
pronoun!possession
Personal pronouns occur instead of possessive prefixes (§ sec:possessive.prefixes ) as first member of compounds with the adverbs -sɯso `as $X$ wish' (from the verb sɯsothink), as in example ( ex:ʑara.sWso ) and -sti `$X$ alone'.

exe

a-zda ra ʑara-sɯso tu-nɯ-nɤŋkɯŋke-nɯ ɲɯ-kʰɯ \\
1sg. poss -companion pl 3pl -as.wish ipfv - auto -go.here.and.there- pl sens -be.possible \\
`The other [snakes] can go here and there as they wish.' (The divination 2002)
0003364#S43
exe

The noun -βra `it is $X$'s turn to' can either take a regular possessive prefix, or a pronoun in bound state form as in ( ex:nAZoBra ), where the bound form nɤʑɤ- occurs instead of nɤʑo 2sg.
exe

wortɕʰi nɤʑɤ-βra a-tɤ-tɯ-ti ra \\
please 2sg. poss -turn irr - pfv -2-say be.needed: fact \\
`It is your turn to say it.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

These constructions are discussed in more detail in § sec.IPN.adverbs and § sec:stWsti.
summary: Personal pronouns can replace possessive prefixes as the first member of compounds with the adverbs -sɯso ‘as X wish’ and -sti ‘X alone.’ The noun -βra ‘it is X’s turn to’ may take either a regular possessive prefix or a bound-form pronoun, as shown by the 2sg bound form nɤʑɤ- instead of nɤʑo.

text:
pronoun!generic generic
tɯʑoone
The generic pronoun tɯʑoone has the same morphological structure as personal pronouns as seen in the previous section, combining the generic possessive prefix tɯ- with the pronominal root -ʑo. Note that this generic possessive has to be strictly distinguished from the homophonous indefinite possessor prefix tɯ- (see § sec:indef.genr.poss ). It has a rare plural variant tɯʑɤraone (see § sec:partitive.indexation, example ex:tWZAra.pWxtCij ).

In Japhug, sentences have at most one generic human referent (§ sec:indef.genr.poss ). If this referent is core argument, the verb has generic indexation ( kɯ- for intransitive subject and object and wɣ- for transitive subject, as in the following example, § sec:indexation.generic.tr ). The generic argument can be realized as the generic pronoun tɯʑo as in ( ex:pjWkWZGAGANgi ) or by a generic noun (such as tɯrmeperson, § sec:tWrme.generic ).

exe

tɯ-zda pjɯ́-wɣ-z-ɣɤtɕa, tɯʑo ntsɯ pjɯ-kɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤŋgi tɕe, pɯ-kɯ-nɯ-ɣɤtɕa kɯ́nɤ pjɯ-kɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤŋgi tɕe, ɯ-mbrɤzɯ kɯ-tu me tu-kɯ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
genr. poss -companion ipfv - inv - caus -be.wrong oneself always ipfv - genr:S/O- refl -be.right lnk aor - genr:S/O- auto -be.wrong also ipfv - genr:S/O- refl -be.right lnk 3sg. poss -result sbj: pcp -have not.exist: fact ipfv - genr -say sens -be \\
`If one considers that one's companion is wrong, and always considers himself to be right even if one is wrong, there is can be no good result.' (lWlu)
0003361#S80
exe

The generic pronoun can occur before a noun with the generic possessive as in tɯʑo tɯ-skɤt `one's language' in example ( ex:tWZo.tWskAt ); this contributes to disambiguating between the indefinite possessive and the generic possessive in the case of inalienably possessed nouns (thus on its own tɯ-skɤt can mean either `a language' or `one's language').

exe

tɕendɤre tɯʑo tɯ-skɤt ʑara ɣɯ-sɯxɕɤt ɲɯ-ra, ʑara nɯ-skɤt tɯʑo kɯ-sɯxɕɤt ɲɯ-ra \\
lnk genr genr. poss -language 3pl inv -teach: fact sens -be.needed 3pl 3pl. poss -language genr genr:S/O-teach: fact sens -be.needed \\
`One has to teach them one's language, and they have to teach you their language.' (150901 tshuBdWnskAt)
0006242#S28
exe

When occurring in A function, the generic pronoun tɯʑo obligatorily receives the ergative kɯ as in ( ex:tWZo.kW ) (note that in example ex:tWZo.tWskAt, although the generic referent is A in the first clause, tɯʑo does not take ergative because it is a determiner of tɯ-skɤt ).

exe

tɯʑo kɯ tɯ-χti ɲɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-ɕar kɯ-maʁ kɯ, tɯ-pʰama ra kɯ tɯ-χti ɲɯ-ɕar-nɯ \\
genr erg genr. poss -spouse ipfv - inv - auto -search inf: stat -not.be erg genr. poss -parent pl erg genr. poss -spouse ipfv -search- pl \\
`One could not choose one's spouse, one's parents chose one's spouse.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S191
exe

Relator nouns (§ sec:relator.nouns ), for example the dative ɯ-ɕki (§ sec:dative ), are grammaticalized from inalienably possessed nouns and like them, take a generic possessive prefix ( tɯ-ɕki or tɯ-pʰe `to one') when following tɯʑo, as in example ( ex:tWZo.tWCki ), which describes the Omaha-type skewing rule in the kinship system (§ sec:omaha ).

exe

tɯ-ɲi ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit nɯra kɯ tɯʑo tɯ-ɕki ``a-rpɯ", tɤ-tɕɯ pɯ-kɯ-ŋu nɤ ``a-rpɯ" tu-ti-nɯ, tɕʰeme pɯ-kɯ-ŋu nɤ ``a-ɬaʁ" tu-ti-nɯ kɯ-ra ŋu \\
genr. poss -FZ gen 3sg. poss -child dem: pl erg genr genr -dat 1sg. poss -MB indef. poss -son pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-be if 1sg. poss -MB ipfv -say- pl girl pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-be if 1sg. poss -MZ ipfv -say- pl inf. stat -be.needed be: fact \\
`One's father's sister's children have to call oneself ``my maternal uncle'' if one is a boy, ``my maternal aunt'' if one is a girl.' (140425 kWmdza03) 0003787
exe

As examples ( ex:pjWkWZGAGANgi ) to ( ex:tWZo.tWCki ) illustrate, generic agreement between pronoun, possessive prefix and verb indexation is very systematic. Examples of 1pl indexation with generic pronouns or vice-versa are, however, attested (§ sec:partitive.indexation ).

Due to the constraint against more than one generic argument per clause (§ sec:indef.genr.poss ), the only case that the generic pronoun can appear two times in the same clause occurs in reflexive constructions (§ sec:reflexive ), as in ( ex:tWZo.kW.tWZo ).

exe

tɯʑo kɯ tɯʑo tu-kɯ-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-βri ra kɤ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
genr erg genr ipfv - genr:S/O- auto - refl -protect be.needed: fact inf -say sens -be \\
`One has to protect oneself.' (04-qala1)
exe

The generic noun tɯrmeperson
generic!noun
The noun tɯrmeperson, also attested to express indefinite humans (§ sec:ci.someone ) or in the meaning `someone else' (§ sec:other.pro ), can occur as a marker of generic person, as in ( ex:kWnA.tuwGndza ).

exe

tɯrme kɯnɤ tú-wɣ-ndza sna. \\
people also ipfv - inv -eat be.good: fact \\
`It is also good for people to eat.' (12-Zmbroko) 0003490#S29
exe

In this function, tɯrmeperson can be indexed on the verb by either generic person (as in ex:kWnA.tuwGndza ) or 3pl markers, a question explored in more detail in § sec:genr.3pl.

There is a slight difference of usage between tɯrmeperson and tɯʑoone in clauses with a generic argument. Both can be followed by a noun or a case marker taking the generic possessive prefix, as in ( ex:genr.tWrme3 ) and ( ex:tWZo.tWfsu ).

exe

tɯrme tɯ-fsu ɕaŋtaʁ tu-mbro mɤ-cʰa. \\
people genr. poss -equal.to until ipfv -be.big neg - fact:can \\
`It cannot grow bigger than a person.' (`as oneself') (11-qarGW)
0003480#S25
exe

exe

ɯ-tɯ-mbro nɯnɯ tɯʑo tɯ-fsu jamar tu-zɣɯt cʰa. \\
3sg - nmlz: deg -be.high dem genr genr -equal.to about ipfv: up -reach can: fact \\
`As for its size, it can reach one's (`a person's') size.' (16-CWrNgo)
0003518#S18
exe

However, tɯrmeperson as a generic noun can alternatively be used with a possessee or a case marker with the third person singular ɯ- prefix, as in ( ex:tWrme.Wfsu ), while this option does not exist for tɯʑoone.

exe

tɯrme ɯ-fsu jamar tu-βze cʰa. \\
people 3sg -equal.to about ipfv -do[III] can: fact \\
`It can grow about the size of a person.' (12-ndZiNgri)
0003488#S4
exe
summary:
The generic pronoun **tɯʑoone** is morphologically parallel to personal pronouns, built from the generic possessive prefix **tɯ-** plus the root **-ʑo**, and it has a rare plural form **tɯʑɤraone**. In Japhug, a clause can contain only one generic human referent, and if this referent is a core argument, the verb shows generic indexation; the generic pronoun may also combine with generic possessive constructions, with ergative marking when it functions as A, and it can occur twice only in reflexive contexts.

The generic noun **tɯrme ‘person’** can also express generic person, and in this function it may be indexed on the verb either with generic person markers or with 3pl markers. Compared with **tɯʑoone**, **tɯrme** can be used with a posses

text:
pronoun!genitive genitive!pronoun
The form of pronouns and personal prefixes undergoes few morphophonological changes in combination with postpositions and relational nouns. However, in combination with the genitive postposition ɣɯ (cf § sec:genitive ), some personal pronouns have special forms indicated in Table tab:pronoun.gen.

While some degree of variation exists with dual and plural pronouns (for instance the regular iʑo ɣɯ is found alongside iʑɤɣ and iʑɤra ɣɯ ), for the singular pronouns only one form is attested.

exe

aʑɯɣ ndʐa ŋu ɕi, nɤʑɯɣ ndʐa ŋu, aj mɯ́j-tso-a \\
1sg: gen reason be: fact qu 2sg: gen reason be: fact 1sg neg: sens -understand- 1sg \\
`I don't know if it is because of me, or because of you.' (that the phone line is not working well) (phone conversation)
exe

In the genitive forms of the pronouns, the vowel of the genitive marker is generally dropped, and the pronominal root -ʑo undergoes vowel change to -ʑɯɣ (in the case of first and second person) and -ʑɤɣ (in other forms). Note that ʑaraɣ is the only case of the rhyme aɣ in Japhug.

When genitive pronouns occur as determiners of nouns (including in the possessive existential construction, § sec:possessive.mihi.est ), these nouns almost always take a possessive prefix coreferent with the genitive pronoun, as in ( ex:tɕithAfkAlAGi ).

exe

tɕiʑɤɣ tɕi-tʰɤfkɤlɤɣi tɯ-ɕkat pɯ-tu tɕe, nɯ kɤ-nɯ-χtɤr-tɕi ɕti wo \\
1du: gen 2du -plant.ash one-load pst. ipfv -exist lnk dem aor - auto -spread- 1du be: aff: fact sfp \\
`We had one load of ash, and we spilled it there.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

The genitive pronouns can be used as possessive pronouns (`mine', `my own' etc) and take the determiner nɯ and the plural ra, as in ( ex:aZWG.nW ) and ( ex:WZAG.nWra ).

exe

``tɕe ɣnɤsqaptɯ-rʑaʁ tu-tsu tɕe ɲɯ-ʁaʁ ŋu" ɲɯ-ti-nɯ ri, aʑɯɣ nɯ ɣnɤsqamnɯz tɤ-rʑaʁ mɤɕtʂa mɯ-nɯ-ʁaʁ. \\
lnk twenty.one-night ipfv -pass lnk ipfv -hatch be: fact sens -say- pl lnk 1sg: gen dem twenty.two one-night until neg - aor -hatch \\
`People say that [chicken eggs] hatch after twenty-one days, mine took twenty-two days to hatch.' (150819 kumpGa)
0006388#S33
exe

exe

ɯʑɤɣ nɯra tu-nɯ-ɣɤ-βdi tɕe, ɕɯ-sɤ-sqɤr mɤ-ra \\
3sg: gen dem: pl ipfv - auto - caus -be.well lnk tral - apass -hire: fact neg -be.needed: fact \\
`He repairs his own [machines] by himself, he does not need to ask other people.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S153
exe
summary:
Pronouns and personal prefixes undergo few morphophonological changes with postpositions and relational nouns, but some personal pronouns have special genitive forms with the postposition ɣɯ. In these genitive forms, the vowel of the genitive marker is usually dropped and the pronominal root changes, with some variation in dual and plural forms but only one attested form for singular pronouns.  

Genitive pronouns can function as possessive pronouns and often appear with the determiner nɯ and plural ra; when they modify nouns, those nouns usually also take a possessive prefix coreferent with the genitive pronoun.

text:
pronoun!emphatic use
In addition to their referential and anaphoric functions, pronouns in Japhug can be used in an emphatic way in combination with the emphatic particle ʑo (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ), as in ( ex:WZo.Zo ).

exe

aʑo ɯʑo ʑo kɤ-mto mɯ-pɯ-rɲo-t-a. \\
1sg 3sg emph inf -see neg - aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I never saw it itself.' (24-kWmu)
0003618#S7
exe

In combination with the autive nɯ- on the verb, pronouns express the meaning `do $X$ on one's own' (§ sec:autoben.proper ). In the case of transitive verbs, third person pronouns in this function does not take the ergative even if the referent is the transitive subject (example ex:pjWnWtCAtnW, where tɕɤttake out is transitive, § sec:tCAt.lv ).

exe

tɕe lu-nɯ-rɤji-nɯ tɕe, nɯ-kɤ-ndza nɯra ʑara pjɯ-nɯ-tɕɤt-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu tɕe \\
lnk ipfv - auto -plant.crops- pl lnk 3pl. poss - obj. pcp -eat dem: pl 3pl ipfv - auto -take.out- pl ifr. ipfv -be lnk \\
`They were working in the fields, and earning their own food by themselves.' (about lepers, who were settled in the special place by the government, 25-khArWm)
0003644#S61
exe

The emphatic pronoun raŋoneself borrowed from Tibetan རང་raŋoneself, can also be used with any person, though this usage is not very common. It can occur with the autive ( ex:aZo.raN ) or without it ( ex:aZo.raN.Zo ).

exe

nɤʑo tu-tɯ-ti mɤ-ra ma aʑo raŋ tu-nɯ-ti-a jɤɣ \\
2sg ipfv -2-say neg -be.neededo: fact lnk 1sg oneself ipfv - auto -say- 1sg be.possible: fact \\
`You don't need to say it, I can say it myself.' (elicited)
exe

exe

aʑo raŋ ʑo ju-ɕe-a ra \\
1sg oneself emph ipfv -go- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`I have to go there myself.' (150830 afanti-zh)
0006380#S94
exe
summary:
In Japhug, pronouns can be used emphatically with the particle ʑo to express contrastive or intensive meaning, as in “it itself.” With the autive prefix nɯ- on the verb, pronouns can also mean “do X on one’s own”; in this use, third-person pronouns do not take the ergative even when they are the subject of a transitive verb.

The borrowed emphatic pronoun raŋ ‘oneself’ from Tibetan can likewise be used with any person, though this is uncommon. It may appear with the autive prefix or without it, both conveying a meaning like “myself” or “on my own.”

text:
pronoun!interrogative
The interrogative pronouns in Japhug are indicated in tab:interrog.pronoun. These pronouns are used in independent interrogative clauses ( ex:tChi.pWNu ), in subordinate clauses ( ex:tChi.kWNu ), and also in correlatives ( ex:NotCu.WsAzrAZi ) (§ sec:interrogative.relative ), and also occur to express non-specific referents (these uses are described in § § sec:interrogative.indef, after the indefinite pronouns).

exe

tɕe mɤʑɯ tɕʰi pɯ-ŋu? \\
lnk yet what pst. ipfv -be \\
`What was there [after this one]?' (12-ndZiNgri) 0003488#S92
exe

exe

ɯʑo tɕʰi kɯ-ŋu nɯ ko-tso-nɯ tɕe tɕe cʰɤ́-wɣ-tɕɤt \\
3sg what sbj: pcp -be dem ifr -understand- pl lnk lnk ifr: downstream - inv -take.out \\
`They understood what he was, and expelled him (from their group).' (140427 hanya yu gezi-zh)
0003842#S18
exe

exe

ɯ-pʰoŋbu tɕʰi kɯ-fse nɯ, ŋotɕu ɯ-sɤz-rɤʑi nɯnɯ ɣɯ kɯ-nɯtsa kɯ-fse ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe \\
3sg. poss -body what sbj: pcp -be.like dem where 3sg - obl: pcp -remain dem gen sbj: pcp -fit sbj: pcp -be.like sens -be: aff lnk \\
`The way its body is like is well-adapted to the place where it lives.' (19-rNamoN)
0003552#S22
exe

In addition to these pronouns, some indefinite pronouns are also marginally used in questions, see for instance ( ex:thWthAci.totia ) in § sec:thWci.

tɕʰiwhat
The interrogative pronoun `what' considerably varies across Japhug dialects. In Kamnyu we find tɕʰi, apparently borrowed from Tibetan tɕʰi. Neighbouring dialects of Gdongbrgyad area have either tsʰi (in Mangi) or tʰi (in Rqaco), which represents the original Gyalrongic root for this interrogative pronoun (cognate with Tibetan ཆི་tɕʰiwhat and Limbu the ). Even in the Kamnyu dialect, the form tsʰi- is directly attested in the indefinite tsʰitsukuwhatever (§ sec:tshitsuku ). Mangi Japhug shares with Kamnyu the sound change *tʰi tsʰi which also affects the verb tsʰidrink (this sound change occurred after the pronoun *tʰi underwent bound state alternation to tʰɯ- and was used to build the indefinite pronoun tʰɯcisomething, see § sec:thWci ). Note that Kamnyu Japhug tɕʰiwhat is homophonous with the noun tɕʰitree-trunk stairs attested for instance in example ( ex:tChi.tukWndW ) -- the readers of Japhug texts have to be aware of this potential ambiguity.

exe

ɕom ɣɟɯ kɯ-mbɯ mbro ʑo, ɯ-ɣmbaj zɯ tɕʰi tu-kɯ-ndɯ ci pɯ-tu ɲɯ-ŋu \\
iron tower sbj: pcp - emph be.high emph 3sg. poss -side loc treetrunk.stairs ipfv: up - sbj: pcp - acaus:spread indef pst. ipfv -be sens -be \\
`There was a huge iron tower, with a tree-trunk stairs on its side.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

The Eastern dialects of Gsardzong and Datshang have xto instead, a word of unknown etymology; these dialects, which share many additional morphosyntactic and phonological commonalities, can be collectively referred to as ``Xtokavian''.

In the Kamnyu dialect, tɕʰiwhat is by far the most common interrogative pronoun in the corpus. In interrogative clauses, it can be used to ask about objects, non-human animals ( ex:nAmbro ) and names of persons ( ex:tChi.tWrmi ), and can occur as prenominal determiner meaning `what (type of)' as in ( ex:tChi.Cku ).

exe

nɤʑo nɤ-mbro nɯ tɕʰi ŋu \\
2sg 2sg. poss -horse dem what be: fact \\
`Who is your horse?' (about a sentient horse) (2003 smanmi2)
exe

exe

tɕʰi tɯ-rmi? \\
what 2-be.called: fact \\
`What is your name?' (heard in context)
exe

exe

tɕendɤre mɤʑɯ tɕʰi ɕku tu \\
lnk yet what allium exist: fact \\
`What other [plants of the genus] Allium are there?' (07-Cku)
0003424#S94
exe

As in many languages, this interrogative pronoun (instead of the pronoun ɕɯwho) is also used in questions about classification of persons, including social affiliation ( ex:tChi.WrWG, and ex:tChi.kWNu above) and biological affiliation ( ex:tChi.tosci ).

exe

ɯtɤz nɯʑo tɕʰi ɯ-rɯɣ tɯ-ŋu-nɯ? \\
finally 2pl what 3sg. poss -race 2-be: fact - pl \\
`Finally, which type [of being] are you?' (smanmi 2003)
exe

There is no specific interrogative pronoun to ask about manner like English `how', and Japhug expresses this meaning by combining tɕʰi with the verbs fsebe like or studo like (§ sec:similative.verb.complementation ) as in ( ex:tChi.Zo.tuwGBzu.phAn ).

exe

nɤ-smɤn tɤ-sɯ-βzu-t-a ri maka mɯ́j-pʰɤn, tɕe tɕʰi ʑo tú-wɣ-stu pʰɤn \\
3sg. poss -medicine aor - caus -make- pst: tr - 1sg but at.all neg: sens -be.efficient lnk what emph ipfv - inv -do.like be.efficient: fact \\
`I had medicine made for you but it does not work, how should we do for it to work?' (nyima wodzer 2002)
exe

When used with tɕʰi, the similative verbs often take an infinitival complement as in ( ex:tChi.tAtWfsendZi ).

exe

a-ʁi, ki kɯ-fse tɤjpɣom kɯ-wxti nɯtɕu, kɤ-ɕe tɕʰi tɤ-tɯ-fse-ndʑi? \\
1sg. poss -younger.sibling this sbj: pcp -be.like ice sbj: pcp -be.big dem: loc inf -go what aor -2-be.like- du \\
`Sister, how did you cross such a big block of ice?' (Kunbzang 2005)
exe

The pronoun tɕʰiwhat on its own can occur in questions about the reason or the purpose of a particular state of affair, as in ( ex:tChi.apWNua ) and ( ex:tChi.YWtWnAre ).

exe

aʑo tɕʰi a-pɯ-ŋu-a? \\
1sg what irr - ipfv -be- 1sg \\
`How can it be me?' (2003 sras)
exe

exe

a-tɤɕime, tɕʰi ɲɯ-tɯ-nɤre ŋu? \\
1sg. poss -lady what sens -2-laugh be: fact \\
`My lady, why are you laughing?' (Not `what are you laughing at?', 2002 qaCpa)
exe

When referring to purpose or reason, it is possible to combine tɕʰiwhat with the nouns ɯ-spamaterial and ɯ-ndʐacause (as the pronoun tɕʰindʐawhy), as in ( ex:tChi.Wspa.pWNu ) and ( ex:tChi.YWtWɣAwu ). Note that examples ( ex:tChi.YWtWnAre ) and ( ex:tChi.YWtWɣAwu ) are from the same story, just a few lines away, in the same context; the construction in ( ex:tChi.YWtWɣAwu ) is a more explicit variant of that in ( ex:tChi.YWtWnAre ).

exe

tɕe tɕʰi ɯ-spa pɯ-ŋu mɤ-xsi ma tɕe nɯ kɯ-fse pjɤ-tu \\
lnk what 3sg. poss -material pst. ipfv -be neg - genr:know lnk lnk dem sbj: pcp -be.like ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`It is not known what it was for, but there was something like that.' (hist140522 GJW)
0004051#S18
exe

exe
summary: Japhug interrogative pronouns are used in independent and subordinate questions, in correlatives, and sometimes to express non-specific referents; some indefinite pronouns are also marginally used in questions. The most common interrogative is **tɕʰi** ‘what,’ whose form varies across dialects and which can ask about objects, animals, names, classification, manner (with similative verbs), and reason or purpose. For ‘why,’ Japhug may use **tɕʰi** alone or combine it with nouns meaning ‘material’ and ‘cause’ to form a more explicit expression.

text:
tɕʰindʐa ɲɯ-tɯ-ɣɤwu ŋu? \\
why sens -2-cry be: fact \\
`Why are you crying?' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

The pronoun tɕʰi takes case marking with genitive ɣɯ and the instrumental/ergative kɯ, as in ( ex:tChi.kW ).

`I don't what [the wasp] uses to make [its nest$_i$], it$_i$ is attached on trees like that.' (26-ndzWrnaR) 0003678#S52
exe

In combination with the adverb jarma / jamarabout, it can be used to indicate a quantity, instead of tʰɤstɯɣhow many (§ sec:thAstWG ), as illustrated by ( ex:tChi.jamar ), and ( ex:tChi.jamar.kondza ).

tu-ɕtʂam-a tɕe tɕʰi jamar ʑo ɣɤʑu kɯ? \\
ipfv -measure[III]- 1sg lnk what about emph exist: sens sfp \\

It is possible to combine tɕʰi jamar with a adjective to express approximate comparison, as in ( ex:tChi.kWzri ).

In correlative clauses, the pronoun tɕʰiwhat can also be used to refer to a quantity without the adverb jamarabout (example ex:tChi.tAkWsci ).

However, in independent interrogative clauses, tɕʰiwhat cannot refer to quantities. Sentence ( ex:tChi.tosci ) thus can only mean `Was it a boy or a girl' not `How many children did she have?'.

3sg. poss -child what ifr -be.born \\
`Was it a boy or a girl?' (elicited)

ɕɯwho
The interrogative pronoun ɕɯwho occurs in questions about the identification of a human referent. It can occur in all syntactic roles, and does not have special ergative or genitive forms (see examples ex:CW.kW.tWwGmbi and ex:CW.GW ). It is the probable cognate of a etymon widespread in the Trans-Himalayan family (for instance, Tibetan སུ་suwho).

ma-tɯ-nɯqaɟy ma ɕɯ tɯ-ŋu mɤ-xsi \\

`Don't fish, I don't who you are.' (gesar)
exe

exe

mɤ-ta-mbi nɤʑo qaɕpa ɕɯ kɯ tɯ́-wɣ-mbi \\
neg -1 2-give: fact 2sg frog who erg 2- inv -give: fact \\
`We won't give her to you, who would give her to you, a frog?' (2002 qaCpa)

The pronoun ɕɯwho can be used in one context with non-human referents, when asking about which object (out of two or more) has the highest value as to a property described by the main verb, as in ( ex:CW.kW.YWzrindZi ); in this construction, the verb receives non-singular indexation (§ sec:partitive.indexation ), such as the dual -ndʑi in this example. Concerning the use of the ergative kɯ in this sentence see § sec:comparative, § sec:sAz.kW and.

nɯ nɤ-ku ɯ-tɯ-rɲɟi nɯ, aki ɕe-tɕi tɕe, mbro ɯ-jme cʰonɤ tú-wɣ-sɤfsu, ɕɯ kɯ ɲɯ-zri-ndʑi kɯ \\

`Your hair is very long, let us go downstairs, and compare it with a horse's tail.' (2002 qaCpa)

Forms related to ɕɯwho in Japhug include the indefinite pronoun ɕɯmɤɕɯwhoever, anybody ( sex:CWmACW ) and ɕɯŋarɯraeach better than the other.

tʰɤstɯɣhow many and tʰɤjtɕuwhen
To ask about precise quantities, tʰɤstɯɣhow many (or `how much') occurs rather than tɕʰi jamar as seen above (§ ex:tChi.jamar ).

exe

nɤʑo tʰɤstɯɣ tɯ-kʰɤm? \\
you how.much 2-give[III]: fact \\
`How much [money] do you give [for it]?' (Bargaining)
exe

It can be used for any countable quantity, including for people, as in ( ex:thAstWG.tWtunW ).

exe

tsʰupa tʰɤstɯɣ tɯ-tu-nɯ ŋu? \\
village how.much 2-exist: fact - pl be: fact \\
`How many [people] are you in the village?' (conversation)
exe
summary:
The passage describes the interrogative pronoun tɕʰi, which takes genitive ɣɯ and instrumental/ergative kɯ case marking and can be combined with jamar/jamaro to express quantities or approximate comparison. In correlative clauses it can refer to quantities without jamar, but in independent interrogative clauses it cannot mean ‘how many,’ only asking about identity or category, and in topicalized clauses it can mean ‘as for how X it becomes.’  

It also presents ɕɯ as the human ‘who’ pronoun, which can occur in all syntactic roles without special ergative or genitive forms, though it can also be used for non-human referents in a comparative construction. For precise quantities, the language instead uses tʰɤstɯɣ ‘how many/how much,’ including for people and other countable items.

text:
The pronoun tʰɤstɯɣ has a conjunct form tʰɤstɯ- when used with counted nouns, including Chinese borrowings (§ sec:other.numeral.prefixes ). For instance, in ( ex:thAstWmaR ) and ( ex:thAstWdian ), it occurs with the classifiers X-maʁsize of shoes (from Chinese 码 mǎ ), and in ( ex:thAstWdian ) with the non-nativized form of 点 diǎnhour (the same meaning can be expressed without borrowing from Chinese, as in ex:thAstWG.kozGWt ).

exe

nɤ-xtsa nɯ tʰɤstɯ-maʁ tu-tɯ-ŋge ŋu \\
2sg. poss -shoe dem how.many-size ipfv -2-wear[III] be: fact \\
`What is the size of your shoes?' (Conversation)
exe

exe

nɯʑo nɯtɕu tʰɤstɯ-<dian> ŋu? \\
2pl dem: loc hour how.many-hour be: fact \\
`What time is it at your place?' (conversation 12-11-2018)
exe

Combined with the noun tɤ-rʑaʁtime, tʰɤstɯɣ can be used to ask about a length of time ( ex:thAstWG ).

exe

nɤʑo tɤ-rʑaʁ tʰɤstɯɣ jamar tɤ-tsu tɕe kɤ-tɯ-spa-t? \\
you indef. poss -time how.many about aor -pass lnk aor -2-be.able- pst: tr \\
`How long did it take you to learn it?' (elicited)
exe

The phrase tɤ-rʑaʁ tʰɤstɯɣ (or alternatively tɯtsʰot tʰɤstɯɣ ) in collocation with the verb zɣɯtarrive, is also employed for asking about clock time, as in ( ex:thAstWG.kozGWt ) (see § sec:hours ) or dates.

exe

tɤ-rʑaʁ tʰɤstɯɣ ko-zɣɯt? \\
indef. poss -time how.many ifr -reach \\
`What is the time?' (heard in context)
exe

Questions about time can also be expressed by the pronoun tʰɤjtɕuwhen, as in ( ex:thAjtCu ) and ( ex:thAjtCu.GW ).

exe

tʰɤjtɕu lɤ-tɯ-nɯɣe pɯ-ŋu ra nɤ? \\
when aor -2-come.back[II] pst. ipfv -be pl sfp \\
`When did you come back home?' (taRrdo conversation)
exe

As shown by ( ex:thAjtCu.GW ), tʰɤjtɕuwhen can be used with the genitive ɣɯ.

exe

<jipiao> nɯ, tʰɤjtɕu ɣɯ tɤ-tɯ-χtɯ-t? \\
plane.ticket dem when gen aor -2-buy- pst: tr \\
`Your plane ticket, for what date did you buy it?' (conversation, 2014.03.19)
exe

The pronoun tʰɤjtɕuwhen also occurs in the meaning `since when' to express impossible events as in ( ex:thAjtCu.pjANgrAl ).

exe

nɤ-wɯ kɯ-rɤrɟit jɤ-ari kɯ ɕi, tɤ-tɕɯ cʰɯ-kɯ-rɤrɟit tʰɤjtɕu pjɤ-ŋgrɤl? \\
3sg. poss -grandfather sbj: pcp -have.a.child aor -go[II] sfp qu indef. poss -son ipfv - sbj: pcp -have.a.child when ifr. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`[You say] that your father-in-law went away to give birth to a child, but since when can a man bear children?' (tAwa kWCqraR)
exe

The element tʰɤ- in the pronouns tʰɤjtɕuwhen and tʰɤstɯɣhow many is the bound state form of proto-Japhug *tʰi, the inherited form of the pronoun `what' (see § sec:tChi ). The element -tɕu in tʰɤjtɕuwhen is related to the locative tɕu (§ sec:core.locative ).

The prefixal form ɕɯstɤ- instead of tʰɤstɯ- is attested in one story told by Kunbzang Mtsho, probably influence from Tshobdun ( ex:CWstAJom ).

exe

nɤmkʰa ɕɯstɤ-ɟom ku-nɯ-tu kɯɣe?\\
sky how.many-fathom dubit - auto -exist sfp \\
`How many fathoms [high] is the sky?' (tAwa kWCqraR)
exe

ŋotɕuwhere

The interrogative pronoun ŋotɕuwhere and its variant form ŋoj (§ sec:locative.j ) can be used to ask either about a location ( ex:NotCu.kutWrAZi ), a direction towards (examples ex:NotCu.tWCe and ex:Noj.nari ) or from ( ex:NotCu.jAtWGenW ) a certain place. The second syllable of this pronoun -tɕu comes from the locative postposition tɕu, but the first part is etymologically obscure.

exe

ŋotɕu ku-tɯ-rɤʑi? \\
where pres. egoph -2-stay \\
`Where are you?' (Conversation)
exe

exe

ŋotɕu tɯ-ɕe? \\
where 2-go: fact \\
`Where are you going to?' (Common greeting used when one meets someone on the road)
exe

exe

qala ŋoj nɯ-ari? \\
rabbit where aor: west -go[II] \\
`Where did the rabbit go?' (qala2002)
exe

exe

nɯʑɤra ŋotɕu jɤ-tɯ-ɣe-nɯ? ŋotɕu ɕ-pɯ-tɯ-tu-nɯ? \\
2pl where aor -2-come[II]- pl where tral - pst. ipfv -2-exist- pl \\
`Where are you from? Where have you been?' (2003 sras)
exe

Likewise, with verbs of manipulation, ŋotɕu can be used both from questions about origin (as in ex:NotCu.jAtWGWt ) or destination.

`Where did you get it from, from where did you bring it?' (150831 renshen wawa-zh)
0006418#S48

With the determiner nɯ, the pronoun ŋotɕu means `which (of several places)', as in ( ex:NotCu.nW.Nu ) and ( ex:NotCu.nW.Wku.Nu ).

exe

kʰa raŋri ɣɯ ʑo ɯ-ftaʁ pjɤ-tu ɕti ma, tɕe ŋotɕu nɯ ŋu, ŋotɕu nɯ maʁ mɯ-pjɤ-saχsɤl. \\

`There was a mark on each of the houses, and one could not tell which [house] was [Alibaba's] and which was not.' (140512 alibaba-zh) 0003965#S183
exe

exe

qaprɤftsa nɯnɯ, cici jɤ-ari tɕe ɯ-ku ju-z-mɤke, cici tɕe ɯ-jme ju-z-mɤke ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe ŋotɕu nɯ ɯ-ku ŋu, ŋotɕu ɯ-jme ŋu, mɯ́j-saχsɤl \\

`The centipede, when it moves, sometimes its head goes first, sometimes its tail goes first, it is not each to tell which is its head and which is its tail.' (21-qaprAftsa)
0003582#S9

With generic nouns such as tɯrmeperson, ŋotɕu can serve as prenominal determiner to mean `a person from where', as in ( ex:NotCu.tWrme ).

ŋotɕu tɯrme tɯ-ŋu? \\
where person 2-be: fact \\
`Where are you from?' (2011-05-nyima)

The pronoun ŋotɕu however has non-spatial uses, in particular to ask about a particular individual (or a subgroup) within a group, as in ( ex:NotCu.Zo.nW ) and ( ex:NotCu.nW.Zo.sAndAG ).

exe

aʑo a-wa nɯ ŋotɕu ʑo nɯ ŋu kɯ? \\
1sg 1sg. poss -father dem where emph dem be: fact sfp \\

0006294#S158

summary:
The pronoun **tʰɤstɯɣ** has a conjunct form **tʰɤstɯ-** used with counted nouns, including Chinese borrowings and classifiers, and it can also occur with **tɤ-rʑaʁ** ‘time’ to ask about duration or clock time. Questions about time may also be formed with **tʰɤjtɕu** ‘when’, which can take the genitive and can also mean ‘since when’ in contexts expressing impossible events.  

The interrogative **ŋotɕu** ‘where’ and its variant **ŋoj** can ask about location, direction, or origin, and with **nɯ** it means ‘which (of several places)’. It also has non-spatial uses, including asking which individual or subgroup within a larger group is intended.

text:
mɤʑɯ ŋotɕu nɯ ʑo sɤndɤɣ mɤ-xsi ma \\
more where dem emph be.poisonous: fact neg -know: genr lnk \\
`(Apart from this one), I don't which other [mushrooms] are poisonous.' (23-grWBgrWBftsa) 0003602#S29
exe

In participial relatives with subject participle (in kɯ, see § sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ), ŋotɕuwhere can occur to express relativization of locative adjuncts, as in ( ex:NotCu.kWtu ); see § sec:interrogative.relative for a discussion of the other available constructions.

exe

kɯ-me nɯra qʰe me, ŋotɕu kɯ-tu nɯ qʰe kɯ-dɯ dɤn tu-ɬoʁ ŋu. \\
sbj: pcp -not.exist dem: pl lnk not.exist: fact where sbj: pcp -exist dem lnk sbj: pcp - emph be.many ipfv -come.out be: fact \\
`In [places] where it is not found, there is none, but in [places] where it is found, it grows in great number.' (21-jmAGni) 0003572#S87
exe

The pronoun ŋotɕuwhere is not exclusively used in question about place or direction, we also find it in the expression in ( ex:NotCu.YWNgrAl ).

exe

kɯki ŋotɕu ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl? \\
this where ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`How could this be possible?' (qajdoskAt 2002) 0003366#S32
exe

This sentence is used to express indignation (as in Chinese 哪有这样的道理？ ). In the story from which it is quoted, the husband says this sentence after his wife, quoting the words of a raven, says that she will have luck, not her husband, who thus reacts in anger.
summary: The passage explains that the interrogative pronoun ŋotɕu ‘where’ can be used not only in questions about place or direction, but also to relativize locative adjuncts in participial relative clauses with subject participles. It gives examples showing its use in clauses like “where it is not found/where it is found,” and notes that it can also appear in an idiomatic expression meaning “How could this be possible?”, used to express indignation.

text:
pronoun!indefinite
Japhug has a handful of indefinite pronouns, indicated in tab:indef.pronoun. They do not form a complete paradigm, and other constructions, in particular generic nouns and free relatives occur to express meanings for which no indefinite pronoun exists (see § sec:headless.relatives.quantification ).

There are no negative indefinite pronouns, and indefinite pronouns are almost never under the scope of negation (except in translations from Chinese). They also never occur as standard of comparison. Examples such as `In Freiburg the weather is better than anywhere in Germany'  would not be expressible with an indefinite pronoun.

ci `someone'
There is no indefinite pronoun `someone' in Japhug, but the numeral cione, which has many additional functions (indefinite article, modifier and partitive pronoun § sec:indef.article, § sec:other.pro, § sec:partitive.pronouns, § sec:identity.modifier, § sec:one.to.ten and § sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ), can express this meaning as in ( ci.kW.thaGWt ) and ( ci.kW.tWrdoR ).

exe

ɯ-lɤcu nɯtɕu qaʑo kɤtsa ci, ci kɯ kɤ-ntsɣe tʰa-ɣɯt ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -upstream dem: loc sheep parent.and.child indef one erg obj: pcp -sell aor:3 -bring sens -be \\
`Upstream from there, [there was] a ewe and her young, that someone had brought them to sell.' (2003 kandZislama)
exe

exe

tɯ-xpa tɕe ci kɯ tɯ-rdoʁ pjɤ-sat. \\
one-year lnk one erg one-piece ifr -kill \\
`One year, someone killed one [wild goose].' (22-qomndroN) 0003598#S37
exe

This use of ci is rare. The preferred construction to express the meaning `someone' involves the combination of the generic noun tɯrmeperson with the indefinite ci.

tʰɯcisomething
The indefinite pronoun tʰɯcisomething derives from the bound state of the proto-Japhug pronoun *tʰi `what' (see § sec:tChi above) with the indefinite determiner and numeral cione. Note that vowel alternation bleeds the sound change *tʰi tsʰi, otherwise a form such as $ $ tsʰɯci would have been expected. Its reduplicated form tʰɯtʰɤci has an irregular vocalism ɤ ($ $ tʰɯtʰɯci would have been expected instead).

It can designate specific referents, whose nature is known to the speaker but unknown to the addressee (as in ex:thWthAci.Zo.pjWtu ), Example ( ex:thWthAci.Zo.pjWtu ) is from a tale about a rabbit tricking a snow leopard; the difference of knowledge between the speaker and the addressee concerning the nature of the `something' is crucial to the plot..

exe

tu-nɯsman-a jɤɣ ri, mɤʑɯ ɯ-ftɕaka tsuku pjɯ-tu ra wo, tɕe tʰɯtʰɤci ʑo pjɯ-tu ra \\
ipfv -treat- 1sg be.possible: fact but yet 3sg. poss -manner some ipfv -exist be.needed: fact sfp lnk something emph ipfv -exist be.needed: fact \\
`I can treat [your illness], but yet another method is needed, something [else] is needed.' (140427 qala cho kWrtsAg) 0003852#S44
exe

The pronoun tʰɯci also occurs to refer to things whose name is unknown to the speaker (as in ex:gser.zhwa and ex:thWci.khWtsa ), even if he/she may have seen the object.

exe

tɕe nɯ nɯ-rte nɯ tɕʰi ŋu ma tʰɯci ci ``-ʑa" tu-ti ŋu, χsɤrʑa! \\
lnk dem 3pl. poss -hat dem what be: fact lnk something indef... ipfv -say be: fact golden.hat \\
`How is their hat [called], something in `ʑa'.... yes, གསེར་ཞྭ་gser.ʑʷagolden hat!' (30-mboR)
0003748#S93
exe

exe

tɕe tɤ-ndʑɯɣ nɯ kɯnɤ, tʰɯci kʰɯtsa kɯ-fse ɯ-ŋgɯ tu-rku-nɯ tɕe \\
lnk indef. poss -resin dem also something bowl sbj: pcp be.like 3sg -inside ipfv -put.in- pl lnk \\
`The resin, people put it into something like a bowl.'' (07-tAtho)
0003432#S40

It is also used for non-specific referents whose nature is entirely unknown, as in ( ex:thWthAci.tannWrkunW ) and ( ex:thWmqlaR ).

lnk yet something aor:3 - auto -put.in- pl sfp \\
`They also probably gave them something else.' (02-deluge 2012)

The reduplicated form tʰɯ tʰɤci, especially in combination with fsebe like, can also mean `whatever (happened)', as in ( ex:thWthAci.kWfse ).

The non-reduplicated form tʰɯci occurs in a correlative construction with the form mɯci to mean `this and that', an expression that is used especially in reporting speech from another person when the speaker does not want to bother reporting in details the exact words that have been said.

The pronoun tʰɯcisomething can also occur as head of a relative clause as in ( ex:thWci.khWtsa ) above with the relative tʰɯci kʰɯtsa kɯ-fse `something which is like a bowl'. With stative verbs in the relative as in ( ex:thWci.kApGWlu ), this construction has a low degree meaning `a little X'.

summary:
Japhug has only a small, incomplete set of indefinite pronouns, and other constructions such as generic nouns and free relatives are used where no pronoun exists. There are no negative indefinite pronouns, and these pronouns do not normally appear under negation or as standards of comparison.

The numeral cione can sometimes express ‘someone,’ though this use is rare and the preferred form combines the generic noun *tɯrmeperson* with indefinite *ci*. The pronoun *tʰɯci* ‘something’ can refer to known-but-unnamed, unknown, or non-specific referents, can form correlative expressions meaning ‘this and that,’ and can head relative clauses, sometimes yielding a low-degree meaning with stative verbs.

text:
tɕe kɯ-wɣrum ɯ-ŋgɯz kɯnɤ tʰɯci kɯ-ɤpɣɯlu kɯ-fse ci ŋu tɕe, \\
lnk sbj: pcp -be.white 3sg. poss -inside: loc also something sbj: pcp -greyish sbj: pcp -be.like indef be: fact lnk \\
`[Silver] is white with a little greyish colour.' (30-Com)
0003736#S173
exe

The reduplicated form of the indefinite pronoun tʰɯtʰɤci can be used as an interrogative pronoun, as in ( ex:thWthAci.totia ). This construction is similar in meaning to Chinese 一些什么 yīxiēshénmewhat kinds of things, and is attested in particular with the verbs tisay and rabe needed. By using this form, the speaker implies that the addressee necessarily knows the answer to the question. For instance, in ( ex:thWthAci.totia ), a sentence from a text enumerating the mountain names in Kamnyu, the names had been written before hand on a piece of paper, and I was reading them one by one to Tshendzin; given the fact that the name had been written down, it was obvious that I necessarily knew the answer to that question (on the use of the Inferential in this example, see § sec:inf.1person ).

exe

nɯ ɯ-pa tʰɯtʰɤci to-ti-a? \\
dem 3sg. poss -down something ifr -say- 1sg \\
`What did I say after that?' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004055#S69
exe

There are very marginal examples of tʰɯcisomething used as an indefinite prenominal determiner (§ sec:indefinite ).

The pronoun tʰɯcisomething can take various modifiers, for instance the identity modifier kɯmaʁother (§ sec:identity.modifier ) as in ( ex:kWmaR.thWci ).

exe

ki mbro ki ɲɯ-kɤ-ntsɣe tɕe, [kɯmaʁ tʰɯci] ɲɯ-kɤ-sɤndu to-nɯkrɤz-ndʑi \\

`They discussed about selling their horse, and exchanging it for something else.' (150822 laoye zuoshi zongshi duide-zh)
0006298#S41
exe

No example of tʰɯci with topic markers contributing to mark definiteness such as nɯ or iɕqʰa (§ sec:definiteness ) have been found in the corpus.

tsʰitsukuwhatever
The pronoun tsʰitsukuwhatever combines the interrogative pronoun tsʰiwhat (replaced by tɕʰiwhat, a borrowing from Tibetan, in Kamnyu Japhug, but still attested in Mangi village, see § sec:tChi above) with the mid-scalar quantifier tsukusome (see § sec:tsuku; also found as a partitive pronoun, § sec:partitive.pronouns ). Unlike tʰɯcisomething, is not used for specific referents. Example ( ex:tshitsuku.kuwGsqa ) illustrates its most common use. The variant form tʰitsuku, without the sound change *tʰi tsʰi, is also used by speakers of the Kamnyu dialect.

exe

kɤ-nɯ-βlɯ tɕe ɕkrɤz wuma ʑo pe ma nɯnɯ, nɯnɯ ɣɯ ɯ-smɯmba nɯ sɤɕke, tɕendɤre tsʰitsuku kú-wɣ-sqa tɕe, ʑaʑa ʑo ku-ɣɤ-smi cʰa, tsʰitsuku tú-wɣ-sɯ-ɤla tɕe, ʑaʑa tu-sɯ-ɤle cʰa. \\

`For burning, oak is very good, the flames [from its wood] are very hot, whatever one cooks, it cooks it quickly, whatever one boils, it boils it quickly.' (08-CkrAz) 0003444#S2

In many cases, it is better translated as `all kinds of things', as in ( ex:tshitsuku.YWznAme ).

As other indefinite pronouns, tsʰitsukuwhatever is not normally used with negation, but such sentences do occur in the corpus in translations from Chinese, as ( ex:tshitsuku.mWtoti ). They are not idiomatic Japhug, and only marginally grammatical.

ɕɯmɤɕɯwhoever, anybody
There is no indefinite pronoun for human referents `somebody' in Japhug corresponding to tʰɯcisomething -- a generic noun with the indefinite determiner cione such as tɯrme ci `a man' is used instead. There is nevertheless a free choice pronoun ɕɯmɤɕɯwhoever, anybody (see on the differences with universal quantifiers), which, however, is not very common. As example ( ex:CWmACW.kW ) shows, it can take the ergative kɯ, and the verb receives plural indexation (§ sec:genr.3pl ).

exe

tɕaχkɤr kʰɯtsa nɯ ʁo tʰam qʰe ɕɯmɤɕɯ kɯ ku-nɯ-ntɕʰoz-nɯ ɕti \\

ciscʰizsomewhere
The indefinite pronoun ciscʰizsomewhere comprises the indefinite cione and the approximate locative (s)cʰiz (see § sec:approximate.locative ). It occurs with or without the locative postposition ri, as in ( ex:cischiz ) and ( ex:cischiz.ri ). It can refer to static location, or motion from or towards a direction.

`One attaches [their noseband] somewhere, like on a nail, on a pillar.' (150902 kAxtCAr) 0006308#S7

`One puts it vertically somewhere.' (14-tasa) 0003510#S58

summary:
The passage describes several indefinite and interrogative pronouns in Japhug and their uses. The reduplicated indefinite pronoun tʰɯtʰɤci can function as an interrogative pronoun implying that the addressee knows the answer, while tʰɯci is an indefinite pronoun meaning ‘something’ that can take modifiers like kɯmaʁ ‘other’ but is not found with definiteness-marking topic particles.  

It also introduces tsʰitsuku ‘whatever,’ formed from the interrogative pronoun and a quantifier, which usually means ‘all kinds of things’ and is not used for specific referents; negated uses are marginal and largely influenced by Chinese. Finally, it notes that Japhug lacks a common indefinite pronoun for human referents ‘somebody,’ using a generic noun instead, but it does have the less common free-choice pronoun ɕɯmɤ�

subsection: Interrogative pronouns used as free-choice indefinites
text:
Non-specific free-choice  indefinite referents can be expressed by interrogative pronouns in Japhug. Constructions where this function is attested include correlatives (§ sec:interrogative.relative ), as in ( ex:NotCu.lAtWrNgW ) and universal concessive conditionals (§ sec:universal.concessive.conditional ) as in ( ex:thAjtCu.fsaN ).

exe

a-pɯwɯ, [ŋotɕu lɤ-tɯ-rŋgɯ ʑo qʰe], nɯtɕu rɤʑi-tɕi ŋu ma, \\
1sg -donkey where aor: upstream -2-lay.down emph lnk dem: loc stay: fact - 1du be: fact because \\
`My donkey, we will stay wherever you lay down.' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S36
exe

exe

[tʰɤjtɕu fsaŋ kɤ-ta tɤ-ra] ʑo tɕe nɯnɯ tu-βlɯ-nɯ tɕe, \\
when fumigation inf -put aor -be.needed emph lnk dem ipfv -burn- pl lnk \\
`Whenever there is need to make fumigations, they burn it.' (15-YaBrWG)
0003516#S28
exe

This meaning also occurs in infinitival subordinate clauses, in particular in the expression tɕʰi kɤ-cʰa `do whatever $X$ can to $Y$', as in example ( ex:tChi.kAcha.Zo ).

exe

[tɕʰi kɤ-cʰa] ʑo cʰɯ-pʰɯt-nɯ, \\
what inf -can emph ipfv -remove- pl \\
`People do whatever they can to remove [this plant].' (12-Zmbroko) 0003490#S116
exe

In both correlative relatives and universal concessive conditionals, the interrogative pronoun often occurs with verb with partial reduplication on the last syllable of the stem and/or the autive nɯ- prefix (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous, § sec:universal.concessive.conditional ).

With tɕʰiwhat, this construction expresses the meaning `whatever; no matter what' in intransitive subject ( ex:tChi.pWnWNWNu ), object ( ex:tChi.tAtWnWtWtWt ) or semi-object ( ex:tChi.kWstWstua, see § sec:ditransitive.secundative ) functions.

exe

lú-wɣ-sti tɕe tɕe nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ [tɕʰi pɯ-nɯ-ŋɯ ŋu] nɯ ɲɯ-mɲɤt mɯ́j-cʰa \\
ipfv - inv -block lnk lnk dem 3sg -inside what pst. ipfv - auto -be dem ipfv -be.spoiled neg: sens -can \\
`One seals [its opening] and whatever [food] is inside will not be spoiled.' (150828 kodAt)
0006392#S13
exe

exe

[tɕʰi tɤ-tɯ-nɯ-tɯ tɯt] ʑo ju-ɣi ɕti \\
what aor -2- auto -say[II] emph ipfv -come be. aff: fact \\
`Whatever you say will come.' (2003 tWxtsa)
exe

exe

nɤʑo tɕʰi kɯ-stɯ stu-a ʑo ŋu \\
2sg what 2 1-do.like: fact - 1sg emph be: fact \\
`Whatever you do to me [will be fine].' (28-qajdoskAt) 0003718#S38
exe

With ɕɯwho, the construction means `whoever; regardless of who; no matter who'. Examples are found with the non-specific referent in intransitive subject ( ex:CW.pWnWNWNu ), transitive subject ( ex:CW.kW.panWmtWmtonW ), or oblique argument ( ex:CW.GW.nWnWkhWkhota ) functions. Note that it often occurs with plural indexation.

exe

tɯsqar nɯ kɯrɯ tɯrme ra mɤ-kɯ-rga maka ʑo me, [ɕɯ pɯ-nɯ-ŋɯ ŋu] ʑo, tɯsqar a-pɯ-tu qʰe, tɕendɤre, nɯ-kɤ-ndza tu-rtaʁ ɕti, \\
tsampa dem Tibetan person pl neg - sbj: pcp -like at.all emph not.exist: fact who pst. ipfv - auto -be emph tsampa irr - ipfv -exist lnk lnk 3pl. poss - obj: pcp -eat ipfv -be.enough be: aff: fact \\
`Among Tibetan people, everybody likes tsampa (`there is no one who does not like it'), no matter who, if they have tsampa, they have enough to eat.' (2002 tWsqar2)
exe

tɕe [ɕɯ kɯ pa-nɯ-mtɯ mto-nɯ] ʑo kɯki ɣɯ, nɯ-kʰa ɣɯ nɯ-mɯntoʁ nɯ cʰondɤre nɯ-ɕoŋpʰu nɯra tɕe, mɤʑɯ nɯ-<cai> nɯra, pjɯ-ɣɤmɯ-nɯ tɕe, \\
lnk who erg aor:3 -see- pl emph dem. prox gen 3pl. poss -house gen 3pl. poss -flower dem comit 3pl. poss -tree dem: pl lnk yet 3pl. poss -vegetable dem: pl ipfv -praise- pl lnk \\
`Whoever saw it, the flowers and the trees and the vegetables of their house, they praised it.' (150824 yuanding-zh) 0006270#S29
