tɤɕime ri tɯ-rdoʁ ma me, tɕendɤre nɯʑo [ɕɯ ɣɯ nɯ-nɯ-kʰɯ kʰo-t-a] ʑo mɯ́j-nɯtɯtʂaŋ ɕti tɕe, \\
lady also one-piece apart.from not.exist: fact lnk 2pl who gen aor - auto -give- pst: tr - 1sg emph neg: sens -be.fair be. aff: fact lnk \\
`There is only one princess, and regardless of whom among you all I give her hand to, it will be unfair.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S223
exe

Universal concessive conditionals are found with the pronoun ŋotɕuwhere, with the meaning `no matter where, wherever' (location or direction from or to), as in ( ex:nWGtWta ). This free-choice indefinite meaning of ŋotɕu in also found in the delocutive expression ŋɤtɕɯkɤti+kʰɯbe obedient, where the interrogative pronoun occurs in bound state form ŋɤtɕɯ- with the infinitive of tisay (§ sec:lexicalized.velar.inf ).

exe

[ŋotɕu nɯ́-wɣ-tɯ ta] ʑo kɯpɤz ɲɯ-βze ɲɯ-ɕti\\
where ipfv - inv - indefinite put emph type.of.bug ipfv -grow sens -be. aff \\
`Bugs will grow wherever you put [the meat].' (28-kWpAz) 0003714#S21
exe

No example of multiple partitive use of interrogatives (as in French qui apportait un fromage, qui un sac de noix, ) is attested in the data at hand; mid-scalar quantifiers such as tsukusome occur instead as partitive pronouns (§ sec:partitive.pronouns ).
summary: Japhug can use interrogative pronouns as non-specific free-choice indefinites, especially in correlatives and universal concessive conditionals, and also in some infinitival subordinate clauses. Forms like **tɕʰi** ‘what’, **ɕɯ** ‘who’, and **ŋotɕu** ‘where’ mean ‘whatever’, ‘whoever’, or ‘wherever’, often appearing with partial verb reduplication and/or the autive **nɯ-** prefix, and they can function as subjects, objects, or oblique arguments. The passage also notes that no examples of multiple partitive interrogative use are attested in the data.

text:
universal quantifier
Several quantifiers meaning `all' exist in Japhug (§ sec:universal.quant ). Among them, kɤsɯfseall can be used in the meaning `everybody', as in example ( ex:kAsWfse.kW ).

exe

kɤsɯfse kɯ ʑo ta-nɯ maʁ \\
all erg emph put: fact - pl not.be: fact \\
`Not everybody puts it.' (160706 thotsi)
0006133#S21
exe

The less common form mɲɯrɯrieverybody, each person (from Tibetan མི་རེ་རེ་mi.re.reeach man also serves as a universal quantifier, as in ( ex:mYWrWri ).

exe

mɲɯrɯri kɯ `nɯnɯ ɲɯ-pe' ntsɯ to-ti-nɯ \\
everybody erg dem sens -be.good always ifr -say- pl \\
`Everybody said `It is nice!'' (140521 huangdi de xinzhuang)
0004047#S192
exe

There are several words meaning `everywhere', such as aʁɤndɯndɤteverywhere, but they are treated as adverbs rather than pronouns (§ sec:everywhere ).
summary: Japhug has several quantifiers meaning “all,” including **kɤsɯfse**, which can also mean “everybody,” and the less common **mɲɯrɯri**, meaning “everybody” or “each person,” which likewise functions as a universal quantifier. Words meaning “everywhere,” such as **aʁɤndɯndɤ**, are treated as adverbs rather than pronouns.

text:
pronoun!partitive partitive
The mid-scalar quantifier tsukusome is used both as a noun determiner (§ sec:tsuku ) and as a partitive pronoun, taking case markers and determiners. This construction expresses a meaning close to that obtained by combining a relative clause with an existential verb (`there is someone who...', § sec:existential.basic ), as can be seen in ( ex:zgri.mWrkuj ) where both constructions are used one after the other.

exe

tsuku kɯ zgri tu-ti-nɯ ŋu, tsuku kɯ mɯrkuj tu-ti-nɯ ŋu. mɯrkuj tu-kɯ-ti tɕi tu, zgri tu-kɯ-ti tɕi tu ma, \\
some erg plant.name ipfv -say- pl some erg plant.name ipfv -say- pl plant.name ipfv - sbj: pcp -say also exist: fact plant.name ipfv - sbj: pcp -say also exist: fact lnk \\
`Some call it zgri, some call it mɯrkuj; there are people who call it mɯrkuj, and also people who call it zgri.' (19-qachGa mWntoR)
0003546#S154
exe

The quantifier tsukusome used as a pronoun generally refers to humans in the corpus, but ( ex:tsuku.YaR ) shows that it can also denote plants for instance.

exe

tsuku ɲaʁ, tsuku aqarŋɯrŋe, \\
some be.black: fact some be.light.yellow: fact \\
`Some are black, some are light yellow.' (140505 stonka mWntoR) 0003917#S5
exe

Numerals (in particular cione) and also counted nouns (§ sec:CN.quantifier ) can be used without head noun with a partitive meaning `one of (a group)' as in ( ex:ci.GW ) and ( ex:ci.thWkWrgAz ).

exe

ci ɣɯ tɤ-tɕɯ, ci ɣɯ tɕʰeme tɯ tɤ-tu nɤ, ʁzɤmi ku-kɤ-sɯ-βzu \\
one gen indef. poss -son one gen indef. poss -son cond aor -exist lnk husband.and.wife ipfv - inf - caus -make \\
`If one of them has a boy, and the other one has a girl, let us make them husband and wife.' (2003 zrAntCW)
exe

exe

ci tʰɯ-kɯ-rgɯ rgɤz ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe, ci kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe, \\
one aor - sbj: pcp - emph be.old C-be. aff lnk one aor - sbj: pcp - emph be.old C-be. aff lnk \\
`One of them has grown very old, and one of them is very small.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

This partitive function is also found in combination with personal pronouns, as in ( ex:nWZora.ci ).

exe

nɯʑora ci kɯ a-tɯci ci ju-tɯ-ɣɯt-nɯ ɯ́-jɤɣ \\
2pl one erg 1sg. poss - indef. poss -water a.little ipfv -2-bring- pl qu -be.possible: fact \\
`Could one of you bring me some water?' (150904 zhongli-zh)
0006348#S47
exe
summary: The quantifier *tsukusome* functions both as a noun determiner and as a partitive pronoun, and in the latter use it can take case markers and determiners. As a pronoun it usually refers to humans in the corpus, though it can also refer to plants, and its partitive meaning is shared by numerals and counted nouns used without a head noun, as well as by personal pronouns.

text:
pronoun!distributive distributive
The pronoun ʑakaeach his own and its variant ʑakastakaeach his own occur as pronouns, especially as possessors in an possessive existential construction. It can be correlated with a third singular ɯ- ( ex:Zaka.WmdoR ) or a third plural nɯ- ( ex:Zaka.nWrmi ) prefix on the possessum.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ li qaʑo nɯ kɯ-ɲaʁ tu, kɯ-wɣrum tu, kɯ-ɤɣɯnɯɕɯr kɯ-fse tu, kɯ-ɤrŋɯlɯz tu, tɕe nɯnɯ ʑaka ɯ-mdoʁ tu ma \\
lnk dem again sheep dem sbj: pcp -be.black exist: fact sbj: pcp -be.white exist: fact sbj: pcp -be.reddish sbj: pcp -be.like exist: fact sbj: pcp -be.blueish exist: fact lnk dem each.his.own 3sg. poss -colour exist: fact lnk \\
`There are black sheep, white ones, reddish ones, blueish ones, each has his own colour (they come in all types of colors).' (05-qaZo) 0003404#S58
exe

exe

li ʑaka nɯ-rmi tu, \\
again each.his.own 3pl. poss -name exist: fact \\
`Each have their own names.' (150903 tWmNu) 0006280#S10
exe

The pronoun ʑaka is built by combining the bound state of the pronominal root -ʑo (§ sec:pers.pronouns ) with the root -ka found in the distributive modifier tɯkaeach (which follows possessums, see § sec:raNri ).
summary: The distributive pronoun ʑaka, with the variant ʑakastaka, means “each his own” and is used especially as a possessor in possessive existential constructions. It can appear with a third-singular ɯ- or third-plural nɯ- prefix on the possessum, and it is formed from the bound state of the pronominal root -ʑo plus the root -ka found in the distributive modifier tɯka.

text:
pronoun!identity
The words kɯmaʁother and kɯɕteother occur as prenominal determiners (see § sec:identity.modifier, also for a discussion on the etymology of the former), but it can also be used as a pronoun and take determiners as in ( ex:kWmaR.nWra ).

exe

ma kɯmaʁ nɯra aj mɯ́j-sɯχsal-a ri, tɤkʰepɣɤtɕɯ nɯ sɯχsal-a \\
lnk other dem: pl 1sg neg: sens -recognize but bird.sp dem recognize: fact - 1sg \\
`The other ones I don't recognize them, but the tɤkʰepɣɤtɕɯ bird, I do recognize it.' (23-scuz)
0003612#S43
exe

The interpretation of both kɯmaʁother and kɯɕteother can be locative `somewhere else' as in ( ex:kWmaR.nWtWtat ), when the main verb ( taput in this example) selects a goal or a locative adjunct (since locative noun phrases are often unmarked, § absolutive.goal, § absolutive.locative ).

exe

kɯmaʁ/kɯɕte nɯ-tɯ-ta-t ŋu ɯ-maʁ? \\
other aor -2-put- tr: pst be: fact qu -not.be: fact \\
`Did you put it somewhere else?' (elicitated1)
exe

Adding the indefinite determiner cione is necessary in this context to convey the meaning `something else':

exe

kɯmaʁ/kɯɕte ci nɯ-tɯ-ta-t ŋu ɯ-maʁ? \\
other indef aor -2-put- tr: pst be: fact qu -not.be: fact \\
`Did you put something else?' (elicitated1)
exe

Example ( ex:kWmaR.ci.juGWt ) illustrates that both kɯmaʁ and kɯmaʁ ci can occur in the meaning `another one' in some contexts (here with the verb ɕarsearch).

exe

χsɯ-sŋi mɤ-kɯ-tsu qʰe li kɯmaʁ ci ju-ɣɯt qʰe, li ɯ-zda ɲɯ-nɯ-ɕar ɲɯ-ɕti. tɕe nɯnɯ maka kɯjka nɯ ŋɤn ma, ɯ-zda nɯ nɯ-me ɯ-qʰu mɤ-kɯ-nɤrʑaʁ tɕe kɯmaʁ ɲɯ-ɕar ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe mɯ́j-pe tu-ti-nɯ ŋgrɤl. \\
three-day neg - inf: stat -pass lnk again other indef ipfv -bring lnk again 3sg. poss -companion ipfv - auto -search sens -be. aff lnk dem completely pyrrhocorax dem be.evil: fact lnk 3sg. poss -companion dem aor -not.exist 3sg. poss -after neg - inf: stat -spend.time lnk other ipfv -search sens -be. aff lnk neg: sens -be.good ipfv -say- pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`Not even three days [after hunters kill its mate, the Pyrrhocorax ] brings another one, it looks for another mate. People say that the Pyrrhocorax is not nice, because not long after its mate has died, it looks for another one, it is not good.' (22-CAGpGa) 0003586#S79
exe

The indefinite cione combined with the demonstrative determiner nɯ (or nɯnɯ ) has the meaning `the other one' (the definite counterpart of kɯmaʁother), as in ( ex:ci.nW.kW ) and ( ex:tWrdoR.ci.nW ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-jaʁ kɯ ki tu-ste lu-z-naʁje ɲɯ-ŋu ri, tɕe ci nɯ kɯ ɯ-jaʁ ku-mtsɯɣ ɲɯ-ɕti qʰe, \\
lnk 3sg. poss -hand erg dem: prox ipfv -do.like[III] ipfv -reach.into[III] sens -be but lnk indef dem erg 3sg. poss -hand ipfv -bite sens -be. aff: fact lnk \\
`[The cat]$_i$ reaches with its$_i$ paw [into the hole] like this, but the other one (the weasel) bites its$_i$ paw.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S47
exe

exe

ɯ-me ʁnɯz pjɤ-tu tɕe, tɯ-rdoʁ nɯ χsɤrlɤsmɤn pjɤ-rmi, ci nɯ rŋɯlɤsmɤn pjɤ-rmi tɕe, \\
3sg. poss -daughter two ifr. ipfv -exist lnk one-piece dem gser.la.sman ifr. ipfv -be.called indef dem dngul.la.sman ifr. ipfv -be.called lnk \\
`He had two daughters, one of them was called Gser.la.sman, and the other Dngul.la.sman.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

Alternatively to the construction in ( ex:tWrdoR.ci.nW ) with tɯ-rdoʁone piece and ci nɯ to express the meaning `one of them.... and the other...', it is possible to use ci nɯ two times in the same sentence to refer to more than one persons or animals, as in ( ex:ci.nW.2 ).

exe

tɕe ci nɯnɯ ju-ɕe ɯ-kʰɯkʰa ci nɯ kɯ ɯ-pu tu-ndze, cʰɯ-rɤɕi. \\
lnk indef dem ipfv -go 3sg -while indef dem erg 3sg. poss -intestine ipfv -eat[III] ipfv -pull \\
`While one of the two (i.e. the prey) is (still) going, the other one (i.e. the predator) eats and pulls its intestine.' (20-RmbroN)
0003560#S69
exe

The dual ci nɯni `the other two' and plural ci nɯra `the other ones' are also attested, as in ( ex:ci.nWni ), showing that ci is here completely bleached of numeral meaning.

exe

ci nɯni ɣɯ nɯ, ndʑi-ta-mar rɟɤɣi pjɤ-ŋu tɕe tɕe nɯnɯ ɯʑo kɯ to-ndza \\
indef dem: du gen dem 3du. poss - indef. poss -butter tsampa ipfv. ifr -be: fact lnk lnk dem 3sg erg ifr -eat \\
`The tsampa of the other two [sisters] was butter tsampa, and she ate it.' (2003-kWBRa)
0006346#S67
exe

It is also possible in this function to use other modifiers such as numerals, as in ( ex:ci.XsWm ) with χsɯmthree.

exe

iɕqʰa ci χsɯm nɯ mɯ-jo-ɣi-nɯ kɯ \\
the.aforementioned indef three dem neg - ifr -come- pl erg \\
`The three other ones, without coming, (said...)' (140515 congming de wusui xiaohai-zh)
0003998#S44
exe

As a prenominal determiner, ci also has the meaning `the other $X$' (see § sec:identity.modifier ).

Finally, the noun tɯrmeperson (which also occurs to express generic person, § sec:tWrme.generic ) can be used in the meaning `someone else' or `other people', in particular in genitival constructions as in ( ex:tWrme.WkhApa.zW ).

exe

tɯrme ɯ-kʰɤpa zɯ, ki kɯ-fse tɯ-rʑaʁ lu-znɯfsoʁspat-a ku-omdzɯ-a. \\
people 3sg. poss -yard loc dem. prox sbj: pcp -be.like one-night ipfv -do.the.whole.night- 1sg ipfv -sit- 1sg \\
`I would spend an entire night from dusk till dawn sitting in someone else's animal yard.' (2010-histoire09)
exe
summary: The passage explains that **kɯmaʁ** and **kɯɕte** can function not only as prenominal determiners but also as pronouns. As pronouns, they can mean **“the other one(s)”**, **“something else”**, or in some contexts **“somewhere else,”** with definiteness or indefiniteness marked by combinations with **ci** and **nɯ**; the text also shows dual and plural forms, indicating that **ci** has lost its numeral meaning in this function. It further notes that **tɯrme** can be used for **“someone else”** or **“other people,”** especially in genitive constructions.

text:
pronoun!demonstrative demonstrative!pronoun
There are two basic demonstratives in Japhug, the proximal kithis and the distal one nɯthat, which also occur as demonstrative determiners (see § sec:demonstrative.determiners ). tab:dem.pronoun illustrates the various demonstrative pronouns that are derived from these basic forms, with reduplicated and emphatic forms. There is in addition a cataphoric pronoun nɤki, discussed in § sec:cataph.pron.

Plural and dual forms, as in the case of determiners, are formed by adding -ra and -ni suffixes (§ sec:number.determiners ) to the demonstrative root, which undergoes bound state change i ɯ in the case of proximal demonstratives. Plural forms are given in the table; dual forms are attested but rare and can be predicted ( kɯnithese two etc).

The distal demonstratives, being the default forms, are simply glossed as dem in the examples: only proximal demonstratives are explicitely marked as such in the glosses.
summary:
Japhug has two basic demonstrative pronouns: the proximal **kithis** and the distal **nɯthat**, both of which can also function as demonstrative determiners. In addition, there is a cataphoric pronoun **nɤki**, and demonstrative pronouns can be formed with reduplication and emphasis.

Plural and dual forms are created by adding the suffixes **-ra** and **-ni** to the demonstrative root, with a bound-state change for proximal forms. Distal demonstratives are treated as the default and are usually glossed simply as **dem**, while proximal forms are explicitly marked.

text:
demonstrative!anaphoric
The basic demonstratives ki and nɯ are less often used as pronouns that the other ones (they mainly occur as determiners). They nevertheless do occur in all syntactic functions, including object (in particular with the verb tisay, as in ex:nW.toti, where it refers to words that have been previously told to another animal), and semi-object (in particular with the verb studo like as in ex:ki.tuste ).

exe

li nɯ to-ti ri, \\
again dem ifr -say lnk \\
`[Gesar] said the same thing to the [snow leopard].' (gesar)
exe

exe

ɯ-mu nɯ ku-rqoʁ tɕe ki tu-ste tɕe \\
3sg. poss -mother dem ipfv -hug lnk dem: prox ipfv -do.like[III] lnk \\
`It hugs its mother like that.' (19-GzW)
0003536#S29
exe

The distal demonstratives nɯ and nɯnɯ serve as anaphoric pronouns with any type of referent, including humans, but also abstract concepts, inanimate objects or plants as in ( ex:nWnW.kW.smi ), though as mentioned in § sec:pers.pronouns, third person pronouns such as ɯʑohe can also have inanimate antecedents.

exe

tʂʰa kɤ-nɯ-ta tɤ-ra, smi kɤ-βlɯ tɤ-ra pɯ-nɯ-ŋu, tʰamaka sko-nɯ pɯ-nɯ-ŋu, tɕe nɯnɯ kɯ smi tu-sɯ-tɕɤt-nɯ. \\
tea inf - auto -put aor -be.needed fire aor -burn aor -be.needed pst. ipfv - auto -be tobacco smoke: fact - pl pst. ipfv - auto -be lnk dem erg fire ipfv - caus -take.out- pl \\
`When they need to boil tea, to make a fire or smoke tobacco, people light up the fire with it.' (15-babW) 0003512#S209
exe

When a third person mentioned in a discussion is present, the pronoun ɯʑohe is not the optimal way of referring to him/her, and a proximal demonstrative, in particular the reduplicated kɯkithis, is used instead. It can occur to present someone to someone else ( ex:kWki.aslama ) (note that a similar usage exists in Western languages such as English in the same context) and even to talk about the actions of this person, as in ( ex:kWki.kW.taBzu ) and ( ex:kWki.nW.ftsWntCi ).

exe

kɯki a-slama ŋu \\
dem. prox 1sg. poss -student be: fact \\
`This a [former] student of mine.' (conversation 140510)
exe

exe

kɯki kɯ ta-βzu? \\
dem. prox erg aor:3 -make \\
`Did she make it?' (conversation 140510)
exe

As other pronouns (see § sec:pers.pronouns ), demonstrative pronouns can take the demonstrative determiner nɯ, as in ( ex:kWki.nW.ftsWntCi ).

exe

mɯ mɤ-pɯ-jɤɣ tɕe mɤ-ɣi-tɕi ma kɯki nɯ fstɯn-tɕi ra ma tɕi-βɣe ɯ-ku tʰɯ-kɯ-ɣɤrndi \\
cond neg - pst. ipfv -be.acceptable lnk neg -come: fact - 1du lnk dem: prox dem serve: fact - 1du be.needed: fact lnk 1du. poss -orphan 3sg. poss -head aor - sbj: pcp -support \\
`If it is not possible [to take the old man with us] we will not come, as we have to serve him, he is the one who adopted us orphans when we were in dire straits.' (The old man is presumably present when this sentence is uttered) (2003nyima2)
exe

The emphatic demonstrative pronouns (which are also used as determiners, § sec:demonstrative.determiners ) are built by combining the reduplicated forms of demonstratives with the third person possessive prefix ɯ-. They are about fifty times less common than corresponding reduplicated forms, but their function is essentially the same. In ( ex:WnWnW.kW ), ɯnɯnɯ is an anaphoric pronoun whose antecedent is present in the immediately preceding clause.

exe

tɕe ɯ-rqʰu kɯ-fse ci ɣɤʑu tɕe, ɯnɯnɯ kɯ ɯ-rdu nɯ tu-ɕɯ-fkaβ kɯ-fse ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -hull sbj: pcp -be.like indef exist: sens lnk dem: emph erg 3sg. poss -eyeball dem ipfv - caus -cover sbj: pcp -be.like sens -be \\
`It has something like a membrane, and it covers its eyeball with it.' (description of the nictitating membrane of birds, 140513 sWNgWrmABja)
0003983#S9
exe

The demonstrative nɯ may not refer anaphorically to a particular entity, but also to an entire situation, as in ( ex:nW.pjArAZindZi ) where it occurs as an adjunct in absolutive form, meaning `this way, like that' (in another version of the same story, we find nɯ kɯ-fse `like that' instead of nɯ in the same context).

exe

nɯnɯ ɯ-mŋu nɯtɕu zɯ li, qapri, nɤki, kɯ-ɲaʁ nɯ kɯ kɯ-wɣrum nɯ ɯ-qiɯ ʑo cʰɤ-mqlaʁ tɕe nɯ pjɤ-rɤʑi-ndʑi. \\
dem 3sg. poss -bank dem: loc loc again snake filler sbj: pcp -be.black dem erg sbj: pcp -be.white dem 3sg. poss -half emph ifr -swallow lnk dem ifr. ipfv -stay- du \\
`On the bank [of the lake], there was again a black snake that had swallowed half of a white snake, and they were staying [stuck] like that.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S99
exe
summary: The basic demonstratives ki and nɯ are mainly determiners, but they can also function as pronouns in all syntactic roles, including object and semi-object positions. Distal demonstratives nɯ and nɯnɯ serve as anaphoric pronouns for humans, abstract concepts, inanimate objects, and plants, while proximal reduplicated forms like kɯkithis are used especially when referring to a person who is present; emphatic demonstrative pronouns are formed by adding the third person possessive prefix ɯ- to reduplicated forms and have essentially the same anaphoric function. The demonstrative nɯ can also refer not just to entities but to entire situations, meaning ‘this way, like that.’

text:
demonstrative!cataphoric
demonstrative!medial
summary: The passage labels demonstratives by two descriptive categories: cataphoric and medial. It does not provide further explanation or examples of these forms.

text:
In addition to the proximal and distal demonstratives, there is a considerably rarer medial demonstrative nɤki, in examples such as ( ex:nAki.nWtɕu ) and ( ex:nAki.nW.aZWG ), which means `your place, near you', as opposed to `here'.

exe

kutɕu ko-qanɯ pʰoʁpʰoʁ ʑo, nɤki nɯtɕu ɯ-kó-qanɯ? \\
dem. prox: loc ifr -be.dark idph (II):completely emph dem: medial dem: loc qu - ifr -be.dark \\
`Here (in Mbarkhams) it is already dark, is it [also] dark at your place (in Paris)?' (phone conversation, 14.12.24, referring to the time lag between Paris and Mbarkham)
exe

exe

ki kɯra ɲɯ-kʰam-a tɕe nɤki nɯ aʑɯɣ nɯ-kʰɤm je \\
dem: prox dem: prox: pl ipfv -give- 1sg lnk dem: medial dem 1sg: gen imp -give sfp \\
`I give [you] these [toys], give me that one.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S116
exe

The medial demonstrative nɤki can be historically analyzed as a combination of the proximal demonstrative ki with the second person possessive nɤ-. However, equivalent dual or plural forms such as $ $ ndʑiki or $ $ nɯki are impossible (the equivalent meaning can only be expressed with the dative, using a form such as ndʑiʑo ndʑi-pʰe `at your$_du$ place', § sec:dative ).
summary: Besides the proximal and distal demonstratives, the language has a much rarer medial demonstrative, **nɤki**, which refers to a place near the addressee, as in “your place, near you,” rather than “here.” It can be historically analyzed as **ki** plus the second-person possessive prefix **nɤ-**, but comparable dual or plural forms are not possible; those meanings must instead be expressed with the dative construction.

text:
In addition to its function as a medial demonstrative (§ sec:medial.dem.pro ), the demonstrative nɤki also occurs to express cataphoric reference. It occurs especially when the speaker hesitates and uses it as a filler, followed by a clause with the same verb (examples ex:nAki.YWNu and ex:nAki.YAXtAr ) or just with the same auxiliary ( ex:nAki.Nu.Ci ).

exe

<luohan> nɯnɯ nɤki ɲɯ-ŋu loβ, skɯ ɲɯ-ŋu loβ \\
Arhat dem dem: cataph sens -be sfp statue sens -be sfp \\
`An Arhat is... it is Buddhist statue.' (150829 jidian)
0006338#S124
exe

exe

tɕe nɯ tɯ-ci ɣɯ ɯ-taʁ nɯnɯtɕu, nɤki ɲɤ-χtɤr, iɕqʰa <yujinxiang> kɤ-ti mɯntoʁ nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-jwaʁ nɯ ɲɤ-χtɤr. \\
lnk dem indef. poss -water gen 3sg -on dem: loc dem: cataph ifr -spread the.aforementionned tulip obj: pcp -say flower dem gen 3sg. poss -leaf dem ifr -spread \\
`She spilled on the water... she spilled the petals of the flower called ``tulip''.' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh) 0006334#S68
exe

exe

tɕe nɯ-nɯŋa ra nɤki ŋu ɕi, tɕe ɲɯ-tɯ-nɤm qʰe, tɕe ʑara ku-n-nɯ-ɣi-nɯ ŋu ɕi? \\
lnk 2sg. poss -cow pl dem: cataph be: fact qu lnk ipfv: west -2-chase[III] lnk lnk 3pl ipfv: east - auto - vert -come- pl be: fact qu \\
`And your cows, are they (still) like that, you let them out of the pen (in the morning), and they come back home on their own (in the evening)?' (taRrdo conversation)
exe

It is also used when the speaker alerts the addressee that a long description follows as in ( ex:nAki.tustunW ), as in English `(he said) the following'. Given the fact the Japhug is strictly verb-final and has pre-verbal complements (§ sec:basic.word.order ), this is a strategy employed to avoid relegating the main verb to the end of the description.

exe

kʰopi kɯ ɴqiazwɤr ci ɲɯ-mɯm rca ɲɯ-saχaʁ ʑo tɕe nɤki tu-stu-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ti, ɲɯ-pʰɯt-nɯ qʰe kɯ-zri... ki jamar ʑo kɯ-zri ɲɯ-pʰɯt-nɯ qʰe nɤki, ɯ-ku ɯ-mtɯ kɯ-fse nɯtɕu kú-wɣ-ndo qʰe tɕe ɯ-pa nɯ, ɯ-jwaʁ nɯ cʰɯ-χɕoʁ-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu... \\
anthr erg bitter.wormwood indef sens -be.tasty unexpect sens -be.extremely emph lnk dem: cataph ipfv -do.like- pl sens -be sens -say ipfv -take.out- pl lnk sbj: pcp -be.long dem: prox about emph sbj: pcp -be.long ipfv -take.out- pl lnk dem: cataph 3sg. poss -head 3sg. poss -crest sbj: pcp -be.like dem: loc ipfv - inv -take lnk lnk 3sg. poss -under dem 3sg. poss -leaf dem ipfv: downstream -take.out- pl sens -be \\
`Kebei says that bitter wormwood is very tasty, and that they prepare it in the following way: they pluck (wormwoods) that are this big, take it by something that looks like a crest on the top, and prune away the leaves under it... (continued by several paragraphs)' (conversation 140510)
exe

The pronoun nɤki is also used as a determiner (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners ) and the speech filler nɤkinɯ (§ sec:fillers ) derives from the combination of nɤki with the determiner nɯ. There are no plural or dual forms of nɤki, but it can be combined with dual or plural determiners as in ( ex:nAki.nWra ).

exe

tɕe nɤki nɯra, mkʰɤrmaŋ ra pjɤ-rɯsɯso-nɯ tɕe, \\
lnk dem: cataph dem: pl people pl ifr -think- pl lnk \\
`And these, the people thought about it.' (150829 jidian-zh)
0006338#S132
exe

It is likely that the cataphoric demonstrative use of nɤki derives from its function as a medial demonstrative, suggesting the historical pathway in ( ex:nAki.hist ).

exe

2sg + dem: prox $ $ dem: medial $ $ dem: cataphoric $ $ speech filler
exe
summary:
The demonstrative **nɤki** is used not only as a medial demonstrative, but also for **cataphoric reference**, often when the speaker hesitates and then continues with a clause repeating the same verb or auxiliary. It can also signal that a long description is coming, helping avoid placing the main verb at the very end in Japhug’s verb-final order.  

The text notes that **nɤki** also functions as a determiner, and that the filler **nɤkinɯ** comes from combining **nɤki** with the determiner **nɯ**; although **nɤki** has no plural or dual forms, it can combine with plural or dual determiners. Its cataphoric use is likely historically derived from its medial demonstrative function.

subsection: Locative forms of the demonstrative pronouns
text:
demonstrative!locative
The locative postposition tɕu (§ sec:core.locative ) can be combined with the demonstrative pronouns nɯ and ki and their reduplicated and emphatic forms, as shown in tab:loc.dem.pronoun.

The locative pronouns in -tɕu can be followed by the postposition zɯ as in ( ex:nWtCu.zW.mbro ), but not by the locative ri.

exe

mbrosta ci tu tɕe, nɯtɕu zɯ mbro nɯ a-ja. \\
stable indef exist: fact lnk dem: loc loc horse dem pass -keep.attached: fact \\
`There are stables (in this palace), and the horse is kept there.' (140507 jinniao-zh) 0003931#S170
exe

The proximal demonstrative ki undergoes bound state (§ sec:status.constructus ) alternation and changes to kɯ- when combined with the locative postposition tɕu (§ sec:core.locative ), with further assimilation to [ u ] due to the regressive vowel assimilation (§ sec:vowel.harmony ) when followed by -tɕu.

In addition to the locative pronouns in -tɕu, there is an entirely parallel series of pronouns in -re; this suffix is probably unrelated to the locative postposition ri, and may rather reflect the plural marker ra (which can be used to mark vague location, see § sec:plural.determiners ) with the proto-Gyalrong locative suffix *-j and regular vowel fusion (§ sec:locative.j ). These locative pronouns are much less commonly used in the corpus than those of the -tɕu series.

Locative pronouns in -re can appear on their own as in ( ex:kWre ), or with the locative postposition ri as in ( ex:ndWchu.kWre.ri ), but never with the other postpositions zɯ and tɕu.

exe

aʑo mɯ-pɯ-rɤʑi-a, kɯre pɯ-ɕti-a. \\
1sg neg - pst. ipfv -stay dem. prox: loc pst. ipfv -be. aff - 1sg \\
`I was not present [there], I was here.' (conversation140510 )
exe

exe

tɕe kukutɕu, <zhuanmen>, nɤkinɯ, tɯ-ɕɣa ɯ-kɯ-nɯsmɤn, tɕetʰi, ndɯcʰu kɯre ri rɤʑi ma, nɯnɯ wuma ʑo mkʰɤz tɕe, \\
lnk dem. prox: loc specially filler indef. poss -tooth 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -treat downstream west: approx. loc dem. prox: loc loc stay: fact lnk dem really emph be.expert: fact lnk \\
`Here (in Mbarkham), there is someone who specially treats teeth in the west (of Mbarkham).' (27-tApGi) 0003706#S130
exe

Locative adverbs, such as those based on the approximate locative -cʰu (§ sec:approximate.locative ) can be combined with the locative pronouns in -re as shown by the phrase ndɯcʰu kɯre ri `on the western side' in ( ex:ndWchu.kWre.ri ).

Both series of locative pronouns can express static location as in examples ( ex:kWre ) to ( ex:nWtCu.kurAzinW ), or motion towards a place as in ( ex:kWre.nWnWGea ) and ( ex:nWnWtCu.pjWwGlAt ).

exe

nɯtɕu ku-rɤʑi-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
dem: loc ipfv -stay- pl sens -be \\
`They live there.' (20-RmbroN) 0003560#S4

The **-tɕu** forms combine with demonstrative pronouns, can take **zɯ** but not **ri**, and the proximal demonstrative **ki** changes to **kɯ-** and then assimilates to [u] in this environment; the **-re** forms can stand alone or combine with **ri**, but not with **zɯ** or **tɕu**.

text:
numeral
This section describes the morphology of cardinal and ordinal numerals in Japhug. Unlike some other languages of the Sino-Tibetan family, which have vigesimal features or substractive numerals, Japhug has a strict decimal system.

In addition to plain numerals, Japhug has a system of numeral prefixes (§ sec:numeral.prefixes ) which occur on a specific type of nouns, counted nouns, discussed in § sec:counted.nouns.
summary: Japhug cardinal and ordinal numerals have a strict decimal system, unlike some other Sino-Tibetan languages that show vigesimal or subtractive numeral patterns. In addition to plain numerals, Japhug also has numeral prefixes that occur with a particular class of nouns called counted nouns.

text:
The basic numerals from one to ten are indicated in tab:numerals.under.10. The corresponding numeral prefixes are discussed in § sec:num.prefixes.1.10.

Some dialects of Japhug other than the Kamnyu variety use tɤɣone instead. In calculations (see § sec:arithmetic ), the generic counted noun tɯ-rdoʁone piece (§ sec:CN.quantifier ) with the numeral prefix `one' (§ sec:numeral.prefixes )
is used instead of cione to express the number `one'.

Apart from cione and sqiten, these numerals have clear cognates in languages outside of the Gyalrongic group, even in Tibetan and Chinese; tab:numerals.under.10 includes the Tibetan equivalent of these numerals (the numerals that are not cognate with their Japhug equivalents are indicated between brackets) and the Japhug pronunciation of these Tibetan words in borrowed words (see § sec:tibetan.numerals, in particular tab:tibetan.ordinals ).

The numerals from 2 to 9 have a prefix, uvular χ-/ʁ- in `two' and `three' and velar kɯ- from `four' to `nine'. These prefixes do not appear in some derived forms such as the numbers 11-19 ( sec:teens below) or approximate numerals (§ sec:approx.numerals ).

The numeral ʁnɯztwo is etymologically related to the dual postnominal determiner ni (§ sec:dual.determiners ). The latter lacks the uvular prefix and the sibilant suffix, but the vowel difference is expected, as after adding the suffix *-s, the proto-Gyalrong rhyme *-is regularly yields Japhug -ɯz. The adverb ʁnaʁnaboth (§ sec:dual.determiners ) is also probably related, though its morphological relationship with ʁnɯztwo does not fit any known pattern.

The superficial resemblance between ʁnɯztwo and kɯɕnɯzseven could suggest the existence of a former quinary system. However, the fact that these two numerals have different vowels in Situ (Cogtse kəniɛ̄s `two' and kəɕnə̄s `seven', from ) makes this assumption less likely; it is in any case irrelevant to the synchronic grammar of Japhug.

Unlike the other numerals in tab:numerals.under.10, the free numeral χsɯmthree is identical to the form found in compound loans such as kɯmtɕʰoχsɯmtriratna from དཀོན་མཆོག་གསུམ་dkon.mtɕʰog.gsumtriratna. Therefore, one cannot exclude the possibility that it is a borrowing from Tibetan གསུམ་gsumthree that replaced the native numeral `three' (which was cognate to the Tibetan form, and phonetically similar to it). In this hypothesis, the alternative forms -fsum and fsɯ- for `three' found in the numerals 11-19 (§ sec:teens ) and tens (§ sec:decades ) could be remnants of the native numeral. Alternatively, it is possible that the native word and the borrowing are true cognates, and happen to have the same form by coincidence.

The numeral kɯngɯtnine has a coda -t which is not found in the cognates of this numeral in Situ and languages outside of Gyalrongic, suggesting analogical spreading of the coda from kɯrcateight.
This innovation is shared by all Northern Gyalrong languages: Tshobdun has kə́nⁿgət and Zbu kənⁿɡə́t. The same analogy independently occurred in the Siyuewu dialect of Khroskyabs, where `nine' is ŋgə́d.
analogy!numerals

Numerals from 1 to 99 are a subclass of unpossessible nouns (§ sec:unpossessible.nouns ), and cannot take possessive prefixes; they differ in this regard from the higher numerals (§ sec.hundred.plus, § sec:approx.numerals ).
summary: Japhug numerals 1–10 have basic forms listed elsewhere, with some dialectal variation for ‘one’ and the use of a generic counted noun in calculations. Most numerals show cognates outside Gyalrongic, and the text discusses several morphological and historical issues: prefixes on numerals 2–9, a possible relation of ‘two’ to dual markers, the uncertain status of ‘three’ as a possible Tibetan borrowing, and an analogically extended final -t in ‘nine’ shared across Northern Gyalrong languages. Numerals from 1 to 99 are unpossessible nouns and cannot take possessive prefixes.

text:
The numerals for tens ( tab:decades ) are relatively straightforward. With the exception of ɣnɤsqitwenty and fsɯsqithirty, they are predictable by combining sqiten with the corresponding numeral prefix (§ sec:numeral.prefixes ). The numeral kɯngɯsqininety is ambiguous, as the same form can also mean `nine or ten' (see tab:approx.num.1to10 ).

The element ɣnɤ- in ɣnɤsqitwenty is related to the numeral ʁnɯztwo, but has a velar ɣ- prefix instead of the uvular ʁ, and has a different vowel. The adverb ʁnaʁnaboth is also relatable, but the alternations are not explainable from a synchronic point of view.

Other numerals under one hundred are built by combining the tens in tab:decades (removing the -sqi element) with the units in tab:teens. For instance, 37 can be obtained by putting together fsɯsqithirty and sqaɕnɯzseventeen as fsɯ-sqa-ɕnɯz.
summary:
The numerals for the tens are mostly regular, formed by combining *sqiten* with the appropriate numeral prefix, except for *ɣnɤsqitwenty* and *fsɯsqithirty*. The form *kɯngɯsqininety* is ambiguous because it can also mean “nine or ten,” and *ɣnɤ-* in *ɣnɤsqitwenty* is historically related to the numeral for “two,” though the sound alternations are not synchronically explainable.

Numbers below one hundred are formed by combining the tens forms, with *-sqi* removed, and the teen numerals. For example, 37 is built from *fsɯsqithirty* and *sqaɕnɯzseventeen* as *fsɯ-sqa-ɕnɯz*.

text:
The numerals 11-19, listed in tab:teens, serve as the basis for indicating units in all following numerals between 21 and 99, by replacing the -sqi element of the tens ( tab:decades ) by the appropriate form. As an example of how to build numerals above 19 with a unit 1-9, tab:teens illustrates the formation of the numerals 21 to 29 from ɣnɤsqitwenty.

The numerals 11-19 present three morphological changes in comparison with the basic numerals 1-9.

First, the form sqiten alternates with sqa-. The origin of this Ablaut is unknown, though it could be a type of bound state (§ sec:status.constructus ); some Gyalrongic languages, such as Khroskyabs have a similar alternation.

Second, the velar kɯ- and uvular χ-/ʁ- prefixes found in the base numerals are lost in all numerals 11-19.

Third, a labial element p ( sqaptɯɣeleven, sqaprɤɣsixteen), m ( sqamnɯztwelve), or w ( sqafsumthirteen) is inserted between the sqa- and the following numeral root. It does not occur in seventeen, eighteen and nineteen (which already have a cluster), fourteen and fifteen (which have a cluster with a labial as first element).

The form sqaptɯɣeleven contains an ablauted form of tɤɣone as second element. The cluster -pt- in this word is the only case in the language of a p followed by an obstruent (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ).

In sqamnɯztwelve, the labial linker is nasalized by the following n. This is not a synchronic rule: for instance, a noun ɕnaβndʑɣisnotty-nosed kid has β allomorph of w before a prenasalized obstruent (§ sec:subject.verb.compounds ). However, there are other cases of nasalization of labial consonants to m before nasal or prenasalized consonants in Japhug (see § sec:causative.m ).

In sqaprɤɣsixteen, not only the prefix kɯ- is lost, the tʂ affricate of the base form kɯtʂɤɣsix is replaced by r, preceded by the linking element -p-. This tʂ r alternation is evidence for a sound change *tr- tʂ (§ sec:Cr.clusters ). The numeral kɯtʂɤɣsix contains two etymological prefixes, kɯ- and a prefix *t- that has fused with the root as -tʂɤɣ. This *t- prefix is possibly related to the d- of its Tibetan cognate དྲུག་drugsix.

The numeral prefixes corresponding to the numerals between 11 and 99 are discussed in § sec:num.prefixes.11.99.
summary:
The numerals 11–19 are the model for forming units in numerals from 21 to 99, where the -sqi element of the tens is replaced by the appropriate unit form. Compared with the basic numerals 1–9, these forms show three main changes: alternation of sqiten with sqa-, loss of the initial velar/uvular prefixes, and insertion of a labial linker consonant (p, m, or w) before the numeral root in many forms.

The passage also notes special phonological details in forms like eleven, twelve, and sixteen, including ablaut, nasalization of the linker before nasal consonants, and replacement of an affricate by r in sixteen. The -pt- cluster in eleven is described as unique in the language, and the tʂ > r alternation is taken as evidence for an earlier sound change.

text:
There are two ways of expressing numbers above 99 in Japhug. First, the noun-like numeral ɣurʑahundred can occur on its own or be followed by another numeral to express a number between 101 and 199, as in ( ex:hundred.and.eight ).

exe

aʑo kɯ-fse kɯ-ɤcʰɯcʰa ʑo ʁʑɯnɯ ɣurʑa kɯrcat ra\\
1sg sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp -be.capable emph young.man hundred eight need: fact \\
`I need one hundred and eight able young men like me.' (Norbzang)
0003768#S16
exe

The numeral ɣurʑahundred cannot be combined with single digit numerals to express numbers between 200 and 900. The counted noun Counted nouns are nouns that take an obligatory numeral prefix (§ sec:counted.nouns ). tɯ-rione hundred is used for this purpose, as in ex:three.hundreds. The two suppletive roots for hundreds are shared with Pumi (the numeral ɕí `hundred' vs. the counted noun -ɻɛj, see; evidence for cognacy with ɣurʑa and tɯ-ri is presented in ).

Numerals above the hundreds are all borrowed from Tibetan: stoŋtsuthousand, kʰrɯtsuten thousands, mbɯmχtɤrhundred thousands originate from སྟོང་ཚོ་stoŋ.tsʰothousand, ཁྲི་ཚོ་kʰri.tsʰoten thousands and འབུམ་ཐེར་ⁿbum.tʰerhundred thousands, respectively. Like other numerals, they are postnominal, as shown by ( ex:stoNtsu ).

The numerals thousand and above can take other numerals as multiplicative modifiers, as in ( ex:stoNtsu.kWtsxAG ), where kɯtʂɤɣsix follows stoŋtsuthousand to express `six thousand'. This use illustrates the difference between the numerals stoŋtsuthousand and above with ɣurʑahundred, as when the latter is followed by a numeral, as ɣurʑa kɯrcatone hundred and eight, it can only be in additive, not multiplicative, relation to it (see example ex:hundred.and.eight above). The multiplicative numeral modifier to stoŋtsuthousand cannot be preposed (Tshendzin says of a combination like $ $ kɯtʂɤɣ stoŋtsu that nɯ mɤ-sɤtso `it does not make sense').

`He can earn about six thousand [renminbi] per year.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S159

In ( ex:khrWtsu.sqi ), a multiplicative modifier sqiten following kʰrɯtsuten thousands is used instead of mbɯmχtɤrhundred thousands. The latter numeral, although known to native speakers, is hardly ever used in speech.

exe
