Unlike numerals under 100, ɣurʑahundred and above are alienably possessed nouns and can take a third person possessive prefix ɯ- to express an approximate number (§ sec:approx.numerals ).
summary: Japhug has two strategies for numbers above 99: the noun-like numeral ɣurʑa ‘hundred’ is used on its own or followed by another numeral to express 101–199 additively, while the counted noun tɯ-ri ‘hundred’ is used for 200–900. Numerals above ‘hundred’ are borrowed from Tibetan and behave postnominally; they can take following numerals as multiplicative modifiers for forms like ‘six thousand,’ but additive meanings require comitative markers such as cʰo or cʰondɤre. Unlike numerals below 100, ɣurʑa and higher numerals are alienably possessed nouns and can take a third-person possessive prefix to express approximation.

text:
numeral!ordinal
There are no native ordinal numbers in Japhug, even for `first', which is expressed by combining the superlative stumost (§ sec:stu.superlative ) with the subject participle (§ sec:subject.participles ) of the verb mɤkube first (§ sec:denom.mA ). This minimal participial relative stu kɯ-mɤku (§ sec:intr.subject.relativization ) can be used as prenominal modifier as in ( ex:stu.kWmAku ), but most commonly occurs adverbially as in ( ex:stu.kWmAku2 ).

exe

stu kɯ-mɤku tɯ-xpa nɯ ɲɯ-rɯmɯntoʁ ma, nɯ ma ɯ-mat me \\
most sbj: pcp -be.first one-year dem ipfv -have.flower lnk dem apart.from 3sg. poss -fruit not.exist: fact \\
`The first year, it has flowers, but no fruits.' (08-qaCti)
0003456#S33
exe

exe

stu kɯ-mɤku nɯ a-pi kɯ pɯ́-wɣ-sat-a, nɯ ɯ-qʰu tɕe, pɣɤtɕɯ tɤ-sci-a, \\
most sbj: pcp -be.first dem 1sg. poss -elder.sibling erg aor - inv -kill- 1sg dem 3sg. poss -after lnk bird aor -be.born- 1sg \\
`First, my elder sister killed me, and then I was reborn as a bird.' (2005-stod-kunbzang)
exe

With counted nouns (§ sec:counted.nouns ), it is strictly prenominal, and the counted noun can be converted to an inalienably possessed noun (§ sec:CN.IPN ); for instance, the noun phrase ( ex:stu.kWmAku.Wxpa ) can be used instead of stu kɯ-mɤku tɯ-xpa in ( ex:stu.kWmAku ). The phrase stu kɯ-mɤku does not occur postnominally.

exe

stu kɯ-mɤku ɯ-xpa \\
most sbj: pcp -be.first 3sg. poss -year \\
`The first year' (elicitation based on ex:stu.kWmAku )
exe

There is no specific word meaning `last' in Japhug either, and the participial relative stu kɯ-maqʰu with the subject participle (§ sec:subject.participles ) of maqʰube after is used instead; as in the case of stu kɯ-mɤku, counted noun to inalienably possessed noun conversion is possible, and for instance both ( ex:stu.kWmaqhu.tWsNi ) and ( ex:stu.kWmaqhu.WsNi ) exist.

exe

stu kɯ-maqʰu tɯ-sŋi \\
most sbj: pcp -be.after one-day \\

stu kɯ-maqʰu ɯ-sŋi \\
most sbj: pcp -be.after 3sg. poss -day \\
`The last day' (elicited)
exe

Given the absence of native ordinals, Chinese ordinals are used (§ sec:chinese.numerals ). Tibetan ordinals are only attested for names of months (§ sec:tibetan.numerals ) and even this use is disappearing, as they are being replaced by their Chinese equivalents.

Unlike many languages of the Sino-Tibetan family, the system of birth-order ordinals is very rudimentary. The eldest son is simply called stu kɯ-wxti `the one who is the biggest' as in ( ex:stu.kWwxti ).

exe

ɯ-rɟit stu kɯ-wxti nɯ rɯntɕʰɯn tʂoma rmi\\
3sg. poss -child most sbj: pcp -be.big dem anthr anthr be.called: fact \\
`Her eldest child is called Rinchen Sgrolma.' (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S59
exe

The only dedicated birth-order ordinal is tɯlɤtsecond sibling (see § sec:kinship and § sec:other.upn ). The inalienably possessed noun ɯ-pa `(the one) below' can be used to designate any following sibling, and the youngest sibling is designated by the superlative form of the participle of xtɕibe small (see example ex:Wpa.nW, which illustrates all these terms).

exe

stu kɯ-wxti cʰondɤre nɯ ɯ-pa nɯ tɯlɤt ni wuma ʑo pjɤ-ɕqraʁ-ndʑi. tɕe nɯ ndʑi-tɕɯ stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯnɯ, dɯxpa ma wuma ʑo pjɤ-kʰe. \\
most sbj: pcp -be.big comit dem 3sg. poss -under dem second.sibling du really emph ifr. ipfv -be.intelligent- du lnk dem 3du. poss -son most sbj: pcp -be.small dem poor lnk really emph ifr. ipfv -be.stupid \\
`The eldest son and the one under him, the second one, were very intelligent. Their smallest son, poor him, was very stupid' (140430 jin e-zh) 0003893#S5
exe
summary: Japhug has no native ordinal numerals, so ‘first’ and ‘last’ are expressed with participial relative constructions built from the superlative *stu* and the verbs meaning ‘be first’ and ‘be after’; these forms can function prenominally, especially with counted nouns, but not postnominally. Chinese ordinals are used instead, while Tibetan ordinals survive only for month names and are fading. Birth-order terms are also limited: the eldest son is described as “the one who is the biggest,” the only dedicated term is ‘second sibling,’ and other siblings are referred to by expressions meaning ‘the one below’ or ‘the smallest.’

text: In addition to the native numerals presented above, Tibetan and Chinese numerals commonly occur in Japhug stories and conversations.
summary: Besides the native numerals described above, Tibetan and Chinese numerals are also commonly used in Japhug stories and everyday conversation.

text:
numeral!Tibetan Tibetan!numeral
In Japhug, Tibetan numerals (see tab:numerals.under.10 above) are mainly used in fixed expressions. Only a minority of Japhug speakers are fluent in Amdo or other Tibetic languages, so that Tibetan loanwords in Japhug, and in particular numerals, cannot be considered to be code-switching.
Some of these expressions exclusively comprise Tibetan words, for instance luskɤr χtɕɯʁɲiztwelve year cycle from ལོ་སྐར་lo.skaryear of the cycle and བཅུ་གཉིས་btɕu.gɲistwelve. Other compounds combine Tibetan numerals with Japhug roots, for instance the possessive compound rnaftɕɯχahaving ears with ten holes from tɯ-rnaear (or Tibetan རྣ་rnaear, the form is ambiguous between cognate and borrowing), the numeral ftɕɯ- (from བཅུ་btɕuten) and the verb aχalacking a piece, which appears as postnominal modifier in the name of a trickster character qala rnaftɕɯχathe rabbit with ten holes in his ears.

The Japhug form -χtɕɯɣ- of the Tibetan numeral གཅིག་gtɕigone occurs in compounds, but is not attested as an independent word; however, it is possible that it used to exist in Japhug at an earlier stage of the language (though perhaps not as a numeral), as the stative verb naχtɕɯɣbe the same is a denominal derivation based on this numeral (§ sec:identity.modifier, § sec:denom.intr.nW ).

The Tibetan ordinal numbers up to ten (and the cardinal numbers for `eleven' and `twelve'), indicated in tab:tibetan.ordinals, can be used for months names. This usage is not attested in conversations, but does occur in texts when speakers consciously try to avoid using Chinese words. In example ( ex:XsWmba ), Tshendzin first used the Chinese 三月份 sānyuèfènthird month and then corrected it to its Tibetan equivalent.

exe

<sanyuefen> jamar zlawa χsɯmba jamar tɕe ci cʰɯ-rɤpɯ, \\
third.month about month third about lnk one ipfv -have.young \\
`It bears young once in the third month.' (21-lWLU)
0003576#S61
exe

The ordinals can be used with the Tibetan word zlawamonth (from ཟླ་བ་zla.bamoon, month) as in ( ex:XsWmba ), or without it as in ( ex:rgWpa ) from the same text.

exe

rgɯpa jamar tɕe ci cʰɯ-rɤpɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
ninth about lnk one ipfv -have.young sens -be \\
`It bears young once in the ninth month.' (21-lWLU)
0003576#S63
exe

In traditional stories of Tibetan origin, complete noun phrases in Tibetan including numerals can be found. For instance, in ( ex:gsum.brgya.drug.bcu ), the numeral χsɯmrɟatʂɯɣftɕɯ from གསུམ་བརྒྱ་དྲུག་བཅུ་gsum.brgʲa.drug.btɕuthree hundred sixty occurs with the noun pja (from Tibetan བྱ་bʲabird; not normally used in Japhug except in compounds) and the adverb mɯndʐamɯχtɕɯɣall kinds (from མི་འདྲ་མི་གཅིག་mi.ⁿdra.mi.gtɕigdiverse, different, § sec:quantifiers.other ).

exe

pja mɯndʐamɯχtɕɯɣ, χsɯmrɟatʂɯɣftɕɯ kɯ pɣɤmbri ɲcɣɤnɤɲcɣɤt ʑo to-lɤt-nɯ, \\
bird all.kinds 360 erg bird.song idph.III:very.noisy emph ifr -throw- pl \\
`Three hundred sixty birds of all kinds sung bird songs.' (2003 smanmi)
exe
summary:
In Japhug, Tibetan numerals are mainly used in fixed expressions and should not be treated as code-switching, since only a minority of speakers are fluent in Tibetan languages. Some expressions are entirely Tibetan, while others combine Tibetan numerals with Japhug roots, and the Tibetan numeral for “one” appears only in compounds, though it may have existed as an independent form in an earlier stage of the language.  

Tibetan ordinal numbers are also used in month names, especially in texts where speakers avoid Chinese forms, and can occur with or without the Tibetan word for “month.” In traditional stories of Tibetan origin, full Tibetan noun phrases with numerals are also found.

text:
numeral!Chinese
Chinese numerals are ubiquitous in Japhug, and many younger people (born after 1990) have trouble counting above twenty, even if they otherwise speak Japhug fairly fluently. Even the most fluent speakers use Chinese numerals (with their appropriate Chinese classifiers) when speaking normally.

In examples ( ex:quanxiang ) and ( ex:liangge ), from a text describing the hamlets in the township of Gdong-brgyad, the Chinese expressions 全乡 quánxiāngthe whole township, 三千多人 sānqiānduōrénthree thousand people and a little more and 两个小队 liǎnggèxiǎoduìtwo groups (with the generic classifier 个 gè cl ) are used instead of Japhug native numerals and quantifiers to count the number of people in the area. Note the use of the Cultural Revolution term 小队 xiǎoduìteam, group as a counting unit. The use of Chinese here is due to the fact that administration-related counting, even in villages, is done in Chinese.

exe

nɯnɯ ʁdɯrɟɤt <quanxiang> nɯnɯ <sanqianduoren> ma maŋe. \\
dem anthr the.whole.township dem three.thousand.people apart.from not:exist: sens \\
`There are only a little more than three thousand people in the township of Gdong-brgyad.' (140522 RdWrJAt)
0004061#S109
exe

exe

kɤmɲɯ nɯ <lianggexiaodui> ma maŋe \\
Kamnyu dem two.groups apart.from not.exist: sens \\
`In Kamnyu there are only two xiaodui.' (140522 RdWrJAt) 0004061#S111
exe

Given the absence of ordinal numerals in Japhug (§ sec:ordinals ), Chinese expressions with the ordinal marker 第 dì are used instead. In example ( ex:stu.kWmAku3 ), the Chinese phrase 第一名 dìyīmíngthe first (in a competition) occurs, directly followed by the participial clause stu kɯ-mɤku `the first one'.

exe

tɕe βʑɯ nɯ kɯ <diyiming> tɕe stu kɯ-mɤku pjɤ-mɟa. \\
lnk mouse dem erg first lnk most sbj: pcp -be.first ifr -take \\
`The mouse obtained the first place.' (150826 shier shengxiao-zh)
0006284#S96
exe
summary: Chinese numerals are widely used in Japhug, even by fluent speakers, and younger speakers often have difficulty counting above twenty in Japhug. In ordinary speech and especially in administrative contexts, Chinese numeral expressions with Chinese classifiers replace native Japhug forms for counting. Because Japhug lacks ordinal numerals, speakers also use Chinese ordinals marked with 第 dì, as in 第一名 “first place.”

text:
numeral
Japhug numerals can occur on their own when counting ( ci, ʁnɯz, χsɯm, kɯβde...) or be used as postnominal attributive modifiers (§ sec:noun.phrases.word.order ). The noun can be elided when the context is clear, especially when the same referent occurs in the previous proposition as in ( ex:WrJit.kWngWt ) with ɯ-rɟither children and ( ex:kWBde.kW ) with 菜 càidish. In this case the numeral constitutes the head of the noun phrase.

exe

ɯ-rɟit kɯngɯt tɤ-tu ri, kɯtʂɤɣ nɯ-si \\
3sg. poss -child nine aor -exist lnk six aor -die \\
`She had nine children, but six [of them] died.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S16
exe

exe

<cai> χsɯm tu-sɯ-lɤt-i tɕe tɕe kɯβde nɯ kɯ χsɯm tu-ndza-j kɯ-fse. \\
dish three ipfv - caus -throw- 1pl lnk lnk four dem erg three ipfv -eat- 1pl sbj: pcp -be.like \\
`We used to order three dishes, and the four of us would eat [the] three [of them].' (140501 tshering skyid)
0003902#S90
exe

Numerals can also be modifiers of dual and plural pronouns as in ( ex:iZo.kWBde ). Since pronouns are never obligatory in Japhug (§ sec:overt.non.overt ), it is also possible to use a bare numeral in core argument function with first or second person indexation on the verb, as in ( ex:kWBde.kW ), where the verb tu-ndza-j `we eat' of the second proposition has the 1pl -j suffix indexing the transitive subject, coreferent with the ergatively-marked phrase kɯβde nɯ kɯ `the four' (standing for iʑo kɯβde nɯ kɯ `the four of us').

exe

tɕe iʑo kɯβde nɯ tɯtɯrca ku-rɤʑi-j tɕe, \\
lnk 1pl four dem together ipfv -stay- 1pl lnk \\
`The four of us were living together.' (140501 tshering skyid) 0003902#S84
exe

Numerals can be used in collocations with two light verbs: the intransitive verb papass $X$ years (§ sec:pa.intr.lv ) and the transitive verb ndotake (§ sec:ndo.lv ).

The numeral cione occurs in many additional functions: as an identity pronoun `the other one' (§ sec:other.pro ), as a partitive pronoun `one of them' (§ sec:partitive.pronouns ), as an indefinite article `a, one' (postnominal, § sec:indefinite.markers ), as an identity modifier `the other X' (prenominal, § sec:identity.modifier ) and as an adverb meaning `once, one time, a little' (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ).
summary: Japhug numerals can stand alone in counting or function as postnominal attributive modifiers, and when the noun is omitted in a clear context, the numeral becomes the head of the noun phrase. They can also modify dual and plural pronouns, or appear as bare numerals in core argument position with verbal indexation marking the person, and they occur in collocations with two light verbs. The numeral *cione* has several additional uses, including as an identity pronoun, partitive pronoun, indefinite article, identity modifier, and an adverb meaning ‘once’ or ‘a little.’

text:
numeral!approximate
To express an approximate number, it is possible in Japhug to use the adverb jamarabout (from Tibetan ཡར་མར་jar.marabout, up and down and/or to combine adjacent numerals in a row as in ( ex:RnWz.XsWm.kWBde ).

exe

tɯ-kʰɤl nɯtɕu ʁnɯz, χsɯm kɯβde jamar ku-ndzoʁ. \\
one-place dem: loc two three four about ipfv - anticaus:attach \\
`In each place [the flowers] are attached in [groups] of about two, three or four.' (16-RlWmsWsi)
0003520#S9
exe

However, Japhug also has five morphological devices to build approximate numerals (Tables tab:approx.num.1to10 and tab:approx.decades ).

First, for numerals under seven ( tab:approx.num.1to10 ), one can build approximate numerals by prefixing a la- or lɤ- element to one (or two) numeral root(s). Not all possibilities are attested (for instance there is no such approximate numeral $ $ lɤtʂɤɣ derived from only kɯtʂɤɣsix). Prefixation of la- / lɤ- occurs with other morphological changes: (i) loss of the velar kɯ- prefix (but not the uvular one in `two' and `three', § sec:one.to.ten ) (ii) loss of the m- preinitial in lɤŋuabout five, but not of the *t- prefix of kɯtʂɤɣ (§ sec:teens ) in lɤŋɤtʂɤɣfive or six (otherwise $ $ lɤŋɤrɤɣ would be have been found). The la- / lɤ- prefix is probably historically related to the -lɤ- element found in dvandva collectives (§ sec:dvandva.coll ).

Above `seven', the lɤ- prefix seem to have some productivity, as in example ( ex:lAkhrWtsusqi ) from a story translated from Chinese, it is found in the form lɤ-kʰrɯtsu-sqi, which translates 数十万 shùshíwànseveral hundred thousands. The normal way to express this meaning in contemporary Japhug would be direct borrowing from Chinese (§ sec:chinese.numerals ), and this Augenblicksbildung was introduced to avoid using a Chinese word.

exe

<zhanghan> kɤ-ti nɯnɯ kɯ ʁmaʁmi lɤ-kʰrɯtsu-sqi jamar ʑo to-ndo. \\
anthr obj: pcp -say dem erg soldier about-10000-ten about emph ifr -take \\
`The [general] called Zhang Han took several hundred thousand soldiers.' (hist160721 pofuchenzhou-zh)
exe

Second, some approximate numerals are built by compounding two numeral roots (in some cases with the la- / lɤ- prefix, tab:approx.num.1to10 ). The first numeral undergoes bound state vowel change (§ sec:status.constructus ), with loss of the codas -z and -t (§ sec:loss.codas.compounds ). In the case of ɕnɤcatseven or eight (illustrated by example ex:CnAcat.ci ), the form ɕnɤ- is irregular ($ $ ɕnɯ- would be expected instead). Note that in this list kɯngɯsqinine or ten is ambiguous: this form can also mean `ninety' (see tab:decades ).

exe

ɯʑo nɯnɯ ɕnɤcat ci tɤ-kɤ-sɯpa jamar ʑo qarma wxti ri, \\
3sg dem seven.or.eight one aor - obj: pcp - caus -do about emph crossoptilon be.big: fact but \\
`Although the crossoptilon is as big as about seven or eight of them (weasels) put together.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S54
exe

Third, for tens ( tab:approx.decades ), approximate forms can be formed using the same rule as tens from 40 to 90 (§ sec:decades ), by combining the bound state of the unit numeral with the root sqiten, for instance lɤŋɤsqiabout fifty from lɤŋuabout five like kɯmŋɤsqififty from kɯmŋufive. These approximate numerals are rare and not attested in the non-elicited corpus.

Fourth, an alternative way of producing approximate tens is to add the numeral prefix tɯ- (§ sec:numeral.prefixes ) to a ten, as for instance tɯɣnɤsqiabout twenty from ɣnɤsqitwenty (see example ex:tWGnAsqi ).

exe

tɯɣnɤsqi jamar tɯtɯrca ju-ɣi-nɯ ŋgrɤl \\
about.twenty about together ipfv -come- pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`They come in groups of about twenty individuals.' (23-qapGAmtWmtW) 0003608#S98
exe

Fifth, in the case of numerals above 99, approximate numerals are built by prefixing a third singular possessive ɯ- prefix, as ɯ-ɣurʑaseveral hundreds ( ex:WGurZa ), ɯ-stoŋtsuseveral thousands ( ex:WstoNtsu ) and higher numerals.

exe

ɯ-ɣurʑa, χsɯ-ri jamar ndɤre tu-nɯ ko, tɯ-tɯpʰu nɯ \\
3sg. poss -hundred three-hundred about top. advers exist: fact - pl sfp one-hive dem \\
`There are about several hundreds, about three hundred of them in one hive.' (26-GZo)
0003668#S48
exe

exe

tɯ-ŋga tɯ-rdoʁ nɯ ɯ-stoŋtsu ɯ-pʰɯ kɯ-fse ŋu ma \\
indef. poss -clothes one-piece dem 3sg. poss -thousand 3sg. poss -price sbj: pcp -be.like be: fact lnk \\
`One piece of clothes [made from it], its price is several thousand [renminbi].' (05-qaZo) 0003404#S72
exe
summary: Japhug can express approximate numbers either with the adverb *jamar* ‘about’ or by combining adjacent numerals, but it also has five morphological strategies for approximate numerals. These include prefixing *la-*/*lɤ-* to numeral roots below seven, compounding two numeral roots, forming approximate tens with the same pattern used for regular tens, adding the prefix *tɯ-* to tens, and prefixing third-person possessive *ɯ-* to numerals above 99.

text:
counted noun noun!counted classifier
The term counted nouns designates a subclass of nouns that differs from inalienably possessed (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ), alienably possessed and unpossessible nouns (§ sec:unpossessible.nouns ) in that they require a numeral prefix, whose paradigm is described in (§ sec:numeral.prefixes ). No other part of speech is compatible with these prefixes.

For instance, the counted noun -xpa `year' occurs in ( ex:XsW.xpa ) with the prefix χsɯ- `three'. It is not possible to express the same meaning by combining the bare stem of the noun -(x)pa with the corresponding numeral numeral χsɯmthree (something like $ $ xpa χsɯm or $ $ pa χsɯm would be agrammatical).

exe

χsɯ-xpa \\
three-year \\
`Three years'
exe

In this grammar, counted noun are cited using the form with the numeral prefix `one' ( tɯ-xpa in the case of `year'). One reviewer pointed out that this choice may be infelicitous, but in my opinion it is preferable in order to avoid confusion with other subclasses of nouns, in particular in the case of conversion from inalienable and alienable nouns to counted nouns (§ sec:CN.parts.of.speech ).

Numeral prefixes are bound forms historically derived from free numerals (§ sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history ). These bound forms strictly precede the nominal stem, unlike free numerals, which generally follow the nouns they modify (§ sec:uses.numerals ). However, the numeral+noun order is attested in some compounds (§ sec:determinative.n.n, § sec:possessive.n.n ).

Only a highly restricted number of nominal stems can take numeral prefixes. For instance, the alienably possessed mbrohorse or the inalienably possessed tɤ-pielder sibling are not compatible with numerals prefixes. To express the meanings `three horses' or `three brothers', one cannot add the numeral prefix χsɯ-: forms such as $ $ χsɯ-mbro, $ $ χsɯ-tɤ-pi or $ $ χsɯ-pi would be unintelligible. Instead, one must use the free numeral χsɯmthree (§ sec:uses.numerals ) as in ( ex:mbro.XsWm ).

exe

mbro χsɯm \\
horse three \\
`Three horses'

exe

A handful of alienably and inalienably possessed nouns can be converted to counted nouns and thus take numeral prefixes, but always with a semantic narrowing (§ sec:CN.IPN, § sec:CN.APN ).

The class of ``counted nouns'' in this grammar is similar to what have elsewhere in the literature been described as `classifiers' (in Chinese 量词 liàngcí ``measure words''). The morphology-based term ``counted noun'', independent of meaning and function, is preferred over ``classifier'' because it is highly contestable that classification is indeed the main function of this class of words (see for instance, and § sec:CN.classification ).
summary: Counted nouns are a special subclass of nouns that must take a numeral prefix, and no other part of speech can combine with these bound prefixes. Only a restricted set of nominal stems can do this; most possessed nouns cannot, so meanings like “three horses” or “three brothers” must be expressed with a free numeral instead. The grammar uses the term “counted noun” rather than “classifier” because it treats the category as a morphological class and does not assume that classification is its main function.

text:
numeral!prefix
In this section, numeral prefixes are described following several categories (1-10, 11-99, approximate numerals and prefixes derived from nouns) and irregular forms are discussed in a separated subsection (§ sec:irregular.numeral.prefixes ). A final subsection presents historical hypotheses to account for the numeral prefixal paradigm and its relationship to that of other Gyalrongic languages.
summary: The section describes numeral prefixes by grouping them into several categories: 1–10, 11–99, approximate numerals, and prefixes derived from nouns. It also treats irregular forms separately and ends with historical hypotheses explaining the numeral prefix paradigm and its relationship to other Gyalrongic languages.

text:
The paradigm of regular numeral prefixes from 1 to 10 in Kamnyu Japhug is indicated in tab:num.prefix.1.to.10. The prefixes are derived from the corresponding numeral by bound state (§ sec:status.constructus ), with loss of the coda and vowel alternation. Vowel alternation is optional for kɯβdefour and kɯmŋufive.

Note that the forms of the numeral prefixes differ in some cases from the corresponding numeral prefixes in tens (cf. tab:decades ), compare kɯɕnɯ-sŋiseven days with kɯɕnɤ-sqiseventy.
summary: In Kamnyu Japhug, the regular numeral prefixes from 1 to 10 are formed from the corresponding numeral in bound state, with coda loss and vowel alternation. The vowel alternation is optional for the prefixes for ‘four’ and ‘five’. Some numeral prefixes also differ from the forms used in tens, as shown by the contrast between ‘seven days’ and ‘seventy’.

text:
Above ten, numeral prefixes present some variation. tab:num.prefix.11.to.20 shows the most common forms of the numeral prefixes between 11 and 20 (from which all numerals between 11 and 99 can be generated following the rules described in § sec:decades ), but many cases without vowel alternation or with preservation of the codas -z ( ex:GnAsqamnWzpArme ) or -ɣ ( ex:GnAsqaptWWGrZaR ) are attested, as in ( ex:GnAsqamnWzpArme ) for instance.

exe

ma ɯ-me kɯnɤ ɣnɤsqamnɯz-pɤrme tʰɯ-azɣɯt. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -daughter also twenty.two-year.old aor -reach \\
`Even his daughter is now twenty-two.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S284
exe

In example ( ex:fsWsqildZa ), we observe the two alternative forms -sqɯ- and -sqi- for the tens in the same sentence. While for the numeral ten only the prefix sqɯ- (or its variant sqɤ, see tab:num.prefix.tArZaR below) is found, for tens between 20 and 90 vowel alternation is optional and there is free variation between the two forms. In the corpus, we find 15 examples of -sqi- and 14 of -sqɯ, suggesting that both are about equally common.

exe

tɯ-pʰɯ nɯ tɕe rcanɯ, li, fsɯsqi-ldʑa jamar, kɯβdɤsqɯ-ldʑa jamar tu. \\
one-tree dem lnk unexp: deg again thirty-long.object about forty-long.object about exist: fact \\
`On one tree, there are about thirty or forty [branches].' (14-sWNgWJu) 0003506#S186
exe

Example ( ex:GnAsqaptWWGrZaR ) illustrates three alternative forms with the counted noun tɤ-rʑaʁone night: ɣnɤsqaptɯ-rʑaʁ with regular loss of coda, ɣnɤsqaptɯɣ-rʑaʁ with preservation of the coda, and ɣnɤsqamnɯz tɤ-rʑaʁ as two words, the numeral being a kind of prenominal modifier. The first form is regular, while the other ones each are hapax legomena.

exe

tɕe nɯ ɣnɤsqaptɯɣ-rʑaʁ tu-tsu ɲɯ-ra. ``tɕe ɣnɤsqaptɯ-rʑaʁ tu-tsu tɕe ɲɯ-ʁaʁ ŋu" ɲɯ-ti-nɯ ri, aʑɯɣ nɯ ɣnɤsqamnɯz tɤ-rʑaʁ mɤɕtʂa mɯ-nɯ-ʁaʁ. \\
lnk dem twenty.one-night ipfv -pass sens -be.needed
lnk twenty.one-night ipfv -pass lnk ipfv -hatch be: fact sens -say- pl lnk 1sg: gen dem twenty.two one-night until neg - aor -hatch \\
`[Eggs] need twenty-two days to hatch; people say `They hatch in twenty-two days' but mine only hatch after twenty two days.' (150819 kumpGa)
0006388#S32
exe
summary: Numeral prefixes above ten show some variation, though the most common forms for numerals 11–20 are given in the table and can be used to form numerals up to 99. Attested variation includes forms without vowel alternation and forms that preserve the codas -z or -ɣ, and for tens between 20 and 90 the alternation between -sqɯ- and -sqi- is optional and appears about equally frequent in the corpus.

text:
Approximate numerals also have corresponding prefixal forms. tab:approx.num.prefixes presents the forms attested in the corpus.

By far the most commonly used approximate numeral prefix is laʁnɯ-X, whose meaning is not `one or two' as could have been expected from the use of the lɤ-/la- prefix in the other examples, but `a few' (see example ex:laʁnWxpa -- life expectancy of goats and sheep is much above two years).

exe

tsʰɤt qaʑo nɯnɯ tɕe laʁnɯ-xpa ma cʰɯ-mdɯ mɯ́j-ŋgrɤl ma tɕe cʰɯ-rgɤz ɕti \\
goat sheep dem lnk a.few-year apart.from ipfv -live.up.to neg: sens -be.usually.the.case lnk lnk ipfv -be.old be. aff: fact \\
`Goats and sheep only live for a few years, and then become old.' (05-qaZo) 0003404#S128
exe

Just like approximate numbers can also be expressed by juxtaposition of numerals (§ sec:approx.numerals ), it is possible to juxtapose counted nouns (the same counted noun with contiguous numeral prefixes, as in ex:XsWzWm.kWBdezWm ), or to combine a numeral with a counted noun whose numeral prefix is contiguous to it, as in ( ex:GnAsqi.fsWqifkur ).

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ χsɯ-zɯm kɯβde-zɯm jamar kɯ-xtɕʰɯt tu. \\
lnk dem three-bucket four-bucket about sbj: pcp -contain exist: fact \\
`There are [jars] that can contain about three or four buckets [of water].' (26-tChWra)
0003690#S4
exe

exe

<tuolaji> tɯ-ɣjɤn ju-ɣɯt nɯ rcanɯ, ɣnɤsqi fsɯsqi-fkur jamar ju-sɯ-ɤzɣɯt cʰa. \\
tractor one-time ipfv -bring dem unexp: deg twenty thirty-burden about ipfv - caus -reach can: fact \\
`Each time the tractor brings [firewood], it can move about twenty or thirty loads (the size a person can carry on his back).' (140430 tWfkur)
0003898#S22
exe

Additionally, the paucal meaning can be expressed by converting the counted noun into an inalienably possessed noun with a third person possessive prefix and reduplication of the noun stem (see § sec:CN.IPN ).
summary: Approximate numerals in the corpus can take prefixal forms, with the most frequent being **laʁnɯ-X**, which means **“a few”** rather than the expected “one or two.” Approximate quantity may also be expressed by juxtaposing counted nouns with contiguous numeral prefixes, or by combining a numeral with such a counted noun. The passage also notes that a **paucal** meaning can be formed by making the counted noun inalienably possessed with a third-person possessive prefix and reduplicating the noun stem.

text:
In addition to the numerals mentioned above, all higher and compound numerals, an interrogative pronoun and a participle form can appear as prefixes of counted nouns.

The numerals above 99 (§ sec.hundred.plus ) occur as numeral prefixes without vowel alternation, as ɣurʑa-xpaa hundred years and stoŋtsu-xpaa thousand years (from ɣurʑahundred and stoŋtsuthousand). Even in the absence of vowel alternation, the prefixal status of these numerals is shown by three pieces of evidence: (i) the fact that they combine with non-free elements like the stem -xpa `year', which require a numeral prefix, (ii) the absence of stress and (iii) the inability to pause or insert any element in between, except in the case of speech errors.

The prefixal form of hundreds based on the counted noun tɯ-rione hundred have double numeral prefixes, such as χsɯ-ri-xpathree hundred years in ( ex:XsWrixpa ).

exe

tɕendɤre χsɯ-ri-xpa tɤ-tsu tɕe, li kɯjŋu pɯ-ta-t-a tɕe, \\
lnk three-hundred-year aor -pass lnk again oath aor -put- tr: pst - 1sg lnk \\
`Three hundred years passed, and I made another oath.' (140512 yufu yu mogui-zh)
0003973#S87
exe

In the case of complex numerals, such as the very common ɣurʑa kɯrcatone hundred and eight, only the last one undergoes bound state, as in ( ex:GurZa.kWrCAJom ) and ( ex:GurZa.kWrCAGdAt ), where we find ɣurʑa as a separate phonological word followed by the counted noun with the numeral prefix kɯrcɤ- (from kɯrcateight).

exe

ɕommbri ɣurʑa kɯrcɤ-ɟom, [...] ɕomtsʰoʁ ɣurʑa kɯrcɤ-ldʑa ra \\
iron.chain hundred eight-length.of.two.outstretched.arms... iron.nails hundred eight-long.object be.needed: fact \\
`[I] need a chain of one hundred and eight fathoms, and one hundred and eight nails.' (2003 tWxtsa)
exe

exe

ɣurʑa kɯrcɤ-ɣdɤt qapri nɯ a-tɤ-ɕe ra \\
hundred eight-section snake dem irr - pfv: up -go be.needed: fact \\
`May the snake be cut into hundred and eight sections!' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S243
exe

The interrogative pronoun tʰɤstɯɣhow many has the prefixal form tʰɤstɯ- with counted nouns (§ § sec:thAstWG ).

The subject participle kɯ-ɤntɕʰɯ of the stative verb antɕʰɯbe many, has the prefixal form kɤntɕʰɯ, as in ( ex:kAntChWtWpW ). This prefix is very common in the corpus.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ kɤntɕʰɯ-tɯpɯ ɣɯ nɯ-tɯrsa ɯ-sta ɲɯ-ŋu ma \\
lnk dem many-household dem 3pl. poss -grave 3sg. poss -place sens -be lnk \\
`It is the grave-place of many families.' (140522 kAmYW tWji)
0004055#S91
exe

It is however not possible to convert any noun, pronoun or quantifier into a numeral prefix; with other words, it is necessary to convert the counted noun to an inalienably possessed noun, with a third singular ɯ- prefix instead of the numeral prefixes, see § sec:CN.IPN.

The nouns tɯ-slaone month and tɯ-xpaone year can be used with a numeral prefix kɤrɤ- not attested with other counted nouns (see § sec:CN.time ).
summary: Higher and compound numerals, an interrogative pronoun, and a participle can function as prefixes on counted nouns. The passage shows that numerals above 99, complex numerals, and forms such as tʰɤstɯ- ‘how many’ and kɤntɕʰɯ- ‘many’ behave as true prefixes, but it also notes that not every noun or quantifier can be turned into a numeral prefix. Only certain counted nouns, especially time nouns like ‘month’ and ‘year’, allow the special prefix kɤrɤ-.

text:
A handful of counted nouns, in particular tɤ-rʑaʁone night, have an alternative paradigm with ɤ instead of ɯ in the prefixes, as shown by the forms ʁnɤ-rʑaʁ `two nights' and χsɤ-rʑaʁ `three nights' in ( ex:RnA.XsArZaR ).

exe

ʁnɤ-rʑaʁ jamar, χsɤ-rʑaʁ jamar to-tsu tɕe tɕendɤre cʰa ɯ-di tu-mnɤm ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
two-night about three-night about ifr -pass lnk lnk alcohol 3sg. poss -smell ipfv -have.a.smell sens -be \\
`After two or three nights, one can smell the smell of alcohol.' (160703 araR)
0006101#S39
exe

The complete paradigm of this noun is presented in
tab:num.prefix.tArZaR.

There is however some degree of variation, and using the regular paradigm is not considered erroneous. In the corpus, the numeral `one' form tɯ-rʑaʁone night is more common than tɤ-rʑaʁ, possibly because of the homophony with the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-rʑaʁtime found in examples such as ( ex:tArZaR.tArYJi ). For other numerals, the forms in Table ( tab:num.prefix.tArZaR ) are considerably more common than the regular ones. In addition, the ɤ vocalism is also found with other numeral prefixes such as the interrogative ( tʰɤstɤ-rʑaʁhow many nights).

exe

tɕe qarma nɯ, tɯ-rʑaʁ tɕe kɯβde kɯmŋu jamar pjɯ-sat-nɯ, tɯ-rdoʁ, tɯrme tɯ-rdoʁ kɯ \\
lnk crossoptilon dem one-night lnk four five about ipfv -kill- pl, one-piece person one-piece erg \\
`Crossoptilons, in one night, each of [the hunters] can kill four or five of them.' (23-qapGAmtWmtW) 0003608#S146
exe

exe

tɤ-rʑaʁ tɤ-rɲɟi tɕe, nɯ-ji ra kɯ-dɯ dɤn kɯ-jɯ jom lo-pɣaʁ-nɯ, ɕoŋtɕa kɯ-dɯ dɤn pjɤ-pʰɯt-nɯ \\
indef. poss -time aor -be.long lnk 3pl. poss -field pl sbj: pcp - emph be.many sbj: pcp - emph be.broad ifr -turn.over- pl timber sbj: pcp - emph be.many ifr -remove- pl \\
`After some time/as time went on, [those people] had ploughed many broad fields for them, and chopped a lot of timber.' (2002 qajdoskAt)
0003366#S115
exe

Apart from tɤ-rʑaʁone night, counted nouns following the paradigm in Table ( tab:num.prefix.tArZaR ) are very rare. The counted nouns tɯ-tɣaone span and tɯ-rtsɤɣone storey have the irregular forms χsɤ-tɣathree spans and χsɤ-rtsɤɣthree storeys (competing with regular χsɯ-tɣa and χsɯ-rtsɤɣ ) as in ( ex:XsAtGa ), but not for other numeral prefixes.

exe

nɯ χsɤ-tɣa kɯβde-tɣa jamar tu-rɲɟi cʰa. \\
dem three-span four-span about ipfv -be.long can: fact \\
`It can grow three or four spans long.' (14-sWNgWJu) 0003506#S181
exe

Another unrelated irregularity concerns the counted noun tɯ-ɣjɤnone time: free variation between -jɤn and -ɣjɤn is observed for the numerals `two' and `three' (both χsɯ-ɣjɤnthree times and χsɯ-jɤn are attested).

A similar case is observed with counted noun tɯ-xpaone year; the form -xpa is obligatory for one to three ( ʁnɯ-xpatwo years, χsɯ-xpathree years), but for `four' on, both stems -xpa and -pa are attested (both sqɯ-xpaten years and sqɯ-paten years are possible, though the former is more common), including for approximate numerals ( ɕnɤcɤ-paseven or eight years).

The counted noun tɯ-zloʁone time (see § sec:arithmetic on its use) is attested in ( ex:RYizloR ) with the special form ʁɲɯ-zloʁtwo times whose first element is a numeral prefix form ʁɲɯ- influenced by the Tibetan numeral གཉིས་gɲistwo (in Japhug pronunciation ʁɲiz- ). The regular form ʁnɯ-zloʁtwo times also exists.

exe

a-zda ɣɯ kɯ-fse ʁɲɯ-zloʁ nɯ tu-ndze-a ɲɯ-tʂaŋ \\
1sg. poss -companion gen sbj: pcp -be.like two-times dem ipfv -eat[III]- 1sg sens -be.fair \\
`It would be fair if I had two times as much to eat as the other one.' (140426 lv he luozi-zh)
0003816#S9
exe

The stem -zloʁ looks like a blend from the two Tibetan words ཟློག་zlogturn around and ཟློzlorepeat. Tibetan numerals are generally post-nominal, but prenominal numerals also exist as in ཉིས་ལྡབ་ɲis.ldabtwo times.
summary: The passage describes several counted nouns with irregular numeral-prefix paradigms, especially **tɤ-rʑaʁ** ‘night,’ which can take an alternative **ɤ**-vocalism in its prefixes (e.g. ‘two nights,’ ‘three nights’), though the regular forms are also possible and sometimes more common. Similar irregular or variable forms are noted for a few other counted nouns, including **tɯ-tɣa** ‘span,’ **tɯ-rtsɤɣ** ‘storey,’ **tɯ-ɣjɤn** ‘time,’ **tɯ-xpa** ‘year,’ and **tɯ-zloʁ** ‘time,’ with some forms showing Tibetan influence or competing stem variants.

text:
The distributed form of counted nouns is built by reduplicating the numeral `one' prefix tɯ, as tɯ-tɯ-rdoʁ from the generic counted noun tɯ-rdoʁone piece (see § sec:CN.classification ) in example ( ex:tWtWrdoR ).

exe

ʑɯrɯʑɤri qʰe, tɕe tɯ-tɯ-rdoʁ nɯ ɲɯ-ʑɣɤ-qɤr-nɯ qʰe \\
progressively lnk lnk one-one-piece dem ipfv -get.separated- pl lnk \\
`Progressively, some of them get separated [from the herd].' (20-RmbroN) 0003560#S55
exe

Example ( ex:tWtWxpa ) with tɯ-tɯ-xpasome years from tɯ-xpaone year clearly illustrates the functional difference with approximate numerals (§ sec:approx.numerals and § sec:approximate.numeral.prefixes ), as the meaning of the distributed counted noun cannot be translated here as `a few years' -- the years when the income is good are not necessarily contiguous in time.

exe

tɯ-tɯ-xpa tɕe a-pɯ-pe tɕe, kʰrɯtsu ɯ-ro jamar ɲɯ-fsoʁ ɲɯ-cʰa \\
one-one-year lnk irr - ipfv -be.good lnk ten.thousand 3sg. poss -excess about ipfv -earn sens -can \\
`Some years if [his income] is good, he can earn more than ten thousands [renminbi].' (14-siblings)
0003508#S161
exe

An alternative distributed form involves partial reduplication of the stem of the counted noun and replacing the numeral prefix by a third singular possessive ɯ, as in the conversion from counted noun to inalienably possessed noun (§ sec:CN.IPN ). In (§ sec:WphWphW ), the counted noun tɯ-pʰɯone tree is changed to ɯ-pʰɯ pʰɯsome trees. The other distributed form tɯ-tɯ-pʰɯ could also be used in the same context without meaning difference.

exe

zgoku kɯ-mbro tɕe, ɕkrɤz kɯ-wxti ra nɯ ɯ-rcʰɤβ ri ɯ-pʰɯ pʰɯ ʑo tu tɕe \\
mountain nmzl:S/A-be.tall lnk oak nmzl:S/A-be.big pl dem 3sg. poss -between loc 3sg. poss - part tree emph exist: fact lnk \\
`On high mountains, among big oaks, there are some [of these little trees].' (16-CWrNgo)
0003518#S168
exe

This distributed form puts emphasis on the non-contiguousness and spread over distribution of the entities designated by the reduplicated counted noun: in (§ sec:WphWphW ) for instance, its presence implies that the little trees are not clustered, but rather scattered among the oaks.

Distributed counted nouns can also be repeated to put even more emphasis on the scattered distribution (see § sec:CN.repetition ).
summary: Distributed counted nouns are formed by reduplicating either the numeral prefix *tɯ-* or the stem of the counted noun, sometimes with replacement by the third-person possessive *ɯ-*. These forms express a distributed, non-contiguous plurality, emphasizing that the entities are scattered rather than grouped together, and they can be repeated for even stronger emphasis.

subsubsection: Historical perspectives on the numeral prefixal paradigm
text:
Most non-Tibetan languages of Western Sichuan/Northern Yunnan have counted nouns (generally called `classifiers', see § sec:CN.classification ) with numeral-counted noun order (see for instance, ). It is striking that among the quasi-isolating languages (Lolo-Burmese, Naish), numeral prefix paradigms are commonly a pocket of irregular morphology (, ); this is also true in some Hmong-Mien languages (see ).

By contrast, while Japhug and the other Gyalrong languages have a richer morphology in general, the numeral prefixal paradigms are, with only few exceptions (§ sec:irregular.numeral.prefixes ), suspiciously regular. The historical interpretation of this observation is not completely straightforward, but in any case counted nouns are morphologically like determinative compounds (§ sec:determinative.n.n ) with a numeral as first element, undergoing bound state in the case of more integrated numerals (some of the numerals under 100, see § sec:num.prefixes.1.10, § sec:num.prefixes.11.99 and § sec:approximate.numeral.prefixes ) and immune from it in the case of higher numerals (§ sec:other.numeral.prefixes ).

One morphological alternation common to all numeral prefixes under 10 is the loss of the codas, otherwise a rare phenomenon in noun compounds (see § sec:loss.codas.compounds ). For numerals above 10, there is some degree of free variation in the preservation of the codas (see for instance example ex:GnAsqaptWWGrZaR p. ex:GnAsqaptWWGrZaR); the forms preserving codas are rarer, and may be ongoing analogical levelling.

Even in the case of lower numerals, there are indirect traces of the former existence of codas, in particular in irregularities (§ sec:irregular.numeral.prefixes ). A few counted nouns like tɯ-xpaone year and tɯ-ɣjɤnone time have velar fricative preinitials x-/ɣ- which are lacking in some forms of the paradigm.

In the case of tɯ-xpaone year, note the alternative stem -pa ( sqɯ-xpaten years vs. sqɯ-paten years), the time ordinals (§ sec:time.ordinals ), the adverb pakukuevery year and the verb papass $X$ years (see example ex:40.topa, § sec:pa.intr.lv ) from which the counted noun tɯ-xpaone year is historically derived. Cognates of this root -pa appear in other Burmo-Gyalrongic languages such as Naish  but are restricted to time ordinals, and do not occur as counted nouns. Even in the closely related Stau language, time ordinals such as javəlast year and pəvəthis year have a root -və cognate to Japhug -pa, but the corresponding counted noun e-fkuone year has a different root which left no trace in the Gyalrong languages. The generalization of the -pa root to the counted paradigm is probably a common Gyalrong innovation (see § sec:CN.verbs ).

A possible explanation for this x-/ɣ- element is that it originates from the coda of the numeral `one' (although replaced by cione, this former numeral is still found in the element -tɯɣ in sqaptɯɣeleven) through false segmentation ( *tɯk-pa $ $ *tɯ-kpa $ $ *tɯ-xpa `one year') and subsequent generalization to the whole paradigm. Note that since proto-Gyalrong *kp- regularly yields βɣ- with metathesis, this false segmentation must have occurred after the *kp- $ $ βɣ- sound change, which is not shared with other Gyalrong languages. It is not an example of x-/ɣ- nominalization (§ sec:G.nmlz ).
summary: Western Sichuan/Northern Yunnan languages often have counted nouns with numeral-counted order, and in several quasi-isolating languages numeral prefixes are irregular, but Japhug and other Gyalrong languages show unusually regular numeral prefix paradigms. The passage explains that counted nouns behave like determinative compounds, with some numerals undergoing bound-state marking and lower numerals commonly losing codas; irregular forms and velar fricative preinitials in a few nouns preserve traces of older forms. It further suggests that the x-/ɣ- element in forms like tɯ-xpa ‘one year’ may come from false segmentation involving the old numeral ‘one,’ though the historical explanation is not fully certain.

text:
This section discusses the use of counted nouns in quantifying function, as noun modifiers, head of a noun phrase or a sentential quantifier.

The main functions of counted nouns include partitive, distributive, restrictive and iterative meanings.
summary: Counted nouns are used in quantifying functions as noun modifiers, as the head of a noun phrase, or as sentential quantifiers. Their main semantic roles include partitive, distributive, restrictive, and iterative meanings.

text:
partitive!counted noun counted noun!partitive
When occurring as postnominal modifiers, most counted nouns are essentially partitive in meaning, referring to a certain number of individuals from a group, and are not used to express indefiniteness (§ sec:CN.definiteness ): the polyfunctional determiner cione (§ sec:indef.article ) occurs instead in this meaning.

Thus, a phrase such as tɯrme tɯ-rdoʁ combining the noun tɯrmeperson with the generic counted noun tɯ-rdoʁone piece (see § § sec:CN.classification on counted noun selection) is generally either to be translated as a partitive `one of them' as in ( ex:tWrme.tWrdoR.RnWz ).

exe

tɯrme ʁnɯz pjɤ-tu tɕe, tɯrme tɯ-rdoʁ nɯ rcanɯ, ɯ-stɤrju ʁɟa ʑo tu-βze tɕe, \\
people two ifr. ipfv -exist lnk people one-piece dem unexp: deg 3sg. poss -truth completely emph ipfv -do[III] lnk \\
`There were two persons, one of them always told the truth (and the other one was a liar).' (140427 yuanhou-zh)
0003870#S3
exe

The partitive meaning is found even when the individual counted noun occurs on its own without overt head noun as in ( ex:tWrdoR.cinA ).

exe

ɯ-tɕɯ kɯβde pɯ-tu ri, ɯʑo kɯ-fse kɯ-ɕqraʁ tɯ-rdoʁ cinɤ pɯ-me ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -son four pst. ipfv -exist but 3sg sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp -be.intelligent one-piece even pst. ipfv -not.exist sens -be \\
`He had four sons, but not even one of them was smart like him.' (2005 tAwa kWcqraR)
exe

The partitive meaning is found in particular when counted nouns modify mass nouns, such as paʁɕapork in ( ex:paʁɕa.tWrdoR ).

exe

pakuku ʑo paʁɕa tɯ-rdoʁ, qʰe tɕe tɕe stoʁ cʰɯ-ɣɯt, \\
every.year emph pork one-piece lnk lnk lnk broad.bean ipfv: downstream -bring \\
`Every year, he would bring a piece of pork and broad beans.' (140501 tshering skyid)
0003902#S34
exe
summary: When used as postnominal modifiers, most counted nouns have a partitive meaning, referring to a specific number of individuals from a larger group, rather than expressing indefiniteness, which is instead marked by the determiner cione. This partitive interpretation can occur both when the counted noun follows an overt head noun and when it appears alone, and it is especially common when counted nouns modify mass nouns, as in phrases meaning “a piece of pork.”

text:
distributive!counted noun counted noun!distributive
Counted nouns can also have a distributive meaning `each of them' when another numeral or counted noun occurs in the same clause, indicating that each of the members of the group performs the same action, the verb can either receive plural (as in ex:tWrme.tWrdoR.kW and ex:tWrZaR ) or singular indexation (example ex:tWrme.tWrdoR2 ). This is a particular case of fluid number indexation (§ sec:agreement.mismatch ).

exe

tɕe tɕe tɯrme tɯ-rdoʁ kɯ kʰɯna ʁnɯz χsɯm jamar tu-ndo-nɯ \\
lnk lnk person one-piece erg dog two three about ipfv -take- pl \\
`Each [of the hunters] takes two or three dogs.' (150829 KAGWcAno)
0006420#S24
exe

exe

tɯrme tɯ-rdoʁ kɯ cʰɤmdɤru tɯ-ldʑa tu-nɯ-ndɤm \\
people one-piece erg drinking.straw one- cl ipfv - auto -take[III] \\
`Each person takes one straw.' (30-tChorzi)
0003760#S33
exe

Counted noun with a collective meaning (§ sec:collective.counted.noun ) such as tɯ-tɯpɯone household also frequently have a partitive meaning, especially when combined with a numeral.

exe

tɕe tɯ-tɯpɯ tɕe, ɯ-qaʑo kɯβdɤsqi, kɯmŋɤsqi jamar pɯ-tu. \\
lnk one-household lnk 3sg. poss -sheep forty fifty about pst. ipfv -exist \\
`Each household used to have about forty or fifty sheep.' (160712 smAG)
0006073#S23
exe

Temporal counted nouns such as tɯ-sŋione day (§ sec:CN.time ) are generally repeated when used in distributive function in the meaning `every (day)' (§ sec:CN.repetition ). However, in combination with other counted nouns, they can mean `per...' as in ( ex:tWkhWtsa.tWrdoR ), even without repetition.

exe

tɯ-sŋi tɕe tɯ-kʰɯtsa jamar tɯ-rdoʁ kɯ pjɯ-tsʰi ɲɯ-cʰa. \\
one-day lnk one-bowl about one- cl erg ipfv -drink sens -can \\
`One [cat] can drink about one bowl of milk per day.' (21-lWLU)
0003576#S44
exe

When no other numeral or counted noun is present, the modifier of Tibetan origin raŋrieach (from རང་རེ་raŋ.reeach; see also § sec:raNri ) can be used to specify the distributive meaning as in ( ex:tWtWpW.rANri ).

exe

tɯ-tɯpɯ raŋri ɣɯ, nɯ-mbro pjɤ-tu... \\
one-household each gen 3pl. poss -horse ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`Each household used to have horses etc.' (150820 kAnWCkat)
exe

Counted nouns can have a combined distributive and partitive meaning `each one of their...', such as tɯ-ntsione of a pair in ( ex:nWXpWm.tWntsi ).

exe

tɕe tɕʰeme ra kɯ nɯ-χpɯm tɯ-ntsi ka-ta-nɯ, tɤ-tɕɯ ra kɯ nɯ-χpɯm ʁnɯz ka-ta-nɯ ri, \\
lnk girl pl erg 3pl. poss -knee one-of.a.pair aor:3 -put- pl indef. poss -son pl erg 3pl. poss -knee two aor:3 -put- pl lnk \\
`[Each of] the girls (in their group) put one of their knees, the boys put their two knees [as a support for the tea kettle].' (2005-stod-kunbzang)
exe
summary: Counted nouns can express distributive meanings like “each of them,” especially when another numeral or counted noun appears in the clause, and in these cases the verb may show either plural or singular agreement. Temporal counted nouns can also mean “per…” in combination with other counted nouns, and without another numeral, the Tibetan-origin modifier raŋri can mark distributive meaning. Counted nouns with collective or paired meanings may further develop partitive or combined distributive-partitive readings, such as “each household” or “each one of a pair.”

text:
Repeating a counted nouns with the same numeral prefix has either a distributive or a distributed meaning. If the numeral prefixes are different however, an approximate numeral interpretation results, see § sec:approximate.numeral.prefixes.

Example ( ex:tWldZa.tWldZa ) illustrates the distributive meaning (`each', `each single', `one by one') of counted noun repetition with an individual counted noun ( tɯ-ldʑaone long object) and also a partitive counted noun ( tɯ-spraone handful). Repeated counted nouns of measure can be used to refer to the unit in which a whole mass of elements (here the hemp stalks) is divided into (`into bundles', `bundle by bundle').

exe

tɤsɤmu nɯ tɕe tɯɲcɣa tú-wɣ-lɤt tɕe, [...] tɯ-ldʑa tɯ-ldʑa ɲɯ́-wɣ-pʰɯt tɕe tɕe nɯnɯ li tɯ-spra tɯ-spra tú-wɣ-xtɕɤr. \\
hemp dem lnk sickle ipfv - inv -throw lnk one-long.object one-long.object ipfv - inv -pluck lnk lnk dem again one-handful one-handful ipfv - inv -tie \\
`As for hemp, one uses a sickle and cuts [the stalks] one by one and then ties them into bundles.' (14-tasa)
0003510#S50
exe

The distributive meaning also occurs with repeated temporal counted nouns, as in ( ex:tWxpa.tWxpa ).

exe

tɕe tɯ-xpa tɯ-xpa tu-ɬoʁ qʰe tɕe qartsɯ tɕe pjɯ-kʰrɯ ɕti. \\
lnk one-year one-year ipfv -come.out lnk lnk winter lnk ipfv -be.dry be. aff: fact \\
`It grows every year (i.e. it is an annual plant), and dies in winter.' (140512 tAzraj)
0003971#S10
exe

Alternatively, rather than juxtaposing counted nouns, coordinating them with the additive nɤ (§ sec:additive.nA ) as in ( ex:tWCha.nA.tWCha ) also results in a distributive meaning.

exe

tɕe nɯŋa ndɤre ɯ-pɯ nɯ tɯ-rdoʁ nɤ tɯ-rdoʁ ma me tɯ-xpa tɯ-ɣjɤn ma ɲɯ-rɤpɯ mɤ-cʰa \\
lnk cow top. advers 3sg. poss -offspring dem one-piece add one-piece apart.from not.exist: fact one-year one-time apart.from ipfv -bear.young neg -can: fact \\
`As for cows, they [have] their young only one by one, and can only bear young once a year.'
0003404#S123
exe

exe

nɯnɯ mɯrmɯmbju nɯ tɯ-tɕʰa nɤ tɯ-tɕʰa ntsɯ tɯtɯrca ntsɯ ku-rɤʑi-nɯ ŋu tɕe \\
dem swallow dem one-pair add one-pair always together always ipfv -stay- pl be: fact lnk \\
`Swallows are always in pairs.' (03-mWrmWmbjW) 0003382#S49
exe

Repeated counted nouns also express a distributed meaning as in ( ex:tWrdoR.tWrdoR ). Like the distributed numeral prefixes (§ sec:numeral.prefixes.distributed ), this construction indicates that the entities referred to by the counted nouns are scattered more or less homogeneously.

exe

tɯ-rdoʁ tɯ-rdoʁ kɯ-fse tu-ɬoʁ ŋu ma mɤ-arɤkʰɯmkʰɤl. \\
one-piece one-piece sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv -come.out be: fact lnk neg -be.heterogeneously.distributed: fact \\
`It grows in scattered fashion, not in clusters here and there.' (22-BlamajmAG)
0003584#S124
exe

It is also possible to repeat counted nouns with distributed numeral prefixes to emphasize even more the scattered distribution as in ( ex:tWtWrdoR.tWtWrdoR ).

exe

tɕeri tɯ-tɯ-rdoʁ tɯ-tɯ-rdoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu ma kɯ-ɤndʑɯrɣa kɯ-fse kɯ-ɤrɤkʰɯmkʰɤl kɯ-fse maŋe. \\

summary:
Repeating a counted noun with the same numeral prefix can express either a distributive meaning, such as “each” or “one by one,” or a distributed meaning, where entities are spread out more or less evenly. If the repeated counted nouns have different numeral prefixes, the result is an approximate numeral interpretation instead.  

The passage illustrates distributive uses with individual objects, measure nouns, and temporal nouns, and shows that coordination with the additive nɤ can also yield distributive meaning. It also notes that repeated counted nouns with distributed numeral prefixes can intensify the sense of scattered distribution.

In negative restrictive constructions with cinɤ(not) even one, individual counted nouns with the numeral tɯ- `one' also occur as in ( ex:Wjwaʁ.tWmpCar.cinA ).

Individual counted nouns can also express a combination of partitive and restrictive meaning, `just $X$ of them', as in ( ex:tWrdoR.mapWwGsat ).

Another type of restricted meaning is, in the case of mass nouns such as rdɤstaʁstone, the meaning `in one piece' as in example ( ex:rdAstaR.tWldZa ), with the individual counted nouns tɯ-ldʑaone long object or tɯ-rdoʁone piece (the storyteller hesitates between the two) occurring here not as noun modifier, but as nominal predicates with the participle of the copula ŋube (§ sec:copula.basic ). Unlike languages such as Chinese, where the meaning `alone' can be expressed by the numeral `one' with a quantifier ( 一个人 yīgèrénone person, alone), this meaning is not normally conveyed by counted nouns in Japhug, but rather by the adverbial root -sti `alone' (see § sec:stWsti ).
summary: The passage explains that in Japhug, the counted noun phrase with tɯ- ‘one’ most consistently means ‘one person’ only in restrictive constructions with the exceptive postposition ma ‘apart from,’ and similar forms also appear in negative restrictive contexts with cinɤ ‘not even one.’ It further shows that counted nouns can carry restrictive or partitive-restrictive meanings such as ‘just one of them’ or ‘in one piece,’ but they do not normally express the meaning ‘alone,’ which is instead conveyed by the adverbial root -sti.

text:
Some counted nouns, rather than being used as postnominal quantifiers, can have scope over the whole sentence. Two constructions can be distinguished: the iterative/semelfactive construction, in which the counted nouns designate the number of time that an action takes place, and the pseudo-object construction.

Only a minority of counted nouns can be used in the iterative/semelfactive construction. This group includes temporal counted nouns like tɯ-ɣjɤnone time (§ sec:CN.time ), counted nouns derived from verbs (§ sec:CN.verbs ) such as tɯ-tɤtɕʰɯhitting with the hoe one time (from tɕʰɯgore, stab) and tɯ-tɤfskɤrone turn (from fskɤrturn around) or from ideophones (§ sec:CN.ideophones ) such as tɯ-tɤxɯrone turn.

Semelfactive counted nouns can either be used as objects of an auxiliary verb, mainly lɤtrelease (§ sec:lAt.lv ), as in ( ex:kAntChWtAtChW ) and ( ex:RnWtAxWr ), or as sentential quantifiers (§ sec:CN.iterative ), as in ( ex:laRnWtAxWr ) with the intransitive verb mtɕɯrturn.

exe

qaʁ kɤntɕʰɯ-tɤtɕʰɯ to-lɤt \\
hoe several-hitting.with.the.hoe ifr -release \\
`He hit several times with the hoe.' (elicited)
exe

exe

ʁnɯ-tɤxɯr to-lɤt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
two-turn ifr -throw sens -be \\
`He ran two laps.' (2003 sras)
exe

exe

χcʰa pɕoʁ laʁnɯ-tɤxɯr ku-mtɕɯr, ʁe pɕoʁ laʁnɯ-tɤxɯr ku-mtɕɯr ŋu. \\
right side a.few-turn ipfv -turn left side a.few-turn ipfv -turn be: fact \\
`It turns several times on the right, and several times one the left.' (150826 qro kWnWkhABGa)

In the pseudo-object construction, counted nouns semantically related to the patient of the main verb (even in intransitive constructions lacking an object) occur to express the meaning `not even one...' (in a negative construction) or `a few...'. This construction is most clearly illustrated with intransitive verbs. In examples ( ex:tWtWkWr.cinA ) and ( ex:laRnWNka.rWCmitCi ), the intransitive verbs with rɯndzɤtsʰihave a meal and rɯɕmispeak cannot take overt object noun phrases (they are not semi-transitive, see § sec:intr.goal ), but occur here with counted noun quantifiers referring to the non-overt patients (the food in ex:tWtWkWr.cinA and the words in ex:laRnWNka.rWCmitCi ), which would be the object of the corresponding transitive verbs ndzaeat and tisay.

tɤ-pɤtso ra tɯ-mu ɯ-xɕɤt kɯ tɯ-tɯ-kɯr cinɤ ʑo kɤ-rɯndzɤtsʰi mɯ-pjɤ-cʰa-nɯ. \\
indef. poss -child pl nmlz:action-be.afraid 3sg. poss -strength erg one- indef. poss -mouth even emph inf -eat neg - ifr. ipfv -can- pl \\
`The children were so afraid that they could not even eat one mouthful.' (160704 poucet4-v2)
0006097#S52

laʁnɯ-ŋka rɯɕmi-tɕi \\
few-word speak: fact - 1du \\
`Let us speak a few words.' (elicited)

In these examples, adding an overt noun would be agrammatical, and the quantifiers tɯ-tɯ-kɯr cinɤ ʑo `not even one mouthful' and laʁnɯ-ŋkaa few words cannot be analyzed as objects. Rather, they are sentential adverbs, whose grammatical status is comparable to that of temporal counted nouns (§ sec:CN.time ).
summary: Some counted nouns can take scope over the whole sentence rather than functioning as postnominal quantifiers. The passage distinguishes an iterative/semelfactive construction, where the counted noun marks the number of times an action occurs and is used by a minority of counted nouns, and a pseudo-object construction, where a counted noun semantically related to an unexpressed patient expresses meanings like “not even one…” or “a few…”. In the pseudo-object construction, the quantifier is not an object but a sentential adverb, and overt noun phrases are ungrammatical.

text:
We also find examples of counted nouns without partitive, distributive, restricted or iterative meaning.

This the case in particular for counted nouns with a collective meaning, denoting a group of entities whose quantity can be precise ( tɯ-tɕʰaone pair) or unspecified ( tɯ-boʁone group, tɯ-tɯpɯone household or tɯ-tɯpʰuone hive). In ( ex:taRrdp.RnWtWpW ) for instance, ʁnɯ-tɯpɯ means `two households', not `two of the households' or `each of the households'. Note also the plural (rather than dual) indexation on the verb tu-nɯ, showing the inherent collective meaning of the counted noun tɯ-tɯpɯone household. Plural indexation here is optional (§ sec:optional.indexation ). In this example, ʁnɯ-tɯpɯ is not a modifier of the placename taʁrdo: this placename is an absolutive locative adjunct (§ absolutive.locative ).

exe

tʰam taʁrdo ʁnɯ-tɯpɯ tu-nɯ \\
now placename two-household exist- pl \\
`Now there are two households in Tarrdo.' (140522 tshupa)
0004053#S19
exe

This number quantification meaning is also attested with non-collective counted nouns. For instance, in ( ex:xCAndZu.XsWldZa ), χsɯ-ldʑa `three (long objects)' occurs in the same context as the numerals cione and χsɯmthree. In ( ex:si.tWphW.pjAtu ) likewise, it is clear from the context that neither a partitive, distributive, nor restrictive interpretation is possible.

However, this function is not very widespread in native texts.

In texts translated from Chinese or elicited material however, this usage is very common, as speakers will easily calque the Chinese noun+classifier construction. In example ( ex:qaJY.tWldZa ) for instance qaɟy tɯ-ldʑa `one fish' is very probably calqued from Chinese 一条鱼 yī-tiáo yú (one- cl fish). The original text from which ( ex:qaJY.tWldZa ) was translated is 不久，老三又看见了一条鱼和一只狐狸. The counted noun tɯ-ldʑaone long object however is really applied to fishes, snakes and worms in Japhug even in non-translated texts (§ sec:CN.classification ).

`He saw a fish and a fox.' (140505 xiaohaitu-zh)

Future studies on the use of counted noun as quantifiers should be therefore exclusively based on texts not translated from Chinese and conversation, not on translations and elicitation.
summary: The passage notes that counted nouns can express simple number quantification without any partitive, distributive, restricted, or iterative meaning, especially when they have a collective sense such as “two households” or “one group.” It also shows that this number-quantifying use occurs with some non-collective counted nouns, though it is uncommon in native texts and much more frequent in Chinese translations or elicited data, where it often reflects a calqued Chinese classifier construction.

definite

text:
noun!counted classification
This section presents the semantic restrictions on the use of particular counted nouns. It also discusses the cases of nouns that are compatible with several counted nouns.
summary: The passage says that this section explains the semantic restrictions governing the use of specific counted nouns. It also covers nouns that can combine with more than one counted noun.

text:
The counted noun tɯ-rdoʁone piece can occur as postnominal modifier with a considerable variety of nouns, designating people, animals, inanimate objects, including mass nouns; it is the counted noun by default.

A minority of nouns select other individual counted nouns referring to specific shapes: tɯ-ldʑaone long object, tɯ-mpɕarone leaf and tɯ-pʰɯone tree.

The counted noun tɯ-ldʑaone long object, like Chinese 一条 yitiáoone long object or 一根 yigēnone long object, occurs in the corpus with nouns belonging to the following semantic categories:

itemize
Stick-like objects: ɯ-ruits stalk, tɤ-zrɤmroot, tɤɲiwalking stick, taqaβneedle, tɯmɲaarrow, dɤrʁɯfern or ndʑustick, `chopsticks' (ex. ex:ndZu.XsWldZa )
Limbs, hair and other protruding body-parts: tɯ-mifoot, leg, tɤ-kɤrmehead hair, tɤ-mujfeather, ta-ʁrɯhorn.
Limbless animals: qaprisnake, qaɟyfish
Towers: ɣɟɯwatchtower
itemize

exe

tɕi-xɕɤndʑu χsɯ-ldʑa pɯ-tu tɕe \\
1du. poss -twig three-long.object pst. ipfv -exist lnk \\
`We had three twigs.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

The counted noun tɯ-mpɕarone leaf occurs with flat objects, including tree leaves (with tɤ-jwaʁleaf as in ex:RnWmpCar ), sheets of cloth (with razcloth) and snowflakes (with tɤjpasnow).

exe

ɯ-jwaʁ nɯ ʁnɯ-mpɕar ma me tɕe \\
3sg. poss -leaf dem two-leaf apart.from not.exist: fact lnk \\
`It only has two leaves.' (16-CWrNgo)
0003518#S176
exe

The counted noun tɯ-mpɕarone leaf can also refer to money (in present-day China, bank notes are by far more common than coins even for small amounts of money), meaning `one renminbi'.

The counted noun tɯ-phɯone tree occurs with the generic noun sitree or names of particular species.
summary:
The counted noun tɯ-rdoʁ ‘one piece’ is the default classifier and can modify a wide range of nouns, including people, animals, inanimate objects, and even mass nouns. A minority of nouns instead select more shape-specific counted nouns such as tɯ-ldʑa ‘one long object,’ tɯ-mpɕar ‘one leaf,’ and tɯ-pʰɯ ‘one tree.’

These shape-based counted nouns are semantically restricted: tɯ-ldʑa occurs with stick-like objects, protruding body parts, limbless animals, and towers; tɯ-mpɕar with flat objects such as leaves, cloth sheets, snowflakes, and also money; and tɯ-pʰɯ with the generic noun for tree or with specific tree species.

text:
counted noun!collective
Most nouns referring to humans and animals can occur with the counted noun tɯ-boʁone group. However, the collective counted noun tɯ-ɟɯɣone pack appears to be exclusively used with horses. Its only attestations in the corpus (for instance ex:tWJWG ) are found in a translated text.

exe

again dem about dem: prox irr - pfv -2-go lnk lnk dem: loc lnk more horse one-herd exist: fact lnk \\
`Continue going again for about that distance, and there will be a pack of horse.' (150824 kelaosi-zh)
0006276#S193
exe
summary: Most nouns referring to humans and animals can combine with the counted noun **tɯ-boʁone** “group.” By contrast, the collective counted noun **tɯ-ɟɯɣone** “pack” seems to be used only with horses, and its few corpus examples occur only in translated text.

text:
Some nouns are compatible with more than one counted noun postnominal modifier, with different connotations. For instance zgomountain can be used with the generic counted noun tɯ-rdoʁone piece as in ( ex:zgo.tWrdoR ), but also with tɯ-ldʑaone long object as in ( ex:zgo.RnWldZa ) in the meaning `mountain range' and also with tɯ-tɤɣmbajone side to mean `mountain face'.

exe

nɯ-kʰa ɯ-rkɯ zgo tɯ-rdoʁ pɯ-ri \\
dem house 3sg. poss -side mountain one-piece aor -be.left \\
`When there was only one mountain left [on his way back] home,...' (Lobzang03)
exe

exe

rŋgɯkɤta nɯ li zgo ʁnɯ-ldʑa tu tɕe, \\
topo dem again mountain two-long.object exist: fact lnk \\
`[As for the placename] Rngukata, there are also two mountain ranges.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo)
0004059#S62
exe

In other cases, the change of counted noun does not entail a radical semantic contrast. For instance, the noun sitree, while generally used with tɯ-pʰɯone tree, is also attested with the counted noun tɯ-ldʑaone long object, as in ( ex:si.tWldZa ), without clear semantic difference.

exe

maka rdɤstaʁ cʰo si rcanɯ tɯ-ldʑa cinɤ ʑo kɯ-me scʰiz kɤ-azɣɯt-ndʑi ɲɯ-ŋu, \\

`They arrived at a place where there was no stones and not even one tree.' (2003 Kunbzang)
