summary: Some nouns can combine with more than one counted noun postnominal modifier, and the choice can create different meanings: for example, *zgo* ‘mountain’ may take the generic counted noun ‘one piece,’ ‘one long object’ to mean ‘mountain range,’ or ‘one side’ to mean ‘mountain face.’ In other cases, changing the counted noun does not produce a clear semantic contrast, as with *si* ‘tree,’ which is normally used with ‘tree’ but can also occur with ‘one long object’ without an obvious difference in meaning.

subsection: Counted nouns and other parts of speech
text: This section presents the derivations from other parts of speech (including other nominal classes, such as inalienably and alienably possessed nouns) into counted noun, and from counted noun into other classes.
summary: The section describes derivational processes that move words from other parts of speech, including other nominal classes such as inalienably and alienably possessed nouns, into the class of counted noun. It also covers derivations that move words from counted nouns into other classes.

subsection: Counted nouns and other parts of speech
subsubsection: Counted nouns and inalienably possessed nouns
text:
Counted nouns and inalienably possessed nouns stand out among other nouns in having an obligatory prefix. Since the citation form of both classes of nouns -- the numeral `one' prefix tɯ- and the indefinite possessor prefixes tɯ-/tɤ- -- are homophonous, it is not unexpected that conversion occurs between the two classes.

Given the fact that numeral prefixes are a closed class (see § sec:numeral.prefixes and in particular § sec:other.numeral.prefixes ), when one needs to use a quantifier without numeral prefix equivalent, it is necessary to convert the counted noun into an inalienably possessed noun in third person singular form, with the quantifier before it. In example ( ex:nW.thamtCAt.WtWphu ), the quantifier nɯ tʰamtɕɤtthat many cannot be converted to a prefix, and therefore the counted noun tɯ-tɯpʰuone type is converted to an inalienably possessed noun in 3sg possessive form ɯ-tɯpʰu.

exe

tɕe paʁ tɯ-ɣjɤn pjɯ́-wɣ-ntɕʰa nɯ nɯ tʰamtɕɤt ɯ-tɯpʰu ɲɯ-ɬoʁ ra \\
lnk pig one-time ipfv - inv -butcher dem dem all 3sg. poss -type ipfv -come.out be.needed: fact \\
`Each time one kills a pig, one will get that many types [of foodstuff from it].' (05-paR)
0003400#S89
exe

Similarly, in ( ex:GurZa.Wro.WtWpW ), the more complex phrase ɣurʑa ɯ-ro `more than one hundred' with the emphatic ʑo occurs with the 3sg prefix.

exe

ɣurʑa ɯ-ro ʑo ɯ-tɯpɯ tu-j \\
hundred 3sg. poss -excess emph 3sg. poss -household exist: fact - 1pl \\
`There are more than one hundred households of us.' (22-kumpGatCW)
0003590#S29
exe

Example ( ex:WtWpW.pjAkAntChWci ) illustrates a third case of conversion from counted noun to inalienably possessed noun: a third singular possessive on the converted counted noun indicates here indefinite number, which makes it possible to specify the quantity as the predicate ( pjɤ-k-ɤntɕʰɯ-ci `they used to be many') instead of the numeral prefix ( kɤntɕʰɯ-tɯpɯmany households, see § sec:other.numeral.prefixes ).

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ nɯ, ɯ-tɯpɯ pjɤ-k-ɤntɕʰɯ-ci nɤ, \\
former.time dem 3sg. poss -household ifr. ipfv - peg -be.many- peg sfp \\
`In former times, the households [there] were many.' (140522 tshupa)
0004053#S67
exe

Conversion from counted noun to inalienably possessed noun is also observed when a prenominal demonstrative or adnominal clause is present, as in ( ex:nW.Wxpa.nW ) and ( ex:arCo.pWNu.WsNi ). Conversion is however not obligatory, as shown by ( ex:nW.tWsNi ) (see additional examples in § sec:ordinals ).

exe

nɯ ɯ-xpa nɯ taχpa wuma pjɤ-pe \\
dem 3sg. poss -year dem harvest really ifr. ipfv -be.good \\
`On that year, the harvest was really good.' (02-montagnes-kamnyu)
0003378#S60
exe

exe

[arɕo pɯ-ŋu] ɯ-sŋi nɯtɕu tɕe \\
be.finished.up: fact pst. ipfv -be 3sg. poss -day dem: loc loc \\
`The day when [the appointed time] was about to be finished,' (2003 sras)
exe

exe

tɕendɤre nɯ tɯ-sŋi nɯnɯ mɯ-pjɤ-ko \\
lnk dem one-day dem neg - ifr -defeat \\
`On that day, he failed in his attempt [to force her to take him with her].' (02-deluge2012)
0003376#S68
exe

Finally, in the case of counted nouns expressing body-based units of length, conversion to an inalienably possessed noun has a very specific meaning. These units have a value that depends on the person of reference (few pairs of people have exactly the same handspan). The possessive prefix serves to indicate the person whose body part serves as the reference as in a-tɣa `my handspan' in ( ex:aZo.atGa ). It is the only case that a counted noun converted to inalienably possessed noun can take a possessive prefix other than 3sg.

exe

kɯ-zri nɯra, tɯ-tɣa ma kɯki ɕaŋtaʁ mɤ-zri, aʑo a-tɣa jamar ci ma me. \\
sbj: pcp -be.long dem: pl one-span apart.from dem. prox up.from neg -be.long: fact 1sg 1sg. poss -span about one apart.from not.exist: fact \\
`As for its length, it is at most one handspan, only the length of my handspan.' (28-tshAwAre)
0003722#S50
exe

Conversion from inalienably possessed noun to counted noun also exists, but is very marginal in Japhug. When inalienably possessed nouns are converted to counted nouns referring to a quantity, they are alienabilized (§ sec:alienabilization ) and the numeral prefixes are added to the noun stem with its indefinite possessor prefix. For instance, the counted noun tɯ-tɯ-kɯrone mouthful (example ex:tWtWkWr.cinA p. ex:tWtWkWr.cinA) or tɯ-tɤ-steone bladder of ( ex:tWci.tWtAste ) are derived from the body part inalienably possessed nouns tɯ-kɯrmouth and tɤ-stebladder.

exe

tɕe ʁdɯxpanaχpu ɣɯ ɯ-me ɣɯ nɯ, tɯ-ci tɯ-tɤ-ste, tɤrcoʁ sɯrna ci to-rku-nɯ, \\
lnk anthr gen 3sg. poss -daughter gen dem indef. poss -water one- indef. poss -bladder clay figurine indef ifr -put.in- pl \\
`They gave to Gdugpa Nagpo's daughter a bladder full of water and a clay figurine (to take with her on the road, as her dowry).' (2003 smanmi2)
exe

Direct conversion from inalienably possessed noun to counted noun without alienabilization is rarer, and it is not always obvious whether the inalienably possessed noun, or the counted noun is primary. For instance, the counted noun tɯ-qiɯone half (see § sec:fractions ) is likely to have been derived from the inalienably possessed noun ɯ-qiɯhalf, but the other directionality cannot be excluded.

Clearer cases is provided by the inalienably possessed ɯ-mdoʁcolour (from Tibetan མདོག་mdogcolour), which derives a counted noun with the numeral prefix kɤntɕʰɯ- `many' (on which see § sec:other.numeral.prefixes ) in ( ex:kAntChWmdoR ), and the native inalienably possessed noun tɤ-ʁarwing from which the counted noun tɯ-ʁarthe length of one arm originates (§ sec:measures ).

exe

tɕeri kɤntɕʰɯ-tɯpʰu, kɤntɕʰɯ-mdoʁ ɣɤʑu. \\
but many-types many-colour exist: sens \\
`There are many types [of the mushrooms called tɯqejmɤɣ ], and with many colours.' (24-zwArqhAjmAG)
0003630#S47
exe
summary: The passage explains that counted nouns and inalienably possessed nouns in Japhug both have obligatory prefixes, and because their citation-form prefixes are homophonous, nouns can convert between the two classes. Conversion from counted noun to inalienably possessed noun is common when a quantifier cannot take a numeral prefix, when prenominal demonstratives or clauses are present, or in some body-based units of length where the possessive prefix marks the reference person; conversion in the opposite direction is possible but marginal, and usually involves alienabilization.

subsection: Counted nouns and other parts of speech
subsubsection: Counted nouns and alienably possessed nouns
text:
Alienably possessed nouns designating containers can be converted to a partitive counted nouns by adding the numeral prefixes to the noun stem. For instance, the noun kʰɯtsabowl has a corresponding counted noun tɯ-kʰɯtsaone bowl as in ( ex:tWkhWtsa ).

exe

tɯ-kri tɯ-kʰɯtsa pjɤ-tu \\
indef. poss -oil one-bowl ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`They had one bowl [full] of oil.' (140501 mdzadi)
0003905#S6
exe

The same is true of nouns borrowed from Tibetan and Chinese such as pʰoŋbottle (from 瓶 píngbottle). As an alienably possessed noun, pʰoŋ designates the bottle itself (not its content), and takes postnominal numerals (as in ex:phoN ).

exe

pʰoŋ kɯβde ɣɤʑu \\
bottle four exist: sens \\
`There are four bottles.' (elicited; can refer for instance to empty bottles)
exe

Converted to a counted noun tɯ-pʰoŋone bottle it refers to the quantity of liquid contained in a bottle, and typically follows a mass noun as in ( ex:kWBdephoN ).

exe

cʰa kɯβde-pʰoŋ pjɤ-k-ɤ-ta-ci. \\
alcohol four-bottle ifr. ipfv - peg - pass -put- peg \\
`There were four bottles [full] of alcohol.' (140510 sanpian sheye-zh)
0003945#S49
exe

The derivation process is quite productive, and potentially new counted nouns meaning `a... full of' can be derived from any alienably possessed noun if a meaning can be made out of it, as in tɯ-co from covalley in ( ex:mbro.tWco ), which means in this particular context `an entire valley full of...'.

exe

mbro tɯ-co kɯ-fse, qaʑo tɯ-co kɯ-fse nɯ, fsapaʁ rmɯrmi ʑo nɯ tɯ-co nɤ tɯ-co ʑo pɯ-tu ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
horse one-valley sbj: pcp -be.like sheep one-valley sbj: pcp -be.like dem animal all.kinds emph dem one-valley lnk one-valley emph pst. ipfv -exist sens -be \\
`There was one valley entirely for each species of animals, like one valley full of horses, one valley full of sheep.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe
summary: Alienably possessed nouns for containers can be converted into partitive counted nouns by adding numeral prefixes to the noun stem, changing the meaning from the container itself to a quantity such as “one bowl full of oil.” This pattern also applies to borrowed nouns like “bottle,” where the possessed form refers to the bottle as an object, while the counted form refers to the amount contained. The derivation is productive and can extend to other alienably possessed nouns when a suitable “a… full of” meaning is available.

subsection: Counted nouns and other parts of speech
text:
The derivation of verbs into counted nouns and that of counted nouns into verbs are both productive processes in Japhug.

Counted nouns of verbal origin are either built by adding a numeral prefix to the verb stem (as tɯ-fkurone load from fkurcarry on the back) or to the verb stem with an additional prefix tɤ- ( tɯ-tɤrmbɯone heap from the transitive verb rmbɯheap up, § sec:action.nominals ). Note also the simultaneous action nominal with two prefixes tɯ-tɯ, which can be analyzed as involving a counted noun derived from a verb (§ sec:simultaneous.action.nominal ).

Most deverbal counted nouns are from transitive verbs, but examples from intransitive verbs are also found. For instance, in ( ex:tWtshoz ) the counted noun tɯ-tsʰozone complete set (from the stative intransitive verb tsʰozbe complete) translates Chinese 一整套 yīzhěngtào one complete set.

exe

nɯnɯ kɯ iɕqʰa rŋɯl kɯ tɯ-ŋga tʰɯ-kɤ-βzu ci tɯ-tsʰoz pjɤ-βde. \\
dem erg the.aforementioned silver erg indef. poss -clothes aor - obj: pcp -make indef one-complete.set ifr -throw.down \\
`[The bird] threw her a complete set of clothes that had been made in silver.' (140504 huiguniang-zh)
0003909#S106
exe

Deverbal counted nouns are either partitive counted nouns (§ sec:CN.partitive ), designating a quantity of objects resulting from the action of the verb (for instance tɯ-fkurone load or tɯ-tɤrtsɯɣone pile from rtsɯɣpile up as in ex:RnWtArtsWG ) or semelfactive counted nouns (§ sec:CN.iterative ), referring to the number of time an iterative/semelfactive action takes place (such as tɯ-tɤtɕʰɯhitting with the hoe one time from tɕʰɯgore, stab).

exe

ɕɤrɯ nɯ ʁnɯ-tɤrtsɯɣ to-βzu-ndʑi tɕe \\
bone dem two-pile ifr -make- du lnk \\
`They had make two piles from the bones.' (2002nyimavodzer)
exe

exe

qaʁ tɯ-tɤtɕʰɯ ta-lɤt \\
hoe one-hitting.with.hoe aor:3 -throw \\
`He used the hoe one time.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S86
exe

There also are more lexicalized and synchronically less obvious examples of counted nouns derived from verbs. For instance the temporal counted noun tɯ-xpaone year originates from the intransitive verb papass $X$ years illustrated in ( ex:12.topa ) (see also example ex:40.topa in § sec:pa.intr.lv and the account of the -x- element in tɯ- x pa proposed in § sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history ).

exe

kʰa na-βde nɯ sqamnɯz to-pa tɕe \\
house aor:3 -leave dem twelve ifr -pass.X.years lnk \\
`Twelve years had passed since she had left home.' (150828 huamulan-zh)
0006396#S127
exe

Since Situ, Zbu and Tshobdun all have cognates of tɯ-xpaone year, this non-trivial derivation must have occurred at the time of their common ancestor, but not earlier. Other Burmo-Gyalrongic languages, even Horpa and Khroskyabs have a root related to Japhug papass $X$ years for time ordinals (§ sec:time.ordinals ), but not for the corresponding counted noun.

Derivation of transitive verbs from counted nouns with the denominal prefix rɤ- is well-attested, for instance rɤtɣameasure by handspan from tɯ-tɣaone span. A complete list of these verbs and the various meanings of this derivation is presented in § sec:denom.tr.rA.
summary:
In Japhug, derivation between verbs and counted nouns is productive in both directions: verbs can form counted nouns, and counted nouns can also be used to derive verbs. Deverbal counted nouns are typically made with numeral prefixes and may denote quantities resulting from an action or the number of times an action occurs, though some forms are more lexicalized and historically less transparent, such as tɯ-xpa “year” from a verb meaning “pass X years.”

The passage also notes that most deverbal counted nouns come from transitive verbs, but some derive from intransitive verbs as well. In the opposite direction, transitive verbs can be derived from counted nouns with the denominal prefix rɤ-, as in rɤtɣa “measure by handspan” from tɯ-tɣa “span.”

subsection: Counted nouns and other parts of speech
text:
Deideophonic counted nouns are quite common, and belong to all major functional categories described above. In the following discussion, ideophones (§ sec:idph ) are by default cited in pattern II (§ sec:ideo.II ), though other patterns are mentioned in some cases where appropriate.

The collective counted nouns tɯ-boʁone group and tɯ-ɟɯɣone pack originate from the ideophonic roots found in boʁboʁin group, in order and ɟɯɣɟɯɣin great number (of long objects), respectively. The presence of plain voiced initial stops in these roots is a clue to their ideophonic origin (§ sec:idph.onsets ).

The semelfactive/iterative counted noun tɯ-tɤxɯrone turn comes from the ideophonic root of xɯrxɯrround (pattern III xɯrnɤxɯrturning around) with an additional prefix tɤ-. This prefix is possibly the trace of an intermediate stage as an inalienably possessed noun, with a two-step derivation ideophone $ $ inalienably possessed noun $ $ counted noun.

Direct derivation from ideophone to semelfactive counted noun is also attested, for instance tɯ-ɬɯmone period of sleep ( ex:tWlhWm.pjAnWZWB ) from the root in ɬɯmɬɯmhave a nice sleep without the tɤ- prefix.

exe

li tɯfsɤkʰa tɕe tɯ-ɬɯm pjɤ-nɯʑɯβ tɕe li ɯ-jmŋo ko-ntɕʰɤr tɕe \\
again dawn lnk one-sleep ifr -sleep lnk again 3sg. poss -dream ifr -appear lnk \\
`(The mother was so worried she could not sleep all night.) At dawn, she had a little sleep and had again a dream.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S159
exe
summary:
Deideophonic counted nouns are common and occur in all major functional categories, with ideophones generally cited here in pattern II. Some collective nouns, such as tɯ-boʁone ‘group’ and tɯ-ɟɯɣone ‘pack,’ derive from ideophonic roots, as shown by their forms and by voiced initial stops that suggest an ideophonic origin.

The semelfactive/iterative noun tɯ-tɤxɯrone ‘turn’ is derived from an ideophonic root with an added tɤ- prefix, possibly reflecting an intermediate inalienably possessed-noun stage. Direct derivation from ideophone to counted noun also occurs, as in tɯ-ɬɯmone ‘period of sleep,’ which comes from the root ɬɯmɬɯm without the tɤ- prefix.

text:
counted noun!measure
Measures of size, weight and volume are mainly expressed by counted nouns, though some unpossessible nouns are also found. Measures of time are discussed in § sec:time. Most or these words are falling out of use, and being replaced by Chinese words, or calques from Chinese.

tab:length.cn presents the counted nouns used in Japhug for measures of lengths. The obsolete forms are indicated in brackets. The counted nouns tɯ-tɣaone span and tɯ-ɟomthe length of two outstretched arms are very commonly used in narratives and conversations (their Chinese equivalents are 一拃 yīzhǎone span and 一庹 yītuǒthe length of two outstretched arms, respectively). There are two ways to measure the handspan, ndzoʁtɣalength between the thumb and the forefinger and ɲaʁtɣilength between the thumb and the middle finger; these nouns are followed by the tɯ-tɣa when one wants to specify which of the measures one chooses, as in ɲaʁtɣi tɯ-tɣa. The counted noun tɯ-ʁarthe length of one arm (related to tɤ-ʁarwing) is less common that the other ones in tab:length.cn but attested for instance in ( ex:tWRar ).

exe

tsuku tɕe tɕe tɯ-ɟom kɯnɤ tu-zri mɯ́j-cʰa, tɯ-ʁar jamar, tɯ-ʁar tɕe tɕe kɯki jamar, kɯki jamar tu-zri ɲɯ-cʰa. \\
some lnk lnk one-length.of.two.outstretched.arms even ipfv -be.long neg: sens -can one-arm.length about one-arm.length lnk lnk dem: prox about dem: prox about ipfv -be.long sens -can \\
`Some of them cannot even grow up to the length of one fathom, they can only grow up to the length of one arm, this much.' (16-RlWmsWsi)
0003520#S115
exe

The counted noun tɯ-tɯnɯnaone mile derives from the tɯ- actional nominal (§ sec:tW.action.nominal ) of the verb nɯnarest, designating a milestone on the road indicating travellers' resting places (at regular intervals). Distances are counted now however only in kilometers using Chinese (including Chinese numerals), as for instance the expression 三公里 sāngōnglǐthree kilometers in ( ex:sangongli ).

exe

a-pi tɕʰeme nɯnɯ mbarkhom ɯ-rkɯ <xiaoshuigou> <sangongli> nɯtɕu tʰɯ-ɣe. \\
1sg. poss -elder.sibling girl dem Mbarkham 3sg. poss -side anthr three.kilometers dem: loc aor: downstream -come[II] \\
`My elder sister came to Xiaoshuigou, three kilometers from Mbarkham.' (140501 tshering skyid)
0003902#S39
exe

Not all nouns of measure are counted nouns. In traditional stories, the unpossessible noun χpaχtsʰɤtyojana from Tibetan དཔག་ཚད་dpag.tsʰadyojana occurs to designate a mythical measure of distance taken from Indian sources. Numerals are indicated as postnominal numeral modifiers as in ( ex:dpag.tshad ).

exe

tɯ-sŋi χpaχtsʰɤt kɯngɯt ɲɯ-tɯ́-wɣ-tsɯm cʰa \\
one-day yojana nine ipfv: west -2- inv -take.away can: fact \\
`[This horse] can carry you (west) nine yojana s in one day.' (2003 smanmi)
exe

For measuring the surface of fields, the term tɯ-rkoŋɕɤl, illustrated by example ( ex:tWrkoNCAl ), is still in use.

exe

mɤʑɯ tɯ-rkoŋɕɤl jamar tɕe kɤ-ɕlu lu-jɤɣ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
more one-unit.of.field.surface about lnk inf -plow ipfv: upstream -finish sens -be \\
`One more unit and the plowing will be finished.' (elicited)
exe

In the traditional society, cereals were more often measured by volume (using containers of various size) than by weight, an action called ɕtʂomeasure by scooping. tab:volume.cn presents the known units of volume. Among these units, tɯ-poone dou apparently comes from Tibetan འབོ་ⁿbounit of measure corresponding to Chinese 一斗 yīdǒuone dou (about ten liter in the metric system). The other units are native words.
Among them, χtsiɯbushel and ɕpɣoten bushels occurs as either alienably possessed or counted nouns. The relationship between the units of volume is described in ( ex:sqWXtsiW ).

exe

sqɯ-χtsiɯ tɕe tɕe nɯ ɕpɣo ɲɯ-ŋu. tɕe tɯ-ɕpɣo ɲɯ-ŋu. ɕpɣo nɯnɯ tɕe tɕe, mɤʑɯ fsɯsqɯ-χtsiɯ a-tɤ-ɤpɯpa tɕe tɕe nɯnɯ tɯ-ɣna. tɕe nɯ tɯ-ɣna pjɤ-ŋu tɕe tɕe nɯ ɕaŋtaʁ ɯ-sɤ-ɕtʂo pjɤ-me tɕe, \\
ten-bushel lnk lnk dem ten.bushels sens -be sens -be ten.bushels sens -be ten.bushels dem lnk lnk even.more thirty-bushel irr - pfv -accumulate lnk lnk dem one-thirty.bushels lnk dem one-thirty.bushels ifr. ipfv -be lnk lnk dem up.from 3sg. poss - obj: pcp blique-measure ifr. ipfv -not.exist lnk \\
`Ten bushels was a ɕpɣo, after the ɕpɣo, thirty bushels put together was a tɯ-ɣna. After that, there was no container used to measure [grains].' (140515 rJama)
0004006#S24
exe

The units of weight include tɯ-sraŋone ounce (from Tibetan སྲང་sraŋounce), rɟɤpɕɤthalf pound (from the first syllable of རྒྱ་མ་rgʲa.mascales with ཕྱེད་pʰʲedhalf) and the counted noun tɯ-tɯrpaone pound derived from tɯrpaaxe (see § sec:CN.APN ). This may be an ancient calque from 斤 jīnpound, which also meant `axe' in Old Chinese. Apart from tɯ-tɯrpaone pound, all technical terms related to weighing are from Tibetan (including rɟamascales and skɤrweigh).

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ rɟama ɯ-taʁ tɕe, kɯrcɤ-sraŋ tɕe rɟɤpɕɤt, sqaprɤ-sraŋ tɕe tɯ-tɯrpa pjɤ-ŋu. \\
in.former.times weighing.scales 3sg. poss -on lnk eight-pound lnk half.pound sixteen-ounce lnk one-pound ifr. ipfv -be \\
`In former times, on the scales, one half pound was eight ounces, and one pound was sixteen ounces.' (140515 rJama)
0004006#S2
exe
summary: The passage explains that Japhug mainly expresses measures of size, weight, and volume with counted nouns, though some unpossessible nouns also occur, and many older forms are being replaced by Chinese words or calques. It gives examples of traditional and current units for length, distance, field area, volume, and weight, noting that several terms come from Tibetan or Chinese and that some older measurement terms are obsolete.

text:
counted noun!temporal
Japhug has native counted nouns for time durations related to solar and lunar cycles: tɯ-xpaone year, tɯ-slaone month, tɯ-sŋione day, tɤ-rʑaʁone night (also used to express 24 hours). There are no native concepts for `weeks' or `ten days'; the expression of hours is presented in § sec:hours. Other temporal counted nouns include tɯ-mɲɯtsione lifetime (from མི་ཚེ་mi.tsʰehuman life), tɯ-tɯpɕɯrtɕʰaʁone generation and tɯ-rzɯɣone section, `one instant', and tɯ-skɤrmaone minute (from Tibetan སྐར་མ་skar.mastar, minute)

The temporal counted nouns tɯ-sŋione day and tɤ-rʑaʁone night are commonly used in apposition with the same numeral prefix to express the meaning `X days and X nights', as in ( ex:XsWsNi.XsArZaR ).

exe

χsɯ-sŋi χsɤ-rʑaʁ ʑo pjɤ-rɤʑi \\
three-day three-night emph ifr. ipfv -stay \\
`He stayed there for three days and three nights.' (2011-13-qala)
exe

To express the meanings corresponding to English `after' or `later' with a time span, the idiomatic way in Japhug is to use verbs such as tsupass (of time), as shown by example ( ex:tWsNi.tAtsu ) and ( ex:tAtsua ). Note that tsupass (of time) is a semi-transitive verb (§ sec:semi.transitive ) whose semi-object is the time period expressed by the counted noun, and whose subject is the person affected by the passing of time (see for instance ex:tAtsua with 1sg indexation).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-ɣɤ-wxti pjɤ-saχaʁ ʑo tɯ-sŋi tɤ-tsu tɕe, χsɯ-sŋi tɤ-kɯ-tsu to-fse. χsɯ-sŋi tɤ-tsu tɕe, tɯ-sla tɤ-kɯ-tsu to-fse. tɯ-sla tɤ-tsu tɕe, tɯ-xpa tɤ-kɯ-tsu to-fse. \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - facil -be.big ifr. ipfv -be.extremely emph one-day aor -pass lnk three-days aor - sbj: pcp -pass ifr -be.like three-day aor -pass lnk one-month aor - sbj: pcp -pass ifr -be.like one-month aor -pass lnk one-year aor - sbj: pcp -pass ifr -be.like \\
`He grew extremely fast, one day after [he was born] he looked like [an infant] who was three days old, after three days he looked like a [baby] who was one month old, after one month he looked like a [toddler] who was one year old.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S103
exe

exe

tɕʰorzi ɯ-ŋgɯ cʰɯ-kɯ-rku-a, χsɤ-rʑaʁ tɤ-tsu-a tɕe ci a-tɤ-kɯ-rtoʁ-a, \\
jar 3sg. poss -inside ipfv: downstream -2 1-put.in- 1sg three-days aor -pass- 1sg lnk once irr - pfv -2 1-look- 1sg \\
`Put me in a jar, and three days later have a look at me.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

The postposition ɕɯŋgɯbefore (§ sec:temporal.postpositions ) occurs after temporal counted nouns in examples such as ( ex:ngWsqWxpa.CWNgW ) (see also ex:sqamNusNi.CWNgW below); the relator noun ɯ-qʰuafter, behind (§ sec:relator.temporal ) is not used in this way except in texts translated from Chinese (where it is likely calqued) as in ( ex:kWBdexpa.Wqhu ).

kɯngɯsqɯ-xpa ɕɯŋgɯ nɯra tɕʰeme ra wuma ʑo kɯ-taʁ pɯ-dɤn \\

`Nine or ten years ago, there were many weavers among women.' (thaXtsa2002)
exe

exe

kɯβdɤ-xpa ɯ-qʰu tɕe kukutɕu tu-kɤ-ɤwɯwum to-nɯ-pa-nɯ. \\
four-year 3sg. poss -after lnk here ipfv - inf - recip:gather ifr - auto -make- pl \\
`They agreed to meet again at this place in four years.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S23
exe

In order to express meanings such as `beginning' or `end' of a time period indicated by a counted noun, verbs such as arɕobe finished are used as in ( ex:tWxpa.YArCo ) instead of nouns or participles like ɯ-sɤɣjɤɣits end.

exe

ɣɯjpa tɯ-xpa ɲɯ-ɤrɕo ɕɯŋgɯ tɕe, <lunwen> kɤ-rɤt pjɯ-jɤɣ ɲɯ-ra. \\

`He has to finish writing his dissertation before the end of this year.' (elicitation)

summary:
Japhug has native counted nouns for several time spans linked to solar and lunar cycles, including year, month, day, and night, as well as lifetime, generation, instant, and minute, but it lacks native terms for weeks or ten-day periods. These temporal counted nouns are used to express spans like “X days and X nights,” to indicate “after/later” with verbs meaning “pass,” and to mark beginnings or ends of periods with verbs such as “be finished.”  

They usually occur without a head noun, though *tɯ-xpa* “year” can sometimes combine with *lu* “year” in traditional stories, and *month* and *year* have special forms meaning “several” or can take an approximate prefix meaning “a few,” which does not apply to other temporal counted nouns.

text:
time ordinal
Japhug has two series of time ordinals, one for days ( tab:day.ordinals ) and another one for years ( tab:year.ordinals ). In the following discussion, I adopt Michailovsky's ( michailovsky03ordinals) notations: $D^- $ `$ $ day(s) ago', $D^+ $ `in $ $ day(s)', $Y^+ $ `$ $ year(s) ago', $Y^+ $ `in $ $ year(s)'.

The Japhug system has relatively few ordinals for past days and years (some Kiranti languages have terms for up to $D^-6$ and $Y^-4$, as shown by ), but stands out by having six ordinals for future years (no Kiranti languages has more than $D^+6$ and $Y^+4$ in Michailovsky's michailovsky03ordinals data). However, the $D^+5$ βʑindiin five days, $D^+6$ pɤtsɤndiin six days and the corresponding year ordinals $Y^+5$ and $Y^+6$ are not used any more in day-to-day speech even by the eldest speakers.

The $D^0$ to $D^-2$ and $Y^0$ to $Y^-2$ordinals have a prefix ji-/jɯ-/ja, which is probably of demonstrative origin. This prefix also occurs in the derived ordinals jɯɣmɯrthis evening and jɯxɕothis morning (see Tables tab:morning.ordinals and tab:evening.ordinals below), as well as in some frozen adverbs, such as jɤxtsʰithis time (from tɯ-xtsʰione time) and jindethese days. Cognates of this prefix are found in other time ordinals elsewhere in Gyalrongic. In the case of ɣɯjpathis year, this prefix surfaces as a preinitial -j- to the root -pa `year' (see § sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history on the etymology of this noun). The ɣɯ- (from *wə- ) prefix may be cognate to the prefix pə- in pəvəthis year and pəsɲətoday in Stau.

The expressions jɯfɕɯndʐitwo days ago and japandʐitwo years ago, which are based on the $D^-1$ and $Y^-1$ forms with a suffix -ndʐi, can be analyzed as time ordinals ($D^-2$ and $Y^-2$, respectively), as in ( ex:japandzxi ). This suffix -ndʐi is not attested elsewhere, but is probably related to the syllable -ri of the relator noun ɯ-ʁɤribefore, in front of, from an earlier *-n-ri with epenthesis ( *-ndri ) and fricativization of the resulting *dr cluster.

exe

nɯ ma kɯ-dɤn japa mɯ-tɤ-χtɯ-t-a. japandʐi alo, ɬaltɕɤm kɯ z-ɲɤ-ɕar tɕendɤre \\
dem apart.from sbj: pcp -be.many last.year neg - aor -buy- tr: pst - 1sg two.years.ago upstream anthr erg tral - ifr -search lnk \\
`Last year, it did not buy a lot [of edible fern]. The year before, up there (in Kamnyu), Lhalcam collected some.' (conversation, 14.05.10)
exe

However, in many cases, they have less specific meanings such as `a few days ago' and `a few years ago', as shown by ( ex:jWfCWndzxi ), referring to an event that had occurred more than one week before. This use reminds of the English expression `a couple of days ago', which can mean up to a week ago.

`Thank you both for the other day, the clothes that you have sent me, the shoes are very nice, I wear them, they are my size.' (conversation, 15.04.18)

Even the $Y^-1$ ordinal japalast year can have a less specific meaning if combined with dalearly and the locative ri as japa dal ria few years ago as in ( ex:japa.dal.ri ). No other time ordinal can be used with dalearly or other modifiers.

japa dal ri, ftɕar ri ʁmbɣɯzɯn ɣɤʑu ɲɯ-ti-nɯ ma \\
last.year early loc summer loc solar.eclipse exist: sens sens -say- pl sfp \\
`A few years ago, they said there was a solar eclipse during summer.' (29-RmGWzWn2)

The day ordinals from $D^+2$ to $D^+5$ contain a suffix -ndi, which attaches to the bound state forms of fsotomorrow in $D^+2$ fsɤndi and ɯ-qʰuafter, behind in $D^+3$ qʰɤndi. The $D^+5$ form βʑindi contains the bound state βʑɯ- of the Japhug pronunciation βʑi of the Tibetan numeral བཞི་bʑifour (see § sec:one.to.ten ), presumably meaning `the fourth day after tomorrow'.

Year ordinals from $Y^+2$ to $Y^+5$ ( tab:year.ordinals ) are built by simply adding the root -pa `year' (see § sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history and § § sec:CN.verbs ) to the bound state of the corresponding day ordinals $D^+2$ to $D^+5$. The $Y^+1$ time ordinal fsaqʰenext year comes from the bound state of fsotomorrow, and the second element may be from the counted noun ɯ-qʰuafter, behind followed by the locative suffix *-j with regular vowel fusion (§ sec:locative.j ).

In addition, there are morning ordinals ( tab:morning.ordinals ) which derive from the corresponding day ordinals by adding the noun sozmorning (with the exception of jɯxɕothis morning), and the evening and night ordinals ( tab:evening.ordinals ) which are built by adding the bound form -mɯr (found in tɯ-ɣmɯrone evening and mɯrkɯrkuevery evening). These ordinals are not attested after $D^+3$, though the forms could be built easily; note the absence of bound state, except for $D^-1$, where jɯfɕɯryesterday loses its coda, as in jɯfɕɯsozyesterday morning.

Note the isolated qʰujthis afternoon tab:evening.ordinals ), which can refer to the time period between noon and the night (including the early evening).

As shown by ( ex:jWfCWndzximWr ), it is also possible to combine day ordinals with other time nouns such as tɯrmɯdusk to indicate particular moments of previous or future days.

exe
summary:
Japhug has separate series of time ordinals for days and years, with relatively few forms for past times but an unusually large set for future years; however, some of the higher future forms are no longer used in ordinary speech. Many of these ordinals are built with a prefix ji-/jɯ-/ja, likely of demonstrative origin, and some forms such as “two days/two years ago” can be analyzed as time ordinals with a special suffix -ndʐi.

The system also includes day ordinals formed with suffix -ndi, year ordinals built from the corresponding day ordinals plus the noun “year,” and morning, evening, and night ordinals derived by adding time nouns or bound forms. Several forms can have both specific and less specific meanings, such as “a few days/years ago,” and some ordinals can combine with modifiers like “early” or with other time nouns to refer to particular moments.

It also explains that time ordinals can be turned into inalienably possessed nouns with the third-singular prefix ɯ-, which shifts the reference from present time to past or hypothetical time, as illustrated by forms like “the next day” and “the next morning.”

text:
Japhug has a series of distributive adverbs meaning `every/each $X$' ( tab:every.time ). These adverbs are derived from time nominals (mainly counted nouns, but also alienably possessed nouns like sozmorning) by adding a suffix -ku and then applying partial reduplication (§ sec:partial.redp ). If the nominal root has a coda such as that of -mɯr `evening' (as in tɯ-ɣmɯrone evening), this coda is resyllabified and undergoes reduplication together with the suffix, as in the form mɯrkɯrkuevery evening (not $ $ mɯrkɯku ).

The ɯ of the preceding syllable tends to become [ u ] due to vowel assimilation (§ sec:vowel.harmony ); since vowel assimilation always occurs in the forms without a reduplicated cluster, the transcriptions sɲikukuevery day and pakukuevery year are used in this grammar ( tab:every.time ) instead of the more phonological representations sɲikɯku and pakɯku.

These adverbs are commonly used with the emphatic marker ʑo, as in ( ex:mWrkWrku ).

exe

mɯrkɯrku ʑo kɤntɕʰaʁ a-pi ɯ-pʰe kɯ-nɤpɤri ɲɯ-ɣi-a,... pɯ-ŋu. \\
every.evening emph street 1sg. poss -elder.sibling 3sg. poss - dat sbj: pcp -have.supper... pst. ipfv -be \\
`Every evening, if would go in the town at my elder brother's home to have supper and...' (140501 tshering skyid)
0003902#S110
exe

This morphological derivation is not productive, and cannot be used with any other temporal counted noun, even tɯ-slaone month -- the distributive modifiers raŋrieach or rɯrieach are used instead (§ sec:raNri ).
summary:
Japhug has distributive adverbs meaning “every/each X” that are formed from certain time nominals by adding the suffix -ku and then applying partial reduplication. When the noun ends in a coda, that coda is resyllabified and included in the reduplication, and vowel assimilation often changes preceding ɯ to [u], which is why the grammar uses spellings like sɲikuku and pakuku.

These adverbs commonly occur with the emphatic marker ʑo. The pattern is not productive and cannot be extended to other temporal nouns such as “month,” which instead require the distributive modifiers raŋri or rɯri.

text:
Japhug has a series of words borrowed from Tibetan that can be used to refer to hours and minutes. The alienably possessed tɯtsʰottime, hour, clock from Tibetan དུས་ཚོད་dus.tsʰodtime, hour (note that tɯ- here is not a prefix, but represents the Tibetan syllable དུས་dustime), if directly followed by a numeral (or the generic counted noun tɯ-rdoʁone piece) refers to hours, as in examples ( ex:tWtshot.sqamnWz ) and ( ex:tWtshot.tWrdoR ).

exe

ɕɤr tɯtsʰot sqamnɯz ʑo tɕe a-jɤ-tɯ-z-nɤtɯɣ tɕe, \\
night hour twelve emph lnk irr - pfv -2- caus -happen.to.be.at lnk \\
`You will have to make sure to be there at midnight.' (2003 qachGa)

`When [nettles] start causing pain, it won't stop for about one hour.' (11-mtshalu) 0003472#S7

To ask about clock time, the interrogative pronoun tʰɤstɯɣhow many, `how much' occurs with the verb zɣɯtarrive as in ( ex:tWtshot.thAstWG ) (see also § sec:thAstWG ).

These expressions, although used in the everyday language in Japhug, are calqued from Chinese since they follow modern time counting units and are all recent. Another calque from Chinese includes tɯ-tɕɯlɤβone unit of tobacco as in ( ex:thamaka.tWtCWlAB ), from the expression 一斗烟的功夫 yī dǒu yān de gōngfūtime of one unit of tobacco.

`One needs about the time of a tobacco smoke.' (elicited)

summary: Japhug uses a set of Tibetan-borrowed words, also calqued from Chinese, to express hours, minutes, and clock time. The word tɯtsʰot ‘time, hour, clock’ followed by a numeral refers to hours, while minutes are expressed by adding tɯ-skɤrma ‘minute’; questions about the time use tʰɤstɯɣ with the verb zɣɯt ‘arrive.’ These time expressions are said to be recent and part of everyday language.

text:
arithmetic

Although Japhug lacks an elaborate mathematical vocabulary, is it possible to express at least the basic arithmetic operations without recourse to Chinese.

The counted noun tɯ-rdoʁone piece is used instead of the numeral cione is calculations (see ex:tWrdoR.pjWwGta below).

Additions are expressed by the construction in ( ex:tWrdoR.pjWwGta ) and ( ex:kWrCat.pjWwGta ), The form kɯɕnɯ-kɯrcat (with the numeral prefix kɯɕnɯ- on the numeral kɯrcateight) in example ( ex:kWrCat.pjWwGta ) is part of a riddle in the story, and is not a normal way to express additions in Japhug. with the verb taput (or alternatively, ɣɤjɯadd) and the locative noun ɯ-taʁon, above, literally `If one puts Y on the top of X, it makes Z' corresponding to $X+Y=Z$.

exe

kɯmŋu ɯ-taʁ tɯ-rdoʁ pjɯ́-wɣ-ta tɕe kɯtʂɤɣ tu-βze ŋu. \\
five 3sg -on one-piece ipfv: down - inv -put lnk six ipfv -do[III] be: fact \\
`Five plus one equals six.' (gram140505 math, elicitation)
exe

exe

nɤʑo kɯɕnɯ-kɯrcat nɯ pɯpɯŋu nɤ, kɯɕnɯz ɯ-taʁ kɯrcat pjɯ́-wɣ-ta tɕe sqamŋu ɲɯ-ŋu sqamŋu tɕe ju-tɯ-nɯ-ɕe ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\

`As for the expression `seven eight' [that your father in law has told] you, seven plus eight equals fifteen, [it means that] you go back [to your husband's home] in fifteen days.' (2005 tAwa kWcqraR)

In the case of subtractions, the main verb is tɕɤttake out combined with the downstream orientation preverb (the preverb cʰɯ- in ex:tWrdoR.chWwGtCAt, § sec:illative.elative ). The minuend ( tɯ-rdoʁ in ex:tWrdoR.chWwGtCAt ) is the object of tɕɤttake out, and the subtrahend ( kɯmŋu in ex:tWrdoR.chWwGtCAt ) is encoded with the relator noun ɯ-ŋgɯinside (§ sec:WNgW ). Alternatively, the verb sɯxtɕʰaʁmake diminish, causative of tɕʰaʁdiminish (§ sec:caus.sWG ) can also occur (selecting the downwards orientation). The construction is exactly the same as in ( ex:tWrdoR.chWwGtCAt ), replacing cʰɯ́-wɣ-tɕɤt by pjɯ́-wɣ-sɯxtɕʰaʁ.

`If one takes out one from five, only four remain = five minus one equals four' (gram140505 math, elicitation)
exe

Japhug is rarely used for multiplication. The counted noun tɯ-zloʁone time can convey a multiplicative meaning as in example ( ex:XsW.zloR ). Note that this counted noun of Tibetan origin has two alternative forms for `two times', the regular ʁnɯ-zloʁ and the hybrid form ʁɲɯ-zloʁ with an irregular numeral prefix that seems influenced by the Tibetan numeral གཉིས་gɲistwo (see § sec:tibetan.numerals, § sec:irregular.numeral.prefixes ). Divisions are treated in the section on fractions (§ sec:fractions ).

exe

kɯngɯt nɯ χsɯm ɣɯ χsɯ-zloʁ ŋu \\
nine dem three gen three-time be: fact \\
`Nine is three times three.' (gram140505 math, elicitation)
exe
summary:
Japhug has limited mathematical vocabulary, but basic arithmetic can be expressed without Chinese. Addition uses a construction meaning roughly “if one puts Y on top of X, it makes Z,” while subtraction uses a verb meaning “take out” or “make diminish,” with the minuend as the object and the subtrahend marked by a relational noun meaning “inside.”

Multiplication is rare, but it can be expressed with the counted noun tɯ-zloʁ ‘one time,’ including special forms for “two times.” Division is treated together with fractions elsewhere.

fraction
Japhug does not have specific names for fractions other than ɯ-qiɯhalf. This inalienably possessed noun has no prefixal form, and to express the meaning `half a $X$', the only available construction is the one illustrated in ( ex:tWJom.WqiW ) and ( ex:tWxpa.WqiW ), combining a counted noun with the numeral prefix `one', the genitive ɣɯ and ɯ-qiɯhalf.

`[Its tail] is about half a fathom (i.e. one arm) long.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
