exe

ki kɯ-fse tɯ-ɟom cʰo ɯ-qiɯ jamar kɯ-zri ra \\
dem. prox sbj: pcp -be.like one-length.of.two.outstretched.arms comit 3sg. poss -half about sbj: pcp -be.long be.needed: fact \\
`They need [a piece of leather] long like one fathom and a half.' (24-mbGo) 0003621
exe

Alternatively, the additive meaning `and a half' can be expressed with the counted noun tɯ-qiɯone half, which derives from ɯ-qiɯhalf (§ sec:CN.IPN ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-pɤrtʰɤβ tɕe, tɯ-pɤrme tɯ-qiɯ jamar, ʁnɯ-pɤrme jamar ma kɯ-me ʁɟa. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -between lnk one-year one-half about, two-year about apart.from sbj: pcp -not.exist completely \\
`(Some women had thirteen or fifteen children) Between each of them, there was only one year and a half or two years.' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR, 89; see the preceding sentence in example ex:tsuku.tWrme.tWrdoR in § sec:tsuku )
exe

For more complex fractions, the counted nouns tɯ-tɯcɯrone part, tɯ-tɤsɯmone part or tɯ-tɯkroone part are used. Two related constructions are possible; in the following discussion, $X$ represents the numerator, $Y$ the denominator (the fraction $ XY$).

The first one is a noun phrase with the structure $Y$- tɯcɯr ɯ-ŋgɯ $X$- tɯcɯr, literally `$X$ parts among $Y$ parts', illustrated by example ( ex:kWmNutWcWr ). This may be a calque of the Chinese construction $Y$ 分之 $X$
($Y$-fēn zhī-$X$) literally `$X$ of $Y$ parts', a way of expressing fractions attested from Han dynasty documents to standard Mandarin.

exe

kɯmŋu-tɯcɯr ɯ-ŋgɯ χsɯ-tɯcɯr \\
five-part 3sg -inside three-part \\
$ 35$ = `Three parts among five parts.' (elicited)
exe

An alternative possibility is to use the auxiliary verb lɤtrelease as in ( ex:XsWtWcWr ), but such construction is biclausal (the second clause lacks a verbal predicate, § sec:non.verbal.predicates ).

exe

χsɯ-tɯcɯr tú-wɣ-lɤt tɕe tɯ-tɯcɯr \\
three-part ipfv - inv -release lnk one-part \\
$ 13$; literally `Making three parts, one part.' (elicited)
exe

Divisions can be expressed using the constructions in ( ex:division ) and ( ex:division2 ).

exe

xlist

sqi nɯ kɯmŋu-tɯcɯr tú-wɣ-lɤt tɕe, ʁnɯz nɤ ʁnɯz ɲɯ́-wɣ-βzu kʰɯ \\
ten dem five-part ipfv - inv -release lnk two lnk two ipfv - inv -make be.possible: fact \\

sqi nɯ kɯmŋu-tɯkro ɲɯ́-wɣ-lɤt tɕe, ʁnɯz nɤ ʁnɯz ɲɯ́-wɣ-sɤβzu kʰɯ \\
ten dem five-part ipfv - inv -throw lnk two lnk two ipfv - inv -transform be.possible: fact \\
xlist
$ 105=2$; literally `Making 5 parts out of 10, one can make them in sets of two'.
exe

In these examples, the numerator is a left-dislocated numeral followed by the determiner nɯ, the denominator a counted noun serving as object of lɤtrelease as in the fraction in ( ex:XsWtWcWr ), and the result of the computation is indicated by a distributive repetition of the numeral with the additive postposition nɤ (§ sec:CN.repetition ).
summary:
Japhug has no special names for fractions beyond the inalienably possessed noun ɯ-qiɯ ‘half’, and ‘half a X’ is expressed by combining a counted noun, the numeral ‘one’, the genitive ɣɯ, and ɯ-qiɯ. The additive meaning ‘and a half’ can be expressed either by coordinating the counted noun with ɯ-qiɯ using the comitative cʰo or by using the derived counted noun tɯ-qiɯ ‘one half’.  

For more complex fractions, Japhug uses counted nouns meaning ‘one part’ and can form either an NP meaning ‘X parts among Y parts’, probably calqued from Chinese, or a biclausal construction with the auxiliary lɤ ‘release’. Divisions are expressed with related constructions in which a numeral and denominator are combined, and the computed result is shown by distributive repetition of the numeral.

text: Japhug is particularly poor in case-marking morphology, and grammatical relations are indicated by verbal morphology (treated in Chapter chap:indexation ) combined with postpositions and relator nouns. Word order also plays a minor role (§ sec:word.order ). In this chapter, I first present the various possible functions of bare (absolutive) noun phrases, and then describe the uses of all postpositions and relator nouns in combination with noun phrases. Some postpositions and relator nouns also occur in various types of subordinate clauses (§ sec:marked.subordinate ).
summary: Japhug has very little case-marking morphology, so grammatical relations are expressed mainly through verbal morphology together with postpositions and relator nouns, while word order plays only a minor role. The chapter first examines the functions of bare absolutive noun phrases and then describes the uses of postpositions and relator nouns with noun phrases, noting that some of these forms also appear in subordinate clauses.

text:
absolutive
In Japhug absolutive refers to the bare form of a noun phrase, without postposition, relator noun or locative suffix. This form is used for intransitive subject, object and various other grammatical functions described in this section, in particular goals and some locative phrases, for which locative postpositions (§ sec:locative ) and relator nouns (§ sec:relator.location ) are optional.
summary: In Japhug, the absolutive is the bare form of a noun phrase, without a postposition, relator noun, or locative suffix. It is used for intransitive subjects, objects, and several other functions, especially goals and some locative phrases, where locative postpositions and relator nouns are optional.

text:
absolutive subject:intrantive
The only argument of morphologically intransitive and syntactically monoactantial verbs, the intransitive subject (S), is in absolutive form and is indexed on the verb, as tɕʰeme nɯra `the women' with plural indexation in ( ex:tCheme.nWra.thWstanW ).

exe

tɕʰeme nɯra tʰɯ-sta-nɯ \\
woman dem: pl aor -wake.up- pl \\
`The women woke up.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

optional case marking
Apparent examples of ergative kɯ with third person intransitive subjects are due to the effect of long distance ergative marking (§ sec:long.distance.kW ), due to bracketing issues between main clause and complement clause (§ sec:complement.clause.case.marking ) or to errors, as in example ( ex:kW.chAsta ): the intransitive stawake up only takes an absolutive argument (as in ex:tCheme.nWra.thWstanW above), and the ergative kɯ is preceded and followed by pauses, reflecting the hesitation of the narrator. As an isolated sentence, the use of ergative is considered to be agrammatical in this example.

exe

nɯ jamar kóʁmɯz nɯ lɯlu nɯ, /kɯ/, cʰɤ-sta. \\
dem about only.then dem cat dem erg ifr -wake.up \\
(150826 shier shengxiao)
0006284#S146
exe

Some morphologically intransitive verbs have a second argument, which can be either absolutive (semi-objects § sec:semi.object or goals § absolutive.goal ) or oblique (dative with rulook at, genitive with rabe needed and existential verbs § sec:gen.beneficiary, comitative with naχtɕɯɣbe the same § sec:comitative ), but in all these cases the argument indexed on the verb is always in absolutive form.

The intransitive subject can only be relativized using subject participial relatives (§ sec:intr.subject.relativization ).
summary:
The only argument of morphologically intransitive verbs, the intransitive subject (S), is in absolutive form and is indexed on the verb. Apparent cases of ergative marking on intransitive subjects are explained by other factors such as long-distance ergative marking, clause-bracketing issues, or errors, and isolated use of ergative here is ungrammatical.  

Some morphologically intransitive verbs can also take a second argument, either absolutive or oblique, but the verb always indexes the absolutive argument. The intransitive subject can only be relativized with subject participial relatives.

text:
absolutive subject:transitive
The transitive subject (A argument) is usually marked by the ergative postposition kɯ (§ sec:erg.kW ). The ergative is optional with first and second person pronouns in transitive subject function, as shown by examples such as ( aZo.absolutive.A ), where mtosee is a transitive verb. The use of ergative on these pronouns is however possible, especially in the case of contrastive focalization (§ sec:A.kW ).

exe

aʑo nɯ mɯ-pɯ-mto-t-a ri nɯ ɯ-sŋi wuma ʑo pɯ-ɣɤndʐo \\
1sg dem neg - aor -see- tr: pst - 1sg lnk dem 3sg. poss -day really emph pst. ipfv -be.cold \\
`I did not see it (the eclipse), but on that day is was very cold.' (29-RmGWzWn2)
0003730#S23
exe

Third person transitive subjects are obligatorily marked with the ergative kɯ (§ sec:A.kW ). Apparent counterexamples in the corpus are due to the emphatic use of third person pronouns (§ sec:pronouns.emph ), or to errors involving hesitations.
summary: In transitive clauses, the A argument is generally marked with the ergative postposition **kɯ**. With first- and second-person pronouns, ergative marking is optional and may be used for contrastive focus, but third-person transitive subjects are obligatorily ergative-marked. Apparent exceptions in the corpus are explained by emphatic pronoun use or hesitation errors.

text:
absolutive object
Morphologically transitive verbs (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ) take an object (O argument) in absolutive form, indexed by the verb morphology (§ sec:polypersonal ). For instance tsuku tɯrme ra `some people' in ( ex:tsuku.tWrme.ra.kuwGmtsWGnW ) has no case marking, and is coreferent with the plural indexation on kú-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-nɯ `they are stung' (with inverse marking, § sec:direct-inverse ). Only absolutive phrases can be indexed as objects; there are no verbs in Japhug indexing a postpositional phrase other than an ergatively marked transitive subjects.

exe

tsuku tɯrme ra kú-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-nɯ tɕe mɯ́j-ʁdɯɣ, \\
some people pl ipfv - inv -bite- pl lnk neg. sens -be.serious \\
`Some people, when they are stung [by bees] are fine.' (26-ndzWrnaR)
0003678#S61
exe

Objects (like semi-objects, § sec:semi.object ) can be relativized by object participial relatives or by finite relatives (like semi-objects, goals § absolutive.goal and locative phrases § absolutive.locative ).

Most transitive verbs have a strict requirement on the semantic role of the object. However, speakers can in limited cases select an object with a different role with stylistic effect. For instance, the verb ʑmbriplay (an instrument), `make noise with' normally takes a object a musical instrument or any other noise-making implement (§ sec:caus.Z ), as in ( ex:taZmbri ). However, in the next sentence of the same story ( ex:taZmbri2 ), this verb appears with the phrase ɯ-mu cʰo ndʑi-kɤ-ndza kɤ-tsʰi kɯ-dɯ dɤn `a lot of food and drink for (him) and his mother' as object, a resultative construction: the direct object is not the instrument used to make the noise, but rather the boon obtained by making noise with the wish-granting pʰantsɯtplate.

exe

xlist

[iɕqʰa pʰantsɯt nɯ] ta-ʑmbri ɲɯ-ŋu \\
the.aforementioned plate dem aor:3 -make.noise sens -be \\
`He made noise with the (magical wish-granting) plate (by hitting on it). (2003 tWxtsa)

[ɯ-mu cʰo ndʑi-kɤ-ndza kɤ-tsʰi kɯ-dɯ dɤn ʑo nɯ] ta-ʑmbri nɤ, \\
3sg. poss -mother comit 3du. poss - obj: pcp -eat obj: pcp -drink sbj: pcp - emph be.many emph dem aor:3 -make.noise add \\
`He [made appear] a lot of food and drink for him and his mother by making noise (with the wish-granting plate).' (2003 tWxtsa)
xlist
exe
summary: Morphologically transitive verbs in Japhug take an absolutive object that is indexed by the verb, and only absolutive phrases can be indexed as objects. The passage also notes that objects may be relativized by object participial or finite relatives, and that although transitive verbs usually require a specific semantic role for the object, speakers can sometimes choose a different role for stylistic effect, as in a resultative construction where the object is the boon obtained rather than the instrument used.

subsection: Sole argument of predicates of natural forces
text:
absolutive dummy subject
While some verbs referring to natural forces are intransitive ( nmushake (of earthquakes)), § sec:volitional.mW ), most are morphologically transitive auxiliary verbs (mainly lɤtrelease, βzumake, taput and rkuput in), used in collocation with a noun in absolutive form, as in ( ex:tWmW.YAsWlAt ) and ( ex:qale.taBzu ).

The presence of the progressive asɯ- prefix in ( ex:tWmW.YAsWlAt ) and of the C-type Aorist ta- preverb (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) in ( ex:qale.taBzu ) show that these verbs are morphologically transitive (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ). The noun in these collocations is also relativized like a direct object (§ sec:semi.object.relativization ).

exe

tɯ-mɯ ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-lɤt \\
indef. poss -sky sens - prog -release \\
`It is raining.' (heard in context)
exe

exe

ɕlaʁ ʑo cʰɯ-mda ɕɯŋgɯ tɕe tɕe qale ta-βzu tɕe tɕe cʰɯ-tʂaβ ŋu tɕe, \\
idph (I):suddenly emph ipfv -be.the.time before lnk lnk wind aor:3 -make lnk lnk ipfv -cause.to.fall be: fact lnk \\
`When there is wind suddenly before [the barley] is fully ripe, it presses them [on the ground, and it cannot grow any more].' (25-cWXCWz)
0003636#S41
exe

However, these constructions have intransitive-like properties: no ergatively marked argument can occur, they are in dental infinitive rather than bare infinitive form when used with phasal complement-taking verbs (see ex:tWlAt.pjAZa, § sec:dental.inf and § sec:bare.inf.dental.complementary ), and they are relativized like intransitive subjects (§ sec:dummy.subj.object.relativization ).
summary:
Verbs referring to natural forces are sometimes intransitive, but more often they are morphologically transitive auxiliary verbs used with a noun in absolutive form. The transitive morphology is shown by markers such as the progressive prefix and aorist preverb, and the noun in these constructions is relativized like a direct object.

At the same time, these constructions behave like intransitives in several respects: they do not allow an ergatively marked argument, appear in the dental infinitive after phasal complement verbs, and are relativized like intransitive subjects.

text:
absolutive semi-object
Some morphologically intransitive verbs in Japhug can take a second absolutive argument (§ sec:semi.transitive,, ). The verb rgalike is such an example; in ( ex:aZo.Ro.nW.mArgaa ) the intransitive subject paʁ ra `pigs' and nɯŋacow are in absolutive form, with 3pl indexation on the verb for the first. The second argument ɕirɴɢoAnisodus tanguticus is topicalized. In ( ex:aZo.Ro.nW.mArgaa ), the subject is topicalized, and the second argument nɯthat appears just before the verb, in absolutive form (in this particular case, the 1sg indexation suffix merges with the verb stem in the Kamnyu dialect, § sec:synizesis ). The semi-transitive rgalike, though it can take an overt object as in ( ex:aZo.Ro.nW.mArgaa ), tends to be used more often with complement clauses or left-dislocated objects, the applicative nɯrgalike being preferred with definite objects, § sec:applicative.promoted. This second argument is called semi-object.

exe

ɕirɴɢo nɯnɯ, paʁ ra mɤ-rga-nɯ ri, nɯŋa wuma ʑo rga.\\
Anisodus.tanguticus dem pig pl neg -like: fact - pl lnk cow really emph like: fact \\
`The Anisodus tanguticus, pigs don't like it, but cows do.' (16-CWrNgo)
0003518#S9
exe

exe

aʑo ʁo nɯ mɤ-rga-a \\
1sg top. advers dem neg -like- 1sg \\
`But as for me, I don't like it.'
exe

Other verbs taking semi-objects include tsoknow, understand ( WYWtWtso ), sɤŋolisten, rmibe called.

exe

naŋrzoŋ ɯ-ɲɯ-tɯ-tso? \\
interior.decoration qu - sens -2-understand \\
`Do you understand [the word] `interior decoration'?' (12-BzaNsa) 0003484#S82
exe

participle!object relative clause!object relative clause!finite
Semi-objects are relativized either with object participles in kɤ- (§ sec:object.participle.relatives ) or with finite relative clauses (§ sec:finite.relatives, § sec:semi.tr.relativization ). Semi-objects are also found is some triactantial verbs. In particular, the theme of secundative verbs is a type of semi-object (§ sec:theme.ditransitive ).
summary:
The passage explains that some morphologically intransitive verbs in Japhug can take a second absolutive argument, called a semi-object. The verb *rgalike* is given as an example: it can appear with an overt semi-object, often in topicalized or left-dislocated structures, though the applicative form is preferred with definite objects. 

It also notes that other verbs such as ‘know,’ ‘understand,’ ‘listen,’ and ‘be called’ can take semi-objects. Semi-objects may be relativized with object participles or finite relative clauses, and they also occur in some tri-argument verbs, including the theme of secundative verbs.

text:
absolutive semi-object theme
There are both secundative and indirective ditransitive verbs in Japhug (§ sec:ditransitive ). In the case of indirective verbs, the theme is the object, while the recipient being marked with an oblique case, as in example ( ex:tAtsxu.YAkho ) with the verb kʰogive, `pass over'. With this type of verbs, the theme is relativized in exactly the same way as the object of a monotransitive verb (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) and is indexed on the verb.

exe

ɯ-mu ɯ-ɕki tɤtʂu nɯ ɲɤ-kʰo. \\
3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss - dat lamp dem ifr -give \\
`He gave the lamp to his mother.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S161
exe

With secundative verbs, the recipient is the object and appears in absolutive form, with object indexation. The theme of these verb is also in the absolutive, as a-me `my daughter' in ( ex:ame.tambi ).

exe

a-me ta-mbi ra \\
1sg. poss -daughter 1 2-give: fact be.needed: fact \\
`I will give you my daughter.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S281
exe

The theme of a secundative verb cannot be indexed by the verb morphology. In ( ex:RnWz.nWtambi ), the theme is the numeral ʁnɯztwo, but dual indexation on nɯ-ta-mbi `I gave $X$ to you' is not possible, as the form nɯ-ta-mbi-ndʑi ( aor -1 2-give- du ) can only mean `I gave $X$ to both of you', the number referring to the recipient and not the theme (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ).

exe

mɤ-ta-mbi ma ʁnɯz nɯ-ta-mbi ri, nɤʑo cʰɤ-tɯ-ɕɣɤz ɕti tɕe \\
neg -1 2-give: fact lnk two aor -1 2-give lnk 2sg ifr -2-give.back be. aff: fact lnk \\
`I won't give her [my youngest daughter] to you, as I gave you two [of my daughters], and you sent them back.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

However, the theme of a secundative verb is relativized like the object of a monotransitive verb (§ sec:object.participle.relatives, § sec:secundative.theme.relativization ), and it can be considered as a sub-type of semi-object (§ sec:semi.object ).
summary: Japhug has both indirective and secundative ditransitive verbs. In indirective verbs, the theme functions as the object and is indexed on the verb, while the recipient is marked obliquely; in secundative verbs, both recipient and theme appear in absolutive form, but only the recipient can be indexed on the verb, not the theme. Nevertheless, the theme of a secundative verb is relativized like the object of a monotransitive verb, so it is treated as a type of semi-object.

text:
essive absolutive
Essive noun phrases are not arguments of the sentence, but are used to indicate `the property of fulfilling the role of an N' (; ).

In Japhug, bare noun phrases without any case marker can be interpreted as essive adjuncts, such as nɤ-rʑaβ `your wife' in ( ex:nArZaB.YWkhotCi ) and nɤ-kɯmtɕʰɯ `your toy' ( ex:nAkWmtChW.YWtambi ). These adjuncts are neither recipients (in both examples the recipient is 2sg, encoded as object of the ditransitive verb mbigive, § sec:ditransitive.secundative ) nor themes (in ex:nArZaB.YWkhotCi the theme is ji-me `our daughter', and it serves as object of the indirective kʰogive, § sec:ditransitive.indirective; in ex:nAkWmtChW.YWtambi the theme is non-overt).

exe

ji-me nɯ nɤ-rʑaβ ɲɯ-kʰo-tɕi je, ɲɯ-ta-mbi je to-ti\\
1pl. poss -daughter dem 2sg. poss -wife ipfv -give- 1du sfp ipfv -1 2-give sfp ifr -say \\
`He said: `We will give you our daughter in marriage.'' (150831 laoshu jianv-zh)
0006374#S53
exe

exe

nɤ-kɯmtɕʰɯ ɲɯ-ta-mbi \\
2sg. poss -toy ipfv -1$ $2-give \\
`I give it to you as a toy.' (28-kWpAz) 0003714#S166
exe

Since essive adjuncts are formally indistinguishable from absolutive arguments such as objects and intransitive subjects, some sentences may appear to be ambiguous. In ( ex:tWrme.YWpe ), the noun tɯrmeperson could be interpreted as the subject, and the phrase kɯki stu kɯ-xtɕi ki as a topic.

exe

kɯki stu kɯ-xtɕi ki tɯrme ɲɯ-pe tɕe \\
dem. prox most sbj: pcp -be.small dem. prox person sens -be.good lnk \\
`The smallest one is very nice as a person.' (31-deluge)
0004077#S122
exe

That tɯrme here is not the subject can be seen if one chooses a first or second person form: in ( ex:tWrme.YWtWpe ), the noun tɯrme is still present despite 2sg indexation on the verb. This piece of evidence demonstrates that the analysis as essive adjunct is the only possible one.

exe

nɤʑo tɯrme wuma ɲɯ-tɯ-pe \\
2sg person really sens -2-be.good \\
`You are very nice as a person.' (elicited)
exe

It is common to have a related word as essive and as the subject or object which it refers to. In ( ex:tWGli.Wuma.Zo.pe ), for instance, the inalienably possessed noun tɯ-ɣlidung occurs as both intransitive subject of the verb pebe good (with 3sg possessive prefix) and as essive adjunct, in the latter in the specialized meaning `fertilizer'. Note that the essive adjunct is closer to the verb than the oblique phrase in ɯ-taʁ (§ sec:word.order.intr ).

exe

tsʰɤt nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-ɣli nɯnɯ tɤ-rɤku ɯ-taʁ tɯ-ɣli wuma ʑo pe. \\
goat dem gen 3sg. poss -manure dem indef. poss -crops 3sg. poss -on indef. poss -manure really emph be.good: fact \\
`Goat manure is very good as a fertilizer for the crops.' (05-qaZo) 0003404#S27
exe

In ( ex:ambro.tArkunW.ra ), the noun mbrohorse occurs both in the object of rkuput in (meaning here `include the dowry') and in the essive adjunct a-mbro `as a horse (for me)'.

exe

mbro tɯ-skɤt kɯ-tso ci, a-mbro tɤ-rku-nɯ ra \\
horse c. poss -speech sbj: pcp -understand indef 1sg. poss -horse imp -put.in- pl be.needed: fact \\
`Give me a horse who understands human speech as my horse.' (2003 kandzWsqhaj)
exe

The essive adjunct can be either closer to the verb than the core argument it refers to, as in ( ex:nArZaB.YWtambi ), ( ex:tWGli.Wuma.Zo.pe ) and ( ex:ambro.tArkunW.ra ) above, or further away as in ( ex:WphW.rNWl ), where the intransitive subject of mɤ-ra `is not needed', rŋɯlsilver, occurs between the verb and the essive ɯ-pʰɯ `as its price'.

exe

aʑɯɣ ɯ-pʰɯ rŋɯl mɤ-ra, \\
1sg: gen 3sg. poss -price silver neg -be.needed: fact \\
`I don't want money as the price [for these clothes].' (140506 shizi he huichang de bailingniao-zh) 0003927#S235
exe

With the monotransitive verb pʰɯttake out, cut, an essive adjunct can be used to express the purpose of the action as in ( ex:paʁndza.YWnWphWtnW ).

exe

tsuku kɯ paʁndza ɲɯ-nɯ-pʰɯt-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu ri, \\
some erg hogwash ipfv - auto -pluck- pl sens -be lnk \\
`Some people cut [ Sambucus ] as hogwash.' (12-ndZiNgri)
0003488#S28
exe

This essive phrase sometimes occurs with the noun ɯ-spamaterial with this verb as in ( ex:zGAmbu.Wspa ), a construction that is in the process of grammaticalizing into a purposive construction when used with a participial clause (§ sec:participial.clause.essive ).

exe

zɣɤmbu ɯ-spa ɲɯ-nɯ-pʰɯt-nɯ ŋgrɤl \\
broom 3sg. poss -material ipfv - auto -cut- pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`They cut it to make brooms. (`as a material for brooms')' (140505 sWjno)
0003919#S21
exe

Some verbs, like sɤrtsicount as (§ sec:sig.caus.other.derivations ), have an essive argument (rather than adjunct), which is not indexed on the verb and receive no case marking, as shown by ( ex:tutanWsArtsi ), where the essive argument is a-tɕɯ `my son'.

exe

aʑo a-tɕɯ tu-ta-nɯ-sɤrtsi ŋu \\
1sg 1sg. poss -son ipfv -1 2- auto -consider.as be: fact \\
`I consider you as my son.' (elicited)
exe

The transitive verb wumgather can also select an essive argument different from the object when used in the meaning `take as a student', as in ( ex:naslama.kukWwuma ). This expression is similar to Chinese 收……为徒 shōu... wéitútake as a disciple, where 收 shōu has the same meaning as wumgather, and where the essive is overtly marked by 为 wéi. In this example the object is 1sg, and the essive is the noun nɤ-slama, with a possessive prefix coreferent with the subject. The verb wum in this meaning requires the orientation eastwards in its centripetal function (see example ex:YWqAt.nA.kuwum, § sec:centripetal.centrifugal ).

exe

wortɕʰi ʑo aʑo nɤ-slama ku-kɯ-wum-a \\
please emph 1sg 2sg. poss -student ipfv -2 1-gather- 1sg \\
`Please take me as your student.' (150907 laoshandaoshi-zh)
0006398#S35
exe
summary: Essive noun phrases in Japhug are not sentence arguments; they express the role or function that a referent fulfills, and bare noun phrases without case marking can be interpreted this way. Because essive adjuncts are formally identical to absolutive arguments, some sentences are ambiguous, but examples with person indexation show that the noun is not the verb’s subject; the passage also shows that some verbs can take essive arguments or use essive phrases for meanings such as “as a material,” “as a price,” or “as a student.”

text:
Verb ellipsis may explain the presence of essive noun phrases with verbs that are not usually used with adjuncts of this type. For instance, in ( ex:pGAtCW.tAmdzu ), the nouns pɣɤtɕɯbird and tɤ-mdzuthorn are not objects (there 1sg object indexation on both pɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-sat-a and tʰɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-sat-a ) and are analyzable as essive adjuncts `me, as a bird/thorn', `while I was a bird/thorn'. This example comes from a story where the main character was repeatedly killed by her sister, and reborn several times, first as a bird, and then as a thorn, as describe in ( ex:pGAtCW.tAmdzu ), from another version of the same story.

exe

a-pi kɯ nɯra pɯ-fse tɕe, pɣɤtɕɯ ri pɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-sat-a, tɤ-mdzu ri tʰɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-sat-a \\
1sg. poss -elder.sibling erg dem: pl pst. ipfv -be.like lnk bird also aor - inv - caus -kill- 1sg indef. poss -thorn also aor - inv - caus -kill- 1sg \\
`Your elder sister was like that, she had me killed [while I was a] bird, and had also me killed [while I was a] thorn.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

The presence of these adjuncts in this particular context is probably due to the ellipsis of tɤ-sci-a `I was born', an intransitive verb which takes essive noun phrases with the meaning `be reborn as, be reincarnated as' as in ( ex:pGAtCW.tAscia ).

exe

nɯ ɯ-qʰu tɕe pɣɤtɕɯ tɤ-sci-a, nɯ ɯ-qʰu tɕe tɤ-mdzu tɤ-sci-a qʰe \\
dem 3sg. poss -after lnk bird aor -be.born- 1sg dem 3sg. poss -after lnk indef. poss -thorn aor -be.born- 1sg lnk \\
`After that I was reborn as a bird, and after that I was reborn as a thorn.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe
summary: The passage argues that certain essive noun phrases may appear with verbs that normally do not take this type of adjunct because an underlying verb has been omitted. In the example, *bird* and *thorn* are analyzed as essive adjuncts meaning “while I was a bird/thorn,” and this is attributed to ellipsis of *tɤ-sci-a* ‘I was born,’ a verb that can take essive phrases meaning ‘be reborn as’ or ‘be reincarnated as.’

text:
goal absolutive
Motion verbs ( ɕego, ɣicome, ɬoʁcome out etc), manipulation verbs ( ɣɯtbring, tsɯmtake away etc) and some perception verbs (like rulook at) have arguments referring to the location towards which the action is directed. These arguments are not indexed in the verb morphology (in particular, motion verbs are intransitive, see § sec:intr.goal ). They can be marked with locative postpositions (§ sec:core.locative ) or dative (§ sec:dative ), but also occur in absolutive form, as tɯrme-kʰaother people's house in ( ex:kha.jari ).

exe

tɕe nɯ-mɤrʑaβ qʰe tɕe tɯrme-kʰa jɤ-ari ɕti qʰe \\
lnk aor -marry lnk lnk people-house aor -go[II] be. aff: fact lnk \\
`She married and went to [live in] other people's (her in laws') house.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S9
exe

Goals can be relativized (§ sec:locative.relativization ) using oblique participial relatives (§ sec:locative.participle.relatives ) or finite relatives (§ sec:locative.relativization.finite ), but not object participial relatives except in a very restricted context (§ sec:locative.relativization.object ), unlike most absolutive arguments.
summary:
Motion, manipulation, and some perception verbs can take goal arguments indicating the destination of the action, but these arguments are not indexed in the verb morphology. They may appear with locative or dative marking, yet they can also surface in absolutive form.  

These goal arguments can be relativized with oblique participial or finite relatives, but not with object participial relatives except in a very restricted context, unlike most absolutive arguments.

text:
absolutive locative
In addition to goals, absolutive noun phrases expressing a static location are found in Japhug, in particular with the verb rɤʑistay as in ( ex:rqaco.pWrAzi ). Locative postpositions can also occur, but are optional (§ sec:core.locative ).

exe

tɕe pjɯ-sɤ-sɯxɕat-a pɯ-ŋu tɕe, rqaco pɯ-rɤʑi-a, tsʰuβdɯn pɯ-rɤʑi-a. \\
lnk ipfv - antipass -teach-ɕ pst. ipfv -be lnk topo pst. ipfv -stay- 1sg topo pst. ipfv -stay- 1sg \\
`When I was teaching, I lived in Rqakyo and in Tshobdun.' (150819 kumpGa) 0006388#S2
exe

Absolutive locative phrases are also found with some transitive verbs, as nɯ-mtʰɤɣ `their waist' with rtɤβattach in ( ex:nɯmthAG.YWrtABnW ).

exe

tɯrme ra kɯ nɯ-mtʰɤɣ ɲɯ-rtɤβ-nɯ. \\
people pl erg 3pl. poss -waist ipfv -attach- pl \\
`People attach [badger skin] around their waist (as a remedy for rheumatism).' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S126
exe

Oblique participial relatives (§ sec:locative.participle.relatives, § sec:locative.relativization.finite ) or finite relatives (§ sec:locative.relativization.finite ) are used to relativize these absolutive locative phrases.
summary: In Japhug, absolutive noun phrases can express static location, not only goals, especially with the verb *rɤʑistay* “stay,” and locative postpositions are possible but optional. Such absolutive locative phrases also occur with some transitive verbs, and they are relativized by oblique participial relatives or by finite relatives.

text:
Postposition are invariable words which necessarily follow a noun phrase, and specify the syntactic function of that noun phrase, be it core argument or adjunct. They cannot be used on their own, and at the very least require a demonstrative pronoun such as nɯ (§ sec:anaphoric.demonstrative.pro ).

Although their uses have commonalities with relator nouns (§ sec:relator.nouns ), they differ from those in lacking a possessive prefix. Postposition stacking is rare; only two cases exist: the sequence of locative postpositions tɕu zɯ and tɕe (§ sec:core.locative ) and also the case of genitive postpositional phrases used in the meaning `the one from/of...' (with an elided head noun), as in ( ex:GW.cho ), where the genitive ɣɯ is followed by the comitative (§ sec:comitative ).

exe

tɕe pɤjka ɣɯ cʰo wuma ʑo naχtɕɯɣ. \\
lnk pumpkin gen comit really emph be.similar: fact \\
`Its [little thorn-like things] are like those of the pumpkin.'
0003518#S55
exe
summary:
Postpositions are invariable elements that obligatorily follow a noun phrase and mark its syntactic role, whether as a core argument or an adjunct. They cannot stand alone and require at least a demonstrative pronoun, and unlike relator nouns they lack a possessive prefix.  

Stacking postpositions is rare, with only two attested patterns: the sequence of locative postpositions *tɕu zɯ* and *tɕe*, and genitive postpositional phrases used with an elided head noun in the sense ‘the one from/of…’, where the genitive marker *ɣɯ* is followed by the comitative.

text:
word!clitic
Since other Gyalrongologists, in particular, treat the postpositions in related languages as clitics rather than as independent words as is done in the present work, a justification of the present analysis is necessary.

In Japhug, the postpositions kɯergative (§ sec:erg.kW ) and ɣɯgenitive (§ sec:genitive ) do have some clitic-like characteristics: they cannot be used without a preceding noun phrase (or a subordinate clause, § sec:marked.subordinate ), are unstressed, and in the case of the genitive have special irregular forms with pronouns (§ sec:pronouns.gen ).

However, a pause can occur between these postpositions ( ex:kW.nAmWmnW ) and the noun phrase they follow. For instance, in example ( ex:kW.nAmWmnW ), a two second pause (with an inspiration) is found between the phrase nɯŋa ra and the following ergative kɯ.

exe

tɕe tɯrtsi nɯ pjɯ́-wɣ-βzu tɕe, nɯŋa ra, kɯ nɤ-mɯm-nɯ cʰo wuma ʑo ɣɯ-ɕɯ-fka-nɯ \\
lnk cow.food dem ipfv - inv -make lnk cow pl erg trop -be.tasty: fact - pl comit really emph inv - caus -be.satiated: fact - pl \\
`They make cow food with flour, the cows find it tasty, and it satisfies their hunger.' (140513 tWrtsi)
0003985#S15
exe

A filler (§ sec:fillers ) can even be inserted between the noun phrase and the following ergative, as in ( ex:nW.nAkinW.kW ).

exe

tɕendɤre iɕqʰa <xifangping> nɯ, nɤkinɯ, kɯ `ɯ-wa ɣɯ nɯnɯ tʰɯci ɯ-tɯtʂaŋ ci a-pɯ-tu ra' ntsɯ ɲɯ-sɯsɤm pjɤ-ŋu. \\
lnk the.aforementioned anthr dem filler erg 3sg. poss -father gen dem something 3sg. poss -justice indef irr - ipfv -exist be.needed: fact always sens -think[III] ifr -be \\
`Xi Fangping wanted to obtain justice for his father.' (150909 xifangping-zh)
0006408#S28
exe

Such cases are by no means exceptional; at least 54+35 examples of ergative and genitive preceded by a pause are attested in the corpus (they can be found by searching kɯ or ɣɯ preceded by a comma). Most of these cases are found in sentences where the speaker hesitates, and are especially common in texts translated from Chinese.

The same is true of all postpositions studied in this section. Examples of pause between the noun phrase and the following postposition can be found for most of them, for instance ( ex:nWnWtCu.zW ) for the locative zɯ (§ sec:core.locative ).

exe

<bageda> kɤ-ti nɯnɯtɕu, zɯ, nɤkinɯ, \\
topo obj: pcp -say dem: loc loc filler \\
`In the [place] called Baghdâd...' (140515 facaimeng-zh) 0004000#S2
exe
summary: The passage argues that Japhug postpositions should be treated as independent words rather than clitics, even though ergative kɯ and genitive ɣɯ have some clitic-like properties such as requiring a preceding noun phrase, being unstressed, and showing irregular pronoun forms. The key evidence is that a pause, and even a filler, can occur between the noun phrase and the postposition, and this is not rare in the corpus; similar pause-separated uses are found with other postpositions as well.

text:
ergative
The ergative kɯ, like genitive ɣɯ, is borrowed from Tibetan and shares with the Tibetan ergative the functions of marking transitive subject, instrument and cause. It has however a series of specific functions not found in Tibetic languages, such as that of comparee (§ sec:comparee.kW ), distributive (§ sec:distributive.kW ), and oblique argument (§ sec:oblique.kW ) marker. It is homophonous with the orientation adverb kɯ eastwards (§ sec:locative.adv ).

Although postpositional phrases in kɯ have a different syntactic status depending on the various sub-functions of this marker (as can be shown with tests like relativization), kɯ is glossed as erg in all cases.

The postposition kɯ does not appear in combination with the additive focus marker kɯnɤalso, even (§ sec:kWnA ), regardless of its function.
summary: The ergative marker **kɯ**, borrowed from Tibetan like the genitive **ɣɯ**, marks transitive subjects, instruments, and causes, but it also has additional functions not found in Tibetic languages, including marking the comparee, distributive, and oblique arguments. It is homophonous with the orientation adverb **kɯ** ‘eastwards,’ and although its syntactic status varies by function, it is glossed as **erg** in all cases. The postposition **kɯ** never combines with the additive focus marker **kɯnɤ** ‘also, even.’

text:
ergative subject:transitive
The core function of kɯ is marking the subject of morphologically transitive verbs. Ergative is obligatory on third person transitive subjects as in ( ex:WtCW.nW.kW ), and is agrammatical on objects and intransitive subjects, except in the case of long distance ergative (§ sec:long.distance.kW ) and some semi-transitive verbs (§ sec:S.kW ). Apparent counterexamples are speech errors (§ sec:absolutive.S ).

exe

tɕeri ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ nɯ pjɤ-sɯχsɤl \\
lnk 3sg. poss -son dem erg dem ifr -recognized \\
`But the son realized it (that she was a râkshasî).' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S19
exe

Transitive subjects in the ergative most often precede the object as in ( ex:WtCW.nW.kW ), but can also follow it as in ( ex:nAZo.tWsqar.kW ), an example illustrating a third person inanimate ( tɯsqar kɯ `tsampa') acting on first/second person (§ sec:indexation.mixed ).

exe

nɤʑo tɯsqar kɯ nɤki nɯ tʰɯ-tɯ́-wɣ-stu ɕti tɕe, \\
2sg tsampa erg dem. medial dem aor -2- inv -do.like be. aff: fact lnk \\
`Tsampa made you the [way you are now].' = `You grew that big by eating tsampa.' (2011-07-tWsqar)
exe

While ergative is obligatory on third persons, it is optional on first and second person pronouns, as shown by example ( ex:aZo.tAmYota ) where aʑo 1sg is in absolutive form with the transitive verb mɲoprepare.

exe

maʁ nɤ, aʑo tɤ-mɲo-t-a, kɯki kɯ tɕi mɤ-βze rca! \\
not.be: fact sfp 1sg aor -prepare- pst: tr - 1sg dem. prox erg also neg -make[III]: fact sfp \\
`No, it is I who prepared [our lunch], she does not do it.' (Answer to the question 'Did she prepare your lunch?) (conversation 140510)
exe

Using the ergative on a first or second person pronoun in transitive subject function is however never impossible, as in ( ex:WZo.kW.aZo.kW ), and more common in the case of contrastive focus (§ sec:focalization.overt ).

exe

nɯ kɯ-fse tɕe tɤscoz ɯʑo kɯ ɲɯ-sɯ-ɣɯt, aʑo kɯ ku-sɯ-tsɯm-a tɕe, \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.like lnk letter 3sg erg ipfv: west - caus -bring 1sg erg ipfv: east - caus -take.away- 1sg lnk \\
`And like that, she sent me letters, and I sent her letters.' (12-BzaNsa) 0003484#S24
exe

Transitive subjects are relativized using subject kɯ- participial relative clauses, the participle taking a possessive prefix coreferent with the object (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ).
summary:
The passage explains that **kɯ** marks the subject of morphologically transitive verbs and is obligatory with **third-person transitive subjects**, while it is ungrammatical on objects and intransitive subjects except in special cases. With **first- and second-person pronouns**, ergative marking is optional, though it can be used and is especially common when the subject is contrastively focused.

It also notes that transitive subjects usually precede the object but may follow it, and that transitive subjects are relativized with **subject kɯ- participial relative clauses** whose participle takes a possessive prefix coreferent with the object.

text:
ergative!long distance subject:intransitive
Postpositional phrases in kɯ referring to the subject of a transitive verb can be stranded from their verb by another clause with an intransitive verb.

In ( ex:long.erg2 ), for instance, the clause nɯ ma ɯ-kɤpa pjɤ-me qʰe `she had no other way' separates the subject tɤɕime nɯ kɯ `the princess' from the main verb to-ti `she said'; note the presence of a pause and of the filler nɤkinɯ after the transitive subject. The transitive subject here also happens to be coreferent with the possessor of ɯ-kɤpa `her method, her way' in the standing clause, resulting in a surface case mismatch.

exe

tɕendɤre tɤɕime nɯ kɯ, nɤkinɯ, nɯ ma ɯ-kɤpa pjɤ-me qʰe `jɤɣ jɤɣ jɤɣ' to-ti ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk young.lady dem erg filler dem apart.from 3sg. poss -method ipfv. ifr -not.exist lnk be.possible: fact be.possible: fact be.possible: fact ifr -say sens -be \\
`The young lady had no other way but to say ``yes, yes, yes".' (140428 mu e guniang-zh) 0003880#S86
exe

Similarly in ( ex:long.erg3 ), the minimal clause jo-ɣi `he came' consisting of a single verb occurs between the subject iɕqʰa rgɤtpu nɯ kɯ `the old man' and the rest of the main clause ɬɤndʐi nɯnɯ jo-tsʰi `he stopped the demon'.

exe

iɕqʰa rgɤtpu nɯ kɯ, jo-ɣi tɕe, nɤki, ɬɤndʐi nɯnɯ jo-tsʰi \\
the.aforementioned old.man dem erg ifr -come lnk filler demon dem ifr -block \\
`The old man came and stopped the demon.' (140512 fushang he yaomo1-zh) 0003969#S59
exe

Here the intransitive subject of jo-ɣi `he came' and the transitive subject of jo-tsʰi `he blocked him' happen to be coreferent. If analyzed superficially, ( ex:long.erg3 ) could seem to be an example of ergative appearing on an intransitive subject. In isolation, however, without context, a clause such as $ $ rgɤtpu nɯ kɯ jo-ɣi is not considered to be correct by native speakers, showing that it is preferable to analyze jo-ɣi as an incision in this context rather than forming a constituent with the preceding postpositional phrase in kɯ.
summary: The passage explains that in kɯ postpositional phrases referring to the subject of a transitive verb can be separated from their verb by an intervening clause with an intransitive verb. In the examples, this creates a surface mismatch and may look like ergative marking on an intransitive subject, but native-speaker judgments show that the intransitive clause is better analyzed as an inserted incision rather than as forming a constituent with the preceding ergative phrase.

text:
ergative subject:intransitive
Genuine examples of intransitive subjects with ergative appear to be nevertheless attested at least with some semi-transitive verbs like tsoknow, understand as in ( ex:kW.tso ). It is optional and much less common than the absolutive form.

exe

ɕɯ kɯ tso ma \\
who erg understand: fact lnk \\
`Who would know.' (150909 xiaocui-zh) 0006386#S59
exe

Ergative marking on the subject of reflexive verbs (which are morphologically intransitive, § sec:reflexive ) is also attested for marking emphasis, with the same pronoun preceding and following the ergative (for instance tɯʑo kɯ tɯʑo in example ex:tWZo.kW.tWZo, § sec:genr.pro ).
summary: The passage notes that ergative marking can appear on subjects of some semitransitive verbs such as *know* and *understand*, but this usage is optional and much less common than the absolutive form. It also reports ergative marking on the subjects of reflexive verbs, where it serves an emphatic function and may occur with the same pronoun both before and after the ergative marker.

text:
ergative subject:intransitive
In addition to marking the transitive subject, the postposition kɯ occurs on instruments, as in ( ex:Wlu.kW.chWsWXse ). It is possible to find examples with postpositional phrases in kɯ, one corresponding to the subject and the other one to the instrument, as in ( ex:rJAlpu.kW.nWnW.kW ). No good examples of instruments in kɯ are found with an intransitive main verb in the corpus (only manner or causal adjuncts are found, § sec:manner.nominal.kW ).

exe

ɯ-pɯ nɯ ɯ-lu kɯ cʰɯ-sɯ-χse ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -young dem 3sg. poss -milk erg ipfv - caus -feed[III] sens -be \\
`[The whale] feeds its young with milk.' (160703 jingyu)
0006169#S14
exe

exe

rɟɤlpu kɯ nɯnɯ kɯ ɯ-βri a-pɯ-sɯ-χtɕi ndɤre, mɤʑɯ nɤ-sɤ-scit tʰaŋ nɤ!\\
king erg dem erg 3sg. poss -body irr - pfv - caus -wash lnk even.more trop - prop -be.happy: fact hypoth sfp \\
`If the king washes his body with this, he will find it even nicer.' (140514 xizajiang he lifashi-zh)
0003996#S83
exe

When an instrument in kɯ occurs in a clause, the main verb generally takes the causative prefix as in ( ex:Wlu.kW.chWsWXse ) and ( ex:rJAlpu.kW.nWnW.kW ), as if the instrument were a type of causee -- it differs from a causee however in that in the case of the latter the postposition kɯ is optional (§ sec:causee.kW ). Causative marking in clauses with instruments is optional, and one can find the two constructions with or without the causative marker side by side in the same narrative, as shown by examples ( ex:instr3 ) and ( ex:instr4 ).

exe

qartsʰaz ɯ-ndʐi kɯ cʰɯ-βzu-nɯ tɕe, nɯ stu kɯ-ʑru. \\
deer 3sg. poss -hide erg ipfv -do- pl lnk dem most sbj: pcp -precious \\
`They make [shoes] with deer hide, it is the most precious [type of skin].' (30-mboR)
0003748#S46
exe

exe

qartsʰaz ɯ-ndʐi ʁɟa kɯ ʑo tʰɯ-kɤ-sɯ-βzu \\
deer 3sg. poss -hide entirely erg emph aor - obj: pcp - caus -do\\
`[It is] entirely made of deer hide.' (30-mboR)
0003748#S51
exe

The instrument is mainly a concrete object, but can also refer to an entire action, as in ( ex:nW.kW.ndZixtu ) where the anaphoric nɯthat refers to the actions described in the previous clauses.

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ sɲikuku ʑo si ʑ-lu-pʰɯt tɕe, nɯ ɲɯ-ntsɣe-ndʑi tɕe, nɯ kɯ ndʑi-xtu cʰɯ-sɯ-χsu-ndʑi pɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
indef. poss -son dem erg every.day emph tree tral - ipfv -fell lnk dem ipfv -sell- du lnk dem erg 3du. poss -belly ipfv - caus -feed- du pst. ipfv -be sens -be \\
`The son went every day to fell trees, they sold [the wood], and they fed their bellies this way.' (2003 tWxtsa)
exe

Instruments differ from transitive subjects in that they are relativized using oblique participles in sɤ(z)- (§ sec:oblique.participle ) rather than subject participles.
summary: The postposition **kɯ** marks transitive subjects and can also mark instruments, and in clauses with instruments the main verb generally takes a causative prefix, as though the instrument were a kind of causee. However, unlike causees, this marking is optional, and the corpus contains no good examples of **kɯ**-marked instruments with an intransitive main verb, only manner or causal adjuncts. Instruments are usually concrete objects but can also refer to an entire action, and they are relativized with oblique participles rather than subject participles.

text:
ergative manner cause
Postpositional phrases in kɯ can also describe the manner in which an action takes place, or its cause. Manner adjuncts in kɯ are generally formed with abstract nouns (§ sec:tA.abstract.nouns ) as tɤ-mqeverbal fight and tɤ-ndɯtdispute in ( ex:tAmqe.tAndWt.kW ) and tɤŋɤmpain in ( ex:tANAm.kW.pjWsi ). Unlike instruments, manner adjuncts do not trigger the addition of a causative prefix on the main verb, and are fully compatible with intransitive verbs.

exe

kumpɣa cʰo kʰɯna ni li tɤ-mqe tɤ-ndɯt kɯ jo-ɣi-ndʑi tɕe, \\
chicken comit dog du again indef. poss -verbal.fight indef. poss -dispute erg ifr -come- du lnk \\
`The chicken and the dog came fighting and arguing [with each other].' (150826 shier shengxiao-zh)
0006284#S119
exe

exe

tɤŋɤm kɯ pjɯ-si ɲɯ-ra. \\
pain erg ipfv -die sens -be.needed \\
`[The animal that is devoured alive by the lions] dies in pain.' (20-sWNgi) 0003562#S45
exe

Causal adjuncts, like manner adjuncts, also take the postposition kɯ without causative form on the verb, as in ( ex:WRrWm.kW ). The inalienably possessed noun ɯ-ndʐacause in particular is often used with the ergative to specify a cause ( ex:nW.Wndzxa.kW ).

exe

kʰa ɯ-ʁrɯm nɯ kɯ tɕe tɕe ɲɯ-ɣɤɕu \\
house 3sg. poss -shade dem erg lnk lnk sens -be.cool \\
`Due to the shade of the buildings, [this road] is not exposed to the heat of the sun.' (conversation 2014-05-10)
exe

exe

qambalɯla nɯ, nɯ ɯ-ndʐa kɯ tʰa ɯβrɤ-si ma \\
butterfly dem dem 3sg. poss -cause erg later rh. q -die: fact sfp \\
`The butterfly might die because of that.' (150818 muzhi guniang)
0006334#S189
exe

Various subordinate clauses with finite or non-finite verbs are also made with the postposition kɯ (see § sec:causality and § sec:rectification.clauses for instance).
summary: Postpositional phrases with **kɯ** in this language can express both **manner** and **cause**. Manner adjuncts are often built from abstract nouns, do not require a causative prefix on the main verb, and can occur with intransitive verbs; causal adjuncts behave similarly and may use the inalienable noun **ɯ-ndʐa** ‘cause’ to specify the reason.

text:
ergative causee
Causative verbs in sɯ(ɣ)-/z- derived from transitive verbs have three arguments: causer, causee and object (§ sec:ditransitive.causative, § sec:sig.caus.tr ). The causer is treated as the transitive subject, and is marked with the ergative. The causee can also receive ergative marking as qapri kɯ-ɲaʁ nɯ kɯ `the black snake' in ( ex:kW.losWqioR1 ) and kɯ-wɣrum nɯ kɯ `the white one' ( ex:kW.losWqioR2 ). The most common word order is to put the causee before the object as in ( ex:kW.losWqioR1 ), but the opposite order is also attested as in ( ex:kW.losWqioR2 ).

exe

li mdaʁʑɯɣ ci to-lɤt tɕe, tɕendɤre, nɤki, qapri kɯ-ɲaʁ nɯ kɯ kɯ-wɣrum nɯnɯ lo-sɯ-qioʁ tɕe tɕe ɲɤ-sɯ-ɤkɤlɤt. \\
again bow one ifr -release lnk lnk filler snake sbj: pcp -be.black dem erg sbj: pcp -be.white dem ifr - caus -vomit lnk lnk ifr - caus -detach \\
`He shot an arrow and caused the black snake to vomit the white one, and separated it [from the other one].' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S100
exe

exe

to-lɤt tɕe tɕendɤre nɯnɯ qapri kɯ-ɲaʁ nɯ, kɯ-wɣrum nɯ kɯ lo-sɯ-qioʁ tɕe ɲɤ-sɯ-ta. \\
ifr -release lnk lnk dem snake sbj: pcp -be.black dem sbj: pcp -be.white dem erg ifr - caus -vomit lnk ifr - caus -put \\
`He shot [an arrow] and caused the white one to vomit the black snake and to release it.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S94
exe

However, the presence of ergative on the causee is optional, as shown by example ( ex:CkozRAru ) where the causee ɯ-tɕɯ stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ `his youngest son' is in absolutive form.

exe

rɟɤlpu kɯ ɯ-tɕɯ stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ ɕ-ko-z-rɯru. \\
king erg 3sg. poss -son most sbj: pcp -be.small dem tral - ifr - caus -guard \\
`The king sent his youngest son to guard [the trees].' (140507 jinniao-zh)
0003931#S37
exe

When the object is third person, and the causee first or second, the causee is obligatorily indexed, as in ( ex:pWwGsWmtoa ) (see § sec:sig.caus.tr for more examples), resulting in a verb form that is identical with that when both causer and causee are third person, and the object is first or second person as in ( ex:kW.pWwGsWmtoa ). With such ambiguous verb forms, the presence of the ergative postposition on the causee as a-tɕɯ kɯ `my son' in ( ex:kW.pWwGsWmtoa ) is a way to disambiguate from the interpretation of the noun as object as in ( ex:pWwGsWmtoa ).

exe

xlist

ɯʑo kɯ a-tɕɯ pɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-mto-a \\
3sg erg 1sg. poss -son aor - inv - caus -see- 1sg \\
`He let me see my son.' (elicited)

ɯʑo kɯ a-tɕɯ kɯ pɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-mto-a \\
3sg erg 1sg. poss -son erg aor - inv - caus -see- 1sg \\
`He let my son see me.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

No minimal pair similar to ( ex:pWwGsWmtoa ) and ex:kW.pWwGsWmtoa ), where the ergative on the causee has a disambiguating function, is attested in the corpus.
summary: Causative verbs derived from transitive verbs have three arguments: causer, causee, and object. The causer is marked ergative, while the causee may also take ergative marking, most commonly before the object but sometimes after it; this marking is optional in some cases and can help disambiguate ambiguous verb forms, especially when person indexing would otherwise make the interpretation unclear.

text:
comparee ergative
In the comparative construction (§ sec:comparison ), in addition to the standard markers (such as sɤz and its variants, see § sec:comparative ), the postposition kɯ can appear on the comparee, although the comparee is syntactically an intransitive subject (indexed on the stative adjectival predicate).

The comparee with kɯ can either precede ( ex:nWnW.kW.aZo.sAz ) or follow the standard, but most often this marker appears when no overt standard is present as in ( ex:nW.kW.xtCi ). In all of these examples, including the last one, the marker kɯ is optional.

exe

mahi nɯnɯ kɯ aʑo sɤz cʰa \\
water.buffalo dem erg 1sg comp can: fact \\
`The water buffalo is stronger than me.' (150831 laoshu jianv-zh)
0006374#S59
exe

exe

ndʑi-tsʰɯɣa nɯra wuma naχtɕɯɣ. tɕeri tɯrgilaŋlaŋ nɯ kɯ xtɕi. \\
2du. poss -form dem: pl really be.similar: fact but fir.cone dem erg be.small: fact \\
`Their shape is similar, but the fir cone is smaller.' (08-tWrgi) 0003464#S74
exe

See for a historical hypothesis explaining how the ergative marker came to be used to mark the comparee.
summary: In comparative constructions, the postposition **kɯ** may appear on the comparee even though the comparee is syntactically an intransitive subject indexed on a stative adjectival predicate. This marker can occur before or after the standard, but it is most common when no overt standard is expressed, and it remains optional in all cases.

text:
ergative distributive!ergative
The postposition kɯ, when occurring with a counted noun designating a quantity, can be used to focus on the distributive meaning (`for one X', `per'). It occurs in constructions with intransitive verbs where no agent or instrument is present, but exclusively to express the price of the quantity designated, as in ( ex:tWtWrpa.kW1 ) (see additional examples in ). It cannot be used with time counted nouns.

exe

tɯ-tɯrpa kɯ sqi jamar ɲɯ-ra. \\
one-pound erg ten about sens -be.needed \\
`You need ten [renminbis] per pound [of Angelica].' (17 ndZWnW)
0003524#S22
exe

As argued in, this construction results from the elision of a verb such as sɤnduexchange, which can take as instrument (§ sec:instr.kW ) the counted noun expressing a quantity, as in ( ex:kW.YWwGsAndu ).

exe

tɯ-tɯrpa kɯ ɣurʑa jamar ɲɯ́-wɣ-sɤndu ɲɯ-kʰɯ \\
one-pound erg hundred about ipfv - inv -exchange sens -be.possible \\
`One can exchange (sell) one pound for a hundred [renminbis].' (elicited)
exe
summary: The postposition **kɯ** can mark distributive meaning with a counted noun, especially in expressions of quantity meaning “for one X” or “per.” In this use, it appears with intransitive verbs only to express the **price** of the quantity, not with time nouns, and the construction is analyzed as arising from the omission of a verb like **sɤndu** ‘exchange,’ which can take the counted noun as an instrument.

text:
ergative partitive!ergative
The intransitive verb mtsʰɤtbe full generally has a dummy subject, and selects a locative argument and a partitive argument, indicating the material / elements that the location is full of. This partitive argument is generally in a absolutive form, as in ( ex:YAmtshAt ), but we also find examples with the ergative, as in ( ex:kW.pjAmtshAt ). Although ( ex:kW.pjAmtshAt ) is translated from Chinese, the original has 下面坐满了观众 xiàmiàn zuòmǎn le guānzhòngBelow, the spectator seats were filled, and there is nothing in the structure of the original sentence that could allow to interpret the ergative as a calque. In addition, Tshendzin confirmed that the ergative is correct here.

exe

tʂapa tʰamtɕɤt, nɯ-mbro nɯ-jla, nɯŋa paʁ nɯra ɲɤ-mtsʰɤt. \\
pen all 3pl. poss -horse 3pl. poss -hybrid.yak cow pig dem: pl ifr -be.full \\
`All the pens had become full of horses, hybrid yak, cows and pigs.' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S125
exe

exe

ɯ-pa nɯtɕu rca, kɯ-nɤmɲo kɯ pjɤ-mtsʰɤt ʑo \\
3sg. poss -down dem: loc unexp: deg sbj: pcp -watch erg ipfv. ifr -be.full emph \\
`Down [the stage], [the seats] were full of spectators.' (150822 yan muouxi de ren-zh)
0006384#S50
exe

Another verb with an optional partitive argument, which can take ergative marking, is the passive amarbe smeared with (example ex:tAse.kW.pjAkAmarci, § sec:passive.agent ).
summary:
The intransitive verb *mtsʰɤt* ‘be full’ typically takes a dummy subject plus locative and partitive arguments, where the partitive denotes the material or beings filling the location. This partitive is usually absolutive, but the text gives examples showing that it can also appear in ergative form, and this ergative use is confirmed as grammatical rather than a calque from Chinese.  

A similar pattern is noted for the passive verb *amar* ‘smeared with’, which also allows an optional partitive argument that may take ergative marking.

text:
ergative
The transitive verb kʰɤtdo repeatedly, `do for a long time' and its causative form sɯ-kʰɤtcause to do repeatedly, `cause to do for a long time' occur in a construction with instrumental-like noun phrases marked with the ergative kɯ, indicating the action which is performed repeatedly or done over a long time. These noun phrases can include either an action nominal derived from a verb with the prefix tɯ- (§ sec:action.nominals ) as in ( ex:tWqioR.kW ), or an underived action noun, as in ( ex:tama.kW.takhAt ) and ( ex:khAcAl.kW.takhata ).

exe

tɯ-qioʁ kɯ tó-wɣ-sɯ-kʰɤt ʑo tɕe, tɕe nóʁmɯz nɤ tɯɣ nɯnɯ ló-wɣ-sɯ-tɕɤt \\
nmlz: action -vomit erg ifr - inv - caus -do.a.long.time emph lnk lnk only.then lnk poison dem ifr - inv - caus -take.out \\
`[The medicine] caused [Gesar] to vomit a long time until he expelled the poison.' (Gesar)
exe

exe

ta-ma kɯ ta-kʰɤt ʑo \\
indef. poss -work erg aor:3 -do.a.long.time emph \\
`He did a lot of work.' (elicited)
exe

Example ( ex:khAcAl.kW.takhata ), with the verb kʰɤtdo repeatedly, `do for a long time' taking 1sg 3 indexation (§ sec:indexation.mixed ), shows that the ergative phrase cannot be analyzed as a transitive subject; moreover, the fact that adding the causative in this case would imply a real causative interpretation (`cause X to repeatedly') also indicates that this phrase is not an instrumental adjunct (see § sec:instr.kW ).

exe

kʰɤcɤl kɯ tɤ-kʰat-a ʑo \\
conversation erg aor -do.a.long.time- 1sg emph \\
`I have a long conversation.' (elicited)
exe

No other verb takes this type of oblique ergative phrase.
summary: The verb kʰɤt ‘do for a long time’ and its causative form occur with noun phrases marked by ergative kɯ that denote the action carried out repeatedly or over an extended period. These noun phrases may be action nominals or underived action nouns, and the construction is shown not to be a transitive subject or an instrumental adjunct because of its indexation patterns and the interpretation of the causative. No other verb takes this kind of oblique ergative phrase.

text:
genitive
With the exception of particular forms for some pronouns (§ sec:pronouns.gen ), the genitive postposition has the invariant form ɣɯ in Kamnyu Japhug. Like the ergative kɯ, it is likely borrowed from the Amdo clitic -ɣə/-kə. It is used in possessive contructions, but also expresses beneficiary and recipient.
summary: In Kamnyu Japhug, the genitive postposition is invariant ɣɯ, except for special forms used with some pronouns. It is likely borrowed from the Amdo clitic -ɣə/-kə and is used not only in possessive constructions but also to mark beneficiaries and recipients.

text:
possession
The genitive ɣɯ occurs in various type of possessive constructions, including genitival noun complements and possessive existential predicates (§ sec:possessive.mihi.est ).

Inside the noun phrase, the genitive occurs between possessor and possessum, and a possessive prefix is found on the possessum (§ ex:prefix.expression.of.possession ), as in ( ex:GZAndza.GW.WjwaR ).

exe

ri ɣʑɤndza ɣɯ ɯ-jwaʁ nɯra mɤ-wxti ri, ɲaʁ ʑo qʰe, \\
lnk Agastache.rugosa gen 3sg. poss -leaf dem: pl neg -be.big: fact lnk be.black: fact emph lnk \\
`The leaves of the Agastache rugosa are not large and quite dark in colour.' (11-qarGW)
0003480#S120
exe

Genitival phrases without possessive prefix on the possessum are rare but do exist, in particular when the possessum is a noun borrowed from Chinese and non-fully nativized like 国语 guóyǔnational language in ( ex:iZo.GW.guoyu ).

exe

iʑo ɣɯ <guoyu> ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, nɯnɯ kɤsɯfse ɣɯ ji-rju ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
1pl gen national.language sens -be lnk dem all gen 1pl. poss -speech sens -be lnk \\
`[Chinese] is our national language, it is our common language.' (150901 tshuBdWnskAt)
0006242#S14
exe

For singular noun possessors, the presence or not of a third person possessive prefix ɯ- is not always easy to tell from recordings, as due to the external sandhi (§ sec:sandhi.word ), ɣɯ ɯ- merges as ɣɯ when no pause occurs between the two. In careful speech, the third person prefix is clearly audible.

Nominal modifiers can sometimes be marked like possessors, with the genitive and/or with a possessive prefix on the following head noun, see § sec:gen.other.

The genitive can also appear between a noun phrase and a relator noun (§ sec:relator.nouns ), and even be followed by focus markers in this position, as in ( ex:GW.kWnA.WrkW.ri ).

exe

tɯ-ci kɯ-wxti ɣɯ kɯnɤ ɯ-rkɯ ri nɯra tu ŋgrɤl. \\
indef. poss -water sbj: pcp -be.big gen also 3sg. poss -side loc dem: pl exist: fact be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`[Dragonflies] are also found near large rivers.' (26-quspunmbro)
0003684#S7
exe

In these constructions, the genitive is always optional, and the prefix on the possessum suffices to express possession, as in ( ex:paXCi.WjwaR ) (see § ex:prefix.expression.of.possession ).

exe

paχɕi ɯ-jwaʁ tsa fse ri, nɯ sɤznɤ artɯm,\\
apple 3sg. poss -leaf a.little be.like: fact lnk dem comp be.round: fact \\
`[Its leaves] are a little like the leaves of an apple tree, but more round.' (09-mi)
0003466#S13
exe

When the possessum is elided however, the genitive postposition becomes obligatory, as in ( ex:baigua.GW.sAz ).

exe

ɯ-rɣi nɯnɯ, nɤki, <beigua> ɣɯ sɤz ɲɯ-jaʁjɯ. \\
3sg. poss -seed dem filler pumpkin gen comp sens -be.thick.and.strong \\
`Its seeds are thicker than those of the pumpkin.' (16-CWrNgo) 0003518#S126
exe

While there are transitive and semi-transitive verbs expressing possession (§ sec:possessive.constructions ), the most common possessive construction involves an existential verb taking the possessum as subject, with the possessor marked by a possessive prefix on the possessum, and optionally with the genitive, as in ( ex:phu.nW.GW.WRrW.GAZu ).

exe

qartsʰaz pʰu nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-ʁrɯ ɣɤʑu \\
deer male dem gen 3sg. poss -horn exist: sens \\
`The male deer has horns.' (27-qartshAz)
0003702#S32
exe

This construction is also used for abstract possession, as in ( ex:aZWG.aBlu.tu ).

exe

aʑɯɣ a-βlu tu \\
1sg: gen 1sg. poss -trick exist: fact \\
`I have an idea.' (140507 tangguowu-zh) 0003933#S28
exe

The causative verbs ɣɤtucause to have and ɣɤmedestroy, `cause not to exist/have' derived from tuexist and menot exist (§ sec:velar.caus.modal ) select an oblique argument with the genitive, as in ( ex:WZo.GW.tuGAtea ). Although this argument could be considered to be a type of beneficiary (§ sec:other.uses.poss.prefixes ), we observe here stability in case marking of the possessor between the base construction and the derived causative one.

exe

ɯʑo kɯ maka kɤ-ntɕʰoz mɤ-kɯ-ɤrɕo kɯ-fse ʑo tɯrɟɯ laχtɕʰa ɯʑo ɣɯ tu-ɣɤ-te-a jɤɣ \\
3sg. poss erg at.all inf -use neg - inf: stat -be.finished inf: stat -be.like emph wealth thing 3sg. poss gen ipfv - caus -exist[III]- 1sg be.possible: fact \\
`[If someone saves me], I will make him have more wealth and riches than he can ever use.' (140512 yufu yu mogui-zh)
0003973#S80
exe

Not all combinations of existential verbs and genitival phrases are existential possessive constructions. For instance, in ( ex:BZW.GW.WqiW ), the second clause could appear to contain a possessive construction meaning `the mouse only has half of it', but the context makes it clear that a different interpretation is necessary (§ sec:existential.comparative ).

exe

qamtɕɯr nɯ ɯ-mtɕʰi nɯnɯ βʑɯ sɤznɤ mɤʑɯ ʑo amtɕoʁ tɕe nɯ βʑɯ ɣɯ ɯ-qiɯ kɯnɤ me \\
shrew dem 3sg. poss -mouth dem mouse comp yet emph be.pointy lnk dem mouse gen 3sg. poss -half even not.exist: fact \\
`The shrew's mouth is even sharper than that of the mouse, and [its size] is not even half that of the mouse.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S192
exe
summary:
The genitive ɣɯ is used in several possessive constructions, including genitival noun complements and possessive existential predicates. Within noun phrases, it typically occurs between possessor and possessum, with a possessive prefix on the possessum; this prefix may be absent in rare cases, especially with some Chinese borrowings, and the genitive becomes obligatory when the possessum is elided.

The most common possessive construction is an existential verb with the possessum as subject and the possessor marked on the possessum by a possessive prefix, optionally with genitive ɣɯ. The genitive is also used with relator nouns and in derived causative possession verbs, but not every existential clause with a genitive phrase is necessarily possessive.

text:
genitive recipient beneficiary

The genitive can be used to mark the recipient by the indirective verb kʰogive, `pass over', as in ( ex:aZWG.nWkhAm ) and ( ex:GW.anWtWkhAm ).

exe

ɕɯ ʑo stu kɯ-mɤku pɯ-tɯ-mto-t nɯnɯ, laχtɕʰa pɯ-nnɯ-ŋu, tɯrme pɯ-nnɯ-ŋu nɯ, aʑɯɣ nɯ-kʰɤm tɕe tɕendɤre, aʑo ɲɯ-ta-lɤt jɤɣ \\
who emph most sbj: pcp -be.first aor -2-see- pst: tr dem thing pst. ipfv - auto -be person pst. ipfv - auto -be dem 1sg: gen imp -give[III] lnk lnk 1sg ipfv -1 2-release be.possible: fact \\
`Give me the first thing that you see [when you arrive home], be it a person or an object, and I will release you.' (140506 shizi he huichang de bailingniao-zh)
0003927#S48
exe

exe

jɤ-tsɯm tɕe iɕqʰa nɯ kɯβʁa nɯ ɣɯ a-nɯ-tɯ-kʰɤm \\
imp -take.away lnk the.aforementioned dem noble dem gen irr - pfv -2-give[III] \\
Take it and give it to the nobleman.' (150831 renshen wawa-zh) 0006418#S43
exe

The recipient of the verb kʰogive, `pass over' can alternatively also be marked by a possessive prefix on the inalienably possessed noun tɯ-jaʁhand, arm (with the meaning `hand over', § sec:semi.grammaticalized.relator ) or, with the dative relator nouns ɯ-ɕki or ɯ-pʰe (§ sec:dative ).

The genitive is selected by a few intransitive modal verbs to indicate the experiencer/beneficiary, in particular rabe needed,`need', ʁzibe necessary, as in ( ex:aZWG.WCArW ) and ( ex:aZWG.Rzi ).

exe

aʑɯɣ ɯ-ɕɤrɯ ra \\
1sg: gen 3sg. poss -bone be.needed: fact \\
`I want its bones.' (07-deluge) 0003426#S9
exe

exe

aʑɯɣ wuma ʑo ʁzi ɲɯ-ŋu, a-kɤ-ntɕʰoz sna ɲɯ-ŋu \\
1sg: gen really emph be.necessary: fact sens -be 1sg. poss - obj: pcp -use be.good: fact sens -be \\
`It will be useful for me, it will have good use of it.' (150902 hailibu-zh) 0006316#S44
exe

The experiencer/beneficiary can also be marked by possessive prefixes on the subject, without genitive, as in ( ex:arNWl.mAra ) (see also § sec:other.uses.poss.prefixes for additional examples).

exe

aʑo a-rŋɯl a-χsɤr ra mɤ-ra \\
1sg 1sg. poss -silver 1sg. poss -gold pl neg -be.needed: fact \\
`I don't need silver or gold.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

Other intransitive verbs selecting genitive arguments include ŋgrɯsucceed. In ( ex:nAZWG.apWNgrW ), in addition to the oblique 2sg argument nɤʑɯɣ, the verb takes the infinitival complement clause βdaʁmu kɤ-ndo as intransitive subject.

exe

[βdaʁmu kɤ-ndo] nɤʑɯɣ a-pɯ-ŋgrɯ qʰe, tɕendɤre tu-tɯ-ŋke maka mɤ-ra \\
queen inf -take 2sg: gen irr - pfv -succeed lnk lnk ipfv -2-walk at.all neg -need: fact \\
`If you succeed in becoming the queen, you will not need to walk anymore.' (140504 huiguniang-zh) 0003909#S188
exe

The genitive also occurs with beneficiaries/maleficiaries as adjuncts, not selected by the main verb, with transitive verbs such as nɤmado ( ex:tChi.tunAmea ) and wumgather ( ex:WZAG.pjAmaR ) or stative intransitive verbs such as pebe good as in ( ex:aZWG.mApe ) with the meaning `be favourable, advantageous to'. It is not the only possible way of expressing beneficiary; the relator noun ɯ-taʁ also has this function in collocation with the stative verb pebe good (§ sec:WtaR ), with the slightly different meaning `be nice to'.

exe

nɤʑɯɣ tɕʰi tu-nɤme-a ra, tɤ-ti \\
2sg: gen what ipfv -do[III]- 1sg be.needed: fact imp -say \\
`Tell me what I shall do for you.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S168
exe

exe

ɯ-fso tʰɯ-wxti tɕe aʑɯɣ mɤ-pe \\
3sg. poss -tomorrow aor -be.big lnk 1sg: gen neg -be.good: fact \\
`In the future, when he will have grown up, he will cause me trouble.' (`he will not be good to me', 2011-05-nyima)
exe

The beneficiary adjunct is not necessarily contiguous with the verb on which it depends, as in ( ex:iZora.GW.tChi.tufsej ) where the genitive phrase iʑora ɣɯ `for us, on our behalf' is separated from the verb tʰuask by a lengthy complement comprising two clauses.

exe

iʑora ɣɯ [tɕʰi tu-fse-j tɕe ji-tɯ-ci ɣɤʑu] tu-tɯ-tʰe ɯ-tɯ́-cʰa? \\
1pl gen what ipfv -be.like- 1pl lnk 1pl. poss - indef. poss -water exist: sens ipfv -2-ask[III] qu -2-can: fact \\
`Can you ask on our behalf how we should do to have water?' (2005 divination)
exe

Beneficiary genitive phrases can occur as predicates with a copula as ɯʑɤɣ 3sg: gen in ( ex:WZAG.pjAmaR ).

exe

tʰoʁtɤm ka-wum tɕe, ɯʑɤɣ pjɤ-maʁ kɯ, tɕoχtsi rɟɤlpu ɣɯ ku-wum, \\
taxes aor:3 -collect lnk 3sg: gen ifr. ipfv -not.be erg anthr king gen ipfv -collect \\
`The taxes that he had collected were not for himself, he was collecting them for the king of Cogtse.' (150901 NAjstsa)
0006248#S28
exe

In this use too, it is alternatively possible to indicate the beneficiary as a possessive prefix on the object, without genitive postposition, as in ( ex:atWci.tArke ).

exe

χsɤr kʰɯtsa ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu a-tɯ-ci ci tɤ-rke ma wuma ɲɯ-ɕpaʁ-a \\
gold bowl 3sg. poss -inside dem: loc 1sg. poss - indef. poss -water a.little imp -put.in[III] lnk really sens -be.thirsty- 1sg \\
`Please pour some water in the golden bowl for me, I am thirsty.' (140428 mu e guniang-zh)
0003880#S44
exe

The genitive is also attested with a noun-verb collocations (§ sec:light.verb ), like ɯ-kɤrnoʁ+mtɕɯrfeel dizzy, in which the possessor of the noun is an experiencer as in ( ex:fsapaR.GW.kWnA ). This example also illustrates the use of the genitive followed by a focus marker, as ( ex:GW.kWnA.WrkW.ri ) above.

exe

tɕeri fsapaʁ ɣɯ kɯnɤ ɯ-kɤrnoʁ ɲɯ-mtɕɯr ɲɯ-ŋu \\
lnk animal gen also 3sg. poss -head sens -turn sens -be \\
`But animals too can feel dizzy.' (29-tAmtshAzkAkWndo)
0004065#S66
exe

Finally, the experiencer subject argument demoted by the proprietive derivation can also in some cases be optionally encoded with the genitive case (see example ex:aZWG.mAsAscit, § sec:proprietive ).
summary:
The genitive marks recipients with the indirective verb kʰo ‘give/pass over’, and this recipient can also be expressed by other means such as a possessive prefix on an inalienably possessed noun or by dative relator nouns. It is also used by certain intransitive modal verbs to mark the experiencer/beneficiary, and can appear as an adjunct with transitive verbs and stative intransitives, including meanings like ‘for X’ or ‘be favorable to X’.

Beneficiary genitive phrases may be separated from the verb, and they can also occur as predicates with a copula. The genitive further appears with some noun-verb collocations to mark an experiencer, and in some cases with experiencer subjects demoted by proprietive derivation.

text:
The genitive ɣɯ occurs with various types of noun complements which are semantically neither possessive or beneficiaries/recipients.

Nouns used as prenominal modifiers are in rare cases followed by a genitive postposition before the head noun. If the head noun is an alienably possessed noun, the presence of a third singular possessive prefix ɯ- is optional, as shown by examples such as ( ex:χsAr.GW.khWtsa ) and ( ex:ftsoR.kWngWt.WphW ).

exe

χsɤr ɣɯ, nɤkinɯ, kʰɯtsa ci to-nɯ-ndo. \\
gold gen filler bowl indef ifr - auto -take \\
`He took a golden bowl' (140508 shier ge tiaowu de gongzhu-zh)
0003937#S152
exe

This type of construction is most common in texts translated from Chinese, but does also occur in more spontaneous material as in ( ex:ftsoR.kWngWt.WphW ), with a complex modifier ftsoʁ kɯngɯt ɯ-pʰɯ `the price of nine female hybrid yaks'.

exe

tɕendɤre ɯ-jaʁ nɯtɕu [ftsoʁ kɯngɯt ɯ-pʰɯ] ɣɯ srɯnloʁ pjɤ-k-ɤ-rku-ci \\
lnk 3sg. poss dem: loc female.hybrid.yak nine 3sg. poss -price gen ring ifr. ipfv - peg -pass-put.in- peg \\
`She had a ring worth nine female hybrid yak in her hand.' (2003gesar)
exe

In a construction with a prenominal modifier marker in the genitive, even when a possessive prefix is present on the head noun (in particular when it is an inalienably possessed noun), that prefix does not necessarily refer to the modifier. For instance, in ( ex:tWpAlAskAr.GW.nWmgozmArAB ), the third plural possessive prefix nɯ- on nɯ-mgozmɤrɤβ `their vegetables' refers to the people eating the vegetable, not the modifier tɯxpalɤskɤrthe whole year (on whose formation see § sec:dvandva.coll ) which would require a third singular prefix instead (an option which is also attested with this noun). Alternatively, it is also possible to have an indefinite possessor prefix on the head noun if inalienably possessed, as in ( ex:tWxpa.GW.tWGli ). Note that both options are attested in the construction with a prenominal modifier without the genitive, as seen in § sec:possessive.prefixes.prenominal.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ tɯxpalɤskɤr ɣɯ nɯ-mgozmɤrɤβ nɯ nɯ ma pjɤ-me. \\
lnk dem whole.year gen 3pl. poss -vegetable dem dem apart.from ifr. ipfv -not.exist \\
`It was the only vegetable that they had the whole year.' (140522 kAmYW tWji)
0004055#S22
exe

exe

tɯ-xpa ɣɯ tɯ-ɣli nɯ cʰɯ́-wɣ-tɕɤt tú-wɣ-rmbɯ \\
one-year gen indef. poss -manure dem ipfv: downstream - inv -take.out ipfv - inv -heap \\
`People take out (from the stable) the whole year's manure and heap it up.' (2010-tArAku)
exe

Some apparently unclassifiable uses of the genitive can be accounted for to some extent by assuming the elision of a head noun. For instance, in ( ex:iZora.GW ), the phrase iʑora ɣɯ, meaning `in our language', can be explained as coming from iʑora ɣɯ ji-skɤt `our language' used as a absolutive locative phrase (§ absolutive.locative ) `in our language', with elision of the head noun. This example does not illustrate a separate function of the genitive: it is simply a particular case of possessive.

exe

<longtoutan> nɯ kupa-skɤt ɕti. tɕe iʑora ɣɯ tɕʰi tu-kɯ-ti ŋu mɤ-xsi. \\
topo dem Chinese-language be. aff: fact lnk 1pl gen what ipfv - genr -say be: fact neg - genr:know \\
`Longtoutan is a Chinese word; I don't know how it is said in our [language].' (150820 qaprANar)
0003798#S2
exe

The same is true of the use of the genitive with the verb mŋɤmfeel pain and its causative ɕɯmŋɤmcause pain, which take a body part (not the person or animal feeling pain) as their subject and object, respectively. In ( ex:aZWG.taCWmNAm ), the genitive first person aʑɯɣ 1sg: gen is not an oblique argument or even a malefactive adjunct. Rather, its presence implies an elided noun a-βri `my body' (`he caused pain to my body'). It is however likely that sentences like this are the pivot constructions which made possible the reanalysis of possessive genitive phrases as benefactive/malefactive adjuncts.

exe

aʑɯɣ ta-ɕɯ-mŋɤm, aʑɯɣ a-laχtɕʰa ra ja-nɯ-tsɯm-nɯ \\
1sg: gen aor:3 - caus -be.painful 1sg: gen 1sg. poss -thing pl aor:3 - vert -take.away- pl \\
`He hurt me and took away my things.' (140426 luozi he qiangdao) 0003814#S31
exe

The genitive can also occur between prenominal relatives (§ sec:genitival.relatives ) and their head noun. In this construction the head noun generally does not take a possessive prefix. This type of relative is particularly common in story translated from Chinese, where it calques the prenominal relatives in 的 <de>, as in ( ex:makWra.GW.sAtCha ). The same situation has been observed in Khroskyabs.

exe

[kɯ-ɣɤndʐo ri kɯ-me], [kɯ-sɤ-mtsɯr ri kɯ-me], [kɤ-nɯsɯmɯzdɯɣ ri mɤ-kɯ-ra] ɣɯ sɤtɕʰa nɯtɕu jo-ɕe-ndʑi ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
sbj: pcp -be.cold also sbj: pcp -not.exist sbj: pcp - prop -be.hungry also sbj: pcp -not.exist inf -worry also neg - sbj: pcp -be.needed gen place dem: loc ifr -go- du sens -be \\
`The two of them went to a place where they was cold cold and hunger, and where one did not need to worry.' (140519 mai huochai de xiao nvhai-zh)
0004036#S171
exe

However, this type of relative is also attested, though rarer, in non-translated texts, for instance in ( ex:tWxpa.tukWlhoR.GW.sWjno ) with intransitive subject relativization.

exe

tɕe [tɯ-xpa tu-kɯ-ɬoʁ] ɣɯ sɯjno nɯ ŋu tɕe, \\
lnk one-year ipfv - sbj: pcp -come.out gen topo dem be: fact lnk \\
`It is an annual plant.' (18-NGolo)
0003530#S98
exe

Genitival prenominal relative clauses are to be distinguished from relatives as possessors, as in ( ex:tWCGA.kWmNAm.GW.WrJAnNgo ), where the possessum ɯ-rɟɤŋgoits radiating pain is not an argument of the relative tɯ-ɕɣa kɯ-mŋɤm `a tooth that hurts'.

exe
summary: The passage explains that the genitive ɣɯ appears in several prenominal constructions that are not straightforwardly possessive, including noun modifiers, relatives, and cases where an omitted head noun must be inferred. In these constructions, possessive prefixes on the head noun may or may not refer to the modifier, and some examples are especially common in texts translated from Chinese, though they also occur in spontaneous speech. It also notes that some uses historically or structurally resemble possessive genitives rather than separate benefactive or malefactive functions.

text:
tɯ-ɕɣa a-tɤ-mŋɤm tɕe tɕe tɤ-rca tɯ-ɣmba, tɯ-ku nɯra tu-mŋɤm ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, nɯnɯ ``[tɯ-ɕɣa kɯ-mŋɤm] ɣɯ ɯ-rɟɤŋgo ɣɤʑu" tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
genr. poss -tooth irr - pfv -be.painful lnk lnk indef. poss -following genr. poss -cheek genr. poss -head dem: pl ipfv -be.painful sens -be lnk dem indef. poss -tooth sbj: pcp -be.painful gen 3sg. poss -radiating.pain exist: sens ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`When one has a toothache, and that one feels pain in one's cheek or a headache, one says `the toothache has a radiating pain.'' (140516 WrJANgo)
0004012#S3

Adnominal complement clauses (§ sec:complement.taking.nouns ) can also take a genitive marker, as in ( ex:mWjnaXtChWG.GW.WtCha ).

exe

[<donggua> cʰo <qiezi> ni tɕʰi ʑo mɯ́j-naχtɕɯɣ] ɣɯ ɯ-tɕʰa a-jɤ-tɯ-ɣɯt ra \\
gourd comit eggplant du what emph neg: sens -be.the.same gen 3sg. poss -information irr - pfv -2-bring be.needed: fact \\
`[Go there and come back to] tell me in what way gourd and eggplant differ from each other.' (2010-02-yitian bi yitian-zh)
exe

Some relative clauses can take possessors marked in the genitive, as in ( ex:stu.WkAnWmga ) and ( ex:slama.ra.GW ). It is debatable whether the genitival phrase belongs to the relative in this type of construction.

exe

tɕe paʁ ɣɯ [stu ɯ-kɤ-nɯmga], iʑora ji-kɤ-nɯmga nɯ ɯ-ɕa ŋu tɕe \\
lnk pig gen most 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -want.from 1pl 1pl. poss - obj: pcp -want.from dem 3sg. poss -meat be: fact lnk \\
`What is most wanted from pigs, what we want from them is their meat.' (05-paR)
0003400#S13
exe

exe

slama ra ɣɯ [tʰɯtʰɤci kɯ-fse], nɯ kɤ-rɤ-βzjoz ra ɲɯ-stu mɯ́j-stu nɯ, nɯ-stu ɲɯ-nɤma-nɯ mɯ́j-nɤma-nɯ, nɯnɯra nɯ-pʰama ra nɯ-ɕki kɯ-rɤ-fɕɤt ɲɯ-ra. \\
student pl gen something sbj: pcp -be.like dem inf - antipass -learn pl sens -be.assiduous sens -be.assiduous dem 3pl. poss -truth sens -work- pl neg: sens -work- pl dem: pl 3pl. poss -parent pl 3pl. poss - dat genr:S/O- antipass -tell: fact sens -be.needed \\
`One has to tell the parents all kinds of things concerning the students, whether they try hard or not, whether they work seriously or not.' (150901 tshuBdWnskAt)
0006242#S17
exe

The genitive ɣɯ can optionally be used after the object in purposive complements (§ sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ) containing a transitive verb as in ( ex:GW.WkWrtoR ); in this type of clauses, the verb is in subject participial form and transitive verbs take a possessive prefix coreferent with the object (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ).

exe

rgɤtpu nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-kɯ-rtoʁ jo-ɣi. \\
old.man dem gen 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -see ifr -come \\
`He came to see the old man.' (150908 menglang-zh)
0006320#S12
exe
summary: The passage notes that genitive marking can appear on adnominal complement clauses and on some relative clauses, including cases where the genitival phrase may or may not be part of the relative clause itself. It also shows that in purposive complements with transitive verbs, the genitive ɣɯ may optionally follow the object, while the verb appears in subject participial form with a possessive prefix coreferential with that object.
