text: locative
summary: The passage identifies **locative** as a grammatical category or term related to location. It refers to forms or constructions that express where something is situated.

text:
There are three locative postpositions in Japhug, zɯ, tɕu and ri, the latter being homophonous with the correlative additive focus ri (§ sec:ri.additive ). The exact conditions of their uses is still an unsolved problem of Japhug grammar. They appear to be always optional (goals and locative adjuncts can always be in absolutive form, see § absolutive.goal and absolutive.locative ) and seem to be interchangeable, as is illustrated in this section.

All three postpositions can be used to express static location, motion into, motion or from a place. Location or motion (into/from/on) a surface, (into/from/in) a container or with/without contact does not seem to be relevant factors for the selection of the locative postpositions.

The locative tɕu is most often used in combination with a demonstrative nɯ as in ( ex:co.nWtCu ), a form identical to the locative of the demonstrative pronoun ( nɯtɕuthere, see § sec:locative.pronoun ). Without demonstrative, tɕu is also found as in ( ex:tsxu.tCu ) and ( ex:khAxtAndo.tCu ).

exe

japa tɕe alo <ercha> nɯtɕu, nɤkinɯ, iɕqʰa tsʰapa co nɯtɕu tɯɲɤt cʰɤ-ɣi. \\
last.year lnk upstream topo dem: loc filler filler topo valley dem: loc rock.slide ifr: downstream -come \\
`Last year, at Ercha, at the valley of Tshapa, there was a rock slide.' (160715 nWNa)
0006067#S1
exe

exe

jo-nɯ-ɕe tɕe, tʂu tɕu ɲɤ-mtsɯr, \\
ifr - auto -go lnk road loc ifr -be.hungry \\
`He went away, and on the road he felt hungry.' (2002 qajdoskAt)
0003366#S109
exe

exe

kʰɤxtɤndo tɕu ko-zo \\
side.of.the.top.terrace loc ifr -land \\
`[The raven] landed on the side of the top terrace.' (2002 qajdoskAt)
0003366#S124
exe

The above examples show tɕu used for location without motion ( ex:co.nWtCu ), motion via a place ( ex:tsxu.tCu ), motion onto a place resulting in contact with the surface ( ex:khAxtAndo.tCu ), and ( ex:WkWm.nWtCu ) illustrates tɕu expressing motion from the inside.

exe

nɯnɯ kɯβʁa ra ɣɯ nɯ-kʰa ɯ-kɯm nɯtɕu cʰɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ tɕe, \\
dem nobleman pl gen 3pl. poss -house 3sg. poss -door dem: loc ifr: downstream - auto -come.out lnk \\
`He went out from the door of the nobleman's house.' (140513 mutong de disheng-zh)
0003977#S153
exe

The same diversity of uses is found with the locative zɯ; ( ex:nAmkha.zW.pjAnWlhoRnW ) shows zɯ expressing static location (`in their hands') and motion from a place (`from the sky'). Example ( ex:Wjme.zW.kAzo ) illustrates zɯ used with the verb zoland, which is attested with tɕu in ( ex:khAxtAndo.tCu ). Note that in another version of the same story by the same speaker, the relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:relator.nouns.3d ) is found instead of a locative postposition (see ex:ambro in § ex:prefix.expression.of.possession ).

exe

tɯmɯkɤrŋi ɯ-me kɯɕnɯz nɯ nɯ-jaʁ zɯ, nɤkinɯ, <shanzi> kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕɤr ʑo, qale ɯ-sɤ-lɤt nɯ pjɤ-k-ɤsɯ-ndo-nɯ-ci tɕe, tɯmɯnɤmkʰa zɯ pjɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ-nɯ. \\
heaven 3sg. poss -daughter seven dem 3pl. poss -hand loc filler fan sbj: pcp - emph be.beautiful emph wind 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -release dem ifr. ipfv - peg - prog -hold- pl - peg lnk sky loc ifr: down - auto -come.out- pl \\
`The seven daughters of heaven, holding beautiful fans in their hands, came down from the sky.' (150828 niulang-zh)
0006318#S47
exe

exe

a-mbro ɯ-jme zɯ kɤ-zo, \\
1sg. poss -horse 3sg. poss -tail loc imp -land \\
`Land on my horse's tail.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

The postposition zɯ is related to the suffix -s in Situ, which expresses motion from an origin or towards a goal. Situ is certainly most archaic in this regard (as it also preserves a locative -j suffix of which only lexicalized traces remain in Japhug, § sec:locative.j ), and the Japhug form has to be explained as debonding from suffix to clitic to independent word (see ex:nWnWtCu.zW in § ex:word.vs.clitic.postp for evidence that zɯ is not a clitic). Japhug-internal evidence for the degrammaticalization is the otherwise unexplainable voicing to z, a process that applied to all fricative codas (§ sec:codas.inventory ), and the fact that some frozen forms preserve a -z suffix, in particular the approximate locative cʰiz (§ sec:approximate.locative ), the related indefinite pronoun ciscʰizsomewhere (§ sec:cischiz ) and the relator ɯ-ŋgɯzinside, among (see ex:kAndZWRi.nWNgWz and ex:arNi.WNgWz in § sec:other.locative.relator ) and the postposition ʁazwhile... still (§ sec:denominal.postposition.s ).

The locative ri also occurs in all the meanings attested above for tɕu and zɯ, though due to homophony with the additive correlative ri (§ sec:ri.additive ), some examples are ambiguous. Examples ( ex:khAXtu.ri.pWrAZia ) and ( ex:kha.ri.kari ) show the locative ri marking static location and motion towards a place, respectively.

exe

kʰɤxtu ri pɯ-rɤʑi-a tɕe tɤ-mtʰɯm tu-ndze-a pɯ-ŋu ri, \\
terrace loc pst. ipfv -stay- 1sg lnk indef. poss -meat ipfv -eat[III]- 1sg pst. ipfv -be lnk \\
`I was on the terrace eating meat.' (150909 qandZGi) 0006358#S4
exe

exe

tɕe nɯ nɯ-kʰa ri ɯʑo kɤ-ari ɯ-qʰu tɕe, \\
lnk dem 3pl. poss -house loc 3sg aor: east -go[II] 3sg. poss -after lnk \\
`After he went to [his wife's family's] house...' (14-siblings) 0003508#S165
exe

The same interchangeability and optionality of the locative postpositions is observed when these are combined with relator nouns (§ sec:relator.postposition.location ). Although the three postpositions are almost identical in their range of uses, there are nevertheless differences in their compatibilities. With the locative demonstrative pronouns kɯrehere, and nɯrethere (§ sec:locative.pronoun ) as well as aʁɤndɯndɤteverywhere, only ri can be added, as in ( ex:nWre.ri.li.akumpGa ). The postpositions tɕu and zɯ can be combined as nɯtɕu zɯ as in ( ex:tCAkW.nWtCu.zW ); no other combination of locative postpositions are possible.

exe

tɕendɤre tsʰuβdɯn kɯ-sɤ-sɯxɕɤt lɤ-ari-a. tɕe nɯre ri li a-kumpɣa pɯ-tu tɕe \\
lnk topo nmlz - antipass -teach aor: upstream -go[II]- 1sg lnk dem: loc loc again 1sg. poss -hen pst. ipfv -exist lnk \\
`I went to Tshobdun to teach. There, I had a hen again.' (150819 kumpGa) 0006388#S69
exe

exe

ɯʑo tɕekɯ nɯtɕu zɯ pjɤ-rɤʑi qʰe \\
3sg east dem: loc loc ifr. ipfv -stay lnk \\
`(When) he was on the east side,...' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S145
exe
summary: Japhug has three locative postpositions, zɯ, tɕu, and ri, whose exact distribution is not yet understood; they are generally optional and often interchangeable, and can mark static location as well as motion into, onto, from, or via a place. The passage notes some tendencies and restrictions: tɕu commonly occurs with the demonstrative nɯ, zɯ may have historical connections to an older suffix, and ri is homophonous with an additive focus particle, which makes some examples ambiguous. Although the three postpositions are largely similar, certain combinations are restricted, such as only ri occurring with some locative demonstratives, while tɕu and zɯ can occur together.

text:
All three postpositions are also used with time adjuncts, but do present some noticeable differences in usage. They can be interchangeably used with temporal relator nouns such as ɯ-raŋduring, the time when (§ sec:relator.temporal ), but in other contexts

With counted nouns expressing time (§ sec:CN.time ), there is not a single example with zɯ in the corpus. The postposition ri is used to express a point in time (as in ex:tWxsoz.ri ), while tɕu mostly means `within (the time period)' as in ( ex:tWxpa.nWtCu ).

exe

tɯ-xsoz ri tɕe jo-ɣi ri, ɯ-βri tɤʑri ɣɤʑu, ɲɯ-ɤci. \\
one-morning loc lnk ifr -come lnk 3sg. poss -body dew exist: sens sens -be.wet \\
`One morning, [our hen] came [back from the forest, where it was laying eggs] and its body was wet from the dew.' (150819 kumpGa) 0006388#S19
exe

exe

tɯ-xpa nɯtɕu [...] tɯ-tɯpʰu, ɣʑo nɯra kɯ, ɣʑɤzga nɯnɯ, nɯnɯ sqɯ-tɯrpa ɯ-ro nɯ ku-sɯ-ɤjtɯ-nɯ ɲɯ-cʰa-nɯ. \\
one-year dem: loc one-hive bee dem: pl erg honey dem dem ten-pound 3sg. poss -excess dem ipfv - caus -accumulate- pl sens -can- pl \\
`In one year, one hive, the bees, the honey, they can gather more than ten pounds of it.' (26-GZo) 0003668#S33
exe

The form tɕe, which is mainly analyzable as a linker (§ sec:coordination ) and in some cases a topic marker (§ sec:tCe.topic ) occurs with locative and temporal adjuncts and could be analyzed as a postposition in these usages (see also § sec:locative.j ). With the temporal counted nouns, like ri it expresses a specific point in time as in ( ex:tWsNi.tCe ) rather than a duration.

exe

tɕe tɯ-sŋi tɕe ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci tɕe, \\
lnk one-day lnk ifr - peg -meet- peg lnk \\
`One day, [the bear finally] met [the rabbit].' (2011-13-qala)
exe
summary: All three postpositions can be used with time adjuncts, and they are interchangeable with temporal relator nouns like ɯ-raŋ “during, the time when,” but they differ in other contexts. With counted time nouns, zɯ is not attested in the corpus, ri marks a point in time, tɕu means “within the time period,” and tɕe can also occur in temporal adjuncts to express a specific point in time rather than a duration.

text:
locative!approximate
The suffix -cʰu is used to indicate approximate location, referring to a broad area rather than a specific place, like the plural ra (§ sec:plural.determiners ). In ( ex:kupa.chu ) it means `area/region', while in ( ex:Wqhu.chu ) it can be translated as `side' and is opposed to ɯ-stustraight ahead.

exe

tɕe kupa-cʰu nɯra, atʰi pɕoʁ nɯra, ɯ-pɕi nɯra kɯ kɯre ri ɣɯ-cʰɯ-sɯ-χtɯ-nɯ ŋu. \\
lnk Chinese- approx. loc dem: pl downstream side dem: pl 3sg. poss -outside dem: loc erg dem. prox: loc loc cisl - ipfv: downstream - caus -but- pl be: fact \\
`People from the Chinese areas downstream, outsiders, send [people] here to buy [these mushrooms]. (20-grWBgrWB) 0003554#S57
exe

It also occurs with various relator nouns, in particular ɯ-qʰuafter, behind and ɯ-ŋgɯinside as in ( ex:Wqhu.chu ) and ( ex:WNgW.chu ), respectively. The form ɯ-qʰu-cʰu exclusively has a locative meaning, unlike ɯ-qʰu which can be used with the temporal meaning `after' Note that ɯ-ŋgɯ undergoes vowel assimilation to [ ɯŋgucʰu ], showing that it must be analyzed as a suffix rather than as a postposition. Most relator nouns cannot be used with cʰu, for instance one cannot say $ $ ɯ-ʁɤri-cʰu.

exe

ɯ-jwaʁ ɯ-ʁɤri ɯ-stu nɯ ɲɯ-ɤrŋi, ɯ-jwaʁ ɯ-qʰu-cʰu nɯ ɲɯ-pɣi, \\
3sg. poss -leaf 3sg. poss -front 3sg. poss -direction dem sens -be.green 3sg. poss -leaf 3sg. poss -behind- approx. loc dem sens -be.grey \\
`The upper side of its leaves is green, and the lower side is grey.' (13-NanWkWmtsWG) 0003492#S7
exe

exe

tɕe ɯ-xtɤpa cʰo ɯ-mi, ɯ-jaʁ, ɯ-ŋgɯ-cʰu nɯra ɲɯ-wɣrum. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -lower.belly comit 3sg. poss -foot 3sg. poss -hand 3sg. poss - inside - approx. loc dem: pl sens -be.white \\
`The lower part of its body, its feet, its paws, the inside part are white.' (20-xsar)
0003568#S23
exe

The approximate locative -cʰu is commonly used in particular with the loupstream / tʰidownstream and kɯeast / ndiwest locative adverbs (§ sec:locative.adv ), as in ( ex:lo.chu ). For the use of mɤɕtʂauntil to express restrictive focalization in ( ex:lo.chu ), see § sec:terminative.

exe

pa jɯl pɕoʁ nɤki, tɯ-ji ɯ-rkɯ nɯra maka me. rɯŋgu kɯnɤ lo-cʰu koŋla ʑo kɯ-ɣɤndʐo mɤɕtʂa tʰi nɯra me \\
down village side filler indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -side dem: pl at.all not.exist: fact pasture also upstream- approx. loc completely emph sbj: pcp -be.cold until downstream dem: pl not.exist: fact \\
`It is not found down in the villages, near the fields. Even on the pastures, it only exists at high altitudes where it is very cold, not lower.' (15-babW)
0003512#S107
exe

The suffix -cʰu is itself related to the indefinite locative postpositions cʰiz and scʰiz `at/in/towards a X, somewhere where X' as in ( ex:schiz.kazGWtnW ), which come from the combination of -cʰu with the locative suffix -z (degrammaticalized as the locative postposition zɯ, see § sec:core.locative ). For the notation -iz (instead of the more etymological -ɯz ) here, see § sec:W.i.contrast. In the case of the variant scʰiz, the root of -cʰu was both prefixed and suffixed by the locative -z.

exe

tɕe tɕekɯ kɯ ʑo scʰiz sɤstoŋ ʑo scʰiz kɤ-azɣɯt-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu, nɤki, si ri kɯ-me, rdɤstaʁ ri kɯ-me scʰiz ʑo kɤ-azɣɯt-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk east emph emph indef. loc desert emph indef. loc aor: east -reach- pl sens -be filler tree also sbj: pcp -not.exist stone also sbj: pcp -not.exist indef. loc emph aor: east -reach- pl \\
`Further east, they arrived at a desert, somewhere where there were neither trees nor stones.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

The postpositions cʰiz and scʰiz have reduced forms cʰɯ and scʰɯ with loss of final -z (see ex:nWrJara.chW below), probably originally sandhi variants.

exe

nɯ-rɟara cʰɯ pjɤ-k-ɤmdzɯ-ci tɕe, \\
3pl. poss -yard indef. loc pst. ipfv - peg -sit- peg lnk \\
`She was sitting in their yard.'(150907 yingning-zh) 0006264#S57
exe

There is also a rarer disyllabic variant of the approximate locative cʰizɯ as in ( ex:chizW ), with the fully syllabic form zɯ of the locative postposition.

exe

tɯ-βzɯr cʰizɯ, nɤki, kɯ-spoʁ ci pjɤ-tu tɕe, \\
indef. poss -corner indef. loc filler sbj: pcp -have.a.hole indef ifr. ipfv -exist lnk \\
`In one of the corners, there was a hole.' (140510 sanpian sheye-zh) 0003945#S62
exe

Some nouns use a suffix -cʰɯ (homophonous with the reduced form of cʰiz in ex:nWrJara.chW ) to indicate direction, and are not compatible with cʰiz and other forms: mɤpɕoʁ-cʰɯtowards the opposite side and tɯ-mɯ-cʰɯtowards the sky, the latter mainly used with the verb rulook at to mean `lying on one's back face up (towards the sky)' as in ( ex:tWmWchW ).

exe

tɕe tɯ-mɯ-cʰɯ nɯ ɯ-kɯ-ru nɯ ɯ-ɣmɤr ɯ-ŋgɯ ʑo ɕ-pjɤ-lɤt, \\
lnk indef. poss -sky-towards dem 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -look.at dem 3sg. poss -mouth 3sg. poss -inside emph tral - ifr -release \\
`It dropped [the medicine] inside the mouth of [Gesar], who was [lying on his back] face up towards the sky.' (Gesar)
exe

tɕe: linker or postposition
The word tɕe is one of the most common words in Japhug, and it has several different morphosyntactic functions, including that of linker (§ sec:coordination ) and topic marker (§ sec:tCe.topic ). In addition, it is also used as a postposition, expressing both motion and location; it especially commonly occurs with an ablative meaning, as in ( ex:kutɕu.zgo.tCe ) and ( ex:pa.tCe.taR ). Its etymology is discussed in the following section (§ sec:locative.j ).

exe

kutɕu zgo tɕe tɕekɯ zgo ku-nɯ-tsɯm ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl ma \\
dem. prox: loc mountain loc east mountain ipfv: east - auto -take.away sens -be.usually.the.case lnk \\
`[The crossoptilon] would take [the weasel] from the mountain here to the mountain over there (on the other side of the river).' (23-qapGAmtWmtW) 0003608#S82
exe

exe

tɯ-ci nɯra pa tɕe taʁ ʁɟa ʑo ɣɯ-tsɯm pjɤ-ra. \\
indef. poss -water dem: pl down loc up completely emph inv -take.away: fact ifr. ipfv -be.needed \\
`One had to bring water from the lower part [of the valley] upwards.' (140522 RdWrJAt)
0004061#S7
exe
summary:
The suffix **-cʰu** marks an approximate locative, referring to a broad area or region rather than a precise place, and it can also combine with certain relator nouns such as **ɯ-qʰu** “behind/after” and **ɯ-ŋgɯ** “inside.” In these combinations it has a locative meaning only, and the assimilation of **ɯ-ŋgɯ** shows that **-cʰu** functions as a suffix; most relator nouns cannot take it.  

The passage also notes related indefinite locative postpositions **cʰiz** and **scʰiz** and their reduced forms, as well as a rarer variant **cʰizɯ**. Finally, it describes **tɕe** as a very common word that can function as a linker, topic marker, and postposition with motion or location meanings, especially ablative ones.

text:
The postposition tɕe is also found with temporal adjuncts, as in ( ex:qartsW.tCe.YWjpum ).

exe

qartsɯ tɕe ɲɯ-jpum ftɕar tɕe tu-mbro ŋu. \\
winter loc ipfv -be.thick summer loc ipfv -be.high be: fact \\
`It grows thicker in winter, and taller in summer. (07-tAtho) 0003432#S19
exe

It appears in the expression ɯ-sɯm tɕe `in his opinion, in his mind' as in ( ex:asWm.tCe ) and ( ex:WsWm.tCe ); the core locative postpositions are not used in this meaning.

exe

aʑo a-sɯm tɕe, nɯ-ʁrɯ ʑo ɣɤʑu ɕti tɕe \\
1sg 1sg. poss -mind loc 3pl. poss -horn emph exist: sens be. aff: fact lnk \\
`In my opinion, [since] they have horns, (they should be able to fight the predators off).' (20-RmbroN)
0003560#S59
exe

exe

tɕe ɯʑo ɯ-sɯm tɕe tɕe tu-tsɯm tɕe tɕendɤre iʑora ji-sɤtɕʰa ra lonba ʑo tɯ-ci ɲɯ-sɯ-ɤβze to-ʁmɯɣ. \\
lnk 3sg 3sg. poss -mind loc lnk ipfv: up -take lnk lnk 1pl 1pl. poss -place pl all emph indef. poss -water ipfv - caus -become[III] ifr -have.the.intention \\
`In his mind, [the snake] wanted to take the water upwards and transform our whole area into water.' (150820 qaprANar)
0006246#S19
exe

Distinguishing between the uses of tɕe as a postposition and as a topic marker (§ sec:tCe.topic ) is not always trivial; it is analyzed as a topic marker when it can be replaced by nɯ § sec:nW.topic, or when two tɕe appear in a row as in ( ex:WsWm.tCe ): in this case, the first one is a postposition and the second one a topic marker.

Traces of the locative suffix *-j
Situ has a locative suffix -j, also used in the possessive construction, which has disappeared in Japhug, though a few traces remain.

The form tɕe, which is mainly used as a linker (§ sec:coordination ) and also occurs as postposition (§ sec:tCe.postposition ) and as a topic marker (§ sec:tCe.topic ), probably originates from the combination of the locative postposition tɕu and the locative suffix *-j, with vowel merger at a stage preceding the sound change *o $ $ u ( *tɕo-j $ $ tɕe; see § sec:historical.phono for a discussion of these sound changes).

Another trace of the locative suffix *-j is found in the linker qʰethen and the time ordinal qʰujthis afternoon (§ sec:time.ordinals ), combining the relator noun ɯ-qʰuafter, behind (§ sec:relator.temporal ) with the coda *-j, in the former with vowel fusion (an earlier lexicalization), and the latter without fusion. The form qʰujthis afternoon shows that the suffix *-j was still productive in Japhug after the sound change *o $ $ u took place.

The interrogative pronoun ŋojwhere, variant of ŋotɕuwhere (§ sec:NotCu ), also has a trace of the *-j suffix without vowel fusion.

Finally, the suffix -re in the locative pronouns kɯrehere, nɯrethere and related forms is most probably the plural marker ra (§ sec:plural.determiners ) to which the locative *-j has been added, with the same vowel fusion as in the forms above (§ sec:locative.pronoun ).
summary:
The postposition tɕe is also used with temporal adjuncts and in the expression ɯ-sɯm tɕe ‘in his opinion, in his mind’; in this latter meaning, the ordinary locative postpositions are not used. Because tɕe can function both as a postposition and as a topic marker, its role must be determined by context, especially when it can be replaced by nɯ or when two tɕe forms occur in sequence.  

The passage also argues that tɕe probably comes from a combination of the locative postposition tɕu and the locative suffix *-j, and it presents several other forms as traces of this old suffix, including qʰethen, qʰuj ‘this afternoon,’ ŋoj ‘where,’ and locative pronouns such as kɯre and nɯre.

text:
comitative
Postpositional phrases with the comitative postposition cʰoand, with and its variants cʰondɤre and cʰonɤ (comprising the additive nɤ and the linker ndɤre ) are selected by verbs with non-singular subjects (§ sec:intrinsically.n.sg.subject ), including naχtɕɯɣbe the same (§ sec:identity.modifier ), amɯmibe on good terms ( ex:cho.kWnaXtCWG ), rɤkrɤzhave a discussion and reciprocal verbs (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ).

exe

[ɯʑo cʰo] kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ [sɯjno, xɕaj ma mɤ-kɯ-ndza nɯra cʰonɤ] amɯmi-nɯ tɕe, \\
3sg comit sbj: pcp -be.the.same vegetables grass apart.from neg - sbj: pcp -eat dem: pl comit be.on.good.terms: fact - pl lnk \\
`[The rabbit] is on good terms with [the animals] which eat only grass and vegetables like him.' (04-qala2)
0003392#S31
exe

exe

[kʰu cʰondɤre] mbro ni to-rɤkrɤz-ndʑi. \\
tiger comit horse du ifr -discuss- du \\
`The tiger and the horse had a discussion.' (20-tArka)
0003566#S31
exe

Postpositional phrases in cʰo can be considered to be oblique arguments, since they are relativized using the oblique participle (§ sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives, § sec:comitative.relativization ). However, verbs that select cʰo phrases index not only the intransitive subject proper, but the sum of the subject and the cʰo phrase, which can be in the dual as in ( ex:cho.YWnaXtCWGndZi ) (the white birch and the red birch) or in the plural ( ex:cho.kWnaXtCWG ) (the rabbit and the other animals).

exe

tɕe ɯ-rqʰu nɯ ɣɯrni laʁma ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯ [sɤjku cʰo] ɲɯ-naχtɕɯɣ-ndʑi ri\\
lnk 3sg. poss -bark dem be.red: fact apart.from.the.fact 3sg. poss -inside dem birch comit sens -be.the.same- du lnk \\
`Apart from the fact that its bark is red, it is identical in the inside with the birch.' (06-mbrAj)
0003414#S11
exe

The verb naχtɕɯɣbe the same with a cʰo phrase can be used in an equative construction (§ sec:nmlz.equative ).

Apart from the function presented above, cʰoand, with is commonly used to link together two nouns inside a single noun phrase, as in ( ex:awW.cho.aRi ). In this case too, the main verb of the clause indexes the whole noun phrase, comprising the sum of referents designated by the nouns linked by cʰo.

exe

a-wɯ cʰo a-ʁi ni cʰɯ-ɣi-ndʑi ra ma ʑɤni-sti kɤ-rɤʑi mɤ-cʰa-ndʑi tɕe, \\
1sg. poss -grand.father comit 1sg. poss -younger.sibling du ipfv: downstream -come- du be.needed: fact lnk 3du -alone inf -stay neg -can: fact - du lnk \\
`My grandfather and my younger brother have to come, they cannot stay by themselves.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

The marker cʰo can also link verb phrases and even entire clauses (see § sec:neutral.addition and ).

Given the apparently equal status of the two linked nouns in ( ex:awW.cho.aRi ), in particular with regard to indexation, it is legitimate to wonder whether analyzing it as a postposition makes more sense than considering it to be a coordinator; this question is explored in § sec:coordinator.cho ).

A cʰo phrase can be followed by the associative plural marker ra (§ sec:number.determiners ) as in ( ex:cho.ra.kW ) to mean `et cetera', and the whole phrase can take case marking such as ergative.

exe

tɕeri ɯʑo ndɤre, qajdo cʰo ra kɯ ndɤ tú-wɣ-ndza ɕti \\
but 3sg advers crow comit pl erg advers ipfv - inv -eat be. aff: fact \\
`But it is eaten by crows and other [animals].' (26-NalitCaRmbWm)
0003676#S134
exe

optional case marking
The ergative kɯ is however optional on comitative phrases, as shown by ( ex:WpW.ra.cho ), where ergative marking would be expected on the phrase ɯ-pɯ ra cʰo.

exe

[ɯ-pɯ ra cʰo] tɯtɯrca to-ndza-nɯ tɕe to-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-fka-nɯ ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -young pl comit together ifr -eat- pl lnk ifr - auto - refl - caus -be.full- pl emph sens -be \\
`[The eagle] ate them together with its fledglings and they ate to their full.' (huli yu shanying-zh)
exe

A postpositional comitative phrase can also serve as a dual or plural possessor, as if from a complex noun phrase `$X$ cʰo $Y$' with elided Y element, as in ( ex:cho.ndZime ). Note that ( ex:cho.ndZime ) does not mean `There is his wife and their daughter' (dual indexation would be expected on the verb). See § sec:coordinator.cho for additional discussion.

exe

tɕe ɯ-rʑaβ cʰo ndʑi-me ci tu tɕe, \\
lnk 3sg. poss -wife comit 3du. poss -daughter one exist: fact lnk \\
`He and his wife have a daughter.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S281
exe

The comitative is also used in the simultaneous action construction (§ sec:simultaneous.action.nominal, § sec:simult.action.nominal.Bzu )
summary: Comitative phrases with cʰo, cʰondɤre, and cʰonɤ are selected by verbs with non-singular subjects, and the verb indexes the combined set of participants rather than just the intransitive subject. These phrases can function as oblique arguments, be used in equative constructions, link nouns within a noun phrase, and even link verb phrases or whole clauses; they may also take plural markers or case marking, with ergative on the comitative phrase being optional in some contexts.

text:
additive
The additive adposition nɤ, possibly from Tibetan ན་nalocative, appears after the protasis of some conditional clauses (§ sec:real.conditional ), but it also occurs in direct adjacency between two nouns (generally identical ones), most commonly to express repeated action as in ( ex:tArpi.nA.tArpi ) and ( ex:cha.nA.cha ).

exe

tɤ-rpi nɤ tɤ-rpi ʑo ɲɯ-sɯ-βzu-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
indef. poss -sutra add indef. poss -sutra emph ipfv - caus -make- pl sens -be lnk \\
`They ask [lamas] to chant sutras after sutras.' (2003kandZislama)
0006147#S81
exe

exe

tɕe ɯ-χti nɯ kɯ cʰa ntsɯ ku-tsʰi pɯ-ŋu tɕe cʰa nɤ cʰa ku-tsʰi pjɯ-ɕti tɕe \\
lnk 3sg. poss -companion dem erg alcohol always ipfv -drink pst. ipfv -be lnk alcohol add alcohol ipfv -drink ipfv -be. aff lnk \\
`Her husband used to drink all the time, drank alcohol again and again.' (17-lhazgron)
exe

It can also be interpreted as gradual increase ( ex:taR.nA.taR ) and/or the meaning `all the way' with locative nouns as in ( ex:tsxu.nA.tsxu ).

exe

tɯ-ci nɯ taʁ nɤ taʁ, taʁ nɤ taʁ tu-ɣi pjɤ-ɕti \\
indef. poss -water dem up add up up add up ipfv: up -come ifr. ipfv -be. aff \\
`The water was raising up and up.' (31-deluge)
0004077#S19
exe

exe

tʂu nɤ tʂu pjɤ-ɕe qʰe, \\
path add path ifr: down -go lnk \\
`He went all the way down.' (140511 alading-zh) 0003953#S102
exe

The additive can also occur between finite verbs with a similar range of meanings (§ sec:distributed.action ), with numerals and counted nouns (§ sec:CN.repetition ) to express distributivity, and with ideophones to describe a rhythmically occurring action (§ sec:ideo.III ).
summary: The additive adposition nɤ can appear after the protasis of some conditional clauses, but it also occurs directly between identical nouns to express repeated action, gradual increase, or the sense of “all the way,” especially with locative nouns. It can additionally occur between finite verbs with similar meanings, with numerals and counted nouns to express distributivity, and with ideophones to describe rhythmically repeated actions.

text:
standard
Japhug has several postpositions that are mainly used to mark the standard in the comparative construction. The most common one is sɤzcompared with, but the variants staʁ, sɤznɤ, staʁnɤ, sɯstaʁ ( ex:WCGa.anWxtCi in § sec:preverb.adjectives.size ) χtanɤ ( ex:nWBde.wo, § sec:fsp.imp ) and sɯχta are also attested (see § sec:denominal.adverb.s.prefix concerning their etymology). Their relative frequency appears to be speaker-dependent, and no meaningful difference could be detected between them.

In the comparative construction (§ sec:sAz.kW ), the comparee is the intransitive subject of the main verb (the parameter, generally an adjectival stative verb) and is indexed on the verb. The comparee is either in the absolutive or in the ergative (§ sec:comparee.kW ). The standard is necessarily marked by one of the postpositions listed above, and cannot be indexed on the main verb. Neither the standard not the comparee are required to be overt. An adjectival stative verb with a standard postpositional phrase as in ( ex:sAznA.YWwxti ) is a well-formed comparative construction. Examples like ( ex:aZo.YWwxti ) with overt comparee and standard are rarer.

exe

qandʑɣi sɤznɤ ɲɯ-wxti, qaliaʁ sɤznɤ ɲɯ-xtɕi \\
falcon comp sens -be.big eagle comp sens -be.small \\
`It is bigger than a falcon, and smaller than an eagle.' (2011-08-kuwu)
exe

exe

ɯʑo nɯ aʑo sɤz tɯ-xpa wxti \\
3sg dem 1sg comp one-year be.big: fact \\
`She is one year older than me.' (12-BzaNsa) 0003484#S85
exe

The standard marker sɤz (and its variants) also occurs in a construction expressing progressive increase throughout the time, where a time counted noun like tɯ-sŋione day or tɯ-xpaone year is followed by the standard marker and then repeated, as tɯ-xpa sɤz tɯ-xpa `more year after year' in ( ex:tWxpa.sAz.tWxpa ). This construction, although attested in non-translated texts, is more common in texts from Chinese, where it calques the construction 一年比一年 yīnián bǐ yīniánmore year after year. The more idiomatic Japhug construction to express the same meaning is through partial reduplication of the first syllable of the main verb (§ sec:redp.gradual.increase ).

exe

nɯ-jwaʁ nɯ, [...] tɯ-xpa sɤz tɯ-xpa lu-dɤn ŋu ma \\
3pl. poss -leaf dem one-year comp one-year ipfv -be.many be: fact lnk \\
`There are more needles (`leaves') each year.' (08-saCW) 0003462#S17
exe

The standard markers can also be used with subordinate clauses (§ sec:incremental.addition ). The standard marker with the distal demonstrative nɯ sɤznɤ has the meaning `rather than that, could... as well' as in ( ex:nW.sAznA.arca ).

exe

nɤ-mu kɤ-fsraŋ mɤ-tɯ-cʰa tɕe, nɯ sɤznɤ, a-rca jɤ-ɣi tɕe, a-rca, nɤki, laχɕi pɯ-βzjoz \\
2sg. poss -mother inf -protect neg -2-can: fact lnk dem comp 1sg. poss -following imp -come lnk 1sg. poss -following filler trade imp -learn \\
`You cannot save your mother, rather than that, come with me to learn some abilities.' (150826 baoliandeng-zh)
0006370#S140
exe

This phrase can also be used as a scalar marker `even' with scope over the following clause, as in ( ex:nW.sAznA.chaa ), and occurs in incremental additive constructions `not only $X$, but also $Y$' (§ sec:incremental.addition ).

exe

ki kɤ-rtsi kɯ-tu me nɤ, aʑo nɯ sɤznɤ, nɤkinɯ, kʰa kɯ-qanɯ nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ zɯ, nɤkinɯ, tɯ-ɕpɤβ kɯβde-rzɯɣ tɤ-kɤ-lɤt nɯnɯ ku-sɤlɤɣi-a cʰa-a ɕti nɤ! \\
dem. prox inf -count sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact sfp 1sg dem comp filler house sbj: pcp - emph be.dark 3sg. poss -inside loc filler indef. poss -corpse four-section aor - obj: pcp -release dem ipfv -combine- 1sg can: fact - 1sg be. aff: fact sfp \\
`[What you ask] is nothing, I am even able to put together a corpse that had been cut into four pieces in a dark house.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S151
exe

The phrase nɯ sɤznɤ is also used as a marker of adversative topic as in ( ex:nW.sAznA.YWwxti ), where it can be replaced by the marker ʁo (§ sec:adversative.topic ).

exe

kɯki sɤlaŋpʰɤn ki nɯ sɤznɤ ɲɯ-wxti wo tɕe kʰa ju-nɯ-tsɯm-a tɕe, \\
dem. prox basin dem. prox dem comp sens -be.big sfp lnk house ipfv - vert -take- 1sg lnk \\
`This basin is really big, I will take it home.' (150831 jubaopen)
0006294#S20
exe
summary:
Japhug uses several postpositions to mark the standard in comparative constructions, with sɤz being the most common, though several speaker-dependent variants are also attested and do not differ in meaning. In these constructions, the comparee is indexed on the main verb and may be in the absolutive or ergative, while the standard must be expressed by a postposition and cannot be indexed; either element may be omitted.  

The standard marker sɤz and its variants also appear in other constructions, including progressive increase over time, subordinate clauses, scalar meaning ‘even,’ incremental additive constructions, and adversative topic marking, with some uses likely influenced by Chinese.

text:
exceptive
The exceptive postposition maapart from and its reduplicated variant mɯma are not selected by any verb, and only used in adjunct postpositional phrases as in ( ex:kWm.ci.mWma ).

exe

kɯm ci mɯma nɯnɯ tɕe znde ʁɟa ʑo ɕti \\
door one apart.from dem lnk wall completely emph be. aff: fact \\
`Apart from one door, there are walls everywhere.' (2011-11-kha)
exe

The exceptive maapart from is used in particular in restrictive focus constructions (§ sec:restrictive.focus ).

When the scope of the restrictive construction is on an entire clause rather than a single noun phrase, the clause is followed by the linker ma (homophonous with the exceptive) and an exceptive phrase limited to the demonstrative pronoun nɯ (here in resumptive use, coreferent with the entire preceding clause) and the postposition ma, as in ( ex:ra.ma.nW.ma ). The first ma in this construction is not to be analyzed as the postposition: while it is possible to reduplicated the second one as in ma nɯ mɯma (example ex:mAspea.ma.nW.ma ), reduplication of the first ma is not attested.

exe

[aʑɯɣ ɯ-ɕa ra] ma nɯ ma kɯ-ra me \\
1sg. gen 3sg. poss -meat be.needed: fact lnk dem apart.from sbj: pcp -be.needed not.exist: fact \\
`I want its meat, and nothing else.' (02-deluge2012)
0003376#S13
exe

exe

tɤ-pɤtso kɯ-ɣɤwu ʑo kɤ-nɯɕpɯz mɤ-spe-a ma nɯ mɯma spe-a \\
indef. poss -child sbj: pcp -cry emph inf -imitate neg -be.able[III]: fact - 1sg lnk dem apart.from be.able[III]: fact - 1sg \\
`I cannot imitate a child crying, but apart from that I can imitate [anything].' (27-kikakCi)
0003700#S134
exe

The postposition maapart from is also found in a periphrastic modal construction (§ sec:cimame.cinAmaRkW ).
summary: The exceptive postposition **ma** ‘apart from’ and its reduplicated form **mɯma** are not governed by any verb and occur only in adjunct postpositional phrases. They are especially used in restrictive focus constructions; when the focus scope extends over a whole clause, the clause is followed by the linker **ma** and an exceptive phrase with **nɯ** plus **ma/mɯma**, and the initial **ma** in this pattern is analyzed as a linker rather than the postposition. The text also notes that **ma** appears in a periphrastic modal construction.

text:
terminative
The postposition mɤɕtʂauntil is used after noun phrases to indicate temporal ( ex:RnWpArme.mACtsxa ) or locative ( ex:akW.mACtsxa ) limit. It can be used in opposition with the egressive postpositions (see ex:tWmAmke.mACtsxa in § sec:egressive ) or with kóʁmɯzonly after (example ex:sqamNuxpa.koRmWz in § sec:temporal.postpositions ).

exe

tɤ-pɤtso kɯ-dɤn nɯra tɕe, tɯ-pɤrme, ʁnɯ-pɤrme jamar mɤɕtʂa tɯ-nɯ ku-tsʰi-nɯ. \\
indef. poss -child sbj: pcp -be.many dem: pl lnk one-year.old two-year.old about until indef. poss -breast ipfv -drink- pl \\
`In [families where] children are numerous, [mothers] breastfeed [the children] until [they are] one or two years old.' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR)
exe

exe

akɯ mɤɕtʂa ɣɯ-ku-ta-lɤt \\
east until cisl - ipfv: east -1 2-release \\
`I will accompany you until the [land of the] east.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S205
exe

In combination with the demonstrative nɯthat, mɤɕtʂauntil means `otherwise', as in ( ex:nW.mACtsxa ).

exe

kɤ-sɤŋo ʁɟa qʰe, nɯ-mtɕʰi kɤ-χpjɤt ʁɟa kɯ kú-wɣ-spa ɕti. nɯ mɤɕtʂa mɤ-kʰɯ. \\
inf -hear completely lnk 3pl. poss -mouth inf -observe completely erg ipfv - inv -be.able be. aff: fact dem until neg -be.possible: fact \\
`(In order to learn the Tshobdun language, since it has no writing system), one has no choice but to listen and observe people's mouth to learn it, otherwise it is not possible.' (150901 tshuBdWnskAt)
0006242#S42
exe

With a verb in negative form, the terminative can express restrictive focalization of locative and temporal adjuncts (§ sec:restrictive.focus ), as in ( ex:01.20hao.mACtsxa ).

exe

iʑora pɤjkʰu <yiyue> <ershiduohao> mɤɕtʂa mɯ́j-lɤt-nɯ kʰi. \\
1pl still January twentieth.plus until neg: sens -release- pl hearsay \\
`[At] our [place], they will only have [vacations] on the twentieth something of January, they say.' = `They won't have [vacations] until the twentieth of January.' (conversation, 14-12-24)
exe

The terminative postposition mɤɕtʂa can also be used to build temporal subordinate clauses (§ sec:terminative.clause ).
summary: The postposition **mɤɕtʂa** ‘until’ follows noun phrases to mark a temporal or locative limit, and it can contrast with egressive postpositions or with **kóʁmɯz** ‘only after.’ With the demonstrative **nɯ** ‘that,’ it means ‘otherwise,’ and with a negative verb it can express restrictive focalization of temporal or locative adjuncts. It can also form temporal subordinate clauses.

text:
egressive
There are six egressive postpositions in Japhug, which are built by combining the root ɕaŋ-/ɕoŋ- (among the words where -aŋ and -oŋ are in free variation; the variant ɕaŋ- is generalized in the orthography, see § sec:aN.oN.free ) with either the root of locative relator nouns (§ sec:relator.location ) or orientation adverbs (§ sec:preverbs.adverbs ) as shown in tab:egressive. There is a one-to-one relationship between the orientations of these postpositions and the six definite orientations found in verb morphology (§ sec:preverbs.adverbs ).

orientation!egressive
The egressive postpositions are mainly used with noun phrases of location expressing length or height ( ex:tWfsu.CaNtaR ) or a reference point marking a limit ( ex:praRwW.CaNdi ). However, ɕaŋtaʁup from and ɕaŋpadown from can also follow noun phrases referring to time reference or durations, as in ( ex:kWmNArZaR, ex:tWGjAn.CaNtaR.pWme ) or more generally any quantity ( ex:XsWm.CaNtaR ). No examples of these postpositions following finite subordinate clauses have been found.

exe

tɯrme tɯ-fsu ɕaŋtaʁ tu-mbro mɤ-cʰa. \\
people genr. poss -same.size up.from ipfv: up -be.high neg -can: fact \\
`It cannot grow bigger than a person.' (11-qarGW)
0003480#S25
exe

exe

ma kɯtɕimke nɯnɯtɕu, akɯ ku-ru tɕe, praʁwɯ ɕaŋdi sɤ-mto,
andi tɕe tɕe, ɕɯfco ɕaŋkɯ nɯ sɤ-mto tɕe, \\
lnk topo dem: loc east ipfv: east -look.at lnk topo west.from prop -see: fact west lnk lnk topo east.from dem prop -see: fact lnk \\
`In Kuchimke, looking towards the east, [the areas] to the west of Praqwu are visible, and in the west, [the areas] to the east of Shyufkyo are visible.' (150904 tshAcim)
0006274#S28
exe

exe

kɯmŋɤsqɤ-rʑaʁ ɕaŋtaʁ cʰɯ-mdɯ-nɯ mɤ-ŋgrɤl tu-ti-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
fifty-day up.from ipfv -live.up.to- pl neg -be.usually.the.case: fact ipfv -say- pl sens -be \\
`They cannot live more than fifty days, it is said.' (26-GZo) 0003668#S39
exe

exe

tɕe stu kɯ-dɤn nɯnɯ tɯ-xpa [tɯ-ɣjɤn ɕaŋtaʁ] kɯ-ɤmɯtɯɣ pɯ-me \\
lnk most sbj: pcp -be.many dem one-year one-time up.from genr - recip:meet pst. ipfv -not.exist \\
`At most, we would only meet once per year (we had no opportunity to meet more than once a year).' (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S38
exe

exe

ɯ-pɯ nɯnɯ χsɯm ɕaŋtaʁ tu mɯ́j-ŋgrɤl\\
3sg. poss -young dem three up.from exist: fact neg: sens -be.usually.the.case\\
`It does not usually have more than three offsprings.' (2011-08-kuwu)
exe

The postposition ɕaŋtaʁup from is by far more common than all the other ones, and is often combined with a negative predicate in a comparative construction (meaning `at most, no more than...', § sec:egressive.comparative, § sec:negative.existential.superlative ), as shown by ( ex:tWfsu.CaNtaR ), ( ex:kWmNArZaR ), ( ex:tWGjAn.CaNtaR.pWme ) and ( ex:XsWm.CaNtaR ) above.

In addition to the locational, temporal and quantitative meanings presented above, ɕaŋtaʁup from and ɕaŋpadown from can be used to refer to relative age (down from the upper generation, up from the lower generation, as shown in ex:CaNpa.CaNtaR ) or social status (up from the lowliest person, as in ex:BGAru.ci.CaNtaR ).

exe

nɤ-mu nɤ-wa ni ɕaŋpa, a-ɣe ɕaŋtaʁ tɤ-rɯndzaŋspa-nɯ je! \\
2sg. poss -mother 2sg. poss -father du down.from 1sg. poss -grandchild up.from imp -be.careful sfp \\
`Be careful, [all of you] from your parents (in the upper generation) to my grandson (in the lower generation).' (conversation, 29-09-2020)
exe

exe

wortɕʰi ʑo βɣɤru ci ɕaŋtaʁ ʑo tɤ-sɯ-ɤwɯwum-nɯ tɕe, \\
please emph miller indef up.from emph ifr - caus - recip:gather- pl lnk \\
`Please gather [everybody], from the miller (i.e. the lowliest of servants) up [to the highest ranking person].' (2003 kandZislama)
exe

The egressive postpositions can be used in contrast with the terminative mɤɕtʂauntil, as in ( ex:tWmAmke.mACtsxa ).

exe

tɯ-mke ɕaŋpa tɕe tɕe ki tɯ-mɤmke mɤɕtʂa kɯ-zɣɯt kɯ-rɲɟi pjɯ-ŋu ra. \\
indef. poss -neck down.from lnk lnk dem. prox indef. poss -ankle until sbj: pcp -reach sbj: pcp -be.long ipfv -be be.needed: fact \\
`[Tibetan clothes] have to be long [enough] so as to reach the ankle down from the neck.' (30-tWNga)
0004069#S3
exe

As other postpositional phrases, egressive phrases followed by demonstratives (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners ) mean `the person(s)/thing(s) from X', with a locative ( ex:TshuBdWn.CaNlo ) or temporal ( ex:sqamnW.pArme.CaNpa ) interpretation.

exe

iʑora kɯ, nɤki, tsʰuβdɯn ɕaŋlo nɯra `stɤtpa-pɯ' tu-ti-j ŋu. \\
1pl erg filler topo upstream.from dem: pl pl.n.-person ipfv -say- 1pl be: fact \\
`We call the people [who live] in Tshobdun and further upstream `Stotpa'.' (23-tCAphW)
0003614#S12
exe

exe

sqamnɯ-pɤrme ɕaŋpa nɯnɯ tɯ-ɕɣa tu-nɤsci kʰɯ \\
twelve-years.old down.from dem genr. poss -tooth ipfv -exchange be.possible: fact \\
`Those under twelve years old, their teeth can be replaced.' (27-tWCGArgu) 0003708#S55
exe

The postposition ɕaŋloupstream from is homophonous with, and historically related to, the noun ɕaŋloseating place (for old people and ladies) (§ sec:orientation.kitchen ).
summary:
Japhug has six egressive postpositions formed by combining the root ɕaŋ-/ɕoŋ- with locative relator nouns or orientation adverbs, and each corresponds one-to-one with a definite orientation in verb morphology. They are mainly used with noun phrases denoting locations, limits, times, durations, or quantities; ɕaŋtaʁ “up from” is especially common and often appears in negative comparative constructions meaning “at most, no more than.”

These postpositions can also express relative age or social status, and when followed by demonstratives they can mean “the person(s)/thing(s) from X,” with either a locational or temporal reading. The form ɕaŋlo “upstream from” is homophonous with, and historically related to, a noun meaning “eating place.”

text:
temporal postposition
Apart from the locative, terminative and egressive postpositions, a certain number of specifically temporal postpositions are found in Japhug, including ɕɯŋgɯbefore, ɕimɯmaimmediately after, kóʁmɯzonly after, pɕintɕɤtsince, jɤzwhen and ɕaŋpɕisince, `from... on'. All can be used with noun phrases and subordinate clauses; the latter use is studied in the section on temporal clauses (§ sec:temporal.clauses ).

The postposition ɕɯŋgɯbefore is an ancient compound containing as first element the bound state of a root cognate to Tangut 𗪘2104śji1.10 `formerly, before' and the relator noun ɯ-ŋgɯinside (§ sec:relator.location ) as second element. It contrasts with ɯ-qʰuafter, behind (§ sec:relator.temporal ), and can follow a noun phrase referring to a point in time, as in the common expression saχsɯ ɕɯŋgɯ `before lunch' (with the noun saχsɯlunch), or a duration, as in ( ex:sqamNusNi.CWNgW ) and ( ex:XsArZaR.CWNgW ). The latter example shows that ɕɯŋgɯbefore can be used to refer to events occurring after the current temporal point of reference (in ex:XsArZaR.CWNgW, before three days from the present in the story).

exe

tɤte sqamŋu-sŋi ɕɯŋgɯ nɯtɕu tɕe, nɤki, nɯ-rlaʁ tɕe nɯ-me pɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ŋu, tɕʰeme nɯ, \\
that.is fifteen-day before dem. loc lnk filler aor -disappear lnk aor -not.exist pst. ipfv -be sens -be girl dem \\
`That is, fifteen days before, she had disappeared, that girl.' (tWxtsa)
exe

exe

χsɯ-sŋi χsɤ-rʑaʁ mɤɕtʂa a-mɤ-tɤ-tɯ-rɤru ra ma tɕe mɤ-pʰɤn nɯra to-ti. matɕi tɕetʰa χsɯ-sŋi χsɤ-rʑaʁ ɕɯŋgɯ ɯʑo ɲɯ-pʰɣo pjɤ-ra lo \\
three-day three-night until irr - neg - pfv -2-get.up be.needed: fact lnk lnk neg -be.efficient: fact dem: pl ifr -say because later three-day three-night before 3sg ipfv -flee ifr. ipfv -be.needed sfp \\
`[The rabbit] said `Don't get up until three days and three nights [have passed]', because [the rabbit was buying time] and had to flee before [the end of] these three days and nights.' (140427 qala cho kWrtsag)
0003852#S28
exe

The postposition ɕɯŋgɯbefore however most commonly occurs with subordinate clauses, and requires a finite verb in the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.temporal, § sec:precedence.CWNgW ). It is attested following personal pronouns, as in ( ex:aʑo.CWNgW ), ɕɯŋgɯbefore refers to an action concerning the referent of the pronoun, whose nature can be determined from the context, as if the main verb of a subordinate clause had been elided.

exe

aʑo ɕɯŋgɯ a-pi ra atu rɤʑi-nɯ tɕe, nɯnɯra ɣɯ nɯ-rmi tɤ-z-mɤke qʰe, \\
1sg before 1sg. poss -elder.sibling pl up.there stay: fact - pl lnk dem: pl gen 3pl. poss -name imp - caus -be.first[III] lnk \\
`Before [you choose a name for] me, [choose] the names of my elder brothers up there first.' (Gesar)
exe

The common adverb kɯɕɯŋgɯin former times comes from the combination of the bound state of the proximal demonstrative kithis (§ sec:demonstrative.pronouns ) with the postposition ɕɯŋgɯbefore. The phrases ki ɕɯŋgɯ `before this' nɯ ɕɯŋgɯ `before that' with the demonstratives kithis and nɯthat are also attested.

While the neutral antonym of ɕɯŋgɯbefore is the relator noun ɯ-qʰuafter, behind (§ sec:relator.temporal ), subsequent temporality can also be expressed by ɕimɯmaimmediately after and kóʁmɯzonly after (one of the rare uninflected words with a non-final stress, § sec:stress ). These postpositions are mainly attested following the demonstrative pronoun nɯ, and often used adverbially as nɯ ɕimɯmaimmediately and nɯ kóʁmɯz nɤonly then, but are also attested with temporal and conditional clauses (§ sec:immediate.subsequence, § sec:only.if ) and with temporal counted nouns or adverbs as in ( ex:sqamNuxpa.koRmWz ), which also illustrates the opposition between kóʁmɯzonly after and the terminate postposition mɤɕtʂauntil (§ sec:terminative.

exe

ɯ-xso ʑɴɢɯloʁ nɯnɯ, tɕe sqamŋu-xpa mɤɕtʂa ɯ-mat ku-tsʰoʁ mɯ́j-cʰa. pɯ́-wɣ-ji ɕimɯma, ɯ-rɣi pjɯ́-wɣ-ji ɯ-qʰu, sqamŋu-xpa kóʁmɯz nɤ ɯ-mat ku-tsʰoʁ ŋu tu-ti-nɯ ŋgrɤl tɕe, \\
3sg. poss -normal walnut dem lnk fifteen-year until 3sg. poss -fruit ipfv -attach neg: sens -can aor - inv -plant just.after 3sg. poss -seed ipfv - inv -plant 3sg. poss -after fifteen-year only.after lnk 3sg. poss -fruit ipfv -attach be: fact ipfv -say- pl be.usually.the.case: fact lnk \\
`Usually, the walnut tree cannot have walnuts until fifteen years [have passed]. Just after one has planted it, after one plants its seeds, it is only fifteen years later that it bears nuts, they say.' (12-ndZiNgri)
0003488#S151
exe

There is an adverb nóʁmɯzonly then (found for instance in ex:tWqioR.kW, § sec:oblique.kW ) whose meaning is identical to nɯ kóʁmɯz nɤonly then, and apparently results from the fusion of the demonstrative nɯ with the root -oʁmɯz. The origin of the k- element in kóʁmɯzonly after is unclear; it could be the fused form of the proximal demonstrative ki (§ sec:anaphoric.demonstrative.pro ).

The postposition pɕintɕɤtsince (from Tibetan ཕྱིན་ཆད་pʰʲin.tɕʰadthereafter) can follow a date ( ex:69nian.pCintCAt ) or a subordinate clause, and is most often used with the relator noun ɯ-qʰuafter, behind to mean `from that time on' as in ( ex:nW.Wqhu.pCintCAt ). Another postposition, ɕaŋpɕisince, `from... on' (combining the ɕaŋ- element found in egressive postpositions § sec:egressive with -pɕi from Tibetan ཕྱི་pʰʲilater) can be used like pɕintɕɤtsince following ɯ-qʰuafter, behind as in ( ex:Wqhu.CaNpCi ), or after temporal clauses (§ sec:since.clause ). The two postpositions pɕintɕɤtsince and ɕaŋpɕisince, `from... on' have the same meaning, but the latter is considered by Tshendzin to be an influence from the Xtokavian dialects (§ sec:tChi, § sec:xtokavian.preverbs ).

exe

tɕe tʰam kɯβdesqi ɯ-ro to-pa ma <liu.jiu.nian> pɕintɕɤt \\
lnk now fourty 3sg. poss -excess ifr -pass.X.years lnk 1969 since \\
`Now it has been forty years [we have known each other], since 1969.' (12-BzaNsa) 0003484#S12
exe

exe

tɕiʑo pɯ-ari-tɕi ŋu, mtsʰukʰa pɯ-ftɕɤt-tɕi ŋu, nɯ ɯ-qʰu pɕintɕɤt tɕe, nɯ-ʁgra nɯ nɯ-me ŋu \\
1du aor: down -go[II]- 1du be: fact lake aor -subdue- 1du be: fact dem 3sg. poss -after since lnk 2pl. poss -enemy dem aor -not.exist be: fact \\
`We went down [into the lake], subdued the [demons in] the lake, and from that time on, your enemy is no more.' (Nyima.'Odzer 2003.2)
exe

exe
summary: Japhug has several specifically temporal postpositions, including forms meaning ‘before,’ ‘immediately after,’ ‘only after,’ ‘since,’ ‘when,’ and ‘from… on,’ which can all occur with noun phrases and subordinate clauses. The passage explains that ɕɯŋgɯ ‘before’ is an ancient compound, is most often used with subordinate clauses requiring an imperfective finite verb, and can also follow time expressions, durations, and even personal pronouns in elliptical contexts. It also notes that pɕintɕɤt and ɕaŋpɕi both mean ‘since/from… on,’ while ɕimɯ and kóʁmɯz express immediate or delayed subsequence, often with the demonstrative nɯ.

text:
tɕe tɤ-mu nɯ, nɯ ɯ-qʰu ɕaŋpɕi ʑo kɤ-rɯndzɤqʰɤjɯ ta-znɯna \\
lnk indef. poss -mother dem dem 3sg. poss -after from.that.time.on emph inf -eat.without.sharing aor:3 -stop \\
`From that [time] on, the mother stopped to eat on her own without sharing.' (tWJo 2005)
exe

The postposition jɤzwhen and its variant jɤznɤwhen follows either subordinate clauses (§ sec:temporal.reference ), temporal adverbs ( ex:jWfCWr.jAznA ) or the noun ɯ-ŋgubeginning (from འགོ་gohead, beginning) as in ( ex:jWfCWr.jAznA ); it is not attested with other noun phrases.

exe

jɯfɕɯr nɯtɕu iɕqʰa tɤtɕɯpɯ nɯnɯra, jɯfɕɯr jɤznɤ tu-ndze-a tɕe pɯ-apa wo ri \\
yesterday dem: loc the.aforementioned boy dem: pl yesterday when ipfv -eat[III]- 1sg lnk pst. ipfv -be.correct sfp lnk \\
`I should have eaten these boys yesterday.' (160705 poucet5-v2)
0006163#S35
exe

exe

tɕe ɯ-ŋgu jɤznɤ tɕe, ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ nɯra mɯ-cʰɯ-pʰaʁ-nɯ tɕe, tɕe nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-ndʐi kɯ-fsɯ fse nɯ pjɯ-qaʁ-nɯ tɕe tɕe \\
lnk 3sg. poss -beginning when lnk 3sg. poss -limb dem: pl neg - ipfv -cut- pl lnk lnk dem gen 3sg. poss -skin sbj: pcp - emph be.like dem ipfv -remove.skin- pl lnk lnk \\
`In the beginning, they don't cut off the limbs (from the cattle's body), and take out the skin [in such a way as to preserve its shape] exactly like [that of the living animal].' (06-BGa) 0003408#S68
exe
summary: The postposition **jɤzwhen / jɤznɤwhen** is used after subordinate clauses, temporal adverbs, and the noun **ɯ-ŋgu** “beginning,” but it is not attested with other noun phrases. The examples show it marking temporal reference such as “from that time on,” “yesterday,” and “in the beginning.”

text:
noun!relator relator noun
Relator nouns are inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ) used to mark the grammatical relations of oblique arguments or adjuncts. They differ from postpositions by at least three properties.

First, they have an obligatory possessive prefix, which is coreferent with the preceding noun phrase or clause when one is present (generally the third person singular ɯ- prefix).

Second, unlike postpositions, which require at the very least a demonstrative (§ ex:postpositions ), they can occur without a preceding noun phrase or clause if the referent indicated by the possessive prefix is definite (including first or second person, as in ex:aCki.jAGe ) or generic (see example ex:tWCki in § sec:indef.genr.poss ).

exe

jɯfɕɯr <gongxun> a-ɕki jɤ-ɣe. \\
yesterday anthr 1sg. poss - dat aor -come[II] \\
`Yesterday Gong Xun came to [see] me.' (160320, conversation)
exe

Third, the genitive ɣɯ (§ sec:genitive ) can optionally occur between the preceding noun phrase and the relator (as in ex:GW.WCki.nWtCu below and ex:GW.kWnA.WrkW.ri ), since relator noun phrases are a subtype of the possessive construction (§ sec:gen.possession ).

exe

tɕe smɤt tɯmda rɟɤlpu ɣɯ ɯ-ɕki nɯtɕu, nɤkinɯ, ɯ-rʑaβ ɯ-kɯ-tʰu cʰɤ-ɕe tɕe, \\
lnk topo topo king gen 3sg. poss - dat dem: loc filler 3sg. poss -wife 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -ask ifr: downstream -go lnk \\
`He went to ask the king of the lower valley for [one his daughter to take as] a wife.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

In addition, most relator nouns still preserve non-grammaticalized uses revealing their diachronic source, and some of them can be followed by the locative postpositions (§ sec:core.locative ) or by other relator nouns.
summary: Relator nouns are inalienably possessed nouns used to mark the grammatical relations of oblique arguments or adjuncts, and they differ from postpositions in several ways. They require an obligatory possessive prefix, can occur without a preceding noun phrase if the referent is definite or generic, and may optionally take a genitive NP before them because they are part of a possessive construction. The text also notes that many relator nouns retain older non-grammaticalized uses, and some can be followed by locative postpositions or other relator nouns.

text:
dative
Two dative markers are attested in Japhug, ɯ-ɕki and ɯ-pʰe; some speakers like Tshendzin prefer the former (as in ex:aCki.jAGe, ex:WCki.zW, ex:WCki.toti ), but most speakers I have recorded favor the latter (for instance, Kunbzang Mtsho who tells the story from which ex:Wphe.toti is taken).

The dative can be followed by the locative postpositions zɯ and tɕu, as in ( ex:WCki.zW ), ( ex:nWCki.zYArNo ) and ( ex:slANe.ZNgri.ra.nWphe ).

exe

nɯ mbro tɯ-skɤt kɯ-tso nɯnɯ ɯ-ɕki zɯ.... to-ti \\
dem horse indef. poss -speech sbj: pcp -understand dem 3sg. poss - dat loc ifr -say \\
`She said... to the horse who could understand speech' (2003kAndzWsqhaj)
exe

The dative is used to mark the recipient or addressee. It occurs with indirective verbs of speech such as tisay ( ex:WCki.zW, ex:WCki.toti and ex:Wphe.toti ), fɕɤttell and tʰuask ( ex:nWCki.tAthe ), and also with some intransitive verbs of speech such as rɯɕmispeak ( ex:WCki.torWCmi ).

exe

iɕqʰa srɯnmɯ nɯ kɯ, [...] smɤnmimitoʁ kuɕana ɯ-ɕki `nɤʑo tɕʰi ɯ-rɯɣ tɯ-ŋu' to-ti ri, \\
the.aforementioned râkshasî dem erg anthr anthr 3sg. poss - dat 2sg what 3sg. poss -race 2-be: fact ifr -say lnk \\
`The râkshasî asked Smanmi Metog Koshana, `What type of being are you?' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S357
exe

exe

tɕe tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ ɯ-wa ɯ-pʰe nɯra pɯ-kɯ-fse nɯra to-ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
lnk indef. poss -son dem erg 3sg. poss -father 3sg. poss - dat dem. pl aor - sbj: pcp -be.like dem. pl ifr -say sens -be \\
`The boy told his father the things that had happened.' (2012-qachGa)
0004087#S171
exe

exe

nɤʑo ɯ-mɤ-ɲɯ-tɯ-stu nɤ, ʑara nɯ-ɕki tɤ-tʰe jɤɣ \\
2sg qu - neg - sens -2-believe lnk 3pl 3pl. poss - dat imp -ask[III] be.possible: fact \\
`If you don't believe it, ask them!' (140508 shier ge tiaowu de gongzhu-zh)
0003937#S181
exe

exe

nɯ tɤ-pɤtso nɯ ɯ-ɕki to-rɯɕmi. \\
dem indef. poss -child dem 3sg. poss - dat ifr -speak \\
`It spoke to the child.' (150831 renshen wawa-zh) 0006418#S36
exe

It also occurs with verbs of giving to mark the recipient as in ( ex:WCki.YAkho ) with the verb kʰogive, `pass over', but also the source as in ( ex:nWCki.zYArNo ) with verbs such as rŋoborrow, sɤmbiask for and χtɯbuy (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective, § sec:sig.caus.inversive ).

exe

ɯ-nmaʁ ɯ-ɕki ɲɤ-kʰo tɕe, \\
3sg. poss -husband 3sg. poss - dat ifr -give lnk \\
`She gave it to her husband.' (qajdoskAt)
exe

exe

kɯ-rɤrma ra nɯ-ɕki nɯtɕu, kuxtɕo ci z-ɲɤ-rŋo, \\
sbj: pcp -work pl 3pl. poss - dat dem: loc basket indef tral - ifr -borrow \\
`[The snow leopard] borrowed a basket from the workers.' (qala2002)
exe

With the verb kʰogive, `pass over' the recipient is more often encoded with the genitive or a possessive prefix on the theme (§ sec:gen.beneficiary ) or with the semi-grammaticalized noun tɯ-jaʁhand, arm (§ sec:semi.grammaticalized.relator ).

The semi-transitive verb rulook at can mark its goal with the dative, as in ( ex:WCki.Cturu ); this is however optional, as this verbs also takes goals in the absolutive (§ absolutive.goal ) or locative (§ sec:locative ).

exe

tɕe tɤŋe nɯ nɯɣ-me tɕe, tɕe tɤŋe ɯ-ɕki ʁɟa ʑo ɕ-tu-ru tɕe, tɯʑo tɯ-ɕki maka ʑo mɤ-ru \\
lnk sun dem appl -be.afraid[III]: fact - 1sg lnk lnk sun 3sg. poss - dat completely emph tral - ipfv: up -look.at lnk genr genr. poss - dat at.all emph neg -look.at: fact \\
`[If the yeti catches you], it is afraid of the sun, it looks at the sun the whole time, and does not look at you.' (140510 mYWrgAt)
0003941#S13
exe
dative grammaticalization!dative
The dative ɯ-ɕki derives from a relator noun meaning `side', `near' or `at $X$'s place' (with or without motion). These locative meanings are still marginally present in Japhug in examples like ( ex:aCki.jAGe ) above and ( ex:WCki.loc ), ( ex:slANe.ZNgri.ra.nWphe ) and ( ex:WCki.kunWrAZi ) below.

exe

ɯ-rte nɯ ɯ-rna ɯ-ɕki pɯ-kɯ-ɴqoʁ nɯnɯ pjɤ-mɟa tɕe ɯ-ku ɯ-taʁ to-ta. \\
3sg. poss -hat dem 3sg. poss -ear 3sg - dat aor: down - nmlz:S/A-hang dem ifr: down -take lnk 3sg. poss -head 3sg -on ifr -put \\
`He took the hat that was hanging on his ear and put it on his head.' (140505 liuhaohan zoubian tianxia-zh)
0003913#S161
exe

exe

tɤŋe cʰo slɤŋe ʑŋgri ra nɯ-pʰe nɯtɕu kɤ-nɤɕqa a-pɯ-tɯ-cʰa ra ma, \\
sun comit moon star pl 3pl. poss - dat dem: loc inf -bear irr - pfv -2-can be.needed: fact lnk \\
`[When you are] close to the sun, the moon and the stars, you will have to bear [the heat and the cold], otherwise...' (2003kandZislama)
exe

exe

li tɕetu tɤ-ɣe qʰe, ɯ-wa ɯ-ɕki ku-nɯ-rɤʑi, tɕeki pɯ-ari qʰe, ɯ-wɯ ɯ-wi ni ndʑi-ɕki ju-nɯ-ɕe qʰe, \\
again up.there aor: up -go[II] lnk 3sg. poss -father 3sg. poss - dat ipfv - auto -stay, down.there aor -go[II] lnk 3sg. poss -grand.father 3sg. poss -grand.mother du 3du. poss - dat ipfv - auto -go lnk \\
`When she comes up there, she stays at her father's house, and when she goes down there, she goes to her grandparent's place.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S283
exe

The dative in combination with a copula can express temporary and alienable possession, as in ( ex:kWre.aCki ). It is marginal in comparison with the genitive mihi est possessive construction (§ sec:possessive.mihi.est ).

exe

kɯre aʑo a-ɕki ɕti ma, ɯʑo ɯ-ɕki me wo. \\
dem: prox: loc 1sg 1sg. poss - dat be. aff: fact lnk 3sg 3sg. poss - dat not.exist: fact sfp \\
`(The key) is with me here, she doesn't have it.' (so she asked me for it) (conversation, 2021-01)
exe
summary:
Japhug has two dative markers, ɯ-ɕki and ɯ-pʰe, with speaker variation in preference. The dative marks recipients or addressees, is used with indirect speech verbs, some verbs of giving and borrowing, and optionally with the verb “look at,” and it can also combine with locative postpositions.

The ɯ-ɕki marker is historically derived from a relator noun meaning “side,” “near,” or “at X’s place,” and these locative meanings remain marginally attested. With a copula, the dative can also express temporary, alienable possession, though this is less common than the genitive possessive construction.

text:
secutive
The secutive relator noun ɯ-rcafollowing is used with verbs of motion such as gicome to express the meaning `follow', `come/go with' as in ( ex:nArca.Gia ).

exe

aʑo kɯnɤ nɤ-rca ɣi-a ɕti \\
1sg also 2sg. poss -following come: fact - 1sg be. aff: fact \\
`I am coming/going with you.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe
comitative adverb
The secutive can have a meaning similar to that of the comitative adverb (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) `together with X', as in ( ex:WBGi.Wrca ).

exe

pɤnmawombɤr ɣɯ ɯ-ɕɤrɯ ɯ-βɣi ɯ-rca tsʰɯntsʰɯn ʑo ta-wum-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
anthr gen 3sg. poss -bone 3sg. poss -ash 3sg. poss -following idph (II):neat emph aor:3 -collect- pl sens -be \\
`They collected all of Padma 'Od-'bar's bones together with his ashes.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

The secutive phrase can follow ( ex:WBGi.Wrca ), or precede ( ex:tWjAGAt.Wrca ) the noun phrase it accompanies.

exe

tɯ-jɤɣɤt ɯ-rca tɤ-se cʰɯ-nɯ-ɬoʁ \\
indef. poss -feces 3sg. poss -following indef. poss -blood ipfv: downstream - auto -come.out \\
`(In the case of this disease), blood comes out together with the feces.' (24-pGArtsAG) 0003624#S109
exe

With the indefinite possessor prefix tɤ-rca and tɯ-tɯ-rca, the secutive appears in adverbial function with the meaning `together' (example ex:iZo.kWBde, § sec:uses.numerals ), though in examples such as ( ex:tArAku.tArca ) the form tɤ-rca retains its nominal status.

exe

ɕoʁ nɯnɯ tɤ-rɤku tɤ-rca ŋu, sɯjno maʁ. \\
buckwheat dem indef. poss -crops indef. poss -following be: fact grass not.be: fact \\
`Buckwheat is a type of crops, it is not a [type of] grass.' (13-NanWkWmtsWG) 0003492#S64
exe

In addition, the unexpected focus marker rcanɯ (§ sec:unexpected ) and the epistemic sentence final particle rca (§ sec:fsp.epistemic ) are historically related to the secutive.
summary: The secutive relator noun ɯ-rca ‘following’ is used with motion verbs to express meanings like ‘follow’ or ‘come/go with,’ and it can also function like a comitative expression meaning ‘together with.’ It may appear either before or after the noun phrase it accompanies, and with indefinite possessor forms such as tɤ-rca and tɯ-tɯ-rca it can have an adverbial meaning ‘together.’ The text also notes that the unexpected focus marker rcanɯ and the epistemic sentence-final particle rca are historically related to the secutive.

text:
deputative
The relator noun ɯ-tsʰɤt has two meanings. First, it can serve as a deputative relator noun `instead of, on behalf of' as in ( ex:nWtAsno.WtshAt ) and ( ex:nWsi.WtshAt ). No verb selects this relator noun.

The deputative adjunct can correspond to the intransitive subject (as in ex:nWtAsno.WtshAt, with the verb tuexist), the transitive subject (as in ex:aZo.nAtshAt, with ɣɯjtsisupport) or the object.

exe

nɯʑora ɣɯ nɯ-tɤ-sno kɯ-fse ɯ-tsʰɤt nɯ, tɕiʑo ɣɯ, tɕi-xɕɤndʑu χsɯ-ldʑa pɯ-tu tɕe, nɯnɯ lɤ-nɯ-βlɯ-tɕi ɕti wo \\
2pl gen 2pl. poss - indef. poss -saddle sbj: pcp -be.like 3sg. poss -instead.of dem 1du gen 1du. poss -twig three-long.object pst. ipfv -exist lnk dem aor - auto -burn- 1du be. aff: fact sfp \\
`Instead of a saddle like yours, we had three twigs, this is what we burned.' (Kunbzang 2003)
exe

exe

aʑo nɤ-tsʰɤt, nɤki, si nɯ tu-ɣɯjtsi-a jɤɣ \\
1sg 2sg. poss -instead.of filler tree dem ipfv -support- 1sg be.possible: fact \\
`I can support the tree for you/instead of you (while you fetch it).' (150830 afanti-zh)
0006380#S132
exe

The noun phrase headed by ɯ-tsʰɤt can be either an adjunct as in ( ex:nWtAsno.WtshAt ) and ( ex:aZo.nAtshAt ), the object of the verb βzumake, or a nominal predicate with a copula as in ( ex:nWsi.WtshAt ) and ( ex:aZo.atshAt ). In the latter case, to express the meaning `do to $X$ instead of to $Y$', a biclausal construction `do to $X$, ($X$) is instead of $Y$' is used as in ( ex:aZo.atshAt ).

exe

si maŋe tɕe tɕe nɯnɯtɕu tɕe, nɯ-si ɯ-tsʰɤt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
tree not.exist: sens lnk lnk dem: loc lnk 3pl. poss -wood 3sg. poss -instead.of sens -be \\
`[Since] there are no trees, [dung] is used there to replace the firewood.' (05-tamar)
0003406#S8
exe

exe

nɯ tɤ-nɯ-ndɤm tɕe aʑo a-tsʰɤt ŋu tɕe \\
dem imp - auto -take[III] lnk 1sg 1sg. poss -instead.of be: fact lnk \\
`Take these [as a compensation] instead of having me [as your wife].' (2003kAndzwsqhaj2)
exe

The examples ( ex:aZo.nAtshAt ) and ( ex:aZo.atshAt ) also show that the relator noun ɯ-tsʰɤtinstead of can occur with a first or second person possessive prefix.

Second, ɯ-tsʰɤt also means `with proper measure', mainly occurring in adverbial function as in ( ex:WtshAt.tsa ) or in collocation with the verb βzumake in the sense `do with proper measure' as in ( ex:WtshAt.tusWBzunW ).

exe

rkaŋraŋ ɯ-tsʰɤt tsa ɲɯ-kɯ-nɤɕtʂaʁli-a-nɯ raʁmaʁ ma \\
anthr 3sg. poss -proper.measure a.little ipfv -2 1-torture- 1sg - pl sfp sfp \\
`Rkangrang, don't go over the top in your torturing of me (`torture me with proper measure'), please? (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S184
exe

exe

ɯ-tsʰɤt tu-sɯ-βzu-nɯ mɯ́j-kʰɯ ma, nɯ-kɤ-kʰo nɯ mɯ-tʰa-ɕkɯt mɤɕtʂa tu-ndze ɲɯ-ɕti. \\
3sg. poss -proper.measure ipfv - caus -make- pl neg: sens -be.possible lnk aor - obj: pcp -give dem neg - aor:3 -eat.completely until ipfv -eat[III] sens -be. aff \\
`They cannot make [the monkey eat] with measure, as it continues eating the [food] that is given to it until there is none.' (19-GzW)
0003536#S58
exe

In some contexts as in ( ex:nWnW.WtshAt ), ɯ-tsʰɤtproper measure in adverbial used is better translated as `depending on the circumstances'. This example is taken from a text describing goats and sheep; goats are called tsʰɤt in Japhug, but it is clear from the context that ɯ-tsʰɤt cannot be the 3sg possessed form of this noun, though the two forms are indeed homophonous.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ ɯ-tsʰɤt nɯnɯ ɯ-pɯ ci ci ʁnɯz tu, ci ci tɯ-rdoʁ ma me tɕe núndʐa ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk dem 3sg. poss -proper.measure dem 3sg. poss -young once once two exist: fact once once one-piece apart.from not.exist: fact lnk for.this.reason sens -be \\
`This is why, depending on the circumstances, sometimes [the goat] has two kids, sometimes only one.' (05-qaZo)
0003404#S25
exe

The inalienably possessed noun ɯ-tsʰɤt (at least in the meaning `proper measure') is borrowed from ཚད་tsʰadmeasure, limit. It occurs as second element in the compound xtɤtsʰɤtrestraint of one's appetite(with the bound state xtɤ- of tɯ-xtubelly).
summary: The relator noun ɯ-tsʰɤt has two main meanings: deputative “instead of, on behalf of” and adverbial “with proper measure.” In its deputative use, it can function as an adjunct, object, or nominal predicate, and it may refer to the intransitive subject, transitive subject, or object; expressing “do to X instead of Y” requires a biclausal construction. In the second meaning, it appears mainly adverbially, sometimes better translated as “depending on the circumstances,” and is borrowed from Tibetan tsʰad “measure, limit.”

text:
relator noun!locative
The dearth of specific locative postpositions (§ sec:locative ) other than the egressive ones (§ sec:egressive ) in Japhug is compensated by the existence of many relator nouns expressing various types of location, as shown in tab:relator.location.

As other relator nouns, they can follow noun phrases (including headless relative clauses), with the possessive prefix agreeing in person and number with the preceding constituant, but can also occur on their own if the referent is definite, as ɯ-taʁon, above in ( ex:WtaR.zW.kAmdzW ) and ( ex:WtaR.nWtCu.YAXtAr ) below.

exe

ɯ-taʁ zɯ kɤ-amdzɯ nɤ tɤ-lu pa-tɕɤt ɲɯ-ŋu\\
3sg. poss -on loc aor -sit lnk indef. poss -milk aor:3 -take.out sens -be\\
`She sat on him and milked.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe
summary: The passage explains that Japhug lacks many specific locative postpositions aside from egressive ones, and this gap is partly filled by numerous relator nouns that express different kinds of location. Like other relator nouns, they can follow noun phrases or headless relative clauses with a possessive prefix agreeing in person and number, but they may also stand alone when the referent is definite.

text:
orientation!relator noun
The first six nouns in tab:relator.location are derived from orientation adverbs (§ sec:locative.adv ). The vertical dimension relator nouns ɯ-taʁon, above and ɯ-pabelow, under are simply built by adding a possessive prefix to the root of the adverb, while the other ones combine the bound state of the adverbial root ( lɤ, tʰɤ, kɤ, ndɤ- from lo, tʰi, kɯ and ndi, respectively) with a suffix -cu. This hexameric system comprising three pairs of elements along three dimensions (vertical, fluvial, solar) is the same as found in verbal morphological (§ sec:preverbs.adverbs ) and also egressive postpositions (§ sec:egressive ).
summary: The first six nouns in the relator-noun set are derived from orientation adverbs. The vertical terms are formed by adding a possessive prefix to the adverb root, while the other relator nouns combine the bound state of the adverbial root with the suffix -cu. This six-part system of paired elements across three dimensions (vertical, fluvial, solar) matches patterns found in verbal morphology and egressive postpositions.

text:
Outside of the tridimensional system, other locative relator nouns also occur in antithetic pairs, in particular ɯ-ʁɤribefore, in front of vs. ɯ-qʰuafter, behind (the latter also occurs as a temporal relator noun, cf § sec:relator.temporal ), ɯ-ŋgɯinside vs. ɯ-pɕioutside and ɯ-mŋuopening, edge, border vs. ɯ-ndoedge, border or ɯ-qabottom of.

A few of these relator nouns are borrowed from Tibetan, as indicated in tab:relator.location ), but most of them are native Gyalrong words. In particular ɯ-ʁɤribefore, in front of is one of the very rare cases of a disyllabic word that has a cognate in Tangut sharing both syllables ( 𘁞𗙷5416-567ɣwə-rjir2.25-2.74 `before', ). The syllable ʁɤ- = 𘁞5416ɣwə2.25 may be a fossilized allomorph of tɯ-kuhead with a uvular as in the Stau cognate ʁəhead. The relator noun ɯ-kutop of (as in ex:Wku.zW ) is transparently grammaticalized from the body part tɯ-kuhead.

exe

tɕetu si ɯ-ku zɯ qaliaʁ ɣɤʑu tɕe, \\
up.there tree 3sg. poss -top.of loc eagle sens:exist lnk \\
`Up there on the top of the tree there is an eagle.' (140427 laoying mao he yezhu-zh)
0003846#S29
exe

Some relator nouns other than ɯ-kutop of have non-grammaticalized uses; for instance ɯ-ŋgɯinside still occurs as a noun meaning `internal part, inside' in ( ex:WNgW.nW.so ).

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ kɯ-spoʁ ŋu, ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯ so tɕe \\
lnk dem sbj: pcp -have.a.hole be: fact 3sg. poss -inside dem be.hollow: fact lnk \\
`Its [inside] has a hole, its inside is hollow.' (12-Zmbroko)
0003490#S21
exe

Some of the relator nouns above can derive verbs of location such as mɤkube first and mɤpɕibe outside with the denominal prefix mɤ- (§ sec:denom.mA ).

The meaning of the relator nouns ɯ-mŋu and ɯ-ndo requires a specific description. These nouns are not antithetic to another in all cases. The basic (non-grammaticalized) meaning of ɯ-mŋu is the border of the opening or mouth of a container / bag ( ex:khWtsa.WmNu ), or the shoreline (of a lake), as in ( ex:mtshu.WmNu ). In this use, it is opposed to ɯ-qabottom of, as in ( ex:mtshu.Wqa ).

exe

tɕendɤre nɯnɯ kʰɯtsa ɯ-mŋu jamar kɯ-wxti tu,\\
lnk dem bowl 3sg. poss -border about sbj: pcp -be.big exist: fact \\
`Some are about as big as the mouth of a bowl.' (22-BlamajmAG)
0003584#S122
exe

exe

tɕendre pɣɤtɕɯ nɯ mtsʰu ɯ-mŋu nɯtɕu `ʂɯt' to-ti to-nɯ-ɬoʁ. \\
lnk bird dem lake 3sg. poss -border dem: loc idph.I:sound ifr -say ifr: up - auto -come.out \\
`The bird came out of the shore of the lake with a noise.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

exe

mtsʰu ɯ-qa zɯ nɤrwɯ mɤ-kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ ci ɣɤʑu tɕe, \\
lake 3sg. poss -bottom loc jewel neg - sbj: pcp -be.similar indef exist: sens lnk \\
`At the bottom of the sea, there is a jewel unlike any other.' (2012 Kunbzang)
0003768#S11
exe

The basic meaning of ɯ-ndo includes `extremity' (for instance, of a limb as in ex:WRar.Wndo ) and also `end' in both the locative and temporal sense ( ex:Wndo.tCe ).

exe

ɯ-ʁar ɯ-ndo nɯra hanɯni ɲɯ-ɲaʁ. \\
3sg. poss -wing 3sg. poss -border dem: pl a.little sens -be.black \\
`The extremities of its wings are a bit black.' (23-scuz)
0003612#S122
exe

exe

ɯ-ndo tɕe maka kɯ-tu ɲɯ-me ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
3sg. poss -border lnk at.all sbj: pcp -exist ipfv -not.exist sens -be lnk \\
`In the end, nothing is left.' (04-xiaocunzhuang-zh)
0003394#S56
exe

In the case of clothes, ɯ-ndo refers to the lower opening (towards the feet), as opposed to the collar, as in ( ex:Wndo.ri.kulAtnW ).

exe

tɕe nɯ ɯ-ndʐi nɯnɯ pjɯ-χtsɤβ-nɯ tɕe tɕe tɯ-ŋga ɯ-ndo ri ku-lɤt-nɯ, tɯ-ŋga ɯ-kuŋa, ɯ-pɤloʁ ɯ-ku, ɯ-ndo nɯra ku-lɤt-nɯ, tu-sɯ-fskɤr-nɯ ŋu. \\
lnk dem 3sg. poss -skin dem ipfv -tan- pl lnk lnk indef. poss -clothes 3sg. poss -border loc ipfv -release- pl indef. poss -clothes 3sg. poss -collar 3sg. poss -sleeves 3sg. poss -top 3sg. poss -border dem: pl ipfv -release- pl ipfv - caus -surround- pl be: fact \\
`They tan its hide (of the otter) and put it on the lower opening of the clothes, on the collar of clothes, the cuffs of the sleeves and the lower opening, and make it around [these openings].' (28-qapar)
0003720#S90
exe

A contrast between ɯ-mŋu and ɯ-ndo occurs in their uses as relator nouns, indicating opposite extremities or sides. In the case of fields (as in ex:tWji.WmNu.Wndo ), ɯ-mŋu designates the higher side of the field (towards the mountain), while ɯ-ndo refers to the side closer to the river (all arable lands in Gyalrong area lie in narrow valleys).

exe

qaʑmbri nɯ, tɯ-ji ɯ-ndo, tɯ-ji ɯ-mŋu nɯra aʁɤndɯndɤt ʑo tu-ɬoʁ ɕti \\
vine dem indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -border indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -border dem: pl everywhere emph ipfv: up -come.out be. aff: fact \\
`The vine, it grows everywhere, on both sides of the fields.' (06-qaZmbri)
0003526#S18
exe

The relator noun ɯ-mŋu can also designates the top extremity of stairs, as in ( ex:rJAskAt.WmNu ); for the lower side, either ɯ-qabottom of or ɯ-ndo can be used (the former more commonly).

exe

cɯŋglɯɣ nɯ rɟɤskɤt ɯ-mŋu zɯ na-ta ɲɯ-ŋu \\
pestle dem stairs 3sg. poss -border loc aor:3 -put sens -be \\
`He put the pestle on the top of the stairs.' (tWJo 2005)
exe

The superlative derivation (§ sec:superlative.XCWX ) can be applied to most locative relator nouns, as ɯ-mŋuɕɯmŋu from ɯ-mŋu in ( ex:WmNuCWmNu ), where it means that the liquid completely fills the bowl to the point of touching the border of its mouth, flowing out at the slightest motion.

exe

tʂʰa tɤ́-wɣ-rku tɕe kʰɯtsa ɯ-mŋuɕɯmŋu stʰɯci tu-zɣɯt mɤ-ra ma kɤ-ndo tɕe sɤ-ɕke \\
tea aor - inv -put.in lnk bowl 3sg. poss -border: superlative so.much ipfv: up -reach neg -be.needed: fact lnk inf -take lnk prop -burn: fact \\
`When one pours tea, it should not reach the limit of the mouth of the bowl, otherwise it will be burning when one holds it.' (elicited)
exe
summary: The passage describes several locative relator nouns in Gyalrong that occur in opposite pairs, such as ‘before/behind,’ ‘inside/outside,’ and ‘opening/edge’ versus ‘bottom.’ It notes that some are borrowed from Tibetan, most are native, and some retain non-grammaticalized noun uses or can derive location verbs; the meanings of ɯ-mŋu and ɯ-ndo are especially variable, depending on the object and context.

text:
In addition to the relator nouns described above, the inalienably possessed noun ɯ-stustraight ahead is mainly used as an adverb, but can also serve as a relator noun to indicate the goal of a motion verb as in ( ex:Wstu.Zo.YAGi ).

exe

tɕe pʰaʁrgot ri li ɯʑo ɯ-stu ʑo ɲɤ-ɣi qʰe, ɕɤmɯɣdɯ kɤ-lɤt mɯ-pjɤ-nɤz qʰe pʰaʁrgot jo-nɯ-ɕe. \\
lnk boar also again 3sg 3sg. poss -straight emph ifr: west -come lnk gun inf -release neg - ifr. ipfv -dare lnk boar ifr - auto -go \\
`The boar came directly at him, but he did not dare to shoot and the boar went away.' (150829 phaRrgot)
0006414#S8
exe

The relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above
The relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above is mainly used to build locative adjuncts or goals (see examples in § sec:relator.postposition.location ), but it is also selected by a certain number of verbs to mark an oblique argument. The relator noun ɯ-taʁ is homophonous with the bare infinitive ɯ-taʁ of the verb taʁweave (§ sec:bare.inf ), as in example ( ex:WtaR.WtWBdi ), § sec:degree.nominal.arguments, but the resemblance between the two forms is fortuitous.

The intransitive verb atsaprick and its causative form sɤtsaprick, pierce encode the piercing object as intransitive subject and object, respectively. The patient (the person or object being pricked) is encoded as an oblique argument in ɯ-taʁ; example ( ex:tWtaR.kotsa ) illustrates the intransitive verb atsa with a generic human argument (§ sec:indef.genr.poss ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-ku kɯ-ɤmtɕoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, tɯ-taʁ ku-otsa tɕe ɲɯ-ɕɯ-mŋɤm. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -head sbj: pcp -be.pointy sens -be lnk genr. poss -on ipfv -prick lnk sens - caus -hurt \\
`[The fir needles] are pointy-headed, they prick people, it hurts.' (08-tWrgi) 0003464#S26
exe

The intransitive verb ɴqoʁhang has an additional volitional meaning of `grab, lean on', taking an object or person with both hands with body contact. It is attested for instance to describe a person who has fallen in the water, reaching for floating pieces of wood in order not to sink as in ( ex:WtaR.kANqoRnW ) or jumping on the back of someone and grabbing her to prevent her from leaving ( ex:WtaR.koNqoR ). The object or person being grabbed is marked with ɯ-taʁ.

exe

nɯnɯ ʑmbrɯ nɯ-kɤ-χtɤr nɯ ɯ-taʁ kɤ-ɴqoʁ-nɯ ra \\
dem ship aor - obj: pcp -scatter dem 3sg. poss -on imp -hang- pl be.needed: fact \\
`Grab the [pieces of the] ship that have been scattered.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S30
exe

exe

tɯrmɯkʰa tɕe tɯlɤt nɯ ɯ-taʁ ko-ɴqoʁ tɕe \\
evening loc second.sibling dem 3sg. poss -on ifr -hang lnk \\
`In the evening, he grabbed the second sister.' (07-deluge) 0003426#S46
exe

Some stative verb also optionally select an oblique argument in ɯ-taʁ, in particular to express a beneficiary/maleficiary with the verbs pebe good and ŋɤnbe evil, in the meaning `be good to $X$, be nice with $X$, treat $X$ well' and `treat $X$ badly', as in ( ex:WtaR.mWpjApendZi ). The genitive can alternatively be used to mark the beneficiary with these verbs (§ sec:gen.beneficiary ), but the meaning is rather `be advantageous' or `be harmful' depending on polarity.

exe

maka ʑo ɯ-taʁ mɯ-pjɤ-pe-ndʑi qʰe, pjɤ-ŋɤn-ndʑi \\
at.all emph 3sg. poss -on neg - ipfv. ifr -be.good- du lnk neg - ipfv. ifr -be.bad- du \\
`They did not treat him well, they treated him badly. (2014-kWlAG)
exe

exe

a-pi ra a-taʁ nɯ-tɯ-pe pɯ-sɤre ʑo tɕe \\
1sg. poss -elder.sibling pl 1sg. poss -on 3pl. poss - nmlz: deg -be.good pst. ipfv -be.ridiculous emph lnk \\
`My elder brothers treated me very well.' (140501 tshering skyid)
0003902#S46
exe

The bipartite verb stu=mbattry hard (§ sec:bipartite ) can also take a beneficiary in ɯ-taʁ, with the meaning `care about $X$ and treat $X$ well' as in ( ex:nAtaR.stua ).

exe

nɤ-taʁ stu-a mbat-a ʑo ɕti\\
2sg. poss -on try.hard(1): fact - 1sg try.hard(2): fact - 1sg emph be. aff: fact \\
`I will treat you well.' (2005lobzang)
exe

Other intransitive verbs selecting oblique arguments in ɯ-taʁ include nɯrɕɤtslightly touch in passing (designating the object touched), ndzoʁbe attached ( ex:WtaR.kondzoR, § sec:anticausative.volitionality ) and the labile verb rpubump into (§ sec:goal.labile ).

The transitive verb lɤtrelease, when used as a light verb (§ sec:light.verb ) in collocation with nouns expressing either objects, weapons or substances that are thrown or that the subject hits people with, selects a phrase in ɯ-taʁ to indicate the recipient, as in ( ex:tWmci.pjWwGlAt ) and ( ex:scoRqhu.tulAt ). This recipient, although syntactically quite different from an object or a semi-object, can however be relativized using the object participle (§ sec:object.participle.other.relative ).

exe

ɯ-taʁ tɯ-mci pjɯ́-wɣ-lɤt \\
3sg. poss -on genr. poss -spit ipfv - inv -release \\
`If one spits on it,' (08-qaJAGi) 0003458#S27
exe

exe

ʁjoʁ ra nɯ-taʁ kɯnɤ kɤ-ari tɕe scoʁ-qʰu ci tu-lɤt, nɯ-ɣe tɕe tɤŋkʰɯt ci tu-lɤt \\
servant pl 3pl. poss -on also aor: east -go[II] lnk ladle-back once ipfv -release aor: west -come[II] lnk fist once ipfv -release \\
`Every time she went right she would hit the servants with the back of the ladle, every time she went left she hit them with the fist.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

In addition, the relator noun ɯ-taʁ is required with some categories of nouns in specific contexts.

First, ɯ-taʁ in combination with a noun designating a type of transport (boat, car etc) can express the transportation used in a particular trip. With the verb ɕego taking the orientation upwards, the meaning is `to take (a boat, a car etc)' as in ( ex:ZmbrW.WtaR.toCe ).

exe

ʑmbrɯ ɯ-taʁ to-ɕe tɕe jo-nɯ-ɕe \\
boat 3sg. poss -on ifr: up -go lnk ifr - vert -go \\
`He took a boat and went back home.' (150907 niexiaoqian-zh) 0006262#S130
exe
