The verb ɬoʁcome out with the orientation downwards in combination with ɯ-taʁ expresses the meaning `take off (a boat, a car etc)' as in ( ex:ZmbrW.WtaR.pjAlhoRnW ); the relator noun itself is neutral as to the type of location (static, motion from, motion towards)), a topic discussed in more detail in § sec:relator.postposition.location.

exe
summary: The inalienably possessed noun ɯ-stu ‘straight ahead’ is mainly used adverbially, but it can also function as a relator noun marking the goal of motion verbs. The relator noun ɯ-taʁ ‘on/above’ is used to form locative adjuncts or goals and is selected by various verbs to mark oblique arguments, including patients, beneficiaries/maleficiaries, and recipients. It is also required in some contexts with transport nouns to indicate taking or leaving by a vehicle, depending on the verb and orientation.

text:
ʑmbrɯ ɯ-taʁ pjɤ-ɬoʁ-nɯ \\
boat 3sg. poss -on ifr: down -come.out- pl \\
`They took off the boats.' (140508 shier ge tiaowu de gongzhu-zh) 0003937#S144
exe

To designate the means of transportation used during the whole travel (as opposed to the begin and end points of the travel as in ex:ZmbrW.WtaR.toCe and ex:ZmbrW.WtaR.pjAlhoRnW ), the relator noun ɯ-ŋgɯinside can also be used (§ sec:WNgW ).

The relator noun ɯ-taʁ also occurs to refer to a written medium, as in ( ex:jWGi.WtaR.tufCAt ).

exe

tɕe jɯɣi ɯ-taʁ tu-fɕɤt tɕe, \\
lnk book 3sg. poss -on ipfv -tell lnk \\
`It is told in a book, that...' (27-qaCpa) 0003716#S5
exe

The relator noun ɯ-ŋgɯinside
The relator noun ɯ-ŋgɯinside is only partially grammaticalized (§ sec:other.locative.relator ). However, it is selected by a few verbs to mark an oblique argument, in particular the goal of the transitive verbs rkuput in (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) and lɤt in the meaning `sow, spread' as in ( ex:khWtsa.WNgW.turkunW ).

exe

kʰɯtsa ɯ-ŋgɯ tɯ-ci tu-rku-nɯ tɕe, \\
bowl 3sg. poss -inside indef. poss -water ipfv -put.in- pl lnk \\
`People used to put water in a bowl, and...' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S117
exe

exe

tɯ-ji ɯ-ŋgɯ zɯ tsʰɤt ɯ-ɣli nɯ cʰɯ́-wɣ-lɤt tɕe, tɤ-rɤku wuma ʑo tu-sɤpe cʰa \\
indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -inside loc goat 3sg. poss -manure dem ipfv: downstream - inv -release lnk indef. poss -crops really emph ipfv -do.well can: fact \\
`If one spreads goat manure on the fields, it can make the crops grow really well.' (05-qaZo) 0003404#S28
exe

It is also found in combination with motion verb to express the means of transportation used during the whole travel, as in ( ex:chuzu.WNgW ).

exe

<chuzu> ɯ-ŋgɯ tʰɯ-ɣe-a tɕe \\
taxi 3sg. poss -inside aor: downstream -come[II]- 1sg lnk \\
`I came on a taxi.' (2010-01- Dpalcan )
exe
summary: The relator noun ɯ-taʁ ‘on’ can mark the means of transportation used for an entire journey, and it may also refer to a written medium, as in ‘It is told in a book.’ The relator noun ɯ-ŋgɯ ‘inside’ is only partly grammaticalized, but it is selected by some verbs to mark an oblique argument such as the goal of verbs like ‘put in’ and ‘sow, spread’. It can also combine with motion verbs to express the means of transportation used during the whole travel, as in ‘I came on a taxi.’

subsubsection: Locative relator nouns and locative postpositions
text:
All locative relator nouns can be also used with the locative postpositions zɯ, ri, tɕu and the fused forms of the latter two with the demonstratives nɯre and nɯtɕu (§ sec:locative ). Example ( ex:WtaR.ri.Wpa.ri ) illustrates the use of ɯ-taʁon, above and ɯ-pabelow, under with the locative ri expressing both static position (with the existential verb tuexist) and motion towards (with the verb lɤtrelease, here specifically meaning `direct water').

exe

ɯ-tʰɤcu maŋtʰi qʰajŋgɯ nɯ kɯ, nɤki, βɣa ɯ-pa ri tɕʰɯŋkʰɤr tu tɕe, tɕʰɯŋkʰɤr ɯ-taʁ ri cʰɯ-lɤt tɕe, tɕʰɯŋkʰɤr ɯ-taʁ nɯre ri βɣɤrnɤjwaʁ kɤ-ti tu tɕe \\
3sg. poss -downstream downstream water.trough dem erg filler mill 3sg. poss -under loc water.wheel exist: fact lnk water.wheel 3sg. poss -on loc ipfv: downstream -release lnk lnk water.wheel dem: loc loc blades obj: pcp -say exist: fact lnk \\
`The inferior water trough -- under the mill there is a water wheel -- [the water trough] directs [the water] onto that water wheel -- on the water wheel there are things called `blades'.' (06-BGa) 0003408#S23
exe

Example ( ex:Wpa.ri.tulhoR ) illustrates ɯ-pabelow, under with the locative ri expressing motion from a place.

exe

ɯ-tʰoʁ ɯ-pa ri tu-ɬoʁ nɯra mɯ́j-cʰa \\
3sg. poss -earth 3sg. poss -below loc ipfv: up -come.out dem: pl neg: sens -can \\
`[Its shoots] cannot come out from under the ground.' (15-babW)
0003512#S41
exe

Examples ( ex:khri.WtaR.zW ) and ( ex:WtaR.zW.kAmdzW ) above show the combination of ɯ-taʁon, above with the locative zɯ, also for static position and motion.

exe

χsɤr kʰri ɯ-taʁ zɯ pjɤ-rɤʑi tɕe ɯ-tɯ-ɣɤχsrɯ pjɤ-saχaʁ ʑo. \\
gold bed 3sg. poss -on loc ifr. ipfv -stay lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.handsome ifr. ipfv -be.extremely emph \\
`He was sitting on the golden bed, very handsome.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

The uses are attested with the locative tɕu, as shown by ( ex:WtaR.nWtCu.pjArAZi ) and ( ex:WtaR.nWtCu.YAXtAr ). No clear criterion accounting for the presence or absence of these locative postpositions in combination with the relator nouns has been found.

exe

rɟɤmtsʰu ɣɯ ɯ-rkɯ qambɯt ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu pjɤ-rɤʑi. \\
ocean gen 3sg. poss -side sand 3sg. poss -on dem: loc ifr. ipfv -stay \\
`He stayed on the beach.' (140511 xinbada-zh)
0003961#S159
exe

exe

tɕe ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu pɣɤmuj tɯ-spra nɯ ɲɤ-χtɤr. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -on dem: loc feather one-handful ifr -scatter \\
`He scattered a handful of feathers on it.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S309
exe

There is one case of a fossilized zɯ locative (§ sec:core.locative ) with the relator noun ɯ-ŋgɯinside, the form ɯ-ŋgɯzinside, among, which is used in particular to single out an element for a group, in particular in a superlative construction ( ex:kAndZWRi.nWNgWz ) (§ sec:stu.superlative ) or to describe an intermediate colour (with stative verbs, as in example ex:arNi.WNgWz ).

exe

kɤndʑiʁi nɯ-ŋgɯz stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯnɯ kɯ... nɯra ntsɯ tu-ti pjɤ-ŋu. \\
coll:siblings 3pl. poss -among: loc most sbj: pcp -be.small dem erg dem: pl always ipfv -say ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The youngest among the sisters was always saying...' (150828 donglang)
0006312#S26
exe

exe

nɯ ɯ-mdoʁ nɯ aj kɤ-ti mɯ́j-spe-a ma arŋi ɯ-ŋgɯz kɯnɤ pɣi kɯ-fse \\
dem 3sg. poss -colour dem 1sg inf -say neg: sens -be.able[III]- 1sg lnk be.green: fact 3sg. poss -inside: loc also be.grey: fact sbj: pcp -be.like \\
`I cannot say its colour, it is somewhere between green and grey.' (06-qaZmbri)
0003416#S50
exe
summary:
The passage explains that locative relator nouns can combine with several locative postpositions, especially zɯ, ri, tɕu, and fused forms with demonstratives nɯre and nɯtɕu. Examples show that these combinations can express both static location and motion from or toward a place, and the text notes that no clear rule has been found for when the postpositions appear or are omitted.  

It also mentions a fossilized form ɯ-ŋgɯz, derived from the locative zɯ with ɯ-ŋgɯ “inside/among,” which is used to single out one element in a group, especially in superlatives, or to describe intermediate colors.

text:
relator noun!temporal
Many temporal postpositions are found in Japhug (§ sec:egressive, § sec:terminative, § sec:temporal.postpositions ), and temporal relator nouns are relatively fewer. The relator ɯ-raŋduring, the time when (from Tibetan རིང་riŋlong, during, when) is very commonly used with subordinate clauses (§ sec:temporal.reference ), but can also follow temporal adverbs and nouns, as in (§ ex:XCitka.WraN ).

exe

χɕitka ɯ-raŋ tɕe, tɕendɤre pɣa ra, nɯ-kɤ-ndza maka cʰɯ-me ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, tɕendɤre ɯ-tɯ-mtsɯr pjɤ-saχaʁ ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
spring 3sg. poss -during lnk lnk bird pl 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -eat at.all ipfv -not.exist sens -be lnk lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.hungry ifr. ipfv -be.extremely emph sens -be \\
`In spring, the birds' food has gone out and [that crow] was extremely hungry.' (kWjujmAlu)
exe

The inalienably possessed noun ɯ-rɤɣ, whose basic meaning is `specific (and predictable) time' as ( ex:WrAG.GAZu ) (see also § sec:denom.arA ), can be used as relator noun as in ( ex:nW.WrAG.tCe.li ) to mean `the exact time when'.

exe

ɯ-rɤɣ ɣɤʑu ma nɤkinɯ sɲikuku ʑo ɲɯ-maʁ \\
3sg. poss -specific.time exist: sens lnk filler every.day emph sens -not.be \\
`[The rut] occurs at a specific time, not every day.' (27-qartshAz) 0003702#S150
exe

exe

tɕendɤre ɯ-fsaqʰe tɕe nɯ ɯ-rɤɣ tɕe li lo-ɣi \\
lnk 3sg. poss -next.year lnk dem 3sg. poss -specific.time lnk again ifr: upstream -come \\
`It came back at exactly the same time the next year.' (22-qomndroN) 0003598#S40
exe

There are two relator nouns that can be used as antonyms of the preposition ɕɯŋgɯbefore (§ sec:temporal.postpositions ), ɯ-mpʰruafter, following (from འཕྲོ་ⁿpʰroremnant, in particular in expressions such as དེའི་འཕྲོར་deɦi.ⁿpʰrornext, after that) and ɯ-qʰuafter, behind, which is also used for spatial relations (§ sec:other.locative.relator ). These two nouns are not synonymous. The former must be used in the expression ci ɯ-mpʰru cione after the other ( ex:ci.Wmphru.ci ), and means `next' as in ( ex:nW.Wmphru.tCe ), and can follow a subordinate clause, expressing temporal subsequence (§ sec:subsequence.neutral ), though most commonly a demonstrative pronoun such as nɯ or nɯnɯ referring to the previous clause is used instead, as in ( ex:nWnW.Wmphru.tWsla ).

exe

ci ɯ-mpʰru ci ʑo ko-nɯpoʁ qʰe lo-sɯ-ɣe. \\
one 3sg. poss -after one emph ifr -kiss lnk ifr: upstream - caus -come \\
`[The mother] kissed [her children] one after the one and had them come inside.' (160701 poucet2) 0006155#S38
exe

exe

tɕe nɯ ɯ-mpʰru tɕe tɕʰi to-ti? \\
lnk dem 3sg. poss -after lnk what ifr -say \\
`What does it say next?' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S103
exe

exe

tɕe tɯ-rdoʁ pjɤ-sat tɕe tɕeri nɯnɯ ɯ-mpʰru tɯ-sla jamar nɯnɯ tɯ-ci ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu ɯ-zda nɯ lo-ɕe nɤ cʰɤ-ɣi, lo-ɕe nɤ cʰɤ-ɣi ɲɤ-ɕar \\
lnk one-piece ifr -kill lnk lnk dem 3sg. poss -after one-month about dem indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -on dem: loc 3sg. poss -mater dem ifr: upstream -go lnk ifr: downstream -come ifr: upstream -go lnk ifr: downstream -come ifr -search \\
`[Someone] killed one of them, and after that, [the other one] flew along the river searching for its mate for about one month.' (22-qomndroN)
0003598#S38
exe

The locative relator ɯ-qʰuafter, behind also has temporal uses, in particular to build temporal subordinate clauses (§ sec:subsequence.neutral ), and it can also be used after noun phrases as in the expression saχsɯ ɯ-qʰu `after lunch, afternoon', or simply following a demonstrative as in nɯ ɯ-qʰuafter that.

Another originally locative relator noun has temporal functions: ɯ-pɤrtʰɤβthe middle of, which is used after the demonstrative nɯ to mean `in the meantime' ( ex:nW.WpArthAB.tCe ) and also occurs with temporal clauses with the meaning `while'.

exe

aʑo ku-ɕe-a tɕe z-ɲɯ-saʁjar-a ŋu tɕe nɯ ɯ-pɤrtʰɤβ tɕe nɯʑo ra kɯ ɕ-pɯ-rla-nɯ je tɕe lɤ-tsɯm-nɯ je \\
1sg ipfv: east -go- 1sg lnk tral - sens -delay- 1sg be: fact lnk dem 3sg. poss -in.the.middle loc 2pl pl erg tral - imp -untie- pl sfp lnk imp: upstream -take.away- pl sfp \\
`I will go there and delay him$_i$, and in the meantime, you go there and untie him$_j$, and take him$_j$ away.' (tWJo 2005)
0003368#S37
exe
summary:
The passage describes several Japhug relator nouns with temporal meanings, noting that temporal relator nouns are fewer than temporal postpositions. It explains that ɯ-raŋ means “during, the time when,” ɯ-rɤɣ means “the exact time when,” and that ɯ-mpʰru and ɯ-qʰu both mean “after” but are not synonymous, with ɯ-mpʰru also used for “next” and in fixed expressions.

It also notes that ɯ-qʰu can form temporal subordinate clauses and expressions like “after lunch” or “after that,” while ɯ-pɤrtʰɤβ, originally locative, can mean “in the meantime” with nɯ and “while” with temporal clauses.

text:
tɯ-jaʁhand, arm
The noun tɯ-jaʁhand, arm occurs with several verbs in fixed collocation, the recipient of the action being indexed by the possessive prefix on this noun.

It is found with kʰogive to express the meaning `hand over to' as in ( ex:ajaR.tAkhAm ) and ( ex:nAjaR.YWkhoj ).

exe

nɤki tɤtʂu nɯ a-jaʁ tɤ-kʰɤm! \\
dem: medial lamp dem, 1sg. poss -hand imp: up -give[III] \\
`Hand over to me (up here) that lamp.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S119
exe

exe

kɯki mbro ki nɤ-jaʁ ɲɯ-kʰo-j ŋu \\
dem. prox horse dem. prox 2sg. poss -hand ipfv -give- 1pl be: fact \\
`(If you succeed), we will give you this horse.' (2012-qachGa)
0004087#S60
exe

The collocation of tɯ-jaʁ with the intransitive verb zɣɯtarrive means `receive' or `obtain', as in ( ex:ajaR.anWzGWt ). With the causative form sɤzɣɯt, the collocation means `get' (with volition and controlability) as in ( ex:WjaR.junWsAzGWt ) -- the recipient marked by the possessive prefix on tɯ-jaʁ is the same referent as the transitive subject of the main verb.

exe

iɕqʰa tɤtʂu nɯ a-jaʁ a-nɯ-zɣɯt ra \\
the.aforementioned lamp dem 1sg. poss -hand irr - pfv -reach be.needed: fact \\
`I have to obtain this lamp.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S203
exe

exe

tɕʰi ra na-sɯso ʑo nɯ, ɯ-jaʁ ju-nɯ-sɯ-ɤzɣɯt pjɤ-cʰa. \\
what pl aor:3 -think emph dem 3sg. poss -hand ipfv - auto - caus -reach ifr. ipfv -can \\
`He was able to get whatever he wanted.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S46
exe

The collocation of the noun tɯ-jaʁhand, arm with the verb ɣicome also means `obtain' or `find', as in ( ex:tWjaR.mWjGi ).

exe

jinde tɕe ɯ-kɯ-sat koŋla maŋe tɕe, nɯ qarma ɯ-muj kɯnɤ tɯ-jaʁ mɯ́j-ɣi wo\\
nowadays lnk 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -kill completely not.exist: sens lnk dem crossoptilon 3sg. poss -feather also genr. poss -hand neg: sens -come sfp \\
`Nowadays, nobody kills them, and one cannot get crossoptilon feathers (to use as ornaments).' (23-qapGAmtWmtW)
0003608#S152
exe

The noun tɯ-jaʁhand, arm does not occur in metaphoric use outside of these collocations; it cannot be used in particular to mark any adjunct. Other noun-verb collocations where an experiencer or a recipient is marked as possessor of the noun are described in § sec:light.verb.
summary:
The noun **tɯ-jaʁ** ‘arm’ occurs in fixed noun-verb collocations, where the recipient of the action is indexed by a possessive prefix on the noun. With **kʰo** ‘give’ it means ‘hand over to’, with **zɣɯt** ‘arrive’ it means ‘receive/obtain’ and with the causative **sɤzɣɯt** it means ‘get,’ while the collocation with **ɣi** ‘come’ also means ‘obtain/find.’  

The noun is not used metaphorically outside these collocations and cannot mark arbitrary adjuncts. Other similar experiencer/recipient possessive constructions are discussed elsewhere in the grammar.

text:
relator noun
cause beneficiary
Two semi-grammaticalized inalienably possessed nouns can be used to express beneficiaries: ɯ-ndʐacause as in ( ex:nAndzxa.pWGea ), and ɯ-skɤtspeech, sound as in ( ex:kWpe.GW.WskAt ), though the latter is very rare. These two nouns also take complement clauses (§ sec:nouns.cause.complement, § sec:nouns.speech.complement ) instead of noun phrases.

exe

nɤʑo nɤ-ndʐa pɯ-ɣe-a ɕti \\
2sg 2sg. poss -reason pst: down -come[II]- 1sg be. aff: fact \\
`I came down [here] for you.' (2003 tWxtsa)
exe

exe

pʰa kɤmɲɯ ɣɯ kɯ-pe ɣɯ ɯ-skɤt nɯtɕu to-βzu-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
all topo gen sbj: pcp -be.good gen 3sg. poss -speech dem: loc ifr -make- pl sens -be \\
`People built it there for the benefit of all of Kamyu.' (150904 tshAcim)
0006274#S30
exe

The noun ɯ-tʰɯrʑimercy (borrowed from Tibetan ཐུགས་རྗེ་tʰugs.rdʑecompassion, also found in a collocation § sec:borrowed.NV ), occurs in a semi-grammaticalized construction meaning `thanks to', in combination with the ergative kɯ as an instrumental adjunct ( ex:nAthWrZi.kW ), or in absolutive form as a nominal predicate ( ex:smAn.WthWrZi ).

exe

pɯ-cʰa-a nɯra nɤj nɤ-tʰɯrʑi kɯ pɯ-cʰa-a \\
aor -can- 1sg dem: pl 2sg 2sg. poss -mercy erg aor -can- 1sg \\
`I succeeded all thanks to you.' (2011 04-smanmi)
exe

exe

ma jinde nɯra kɯ-fse kɤ-mtsʰɤm maŋe tɕe, smɤn ɯ-tʰɯrʑi ɯmɤ-ŋu ma \\
lnk nowadays dem: pl sbj: pcp -be.like inf -hear not.exist: sens lnk medicine 3sg. poss -mercy prob -be: fact lnk \\
`Nowadays we do not hear about [this disease], probably thanks to the medicine.' (27-tWfCAl)
0003710#S48
exe

The noun ɯ-xɕɤtstrength is also often used in instrumental adjuncts with the ergative to express cause, as in ( ex:WxCAt.kW2 ).

exe

tɤ-zdɯɣ ɯ-xɕɤt kɯ pjɯ-si ɕti, \\
indef. poss -toil 3sg. poss -strength erg/instr ipfv -die be: aff: fact \\
`[The bees] die of exhaustion.' (26 GZo) 0003668#S40
exe
summary: The passage describes several semi-grammaticalized nouns used to express beneficiary or cause meanings. Two inalienably possessed nouns, ɯ-ndʐa ‘reason/cause’ and the very rare ɯ-skɤt ‘speech, sound,’ can mark beneficiaries and also take complement clauses rather than noun phrases. It also notes that ɯ-tʰɯrʑi ‘mercy’ can mean ‘thanks to’ with ergative kɯ, and ɯ-xɕɤt ‘strength’ is often used similarly in instrumental adjuncts to express cause.

text: This section discusses all noun modifiers and determiners except those involving subordinate clauses (relative and complement clauses, discussed in chapter chap:relatives and § sec:complement.taking.nouns, respectively).
summary: This section covers all noun modifiers and determiners except those that involve subordinate clauses. Relative clauses and complement clauses are excluded and are discussed elsewhere in the grammar.

text: Japhug has two number markers, the dual ni and the plural ra. These clitics are not obligatory for non-singular arguments (even when these have human referents), and do not necessarily trigger plural or dual agreement on the verb (§ sec:optional.indexation ). Cognates of these markers in Gyalrong languages and beyond are discussed in § sec:indexation.suffixes.history.
summary: Japhug has two number markers: the dual clitic **ni** and the plural clitic **ra**. These markers are optional with non-singular arguments, including human ones, and they do not necessarily cause dual or plural agreement on the verb.

text:
dual number!dual
The dual ni is historically related to the numeral ʁnɯz (§ sec:one.to.ten ), but their relationship is synchronically opaque. It combines with the proximal and distal demonstratives ki and nɯ to form the dual demonstratives kɯni and nɯni, respectively (§ sec:demonstrative.pronouns, § sec:demonstrative.determiners ).

There is no semantic restriction on the use of ni, it most often occurs with human referents ( ex:awW.cho.aRi.ni, ex:Wmu.Wwa.ni, ex:tCiZo.ni, ex:ni.ndZisroR ), but is also commonly attested with animals ( ex:ʁnWz.ni ) inanimate objects ( ex:ni.RnaRna ), and placenames ( ex:rgWnba.ni ).

exe

prɤɕta cʰo rgɯnba ni ndʑi-pɤrtʰɤβ ri ŋu \\
topo comit monastery du 3du. poss -between loc be: fact \\
`It is between Prashta and the monastery.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo)
0004059#S112
exe

The marker ni can appear with a noun phrase comprising two nouns (each with singular referents) linked by the comitative cʰo (§ sec:comitative ) as in ( ex:rgWnba.ni ) and ( ex:awW.cho.aRi.ni ).

exe

tɕe a-wɯ cʰo a-ʁi ni pjɯ-tɯ-sat mɤ-jɤɣ \\
lnk 1sg. poss -grandfather comit 1sg. poss -younger.sibling du ipfv -2-kill neg -be.possible: fact \\
`You cannot kill my grandfather and my younger brother.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

The dual can follow the numeral ʁnɯztwo, as in ( ex:ʁnWz.ni ). This combination is however very rare (only 13 examples in the corpus out of hundreds of dual ni ). The opposite order (dual followed by numeral) is not grammatical.

exe

mbɣɤru nɯ jla ʁnɯz ni ndʑi-tʰɤβ ri ɲɯ-ɕe tɕe \\
plough.beam dem hybrid.yak two du 3du. poss -between loc ipfv: west -go lnk \\
`The beam of the plough goes between the two hybrid yaks.' (24-mbGo) 0003621
exe

The adverb ʁnaʁnaboth commonly co-occurs with dual, as in ( ex:ni.RnaRna ). It is exterior to the noun phrase, and must thus follow ni and all other postnominal determiners.

exe

zaŋ cʰo raʁ ni ʁnaʁna ʑo ʁja ku-te ɲɯ-ŋu \\
copper comit brass du both emph verdigris ipfv -put[III] sens -be \\
`Both copper and brass get verdigris.' (30-Com)
0003736#S99
exe

The dual can also be used with noun dyads (§ sec:dyads ), as in ( ex:Wmu.Wwa.ni ).

exe

ɯ-mu ɯ-wa ni kɯ ɲɯ-z-nɤja-ndʑi qʰe \\
3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss -father du erg ipfv - caus -be.a.pity- du lnk \\
`Her parents could not stand to part with her.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S275
exe

The third person dual pronoun ʑɤni is built by combining the pronominal root -ʑo- with the dual ni (§ sec:pers.pronouns ), and is not attested in combination with the dual. The first and second dual pronouns tɕiʑo and ndʑiʑo, do occur with the dual marker as in ( ex:tCiZo.ni ), though examples are very rare.

exe

tɕiʑo ni wuma ʑo pɯ-amɯmi-tɕi tɕe \\
1du du really emph pst. ipfv -be.on.good.terms- 1du lnk \\
`We were in harmony together.' (140512 fushang he yaomo-zh)
0003967#S78
exe

Noun phrases with the dual ni are always correlated with a dual prefix on the following noun in possessive constructions or with relator nouns, as in ( ex:rgWnba.ni ), ( ex:ʁnWz.ni ) and ( ex:ni.ndZisroR ). Not a single example of a noun phrase in ni followed by a noun with a singular or plural possessive prefix is found in the corpus.

exe

ɯ-pi ni ndʑi-sroʁ ko-ri tɕe \\
3sg. poss -elder.sibling du 3du. poss -life ifr -save lnk \\
`He saved the life of his two brothers.' (2012-qachGa)
0004087#S136
exe

The marker ni is not obligatory with dual referents, in particular when the numeral ʁnɯztwo is present.
There are in particular intrinsically collective nouns referring to a pair of individuals such as ʁzɤmihusband and wife, which can trigger dual indexation as in ( ex:RjWmbrWg.RzAmi ).

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe tɕe atu <qinghai> ʑɴɢɯloʁ nɯtɕu tɕe, ʁjɯmbrɯɣ ʁzɤmi ci pjɤ-tu-ndʑi tɕe, \\
in.former.times lnk lnk up.there anthr anthr dem: loc lnk dragon husband.and.wife one ifr. ipfv -exist- du lnk \\
`In former times, in Qinghai, in the Mgolog area, there was a couple of dragons.' (150820 qaprANar)
0006246#S40
exe

Such examples are however rare in the corpus; dual indexation is most often correlated with a dual marker on the corresponding noun phrase, if overt.

The numeral ʁnɯztwo without the dual also triggers dual indexation, as in ( ex:RnWz.tundZi ).

exe

sɯŋgɯ zɯ tɯrme wuma ʑo kɯ-wxti ʁnɯz tu-ndʑi tɕe\\
forest loc person really emph sbj: pcp -be.big two exist: fact - du lnk \\
`In the forest, there are two giants.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh)
0003886#S160
exe

Dual marking on a noun phrase is not necessarily correlated with dual indexation on the verb, especially, but not exclusively, with inanimate referents, as in ( ex:ni.tomto ) (§ sec:optional.indexation ).

exe

ɯ-mɲaʁ χcʰoʁe ni to-mto. \\
3sg. poss -eye left.and.right du aor -have.sight \\
`His left and right eyes recovered sight.' (140517 mogui de jing-zh) 0004022#S100
exe

However, a noun phrase with ni is never correlated with a plural indexation marker on the verb. Apparent exceptions are either speech errors, or cases of ambiguous indexation, as in ( ex:paznAkharnW ).

exe

nɤ-pi ni kɯ nɤʑo nɯɣi kɤ-sɯso kɯ ʁmaʁ χsɯ-tɤxɯr kɯ pa-z-nɤkʰar-nɯ ɕti tɕe, \\
2sg. poss -elder.sibling du erg 2sg come.back: fact inf -think erg soldier three-round erg aor:3 - caus -surround- pl be. aff: fact lnk \\
`Your two elder brothers, thinking that you are coming back, had [the palace] guarded on all sides by three rows of soldiers.' (2012-qachGa)
0004087#S154
exe
summary:
The dual marker **ni** is historically related to the numeral **ʁnɯz** ‘two’, though this connection is no longer synchronically transparent. It combines with demonstratives to form dual demonstratives, occurs with many kinds of referents, and can follow a numeral or a comitative-linked noun phrase, though numeral-plus-dual is rare and the reverse order is ungrammatical.

Dual **ni** often correlates with dual agreement/indexation, especially in possessive constructions, but this is not obligatory and is especially variable with inanimate referents. It is not required when duality is already clear from the numeral, and noun phrases with **ni** never take plural verbal indexation.

text:
Example ( ex:paznAkharnW ) is not completely straightforward, and deserves a detailed comment. The form paznɤkʰarnɯ can be parsed either as pɯ-az-nɤkʰar-nɯ pst. ipfv - prog -surround- pl `They were guarding it' with vowel fusion (§ sec:contraction ) or as pa-z-nɤkʰar-nɯ aor:3 - caus -surround- pl `(He/they) had them guard it'. Context makes it clear here that the second option is the correct one, in particular because in the same passage in another version of the same story, we find the verb pa-sɯ-lɤt ( aor:3 - caus -release) `he had (them) make' with the perfective 3 form of a causative verb (, § sec:sig.caus.allomorphs ). Moreover, while the phrase nɤ-pi ni kɯ `your two elder brothers' could in principle belong to the infinitival clause in kɤ-sɯso Incidentally, note that this infinitival clause contains another complement in Hybrid Reported Speech (§ sec:hybrid indirect )., it is clear from the context and the explanations provided by native speakers that nɤ-pi ni kɯ is the causer, and ʁmaʁ χsɯ-tɤxɯr kɯ `three rows of soldiers' is the causee (also marked by the ergative, see § sec:causee.kW ).

We thus observe plural indexation -nɯ on the main verb pa-z-nɤkʰar-nɯ, while the subject nɤ-pi ni kɯ has a dual marker. However, this is neither a counterexample to the number indexation rule stated above, nor a speech error: rather, it is a consequence of the fact that causees rather than causers can trigger number indexation on the verb.
summary: The passage clarifies an apparently ambiguous example by showing that the verb form is best analyzed as a causative meaning “had them guard it,” not as “they were guarding it,” based on context and a parallel form in the same story. It also explains that although the causer phrase is dual while the verb shows plural indexation, this does not violate the number-indexation rule, because in causative constructions the causee—not the causer—controls number marking on the verb.

text:
plural number!plural
The plural marker ra, like the dual, follows the noun and most of its modifiers, and fuses with the demonstratives ki and nɯ to build the plural demonstratives kɯra and nɯra, respectively (§ sec:demonstrative.pronouns, § sec:demonstrative.determiners ). It should not be confused with the auxiliary verb rabe needed, `be necessary' (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ), though there are cases where some ambiguity may occur.

Like the dual ni, the plural ra is compatible with both animate and inanimate referents, as in ( ex:si.ra.cho ) and ( ex:rdAstaR.ra ). It can be a plain marker of plurality as in ( ex:si.ra.cho ).

exe

kɯmaʁ si ra cʰo nɯ-mdoʁ mɤ-naχtɕɯɣ \\
other tree pl comit 3pl. poss -colour neg -be.the.same: fact \\
`Its colour is different from that of the other trees.' (`this tree and other trees, their colours are different') 11-qrontshom)
0003482#S52
exe

The marker ra is also often a similative plural, understandable as `and other things', `all kinds of' as in ( ex:rdAstaR.ra ).

exe

rdɤstaʁ ra pjɯ-tʂaβ-nɯ qʰe tɯrme tu-xtsɯɣ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
stone pl ipfv -cause.to.fall- pl lnk people ipfv -hit sens -be \\
`[Goats and sheep], (as they climb high) cause stones (and other things) to fall and these hit people.' (tshAt-qaZo-kAlAG) 0003420#S3
exe

The plural can follow numerals (even without head noun) to express an approximative number, as in ( ex:XsWm.kWBde ). Note that in ( ex:XsWm.kWBde ) ci ci is the expression for `sometimes' (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ), not used as a numeral.

exe

ci ci χsɯm kɯβde ra ɲɯ-lɤt ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl. tsuku tɕe ʁnɯz jamar ma mɯ́j-lɤt,\\
one one three four pl sens -throw sens -be.usually.the.case. some lnk two about apart.from neg: sens -throw \\
`Sometimes [dogs] have three or four [puppies], some only have two.' (05-khWna)
0003398#S18
exe

The plural marker ra can also indicate approximate location, with or without locative markers. In ( ex:kha.ra ), we find approximate location ra in kʰa ra `(everywhere) in the house, around the house' and tɯ-ji ɯ-ngɯ ra `in the fields', and in ( ex:nWrNa.ra ) with body parts.

exe

βʑɯ nɯ wuma ʑo ŋɤn tɕe, tɕendɤre aʁɤndɯndɤt ʑo kʰa ra cʰɯ-rɤpɯ. tɯ-ji ɯ-ngɯ ra cʰɯ-rɤpɯ, \\
mouse dem really emph be.evil: fact lnk lnk everywhere emph house pl ipfv -bear.young indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -inside pl ipfv -bear.young \\
`The mouse is fierce, it has pups everywhere in the house, and has pups in the fields.' (27-spjaNkW)
0006330#S46
exe

This use of ra can convey a meaning of distributed location, and is often combined with the adverb aʁɤndɯndɤteverywhere (§ sec:aRandWndAt ). It is reminiscent of plural markers in Kirghiz and Old Japanese, which combine collective, hypocoristic and approximate locative meanings.

exe

nɯ-βri ra ɲɯ-ɬoʁ, nɯ-mke nɯra ɲɯ-ɬoʁ nɯ-rŋa ra brɤβbrɤβ ʑo ɲɯ-ɬoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3pl. poss -body pl ipfv -come.out 3pl. poss -neck dem: pl ipfv -come.out 3pl. poss -face pl idph (II):covered.by.tiny.bumps emph ipfv -come.out sens -be \\
`[People who suffer from this disease have little blisters] appearing on their body, on their neck and all over their face.' (27-kharwut)
0003698#S56
exe

The marker ra even occurs with referents which are clearly singular, not only in the approximative location function, but also in examples such as ( ex:tAwi.ra ) where the reason for the presence of ra is less immediately obvious. In ( ex:tAwi.ra ), a sentence taken from the translation of Rotkäppchen into Japhug (however, the presence of ra cannot be due to calque since there is no plural marker in the original), the function of the plural on the phrase tɤ-wi ra `the grandmother' is more subtle: it conveys the idea that the impersonation takes on several aspects of the grandmother, not only her physical appearance, but also her voice, as implied by the second clause.

exe

qapar nɯ kɯ li, [...] tɤ-wi ra to-nɯɕpɯz tɕe, tɕe ɯ-skɤt ra cʰɤ-sɯ-ɤmtɕoʁ ʑo tɕe nɯra to-ti. \\
dhole dem erg again indef. poss -grandmother pl ifr -impersonate lnk lnk 3sg. poss -voice pl ifr - caus -be.sharp emph lnk dem: pl ifr -say \\
`The wolf was pretending to be the grandmother, and said these [words] with a sharp voice.' (140428 xiaohongmao-zh) 0003884#S91
exe

Just like noun phrases with dual ni correlate with dual possessive prefixes (see ex:ni.ndZisroR in § sec:dual.determiners ), those with plural ra can only be coreferent with a plural possessive prefix, as nɯ- in ( ex:si.ra.nWmat ).

exe

sɯku tɕe tʰɣe kɯ-fse, kɯmaʁ si ra nɯ-mat nɯra ɕ-pjɯ-nɯ-pʰɯt tɕe tu-ndze ɲɯ-ŋu.\\
tree lnk acorn sbj: pcp -be.like other tree pl 3pl. poss -fruit dem: pl tral - ipfv: down - auto -pluck lnk ipfv -eat[III] sens -be \\
`On the trees, [the bear] plucks acorn or fruits from other trees to eat.' (21-pri)
0003580#S43
exe

Apparent counterexamples such as ( ex:WtaR.ra.Wmat ), where ra is followed by a noun with the singular possessive prefix ɯ, occur when the preceding noun phrase is not the possessor of the following noun. For instance, in ( ex:WtaR.ra.Wmat ) ra in the locative phrase tɯ-ŋga ɯ-taʁ ra `on the clothes' has a vague locative function. The is a locative adjunct. The phrase tɯ-ŋga ɯ-taʁ ra cannot be analyzed as the possessor of ɯ-mat `its fruits', otherwise the 3pl possessor prefix nɯ- would be expected.

exe

tɯ-ŋga ɯ-taʁ ra ɯ-mat bɤbɤβ ʑo ku-ndzoʁ. \\
indef. poss -clothes 3sg. poss -on pl 3sg. poss -fruit idph (II):in.clusters emph ipfv - anticaus:attach \\
`Its seeds attach in clumps to one's clothes.' (18-qromJoR)
0003532#S159
exe

The plural ra very commonly occurs with headless relatives, with or without a demonstrative, as in ( ex:nW.tCaGi ), where we find both relatives followed by nɯnɯra and another one followed by ra.

exe
summary: The plural marker ra follows the noun and most modifiers, and combines with demonstratives ki and nɯ to form plural demonstratives kɯra and nɯra. It can mark plurality with animate or inanimate referents, but also has broader uses: it may express similative plurality (“and other things,” “all kinds of”), approximate number after numerals, approximate or distributed location, and occasionally occurs with singular referents to convey a more complex, collective-like meaning.

text:
[kɤ-ti mɤ-kɯ-pe kɯ-fse tu-kɯ-ti] nɯnɯra tɕe, [[kɤ-nɯtsɯ kɯ-ra] ra kɯnɤ tu-kɯ-ti] nɯnɯra,
tɯrme ra kɯnɤ, tɕaɣi tu-sɤrmi-nɯ ŋgrɤl. \\
inf -say neg - nmlz.S/A-be.good nmlz.S/A-be.like ipfv - nmlz.S/A-say dem: pl lnk inf -hide nmlz.S/A-be.needed pl also ipfv - nmlz.S/A-say dem: pl people pl also parrot ipfv -call- pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`Those who say things that one should not say, who say even what should be concealed, even [if they are] people, they call them `parrots'. (24-qro)
0003626#S113
exe

The plural ra also occurs between auxiliaries and the preceding complement clause with a verb in finite ( ex:GWkWnWru.ra ) or non-finite ( ex:kAnAjaR.ra ) form, with a vague implication that additional related actions are concerned.

exe

li tɯ-ji ɯ-ŋgɯ ra ɣɯ-ku-nɯru ra ŋgrɤl. \\
again indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -inside pl cisl - ipfv -eat.crops pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`It also usually comes to eat crops in the fields.' (24-ZmbrWpGa) 0003628#S35
exe

exe

ɣɤmdzu tɕe nɯnɯ kɤ-nɤjaʁ ra mɤ-sɤ-nɤz tɕe \\
be.thorny: fact lnk dem inf -touch pl neg - prop -dare: fact lnk \\
`It is thorny and one does not dare to touch it with the hand.' (11-qrontshom) 0003482#S85
exe

The marker ra following a locative noun or adverb can have the meaning `the people/things from X', as in ( ex:alo.ra ), without the need to add a demonstrative (cf ex:aki.nW § sec:demonstrative.determiners ).

exe

alo ra ɲɯ-mbɣom-nɯ qʰe \\
upstream pl sens -be.in.a.hurry- pl lnk \\
`Those in the village, they [do things] in a hurry.' (conversation140510 tshering)
exe
summary: The plural marker *ra* can appear between auxiliaries and a preceding complement clause, whether the verb is finite or non-finite, with a vague sense that additional related actions are included. It also occurs after locative nouns or adverbs to mean ‘the people/things from X,’ without requiring a demonstrative.

text:
plural!honorific
The plural marker ra is also used as an honorific marker on terms of address as a-ʑi ra `my young lady' in ( ex:aZi.ra ), correlating with the plural possessive prefix nɯ- and sometimes plural indexation (§ sec:honorific.indexation ).

exe

a-ʑi ra nɯ-<bandeng> ɲɯ-ɕar-a ɕi aʑo tu-ozgrɯ-a ma \\
1sg. poss -young.lady pl 3pl. poss -seat ipfv -look.for- 1sg qu 1sg ipfv -bend- 1sg lnk \\
`Young lady, should I look for a seat for you, or bend down [for you to sit on my back]?' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

The honorific function of plural number is also attested with the pronoun nɯʑo (§ sec:honorific.pronouns ).
summary: The plural marker **ra** can also function as an **honorific** on terms of address, as in *a-ʑi ra* “my young lady,” and this use correlates with the plural possessive prefix **nɯ-** and sometimes plural indexation. The text also notes that plural number has an honorific function with the pronoun **nɯʑo** as well.

text:
demonstrative!determiner
Japhug demonstrative determiners are formally identical to the demonstrative pronouns (§ sec:demonstrative.pronouns ). They distinguish between proximal and distal demonstratives with different roots, and fuse with the dual and plural markers studied in § sec:number.determiners; the proximal ki undergoes change to kɯ- in those fused forms.

As with the demonstrative pronouns, there are three sets of demonstratives, the base form, the reduplicated one (obtained by reduplicating the first syllable), and the emphatic one, with added ɯ- prefix. Note that the latter two sets are not attested in the dual for determiners in the corpus, but the forms exist and are easily deducible from the corresponding plural ones. In addition, there is a medial demonstrative nɤki which occurs in prenominal position.

In Japhug, as in other Gyalrong languages, demonstrative determiners can be either/both pre- and postnominal as shown by an example such as ( ex:ki.srWnloRpW.ki ), with the proximal ki both before and after the noun srɯnloʁpɯlittle ring.

exe

aʑo ɣɯ-ɕaβ-a tɤ-ŋu tɕe, ki srɯnloʁ-pɯ ki ɲɯ-ɕtʰɯz-a tɕe, \\
1sg inv -catch.up: fact - 1sg aor -be lnk dem. prox ring- dim dem. prox ipfv: west -turn.toward- 1sg lnk \\
`When [the râkshasas] are about to catch up with me, I will turn this little ring towards west [in their direction].' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S209
exe

All possible combinations of base demonstratives (B) and reduplicated demonstratives (R) are attested as pre- or postnominal determiners:

itemize
BNB: ki N ki, nɯ N nɯ ( ex:ki.srWnloRpW.ki )
RNB: kɯki N ki, nɯnɯ N nɯ ( ex:kWki.tAYi.ki )
BNR: ki N kɯki, nɯ N nɯnɯ ( ex:ki.rgAtpu.kWki )
RNR: kɯki N kɯki, nɯnɯ N nɯnɯ ( ex:kWki.qingjiao.kWki )
itemize

The types BNB and RNB, with the postnominal determiner as a base demonstrative, are by far the most common ones in the corpus.

exe

aʑo kɯki tɤɲi ki lu-nɤkʰɯkʰrɯt-a tɕe \\
1sg dem. prox staff dem. prox ipfv: upstream -drag- 1sg lnk \\
`I will drag along this staff [on the ground].' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

exe

iɕqʰa kɯki <qingjiao> kɯki tɕe, ɯ-qa kɯ-wɣrum ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
the.aforementioned dem. prox plant.name dem. prox lnk 3sg. poss -root sbj: pcp -be.white sens -be \\
`This [plant that is called] qingjiao (in Chinese), its root is white (unlike the other qingjiao whose root is red).' (17-ndZWnW) 0003524#S75
exe

exe

ki rgɤtpu kɯki kɯ, iɕqʰa, qaʑo nɯ to-mtsʰi qʰe, li tʂu kɯ-wxti nɯtɕu jo-ɕe tɕe, \\
dem. prox old.man dem. prox erg the.aforementioned sheep dem ifr -lead lnk again road sbj: pcp -be.big dem: loc ifr -go lnk \\
`The old man, leading the sheep, went to the big road.' (150822 laoye zuoshi zongshi duide-zh)
0006298#S98
exe

The emphatic form is very rare prenominally. In ( ex:WkWki.arZaB.kWki ), prenominal ɯkɯki occurs to put contrastive focus on the noun to avoid potential confusion with the subject of the sentence (` this wife of mine, not his wife').

exe

nɯ ɯ-rʑaβ nɯ kɯ, ɯkɯki a-rʑaβ kɯki, kɯki ɕkom ki na-sɯ-ɤβzu tɕe, \\
dem 3sg. poss -wife dem erg dem. prox. emph 1sg. poss -wide dem. prox dem. prox muntjac dem. prox aor:3 - caus -become lnk \\
`[My son's] wife turned this wife of mine into this muntjac.' (140512 fushang he yaomo-zh)
0003967#S173
exe

When the postnominal demonstrative is in plural or dual form, the prenominal one is generally unmarked for number, as in ( ex:kWki.tCheme.kWra ).

exe

kɯki tɕʰeme kɯra nɯ-rca aʑo tu-ɕe-a ɲɯ-ntsʰi ma mɯ́j-pe \\
dem girl dem: pl 3pl. poss -following 1sg ipfv: up -go- 1sg sens -have.better apart.from neg: sens -be.good \\
`I have no other choice but to go [to heaven] with these girls.' (31-deluge)
0004077#S61
exe

However, there are also a few examples with plural marking on both pre- and postnominal demonstratives, as in ( ex:nWnWra.pGa.nWra ), a remarkable phenomenon given the fact that the number markers are strictly postnominal. This raises the question whether nɯnɯra should be analyzed as a prenominal demonstrative, forming a constituent with pɣa nɯra. There is no pause between nɯnɯra and pɣa in the sound file, but I cannot exclude the possibility that nɯnɯra here as a left-dislocated demonstrative (and should be followed by a comma). Plural marking on the prenominal demonstrative with a singular postnominal demonstrative is not attested.

exe

nɯnɯra pɣa nɯra lonba ʑo ɲɤ-me-nɯ tɕe, ʁʑɯnɯ sqaptɯɣ ɲɤ-k-ɤpa-nɯ-ci. \\
dem. pl bird dem. pl all emph ifr -not.exist lnk young.man eleven ifr - peg -become- pl - peg \\
`All those birds disappeared, and became eleven young men.' (140520 ye tiane-zh)
0004044#S113
exe

Proximal prenominal demonstratives can be combined with the postnominal nɯ, as in ( ex:kWki.Xpi.nW ), where the latter one is used as a topic marker. The opposite combination, a distal prenominal demonstrative with proximal postnominal one, is not attested in the corpus and presumably agrammatical.

exe

kɯki χpi nɯ pɯpɯŋu nɤ, \\
dem. prox story dem top lnk \\
`As far as this story goes,' (11 examples in the corpus)
exe

The medial demonstrative nɤki, used to designate referents closer to the addressee than to the speaker, is found as a pronoun (§ sec:medial.dem.pro ), but also occurs as a prenominal determiner, with or without postnominal demonstrative (either proximal or distal), as in ( ex:nAki.nAtAYi ) and ( ex:nAki.nAtAri ). It is frequently used with a noun taking a second person possessive prefix -- note that the first syllable nɤ- of the demonstrative nɤki itself probably originates from the second singular possessive, as proposed in § sec:medial.dem.pro.

exe

nɤki nɯ-tɤɲi ɯ-taʁ kɤ-rɤt nɯ ɯβrɤ-kɯ-z-nɤmɲo-a-nɯ \\
dem: medial 2pl. poss -staff 3sg. poss -on obj: pcp -write dem rh. q -2 1- caus -watch- 1sg - pl \\
`You wouldn't show me what is written on that staff of yours, would you?' (2003 sras)
exe

exe

nɤki nɤ-tɤ-ri nɯ ŋotɕu pɯ-tu \\
dem: medial 2sg. poss - indef. poss -thread dem where pst. ipfv -exist \\
`That thread of yours, where is it from?' (2005 Norbzang)
exe
summary:
Japhug demonstrative determiners are formally identical to demonstrative pronouns and distinguish proximal and distal forms, with the proximal ki changing to kɯ- when fused with dual or plural markers. They occur in base, reduplicated, and emphatic forms, and can appear both before and after the noun; the most common patterns are those with a base postnominal demonstrative, while emphatic prenominal forms are rare and used for contrast.

The medial demonstrative nɤki also functions as a prenominal determiner, sometimes combined with other demonstratives, especially in contexts involving second-person possessive prefixes. The passage also notes some unusual number-marking patterns, including a few cases where both pre- and postnominal demonstratives carry plural marking.

text:
The relative position of prenominal demonstratives and other pronominal elements is not free. The aforementioned topic marker iɕqʰa (§ sec:iCqha ) strictly occurs before prenominal demonstratives (as in ex:kWki.qingjiao.kWki ), while nominal modifiers such as χsɤrgold in ( ex:kWki.XsAr.pGAtCW ) appear closer to the noun.

exe

kɯki χsɤr pɣɤtɕɯ ki nɤ-jaʁ ɲɯ-kʰam-a ŋu \\
dem. prox gold bird dem. prox 1sg. poss -hand ipfv -give[III]- 1sg be: fact \\
`(If you succeed) I will give you this golden bird.' (2012-qachGa)
0004087#S45
exe

exe

nɯtɕu a-tɯrsa ŋu, tɕe nɤʑo kɯ [nɯ aʑo a-ɕɤrɯ nɯnɯra] a-tɤ-tɯ-tɕɤt tɕe, \\
dem: loc 1sg. poss -tomb be: fact lnk 2sg erg dem 1sg 1sg. poss -bone dem: pl irr - pfv -2-take.out lnk \\
`My tomb is there, if you take out my bones,...' (150907 niexiaoqian-zh)
0006262#S105
exe

Pronouns coreferent with a possessive prefix on the head noun, however, can be placed either after ( ex:nW.aZo.aCArW.nW ) or before ( ex:aZo.ki.aku.ki ) prenominal demonstratives.

exe

kɯki, aʑo [ki a-ku ki] pɯ-pʰɯt ra \\
dem. prox 1sg dem. prox 1sg. poss -head dem. prox imp -cut be.needed: fact \\
`Please behead me!' (140507 jinniao-zh)
0003931#S297
exe

The principles governing the presence and absence of the demonstrative determiners, and the choice of the various patterns described above, is particularly complex to describe and will be a topic for future research, when a larger corpus of texts will become available. While the proximal demonstratives always have some deictic function (although it may not always be appropriate to translate them with a demonstrative in other languages such as English), the distal demonstratives clearly contribute to marking topic (§ sec:topic ) and definiteness (§ sec:definiteness ), and disentangling these various functions is a complex matter.

The distal demonstratives nɯ and nɯnɯ are particularily common after relative clauses (either participial § sec:participial.relatives or finite ones § sec:finite.relatives ) and complement clauses, where arguments against analysing these forms as complementizers are provided (§ sec:complement.determiner ).

Following locative adverbs or locative postpositional phrases, the distal and proximal demonstratives can be used to express the meaning `the one/those (at) $X$' as in ( ex:athi.ki ) and ( ex:aki.nW ). Note that the number determiner ra can also be used in the same way (example ex:alo.ra in § sec:plural.determiners ) even without being combined with a demonstrative.

exe

amaŋ amaŋ, atʰi ki kɯ `a-βɣo mɤ-a<nɯ>tɯɣ-a tɕe a-scawa' ɲɯ-sɯsɤm ɲɯ-ŋu ɣe \\
interj: surprise interj: surprise downstream dem. prox erg 1sg. poss -uncle neg -<auto>meet: fact - 1sg lnk 1sg. poss -poor sens -think[III] sens -be sfp \\
`The one down there, he is thinking `Poor me, I will not meet my lama', isn't he?' (2003kandZislama)
0006147#S142
exe

exe

a-pa, aki nɯ staʁlupa kɤ-βde ɯ-spa nɯ mɤ-nɯ-xsi ri, \\
1sg. poss -father down dem born.in.the.year.of.the.tiger obj: pcp -throw.away 3sg. poss -material dem neg - auto - genr:know lnk \\
`Father, the one down there, I don't know if he is a [boy] born in the year of the Tiger, to be thrown [into the lake], but...' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

Note however that demonstratives or number markers are not absolutely necessary in such a context. A few (rare) examples of locative postpositional phrases meaning `the one at/in/from' without any modifier can be found, as in ( ex:sWkAku.nWtCu ), where the postpositional phrase is directly followed by the dative, here used in its locative meaning `by (the side of), near, at' (§ sec:dative ). In this example, the phrase sɯkɤku nɯtɕu does not mean `on the treetop', but `the man who is on the treetop'. The story from which this example is taken is about three thieves who mistakenly steal a tiger during the night, believing it was an ox; one of the three thieves flees on the top of a tree -- his manner of fleeing being here the characteristic distinguishing him from the other two thieves.

exe

[sɯkɤku nɯtɕu] ɯ-pʰe nɯtɕu lo-zɣɯt-ndʑi tɕe\\
treetop dem: loc 3sg. poss - dat dem: loc ifr: upstream -reach- du lnk \\
`[The tiger and the fox] arrived at [the place where the one who was] on the treetop [was].' (2012-x1-khu)
0004085#S45
exe
summary: Prenominal demonstratives have a fixed position relative to other elements: the topic marker iɕqʰa must come before them, while nominal modifiers such as adjectives or nouns like “gold” occur closer to the noun. Pronouns coreferent with a possessive prefix may appear either before or after prenominal demonstratives, and the overall system of demonstratives is complex, with proximal forms mainly deictic and distal forms marking topic and definiteness. Distal demonstratives are especially common after relative and complement clauses, and demonstratives or even just locative phrases can express meanings like “the one at X.”

text: This section only discusses universal, mid-scalar and specifically distributive quantifiers; numerals and counted nouns, which also serve as quantifiers (in particular distributive ones), are described in chapter chap:numerals.
summary: This section focuses only on universal, mid-scalar, and specifically distributive quantifiers. Numerals and counted nouns are also quantifiers, especially distributive ones, but they are treated separately in the chapter on numerals.

text:
universal quantifier!determinier quantifier!universal
The determiner tʰamtɕɤtall, from Tibetan ཐམས་ཅད་tʰams.cadall, is strictly postnominal, as in ( si.thamCAt.kW ). It cannot be used as a pronoun, and there are no examples in the corpus of tʰamtɕɤtall following a personal pronoun.

exe

sɯŋgɯ kɤ-kɯ-nɯχtɕɤn tɕe tɕe si tʰamtɕɤt kɯ nɯnɯ pjɯ-kɯ-sat kɯ-ŋgrɤl ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
forest aor - sbj: pcp -be.dangerous lnk lnk tree all erg dem ipfv - genr:S/O-kill sbj: pcp -be.usually.the.case sens -be \\
`The fierce/dangerous forest, it was (a place where) all the trees would kill [people thrown into it].' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S176
exe

The combination of a demonstrative such as nɯthat with tʰamtɕɤtall does not mean `all of this', but `so much, so many', as in ( kha.nW.thamCAt ). In this function, the prefixed form stʰamtɕɤtso much (§ sec:denominal.adverb.s.prefix ) is generally used, resulting in the form nɯstʰamtɕɤtthat much (§ sec:nWtshWci ).

exe

iʑora tʰɯ-dɤn-i qʰe, kʰa nɯ tʰamtɕɤt mɯ-ɲɯ-ɤmɯ-xtɕʰɯt-i qʰe \\
1pl aor -be.many- 1pl lnk house dem all neg - sens - recip -have.enough.place- 1pl lnk \\
`There was more of us [than before], and so many of us could not fit in the house.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S94
exe

Another universal quantifier, kɤsɯfseall, is common as a pronoun (§ sec:quantifiers.pronouns ). It is analyzable as a determiner in examples like ( ex:kAtsa.ra.kAsWfse.kW ) where it follows the plural marker ra, and takes the ergative kɯ. It is restricted to human human referents.

exe

kɤtsa ra kɤsɯfse kɯ wuma ʑo pjɤ-nɯ-rga-nɯ \\
parents.and.children pl all erg really emph ifr. ipfv - appl -like- pl \\
`Everybody in the family liked her very much.' (140429 qingwa wangzi) 0003890#S5
exe

The universal quantifier lonbaall (from Tibetan ལོན་པ་lon.pareached, enough, completed), like kɤsɯfseall, also occurs after (never before) demonstratives and number markers as in ( ex:aRi.lonba ).

exe

aʑo a-ʁi nɯra lonba aʑo kɯ tɤ-nɤpɯpa-t-a \\
1sg 1sg. poss -younger.sibling dem: pl all 1sg erg aor -take.care- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`It was I who took care of all my younger brothers and sisters.' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR4)
exe

In ( ex:lonba.akhAcAl ), lonba follows and has scope over the complement clause of the noun of speech kʰɤcɤldiscussion (§ sec:nouns.speech.complement ).

exe

[a-wa nɯ tɕʰi kɯ-fse ci pɯ-ŋu kɯ] lonba a-kʰɤcɤl pɯ-fɕɤt ra \\
1sg. poss -father dem what sbj: pcp -be.like indef pst. ipfv -be sfp all 1sg. poss -discussion imp -tell be.needed: fact \\
`Tell me all about what happened to my father.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

In ( ex:nWrmi.lonba ), it has scope over the possessor of the head noun nɯ-rmi `their names' redundantly with tʰamtɕɤt. Here nɯ-rmi lonba could be glossed as nɯ-rmi nɯ-tɤngɯt `their name as a whole', `their collective name' (example ex:nWrmi.nWtAngWt, § ex:attributive.postnominal ).

exe

nɯ-zda rɯdaʁ ɯ-kɯ-ndza tʰamtɕɤt nɯnɯra nɯ-rmi lonba kɯrŋi tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
3pl. poss -companion animal 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -eat all dem: pl 3pl. poss -name all beast ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`All those that eat the other animals, their generic name is `beast'.' (150822 kWrNi)
0006260#S7
exe

An alternative construction with a meaning similar to a universal quantifier is totalitative reduplication (§ sec:totalitative.redp ). In particular, the totalitative participle kɯ kɯ-tu `all who exist' (§ sec:headless.relatives.quantification ) of the existential verb tuexist commonly occurs with a preceding noun phrase (in a head-internal relative, as in ex:Wzda.kWkWtu.kW ) or on its own (as a headless relative) as a semi-lexicalized quantifier `all'.

exe

tɕe [ɯ-zda ra kɯ kɯ-tu] kɯ nɯ-rʑaβ na-nɯ-ɕar-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
lnk 3sg. poss -companion pl total sbj: pcp -exist erg 3pl. poss -wife aor:3 - auto -look.for- pl sens -be \\
`All of his companions took [other women] as their wives.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

The semantic proximity between totalitative reduplication and universal quantifiers such as tʰamtɕɤtall is shown by examples such as ( ex:tWrju.kWkWpe.thamtCAt ), where both are used redundantly.

exe

<wangbapi> nɯ kɯ, tɯrju kɯ kɯ-pe, kɯ-mpɕɤr tʰamtɕɤt spɯ spe ʑo to-ti ri \\
anthr dem erg word total sbj: pcp -be.good sbj: pcp -be.beautiful all total be.able: fact emph ifr -say lnk \\
`Wang Bapi had said all the nice and pleasant words that he could [to convince the old man].' (150831 jubaopen-zh)
0006294#S82
exe

The marker pʰawhole is exceptional in terms of word order, as it is the only strictly prenominal quantifier, occurring directly before the noun on which it has scope, as the following examples illustrate. It partially overlaps in meaning with the previous markers, as it can express the totality of individuals in a group as in ( ex:pha.mkhArmaN ) (see also for instance ex:chAsAwWwum, § sec:reciprocal.other ), and also occurs with names of localities to refer to all the persons living in the place ( ex:pha.RdWrJAt, § sec:place.names ).

exe

ʑara kɯ iɕqʰa sɤtɕʰa ɣɯ ɯ-rɟɤlpu tʰa-nɯ-ndo-nɯ ndɤre pʰa mkʰɤrmaŋ ʑo ta-sɤpe-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3pl erg the.aforementioned place gen 3sg. poss -king aor:3 - auto -take- pl lnk whole population emph aor:3 -do.good- pl sens -be \\
`They became kings of this place, and treated well the whole population.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

Its core meaning however is to express the entirety of an object/entity, as in the noun phrase pʰa ɯ-pʰoŋbu `its whole body' in ( ex:pha.WphoNbu ). If an overt possessor (for instance, the 3sg pronoun ɯʑo ) is present, it occurs stranded before pʰawhole, as in ( ex:WZo.pha.WphoNbu ).

exe

ma pʰa ɯ-pʰoŋbu ʑo ɯ-mdzu tu ri, ɯ-mat ɯ-taʁ ʑo ɯ-mdzu me, \\
lnk whole 3sg. poss -body emph 3sg. poss -thorn exist: fact lnk 3sg. poss -fruit 3sg. poss -on emph 3sg. poss -thorn not.exist: fact \\
`It has thorns on its whole body, but no thorns on its fruits.' (15-babW)
0003512#S245
exe

exe

ɯʑo$_i$ pʰa ɯ$_i$-pʰoŋbu \\
3sg whole 3sg. poss -body \\
`Its whole body' (several attestations)
exe
summary: The passage describes several quantifier-like forms in the language and their distribution. The determiner **tʰamtɕɤt** ‘all’ is strictly postnominal, cannot be used as a pronoun, and with demonstratives it means ‘so much/many’ rather than ‘all of this’; another universal quantifier, **kɤsɯfse**, is common as a pronoun and is limited to human referents, while **lonba** also follows demonstratives and number markers and can have scope over larger noun phrases or clauses. It also notes that **totalitative reduplication** can function similarly to a universal quantifier, and that **pʰa** is exceptional as the only strictly prenominal quantifier, expressing the entirety of an entity or all persons in a place.

text:
quantifier!mid-scalar
The quantifier tsukusome is generally used as a pronoun (§ sec:partitive.pronouns ), but it does occur as a prenominal determiner as in ( ex:tsuku.tWrme ), or a postnominal one as in ( ex:kWmtChW.tsuku ) and ( ex:kWmWrkW.tsuku ). It is most often used in the corpus with human referents, but is compatible with inanimate objects, as shown by ( ex:kWmtChW.tsuku ).

exe

tsuku tɯrme ra kú-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-nɯ tɕe mɯ́j-ʁdɯɣ, tsuku tɯrme ra [...] kú-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-nɯ tɕe tɕe, wuma ʑo cʰɯ́-wɣ-z-nɯɣmbɤβ-nɯ qʰe ɲɯ́-wɣ-z-nɯtɯfɕɤl-nɯ qʰe ku-rŋgɯ-nɯ ɲɯ-ra.\\
some people pl ipfv - inv -bite- pl lnk neg. sens -be.serious some people pl ipfv - inv -bite- pl lnk lnk really emph ipfv - inv - caus -swell- pl lnk ipfv - inv - caus -have.diarrhea- pl lnk ipfv -lie.down- pl sens -be.needed\\
`Some people, when they are stung (by bees) are fine, other people, when they are stung, it causes them swelling and diarrhea and they have to lie down.' (26-ndzWrnaR)
0003678#S61
exe

exe

`pjɯ-nɯβle-a ɲɯ-ra' ɲɤ-sɯso tɕe, kɯmtɕʰɯ tsuku ɲɤ-kʰo tɕe, \\
ipfv -cheat[III]- 1sg sens -be.needed ifr -think lnk toy some ifr -give lnk \\
`She thought `Let's cheat him' and gave him some toys.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S115
exe

exe

ri kɯ-mɯrkɯ tsuku pjɤ-tu-nɯ tɕe tɕe, \\
lnk sbj: pcp -steal some ifr. ipfv -exist- pl lnk lnk \\
`There were some thieves.' (X1-khu)
0004085#S8
exe

Note in ( ex:tsuku.tWrme.tWrdoR ) the combination of the quantifier tsukusome with the counted noun tɯ-rdoʁone piece, which expresses here a restrictive meaning (thirteen or fifteen children for a single person, § sec:CN.restrictive ).

exe

tsuku tɯrme tɯ-rdoʁ ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit, sqafsum jamar, sqamŋu jamar tu-kɯ-tu pjɤ-tu. \\
some person one-piece gen 3sg. poss -offspring thirteen about fifteen about ipfv - genr:S/A-exist ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`[In] some [cases], a single [woman] had thirteen or fifteen children.' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR)
exe
summary: The quantifier **tsukusome** is normally used as a pronoun, but it can also appear as a prenominal or postnominal determiner. In the corpus it most often refers to humans, though it can also modify inanimate nouns, and when combined with a counted noun such as **tɯ-rdoʁ** ‘one piece,’ it can express a restrictive meaning.

text:
quantifier!distributive distributive!quantifier
Although distributive meaning is generally expressed in Japhug with a counted noun (§ sec:CN.distributive ), the postnominal determiner raŋrieach and its variant rɯrieach (from Tibetan རང་རེ་raŋ.reeach and རེ་རེ་re.reeach) can also express distributive meaning, as in ( ex:tWtWpW.raNri ).

exe

paʁ rcanɯ, tɯ-tɯpɯ raŋri kɯ ʑo pjɯ-χsu-nɯ ra.\\
pig unexp: deg one-household each erg emph ipfv -raise- pl be.needed: fact \\
`Each single household has to raise pigs.' (05-paR) 0003400#S4
exe

It can also be used with numerals, as in ( ex:sqamNu.raNri ), where it refers specifically to days.

exe

sqamŋu raŋri ʑo zgo tu-ɕe pɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
fifteen each emph mountain ipfv: up -go pst. ipfv -be sens -be \\
`Every fifteen days, she would go up the mountain.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

When the quantifier raŋrieach occurs in the same sentence with a counted noun, the scope of the two quantifiers is ambiguous, as in ( ex:rirAB.raNri ).

exe

rirɤβ raŋri χsɯ-tɤxɯr a-tɤ-tɯ-sɯ-lɤt tɕe, \\
mountain each three-lap irr - pfv -2- caus -throw lnk \\
`Drag her three times around each mountain.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

In the predicative possessive construction (§ sec:possessive.mihi.est ), when the possessor takes the determiner raŋri, its possessum is often followed by the distributive determiner tɯkaeach (and its reduplicated variant tɯkaka ) as in ( ex:Wmat.raNri ).

exe

iɕqʰa ɯ-mat raŋri ʑo nɯ ɯ-ru tɯka ntsɯ tu. \\
the.aforementioned 3sg. poss -fruit each emph dem 3sg. poss -stalk own always exist: fact \\
`Each of its fruits has its own stalk.' (17-thowum)
0003526#S34
exe

The determiner tɯkaeach can also be used without a possessor in raŋri, for example with the distributive pronouns ʑakaeach his own and ʑakastakaeach his own (§ sec:distributive.pronouns ) as in ( ex:nWkho.tWka ).

exe

ʑakastaka nɯ-kʰo tɯka pjɤ-tu tɕe \\
each.his.own 3pl. poss -room each ifr. ipfv -exist lnk \\
`Each of them had her own room.' (140508 shie ge tiaowu de gongzhu)
0003937#S81
exe

In addition to the possessive construction, tɯkaeach also occurs in transitive constructions, following objects, with broad scope over the whole action ( ex:pCaR.tWka ).

exe

pɕaʁ tɯka to-βzu-nɯ tɕe jo-nɯ-ɕe-nɯ. \\
reverence each ifr -make- pl lnk ifr - vert -go- pl \\
`Each of them made a reverence and went back.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S162
exe

The aspectual adverb ntsɯalways, which generally has scope over the whole sentence (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs, § sec:postverbal.adv ), can also be used as a distributive quantifier as in ( ex:RnWpArme.machAti ), where its scope is restricted to the temporal phrase ʁnɯ-pɤrme nɤ ʁnɯ-pɤrme `by two years' (with the additive nɤ, § sec:additive.nA ). On the morphosyntax of the verb acʰɤtbe $X$ years apart, see § sec:a.non.passive.denominal.

exe

tɕe iʑo kɤndʑiʁi ra ʁnɯ-pɤrme nɤ ʁnɯ-pɤrme ntsɯ ma mɤ-acʰɤt-i \\
lnk 1pl coll:sibling pl two-year add two-year always apart.from neg -differ.in.age: fact - 1pl \\
`We brother and sisters were born in intervals of two years each.' (if ranked by birth order, adjacent siblings differ in age from each other by two years each) (14-siblings) 0003508#S220
exe
summary: The passage explains that Japhug can express distributive meaning not only with counted nouns but also with the postnominal determiner **raŋrieach/rɯrieach**, which can combine with nouns and numerals and may yield ambiguous scope when used alongside a counted noun. It also describes the distributive determiner **tɯka**, which appears in possessive and transitive constructions and can have broad scope over an entire action, as well as the adverb **ntsɯ**, which can function distributively with a restricted temporal scope.

text:
The intensifier kʰromuch and ʑimkʰɤmmuch can have both scope over the predicate (§ sec:khro ) or serve as postnominal modifiers meaning `many, a lot of'. They can undergo emphatic reduplication to kʰɯ kʰro and ʑɯ ʑimkʰɤm, respectively.

When following a noun in absolutive form as in ( ex:tWNgo.ZimkhAm ), these intensifiers are syntactically ambiguous, as they can be analyzed as having scope over the preceding noun phrase, or on the whole predicate.

exe

<baisuzhen> nɯ kɯ, nɤki, sŋaʁ pjɤ-spa tɕe (...) tɯ-ŋgo ra ʑimkʰɤm ʑo to-ɣɤ-mna \\
anthr dem erg filler magic ifr. ipfv -be.able lnk indef. poss -disease pl many emph ifr - caus -be.better \\
`Bai Suzhen knew magic, and healed many diseases.' (150825 baishe zhuan-zh)
0006342#S64
exe

In ( ex:khWkhro.kW ) however, kʰɯ kʰro unambiguously occurs inside of the ergative postpositional phrase, showing that it cannot be analyzed here as a clausal intensifier.

exe

[tɯrme kʰɯ kʰro] kɯ ʑo ɣɯ-to-rɤtsʰɤt-nɯ \\
person emph much erg emph cisl - ifr -try- pl \\
`Many people came and tried it.' (140505 xiaohaitu-zh)
0003921#S16
exe
summary: The intensifiers **kʰromuch** and **ʑimkʰɤmmuch** can function either as clausal intensifiers with scope over the predicate or as postnominal modifiers meaning “many, a lot of,” and they may undergo emphatic reduplication to **kʰɯ kʰro** and **ʑɯ ʑimkʰɤm**. When they follow a noun in absolutive form, they are syntactically ambiguous between noun-phrase scope and predicate scope, but in examples where **kʰɯ kʰro** appears inside an ergative postpositional phrase, it must be analyzed as internal to that phrase rather than as a clausal intensifier.

text:
In addition to the quantifiers discussed above, there are several markers which combine quantificational function with additional specific meanings.

The marker ɕiŋarɯraeach better than the other is used as postnominal attribute (§ ex:attributive.postnominal ). In transitive constructions, is occurs between the noun and the ergative kɯ as in ( ex:CWNArWra.kW ). It is probably built by combining the pronoun ɕɯwho (§ sec:CW.pronoun ), the bound form of the copula ŋube (§ sec:copula.basic, *ŋɤ- $ $ ŋa- due to assimilation with the following -ra ) and the plural ra (§ sec:plural.determiners ) in reduplicated form.

exe

rɟɤlpu ɕiŋarɯra kɯ ta-tʰu-nɯ ɕti ri, mɯ-tɤ-nɤla-j ɕti tɕe, \\
king each.better.than.the.other erg aor:3 -ask- pl be. aff: fact lnk neg - aor -agree- 1sg \\
`[Many] kings, all better than the other, asked for [my daughters in marriage], but we did not agree.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S74
exe

The adverbs mɯtɕʰimɯrɯzall kinds and mɯndʐamɯχtɕɯɣall kinds (from Tibetan མི་འདྲ་མི་གཅིག་mi.ⁿdra.mi.gtɕigdiverse, different) are also used as postnominal attributes, located closer to the noun than numerals and demonstratives ( ex:mWndzxamWXtCWG.kW ). These forms are only found in traditional narratives.

exe

ɕoŋpʰu mɯndʐamɯχtɕɯɣ χsɯ-ri kɯtʂɤsqi a-pɯ-tu, ɯ-ku zɯ pɣa mɯndʐamɯχtɕɯɣ χsɯ-ri kɯtʂɤsqi nɯ] kɯ pɣɤmbri a-tɤ-lɤt-nɯ ɲɯ-ra \\
tree all.kinds three-hundred sixty irr - ipfv -exist 3sg. poss -on loc bird all.kinds three-hundred sixty dem erg bird.song irr - pfv -release- pl sens -be.needed \\
`May there be three hundred and sixty trees of all kinds, and on them three hundred and sixty bird of all kinds of species singing.' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

The universal quantifier rmɯrmiall, all kinds of ( rmWrmi.GW.nWrmi ), a borrowing from Situ (meaning `everybody'), has a very close meaning, but is very rarely attested.

exe

maka tɤ-rɤku rmɯrmi ɣɯ nɯ-rmi nɯ to-nɤrmi ri maka kɯm mɯ-pjɤ-ɲɟɯ \\
at.all indef. poss -crops all gen 3pl. poss -name dem ifr -say.name lnk at.all door neg - ifr - anticaus:open \\
`He said the names of all kinds of crops, but the door did not open.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S102
exe
summary:
The passage describes several quantificational markers that also have additional lexical meanings. The marker ɕiŋarɯraeach better than the other functions as a postnominal attribute, while the adverbs mɯtɕʰimɯrɯz and mɯndʐamɯχtɕɯɣall kinds also appear as postnominal attributes, closer to the noun than numerals and demonstratives, though they occur only in traditional narratives.  

It also mentions rmɯrmiall, all kinds of, a rare borrowing from Situ with a meaning close to universal quantification.

text:
indefinite!determiner
The form cione has among its many functions (in addition to pronoun, numeral and adverb, see § sec:ci.someone, § sec:other.pro, § sec:partitive.pronouns, § sec:identity.modifier, § sec:one.to.ten, § sec:tense.aspect.adverbs, § sec:cimame.cinAmaRkW ) that of singular indefinite determiner, as in ( ex:ci.indef ) and ( ex:ci.chAGi ). It is typically used to introduce a new referent in a story.

exe

tɕʰeme kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕɤr ci ɲɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ \\
girl sbj: pcp - emph beautiful indef ifr - auto -come.out \\
`A very beautiful girl came [out of the skin].' (31-deluge) 0004077#S50
exe

exe

tɕelo tɕe tɤ-tɕɯ ci cʰɤ-ɣi qʰe, \\
upstream lnk indef. poss -son indef ifr: downstream -come lnk \\
`A boy came from upstream.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

Although ci can be used as a partitive pronoun `one of them' (§ sec:partitive.pronouns ), as a postnominal determiner it does not have partitive meaning. To express a meaning such as `one of the boys', a counted noun such as tɯ-rdoʁone piece is used instead (§ sec:CN.partitive ).

Note that when used as a prenominal modifier, ci has a completely different (definite) meaning `the other $X$' (§ sec:identity.modifier ). However, the indefinite ci is attested in prenominal position if preceded by the prenominal identity modifier kɯmaʁother, as in ( ex:kWmaR.ci.nArZaB ), though the exact syntactic analysis of such sentences may require more research (it is possible that nɤ-rʑaβ here is an essive adjunct § sec:essive.abs, and does not belong to the same constituent as kɯmaʁ ci ).

exe

nɤʑo kɯmaʁ ci nɤ-rʑaβ nɯ-nɯ-ɕar kɯ mna \\
2sg other indef 2sg. poss -wife imp - auto -search erg be.better: fact \\
`It would be better if you looked for another wife.' (150909 xiaocui-zh)
0006386#S150
exe

There are no dual or plural indefinite determiners in Japhug. The plural marker ra can occur after the indefinite ci, but with a vague similative meaning `and other things' as in ( ex:ci.ra ).

exe

ndʑi-tɕɯ ci, ndʑi-me ci ra to-tu. \\
3du. poss -son indef 3du. poss -girl indef pl ifr -exist \\
`They$_du$ had a boy and a girl (etc).' (150827 tianluo-zh)
0006250#S153
exe

The indefinite ci is not obligatory for indefinite referents (whether specific or non-specific), and bare NPs can used as fsapaʁanimal and qapardhole in example ( ex:ci.ra2 ).

exe

fsapaʁ nɯ-me, a-pɯ-si qʰe, `nɯ qapar kɯ ta-ndza ŋu ma' tu-ti-nɯ ɕti ma, \\
animal aor -not.exist irr - pfv -die lnk dem dhole erg aor:3 -eat be: fact sfp ipfv -say- pl be. aff: fact lnk \\
`When an animal disappears, dies, people say `A dhole ate it.' (28-qapar)
0003720#S25
exe
summary: The form **ci** can function as a **singular indefinite determiner**, typically used to introduce a new referent in discourse. However, it is not required for indefinite reference, and bare noun phrases can also express indefinite meanings; Japhug has no dual or plural indefinite determiners, though **ci + ra** may give a vague “and other things” interpretation.

text:
indefinite!determiner
The indefinite pronoun tʰɯcisomething (§ sec:thWci ) has marginal uses as a prenominal indefinite modifier, as in ( ex:thWci.laXCi ), ( ex:thWci.WjmNo ) and ( ex:laXtCha.ci.nWnW ) below.

exe

tʰɯci laχɕi ci ɕ-pɯ-nɯ-βzjoz-nɯ tɕe, jɤ-ɕe-nɯ ra \\
something trade indef tral - imp - auto -learn- pl lnk imp -go- pl be.needed: fact \\
`Go and learn some trade!' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S29
exe

This construction arose perhaps from the use of the pronoun tʰɯci as head of a postnominal relative clause with the verb fsebe like, as illustrated by examples like ( ex:thWci.kAnWsaXCWB ) or ( ex:thWci.akAspa ) in § sec:thWci. Turning the verb fsebe like to a finite form as in ( ex:thWci.WjmNo ) could cause the indefinite tʰɯci, head of the relative in ( ex:thWci.kAnWsaXCWB ), to be reanalyzed as the prenominal modifier of the immediately adjacent noun in ( ex:thWci.WjmNo ).

exe

nɯra [tʰɯci [kɤ-nɯsaχɕɯβ kɯ-fse]] pɯ-ŋu wo. \\
dem: pl something inf -have.a.contest sbj: pcp -be.like pst. ipfv -be sfp \\
`It was like a kind of contest.' (160706 thotsi)
0006133#S16
exe

exe

[tʰɯci ɯ-jmŋo] ci ʑo pɯ-fse ri \\
something 3sg. poss -dream one emph pst. ipfv -be.like lnk \\
`It looked like [he had had] some dream.' (Lobzang2005)
0003370#S74
exe
summary: The indefinite pronoun *tʰɯci* ‘something’ has only marginal use as a prenominal indefinite determiner. The passage suggests this construction may have developed from *tʰɯci* functioning as the head of a postnominal relative clause with *fse* ‘be like’; when *fse* was made finite, *tʰɯci* could be reanalyzed as an indefinite modifier of the neighboring noun.

text:
definite
Japhug has no dedicated definite determiner, but nɯ and nɯnɯ as demonstrative determiners (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners ) and as topic markers (§ sec:topic ) and the prenominal aforementioned topic marker iɕqʰa (§ sec:iCqha ) are generally used with definite referents.

Example ( ex:ci.joGi ) illustrates a typical example with the determiner nɯ; the indefinite determiner ci (§ sec:indef.article ) occurs in the first introduction of a new referent in the story as in the first clause of example ( ex:ci.joGi ), but on the following occurrence of the same noun nɯ is found.

exe

tɕe qajdo ci jo-ɣi tɕe, tɕe qajdo nɯ kɯ `mo laz tu, pʰo laz me' to-ti. \\
lnk crow indef ifr -come lnk lnk crow dem erg girl karma exist: fact boy karma not.exist: fact ifr -say \\
`A crow came. The crow said: `The girl will have chance, the boy won't.'' (28-qajdoskAt) 0003718#S10
exe

However, although noun phrases followed by nɯ and nɯnɯ more often than not denote definite referents, these determiners cannot be analyzed as definite determiners, as noun phrases with nɯ or nɯnɯ can in certain cases have indefinite referents.

A very clear case of use of nɯ with an indefinite referent occurs on nouns serving as heads of head-internal relative clauses. A well-attested typological generalization is that in this type of relative clauses, definiteness marking is agrammatical (see ). In Khroskyabs, reports that the definiteness marker =tə is indeed not accepted on the head noun of head-internal relatives. In Japhug however, nɯ does occur in such a syntactic context. For instance, in ( ex:tAnmaR.nW.kW ), the head tɤ-nmaʁ nɯ kɯ is subject of the participle ɲɯ-kɯ-nɯ-ɕar `looking for', and is embedded in the participial relative clause indicated in brackets -- the presence of the ergative kɯ precludes to analyze it as a post-nominal relative (§ sec:head-internal.relative.prenominal ). From the meaning of the sentence the head tɤ-nmaʁhusband is clearly indefinite non-specific non-generic (see ). The fact that it takes the marker nɯ shows that this marker, unlike Khroskyabs =tə, is not primarily marking definiteness.

exe

tɕeri [tɤ-nmaʁ nɯ kɯ ɯ-rʑaʁ kɯ-ɤntɕʰɯ ɲɯ-kɯ-nɯ-ɕar], aʁɤndɯndɤt tɤndɤɣri tu-kɯ-βzu pjɤ-tu. \\
but indef. poss -husband dem erg 3sg. poss -wife sbj: pcp -be.many ipfv - sbj: pcp - auto -search everywhere illegitimate.child ipfv - sbj: pcp -make ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`However there were husbands who were looking for several women and had illegitimate children.' (140427 tAndAGri) 0003858#S4
exe

Other cases of indefinite noun phrase with nɯ are observed with left-dislocated topics. In example ( ex:RnWz.nWnW ), we find a type of tail-head linkeage (§ sec:tail.head.linkeage ) where both the noun phrase spjaŋkɯ ʁnɯz `two wolves' and the verb ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci `he met' are repeated; in the second occurrence, the noun phrase is topicalized and is followed by the topic marker nɯnɯ, with a slight pause of hesitation. The determiner nɯnɯ in this clause, unlike nɯ in ( ex:ci.joGi ), does not mark definiteness: that clause cannot be understood as `He met the two wolves'.

exe

spjaŋkɯ ʁnɯz ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci. spjaŋkɯ ʁnɯz nɯnɯ, tɕendɤre ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci tɕe iɕqʰa, kɯ-rɤ-ntɕʰa nɯ wuma ʑo ɲɤ-mu. \\
wolf two ifr - peg -meet- peg wolf two dem lnk ifr - peg -meet- peg lnk the.aforementioned sbj: pcp - a. pass: n. hum -kill dem really emph ifr -be.afraid \\
`He$_i$ (i.e. the butcher) met two wolves. He$_i$ met two wolves, and the butcher$_i$ was very much afraid.' (150902 liaozhai lang-zh) 0006340#S7
exe

The determiners nɯ or nɯnɯ are rarely adjacent to the indefinite singular determiner ci in the corpus. In all cases with ci followed by nɯ (other than the identity pronoun in § sec:other.pro ), or with nɯ followed by ci in the corpus, they belong to different constituents. For instance, in ( ex:ci.YAZGAsAphAr ), ci is in adverbial use (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ) and does not belong to the preceding noun phrase.

exe

[tɕʰeme nɯ] ci ɲɤ-ʑɣɤ-sɤpʰɤr qʰe \\
girl dem one ifr - refl -shake lnk \\
`The girl shook herself.' (02-deluge2012) 0003376#S115
exe

In ( ex:laXtCha.ci.nWnW ) although nɯnɯ follows ci, it has scope over the both preceding phrases, which are left-dislocated and followed by a pause.

exe

kɤ-xtɕɤr tɕe nɯnɯ tɕe tɕe iɕqʰa, [[tʰɯci tɯmbri tɤ-ri kɯ-fse kɯ] [laχtɕʰa ci] nɯnɯ], ci kú-wɣ-sɯ-pa tɕe, kú-wɣ-xtɕɤr, \\
inf -attach lnk dem lnk lnk the.aforementioned something rope indef. poss -thread sbj: pcp -be.like erg thing indef dem one ipfv - inv - caus -do lnk ipfv - inf -attach \\
``To attach' [means] `to put together', `to attach something with something like a rope or a thread.'' (150902 kAxtCAr)
0006308#S2
exe

However, the indefinite determiner ci can be followed by nɯ as in ( ex:kWrZi.ci.nW ).

exe

nɯ, kɯ-rʑi ci nɯ ɣɤʑu maʁ kɯ \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.heavy indef dem exist: sens not.be: fact sfp \\
`This is not a difficult thing [to do].' (divination2005)
exe

The aforementioned topic marker iɕqʰa (§ sec:iCqha ) is almost always used with definite referents when prenominal, as in ( ex:RnWz.nWnW ) above, and is the closest candidate to be analyzed as a definiteness marker in Japhug. However, it does occur with non-specific generic referents as in ( ex:lWlAmu ), including some that are very clearly indefinite as in ( ex:lApWG ); note the absence of postnominal determiner nɯ ( ex:lApWG ).

exe

iɕqʰa lɯlɤmu nɯ tʰɯ-rɤpɯ tɕe tɕe ɯ-sŋi tɕe kɤ-nɯ-rŋgɯ nɯ stʰɯci mɯ́j-tsu ma ɯ-pɯ ra χse ɲɯ-ra \\
the.aforementioned female.cat dem ipfv -bear.young lnk lnk 3sg. poss -day lnk inf - auto -lie.down dem so.much neg: sens -have.time.to lnk 3sg. poss -young pl feed: fact sens -be.needed \\
`A/the female cat (unlike male cats), when it had had kittens, does not have time to sleep during the day, as it has to feed its kittens.' (21-lWLU)
0003576#S35
exe

exe

iɕqʰa lɤpɯɣ ɯ-rɣi ʑo fse. \\
the.aforementioned radish 3sg. poss -seed emph be.like: fact \\
`It looks like a radish seed.' (hist-26-qro-fourmi)
0003682#S60
exe
summary: Japhug has no dedicated definite determiner, but nɯ, nɯnɯ, and the prenominal topic marker iɕqʰa are generally associated with definite referents. However, these forms cannot be analyzed as definite determiners, because they can also appear with indefinite, non-specific, or generic noun phrases, including in head-internal relative clauses and left-dislocated topics. The corpus also shows that nɯ and nɯnɯ are rarely adjacent to the indefinite determiner ci when they belong to the same noun phrase, and iɕqʰa is the closest form to a definiteness marker but still occurs with clearly indefinite referents.

text: In ( ex:laXtCha.ci.nWnW ), iɕqʰa also precedes two phrases involving indefinite referents, but there is a marked pause, and this is a case of iɕqʰa in its function as speech filler (§ sec:fillers ).
summary: The passage notes that in the example, *iɕqʰa* precedes two phrases with indefinite referents. However, there is a marked pause, indicating that in this case *iɕqʰa* is being used as a speech filler rather than in its ordinary connective function.

text:
Like many languages, Japhug uses bare nouns without any definiteness marking. Bare nouns are most often non-referential, as tɕʰemegirl in ( ex:tCheme.tWtAtu ).

exe

ʁnaʁna tɕʰeme tɯ tɤ-tu nɤ, kɤndʑisqʰaj tu-kɤ-sɯ-βzu \\
both girl cond aor -exist lnk coll:sister ipfv - inf - caus -make \\
`If both of them have girls, let them be sisters.' (2003 zrAntCW)
exe

Bare nouns are less common with referential nouns (except in answers to questions), but examples can be found, as qacʰɣafox in ( ex:qachGa.kW ).

exe

qacʰɣa kɯ maχtɕɯ tɤ-tɯt-a nɯ mɤ-tɯ-ste ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
fox erg I.told.you.so aor -say[II]- 1sg dem neg -2-do.like[III]: fact say: fact sens -be \\
`The fox says: `You do not do as I told you to." (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S42
exe

Personal names generally occur as bare nouns, without any definiteness marker as in ( ex:WrJAnpanma ), but there are no constraints against co-occurrence of personal names with the determiner nɯ either (see § sec:personal.names.modifiers ).

exe

ɯrɟɤnpanma kɯ ʁlaŋsaŋtɕʰin ɯ-ɕki \\
Padmasambhava erg Gesar 3sg - dat \\
`Padmasambhava [told] Gesar.' (Gesar)
exe
summary: Japhug, like many languages, uses bare nouns without definiteness marking. These bare nouns are usually non-referential, though they can sometimes be referential, especially in answers to questions, and personal names typically appear as bare nouns as well. However, personal names may also co-occur with the determiner nɯ, so this is not obligatory.

text:
topic!deliminative
The delimitative topic marker pɯ pɯ-ŋu nɤ `as for..., concerning...' is transparently derived from the past imperfective of the verb `be' in conditional form `if it was...' (with verb-initial reduplication, § sec:verb.initial.redp ), as other copulas such as affirmative ɕtibe and maʁnot be in ( ex:pWpWmaʁ ).

exe

nɯnɯ koŋla ʑo tɤɕime pɯ pɯ-maʁ nɤ \\
dem really emph princess cond pst. ipfv -not.be lnk \\
`If she was not really a princess,...' (140519 wandou gongzhu-zh) 0004038#S68
exe

The delimitative construction generally has scope over a noun phrase, which can have an additional demonstrative nɯ as topicalizer as in ( ex:nW.pWpWNunA ) (see § sec:nW.topic ).

exe

a-mu nɯ pɯ pɯ-ŋu nɤ, qʰlɯ ʁdɯxpakɤrpu ɣɯ ɯ-me stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ a-mu ɲɯ-pe, \\
1sg. poss -mother dem cond pst. ipfv -be lnk nâga p.n gen 3sg. poss -daughter most sbj: pcp -be.small dem 1sg. poss -mother sens -be.good \\
`As for my mother, the youngest daughter of the Nâga Gdugpa dkarpo is good to be my mother.' (Gesar)
exe

In this construction, the verb is in the process of becoming grammaticalized as a topic particle. It is possible to find examples where the verb still takes person indexation in the delimitative construction when the topicalized element is a first or second person pronoun, as in ( ex:pWpWNuanA ).

exe

aʑo pɯ pɯ-ŋu-a nɤ, kɤndʑiʁi kɯmŋu tu-j, \\
1sg cond pst. ipfv -be- 1sg lnk siblings five exist: fact - 1sg \\
`Concerning me, we are five brothers and sisters.' (hist140501 tshering skyid) 0003902#S1
exe

However, there are also examples with first or second person pronoun without indexation on the delimitative marker, as in ( ex:pWpWNunA ), ( ex:pWpWNunA2 ) and ( ex:pWpWNunA3 ), where a first person singular form pɯ pɯ-ŋu-a nɤ or second person pɯ pɯ-tɯ-ŋu nɤ would have been expected. Such examples show that pɯpɯŋunɤ has ceased to be analyzed as a verb form at least in these cases. Moreover, third person plural and dual indexation is hardly ever found in the delimitative construction.

exe

nɤʑo pɯpɯŋunɤ, ɬɤndʐi ra ɣɯ nɯ-kɯ-βʁa, nɯ-rɟɤlpu tɯ-ŋu \\
2sg as.for demon pl gen 3pl. poss - sbj: pcp -be.victorious 3pl. poss -king 2-be: fact \\
