The delimitative topic construction can be used to introduce the main topic of a following discourse (as in ex:pWpWNuanA and ex:pWpWNunA2 ), but can be used for contrastive topics, as in example ( ex:pWpWNunA3 ) where the speaker expresses a contrast between his and the addressee's action (`you, you were fighting for the sake of other people').
summary: The delimitative topic marker pɯ pɯ-ŋu nɤ ‘as for..., concerning...’ is transparently derived from the past imperfective of the verb ‘be’ in a conditional form, and it is undergoing grammaticalization into a topic particle. It usually takes scope over a noun phrase and may still show person indexation with first- or second-person pronouns, though many examples lack such marking, indicating that it is no longer analyzed as a verb in those cases. The construction can introduce a new discourse topic or mark a contrastive topic, and a shortened form ŋunɤ is also attested.

text:
topic!aforementioned
The marker iɕqʰathe aforementioned is used on referents that have been previously mentioned in the same story, usually only a few sentences back. It is strictly prenominal.

Example ( ex:iCqha.aforementioned ) illustrates the most typical use of this marker. Sentence ( ex:kAtWm ) introduces a new referent, kɤtɯmball of thread marked with the indefinite determiner ci (§ sec:indef.article ). Three clauses later in ( ex:iCqha.kAtWm ), the same referent occurs again as an overt noun with two topic markers, the postnominal nɯ and the prenominal iɕqʰa.

exe

`He told [Rgyabza] `I need a ball of thread and a needle.''

tɕendɤre ɲɤ-kʰo qʰe, \\
lnk ifr -give lnk \\
`She gave it to him.'

lnk 3sg. poss -meal aor:3 -bring- pl dem: loc lnk lnk \\
`When they brought his meal,'

iɕqʰa kɤtɯm nɯ ɯʑo kɯ ko-ndo, \\
the.aforementioned ball dem 3sg erg ifr -take \\
`he took the ball of thread, and...' (Gesar 270-272)

A systematic study of the use of the topic marker iɕqʰa in Japhug must overcome two inherent difficulties. First, this topic marker is homophonous with (and historically related to) the speech filler iɕqʰa (§ sec:fillers ) and with the adverb iɕqʰajust now, which can also precede noun phrases. Listening to the sound files can help distinguishing between the three, as the speech filler is always followed by a pause (and optionally by the demonstrative nɯ ), but there are still ambiguous sentences (see below). Second, iɕqʰa occurs on nouns designating entities that the speaker considers to have been previously referred to in the conversation, even if they are not present in the same recording.

For instance in ( ex:iCqha.pɣArnoR ) the noun pɣɤrnoʁa species of fungus is used with iɕqʰa, although this name does not occur before in the same text; it was however mentioned the day before in another recording.

exe

dem fungi.sp. comit the.aforementioned fungi.sp. dem: du 3du. poss -form really emph be:identical: fact \\
`The zdɯmqe and the pɣɤrnoʁ are very similar.' (23-mbrAZim)
0003604#S75

The topic marker iɕqʰa transparently comes from the adverb iɕqʰajust now (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ). The pivot constructions that allowed reanalysis from adverb to prenominal topic marker are very probably headless relatives (§ sec:headless.relative ) as in ( ex:iCqha.tAtWta ), or complement clauses as in ( ex:iCqha.ZnWzmWnmuta ).

exe

[iɕqʰa tɤ-tɯt-a] nɯ tú-wɣ-stu qʰe, \\
just.now ifr -say[II]- 1sg dem ipfv - inv -do.like lnk \\
`One does as I just said, and...' (2002 tWsqar)
exe

exe

iɕqʰa [ʑ-nɯ-z-mɯnmu-t-a] nɯ mɯ-pjɤ-pe rcama. \\
the.aforementioned tral - aor - caus -move- pst: tr - 1sg dem neg - ifr. ipfv -be.good fsp \\
`It was probably not a good thing that I had [gone and] moved them (as I said above).' (150819 kumpGa) 0006388#S41
exe

These sentences are still synchronically ambiguous in Japhug; in ( ex:iCqha.ZnWzmWnmuta ) the context makes it clear that iɕqʰa is the topic marker (since the fact of having moved (the eggs) had been told a few sentences back) and not an adverb `just now' with a temporal reference in the past, as the meaning would be `it was probably not a good thing that I had just moved them' (an impossible interpretation in this context, since this sentence is an explanation why several eggs had not given chicks, several days after they had been brought to another place). However, extracted from the context, both interpretation would be equally possible for ( ex:iCqha.ZnWzmWnmuta ), and correspond to two different syntactic structures.

With postnominal relative clauses (§ sec:postnominal.relative ) or head-internal relative clauses (§ sec:head-internal.relative ) whose head noun happens to be located on the left edge of the clause as in ( ex:tWrpa.thafse ), iɕqʰa can also be ambiguous. Since the adverb iɕqʰajust now can occur both before the object ( ex:tWrpa.thWfseta ) or before the verb ( ex:tWrpa.thWfseta2 ) in an independent clause, a relative such as ( ex:tWrpa.thafse ) can be either interpreted `the axe (mentioned above) that he had whetted' (with the topic marker iɕqʰa outside of the relative clause, having scope over its head) and `the axe that he had just whetted' with the adverb iɕqʰajust now inside the relative clause.

reanalysis ambiguity!relative clause
The use of iɕqʰa as a topic marker with nouns (as in ex:iCqha.kAtWm above) probably took place by reanalysis of the adverb in headless or postnominal relatives, or in complement clauses as above, then generalized to all noun phrases even those without a subordinate clause.
summary: The marker iɕqʰa indicates an aforementioned referent, typically one mentioned a few sentences earlier, and it is strictly prenominal. It can be difficult to analyze because it is homophonous with the speech filler iɕqʰa and the adverb meaning “just now,” and some sentences remain synchronically ambiguous between a topic-marker and adverb interpretation. The text suggests that the topic marker likely arose through reanalysis of the adverb in headless relative clauses or complement clauses, and then extended to noun phrases without subordinate clauses.

text:
topic!adversative
There are two adversative topic markers in Japhug, ʁo and ndɤre. The former is similar in meaning to Mandarin 倒 dàoinstead, on the other hand, and occurs in contexts with a strong adversative meaning `however, but, on the other hand' as in ( ex:Ro.pWtu ).

exe

jinde ku-nɯ-tu ɕi kɯma mɤ-xsi ma kɯɕɯŋgɯ ʁo pɯ-tu, \\
nowadays dubit - auto -exist qu sfp neg - genr:know lnk in.former.times top. advers ipfv. pst -exist \\
`It is not clear whether it is still to be found nowadays, but it did exist in former times.' (23-scuz)
0003612#S27
exe

The marker ʁo also occurs in two constructions meaning `of course'. First, it is found in the `X ʁo X' construction meaning `of course (it is) X', as in ( ex:nAZo.Ro.nAZo ), the answer to the question in ( ex:nABJu.YWCara.Ci ) which presents two alternatives.

exe

xlist

`a-tɤɕime, nɤ-βɟu ɲɯ-ɕar-a ɕi, aʑo tu-ozgrɯ-a' nɯra to-ti, `ma nɤ-pi ɣɯ aʑo tɤ-azgrɯ-a ɕti' to-ti \\
1sg. poss -lady 2sg. poss -mat ipfv -search- 1sg qu 1sg ipfv -bow- 1sg dem: pl ifr -say lnk 1sg. poss -elder.sibling gen 1sg aor -bow- 1sg be. aff: fact ifr -say \\
`He said `My lady, should I look for a cushion for you, or should I bow [for you to sit on my back]', and he said `Because I bowed for your elder sister [to sit].'

`nɤʑo ʁo nɤʑo ma, a-βɟu ɲɯ-tɯ-ɕar kɯ-ɤtsɯtsu me' to-ti. \\
2sg top. advers 2sg lnk 1sg. poss -mat ipfv -2-search inf. stat -have.time not.exist: fact ifr -say \\
`Of course [I will sit on] you, there is no time to look for a mat for me.' (2014-kWlAG)

Second, ʁo is commonly used with the adverb lɯskiof course, as in ( ex:Ro.lWski ), not necessarily with any adversative meaning.

The phrase nɯ sɤznɤ `even, rather than that etc' (§ sec:comparative ) is also used as an adversative topic marker similar to ʁo (see in particular example ex:nW.sAznA.YWwxti ).

The demonstrative nɯ as a topic marker
topic demonstrative
The postnominal determiner nɯ and its reduplicated form nɯnɯ is one of the most common words in Japhug, and has a considerable number of functions. It is used as a demonstrative (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners ), contributes to expressing definiteness (§ sec:definiteness ) and could be argued to be a subordinator (an analysis not adopted in the present work, see § sec:complement.determiner ).

In addition, it is commonly used to mark topic: left-dislocated noun phrases generally (though not compulsorily) take this determiner. For instance, in texts presenting animals or plants, their name on first occurrence is left dislocated and followed by the determiner nɯ, as in ( ex:qawWz.nW ).

exe

qawɯz nɯ, (qawɯz nɯ pɯ-tɯ-mto-t, ɣe?) qawɯz nɯnɯ, nɤki, kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe, \\
Edelweiss dem Edelweiss dem aor -2-see- pst: tr sfp Edelweiss dem filler before lnk \\
`The edelweiss, (you saw Edelweiss before, right?)... The edelweiss, in former times,' (15-babW) 0003512#S164
exe

It also occurs with personal pronouns, as in ( ex:mWNi.zW ), a sentence where the narrator talks about his personal situation, as opposed to that of his parents who were mentioned in the previous lines.

exe

aʑo nɯ, mɯŋi zɯ kɯ-rɤ-βzjoz ɲɯ-ɕe-a pɯ-ŋu. \\
1sg dem topo loc sbj: pcp - antipass -learn ipfv: west -go- 1sg pst. ipfv -be \\
`As for me, I was going to school in Mungi.' (2010-09)
exe

In its function as a topicalizer, the determiner nɯ can follow a noun with postnominal demonstratives, as in ( ex:kWki.nW ). However, due to the difficulty of systematically sorting out the topicalization and demonstrative functions of this marker, I do not attempt to reflect this distinction in the glosses, and use dem everywhere.

exe

tɕeri kɯki mɯntoʁ kɯki nɯ pɯpɯŋunɤ, wuma ʑo kɯ-ʑru, kɯ-pe, \\
lnk dem. prox flower dem. prox dem as.for really emph sbj: pcp -be.strong sbj: pcp -be.good \\
`But concerning this flower, so precious and nice' (150820 meili de meiguihua-zh) 0006286#S55
exe
summary:
Japhug has two adversative topic markers, **ʁo** and **ndɤre**. **ʁo** expresses a strong adversative meaning like “however” or “but,” but it also appears in constructions meaning “of course,” including the **X ʁo X** pattern and with **lɯski** “of course”; **ndɤre** has a milder adversative sense such as “as far as X is concerned” or “unlike others,” and can contrast one situation with another.  

The passage also notes that the postnominal determiner **nɯ / nɯnɯ** commonly marks topicalized noun phrases, especially left-dislocated topics and personal pronouns. In this topicalizing function it follows noun phrases and is glossed as a demonstrative because its topical and demonstrative uses are difficult to separate systematically.

text:
The linker tɕe as a topic marker
The word tɕe, which originates from a locative postposition (§ sec:locative.j ), is mainly used in Japhug as a linker (§ sec:coordination ) and as a postposition (§ sec:tCe.postposition ). It is one of the most common words in the corpus.

In addition, it can serve as a topic marker, following left-dislocated noun or postpositional phrases ( ex:tsuku.kW.tCe ).

exe

tsuku kɯ tɕe lɤpɯɣ ra mbɯsɯt cʰɯ-lɤt-nɯ tɕe nɯra ɲɯ-rku-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
some erg lnk radish pl grating ipfv -throw- pl lnk dem. pl ipfv -put.in- pl sens -be \\
`Some people, they grate radish and use it as filling [for the sausage].' (05-paR) 0003400#S74
exe
summary: The word **tɕe**, originally a locative postposition, is mainly used in Japhug as a linker and as a postposition, and it is very common in the corpus. It can also function as a **topic marker**, occurring after left-dislocated noun phrases or postpositional phrases.

text:
There are several focalization strategies in Japhug, including pseudo-cleft sentences (§ sec:pseudo.cleft ) and sentence-final copulas (§ sec:focalization.final.copula ), but focalized constituents are sometimes also unmarked, though they have to be overt (§ sec:focalization.overt ).

This section presents the markers used to express different types of focus on noun phrase constituents.

Additive and scalar focus marker kɯnɤ
focus marker!scalar focus marker!additive
The additive and scalar focus marker kɯnɤalso, even follows the constituent over which it has scope, which can be noun phrases, postpositional phrases but also subordinate clauses (§ sec:scalar.concessive.conditional ). As with other function words with the syllable nɤ as last element (§ sec:stress ), the stress is on the first syllable ( kɯ́nɤ ) and the vowel on the second syllable is often elided (a pronunciation kɯn is often heard).

The marker kɯnɤ expresses both additive focus, as in ( ex:aZo.kWNA.staRlupa ), and scalar focus, as in ( ex:WNgWz.kWnA.tunAndWtnW ) in affirmative sentences. It is also compatible with negative verb forms, as in ( ex:tWrdoR.kWnA ), expressing the meaning `not even' (see also cinɤ(not) even one in § sec:cinA ).

exe

aʑo kɯnɤ staʁlupa ŋu-a tɕe \\
1sg also born.in.the.tiger.year be: fact - 1sg lnk \\
`Me too (like you), I am of the Tiger year.' (2011-05-nyima)

`Even among themselves, they fight, and there are winners and losers.' (20-sWNgi)

`Sometimes one cannot finish even one pattern (on the belt) in one day.' (2011-06-thaXtsa)

The scope of kɯnɤ is generally exclusively on the constituent that it immediately follows, but there are cases where the scope is more extensive. In ( ex:aZo.kWnA.akAsWso ), kɯnɤ occurs between the pronoun aʑo and the following participial verb form, which bears a 1sg possessive prefix a- coreferent with that pronoun (see also ex:aZWG.kWnA below). The semantic scope of kɯnɤ here is on the whole relative aʑo a-kɤ-sɯso `(the things) that I want' rather than exclusively on the pronoun aʑo.

exe

`(I will do as you say, but) do also the things that I want.' (2003kAndzwsqhaj2)
exe

As an additive focus marker, kɯnɤ can be repeated on all the nouns designating the members of a group sharing a particular property, in the construction $X$ kɯnɤ, $Y$ kɯnɤ `both $X$ and $Y$', as in ( ex:Dpalcan.kWnA ).

The focus marker kɯnɤ is found with nouns or pronouns in core argument function, including S ( ex:kWnA.nArca ), O ( ex:nWXpWm.kWnA ), and semi-objects ( ex:kWnA.mAsna ). Examples with transitive subjects are presented below ( ex:nWra.kWnA and ex:Wzda.ra.kWnA ).

summary:
Japhug has several focalization strategies, including pseudo-clefts and sentence-final copulas, but focalized constituents can also be unmarked as long as they are overt. The passage then focuses on the additive and scalar focus marker **kɯnɤ** ‘also, even’, which follows the constituent in its scope and can attach to noun phrases, postpositional phrases, subordinate clauses, and a wide range of core, oblique, and adjunct constituents.  

In affirmative clauses it marks additive or scalar focus, and with negative verb forms it can mean ‘not even’. Although its scope is usually the immediately preceding constituent, it can sometimes extend over a larger phrase, and it may be repeated on coordinated nouns to mean ‘both X and Y’.

`The maldzɯ plant, it is also found in places of slightly lower altitude, but grows also in the same places as qarɣɤpɤt plants.' (18-qromJoR)

Although kɯnɤalso, even can be combined with most postpositions and relator nouns as shown by the examples above, it is however incompatible with the ergative kɯ. For instance, in ( ex:nWra.kWnA ), although the demonstrative pronoun nɯra `they, those' in the second clause is the subject of the transitive verb ndzaeat, it does not take the ergative kɯ as would be expected (§ sec:A.kW ). The same applies to ɯ-zda ra `his companions', subject of the transitive verb na-nɯ-ɕar-nɯ `they looked for themselves' in ( ex:Wzda.ra.kWnA ).

exe

ɯ-pɯ nɯra li ju-ɣi-nɯ qʰe, nɯra kɯnɤ ɣɯ-tu-ndza-nɯ. \\
3sg. poss -young dem: pl again ipfv -come- pl lnk dem: pl also cisl - ipfv -eat- pl \\
`Its cubs also come and they too eat it.' (20-sWNgi) 0003562#S56

exe

ɯ-zda ra kɯnɤ nɯ-rʑaβ tɯka na-nɯ-ɕar-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -companion pl also 3sg. poss -wife each aor:3 - auto -search sens -be \\
`His companions also took each a wife for himself (among the women of the island).' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

The combinations $ $ kɯ kɯnɤ or $ $ kɯnɤ kɯ are unattested, and not accepted by native speakers. The contrast between absolutive and ergative noun phrases is therefore neutralized in additive or scalar focus with kɯnɤ. Note that other focus markers, such as ri and tɕi (see ex:tCi.ndze in § sec:ri.additive ) differ from kɯnɤ in this regard.

Four pieces of evidence converge to suggest that the first syllable of kɯnɤ is historically related to the ergative postposition kɯ: (i) the incompatibility of co-occurrence of kɯnɤ and kɯ; (ii) the stress on the first syllable in kɯ́nɤ; (iii) the similar -nɤ element in the other scalar focus marker cinɤ(not) even one (§ sec:cinA ) (iv) the existence of the linker nɤ, possibly of Tibetan origin (§ sec:additive.nA ). A detailed examination of this topic is however impossible on the basis Japhug-internal evidence, and will require extensive syntactic comparison between Gyalrong languages.

The adverb tɤmtɯkɯnɤspecially, on purpose appears to be a lexicalized combination of the noun tɤ-mtɯknot and the focus marker kɯnɤ.

Correlative additive focus markers ri and tɕi
focus marker!correlative additive
The additive focus markers ri and tɕi are used in enumerations, repeated after each noun referring to members of a group, to focus on the fact that their referents share a common property (or properties that are semantically close enough), as in ( ex:tCi.tulhoR.cha ) (see additional examples in ). In addition to their uses in the noun phrase presented in this section, ri and tɕi can also have scope over verbs, as discussed in § sec:correlative.addition.

exe

ɴqiaβ tɕi tu-ɬoʁ cʰa, zrɯ tɕi tu-ɬoʁ cʰa, \\
dark.side.of.the.mountain also ipfv -come.out can: fact sunny.side.of.the.mountain also ipfv -come.out can: fact \\
`It can grow in both the dark and the sunny sides of the mountains.' (17-thowum)
0003526#S14
exe

The correlative focus markers ri and tɕi can occur after any noun phrase or postpositional phrase, including with the ergative kɯ as shown by ( ex:tCi.ndze ), unlike the marker kɯnɤalso, even (see examples ex:nWra.kWnA and ex:Wzda.ra.kWnA, § sec:kWnA ).

exe

paʁ kɯ tɕi ndze, nɯŋa kɯ tɕi ndze, jla kɯ tɕi ndze. \\
pig erg also eat[III]: fact cow erg also eat[III]: fact hybrid.yak erg also eat[III]: fact \\
`Pigs eat it, cows eat it, hybrid yaks eat it.' (18-NGolo)
0003530#S159
exe

They can have scope over only part of the noun/propositional phrase, and even on the relator nouns as in ( ex:WNgW.tCi ).

exe

sɤtɕʰa ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕi ɣɤʑu, sɤtɕʰa ɯ-taʁ tɕi ʑo ɣɤʑu \\
ground 3sg. poss -inside also exist: sens ground 3sg. poss -inside also emph exist: sens \\
`It is found both inside the ground, and on the ground.' (25-GdAso)
0003638#S17
exe

Alternatively, it is possible to enumerate several properties of the same referent using ri (this usage is not found with tɕi ), but that marker still follows the noun phrase. In this case the referent cannot be elided, and must be repeated in both clauses, at least as a third person pronoun ɯʑo as in ( ex:WlWz.ri.pjAxtCi ).

exe

pʰaʁrgot nɯnɯ ɯʑo ri pjɤ-rʑi, ɯʑo ri pjɤ-tsʰu tɕe \\
boar dem 3sg also ifr. ipfv -be.heavy 3sg also ifr. ipfv -be.fat lnk \\
`The boar, it was heavy and fat.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh)
0003886#S228
exe

This construction can be relativized with internally-headed relative clauses in apposition, keeping the third person ɯʑo as a resumptive pronoun (§ sec:resumptive ).

The correlative construction can involve the possessor of an inalienably possessed noun, as in ( ex:WlWz.ri.pjAxtCi ), where in the first clause the referent `the girl' is possessor of the intransitive subject (literally `her age was small') and in second it corresponds to the intransitive subject, realized as a third person pronoun ɯʑo `she'.

exe

tɕʰeme nɯ ɯ-lɯz ri pjɤ-xtɕi, ɯʑo ri pjɤ-mpɕɤr, \\
girl dem 3sg. poss -age also ifr. ipfv -be.small 3sg also ifr. ipfv -be.beautiful \\
`The girl was young and beautiful.' (150909 hua pi-zh)
0006278#S10
exe
summary:
The passage explains that the additive focus marker **kɯnɤ** ‘also, even’ can combine with most postpositions and relator nouns, but it is **incompatible with the ergative marker kɯ**. This means that in additive or scalar focus, the contrast between absolutive and ergative noun phrases is neutralized; the text also notes possible historical links between the first syllable of **kɯnɤ** and ergative **kɯ**.

It then describes the correlative additive focus markers **ri** and **tɕi**, which are used in enumerations to mark shared properties across members of a group. Unlike **kɯnɤ**, they can occur after any noun phrase or postpositional phrase, including ergative ones, and **ri** can also enumerate multiple properties of the same referent with a repeated or resumptive third-person pronoun.

text:
More complex correlations, involving different subjects and predicates related to another referent, are also possible as shown by example ( ex:lWlu.kW ), where ri occurs after the intransitive subject tɯ-ciwater, after the transitive subject lɯlucat with the ergative and after the finite verb tu-ɕe `it goes up'.

exe

<yancong> ku-kɯ-rɤloʁ tɕe ɯ-taʁ tɯ-ci ri mɯ́j-ɣi lɯlu kɯ ri mɯ-ɲɯ́-wɣ-ɕaβ qapri tu-ɕe ri mɯ́j-cʰa tɕe \\
chimney ipfv - genr:S/O-make.a.nest lnk 3sg. poss -on indef. poss -water also neg: sens -come cat erg also neg - ipfv - inv -catch snake ipfv: up -go also neg: sens -can lnk \\
`[The sparrows] make their nest in the chimney, [because] water cannot come up there, the cats cannot catch them, and the snakes cannot go up there.' (22-kumpGatCW)
0003590#S59
exe

The marker ri is homophonous with the locative ri (§ sec:locative ), and in cases with an enumeration of locative adjuncts, there can be ambiguity between the two. In ( ex:Xcha.ri.ci ), ri is analyzed as a locative because of the position of the determiner ci, and also because it can be replaced with other locative postpositions.

exe

χcʰa ri ci, ɯ-ʁe ri ci ɯ-jme cʰɯ-ɬoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
right loc one 3sg. poss -left loc one 3sg. poss -tail ipfv: downstream -come.out sens -be \\
`It has one tail on the right, and one on the left.' (26-qro)
0003682#S109
exe
summary: The passage shows that **ri** can mark repeated correlations across multiple clauses or predicates, appearing after different subjects and even after a finite verb when they refer to the same additional referent. It is also noted that **ri** is homophonous with the locative **ri**, so in strings of locative adjuncts there can be ambiguity; in such cases, the surrounding structure and substitutability with other locative postpositions help identify the locative use.

text:
Three markers are used to express the meaning `not only $X$, but also $Y$', where $X$ and $Y$ stand for noun phrases: ʁo alala ri/ma ( ex:nWnWra.Roalalari ), mɤra ma ( ex:WkAphaR.mArama ) and ɯ-tɤjɯ tɕe. The etymology of these markers is discussed in § sec:incremental.addition.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯra ʁo alala ri ɯʑo sɤz kɯ-xtɕi pɣa nɯra kɯnɤ ku-ndɤm qʰe tu-ndze \\
lnk dem: pl advers not.only lnk 3sg comp sbj: pcp -be.small bird dem: pl also ipfv -take[III] lnk ipfv -eat[III] \\
`Apart from those, [the eagle] also catches birds that are smaller than itself and eats them.' (19-qandZGi)
0003548#S55
exe

The combination of these markers with the scalar focus marker cinɤ(not) even one (§ sec:cinA ) on the second noun phrase means `not even $X$, let alone $Y$', as shown by ( ex:WkAphaR.mArama ).

exe

ɯ-kɤ-pʰaʁ mɤra ma, ɯ-kɤ-skraβ cinɤ ʑo mɯ-ja-sɯ-ɤzɣɯt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -head-half not.only lnk 3sg. poss -head-fine.hair not.even.one emph neg - aor: 3sg 3- caus -arrive sens -be \\
`[This time, the horse] did not even bring back one fine hair from the [evil woman's] head, let alone half her head.' (Kunbzang)
exe

These three markers also occur as clausal subordinators (§ sec:incremental.addition ).

Scalar focus marker cinɤ
focus marker!scalar
The focus marker cinɤ(not) even one exclusively occurs with a negative verb. Like kɯnɤalso, even, this marker has stress on the first syllable cínɤ (§ sec:stress ), which is obviously related to the numeral cione (§ sec:one.to.ten, § sec:indef.article ).

The marker cinɤ has scope over the constituent that immediately precedes it, generally a noun phrase including or consisting of a counted noun, as in ( ex:tWrdoR.cinA3 ), but also headless participial relative clauses as in ( ex:zrWG.kAmto.cinA ), and ( ex:WrNa.WkWru.cinA ).

exe

tsuku kɯ qʰe tɯ-rdoʁ cinɤ mɤ-kɯ-mto tu. \\
some erg lnk one-piece even neg - sbj: pcp -see exist: fact \\
`There are some people who [cannot] even find a single one.' (20-grWBgrWB)
0003554#S35
exe

exe

ma tɕe jinde nɯ zrɯɣ kɤ-mto cinɤ maŋe. \\
lnk lnk nowadays dem louse obj: pcp -see even not.exist: sens \\
`Nowadays there isn't even a single louse to be seen/one cannot even see a single louse.' (21-mdzadi)
0003578#S67
exe

exe

ɯ-rŋa ɯ-kɯ-ru cinɤ ʑo pjɤ-me \\
3sg. poss -face 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -look even emph ipfv. ifr -not.exist \\
`Not even one [of the thieves] looked at it.' (`The thieves did not even so much as looked at it.') (140426 luozi he qiangdao-zh)
0003814#S28
exe

It is also possible to have both a headless relative clause and the counted noun tɯ-rdoʁ combined with cinɤ as in ( ex:lukWpGaR.nW.cinA ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-ɲɯ-kɯ-ɣɤ-rkɯn nɯ ɲɯ-dɤn ma lu-kɯ-pɣaʁ nɯ tɯ-rdoʁ cinɤ ʑo maŋe\\

`A lot of people diminish their fields, and not a single of them opens new fields.' (150903 friche)
0006400#S6
exe

In the case of relative clauses before cinɤ, there is some ambiguity as to whether the scope of the focus marker is on the head of the relative or on the main verb of the relative clause. Hence the two proposed translations above for ( ex:zrWG.kAmto.cinA ) and ( ex:WrNa.WkWru.cinA ).

It is not possible to use cinɤ with scope over transitive subjects, followed by the ergative.

The form cinɤ also occurs in the expression cinɤ maʁ kɯ `in any case it is not' (§ sec:cimame.cinAmaRkW ).
summary:
The passage describes three markers used to express the meaning “not only X, but also Y” with noun phrases, and notes that they can also function as clausal subordinators. When combined with the scalar focus marker cinɤ “not even one” on the second noun phrase, they yield the meaning “not even X, let alone Y.”  

It then explains that cinɤ is a focus marker that occurs only with negative verbs and usually takes scope over the immediately preceding constituent, especially counted noun phrases or headless participial relative clauses. The text also notes ambiguity in some relative-clause uses, states that cinɤ cannot take scope over transitive subjects followed by the ergative, and mentions its use in the fixed expression cinɤ maʁ kɯ “in any case it is not.”

text:
The most common way to express restrictive focus in Japhug is to combine the exceptive maapart from (and its reduplicated variant mɯma § sec:exceptive ) with a negative predicate. This can be a verb with a negative prefix as in ( ex:XsArZaR ), or a negative existential verb as in ( ex:Wmi.Wntsi.ma.me ).

exe

χsɤ-rʑaʁ ma mɯ-pɯ-tsu-a ɲɤ-sɯso ri χsɯ-xpa pjɤ-tsu tɕe, \\
three-day apart.from neg - aor -pass- 1sg ifr -think lnk three-year ifr -pass lnk \\
`He thought that he had spent only three days, but three years had passed.' (2011-4-smanmi)
exe

exe

rkoŋɟɤl nɯnɯ, ɯ-mi ɯ-ntsi nɯ ma me kʰi. \\
one.legged.demon dem 3sg. poss -leg 3sg. poss -one.of.a.pair dem apart.from not.exist: fact hearsay \\
`It is said that one-legged demons only had one leg.' (140510 rkoNJAl)
0003943#S5
exe

In the case of restrictive focalization on locative or temporal phrases, the terminative mɤɕtʂauntil (§ sec:terminative ) occurs instead of the exceptive.

exe

nɯnɯtɕu mɤɕtʂa mtsʰalu pjɤ-me qʰe \\
dem: loc until nettle ifr. ipfv -not.exist lnk \\
`It was only there that there was nettle.' = `There was no nettle until there.' (140520 ye tian'e-zh)
0004044#S301
exe

The restrictive focus construction implies the presence of a noun phrase with a numeral or a counted noun when the restriction bears on the quantity as in ( ex:XsArZaR ) and ( ex:Wmi.Wntsi.ma.me ) above, but restriction can also be qualitative, without quantifier, as in ( ex:karGi.Zo.kWfse.ma.me ).

exe

ɯ-mat nɯnɯ na-lɤt ɕimɯma nɤ kɯ-ndɯ ndɯβ ʑo ma me, karɣi ʑo kɯ-fse ma me \\
3sg. poss -fruit dem aor:3 -throw just lnk sbj: pcp - emph small emph apart.from not.exist: fact turnip.seed emph sbj: pcp -be.like apart.from not.exist: fact \\
`When the fruit of [xanthoxyllum] has just come out, there is only something very small, only like a turnip seed.' (07-tCGom) 0003434#S6
exe

The restrictive focus construction can be combined with a scalar focus in kɯnɤ (see § sec:kWnA ), as in ( ex:ma.kWme.kWnA ). In this example, kɯnɤ has scope over the subordinate clause stɯsti ma kɯ-me, which is ambiguous between a participial headless relative (§ sec:headless.relative ) `consisting of only a female all alone' and a manner infinitival clause (§ sec:manner.converbs; in this case the gloss of kɯ-me would be inf: stat -not.exist) `even (when) there is only a female all alone'.

exe

mu ma, stɯsti ma kɯ-me kɯnɤ cʰɯ-rɤŋgɯm ɲɯ-ɕti. \\
female apart.from alone apart.from sbj: pcp -not.exist also ipfv -lay.eggs sens -be. aff \\
`Even only a female [hen] alone does lay eggs.' (150819 kumpGa)
0006388#S10
exe

A second possibility to express restrictive focus is the use of the adverb ʁɟacompletely, `all' (§ sec:restrictive.adverbs ) with scope over a noun phrase rather than the whole clause as in ( ex:RJa.tunWndze ). The form ʁɟa possibly originates from the first syllable of Tibetan གཡའ་མ་gja.mastone slab, through a meaning `bare rock'.

exe

alo mbroχpa ra tɕe tɕe nɤki qra cʰo qambrɯ ra ɣɯ nɯ-ɣli nɯnɯ tɕe nɯ tu-wum-nɯ, tu-sɯɣ-rom-nɯ mbroχpa sɤtɕʰa tɕe stɤmku ʁɟa ɲɯ-ɕti ma si maŋe tɕe tɕe \\
upstream nomad pl lnk lnk filler female.yak comit male.yak pl gen 3pl. poss -dung dem lnk dem ipfv -gather- pl ipfv - caus -be.dry- pl nomad place lnk grassland completely sens -be. aff lnk tree not.exist: sens lnk lnk \\
`Upstream, in the nomad areas, they gather and dry yak dung, as in nomad places there is only grassland, there are no trees.' (05-tamar) 0003406#S7
exe

The adverb ʁɟa (here used rather as a noun modifier) is related to the denominal verb aʁɟabe bald, be bare (see § sec:denom.a on the a- derivation), which can be applied to nouns such as stɤmkugrassland and zgomountain.

exe

qajɯ ʁɟa tu-nɯ-ndze, ma nɯ ma tɤ-rɤku kɯ-fse ra ndze mɤ-ŋgrɤl. \\
bug completely ipfv - auto -eat[III] lnk dem apart.from indef. poss -harvest sbj: pcp -be.like pl eat[III]: fact neg -be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`It only eats insects, it does not eat cultivated plants.' (140511 qamtsWrmdzu)
0003957#S16
exe

While in ( ex:RJa.tunWndze ) and ( ex:stAmku.RJa ) we lack decisive evidence that ʁɟa forms a syntactic constituent with the previous nouns or the following verb, in ( ex:RJa.kW ) the presence of the ergative makes it clear that ʁɟa is not a clausal adverb, and belongs to the postpositional phrase headed by kɯ.

exe

[tɤ-lu cʰo tɯkrimgo ʁɟa kɯ] cʰɯ-z-ɣɤ-wxti-nɯ. \\
indef. poss -milk comit doughnut completely erg ipfv - caus - caus -be.big- pl \\
`They [used to] raise up [the babies] by feeding them milk and doughnuts only.' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR)
exe

The same applies to ( ex:Wru.RJa.nW ), where the presence of the demonstrative nɯ after ʁɟa shows that it belongs to the same noun phrase.

exe

ɯ-rdoʁ nɯ-me tɕe, [ɯ-ru ʁɟa nɯ], pɯ-kɤ-tɤβ nɯnɯ, taʁndzɤr ɯ-ŋgɯ tú-wɣ-rku tɕe, \\
3sg. poss -grain aor -not.exist lnk 3sg. poss -stalk completely dem aor - obj: pcp -thresh dem feeding.emmer 3sg. poss -inside ipfv - inv -put.in lnk \\
`When all the grains have been removed, the bare stalks, the one that have been threshed, one puts them in a feeding emmer.' (140513 tWrtsi)
0003985#S5
exe

A reduplicated emphatic form ʁɟɯ ʁɟa is also found as in ( ex:RJWRJa.kW )

exe

χtɕɤnzɤn ʁɟɯ ʁɟa kɯ ʑo pɯ́-wɣ-nɤjo ɕti ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
beast emph completely erg emph pst. ipfv - inv -wait be. aff: fact sens -be \\
`It was all wild beasts waiting for him [there].' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

A third option to express restrictive focus is the inalienable noun ɯ-jlu, which is used in the meaning `uncooked' as a property noun (§ sec:property.nouns ), but has become grammaticalized as a restrictive marker `exclusively, without anything else' (presumably from an intermediate meaning `plain, simple'), as in ( ex:Wjlu.Zo ).

exe
summary:
Restrictive focus in Japhug is most commonly expressed with the exceptive ma or mɯma plus a negative predicate, and with the terminative mɤɕtʂa in locative or temporal phrases. The construction can indicate either quantity-based restriction with numerals/counted nouns or qualitative restriction without quantifiers, and it may combine with scalar focus markers like kɯnɤ.  

A second strategy uses the adverb ʁɟa ‘completely, all’, which can scope over a noun phrase rather than the whole clause and sometimes appears in emphatic or noun-modifying uses; a reduplicated emphatic form ʁɟɯ ʁɟa is also attested. A third restrictive marker is the inalienable noun ɯ-jlu, grammaticalized to mean ‘exclusively, without anything else’.

text:
srɤz nɯ kɯ tɕʰoz ɯ-jlu ʑo pjɯ-nɯjɤntɤn pɯ-ɕti ma jɯm nɯ mɯ-pjɤ-ɕar ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
prince dem erg religion 3sg. poss -exclusively emph ipfv -be.assiduous.in pst. ipfv -be. aff lnk wife dem neg - ifr. ipfv -look.for sens -be \\
`The prince was focused exclusively in the study of religion, and was not looking for a wife.' (2003 sras)
exe

For the expression of restrictive focus with temporal noun phrases or clauses, the postposition kóʁmɯzonly after can also be used, especially with the demonstrative in the expression nɯ kóʁmɯz nɤonly then (§ sec:temporal.postpositions, § sec:immediate.subsequence ).
summary: The passage gives an example of restrictive focus, showing that the prince was “focused exclusively” on studying religion and not seeking a wife. It also notes that with temporal noun phrases or clauses, the postposition **kóʁmɯz** ‘only after’ can be used to express restrictive focus, especially with the demonstrative in the expression **nɯ kóʁmɯz** ‘only then.’

text:
identity modifier
There is no specific identity modifier `the same' in Japhug. The only way to express this meaning is to use the subject participle of the verb naχtɕɯɣbe the same (a denumeral verb of Tibetan origin, § sec:tibetan.numerals, see also § sec:comitative and § sec:nmlz.equative on the syntax of this stative verb) in a relative clause, as in ( ex:tArmi.kWnaXtCWG ) (a possessor relative, § sec:possessor.relativization ). This participle competes with the borrowed identity adverb anamanaidentical (§ sec:identity.adverbs ).

exe

tɤ-rmi kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ pjɤ-dɤn wo kɤmɲɯ, nɤki kɯrɯ ra tɕe. \\
indef. poss -name sbj: pcp -be.the.same ifr. ipfv -be.many sfp topo filler Tibetan pl lnk \\
`There were many people who had identical names, in Kamnyu, among the Tibetans.' (140522 tshupa) 0004053#S155
exe

There are two prenominal modifiers expressing non-identity in Japhug: kɯmaʁother and the numeral cione, which in prenominal position means `the other one' (in postnominal position, it is used as an indefinite determiner, see § sec:indef.article ). Both of these words can also be used as pronouns, though ci requires to be combined with the demonstrative nɯ in this usage (see § sec:other.pro ).

The modifier kɯmaʁ is prenominal in its meaning `other', as in ( ex:kWmaR.tWrme ).

exe

tɯ-zda nɯ ma kɯmaʁ tɯrme a-pɯ-me tɕe, kʰa ra aʁɤndɯndɤt ɲɯ-ɤ<nɯ>ɣro ɲɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ti. \\
genr. poss -companion dem apart.from other person irr - ipfv -not.exist lnk house pl everywhere ipfv -< auto >play sens -be sens -say \\
`[Our neighbour] says that if there are no other persons apart from family members, [the monkey] would play everywhere in the house.' (19-GzW2)
0003538#S10
exe

There are apparent examples of kɯmaʁother in postnominal position, as in ( ex:kWmaR.taXtW ) and ( ex:kWmaR.tanWsWBzu ), but in such sentences kɯmaʁ is a preverbal adverb, not a noun modifier, with a slightly different meaning `anew'. In ( ex:kWmaR.taXtW ), the usage of kɯmaʁ is very similar to its Chinese equivalent 另外 lìngwàiother in the corresponding Chinese sentence 阿兰另外给我买了一部手机, where the preverbal position of 另外 lìngwàiother clearly shows that it is not a noun modifier.

exe

<alan> kɯ a-<dianhua> kɯmaʁ ta-χtɯ \\
anthr erg 1sg. poss -phone other aor:3 -buy \\
` Alan bought me a new phone.' (conversation, 17-03-27)
exe

exe

a-ʁi kɯ kʰa kɯmaʁ ta-nɯ-sɯ-βzu\\
1sg. poss -younger.sibling erg house other aor:3 - auto - caus -make\\
`My brother made himself a new house.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S279
exe

The identity determiner kɯmaʁother is grammaticalized from the subject participle of the verb maʁnot be, kɯ-maʁ `who/which is not X' (see also § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ), which is still widely used, as in ( ex:tChWrtsAm.kWmaR ) and ( ex:sthWci.kWmaR ).

exe

mɤʑɯ [tɕʰirtsɤm kɯ-maʁ] nɯnɯ tɕe, tú-wɣ-χtɕi ma nɯ ma kɤ-sqa (mɤ-ra) \\
yet type.of.tsampa sbj: pcp -not.be dem lnk ipfv - inv -wash lnk dem apart.from inf -boil neg -be.needed: fact \\
`The tsampa that is not `chu.rtsam', one needs to wash it, but not to boil it.' (2002 tWsqar)
exe

exe

[ɯ-rkɯ wuma ʑo stʰɯci kɯ-maʁ] nɯtɕu tɤ-ri ci kú-wɣ-lɤt \\
3sg. poss -side really emph so.much sbj: pcp -not.be dem: loc indef. poss -thread once ipfv - inv -throw \\
`One sews a thread at a place which is not too much on the border [of the patch]'. (12-kAtsxWb)
0003486#S16
exe

The modifier ci differs from kɯmaʁ in that it is necessarily definite, meaning `the other one', as in ( ex:ci.rWdaR ), where it refers to an animal that is chased by lions, which was previously mentioned in the text.

exe

ʑɯrɯʑɤri qʰe ci rɯdaʁ nɯ dɯxpa ma nɯ-kɤ-ndza ɯ-spa ɲɯ-ɕti qʰe, qʰe pjɯ-ndʐaβ qʰe mɯ-ɲɯ-cʰa qʰe, \\
progressively lnk other.one animal dem poor lnk 3pl. poss - obj: pcp -eat 3sg. poss -material sens -be. aff lnk lnk ipfv - anticaus:make.fall lnk neg - ipfv -can lnk \\
`The other animal, poor him, it is their prey, progressively it falls down and cannot stand it anymore.' (20-sWNgi)
0003562#S41
exe

Interestingly, the determiner ci does not have scope over other noun modifiers. For instance, in ( ex:ci.tCheme.kWNAn ), the noun tɕʰemegirl occurs with an attributive adjective in participial form kɯ-ŋɤn `who is evil' (a relative clause, see § sec:attributes ), but the meaning is not `the other evil woman' as could have been expected (this interpretation is excluded since the woman who is the subject of the sentence is, by contrast, a kind person), and rather must be `the other woman, the evil one'. There is no pause in the recording that could lead us to suppose that kɯ-ŋɤn here is an apposition -- it is rather a postnominal relative.

exe

nɤki, tɕʰeme nɯ ɯ-ɕki ɯ-kɯ-sɤja jo-ɕe, ci tɕʰeme kɯ-ŋɤn nɯ ɯ-ɕki. \\
filler women dem 3sg - dat 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -give.back ifr -go other.one woman sbj: pcp -be.evil dem 3sg - dat \\
`She went to give it back to the woman, the other one, the evil woman.' (140515 jiesu de laoren-zh)
0004004#S84
exe
summary: Japhug has no dedicated modifier meaning “the same”; this sense is expressed instead by the subject participle of the verb *naχtɕɯɣ* “be the same” in a relative clause, and this form competes with the borrowed adverb *anamana* “identical.” For non-identity, Japhug uses prenominal *kɯmaʁ* “other” and *ci* “the other one,” with *ci* being definite and unable to take scope over following noun modifiers. The form *kɯmaʁ* is grammaticalized from a participle meaning “not be X,” and when it appears after the noun it functions as a preverbal adverb meaning “anew,” not as a modifier.

text:
Japhug has several sub-parts of speech which could be described as ``adjectives'': stative verbs, adverbs and nouns which express properties (rather than actions or entities). Property words used as noun modifiers are collectively designated by the term attributes. This heterogenous class excludes the property nouns described in § sec:property.nouns, which are the syntactic heads of the noun phrase.

Three types of attributes are distinguished: attributive postnominal (noun or adverb) modifiers, prenominal modifiers and participial kɯ- relatives (mainly postnominal or head-internal). The constructions mentioned in this section are all described in more detail elsewhere in the grammar, and for this reason the discussion is kept brief.
summary:
Japhug has several word types that can function like “adjectives,” including stative verbs, adverbs, and property-denoting nouns. These are grouped together as attributes when they modify nouns, but this category excludes property nouns that serve as syntactic heads of noun phrases.

The grammar distinguishes three kinds of attributes: postnominal modifiers, prenominal modifiers, and participial kɯ- relatives, which are mainly postnominal or head-internal. These constructions are only briefly discussed here because they are treated in more detail elsewhere in the grammar.

text:
attribute!postnominal
In addition to the postnominal markers studied above (numeral and number § sec:number.determiners, demonstratives § sec:demonstrative.determiners, quantifiers § sec:quantifiers.determiners, definiteness markers § sec:indef.article, topic and focus markers), there are a certain number of nouns that can serve as post-nominal modifiers.

The terms tɕʰemegirl and tɤ-tɕɯson, `boy' can be used as modifiers to specify the gender of a person, in particular in combination with gender-neutral kinship terms such as tɤ-ftsasister's child or relative age sibling terms (§ sec:siblings.age ).

Some compound nouns occur as postnominal modifiers, specific to a particular head-noun, for instance tʰɤlwɤɕtʂatsparing earth or rnɤftɕɯχawhose ear has ten holes, used as attributes of qandʐeearthworm (example ex:qandzxe.thAlwACtsxat, § sec:object.verb.compounds ) and qalarabbit (§ sec:subject.verb.compounds ), respectively. Some compounds from Tibetan such as the nouns of the twelve year cycle (such as staʁluyear of the tiger from སྟག་ལོ་stag.loyear of the tiger in ex:WGe.staRlu ) also occur postnominally.

exe

tɕelo prɤmzi rgɤtpu ɣɯ ɯ-ɣe staʁ-lu ci ɣɤʑu tɕe, \\
upstream anthr old.man gen 3sg. poss -grandchild tiger-year indef exist: sens lnk \\
`Up there, the old Bramze has a grandchild who is born in the year of the tiger.' (2003nyima2)
exe

Privative nouns in -lu `...less' (§ sec:privative ) and nouns of relative location in maŋ- (§ sec:relative.location ) are mainly used as postnominal modifiers.

The nouns χcʰaright and ʁeleft are mainly used with the noun tɯ-jaʁhand, arm (or with other paired body parts), and can either be used as pre- ( ex:Re.ajaR ) or postnominal modifiers (§ ex:tWjaR.Xcha ).

exe

ʁe a-jaʁ tu-ntɕʰoz-a ŋu \\
left 1sg. poss -hand ipfv -use- 1sg be: fact \\
`I use my left hand.' (elicited)
exe

exe

tɯ-jaʁ χcʰa nɯ kɯ, taqaβ cʰo tɤ-ri nɯ tú-wɣ-ndo, tɯ-jaʁ ʁe nɯ kɯ kɤ-ɕpʰɤt ɯ-spa nɯ pjɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-stʰoʁ ŋu \\
genr. poss -hand right dem erg needle comit indef. poss -thread dem ipfv - inv -take genr. poss -hand left dem erg inf -patch 3sg. poss -material dem ipfv - inv - caus -press be: fact \\
`One takes the needle and the thread with one's right hand, and one presses the [cloth] to be patched with the left hand.' (12-kAtsxWb)
0003486#S32
exe

The word wumareal, really from Tibetan ངོ་མ་ŋo.mareal, true (§ sec:zero.onset ) is generally used as an intensifier, in particular with stative verbs (§ sec:wuma ), but also occurs as a postnominal modifier meaning `real', its original meaning, as in ( ex:lhAndzxi.wuma ) and ( ex:tAtsoR.wuma ).

exe

ɬɤndʐi wuma nɯ nɤʑo ɲɯ-tɯ-ŋu ma aʑo ɬɤndʐi ɲɯ-maʁ-a \\
demon real dem 2sg sens -2-be lnk 1sg demon sens -not.be- 1sg \\
`You are the real demon, not me.' (2002 lhandzi)
exe

exe

ɯ-qa nɯ qarŋe, tɤtsoʁ wuma nɯ. \\
3sg. poss -root dem be.yellow: fact silverweed real dem \\
`Its root is yellow, the real silverweed.' (19-khWlu)
0003540#S68
exe

The inalienably possessed noun nɯ-tɤngɯtcommon possession, which requires a non-singular possessor, can be used as a postnominal attribute, sharing the same possessive prefix as the preceding noun, as in nɯ-rmi nɯ-tɤngɯt `their collective name' in ( ex:nWrmi.nWtAngWt ).

exe

nɯnɯ tʂu nɯ ɕaŋtaʁ nɯnɯ tɕetu, (...) rɯŋgu mɯ-tu-tɯɣ mɤɕtʂa, nɯnɯ tɯ-ji tʰamtɕɤt ʑo nɯ-rmi nɯ tɯtɯrca nɯ-rmi nɯ tɯmŋu rmi. tɕeri tɯmŋu nɯnɯ, nɯ-rmi nɯ-tɤngɯt kɯ-fse ŋu. \\
dem road dem up.from up.there dem pasture neg - ipfv: up -touch until dem indef.poss-field all emph 3pl. poss -name dem together 3pl. poss -name dem topo be.called: fact lnk topo dem 3pl. poss -name 3pl. poss -in.common sbj: pcp -be.like be: fact \\
`Up from that path until the pasture, all the fields in there put together, their collective name is tɯmŋu.' (150903 tWmNu)
0006280#S7
exe
comitative adverb
In addition, some adverbs, which are more often used with scope over the whole clause, can occur as postnominal modifiers, in particular the comitative adverbs (§ sec:comitative.adverb ) and adverbs of quantification (§ sec:quantifiers.determiners ).
summary:
The passage describes several kinds of nouns and adverbs that can function as postnominal modifiers. These include gender-specifying nouns like “girl” and “boy,” certain compound nouns and Tibetan borrowings, privative and relative-location nouns, left/right terms used with paired body parts, the intensifier wuma used attributively as “real,” and the inalienably possessed noun nɯ-tɤngɯt ‘in common’ with a shared possessive prefix.

It also notes that some adverbs, especially comitative adverbs and quantificational adverbs, may appear after the noun as postnominal modifiers.

text:
attribute!penominal
Noun phrases serving as prenominal modifiers are not easily distinguishable from possessors, the only difference being the absence of a coreferent possessive prefix on the following noun (§ ex:prefix.expression.of.possession ).

The most common type of prenominal modifiers are place-names and other unpossessible nouns (§ sec:place.names ) and nouns expressing the material from which an object is a made, as χsɤrgold, rŋɯlsilver and siwood in ( ex:rNWl.rJAskAt ).

exe

a-tɤɕime, nɤʑo rŋɯl rɟɤskɤt ɯ-taʁ tɯ-ɕe ɕi, χsɤr rɟɤskɤt ɯ-taʁ tɯ-ɕe ɕi, ɕom rɟɤskɤt ɯ-taʁ tɯ-nɯ-ɕe? \\
1sg. poss -lady 2sg silver stair 3sg. poss -on 2-go: fact qu gold stair 3sg. poss -on 2-go: fact qu wood stair 3sg. poss -on 2- auto -go: fact \\
`My lady, will you go on the silver stairs, the golden stairs or the wooden stairs?' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

Prenominal modifiers can be more complex phrases. In ( ex:CkrAz.RJa.Zo ), the prenominal modifier ɕkrɤzoak takes the restrictive focus marker ʁɟacompletely (§ sec:restrictive.focus ). A superficially similar construction in found in ex:tAtCW.RJa.Zo (§ sec:restrictive.adverbs ); in that example, the constituent [noun+ ʁɟa ʑo ] is a preposed nominal predicate. That analysis is not possible in ( ex:CkrAz.RJa.Zo ), since the subject is the demonstrative nɯ, and the nominal predicate is ɕkrɤz ʁɟa ʑo sɯŋgɯ.

exe

nɯ [ɕkrɤz ʁɟa ʑo] sɯŋgɯ ŋu tɕe \\
dem oak completely emph forest be: fact lnk \\
`It is a forest exclusively of oaks.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo)
0004059#S88
exe

In ( ex:nWsakaB.tsxu ), the prenominal modifier of tʂuroad has three degrees of embedding.

exe

[[[smɤt tɯmda] rɟɤlpu nɯra ɣɯ] nɯ-sakaβ] tʂu nɯtɕu ɕ-kɤ-rɤʑi ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
topo topo king dem. pl gen 3pl. poss -well path dem. loc tral - aor -stay sens -be \\
`He went (there) and stayed on the way to the well of the king of Smad.mda.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

When a prenominal modifier is present, possessive prefixes on inalienably possessed head nouns can be neutralized, becoming an indefinite possessor (§ sec:possessive.prefixes.prenominal ).

At least in the case of some prenominal modifiers limited to single nouns, Attempts to test this possibility with larger prenominal phrases such as that in ( ex:CkrAz.RJa.Zo ) are inconclusive. possessive prefixes can either be prefixed on the head noun ( ex:XsAr.akWmtChW2 ), or on the modifier ( ex:aXsAr.kWmtChW2 ) (§ sec:possessive.prefixes.prenominal ).

exe

xlist

χsɤr a-kɯmtɕʰɯ \\
gold 1sg. poss -toy \\

a-χsɤr kɯmtɕʰɯ \\
1sg. poss -gold toy \\
`My golden toy' (see example ex:XsAr.akWmtChW, § sec:possessive.prefixes.prenominal )
xlist
exe

Since in ( ex:XsAr.kWmtChW ) no stress can be heard on the modifier χsɤrgold, it could be possible to argue that χsɤr kɯmtɕʰɯ in ( ex:aXsAr.kWmtChW2 ) should rather be analyzed as a noun compound (§ sec.n.n.compounds ) χsɤr-kɯmtɕʰɯ: this is one of the domains of Japhug grammar in which the boundary between syntax and morphology is unclear (§ sec:wordhood ).

The adverb koŋlareally, `completely' (§ sec:intensifier.adverbs ) can be used as a prenominal modifier in the sense of `real'.

exe

koŋla tɯrme ci, kɯ-pɯ pe tɕʰeme ci, nɤ-ɕɣa kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕɤr a-nɯ-tɯ-aβzu smɯlɤm \\
really person indef sbj: pcp - emph be.good girl indef 2sg. poss -age sbj: pcp - emph be.small sbj: pcp - emph be.beautiful irr - pfv -2-become prayer \\
`May you become a real human, a nice, young and beautiful girl.' (said to a râkshasî) (2005 Norbzang)
exe
summary: Prenominal modifiers in this language are often hard to distinguish from possessors, since the main difference is that the following noun lacks a coreferent possessive prefix. The most common prenominal modifiers are place names, other unpossessible nouns, and material nouns, but they can also be more complex phrases, sometimes with restrictive focus markers; in some cases possessive prefixes may appear either on the head noun or on the modifier, blurring the boundary between syntax and compounding. The adverb *koŋla* can also function prenominally with the meaning ‘real.’

text:
attribute!participial relative relative clause!attribute
Most words expressing properties in Japhug are a subclass of stative verbs, and cannot serve as attributes without being embedded into a relative clause. Since intransitive subjects can only be relativized using kɯ- participial relative clauses (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ), attributive adjectival stative verbs are always in this form, as kɯ-pe `good one, which is good' in ( ex:wuma.Zo.kWpe ); the relative wuma ʑo tɕʰeme kɯ-pe in this example is head-internal (§ sec:head-internal.relative ), as shown by the position of the intensifier wuma ʑo (§ sec:wuma ), and literally means `(a) woman who is/was really nice.'

exe

ɯ-rʑaβ βdaʁmu nɯ [wuma ʑo tɕʰeme kɯ-pe] ci pjɤ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -wife lady dem really emph woman sbj: pcp -be.good indef ifr. ipfv -be \\
`His wife, the queen, was a very nice woman.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S4
exe

In the case of shorter relative clauses it is not always clear whether we have a head-internal, or a postnominal one (§ sec:postnominal.relative ). Prenominal relatives with an adjectival stative verb such as stu kɯ-mna `the best one, the leader' in ( ex:stu.kWmna.tCheme ) are less common.

exe

rɟɤlpu nɤrɯβzaŋ nɯ kɯ, nɤki, [stu kɯ-mna tɕʰeme] nɯ ɲɤ-nɯ-ɕar ɲɯ-ŋu \\
king anthr dem erg filler most sbj: pcp -be.better woman dem ifr - auto -search sens -be \\
`King Norbzang chose for himself the woman leader.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S37
exe

The presence of an adjunct, such as a standard marker, can disambiguate between postnominal and head-internal relatives (§ comparee.relativization ); in ( ex:WZo.sAznA.pGa.kWxtCi ) for instance, the head pɣabird is clearly internal.

exe

βʑar ndɤre ŋɤn ma [ɯʑo sɤznɤ pɣa kɯ-xtɕi] nɯra ʁɟa ʑo tu-ndze ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
buzzard lnk be.evil: fact lnk 3sg comp bird sbj: pcp -be.small dem: pl completely emph ipfv -eat[III] sens -be lnk \\
`The buzzard is fierce, its eats all the birds that are smaller than itself.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S80
exe

As shown in § sec:head-internal.relative.determiners, in head-internal relative clauses the same determiner can appear on the head noun and repeated after the whole relative. The same is found with adjectival participial relatives, as in ( ex:qajW.ci.kArNi.ci ) with the indefinite cione, though this usage is rare, in most cases only one of the two determiners is used (either the one inside the relative or the external one).

exe

tɕe [qajɯ ci kɯ-ɤrŋi] ci ŋu. \\
lnk bug indef sbj: pcp -be.green indef be: fact \\
`It is a green/black bug.' (26-zrWGndza)
0003696#S6
exe

In prenominal position, subject relatives are almost not attested with stative verbs, but are found with some intransitive dynamic verbs. In the lexicalized expression in ( ex:kWrlaR.kha ), prenominal placement of the participle kɯ-rlaʁ is required.

exe

kɯ-rlaʁ kʰa \\
sbj: pcp -disappear house \\
`An abandonned house.'
exe
summary:
In Japhug, most property-denoting words are stative verbs, so they cannot modify a noun directly and must appear inside a relative clause. These adjectival stative verbs are typically relativized with kɯ- participial relatives, often as head-internal clauses, though shorter cases can be ambiguous and prenominal relatives of this type are less common.

The passage also notes that adjuncts such as standard markers can help distinguish head-internal from postnominal relatives, and that determiners may appear both inside and outside head-internal relatives, though this is rare. Prenominal subject relatives are generally uncommon with stative verbs, but some occur with intransitive dynamic verbs and in lexicalized expressions.

text:
coordination!noun phrase
Japhug lacks a dedicated noun coordinator. Nouns can be either coordinated by using the comitative postposition cʰo (§ sec:coordinator.cho ), or by juxtaposition without any linking element (§ sec:bare.coordination ).
summary: Japhug does not have a special coordinator for noun phrases. Instead, nouns are coordinated either with the comitative postposition **cʰo** or by simple juxtaposition without any linking element.

text:
The closest thing to a noun coordinator in Japhug is the comitative marker cʰo; it can be used both to connect finite clauses (§ sec:neutral.addition ) or nouns as in ( ex:dpalcan.cho.alan ).

When the constituent comprising two noun phrases connected by cʰo is in subject or object function, number indexation on the verb reflects the sum of all individuals referred to by this coordinated constituent, dual in the case of ( ex:dpalcan.cho.alan ).

exe

[χpɤltɕin cʰo alan] kɯ ko-ndo-ndʑi tɕe, \\
n.p. comit n.p. erg ifr -take- du lnk \\
` Dpalcan and Alan caught [one].' (24-qro)
0003626#S94
exe

Number markers like ra (§ sec:plural.determiners ) have scope over the whole coordinated constituent, as in ( ex:qandZGi.cho.qaliaR ).

exe

[qandʑɣi cʰo qaliaʁ] ra kɯ cʰɯ-nɯ-tsɯm-nɯ tu-ndza-nɯ ŋgrɤl. \\
falcon comit eagle pl erg ipfv: downstream - vert -take.away- pl ipfv -eat- pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`Falcons and eagles take [the moles] and eat them.' (28-qapar)
0003720#S192
exe

There is however evidence that cʰo is a postposition rather than conjunction. First, while cʰo cannot be used without a preceding noun phrase or clause, the noun following it (for instance, qaliaʁeagle in ex:qandZGi.cho.qaliaR ) is optional, as illustrated by ( ex:cho.torWstWnmWndZi ) and several additional examples in § sec:comitative.

exe

nɯ cʰo to-rɯstɯnmɯ-ndʑi. \\
[ dem comit ] ifr -marry- du \\
`He married her.' (140511 alading-zh) 0003953#S183
exe

Second, the fact that the noun followed by cʰo is a constituent can be shown by the fact that it can be relativized with an oblique participle (§ sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ).

For these reasons, rather than assuming a `flat' structure as in fig:qanZGi, I consider qandʑɣi cʰo to be a postpositional phrase used as an adnominal modifier of the noun qaliaʁeagle, as in fig:qanZGi2.
summary:
In Japhug, the comitative marker **cʰo** functions as the closest equivalent to a noun coordinator and can link either clauses or nouns. When it joins two noun phrases in subject or object position, verbal number marking reflects the total number of individuals involved, and plural markers such as **ra** scope over the entire coordinated constituent.  

However, the text argues that **cʰo** is better analyzed as a **postposition** than as a conjunction, because it cannot occur without a preceding noun phrase or clause, while the following noun is optional and behaves as a constituent that can be relativized. On this view, sequences like **qandʑɣi cʰo** form a postpositional phrase modifying the following noun rather than a flat coordination structure.

text:
noun!enumeration
Enumerations are the listing of a series of nouns, often with a specific (rising) intonation and a pause between items, and without any coordinating element (such as the postposition cʰo seen above). In Japhug, quite lengthy enumerations are attested in the corpus, as shown by ( ex:mbro.etc ) with seven nouns.

exe

mbro, jla, nɯŋa, mbala, tsʰɤt, qaʑo, paʁ, nɯra nɯtɕu ʁɟa z-ɲɯ́-wɣ-lɤɣ pɯ-ŋu. \\
horse hybrid.yak cow bull goat sheep pig dem: pl dem: loc completely tral - ipfv - inv -graze pst. ipfv -be \\
`People used to graze their horses, hybrid yaks, cows, bulls, goats, sheep and pigs.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo)
0004059#S151
exe

Enumerations are generally understood as non-exhaustive, implying the potential inclusion of other referents to the list, especially when each noun occurs with the participle kɯ-fse `like' as in ( ex:qala.kWfse ).

exe

nɯnɯ tɤ-mu nɯ kɯ qala kɯ-fse, ca kɯ-fse, nɯnɯ rɯdaʁ kɯ-xɕti nɯra pjɯ-sat. \\
dem indef. poss -mother dem erg rabbit sbj: pcp -be.like deer sbj: pcp -be.like dem animal sbj: pcp -be.small dem: pl ipfv -kill \\
`The mother kills small animals like rabbits or deer.' (20-sWNgi)
0003562#S77
exe

However, enumerations with only two nouns and without specific intonation, as in ( ex:tshAt.qaZo ), can also express exhaustive enumeration.

exe

qʰe tsʰɤt qaʑo ra ɣɯ nɯ-ndza nɯra ɲɯ-sna. \\
lnk goat sheep pl gen 3pl. poss -food dem: pl sens -be.good \\
`It is good as fodder for goats and sheep.' (16-RlWmsWsi)
0003520#S62
exe

When the order of the nouns is rigid (which is not the case in ex:tshAt.qaZo, since qaʑo tsʰɤt `sheep and goats' is also attested), the construction belongs to a different category: that of noun dyads (§ sec:dyads ).
summary: Enumerations in Japhug are lists of nouns, typically marked by rising intonation and pauses between items, and they do not include a coordinating element; very long examples are attested. They are usually interpreted as non-exhaustive, though two-item lists without special intonation can be exhaustive. If the noun order is fixed, the construction is not an enumeration but a noun dyad.

text:
noun!dyad
Noun dyads are a pair of nouns occurring in a fixed order, without intervening linker or postposition, and sharing their number and case markers. A good example is provided by the expression `parents' comprising the kinship terms tɤ-mumother and tɤ-wafather, as in ( ex:amu.awa.ni.GW ). Note that while number and case markers are shared by both nouns, each of them takes its own possessive prefix, and both prefixes are coreferent.

exe

nɯ a-mu a-wa ni ɣɯ ŋu \\
dem 1sg. poss -mother 1sg. poss -father du gen be: fact \\
`This is for my parents.' (meimei de gushi)
exe

The dyad for `parents' has a honorific variant, originally used for noblemen in the traditional society. It comprises the terms tɤ-pafather and tɤ-mamother, which are borrowed from Tibetan ཨ་ཕ་ʔa.pʰafather and ཨ་མ་ʔa.mamother, respectively. Interestingly, the honorific expression follows the `father-mother' order (as in example ex:apa.ama ), while the native one reverses the order with `mother' first, as in `mother-father'.

exe

nɯ kɯ-fse a-pa a-ma ni kɯ ɲɯ-ti-ndʑi tɕe \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.like 1sg. poss -father 1sg. poss -mother du erg sens -say- du lnk \\
`My parents say this.' (2003nyima2)
exe

Other common dyads referring to humans, but alienably possessed, include rgɤtpu rgɤnmɯ `old man(men) and woman(women)', tɤ-tɕɯ tɕʰeme `boy(s) and girl(s)'. They are most commonly used as collectives with indefinite referents as in ( ex:tAtCW.tCheme.tWsAmdzW ), but are also attested with definite ones, as in ( ex:rgAtpu.rgAnmW ), with the aforementioned topic marker iɕqʰa (§ sec:iCqha ).

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ tɕʰeme tɯ-sɤ-ɤmdzɯ ʑaka tu \\
indef. poss -son girl genr. poss - obl: pcp -sit each exist: fact \\
`Gentlemen and ladies each have [different] seating places.' (31-khAjmu)
0004079#S10
exe

exe

tɤ-rɟit nɯ li iɕqʰa rgɤtpu rgɤnmɯ ni kɯ pjɤ-mto-ndʑi \\
indef. poss -offspring dem again the.aforementioned old.man old.woman du erg ifr -see- du \\
`That child, the old man and the old woman saw him.' (140514 huishuohua de niao-zh)
0003992#S51
exe

Dyads are not restricted to humans, as shown by the dyad tɤɕi qaj `barley and wheat' ( ex:rCWB4.pjWlAt, § sec:ideo.X ).

Another type of noun dyad comprises two abstract nouns, which can be used as manner adjuncts with the ergative (see example ex:tAmqe.tAndWt.kW § sec:manner.nominal.kW ) or in the degree construction as in ( ex:tAre.tAJaR ) with the dyad tɤ-re tɤ-ɟaʁ `chatting and laughing' (only tɤ-relaugh (n) exists as an independent word). Some of these dyads are nominalized forms of bipartite verbs (§ sec:bipartite ).

exe

nɯtɕu rcanɯ maka tɤ-re tɤ-ɟaʁ pjɤ-saχaʁ \\
dem: loc unexp: deg completely indef. poss -laugh indef. poss -laugh ifr. ipfv -be.extremely \\
`There, [the râkshasî] were chatting and laughing a lot.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe
summary: Noun dyads are fixed pairs of nouns that occur without a linker or postposition and share number and case marking, though each noun keeps its own possessive prefix. The passage illustrates kinship dyads such as “parents,” including a native mother–father order and an honorific father–mother variant, and notes that other dyads can refer to human groups, nonhuman pairs like “barley and wheat,” or abstract concepts used as manner or degree expressions.

text:
There is no dedicated linker for expressing inclusive and/or exclusive disjunction of noun phrases in Japhug. The clausal linker nɯmaʁnɤotherwise can exceptionally occur between nouns as in ( ex:arpW.nWmaRnA ), but such rare constructions are the result of the elision of the non-final verb(s) in a string of clauses sharing the same verb forms such as ( ex:luwɣlAt.nWmaRnA ) (§ sec:disjunction.clauses ).

exe

tɕe aʑo a-rɟit nɯ kɯ a-wɤmɯ ɯ-rɟit nɯ tɕe ``a-rpɯ" nɯmaʁnɤ ``a-ɬaʁ" tu-ti kɯ-ra. \\
lnk 1sg 1sg. poss -child dem erg 1sg. poss -brother 3sg. poss -child dem loc 1sg. poss -MB otherwise 1sg. poss -MZ ipfv -say sbj: pcp -be.needed \\
`Then my son has to say `my uncle' or `my aunt' to my brother's son.' (140425 kWmdza04) 0003788
exe

exe

tɤ-ŋgɤr lú-wɣ-lɤt, nɯmaʁnɤ tɤ-ŋkɯ lú-wɣ-lɤt, nɯmaʁnɤ ɕɤrɯ lú-wɣ-lɤt, \\
indef. poss -fat ipfv - inv -release otherwise indef. poss -pig.skin ipfv - inv -release otherwise bone ipfv - inv -release \\
`One puts pig fat, pig skin or bones in it.' (140428 mtshalu) 0003878#S18
exe

The reduced form maʁ (homophonous with the 3sg Factual non-past of maʁnot be) of nɯmaʁnɤotherwise is also attested to express disjunction between nouns as in ( ex:mboR.maR.tWwWr ).

exe

nɯnɯ mboʁ maʁ tɯwɯr nɯ tʰɯ́-wɣ-nɤqʰɤŋga tɕe χcʰoʁe nɯ ɯ-jŋoʁ nɯ kɯ kú-wɣ-sɯ-ndo. \\
dem square.cloth otherwise raincoat dem ipfv - inv -put.on lnk right.and.left dem 3sg. poss -hook dem erg ipfv - inv - caus -take \\
`When one puts on a square cloth or a raincoat (to protect oneself from the rain), one attaches it with the hooks on the left and on the right.' (140429 NoR)
0003888#S14
exe

Another way of expressing disjunction with nouns is the polar sentence final particle ɕi (§ sec:fsp.interrog ) but the verb is repeated in both clauses with elision, as in ( ex:tWtWphu.Nu.Ci ).

exe

tɯ-tɯpʰu ŋu ɕi ʁnɯ-tɯpʰu ŋu mɤ-xsi. \\
one-species be: fact qu two-species be: fact neg - genr:know \\
`I dont know if it is one or two species.' (23-RmWrcWftsa) 0003610#S43
exe
summary: Japhug has no dedicated linker for inclusive or exclusive disjunction between noun phrases. Instead, the clausal linker nɯmaʁnɤ ‘otherwise’ can sometimes appear between nouns, and the reduced form maʁ is also used, but these constructions are rare and are analyzed as resulting from elided verbs in coordinated clauses. Another strategy is the sentence-final particle ɕi, with the verb repeated in both clauses, as in expressions like “one species or two species.”

section: Word order in the noun phrase
text:
word order
The order of the elements in the noun phrase in Japhug is relatively rigid. Examples of complex noun phrases such as ( ex:N.Adj.Num ) and ( ex:Dem.N.Num.Dem ) illustrate the orders N(oun)-Adj(ective)-Num(eral) and Dem(onstrative)-N(oun)-Num(eral)-Dem(onstrative), respectively. The term ``adjective'' here refers to attributive adjectival stative verbs in participial form (§ ex:attributive.participles.stative.verbs ).

exe

sɯŋgɯ zɯ, [tɯrme wuma ʑo kɯ-wxti ʁnɯz] tu-ndʑi tɕe\\
forest loc people really emph sbj: pcp -be.big two exist: fact - du lnk \\
`In the forest, there are two giants.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh)
0003886#S160
exe

exe

[ɯkɯki ɕnat ʁnɯz kɯni] kɯ, \\
dem. prox heddle two dem. prox: du erg \\
`[The weaving is done] with these two heddles.' (vid-20140429090403)
0003776#S46
exe

From such examples, it can be extrapolated that the most basic word order in the noun phrase in Japhug is Dem-N-Adj-Num-Dem. Although no noun phrase in the corpus presents all five elements, it is easy to elicit such an example. This order is not unusual crosslinguistically: notes that the orders Dem-N-Adj-Num and N-Adj-Num-Dem are both widely attested.

All of the elements in the noun phrases are optional, even the nominal head.

Although the indefinite marker cione and the topic nɯ can appear between the noun and the adjective (being here a head-internal participial relative clause, § ex:attributive.participles.stative.verbs ), as shown by examples ( ex:qajW.ci.kArNi.ci ) above and ( ex:GJW.ci.kWmbWmbro ) below, numerals are not attested in this position.

exe

ɣɟɯ ci kɯ-mbɯ mbro ʑo pjɤ-tu ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe \\
watchtower indef sbj: pcp - emph be.high emph ifr. ipfv -exist sens -be lnk \\
`There was a very big tower.' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S49
exe

There are attributes other than adjectival stative verbs in Japhug (§ ex:attributive.postnominal and § ex:attributive.prenominal ), in particular prenominal attributes as rŋɯlsilver in ( ex:rNWl.qhoRqhoR ), but it is problematic to use such examples as evidence for a Adj-N-Num-Dem, given the fact that prenominal attributes are always essentially nouns used as modifiers.

exe

rŋɯl qʰoʁqʰoʁ χsɯm nɯ ɲɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ. \\
silver ingot three dem ifr - auto -come.out \\
`The three silver ingots had come out.' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S169
exe

The prenominal slot can be filled by demonstratives (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners ) and identity modifiers kɯmaʁother or cione (§ sec:identity.modifier ). These elements can be preceded by either a comitative cʰo phrase (§ sec:coordinator.cho ) or by the aforementioned topic marker iɕqʰa (§ sec:iCqha, cf. example ex:iCqha.ci.rJAlpu ), the leftmost element of a noun phrase.

exe

rɟɤlpu ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ, iɕqʰa ci rɟɤlpu nɯnɯ, <xila> rɟɤlpu nɯ ɯ-ɕki, \\
king 3sg. poss -son dem erg the.aforementioned other.one king dem topo king dem 3sg. poss - dat \\
`The king's son [told] the other king, the king of Greece.' (140518 huifei de muma-zh)
0004026#S39
exe
summary: Japhug noun phrases have a relatively rigid word order, with the basic pattern extrapolated as Dem-N-Adj-Num-Dem, although all elements are optional, including the nominal head. The passage also notes that some prenominal modifiers and markers can occur before the noun, but numerals are not attested in that position, and prenominal attributes are not good evidence for a separate adjective-like order because they are essentially noun modifiers.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text: This chapter comprises four sections: § sec:idph discusses ideophones, § sec:other.expressive presents expressive words lacking specific ideophonic properties (interjections and calling sounds), § sec:fillers and § sec:sfp describe sentence final particles and their contribution to the expression of modality and evidentiality.
summary: This chapter is divided into four sections. It covers ideophones, other expressive words such as interjections and calling sounds, and then sentence-final particles, which are discussed in relation to modality and evidentiality.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
ideophone
Ideophones in Japhug constitute a particularly large part of speech, and can be unambiguously defined on the basis of morphological criteria. The present section builds on previous research ), but is based on a larger corpus of ideophones.
summary: Ideophones make up a particularly large part of speech in Japhug and can be identified unambiguously by morphological criteria. The discussion in this section draws on previous research but is based on a larger corpus of ideophones.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
ideophone!stem morphology!ideophone
Cross-linguistic definitions have been proposed for ideophones; for instance, according to, they are `marked words that depict sensory imagery'. While Japhug ideophones do indeed fit this description, in this grammar a language-particular definition is adopted.

Ideophones often have specific morphology, which differs from the rest of the lexicon ( and ). This is the case in Gyalrong languages, and ideophones are thus defined in this grammar (following ) as words derived from monosyllabic ideophonic roots that can undergo the morphological alternations described in this section.

tab:ideo.morpho1 presents the ten ideophonic patterns attested in Japhug. Since these patterns involve several types of partial reduplication, a set of symbols are used to represent the elements of the root that are targeted by reduplication: $C_i$ represents initial clusters (or single consonants), $C_f$ codas, $V$ the main vowel and $R$ the complete ideophonic root.

This system is not specific to Japhug: patterns I, II, III, IV and VII have direct correspondences in Tshobdun. Patterns V and VI express an intensive meaning in comparison with the corresponding semelfactive (pattern I) and stative (pattern II). No equivalent pattern exists in Tshobdun. The -nɤ- element in patterns III, IV and IX is related to the additive nɤ (§ sec:additive.nA ).

All patterns (except X) are illustrated with an example using the root zjaŋ `tall'. Example sentences for each of these forms and more detailed accounts of their semantics are provided in § sec:ideo.regular.
summary: The grammar adopts a language-specific definition of Japhug ideophones as words derived from monosyllabic ideophonic roots that undergo special morphological alternations. It describes ten ideophonic patterns in Japhug, many involving partial reduplication, and notes that several patterns correspond to those in Tshobdun, while patterns V and VI are intensive forms and the -nɤ- element in patterns III, IV, and IX is related to the additive nɤ.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Although most ideophonic patterns are attested in the text corpus, it is difficult to find real examples of all regular derivations from one particular root. For ease of presentation, we cite example sentences with complex ideophones based on a single root, zjaŋ `tall', This root is not used to illustrate pattern X (§ sec:ideo.X ), which is semantically restricted. and thus most of these examples are elicited. They are however not translated: I asked my main consultant Tshendzin to produce sentences illustrating each of the possible patterns of the root zjaŋ. Ideophones are glossed by idph, followed by the number of the pattern, and a brief translation of the general meaning of the ideophonic root.

The basic meaning of the ideophonic root zjaŋ `tall' was glossed by Tshendzin as ( ex:zjaN.expl ).

exe

ɯ-zda ra sɤz kɯ-mbro kɯ-fse \\
3sg. poss -companion pl comp sbj: pcp -be.tall sbj: pcp -be.like \\
`Taller or higher than the others.' (elicited)
exe

There is a series of ideophonic roots that are related to zjaŋ by other type of processes ( tab:zjaN.tsjaN, § sec:idph.gradation ).
summary: The passage explains that while most ideophonic patterns are found in the corpus, it is hard to find fully attested examples of every regular derivation from a single root. For clarity, the author uses elicited examples based on the ideophonic root *zjaŋ* ‘tall,’ which is not used for one semantically restricted pattern, and notes that ideophones are glossed with pattern numbers and a general meaning. It also mentions that some ideophonic roots are related to *zjaŋ* through other processes.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern I, which consists of the bare ideophonic root, is combined with predicates in the Aorist or Inferential to express an action occurring suddenly, as in ( ex:ideo1 ). The form zjaŋ means that the action of the sentence resulted in the main referent becoming taller than its surrounding.

exe

zjaŋ ʑo tɤ-ndzur \\
idph (I):tall emph aor -stand \\
`He stood up suddenly, and [appeared to be] very tall.' (elicited)
exe
summary: Pattern I uses the bare ideophonic root with Aorist or Inferential predicates to express a sudden action. In the example, *zjaŋ* indicates that the referent became taller than its surroundings, meaning “He stood up suddenly, and [appeared to be] very tall.”

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern II with plain reduplication indicates a state. It is by far the most common ideophonic pattern in texts and it is attested for most ideophonic roots. It generally describes a permanent state (as in ex:RJWRJri below).

When an ideophone in pattern II is used with a lexical verb, it can describe a state resulting from the action indicated by the main verb ( rmbɯheap up in ex:zjaNzjaN3 ).

exe

tɕe zjaŋzjaŋ ʑo kɯ-pa to-rmbɯ-nɯ \\
lnk idph (II):tall emph inf: stat - aux ifr -pile.up- pl \\
`[The villagers] had piled [the hay] up very high.' (150902 liaozhai lang-zh)'
0006340#S24
exe

A handful of deideophonic verbs in a- and nɤ- can be built from pattern II ideophones (§ sec:a.nA.deidph ).

The reduplicated form in pattern II is in most cases a complete reduplication. Not only the onset, but also the vowel as well as the final consonant are copied, even in the case of initial clusters, as in zɟraŋ $ $ zɟraŋzɟraŋ `bulging, swollen'.

Nevertheless, we do observe some phonetic attrition in the case of the codas -t, -ɣ and -β. Final -t is generally deleted regardless of the following consonant, as in xʂɤt $ $ xʂɤxʂɤt `long, thin and flexible'. An exception, which involves an ideophone without initial cluster, is cotcot `small and cute'.

Final -β generally disappears in the reduplicated syllable when the onset of the ideophonic root contains a labial (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ), as in bɤβ $ $ bɤbɤβ `stubborn, bulky'. This rule is however only optional, and bɤβbɤβ is also attested.

Final -ɣ is generally deleted when the onset contains a velar (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ) as in gɤɣ $ $ gɤgɤɣ `moving with difficulty, unstable on its feet'. This rule is also optional.

Another type of phonetic reduction optionally appears with a few ideophones with open rhymes in -i and a initial cluster with medial -l- or -r-. The medial is deleted and the rhyme is replaced by -ɯ, following the regular process of partial reduplication common in verbal morphology (§ sec:partial.redp ). Examples of this phenomenon include for instance ʁɟri $ $ ʁɟɯʁɟri `fat, soft and wet' and qli $ $ qɯqli `staring without moving'.

exe

ɯ-βri nɯra kú-wɣ-rtoʁ qʰe ɲɯ-ɤcilaj ʑo qʰe, nɤkinɯ, ʁɟɯʁɟri ʑo ɲɯ-pa. \\
3sg. poss -body dem: pl ipfv - inv -look lnk sens -be.wet emph lnk filler idhp:II:fat.soft.wet emph sens - aux \\
`The body [of the gecko] looks wet, it is wet and soft.' (28-tshAwAre) 0003722#S37
exe
summary:
Pattern II ideophones with plain reduplication express states, usually permanent ones, and they are the most common ideophonic form in texts, occurring with most ideophonic roots. When combined with a lexical verb, they can also describe a resulting state caused by the action of that verb.  

The reduplication is usually complete, copying the onset, vowel, and final consonant, though there are optional or regular reductions for certain codas such as -t, -β, and -ɣ. A smaller set of ideophones with open rhymes in -i and initial clusters with medial -l- or -r- show another reduction pattern, in which the medial is deleted and the rhyme becomes -ɯ.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern III is formed by reduplicating the ideophonic root with the additive marker nɤ (§ sec:additive.nA ) inserted in between. It depicts a rhythmic action or a constant motion as in ( ex:ideo3 ), depending on the semantics of the root.

exe

mbro ɯ-taʁ to-ɕe tɕe zjaŋnɤzjaŋ jɤ-ari-ndʑi \\
horse 3sg -on ifr: up -go lnk idph (III):tall aor -go[II]- du \\
`He mounted the horse, and they went there, very tall.' (elicited)
exe

Deideophonic verbs in ɣɤ- and sɤ- (§ sec:GA.sA.deidph ) and nɯ- (§ sec:nW.deidph ) are built from pattern III ideophones, without additive nɤ.

Pattern III also allows a variant $RR$- nɤ -$RR$ with double reduplication of the ideophonic root, with an intensive meaning. For instance pɣɤlnɤpɣɤl `(walking) with big strides' has the slightly different meaning `(running) with big strides' with double reduplication ( ex:pGAlnApGAl ).

exe

`wo a-mu ma-pɯ-tɯ-ʑɣɤ-sat tɕe aʑo pjɯ-nɯ-ɣi-a ŋu' to-ti. pɣɤlpɣɤlnɤpɣɤlpɣɤl pjɤ-nɯ-ɣi. \\
interj 1sg. poss -mother neg - imp -2- refl -kill lnk 1sg ipfv: down - vert -come- 1sg be: fact ifr -say idph (III):with.big.strides ifr: down - auto -come \\
`She said ``Mother, don't commit suicide, I am coming back'' and came back running in big strides.' (2003 kAndZWsqhaj2)
exe
summary: Pattern III is formed by reduplicating an ideophonic root with the additive marker *nɤ* inserted between the copies, and it expresses either rhythmic action or constant motion depending on the root’s semantics. Deideophonic verbs built with *ɣɤ-* and *sɤ-* or *nɯ-* are derived from Pattern III ideophones but without the additive marker. The pattern also has a double-reduplication variant, *RR-nɤ-RR*, which adds an intensive meaning.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern IV is formed by combining with the ideophonic root, the additive nɤ (§ sec:additive.nA ) and a partial copy of the ideophonic root replacing the onset by l, a pattern reminiscent of some distributed action verbs (§ sec.distributed.action.l ). It describes an action involving motion occurring in disorderly fashion with intermittent changes of state. In ( ex:ideo4 ) the form zjaŋnɤlaŋ can be used to depict a drunk person who stumbles from time to time while walking, so that he seems taller at one time and shorter at another time.

exe

zjaŋnɤlaŋ ɲɯ-ŋke \\
idph (IV):tall sens -go \\
`He is walking unsteadily, very tall.' (elicited)
exe

Deideophonic verbs in ɣɤ- and sɤ- can be build from pattern IV ideophones (§ sec:GA.sA.deidph ), without insertion of the additive.
summary: Pattern IV is formed by combining an ideophonic root with the additive nɤ and a partial copy of the root whose onset is replaced by l, a shape reminiscent of certain distributed action verbs. It denotes disorderly motion with intermittent changes of state, as in a drunken person who stumbles and appears alternately taller and shorter. Deideophonic verbs in ɣɤ- and sɤ- can also be formed from Pattern IV ideophones, without the additive.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern V, made of the ideophonic root prefixed with the element pʰɯ, is similar to pattern I (§ sec:ideo.I ) semantically, but it is more rarely used; it indicates a more sudden action and/or one carried out to a higher degree.

exe
