pʰɯzjaŋ ʑo tɤ-ndzur \\
idph (V):tall emph aor -stand \\
`He stood up suddenly, and [appeared to be] very tall.' (elicited)
exe

This pattern occurs in particular with onomatopoeic ideophones, such as qʰloŋ `splashing' ( ex:phWqhloN ).

exe

nɯ pʰɯqʰloŋ ʑo pjɤ-ɣɤrɤt \\
dem idph (V):splashing emph ifr -throw \\
`He threw [the bag into the water], making a sudden splashing noise.' (150824 kelaosi-zh) 0006276#S146
exe

The most common pattern V ideophone is pʰɯɕlaʁ from ɕlaʁ `suddenly', which has the ɣɤ- and sɤ- denominal forms (§ sec:GA.sA.deidph ) ɣɤpʰɯɕlaʁ `moving/working quickly, hardworking' and sɤpʰɯɕlaʁ `do $X$ quickly (not lingering)'.
summary: Pattern V consists of an ideophonic root prefixed with pʰɯ and is semantically similar to Pattern I, but it is used less often. It denotes a more sudden action and/or one performed to a greater degree, and is especially common with onomatopoeic ideophones. The most common example is pʰɯɕlaʁ from ɕlaʁ “suddenly,” which also appears in denominal forms meaning “moving/working quickly” and “do X quickly (not lingering).”

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern VI, with the root prefixed by mɤlɤ, describes a state like pattern II, but differs from it in that it expresses a higher degree. In addition, it can be used to express the result of a change of state with the verb aβzubecome, grow as in ( ex:ideo6 ). It is the rarest of all ideophonic patterns, not attested in the Japhug text corpus.

exe

a-ɣe mɤlɤzjaŋ ʑo tʰɯ-aβzu \\
1sg. poss -grandson idph (VI):tall emph aor -become \\
`My grandson has become very tall.' (elicited)
exe
summary: Pattern VI, marked by the prefix **mɤlɤ-**, describes a state like Pattern II but indicates a higher degree. It can also express the result of a change of state with **aβzu** ‘become, grow.’ This is the rarest ideophonic pattern and is not attested in the Japhug text corpus.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
In pattern VII, the coda of the root ($C_f$; if no coda is present, a w is inserted, § sec:ideo.VIII ) is resyllabified as onset of a syllable with the vowel ɯ, and then reduplicated with the vowel i following the pattern $C_fV$.$C_f$ ɯ.$C_f$ i. It expresses a progressive change of state, involving in some case slow motion as in ( ex:ideo7 ).

exe

zjaŋɯŋi ʑo jɤ-ari \\
idph (VII):tall emph aor -go[II] \\
`He went away slowly, looking taller than rest.' (elicited)
exe
summary: In pattern VII, the root coda is resyllabified as the onset of a syllable with ɯ and then reduplicated with i, following the template \(C_fV.C_f\ ɯ.C_f\ i\); if no coda is present, a w is inserted. This pattern expresses a progressive change of state and can, in some cases, convey slow motion.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern VIII depicts a state involving a lot of referents having the property described by the ideophone, but spread out spatially in a disorderly fashion.

The formula $R$ ɯ.$C_i$ a $C_f$ i in tab:ideo.morpho1 applies to ideophonic roots which do not have a as their main vowel, for instance zjɤɣ (whose meaning is almost identical to that of zjaŋ) has the form zjɤɣ.ɯ.zjaɣ.i. When the main vowel is a, the formula is $C_i$ ɯ $C_f$ ɯ.$C_i$ a $C_f$ i. Thus, the pattern VIII of zjaŋ is zjɯ.ŋɯ.zja.ŋi. This form means that in a group of unique entities, some are tall and some are short, but they are unevenly spread ( ex:ideo8 ).

exe

zjɯŋɯzjaŋi ɲɯ-xcat \\
idph (VIII):tall sens -be.many \\
`There are many [people], some taller and some shorter.' (elicited)
exe

Tshendzin glossed the meaning of ( ex:ideo8 ) as follows ( ex:zjWNWzjaNi:expl ).

exe

tsuku kɯ-mbro tsuku kɯ-mbɤr kɯ-fse \\
some sbj: pcp -be.tall some sbj: pcp -be.short sbj: pcp -be.like \\
`Some tall and some short.' (elicited)
exe

In cases where the ideophonic root has no coda, the consonant w replaces $C_f$ in patterns VII and VIII. For instance, / ʂχi / `with big holes, with big nostrils' has the pattern VIII form ʂχɯwɯʂχawi `full of holes everywhere' ( ex:sxXwwWsxWawi ).

exe

nɯnɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ ri ɕ-tu-ndze tɕe ku-rɤʑi ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe, (...) nɯnɯtɕu aʁɤndɯndɤt ʂχɯwɯʂχawi ɲɯ-sɯ-spoʁ tɕe \\
dem 3sg. poss -in loc tral - ipfv -eat[III] lnk ipfv -stay sens -be. aff: fact lnk dem: loc everywhere idph (VIII):with.holes ipfv - caus -have.a.hole lnk \\
`[The species of ants called cɤmi qro ] goes into wood and eats it, and stays in there, (...) and makes holes everywhere in it.' (26-qro)
0003682#S89
exe
summary: Pattern VIII expresses a state in which many referents have the property indicated by the ideophone, but are spread out irregularly in space. Its morphological shape depends on the root’s vowel and coda: roots without main vowel *a* take one pattern, roots with *a* take another, and roots without a coda use *w* in place of the final consonant. Examples show this pattern used for meanings like “some tall and some short” or “full of holes everywhere.”

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern IX is formally similar to pattern III except that i is added after each reduplicant of the ideophonic root. Semantically, it indicates that the entity presenting the property described by the ideophonic root undergoes a fast motion.

exe

mbro ta-nɯmbrɤpɯ tɕe zjaŋinɤzjaŋi ʑo jɤ-ɕqʰlɤt \\
horse aor:3 -ride lnk idph (IX):tall emph aor -disappear \\
`He mounted the horse and disappeared quickly (in the horizon), very tall.' (elicited)
exe
summary: Pattern IX is formally like pattern III, but with an added **i** after each reduplicant of the ideophonic root. Semantically, it marks that the entity described by the ideophonic root undergoes fast motion.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern X involves reduplication of the ideophonic root three or more times (it was not considered to be an ideophonic pattern in ). It is the only domain of Japhug grammar where triplication is allowed, Another language in which ideophone triplication has been documented is Chintang.
unlike the Mazur variety of Stau, where triplication occurs in finite verb forms.

Pattern X differs from all preceding patterns in that it is semantically restricted to onomatopoeia ( ex:cutcutcut ) and endopathic ideophones (ie. ideophones expressing inner sensations such as cold or pain) ( ex:zWrzWrzWr ), and nearly always select tisay as light verb (§ sec:idph.ti ). Lexical verbs are also attested with pattern X ideophones ( ex:rCWB4.pjWlAt ), though more rarely.

exe

tu-mbri nɯra cutcutcut ʑo tu-ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
ipfv -call dem: pl idph (X):cry emph ipfv -say sens -be \\
`When it calls it makes ` cut cut cut '.' (24-ZmbrWpGa) 0003628#S8
exe

exe

ɲɯ-kɯ-sɤŋo tɕe, nɯ nɯ-ɬoʁ tɕe, zɯrzɯrzɯr tu-ti qʰe tɕendɤre tɤ-ndɤr ɲɯ-ɬoʁ ɕti. \\
ipfv - genr:S/O-listen lnk dem aor -come.out lnk idph (X):itchy.feeling ipfv -say lnk lnk pimple ipfv -come.out be: aff: fact \\
`When it appears, one has an itchy feeling, and a pimple appears.' (25-khArWm) 0003644#S4
exe

The triplication (reduplication at will) of the root expresses either repeated action like pattern III, or a continuous and unceasing state. Some pattern X ideophones are reduplicated four ( ex:rCWB4.pjWlAt ) or more ( ex:ZeZeZeZe ) times.

exe

tɤɕi qaj nɯ tɤtɤɣ ɯ-ŋgɯ rɕɯβrɕɯβrɕɯβrɕɯβ ʑo pjɯ-lɤt nɯ, ɯ-zgra nɯ pjɤ-sɤ-mtsʰɤm. \\
barley wheat dem cupboard 3sg. poss -in idph (X):rustling emph ipfv -release dem 3sg. poss -noise dem ifr. ipfv -pro-hear \\
`(In the night), one could hear the rustling noise of the [one-legged demon]$_i$ pouring barley and wheat grains into the cupboard (of the woman with whom he$_i$ was having a relationship). (140510 rkoNJAl) 0003943#S30
exe

Not all onomatopoeia are realistic descriptions of natural sounds. In ( ex:ZeZeZeZe ) we find an ideophonic root ʑe* describing the supposed minute sound made by the quick motion of the legs of a millipede.

exe

kú-wɣ-rtoʁ tɯ-mɲaʁ kɯ ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ ra mɯ́j-saχsɤl ʑo ri, ``ʑeʑeʑeʑeʑeʑe" ʑo tu-ti ju-ɕe qʰe, ɯ-tɯ-mbjom sɤre ʑo \\
ipfv - inv -look genr. poss -eye erg 3sg. poss -limb pl neg: sens -be.clear emph lnk idph (II):sound emph ipfv -say ipfv -go lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.quick be.ridiculous: fact emph \\
`(Of a type of small millipede) Looking at it, its feet are not clearly visible, but it moves making ʑeʑeʑeʑeʑeʑe, extremely quickly.' (28-kWpAz)
0003714#S142
exe

Some of the roots used in pattern X are polysyllabic (see for instance dudut in § sec:underived.expressive.nouns ), in which case the ideophone can only be reduplicated two times.
summary:
Pattern X is a Japhug ideophonic pattern characterized by reduplication three or more times, and it is the only area of Japhug grammar where triplication is allowed. It is semantically restricted mainly to onomatopoeia and endopathic ideophones, usually takes *tisay* as the light verb, and can also appear with lexical verbs, though less often.  

The triplication or greater reduplication can express repeated action or a continuous, unceasing state, and some roots may be repeated four or more times. Some pattern X ideophones imitate natural sounds, while others describe very small or non-realistic sounds; polysyllabic roots in this pattern can only be reduplicated twice.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
ideophone!semantic
Japhug ideophones are used for describing various features including sound, colour, shape, texture, attitude or mood, and some ideophones are multimodal, referring to combination of several types of sensory information.

proposed the hierarchy ( ex:ideo.hierarchy ) according to which, if a particular language possesses ideophones belonging to a particular class in this hierarchy, it will also present ideophones for all the lower classes. All categories are exemplified in Japhug.

exe

sound > motion > visual patterns > other sensory perceptions > inner feelings and cognitive states
exe

Onomatopoeic ideophones include for instance qʰloŋ `splashing' ( ex:phWqhloN, § sec:ideo.V ) or tɕʰɯŋ `metal clinking'.

In addition to sounds, ideophonic roots also describe shapes (for instance boŋboŋ `ovoid'), specific hues of colour ( smɯɣsmɯɣ `fresh green'), touch ( brɯɣbrɯɣ `rough, covered in small pimples'), temperature ( xɯβxɯβ `warm'), size ( scraʁscraʁ `very small, close to the ground'), quantity ( ʑɯβʑɯβ `many (people, object) standing/in upright position'), attitudes ( dɣɤrdɣɤr `agape, in a daze, looking stupid', ɕquɕqu `frowning'), pain ( ɕɲɯɣ `intense and sudden pain'), body position ( ɕpʰɤβɕpʰɤβ `lying on the ground, motionless') and also cognitive states ( ɬɤɬɤt `free from worry').

Ideophonic roots often combine several parameters. For instance, ɕɣaʁɕɣaʁ `sharp and shiny (of fangs)' encodes both shape and hue.

It appears that there are no ideophonic roots specifically dedicated to expressing motion; however, dynamic ideophonic patterns (I, III, IV, IX) applied to ideophones describing sound or shapes often add a motional imagery. For instance, the root xɯr means `round' in pattern II, but `rotating, turning' in pattern III ( ex:xWrnAxWr, § sec:nW.deidph ) and IX ( ex:xWrinAxWri ).

exe

ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ kɯra nɤ kɯra tu-ste qʰe tɕe, iɕqʰa staχpɯrɟɤskʰi ɣɯ ɯ-jwaʁ nɯ xɯrinɤxɯri ʑo tu-sɯ-mtɕɯr. \\
3sg. poss -limb dem. prox: pl add dem. prox: pl ipfv -do.like[III] lnk lnk the.aforementioned plant.name gen 3sg. poss -leave dem idph (IX):round emph ipfv - caus -turn \\
`[There is a species of insect which] does this with its legs repeatedly, and rotates the leaves of the staχpɯrɟɤskʰi very quickly.' (18-NGolo)
0003530#S128
exe

Some ideophones, however, can have an auditory interpretation competing with many other ones. Thus, bɤβ in pattern II form bɤbɤβ can designate many objects clustered together (like mushrooms) ( ex:kAmWsthWsthaB, § sec:recip.amW.indirective and ex:WtaR.ra.Wmat, § sec:plural.determiners ), a stubborn person or a heavy and cumbersome object depending on the context.

With a dynamic pattern such as I or III, it can be interpreted as designating the noise made by a heavy object falling from a high place as in ( ex:bAB.Zo.paBde ), a meaning shared with the deideophonic verbs sɤbɤbɤβ and nɯbɤβ (see the examples in ex:nWbAB.bABnAbAB, § sec:nW.deidph ).

exe

mbro kɯ [...] tɕʰeme nɯ bɤβ ʑo pjɤ-βde qʰe \\
horse erg girl dem idph (I):heavy.object.falling emph ifr: down -throw lnk \\
`The horse (...) and threw the girl down, making `bom' (on the ground).' (2003 kAndZWsqhaj)
exe
summary: Japhug ideophones are used to describe a wide range of sensory and mental experiences, including sound, colour, shape, texture, temperature, size, attitude, pain, body position, and cognitive states, and some are multimodal. The passage presents a hierarchy of ideophonic categories and notes that Japhug has examples for all of them, though there do not seem to be ideophones specifically dedicated to motion; instead, some dynamic patterns add motion imagery to ideophones based on sound or shape. It also shows that many ideophonic roots are context-dependent and may have multiple interpretations, such as describing clustered objects, stubbornness, heaviness, or noises made by falling objects.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
ideophone!irregularity irregularity!ideophone
In practice, very few ideophonic roots allow the application of all the ten patterns exemplified in § sec:ideo.regular. In many cases, a particular pattern is not attested because there is no imaginable context where the situation could exist.

The meaning of some ideophonic roots can be incompatible with stative patterns (II, VI and VIII). For instance, the very common ɕlaʁ `suddenly' is only attested in patterns I, III and V.

Even in the case of ideophonic roots which allow several different patterns, the semantics of a particular pattern cannot always be predicted from that of the other ones. In other words, not all ideophonic roots have a basic meaning from which the semantics of all patterns can be regularly derived. In this section, we provide two examples with such unpredictable semantics.

First, the root rɯβ has a pattern III rɯβnɤrɯβ meaning `dripping (drop by drop) continuously' ( ex:rWBnArWB ).

exe

li mbalɤ-pɯ nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-qom ra rɯβnɤrɯβ ʑo ɲɤ-ɬoʁ ɕti qʰe \\
again bull- dim dem gen 3sg. poss -tear pl idph (III):dripping.continuously emph ifr -come.out be. aff: fact lnk \\
`The tears of the calf flowed, dripping without stop.' (140512 fushang he yaomo-zh)
0003967#S127
exe

The regular ɣɤ- deideophonic verb (§ sec:GA.sA.deidph ) ɣɤrɯβrɯβdrip continuously deriving from rɯβnɤrɯβ is also attested (example ex:nWrqo.YWmNAm, § sec:sensory.endopathic ). In addition, the compound noun mcirɯβrɯβperson whose saliva drips continuously (§ sec.n.idph.compounds ) has the same form with compatible semantics.

However, the pattern VIII rɯwɯrawi from the same root has an entirely different meaning `upset and confused'. It occurs in collocation with tɯ-sɯmmind ( ex:rWwWrawi ) and cannot be combined with nouns referring to liquids. Although it could originally have been a metaphorical extension of the concrete meaning of this root, the exact pathway of semantic change is by no means obvious.

exe

ɯ-kɤ-nɯzdɯɣ ɲɯ-dɤn tɕe, ɯ-sɯm rɯwɯrawi ɲɯ-xtsu \\
3sg. poss - obj: pcp -be.worried.about sens -be.many lnk 3sg. poss -mind idph (VIII):confused ipfv -ferment \\
`He is worried about many things, and he feels upset and confused.' (elicited)
exe

Second, the root dzoŋ has a pattern II dzoŋdzoŋ meaning `having bristling hair' ( ex:dzoNdzoN.YWpa ).

exe

tɕeri nɯnɯ ɯ-rme nɯ dzoŋdzoŋ ɲɯ-pa\\
lnk dem 3sg. poss -hair dem idph (II):bristling.hair sens - aux \\
`The hair [on the squirrel's tail] is bristling.' (28-qapar)
0003720#S129
exe

However, the pattern III form dzoŋnɤdzoŋ has an entirely different meaning: it refers to the itchy feeling one experiences when blood flows into a limb that has fallen asleep (due to a sitting position for instance) and blood flows back into the numb limb, as in ( ex:dzoNnAdzoN ).

exe

tu-ŋke-a tɕe a-mi dzoŋnɤdzoŋ ʑo ɲɯ-ti ma cʰɤ-ndʑɯrpɯt \\
ipfv: up -walk- 1sg lnk 1 sg. poss -foot idph (III):feel.itchy emph sens -say because ifr -be.numb \\
`My foot feels itchy as I walk, because it was numb.' (elicited)
exe

These two examples are in no way exceptional; while ideophonic morphology is productive, one should not assume that semantics is predictable.
summary: Very few ideophonic roots can occur in all ten patterns, and some patterns are absent simply because no suitable context exists. The semantics of some patterns are incompatible with certain root meanings, and even when multiple patterns are available, their meanings may not be predictable from one another: the passage illustrates this with roots like *rɯβ* and *dzoŋ*, where different patterns yield unrelated meanings. The general point is that ideophonic morphology is productive, but its semantics should not be assumed to be regular or fully predictable.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
ideophone!phonology
The phonological markedness of Japhug ideophones is relatively easy to assess, as ideophonic roots (and all the form derived from them present uncommon features from in both onsets and codas.
summary: Japhug ideophones are phonologically marked and easy to recognize because their roots and derived forms contain uncommon features in both onsets and codas. The passage emphasizes that these unusual phonological patterns make ideophones stand out from more ordinary forms in the language.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Of all 423 known onsets in Japhug, 63 (including 45 two-consonant and 18 three-consonant clusters) are exclusively attested in ideophones or ideophonic verbs. These onsets present four types of unusual combinations which are completely absent from the native vocabulary and/or Tibetan borrowings.

First, palatal stops can be combined with the medials r, l in clusters such as cr, cʰr, ɟr, cl, ɲɟl- (§ sec:Cl.clusters, § sec:Cr.clusters ) in ideophones. The only medial consonant compatible with palatal stops in the non-ideophonic lexicon is ɣ (§ sec:CG.clusters ).

Second, dental stops are found with the medials r, j and w in clusters such as dr, dj, dw- and tʰj- in ideophones. In the non-ideophonic lexicon, the only attested medial after dental stops is ɣ (§ sec:CG.clusters ). The noun qɯmdroŋcrane also has such a cluster, but an onomatopoeic origin of the second syllable is not impossible, compare the Tibetan name of the same bird ཁྲུང་ཁྲུང་kʰruŋkʰruŋcrane. There is evidence that proto-Gyalrong *tr- became a retroflex affricate tʂ- (§ sec:second.member.alternation, § sec:teens ), and that clusters of this type have been removed by regular sound change (§ sec:Cr.clusters ).

Third, the unvoiced fricatives ʂ and χ occur as preinitial consonants in clusters with voiced main consonant such as ʂɣ, ʂɲ- and χɲ- ( χɲɯχɲi `soft and thin (of food); dizzy, listless'). In the non-ideophonic vocabulary, ʂ and χ as first element of clusters are in complementary distribution with their voiced counterparts r and ʁ, respectively (§ sec:rC.clusters, § sec:XC.clusters ).

Fourth, l is common as first element of clusters in ideophonic roots, as in lbjɯlbjɯɣ `soft, hanging down'. Comparison with other Gyalrongic languages reveals that *l- preinitial has changed to j- in the non-ideophonic vocabulary (§ sec:jC.clusters ).

Another conspicuous phonological feature in ideophones is the very high relative frequency of non-prenasalized voiced stops. In native (non-Tibetan and non-deideophonic) nouns and verbs, the simple stop onsets b and g are extremely rare (§ sec:consonant.phonemes ). The onsets d and ɟ are more common in the non-ideophonic vocabulary, but almost all originate from clusters containing laterals (see ).

While Japhug ideophones, unlike calling/chasing sounds (§ sec:call ) do not contain independent phonemes that are not found in the non-ideophonic vocabulary, they enrich the complexity of the phonological system by filling gaps in the phonological system caused by sound changes (see for instance ) and by favouring rare phonemes and phoneme combinations.
summary: In Japhug, 63 of the 423 known onsets are found only in ideophones or ideophonic verbs, and they include several consonant combinations absent from native vocabulary and Tibetan borrowings. These include unusual clusters with palatal and dental stops, voiceless fricatives as preinitials before voiced consonants, and initial l-, as well as a high frequency of non-prenasalized voiced stops. Although ideophones do not introduce new phonemes, they preserve or favor rare phonological patterns and combinations that have been lost or are uncommon elsewhere in the language.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
The phonological specificities of ideophonic roots are not limited to onsets: the rhymes present also some unusual features, especially the codas.

The Kamnyu dialect of Japhug lacks a labial stop coda in the non-ideophonic vocabulary (§ sec:codas.inventory ), due to a sound change *-p $ $ -β. However, some ideophones allow a stop final -p instead of -β; there is considerable variation across speakers as to which ideophones allow this pronunciation. Tshendzin optionally uses final -p with six ideophones in combination with the main vowel ɯ: tsʰɯptsʰɯp `feeling of humidity in the air', tɕʰɯptɕʰɯp `with water drops', ʑɯpʑɯp `many objects/persons standing upright', cʰɯpcʰɯp `filthy', rsɯprsɯp `very hairy' and rkʰɯprkʰɯp `knocking noise'.

Another remarkable property of ideophones is the frequency of the codas -ŋ, -l and -n (§ sec:codas.inventory ). These codas have been eliminated by a series of sound changes, merging with the vowels in complex ways (for instance, proto-Gyalrongic *-aŋ became Japhug -o, § sec:historical.phono ). They are also found in loanwords from Tibetan, but some rhymes such as -ɯŋ are only attested in ideophones.
summary: Ideophonic roots in Japhug show unusual phonological behavior not only in their onsets but also in their codas. In the Kamnyu dialect, most non-ideophonic words lack a labial stop coda, but some ideophones optionally preserve final -p, and ideophones also frequently use codas like -ŋ, -l, and -n, some of which survive only in ideophones.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
This section focuses on relative iconicity, namely the correlation between a more or less gradient phonological feature and a semantic dimension, a phenomenon also known as sound symbolism  or synesthesia.

Japhug lacks regular patterns of consonant gradation such as the alternations described in Lakhota. Gradation in place of articulation is attested, but specific to a particular family of ideophones. For instance, the roots in tab:gradation.fric have a dental -- retroflex -- velar -- uvular gradation which does correlate with the degree of whiteness, but the same gradation is not generalizable to all ideophones with coronal fricatives.

In addition to consonant gradation, even more puzzling phenomenon is ideophonic hybridization, namely the merger between several ideophonic families by combining rhymes and initial consonant clusters. The `clear, bright, white' family (unvoiced coronal initial fricative, -ɯ/aŋ rhyme) of tab:gradation.fric has intersections with two other ideophonic families shown in Tables tab:zjaN.tsjaN and tab:slaN.rloR.

tab:zjaN.tsjaN presents the ideophonic family of zjaŋ `tall', the ideophone used as example in § sec:ideo.regular. The members of this family mean `high, lofty', and have the shape a dental fricative initial, followed by a j + medial and a velar coda. The root sjɯŋ combines these phonological features with the unvoiced fricative s and the rhyme -ɯŋ of the family `white' in tab:gradation.fric. Its meaning also combines `white' and `high' from both families.

The ideophonic family meaning `round, spherical' ( tab:slaN.rloR ) is particularly rich. Its intersection with the `white' family comprises four ideophones ( slɯŋ, slaŋ, ɕlaŋ and claŋ), which share the initial consonant, the vowel and the coda with the ideophones in tab:gradation.fric, and integrate both the meanings `white, bright, shiny' and `round'.

The two ideophonic families presented in Tables tab:zjaN.tsjaN and tab:slaN.rloR have intersections with yet other families; a comprehensive account of ideophones however goes beyond the scope of this grammar, as a considerable amount of elicitation will be necessary to fully reveal the structure of ideophonic vocabulary. Rather than isolated lexemes, ideophonic roots are organized in a network of similar forms, with gradual phonetic resemblances associated with gradual shades of meanings. A historical scenario accounting for how this type of pattern may have come into being is presented in § sec:genesis.idph.
summary: The passage describes relative iconicity, or sound symbolism, in Japhug ideophones, where gradual phonological differences correlate with meaning differences. Japhug does not show general consonant gradation like Lakhota, though one ideophonic family has a dental–retroflex–velar–uvular pattern linked to degrees of whiteness, and ideophonic “hybridization” creates forms that combine phonological material and meanings from multiple families, such as associations of “white,” “high,” and “round.”

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Pattern II ideophones (§ sec:ideo.II ) have in some cases an emphatic pronunciation, in which the first member of the reduplicated ideophone receives a peak in F0 and intensity. In (§ sec:xtsxoNxtsxoN ) for instance, the first syllable of the ideophone xtʂoŋ- has the highest pitch (315 Hz) in the whole sentence, and there is a sharp pitch drop on the second syllable (267 Hz), as shown in fig:xtsxoN. There is possibly a difference in voice quality, though this remains to be demonstrated.

exe

xɕelwi rcanɯ, tɯ-se nɯ ku-tsʰi nɤ ku-tsʰi, (...) ɯ-xtu nɯ xtʂóŋ.xtʂoŋ ʑo ɲɯ-pa ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
tick unexp: deg genr. poss -blood dem ipfv -drink add ipfv -drink (...) 3sg. poss -belly dem idph (II):bloated emph ipfv - aux sens -be \\
`The tick drinks one's blood again and again, (...) so that its belly become bloated.' (25-xCelwi) 0003664#S42
0003664#S39
exe

This emphatic pronunciation is not uncommon, but in most cases the ideophones do not have any special intonation. Example (§ sec:xtsxoNxtsxoN2 ) illustrates the same ideophone xtʂoŋxtʂoŋ a few sentence later in the same text, without any emphasis.

exe

tɕe ma nɯnɯ tu-fka xtʂoŋxtʂoŋ ʑo ŋu. \\
lnk lnk dem ipfv -be.full idph (II):bloated emph be: full \\
`[The tick] is full [from having drunk blood] and bloated.' (25-xCelwi)
0003664#S57
exe
summary: Pattern II ideophones can sometimes be pronounced emphatically, with the first part of the reduplicated form receiving the highest F0 and intensity; in one example, the first syllable of *xtʂoŋ-* has the highest pitch in the sentence and the pitch drops sharply on the second syllable. The passage notes that a difference in voice quality may also exist, though this is not yet demonstrated. However, most instances of these ideophones show no special intonation, as illustrated by the same ideophone later in the text.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
ideophone!genesis
While it cannot be a priori excluded that some ideophones could be ancient, their phonological markedness is a sign that they are constantly renewed, using processes different from those found in non-ideophonic words. In this section, I propose a scenario account for one of the origins of ideophonic roots, and ideophonic hybridization (§ sec:idph.gradation ).

Some ideophonic roots are obviously built from Tibetan loanwords, but with slight phonetic changes. The most obvious case is ldʑɯŋ `skyblue', which originates from the first syllable of ལྗང་ཁུ་ldʑaŋ.kʰugreen (also borrowed as the unpossessible noun ldʑaŋkɯgreen, § sec:tibetan.colours ) with a slight modification of the vowel. The semantic relationship between the ideophone and the Tibetan borrowing is not always as obvious. For instance, zɟaŋ and zɟraŋ, both meaning `filled up, looking soft' (of a person's belly, a bag filled with objects) are reminiscent of the verb βrɟaŋstretch tight (of skin), which is borrowed from the past tense of རྒྱོང་བརྒྱངས་rgʲoŋ.brgʲaŋsstretch, distend: the ideophones describe a skin or membrane that is overstretched and distended, like the result of the action expressed by the verb βrɟaŋ. The form zɟaŋ could either have been independently borrowed from a Tibetan variety where r- and s- merge, or directly based on βrɟaŋ with further consonant modification. The root zɟraŋ is derived from zɟaŋ by insertion of -r- (see below for a possible account of these sporadic sound changes).

The Tibetan origin of some ideophones is one possible reason for the frequency of voiced stops in ideophones (§ sec:idph.onsets ), as b, d, ɟ and g are common in clusters in the borrowed layer.

However, in many case the lexical origin of ideophones has been completely blurred by a variety of mechanisms which can only be hypothesized. The four synonymous ideophones dzoʁ ( ex:dzoR.Zo.pjAtshoR ), zgoʁ, goʁ and dzɯr ( ex:dzWr.Zo.tanWtshoR ) exclusively occur in collocation with the transitive verb tsʰoʁattach and the noun tɯ-χpɯmknee (§ sec:tshoR.lv ) to express both the speed of the kneeling motion and the highly deferential attitude of the kneeling person.

exe

ɯ-χpɯm dzoʁ ʑo pjɤ-tsʰoʁ \\
3sg. poss -knee idph (I):kneeling emph ifr -attach \\
`[The demon] immediately knelt down.' (140513 abide he mogui-zh) 0003975#S45
exe

exe

ɯ-χpɯm dzɯr ʑo ta-nɯ-tsʰoʁ ndɤre, tɤ-lu pa-nɯ-tɕɤt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -knee idph (I):kneeling emph aor:3$'$ 3- auto -attach lnk indef. poss -milk aor:3$'$ 3- auto -take.out sens -be \\
`She immediately knelt down and milked [the cow].' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

In addition to pattern I, they also occur in pattern III as in ( ex:zgoRnAzgoR.Zo.tatshoRnW ).

exe

tɤ-pɤtso ra dɯxpa-nɯ matɕi tɕendɤre, zgoʁnɤzgoʁ ʑo nɯ-χpɯm ta-tsʰoʁ-nɯ tɕe \\
indef. poss -child pl poor- pl because lnk idph (II):kneeling emph 3pl. poss -knee aor:3$'$ 3-attach- pl lnk \\
`The poor children, they knelt [before the ogre] one after the other.' (160704 poucet4-v2)
0006097#S23
exe

reanalysis
I propose that one of the mechanism of ideophone creation is by playful reanalysis from lexical verb roots. The four ideophones dzoʁ, zgoʁ, goʁ and dzɯr, which have either the onset (z)g- or dz- and the rhymes -oʁ and -ɯr, originate in my opinion from the verbs ndzoʁbe attached (the anticausative of tsʰoʁattach, § sec:anticausative.dummy ) and azgɯrbow, bend down (the latter borrowed from སྒུར་sgurbend down). The development of these ideophones occurred in three steps, as illustrated in fig:idph.dzoR.

First, the ideophone roots dzoʁ `kneeling' (with alternation to the more marked plain voiced dz- onset, § sec:consonant.phonemes ) and an unattested *zgɯr (perhaps `kneeling and bowing') were directly created from the two verbs. The forms zgoʁ and dzɯr result from blending from the two primary ideophones dzoʁ and *zgɯr by exchanging rhyme and onset. Third, goʁ was derived from zgoʁ by simplification of the onset.

This process is not a derivation in the proper sense, since it is neither regular nor predictable, and involves processes such as blending which do not normally occur in the verbal and nominal morphology of the Japhug language.

In addition to native roots and Tibetan loanwords, an obvious source of ideophones are onomatopoeic imitations of natural sounds. However, given the fact that ideophonic changes do not follow regular rules unlike the normal vocabulary on the one hand, and that northern Gyalrong languages lack historical records on the other hand, it is unlikely that the prehistory of this type of ideophones can be recovered.
summary: The passage argues that ideophones are constantly renewed rather than necessarily ancient, because their marked phonology suggests they arise through special processes distinct from ordinary vocabulary. It gives two main origins: some ideophones are slightly modified Tibetan loanwords, while others may have been created by playful reanalysis, blending, and simplification from verb roots, though these changes are irregular and hard to reconstruct historically. The text also notes that some ideophones may be imitations of natural sounds, but their prehistory is largely unrecoverable.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
ideophone!syntax
As pointed out by, the markedness of ideophones is not limited to their phonology, but is also manifested in their syntactic behaviour.

Ideophones nearly always occur as verb adjuncts in Japhug. They are most commonly found with the intransitive light verb pa, the quotative verb tisay and the similative verb studo like, following a cross-linguistically well-attested pattern. They can also be used as adjunct of any lexical verb in either nominalized or finite form, and in a handful of examples, as noun modifiers. Ideophones commonly occur with the emphatic ʑo (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ), which follows them.

The auxiliary pa
The intransitive verb pa (also attested in collocation with numerals, § sec:pa.intr.lv ) is one of the most common light verb used with ideophones. It is the labile intransitive counterpart (§ sec:lability.pass ) of the verb pado, which also occurs as a light verb in noun-verb collocations (§ sec:pa.lv ).

It can either appear as an inflected form as in ( ex:RYJli.Zo.YWpa ), or as the participle kɯ-pa as in ( ex:XploR.kWpa ) (see also ex:zjaNzjaN3, § sec:ideo.II ). It is mainly used with pattern II ideophones describing colour, shape or spatial disposition.

exe

ɯ-pʰoŋbu nɯ rcanɯ ʁɲɟlíʁɲɟli ʑo ɲɯ-pa. \\
3sg. poss -body dem unexp: deg idph (II):huge emph sens - aux \\
`Its body, it is enormous.' (20-sWNgi) 0003562#S16
exe

exe

aʑo grɯβgrɯβ ɯ-ftsa nɯ tɤ-kɯ-qawɤr ma nɯ ma χploʁχploʁ kɯ-pa mɯ-pɯ-mto-t-a \\
1sg matsutake 3sg. poss -nephew dem aor - sbj: pcp -open.cap apart.from dem apart.from idph (II):small.and.spherical sbj: pcp - aux neg - aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`(The mushroom called) `the matsutake's nephew', I have seen ones with opened caps, but never seen one in ball shape (before the cap opens).' (23-grWBgrWBftsa)
0003602#S5
exe

Like other stative verbs, pa has an inchoative meaning in the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.inchoative ), the Aorist (§ sec:aor.inchoative ) and the Inferential (§ sec:ifr.inchoative ). It is attested with the upwards ( tu-pa, example ex:tupa.YWNu ) and the westwards ( ɲɯ-pa, example § sec:xtsxoNxtsxoN in § sec:emphatic.idph ) orientation preverbs.

exe

ɯ-ru nɯra nɯ-rom tɕe rʁɤβrʁɤβ tu-pa ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -stalk dem: pl aor -dry lnk idph (II):rough ipfv - aux sens -be \\
`Once it has dried, its stalk becomes very rough.' (14-sWNgWJu)
0003506#S21
exe

While pa is mainly found with pattern II ideophones, it is not restricted to these, and attested in a handful of examples with other patterns, such as III ( ex:dWrnAdWr.pjApa ) and IV ( ex:ckArnAlAr ).

exe

ʑɯrɯʑɤri qʰe li tɤ-se nɯ to-mbat qʰe, li tɤrmbɣo nɯ dɯrnɤdɯr pjɤ-pa \\
progressively lnk again indef. poss -blood dem ifr -diminish lnk again drum dem idph (III):drumming.far.away ifr. ipfv - aux \\
`Progressively, the blood [in the lake] started to recede, and there was again a drumming sound far away.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

exe

ɕkɤrnɤlɤr ʑo kɯ-pa nɯ jo-nɯ-ɣi \\
idph (IV):limping emph sbj: pcp - aux dem ifr - vert -come \\
`He came back home limping.' (140429 jiedi-zh)
exe

Quotative tisay
The verb tisay occurs as a light verb with ideophones expressing sound ( ex:zJWG.Zo, ex:tCRWz.nA.tCRWz ) and endopathic sensations (especially itching or pain as in ex:CYWG.Zo ), in patterns I ( ex:zJWG.Zo, ex:CYWG.Zo ), III ( ex:tCRWz.nA.tCRWz ) and X (§ sec:ideo.X ).

exe

ɯ-tʰoʁ tɕu zɟɯɣ ʑo ti ɲɯ-ŋu\\
3sg. poss -ground loc idph (II):heavy.object.falling emph say: fact sens -be\\
`[The stone] made a loud noise [as it fell] on the ground.' (2003 tWxtsa)
exe

exe

cʰɯ-tɯt ɕɯŋgɯ tɕe tɕe tú-wɣ-ndza tɕe, tɕʁɯznɤtɕʁɯz tu-ti ɲɯ-ŋu tʰɯ-tɯt ɯ-qʰu tɕe tɕe tɤ́-wɣ-ndza tɕe, zwaʁnɤzwaʁ tu-ti ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, nɯ ɲɯ-mɯm. \\
ipfv -be.ripe before lnk lnk ipfv - inv -eat lnk idph (III):crunchy.sound ipfv -say sens -be: fact aor -be.ripe 3sg. poss -after lnk lnk aor - inv -eat lnk idph (III):not.crunchy ipfv -say sens -be lnk dem sens -be.tasty \\
`If one eats [an apple]$_i$ before it$_i$ is ripe, it makes a crunchy sound, when it is ripe, it makes a soft (i.e. not crunchy) sound, it is [more] tasty (in this case because it has become sweeter and less sour).' (07-paXCi)
0003430#S22
exe

exe

tu-kɯ-ti kɯnɤ ɕɲɯɣ ʑo tu-ti tu-mŋɤm ŋu \\
ipfv - genr:S/O-say also idph (I):intense.pain emph ipfv -say ipfv -hurt be: fact \\
`(When suffering from this disease), one feels intense pain even when one talks.' (29-RzAr)
0003732#S35
exe

The similative verb studo like
The transitive similative verb studo like (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative, § sec:svc.similative.verb ) most commonly appears with the non-stative ideophonic patterns III ( ex:lhWG.nA.lhWG ) and IV ( ex:rloR.nA.rloR ). It expresses volitional actions, unlike pa and ti. The syntactic function of the ideophones when used with studo like is possibly that of semi-object, as they replace the demonstratives that usually occur with this verb (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ).

exe

ɯ-sŋɯro lu-lɤt tɕe ɬɯɣnɤɬɯɣ, ɬɯɣnɤɬɯɣ tu-ste ɲɯ-ŋu.\\
3sg. poss -breath ipfv -release lnk idph (III):breathing.movement idph (III):breathing.movement ipfv -do.like[III] sens -be \\
`When [the frog]$_i$ breathes, it$_i$ expands and retracts [its whole body] with each breath.' (27-qaCpa)
0003716#S3
exe

The ideophone can describe the action as a whole ( ex:lhWG.nA.lhWG ), or an aspect of the action on the object of stu as in ( ex:rloR.nA.rloR ), where the root rloʁ depicts the shape of the fly's head ( tab:slaN.rloR, § sec:idph.gradation ), and pattern III morphology (§ sec:ideo.III ) the motion of the head.

exe

ɯ-jaʁ tu-tsɯm tɕe, ɯ-ku ra pjɯ-nɯ-χtɕi tɕe ɯ-ku ra rloʁnɤrloʁ tu-ste ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -hand ipfv: up -take.away lnk 3sg. poss -head pl ipfv - auto -wash lnk 3sg. poss -head pl idph (III):round ipfv -do.like[III] sens -be \\
`[The fly] stretches up its forelegs to clean its head (and the area around it), making (at the same time) a rhythmic rolling motion [with its head, round and minute].' (25-akWzgumba)
0003632#S46
exe
summary:
Ideophones in Japhug are syntactically marked as well as phonologically marked: they nearly always function as verb adjuncts, most often with the light verb *pa*, the quotative verb *tisay*, or the similative verb *studo*. They can also modify other lexical verbs, occasionally act as noun modifiers, and commonly co-occur with the emphatic particle *ʑo*.

The light verb *pa* is especially frequent with ideophones, especially pattern II forms describing colour, shape, or spatial disposition, though it also appears with some other patterns. *Tisay* is used mainly with sound ideophones and endopathic sensations, while *studo* occurs with non-stative ideophones and expresses volitional actions, with the ideophone functioning like a semi-object.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
The reflexive form ʑɣɤ-stu (§ sec:lexicalized.refl ) is almost exclusively attested with ideophones, in particular in the manner serial verb construction (§ sec:svc.manner ) with other intransitive verbs, such as ku-rɤʑi in ( ex:XtshAXtshAt.Zo.tuZGAstu ). With pattern II ideophones, it means `make/have a $X$ look', generally expressing an attitude made on purpose.

exe

spɣi ɲɯ-nɯ-te ndɤre, nɤki rɟɤlpu tu-ɕe rcanɯ, tu-rɤjoʁβzɯr kɯ-fse rcanɯ, nɤki, χtsʰɤχtsʰɤt ʑo tu-ʑɣɤ-stu tɕe, ku-rɤʑi pɯ-ŋu, βdaʁmu tu-ɕe rcanɯ, pʰɤtɕʰɯχtɤr ʑo pjɯ-te tɕe, qɯqlɯ ʑo tu-ʑɣɤ-stu tɕe ku-rɤʑi pɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
attic 3sg -inside ipfv: east - auto -put[III] lnk king ipfv: up -go unexp: deg ipfv -clean.up inf: stat -be.like unexp: deg filler idph (II):lively.small emph ipfv - refl -do.like lnk ipfv -stay pst. ipfv -be lady ipfv: up -go unexp: deg mess emph ipfv -put[III] lnk idph (II):hangdog.look emph ipfv - refl -do.like lnk ipfv -stay pst. ipfv -be sens -be \\
`[The king]$_i$ put [the bird]$_j$ in the attic. When the king$_i$ would go up there, it$_j$ would clean everything up and would be lively; when the queen would go up there, it$_j$ would make a mess and have a hangdog look.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

It is also compatible with pattern I ( ex:CNAB.Zo.tuZGAstu ) or III ideophones, expressing motion and/or sound.

exe

tɕe nɯ kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ʑo ɲɯ́-wɣ-mbi tɕe ma ɕŋɤβ ʑo tu-ʑɣɤ-stu tɕe ju-nɯ-mɟe tɕe tu-ndze ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk dem sbj: pcp - emph be.small emph ipfv - inv -give lnk lnk idph (I):snapping emph ipfv - refl -do.like lnk ipfv - auto -take[III] lnk ipfv -eat[III] sens -be \\
`We would give [our turtle]$_i$ a little piece$_j$ [of meat], and it$_i$ would grab it$_j$ with a snapping noise and eat it$_j$.' (140510 wugui)
0003951#S22
exe
summary: The reflexive form ʑɣɤ-stu is almost exclusively used with ideophones, especially in manner serial verb constructions with intransitive verbs. With pattern II ideophones it means ‘make/have X look,’ typically conveying a deliberately produced attitude, and it can also occur with pattern I or III ideophones to express motion and/or sound.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Ideophones are not restricted in use to the light verbs cited above, and can appear with other types of verbs with compatible semantics. There are strict collocation restrictions, and most ideophones can only be used with one one or a handful of verbs.

With the three light verbs discussed above (§ sec:idph.pa, § sec:idph.ti, § sec:stu.idph ), ideophones are strictly preverbal, but when employed with other verbs, postverbal order is common, in particular in the case of stative adjectival verbs ( ex:YWGWrni.tsGaRtsGaR ).

exe

ɯ-mɲaʁ wuma nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rkɯ nɯra ɲɯ-ɣɯrni, ɲɯ-ɣɯrni tsɣaʁtsɣaʁ ʑo \\
3sg. poss -eye really dem gen 3sg. poss -side dem: pl sens -be.red sens -be.red idph (II):brilliant.red emph \\
`The sides of its eye proper are red, brilliant red.' (23-qapGAmtWmtW) 0003608#S47
exe

Ideophones can be postverbal even in particpial and finite relative clauses (§ sec:relative.postverbal ), and can be located loser to the verb than determiners such as the indefinite ci (§ sec:indef.article ), as in ( ex:kWGWrni.tsGaRtsGaR ).

exe

[kɯ-ɣɯrni ʑo tsɣaʁtsɣaʁ] ci ŋu tɕe \\
sbj: pcp -be.red emph idph (II):brilliant.red indef be: fact lnk \\
`[This species of millipede] is brilliant red.' (28-kWpAz)
0003714#S139
exe

When their semantic scope is more focalized on one of the arguments, the ideophone can directly follow a noun as in ( ex:bAbAB.Zo.kundzoR ) or ( ex:brWGbrWG.Zo.tutCAt ).

exe

tɯ-ŋga ɯ-taʁ ra ɯ-mat bɤbɤβ ʑo ku-ndzoʁ. \\
genr. poss -clothes 3sg -on pl 3sg. poss -fruit idph (II):clumping.together emph ipfv - acaus:attach \\
`When one walks among [these plants], their seeds attach in clumps to one's clothes.' (18-qromJoR)
0003532#S159
exe

exe

rtɕʰɯʁjɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rme nɯ kɯ ɲɯ-kɯ-z-rɤʑa. nɯ tɯ-ɕa a-mɤ-nɯ-ɤtɯɣ ra ma tɤndɤr brɯɣbrɯɣ ʑo tu-tɕɤt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
caterpillar gen 3sg. poss -hair dem erg ipfv - genr:S/O- caus -itch dem genr. poss -flesh irr - neg - pfv -touch be.needed: fact lnk pimple idph (II):little.pimples emph ipfv -take.out sens -be \\
`The caterpillar's hair itches people, it should not touch one's flesh, otherwise it will cause a lot of little pimples to appear.' (25-rtchWRjW)
0003656#S82
exe
summary: Ideophones are not limited to the light verbs previously discussed; they can also occur with other verbs whose meanings are compatible, though each ideophone is typically restricted to only one or a few verbs. With the three light verbs, ideophones are strictly preverbal, but with other verbs they are often postverbal, including in stative adjectival verbs and even in participial and finite relative clauses. When the ideophone has a more focal relation to a noun or argument, it may directly follow that noun.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
In examples such as ( ex:bAbAB.Zo.kundzoR ) or ( ex:brWGbrWG.Zo.tutCAt ) (§ sec:ideophone.plus.lexical.verb ), the syntactic status of the ideophone is ambiguous between a sentential adverb and a postnominal modifier.

Examples ( ex:zJAGzJAG.ma ) and ( ex:ndzArndzAr.ma ) are incontrovertible evidence that ideophones can serve as noun modifier: in ( ex:zJAGzJAG.ma ) is embedded within an exceptive (§ sec:exceptive ) postpositional phrase which does not contain any verb, and must be analyzed as modifier of the counted noun tɯ-rdoʁ `one piece'.

exe

ma nɯnɯ ɕawurambɯm tu-ti-nɯ tɕe nɯnɯ, nɤkinɯ, [[tɯ-rdoʁ ʑo zɟɤɣzɟɤɣ ] ma] kɯ-me ɲɯ-ŋu kʰi \\
lnk dem Shwa.ba.rwa.mbum ipfv -say- pl lnk dem filler one-piece emph idph (II):short.and.thick apart.from sbj: pcp -not.exist sens -be hearsay \\
`People call it `Shwaba rwa'bum', it is [a kind of deer antler] with only one [branch], short and thick.' (27-qartshaz) 0003702#S72
exe

In ( ex:ndzArndzAr.ma ), the ideophone ndzɤrndzɤr is in the emphatic exceptive construction, with the linker ma (§ sec:exceptive ).

exe

<donglang> ɯʑo-sti nɯnɯ, [tɤ-tɕɯ tɯ-rdoʁ ndzɤrndzɤr] ma nɯ ma kɯ-tu pjɤ-me. \\
anthr 3sg -alone dem indef. poss -son one-piece idph (II):alone lnk dem apart.from sbj: pcp -exist ifr. ipfv -not.exist \\
`There remained only Donglang, the boy, all alone (on earth after his family had been taken away).' (150828 donglang)
0006312#S129
exe

However, ideophones as postnominal modifiers are rare, and only occur in combination with a singular counted noun such as tɯ-rdoʁ in the meaning `alone'.
summary: The passage argues that ideophones can function as noun modifiers, not just as sentential adverbs, as shown by examples where they occur inside exceptive constructions without any verb and modify a counted noun. However, such postnominal modifier uses are rare and seem limited to combinations with singular counted nouns like tɯ-rdoʁ, especially with the meaning ‘alone.’

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Ideophones are non-essential to communication in the sense that any sentence containing an ideophone can be glossed with another sentence of identical truth value without using any ideophone. The frequency of ideophones and ideophonic verbs presents considerable variation in the corpus: some stories and procedural texts are almost devoid of them, while some episodes of traditional narratives are densely packed with them.

Ideophones convey rich and intricate meanings in a succinct way. In traditional stories, their use contributes to the vividness of the description. For instance, in ( ex:ndArndAr ), the choice of the pattern II ndɤrndɤr `huge and imposing' and the pattern III ɲcɣɤnɤɲcɣɤt `loud and moving around' evokes a much more expressive picture than the translation provided here in plain language. Native speakers, upon hearing such a sentence, visualize the vivid picture of huge lush trees and flocks of birds flying around, tweeting and chirping.

exe

nɯra tɤ-stu-t-a tɕe, sɯŋgɯnaχtɕɯn ndɤrndɤr ʑo nɯ-stu-t-a, ɯ-taʁ, pɣa ɲcɣɤnɤɲcɣɤt ʑo ɲɯ-mbri tɕe \\
dem: pl aor -do.like- pst: tr - 1sg lnk deep.forest idph (II):huge emph aor -do.like- pst: tr - 1sg 3sg -on birds idph (III):loud emph sens -call lnk \\
`I acted this way, I created a huge and deep forest on the top of whose trees birds are tweeting and chirping and flying around.' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe
summary: Ideophones are not essential for conveying truth conditions, since any sentence with an ideophone can be paraphrased without one, but their use varies greatly across texts: some are nearly absent, while others, especially in traditional narratives, are rich in them. They pack vivid and intricate meanings into a compact form and make descriptions more expressive, as in the example where ideophones evoke a striking image of a huge forest with birds flying, tweeting, and chirping.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Two classes of words present common properties with, but are different from, real ideophones: interjections (§ sec:interjections ) and calling sounds (§ sec:call ). Although both also present phonological markedness and some degree of iconicity, they are not subject to ideophonic morphology (§ sec:ideo:morpho ) and do not share the same syntactic properties.

In addition, we find some nouns which, unlike deideophonic verbs (§ sec:GA.sA.deidph ), ideophonic counted nouns (§ sec:CN.ideophones ) and nominal ideophonic compounds (§ sec.n.idph.compounds ), are directly built on an expressive root without derivational morphology (§ sec:underived.expressive.nouns ).
summary: Interjections and calling sounds share some properties with ideophones, such as phonological markedness and some iconicity, but they are not true ideophones because they do not undergo ideophonic morphology or show the same syntactic behavior. The passage also notes that some nouns are directly formed from expressive roots without derivational morphology, unlike deideophonic verbs, ideophonic counted nouns, and nominal ideophonic compounds.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
interjection
Interjections are marked words expressing a feeling or an emotion like ideophones, but differ from them in that they cannot serve as verb adjuncts, cannot receive ideophonic morphology and are mainly used in isolation, either in their own clause or as the reported speech complements of verbs of speaking like tisay ( ex:atsatsa, ex:wudzWdzi ).

exe

tɤ-ɣɤndʐo tɕe `ɯtɕʰɯtɕʰɯ' ma-tɯ-ti, tɤ-sɤɕke tɕe (nɤkinɯ) `atsatsa' ma-tɯ-ti, kɯ-mŋɤm tɤ-tu tɕe `atsatsa' ma-tɯ-ti ra \\
aor -be.cold lnk interj:cold neg: imp -2-say aor - prop -burn lnk filler interj:pain neg: imp -2-say sbj: pcp -hurt aor -exist lnk interj:pain neg: imp -2-say be.needed: fact \\
`When you feel cold, don't say ``Ah'', when you feel hot, don't say ``ouch'', when you feel pain, don't say ``ouch''.' (07-deluge) 0003426#S64
exe

exe

srɯtpʰu srɯnmɯ kɯ-fse kɯ-sɤ-ɣmɯ ɣmu ʑo ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ndʑi-ci ri, `wudzɯdzi' mɯ-to-ti. \\
râkshasa râkshasî sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp - prop - emph fear emph ifr - peg -meet- du - peg lnk interj:fear neg - ifr -say \\
`They met fearsome râkshasas and râkshasîs, but he did not say `how frightful!'.' (31-deluge) 0004077#S114
exe

Interjections can however be followed by full clauses, but with a pause as in ( ex:aCi ) (see also for instance ja in example ex:thWnWmblWmnW.je, § sec:reported.speech.sfp ).

exe

aɕi! ɲɯ-tɯ-ɣɤŋgi. \\
interj:correction sens -2-be.right \\
`Of course (I take back what I have said)! You are right.' (2003 tWxtsa)
exe

The marker wo can precede without pause a noun in vocative function ( ex:wo.amu ) (see also ex:pGAlnApGAl, § sec:ideo.III ).

exe

wo a-mu a-kɯm ɣɯ-tɤ-ci \\
interj 1sg. poss -mother 1sg. poss -door cisl - imp -open[III] \\
`Mother, come and open the door for me!' (2012 tWJo) 0004089#S21
exe

Some interjections cannot form a complete utterance on their own: χawoif only introduces a clause in the Irrealis expressing a wish (see examples ex:apWsatnW.YWsWsama, § sec:irrealis.complement.clauses and ex:atWrme, § sec:frozen.indef ). The form tsatsatsa is used in a correlative construction meaning `one can say that $X$, but one can also say that $ X$, with the positive $X$ and negative $ X$ forms of the same verb followed by the additive nɤ, as in ( ex:tsatsatsa ).

exe

ɲɯ-tɯ-fse nɤ tsatsatsa, mɯ́j-tɯ-fse nɤ tsatsatsa \\
sens -2-be.like add interj neg: sens -2-be.like add interj \\
`One can say that you look like her, but one can also say that you don't.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

Interjections can be classified into four categories ( tab:interjections ): involuntary responses to stimuli (interjections in the proper sense, ), and uninflected words expressing comments on words uttered by oneself or others, short orders or polite expressions.

Among these forms, pɤkʰijewait is the only one with a clear internal etymology (from pɤjkʰu je, § sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ). Some interjections are from Tibetan, including the polite expressions and mtsʰɤrihow strange (§ sec:mirative ), which is originally a uniflected predicate borrowed from མཚར་mtsʰarfeel strange.

Although interjections lack morphological alternation, the additive nɤ can be inserted within wortɕʰi wojɤr (which is borrowed from འོར་ཆེ་ɦor.tɕʰethanks) to express repeated action as in ( ex:wortChi.nA.wojAr ) (see also ex:wojAr.ntsW.toti, § sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ), a use reminiscent of the Ideophonic patterns III (§ sec:ideo.III ) and IV (§ sec:ideo.IV )

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ ``wortɕʰi nɤ wojɤr ʑo" to-ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
indef. poss -boy dem erg please add please emph ifr -say sens -be \\
`The boy said `please' several times.' (2012-qachGa)
0004087#S79
exe

The phatic expressions and sɤrmagood night and kɤnɤβditake care, though originally non-inflecting, can take number indexation suffixes (§ sec:phatic.inflectionalization ) and have become quasi-verbs, though they are highly anomalous and defective. The interjection woːwe can be used as a response to these expressions.

The expression kʰɤβzaŋ `here I am' is uttered by the guest when he arrives at someone else's home; the hosts invites the guest inside by saying nɤ-tʂu `your way'.

The interjection woja `yes, right' occurs to confirm the validity of a previous statement, sometimes assertive as in ( ex:woja.nW.kWfse ) but also with interrogative markers such as ɣe (see ex:totsu.Ge, § sec:fsp.interrog ). It can be used whether the addressee had a vocal reaction or not.

exe

ɯnɯnɯ tɕendi <wazi> nɯ ɯ-mdoʁ wuma ʑo ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-ndo. woja, nɯnɯ kɯ-fse ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
dem west socks dem 3sg. poss -colour really emph sens - prog -take interj dem sbj: pcp -be.like sens -be \\
`It has the colour of the socks over there. Yes, it is like that.' (23-grWBgrWBftsa)
0003602#S44
exe
summary:
Interjections are marked words that express feelings or emotions, but unlike ideophones they cannot function as verb adjuncts or take ideophonic morphology, and they are used mainly in isolation or as reported speech complements. The passage also notes that some interjections can be followed by a full clause with a pause, while others occur in vocative or special correlative constructions and may not form complete utterances on their own.

The text further classifies interjections into four types: involuntary responses to stimuli, uninflected comment words, short orders, and polite expressions. Some forms are borrowed from Tibetan, a few have internal etymology, and certain originally uninflecting expressions have become quasi-verbs or allow limited insertion of the additive nɤ.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
summon dispersal calling sound chasing sound
Calling and chasing sounds, also referred to as `summons' and `dispersals'  are sounds used by people to interact with animals. French has the more colorful term huchement de berger to designate this class of utterances. They are used either to incite the animals to come forward in the direction of the speaker (calling sounds, as in ex:tCitCi3 ) or to advance or go away (chasing sounds, as in ex:tCha.lWlu ).

exe

xlist

lɯlu ɲɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-ɤkʰɤzŋga qʰe tɕítɕi tɕítɕi tɕítɕi nɯra tu-kɯ-ti qʰe ju-ɣi ŋu \\
cat ipfv - inv - appl -shout lnk call:cat dem: pl ipfv - genr -say lnk ipfv -come be: fact \\
`When one calls a cat, one says tɕítɕi tɕítɕi tɕítɕi and it comes.' (06-huchements1) 0003412

lɯlu jú-wɣ-no tɕe ``tɕʰa" tu-kɯ-ti ŋu \\
cat ipfv - inv -chase lnk chase:cat ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`When one chases a cat, one says tɕʰa.' (06-huchements2)
xlist
exe

In Japhug, nearly all farm animals and pets, whether mammals or birds, have special dedicated calling sounds, a list of which is provided in tab:calling.sounds. In addition, a click sound for which no IPA symbol exists is used to call puppies.

Given the rudimentary nature of man-animal interactions, it is not surprising that these sounds cannot be subjected to any morphological operation other than reduplication. They cannot be used with any light verbs or occur as adjuncts. However, if the animal has a name, it can be added after the calling/chasing sound ( ex:aBleBle.rgWskW ).

exe

tɕe ɯʑo kɯ-ɤskɯ a-pɯ-ŋu qʰe ``aβleβle rgɯskɯ" tu-kɯ-ti qʰe tɕe ɯʑo tso ɕti qʰe ju-nɯ-ɣi ɕti \\
lnk 3sg sbj: pcp -having.white.colour.on.the.back irr - ipfv -be lnk calling:cow cow.name ipfv - genr -say lnk lnk 3sg understand: fact be. aff: fact lnk ipfv - auto -come be. aff: fact \\
`If [the cow] has white colour on the back (and is given the name rgɯskɯ ), one says aβleβle rgɯskɯ and she understands, and comes by herself.' (06-huchements1) 0003412
exe

Phonologically, these words contain very unusual sounds: they make use of consonants and vowel that are not found at all in the standard lexicon: the dental click ǀ, the glottal stop in a cluster ʔw or as a coda and breathy voice.

Only one of these words appears to have an identifiable etymology: soŋ `chasing sound for dogs' is possibly related to Tibetan སོང་soŋgo. However, there is a striking resemblance between some of the chasing/calling sounds in Japhug and Khroskyabs, as illustrated by tab:calling.sounds.japhug.khroskyabs. It is unlikely that these resemblances are due to common inheritance.
summary: The passage describes special “calling” and “chasing” sounds used to interact with animals in Japhug, equivalent to summons and dispersals. These utterances are highly restricted: they are usually just reduplicated forms, cannot take light verbs or function as adjuncts, and may be followed by an animal’s name; phonologically, they include unusual sounds absent from the standard lexicon, and only one form has a possible etymology, while similarities with Khroskyabs are likely not inherited.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
noun!expressive
A certain number of bird names are based on onomatopoeia imitating their song. For instance, qusputcuckoo (example ex:ntsW.tuti, § sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ) and tsɯʁotpheasant ( ex:tsWRot.tuti ) are described as making a sound identical to their Japhug name.

exe

tsɯʁot pʰu nɯ tu-mbri tɕe, ``tsɯʁot tsɯʁot tsɯʁot" ntsɯ tu-ti ŋu. \\
pheasant male dem ipfv -make.sound lnk idph (X):cry always ipfv -say be: fact \\
`When the male pheasant sings, it says tsɯʁot tsɯʁot tsɯʁot.' (24-kWmu) 0003618#S104
exe

In the case of dɯdɯtturtle dove, its calling sound is described as being slightly different from its name, with various interpretations ( ex:dudut.tuti ). In Tshobdun, `pheasant' and `turtle-dove' are called tsəʁot and dudut, respectively. These words cannot be inherited from the common ancestor of Japhug and Tshobdun however, since Tshobdun -ot should correspond to either -ɤt or -ɯt.

exe

tɕe dɯdɯt kɤ-ti ci tu tɕe, tɕe ``dudut dudut" ntsɯ tu-ti. tsuku kɯ ``dudut cɯŋglɯɣ" tu-ti ŋu ra tu-ti-nɯ ri, nɯ mɤ-xsi ri, ``dudu wu" kɯ-fse tu-ti ŋgrɤl. \\
lnk turtle.dove obj: pcp -say indef exist lnk lnk onomatopoeia always ipfv -say some erg onomatopoeia mortar ipfv -say be: fact pl ipfv -say- pl lnk dem neg - genr:know lnk onomatopoeia sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv -say be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`There is [a bird] called turtle-dove, it always makes dudut dudut. Some people say that it makes dudut cɯŋglɯɣ, I don't know [if it is true], [in any case] it makes dudut wu.' (22-CAGpGa)
0003586#S24
exe

The bird name tacoʁcoʁ is based on the onomatopoeia describing its song (see example ex:tWrtsAG.tAmbro, § sec:imp.function ), but with the addition of a ta- prefix, which may or may not be related to the action nominal tɯ- prefix (§ sec:action.nominals ).
summary: The passage explains that several bird names in Japhug are formed from onomatopoeic imitations of their calls, such as *qusput* ‘cuckoo’ and *tsɯʁot* ‘pheasant,’ whose names are said to match their song exactly. It also notes that *dɯdɯt* ‘turtle dove’ is associated with a somewhat variable calling sound, and that *tacoʁcoʁ* is based on an onomatopoeia but includes an added *ta-* prefix of uncertain origin.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
filler
In Japhug speech fillers, rather than a central vowel, are used to mark pause during speech either due to hesitation, or to give the speaker more time to reflect on what he or she is about to say.

The cataphoric demonstrative nɤki, used both as a pronoun (§ sec:cataph.pron ) and as a noun modifier (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners ), is the most frequent speech filler (examples in this grammar include ex:YWwGrWwGrum in § sec:emph.redp, ex:tWNgo.ZimkhAm in § sec:nominal.intensifier and ex:lurYJi.tsa.Nu in § sec:preverb.adjectives.size ). It can be combined with the determiner nɯ (§ sec:nW.topic ) as nɤkinɯ ( ex:pjAkAtaci.passive, § sec:preverbs.contracting.verbs ) or with the indefinite ci (§ sec:indef.article ) as nɤki ci nɯ.

The aforementioned anaphoric topic marker iɕqʰa (§ sec:iCqha ), which derives from the adverb iɕqʰajust now, also occurs as speech filler (example ex:CkunWrtCe, § sec:echo.multiple.AM ), likewise frequently followed by the determiner nɯ ( ex:WphWNgW.nWtCu.YAtCAt, § sec:manipulation.verbs and ex:CtuBzdWnW, § sec:AM.goal ).

exe

nɯnɯ tɕe, pɕi ku-rɤʑi ɕti tɕe, nɤki nɯ, iɕqʰa nɯ, kʰa ɯ-ŋgɯ ju-ɣi mɤ-ŋgrɤl \\
dem lnk outside ipfv -stay be. aff: fact lnk filler dem filler dem house 3sg. poss -in ipfv -come neg -be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`That one (the wild cat), it stays outside, it does not come inside houses (unlike the domestic cat).' (21-lWLU) 0003576#S5
exe

The interjection ja (§ sec:interjections ) is used as speech filler by persons listening to traditional stories, as a sign that they are following the narrative of the storyteller. Traditional storytellers require their audience to respond in this way, as shown by ( ex:ja.tAti.ma.tCe ).

exe

``ja" tɤ-ti ma tɕe mɯ́j-kʰɯ. \\
filler imp -say lnk lnk neg: sens -be.possible \\
`Say `ya', otherwise [I] can't [tell the story].' (160720 kandZislama)
0006147#S3
exe
summary: Japhug speech fillers are used to mark pauses caused by hesitation or to give the speaker time to think. The most frequent filler is the cataphoric demonstrative **nɤki**, which can also combine with **nɯ** or **ci**; the anaphoric topic marker **iɕqʰa** is also used this way, often with **nɯ**. In addition, the interjection **ja** functions as a filler for listeners in traditional storytelling, signaling attention and participation.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
Japhug has a rich system of sentence final particles, which combine with verbal morphology to express modality, evidentiality, interrogation and the attitude of the speaker.

Given the fact that the meaning of most sentence final particles is rather difficult to pinpoint with precision, the non-specific gloss sfp is used for all of them.
summary: Japhug has a rich set of sentence-final particles that combine with verbal morphology to express modality, evidentiality, interrogation, and the speaker’s attitude. Because the meanings of most of these particles are difficult to define precisely, they are all glossed nonspecifically as sfp.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
command!particle
The particle je conveys a milder tone to orders expressed with Imperative (§ sec:imperative ), Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis ) and Prohibitive (§ sec:prohibitive ), as shown by ( ex:guan.makAtWBze ) (see also ex:jAlAt.je in § sec:imp.function and § sec:imp.autive in § ex:tAnWndAm.je ).

exe

pɤkʰije tɕe <guan> ma-kɤ-tɯ-βze je! \\
wait lnk turn.off neg - imp -2-make[III] sfp \\
`Wait, don't hang up [your phone].' (conversation, 2015-07-05)
exe

It combines with first person Imperfective verb forms to express hortative meaning (§ sec:ipfv.hortative ) as in ( ex:chWGia.je ).

exe

aʑo cʰɯ-ɣi-a je ma mɤ-pʰan-a nɤ mɤ-ʁdɯɣ-a tʰaŋ nɤ \\
1sg ipfv: downstream -come- 1sg sfp lnk neg:be.efficient: fact - 1sg add neg -harm: fact - 1sg sfp sfp \\
`Let me come along, even if I am of no use, I will not do any harm.' (several occurrences)
0003368#S20
exe

It is also used with 2 1 Imperfective forms to express commands with a first person object as in ( ex:pjWkWrkua.je ), since Imperative lacks 2 1 forms (§ sec:imperative ).

exe

a-wi tɕʰorzi ɯ-ŋgɯ pjɯ-kɯ-rku-a je\\
1sg. poss -grandmother jar 3sg. poss -in ipfv: down -2 1-put.in- 1sg sfp \\
`Grandmother, put me in the jar, and...' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

In addition, the particle je is often added to phatic expressions such as tɤ-ɤstu `goodbye', sɤrmagood night and kɤnɤβditake care (§ sec:phatic.inflectionalization ) as in ( ex:kAnABdi.je ).

exe

kɤnɤβdi je a-mu! \\
take.care sfp 1sg. poss -mother \\
`Take care, mother!' (Gesar,54)
exe

Other postverbal elements used with Modal categories include the noun smɯlɤmprayer which occurs with the Irrealis (§ sec:smWlAm.TAME ) and the softened command particle wo (originally an interjection) as in ( ex:nWBde.wo ). This particle can be cliticized to the verb stem (§ sec:verb.enclitics ).

exe

kʰu nɯ ʁo nɯ-βde wo, a-me nɯ χtanɤ a-ftsaʁ ɯβrɤ-ɣi ma \\
tiger dem advers imp -throw sfp 1sg. poss -daughter dem comp 1sg. poss -roof.leak rh. q -come sfp \\
`My daughter, don't worry about the tiger, [I am more worried] that my [house] could have a roof leak.' (khu 2005)
0004085#S4
exe

The je and wo particles are curiously similar to the Imperative and Hortative suffixes -(j)e and -(w)ɵ in the Kiranti language Khaling, though it is extremely unlikely that this could reflect common inheritance, and is rather a pure coincidence. In any case, Proto-Gyalrong *-o yields Japhug -u (§ sec:historical.phono ).
summary:
The particle **je** softens orders formed with the Imperative, Irrealis, and Prohibitive, and it also combines with first-person imperfective forms to express hortative meaning. It is further used with 2→1 imperfective forms to make commands with a first-person object, and it often appears in phatic expressions such as “goodbye,” “good night,” and “take care.”  

The passage also notes another softened command particle, **wo**, which can cliticize to the verb stem; although **je** and **wo** resemble certain Kiranti suffixes, this similarity is described as coincidental rather than evidence of common inheritance.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
question!particle
In addition to the interrogative prefix ɯ- (§ sec:interrogative.W ), and interrogative pronouns (§ sec:interrogative.pronouns ), questions can be marked by a series of several interrogative particles.

The particle ɕi is the most common way of expressing a polar question, in combination with a verb in assertive form as in ( ex:pjWmnata.Ci ) and ( ex:nAZWB.WYWGi.Ci ). In this function, it is equivalent to the prefix ɯ- (§ sec:interrogative.W ).

exe

kɯki li pjɯ-mnat-a ɕi? \\
dem. prox again ipfv -repeat- 1sg qu \\
`Do I tell [the story] again?' (150908 menglang-zh) 0006320#S1
exe

exe

nɤ-ʑɯβ ɲɯ-ɣi ɕi? \\
2sg. poss -sleep sens -come qu? \\
`Are you feeling sleepy?' (09-stoR, 65) 0003470#S60
exe

It can be used to express an alternative between two possibilities ( ex:chWtWnWBlWnW.Ci ), often with an assertive verb form followed by the corresponding negative one ( ex:YWmpCAr.Ci ).

exe

nɯʑora smi cʰɯ-tɯ-nɯ-βlɯ-nɯ ŋu ɕi, <dian> cʰɯ-tɯ-nɯmbjɯm-nɯ ŋu? \\
2pl fire ipfv -2- auto -burn- pl be: fact qu electricity ipfv -2-get.warm- pl be: fact \\
`Do you burn a fire, or do you get warm with an electric [radiator]?' (conversation, 2013-12-13)
exe

exe

kɯki a-χpi ki ɲɯ-mpɕɤr ɕi mɯ́j-mpɕɤr? \\
dem. prox 1sg. poss -story dem. prox sens -be.beautiful qu neg: sens -be.beautiful \\
`Is this story of mine beautiful or not?' (140512 fushang he yaomo-zh)
0003967#S176
exe

Furthermore, ɕi can indicate a disjunction between more than two options. In this function, it is repeated after each clause in the disjunction, except the last one, as in ( ex:tAnWmdzW.Ci ) (see also ex:tWnWCe.Ci, § sec:disjunction.clauses ).

exe

χsɤr kʰri ɯ-taʁ tɯ-ɤ<nɯ>mdzɯ ɕi, rŋɯl kʰri ɯ-taʁ tɯ-ɤ<nɯ>mdzɯ ɕi, (...) ɕom kʰri ɯ-taʁ tɯ-ɤ<nɯ>mdzɯ ɕi, si kʰri ɯ-taʁ tɯ-ɤ<nɯ>mdzɯ? \\
gold seat 3sg. poss -on 2-< auto >sit: fact qu silver seat 3sg. poss -on 2-< auto >sit: fact qu iron seat 3sg. poss -on 2-< auto >sit: fact qu wood seat 3sg. poss -on 2-< auto >sit: fact \\
`Will you sit on the golden seat, the silver seat, the iron seat or the wooden seat?' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

The apprehensive prefix ɕɯ- is likely to have been grammaticalized from this particle (§ sec:apprehensive.history ).

The particle kɯ occurs in questions to oneself ( ex:nanWri.kW ), rhetorical questions and confirmation-seeking questions ( ex:future.GAZu, § sec:sensory.functions ). Unlike ɕi, it occurs together with either an interrogative pronoun or in combination with an interrogative verb form. Example ( ex:nanWri.kW ) could be translated into French using the marker donc as `Mais où est donc passé mon mendiant (de mari)?' It is particularly common with the Dubitative (§ sec:dubitative ).

exe

a-rcɤmbe-ŋga nɯ ŋotɕu nɯ-a<nɯ>ri kɯ? \\
1sg. poss -old.jacket-wear dem where aor: west -< auto >go[II] qu \\
`Where did my beggar (`wearer of an old jacket") of a husband vanish?' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

It can be combined with the particles ma (§ sec:fsp.epistemic ) and ɣe (see below) as kɯma ( ex:mWpWfCAttCi.kWma ) and kɯɣe.

exe

mɤʑɯ tɕʰi mɯ-pɯ-fɕɤt-tɕi kɯma? \\
even.more what neg - aor -tell- 1du qu \\
`Which [trees] are there which we have not yet told [a story] about?' (13-tApWpjoR) 0003494#S60
exe

Several particles mark a question inviting the addressee to confirm what the speaker has said: ɣe, which even resembles an interjection in that it can be preceded by a pause as in ( ex:totsu.Ge ), nétɕi ( ex:YWNu.netCi, ex:totia.Nu.netCi ) and loβtɕi ( ex:tWsla.tomtshAt.loBtCi ).

exe

kɯβdesqafsum-pa to-tsu, ɣe? woja, nɯ to-tsu \\
43-year ifr -pass sfp interj dem ifr -pass \\
`(How many years have passed since 1969?), 43 years have passed, right? Yes, that many years have passed.' (12-BzaNsa) 0003484#S13
exe

exe

hehe kɯ-lɤɣ acɤβ, kɯ-sat-a ɲɯ-ŋu nétɕi? \\
interj sbj: pcp -herd anthr 2 1-kill: fact - 1sg sens -be sfp \\
`Shepherd Askyabs, you are preparing to kill me, right?' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

exe

``tʂʰa mbuz ɲɯ-ŋu" to-ti-a ŋu nétɕi? \\
tea spill.overt: fact sens -be ifr -say- 1sg be: fact sfp \\
`I said `The tea is abouyt to spill over', didn't I?' (26-tAGe) 0003686#S14
exe

exe

nɤʑo nɤ-tɕɯ tɯ-sla to-mtsʰɤt loβtɕi? \\
2sg 2sg. poss -son one-month ifr -full sfp \\
`Your son is now more than one month old, right? (conversation 2013-12-02)
exe

The particle raʁmaʁ also invites the addressee to give a positive answer to the speaker's suggestion like aforementioned markers, but with an additional overtone `How about...?' ( ex:tuwGqurnW.raRmaR ).

exe

tɯ-rdoʁ tsa rɤʑi-j tɕe tú-wɣ-qur-nɯ raʁmaʁ \\
one-piece a.little stay: fact - 1pl lnk ipfv - inv -help- pl sfp \\
`How about only one of us staying [here] and helping them?' (180503 xiyouji 12-zh)
0006189#S74
exe

It can be used to express supplication, as in ( ex:raRmaR.ma ) (see also the nearly identical example ex:WtshAt.tsa, § sec:deputative ).

exe

a-rɟit a-nmaʁ ʑo nɯ tɤ-tɯ-stu-nɯ ɕti tɕe, aʑo ɯ-tsʰɤt tsa ɲɯ-kɯ-nɤɕtʂaʁli-a-nɯ raʁmaʁ ma \\
1sg. poss -offspring 1sg. poss -husband emph dem aor -2-do.like- pl be. aff: fact lnk 1sg 3sg. poss -proper.measure a.little ipfv -2 1-torture- 1sg - pl sfp sfp \\
`Rkangrang, you dealt with my son in the same way as you did with my husband (i.e. had him killed), don't go over the top in your torturing of me (torture me with proper measure), please?' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S185
exe

The second syllable -maʁ in raʁmaʁ probably originates from the negative copula maʁnot be (§ sec:suppletive.negative, § sec:copula.basic ) as postverbal negation (§ sec:postverbal.copulas; perhaps from an interrogative form ɯ́-maʁ `is it not...'). The source of the first syllable raʁ- is less clear, but may be from the auxiliary rabe needed (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ), the original meaning being `is it not the case that $X$ have/has to...'
summary:
The passage describes several interrogative particles in addition to the interrogative prefix ɯ- and interrogative pronouns. The particle ɕi is the most common marker of polar questions, can also mark alternatives between two or more possibilities, and may have given rise to the apprehensive prefix ɕɯ-. 

The particle kɯ is used in self-addressed, rhetorical, and confirmation-seeking questions, often with interrogative pronouns or interrogative verb forms, and can combine with ma and ɣe. Other particles such as ɣe, nétɕi, loβtɕi, and raʁmaʁ are used to invite confirmation, with raʁmaʁ additionally expressing a suggestion or supplication and probably historically related to negation.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
hearsay
The particle kʰi expresses hearsay, and often occurs when the original narrator is left unidentified by the speaker ( ex:mWpjAcha.khi ).

exe

ɯ-jaʁmu ra to-tɕɤt kʰi, wo, tɕendɤre kɯ-ɣɤrʁaʁ nɯ kɯ kɤ-nɯɕɤmɯɣdɯ mɯ-pjɤ-cʰa kʰi. \\
3sg. poss -thumb pl ifr -take.out sfp interj lnk sbj: pcp -hunt dem erg inf -shoot neg - ifr -can sfp \\
`[They say that the monkey mother] stuck out her thumb (as a sign meaning `now you can shoot'), For the context of this example, see ( ex:ra.WskAt.ra.toBzu ) (§ sec:nouns.speech.complement ). but the hunter could not shoot.' (19-GzW) 0003536#S71
exe

Sentences marked with this particle ( ex:khu.pjAtu.khi ) can be reformulated using a reported speech clause with the complement-taking noun ɯ-fɕɤtstory (§ sec:nouns.speech.complement ), as in ( ex:khu.pjAtu.WfCAt ).

exe

xlist

iʑo ji-sɤtɕʰa kʰu pjɤ-tu kʰi \\
1pl 1pl. poss -place tiger ifr. ipfv -exist sfp \\

iʑo ji-sɤtɕʰa kʰu pjɤ-tu ɯ-fɕɤt tu.\\
1pl 1pl. poss -place tiger ifr. ipfv -exist 3sg. poss -story exist: fact \\
xlist
`People say that there used to be tigers in our place.' (elicited)
exe

The particle kʰi can be treated as an afterthought, and undergo right-dislocation (§ sec:right.dislocation ) together with an auxiliary verb as in ( ex:YWNu.khi ), or with a full pause and the beginning of a new sentence as in ( ex:YWNu.khi.ma ), when the speaker realizes as s/he is speaking that s/he only knows this information from second-hand sources, as explicitly stated in ( ex:YWNu.khi.ma ).

exe

kɯ-dɤn tsa tɯtɯrca ku-rɤʑi-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu, ɲɯ-ŋu kʰi \\
sbj: pcp -be.many a.little together ipfv -stay- pl sens -be sens -be sfp \\
`They stay together in great number (on remote cliffs), it is said' (20-ldWGi)
0003558#S12
exe

exe

ki kɯ-fse kɯ-ɤrɤmbɯmbri ʑo kɯ-fse tu-ɬoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu. ɲɯ-ŋu kʰi ma, aj mɯ-pɯ-mto-t-a \\
dem. prox sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp -spread.in.patches emph sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv -come.out sens -be sens -be sfp lnk 1sg neg - aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`[The mushroom Hericium erinaceus ] grows in patches (i.e. not spread evenly). So they say, I have not seen it.' (23-mbrAZim) 0003604#S172
exe

In the immense majority of examples, kʰi occurs with verbs in the Inferential ( ex:mWpjAcha.khi ) or Sensory ( ex:YWNu.khi and ex:YWNu.khi.ma ) (§ sec:ifr, § sec:sensory ). However, this not a morphosyntactic constraint, and kʰi can in principle be combined with verbs in other TAME categories, such as the Factual (§ sec:factual ) in ( ex:cha.khi ) ( cʰa rather than the Sensory ɲɯ-cʰa ), confirming Tournadre and LaPolla's ( tournadre14evidentiality) insight of the necessity of distinguishing source and access to information when describing evidential systems.

exe

pɣɤkʰɯ nɯ kɯ qaɲi kɤ-sat wuma ʑo cʰa kʰi. \\
owl dem erg mole inf -kill really emph can: fact sfp \\
`The owl is very good at killing moles, it is said.' (28-qapar)
0003720#S196
exe

The archaic inferential kʰɯ-ti `s/he said' found in a handful of stories may result from the fusion of this particle with the prefixless stem of the verb tisay (§ sec:khWti ).

In addition, the noun kʰicʰorumour, hearsay is a delocutive noun derived from the particle kʰi and the comitative cʰo (§ sec:comitative ). The etymological relationship between kʰicʰo and kʰi is made clear by examples like ( ex:khicho ), where kʰicʰo is glossed as `saying pjɤ-ŋu kʰi ', i.e. using the hearsay particle and the Inferential to insist on the fact that one has only heard this information from second-hand sources.

exe

tɕeri ɯ-pɯ-kɯ-mto tɕi pjɤ-me wo ma, kʰicʰo ma nɯ ma ɯ-kɯ-sɯz maŋe. ``pjɤ-ŋu kʰi,... pjɤ-ŋu kʰi" nɯra tu-ti-nɯ ma nɯ ma ɯ-kɯ-ti pɯ-me. \\
lnk 3sg. poss - aor - sbj: pcp -see also ifr. ipfv -not.exist sfp sfp rumour lnk dem apart.from 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -know not.exist: sens ifr. ipfv -be sfp ifr. ipfv -be sfp dem: pl ipfv -say- pl lnk dem apart.from 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -say pst. ipfv -not.exist \\
`Nobody has ever seen [one-legged demons], there are only rumours, apart from that nobody knows about them. People used to say `it was [allegedly]...', but apart from that nobody said anything.' (140510 rkoNJAl)
0003943#S80
exe

The hearsay particle can be followed by other sentence final particles (such as wo, § sec:verb.enclitics ), but there are no examples of it being preceded by other particles.
summary: The particle **kʰi** marks **hearsay** and is used when the speaker reports information from second-hand sources, often without identifying the original narrator. It most often appears with **Inferential** or **Sensory** verbs, though it is not restricted to those categories and can also occur with other TAME forms; it may also be treated as an afterthought and can be followed by other sentence-final particles.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
modality!epistemic
In addition to verbal morphology (§ sec:TAME.modal, § sec:second.modal ), epistemic modality is expressed in Japhug by sentence final elements, including the grammaticalized noun ɯ-mdoʁcolour (§ sec:WmdoR.TAME ) and the particles tʰaŋ, rca and ma.

The particle tʰaŋ is borrowed from Amdo Tibetan, where it appears in the complex ending na.tʰaŋ.gi expressing possibility (translated as ……かもしれない `maybe...' in ).

Semantically tʰaŋ is close to the possible modality prefix (§ sec:WmA ), as illustrated by ( ex:GWmtsWGa.thaN ) and ( ex:WmAwGmtsWGa ) (see also ex:WmAjazGWt.gloss and ex:WmAjazGWt in § sec:peg.circumfix ). It is often followed by the exclamative nɤ (allomorph of nɯ, § sec:fsp.attitude ).

exe

xlist

qapri kɯ ɣɯ-mtsɯɣ-a tʰaŋ nɤ! \\
snake erg inv -bite: fact - 1sg sfp sfp \\

qapri kɯ ɯmɤ́-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-a \\
snake erg prob - inv -bite: fact - 1sg \\
`The snake will perhaps bite me.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

In the overwhelming majority of cases, tʰaŋ follows a verb in the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ) to indicate either a probable future event ( ex:GWmtsWGa.thaN and ex:mAwGndzaj.thaN; see also ex:Gi.thaN, § sec:fact.main.clauses ) or a general statement of uncertain truth value ( ex:mAndze.thaN ).

exe

si ɯ-mat ra tu-ndze ɲɯ-ɕti. xɕaj nɯ mɤ-ndze tʰaŋ nɤ. nɤj ɯ-tɯ́-sɯz? \\
tree 3sg. poss -fruit pl ipfv -eat[III] sens -be. aff grass dem neg -eat[III]: fact sfp sfp 2sg qu -2-know: fact \\
`[The monkey] eats fruits. It probably does not eat grass. Do you know [whether it does or not]?' (19-GzW)
0003536#S6
exe

It can also express uncertain result in the apodosis of conditional constructions (with a protasis in the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.conditional, § sec:real.conditional ), as in ( ex:mAwGndzaj.thaN ) In addition, ( ex:mAwGndzaj.thaN ) is an interesting example of hybrid indirect speech (§ sec:hybrid indirect ), with the verb form ɲɯ-ŋu reflecting the point of view of the ogre, while the 1pl pronoun iʑora and the 3sg possessive ɯ-me `his daughters' represent that of the children. (see also ex:pjWwGnWXtCi.apWNu, § sec:irrealis.periphrastic ).

exe

nɯ a-tɤ-fse tɕe tɕetʰa, ɬɤndʐi nɯ kɯ tʰa ``iʑora ɯ-me ɲɯ-ŋu" a-nɯ-sɯsɤm tɕe, mɤ́-wɣ-ndza-j tʰaŋ \\
