dem irr - pfv -be.like lnk later demon dem erg later 1pl 3sg. poss -daughter sens -be irr - pfv -think[III] lnk neg - inv -eat- 1pl sfp \\
`[If we do it] this way, the ogre$_i$ will think that we are his$_i$ daughters and maybe he$_i$ will not eat us. (160705 poucet5-v2)
0006163#S31
exe

It can also express a possibly undesirable result as in ( ex:zayin.tu.thaN ) (§ sec:precautioning.clauses ).

exe

tɕetʰa tu-ɕe-a ma kʰapa ri ku-nɤŋkɯŋke-a tɕetʰa, nɤkinɯ, <zayin> tu tʰaŋ \\
later ipfv: up -go- 1sg lnk yard loc prs - distr:walk- 1sg later filler noise exist: fact sfp \\
`I will go up [to my house] because [now] I am walking in the yard, there could be noise (so that we won't hear each other on the phone).' (conversation 2016-02-21)
exe

Other TAME categories are also compatible with tʰaŋ, including the Past Imperfective ( ex:pWsaXaR.thaN ) and the Aorist (examples ex:WmAjazGWt.gloss in § sec:peg.circumfix and ex:OSV.janWtsWm in § sec:monotransitive.word.order ).

exe

tɕe nɯŋa dɯxpa ma (...) ɯ-tɯ-mu nɯ pɯ-saχaʁ ʑo tʰaŋ ɲɯ-sɯsam-a ŋu. \\
lnk cow poor lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -fear dem pst. ipfv -be.extremely emph sfp ipfv -think[III] be: fact \\
`I am thinking that the poor cow, she probably was extremely afraid (after escaping from a flood and losing a horn in the process).' (160715 nWNa)
0006067#S14
exe

The particle rca, which is probably related to the secutive relator noun ɯ-rcafollowing (§ sec:secutive ) and the unexpected focus marker rcanɯ (§ sec:unexpected ), occurs with verbs in the Sensory or Inferential ( ex:pjAsi.rca, ex:pjAtu.rca ), expressing high probability `presumably, probably'.

exe

jinde kɤntɕʰɯ-sŋi kɤ-mto pɯ-me tɕe, pjɤ-si rca \\
nowadays several-day obj: pcp -see pst. ipfv -not.exist lnk ifr -die sfp \\
`[We] haven't seen him for several days, he probably died.' (150827 mengjiangnv-zh)
0006290#S154
exe

exe

tɕe kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe, nɤki, tɯ-tɯpɯ raŋri ɣɯ nɯ-kʰa nɯtɕu kʰɤβɣa pjɤ-tu rca. \\
lnk former.times lnk filler one-household each gen 3pl. poss -house dem: loc hand.mill ifr. ipfv -exist sfp \\
`In former times, there used to be handmills in every house, presumably (now they have disappeared).' (160705 khABGa)
0006207#S23
exe

High degree of certainty can be indicated by ko, which can be translated as `indeed, certainly' ( ex:mWjpe.ko, ex:mWjtWntCHWG.ko ).

exe

mŋɤm mɤ-mŋɤm mɤ-xsi ri, kú-wɣ-rtoʁ ndɤre mɯ́j-pe ko. \\
hurt: fact neg -hurt: fact neg - genr:know lnk ipfv - inv -look lnk neg: sens -be.good sfp \\
`I don't know whether [leprosy] hurts or not, but in any case it does not look good indeed.' (25-khArWm) 0003644#S53
exe

exe

wo, nɤki, ɲɯ-tɯ-ɕqraʁ ko, mɯ́j-tɯ-naχtɕɯɣ, nɤ-wa nɯ mɯ́j-tɯ-ntɕʰɯɣ ko. \\
interj filler sens -2-be.intelligent sfp neg: sens -2-be.identical 2sg. poss -father dem neg: sens -2-soil sfp \\
`You are really intelligent, you are not a common man, you are your father's son indeed.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S119
exe

Low degree of certainty on the other hand can be marked by ma and matɕi. They are particularly common with the defective verb mɤ-xsione does not know (§ sec:irregular.transitive ). Their scope is on the complement clause(s) of this verb as in ( ex:mAxsi.matCi ) (see also ex:kunWphAn.mWkunWphAn, § sec:dubitative ).

exe

kɤ-mto a-pɯ-kɯ-cʰa tɕe nɯnɯ wuma ʑo pe tu-ti-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl.
tɕeri ŋu maʁ mɤ-xsi matɕi. \\
inf -see irr - ipfv - genr:S/O-can lnk dem really emph be.good: fact ipfv -say- pl sens -be.usually.the.case lnk be: fact not.be: fact neg - genr:know sfp \\
`People say that if you succeed in finding it, it is very good [against poison], but I don't know if it is true or not.' (22-kuwu)
0003592#S43
exe

Additionally, ma is often found with verbs in the Probabilitative (§ sec:WmA ) or the Rhetorical Interrogative (§ sec:WBrA ) prefixes, as in ( ex:WmAkWNuci.ma ) and ( ex:WBrAYWjmWta.ma ).

exe

ɲɯ-mbri ɯmɤ-kɯ-ŋu-ci ma. \\
sens -make.noise prob - peg -be- peg sfp \\
`It looks like [my phone] is ringing.' (160630 aba-zh) 0006197#S95
exe

exe
summary: Epistemic modality in Japhug is expressed not only by verbal morphology but also by sentence-final elements, notably the grammaticalized noun ɯ-mdoʁ and the particles tʰaŋ, rca, ma, and matɕi. The passage describes tʰaŋ as a borrowed particle meaning ‘maybe/probably,’ used mainly with the Factual Non-Past for probable future events, uncertain statements, conditional results, and even possibly undesirable outcomes; it can also occur with other TAME categories. By contrast, rca marks high probability or ‘presumably,’ while ma and matɕi mark low certainty, especially with the verb ‘not know,’ and ma also appears with probabilitative or rhetorical-interrogative forms.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
li ɯβrɤ-ɲɯ-jmɯt-a ma. \\
again rh. q - ipfv -forget- 1sg sfp \\
`I might forget again (some details of the story that I am about to tell again).' (160704 poucet4-v2) 0006097#S1
exe

The particle kɯma results from the fusion of this dubitative ma with the interrogative kɯ (§ sec:fsp.interrog ).

It is possible that these particles originate from the causal linkers ma and matɕibecause (§ sec:causal.clauses ), and that their use as dubitative particles arose from an elided causal clause (`I don't know whether it is true or not because...') or justification clause (§ sec:justification.clauses ) (`It looks like... since').
summary: The passage gives an example of the dubitative particle **ma**, which marks uncertainty in a statement such as “I might forget again.” It also notes that **kɯma** is a fusion of this dubitative **ma** with the interrogative **kɯ**. The text further suggests that these particles may have originated from causal linkers, perhaps first used in elided causal or justification clauses before developing into dubitative markers.

chapter: Expressive words and sentence final particles
text:
speaker attitude
The particles described in this section have meanings that are not easily classifiable into any of the previous categories, but some of which contribute to express modality.

The particle nɯ, sometimes realized as nɤ, occurs in exclamative sentences, in particular with degree nominals (§ sec:degree.monoclausal ) and exclamative nouns (§ sec:exclamative.IPN ).

exe

nɯ ɯ-tʰoʁ nɯra nɯ-kʰi nɯ ɣe, nɯ-tɯ-scit nɯ! \\
dem 3sg. poss -ground dem: pl 3pl. poss -luck sfp sfp 3pl. poss -2-be.happy sfp \\
`The people on earth (`on the ground'), how lucky they are, right? How happy there are!' (150828 donglang)
0006312#S26
exe

The particle ja is used to express regret that the action in the clause has taken place ( ex:mWpWmda.ja ).

exe

pɤjkʰu hanɯni ci nɯ ma-tɤ-tɯ-fse pɯ-ra ja, hanɯni ci mɯ-pɯ-mda ja ri \\
still a.little indef dem neg - imp -2-be.like pst. ipfv -be.needed sfp
a.little indef neg - pst. ipfv -be.the.time sfp lnk \\
`What a shame, if you could just have [waited] a little bit [before] doing that, the time was not yet ready.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

The function of lo / loβ is more difficult to pinpoint. It can serve as a marker of low degree of certainty ( ex:GAZu.loB ) and as a rhetorical interrogative (in particular the form loβtɕi, § sec:fsp.interrog )

exe

ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ nɯ kɯtʂɤ-ldʑa jamar ɣɤʑu loβ. ma koŋla mɯ-kɤ-rtoʁ-a ri, ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ nɯra ɲɯ-dɤn \\
3sg. poss -limb dem six-long.object about exist: sens sfp lnk really neg - aor -look- 1sg lnk 3sg. poss -limb dem: pl sens -be.many \\
`It has about six legs, (I think...) I did not have a good look, but in any case it has a lot of legs.' (21-mdzadi) 0003578#S7
exe

It is also found in enumerations (§ sec:noun.enumeration ) on each of the elements (nouns or clauses) in the list ( ex:enumerate.loB ) with a continuative intonation, followed a pause.

exe

ɯ-pi ni ɣɯ fsapaʁ loβ, tɯjpu loβ, ɯ-grɤl kɯ-me ʑo ta-rku-nɯ \\
3sg. poss -elder.sibling du gen cattle sfp flour.based.food sfp 3sg. poss -order sbj: pcp -not.exist emph aor:3 -put.in- pl \\
[Their parents] gave her two elder sisters cattle and food in great quantity.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe
summary:
The particle **nɯ** (also **nɤ**) is used in exclamative sentences, especially with degree nominals and exclamative nouns. The particle **ja** expresses regret that the event in the clause has already happened.  

The function of **lo / loβ** is less clear, but it can mark low certainty, serve as a rhetorical interrogative, and appear in enumerations on each listed item with continuative intonation and a pause.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
Japhug is a verbocentric language: nearly half of this grammar (eleven chapters) is devoted to verbal morphology.

This chapter first presents an overview of the structure of the verb in Japhug, including the prefixal (§ sec:prefixal.chain ) and suffixal (§ sec:suffixes, § sec:peg.circumfix ) chains. The final sections discuss the templatic structure of Japhug verbal morphology (§ sec:templatic.verb ) and word boundaries (§ sec:wordhood.verb ).
summary: Japhug is described as a verbocentric language, with nearly half of the grammar devoted to verbal morphology. This chapter gives an overview of the structure of the Japhug verb, including its prefixal and suffixal chains, and concludes with discussion of the templatic organization of verbal morphology and verb word boundaries.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
prefix!chain
Like other Gyalrongic languages, Japhug has a strongly prefixing verbal morphology. Inflectional and derivational prefixes constitute two different groups with almost no overlap, the latter closer to the verb root, and the former further away from it. For this reason, these two groups are referred to as `outer' and `inner' prefixes. Previous accounts of the Japhug verbal template such as do not clearly distinguish between these two prefixal domains.

Not all prefixes are tautosyllabic; some only comprise a consonant (for instance some allomorphs of the translocative such as ɕ- ), and due to vowel contraction rules (§ sec:contraction, § sec:allomorphy.inv ), some combinations of prefixes merge into a single syllable. The transcription used in this grammar however undoes the effect of vowel merger to bring clarity to the morphological analysis, and avoid a proliferation of portmanteau affixes.
summary: Japhug, like other Gyalrongic languages, has strongly prefixing verbal morphology, with inflectional and derivational prefixes forming two largely separate domains: “outer” prefixes farther from the verb root and “inner” prefixes closer to it. Some prefixes are not full syllables, and vowel contraction can fuse prefix combinations into one syllable, but this grammar’s transcription reverses such mergers to make the morphology clearer and avoid treating these as portmanteau affixes.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
prefix!outer
The template of outer prefixes in finite verb forms is summarized in tab:template.inflectional.pref. It contains six slots, as compared to the four slots in the suffixal chain (§ sec:suffixes ). This table does not represent inner prefixes, which are contained within the `extended verb stem', and discussed below in § sec:inner.prefixal.chain.

The minimal verb form only contains the verb stem without any prefix. The only finite verb forms with empty prefixal slots are the first or third persons (§ sec:intransitive.paradigm ) or 1/3 configurations (§ sec:indexation.mixed, § sec:indexation.non.local ) of the affirmative Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ), as in ( ex:Gi ). All other finite verb forms require the presence of at least one prefix.

exe

ɣi / ɣi-a \\
come: fact come: fact - 1sg \\
`He comes/will come; I (will) come.'
exe

Slot -6 can be filled by the Irrealis a- (§ sec:irrealis.morphology ), the Rhetorical Interrogative ɯβrɤ, the Polar Interrogative ɯ, the Probabilitative ɯmɤ- and the Proximative Aspect jɯ- prefixes (§ sec:proximative ). These prefixes are mutually exclusive.

Slot -5 contains the negative prefixes (§ sec:negation ), which also partially encode TAME. Only one negative prefix can appear in this position; double negation must be expressed with a negative auxiliary (§ sec:double.negation ).

Slot -4 is restricted to the translocative ɕɯ- and cislocative ɣɯ- Associated Motion prefixes (§ sec:am.prefixes ). These two prefixes are mutually exclusive, and also incompatible with motion or manipulation verbs with opposite deixis (§ sec:motion.verbs.AM ).

Slot -3 corresponds to orientation preverbs (§ sec:orientation.preverbs ). It must be filled in all finite forms other than the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:fact.morphology ) and the negative Sensory (§ sec:negation, § sec:sensory.morphology ), and only one preverb is allowed in this position. Xtokavian dialects of Japhug have an additional slot -3$'$ containing the Inferential a- prefix (§ sec:xtokavian.preverbs ) and the Aorist a- (§ sec:indexation.non.local ), but since these two prefixes have merged with the orientation preverbs in Kamnyu Japhug, this slot is not treated as different from -3 in this grammar. Although not an orientation preverb, the Apprehensive ɕɯ- (§ sec:apprehensive ) also appears in slot -3.

Slot -2 includes indexation prefixes, including second person tɯ- (§ sec:intr.23 ), the ta- 1 2 and kɯ- 2 1 portmanteau prefixes (§ sec:indexation.local ) and the generic S/O prefix kɯ- (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ). The prefixal element k(ɯ)- of the peg circumfix (§ sec:peg.circumfix ) is also located in this slot.

Slot -1 comprises the inverse -wɣ (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ) and the Progressive asɯ- (§ sec:progressive.morphology ) prefixes.Tthese two prefixes only appear on transitive verbs, since they are incompatible with morphologically intransitive verbs. This slot is the only one that can be filled by more than one prefix simultaneously, as shown by forms such as pjɤ-k-ɤ́<wɣ>z-nɤjo-ci `he was waiting for him' in ( ex:pjAkAwGznAjoci ) where the inverse -wɣ (see § sec:indexation.non.local and § sec:obviation.saliency on the function of the inverse prefix in this example) is infixed within the -ɤz- allomorph of the Progressive (§ sec:contraction, § sec:progressive.morphology ).

exe

tɕe pjɤ-ɣi tɕe qala kɯ pjɤ$^-3$-k$^-2$- ɤ́< wɣ> z$^-1$-nɤjo-ci tɕe\\
lnk ifr: down -come lnk rabbit erg ifr. ipfv $^-3$- peg $^-2$-< inv > prog $^-1$-wait- peg lnk \\
`[The snow leopard]$_i$ came down. The rabbit was waiting for him$_i$ (there).' (140427 qala cho kWrtsAG) 0003852#S60
exe

In addition, since the autive nɯ- can also be infixed within the progressive (§ sec:autoben.position, § sec:inner.prefixal.chain ), slot -1 actually lies at the border between the inner and outer prefixal domains.

All of these slots can be filled, as in example ( ex:amAGWtAtWwGndza ). Although there are co-occurrence restrictions across slots (for instance, some prefixes in -6 such as the Rhetorical Interrogative ɯβrɤ- are incompatible with the negative prefixes in -5; additional examples are presented in § sec:templatic.verb ), it is possible to build verb forms with nearly any subset of the six prefixal slots of the outer domain.

exe

qapar kɯ nɤʑo a$^-6$-mɤ$^-5$-ɣɯ$^-4$-tɤ$^-3$-tɯ́$^-2$-wɣ$^-1$-ndza \\
dhole erg 2sg irr $^-6$- neg $^-5$- cisl $^-4$- pfv $^-3$-2$^-2$- inv $^-1$-eat \\
`(Let us hope that) the dhole will not come to eat you.' (elicited)
exe

The Sensory Evidential existential verbs ɣɤʑuexist and maŋenot exist are only compatible with the affixes of slot -2 (the second person and generic kɯ- ), but in this case these appear as infixes rather than prefixes (§ sec:intr.person.irregular ). The defective verb kɤtɯpatell cannot take any prefix (§ sec:irregular.transitive ).

Non-finite verb forms follow a similar but slightly different template. As shown in tab:template.nmlz (§ sec:participles ), participles lack the -2 slot, have strong restrictions on the other slots: in -6 only the prospective jɯ- is possible), in -5 only mɤ- or mɯ, in -3 only type A and B preverbs, and in rare cases in -1 only the progressive. Participial prefixes occur between slot -1 and the extended verb stem, and in addition some participle forms take a possessive prefix before slot -6.
summary:
The passage describes the template for outer prefixes in finite Japhug verb forms, which has six slots rather than the four-slot suffixal chain, and notes that the minimal verb form may lack prefixes only in a few finite configurations. It then specifies the contents and constraints of each slot, including mutually exclusive prefixes, co-occurrence restrictions, and the special behavior of slot -1 at the boundary between outer and inner prefixes.  

It also briefly outlines the template for non-finite forms, especially participles, which lack slot -2 and allow only a restricted set of prefixes in the remaining slots, with participial prefixes positioned between slot -1 and the extended verb stem.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
prefix!inner
Unlike outer prefixes, inner prefixes do not follow a rigid template. The sigmatic causative, in particular, can occur recursively (§ sec:sig.caus.other.recursion ) and its relative position vis-a-vis the facilitative (§ sec:facilitative.nWGW ) and reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ) derivations is determined by semantic scope (§ sec:sig.caus.other.derivations ).

fig:map.inner.prefixes represents the possible ways in which most inner prefixes (excluding the autive, the denominal prefixes, the human antipassive, the distributed action derivation and the subject-oriented facilitative) can be combined with each other, excluding cases of lexicalized derivations. Lexicalized derivations do not necessarily follow these ordering rules, see § sec:sig.caus.lexicalized and § sec:autoben.lexicalized. Examples of attested complex forms can be found in the following sections:

itemize
Antipassive rɤ- ( apass ): § sec:antipassive.compatibility
Applicative nɯ(ɣ)- ( appl ): § sec:appl.other.derivations
Sigmatic causative sɯ(ɣ)- ( caus ): § sec:sig.caus.other.derivations
Velar causative ɣɤ- ( caus2 ): § sec:velar.caus.other
Facilitative nɯɣɯ- ( facil ): § sec:facilitative.nWGW
Passive a- ( pass ): § sec:passive.other.derivations
Proprietive sɤ- ( prop ): § sec:proprietive.compatibility
Reflexive ʑɣɤ- ( refl ): § sec:refl.caus, § sec:refl.tropative, § sec:reciprocal.other
Tropative nɤ(ɣ)- ( trop ):
§ sec:tropative.other.construction
itemize

Combinations of more than two inner prefixes are very rare, and mainly involve lexicalized derivations. Examples include asɤmɯmtsʰɯmtsʰɤminform each other(from mtsʰɤmhear) ( ex:ZnasAmWmtshWmtshAmnW2 ), which combines an amɯ- reciprocal, a sigmatic causative, and a reduplicated reciprocal derivations (see further discussion in § sec:sAmW; in ex:ZnasAmWmtshWmtshAmnW2 and following examples, inner prefixes are colored in red and outer prefixes in blue).

exe

ɣurʑa kɯrcat nɯ ʑ-nɯ- a-sɯ-ɤmɯ-mtsʰɯ mtsʰɤm-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
hundred eight dem tral - aor - recip - caus - recip -hear- pl sens -be \\
`[All] one hundred and eight [boys] went and informed each other.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

A common case of non-lexicalized triple derivation is found when a doubly derived verb additionally takes the highly productive autive prefix, as in ( ex:tonWZGACWfkanW ).

exe

to- nɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-fka-nɯ ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
ifr - auto - refl - caus -be.full- pl emph sens -be \\
`They ate to their full.' (huli yu shanying-zh)
exe

The position of the autive prefix is very unusual (§ sec:autoben.position ), and not easily representable in fig:map.inner.prefixes. In non-contracting verb forms (§ sec:contraction ), it occurs on the border between the outer and inner prefixal domain, following the inverse (as shown by example ex:amAGWnWtWwGnWmbi, with all six outer prefixal positions filled) and preceding the reflexive ʑɣɤ- (example ex:tonWZGACWfkanW above, see also § sec:refl.autoben ).

exe

ɯ-ɲɯ-ra nɤ, a-mɤ-ɣɯ-nɯ-tɯ́-wɣ- nɯ-mbi \\
qu - sens -be.needed add irr - neg - cisl - pfv -2- inv - auto -give \\
`If he$_i$ needs it$_j$, then he$_i$ does not have to come and give it$_j$ to you (if he does not want to).' (elicited)
exe

In the case of contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction ), the autive is however inserted after the a- element (§ sec:autoben.position ), even in verbs such as atɤrfall ( ex:pjAnWtAr ) where it is not analyzable as a prefix synchronically -- the autive is thus infixed within the verb stem.

exe

ɯʑo pjɯ-ɤ< nɯ>tɤr mɤ-cʰa. \\
3sg ipfv -< auto >fall neg -can: fact \\
`It cannot fall (detach) on its own (as its sticks on the clothes).' (18-qromJoR) 0003532#S171
exe

In addition, the autive is infixed within the progressive asɯ- (§ sec:autoben.position, § sec:allomorphy.inv, § sec:progressive.morphology ), stranded between the outer and inner domain, as shown by ( ex:konWsWndzaj ). The autive is also infixed when used with the Sensory existential verbs (§ sec:intr.person.irregular, § sec:autoben.position ).

exe

ɕa ʁɟa ʑo ku-o< nɯ> sɯ-ndza-j \\
meat completely emph prs - prog < auto >-eat- 1pl \\
`We are eating only meat.' (2003 kandZislama)
exe

While most of the prefixes in the inner domain follow a layered structure, the position of the autive, which is determined by phonology and morphology rather than semantics, is clearly templatic (, § sec:templatic.verb ).
summary: Inner prefixes generally do not follow a rigid template, unlike outer prefixes; instead, their ordering is often determined by semantic scope, and some, such as the sigmatic causative, can recur recursively. Most inner prefixes can combine in layered ways, but combinations of more than two are rare and usually occur only in lexicalized or highly productive forms; by contrast, the autive prefix has an exceptional position governed by phonology and morphology rather than semantics.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
prefix!stress stress
Unlike most Gyalrong languages (,, ), Japhug lacks tonal alternations, and stress retraction is very rare. Stress is located by default on the last syllable of the verb stem (all suffixes from slots +1 to +4, are unstressed, § sec:suffixes ), and stress retraction only occurs with three prefixes: the inverse -wɣ (slot -1, § sec:allomorphy.inv ), the negative sensory mɯ́j- (slot -5, § sec:neg.allomorphs ) and the interrogative ɯ- (slot -6, § sec:interrogative.W.morpho ).
summary: Japhug, unlike most Gyalrong languages, has no tonal alternations, and stress retraction is very rare. By default, stress falls on the last syllable of the verb stem, while suffixes in slots +1 to +4 are unstressed. Stress retraction occurs only with three prefixes: the inverse -wɣ, the negative sensory mɯ́j-, and the interrogative ɯ-.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
prefix!phonotactic constraints
There are very strong phonotactic contraints on prefixes in Japhug. Of the fifty consonant phonemes that are contrastive in onset position (§ sec:consonant.phonemes ), only ten are attested in inner prefixes (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ): the nasal m and n (but not ŋ and ɲ), the glides j and w, the dental and alveolo-patalal fricatives ( s, z, ɕ and ʑ), the rhotic r (but not the lateral l) and the velar spirant ɣ (but not its uvular counterpart ʁ). The vowels of the inner prefixes are limited to a, ɯ and ɤ. Outer prefixes (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) other than person indexation (§ sec:intr.23 ) and orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) show the same restriction.

Person indexation prefixes (second person tɯ, generic kɯ- and the portmanteau ta- and kɯ, § sec:intr.23, § sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history ), are exclusively built from two unvoiced unaspirated stops, k and t. This characteristic is shared with a subgroup of non-finite verb forms (§ sec:velar.nmlz.history, § sec:dental.nmlz.history ).

Orientation preverbs stand out among prefixes in allowing aspirated stops, palatal and labial stops, the lateral l- and the palatal nasal (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs, § sec:khWti ), as well as the vowels u and o, which suggest a more recent grammaticalization (§ sec:preverbs.adverbs, ).
summary:
Japhug has very strong phonotactic restrictions on prefixes: among the many consonants contrastive in onset position, only ten occur in inner prefixes, and prefixal vowels are limited to a, ɯ, and ɤ. Outer prefixes show the same restriction except for person indexation prefixes and orientation preverbs.

Person indexation prefixes are made only of the unvoiced unaspirated stops k and t, a pattern shared with some non-finite verb forms. By contrast, orientation preverbs allow a wider range of consonants and the vowels u and o, which suggests a more recent grammaticalization.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
suffix!chain
Japhug has four inflectional suffixal slots, fewer than the six slots of the outer prefixal domain (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ). tab:template.suff presents the suffixal template.

Slot +1 only contains the -t suffix found in 1sg 3 and 2sg 3 of the Aorist, Inferential, Past Imperfective and Apprehensive (§ sec:other.TAME ) of the transitive paradigm (§ sec:indexation.mixed ). It can only be added on open syllable verb stems. It can only be followed by the 1sg -a indexation suffix. The form -t is only found in the dialects of Ercha, Kamnyu and Mangi, all dialects east of Rqakyo (including all Xtokavian dialects) have -z instead. A sound change *-s -t seems to have occurred in Kamnyu, but its conditioning is unclear. This suffix is cognate to the suffix -z in Zbu, which also occurs in 3sg forms.

Slot +2 corresponds to the first person indexation prefixes 1sg -a, 1du -tɕi and 1pl -ji (§ sec:intr.1, § sec:indexation.mixed ).

Slot +3 comprises the second and third person dual -ndʑi and plural -nɯ indexation suffixes (§ sec:intr.23 ). This slot cannot be filled if a non-singular first person suffix occurs in slot +2, and only contains at most one suffix. As a result of the second constraint, in 3$ $3 and 2$ $3 configurations, it is not possible to index the number of both arguments. As shown in § sec:double.number.indexation, these constraints are morphological and cannot be accounted for by purely phonological rules.

Slot +4 is restricted to the suffixal element -ci of the peg circumfix, which always occur in combination with the prefixal element k(ɯ)- in slot -2, and can be elided (§ sec:peg.circumfix ).

When no stress-bearing prefix is present (§ sec:stress.prefixal.chain ), the stress invariably falls on the last syllable of the verb stem. The prefixal slots +2 to +4 are always unstressed, and their vowel can become unvoiced (§ sec:stress ).

Combinations of 1du / 1pl -tɕi / -j (slot +2) with third or second dual or plural -ndʑi/-nɯ (slot +3) suffixes are prohibited (§ sec:double.number.indexation ): for instance, $ $ pɯ-mto-tɕi-nɯ ( aor -see- 1du - pl, intended meaning: `The two of us saw them') is categorically rejected. The only possible form is pɯ-mto-tɕi ( aor -see- 1du ), with neutralization of the number of the object.

The only verb forms where slots +1, +2 and +3 are filled are the Aorist or Inferential 1sg 3 du/pl, as in ( ex:pWmtotandZi ). This is the verb form with the highest suffix-to-prefix ration (3/1).

exe

pɯ-mto-t$^+1$-a$^+2$-ndʑi$^+3$\\
aor -see- pst: tr $^+1$- 1sg $^+2$- du $^+3$ \\
`I saw the two of them.' (elicited)
exe

The +4 slot is generally empty, except in two cases: the Inferential of contracting (intransitive) verbs, as in ( ex:tokAlWlAtndZici2 ), and in combination with the ɯmɤ- and ɯβrɤ- modal prefixes (§ sec:peg.circumfix ). In the latter case, it is potentially compatible with transitive verbs in the Aorist, and verb forms such as ( ex:WmApWkWmtoandZici ) with all four suffixal slots filled are acceptable, though no example is found in the corpus.

exe

to-k-ɤlɯlɤt-ndʑi$^+3$-ci$^+4$ \\
ifr - peg -fight- du $^+3$- peg $^+4$ \\
`The two of them fought.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh) 0003886#S179
exe

The maximal suffixal chain as in ( ex:WmApWkWmtoandZici ) can only be built by integrating the circumfix kɯ-...-ci and the modal ɯmɤ- prefix, so that the prefixal chain has at least three elements ( ɯmɤ-pɯ-kɯ- ) constituting four syllables, as compared to the suffixal chain which contains four elements ( -t-a-ndʑi-ci ) and three syllables (4/3 suffix-to-prefix ratio).

exe

ɯmɤ-pɯ-kɯ-mto-t$^+1$-a$^+2$-ndʑi$^+3$-ci$^+4$ \\
prob - aor - peg -see- pst: tr $^+1$- 1sg $^+2$- du $^+3$- peg $^+4$ \\
`It looks like I have seen the two of them.' (elicited)
exe

Stem alternation (§ sec:stem.alternation ) involves in some cases suffixal elements such as -t in stem II (§ sec:stem2; see also § sec:t.free.variation ) and -m in stem III ( (§ sec:stem3 ) which are not considered as part of this suffixal template. However, even if one were to analyze those elements as separate suffixes, they would occupy slot +1: the -t Past Tense transitive suffix and stem III are mutually incompatible, and in any case -t can only surface if the preceding verb stem has an open syllable. Moreover, evidence from bipartite verbs (§ sec:bipartite ), in particular example ( ex:mAtWspe2 ) suggests that stem III is not suffixal.

Derivational suffixes are very rare in Japhug, and only found in a handful of lexicalized examples such as the -t applicative (§ sec:applicative.t, § sec:antipassive.t ). Since applicative suffix generates a closed syllable stem (for instance ɣɯtbring from ɣicome), this suffix and the transitive Past tense -t suffix are mutually incompatible, and no verb form has more than four suffixes, even counting frozen morphology.

All of the suffixes presented in tab:template.suff occur in finite verb forms. Non-finite verbs in Japhug cannot take any suffix (§ sec:participles ).

Japhug clearly is a strongly prefixing language: it is possible to reach seven to even potentially nine prefixes in a single verb form by combining the six slots of the outer prefixal domain (§ sec:prefixal.chain ) with one to three prefixes of the inner domain (see for instance ex:amAGWnWtWwGnWmbi ), while four suffixes is the upper limit for the suffixal domain.
summary:
Japhug has four inflectional suffixal slots, and the suffixal domain is much smaller than the prefixal domain. Slot +1 contains a transitive -t/-z suffix in certain TAM forms, slot +2 has first-person indexation suffixes, slot +3 has dual/plural suffixes for second and third person, and slot +4 is reserved for the -ci element of the peg circumfix.  

The language places several restrictions on these suffixes: some combinations are impossible, especially when a first-person non-singular suffix in slot +2 would conflict with dual/plural marking in slot +3, and the fullest suffixal chains are rare. The passage concludes that Japhug is strongly prefixing, since verbs can have many more prefixes than suffixes, and non-finite verbs take no suffixes.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text: circumfix!peg
summary: The passage appears to be an incomplete or malformed fragment rather than a full discussion. It does not provide enough information to summarize any linguistic facts or arguments.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
The peg circumfix kɯ-...-ci comprises a prefixal element k(ɯ)- inserted in slot -2 of the outer domain (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ), and a suffixal element -ci, which appears last in the suffixal chain, after all indexation suffixes, as shown by ( ex:mWYAkAtWGnWci ).

exe

ndʑi-ɣi ra, nɯni mɯ-ɲɤ- k-ɤtɯɣ-nɯ- ci \\
3du. poss -relative pl dem: du neg - ifr - peg -meet- pl - peg \\
`Their relatives did not meet them (again).' (2003 zrAntCW tWrme)
exe
summary: The peg circumfix consists of a prefixal element k(ɯ)- placed in slot -2 of the outer domain and a suffixal element -ci that occurs last in the suffixal chain, after all indexation suffixes. The example shows this circumfix in use in a sentence meaning “Their relatives did not meet them (again).”

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
The -ci element of the circumfix is not always present, and thus in some cases only the peg prefix k- occurs.
Elision of prefixal kɯ- is also found in some rare forms, see ( ex:WmAnWtWnWjmWtci ) below.
Example ( ex:YAkAtWGci.YAkAtWG ) with tail-head linkage (§ sec:tail.head.linkeage ) for instance shows that the Inferential of atɯɣmeet can be either ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci (the most common form) or ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ without the -ci, without change of meaning. In the whole corpus, out of 40 examples of atɯɣmeet in the Inferential, nine lack the -ci suffix.

exe

tɕendi tɕendi tɕe mtsʰu ci ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci. mtsʰu kɯ-ɲɯ ɲaʁ ci ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci. tɕendɤre mtsʰu kɯ-ɲɯ ɲaʁ ci ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ tɕe tɕe, \\
west west loc lake indef ifr - peg -meet- peg lake sbj: pcp - emph be.black indef ifr - peg -meet- peg lnk lake sbj: pcp - emph be.black indef ifr - peg -meet lnk lnk \\
`In the west, he found a lake, he found a lake that was very black. He found a lake that was very black, and...' (28-smAnmi 92-94) 0004063#S87
exe

Forms with the simple prefixal peg k- without -ci are however never found in utterance-final contexts: they are always followed by a linker such as tɕe (§ sec:coordination ), as in ( ex:YAkAtWGci.YAkAtWG ) above, where the two instances of ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci have utterance final intonation and are followed by a pause, while ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ starts a new utterance group.
summary: The circumfixal -ci is sometimes absent, so the form may appear with only the peg prefix k-, and rare forms also show elision of prefixal kɯ-. In the Inferential of atɯɣmeet, both ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci and ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ occur without any change in meaning, though in the corpus 9 of 40 examples lack -ci. However, the simple prefixal form without -ci is never used utterance-finally; it is always followed by a linker such as tɕe.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
The circumfix has two different functions in the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug.

First, it occurs in contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction ) to prevent vowel fusion when a D-type preverb is found before a contracting verb stem or prefix (§ sec:preverbs.contracting.verbs ). In ( ex:mWYAkAtWGnWci ) for instance, without the k- prefixal element, the inferential ɲɤ- would merge with the verb stem atɯɣ as ɲɤtɯɣ, becoming undistinguishable from the corresponding Imperfective ɲɯ-ɤtɯɣ (§ sec:ipfv.morphology ). This function is not found in Xtokavian dialects of Japhug.

Second, the peg circumfix is found together with Rhetorical Interrogative ɯβrɤ- and Probabilitative ɯmɤ- prefixes. In these configurations, the negative prefixes cannot occur, and only type A orientation preverbs (Aorist, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) are possible.

The minimal pair in ( ex:kAtWnWtsxWB.WBrA ) between ɯβrɤ-ŋu and ɯβrɤ-kɯ-ŋu-ci provides an illustration of the semantic function of the circumfix: without it, the Rhetorical Interrogative generally denotes worry/apprehension that the action could take/have taken place ( ex:kAtWnWtsxWB.WBrANu ), while the combination of the Rhetorical Interrogative and the circumfix has the negative epistemic modality value `it seems like $X$ did/does not $Y$' ( ex:kAtWnWtsxWB.WBrAkWNuci ).

exe

xlist

nɤ-ŋga kɤ-tɯ-nɯ-tʂɯβ ɯβrɤ-ŋu ma \\
2sg. poss -clothes aor -2- auto -sew rh. q - peg -be- peg lnk \\
`You didn't sew your garment, did you? (worried that the subject might have sewed his/her garment)' (elicited)

nɤ-ŋga kɤ-tɯ-nɯ-tʂɯβ ɯβrɤ- kɯ-ŋu- ci ma ɲɯ-nɯ-spoʁ ɕti \\
2sg. poss -clothes aor -2- auto -sew rh. q - peg -be: fact - peg lnk sens - auto -have.a.hole be. aff: fact \\
`It looks like you haven't sewed your garment, it still has a hole.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

With the Probabilitative ɯmɤ, the use of the circumfix ( ex:WmAjAkWzGWtci ) is associated with a lesser degree of confidence than the corresponding form without it ( ex:WmAjazGWt ). Tshendzin explains the meaning of ( ex:WmAjAkWzGWtci ) with the Inferential ( ex:WmAjakWzGWtci.gloss ).
Note that the Inferential preverbs are not compatible with the Probabilitative prefix (§ sec:WmA ).

exe

xlist

ɯmɤ-jɤ-azɣɯt \\
prob - aor -arrive \\

tʂʰɯɣ jɤ-azɣɯt tʰaŋ\\
probably aor -arrive sfp \\
`He probably has already arrived.' (elicited)

ɯmɤ-jɤ- kɯ-zɣɯt- ci \\
prob - aor - peg -arrive- peg \\

jo-zɣɯt ɯ-mdoʁ \\
ifr -arrive 3sg. poss -colour \\
`It seems that he has probably arrived.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

The minimal pair above shows that the circumfix is not a simple secondary morphological exponent of the Inferential, but has a specific modal and evidential value. However, it is not obvious at this stage that the combination of the circumfix with Rhetorical Interrogative and Possible modality prefixes can be analyzed compositionally at the synchronic level in the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug, and I therefore use the arbitrary gloss `peg' for this formative.

The kɯ- prefixal element competes with indexation prefixes in slot -2 (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ). Since the 2 1 portmanteau kɯ- prefix has the same shape as the peg prefix, transitive verbs can present ambiguity between 2 1 (§ sec:indexation.local ) and 1 3 (§ sec:indexation.mixed ) configurations, as in ( ex:WmAnWkWnWjmWta ), a verb forms with two possible interpretations.

exe

ɯmɤ-nɯ- kɯ-nɯ-jmɯt-a- ci \\
prob - aor - peg /2 1- auto -forget- 1sg - peg \\
`It looks I forgot about it.' ( kɯ- = peg )
`It looks like you have forgotten me.' ( kɯ- = 2 1)
exe

The second person tɯ- and 1 2 portmanteau ta- are dominant in slot -2, and the peg prefixal element kɯ- disappears in 2 3 ( ex:WmAnWtWnWjmWtci ) and 1 2 configurations ( ex:WmApWtamto ).

exe

ɯmɤ-nɯ-tɯ-nɯ-jmɯt- ci \\
prob - aor -2- auto -forget- peg \\
`It looks like you have forgotten about it.' (elicited)
exe

exe

ɯmɤ-pɯ-ta-mto- ci \\
prob - aor -1 2-see- peg \\
`It looks like I have seen you.' (elicited)
exe

The inverse prefix, although located in slot -1, is incompatible with the peg circumfix: both $ $ ɯmɤ-nɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-jmɯt-a-ci ( prob - aor - inv - auto -forget- 1sg - peg ) and $ $ ɯmɤ-nɯ-kɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-jmɯt-a-ci ( prob - aor - peg - inv - auto -forget- 1sg - peg ) are incorrect, and the only way to express this meaning is with the Inferential in combination with the complement-taking noun ɯ-mdoʁ ( ex:YAwGnWjmWta.WmdoR ) (§ sec:WmdoR.TAME ).

exe

ɯʑo kɯ ɲɤ́-wɣ-nɯ-jmɯt-a ɯ-mdoʁ \\
3sg erg ifr - inv - auto -forget- 1sg 3sg. poss -colour \\
`It looks like he has forgotten about me.' (elicited)
exe

Although complex forms such as ( ex:WmAjAkWzGWtci ), ( ex:WmAnWkWnWjmWta ), ( ex:WmAnWtWnWjmWtci ) or ( ex:WmApWtamto ) can be elicited, in the corpus the combination of circumfix with Rhetorical Interrogative or Probabilitative prefixes only occur on stative verbs in 3sg form, and mainly with copulas, existential or modal auxiliaries.

The Japhug -ci suffixal element is probably cognate with the Mediative -cə in Tshobdun and the non-egophoric ki in Zbu, which however have a much larger distribution. The k(ɯ)- prefixal element is relatable to the non-finite kɯ- prefixes (§ sec:velar.nmlz.history ) and some related finite forms (§ sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history ).
summary: The Kamnyu dialect of Japhug has a circumfix with two functions: in contracting verbs, it prevents vowel fusion when a D-type preverb precedes the stem, and this use is absent in Xtokavian dialects. It also appears with Rhetorical Interrogative ɯβrɤ- and Probabilitative ɯmɤ- prefixes, where it blocks negative prefixes, restricts preverb types, and adds a distinct modal/evidential meaning, often indicating that something seems not to have happened or is less certain.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
morphology!templatic morphology!layered
While the inner prefixal domain follows a layered structure (except for the autive prefix, § sec:inner.prefixal.chain ), the outer prefixal chain (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) and the suffixal chain (§ sec:suffixes ) are rather to be described in terms of templatic morphology. Each of the slots in these chains is rigid in the Kamnyu dialect: there is no free affix ordering as in Kiranti languages like Chitang. We observe four specifically templatic features.

First, several non-adjacent dependencies (or mutual incompatibilities) are observed between prefixes, suffixes and stems, reflecting the fact that some TAME categories and person configurations are encoded by formatives in different slots. Some conspicuous examples are listed below.

itemize
Morphological transitivity is encoded by seven independent morphological and redundant features in various slots (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ).
The Aorist is marked by combining A-type orientation preverbs (slot -3, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), Stem II (§ sec:stem2 ) and the past transitive -t (slot +1, § sec:suffixes ).
The Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.morphology ) requires a- in slot -6, a type A preverb in slot -3 and stem III (§ sec:stem3.distribution ) when the person configuration allows it, as in ( ex:aGWtAtWthe ) below.
The peg circumfix (slots -2 and +4, § sec:peg.circumfix ) occurs in conjunction with either some modal prefixes (slot -6) or type D preverbs (slot -3).
Person configuration (direct vs. inverse, § sec:direct-inverse ) is marked by the inverse prefix (slot -1, § sec:allomorphy.inv ), the contrast between stem I and stem III (§ sec:stem3.distribution ) and the past transitive -t (slot +1, § sec:suffixes ). The former is incompatible with the latter two (which occur in complementary distribution).
itemize

Example ( ex:aGWtAtWthe ) illustrates (coloured in red) the non-adjacent dependency between a- (-6), the type A preverb (-3) and stem III.

exe

a-ɣɯ- tɤ-tɯ- tʰe \\
irr - cisl - aor -2-ask [III] \\
`Come and ask [for her hand in marriage].' (150826 liangshanbo zhuyingtai-zh) 0006244#S124
exe

Second, the position of some prefixes in the chain is independent of the semantic scope of the outer prefixes between themselves, and of their scope with regards to the inner prefixes. In particular, the causative prefix, located in the inner domain (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ), has ambiguous scope with the negative (§ sec:sig.caus.negation ) and associated motion prefixes (§ sec:sig.caus.AM ).

Third, the allomorphy of more inwards prefixes is in some cases sensitive to more outward prefixes: for instance, the allomorphy of the inverse (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ) in slot -1 depends on the preceding prefixes: in particular, modal prefixes in slot -6 do not select the same allomorph as the other prefixes.

Fourth, bipartite verbs (§ sec:bipartite ) offer cases of verb forms with more than one head.
summary: The passage argues that, unlike the layered inner prefixal domain, the outer prefixal chain and suffixal chain in the Kamnyu dialect are templatic and rigidly ordered, with no free affix ordering. It highlights four templatic properties: non-adjacent dependencies across slots for categories like transitivity, tense/aspect/mood, and person configuration; scope interactions involving the causative prefix; sensitivity of inward prefix allomorphy to outer prefixes; and bipartite verbs with more than one head.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
word!wordhood
Some languages of the Trans-Himalayan family like Bantawa or Galo present conflicting morphosyntactic and phonological domains  making an unambiguous definition of `words' problematic.

In Japhug, the verb presents several phonological and morphological domains, represented in tab:verbal.complex.domain. Each of the domains is coloured in grey; slots partially included in the domain in certain contexts are represented in light grey.

Domain A represents non-adjacent dependencies: as argued in § sec:templatic.verb, the suffixal element -ci of the peg circumfix in slot +4 (§ sec:peg.circumfix ) is selected by some modal prefixes in slot -6, showing that dependencies across formatives cover the whole verb complex from the beginning of the outer prefixal chain (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) to the end of the suffixal chain (§ sec:suffixes ).

Domain B corresponds to the minimal obligatory free form: the suffixal element -ci is not included because it is optional (§ sec:peg.circumfix ) and the dual and plural suffixes in slot +3 are also optional in specific conditions (§ sec:optional.indexation ).

Domain C indicates the slots that can receive stress. It general is found on the last syllable of the verb stem by default, but some prefixes attract stress (§ sec:stress.prefixal.chain ). Slot -6 receives stress when it is filled by interrogative prefix ɯ́- followed by a monosyllabic verb form (§ sec:factual ), or when the other prefixes merge with the inverse -wɣ. Tautosyllabic suffixes are never stressed (§ sec:suffixes ), but 1sg suffix -a merges with the last syllabe in some cases (§ sec:synizesis ).

Domain D correspond to the prefixal slots selecting the allomorph -wɣ of the inverse prefix when directly followed by it, and able to interact with the contracting vowel of the verb stem (§ sec:contraction ), either by undergoing vowel fusion or by insertion of an epenthetic -j-.

These four domains, to which the extended verb stem (including the inner prefixes, § sec:inner.prefixal.chain ) can be added, are concentric: the domain boundaries do not overlap. In this grammar, domain A is chosen as the verbal word, because in addition to non-adjacent dependencies, all formatives contained within it have a fixed position, and no external element can be inserted.

There are no proclitic markers which could be candidates to be analyzed as prefixes in Japhug. Some enclitic linkers and particles are phonologically attached on the verb, but there is clear evidence that they cannot be analyzed as suffixes (§ sec:verb.enclitics ). Bipartite verbs (§ sec:bipartite ) offer a more serious challenge to the definition of wordhood, but problematic forms are extremely rare and limited.
summary:
In Japhug, the verb contains several concentric phonological and morphological domains, each with different properties: domain A spans long-distance dependencies across the whole verb complex, domain B is the minimal obligatory free form, domain C marks the positions that can bear stress, and domain D includes prefixal slots interacting with the inverse prefix and stem contraction. The grammar identifies domain A as the verbal word because it combines non-adjacent dependencies with fixed internal ordering and excludes external insertion.  

The passage also notes that Japhug has no proclitics that should be treated as prefixes, and that although some enclitic elements attach phonologically to the verb, they are not suffixes. Bipartite verbs pose a potential problem for wordhood, but such forms are rare and limited.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
word!enclitic
Some particles and linkers are cliticized on the verb stem, and could seem to behave as suffixes.

The sentence final particle wo (§ sec:fsp.imp ) is generally a free-standing word, but it can optionally be phonologically attached to the verb as in ( ex:pWfCAto ). In these cases, it bears a stress, possibly analyzable as a effect of intonation.

exe

a-χpi ci pɯ-fɕɤt=ó \\
1sg. poss -story indef imp -tell= sfp \\
`Tell me a story.' (140511 yiqianlingyiye yinzi-zh) 0003963#S30
exe

There are two pieces of evidence showing that =o is not a verbal suffix. First, even in cliticized form, its locus is not specifically the verb, but rather the last word of the sentence: in ( ex:WmdoRo ), =o cliticized on the predicative noun ɯ-mdoʁcolour, `it looks like...' (§ sec:WmdoR.TAME ).

exe

ma qacʰɣa ɣɯ ɯ-me pjɤ-ɕti ɯ-mdoʁ=o. \\
lnk fox gen 3sg. poss -daughter ifr. ipfv -be. aff 3sg. poss -colour= sfp \\
`It looks like she (the main character of the story) was the daughter of a fox.' (150909 xiaocui-zh) 0006386#S161
exe

Second, wo actually occurs last in the chain of sentence final particles. It follows for instance the hearsay particle kʰi in ( ex:YWphAn.khi.wo ),

exe

<aizheng> ɲɯ-pʰɤn kʰi wo\\
cancer sens -be.efficient hearsay sfp \\
`It can cure cancer, it is said.' (20-grWBgrWB) 0003554#S68
exe

This hearsay particle is never phonologically cliticized on the verb, and moreover can be separated from the verb by the emphatic particle ʑo (§ sec:degree.adverbs ), as in ( ex:saXaR.Zo.khi ).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-ɣɤndʐo saχaʁ ʑo kʰi. \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.cold be.extremely: fact emph hearsay \\
`It is said that [during an eclipse], it is extremely cold.' (29-mWBZi) 0003728#S104
exe

The additive linker nɤ occurs in additive repetition (§ sec:distributed.action ) and in conditionals (§ sec:real.conditional ). It is always an enclitic, as indicated by the vowel ɤ, which can never stressed in word-final position in Japhug (§ sec:vowels ). Were nɤ analyzed as a suffix, an additional +5 slot would be necessary, since it can follow the -ci suffixal element, as in ( ex:tokAtChWzci ).

exe

to-kɯ-ɤtɕʰɯz-ci=nɤ to-kɯ-ɤtɕʰɯz-ci \\
ifr - peg -sneeze- peg = add ifr - peg -sneeze- peg \\
`He sneezed again and again.' (140515 jiesu de laoren-zh) 0004004#S132
exe

In conditional constructions, this linker co-occurs with initial reduplication (§ sec:redp.protasis, § sec:real.conditional ). However, although nɤ is the most common linker on the protasis on conditionals, it is not required, and other linkers such as tɕe are also attested, as in ( ex:tWtAtWtWt.tCe ), and there is no strict non-adjacent dependency between nɤ and reduplication (§ sec:wordhood.criteria.verb ).

exe

nɯ tɯ tɤ-tɯ-tɯt tɕe qʰe tɕe rcanɯ nɤʑo rdɤstaʁ ɲɯ-tɯ-ɤβzu \\
dem cond aor -2-say[II] lnk lnk lnk unexp: deg 2sg stone ipfv -2-become \\
`If you tell [them] about it, you will be turned into stone and...' (150902 hailibu-zh)
0006316#S81
exe

In additive function, nɤ is not specific to verbs (§ sec:additive.nA ), and the emphatic ʑo can be inserted between the verb and this linker ( ex:jari.Zo.nA ).

exe

tɕendɤre jɤ-ari nɤ jɤ-ari ʑo nɤ \\
lnk aor -go[II] add aor -go[II] emph add \\
`He went again and again.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

For these reasons, nɤ is not analyzed as a part of the verbal word in Japhug.
summary: The passage argues that some particles and linkers can attach phonologically to verbs and look like suffixes, but they are not actually verbal suffixes. The sentence-final particle =o can attach to the last word of a sentence, not specifically to verbs, and the additive linker nɤ is always an enclitic that can follow suffixal material and occur outside the verbal word. For these reasons, neither =o nor nɤ is analyzed as part of the verbal word in Japhug.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
word!bipartite verbs verb!bipartite indexation!bipartite
Bipartite verbs comprise two morphologically active stems, which despite having affixes of their own are combined together in one phonological word, sharing in some cases whole prefixal or suffixal chains. Following the Kirantological tradition (for instance or ), the first verb stem is referred to as $V_1$, and the second one as $V_2$.

The main features of bipartite conjugation can be explained using stu=mbattry hard, `do one's best', the most common bipartite verb. This verb has four possible conjugation patterns, illustrated in tab:bipartite.ABCD imperative second dual form `try hard (the two of you)', which contains one prefix (orientation preverb, slot -3, § sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) and one suffix (indexation suffix, slot +3, § sec:suffixes ).

Type A bipartite verbs are lexicalized serial verb constructions (§ sec:svc ): the two verb stems are not phonologically integrated, and each of them takes both prefixes and suffixes. No word can be inserted between stu and mbat in the corpus, unlike other examples of SVC in Japhug. This is however not the case with all bipartite verbs. For instance, in the case of fse=raŋhappen so many things, it is possible to repeat the subject, as in ( ex:fse.rang ).

exe

nɯra pɯ-fse nɯra pɯ-raŋ\\
dem: pl pst. ipfv -be.like dem: pl pst. ipfv -last.a.long.time \\
`All these things happened.' (many attestations of this sentence, occurs in traditional stories typically to avoid repeating sentences when a character tells another character what has happened previously)
exe

In types B and C, the two conjugated verb forms merge phonologically, and either the suffixal chain of the first verb (in the case of the right-dominant B type, where the $V_1$ has a reduced form and the $V_2$ preserves the full form) or the prefixal chain of the second one (left-dominant) are removed. For instance, in ( ex:atAtWstunatAtWmbatndZi ) the right-dominant bipartite verb has only one dual suffix -ndʑi $^+3$ on the $V_2$, while the prefixal chain a$^-6$-tɤ$^-3$-tɯ$^-2$ ( irr - pfv -2) is repeated on both the $V_1$ and the $V_2$. The boundary between the $V_1$ and the $V_2$, transcribed with a clitic sign =, does not conform to the phonological rules of word-internal morpheme boundaries: for instance, no vowel contraction occurs between the Irrealis a- and the preceding -u in ( ex:atAtWstunatAtWmbatndZi ), either as u-a $ $ o (§ sec:contraction ) or u-a $ $ wa (§ sec:intr.1 ). In addition, this bipartite verb form has two stresses, one on each verb stem.

exe

a-tɤ-tɯ-stu= a-tɤ-tɯ-mbat- ndʑi \\
irr - pfv - 2 -try.hard(1)= irr - pfv - 2 -try.hard(2)- du \\
`(While I am gone), may the two of you do your best.' (smanmi 2003.2)
exe

The prefixal chain must be complete: a partial copy such as $ $ a-tɤ-tɯ-stu=tɯ-mbat-ndʑi with only the second person tɯ- prefix on the $V_2$ is categorically rejected. Likewise, in left-dominant bipartite verbs, the suffixal chain has to be complete on both the $V_1$ and the $V_2$. This specificity is by no means universal even in Trans-Himalayan: in Kiranti languages for instance, the $V_1$ generally only preserves a sub-set of the suffixal chain, as illustrated by the Bantawa example ( ex:kharin ) below, where the chain -in-ka occurs in reduced form -in on the $V_1$ kʰat- `go'.

exe

kʰar- in lont- in-ka \\
go- 1/2pl come.out- 1/2pl-excl \\
`We shall rise again.' 
exe

In type D, the two verbs come to share the same prefixal and suffixal chain, with no intervening affix between the two verb stems.

tab:bipartite summarizes all bipartite verbs discovered up to now in Japhug. Type C conjugation is only attested with stu=mbat. In Kiranti languages, by contrast, right-dominant bipartite verbs (with partial suffixal chain on the $V_1$, as in ex:kharin ) are by far the most common option. Question marks indicate that the forms in question are only attested in a few non-finite forms.

The important proportion of Tibetan loanwords in this list is particularly noteworthy: =raŋ, zdɯɣ=sŋɤl, ntsʰɤβ=, rga=, are from རིང་riŋlong, སྡུག་བསྔལ་sdug.bsŋaltorment, འཚབ་ⁿtsʰabanxious, དགའ་dgaglad, respectively.

Bipartite verbs cannot be easily subjected to verbal derivations. The only example that could be elicited is the tropative verb (§ sec:tropative ) nɤ-stu-mbat `consider that X tries hard'. Only the quasi-compound form of the bipartite verb can be derived. The derivational prefix nɤ- cannot be repeated on the $V_1$ and the $V_2$ (a form such as $ $ nɤ-stu=nɤ-stu is incorrect).

There is only one bipartite transitive verb, neg +spa= neg +rka=tu/mebe guilty/innocent, which is actually even tripartite, since its always occur with an existential verb. It means `be guilty' when used with the affirmative existential verb tuexist and `be innocent' with the negative one menot exist (§ sec:suppletive.negative ). The $V_1$ and $V_2$ require a negative prefix (§ sec:obligatory.negative ). Both type A ( ex:mAtWspe1, ex:mAspanW.mArkAnW.kWme ) and type D ( ex:mAtWsparkandZi ) conjugations are attested. The existential verb is always an independent word, and never takes person/number indexation in this collocation.

exe

mɤ-tɯ-spe mɤ-tɯ-rke me \\
neg -2-be.innocent(1)[III]: fact neg -2-be.innocent(2)[III]: fact not.exist: fact \\
`You$_sg$ are innocent.' (elicited)
exe

exe

mɤ-tɯ-spa=rka-ndʑi me \\
neg -2-be.innocent(1)-be.innocent(2): fact - du not.exist: fact \\
`You$_du$ are innocent.' (elicited)
exe

The verb stems spa and rka are always in finite form: only the existential verb takes non-finite prefixes. In ( ex:mAspanW.mArkAnW.kWme ) the subject participle prefix kɯ- occurs on the negative existential me, while spa and rka are found in Factual Non-Past. This example suggests that spa and rka are located in a subject complement clause selected by the existential verb (§ sec:existential.basic ).

exe

[mkʰɤrmaŋ [mɤ-spa-nɯ mɤ-rka-nɯ] kɯ-me] nɯ ʑimkʰɤm pjɤ-sɯ-sat pjɤ-ra rcanɯ, tɯrme ra kɯ wuma ʑo pjɤ-qʰa-nɯ \\
people neg -be.innocent(1): fact - pl neg -be.innocent(2): fact - pl sbj: pcp -not.exist dem a.lot ifr - caus -kill ifr. ipfv -be.needed unexpected man pl erg really emph ifr -hate- pl \\
`As he had to have many innocent people killed, people hated him.' (hist140514 xiee de shewang-zh)
0003994#S76
exe
summary:
Bipartite verbs in Japhug consist of two morphologically active stems, V1 and V2, that form a single phonological word and may share prefixal or suffixal material. The passage distinguishes four conjugation types: type A, where both stems keep their own affixes; types B and C, where the two stems merge phonologically and one affixal chain is reduced; and type D, where both stems share the same prefixal and suffixal chains.

The best-known bipartite verb is *stu=mbat* ‘do one’s best’, and the text notes that bipartite verbs are difficult to derive, with only a tropative derivative attested for this class. It also describes a single bipartite transitive verb, *spa=rka* ‘be guilty/innocent’, which behaves tripartitely with an existential verb and requires negative marking on both stems.

chapter: The structure of the Japhug verb
text:
Although morphologically transitive (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ), as shown by the presence of stem III alternation in sg $ $3 non-past forms (§ sec:stem3.form ), in examples ( ex:mAtWspe1 ) and ( ex:mAspea ), the direct object is dummy and cannot be overt.

exe

mɤ-spe-a mɤ-rke-a me \\
neg -be.innocent(1)[III]: fact - 1sg neg -be.innocent(2)[III]: fact - 1sg not.exist: fact \\
`I am innocent.' (elicited)
exe

Example ( ex:mAtWspe2 ), where both spa and rka are in stem III form ( spe= and =rke, respectively) reveals two facts about type D conjugation. First, stem III alternation, although historically partially suffixal in origin (§ sec:stem3.form ), is synchronically disjunct from the suffixal chain. Second, although type D forms could appear at first glance to be simple compound verbs (§ sec:denom.compound.verbs ), the presence of stem alternation on both $V_1$ and $V_2$, instead of having $ $ mɤ-tɯ-spa-rke with alternation on the $V_2$ only, shows that the two verb roots are still morphologically active.

exe

mɤ-tɯ-spe=rke me \\
neg -2-be.innocent(1)[III]-be.innocent(2)[III]: fact not.exist: fact \\
`You$_sg$ are innocent.' (elicited)
exe
summary: The passage says that although these forms are morphologically transitive, their direct object is a dummy argument that cannot be overtly expressed. It also shows that type D conjugation involves stem III alternation that is synchronically separate from the suffixal chain, and that both verb roots remain morphologically active rather than forming a simple compound verb.

text:
While Japhug lacks tonal alternations like most Gyalrongic languages, non-concatenative segmental alternations are common.

This chapter briefly presents derivation onset alternations (§ sec:onset.alternations ), and then provides a detailed account of inflectional stem alternations (§ sec:stem.alternation ), vowel contraction (§ sec:contraction ) and partial reduplication (§ sec:redp.verb ) in verbal morphology.
summary: Japhug does not have tonal alternations like most other Gyalrongic languages, but it does show common non-concatenative segmental alternations. The chapter first introduces derivational onset alternations and then gives a more detailed discussion of inflectional stem alternations, vowel contraction, and partial reduplication in verbal morphology.

text:
consonant!alternation
While most of the prefixal derivation morphology in Japhug is fairly concatenative, a handful of prefixal morphological processes involve consonantal alternations.

Prenasalization is found in the anticausative (§ sec:anticausative ) and a handful of frozen verb forms (§ sec:fossil.prenasalization, § sec:caus.Z ). In all cases, it is probably the result of the fusion of a nasal prefix with an unvoiced stop/affricative, turning it into the corresponding voiced prenasalized obstruent (§ sec:anticausative.direction ).

Another type of consonant alternation is the β- b- fortition in the causative verb zbraʁattach together (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ).
summary: Although Japhug prefixal derivation is mostly concatenative, some prefixal processes involve consonant alternations. These include prenasalization in the anticausative and a few frozen verb forms, which is likely due to fusion of a nasal prefix with an unvoiced stop or affricate, and a β- to b- fortition seen in the causative verb zbraʁ ‘attach together’.

text:
vowel!alternation stem alternation
Northern Gyalrong languages have three verbal stems, labeled I, II and III following (Situ dialects lack stem III, but some varieties have additional stems I' and II', see ). Stem I is the default form, stem II mainly occurs in Aorist and Past Imperfective, and stem III occurs in the Non-Past sg 3 direct forms of some transitive verbs (§ sec:indexation.mixed ).

In Japhug, no verb has more than two different stems. Stem II is different from stem I in only a handful of irregular verbs (§ sec:stem2 ), while stem III has been regularized (§ sec:stem3 ).
summary: Northern Gyalrong languages generally have three verbal stems: stem I as the default form, stem II mainly in the Aorist and Past Imperfective, and stem III in certain Non-Past singular third-person direct forms of some transitive verbs. In Japhug, however, no verb has more than two stems; stem II differs from stem I only in a small set of irregular verbs, and stem III has been regularized.

text:
Unlike in Tshobdun, Zbu  and Situ, stem II in Japhug is very limited, and only found in three irregular verbs and in a few derivations from them ( tab:stem2 ).

The ɣi/ɣe alternation has an exact correlate in Tshobdun ( wi/wɛʔ, ). The verb tisay has an irregular correspondence with other Gyalrong languages, where an affricate onset is found (Tshobdun ´tsə `say',, Situ tsə̂, tsīs, ). In Zbu however, a unique alternation between affricate and stop is found in this verb (stem I ´tsʰə, stem II ´tʰit, ). The correspondence between the Japhug stem II -tɯt and its Zbu equivalent ´tʰit is regular (apart from the aspiration). The irregular paradigm of this verb in Zbu certainly has to be reconstructed to proto-Gyalrong. Situ and Tshobdun have generalized the affricate to stem II, while Japhug has remade the stem I by generalizing the dental stop.

Suppletion is observed in the paradigm of ɕego, whose stem II -ari is perhaps related to the stem I of the verb `go' found in some dialects of Zbu ( rî, ). Xtokavian dialects of Japhug have tʰɐl as the stem II of this verb, a form borrowed from Tibetan ཐལ་tʰalgo beyond, pass.

The transitive verb sɯxɕesend, `let go' is the causative of ɕego, and its stem II presents an irregular vowel merger sɯɣ+ari $ $ sɤɣri, instead of expected $ $ sɤri or $ $ asɯɣri (§ sec:caus.sAG ). Other derivations from ɕego also have suppletion, but the alternations are regular. The autive and the vertitive nɯ- prefixes (§ sec:autobenefactive, § sec:vertitive ) in nɯ-ɕe `go by oneself'/`go back' are predictably infixed (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ) within the stem II ari as a<nɯ>ri (see examples ex:Wrte.YAnWBde2 in § sec:autoben.lexicalized and ex:tWZo.kW in § sec:genr.pro ). the distributed action derivation nɤɕɯɕego around likewise has the expected reduplicated stem -anɤrɯri.

The verb nɯɣicome back, vertitive of ɣicome, shows the expected stem II nɯɣe with vowel alternation. Its lexicalized causative sɯɣeinvite on the other hand, has lost stem alternation, but appears to have generalized stem II (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ).
summary: Japhug has a very restricted stem II system, unlike Tshobdun, Zbu, and Situ, where it is more extensive: in Japhug it occurs only in three irregular verbs and a few derivatives. The passage describes several irregular paradigms and correspondences with other Gyalrong languages, including *tisaye* and *ɕego*, showing cases of suppletion, borrowed forms, and regular or irregular stem alternations. It also notes that some derivatives preserve expected alternations or infixation, while others have generalized stem II forms or lost alternation altogether.

text:
Xtokavian
In Japhug, stem II is mainly found in the Aorist (§ sec:aor.morphology ) and in the Apprehensive (§ sec:apprehensive.morphology ). The verb tisay also has stem II tɯt in the irregular Progressive Sensory form ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-tɯt, ɲɯ-ɤs-tɯt `he is/was saying' (§ sec:sensory.morphology ). In Zbu, stem II is also found in the Progressive (, ).

Unlike Stem III (§ sec:stem3.distribution ), Stem II is insensitive to person and number in all known Gyalrong languages.
summary: In Japhug, stem II is mainly used in the Aorist and Apprehensive, and the verb *tisay* also shows stem II *tɯt* in the irregular Progressive Sensory form meaning ‘he is/was saying.’ In Zbu, stem II also appears in the Progressive. Unlike Stem III, Stem II does not vary according to person or number in any known Gyalrong languages.

text:
In the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug, stem III is fully regular, and applies to all transitive verbs with an open syllable stem ending in a non-front vowel in the expected contexts (§ sec:stem3.distribution ).

As presented in tab:stem3, two types of alternations are attested: (i) vowel fronting in the case of stems in -a, -u, -ɯ and (ii) -m suffixation with vowel unrounding for stems in -o. In Xtokavian dialects, the alternations are less predictable, as some verbs in -u and -ɯ can take the -m suffix (, ). Kamnyu, by comparison, has regularized the alternations by analogical levelling. A cognate suffix -m in stem III is also attested in Zbu.
analogy!stem alternation

Stem III in -ɤm undergoes regular vowel assimilation to -am- when followed by a 1sg -a suffix (§ sec:intr.1 ). For instance, the 1sg 3sg Factual Non-Past of mtosee is mtam-a `I (will) see it/him/her' rather than $ $ mtɤm-a. Stem III with the fronted vowel -e change to -i when followed by -a: ndze-a `I (will) eat it' is realized as ndzia.

Vowel fronting in stem III originates from the fusion of the verb stem with a *-j suffix (§ sec:historical.phono,, ), cognate to the ``transitivity marker'' -jə in Tshobdun.

Rather than analyzing the -m suffix as a part of the stem III, it could alternatively be possible to view it as part of the suffixal chain. Under such an analysis, it would be located in slot +1 (§ sec:suffixes ). Bipartite verbs provide evidence against such an analysis however (§ sec:bipartite ).
summary:
In the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug, stem III is fully regular for transitive verbs with open-syllable stems ending in a non-front vowel, unlike the less predictable alternations found in Xtokavian dialects. Kamnyu shows two main alternations: vowel fronting for stems in -a, -u, and -ɯ, and -m suffixation with vowel unrounding for stems in -o; these patterns have been regularized by analogical levelling, with a cognate -m suffix also found in Zbu.

The text also notes that stem III in -ɤm assimilates to -am- before a 1sg -a suffix, and that fronted vowels like -e change to -i in this environment. It suggests that vowel fronting comes historically from fusion with a *-j suffix, and rejects an analysis of -m as part of the suffixal chain because bipartite verbs argue against it.

text:
Stem III only occurs in finite verb forms. It is found in Factual Non-Past (§ sec:fact.morphology ), Egophoric Present (§ sec:egophoric.morphology ), Sensory (§ sec:sensory.morphology ), Imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ), Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.morphology ) and Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.morphology ) of transitive verbs in the 1sg 3, 2sg 3 and 3sg configurations (§ sec:indexation.mixed ).

tab:stem3.mto.mtAm illustrates all five person configurations of the Factual Non-Past where stem III appears and a selection of other configurations where stem I is used instead. It has exactly the same distribution in the other TAME categories listed above.

Stem III encodes four morpholosyntactic features, comprising both TAME and person indexation: direct configuration (§ sec:direct-inverse ), singular transitive subject, third person object and Non-Past tense.
summary: Stem III occurs only in finite verb forms, appearing in the Factual Non-Past, Egophoric Present, Sensory, Imperative, Irrealis, and in the Imperfective of transitive verbs in the 1sg>3, 2sg>3, and 3sg configurations. In these contexts, it has the same distribution across the relevant TAME categories, while stem I is used elsewhere. Stem III encodes four morphosyntactic features: direct configuration, singular transitive subject, third person object, and Non-Past tense.

text:
backformation analogy!stem alternation
An indirect consequence of the perfect regularity of stem III formation (§ sec:stem3.form ) is that in some rare cases, the stem I has been generated from the stem III by applying the alternations backwards.

The stem I of kʰogive, `pass over' (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) regularly corresponds to Tshobdun ´kʰi (as if from proto-Gyalrong *kʰaŋ ). On the other hand, Zbu kʰɐ̂m, kʰə̂m, ´kʰəm `give'  and Tangut 𘓯1105kʰjow1.56 (, proto-Tangut *khjVm ) match the Japhug stem III kʰɤm. A possible hypothesis to account for these diverging correspondences would be that Japhug and Tshobdun have preserved the original verb root, and that Zbu and Tangut have generalized stem III to the whole paradigm. However, there are three reasons why such an explanation is problematic.

First, the verb 𘓯1105kʰjow1.56 is highly irregular, and therefore unlikely to have been analogized. Second, Zbu is phylogenetically closer to Tshobdun and Japhug than it is to Tangut, and therefore shared features between Zbu and Tangut are more likely to be due to common retention than to common innovation. Third, there is Japhug-internal evidence that the stem I -o is secondary.

The transitive verb fkroput in order, arrange', whose stem III is fkrɤm is borrowed from the past tense of the Tibetan verb འགྲེམ་བཀྲམ་ⁿgrem-bkramspread out. The stem I fkro is clearly backformed from the stem III, by overapplication of the -o/-ɤm alternation. Some speakers treat this verb as having a non-alternating stem fkrɤm, showing that backformation is still an ongoing process.

The case of fkro offers a model to analyze Japhug kʰogive, `pass over' and Tshobdun ´kʰi: this verb originally had a stem I *kʰɐm in proto-Gyalrong, preserved in Zbu, but underwent backformation to *kʰaŋ in the common ancestor of Japhug and Tshobdun, subsequently evolving to kʰo and ´kʰi by the application of regular sound laws. This is one piece of evidence that Tshobdun is closer to Japhug than it is to Zbu.

The regular stem III βze of the verb βzumake does appear in some non-finite forms such as cʰɯ-kɯ-βze in ( ex:Wmat.chWkWBze ) (see also ex:YWkWnWBze in § sec:autoben.spontaneous ), in the dummy transitive subject construction (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), meaning `grow' or in collocation with the noun ɯ-tsa (in the meaning `be suitable', § sec:Bzu.lv ) for instance.

gourd dem tree indef sens -be 3sg. poss -fruit ipfv - sbj: pcp -make[III] indef lnk 3sg. poss -fruit dem 3sg. poss -top ipfv: east - sbj: pcp -be.thin 3sg. poss -bottom ipfv: west - sbj: pcp -be.thick indef ipfv -make[III] sens -be lnk dem gourd ipfv -call- pl \\
`The gourd is a tree, one which grows fruits. It grows fruits that are thinner on the top part and thicker in the bottom, they are called `gourd'.' (150825 huluwa-zh)
0006346#S2
exe

Rather than an exception to the rules described in § sec:stem3.distribution, it is simpler to consider that a synchronic verb root βzegrow different from βzumake has been created by backformation (§ sec:stem3.backformation ) from finite imperfective forms such as cʰɯ-βze `it grows' in ( ex:Wmat.chWkWBze ). The stem βze however never occurs in past tenses (Inferential and Aorist), so that this verb is an example of partial and ongoing backformation.

Another possible example of the same type of backformation is discussed in § sec:pWrndeta.

Frozen -t suffix
Three verbs presented in tab:frozen.t have two alternative stem forms in free variation, with an optional -t suffix. This suffix appears in all person and TAME forms without any semantic change; compare for instance the Imperfective 1pl forms ku-rɤʑit-i ( ipfv -stay- 1pl, example ex:jisAxCe.maNe, § sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ) and ku-rɤʑi-j ( ipfv -stay- 1pl, example ex:iZo.kWBde, § sec:uses.numerals ), uttered by the same speaker. The two variants are freely interchangeable, but some speakers use the -t suffixed forms more frequently that others.

The optional -t is not synchronically relatable to the past tense -t, which is restricted to 1sg 3 and 2sg 3 Aorist and Inferential (§ sec:indexation.mixed ), and never appears on intransitive forms, or to any of the frozen derivation -t suffixes (§ sec:applicative.t, § sec:antipassive.t ).

It could be a trace of the stem II -t suffix, attested in the verb ti, tɯt `say' in Japhug (§ sec:stem2 ), and in a handful of other verbs in Zbu. In this hypothesis, these three verbs used to have a stem II with the -t suffix, but at the present stage the two stems have ceased to be morphologically contrastive.
summary:
The passage argues that some irregular stem correspondences in Japhug and related languages are best explained by backformation rather than by simple retention or innovation. It uses examples such as **fkro** and **βze** to show that a stem I can be re-created from stem III or finite forms by analogy, and it suggests that Japhug and Tshobdun shared a historical backformation while Zbu preserved the older form.

It also discusses a set of verbs with an optional, frozen **-t** suffix that appears across forms without semantic effect. This suffix is not synchronically the same as the past tense **-t**, and may be a relic of an older stem II **-t** suffix that has lost its morphological contrast.

text:
contracting verb vowel!contraction
Contracting verbs have polysyllabic stems whose first syllable is a-. All of these verbs are morphologically intransitive (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ), but some of them can have semi-objects or oblique arguments (§ sec:semi.transitive ). The a- element can be a valency-decreasing prefix (including the passive § sec:passive, reciprocal (§ sec:reciprocal or distributed property § sec:distributed.amW prefixes), a denominal prefix (the stative denominal a- § sec:denom.a or a disyllabic denominal prefix with a- as its first syllable, § sec:denom.contracting ), a deideophonic prefix (§ sec:a.nA.deidph ) or a synchronically non-analyzable element (as in aroown or amdzɯsit).

To represent vowel contraction in a straightforward way, the notation employed in this grammar separates the vowel of the preceding prefix and the contracting by a hyphen, the prefix is transcribed in its base form, and the result of the vowel contraction is indicated after the hyphen. For instance pɯ-a- is to be read as `prefix pɯ- merging with the contracting vowel as pa', while pɯ-ɤ- indicates merger of the preverb with the contracting vowel as pɤ. This orthographic rule transcribes contracting vowels in several ways ( -ɤ, -a- or -o- ) depending on the prefix with which they merge (see tab:preverb.contraction below). It is important to note however that there is no contrast between -a, -ɤ- and -o- as contracting vowels: there are simply morphologically-conditioned allomorphs. The a- allomorph is used as citation form of contracting verbs.

This convention has the advantage of disambiguating verb forms that have become identical due to vowel contraction (for instance, tɤ-ɤ- vs. tɯ-ɤ, both of which surface as tɤ), and making the verb forms more easily parseable in the corpus.

In Factual Non-Past unprefixed verb forms, the a- element surfaces without alternation, as in (§ ex:aroa.me ).

exe

nɯ ma aro-a me qʰe, \\
dem apart.from possess: fact - 1sg not.exist: fact lnk \\
`I don't have anything else.' (2003 divination)
0003364#S114
exe

The prefixes in slots -6, -5 and -4 can occur in direct contact with the contracting vowel a- only in Factual Non-Past non-second person forms (§ sec:fact.morphology ). The vowel of Rhetorical Interrogative ɯβrɤ, Proximative aspect jɯ- (-6) negative mɤ- (-5) and associated motion prefixes ɕɯ- and ɣɯ- (-4) merge as a-: ɯβrɤ-a- $ $ ɯβra, jɯ-a- $ $ ja, mɤ-a- $ $ ma, ɕɯ-a- $ $ ɕa- and ɣɯ-a- $ $ ɣa, as shown in ɕɯ-anbaʁ-i `we go and hide' ɕanbaʁi in ( ex:CanbaRi ), mɤ-a-rɤt `it has not yet been written' marɤt (example ex:marAt, § sec:passive.stative ).

rŋgɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu ɕɯ-anbaʁ-i ɯmɤ-kɯ-ntsʰi-ci ma, \\
boulder 3sg. poss -in dem: loc tral -hide: fact - 1pl prob - peg -be.better- peg lnk \\
`It looks like we should go and hide in the [hollow] boulder.' (160706 poucet6) 0006109#S61

The interrogative ɯ- in slot -6 does not merge with a-. Rather, an epenthetic -j- consonant is inserted between the two, as in ( ex:WjatsWtsu ) with the verb atsɯtsuhave time.

a-wa tɯrju χsɯ-ŋka tu-ti-a ɯ-j-átsɯtsu \\
1sg. poss -father word three-word ipfv -say- 1sg qu -X-have.time: fact \\
`Father, do I have time to say three sentences?' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S175
