In finite relatives, the verb lacks any overt nominalization marker other than the reduplication itself. In this construction, the relativized elements are either direct objects (as in ex:pWpWfCata.nWra.kW and ex:spWspe below), semi-objects or goals, but never subjects (§ sec:finite.relatives ).

exe

ɯ-ro nɯra [iɕqʰa pɯ pɯ-fɕat-a] nɯra kɯ tɕe tɕe sɯjno tu-ndza-nɯ \\
3sg. poss -rest dem: pl just.before total aor -tell- 1sg dem: pl erg lnk lnk grass ipfv -eat- pl \\
`The rest, all the [other animals] that I have told about just before eat grass.' (05-khWna, 46
0003398#S38
exe

exe

nɯ [spɯ spe] nɯ to-nɤrmi ri tɤte <zhima> kɤ-ti nɯ ɲɤ-nɯ-jmɯt \\
dem total be.able.to: fact dem ifr -call.name lnk that.is sesame inf -say dem ifr - auto -forget \\
`He called the names of all [the crops] he knew, but forgot to say `sesame'.' (140512 alibaba-zh) 0003965#S103
exe

Finite transitive verbs with totalitative reduplication and a 1sg subject can optionally take plural indexation (§ sec:indexation.mixed ) corresponding to the relativized direct object with universal quantification. Object plural indexation in this case is rare (it is absent for instance in ex:pWpWfCata.nWra.kW above), and only one example is attested in the corpus: pɯ pɯ-mto-t-a-nɯ ( total aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg - pl ) `all those that I have seen' ( ex:pWpWmtotanW, § sec:double.number.indexation ).

The totalitative subject participle of the existential verb tuexist can take a possessive prefix, which is interpreted as a possessor, as in a-kɯ kɯ-tu 1sg. poss - total sbj: pcp -exist `everything that I have'. No other totalitative verb form allows possessor prefixation. In particular, since the subject participles of transitive verbs require a possessive prefix coreferent with the object (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ), totalitative reduplication is incompatible with these forms. For instance, to express the meaning `all those who help me', forms such as $ $ a-tɯ tu-kɯ-qur ( 1sg. poss - total ipfv - sbj: pcp -help) with reduplicated orientation preverb or $ $ a-kɯ kɯ-qur ( 1sg. poss - total sbj: pcp -help) with reduplicated participial prefix are unacceptable, and universal quantification has to be expressed with other means, for instance a-tu-kɯ-qur tʰamtɕɤt ( 1sg. poss - ipfv - sbj: pcp -help all).

Totalitative reduplication of transitive subject participle is only possible if no possessive prefix is present (see ex:tWrme.pWpWkWmto, § sec:totalitative.relatives ).
summary: Totalitative reduplication is a form of reduplication on the main verb of relative clauses that marks universal quantification of the relativized referent, and it occurs in participial relatives, finite relatives, and some lexicalized participles. In participial relatives, the reduplicated syllable is the first syllable of the verb after any possessive prefix, while in finite relatives the verb has no overt nominalization marker besides the reduplication, and the relativized element is typically a direct object, semi-object, or goal rather than a subject. The construction has restrictions on indexation and possession: object plural indexation is rare, only the existential verb allows possessor prefixation in totalitative form, and transitive subject participles can take totalitative reduplication only when no possessive prefix is present.

text:
reduplication!emphatic autive!reduplication
When occurring in word-initial position, the autive prefix nɯ- can be reduplicated to express emphatic permansive `still $X$ (regardless of whatever may happen)', and such verb form can be repeated with the additive linker nɤ, as in ( ex:nWnWtu ).

exe

tɤtʰo nɯ pɯpɯŋunɤ, tɕe nɯ mɤ-fse tɕe tɕendɤre ɯ-jwaʁ nɯ nɯ nɯ-tu nɤ nɯ nɯ-tu qʰe \\
pine dem as.for lnk dem neg -be.like: fact lnk lnk 3sg. poss -leaf dem emph auto -exist: fact add emph auto -exist: fact lnk \\
`As for the pine, it is not like [the other trees], [whatever happens], its leaves (needles) are still there.' (07-tAtho) 0003432#S14
exe

The reduplicated autive should not be mistaken with the combination of a type A `westward' orientation preverb nɯ- with the autive in spontaneous function (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ) as in ( ex:nWnWme ).

exe

ɯʑo nɯ-nɯ-me ɕti. \\
3sg aor - auto -not.exist be. aff: fact \\
`[The wart] disappeared by itself.' (24-pGArtsAG) 0003624#S52
exe
summary: When the autive prefix nɯ- occurs in word-initial position, it can be reduplicated to mark emphatic permansive meaning, roughly ‘still X, regardless of whatever may happen.’ This reduplicated autive can also be repeated with the additive linker nɤ. It should not be confused with the sequence of a type A “westward” orientation preverb nɯ- plus the autive in its spontaneous function, which has a different meaning such as ‘disappeared by itself.’

subsection: Verb stem reduplication as secondary exponence
text:
reduplication!secondary exponence
Prefixal partial reduplication of the verb stem is a secondary exponence, used in combination with a prefix, in several productive verbal forms listed in tab:verb.redp.prefix.

Stem reduplication occurs in two converbs, the gerund (§ sec:gerund and the purposive converb (§ sec:purposive.converb ), together with a sɤ(z)- prefix cognate to that of the oblique participle (§ sec:oblique.participle ).

It is also found in four regular derivations: reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal, on the a- prefix see § sec:applicative.history ), distributed action (§ sec:distributed.action ), auto-evaluative (§ sec:autoevaluative ) and attenuative (§ sec:attenuative ). The attenuative differs from all other cases in that the vowel of the reduplicated syllable is in some cases -ɤ- rather than -ɯ-.

The locus of reduplication is the last syllable of the verb stem, disregarding indexation suffixes. When the verb stem contains more than one syllable, the reduplicated syllable is infixed. For instance, the gerund of nɤrelaugh is sɤz-nɤ rɯ re `laughing': the partially replicated material -rɯ- occurs between the two syllables nɤ- and -re of the verb stem. Additional reduplication is blocked on lexically reduplicated verb stems such as rɯruguard (§ sec:redp.voice ) or nɯqambɯmbjomfly: triplication is not attested in Japhug, unlike in Stau.

Non-productive suffixal partial reduplication is found in a handful of antipassive (§ sec:antipassive.redp ) and distributed action derivations (§ sec.distributed.action.l ).

Irregular partial reduplication with -oʁ or -ɯm in the replicated syllable instead of regular -ɯ are also attested (for instance nɤʁɯmʁaʁplay around from nɤʁaʁhave a good time, § sec.distributed.action.oR ).
summary:
The passage describes prefixal partial reduplication of the verb stem as a secondary exponent used with a prefix in several productive verbal forms, including two converbs and four regular derivations. The reduplicated material is normally the last syllable of the stem and is infixed in multisyllabic stems, while additional reduplication is blocked on already reduplicated stems.

It also notes some non-productive suffixal partial reduplication in a few antipassive and distributed-action forms, and mentions irregular cases where the reduplicated syllable contains -oʁ or -ɯm instead of the usual -ɯ. The attenuative is exceptional in sometimes using -ɤ- in the reduplicated syllable.

text:
reduplication!emphatic
Emphatic reduplication is a partial reduplication in -ɯ targeting the final syllable of the stem like other cases of verb stem reduplication (§ sec:verb.stem.redp ). This inflectional reduplication has several related functions.

With adjectival stative verbs, emphatic reduplication indicates a high degree, opposite of the attenuative reduplication (§ sec:attenuative ): compare for instance qarŋɯ rŋe `be deep yellow' vs. aqarŋɯ rŋe `be yellowish'. Reduplicated adjectival verbs are almost always attested in participial form, as in ( ex:kWmpCWmpCAr.kWpWpe ).

exe

tɕʰeme kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕɤr kɯ-pɯ pe ci nɤ-ɕɣa kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ci a-nɯ-tɯ-ɤβzu smɯlɤm \\
girl sbj: pcp - emph be.beautiful sbj: pcp - emph be.good indef 2sg. poss -tooth/age sbj: pcp - emph be.small indef irr - pfv -2-become prayer \\
`May you become a very beautiful, nice young girl.' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S237
exe

Rare examples of emphatic adjectival verbs in finite form are however also found in the corpus, in ( ex:YWwGrWwGrum ).

exe

ɯ-ku nɯra tɕe nɤki, ɯ-kɤχcɤl nɯra li ɲɯ-qarŋe qʰe ɲɯ-wɣrɯ wɣrum kɯ-fse. \\
3sg. poss -head dem: pl lnk filler 3sg. poss -top.head dem: pl again sens -be.yellow lnk sens - emph be.white sbj: pcp -be.like \\
`It is yellow and very white on the top of its head.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S24
exe

With the negative existential verb menot exist, emphatic reduplication indicates radical non-existence `not (have/exist)... at all', as in ( ex:nAwa.pWnnWmWme ). In ( ex:nAwa.pWnnWmWme ), the mother of the character Padma 'Od'bar, who asked her about the identity of father, gives this answer in the hope that her son will not try to find the truth about the disappearance of his father and thereby run into a mortal danger.

exe

nɤ-wa pɯ-nnɯ-mɯ me ɕti \\
2sg. poss -father pst. ipfv - auto - emph not.exist \\
`You never had a father at all.' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S123
exe

Emphatic reduplication also occurs with modal verbs such as the semi-transitive rgalike ( ex:kWrgWrga.tWrme ) and the transitive spabe able ( ex:kArWCmi.kWspWspa ) to express high degree.

exe

kɯ-rgɯ rga ʑo tɯrme ra maŋe-nɯ ma \\
sbj: pcp - emph like emph people pl not.exist: sens - pl lnk \\
`There are no people who like it a lot.' (160706 thotsi) 0006133#S24
exe

exe

pɣa kɤ-rɯɕmi kɯ-spɯ spa nɯ kɯ... \\
bird inf -speak sbj: pcp - emph be.able dem erg \\
`The bird who was able to speak very well (said....).' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S25
exe

Often in combination with the autive nɯ- (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ), emphatic reduplication occurs in free-choice correlatives and in universal concessive conditional constructions (§ sec:universal.concessive.conditional ) as in ( ex:tChi.lAwGnWjWji.Zo ), without any constraint of the verb category. In ( ex:tChi.lAwGnWjWji.Zo ), the subject of the verb pe `(it) is good' is not the crop referred to by the interrogative pronoun tɕʰi, but the planting activity. To analyze this example as a correlative, one would have to suppose that a complement clause such as nɯnɯ kɤ-ji `planting that' has been elided before pe (on pebe good as a complement-taking verb, see example ex:kAji.mApe (§ sec:adjective.complement ).

exe

tɯ-ji sna tɕe, [tɕʰi lɤ́-wɣ-nɯ-jɯ ji] ʑo pe \\
indef. poss -field be.good lnk what aor - inv - auto - emph plant emph be.good: fact \\
`(The type of earth called tɤtʂo ) is fit (to be used) as fields, whatever one plants in it, [the planting] will be good (successful).' (25-cWXCWz) 0003636#S61
exe

Although emphatic reduplication is highly productive and regular, a handful of verbs have irregular reduplication patterns. The transitive verb rɤtɕaʁtread on has the emphatic form rɤtɕɯmtɕaʁtrample (compare example ex:kWNGio.YWsaRdAt, § sec:proprietive.generic with ex:amAtAndonW.ma.GWznAndAGnW, § sec:genr.3pl ) with -ɯm reduplicated syllable (§ sec.distributed.action.oR ). The stative verb mdibe complete has the emphatic form mdoʁmdi with -oʁ reduplication (§ sec.distributed.action.oR ), and tsʰube fat has the suffixed -e reduplicated form tsʰutsʰebe very fat.

The verb fsebe like has the irregular reduplicated form -fsɤ fse alonside -fsɯ fse in universal concessive conditionals ( tɕʰi pɯ-nɯ-fsɤ fse`in any case', example ex:tChi.pWnWfsAfse.Zo, § sec:universal.concessive.conditional ).
summary: Emphatic reduplication is a productive partial reduplication in -ɯ that targets the final syllable of a verb stem and serves several related functions. With adjectival stative verbs it marks a high degree, with the negative existential verb it expresses radical non-existence, and with certain modal verbs it conveys high degree; it also appears in free-choice correlatives and universal concessive conditionals, often with the autive nɯ-. Although regular overall, a few verbs show irregular emphatic reduplication patterns.

text:
Negation in Japhug is mainly expressed by negative prefixes (§ sec:negation ). It is symmetrical: the presence of these prefixes is not systematically correlated with finiteness or TAME alternations.

In addition to negative prefixes, a periphrastic negative construction with sentence-final negative auxiliary is also attested (§ sec:periphrastic.negation ), and it is required in particular to mark double negation (§ sec:double.negation ).
summary: Negation in Japhug is mainly expressed through negative prefixes, and this system is symmetrical in that their use is not systematically tied to finiteness or TAME alternations. A periphrastic negative construction with a sentence-final negative auxiliary also exists, and it is especially required to express double negation.

text: negation!prefix prefix!negation
summary: The passage indicates that negation can be expressed through a prefix, specifically a negation prefix. It simply labels the relationship between negation and prefixation without providing further detail.

text:
morphology!allomorphy allomorphy!negative prefixes
Four negative prefixes are found in Japhug: mɤ, mɯ, ma- and mɯ́j-. Their distribution is determined by TAME and finiteness.

The ma- prefix is restricted to prohibitive verb forms (§ sec:prohibitive.morpho ), and always combined with type A orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ).

The stress-bearing (§ sec:stress.prefixal.chain ) mɯ́j- prefix (see ex:WmAtaZa below) is a portmanteau of negation and Sensory evidental (§ sec:sensory ). The Sensory prefix ɲɯ- has the expected negative form mɯ-ɲɯ- only in the case of contracting verbs (§ sec:sensory.morphology ). Otherwise, when the prefixal sequence mɯ-ɲɯ- occurs, the ɲɯ- preverb marks the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.morphology ).

The form mɤ- is found on non-finite verbal forms without any orientation preverb (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:object.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:infinitives.other.prefixes, § sec:degree.nominal.prefixes ), in Factual Non-Past and Irrealis form (see ex:amAGWtAtWwGndza above in § sec:outer.prefixal.chain ), and also when preceded by the interrogative ɯ- (§ sec:interrogative.W.morpho ) as in ( ex:WmAtaZa ) and the Proximative jɯ- (§ sec:proximative ) as in ( ex:jWmACtAthuta ).

exe

tɕe tɯ-ŋke ɯ-mɤ-ta-ʑa, ɯ-mɤ-nɯ-mɯnmu qʰe mɯ́j-sɤ-mto \\
lnk inf:II-walk qu - neg - aor:3 -start qu - neg - aor -move lnk neg: sens - prop -see \\
`If it has not started walking, if it has not moved, it is not visible.' (26-NalitCaRmbWm) 0003676#S102
exe

exe

jɯfɕɯr jɯ-mɤ-ɕ-tɤ-tʰu-t-a ʑo \\
yesterday proxm - neg - tral - aor -ask- pst: tr - 1sg emph \\
`Yesterday I almost did not go and ask about it.' (elicited)
exe

The allomorph mɯ- is found elsewhere, including non-finite verb forms with orientation preverbs (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:object.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:inf.exist ) and all finite verb forms with orientation preverbs other than the Prohibitive and the verbal forms where slot -6 is filled (Irrealis, Interrogative, Proximative etc).

The partial reduplication (§ sec:verb.initial.redp ) of mɯ- (which occurs in particular in the protasis of conditionals, § sec:redp.protasis ) does not yield expected $ $ mɯ mɯ, but rather mɯ mɤ- with vowel alternation: compare for instance mɯ-nɯ-si `she did not die' with the mɯ- prefix (as expected in the Aorist) with mɯ mɤ-nɯ-si-a `if I do not die' in ( ex:mWmAnWsia ).

exe

tɤ-mu nɯ ɣɯjpa kɯre mɤɕtʂa mɯ-nɯ-si \\
indef. poss -mother dem this.year dem. loc until neg - aor -die \\
`The old woman only died this year.' (`she did not die until this year') (14-siblings)
0003508#S318
exe

exe

mɯ mɤ-nɯ-si-a nɤ, a-tɤ-kɯ-nɯlaʁrdaβ-a ra \\
cond neg - aor -die- 1sg add irr - pfv -2 1-hit.with.forelegs- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`If [after that] I have not died [yet], hit me with your forelegs.' (2003kAndzwsqhaj2)
exe

The Interrogative ɯ- prefix, like conditional reduplication, requires the mɤ- negative prefix (see ex:WmAtaZa above), and this commonality in morphophonology is correlated with a similarity in function, since both the prefix ɯ- and reduplication are used to mark the verb of the protasis of conditional clauses (§ sec:real.conditional ).

The -6 slot ɯmɤ- prefix of possible modality (§ sec:WmA ) has a surface form identical to the combination of the interrogative ɯ- with the negative prefix mɤ, as in ( ex:tundze.WmANu ). The ɯmɤ- synchronically differs from ɯ-mɤ- (from which it historically derives) in that it can occur with the peg circumfix (§ sec:peg.circumfix, § sec:WmA.kW.ci ). It is not compatible with a negative prefix.

exe

qajɯ kɯ-fse ra tu-ndze ɯmɤ-ŋu ma \\
bug sbj: pcp -be.like pl ipfv -eat[III] prob -be: fact lnk \\
`It presumably/maybe eats bugs.' (23-pGAYaR) 0003606#S28
exe

Negative prefixes are restricted to verb forms, and cannot be prefixed on nouns (§ sec:negation.noun ). However, they occur on most non-finite verb forms, including participles (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:object.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:oblique.participle.orientation ), infinitives (§ sec:infinitives.other.prefixes, § sec:inf.exist, § sec:dental.inf.polarity ), degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominal.prefixes ), converbs (§ sec:gerund.neg, § sec:purposive.converb ), but not action nominals (§ sec:action.nominals ) and fossilized deverbal nouns (§ sec:fossil.nmlz ).
summary: Japhug has four negative prefixes—mɤ, mɯ, ma-, and mɯ́j-—whose distribution depends on TAME and finiteness. Ma- is limited to prohibitive forms, mɯ́j- combines negation with Sensory evidential meaning, mɤ appears in certain non-finite forms and some finite contexts such as Factual Non-Past and Irrealis, and mɯ- is used in other negative environments, especially with orientation preverbs. The passage also notes that negative prefixes are confined to verb forms, though they occur on many non-finite verbal categories and not on nouns or some nominalized forms.

text:
negation!suppletion verb!suppletion
Negative prefixes can occur on most verbs, with the exception of copulas and existential verbs, which have suppletive negative forms (§ sec:intr.person.irregular ), as illustrated in tab:neg.suppletion. Another verb lacking negative forms is kɤtɯpatell, though for a different reason (§ sec:irregular.transitive ). The contrast between the neutral copula ŋube and the Emphatic Affirmative ɕtibe is neutralized in the negative, where only one negative copula maʁnot be is present (§ sec:copula.basic ).

For instance, the negation of ŋube and tuexist can only be maʁnot be ( ex:aZo.maRa ) and menot exist ( ex:tWtshot.pWme ).

exe

aʑo maʁ-a \\
1sg not.be: fact - 1sg \\
`I am not [that girl].' (2003 sras)
exe

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe tɯtsʰot pɯ-me tɕe, \\
former.times loc clocks pst. ipfv -not.exist lnk \\
`In former times, there were no clocks.' (29-LAntshAm) 0003726#S60
exe

Combining ŋu and tu with negative prefixes (for instance $ $ mɤ-ŋu-a instead of maʁ-a `I am not/It is not me' and $ $ mɯ-pɯ-tu instead of pɯ-me ) is utterly incorrect and categorically rejected by all speakers. Likewise, negative copulas cannot take negative prefixes ($ $ mɤ-maʁ-a is agrammatical).

It is however possible to combine affirmative copulas or existential verbs with their negative counterparts as postverbal periphrastic negations (§ sec:periphrastic.negation ). The copulas ŋu and maʁ occur together in the phrase ŋu cinɤ maʁ kɯ `in any case it is not true' (example ex:Nu.cinA.maR.kW, § sec:cinA ). The negative existential menot exist is very commonly found with the participle of its antonym kɯ-tu to express emphasis on the non-existence, as in ( ex:pWkWtu.me ) in comparison with ( ex:tWtshot.pWme ) (§ sec:existential.basic ).

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ mkʰɯrlu kɯ-fse ra pɯ-kɯ-tu me. \\
former.times machine sbj: pcp -be.like pl pst. ipfv - sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact \\
`In former times, there were no machines or things like that at all.' (140430 tWfkur)
0003898#S4
exe
summary: Negative prefixes occur on most verbs, but copulas and existential verbs instead use suppletive negative forms, and one verb, kɤtɯpatell, lacks negative forms for a different reason. The neutral and emphatic affirmative copulas are neutralized in negation, where only the negative copula maʁ is used, and speakers reject combining these verbs with negative prefixes or double negation of the copula. However, affirmative and negative copulas or existential verbs can co-occur in periphrastic negation, and the negative existential me is often paired with the participle of its antonym kɯ-tu for emphasis.

text:
Some verbs are defective and lack affirmative forms: they only appear in conjunction with negative prefixes. Two categories can be distinguished.

First, a handful of defective verb roots are only attested with negative prefixes, listed in tab:defect.verbs.neg. The verb roots in this table are not found in any derived form without negation, except for mɤ-xsione does not know, a highly defective verb (§ sec:irregular.transitive ) historically related to the transitive verb sɯzknow (whose paradigm is not defective).

The complex collocation neg +spa= neg +rka=tu/me `be guilty/be innocent' contains a bipartite verb (§ sec:bipartite ) whose first component -spa may be related to the modal auxiliary spabe able (§ sec:abilitative.lexicalized, § sec:spa.verb ) and whose second component -rka is an orphan verb.

The verb neg +ʑɯnot just be, `not be/have only' ( ex:mAZW.ma ) is most commonly used in one of the comparative constructions (§ sec:mAZW ) and has even been further grammaticalized as an adverb mɤʑɯeven more ( ex:mAZW.Zo.chWtshu ).

exe

kʰɤjmu nɯtɕu mɤ-ʑɯ ma, tɤrɲɟo tu tɕe, \\
kitchen dem: loc neg -be.just lnk shelf exist: fact lnk \\
`In the kitchen, there are not just [the aforementioned objects], there is also a shelf (to store the cooking implements).' (2011-11-kha2)
exe

exe

nɯnɯ paʁ kɯ tu-ndze tɕe, mɤʑɯ ʑo cʰɯ-tsʰu cʰa \\
dem pig erg ipfv -eat[III] lnk even.more emph ipfv -be.fat can: fact \\
`When the pig eats it [acorns], it can grow even fatter.' (08-CkrAz)
0003444#S43
exe

Second, most sɯ-/z- abilitative verbs (§ sec:abilitative ) are only found in negative forms. For instance the abilitative z-nɤjo from nɤjowait only occurs with a negation in the meaning `cannot wait to' (due to hurry/impatience) as in ( ex:juzGWt.mWpjAznAjo ).

exe

spjaŋkɯ nɯ kɯ ju-zɣɯt mɯ-pjɤ-z-nɤjo ʑo tɕe, \\
wolf dem erg ipfv -arrive neg - ifr. ipfv - abil -wait emph lnk \\
`The wolf could not wait [for the fox] to arrive.' (140516 huli de baofu-zh) 0004010#S39
exe

This constraint is also observed with the lexicalized abilitative spʰɯtcan cut (from pʰɯttake out, cut, § sec:abilitative.lexicalized) as in ( ex:WndzrW.mWjsphWt ).

exe

tsɯntu kɯ ɯ-ndzrɯ mɯ́j-spʰɯt ma ɯ-tɯ-rko ɯ-tɯ-jaʁ ɲɯ-sɤre ʑo \\
scissors erg 3sg. poss -nail neg: sens -can.cut lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.hard 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.thick sens -be.ridiculous emph \\
`The scissors cannot cut through her nails, as they are extremely hard and thick.' (2012, heard in context)
exe
summary:
The passage describes two kinds of defective verbs that appear only with negative prefixes. First, a small set of verb roots are attested only in negative forms, including a few special cases such as a bipartite expression meaning ‘be guilty/be innocent’ and the verb mɤʑɯ ‘not be just,’ which is also used in comparative constructions and has been further grammaticalized.  

Second, most sɯ-/z- abilitative verbs likewise occur only in negative forms, as shown by examples like z-nɤjo ‘cannot wait to’ and the lexicalized abilitative spʰɯt ‘cannot cut,’ which are used only in negated contexts.

text:
negation!lexicalized
Some verb roots have negative forms with unpredictable lexicalized meanings. Three subtypes can be distinguished.

First, the negative form of the underived form of the root can have an extended meaning. For instance, the verb rkaŋbe strong, `be in good physical condition' can mean `be pregnant' in the negative as in ( ex:mWYArkaN ).

exe

ki tɕʰeme ki mɯ-ɲɤ-rkaŋ \\
dem. prox girl dem. prox neg - ifr -be.in.good.shape \\
`This woman became pregnant.' (elicited)
exe

Second, the special meaning of the negation appears in derivations: for instance, the stative verb ftsʰifeel better has a negative causative neg +sɯftsʰiforce, `coerce' (§ sec:sig.caus.lexicalized ) and a lexicalized negative participle mɤkɯftsʰiforcibly used as an adverb (§ sec:velar.inf.adverb ).

Third, some lexicalized noun-verb collocations require a negative prefix on the verb (§ sec:other.collocation.intr ), for instance tɯ-skʰrɯ= neg -βdi `be pregnant' from tɯ-skʰrɯbody and βdibe well as in ( ex:ndZiskhrW.mWYABdi ).

exe

ndʑi-rʑaβ ʁnaʁna ʑo ndʑi-skʰrɯ mɯ-ɲɤ-βdi \\
3du. poss -wife both emph 3du. poss -body neg - ifr -be.well \\
`Both of their wives got pregnant.' (2005 Lobzang)
0003370#S2
exe
summary: Some verb roots have negative forms with unpredictable lexicalized meanings, and three subtypes are distinguished. These include cases where the negative form of the basic verb has an extended meaning, where special meanings appear in derived forms such as causatives or participles, and where certain noun-verb collocations require a negative prefix on the verb.

text:
negation!periphrastic
Aside from negative prefixes ( ex:mWpWmtota ), negation can be expressed by the negative copula maʁnot be ( ex:pWmtota.maR ) and the negative existential verb menot exist ( ex:pWmtota.me ) in postverbal position.

exe

xlist

mɯ-pɯ-mto-t-a \\
neg - aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I have not seen it.' (several examples)

pɯ-mto-t-a maʁ\\
aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg not.be: fact \\
`I have not seen it, (but rather...).'

pɯ-mto-t-a me \\
aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg not.exist: fact \\
`I have seen none/I haven't seen anything.' (several examples)
xlist
exe

The negative copula maʁnot be occurs postverbally in Periphrastic TAME categories requiring a copula (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ), or to express emphatic negation, contrasting with an assertative postverbal copula (§ sec:affirmative.copula.function ) as in ( ex:YWGAwua.maR ).

exe

xlist

tɕʰindʐa ɲɯ-tɯ-ɣɤwu ŋu? \\
why sens -2-cry be: fact \\
`Why are you crying?'

ɲɯ-ɣɤwu-a maʁ nɤ, tɯ-mɯ pjɯ-lɤt ɲɯ-ɕti ma \\
sens -cry- 1sg not.be: fact sfp indef. poss -sky ipfv -release sens -be. aff lnk \\
`It is not that I am crying, [I look like I am crying because] it has been raining.' (2005-stod-kunbzang)
xlist
exe

The postverbal negative existential me (§ sec:existential.basic ) has a universal negative meaning `nothing' or negative indefinite `none, not any' as in ( ex:pWmtota.me ) (§ sec:negation.existential ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-mdoʁ tɕʰi ʑo fse mɤ-xsi, a-kɤ-ti me ma mɯ-pɯ-mto-t-a. ɯ-ndʐi kɯnɤ pɯ-mto-t-a me \\
lnk 3sg. poss -colour what emph be.like: fact neg - genr:know 1sg. poss - obj: pcp -say not.exist: fact lnk neg - aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg 3sg. poss -skin also aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg not.exist: fact \\
`I don't know which colour it$_i$ has, I can't say because I have not seen it$_i$, I have not even seen any of its$_i$ hides.' (27-kikakCi)
0003700#S21
exe

It is also found in one of the superlative constructions, illustrated by example ( ex:tuqhea.me ) (§ sec:negative.existential.superlative ).

exe

βʑɯ kɯ-fse tu-qʰe-a me \\
mouse sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv -hate[III]- 1sg not.exist: fact \\
`Mice is what I hate most.' (`there is nothing that I hate like a mouse') (140427 bianfu yu huangshulang-zh) 0003838#S13
exe
summary: Besides negative prefixes, negation can also be expressed with the postverbal negative copula **maʁ** ‘not be’ and the negative existential verb **me** ‘not exist’. **Maʁ** is used in periphrastic TAME categories requiring a copula and can also serve for emphatic, contrastive negation, while **me** has a universal negative meaning such as ‘nothing’ or ‘none’ and also appears in a superlative construction.

text:
negation!double
Since negative prefixes are not recursive, there are only two ways to express double negation in Japhug: either is by combining a negative verb form with a negative auxiliary ( menot exist or maŋenot exist), or a negative verb form in a complement clause with a negative complement-taking verb.

Double negation with existential verbs can indicate universal quantification, in particular when the verb taking the negative prefix is transitive (or semi-transitive) and no overt object (or semi-object) is present as in ( ex:mAndze.Zo.me ) (see also § sec:negation.existential ).

exe

paʁ aɣɯɣli ma rcanɯ mɤ-ndze ʑo me \\
pig produce.a.lot.of.manure: fact lnk unexp: deg neg -eat[III] emph not.exist: fact \\
`Pigs produce a lot of manure, as they eat everything (there is nothing they don't eat).' (05-paR)
0003400#S27
exe

Negative participial forms with a negative auxiliary express mild assertion, as in ( ex:mAkWpe.me ) and ( ex:mAkWkhW.me ).

exe

aʑɯɣ mɤ-kɯ-pe me \\
1sg: gen neg - sbj: pcp -be.good not.exist: fact \\
`I am fine (I don't have any particular problem).' (140506 shizi he huichang de bailingniao-zh) 0003927#S70
exe

exe

mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ me \\
neg - sbj: pcp -be.possible not.exist: fact \\
`There is nothing wrong with it.' (common in metalinguistic judgments about the grammaticality of sentences)
exe

Another type of double negation construction is observed when both the complement-taking verb and the verb in the complement clause take a negative prefix. The most common verb in this type of configuration is the modal verb kʰɯbe possible (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ), either with finite complements (§ sec:finite.complement ) as in ( ex:mAGia.mAkhW ), or with negative infinitival complements (example ex:mAkACe.mAkhW, § sec:infinitives.other.prefixes ), expressing the meaning `have no choice but to $X$'.

exe

nɤ-rca mɤ-ɣi-a mɤ-kʰɯ qʰe \\
2sg. poss -together.with neg -come: fact - 1sg neg -be.possible: fact lnk \\
`It have no other choice but to go with you/follow you.' (Nyima Wodzer 2003.2)
exe

Other verbs attested in this type of construction include nɤzdare (§ sec:nAz.verb ) as in ( ex:mAkAGi.mAnAzi ) and cʰacan (with the meaning `cannot help but' as in ex:mACWkAtshi, § sec:am.complement ).

exe

rɟɤlpu fka ɕti tɕe, mɤ-kɤ-ɣi mɤ-nɤz-i ri \\
king order be. aff: fact lnk neg - inf -come neg -dare: fact - 1pl lnk \\
`It is the king's order, we do not dare not to come.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe
summary: Because negative prefixes are not recursive, Japhug expresses double negation only in two main ways: by combining a negative verb form with a negative auxiliary, or by using a negative verb in a complement clause with a negative complement-taking verb. The first type can express universal quantification with existential verbs, or mild assertion with negative participial forms. The second type, often with the modal verb meaning “be possible,” can mean “have no choice but to X,” and other verbs in this construction also convey similar necessity or lack of avoidance.

section: Negation and parts of speech other than verbs
text: Verbs are the only part of speech than can take negative prefixes. This section describes the constructions used in Japhug to express meaning corresponding to that of negative nouns or pronouns, and also discusses negative intensifiers adverbs.
summary: Verbs are the only part of speech that can take negative prefixes. The section describes how Japhug expresses meanings equivalent to negative nouns or pronouns, and also discusses negative intensifier adverbs.

section: Negation and parts of speech other than verbs
text:
negation!noun
Although there is a privative nominal derivation in Japhug (§ sec:privative ), there is no way of building a negative noun like English `non-$X$' or `un-$X$' meaning `which is not $X$' (rather than $X$-less). The only way to express such a meaning is build using a participial relative (§ sec:subject.participles ) with the negative copula $X$ kɯ-maʁ `something/someone who/that is not $X$' (§ sec:copula.basic ), for instance tɤ-rɟit kɯ-maʁ `someone who is not a child' in ( ex:tArJit.kWmaR ).

exe

ɯʑora nɯ-rɟit ʑo cʰɯ-βri-nɯ qʰe kɯmaʁ ra nɯ-rɟit nɯ pɯpɯŋunɤ [tɤ-rɟit kɯ-maʁ] tú-wɣ-sɯpa qʰe \\
3pl 3pl. poss -offspring emph ipfv -protect- pl lnk other pl 3pl. poss -offspring dem top indef. poss -child sbj: pcp -not.be impf - inv -consider lnk \\
`(At school), [some parents] protect their own children, and as for the children of other people, they consider them as if they were not children (`as non-children').' (140501 01)
exe
summary: Japhug has a privative nominal derivation, but it does not have a direct way to form a negative noun meaning “not X” like English *non-X* or *un-X*. Instead, this meaning is expressed with a participial relative construction plus the negative copula, yielding expressions such as *tɤ-rɟit kɯ-maʁ* “someone who is not a child.”

section: Negation and parts of speech other than verbs
text:
negation!prnoun
Japhug lacks negative pronouns (§ sec:indef.pro ), and headless relative clauses (§ sec:headless.relatives.quantification ) combined with a negative existential copula (§ sec:suppletive.negative ) are used to express the meanings `nothing', `nobody' ( ex:nAkWCaB.me, ex:WkWntChoz.maNe ) or `nowhere' ( ex:WsArNgW.maNe ).

exe

nɤ-kɯ-ɕaβ me \\
2sg. poss - sbj: pcp -catch.up not.exist: fact \\
`Nobody will [be able] to catchup with you.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S112
exe

exe

tɯmɯrkʰa tɕe ɯ-sɤ-rŋgɯ maŋe \\
evening loc 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -lie.down not.exist: sens \\
`In the evening, it has no place to stay.' (26-NalitCaRmbWm) 0003676#S37
exe

In negative existential constructions, the headless relative can also mean `not any of' as kɤ-mto `any (amadou) to be seen' in ( ex:WkWntChoz.maNe ).

exe

jinde tɕe nɯ [ɯ-kɯ-ntɕʰoz] maŋe qʰe, [kɤ-mto] kɯnɤ maŋe \\
nowadays lnk dem 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -use not.exist: sens lnk obj: pcp -see also not.exist: sens \\
`Nowadays nobody uses [amadou], there isn't even any to be seen.' (15-babW)
0003512#S214
exe
summary: Japhug does not have negative pronouns; instead, meanings such as “nothing,” “nobody,” and “nowhere” are expressed with headless relative clauses plus a negative existential copula. In negative existential constructions, the headless relative can also mean “not any of,” as in examples like “there isn’t even any to be seen.”

section: Negation and parts of speech other than verbs
text:
negation!adverb
Japhug lacks an all-purpose negative adverb, but there a few negative intensifiers.

The adverb maka is generally used with negative verb forms to express emphatic negation `not... at all' as in ( ex:maka.mWpWjAG ), in particular with negative existential verbs (§ sec:negation.existential ).

exe

tɕʰeme kʰɤɕkʰɤr ku-kɯ-ɕe maka mɯ-pɯ-jɤɣ \\
girl man.seating.place ipfv: east - genr:S/O-go at.all neg - pst. ipfv -be.allowed \\
`Ladies were not allowed to go to the men's seating place.' (31-khAjmu)
0004079#S39
exe

It is however attested in non-negative sentences as in ( ex:maka.nWnACqe ), in adversative contexts.

exe

jɤxtsʰi ndɤre maka nɯ-nɤɕqe ra \\
this.time advers at.all imp -endure[III] be.needed: fact \\
`This time (unlike the previous times), you have absolutely to bear [the cold of the moon and the heat of the sun without making a word, otherwise we will not succeed].' (tWxtsa)
exe

This adverb is built from the root -ka found in the distributive determiner tɯkaeach (§ sec:raNri ) and the distributive pronoun ʑakaeach his own (§ sec:distributive.pronouns ). The first syllable ma- resembles the negative prefix mɤ- (§ sec:negation ), but given the fact that negative prefixes (§ sec:negation ) are strictly restricted to verb forms, it is not likely that the first syllable of maka is from a negative prefix.

Rather, it is from the intensifier mu, This form is related to the denominal verb mɤmube the most important. also attested as intensifier `not... at all' in negative contexts ( ex:muZo.me ), in bound state form mɤ- (§ sec:vowel.alternations.compounds ), followed by vowel assimilation with the following syllable -ka.

exe

nɯ ma kɯ-ra mu ʑo me \\
dem apart.from sbj: pcp -be.needed at.all emph not.exist: fact \\
`I don't need anything else at all.' (2003 tWxtsa)
exe

We find in addition the compound form mucin `not even one at all' ( ex:mucin.Zo.marCAttCi ) from mu and cinɤ(not) even one (§ sec:cinA ).

exe

kɯmdza ra mucin ʑo mɤ-arɕɤt-tɕi \\
relative pl at.all emph neg -have.a.kinship.relationship: fact - 1du \\
`We don't have any kinship relationship at all.' (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S52
exe
summary: Japhug does not have a general negative adverb, but it does have several negative intensifiers. The adverb *maka* is mainly used with negative verb forms to mean “not... at all,” though it can also occur in adversative non-negative contexts; it is analyzed as coming from the intensifier *mu* plus *-ka*, rather than from the negative prefix. The language also has the compound *mucin* meaning “not even one at all,” formed from *mu* and *cinɤ* “not even one.”

text:
In Japhug, person indexation is the defining feature of finite verbs, as opposed to non-finite verbs (§ chap:non-finite ) and other parts of speech. Japhug finite verb forms index one or two arguments, depending on the transitivity of the verb, using a combination of prefixes, suffixes and stem alternation. No verb indexes more than two arguments. The indexation system is very close to a canonical direct-inverse system (§ sec:direct-inverse ).

This chapter first presents intransitive and transitive conjugations, investigates the issue of agreement mismatch, and then discusses the origin of person indexation affixes. In addition, it documents the analogical extension of person indexation suffixes to non-finite verb forms in some specific contexts.
summary: In Japhug, person indexation is the defining property of finite verbs, which mark one or two arguments depending on transitivity through prefixes, suffixes, and stem alternation; no verb indexes more than two arguments. This system is very close to a canonical direct-inverse system. The chapter then outlines intransitive and transitive conjugations, agreement mismatch, the origin of the person indexation affixes, and the extension of some suffixes to non-finite verb forms in certain contexts.

text:
verb!intransitive
Intransitive verbs comprise dynamic, stative and semi-transitive verbs. All of the verbs have in common the property of indexing one argument, the intransitive subject, which when overt is in absolutive form (§ sec:absolutive.S ).
summary: Intransitive verbs include dynamic, stative, and semi-transitive types. They all share the property of indexing a single argument, the intransitive subject, which is in absolutive form when expressed overtly.

text:
tab:intransitive.indexation illustrates the paradigm of intransitive verbs in Kamnyu Japhug, using the verb ɕego in the Factual non-past This TAM category is chosen to illustrate the paradigms due to the fact that it does not bear any orientation preverb, but at the same time presents stem alternation in the transitive paradigm. as an example. Other Japhug dialects have slightly different indexation suffixes, a question discussed in § sec:indexation.suffixes.history with comparative evidence from other Gyalrong languages.

There is no stem alternation related to person indexation in the intransitive paradigm in any Japhug dialect. The invariable stem is represented with the symbol in tab:intransitive.indexation. This notation follows the Kirantological tradition (for instance ).

With a few well-identified exceptions, the indexation suffixes agree in person and number with the intransitive subject in Japhug. There is no indexation with possessors or oblique arguments, unlike closely related languages like Khroskyabs or Tangut.

In the intransitive paradigm, five suffixes and two prefixes are found. The stress is always on the last syllable of the verb stem (§ sec:suffixes, except in a handful of forms, § sec:stress ), and all person indexation suffixes, including -a, are unstressed and sometimes are even devoiced (§ sec:stress ). Unlike other languages of the Trans-Himalayan, such as Khaling (where the dual inclusive and the third dual are homophonous, see ), in Japhug all slots in the intransitive paradigm are distinct, without ambiguity.
summary:
The passage describes the intransitive indexation paradigm in Kamnyu Japhug, illustrated with the verb ɕego in the Factual non-past because this TAM has no orientation preverb, though the transitive paradigm shows stem alternation. In Japhug, there is no stem alternation tied to person indexation in any intransitive paradigm, and the verb stem is invariable in this respect.  

The suffixes generally agree with the intransitive subject in person and number, with no indexing of possessors or oblique arguments, and the paradigm contains five suffixes and two prefixes. Stress normally falls on the final syllable of the stem, the person suffixes are unstressed, and all slots in the intransitive paradigm are distinct without homophony.

text:
person!first
First person subjects are indexed by a set of three suffixes marking both person and number: -a, -tɕi and -ji for first singular, dual and plural, respectively. As in the pronominal paradigms (§ sec:pers.pronouns ), there is no inclusive/exclusive distinction in Japhug; inclusive first+second person is indexed as 1du or 1pl, as shown by examples such as ( ex:CWnARaRtCi ) where the 1du indexation corresponds to the sum of the 2sg and 1sg pronouns in the phrase nɤʑo cʰo aʑo ni. Equivalent examples with exclusive meaning ( 1sg + 3sg ) can be found in the corpus, for instance ( ex:cho.aCGAtCi ) below in § sec:intrinsically.n.sg.subject. In the transitive paradigm, the inclusive/exclusive distinction is not present either, but note the case of inclusive semi-reflexive configurations (§ sec:incl.semi.reflexive ).

exe

nɤʑo cʰo aʑo ni, nɤki, rɟɤmtsʰu ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu χsɯ-sŋi ɕɯ-nɤʁaʁ-tɕi, ɕɯ-nɤmɲole-tɕi. \\
2sg comit 1sg du filler sea 3sg. poss -on dem: loc three-day tral -have.a.good.time: fact - 1du tral -do.sightseeing: fact - 1du \\
`You and I will go on a three day tour on the sea.' (150827 mengjiangnv-zh)
0006290#S213
exe

The 1sg -a suffix is the only suffix in Japhug with a vowel other than ɯ (or i after palatal and alveolo-palatal consonants, § sec:W.i.contrast ), and is the only indexation suffix that can be followed by another indexation suffix in the transitive paradigm (§ sec:double.number.indexation ). The -a 1sg person index is among the suffixes revealing the underlying form of the codas: -β, -ɣ, -ʁ, -z, which become unvoiced in some contexts (§ sec:codas.inventory ) are realized as voiced (see for instance in tab:verb.stem.1sg below; -β is realized -w- in this context, since it becomes an onset, § sec:consonant.phonemes ), but the coda -t remains unvoiced (for instance scit-a be.happy- 1sg `I am happy'). The codas are resyllabified; for instance scit-a is syllabified as sci/ta ).

Some verb stems (independently of transitivity) undergo predictable phonological alterations when followed by -a. With verb stems whose last syllable is an open syllable, the -a suffix merges its vowel. With closed syllable verb stem in -ɤC (C representing a coda), the 1sg suffix causes vowel assimilation. These phonological rules are presented in tab:verb.stem.1sg.

When the verb stem ends in -a, the 1sg suffix merges with the stem as a in Kamnyu Japhug, resulting in homophony between the 1sg and the 3sg forms. The surface form rga corresponds to both 1sg rga-a `I like it' and 3sg rga `he likes it'. The fused and invisible suffix is systematically indicated in the orthography used in this grammar. In the Sarndzu of Japhug, a long vowel occurs in the 1sg, which thus remains different from the 3sg.

When the verb stem ends in vowels other than -a, these vowels undergo synizesis with the -a suffix (§ sec:synizesis ), merging into one syllable. In addition, the mid-high vowels -e and -o become the corresponding high vowels -i and -u in this context.

These vowel mergers are obligatory in the Kamnyu dialect. However, there are not attested in all Japhug dialects, which may favor hiatus.

With verb stem ending in -ɤt, -ɤn, -ɤβ, -ɤm, -ɤr, -ɤl and -ɤz, the 1sg suffix causes non-optional vowel assimilation -ɤC-a $ $ -aCa (§ sec:vowel.harmony ). tab:verb.stem.1sg provides examples for all rhymes of this type. In the orthography employed in this grammar, these forms are transcribed as aC-a rather than the underlying ɤC-a ( jɣat-a rather than jɣɤt-a ), to indicate the fact that ɤ $ $ a assimilation is obligatory in this context.

The first dual -tɕi suffix ( -tsə in some dialects of Japhug, § sec:indexation.suffixes.history ) only causes regular devoicing assimilation on the coda of the verb stem: -z, -r, -ɣ, -ʁ are realized as -s, -ʂ, -x, -χ when followed by -tɕi (for instance mkʰɤz-tɕi is pronounced mkʰɛ́stɕi ). The labial coda -β is not affected.

The first plural -ji has two allomorphs, -j and -i. The first one occurs on verb stems ending in open syllables, for instance ɕe-j `we (will) go', and the second follows verb stems in closed syllables, such as scit-i `we are happy', with resyllabification of the coda ( sci/ti ). Like the -a suffix discussed above, the suffix -i reveals the underlying form of the codas. The contrast between -ɯ and -i is neutralized as i when followed by the 1pl suffix: for instance, the last syllable of smi tʰɯ-βlɯ-j `we made a fire' and lɤpɯɣ pɯ-βli-j `we planted radish' is considered to be homophonous (the last syllable is realized as βlij ) by Tshendzin (§ sec:rhyme.inventory ).
summary: Japhug marks first-person subjects with three suffixes indicating person and number: -a for 1sg, -tɕi for 1du, and -ji/-j/-i for 1pl, with no inclusive/exclusive distinction in either the intransitive or transitive paradigms. The passage also describes how these suffixes trigger various phonological changes in verb stems, including resyllabification, vowel merger or assimilation, devoicing of final consonants, and in some cases homophony between 1sg and 3sg forms.

text:
person!second person!third
Second and third person forms have the same set of suffixes (zero, -ndʑi and -nɯ for singular, dual and plural, respectively) and only differ by the presence of a tɯ- prefix in second person forms. Unlike in Situ, there is no second person suffix in the 2sg.

The non-first person dual and plural suffixes -ndʑi and -nɯ (some Japhug dialects have -ndzə in the dual instead, see § sec:indexation.suffixes.history ) nasalize the coda -t to n, which is not audible before -ndʑi and results in a geminate in the plural. For instance, scit-ndʑi and scit-nɯ are realized as scíndʑi and scínnɯ, respectively. The vowel -i and -ɯ is often elided, resulting in apparent -n codas. The contrast between the codas -n and -t is neutralized in these forms: the last two syllables of both tu-nɤndɯt-nɯ ipfv -fight- pl `they fight (over it)' and pjɯ-ndɯn-nɯ ipfv -read- pl `they read/recite it' are thus realized as -ndɯ́nnɯ.

By contrast, the codas -β, -ɣ and -ʁ are not nasalized to m, ŋ and ɴ when followed by the suffixes -ndʑi and -nɯ, respectively.

The second person tɯ- prefix fuses with the initial a- of contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction ). The result of vowel fusion is tɯ-a- $ $ ta in the Factual Non-past ( tɯ-atɤr `you will fall down') or the Aorist ( jɤ-tɯ-ari `you went there'), but tɯ-ɤ- $ $ tɤ in Irrealis, Imperative, Imperfective or Prohibitive ( ma-tɤ-tɯ-ɤɕqʰe `don't cough') forms. Some irregular verbs have unpredictable second person forms (§ sec:intr.person.irregular ). The generic intransitive subject prefix kɯ- (also used for the object of transitive verbs, see § sec:indexation.generic.tr ) follows the same rules of vowel fusion as the second person prefix.
summary: Second- and third-person forms use the same suffixes for singular, dual, and plural, and differ only in that second person adds a tɯ- prefix; unlike in Situ, there is no special second-person suffix in the 2sg. The dual and plural suffixes -ndʑi and -nɯ nasalize a preceding -t, though this can be obscured by vowel elision, while codas -β, -ɣ, and -ʁ are not nasalized in this context. The tɯ- prefix also undergoes vowel fusion with initial a- in contracting verbs, and the generic intransitive subject prefix kɯ- follows the same fusion rules.

text:
morphology!irregular infix
In comparison with Zbu, Japhug only has very few irregular verbs. Irregularities related to person marking in Japhug all involve the prefixes.

The second person forms of Sensory Evidential existential verbs ɣɤʑuexist and maŋenot exist (§ sec:sensory.morphology ) are infixed rather than prefixed. The infixed forms are ɣɤtɤʑu and mataŋe, as in ( ex:GAtAZu ) (from ) and ( ex:kAmtshAm.mataNe ). These two verbs lack non-finite morphology (§ sec:nmlz.defective ) and do not occur in other tenses (§ sec:verbs.no.preverbs ) and can be considered to be suppletive forms of the existential verbs tuexist and menot exist (§ sec:suppletive.negative ).

exe

iɕqʰa tɯrme ra nɯ-rca ɣɤ<tɤ>ʑu \\
the.aforementioned person pl 3pl. poss -following <2sg>exist: sens \\
`[I saw] you among these people.' (elicited)
exe

exe

kɤ-mtsʰɤm maka ma<ta>ŋe tɕe, nɤ-kɯ-mŋɤm tu ɯβrɤ-ŋu ma, mɤ-kɯ-pe tu ɯβrɤ-ŋu ma nɯra nɯ-sɯso-t-a. \\
inf -hear at.all < 2sg >not.exist: sens lnk 2sg. poss - sbj: pcp -hurt exist: fact rh. q -be: fact sfp neg - sbj: pcp -be.good: fact exist: fact rh. q -be: fact sfp dem: pl aor -think- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`[I] have not heard at all about you [for some time], I was wondering whether you have some disease, whether something bad happened to you.' (phone conversation, 16-12-28)
exe

These are not the only infixed forms in the paradigm of these verbs: the generic person kɯ- is also infixed ( ɣɤkɤʑu, makaŋe ) as is the autive nɯ- (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ).

The verb zɣɯtarrive has in part of its paradigm forms that are identical to those of contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction ). In the Aorist, it has two alternative second person forms in free variation, the regular jɤ-tɯ-zɣɯt and the form jɤ-tɯ-azɣɯt with an additional a, illustrated by ( ex:jAtWzGWt.tCe ) and ( ex:jAtazGWt.mACtsxa ), coming from two versions of the same story by the same speaker.

exe

a-rkɯ mɯ-jɤ-tɯ-azɣɯt mɤɕtʂa mɯ-pɯ-ta-mtsʰɤm tɕe \\
1sg. poss -side neg - aor -2-arrive until neg - aor -1 2-hear lnk \\
`I did not feel your [presence] until you arrived near me.' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S224
exe

exe

jɤ-tɯ-zɣɯt tɕe, nɤki, aʑo a-kʰa a-jɤ-tɯ-z-mɤke ma nɤj nɤ-kʰa a-mɤ-jɤ-tɯ-z-mɤke ra mɯ-tɤ-tɯ-tɯt \\
aor -2-arrive lnk filler 1sg 1sg. poss -house irr - pfv -2- caus -be.first[III] lnk
2sg 2sg. poss -house irr - neg - pfv -2- caus -be.first[III] be.needed: fact neg - aor -2-say[III] \\
`You did not say ``When you arrive, don't go first to your house, come to my house first.'' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

The paradigm of this verb otherwise includes non-optional contracting ( jɤ-azɣɯt `he arrived') and non-contracting forms (the immediate converb ju-tɯ-zɣɯt `as soon as X arrived', § sec:immediate.converb ).
summary:
Japhug has very few irregular verbs, and the irregular person-marking forms all involve prefixes. In the Sensory Evidential existential verbs ɣɤʑuexist and maŋenot exist, the second-person forms are infixed rather than prefixed, and these verbs also show other infixed person markers such as generic kɯ- and autive nɯ-.  

The verb zɣɯtarrive also shows irregularity in part of its paradigm: in the Aorist, it has two free-variant second-person forms, one regular and one with an extra a. Elsewhere, its paradigm includes both contracting and non-contracting forms.

text:
verb!semi-transitive
Semi-transitive verbs have the same paradigm as plain intransitive verbs, and lack the morphological properties of transitive verbs (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ). Their intransitive subject is in absolutive form. However, they take a semi-object (§ sec:semi.object ), also in absolutive form, as paχɕiapple in ( ex:paXCi.ci.taroa ). These semi-objects do present some objectal properties (§ sec:semi.object, § sec:semi.tr.relativization ).

exe

tɕe aʑo tʰam kɯki, paχɕi ci tɤ-aro-a tɕe tɕendɤre,
[...] nɯʑora kɯnɤ ta-sɯ-ɤʁe-nɯ ra \\
lnk 1sg now dem. prox apple indef aor -have- 1sg lnk lnk 2pl also 1 2- caus -be.needed.eat: fact - pl be.needed: fact \\
`Now that I have (i.e. was given) this apple, I will give it to you also to eat.' (150904 zhongli-zh)
0006348#S32
exe

Unlike transitive verbs, which can index the number of the object if the subject is 1sg (§ sec:double.number.indexation ), semi-transitive verbs cannot add a person index after the 1sg -a. For instance, in ( ex:XsWm.aroa ), although the object is plural, a form such as $ $ aroa-a-nɯ with the -nɯ plural prefix is strictly prohibited.

exe

aʑo tɤ-rɟit χsɯm aro-a \\
I indef. poss -child three have: fact - 1sg \\
`I have three children.' (elicited)
exe

optional case marking
The subject of some semi-transitive verbs, in particular tsoknow, understand and ʑɣɤpapretend, can optionally be marked with the ergative like a transitive subject (§ sec:S.kW ), as tɤ-mu nɯ kɯ in ( ex:kW.mWpjAtso ) and βdaʁmu nɯ kɯ in ( ex:kW.toZGApa ).

exe

tɕendɤre [tɤ-mu nɯ kɯ] ɕɯ ŋu nɯ maka mɯ-pjɤ-tso tɕeri \\
lnk indef. poss -mother dem erg who be: fact dem at.all neg - ifr. ipfv -know lnk \\
`The old woman did not realize who it was.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

exe

iɕqʰa βdaʁmu nɯ kɯ [wuma ʑo ɯ-sɯm kɯ-sna] to-ʑɣɤpa \\
the.aforementioned lady dem erg really emph 3sg. poss -mind sbj: pcp -be.good ifr -pretend \\
`The lady pretended to be a good person.' (140520 ye tiane-zh) 0004044#S41
exe

Some semi-transitive verbs can take both nominal semi-objects and complement clauses. For instance, tso (which can be translated as `know', `understand' or `realize' depending on the context) occurs with nouns referring to speech or meaning as semi-object (as in ex:apWtWtso.smWlAm ), finite relative clauses ( ex:rCanW.mWkAtsoa ) and also participial clauses ( ex:kWNu.kutsoa, § sec:tso.sWXsAl ).

exe

pja mɯndʐamɯχtɕɯɣ nɯ-skɤt a-pɯ-tɯ-tso smɯlɤm\\
bird all.kinds 3pl. poss -speech irr - ipfv -2-understand prayer\\
`May you understand the speech of all species of birds!' (2003kandZislama)
exe

exe

ci kɤ-pa-tɕi, nɯstʰɯci tɤ-nɤrʑaʁ ri, [nɯstʰɯci nɤ-ku ʑru rcanɯ] mɯ-kɤ-tso-a \\
one aor -do- 1du so.much aor -pass(time) lnk so.much 2sg. poss -head be.strong: fact unexp: deg neg - aor -know- 1sg \\
`So much time has passed since we have married, I did not realize that your hair was so long.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

exe

tɕe [tɕʰi ɯ-skɤt kɯ-ŋu ra] ku-tso-a ɲɯ-ra ma tu-tɯ-ti stɯsti, mɯ́j-ɕɯftaʁ-a ɲɯ-ti \\
lnk what 3sg. poss -speech sbj: pcp -be pl ipfv -understand- 1sg sens -be.needed lnk ipfv -2-say alone neg: sens -remember- 1sg sens -say \\
`He says: `I need to understand what it is about (what objects these words refer to), otherwise if you only speak (if you only explain orally) I won't remember.'' (conversation 14-05-10)
exe

Among semi-transitive verbs, we find the following subclasses:

itemize
Verbs of cognition and perception: tsoknow, understand, `know' sɤŋolisten
Verbs of evaluation: rgalike, stubelieve, dɯɣhave enough of
Modal verbs: cʰacan
Verbs of possession: aroown
Copulas: ŋube, maʁnot be, apabecome (§ sec:copula.basic )
Verbs of assignation: rmibe called, artsibe counted as, fsebe like
Verbs requiring an argument expressing time: acʰɤtbe $X$ years apart, tsupass (of time)
Verbs of pretence: ʑɣɤpapretend
Verbs of obtaining (§ sec:preverb.gain ): aʁehave to eat/drink, βɟɤtobtain
Some adjectival stative verbs: mkʰɤzbe expert, pʰɤnbe efficient
itemize

The Tshobdun verbs cʰɐ `can, be able' and rge `like', cognates of the Japhug semi-transitive verbs cʰacan and rgalike, are fully transitive, as shown by the forms mɐ-koɣ-cʰɐ-aŋ ( neg -2 1-can- 1sg ) `you cannot (kill) me' and ne-tɐ-rge ( ipfv -1 2-like) `I love you', which occur with local portmanteau prefixes (§ sec:indexation.local ).

Most semi-transitive verbs are underived bare roots. The only obviously derived verbs are ʑɣɤpapretend, which comes from the reflexive of the verb pado (§ sec:lexicalized.refl ) and artsibe counted as, passive of rtsicount. The verb aroown is possibly analyzable as a denominal verb historically derived from tɤ-rosurplus, leftover (§ sec:bare.action.nominals, § sec:denom.a ).

Most semi-transitive verbs do not usually take a human semi-object, so that sentences with a first or second person semi-object are generally clumsy to build. For some of the verbs above, applicative forms are used when a first or second person object is needed, for instance nɯrgalike and nɤstubelieve(§ sec:applicative.promoted ). The verbs stubelieve and nɤstubelieve differ in that the semi-object of the former refers to words (in general, a complement clause; `believe that X') while the object of the latter is a person (`believe him').

However, examples with subjects and semi-objects both either first or second person are attested. For instance, ( ex:WYWfsea ) shows a very spontaneous use of a 2sg semi-object with a 1sg subject with the verb fsebe like. Only the subject is indexed (with the suffix -a ) and the use of the transitive ta- 1 2 portmanteau prefix (§ sec:indexation.local ) here would be nonsensical.

exe

a-ʁi, nɤʑo ɯ-ɲɯ-fse-a? \\
1sg. poss -younger.sibling 2sg qu - sens -be.like- 1sg \\
`Sister, do I look like you?' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

The same is observed with the copulas ŋube, maʁnot be and also apabecome as in ( ex:nAZo.napaa ) and ( ex:aZo.nWtapa ). (see also § sec:copula.basic ) The copulas always index the subject, never the semi-object, independently of any person hierarchy (see ex:empathy.hierarchy.japhug in § sec:direct-inverse below), and cannot take the ta- 1 2 and kɯ- 2 1 portmanteau prefixes.

exe

nɤʑo nɯ-apa-a \\
2sg aor -become- 1sg \\
`I became you.' (elicited)
exe

exe

aʑo nɯ-tɯ-apa \\
1sg aor -2-become \\
`You became me.' (elicited)
exe
summary: Semi-transitive verbs in Japhug use the same paradigm as intransitive verbs and do not show the morphological properties of transitive verbs; their subject is absolutive, and they take an absolutive semi-object that still behaves somewhat like an object. They cannot index object number like transitive verbs do, though some semi-transitive verbs optionally allow ergative marking on the subject, and a few can combine with either nominal semi-objects or complement clauses. The passage also lists several subclasses of semi-transitive verbs, notes that most are bare roots, and says that when first- or second-person semi-objects are needed, applicative forms are often used, though some direct examples with such semi-objects are attested.

text:
Some semi-transitive verbs are labile; some have a transitive counterpart, while others have a plain intransitive one (§ sec:semi.tr.labile ). The meaning of the verb also slightly changes depending on transitivity (for instance, rga means `like' when semi-transitive, and `be happy' when stative intransitive).

The antipassive form of secundative verbs (§ sec:secundative.theme ), such as rɤmbigive to someone have a status intermediate between semi-transitive and monotransitive verbs: they lack most transitive features (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ), but can index first and second person objects (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative, § sec:antipassive.ditransitive ).
summary: Some semi-transitive verbs are labile, with either a transitive or a plain intransitive counterpart, and their meaning changes slightly with transitivity; for example, *rga* means “like” as a semi-transitive verb and “be happy” as a stative intransitive. The antipassive form of secundative verbs, such as *rɤmbi* “give to someone,” has an intermediate status between semi-transitive and monotransitive verbs: it lacks most transitive features but can still index first- and second-person objects.

text:
verb!intransitive argument!oblique
Semi-transitive verbs have to be distinguished from motion verbs (or perception verbs) with a goal (§ absolutive.goal ), such as ɕego, ɣicome or rulook at. These verbs are morphologically intransitive, lacking the morphological characteristics of transitive verbs (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ).

With these verbs, the goal can occur in absolutive form, and superficially resembles a semi-object, as sɯŋgɯforest in ( ex:sWNgW.joCendZi ). Indexation obligatorily occurs with the subject (for example, the 3du form in ex:sWNgW.joCendZi ), never with the goal. As in the case of semi-transitive verbs, number stacking on the 1sg -a is not possible (§ sec:semi.transitive, example ex:XsWm.aroa ).

exe

ʁnɯz ni, [sɯŋgɯ] jo-ɕe-ndʑi. \\
two du forest ifr -go- du \\
`Two [men] went into the forest.' (26-tAGe) 0003686#S1
exe

However, unlike semi-objects, these goals can optionally take locative postpositions, such as zɯ in ( ex:sWNgW.zW.joCe ).

exe

tɤ-pɤtso nɯnɯ li [sɯŋgɯ zɯ] jo-ɕe. \\
indef. poss -child dem again forest loc ifr -go \\
`The child went again into the forest.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifen-zh) 0003886#S217
exe

Dative marking on the goals is also well-attested, as in ( ex:sWNgW.WCki.joCe ) -- with motion verbs, it translates as `towards X'.

exe

tɕʰemɤpɯ nɯ kɯ ɯ-wa cʰo ɯ-pi nɯra ɲɤ-βde tɕe, sɯŋgɯ ɯ-ɕki tɕe jo-ɕe. \\
girl dem erg 3sg. poss -father comit 3sg. poss -elder.sibling dem: pl ifr -leave lnk forest 3sg. poss - dat loc ifr -go \\
`The girl left her father and her brothers, and went toward the forest.' (140506 shizi he huichang de bailingniao)
0003927#S72
exe

The subject of intransitive verbs with goals is in absolutive form, except when shared with a transitive verb in another clause, as tɕʰemɤpɯ nɯ kɯ in ( ex:sWNgW.WCki.joCe ), which owes its ergative marking to the transitive verb ɲɤ-βde `She left them'. The verb rpubump into (which takes as goal the surface of physical contact) however can take ergative subjects, as it is labile and can be conjugated transitively (§ sec:goal.labile ). Transitive verbs of manipulation can optionally take goals that are formally similar to those of ɕego and ɣicome (§ sec:secundative.monotransitive ).

Some intransitive verbs of speech, rɯɕmispeak and akʰucall, can optionally take a dative argument, as in ( ex:WCki.turWCmia ).

exe

tɯrme ɯ-ɕki tu-rɯɕmi-a ɕti wo \\
person 3sg. poss - dat ipfv -speak- 1sg be. aff: fact sfp \\
`I am talking to someone [else].' (phone conversation, 2013-12-02)
exe

Other than locative and dative, some intransitive verbs select oblique arguments with the genitive (§ sec:genitive ) the relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:WtaR ) and verbs with intrinsically non-singular subjects often occur with comitative postpositional phrases in cʰo (§ sec:intrinsically.n.sg.subject ).

Some intransitive verbs which cannot take semi-objects do occur with counted nouns (in particular, rɯɕmispeak); these counted nouns however have scope over the whole sentence, and are not arguments of these verbs, as argued in § sec:CN.iterative.
summary:
Semi-transitive verbs must be distinguished from motion and perception verbs that take a goal, because these verbs are morphologically intransitive but allow an absolutive goal that may look superficially like a semi-object. The subject is obligatorily indexed, never the goal, and the goal may optionally take locative or dative marking; in some cases, intransitive speech verbs can also take dative arguments.  

The passage also notes that intransitive verbs may select other oblique arguments, such as genitive phrases, relator nouns, or comitative phrases, and that some verbs can occur with counted nouns that have sentence-wide scope rather than functioning as arguments.

subsection: Semi-transitive verbs with additional oblique arguments
text:
verb!intransitive argument!oblique
Some semi-transitive verbs can have up to three arguments, and are therefore trivalent.
This shows that trivalent verbs in Japhug are not necessarily ditransitive (§ sec:ditransitive ).
This is the case of rogative verbs (§ sec:rogative.derivation ) such as sɤmbiask for (derived from the secundative verb mbigive), which have both a dative argument and a semi-object, as shown by ( ex:Wphe.piaozi ), but are yet conjugated intransitively (the generic subject is marked by kɯ, § sec:indexation.generic.tr ).

exe

<guojia> ɯ-pʰe <piaozi> ɲɯ-kɯ-sɤ-mbi \\
country 3sg. poss - dat money ipfv - genr:S/O- rog -give \\
`Ask the government for money.' (2010)
exe
summary: Some semi-transitive verbs in Japhug can take up to three arguments and are therefore trivalent, but this does not mean they are ditransitive. An example is the rogative verb sɤmbi ‘ask for,’ derived from the secundative verb mbi ‘give’: it takes both a dative argument and a semi-object, yet is still conjugated intransitively, with the generic subject marked by kɯ.

text:
verb!intransitive subject!intransitive subject!non-singular
Some intransitive verbs have an intrinsic reciprocal meaning, and do not occur in singular form. This category includes most derived reciprocal verbs (§ sec:reciprocal ), but also some historical reciprocal verbs that are synchronically non-analyzable such as amɯmibe on good terms, and denominal verbs in a- like anɯmqajfight or aɕɣabe the same age (§ sec:denom.a ). Example ( ex:atAtAnWmqajnW ) provides some examples of verbs of this type. In the corpus, these verbs only occur in dual or plural form.

exe

tɕe a-pi a-ʁi ra kutɕu a-nɯ-tɯ-ɤnɯɣro-nɯ, ci ci a-tɤ-tɯ-ɤnɯmqaj-nɯ, ci ci a-tɤ-tɯ-ɤmɯmi-nɯ qʰe a-kɤ-tɯ-nɯ-rɤʑi-nɯ, \\
lnk 1sg. poss -elder.sibling 1sg. poss -younger.sibling pl here irr - pfv -2-< auto >play- pl once once irr - pfv -2-fight- pl once once irr - pfv -2-be.on.good.terms- pl lnk irr - pfv -2- auto -stay- pl \\
`Brothers, stay here and play, fight from time to time, reconcile with each other from time to time.' (2003kandzwsqhaj)
exe

The subject of these verbs can be a noun phrase comprising a comitative postpositional phrase in cʰo (see § sec:comitative and § sec:coordinator.cho ), in particular with reciprocal verbs (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ); number indexation on the verb reflects the addition of the added number of all nominals in the noun phrase. For example, in ( ex:cho.pjAkAmWmindZi ) and ( ex:cho.aCGAtCi ), the verbs have dual indexation, referring to the total number of individuals in the subject noun phrase connected by the comitative cʰo.

exe

<maerjina> nɯ cʰo <alibaba> ni wuma ʑo pjɤ-k-ɤmɯmi-ndʑi tɕe \\
anthr dem comit anthr du really emph pst. ifr - peg -be.on.good.terms- du lnk \\
`Maerjina and Alibaba were in very good terms.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S291
exe

exe

nɤj nɤ-mu cʰo aʑo ni aɕɣa-tɕi \\
2sg 2sg. poss -mother comit 1sg du be.of.the.same.age: fact - 1du \\
`I have the same age as your mother.' (`You mother and I have the same age') (elicited)
exe

The verb acʰɤtbe $X$ years apart has an intrinsically non-singular subject, and is at the same time semi-transitive (§ sec:semi.transitive ), taking as semi-object a temporal noun phrase expressing the age difference between the members of the group referred to by the subject (§ sec:a.non.passive.denominal ).

The verb alɯlɤtfight, historically the reciprocal of lɤtrelease (§ sec:redp.lexicalized ), almost always has non-singular indexation, either with a non-singular intransitive subject as in ( ex:qro.ni.YAlWlAtndZi ), or with a comitative phrase ( ex:cho.tokAlWlAtndZi ) as in examples ( ex:cho.pjAkAmWmindZi ) and ( ex:cho.aCGAtCi ) above.

exe

tɕeki qro ni ɲɯ-ɤlɯlɤt-ndʑi \\
down ant du sens -fight- du \\
`Down there two ants are fighting.' (conversation140501-01)
exe

exe

ʁdɯxpakɤrpu ɯ-tɕɯ cʰondɤre a-tɕɯ ni to-k-ɤlɯlɤt-ndʑi \\
anthr 3sg. poss -son comit 3sg. poss -son du ifr - peg -fight- du \\
`The son of Gdugpa Dkarpo fought with my son.' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

However, examples with singular indexation are also attested, for instance ( ex:tAtalWlAt ) and ( ex:tutalWlAt ) with 2sg form. Both are from texts translated from Chinese, but were not considered infelicitous by Tshendzin. While direct Chinese influence on indexation is unlikely, the use of alɯlɤtfight with the person one fights against left unexpressed (as in ex:tAtalWlAt ) or marked in the dative (as in ex:tutalWlAt ), is not attested elsewhere. The Chinese original sentences of examples ( ex:tAtalWlAt ) and ( ex:tutalWlAt ) are 你是为众人的利益而战 nǐ shì wèi zhòngrén de lìyì érzhànYou were fighting for the interest of the people and 你不该和舅舅动手 nǐ bùgāi hé jiùjiù dòngshǒuYou should not get into a fight with your uncle.

exe

ki ɕɯŋgɯ ki pɯpɯŋunɤ, nɤʑo kɯ iɕqʰa mkʰɤrmaŋ ɣɯ nɯ-ndʐa kɯ tɤ-tɯ-alɯlɤt pɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
dem. prox before dem. prox top 2sg erg filler people gen 3pl. poss -reason erg aor -2-fight pst. ipfv -be lnk \\
`The previous time, you fought for the sake of the people.' (140512 abide he mogui-zh)
0003975#S86
exe

exe

tɕe nɤʑo nɤ-rpɯ ɯ-ɕki, nɤkinɯ, tu-tɯ-ɤlɯlɤt ndɤre mɤ-pe \\
lnk 2sg 2sg. poss -MB 3sg. poss - dat filler ipfv -2-fight lnk neg -be.good: fact \\
`It is not good for you to fight with your uncle.' (150826 baoliandeng-zh)
0006370#S178
exe

The verb naχtɕɯɣbe the same, although requiring the comparison of at least two entities, most often occurs with singular indexation, as shown by examples like ( ex:WGli.cho.naXtCWG ) and ( ex:ndZitWwxti.YWnaXtCWG ). This may be due to the fact naχtɕɯɣbe the same is commonly used with inanimate referents (§ sec:optional.indexation ), and also because it commonly takes degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominals ) as subjects in the equative construction (§ sec:nmlz.equative ). These degree nominals can take non-singular possessors (dual in ex:ndZitWwxti.YWnaXtCWG ), but remain themselves singular arguments.

exe

lnk dem sheep 3sg. poss -dung dem again goat 3sg. poss -dung comit be.the.same: fact emph lnk \\

The passage also notes that while verbs like *acʰɤtbe* ‘X years apart’ and *alɯlɤt* ‘fight’ usually show non-singular indexation, singular forms are occasionally attested for *alɯlɤt*, whereas *naχtɕɯɣbe* ‘be the same’ often takes singular indexation despite requiring comparison between at least two entities.

verb!intransitive verb!invariable
A non-negligible amount of intransitive verbs are only attested in 3sg form. Four categories must be distinguished.

First, we find intransitive auxiliary verbs taking complement clauses as intransitive subjects (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ), for instance jɤɣbe allowed, which has 3sg indexation regardless of the person of the subject or the object in the complement clause, as shown by example ( ex:YWkhama.jAG ). For verbs of this type, the indexation restriction is structurally determined and independent of semantics.

aʑo a-me nɯ [nɤʑɯɣ nɤ-rʑaβ ɲɯ-kʰam-a] jɤɣ, [nɤ-rʑaβ a-kɤ-βze] jɤɣ \\

A second type of invariable verbs are those exclusively attested in noun-verb collocations where the noun is the intransitive subject. For instance, the intransitive verbs mbi and ŋgɯ are only found There are homophonous verbs such as the transitive mbigive and the adjectival stative verb ŋgɯbe poor but these are synchronically and even historically unrealted ( mbi is an anticausative verb, see § sec:anticausative.collocation ). in collocation with tɤ-mbrɯanger and the orphan noun tɯ-ʁo, meaning `be angry' and `be discouraged be frustrated, lose heart', respectively. The person and number of the experiencer are marked by the possessive prefix on the nouns, as in ( ex:nWRo.amAnWmbi ), and since these nouns are always singular, the verb indexation is also always in 3sg form.

The verb ɣi is compatible with all person indexation affixes, but in this collocation it is only found in 3sg, regardless of the person of the possessive prefix on tɯ-ʁjiz, as shown by ( ex:aRjiz.Gi.Cti ).

It also notes that some verbs seem invariant only because non-3sg forms are rare, since at least one such verb can in fact appear with non-3sg indexation.
