subsection: The morphological marking of transitivity in Japhug
text:
transitivity!morphology morphology!transitivity
Transitivity in Japhug can be defined exclusively on the basis of verbal morphology. Transitive verbs have the following six common properties.

Aorist
First, the Aorist 3 sg 3$'$ (§ sec:aor.morphology, § sec:preverb.TAME.morphology ), The notation 3 sg 3$'$ means `third singular subject with another third person object', see § sec:polypersonal. a form that is attested on all transitive verbs except for one (§ sec:irregular.transitive ) requires a C-type orientation preverb (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) in Kamnyu Japhug. This test can always be applied to distinguish a transitive verb from an intransitive one. For instance, the Aorist 3 sg 3$'$ of ndzaeat is ta-ndza `he ate it' with the C-type prefix ta, while an A-type prefix tɤ- would be expected if the verb were intransitive (the incorrect form $ $ tɤ-ndza ). A potential problem with this test is the fact that the result of the merger of A-type orientation preverbs with the initial a- of contracting verbs (which are always intransitive, see § sec:contraction ) is formally identical to a C-type prefix, for instance the Aorist 3sg tɤ-ala `it boiled up' is realized tala, the first syllable ta- being homophonous with that of ta-ndza `he ate it'. It is therefore necessary to take into consideration the Factual Non-Past form (§ sec:fact.morphology ) to determine whether the stem has initial a-. A contrast similar to the one between A-type and C-type orientation preverbs is also found on the apprehensive prefix ɕɯ, which has a form ɕa- in the 3 sg 3$'$ Past form of transitive verbs (§ sec:apprehensive ).

Second, verbs with open-syllable stems allowing stem III alternation ( -a, -o, -u and -ɯ, § sec:stem3.form ) have stem III in all sg 3 non-past finite forms (§ sec:stem3.distribution ). For instance, the Factual Non-Past 3 sg 3$'$ of ndzaeat has the stem III form ndze `he will eat it'. If this were intransitive, the stem I ndza would be found instead. This alternation is an effective test to determine if a verb is transitive or not, but its applicability depends on the form of the stem.

infinitive!bare
Third, transitive verbs require a bare infinitive (§ sec:bare.inf ) when occurring in specific complement clauses, while intransitive verbs select dental infinitives (§ sec:dental.inf ). In ( ex:Wndza.tuZanW ) for example, ndzaeat occurs in a complement clause governed by the phasal verb tu-ʑa-nɯ `they start' in bare infinitive form. If it were an intransitive verb, a dental infinitive ($ $ tɯ-ndza tu-ʑa-nɯ ) would be found instead. This criterion is not applicable to all verbs, since some of them cannot occur in the subtype of complement clauses where bare infinitives are found for semantic reasons.

exe

ɕlaʁ pjɯ-si ɕɯŋgɯ qʰe ɯ-ɕa ɯ-ndza tu-ʑa-nɯ. \\
idph (I):immediately ipfv -die before lnk 3sg. poss -meat 3sg. poss - bare. inf:eat ipfv -start- pl \\
`They start eating its flesh just before it dies.' (20-sWNgi)
0003562#S54
exe

participle!transitive
Fourth, the subject participles of transitive verbs require a possessive prefix coreferent with the object, unless another inflectional prefix (marking orientation, polarity or associated motion) precedes the participle prefix kɯ- (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ). The subject participle of ndzaeat is thus ɯ-kɯ-ndza `the one who eats it', and the prefix ɯ- cannot be removed. In the negative form mɤ-kɯ-ndza ( neg - pcp: sbj -eat) `the one who does not eat it', by contrast, the possessive prefix ɯ- is optional.

past tense!suffix
Fifth, transitive verbs with open-syllable stems require the past tense -t suffix (§ sec:suffixes, § sec:indexation.mixed, § sec:other.TAME ) in Aorist and Past Imperfective 1sg 3 and 2sg 3 forms. For example, tɤ-ndza-t-a `I ate it' has this past suffix; if this verb were intransitive, a form such as $ $ tɤ-ndza-a would be found instead. This criterion only applies to open-syllable transitive verbs allowing first and second person subjects.

Progressive
Sixth, the Progressive asɯ- (§ sec:progressive.morphology ) is only found on transitive verbs. For instance, the transitive verb ndzaeat has a Progressive Sensory 3 sg 3$'$ form ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-ndza `He is eating it', which would not exist if this verb were intransitive.

Seventh, only transitive verbs Antipassive secundative verbs such as rɤmbigive to someone are the only exception, see § sec:secundative.theme, examples ( ex:nWwGrAmbia ) and ( ex:YAkWrAmbia ). can take the inverse wɣ- (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ) and the portmanteau kɯ- 2 1 and ta- 1 2 prefixes (§ sec:indexation.local ). The portmanteau prefixes are only found on verbs allowing human subjects and objects.

These seven criteria are almost completely congruent. With the exception of a handful of defective verbs (§ sec:irregular.transitive ), the dummy transitive subject construction (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), and the antipassive forms of some secundative verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative, § sec:antipassive.ditransitive ), if a verb satisfies one of these criteria, it will satisfies them all. This excludes cases when particular tests are not applicable, in particular criteria 2 and 5 if the verb has a closed-syllable stem or 3, 5, 6 and 7 due to semantic incompatibility. Only criteria 1 and 4 apply to all verbs.

Intransitive verbs, including semi-transitive verbs (§ sec:semi.transitive ) do not satisfy any of these seven criteria, as can be exemplified with the verb tsoknow, understand ( tab:tso.tests and example ex:tWtso.kAZata illustrating test 3).

exe

aʑo tɯ-tso kɤ-ʑa-t-a \\
1sg inf:II-understand aor -start- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I began to understand.' (elicited)
exe

The morphosyntactic specificities of transitive verbs are not limited to inflectional verbal morphology. Some derivational processes, such as antipassivization (§ sec:antipassive ) and anticausativization (§ sec:anticausative.direction ) can only be applied to transitive verbs, and conversely other derivations (such as the applicative, § sec:applicative ) are only attested on intransitive verbs. Since derivational morphology however, is not as productive as inflectional morphology and can be sometimes ambiguous, these characteristics cannot be used to define transitivity in Japhug.
summary:
In Japhug, transitivity is defined entirely by verbal inflectional morphology, and transitive verbs are identified by a set of seven largely overlapping diagnostic properties. These include special Aorist orientation marking, stem III alternation in certain non-past forms, use of bare infinitives in some complement clauses, obligatory possessive marking on transitive subject participles, a past suffix in certain open-syllable forms, the Progressive prefix asɯ-, and the ability to take inverse and certain portmanteau prefixes.

The passage notes that most verbs matching one criterion match the others as well, except for a few defective or semantically restricted cases, and that intransitive and semi-transitive verbs do not show any of these properties. It also says some derivational processes are restricted to transitive or intransitive verbs, but these are not used to define transitivity because they are less productive and can be ambiguous.

subsection: The morphological marking of transitivity in Japhug
text: Another distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs is the fact that transitive subjects require ergative marking (§ sec:A.kW ), whereas intransitive subjects are generally in absolutive form (§ sec:absolutive.S ). This is not an absolute criterion to distinguish between transitive and intransitive verbs, however, since some transitive verbs have a dummy subject (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), and since intransitive verbs with ergative marking are attested in specific contexts (§ sec:S.kW, § sec:long.distance.kW ).
summary: Transitive subjects are typically marked with ergative case, while intransitive subjects are generally in absolutive form. However, this is not an absolute diagnostic, because some transitive verbs take dummy subjects and some intransitive verbs can appear with ergative marking in certain contexts.

text:
In Japhug, as in other Gyalrongic languages, transitive verbs index two arguments, the transitive subject and the object. This section provides a detailed analysis of the transitive indexation paradigm in comparison with the intransitive conjugation.

The transitive conjugation comprises 31 different forms for each TAME category, as listed in tab:japhug.tr on p. tab:japhug.tr. tab:mto.paradigm exemplifies this paradigm using the Factual Non-Past of the verb mtosee. These two-dimensional tables (and all other such tables in this chapter) list the subjects as rows and the objects as columns. The polypersonal configurations are represented using the notation $A$ $P$, where $A$ stands for the person and number of the transitive subject, and $P$ for that of the object; for instance 1sg 3du means `first singular subject with third du object'. 3$'$ represents obviative third person, a concept described in more detail in § sec:indexation.non.local. The shaded cells 1 1, 2 2, 3 3 and 3$'$ 3$'$ correspond to reflexive forms, which are not transitive in Japhug, and are expressed by deriving an intransitive verb using the prefix ʑɣɤ- (§ sec:reflexive ). Generic person (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ) is not included in tab:japhug.tr.

One of the most fundamental features of the Japhug indexation system is the fact that the affixes found in the intransitive paradigm also occur in the transitive conjugation, and can index either the subject (intransitive S or transitive A) or the object (O) (depending on the presence or absence of direction marking, § sec:direct-inverse ) as illustrated in tab:neutral.alignment with the suffix -a and the prefix tɯ-. In other words, the indexation affixes reflect neutral alignment.

When studying indexation systems of this type, it is useful to divide the space of bipersonal indexation into three domains: the local domain (when both subject and object are first or second person), the non - local domain (when both subject and object are third person) and the mixed domain (one argument is first or second person and the other one is third person). tab:domain represents these three domains in blue, red and green, respectively.

In the following sections, we first present the forms of the transitive paradigm in each of the three domains, then discuss some specific issues (generic and double number indexation) and then analyze the structure of the Japhug indexation system in a typological perspective.

landscape

landscape
summary:
Japhug transitive verbs index both the subject and the object, and the transitive paradigm has 31 forms in each TAME category. The same affixes used in the intransitive paradigm can mark either the transitive subject or the object depending on direction marking, showing neutral alignment.  

The system is organized into local, non-local, and mixed domains according to the person values of the two arguments, and reflexive combinations are excluded because they are expressed with derived intransitive forms.

text:
person!mixed configuration
In the mixed domain, we have to distinguish between direct configurations, where the subject is first or second person and the object is third person (1 3, 2 3) and inverse configurations, where the opposite holds true (3 1, 3 2). This terminology will be justified in § sec:direct-inverse.

tab:mixed.direct presents all 1 3 and 2 3 forms (except 1sg 3 du/pl, which are discussed in § sec:double.number.indexation ) of mtosee in the Factual Non-Past and the Aorist, compared with the corresponding forms of the intransitive verb ngobe ill. The downwards pɯ- and upwards tɤ- preverbs are lexically selected by these verbs (§ sec:preverb.perception ).

With the exception of 1sg 3 forms (on which see § sec:double.number.indexation ), the number of the third person argument is never expressed in the mixed domain. Examples ( ex:kAfstWni ) and ( ex:ni.pjWsati ) illustrate 1pl 3sg and 1pl 3du forms, respectively. Whether the third person object is singular or dual, person indexation is restricted to the 1pl -ji suffix in both cases. The same is true of the -tɕi suffix, and also in inverse configurations.

exe

tɕe iʑo ji-kʰa kɯnɤ kɤ-fstɯn-i pɯ-ra \\
lnk 1pl 1pl. poss -house also aor -serve- 1pl pst. ipfv -be.needed \\
`We also had to take care of him in our house.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S324
exe

exe

nɤ-wɯ cʰo nɤ-ʁi ni pjɯ-sat-i ŋu \\
2sg. poss -grandfather comit 2sg. poss -younger.sibling du ipfv -kill- 1pl be: fact \\
`We will kill your grandfather and your brother.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

Although the indexation suffixes -ndʑi and -nɯ are the same for second and third person (§ sec:intr.23 ), in 2 3 and 3 2 configurations, they can only index the number of the second person argument, never that of the third person. For instance, in ( ex:ra.totWGWt ), to-tɯ-ɣɯt is 2sg 3pl, and adding a plural -nɯ here would change the meaning to `you$_pl$ brought people' and be incompatible with the singular pronoun nɤʑo.

exe

nɤʑo tɯrme ra to-tɯ-ɣɯt tɕe, \\
2sg people pl ifr: up -2-bring lnk \\
`You( sg ) brought people [here].' (150901 changfamei)
0006352#S146
exe

The direct forms of the transitive paradigm are nearly all identical to the corresponding intransitive paradigm. The 1sg 3 and 2sg 3 forms are the only ones that show morphological features absent from the corresponding intransitive paradigm: the Stem III alternation in the Factual Non-Past (and other tenses, § sec:stem3.distribution, § sec:stem.TAME ) Note in addition the allomorph mtam- of stem III when followed by the 1sg suffix -a, following regular vowel assimilation (§ sec:intr.1 ).
and the -t suffix in the Past. These features are highlighted in red in tab:mixed.direct. Most dialects of Japhug, including those of Gdongbrgyad township, have -z instead of -t as Past suffix (§ sec:suffixes ).

Stem III alternation and the -t suffix mark at the same time TAME (§ sec:other.TAME, § sec:suffixes ) and person of both subject and object, and must be considered to be an integral part of the person indexation system.

Not all transitive verbs present these two features, however; in particular, verb with close syllable stems lack both of them. Stem alternation is restricted to a few open-syllable stem types ( -o, -a, -u and -ɯ, § sec:stem3.form ), and the -t suffix cannot surface in close syllable stems. For instance, the Aorist 1sg 3sg of the verbs joʁraise and ɕlɯɣdrop are tɤ-joʁ-a `I raised it' and pɯ-ɕlɯɣ-a `I dropped it', not the completely incorrect $ $ tɤ-joʁ-t-a or $ $ pɯ-ɕlɯɣ-t-a (with automatic regressive devoicing of ʁ and ɣ before t, § sec:codas.inventory ). These incorrect forms would not violate Japhug phonotactics, since clusters such as -χt- and -xt- are well attested (§ sec:xC.clusters, § sec:XC.clusters ), showing that the rules governing the use of the -t suffix are not purely phonological.

The direct forms of transitive verbs with closed syllable stems (such as joʁraise and ɕlɯɣdrop) in the mixed domain are thus identical to that of intransitive verbs.

The inverse forms of the mixed domain of the verb mtosee are presented in tab:mixed.inverse. All forms in this section of the paradigm, regardless of the TAME category, take the prefix ɣɯ́-/wɣ, whose distribution and allomorphy ( ɣɯ́- vs. wɣ- ) is discussed in more detail in § sec:allomorphy.inv.

Aside from the prefix ɣɯ́-/wɣ, the inverse forms in the mixed domain present the same affixes as those of the corresponding intransitive forms (except in the case of double number indexation, treated in § sec:double.number.indexation ), and lack stem alternation (only stem I occurs).

The imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ) is only attested in the direct mixed 2 3 configurations, and is the only finite form involving a second person that neither takes the second person prefix nor a portmanteau prefix. To express 2 1 imperative, the imperfective is used instead (§ sec:ipfv.hortative ).
summary:
In the mixed person domain, Japhug distinguishes direct configurations (1/2 person subject with 3rd person object) from inverse configurations (3rd person subject with 1/2 person object). In direct forms, the paradigm is mostly identical to the intransitive one, with 1sg 3 and 2sg 3 forms showing additional stem alternation and a Past -t suffix that encode both TAM and person; number of the third person object is generally unexpressed, while the number marker refers to the 1st/2nd person argument in 2 3 and 3 2 configurations.  

Inverse forms all take the prefix ɣɯ́-/wɣ and otherwise resemble the corresponding intransitive forms, lacking stem alternation and using only stem I. The imperative occurs only in direct 2 3 configurations, and 2 1 imperative meanings are expressed with the imperfective instead.

text:
person!non-local configuration
tab:non.local presents the Non-local domain of the paradigm of mtosee in the Factual Non-Past and the Aorist, compared with the intransitive paradigm as exemplified by ngobe ill.

There are two types of non-local forms: those taking the ɣɯ́-/wɣ- prefix, the inverse configurations (§ sec:direct-inverse ), and those without it, the direct configurations.

Direct forms present two features distinguishing them from the corresponding third person intransitive forms. First, in non-past tenses such as the Factual Non-Past, the 3sg subject form has Stem III (like the 1sg 3 and 2sg 3 forms of the mixed domain, § sec:indexation.mixed ). Second, in the Aorist, a C-type orientation preverb, with -a- vocalism is used instead of the A-type orientation preverbs in -ɯ- and -ɤ- found in the mixed and local domains ( pɯ- in the case of the verb mtosee). C-type orientation preverbs, only found in this section of the transitive paradigm (§ sec:transitivity.morphology, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), result from the fusion of A-type prefixes with another prefix which is only otherwise attested in the Apprehensive (§ sec:apprehensive ).

The -t suffix found in some direct forms in the mixed domain (§ sec:indexation.mixed ) is not attested in the non-local domain.

Inverse forms of the non-local domain only differ from the third person intransitive forms by the presence of the ɣɯ́-/wɣ- prefix, lacking stem alternation or additional affixes, like the inverse forms of the mixed domain (§ sec:indexation.mixed ).

Number indexation in the non-local domain encodes only one of the two arguments: the subject in the direct configurations and the object in the inverse configurations. For instance, in ( ex:pjAwGnAsmandZi ), the subject of the verb pjɤ́-wɣ-nɤsma-ndʑi is plural ( 3pl 3du ), but plural indexation -nɯ here instead of the dual would be incorrect, as this verb form has the ɣɯ́-/wɣ- prefix and thus agrees in number with the object.

exe

ndʑi-jɯlco ra kɯ wuma pjɤ́-wɣ-nɤsma-ndʑi. \\
3du. poss -neighbour pl erg really ifr - inv -envy- du \\
`Their neighbours envied the two of them.' (qajdoskAt)
exe

The third person argument whose number is indexed (the 3du argument in ex:pjAwGnAsmandZi ) is called proximate, and the one that is not indexed on the verb (corresponding to the noun phrase ndʑi-jɯlco ra in ex:pjAwGnAsmandZi ) is called obviative (glossed as 3$'$), using terminology from Algonquian linguistics. While in Algonquian the term obviative (coined by ) originally refers to a category marked on both nouns and verb indexation (including intransitive verbs), in Gyalrong languages the proximate/obviative contrast is only reflected in transitive verbal morphology (see § sec:direct-inverse and § sec:inverse.3.3.saliency )

Direct configurations are by far more common in the corpus than inverse ones. Inverse non-local forms have two functions: marking the relative saliency of the subject and the object (a question detailed in § sec:inverse.3.3.saliency ) and indexing a generic subject (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ).
summary:
The non-local domain of the mtosee paradigm has two kinds of forms: direct forms without the ɣɯ́-/wɣ- prefix and inverse forms with it. Direct forms differ from the corresponding intransitive third-person forms in having Stem III in the 3sg subject Factual Non-Past and C-type orientation preverbs in the Aorist, while inverse forms show only the ɣɯ́-/wɣ- prefix and otherwise no stem alternation or extra affixes.

In this domain, number agreement indexes only one argument: the subject in direct configurations and the object in inverse configurations. The indexed third-person argument is termed proximate, while the unindexed one is obviative, and inverse forms are said to mark saliency relations and sometimes a generic subject.

text:
person!local configuration person!first indexation!portmanteau
Local configurations stand out in Japhug verbal paradigms in being the only forms involving the second person without a tɯ- prefix. Instead, synchronically unanalyzable portmanteau prefixes are found: ta- for 1 2, and kɯ- for 2 1. The ta- co-occurs with the non-first person dual and plural suffixes ( -ndʑi and -nɯ, § sec:intr.23 ), and kɯ- with first person suffixes ( -a, -tɕi and -ji, § sec:intr.1 ), indexing in all cases the person and number of the object. In 2 1 forms, the first person is redundantly indexed both by the suffixes and the portmanteau prefix kɯ-.

The presence of portmanteau prefixes in the local domain is not typologically unusual. Typologists have long noticed that languages with polypersonal indexation tend to have unanalysable affixes in 1 2 and 2 1 forms in part due to pragmatic factors. The historical origin of these prefixes is discussed in and § sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history.

In 1 2 configurations, since 2sg is exclusively indexed by the tɯ- prefix in the intransitive paradigm, without any suffix (unlike Situ, § sec:indexation.suffixes.history ), the 1 2sg also lacks any indexation suffix. tab:local.paradigm presents all local configurations of the verb mtosee in the Factual Non-Past and the Aorist, except for those with double suffixation ( 2du 1sg and 2pl 1sg ) which are treated in § sec:double.number.indexation.

There is no stem alternation, -t past tense suffix or ɣɯ-/wɣ- prefix in the local domain in Japhug. Aorist and Factual Non-Past only differ from each other by the presence of the A-type orientation preverb in the former, as can be seen in tab:local.paradigm.

In Japhug, the forms of the local domain are always different from those of the mixed domain, and the person of the subject and the object is never ambiguous. In this regard, Japhug differs from many languages of the Trans-Himalayan family, in particular those of the Kiranti branch. In Khaling, for instance, the same forms are used for 2 1 and 3 1 configurations on the one hand, and for 3 2 and 1nsg 2 on the other hand. In that language, the only local configuration to have specific unambiguous forms is 1sg 2.

In Japhug, while person is unambiguously expressed in the local domain, only the number of the object is specified, with the exception of 2 1sg configurations (§ sec:double.number.indexation ). Examples ( ex:aZo.tutafsraN ) and ( ex:iZora.tutafsraN ) illustrate the same form tu-ta-fsraŋ meaning in the first case 1sg 2sg `I will save you$_sg$' and in the second one 1pl 2sg `We will save you$_sg$', showing that the form remains identical regardless of the number of the subject.

exe

tɕe aʑo tu-ta-fsraŋ ra tɕe, \\
lnk 1sg ipfv -1 2-protect be.needed: fact lnk \\
`I have to save you.' (150901 changfamei-zh) 0006352#S205
exe

exe

iʑora nɯnɯ koŋla ʑo tu-ta-fsraŋ, tu-ta-βri ɲɯ-sɯso-j ɕti ri, \\
1pl dem really emph ipfv -1 2-protect ipfv -1 2-save ipfv -think- 1pl be. aff: fact lnk \\
`We really want to save you.' (niulan li de lu-zh)
exe

Similarly, ( ex:tukWquri.ra ) and ( ex:GWtukWquri ) show the form tu-kɯ-qur-i meaning 2sg 1pl `You$_sg$ help us' in the first example and 2pl 1pl `You$_pl$ help us' in the second one.

wortɕʰi wojɤr ʑo tu-kɯ-qur-i ra \\
please please emph ipfv -2 1-help- 1pl be.needed: fact \\
`Please, help us.' (150827 taisui-zh)
0006390#S21

<chuhuaiwang> cʰo nɯra, kɯmaʁ nɯra nɯ-ɕki, ``ɣɯ-tu-kɯ-qur-i ɲɯ-ntsʰi" z-jo-sɯ-ti. \\

`He sent [someone] to the king Huai of Chu and the other ones to tell them `Come and help us'. (160721 pofuchenzhou-zh)

The 2 1 configuration can occur in the prohibitive with the prefix ma- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ) as in the form ma-tʰɯ-kɯ-βlɯ-a `don't burn me' in ( ex:mathWkWBlWa ), but not in the imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ). Instead, the Imperfective is used (§ sec:ipfv.hortative ), most often with a modal verb, as in ( ex:tukWquri.ra ) and ( ex:GWtukWquri ) and in the form cʰɯ-kɯ-rku-a in ( ex:mathWkWBlWa ). Attempts to produce 2 1 Imperative forms such as $ $ tɤ-kɯ-qur-i (instead of the correct tu-kɯ-qur-i ra `help us') are rejected by native speakers.

`Don't burn me, put me in a wine jar.' (2003 Kunbzang)

summary:
Japhug local verbal forms are marked by unanalyzable portmanteau prefixes in the 1→2 and 2→1 configurations: ta- for 1→2 and kɯ- for 2→1, with the object’s person and number indexed by the accompanying suffixes. In these forms, the local domain has no stem alternation or certain other prefixes/suffixes found elsewhere, and the Aorist differs from the Factual Non-Past only by the A-type orientation preverb.  

The passage also notes that Japhug local forms are always distinct from mixed-domain forms, so subject and object person are never ambiguous, unlike in some other Trans-Himalayan languages. However, only the object’s number is generally expressed, since the same forms can be used with different subject numbers, and 2→1 forms are restricted in mood: they occur in prohibitives and imperfective hortatives, but not in the imperative.

text:
indexation!semi-reflexive
Japhug lacks inclusive / exclusive contrast in both pronouns and indexation system (§ sec:intr.1 ), and inclusive persons are treated the same way as 1du and 1pl exclusive. While inclusive persons could in principle exist in the local domain, configuration of this type are problematic: if the subject or object of a transitive verb is inclusive, and the other argument strictly first or second person, the resulting configuration is partially reflexive, since the inclusive contains both first and person referents.

In a language like Japhug where reflexivity is marked by an intransitivizing derivation (§ sec:reflexive ), there is therefore a conflict between the absence of reflexive forms in the transitive paradigm and the need to express inclusive$ $first/second person configurations in a way that is different from plain reflexives.

The following list provides the four theoretically possible inclusive semi-reflexive configurations, displaying the referent shared by subject and object in red. This list neglects possible additional third person referents in 1du exclusive, 1pl, 2du and 3pl arguments, which would artificially increase the number of configurations.

itemize
1+2 1 `You and I verb me'
1+ 2 2 `You and I verb you'
1 1+2 `I verb you and me'
2 1+ 2 `You verb you and me'
itemize, in his review of, argues that Kiranti languages and Limbu in particular cannot express inclusive semi-reflexive configurations using transitive verbal morphology, and must resort to periphrases; for instance, in order to express the meaning of the 2 1+ 2 configuration `you saw both of us in the mirror', Limbu uses a complement clause containing an intransitive verb meaning `you and I appear in the mirror', object of the transitive verb `see', as in ( ex:adhaapsiba ).

exe

khɛnɛʔ anchi aina-o a-dha:p-si-ba kɛ-ni \\
2sg 1di mirror- loc incl -be.visible- du - nmlz 2-see \\
`You(sg) saw both of us in the mirror.’ 
exe

In Japhug, a similar strategy (though with a finite clause instead of a nominalized verb form) is employed to express the 1 1+2 configuration in ( ex:kAntChArtCi ), with the finite complement clause χɕɤlzgoŋ ɯ-ŋgɯ kɤ-ntɕʰɤr-tɕi `we appear in the mirror' as object of the transitive perception verb mtosee.

exe

[χɕɤlzgoŋ ɯ-ŋgɯ kɤ-ntɕʰɤr-tɕi] nɯra pɯ-mto-t-a \\
mirror 3sg. poss -in aor -appear- 1du dem: pl aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I saw both of us in the mirror.' (elicitation, )
exe

Nevertheless, there are cases in Japhug where inclusive semi-reflexive meanings can be expressed by simple verb forms of the local domain. In example ( ex:tha.kWzmaqhutCi ), the verb kɯ-z-maqʰu-tɕi presents a 2 1du configuration (§ sec:indexation.local ); it is clear in this particular case that the object is first dual inclusive `you and I' rather than first exclusive, and that we therefore have a semi-reflexive configuration 2 1+ 2.

exe

mɯ́j-tɯ-mbɣom ri tʰa kɯ-z-maqʰu-tɕi \\
neg: sens -2-be.in.a.hurry lnk later 2 1- caus -be.after: fact - 1du \\
`[If] you don't hurry [up], you will get us late.' (elicited)
exe

No example of this type is found in the corpus, and such pragmatically clumsy configurations are on the borderline of the Japhug person indexation system.

Semi-reflexive indexation also occurs with third person referents, in particular in causative constructions (see ex:toWGsWndzandZi.pjAra, § sec:sig.caus.morphosyntax ).
summary:
Japhug has no inclusive/exclusive distinction in pronouns or indexation, so inclusive persons are treated like first dual/plural exclusive, but this creates “semi-reflexive” situations when an inclusive argument combines with a strict 1st or 2nd person argument. Because reflexivity is expressed by an intransitivizing derivation, such meanings are often hard to encode in transitive morphology, and Japhug may instead use a complement clause, though some local-domain verb forms can express them directly.

The passage gives examples of the four possible inclusive semi-reflexive configurations and notes that Japhug’s corpus lacks examples of this type, suggesting they are pragmatically awkward and marginal in the person indexation system. It also says that semi-reflexive indexation can involve third person referents, especially in causative constructions.

text:
indexation!generic generic inverse
The prefix kɯ, which appears in the intransitive paradigm to express generic intransitive subject (§ sec:intr.23 ), is also attested in the transitive paradigm to refer to generic object. For instance, in example ( ex:amAjAkWphGo.kWmto.kWndo ), The generic person in ( ex:amAjAkWphGo.kWmto.kWndo ) is translated into English by the second person `you'. the transitive verbs kɯ-mto `(the yeti) will see one' and kɯ-ndo `(the yeti) will catch one' have the same kɯ- prefix as the intransitive verb a-mɤ-jɤ-kɯ-phɣo `one should not flee'. This example also shows that stem I is selected in the 3 genr form, as the stem III of mtosee and ndotake, `catch' are mtɤm and ndɤm, respectively. Combining the generic kɯ- prefix with stem III is impossible, and kɯ-mto cannot be replaced by a form such as $ $ kɯ-mtɤm, which would be unintelligible.

exe

ɯ-qʰu-cʰu ɯ-stu ʑo a-mɤ-jɤ-kɯ-pʰɣo ra ma tɕe kɯ-mto tɕe kɯ-ndo ɕti tu-ti-nɯ \\
3sg. poss -behind- approx. loc 3sg. poss -direction emph irr - neg - pfv - genr:S/O-flee be.needed: fact lnk lnk
genr:S/O-see: fact lnk genr:S/O-take: fact be. aff: fact ipfv -say- pl \\
`People say that you should not flee in the direction behind[the yeti], as it would see you and catch you.' (140510 mYWrgAt)
0003941#S20
exe

Unlike in Tshobdun, generic transitive subjects in Japhug are not indexed by the same prefix as generic intransitive subjects. Apart from a handful of irregular verbs (§ sec:irregular.transitive ), the inverse prefix wɣ- occurs instead of kɯ- to express generic transitive subject, as in the verb tú-wɣ-ndza `one eats it' in ( ex:YWkWznWtWfCAl ), whose object is definite (anaphorically referring to the noun kʰɯrwummold in a previous clause). Note that the generic subject of tú-wɣ-ndza is co-referent with the object of the verb ɲɯ-kɯ-z-nɯtɯfɕɤl `it causes one to have diarrhea' (causative of the intransitive verb nɯtɯfɕɤlhave diarrhea, on which see § sec:denominalization.action.nominal ) in the following clause, indexed with the kɯ- as in ( ex:amAjAkWphGo.kWmto.kWndo ) above, and that conversely the (inanimate) object of tú-wɣ-ndza corresponds to the subject of ɲɯ-kɯ-z-nɯtɯfɕɤl.

exe

ma tú-wɣ-ndza tɕe, ɲɯ-kɯ-z-nɯtɯfɕɤl ɕti\\
lnk ipfv - inv -eat lnk ipfv - genr:S/O- caus -have.diarrhea be. aff: fact \\
`If you eat [mold], it causes you diarrhea.' (20-sWrna) 0003564#S51
exe

Generic person indexation is remarkable in Japhug morphosyntax in being one of the very few examples of ergative-absolutive alignment outside of the case marking system, since the intransitive subject and the object are marked by the same prefix kɯ, while the transitive subject is not ($S=P A$).

A generic person subject or object is only compatible with a third person argument ( genr 3 or 3 genr ). Combinations with first or second persons are not possible. However, number indexation of the non-generic third person argument is possible when the generic argument is subject. Dual or plural suffixes in genr du or genr pl configurations are attested in procedural texts. For instance, ( ex:YWwGznWNGAtndZi ) has dual indexation (referring to the turnip leaves and the turnip root) with generic human subject.

exe

rasti cʰo rɤjndoʁ ni, pjɯ́-wɣ-ʁndzɤr-ndʑi tɕe ɲɯ́-wɣ-z-nɯɴɢɤt-ndʑi ŋu. \\
turnip comit turnip.root du ipfv - inv -cut- du lnk ipfv - inv - caus - acaus:separate- du be: fact \\
`One separates the turnip from its root by cutting them.' (150903 kAJar)
0006412#S7
exe

Number indexation occurs in particular in the case of generic subject indexation referring to a first person (§ sec:1.genr ). In ( ex:tuwGqurnW ), the generic subject of the verb tú-wɣ-qur-nɯ corresponds to the first person plural, as indexed on the preceding verb rɤʑi-j, and the plural object is overtly indexed.

exe

tɯ-rdoʁ tsa rɤʑi-j tɕe tú-wɣ-qur-nɯ raʁmaʁ \\
one-piece a.little stay: fact - 1pl lnk ipfv - inv -help- pl sfp \\
`How about only one of us staying [here] and helping them?' (hist180503 xiyouji 12-zh)
0006189#S74
exe

On the other hand, when the generic argument is in object or intransitive subject function, no person indexation suffix can appear on the verb, even if this argument is realized as an overt noun phrase with plural marking in addition to generic indexation.

For instance, in ( ex:Wku.kukWsWndo ), the verb form with generic object indexation ku-kɯ-sɯ-ndo lacks any indexation suffix, although both the causer (`the elders') and the causee (the generic argument, tɤ-pɤtso ra `us, the children') are plural.

exe

qaʑo cʰɯ-krɤɣ-nɯ tɕe tɤ-pɤtso ra kɯ nɯ qaʑo ɣɯ ɯ-ku nɯ ku-kɯ-sɯ-ndo. \\
sheep ipfv -shear- pl lnk indef. poss -child pl erg dem sheep gen 3sg. poss -head dem ipfv - genr:S/O- caus -take \\
`[Every time the adults] sheared the sheep's wool, they would ask the children (us) to grab the sheep's head.' (160712 smAG)
0006073#S2
exe
summary:
Japhug uses the prefix **kɯ-** for generic intransitive subjects and generic objects, but **generic transitive subjects** are usually marked instead by the **inverse prefix wɣ-** (with a few irregular exceptions). This generic indexation pattern is notable because it creates an ergative-absolutive-like alignment in agreement: the intransitive subject and object share **kɯ-**, while the transitive subject is treated differently.  

Generic person forms are only possible with **third-person** arguments; first and second persons cannot combine with generic marking. Number suffixes can occur when the non-generic third-person argument is indexed, especially with generic subjects, but when the generic argument is an object or intransitive subject, no person-number suffix appears on the verb even if the noun phrase is overtly plural.

text:
indexation!number
The transitive paradigm contains six doubly suffixed forms, two in the local domain, and four in the mixed domain, as summarized in tab:double.indexation. Japhug is not the only Gyalrong language with double number indexation. The same set of doubly suffixed forms is found in Tshobdun and Zbu.

The forms corresponding to those in tab:double.indexation without additional -ndʑi or -nɯ suffix generally have a singular third or second person argument, for instance pɯ-mto-t-a `I saw him' (§ sec:indexation.mixed ) or pɯ-kɯ-mto-a `You$_sg$ saw me.' (§ sec:indexation.local ). There are however also cases of optional number indexation, a topic discussed in § sec:optional.indexation.

The 1sg 3du and 1sg 3pl forms have stem III alternation in non-past tenses ( mto -mtam- in tab:double.indexation ) and the suffix -t in the Aorist, like the corresponding 1sg 3sg form (§ sec:indexation.mixed ).

Examples ( ex:tundzeandZi ), ( ex:tAwGnWmGlaandZi ), ( ex:tukWquranW.YWntshi ) illustrate 1sg 3du (with stem III, ndza ndze ), 3du 1sg and 2pl 1sg configurations, respectively. All these forms have double suffixation, comparable to mtam-a-nɯ, pɯ́-wɣ-mto-a-ndʑi and kɯ-mto-a-nɯ in tab:double.indexation (with the Imperfective instead of the Factual Non-Past).

exe

tu-ndze-a-ndʑi ra \\
ipfv -eat[III]- 1sg - du be.needed: fact \\
`I'd like to eat them.' (lWlu 2002)
0003361#S69
exe

exe

tu-kɯ-nɯmɢla-a jɤɣ ma nɤ-pi ni kɯ tɤ́-wɣ-nɯmɢla-a-ndʑi ɕti \\
ipfv -2 1-step.over- 1sg be.allowed: fact lnk 2sg. poss -elder.sibling du erg aor - inv -step.over- 1sg - du be. aff: fact \\
`You can step over me, your two elder sister stepped over me.' (Kunbzang)
exe

exe

a-pi ra, aʑɯɣ kukutɕu a-mɤ-kɤ-cʰa ci ɣɤʑu tɕe [...] tu-kɯ-qur-a-nɯ ɲɯ-ntsʰi \\
1sg. poss -elder.sibling pl 1sg: gen here 1sg. poss - neg - obj: pcp -can indef exist: sens lnk ipfv -2 1-help- 1sg - pl sens -be.better \\
`Sisters, I have a problem (something that I cannot do) here, help me!' (150828 donglang)
0006312#S106
exe

Double number indexation also occurs on relativized verbs with totalitative reduplication (§ sec:totalitative.redp ), such as pɯ pɯ-mto-t-a-nɯ in ( ex:pWpWmtotanW ). In this example, the suffix -nɯ indexes the number of the object tɕʰemegirl, which is also the head of this head-internal relative (§ sec:head-internal.relative ). It is redundant with the verb-initial reduplication, which expresses universal quantification of the object.

exe

nɯnɯ [tɕʰeme pɯ pɯ-mto-t-a-nɯ] ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯ kɯ-fse kɯ-mpɕɤr maŋe \\
dem girl total aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg - pl 3sg. poss -inside dem sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp -be.beautiful not.exist: sens \\
`This is the most beautiful among all the girls I have ever seen.' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh)
0006334#S469
exe

All forms with double number indexation in Japhug ( tab:double.indexation and examples ex:tundzeandZi to ex:tukWquranW.YWntshi above) contain the first person -a suffix. This includes 1sg $ $3, 3$ $ 1sg and 2$ $ 1sg configurations, but not 1sg $ $2: the 1$ $2 forms, unlike other configuration involving a first person, do not take person indexation suffixes coreferent with their first person subject (§ sec:indexation.local ). Two hypotheses could be proposed to account for this relationship between -a suffix and double number indexation.

First, this constraint could be seen as a (haplological) prohibition against the presence of two identical suffixes in the same verb form. Since second and third person number markers are identical, the only way to express a form such as 2du$ $3du in a fully explicit way would be $ $ - ndʑi-ndʑi with two times the same suffix, a form which would be excluded by the hapological rule. Such a rule however would not account for the absence of second number marker in verb forms suffixed with the 1du -tɕi or the 1pl -ji.

Second, it could be argued to be a question of phonology: all person indexation suffixes apart from -a have the high vowels i or ɯ (which are not contrastive in this context, § sec:W.i.contrast ), and one could suppose that the ban on double suffixation in this paradigm is due to a constraint against two unstressed suffixes with high vowels (since the stress is on the last syllable of the stem, except in a limited number of cases, § sec:stress ).

However, this hypothesis is contradicted by the fact that other verbal paradigms in Japhug do contain verb forms with two suffixes in high vowels, as in example ( ex:tokAlWlAtndZici ). See § sec:preverbs.contracting.verbs and § sec:peg.circumfix on the peg circumfix kɯ-...-ci.

exe

to-k-ɤlɯlɤt-ndʑi-ci \\
ifr - peg -fight- du - peg \\
`They fought each other.'
exe

Given the fact that the combination of two unstressed suffixes in high vowel are possible in Japhug, phonology cannot explain the absence of a form such as $ $ kɯ- - tɕi-ndʑi (intended for 2du$ $1sg ).

A third approach to explain the unique properties of the -a suffix, involving the notion of person hierarchy, is explored in § sec:direct-inverse.
summary:
The passage describes double number indexation in Japhug transitive verbs, noting that six doubly suffixed forms occur in the local and mixed domains, and that the same pattern is also found in Tshobdun and Zbu. These forms usually involve a singular third- or second-person argument, though some optional number indexation also exists, and all Japhug forms with double number indexation include the first-person suffix -a, except for 1>2 forms.

The text considers two possible explanations for this restriction: a haplological ban on repeated identical suffixes, and a phonological constraint against two unstressed high-vowel suffixes. It rejects the phonological account because other Japhug paradigms do allow two such suffixes, and concludes by pointing to a person-hierarchy explanation discussed elsewhere.

subsubsection: The allomorphy of the inverse prefix
text:
inverse morphology!allomorphy allomorphy!inverse
The inverse prefix The possible origins of the inverse prefix are discussed in § sec:3sg.possessive.form and § sec:inverse.history. has the allomorph ɣɯ́- when occurring in word-initial position, something which is only possible in the Factual Non-Past (as it is the only TAME category without any orientation preverb, § sec:fact.morphology ) when no other inflectional prefix is present. It surfaces as wɣ- in all other cases, merging with the vowel of the preceding prefix, which then bears the accent; the inverse is one of the very few stress-attracting prefixes in Japhug (§ sec:stress.prefixal.chain ).

The allomorph wɣ- also occurs in Factual Non-Past forms with the following prefixes:

itemize
Second person tɯ- (§ sec:indexation.mixed ): tɯ́-wɣ-mto (2- inv -see: fact ) `he will see you'
Negative mɤ- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ): mɤ́-wɣ-mto-a ( neg - inv -see: fact - 1sg ) `he will not see me'
Apprehensive ɕɯ- (§ sec:apprehensive ): ɕɯ́-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-a ( appr - inv -bite: fact - 1sg ) `(I fear) that it could bite me'
Associated motion ɕɯ-/ɣɯ- (§ sec:associated.motion ): ɣɯ́-wɣ-ndza-j ( cisl - inv -eat: fact - 1pl ) `it will come to eat us'
Proximative aspect: jɯ- (§ sec:proximative ) jɯ́-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-a proxm - inv -bite: fact - 1sg `it is about to bite me'
Possible modality: ɯmɤ- (§ sec:WmA ) ɯmɤ́-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-a ( prob - inv -bite: fact - 1sg ) `it will perhaps bite me' ( ex:WmAwGmtsWGa, § sec:fsp.epistemic )
Rhetorical Interrogative: ɯβrɤ- (§ sec:WBrA.morphology ) ɯβrɤ́-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-a ( rh. q - inv -bite: fact - 1sg ) `it will not bite me, will it?'
Interrogative: ɯ- (§ sec:interrogative.W.morpho ) ɯ́-wɣ-ndza-a ( qu - inv -eat: fact - 1sg ) `Will it eat me?'
itemize

With the progressive prefix asɯ- (§ sec:progressive.morphology ), the inverse is infixed rather than being prefixed, for instance in a form such as ɲɯ-tɯ-ɤ́<wɣ>sɯ-zgroʁ ( sens -2- prog < inv >-attach) `he is attaching you'. This question is discussed in more detail in § sec:outer.prefixal.chain.

The merger of the w of the inverse prefix with the vowels ɯ and ɤ of the preceding prefixes yields u and o, respectively. Although the transcription wɣ is chosen in the present orthography, the fricative ɣ is most often elided, and the stress and vowel rounding are the main clues of the presence of the inverse prefix.

Due to the vowel merger, the contrasts between several series of prefixes are neutralized when preceding the inverse prefix, causing homophony between morphologically different forms (our orthography however keeps the distinction between the rounded and unrounded vowels in this context). There are potential ambiguities in three situations.

First, since the B-type (imperfective) upwards preverb tu- (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) and the second person tɯ- (§ sec:intr.23 ) both become neutralized as tú- before the inverse prefix, transitive verbs whose intrinsic orientation is upwards (§ sec:lexicalized.orientation ) have the same surface form in the Imperfective 3$'$ 3 (and also 3sg 1sg with verbs whose stem ends in -a, due to vowel merger, see § sec:synizesis and § sec:intr.1 ) on the one hand and the Factual Non-Past 3 2sg on the other hand. The two examples in ( ex:tuwGndza.ambiguity ) illustrate this ambiguity with the verb ndzaeat (which selects the orientation upwards, § sec:preverb.ingestion ) with the Factual Non-Past 3 2sg tɯ́-wɣ-ndza `it will eat you' in ( ex:ma.tWwGndza ) and the Imperfective tú-wɣ-ndza-a 3sg 1sg `it eats me', For the use of the Imperfective in subject complement clause of the verb jɤɣbe allowed, see § sec:ipfv.complement. both pronounced túɣndza in two immediately adjacent sentences in the same text.

exe

The inverse prefix has the allomorph ɣɯ́- word-initially, which occurs only in Factual Non-Past forms without any other inflectional prefix; elsewhere it surfaces as wɣ-, merging with the preceding prefix’s vowel and attracting stress. With the progressive prefix, the inverse is infixed rather than prefixed, and vowel merger often reduces the fricative ɣ, leaving stress and rounding as the main signs of the inverse.

This merger neutralizes distinctions among several prefix series and can create homophony, especially between the upward preverb tu- and second-person tɯ- before the inverse. The passage illustrates how such ambiguities arise and how they may sometimes be resolved by meaning or by the syntactic context of surrounding verbs.

person!hierarchy hierarchy!person person!first direct-inverse inverse
The mixed and non-local domains of the Japhug indexation system present a remarkable symmetry, illustrated in tab:symmetrical: direct X 3 and inverse 3 X forms have the same person indexation affixes, and only differ by the presence of the prefix wɣ- in inverse configurations, and of stem III in (Non-Past) X sg 3 configurations.

Although this symmetry is broken in the local domain, where neither the wɣ- prefix nor stem III alternation occur (§ sec:indexation.local ), Japhug has an indexation system very close to the canonical direct-inverse, as presented in tab:inverse-canon: all configurations of the lower half of the bipersonal indexation space except 2 1 take the wɣ- prefix, while this prefix is not found in the upper half.

As mentioned above, person indexation affixes in Japhug have neutral alignment, and can be used to index either subjects (of transitive or intransitive verbs) or objects. With transitive verbs, the wɣ- prefix (whose allomorphy is described in § sec:allomorphy.inv ) and Stem III (§ sec:stem3 ) serve to disambiguate the function of the indexation affixes closest to the verb stem: If two indexation suffixes are present, the second suffix indexes the number of the other argument (§ sec:double.number.indexation ). if the wɣ- prefix is present, the affix(es) index the object, while if Stem III is present, they index the subject. The wɣ- prefix and stem III mark inverse and direct configurations, respectively.

A way to describe the distribution of the inverse and direct markers is the notion of person or empathy hierarchy. A typical example of person hierarchy is ( ex:empathy.hierarchy ), on which first person ranks higher than second person, discourse participants (first of second persons) higher than third persons, On the difference between third person on the one hand, and first and second persons on the other hand, see also. and among animate third persons (in particular humans) higher than inanimate third persons.

This type of hierarchies, Other hierarchies have been suggested; for instance, slot accessibility in most Algonquian languages requires to posit a hierarchy 2 > 1 > 3. originally proposed to account for splits in pronominal systems, have been invoked to explain various morphosyntactic phenomena, including slot accessibility (for instance, the prefixal slot in the Independent Order paradigms of Algonquian languages, ) and direct/inverse marking.

In this framework, when the subject and the object compete for the same morphological slot, the one that is higher on the hierarchy is indexed. In addition, inverse markers occur when the object is higher on the hierarchy than the subject (2 1, 3 1, 3 2), and direct markers when the subject is higher (1 2, 1 3, 2 3).

The explanatory power of hierarchies to analyze indexation systems has been challenged, in particular due to the fact that in some languages one would need to posit contradictory hierarchies (see Zúñiga's zuniga06 discussion of Plains Cree).

Independently of the cross-linguistic validity of the notion of person hierarchies, the Japhug indexation system is amenable to an analysis in terms of the two non-contradictory hierarchies in ( ex:empathy.hierarchy.japhug ). The nature of the contrast between 3 proximate and 3$'$ obviative is discussed in § sec:inverse.3.3.saliency.

Hierarchy ( ex:hierarchy.3 ) describes the distribution of the inverse wɣ- prefix and Stem III in the mixed and non-local domains:

itemize
The inverse prefix occurs whenever the subject is lower than the object (3 1, 3 2, 3$'$ 3), a rule that also accounts for its function to mark the generic transitive subject genr 3 (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ).
Stem III is found when the subject is singular and higher than the object ( 1sg 3, 2sg 3, 3sg 3$'$).
Neither the inverse prefix nor Stem III are found when the subject and the object are equal on the hierarchy ( ex:hierarchy.3 ), in particular in the local domain (2 1, 1 2), where portmanteau prefixes occur to indicate person configuration (§ sec:indexation.local ), and the suffix closest to the verb stem indexes the object. Generic object configurations, which are marked with the kɯ- generic prefix and lack Stem III (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ),
are analyzed as 3$'$ genr, as third person obviative and generic are equal on ( ex:hierarchy.3 ).
itemize

Additional evidence for the existence of ( ex:hierarchy.3 ) is presented in § sec:ditransitive.causative.

Hierarchy ( ex:hierarchy.1sg ) accounts for the special status of the 1sg: whenever one of the core arguments is 1sg, the number of the other argument is indexed on the verb. In 2 1sg, 3 1sg and 1sg 3 configurations, an additional suffix can follow the -a 1sg to index the number of the third or second person argument (§ sec:double.number.indexation ). In the 1sg 2 configurations, the suffix is coreferent with the number of the object like all forms in the local domain (§ sec:indexation.local ).

The hierarchies in ( ex:empathy.hierarchy.japhug ) are only valid for Japhug. In other Gyalrong languages, including Situ, Tshobdun and Zbu, the inverse prefix is also found in the 2 1 configuration and does not appear in the generic subject form, suggesting a hierarchy closer to ( ex:empathy.hierarchy ).

A different approach to explain the structure of the Japhug direct-inverse indexation system is to analyze it in terms of historical linguistics. Some preliminary ideas on the topic are presented in § sec:indexation.suffixes.history and § sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history.
summary:
Japhug’s indexation system is highly symmetrical in the mixed and non-local domains: direct and inverse forms use the same person affixes, with the inverse distinguished by the prefix wɣ- and direct forms by Stem III in certain non-past 3rd-person configurations. The system can be described with person hierarchies, where the higher-ranked argument is indexed and inverse marking appears when the object outranks the subject, while direct marking appears when the subject outranks the object.  

A Japhug-specific hierarchy also accounts for the special behavior of 1sg and of proximate versus obviative 3rd person, including cases where the number of the other argument is indexed. The passage notes that these hierarchies are language-specific and that other Gyalrong languages show different inverse-marking patterns.

subsection: The function of the direct/inverse contrast in non-local configurations
text:
inverse person!non-local configuration
Like most Gyalrong languages, including Tshobdun, Zbu, but excluding West Gyalrongic and some dialects of Situ, Japhug has a contrast between inverse and direct forms in the non-local configurations.

The clearest function of the inverse prefix in this context in Japhug is marking generic subject (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ). In non-generic forms, the choice of inverse or direct configurations is determined by several factors, including animacy, possession and saliency of the core arguments.

Japhug lacks obviative marking on nouns (§ sec:possessive.prefix.obv.def ), but in the present work I use the terms `obviative' (abbreviated as 3$'$) to refer to the third person object of a verb in direct non-local configuration or to the third person subject of a transitive verb with inverse configuration, and `proximate' (3) for the subject of a verb in direct form or object of a verb in inverse form (the choice of these terms is discussed in § sec:indexation.non.local ).
summary: Japhug, like most Gyalrong languages, distinguishes inverse and direct forms in non-local configurations, though this contrast is absent in West Gyalrongic and some Situ dialects. In Japhug, the inverse prefix most clearly marks generic subjects, while in non-generic forms the choice between inverse and direct depends on factors such as animacy, possession, and the saliency of core arguments. The author also uses the terms “obviative” and “proximate” to refer to third-person roles in direct and inverse configurations, since Japhug itself lacks obviative marking on nouns.

subsection: The function of the direct/inverse contrast in non-local configurations
text:
inverse
The clearest factor determining the proximate or obviative status of a noun phrase in Japhug is animacy. Whenever one of the core arguments (whether a noun phrase or a clause) is inanimate and the other animate, the former will almost always be obviative, and the latter proximate.

When the subject is animate and the object inanimate (with the exception of generic subjects § sec:indexation.generic.tr and pseudo-passive constructions § sec:pseudo.passive ), the verb must be in direct form. Thus, indirective verbs of speech (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) such as tisay, or transitive modal verbs such as spabe able (§ sec:spa.verb ), whose object is always a complement clause (or an abstract noun for some of these verbs), Complement clauses, being inanimate arguments, are always obviative when used as objects of complement-taking verbs. and whose subject is necessarily human or higher animal, will always have a proximate subject and an obviative object (3 3$'$), and thus never appear in (non-generic) inverse configurations.

Conversely, in nearly all the cases when the subject is an inanimate entity (including plants) and the object an animate one (including humans and non-human animals), the verb appears in inverse form, as illustrated by examples ( ex:nWNa.chowGWt ), ( ex:YAwGsWGYARnW ) and ( ex:pANAxCaj ).

Inanimate agents are usually natural forces, such as tɯ-ciwater (subject of cʰɤ́-wɣ-ɣɯt `it brings her downstream' in ex:nWNa.chowGWt ) or tɯ-mɯ `the rain' (subject of the verb pjɯ́-wɣ-χtɕi-nɯ `(they) wash them away' in ex:YAwGsWGYARnW ).

In Japhug, animacy is the main factor determining whether a noun phrase is proximate or obviative: when one core argument is animate and the other inanimate, the inanimate one is usually obviative and the animate one proximate. As a result, clauses with animate subjects and inanimate objects are normally in direct form, while clauses with inanimate subjects and animate objects are usually in inverse form, especially when the inanimate subject is a natural force or other agentive inanimate.  

The passage also notes some exceptions and intermediate cases: a few natural-force subjects take direct marking, but these are rare, and when both core arguments are animate, either direct or inverse is possible; when both are inanimate, the verb is generally direct.

text:
obviative possessor
In Algonquian languages, there are two main constraints governing the use of obviation on nouns: on the other hand, third persons possessed by another third person are automatically obviative (, ), and on the other hand, at most one argument can be proximate in any given clause. A consequence of these constraints is that whenever a transitive verb takes as subject a possessed noun, and as object a (proximate) noun coreferent with the possessor of the subject, If the object noun is not co-referent with the possessor of the subject, it will be obviative too due to the second constrain. the verb will necessarily have an inverse form, as in the Cree example in ( ex:cree.kiimaakwamik ). Conversely, if the subject is a proximate noun and the object a possessed noun whose possessor is coreferent with the subject, the verb will necessarily be direct.

Though similar phenomena have been reported outside of Algonquian, not all languages with direct-inverse indexation display such relationship between possession and obviation.

Japhug lacks obviation marking on nouns (§ sec:possessive.prefix.obv.def ), but the presence of direct or inverse morphology can nevertheless be used to test whether possession has an effect on the obviation status of nominal arguments.

There is a very clear tendency for inverse marking to occur when the subject is a possessed noun and the object its possessor (henceforth SPO `subject possessed by third person object'), as shown by examples such as ( ex:towGnAmqe ), ( ex:mWpjAwGsWXsAl ) and ( ex:pjAwGnAZAmNAn ).

However, the fact that a correlation between inverse marking and SPO configurations exists does not necessarily imply that the inverse is actually triggered by SPO.

First, there are also many examples of SPO with direct marking. For instance, in ( ex:YWznAjandZi.mWtasWGendZi ), the verbs ɲɯ-z-nɤja-ndʑi and mɯ-ta-sɯ-ɣe-ndʑi with SPO lack inverse prefixes and have direct morphology (subject number indexation § sec:indexation.non.local and the C-type orientation preverb ta, § sec:transitivity.morphology ). In addition, the examples ( ex:prox.naBde ) and ( ex:obv.nWwGBde ) in § sec:possessive.prefix.obv.def provide a minimal of SPO configuration with direct vs. inverse configuration in exactly the same context.

exe

girl really emph sbj: pcp -be.good indef pst. ipfv -be lnk 3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss -father du erg sens - caus -be.regrettable- du lnk neg - aor:3 3$'$- caus -come[II]- du \\
`[His wife]$_i$ was a very nice girl, her$_i$ parents were unwilling to part with her$_i$ and did not let her$_i$ come.' (14-siblings)

Second, the presence of inverse marking in examples ( ex:towGnAmqe ), ( ex:mWpjAwGsWXsAl ) and ( ex:pjAwGnAZAmNAn ) above (and in most cases of SPO with inverse) can be accounted for by factors other than possession, in particular the relative saliency of the subject and the object (§ sec:obviation.saliency ): in all three examples, the object corresponds to the main character of the story; notice in particular in ( ex:towGnAmqe ) the presence of inverse marking on the previous verb kó-wɣ-ndʑɯ `he complained about him', which does not have SPO.

In stories, non-salient characters tend to be described on the basis of their relationship with a salient character (rather than by a different name), and are therefore expressed by nouns with third person possessor. Many, if not most SPO configurations in the corpus involve non-salient referents acting upon salient referents related to them; the apparent correlation between SPO and inverse marking in texts may therefore be a side-effect of argument saliency rather than a specific morphosyntactic phenomenon.
summary: In Algonquian languages, third persons possessed by another third person are automatically obviative, and only one argument may be proximate in a clause; as a result, certain subject–object possession configurations force inverse or direct verb forms. The passage notes that Japhug shows a strong tendency for inverse marking in subject-possessed/object-possessor (SPO) contexts, but this does not prove that possession itself triggers the inverse. Instead, many of the observed cases may reflect argument saliency, since SPO examples often involve non-salient characters described through their relationship to a salient one.

subsection: The function of the direct/inverse contrast in non-local configurations
text:
inverse inverse!saliency
When both core arguments are third person animate, both are potentially proximate or obviative, and the verb can thus be either in direct of inverse form, and the choice between one or the other is determined, as we will discuss in this section, by pragmatics. In this section, I mainly focus on human or anthropomorphized non-human referents; animals are briefly treated at the end of the section.

Transitive verb forms where such a choice between inverse and direct forms exist are however a minority. For instance, in ( ex:towGtsWm.tonWqambWmbjom ), the verbs to-ti `she said', to-nɯ-ŋga `she wore it' and ko-rqoʁ `he hugged (her neck)' are in the direct form due to animacy constraints (since the subjects of all three verbs are animates and their object inanimates, see § sec:obviation.animacy ). Note that a subject shift takes place between to-nɯ-ŋga `she wore it' and ko-rqoʁ `he hugged (her neck)' without inverse marking.

The only verb in this passage taking two animate referents is tó-wɣ-tsɯm `she took him up', whose subject is stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ `the smallest (of the daughters of heaven)' and whose object is a human boy. Compare example ( ex:towGtsWm.tonWqambWmbjom ), where this referent is in 3sg, with ( ex:jWfCWndzximWr ) in § sec:time.ordinals and ( ex:jWGmWr.ndAre ) in § sec:adversative.topic, where it appears in 1sg.

exe

stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ kɯ `...' to-ti tɕendɤre qro nɯnɯ ɯ-ŋga nɯ to-nɯ-ŋga qʰe, tɕe nɯ ɯ-mke ko-rqoʁ qʰe tɕendɤre tó-wɣ-tsɯm to-nɯqambɯmbjom qʰe \\
most sbj: pcp -be.small dem erg ifr -say lnk pigeon dem 3sg. poss -clothes top ifr - auto -wear lnk lnk dem 3sg. poss -neck ifr -hug lnk lnk ifr - inv -take.away ifr: up -fly lnk \\
`The smallest [daughter]$_i$ said `...', she$_i$ wore the pigeon skin, he$_j$ hugged her$_i$ neck, and she$_i$ took him$_j$ and flew away [with him].' (07-deluge)
0003426#S68
exe

The presence of inverse marking on tó-wɣ-tsɯm `she took him up' in ( ex:towGtsWm.tonWqambWmbjom ) is neither due to semantic nor syntactic factors. Rather, animate (in particular, human/sentient) referents in a particular passage (the subsection of a story, or a complete) are classified along a scale of obviativity. The main character(s) is/are ascribed proximate status, while characters which the narrator considers to be more secondary receive obviative status.

Example ( ex:towGtsWm.tonWqambWmbjom ) is taken from a flood story whose main character is a human boy (the only survivor of the flood). This character remains proximate in the whole story, and thus by comparison, the daughter of heaven (the other character found in the passage in ex:towGtsWm.tonWqambWmbjom ) is obviative. The proximate/obviative constrast on these animate referents is not visible when they occur as subjects with inanimate objects: the inanimate referents are necessarily always more obviative that any animate referent, and therefore direct forms are found. This contrast is only revealed when a verb takes two animate referents, namely the verb tó-wɣ-tsɯm. The apparent shift between direct and inverse forms found in ( ex:towGtsWm.tonWqambWmbjom ) is not an effect of the animate referent changing their obviation status across sentences, but is rather a consequence of the fact that Gyalrong languages lack a special conjugation class used with inanimate objects, such as the VTI (transitive inanimate) verbs in Algonquian.

The scale of obviation ( ex:scale.toWGtsWm ) accounts for the distribution of direct and inverse marking in ( ex:towGtsWm.tonWqambWmbjom ) (and in the rest of the story): direct marking is found when the subject is higher than the object on the scale, and inverse marking when it is lower.

exe

human boy > daughter of heaven$_i$ > inanimate referents ( qro ɯ-ŋga `pigeon clothes'; ɯ-mke `her$_i$ neck')
exe

The degree of obviativity of each referent, while generally stable within a particular passage, can be fluid in longer narratives. For instance, in the story `Norbzang and Padma 'Od'bar', the analysis of direct vs. inverse forms reveals several scales.

In ( ex:Padma.nWGznARaR ), the subject is the king and the object the character Padma 'Od'bar, and inverse marking indicates that the latter is proximate.

exe

kɯɕnɯ-sŋi kɯɕnɤ-rʑaʁ nɯ́-wɣ-z-nɤʁaʁ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
seven-day seven-night ipfv - inv - caus -have.a.good.time sens -be \\
`[The king] let [Padma 'Od'bar] have a good time for seven days and seven nights.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

Examples ( ex:Padma.pasWxCAt ) and ( ex:Padma.nWwGCWrNonW ) have the secundative verbs pa-sɯxɕɤt `he taught (it) to them' (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ) and nɯ́-wɣ-ɕɯ-rŋo-nɯ `he lent it to them' (§ sec:ditransitive.causative ) in direct and inverse forms, respectively. From these examples, one could further propose the scale ( ex:Padma.scale ) showing the relative obviativity of the three groups of characters (Padma 'Od'bar, the three girls, and the king).

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ, [...] nɯnɯ tɕʰeme χsɯm nɯ lonba pa-sɯxɕɤt ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
indef. poss -boy dem erg dem girl three dem all aor:3 3$'$-teach sens -be \\
`The boy (Padma 'Od'bar) taught the whole [mantra] to the three girls.' (2005 Norbzang, 380; Padma 'Od'bar > girls)
exe

lnk be.possible: fact say: fact lnk artefact aor - inv - caus -borrow sens -be \\

exe

However, while ( ex:Padma.scale ) is indeed valid in some sections of the story, we also find examples such as ( ex:Padma.nanWsNom ) and ( ex:Padma.katCABnW ) with a verb in direct form, despite the fact that the subject (the king) is lower on the scale ( ex:Padma.scale ) than the object (Padma 'Od'bar): an inverse configuration would be expected.

tɕendɤre rɟɤlpu kɯ na-nɯsŋom ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk king erg aor:3 3$'$-envy sens -be \\
`The king envied [Padma 'Od'bar].' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

exe

tɕendɤre tɕetu ndɤre, pɤnmawombɤr ka-tɕɤβ-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\

`[The king and his servants] burned Padma 'Od'bar up there.' (2005 Norbzang)

In ( ex:Padma.nanWsNom ) and ( ex:Padma.katCABnW ), a different scale ( ex:Padma.scale2 ) has to be posited.
summary: The passage explains that when both core arguments are third-person animate, a verb may appear in either direct or inverse form, with the choice governed by pragmatics and obviation rather than by syntax or semantics. Direct and inverse marking reflect a scale of proximate vs. obviative status: direct is used when the subject ranks higher than the object, inverse when it ranks lower, and this can vary within narratives depending on which characters are treated as main or secondary.

subsection: The function of the direct/inverse contrast in non-local configurations
text:
exe

King > Padma 'Od'bar
exe

Thus, a particular character of this story (the king), which has obviative status in ( ex:Padma.nWGznARaR ) and ( ex:Padma.nWwGCWrNonW ), becomes proximate in ( ex:Padma.nanWsNom ) and ( ex:Padma.katCABnW ), in a passage where he temporarily becomes the `main character'.

Within each of the scenes of a narrative, the obviativity status of each referent generally remains stable. Thus, in chains of verbs sharing coreferent pairs of subject and object, all of the verbs are either in direct or in inverse form. In ( ex:YowGmbi.Yowjtshi.towGCWfka ) for instance, we find four verbs in inverse form in a row; each of them takes tɤ-wɯ `grandfather, old man' as obviative subject and the main character of the story Nyima 'Odzer as proximate object.

exe

tɕendɤre tɤ-wɯ nɯ kɯ ɲɤ́-wɣ-ngɤjtsʰi tɕe, nɤki, tɯmgo ɲɤ́-wɣ-mbi, tɯ-ci ra ɲɤ́-wɣ-j-tsʰi tó-wɣ-ɕɯ-fka tɕe tɕe \\
lnk indef. poss -grandfather dem erg ifr - inv -give.to.eat.and.drink lnk filler food ifr - inv -give indef. poss -water pl ifr - inv - caus -drink ifr - inv - caus -be.full lnk lnk \\
`The old man gave him food and drinks, gave him food to eat, water to drink, gave him enough for him to eat his fill.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

However, alternations between direct and inverse can also be found across adjacent clauses with constant subjects and objects within a single passage. In ( ex:RnaRna.Zo.chAwGndzandZi ), the noun lɯlucat This story is about humanized animals depicted as able to think and speak, and can be considered to be similar to human referents. is the proximate referent of the verbs ko-mɟa and ɲo-mɟa, since they are in direct form, but then a shift to inverse occurs and its preys (in the dual, the mouse and the sparrow) become proximate instead. The switch between direct and inverse marking gives native speakers flexibility to change the perspective of the narration.

exe

tɕe nɯ jamar tɕe ci nɯni kɯ ``lɯlu kɯ ɣɯ́-ndza-tɕi" ra mɯ-ɲɤ-sɯso-ndʑi kɯ, ``aʑo ɣɤŋgi-a nɤ aʑo ɣɤŋgi-a" ɲɤ-sɯso-ndʑi, tɕendɤre lɯlu nɯ kɯ ci ko-mɟa, ci ɲo-mɟa tɕe, ndɤre ʁnaʁna ʑo cʰɤ́-wɣ-ndza-ndʑi tɕe, \\

`The other two were not thinking `The cat will eat us', but rather `I am right, I am right', and the cat grabbed one on his left and one on his right, and both ended up eaten by him.' (lWlu 2002)
0003361#S76
exe

In other cases, alternations between direct and inverse forms without change in subjects and objects appear to be due to hesitations on the part of the speaker. For instance, in ( ex:GArAtnW.pjANu ) the speaker first chooses a direct 3pl 3$'$ verb form ɣɤrɤt-nɯ, with rɟɤlpu ɣɯ ɯ-ʁjoʁ nɯra `the king's servants' being the proximate referent, but then switches to the inverse 3$'$ 3sg form ɣɯ-tsɯm, with the character Nyima 'Odzer as proximate referent instead.

exe

rɟɤlpu ɣɯ ɯ-ʁjoʁ nɯra kɯ ɲimawozɤr, nɯnɯ ɣɤrɤt-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu, ɣɯ-tsɯm pjɤ-ŋu tɕeri, \\
