`As the king's servants were about to throw him [into the lake], as they were about to take him away.' (Nyima wodzer2002)
exe
summary: The passage explains that within a narrative scene, a referent’s proximate or obviative status usually stays stable, so sequences of verbs with the same subject and object are consistently either direct or inverse. However, speakers can shift between direct and inverse marking to change narrative perspective or because of hesitation, allowing a character who is normally obviative to become proximate when they temporarily take center stage.

subsection: The function of the direct/inverse contrast in non-local configurations
text:
inverse!pseudo-passive
In some texts translated from Chinese, inverse verb forms are used in configurations with an inanimate object and an animate subject, an exception to the animacy constraints described in § sec:obviation.animacy, according to which a direct form would be expected. This usage is similar to the generic subject construction (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ) where the inverse also occurs with animate subjects and inanimate objects, but semantically differs in that the subject is not generic, but rather an unknown referent.

Example ( ex:jowGkio.towGcW ) illustrates this construction with the verbs jó-wɣ-kio and tó-wɣ-cɯ, whose object is the jar's cover and subject the girl inside the jar (whose presence was unknown to the observer from whose point of view this passage is narrated).

exe

ɯ-tɕʰira [...] ɣɯ ɯ-fkaβ nɯnɯ jó-wɣ-kio. tɕe nɯ tó-wɣ-cɯ tɕe nɯtɕu tɕe tɕe li, nɯɕimɯma tɕe li, ɯ-ŋga ra kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕɤr ci, ɯ-ʁzɯɣ ra kɯ-βdɯ βdi ci, tɕʰemɤpɯ ci, iɕqʰa tɕʰira ɣɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu to-nɯ-ɬoʁ.\\
3sg. poss -jar gen 3sg. poss -cover dem ifr - inv -slide lnk dem ifr - inv -open lnk dem: loc lnk lnk again immediately lnk again 3sg. poss -clothes pl sbj: pcp - emph be.beautiful indef 3sg. poss -appearance pl sbj: pcp - emph be.nice indef girl indef the.aforementioned jar gen 3sg. poss -in dem: loc ifr: up - auto -come.out \\
`The jar's cover slid over and opened, and a girl with beautiful clothes and a very nice appearance came immediately out of it.' (150827 tianluo-zh)
0006250#S98
exe

The first two clauses translate Chinese 发现水缸盖被推开了 fāxiàn shuǐgānggài bèi tuīkāi leHe realized that the jar's cover had been pushed open. The inverse forms correspond here to a 被 bèi `passive' construction, and nearly all of the examples of inverse expressing unknown (rather than generic) animate subjects have been found in the translation of sentences containing this construction in Chinese. This pseudo-passive construction appears to be an effect of calque from the original, although Tshendzin, when asked about these examples, did not consider them to be ungrammatical.

In addition, there are a few cases in translated texts like ( ex:pjAwGlwoR.kWme.pjAme ) with inverse marking and unknown human subject (on the verb pjɤ́-wɣ-lwoʁ `someone spilled it') where no 被 bèi construction is found in the original: this example translates 他发现水罐空了 tā fāxiàn shuǐguàn kōng leHe realized that his water jar was empty. The fact that the translation in this example is somewhat removed from the original would support the idea that the pseudo-passive inverse is a native grammatical construction.

exe

tɕendɤre ri, ku-rtoʁ tɕe ɯ-tɯ-ci nɯra pjɤ́-wɣ-lwoʁ tɕe kɯ-tu pjɤ-me qʰe, \\
lnk lnk ipfv -look lnk 3sg. poss - indef. poss -water dem: pl ifr - inv -spill lnk sbj: pcp -exist ifr. ipfv -not.exist lnk \\
`He$_i$ realized that someone had spilled the water [in his$_i$ gourd], and none was left.' (140505 liuhaohan zoubian tianxia-zh)
0003913#S188
exe

Thus, it is unclear at present whether the extension of the generic subject construction to express unknown subjects (the `pseudo-passive'), is the result of translatese, or whether it reflects a genuine but rare native construction.
summary: Some translated texts from Chinese use inverse verb forms with inanimate objects and animate, but unknown, subjects, even though a direct form would normally be expected. This “pseudo-passive” use resembles the generic subject construction formally, but differs in that the subject is not generic; it may be a calque from Chinese 被 bèi passives, though some examples without a Chinese passive source suggest it could also be a rare native construction.

text:
morphology!irregular verb!defective
Unlike in Zbu, there are no transitive verbs in Japhug with irregular 1sg forms. The only irregularities related to person indexation are either found in generic forms or defective conjugations.

The verb tisay takes the prefix kɯ- to express generic human subject as in ( ex:tukWti.Nu ) as if it were an intransitive verb (§ sec:intr.23 ) instead of the inverse ɣɯ- found on regular transitive verbs (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ); a form such as $ $ tú-wɣ-ti would be incorrect. It is not the only irregularity of tisay: this is also the only underived transitive verb with a separate stem II in Japhug (§ sec:stem2.form ).

exe

tɕe ɕkrɤz ɣɯ ɯ-mat nɯ tʰɣe tu-kɯ-ti ŋu \\
lnk oak gen 3sg. poss -fruit dem acorn ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`The fruit of the oak is called an acorn.' (08-CkrAz)
0003444#S39
exe

Although the prefix kɯ- expresses generic object on other transitive verbs (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ), in the case of tisay there is no ambiguity: the object of this verb is necessarily a complement clause or a noun, and can never have a first, second or generic person referent. The use of kɯ- to mark the transitive subject is reminiscent of Tshobdun, where both transitive and intransitive verbs mark generic subject by the same prefix.

The defective verb mɤ-xsione does not know only occurs in Factual Non-Past negative with a generic subject. This transitive verb takes nouns or complement clauses as object, usually with either an interrogative pronoun or a polar opposition as in ( ex:tukWti.Nu ), sometimes with the dubitative (§ sec:dubitative ). It cannot take any additional affix (including nominalization prefixes, § sec:nmlz.defective and orientation preverbs, § sec:verbs.no.preverbs ), except for the autive nɯ- in the form mɤ-nɯ-xsi, as in ( ex:mAnWxsi.ri ).

exe

tu-ndze ŋu maʁ mɤ-xsi. \\
ipfv -eat[III] be: fact not.be: fact neg - genr:know \\
`I don't know whether [bears] eat [humans] or not.' (21-pri) 0003580#S112
exe

exe

a-pa, aki nɯ staʁlupa kɤ-βde ɯ-spa nɯ mɤ-nɯ-xsi ri, \\
1sg. poss -father down dem born.the.year.of.the.tiger obj: pcp -throw 3sg. poss -material dem neg - auto - genr:know lnk \\
`Father, I don't know whether the [boy] down there is someone born in the year of the tiger, [who must] to be thrown [into the lake as a sacrifice to the lake monster], but...' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

The stem -xsi contains the same root as sɯzknow but without -z suffix and with a x- prefix which represents a fossilized allomorph of the regular generic kɯ-. The verb sɯzknow is attested in generic form, as in ( ex:pWwGsWz.me.ri ). Although such examples are very rare, they show that mɤ-xsi cannot be considered to be a suppletive form in the paradigm of sɯzknow.

exe

nɯ ma kɯ-pe tɕi pɯ́-wɣ-sɯz me, mɤ-kɯ-pe tɕi pɯ́-wɣ-sɯz me. \\
dem apart.from sbj: pcp -be.good also aor - inv -know not.exist: fact neg - sbj: pcp -be.good also aor - inv -know not.exist: fact \\
` `Apart from that, I don't know about the good or the bad things [that the butterfly does].' (26-qambalWla)
0003680#S51
exe

The verb kɤtɯpatell, which presents a unique case of incorporation (§ sec:lexicalized.object.participle, § sec:incorp.denom ), only occurs in non-prefixed forms. Its paradigm is thus restricted to the Factual Non-Past (the only tense without orientation preverb, § sec:fact.morphology ), excluding second person forms (which always take a prefix, whether in the mixed or local domain), all inverse forms (which take the wɣ- inverse prefix) and non-finite forms (§ sec:nmlz.defective ). tab:kAtWpa (from ) presents the defective paradigm of kɤtɯpatell, with the regular stem III kɤtɯpe in 1sg 3 and 3sg 3$'$ forms, alongside that of ndzaeat.
summary: Japhug has no transitive verbs with irregular 1sg forms; instead, the relevant irregularities concern generic indexation or defective paradigms. The verb *tisay* uses *kɯ-* with generic human subjects and has a separate stem II, while *mɤ-xsi* ‘not know’ is a defective transitive verb restricted to negative Factual Non-Past generic forms and cannot take most affixes. Another defective verb, *kɤtɯpatell*, occurs only in non-prefixed forms, so its paradigm is limited to Factual Non-Past and excludes second person, inverse, and non-finite forms.

text:
verb!transitive subject!dummy
A handful of transitive light verbs ( βzumake § sec:Bzu.lv, lɤtrelease § sec:lAt.lv, tɕɤttake out § sec:tCAt.lv, ndotake § sec:ndo.lv, taput § sec:ta.lv and tsʰoʁattach) occur in the dummy subject construction, expressing natural phenomena, in particular meteorological ones. These dummy subjects, which cannot be realized, correspond to expletive pronouns in languages which require overt subjects.

In this construction, the verb only has one overt (always singular) absolutive nominal argument. The only form of the paradigm is the direct 3sg 3$'$ (§ sec:indexation.non.local ), with Stem III alternation in non-past tenses as in ( ex:kWwGrum.kute ), and C-type preverbs in Aorist as in ( ex:tANe.naBzu ), showing that the verb, despite its lack of ergatively-marked subject, is unambiguously transitive (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ).

exe

tɤŋe na-βzu qʰe ɲɯ-me ɕti. \\
sun aor:3 3$'$-make lnk ipfv -not.exist be. aff: fact \\
`It disappears when the sun appears.' (25-RmArYWG)
0003652#S35
exe

exe

ɯ-taʁ ri kɯ-wɣrum ku-te, ku-kɯ-ta ci tu qʰe, nɯnɯ li kʰɯrwum ŋu \\
3sg. poss -on loc sbj: pcp -be.white ipfv -put[III] ipfv - sbj: pcp -put indef exist: fact lnk dem again mold be: fact \\
`A white thing grows on [meat that has been left to rot], there is something that grows on it, this is also mold.' (20-sWrna)
0003564#S54
exe

The unique absolutive argument of this construction superficially resembles an object. However, in ( ex:kWwGrum.kute ), note that the subject participle ku-kɯ-ta `(the thing) that grows (on it)' (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ) is used to relativize this argument instead of an object participle (§ sec:dummy.subj.object.relativization ) as would have been expected (see also § sec:subject.participle.other.relative ).

Moreover, despite the unambiguous morphological transitivity of the verb, the ergative is strictly impossible on the noun, even in the case of personified natural forces. For instance, in the retellings of Aesop's story `The North Wind and the Sun', although akɯcʰoʁleeast wind This term was chosen to translate `Northern Wind'. occurs with the ergative with other verbs, and although here the North Wind is anthropomorphized and is described as blowing on purpose (to compete with the sun), the ergative is not accepted when the main verb is βzumake as in ( ex:akWchoRle.toBzu ).

exe

akɯcʰoʁle nɯ to-βzu tɕe rcanɯ, \\
east.wind dem ifr -make lnk unexp: deg \\
`The East (North) Wind blew.' (aesop feng he taiyang-zh)
exe

In addition, the light verbs in this construction lack one of the seven morphological properties of transitive verbs (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ): they select dental infinitives instead of bare infinitives (§ sec:dental.inf ). Compare for instance ( ex:tArtsa.tWBzu.toZa ) where βzumake occurs in the bare infinitive tɯ-βzu with ( ex:WBzu.loZa ), where the bare infinitive ɯ-βzu is found instead, as βzumake is in a plain transitive construction.

exe

tɤrtsa kɯ-wxti tsa tɯ-βzu to-ʑa. \\
wave sbj: pcp -be.big a.little inf:II-make ifr -start \\
`There started to be big waves [on the sea].' (140430 yufu he tade qizi-zh)
0003900#S96
exe

exe

tɕendɤre cʰa ɯ-skɤt ɯ-βzu lo-ʑa. \\
lnk alcohol 3sg. poss -speech 3sg. poss - bare. inf:make ifr -start \\
`He started drunk-talking.' (150906 qingfeng-zh)
0006366#S60
exe

The list of the verbs which allow the dummy transitive subject construction is not closed. For instance the causative of amɲɤmbe homogeneous, `be even' occurs with the noun tɯ-mɯsky, weather in ( ex:tWmW.thasAmYAm ).

exe

jisŋi tɯ-mɯ nɯ kɯ-fse tʰa-sɯ-ɤmɲɤm ʑo, tɤŋe tɕi mɯ-na-βzu, tɯ-mɯ tɕi mɯ-ka-lɤt \\
today indef. poss -sky dem sbj: pcp -be.like aor:3 3$'$-be.homogeneous emph sun also neg - aor:3 3$'$-make indef. poss -weather also neg - aor:3 3$'$-release \\
`Today the weather was uniform, there was neither sun nor rain.' (elicited)
exe
summary: A small set of transitive light verbs occurs in a dummy subject construction used mainly for natural and meteorological phenomena, where the subject is unrealized and corresponds to an expletive pronoun in languages that require overt subjects. In this construction, the verb has only one overt singular absolutive argument and shows transitive morphology, but the ergative is impossible even with personified natural forces; the construction also selects dental infinitives rather than bare infinitives. The set of verbs that can appear in this construction is open, as shown by additional examples beyond the core verbs listed.

text:
ditransitive verb
Ditransitive verbs are trivalent verbs which follow the transitive conjugation (unlike trivalent semi-transitive verbs, § sec:semi.transitive.dative ). Both indirective and secundative transitive verbs are attested, and causative verbs deriving from monotransitive verbs also belong to this category.
summary: Ditransitive verbs are trivalent verbs that follow the transitive conjugation, unlike trivalent semi-transitive verbs. The category includes both indirective and secundative transitive verbs, as well as causative verbs derived from monotransitive verbs.

text:
verb!indirective ditransitive verb!indirective
Most non-derived ditransitive verbs in Japhug are indirective. The theme is in the absolutive and is indexed as an object. The recipient either takes dative (§ sec:dative ) or genitive (§ sec:gen.beneficiary ) flagging, as in ( ex:zYArNo ), or is encoded as a possessive prefix on the object.

exe

kɯ-rɤrma ra nɯ-ɕki nɯtɕu, nɤki, kuxtɕo ci z-ɲɤ-rŋo, \\
sbj: pcp -work pl 3pl. poss - dat dem: loc filler basket indef tral - ifr -borrow \\
`[The leopard] borrowed a basket from the workers.' (2002 qalakWcqraq)
exe

The indirective category can be divided into four semantic subgroups.

First, it comprises verbs of speech, such as tisay, tʰuask, ndʑɯaccuse and fɕɤttell, which mark the adressee with the dative.

Second, it includes verbs expressing gift or temporary transfer of objects such as kʰogive, `pass over' (§ sec:stem3.backformation ) and pʰɯloffer and rŋoborrow and nɤŋgɯborrow. Th first two encode the source as their subject while their recipients takes the dative case, whereas the latter encode the recipient as their subject, and their source appear in the dative.

The two verbs translated as `borrow' differ in that the former ( rŋo ) expresses the lending of an object which can be returned in its original shape to the original owner, while the latter ( nɤŋgɯ ) is used with grain or money, for which an equivalent amount is given back instead of the original object (which has presumably already been consumed). The meaning `lend' is expressed with the corresponding causatives, see § sec:ditransitive.causative. In addition, verbs of manipulation such as ɣɯtbring and tsɯmtake away can optionally take a dative beneficiary and convey a meaning similar to verbs of giving, as in example ( ex:Wphe.latsWm ).

exe

tɕendɤre rɟɤlpu ɯ-pʰe la-tsɯm ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
lnk king 3sg. poss - dat aor:3 3: upstream -take.away sens -be \\
`He brought[the shoe] to the king.' (tWxtsa 2003)
exe

Third, verbs expressing hitting or throwing can also be indirective, for instance βdethrow, and also lɤtrelease, which occurs in many light verb constructions (§ sec:light.verb ).

Fourth, some verbs of manipulation have an obligatory indirect argument expressing the goal, in particular the verb rkuput in which selects the relator noun ɯ-ŋgɯinside (§ sec:WNgW ). For most verbs of manipulation the goal is optional (§ sec:secundative.monotransitive ).

The object of indirective verbs is nearly always third person, and local and inverse configurations are almost never attested (except for inverse generic forms, § sec:indexation.generic.tr ). For instance in (§ sec:tAthe.jAG ), the recipient is 1sg (`ask me'), but the verb tʰuask has the imperative 2sg 3 form (§ sec:imp.morphology ) because the non-overt theme corresponds to the questions that the adressee is about to ask, and using a 2 1 configuration here would be non-sensical.

exe

tɤ-tʰe jɤɣ \\
imp -ask[III] be.allowed: fact \\
`Ask [me your questions]!' (conversation, several attestations)
exe

Local or inverse configurations are attested with indirective verbs of giving in the corpus to refer to asking or giving a girl in marriage, as in ( ex:nWwGkhoa ), as this is the most common situation when a human can occur as theme of a verb of this type.

exe

a-wa kɯ, tɯrme ɣɯ ɯ-rʑaβ nɯ́-wɣ-kʰo-a ɕti nɤ \\
1sg. poss -father erg person gen 3sg. poss -wife aor - inv -give- 1sg be. aff: fact sfp \\
`My father has offered me in marriage to someone.' (150828 liangshanbo zhuyingtai-zh)
0006244#S157
exe

The only indirective verb of speech which is commonly used with a human theme is ndʑɯaccuse: the object and the dative argument correspond to the persons about whom and to whom one complains, respectively. For instance in (§ sec:Wɕki.tandZW ), the object is 2sg, and the dative argument a third person referrent.

exe

aʑo <laoshi> ɯ-ɕki ta-ndʑɯ \\
1sg professor 3sg. poss - dat 1 2-accuse: fact \\
`I will issue a complain against you to the professor.' (150826 liangshanbo zhuyingtai-zh) 0006244#S81
exe

Indirective verbs of manipulation can be used with animate or even human objects, and do occur in local configurations, as in (§ sec:axtu.WNgW.chWtarku ).

exe

aʑo a-xtu ɯ-ŋgɯ cʰɯ-ta-rku \\
1sg 1sg. poss -belly 3sg. poss -in ipfv: downstream -1 2-put.in \\
`I will put you in my belly.' (140505 xiaohaitu-zh) 0003921#S80
exe
summary:
Most non-derived ditransitive verbs in Japhug are indirective: the theme is absolutive and indexed as an object, while the recipient is marked by dative or genitive flagging, or sometimes by a possessive prefix on the object. The passage divides these verbs into four semantic groups: speech verbs, verbs of giving or temporary transfer, verbs of hitting/throwing, and some manipulation verbs with an obligatory or optional goal argument.  

It also notes that indirective verbs usually take third-person objects, with local or inverse configurations being rare, though they can occur in special contexts such as marriage or complaints. Some manipulation verbs can take animate or human objects and may appear in local configurations.

text:
verb!secundative ditransitive verb!secundative
Secundative verbs have two absolutive arguments, one of which (the recipient) is indexed on the verb, and the other one (the theme) is not. The theme is a semi-object, and presents some objectal properties (§ sec:object.participle.relatives, § sec:secundative.theme.relativization ).
summary: Secundative verbs have two absolutive arguments: the recipient, which is indexed on the verb, and the theme, which is not. The theme functions as a semi-object and shows some object-like properties.

text:
Most secundative verbs express temporary or permanent giving: mbigive and ɕtʂɯentrust with. Since these verbs index the recipient, they commonly occur in local configurations (§ sec:indexation.local ), as in (§ sec:kAkWCtsxWa ).

exe

sɯmat kɤ-kɯ-ɕtʂɯ-a \\
fruit aor -2 1-entrust.with- 1sg \\
`You had left me [a jar of] fruit.' (140516 yiguan ganlan-zh) 0004014#S73
exe

The verb mbigive can in addition take an essive adjunct (give as $X$, § sec:essive.abs ), as nɤ-rʑaβ `your wife' in ( ex:nArZaB.YWtambi ); in this sentence the object (theme) is a-me nɯ `my daughter'.

exe

a-me nɯ nɤ-rʑaβ ɲɯ-ta-mbi ŋu \\
1sg. poss -daughter dem 2sg. poss -wife ipfv -1$ $2-give be: fact \\
`I will give you my daughter in marriage.' (`I will give her to you as your wife') (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh)
0003886#S164
exe

Most verbs of speech are indirective, but sɯxɕɤtteach has secundative alignment (see example ex:pjWtasWxCAt, § sec:antipassive.ditransitive ). This verb is perhaps historically a causative (§ sec:caus.sWG ), but it is not analyzable as such synchronically.

The similative verb studo like can also be considered to be secundative. It takes a semi-object designating the manner (generally a demonstrative), and its object refers to the entity (human, animal or inanimate) subjected to the action (with infinitival complement clauses however, there is no raising of the object from the complement, see § sec:similative.verb.complementation ). In ( ex:tAwGstuandZi ), this verb occurs in a 3du 1sg configuration (§ sec:double.number.indexation ), and takes as semi-object the demonstrative nɯra `these (things)'. In serial verb constructions, it occurs with transitive verbs, sharing the subject and the object of its counterpart, but taking an additional (generally demonstrative) manner semi-object (§ sec:svc.similative.verb ).

exe

a-pi ni kɯ nɯra tɤ́-wɣ-stu-a-ndʑi ndʐa ɕti ma, \\
1sg. poss -elder.sibling du erg dem: pl aor - inv -do.like- 1sg - du reason be. aff: fact lnk \\
`[This is because] my two brothers treated me like that.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S177
exe
summary:
The passage describes several verbs with secundative alignment. Most secundative verbs express temporary or permanent giving, such as *mbi* ‘give’ and *ɕtʂɯ* ‘entrust with’, which index the recipient and often appear in local configurations; *mbi* can also take an essive adjunct, as in giving someone a daughter “as your wife.”  

It also notes that *sɯxɕɤt* ‘teach’ has secundative alignment despite most speech verbs being indirective, and that *studo* ‘like’ can be treated as secundative because it takes a manner semi-object and an object referring to the affected entity. In serial verb constructions, *studo* shares the subject and object of the main verb while adding a demonstrative-like manner semi-object.

text:
The theme of secundative verbs cannot be indexed, unlike that of indirective verbs, and first or second person themes are not appropriate with the verb mbigive. To express meanings such as `$X$ gave me/you to $Y$', either an indirective verb has to be used (see ex:nWwGkhoa above), or alternatively the antipassive form rɤmbigive to someone. This antipassive form is the only verb form in Japhug lacking morphological transitivity (§ sec:transitivity.morphology, § sec:antipassive.ditransitive ) that can be used with inverse and local person indexation, as shown by ( ex:nWwGrAmbia ) and ( ex:YAkWrAmbia ).

exe

xlist

a-wa kɯ aʑo nɯ́-wɣ-rɤ-mbi-a \\
1sg. poss -father erg 1sg aor - inv - apass -give- 1sg \\
`My father gave me away.' (elicited)

nɤʑo kɯ aʑo ɲɤ-kɯ-rɤ-mbi-a \\
2sg erg 1sg ifr -2 1- apass -give- 1sg \\
`You gave me away (without me knowing).' (elicited)
xlist
exe
summary:
In Japhug, the theme of secundative verbs cannot be indexed, unlike indirective verbs, and first- or second-person themes are not compatible with *mbigive*. To express meanings like “X gave me/you to Y,” speakers must either use an indirective verb or the antipassive form *rɤmbigive to someone*.  

This antipassive is notable because it is the only Japhug verb form without morphological transitivity that can still combine with inverse and local person indexation.

text:
verb!transitive causative!sigmatic causee causer ditransitive verb
The sigmatic causative is the only valency-increasing derivation in Japhug which can be applied to transitive (unlike applicative § sec:applicative and tropative § sec:tropative ) verbs. When the base verb is transitive, its causative form is ditransitive. I use the notation $C$ $C'$ $P$ to describe causative configurations with three participants: $C$ represents the causer (corresponding to the initiator of the causation, the argument that is added by the causative derivation), $C'$ the causee (corresponding to the subject of the base verb) and $P$ the patientive (corresponding to the object of the base verb); for instance, if the base verb is `help', a 1sg 3pl 2sg configuration can be interpreted as `I made them help you.'

Lexicalized causatives are like underived secundative verbs, and index the recipient as the object. This category includes jtsʰigive to drink, which derives from the monotransitive verb tsʰidrink, and ɕɯrŋolend, which comes from the indirective verb rŋoborrow (see ex:YWkWCWrNoj below for a more detailed discussion on this derivation).

Examples ( ex:YWkWjtshitCi ) and ( ex:YWkWCWrNoj ) illustrate the 2 1 3 configuration with the verbs jtsʰigive to drink and ɕɯrŋolend, expressed in the same way as the local 2 1 configurations of a monotransitive verb (§ sec:indexation.local ).

exe

a-wɯ tɯ-ci ɲɯ-kɯ-j-tsʰi-tɕi ɯ́-jɤɣ? \\
1sg. poss -grandfather indef. poss -water ipfv -2 1- caus -drink- 1du qu -be.allowed: fact \\
`Grandfather, could you give us water to drink?' (nyima wodzer 2002)
exe

In the case of non-lexicalized sigmatic causatives, the status of the causee is more complex, since it can optionally receive ergative flagging (§ sec:causee.kW ), and cannot be relativized like an object (see § sec:instrument.relativization ). The direct object of such verbs can also be relativized using constructions unavailable for the direct object of monotransitive verbs (§ sec:object.causative.relativization ).

In addition, unlike secundative verbs, triactantial causatives can either index the causee or the argument corresponding to the object of the base verb, depending on their person: if the causee or object is first or second person, and the other argument is third person, the first or second person will be indexed regardless of its syntactic function.

For instance, all three examples ( ex:pWkWsWxtCia ), ( ex:kWsWRndWa ) and ( ex:YWkWznWntshoa ) show 2 1 indexation, but the first two has a 2 3 1 configuration, and index the patientive argument as the object, while the last one is an instance of a 2 1 3 configuration, and it indexes the causee as object (see also § sec:sig.caus.morphosyntax and ex:pGAtCW.tAmdzu, § sec:essive.abs for additional examples of the same type). The prevalence of first and second persons over third persons in this context might support the person hierarchy ( ex:hierarchy.3 ) postulated in (§ sec:direct-inverse ).

exe

aʑo tɯ-mɯ kɯ pɯ-kɯ-sɯ-χtɕi-a, tɤndʐo nɯ! \\
1sg indef. poss -weather erg aor -2 1- caus -wash- 1sg cold sfp \\
`You caused me to be drenched by the rain, it is so cold!' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

exe

nɤʑo tɤ-ndze ma alo ma-lɤ-tɯ-tsɯm ma tʰa li kɯ-sɯ-ʁndɯ-a \\
2sg imp -eat[III] lnk upstream neg - imp: upstream -2-take.away lnk later again 2 1- caus -hit- 1sg \\
`Eat it, don't take it up there, you would cause me to be beaten again.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

exe

aʑo ɕɤrɯ ɲɯ-kɯ-z-nɯntsʰo-a \\
1sg meat ipfv -2 1- caus -eat- 1sg \\
`You make me eat the bones.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

While indexation is ambiguous in such cases, ergative flagging helps distinguish between 2 3 1 and 2 1 3 configurations: the ergative is present on the causee in ( ex:pWkWsWxtCia ), and absent on the patientive argument in ( ex:YWkWznWntshoa ) (see also § sec:causee.kW ).

Configurations with both causee and patientive argument being first or second person (3 2 1 and 3 1 2) are not attested in the corpus, See however ( ex:nACki.jAwGsWGWta ) below, quadrivalent configuration with a second person beneficiary in the dative and 3 sg 1 sg verb indexation. and are not easy to elicit. The elicited examples ( ex:WZo.kW.pWwGsWmtoa ) and ( ex:WZo.kW.pWtWwGsWmto ) show that 3 1 2 and 3 2 1 configurations are expressed using mixed 3 1 and 3 2 forms, respectively. In other words, the causee is indexed as object, and the patientive argument is not indexed.

exe

xlist

ɯʑo kɯ nɤʑo pɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-mto-a \\
3sg erg 2sg ipfv - inv - caus -see- 1sg \\
`He made me see you.' (3 sg 1 sg 2 sg, elicited)

ɯʑo kɯ aʑo pɯ-tɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-mto \\
3sg erg 1sg aor -2- inv - caus -see \\
`He made you see me.' (3 sg 2 sg 1 sg elicited)
xlist
exe

The causative derivation of indirective verbs has several different effects on argument structure. In the case of the lexicalized causative ɕɯrŋolend, the relationship between its three arguments and those of the base verb rŋoborrow can be summarized as follows (compare ex:YWkWCWrNoj with ex:zYArNo in § sec:ditransitive.indirective ).

itemize
The subject of rŋoborrow, the receiving person, corresponds to the object of ɕɯrŋolend.
The object of rŋo, the thing that is borrowed, corresponds to the semi-object of ɕɯrŋolend.
The dative oblique argument of rŋo, the giving person, corresponds to the subject of ɕɯrŋolend, which is semantically both causer and source.
itemize

exe

wortɕʰi ʑo, nɤ-χsɤrzaŋ ɲɯ-kɯ-ɕɯ-rŋo-j \\
please emph 2sg. poss -magical.object ipfv -2 1- caus -borrow- 1pl \\
`Please, lend us you magical object.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

This `inversive' causative derivation reverses the direction of the borrowing action and modifies the argument structure and the alignment (indirective to secundative) without adding any new referent, by merging the source and causer roles, interpreting ɕɯrŋo as `$X_i$ causes $Y$ to borrow $Z$ from himself$_i$'. Other cases of this type of `inversive' causative are presented in § sec:sig.caus.inversive.
summary:
The sigmatic causative is the only valency-increasing derivation in Japhug that can apply to transitive verbs; with a transitive base verb, the causative becomes ditransitive, with three roles: causer, causee, and patientive. For non-lexicalized causatives, the causee may take ergative marking and is not relativizable like an object, while indexation can vary according to person hierarchy so that first- or second-person arguments are indexed over third persons, sometimes making the causee or the patientive appear as the object.

The passage also describes lexicalized causatives such as jtsʰi- ‘give to drink’ and ɕɯrŋo- ‘lend’, which behave like secundative verbs. In the case of ɕɯrŋo- ‘lend’, the causative reverses the borrowing relation and changes the alignment without adding a new

text:
For most indirective verbs however, recipients and beneficiaries are marked with the dative and/or with a coreferent possessive prefix. Thus, the causative derivation does turn them into absolutive patientive arguments. For instance, the beneficiary of the verb sɯɣɯtsend, cause to bring is in the dative as that of its base verb ɣɯtbring, as shown by ( ex:nACki.jAwGsWGWta ), where dative marking on the 2sg is obligatory.

exe

aʑo a-βdaχpu nɯ kɯ pjɤ-nɯmto tɕe tɕendɤre nɤ-ɕki jɤ́-wɣ-sɯ-ɣɯt-a ŋu tɕe, \\
1sg 1sg. poss -master dem erg ifr -find lnk lnk 2sg. poss - dat aor - inv - caus -bring- 1sg be: fact lnk \\
`My master found it and sent me to bring it to you.' (140513 qianshang he xiaotou-zh)
0003979#S65
exe
summary: The passage says that for most indirective verbs, recipients and beneficiaries are marked with the dative and/or a coreferent possessive prefix, and that the causative derivation makes them absolutive patientive arguments. It illustrates this with a causative verb meaning “cause to bring,” where the beneficiary still appears in the dative, and notes that the dative marking on the second person singular is obligatory.

text:
verb!semi-transitive causative!sigmatic causee causer
Causative verbs derived from semi-transitive ones (§ sec:semi.transitive ) show secundative alignment: the causee is treated as object, and the semi-object of the base verb as an absolutive oblique, not indexed on the verb. For instance, the causative sɤrmigive a name (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ) of the verb rmibe called selects the entity to which a name is given as direct object, the 1pl in example ( ex:tuwGsArmij ).

exe

sɤrndzu cʰo tatsʰi ra kɯ sɤŋu-pɯ tu-nɯ-ti-nɯ tɕe, ʁdɯrɟɤt ra sɤŋu-pɯ tú-wɣ-sɤrmi-j ŋu. \\
topo comit topo pl erg pl.p-person.from ipfv - auto -say- pl lnk topo pl topo -person.from ipfv - inv -give.name- 1pl be: fact \\
`Those from Gsar-rdzong and Da-tshang say `Sangu people', they name us, [those] of Gdong-brgyad, `Sangu people'.' (23-tCAphW)
0003614#S1
exe
summary: Causative verbs derived from semi-transitive verbs show secundative alignment: the causee is treated as the direct object, while the semi-object of the base verb is realized as an absolutive oblique and is not indexed on the verb. In the example of *sɤrmigive a name* from *rmibe called*, the entity receiving the name is the direct object, while the 1pl referent appears as the oblique participant.

text:
verb!labile lability
Most Japhug verbs strictly follow either the intransitive, or the transitive conjugations, and voice alternations such as causative (§ sec:sig.causative, § sec:velar.causative ), applicative (§ sec:applicative ) and antipassive (§ sec:antipassive ) are needed to change their valency. A limited number of labile verbs are compatible with both conjugations; three groups can be distinguished: plain labile, labile with oblique arguments and labile with semi-object.
summary: Most Japhug verbs belong either to the intransitive or transitive conjugation, and changes in valency normally require voice alternations such as causative, applicative, or antipassive forms. However, a limited set of verbs is labile and can occur in both conjugations, with three types distinguished: plain labile verbs, labile verbs with oblique arguments, and labile verbs with semi-object arguments.

text:
Plain labile verbs are compatible with both the intransitive and the transitive conjugations. When conjugated intransitively, they only have one argument (no semi-object or oblique argument). When conjugated transitively (following the features in § sec:transitivity.morphology ), their subject corresponds to the intransitive subject, and the added argument is the object, except for a handful of examples (§ sec:lability.pass ).

Compare for instance the intransitive and transitive use of the verb βlɯburn in ( ex:BlW.tr.intr ). In the ( ex:tABlWa ), the verb has 1sg indexation, and since it lacks the 12 sg 3 past -t suffix (§ sec:indexation.mixed ), cannot be a transitive verb form (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ). This intransitive verb form cannot take an object, and means `make a fire'. In ( ex:smi.tABlWta ), the verb has the -t suffix and is therefore a 1sg 3 transitive configuration (§ sec:indexation.mixed ), and can take an overt object (here smifire, but it can also occur with a noun referring to the object being burned).

exe

xlist

tɤ-βlɯ-a \\
aor -burn- 1sg \\
`I made a fire'. (elicited; 1sg: intr )

smi tɤ-βlɯ-t-a \\
fire aor -burn- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I made a fire'. (elicited; 1sg 3)
xlist
exe

tab:labile1 gives additional examples of labile verbs with open syllable stems in transitive and intransitive conjugations.

All criteria listed in § sec:transitivity.morphology (when applicable) are congruent to distinguish between the transitive and intransitive forms of labile verbs; tab:labile.test presents the application of the seven tests to the verb βlɯburn.

Tests 2 and 5 are not operational with verbs whose stem ends in close syllable, but at least test 1 (in the case of taʁweave in ex:taR.tr.intr ) is always applicable. Some labile verbs can even be used with the non-periphrastic Past Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv ), as in ( ex:tCheme.pWtaR ). The presence or absence of the ergative on third person overt subjects is also a useful confirmation of the valency of the verb; for instance, in ( ex:tCheme.pWtaR ) the subject tɕʰemegirl lacks ergative marking, confirming the fact that taʁweave is used here intransitively.

exe

xlist

tɕʰeme ci pɯ-taʁ ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
girl indef pst. ipfv -weave sens -be \\
`A girl was weaving.' (tWxsta2003)

summary:
Plain labile verbs can appear in both intransitive and transitive conjugations. In the intransitive use, they have only one argument, whereas in the transitive use the subject corresponds to the intransitive subject and a new object is added, with a few exceptions.  

The passage illustrates this with βlɯburn, whose intransitive form lacks the transitive -t suffix and cannot take an object, while the transitive form has -t and allows an overt object such as “fire.” Various morphology-based tests, including ergative marking and special past forms, help distinguish the two valency patterns, though some tests are not available for certain stem types.

text:
verb!labile
In addition to those in tab:labile1, the following verbs are labile: ɣndʑɯrgrind, lɤɣgraze, nbraʁloosen the earth, ntʂuweed with a hoe, nɤrelaugh, nɯɣɤjatalk back, oppose, nɯkʰɤjatalk back, oppose, nɯproʁmbaimitate, rŋuparch, sɯlaʁrdɤβkick (kick with forelegs), sɯqartsɯkick, sɯsothink, taʁweave, tɤβthresh.

The majority of plain labile verbs denote actions modifying the substance or shape of a material ( ɣndʑɯrgrind, ɕluplough etc), in particular activities related to agriculture and traditional trades. When used intransitively, these verbs do not specify any object, and generally express atelic actions. For instance in ( ex:tCheme.pWtaR ), pɯ-taʁ means `do weaving', without intrinsic endpoint and without reference to a particular piece of cloth.

Another category of labile verbs express action negatively affecting people (such as nɯɣɤjatalk back, oppose etc), some with animal subjects ( sɯlaʁrdɤβkick (kick with forelegs) etc). These verbs take humans as objects in the transitive conjugation; The verb mɯrkɯsteal, though adversely affecting the persons whose possession are stolen, does not belong to this category since it takes the possession as object, not the victim of the theft. when used intransitively, they express a general propensity of the subject to do these negative actions.

The perception verb mtosee also has an intransitive stative use, meaning `have sharp eyesight', taking the noun tɯ-mɲaʁeye as subject, and expressing the experiencer as subject possessor). Example ( ex:WmYaR.YWmto ) shows that the verb mto is conjugated intransitively (without stem III alternation, otherwise ɲɯ-mtɤm `he sees it' would be expected). Some verbs derived from the root mto, such as the velar causative ɣɤmtocause to recover eyesight (§ sec:velar.causative.vs.sigmatic.causative ), come from this stative intransitive use rather than the more common transitive one.

summary:
The passage explains that several verbs are labile, with many plain labile verbs describing actions that alter the substance or shape of a material, especially in agriculture and traditional trades. When used intransitively, these verbs typically lack a specific object and denote atelic actions.  

It also notes a second group of labile verbs that express actions negatively affecting people or animals, where the transitive form takes human objects and the intransitive form expresses a general propensity. Finally, the perception verb *mto* ‘see’ has an intransitive stative meaning ‘have sharp eyesight,’ and some derived verbs come from this stative use rather than the transitive one.

text:
alignment!nominative-accusative lability
Most labile verbs in intransitive use have a meaning and syntactic function reminiscent of antipassive (§ sec:antipassive ) derivations, and share with them the ability to take the non-periphrastic Past Imperfective pɯ- (§ sec:antipassive.pst.ipfv ). Nevertheless, it is unclear whether the transitive use of labile verbs is primary; one could also consider the intransitive use to be the basic function, and compare their transitive use to the Applicative derivation (§ sec:applicative ) instead. Since the alignment of the subjects between the transitive and intransitive uses of these verbs follows nominative-accusative, it is referred to as `accusative lability' in this work. The term `agent-preserving lability' is less felicitous, since the subjects of labile verbs are not always agents.

Two plain labile verbs, nɤrelaugh and sɯsothink, have an antipassive form. This feature is shared with the semi-transitive labile verb sɤŋolisten see § sec:semi.tr.labile. On the other hand, no labile verb is compatible with applicative derivation. These two verbs also differ from other labile verbs in having idiosyncratic semantic differences in their intransitive and transitive uses.

The verb nɤrelaugh is a denominal verb deriving from the inalienable noun tɤ-relaugh (n). In its transitive use `laugh at, mock', it encodes the stimulus as direct object. Both the intransitive meaning and the transitive one are well-attested functions of the nɯ-/nɤ- denominal prefix: parallel examples include nɤʁaʁhave a good time (from tɤ-ʁaʁgood time, § sec:denom.intr.nW ) for the intransitive use of nɤ- and nɤmbrɯget angry with (from tɤ-mbrɯanger, § sec:denom.tr.nW ) for it transitive use. Therefore, the most likely way to account for the lability of nɤre is to posit that it represents the conflation of two denominal derivations from the same base noun.

The antipassive form sɤnɤrelaugh at people is semantically connected with the meaning of the transitive use, and semantically quite different from the intransitive use of nɤrelaugh.

The intransitive use of sɯsothink is restricted to the meaning `in $X$'s opinion', as in ( ex:pjWsWsoa ), The intransitivity of sɯsothink in ( ex:pjWsWsoa ) is shown by the absence of Stem III, which would be expected in the Imperfective 1sg 3 (§ sec:ipfv.morphology ). Note that the orientation downwards is selected, instead of westwards in the transitive use (§ sec:orientation.lability ). and has no semantic overlap with the antipassive rɯsɯsothink, `ponder' ( ex:pjWrWsWso ). Note that this antipassive form is irregular, § sec:antipassive.rA.

summary:
Most labile verbs in their intransitive use resemble antipassive derivations and can take the non-periphrastic Past Imperfective pɯ-, but it is unclear whether the transitive or intransitive use is basic. Because their subject alignment is nominative-accusative, the book calls this pattern “accusative lability,” and notes that “agent-preserving lability” is less accurate since the subjects are not always agents.

Among labile verbs, only nɤre ‘laugh’ and sɯso ‘think’ have antipassive forms, and neither is compatible with applicative derivation; both also show idiosyncratic semantic differences between their intransitive and transitive uses. The intransitive use of nɤre is best analyzed as the conflation of two denominal derivations from the same noun, while the very restricted intransitive use of sɯso appears to be derived from

text:
alignment!ergative-absolutive lability
A handful of labile verbs have ergative (or passive-like) lability: the subject of the verb when used intransitively corresponds to its object when used transitively.

The clearest example is provided by the denominal verb nɯʁjoʁ from ʁjoʁservant, which means `give orders to' in transitive use (from `treat as a servant', § sec:denom.tr.nW ), and `work as a servant' in intransitive use. In ( ex:YWnWRjoR.tuzrAme ), the transitive nɯʁjoʁ shares its subject and object with causativized verbs, while in ( ex:zYWnWRjoR.ZYWnAme ) the intransitive subject of nɯʁjoʁ has the same referent as the subject of z-ɲɯ-nɤme, as shown by the presence of a translocative echo (§ sec:echo.multiple.AM ) on both verbs (which cannot target the direct object, § sec:AM.argument.motion ).

exe

tɕʰeme nɯ tɕe tɕe ɯ-kʰa nɯtɕu ko-z-rɤʑi tɕe, ɲɯ-nɯʁjoʁ tu-z-rɤme pjɤ-ŋu. \\
girl dem lnk lnk 3sg. poss -house dem: loc ifr - caus -stay lnk ipfv -give.orders ipfv - caus -work[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The witch kept the girl in the house, and gave her orders and put her to work.' (140507 tangguowu-zh) 0003933#S107
exe

exe

sŋi qʰe z-ɲɯ-nɯʁjoʁ tɕe kɯβʁa ra nɯ-ma z-ɲɯ-nɤme \\
day lnk tral - ipfv -work.as.servant lnk noble pl 3pl. poss -work tral - ipfv -do.work[III] \\
`In the day, he would work as a servant, and do work for the nobles.' (150828 donglang)

Since the nɯ-/nɤ- denominal prefixes occur with similar meanings (`treat as $X$' and `become/serve as $X$) on other base nouns (see § sec:denom.intr.nW and § sec:denom.tr.nW ), the lability of nɯʁjoʁ can be accounted for by assuming a conflation of two homophonous denominal derivations from the same base noun, as in the case nɤrelaugh discussed above (§ sec:lability.apass ). The fact that double denominal derivation yields accusative lability in one case and ergative lability in the other is a consequence of the high diversity of meanings associated with the hyper-productive nɯ-/nɤ- prefix (§ sec:denom.nW ).

The other examples of ergative lability are highly lexicalized, and the transitive vs. intransitive functions have to be treated as different lexical entries synchronically.

The intransitive riremain `be left' ( ex:tWrdoR.YAri ) (see also ex:zgo.tWrdoR, § sec:multiple.CN ) is related to the transitive homophonous verb root ri, which is exclusively found in collocation with tɯ-sroʁlife (§ sec:orphan.verb ) in the meaning `save $X$'s live' ( ex:asroR.kAtWrit ). The entity whose life is spared is encoded as subject of the intransitive ri, and as possessor of the object tɯ-sroʁ of transitive ri (see also ex:ni.ndZisroR, § sec:dual.determiners ).

exe

ɯ-tɕɯ ʁnɯz nɯ pjɤ-si, tɯ-rdoʁ nɯ ɲɤ-ri qʰe \\
3sg. poss -son two dem ifr -die one-piece dem ifr -remain lnk \\
`Two of her sons died, and one remained [alive].' (Gesar 2003)
exe

exe

a-sroʁ kɤ-tɯ-ri-t \\
1sg. poss -life aor -2-save- pst: tr \\
`You saved my life.' (150906 qingfeng-zh) 0006366#S109
exe

Given the more specific meaning of transitive ri, it is more likely that it derives from intransitive ri rather than the other way round. A further piece of evidence in favour of this hypothesis is the irregular causative βriprotect, which also appears to derive from the intransitive riremain (§ sec:causative.m ). The relationship between intransitive ri, transitive ri and causative βri is purely historical. These three verbs are synchronically completely distinct, and select different orientation preverbs ( westwards, eastwards and upwards, respectively).

The verb pado is one of the most common verbs in Japhug, with a wide range of meanings including `close (door)', `become (friend, spouses)' and `discuss' (§ sec:pa.lv ). It selects not only nouns, but also infinitive complements as objects (§ sec:pa.complements ).

Two intransitive verbs with the same root form pa, but only attested in 3sg, also exist: the verb papass $X$ years, which selects as subject a numeral referring to a number of years (see example ex:40.topa, § sec:pa.intr.lv and the discussion in § sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history ), and the light verb pa used as light verb with ideophones (§ sec:idph.pa ). Both of these functions are derivable from the meaning `do' of the transitive verb (§ sec:CN.verbs, § sec:pa.lv ). The conversion to the intransitive conjugation may have occurred through third person ambiguous forms in a dummy subject construction (§ sec:transitive.dummy ).

The discussion above shows that in the cases of ergative lability, either the intransitive verb ( riremain) or the transitive one ( pado) can potentially be the primary form, with transitivization or intransitivization by zero-derivation due to reanalysis in ambiguous contexts (on this topic, see also § sec:stem3.backformation ).
summary: The passage describes a small set of Japhug verbs with ergative-absolutive lability, where the subject of the intransitive use corresponds to the object of the transitive use. The clearest case is the denominal verb nɯʁjoʁ, whose transitive and intransitive meanings can be explained as two homophonous denominal derivations from the same noun, while the other examples are highly lexicalized and must be treated as separate lexical entries synchronically. It concludes that in such cases either the intransitive or the transitive form may be historically primary, with zero-derivation arising through reanalysis in ambiguous contexts.

When used transitively, rpubump into takes an object corresponding to the body parts suffering the impact ( ex:WtaR.kAnWrputa, with the 12 sg 3 past -t suffix), while in its intransitive use as in ( ex:kArpua ) no body part is specified.

When transitively conjugated, rpubump into does not have a causative meaning `cause X to bump into Y' (the causative sɯ-rpu is used for this meaning). Although one could be tempted to translate rpubump into in this way in examples like ( ex:WtaR.kunWrpea ) (`I caused my bracelet to knock on the tripod'), here the bracelet, which is worn on the body, is construed as an extended part of the body (note the autive, which conveys both the meaning of non-volitionality and of action affecting the subject, § sec:autoben.proper, § sec:autoben.spontaneous ).

summary:
The verb *rpu* ‘bump into’ is labile and takes the relator noun *ɯ-taʁ* ‘on/above’ to mark the thing or person that is bumped into. In transitive use, it takes an object naming the body part that receives the impact, whereas in intransitive use no body part is specified.  

The passage also notes that transitive *rpu* does not mean ‘cause X to bump into Y’; that causative meaning is expressed by *sɯ-rpu*. In examples where an apparently external object is involved, such as a bracelet, the object is treated as an extended part of the body, and the autive marks the event as non-volitional and affecting the subject.

The verb sɤŋolisten can be conjugated transitively or intransitively, but selects a semi-object in the second case. In addition, its meaning and the orientation preverbs it selects are different depending on its valency.

In the intransitive conjugation, sɤŋo means `listen' and selects the orientation `towards west', as in ( ex:nWsANo ) (without Stem III alternation). In ( ex:YWkWsANo ), it occurs with the semi-object ɯ-skɤt.

There are two subtypes of ditransitive-monotransitive lability in Japhug: secundative-monotransitive and indirective-monotransitive.

Monotransitive-secundative lability is illustrated by verbs such as ɕɣɤzgive back, fsɯɣrepay (gratitude) and sɤjagive back: they index as object either the recipient or the theme, as shown by examples ( ex:nAtsxWnlAn.YWtafsWG ) and ( ex:nAtsxWnlAn.YWnWfsWGa ). The autive is optional in ( ex:nAtsxWnlAn.YWnWfsWGa ).

Indirective-monotransitive lability is more common: this phenomenon refers to verbs which optionally take an oblique goal argument similar to that of intransitive verbs (§ sec:intr.goal ). Typical examples include allative verbs of manipulation (§ sec:manipulation.verbs ) such as ɣɯtbring or tsɯmtake away, which are often found with absolutive or locative postpositional phrases expressing the goal of the motion as in ( ex:kha.WNgW.jowGtsWmndZi ), but also commonly occur without any locative argument ( ex:jWGmWr.nArca.tukWtsWma ).

In the secundative type, verbs such as ‘give back,’ ‘repay,’ and ‘give back’ can index either the recipient or the theme as object, while in the more common indirective type, verbs of manipulation such as ‘bring’ or ‘take away’ optionally take an oblique goal argument but can also occur without any locative phrase.

section: Additional questions on the generic and number indexation
text: The previous sections focused on person and number indexation in relation to verb argument structure. This section discusses some properties of number and generic indexation that are observed on both intransitive and transitive verbs.
summary: The passage states that the earlier sections dealt with person and number indexing as related to verb argument structure. It then introduces a new section on number and generic indexing, noting that these properties occur on both intransitive and transitive verbs.

section: Additional questions on the generic and number indexation
text:
indexation!mismatch
This section investigates various types of mismatch between person indexation on the verb and nominal and pronominal elements in the clause: optional number indexation, honorific plural, partitive indexation and the interaction between first person and generic person. There are two additional types of indexation mismatch not discussed here: hybrid indirect speech (§ sec:hybrid indirect ), and affixal chains in bipartite verbs (§ sec:bipartite ).
summary: The section examines mismatches between person indexation on the verb and nominal or pronominal elements in the clause, including optional number indexation, honorific plural, partitive indexation, and the interaction between first person and generic person. It also notes two further mismatch types not discussed here: hybrid indirect speech and affixal chains in bipartite verbs.

section: Additional questions on the generic and number indexation
text:
indexation!optional
The default situation in Japhug is for the third person core arguments to be indexed in number on the verb in intransitive or non-local configurations (the number of the subject in direct configurations, and that of the object in inverse configurations, § sec:indexation.non.local ). This is the case in particular in series of verbs sharing the same subject, as in example ( ex:tonWndzondZi.konWGindZi ) with dual ( 3du 3$'$ or 3du intransitive) indexation on five verbs in a row, referring to the same pair of persons.

exe

tɕendɤre <yinliao> to-nɯ-ndo-ndʑi, kɤndza ra to-nɯ-ndo-ndʑi qʰe,
qrɤŋgɤɣ ɯ-tʰɤcu tɕe, to-nɯna-ndʑi qhe, ɲɤ-nɤmɲole-ndʑi qʰe, tɕe ko-nɯ-ɣi-ndʑi \\
lnk drink ifr - auto -take- du food pl ifr - auto -take- du lnk topo 3sg. poss -downstream loc ifr -rest- du lnk ifr -do.sightseeing- du lnk lnk ifr: east - vert -come- du \\
`The two of them took with them drinks and food, and rested and did sightseeing further down from Qrangak, and then came back.' (conversation 140510)
exe

However, non-singular third person core arguments do not necessarily trigger number indexation in all cases. Several syntactic, semantic and discourse factors interfere with number indexation.

With existential verbs, number indexation of the subject is nearly always observed in the case of human referents in the existential construction, even in the case of collective nouns without number markers, such as the counted noun tɯ-tɯpɯone household in ( ex:tWtWpW.pjAtunW ). Dual or plural indexation is generally observed when the subject has a numeral modifier, as in ( ex:XsWm.pjAtunW ).

exe

ɯnɯnɯtɕu tɯ-tɯpɯ pjɤ-tu-nɯ \\
dem: loc one -household ifr. ipfv -exist- pl \\
`there was one household there.' (140512 yufu yu mogui-zh) 0003973#S3
exe

exe

kɤndʑi-xtɤɣ χsɯm pjɤ-tu-nɯ \\
coll -brother three ifr. ipfv -exist- pl \\
`There were three brothers.' (31-deluge) 0004077#S7
exe

On the other hand, with inanimate referents, number indexation is rarely observed. In ( ex:ʁnWz.tu ) for instance, no dual indexation is found on the verb despite the numeral ʁnɯztwo.

exe

nɯnɯreri tsʰɤko ʁnɯz tu. \\
dem: loc stone.mount two exist: fact \\
`There are two stone mounts there.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S133
exe

In the possessive construction (§ sec:gen.possession, § sec:possessive.constructions ), however, the subject of existential verbs (the possessum) rarely triggers number indexation, even in the case of human referents: compare for instance in ( ex:pjAtundZi.pjAtu ) the first verb form pjɤ-tu-ndʑi (existential construction with dual indexation) vs. the second one pjɤ-tu (possessive construction with plural possessum, no indexation).

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe, ʁzɤmi ci pjɤ-tu-ndʑi tɕe, ndʑi-tɕɯ χsɯm pjɤ-tu. \\
long.ago loc husband.and.wife indef ifr. ipfv -exist- du lnk 3du. poss -son three ipfv. ipfv -exist \\
`Long ago, there was a husband and his wife, and they had three sons.' (140430 jin e-zh)
0003893#S2
exe

With dynamic verbs, as in the existential construction, core arguments generally triggers number indexation when they have animate referents. This is in particular the case with the adverb tɯtɯrcatogether (§ sec:secutive ), even to describe group actions where all individuals act exactly in the same way as in ( ex:tWtWrca.luzonW ).

exe

tɕe lɤ-zo-nɯ kɯnɤ tɯtɯrca lu-zo-nɯ, tʰɯ-nɯqambɯmbjom-nɯ kɯnɤ tɯtɯrca cʰɯ-nɯqambɯmbjom-nɯ, \\
lnk aor: upstream -land- pl also together ipfv: upstream -land- pl aor: downstream -fly- pl also together ipfv: downstream -fly- pl \\
`When they land they all land together, when they fly they all fly together.' (24-qro)
0003626#S9
exe

Number indexation is optional with tɯtɯrcatogether in the case of inanimate referents (including plants). Examples ( ex:tulhoRnW.Nu ) and ( ex:tulhoR.Nu ) from the same text shows verb forms with and without plural indexation in the same context (referring to a species of mushroom).

exe

xlist

tɯtɯrca kɯ-dɯ dɤn tu-ɬoʁ-nɯ ŋu. \\
together sbj: pcp - emph be.many ipfv -come.out- pl be: fact \\
`They grow together in great numbers.' (21-jmAGni) 0003572#S78

kɯ-dɯ dɤn ʑo tɯtɯrca tu-ɬoʁ ŋu. \\
sbj: pcp - emph be.many emph together ipfv -come.out be: fact \\
`They grow together in great numbers.' (21-jmAGni) 0003572#S80
xlist
exe

Optional number indexation is however also attested, though uncommon, with dynamic verbs in reference to humans, as in ( ex:kWtsxAG.nWsi ), where verb `die' occurs without plural indexation in its first occurrence (just after a possessive construction, where indexation on the existential verb tɤ-tu is not found either), and with the plural suffix -nɯ in the second occurrence.

exe

ɯ-rɟit kɯngɯt tɤ-tu ri, kɯtʂɤɣ nɯ-si. kɯtʂɤɣ nɯ-si-nɯ qʰe \\
3sg. poss -child nine aor -exist lnk six aor -die six aor -die- pl lnk \\
`She had nine children, but six [of them] died. Six died, and...' (14-siblings) 0003508#S16
exe

The conditions for optional number indexation of human referents with dynamic verbs are not completely clear. Absence of number indexation is rare in intransitive and direct forms, and may be due in part to speech errors (§ sec:mismatch.errors ).

With generic human subjects, the indexation of the number of the object, though attested (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ), is not common. For instance in ( ex:ni.schWwGqru ), despite an overt dual object, the verb lacks number indexation.

exe

kɤndʑi-ʁi ni s-cʰɯ́-wɣ-qru ŋu \\
coll -sibling du tral - ipfv: downstream - inv -welcome be: fact \\
`Let's invite the two brothers down here.' (Nyima wodzer2003-2)
exe
summary:
In Japhug, third-person core arguments are usually indexed for number on the verb in intransitive or non-local configurations, especially across chains of verbs with the same subject. However, number indexation is not obligatory: it is strongly favored with animate or human referents in existential and dynamic verbs, but is much rarer with inanimate referents and in possessive constructions.

Several factors condition whether number is marked, including animacy, numerals, collective nouns, and discourse context. The passage also notes that with generic human subjects, object number indexation is attested but uncommon.

section: Additional questions on the generic and number indexation
text:
number!honorific plural!honorific indexation!plural
Plural marking on nouns (§ sec:ra.honorific ) and pronouns (§ sec:honorific.pronouns ) can be used to express singular honorific in Japhug. Similarly, honorific plural indexation is found with second ( ex:atACime.kAnWrNgWnW ) or third ( ex:rJAlpu.mArAZinW ) person referents, with or without plural ra marking on the noun. Honorific plural is mainly attested in traditional stories, but it is still used to address lamas.

exe

a-tɤɕime ra, ci ɲɯ-ɣɯtsʰɤdɯɣ tɕe, kɤ-nɯ-rŋgɯ-nɯ \\
1sg. poss -lady pl a.little sens -be.hot lnk imp - auto -lie.down- pl \\
`My lady, it is a bit hot, lie down [to sleep].' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

exe

tɕeri tɤ-mu nɯ kɯ rɟɤlpu ra mɤ-rɤʑi-nɯ tɕe, pɣɤtɕɯ nɯ pjɤ-sɯ-sat. \\
lnk indef. poss -mother dem erg king pl neg -stay: fact - pl lnk bird dem ifr - caus -kill \\
`The woman had the bird killed while the king was away.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

Honorific plural indexation on the noun does not always correlate with plural indexation on the verb, as in ( ex:aZi.ra.YWtWnAre ), where the verb has a singular form.

exe

wo a-ʑi ra tɕʰindʐa ɲɯ-tɯ-nɤre ŋu \\
interj 1sg. poss -young.lady pl why ipfv -2-laugh be: fact \\
`My lady, why are you laughing?' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe
summary: In Japhug, plural marking on nouns and pronouns can also express singular honorific, and honorific plural indexation may appear with second- or third-person referents, whether or not the noun itself is marked with plural *ra*. This usage is mainly found in traditional stories but is still used when addressing lamas. Honorific plural on the noun does not always match plural marking on the verb, since the verb may remain singular.

section: Additional questions on the generic and number indexation
text:
indexation!partitive partitive!indexation
Number indexation with a with first person core argument, unlike that of second and third person, is compulsory.

Apparent examples of mismatch however do exist, but are confined to a very specific partitive use of dual of plural number. With the interrogative pronoun ɕɯwho (§ sec:CW.pronoun ), in particular, indexation on the verb can be non-singular with the specific partitive meaning `who among $X$', in particular in comparative constructions as in ( ex:CW.kW.YWmpCArtCi ), with 1du indexation on the verb although this sentence implies that only one of the two sisters is the most beautiful (see § sec:sAz.kW on this comparative construction, and and § sec:comparee.kW on the use of the ergative here).

exe

a-ʁi, nɤki tɕetʰi tɕe, tɯ-ci ɯ-ŋgɯ ɕ-pɯ-ru tɕe, ɕɯ kɯ ɲɯ-mpɕɤr-tɕi kɯ? \\
1sg. poss -younger.sibling filler downstream loc indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -inside tral - imp: down -look lnk who erg sens -be.beautiful- 1du sfp \\
`Sister, go and look down there in the water, who is the most beautiful of us?' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

Similarly, non-singular indexation on the verb with a counted noun core argument can have a partitive meaning, for instance tɯ-rdoʁone piece (§ sec:CN.partitive ) with plural -nɯ on the verb in ( ex:tWrdoR.kW.asci.athWndonW ) can only be interpreted as meaning `one of them should take it'.

exe

``tɯ-rdoʁ kɯ a-sci a-tʰɯ-ndo-nɯ ntsʰi" ɲɯ-sɯsɤm pjɤ-ŋu \\
one-piece erg 1sg. poss -instead irr - pfv -take- pl be.better: fact ipfv -think[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`[The king] was thinking: `One of [my sons] should inherit the throne.'' (140510 sanpian yumao-zh)
0003947#S7
exe

Another type of partitive indexation is the use of 1pl pronouns with third person indexation, as in ( ex:iZora.tutinW ), with two verbs in 3pl 3 form and the 1pl pronoun in topicalized position meaning `some among us'.

exe

iʑora tɕe ɕkɤpʰɤr tu-ti-nɯ tsuku kɯ ɕkɤjwaʁ tu-ti-nɯ ŋu ma \\
1pl lnk wild.chives ipfv -say- pl some erg wild.chives ipfv -say- pl be: fact lnk \\
`Among us, some call it ɕkɤpʰɤr, some ɕkɤjwaʁ.' (07-Cku)
0003424#S63
exe
summary: Number indexation with a first-person core argument is compulsory, unlike with second- and third-person arguments. The passage notes, however, that non-singular indexation can occur in limited partitive uses: with the interrogative pronoun “who” in the sense ‘who among X,’ with counted nouns meaning ‘one of X,’ and with first-person plural pronouns indexed as third person to mean ‘some among us.’

section: Additional questions on the generic and number indexation
text:
person!first indexation!generic
Another type of agreement mismatch observed with first person concerns 1pl and generic person. Before examining the examples of mismatch between pronouns and verb indexation in Japhug, it is important to note that generic person often occurs in gnomic statements applying to the speaker himself (§ sec:genr.3pl ), and can be used as an indirect way to express a first person, as has been described in some Kiranti languages. It is even found in contexts where it unambiguously refers to the first person singular, as in ( ex:mAxsi.YAnWjmWta ).

exe

mɤ-xsi ko, nɯra ɲɤ-nɯ-jmɯt-a \\
neg - genr:know sfp dem: pl ifr - auto -forget- 1sg \\
`I don't know, I forgot about these things.' (phone conversation, 2013-12-24)
exe

Generic inverse Imperfective verb forms with modal verb such as ntsʰihave better or rabe needed (example ex:jinWNa.pjWwGnWntCha ) or even without auxiliary ( ex:iZo.ci.YWwGphWt ) is a common way to express 1pl hortative (§ sec:ipfv.complement, § sec:ipfv.hortative ), and in such contexts 1pl pronouns or possessive prefixes can be found.

In ( ex:jinWNa.pjWwGnWntCha ), generic inverse marking on the verb corresponds to the 1pl possessive on the object nɯŋacow. The presence of the autive nɯ- (§ sec:autobenefactive ) is a further clue to the equivalence of the generic subject and the 1pl in this example.

exe

skalpa ndʑɯɣ nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, ji-nɯŋa pjɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-ntɕʰa ɲɯ-ntsʰi \\
world be.destroyed: fact dem sens -be lnk 1pl. poss -cow ipfv - inv - auto -butcher sens -be.better \\
`The world is about to be destroyed, let us kill our cow.' (07-deluge) 0003426#S7
exe

In ( ex:iZo.ci.YWwGphWt ), the 1pl pronoun iʑo directly co-occurs with a verb in transitive subject generic form (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ).

exe

iʑo kɯ-mɤku pɤjkʰu, ɯ-ɕɣa kɯ-mtɕoʁ nɯ ci ɲɯ́-wɣ-pʰɯt \\
1pl sbj: pcp -be.first still 3sg. poss -tooth sbj: pcp -be.sharp dem a.little ipfv - inv -take.out \\
`Let us first take out its sharp teeth.' (150908 menglang-zh)
0006320#S71
exe

Co-occurrence of generic indexation with a 1pl pronoun is also found in procedural texts; in such contexts the 1pl pronouns occur in apposition with place names (§ sec:place.names ), ethnic groups or classes of people, for instance iʑo kɯrɯ ra `we Tibetans' in ( ex:iZo.luWGnWBzu ).

exe

iʑo kɯrɯ ra, nɤkinɯ, qajɣi lú-wɣ-nɯ-βzu tɕe \\
1pl Tibetan pl filler bread ipfv - inv - auto -make lnk \\
`We Tibetans, when we make bread,' (160706 thotsi)
0006133#S1
exe

The opposite situation, a generic pronoun in combination with 1pl indexation, is much rarer, but also attested. For instance, in ( ex:tWZAra.pWxtCij ), the adjectival stative verb xtɕibe small bears 1pl -j suffix, but the corresponding overt pronoun in the sentence is the generic person tɯʑɤraone (§ sec:genr.pro ). The generic form pɯ-kɯ-xtɕi, as in ( ex:pWkWxtCi.tCe.pWwGmto ) would be possible in the exactly the same context, clearly including the first person.

exe

tɯʑɤra pɯ-xtɕi-j tɕe, \\
genr pst. ipfv -be.small- 1pl lnk \\
`When we were young.' (17-ndZWnW) 0003524#S50
exe

exe

tɕe jinde aj pɯ-mto-t-a me ri, pɯ-kɯ-xtɕi tɕe pɯ́-wɣ-mto \\
lnk now 1sg aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg not.exist: fact lnk pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-be.small lnk aor - inv -see \\
`I have not seen any [wild crane] recently, but when we were young, we did see (some).' (22-qomndroN)
0003598#S31
exe

Dual or plural indexation can occur with generic transitive subject indexation marking a first person, as in example ( ex:tuwGqurnW ) in § sec:indexation.generic.tr.

In addition to the generic person, the proprietive derivation is another possible strategy to indirectly refer to the first person (§ sec:proprietive.generic ).
summary: The passage describes agreement mismatches involving first person, especially between generic person and 1pl indexation in Japhug. Generic marking can refer indirectly to first person, including unambiguous 1sg contexts, while 1pl hortative expressions often use generic inverse imperfective forms alongside 1pl pronouns or possessive prefixes. It also notes the rarer reverse pattern, where a generic pronoun appears with 1pl verbal indexation, and mentions that dual or plural indexation and the proprietive derivation can likewise indirectly express first person.

section: Additional questions on the generic and number indexation
text:
speech error!indexation indexation!speech error
Speech errors are inevitable in any corpus, and are a factor to take into consideration to explain inconsistencies in person indexation.

The clearest examples of erroneous indexation are self-corrections. In ( ex:YotanW.Yota ) for instance, the speaker first chooses a plural 3pl 3$'$ with -nɯ suffix and then corrects herself to the appropriate form 3sg 3$'$ ɲo-ta. The error here is due without doubt to the presence of the overt object ʁʑɯnɯ tɕʰemɤli ra bearing a plural marker: plural objects in non-local configuration are only indexed in the case of inverse forms (§ sec:indexation.non.local ), but examples of this type show that speakers may nevertheless be tempted to index them in direct configurations too (as if the verb were intransitive).

exe

ʁʑɯnɯ tɕʰemɤli ra, ɲo-ta-nɯ tɕe, ɲo-ta tɕe, \\
young.man young.woman pl ifr -put- pl lnk ifr -put lnk \\
`She left [there] the young men and women.' (2003kandzWsqhaj)
exe

In ( ex:YAnArWrandZi.pl ) from a text translated from Chinese, Tshendzin realised that the number of daughters was different from what she had remembered, and hesitated between the dual and the plural on the indexation of the intransitive verb nɤrɯralook around.

exe

oma, kɯβde pjɤ-sɯ-ɣe nɤ! kɯβde pjɤ-sɯ-ɣe qʰe, nɯnɯra ɲɤ-nɤrɯra-ndʑi ri, ɲɤ-nɤrɯra-nɯ ri, \\
interj four ifr: down - caus -come sfp four ifr: down - caus -come lnk dem: pl ifr -look.around- du lnk ifr -look.around- pl lnk \\
`He sent four (of his daughters, not three), he sent four of them, and they looked around.' (150826 baoliandeng-zh) 0006370#S214
exe

Without self correction, indexation errors are less obvious and have to be rechecked with a native speaker. In ( ex:lAwGCaBndZi ), the first verb lɤ́-wɣ-ɕaβ-ndʑi has inverse marking (§ sec:obviation.possessor ) and indexes the non-overt object (the youngest daughter and her husband). The second (intransitive) verb has dual indexation, but its subject is coreferent with that of the previous verb ( ɯ-pi ra `her elder sisters etc') and plural indexation would therefore be expected here, and Tshendzin indeed proposes to correct the verb form to kɤ-akʰu-nɯ aor -call- pl. The confusion between dual and plural here is a combination of two factors: the presence of a verb with dual indexation just before (indexation attraction), and the ambiguity of the subject: the youngest sister has two eldest daughters (the plural here refer to her husbands and servants), and one could construe the subject of kɤ-akʰu-ndʑi as referring only to the two elder sisters, without the additional people, hence the dual indexation.

exe

ndɤre ɯ-pi ra kɯ lɤ́-wɣ-ɕaβ-ndʑi nɤ kɤ-akʰu-ndʑi ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -elder.sibling pl erg aor: upstream - inv -catch.up- du lnk aor -call- du sens -be \\
`Her elder sisters and the others caught up with them and called.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

Some apparent cases of optional number indexation (§ sec:optional.indexation ) should also be analyzed as speech errors, as in (§ sec:optional.indexation ), where the first verb jɤ-ɣe-ndʑi bears correct dual indexation, but the second one lacks it, presumably due to hesitation on the part of the speaker.

exe

nɯnɯ kɯ-fse ʁnɯz jɤ-ɣe-ndʑi tɕe, ji-kʰa zɯ jɤ-ɣe tɕe \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.like two aor -come[II]- du lnk 1pl. poss -house loc aor -come[II] lnk \\
`Two [ghosts] like that came, came to our house.' (150902 qixian-zh) 0006258#S136
exe

Generic person vs. 3pl indexation
indexation!generic indexation!plural
In Japhug, both generic marking (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ) and third person plural indexation can be used to express generic referents. In particular, both can agree with the generic/indefinite noun tɯrmeperson (§ sec:tWrme.generic ), as illustrated by examples ( ex:tWrme.kW.tuwGndza ) The generic transitive subject marker is the inverse prefix (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ). In this section, it is however glossed as genr:A for clarity. and ( ex:tWrme.ra.kW.nWrganW ).

exe

nɯŋa ra tɕi kɤ-ndza rga-nɯ, tɯrme kɯ tú-wɣ-ndza mɤ-sna. \\
cow pl erg inf -eat like: fact - pl people erg ipfv - genr: A -eat neg -be.good: fact \\
`Cows like to eat it, but it is not good for people.' (11-paRzwamWntoR)
0003476#S37
exe

exe

tɕe lɯlu nɯ wuma ʑo pe tɕe, nɯnɯ, tɯrme ra kɯ nɯ nɯ-rga-nɯ tɕe \\
lnk cat dem really emph be.good: fact lnk dem people pl erg dem appl -like: fact - pl lnk \\
`The cat is a very nice [animal], people like it.' (21-lWLU)
0003576#S39
exe

The aim of this section is to examine the semantic difference between generic person vs. 3pl in contexts like those illustrated by the examples above.

Generic indexation (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ) is most commonly used to express general or gnomic statements applying to most humans, including the speaker. No more than one argument in a particular sentence can be generic: In particular, it is not possible to have both generic subject and object on the same verb form (§ sec:indef.genr.poss and § sec:genr.pro ), except in reflexive constructions (example ex:tWZo.kW.tWZo, § sec:genr.pro ).

There is obligatory agreement between all generic person markers, whether indexation on the verb, pronouns or possessive prefixes inside a clause, and across contiguous clauses. In ( ex:nA.mAwGmto ) for instance, the generic intransitive subject of the verb mɯ mɤ-pɯ-kɯ-tso is coreferent with the transitive subject of mɤ́-wɣ-mto.

exe

tɕe wuma ʑo mɯ mɤ-pɯ-kɯ-tso nɤ mɤ́-wɣ-mto \\
lnk really emph cond neg - pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-know lnk neg - genr: A -see: fact \\
`If you do not know it well, you won't see it.' (07-Cku) 0003424#S57
exe

In ( ex:tCheme.tukWnAkhe ), the generic possessor prefix on tɯ-laχtɕʰa is also coreferent with the object of ɲɯ-kɯ-nɯsɯkʰo `they rob people of X'. Note however in this example that the generic person on tu-kɯ-nɤkʰe is not exactly identical to the referent of the previous verb, referring to a subset of it (only women).

exe

tɯrme pjɯ-sat-nɯ, tɯ-laχtɕʰa ɲɯ-kɯ-nɯsɯkʰo, tɕʰeme tɕe tu-kɯ-nɤkʰe kɯ-fse ɲɯ-ŋu \\
people ipfv -kill- pl genr. poss -thing ipfv - genr:S/O-rob woman lnk ipfv - genr:S/O-bully sbj: pcp -be.like sens -be \\
`They did things like killing people, robbing people's things, raping women.' (17-lhazgron)
exe
summary: The passage explains that speech errors must be considered when analyzing person and number indexation in Japhug, since speakers may temporarily choose the wrong plural, dual, or optional form and then self-correct; some apparent optional omissions are also likely just hesitation. It then turns to the relation between generic person and 3pl indexation, noting that both can express generic referents, but that generic marking is typically used for general statements applying to humans and requires consistent agreement across related forms within and across clauses.

section: Additional questions on the generic and number indexation
text:
Example ( ex:tWZo.tukWrWCmi ) show the agreement between the generic pronoun tɯʑoone and generic marking on the verb.

exe

tɯʑo tu-kɯ-rɯɕmi nɯra ɯ-ɲɯ́-tso? \\
genr ipfv - genr:S/O-speak dem: pl qu - sens -understand \\
`Does [you son] understand when people speak?' (phone conversation 15-01-13)
exe

Generic human marking can sometimes be used as a substitute for first person, both as indexation prefix (§ sec:1.genr ) or as possessive prefix (§ sec:generic.tW.1sg ). Example ( ex:tApAtso.pWkWNu ) illustrates this function.

exe

tɕeri tɤ-pɤtso pɯ-kɯ-ŋu tɕe, nɯ kɤ-ndza wuma ʑo pɯ-kɯ-rga. \\
lnk indef. poss -child pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-be lnk dem inf -eat really emph pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-like \\
`When we were children, we used to like eating it a lot.' (12-ndZiNgri) 0003488#S126
exe

The commonality between all the uses of generic person marking is that it always refers to a group including the speaker. Example ( ex:tWZo.tukWrWCmi ) above could seem to be a counterexample, but the question here is about the ability to understand speech in general, not restricted to the people in contact with my son at the moment this question was uttered. It is particularly clear in ( ex:tCheme.tukWnAkhe ), where the generic prefix kɯ- on tu-kɯ-nɤkʰe is coreferent with the overt object tɕʰemegirl; this verb form is appropriate in this particular instance because the speaker is a woman, and tɕʰemegirl is used here as a generic noun.

Example ( ex:Juli.chWlAtnW ) further illustrates the same phenomenon. The speaker, also a woman, includes herself among the potential Jews' harp players (though she has never played the instrument) and thus employs generic subject marking on the first verb (note also the presence of the 1pl pronoun, § sec:1.genr ). Conversely, she excludes herself from potential flute players (traditionally, only men) and selects 3pl marking on the second verb.

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe, iʑora tɕʰeme kɯ ʑɴɢro ɲɯ́-wɣ-lɤt, tɤ-tɕɯ ra kɯ ɟuli cʰɯ-lɤt-nɯ. \\
long.ago lnk 1pl girl erg Jews'.harp ipfv - genr: A -release indef. poss -boy pl erg flute ipfv -release- pl \\
`Long ago, among us women used to play the Jews' harp, while men used to play the flute.' (150907 ZNGro)
0006252#S13
exe

This example is typical of procedural texts: the generic is consistently used by women speakers to refer to activities typically performed by women, and the 3pl for men's duties (and vice-versa with men speakers).

This contrast is also found when discussing differences between Tibetan and Chinese people, in particular the names given to animals and plants. In ( ex:khWnajme ), Chinese are referred to collectively in the 3sg (the plural would also be possible in the same context), while Tibetans (the ethnic group to which the speaker associates herself) are indexed on the verb by the generic kɯ- prefix (§ sec:irregular.transitive ).

Another crucial difference between speaker-inclusive generic and 3pl, is that unlike the former, the latter can refer to several different referents in the same sentence. In example ( ex:amAtAndonW.ma.GWznAndAGnW ) for instance, the 3pl on the verbs a-mɤ-tɤ-ndo-nɯ `let them not take it' and ɣɯ-z-nɤndɤɣ-nɯ `it will poison them' The inverse on this verb does mark generic subject (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ), since the subject of this verb is the poisonous mushroom.
