The passage explains that generic person marking with tɯʑo and the verbal generic prefix kɯ- agrees with a speaker-inclusive group, not just with the immediate addressee or the people mentioned in a specific situation. It can also substitute for first person in both subject and possessive marking, especially when speakers refer to shared human activities or roles typical of their own group.  

It contrasts this generic marking with 3pl indexation, which is speaker-exclusive and can refer to multiple distinct third-person referents in the same sentence. Thus, generic person marking is described as speaker-inclusive, whereas 3pl marking is speaker-exclusive.

section: Person indexation on non-finite predicative words
text:
inflectionalization indexation!non-finite
Despite being a highly verb-prominent language, Japhug has some non-verbal predicates (§ sec:non.verbal.predicates ). There is evidence that a few nominals occurring as predicates, including nominalized verb forms and nouns, have acquired person indexation markers.

Phenomena of this type are uncommon, but clear examples do exist in Indo-European. For instance, in Greek, the adverbs δεῦρο `hither' and τῆ `here, take it' have developed the plural forms δεῦτε and τῆτε, with the plural present imperative suffix -τε (and unexplainable loss of the syllable -ρο in δεῦτε), by contamination with imperative verb forms ( φέρε, φέρετε), which occur in the same contexts. A similar case is found in Gothic, where the adverb hiri `hither' (which incidentally translates Greek δεῦρο) has dual hirjats and plural hirjiþ, modelled on imperatives.

Inflectionalization of nominals is attested in the case of a few phatic (§ sec:phatic.inflectionalization ) and exclamative (§ sec:exclamative.inflectionalization ) expressions in Japhug.
summary: Japhug is highly verb-prominent, but it also has some non-verbal predicates, and a few nominals used as predicates—including nominalized verb forms and nouns—have acquired person indexation markers. The passage notes that such inflectionalization is uncommon but parallels exist in Indo-European, and it gives Japhug examples of phatic and exclamative expressions that have become inflected.

section: Person indexation on non-finite predicative words
text:
phatic
The expression sɤrmagood night, used to address someone leaving one's house in the evening, transparently derives from the oblique participle sɤ-rma `place where/time when one stays overnight' (§ sec:oblique.participle ) from the verb rmastay the night, live, as illustrated by example ( ex:Ckurma ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-sɤ-rma nɯnɯ, praʁ, praʁpa tɕe ɕ-ku-rma ɲɯ-ŋu \\
lnk 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -stay.the.night dem cliff cavern lnk tral - ipfv -stay.the.night sens -be \\
`The place where its spends the night is the cliffs, it goes to spend the night in caverns under the cliffs.' (20-xsar)
0003568#S36
exe

This expression is probably the abbreviation of a phrase such as `go back to your resting place' (which would be nɤ-sɤrma jɤ-nɯɕe ).

Yet, when addressing more than one person, the dual form sɤrma-ndʑi and the plural sɤrma-nɯ are used, with the 2/3 dual -ndʑi and plural -nɯ suffixes found in verb paradigms (§ sec:intr.23 ). These suffixes normally only appear on finite verbs. The forms sɤrma, sɤrma-ndʑi and sɤrma-nɯ could in principle be analyzed as a Factual Non-Past form (§ sec:fact.morphology ), but there are three problems with this hypothesis.

First, the meaning of the expression (`have a good night') is hardly compatible with the Factual Non-Past; an Imperative or Irrealis form would be expected instead, and a second person prefix tɯ- would in any case be required. Second, while there are several sɤ- verbal derivational prefix, none of them (proprietive § sec:proprietive.allomorphy, antipassive § sec:antipassive.sA and causative § sec:caus.sA ) has a function which could account for a derivation such as `spend the night' $ $ `(have a) good night'. Third, no other verb forms (including first or third person), finite or non-finite, are attested for sɤrma.

analogy
A more promising approach to account for these verb forms is analogy with other phatic expressions involving finite verb forms. The most probable one is the verb astube straight, whose Imperative is used to mean `goodbye' (literally `(walk) straight') as in ( ex:tAstundZi ). These verb forms optionally occur with the sentence final particle je (§ sec:fsp.imp ), another commonality with sɤrmagood night.

exe

xlist

tɤ-ɤstu (je) \\
imp -be.straight sfp \\
`Goodbye' = `(walk) straight' (singular)

tɤ-ɤstu-ndʑi (je) \\
imp -be.straight- du sfp \\
`Goodbye' (dual)
xlist
exe

The dual and plural forms of sɤrmagood night can thus be explained as trivial four-part analogy as in tab:analogy.sArma.

The expression kɤnɤβditake care, used when leaving from someone's place, and which also has a dual kɤnɤβdi-ndʑi and a plural kɤnɤβdi-nɯ, might also be a inflectionalized form of the kɤ- infinitive (§ sec:velar.inf ) of the tropative nɤ- (§ sec:tropative ) of the stative verb βdibe well.

However, this case is less compelling than sɤrmagood night, because kɤ-nɤβdi-ndʑi and kɤ-nɤβdi-nɯ can alternatively be formally analyzed as imperatives with the eastwards kɤ- preverb (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), and because nɤβdi is also found in regular finite forms (as in ex:WkutWnABdi ).

exe

ɯ-ku-tɯ-nɤβdi? ɯ-ku-tɯ-pe? \\
qu - prs -2-feel.well qu - prs -2-good \\
`Do you feel well, are you fine?' (conversation, 16-12-28)
exe
summary:
The passage explains that the greeting sɤrma ‘good night’ is transparently based on the oblique participle of the verb rmastay the night, though it may be an abbreviated phrase like “go back to your resting place.” Its dual and plural forms, sɤrma-ndʑi and sɤrma-nɯ, are unusual because they use person-number suffixes normally found only on finite verbs, and the author rejects a straightforward factual non-past analysis in favor of analogy with other phatic expressions such as astube straight ‘goodbye.’

It also notes that kɤnɤβdi ‘take care’ has similar dual and plural forms and may be related to a derivational form of the stative verb βdibe well, but this analysis is less convincing because the forms can also be interpreted as ordinary imperatives and because nɤβdi appears in regular finite forms.

section: Person indexation on non-finite predicative words
text:
exclamative
The expression dɯxpapoor... seems at first glance to be a verb, as it not only takes dual and plural suffixes ( dɯxpa-nɯ `poor them', example ex:dWxpanW ), but it can also receive first person indexation (such as 1du in ex:dWxpatCi ). The variant form zdɯxpa is also attested (see ex:kuZGACthWza, § sec:ipfv.hortative ).

exe

wo a-rɟit ra dɯxpa-nɯ ma nɯ ɯ-xtu ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu ɣɤʑu-nɯ rca \\
interj 1sg. poss -offspring pl poor- pl because dem 3sg. poss -belly dem: loc exist: sens - pl sfp \\
`My poor children, there are in his [the wolf's] belly' (140430 lang he qizhi xiaoshanyang-zh)
0003895#S126
exe

exe

tɕiʑo ndɤ dɯxpa-tɕi ɣe, nɤ tɕendɤre, kɤ-ntɕʰa ɯ-spa ʑo ɕti-tɕi \\
1du on.the.other.hand poor- 1du sfp lnk lnk obj: pcp -kill 3sg. poss -material emph be. assert: fact - 1du \\
`We, on the other hand, poor us! We are to be butchered.' (kandZislama2003.210)
exe

Yet, dɯxpa has a defective paradigm: it cannot take any prefix, including the second person tɯ, any TAM marker or any nominalization prefix. In addition, if dɯxpa were to be analyzed as a verb, it would be anomalous, as it is borrowed from Tibetan སྡུག་པ་sdug.pasuffering (also spelled sdug.ga ), For an account of the alternation between p/b and g in the spelling, see and the references therein. a nominalized form taking the -pa/-ba suffix.

While examples of verbs directly borrowed from Tibetan into Japhug are numerous, at least in the earliest layer (for instance rɟɯɣrun, βzɟɯrchange, correct etc, see ), nouns or nominalized verbs borrowed from Tibetan are never converted to verbs without denominal prefixes. Incidentally, we find in Japhug two verbs derived from the same Tibetan etymon (in the variant °zdɯxpa, from an earlier layer of borrowing) by means of denominal prefixes, the intransitive stative verb sɤzdɯxpabe pitiful and the transitive verb nɯzdɯxpahave pity for. The word dɯxpa cannot be analyzed either as a verb derived from a noun by zero-derivation, as zero denominal derivation does not exist in Japhug (§ sec:verb.backformation ).

A better account of the defectiveness of dɯxpa and its etymology is that it originally was an exclamative noun (§ sec:exclamative.IPN, § sec:non.verbal.predicates ), and that the third person and first person indexation suffixes were added by contamination with finite stative verbs used in exclamative sentences, as sɤzdɯxpabe pitiful in ( ex:pjAsAzdWxpanW ).

exe

ndʑi-ɣi ra, nɯni mɯ-ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-nɯ-ci, pjɤ-sɤzdɯɣpa-nɯ ma \\
3du. poss -relatives pl dem: du neg - ifr - peg -meet- pl - peg ifr. ipfv -be.pityful- pl lnk \\
`Their relatives did not meet them [again], poor them.' (2003 zrAntCW tWrme)
exe
summary: The passage argues that **dɯxpa** may look like a verb because it can take dual/plural suffixes and even first-person indexation, but its paradigm is defective since it cannot take prefixes, TAM marking, or nominalization prefixes. The author concludes that **dɯxpa** is better analyzed as an originally exclamative noun borrowed from Tibetan, with its verbal-looking forms arising by contamination from finite stative verbs in exclamative contexts.

text:
This section explores a range of hypotheses to account for the synchronic resemblance between indexation markers (indexation suffixes, the inverse prefix and the local scenario portmanteau prefixes) and other morphemes that are possibly historically related in Japhug, drawing on comparative data from other Gyalrong languages and beyond.
morphology!Trans-Himalayan comparison
summary: The section examines several hypotheses explaining the synchronic similarity in Japhug between indexation markers—such as indexation suffixes, the inverse prefix, and local scenario portmanteau prefixes—and other morphemes that may be historically related. It uses comparative evidence from other Gyalrong languages and from Trans-Himalayan languages more broadly to evaluate these possible connections.

subsection: Indexation suffixes, pronouns and possessive prefixes
text:
indexation pronoun prefix!possessive possession!prefix
The indexation suffixes (§ sec:intransitive.paradigm ) are similar to the corresponding possessive prefixes (§ sec:possessive.paradigm ) and pronouns (§ sec:pers.pronouns ) in Japhug, as shown by the data in tab:personal.suffixes.japhug. In addition to the Kamnyu dialect, this table includes data on the Tatshi dialect (from, and personal communication) between brackets. The two dialects differ mainly in the presence of alveolo-palatal affricates in Kamnyu Japhug in the dual, while dental affricates are found in Tatshi.

In the other Gyalrong languages, very similar affixes are found, as shown by tab:person.suff.pref.rgyalrong (data from,,, ).

The main differences between the indexation systems of the four Gyalrong languages include the following observations: (i) only Situ has a 2sg suffix (intransitive and 2sg object) In Situ, the second person singular is indexed by both a prefix and a suffix, while in the other languages including Japhug, it is only indexed by the prefix (§ sec:intr.23 ). and a third person object suffix, (ii) the 1sg suffix presents unique correspondences, and has many allomorphs in Zbu and Situ, (iii) Zbu has a 1pl possessive prefix that is unrelated to the 1pl suffix, (iv) Situ has no distinction between 1du and 2/3du possessive prefixes, and (v) the 1du, 2/3du and 2/3pl affixes are either (alveolo)-palatal or dental across the languages.

As shown by tab:palatalized.dual.plural.rgyalrong, Tshobdun and Tatshi Japhug only have dental person indices, Zbu and Situ only (alveolo-)palatal ones, and Kamnyu Japhug is intermediate between the two groups, with alveolo-palatal dual affixes -tɕi/-ndʑi and dental plural affixes -nɯ. It is noteworthy that Kamnyu Japhug, the dialect geographically closest to Tshobdun, is less similar to that language in this regard than the Tatshi dialect, which is not in direct contact with Tshobdun.

A possible explanation to account for the resemblances between the suffixes, the possessive prefixes and the pronouns is to argue that the former were grammaticalized from the latter, as has been proposed by. In the same line of reasoning, the second and third person dual and plural suffixes, which are similar to the dual and plural nominal markers in Situ and Tatshi Japhug, could be argued to have originated from them. In Tatshi Japhug for instance, the dual -ndzə and plural -nə suffixes could be analyzed as deriving from the dual ndzə and plural nəjo nominal clitics (which differ from those of Kamnyu Japhug, § sec:number.determiners ).

The idea of transparent grammaticalization from pronouns or number markers in indexation suffixes is however not as straightforward as it might appear at first glance. Leaving aside extra-Gyalrong comparative evidence, and the fact that most of the pronouns in Gyalrong languages are derived from possessive prefixes rather than the opposite (, § sec:pers.pronouns ), if the similarity between the three series of person markers were to be explained as resulting exclusively from a recent grammaticalization, the pattern in tab:person.suff.pref.rgyalrong, where the place of articulation (alveolo-palatal vs. dental) of dual and plural indexation suffixes is aligned on that of the pronouns and possessive prefixes and draws an isogloss across the dialects of Japhug ( tab:palatalized.dual.plural.rgyalrong ), would imply that the grammaticalization postdated not only the breakup of proto-Gyalrong, but even that of the common ancestor of modern Japhug dialects.

The indexation system of Gyalrong languages cannot however be that recent, in particular because the stem alternation system, which contributes to person indexation (§ sec:stem3.distribution, § sec:indexation.mixed ) is clearly reconstructible to the common ancestor of Gyalrong languages and Tangut and is too complex and irregular (in particular in Zbu, see and ) to be a recent development.

Three alternative types of explanation can be explored to account for the correspondences between affixes and pronouns: analogical simplification of allomorphy, contamination and degrammaticalization.

First, there is evidence that in proto-Gyalrong, the suffixes had phonetically conditioned allomorphs: the 1sg suffix has maintained some allomorphy in Zbu and Situ. Analogical levelling is thus a likely explanation for the diverging forms of the 1sg suffix. Note that the form -aŋ in Tshobdun cannot derive from proto-Gyalrong *-aŋ (which yields Tshobdun -i ), and the Zbu and Situ -ŋ cannot be a phonetic reflex of *-ŋ in most cases, otherwise for instance stems in -a should alternate with -o $ $ *-aŋ in Situ in the 1sg. In Situ and Zbu, the final -ŋ in open syllables must have been restored, due to analogical spread from a particular context where the *-ŋ was maintained.

Second, the similarity between possessive prefixes, indexation suffixes and pronouns could be the result of mutual contamination and convergence. Cases of contamination between indexation systems and possessive affixes are attested. In Hebrew and Phoenician, for instance, the first person singular perfect suffix -tî has an unexpected vocalism, as it is commonly agreed that proto-North-West Semitic suffix was *-tu, whose outcome should have been $ $ -t. The irregular Hebrew form is explained as due to contamination from either the 1sg pronoun ʔănî or the 1sg possessive suffix -î (, ).

Contamination could account for the 1sg affixes in Japhug. The possessive prefix a- is the regular outcome of earlier *ŋa, a proto-form which also account for the 1sg prefixes in the other languages. The 1sg suffix -a however does not regularly correspond to the suffixes -aŋ and -ŋ found in Tshobdun, Zbu and Situ. One possibility is that *-ŋɐ was one of the proto-Gyalrong allomorphs of the 1sg suffix, In Bantawa for instance, the 1sg suffix has three allomorphs -ŋ, -ŋ, and -ŋa. and was generalized. Another explanation is that only *-ŋ was present in proto-Gyalrong, and that the *-ŋɐ precursor of Japhug -a arose by contamination of *-ŋ with the (historically related) possessive prefix *ŋɐ-.
summary:
The passage compares Japhug indexation suffixes with possessive prefixes and pronouns, showing that the Gyalrong languages share similar person-marking affixes but differ in several specific ways, especially in second- and third-person dual and plural forms and in whether affixes are dental or (alveolo-)palatal. It argues that while these similarities may reflect grammaticalization from pronouns or number markers, the indexation system is probably not that recent because it is tied to an older, reconstructible stem-alternation system.

The author therefore considers alternative explanations, especially analogical leveling, contamination, and degrammaticalization. In particular, the irregular forms of the 1sg suffix are treated as likely cases of analogical change or contamination involving possessive prefixes and pronouns.

subsection: Indexation suffixes, pronouns and possessive prefixes
text:
Third, the possibility of degrammaticalization from person indexation suffixes to nominal number markers in Tatshi Japhug and Situ should be taken into consideration. Kamnyu Japhug, Tshobdun and Zbu have dual and plural markers that are completely different from indexation suffixes (Kamnyu ni / ra, Tshobdun niʔ / rɐʔ and Zbu ɲi / réʔ, see § sec:number.determiners, and ). The plural marker is cognate to Pumi =ɹə: Japhug -a regularly corresponds to Pumi -ə in the native vocabulary, and it is therefore unlikely to be a Northern Gyalrong innovation.

If the Zbu, Tshobdun and Kamnyu Japhug number markers above are conservative, the corresponding Tatshi Japhug ndzə / nəjo and Cogtse Situ ndʒe / ɲe forms must therefore be innovations, and by consequence, it cannot be argued that the 2/3 indexation suffixes derive from these number markers. The opposite scenario is possible: discusses the case of the Irish 1pl pronoun muid which comes from one of the allomorphs of the 1pl future indexation suffix. A similar type of debonding can account at least for the Tatshi Japhug dual ndzə nominal marker, from the 2/3 dual -ndzə indexation suffix. The case of plural nəjo is more complicated: the nə- element here probably rather derives from the distal demonstrative. The acquisition of indexation suffixes by several non-verbal words discussed in § sec:non.finite.indexation may have contributed to the reanalysis of indexation suffixes as number-marking enclitics.

Much remains unclear about the history of person indexation suffixes and the nature of their relationship with pronouns, possessive prefixes and number markers in Gyalrong languages. A more satisfying account of these data will only become possible when a fully explicit system of proto-Gyalrong reconstruction, and complete data on as many varieties as possible becomes available.
summary:
The passage argues that degrammaticalization from person indexation suffixes to nominal number markers should be considered in Tatshi Japhug and Situ, because comparable number markers in Kamnyu Japhug, Tshobdun, and Zbu appear to be conservative rather than innovations. If so, the Tatshi Japhug and Cogtse Situ forms are likely innovations, and the 2/3 indexation suffixes cannot be derived from them; instead, a reverse development may explain at least the Tatshi Japhug dual marker, though the plural form is less clear.  

It also suggests that the spread of indexation suffixes to non-verbal words may have helped reanalyse them as number-marking enclitics, but the historical relations among indexation suffixes, pronouns, possessive prefixes, and number markers remain uncertain pending fuller proto-Gyalrong reconstruction and broader comparative data.

text:
inverse
Two Gyalrong-internal scenarios could be proposed to account for the origin of the inverse prefix.

First, it could be proposed that the inverse comes from the 3sg possessive prefix. In Tshobdun, Zbu and Situ, the inverse prefix ( o, və- and wə, respectively) is homophonous with the 3sg possessive prefix (see tab:3sg.inv in § sec:3sg.possessive.form ). This is not the case in Japhug, where the inverse ɣɯ- / -wɣ is clearly different from the 3sg ɯ, but it is possible that the 3sg possessive underwent an irregular development, as argued in § sec:3sg.possessive.form. The 3$'$ 3 sg form would originally be a non-finite form taking a possessive prefix (for instance a predecessor of the bare infinitive, § sec:bare.inf ), and the inverse prefix would have spread from the 3$'$ 3 to the mixed scenarios 3 2 and 3 1, following the pathways described in.

Second, the partial resemblance between the Japhug allomorph ɣɯ- and the associated motion cislocative ɣɯ- prefix (§ sec:cislocative.morpho ) could support the idea that the inverse derives from the cislocative, following a well-known grammaticalization pathway. This hypothesis is however less likely, as the cislocative itself may be an innovation in Gyalrong languages (§ sec:am.prefixes ).

In any case, cognates of the inverse prefix are found in other Gyalrongic languages and in Kiranti, so that whatever the ultimate origin of this prefix, it was already grammaticalized at the proto-Gyalrongic level.
summary: The passage proposes two possible Gyalrong-internal origins for the inverse prefix: it may derive from the 3sg possessive prefix, or less likely from the cislocative prefix because of a partial formal resemblance in Japhug. Although the exact source is uncertain, the inverse prefix was already grammaticalized at the proto-Gyalrongic level, since cognates occur in other Gyalrongic languages and in Kiranti.

text:
indexation!portmanteau person!local configuration
The presence of portmanteau prefixes in the local 1 2 and 2 1 configurations in Japhug is not unusual crosslinguistically. However, the resemblance of the 1 2 prefix ta- to the second person tɯ- prefix on the one hand, and of the 2 1 prefix kɯ- to various non-finite velar prefixes (§ sec:velar.nmlz.history ) on the other hand, raises the question of their potential historical relatedness.

The form of the local configuration prefixes is very similar in other Gyalrong languages, as shown by tab:local.rgy (data from, and ).

Only two differences are found in the local domain across the Gyalrong languages: Japhug does not have the inverse wɣ- prefix in the 2 1 form, and Zbu and Tshobdun allow an alternative form with the second person prefix tə- and the inverse prefix. In all four languages, the verb takes suffixes that are coreferent with the object (second person in 1 2 and first person in 2 1). Situ is the only language with a suffix -n in the 1 2sg form, the same as that found in intransitive 2sg and 3 2sg.

proposes that the 1 2 prefix originates from the fusion of the second person prefix tɯ- with the agentless passive a- (from *ŋa, ), which yields the expected form in all four languages. In this view, a form like Japhug ta-mbi 1 2-chase- sg `I will give it to you$_SG$' would have developed through the following stages:

reanalysis
itemize
* tə-ŋa-mbi-nə 2- pass -give- 2sg `it will be given to you' (Passive form)
* ta-mbi-nə 2: pass -give- 2sg (Regular phonological fusion between the person marker and the passive prefix, attested in all four Gyalrong languages, § sec:contraction )
* ta-mbi-nə 1 2-give- 2sg `I will give it to you' (reanalysis of the fused form as a portmanteau prefix; the unspecified agent of the passive construction is construed as being first person)
ta-mbi 1 2-give `I will give it to you' (loss of 2sg suffix in Japhug)
itemize

passive
This scenario is not completely straightforward; in particular, the passive ambibe given of the verb mbigive takes the theme, not the recipient, as intransitive subject (§ passive.ditransitive ), and passives in Japhug are only rarely attested with first or second person subjects (§ sec:passive ). However, there are no major phonological or morphological obstacles against this hypothesized scenario, and good typological parallels have been described.

In the case of 2 1 kɯ, originally proposed that this prefix might be an archaism of Gyalrong languages, based on the principle of archaic heterogeneity, using the data in tab:second.japhug.kiranti. In second person forms other than 1 2, some Kiranti languages have a dental stop prefix (Bantawa tɨ, ), and Limbu has the velar prefix kɛ-, correspondance to Japhug tɯ- in intransitive second person and 2 3, and kɯ- in 2 1 configurations. A possible way of interpreting this corresponding would be to suppose that a pattern similar to that found in Gyalrongic (with a velar prefix in 2 1 and a dental stop prefix in other second person forms) has to be reconstructed in proto-Kiranti: Bantawa would have generalized the tɨ- prefix to the 2 1 slot (a type of analogical levelling attested in Zbu and Tshobdun, see tab:local.rgy ), and Limbu the velar prefix to the 2 3 and intransitive forms.

This hypothesis raises three issues: (i) the 2 1 form is less common than second intransitive and 2 3, and is unlikely to have served as the basis for analogical levelling in Limbu, (ii) the presence of an inverse prefix in the 2 1 form in other Gyalrong languages is unexplained and (iii) the homophonies between the second person possessive prefix kɛ- and the indexation prefix in Limbu on the one hand, and the kɯ- 2 1 portmanteau prefix and the non-finite kɯ- prefixes on the other hand, would be due to chance.

Since the kɛ- second person indexation prefix in Limbu can be explained as an internal innovation, it is necessary to explore the possibility that Japhug the 2 1 kɯ- portmanteau is also an Gyalrong innovation, especially since no other traces of such a putative prefix are found elsewhere in the Trans-Himalayan family.

As mentioned above, Japhug 2 1 kɯ- differs from the 2 1 portmanteau prefixes found in the three other Gyalrong languages, which co-occur with the inverse prefix ( tab:local.rgy ). An identical difference appears in the generic object form, which takes of a simple kɯ- prefix in Japhug (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ) but has an additional inverse prefix kə-o- in Tshobdun ( tab:genr.japhug.tshobdun, ).

The resemblance between the 2 1 portmanteau prefix, the generic person prefixes, and the nominalization prefixes in Japhug and Tshobdun is striking. However, since in these two languages velar participles (§ sec:subject.participles, § sec:object.participle ) and infinitives (§ sec:velar.inf ) are compatible with neither first person indexation suffixes nor the inverse prefix, it is not possible to propose a direct path of reanalysis from participial or infinitive forms to 2 1 (which co-occur with first person suffixes, § sec:indexation.local ) or generic (which appear with inverse in Tshobdun) prefixes.

However, in Situ, unlike other Gyalrong languages, semi-finite nominalized forms combining a prefix kə- and person indexation suffixes ( ex:kESiN ) and/or inverse marking ( ex:nokombEng, in 3 1sg configuration) are also attested, in particular to build certain types of relative clauses.

Bsod.nams-Skyid erg aor. inv - nmlz - inv -give- 1sg det name 3sg. poss -book sens -be[I] \\

summary: The passage argues that Japhug’s local person indexation prefixes, especially the 1→2 ta- and 2→1 kɯ- forms, may be historically related to other person-marking and nominalizing prefixes, rather than being simple inherited portmanteaux. It presents a possible derivation of 1→2 ta- from fusion of a second-person prefix with a passive prefix, while treating the origin of 2→1 kɯ- as unclear but possibly an innovation within Gyalrong, since comparable forms and inverse marking patterns differ across the related languages.

text:
If one accepts the hypothesis that semi-nominalized verb forms did already exist in proto-Gyalrong, and could be used to mark indefinite core arguments in addition to the functions they have in modern Situ, it becomes possible to account for the forms in Tables tab:local.rgy and tab:genr.japhug.tshobdun.

A nominalized form combining the prefix kə, the inverse and a first person suffix like no-kə-o-mbə̂-ŋ in example ( ex:nokombEng ), originally meaning `someone gave it to me', could have become a less abrupt way of saying `you gave it to me' and have been progressively reanalyzed as a 2 1 prefix. The absence of inverse in Japhug in the 2 1 form may be explained by supposing that in the ancestor of Japhug, semi-finite forms became incompatible with inverse marking, while still taking indexation suffixes. This idea is not outlandish, as semi-finite inverse forms are very rare in Situ (only one example is found in Lin's linyj16cogtse text corpus).

The velar nominalization prefixes in semi-finite indefinite forms could also have become reanalyzed as generic person prefixes. This hypothesis implies that Tshobdun is more conservative than Japhug, and that Japhug has later innovated by replacing generic transitive subjects by inverse forms, perhaps to avoid confusion between generic subjects and object caused by the constraint against inverse in semi-finite forms already posited above to explain the 2 1 portmanteau kɯ-. The idea that the Japhug pattern is innovative is supported by the existence of irregular verbs whose generic transitive subjects are marked by kɯ- prefix rather than the inverse (§ sec:irregular.transitive ); these verbs would be the remnants of the stage attested in Tshobdun.
summary:
The passage argues that if proto-Gyalrong already had semi-nominalized verb forms, these could explain certain forms in local Rgyalrong and in Japhug/Tshobdun. It proposes that a nominalized form with kə-, inverse, and a first-person suffix was reanalyzed as a 2→1 prefix, while the lack of inverse in Japhug may reflect a historical restriction on inverse marking in semi-finite forms.

It further suggests that velar nominalization prefixes in semi-finite indefinite forms were later reanalyzed as generic person prefixes. On this account, Tshobdun is more conservative, whereas Japhug innovated by replacing generic transitive subjects with inverse forms, with some irregular verbs preserving an older pattern marked by kɯ-.

text:
prefix!orientation orientation!preverb
In Japhug, orientation preverbs have main fundamental functions. First, they are a fundamental element of the TAME system; all finite verb forms, except the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ) and the Apprehensive (§ sec:apprehensive ), require one (and only one) orientation preverb. Nearly all verbs (§ sec:verbs.no.preverbs ) have at least one lexically determined orientation, used to build preverb-requiring tenses. Second, preverbs can in some cases also serve to indicate the spatial direction or orientation of a motion event or an action expressed by the verb form.

This section first presents the morphological features of orientation preverbs and their historical relationship with other words expressing orientation, and then discusses the expression of spatial direction with motion verbs, some common extended uses of the preverbs, and lexicalized orientations.
summary: In Japhug, orientation preverbs are a central part of the TAME system: nearly all finite verb forms require exactly one, except the Factual Non-Past and Apprehensive, and most verbs have at least one lexically specified orientation used in such forms. These preverbs can also mark the spatial direction or orientation of a motion event or action.

text: The morphology of orientation preverbs presents significant differences across Japhug dialects. This section first describes the system of preverbs in Kamnyu Japhug, in particular with contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction ), presents comparative data from Eastern dialects, and then discusses the historical relationship of preverbs with the corresponding locative nouns and adverbs.
summary: The passage says that orientation preverbs vary significantly across Japhug dialects. It outlines the system in Kamnyu Japhug, especially with contracting verbs, compares it with Eastern dialect data, and then examines the historical connection between these preverbs and the corresponding locative nouns and adverbs.

text:
orientation!preverb
This section deals with the form of orientation preverbs in the Kamnyu dialect in non-contracting verbs. In the Kamnyu dialect, four series of preverbs can be distinguished, as in tab:orientation.preverbs. The choice of a particular series depends on TAME and person indexation; capital letters are used as labels, because functional labels (such as `perfective' or `imperfective') would be potentially misleading, since series B preverbs in particular occur in functionally unrelated verb forms. Series C and D historically result from the merger of vowel-initial prefixes with A and B preverbs, respectively (§ sec:xtokavian.preverbs ).

Only A and B-type preverbs are found in non-finite verb forms.

Preverbs occur in slot -3 of the verbal template (§ sec:prefixal.chain ), following Associated Motion prefixes (§ sec:am.prefixes ), but preceding inverse and indexation prefixes (§ sec:intr.23, § sec:indexation.local, § sec:allomorphy.inv ).

The four series of preverbs each comprise seven orientations, which can be divided into four subsets (including three spatial dimensions, § sec:tridimensional.preverb ): vertical (up / down), riverine (upstream / downstream), solar (east /west) and the unspecified orientation. Only orientable verbs (including motion and manipulation verbs, § sec:orientable.verbs ) are compatible with the unspecified orientation preverbs.

Each of the three spatial dimensions are encoded by a pair of preverbs: upper (upwards, upstream, east) vs. lower (downwards, downstream, west) orientations. In addition to formal differences between upper and lower orientation preverbs, this contrast reflects the fact that each of the three dimensions has an intrinsic directionality, encoding the direction of gravity, the flow of water and the apparent trajectory of the sun in the sky, respectively. The lower orientations correspond to the direction of natural motion along these dimensions: downwards (drawn by gravity), downstream (drawn by water flow) and westwards (towards the point where the sun sets). The upper orientations encode the opposite directions, reflecting the source from which natural motion takes place.

The A-type preverbs have either ɤ or ɯ vocalism, corresponding to upper and lower orientations, respectively. They occur in the Aorist (§ sec:aor.morphology, except for the 3sg configurations (where the C series is used instead, § sec:indexation.non.local ), the Imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ) and the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.morphology ). In addition, the Past Imperfective pɯ- corresponds to the downwards A-type preverb (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology, ). With subject and object participles, A-type preverbs are used to build perfective participles (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:object.participle.other.prefixes ); they do not occur on oblique participles (§ sec:oblique.participle.orientation ) or infinitives (§ sec:infinitives.other.prefixes ).

The B-type preverbs have u vocalism in upper orientations, and ɯ in lower orientations. In addition, lower orientations preverbs have a palatalized form. This palatalization is either reflected by the addition of a -j- medial in the case of pjɯ- downwards or by a shift of from dental (in the A-type preverb) to the corresponding palatal for cʰɯ- downstream and ɲɯ- eastwards. In the synchrony of Japhug, clusters involving a dental stop followed by j are attested, though only in ideophones (§ sec:Cj.clusters ). The alternation between tʰ and cʰ is unique in the grammar of Japhug. The vowel transcribed ɯ is mostly realized as i in this context (§ sec:W.i.contrast ). The B series occurs in the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.morphology ) and in the Immediate Perfective Converb (§ sec:immediate.converb ). In addition, the ɲɯ- prefix marking the Sensory evidential (§ sec:sensory.morphology ) and the ku- prefix of the Egophoric Present (§ sec:egophoric.morphology ) and the Dubitative (§ sec:dubitative ) are specialized uses of the westwards and eastwards B-type preverbs. B-type preverbs are found with subject, object and oblique participles (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:object.participle.other.prefixes, § sec:oblique.participle.orientation ) as well as velar infinitives (§ sec:infinitives.other.prefixes, § sec:inf.exist ).

The C-type preverbs have the same onset as the corresponding A-type preverbs, but their vocalism is neutralized to a. This series only occurs in the Aorist 3sg configuration of the transitive paradigm (§ sec:indexation.non.local ).

The D-type preverbs are exclusively used to build the Inferential (Perfective § sec:ifr.morphology and Imperfective § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ). These preverbs have the same onsets as those of the B series, with a division between non-palatalized upwards preverbs and palatalized downwards preverbs. The preverbs of the upwards series have o vocalism, but those of the `downward' series have two variants, with either o or ɤ vocalism in free variation, as illustrated by the 3sg Inferential ɲɤ-me and ɲo-me of the verb menot exist in ( ex:preverb.YAme ) and ( ex:preverb.Yome ), respectively.

exe

tɕe mtsʰu nɯ ɲɤ-me tɕe, \\
lnk lake dem ifr -not.exist lnk \\
`Then the lake disappeared.' (2003nyima-2)
exe

exe

ɯ-ftsoʁ nɯ ɲo-me, ɲo-nɯ-ɣɤ-me qʰe \\
3sg. poss -female.hybrid.yak dem ifr -not.exist ifr - auto - caus -not.exist lnk \\
`Her female hybrid yak was gone, she lost it.' (gesar 2003)
exe

Since the contrast between ɤ and o is neutralized before the inverse wɣ prefix (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ), A- and D-type upwards preverbs have the same surface form when they directly precede it, as shown in tab:A.D.inv. The contrast is however maintained in the transcription system used in this grammar.

With downwards preverbs the contrast is not lost in this context, since both vowels and consonants remain different (for instance pɯ́-wɣ- vs. pjɤ́-wɣ- ).

In all four series, the unspecified orientation preverbs behave like the upper orientation preverbs ( ɤ, u and o vocalism in series A, B and D, respectively).

The isolated preverb kʰɯ, which cannot be included in the system described above is found in the archaic form kʰɯ-ti `s/he said' of the verb tisay (§ sec:khWti ).
summary:
The passage describes four series of orientation preverbs in the Kamnyu dialect, whose form depends on TAME and person indexing rather than simple functional labels. Series A and B occur in non-finite forms, while C and D are historically merged forms; the preverbs occupy slot -3 in the verbal template and encode seven orientations organized into vertical, riverine, solar, and unspecified types.

It further explains that upper and lower orientations are marked differently across the series, with lower forms often showing palatalization in B and D, and specifies which verb forms each series appears in: A in aorist, imperative, irrealis, and certain participles; B in imperfective, immediate perfective converb, and several participles and infinitives; C only in 3sg aorist transitive forms; and D only in inferential forms. Unspecified orientation preverbs pattern like upper ones, and an isolated archaic preverb kʰɯ survives only

text:
vowel!contraction
Vowel contraction occurs when a type A or B preverb (in tenses forms such as the pɯ- Past Imperfective § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology, the ɲɯ- Sensory § sec:sensory.morphology and the ku- Egophoric Present § sec:egophoric.morphology which require the same preverb for all verbs) directly precedes either the stem of a contracting verb (§ sec:contraction ) or the progressive prefix asɯ-. Vowel contraction occurs in an idiosyncratic way depending on the type of preverb. The a- of contracting verb or of the progressive prefix merges with A-type preverbs as -a- in the Aorist, and as -ɤ- in the Irrealis and Imperative. With B-type preverbs the result of the contraction depends on the preceding vowel: -o- with upper Cu- preverbs, and -ɤ- with lower C(j)ɯ- preverbs. tab:contraction.preverb.AB summarizes the resulting forms (not including Irrealis or Imperative); the spelling adopted in this grammar uses the intermediate `contracting form'.

The surface forms resulting from vowel contraction of A- and B-type preverbs are identical to C-type and D-type preverbs, respectively. The only immediate difference between D-type preverbs and contracting B-type preverbs is that the former show free variation between Cɤ- and Co- in the downwards series, while the latter only have the Cɤ- form. For instance, while the Inferiential of menot exist is either ɲɤ-me or ɲo-me (see ex:preverb.YAme and ex:preverb.Yome above) with the two variants of the D-type preverbs, the result of the fusion of the B-type preverb ɲɯ- (either Sensory or Imperfective) with either a contracting a- initial verb or a progressive asɯ- prefix is ɲɯ-ɤ- ɲɤ- and cannot be realized as ɲo- except in the case of inverse wɣ infixation within the progressive ɤ́<wɣ>sɯ/z- (§ sec:allomorphy.inv, § sec:progressive.morphology ).

C-type preverbs never appear in contracting contexts, because on the one hand contracting verbs are all intransitive and thus do not take C-type preverbs in the Aorist (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ), and on the other hand the progressive asɯ- removes all marks of morphological transitivity, including the alternation between A- and C-type preverbs (§ sec:transitivity.morphology, § sec:aor.morphology ).

Confusion between C-type preverbs and A-type preverbs with vowel fusion can arise in two cases with transitive verbs selecting the downwards orientation. First, the 3 Aorist form (for instance pa-rku `he put it into it') can have the same surface form (in this case parku ) as the Past Imperfective of the Passive (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology, § sec:passive.stative ) of the same verb ( pɯ-a-rku `it was put in it'). Second, the 3 Aorist Causative ( pa-sɯ-rɤt `he wrote it with it, he used it to write it') can be homophonous (here pasɯrɤt ) with the Past Imperfective Progressive ( pɯ-asɯ-rɤt `he was writing it').

Unlike C-type preverbs, D-type preverbs often occur with contracting verbs or with the progressive prefix. In such cases, the result of vowel contraction is not distinguishable from that with a B-type preverb. For instance, in ( ex:pjAAwGronW ) the Inferential Imperfective pjɤ-ɤ<nɯ>ɣro-nɯ of the verb anɯɣroplay has the same surface form pjɤnɯɣrónɯ as the corresponding Imperfective pjɯ-ɤ<nɯ>ɣro-nɯ. It is clear from context however that the form here must be interpreted as Inferential Imperfective, because the other verbs in the same passage pjɤ-nɯ-rɤ-rɤt-nɯ and pjɤ-scit-nɯ are in this form, not in the simple Imperfective.

`In her dream, her elder brothers were drawing, they were playing, they were very happy.' (140520 ye tiane-zh)

In the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug, however, although vowel contractions involving D-type preverbs are attested, such ambiguous forms are rare and avoided. More commonly, a peg circumfix kɯ-...-ci occurs in these forms: the kɯ- element prevents fusion between the D-type prefix and the following vowel, which is realized -ɤ- in this context.

For instance, instead of pjɤ-ɤ<nɯ>ɣro-nɯ, the more common Imperfective Inferential form of anɯɣroplay is pjɤ-k-ɤ<nɯ>ɣro-nɯ-ci as in ( ex:pjAkAwGronWci ). The -ci suffix is originally an evidential marker (cognate to the Tshobdun =cə Mediative suffix, on which see ), but in Kamnyu Japhug it only occurs in combination with the kɯ- prefix as a peg element (§ sec:peg.circumfix ).

lnk dem: pl ifr. ipfv - peg -< auto >play- pl - peg lnk \\
`They were playing.' (140510 fengwang-zh) 0003939#S33
exe

Inferential forms with the peg circumfix kɯ-...-ci regularly occur with contracting verbs or verbs bearing the progressive prefix in the same contexts as the corresponding non-contracting forms without the peg. For instance, in ( ex:pjAkArNici.Zo ), the verb pjɤ-k-ɤrŋi-ci `it was green' with the peg circumfix clearly belongs to the same TAME category as the two preceding verbs pjɤ-tu `there was' and pjɤ-rom `it was dry'.

In the Inferential, the peg circumfix becomes a morphological exponent of the Passive in addition to the Passive prefix ɤ- itself: without the peg, the passive would not be easily differentiable from the base transitive verb. For instance, without the peg element, the Inferential Imperfective Passive pjɤ-k-ɤ-ta-ci `It had been put there' in ( ex:pjAkAtaci.passive ) would be identical to the Inferential pjɤ-ta `he put it there' with the downwards orientation.

In the Kamnyu dialect, such ambiguity is often avoided by using the peg circumfix kɯ-...-ci, which blocks fusion and also serves as a passive marker in the Inferential.
