text:
Xtokavian
The Kamnyu dialect of Japhug stands apart from most varieties in terms of its system of preverbs in two regards: the status of C- and D-type preverbs and the form of the downwards orientation preverbs.

The Xtokavian (§ sec:tChi ) dialects of Japhug spoken in Sarndzu and Tatshi are better analyzed with only two series of preverbs: the A- and B-types (, with a different terminology). Instead of the C- and D-type preverbs, and posit two additional vowel-contracting a- prefixes in these dialects, one occurring in the 3 Aorist configuration, and the other one in the Inferential.

These prefixes occur with the A- and B-type preverbs, respectively. In third and first person forms, the surface forms (resulting from the fusion of these preverbs with the a- 3 Aorist or Inferential) are identical (minor pronunciation differences excepted) to the corresponding C-type and D-type preverbs in Kamnyu Japhug, following fusion rules similar to those presented in tab:contraction.preverb.AB

For instance, in ( ex:YEACe.Tatshi ) and ( ex:YACe.Kamnyu ), the verb forms transcribed as ɲə-a-ʃe (in Tatshi) and ɲɤ-ɕe (in Kamnyu) are near-identical in surface pronunciation and function.

exe

xlist

l̥amu ɲə-a-ʃe \\
anthr ifr: west - ifr -go \\
`Lhamu went westwards.' (Tatshi dialect, )

ɬamu ɲɤ-ɕe \\
anthr ifr: west -go \\
`Lhamu went westwards.' (Kamnyu dialect)
xlist
exe

In second person forms, on the other hand, the second person prefix in Tatshi is inserted between the B-type preverb and the a- Inferential prefix (A-type preverb and a- 3 prefix, respectively), as can be seen by comparing the Inferential second person intransitive in Tatshi ( ex:YEtanWYAmkhe ) and Kamnyu ( ex:YAtWnWYAmkhe ). The change in the relative ordering between the vowel-contracting prefixes and the second person prefix has modified the structure of the preverbal system: the Kamnyu dialect has gained two additional series of preverbs, but lost one slot in the verbal template (§ sec:prefixal.chain ).

exe

xlist

ɲə-tə-a-nɯɲɐmkʰe \\
B. preverb -2- ifr -be.lean \\
`You got lean.' (Tatshi dialect, heard in context)

ɲɤ-tɯ-nɯɲɤmkʰe \\
ifr -2-be.lean \\
`You got lean.' (Kamnyu dialect)
xlist
exe

Alternatively, it is possible to analyze C- and D-type preverbs in Kamnyu Japhug as A- and B-type preverbs with vowel fusion following, but there is little Kamnyu-internal data to support such an analysis, since D-type preverbs are not segmentable synchronically in this variety.

While in the case of D-type preverbs the vowel fusion approach proposed by is less attractive in Kamnyu Japhug than in the Tatshi dialect, for the C-type preverbs it is equally applicable to both dialects. First, there is no prefix ordering difference between Kamnyu and Tatshi: the 3 Aorist a- prefix posited by Lin Youjing never occurs in verb forms with prefixed person indexation markers (second person and/or inverse configurations). Second, there is arguably one additional trace of the 3 Aorist a- prefix in the Kamnyu dialect: the ɕa- variant of the Apprehensive ɕɯ- prefix (§ sec:apprehensive ) when used with transitive verbs in 3 form.

There can be little doubt that the fusion hypothesis is correct historically -- there was a stage where a 3 Aorist prefix did exist. However, from a synchronic point of view, it is not necessary to analyze this prefix as a separate morpheme. Furthermore, I decided to favour the non-contracting analysis of the preverbs to avoid potential confusion with the a- Denominal (§ sec:denom.contracting ), Passive (§ sec:passive ) and Reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ) prefixes.

Another substantial difference between Kamnyu Japhug and the Xtokavian dialects concerns the B-type downwards preverb. As shown by tab:orientation.preverbs.tatshi (based on ), the A- and B-type preverbs in Tatshi are nearly completely identical to the corresponding Kamnyu preverbs (except for notational differences such as ɐ and ə instead of ɤ and ə ). The only real difference is the downwards B-type preverb, which is pjɯ- in Kamnyu but has the form cə- with a palatal stop instead of a cluster in Tatshi. It is possible that the Tatshi palatal results from the palatalization of p, but no other examples of *pj- c- are known to me. Alternatively, Kamnyu pjɯ- (and D-type pjɤ- ) could be analogically based on the A-type preverb pɯ-. Another possible origin for the cə- of xtokavian dialects is the base -ki downwards found in the adverbs aki and tɕeki (§ sec:preverbs.adverbs ).
summary:
The Xtokavian dialects of Japhug are analyzed as having only A- and B-type preverbs, with the forms traditionally called C- and D-type better explained as A- and B-type preverbs fused with extra vowel-contracting a- prefixes in the 3 Aorist and Inferential, respectively. In third and first person forms, this fusion yields surface forms nearly identical to those in Kamnyu Japhug, but in second person forms the different placement of the person prefix changes the preverbal template and gives the dialects a different structural analysis.

A further difference is the B-type downwards preverb: Kamnyu has pjɯ-, whereas the Xtokavian dialects have cə-. The passage notes that the historical origin of these forms is uncertain, though the fusion analysis is likely correct historically even if it is not necessary for a synchronic description.

subsubsection: Orientation preverbs and orientation nouns and adverbs
text:
orientation!preverb orientation!noun orientation!adverb
Excluding the unspecified orientation, there is a one-to-one relation between the orientation preverbs, the egressive postpositions (§ sec:egressive, tab:egressive ), locative relator nouns (§ sec:relator.nouns.3d ) and orientation adverbs (§ sec:locative.adv ), as the data in tab:orientation.preverbs.locatives show.

The initial consonant of the orientation preverbs is identical to that of the locative adverbs ( tab:orientation.preverbs.locatives ), except for (i) the westwards orientation with a nasal n- instead of a prenasalized nd- (ii) the downwards orientation, which corresponds to -ki in some adverbial forms ( aki and tɕeki ).

The vocalism of the preverbs is only partially predictable from that of the corresponding adverbs: the prefixes tʰɯ- and nɯ- could be seen as the bound state of the adverbs tʰidownstream and ndiwestwards with -i -ɯ alternation, but the pattern is less clear in the remaining preverbs. In the case of the upwards preverbs, the t- prefixes are more likely to be related to the -tu root found in the adverbs atu and tɕetu rather than the -taʁ root found in the locative noun ɯ-taʁ (on which see § sec:WtaR ).

The irregular consonantal correspondence between the preverb nɯ- and the adverb ndi of the downwards orientation could be interpreted in three ways.

First, the preverb could have been grammaticalized from the adverb, and a sound change *ndi- nɯ- could have taken place one it had become a prefix, due to a phonotactic constraint against prenasalized stops (and complex segments in general) in prefixal position (§ sec:prefix.phonotactic ). This hypothesis is unlikely however, because orientation preverbs are precisely the only prefixes that appear to violate the phonotactic constraints observed by all other elements of the prefixal chain, as shown in particular by the presence of aspirated segments ( tʰɯ- ), laterals ( lɤ- ) and clusters ( pjɯ- ).

Second, the adverb ndi could originate from a compound, whose first element n- would come from the same etymon as the westwards preverb nɯ-.

Finally, the possibility that the preverb nɯ- and the adverb ndi are historically unrelated should also be considered.

The strong resemblance between the preverbs and the locative adverbs could be interpreted as due to a relatively recent grammaticalization. However, just as in the case of the relation between pronouns and indexation suffixes (§ sec:indexation.suffixes.history ), the possibility of mutual contamination between partially cognate paradigms has to be taken into consideration.
summary:
The passage states that, apart from the unspecified orientation, there is a one-to-one correspondence between orientation preverbs, egressive postpositions, locative relator nouns, and orientation adverbs. It also notes that the initial consonants of the preverbs generally match those of the adverbs, though there are exceptions, and that the vowel correspondences are only partly predictable, especially in the forms for upwards and downwards orientation.

It then discusses the irregular relation between the downwards preverb nɯ- and the adverb ndi, proposing several possible explanations: derivation with a later sound change, origin from a compound, or historical unrelatedness. Overall, the close similarity between preverbs and adverbs may reflect recent grammaticalization, though mutual contamination between partially cognate paradigms is also possible.

text:
orientation!incomptability verb!defective
In the West Gyalrongic languages, including Stau  or Khroskyabs, some verbs never take orientation preverbs even in the Imperative and Aorist. This appears to be an archaic feature, as it is restricted to a very small set of cognate verbs, for instance Stau vdɞ `see' and Khroskyabs vdê `see'. No such phenomenon exists in Japhug.
Still, there are some indirect clues that tisay could have had irregular preverbless forms at an earlier stage (§ sec:fact.periphrastic ). The Japhug cognates of West Gyalrongic preverb-less verbs regularly take orientation preverbs (for instance, mtosee selects the downwards orientation, see § sec:preverb.perception ).

A handful of verbs never occur with orientation preverbs in Japhug, but this phenomenon is completely different from the West Gyalrongic case. In Japhug, preverb-less verbs have a defective paradigm, and only occur in one TAME category. Two of them ( mɤ-xsione does not know and kɤtɯpatell, § sec:irregular.transitive ) are only attested in the Factual Non-Past, and the absence of preverbs is thus regular. The existential verbs ɣɤʑuexist and maŋenot exist are only found in the Sensory Evidential (§ sec:intr.person.irregular, § sec:sensory ), which is normally marked by the preverb ɲɯ, and can be considered to be the suppletive forms of tuexist and menot exist, respectively.
summary:
In West Gyalrongic languages such as Stau and Khroskyabs, a very small set of cognate verbs never takes orientation preverbs even in the Imperative and Aorist, which seems to be an archaic feature. Japhug does not show this pattern: its cognates normally take orientation preverbs, though there are hints that an earlier stage may have had irregular preverb-less forms.

In Japhug, the few verbs that never occur with orientation preverbs do so for a different reason: they have defective paradigms and are restricted to a single TAME category. Some are only attested in the Factual Non-Past, while the existential verbs occur only in the Sensory Evidential and are treated as suppletive forms.

text:
verb!orientable
Most verbs in Japhug have one or several lexicalized orientation(s) (§ sec:lexicalized.orientation ), and when used with preverbs, these no longer express spatial orientation or direction. Yet, there is a subclass of verbs, in which the preverbs retain their original spatial meaning: these are called in this grammar ``orientable verbs''.

The defining feature of these verbs is not simply the ability to take any of the six orientation preverbs, but more importantly their compatibility with the unspecified orientation (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), which is never used as a lexicalized orientation.

Orientable verbs can be subdivided into three main categories: motion verbs (`go, `come' etc), manipulation verbs (`bring', `take' etc) and orienting verb (`look towards', `turn towards' etc). In addition, some stative verbs can be converted into orientable verbs. This section presents the specificities of a sample of these categories, and then describes the uses of preverbs to express spatial direction.
summary:
In Japhug, most verbs have lexicalized orientations, so preverbs no longer indicate spatial direction; however, a subclass called orientable verbs preserves the original spatial meaning of preverbs. The key diagnostic for orientable verbs is not just taking orientation preverbs, but also compatibility with the unspecified orientation, which is never lexicalized.  

Orientable verbs fall into three main types: motion verbs, manipulation verbs, and orienting verbs, and some stative verbs can also be converted into orientable verbs. The section then examines examples of these categories and how preverbs are used to express spatial direction.

text:
verb!motion
Motion verbs in Japhug can be subdivided into four categories, depending on their transitivity and on whether they select a local phrase.

First, allative motion verbs select a locative phrase (in the absolutive § absolutive.goal, with a locative postposition § sec:locative and/or a relator noun § sec:relator.location ) expressing the goal / direction of the motion. The most common allative verbs are ɕego and ɣicome (§ sec:motion.deixis ), which can also take a purposive complement (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation ).

Other allative verbs include zɣɯtarrive ( ex:WkAcu.kozGWtndZi ), citmove, pʰɣoflee, mtsaʁjump, ɕqʰlɤtdisappear and jɣɤtturn around, and derived vertitive verbs (§ sec:vertitive ) such as nɯɕego back.

The orientation preverbs of allative verbs express the trajectory towards the goal, as in ( ex:WkAcu.kozGWtndZi ). Note here the orientation concord between the eastwards preverb ko- and the locative relative noun ɯ-kɤcueast of (§ sec:orientation.concord ).

exe

ɯ-kɤcu tɕe iɕqʰa mtsʰu kɯ-wɣrum nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu ko-zɣɯt-ndʑi. \\
3sg. poss -east loc the.aforementioned lake sbj: pcp -be.white dem gen 3sg. poss -on dem: loc ifr: east -reach- du \\
`They arrived at the white lake east of there.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S256
exe

In addition, reflexive-causative derivations from allative verbs, or from verbs of relative location, such as ʑɣɤsɤzɣɯtmanage to reach and ʑɣɤsɤrmbatmove closer from zɣɯtarrive and armbatbe near (§ sec:convertion.orientable.verbs, § sec:refl.caus.motion ), can also be allative verbs.

There is always an implicit goal with ɕego, ɣicome and zɣɯtarrive, even when it is not overt, as in ( ex:alo.nA.alo.kAGea ). In this example, the locative adverb aloupstream (here `closer to the mountain', see § sec:riverine.dimension ) refers to the path of the motion, not its goal. The goal, being encoded by the eastwards preverb, would have to be expressed with a eastwards locative noun or adverb (§ sec:orientation.concord ).

exe

alo nɤ alo kɤ-ɣe-a ma ɯ-ʁɤri ku-kɯ-ɣi tɕe, ɲɯ-ɣɯtsʰɤdɯɣ. \\
upstream add upstream aor: east -come[II]- 1sg lnk 3sg. poss -front ipfv: east - genr:S/O-come lnk sens -be.hot \\
`I came [here], (eastwards from the point of origin) by [the road that lies] closer to the mountain, when one comes by the [road that is located] in the front (closer to the river), it is too hot.' (conversation, 140510)
exe

Second, the verb ɬoʁcome out is an ablative motion verb, selecting a locative phrase expressing the point of departure of the motion event, as ndzom ɯ-pa nɯtɕu `from under the bridge' and tɯ-ci ɯ-rkɯ nɯtɕu `from the side of the river' in ( ex:Wpa.nWtCu.tonWlhoR ) and tɯmɯnɤmkʰa zɯ `from heaven' in ( ex:tWmWnAmkha.zW.pjAnWlhoRnW ). The preverb refers to the direction from this point of origin to the goal (which may be left unspecified), a motion upwards in ( ex:Wpa.nWtCu.tonWlhoR ), and downwards in ( ex:tWmWnAmkha.zW.pjAnWlhoRnW ).

exe

tɕe ndzom ɯ-pa nɯtɕu tɯ-ci ɯ-rkɯ nɯtɕu pɣɤtɕɯ nɯ to-nɯ-ɬoʁ tɕe \\
lnk bridge 3sg. poss -under dem: loc indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -side dem: loc bird dem ifr: up - auto -come.out lnk \\
`The bird came out from under the bridge, near the river.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

exe

tɯmɯnɤmkʰa zɯ pjɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ-nɯ. \\
heaven loc ifr: down - auto -come.out- pl \\
`[They] came down from heaven.' (150828 niulang-zh) 0006318#S48
exe

The verb ɣicome sometimes selects a locative phrase referring to the source of the motion, rather than to the goal, as shown by ( ex:tWmWnAmkha.nWtCu.pjWGinW ), describing an action similar to ( ex:tWmWnAmkha.zW.pjAnWlhoRnW ).

exe

sɲikuku ʑo tɕe tɯmɯnɤmkʰa nɯtɕu, qro χsɯm pjɯ-ɣi-nɯ \\
every.day emph lnk heaven dem: loc pigeon three ipfv: down -come- pl \\
`Everyday, three pigeons came down from heaven.' (31-deluge)
0004077#S47
exe

Another ablative verb is the reflexive-causative ʑɣɤsɤrqʰimove further away derivation from the stative verb arqʰibe far (see § sec:convertion.orientable.verbs ).

Third, atelic motion verbs do not select a locative phrase. This category includes verbs expressing the speed of motion ( rɟɯɣrun, ŋkewalk), or non-terrestrial motion ( nɯqambɯmbjomfly, ndʑaʁswim). With these verbs, when a locative phrase is present, it generally indicates the path of the motion, not the goal, as in ( ex:WNgW.ri.tANkea ).

exe

<bazi> ɯ-ŋgɯ ri tɤ-ŋke-a ma, kɯ-ɤrqʰi kɤ-ɕe mɯ-ku-cʰa-a. \\
yard 3sg. poss -in loc aor -walk- 1sg lnk sbj: pcp -be.far inf -go neg - prs -can- 1sg \\
`I had a walk in the yard, I cannot go very far.' (conversation, 2017-09-21)
exe

To specify a goal, the atelic motion verb is usually conjoined with an allative verb, in particular ɕego or ɣicome, as in ( ex:jondZaR.tCe.joCe ).

exe

rɟɤmtsʰu ɯ-pɕoʁ tɕe jo-ndʑaʁ tɕe jo-ɕe. \\
sea 3sg. poss -side loc ifr -swim lnk ifr -go \\
`He swam towards the sea.' (150830 baihe jiemei-zh)
0006368#S201
exe

With the verb rɟɯɣrun there are apparent examples of locative phrases indicating the goal as in ( ex:WNgW.chArJWG ), but only in texts translated from Chinese, and this may be a calque, though such examples are not considered clumsy by Tshendzin.

exe

rɟara ɯ-ŋgɯ cʰɤ-rɟɯɣ ri, \\
yard 3sg. poss -in ifr: downstream -run lnk \\
`He ran out into the yard.' (140505 bulaimei-zh) 0003911#S104
exe

The verb ŋkewalk is barely attested with the unspecified orientation preverbs. It only occurs with them when in a serial verb construction (§ sec:svc.manner ) with an allative motion verb, as in ( ex:joNke.joCe ). When used on their own, the upwards preverbs occur to express unspecified orientation, as in ( ex:WNgW.ri.tANkea ) above.

exe

tɕe jo-ŋke jo-ɕe tɕe tɕe, <changcheng> [...] ɯ-kɯ-βzu ra nɯ-ɕki tɕe jo-zɣɯt. \\
lnk ifr -walk ifr -go lnk lnk great.wall 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -make pl 3pl. poss - dat loc ifr -arrive \\
`She went [there] on foot and arrived where people were building the Great Wall.' (150827 mengjiangnv-zh) 0006290#S145
exe

The distributed action verb nɤɕɯɕego around (from ɕego) does not take definite goals (§ sec:distributed.action ), and in addition is only compatible with unspecified orientation preverbs.
summary:
Japhug motion verbs are divided into four types according to transitivity and whether they take a local phrase: allative verbs, ablative verbs, atelic motion verbs, and a distributed-action verb. Allative verbs like ɕego, ɣicome, and zɣɯtarrive select a locative phrase expressing the goal or direction of motion, while ɬoʁcome out is ablative and selects a source phrase; ɣicome can also sometimes mark the source, and some derived verbs behave similarly.

Atelic motion verbs such as rɟɯɣrun, ŋkewalk, nɯqambɯmbjomfly, and ndʑaʁswim do not select a locative phrase, so any locative phrase usually indicates the path rather than the goal. To express a goal with these verbs, Japhug commonly combines them with an allative verb

text:
Fourth, transitive motion verbs include βɟichase, pjɤlgo around, cross, avoid, pɣaʁturn over and nɯmɢlastep over, which can also occur with the non-specific orientation preverbs, as in ( ex:jannWpGaRndZi.jannWmGlandZi ). The object of these verbs is the location or entity around which (or through/towards which) the motion event takes place.

exe

zgo tʰɤstɯɣ ja-nnɯ-pɣaʁ-ndʑi, tɯ-ci tɕʰi jarma ja-n-nɯmɢla-ndʑi mɤ-xsi ma, \\
mountain how.many aor:3 - auto -turn.over- du indef. poss -water what about aor:3 - auto -cross- du neg - genr:know lnk \\
`It is not known how many mountains and rivers they crossed.' (qajdoskAt 2002) 0003366#S50
exe

The transitive verb nɯɴqʰugo along, follow (§ sec:denom.tr.nW ) is also compatible with the unspecified orientation preverbs, but can also selects the upwards preverbs as default, like ŋkewalk.
summary: The passage says that several transitive motion verbs, including ‘chase,’ ‘go around,’ ‘cross,’ ‘avoid,’ ‘turn over,’ and ‘step over,’ can occur with non-specific orientation preverbs. Their object is the place or entity around, through, or toward which the motion happens. It also notes that the verb meaning ‘go along/follow’ is compatible with unspecified orientation preverbs, but usually takes upward preverbs by default like the verb ‘walk.’

text:
verb!manipulation
verb!caused accompanied motion
Manipulation verbs are transitive verbs expressing a motion involving two entities. The term ``caused accompanied motion'' has been suggested to replace ``manipulation''. The subject, generally (but not exclusively) animate causes the object (prototypically, an inanimate) to move (in some case together with him/her/it). As in the case of motion verbs, there are several categories depending on whether a locative phrase is selected and the nature of the motion causation.

Allative manipulation verbs select a locative phrase indicating the goal of the motion, such as <xuexiao> ɣɯ ɯ-<caochang> ɯ-χcɤl `the middle of the school playground' in ( ex:WXcAl.Zo.natsWmnW ) or sɤtɕʰa kɯ-ɤrqʰi zɯ `to a place far away' in ( ex:WpCi.zW.juwGsco ). The presence of a locative phrase is however always optional (§ sec:secundative.monotransitive ).

exe

ji-kʰɯtsa sɤ-rku tsʰaŋ nɯnɯ, ta-nɤjoʁjoʁ-nɯ ta-nɯtʰaj-nɯ qʰe rcanɯ, <xuexiao> ɣɯ ɯ-<caochang> ɯ-χcɤl ʑo na-tsɯm-nɯ. \\
1pl. poss -bowl obl: pcp -put.in cupboard dem aor:3 -lift.up.and.go.around- pl aor:3 -lift.up.and.carry- pl lnk unexp: deg school gen 3sg. poss -playground 3sg. poss -center emph aor:3: east -take.away- pl \\
`They lifted up the cupboard where we put our bowls, and carried it to the middle of the school playground.' (150831 BZW kAnArRaR)
0006378#S20
exe

exe

ɯ-pɕi zɯ jú-wɣ-sco, sɤtɕʰa kɯ-ɤrqʰi zɯ pjɯ́-wɣ-lɤt ma-pɯ́-wɣ-sat ra tu-kɯ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -outside loc ipfv - inv -send place sbj: pcp -be.far loc ipfv: down - inv -release neg - imp - inv -kill be.needed: fact ipfv: down - genr:S/O-say sens -be \\
`One has to send [the snake] outside, to a place far away without killing it, people say.' (2010-11)
exe

Allative manipulation verbs can be divided into several subcategories. Verbs of transportation, in which the subject carries the object and moves together with it/him include tsɯmtake away and ɣɯtbring, the transitive counterparts of the motion verbs ɕego and ɣicome (§ sec:motion.deixis ), rufetch, bring (discussed in more detail in § sec:ru.fetch ). Verbs of accompanied motion, whose subject and objects move together along the same trajectory, include mtsʰilead, nodrive, scosee off and lɤtrelease. This verb has many functions as a light verb (§ sec:lAt.lv ), but one of its basic meanings when used on its own is `see off' like sco. The latter two verbs can also refer to transportation in a vehicle, as in ( ex:GWlAwGlAti ). Verbs of accompanied motion can occur with a locative phrase, but such uses are very rare.

exe

ɯ-wa kɯ ɣɯ-lɤ́-wɣ-lɤt-i \\
3sg. poss -father erg cisl - ifr: upstream - inv -release- 1pl \\
`His father give us a ride here (from Chengdu to Mbarkham).' (elicited)
exe

Allative verbs of induced motion comprise the causative derivations of motion verbs, in particular sɯɣeinvite, `cause to come'and sɯxɕesend, `cause to go'. Only the object undergoes the motion, as in ( ex:WtaR.tAwGsWxCe ). However, the motion verb rɟɯɣrun has a causative form sɯrɟɯɣrun away with which expresses motion of both subject and object (§ sec:sig.caus.appl.comitative ).

exe

rŋɯl rɟɤskɤt ɯ-taʁ tɤ́-wɣ-sɯx-ɕe ɲɯ-ŋu \\
silver stairs 3sg. poss -on ifr: up - inv - caus -go sens -be \\
`They made her go up the silver stairs.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

The verbs mɟatake (§ sec:antipassive.t ) and tɕɤttake out when used as manipulation verbs select a locative phrase which can refer to the goal, as in ( ex:WmNu.zW.jutCAtnW ), but also in some cases to the point of origin of the motion, as in ( ex:WphWNgW.nWtCu.YAtCAt ). These verbs do not necessary imply translational motion of the subject (only motion of the hands).

exe

ɲɤ-mtsɯr qʰe tɕendɤre ɯ-pʰɯŋgɯ nɯtɕu iɕqʰa nɯ, qajɣi ci ɲɤ-tɕɤt tɕe to-nɯ-ndza. \\
ifr -be.hungry lnk lnk 3sg. poss -fold.of.clothes dem. loc filler dem bread indef ifr -take.out lnk ifr - auto -eat \\
`He became hungry, took a piece of bread from the folds of his clothes and ate it.' (150830 san ge heshang-zh) 0006416#S129
exe

exe

rɟɤmtsʰu ɯ-mŋu zɯ ju-tɕɤt-nɯ tɕe \\
ocean 3sg. poss -border loc ipfv -take.out- pl lnk \\
`[The whalers] take [the whale] to the shore.' (160703 jingyu)
0006169#S35
exe

Atelic manipulation verbs cannot select a locative phrase. Some atelic verbs are not orientable, and cannot take the unspecified orientation preverbs. For instance, nɯtʰajcarry (a verb borrowed from Chinese, see § sec:zh.loanverbs ) is only compatible with the upwards orientation, and requires to be used with an allative verb such as tsɯmtake away to specify the goal and the orientation, as in ( ex:WXcAl.Zo.natsWmnW ) above.
summary:
Manipulation verbs are transitive verbs expressing caused accompanied motion, where an animate subject causes an object to move, sometimes together with it. They are divided into types such as allative verbs, which optionally take a locative goal phrase, verbs of transportation and accompanied motion, verbs of induced motion, and verbs like *take* and *take out* that may refer to the goal or origin of motion.

Atelic manipulation verbs cannot select a locative phrase. Some are not orientable and therefore cannot take unspecified orientation preverbs, so a borrowed verb like *carry* must combine with an allative verb to express both the goal and the direction of motion.

text:
deixis!motion
Motion and manipulation verbs both have a contrast between translocative ( ɕe § sec:motion.verbs, tsɯm § sec:manipulation.verbs ) and cislocative ( ɣi § sec:motion.verbs, ɣɯt § sec:manipulation.verbs ), like the corresponding associated motion prefixes ( ɕɯ- § sec:translocative.morpho, ɣɯ- § sec:cislocative.morpho ).

The translocative and cislocative verbs can often be translated as `go/take away' and `come/bring', respectively. However, these translations may be misleading, as the criteria for determining the deictic center in Japhug are not identical to those of Chinese or English.

The cislocative verbs are required not only in case of motion towards the location of the speaker, they have to be used whenever a motion is directed towards a spatial location related either to the speaker or the addressee, even in the case of motion from the location of the speaker to that of the addressee. For instance, while in Chinese (and most languages of Europe) both 来你家 lái nǐ jiācome to your house and 去你家 qù nǐ jiāgo to your house are grammatical, in Japhug only the cislocative verbs are employed in this case. In ( ex:nAkha.juGia ) for instance, replacing ju-ɣi-a by ju-ɕe-a would result in a very clumsy clause.

exe

aʑo tʰɤjtɕu jamar nɤ-kʰa ju-ɣi-a pe? \\
1sg when about 2sg. poss -house ipfv -come- 1sg be.good: fact \\
`What time should I go to your house?' (elicited)
exe

Similarly, the cislocative is necessary when both addressee and speaker go together, in sentences with the secutive ɯ-rca (§ sec:secutive ) such as ( ex:arca.jAGi ), ( ex:nArca.tuGia ) (see also ex:nArca.YWGia in § sec:solar.dimension ). The translocative ɕego is never attested is such contexts.

exe

a-rca jɤ-ɣi \\
1sg. poss -following imp -come \\
`Come with me.' (several attestations)
exe

exe

nɤ-rca tu-ɣi-a ra ma kutɕu aʑo-sti ku-rɤʑi-a mɯ́j-cʰa-a \\
2sg. poss -following ipfv: up -come- 1sg be.needed: fact lnk here 1sg -alone ipfv -stay- 1sg neg: sens -can- 1sg \\
`I am going [to heaven] with you, I cannot stay here alone.' (02-deluge) 0003376#S74
exe

The translocative manipulation verb tsɯmtake away however can be used with a second person secutive, as in ( ex:nArca.tukWtsWma ).

exe

nɤ-rca tu-kɯ-tsɯm-a ra \\
2sg. poss -following ipfv: up -2 1-take.away- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`Take me with you [to heaven].' (31-deluge) 0004077#S71
exe
summary:
Japhug has a translocative/cislocative contrast in both motion verbs and manipulation verbs, roughly corresponding to ‘go/take away’ versus ‘come/bring.’ However, the cislocative is used more broadly than in Chinese or English: it is required not only for motion toward the speaker, but also for motion toward a location associated with either speaker or addressee, including motion from speaker to addressee.

This is seen in examples where only the cislocative is natural for going to the addressee’s house or for moving together with the addressee under the secutive construction. By contrast, the translocative manipulation verb tsɯm ‘take away’ can occur in a second-person secutive context.

text:
orientation!orienting verb verb!orienting
Orienting verbs express change of orientation without translational motion, involving a pointing/aiming gesture towards a goal. This category includes the intransitive rulook at (§ sec:intr.goal ), the transitive verbs ɕtʰɯzturn towards and tʰɯbuilt (of roads or bridges; this verb also has additional meanings such as `leave (a trace)' as in ex:WjroR.juthi in specific contexts), as well as the anticausative ndɯbe spread (§ sec:anticausative ).

With the verb ɕtʰɯz for instance, the preverb indicates the orientation towards which the object is directed, and it can correlate with locative adverbs ( ex:YACthWz.koCthWz ) or locative phrases ( ex:khWtsa.tuCthWznW ).

exe

tɕe tɕekɯ zɯ rŋɯl-kʰri ndi ɲɤ-ɕtʰɯz, tɕendi zɯ kɯ ko-ɕtʰɯz tɕe, \\
lnk east. distal loc silver-seat west ifr: west -turn.towards west. distal loc east ifr: east -turn.towards lnk \\
`On the eastearn side, he turned the silver seat towards the west, and on the western side he turned [the other seat] towards the east.' (smAnmi2003)
exe

exe

tɕe nɯ kʰɯtsa nɯ tu-ɕtʰɯz-nɯ, tɯ-mɲaʁ ɯ-pa ri tu-ɕtʰɯz-nɯ kɯ-fse tɕe, \\
lnk dem bowl dem ipfv: up -turn.towards- pl indef. poss -eye 3sg. poss -below loc ipfv: up -turn.towards- pl inf: stat -be.like lnk \\
`[The lamas] turn the bowl upwards below the eye [of the patient].' (27-tApGi)
0003706#S18
exe

Orienting verbs are also compatible with unspecified orientation preverbs, as example ( ex:WjroR.juthi ) shows.

exe

kɯ-fsoʁ ɯ-jroʁ kɯ-fse ci ju-tʰi tɕe, \\
sbj: pcp -be.bright 3sg. poss -trace sbj: pcp -be.like indef ipfv: unspecified -leave.trace[III] lnk \\
`The shooting star leaves something like a bright trail.' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S86
exe
summary:
Orienting verbs express a change of orientation without translational motion, typically involving a pointing or aiming gesture toward a goal. The category includes the intransitive *rulook at*, the transitive verbs *ɕtʰɯz* ‘turn towards’ and *tʰɯb* ‘built’ (also with other meanings in some contexts), and the anticausative *ndɯ* ‘be spread’.  

For *ɕtʰɯz*, the preverb marks the direction toward which something is oriented and may cooccur with locative adverbs or phrases; these verbs can also take unspecified orientation preverbs.

text:
verb!orientable
A handful of stative verbs can take the unspecified orientation preverbs and be converted to dynamic orientable verbs. The stative verbs of relative location armbatbe near and arqʰibe far can be used in the meanings `move closer' and `move further away' identical to the reflexive-causative derived verbs ʑɣɤsɤrmbatmove closer and ʑɣɤsɤrqʰimove further away(§ sec:motion.verbs, § sec:refl.caus ), as in ( ex:jarmbat.kurtoR ).

exe

jɤ-armbat tɕe ku-rtoʁ tɕe, tɕeri ɯʑo ɯ-pi ʁnɯz nɯni pjɤ-ŋu-ndʑi. \\
aor -be.close lnk ipfv -look lnk lnk 3sg 3sg. poss -elder.sibling two dem: du ifr. ipfv -be- du \\
`As he moved closer, he saw that [the people about to be executed] were his brothers.' (140507 jinniao-zh) 0003931#S318
exe

Finally, the stative verb ɲatbe tired occurs with the indefinite orientation preverbs in the meaning `become tired (from walking/running)', as in ( ex:mWjAYat.joCe ).

exe

mɯ-jɤ-ɲat ʑo mɤɕtʂa jo-ɕe \\
neg - aor -be.tired emph until ifr -go \\
`He went [after them] until he became tired.' (160706 poucet6) 0006109#S45
exe
summary: A small number of stative verbs can combine with unspecified orientation preverbs to become dynamic orientable verbs. In particular, the location verbs *armbat* ‘be near’ and *arqʰi* ‘be far’ can mean ‘move closer’ and ‘move further away,’ like their reflexive-causative counterparts. The stative verb *ɲat* ‘be tired’ can also occur with indefinite orientation preverbs to mean ‘become tired (from walking/running).’

text: Some complement-taking verbs, in particular phasal verbs (§ sec:phasal.complements ) such as ʑabegin, select the orientation of the verb in the complement clause, and can be used with indefinite orientation preverbs (§ sec:orientation.raising ).
summary: Some complement-taking verbs, especially phasal verbs like ʑabegin, determine the orientation of the verb in their complement clause. They can also occur with indefinite orientation preverbs.

text:
orientation!concord
Clauses containing a orientable verb generally show agreement between the orientation of the preverb and that of orientation nouns and adverbs
(§ sec:relator.nouns.3d, § sec:preverbs.adverbs ).

In ( ex:alo.lorJWG.athi.chArJWG ) for instance, the upstream lo- and cʰɤ- downstream preverbs correlate with the adverbs aloupstream and atʰidownstream, respectively, expressing here a back and forth motion.

exe

alo nɤ lo-rɟɯɣ atʰi nɤ cʰɤ-rɟɯɣ \\
upstream add ifr: upstream -run downstream add ifr: downstream -run \\
`He ran upstream and downstream.' (160720 kandZislama)
0006147#S66
exe

In ( ex:WndAcu.YAkAtWGci ), the westwards ɲɤ- preverb corresponds to the orientation relator noun ɯ-ndɤcuwest of. In the same story, the main character comes back to the same place on the return trip, from the opposite direction, and the eastwards orientation preverb and relator noun are found instead (example ex:WkAcu.kozGWtndZi, § sec:motion.verbs ).

exe

ɯ-ndɤcu tɕe, mtsʰu kɯ-wɣrum ci ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-ci. \\
3sg. poss -west loc lake sbj: pcp -be.white indef ifr: west - peg -meet- peg \\
`In the west from there, he came upon a white lake.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S97
exe
summary: Clauses with an orientable verb typically show agreement between the orientation of the preverb and the orientation expressed by nouns or adverbs. The passage illustrates this with upstream/downstream preverbs matching upstream/downstream adverbs in a description of back-and-forth running, and with a westward preverb corresponding to a “west of” relator noun, later replaced by eastward forms when the character returns from the opposite direction.

text:
orientation!tridimensional system
Orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) in Japhug are organized in a three-dimensional system like spatial postpositions, relator nouns and adverbs (§ sec:egressive, § sec:relator.nouns.3d, § sec:locative.adv ). Very similar orientation systems are found in other Gyalrong languages, in particular Tshobdun and the Cogtse dialect of Situ. Not all Core Gyalrong languages, however, have a tridimensional orientation system: Zbu and the Bragbar dialect of Situ are exceptions.

The present section describes the concrete spatial uses of each of the three dimensions (vertical, riverine and solar) The labels `riverine' and `solar' follow Sun's ( jackson00sidaba) and Lin's ( lin02dimension) work on Tshobdun and Situ. Previous authors have analyzed the `riverine' and `solar' dimensions as `river-mountain' and `upstream-downstream', respectively (see the discussion in § sec:riverine.dimension ). with orientable verbs. The discussion here not only applies to orientation preverbs, but also to all nouns, postpositions and adverbs encoding orientation.
summary:
Japhug orientation preverbs are part of a tridimensional spatial system, parallel to the system found in spatial postpositions, relator nouns, and adverbs. Similar systems occur in other Gyalrong languages such as Tshobdun and Cogtse Situ, though Zbu and Bragbar Situ lack this tridimensional orientation system.

The section explains the spatial uses of the three dimensions—vertical, riverine, and solar—and notes that the labels “riverine” and “solar” follow earlier studies. It also states that the discussion applies not only to orientation preverbs but to all nouns, postpositions, and adverbs expressing orientation.

text:
orientation!vertical dimension
The basic meaning of the upwards and downwards preverbs, adverbs and locator nouns is to encode relative position or motion on the axis that is perpendicular to the ground. A typical use of these preverbs with orientable verbs for instance is to describe motion up and down trees or stairs, as shown by ( ex:WtaR.tari ) and ( ex:rJAskAt.pjACe ).

exe

tɕʰi nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-taʁ tɤ-ari ɲɯ-ŋu \\
tree.trunk.stairway dem gen 3sg. poss -on aor: up -go[II] sens -be \\
`He went up the tree trunk stairway.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

exe

rɟɤskɤt to-sɤglɤglɤɣ ʑo pjɤ-ɕe tɕe, \\
stairs ifr -make.trampling.noise emph ifr: down -go \\
`She hurtled down the stairs.' (Nyima wodzer2002)
exe

The downwards preverb also expresses downwards motion into another medium such as water, as in ( ex:pjAmtsaR.pjAsi ).

exe

tɕendɤre tɯ-ɲɟɤt kɯ tɯ-ci ɯ-ŋgɯ pjɤ-mtsaʁ qʰe pjɤ-si. \\
lnk nmlz: action -regret erg indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -in ifr: down -jump lnk ifr -die \\
`(Desperate from) regret, he jumped into the water and died.' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S177
exe

The rising and setting of the sun is also expressed with the vertical preverbs ( to-ɬoʁ ifr: up -come.out `(the sun) rose' vs. pjɤ-ɕqʰlɤt ifr: down -disappear `(the sun) set'); alternatively, the solar dimension is also used (§ sec:solar.dimension ).

The vertical dimension preverbs also express relative altitude, in particular when the slope between two places is particularly steep. Alternatively, the riverine preverbs upstream / downstream (§ sec:riverine.dimension ) occur either when the slope is less steep, or when following a water stream. This dimension can also be used between far away places when the difference in altitude is perceived to be particularly conspicuous. For instance, the orientation upwards is selected to describe a journey from Gyalrong areas to central Tibet, and downwards for a trip to Chinese areas, as in ( ex:pot.tari ) and ( ex:rJa.pjACe ) (see also ex:CpjWntGea in § sec:orientation.AM ). The riverine dimension is alternatively possible however to refer to motion between Gyalrong and Chinese areas (§ sec:riverine.dimension ).

exe

pot stʰɯci kɯ-ɤrqʰi me ri, nɯtɕu tɤ-ari ɕti tɕe \\
Tibet such.as sbj: pcp -be.far not.exist: fact lnk dem. loc aor: up -go[II] be. aff: fact lnk \\
`There is no [place] further away [from here] than Tibet, but he went there.' (meimeidegushi)
exe

exe

rɟa pjɤ-ɕe tɕe \\
Chine ifr: down -go lnk \\
`He went to China.' (Gesar)
exe

In some cases, the orientation downwards is selected when the path includes a section down a mountain, even if the axis is oriented in the upstream/downstream or east/west directions. For instance, the downwards orientation preverb appears to express a motion from kɤmɲɯ Kamnyu to smɯlju Smeliu village, as explained in example ( ex:rqaco.pjWCea ), although the path between them follows the east-west axis. It is however alternatively possible to use the eastwards preverbs to describe the trip from Kamnyu to Smeliu (and the westwards preverbs for the opposite journey).

exe

``rqaco pjɯ-ɕe-a" tu-kɯ-ti, ``smɯlju pɯ-ari-a" tu-ti-nɯ. tɕe ma nɯnɯ zgo nɯ tu-kɯ-ɕe tɕe, akɯ tɕe pa pjɯ-kɯ-ɕe ɲɯ-ra loβ, tɕe núndʐa ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
topo ipfv: down -go- 1sg ipfv - genr -say topo aor: down -go[II]- 1sg ipfv -say- pl lnk lnk dem mountain dem ipfv: up - genr:S/O-go lnk east loc down ipfv: down - genr:S/O-go sens -be.needed sfp lnk for.this.reason sens -be \\
`People say `I will go (down) to Rqakyo', or `I went [down] to Smeliu', this is because one has to go up a mountain and back down its eastern side.' (150904 akW andi-zh) 0006372#S15
exe
summary: The basic function of the upward and downward preverbs, adverbs, and locator nouns is to mark relative position or motion along the vertical axis, especially in motion up and down trees, stairs, water, or other media. They also describe the rising and setting of the sun and can indicate relative altitude between places, including routes where a steep mountain slope makes vertical orientation more salient than riverine or east-west orientation.

text:
orientation!riverine dimension
The basic meaning of the upstream and downstream preverbs, adverbs and locator nouns is to express motion or relative position along the axis of a flowing river or streamlet.

The downstream preverbs are systematically used to refer to the direction of water flow. In particular, the imperfective participles cʰɯ-kɯ-ɣi or cʰɯ-kɯ-ɕe with the downstream preverb are sometimes added to the noun tɯ-ciwater to specify the meaning `river, stream' ( tɯ-ci cʰɯ-kɯ-ɣi, literally `the water that is coming downstream') as in ( ex:tWci.chWkWGi ) and ( ex:tunWNqhu.lukWCe ).

exe

alo ji-tɯ-ci cʰɯ-kɯ-ɣi, <jiaomujiao> tɯ-ci nɯ \\
upstream 1pl. poss - indef. poss -water ipfv: downstream - sbj: pcp -come pl.n indef. poss -water dem \\
`Our river upstream [in Kamnyu], the Kyomkyo river...' (150820 ZNGWloR)
0006292#S10
exe

In ( ex:tWYAt.nWNA.chAwGGWt ), the downstream preverb is not only used with motion verbs in the collocation with the nouns tɕʰitʰɤnmudslide or tɯɲɤtlandslide, it is also found on the verb cʰɤ́-wɣ-ɣɯt to describe a mudslide taking away an animal with it.

exe

tɕe tɕʰitʰɤn cʰɤ-ɣi tɕendɤre <dianchang> cʰɤ-pʰɯt. <dianchang> cʰɤ-pʰɯt, nɯnɯ tɯɲɤt tʰɯ-ɣe nɯ ɯ-rca nɯtɕu tɕe,
nɯŋa pɯ-kɯ-nɯrɯ nɯ tɤrca cʰɤ́-wɣ-ɣɯt, tɯ-rdoʁ. \\
lnk mudslide ifr: downstream -come lnk power.station ifr: downstream -take.out power.station ifr: downstream -take.out dem landslide aor: downstream -come[II] dem 3sg. poss -together dem. loc loc cow pst. ipfv - sbj: pcp -grazing dem together ifr: downstream - inv -bring one.piece \\
`The mudslide swept away the power station. It swept away the power station, and when the landslide occurred, it took away a cow that was grazing [there].' (160715 nWNa)
0006067#S3
exe

The direction opposite to that of the flow of water is normally referred to with the upstream preverbs, as in ( ex:tunWNqhu.lukWCe ). In ( ex:tunWNqhu.lukWCe ), the upwards preverb on nɯɴqʰugo along, follow is the default orientation, see § sec:motion.verbs. As shown by ( ex:tChiphWG ), the upstream preverbs and adverbs are understood by speakers as specifically referring to the direction towards the source of the river ( tɕʰipʰɯɣ, a noun borrowed from ཆུ་ཕུགས་tɕʰu.pʰugswater source).

exe

kɯki tɯ-ci cʰɯ-kɯ-ɣi kɯki tú-wɣ-nɯɴqʰu lu-kɯ-ɕe tɕe, \\
dem. prox indef. poss -water ipfv: downstream - sbj: pcp -come dem. prox ipfv - inv -follow ipfv: upstream - genr:S/O-go lnk \\
`[If] you follow this creek upstream...' (04-cuiniao-zh)
0003390#S60
exe

exe

tɕʰipʰɯɣ ɯ-pɕoʁ lu-kɯ-ɕe nɯ tɕe ``lo", tɕʰimtʰa ɯ-pɕoʁ cʰɯ-kɯ-ɕe nɯ tɕe ``tʰɯ-ari-a", ``tʰi'' tú-wɣ-nɯ-sɤrmi ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
source.of.the.river 3sg. poss -side ipfv: upstream -gen:S/O-go dem lnk upstream lower.reaches 3sg. poss -side ipfv: downstream - genr:S/O-go dem lnk aor: downstream -go[II]- 1sg downstream ipfv - inv - auto -call sens -be \\
`One calls going towards the source of the river upstream, and going towards the lower reaches of the river `downstream.' (150904 akW andi)
0006372#S24
exe

For motion between localities in the Gyalrong areas located along a river, the upstream and downstream orientation are selected in some cases. For instance, the upstream preverbs occur to describe trips from Kamnyu to Tshobdun (or Zbu) as in ( ex:tshuBdWn.laria ), and the downstream preverbs for the opposite trip.

exe

tsʰuβdɯn kɯ-sɤ-sɯxɕɤt lɤ-ari-a. \\
topo sbj: pcp - apass -teach aor: upstream -go[II]- 1sg \\
`I went to Tshobdun to teach.' (150819 kumpGa) 0006388#S69
exe

The riverine dimension preverbs can also be used in the case of trips to far away places up or down the course of a river. For instance, a journey to Chinese areas can be described using the downstream orientation as in ( ex:rJa.thari ), though due to the considerable altitude difference the orientation downwards is often preferred (compare with example ex:rJa.pjACe, § sec:vertical.dimension ).

exe

rɟa sɤz kɯ-ɤrqʰi me ri, nɯtɕu tʰɯ-ari ɕti \\
China comit sbj: pcp -be.far.away not.exist: fact lnk dem: loc aor: downstream -go[II] be. aff: fact \\
`There is no [place] further away [from here] than China, but he went there.' (meimeidegushi)
exe

However, in valleys where the main river flows along the east-west axis, the solar dimension (§ sec:solar.dimension ) takes over the riverine dimension. In Mbarkham and the towns around it, where the Somang river flows from east to west, the upstream and downstream preverbs cannot be used to refer to the places along the river. Rather, the eastwards preverbs occur for the upstream direction and the westwards preverb for the downstream orientation. For instance, from Mbarkham to Cogtse, located upstream, the eastwards preverb is selected as in ( ex:tCWXtsi.karij ). For Rdzonggag and Bragbar, further downstream (and southwest from Mbarkham), the westwards preverb is used. For shorter trips (on foot or on vehicles) inside Mbarkham city, the solar dimension preverbs are also systematically used.

exe

tɕɯχtsi kɤ-ari-j, kɯ-nɤmɲo \\
topo aor: east -go[II]- 1pl sbj: pcp -watch \\
`We went to Cogtse, to visit.' (conversation, 2013-10-15)
exe

In this environment, the riverine preverbs are used to encode the mountain-river slope axis, which is perpendicular to the river axis. This phenomenon has been observed in other Gyalrong languages., in an article about Situ where the same reorganisation of preverb dimensions occurs, argues that `the riverine pair has become generalized for cases where there are no mountain creeks in sight, and the orientation markings then encode an opposition between higher and lower parts of a slope via metaphorical extension.'

A further extension of the riverine dimension in such geographical environments is to encode the orientation perpendicular to that river even in places with relatively flat ground without any slope. In localities where the river is exactly aligned on the East-West axis, the riverine preverbs thus started to encode the North-South axis, with the downstream preverb for the orientation towards the river on this axis, and the upstream preverb from that away from the river.
summary:
The upstream and downstream preverbs, adverbs, and locator nouns primarily express motion or position along a river’s flow, with downstream marking the direction of water flow and upstream marking the opposite direction toward the river source. They are also used in fixed collocations and broader geographical reference, including trips between localities along a river and even faraway places, though in some east-west river valleys the solar dimension replaces this system for along-river orientation.

In such valleys, the riverine preverbs can be reinterpreted to mark the mountain-river slope axis, and in some places they extend further to encode a perpendicular North-South axis even on flat ground. The passage notes that this kind of reorganization has parallels in other Gyalrong languages.

text:
This perpendicular orientation grid is applied not only on streets (where a mild slope is generally perceptible in Gyalrong-speaking valleys), but even extended within houses, where the ground is even. For instance, if the toilets are located on the side of the building that is closer to the river, and if one happens to be on the opposite side of the apartment, one can say ( ex:jAGAt.ci.chWCea ), even though one remains at the same vertical level (all solar and riverine prefixes would also be appropriate, depending on the absolute orientations).

exe

jɤɣɤt ci cʰɯ-ɕe-a \\
toilet a.little ipfv: downstream -go- 1sg \\
`I am going to the bathroom.' (heard several times in context)
exe

Some journeys involve a change of orientation. In such cases, the choice of the preverb depends on the longest section during the trip. For instance, the road from Mbarkham to Kamnyu first goes downstream the Somang river (westwards) and then, for a longer distance, upstream the Kyomkyo river (northwards), and therefore the upstream preverbs are required ( ex:kAmYW.mWlAtsWma ).

exe

kɤmɲɯ mɯ-lɤ-tsɯm-a \\
topo neg - aor: upstream -take.away- 1sg \\
`I did not take [my mobile phone] to Kamnyu.' (said after having come back to Mbarkham, conversation, 16-02-21)
exe

For the opposite journey (from Kamnyu to Mbarkham), the orientation downstream is always selected, as in ( ex:kWrABzjoz.thWGea ).

exe

tɕe mbarkʰom kɯ-rɤ-βzjoz tʰɯ-ɣe-a, \\
lnk topo sbj: pcp - apass -study aor: downstream -come[II]- 1sg \\
`I came to Mbarkham to study.' (140501 tshering skyid) 0003902#S48
exe

Given the fact that several contradictory constraints are involved in the choice of the riverine vs. solar orientation preverbs, it is not surprising that the orientations chosen to describe motion from one locality to another in the Japhug speaking area is not completely predictable, and that some orientations must be analyzed as having been completely lexicalized (§ sec:lexicalized.orientation ).

The downstream preverbs can be used also for motion into water as in ( ex:chAmtsaR.pjAZGAsat ) and ( ex:tWci.WNgW.schWlAtnW ). They compete in this function with the vertical dimension downwards preverbs (see ex:pjAmtsaR.pjAsi in § sec:vertical.dimension, an example describing the event referred to in ex:chAmtsaR.pjAZGAsat in another version of the same story).

exe

ɕlaʁ ʑo tɯ-ci ɯ-ŋgɯ cʰɤ-mtsʰaʁ tɕe pjɤ-ʑɣɤ-sat. \\
idph (I):immediately emph indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -in ifr: downstream -jump lnk ifr - refl -kill \\
`He immediately jumped into the water to commit suicide and died.' (qajdoskAt 2002) 0003366#S117
exe

exe

βlama nɯra kɯ [...] tsʰɤtʰɤr lu-lɤt-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. tɕe tɯ-ci ɯ-ŋgɯ s-cʰɯ-lɤt-nɯ tɕe, \\
lama dem: pl erg life.release ipfv -release- pl sens -be lnk indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -in tral - ipfv: downstream -release- pl lnk \\
`The lamas perform life release and release [aquatic animals] into the water.' (140510 wugui) 0003951#S14
exe

The upstream preverbs occur to express motion out of the water, as in ( ex:tWci.WNgW.lonWlhoR ).

exe

<wugui> nɯ tɯ-ci ɯ-ŋgɯ lo-nɯ-ɬoʁ \\
turtle dem indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -in ifr: upstream - auto -come.out \\
`The turtle came out of the water.' (elicited, based on a text example)
exe

Metaphorical extensions of the riverine preverbs include the illative/elative functions (§ sec:illative.elative, § sec:orientation.position ), the orientation in the living room (§ sec:orientation.kitchen ), the loom (§ sec:orientation.loom ) and various lexicalized uses (§ sec:preverb.ingestion ).
summary: The passage explains that Japhug uses riverine orientation preverbs even in contexts where the physical slope is not relevant, such as inside houses, and that the choice of orientation can depend on broader path structure rather than simple local direction. Because multiple constraints interact, motion between localities is not fully predictable and some orientations have become lexicalized. It also notes that downstream preverbs are used for motion into water, upstream preverbs for motion out of water, and that these preverbs have further metaphorical extensions in several domains.

text:
orientation!solar dimension
The basic meaning of the eastwards and westwards preverbs, adverbs and locator nouns is to encode the east-west axis. Example ( ex:tCendi.ri.tANe ) for instance shows that the orientation encoded by the distal locative adverb tɕendi is the same as that of the place where the sun sets.

exe

tɯrmɯkʰa ri tɕe tɕendi ri tɤŋe ɯ-sɤ-ɕqʰlɤt pɕoʁ ri tu. \\
dusk loc lnk west loc sun 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -disappear side loc exist: fact \\
`[This star] is found in the west at dusk, at the place where the sun sets.' (29-mWBZi,76)
0003728#S71
exe

The selection of the eastwards and westwards preverbs is observed not only with the orientational adverbs tɕendi, tɕekɯ (§ sec:locative.adv ) and related forms, but also with the borrowed cardinal point ɕɤrpɕoʁeast (from ཤར་ཕྱོགས་ɕar.pʰʲogseast) or descriptive relative clauses meaning `place where the sun sets' or `place where the sun rises' as shown by example ( ex:koCe.YACqhlAt ).

exe

tɯ-rdoʁ nɯnɯ, ɕɤrpɕoʁ ko-ɕe, tɯ-rdoʁ nɯnɯ ʁmbɣi ɯ-sɤ-ɕqʰlɤt nɯtɕu ɲɤ-ɕqʰlɤt. \\
one-piece dem east ifr: east -go one-piece dem sun 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -disappear dem: loc ifr: west -disappear \\
`One [of the feathers] went to the east, another one disappeared in the direction where the sun sets.' (140510 sanpian yumao-zh) 0003947#S16
exe

The westwards orientation is found to express the motion of the sun with both the verbs ɬoʁcome out and ɕqʰlɤtdisappear, as in ( ex:tANe.YAnWlhoR ). Alternatively, the vertical dimension is also used (§ sec:vertical.dimension ).

exe

tɤŋe ɲɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ \\
sun ifr: west - auto -come.out \\
`The sun rose (from the east, towards the west)'. (elicited)
exe

The eastwards orientation is selected to describe trips between localities from west to east, for instance from Kamnyu (32°12'N, 101°57'E) to Sarndzu township (32°09'N, 102°07'E) ( ex:sArndzu.karia ), and the westwards orientation for the return journey.

exe

iʑora tɕe ``sɤrndzu kɤ-ari-a" tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
1pl lnk topo aor: east -go[II]- 1sg ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`We (in Kamnyu) say ``I went (eastwards) to Sarndzu.' (150904 akW andi) 0006372#S21
exe

In locations where the river is oriented on this axis, the solar dimension is dominant and the riverine dimension recessive (§ sec:riverine.dimension ). In Mbarkham city, where the river flows from east to west, the eastwards and westwards preverbs are used for the upstream and downstream directions, respectively. This overlap has caused previous linguists working on Gyalrong languages (in particular Situ) to analyze the solar dimension preverbs and adverbs as encoding the `upstream/downstream' axis (see the discussion in ).

The solar dimension remains dominent even when the path is not parallel to the east-west axis, but oriented southwest-northeast or southeast-northwest. For instance, a journey from Mbarkham to Jinchuan or Danba along the Somang river, which has a clear southwest orientation, the westwards orientation is still preferred over the downstream orientation.

exe

<jinchuan> nɯ-azɣɯt-i ri \\
topo aor: west -arrive- 1pl lnk \\
`When we arrived in Jinchuan...' (2010-1)
exe

The east/west dimension can even be used in the case of far away countries, as between France and China, as shown by the choice of the westwards preverb in ( ex:nArca.YWGia ).

exe

nɤ-rca aʑo kɯnɤ <faguo> ɲɯ-ɣi-a. \\
2sg. poss -following 1sg also France ipfv: west -come- 1sg \\
`I am going with you to France.' (conversation, 2013)
exe

This usage is also found with lɤtrelease in its meaning `phone' (when occurring in collocation with the Chinese noun 电话 diànhuàphone), which takes the orientation eastwards to describe a phone call from France to China, and westwards for the opposite direction.

exe

ɯʑo kɯ (<dianhua>) ku-lɤt ɕti ma, aʑo ɲɯ-lat-a mɤ-kʰɯ tɕe, andi ku-rɤʑi tɕe ɯ-<dianhuahaoma> a-kɤ-ti mɤ-kʰɯ \\
3sg erg phone ipfv: west -release be. aff: fact lnk 1sg ipfv: west -release- 1sg neg -be.possible: fact lnk west ipfv -stay lnk 3sg. poss -phone.number 1sg. poss - inf -say neg -be.possible: fact \\
`It is he who calls [me on the phone], I cannot call him, he lives in the west (in France), I cannot say his phone number.' (conversation, 16-12-28)
exe

The west is the orientation of the mythical countries in traditional stories, as in ( ex:andi.smanmi ). This use probably reflects the geographical location of India as in ( ex:rJAkAr.YWCe ).

exe

andi smɤnmimitoʁkuɕana ɕɯ-nɤʁdan-a ra tɕe, ɲɯ-ɕe-a tɕe, kɤ-ɣe-a tɕe a-pɯ-ŋu \\
west anthr tral -invite: fact - 1sg be.needed: fact lnk ipfv: west -go- 1sg lnk aor: east -come[II]- 1sg lnk irr - ipfv -be \\
`I am going to the west to invite Smanmi Metog Koshana [to our realm], let us do [the wedding] when I come [back].' (smAnmi 2003)
exe

exe

nɯ rɟɤkɤr ɲɯ-ɕe kɯ-ra, \\
dem India ipfv: west -go sbj: pcp -be.needed \\
`That [daughter] has to go to India.' (Gesar)
exe

The eastwards orientation is selected to refer to Hor (Mongolia) in the Japhug version of Gesar, as in ( ex:XwAr.kuCe ).

exe

nɯ χwɤr ku-ɕe kɯ-ra ɕti, \\
dem topo ipfv: east -go sbj: pcp -be.needed be. aff: fact \\
`That [daughter] has to go to Hor.' (Gesar)
exe

There is one case in which the solar dimension preverbs are selected to encode the axis that is perpendicular to the river: to refer to motion toward the opposite bank of the river at the same altitude level (by walking on a bridge, by boat or wading), the eastwards and westwards preverbs are selected, as in ( ex:kWchu.phAri.kAwGtCAt ) and ( ex:nWtCu.kotsWm ). In this context, both orientations are appropriate, and there is no strict rule to choose eastwards or westwards to cross a river, unless the river is oriented north-south and the axis perpendicular to it corresponds to the east-west axis.

exe

qapri nɯ kɯ kɯ-cʰu pʰɤri li kɤ́-wɣ-tɕɤt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
snake dem erg east- approx. loc opposite.bank again aor: east - inv -take.out sens -be \\
`The snake took him to the opposite bank.' (divination 2005)
exe

exe
summary: The passage explains that eastward and westward preverbs, adverbs, and locator nouns primarily encode the east–west solar axis, often referring to the direction of sunrise or sunset. This orientation is used not only for literal movement but also for journeys between places, some river-related contexts, distant countries, phone calls, and mythical places, although in some river settings the upstream/downstream interpretation overlaps with the solar dimension.

text:
kɯ-cʰu pʰɤri nɯtɕu ɯ-wa ko-tsɯm tɕe, \\
east- approx. loc opposite.bank dem. loc 3sg. poss -father ifr: east -take.away lnk \\
`He took his father to the opposite bank of the river.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

The eastwards and westwards preverbs have many other extended uses, in particular to express centripetal/centrifugal directions (§ sec:centripetal.centrifugal ) and meanings further derived from them (§ sec:preverb.loss, § sec:preverb.giving, § sec:vertical.preverbs.time ). In addition, the Sensory ɲɯ- (§ sec:sensory.morphology ) and Egophoric Present ku- (§ sec:egophoric.morphology ) prefixes originate from the B-type westwards and eastwards preverbs, respectively.
summary: The passage gives an example showing the eastwards preverb used in a clause meaning “he took his father to the opposite bank of the river.” It then notes that the eastwards and westwards preverbs have many extended functions, including centripetal and centrifugal direction meanings and further derived senses, and that the Sensory ɲɯ- and Egophoric Present ku- prefixes historically come from the B-type westwards and eastwards preverbs, respectively.

text:
verb!deadverbial derivation!verbalizing deadverbial
Deadverbial verbs of relative location express the position of the subject (in comparison to that of other referents) on one of the three dimensions. These verbs are built by adding the prefix maŋ- to the adverbial stems, as indicated in tab:verbs.location, and their stems are homophonous with the corresponding nouns of relative location (§ sec:relative.location ).

The maŋ- prefix has a function that is similar to that of the denominal mɤ- prefix, which derives verbs of relative location from relator nouns (§ sec:denom.mA ).

Each of the six verbs in tab:verbs.location selects the orientation preverbs corresponding to their own orientation, for instance maŋlobe upstream can only select the upstream orientation, as in shown by ( ex:lumaNlonW ) and ( ex:sAz.lukWmaNlo ). They are not compatible with the indefinite orientation preverbs, and should not be confused with orientable (§ sec:orientable.verbs ) and orienting (§ sec:orienting.verbs ) verbs.

exe

nɯ-<beifen> kɯ-mbro nɯra lu-maŋlo-nɯ, \\
3pl. poss -seniority sbj: pcp -be.high dem. pl ipfv: upstream -be.upstream- pl \\
`The elders [sit] higher (i.e. upstream).' (31-khAjmu) 0004079#S59
exe

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ tɤ-ftsa nɯ tɤ-rpɯ sɤz lu-kɯ-maŋlo mɯ-pjɤ-ŋgrɤl \\
lnk dem indef. poss -ZS dem indef. poss -MB comp ipfv - genr:S/O-be.upstream neg - ifr. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`(In former times) nephews (were not allowed to) be seated higher (i.e. upstream) than their maternal uncles.' (08-saCW) 0003462#S12
exe

These verbs are however compatible with tenses where the orientation preverbs are neutralized, such as the Sensory ɲɯ- as in ( ex:YWtWmaNlo.YWmaNthia ).

exe

nɤʑo ɲɯ-tɯ-maŋlo ɕti ma aʑo ɲɯ-maŋtʰi-a ɕti tɕe, \\
2sg sens -2-be.upstream be. aff: fact lnk 1sg sens -be.downstream- 1sg be. aff: fact lnk \\
`You are upstream and I am downstream.' (2014, lang he yang-zh)
exe

Deadverbial verbs of relative location are either used in comparative sentences ( ex:sAz.lukWmaNlo ), in superlative constructions with stumost (§ sec:stu.superlative ), with contrasting orientations such as ( ex:YWtWmaNlo.YWmaNthia ) or in sentences with an implicit comparison such as ( ex:lumaNlonW ).
summary:
Deadverbial verbs of relative location describe the subject’s position relative to other referents along one of three dimensions, and they are formed by adding the prefix **maŋ-** to adverbial stems whose stems are homophonous with the corresponding nouns of relative location. This prefix functions similarly to the denominal **mɤ-** prefix, which derives verbs of relative location from relator nouns.

Each of the six verbs selects only the orientation preverb matching its own orientation and is incompatible with indefinite orientation preverbs, so they should not be confused with orientable or orienting verbs. They can occur with neutralized orientation tenses such as the Sensory **ɲɯ-** and are used in comparative, superlative, contrasting, or implicitly comparative contexts.

text:
orientation!time
The flow of time can be expressed in Japhug using the vertical dimension, in particular to refer to a following period, as shown by the verb pɯ-ari in ( ex:xiayidai.Wpa.pari ), which is translated as 到了他们的下一代 dào le tāmen de xiàyīdàiin the following generation by Tshendzin in this context (see § sec:G-1 concerning this aspect of the kinship system).

exe

nɯ ɯ-pa pɯ-ari tɕe tɕe, a-wɤmɯ ɯ-ɣe pɯ-nɯ-ŋu, a-sqʰaj ɣɯ ɯ-ɣe pɯ-nɯ-ŋu tɕe aʑo tɤrcɯrca ``a-ɣe" tu-ti-a ɕti. \\
dem 3sg. poss -down aor: down -go[II] lnk lnk 1sg. poss -brother 3sg. poss -grandchild pst. ipfv - auto -be 1sg. poss -sister gen 3sg. poss -grandchild pst. ipfv - auto -be lnk 1sg together 1sg. poss -grandchild ipfv -say- 1sg be. aff: fact \\
`In the [generation] below [that of my nephews], I say a-ɣe `my grandchild' (to all grandnephews), whether they are my brother's grandchildren or my sister's granchildren.' (140425 kWmdza02) 0003786
exe

However, motion verbs in collocations with temporal nouns in the sense of `pass (of time)' select the orientation westwards, as in ( ex:tArZaR.nari ) and ( ex:kAntChWsla.YACqhlAt ). This use could also be a metaphorical extension of the apparent westward motion of the sun in the sky during day time (§ sec:solar.dimension ), or derived from the centrifugal function of the `westward' orientation
(§ sec:centripetal.centrifugal ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-tɯ-sɤ-scit kɯ nɯ tɤ-rʑaʁ nɯ-ari mɯ-pjɤ-tso. \\
lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - prop -be.happy erg dem indef. poss -time aor: west -go[II] neg - ifr -understand \\
`It was so nice there that he did not realize that [a lot of] time had passed.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S273
exe

exe

kɤntɕʰɯ-sla ɲɤ-ɕqʰlɤt ri \\
several-months ifr: west -disappear lnk \\
`Several months passed, but...' (140513 mutong de disheng-zh) 0003977#S11
exe

The semi-transitive verbs mdabe the time and tsupass (of time) however generally select the orientation upwards (see ex:tWsNi.tAtsu and ex:tAtsua in § sec:CN.time ), though the unspecified orientation is also attested for the latter, as in ( ex:XsWxpa.jAtsuj ). The verb mdɯlive up to is used with the downstream orientation preverbs (see ex:chWmdW and ex:chWmdWa, § sec:applicative.t ).

exe

χsɯ-xpa jɤ-tsu-j, \\
three-year aor: unspecified -pass- 1sg \\
`We have been [together] for three years [now], and...' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

For these semi-transitive verbs, the noun phrase referring to a time period is the semi-object, not the subject.
summary: Japhug expresses the flow of time with vertical spatial orientation, especially for future or following periods, as shown by a verb meaning “go down” used in the sense “in the following generation.” By contrast, motion verbs used with temporal nouns meaning “pass (of time)” normally take a westward orientation, possibly linked to the sun’s movement or to a westward centrifugal orientation. Semi-transitive verbs meaning “spend time” or “pass (of time)” generally select an upward orientation, and in these constructions the noun phrase for the time period functions as a semi-object rather than a subject.

text:
orientation!illative
A common extended function of the riverine dimension preverbs is to express motion through an opening. The upstream preverbs can have an illative meaning, describing motion into a building or a natural cave (through a door, a window or any other opening) as in ( ex:praRkhaN.WNgW.loCe ), ( ex:WNgW.lAGindZi ) and ( ex:kWm.losthoR ).

exe

praʁkʰaŋ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu lo-ɕe ɲɯ-ŋu tɕeri \\
cave 3sg. poss -in dem: loc ifr: upstream -go sens -be lnk \\
`He went into the cave.' (140425 shizi huli he lu-zh)
exe

exe

kʰa ɯ-ŋgɯ lɤ-ɣi-ndʑi tɕe, \\
house 3sg. poss -in imp: upstream -come- du lnk \\
`Come inside the house.' (140507 tangguowu-zh) 0003933#S87
exe

The combination of the upstream orientation with stʰoʁpush in ( ex:kWm.losthoR ) means `push (the door) towards the inside of the house'.

exe

spjaŋkɯ nɯ kɯ kɯm lo-stʰoʁ tɕe, ɯ-ŋgɯ lo-ɕe. \\
wolf dem erg door ifr: upstream -push lnk 3sg. poss -in ifr: upstream -go \\
`The wolf pushed the door open and went in.' (140428 xiaohongmao-zh)
0003884#S76
exe

The opposite downstream orientation preverbs have an elative meaning, expressing motion out of a building, as in ( ex:WpCi.chAlhoR ).

exe

kʰa ɯ-pɕi cʰɤ-ɬoʁ. \\
house 3sg. poss -outside ifr: downstream -come.out \\
`She came out of the house.' (140428 xiaohongmao-zh) 0003884#S27
exe

However, in the case of tubular or pipe-like objects like the trunk of a musket, the orientation is the opposite: the downstream preverbs are used for motion toward the inside ( ex:qandZi.chWrkunW ), and the upstream preverbs occur for motion towards the outside ( ex:qandZi.luBde ).

exe

ɕɤmɯɣdɯ ɯ-lɤcu ɯ-mŋu ri qandʑi cʰɯ-rku-nɯ \\
musket 3sg. poss -upstream 3sg. poss -opening loc bullet ipfv: downstream -put.in- pl \\
`They load the bullet into the [barrel] of the musket from the opening [the muzzle]' (28-CAmWGdW) 0003712#S37
exe

exe

nɯnɯ mɯzi nɯ tu-nɯt tɕe tɕe qandʑi nɯ lu-βde tɕe ju-ɕe ɲɯ-ŋu \\
dem gunpowder dem ipfv -burn lnk lnk bullet dem ipfv: upstream -throw lnk ipfv: unspecified -go sens -be \\
`The gunpowder flares and drives the bullet out (of the barrel of the muzzle).' (28-CAmWGdW)
0003712#S103
exe

Likewise, the upstream preverbs occur to express motion out of a sheath, as in ( ex:scapa.loXCoR ).

exe

scapa lo-χɕoʁ \\
sword ifr: upstream -take.out \\
`He unsheathed his sword.' (140514 huishuohua de niao-zh) 0003992#S166
exe

The same applies with containers having a small (and tubular) opening, like bags or bottles for instance. The downstream orientation preverbs have the illative meaning `go/put into' and the upstream preverbs the elative meaning `come out of/take out of' as illustrated by ( ex:tAfkWm.WNgW.chArku ) and ( ex:phoN.WNgW.thWwGrkua ). By extension, the verb ɣɤmɯtblow (for instance, into a pipe) also selects the downstream preverbs (§ sec:preverb.speech ).

exe

tɕendɤre ``tɤ-fkɯm ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕe tʰɯ-ɕe ɲɯ-ntsʰi wo" to-ti. tɕendɤre <dongguoxiansheng> nɯ kɯ iɕqʰa tɤ-fkɯm ɯ-ŋgɯ jɯɣi nɯra tsuku lo-tɕɤt, [...] spjaŋkɯ nɯ nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ cʰɤ-rku. \\
lnk indef. poss -bag 3sg. poss -in loc imp: downstream -go sens -be.better sfp ifr -say lnk anthr dem erg the.aforementioned indef. poss -bag 3sg. poss -in book dem: pl some ifr: upstream -take.out wolf dem dem 3sg. poss -in ifr: downstream -put.in \\
`Mr. Dongguo said: `Why don't you go into the bag [to hide]', took out some of the books from the bag, and put the wolf into it.' (150901 dongguo xiansheng he lang-zh)
0006336#S45
exe

exe

<suoluomen> nɯ kɯ aʑo kɯki pʰoŋ ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕe tʰɯ́-wɣ-rku-a ŋu,\\
anthr dem erg 1sg dem. prox bottle 3sg. poss -in loc aor: downstream - inv -put.in- 1sg be: fact \\
`Solomon put me in this bottle.' (140512 yufu yu mogui-zh)
0003973#S73
exe

In the case of boxes with large openings on the top, the riverine orientation preverbs are not used, and the vertical dimensions preverbs occur instead: the downwards preverbs express motion into the box, as in ( ex:rgAm.WNgW.pjArku ), and the upwards preverbs motion out of it, as shown by example ( ex:rgAm.WNgW.totCAt ).

exe

mar-rgɤm ɯ-ŋgɯ zɯ χwɤr ra ɣɯ nɯ-rɟɤβlun tʰamtɕɤt ɣɯ nɯ-ku nɯ pjɤ-rku \\
butter-box 3sg. poss -in loc topo pl gen 3pl. poss -ministers all gen 3pl. poss -head dem tral - ifr: down -put.in \\
`He had put the heads of all the ministers of Hor in a butter box.' (gesar)
exe

exe

ɯ-sloχpɯn nɯ kɯ rgɤm ɯ-ŋgɯ zɯ, nɤkinɯ, χɕɤlmdoŋ ci to-tɕɤt tɕe ɲɤ-mbi \\
3sg. poss -teacher dem erg box 3sg. poss -in loc filler spyglass indef ifr: up -take.out lnk ifr -give \\
`His teacher took a spyglass from a box and gave it to him.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S72
exe

The westwards preverbs are selected in the case of an object passing through a hole with openings on both sides, for instance a needle's eye, as in ( ex:taqaB.Wrna.YWwGrRe ).

exe

taqaβ nɯ ɯ-rna ri spoʁ tɕe, tɕe nɯtɕu tɤ-ri ɲɯ́-wɣ-rʁe, \\
needle dem 3sg. poss -ear loc have.a.hole: fact lnk lnk dem: loc indef. poss -thread ipfv: west - inv -pass.through \\
`The needle has an eye at its tip, and one passes the thread though it.' (12-kAtsxWb) 0003486#S29
exe

The orientation eastwards can be used for motion into a small cavity whose opening is as large as the inside and is located on the side, as shown by examples ( ex:Wndzri.WNgW.koCe ) and ( ex:Wrna.WNgW.koCe ).

exe

nɯŋa ɯ-ndʐi tʰɯ-kɤ-rɤɣdɯt ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu ko-ɕe. \\
cow 3sg. poss -skin ipfv - obj: pcp -distend 3sg. poss -in dem: loc ifr: east -go \\
`He went into the distended hide of the cow.' (31-deluge)
0004077#S25
exe

exe

nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rna ɯ-ŋgɯ xɕelwi ko-ɕe ɲɯ-ŋu \\
dem gen 3sg. poss -ear 3sg. poss -in tick ifr: east -go sens -be \\
`A tick went into his ear.' (kAndZislama 2003)
exe

The eastwards orientation also occurs for piercing motion into a surface (like skin), as in ( ex:WNgW.kari ) (see also ex:fsapaR.ra.kW.nAsAGdWGnW, § sec:tropative.other.derivations ).

exe
summary: The passage describes how riverine orientation preverbs encode spatial motion, especially through openings. Upstream preverbs typically mark illative motion into buildings, caves, sheaths, bags, bottles, and similar containers, while downstream preverbs mark elative motion out of them; however, tubular objects like gun barrels reverse this pattern, and other dimensions or directions are used for boxes, holes, side openings, and piercing motions when the riverine system does not apply.

text:
tɯ-ɕa ɯ-ŋgɯ kɤ-ari qʰe, koŋla ɯ-ŋgɯ ʑo ku-ɕe ɕti. \\
indef. poss -flesh 3sg. poss -in aor: east -go[II] lnk completely 3sg. poss -in emph ipfv: east -go be. aff: fact \\
`When [its thorn] goes into the flesh, it penetrates completely.' (17-xCAj)
0003528#S66
exe

The data above show that no orientation preverb intrinsically encodes illative or elative meaning in Japhug. The interpretations `towards the inside' or `towards the outside' depend on the shape of the object and the location and the relative size of the opening.
summary: The data indicate that Japhug orientation preverbs do not themselves encode illative or elative meaning. Instead, whether an event is interpreted as moving “into” or “out of” something depends on the shape of the object, the location of the opening, and their relative size.

text:
orientation!centripetal
In Gyalrong languages, the westwards and eastwards preverbs in some cases express centrifugal vs. centripetal directions, respectively. This phenomenon was first noticed in Situ by.

Example ( ex:WpCi.YACthWz.WNgW.koCthWz ) This example is very freely translated from ……把羊毛朝外面翻出来 bǎ yángmáo cháo wàimiàn fānchūláihe turned over the jacket so that the sheep fur was on the outside. Given the distance from the original, there is no suspicion of calque from Chinese here. illustrates this extension of the solar dimension with the verb ɕtʰɯzturn towards (§ sec:orienting.verbs ): the orientation towards the subject of the verb (centripetal) is expressed by the eastwards preverb ( ko-ɕtʰɯz ), and the opposite orientation away from the subject (centrifugal) is encoded by the westwards preverb ( ɲɤ-ɕtʰɯz ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-rme nɯ ɯ-pɕi ɲɤ-ɕtʰɯz, ɯ-ndʐi nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ ko-ɕtʰɯz tɕe tɕe to-ŋga. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -hair dem 3sg. poss -outside ifr: west -turn.towards 3sg. poss -skin dem 3sg. poss -in ifr: east -turn.towards lnk lnk ifr -wear \\
`He turned the fur [of the jacket]$_i$ towards the outside, and the leather towards the inside and wore it$_i$.' (140513 mutong de disheng-zh)
0003977#S52
exe

The centrifugal use of the westwards preverbs has been further lexicalized and extended to verbs expressing loss or transfer of property (§ sec:preverb.loss, § sec:preverb.giving ) and passing of time (§ sec:vertical.preverbs.time ).

The centripetal use of the eastwards preverbs also accounts for the presence of the eastwards preverbs with verbs meaning `close', `wrap up' or `fold'. Compare for instance the eastwards preverb on wumgather (in the meaning `fold wings') with the westwards one on qɤtseparate in ( ex:YWqAt.nA.kuwum ).

exe

tɤ-mbri ɯ-kʰɯkʰa ɯ-ʁar nɯ kɯra ntsɯ tu-ste ŋu ma jɯ-kɯ-nɯqambɯmbjom tɤ-kɯ-rɤŋgat nɯ kɯ-fse, ɯ-ʁar nɯ ɲɯ-qɤt nɤ ku-wum [...] ŋu \\

`When it sings, it does this with its wings, as if it is about to fly, it [repeatedly] spreads its wings and then folds them back.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S109

A separate use of the solar dimension preverbs is to express alternation between left and right motion, with two verbs either linked by nɤ as in ( ex:kuCe.nA.YWGi ) or in paratactic relation as in ( ex:korACinW.YArACinW ) and ( ex:komJA.YomJa ). In this function, the eastwards preverbs occur on the first verb and the westwards preverbs on the second one.

exe

pjɤ-ɣɤrɤt tɕe ɯ-rɟit ra kɯ ko-rɤɕi-nɯ ɲɤ-rɤɕi-nɯ ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu \\

`She threw them$_i$ down there, and her children tore them$_i$ apart (pulled them$_i$ right and left in a disorderly way).' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S349
exe

exe

lɯlu nɯ kɯ ci ko-mɟa, ci ɲo-mɟa tɕe \\
cat dem erg one ifr: east -grab one ifr: west -grab lnk \\
`The cat grabbed one from his left and one from his right.' (lWlu 2002)
0003361#S78
exe

With the deictic motion verbs, the eastwards - westwards alternation also occurs between ɕego and ɣicome as shown by ( ex:kuCe.nA.YWGi ). Since in this construction the motion verb with translocative deixis always takes the eastwards preverbs, while the one with cislocative deixis is found with the westwards preverbs, it is not possible to argue that these preverbs here have centripetal vs. centrifugal functions as in this case the deixis of the preverbs would contradict that of the motion verb.

exe

ɟiga ki kɯ-fse ku-ɕe nɤ ɲɯ-ɣi, ku-ɕe nɤ ɲɯ-ɣi, \\
zigzag dem sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv: east -go add ipfv: west -come ipfv: east -go add ipfv: west -come \\
`The zigzags go left and right.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S37
