summary: In Gyalrong languages, westwards and eastwards preverbs sometimes mark centrifugal versus centripetal direction, with eastwards forms indicating movement toward the subject and westwards forms movement away from it. This use has been extended to verbs of loss, transfer, time, and actions like closing, wrapping, and folding, but in other constructions the same preverbs simply alternate to express left-right motion, so they cannot always be analyzed as centripetal versus centrifugal.

text:
traditional houses
In the traditional living room ( kʰɤjmu ), the seating places around the hearth and the tripod ( sqʰi ) have specific names and functions: kʰɤɕkʰɤr for the men, kʰɤdi for the lady (in charge of preparing the meal), ɕaŋlo for elderly ladies This noun is related to the egressive postposition ɕaŋloupstream from (§ sec:egressive ). and saŋdi for servants and for putting firewood. The use of the riverine and solar dimension preverbs, adverbs and locative nouns in the living room is unrelated to the cardinal east-west axis or the direction of the mountain slope, and is rather completely determined by these conventional seating places, as explained in ( ex:khAjmu.orientation ), and summarized in fig:kitchen.

exe

kʰɤdi nɯnɯ tɕe atʰi tu-ti-nɯ. ɕaŋlo nɯ tɕe alo tu-ti-nɯ,
kʰɤɕkʰɤr nɯ tɕe kutɕu pɕoʁ pɯ-nɯ-ŋu, kutɕu pɕoʁ pɯ-nɯ-ŋu,
tɕekɯ tu-ti-nɯ. tɕe ``nɤʑo tɕekɯ kɤ-nɯ-ɕe" nɯra tu-ti-nɯ. \\
lady.seating.place dem lnk downstream ipfv -say- pl elder.lady.seating.place dem lnk upstream ipfv -say- pl man.seating.place dem lnk here side pst. ipfv - auto -be here side pst. ipfv - auto -be eastwards ipfv -say- pl lnk 1sg eastwards imp: east - auto -go dem: pl ipfv -say- pl \\
`For the seating of the ladies, they say downstream, for that of the elder ladies they say upstream, for that of the men, whether it is here or here, they say eastwards, they say `go over there eastwards '. (31-khAjmu)
0004079#S53
exe

The preverbs corresponding to the orientation indicated in fig:kitchen are always selected when the goal of the motion is one of the seating places in the living room, for instance eastwards in ( ex:khACkhAr.tCu.kuCenW ) or westwards in ( ex:saNdi.nWtCu.YWtanW ).

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ pɯ-nɯ-xtɕi-nɯ pɯ-nɯ-wxti-nɯ tɕe kʰɤɕkʰɤr tɕu ku-ɕe-nɯ. \\
indef. poss -son dem pst. ipfv - auto -be.small- pl pst. ipfv - auto -be.big- pl lnk men.seating.place loc ipfv: east -go- pl \\
`Men, whether they are young or older, go to the men's eastward seating place.' (31-khAjmu)
0004079#S49
exe

exe

saŋdi nɯtɕu si ɲɯ-ta-nɯ \\
seating.place dem: loc wood ipfv: west -put- pl \\
`They put the firewood on the westward seating place (that is opposite the men's eastward seating place).' (31-khAjmu) 0004079#S36
exe
summary: In the traditional living room, the seating places around the hearth and tripod have fixed names and roles: the men’s place, the lady’s place for meal preparation, the elder ladies’ place, and the servants’ place for firewood. The use of riverine and solar orientation terms in this space is not based on cardinal directions or slope direction, but is entirely determined by these conventional seating positions.

text:
weaving loom
The riverine dimension is metaphorically extended to refer to the axis of the warp threads in the loom. The downstream orientation corresponds to the end of the warp closer to the weaver (where Tshendzin 's hands are located in fig:loom1 ), and the upstream orientation to the opposite end, where the threads are attached.

The downstream preverbs are required on all verbs expressing motion towards the lower side, for instance to express the tamping of the intersections between the threads (using the tool called tʰaʁmu, which is located between upper and lower warp threads to maintain them apart from each other in fig:loom1 ) towards the waist of the weaver, as in ( ex:thari.chWGnda ).

exe

ɯ-sqar nɯ tʰɯ-ari tɕe tɕe, nɤki, kɯki tú-wɣ-stu tɕe cʰɯ́-wɣ-ɣnda. \\
3sg. poss -intersection.of.warp.threads dem aor: downstream -go[II] lnk lnk filler dem. prox ipfv - inv -do.like lnk ipfv: downstream - inv -tamp \\
`As the intersection of the [upper and lower] warp threads goes down, one does this to tamp it down.' (vid-20140429090403) 0003776#S57
exe

The axis that is perpendicular to that of the warp threads and parallel to the ground, through which the weft is inserted (the action depicted in fig:loom1 ), is described using the solar dimension, as shown by the selection of the westwards preverb in ( ex:tWjlAB.YWwGrRe ).

exe

ɯ-taʁ cʰo ɯ-pa ɣɯ ɯ-ʁjar ni pjɯ-ɤqɤtʂʰa-ndʑi, nɯtɕu tɯ-jlɤβ ɲɯ́-wɣ-rʁe tɕe \\
3sg. poss -top comit 3sg. poss -bottom gen 3sg. poss -warp du ipfv -be.crossed- du dem. loc indef. poss -weft ipfv: west - inv -insert lnk \\
`The upper and lower warp threads are crossed, and at [the crossing place] one inserts the weft.' (additional explanation provided while transcribing the video from which fig:loom1 is taken).
exe

The vertical dimension preverbs refer to the third axis that is perpendicular with the two previous ones, with the downwards orientation towards the ground. The upwards preverbs occur to describe the lifting of the warp threads using the heddles, as in ( ex:Cnat.kW.tuwGsWjoR ).

exe

ɕnat kɯ tɤ-ri ra tɕe nɯ kɯ tú-wɣ-sɯ-joʁ tɕe,\\
heddle erg indef. poss -thread pl lnk dem erg ipfv: up - inv - caus -raise lnk \\
`One lifts the [warp] threads with the heddles.' (2011-06-thaXtsa)
exe
summary: The passage explains how spatial preverbs are mapped metaphorically onto the axes of a weaving loom. The riverine dimension is used for the warp thread axis, with downstream referring to the end near the weaver and upstream to the opposite end, while the solar dimension describes the perpendicular weft-insertion axis, using a westwards preverb. A vertical dimension is also used for the third axis, with upwards preverbs marking actions such as lifting the warp threads with heddles and downwards preverbs marking motion toward the ground.

text: A complete description of the lexicalized orientation preverbs in Japhug would require a monograph-length treatment taking into account all verbs, basic and derived, and including complex predicates. In order to keep this chapter within a reasonable size, I therefore only focus on a few selected semantic categories comprising the most common non-orientable verbs of the language.
summary: A full description of lexicalized orientation preverbs in Japhug would require a monograph-length study covering all basic and derived verbs, as well as complex predicates. To keep the chapter manageable, the author limits the discussion to a selection of semantic categories, focusing on the most common non-orientable verbs in the language.

subsubsection: Spatial use of preverbs with non-orientable verbs
text:
While non-orientable verbs generally select only one or two orientations (§ sec:lexicalized.orientation ), orientation preverbs that are different from the lexical ones can occur in specific contexts to indicate either a motion event linked with the action of the verb (normally with an additional associated motion prefix, § sec:orientation.AM ), the motion of a body part or the position of the body.

The intransitive verb cɯhibernate provides an interesting example of this use of the preverbs. The lexically selected orientation of this verb is eastwards (like other verbs from the same semantic category), as shown by the preverb ku- in ( ex:qartsW.tCe.kucW ).

exe

qartsɯ tɕe ku-cɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
winter loc ipfv -hibernate sens -be \\
`In winter, [the bear] hibernates.' (21-pri) 0003580#S49
exe

However, the orientations upstream and upwards are also attested with this verb, with more specific readings. The upstream orientation is found in ( ex:praRpa.WNgW.lucW ) and also in ( ex:luCe.tCe.lucW ) above, § sec:am.prefixes, and expresses hibernation in a cave. These examples reflect the illative use of the upstream preverbs (§ sec:illative.elative ). The upwards orientation, also shown by ( ex:praRpa.WNgW.lucW ), is used when hibernation takes place in a hollow tree, with vertical motion up the tree (§ sec:vertical.dimension ).

exe

tɕe qartsɯ tɕe nɯnɯ si kʰoŋrɤl tɤ-kɯ-ɤri nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯmaʁ tu-cɯ,
nɯmaʁnɤ, praʁpa ɯ-ŋgɯ lu-ɕe tɕe lu-cɯ. \\
lnk winter loc dem wood hollow.tree aor: up - sbj: pcp -go[II] dem 3sg. poss -in otherwise ipfv: up -hibernate otherwise cave 3sg. poss -in ipfv: upstream -go lnk ipfv: upstream -hibernate \\
`In winter, it either hibernates in a hollow tree, or goes into a cave and hibernates (there).' (21-pri)
0003580#S100
exe

The forms with upstream and upwards preverbs often occur with either motion verbs or associated motion prefixes, as in ( ex:si.WNgW.tAkWso.WNgW.CtucW ).

exe

si ɯ-ngɯ tɤ-kɯ-so, ɯ-ŋgɯ tɤ-kɯ-rom, nɯnɯ pjɯ-saχsi tɕe, nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ ɕ-tu-cɯ ɲɯ-ŋu.\\
wood 3sg. poss -in ipfv: up - sbj: pcp -be.hollow 3sg. poss -in ipfv: up - sbj: pcp -be.dried dem ipfv -do.completely lnk dem 3sg. poss -in tral - ipfv: up -hibernate sens -be \\
`Trees whose inside is hollow, whose inside is dried out, [the bear] hollows it completely, goes up [the hole] and hibernates there.' (21-pri) 0003580#S53
exe

The use of preverbs to express spatial position or motion as in the case of the upstream and upwards orientations with cɯhibernate above are not unusual with non-orientable verbs, but are lexicalized, and restricted to highly specific and well-identified situations. Only orientations that are pragmatically and culturally plausible and compatible with the speaker's knowledge of the world can be used: with cɯhibernate for instance, the other series of orientation preverbs ( downwards, downstream, westwards ) are not attested. It is not possible to predict which non-orientable verb will be compatible with the spatial use of preverbs, and this information has to be specified in dictionaries in a systematic way. The following sections (§ sec:preverb.ingestion to § sec:preverb.cover ) present a series of examples of similar phenomena.
summary: Although non-orientable verbs usually select only one or two orientations, different orientation preverbs can appear in special contexts to express motion related to the event, motion of a body part, or body position. The verb cɯhibernate normally takes the eastward preverb, but upstream and upwards forms occur in specific, lexicalized situations: hibernating in a cave or in a hollow tree. Such uses are restricted to culturally and pragmatically plausible contexts, are not predictable, and must be recorded in dictionaries.

text:
A handful of labile verbs select different preverbs and have slightly different meanings in their transitive and intransitive/semi-transitive uses.

The verb sɤŋolisten takes the westwards preverbs when semi-transitive, and the eastwards preverbs when transitive with the meaning `listen to, obey' (§ sec:semi.tr.labile ).

The verb sɯsothink is normally transitive and selects the westwards preverbs. It can also occurs with the downwards preverbs, but in this case it is intransitive, and means `in $X$'s opinion' (§ sec:labile.tr-intr ).
summary: A few labile verbs use different preverbs and have slightly different meanings depending on whether they are transitive or intransitive/semi-transitive. For example, sɤŋolisten takes westwards preverbs when semi-transitive, but eastwards preverbs when transitive with the meaning ‘listen to, obey.’ Similarly, sɯsothink is usually transitive with westwards preverbs, but with downwards preverbs it is intransitive and means ‘in X’s opinion.’

text:
Motion from one locality to another is nearly always expressed using the vertical, riverine and solar dimensions in their basic spatial functions (§ sec:vertical.dimension, § sec:riverine.dimension and § sec:solar.dimension, respectively). While in some cases there are conflicts between several possible orientations, especially between the riverine and the solar preverbs, the choice of the preverbs is nearly always motivated.

However, there are also cases where the choice of the preverbs is unrelated to the actual spatial orientation of the trip from one particular place to another. For instance, Kamnyu kɤmɲɯ ( 32° 12′ 43″ N, 101° 57′ 42″ E ) is located to the west of Mengi mɯŋi ( 32° 12′ 32″ N, 102° 0′ 14″ E, 蒙岩 ).

However, the preverbs corresponding to orientations that are exactly opposite to the geographical orientations are used between these two villages: the orientation westwards is used for motion from Kamnyu to Mengi (to describe a trip from west to east), and eastwards from Mengi to Kamnyu (whereas the actual trip is from east to west), as shown by ( ex:kAmYW.mWNi ) and ( ex:mWNi.YWsAxCe ).

exe

kɤmɲɯ tɕe tɕe mɯŋi kɤ-ɕe tɤ-ra tɕe, ``mɯŋi ɲɯ-ɕe-a" tu-kɯ-ti ŋu.
tɕe mɯŋi tɕe kɤmɲɯ nɯ tɕe tɕe, nɤki, ``kɤmɲɯ kɤ-ɣe-a, kɤmɲɯ ku-ɕe-a ŋu" nɯra tu-ti-nɯ. \\
topo loc lnk topo inf -go aor -be.needed lnk topo ipfv: west -go- 1sg ipfv - genr:S/O-say be: fact lnk topo loc topo dem lnk lnk filler topo aor: east -come[II]- 1sg pl.n ipfv: east -go- 1sg be: fact dem: pl ipfv -say- pl \\
`When one has to go from Kamnyu to Mengi, one says `I am going (westwards) to Mengi, and from Mengi to Kamnyu, people say `I came (eastwards) to Kamnyu, I am going (eastwards) to Kamnyu.' (150904 akW andi)
0006372#S6
exe

exe

mɯŋi ɲɯ-sɤx-ɕe tʂu nɯnɯre ri, \\
topo ipfv: west - obl: pcp -go path dem: loc loc \\
`On the road (from Kamnyu) towards Mengi...' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S2
exe

This contradiction is clear in example ( ex:akW.mWNi ), where Mengi is explicitly described as being located on the akɯ (east) side of Kamnyu.

exe

akɯ pɕoʁ nɯ mɯŋi ŋu, andi pɕoʁ praʁwɯ ŋu. \\
east side dem topo be: fact west side topo be: fact \\
`Mengi is in the east, and Praqwu (a small locality in Kamnyu) is in the west.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S21
exe

Ercha village (in Japhug ɣɟɯ tsʰapa, most often called using its Chinese name 二茶村 èrchácūn, 32° 13′ 10″ N, 101° 55′ 55″ E ),

located to the west of Kamnyu, also presents orientation inversion: as shown by ( ex:erchacun.kukWCe ), the eastwards preverbs are used for trips from Kamnyu to Ercha, and the westwards preverbs for the opposite trip. This fact has been rechecked with several speakers (note in particular the anecdote reported in § sec:MBChCh.Dpalcan ).

In ( ex:erchacun.kukWCe ) Tshendzin hesitates: she was about to say ɲɯ-kɯ-ɕe with a westwards preverb (the expected form, based on the geographical location of these localities), followed by the correct ku-kɯ-ɕe with the irregular orientation.

exe

tɕe kɤmɲɯ tɕe tɕe <erchacun> ɲɯ-kɯ... ku-kɯ-ɕe tɕe tɕe, nɯnɯ ``ku-ɕe-a" tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. <erchacun> tɕe kɤmɲɯ a-nɯ-ɣi-nɯ tɕe nɯ `kɤmɲɯ nɯ-ari-a, kɤmɲɯ nɯ-ɣe-a" nɯra tu-ti-nɯ ŋu. \\
lnk topo loc lnk topo ipfv: east - genr:S/O-go lnk lnk dem ipfv: east -go- 1sg ipfv - genr:S/O-say be: fact topo loc topo irr - pfv: west -come- pl lnk dem topo aor: west -go[II]- 1sg topo aor: west -come[II]- 1sg dem: pl ipfv -say- pl be: fact \\
`When one goes from Kamnyu to Erchacun, one says `I go (eastwards)', and when people come to Kamnyu from Erchacun, they says `I went, I came (westwards).'
(150904 akW andi)
0006372#S9
exe

This puzzling irregularity has not been observed for other toponyms, especially those located further away from Kamnyu. For instance, the upstream orientation is used for trips to Tshobdun and Zbu, the downstream orientation to Mbarkham (§ sec:riverine.dimension ) and the eastwards orientation to Sarndzu and Tatshi (§ sec:solar.dimension ).
summary: Motion between localities is usually expressed with preverbs whose vertical, riverine, or solar orientation matches the actual direction of travel, though there can be some competition between riverine and solar forms. In a few cases, however, the preverb choice is inverted relative to geography: between Kamnyu and Mengi, and between Kamnyu and Ercha, speakers use east/west forms opposite to the real directions of travel. This irregularity is noted as unusual and has not been observed with other, more distant toponyms.

text:
The most common verb of ingestion, ndzaeat, generally selects the upwards preverbs, as shown for instance by ( ex:chWnWtsWm.Ctundze ) (in § sec:AM.goal ) and ( ex:nWtCu.Ctundze ) (in § sec:nature.of.motion.AM ). The same is true of verbs derived from it, such as the compound verb rɯndzɤtsʰihave a meal (§ sec:denom.compound.verbs ), as shown by ( ex:ri.CtArWndzAtshij ) in § sec:AM.goal, and of other more specialized verbs of food ingestion such as moʁeat (powdery food), nɯtɕʰaʁeat fodder (of horses), nɯtʂʰɤɣndʑɤreat a tsampa meal, zmɤrɤβeat (mixing with) or χsɤleat (honorific).

The downstream preverbs can occur with ndzaeat to refer to eating by wild beasts and birds of prey, as in ( ex:kWrtsAG.nW.kW.chWndze ), probably due to the fact that this orientation is also selected by ɕkɯteat/drink completely, a verb which can also describe the actions of ferocious animals as in example ( ex:khu.kW.thaCkWt ) in § sec:obviation.animacy. See also the discussion on the use of the downstream orientation with tsʰidrink below, above example ex:cha.ntsW.chWtshi ).

exe

kɯrtsɤɣ nɯ kɯ, nɤki, tɯrme ra ɣɯ nɯ-fsapaʁ nɯ cʰɯ-ndze, [...] qaʑo tsʰɤt nɯ cʰɯ-ndze pjɤ-ŋu, \\
leopard dem erg filler people pl gen 3pl. poss -animal dem ipfv: downstream -eat[III] sheep goat dem ipfv: downstream -eat[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The snow leopard was eating farm animals, eating...., sheep and goats.' (qala kWCqraR 2002)
exe

This orientation is also attested to describe the eating of earth by earthworm as in ( ex:qandzxe.nW.kW.chWndze ), though in this case the preverb is used spatially (§ sec:orientation.position ), reflecting the burrowing motion of the earthworm (§ sec:illative.elative ).

exe

tɕeri qandʐe kɯ tʰɤlwa ʁɟa cʰɯ-ndze ɲɯ-ɕti. \\
lnk earthworm erg earth completely ipfv: downstream -eat[III] sens -be. aff \\
`The earthworm only eats earth.' (25-akWzgumba)
0003632#S115
exe

The eastwards orientation is exclusively attested with ndza to describe eclipses, as in ( ex:mWkarCo.mACtsxa.kundze ), also a spatial use of the preverbs (expressing motion from the left side to the right side or vice-versa, § sec:centripetal.centrifugal ).

exe

ɯ-rkɯ kɯ-fse ku-ʑe tɕe, mɯ-kɤ-arɕo mɤɕtʂa ku-ndze ɣɤʑu, \\
3sg. poss -side sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv: east -being[III] lnk neg - aor: east -be.finished until ipfv: east -eat[III] exist: sens \\
`Sometimes [the eclipse] starts on one side, and `eats' [the moon] until it [disappears] completely.' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S138
exe

The orientation westwards occurs with verbs referring to animals eating grass, such as the intransitive verb nɯrɯeat grass as in ( ex:YWnWrWnW ) and its synonym nɯsɤlɤɣ.

exe

nɯŋa qʰe qaʑo tsʰɤt nɯra pjɤ-dɤn-nɯ tɕe, nɯtɕu ɲɯ-nɯrɯ-nɯ tɕe sɯjno tu-ndza-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu, \\
cow lnk sheep goat dem: pl ifr. ipfv -be.many- pl lnk dem: loc ipfv: west -eat.grass- pl lnk grass ipfv: up -eat- pl ifr. ipfv -be \\
`There were many cows, sheep and goats, and they were eating grass there.' (150819 woniu-zh)
0006254#S8
exe

Verbs related to the ingestion of liquids select the eastwards preverbs as default, as in ( ex:konWkhWG.Zo.kotshi ), including the deideophonic nɯkʰɯɣgulp (§ sec:nW.deidph ).

exe

tɯ-ci ko-nɯkʰɯɣ ʑo ko-tsʰi. \\
indef. poss -water ifr: east -gulp emph ifr: east -drink \\
`He gulped the water.' (140429 jiedi-zh)
exe

The verb tsʰidrink is also found with the downwards orientation to refer to drinking with the head down on the grounds (like animals, or from a jar with a straw), for instance in ( ex:GWpjWnWtshinW ) and ( ex:CpjAnWtshi ) in § sec:am.prefixes and ( ex:WtAlu ) in § sec:alienabilization. The denominal verb nɯcidrink from the ground also selects this orientation.

The downstream preverbs occur with this verb in two contexts. First, following the basic spatial meaning of these preverbs (`direction of the flow of water', § sec:riverine.dimension ), they can be used to insist on the flow of liquid through the oesophagus during ingestion, as in ( ex:tWci.chWtshi ).

exe

tɯ-ci kɯnɤ cʰɯ-ɕe mɯ-ɲɤ-kʰɯ. tɯ-ci cʰɯ-tsʰi mɯ-ɲɤ-kʰɯ \\
indef. poss -water also ipfv: downstream -go neg - ifr -be.possible indef. poss -water ipfv: downstream -drink neg - ifr -be.possible \\
`Even water could not go [down his throat], he could not drink anymore.' (of a person suffering from throat cancer) (27-tWfCAl) 0003710#S87
exe

Second, the downstream orientation is found to express excessive alcohol drinking, as in ( ex:cha.ntsW.chWtshi ), possibly by analogy with ɕkɯteat/drink completely which also takes this orientation (see also the discussion concerning example ex:kWrtsAG.nW.kW.chWndze above).

exe

ɯ-wa nɯ kɯ cʰa ntsɯ cʰɯ-tsʰi qʰe, ɯ-me mɯ́j-nɯβdaʁ \\
3sg. poss -father dem erg alcohol always ipfv: downstream -drink lnk 3sg. poss -daughter neg: sens -take.care \\
`Her father was drinking alcohol all the time, and did not take care of his daughter.' (17-lhazgron)
exe

The downstream preverbs are also selected by the denominal verb nɯcʰɤmdadrink with a straw (example ex:chWwGnWchAmdaj, § sec:svc ), probably reflecting the illative (through tubular opening) function of the downstream preverb (§ sec:illative.elative ). It is noteworthy that tsʰidrink takes the downwards orientation instead when referring to drinking from a straw.

The upstream preverbs occur with the verb χɤβ, which can mean `drink until the last drop in one gulp', or `breathe in, suck up, draw up' as in ( ex:WsnWro.luXAB ), a special case of the illative (through large opening) function of this orientation (§ sec:illative.elative; note that the illative is expressed with the opposite orientation as that of nɯcʰɤmdadrink with a straw, due to the difference of the shape of the opening).

exe

ɯ-sŋɯro lu-χɤβ ʑo tɕe nɯ βɣɤza nɯ ɯ-kɯr ɯ-ŋgɯ lu-nɯ-ɕe ɕti \\
3sg. poss -breath ipfv: upstream -suck emph dem lnk fly dem 3sg. poss -mouth 3sg. poss -in ipfv: upstream - auto -go be. aff: fact \\
`[The frog]$_i$ breathes in and the fly goes into its$_i$ mouth by itself.' (27-qaCpa)
0003716#S7
exe
summary:
The passage describes how different ingestion verbs in the language systematically select particular directional preverbs. The common verb for eating, ndza, and related verbs generally take upward preverbs, but downstream, eastward, and westward orientations appear in more specialized contexts, such as eating by wild animals, eclipses, animals eating grass, and liquid ingestion.  

For drinking, eastward preverbs are the default, while downstream and downward orientations occur with meanings such as drinking with the head down, drinking through the throat, drinking excessively, or drinking through a straw; upstream preverbs are used with a verb meaning ‘drink until the last drop’ or ‘suck up, draw in.’

text:
Adjectival verbs describing size, like other stative verbs, become dynamic verbs (`become X') in the Imperfective (§ sec:imperfective ), the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis ), the Aorist (§ sec:aor.inchoative ) and the Inferential (§ sec:ifr ). The most neutral orientation preverbs for these verbs are indicated in tab:size.adj.preverbs. Most positive adjectival verbs select the upwards orientation, except for those describing radial size ( jpumbe thick, rɟumbe broad) which are found with the westwards orientation, and those expressing length (see below).

It is much more difficult to ascertain the lexically selected orientation of negative adjectival verbs, since the situations in which their use as dynamic verbs is appropriate (`become small(er)', `become short(er)') are less common. The downwards orientation does occur as lexically selected orientation (with xtɕibe small and mbɤrbe low), resulting in forms that are homophonous with the Past Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv ). Perhaps due to this homophony, the westwards orientation is also used instead with xtɕibe small, as in ( ex:WCGa.anWxtCi ).

exe

ki ɯ-ʁɤri sɯstaʁ ʑo ɯ-ɕɣa a-nɯ-xtɕi ra \\
dem. prox 3sg. poss -before comp emph 3sg. poss -age irr - pfv: west -small be.needed: fact \\
`May she become younger than before!' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

In addition to the orientations in Table ( tab:size.adj.preverbs ), the downstream preverbs can occur to express a progressive increase (§ sec:orientation.preverb.aspect ). Compare for instance the use of wxtibe big with the upwards orientation in ( ex:Wkha.towxti ) with that in ( ex:ZWrWZAri.chAwxti ) with the downstream orientation, describing a process taking place progressively over many years.

exe

mɤʑɯ ʑo ɯ-kʰa ra to-wxti tɕe, \\
even.more emph 3sg. poss -house pl ifr: up -be.big lnk \\
`His house had become even bigger.' (140430 yufu he tade qizi-zh)
0003900#S212
exe

exe

tɕeri ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ ʑɯrɯʑɤri cʰɤ-wxti \\
lnk 3sg. poss -son dem progressively ifr: downstream -be.big \\
`His son progressively grew up.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S10
exe

Some of these verbs are compatible with more than one orientation. For instance, rɲɟibe long is attested with the upwards orientation to refer to the length of a vertical object, as in ( ex:turYJi.mAcha ) (where it is synonymous with mbrobe high). With the upstream preverbs, it describes for instance (elongated) fruits or leaves growing out of the branch of a plant, as in ( ex:lurYJi.tsa.Nu ).

exe

tɕe <yimi> jamar ma tu-rɲɟi mɤ-cʰa ma \\
lnk one.meter about apart.from ipfv: up -be.long neg -can: fact lnk \\
`It cannot grow longer than about one meter.' (11-qarGW)
0003480#S98
exe

exe

tɯrgi ɣɯ ɯ-mat lu-rɲɟi tsa ŋu tɕe, nɤki jima popo tsa fse. \\
fir gen 3sg. poss -fruit ipfv: upstream -be.long a.little be: fact lnk filler maize cob a.little be.like: fact \\
`The fir cone is elongated, a bit like the corncob (07-tAtho)
0003432#S28
exe

The downstream preverbs are found to express progressive increase (example ex:ZWrWZAri.chAwxti, § sec:redp.gradual.increase, § sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ), as in ( ex:chWxtWt.Nu ), but can also refer to the growth of thread-like objects like hair, as in ( ex:tWkArme.chWrYi ). Note in this example that rɤɕipull shares the same preverb to refer to the pulling of hairs.

exe

ɕɤr nɯ cʰɯ-rɲɟi, sŋi nɯ cʰɯ-xtɯt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
night dem ipfv: downstream -be.long day dem ipfv: downstream -be.short sens -be \\
`The nights are becoming longer, and the days shorter.' (elicited)
exe

exe

pɯ-kɯ-xtɕi tɕe, nɯnɯ ʑŋgri nɯ nɯ-mɤrʑaβ ɯ-raŋ tɕe, tɯ-kɤrme cʰɯ́-wɣ-rɤɕi tɕe, cʰɯ-rɲɟi ŋu to-ti-nɯ tɕe,\\
pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-be.small lnk dem star dem aor -marry 3sg. poss -time lnk genr. poss -hair ipfv: downstream - inv -pull lnk ipfv: downstream -be.long be: fact ifr -say- pl lnk \\
`When we were young, people said that when there is a shooting star, if you pull your hair, it will grow longer.' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S93
exe
summary: Adjectival verbs of size behave like other stative verbs by becoming dynamic “become X” verbs in the Imperfective, Irrealis, Aorist, and Inferential, with most positive forms selecting an upwards orientation, though radial-size and some length terms show other orientations. Negative size adjectives are harder to classify, but some select downwards orientation while others use westwards, possibly to avoid homophony with Past Imperfective forms. The downstream preverbs can additionally mark progressive increase, and some verbs allow more than one orientation depending on the object or meaning involved.

subsubsection: Verbs related to growth, gain or birth
text:
Adjectival verbs of size can be used to express growth (§ sec:preverb.adjectives.size ), but another constructions expressing the same meaning involves the transitive verb βzumake with a dummy subject (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), and an adjectival verb in participial form (§ sec:subject.participles ), as in ( ex:kWmbWmbro.tuBze ), with the upwards orientation (compare with ex:turYJi.mAcha above and ex:YWwGzmaqhu in § sec:obviation.animacy ).

exe

ɕɤɣ nɯ li kɯ-mbɯ mbro tu-βze cʰa \\
juniper dem again sbj: pcp - emph be.high ipfv: up -make[III] can: fact \\
`The juniper grows very high.' (08-CAG) 0003442#S1
exe

The upstream orientation appears to describe fruits or leaves growing out of a plant, as in ( ex:tWrgi.laNlaN.laBzu ) (compare with ex:lurYJi.tsa.Nu above).

exe

tɯrgi laŋlaŋ nɯnɯ, la-βzu ɕimɯma nɯ ɲɯ-ɤrŋi, \\
fir cone dem aor: upstream:3 -make immediately dem sens -be.green \\
`The fir cone is green when it has just come out.' (08-tWrgi) 0003464#S67
exe

The downstream orientation is found with long and thin thread-like objects, like the stalks of some plants as in ( ex:Wru.chWBze ) (compare with ex:tWkArme.chWrYi ), but also occur to refer to fruits or grains ( ex:Wmat.kWfse.chWBze ), probably as an extension of the progressive incrementation function of this orientation ( ex:ZWrWZAri.chAwxti above, § sec:preverb.adjectives.size ).

exe

ɯ-ru ra kɯ-xtsʰɯ xtsʰɯm ŋu ri, kɯ-zɯ zri ʑo cʰɯ-βze qʰe, \\
3sg. poss -stalk pl sbj: pcp - emph be.thin be: fact lnk sbj: pcp - emph be.long emph ipfv: downstream -make[III] lnk \\
`Although its stalk is very thin, it grows very long.' (19-qachGa mWntoR)
0003546#S66
exe

exe

sɯŋgɯpɤjka nɯ ɯ-mat nɯnɯ pɤjka kɯ-fse cʰɯ-βze, \\
wild.squash dem 3sg. poss -fruit dem squash sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv: downstream -make[III] \\
`Wild squash grows fruits like those of the [cultivated] squash.' (16-CWrNgo)
0003518#S37
exe

The intransitive verb ndzɤtgrow also selects the upwards orientation to describe the growth of a plant, and the downstream preverbs for children, as in ( ex:tApAtso.chondzAt ).

exe

tɤ-pɤtso cʰo-ndzɤt \\
indef. poss -child ifr: downstream -grow \\
`The child grew up.' (elicited)
exe

For growth in quantity rather than size, the upwards orientation is selected, for instance with the verb dɤnbe many in ( ex:tAdAnnW2 ).

exe

tʰam tɕe mɤʑɯ tɤ-dɤn-nɯ \\
now lnk even.more aor: up -be.many- pl \\
`Now they are even more numerous than before.' (140522 tshupa) 0004053#S84
exe

The upwards orientation is also selected by verbs expressing birth and coming into existence such as tuexist in ( ex:ci.totu ) and ( ex:tWci.paRea ) (note that its antonym menot exist rather selects the westwards orientation, § sec:preverb.loss ), and verbs of Tibetan origin such as scibe born ( ex:WtCW.tosci ) and the honorific mkʰroŋbe reincarnated ( ex:GWtomkhroN ).

exe

ndʑi-tɕɯ ci to-tu \\
3du. poss -son indef ifr: up -exist \\
`They had one son.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

exe

ɯ-tɕɯ to-sci ɕi, ɯ-me to-sci? \\
3sg. poss -son ifr -be.born qu 3sg. poss -girl ifr -be.born \\
`Did she have a boy or a girl?' (elicited)
exe

exe

nɯʑora nɯ-ɕki ɣɯ-to-mkʰroŋ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
2pl 2pl. poss - dat cisl - ifr: up -be.born sens -be \\
`He had come to be born in their [family].' (150825 nezha naohai-zh) 0006272#S35
exe

The downstream orientation however occurs with verbs expressing humans or animals giving birth, such as the intransitive denominal verbs rɤpɯhave young, rɤŋgɯmlay eggs and rɤrɟithave a child (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ) and the light verb lɤtrelease in the meaning `give birth to' in ( ex:thWrApW.chWlAt ). This may be an extension of the elative function of the downstream preverbs (§ sec:illative.elative ).

exe

tsʰɤt nɯ tʰɯ-rɤpɯ tɕe, ʁnɯz ntsɯ cʰɯ-lɤt ŋgrɤl \\
goat dem aor: downstream -have.young lnk two always ipfv: downstream -release be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`When goats have young, they give birth to two [kids] at a time.' (05-qaZo)
0003404#S6
exe

exe

tɯ-ji ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯra cʰɯ-rɤŋgɯm ŋgrɤl \\
indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -in dem: pl ipfv: downstream -lay.eggs be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`It lays eggs in the fields.' (24-kWmu) 0003618#S80
exe

Verbs expressing gain select the downwards orientation, including the orientable verb mɟatake (§ sec:manipulation.verbs ) when used in the meaning `obtain, get' (example ex:pjWGmJa.ma.mWpWkWcha in § sec:antipassive.t ), βɟɤtobtain (§ sec:antipassive.t ), mtosee (which can mean `find' especially when used with the autive prefix, see § sec:preverb.perception and § sec:autoben.spontaneous ) as well as the semi-transitive aʁehave to eat/drink This verb can be translated into Chinese as 吃到 chīdàohave to eat or 喝到 hēdàohave to drink. as in ( ex:tWci.paRea ).

exe

a-kɯr ɯ-ŋgɯ tɯ-ci pɯ-aʁe-a tɕe, a-sroʁ to-tu \\
1sg. poss -mouth 3sg. poss -in indef. poss -water aor: down -be.needed.eat- 1sg lnk 1sg. poss -life ifr: up -exist \\
`I have water in my mouth to drink, my life is back.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe
summary: The passage describes how different orientational preverbs and verbal constructions are used to express growth, emergence, and increase. Upwards orientation is associated with growth in size or quantity, plant growth, birth, and coming into existence, while downstream orientation is linked to growth in length, the appearance of fruits or leaves, children or animals giving birth, and expressions of gain or obtaining.

subsubsection: Verbs related to loss or death
text:
Verbs expressing loss, with meanings such as `disappear' or `lose' generally select the orientation westwards, probably as an extension of its centrifugal use (§ sec:centripetal.centrifugal ). For instance, the verb βdethrow, which can also be interpreted as meaning `lose' when used non-volitionally (especially with the autive § sec:autoben.lexicalized ), selects this orientation, as shown by ( ex:Wrte.YAnWBde ), even though the loss of the hat (in the pear story movie) involved a motion downwards.

exe

tɕe ɯ-rte ra ɲɤ-nɯ-βde tɕe, \\
lnk 3sg. poss -hat pl ifr: west - auto -lose lnk \\
`[The boy] lost his hat' (Pear story 2010, Tshendzin, 12)
exe

The same is observed with the verb menot exist in ( ex:mtshu.YAme ), here also despite a clear downward motion of the water level until the lake disappears.

exe

mtsʰu nɯ cʰɯmcʰɯm ʑo, tɕe, tɯ-skɤm pjɤ-sɤʑa tɕe mtsʰu nɯ ɲɤ-me tɕe \\
lake dem idph (II):slowly emph lnk inf:II-dry.up ifr: down -start lnk lake dem ifr: west -not.exist lnk \\
`The level of the lake started to go down slowly and the lake disappeared.' (nyima2003)
exe

Verb expressing partial disappearance, such as rkɯnbe few in ( ex:si.YWYArkWn ), also occur with the westwards orientation.

exe

zgoku nɯtɕu si nɯ ʑɯrɯʑɤri ɲɯ ɲɤ-rkɯn ʑo \\
mountain dem: loc tree dem progressively incr ifr: west -be.few emph \\
`There were fewer and fewer trees on the mountain.' (04-xiaocunzhuang-zh) 0003394#S24
exe

The verb ɕqʰlɤtdisappear, also semantically related to these verbs, is an orientable motion verb (§ sec:motion.verbs ). It does not usually select the westwards orientation in a non-spatial way, except for the express the passing of time (§ sec:vertical.preverbs.time ). In example ( ex:tANe.YWCqhlAt ), there is however some ambiguity as to whether the westwards orientation is purely spatial (the setting of the sun in the west, see § sec:solar.dimension; note that the vertical dimension is more commonly selected, § sec:vertical.dimension ), or whether it could also be analyzed as centripetal.

exe

tɤŋe nɯ ɲɯ-ɕqʰlɤt ku-nɤjɤm ra kʰi ma tɤŋe nɯ wuma ʑo nɯɣ-me kʰi. \\
sun dem ipfv: west -disappear ipfv -wait[III] be.needed: fact hearsay lnk sun dem really emph appl -be.afraid[III]: fact hearsay \\
`[The yeti] waits for the sun to disappear [before eating the man he has caught], because he fears the sun, it is said.' (140510 mYWrgAt)
0003941#S7
exe

It is possible that the centripetal function of the westwards orientation has originated from a metaphoric extension of the disappearance of the sun in the west at dusk, in which examples like ( ex:tANe.YWCqhlAt ) would be the pivot construction allowing reanalysis from a purely spatial marker to a more abstract meaning such as `away from the deictic center' or `loss'.

Verbs expressing a more abstract type of disappearance, such as the cognition verb jmɯtforget (memory loss), likewise select the westwards prefixes, as in ɲɤ-nɯ-jmɯt-a ifr: west - auto -forget- 1sg `I forgot (about it)' (see ex:mAxsi.YAnWjmWta, § sec:1.genr ).

The verb menot exist has another set of forms with the upwards orientation, as in ( ex:si.tAme ). With the upwards vertical preverbs, this verb does not entail the presupposition that loss occurred; in the perfective, the tɤ-me with upwards orientation means `when there this no X' (a usage found with other stative verbs, § sec:orientation.preverb.aspect ), while nɯ-me with westwards orientation can only be interpreted as `(when) X disappeared/was lost'.

exe

nɯ ma si tɤ-me tɕe li nɯ ɲɯ-pʰɯt-nɯ\\
dem apart.from wood aor: up -not.exist lnk again dem ipfv -take.out- pl \\
`When there is no other wood than this, people cut it.' (07-Zmbri)
0003438#S59
exe

As in many languages (for instance Indo-European *mer, ), me in the meaning `disappear' is commonly used as a euphemism for passing away, as in ( ex:WXti.YAme ).

exe

ɯʑo ɯ-χti ɲɤ-me tɕe, \\
3sg 3sg. poss -companion ifr: west -not.exist lnk \\
`Her husband passed away.' (12-BzaNsa) 0003484#S111
exe

Likewise, verbs expressing death and destruction, such as sidie and χɕaʁpass away (a borrowing from གཤེགས་gɕegsgo away), plɯtdestroy, ndʑɯɣbe destroyed select the westwards orientation, as shown by ( ex:tongo.YAsi ), ( ex:WrGi.nWplWti ) and ( ex:Ctusci.YWNu ) further below (in § sec:nature.of.motion.AM ).

exe

βdaʁmu nɯ to-ngo tɕe ɲɤ-si. \\
lady dem ifr -be.ill lnk ifr: west -die \\
`The lady became ill and died.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

exe

jima ɯ-rɣi nɯ-plɯt-i \\
maize 3sg. poss -grain aor: west -destroy- 1pl \\
`We have used up all the maize grains.' (elicited)
exe

The verb sidie alternatively also occur with the downwards preverbs, in particular in the case of animals as in ( ex:nWNGarmW.pjAsi ). With humans, using the downwards preverbs is not rude, but considered to be blunter than with the westwards' preverbs.

exe

tɕetu ʑara nɯ-ɴɢarmɯ nɯ pjɤ-si kʰi tɕe, \\
up.there 3pl 3pl. poss -hybrid.cow dem ifr: down -die hearsay lnk \\
`Those up there, their cow died, it is said.' (Tagrdo conversation, 2003)
exe

The transitive verb satkill also selects the downwards orientation preverbs, even when taking an associated motion prefix and an overt goal pointing to an orientation other than downwards, as in ( ex:pGAtCW.CpWsatnW ).

exe

atu pɣɤtɕɯ nɯ ɕ-pɯ-sat-nɯ ra \\
up.there bird dem tral - imp: down -kill- pl be.needed: fact \\
`Go and kill the bird up there.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

Likewise, ntɕʰakill, butcher (on whose etymology see ) occurs with the downwards preverbs in the meaning `kill (an animal)', as shown by ( ex:nWNa.pjAnWnWntChanW ).

exe

tɕe nɯ-nɯŋa pjɤ-nɯ-ntɕʰa-nɯ \\
lnk 3pl. poss -cow ifr: down - auto -butcher- pl \\
`They killed their cow (for themselves to eat).' (02-deluge2012) 0003376#S16
exe

The orientation westwards also occurs with this verb in the meaning `butcher', as illustrated by ( ex:natChanW.tutCAtnW ) and ( ex:YWtChanW ). On the other hand, satkill is not found with the westwards preverbs.

exe
summary: Verbs of loss, disappearance, forgetting, death, and destruction generally select the westwards orientation, which seems to extend from a centrifugal use. The passage notes that this holds even when the relevant event involves downward motion, as with verbs like βde ‘lose’ and me ‘not exist,’ while me with westwards orientation specifically implies actual disappearance or loss, unlike its upwards forms. Some verbs, such as sidie ‘die,’ can also occur with downwards preverbs, and transitive killing verbs like sa ‘kill’ and ntɕʰa ‘butcher’ select downwards orientation, though ntɕʰa can also occur with westwards in the sense ‘butcher.’

subsubsection: Verbs related to loss or death
text:
fsapaʁ ɯ-ŋgru pɯ-nɯ-ŋu, rɯdaʁ ɯ-ŋgru pɯ-nɯ-ŋu, nɯnɯ na-ntɕʰa-nɯ tɕe tu-tɕɤt-nɯ tɕe tɕe tu-sɯɣ-rom-nɯ. \\
farm.animals 3sg. poss -sinew pst. ipfv - auto -be 3sg. poss -sinew wild.animals pst. ipfv - auto -be dem aor: west:3 -butcher- pl lnk ipfv: up -take.out- pl lnk lnk ipfv - caus -be.dry- pl \\
`Whether it is sinew$_i$ from a farm or a wild animal,$_j$ after they butcher them,$_j$ they take it$_i$ out and dry it$_i$.' (150906 tWNgru) 0006304#S5
exe

exe

nɯnɯ pa-sat-nɯ tɕe tɕe ju-nɯ-ɣɯt-nɯ tɕe ɲɯ-ntɕʰa-nɯ \\
dem aor: down:3 -kill- pl lnk lnk ipfv - vert -bring- pl lnk ipfv: west -butcher- pl \\
`After [the hunters] have killed [the animals]$_i$, they bring them$_i$ home and butcher them$_i$.' (150829 KAGWcAno) 0006420#S17
exe
summary: The passage illustrates a sequence of actions involving animals or animal products: after killing or butchering them, people bring them home, take out the sinew, and dry it. It also shows the same referents being tracked across clauses with pronominal marking, referring to either farm or wild animals.

text:
Verbs of speech mainly select either the orientation upwards ( tisay, rɯɕmispeak, arjuspeak, see for instance ex:tWkArme.chWrYi in § sec:preverb.adjectives.size and ex:WCki.turWCmia in § sec:intr.goal; their etymology is discussed in § sec:denom.a and § tab:denom.rA.intr ), with the exception of fɕɤttell (borrowed from བཤད་bɕadtell), which occurs with the downwards preverbs (see the Inferential pjɤ-fɕɤt ifr: down -tell `she told it' in ex:WsAfCAt, § sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ). The intransitive verb mbrimake a sound, used for animals or objects, is also found with the upwards preverbs (see to-mbri ifr: up -make.noise in ex:tAkWmbri.kWme, § sec:subject.participle.other.relative )

The intransitive denominal verb nɯrɤɣosing (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ) on the other hand appears with the orientation downstream, as in ( ex:chWnWrAGo ), and this applies to transitive verbs taking the base noun rɤɣosong as objects (such as cʰɯ-tɯ-ʑa and cʰɯ-ti in ex:chWtinW.tochanW ).

exe

qartsʰi nɯ sŋi tɕe cʰɯ-nɯrɤɣo nɤ cʰɯ-nɯrɤɣo ŋu tɕe \\
cicada dem day loc ipfv: downstream -sing add ipfv: downstream -sing be: fact lnk \\
`The cicada [was] singing all day long. (26-NalitCaRmbWm)
0003676#S29
exe

exe

nɯnɯ rɤɣo cʰɯ-tɯ-ʑa qʰe, tɤrcɯrca ʑo cʰɯ-ti-nɯ to-cʰa-nɯ. \\
dem song ipfv: downstream - conv: imm -start lnk together emph ipfv: downstream -say ifr -can- pl \\
`They became able to sing along as soon as it started its song.' (140519 yeying-zh)
0004040#S148
exe

The choice of the downstream preverbs on verbs related to songs and music is probably an analogical extension of its use with verbs related to wind instruments, as in ( ex:Juli.chAlAt ) and ( ex:rdAdWt.chWZmbrinW ) (see also ex:Juli.chWlAtnW, § sec:genr.3pl ).

exe

ɟuli nɯ cʰɤ-lɤt. \\
flute dem ifr: downstream -release \\
`He played the flute' (140513 mutong de disheng-zh) 0003977#S77
exe

exe

nɯnɯra kɯ rkɤdɯt cʰɯ-ʑ-mbri-nɯ pjɤ-mtsʰɤm. \\
dem: pl erg horn ipfv: downstream - caus -make.noise- pl ifr -hear \\
`She heard [the hunters] blowing the horn.' (140520 ye tiane-zh) 0004044#S234
exe

The downstream preverbs on verbs of this type itself derives from their use with ɣɤmɯtblow as in ( ex:WlAcu.chWwGGAmWt ), itself an extension of their illative meaning (`into a tubular object', see § sec:illative.elative ).

exe

ɯ-lɤcu cʰɯ́-wɣ-ɣɤmɯt tɕe tɯ-rtsʰɤz nɯ ɲɯ-fka ŋu \\
3sg. poss -upstream ipfv: downstream - inv -blow lnk indef. poss -lung dem sens -be.full be: fact \\

summary:
The passage says that most verbs of speech take upward-oriented preverbs, with the exception of **fɕɤt** ‘tell,’ which instead occurs with downward preverbs. The intransitive verb **mbri** ‘make a sound’ also appears with upward preverbs, while the denominal verb **nɯrɤɣo** ‘sing’ and related transitive verbs take downward preverbs.  

It further suggests that the downward preverbs used with singing and music verbs are probably an analogical extension from verbs involving wind instruments, and that this usage ultimately derives from the verb **ɣɤmɯt** ‘blow,’ which itself has an illative sense of movement into a tubular object.

text:
With the exception of the orientable verb rulook at (§ sec:orienting.verbs ), most verbs of perception generally select only one orientation. The downwards preverbs are selected by the non-volitional verbs mtosee and mtsʰɤm, which generally means `hear', but is also used for all non-visual non-volitional perception, including olfaction (example ex:nWdi.tunAmnAm, § sec:tropative.lexicalized ), touch and the perception of vibrations as in ( ex:NGoCna.nWkW.pjWmtshAm ).

exe

ɲɯ-mɯnmu nɤ ɲɯ-mɯnmu tɕe tɕe, nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ ɴɢoɕna kɯ-rɤʑi nɯ kɯ pjɯ-mtsʰɤm tɕe \\
ipfv -move add ipfv -move lnk lnk dem 3sg. poss -in spider sbj: pcp -stay dem erg ipfv: down -feel lnk \\
`[The fly that has been caught in the spider's web] moves and moves, and the spider inside feels it.' (26-mYaRmtsaR)
0003674#S58
exe

The other verbs each have a different orientation: the semi-transitive sɤŋolisten selects the westwards preverbs (§ sec:orientation.lability, § sec:semi.tr.labile ), and the tropative verb nɤmnɤmsmell (§ sec:tropative.lexicalized ) the upwards preverbs (examples ex:nWdi.tunAmnAm and ex:tutanAmnAm, § sec:tropative.lexicalized ). This orientation simply reflects that of the base intransitive verb mnɤmsmell.
summary: Most verbs of perception select a single orientation, with the exception of the orientable verb *rulook at*. Downwards preverbs are used with the non-volitional verbs *mtosee* and *mtsʰɤm*, the latter covering hearing as well as other non-visual, non-volitional perceptions such as smell, touch, and vibrations. Other perception verbs have their own orientations: *sɤŋolisten* takes westwards preverbs, and *nɤmnɤmsmell* takes upwards preverbs, reflecting the orientation of its intransitive base verb *mnɤmsmell*.

text:
Ditransitive verbs expressing permanent or temporary transfer of property, including mbigive, kʰogive, `pass over', rŋoborrow and nɤŋgɯborrow (and verbs derived from these), have different argument structures (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective and § sec:ditransitive.secundative ), but most of them select the westwards preverbs as default orientation, perhaps reflecting the centripetal function of this orientation (§ sec:centripetal.centrifugal ), as in English `give away' or `give out'.

For instance, the most common Inferential 3 forms of these verbs are ɲɤ-mbi, ɲɤ-mbi, ɲɤ-rŋo and ɲɤ-nɤŋgɯ (examples are plentiful elsewhere in this grammar, for instance ex:nArZaB.YWkhotCi in § sec:essive.abs, ex:zYArNo and ex:nWwGkhoa in § sec:ditransitive.indirective and ex:WCki.YAkho and ex:nWCki.zYArNo in § sec:dative ).

However, it is alternatively possible to choose a prefix reflecting the spatial direction of the transfer of property. In ( ex:pWwGmbia ), we find thus a downwards orientation preverb to describe a present (downwards) from heaven, and in ( ex:Wphe.tokho ) an upwards preverb expresses the relative vertical position of the recipient and the subject: the latter being on the ground, while the former rides a tiger, the transfer of property involves a motion upwards.

exe

tɯmɯkɯmpɕi kɯ pɯ́-wɣ-mbi-a ŋu \\
heaven erg aor: down - inv -give be: fact \\
`The heavens gave it to me.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

exe

laʁjɯɣ nɯ ɯ-taʁ nɯ ɯ-pʰe to-kʰo tɕe, \\
staff dem 3sg. poss -on dem 3sg. poss - dat ifr: up -give lnk \\
`He gave the staff to the [thief] who was on [the tiger].' (khu2012)
0004085#S15
exe

The downwards orientation can also be used more metaphorically to express gift from someone higher up in the social hierarchy, as in ( ex:piaozi.pWwGmbij ).

exe

taʁ kɯ, <piaozi> pɯ́-wɣ-mbi-j. \\
up erg money aor: down - inv -give- 1pl \\
`The ones above (i.e. the government) gave us money.' (2010-09)
exe

The riverine axis is also metaphorically use to express relative social status with the verb kʰogive, `pass over'. The downstream preverbs express transfer of property from someone higher in the hierarchy (in particular, nobles or lamas) to someone lower than himself. For instance in ( ex:laftaR.chAtWkhonW ), the subject of cʰɤ-tɯ-kʰo-nɯ `you gave it to her' is a prince, and the recipient an unknown girl; note that the downstream preverb co-occurs here with the honorific plural (§ sec:honorific.indexation ), another linguistic clue to the social status of the subject.

exe

nɯtɕu zɯ laftaʁ cʰɤ-tɯ-kʰo-nɯ tɕe, nɯnɯ nɯ-jɯm nɯ ɕɯ-ɕar-i ra \\
dem: loc loc token ipfv: downstream -2-give- pl lnk dem 3pl. poss -wife.of.lama dem tral -look.for: fact - 1pl be.needed: fact \\
`[Since] you have given her a token, we will go and look for (this woman, who is to be) your wife.' (sras 2003)
exe

The opposite upstream orientation is found to express gift from someone lower in the hierarchy to an important person. In particular, it is the orientation selected by the honorific verb pʰɯloffer, which is borrowed from ཕུལ་pʰuloffer.
summary: Ditransitive verbs of giving, borrowing, and related transfer meanings have different argument structures, but most default to westward preverbs, likely because this orientation has a centripetal function. However, speakers can also choose preverbs that match the spatial direction of transfer, such as downward or upward forms. These directional preverbs are also extended metaphorically to signal social hierarchy: downward or downstream forms mark transfer from higher-status figures to lower ones, while upward forms mark transfer from lower-status people to important recipients, including the honorific verb for “offer.”

text:
The verb fkaβcover occurs with both the downwards and downstream preverbs. The former are selected when the covering action involves a downwards motion (as in ex:pjWGi.tCe.pjWfkaB ), or when describing the feeling of being completely covered by a roof ( ex:pjWkWfkaB ) or by the sky.

exe
