summary:
The verb **fkaβ** ‘cover’ combines with different preverbs depending on the kind of covering action. The **downward** preverb is used for covering involving downward motion or complete enclosure from above, while the **downstream** preverb is used for covering by growing or building; an **eastward** preverb can also mark complete covering, including the top and sides, even when the action is physically downward.

The verb **mpʰɯr** ‘wrap’ likewise takes different preverbs with different meanings: **eastward** for wrapping something inside, **upward** for binding up a wound, and **downstream** for wrapping into a roll.

text:
associated motion
An associated motion marker, following Guillaume's ( guillaume16am) definition, is `a grammatical morpheme that is associated with the verb and that has among its possible functions the coding of translational motion.' This definition excludes both motion verbs, which are not morphologically tied to the verb stem in the purposive construction (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation, § sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ) and orientation preverbs (§ sec:orientation.preverbs ), which do not express translational motion (of the whole body) by themselves in Japhug, though they can indicate in specific cases the direction of gestures involving the motion of a body part (§ sec:orienting.verbs ).
summary: An associated motion marker is a grammatical morpheme linked to the verb that can code translational motion. Under Guillaume’s definition, this excludes motion verbs, since they are not morphologically attached to the verb stem in the purposive construction, and orientation preverbs, since they do not by themselves express translational motion of the whole body in Japhug.

text:
prefix!associated motion
Unlike Arandic ( and ) and Tacanan  languages, Japhug and other Gyalrong languages have simpler AM systems with only two prefixes, andative/translocative and venitive/cislocative as illustrated by examples ( ex:GWpjWnWtshinW ) and ( ex:CpjAnWtshi ), respectively.

exe

tɕe tɯ-ci ɣɯ-pjɯ-nɯ-tsʰi-nɯ \\
lnk indef. poss -water cisl - ipfv - auto -drink- pl \\
`[The wild yaks] come and drink water.' (20-RmbroN) 0003560#S43
exe

exe

tɕe tɯ-ci ɕ-pjɤ-nɯ-tsʰi. \\
lnk indef. poss -water tral - ifr - auto -drink \\
`She went [there] and drank water.' (140428 mu e guniang-zh) 0003880#S66
exe

AM prefixes in Japhug and other Gyalrong languages refer to a motion event occurring before the action of the main verb, resulting in a prior temporal relation with respect to the main verb, as in ( ex:GWpjWnWtshinW ) and ( ex:CpjAnWtshi ). There are no AM markers for subsequent or concurrent motion.

tab:am-gyalrong presents the forms of AM prefixes in all four Gyalrong languages (; data from,,,,, ).

As shown by the close phonetic resemblance between the motion verbs and the corresponding AM prefixes, there is little doubt that the latter have been grammaticalized from the former, Exceptions however include the cislocative ɟɐ- in Bragbar Situ, whose origin is not straightforward, and the case of Zbu, where the motion verb xwéʔ is unrelated to the AM prefix. probably through a paratactic or serial verb construction in which motion verbs occurred in direct contact with the lexical verb without intervening linker.

Although attested, as in (§ sec:toCe.tonWrRWrRa ), parataxis is rare in Japhug. It can also found when the second verbs takes an AM marker (see ex:GWYWsloR, § sec:AM.echo ). The preferred order is to-nɯrʁɯrʁa to-ɕe, and despite the absence of pause, to-nɯrʁɯrʁa here is an afterthought.

exe

tɕendɤre tɕetu zgo kɯ-mbɯ mbro mɤɕtʂa to-ɕe, to-nɯrʁɯrʁa. \\
lnk up.there mountain sbj: pcp - emph be.high until ifr: up -go ifr: up -climb \\
`He went up there, climbing the very high mountain.' (150825 huluwa-zh) 0006346#S151
exe

Usually, when a motion verb is followed by or follows another verb, a linker such as tɕe almost always occurs between them, as in ( ex:luCe.tCe.lucW ).

exe

praʁpa ɯ-ŋgɯ lu-ɕe tɕe lu-cɯ. \\
cave 3sg. poss -inside ipfv: upstream -go lnk ipfv: upstream -hibernate \\
`(Otherwise), [the bear] goes into a cave and hibernates [there].' (21-pri)
0003580#S101
exe

The grammaticalization of motion verbs to AM prefixes, from a construction similar to that in (§ sec:toCe.tonWrRWrRa ), occurred in the common ancestor of all Gyalrong languages, rather than independently in each language, as is shown by the fact that the transitive verb `to bring, to fetch' (Japhug ru, Bragbar Situ ró / rô ) shares a common irregularity in all languages: it must appear with an associated motion prefix. In examples (§ sec:CtAruta ) and (§ sec:rECAroN ) from Japhug and Situ removing the AM prefix would result in incorrect forms (§ sec:ru.fetch ).

exe

ɕ -tɤ-ru-t-a \\
transl - aor: up -bring- pst: tr -1 sg \\
`I fetched it.' (Japhug)

rə- ɕɐ -rô-ŋ \\
aor: up - transl -bring[II]-1 sg \\
`I fetched it.' (Situ)
exe

In the Japhug verbal template, AM prefixes occupy slot -4, just after modal and negative prefixes (§ sec:prefixal.chain ), but before orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs, see also ( ex:GWpjWnWtshinW ) and ( ex:CpjAnWtshi ) above) unlike in Situ, where AM occur closer to the verb stem than the orientation preverbs (as shown by § sec:rECAroN ).

The translocative and cislocative prefixes however may not be equally ancient. There is no doubt that the translocative prefix can be reconstructed to proto-Gyalrong, because in addition to the irregular verb `fetch', it does not superficially resemble the verb `to go' in Situ and Zbu (see tab:am-gyalrong ) and therefore cannot have been recently grammaticalized. This idea is supported by the high allomorphy of this prefix (§ sec:translocative.morpho ). The only language with a translocative prefix that is not cognate with the rest of Gyalrong is the Cogtse dialect of Situ, where the prefix j- originates from the indefinite orientation preverb (Japhug jɤ- ), replacing the inherited prefix.

The cislocative prefix on the other hand lacks any allomorphy, and its initial consonant is identical to that of the verb `come' (with its main vowel either converted to a schwa or identical to that of the verb stem in the case of Cogtse) in almost all languages including Tshobdun (where o- comes from *wə, the reduced form of wî `come'), the only possible exception being the Bragbar dialect of Situ. It is therefore possible that each Gyalrong language has independently innovated a cislocative prefix from its verb `come' after the breaking up of proto-Gyalrong, and that the proto-Gyalrong only had one AM prefix with neutral deixis. The introduction of a cislocative AM affix grammaticalized from the verb `come' in a system which originally only comprised a single AM marker is attested in Manchu, and a similar process may have taken place in Gyalrong languages.
summary:
Japhug and other Gyalrong languages have a relatively simple associated motion system with only two prefixes: an andative/translocative prefix and a venitive/cislocative prefix. These prefixes indicate that a motion event occurs before the main verb’s action, and there are no markers for subsequent or simultaneous motion.

The text argues that these prefixes were grammaticalized from motion verbs, probably through a construction in which a motion verb directly preceded another verb. It further suggests that the translocative prefix may go back to Proto-Gyalrong, while the cislocative prefix may have been innovated separately in the individual languages from the verb meaning ‘come.’

text:
The cislocative (or venitive) ɣɯ- is superficially homophonous with one of the allomorphs of the inverse prefix ɣɯ- (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ) and with one denominal prefix (§ sec:denom.GW ), but cannot be confused with either one; nevertheless some discussion concerning the distinction between the inverse and the cislocative can be useful to readers of Japhug texts.

Since the cislocative and the inverse do not occur in the same slot, and in particular before and following the orientation preverbs, they two are easily distinguishable in forms having orientation preverbs such as ( ex:GWtundze ) (where ɣɯ- can only be the cislocative, not the inverse, since it occurs on the left of the orientation preverb tu- ).

exe

qajɯ ra tu-ndze ma tɤ-rɤku ɣɯ-tu-ndze mɤ-ŋgrɤl \\
bugs pl ipfv -eat[III] lnk indef. poss -crops cisl - ipfv -eat[III] neg -be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`It eats bugs, and it does not come and eat the crops.' (24-ZmbrWpGa) (Japhug)
0003628#S119
exe

The only type of forms where a confusion could potentially arise is in the non-past factual, without second person arguments (which are indexed by prefixes, see § sec:intr.23 ). Even in such forms, since the inverse receives stress, and since it is incompatible with stem III (§ sec:stem3.distribution, § sec:direct-inverse ), verbs with stem alternation will not have ambiguous forms at least in the singular, as illustrated by the contrast between ɣɯ́-ndza (inverse, stem I) in ( ex:GWndza ) and ɣɯ-ndze (cislocative, stem III) in ( ex:GWndze ).

exe

tɕe ɯʑo nɯ ɲɤ-nɯ-pʰɣo matɕi tɕe, nɯmaʁnɤ ɣɯ́-ndza pjɤ-ŋu. \\
lnk 3sg dem ifr - auto -flee lnk lnk otherwise inv -eat: fact ifr -be \\
`[The rabbit], he had fled, otherwise he would have been eaten.' (140427 qala cho kWrtsAG) 0003852#S71
exe

exe

tɤ-rɤku kɯ-fse ɣɯ-ndze mɤ-ŋgrɤl \\
indef. poss -crop sbj: pcp -be.like cisl -eat[III]: fact neg -be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`It does not come and eat crops.' (23-pGAYaR) 0003606#S21
exe

It is perfectly possible for the inverse (in its non-initial allomorph wɣ ) to directly follow the cislocative, which in this case receives the stress, as ɣɯ́-wɣ-ndza in ( ex:GwWGndza ).

exe

kʰu a-jɤ-ɤzɣɯt ndɤ ɣɯ́-wɣ-ndza ɲɯ-ŋu \\
tiger irr - pfv -arrive lnk cisl - inv -eat: fact sens -be \\
`If the tiger comes, it will eat him [the man].' (kandZislama 2003)
exe
summary: The cislocative/venitive prefix ɣɯ- is homophonous with an inverse prefix allomorph and a denominal prefix, but it is not actually confusable with them because it occupies a different position in the verb template. In forms with orientation preverbs, the cislocative appears to the left of the preverb, unlike the inverse, and the main possible ambiguity is in some non-past factual forms without second-person arguments. Even there, stress and stem distribution usually disambiguate the two, and the inverse can also follow the cislocative, with the cislocative bearing the stress.

text:
Unlike the cislocative, the translocative (or andative) prefix presents an important degree of allomorphy. Besides the main allomorph ɕɯ, the consonantal allomorphs ɕ, ʑ, s- and z- are also found. These allomorphs are only attested in direct contact with orientation preverbs, following the rules in tab:translocative.allomorphs.

The dental allomorphs s- and z- are only found with orientation preverbs with a palatal consonant, and result from dissimilation in place of articulation from their alveolo-palatal counterparts. They harmonize in voicing with the following orientation preverb, s- being found before the orientation preverbs in cʰ- and pj, and z- before those in j- and ɲ-.

The alveolo-palatal allomorphs are found with non-palatal orientation preverbs, and also harmonize in voicing with the following consonant, ɕ- occurring before unvoiced prefixes ( ɕ-tu-kʰat-a in ex:ZYWlata below) and ʑ- before voicing ones as in ( ex:ZnaCar ).

exe

tɕendɤre ɯ-pɯ ra nɯ-ndza ʑ-na-ɕar \\
lnk 3sg. poss -young pl 3pl. poss -food tral - aor:3 -search \\
`The [cat mother] went to look for food for her [kitten].' (21-lWLU)
0003576#S75
exe

The alveo-palatal allomorphs are also used with the palatal orientation preverbs, as shown by the form ʑ-ɲɯ-lat-a (instead of z-ɲɯ-lat-a ) in ( ex:ZYWlata ) (for an example of ɕ-cʰɯ, see ex:CchWZGABdea, § sec:shC.clusters ). With cʰ, j- and ɲ- prefixes, the alveolo-palatal allomorphs are very rare, but with pj- prefixes interestingly, the dissimilatory effect is much more limited and ɕ- is more common than s- (§ sec:Cj.clusters ), as shown by the counts in tab:transloc.allomorphs.counts.

exe

nɯnɯ ʑakastaka kɯ-tu nɯnɯ ɣɯ nɯ-<gongfen> ra ʑ-ɲɯ-lat-a ɕ-tu-kʰat-a pɯ-ra.\\
dem each sbj: pcp -exist dem gen 3sg. poss -work.point pl tral - ipfv -throw- 1sg tral - ipfv -do.everywhere- 1sg pst. ipfv -be.needed\\
`I had to go everywhere to count work points for every single person.' (2010-09)
exe

Some clusters, such as ɕpj, ʑn, ɕcʰ- and zɲ, are only attested in translocative + orientation preverb combinations (§ sec:shC.clusters ).

With prefixes other than orientation preverbs, such as infinitive kɤ- ( ex:CWkArANgWm ) or second person tɯ- ( ex:maCWtWnAtWi ), only the allomorph ɕɯ- is found. The infinitive kɤ- and the east/centripetal orientation preverb kɤ- can thus be distinguished by their compatibilities with the allomorphs of the translocative prefix, the former occurring with ɕɯ, and the latter with ɕ-.

exe

tɕendɤre nɯtɕu ɕɯ-kɤ-rɤŋgɯm ndɤre kumpɣɤtɕɯ mɯ́j-nɤz \\
lnk dem: loc tral - inf -lay.eggs lnk sparrow neg: sens -dare \\
`The sparrow does not dare to lay eggs there (on the ground).' (22-kumpGatCW) 0003590#S80
exe

exe

ma-ɕɯ-tɯ-nɤtɯti \\
neg - tral -2-tell.everywhere \\
`Do not go around talking about it.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

In Factual Non-Past prefixless forms, the allomorph ɕɯ- is also the only possible one, as in ( ex:CWte.pjAra ) ($ $ ɕ-te would be an incorrect form).

exe

tɕe ndʑi-ŋga ɕɯ-te pjɤ-ra \\
lnk 3du. poss -clothes tral -put[III]: fact pst. ifr -be.needed \\
`She had to make their beds (cover them with a quilt)'. (2003 kWBRa)
exe
summary:
The translocative (andative) prefix shows considerable allomorphy, with a main form ɕɯ and consonantal allomorphs ɕ-, ʑ-, s-, and z- that appear only in direct contact with orientation preverbs. The dental allomorphs s- and z- occur only with palatal orientation preverbs and reflect place dissimilation, while the alveolo-palatal allomorphs ɕ- and ʑ- occur with non-palatal preverbs and agree in voicing with the following consonant.  

With non-orientation prefixes such as kɤ- or tɯ-, only ɕɯ- appears, and in Factual Non-Past prefixless forms ɕɯ- is likewise the only possible form. The text also notes that some consonant clusters are attested only in translocative plus orientation-preverb combinations, and that ɕ�

text:
subject associated motion!argument of motion
The argument undergoing the motion event is always the subject in the case of intransitive, semi-transitive ( ex:aki.CpWsANo ), and transitive verbs ( ex:phaʁrgot.CpWsat ). It is thus impossible to interpret ɕ-pɯ-sɤŋo in ( ex:aki.CpWsANo ) as meaning something like `listen to $X$, after $X$ has gone there' (motion of semi-object) or ɕ-pɯ-sat in ( ex:phaʁrgot.CpWsat ) as meaning `kill the boar, after it has gone there' (motion of object).

exe

aki ɕ-pɯ-sɤŋo \\
down tral - imp -listen \\
`Go down there and listen' (many attestations).
exe

exe

pʰaʁrgot ci tu tɕe, nɯ ɕ-pɯ-sat ra \\
boar indef exist: fact lnk dem tral - imp -kill be.needed: fact \\
`There is a boar, go and kill it.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh) 0003886#S214
exe

This is also true in inverse (mixed and non-local) verb forms. In ( ex:GWtWwnWGnWsnWYaR ) for instance, the argument whose motion is indicated by the cislocative prefix is necessarily ɬɤndʐi tɤ-mu `the ghost woman', the subject of the transitive verb ɣɯ-tɯ́-wɣ-nɯsnɯɲaʁ, and also the subject the preceding motion verb ɣi (a case of AM echo, § sec:AM.echo ). The cislocative ɣɯ- cannot be interpreted as expressing the motion of the object ( 2sg ) (`you will come and she will do you harm').

exe

tɕetʰa nɯ ɬɤndʐi tɤ-mu nɯnɯ ɣi tɕe nɤʑo ɣɯ-tɯ́-wɣ-nɯsnɯɲaʁ ɕti \\
later dem ghost indef. poss -mother dem come: fact lnk 2sg cisl -2- inv -do.harm be. aff: fact \\
`The ghost woman will come and cause you harm.' (150907 niexiaoqian-zh)
0006262#S88
exe

The same rule is observed in local configurations. In ( ex:GWpjWkWmJaa ), the verb form ɣɯ-pjɯ-kɯ-mɟa-a cannot be interpreted as meaning `Now that I have come here, take me': the cislocative motion event concerns the subject, not the object.

exe

aʑo kɯre rɤʑi-a, tɕe ɣɯ-pjɯ-kɯ-mɟa-a wo \\
1sg here stay: fact - 1sg lnk cisl - ipfv -2 1-take- 1sg sfp \\
`I am here, come and take me!' (150825 huluwa-zh)
0006346#S186
exe

In causative constructions however, the argument of motion can be either the causer or the causee (§ sec:sig.caus.AM; on the syntactic status of the causee, see § sec:ditransitive.causative and § sec:sig.caus.tr ). For instance, the form ɣɯ-cʰɯ-sɯ-χtɯ-nɯ could either mean `they send (cause to come) $X$ here to buy $Y$' or `they come and make $X$ buy $Y$'; ( ex:GWchWsWXtWnW ) illustrates the first interpretation.

exe

tɕe kupa-cʰu nɯra atʰi pɕoʁ nɯra, ɯ-pɕi nɯra kɯ kɯre ri ɣɯ-cʰɯ-sɯ-χtɯ-nɯ ŋu. \\
lnk Chinese- loc dem: pl downstream direction dem: pl 3sg -outside dem: pl erg here loc cisl - ipfv: downstream - caus -buy- pl be: fact \\
`People from the Chinese areas downstream, outsiders, send people here to buy [matsutake].' (20 grWBgrWB 58) 0003554#S57
exe

In the case of manipulation verbs, the motion can involve both the subject and the object. In ( ex:Wscun.GWpjAWGlAt ) for instance, the cislocative does refer to the motion of the object (the character who has been sent down), but it is implied that he did not come alone, and was brought to his current place by the unspecified subject of the verb ɣɯ-pjɤ́-wɣ-lɤt `s/he/they sent/brought him down'.

exe

ɯ-scun pjɤ-tu tɕe,... kutɕu ɣɯ-pjɤ́-wɣ-lɤt pjɤ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -fault pst: ipfv -exist lnk here cisl - ifr: down - inv -release pst: ipfv -exist \\
`He had broken the law,... and had been sent (down) here [to earth, as punishment].' (180501 xiyouji 08-zh)
exe

A similar use of the cislocative with the verb lɤtrelease in the sense of `bring, send' (someone) in found in example ( ex:GWlAwGlAti ) above.
summary: The passage states that in intransitive, semi-transitive, and transitive verbs, the participant undergoing the motion event is always the subject, not the object or semi-object. This pattern also holds in inverse and local forms, while causative constructions allow the motion argument to be either the causer or the causee. In manipulation verbs, however, motion may involve both subject and object, as when the cislocative can refer to the object being brought or sent.

text:
associated motion!motion verbs
In Japhug, there is no constraint on AM prefixes occurring on motion verbs with the same deixis. Examples ( ex:GWjuGinW ) and ( ex:CpjACe ) illustrate the cislocative on the verb ɣicome and the translocative on the verb ɕego, respectively. Such examples are not common enough to allow a clear analysis of the semantic value of the redundant AM in these examples.

exe

<jiazhang> ra ju-ɣi-nɯ tɕe <laoshi> ɯ-ɕki, tɯ-ɕki ʑo ɣɯ-ju-ɣi-nɯ ɕti netɕi? \\
parents pl ipfv -come- pl lnk teacher 3sg. poss - dat genr. poss - dat emph cisl - ipfv -come- pl be. aff: fact sfp \\
`The parents come, they come to (us) the teachers, right?.' (conversation140501 01)
exe

exe

li nɤki iɕqʰa nɯ tɤjlu kɤ-rku ɯ-ŋgɯ zɯ ɕ-pjɤ-ɕe \\
again dem the.aforementioned dem flour obj: pcp -put.in 3sg. poss -inside loc tral - ifr: down -go \\
`He went into [a bag of] flour.' (140519 chou xiaoya-zh)
0004034#S133
exe

The opposite combinations, namely cislocative with ɕego and translocative with ɣicome, are not grammatical.

In the case of motion verbs without an intrinsic locative goal such as ŋkewalk, the presence of the translocative does not add a locative goal (unlike when used with non-motion verbs, see § sec:AM.goal ). In ( ex:CpjANkenW ) for instance, no specific location is specified even in the previous clauses, and the translocative on ŋke indicates that the motion took place far away from the deictic center (the king's palace).

exe

tɕendɤre nɯnɯ ɕ-to-nɯ-ŋke-nɯ tɕe, lu χsɯ-xpa ɕ-pjɤ-ŋke-nɯ, \\
lnk dem tral - ifr - appl -walk- pl lnk year three-year tral - ifr -walk- pl \\
`The ministers went to look for [the girl], they walked for three years.' (sras 2003)
exe

Participles used in the purposive complements of motions verbs (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation ) do not take AM prefixes.
summary: In Japhug, associated motion prefixes can occur on motion verbs with the same deixis, such as cislocative on ɣi ‘come’ and translocative on ɕe ‘go’, but the reverse combinations are ungrammatical. For motion verbs like ŋke ‘walk’ that do not inherently encode a locative goal, the translocative does not add a specific destination but instead indicates movement away from the deictic center. Participles in purposive complements of motion verbs do not take associated motion prefixes.

text:
associated motion!orientation orientation!associated motion
In Japhug, AM markers only specify deixis and the temporal relation between motion event and verbal action, but are neutral as far as the orientation of the motion event is concerned.

Orientation and AM markers occupy different prefixal slots. Apart from orientable verbs (§ sec:orientable.verbs ), most verbs select one or two lexicalized orientations (see § sec:lexicalized.orientation ). For instance, the transitive mɯrkɯsteal occurs with the orientation upwards (with the orientation preverbs tɤ, ta, tu, to, see § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ).

When non-orientable verbs occur with AM, the verb normally keeps its lexicalized orientation preverb, as in ( ex:CtumWrki ), where mɯrkɯsteal is used with the expected tu- upwards prefix. In this context, the motion related to the act of stealing occurs at the same horizontal level and there is no upward motion; the orientation preverb here encodes the default lexicalized orientation for the verb mɯrkɯsteal, and is thus irrelevant to the motion event itself.

exe

kɯ-nŋo nɯ qʰe ci ci ɕ-tu-mɯrki kɯ-fse ma nɯ ma mɯ-ɲɯ-ɤʁe. \\
sbj: pcp -be.defeated dem lnk one one tral - ipfv -steal[III] sbj: pcp -be.like apart.from dem apart.from neg - sens -be.needed.eat \\
`The [lion] which is defeated steals a little [meat], but apart from that has nothing to eat.' (20-sWNgi)
0003562#S62
exe

Similarly, in ( ex:CpjWskia ), the verb skɯbury appears with the lexical orientation downwards, although the associated motion event is oriented towards the opposite direction, as indicated by the adverb tɕetuup there.

exe

ki a-tɕɯ ki tɕetu zgoku tɕe ɕ-pjɯ-ski-a ɲɯ-ntsʰi \\
dem. prox 1sg. poss -son dem. prox up.there mountain loc tral - ipfv: down -bury[III]- 1sg sens -be.better \\
`Let's bury my son up there on the mountain.' (150904 cuzhi-zh)
0006322#S107
exe

However, alternatively, the orientation preverbs of verbs with an AM marker can also reflect the orientation of the motion event. In ( ex:CpjWntGea ), the verb ntsɣesell occurs with the orientation preverbs upwards ( ɕ-tu-ntsɣe-a ) and downwards ( ɕ-pjɯ-ntsɣe-a ). The lexicalized orientation normally selected by ntsɣesell is the `westward; centrifugal' one (§ sec:centripetal.centrifugal ). In ( ex:CpjWntGea ) the upwards and downwards prefixes clearly correlate with those found on the manipulation verb ɣɯtbring and express the direction of the motion event.

exe

rɟa ɣɯ ɯ-laχtɕʰa tu-ɣɯt-a tɕe pot zɯ ɕ-tu-ntsɣe-a, pot ɣɯ ɯ-laχtɕʰa pjɯ-ɣɯt-a tɕe, rɟa zɯ ɕ-pjɯ-ntsɣe-a. \\
China gen 3sg. poss -thing ipfv: up -bring- 1sg lnk Tibet loc tral - ipfv: up -sell- 1sg Tibet gen 3sg. poss -thing ipfv: down -bring- 1sg lnk China loc tral - ipfv: down -sell- 1sg \\
`I bring things [down] from central Tibet, and sell them in China.' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S15
exe

Overriding of the lexical orientation by the motion event is found in particular in the case of AM prefixes expressing round trips (§ sec:round.trip.AM ). In ( ex:ZlumWrkia ) for instance, the translocative ʑ-lu-mɯrki-a with the upstream preverb expresses the fact that the main character of the story steals from a place located downstream (first motion event, indicated by the AM prefix) and then brings it upstream (second motion event, whose orientation is encoded by the preverb). Interestingly, after a few occurrences of the verb mɯrkɯsteal with AM and upstream orientation, one finds examples of that verb with the same non-lexicalized orientation upstream but without the AM prefix in the same text, as in ( ex:lomWrkW ).

exe

tɕetʰi tɤmuj jlɤrɯcɤrna ɣɯ ɯ-pʰe nɯtɕu kɯ-mɯrkɯ cʰɯ-ɕe-a ŋu tɕe. tsʰɤt ɯ-ʁrɯ ɣɯ ɯ-ci nɯnɯ ʑ-lu-mɯrki-a ri a-qʰu zɯ lɤ-ɣe-nɯ tɕe \\
downstream topo topo gen 3sg. poss - dat dem: loc sbj: pcp -steal ipfv: downstream -go- 1sg be: fact lnk goat 3sg. poss -horn gen 3sg. poss -water dem tral - ipfv: upstream -streal[III]- 1sg lnk 1sg. poss -after loc aor: upstream -come[II]- pl lnk \\
`(Tomorrow morning) I will go downstream to steal from Tamuj Jlarukyarna, and I will steal the water from the goat's horn, but when [the mountain god] comes after me...' (25-kAmYW-XpAltCin)
0003642#S29
exe

exe

lo-mɯrkɯ pjɤ-cʰa tɕe lo-ɣɯt ri \\
ifr: upstream -steal ifr -can lnk ifr: upstream -bring lnk \\
`He was able to steal it and brought it upstream.' (02-montagnes-kamnyu-cz)
0003378#S28
exe

In some limited contexts, it is thus possible for verbs without associated motion markers to use their orientation preverb to indicate the direction of the action, with or without motion, as in ( ex:lomWrkW ).

In ( ex:lupea.je ), similarly, we find the verb lu-pe-a with the upstream orientation without an associated motion marker; when this sentence was uttered, we were sitting far from the door, and to close the door it was necessary to get up and walk a few meters (we were seated at a place closer to the river, so the door was upstream, § sec:riverine.dimension ). The same sentence could have been uttered if the door had been at a hand's reach, and could thus have been closed without walking. Replacing lu-pe-a in ( ex:lupea.je ) by ʑ-lu-pe-a tral - ipfv: upstream -close[III]- 1sg, with an associated motion marker, would make the second interpretation impossible.

exe

tɕi-kɯm lu-pe-a je! \\
1du. poss -door ipfv: upstream -close[III]- 1sg sfp \\
`Let me close the door (for us).' (conversation, 03-05-2018, Tshendzin )
exe

It is debatable whether the orientation preverbs in examples like ( ex:lomWrkW ) and ( ex:lupea.je ) could be analyzed as marking associated motion (in Guillaume's guillaume16am definition), as these prefixes do not actually specify that a motion event takes or does not place. What they specify is that if the main action is linked with a translational motion event, that motion event follows the direction indicated by the prefix. In this grammar, the use of orientation preverbs in examples such as ( ex:lomWrkW ) and ( ex:lupea.je ) are therefore not considered to be cases of associated motion.
summary: In Japhug, associated motion markers encode deixis and the temporal relation between motion and the verbal action, but they do not themselves specify motion orientation. Orientation preverbs usually belong to the verb’s lexical class, yet in some cases they can either retain that lexical orientation despite associated motion or reflect the direction of the motion event, especially with round-trip AM forms. The grammar therefore treats uses of orientation preverbs without an AM marker as not genuinely associated motion, since they only indicate the direction of a possible translational motion linked to the action.

text:
The combination of some verbs with AM prefixes implies a round trip when the lexical orientation (§ sec:lexicalized.orientation ) is overridden by the orientation of the motion event (§ sec:orientation.AM ).

With the verb χtɯbuy for instance, the translocative expresses a first trip to the goal indicated by the locative ri (§ sec:AM.goal ), but a second trip back to the deictic center (here, Kamnyu) is implied by the selection of the downstream orientation (§ sec:orientation.AM ).

exe

tɕe mbroχpa ri jla nɯ s-cʰɯ-χtɯ-nɯ ʁɟa pɯ-ra. \\
lnk nomad loc hybrid.yak dem tral - ipfv: downstream -buy- pl completely pst. ipfv -be.needed \\
`People had to buy hybrid yaks from the nomads.' (150820 kAnWCkat)
0006256#S23
exe

In ( ex:kWre.ri.GWchWsWXtWnW ), the cislocative indicates a first trip from Chinese areas up to Mbarkham (the deictic center, kɯre ri `here'), and then back to Chinese areas, as indicated by the choice of the downstream preverb (§ sec:riverine.dimension ).

exe

ɯ-pɕi nɯra kɯ kɯre ri ɣɯ-cʰɯ-sɯ-χtɯ-nɯ ŋu. \\
3sg -outside dem: pl erg here loc cisl - ipfv: downstream - caus -buy- pl be: fact \\
`Outsiders send people to come here and buy [matsutake].' (20 grWBgrWB)
0003554#S58
exe

AM markers expressing round trips are found with a handful of verbs, for instance mɯrkɯsteal ( ex:ZlumWrkia ), expressing actions which can be considered to have been fully completed only when the subject comes back to his starting point with the object. The verb rufetch, bring, which requires to be used with an AM prefix, always implies a two way trip (§ sec:ru.fetch ). As in examples ( ex:mbroXpa.ri.schWXtWnW ) and ( ex:kWre.ri.GWchWsWXtWnW ), the AM prefix encodes the deixis of the first trip, and the orientation preverb the direction of the second trip back -- hence the motion of the first trip is always in a direction opposite to that indicated by the preverb.
summary: Some verbs with AM prefixes imply a round trip when the lexical orientation is overridden by the motion-event orientation. In examples with **χtɯbuy** and **cʰɯ-χtɯ** ‘buy’, the AM prefix marks the first trip, while the downstream or cislocative orientation indicates the return trip, so the overall motion involves going to a goal and then back to the deictic center.

text:
In Japhug, AM prefixes express physical translation from one place to another, and unlike other Gyalrong languages do no have grammaticalized uses like prospective.

The cis- and translocative prefixes only refer to motion events occurring before the action of main verb (§ sec:am.prefixes ). The verbal action does not necessarily take place immediately after the motion. In ( ex:ri.CpaBjoz ) for instance, `learning computers' is one of the many activities that the referent did in Chengdu, and took place a considerable amount of time after the travel from Mbarkham to Chengdu itself. Here the translocative specifies that the action took place at such a distance from the deictic center that motion was necessary.

exe

atʰi ɯ-pɕi ri <chengdu> ri <diannao> ci ɕ-pa-βzjoz \\
downstream 3sg. poss -outside loc Chengdu loc computer indef tral - aor:3 -learn \\
`He went outside of [Tibetan areas, downstream], to Chengdu, and studied computers there a little bit.' (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S73
exe

AM markers are not exclusively used to describe walking or motion on land ( ex:ri.CpaBjoz ). They can also be applied to flying, as in ( ex:nWtCu.Ctundze ), where nɯtɕu ɕ-tu-ndze literally means `it flies there and eats it'. In this example, the translocative is in echo with the manipulation verb tsɯmtake away (§ sec:redundant.AM ).

exe

pʰɤri praʁ ɯ-ŋgɯ mɤɕtʂa ku-tsɯm qʰe, tɕe nɯtɕu ɕ-tu-ndze ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
the.opposite.side cliff 3sg. poss -in until ipfv: east -take.away lnk lnk dem: loc tral - ipfv -eat[III] sens -be \\
`[The eagle] takes [the young animal] to the cliff on the other side [of the river] and eats it there.' (19-qandZGi)
0003548#S48
exe

Additionally, they are attested in the case of motion in a liquid (involving for instance swimming), as in example ( ex:CpjAmto ) in § sec:AM.volitionality, and also plants growing from one place to another ( ex:WzrAm.CtulhoR ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-zrɤm ju-ɕe qʰe nɯre ri, kɯmaʁ ɯ-pɕoʁ ɕ-tu-ɬoʁ ɲɯ-ɕti ma \\
lnk 3sg. poss -root ipfv -go lnk dem: loc loc other 3sg. poss -place tral - ipfv -come.out sens -be. aff lnk \\
`Its root spreads and it grows there, at a different place.' (15-babW)
0003512#S42
exe

In ( ex:Ctusci.YWNu ), the motion implied by the translocative is more metaphorical, as it refers to the reincarnation of a lama in a house different from the one he was born in his previous life. In ( ex:GWtomkhroN ) above (§ sec:preverb.gain ), the cislocative occurs in this meaning.

exe

a-nɯ-χɕaʁ, a-nɯ-si tɕe tɕe, kɯmaʁ pɕoʁ ri li ɕ-tu-sci ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
irr - pfv -pass.away irr - pfv -die lnk lnk other place loc again tral - ipfv -be.born sens -be \\
`When [the reincarnated lama] passes away, he is born in another place.' (160722 skWBli)
0006227#S2
exe

In the case of ( ex:saCW.CtolhoR ), the translocative may be interpreted as referring to the motion of the seed, but since this example comes from a traditional story where the larch is humanized (since its relation to the fir is compared to that of a nephew to its uncle), it may also be viewed here as a metaphorical human-like motion.
In the context of nephews and uncles, the upstream-downstream dimension here refers to the relative position of the adult males on the seating position called kʰɤɕkʰɤr (§ sec:orientation.kitchen ) in the traditional society.

exe

tɕe saɕɯ nɯ tɯrgi ɯ-locu zɯ ɕ-to-ɬoʁ tɕe, tɕe nɯnɯ tɤ-ftsa nɯ tɤ-rpɯ sɤz lu-kɯ-maŋlo mɯ-pjɤ-ŋgrɤl\\
lnk larch dem fir 3sg. poss -upstream loc tral - ifr -come.out lnk lnk dem indef. poss -nephew dem indef. poss -MB comp ipfv: upstream - genr:S/O-be.upstream neg - ifr. ipfv -be.usually.the.case\\
`The larch grew in a place higher than the fir, but nephews could not be seated higher (i.e. upstream) than their maternal uncles (and this is why the larch became deciduous).' (08-saCW) 0003462#S11
exe
summary: In Japhug, AM prefixes mark physical translation from one place to another and do not have grammaticalized uses such as the prospective found in some other Gyalrong languages. The cis- and translocative prefixes indicate motion that occurs before the main verb’s action, and they can apply not only to ordinary walking but also to flying, movement in liquid, plant growth, and even metaphorical contexts such as reincarnation.

text:
associated motion!goal
Verbs taking the translocative prefix very often appear with a locative phrase (adverb, noun in the absolutive or locative case and/or a locative relator noun) expressing the goal of the motion, which at the same time corresponds to the location where the action takes place, as for instance in ( ex:ri.CtArWndzAtshij ). The locative ri is particularly common to express the goal of an AM-prefixed verb (see also for instance ex:mbroXpa.ri.schWXtWnW and ex:kWre.ri.GWchWsWXtWnW in § sec:round.trip.AM and ex:ri.CpaBjoz in § sec:nature.of.motion.AM above).

exe

<guanzi> ɯ-ŋgɯ ri ɕ-tɤ-rɯndzɤtsʰi-j. \\
restaurant 3sg. poss -in loc tral - aor -east- 1pl \\
`We went to a restaurant and ate there.' (2010-1)
exe

Even if it is not present in the same clause as the verb with the translocative, the goal generally appears in previous clauses. For instance in ( ex:CtuBzdWnW ), the verb ɕ-tu-βzdɯ-nɯ `they (went and) collected it there' is not directly preceded by the goal, but it shares the goal sɯŋgɯ `in the forest' of the motion verb ɕego.

exe

tɯrme kɯ-xtɕi nɯnɯra sɲikuku ʑo sɯŋgɯ ju-ɕe-nɯ tɕe, iɕqʰa nɯ, tsʰitsuku z-ɲɯ-ɕar-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu tɕe, χsɤr ra ɕ-tu-βzdɯ-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu. \\
people sbj: pcp -be.small dem: pl every.day emph forest ipfv -go- pl lnk filler dem whatever tral - ipfv -search- pl ifr. ipfv -be lnk gold pl tral - ipfv -collect- pl ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The dwarves went into the forest every day, searching around and collecting gold there.' (140504 baixuegongzhu-zh)
0003907#S94
exe

Verbs with the cislocative, on the other hand, are more rarely used with an overt goal. As an example, the verb ndzaeat appears 7 times in the corpus with the translocative, and 16 times with the cislocative. The goal is explicit with the translocative (either in the same clause or in the previous clause) in 6 times out of 7 (the only exception being ex:chWnWtsWm.Ctundze; note that here the goal can be understood as the nest of the eagle), whereas it is overt in only 4 of the 16 examples with the translocative.

exe

qaliaʁ kɯ, [...] kɯ-mɤku tɕe tɕe ɯ-tʰoʁ nɯ tɕe pjɯ-nɤʁarpʰɤβ tɕe pjɯ-sat, tɕe nɯ koʁmɯz nɤ cʰɯ-nɯ-tsɯm tɕe ɕ-tu-ndze ɲɯ-ra ma, \\
eagle erg sbj: pcp -be.first lnk lnk 3sg. poss -ground dem loc ipfv -hit.with.wings lnk ipfv -kill lnk dem only.after lnk ipfv: downstream - vert -take.away lnk tral - ipfv -eat[III] sens -be.needed lnk \\
`The eagle, (in the case of prey that is too big), it has to kill them by hitting them with its wings, and then take them away and eat them.' (50819 RarphAB)
0006356#S3
exe

The reason for the more common absence of locative phrases with the cislocative, as in ( ex:GWtundze.mANgrAl ), is because in the case of motion towards the deitic center, the goal can generally be inferred on the basis of the context: it is most often either the current location, or the house of either the speaker or the addressee.

exe

jaʁmɤzdoʁzdoʁ nɯ kɯ qajɯ ra tu-ndze ma tɤ-rɤku ɣɯ-tu-ndze mɤ-ŋgrɤl \\
bird.sp dem erg bug pl ipfv -eat[III] lnk indef. poss -crops cisl - ipfv -eat neg -be.usually.the.case \\
`The bird jaʁmɤzdoʁzdoʁ eats bugs, and it does not come and eat the crops.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S119
exe

The examples above illustrate the most typical uses of the AM prefixes. However, the translocative can also be used in cases where the goal is unspecified and not recoverable from the context, simply as a way to indicate that the action takes place at a distance from the deictic center. In ( ex:BGWz.CpjAsat ) for instance, the presence of the translocative implies that the action did not take place immediately near the house, but that the subject had to look for the badgers (see also ex:CpjANkenW in § sec:motion.verbs.AM ).

exe

ji-me nɯ kɯ βɣɯz ʁnɯz ʑo ɕ-pjɤ-sat. \\
1pl. poss -daughter dem erg badger two emph tral - ifr -kill \\
`Our daughter-in-law went (to look for badgers) and killed two badgers.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S102
exe

The exact location of the event is left vague, as shown by ( ex:joCe.tCe.pjAsat ), a comment on ( ex:BGWz.CpjAsat ).

exe

nɯnɯ ŋotɕu ŋu, kɯ-χsɤl kɯ-me kɯ-fse ɲɯ-ɕti, ``jo-ɕe tɕe pjɤ-sat" tu-kɯ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
dem where be: fact sbj: pcp -be.clear sbj: pcp -exist sbj: pcp -be.like sens -be. aff ifr -go lnk ifr -kill ipfv - genr -say sens -be \\
`It is like it is unclear where it is, it means `she went (somewhere) and killed them'.' (explanation of ex:BGWz.CpjAsat ).
exe
summary: Verbs with the translocative prefix very often co-occur with an explicit or previously mentioned locative phrase expressing the goal of motion, which also marks where the action happens, and the locative *ri* is especially common in this function. Cislocative verbs, by contrast, more often lack an overt goal because the destination toward the deictic center is usually inferable from context, and the goal is often the speaker’s or addressee’s location or the current place. The passage also notes that translocative can be used even when the goal is unspecified, to indicate that the action occurred at a distance from the deictic center.

text:
associated motion!echo
Previous literature on AM has reported the existence of `echo phenomena' in the use of AM markers (,,, ), namely that the same motion event can be expressed by more than one AM marker. This phenomenon is common in Japhug narratives. Two subtypes of AM echo can be distinguished: motion verb with redundant AM, and multiple AM marking.
summary: Previous literature on associated motion (AM) has noted “echo phenomena,” in which the same motion event can be expressed by more than one AM marker. This is common in Japhug narratives, where two subtypes are distinguished: a motion verb with redundant AM, and multiple AM marking.

text:
In examples such as ( ex:tari.CtatWt ), ( ex:toCE.tCe.CtAru ) and ( ex:GWYWsloR ), a motion verb is followed by clause containing a verb with an AM prefix with the same deixis: translocative after ɕego (in the Aorist form tɤ-ari in ex:tari.CtatWt ) and cislocative after ɣicome, respectively. It is however clear from the context, in all of these examples, that only one motion event took place, and that the AM marker could be dispensed with.

exe

zgoku tɤ-ari nɤ, `hehe a-ʑi ra cʰɤ-tɯ-nɯ-rɤrɟit-nɯ mɯ́j-tɯ-nɯ-sɯχsɤl-nɯ' ɕ-ta-tɯt ɲɯ-ŋu \\

`He went up the mountain top and said: `My lady, you had a child and did not notice it.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

The motion verb and the verb with AM are not necessarily adjacent, as in ( ex:tari.CtatWt ) where they are separated by a complement clause, but AM echo is common when the AM-marked verb directly follows the motion verb, with an intervening linker such as tɕe (as in ex:toCE.tCe.CtAru ) or more rarely with parataxis (as in ex:GWYWsloR ).

exe

tɕʰi ɯ-taʁ to-ɕe tɕe ɕ-tɤ-ru \\
stairs 3sg. poss -on ifr: up -go lnk tral - aor: up -look \\
`He went up the stairs and looked up.' (08-kWqhi)
0003454#S17
exe

exe

kʰa mɯ-pɯ-rɤʑi tɕe tɕe, ftɕar nɯ wuma ʑo βɣɯz pjɤ-rɯŋɯŋɤn tɕe maka, kɯmtʰoʁ ra kɯnɤ ju-ɣi ɣɯ-ɲɯ-sloʁ pjɤ-ŋu. \\

`He was not at home, and badgers were causing a lot of damage that summer, they came and even dug up the threshold of the house.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S99
exe

Since, with some exceptions, verbs taking AM prefix do not indicate the direction of the motion using their orientation preverbs (§ sec:motion.verbs.AM ), this echo construction makes it possible to indicate the orientation on the motion verb (for instance, upwards in ex:tari.CtatWt, ex:toCE.tCe.CtAru and ex:toCE.tCe.CpjAru ) while keeping that on the AM-taking verb, something which would neither be possible with only AM or with a purposive motion verb construction (§ sec:am.vs.mvc, § sec:subject.participle.complementation ). Specifying both orientations can be informative when the other verb is compatible with more than one orientation, as illustrated by the contrast between ( ex:toCE.tCe.CtAru ) and ( ex:toCE.tCe.CpjAru ) with the orientations upwards and downwards on the AM-taking verb rulook at, respectively. In principle, all $7 7$ theoretical combinations would be possible with this pair of verbs.

indef. poss -son dem ifr: up -go lnk tral - aor: down -look lnk \\
`The boy went up and looked down.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S51

Echo AM is however completely optional; in ( ex:toCe.tCe.kurAZi ) for instance, even though the verbs ku-rɤʑi and pjɯ-ru, share the same subject as to-ɕe, they lack the translocative. Note that in this example the anaphora could be potentially ambiguous, and that adding the translocative on these verbs could have contributed to disambiguating the sentence.

Echo can also occur between a manipulation verb and an AM prefix, as in ( ex:jAtsWm.CpWsat ) (see also ex:nWtCu.Ctundze, § sec:nature.of.motion.AM ).

dem girl dem imp -take.away lnk tral - imp -kill be.needed: fact \\
`Take this girl [to the forest] and kill her.' (140504 baixuegongzhu-zh) 0003907#S38

summary: The passage describes an “echo” construction in which a motion verb is followed by another verb bearing the same directional AM prefix, such as translocative or cislocative, even though only one motion event is involved and the AM marker is often optional. This pattern can occur with intervening material, and it lets speakers specify orientation both on the motion verb and on the following AM-marked verb, which can be informative when the second verb allows more than one directional interpretation.

text:
The second type of AM echo construction is found when two (or more) verbs are redundantly prefixed with the same AM marker, for instance the cislocative ɣɯ- in ( ex:GWtaBzu ), though only a single motion event is supposed to have taken place.

exe

tɕe a-kʰa ra ɣɯ-ta-rɤroʁrɯz, a-mgo ra ɣɯ-ta-βzu ŋu ɕi \\
lnk 1sg. poss -house pl cisl - aor:3 -tidy
1sg. poss -food pl cisl - aor:3 -make be: fact qu \\
`Is it [the neighbour's wife who took pity on me] and came and tidied my house and made food for me?' (150827 tianluo-zh)
0006250#S76
exe

AM echo is almost obligatory in serial verb constructions (, § sec:svc.manner ), as shown by ( ex:CkunWrtCe ) and ( ex:zjusWmtshAt.Zo.zjuski ), where the pairs of verbs ɕ-tu-ste / ɕ-ku-nɯrtɕe and z-ju-sɯ-mtsʰɤt / z-ju-ski share the same person (3 ), TAM (imperfective) and AM (translocative) markers.

exe

ci ci ɯ-mi kɯ iɕqʰa, lɯlu ɣɯ ɯ-mi nɯra z-ɲɯ-z-nɤtsʰɣɤz. kɯra ɕ-tu-ste tɕe ɕ-ku-nɯrtɕe ra pjɤ-ŋu. \\

`[The mouse] sometimes went and touched the cat's legs with its paw, it [went and] teased [the cat] like that.' (150902 dashu-zh)
0006330#S31
exe

exe

ɯ-loʁ ɯ-ŋgɯ ri z-ju-sɯ-mtsʰɤt ʑo z-ju-ski \\

However, not all adjacent verb pairs sharing the same AM markers are necessarily cases of AM echo. Repetition of an AM prefix can also refer to different motion events. In ( ex:CtunWrdoR.Zo.zjuski ) for instance, the first translocative prefix on ɕ-tu-nɯrdoʁ refers to the motion of the animal to the place where the walnut tree is found, and the second one on z-ju-ski to the motion back to its nest. The translocative appears in both cases because both places are away from the deictic center (people's houses), and there is no ambiguity that the two places are distinct.

tral - ipfv -collect.one.by.one lnk dem: pl tral - ipfv -bury[III] \\
`It goes and collects the walnuts that have fallen [on the ground] one by one, and goes [to its nest] and buries them [there].' (28-qapar) 0003720#S174

The verb rufetch, bring
irregularity!associated motion
The manipulation verb rufetch, bring (homophonous with the semi-transitive rulook at) is peculiar, as it generally requires the use of AM prefixes (with very few counterexamples, see below), a feature shared with Situ (§ sec:am.prefixes ).

With the translocative, the verb ru means `go to $X$ and bring $Y$ here', expressing two motion events (§ sec:round.trip.AM ): first, a trip away from the present location (to look for an object), and second, the way back to the point of departure (bringing the object). The translocative refers to the first motion event. On the other hand, the orientation preverb encodes the direction of the way back to the deictic center, as shown by ( ex:pari.Ctaru ): the first trip (to the bottom of the ocean) has the downwards orientation, indicated by the prefix on the first verb pɯ-ari, while the second one on ru has the opposite orientation upwards.

exe

pɯ-ari ndɤre jɯɣi nɯ ɕ-ta-ru ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
aor: down -go[II] lnk book dem tral - aor: up:3 -bring sens -be \\
`He went down [to the bottom of the ocean] and brought up the sutra.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

Locative phrases/adverbs or the locative interrogative pronoun ŋotɕuwhere (§ sec:NotCu ), when occurring with ru, refer to the destination of the first motion event (the place where the object was originally/is still found), not the destination of the trip back, as illustrated by ( ex:NotCu.zjAtWrut ) and ( ex:tAmthWm.CpWre ). In ( ex:tAmthWm.CpWre ), the destination of the first trip ( upwards ) is the opposite orientation as that found on the verb ( downwards ), confirming what has been observed in ( ex:pari.Ctaru ) above.

dem. prox basin dem. prox 2sg where tral - aor -2-bring- pst: tr be: fact \\
`Where did you get this washbasin from?' (150831 jubaopen-zh)

up.there indef. poss -meat tral - imp: down -bring[III] \\
`Bring [down] the meat from up there.' (meimeidegushi)
exe

Similarly, the person pronouncing ( ex:zYWrea ) was going towards the east to fetch the key; the orientation westwards on the verb indicates the orientation of the way back to the current location.

sɤcɯ z-ɲɯ-re-a \\
key tral - ipfv: west -bring[III]- 1sg \\

With the cislocative, the meaning of ru can be rather translated as `come (to the current deictic center) and take $X$ away', as in ( ex:arJit.GWnWre ) and ( ex:rdAstaR.GWYWrundZi ); as with the translocative, two motion events take place (§ sec:round.trip.AM ), but their relationship to the deictic center is reversed: the first trip is from some place to the present location, and the second trip is back to that original place.

summary: The passage explains that AM echo construction can involve two or more verbs redundantly taking the same AM prefix, even though only one motion event is intended, and that this is especially common in serial verb constructions. It also notes that not every repeated AM prefix counts as AM echo, since adjacent verbs may each refer to different motion events; this is illustrated with the verb *ru* ‘bring,’ which typically requires AM prefixes and can encode two motion events depending on whether the translocative or cislocative is used.

text:
The orientation preverb, when present, refers to the motion of the second trip away from the deictic center. For instance, in ( ex:rdAstaR.GWYWrundZi ), the two people who are subjects of the verb ɣɯ-ɲɯ-ru-ndʑi (with westwards orientation ɲɯ- ) came from their houses in a place called tɯlu to another location called taʁrdo to take stones (both in Kamnyu village).

exe

kutɕu ʑo rdɤstaʁ ɣɯ-ɲɯ-ru-ndʑi iʑora ɣɯ ra mɤ-ŋgrɤl ɯ-maʁ ma \\

`They come here to take stones away, as if we did not need them.' (conversation, 14-05-10)
exe

As shown by ( ex:taRrdo.kAGendZi ) (a few sentences before ex:rdAstaR.GWYWrundZi ), this trip is oriented from west to east; having taken the stones in taʁrdo (in the east), the two referents go back home to tɯlu (westwards).

exe

tɕekɯ taʁrdo ra kɤ-ɣe-ndʑi \\
east topo pl aor: east -come[II]- du \\
`They came to Tagrdo (and looked for stones).' (conversation, 14-05-10)
exe

The examples from ( ex:pari.Ctaru ) to ( ex:rdAstaR.GWYWrundZi ) discussed above show that regardless of the AM prefix, the transitive verb ru expresses a two-way motion event: first from point $A$ to point $B$, where an object is retrieved, and then back to $A$ with the object. The AM prefix always indicate the deixis of the first trip (either away or towards the deictic center), and the orientation preverb encodes the direction of the second trip, whose deixis is the opposite of that of the first trip (§ sec:round.trip.AM ).

The manipulation rufetch, bring passes all transitivity tests (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ), for instance C-type orientation preverbs ( ex:pari.Ctaru ), the past suffix -t ( ex:NotCu.zjAtWrut ) and Stem III alternation. These tests are generally sufficient to distinguish it from the semi-transitive rulook at, but there are still a few ambiguous cases, in particular in the Inferential, where neither stem alternation nor prefix alternation reveals the transitivity difference. For instance, the surface form ʑ-lo-ru can either correspond to the transitive verb `she went down(stream) and brought it up(stream)' as in ( ex:tWci.Zloru ) or to the translocative of the semi-transitive verb `he went there and looked upstream' as in ( ex:look.Zloru ).

However, in the purposive motion verb construction with ɕego and ɣicome (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation, § sec:am.vs.mvc ), the subject participle ɯ-kɯ-ru is used without an AM marker, as in ( ex:WkWru.loCenW ), as part of a more general constraint against AM prefixes in this construction (§ sec:motion.verbs.AM ).

summary:
The passage explains that the orientation preverb marks the direction of the second leg of a round-trip motion, while the AM prefix marks the deixis of the first leg. In transitive *ru* ‘fetch, bring’, the motion is understood as going from point A to point B to retrieve something and then returning to A with it, and the orientation preverb indicates the direction of that return trip.

It also notes that *ru* generally behaves like a fully transitive verb and usually appears with AM prefixes, including in infinitival and participial forms. However, in the purposive motion construction with *ɕego* and *ɣicome*, the participial form occurs without an AM prefix, and some surface forms can be ambiguous between transitive *bring* and semi-transitive *look at*.

subsection: Associated motion vs. motion verb construction
text:
associated motion!purposive
To express the meaning of motion prior to an action, associated motion prefixes are nearly two times as common as corresponding motion verb constructions (henceforth MVC) in the Japhug corpus. There is however a clear semantic difference between the two constructions, which was briefly described in, but is presented here in more detail.

AM and MVC differ from each other in that in the former, the completion of both motion event and verbal action is presupposed, whereas in the case of the latter, the two can be separated. This difference in degree of event integration is most conspicuous in Aorist forms, and can be observed in four types of constructions: concessives (with negation of the verbal action), interrogatives, conditionals and complement clauses.

Another difference between MVC and AM is the fact that while MVC require a volitional verb in the purposive complement, there is no such requirement for the AM markers.
summary: Associated motion prefixes are nearly twice as frequent as corresponding motion verb constructions in the Japhug corpus, but the two constructions differ semantically. In associated motion, the completion of both the motion event and the verbal action is presupposed, whereas in motion verb constructions the two events can be separated; this difference is especially clear in Aorist forms and appears in concessives, interrogatives, conditionals, and complement clauses. In addition, motion verb constructions require a volitional verb in the purposive complement, but associated motion markers do not.

subsection: Associated motion vs. motion verb construction
text:
associated motion!concessive clause concessive clause!associated motion
A MVC with the motion verb in perfective form can be followed by a clause negating the purposive action, as in ( ex:nAkWrtoR ). In this example, only the motion is realized, while the action expressed by the verb rtoʁlook could not be accomplished.

exe

nɤ-kɯ-rtoʁ jɤ-ɣe-a ri, mɯ-nɯ-atɯɣ-tɕi, mɯ-pɯ-ta-mto. \\
1sg. poss - sbj: pcp -see aor -come[II]- 1sg lnk neg - aor -meet- 1du neg - aor -1 2-see \\
`I came to see you but I did not see you.'
exe

With the corresponding AM verb form ɣɯ-jɤ-ta-rtoʁI came and saw you, negating the action of the verb is self-contradictory and nonsensical, and a sentence such as ( ex:GWjAtartoR ) is incorrect.

exe

$ $ɣɯ-jɤ-ta-rtoʁ ri mɯ-pɯ-ta-mto \\
cisl - aor -1 2-look lnk neg - aor -1 2-see \\
Intended meaning: `I came to see you but I did not see you.'
exe

Additional minimal pairs of the same type are presented in.

Example ( ex:mWjsWntsGe ) from a conversation illustrates this property also with a manipulative verb ɣɯtbring: the action of the essive participial complement kɤ-ntsɣesell (§ sec:participial.clause.essive ) is negated in the following clause (with an abilitative sɯ, see § sec:abilitative ).

exe

sɤnɤmmtsʰu kɯ kɤ-ntsɣe cʰɤ-ɣɯt ri mɯ́j-sɯ-ntsɣe ndɤre, \\
anthr erg obj: pcp -sell ifr: downstream -bring lnk neg: sens - abil -sell lnk \\
`Bsod.nams.mtsho brought them [to Mbarkham] to sell, but could not sell them.' (conversation, 14.05.10)
exe
summary: A motion verb in perfective form within a multiverb construction can be followed by a clause that negates the intended purposive action, so that only the motion is realized and the goal action fails. The passage contrasts this with the associated-motion verb form, where negating the action would be contradictory, and notes that the same pattern also occurs with a manipulative verb, as in an example meaning “brought them to sell, but could not sell them.”

subsection: Associated motion vs. motion verb construction
text:
The difference between MVC and AM in interrogatives can be illustrated by the minimal pair ( ex:tChi.WkWpa ) and ( ex:tChi.GWtAtWpat ).

In interrogative, MVCs are required to express meanings such as `What/who have you come/gone to X', as in example ( ex:tChi.WkWpa ), an example which occurs nine times in the corpus.

Example ( ex:tChi.WkWpa ) presupposes that the addressee has not done anything yet, while ( ex:tChi.GWtAtWpat ) with associated motion can only be used if the presupposition is that the action has already taken place, requiring a different translation.

exe

tɕʰi ɯ-kɯ-pa jɤ-tɯ-ɣe? \\
what 3sg. poss -do aor -2-come[II] \\

summary: The passage contrasts MVCs and associated motion (AM) in interrogatives: MVCs are used for questions like “What/who have you come/gone to do?”, and they presuppose that the addressee has not yet done the action. By contrast, AM forms imply that the relevant action has already taken place, as shown in the examples with eating or sewing after motion. The text also notes that this semantic restriction is not universal, since in languages like Nanai AM markers can be used even when only the motion event is presupposed to have been completed.

subsection: Associated motion vs. motion verb construction
text:
The presuppositional difference between a MVC and AM is also perceptible in the protasis of conditional clauses.

With a MVC in the protasis as in ( ex:mWmAjAtWGe ), there is no presupposition that the verbal action took place, and the motion event alone constitutes a condition to the state of affair described in the apodosis.

exe

nɤ-wa ɯ-kɯ-rtoʁ mɯ mɤ-jɤ-tɯ-ɣe nɤ aʑo mɯ-pɯ-kɯ-mto-a. \\
2sg. poss -father 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -look cond neg - aor -2-come[II] lnk 1sg neg - aor -2 1- 1sg \\
`If you had not come to see your father, you would not have seen me.' (you saw me, but your father was not here)
exe

By contrast, with AM, the verbal action necessarily took place, as in example ( ex:mWmAGWjAtWrtoR ).

exe

nɤ-wa mɯ mɤ-ɣɯ-jɤ-tɯ-rtoʁ nɤ pɯ-sɤzdɯxpa \\

`If you had not come and seen your father, he would have been sorry.' (but you did see him, so he does not feel sorry)
exe
summary: The passage explains that MVCs and AMs differ in conditional protases because they carry different presuppositions. With an MVC, the motion event alone serves as the condition and there is no presupposition that the verbal action occurred, whereas with an AM, the verbal action is presupposed to have taken place.

subsection: Associated motion vs. motion verb construction
text:
associated motion!complement clause complement clause!associated motion
In complement clauses, verbs with AM prefixes are attested, and complement-taking verbs always have scope over both the action of the verb and motion event.

The combination ofodal verbs such as cʰacan with double negation, with the specific meaning `cannot help', § sec:double.negation, have scope over both the motion event and the verbal action.

This is illustrated in example ( ex:mACWkAtshi ), which is taken from a passage in a story where the king scolded a small child, who had just returned from a mission he himself send him on, because the child did not come to greet him first upon his return. Example ( ex:mACWkAtshi ) shows the answer the child uses to justify why he went to see his mother first before greeting the king. From context it is clear that both the motion event (to his mother's house, explaining the child's failure to go to see the king) and the action `drink milk' (the reason for that motion event) are equally important to the plot and inseparable.

In complement clauses, verbs with associated-motion (AM) prefixes show that complement-taking verbs can scope over both the motion event and the verbal action. The same broad scope is found with certain modal, aspectual, and conditional constructions, where the motion and action are inseparable in meaning and both are affected by negation, ability, or time.

By contrast, in one purposive-clause example with an infinitival complement, the auxiliary only scopes over the motion event, not the work itself. This contrast shows that the scope of these verbs can differ depending on the clause type.

subsection: Associated motion vs. motion verb construction
text:
associated motion!volitionality volitionality!associated motion
An additional difference between AM and MVC has to do with volitionality and/or controllability. In the case of an MVC, the verb in the purposive clause, whose action follows the motion event, is always necessarily volitional and controllable. By contrast, in the case of AM, it is possible to find examples where the verbal action expresses a non-controllable event.

For example in ( ex:CpjAmto ) and ( ex:CpWrndutCi ), the verbs ɕ-pjɤ-mto `he (went and) saw/found it there' (with verb echo, § § sec:AM.echo ) and ɕ-pɯ-rndu-tɕi `we (went and) obtained it' express the action of finding something or someone, whose outcome is not controllable. Note that there are no examples of the non-volitional verb mtosee with the MVC in the corpus (the volitional rtoʁlook or rulook at occur instead).

subsection: Associated motion vs. motion verb construction
text:
associated motion!relative clause relative clause!associated motion
Another difference between MVC and AM is related to the relativizability of core arguments. In the MVC, the common subject of the motion verb and the verb of the purposive clause (including transitive subject) can be relativized, and if overt, the head can be internal, between the purposive clause and the nominalized motion verb, as tɤ-tɕɯson, boy in ( ex:tAtCW.jAkAri ), or occur after the whole clause.

exe

[[tɤ-mu ɯ-kɯ-rtoʁ] tɤ-tɕɯ jɤ-kɯ-ɤri] nɯ a-ʁi ŋu \\
indef. poss -mother 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -see indef. poss -son aor - sbj: pcp -go[II] dem 1sg. poss -younger.sibling be: fact \\
`The boy who went to see the old lady is my brother.' (elicited)
exe

On the other hand, when the verb of the purposive clause is transitive, it is not possible to relativize the object. Example ( ex:WkWrtoR.incorrect ), with an overt transitive subject a-ʁi kɯ is thus non-grammatical, and the phrase ɯ-kɯ-rtoʁ jɤ-kɯ-ɤri tɤ-mu can only be interpreted as a subject relative `the old lady who went to see him'.

exe

†a-ʁi kɯ ɯ-kɯ-rtoʁ jɤ-kɯ-ɤri tɤ-mu nɯ a-ɬaʁ ŋu \\
1sg. poss -younger.sibling erg 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -see aor - sbj: pcp -go[II] indef. poss -mother dem 1sg. poss -MZ be: fact \\
Intended meaning: `The old lady that my younger brother went to see is my aunt.'
exe

The only way to build a relative clause with this meaning is to use AM prefixes. In ( ex:zjartoR ) for instance, the prenominal finite relative (a subtype that is restricted to object or goal relativization, § sec:finite.relatives ) a-ʁi kɯ z-ja-rtoʁ does not contain any additional embedded clause, and is a simple case of object relativization.

exe

[a-ʁi kɯ z-ja-rtoʁ] tɤ-mu nɯ a-ɬaʁ ŋu \\
1sg. poss -younger.sibling erg tral - aor:3 -see indef. poss -mother dem 1sg. poss -MZ be: fact \\
`The old lady that my younger brother went to see is my aunt.' (elicited)
exe

The fact that by contrast ( ex:WkWrtoR.incorrect ) is not grammatical shows that relativization out of purposive clauses is prohibited in Japhug grammar, unlike some complement clauses (§ sec:out.complement.relativization ).
summary:
The passage contrasts MVCs with associated motion (AM) in terms of relativization: in MVCs, the shared subject of the motion verb and purposive clause can be relativized, and the head noun may appear internally or outside the clause. However, if the purposive verb is transitive, its object cannot be relativized; only the subject can be, and the example intended to relativize the object is ungrammatical.

To express that meaning, Japhug must use AM prefixes and a finite relative clause, which functions as ordinary object relativization without an embedded purposive clause. This shows that relativization out of purposive clauses is not allowed in Japhug grammar.

text:
The distinction between finite and non-finite verb forms is easy to draw in Japhug: the former have person indexation (see chapter § chap:indexation ), while the latter do not. The only personal markers found on non-finite verb forms are possessive prefixes, the same set as in underived nouns (§ sec:possessive.prefixes ).

In this chapter, I distinguish between several sub-categories of non-finite verb forms, including participles, infinitives, degree and action nominals as well as several converbs. In addition to describing the morphology of these verb forms, I also present their functions to build various types of subordinate clauses, including relative, complement and purposive clauses.
summary: In Japhug, finite verb forms are distinguished from non-finite ones by the presence of person indexation on finite forms, whereas non-finite forms lack it and may only take possessive prefixes, the same ones used with underived nouns. The chapter distinguishes several kinds of non-finite verb forms—such as participles, infinitives, degree and action nominals, and several converbs—and describes both their morphology and their role in forming subordinate clauses like relative, complement, and purposive clauses.

text:
Japhug speakers, like Ancient Greeks, can be aptly described as φιλομέτοχοι `participle lovers': Japhug and other Gyalrong languages have a rich system of participles, and these non-finite forms play a central role in the syntax of the language.

Participles are nominalized verb forms that keep some verbal characteristics: they can serve as predicates of subordinate clauses (in particular relative and complement clauses), take TAM, polarity and associated motion marking, and preserve the verb's argument structure.

Participles differ from finite verbs in three ways. First, they cannot serve as the predicate of a main clause. Second, they are not compatible with the personal indexation of the intransitive and transitive conjugations (including direct/inverse marking, § sec:allomorphy.inv ), and with all inflectional suffixes without exception (§ sec:suffixes ). Japhug is identical in this regard to Tshobdun and Zbu, but crucially differs from Situ, where nominalized forms in kə- can bear indexation suffixes. Rather, like nouns, they can take a possessive prefix which can be coreferent with one of the arguments. Due to the general impossibility of stacking possessive prefixes (§ sec:possessive.paradigm ), at most only one argument can be indexed this way. Third, there are restrictions on TAM marking on participles: they have at most three forms (neutral, perfective and imperfective), and completely lack Inferential (§ sec:ifr ), Egophoric Present (§ sec:egophoric ) or Sensory (§ sec:sensory ) forms.

There are three participles in Japhug; the subject S/A participle in kɯ, the object participle in kɤ- and the oblique participle in sɤ-.

Complex participial forms, including negative, associated motion or TAM prefixes are possible, as shown by example ( ex:WGWjAkWqru ). However, never more than four inflectional prefixes are found; forms with all five prefixal slots filled (such as $ $ ɯ-ɣɯ-jɤ-kɯ-qru ) are not accepted by Tshendzin.

exe

ɯ-ɣɯ-jɤ-kɯ-qru tɤ-tɕɯ \\
3sg - cisl - aor - sbj: pcp -meet indef. poss -boy \\
`The boy who had come to look for her' (The three sisters)
exe

tab:template.nmlz summarizes the template of participial verb forms; more details are provided on possible and attested forms for each participle type in the following sections.

Stem alternation is reduced in participle forms: stem III (§ sec:stem3.distribution ) never occurs. The few verbs that have an alternation between stem I and stem II ( ɕego, ɣicome, tisay and derived forms, § sec:stem2 ), however, use stem II in subject and object participles with perfective orientational prefixes (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), in forms like jɤ-kɯ-ɣe aor - sbj: pcp -come[II] `the one who came'
or tɤ-kɤ-tɯt aor - obj: pcp -say[II] `what was said'.
summary:
Japhug has a rich system of participles that are central to subordinate clause syntax, where they can function in relative and complement clauses while retaining some verbal properties such as TAM, polarity, associated motion, and argument structure. They differ from finite verbs because they cannot be the predicate of a main clause, lack personal indexation and all inflectional suffixes, and have only limited TAM forms; instead, they may take a possessive prefix coreferential with one argument, and Japhug has three participles: subject, object, and oblique.

Participial forms can also combine with prefixes for negation, associated motion, or TAM, though not with more than four inflectional prefixes, and stem alternation is reduced: stem III never appears. In the few verbs that alternate between stem I and stem II, stem II is used in subject and object participles with perfective orientational prefixes.

text:
participle!subject
The subject participle, built by adding the prefix kɯ- to the verb stem, designates an entity corresponding to the intransitive subject ( ex:kWsi, § sec:absolutive.S and § sec:intr.subject.relativization ), a possessor of the subject (§ sec:S.possessor.relativization ), or the transitive subject ( ex:WkWndza, § sec:A.kW, § sec:tr.subject.relativization ) of the base verb.

exe

kɯ-si \\
sbj: pcp -die \\
`The dead one' (many attestations)
exe

exe

ɯ-kɯ-ndza \\
3sg - sbj: pcp -eat \\
`The one who eats it' (many attestations)
exe

With a- initial verbs the kɯ- prefix regularly merge with a- as kɤ, a form which resembles an object participle. There is almost no ambiguity since all a- initial verbs are intransitive, § sec:contraction ). The only exception are the semi-transitive verbs in a, such as aroown, whose subject participle kɯ-ɤro `having, the one who has' and object participle kɤ-ɤro both surface as kɤro.

The subject participle kɯ- prefix is historically related to that of object participles (§ sec:object.participle ), velar infinitives (§ sec:velar.inf ) and deverbal nouns in x-/ɣ- (§ sec:G.nmlz ), and has cognates elsewhere in the family (§ sec:velar.nmlz.history ).

In this section, I discuss first morphological issues (possessive prefixes § sec:subject.participle.ambiguities, other prefixes § sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes and ambiguous forms § sec:subject.participle.ambiguities ), and then present the various functions of subject participles, including participial relatives (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative and § sec:subject.participle.other.relative ), complementation strategies (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation ), as well as the case of lexicalized participles (§ sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ).

Examples which could potentially be viewed as subject participles in converbial use are analyzed as kɯ- infinitives (§ sec:inf.converb ).
summary:
The subject participle is formed with the prefix kɯ- attached to the verb stem and refers to the intransitive subject, a possessor of the subject, or the transitive subject of the base verb. With a- initial verbs, kɯ- normally merges with a- to give kɤ, which can resemble an object participle, though this is rarely ambiguous because such verbs are generally intransitive.  

The passage also notes that the subject participle prefix is historically related to prefixes used in object participles, velar infinitives, and deverbal nouns, and has cognates elsewhere in the family. The section then outlines the topics to be discussed: morphology, various functions of subject participles, and lexicalized forms, while excluding cases better analyzed as kɯ- infinitives.

text:
participle!subject prefix!possessive
In the case of transitive verbs, a possessive prefix coreferent with the object is obligatory when no overt object is present ( 3sg ɯ- in ex:WkWndza ), and when no other prefix is added to the participle.

When another prefix (polarity, associated motion or orientation preverb) is present, the possessive prefix is optional, as shown by forms like mɤ-kɯ-ndza `the one which does not eat (it)' in ( ex:mAkWndza ), as opposed to ɯ-mɤ-kɯ-mto `the one who does not see it' in ( ex:WmAkWmto ) with both possessive ɯ- and the negative prefix mɤ-.
