exe

exe

aʑo a-kɯ-ra nɯra a-tɤ-tɯ-ste qʰendɤre aʑo nɯnɯ, nɤki, ku-nɤtsi-a jɤɣ \\
1sg 1sg. poss - sbj: pcp -be.needed dem: pl irr - pfv -2-do.like[III] lnk 1sg dem filler ipfv -hide[III]- 1sg be.possible: fact \\
`If you do the things I need, I will keep it secret.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

Since participles are also noun-like, the possessive prefixes can be real possessive, and be preceded with a genitive phrase as in ( ex:tCaXpa.ra.GW.nWkWmna ) with nɯ-kɯ-mna `the best among them' = `their chief' (on the verb mnabe better, see § sec:mna.sna ).

exe

tɕaχpa ra ɣɯ nɯ-kɯ-mna nɯ wuma ʑo pjɤ-nɯrɤŋom.\\
bandit pl gen 3pl. poss - sbj: pcp -be.better dem really emph ifr -be.upset\\
`The chief of the bandits was very upset.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S186
exe

This construction is used as a type of superlative (§ sec:possessed.superlative ).
summary:
For transitive participles, a possessive prefix coreferent with the object is required when no overt object is expressed and no other prefix is present; if another prefix such as negative, polarity, associated motion, or orientation is present, the possessive prefix becomes optional. The possessive prefix in ditransitives refers strictly to the object: with indirective verbs it must denote the theme rather than the recipient, while with secundative verbs it obligatorily refers to the recipient.

The passage also notes that intransitive and adjectival stative participles may take possessive prefixes referring to a semi-object or beneficiary. Because participles are noun-like, these prefixes can also have genuine possessive force and combine with genitive phrases, yielding constructions used as a type of superlative.

subsubsection: Associated motion, polarity and orientation preverbs on subject participles
text:
participle!subject associated motion orientation!preverb
Of all non-finite verb forms, subject participles allow the richest possible combinations of inflectional prefixes: associated motion (§ sec:associated.motion, example ex:WCWkWphWt ) below with the translocative ɕɯ- ), polarity (§ sec:negation, see ex:WmAkWmto above) and orientation preverbs marking TAME (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) all can be prefixed.

exe

tɕeri nɯra ɯ-ɕɯ-kɯ-pʰɯt ra kɯ-tu me ma, \\
lnk dem: pl 3sg. poss - tral - sbj: pcp -cut pl sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact lnk \\
`But nobody goes and picks it.'(11-paRzwamWntoR)
0003476#S81
exe

Two of the four series of orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) are possible with subject participles. With A-type prefixes ( tɤ- upwards, pɯ- downwards etc), the participle of dynamic verbs is perfective as tʰɯ-kɯ-ɣe `the one who came' in ( ex:WkWntsGe.thWkWGe ), and takes stem II (§ sec:stem2 ). With B-type prefixes ( tu- upwards, pjɯ- downwards ), it has a habitual imperfective meaning with dynamic verbs as ju-kɯ-ɣi `the one who (usually) comes' in ( ex:WkWndza.jukWGi ). These two examples also illustrate the use of subject participles as purposive complements with the forms ɯ-kɯ-ntsɣe and ɯ-kɯ-ndza (see § sec:subject.participle.complementation, § sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ). The prefixes ɲɯ- and ku- do appear on subject participles, but only to express imperfective: there are no Egophoric (§ sec:egophoric ) or Sensory (§ sec:sensory ) subject partiples.

exe

iɕqʰa qaʑo ɯ-kɯ-ntsɣe tʰɯ-kɯ-ɣe nɯ ɯ-pʰe \\
the.aforementioned sheep 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -sell aor: downstream - sbj: pcp -come[II] dem 3sg. poss - dat \\
`[He told] the person who had come to sell the sheep.' (2003kandZislama)
exe

exe

ɯ-kɯ-ndza ju-kɯ-ɣi nɯ pɣa ci ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -eat ipfv - sbj: pcp -come dem bird indef sens -be \\
`The one who comes to eat [the fruits] is a bird.' (2012-qachGa)
0004087#S22
exe

The participles of stative verbs with series A and B orientation preverbs have an inchoative meaning, exactly like their finite counterpart (§ sec:aor.inchoative and § sec:ipfv.inchoative ). In ( ex:YWkWjpum ) for instance, the imperfective participle ɲɯ-kɯ-jpum from jpumbe thick means `the one which becomes thicker', as opposed to the basic participle kɯ-jpum `the thick one'.

exe

ndʑu ɯ-ku jamar ɲɯ-kɯ-jpum ɣɤʑu nɤ, kɯ-wxti. \\
chopsticks 3sg. poss -head about ipfv - sbj: pcp -be.thick exist: sens sfp sbj: pcp -be.big \\
`There are [maggots] that grow as thick as the tip of a chopstick, the big ones.' (25-akWzgumba)
0003632#S73
exe

Imperfective participles of stative adjectival verbs are also can also describe the gradient variation of a property across space rather than time. For instance, in ( ex:YWkWjpum2 ), the imperfective subject participles ku-kɯ-xtsʰɯm and ɲɯ-kɯ-jpum are used not to indicate a change across time, but to describe the shape of the gourd, which is progressively thinner towards the top and thicker towards the bottom (on the contrast between the eastwards ku- vs. westwards ɲɯ- preverbs in this context, see § sec:centripetal.centrifugal ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-mat nɯnɯ, ɯ-taʁ ku-kɯ-xtsʰɯm, ɯ-pa ɲɯ-kɯ-jpum ci cʰɯ-βze ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, nɯ <hulu> tu-sɤrmi-nɯ. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -fruit dem 3sg. poss -up ipfv - sbj: pcp -be.thin 3sg. poss -down ipfv - sbj: pcp -be.thick indef ipfv -make[III] sens -be lnk dem gourd ipfv -call- pl \\
`It has a fruit that is thinner [in diameter] on the upper part, and thicker on the lower part, people call it `gourd'.' (150825 huluwa-zh)
0006346#S3
exe

The past imperfective of stative verbs is built using the series A prefix pɯ- as in the corresponding finite forms (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ). For instance, the past imperfective participle of ŋube is pɯ-kɯ-ŋu `the one who used to be....' (§ sec:non.existing.derivation ), as in ( ex:pWkWNu ).

exe

ɯʑɤɣ nɯ ɕɯŋgɯ ɯ-nmaʁ pɯ-kɯ-ŋu tsʰɯraŋ nɯ pjɤ-mto \\
3sg: gen dem before 3sg. poss -husband pst. ipfv - sbj: pcp -be anthr dem ifr -see \\
`She saw Tshering, who used to be her husband.' (qajdoskAt 2002) 0003366#S101
exe

Most examples in the corpus have one or two prefixes, either combining a possessive prefix with another prefix (as in ex:WmAkWmto and ex:WCWkWphWt ), or combining a negative prefix with an orientation preverb, as in ( ex:mWnWkWsna ).

exe

tɕe kʰa ɣɯ ɯ-ndzɤtsʰi ɯ-ro nɯ-kɯ-ri nɯra, mɯ-nɯ-kɯ-sna nɯra, nɯra paʁ kɯ ʁɟa tu-ndze ɲɯ-ŋu \\
lnk house gen 3sg. poss -food 3sg. poss -excess aor - sbj: pcp -left dem: pl neg - aor - sbj: pcp -be.good dem: pl dem: pl pig erg completely ipfv -eat[III] sens -be \\
`Leftover food from the house, or food which is not good any more, pigs eat all of it.' (05-paR)
0003400#S32
exe

Subject participles with three prefixes before the participle prefix kɯ- are possible, but attestations are rare. Example ( ex:WGWjAkWqru ) above shows the combination of a possessive, an associated motion and an orientation preverbs ( ɯ-ɣɯ-jɤ-kɯ-qru `the one who had come to meet/look for her'), and ( ex:WmApjWkWnWfkAB ) below that of a possessive, a polarity and an orientation preverbs.

exe

ɯ-pjɯ-kɯ-nɯ-fkaβ tu, ɯ-mɤ-pjɯ-kɯ-nɯ-fkaβ tu ri nɯ kɯ-fse tu-nɯ-ndza-nɯ ɕti. \\
3sg. poss - ipfv - sbj: pcp - auto -cover exist: fact 3sg. poss - neg - ipfv - sbj: pcp - auto -cover exist: fact lnk dem sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv - auto -eat- pl be. aff: fact \\
`There are people who cover it (with a lid while cooking), and people who don't, they eat it as is.' (23-mbrAZim)
0003604#S20
exe

In addition to imperfective orientation preverbs as in ( ex:WmApjWkWnWfkAB ), it is possible for subject participles to combine possessive prefixes with perfective orientation preverbs, as in ( ex:WnWkWCar ). Subject participles are the only non-finite forms attested with such a combination: the object participles do not allow combination of possessive and orientation preverbs (§ sec:object.participle.possessive ) and the oblique participles cannot take perfective orientation preverbs (§ sec:oblique.participle.orientation ).

exe
summary:
Subject participles allow the widest range of prefix combinations among non-finite verb forms, including associated motion, polarity, and orientation preverbs, and sometimes up to three prefixes before the participle marker. With dynamic verbs, A-type orientation preverbs give a perfective meaning and B-type preverbs give a habitual imperfective meaning; with stative verbs, the same preverbs yield an inchoative interpretation, while past imperfective forms are built with the A-type prefix pɯ-.  

Imperfective subject participles of stative adjectives can also describe gradual spatial variation in a property, not just change over time. The passage further notes that while possessive prefixes can combine with orientation preverbs in subject participles, this pattern is rare and is not attested for object or oblique participles.

subsubsection: Associated motion, polarity and orientation preverbs on subject participles
text:
nɯnɯ ɯ-nɯ-kɯ-ɕar ɯ-pɯ-kɯ-mto nɯ ɣɯ ɲɯ-tʂaŋ ma nɯnɯ, nɤkinɯ, ɯ-ɕɯ-kɯ-βɟi nɯ ɣɯ mɯ́j-tʂaŋ \\
dem 3sg. poss - aor - sbj: pcp -search 3sg. poss - aor - sbj: pcp -see dem gen sens -be.fair lnk dem filler 3sg. poss - tral - sbj: pcp -chase dem gen neg: sens -be.fair \\
`It is fair that she would [be given] to the one who looked for her and found her, not to the ones chasing her.' (140517 buaishuohua-zh)
0004018#S117
exe

The negative prefix has the form mɯ- when occurring with a perfective orientation preverb as mɯ-nɯ-kɯ-sna `the one that is not good anymore' in ( ex:mWnWkWsna ) and mɤ- when no orientation preverb is present (examples ex:WmAkWmto and ex:mAkWndza above). With the imperfective orientation preverbs, the allomorph mɤ- occurs when preceded by a possessive prefix ( ex:WmApjWkWnWfkAB ) and mɯ- is found when no possessive prefix is present: compare the elicited forms ( ex:WmAkukWtshi ) and ( ex:mWkukWtshi ). The allomorphs of the negative prefix are not in free variation: forms such as $ $ ɯ-mɯ-ku-kɯ-tsʰi or $ $ mɤ-ku-kɯ-tsʰi would be incorrect in Kamnyu Japhug.

exe

ɯ-mɤ-ku-kɯ-tsʰi \\
3sg. poss - neg - ipfv - sbj: pcp -drink \\

mɯ-ku-kɯ-tsʰi \\
neg - ipfv - sbj: pcp -drink \\
`The one who drinks it.' (elicited)
exe

There are no constraints on the number of derivational prefixes in participial forms. The derivational prefixes are all closer to the verb root than the participle prefix kɯ, and thus follow it as shown by ( ex:WmApjWkWnWfkAB ), where the autive -nɯ, the leftmost of all derivational prefixes (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ), is placed after kɯ-.

Aside from possessive, orientation, associated motion and polarity prefixes, subject participles can also receive the Proximative aspect prefix jɯ- (see ex:jWtukWwGrum, § sec:proximative ).

Subject participles can undergo totalitative reduplication (§ sec:totalitative.redp, § sec:totalitative.relatives ), which applies to the first syllable of the word, whether it is the participle kɯ- or an orientation preverb as in ( ex:jWjAkWGe ), meaning `all of those who/that X'.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ ɯ-taʁ jɯ jɤ-kɯ-ɣe nɯ ku-ndɤm ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk dem 3sg. poss -on total aor - sbj: pcp -come[II] dem ipfv -take[III] sens -be \\
`[The spider] catches all of the [insects] that have come onto [its web].' (26-mYaRmtsaR) 0003674#S99
exe
summary:
The passage explains that the negative prefix in Kamnyu Japhug has context-sensitive allomorphs: mɯ- appears with perfective orientation preverbs, while mɤ- appears when no such preverb is present, and with imperfective orientation preverbs the choice depends on whether a possessive prefix precedes it. These forms are not free variants, since incorrect combinations are ungrammatical.

It also states that participial forms can contain multiple derivational prefixes, all of which occur closer to the verb root than the participle prefix kɯ-. In addition, subject participles may take the proximative prefix jɯ- and can undergo totalitative reduplication of the first syllable, expressing a meaning like ‘all of those who/that X.’

text:
ambiguity!participle
The subject participle kɯ- prefix is homophonous with the generic person marker for intransitive subject and object (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr; note that these two prefixes are probably historically related, § sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history ). In the case of intransitive verbs, some subject participles are therefore homophonous with generic person forms.

For instance, the past imperfective generic pɯ-kɯ-ŋu `one used to be' in ( ex:pWkWNu.genr ) is identical to the past imperfective participle pɯ-kɯ-ŋu `the one who used to be....', discussed above (example ex:pWkWNu in § sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes ). In this example, it is obvious that kɯ- is the generic person marker because the verb pɯ-kɯ-rga `one used to be' occurs as the main verb; outside of any context, tɤ-pɤtso pɯ-kɯ-ŋu could be understood as a relative clause `the one who used to be a child', but this is not the meaning of this sentence.

exe

tɕeri tɤ-pɤtso pɯ-kɯ-ŋu tɕe, nɯ kɤ-ndza wuma ʑo pɯ-kɯ-rga. \\
lnk indef. poss -child pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-be lnk dem inf -eat really emph pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-like \\
`When [we] were children, [we] used to like eating it.' (12-ndZiNgri) 0003488#S126
exe

More generally, the Factual, Imperfective, Past Imperfective and Aorist forms of intransitive verbs in generic person forms are homophonous with unmarked, Imperfective, Past Imperfective and Aorist participles, respectively. In the case of transitive verbs, the subject participle can be identical to the object generic form. For instance, the participle nɯ-tu-kɯ-ndza `the one who eats them' in ( ex:tukWndza.nmlz ) only differs from the generic tu-kɯ-ndza `it eats us/people' in ( ex:tukWndza.genr ) by the possessive prefix nɯ, and that prefix being optional, there are forms that are really ambiguous between participle and generic.

exe

nɯ ɯ-rkɯ jɤ-azɣɯt-nɯ tɕe, ʑara nɯ-tu-kɯ-ndza srɯnmɯ ci pjɤ-tu, \\
dem 3sg. poss -side aor -reach- pl lnk 3pl 3pl. poss - ipfv - sbj: pcp -eat râkshasî indef ifr. ipfv -be \\
`There was a râkshasî who ate those who came near her.' (2012 Kunbzang) 0003768#S219
exe

exe

tɕe ndzɤpri kɤ-ti nɯ tɕe tɯrme tu-kɯ-ndza ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl \\
lnk brown.bear obj: pcp -say dem lnk people ipfv - genr:S/O sens -be.usually.the.case \\
`The one called `brown bear', it eats people.' (21-pri)
0003580#S91
exe

The irregular generic tu-kɯ-ti `one says' of the verb tisay is also identical with the participle `the one who says'.

The 2sg 1sg form of transitive verbs in -a, due to the vowel fusion rule -a-a -a, are also superficially identical to subject participles. For instance tu-kɯ-ndza-a `you eat me' is pronounced tukɯndza exactly like the generic and the participle tu-kɯ-ndza in the Kamnyu dialect (in the dialects of Japhug where this vowel fusion does not occur, the forms remain distinct).

exe

nɯ kóʁmɯz nɤ tu-kɯ-ndza-a \\
dem only.after lnk ipfv -2 1-eat- 1sg \\
`Eat me only after [having taken the thorn from my foot].' (140426 lang yisheng-zh)
0003808#S16
exe

In the case of stative verbs and some auxiliary verbs, the infinitive has in some cases the form kɯ, and there is thus ambiguity between infinitive and subject participial forms for these verbs (§ sec:velar.inf ).
summary: The subject participial prefix kɯ- is homophonous with the generic person marker for intransitive subjects and objects, so some intransitive participles and generic forms are identical. The passage shows that this ambiguity also occurs with certain transitive and irregular verb forms, where participles can match generic forms except for an optional possessive prefix or, in some dialects, vowel fusion. For some stative and auxiliary verbs, the infinitive form kɯ further creates ambiguity between infinitive and subject participial forms.

text:
participle!subject relative clause!subject
The most common use of subject participles is to build participial relative clauses whose head noun is the subject; it is the only way to relativize the subject in Japhug (§ sec:intr.subject.relativization ). Headless relatives are most common (§ sec:headless.relative ), but when the head noun is overt, the relative can be either prenominal, postnominal or head-internal. With intransitive verbs the difference between postnominal or head-internal relatives is often difficult to ascertain, and many examples are ambiguous; for instance in ( ex:tCheme.RnWz.kWrWCmi ), the relative clause could be argued to be postnominal (limited to the participle kɯ-rɯɕmi `speaking') or head-internal (including tɕʰeme ʁnɯz `two girls', and possibly even the previous adjunct).

exe

kʰa ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu tɕʰeme ʁnɯz kɯ-rɯɕmi pjɤ-tu. \\
house 3sg. poss -inside dem: loc girl two sbj: pcp -speak ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`There were two girls speaking in the house.' (150909 xiaocui-zh)
0006386#S144
exe

Other examples such as ( ex:kWm.WrkW.zW.pGa ) are unambiguously head-internal, since the locative adjunct kɯm ɯ-rkɯ zɯ cannot belong to the matrix clause. This example additionally illustrates the necessity of using a subject relative clause with an existential verb to connect a noun with an postpositional phrase ($ $ kɯm ɯ-rkɯ zɯ pɣa would not be a complete sentence).

exe

kumpɣa nɯnɯ tɕe [kɯm ɯ-rkɯ zɯ pɣa kɯ-tu] kɤ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
fowl dem lnk door 3sg. poss -side loc bird sbj: pcp -exist inf -say sens -be \\
`The word kumpɣafowl means `the bird that is next to the door'.' (22-kumpGa).
0003588#S3
exe

With transitive verbs, subject head-internal relatives can be distinguished from postnominal ones by the presence of the ergative kɯ on the head noun (§ sec:head-internal.relative ), as in ( ex:WrdWrdoR.kW.thotsi.WkWta ).

exe

[tsuku ɯ-rdɯ rdoʁ kɯ ʑo tʰotsi ɯ-kɯ-ta] ɣɤʑu. \\
some 3sg. poss -piece erg emph decorative.stamp 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -put exist: sens \\
`There are people who put a decorative mark [on their bread].' (160706 thotsi) 0006133#S20
exe

Prenominal relatives are relatively rare with intransitive verbs, but commonly occur with transitive verbs, as in ( ex:tWnW.WkWtshi ). Note the presence of indefinite person possessive marking on the head noun tɤ-pɤtsochild in this example; unlike in Situ, the head noun of prenominal relatives in Japhug does not take a third person singular prefix as in a possessive construction (in which case the form $ $ ɯ-pɤtso would have been found).

exe

[tɯ-nɯ ɯ-kɯ-tsʰi] tɤ-pɤtso ɣɯ ɯ-kɯ-mŋɤm ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
indef. poss -breast 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -drink indef. poss -child gen 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -hurt sens -be lnk \\
`It is a disease [that affects] infants who still drink their mother's milk.' (25-kACAl)
0003640#S54
exe

There are nevertheless prenominal genitival subject relative clauses, containing a subject participle, with the genitive ɣɯ occurring between the relative clause and the head noun. This construction is especially common in texts translated from Chinese (due to calquing with 的 <de>-relatives, § sec:genitival.relatives ), but also attested in natural speech, as in ( ex:kWsAndza.GW ).

exe

nɯnɯ kɯ-sɤ-ndza ɣɯ rɯdaʁ nɯnɯ tɕe kɯrŋi tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
dem sbj: pcp - apass -eat gen animal dem lnk beast ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`Animals eating [other animals] are called `beasts'.' (150822 kWrNi)
0006260#S6
exe

When subject relative clauses contain a complement clause, the main verb of the complement clause can be in subject participle form (see example ex:ndZikWsAndu in § sec:participial.complements.negative ).
summary: Subject participles are most commonly used to form subject relative clauses in Japhug, and they are the only way to relativize subjects. When the head noun is overt, these relatives may be prenominal, postnominal, head-internal, or genitival, with headless relatives being most common overall; the passage notes that some intransitive examples are ambiguous, while transitive head-internal relatives can be identified by ergative marking on the head noun.

text:
participle!subject relative clause!possessor
In addition to subject relativization, the subject participle is also used in possessor relatives, when the relativized element is the possessor of the subject (§ sec:S.possessor.relativization ). The head-internal clause in ( ex:kWkWtu.head.internal ) is such a possessor relative; its head noun sitree, possessor of the subject ɯ-mat `its fruits', is marked with the genitive, showing that it belongs to the relative.

exe

[si ɣɯ ɯ-mat kɯ kɯ-tu] nɯ ɯ-ku ri ɕ-ku-zo ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe. \\
tree gen 3sg. poss -fruit total sbj: pcp -exist dem 3sg. poss -top loc tral - ipfv -land sens -be lnk \\
`It lands on the top of all trees that have fruits.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S41
exe

Headless possessor relative clauses, such as nɯ-mtɕʰi mɤ-kɯ-pe `those with a big mouth' in ( ex:nWmtChi.mAkWpe ), are even more common.

exe

nɯ-mtɕʰi mɤ-kɯ-pe, kɤ-nɤtsɯ kɯ-ra ra kɯnɤ tu-kɯ-nɯ-ti nɯnɯra tɕaɣi tu-sɤrmi-nɯ ŋgrɤl. \\
3pl. poss -mouth neg - sbj: pcp -be.good inf -hide sbj: pcp -be.needed pl also ipfv - sbj: pcp - auto -say dem: pl parrot ipfv -call- pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`People call `parrots', those with a big mouth, who tell [everything], including things that should [remain] hidden.'
(24-qro) 0003626#S121
exe

In addition, there are also participial relative clauses in kɯ- whose relativized element is neither the subject or the possessor of the subject, in particular locative adjuncts with the relator noun ɯ-stuplace (§ sec:Wstu.relativization.subject ), the only argument of dummy subject verbs (§ sec:dummy.subj.object.relativization ) or arguments from complement clauses embedded within the relative (§ sec:relativization.complement.type ).
summary:
The subject participle is not only used for subject relativization, but also for possessor relatives, where the relativized element is the possessor of the subject; in such cases, the head noun is marked with the genitive to show that it belongs to the relative clause. Headless possessor relative clauses are also common.  

The passage also notes that participial relative clauses in kɯ- can relativize elements other than the subject or its possessor, including locative adjuncts with the relator noun ɯ-stu `place`, the sole argument of dummy-subject verbs, and arguments from embedded complement clauses.

subsubsection: Purposive clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
participle!subject purposive clause motion verb!purposive clause
Subject participles occur in three types of complement clauses and complementation strategies (§ sec:participial.clause.complementation strategies ).

First, the three motion verbs ɕego, ɣicome and ɬoʁcome out (§ sec:motion.verbs ) use subject participle clauses as purposive clauses (§ sec:am.vs.mvc ), such as ndʑi-kɯ-qur in ( ex:ndZikWqur.chWGia ), whose (transitive or intransitive) subject is coreferent with that of the matrix verb.

exe

aʑo [ndʑi-kɯ-qur] cʰɯ-ɣi-a je \\
1sg 2du - sbj: pcp -help ipfv: downstream -come- 1sg sfp \\
`Let me come to help you.' (tWJo 2005) 0003368#S26
exe

posits the category of supine to refer to the cognate construction in Tshobdun. However, given the existence of object participle purposive clauses (§ sec:object.participles.complement, § sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ) above, I consider the supine to be only a specific use of the subject participle, rather than an independent morphology category.

Second, subject participle relative clauses (§ sec:relative.pretence, § sec:constr.participial.clause ) are selected as objects or semi-objects by some verbs such as nɯɕpɯzpretend, `imitate', as in ( ex:kukWtshi.tonWCpWznW ).

exe

ʑara kɯ [cʰa nɯ ku-kɯ-tsʰi] to-nɯɕpɯz-nɯ, \\

summary: Subject participles occur in three kinds of complement or related clause constructions. They function as purposive clauses with motion verbs such as ɕego, ɣicome, and ɬoʁcome out, as object or semi-object complements with verbs like nɯɕpɯz ‘pretend’ or ‘imitate’, and as genuine complements in constructions such as negative existential clauses and cases where the matrix verb is also in subject participle form.

text:
A certain number of subject participles have developed specialized meanings and can be considered to have been lexicalized. Some of these lexicalized participles are formally identical to the regular participle (Table tab:lexicalized.S.nmlz, for instance the noun kɯcʰicandy in ( ex:akWchi ) as compared to the non-lexicalized participle kɯ-cʰi `the one that is sweet' in ( ex:kWchi.tu ). For such nouns, lexicalization is shown by the meaning specialization and the inability to take orientation, associated motion and polarity prefixes (but not possessive prefixes, as shown by he prefix a- on kɯcʰicandy in ex:akWchi ).

exe

aʑo a-ŋgra a-kɯcʰi ci tɤ-χti ra \\
1sg 1sg. poss -salary 1sg. poss -candy indef imp -buy[III] be.needed: fact \\
`Give me a candy as a reward.' (140515 congming de wusui xiaohai-zh) 0003998#S78
exe

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ li tú-wɣ-ndza tɕe, kɯ-cʰi tu, mɤ-kɯ-cʰi tu. \\
lnk dem again ipfv - inv -eat lnk sbj: pcp -be.sweet exist: fact neg - sbj: pcp -be.sweet exist: fact \\
`When one eats them, some are sweet, some are not.' (08-rasti)
0003460#S49
exe

tab:lexicalized.S.nmlz does not include the many names of profession / occupation built from the subject participles which are semantically transparent. We can distinguish two cases.

First, labile verbs derive participial forms such as kɯ-lɤɣshepherd or kɯ-mɯrkɯthief (from lɤɣgraze and mɯrkɯsteal) without an obligatory possessive prefix; the absence of these prefixes cannot be attributed to lexicalization, since these verbs can also be used intransitively (§ sec:lability.categories ).

Second, plain transitive verbs have to undergo antipassive derivation (§ sec:antipassive ) for their subject participles to be usable as names of professions. For instance, kɯrɤrɤtwriter and kɯrɤtʂɯβtailor are from the rɤ- non-human antipassive forms of rɤtwrite, draw and tʂɯβsew, while kɯ-sɤ-sɯxɕɤtteacher comes from the sɤ- human antipassive of sɯxɕɤtteach(see tab:kWrAverb, § sec:antipassive.participle ). Without antipassive prefixes, the subject participles of (non-labile) transitive verbs require either an overt object or a definite and anaphorically recoverable object, and are used as names of professions. For instance, in ( ex:tArmi.WkWrAt ), the participle ɯ-kɯ-rɤt `the one writing it' is used with tɤ-rminame as its object.

exe

[tɤ-rmi ɯ-kɯ-rɤt] tɤ-pɤtso nɯ ɯ-rkɯ ʑo, [...] pjɤ-zɣɯt tɕe, \\
indef. poss -name 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -write indef. poss -child dem 3sg. poss -side emph ifr -reach lnk \\
`It arrived near the boy who wrote the names (of the contestants).' (150826 shier shengxiao)
0006284#S109
exe

Moreover, I do not include among lexicalized participles cases like `shooting star' ( ex:ZNgri.YWkWmArZaB ): although this expression is not compositional, the participle here is not frozen; the verb mɤrʑaβmarry can also occur in finite forms with the noun ʑŋgristar in the meaning `appear, fall (of a shooting star)' as in ( ex:ZNgri.nWmArZaB ).

In the case of kɯŋuright thing and kɯmaʁbad thing, lexicalization is very advanced, and the meanings of the nouns are very different from those of the corresponding participles kɯ-ŋuthe one that is and kɯ-maʁthe one that is not. Examples such as ( ex:kWNu.mAtWnAme ) and ( ex:kWNu.mAtWnAme ) illustrate their use in collocation with verbs like nɤmado and fsebe like.

exe

mɤ-ti-a ma kɯŋu mɤ-tɯ-nɤme \\

`I won't say it, because you will not do the right thing.' (2005 Kunbzang)

The participle kɯ-maʁthe one that is not has been independently grammaticalized as an identity pronoun/determined kɯmaʁother (see § sec:other.pro and § sec:identity.modifier ).

From the nouns kɯŋuright thing and kɯmaʁbad thing, the intransitive verbs rɯkɯŋudo the right thing, `take good care of one's family' and rɯkɯmaʁdo bad things, `happen bad things', `be clumsy' and the transitive verb nɯkɯmaʁmake a mistake have been derived by denominal derivation with rɯ- and nɯ- (§ sec:denom.intr.rA, § sec:denom.nW.pairing ).

The subject participle kɯ-mpɕɤr `the beautiful one' of the verb mpɕɤrbe beautiful has a derived denominal transitive verb nɯkɯmpɕɤrwear (on important occasions) with highly derived semantics, reflecting the lexicalized use of the participle in the meaning `decoration' as in ( ex:WkWmpCAr.tAkABzu ).

`[The mark on breads] is used for decoration.' (160706 WzbroN)
0006131#S5

Several names of diseases only exist as intransitive verbs, and the disease itself or the person suffering from the disease can only be referred to by using a participial or infinitive form. In particular, the word kɤ-kɯ-nɤndzaleper is the perfective subject participle of nɤndzahave leprosy; this word has some degree of lexicalization (in particular, it is a common insult), but it behaves like a participle grammatically; in particular, it can undergo totalitative reduplication (§ sec:totalitative.redp, § sec:totalitative.relatives ), as in ( ex:kWkAkWnAndza ).

Other disease names such as tɤkɤzbɣaʁheadache (as in ex:tAkAzbGaR ), although clearly the perfective participle or infinitive of a verb root *azbɣaʁ, is hardly ever attested in finite form.

exe
summary: The passage explains that some subject participles have developed specialized, lexicalized meanings, shown by semantic narrowing and by their inability to take orientation, motion, or polarity prefixes, though they may still take possessive prefixes. It distinguishes these lexicalized forms from semantically transparent participles used for professions or occupations, noting that transitive verbs often require antipassive derivation for such uses, while some partially lexicalized participles also serve as nouns for things like “right thing,” “bad thing,” “decoration,” or disease names.

tɤkɤzbɣaʁ nɯ tɤ-mŋɤm qʰe, tɕe nɯ ɯ-qʰu nɤ, ŋgɯsqɤ-rʑaʁ ʑo mɯ-tu-mna \\

`After the migraine starts, it does not recede for nine or ten days. (conversation taRrdo 2003)

In addition, we find nouns in kɯ- that can be suspected to be former lexicalized participles, such as kɯjŋuoath, which appears to contain the root of the verb ŋube, though the segment -j- cannot be accounted for at the present moment, In any case, the Tangut cognate 𗡔4600ŋwụ1.58 `oath' shows that this derivation is very ancient and reflects a non-productive morphological process. and kɯmtɕʰɯtoy, whose verbal root cannot be identified. The name kɯsɤɣrumirror (an archaic word in the process of being replaced by the Tibetan χɕɤlzgoŋmirror) could also be a frozen subject participle of the verb rulook at, but the nature of the prefix sɤɣ- is unclear: it could be proprietive prefix (§ sec:proprietive ), or alternatively, be analyzed as a frozen oblique participle prefix (§ sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle ). In the second view, the prefix kɯ- would not be identifiable.

Lexicalized subject participles appearing in compounds are also found. Several cases must be distinguished. First, we find subject participles of transitive verbs as the second member of a compound, with their object as the first member. This type of compounds are lexicalized headless relative clauses, like qalekɯtsʰispecies of kite, which combines qalewind and the participle ɯ-kɯ-tsʰi of the transitive verb tsʰiblock, literally `blocking the wind' (§ sec:determinative.n.n ), a designation referring to this bird's ability to apparently remain unmoving in the sky, as described in ( ex:kAnWqambWmbjom.mWjCe ).

A second type involves two participles in apposition, as kɯrŋukɯɣndʑɯrharvestman, built from the subject participles of the verbs rŋuparch and ɣndʑɯrgrind (§ sec:coordinative.n.n ). Both verbs being transitive, the absence of a possessive prefix ɯ- is an additional clue that the form is fully lexicalized.

Third, there are compounds with the subject participle of transitive or intransitive verbs as first element (see also § sec.v.n.compounds ), for instance kɯqurʑŋgrievening star from ɯ-kɯ-qur `the one helping him' ( qurhelp) and ʑŋgristar literally `the star of the helper', for reasons explained in the following excerpt ( ex:kWqur.ZNgri ).
