Nominalizations with the x-/ɣ- prefix (§ sec:G.nmlz ) are ancient lexicalized subject participles that have undergone a syllable reduction rule (§ sec:velar.class.prefix, ) and have become completely separated from their base verbs synchronically.

There are also a few adverbs derived from verbs with a kɯ- prefix, but these are best analyzed as lexicalized stative infinitives (§ sec:velar.inf.adverb ).
summary: The passage describes several kinds of lexicalized participial nouns and compounds formed with the kɯ- prefix. Some appear to be ancient, non-productive derivations from verbs, while others are frozen compounds built from subject participles in apposition or as the first element, often with meanings that can still be traced back to the verbal root. It also notes that nominalizations with the x-/ɣ- prefix are historically older lexicalized subject participles that have become synchronically detached from their base verbs, and that a few kɯ- adverbs are better treated as lexicalized stative infinitives.

text:
The object participle is a nominalized form which refers to an entity corresponding to the object (§ sec:absolutive.P ) or semi-object (§ sec:semi.object ) of the base verb. Nearly all transitive and semi-transitive verbs (except for a handful of exceptions, § sec:nmlz.defective ) can build an object participle by adding the prefix kɤ- (for instance kɤ-ndza from the verb ndzaeat in ex:kAndza ). This form is homophonous with, and historically related to the velar infinitive (§ sec:velar.inf, § sec:velar.nmlz.history ).

exe

kɤ-ndza \\
obj: pcp -eat \\
`The one that is eaten.' (many attestations)
exe

In the case of secundative verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ), the object participle can either refer to the recipient or the theme, as in ( ex:nWkAmbi ); this question is discussed in more detail in § sec:object.participle.relatives.

exe

nɯ-kɤ-mbi \\
aor - obj: pcp -give \\
`The one that he has given it to.'
`The one that has been given to him.' (many attestations)
exe

In this section, I first describe the morphological properties of object participles (compatibility with possessive prefixes § sec:object.participle.possessive and other prefixes § sec:object.participle.other.prefixes ). Then, I discuss several cases of ambiguity between object participles and other kɤ- prefixed forms in § sec:object.participle.ambiguity (see also § sec:infinitives.participles ). The uses of object participles to build relative clauses and complement clauses are described in § sec:object.participle.relatives and § sec:object.participles.complement. Finally, I present a few cases of lexicalized object participles in § sec:lexicalized.object.participle.
summary:
The object participle is a nominalized form referring to the object or semi-object of a verb, and most transitive and semi-transitive verbs form it with the prefix **kɤ-**. It is homophonous with and historically related to the velar infinitive.

For secundative verbs, the object participle may refer either to the recipient or to the theme. The passage also notes that the section will cover its morphological properties, ambiguities with other **kɤ-** forms, its use in relative and complement clauses, and a few lexicalized forms.

text:
participle!object prefix!possessive
Unlike subject participles, object participles never require a possessive prefix. An optional possessive prefix coreferent with the transitive subject, as in ( ex:akAsWz ), can however be added.

exe

a-kɤ-sɯz \\
1sg - nmlz:P-know \\
`The one that I know.' (many attestations)
exe

In the case of semi-transitive verbs, the possessive prefix is also coreferent with the subject, as in the form ɯ-kɤ-rga `the one that he likes' in ( ex:stu.WkArga ), built in the same way as the object participle of the transitive (tropative, § sec:tropative ) verb nɤmɯmfind tasty.

exe

ri nɯnɯ stu ɯ-kɤ-rga, ɯ-kɤ-nɤ-mɯm pjɤ-ɕti. \\
lnk dem most 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -like 3sg. poss - obj: pcp - trop -be.tasty ifr. ipfv -be. aff \\
`But it was what he liked most, what he found most tasty.' (160703 poucet3) 0006107#S72
exe

In addition to semi-transitive verbs, the complement-taking verb cʰacan has object participles taking possessive prefixes meaning `the one that $X$ can $Y$', $X$ being the subject (marked by the possessive prefix), and $Y$ the verb in the complement clause, which can be overt or not as in ( ex:nWmAkAcha ), where nɯ-mɤ-kɤ-cʰa stands for kɤ-ndo nɯ-mɤ-kɤ-cha `the one(s) that they are able to catch' (see additional examples in § sec:out.complement.relativization.cha ).

exe

tɕe nɯ-mɤ-kɤ-cʰa nɯ kʰɯna χsɯm pɯ-tu qʰe, nɯra kɯ rcanɯ ɕlaʁ ʑo ku-ndo-nɯ ɲɯ-ɕti. \\
lnk 3pl. poss - neg - inf -can dem dog three pst. ipfv -exist lnk dem: pl erg unexp: deg ideo.I:immediately emph ipfv -catch- pl sens -be. aff \\
`The [rats] that [the people] had been unable to [catch], there were three dogs, and these [dogs] caught them at once.' (150831 BZW kAnArRaR)
0006378#S41
exe
summary: Object participles never require a possessive prefix, unlike subject participles, though an optional possessive prefix may be added when it is coreferent with the transitive subject. The same pattern appears with semi-transitive verbs, where the possessive prefix refers to the subject, and with the complement-taking verb *cʰacan*, whose object participles can mean “the one that X can Y,” with *X* marked by the possessive prefix and *Y* expressed in the complement clause, overtly or implicitly.

subsubsection: Associated motion, polarity and orientation preverbs on object participles
text:
associated motion orientation!preverb participle!object
Object participles, like subject participles, are compatible with polarity ( ex:amAkAsWz ), associated motion ( ex:WCWkAnAma ) and orientation preverbs ( ex:WCWkAnAma ).

exe

tɕe aʑo a-mɤ-kɤ-sɯz tɤjmɤɣ nɯ kɤ-ndza mɤ-naz-a \\
lnk 1sg 1sg. poss - neg - obj: pcp -know mushroom dem inf -eat neg -dare: fact - 1sg \\
`I do not dare to eat mushrooms that I do not recognize.' (23-mbrAZim)
0003604#S105
exe

exe

ɯ-pɕi tɕe ɯ-ɕɯ-kɤ-nɤma ci pjɤ-tu tɕe, \\
3sg. poss -outside lnk 3sg. poss - tral - obj: pcp -work indef ifr. ipfv -exist lnk \\
`[The mouse] had something to do outside.' (140518 mao he laoshu-zh)
0004030#S77
exe

Associated motion and polarity prefixes on object participles co-occur with possessive prefixes, as shown by ( ex:amAkAsWz ) and ( ex:WCWkAnAma ) above, but orientation preverbs (whether perfective or imperfective) do not. This is an important difference between subject and object participles (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes ). Object participles only have at most two prefixes.

exe

tɕe pɤjka wuma nɯnɯ tɕe, pjɯ-kɤ-nɯ-ji ŋu tɕe, \\
lnk gourd really dem lnk ipfv - obj: pcp - auto -plant be: fact lnk \\
`The gourd proper is cultivated (it does not grow on its own).' (16-CWrNgo) 0003518#S61
exe

Finite relative clauses, instead of object participles, can be used to specify both TAME and the subject (§ sec:finite.relatives ).

Unlike subject participles, object participles are attested with the progressive asɯ- prefix, as in ( ex:pWkASWndo ). It is the only non-finite form compatible with this prefix.

exe

tɕʰeme nɯ kɯ iɕqʰa, ɯ-jaʁ <meihua>, mɯntoʁ pɯ-kɤ-ɤsɯ-ndo nɯ pjɤ-ɣɤrɤt. \\
girl dem erg the.aforementioned 3sg. poss -hand plum.blossom flower pst. ipfv - obj: pcp - prog -take dem ifr -throw \\
`The girl threw down the plum blossom, the flower that she was holding in her hand.' (150907 yingning-zh)
0006264#S28
exe

These forms are rare and difficult to identify, as they are always ambiguous with object participles or infinitive of causativized verbs. In the case of ( ex:pWkASWndo ), the context makes it clear that interpretation as the participle of a progressive form is the only possibility, as the same verb with the progressive appears a few sentences before in ( ex:meihua.ci.pjAkAsWndoci ).

exe

ɯ-jaʁ nɯtɕu, iɕqʰa, <meihua> ci pjɤ-k-ɤsɯ-ndo-ci, \\
3sg. poss -hand dem: loc filler plum.blossom indef ifr. ipfv - peg - prog -take- peg \\
`She was holding a plum blossom in her hand.' (150907 yingning-zh) 0006264#S19
exe
summary: Object participles, like subject participles, can co-occur with polarity prefixes and associated motion, and they are also compatible with the progressive asɯ- prefix. However, orientation preverbs do not occur with object participles, and unlike subject participles they can take only at most two prefixes; finite relative clauses may be used instead when both TAME and the subject need to be specified.

text:
ambiguity!participle ambiguity!infinitive
There is rampant ambiguity between object participles, kɤ- infinitives and subject participles of passive verbs. The question of the ambiguity between object participles and kɤ- infinitives is discussed in § sec:velar.inf.ambiguity.

The passive a- merges with the subject participle as kɤ, homophonous with the infinitive and the object participle. Potentially ambiguous examples are very common. For instance, in ( ex:kArku.passive ), the form kɤrku could be argued to be an object participle kɤ-rku or a passive subject participle kɯ-ɤ-rku; the second option is chosen here due to the semantics, which fits the passive arkube in better (as this passive verb is in the process of becoming a locative existential verb, § sec:existential.basic ). In the absence of any argument in favour of the passive analysis, the ambiguous kɤ- forms are analyzed as object participles by default.

exe

sɤtɕʰa ɯ-ŋgɯ kɯ-ɤ-rku <yangyu> cʰo lɤpɯɣ nɯra tu-ndze ŋgrɤl. \\
earth 3sg. poss -inside sbj: pcp - pass -put.in potato comit radish dem: pl ipfv -eat[III] be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`It eats the radish and the potatoes that are in the ground.' (25-akWzgumba)
0003632#S21
exe

Due to the fact that passive verbs in Japhug are barely attested in perfective forms (§ sec:passive.stative ), participles with perfective prefixes can be considered to be object participles, especially in cases like ( ex:YAXtAr.nWkAXtAr ), where the participle nɯ-kɤ-χtɤr `(those) that have been scattered' occurs in a sentence following the transitive form ɲɤ-χtɤr `it scattered, it smashed'.

exe

to-ɣi tɕe nɯ-ʑmbrɯ ɲɤ-χtɤr ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, ɯ-zda ra nɯ-pʰe, nɤki, ``nɯnɯ ʑmbrɯ nɯ-kɤ-χtɤr nɯ ɯ-taʁ kɤ-ɴqoʁ-nɯ ra'' to-ti\\
ifr: up -come lnk 3pl. poss -ship ifr -scatter emph sens -be lnk 3sg. poss -companion pl 3pl. poss - dat filler dem ship aor - obj: pcp -scatter dem 3sg. poss -on imp -hang- pl be.needed: fact ifr -say\\
`The [monster] came up and smashed their ship, and [Norbzang] said to his companions: ``Grab the [pieces of the] ship that have been scattered''.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S29
exe

The same analysis as object participles, rather than passive subject participles is applied to examples of perfective kɤ- forms also when the transitive verb is not found in finite form in a neighbouring sentence, such as ( ex:pWkAprAt ).

exe

fsapaʁ ɯ-ŋgo rcanɯ, pɯ-kɤ-prɤt ʑo tɤ-fse ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
animals 3sg. poss -disease unexp: deg aor - obj: pcp -break emph aor -be.like sens -be \\
`It was like the disease of the cattle had been [suddenly] stopped.' (2003 kAndZislama)
exe

A more marginal case of homophony occurs between object participles and velar infinitives on the one hand, and several finite forms taking the series A orientation preverb kɤ- on the other hand (§ sec:infinitives.participles ).
summary: The passage explains that Japhug has frequent homophony between object participles, kɤ- infinitives, and passive subject participles, since the passive prefix a- merges with the subject participle as kɤ-. Because these forms are so similar, ambiguous kɤ- forms are normally analyzed as object participles unless the context clearly supports a passive interpretation, while perfective forms with kɤ- are especially likely to be treated this way because passive verbs are rarely attested in the perfective.

text:
participle!object relative clause!object
Object participles can be used to build object relative clauses, but compete in this function with finite relatives (§ sec:object.relativization ). They differ in this regard from subject relatives, which are the only available construction to relativize transitive and intransitive subjects.

As was described in § sec:object.participle.other.prefixes, object participles, unlike subject and oblique participles, cannot combine possessive and orientation preverbs.

Object participles with orientation preverbs are used in relative clauses with indefinite subjects, or with definite third person subjects as in ( ex:qajGi.nWkAmbi ).

exe

[ɬamu kɯ qajɣi nɯ-kɤ-mbi] nɯ tu-ndze pjɤ-ŋu \\
anthr erg bread aor - sbj: pcp -give dem ipfv -eat[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`[As] he was eating the [pieces of] bread that Lhamo had given him.' (2002 qajdoskAt)
0003366#S110
exe

The only example of first or second person that could be interpreted as subject in a perfective object participle relative in the corpus is ( ex:aZo.kW.pWkAsWrAt ), but in this example (translated from Chinese), the referent of the first person is a pen that has been used to write a poem; the ergative postpositional phrase aʑo kɯ here can be either analyzed as an instrument (`the poem that has been written using me') or as a causee (§ sec:causee.kW, `the poem that he has made me write'), as shown by the presence of the causative sɯ- prefix, not a subject.

exe

[aʑo kɯ pɯ-kɤ-sɯ-rɤt] nɯnɯ pjɯ-ndɯn ɲɯ-ŋu nétɕi \\
1sg erg aor - obj: pcp - caus -write dem ipfv -read sens -be sfp \\
(The pen said): [the poet is reading the poem] that has been written using me.' (150818 bi he moshuihu-zh)
0006382#S131
exe

When the subject is first or second person, an object participle with a possessive prefix is used instead. In ( ex:iZo.jikArku ) for instance, we find ji-kɤ-rku `the thing that we give' (see § sec:z.nmlz concerning the meaning of this verb) and nɤ-kɤ-sɯso `the thing that you think / that you want' with a first plural and a second singular possessive prefix, respectively.

exe

nɯ ma iʑo ji-kɤ-rku me, atu spɣi tɤ-ɕe qʰe, laχtɕʰa ŋotɕu nɤ-kɤ-sɯso ʑo nɯnɯ,
nɤ-mɲaʁ, nɤ-rna, nɤ-ɕna cʰo ra kɯ kɯ-spoʁ nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕe a-kɤ-tɯ-rke qʰe, \\
dem apart.from 1pl 1pl. poss - obj: pcp -put.in not.exist: fact up.there granary imp: up -go lnk thing where 2sg. poss - obj: pcp -think emph dem 2sg. poss -eye 2sg. poss -ear 2sg. poss -nose comit pl total sbj: pcp -have.a.hole dem 3sg. poss -inside loc irr - pfv -2-put.in[III] lnk \\
`We don't have anything else to give you as a departing present, so go up there in the granary, and whatever you want, put it in all the holes [in your body], your eyes, your ears, your nose etc.' (31-deluge) 0004077#S134
exe

When the subject is a definite third person, it is also possible to have a third person possessive prefix on the object participle, as in ( ex:WkWnWmbrApW2 ) (or ex:WCWkAnAma above).

exe

lɤ-fsoʁ ɯ-jɯja nɯ pjɯ-ru tɕe [ɯ-kɤ-nɯmbrɤpɯ] nɯ kʰu pɯ-ɕti ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
aor -be.clear 3sg -along dem ipfv: down -look lnk 3sg. poss - obj: pcp --ride dem tiger pst. ipfv -be. aff sens -be \\
`As the day broke, looking down, [it dawned on him that] what he was riding was a tiger.' (2005 khu)
exe

Unlike in Tshobdun, in Japhug object participial relatives with possessive prefixes are not restricted to generic state of affairs, but can refer to particular situations as in examples such as ( ex:WkWnWmbrApW2 ) and ( ex:nAkAti.nWra ).

exe

a-ɬaʁ, tɕe nɤ-kɯ-mŋɤm tɕʰi ɲɯ-fse ma [alo qʰaqʰu nɤ-kɤ-ti] nɯra tɤ-stu-t-a \\
1sg. poss -aunt lnk 2sg. poss - sbj: pcp -hurt what sens -be.like lnk upstream behind.the.house 2sg. poss - obj: pcp -say dem: pl aor -do.like- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`Stepmother, how do you feel, I did the things you said [about creating a lake] up there behind the house.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S341
exe

In object participial relatives, when the relativized element is overt, it is generally located before the participle, as in ( ex:thWkAraGdWt ).

exe

[nɯŋa ɯ-ndʐi tʰɯ-kɤ-rɤɣdɯt], tʰɯ-kɤ-tʂɯβ nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu ko-ɕe \\
cow 3sg. poss -skin aor - obj: pcp -skin aor - obj: pcp -sew dem 3sg. poss -inside dem: loc evd: east -go \\
`He [crawled] into the cow hide that had been skinned and sewed.' (2-deluge2012) 0003376#S30
exe

While the relative clause in ( ex:thWkAraGdWt ) can either be interpreted as head-internal or post-nominal, clear examples of head-internal object relative clauses are attested (§ sec:head-internal.relative.postnominal ), as in ( ex:kha.tAkAsWBzu ), where the head noun kʰa is located between the instrumental adjunct kɯ-cʰi kɯ and the participle.

exe

[kɯ-cʰi kɯ kʰa tɤ-kɤ-sɯ-βzu] ci pjɤ-mto-ndʑi\\
sbj: pcp -be.sweet erg house aor - obj: pcp - caus -make indef ifr -see- du \\
`They saw a house that was made of sweets.' (140507 tangguowu-zh)
0003933#S75
exe

Prenominal object participial relatives are mainly attested with participles with a possessive prefix, such as a-kɤ-sɯz in ( ex:paXCi.akAsWz ).

exe

nɯnɯ paχɕi [aʑo a-kɤ-sɯz] nɯ nɯra ɣɤʑu \\
dem apples 1sg 1sg. poss - obj: pcp -know allium dem dem: pl exist: sens \\
`Of the apples, [the aforementioned] are the ones I know about.' (07-paXCi)
0003430#S67
exe

Examples of prenominal object participial relatives with orientation preverbs are also attested, as in ( ex:nWkAsWBzu.kha ) (a near minimal pair with ex:kha.tAkAsWBzu ) and ( ex:khru.kW.thWkAsWlAt ). This type of relative clauses are considerably less common that the corresponding head-internal ones, especially in texts that have not been translated from Chinese as in ( ex:khru.kW.thWkAsWlAt ).

exe

[lonba ɕom kɯ nɯ-kɤ-sɯ-βzu] kʰa pjɤ-ŋu \\
all iron erg aor - obj: pcp - caus -make house ifr. ipfv -be \\
`It was a house made completely of iron.' (140505 liuhaohan zoubian tianxia-zh)
0003913#S149
exe

exe

tɕe [kʰru kɯ tʰɯ-kɤ-sɯ-lɤt] laʁdɯn kɯnɤ tu ma\\
lnk cast.iron erg aor - obj: pcp - caus -release tool also exist: fact lnk \\
`There are also tools that are made of cast iron.' (30-Com)
0003736#S28
exe
summary:
Object participles can form object relative clauses, but they compete with finite relatives and differ from subject relatives, since subject relatives are the only option for relativizing subjects. Object participles cannot combine possessive and orientation preverbs, and with orientation preverbs they are used for relative clauses with indefinite subjects or definite third-person subjects.

When the subject is first or second person, a possessive prefix is used instead; with definite third-person subjects, possessive prefixes are also possible and can refer to particular situations, not just generic ones. In object participial relatives, an overt relativized element usually appears before the participle; prenominal relatives are less common than head-internal ones, though both are attested.

text:
As mentioned above (example ex:nWkAmbi ), the object participles of secundative verbs can either refer to their object proper (the recipient, § sec:ditransitive.secundative ) or to the theme, which is not indexed on the verb but occurs in absolutive form (§ sec:theme.ditransitive ). In fact, in the corpus examples of theme relativization with the object participle are quite common (as ex:qajGi.nWkAmbi above and ex:WkAmbi.maNe and ex:pWkAsWxCAt.nWra below), but recipient relativization is rare ( ex:xCiri.nWkAsWxCAt ). Examples can however be elicited without difficulty.

exe

nɯ ma ɯ-kɤ-mbi maŋe tɕe, ``a-me ta-mbi ra" to-ti tɕe, \\
dem apart.from 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -give not.exist: sens lnk 1sg. poss -daughter 1 2-give: fact be.needed: fact ifr -say lnk \\
`He had nothing else to give him, and said `I give you my daughter'.' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

exe

tɕendɤre [tɯmɯkɤrŋi kɯ pɯ-kɤ-sɯxɕɤt] ra ɲɤ-nɤxtʂɯn tɕe tɕe nɯɕimɯma ʑo pjɤ-nɯ-ɕe. \\
lnk heaven erg aor - obj: pcp -teach pl ifr -be.grateful lnk lnk immediately emph ifr: down - vert -go \\
`[Pu'an] was thankful for the things that the god of heaven had taught him and went back [to earth] immediately.' (150827 taisui-zh)
0006390#S134
exe

exe

iɕqʰa, [kɤntɕʰɯ-xpa ʑo, nɤki, xɕiri nɯ-kɤ-sɯxɕɤt] nɯ pjɤ-sat, \\
the.aforementioned several-year emph filler weasel aor - obj: pcp -teach dem ifr -kill \\
`He killed the weasel that he had trained for several years.' (140518 xuezhe he huangshulang-zh)
0004032#S28
exe

With indirective verbs, the object participle can only refer to the theme, as in ( ex:nAkAthu.WGAZu ), for these verbs the recipient must be relativized with the oblique participle (§ sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ).

exe

nɤ-kɤ-tʰu ɯ-ɣɤʑu nɤ, tɤ-tʰe jɤɣ \\
2sg. poss - obj: pcp -ask qu -exist: sens lnk imp -ask[III] be.allowed: fact \\
`If you have and questions, you can ask them.' (conversation 14-11-08)
exe

The semi-object of semi-transitive verbs (§ sec:semi.object ) can also be relativized with a object participial relative, as ji-kɤ-rga `the one that we like' in ( ex:stu.jikArga ).

exe

iɕqʰa <macha> kɤ-ti nɯ [iʑora stu ji-kɤ-rga] ŋu \\
the.aforementioned macha.tea obj: pcp -say dem 1pl most 1pl. poss - obj: pcp -like be: fact \\
`The [type of tea] called `macha' is what we like best.' (30-macha)
0003746#S1
exe

Secundative verbs undergoing antipassivization become semi-transitive verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative, § sec:antipassive.ditransitive ) with the theme remaining the semi-object. Like other semi-transitive verbs, these antipassive verbs can build an object participle, which can then be used to relativize the theme, as in ( ex:nAkArAmbi ).

exe

nɤ-kɤ-rɤ-mbi nɯ tɕʰi pɯ-ŋu? \\
2sg. poss - obj: pcp - apass -give dem what pst. ipfv -be \\
`What was it that you gave (to people)?' (elicited)
exe

Object participles also occur in genitival relatives (§ sec:genitival.relatives, postnominal relative with the genitive postposition ɣɯ occurring between the relative clause and the head noun), as in example ( ex:tAkAsWBzu.GW.tWxtsa ). This type of examples is frequently found in texts translated from Chinese, but unattested in the rest of the corpus for object relativization, and is a clear case of calque (§ sec:genitival.relatives ). Although speakers do accept these examples, they cannot be considered to be representative of the normal grammar of the language.

exe

tɕe [<shuijing> kɯ tɤ-kɤ-sɯ-βzu] ɣɯ tɯ-xtsa nɯra jo-ɣɯt. \\
lnk crystal erg aor - obj: pcp - caus -make gen indef. poss -shoe dem: pl ifr -bring \\
`[The bird] brought shoes made of crystal.' (140504 huiguniang-zh)
0003909#S155
exe
summary: The passage explains that in secundative verbs, object participles can relativize either the recipient or the theme, though corpus examples mainly show theme relativization and recipient relativization is rare but possible. For indirective verbs, the object participle can only refer to the theme, while the recipient must be relativized with an oblique participle. It also notes that semi-transitive verbs and antipassivized secundative verbs can use object participles to relativize the semi-object/theme, and that genitival relatives with object participles are largely calqued from Chinese and not representative of normal grammar.

text:
Just like subject participles can relativize the possessor of subjects § sec:subject.participle.other.relative ), object participles can be used to relativize possessors of objects, as in ( ex:ndZimYaR.mWtAkArAt ), where the head of the relative ndʑi-mɲaʁ mɯ-tɤ-kɤ-rɤt is not the object `their eyes' (which would result in a non-sensical sentence `their eye which had not been drawn were still on the wall') but rather the possessors (the dragons).

exe

[ndʑi-mɲaʁ mɯ-tɤ-kɤ-rɤt] nɯni tɕetu, znde ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu nɯnɯ pjɤ-nɯ-tu-ndʑi. \\
3du. poss -eye neg - aor - obj: pcp -draw dem: du up wall 3sg. poss -on dem: loc dem ifr. ipfv - auto -exist- du \\
`The two [dragons] whose eyes had not been drawn were still on the wall.' (160718 hualongdianjing-zh)
0006153#S59
exe

In light verb constructions with lɤtrelease (§ sec:light.verb ), the oblique argument encoded with the relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:WtaR ) can be relativized with the object participle. For instance, in ( ex:tWsNaR.tAkAlAt ) and ( ex:WtaR.tWsNaR.tolAt ), although the noun tɯsŋaʁenchantment is the object of the verb lɤtrelease in the collocation meaning `cast a spell', the participial relative tɯsŋaʁ tɤ-kɤ-lɤt means here `(prince) who has been enchanted', not `the spell that has been cast'. The second interpretation is however possible, and these relatives are ambiguous. The head of this relative is therefore not the object, but the recipient, although this oblique argument is marked with ɯ-taʁon, above, as shown by example ( ex:WtaR.tWsNaR.tolAt ).

exe

qaɕpa nɯnɯ, iɕqʰa nɯ, rɟɤlpu ci ɣɯ ɯ-tɕɯ nɯnɯ, nɤkinɯ, tɯ-sŋaʁ tɤ-kɤ-lɤt tɕe qaɕpa nɯ-kɤ-sɤβzu pjɤ-ŋu. \\
frog dem filler dem king indef gen 3sg. poss -son dem filler nmlz: action -enchant aor - obj: pcp -release lnk frog aor - obj: pcp -transform ifr. ipfv -be \\
`This frog was the son of a king who had been enchanted and transformed into a frog.' (140429 qingwa wangzi-zh, 180-181) 0003890#S176
exe

exe

a-tɕɯ nɯ ɯ-taʁ tɯ-sŋaʁ to-lɤt tɕe nɯ mbalɤ-pɯ ci ɲɤ-sɤβzu. \\
1sg. poss -son dem 3sg. poss -on nmlz: action -enchant ifr -release lnk dem bull- dim indef ifr -transform \\
`She cast a spell on my son and turned him into a calf.' (140512 fushang he yaomo-zh)
0003967#S98
exe

In addition, there are cases where an object participle can relativize a locative adjunct (§ sec:locative.relativization.object ). The object participle of the perception verbs mtosee and mtsʰɤmhear can be used to make headless locative relative clauses meaning `(a place) where $X$ can see/hear $Y$, in particular when occurring as the goal of a motion verb as in ( ex:tCirna.mAkAmtshAm ). Note the optionality of the ergative on the nouns tɕi-rna `our ears' and tɕi-mɲaʁ `our eyes' in ( ex:tCirna.mAkAmtshAm ).

exe

[tɕi-rna mɤ-kɤ-mtsʰɤm], [tɕi-mɲaʁ mɤ-kɤ-mto] a-jɤ-ɕe-ndʑi ra \\
1du. poss -ear neg - obj: pcp -hear 1du. poss -eye neg - obj: pcp -see irr - pfv -go- du be.needed: fact \\
`May they go away [to a place] where our ears cannot hear them, where our eyes cannot see them.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

It is not possible in ( ex:tCirna.mAkAmtshAm ) to replace the object participle by an oblique participle sɤ-.
summary: The passage explains that object participles can relativize possessors of objects, as in examples where the relative head is the possessor rather than the possessed noun itself, yielding meanings like “the dragons whose eyes had not been drawn.” It also shows that in certain light-verb constructions, an oblique argument marked with ɯ-taʁ can be relativized by the object participle, producing sometimes ambiguous relatives, and that object participles can relativize locative adjuncts in headless relative clauses meaning places where someone can see or hear something. Finally, it notes that in these locative relativizations, the object participle cannot be replaced by an oblique participle sɤ-.

text:
participle!subject purposive clause
While kɤ- prefixed non-finite verb forms are very common in complement clauses, most of these forms are infinitives rather than object participles (§ sec:inf.complementation ), since there are no restrictions on intransitive verbs (§ sec:velar.inf ).

The only complementation strategy where an object participle, rather than an infinitive, has to be posited occurs in the purposive clause of motion verbs when the verb of the purposive clause is transitive and coreference occurs between its object (rather than subject) and the subject of the matrix motion verb, as kɤ-nɤkʰu in ( ex:kAnAkhu.juGi ).

exe

<xingqi> raŋri ʑo tɕe nɯnɯ sɤβʑɯ ɣɯ ɯ-kʰa nɯtɕu kɤ-nɤkʰu ju-ɣi pjɤ-ŋu \\
week each emph lnk dem mouse gen 3sg. poss -house dem: loc obj: pcp -invite ipfv -come ipfv. ifr -be \\
`He would come to the mouse's house as a guest.' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh).
0006334#S291
exe

A possessive prefix coreferent with the transitive subject of nɤkʰu can be optionally added on this object participle, as in ( ex:akAnAkhu ).

exe

a-kɤ-nɤkʰu jɤ-ɣe \\
1sg. poss - obj: pcp -invite aor -come[II] \\
`He came to my house as a guest (following my invitation).' (elicited)
exe

In purposive clauses, the rule is thus that the subject participle is used when there is subject-subject coreference (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation ), and the object participle in cases of object-subject coreference.
summary:
In complement clauses, kɤ- prefixed non-finite verb forms are common, but most are infinitives rather than object participles because intransitive verbs place no restrictions on the use of the infinitive. The one complementation strategy that requires an object participle is the purposive clause of motion verbs when the purposive verb is transitive and its object, rather than its subject, corefers with the subject of the matrix verb.

In these purposive clauses, a possessive prefix coreferent with the transitive subject may optionally appear on the object participle. The overall rule is that subject participles are used for subject-subject coreference, while object participles are used for object-subject coreference.

text:
While some object participles are commonly used as headless relative clauses, few can be considered to be fully lexicalized.

The verbs related to food ingestion such as ndzaeat, tsʰidrink, ndzɤtsʰieat and drink, moʁeat (powdery food) have object participles such as kɤ-ndza `food', kɤ-tsʰi `drink (n), beverage', kɤ-ndzɤtsʰi `food and drink' and kɤmoʁdry tsampa, which commonly occur in enumerations (§ sec:noun.enumeration ) with nouns not derived from verbs, as in ( ex:WkAndza.WkAtshi ).

exe

ɯ-kɤ-ndza ɯ-kɤ-tsʰi ɯ-tɯkrimgo ra to-ɣɯt qʰe, tɕendɤre, nɯra ɲɤ́-wɣ-mbi qʰe, \\
3sg. poss - obj: pcp -eat 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -drink 3sg. poss -butter.bread pl ifr: up -bring lnk lnk dem: pl ifr - inv -give lnk \\
`She brought food, drinks and butter bread for her and gave them to her.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

In these enumerations, sometimes only the first element takes a possessive prefix, as in ( ex:ndZikAndza.kAtshi ), where we find ndʑi-kɤ-ndza kɤ-tsʰi instead of the equally possible ndʑi-kɤ-ndza ndʑi-kɤ-tsʰi (however, if the first kɤ- participle in the enumeration has no possessive prefix, the following participle cannot take one).

exe

ndʑi-kɤ-ndza kɤ-tsʰi mɤ-mbrɤt, ndʑi-kɯ-ndzɤtsʰi a-pɯ-me smɯlɤm \\
2du. poss - obj: pcp -eat obj: pcp -drink neg - acaus:cut 2du. poss - sbj: pcp -eat.and.drink irr - ipfv -not.exist prayer \\
`May you never lack food or drink, may there nobody [coming to] eat you.' (2003kAndZWslama)
exe

In these examples, the possessive prefix always refer to the person or animal ingesting the food (not the person giving the food), and although these forms are very common, since their semantics is completely predictable from the base verb, and since the possessive prefix behaves like that of a normal oblique participle, there is no specific reason to consider that they have become nouns and constitute lexical entries that must be distinguished from the verb (except in the case of kɤmoʁdry tsampa, whose meaning has become more specific).

The forms kɤ-pa and kɤ-stu, derived from the verbs from the verbs pado and studo like, both meaning `manner, method (to solve a problem)' (like Chinese 办法 bànfǎmethod), are other potential candidates to be analyzed as lexicalized object participles (or infinitives). They are particularly commonly used with existential verbs to mean `$X$ has (no/a) way to do it' ($X$ being referred to by the possessive prefix on kɤ-pa or kɤ-stu ), as in ( ex:akApa.maNe ).

exe

a-kɤpa maŋe \\
1sg. poss -method not.exist: sens \\
`I have no way of doing it.' (many attestations)
exe

However, collocation in texts of kɤ-pa and kɤ-stu with the finite forms of the verbs pado and studo like, as in ( ex:nAkApa.tWtu ) and, suggest that these forms are still synchronically linked with these verbs, and that it may be more economical to analyze them as participles rather than derived nouns.

exe

nɤ-kɤ-pa tɯ tu nɤ, tɤ-pe ma mtsʰoʁlaŋ tɤ-ɣe \\
2sg. poss - obj: pcp -do cond exist: fact lnk imp -do[III] lnk water.monster aor: up -come[II] \\
`If you have some way [to protect us], use it, because the water monster has come.' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S26
exe

exe

nɯnɯ ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu nɤ-kɤ-stu ɯ-ɣɤʑu tɕe a-tɤ-tɯ-ste ma tɕe \\
dem 3sg. poss -on dem: loc 2sg. poss - obj: pcp -do.like qu -exist: sens lnk irr - pfv -2-do.like[III] lnk lnk \\
`If you have a way to deal with him, use it.' (25-kAmYW-XpAltCin)
0003642#S35
exe

The object participle kɤ-ti from the verb tisay, although transparently derived, has an unpredictable meaning in the existential construction. With a negative existential verb, in addition to the expected meaning `have nothing to say', it can be interpreted as `be unable to say for sure', as in ( ex:akAti.maNe ).

exe

a-kɤ-ti ci maŋe \\
1sg. poss - obj: pcp -say indef not.exist: sens \\
`I cannot say for sure.' (many examples)
exe

In addition, there are highly lexicalized object participles occurring as members of compounds; these cases are generally ambiguous, and alternatively analyzable as lexicalized velar infinitives (§ sec:lexicalized.velar.inf ). The incorporating verb kɤtɯpatell is an interesting case: it combines the form kɤ-ti (either the participle `what one says' or the infinitive `to say') in bound state kɤtɯ- (the alternative form kɤtipa is also attested) with the auxiliary pado (§ sec:pa.lv ).
summary: Some object participles are commonly used in headless relative clauses, but few are fully lexicalized. The passage argues that forms like food-ingestion participles and kɤ-pa/kɤ-stu are still synchronically linked to their verbs because their meanings are predictable or they regularly collocate with verbal forms, though kɤmoʁ has a more specific meaning and kɤ-ti shows an unpredictable meaning in existential constructions. It also notes that some highly lexicalized object participles occur in compounds, where they may instead be analyzed as lexicalized infinitives.

text:
participle!oblique
The sɤ -prefix (and its allomorphs sɤɣ, sɤz- and z -) is used for non-core argument nominalization, in particular recipients of indirective verbs (§ sec:gen.beneficiary, § sec:dative ), instruments (§ sec:instr.kW ), place and time adjuncts, as in ( ex:come ). It takes a possessive prefix which can be coreferent with any core argument (subject or object).

exe

ɯ-sɤ-ɣi \\
3sg. poss - obl: pcp -come \\
`The place/moment from where/when he/it comes.' (elicited)
exe

Related forms include the gerund (§ sec:gerund ) and the purposive converb (§ sec:purposive.converb ); the historical relationship between these categories is discussed in § sec:sigmatic.nmlz.history.
summary: The sɤ- nominalizing prefix, with allomorphs sɤɣ, sɤz-, and z-, is used to form oblique nominals for non-core arguments such as recipients of indirective verbs, instruments, and place or time adjuncts. It takes a possessive prefix that may be coreferential with either the subject or object, and it is related to the gerund and purposive converb.

text:
participle!oblique
The base form of the oblique participle is sɤ, but three additional allomorphs are also found: sɤz, z- and sɤɣ-.

The allomorph sɤɣ- or sɤx- (depending on the voicing of the next consonant) is attested with intransitive (or labile) monosyllabic verbs with an onset without velar/uvular consonant, and without consonant cluster involving a preinitial (§ sec:caus.sWG ). This allomorph is to some extent lexicalized, and is not found with all verbs fulfilling these criteria. tab:sAG.participle presents some of the most common examples of sɤɣ- participles in Kamnyu Japhug.

Some of the verbs taking the sɤɣ- allomorph do also occur with sɤ-. For instance, menot exist is attested with both ɯ-sɤɣ-me as in ( ex:WsAGme ) and ɯ-sɤ-me in ( ex:WsAme ). However, most verbs in tab:sAG.participle are only compatible with the sɤɣ- allomorph.

exe

ʑmbɯlɯm ɯ-sɤɣ-ɬoʁ nɯra tu-ɬoʁ ŋu. ʑmbɯlɯm ɯ-sɤɣ-me ra kɯnɤ tu-ɬoʁ ɕti. \\
species.of.mushroom 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -come.out dem: pl ipfv -come.out be: fact species.of.mushroom 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -not.exist \ pl also ipfv -come.out be. aff: fact \\
`It grows in the places where the youlaku mushroom grows, and also in the places where there are no youlaku.' (22-BlamajmAG)
0003584#S55
exe

exe

tɤjmɤɣ ɯ-sɤ-tu ɯ-sɤ-me ɣɤʑu. \\
mushroom 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -exist 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -not.exist exist: sens \\
`There are places where there are mushrooms, and other places where there aren't.' (20-grWBgrWB) 0003554#S45
exe

The allomorphs sɤz- and z- occur in the same context, with non-monosyllabic verb stems, where the first syllable (either a productive or a frozen prefix) is sonorant-initial. These two allomorphs are completely interchangeable, without restriction on particular verbs or the function of the relativized element (instrument, locative or temporal adjunct). For instance, the locative participle of rɤʑistay is attested as both ɯ-sɤz-rɤʑi and ɯ-z-rɤʑi `the place when he/it stays' in the corpus, as shown by examples ( ex:WsAzrAZi ) and ( ex:WzrAZi ), a few sentences away from each other in the same story.

exe

tɕeri nɯnɯ sɤtɕʰa nɯ li iɕqʰa qapribɯxsi ɯ-sɤz-rɤʑi pjɤ-ɕti. \\
but dem place dem again the.aforementioned python 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -stay ifr. ipfv -be. aff \\
`But that place was the abode of a python.' (140511 xinbada-zh)
0003961#S89
exe

exe

tɕe <xinbaba> rcanɯ, maka nɯtɕu ɯ-z-rɤʑi ɯ-tɯ-sɤɣ-mu pjɤ-sɤre ʑo tɕe,\\
lnk Sinbad unexp: deg at.all dem: loc 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -stay 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - prop -be.afraid ifr. ipfv -be.ridiculous emph lnk \\
`Sinbad, the place where he stayed was extremely terrifying.' (140511 xinbada-zh)
0003961#S95
exe

The sɤ- allomorph, rather than sɤz- or z, is however found when preceding the vertitive (§ sec:vertitive ) and autive (§ sec:autobenefactive ) prefixes, as in ( ex:sAnWlhoR.kWme ).

exe

qʰe tú-wɣ-cɯ mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ, sɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ ri kɯ-me ta-βzu. \\
lnk ipfv - inv -open neg - sbj: pcp -be.possible obl: pcp - auto -come.out also sbj: pcp -not.exist aor:3 -make \\
`(He put tape on the drawers so that) they could not be opened, and there was no way to come out of them (to prevent the rats inside from escaping).' (150831 BZW kAnArRaR)
0006378#S18
exe

The allomorph sɤɣ- is also (though more rarely) attested with the autive nɯ- of verbs that take sɤɣ- in their simplex form. For instance, next to sɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ, the oblique participle sɤɣ-nɯ-ɬoʁ is found in ( ex:WsAGnWlhoR ) (without autive prefix the oblique participle is ɯ-sɤɣ-ɬoʁ, see tab:sAG.participle ).

exe

ɯ-sɤɣ-nɯ-ɬoʁ ɣɯ ɯ-kɯ-spoʁ pjɤ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss - obl: pcp - auto -come.out gen 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -have.a.hole ifr. ipfv -be \\
`It was the hole from which [the animal] came out [of the cave]. (140511 xinbada-zh) 0003961#S80
exe

The sɤz- allomorph is not completely impossible with the autive nɯ- prefix, but only one example, nɯ-sɤz-nɯ-ɴɢɤt `the place where they (had) parted ways' ( ex:nWsAznWNGAt ), is found in the whole corpus (and the form sɤ-nɯ-ɴɢɤt is also attested, see example ex:YWsAnWNGAt in § sec:locative.participle.relatives ).

exe

nɯ-sɤz-nɯ-ɴɢɤt ɣɯ iɕqʰa, tʂɤsɤɴɢɤt nɯtɕu jɤ-azɣɯt-nɯ tɕe, \\
3pl. poss - obl: pcp - auto - acaus:separate gen filler crossroads dem: loc aor -reach- pl lnk \\
`They arrived at the crossroads where they had parted ways.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi)
0003935#S106
exe
summary:
The oblique participle has a basic form sɤ and three additional allomorphs: sɤz-, z-, and sɤɣ- (or sɤx- before a voiceless consonant). The sɤɣ- allomorph is mainly used with certain intransitive or labile monosyllabic verbs under specific phonological conditions, while sɤz- and z- occur freely and interchangeably with non-monosyllabic stems whose first syllable is sonorant-initial.  

The plain sɤ- form appears instead before vertitive and autive prefixes, and sɤɣ- can also occur with autive nɯ- in some verbs, though this is rarer.

text:
Like subject and object participles, oblique participle keep the verb transitivity, and transitive verbs can take an overt object as qaj ɯ-sɤ-ji `place for planting wheat' Note that participle ɯ-sɤ-ji can have other interpretations, including `the period when it is planted', as in ( ex:WsAji ) below. in ( ex:qaj.WsAji ).

exe

qajsta nɯnɯ kɯɕɯŋgɯ qaj ɯ-sɤ-ji pjɤ-pe tɕe tɕe núndʐa qajsta tu-ti-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
topo dem in.former.times wheat 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -plant ifr. ipfv -be.good lnk lnk for.this.reason topo ipfv -say- pl sens -be \\
`Qaysta, in former times it was a wheat field which was good, and for this reason, it is called `Qaysta' `the place of the wheat'.' (140522 kAmYW tWji2) 0004057#S101
exe

An antipassive form (§ sec:antipassive ) is necessary if there is no definite object. For instance in ( ex:sAZrAji ), sɤz-rɤ-ji `place for planting, field' is based on the rɤ- antipassive of jiplant; this form, unlike ɯ-sɤ-ji in ( ex:qaj.WsAji ), is used without (and cannot occur with) any noun specifying the crop planted in the field.

exe

tɕe tɯmgri sɤz-rɤ-ji nɯ koŋla ɲɤ-ɣɤ-me-nɯ ma kʰa ʁɟa ʑo to-βzu-nɯ. \\
lnk topo obl: pcp - apass -plant dem completely ifr - caus -not.exist- pl lnk house completely emph ifr -make- pl \\
`They removed all the fields in Temgri, and built houses there [instead].' (140522 kAmYW tWji2) 0004057#S17
exe
summary:
Oblique participles preserve verb transitivity, so transitive verbs can still take an overt object, as in forms meaning “place for planting wheat.” These participles may also have other interpretations, such as referring to the time when something is planted.  

If there is no definite object, an antipassive form is required; for example, the form meaning “field” is based on the antipassive of “plant” and cannot occur with a noun specifying the crop.

text:
prefix!possessive participle!oblique
Possessive prefixes on oblique participles are optional, though their presence is preferred in careful speech.

With intransitive verbs, the possessive prefix refers to the subject, as a-sɤz-nɤri `the place where I stay' in ( ex:asAzrAZi.ri.GAZu ).

exe

a-kɤ-ndza ri ɣɤʑu, a-sɤz-rɤʑi ri ɣɤʑu qʰe \\
1sg. poss - obj: pcp -eat also exist: sens 1sg. poss - obj: pcp blique-stay also exist: sens lnk \\
`(There), I have food to eat and a place to stay.' (150831 renshen wawa) 0006418#S22
exe

With transitive verbs, the possessive prefix can be coreferent with the object. For instance, in ( ex:nWsthamtCAt.GW.nWsAtsxWB ), the plural nɯ- on nɯ-sɤ-tʂɯβ refers to the many types of clothes and shoes mentioned just before in the same text.

exe

nɯstʰamtɕɤt ɣɯ nɯ-sɤ-tʂɯβ nɯ tɯ-ŋgru tu-sɯ-βzu-nɯ. \\
so.many gen 3pl. poss - obj: pcp blique-sew dem indef. poss -sinew ipfv - caus -make- pl \\
`People use sinew to sew that many [types of clothes and shoes].' (150906 tWNgru) 0006304#S17
exe

However, it is also possible for the possessive prefix to be coreferent with the subject. This is particularly common when the subject is first or second person, and no overt object is present, as nɤ-sɤ-ta `the place where you put it' in ( ex:nAsAta.me ).

exe

kɯɕte nɯtɕu nɤ-sɤ-ta me ɯ́-ŋu \\
other dem: loc 2sg. poss - obl: pcp -put not.exist: fact qu -be: fact \\
`Isn't there any other place where you put [the food]?' (meimei de gushi)
exe

There is no person hierarchy in slot accessibility to the possessive prefix however; in ( ex:nWsAntChoz ), the possessive prefix on nɯ-sɤ-ntɕʰoz marks the subject, although the object is first person plural.

exe

tɕe iʑora ɣɯ nɯ-sɤ-ntɕʰoz a-pɯ-tu tɕe ɲɯ-tʂɯn \\
lnk 1pl gen 3pl. poss - obl: pcp -use irr - ipfv -exist lnk sens -be.grateful \\
`We are glad that [some] of us have an opportunity to be useful to them.' (conversation)
exe

When the object is overt (§ sec:oblique.participle.transitivity ), it is rare to put a first or second person possessive prefix coreferent with the subject on the participle. Rather, a possessive prefix occurs on the object, as in ( ex:jikhWtsa.sArku ) and ( ex:ambrAz.sArku ), as if kʰɯtsa sɤ-rku `place where one puts the bowls' and mbrɤz sɤ-rku `rice container' were compounds.

exe

tɕe tɕe ji-kʰɯtsa sɤ-rku ɣɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯ, <chouchou> ɯ-ŋgɯ pɯ-nnɯ-ŋu, nɯ kɯmaʁ nɯra pɯ-nnɯ-ŋu kɯnɤ maka, laχtɕʰa kɤ-rku me, kɤ-ndza kɤ-rku me, nɯra tu-ndze nɤ tu-ndze, \\
lnk lnk 1pl. poss -bowl obl: pcp -put.in gen 3sg. poss -inside dem drawer 3sg. poss -inside pst. ipfv - auto -be dem other dem: pl pst. ipfv - auto -be also at.all thing obj: pcp -put.in whether obj: pcp -eat obj: pcp -put.in whether dem ipfv -eat[III] lnk ipfv -eat[III] \\
`Whether it was in the cupboard in which we put [our] bowls, or in the drawers or elsewhere, whether it was food or objects in there, [the mice] ate/gnawed them again and again.' (150831 BZW kAnArRaR)
0006378#S7
exe

exe

nɯ sɤznɤ a-mbrɤz sɤ-rku a-pɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ra \\
dem comp 1sg. poss -rice obl: pcp -put.in irr - ipfv -be sens -be.needed \\
`Why don't I use [this basin] as a rice container?' (150831 jubaopen-zh)
0006294#S23
exe

Using the possessive on the verb is never preferred, but appears to be grammatical in elicitation in negative existential constructions, thus next to ( ex:jikhWtsa.sAta ), ( ex:khWtsa.jisAta ) is also possible.
exe

xlist

iʑo ji-kʰɯtsa sɤ-ta me. \\
1pl 1pl. poss -bowl obl: pcp -put not.exist: fact \\

iʑo kʰɯtsa ji-sɤ-ta me \\
1pl bowl 1pl. poss - obl: pcp -put not.exist: fact \\
`We don't have any place to put the bowls.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

If the object is an inalienably possessed noun, it can be alienabilized (§ sec:alienabilization ). For instance, the 1pl possessive form of tɯ-ŋga sɤ-χtɕi `washing machine' can be either ( ex:jitWNga.sAXtCi ) with alienabilization or ( ex:jiNga.sAXtCi ) without it.

exe

xlist

ji-tɯ-ŋga sɤ-χtɕi \\
1pl. poss - indef. poss -clothes obl: pcp -wash \\

ji-ŋga sɤ-χtɕi \\
1pl. poss -clothes obl: pcp -wash \\
xlist
`Our washing machine' ( ex:jitWNga.sAXtCi heard in context, ex:jiNga.sAXtCi elicited)
exe
summary:
Possessive prefixes on oblique participles are optional, though they are preferred in careful speech. With intransitive verbs, the prefix refers to the subject; with transitive verbs, it may refer either to the object or, especially with first/second person subjects and no overt object, to the subject.  

The text also notes that when the object is overt, subject agreement on the participle is rare and the possessive prefix more often marks the object, sometimes resembling a compound. In negative existential constructions, putting the possessive on the verb is possible but not preferred, and inalienably possessed nouns may be alienabilized before being used with these participles.

text:
participle!oblique orientation!preverb
Unlike subject and object participles, the only prefixes (other than possessive prefixes) that oblique participles can take are the polarity prefixes and series B orientation preverbs.

It is thus not possible to have perfective or past imperfective oblique participles, and alternative strategies are used to express the corresponding meanings. For instance, from the verb sqacook, the form $ $ ɯ-pɯ-sɤ-sqa (intended meaning: `the thing that has been used to cook') is incorrect, and the solution to circumvent this morphological constraint is to combine the plain oblique participle ɯ-sɤ-sqa with pɯ-kɯ-ŋu (the past imperfective subject participle of ŋube) and with the phrase nɯ ɕɯŋgɯ `before that', as in ( ex:WsAsqa.pWkWNu ).

exe

nɯ ɕɯŋgɯ ɯ-sɤ-sqa pɯ-kɯ-ŋu ɯ-ŋgɯ (tu-rku-nɯ) \\
dem before 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -cook pst. ipfv - sbj: pcp -be 3sg. poss -inside ipfv -put.in- pl \\
`[They put it] in the [pan] that had been used to cook [the barley grains] previously.' (31-cha) 0003764#S58
exe

Negative forms of the oblique participle are not very common, but examples are found in the corpus (as in ex:WmAsApe ) and there is no difficulty to elicit them.

exe

qaʑmbri nɯ, nɤkinɯ, ɯ-sɤ-pe ra me, ɯ-mɤ-sɤ-pe ra me, \\
vine dem filler 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -be.good pl not.exist: fact 3sg. poss - neg - obl: pcp -be.good pl not.exist: fact \\
`The vine is neither a boon nor a harm (to the plants on which it grows).' (06-qaZmbri) 0003416#S17
exe
summary: Oblique participles can take only possessive prefixes, polarity prefixes, and series B orientation preverbs; they cannot form perfective or past imperfective participles directly. To express those meanings, speakers use alternative constructions, such as combining a plain oblique participle with a past imperfective subject participle and an adverbial phrase like “before that.” Negative oblique participles are uncommon in the corpus but are attested and can be elicited without difficulty.

text:
participle!oblique relative clause!locative
The oblique participle can be used to build many different types of relative clauses, with various non-core arguments and adjuncts as relativized elements, including locative, temporal, instrumental adjuncts and dative arguments. The most common ones are the locative relative clauses.

With motion verbs like ɕego or verbs of manipulation, the relativized element can be either the goal (the endpoint of the motion, as in ex:ndZisAxCe ), or the path through which the motion event takes place: in ( ex:tsxu.kusAxCe ) for instance, the head tʂu is a locative adjunct (`the road through which one goes to $X$') different from the goal (the placename prɤɕta ).

exe

ndʑi-sɤx-ɕe nɯtɕu jo-zɣɯt tɕe \\
3du. poss - obl: pcp -go dem: loc ifr -reach lnk \\
`[The ox] arrived at the place where the two of them were going.' (150826 shier shengxiao-zh) 0006284#S85
exe

exe

[prɤɕta tʂu ku-sɤx-ɕe] nɯre ri tɯ-ji ci tu tɕe, nɯ cɤŋgɤɣ rmi. \\
topo path ipfv:east- obl: pcp -go dem: loc loc indef. poss -field indef exist: fact lnk dem topo be.called: fact \\
`On the road towards Prashta there is a field, it is called Kyangag.' (140522 kAmYW tWji) 0004055#S110
exe

In ( ex:WsAznACWCe ), the oblique participle designates the areas in which the subject (a plant) grows, without a specific goal.

exe

pɤjka wuma ʑo a-pɯ-pe, tɕe ɯ-sɤx-ɕe nɯra a-pɯ-dɤn ɯ-sɤz-nɤɕɯɕe a-pɯ-dɤn tɕe, pɤjka tɯ-pʰɯ ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu kɯβdɤsqi jamar, ɯ-mat ku-tsʰoʁ ɲɯ-cʰa \\
pumpkin really emph irr - ipfv -be.good lnk 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -go dem: pl irr - ipfv -be.many 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -go.around irr - ipfv -be.many lnk pumpkin one -tree 3sg. poss -on dem: loc fourty about 3sg. poss -fruit ipfv -attach sens -can \\
`When the pumpkin [grows] well, and when there are a lot of [places] for it to spread, one plant can yield about fourty pumpkin.' (16-CWrNgo)
0003518#S95
exe

The relativized locative adjunct can also be the place of origin rather than the goal in the case of the verb ɣicome as in ( ex:jisAGi ).

exe

iʑora nɯ ji-sɤ-ɣi nɯtɕu pjɤ-ŋu tɕe. \\
1pl dem 1pl. poss - obl: pcp -come dem: loc ifr. ipfv -be lnk \\
`The place from where we come was there.' (2010-06)
exe

With stative verbs or dynamic verbs implying no motion, the oblique participle has a static locative meaning, as in ( ex:tWsAmdzW ).

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ tɕʰeme tɯ-sɤ-ɤmdzɯ ʑaka tu. \\
indef. poss -son girl indef. poss - obl: pcp -sit each exist: fact \\
`Gentlemen and ladies each have [different] seating places.' (31-khAjmu)
0004079#S10
exe

Participial locative relative clauses are used to describe non-transient properties of places: directions, locations or places of origin that are unchanging characteristics of things or persons ( ex:tsxu.kusAxCe and ex:jisAGi ), places where some state of affair generally occurs due to a natural law ( ex:WsAznACWCe and ex:WsAdAn ) or places used for a specific purpose, as in ( ex:tWsAmdzW ), and even more clearly in ( ex:WsAta.Wrkoz ) with the property noun ɯ-rkozsomething special (§ sec:z.nmlz ).

exe

tɕe saŋdi nɯ tɕe, nɯnɯ si ɯ-sɤ-ta ɯ-rkoz ʑo pjɤ-ŋu. \\
lnk lower.side.of.the.hearth dem lnk dem firewood 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -put 3sg. poss -special emph ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The lower side of the hearth was specifically where [people] put firewood.' (2011-11)
exe

For transient properties of places, finite relatives are used instead (§ sec:locative.relativization.finite ). In example ( ex:nWNga.sAta ) translated from Chinese, The original text has ……走到仙女们放衣服的地方 zǒu dào xiānnǚmen fàng yīfú de dìfāng...went to the place where the sky goddesses put/had put their clothes; both interpretations are possible. Tshendzin hesitates between a participial relative (implying that there was a specific place where the sky goddesses put their clothes each time they came to earth) and a finite relative (suggesting that they put their clothes in some unspecific place, perhaps in a casual way as the autive -nɯ- could indicate, § sec:autobenefactive ).

exe

tɕʰemɤpɯ nɯra, [nɯ-ŋga sɤ-ta] nɯtɕu ko-ɕe, [nɯ-ŋga na-nɯ-ta-nɯ] nɯtɕu ko-ɕe matɕi, \\
girl dem: pl 3pl. poss -clothes obl: pcp -put dem: loc ifr: east -go 3pl. poss -clothes aor:3 - auto -put- pl dem: loc ifr: east -go lnk \\
`He went to the place where the girls put their clothes, where they had put their clothes.' (150828 niulang-zh) 0006318#S58
exe

Locative participial relative clauses with overt head can be prenominal, in particular with genitival relatives as in ( ex:sAnWCe.GW.Wtsxu ).

exe

pjɤ-nɯkɯlu-nɯ ma sɤ-nɯ-ɕe ɣɯ ɯ-tʂu nɯ mɯ-ɲɤ-nɯ-mto-nɯ. \\
ifr -be.lost- pl lnk obl: pcp - vert -go gen 3sg. poss -path dem neg - ifr - auto -see- pl \\
`They were lost, and could not find their way back home.' (160630 poucet1) 0006065#S52
exe

However, head-internal relatives are also attested: in ( ex:tsxu.kusAxCe ) above and ( ex:YWsAnWNGAt ), the head of the participial relatives, the noun tʂuroad, occurs between the verb in oblique participle form and a place name marking the goal. Note in addition that ( ex:YWsAnWNGAt ) illustrates two locative oblique participial relative clauses embedded within another participial relative. In ( ex:YWsAnWNGAt ), the orientation preverbs reflect the basic meanings of the tridimensional system (§ sec:tridimensional.preverb ).

exe

[[rpɤŋgɯ tʂu lu-sɤx-ɕe] cʰo [prɤscʰɯ tʂu lu-sɤ-ɣi] ɲɯ-sɤ-nɯ-ɴɢɤt] nɯtɕu, \\
topo path ipfv: upstream - obl: pcp -go comit topo path ipfv: upstream - obl: pcp -come ipfv: west - obl: pcp - auto - acaus:separate dem: loc \\
`At the place where the road towards Rpangu and the road towards Praskhyu separate.' (140522 kAmYW tWji2)
0004057#S122
exe
summary:
The oblique participle is used to form many kinds of relative clauses, especially locative ones, in which the relativized element may be a goal, path, origin, or a static place. With motion verbs it can refer either to the endpoint or the route of motion, while with stative or non-motion verbs it expresses a static locative meaning.  

These locative participial relatives describe non-transient properties of places, such as fixed directions, origins, habitual locations, natural settings, or places used for a specific purpose. For transient or less specific place properties, finite relatives are preferred, though both participial and finite interpretations may sometimes be possible.

text:
participle!oblique relative clause!instrumental
Another very productive type of oblique participial relatives are the instrumental relative clauses (§ sec:instrument.relativization ). Although instruments, like transitive subjects, receive ergative case (§ sec:instr.kW ), they are usually relativized with oblique participles.

There is often ambiguity between instrument relativization and locative adjunct relativization; for instance, while the participle ɯ-z-rɤ-rɤt can mean `pen (the tool used to write)' as in ( ex:WzArAt ), this form can also designate the paper on which one writes or even one's office.

exe

ɯ-slamaχti nɯ ɣɯ, [ɯ-z-rɤ-rɤt] ci to-nɯ-ndo tɕe jo-nɯ-tsɯm ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
3sg. poss -classmate dem gen 3sg. poss - obl: pcp - apass -write indef ifr - auto -take lnk ifr - vert -take.away sens -be lnk \\
`He took away the pen of a classmate.' (2014-tou dongxi de xiaohai-zh)
exe

Instrumental relative clauses built with oblique participles can occur as objects of the causativized verb sɯ-βzucause to make; use X to make, as in ( ex:tWthW.sAXtCi.tWNga.sApCiz ).

exe

nɯnɯ [tɯtʰɯ sɤ-χtɕi], [tɯ-ŋga sɤ-pɕiz] nɯra tu-sɯ-βzu-nɯ pɯ-ŋgrɤl. \\
dem pan obl: pcp -wash indef. poss -clothes obl: pcp -wipe dem: pl ipfv - caus -make- pl pst. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`People used to employ [ Usnea ] as tools to wash pans or wipe clothes.' (20-sWrna) 0003564#S141
exe

In this construction, the material used to make the tool is marked with the ergative (§ sec:instr.kW ), as in ( ex:WsACmi ).

exe

ɯnɯnɯ kɯ [ɯ-sɤ-ɕmi] tu-sɯ-βzu-nɯ pɯ-ŋgrɤl \\
dem erg 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -mix ipfv - caus -make- pl pst. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`People used to employ it (a boat oar) to mix [the alcohol].' (31-cha) 0003764#S42
exe

Oblique participles are used to make instrumental relative clauses, used like nouns of instruments, from both transitive and intransitive verbs. If the base verb is transitive, the participle retains its transitivity: thus in ( ex:WsACmi ), the absence of object in the one-word relative clause ɯ-sɤ-ɕmi `the tool used to mix it' is the result of zero-anaphora, and implies a definite object. Instrumental relative clauses with a transitive verb more often have an overt object, as in ( ex:tWthW.sAXtCi.tWNga.sApCiz ). For indefinite objects, antipassivization is necessary, as in ɯ-z-rɤ-rɤt `the tool used to write' in ( ex:WzArAt ) above (see also § sec:oblique.participle.transitivity ).

The relativized instrument need not be an entity, but can also be an action. For instance, in the pseudo-cleft ( ex:WsAznWrmAZu ), what is referred to by the participial relative is the infinitival clause mɲɤm kɤ-pʰaʁ.

exe

qajdo [ɯ-rʑaβ ɯ-ɕki ɯ-sɤz-nɯrmɤʑu] nɯ mɲɤm kɤ-pʰaʁ pjɤ-ŋu \\
crow 3sg. poss -wife 3sg. poss - dat 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -show.off dem type.of.tree inf -chop ifr. ipfv -be \\
`What he was showing off with to his wife was chopping the wood of the mɲɤm tree (which is easy to cut).' (11-mYAm)
0003474#S22
exe
summary:
Instrumental relative clauses are a very productive type of oblique participial relative clause. Although instruments take ergative case like transitive subjects, they are usually relativized with oblique participles, and these forms can be ambiguous with locative adjunct relatives.

These relatives can function as objects of causativized “make/use X to do Y” constructions, and the material used to make the tool is marked with ergative. They are built from both transitive and intransitive verbs; with transitive verbs, the participle retains transitivity, often with an overt object or with zero-anaphora, while indefinite objects require antipassivization. The relativized instrument may also denote an action rather than an entity.

text:
participle!oblique
In addition to goals, locative adjuncts and instruments, oblique participles are used to relativize various other types of arguments and adjuncts, though those cases are considerably less common in the corpus.

Dative arguments (in ɯ-ɕki or ɯ-pʰe, § sec:dative ) are relativized with an oblique participle (§ sec:dative.relativization ), as is shown by ( ex:WsAfCAt ), where the verb fɕɤttell also occurs as the main verb of the second clause with an overt recipient marked with the dative.

exe

[ɯ-sɤ-fɕɤt] pjɤ-me qʰe tɕe tɤ-pɤtso ɯ-ɕki nɯ tɕu nɯra tɕʰi pɯ-kɯ-fse nɯra pjɤ-fɕɤt. \\
3sg. poss - obl: pcp -tell ipfv. ifr -not.exist lnk lnk indef. poss -child 3sg - dat dem loc dem: pl what pst - sbj: pcp -be.like dem: pl ifr -tell \\
`She had no one [else] to tell, so she told the boy everything that had happened.' (140515 congming de wusui xiaohai-zh) 0003998#S74
exe

Likewise, comitative phrases in cʰo (§ sec:comitative ) and occurring with verbs with intrinsically non-singular subjects (§ sec:intrinsically.n.sg.subject ), are relativized with an oblique participle. For instance, the participle ɯ-sɤ-ɤmɯmi in ( ex:WsAmWmi ) is a headless relative meaning `those with whom it is on good terms with'.

exe

tɕe ɯʑo [ɯ-sɤ-ɤmɯmi] nɯ dɤn ma ca kɯ-fse qaʑo kɯ-fse, tsʰɤt kɯ-fse, ɯʑo cʰo kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ sɯjno, xɕaj ma mɤ-kɯ-ndza nɯ ra cʰo nɯ amɯmi-nɯ tɕe, \\
lnk it 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -be.on.good.terms dem be.many: fact because musk.deer obl: pcp -be.like sheep obl: pcp -be.like goat obl: pcp -be.like it with obl: pcp -be.identical herbs grass apart.from neg - obl: pcp -eat dem pl with dem be.in.good.term: fact - pl lnk \\
`The [animals] that are on good terms with the rabbit are many, it is on good terms with those that only eat grass, like musk deer, sheep or goats.' (04 qala1)
0003392#S30
exe

Time adjuncts are also possibly relativized using oblique participles, as ɯ-sɤ-ji, which means `the period when it is planted' in ( ex:WsAji ). However, finite relative clauses are the preferred way of relativizing time adjuncts (§ sec:time.relativization ). As in the case of locative relative clauses (§ sec:locative.participle.relatives ), participial relative clauses are only used to refer to specific dates and time periods that are intrinsic properties of the event.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ ʑaka [ɯ-sɤ-ji] ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe \\
lnk dem each 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -plant sens -be lnk \\
`These are the [periods] when people plant each of these [crops].' (15 tChWma)
0003514#S18
exe

Temporal relative clauses are generally headless, but ( ex:WsAsna ) shows an example of head-internal (or postnominal) relative clause, with skɤrmaminute, date as its head noun. In addition, this participial relative has here a superlative interpretation (§ sec:possessed.superlative ).

exe

lɤsɤr χsɯm ɯ-raŋ tɕe, tɯxpalɤskɤr ɣɯ, nɤkinɯ, [skɤrma ɯ-sɤ-sna] ŋu tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
new.year three 3sg. poss -time loc whole.year gen filler date 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -be.good be: fact ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`We say that the third day of the year is the [most] auspicious day in the whole year.' (2010-10)
exe

A further derived meaning of the oblique participle is that of `opportunity to do X', as in ( ex:sAznWNgra.GAZu ) and ( ex:nWsAntChoz ) above.

exe

tɕe [sɤz-nɯŋgra] ɣɤʑu ri, li sɤɣʑɯr \\
lnk obl: pcp -earn.wages exist: sens lnk again be.dangerous: fact \\
`Although it [provides] an opportunity to earn wages, it is also dangerous.' (conversation 140510)
exe

Even in context, the exact meaning of a particular oblique relative clause may allow some leeway in interpretation. For instance, the participle ji-sɤx-ɕe in the negative existential construction in ( ex:jisAxCe.maNe ) could be understood as a locative relative clause `(we had no) place to go' but also alternatively as `(we had no) opportunity to go (anywhere)' in this particular context.

exe

iʑora tɕe kʰa ɯ-ŋgɯ kɤ-kɤ-ja ʑo ɲɯ-fse-j ku-rɤʑit-i ma [ji-sɤx-ɕe] maŋe \\
1pl lnk house 3sg. poss -inside aor - obj: pcp -close emph sens -be.like- 1pl ipfv -stay- 1pl lnk 1pl. poss - obl: pcp -go not.exist: sens \\
`It was like we were locked in the house, with nowhere to go.' (140501 tshering skyid)
0003902#S115
exe
summary: Oblique participles are used not only for goals, locatives, and instruments, but also to relativize less common argument and adjunct types. They can relativize dative arguments and certain comitative phrases, and they may also be used for time adjuncts, though finite relative clauses are preferred for time expressions. The passage further notes that oblique participles can express meanings such as “the period when X happens” or “opportunity to do X,” with some cases allowing more than one interpretation depending on context.

text:
participle!oblique causative!periphrastic
The oblique participles can occur as object of the verb βzumake, with a purposive ( ex:WmAsAxCe.tuBzunW ) or causative ( ex:WsARjWRjit ) interpretation. These meanings derive from the instrumental nominalizing uses of the oblique participle.

exe

tɯ-ji ɯ-rkɯ ra tɤ-ɣur pjɯ-ta-nɯ tɕe, fsapaʁ ɯ-mɤ-sɤx-ɕe tu-βzu-nɯ ŋgrɤl \\
indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -side pl indef. poss -fence ipfv -put- pl lnk animals 3sg. poss - neg - obl: pcp -go ipfv -make- pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`They put a fence around the fields, so as to prevent farm animals from going there.' (140427 qamtsWrmdzu) 0003854#S13
exe

In ( ex:WmAsAxCe.tuBzunW ), the phrase fsapaʁ ɯ-mɤ-sɤx-ɕe can be interpreted as `(something made so) that animals do not go (there)', while in ( ex:WsARjWRjit ) rgargɯn nɯnɯ ɯ-sɤ-ʁjɯ ʁjit means `(something used to) remind the old man'.

exe

tɕʰeme kɯ-ŋɤn nɯ kɯ iɕqʰa nɯ, rgargɯn nɯnɯ ɯ-sɤ-ʁjɯ ʁjit to-βzu tɕe, \\
woman sbj: pcp -be.evil dem erg filler dem old.man dem 3sg. poss - obl: pcp - emph remember ifr -make lnk \\
`The evil woman reminded the old man.' (140515 jiesu de laoren-zh)
0004004#S118
exe
summary: The oblique participle can serve as the object of **βzumake** ‘make,’ yielding either purposive or causative meanings. These interpretations are said to come from the participle’s older instrumental nominalizing function, as shown by examples meaning roughly ‘so that animals do not go there’ and ‘used to remind the old man.’

text:
The various allomorphs of the oblique participle do resemble other prefixes found in Japhug. The sɤ- and sɤɣ- allomorphs are also found with the proprietive derivation (§ sec:proprietive ), and sɤ- is also similar to the human antipassive, or the sigmatic causative of a- initial verbs (§ sec:contraction ). Finally, the z- allomorph of the oblique participle can resemble the causative (§ sec:caus.z ) or one allomorph of the translocative prefix (§ sec:translocative.morpho ).

However, unlike subject (§ sec:subject.participle.ambiguities ) and object (§ sec:object.participle.ambiguity ) participles, these surface ambiguities are only very superficial, as the forms with which the oblique participle could potentially be confused are all finite, and hardly ever occur in the same syntactic context as the oblique participle (and except for their bare infinitive form, in the case of transitive verb, never occur with a possessive prefix).

In the case of the z- allomorph of translocative prefix, note that it only occurs before a few orientation preverbs ( ɲɯ, ɲɤ, ju, jɤ, jo, ja- ), whereas the oblique participle z- can only follow an orientation preverb, as in ɯ-cʰɯ-z-raʁrɯz in ( ex:WchWzraRWz ), so that the two forms can never be confused.

exe

nɯnɯ ɣɯ ɯ-cʰɯ-z-raʁrɯz nɯ ɯ-sɤ-pɕiz rmi \\
dem gen 3sg. poss - ipfv: downstream - obl: pcp -sweep dem 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -wipe be.called: fact \\
`[The tool used to] sweep [the flour] is called a ``wiper''.' (06-BGa) 0003408#S149
exe
summary: The allomorphs of the oblique participle resemble several other Japhug prefixes, including the proprietive, human antipassive, sigmatic causative, causative, and translocative prefix. However, these similarities are only superficial, because the potentially confusing forms are finite and rarely share the same syntactic contexts, and the z- allomorph of the translocative cannot be confused with the oblique participle since their positions relative to orientation preverbs are different.

text:
Nouns of instruments and of location, including placenames, are often made from oblique participles.

The noun sɤcɯkey, although transparently originating from the instrumental use of the oblique participle of cɯopen, is lexicalized as shown by the fact that it cannot take orientation preverbs, and that it occurs in collocation with the auxiliary lɤt to mean `lock (the door)' as in ( ex:sAcW.malAt2 ).

exe

ɯ-ŋgɯ lɤ-ɣi jɤɣ ma sɤcɯ mɤ-a-lɤt \\
3sg.poss-inside imp: upstream -come be.allowed: fact lnk key neg - pass -throw \\
`Come in, the door is not locked.' (140428 xiaohongmao-zh) 0003884#S73
exe

Place names built from oblique participle include Znɤrɣɤma, from the locative participle z-nɤrɣɤma of the verb nɤrɣɤmapray for rain (probably a denominal verb from a compound * rɣɤma based on tɯ-rɣiseed and ta-mawork, § sec:denom.intr.nW ), as it was the place where people used to perform this activity in Kamnyu in the traditional society, as explained in § sec:antipassive.avoidance.

Another example is the uninhabited place called kɯlɤɣsɤmdzɯ, a transparent combination kɯ-lɤɣshepherd (§ sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ) and ɯ-sɤ-ɤmdzɯsitting place reflecting the use of this place (as described in ex:kWlAG.sAmdzW ).

exe

kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ci ʑo antɤm, tɕe nɯ kɯ-lɤɣ ra nɯtɕu ku-rɤʑi-nɯ pjɤ-ŋgrɤl \\
inf: stat - emph be.small a.little emph be.flat: fact lnk dem sbj: pcp -graze pl dem: loc ipfv -stay- pl ifr. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`[The place called kɯlɤɣsɤmdzɯ ] is a bit flat, and shepherds used to stay there.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S269
exe

There are also case of nouns of instruments in sɤ- whose base verb is not identifiable. For instance, the noun sɤɕtɕɯɣstrap (to carry children on the back), which is glossed using an oblique participle as in ( ex:tApAtso.WsAzbWwa ), is most certainly a frozen oblique participle, but there is no verb *ɕtɕɯɣ in Japhug.

exe

tɤ-pɤtso ɯ-sɤz-bɯwa \\
indef. poss -child 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -carry.on.the.back \\
`Something used to carry children on the back' (definition given for the noun sɤɕtɕɯɣ )
exe

Some nouns originating from lexicalized participles have an irregular s- allomorph ( tab:spa.sta.stu ). Their antiquity is shown by the existence of exact cognates in Tangut  and Khroskyabs. All three nouns are used as relators in relative clauses (§ sec:Wspa.relative, § sec:Wstu.relativization.subject ), and ɯ-spamaterial additionally occurs to build a type of purposive clauses (§ sec:purposive.clauses ).

In addition from the general meaning of `place', the nominal stem -sta has three highly specific meanings: tɯ-sta `bed', tɤ-sta `designated place (for burying a dead person)' and ɯ-sta `habit, state', a complement-taking noun (§ sec:nouns.manner.complement ) always selecting a third singular possessor, used in particular in a collocation meaning `return to one's previous state, recover (from a disease)' with fsebe like, as in ( ex:Wsta.pWnWfse ).

exe

ki ɯ-ʁɤri kɯ-fse nɯ ɯ-sta ʑo pɯ-nɯ-fse nɤ \\
dem. prox 3sg. poss -before sbj: pcp -be.like dem 3sg. poss -state emph pst. ipfv - auto -be.like add \\
`She had become again like she was before.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

More speculatively, it is possible that other allomorphs of the oblique nominalization are preserved in some nouns, even when the base is lost. For example, ʑmbrɯboat might be the lexicalized participle of a verb *mbrɯ `float' (cognate of 浮 bjuw $ $ *m.b(r)u `float', ) with a fronted ʑ- allomorph (like that of the sigmatic causative, § sec:caus.Z ).

An even more pronounced type of lexicalization occurs when an oblique participle becomes member of a compound with status contructus vowel alternation. In these cases, it is probable that the compound is genitival, rather than a reduced relative clause.

As first element of compound, we find the oblique participle ɯ-sɤ-qru (from the verb qrugreet, welcome, receive) in bound state combined with the noun cʰaalcohol into
sɤqrɤcʰaalcohol offered to one's guests (§ sec:determinative.n.n ). There are also cases of undetectable bound state, as in sɤrŋgɯŋgabed cover from the oblique participle of rŋgɯlie down and the inalienably possessed noun tɯ-ŋgaclothes: since the first element of this compound sɤ-rŋgɯ ends in -ɯ, it would not have a different bound form.

Oblique participles are also attested as second element of compounds from both transitive and intransitive verbs.

As an example of lexicalized participle from an intransitive verb, the compound tʂɤsɤɴɢɤtcrossroad combines the participle ɯ-sɤ-ɴɢɤtplace where X part ways from the anticausative verb ɴɢɤtpart ways, part company) with the bound state of the noun tʂuroad, from an earlier locative participial relative *tʂu ɯ-sɤ-ɴɢɤt `the place where roads separate'.

With a transitive verb, we find the noun βɣɤsɤprɤtwatermill valve, from an earlier instrumental relative *βɣa ɯ-sɤ-prɤt `the tool used to stop (water) in the mill' from the bound state βɣɤ- of βɣamill combined with the oblique participle ɯ-sɤ-prɤt of the verb prɤtbreak. With undetectable bound state, we have for instance pʰɯsɤtibelows from the onomatopoeia pʰɯ and the oblique participle of tisay, literally `the tool used to make `pff' sound'.

The noun tɤresɤtɕɯtɕɤtjoke is an example of compound without bound state on the first element. It comes from the reduplicated oblique participle of the verb tɕɤttake out, which occurs in collocation with the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-relaugh (n) to mean `mock', as in ( ex:are.matWtCAt ). The original meaning of this compound presumably was `something/someone to make fun of'.

exe

a-re ma-tɯ-tɕɤt \\
1sg. poss -laugh neg: imp -2-take.out \\
`Don't laugh at me!' (elicited)
exe

In the lexicalized compound tɤresɤtɕɯtɕɤt, tɤ-re is alienabilized (§ sec:alienabilization ); this noun occurs in collocation with the verb βzumake or the causative sɯβzucause to make in the sense of `joke'. It can specifically mean `mock', in which case the compound tɤresɤtɕɯtɕɤt takes a possessive prefix coreferent with the subject of βzu (the person making the joke, not the object of mockery), as shown by the presence of the third dual possessive prefix ndʑi- in ( ex:ndZitAresAtCWtCAt ) and the second singular nɤ- in ( ex:nAtAresAtCWtCAt ).

exe
summary: Nouns of instruments and locations, including place names, are often derived from oblique participles, and many of these forms are lexicalized, so their participial origin is no longer fully transparent. The passage gives examples of such nouns and compounds, including cases where the base verb is lost or where the participle appears in a fixed compound with irregular bound-state forms. It also notes that some of these lexicalized forms have specialized meanings and can participate in later collocations, such as nouns meaning “lock,” “crossroad,” or “joke/mock.”

text:
ɯ-pi ʁnɯz ni kɯnɤ tsʰɯrɟɯn ʑo, nɤkinɯ, pjɯ́-wɣ-ɣɤ-kʰe tɕe ndʑi-tɤresɤtɕɯtɕɤt ra tu-βzu-ndʑi pjɤ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -elder.sibling two du also often emph filler ipfv - inv - caus -be.stupid lnk 3du. poss -joke pl ipfv -make- du ifr. ipfv -be \\
`His two elder brothers often called him stupid and mocked him.' (140430 jin e-zh)
0003893#S9

exe

nɤ-tɤresɤtɕɯtɕɤt ma-tɤ-kɯ-sɯ-βzu-a \\
2sg. poss -joke neg: imp - imp -2 1- caus -make- 1sg \\
`Don't mock me!' (elicited)

In these cases, the noun occurring as first element of the compound corresponds to the object of the verb.

The expression sɤrmagood night derives from the oblique participle of the verb rmastay the night, live, and presents unusual morphological properties (§ sec:phatic.inflectionalization ).

text:
infinitive!velar
The most common infinitives in Japhug are the velar infinitives, built from the stem I of the verb and prefixed either with kɤ- or kɯ-; they are homophonous with participles (and historically related to them, § sec:velar.nmlz.history ) and not always easily distinguishable from them (§ sec:infinitives.participles ). They are in particular the preferred citation form of the verbs (§ sec:inf.citation ), though not with all speakers.

The kɯ- infinitives are found with stative verbs (including adjectives and existential verbs), impersonal modal verbs and some anticausative verbs; other verbs take the kɤ- infinitives. In Tshobdun, reports that the kə- and kɐ- infinitives (corresponding to kɯ- and kɤ- in Japhug) occur with non-human and human arguments, respectively (in the case of dynamic verbs). It seems that this criterion is not applicable to Japhug.

Stative verbs in a- have regular fusion of kɯ- and a- as kɤ, and thus superficially appear to have kɤ- infinitives (for instance, the infinitive of arŋibe green is kɯ-ɤrŋi kɤrŋi).
summary: The most common infinitives in Japhug are velar infinitives formed from stem I with either the prefix kɤ- or kɯ-, and they are homophonous with participles; they are also the preferred citation form of verbs, though not for all speakers. The kɯ- form is used with stative verbs, impersonal modal verbs, and some anticausative verbs, while other verbs take kɤ-, and a criterion reported for Tshobdun based on argument type does not seem to apply in Japhug. Stative verbs in a- can undergo fusion with kɯ- so that they superficially appear to have kɤ- infinitives.

text:
ambiguity!participle ambiguity!infinitive
It is not immediately obvious that a category of `velar infinitives' needs to be distinguished from participles in Japhug, as both are non-finite verbal categories prefixed in kɤ- or kɯ- (§ sec:object.participle.ambiguity and § sec:subject.participle.ambiguities ).

The necessity to set kɤ- infinitives apart from object participles stems from the fact that the latter can only be built from transitive or semi-transitive verbs, while the former also occurs with strictly intransitive verbs. Thus, if one were to argue that all kɤ- prefixed non-finite forms of transitive verbs are object participles, including in the case of complement clauses (for instance kɤ-ndza in ex:kAndza.mWpWrYota ), one would not be able to account for the kɤ- prefixed forms of intransitive verbs occurring in the same context such as kɤ-ɕe in ( ex:kACe.mWpWrYota ) -- even though ɕego could be considered to be a kind of semi-transitive verb (since it can take a goal, which can be relativized with a finite relative clause, § sec:locative.relativization.finite ), it is not possible to build a participial relative clause by prefixing kɤ- on this verb (the oblique participle sɤ- must be used instead, § sec:oblique.participle ).

exe

aʑo kɤ-ndza mɯ-pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
1sg???-eat neg - aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I never ate that.' (many attestations)
exe

exe

aj kɤ-ɕe mɯ-pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
1sg inf -go neg - aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I never went there.' (150820 ZNGWloR) 0006292#S3
exe

I therefore adopt the following criteria to distinguish between a kɤ- infinitive and an object participle: kɤ- non-finite forms of (non-semi-transitive) intransitive verbs are infinitives; kɤ- non-finite forms of transitive and semi-transitive verbs occurring in the same contexts as the infinitives of intransitive verbs are infinitives.

By systematically applying these criteria, we can identify three contexts where infinitives are attested: citation form (§ sec:inf.citation ), complementation (§ sec:inf.complementation; object participles used in complement clauses are discussed in § sec:object.participles.complement ), and manner converbs (§ sec:inf.converb ).

Distinguishing between subject participles and kɯ- infinitives in Japhug is less straightforward, unlike in other Gyalrong languages such as Tshobdun for instance,, since even stative verbs take the kɤ- infinitive in complement clauses (§ sec:inf.complementation ). The only clear contexts where kɯ- infinitives do occur is that of citation forms (§ sec:inf.citation ) and complement clauses containing impersonal modal verbs (§ sec:inf.complementation ). Converbs in kɯ- are analyzed as infinitives rather than subject participle because they are only attested with stative verbs or other verbs taking the kɯ- infinitives (§ sec:inf.converb ).
summary:
The passage argues that Japhug needs a category of “velar infinitives” distinct from participles, even though both are non-finite forms prefixed with kɤ- or kɯ-. The key diagnostic is distribution: kɤ- forms with intransitive verbs are infinitives, and kɤ- forms of transitive or semi-transitive verbs are also infinitives when they occur in the same contexts as intransitive infinitives, whereas object participles are restricted to transitive or semi-transitive verbs.

Using these criteria, the text identifies three contexts for infinitives: citation forms, complementation, and manner converbs. It also notes that distinguishing kɯ- infinitives from subject participles is harder in Japhug, since kɯ- appears clearly only in citation forms, in certain complement clauses with impersonal modal verbs, and in converbs with stative or otherwise kɯ- infinitive-taking verbs.

subsubsection: Associated motion, polarity and orientation preverbs on infinitives
text:
infinitive!velar associated motion orientation!preverb
