With the exception of the construction in § sec:inf.exist and some converbial uses (§ sec:inf.converb ), kɤ- infinitives do not take possessive prefixes. However, like participles, they are compatible with associated motion ( ex:CWkAXtW ), negative prefixes ( ex:mAkACe.mAkhW ) (with double negation, § sec:double.negation ) and B-type orientation preverbs ( mWpjWkAlhoR.ftCaka ), with combinations of two prefixes.

exe

a-mgɯr ɲɯ-mŋɤm tɕe ɕɯ-kɤ-χtɯ mɯ́j-cʰa-a \\
1sg. poss -back sens -hurt lnk tral - inf -buy neg: sens -can- 1sg \\
`My back hurts and I cannot go to buy [apples].' (conversation, 30-04-2018)
exe

exe

rɟɤlpu fka ɕti tɕe, mɤ-kɤ-ɕe mɤ-kʰɯ \\
king order be. aff: fact lnk neg - inf -go neg -be.possible: fact \\
`This is the king's order, [I] have no choice but to go.' (2005 Norbzang)
0003768#S146
exe

exe

tɤ-se mɯ-pjɯ-kɤ-ɬoʁ ftɕaka tu-βze-a tu-mdzoz-a pɯ-ŋu ma, \\
indef. poss -blood neg - ipfv - inf -come.out manner ipfv -make[III]- 1sg ipfv -avoid- 1sg pst. ipfv -be lnk \\
`I avoided by all means to let the blood come out.' (of a skin disease, of which it is said that if the blood comes out and gets into contact with other parts of the skin, it will spread) (24-pGArtsAG) 0003624#S56
exe

Negative infinitives take the allomorph mɤ- (as in ex:mAkACe.mAkhW ), unless an imperfective orientation preverb is present, in which case the negative is mɯ- as in ( mWpjWkAlhoR.ftCaka ).

Impersonal and stative infinitives in kɯ- are only attested with the negative prefix mɤ-.
summary: Kɤ- infinitives generally do not take possessive prefixes, except in the construction discussed in § sec:inf.exist and in some converbial uses. They can, however, combine with associated motion, negative prefixes, and B-type orientation preverbs, sometimes with two prefixes; negative infinitives normally use mɤ-, but mɯ- appears when an imperfective orientation preverb is present. Impersonal and stative kɯ- infinitives are only attested with the negative prefix mɤ-.

text:
ambiguity!infinitive ambiguity!orientation preverb
Aside from the homophony between infinitives and participles (§ sec:infinitives.participles ), another type of ambiguity occurs with verbs selecting the orientation preverb eastwards, whose A form is kɤ- (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). Intransitive verbs in imperative singular and perfective third singular forms (for instance kɤ-rŋgɯ `he laid down') and transitive verbs without stem alternation in imperative singular ( kɤ-tsʰi `drink!', § sec:imp.morphology ) have forms that are homophonous with the corresponding infinitives ( kɤ-rŋgɯ `to lie down', kɤ-tsʰi `to drink'), but these cases are never really ambiguous, as it is trivial to distinguish between a finite verb form and a non-finite one, for instance by changing from singular to dual or plural.

For instance, in a particular context, if a form such as kɤ-rŋgɯ can be changed to the corresponding plural kɤ-rŋgɯ-nɯ (which can be either perfective aor -lie.down- pl `they laid down' or imperative `lie down!'), it is possible to conclude that this kɤ-rŋgɯ is necessarily finite (since non-finite verb forms in Japhug never take indexation affixes, § sec:indexation.finiteness.intro ) and cannot be an object participle or an infinitive.
summary: The passage notes that verbs with the orientation preverb **kɤ-** can be homophonous with their infinitives: intransitive verbs in imperative singular and perfective third singular forms, and some transitive imperative singular forms without stem alternation, may look identical to the corresponding infinitive. However, this is not considered a true ambiguity because the forms can be distinguished by inflectional changes such as switching from singular to dual or plural, since non-finite forms in Japhug never take indexation affixes.

text:
infinitive!velar citation form
The infinitive is the preferred form to refer to a verb in metalinguistic discourse as a citation form. In this context stative and impersonal verbs consistently take the kɯ- prefix as in ( ex:mAkWBdi ), and the rest of verbs the kɤ- prefix, as in ( ex:kAnARarphAB ) and ( ex:WkAlAjme.pjWkACthWz ). Even in citation form, the infinitive verb can take orientation ( ex:WkAlAjme.pjWkACthWz ) and polarity prefixes ( ex:mAkWBdi ).

exe

ɯnɯnɯ tɕe tɕe [ɯ-tɯ-tʂɯβ mɤ-kɯ-βdi] tu-kɯ-ti ŋu \\
dem lnk lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: action -sew neg - inf: stat -be.good ipfv - genr:A-say be: fact \\
`People call this `badly sewn'.' (12-kAtsxWb-zh)
0003486#S28
exe

exe

pjɯ-sɯ-ʁndi tɕe pjɯ-sɯ-sat tɕe nɯ kóʁmɯz nɤ cʰɯ-nɯtsɯm ɲɯ-ra tɕe nɯnɯ [kɤ-nɤʁarpʰɤβ] tu-kɯ-ti ŋu \\
ipfv - caus -hit[III] lnk ipfv - caus -kill lnk dem only.after lnk ipfv: downstream -take.away sens -be.needed lnk dem inf -strike.with.wings ipfv - genr:A-say be: fact \\
`It strikes it and kills it [with its wings] and only then takes it away. This is called kɤ-nɤʁarphɤβstrike with one's wings.' (150819 RarphAB-zh)
0006356#S9
exe

The infinitive is commonly used in metalinguistic discussions about collocations, and in those cases can appear together with intransitive subjects ( ex:mAkWBdi ) or objects ( ex:WkAlAjme.pjWkACthWz ). In the latter, the focus is on the noun ɯ-kɤlɤjmehead upside down (§ sec:dvandva.coll ), the verb ɕtʰɯzturn towards being present only because it is selected by ɯ-kɤlɤjme.

exe

ɯ-mŋu nɯ pa pjɯ́-wɣ-ɕtʰɯz tɕe nɯ [ɯ-kɤlɤjme pjɯ-kɤ-ɕtʰɯz] tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -mouth dem down ipfv: down - inv -turn.towards lnk dem 3sg. poss -head.upside.down ipfv: down - inf -turn.toward ipfv - genr:A-say be: fact \\
`One turns the mouth [of the container] downwards, it is called `to turn upside down'.' (30-macha)
0003746#S64
exe

The infinitive is not the only possible choice as a citation form; some speakers sometimes cite a generic form (especially with the imperfective, as pjɯ́-wɣ-ɕtʰɯz in ex:WkAlAjme.pjWkACthWz ) or other finite forms (even imperatives).

Outside of metalinguistic discourse, the stative/impersonal infinitive is also used as subject of adjectival stative verbs such as pebe good as in ( ex:kArAt.kWkhW ), expressing the meaning `the fact of... is good'.

exe

tɕe [[kɤ-rɤt] kɯ-kʰɯ] nɯ tɕe tɕe ɲɯ-pe ma, tɕe nɯ tɤ-scoz nɯ pjɯ-kɯ-ru ɲɯ-kʰɯ. \\
lnk inf -write inf: stat -be.possible dem lnk lnk sens -be.good lnk lnk dem indef. poss -writing dem ipfv - genr:S/O-look sens -be.possible \\
`It is good to have the possibility to write [a language], because then one can look at the writing (to learn that language; otherwise, one has to learn just by listening). (150901 tshuBdWnskAt)
0006242#S44
exe

In the verb doubling construction, the infinitive of stative verbs can be neutralized to the kɤ- form, as in ( ex:kArZi ) with an adjectival stative verb and ( ex:kAtu.nW.tu ) with the existential verb tuexist.

exe

kɤ-rʑi ri pjɤ-rʑi, \\
inf -be.heavy also ifr. ipfv -be.heavy \\
`As for being heavy, [the old man] was heavy.' (140511 xinbada-zh) 0003961#S179
exe

exe

ɯʑo rkɯn, ri kɤ-tu nɯ tu \\
3sg be.rare: fact lnk inf -exist dem exist: fact \\
`It is rare, but as for existing, it does exist.' (140511 qamtsWrmdzu)
0003957#S17
exe
summary: The infinitive is the preferred citation form for verbs in metalinguistic discussion: stative and impersonal verbs consistently take the kɯ- prefix, while other verbs take kɤ-, and the infinitive may also combine with orientation and polarity prefixes. It is also used to discuss collocations, where it may appear with intransitive subjects or objects, and outside metalinguistic contexts the stative/impersonal infinitive can function as the subject of adjectival stative verbs to mean ‘the fact of... is good.’ Some speakers may instead cite generic or other finite forms, and in verb doubling constructions the stative infinitive may be neutralized to the kɤ- form.

text:
infinitive!velar complement clause!velar infinitive
The most common function of the velar infinitive is to build complement clauses (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ). Apart from a handful of well-identified cases (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation ), all kɤ- prefixed verb forms in complement clauses are infinitive rather than object participles (using the criteria in § sec:infinitives.participles ).

Velar infinitives occur with a great variety of auxiliaries and other complement-taking verbs (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ) as well as a few complement-taking nouns (§ sec:complement.taking.nouns ). Few verbs however require the infinite in complement clauses. Some complement-taking verbs like cʰacan occur with either infinitival complement clauses as in ( ex:kAnWCe.YWCti ) or finite complement clauses (§ sec:finite.complement ), and other verbs like rɲoexperience are compatible with both velar infinitives and bare infinitives (§ sec:dental.inf ). The constraints on co-reference between the subject of the matrix verb and the participants of the complement clause is treated in § sec:velar.inf.coreference.

exe

ɯ-kɤχcɤl ɯ-ʁrɯ nɯ a-nɯ-pʰɯt tɕe kɤ-nɯ-ɕe cʰa ɲɯ-ɕti \\
3sg. poss -top.of.the.head 3sg. poss -horn dem irr - pfv -take.out lnk inf - vert -go can: fact sens -be. aff \\
`If one takes out the horn on his head, he will be able to go back [to the heavens].' (divination 2005)
exe

Complex velar infinitive forms with polarity, orientation and associated motion prefixes are attested in complement clauses, as in ( ex:CWkACar.pWrYota ) (see also for instance ex:CWkAXtW and ex:mAkACe.mAkhW in § sec:infinitives.other.prefixes ).

exe

aʑo [ɕɯ-kɤ-ɕar] pɯ-rɲo-t-a. \\
1sg tral - inf -search aor -experience- tr: pst - 1sg \\
`I did go to search [for Amanita caesarea ].' (22-BlamajmAG) 0003584#S30
exe

Stative verbs, when occurring in a complement clause, generally take the kɤ- infinitive, as in example ( ex:rYo ) and ( ex:kAscit ). The main verb of the complement clauses in these examples have the kɤ- infinitive, even though both tuexist and scitbe happy are stative verbs and have a citation form with the kɯ- prefix.

exe

[a-rŋɯl kɤ-tu] pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
1sg. poss -money inf -exist pst: ipfv -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I used to have money'. (elicited)
exe

exe

[kɤ-scit] pjɤ-ŋgrɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
inf -be.happy ifr -succeed sens -be \\
`She succeeded in being happy.' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh) 0006334#S6
exe

The conversion to kɤ- infinitive only applies to stative verbs, not to impersonal modal verbs such as rabe needed. When the latter occur in a complement clause, as in example ( ex:kAndza.kWra ), they always have the kɯ- prefix.

exe

[[smɤn kɤ-ndza] kɯ-ra] pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
medicine inf -eat inf: impers -be.needed pst: ipfv -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I used to have to take medicine.' (elicited)
exe

The velar infinitive is also found in some adnominal complement clauses, for instance in the collocation comprising the nouns ftɕakamethod or kowamanner with the transitive verb βzumake (§ sec:nouns.manner.complement ), as ( ex:kAndza.kowa.tWwGBzu ) below (see also mWpjWkAlhoR.ftCaka above).

In infinitive complement clauses, the complement verb lacks person/number indexation. However, in the case of the verbs that require coreference between the core arguments of the matrix clause and those in the complement clause, the person and number of the subject (and sometimes also the object) of the complement clauses are reflected on the indexation of the verb in the matrix clause (§ sec:velar.inf.coreference ). For instance, in ( ex:kAti.mWjspea ), both the infinitive kɤ-ti `to say' and the matrix verb mɯ́j-spe-a `I am not able' share the same 1sg subject and 3sg object ( ɯ-mdoʁ `its colour').

exe

nɯ ɯ-mdoʁ nɯ aj [kɤ-ti] mɯ́j-spe-a \\
dem 3sq. poss -colour dem 1sg inf -say neg: sens -be.able[III]- 1sg \\
`I don't know how to say (describe) its colour.' (06-qaZmbri)
0003416#S50
exe

This is also the case with noun+verb collocations taking complement clauses: in ( ex:kAndza.kowa.tWwGBzu ), the verb form tɯ́-wɣ-βzu reflects the 3pl 2sg configuration of the infinitive kɤ-ndza `to eat' in the complement clause.

exe

a-rɟit ra nɯ-ɣi-nɯ ɕti tɕetʰa, kɤ-ndza kowa tɯ́-wɣ-βzu ɕti \\
1sg. poss -children pl vert -come: fact - pl be. aff: fact in.a.moment inf -eat manner 2- inv -make: fact be. aff: fact \\
`My children are coming back home soon, and they will try to eat you.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S258
exe

With velar infinitive complements, some auxiliary verbs take the orientation preverb selected by the verb in the complement clause (§ sec:orientation.raising ).
summary:
The velar infinitive is most commonly used to form complement clauses, and in such clauses kɤ- prefixed verb forms are generally infinitives rather than object participles. It appears with many auxiliaries and complement-taking verbs, though only a few verbs require it, and some verbs can also take finite or bare-infinitive complements.

Stative verbs in complement clauses usually take the kɤ- infinitive, but impersonal modal verbs such as *rabe* ‘need’ do not and instead keep the kɯ- prefix. In these infinitival complements, the verb itself lacks person/number marking, though some matrix verbs or noun+verb collocations show agreement reflecting coreference with the complement clause, and some auxiliaries take the orientation preverb selected by the complement verb.

subsubsection: Doubly prefixed velar infinitives with negative existential verbs
text:
infinitive!velar
The infinitive in kɤ- can take two prefixes in a construction combining the negative existential verb menot exist (§ sec:existential.basic ) with a verb in the infinitive prefixed with a B-type orientation preverb and a possessive prefix coreferent with the subject, The assertion in that infinitives cannot take possessive prefixes is thus wrong. meaning `have no way to $X$, be completely unable to $X$', as in ( ex:ndZijukACe ) and ( ex:WpjWkAnWZWB ). Note that since in both of these examples, the verbs are intransitive and lack an object participle, the kɤ- form can only be analyzed as an infinitive here. This construction is also possible with transitive verbs, in which case the possessive prefix corresponds to the transitive subject.

exe

tɕe ndʑi-ju-kɤ-ɕe pjɤ-me \\
lnk 3du. poss - ipfv - inf -go ifr. ipfv -not.exist \\
`They could not go.' (150908 menglang-zh) 0006320#S41
exe

exe

tɯ-rʑaʁ nɯ ɯ-pjɯ-kɤ-nɯʑɯβ pjɤ-me matɕi, \\
one-night dem 3sg. poss - ipfv - inf -sleep ifr. ipfv -not.exist lnk \\
`He could not sleep the whole night, because...' (150831 BZW kAnArRaR)
0006378#S12
exe

A derived construction involves the causative ɣɤmedestroy, `cause not exist/have', `suppress' with doubly prefixed infinitives to `make it impossible for $X$ to $Y$' as in ( ex:apjWkAnWZWB.naGAme ).

exe

a-pjɯ-kɤ-nɯʑɯβ na-ɣɤ-me \\
1sg. poss - ipfv - inf -sleep aor:3 - caus -not.exist \\
`It kept me from sleeping.' (elicited)
exe

There is a variant of this construction with imperfective subject participles in kɯ- instead of infinitives (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation ).
summary:
The passage explains that the infinitive in kɤ- can actually take two prefixes in a construction with the negative existential verb, an orientation preverb, and a possessive prefix coreferent with the subject. This construction means ‘have no way to X, be completely unable to X,’ and it shows that the claim that infinitives cannot take possessive prefixes is incorrect.  

It also notes a derived causative construction meaning ‘make it impossible for X to Y,’ and mentions a variant of the same pattern that uses imperfective subject participles in kɯ- instead of infinitives.

text:
infinitive!velar converb!velar infinitive
Velar infinitives in kɤ- can also be used as converbs, in subordinate clauses that are neither relatives nor complement clauses, with a variety of meanings.

The most common function of converbial infinitives is similar to the gerund (§ sec:gerund.clauses ), expressing either the manner in which an action takes place (as in ex:kANke.lAGea, ex:tChi.kAcha.Zo.tokAndzWtci and ex:kANke.RJa.Zo ) or describing an additional action occurring at the same time as that referred to by the main verb (as laχtɕʰa kɤ-fkur, with an overt object, in ex:kAfkur.tutWNke ) (additional examples are presented in § sec:manner.clauses ).

exe

kɤ-ŋke lɤ-ɣe-a \\
inf -walk aor: upstream -come[II]- 1sg \\
`I came on foot.' (17-lhazgron)
exe

exe

nɤʑo [laχtɕʰa kɤ-fkur] tu-tɯ-ŋke ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe \\
2sg thing inf -carry.on.the.back ipfv -2-walk sens -be lnk \\
`You are walking carrying things on your back.' (150909 hua pi-zh)
0006278#S12
exe

Converbial infinitives also indicate the degree to which an action is undertaken, as in the common expression tɕʰi kɤ-cʰa ʑo `do whatever $X$ can to $Y$' in ( ex:tChi.kAcha.Zo.tokAndzWtci ).

exe

[tɕʰi kɤ-cʰa] to-k-ɤndzɯt-ci ri, maka ʑo kɯ-pʰɤn pjɤ-me \\
what inf -can ifr - peg -bark- peg lnk completely emph sbj: pcp -be.efficient ipfv. ifr -not.exist \\
`[The dog] barked as much as it could, but it was all for nothing.' (140426 gou he qingwa-zh)
0003802#S20
exe

The converbs can also be followed by adverbs of quantification like ʁɟacompletely (§ sec:universal.quantification.adverbs ), as illustrated by ( ex:kANke.RJa.Zo ).

exe

<kaihui> kɯ-fse tɤ-ra tɕe, kɤ-ŋke ʁɟa ʑo ju-kɯ-ɕe pɯ-ra. \\
meeting sbj: pcp -be.like aor -be.needed lnk inf -walk completely emph ipfv - genr:S/O-go pst. ipfv -be.needed \\
`When one had to [take part in] a meeting for instance, one had to go on foot.' (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S20
exe

Infinitives in these functions can optionally be followed by the ergative kɯ, like the gerunds (§ sec:gerund.clauses ), as shown by ( ex:kArJWG.kW.Zo ).

exe

maka to-nɯmbrɤpɯ-nɯ tɕe li kɤ-rɟɯɣ kɯ ʑo jo-ɕe-nɯ. \\
completely ifr -ride- pl lnk again inf -run erg emph ifr -go- pl \\
`They mounted their horses and galloped away.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S39
exe

Unlike gerunds (§ sec:gerund.clauses ), infinitive converbs do not necessarily imply that two different actions take place at the same time. In ( ex:kANke.RJa.Zo ) and ( ex:kArJWG.kW.Zo ) for instance, the converbs kɤ-ŋke and kɤ-rɟɯɣ do not express a motion event distinct from that described by the main verb; rather, the verb ɕego indicates the direction and deixis of the motion, while the converbs specify the speed and manner of realization of the action. Note that in this particular example, using the gerund is not possible.

The converbial infinitives are attested with the negative prefix mɤ, meaning `without $X$ing', and generally refer to the way in which the action is performed as in ( ex:mAkArWsWso.kW.Zo ).

exe

maka mɤ-kɤ-rɯsɯso kɯ ʑo `jɤɣ' to-ti, to-nɤla. \\
at.all neg - inf -think erg emph be.allowed: fact ifr -say ifr -agree \\
`She said `yes', she agreed without thinking at all.' (140429 qingwa wangzi-zh)
0003890#S65
exe

Negative infinitive converbs can have an adversative interpretation (§ sec:concessive.clauses ). In ( ex:mAkAtWG.kuwWGsWjGatandZi ), mɤ-kɤ-ɤtɯɣ `not meeting' expresses the non-realization of a telic event that was the original purpose of the previous actions of the main referent.

exe

[a-mu a-wi ni mɤ-kɤ-ɤtɯɣ] kú-wɣ-sɯ-jɣat-a-ndʑi. \\
3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss -grand.mother du neg - inf -meet ipfv: east - inv - caus -go.back- 1sg - du \\
`[My uncles] forced me to go back [to school] without having seen my mother and my grandmother (even though I had not met them).' (2010-Dpalcan-09)
exe

Converbial infinitival clauses can contain an object or a semi-object which does not belong to the main clause, as a-mu a-wi ni `my mother and my grandmother' in ( ex:mAkAtWG.kuwWGsWjGatandZi ). The dual on kú-wɣ-sɯ-jɣat-a-ndʑi refers to the subject (`the uncles', mentioned in the previous clause), not the mother and the grandmother.

In nearly all examples, there is subject (S/A) coreference between the matrix clause and the converbial clause, but examples like ( ex:mAkAtWG.kuwWGsWjGatandZi ), where we rather observe coreference between the object of the main clause and the subject of the subordinate clause, shows that there is no syntactic constraint on subject coreference in this construction.

Infinitives in kɯ- (impersonal or stative) also occur as converbs, though these forms could in principle also be analyzed as subject participles (§ sec:subject.participles ). For instance, in ( ex:mAkWmbrAt.YWrAma ) mɤ-kɯ-mbrɤt `without stop' is considered to be an impersonal infinitive serving as a manner converb, but it could be possible to propose an alternative analysis as a kɯ- subject participle `the one which does not stop' used adverbially. The analysis as infinitives however better accounts for the fact that only the verbs whose infinitive is in kɯ- have converbial forms in kɯ-.

exe

nɯ maka mɤ-kɯ-mbrɤt ʑo ɲɯ-rɤma ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe, \\
dem at.all neg - inf: impers:S/A- acaus:break emph ipfv -work sens -be. aff lnk \\
`It works without stopping at all.' (26-GZo)
0003668#S62
exe

The existential verbs also occur in converbial use. For instance, tuexist in infinitive form kɯ-tu following a noun or a pronoun can mean `in the presence of...' as in ( ex:Zara.kWtu.Zo ).

exe

[ʑara kɯ-tu] ʑo to-sɤrɯru tɕe, \\
3pl inf: stat -exist emph ifr -compare lnk \\
`He compared [his testimony with theirs] in their presence.' (150909 xifangping-zh) 0006408#S147
exe

Similarly, the negative existential verb menot exist in infinitive converbial form means `without...', as in example ( ex:nAzo.kWme ).

exe

tɕe nɤj a-pi [nɤʑo kɯ-me] aʑo kɤ-rɤʑi mɤ-cʰa-a \\
lnk 2sg 1sg. poss -elder.sibling 2sg inf: stat -not.exist 1sg inf -stay neg -can: fact - 1sg \\
`Brother, without you I cannot stay [here].' (2011-05-nyima)
exe
summary: Velar infinitives in kɤ- can function as converbs in subordinate clauses that are neither relatives nor complement clauses, with uses similar to gerunds: they can express manner, simultaneous additional action, degree, and can be modified by adverbs like ‘completely’ or take the ergative marker kɯ. Unlike gerunds, these converbial infinitives do not always imply two simultaneous actions, and in some cases they instead specify how a motion is carried out; they also occur with negative meaning (‘without X-ing’), adversative readings, and occasionally with kɯ- impersonal/stative or existential verbs.

text:
The kɯ- infinitive of stative verbs can be used to create adverbs. The most common example is the degree adverb kɯxtɕɯxtɕia little from xtɕibe small in sentences such as ( ex:kWxtCWxtCi.wxti ). In this example, the co-occurrence of an adverb derived from xtɕibe small with the verb wxtibe big shows that this adverb is already fully grammaticalized, otherwise such a sentence would be self-contradictory.

exe

βʑɯ sɤz kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi wxti. \\
mouse comp inf: stat - emph be.small be.big: fact \\
`It is a little bigger than a mouse.' (21-GzWLa) 0003570#S4
exe

An even more lexicalized example is mɤkɯftsʰiforcibly, which occurs in particular with causative verbs to express coercive causation (§ sec:sig.caus.coercitive ), as in ( ex:mAkWfsthi.chAsWrku ).

exe

tɕendɤre mɤkɯftsʰi ʑo, nɤki ɯ-me ɣɯ ɯ-mi nɯ iɕqʰa tɯ-xtsa ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu cʰɤ-sɯ-rku \\
lnk forcibly emph filler 3sg. poss -daughter gen 3sg. poss -foot dem the.aforementioned indef. poss -shoe 3sg. poss -in dem: loc ifr: downstream - caus -put.in \\
`She forced her daughter to put her foot into that shoe.' (140504 huiguniang-zh)
0003909#S219
exe

This adverb is formally the negative stative infinitive of the verb ftsʰifeel better (of a disease) (§ sec:sig.caus.lexicalized ).

These adverbs are probably lexicalized from infinitival converbs (§ sec:inf.converb ), but differ from them in lacking any argument structure.
summary: The kɯ- infinitive of stative verbs can form adverbs, such as kɯxtɕɯxtɕia little from xtɕibe small, and this form is shown to be fully grammaticalized by its use in a sentence that would otherwise be contradictory. A more lexicalized example is mɤkɯftsʰiforcibly, used especially with causative verbs to express coercive causation. These adverbs are likely lexicalized from infinitival converbs, but unlike them they lack argument structure.

text:
Lexicalized velar infinitives in kɤ- found in some compounds, though some cases could alternatively be analyzed as lexicalized object participles, and are treated in § sec:lexicalized.object.participle.

The delocutive expression ŋɤtɕɯkɤti+kʰɯbe obedient provides an unambiguous example of lexicalized velar infinitive. The compound ŋɤtɕɯkɤti combines the pronoun ŋotɕuwhere in bound state form ŋɤtɕɯ- with the infinitive kɤ-ti of the verb tisay, and is exclusively used in collocation with kʰɯbe possible, `agree', as in ( ex:NAtCWkAti ). The causative ŋɤtɕɯkɤti+sɯkʰɯcause to be obedient also exists.
This expression originates presumably from a phrase such as `agree ( kʰɯ ) to whatever ( ŋotɕu ) $X$ says ( kɤ-ti )'. However, it should be noted that the pronoun tɕʰiwhat, not ŋotɕuwhere is used in Japhug in the free-choice indefinite construction meaning `whatever' as in examples ( ex:tChi.pWnWNWNu ) to ( ex:tChi.kWstWstua ) in § sec:interrogative.indef ). The form kɤ-ti in any case was originally the complement of the verb kʰɯbe possible, which takes infinitival complements (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ), and thus is not analyzable as a former object participle.

exe

ɯ-tɕɯ kɯβde nɯra wuma ʑo ŋɤtɕɯkɤti pjɤ-kʰɯ-nɯ \\
3sg. poss -son four dem: pl really emph obey.to.everything(1) ifr. ipfv -obey.to.everything(2)- pl \\
`His four sons were very obedient.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S15
exe
summary: Some compounds in kɤ- are lexicalized velar infinitives, though a few could also be interpreted as lexicalized object participles. A clear example is ŋɤtɕɯkɤti+kʰɯbe obedient, where ŋɤtɕɯkɤti combines a bound pronoun with the infinitive kɤ-ti ‘say’ and occurs only with kʰɯ ‘be possible, agree’; a causative form ŋɤtɕɯkɤti+sɯkʰɯ ‘cause to be obedient’ also exists. The passage argues that this expression likely developed from a phrase meaning ‘agree to whatever X says,’ and that kɤ-ti is best analyzed as an infinitival complement rather than a former object participle.

text:
infinitive!bare
Bare infinitives are formed by combining the stem I of the verb with a possessive prefix coreferential with the object of the complement clause, as in example ( ex:Wmto.mWpWrYota ). Bare infinitives are not attested with orientation, polarity or associated motion prefixes. They historically derive from bare action nominal (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ), which have become a very restricted subclass.

exe

nɤʑo kɯ-fse a-ŋkʰor nɯ ɯ-mto mɯ-pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
you nmlz: stat -be.like 1sg. poss -subject top 3sg. poss - bare. inf:see neg - aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I never saw anyone like you among my subjects.' (28-smAnmi, 393) 0004063#S373
exe

With ʁzɤβbe careful as matrix verb however, the possessive prefix can also index the transitive subject as in ( ex:ndZipa.YWRzAB ) (expressing an indefinite object).

exe

kɤtsa ni ndʑi-pa ɲɯ-ʁzɤβ rca \\
parents.and.children du 3du. poss - bare. inf:do sens -be.careful sfp \\
`The two of them do things very carefully.' (14-05-10)
exe

Intransitive verbs do not have bare infinitives. Complement-taking verbs selecting bare infinitives for transitive verbs either take tɯ- infinitives (§ sec:dental.inf ) or velar infinitives (§ sec:velar.inf ) when occurring with intransitive verbs.
summary:
Bare infinitives are formed from the stem of the verb plus a possessive prefix that is coreferential with the object of the complement clause. They do not occur with orientation, polarity, or associated motion prefixes, and are historically derived from a now highly restricted subclass of bare action nominals.  

With the matrix verb ʁzɤβ ‘be careful,’ the possessive prefix can instead index the transitive subject, yielding an indefinite-object interpretation. Intransitive verbs do not form bare infinitives; verbs that take bare infinitival complements with transitives instead use tɯ- or velar infinitives with intransitives.

text:
infinitive!bare complement clause!bare infinitive
Bare infinitives only occur in complement clauses (§ sec:bare.dental.inf ). Apart from the aspectual verb rɲoexperience, `have already $X$' mentioned above in ( ex:Wmto.mWpWrYota ), bare infinitives are found with two categories of complement-taking verbs.

First, they are compatible with some phasal verbs (§ sec:phasal.complements ) such as ʑabegin, sɤʑabegin, stʰɯtfinish and jɤɣfinish as in ( ex:WtsxWB.thWjAG ).

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ tɯ-ŋga nɯ ɯ-tʂɯβ tʰɯ-jɤɣ \\
lnk dem indef. poss -clothes dem 3sg. poss - bare. inf:sew aor -finish \\
`When one has finished sewing the clothes,...' (30-tWNga)
0004069#S29
exe

Second, they are found with some adjectives such as βdibe well and derived sigmatic or velar causative verbs such as ɣɤ-βdi `repair, cause to be good, do $X$ well' as in ( ex:WnApWpa.tuGABdinW ) (see § sec:velar.caus.complement, § sec:causative.manner.complement ).

exe

lu-ji-nɯ qʰe ɯ-nɤpɯpa tu-ɣɤ-βdi-nɯ, ɯ-ɣli ra ku-sɤpe-nɯ qʰe, cʰɯ-do ɲɯ-cʰa. \\
ipfv -plant- pl lnk 3sg. poss - bare. inf:take.care ipfv - caus -be.good- pl 3sg. poss -dung pl ipfv -do.well- pl lnk ipfv -be.fibrous sens -can \\
`[Now people] plant [pumpkin also in higher areas], [if] they take good care of it and add enough fertilizer, it becomes fibrous (so that it can be sowed for the next year).' (140522 kAmYW tWji)
0004055#S46
exe

The same set of verbs take complement clauses with dental infinitives when the verb of the complement is intransitive (§ sec:dental.inf.complement ).

The bare infinitives also occur in adnominal complement clauses with the noun ɯ-tsʰɯɣashape, manner, as in ( ex:bare.inf.noun ).

exe

ndʑi-mi ɯ-tsʰoʁ ɯ-tsʰɯɣa nɯra wuma ʑo naχtɕɯɣ-ndʑi. \\
3du. poss -foot 3sg - bare. inf: attach.to 3sg. poss -form dem: pl very emph be.the.same: fact - du \\
`The way their legs [of fleas and crickets] touch the ground is very similar.' (26-mYaRmtsaR)
0003674#S17
exe

No verb requires a bare infinitive: all complement-taking verbs selecting it are either alternatively compatible with velar infinitives (§ sec:inf.complementation ) or a finite complement (§ sec:finite.complement ).
summary: Bare infinitives occur only in complement clauses and, aside from the aspectual verb *rɲo* ‘have already X’, they appear with two main types of complement-taking verbs: certain phasal verbs like ‘begin’ and ‘finish’, and some adjectives and derived causative verbs such as *βdi* ‘well’ and *ɣɤ-βdi* ‘repair, do X well’. The same verbs can also take dental-infinitive complements when the embedded verb is intransitive, and bare infinitives may appear in adnominal complement clauses with the noun *ɯ-tsʰɯɣa* ‘shape, manner’. No verb strictly requires a bare infinitive, since all such verbs can also take velar-infinitive or finite complements.

subsubsection: Bare verb stem in negative existential construction
text:
verb!bare stem
A non-finite form resembling bare infinitives without possessive prefix is found in an unusual construction with the negative existential verbs menot exist and maŋenot exist(§ sec:suppletive.negative ) with alternative concessive meaning `whether or not $X$, it amounts to the same' (§ sec:alt.concessive.conditional ), in which the bare verb stem occurs in affirmative and in negative form with the negative prefix mɤ-. Unlike bare infinitives proper, this form exists with both transitive ( ndza.mea ) and intransitive verbs ( mACe.me ).

exe

ndza mɤ-ndza me-a \\
bare. inf:eat neg - bare. inf:eat not.exist: fact - 1sg \\
`Whether [you] eat me or not, it amounts to the same.' (sentence obtained as the correction of a sentence I produced to translate a story in Japhug)
exe

exe

tɕe ɯ-qiɯ ɲɯ-mtsʰam-a, ɯ-qiɯ mɯ́j-mtsʰam-a qʰe, ɕe mɤ-ɕe maŋe \\
lnk 3sg. poss -half sens -hear- 1sg 3sg. poss -half neg: sens -hear- 1sg lnk bare. inf:go neg - bare. inf:go not.exist: sens \\
`I can hear half of it, can't hear the other half, whether or not [I] go, it amounts to the same.' (conversation 140510)
exe

In this construction, the negative auxiliaries can take person marking, and are obligatorily coreferential with the object if the verb in the complement clause is transitive, as in ( ndza.mea ). With intransitive verbs, no person marking appears on the negative verb as in ( mACe.me ). The fact that only the object is indexed on the auxiliary verb suggests here that this construction displays nominative-accusative alignment.
In this construction, the transitive subject (whether of transitive or intransitive verbs) cannot be overt.

Although the non-finite form ɕe in ( mACe.me ) superficially resembles a 3sg Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ), the absence of stem III alternation (§ sec:stem3 ) on ndza in ( ndza.mea ) shows that this cannot be a finite form (otherwise ndze `s/he/it will eat/eats it' would be expected).
summary:
A special non-finite bare verb stem appears in a concessive construction with the negative existential verbs *meno* ‘not exist’ and *maŋe* ‘not exist,’ meaning roughly ‘whether or not X, it amounts to the same.’ This form can occur with both transitive and intransitive verbs, and in the transitive case the negative auxiliary can show person marking and must agree with the object, while the subject cannot be overt.  

The construction therefore suggests nominative-accusative alignment, since only the object is indexed on the auxiliary. Although the form ɕe may look like a finite factual non-past form, the absence of expected stem alternation shows that it is not finite.

text:
infinitive!dental
Dental infinitives (glossed as `second infinitives' inf:II) are built by prefixing tɯ- with the verb stem. Dental infinitives occur with intransitive verbs, including dynamic ( ex:tWNke.taZa.tCe ) and stative verbs ( ex:tArNi.YoZa ), including semi-transitive verbs, but are not attested with transitive verbs, which take bare infinitives or velar infinitives instead.

exe

tɯ-ŋke ta-ʑa tɕe \\
inf: II -walk aor:3 -start lnk \\
`When it starts moving...' (26-NalitCaRmbWm) 0003676#S76
exe

With contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction ), regular vowel fusion between the tɯ- prefix and stem-initial a- occurs, resulting in the surface form tɤ- as in ( ex:tArNi.YoZa ).

exe

si nɯ daltsɯtsa nɯ tɯ-ɤrŋi ɲo-ʑa tɕe \\
tree dem slowly dem inf:II-be.green ifr -start lnk \\
`The tree slowly started to become green.' (divination 2003)
exe

However, a few morphologically transitive verbs selecting dummy subjects (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), in particular lɤtrelease and βzumake do take tɯ- infinitives as in ( ex:tWlAt.pjAZa ). Note that in these complex predicates, the light verbs lɤtrelease and βzumake, although transitively conjugated, cannot take an overt subject marked with the ergative, and only have one argument.

dummy subject
exe

tɯ-mɯ kɯ-wxtɯ wxti ʑo tɯ-lɤt pjɤ-ʑa \\
indef. poss -sky sbj: pcp - emph be.big emph inf -throw ifr -start \\
`A heavy rain started.' (150819 haidenver-zh) 0006314#S101
exe

It is possible that dental infinitives are historically related to degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominals ) and action nominals (§ sec:action.nominals ), which however do not display the same transitivity restrictions. Several hypotheses accounting for the origin of dental infinitives are presented in § sec:dental.nmlz.history.
summary: Dental infinitives are formed by prefixing **tɯ-** to the verb stem and are used mainly with **intransitive verbs**, including dynamic, stative, and semi-transitive verbs, but they are not normally attested with transitive verbs, which instead take bare or velar infinitives. With contracting verbs, vowel fusion with stem-initial **a-** yields the surface form **tɤ-**; however, a few morphologically transitive dummy-subject verbs such as **lɤ** ‘release’ and **βzu** ‘make’ can also take dental infinitives because they function as one-argument predicates. The passage also notes a possible historical connection to degree and action nominals, though these do not share the same transitivity restrictions.

text:
Dental infinitives are only compatible with polarity prefixes (as in example ex:mAtWrga ), and cannot take orientation or associated motion. Possessive prefixes on dental infinitives only occur in the simultaneous construction with the verb sɯpacause to do (§ sec:bare.dental.inf.sWpa ).

exe

qaɟy ɯ-me nɯnɯ, tɕendɤre kʰro mɤ-tɯ-rga to-ʑa\\
fish 3sg. poss -daughter dem lnk a.lot neg - inf: II -like ifr -start \\
`He started not liking the mermaid that much [anymore].' (150819 haidenver-zh)
0006314#S149
exe

Degree nominals present the same constraints on orientation and associated motion prefixes (§ sec:degree.nominal.prefixes ).
summary: Dental infinitives can occur only with polarity prefixes; they do not take orientation or associated motion prefixes. Possessive prefixes on dental infinitives are restricted to the simultaneous construction with *sɯpa* ‘cause to do,’ and degree nominals show the same restrictions on orientation and associated motion prefixes.

text:
infinitive!dental complement clause!dental infinitive
Dental tɯ- infinitives are only attested in complement clauses (§ sec:bare.dental.inf ), and are only found with the verbs that select a bare infinitive (§ sec:bare.inf.complement ) when the verb in the complement clause is transitive. This complementary distribution suggests that bare infinitive and dental infinitives could be treated as two variants of the same grammatical category.

Dental infinitives are more often attested with phasal verbs, in particular ʑabegin and sɤʑabegin as in ( ex:tWskAm.pjAsAZa ).

exe

mtsʰu nɯ cʰɯmcʰɯm ʑo, tɕe, tɯ-skɤm pjɤ-sɤʑa \\
lake dem idph (II):slowly.retreating emph lnk inf:II-be.dry ifr -start \\
`The [water of the] lake started to retreat slowly.' (nyima wodzer 2003)
exe

Non-phasal verbs selecting bare infinitive such as rɲoexperience never occur with the dental infinitive in the corpus, but such forms can be elicited, as in ( ex:tWGi.pWrYota ). In the corpus, intransitive complements of the verb rɲoexperience rather velar infinitives; it is also possible in ( ex:tWGi.pWrYota ) to replace the dental infinitive tɯ-ɣi with a velar infinitive kɤ-ɣi.

exe

mbarkʰom tɯ-ɣi pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
topo inf:II-come aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I came to Mbarkham before.' (elicited)
exe

Like other intransitive verbs, antipassivized transitive verbs can take a dental infinitive (as in ex:tWrArAt.paZa ), unlike the base verb from which they are derived (as in ex:WrAt.paZa, where a bare infinitive is used instead).

exe

tɯ-rɤ-rɤt pa-ʑa \\
inf:II- apass -write aor:3 -start \\
`He started writing.' (elicited)
exe

exe

tɤscoz ɯ-rɤt pa-ʑa \\
letter 3sg. poss - bare. inf: write aor:3 -start \\
`He started writing the/a letter.' (elicited)
exe

In addition, dental infinitives also occur in complements of causativized verbs (§ sec:bare.dental.inf.sWpa, § sec:causative.manner.complement ), and in the construction expressing simultaneous actions with sɯpacause to do described in § sec:bare.inf.complement.
summary: Dental tɯ- infinitives occur only in complement clauses and only with verbs that otherwise select a bare infinitive when the complement verb is transitive, suggesting that bare and dental infinitives may be two variants of the same grammatical category. They are especially common with phasal verbs such as “begin,” while some non-phasal verbs selecting bare infinitives do not normally take dental infinitives in the corpus, though such forms can be elicited. Dental infinitives also appear with antipassivized transitive verbs, causativized verbs, and in constructions expressing simultaneous actions.

text:
nominalization!degree
Degree nominals are built by combining the verb stem with a nominalizing tɯ- prefix and a possessive prefix coreferent with the subject, as the dual ndʑi- in ( ex:ndZitAmWmi ). The form ndʑi-tɯ-ɤmɯmi also shows that the nominalization tɯ- prefix undergoes regular vowel fusion with stem-initial a- to tɤ.

exe

tɕendɤre ndʑi-tɯ-ɤmɯmi ndʑi-tɯ-scit pɯ-saχaʁ ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu \\
lnk 3du. poss - nmlz: deg -be.on.good.terms 3du. poss - nmlz: deg -be.happy pst. ipfv -be.extremely emph sens -be \\
`They were very happy together.' (2005 Lobzang)
0003370#S14
exe

All gradable stative verbs can form degree nominals. They most typically occur in constructions expressing degree as in ( ex:ndZitAmWmi ) (§ sec:degree.nominal.construction, § sec:degree.nominal.subject ), but can also indicate manner as in ( ex:WtAjRu ).

exe

nɯ-mi ɯ-tɯ-ɤjʁu kɯnɤ mɯ́j-naχtɕɯɣ. \\
3pl. poss -leg 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.curved also neg: sens -be.the.same \\
`[People with clubfoot] also differ in the way that their feet are curved (some have both legs curved, some only one, some have the legs rotated inwards, others rotated outwards) (160719 kAmARu)
exe

With dynamic verbs, degree nominals express either the intensity or the frequency of an action as in ( ex:WtWnAru ), or the manner of the action ( ex:tWtAmdzW.kWBdi ). Such examples are however uncommon in the corpus.

exe

japa tɕe pʰaʁrgot ɯ-tɯ-nɤru ɲɯ-saχaʁ ʑo tɕe \\
last.year loc boar 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -eat.crops sens -be.extremely emph lnk \\
`Last year, a boar was causing a lot of damages to the crops.' (150829 phaRrgot)
0006414#S1
exe

exe

tɯ-tɯ-ɤmdzɯ kɯ-βdi mɤ-kɯ-βdi kɯnɤ ʑo cʰɯ-sɤfɕɤra-nɯ pɯ-ɕti. \\
genr: poss - nmlz: deg -sit inf: stat -be.well neg - inf: stat -be.well also emph ipfv -discuss- pl pst. ipfv -be. aff: fact \\
`People would discuss whether one sat properly or not.' (31-khAjmu) 0004079#S28
exe

Degree nominals from transitive verbs are extremely rare, but do occur in particular for tropative verbs (§ sec:tropative ) as in ( ex:WtWnAmpCAr ). It is possible to elicitate degree nominals for most transitive verbs, even if such forms are not attested in the corpus.

exe

maka ɯ-tɯ-nɤ-mpɕɤr kɯ pjɤ-nɤscɤr ʑo. \\
completely 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - trop -be.beautiful erg ifr -be.startled emph \\
`He found her so beautiful that he was startled.' (140429 jiedi-zh)
exe

Although similar in form to dental infinitives (§ sec:dental.inf ) and action nominals (§ sec:action.nominals ), they differ from both categories in requiring the presence of a possessive prefix (see § sec:dental.nmlz.history concerning the historical relationship between these forms). In addition, unlike dental infinitives, degree nominals are compatible with both intransitive and transitive verbs. Their semantics is also fully predictable, unlike action nominals which tend to be lexicalized (§ sec:lexicalized.action.nominals ).

Degree nominal occur in exclamative nominal predicates (§ sec:degree.nominal.predicates ), degree constructions (§ sec:degree.nominal.construction ) and also several types of complement clauses (§ sec:degree.nominal.complement ).

Another type of degree nominal is built by compounding the stems of two antonyms, for instance jaʁmbathickness (of a sheet) from jaʁbe thick and mbabe thin (§ sec.v.v.compounds.degree ). The corresponding regular degree nouns also exist ( ɯ-tɯ-jaʁ and ɯ-tɯ-mba ).
summary:
Degree nominals are formed by combining a verb stem with the nominalizing prefix tɯ- and a possessive prefix coreferent with the subject; the prefix regularly fuses with stem-initial a- to give tɤ. They are available for all gradable stative verbs and can also occur with dynamic verbs to express intensity, frequency, or manner, while transitive degree nominals are rare but possible, especially with tropative verbs.

Although they resemble dental infinitives and action nominals, degree nominals differ in requiring a possessive prefix and in being compatible with both intransitive and transitive verbs; their meaning is also predictable. They occur in exclamative nominal predicates, degree constructions, complement clauses, and can also be formed by compounding antonymous stems.

text:
Like dental infinitives (§ sec:dental.inf.polarity ), degree nominals cannot be used with orientation or associated motion prefixes, but can be found with the negative prefix mɤ, as in ( ex:WmAtWnWGWNke2 ).

exe

maka ɯ-mɤ-tɯ-nɯɣɯ-ŋke pjɤ-saχaʁ ʑo \\
at.all 3sg. poss - neg - nmlz: deg - facil -walk ifr. ipfv -be.extremely emph \\
`It was extremely inconvenient to walk [on the soft earth].' (2014-kWlAG)
exe
summary: Degree nominals, like dental infinitives, cannot occur with orientation or associated-motion prefixes. However, they can combine with the negative prefix mɤ, as shown by the example meaning that it was extremely inconvenient to walk on the soft earth.

text:
nominalization!degree
Unlike action nominals, degree nominals still keep their argument structure intact. They can take complements exactly in the same way as finite verb forms. For instance, βdibe well takes the bare infinitive ɯ-taʁ in ( ex:WtaR.WtWBdi ). Note that the bare infinitive ɯ-taʁ from the verb taʁweave is homophonous with the relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:WtaR ) and that this construction is potentially ambiguous.

exe

maka nɯ raz rcanɯ, ɯ-tɯ-pe ɲɯ-saχaʁ ʑo, ɯ-taʁ ɯ-tɯ-βdi, ɯ-tɯ-mpɕɤr ɲɯ-saχaʁ \\
at.all dem cloth unexp: deg 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.good sens -be.extremely emph 3sg. poss - bare. inf:weave 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.well 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.beautiful sens -be.extremely \\
`This piece of cloth is very nice, it is extremely well woven, it is extremely beautiful.' (140521 huangdi de xinzhuang-zh)
0004047#S77
exe

In ( ex:chWwxti.WtWmbat ), the verb mbatbe easy selects a finite complement clause comprising the verb cʰɯ-wxti `it grows bigger' in imperfective third singular form.

exe

cʰɯ-wxti ɯ-tɯ-mbat ɲɯ-sɤre ʑo \\
ipfv -be.big 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.easy sens -be.ridiculous emph \\
`It grows very easily.' (25-akWzgumba)
0003632#S70
exe

Degree nominals can also be used with oblique arguments, such as the first person marked by the relator noun a-taʁ (unrelated to the bare infinitive ɯ-taʁ from the previous example) in ( ex:ataR.WtWGWtsxWn ).

exe

a-wi a-taʁ ɯ-tɯ-ɤɣɯtʂɯn ɯ-grɤl me \\
1sg. poss -grandmother 1sg -on 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.kind 3sg. poss -order not.exist: fact \\
`My grandmother was extremely kind to me (so that I have to repay her).' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe
summary: Degree nominals retain their argument structure, so they can take complements in the same way as finite verbs. The passage gives examples of degree nominals selecting a bare infinitive, a finite complement clause, and an oblique argument introduced by a relator noun. It also notes that the bare infinitive ɯ-taʁ is homophonous with an unrelated relator noun, making one construction potentially ambiguous.

text:
nominalization!degree noun!predicative
Degree nominals commonly occur as nominal predicates (§ sec:non.verbal.predicates ), either with the sentence final particle nɯ as in ( ex:nWtWmtsWrCpaR ), or as a bare noun phrase as in ( ex:WtWBdi.WtWmpCAr ). In this predicative use, degree nominals express an exclamation, possibly including surprise as in ( ex:mtshAri.ataR.WtWpe ) and ( ex:WtWBdi.WtWmpCAr ).

exe

lɤ-ɣi-nɯ wo tɤ-rɯndzɤtsʰi-nɯ ma, nɯ-tɯ-mtsɯr-ɕpaʁ nɯ, nɯ-tɯ-ɲat nɯ\\
imp: upstream -come- pl sfp imp -have.a.meal- pl C 2pl. poss - nmlz: deg -be.hungry-be.thirsty sfp 2pl. poss - nmlz: deg -be.tired sfp \\
`Come in and have a meal, you [must be] so hungry, thirsty and tired!' (160701 poucet2) 0006155#S39
exe

Example ( ex:WtaR.WtWBdi ) can be compared with ( ex:WtWBdi.WtWmpCAr ) with the verb of degree saχaʁbe extremely in sensory form. It is possible that the use of degree nominal as nominal predicates historically results from the ellipsis of the degree predicate. The high frequency of the predicative use of degree nominals in the corpus however indicates that this usage has been constructionalized.

exe

ɯ-taʁ ɯ-tɯ-βdi, ɯ-tɯ-mpɕɤr! \\
3sg. poss - bare. inf:weave 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.well 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.beautiful \\
`It is woven so well, it is so beautiful!' (140521 huangdi de xinzhuang-zh) 0004047#S162
exe
summary: Degree nominals commonly function as nominal predicates, either with the sentence-final particle **nɯ** or as a bare noun phrase. In this predicative use, they express an exclamation and may convey surprise; although this use may historically come from ellipsis of a degree predicate, its high frequency in the corpus suggests it has become constructionalized.

text:
nominalization!degree degree
The most common use of the degree nominals is in the degree construction, where they occur as intransitive subjects of degree verbs like saχaʁbe extremely, which are always in 3sg form as in ( ex:WtWjpum.pjAsaXaR ). The possessive prefix on the degree noun is coreferent with the referent having the property described by the nominalized verb, often 3sg as in ( ex:WtWjpum.pjAsaXaR ), but not exclusively, for instance with a 3du in ( ex:ndZitAmWmi ) above.

exe

nɯnɯ si nɯ ɯ-tɯ-jpum pjɤ-saχaʁ ʑo tɕe,\\
dem tree dem 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.thick ifr. ipfv -be.extremely emph lnk \\
`That tree was extremely thick.' (150902 luban-zh)
0006268#S90
exe

This construction is described in more details in (§ sec:degree.nominal.subject ).
summary: Degree nominals are most commonly used in degree constructions, where they function as intransitive subjects of degree verbs such as *saχaʁ* ‘be extremely,’ which always appear in 3sg form. The possessive prefix on the degree noun is coreferential with the entity described by the nominalized verb, usually in 3sg but sometimes in other numbers such as 3du.

text:
nominalization!degree complementation strategy!degree nominal
Degree nominals are marginally attested in a complementation strategy, as subject clauses of the modal verb ra `need, have to' in negative form, meaning `$X$ should not be so $Y$', where $X$ is the subject indexed by the possessive prefix preceding the -tɯ- nominalization prefix, and $Y$ the verb in degree nominal form. For instance, the common expression in ( ex:nAtWsAre.nW.mAra ) with the degree nominal nɤ-tɯ-sɤre literally means `You should not be so ridiculous'.

exe

nɤ-tɯ-sɤre nɯ mɤ-ra \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.ridiculous dem neg -be.needed \\
`What you [did/said)] is outrageous.' (several examples) 0004087#S76
exe

This construction also occurs with the antipassive verb sɤnɤkʰebully people, as in ( ex:nAtWsAnAkhe.nW.mAra ). The meaning of this sentence is close to Chinese 你太欺负人了 nǐ tài qīfù rén leyou are out of line.

exe

nɤ-tɯ-sɤ-nɤkʰe nɯ mɤ-ra \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - apass: hum -bully dem neg -be.needed \\
`You are out of line (`you should not bully people like that').' (28-qajdo)
0003718#S14
exe

The degree nominals also seem to occur as adnominal complement of ɯ-tsʰɯɣashape, manner as in ( ex:WtWrRom.WtshWGa ). Note however that since bare infinitives are attested in complement clauses of this noun (see example ex:bare.inf.noun, § sec:bare.inf.complement ), it is also conceivable that the forms ɯ-tɯ-tsʰu and ɯ-tɯ-rʁom could be alternatively analyzed as dental infinitives (§ sec:dental.inf ).

exe

paʁ nɯ ɯ-βri, nɤki, ɯ-rme kɯ-me ʑo ɯ-tsʰɯɣa ɲɯ-fse ma ɯ-tɯ-tsʰu cʰondɤre ɯ-tɯ-rʁom ɯ-tsʰɯɣa nɯ ʑo ɲɯ-fse \\
pig dem 3sg. poss -body filler 3sg. poss -hair inf: stat -not.exist emph 3sg. poss -shape sens -be.like lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.fat comit 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.rough 3sg. poss -shape dem emph sens -be.like \\
`[The body of the elephant] resembles that of the pig in that it has no hair, in that it is fat and [its skin] is rough.' (19-RloNbutChi)
0003550#S44
exe
summary: Degree nominals are only marginally attested, mainly as complement clauses of the negative modal *ra* `need, have to’ to express meanings like “X should not be so Y,” with the subject marked by a possessive prefix before the *-tɯ-* nominalization prefix. They also occur with the antipassive verb *sɤnɤkʰe* `bully people’ in a construction meaning roughly “you are out of line,” and may appear as adnominal complements of *ɯ-tsʰɯɣa* `shape, manner,’ though some such forms could alternatively be analyzed as dental infinitives.

text:
tɯ- action nominals
nominalization!action
There are two types of action nominals in Japhug: action nominals in tɯ, a very productive formation which is the main topic of this section, and the bare action nominals, treated in § sec:bare.action.nominals.

Action nominals in tɯ- can be built from both intransitive and transitive verbs. They differ from both participles and infinitives in that the argument structure of the verb is lost and the transitivity contrast neutralized, and cannot take objects or oblique arguments other than possessors like normal alienably possessed nouns.

The action nominal has three potential meanings. First, it can refer to the action itself, for instance tɯjiplanting and sowing This action noun should not be confused with the related inalienably possessed noun tɯ-jifield, which is a different nominalized form. from the verb jiplant, tɯɣɟaβaction of churning from ɣɟaβchurn, tɯrɟaʁdance (n) from rɟaʁdance (intransitive verb), tɯsideath from sidie or tɯmufear from mufear. In this function, it can be used in a collocation with βzumake (§ sec:action.nominal.Bzu ).

Second, it can mean an object affected by, or resulting from the action. This is also the case with some intransitive verbs, for instance tɯqioʁ from the intransitive qioʁvomit which can either mean `the action of vomiting' or `vomitus' or tɯɕkʰo from ɕkʰospread, `dry in the sun' which can either be `action of drying in the sun' or `grain that are dried in the sun' (see ex:tWCkho.chWBze in § sec:action.nominal.Bzu ).

Third, it can also refer to the way an action is performed, for instance tɯ-rɤt which means `style of writing, way of writing' as in ( ex:er.WtWrAt ). This function is probably the direct historical origin of the degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominals ).

exe

tɕe <er> ɯ-tɯ-rɤt tsa ɲɯ-fse ri, nɯ stʰɯci mɯ-ɲɯ-ŋgɤɣ \\
lnk two 3sg. poss - nmlz: action -write a.little sens -be.like lnk dem so.much neg - sens - acaus:warp \\
`[The constellation] looks a little bit like the way `two' is written, but not as curved.' (29-LAntshAm)
0003726#S50
exe

Stative verbs can also have tɯ- nominals, expressing abstract nouns, for instance tɯtʂaŋjustice from tʂaŋbe fair.

When the base verb has a stem in a, the action nominal prefix tɯ- undergoes regular vowel fusion to tɤ- as in tɤɣrogame from the intransitive verb aɣroplay (however, this verb is also potentially analyzable as a a- denominal verb, see § sec:denom.a and § sec:bare.action.nominals below).

The direction of derivation between noun and verb is not always trivial to determine. For instance, the noun tɯtsɣecommerce could seem to be the action nominal of the transitive verb ntsɣesell. However, in this case it is better to analyze the noun as the base form, and the verb as denominal (the n- element being an irregular allomorph of the nɯ- denominal prefix, § sec:antipassive.irr.form ).

Action nominals can occur as prenominal modifiers, as in tɯtaʁ mtʰɯxtɕɤrweaving belt (the belt used to attach the back-tension loom), comprising the action nominal tɯtaʁweaving (from taʁweave) and the compound noun mtʰɯxtɕɤrbelt.

tɤ- abstract nouns
nominalization!abstract noun noun!abstract
Abstract nouns in tɤ- can be exclusively derived from adjectival stative verbs. The derivation is generally regular but there are exceptions like tɤɣɲattiredness from ɲatbe tired with an additional -ɣ- or tɤŋɤmpain from mŋɤmfeel pain with a missing -m-. In the case of tɤŋɤmpain it is possible that the verb mŋɤmfeel pain derives from the noun with the irregular allomorph of a denominal prefix, which could be either ɣɤ- (§ sec:denom.GW ) or mɤ- (§ sec:denom.mA ). Note also the existence of the compound noun tɯxtɤŋɤmdysentery from the bound state of tɯ-xtubelly with the root -ŋɤm.

Abstract nouns mainly occur with the ergative kɯ. These postpositional phrases express either the manner in which an action takes place (§ sec:manner.nominal.kW ) as in ( ex:tArga.kW.Zo ), or the cause of the action describe by the main verb due to a high degree as in ( ex:tAGYat.tAmtsWr.kW.Zo ) (see also § sec:degree.monoclausal ).

exe

tɤ-rga kɯ ʑo tʰɯ-ari ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
nmlz: abstract -be.happy erg emph aor: downstream -go[II] sens -be \\
`She went there happily.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

Example ( ex:tAGYat.tAmtsWr.kW.Zo ) also illustrates that one ergative postposition can follow several abstract nouns linked with the comitative cʰo or in bare coordination (§ sec:bare.coordination ).

exe

a-ʁi, tɤ-ɣɲat cʰo tɤ-mtsɯr tɤ-ɕpaʁ kɯ mɯ́j-sɤ-cʰa tɕe, nɯna-j je \\
1sg.poss-younger.sibling nmlz: abstract -be.tired comit nmlz: abstract -be.hungry nmlz: abstract -be.thirsty erg neg: sens - prop -can lnk rest: fact - 1pl hort \\
`Brother, we are so tired, hungry and thirsty that we can't [go any further], let us rest!' (2012-qachGa) 0004087#S138
exe

The meaning of the abstract nouns in ( ex:tAGYat.tAmtsWr.kW.Zo ) is very similar to that of degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominal.construction ) combined with the ergative in examples such as ( ex:WtWmtsWr.kW ).

exe

maka ɯ-tɯ-mtsɯr kɯ kɤ-ŋke mɯ-ɲɤ-cʰa \\
at.all 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -hungry erg inf -go neg - ifr -can \\
`It was so hungry that it could not walk anymore.' (140515 huli he yelv-zh)
0004002#S37
exe

Abstract nouns in tɤ- are also attested without ergative to express the state or condition described by the adjective, for instance tɤ-mtsɯrhunger from mtsɯrbe hungry, as in ( ex:atAmtsWr.anWsWGZi ) and ( ex:tWtAmtsWr.YWGAphAn ). Note in both example the possibility of adding a possessive prefix on the noun.

exe

a-tɤ-mtsɯr nɯra ci a-nɯ-sɯɣ-ʑi ɲɯ-ra \\
1sg. poss - nmlz: abstract -be.hungry dem: pl a.little irr - pfv - caus -ease sens -be.needed \\
`Let's [catch the mouse] to ease my hunger.' (140518 mao he laoshu-zh) 0004030#S17
exe

exe

nɯnɯ ɕoʁɕoʁ ɯ-taʁ pɯ-kɤ-rɤt qajɣi nɯ kɯ tɯ-tɤ-mtsɯr ɲɯ-ɣɤ-pʰɤn mɤ-cʰa \\
dem paper 3sg. poss -on aor - obj: pcp -write bread dem erg genr. poss - nmlz: abstract -be.hungry ipfv - caus -be.efficient neg -can: fact \\
`Bread drawn on a piece of paper cannot ease one's hunger.' (160718 huabingchongji-zh)
0006087#S35
exe

In addition, we find abstract alienably possessed nouns in tɤ- expressing an abstract state, but which are not synchronically derived from a verb, and whose corresponding verbs are denominal. tab:abstract.nouns.denominal presents some examples.
summary:
Japhug has two kinds of action nominals, with the productive tɯ- form being the main type; these can derive from both transitive and intransitive verbs, but they lose the verb’s argument structure and cannot take objects or oblique arguments. They can denote the action itself, the result or affected object, or the manner of performing the action, and they may also function as prenominal modifiers.  

A separate tɤ- formation derives abstract nouns from adjectival stative verbs, typically expressing manners, causes, or states/conditions, often with ergative kɯ but sometimes without it. The passage also notes regular vowel fusion in some forms and that in a few cases the direction of derivation between noun and verb is unclear.

text:
The relator noun ɯ-tɤjɯaddition, which is essentially attested as an incremental addition linker (`in addition to $X$', § sec:incremental.addition ) is a trace of the abstract noun from which the denominal verb ɣɤjɯadd was built (§ sec:denom.tr.GA ).

These nouns possibly derive from base verbs which disappeared and were replaced by the corresponding denominal verbs.

The noun tɤkʰeidiot, fool deriving from kʰebe stupid formally resembles an abstract noun, but semantically differs from the other nouns in this category; it is possibly an alienabilized form of the property noun ɯ-kʰesomething nasty (§ sec:property.nouns, § sec:bare.action.nominals ).
summary: The passage notes that the relator noun ɯ-tɤjɯaddition is mainly used as an incremental addition linker and is a trace of the abstract noun that underlies the denominal verb ɣɤjɯadd. It suggests that such nouns may come from older base verbs that later disappeared and were replaced by corresponding denominal verbs. It also mentions that tɤkʰeidiot, fool, though formally like an abstract noun and derived from kʰebe stupid, is semantically different and may be an alienabilized form of the property noun ɯ-kʰesomething nasty.

text:
simultaneity nominalization!action
The simultaneous action nominal is built by prefixing an additional tɯ- to the base form of the action nominal, resulting in a double tɯ-tɯ- prefixed form. It is found in collocation with the verb βzumake (§ sec:tr.light.verbs ), and optionally with the comitative cʰo (§ sec:comitative ), linking two noun phrases referring to the entities undergoing the action together as in ( ex:tWtWrqoR.koBzu ).

exe

tɤ-wa nɯ kɯ ɯ-tɕɯ cʰo ɯ-me ni ʁnaʁna ʑo tɯ-tɯ-rqoʁ ko-βzu. \\
indef. poss -father dem erg 3sg. poss -son comit 3sg. poss -daughter du both emph simult - nmlz: action -hug ifr -make \\
`The father hugged both his son and his daughter at the same time.' (140427 xiong he mei-zh)
0003862#S21
exe

In this construction, the orientation preverb on βzumake is the one that is lexically selected by the verb in simultaneous action nominal form ( eastwards in ex:tWtWrqoR.koBzu, reflecting the centripetal function of this orientation, § sec:centripetal.centrifugal ). With orientable verbs (§ sec:orientable.verbs ), the unspecified orientation ja- can be selected ( ex:tWtWCe.jaBzundZi ).

exe

ʑɤni tɯ-tɯ-ɕe ja-βzu-ndʑi \\
3du simult - nmlz: action -go aor:3 -make- du \\
`They went at the same time.' (elicited)
exe

Example ( ex:tWtWCe.jaBzundZi ) also illustrates the fact that, when the verb in simultaneous action nominal form is intransitive, the shared subject (here ʑɤni ) is in absolutive form, even though βzu is transitive. This type of construction is described in more detail in § sec:simult.action.nominal.Bzu.

The first tɯ- prefix in the simultaneous construction is probably from the numeral tɯ- `one' prefix (§ sec:num.prefixes.1.10 ), added to a tɯ- action nominal. With intransitive verbs, the dental infinitives in tɯ- (with a possessive prefix coreferent with the subject) also occur to express simultaneous actions in collocation with the light verb sɯpacause to do, as shown by ( ex:Wti.cho.WtWCe ) in § sec:bare.inf.complement. The action nominal simultaneous construction differs however from the dental/bare infinitive simultaneous construction in that in the former the action of the same verb applies to different subject/objects, while in the latter the same subject performs actions expressed by different verbs.
summary: The simultaneous action nominal is formed by adding an extra tɯ- prefix to the action nominal, yielding a double tɯ-tɯ- form, and it occurs with the light verb βzumake, sometimes with comitative cʰo to link two noun phrases affected by the action. In this construction, the orientation preverb on βzu is the one selected by the verb, and with intransitive verbs the shared subject appears in absolutive form. The text also notes that the first tɯ- may come from the numeral prefix meaning ‘one,’ and contrasts this construction with simultaneous infinitival constructions, which involve one subject performing different verbs rather than the same verb applying to different participants.

text:
Some tɯ- action nominals can serve as base for denominal derivation in nɯ- or rɯ- (§ sec:denom.rA.pairing ), resulting in a verb with a double derivation nɯ-tɯ- or rɯ-tɯ. This category is highly heterogeneous, and unlike voice derivations originating from denominal prefixes, has not developed a consistent meaning and grammatical function.

In some cases, the meaning of the (doubly) derived verb is predictable from the base verb, but the two verbs differ in their argument structure. For instance, in fɕɤlhave diarrhea $ $ tɯfɕɤldiarrhea $ $ nɯtɯfɕɤlhave diarrhea. In this particular case, the base verb (from Tibetan bɕaldiarrhea) and the doubly derived verb nɯtɯfɕɤlhave diarrhea are both intransitive verbs, but differ in that the former select a body part as subject (the person being indicated by a possessive prefix), while the latter selects the person suffering the disease.

exe

a-xtu ɲɯ-fɕɤl \\
1sg. poss -belly sens -have.diarrhea \\

ɲɯ-nɯtɯfɕal-a \\
sens -have.diarrhea- 1sg \\
`I have diarrhea.' (elicited)
exe

Note that a collocation with βzumake is also attested with the action nominal tɯfɕɤldiarrhea (as in § sec:action.nominal.Bzu ), but the experiencer is encoded as a possessive prefix on that noun, as nɯ-tɯ-fɕɤl in ( ex:nWtWfCAl.YWBze ). Given the parallelism between denominal derivations and noun-light verb collocations (§ sec:Bzu.lv ), is possible that the denominal verb nɯtɯfɕɤlhave diarrhea came into existence as the verbalized form of this collocation.

exe

nɤrŋi nɯra, nɯ-tɯ-fɕɤl ci ɲɯ-βze ŋgrɤl tɕe \\
infant dem: pl 3pl. poss - nmlz: action -have.diarrhea indef sens -make[III] be.usually.the.case: fact lnk \\
`Infants, they often suffer from diarrhea.' (17-xCAj) 0003528#S107
exe

In other cases, the doubly derived verb may have a much more restricted meaning than the base verb, especially when the action nominal on which it is based is more lexicalized (§ sec:lexicalized.action.nominals ).

For instance, the noun tɯsqawheat gruel derived from the transitive verb sqacook is denominalized as the intransitive rɯtɯsqaeat wheat gruel (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ), whose semantic relationship with the base verb is more remote.

This category is difficult to distinguish from denominal verbs from bare action nominals (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ) taking an indefinite possessor prefix tɯ-. For instance, the transitive verb tɕʰɯgore, stab can be used in a light verb construction in lɤtrelease in bare infinitive form, as in ( ex:WtChW.tolAt ).

exe

ɯ-tɕʰɯ to-lɤt \\
3sg. poss - bare. inf:gore ifr -throw \\
`He stabbed him.' (elicited)
exe

The denominal verb nɯtɯtɕʰɯstab (attested in ex:tonWtWtChW.pjAsat ) is most probably derived from the indefinite form tɯ-tɕʰɯ of the bare infinitive in the construction in ( ex:WtChW.tolAt ), though it is also conceivable that this form comes from the action nominal.

exe

to-nɯtɯtɕʰɯ tɕe pjɤ-sat \\
ifr -stab lnk ifr -kill \\
`She stabbed and killed him.' (140512 alibaba) 0003965#S285
exe
summary:
Some tɯ- action nominals can serve as bases for denominal derivation in nɯ- or rɯ-, producing doubly derived verbs of the form nɯ-tɯ- or rɯ-tɯ, but this class is highly heterogeneous and has no consistent semantic or grammatical function. In some cases the meaning is predictable yet the argument structure changes, as with verbs meaning ‘have diarrhea,’ while in others the derived verb has a more restricted or more lexicalized meaning, as with ‘eat wheat gruel’ from ‘wheat gruel.’  

The passage also notes that these denominal verbs can be hard to distinguish from verbs derived from bare action nominals with an indefinite possessor prefix tɯ-, and some forms may have arisen from collocations with light verbs.

text:
Action nominals in tɯ- are prone to lexicalization, developing meanings that are impredictable from the base verb.

Action nominals from verbs related to preparation or ingestion of food can become names of specific types of food. For instance, tɯsqawheat gruel and tɯtsʰirice gruel originate from the transitive verbs sqacook and tsʰidrink, though the synchronic link between these nouns and the base verbs has ceased to be completely obvious. Other cases of unpredictable meanings are found with tɯpumoxibustion (with the verb taput § sec:ta.lv, as in ex:tWpu.kutanW ), which derives from pucook (especially of potatoes in hot ashes, but is not used in reference to moxibustion).

exe

tɯpu ku-ta-nɯ tɕe, tɤ-pɤtso ɣɯ ɯ-laz ci ku-ta-nɯ, \\
moxibustion ipfv -put- pl lnk indef. poss -child gen 3sg. poss -forehead one ipfv -put- pl \\
`(To treat this disease), they apply moxibustion, they apply it to the forehead of the child.' (25-kACAl) 0003640#S64
exe

In some cases, the action noun has a highly restricted meaning in comparison with the base verb, limited to one particular sub-meaning. For instance, the noun tɯpɣaʁland clearing ( ex:tWpGaR.lotCAtndZi ) (used in collocation with tɕɤttake out, § sec:tCAt.lv ) derives from the transitive verb pɣaʁturn over, which has the meaning `plough' when occurring with the orientation preverb upstream (see example ex:nWji.lopGaRnW in § sec:antipassive.lexicalized ). This noun lacks the basic meaning of the base verb and its additional extended meanings (such as `go across (a mountain)', like Chinese 翻山 fānshāncross a mountain). The antipassive rɤpɣaʁreclaim land has the same meaning restriction as the action noun, an observation whose significance is developed in § sec:antipassive.irr.semantic.

exe

tɯpɣaʁ lo-tɕɤt-ndʑi \\
field.clearing ifr: upstream -take.out- du \\
`They cleared fields.' (07-deluge) 0003426#S109
exe

The divergence in meaning between the action nominal and the base verb can also be due to semantic innovation in the verb. For instance, the verb rma means in Japhug `to stay at someone else's place (for a few nights), as in ( ex:CpWnWrmaa ), but the action nominal tɯrmahousehold ( ex:tWrma.kondondZi ), suggesting that the original meaning of the verb used to be `live' and became more restricted semantically, while the derived noun preserved its original meaning.

exe

sɤndzɯn <laoshi> ɯ-ɕki ri kɤ-ari-a tɕe, tɯ-rʑaʁ ɕ-pɯ-nɯ-rma-a \\
anthr teacher 3sg. poss - dat loc aor -go[II]- 1sg lnk one -night tral - aor - auto -stay.at- 1sg \\
`I went to Sandzin's [house], and stayed there for one night.' (conversation 160811)
exe

exe

kʰa ra cʰɤ-fkaβ-ndʑi qʰe tɯrma ko-ndo-ndʑi \\
house pl ifr -cover- du lnk household ifr -take- du \\
`They built a house and established a family.' (02-deluge 2012)
0003376#S121
exe

Note the barely translatable use of the action nominals tɯrma and tɯβlɯ (the latter from the transitive verb βlɯburn) in the expression used as the conclusion of most traditional stories in ( ex:tWrma.tWBlW ).

exe

tɯrma tɯ-βlɯ cʰɤ-nɯ-sɤɲcɣɤɲcɣɤt-nɯ kɤ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
household nmlz: action -burn ifr - auto -cause.to.be.prosperous- pl inf -say sens -be \\
`They lead a prosperous life = they live happily ever after' (many examples)
exe

There are cases where an alienably possessed noun in tɯ- lacks a corresponding base verb; for instance, no verb *qartsɯ `kick' is attested besides the noun tɯqartsɯkicking, which is used with lɤtrelease as in ( ex:tWqartsW.thalAt ) (note that the tɯ- prefix here is neither the indefinite possessor nor the numeral `one' prefixes). The only related verb is the denominal labile verb sɯqartsɯkick (used only for animals, kicking with the rear limbs), which comes from the action nominal tɯqartsɯkicking (§ sec:denom.sW.caus.instr ).

exe

ɯ-rqo nɯtɕu tɯqartsɯ tʰa-lɤt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -throat dem: loc kick aor:3 -throw sens -be \\
`He kicked her in the throat.' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S253
exe

In this case, it is most likely that the base verb *qartsɯ `kick' did exist at some stage but was lost, only leaving derived words.
summary: Action nominals in tɯ- often lexicalize with meanings that cannot be predicted from the base verb. The passage illustrates this with nouns for foods and other specialized items, with cases where the action nominal preserves an older meaning, narrows the verb’s sense, or survives even when the corresponding verb is no longer attested.

text:
nominalization!bare action nominal
Bare action nominals lack any nominalization affix. They are inalienably possessed (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ), and take the indefinite possessor prefixes tɯ- or tɤ, very similar in function to the tɯ- action nominals and in form to the bare infinitives (§ sec:bare.inf ).

They can refer to the action itself, as in tɯ-sɯsothought from the transitive verb sɯsothink or the way an action is performed, as ɯ-tiway of saying, `wording', `expression' from tisay. They can also be concrete nouns ( tab:concrete.action.IPN.verbs ). In the case of transitive verb, these nouns refer to an instrument used to perform the action, or resulting from the action ( tɤ-tsʰoʁnail from tsʰoʁattach, on which see § sec:anticausative.dummy ). In the case of intransitive verbs, bare action nominals can refer to an object having a property described by the verb (for instance tɤ-rosurplus, leftover from robe in surplus). Note the presence of a borrowing from Tibetan among these verbs ( fkaβcover from བཀབ་bkabcover (past)), showing the productivity of this type of derivation.

For some examples, the semantic relationship between the bare action nominal and the base verb is not transparent anymore; for instance, tɯ-ɲɟoʁhelper apparently derives from ɲɟoʁglue, paste (possibly through the sense `(person) attached to oneself').

Some property nouns, which are derived from adjectival stative verbs (§ sec:property.nouns ) without nominalization x-/ɣ- prefix (§ sec:G.nmlz ), are also bare action nominals. tab:property.nouns.verbs presents a list of these property nouns and their respective base verbs (among which maŋbe many is borrowed from མང་maŋbe many).

Intransitive verbs in a- are correlated with inalienably possessed action nominals with the tɤ- indefinite possessor prefix, for instance aɕqʰecough (vi) and tɤ-ɕqʰecough (n). Two hypotheses can be proposed to account for such pairs.

First, one can argue that the base forms are the verbs, and that the inalienably possessed noun are derived from them; in this view the a- element is absorbed the possessive prefixes, and leaves no trace in the possessive paradigm: the 2sg and 2pl of tɤ-ɕqʰecough are nɤ-ɕqʰe `your$_SG$ cough' ( ex:nACqhe.WBRAGAZu ) nɯ-ɕqʰe `your$_PL$ cough', whereas one would have expected these two forms to have become homophonous due to vowel fusion ( 2pl $ $ nɯ-ɤɕqʰe realized as nɤɕqʰe like the 2sg, § sec:a.nouns, § sec:contraction ).

Second, it is also possible that aɕqʰecough (vi) (and other verbs of the same type) derives from tɤ-ɕqʰecough by the a- denominal prefix (§ sec:denom.a ).

exe

nɤ-ɕqʰe ɯβrɤ-ɣɤʑu? \\
2sg. poss -cough rh. q -exist: sens \\
`You don't have a cough, do you?' (conversation, 2013-11-12)
exe

The functional proximity between bare action nominals and tɯ- action nominals is illustrated by example ( ex:Wti.WtWsAZirja ), where both types of nominals (from different verbs) appear in parallel contexts. This sentence is a metalinguistic comment on the phenomenon described in § sec:dyads, examples ( ex:apa.ama ) and ( ex:amu.awa.ni.GW ).

exe

ɯ-ti tɕi mɯ-pjɤ-naχtɕɯɣ, ɯ-tɯ-sɯ-ɤʑirja kɯnɤ mɯ-pjɤ-naχtɕɯɣ ma, \\
3sg. poss -expression also neg - pst. ipfv -be.the.same 3sg. poss - nmlz: action - caus -be.aligned also neg - pst. ipfv -be.the.same lnk \\
`The words for [father and mother] were different [between common and honorific register], and the respective orders [in which `mother' and `father' appear] were also different.' (160706 apa ama) 0006211#S8
exe

Given the fact that the only formal difference between the verb and the noun in this formation is the presence of a possessive prefix on the noun, there are cases where the historical relationship between the noun and the verb is ambiguous. The inalienably possessed nouns tɤ-rminame and tɤ-rʑaʁtime synchronically look like bare action nominals derived from the semi-transitive verbs rmibe called and rʑaʁspend a night. However, there may be comparative evidence that these verbs are back-formations from the nouns (§ sec:verb.backformation ).

Formally irregular bare action nominals are rare. The inalienably possessed noun tɯ-nŋadebt derives from the transitive verb ŋabuy on credit, owe, which takes as object the amount of money owed (§ sec:antipassive.history ). The stem of the noun has an additional n- prefix, which may reflect a reduced allomorph *t- of the tɯ- action nominal prefix, with further automatic nasalization to n- before nasal consonant.

Bare action nominals are restricted to a few verbs. However, it is likely that they were more common at an earlier stage, as suggested by the existence of bare infinitives (§ sec:bare.inf ) and by the development of voice derivations from the reanalysis of denominal prefixes (§ sec:voice.denominal ).

In some cases, the direction of derivation between inalienably possessed noun and verb deserves a more detailed discussion. The noun tɯ-ŋgodisease could be analyzed as deriving from the verb ngobe ill, but it is preferable to suppose that the noun is primary, and that the verb takes an irregular allomorph of the denominal nɯ- prefix (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ).

We also find inalienably possessed nouns without a corresponding base verb, but which may originate from bare action nouns of lost base verbs. For instance tɤ-relaugh (n) is a noun expressing an action, but whose tɤ- is an indefinite possessor prefix and not the action or abstract noun prefix, as shown by ( ex:Wre.CmWG.YAClWG ) where it is replaced by the 3sg possessive ɯ- prefix.

exe

ɯ-re ci ɕmɯɣ ɲɤ-ɕlɯɣ \\
3sg. poss -laugh indef idph (I):laugh.suddenly ifr -drop \\
`She giggled despite herself.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

The verbs related to tɤ-relaugh (n), the adjectival stative verb sɤrebe ridiculous and the labile verb nɤrelaugh (§ sec:labile.tr-intr ), are both denominal and derive from it. However, comparative evidence suggests that this noun itself derives at an earlier stage from a verb, which was replaced by denominal verbs in Japhug.
summary:
Bare action nominals are nominal forms without a nominalization affix; they are inalienably possessed and take the indefinite possessor prefixes tɯ- or tɤ-, much like tɯ- action nominals. They can denote the action itself, the manner of an action, or concrete nouns such as instruments, resulting objects, or properties, and some show semantic links to the base verb that are no longer transparent.  

The passage also notes that bare action nominals are limited in number but may have been more common historically, and that in some cases it is unclear whether the noun or the verb is primary. Several examples suggest possible back-formation or denominal derivation in either direction, including forms with irregular morphology and nouns that survive even when the corresponding base verb is no longer present.

text:
nominalization!action nominal compound compound!action nominal
Action nominal compounds, like bare action nominals (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ), lack any nominalization affixes. Unlike other noun-verb compounds such as actor nominal compounds, which are rare and sporadic (§ sec:object.verb.compounds ), action nominal compounds are a well-identified grammatical category. As with other compound nouns, the first element (the nominal root) is nearly Vowel alternation does not take place in the case of some very productive constructions, such as that with kʰrambalie treated below and in § sec:compound.action.nominal.Bzu. always in bound state form (§ sec:status.constructus ). For instance, the action nominal cʰɤtsʰialcohol drinking is built from the noun cʰaalcohol (with regular vowel alternation to cʰɤ- ) and the transitive verb tsʰidrink. When the incorporated noun is originally inalienably possessed, the indefinite possessor prefix (§ sec:inalienably.possessed.morpho ) is removed, as in ɣlɯtɕɤtremoving dung out of the stable (to be used as fertilized) from tɯ-ɣlidung and tɕɤttake out.

The nominal element generally corresponds to the object of the verb as in cʰɤtsʰi or ɣlɯtɕɤt (§ sec:object.verb.compounds ). There are however also cases of goal or adjunct being incorporated, as in qʰarulook back from ɯ-qʰuafter, behind (bound state qʰa- ) with the intransitive verb rulook at (§ sec:intr.goal ) and kɤtɕʰɯheadbutt from the inalienably possessed noun tɯ-kuhead (bound state kɤ- ) and the verb tɕʰɯgore, stab (§ sec:adjunct.verb.compounds ).

These nouns mainly occur with light verbs such as lɤtrelease (§ sec:lAt.lv ) or βzumake (§ sec:Bzu.lv ) as in ( ex:qharu ), but are also found in other constructions as in ( ex:chAtshi.koGAtChom ), where a free object cʰaalcohol with the bare infinitive ɯ-tsʰi can also be used (see § sec:velar.caus.complement ).
