It is thus likely that the action nominal compounds originate (at least in part) from the coalescence of nouns with bare infinitives.

exe

ɯʑo nɯ tatpa ta-ta ma qʰaru mucin ʑo mɯ-pa-lɤt nɤ tɤ-ari ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3sg dem faith aor:3 -put lnk look.back at.all emph neg - aor:3: down -release lnk aor: up -go[II] sens -be \\
`He had faith, did not look back (downwards) at all and [succeeded in] going up to [the abode of the gods]. (Norbzang)
exe

exe

cʰɤtsʰi ko-ɣɤ-tɕʰom tɕe \\
alcohol.drinking ifr - caus -be.too.much lnk \\
`He had drunk too much alcohol.' (150829 jidian-zh)
0006338#S16
exe

Compounds with rpubump into or tɕʰɯgore, stab as second element can be built productively with the meaning `hit with $X$' and `stab with $X$' in collocation with lɤtrelease, $X$ corresponding to the first element of the compound. For instance, in ( ex:RzAnrpu ) we find the nonce formation ʁzɤn-rpu `hitting with a monastic robe', whose first element ʁzɤnmonastic robe comes from Tibetan གཟན་gzanmonastic robe, a rather incongruous action which cannot possibly have been lexicalized.

exe

ɯ-βɣo nɯ pɯ-ari nɤ, ʁzɤn-rpu ʁɟa ʑo ɕ-ta-lɤt ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -FB dem aor: down -go[II] add robe-bump completely emph tral - aor:3 sens -be \\
`(As he$_i$ fell down the throat of the giant snake$_j$) his lama$_k$ went down [to the place where the snake was] and hit it$_j$ repeatedly with his$_k$ monastic robe [to force it$_j$ to spit him$_i$ out].' (2003 kandZislama)
exe

The patient of the hitting action, if overt, is marked with the relator ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:WtaR ) as in ( ex:RrWrpu ), with the compound ʁrɯrpuhitting with horns (sideways, not goring) from ta-ʁrɯhorn.

exe

jla kɯ a-taʁ ʁrɯ-rpu ta-lɤt \\
hybrid.yak erg 1sg -on horn-bump aor:3 -throw \\
`The hybrid yak hit me with his horn.' (elicited)
exe

In addition, we find action nominal compounds whose incorporated noun expresses the manner of the action, rather than the object, the goal or the instrument as in the previous cases.

First, the noun kʰrambalie can be compounded (without bound state alternation) with transitive or intransive verbs, in forms as kʰramba-tsʰi with the verb tsʰidrink in ( ex:khramba.tshi ). These compound nouns, in collocation with βzu (§ sec:Bzu.lv ), have the meaning `pretend to $X$'. Note that the compounding with kʰramba does not saturate the object position, and has no antipassivization effect: the object cʰaalcohol is overt in ( ex:khramba.tshi ).

exe

ʑara kɯ [cʰa nɯ kʰramba-tsʰi] ka-βzu-nɯ \\
3pl erg alcohol dem lie-drink aor:3 -make- pl \\
`They pretended to drink alcohol.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

Second, the lexicalized participle kɯzɣaa long time can be compounded with a verb root as kɯzɣɤ- (here with vowel alternation). These compounds also occur with light verb βzu, and the collocation means `do $X$ for a long time' as in ( ex:kWzGACar ).

exe

kɯzɣɤ-ɕar ʑo ɲɤ-βzu-nɯ \\
long.time-search emph ifr -make- pl \\
`They searched for it for a long time.' (elicited)
exe

In these constructions, the verb βzumake takes the person indexation of subject and object (§ sec:orientation.raising ), as well as the orientation preverbs selected by the verb in the compound, for instance eastwards like tsʰidrink in ( ex:khramba.tshi ) and westwards like ɕarsearch in ( ex:kWzGACar ). Additional examples of these constructions are discussed in § sec:compound.action.nominal.Bzu (see also ).

Some action nominal compounds can serve as basis for incorporating denominal verbs. The incorporated object sometimes saturates the object function, and the resulting incorporating verbs are intransitive, as in the case of ɣɯcʰɤtsʰidrink alcohol or ɣɯɣlɯtɕɤtremove dung out of stable from cʰɤtsʰialcohol drinking and ɣlɯtɕɤtremoving dung out of the stable, respectively. In the case of ʁrɯrpuhitting with horns however, the resulting verb nɯʁrɯrpuhit with horns is transitive, the oblique argument marked with ɯ-taʁon, above in the construction in ( ex:RrWrpu ) being promoted to direct object status. It is not possible to derive a denominal verb from all of the Noun+ rpu or Noun+ tɕʰɯ compounds.

A complete list of incorporating denominal verbs and the corresponding action nominal compounds is provided in § sec:incorporation. There are also action nominals built by compounding two verb roots (§ sec.v.v.compounds.action ), which serve as the basis for compound verbs by way of denominal derivation (§ sec:denom.compound.verbs ).
summary:
Action nominal compounds are a well-established category of noun-verb compounds that, like bare action nominals, lack nominalization affixes; the nominal element is usually in bound form and most often corresponds to the verb’s object, though it can also express a goal, adjunct, or instrument. Some compounds are used with light verbs such as *lɤ* ‘release’ or *βzu* ‘make’, and the text suggests these forms may partly arise from nouns combining with bare infinitives.

The passage also describes special productive patterns: with *rpu* ‘bump into’ or *tɕʰɯ* ‘gore, stab*, compounds can mean ‘hit with X’ or ‘stab with X’, while other compounds with *kʰramba* and *kɯzɣa* express ‘pretend to X’ and ‘do X for a long time’. Some action nominal compounds also serve as bases for denominal verbs

text:
This section present vestigial nominalization affixes, which despite of their rarity are however important for historical linguistics: the -z suffix and the x/ɣ- prefix.

Nominalization -z suffix
nominalization!suffix suffix!nominalization
Japhug has five inalienably possessed nouns derived from verbs by means of a nominalizing -z The -z nominalizing suffix, though rare in Japhug, is of Sino-Tibetan origin. In Situ, the corresponding nominalizing -s suffix is much more common, and Tibetan and Chinese have traces of a cognate suffix.
( tab:z.nmlz ), three of which take the indefinite possessor prefix tɤ- (§ sec:inalienably.possessed.morpho ). Nouns in -z such as tɤ-rtsɯznumber cannot be counted as a Japhug-internal derivation from rtsicount: both the noun and the verb come from Tibetan, respectively from རྩིས་rtsiscalculation and རྩི་rtsicalculate.

The first two nouns tɤ-rkuzparting present and tɤ-scozletter, writing
This noun is possibly borrowed from Situ. are object nominalizations. The former tɤ-rkuzparting present is biactantial possessed noun, whose possessor corresponds to the recipient (§ sec:biactantial.ipn ). The etymological relationship between tɤ-rkuz and rkuput in is obvious when the use of this verb in the sense of `give as a present to take away' (put in someone's luggage) is considered, as in ( ex:kWki.nArkuz.Nu ).

exe

tɕe tó-wɣ-z-rɤŋgat tɕe, tɕendɤre nɯnɯ kɯ, iɕqʰa nɯ, tɯ-ci tɯ-tɤ-ste to-rku. tɕe `kɯki nɤ-rkuz ŋu' to-ti. \\
lnk ifr - inv - caus -prepare.to.leave lnk lnk dem erg filler dem indef. poss -water one - indef. poss -bladder ifr -put.in lnk dem. prox 2sg. poss -present be: fact ifr -say \\
`He prepared his departure, and gave him a bladder full of water to take with him, and said `this is your departing present'.' (28-smAnmi.txt)
0004063#S247
exe

The verb rkuput in can even occur with its derived noun tɤ-rkuzparting present in the figura etymologica construction in ( ex:arkuz.tarku ) (the verb βzumake can alternatively be used instead of rkuput in).

exe

a-me kɯ a-rkuz rŋɯl ta-rku \\
1sg. poss -daughter erg 1sg. poss -present money aor:3 -put.in \\
`My daughter gave me some money (as a present for my departure) (elicited)
exe

The other nominalizations in -z are all abstract nouns. The form ɯ-ʁjiz, which derives from the transitive verb ʁjitthink of, `miss', `remember', results from the simplification of a complex coda *-ts to -z. This noun only occurs in collocation with motion verbs, and is preceded by a finite or infinitive complement clause (§ sec:nouns.cognition.complement ). The whole construction has the meaning `want to X', where X refers to the content of the complement clause; the experiencer is encoded by the possessive prefix on ɯ-ʁjiz, as illustrated by ( ex:aRjiz.mWjGi ).

exe

tɕe aʑo nɯtɕu kɤ-ɕe a-ʁjiz mɯ́j-ɣi tɕe \\
lnk 1sg dem: loc inf -go 1sg. poss -want neg: sens -come lnk \\
`I don't want to go there.' (150909 hua pi-zh)
0006278#S20
exe

The noun ɯ-mɲozpreparation is also only attested in a collocation (with the verb βzumake as in ex:WmYoz.tuwGBzu ). The transitive verb mɲoprepare from which it derives is itself the irregular causative of ɲobe prepared (§ sec:causative.m ). A -z -less bare action nominal ɯ-mɲopreparation (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ) is also attested.

exe

pjɯ-ɲɟo ɕɯŋgɯ tɕe ɯ-mɲoz tú-wɣ-βzu ra \\
ipfv -be.damaged before lnk 3sg. poss -preparation ipfv - inv -make be.needed: fact \\
`One has to make preparations before it gets damaged.' (elicited)
exe

The property noun ɯ-rkozsomething special ( ex:Wrkoz.me ), probably derived from rkobe hard, This etymology is however uncertain, as it would be the only noun of this type from an intransitive verb, and besides the semantic relationship is not entirely transparent. is used adverbially (with the 3sg or the indefinite possessor prefix) as tɤ-rkozspecially, `on purpose'. This meaning is however frequently expressed by the borrowing 专门 zhuānménspecially, on purpose).

exe

ɯ-rmi ɯ-rkoz me. \\
3sg. poss -name 3sg. poss -special not.exist: fact \\
`There is no specific name (for this type of kinship relationship).' (140425 kWmdza06) 0003790
exe

Nominalization ɣ-/x- prefix
nominalization!velar prefix
A handful of nouns, most of them inalienably possessed, are derived from intransitive verbs by means of a velar prefix ɣ- or x, harmonizing in voicing with the initial consonant of the stem since the voicing contrast is neutralized in preinitial position (§ sec:xC.clusters ). These nouns are lexicalized ancient subject participles (§ sec:subject.participles, § sec:velar.nmlz.history ) which underwent the same phonological change as that observed with the velar animal class prefix (§ sec:velar.class.prefix ), that has a syllabic allomorph kɯ- and reduced allomorphs ɣ- or x -.

The reduced ɣ- / x- prefix only derives nouns from intransitive verbs with monosyllabic stems, without consonant clusters. Some of the nouns in tab:irregular.nmlz have cognates in other Gyalrong languages with reduced prefixes. For instance, ɣndʑɤβ has an exact cognate in Tshobdun: ɣⁿdʒov `fire'. The noun ɯ-ɣɲɟɯ has two corresponding forms in Tshobdun: -ʁⁿɟúʔ `window' with a reduced uvularized prefix, and kəⁿɟuʔ `hole' with a non-reduced prefix.

The noun tɯ-xpaone year, although derived from the verb papass $X$ years and having an additional x- element, does not belong to this category, see § sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history and § sec:CN.verbs.

The noun tɯ-ɣɲifriend, ally also belongs to this category, though the base verb does not exist in Japhug. It is a near-exact cognate of Tibetan གཉེན་gɲenfriend, relative, a noun derived from the adjective ཉེ་ɲenear.
summary: The passage describes two rare but historically important vestigial nominalization patterns in Japhug: a nominalizing **-z suffix** and a **ɣ-/x- prefix**. The -z suffix forms a small set of inalienably possessed nouns, including some object and abstract nominalizations, while the ɣ-/x- prefix derives a few nouns from intransitive verbs and is analyzed as a reflex of ancient subject participles with historical cognates in other Gyalrong languages and Tibetan.

text: This section discusses several non-finite verb forms which exclusively occur in subordinate clauses other than relative and complement clauses. Other verb forms which might be labeled as converbs, in particular some uses of the velar infinitive, are treated in previous sections (§ sec:inf.converb ).
summary: The section discusses several non-finite verb forms that occur only in subordinate clauses other than relative and complement clauses. It notes that other forms that might be considered converbs, especially some uses of the velar infinitive, were treated earlier.

text:
gerund
The gerund is built by prefixing sɤ- or sɤz- to the verb stem with partial reduplication of the final syllable. It clearly derives from the oblique participle (§ sec:oblique.participle, § sec:sigmatic.nmlz.history ), but differs from the latter by the impossibility of adding orientation or possessive prefixes, by the obligatory reduplication, and by the absence of the allomorphs z- and sɤɣ-.

Given the fact that the gerund is marked by both the prefix sɤ-/sɤz- and the reduplication, I only gloss ger under the prefix, and leave the reduplication unglossed; for instance in ( ex:sArgWrga.jonWCe ) sɤ-rgɯ rga is glossed ger -be.happy instead of the more explicit but burdensome ger - ger be.happy.

exe

[sɤ-rgɯ rga] kɯ jo-nɯ-ɕe \\
ger -be.happy erg ifr - vert -go \\
`He went back home happy.' (140516 yiguan ganlan-zh) 0004014#S134
exe

This section reviews the morphology of the gerund (§ sec:gerund.allomorphs ), § sec:gerund.neg ), then discusses the syntactic properties of gerundive clauses (§ sec:gerund.clauses ), and finally presents some cases of lexicalized gerunds (§ sec:gerund.lexicalized ).
summary:
The gerund is formed with the prefix sɤ- or sɤz- attached to the verb stem, together with partial reduplication of the final syllable. Although it derives from the oblique participle, it differs in that it cannot take orientation or possessive prefixes, requires reduplication, and lacks the allomorphs z- and sɤɣ-.

The author glosses only the prefix as ger and leaves the reduplication unglossed. The section then goes on to survey gerund morphology, negation, syntactic properties, and lexicalized forms.

text:
gerund
The distribution of the sɤ- and sɤz- allomorphs is illustrated in tab:gerund. The sɤz- allomorph of the gerund prefix is found when the verb stem contains a sonorant initial syllabic prefix (like nɯ/ɤ, rɯ/rɤ, ɣɯ-/ɣɤ- etc), while the sɤ- allomorph appears in all other contexts, in particular with monosyllabic stems. Verbs with a stem in a- undergo vowel merger sɤ-ɤ- to sɤ, as in sɤmdzɯdzɯ `sitting' from amdzɯsit. The sɤ- allomorph can also optionally be used in all contexts.

Verbs whose stem already contains a reduplication are not triplicated. For instance, the gerund of nɯqambɯmbjom is sɤ(z)-nɯqambɯmbjom, not the impossible form $ $ sɤ(z)-nɯqambɯmbɯmbjom.

As in other reduplicated forms (§ sec:partial.redp ), partial reduplication in the gerund disregards morpheme boundaries. In ( ex:sAznWGmWGmu.kuXse ), the allomorph nɯɣ- of the applicative has a coda -ɣ- (§ sec:caus.sWG, § sec:allomorphy.applicative ) which resyllabifies and becomes the preinitial of the next syllable of the verb stem; as such it undergoes partial reduplication, resulting in sɤznɯɣmɯɣmu rather than the incorrect form $ $ sɤznɯɣmɯmu.

exe

tɕe [sɤz-nɯɣ-mɯ ɣmu] ʑo ku-χse ɲɯ-ra. \\
lnk ger - appl -fear emph ipfv -feed[III] sens -be.needed \\
`It$_i$ has to feed it$_i$ while being afraid of it.$_i$ ' (24-ZmbrWpGa) 0003628#S101
exe

Some lexicalized gerunds have slightly irregular forms (§ sec:gerund.lexicalized ), but otherwise gerund formation is very regular. However, there are traces of the sɤɣ/x- allomorph remaining as alternative gerund forms of some verbs. For instance, the intransitive motion verb ɕego, next to the regular gerund sɤɕɯɕe, also has the form sɤxɕɯxɕe. Like the oblique participle ɯ-sɤx-ɕe (§ sec:oblique.participle.allomorphy ), the gerund sɤxɕɯxɕe was derived with the sɤx- allomorph, with resyllabification of the final -x- and its inclusion in the partial reduplication of the last syllable, like sɤznɯɣmɯɣmu above. Since in the case of oblique participles the sɤɣ- allomorph is only found with monosyllabic verbs, in the corresponding gerund form the -ɣ/x- excrescent element necessarily resyllabifies and undergoes partial reduplication.
summary:
The gerund prefix has two main allomorphs: sɤz- appears before stems with a sonorant-initial syllabic prefix, while sɤ- occurs elsewhere, especially with monosyllabic stems, though sɤ- may also be used optionally in all contexts. In forms with stem-internal reduplication, the gerund does not add a second triplication, and partial reduplication ignores morpheme boundaries, so segments that resyllabify can be copied as part of the reduplicated syllable.  

Gerund formation is otherwise regular, though some lexicalized forms are slightly irregular and a few verbs preserve alternative sɤɣ/x- forms, as in the motion verb ɕego, whose gerund may surface as sɤxɕɯxɕe.

text:
Gerunds cannot bear possessive or orientation preverb, but are attested with the negative prefix mɤ, as in ( ex:ndZisWm.mAsACWCe ) with the negative gerund mɤ-sɤ-ɕɯ ɕe `not going' in collocation with the noun tɯ-sɯmmind, here meaning `not willing, unwillingly, reluctantly'.

exe

tɕendɤre tɤ-pi ni kɯ li [ndʑi-sɯm mɤ-sɤ-ɕɯ ɕe] ʑo ɲɤ-ta-ndʑi \\
lnk indef. poss -elder.sibling du erg again 3du. poss -mind neg - ger -go emph ifr -put- du \\
`The two elder brothers reluctantly left [the ducks] alone.' (140510 fengwang-zh)
0003939#S40
exe

The form of the negative prefix is mɤ- with all verbs, except for the lexicalized masɤrɯrjuquietly, in secret (§ sec:gerund.lexicalized ); the form ma- is perhaps due to the fact that the base verb arjuspeak has an initial a- vowel; however, other verbs in a- have the mɤ- allomorph, for instance mɤ-sɤ-ɤɕqʰɯ ɕqʰe `without coughing' from aɕqʰecough.
summary: Gerunds cannot take possessive or orientation preverbs, but they can occur with the negative prefix mɤ-, as in the negative gerund mɤ-sɤ-ɕɯ ɕe ‘not going,’ which appears in a construction meaning ‘unwillingly, reluctantly.’ The text also notes that mɤ- is the regular negative prefix with verbs, while the lexicalized form ma- is exceptional and possibly conditioned by the initial vowel of the verb base.

text:
Gerunds are non-finite forms but preserve the verb's argument structure, and gerundive clauses can contain overt intransitive subjects ( ex:Wqom.sAlhWlhoR and ex:ndZisWm.mAsACWCe above) or, very rarely, objects ( ex:Wrte.sAznWtWta ).

exe

tɤɕime nɯnɯ kɯ [ɯ-qom sɤ-ɬɯ ɬoʁ] kɯ nɯra tʰɯtʰɤci pɯ-kɯ-fse ra lonba ʑo pjɤ-fɕɤt ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
young.lady dem erg 3sg. poss -tear ger -come.out erg dem: pl something aor - sbj: pcp -be.like pl all emph ifr -tell sens -be \\
`The young lady told him everything that had happened while shedding tears.' (140428 mu e guniang-zh)
0003880#S198
exe

exe

[ɯ-rte sɤz-nɯ-tɯ ta] jɤ-ari \\
3sg. poss -hat ger - auto -put aor -go[II] \\
`He went away wearing his hat.' (elicited)
exe

Gerundive clauses are always subordinate to a main finite clause, and express a background action or state occurring at the same time as that referred to by the main verb; they can nearly always be translated either by a gerund in English or by a `while' clause (§ sec:simultaneity, § sec:manner.clauses ).

Gerundive clauses, like converbial infinitival clauses (§ sec:inf.converb ), can be followed by the ergative kɯ (example ex:Wqom.sAlhWlhoR above), the emphatic ʑo ( ex:sAznWGmWGmu.kuXse and ex:ndZisWm.mAsACWCe, § sec:emphatic.Zo ) or both (as in ex:sAmbWmbGom.YABdenW below). Bare gerundive clauses are also common, as in ( ex:Wrte.sAznWtWta and ex:sAmdzWmdzW.kuzrAZinW below). No semantic difference between bare gerundive clauses and gerundive clauses followed by kɯ or ʑo can be brought to light.

The focus marker kɯnɤ can also follow a gerundive clause with the meaning `even $X$ing' as in ( ex:sArNgWrNgW.tWkArnoR ) below.

The (intransitive or transitive) subject of the gerundive clauses is often coreferent with that of the main clause, as in ( ex:Wrte.sAznWtWta ) above and ( ex:sAmbWmbGom.YABdenW ) below.

exe

tɤɕime ra rca sɤ-mbɯ mbɣom ʑo kɯ, iɕqʰa nɤki, rɟɤlpu ɯ-tɕɯ nɯra ɲɤ-βde-nɯ tɕe jo-nɯ-ɕe-nɯ \\
young.lady pl unexp: deg ger -be.in.a.hurry emph erg the.aforementioned filler king 3sg. poss -son dem: pl ifr -leave- pl lnk ifr - vert -go- pl \\
`The princesses left the princes in a hurry and went back home.' (140508 shier ge tiaowu de gongzhu-zh) 0003937#S156
exe

There is however no strict syntactic constraint on coreference between the subject of the gerundive clause and that of the main clauses. Other types of configurations are attested. In ( ex:sAmdzWmdzW.kuzrAZinW ), the intransitive subject of the gerundive clause tɤ-pɤtso nɯ `child(ren)' is the object, not the subject, of the main clause verb ku-z-rɤʑi-nɯ. In this example I assume that tɤ-pɤtso nɯ belongs to the gerundive clause, with zero anaphora in the main clause; the opposite analysis could also be considered.

exe

[tɤ-pɤtso nɯ sɤ-ɤmdzɯ mdzɯ] ku-z-rɤʑi-nɯ \\
indef. poss -child dem ger -sit ipfv - caus -stay- pl \\
`They [used to] put the children in sitting position (after having covered them in cloth).' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR 2)
exe

Coreference between the possessor of the subject in the gerundive clause and the object of the main clause as in ( ex:Wqom.sAlhWlhoR ) and ( ex:ndZisWm.mAsACWCe ) above is also attested. It is particularly common in inalienably possessed noun+intransitive verb collocations where the experiencer is marked as the possessor on the inalienably possessed noun (§ sec:light.verb ), such as tɯ-sɯm+ɕewant, tɯ-ʁjiz+ɣiwish (§ sec:motion.light.verbs ) or tɤ-mbrɯ+ŋgɯget angry as in ( ex:WmbrW.sANgWNgW ) (§ sec:other.collocation.intr ).

exe

ɯ-mbrɯ sɤ-ŋgɯ ŋgɯ kɯ ʑo jo-nɯ-ɕe. \\
3sg. poss -anger ger -get.angry erg emph ifr - vert -go \\
`He went back home angry.' (150826 baoliandeng-zh) 0006370#S89
exe

The opposite configuration, with the possessor in the main clause coreferent with the subject of the gerundive clause, is also attested, as in ( ex:sArNgWrNgW.tWkArnoR ).

exe

sɤ-rŋgɯ rŋgɯ kɯnɤ tɯ-kɤrnoʁ ɲɯ-mtɕɯr tɕe, \\
ger -lie.down also genr. poss -brain ipfv -turn lnk \\
`Even lying down, one feels dizzy [one's head is turning].' (29-tAmtshAzkAkWndo)
0004065#S55
exe

The only example of gerund without apparent coreference between any participant of the gerundive clause and of the main clause in the corpus is ( ex:sArkWrkWn.chWwGtCAt ). However, even here one can interpret the gerundive clause as having a non-overt subject whose possessor would be coreferent with the subject or the object of the main clause.

exe

nɯ sɤ-rkɯ rkɯn ʑo tɤ-pɤtso cʰɯ́-wɣ-tɕɤt pjɤ-ra tɕe, \\
dem ger -be.few emph indef. poss -child ipfv - inv -take.out ifr. ipfv -be.needed lnk \\
`People had to raise children with few [resources].' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR)
exe
gerund
While gerunds can be built for motion verbs, in the corpus the velar infinitive converbs kɤ- (§ sec:inf.converb ) are more common than gerunds to express meanings such as `running' ( kɤ-rɟɯɣ (kɯ ʑo) ), `walking' ( kɤ-ŋke (kɯ ʑo) ) when occurring in a main clause with another motion verb (for instance with jo-nɯ-ɕe-nɯ `they went away' in ex:kArJWG.kW.Zo ). Motion verbs are only attested in non-motional collocations (as in ex:ndZisWm.mAsACWCe ) above). Gerunds of motion verbs are however possible if the motion is different from the action of the main verb, as in ( ex:sANkWNke.YAsWndza ).

exe

sɤ-ŋkɯ ŋke ʑo ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-ndza \\
ger -walk emph sens - prog -eat \\
`He is eating it while walking.' (elicited)
exe
summary:
Gerunds are non-finite forms that retain verbal argument structure, and gerundive clauses can include overt subjects and, more rarely, objects. They are subordinate to a main finite clause and describe a simultaneous background action or state, often translatable with English gerunds or *while*-clauses; they may appear bare or with markers such as ergative *kɯ*, emphatic *ʑo*, or focus marker *kɯnɤ*, with no clear semantic difference between bare and marked forms.

Coreference between the gerundive clause and the main clause is common but not strictly required, and several participant-sharing configurations are attested, including possessor coreference. Motion verbs are less often expressed with gerunds than with infinitival converbs, though gerunds of motion verbs do occur when the motion is separate from the main action.

text:
gerund
There are a few examples of adverbs from lexicalized gerunds, whose form and meaning is not completely predictable from the base verb.

The gerund sɤ-xtɕɯ-xtɕi, from the stative verb xtɕibe small means `in childhood, when $X$ was young, since childhood', as in ( ex:sAxtCWtCi.YAme ). Since the verb xtɕibe small includes `be young' among its range of meanings, the use of this gerund to refer to young age is not unexpected (`while being young'), but the additional meaning `since childhood' does not correspond to the usual function of the gerund, which expresses an action or state taking place simultaneously with the action of the main verb.

exe

sɤ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ʑo ɯ-mu ɯ-wa ɲɤ-me. \\
ger -be.small emph 3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss -father ifr -not.exist \\
`He lost his parents when he was young.' (150827 tianluo) 0006250#S4
exe

The adverb masɤrɯrjuquietly, in secret from arjuspeak is formally an ancient negative gerund, with the negative prefix ma- rather than mɤ- ). It originally meant `without speaking', but its meaning has become `in secret, without someone knowing' as in ( ex:masArWrju.pjAlwoR ), and it can even be applied to acts involving speech as in ( ex:masArWrju.khAndWn ), showing that it is not semantically linked to its base verb anymore.

exe

tɕʰemɤpɯ nɯra, nɤkinɯ, mɯ-tɤ-rɯndzaŋspa-nɯ jamar tɕe tɕe,
ɯʑo kɯ masɤrɯrju iɕqʰa cʰa nɯ pjɤ-lwoʁ. \\
girl dem: pl filler neg - aor -pay.attention- pl about loc lnk 3sg erg quietly the.aforementioned alcohol dem ifr -spill \\
`While the girls were not paying attention, he poured the alcohol in secret.' (140508 shier ge tiaowu de gongzhu-zh)
0003937#S75
exe

exe

ɯʑo kɯ masɤrɯrju kʰɤndɯn nɯ ɲɤ-ndɯn \\
3sg erg quietly mantra dem ifr -recite \\
`He recited the mantra in secret.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S170
exe

The adverb mɤsɤmdɤlain advance (example ex:masAmdAla.toNke ), related to the verb mdabe the time, might also be an ancient negative gerund, but its morphological structure is not completely clear, in particular the element -la and the absence of reduplication.

exe

nɤki tɤ-rɟit nɯ mɤsɤmdɤla ʑo to-ŋke \\
dem indef. poss -child dem in.advance emph ifr -walk \\
`This child started walking early.' (elicited)
exe

stɤ- Gerund
gerund
The Tibetan loan verb rɟɯɣrun has a regular gerund sɤ-rɟɯ rɟɯɣ `running'; however, the adverb stɤrɟɯɣrunning can also be derived from this verb, with a meaning identical to that of the gerund, as in ( ex:stArJWG ). In addition, the velar infinitive converb kɤ-rɟɯɣ can be used in the same contexts ( ex:kArJWG.kW.Zo, § sec:inf.converb ). It is the only verb with the prefix stɤ-; an exact cognate stɐrɟəɣʔ is found in Tshobdun.

exe

stɤrɟɯɣ nɤ stɤrɟɯɣ ʑo jo-nɯ-pʰɣo \\
running add running emph ifr - vert -flee \\
`She fled back home running.' (140504 huiguniang-zh)
exe
summary: The passage describes several adverbs derived from lexicalized gerunds whose forms and meanings are not fully predictable from their base verbs. It notes that some, such as *sɤ-xtɕɯ-xtɕi* ‘in childhood’ and *masɤrɯrju* ‘quietly, in secret,’ have meanings that have drifted beyond the normal simultaneous-function of gerunds, and that *mɤsɤmdɤla* ‘in advance’ may also be an ancient negative gerund though its structure is unclear. It also mentions the special prefix *stɤ-* with the Tibetan loan verb *rɟɯɣ*, where *stɤrɟɯɣ* forms an adverb meaning the same as the regular gerund, with a cognate in Tshobdun.

text:
converb!purposive
The purposive converb is used in clauses meaning `in order to', `for $X$ to $Y$', `so that $X$ does $Y$'. This converb originates from the oblique participle (§ sec:sigmatic.nmlz.history ). It combines the sɤ- / sɤz- with a reduplicated verb stem like the gerund, but in addition takes a B type orientation preverb preceded by a possessive prefix coreferent with a core argument, as for instance a-ɲɯ-sɤ-stɯ stu `in order for me to believe in it' from the semi-transitive stubelieve in ( ex:aYWsAstWstu ).

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ a-ɲɯ-sɤ-stɯ stu nɯra tu-nɤme pjɤ-ŋu \\
lnk dem 1sg - ipfv - purp -believe dem: pl ipfv -make[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`He was doing these things so that I would believe [his predictions].' (150904 yaoshu-zh) 0006394#S96
exe

Purposive converbs without reduplication are attested, for instance ɯ-mɤ-pjɯ-sɤ-sɯ-spoʁ from sɯspoʁpierce (the form with reduplication ɯ-mɤ-pjɯ-sɤ-sɯ-spɯ-spoʁ `so that it would not pierce it' is also possible) in ex:WmApjWsAsWspoR ) or without orientation preverb such as ɯ-mɤ-sɤ-jmɯ jmɯt `so that he would not forget it' from jmɯtforget in ( ex:WmAsAjmWjmWt ) (the complete form with orientation preverb is found in another version of the same story, for instance in ex:amAYWsAjmWjmWt.nWrkuta ).

exe

tɕe nɯ ɯ-pa nɯnɯ li kʰɤxtu nɯnɯ, tɯ-ci, tɯftsaʁ kɯ pjɯ-sɯ-spoʁ ŋgrɤl tɕe, tɕe ɯ-mɤ-pjɯ-sɤ-sɯ-spoʁ, nɯnɯtɕu tɤrɤm kɯ-fse ɲɯ́-wɣ-ta nɯmaʁnɤ cupa kɯ-fse ɲɯ́-wɣ-ta tɕe, \\
lnk dem 3sg. poss -under dem again platform dem indef. poss -water leaking.water erg ipfv - caus -have.a.hole be.usually.the.case: fact lnk lnk 3sg - neg - ipfv - conv: purp - caus -have.a.hole dem: loc topo sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv - inv -put otherwise flat.stone sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv - inv -put lnk \\
`Under the top platform, the water, the leaking water can leak through [the roof], and in order to prevent it from leaking through, people put planks or flat stones there.' (26-tChWra)
0003690#S11
exe

exe

[kɯ-lɤɣ acɤβ nɯ kɯ ɯ-mɤ-sɤ-jmɯ jmɯt], ɯ-pʰɯŋgɯ nɯ tɕu rdɤstaʁ-pɯpɯ tɕʰirdu ci ɲɤ-rku, \\
sbj: pcp -herd Askyabs dem erg 3sg - neg - purp: conv -forget 3sg. poss -inside.clothes dem loc stone-little pebble indef
ifr -put.in\\
`The shepherd Askyabs put a little pebble inside his clothes so that he would not forget [to tell it].' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

Purposive converbs are most commonly found with the negative prefix mɤ, as ( ex:WmApjWsAsWspoR ) and ( ex:WmAsAjmWjmWt ) above. Non-negative purposive converbs, as in ( ex:aYWsAstWstu ), are comparatively much rarer.

With transitive verbs, the possessive prefix can refer either to the subject (with 1sg possessive a- in ex:amAYWsAjmWjmWt.nWrkuta ) or the object ( 3sg possessive ɯ- in ex:WmAtusArpWrpu.pWphaBa ).

exe

jisŋi tɕe tɕendɤre a-mɤ-ɲɯ-sɤ-jmɯ jmɯt nɯ nɯ-rku-t-a ŋu \\
today lnk lnk 1sg - neg - purp: conv -forget dem aor -put-in- pst: tr - 1sg be: fact \\
`Today I put [the pebble in my clothes] so that I would not forget [to tell you].' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

In example ( ex:WmAtusArpWrpu.pWphaBa ), the purposive form a-mɤ-tu-sɤ-rpɯ rpu with subject indexation is also possible, without meaning difference.

exe

kɯm ɲɯ-mbɤr tɕe, a-ku ɯ-mɤ-tu-sɤ-rpɯ rpu pɯ-pʰaβ-a \\
door sens -low lnk 1sg. poss -head 3sg - neg - ipfv - conv: purp -bump aor -lower- 1sg \\
`As the door is low, I lowered my head so as not to bump on it.' (elicited)
exe

Although most examples of purposive converbs have the same subject as the main clause, this is not a syntactic constraint. In ( ex:amAkusAmtsWmstWG ), it is the object of the main clause kʰɯnadog that corresponds to the subject of the purposive clause. Furthermore, in ( ex:WmApjWsAsWspoR ) above, the subject and object of the purposive clause are not even arguments of the main clause.

exe

a-mɤ-ku-sɤ-mtsɯ mtsɯɣ ɯʑo kɯ kʰɯna ka-βraʁ \\
1sg - neg - ipfv - conv: purp -bite 3sg erg dog aor:3 -attach \\
`He tied up the dog so that it would not bite me.' (elicited)
exe

Purposive converbs, although they can be generated for most verbs without difficulty, are very rare in the corpus, and several alternative constructions are preferred to build purposive clauses (§ sec:purposive.clauses ).
summary:
The purposive converb is used in clauses meaning “in order to,” “for X to Y,” or “so that X does Y,” and it historically comes from the oblique participle. It is formed with sɤ- / sɤz- plus a reduplicated verb stem, often with a B-type orientation preverb and a possessive prefix coreferent with a core argument; however, reduplication or the orientation preverb may be absent in some forms.  

These converbs most commonly appear with the negative prefix mɤ, and with transitive verbs the possessive prefix may refer to either the subject or the object. Although purposive converbs usually have the same subject as the main clause, this is not required, and the construction is rare in the corpus, with other purposive strategies often preferred.

text:
converb!immediate perfective
The immediate perfective converb expresses that the action in the converbial clause is immediately followed by that in the main clause (`as soon as'). It is built by adding the B type orientation preverb and a tɯ- prefix (which may be historically related to the homophonous prefix of action nominals, see § sec:dental.nmlz.history ) and the verb stem I. It is the only verb form with a type B orientation preverb (which in all other cases occurs with imperfective TAM categories) that has a perfective value. The immediate converb cannot take any additional prefix, even possessive or negative prefixes.

Since there is a homophonous prefix tɯ- for second person (§ sec:intr.23 ), the immediate converb is formally identical to the second person singular (the intransitive 2sg and the transitive 2sg$ $3 forms) of the Imperfective for all verbs whose stem I and stem III are identical (all intransitive verbs and some transitive ones, § sec:stem3.form ). These forms are distinct in the case of transitive verbs with stem III alternation, as illustrated by tab:imm.converb.

The converbial clause can contain overt arguments, including absolutive arguments as in ( ex:YWtWRaR ) or transitive subjects marked with the ergative as in ( ex:pjWtWmto ).

exe

ɯ-pɯ ɲɯ-tɯ-ʁaʁ nɤ kumpɣɤtɕɯ jamar ma me \\
3sg. poss -child ipfv - conv: imm -hatch.out lnk sparrow about apart.from not.exist: fact \\
`Just after its chick has hatched, it is just [as big as] a sparrow.' (24-kWmu) 0003618#S85
exe

exe

tɯrme ra kɯ pjɯ-tɯ-mto ʑo sat-nɯ ɕti. \\
people pl erg ipfv - conv: imm -see emph kill: fact - pl be. aff: fact \\
`People kill it as soon as they see it.' (28-qapar)
0003720#S15
exe

exe

nɯ pjɯ-tɯ-βde ʑo tɯrme nɯ pjɯ-kɯ-si pjɤ-ŋgrɤl. \\
dem ipfv - conv: imm -throw emph person dem ipfv - genr:S/O-die ifr. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`As soon as one was thrown in there, one would die.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S154
exe

There is often coreference between the arguments of the converbial clause and those of the main clause. In ( ex:YWtWRaR ) and ( ex:pjWtWBde ), the subjects of the main clauses correspond to the intransitive subject and the object of the converbial clause, respectively. In ( ex:pjWtWmto ) above and ( ex:kutWndo ) below, both the subject and the object of the subordinate clauses are coreferent with those of the main clauses. Example ( ex:kutWndo ) also shows that immediate converbs can have non-third person subjects, though this is rare in the corpus.

exe

tɯtʰɯ ɲɯ-sɤ-ɕke tɕe, aʑo a-jaʁ ku-tɯ-ndo ʑo pɯ-nɯ-ɕlɯɣ-a \\
pot sens - prop -burn lnk 1sg 1sg. poss -hand ipfv - conv: imm -take emph aor - auto -drop- 1sg \\
`As the pot was burning hot, I dropped it as soon as I had grabbed it.' (elicited)
exe

There is however no strict syntactic constraint on subject or object coreference, as we also find examples where the subject of the converbial clause is not a participant of the main clause, such as ( ex:lutWfsoR ).

exe

lu-tɯ-fsoʁ ʑo qʰe tɯ-rɤma tu-ʑe ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
ipfv - conv: imm -be.clear emph lnk inf: II -work ipfv -begin[III] sens -be \\
`It starts working as soon as the day breaks.' (26-GZo)
0003668#S64
exe

This type of converbial clause is nearly always followed either by the emphatic ʑo (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ) and/or by a linker such as tɕe, qʰe ( ex:lutWfsoR ) or nɤ ( ex:YWtWRaR ).

The immediate converb commonly occurs in the corpus, but it is not the only way to express immediate succession. Several constructions have a very close meaning (§ sec:immediate.subsequence ), involving in particular the postposition ɕimɯmaimmediately after (§ sec:temporal.postpositions ).
summary:
The immediate perfective converb expresses that the event in the converbial clause is immediately followed by the event in the main clause, meaning ‘as soon as.’ It is formed with a type B orientation preverb, a tɯ- prefix, and verb stem I, and unlike other forms with type B preverbs, it has perfective meaning and cannot take additional prefixes such as possessive or negative ones.

It can include overt arguments, and while coreference between the converbial and main clauses is common, it is not strictly required; the converbial subject may even be unrelated to the main clause. This converb often appears with the emphatic ʑo and/or a linker, and although it is common, other constructions can also express immediate succession.

text:
The adverb nɯfsejust like that does not derive from a non-finite verb form, but rather has been lexicalized from the demonstrative nɯ (§ sec:anaphoric.demonstrative.pro ) with the 3sg form of the Factual Non-Past of fsebe like in manner clause from a serial verb construction (§ sec:svc.similative.verb ). The range of meanings of nɯfse is however not predictable from those of the base verb.

The main meaning of nɯfse is `just like that, for no particular reason' as in ( ex:nWfse.pjAsi ).

exe

tɯ-rdoʁ tɕʰi mɯ-pɯ-nnɯ-pe mɤ-xsi ma nɯnɯ nɯfse pjɤ-si \\
one-piece what neg - pst. ipfv - auto -be.good neg - genr:know lnk dem like.that ifr -die \\
`One [of them] died just like that, I don't know what went wrong.' (140510 wugui)
0003951#S51
exe

text:
morphology!defective verb verb!defective
Nearly all Japhug verbs have participles, infinitives and the other non-finite forms described in this chapter. There is however a handful of defective verbs lacking non-finite categories.

The sensory existential verbs ɣɤʑuexist and maŋenot exist, which present other types of irregularities (§ sec:intr.person.irregular ), lack all non-finite forms; the nominalized forms of the existential verbs tuexist and menot exist are used instead.

The transitive verb kɤtɯpatell cannot be prefixed (§ sec:irregular.transitive ), and therefore lacks all non-finite forms.

The verb mɤ-xsione does not know is only found in the generic negative Factual Non-Past (§ sec:irregular.transitive ), and the corresponding non-finite forms are provided by the verb sɯzknow.
summary: Most Japhug verbs have participles, infinitives, and other non-finite forms, but a small number of defective verbs lack these categories. The sensory existential verbs ɣɤʑuexist and maŋenot exist have no non-finite forms, so the nominalized forms of tuexist and menot exist are used instead; the transitive verb kɤtɯpatell also lacks non-finite forms because it cannot be prefixed. The verb mɤ-xsione does not know occurs only in the generic negative Factual Non-Past, and its non-finite forms are supplied by sɯzknow.

text: The great majority of non-finite verb forms studied in this chapter take either a velar, a sigmatic or a dental prefix. While it is necessary to distinguish many sub-categories from a synchronic point, it is equally obvious that a diachronic relationship exists between some of these non-finite forms. While a complete account of the history of nominalized forms in Japhug will have to wait a proper reconstruction of proto-Gyalrongic, it is nevertheless possible to offer some preliminary thoughts on the relationship between these morphological categories.
summary: Most of the non-finite verb forms discussed in this chapter use a velar, sigmatic, or dental prefix. Although many subcategories must be distinguished synchronically, some of these forms also appear to be historically related. A full history of Japhug nominalized forms will require reconstruction of Proto-Gyalrongic, but the passage offers some preliminary observations on how these morphological categories may be connected.

text:
morphology!Trans-Himalayan comparison
infinitive!velar participle!origin

Many Trans-Himalayan languages, including Karbi and Kiranti, have productive velar nominalization prefixes, and traces of such prefixes can also be found in other languages such as Tibetan. These forms are very probably historically related to the velar nominalization prefixes found in Gyalrong languages, but the present chapter focuses on Gyalrong-internal evidence.

In Japhug, non-finite verb forms with velar prefixes include the following ones:

itemize
kɯ- subject participles (§ sec:subject.participles )
kɤ- object participles (§ sec:object.participle )
kɯ- and kɤ- velar infinitives (§ sec:velar.inf )
Infinitival converbs (§ sec:inf.converb )
x-/ɣ- deverbal nouns (§ sec:G.nmlz )
itemize

In addition, three finite prefixes are likely to be related to these forms: the 2 1 kɯ- prefix (§ sec:indexation.local, § sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history ), the generic S/O kɯ- prefix (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ), and the circumfix kɯ-...-ci occurring in several morphological contexts (§ sec:peg.circumfix ).

Given the difficulty of distinguishing infinitives from participles even synchronically (§ sec:infinitives.participles ), it is quite obvious that these forms are ultimately related, but accounting for the precise distribution of the forms is not trivial.

In addition to the categories mentioned above, shared by all core Gyalrong languages, Situ has a type of semi-finite participles in kə, used in various types of relative clauses. In ( ex:nEkEmaSentS ) for instance, the form nǝ-kǝ-maʃe-ntʃ has both a participle kə- and a dual suffix -ntʃ; in Japhug, such combination is impossible: indexation suffixes (and the second person prefix tɯ- ) are incompatible with all non-finite forms studied in this chapter.

`The two hardworking ones then became rather rich.'

In the following, I assume that in proto-Gyalrong both semi-finite participles of the type exemplified in ( ex:nEkEmaSentS ) and subject participles as in Japhug (§ sec:subject.participles ) did exist, and were marked by the ancestor of the kɯ- prefix.

The object participle in kɤ, which is synchronically still homophonous with the subject participle of a passivized transitive verb (§ sec:object.participle.ambiguity ), likely originates from the fusion of the *kə- participle with the passive *ŋa- prefix (see also for a suggestion in the same lines).

Since only transitive verbs can have a passive form, the use of the object for semi-transitive verbs (for instance example ex:stu.jikArga in § sec:object.participle.relatives ) must have been an analogical extension occurring after the merger of the participle prefix and the passive was complete.

The kɤ- infinitive possible derives from the object participles. The pivot construction where such a reanalysis could have taken place is the object of verbs of perception such as mtosee. When an object participial clause occurs as the object of a verb of perception, while in some case there is no ambiguity (as in ex:pWkAsAt.nW.kAmto ), in examples such as ( ex:kAntsGe.nW.mWpWmtota ) it is possible to analyze the kɤ- prefixed form either as an object participle (entailing a translation `grains that are sold like that') or as an infinitive (`selling grains like that', referring to the whole action rather than the object).

reanalysis
After such reanalysis took, the kɤ- infinitive, originally restricted to transitive verbs, was extended to dynamic intransitive verbs.

The nominalization x/ɣ- prefix is probably the result of the application of a sound law of presyllable reduction on monosyllables without initial cluster (§ sec:velar.class.prefix, § sec:G.nmlz ) to the subject participle prefix. The regular kɯ- subject participle on monosyllabic clusterless verb stems is due to the analogical generalization of the kɯ- allomorph to all verb forms.

The generic kɯ- and the 2 1 kɯ- prefixes, which occur in finite verb forms in Japhug, are less likely to come from subject participles. Instead, as argued in and § sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history, they are traces of the semi-finite participles in Japhug and other Northern Gyalrong languages.

fig:velar.nmlz.history summarizes the pathways of reanalysis proposed in this section and in § sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history. The semi-finite participle and subject participle forms are without doubt historically related, but both have to be reconstructed at the proto-Gyalrong level and the function of the original prefix from which they derive is unclear -- it is conceivable that the original prefix was completely non-finite like the Japhug subject participle, and that the semi-finite participle is an innovation (on the addition of person indexation markers on non-verbal predicative words, see § sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history ), but the opposite is equally possible.
summary:
The passage argues that many velar prefixes in Gyalrong languages are historically related, with Japhug non-finite forms such as subject participles, object participles, infinitives, converbs, and deverbal nouns all likely descending from earlier velar nominalization morphology. It proposes that the Japhug kɤ- infinitive probably arose by reanalysis of object participles in perception-object constructions, and that the x-/ɣ- nominalizer and some finite kɯ- prefixes reflect further historical developments from older participial or semi-finite forms.

The author also notes that proto-Gyalrong likely had both semi-finite participles and subject participles marked by an ancestor of kɯ-, though the exact original function of that prefix remains unclear.

text:
participle!origin gerund participle!oblique converb!purposive
Nominalized forms involving a coronal fricative prefix, or a trace thereof, have been described in Old Chinese (, ), Tibetan and Jinghpo.

In Japhug, non-finite verb forms with dental fricative prefixes are very widespread, and include the following ones:

itemize
Oblique participle (§ sec:oblique.participle )
Gerund (§ sec:gerund )
Purposive (§ sec:purposive.converb )
itemize

It is quite obvious that both gerund and purposive converbs derive from the oblique participle. The reduplication found in these forms (optional in the case of the purposive, see ex:WmApjWsAsWspoR in § sec:purposive.converb ) presumably reflects the emphatic reduplication (§ sec:emph.redp ) that can be applied to nearly all verb forms.

While derivation of gerunds from oblique participle is not a problem from a formal point of view, the exact pathway of reanalysis deserves some discussion. Given the fact that oblique participles are used to build temporal relatives `the time when...' (§ sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ), it is tempting to suppose that the gerund derives from this function, in absolutive locative form (§ absolutive.locative ). In this view, a gerund like sɤ-ɤmdzɯ mdzɯ `sitting' would come from an original construction meaning `at the time when $X$ was sitting'. However, this hypothesis is difficult, because of the very restricted nature of participial temporal relatives, which are only found for very specific time periods that belong to common knowledge (for instance ɯ-sɤ-ji `the period when it is planted' in example ex:WsAji in § sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ), and are not compatible with most types of temporal clauses.

Other possibilities to explain the origin of the gerund include the locative (§ sec:locative.participle.relatives ) and instrumental (§ sec:instrumental.participle.relatives ) uses of the oblique participles. Locative participles could account for the use of gerund with psychological verbs; for instance sɤ-mɯ mu `fearing' from mufear could originate from a metaphorical locative similar to English `in fear'. However, the hypothesis that gerunds derive from instrumental oblique participles is more probable due to the optional presence of the ergative kɯ with the gerunds (§ sec:gerund.clauses ) while locative postpositions are never found in this context. The gerunds thus probably originated from subordinate clauses expressing reason or cause, from which they came to express manner or simultaneous action (`by sitting' $ $ `sitting').

The purposive converbs probably also come from the instrumental use of oblique participles, but through a different pathway. As suggested in, examples such as ( ex:tWthW.sAXtCi ) may constitute the pivot construction between instrumental participial relatives and purposive converbs.

ɣzɯtʰɯz nɯ kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe [tɯtʰɯ sɤ-χtɕi] ɲɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-pʰɯt pɯ-ŋgrɤl \\
Selaginella dem in.the.past lnk pan obl: pcp -wash ipfv - inv - auto -uproot pst. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`In the past, people would dig up Selaginella [to use as] a pan cleaner.' (16-RlWmsWsi)

In ( ex:tWthW.sAXtCi ), the participial relative clause tɯtʰɯ sɤ-χtɕi `pan cleaner' is an essive adjunct (in absolutive form, § sec:essive.abs ) which can be translated as `(to use) as a pan cleaner'. This meaning is very close to that of a purposive clause `in order to clean pans'. An instrumental participial relative clause in essive function could thus easily be reanalyzed as a purposive clause, and hence the oblique participle as a purposive converbal.
summary: The passage explains that Japhug has several widespread non-finite verb forms with dental fricative prefixes, including the oblique participle, gerund, and purposive converb, and argues that the latter two derive from the oblique participle. It suggests that gerunds probably arose from instrumental participial clauses that were reanalyzed from subordinate clauses of cause or manner, while purposive converbs likely developed through a similar pathway, perhaps via a pivot construction in which an essive participial relative clause was reinterpreted as expressing purpose.

text:
infinitive!dental nominalization!degree nominalization!action converb!immediate perfective
Non-finite verbal forms taking a dental stop prefix tɯ- or tɤ- in Japhug include the following ones:

itemize
Dental infinitive (§ sec:dental.inf )
Degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominals )
tɯ- action nominals (§ sec:action.nominals )
tɤ- abstract nouns (§ sec:tA.abstract.nouns )
Simultaneous action nominal (§ sec:simultaneous.action.nominal )
Immediate perfective converb (§ sec:immediate.converb )
itemize

It is possible that all of these forms are historically related. However, given the fact that some of the non-finite verb forms in Japhug are inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ) derived by adding a possessive prefix to the bare verb stem (bare infinitives § sec:bare.inf and bare action nominals § sec:bare.action.nominals ), it is likely that at least some of the categories listed above originate from the indefinite possessive form of a bare infinitive or a bare action nominal, as suggested in concerning the bare infinitives.

Since bare infinitives and dental infinitives are in complementary distribution, the former being used with transitive verbs and the latter with intransitive ones (see § sec:bare.inf.complement and § sec:dental.inf.complement ), it is legitimate to consider the possibility that both forms go back to a single category. The bare infinitive takes a possessive prefix that is coreferent with the object of the verb; intransitive verbs lack an object (semi-transitive verbs have a semi-object § sec:semi.object, but its morphosyntactic properties are different from those of canonical objects), and thus if a bare infinitive were built from an intransitive verb, one would only have three choices: (i) index the subject, (ii) use the bare stem with any possessive prefix or (iii) use a `dummy' possessive prefix indicating the absence of object. It is possible to argue that dental infinitives correspond to solution (iii), and that the tɯ- prefix in this form is the indefinite possessor tɯ- (§ sec:indef.genr.poss ). In this hypothesis, dental infinitives taking a possessive prefix (see example ex:tWtAmdzW.kWBdi in § sec:dental.inf.complement ) are later creations, made after the etymological origin of the tɯ- had become obscured.

Proposing that tɯ- action nominals and tɤ- abstract nouns come from alienabilized bare action nominals is not to be excluded, but appears to be less compelling, since there is no complementary distribution between the former and the latter, unlike in the case of bare vs. dental infinitives.

It is also conceivable that dental infinitives come from tɯ- action nominals, and bare infinitives from bare action nominals, respectively. In the absence of evidence from languages other than Japhug, I leave this issue unresolved.

Regardless of the origin of action nominals, it is clear that degree nominals on the one hand, and simultaneous action nominals on the other hand, derive from them by prefixing possessive prefixes (in degree nominals) and the numeral tɯ- prefix, respectively (in simultaneous action nominal, § sec:simultaneous.action.nominal ).

The origin of the immediate perfective converbs is quite puzzling. While immediate converb take an obligatory type B orientation preverb, no other tɯ- non-finite form is compatible with orientation preverbs, and moreover type B prefixes normally occur with imperfective TAME categories (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs, § sec:preverb.TAME ). It is conceivable that these converbs ultimately originate from action nominals, but the pathway of morphological evolution that has lead to their creation is unclear.

fig:dental.nmlz.history summarizes the hypotheses presented in this section; the dotted arrows represent uncertain derivations.
summary: The passage explains that several Japhug non-finite verbal forms share a dental prefix tɯ- or tɤ-, including dental infinitives, degree nominals, action nominals, abstract nouns, simultaneous action nominals, and immediate perfective converbs, and suggests they may be historically related. It argues that dental infinitives may come from an indefinite possessive form of bare infinitives, while the origins of action nominals and abstract nouns are less certain; degree nominals and simultaneous action nominals clearly derive from action nominals, but the origin of immediate perfective converbs remains unclear.

text: Japhug has much fewer valency-increasing derivations than valency-decreasing ones: leaving aside fossil derivations (§ sec:marginal.derivations ), only four clearly identified prefixes are found: sigmatic causative (§ sec:sig.causative ), velar causative (§ sec:velar.causative ), applicative (§ sec:applicative ) and tropative (§ sec:tropative ). The sigmatic causative however is probably the most productive of all derivational processes in Japhug, and can be combined with the other three (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain, § sec:sig.caus.other.derivations, § sec:appl.other.derivations, § sec:velar.caus.other ).
summary: Japhug has relatively few valency-increasing derivations compared with valency-decreasing ones, and apart from fossilized forms, only four clearly identified prefixes are found: the sigmatic causative, velar causative, applicative, and tropative. Among these, the sigmatic causative is probably the most productive derivational process in the language and can combine with the other three.

text:
causative!sigmatic
Despite the existence of periphrastic causative constructions (§ sec:sWpa.sABzu ), the main morphosyntactic device to express causation in Japhug is the causative verbal derivation by dental or alveolo-palatal fricative prefixes, referred to as `sigmatic' causative in this work.
summary: Although Japhug has periphrastic causative constructions, its main morphosyntactic way of expressing causation is through causative verbal derivation. This derivation uses dental or alveolo-palatal fricative prefixes, which the text calls the “sigmatic” causative.

text:
causative!allomorphy morphology!allomorphy allomorphy!causative
Although not as complex as the causative derivations in Stodsde or in Khroskyabs, the sigmatic causative prefix is the derivation with the greatest number of allomorphs in Japhug.

It has five regular allomorphs sɯ, sɯɣ, z, s- and sɤ- depending on the following element, and a number of irregular ones (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular ). The allomorph sɯ- occurs in most environments, and can be considered to be the default form.

z- allomorph
The z- allomorph appears in non-monosyllabic verb bases, when the first syllable (generally a derivational prefix, or a synchronically non-analysable prefixal element belonging to the verb root) has a sonorant initial (in practice only mV, nV, ɣV- or rV- ). tab:causative.z illustrates some examples of this allomorph.

On the other hand, monosyllabic verbs with single sonorant initials, whether nasals, rhotics or semi-vowels, never select the z- allomorph. Monosyllabic bases with these initials take the allomorph sɯ- (§ sec:caus.sWG ): nodrive and marsmear have the causative forms sɯnomake/let drive, `drive with' and sɯmarmake/let smear, not $ $ zno and $ $ zmar. The same constraint on monosyllabicity is observed with the regular s- allomorph (§ sec:caus.s.allomorph ), but does not apply to the irregular vowel-less allomorphs of the causative ( ɕ- § sec:caus.C, ʑ- § sec:caus.Z, and j- § sec:caus.j ).

Intransitive bases with nasal (except ŋ- ), rhotic and semi-vowel initial consonants select the sɯɣ- allomorph, as illustrated by jɤɣfinish, rulook at and ɲobe prepared, whose sigmatic causative forms are sɯɣjɤɣfinish, sɯɣrumake/let look at and sɯɣɲoprepare, respectively.

In the case of intransitive verbs with the velar sonorant ɣ, the allomorph sɯ- occurs. For instance, ɣicome has the causative form sɯɣeinvite (with irregular ablaut, § sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ).

Causative verbs with the z- allomorph in irregular contexts are discussed in § sec:sig.caus.irregular.other.
s- allomorph
The s- allomorph is only found with base verbs whose first syllable is qa- ( tab:causative.sqa ). All of these verbs are intransitive; it is unclear whether this qa- element is analyzable as a prefix historically.

Monosyllabic verbs with initial q- always select the sɯ- allomorph. For example, the causative of qaʁpeel is sɯqaʁmake peel, not $ $ sqaʁ.
summary:
The sigmatic causative prefix in Japhug has the greatest number of allomorphs among causative derivations, with five regular forms: sɯ, sɯɣ, z, s-, and sɤ-, plus irregular forms. The default allomorph is sɯ-, while z- appears in non-monosyllabic verb bases whose first syllable begins with a sonorant, and sɯɣ- occurs with intransitive bases beginning with nasal, rhotic, or semi-vowel consonants; monosyllabic sonorant-initial verbs instead take sɯ-.  

The s- allomorph is restricted to verbs whose first syllable is qa-, and all such verbs are intransitive. Monosyllabic verbs with initial q- do not take s-, but instead use the default sɯ- allomorph.

text:
With verbs whose stem begins in a- (contracting verbs, § sec:contraction ), the sigmatic causative prefix merges with this vowel as sɤ, as shown in tab:causative.sA. In the glosses, this vowel merger is represented as sɯ-ɤ, following the orthographic rules in (§ sec:contraction ). Only one contracting verb has an irregular causative with intrusive -ɣ- (§ sec:caus.sAG ).

There are two irregular causative verbs in sɤ, whose base verb is not a contracting verb (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ).

sɯɣ- allomorph
For all other types of verb stem, the choice between the sɯ- and sɯɣ-/sɯx- allomorphs depends on both phonology and morphology. The sɯɣ-/sɯx- allomorphs occur when the base verb is intransitive, monosyllabic, has no initial cluster and no velar or uvular initial consonant, while sɯ- appears in all other cases, in particular in all bases with consonant clusters.

With the intransitive verb ʁaʁhatch (the only verb with the single ʁ- onset), some speakers (such as Tshendzin ) select the sɯɣ- allomorph and use the causative form sɯɣʁaʁcause to hatch ( ex:nWnWsWGRaRa ) with an internal -ɣʁ- cluster (§ sec:heterosyllabic.clusters ), while other speakers select the sɯ- allomorph.

lnk dem aor: east -bring- 1sg lnk lnk aor - auto - caus -hatch- 1sg \\
`I brought [the eggs] and made them hatch by myself (without a hen).' (150819 kumpGa)

tab:causative.sW illustrates the correlation between the sɯ- / sɯɣ-/sɯx- contrast and transitivity. The intrusive -ɣ- element undergoes regressive voice assimilation to -x- when the initial of the verb root is unvoiced.

The intrusive -ɣ- also appears in one of the irregular allomorphs of the sigmatic causative (§ sec:caus.CWG ).

Other derivational prefixes, including the velar causative ɣɤ- (§ sec:allomorphy.applicative ), the applicative nɯ- (§ sec:allomorphy.applicative ), the tropative nɤ- (§ sec:tropative.allomorphy ), the proprietive sɤ- (§ sec:proprietive.allomorphy ) and some denominal derivations (§ sec:denom.sW.caus.instr ), present an allomorphy involving the insertion of the -ɣ- element, originally in the same context as that of the sɯɣ- allomorph of the sigmatic causative. However, in the case of the proprietive and tropative derivation, this -ɣ- insertion has ceased to be productive.
summary:
With contracting verbs whose stems begin in a-, the sigmatic causative prefix merges with the stem vowel to form sɤ, and this merger is represented in glosses as sɯ-ɤ; one contracting verb also has an irregular causative with intrusive -ɣ-. For other verbs, the choice between sɯ- and sɯɣ-/sɯx- depends on phonological and morphological factors: the sɯɣ-/sɯx- allomorphs occur especially with intransitive, monosyllabic verbs lacking initial clusters and velar/uvular initials, while sɯ- appears elsewhere, particularly with cluster-initial stems.

The intrusive -ɣ- assimilates to -x- after unvoiced initials, and some speakers vary in their choice of allomorph, as shown with the verb ʁaʁ ‘hatch.’ Similar -ɣ- insertion is found in other

text:
causative!allomorphy morphology!allomorphy
In addition to the regular allomorphs described in the previous section, the sigmatic causative has five irregular allomorphs with alveolo-palatal or palatal consonants instead of alveolar fricatives: ɕɯ, ɕɯɣ, ɕ, ʑ- and j-. All known examples are presented in tab:causative.irregular.

ɕɯ- allomorph
The ɕɯ- allomorph is the most common of all alveolo-palatal allomorphs. It occurs on verb bases with initial clusters with nasal, f- or r- preinitials, contexts where the regular sɯ- allomorph would be expected (§ sec:caus.sWG ). The only clusterless verb root which selects the ɕɯ- allomorph is the orphan verb ŋgɯ in the complex predicate tɤ-mbrɯ+ŋgɯget angry (§ sec:orphan.verb ).

The ɕɯ- allomorph derives causatives mainly from intransitive verbs, except for rŋoborrow (with the inversive causative ɕɯrŋolend, § sec:sig.caus.inversive ) and fkaβcover (which has the instrumental causative ɕɯfkaβcover with, § sec:sig.caus.instrumental ).

The base verb ɴqoʁhang has three causative forms, ɕɯ-ɴqoʁ (for the most common meaning corresponding to transitive `hang'), ʑ-ɴɢoʁ
(with a more restricted meaning, § sec:caus.Z ) and the regular sɯ-ɴqoʁ for instrumental (`hang with') or indirect causation.

ɕɯɣ- allomorph
The verb mube afraid has the causative ɕɯɣmufrighten, the only example of the ɕɯɣ- allomorph of the sigmatic causative. The intrusive -ɣ- is expected since the base verb is intransitive and has a labial initial consonant with no cluster (§ sec:caus.sWG ), and appears in other derivations such as applicative ( nɯɣmube afraid of, § sec:allomorphy.applicative ) and proprietive ( sɤɣmube frightening, § sec:proprietive.allomorphy ).

ɕ- allomorph
The ɕ- allomorph is one of the three irregular vowel-less allomorphs of the causative. It occurs on two monosyllabic verbs, ɕpʰɣoflee with An alternative form ɕɯpʰɣo with the ɕɯ- allomorph is also attested. (from pʰɣoflee) and ɕlɯɣdrop (from lɯɣget loose), unlike the vowel-less regular allomorphs z- and s- which are never found on monosyllabic bases (§ sec:caus.z, § sec:caus.s.allomorph ). The contrast between ɕ- and ʑ- is not determined by the voicing of the initial consonant of the base verb (since lɯɣget loose has a sonorant initial l- ). Rather, ʑ- exclusively occurs with voiced prenasalized obstruents (§ sec:caus.Z ), and j- derives from ɕ- by a recent sound change (§ sec:caus.j ).

Like other irregular allomorphs, ɕ- is not restricted to one particular sub-function of the sigmatic causative. The verb ɕpʰɣoflee with, `help $X$ flee with oneself' reflects the adjutative function of causative (§ sec:sig.caus.adjutative ), indexing as direct object the entity helped by the subject, as shown by the 3sg 2pl configuration in ( ex:ajAtWwGCphGonW ).

ʑ- allomorph
The ʑ- allomorph of the causative is only attested with verb bases having prenasalized onsets. In each of the three verbs, the meaning of the prefix is slightly different.

The causative ʑmbriplay (an instrument), `make noise with' from the intransitive mbricry, sing, `make noise', is a plain instrumental causative (§ sec:sig.caus.instrumental ), which selects as object the musical instrument (see for instance ex:taZmbri, § sec:absolutive.P ), while ʑŋgahelp wearing, `make/force to wear' (from the transitive ŋgawear) reflects the adjutative (§ sec:sig.caus.adjutative ) function rather than the instrumental one, since it selects as object the person wearing the clothes (the 3du object indexation in ex:tuwWGZngandZi ), while the clothes are a semi-object ( tɯ-ŋga nɯra ɯ-mbe tʰɯ-kɯ-ɴɢraʁ nɯra `old and torn clothes', without ergative marking).

The causative ʑɴɢoʁ from ɴqoʁhang (vi) presents an irregular voicing of the onset, possibly the effect of a phonotactic constraint against clusters comprising a preinitial fricative with a unvoiced prenasalized obstruent such as *ɕɴq, since only voiced prenasalized obstruents are monophonemic (§ sec:consonant.phonemes ).

The meaning of ʑɴɢoʁ is not completely predictable from that of the base verb ɴqoʁhang. summary:
The sigmatic causative has five irregular allomorphs with alveolo-palatal or palatal consonants: ɕɯ, ɕɯɣ, ɕ, ʑ-, and j-. These allomorphs occur in specific phonological environments and on particular verb bases, with ɕɯ- being the most common and used mainly with intransitive verbs, while the rare ɕɯɣ- appears only with *mube* `afraid`.  

The ɕ- allomorph occurs on two monosyllabic verbs and can express different causative functions, including adjutative and non-volitional causation; ʑ- is limited to bases with prenasalized onsets and shows meaning differences across the few verbs that take it. The verb *ɴqoʁ* `hang` illustrates irregularity in that it has three causative forms with distinct meanings,

j- allomorph
In the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug, the verb tsʰidrink has the irregular causative form jtsʰigive to drink with the j- allomorph. In dialects of Japhug which have not undergone the tʰi tsʰi sound change, the base verb is tʰi and its causative ɕtʰi with the ɕ- allomorph (§ sec:caus.C ). This suggests that a sound change *ɕtsʰ- jtsʰ- took place in this word by dissimilation of mode of articulation (§ sec:shC.clusters ).

The causative jtsʰigive to drink is highly lexicalized, and can occur as input for other derivations such as antipassive (§ sec:sig.caus.other.derivations, § sec:antipassive.ditransitive ). The regular causative sɯ-tsʰi can be used with a neutral factitive meaning `make drink' ( ex:qajW.smAnba.kAsWtshi ) or in the instrumental function `drink with/using' (§ sec:sig.caus.instrumental ).

It also discusses an irregular causative form in the Kamnyu dialect, where *tsʰi* “drink” becomes *jtsʰi* “give to drink,” reflecting a sound change by dissimilation, and says this form is highly lexicalized and can serve as input to other derivations. By contrast, the regular causative *sɯ-tsʰi* has a more general factitive meaning “make drink” or an instrumental meaning “drink with/using.”

summary: The causative verb **sɯxɕesend** (from **ɕego**) has a stem II form **sɤɣri**, which is derived from the base verb’s stem II **ari**. This form seems to reflect a merger of the **sɯɣ-** allomorph with the **a-** prefixal element as **sɤɣ**, while retaining the **-ɣ-** element, rather than the expected **sɤri**.

The sɤ- allomorph (§ sec:caus.sA ) is found on two bases with contracting a-: pebe good and rmibe called, whose corresponding causative forms are sɤpedo well and sɤrmigive a name (§ sec:semi.transitive.causative ), respectively. In the case of sɤrmi, this irregularity is a clue that it is in fact a denominal verb derived from the noun tɤ-rminame by the causative denominal (§ sec:sW.caus.history ), rather than a causative directly derived from the intransitive verb rmibe called.

The causative verb sɯɣeinvite from ɣicome has the expected allomorph sɯ, but presents ablaut ( ɣi ɣe ) with the same vowel alternation as that of stem II (§ sec:stem2.form ). This is a trace of a vowel alternation system which used to be more widespread, and is better preserved in Zbu and some varieties of Situ.

a- / z- alternation
Verbs whose stem has three or more syllables, whose initial syllable is a- followed by a prefixal syllable with a sonorant initial such as ɣɯ/ɣɤ- or rɯ/rɤ, have sigmatic causative forms with deletion of the a- element rather than regular vowel fusion (§ sec:caus.sA ). For instance, the causative of arɤtsʰibe cooked like rice gruel is zrɤtsʰicook like rice gruel instead of expected $ $ sɤrɤtsʰi.

Other pairs of the same type include aɣɯrɯruthat can be done at the same time as / zɣɯrɯrudo at the same time as, arɤtɕʰabe determined from / zrɤtɕʰadetermine from (see examples ex:pe.mApe.arAtCha and ex:rtaR.mArtaR.zrAtCha, § sec:multiclausal.complements ) and aɣɯŋgɯŋgɯhave a lot of layers / zɣɯŋgɯŋgɯput on a lot of layers.

Some of the verbs with this a/z- alternation are transparently denominal verbs with the compound prefixes arɤ- (§ sec:denom.arA ) and aɣɯ- (§ sec:denom.aGW.caus ).
summary: The passage describes several irregular causative formations, especially cases where the sigmatic causative appears as infixed or replaces part of the stem rather than following the regular pattern. It notes that some forms, such as sɤrmigive a name and sɯɣeinvite, preserve traces of older derivational or vowel-alternation patterns, and that verbs with longer stems beginning in a- plus a sonorant-initial prefix often show an a-/z- alternation with deletion of the a- element.

The secundative verb nɯsɯkʰorob, extort, is the lexicalized autive (§ sec:autoben.lexicalized ) of the causative sɯkʰocause to give of the indirective verb kʰogive (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ). This derivation dates back to the common ancestor of Northern Gyalrong languages, as shown by the Tshobdun cognate nsəkʰi `snatch away'. The original meaning of nɯsɯkʰo was presumably `$X$ causes $Y$ to give $Z$ to himself$_i$', its grammatical subject being thus originally both agent (causer) and recipient at the same time, reflecting the inversive function of the causative (§ sec:ditransitive.causative, § sec:sig.caus.inversive ).

The transitive subject, object and dative arguments of kʰo correspond to the object, semi-object and subject of nɯsɯkʰo, respectively. Example ( ex:YWkWnWsWkhoa ) shows this verb with 2 1sg indexation, with a meaning that can still be interpreted as `you cause me to give it to you'.

It gives examples of causatives that have shifted meanings, such as z-nɯna meaning both ‘let rest’ and more commonly ‘stop,’ sɯqaʁ meaning ‘delimit the boundaries of,’ and nɯsɯkʰo ‘extort,’ which historically derived from a causative with an inversive function. causative!sigmatic causative!intransitive verb
The causative derivation increases the valency of the base verb by one argument. In the case of intransitive bases, the resulting verb is monotransitive. The intransitive subject of the base verb corresponds to the object of the causative verb. For instance, in ( ex:kutasAnbaR ) the causative verb sɤnbaʁhide (vt) (from the intransitive anbaʁhide (vi), ex:kanbaRa ) takes the portmanteau prefix 1 2 ta- (§ sec:indexation.local ), indexing the person hiding as object, and the causer (the person helping him/her, § sec:sig.caus.adjutative ) as transitive subject.

summary: The causative derivation adds one argument to the base verb’s valency, so when it is formed from an intransitive verb, the result is monotransitive. In such cases, the original intransitive subject becomes the object of the causative verb, while the causer functions like the subject of a normal transitive verb, including ergative marking when overt.

text:
causative!sigmatic causative!transitive verb
The causativization of monotransitive verbs The causativization of semi-transitive and ditransitive verbs is discussed in § sec:semi.transitive.causative and § sec:ditransitive.causative, and is not repeated here. is more complicated. While the causer is always treated like a transitive subject in terms of indexation, ergative marking and relativization (§ sec:ditransitive.causative ), the status of the causee (corresponding to the transitive subject of the base verb) and of the patientive argument (object of the base verbs) are less straightforward.

From the point of view of indexation (§ sec:ditransitive.causative ), both causees ( ex:pjWkWsWfCatandZi ) and patientive arguments ( ex:tAkWsWRndWa ) can be indexed as direct objects (in these examples with 2 1sg configurations, § sec:indexation.local ).

The indexation of these verbs is determined by a person hierarchy: when the causee (or patientive) is first/second person, and the patientive (or causee) is third person, the causative verb takes first/second object indexation (§ sec:ditransitive.causative ).

From the point of view of case marking, patientive arguments never take the ergative, while causees can take it optionally (§ sec:causee.kW ). In example ( ex:kW.pjAsWGWtnW ), the first causee ɕɤɣpɣa `bird sp.' in left-dislocated position has no ergative marking, while the second one qajdocrow takes it (note that the plural indexation on pjɤ-sɯ-ɣɯt-nɯ shows that qajdo is causee and not causer).

Both causees and patientive arguments can be indexed as direct objects, with their indexation determined by a person hierarchy, and patientive arguments never take ergative marking while causees may do so optionally.

summary: The passage describes a special subtype of semi-reflexive indexation in causative forms derived from transitive verbs. When the dual or plural marker includes both causer and causee, the number suffix indexes the two participants together, as in a 3du causative form where the dual ending refers to both the wife and her husband.

text:
The relative position of the negative and causative prefixes in the prefixal chain is fixed (§ sec:prefixal.chain ) and independent of the semantic scope. The same is true of associated motion prefixes (§ sec:sig.caus.AM ). Thus, a negative causative verb can be either interpreted as `not cause to $X$' or as `cause not to $X$' (prohibition). For instance, mɤ-sɯx-ɕe-nɯ ( neg - caus -go: fact - pl ) can either mean `they don't send him/them' or `they prevent/forbid/don't let him/them go' as in ( ex:mAkWspa.mAsWXCenW ).

exe

nɯ ɕɤmɯɣdɯɣ kɤ-lɤt kɯ-mkʰɤz nɯra ra ma mɤ-kɯ-spa nɯra mɤ-sɯx-ɕe-nɯ. \\
dem gun inf -release sbj: pcp -be.expert dem: pl be.needed: fact lnk neg - sbj: pcp -be.able dem: pl neg - caus -go: fact - pl \\
`They need people who are good at shooting with guns, they don't let those who are not able (to shoot) go.' (150829 KAGWcAno)
0006420#S13
exe

The negative verb form mɯ-pa-sɯ-pʰɯt ( neg -pfv:3 - caus -take.off) an also either mean `he did not make him/them destroy it' or `he prevented him/them from destroying it', as in ( ex:mWpasWphWt ).

exe

ɣʑo ɯ-kʰo ta-fsraŋ nɯnɯ, [ɯ-pi ni mɯ-pa-sɯ-pʰɯt] ra ɣɯ, ɣʑo ra ɣɯ nɯ-rɟɤlpu nɯ jo-ɣi. \\
bee 3sg. poss -house aor:3 -protect dem 3sg. poss -elder.sibling du neg -pfv:3 - caus -take.off pl gen bee pl gen 3pl. poss -king dem ifr -come \\
`The king of the bees whose hive he had protected and prevented his brothers from destroying came.' (140510 fengwang-zh)
0003939#S129
exe

Another possible interpretation of the combination of causative and negative prefixes is `make sure $X$ does not need to $Y$', `take care of $X$ and ensure $Y$ does not need to happen' (where $X$ represents the causee and $Y$ the base verb), as in ( amApWtWsqlWtnW ).

exe

a-mu rcanɯ ndʑu tɯ-ldʑa cinɤ a-mɤ-pɯ-tɯ-sɯ-qlɯt-nɯ ra \\
mother unexp: deg chopsticks one-stick even irr - neg - pfv -2- caus -break- pl be.needed: fact \\
`Make sure that my mother does not even need to break chopsticks.' (an idiomatic expression meaning ``please take care of my mother's every need'', 2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S207
exe

The same type of ambiguity is also found with the velar causative (§ sec:velar.causative.negation ).
summary: The passage says that the order of the negative and causative prefixes in the prefix chain is fixed and does not determine semantic scope, and the same is true for associated motion prefixes. As a result, forms with both negative and causative can be ambiguous, meaning either ‘not cause to X’ or ‘cause not to X’ (prohibition), and in some cases also ‘make sure X does not need to Y.’ The text notes that this kind of ambiguity also occurs with the velar causative.

text:
causative!associated motion associated motion!causative
As in the case of the negation (§ sec:sig.caus.negation ), the relative ordering of the associated motion and causative prefixes in the template is fixed and independent of semantic scope, and both `go/come and cause to $X$' and `cause to go/come and $X$' are possible interpretations.

Thus, either the causer or the causee can be the argument undergoing motion (§ sec:AM.argument.motion ). For instance, the verb ɕ-ko-z-rɯru in ( ex:CkozrWru ) can either mean `he sent him to guard it' (causee motion, the correct interpretation in this context) or `he went and made him guard it' (causer motion).

exe

rɟɤlpu kɯ ɯ-tɕɯ stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ ɕ-ko-z-rɯru. \\
king erg 3sg. poss -son most sbj: pcp -be.small dem tral - ifr - caus -guard \\
`The king sent his youngest son to guard [the trees].' (140507 jinniao-zh)
0003931#S37
exe
summary:
The passage says that the relative order of the associated motion and causative prefixes is fixed in the verb template and does not correspond to semantic scope. As a result, both interpretations are possible: either “go/come and cause to X” or “cause to go/come and X.”  

It also notes that either the causer or the causee may be the one undergoing motion. The example verb ɕ-ko-z-rɯru can mean either “he sent him to guard it” or “he went and made him guard it,” though the context here supports the first reading.

text:
causative!serial verb construction serial verb construction!causative
In the serial verb construction with the similative verb studo like, the instrumental causative can be repeated on both verbs, as in ( ex:chWsWste.chWsWBde ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-jaʁ nɯ kɯ tʰɤlwa ki cʰɯ-sɯ-ste nɯ ɯ-tʰɤcu cʰɯ-sɯ-βde \\
lnk 3sg. poss -hand dem erg earth dem. prox ipfv: downstream - caus -do.like[III] dem 3sg. poss -downstream ipfv: downstream - caus -throw \\
`[The mole] does this with its forepaws, and throws the earth below.' (28-qapar)
0003720#S148
exe

In other serial verb constructions (§ sec:svc.manner ), intransitive stative verbs generally have to be causativized to be used with transitive verbs to ensure transitivity harmony. These causative verbs expressing manner can appear before the lexical verbs as in ( ex:pWzmAke ) (where the causative of mɤkube first expresses the meaning `do $X$ first', § sec:denom.mA ) or follow it ( ex:koxtCAr.kosAsWG, ex:toti.tosApe ).

exe

a-tʂʰa ci pɯ-z-mɤke pɯ-rke \\
1sg. poss -tea once imp - caus -be.first[III] imp -put.in[III] \\
`Serve me some tea first.' (elicited)
exe

exe

ɯ-mŋu nɯra koŋla ʑo ko-xtɕɤr ko-sɯ-ɤsɯɣ ʑo. \\
3sg. poss -opening dem: pl completely emph ifr -tie ifr - caus -be.tight emph \\
`He tied the opening [of the bag] very tightly.' (150824 kelaosi-zh)
0006276#S279
exe
