The irregular causative of pebe good, sɤ-pe (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ), is common in the manner SVC (and in the corresponding complement clause construction, see ex:alAn.kAkho.WtAtWsApet in § sec:sig.caus.complement ) to express the meaning `do $X$ well' ( ex:toti.tosApe ).

exe

<luban> kɯ rcanɯ kɯ-pɯ-pe ʑo, maka mɤ-kɯ-ɤntɕʰoʁjɤr ʑo to-ti to-sɤ-pe. \\
anthr erg unexp: deg inf: stat - emph be.good emph at.all neg - inf: stat -be.incomplete emph ifr -say ifr - caus -be.good \\
`Luban said [the answers] very well, without missing anything.' (150902 luban-zh)
0006268#S56
exe
summary: In serial verb constructions with the similative verb *studo* ‘like,’ the instrumental causative can be marked on both verbs. More generally, in manner serial verb constructions, intransitive stative verbs usually need to be causativized to combine with transitive verbs, either before or after the lexical verb, and the irregular causative of *pebe* ‘good’ is commonly used to mean ‘do X well.’

subsubsection: Complement clauses with sigmatic causative of manner
text:
causative!complement clause complement clause!causative
Causative forms from adjectival stative verbs occur as complement-taking verbs to express the manner in which the action takes place (§ sec:causative.manner.complement ). This causative complement construction competes with the manner serial verb construction (§ sec:sig.caus.serial, § sec:svc.manner ) and the use of infinitive converbs (§ sec:inf.converb, § sec:manner.converbs ). The same construction is found with velar causatives (§ sec:velar.caus.complement ).

For instance in ( ex:alAn.kAkho.WtAtWsApet ) the meaning `give a good answer' is expressed with the causative sɤ-pe of pebe good (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ) and an infinitival complement clause with the verb kɤ-kʰo `to give'.

exe

[a-lɤn kɤ-kʰo] ɯ-tɤ-tɯ-sɤ-pe-t nɤ tɕe ku-ta-wum ŋu \\
1sg. poss -answer inf -give qu - aor -2- caus -be.good- pst: tr add lnk ipfv -1 2-gather be: fact \\
`If you give a good answer [to all my questions], I will take you [as my disciple].' (150902 luban-zh)
0006268#S44
exe

With the exception of a few verbs like sɤpedo well, most complement-taking causative verbs select the lexicalized orientation of the verb in the complement clause (§ sec:orientation.raising ). For instance, in ( ex:kAGndZWr.chAsAmYAm ), the causative verb cʰɤ-sɯ-ɤmɲɤm has the downstream orientation preverb cʰɤ- (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) selected by ɣndʑɯrgrind in the infinitival clause.

exe

kɤ-ɣndʑɯr cʰɤ-sɯ-ɤmɲɤm \\
inf -grind ifr: downstream - caus -be.homogeneous \\
`He ground [the flour] very homogeneously.' (elicited)
exe

The causative form is also required when the infinitival complement clause contains a transitive verb with dummy subject (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), as in ( ex:kAlAt.YWzmAke ).

exe

paχɕi nɯ ɯ-jwaʁ kɤ-lɤt ɲɯ-z-mɤke, nɯ ɯ-qʰu tɕe ɲɯ-rɯmɯntoʁ, \\
apple dem 3sg. poss -leaf inf -release ipfv - caus -be.first[III] dem 3sg. poss -after lnk ipfv -bloom \\
`The apple [tree] first grows leaves, and after that blooms.' (07-paXCi)
0003430#S11
exe
summary: Causative forms derived from adjectival stative verbs can function as complement-taking verbs to express the manner of an action, and this construction competes with manner serial verbs and infinitive converbs. The same pattern also occurs with velar causatives, and in most cases the causative verb selects the lexicalized orientation of the verb in the complement clause. In addition, the causative form is required when the infinitival complement contains a transitive verb with a dummy subject.

text:
A few auxiliary verbs can take the sigmatic causative, and are used with complement clauses in a way that is different from those treated in § sec:sig.caus.complement.

The causative sɯxcʰa from the modal verb cʰacan often occurs in inverse form with a dummy subject (§ sec:transitive.dummy ) with the specific meaning of `(cause to) be physically able to $X$', `(cause to) be strong enough to $X$', as in example ( ex:mWjtWwGsWxcha ) (see also § sec:sWxcha ). The agent is not expressed, but implicitly refers to the heavy object in ( ex:mWjtWwGsWxcha ).

exe

ɲɯ-rʑi tɕe [kɤ-fkur] mɯ́j-tɯ-wɣ-sɯx-cʰa. \\
sens -be.heavy lnk inf -carry.on.the.back neg: sens - 2 - inv - caus -can \\
`It is heavy, you won't be able to carry it on your back.' (elicitation)
exe

This complement-taking verb is exceptional in being the only one in Japhug requiring coreference between object of the matrix clause and subject of the complement clause (§ sec:sWxcha ).

This verb is attested in direct forms, as in ( ex:mWYWsWxche ), but only in the meaning `cause to be able to bear' without infinitival complement. The base verb cʰacan, among other functions, is attested with the meaning `be fine, be all right' (Chinese 行 xíngbe all right), in which case it does not take any complement clause or overt semi-object.

exe

kumpɣa pʰu nɯ ɲɯ-βʁa tɕe, mu nɯra mɯ-ɲɯ-sɯx-cʰe\\
fowl male dem sens -win lnk female dem: pl neg - sens - caus -can[III] \\
`(Otherwise) the roosters are too strong, and the hens cannot bear it.' (150819 kumpGa)
0006388#S8
exe

The intransitive phasal jɤɣfinish (§ sec:aspectual.complement, unrelated to the modal verb jɤɣbe allowed, § sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ) has the causative form sɯɣjɤɣfinish, used as a synonym of the transitive verb stʰɯtfinish (§ sec:aspectual.complement ).

Some modal verbs also appear in the same construction with a velar, instead of a sigmatic causative (§ sec:velar.caus.modal ).
summary: A few auxiliary verbs can take the sigmatic causative and combine with complement clauses in ways distinct from the patterns discussed elsewhere. In particular, the causative form of the modal verb cʰacan, sɯxcʰa, is often used with a dummy subject and means ‘(cause to) be physically able to X’ or ‘(cause to) be strong enough to X’; it is exceptional in requiring coreference between the matrix object and the complement subject. The intransitive phasal verb jɤɣ ‘finish’ also has a causative form, sɯɣjɤɣ, used synonymously with the transitive verb stʰɯt, and some modal verbs can appear in a similar construction with a velar rather than a sigmatic causative.

text:
causative!collocation collocation!causative
Verbs in noun-verb collocations can undergo sigmatic causative derivation. For instance, the combination of tɯ-χpɯmknee and tsʰoʁattach (§ sec:tshoR.lv ), which means `kneel' ( ex:WXpWm.pjAtshoR ), can be causativized to tɯ-χpɯm+sɯ-tsʰoʁ `cause/make/force to kneel' ( ex:pjWsWtshoR.tusWndze ).

exe

ɯ-χpɯm pjɤ-tsʰoʁ \\
3sg. poss -knee ifr -attach \\
`He knelt down.' 0003939#S88
exe

exe

ɯ-rkɯ nɯtɕu nɯ-χpɯm pjɯ-sɯ-tsʰoʁ, tɕe ɯ-ndzɤtsʰi ɯ-ro nɯ-kɯ-ri nɯnɯra, nɯ-ʁɤri pjɯ-χtɤr tɕe, tu-sɯ-ndze pjɤ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -side dem: loc 3pl. poss -knee ipfv - caus -attach lnk 3sg. poss -food 3sg. poss -excess aor - sbj: pcp -remain dem: pl 3pl. poss -front ipfv: down -scatter lnk ipfv - caus -eat[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`[The evil prince] forced them to kneel at his side, and would throw them leftovers from his food and force them to eat them.' (150821 edu de wangzi-zh)
0006402#S58
exe

The possessive prefix on the inalienable noun tɯ-χpɯmknee, which is obligatorily coreferential with the transitive subject in the base construction ( ex:WXpWm.pjAtshoR ), must be coreferential with the causee in the causativized construction ( ex:pjWsWtshoR.tusWndze ).

Causativization of complex predicates is also possible with the velar causative prefix (§ sec:velar.causative.collocation ).
summary: Verbs in noun-verb collocations can take sigmatic causative derivation, as in *kneel* from *knee + attach* becoming *cause/make/force to kneel*. In this process, the possessive prefix on the inalienable noun changes its coreference from the transitive subject in the base form to the causee in the causativized form. The passage also notes that complex predicates can be causativized with the velar causative prefix.

text:
The basic meaning of the sigmatic causative is a factitive `make $X$' or `have someone/something $X$'.

Depending on the volition of the causer and causee and the nature of the action, several specific cases can be distinguished: missive `sent to' (§ sec:sig.caus.missive ), coercive `force to' (§ sec:sig.caus.coercitive ), adjutative `help $X$ing' (§ sec:sig.caus.adjutative ), rogative `ask $X$ing' (§ sec:sig.caus.rogative ), permissive `let, allow' (§ sec:sig.caus.permissive ) and indirect causation (§ sec:sig.caus.indirect ). This classification is intended as a convenient way of exploring the uses of the causative in Japhug, and makes no claim to reveal the instanciations of universal categories.

In addition, the sigmatic causative has extended and more grammaticalized functions, such as inversive (§ sec:sig.caus.inversive ), instrumental (§ sec:sig.caus.instrumental ) and also tropative (§ sec:sig.caus.tropative ), as well as purely syntactic functions in serial verb constructions (§ sec:sig.caus.serial above) and complementation (§ sec:sig.caus.complement ).
summary:
The sigmatic causative basically means ‘make X’ or ‘have someone/something X’. Its uses vary according to the volition of the causer and causee and the nature of the action, yielding cases such as missive, coercive, adjutative, rogative, permissive, and indirect causation, though this is presented as a descriptive classification for Japhug rather than a universal one.  

The causative also has more grammaticalized extensions, including inversive, instrumental, and tropative uses, as well as purely syntactic roles in serial verb constructions and complementation.

text:
causative!missive
With motion (§ sec:motion.verbs ) and manipulation verbs (§ sec:manipulation.verbs ), the causative has a missive meaning. For instance, the causative sɯ-ɣɯt from ɣɯtbring means `send' in the sense of `have someone bring $X$' (either by directly asking a person or by mail), as in ( ex:jWfCWndzxi2 ) (see also ex:kW.pjAsWGWtnW above in § sec:sig.caus.tr ).

exe

a-ŋga lɤ-tɯ-sɯ-ɣɯt-ndʑi nɯ, a-xtsa nɯ wuma ɲɯ-pe \\
1sg. poss -clothes aor -2- caus -bring- du dem 1sg. poss -shoe dem really sens -be.good \\
`The clothes that you have sent me, the shoes are very nice.' (conversation, 15.04.18)
exe

The missive meaning of the causative is also found with non-motional bases taking an associated motion prefix, as in ( ex:CkozrWru ) above (see also § sec:sig.caus.AM ).
summary: With motion and manipulation verbs, the causative can have a missive meaning, as in *sɯ-ɣɯt* from *ɣɯt* ‘bring,’ which means ‘send’ in the sense of ‘have someone bring something.’ This missive use also occurs with non-motional bases when they take an associated motion prefix.

text:
causative!coercive
The sigmatic causative also occurs to express coercive causation `force to' against the will of the causee, as in ( ex:kWjNu.pasWtandZi ) (see also ex:pjWsWtshoR.tusWndze in § sec:sig.caus.collocations ).

exe

tɕʰeme nɯ kɯjŋu kɯ-wxtɯ wxti ʑo na-sɯ-ta-ndʑi ɲɯ-ŋu \\
girl dem oath sbj: pcp - emph be.big emph aor:3 - caus -put- du sens -be \\
`They$_DU$ forced the girl to swear a big oath.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S142
exe

This meaning occurs in particular with the adverb mɤkɯftsʰiforcibly ( ex:mAkWftshi.tAsWndzata ) (see also ex:mAkWfsthi.chAsWrku, § sec:velar.inf.adverb ), and the related lexicalized causative verb sɯftsʰiforce (see ex:mWtowGsWftshi, § sec:sig.caus.lexicalized ).

exe

tɤ-pɤtso smɤn mɤkɯftsʰi tɤ-sɯ-ndza-t-a \\
indef. poss -child medicine forcibly aor - caus -eat- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I forced the child to eat the medicine.' (elicited)
exe

In this function, the causee generally does not take the ergative, as shown by the examples above.
summary: The sigmatic causative can express coercive causation, meaning ‘force to’ against the causee’s will. This use is especially found with the adverb **mɤkɯftsʰi** ‘forcibly’ and with the related lexicalized causative verb **sɯftsʰi** ‘force.’ In this function, the causee generally does not take the ergative.

text:
causative!adjutative
The adjutative meaning of the causative `help $X$ing' occurs with verbs whose action is in the interests of the causee, and can only be successfully performed by collaboration between causer and causee. A typical example is the causative sɤnbaʁhide, `help to hide' from anbaʁhide (vi) (see ex:kutasAnbaR and ex:kosAnbaR above, § sec:sig.caus.morphosyntax ).

Some verbs with irregular allomorphs have the adjutative function, in particular ɕpʰɣoflee with (from the intransitive pʰɣoflee, § sec:caus.C ) and ʑŋgahelp wearing (from ŋgawear, § sec:caus.Z ).
summary: The causative can have an adjutative meaning, ‘help X-ing,’ when the action benefits the causee and can only be completed through collaboration between causer and causee. A typical example is *sɤnbaʁhide* ‘help to hide,’ derived from the intransitive *anbaʁhide*. Some verbs with irregular allomorphs also show this adjutative function, including forms meaning ‘help to flee’ and ‘help wearing.’

text:
causative!rogative
Rogative causation occurs when the causer asks a causee for help in performing an action, for instance for medical treatment as in ( ex:aZWG.tAznWsmana ).

exe

aʑɯɣ kɯnɤ tɤ-z-nɯsman-a qʰe tɤ-mna ɕti \\
1sg: gen also aor - caus -treat- 1sg lnk aor -be.better be. aff: fact \\
`I had my own [bellyache] treated and it got better.' (2011-13-qala)
exe

The rogative sɤ- prefix derives from this use of the causative (§ sec:rogative.derivation ).
summary: Rogative causation is a type of causation in which the causer asks the causee to help carry out an action, such as receiving medical treatment. The passage gives an example meaning “I had my own bellyache treated and it got better,” and notes that the rogative **sɤ-** prefix is derived from this use of the causative.

text:
causative!permissive
The sigmatic causative occurs with a permissive interpretation `let/allow $X$', when the causer does not prevent the causee from performing an action. This meaning of the causative is common for instance in 2 1 verb forms such as ( ex:kukWzrAZianW.YWntshi ) and ( ex:tukWsWrtoRi.ra ).

exe

ku-kɯ-z-rɤʑi-a-nɯ ɲɯ-ntsʰi \\
ipfv -2 1- caus -stay- 1sg - pl sens -be.better \\
`Please let me stay [here].' (qajdoskAt 2002) 0003366#S67
exe

exe

a-mu nɤ-ndzɣi ɯ-rcʰɤβ tu-kɯ-sɯ-rtoʁ-i ra \\
2sg. poss -mother 2sg. poss -fang 3sg. poss -interstice ipfv -2 1- caus -look- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`Mother, let us look at [the thing] that is in the interstice between your fangs?' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S265
exe

Additional examples of permissive causatives include for instance z-nɯna `allow to rest' (§ ex:kAznWna.amAtAtWkhW, § sec:sig.caus.lexicalized ) and sɯ-ndza `let eat, give to eat' ( ex:toWGsWndzandZi.pjAra, § sec:sig.caus.morphosyntax ).
summary: The sigmatic causative can have a permissive meaning, ‘let/allow X,’ when the causer does not stop the causee from carrying out the action. This use is common in certain 2/1 verb forms, and the passage gives examples such as ‘Please let me stay here’ and ‘Mother, let us look at it.’ It also notes additional permissive causatives like ‘allow to rest’ and ‘let eat, give to eat.’

text:
causative!indirect
The sigmatic causative can be used to express the unintended result of an (erroneous) action on the part of the causer, as in ( ex:kWsWRndWa2 ) (see also ex:tAkWsWRndWa, § sec:sig.caus.morphosyntax ).

exe

nɤʑo tɤ-ndze ma alo ma-lɤ-tɯ-tsɯm ma tʰa li kɯ-sɯ-ʁndɯ-a \\
2sg imp -eat[III] lnk upstream neg - imp: upstream -2-take.away lnk later again 2 1- caus -hit- 1sg \\
`Eat it, don't take it up there, you would cause me to be beaten again.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

It can even be used to express a detrimental result for the causer due to his negligence and failure to take proper preventive measures ( ex:tuzmWrki ).

exe

kɯm mɯ-cʰɯ-pe qʰe... kɯm kɯ-ɲɟɯ ɲɯ-βde qʰe laχtɕʰa ra tu-z-mɯrki \\
door neg - ipfv -close lnk door sbj: pcp - acaus:open ipfv -leave lnk thing pl ipfv - caus -steal[III] \\
`(Due to being a heavy drinker), he would [forget] to close the door, leave it open, and [as a result] have his things stolen [by other people].' (17-lhazgron)
exe

It also occurs when the causer only suggests that the causee undertake an action of his own volition, with unexpected consequences for the causee. In ( amphWz.nWtWsWphWt ), the causative on nɯ-tɯ-sɯ-pʰɯt `you had it taken off' refers to the fact that the causer (a trickster rabbit from a traditional story) cheated the referent in 1sg (a fierce bear) by suggesting that he treat his belly ache in such a way that he would wound his own bottom. Note that the absence of 2 1 indexation on the verb nɯ-tɯ-sɯ-pʰɯt means that the bear does not regard himself as causee, and expresses it as if the wound resulted from an event independent of him.

exe

pjɤ-kɯ-nɯβlu-a tɕe mɤ-jɤɣ ma tɕe a-xtu kɯ-mna sɤznɤ a-mpʰɯz ɯ-ntɕʰɯr nɯ-tɯ-sɯ-pʰɯt tɕe \\
ifr -2 1-cheat- 1sg lnk neg -be.allowed: fact lnk lnk 1sg. poss -belly inf: stat -be.better comp 1sg. poss -buttock 3sg. poss -piece aor -2- caus -take.off lnk \\
`You cheated me, it is outrageous, not only did my belly not get better, but [by misleading me] you caused a piece of my buttocks to be ripped off.' (2011-13-qala)
exe

The causative can also express an event resulting not from an action, but from the absence of action on the causer's part, with unintended consequences for the patientive argument. For instance, in ( ex:kWsWsata.YWNu ), the 2sg causer (a bird) is about to (unwillingly) cause the 1sg (patientive argument) to be killed by not appearing to the king.

exe

nɯ maʁ nɤ, mɯ́j-tɯ-ɣi tɕe kɯ-sɯ-sat-a ɲɯ-ŋu \\
dem not.be: fact add neg: sens -2-come lnk 2 1- caus -kill: fact - 1sg sens -be \\
`Otherwise, by not coming, you are about to get me killed.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

In ( ex:YAzGAdita ), the causative expresses a non-expected result due to the negligence of the causer.

exe

tɤ-mtʰɯm ɲɤ-z-ɣɤdi-t-a \\
indef. poss -meat ifr - caus -have.a.stench- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I let the meat spoil.' (elicited)
exe
summary: The sigmatic causative can mark unintended or detrimental results caused by an action, an error, or even negligence on the part of the causer. It may also be used when the causer merely suggests an action that the causee performs voluntarily, but which leads to an unexpected harmful outcome for the causee.

text:
causative!inversive
The inversive function of the causative occurs with verbs expressing a transfer of property, reversing the recipient/source relation of the base verb. Two possible cases exist, depending on how source and recipient are encoded by the base verb's argument structure.

First, most inversive causatives are recipient-source inversive: the argument with oblique case of the base verb (the source of the transfer) corresponds to the causer of the causative verb, and the subject of the base verb (the recipient of the transfer) to the causee of the causative verb (indexed as direct object) (see § sec:ditransitive.causative for a more detailed discussion). Examples of goal inversives include the irregular ɕɯrŋolend (§ sec:caus.CW ) from rŋoborrow and znɤŋgɯlend from nɤŋgɯborrow (see § sec:ditransitive.indirective on the semantic difference between nɤŋgɯ and rŋoborrow),

Second, the highly lexicalized nɯsɯkʰorob, extort from kʰogive is a source-recipient inversive: the dative argument of the base verb (recipient) corresponds to the transitive subject (causer/recipient) of the causative verb, and the subject of the base verb to the direct object (source) of the causative verb (§ sec:sig.caus.lexicalized ). For other secundative verbs, the rogative sɤ- derivation is used instead to express source-recipient inversion (§ sec:rogative.derivation ).

Although inversive causative mostly occurs with ditransitive bases, the causative of the monotransitive verb χtɯbuy can also be interpreted as a recipient-source inversive. Although χtɯbuy lacks a dative argument, the source can be optionally specified with the dative as in ( ex:nWCki.kAXtW ) in the case of people, or as a locative adjunct, as in ( ex:shangdian.kAXtW ).

exe

<wugui> ɯ-kɯ-ntsɣe ɣɤʑu tɕe, nɯnɯra nɯ-ɕki li ɯ-ndza ra kɤ-χtɯ ɣɤʑu. \\
turtle 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -sell exist: sens lnk dem. pl 3pl. poss - dat again 3sg. poss -food pl obj: pcp -buy exist: sens \\
`There are people$_i$ who sell turtles$_j$, and one [can] buy their$_j$ food from them$_i$.' (140510 wugui)
0003951#S33
exe

exe

<shangdian> ɯ-ŋgɯ kɤ-χtɯ ɣɤʑu \\
shop 3sg. poss -inside obj: pcp -buy exist: sens \\
`It [can] be bought in a shop.' (28-CAmWGdW)
0003712#S101
exe

The causative form sɯ-χtɯ has several meanings, including the factitive `cause to buy' and instrumental `buy with' (see ex:WCki.CtosWXtW below), but can also mean `sell'. This meaning is found in ( ex:tAwGsWXtWa ) with 3 1sg indexation: the transitive subject of sɯχtɯ in this construction is both causer and source, while its direct object is the recipient.

exe

pɤnmawombɤr kɯ [...] tɤ́-wɣ-sɯ-χtɯ-a ŋu \\
anthr erg aor - inv - caus -sell- 1sg be: fact \\
`It is Padma 'Od'bar who sold it to me.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S133
exe

Case marking is completely different when sɯ-χtɯ has the factitive function `cause to buy', as in ( ex:WCki.CtosWXtW ): the source of the transaction ( tɤ-mthɯm ɯ-kɯ-ntsɣe `the meat seller') is marked with the dative as with the base verb above in ( ex:nWCki.kAXtW ). One should note however that the verb in ( ex:WCki.CtosWXtW ) has the translocative prefix, and that the dative argument could also in principle be analyzed as a goal (§ sec:AM.goal ), though in this case the locative ri would rather be expected -- compare with examples ex:mbroXpa.ri.schWXtWnW and ex:kWre.ri.GWchWsWXtWnW in § sec:round.trip.AM. The causative sɯχtɯ therefore has two different argument structures depending on whether it reflects the inversive (`sell', ex:tAwGsWXtWa ) or factitive/missive (with associated motion `send to buy' as in ex:WCki.CtosWXtW, § sec:sig.caus.missive ) functions of this derivation.

exe

tɤ-mtʰɯm ɯ-kɯ-ntsɣe ɯ-ɕki tɕe tɤ-mtʰɯm ɕ-to-sɯ-χtɯ qʰe, \\
indef. poss -meat 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -sell 3sg. poss - dat loc indef. poss -meat tral - ifr - caus -buy lnk \\
`She sent him to buy meat at the butcher's.' (160701 poucet2)
0006155#S15
exe
summary:
The passage explains that the causative can have an inversive function with transfer verbs, reversing the normal source-recipient relation of the base verb. Most inversive causatives are recipient-source inversive, but a few lexicalized forms are source-recipient inversive; the monotransitive verb *χtɯ* ‘buy’ can also be interpreted inversively, with the source optionally marked by dative or locative expressions.

It also notes that *sɯ-χtɯ* has different argument structures depending on meaning: as an inversive form it can mean ‘sell,’ where the subject is both causer and source and the object is the recipient, while as a factitive or missive form meaning ‘cause/send to buy,’ the source is marked differently.

text:
causative!instrumental instrumental!causative
The causative prefix occurs on transitive verbs to mark an instrument, syntactically treated as a causee as in ( ex:fenbi.kW.tosWrAtndZi ), where the Chinese loanword 粉笔 fěnbǐchalk occurs with ergative marking (§ sec:instr.kW ).

exe

tɕaχpa ʁnɯz nɯ kɯ, nɤki, <alibaba> ɣɯ ɯ-kɯm nɯtɕu <fenbi> kɯ, nɤkinɯ, kɯ-ɤrtɯm ci to-sɯ-rɤt-ndʑi \\
thief two dem erg filler anthr gen 3sg. poss -door dem: loc chalk erg filler sbj: pcp -be.round indef ifr - caus -write- du \\
`The two thieves drew a circle on Alibaba's door.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S121
exe

However, the causative prefix is not required with overt instruments, as in ( ex:WjaR.kW.jumWrRWz ).

exe

ɯ-jaʁ kɯ ju-mɯrʁɯz ɲɯ-cʰa, \\
3sg. poss -hand erg ipfv -scratch sens -can \\
`[The mole] can scratch it with its claws.' (28-qapar)
0003720#S152
exe

instrumental
The co-existence of an overt instrument in the ergative with an overt transitive subject in the same clause (without any pause) is clumsy. Example ( ex:sYWGjW.kW.pasWrAt ) for instance is considered infelicitous if borderline ungrammatical, and the alternative construction with two clauses ( ex:sYWGjW.tando ) is highly preferred.

exe

xlist??ɯʑo kɯ sɲɯɣjɯ kɯ tɤscoz pa-sɯ-rɤt \\
3sg erg pen erg letter aor:3 - caus -write \\
(intended meaning:) `S/he wrote the letter with the pen.' (elicited)

ɯʑo kɯ sɲɯɣjɯ ta-ndo tɕe tɤscoz pa-sɯ-rɤt\\
3sg erg pen aor:3: up -take lnk letter aor:3 - caus -write\\
`S/he took the pen and wrote the letter with it.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

With intransitive bases (such as βziget drunk in ex:lowGsWBzi ), the causative expresses a cause (§ sec:manner.nominal.kW ) rather than an instrument.

exe

cʰa kɯ ló-wɣ-sɯ-βzi \\
alcohol erg ifr - inv - caus -become.drunk \\
`He became drunk from the alcohol.' (elicited)
exe

The irregular causative ɕɯfkaβcover with (from the transitive fkaβcover, § sec:caus.CW ) has an instrumental function, and the instrument is marked with the ergative as in ( ex:pWCWfkaB ).

exe

kʰɤlɤβ kɯ tɯtʰɯ pɯ-ɕɯ-fkaβ-a \\
cover erg pan aor - caus -cover- 1sg \\
`I covered the pan with a cover.' (elicited)
exe

Another irregular causative, ʑmbriplay (from mbricry, sing), can also be interpreted as an instrumental causative, but this verb treats the instrument as the object (§ sec:caus.Z ) without ergative.
summary: The passage explains that the causative prefix on transitive verbs can mark an instrument, which is syntactically treated like a causee and often appears with ergative marking. However, overt instruments do not always require the causative, and clauses containing both an overt instrument and an overt transitive subject in the same clause are generally awkward, so a two-clause alternative is preferred. With intransitive bases, the causative instead expresses a cause rather than an instrument, and some irregular causatives show special instrumental patterns, including one that marks the instrument with ergative and another that treats it as the object without ergative.

text:
causative!tropative tropative!causative
A handful of verbs with a sigmatic causative prefix have a tropative `find X, consider X' rather than a factitive meaning, the same as what would have been expected from a nɤ- tropative derivation (§ sec:tropative ).

The most common tropative causative is znɤjafind $X$ a shame, `hate to part with' ( ex:YWznAjandZi ) (in Chinese 舍不得 shěbùdéhate to part with), which derives from the intransitive nɤjabe a shame ( ex:tWji.YWnAja ).

exe

ɯ-mu ɯ-wa ni kɯ ɲɯ-z-nɤja-ndʑi qʰe mɯ-ta-sɯ-ɣe-ndʑi, \\
3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss -father du erg sens - caus -be.a.shame- du lnk neg - aor:3: up - caus -come- du \\
`Her parents could not stand to part with her, and did not let her come.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S275
exe

exe

tɕe tɯ-ji ɲɯ-nɤja. \\
lnk indef. poss -field sens -be.a.shame \\
`These fields, what a shame (nobody is taking care of them).' (150903-friche)
0006400#S7
exe

Other examples of tropative causative include zɣɤtɕaconsider to be wrong from ɣɤtɕabe wrong ( ex:pjWkWZGAGAtCa, § sec:refl.intr ), zɣɤŋgiconsider to be right from ɣɤŋgibe right and znɤkɤrofind okay from nɤkɤrobe okay (itself a denominal verb, § sec:denom.intr.nW ). The velar causative also has tropative uses (§ sec:velar.causative.tropative ).

The expected tropative forms $ $ nɤnɤja, $ $ nɤɣɤtɕa, $ $ nɤɣɤŋgi and $ $ nɤnɤkɤro are not attested.

In addition, the verbs sɯpaconsider and sɤrtsicount as, causatives of pado (§ sec:pa.lv, § sec:idph.pa ) and artsibe counted as (§ sec:sig.caus.other.derivations ) are used in the periphrastic tropative construction (§ sec:tropative.sWpa ).

The causative of the denominal verb afsujabe of the same size (§ sec:denom.a ) has the near-tropative meaning `compare the length/size of $X$ and $Y$' (rather than `make $X$ and $Y$ have the same length' or `consider that $X$ and $Y$ have the same length') as in ( ex:tuWGsAfsuja ).

exe

mbro ɯ-jme cʰo nɤ-kɤrme tú-wɣ-sɯ-ɤfsuja ra \\
horse 3sg. poss -tail comit 2sg. poss -hair ipfv - inv - caus -be.of.same.size be.needed: fact \\
`Let us compare [the length of] the horse's tail and that of your hair.' (`Let us see which is longest.') (2014-kWlAG)
exe
summary:
A small set of verbs with a sigmatic causative prefix have tropative meanings such as “find X,” “consider X,” or “compare X,” rather than the expected factitive meaning. The clearest example is **z-nɤja** ‘find X a shame, hate to part with,’ derived from intransitive **nɤja** ‘be a shame,’ and similar cases include forms meaning ‘consider wrong,’ ‘consider right,’ and ‘find okay.’  

The passage notes that the expected corresponding tropative forms are unattested, and that some verbs also appear in a periphrastic tropative construction. It further gives a denominal causative whose meaning is near-tropative: ‘compare the length/size of X and Y.’

text:
causative!applicative applicative!causative
The sɯ- prefix has a value that can be described as applicative comitative when used with the motion verb rɟɯɣrun.

Its causative form sɯrɟɯɣ, in addition to the regular missive meaning `cause to gallop', can also serve as an allative transitive verb of manipulation `run away with' (§ sec:manipulation.verbs ), as in ( ex:WpCi.chAsWrJWG ).

exe

jɯlpa ɯ-pɕi tɕe cʰɤ-sɯ-rɟɯɣ. \\
village 3sg. poss -outside loc ifr: downstream - caus -run \\
`He ran away from the village carrying her [on his back].' (150829 jidian-zh)
0006338#S79
exe
summary: The prefix **sɯ-** has an **applicative comitative** meaning when used with the motion verb **rɟɯɣrun**. Its causative form **sɯrɟɯɣ** can mean not only “cause to gallop,” but also an **allative transitive manipulation verb** meaning “run away with,” as in the example glossed “He ran away from the village carrying her [on his back].”

text:
Although the velar causative ɣɤ, rather than the sigmatic prefixes, occurs with most stative verbs, some stative verbs only appear with allomorphs of the sigmatic causative. See § sec:sig.caus.serial and § sec:sig.caus.complement concerning some uses of the causativized stative verbs. tab:causative.sW.stative presents a list of representative examples.

Stative verbs with a prefixal syllable ( mɤ, rɤ, ɣɯ- etc), always appear with z, never with ɣɤ- (except some examples with the prefixal element a- ). This constraint explains for instance why the causative of mɤrtsaβbe spicy is in z- rather than ɣɤ, while almost all other stative verbs denoting feelings or taste have a causative in ɣɤ, for instance tɕurbe sour ɣɤtɕurmake sour and tsribe salty ɣɤtsrimake salty'.

Color stative verbs and stative verbs related to disease and pain ( ngobe ill, mŋɤmfeel pain etc) also form their causative with sɯ- and its variants rather than with ɣɤ, as seen in the table above.

Only a handful of stative verbs are compatible with both velar and sigmatic causative prefixes. The semantic contrast between them is treated in § sec:velar.causative.vs.sigmatic.causative.
summary: Most stative verbs take the velar causative ɣɤ, but some instead occur with allomorphs of the sigmatic causative, and a few verbs can take either type. Stative verbs with a prefixal syllable such as mɤ-, rɤ-, or ɣɯ- always take z- rather than ɣɤ-, which explains forms like the causative of mɤrtsa ‘spicy’; color statives and statives related to disease or pain also use sɯ- and its variants instead of ɣɤ-.

text:
causative!recursion recursion!causative
The causative is the only derivation in Japhug that can occur twice in the same form. A second causative prefix can appear on lexicalized causative verbs, in particular those with irregular allomorphs (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular ), such as ɕɯɴqoʁhang in ( ex:tosWCWNqoR ), where the additional sɯ- prefix has a factitive function.

exe

mbro nɯnɯ ɯ-ku pjɤ-sɯ-pʰɯt tɕe, ɯ-ku nɯnɯ ʑara ɣɯ nɯ-kɤntɕʰaʁ ɣɯ ɯ-kɯm nɯtɕu to-sɯ-ɕɯ-ɴqoʁ. \\
horse dem 3sg. poss -head ifr - caus -take.off lnk 3sg. poss -head dem 3pl gen 3pl. poss -street dem 3sg. poss -door dem: loc ifr: up - caus - caus -hang \\
`She had [people] behead the horse, and hang its head on the city gate.' (140428 mu e guniang-zh)
0003880#S101
exe

The rogative verb sɤjtsʰiask for something to drink (§ sec:rogative.derivation ) also contains two instances of the sigmatic causative (at least historically), the irregular j- (§ sec:caus.j ), preceded by the passive a/ɤ- whose vowel merges with another causative. The underlying form of this verb is thus sɯ-ɤ-j-tsʰi ( caus - pass - caus -drink).

However, double causativization also occurs with non-lexicalized causatives. For instance, in ( ex:pjWGsWsWspoR ) and ( ex:kuwGsWsWBGWt ), the sɯ- prefix closest to the stem is factitive, and the one added to it has the instrumental function (§ sec:sig.caus.instrumental ), meaning `cause to $X$ with'.

exe

nɯnɯ kɯ pjɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-sɯ-spoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
dem erg ipfv - inv - caus - caus -have.a.hole sens -be \\
`One makes a hole [into it] with this.' (24-mbGo) 0003621
exe

exe

ci nɯ tɕe tɕe smi pjɯ́-wɣ-βlɯ tɕe nɯ smɯmba nɯ kɯ ɯ-rme nɯ kú-wɣ-sɯ-sɯ-βɣɯt ɲɯ-ra. \\
one dem lnk lnk fire ipfv - inv -burn lnk dem flame dem erg 3sg. poss -hair dem ipfv - inv - caus - caus -burn.off sens -be.needed \\
`The other [method to remove chicken feathers] is to make a fire and burn off the feathers with the flames.' (150907 kAnWtChWwWt)
0006282#S20
exe

In ( ex:pjWGsWsWspoR ) and ( ex:kuwGsWsWBGWt ), the base verbs spoʁhave a hole and βɣɯtbe burned off (of hairs/feathers) are intransitive, but double causativization is also possible with transitive bases, as in ( ex:pWtAsWsWrAt ).

exe

pɯ-ta-sɯ-sɯ-rɤt \\
aor -1 2- caus - caus -write \\
`I made you write it$_i$ with it$_j$.'
exe

Another type of double causative occurs when sigmatic and velar causative prefixes are combined (§ sec:velar.caus.other ).
summary: The causative is the only Japhug derivation that can appear twice in the same form. A second causative prefix may occur on lexicalized causative verbs, especially those with irregular allomorphs, where the added prefix can have a factitive function, and it can also occur with non-lexicalized verbs, where one causative is factitive and the other is instrumental (“cause to X with”). The passage also notes that double causativization is possible with both intransitive and transitive bases, and that another kind of double causative arises from combining sigmatic and velar causative prefixes.

text:
causative!compatibility
As the most productive verbal derivation, the sigmatic is also the one that is compatible with the greatest number of other derivations.

tab:sig.caus:after lists the derivational prefixes that can follow the causative in the prefixal chain (following the regular allomorphy described in § sec:sig.caus.allomorphs ). Since all cases are exemplified and discussed in the relevant sections, the data is not reproduced here. Despite the considerable number of prefixes that are compatible with the sigmatic causative, the reflexive ʑɣɤ- (§ sec:refl.caus ), sɤ- antipassive (§ sec:antipassive.sA ) and proprietive (§ sec:proprietive ) derivations are never preceded by the sigmatic causative. The autive does not normally follow the causative, except in a handful of lexicalized examples (§ sec:autoben.lexicalized ).

Fewer derivations can occur before the causative in the prefixal chain. The other valency-increasing derivations (applicative, tropative, velar causative) never take a sigmatic causative verb as input. Among valency-decreasing derivations, the anticausative prenasalization is never attested on causative verbs.

Three valency-decreasing derivations precede the causative only in a handful of lexicalized verbs. The antipassive and passive derivations are only found on rɤjtsʰigive to someone to drink (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ) and ajtsʰibe given to drink (§ passive.ditransitive ), from the irregular causative jtsʰigive to drink (§ sec:caus.j ) of tsʰidrink and sɤnɯsɯkʰorob people from the autive-causative nɯsɯkʰorob, extort (§ sec:antipassive.compatibility ).

In addition, the progressive prefix asɯ- probably derives from the combination of the passive with the sigmatic causative (§ sec:progressive.history ), but cannot be analyzed this way synchronically.

The derivations that can productively take a sigmatic causative verb as input are presented in tab:sig.caus:before.

From Tables tab:sig.caus:after and tab:sig.caus:before, we see that only two derivations, the reduplicated reciprocal (§ sec:reciprocal.other ) and the nɯɣɯ- object-oriented facilitative (§ sec:facilitative.nWGW ) can both freely precede and follow the sigmatic causative in the prefixal chain. Unlike negation (§ sec:sig.caus.negation ) and associated motion (§ sec:sig.caus.AM ) prefixes, whose semantic scope with the causative is independent of their relative position in the template, in the case of the reciprocal and facilitative, the relative position influences the semantic scope of the prefixes (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ).
summary:
The sigmatic causative is the most productive verbal derivation and is compatible with the widest range of other derivations, but some prefixes never occur with it in certain positions. In particular, the reflexive, antipassive, and proprietive never precede the causative, and the autive only rarely follows it; several other derivations can appear before the causative only in a few lexicalized verbs, while others cannot productively take a causative verb as input.  

Only the reduplicated reciprocal and the nɯɣɯ- object-oriented facilitative can freely occur both before and after the sigmatic causative, and for these two derivations their position relative to the causative affects semantic scope.

text:
causative!velar
The velar causative prefix ɣɤ- (in the Kamnyu dialect, corresponding to wɤ- in eastern dialects) is the second causative derivation found in Japhug. Unlike the sigmatic causative (§ sec:sig.causative ), it is restricted to stative verb bases. Not all stative verbs, however, build their causative form with the velar causative. In particular, polysyllabic bases, including those whose non-final syllable is a derivation prefix or an unanalyzable element (such as a, nV, rV, sV- etc) can only be causativized with sigmatic prefixes (§ sec:sig.caus.stative ). A handful of verbs are compatible with both velar and sigmatic causative prefixes (§ sec:velar.causative.vs.sigmatic.causative ).

tab:velar.caus presents a representative sample of velar causative verbs, including adjectival stative verbs, existential verbs and modal verbs. The presence of Tibetan loanwords such as dɤnbe many, βdibe well and tsʰozbe complete (from ལྡན་ldanpossessing, བདེ་bdewell and ཚངས་tsʰaŋscomplete) in the list shows that this prefix is productive.

The velar causative ɣɤ- prefix is homophonous with a few other derivational prefixes, including denominal (§ sec:denom.GW ), deideophonic (§ sec:GA.sA.deidph ) and subject-oriented facilitative (§ sec:facilitative.GA ). The latter derives intransitive verbs whose stems are identical (with different conjugations however) to those of velar causatives, for instance ɣɤwxtibecome big easily vs. ɣɤwxtimake bigger from wxtibe big.

The causative verbs from complement-taking modal verbs such as kʰɯbe possible can occur with nominal objects, especially abstract nouns as in ( ex:tWtsGe.mWYWkAGAkhW ), but are more commonly found with complement clauses as objects (§ sec:velar.caus.modal ).

exe

ndʑi-tɯtsɣe ra mɯ-ɲɯ-kɤ-ɣɤ-kʰɯ ftɕaka ntsɯ tu-βze pjɤ-ŋu. \\
2du. poss -commerce pl neg - ipfv - inf - caus -be.possible manner always ipfv -make[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`He was always trying [by all means] to make it impossible for them to manage their business.' (150825 baishe zhuan-zh)
0006342#S99
exe
summary:
The velar causative prefix ɣɤ- (wɤ- in eastern dialects) is the second causative derivation in Japhug and is restricted to stative verb bases. However, not all stative verbs take it: polysyllabic bases and those containing derivational or unanalyzable syllables must use the sigmatic causative, though some verbs allow both forms.

The prefix is productive, as shown by its use with adjectival, existential, and modal verbs, including Tibetan loanwords. It is homophonous with several other prefixes, and one of these, the subject-oriented facilitative prefix, forms intransitive verbs with stems identical to velar causatives but different conjugations. Causatives derived from modal verbs can take nominal objects, though they more often take complement clauses.

text:
causative!allomorphy morphology!allomorphy
Irregular allomorphs of the velar causative are very rare and highly lexicalized. The ɣɤ- prefix clearly originates from earlier *wɐ, as shown by the form wɤ- in eastern Japhug dialects and the cognate prefixes wɐ- in Tshobdun and Zbu. The vowel-less irregular allomorphs originate from earlier *w, nasalized to m before nasal and prenasalized stops.

A w- allomorph, realized as β, is found in the verb βriprotect, `save' ( ex:tatWBrit ), This verb can take as object the entity being protected as in ( ex:tatWBrit ) (see also ex:iZora.tutafsraN, § sec:indexation.local ), but also in some cases the entity one protects something from; for instance the participial clause qale ɯ-kɯ-βri (wind 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -protect) means `(hedge) that protects from the wind'. which derives from the intransitive riremain, `be left' (see examples ex:zgo.tWrdoR, § sec:multiple.CN and ex:tWrdoR.YAri, § sec:lability.pass ). The bare root ri is also attested in the transitive verb ri `save' (always in collocation with tɯ-sroʁlife, § sec:orphan.verb ), a zero derivation from riremain (§ sec:lability.pass ).

exe

nɤ-pi ni tɤ-tɯ-βri-t ŋu \\
2sg. poss -elder.sibling du aor -2-save- pst: tr be: fact \\
`You saved your two elder brothers.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S133
exe

The lexicalized causative βri can be subjected to reflexivization (§ sec:refl.caus ) in ʑɣɤβriprotect oneself (example ex:tWZo.kW.tWZo, § sec:genr.pro ).

The regular sigmatic causative sɯɣ-ri from the base verb riremain also exists, and predictably means `leave, not use up completely' as in ( ex:tWndzrW.anWtWsWGri ). It is probable that βri originally also had a meaning close to that of sɯɣ-ri, and then changed to `save, protect'.

exe

ki a-tɤ-tɯ-ndze qʰe qʰe ɯ-qa nɯtɕu tɯ-ndzrɯ jamar ci ʑo a-nɯ-tɯ-sɯɣ-ri ma \\
dem. prox irr - pfv -2-eat[III] lnk lnk 3sg. poss -bottom dem: loc indef. poss -nail about indef emph irr - pfv -2- caus -remain lnk \\
`When you eat this, leave a [quantity of] about a nail [from it in the bowl].' (2003kandZislama)
exe

The m- allomorph of the velar causative occurs in the verb mɲoprepare (see ex:aZo.tAmYota in § sec:A.kW, and the discussion in § sec:z.nmlz ), a causative of the intransitive stative verb ɲobe prepared (with nasalization *w-ɲo mɲo ). This intransitive verb is particularly common in the participle form kɯ-ɲo `already prepared, ready to (eat)' (corresponding to Chinese 现成 xiànchéngready-made), as in ( ex:kWYo.tundzaj ).

exe

ma jinde tɕe ku-χsu-j me kɯ-ɲo ntsɯ tu-ndza-j ɕti ma \\
lnk nowadays lnk ipfv -raise- 1pl not.exist: fact sbj: pcp -be.ready always ipfv -eat- 1pl be. aff: fact lnk \\
`Nowadays we do not raise [chicken] anymore, we eat `ready-made' [eggs].' (22-kumpGa)
0003588#S79
exe

Like βri above, the causative mɲo can be reflexivized to ʑɣɤmɲoprepare oneself (§ sec:refl.caus ). A regular causative form sɯɣ-ɲo `prepare' is also attested, but it is much rarer than mɲo, and the semantic difference between these two causative forms has not been elucidated.

Another example of the nasalized m- allomorph is the rare transitive verb mdzardrip dry ( ex:pWmdzara ) This verb also appears in participial form in the compound kɯndzarmɯtype of rain (see ex:kWndzarmW, § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ). which derives from the intransitive verb ndzardrip dry ( ex:apWndzar ). The intransitive ndzardrip dry itself is the anticausative form of sarfilter out, `drip dry' (§ sec:anticausative.pairs ). The onset mdz- is phonologically mndz, with the causative *w- prefix nasalized by the prenasalized voiced affricate ndz, a unitary phoneme (§ sec:NC.clusters ).

exe

tɯ-ŋga nɯ-χtɕi-t-a tɕe a-pɯ-ndzar tɕe cʰɯ́-wɣ-ɕkʰo jɤɣ \\
indef. poss -clothes aor -wash- pst: tr - 1sg lnk irr - pfv -drip.dry lnk ipfv: downstream - inv -spread be.allowed: fact \\
`I have washed the clothes, let them first drip dry before putting them in the sun to dry.' (elicited)
exe

exe

mbrɤz kɯ-fse lo, <cai> kɯ-fse nɯnɯra tɕe, ɯ-ŋgɯ tɯ-ci kɯ-tu nɯra pjɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-ɤrɕo tɕe, nɯnɯ ``pɯ-mdzar-a" tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
rice sbj: pcp -be.like sfp dish sbj: pcp -be.like dem: pl lnk 3sg. poss -inside indef. poss -water sbj: pcp -exist dem: pl ipfv - inv - caus -be.finished lnk dem aor -drip.dry- 1sg ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`When one has completely removed the water in the rice or in a dish, one says pɯ-mdzar-a.' (definition)
exe
summary: The passage says that irregular allomorphs of the velar causative are very rare and mostly lexicalized, with the ɣɤ- prefix coming from earlier *wɐ and the vowel-less forms from earlier *w, which nasalized to m before nasal and prenasalized stops. It gives examples such as βri `save/protect`, mɲo `prepare`, and mdzar `drip dry`, noting that some of these forms can also be reflexivized and that regular causative counterparts exist, though they may be rarer or semantically different.

text:
The combination of the velar causative with negation prefixes is ambiguous. As in the case of the sigmatic causative (§ sec:sig.caus.negation ), the scope of the negation can either include the causation (`not cause to $X$') or not (`cause not to $X$'). For instance, the causative ɣɤwxtimake bigger in negative form can either be `not make bigger', or `make smaller' as in ( ex:matAtWGAwxti ).

exe

ɯ-pʰɯ ɲɯ-wxti tɕe, nɯra tʰamtɕɤt ma-tɤ-tɯ-ɣɤ-wxti \\
1sg. poss -price sens -be.big lnk dem: pl all neg - imp -2- caus -be.big \\
`It is expensive, make it less expensive.' (2010-12)
exe

With the velar causative from modal verbs, the broad scope interpretation of the negation is very common. For instance, ɣɤracause to have to and ɣɤkʰɯmake it possible to in the negative form generally mean `cause not to have to' and `make it impossible to' (§ sec:velar.caus.modal ).
summary:
The passage says that combining the velar causative with negation prefixes is ambiguous: negation can scope over the causation itself (“not cause to X”) or over the embedded event (“cause not to X”). For example, the negative causative of *wxti* ‘make bigger’ may mean either ‘not make bigger’ or ‘make smaller’.  

It also notes that with modal verbs, the broad-scope reading of negation is especially common, so forms meaning ‘cause to have to’ or ‘make it possible to’ in negative form usually mean ‘cause not to have to’ and ‘make it impossible to’.

subsubsection: Complement clauses with causative of manner
text:
As with the sigmatic causative (§ sec:sig.caus.complement ), the velar causative can derive complement-taking verbs expressing manner (§ sec:causative.manner.complement ), selecting complement clauses with velar infinitive (§ sec:inf.complementation ) or bare infinitive (§ sec:bare.inf.complement ).

The examples in ( ex:GAtChom ) illustrate the possible constructions with the causative ɣɤtɕʰomcause to be too much, `do $X$ too much' from tɕʰombe too much and the verb tsʰidrink expressing the main action in the complement clauses. The velar infinitive ( ex:kAtshi.koGAtChom ) and bare infinitive ( ex:Wtshi.loGAtChom ) constructions have the same meaning `drink too much', and the causative verb takes the orientation prefix normally selected by the verb in the complement clause, in this case either eastwards ( ex:kAtshi.koGAtChom ) or upstream ( ex:Wtshi.loGAtChom ).

exe

xlist

[cʰa kɤ-tsʰi] ko-ɣɤ-tɕʰom \\
alcohol inf -drink ifr - caus -be.too.much \\

[cʰa ɯ-tsʰi] lo-ɣɤ-tɕʰom \\
alcohol 3sg. poss - bare. inf:drink ifr - caus -be.too.much \\
`He drank too much alcohol.' (elicited)

cʰɤtsʰi ko-ɣɤ-tɕʰom \\
alcohol.drinking ifr - caus -be.too.much \\
`He had drunk too much alcohol.' (150829 jidian-zh)
0006338#S16
xlist
exe

In addition, example ( ex:chAtshi.koGAtChom2 ) shows that object-verb action nominal compounds (§ sec:object.verb.compounds, § sec:action.nominal.compounds ) can occur with causative verbs instead of complement clauses.

While action nominal compounds are rare, the causative complement construction with velar and bare infinitive is very common and compatible with all verb categories. Even noun-verb collocations such as tɯ-xɕɤt+lɤt `exert strength, do $X$ forcibly' can occur in these complement clauses as in ( ex:WxCAt.WlAt.toGAtChom ) (with an upwards orientation preverb).

exe

rgɤtpu nɯ kɯ ɯ-tɕɯ ja-stʰoʁ tɕe, ɯ-xɕɤt ɯ-lɤt to-ɣɤ-tɕʰom tɕe \\
old.man dem erg 3sg. poss -son aor:3 -push lnk 3sg. poss -strength 3sg. poss -release ifr - caus -be.too.much lnk \\
`The old man pushed his son, but exerted too much strength and...' (150831 jubaopen-zh)
0006294#S143
exe

All velar causative verbs, even those that are generally used with a concrete factitive meaning, can be used in these complement-taking constructions. For instance, ɣɤ-βdi (from βdibe well), which can mean `repair' with a nominal object (see ex:WZAG.nWra, § sec:pronouns.gen ), occurs in the sense of `do $X$ well, do $X$ nicely' with a complement clause as in ( ex:akAtWGABdi ).

exe

kʰa ɯ-ʁɤri nɯtɕu ɯ-fkrɤm a-kɤ-tɯ-ɣɤ-βdi \\
house 3sg. poss -front dem: loc 3sg. poss - bare. inf:place irr - pfv -2- caus -be.well \\
`Place these nicely [in order] in front of the house.' (smanmi 2003.1)
exe
summary: The velar causative can form complement-taking verbs of manner, selecting either velar infinitive or bare infinitive complement clauses. These constructions mean the same thing and the causative verb carries the orientation prefix normally required by the complement verb; they are common and work with all verb categories, unlike the rarer object-verb action nominal compounds.

text:
Velar causative forms of modal verbs, in particular ɣɤracause to have to and ɣɤkʰɯmake it possible to, are found with velar infinitive or finite complement clauses (§ sec:sWpa.sABzu ) like the corresponding base verbs rabe needed and kʰɯbe possible (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ) as in ( ex:mWtAGAkhWta ), but not with bare or dental infinitives.

exe

[kɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ] mɯ-tɤ-ɣɤ-kʰɯ-t-a. \\
inf - auto -come.out neg - aor - caus -be.possible- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I prevented it/him from coming out.' (elicited)
exe

The object of the causative verb is most often the (transitive or intransitive) subject of the complement clause as in ( ex:mWtAGAkhWta ), but not necessarily; in ( ex:kAtu.tAGAkhWta ), the object of tɤ-ɣɤ-kʰɯ-t-a is the possessor of the subject (in the possessive construction, § sec:possessive.mihi.est ).

exe

[ɯ-rŋɯl kɤ-tu] tɤ-ɣɤ-kʰɯ-t-a. \\
3sg. poss -money inf -exist aor - caus -be.possible- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I made it possible for him/her to have money.' (elicited)
exe

In ( ex:mWYAGAra ), the causative ɣɤra occurs with a clause containing the form kɯ-ra that can either be interpreted as a relative (with a subject participle) or as a complement clause (in which case the kɯ- prefix is preferably analyzed as a stative infinitive).

exe

<xianling> nɯ nɯ-rga qʰendɤre, [...] [nɯ-ʁjoʁ kɯ-ra] nɯ mɯ-ɲɤ-ɣɤ-ra qʰe, \\
magistrate dem aor -be.happy lnk 3pl. poss -servant sbj: pcp -be.needed dem neg - ifr - caus -be.needed lnk \\
`The magistrate was happy, and cancelled the duties that they had to do.' (150904 cuzhi-zh)
0006322#S173
exe

The existential verb tu (§ sec:existential.basic ) can also be subjected to the ɣɤ- derivation, which yields the verb ɣɤtucause to have. This form is used to causativize possessive constructions (§ sec:possessive.constructions) or noun-verb collocations (§ sec:intr.light.verbs ) as in ( ex:axCAt.Zo.tuGAte ).

exe

a-xɕɤt ʑo tu-ɣɤte tɕe \\
1sg. poss -strength emph ipfv - caus -exist[III] lnk \\
`[The rain] gives me (`makes me have') strength.' (150819 woniu-zh)
0006254#S49
exe
summary: Velar causative forms of modal verbs, especially ɣɤra ‘cause to have to’ and ɣɤkʰɯ ‘make it possible to,’ occur with velar infinitive or finite complement clauses, but not with bare or dental infinitives. The causative object is usually the subject of the complement clause, though it can also be the possessor of that subject; in addition, the existential verb tu can take the ɣɤ- derivation to form ɣɤtu ‘cause to have,’ which is used to causativize possessive constructions and noun-verb collocations.

text:
causative!collocation collocation!causative
Complex predicates comprising a noun-verb collocation can undergo causativization with the ɣɤ- prefix. The causativization of complex predicates with the sigmatic prefixes is treated in § sec:sig.caus.collocations.

For instance, the combination of the lexicalized object participle kɤ-ti ( obj: pcp -say) with the existential verb menot exist, which means `have nothing to say' or `be unable to say for sure' (see example ex:akAti.maNe, § sec:lexicalized.object.participle ), can be causativized to kɤ-ti+ɣɤ-me `cause $X$ to have nothing to say' as ( ex:WkAti.naGame ).

exe

rɟɤlpu nɯ ɯ-kɤ-ti na-ɣɤ-me \\
king dem 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -say aor:3 - caus -not.exist \\
`He made the king unable to say anything.' (2005 tAwakWcqraR)
exe
summary: Complex predicates built from a noun-verb collocation can be causativized with the ɣɤ- prefix. The passage illustrates this with the collocation kɤ-ti menot ‘have nothing to say’ / ‘be unable to say for sure,’ which becomes kɤ-ti+ɣɤ-me ‘cause X to have nothing to say,’ as in “He made the king unable to say anything.”

text:
causative!tropative tropative!causative
The velar causative does have a tropative interpretation in specific contexts, like the sigmatic causative (§ sec:sig.caus.tropative ). The verb ɣɤwxtimake bigger from wxtibe big for instance can mean `find/consider to be bigger' as in ( ex:mWpjAnWGAwxti ).

exe

kɯmaʁ ɯ-ɣi nɯra nɯ-rtsawa mɯ-pjɤ-nɯ-ɣɤ-wxti \\
other 3sg. poss -relative dem: pl 3pl. poss -importance neg - ifr. ipfv - auto - caus -be.big \\
`He did not consider his other relatives to be as important [as his wife].' (kWjujmAlu 2003)
exe

A tropative velar causative with a slightly lexicalized meaning is ɣɤkʰedepreciate, demean ( ex:WkWGAkhe.YWxcat ) (see also ex:ndZitAresAtCWtCAt, § sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle ), from kʰebe stupid.

exe

ɯ-kɯ-n-nɤmqe, ɯ-kɯ-nɤre, ɯ-kɯ-ɣɤ-kʰe nɯra ɲɯ-xcat ʑo. \\
3sg. poss - auto -scold 3sg. poss -laugh.at 3sg. poss - caus -be.stupid dem: pl sens -be.many emph \\
`There were many people scolding him, making fun of him, calling him stupid.' (150829 phaRrgot)
0006414#S11
exe
summary: The velar causative can have a tropative reading in certain contexts, similar to the sigmatic causative. For example, ɣɤwxti “make bigger” from wxti “big” can mean “find/consider to be bigger,” and ɣɤkʰe “depreciate, demean” is a more lexicalized tropative form from kʰe “stupid.”

text:
causative!velar causative!sigmatic
Some stative verbs are compatible with both sigmatic (§ sec:sig.caus.stative ) and velar causative prefixes, an observation which raises the question of the semantic distinction between these two derivations when contrastive. The contrast between the two causative derivations in the case of the irregular allomorphs β- and m- is discussed in § sec:causative.m., with regard to the causative prefixes sə and wɐ- in Tshobdun, proposes that in the case of some stative verbs, the former indicates an increase of degree ( ex:nekAsEGchi ), while the latter expresses a change of state ( ex:nekAwAchi ).

exe

xlist

cʰɐ́ɟi ne-kɐ-səɣ-cʰiʔ=nəʔ mimʔ=cə \\
beer ipfv - genr - caus -be.sweet= dem be.tasty= med \\
‘Beer is tasty when one allows it to sweeten (naturally and gradually).’

cʰɐ́ɟi ne-kɐ-wɐ-cʰiʔ=nəʔ mimʔ=cə \\
beer ipfv -genr- caus -be.sweet= dem be.tasty= med \\
‘Beer is tasty when one sweetens it (e.g. by adding sugar).’
xlist
exe

In Japhug, it is not completely clear whether a semantic contrast of the same type is attested. Minimal pairs such as sɯx-cʰi and ɣɤ-cʰi from cʰibe sweet or sɯx-tɕur and ɣɤ-tɕur from tɕurbe sour do exist, but no consistent semantic difference appears to exist between them.

Examples ( ex:pjWsWxtCur ) and ( ex:YWsWxtCur ) suggest that the causative sɯx-tɕur means `make sour' rather than `make more sour' as would be expected following Sun's analysis of Tshobdun. In the case of ( ex:pjWsWxtCur ), it is possible that tɤjko mɯ-tɤ-tɕur can be contextually translated as `when the pickle is not sour enough ', and that therefore the verb pjɯ-sɯx-tɕur does indeed mean `make more sour'. Tshendzin proposed conflicting interpretations of this example. The occurrence of sɯx-tɕur in ( ex:YWsWxtCur ) however is incompatible with an analysis in terms of heightened degree.

exe

tɕe tɤjko mɯ-tɤ-tɕur tɕe, ɴɢolo ɯ-mat nɯ ɲɯ́-wɣ-pʰɯt tɕe, tɕe tɤrca pjɯ́-wɣ-ɣɤ-la tɕe, tɕe tɤjko pjɯ-sɯx-tɕur cʰa. \\
lnk pickle neg - aor -be.sour lnk Ribes.stenocarpum 3sg. poss -fruit dem ipfv - inv -take.off lnk lnk together ipfv - inv - caus -soak lnk lnk pickle ipfv - caus -be.sour can: fact \\
`When the pickle$_i$ is not sour, one picks fruits from the Ribes stenocarpum $_j$, soaks them together [with it$_i$], and it$_j$ can make the pickle sour.' (18-NGolo)
0003530#S25
exe

exe

ɯ-tɯ-tɕur kɯ tɯ-kɯr ɯ-ŋgɯ lú-wɣ-rku qʰe maka ɲɯ-sɯ-ɤmɯ-zɣɯt qʰe, tɯ-pʰoŋbu ra kɯnɤ ɲɯ-sɯx-tɕur kɯ-fse ɕti\\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.sour erg genr. poss -mouth 3sg. poss -inside ipfv: upstream - inv -put.in lnk at.all ipfv - caus - distr -reach lnk genr. poss -body pl also sens - caus -be.sour sbj: pcp -be.like be. aff: fact \\
`It is so sour that when one puts it into one's mouth, it makes everything [sour in an even way], as if one's whole body becomes sour.' (09-mi)
0003466#S60
exe

In addition, example ( ex:pWGAtCura ) shows that the velar causative ɣɤ-tɕur is not incompatible with the meaning `make more sour'. It is possible that other semantic parameters (such as direct/indirect causation and volitionality) are at play in the choice of the two prefixes.

exe

<cai> ɯ-tɯ-tɕur mɯ́j-rtaʁ tɕe, <cu> pɯ-lat-a tɕe pɯ-ɣɤ-tɕur-a \\
dish 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.sour neg: sens -be.enough lnk, vinegar aor -release- 1sg lnk aor - caus -be.sour- 1sg \\
`As the dish was not sour enough, I added vinegar to make it sourer.' (elicited)
exe

The only verb root that has sigmatic and velar causative forms with clearly different meanings is mto, a labile verb meaning `see' when conjugated transitively, and `have sharp eyesight' when intransitive (§ sec:lability.categories ). The sigmatic causative sɯ-mto, based on the transitive use of mto, means `let see, show' as in ( ex:pjWtWwGsWmto.cha ).

exe

kɯki tɤ-ndɤm tɕe, [...] ʑimkʰɤm ɯ-ku, tɕʰi kɯ-tu ʑo nɯ pjɯ-tɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-mto cʰa \\
dem. prox imp -take[III] lnk world 3sg. poss -head what sbj: pcp -exist emph dem ipfv -2- inv - caus -see can: fact \\
`Take this [spyglass], it will make you able to see everything that exists in the world.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S74
exe

The velar causative ɣɤmtocause to recover eyesight is based on the stative use `have sharp eyesight'. Just as the base verb requires the noun tɯ-mɲaʁeye as intransitive subject (example ex:WmYaR.YWmto, § sec:lability.categories ), ɣɤmto requires it as object as in ( ex:tuGAmtAm.cha ).

exe

nɯnɯ kɯ maka nɯ-mɲaʁ tu-ɣɤ-mtɤm cʰa ri, \\
dem erg completely 3pl. poss -eye ipfv - caus -have.sharp.eyesight[III] can: fact lnk \\
`That [plant] can cure their blindness (cause their eyes to recover eyesight).' (140517 mogui de jing-zh)
0004022#S81
exe
summary:
The passage discusses two causative derivations in Japhug, sigmatic and velar, and notes that with some stative verbs the semantic contrast between them is unclear. While Tshobdun has been analyzed as contrasting increased degree versus change of state, Japhug examples such as *sɯx-tɕur* and *ɣɤ-tɕur* do not show a consistent difference, though some cases suggest the sigmatic form may mean “make more sour” and the velar form may also sometimes mean “make sour.”

The only root with clearly distinct sigmatic and velar causatives is *mto*: the sigmatic form *sɯ-mto* means “let see, show,” while the velar form *ɣɤ-mto* means “cause to recover eyesight,” based on the intransitive stative meaning “have sharp eyesight.”

text:
causative!compatibility
Due to the constraint on monosyllabic bases (§ sec:sig.caus.stative ), the velar causative can only take bare verb roots (or at least verb roots containing frozen prefixes) as input, unlike the sigmatic causative which can precede a dozen derivational prefixes (§ sec:sig.caus.other.derivations ).

The velar causative prefix can be preceded by the reflexive ʑɣɤ- as in ( ex:YWZGAGAxtCindZi ) (see also ex:atAtWGAZo.AtAZGAGAmbjom, § sec:refl.caus.volitional and § sec:refl.trop.caus ).

exe

iɕqʰa tɯ-xtsa nɯni tɤ-kɤ-sŋaʁ pjɤ-ɕti tɕe tɕendɤre, ɲɤ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-xtɕi-ndʑi \\
the.aforementioned indef. poss -shoe dem: du aor - obj: pcp -enchant ifr. ipfv -be. aff lnk lnk ifr - refl - caus -be.small- du \\
`The shoes had been enchanted, and became small by themselves.' (160706 poucet6)
0006109#S92
exe

It can also undergo reduplicated reciprocal derivation ( ex:chAGArlWrlaRnW, § sec:reciprocal.other ), and occurs with the autive nɯ- ( ex:mWpjAnWGAwxti in § sec:velar.causative.tropative above) and the z- allomorph of the sigmatic causative (§ sec:caus.z ) as in ( ex:YAtWzGABdit ).

exe

tɕe tʂu ri ɲɤ-tɯ-z-ɣɤ-βdi-t ɕti tɕe, tɕe nɯtɕu a-kɤ-tɯ-ɕe \\
lnk road also ifr -2- caus - caus -be.well- pst: tr be. aff: fact lnk lnk dem: loc irr - pfv: east -2-go \\
`[Since] you have already had the road repaired (by someone else), [take that road] to go [east].' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

The tropative causative ɣɤkʰedepreciate, demean (derived from kʰebe stupid, § sec:velar.causative.tropative ) also has the sɤ- antipassive form (§ sec:antipassive.sA ) sɤz-ɣɤ-kʰe ( apass - caus -be.stupid) `demean people'.
summary: The velar causative is more restricted than the sigmatic causative because, due to a constraint on monosyllabic bases, it can take only bare verb roots or roots with frozen prefixes, not the many derivationally prefixed forms that the sigmatic causative can combine with. It can, however, cooccur with the reflexive ʑɣɤ-, reduplicated reciprocal derivation, the autive nɯ-, and the z- allomorph of the sigmatic causative. The tropative causative ɣɤ-kʰe also has an antipassive form sɤ-z-ɣɤ-kʰe meaning ‘demean people.’

text:
applicative
The applicative nɯ- is a valency-increasing derivation by means of which an oblique argument, an adjunct or even a non-participant (including comitative or dative adjuncts and semi-objects, § sec:applicative.promoted ) is promoted to object function. In Japhug, the base verb is always morphologically intransitive, and the applicative verb transitive (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ). The subject of the applicative verb corresponds to the same referent as that of the base verb, though it receives ergative case marking instead of absolutive (see examples ex:YWkWnWGmu and ex:YWmunW.chWphGonW in § sec:applicative.promoted below).

The nɯ- applicative is only attested by a limited number of examples (exhaustively listed in tab:applicative; the allomorphy is discussed in § sec:allomorphy.applicative ), but the fact that it includes the Tibetan loanword rgalike, `be happy' (from དགའ་dgabe happy) shows that it has some degree of productivity.

Cognates of the applicative prefix are found in other Gyalrong languages (in Tshobdun, see ), and one potential example is found in Khroskyabs. This prefix probably originates from the denominal nɯ- (§ sec:denom.tr.nW ), and replaced the older suffixal applicative, which only remains in a handful of examples (§
sec:applicative)

In addition to these examples, the nɤ- deideophonic verbs can be analyzed as applicative derivations from their a- deideophonic counterpart (§ sec:a.nA.deidph ).
summary:
The applicative prefix nɯ- increases valency by promoting an oblique argument, adjunct, or even non-participant to object function. In Japhug, the base verb is morphologically intransitive and the applicative verb transitive, while the subject remains the same referent but takes ergative rather than absolutive case.

The prefix is attested only in a limited set of examples, though its presence in a Tibetan loanword suggests some productivity. It has cognates in other Gyalrong languages and likely comes from an earlier denominal nɯ-, replacing an older suffixal applicative; some nɤ- deideophonic verbs may also be analyzed as applicative derivations.

subsection: The syntactic and semantic functions of the promoted argument
text: Despite the limited number of applicative verbs, there is a considerable diversity in the syntactic functions of the non-core arguments (of the base verbs) that are promoted to object status by the applicative derivation.
summary: Although applicative verbs are limited in number, they show considerable diversity in the syntactic roles of the non-core arguments they promote to object status. In other words, applicative derivation can objectivize a wide range of non-core arguments from the base verb.

subsection: The syntactic and semantic functions of the promoted argument
text:
promotion to object function
The verb aʑɯʑuwrestle, historically a reciprocal verb (§ sec:redp.lexicalized ), requires a non-singular subject and can select a comitative argument in cʰo (§ sec:comitative ). The object of the applicative form nɤʑɯʑuwrestle with corresponds to this comitative argument, as shown by the minimal pair ( ex:YAZWZundZi ) vs. ( ex:YAznAZWZu ).

exe

ɯ-zda cʰo ɲɯ-ɤʑɯʑu-ndʑi \\
3sg. poss -companion comit sens -wrestle- du \\
`He is wrestling with his friend.' (elicited)
exe

exe

ɯ-zda ɲɯ-ɤz-nɯ-ɤʑɯʑu \\
3sg. poss -companion sens - prog - appl -wrestle \\
`He is wrestling his friend.' (elicited)
exe
summary: The verb *aʑɯʑu* ‘wrestle’ is historically reciprocal, requires a non-singular subject, and can take a comitative argument marked in *cʰo*. In the applicative form *nɤʑɯʑu* ‘wrestle with,’ the object corresponds to this comitative argument, as shown by the contrast between ‘He is wrestling with his friend’ and ‘He is wrestling his friend.’

subsection: The syntactic and semantic functions of the promoted argument
text:
promotion to object function
In the case of the semi-transitive rgalike, the argument added by the applicative is the semi-object (§ sec:semi.transitive ). The base verb rga and its applicative form nɯrgalike are in some contexts semantically identical, for instance in the pseudo-clefts (§ sec:pseudo.cleft ) stu ji-kɤ-rga and stu ji-kɤ-nɯ-rga in ( ex:stu.jikArga.Cti ) and ( ex:stu.jikAnWrga.Cti ) which both mean `the one that we like most' (both objects and semi-objects can be relativized with the object participle § sec:object.participle.relatives, and the possessive prefix in both cases refers to the subject § sec:object.participle.possessive ).

exe

tɕe iʑo kɯrɯ ra tɕe tʂʰɤlu nɯ stu ji-kɤ-rga ɕti \\
lnk 1pl Tibetan pl lnk milk.tea dem most 1sg. poss - obj: pcp -like be. aff: fact \\
`Milk tea is [the type of tea] that we Tibetans like best.' (05-qaZo)
0003404#S152
exe

exe

tʰaχtsa nɯ iʑo kɯrɯ tɕʰeme ra ɣɯ, nɯnɯ mɤlɤn ʑo pjɯ-tu kɯ-ra tɕe, stu ji-kɤ-nɯ-rga ɕti, \\
coloured.belt dem 1pl Tibetan woman pl gen dem absolutely emph ipfv -exist sbj: pcp -be.needed lnk most 1pl. poss - obj: pcp - appl -like be. aff: fact \\
`Coloured belts are something that we Tibetan woman must absolutely have, and it is what we like best.' (thaXtsa 2002)
exe

In addition to morphological (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ) differences, as well as absolutive vs. ergative marking of the subject (§ sec:A.kW ), the base verb rga and its applicative nɯrga differ from each other in three regards.

First of all, rga displays lability between a semi-transitive use `like' and a stative intransitive use meaning `be happy' (compare ex:cha.pjArga and ex:wuma.Zo.pjArgandZi in § sec:semi.tr.labile ), while the applicative nɯrga does not mean `be happy because/for'.

Second, whereas the base verb rga can take infinitival complement clauses (§ sec:inf.complementation, § sec:velar.inf.coreference ), as in ( ex:kAnArtoXpjAt.pWrgaa2 ) (see also ex:tApAtso.pWkWNu, § sec:genr.3pl ), its applicative form nɯ-rga cannot: the applicative derivation thus removes complement-taking ability (at least in this case).

exe

ma aʑo [qajɯ nɯra kɤ-nɤrtoχpjɤt] pɯ-rga-a tɕe \\
lnk 1sg bug dem: pl inf -observe pst. ipfv -like- 1sg lnk \\
`I liked to observe bugs.' (26-quspunmbro)
0003684#S15
exe

Third, with first or second person objects, only the applicative nɯrga is possible. The local scenario 1 2 ( ex:YWtanWrga ) and 2 1 configurations (example ex:nAstu.Zo.WYWkWnWrgaa, § sec.IPN.adverbs ), as well as the mixed scenario inverse configurations ( ex:apWwGnWrgaa ) cannot be expressed with the base verb rga.

exe

ɲɯ-ta-nɤ-pe ɕti qʰe, aʑo ɲɯ-ta-nɯ-rga \\
sens -1 2- trop -be.good be. aff: fact lnk 1sg sens -1 2- appl -like \\
`I like you, I love you.' (160630 abao-zh)
0006197#S108
exe

exe

nɯnɯ rɟɤlpu ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ a-pɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-rga-a ra \\
dem king 3sg. poss -son dem erg irr - ipfv - inv - appl -like- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`May the prince love me!' (150819 haidenver-zh)
0006314#S497
exe
summary: The applicative of the semi-transitive verb *rga* adds a semi-object, and in some contexts the base form *rga* and applicative *nɯrga* are semantically equivalent, as in pseudo-cleft constructions meaning “the one that we like best.” However, they differ in several ways: *rga* is labile and can also mean “be happy,” while *nɯrga* cannot, and the applicative form loses the ability to take infinitival complement clauses. In addition, only *nɯrga* can be used with first- or second-person objects.

subsection: The syntactic and semantic functions of the promoted argument
text:
promotion to object function
The verbs andzɯtbark and akʰɤzŋgacall optionally select a dative argument ( tɯrme mɤ-kɤ-nɯfse nɯ `the person that it does not know' in ex:WCki.YAndzWt ), which is promoted to object status by the applicative ( ex:YAznAndzWt ).

exe

tɯrme mɤ-kɤ-nɯfse nɯ ɯ-ɕki ɲɯ-ɤndzɯt \\
person neg - obj: pcp -know dem 3sg. poss - dat sens -bark \\
`[The dog] is barking at the unknown person.' (elicited)
exe

exe

tɯrme mɤ-kɤ-nɯfse nɯ ɲɯ-ɤz-nɯ-ɤndzɯt \\
person neg - obj: pcp -know dem sens - prog - appl -bark \\
`[The dog] is barking at the unknown person.' (elicited)
exe
summary: The verbs *andzɯt* ‘bark’ and *akʰɤzŋga* ‘call’ can optionally take a dative argument, such as ‘the unknown person.’ With the applicative, this dative argument is promoted to object status, as shown in the example meaning ‘The dog is barking at the unknown person.’

subsection: The syntactic and semantic functions of the promoted argument
text:
For most applicative verbs, the object corresponds to an entirely new referent, without equivalent in the argument structure of the base verb. Based on the semantic role of the added argument, four sub-cases can be distinguished.

The semi-transitive verb stubelieve, like rgalike, is semi-transitive (§ sec:semi.transitive ). Its semi-object is either a complement clause or a noun such as ɯ-rju `his words', expressing the content of the utterance that is believed by the subject. Its (morphologically irregular, § sec:allomorphy.applicative ) applicative nɤstu takes as object the person uttering the words that are believed by the subject, as in ( ex:WYWkWnAstua ), which is not expressed as an argument of the base verb (with stubelieve the only way to express the person saying the words that are believed is as possessor of the semi-object).

exe

nɯnɯ aʑo ɯ-ɲɯ-kɯ-nɤ-stu-a nɤ, tɕendɤre, nɯɕimɯma ʑo ɕe-tɕi tɕe, \\
dem 1sg qu - sens -2 1- appl -believe- 1sg add lnk immediately emph go: fact - 1du lnk \\
`If you believe me, let us go [there] immediately.' (140425 shizi huli he lu-zh)
0003794#S41
exe

Examples like ( ex:manWtWnAste ) with the relative clause ɯʑo kɯ ta-tɯt `(the words) that he said' appearing before the verb could seem to imply that nɤstu can also select as object the words uttered. If this analysis were correct, the applicative nɤstu would be similar to nɯrgalike above in promoting the semi-object of its base verb as object. However, if the relative clause takes a second person subject as in ( ex:tAtWtWt.nW.mAstua ), it is possible either to use the base verb stubelieve or the applicative nɤstu with a second person object ( mɤ-ta-nɤstu `I don't believe you'), but not with a third person object, showing that in ( ex:manWtWnAste ) the relative clause is not the object, but an adjunct (the object of nɤstu in this example is the referent corresponding to the subject of the relative clause).

exe

[ɯʑo kɯ ta-tɯt] nɯ ma-nɯ-tɯ-nɤ-ste \\
1sg erg aor:3 -say[II] dem neg - imp -2- appl -believe[III] \\
`Don't believe what he said.' (elicited)
exe

exe

[nɤʑo tɤ-tɯ-tɯt] nɯ mɤ-stu-a \\
2sg aor -2-say[II] dem neg -believe: fact - 1sg \\
`I don't believe what you said.' (elicited)
exe

Other intransitive verbs with experiencer subject, such as bɯɣmiss home, mube afraid and sŋomenvy, have applicative forms that promote the stimulus as object. The base verb forms cannot select a noun or a complement clause to specify this stimulus, even as adjunct; the stimulus can only be indirectly expressed in a separate clause. In ( ex:YWmunW.chWphGonW ) for instance, the clause tɤ-tɕɯ... tu-ɣɤɕqali-nɯ `the men... shout' describes the reason for the fear of the animals; though it could be analyzed as the stimulus of the verb ɲɯ-mu-nɯ, the relationship between the two clauses is simply one of temporality/causation, and the verb mube afraid is unable to take any overt stimulus.

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ tʰamtɕɤt kɯ-dɯ dɤn nɯ ɣɯrnɤɣɯr ʑo tu-ɣɤɕqali-nɯ tɕe, tɕendɤre rɯdaʁ nɯra ɲɯ-mu-nɯ tɕe cʰɯ-pʰɣo-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
indef. poss -boy all sbj: pcp -be.many dem idph (III):noisy.and.crowded emph ipfv -shout- pl lnk lnk wild.animal dem: pl ipfv -be.afraid- pl lnk ipfv: downstream -flee- pl sens -be \\
`The men (i.e. the hunters) all shout together in great numbers, and the wild animals being afraid flee downstream.' (150829 KAGWcAno)
0006420#S9
exe

The corresponding applicative verb nɯɣmube afraid of marks the experiencer in the ergative, and takes the stimulus (in ex:YWkWnWGmu, tɯrmeperson) as object (note the generic object indexation, § sec:indexation.generic.tr ). The referent promoted as object by the applicative derivation in this verb is the same as that promoted to subject status by the proprietive sɤ(ɣ)- (see ex:pjAsAGmu.pjAnWGmu, § sec:proprietive ).

exe

nɯnɯ kɯ tɯrme wuma ʑo ɲɯ-kɯ-nɯɣ-mu. \\
dem erg people really emph ipfv - genr:S/O- appl -be.afraid \\
`It is very afraid of people.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S26
exe

The verb aɣroplay (almost always attested as a<nɯ>ɣro with infixation of the autive, § sec:autoben.position ), rarely occurs in the singular, and can select comitative arguments (§ sec:comitative ), as in ( ex:cho.YAnWGrondZi ).

exe

<xiaocui> nɯ tɤ-rɯstɯnmɯ ɯ-qʰu qʰe tɕe iɕqʰa [<yuanfeng> nɯ, taʁndo mɤ-kɯ-tso nɯ cʰo] sɲikuku ʑo tɯtɯrca ɲɯ-ɤ<nɯ>ɣro-ndʑi qʰe \\
anthr dem aor -marry 3sg. poss -after lnk lnk the.aforementioned anthr dem speech neg - sbj: pcp -understand dem comit every.day emph together ipfv -< auto >play- du lnk \\
`After she married, Xiaocui played every day with Yuanfeng, who did not understand speech.' (150909 xiaocui-zh)
0006386#S60
exe

However, unlike aʑɯʑuwrestle above, its applicative nɤɣroplay with does not promote the comitative argument (the person one plays with) to object status. Rather, it selects the instrument (the toy one plays with) as object. In ( ex:YWnAGrondZi ), the object of nɤɣro is not overt in the same clause, but anaphorically refers to kɯmtɕʰɯtoy in the previous clause.

exe

mɤʑɯ kɯmtɕʰɯ kɯ-fse tɤ-tu nɤ, tɯɣrɤz ɲɯ-nɯ-ɤɣro-ndʑi nɯra pjɤ-ŋgrɤl,\\
again toy sbj: pcp -be.like aor -exist add together ipfv - appl -play- du dem: pl ipfv. ifr -be.usually.the.case \\
`Whenever there was a toy$_i$, they( du ) played with it$_i$ together.' (lWlu)
exe
summary: The passage explains that applicative verbs often introduce a new object referent not present in the base verb’s argument structure, and that the added object can vary according to semantic role. In the case of *stubelieve*, the applicative *nɤstu* takes the speaker as object rather than the content believed, while with verbs like *mube afraid* the applicative promotes the stimulus to object status, since the base verb cannot overtly express that stimulus. It also notes that *aɣroplay* does not promote the comitative participant as object; instead, its applicative selects the instrument, such as a toy, as object.

subsection: The syntactic and semantic functions of the promoted argument
text:
The relationship between the transitive verb nɯzdɯɣworry about and the base verb zdɯɣsuffer (from སྡུག་sdugsuffering) is slightly different from the preceding cases, and it is disputable whether this verb is to be classified as applicative. The intransitive verb zdɯɣ has two different meanings: `be sad' when used with the nouns tɯ-sɯmmind or tɯ-sniheart as subjects, and the experiencer as possessor as in ( ex:Wsni.YAzdWG ), and `endure hardship' when taking a human (or non-human animal) subject ( ex:pjAzdWGndZi ). The meaning `worry' of the verb nɯzdɯɣ is not directly derivable from either. It is close to `to be sad about', but the transitive subject of nɯzdɯɣ corresponds to the possessor of the subject of zdɯɣ, making it a unique type of derivation.

exe

tɕʰemɤpɯ nɯ ɯ-sni ɲɤ-zdɯɣ \\
little.girl dem 3sg. poss -heart ifr -suffer \\
`The little girl was very sad.' (140504 huiguniang-zh)
0003909#S96
exe

exe

laʁnɯ-sŋi pjɤ-zdɯɣ-ndʑi tɕe, \\
one.or.two-day ifr. ipfv -suffer lnk \\
`They had [worked] hard for several days.' (qajdoskAt 2002) 0003366#S18
exe
summary: The verb **nɯzdɯɣ** ‘worry about’ is related to the intransitive base verb **zdɯɣ** ‘suffer,’ but its status as an applicative is uncertain. The base verb has two meanings: ‘be sad’ with subjects like ‘mind’ or ‘heart’ where the experiencer is expressed as a possessor, and ‘endure hardship’ with human or animal subjects; **nɯzdɯɣ** ‘worry’ is not directly derived from either, though its transitive subject corresponds to the possessor of the subject in **zdɯɣ**, making it a distinctive kind of derivation.

text:
applicative!allomorphy morphology!allomorphy allomorphy!applicative
The applicative prefix has three regular allomorphs: nɯ, nɯɣ- and nɤ-. A similar allomorphy is found in other Gyalrong languages, see on Tshobdun. The allomorph nɯɣ- has the same distribution as the sɯɣ- allomorph of the causative (§ sec:caus.sWG ), occurring with monosyllabic intransitive verb roots whose onset does not contain a cluster and/or a velar consonant. The allomorph nɤ- (homophonous with the tropative, § sec:tropative.allomorphy ) is due to vowel fusion with the contracting a- in some verb stems (§ sec:contraction; the de-contracted form nɯ-ɤ- is used in some of the discussion in this section), with the exception of the verb stubelieve whose applicative is irregular.

The allomorph nɯ- occurs in all other contexts. It is homophonous with the autive (§ sec:autobenefactive ), the vertitive (§ sec:vertitive ) and various other prefixes, including the westwards orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) and the denominal nɯ- (§ sec:denom.nW ), but ambiguity is rare as these prefixes belong to different slots (§ sec:prefixal.chain ). For an example of partial ambiguity between autive and applicative, see examples ( ex:CtAnWNke ) and ( ex:tukWnWNke ) in § sec:applicative.lexicalized.
summary:
The applicative prefix has three regular allomorphs: nɯ, nɯɣ-, and nɤ-.
