The allomorph nɯɣ- occurs with monosyllabic intransitive verb roots lacking a cluster or velar in the onset, while nɤ- results from vowel fusion with a contracting a- in certain verb stems; one verb, *believe*, has an irregular applicative.

The default form nɯ- appears elsewhere. Although nɯ- is homophonous with several other prefixes, ambiguity is usually limited because these prefixes occupy different positions in the prefix chain.

text:
Three of the applicative verbs in tab:applicative are highly lexicalized and cannot be considered to be synchronically analyzable as related to their base verbs.

First, the transitive verb nɤkʰuinvite (to one's home as a guest, see examples in § sec:bare.inf.coreference and § sec:object.participles.complement ) originates from the applicative nɯ-ɤkʰu of akʰucall, meaning `call (someone), shout at'. The verb akʰu can select a locative goal (referring to the direction where one calls), as in ( ex:CtokAkhuci ), and its applicative nɯ-ɤkʰu presumably originally promoted this oblique argument to object status.

exe

kʰa nɯtɕu ɕ-to-k-ɤkʰu-ci \\
house dem: loc tral - ifr - peg -call- peg \\
`He went and called in the direction of the house.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

At that earlier stage, nɯ-ɤkʰu probably used to have a meaning similar to that of nɯ-ɤkʰɤzŋga `shout at', the applicative of akʰɤzŋgacall, `shout' (a verb related to and synonymous with akʰucall). As shown by ( ex:tuwGnAkhAzNganW ), the applicative nɤkʰɤzŋgashout at selects the goal/addressee as object (the plural marking on the verb form which here indexes the object being due to the presence of the inverse prefix, see 3$'$ 3pl in § sec:indexation.non.local ).

exe

tɕʰeme ɯ-skɤt kɯ-snɯ sna ci kɯ ʑo tú-wɣ-nɯ-ɤkʰɤzŋga-nɯ ntsɯ. \\
girl 3sg. poss -voice sbj: pcp - emph nice indef erg emph ipfv - inv - appl -call- pl always \\
`A girl who had a beautiful voice was calling them.' (2003kandZislama)
exe

The applicative nɯ-ɤkʰu however underwent the semantic change `call $X$' $ $ `call $X_i$ to invite him/her$_i$ to come as guest' $ $ `invite $X$ to come as guest', so that its etymological relationship with its base verb akʰucall is not synchronically obvious anymore.

Second, nɯŋkelook for is formally an applicative of the atelic motion verb ŋkewalk (§ sec:motion.verbs ). The promoted object corresponds to the aim of the motion (the entity that the subject is searching), as in ( ex:CtAnWNke ).

exe

ji-<baogao> tɤ-lɤt, <piaozi> ɕ-tɤ-nɯŋke, <dianzhan> βzu-j ŋu \\
1pl. poss -report imp -release money tral - imp -look.for electric.station make: fact - 1pl be: fact \\
`Make a report for us, go and look for money, and we will build an electrical station.' (2010-09)
exe

This verb should not be confused with the regular autive nɯ-ŋke of the verb ŋkewalk, which is intransitive, as shown by the generic kɯ- in ( ex:tukWnWNke ) (§ sec:intr.23 ).

exe

tɯ-ji ɯ-ŋgɯ aʁɤndɯndɤt tu-kɯ-nɯ-ŋke kʰɯ tɕe \\
indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -in everywhere ipfv - genr:S/O- auto -walk be.possible: fact lnk \\
`One can walk [on this path] everywhere in the fields [as one wishes].' (15-06-05)
exe

Third, the transitive verb nɤmdzɯlook after historically derives from the intransitive amdzɯsit by the applicative derivation. Its original meaning probably was `sit by', with a locative adjunct promoted to object status, but in Japhug it rather means `stay near $X$ and look after $X$' without necessary implication of remaining seated, as in ( ex:kuWGnAmdzW.YWra ).

exe

tɤ-lu koŋla ʑo kú-wɣ-nɤmdzɯ ɲɯ-ra ma ʁlɤwur ʑo tu-mbuz ɲɯ-ŋu \\
indef. poss -milk completely emph ipfv - inv -look.after sens -be.needed lnk immediately emph ipfv -spill.out sens -be \\
`One has to look after the milk [in the pan], otherwise it will overflow as soon as [it boils].' (elicited)
exe
summary: Three applicative verbs in the table are now highly lexicalized and no longer transparently analyzable as derivatives of their base verbs. The verbs **nɤkʰu** ‘invite’, **nɯŋke** ‘look for’, and **nɤmdzɯ** ‘look after’ each historically involved applicative promotion of an oblique argument, but their meanings have shifted enough that their relation to the original verbs is no longer synchronically obvious.

text:
applicative!compatibility
The applicative derivation cannot take any other derived verb form as input. The only partial exception is the applicative nɤʑɯʑuwrestle with, whose base form aʑɯʑuwrestle historically was a reciprocal verb (§ sec:redp.lexicalized ), but since it is an already fossilized reciprocal, it does not demonstrative the ability of the applicative to apply to reciprocal forms in general.

On the other hand, applicative verb forms can be subjected to further derivations, including the reflexive ʑɣɤ- ( ʑɣɤ-nɤ-stu refl - appl -believe `believe in oneself', see example ex:mWYAZGAnAstu, § sec:refl.tropative ) and the sigmatic causative ( ex:YWznWsNomanW ). In this example, the 1sg is both causer (indexed as transitive subject) and patient, while the causee (`the people') is indexed as object..

exe

tɯrme ra, ʑimkʰɤm ʑo, ɲɯ-z-nɯ-sŋom-a-nɯ cʰa-a \\
people pl many emph ipfv - caus - appl -envy- 1sg - pl can: fact - 1sg \\
`I will be able to make a lot of people envy [me for my dress].' (jinai de guniang-zh)
exe

The problematic verb nɯzdɯɣworry about (§ sec:nWzdWG ) can in addition serve as input to the proprietive derivation (§ sec:proprietive.compatibility ).
summary: The applicative derivation generally cannot take another derived verb as its input, with only a historical fossilized reciprocal form as a partial exception. However, applicative forms can themselves undergo further derivations, such as the reflexive and sigmatic causative, and the verb nɯzdɯ “worry about” can also function as input to the proprietive derivation.

text:
tropative
The tropative This term is taken from Arabic linguistics, see for instance. Another possible term for this derivation would be `estimative'. nɤ- prefix is a valency-increasing derivation creating a transitive verb meaning `find/consider to be $X$' out of an intransitive stative verb. Cognate prefixes are found in other Gyalrong languages, (, ).

The tropative resembles the causative derivations in that the subject of the base verb becomes the object of the derived verb, and the added argument is the transitive subject (unlike the applicative). However, the semantic role of the transitive subject is not an agent (causer), but an experiencer.

For instance, the tropative of the stative verb mpɕɤrbe beautiful is the transitive nɤmpɕɤrfind beautiful, whose object is the entity considered to be beautiful ( iɕqʰa tɕʰeme `the girl' in ex:YAnAmpCAr.YAnApe ), and whose transitive subject in the ergative is the person feeling the beauty of the object ( tɤru ɯ-tɕɯ `the prince' in ex:YAnAmpCAr.YAnApe ).

exe

tɕe nɯ tɤru ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ nɯɕimɯma ʑo iɕqʰa tɕʰeme nɯ ɲɤ-nɤ-mpɕɤr,
tɕe ɲɤ-nɤ-pe. \\
lnk dem chieftain 3sg. poss -son dem erg immediately emph the.aforementioned girl dem ifr - trop -be.beautiful lnk ifr - trop -be.good \\
`The prince immediately found the girl very beautiful and fell in love with her.' (140518 huifei de muma-zh)
0004026#S51
exe

The tropative derivation is extremely productive, and tab:tropative illustrates a few representative examples.

The semantics of the derived verb is not always simply `consider/find $X$'. In the case of stative verbs whose meaning is neutral (not explicitly positive like `beautiful'), the tropative often has the additional meaning `find too $X$', as in ( ex:WYWtWnAxtCi ) for instance.

exe

nɤ-sɤtɕʰa ɯ-ɲɯ-tɯ-nɤ-xtɕi nɤ, aʑo a-βlu ci tu tɕe, \\
2sg. poss -place qu - sens -2- trop -be.small add 1sg 1sg. poss -trick indef exist: fact lnk \\
`If you find this place too small for you, I have an idea.' (150829 taishan zhi zhu-zh,203)
0006350#S196
exe

The tropative nɤ- cannot be prefixed to non-adjectival stative verbs like copulas ( ŋube, ɕtibe) or existential verbs ( tuexist, menot exist). A meaning such as `consider $X$ to be $Y$', where both $X$ and $Y$ are nouns, cannot be expressed in Japhug using a tropative derivation (forms such as $ $ nɤ-ŋu or $ $ nɤ-tu are utterly incorrect), and a synthetic construction must be used instead (§ sec:tropative.sWpa ).

An apparent exception could seem to be nɤɣmaʁconsider wrong from the negative copula maʁnot be. However, this verb never means `consider $X$ not to be $Y$', and it seems that one of the original meanings of maʁ was `not to be right', as shown by a lexicalized form such as the fossilized participle kɯmaʁbad thing (from `(something) which is not right', § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ). In this example the tropative preserved the original meaning of the verb, while the base verb underwent an independent semantic change (already at the common Gyalrong stage).

The ability to undergo tropativization is thus a criterion for identifying a sub-class of adjectives among stative verbs (with the exception of some derived adjectives, which are not compatible with the tropative possibly for morphological reasons, § sec:tropative.other.derivations ).
summary:
The tropative is a productive valency-increasing derivation in Japhug, marked by the prefix **nɤ-**, which turns an intransitive stative verb into a transitive verb meaning ‘find/consider to be X.’ In this construction, the base verb’s subject becomes the object of the derived verb, while the added transitive subject is an experiencer rather than an agent.  

The passage notes that tropativization is not possible with non-adjectival stative verbs such as copulas or existential verbs, and that constructions like ‘consider X to be Y’ with two nouns cannot be formed this way. Because of this restriction, the ability to take the tropative serves as a diagnostic for a subclass of adjectives among stative verbs.

text:
tropative!allomorphy morphology!allomorphy allomorphy!tropative
As shown by tab:tropative, aside from the regular nɤ- allomorph, a few verbs select a nɤɣ- / nɤx- allomorph. A similar allomorphy is observed on the sigmatic causative (§ sec:caus.sWG ) and the applicative (§ sec:allomorphy.applicative ) prefixes. The sɯ- / sɯɣ- alternation of the sigmatic causative is still productive: the latter allomorph occurs when the original verb is intransitive, without an initial consonant cluster and without initial velar or uvular. It is possible that a similar distribution used to exist at a former stage for the nɤ- / nɤɣ- allomorphs, but the data at hand do not permit a firm conclusion.

The nɤ- allomorph of the tropative is homophonous with that of the applicative before a- contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction, § sec:allomorphy.applicative ), but there are no cases of forms that are ambiguous between these two derivations.

When two base verbs have stems that only differ in the presence vs. absence of an a- prefixal element, their tropative form is identical. For instance, the stative verbs amtɕoʁbe pointy and mtɕoʁbe sharp (§ sec:a.non.passive.denominal ) have the same tropative nɤmtɕoʁ, which can be interpreted as either `find pointy' or `find sharp'.
summary:
The tropative prefix normally appears as nɤ-, but a small number of verbs take an alternant nɤɣ- / nɤx-. This alternation resembles patterns found in the sigmatic causative and applicative prefixes, although only the causative alternation is still productively conditioned by the phonological shape of the base verb; the text says a similar historical conditioning for the tropative is possible but unproven.  

The nɤ- allomorph is homophonous with the applicative prefix before a-contracted verbs, but no forms are actually ambiguous between the two analyses. When two verbs differ only by the presence or absence of an a- prefix, their tropative forms are identical, as shown by pairs like amtɕoʁbe and mtɕoʁbe, both yielding nɤmtɕoʁ.

text:
Past Imperfective!tropative tropative! Past Imperfective
Tropative verbs stand out among transitive verbs in that they are compatible with Past Imperfective pɯ- and Inferential imperfective pjɤ- forms as in (§ sec:pWwGnAmWm ) (see also ex:mWpWnAsAscita in § sec:tropative.other.derivations below), unlike most transitive verbs which require the progressive asɯ- to occur with these TAME prefixes (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv ).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-tɕur mɤ-tɕʰom tɕe, pɯ́-wɣ-nɤ-mɯm ɕti. \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -sour neg -be.exceedingly: fact lnk pst. ipfv - inv - trop -be.tasty be. aff: fact \\
`It is not too sour, and we used to find it tasty.' (17-ndZWnW)
0003524#S54
exe

The use of the Inferential or the Perfective with tropative verbs indicates a change of state. For instance, to-nɤ-mɯm ifr - trop -be.tasty) means `(he used not to find it tasty, but now) he finds it tasty'.
summary: Tropative verbs are exceptional among transitive verbs because they can combine with Past Imperfective pɯ- and Inferential imperfective pjɤ- forms, whereas most transitive verbs require the progressive asɯ- with these TAME prefixes. The Inferential or Perfective with tropative verbs signals a change of state, indicating that something that was previously not perceived as tasty is now found tasty.

text:
Some tropative verbs have specialized meanings that are not completely predictable from the base verb. Thus, nɤ-pe (tropative of pebe good), in addition to its regular meaning `consider to be good', can also used in the sense of `love', as in ( ex:YAnAmpCAr.YAnApe ) above. The tropative of the modal auxiliary ntsʰihave better (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ), nɤntsʰi, also has this meaning ( ex:anWwGnAntshia ). Since the etymological relationship between the base verb ntsʰihave better and nɤntsʰilove is not synchronically transparent, the nɤ- is not analyzed as a prefix in the glosses.

exe

aʑo a-nɯ́-wɣ-nɤntsʰi-a ra \\
1sg irr - pfv - inv -love- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`[Aladin thought] `May the princess love me.'' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S187
exe

The transitive verb nɤkʰebully from kʰebe stupid, probably also used to be a tropative verb `consider to be stupid', with a quite unpredictable semantic evolution.

The perception verb nɤmnɤmsmell (vt) is formally a tropative derived from the intransitive mnɤmsmell (vi), a verb that can only take nouns meaning `smell' (such as the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-dismell) as subject, as shown by ( ex:Wdi.mnAm ).

exe

nɯnɯ ɕɤɣ nɯ wuma ʑo pe, tɕe pjɯ́-wɣ-βlɯ tɕe ɯ-di wuma mnɤm \\
dem juniper dem really emph be.good: fact lnk ipfv - inv -burn lnk 3sg. poss -smell really have.a.smell: fact \\
`The juniper is very nice, when one burns it, it has a strong smell.' (08-CAG)
0003442#S13
exe

The tropative nɤmnɤm can take as object a noun meaning `smell', with the referent whose smell is perceived encoded as a possessive prefix on the object (for instance the 3pl prefix on the noun nɯ-di `their smell' in ex:nWdi.tunAmnAm ). However, unlike its base verb, nɤmnɤm can also directly select as object the referent whose smell is perceived, including even a first or second person as in ( ex:tutanAmnAm ).

exe

srɯtpʰu nɯ kɯ, ŋotɕu rɤʑi-nɯ pjɤ-sɯχsɤl matɕi, nɯ-di tu-nɤ-mnɤm pjɤ-ɕti tɕe pjɤ-mtsʰɤm. \\
râkshasa dem erg where stay: fact - pl ifr -realize lnk 3pl. poss -smell ipfv - trop -have.a.smell ifr. ipfv -be. aff lnk ifr -feel \\
`The ogre realized where they where, as it was sniffing them out and perceived [their smell].' (160706 poucet6)
0006109#S49
exe

exe

jɤ-ɣi tɕe, pɤjkʰu tu-ta-nɤ-mnɤm \\
imp -come lnk still ipfv: up -1 2- trop -have.a.smell \\
`Come (here), I will smell you (to see if you have had alcohol).' (140506 loBzi)
0003923#S11
exe

Example ( ex:nWdi.tunAmnAm ) also shows that nɤmnɤm expresses volitional olfactory perception (looking for something by paying attention to smell). Its non-volitional counterpart is mtsʰɤm in the sense of `perceive (a smell) inadvertently; find (by smell)'. The verb mtsʰɤm expresses non-visual non-volitional perception (§ sec:preverb.perception ), not only auditory (in the meaning `hear'), but also olfactory as in ( ex:nWdi.tunAmnAm ).
summary:
Some tropative verbs have meanings that go beyond the predictable “consider X to be Y” sense. For example, the tropatives nɤ-pe and nɤntsʰi can mean “love,” and nɤkʰe may have developed a similarly unpredictable meaning from “stupid.”  

The passage also explains that nɤmnɤm is a tropative based on the intransitive verb “smell,” but it differs from its base verb in allowing either a possessed noun meaning “smell” or directly the referent being smelled as object. It further contrasts volitional olfactory perception with the non-volitional verb mtsʰɤm, which means perceiving a smell inadvertently.

text:
tropative!compatibility
In addition to underived stative verbs as in tab:tropative above, the tropative derivation can also take verbs with the proprietive sɤ- derivation (§ sec:proprietive )

One of the most common of such verbs is nɤsɤscitfind pleasant (of a place, a situation, an event) from the proprietive sɤscitbe pleasant (`be such that people feel happy with/in it') of the stative verb scitbe happy. In the excerpt from a conversation in ( ex:sAscit.nAsAscit ), we see that the tropative mɯ-pɯ-nɤ-sɤ-scit-a ( ex:mWpWnAsAscita ) occurs in answer to a question with the proprietive verb ɯ-pɯ́-sɤ-scit ( ex:WpWsAscit ).

exe

xlist

(T) atu tɤʁaʁ ɯ-pɯ́-sɤ-scit? [...] \\
up.there party qu - pst. ipfv - prop -be.happy \\
`Was the party up there nice?'

(L) pɯ-sɤ-scit a-ɬaʁ, mɤ-kɯ-sɤ-scit pɯ-me \\
pst. ipfv - prop -be.happy 1sg. poss -MZ neg - sbj: pcp - prop -be.happy pst. ipfv -not.exist \\
`It was nice, mother-in-law, there was nothing that was not nice.'

(A) aʑo ndɤre mɯ-pɯ-nɤ-sɤ-scit-a, lo-nɯtɕʰomba-a \\
1sg lnk neg - pst. ipfv - trop - prop -be.happy- 1sg ifr -have.a.cold- 1sg \\
`As far as I am concerned, I did not find [that party] nice, I caught a cold.' (TaRrdo2003)
xlist
exe

The antonym of nɤsɤscit, nɤsɤɣdɯɣfind unpleasant, is also the tropative of a proprietive verb sɤɣdɯɣbe unpleasant from the base verb dɯɣhave enough of, `be upset'. Both scit and dɯɣ are Tibetan loanwords (from སྐྱིད་skʲidbe happy and སྡུག་sdugsuffer, respectively), showing the productivity of this double derivation. While no other examples of this double derivation are found in the corpus, it is possible to elicit additional examples (§ sec:proprietive.compatibility ).

exe

nɯnɯ ɯ-rme ɯ-ŋgɯ ri ku-ɕe tɕe tɕendɤre ku-ɕe nɤ ku-ɕe tɕe tɕe ɯ-ndʐi ɯ-ŋgɯ ri ku-otsa ɲɯ-ŋu. tɕe fsapaʁ ra kɯ nɯ nɤ-sɤɣ-dɯɣ-nɯ ŋgrɤl ma \\
dem 3sg. poss -hair 2sg. poss -in loc ipfv: east -go lnk lnk ipfv: east -go add ipfv: east -go lnk lnk 3sg. poss -skin 3sg. poss -in loc ipfv -prick sens -be lnk animal pl erg dem trop - prop -be.upset: fact - pl be.usually.the.case: fact lnk \\
`[Its seeds] go into the hair [of the sheep], deeper and deeper, and stick into their skin, and the animals find this unpleasant.' (19-khWlu)
0003540#S96
exe

The tropative-proprietive verbs nɤsɤscit and nɤsɤɣdɯɣ take as transitive subject (with the ergative in ex:fsapaR.ra.kW.nAsAGdWGnW ) the experiencer (like the base verbs scitbe happy and dɯɣhave enough of) and as object the stimulus (the situation or place causing the feeling, like the proprietive verbs sɤscitbe pleasant and sɤɣdɯɣbe unpleasant).

The tropative is also attested with the subject-oriented facilitative ɣɤ- (§ sec:facilitative.GA ). For instance, from ɣɤβzibecome drunk easily (facilitative of βziget drunk) one can derive the tropative nɤɣɤβzi `consider that $X$ becomes drunk easily' ( ex:YWtAnAGABzi ).

exe

nɤʑo ndɤre ɲɯ-ta-nɤ-ɣɤ-βzi \\
2sg lnk sens -1 2- trop - facil -be.drunk \\
`You, I think that you get drunk easily.' (elicited)
exe

Distributed property verbs such amɯzɣɯtbe evenly distributed (§ sec:distributed.amW ) can undergo the tropative derivation ( nɤmɯzɣɯt `consider that $X$ is evenly distributed', for instance about colours), though such uses are uncommon.

The tropative cannot take as input any other type of derived stative verbs, such as the passive (§ sec:passive ), and more surprisingly the nɯɣɯ- facilitative (§ sec:facilitative.nWGW ).

Tropative verbs can in their turn serve as input for other derivations, including causative (§ sec:sig.caus.other.derivations ), reflexive (§ sec:refl.tropative ) and reciprocal (§ sec:reciprocal.other ). A related derivation whose meaning is close to that of a reflexivized tropative is the auto-evaluative znɤ- (§ sec:autoevaluative ).
summary:
The tropative derivation can also apply to certain derived stative verbs, especially those built with the proprietive sɤ- and, more rarely, the facilitative ɣɤ- or distributed-property verbs. In these cases, the tropative keeps the experiencer as transitive subject and the stimulus as object, as shown by forms meaning ‘find pleasant/unpleasant’ or ‘consider that someone gets drunk easily.’  

This double derivation appears productive, though only a few examples occur in the corpus, and the tropeative cannot take some other derived statives such as passives or nɯɣɯ- facilitative forms. Tropative verbs can themselves undergo further derivations, including causative, reflexive, and reciprocal.

text:
causative!tropative tropative!causative
Apart from the tropative nɤ, tropative meaning can be expressed in Japhug by the sigmatic causative in a few cases (§ sec:sig.caus.tropative ), the velar causative (§ sec:velar.causative.tropative ) and by periphrastic constructions (§ sec:tropative.sWpa ).

Other derivations with a tropative meaning include the rɤ(ɣ)- prefix in rɤɣrɯɣcherish (from rɯɣbe precious, § sec:rA.non.apass ), and the reflexive ʑɣɤ- of some intransitive verbs (§ sec:refl.intr ).
summary: Besides the tropative nɤ, Japhug can express tropative meaning in a few other ways: the sigmatic causative, the velar causative, and periphrastic constructions. Additional tropative-like derivations include the rɤ(ɣ)- prefix in rɤɣrɯɣ “cherish” and the reflexive ʑɣɤ- used with some intransitive verbs.

text:
passive contracting verb vowel!contraction
The passive derivation is marked by the prefix a, a formative also found in the reciprocal derivation (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ) and probably of denominal origin (§ sec:applicative.history ). It derives an intransitive verb from a transitive one, whose intransitive subject corresponds to the object of the base verb ( tɤscozletter in ex:rAt and ex:arAt ). The derivation also affects the dynamicity of the verb and the TAME (§ sec:passive.stative ). The transitive subject cannot be expressed: passive verbs do not take overt agents.

exe

xlist

ɯʑo kɯ tɤscoz rɤt \\
3sg erg letter write: fact \\
`S/he will write a/the letter.' (elicited)

tɤscoz a-rɤt \\
letter pass -write: fact \\
`The letter is written/has been written.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

Like other verbs in a, passive verbs present vowel contraction and insertion of the peg circumfix k-...-ci in Inferential forms (§ sec:ifr.morphology, § sec:preverbs.contracting.verbs ), as in ( ex:pjAkAGAtWGci ) (where it is realized as -ɤ, following the rule in § sec:contraction ). In the Kamnyu dialect, the peg circumfix, although originally a secondary marker, has almost become the main exponent of the passive in the Inferential tenses.

exe

kɯm ɲɤ-stʰoʁ ri, kɯm pjɤ-k-ɤ-ɣɤtɯɣ-ci ɕti tɕe, \\
door ifr -push lnk dem ifr. ipfv - peg - pass -lock- peg be: aff: fact lnk \\
`He pushed the door, but the door was locked.' (tWJo 2012) 0004089#S20
exe

tab:passive presents a few representative examples of passive verbs, including lexicalized ones whose meaning has become slightly shifted from that of the base verb (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ). The presence of Tibetan loanwords such as rtsicount (from རྩི་rtsicount) among the base verbs shows that the passive derivation is still productive.

The passive derivation only removes transitive subjects, and passivized verbs preserve oblique arguments or adjuncts. For instance, like the verb βraʁattach to, which includes a locative argument in its argument structure, the passive form aβraʁbe attached to also selects a locative phrase, with a locative case as in ( ex:xtWrkW.aBraR ) or in absolutive form as in ( ex:kWmqhu.pjAkABraRci ).

exe

stuxsi ɣɯ ɯ-χcɤl ri xtɯrkɯ a-βraʁ, \\
double.yoke gen 3sg. poss -middle loc hide.ripe pass -attach: fact \\
`The hide rope [connecting the yoke to the plough] is attached in the middle of the double yoke.' (24-mbGo) 0003621
exe

exe

tɤ-mu nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯm-qʰu pjɤ-k-ɤ-βraʁ-ci tɕe,\\
indef. poss -mother dem gen 3sg. poss -son dem door-back ipfv - peg - pass -attach- peg lnk \\
`The old woman's son was attached on the back of the door.' (tWJo 2012) 0004089#S61
exe

The passive derivation also applies to some noun-verb collocations. For instance, in ( ex:sAcW.malAt ), passivized verb a-lɤt, meaning `be locked' in collocation with the noun sɤcɯkey, has a meaning directly derived from that of the collocation of sɤcɯ with the base verb lɤtrelease, which means `lock (the door)' (§ sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle ). The noun sɤcɯkey is a semi-object (§ sec:semi.object ) in this collocation. The intransitive subject of (sɤcɯ) a-lɤt `be locked' in ( ex:sAcW.malAt ) is kɯmdoor.

exe

kɯm sɤcɯ mɤ-a-lɤt \\
door key neg - pass -release: fact \\
`The door is not locked/has not been locked.' (140428 xiaohongmao-zh) 0003884#S74
exe

Passive verb forms are almost never attested in first or second person forms, except for the highly lexicalized passives apabecome and aβzubecome, grow (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ). Example ( ex:parkua ) with arkube in Although this passive verb is used as a semi-lexicalized existential verb (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ), in this particular context it can be interpreted as expressing a resultative state with a definite agent. shows that there is not absolute constraints against first or second person indexation on passive verbs.

exe

nɯnɯ pʰoŋ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu pɯ-a-rku-a \\

dem bottle 3sg. poss -in dem: loc pst. ipfv - pass -put.in- 1sg \\

`(You don't believe that) I had been put inside this bottle.' (140512 yufu yu mogui-zh) 0003973#S111
exe

The historical hypothesis in (§ sec:portmanteau.prefixes.history ) proposes that the 1 2 portmanteau prefix ta- originates from the fusion of the passive a- with the second person tɯ- prefix indexing the object. If correct, this scenario implies that first or second person indexation on passive verbs may have been more common in proto-Gyalrong than in Japhug.
summary:
The passive derivation is marked by the prefix a-, which also appears in the reciprocal derivation and likely has denominal origin. It turns a transitive verb into an intransitive one whose subject corresponds to the base verb’s object, removes overt agents, and can affect the verb’s dynamicity and TAM interpretation; passive forms also show vowel contraction and, in Inferential forms, may use the peg circumfix k-...-ci, especially in the Kamnyu dialect.

The passive remains productive, as shown by regular use with both native and Tibetan loan verb bases, and it preserves oblique arguments or adjuncts rather than deleting them. Although passive forms are rarely attested with first- or second-person indexing, such forms do occur, particularly with lexicalized passives, and this has been linked to a historical hypothesis about the origin of the 1/2 portmanteau prefix ta-.

subsection: The interaction of the Passive derivation with Dynamicity and TAME
text:
passive!TAME
With the exception of apabecome and aβzubecome, grow (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ), passive verbs express resultative states. They are mainly attested in the Past Imperfective ( ex:parkua ) and in the Inferential Imperfective ( ex:kWmqhu.pjAkABraRci, see also ex:pjAkAmphWrci in § sec:passive.agent ). In combination with the Factual Non-Past the passive means `$X$ has already been $Y$ed' or `$X$ is $Y$ed' (where $X$ represents the object of the base verb $Y$) as in ( ex:marAt ) (see also ex:arAt and ex:sAcW.malAt above).

exe

jaʁmɤzdoʁzdoʁ nɯ kɯnɤ pɣa ŋu, mɤ-a-rɤt \\
bird.sp. dem also bird be: fact neg - pass -write: fact \\
`The jaʁmɤzdoʁzdoʁ is also a bird, it is not written (in the list of bird's names that had been prepared beforehand to ask about all known bird species).' (23-RmWrcWftsa) 0003610#S80
exe

Examples of passive verbs in Perfective or Inferential forms are very rare. In ( ex:koKAYJoRci ), the form ko-k-ɤ-ɲɟoʁ-ci can only be interpreted as the Inferential of the passive of ɲɟoʁglue, paste, with a meaning `(the spit) got glued (on her)' that does not seem interpretable as resultative.

exe

tɕelo kutɕu a-mci ci s-cʰɯ-βde-a, nɯ ɕɯ ɣɯ ndʑi-taʁ kɤ-kɯ-ɤ-ɲɟoʁ nɯ a-rʑaβ a-pɯ-tɯ-ŋu-ndʑi to-ti ri [...] tɕe ci s-cʰo-βde ri, rŋɯlɤsmɤn ɯ-taʁ ko-k-ɤ-ɲɟoʁ-ci ɕti ri, jaʁmɤcʰɯqa kɯ ɲɤ-nɯ-pɕiz qʰe ɯʑo ɯ-taʁ ko-nɯ-ɲɟoʁ. \\
upstream dem. prox: loc 1sg. poss -saliva once tral - ipfv: downstream -throw- 1sg, dem who gen 2du. poss -on aor - sbj: pcp - pass -glue dem 1sg. poss -wife irr - ipfv -2-be- du ifr -say lnk lnk once tral - ifr: downstream -throw lnk anthr 3sg. poss -on ifr - peg - pass -glue- peg be. aff: fact lnk anthr erg ifr - auto -wipe lnk 3sg 3sg. poss -on ifr - auto -glue \\
`He said `I will spit from here, and whoever of you two gets glued by my spit will be my wife.' He spat, and although [his spit] got glued on Rngulasman, Yagmakhyiqa wiped it off and pasted it onto herself.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

The participle kɤkɤɲɟoʁ in this example could in principle either be parsed as a an perfective object participle kɤ-kɤ-ɲɟoʁ ( aor - obj: pcp -glue) or perfective subject passive participle kɤ-kɯ-ɤ-ɲɟoʁ ( aor - sbj: pcp - pass -glue), but only the second option is likely, due to the fact that the gluing action is spontaneous and lacks an agent. Note in addition that the relativized element is the referent marked with the oblique relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:WtaR ). The fact that ɲɟoʁglue, paste lacks an anticausative (§ sec:anticausative ) and that the passive form aɲɟoʁ is used with an anticausative-like meaning (§ sec:passive.agent ) may explain why the perfective forms are possible with this verb.
summary:
Passive verbs generally express resultative states, except for the lexicalized forms apabecome and aβzubecome, grow. They are most commonly found in the Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective, and with the Factual Non-Past they mean either that something has already been done to X or that X is currently in the state of being Y-ed.  

Passive forms in the Perfective or Inferential are very rare; when they do occur, they may be interpreted as spontaneous or agentless events rather than straightforward resultatives. The passage illustrates this with forms of ɲɟoʁ ‘glue, paste,’ whose passive can appear in such contexts because the verb lacks an anticausative and the passive can take on an anticausative-like meaning.

text:
The verbs pado (§ sec:pa.lv ) and βzumake (§ sec:Bzu.lv ) have lexicalized passive forms that are used as quasi-copulas apabecome and aβzubecome, grow taking a semi-object serving as nominal predicate (§ sec:copula.basic ), for instance tɕʰiwhat in ( ex:anWtABzu ) or tɯrme (ci) `a human' in ( ex:anApa ) (for additional examples, see ex:nWnWra.pGa.nWra in § sec:demonstrative.determiners, ex:YAkABzuaci and ex:YAtABzu in § sec:preverbs.contracting.verbs ). In addition, aβzu is also used as a plain intransitive verb meaning `grow'.

exe

nɤʑo tɕʰi a-nɯ-tɯ-ɤβzu ra? \\
2sg what irr - pfv -2-become be.needed: fact \\
`What do you [want to] become?' (2003kandZislama)
exe

exe

tɯrme ci a-nɯ-ɤpa-a kɯ, tɯrme ɲɯ-ɤβzu-a ci a-pɯ-kʰɯ kɯ \\
human indef irr - pfv -become- 1sg sfp human ipfv -become- 1sg a.little irr - ipfv -be.possible sfp \\
`If only I could become a human!' (150819 haidenver-zh)
0006314#S229
exe

In the perfective, the third person forms of aβzubecome, grow have an identical surface form with those of the transitive βzumake: for instance naβzu can be either parsed as nɯ-aβzu ( aor -become) or as na-βzu ( aor:3 -make). Since the transitive βzu has dummy subject functions (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), in examples such as ( ex:Wmat.thaBzu ), it is possible to analyze the form tʰaβzu as tʰa-βzu ( aor:3 -make) instead.

exe

ɯ-mat tʰɯ-aβzu tɕe tɕe \\
3sg. poss -fruit aor -grow lnk lnk \\
`When its fruits grow...' (06-zrAntCW) 0003422#S25
exe

The verbs taput and rkuput in have passive forms whose meaning is still predictable from the base verb, atabe on and arkube in. However, these passive forms generally serve as existential verbs (§ sec:existential.basic ) as in ( ex:Wsno.ata ) and ( ex:WNgW.arku ), without the implication that the state results from a manipulative action. While in ( ex:Wsno.ata ) one could argue that an alternative translation such as `a saddle has been put there' would be possible, In this example, the Factual actually can be construed as having a future interpretation (§ sec:fact.main.clauses ): a character describes to another character what he will see when he arrives at a place. I translate here a-ta as `there is' in the present tense rather than `there will be' because at the time of utterance, the wooden saddle is already placed next to the horse, and there is no implication that a change of state will occur. in the case of ( ex:WNgW.arku ) it is obvious the presence of a sweet substance inside of a plant leaf is not attributable to an external agent.

exe

ɯ-rkɯ nɯtɕu si ɯ-sno ci a-ta tɕe, \\
3sg. poss -side dem: loc wood 3sg. poss -saddle indef pass -put: fact lnk \\
`Next to [the horse], there is a wooden saddle.' (2012-qachGa2012-qachGa) 0004087#S50
exe

exe

nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯ kɯ-cʰi ɣʑɤzga kɯ-fse a-rku tɕe \\

dem 3sg. poss -in dem sbj: pcp -be.sweet honey sbj: pcp -be.like pass -put.in: fact lnk \\

`(When one presses on the flower of the Habenaria glaucifolia ), inside of it there is something sweet like honey.' (16-CWrNgo) 0003518#S192
exe

A piece of evidence suggesting that the verbs atabe on and arkube in are in the process of becoming specialized existential verbs (§ sec:existential.basic ) is the fact that they alternate with the suppletive Sensory forms of the existential verbs ( ɣɤʑuexist and maŋenot exist, § sec:intr.person.irregular ), as in ( ex:pata.ri.maNe ).

exe

nɯtɕu pɯ-a-ta ri maŋe \\
dem: loc pst. ipfv - pass -put lnk not.exist: sens \\
`[The meat] used to be there, but now it is not there [any more].' (meimeidegushi)
exe

However, unlike the existential verbs tuexist and menot exist, both atabe on and arkube in have regular sensory forms, as in ( ex:tWtaNGoR.YArku ).

exe

sɤtɕʰa ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu rŋɯl tɯ-taɴɢoʁ ɲɯ-ɤ-rku tɕe, \\
ground 3sg. poss -in dem: loc silver one-basket sens - pass -put.in lnk \\
`Inside the ground, there is a basketful of silver.' (2003 divination)
exe
summary:
The passage describes two sets of verbs with passive forms that have developed specialized nonliteral uses. First, the passive forms of *pado* and *βzumake* function as quasi-copulas meaning ‘become’ or ‘grow,’ taking a nominal predicate, though *aβzu* also still works as an ordinary intransitive verb meaning ‘grow’; in the perfective, some forms are formally ambiguous with the transitive verb *βzu* ‘make.’  

Second, the passive forms of *taput* and *rkuput* still have meanings predictable from the base verbs, but they are mainly used as existential verbs meaning ‘there is,’ without implying an externally caused change of state. The text argues that these forms are becoming specialized existential verbs because they alternate with sensory forms of the existential paradigm, although unlike the ordinary existential verbs they still have regular sensory forms.

text:
The a- derivation demotes the transitive subject, and the agent is not expressible in the same clause. However, the agent is not necessary semantically deleted by the passive derivation. In ( ex:pjAkAmphWrci ) for instance, the agent of the wrapping action is clear from the context both to the narrator of the story and to the person discovering the silver ingots inside the pieces of bread -- it is therefore semantically recoverable.

exe

ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu rŋɯl qʰoʁqʰoʁ tɯ-rdoʁ pjɤ-k-ɤ-mpʰɯr-ci, \\
3sg. poss -in dem: loc silver ingot one-piece ifr. ipfv - peg - pass -wrap- peg \\
`A silver ingot had been wrapped inside.' (qajdoskAt 2002) 0003366#S108
exe

Many of the verbs that have an anticausative form (built by prenasalizing the onset, see Tables tab:anticausative.unaspirated and tab:anticausative.aspirated, § sec:anticausative below) also have a passive. The passive is required in these cases when the agent is implicit and recoverable (for instance, aprɤthave been broken from prɤtbreak (vt), example ex:pjAkAprAtci in § sec:anticausative.function ), while the anticausative is selected when the action occurs spontaneously without external agent ( mbrɤtbreak (vi), example ex:nWmbrAt.pWmbrAt in § sec:anticausative.function ).

In some contexts, both passive and anticausative forms are possible. For instance, to express the fact that a piece of iron is attached to an object, both the passive atsʰoʁbe attached ( ex:Com.atshoR ) and the anticausative ndzoʁbe attached ( ex:Com.kWndzoR ) (from
tsʰoʁattach) are attested.

exe

ɯ-pa, tɕʰɯŋkʰɤr ɣɯ ɯ-spjɯŋ tu-kɯ-ɣi nɯnɯre ri li ɕom a-tsʰoʁ tɕe \\
3sg. poss -down water.wheel gen 3sg. poss -axle ipfv: up - sbj: pcp -come dem: loc loc again iron pass -attach: fact lnk \\
`On the [top extremity of] the axle of the mill coming up from below, a piece of iron is attached.' (06-BGa) 0003408#S50
exe

exe

nɯ ɯ-tʰɤcu ri ɕom kɯ-ndzoʁ ci tu tɕe, nɯ tʰaʁmu rmi. \\
dem 3sg. poss -downstream loc iron sbj: pcp - acaus:attach indef exist: fact lnk dem weaving.blade call: fact \\
`Below, there is [a weaving implement] that has a piece of iron attached to it, it is called tʰaʁmu.' (thaXtsa 2002)
exe

The anticausative ndzoʁbe attached is required in cases when the entity that is attached on a surface has grown on it, rather than having been attached by someone, as in ( ex:WmWntoR.kundzoR ). In this function, it can be considered to be a subtype of existential verb (§ sec:existential.basic ).

exe

ɯ-mɯntoʁ nɯ kɯnɤ cʰɯ-ɤʑirja tɕe tɯ-kʰɤl nɯtɕu ʁnɯz, χsɯm kɯβde jamar ku-ndzoʁ. \\
3sg. poss -flower dem also ipfv: downstream -be.aligned lnk one-place dem: loc two three four about ipfv - acaus:attach \\
`Its flowers are also aligned, in each place they are attached in [groups] of about two, three or four.' (16-RlWmsWsi)
0003520#S9
exe

Another difference between ndzoʁbe attached and atsʰoʁbe attached is that the former only occurs as a resultative (like most passive verbs in Japhug, see § sec:passive.stative ), while ndzoʁbe attached can also mean `cling onto, lean on, grab' as in ( ex:WtaR.kondzoR ) (§ sec:anticausative.volitionality ).

In the case of verbs lacking an anticausative form however, such as ɲɟoʁglue, paste, the passive forms can be used with an anticausative function, with a semantically deleted agent, as shown by examples such as ( ex:koKAYJoRci ) in § sec:passive.stative.

Passive verbs are as a rule incompatible with an overt agent, even when semantically recoverable. Other morphosyntactic devices such as a direct-inverse marking are used to express the relative saliency of the agent and the patient in Japhug (see the discussion in § sec:inverse.3.3.saliency ).

In example ( ex:tAse.kW.pjAkAmarci ) with a passive verb, the ergative postpositional phrase tɤ-se kɯ could appear to be an example of overt agent. In the Chinese original from which this story is translated, the corresponding passage is 满嘴鲜血 mǎnzuǐ xiānxuèthe mouth covered in blood; the presence of ergative in ( ex:tAse.kW.pjAkAmarci ) cannot be explained as calquing from Chinese. However, note that the base verb marsmear can encode the material used to smear a surface as a semi-object ( taʁɟazsoot in ex:taRJAz.tomar ) rather than as an instrument. Likewise, the ergative is optional on tɤ-seblood (compare with ex:tAse.ra.pjAkAmarci ).

exe

xɕiri ɣɯ ɯ-mtɕʰi ra [tɤ-se kɯ] pjɤ-k-ɤ-mar-ci ʑo \\
weasel gen 3sg. poss -mouth pl indef. poss -blood erg ifr. ipfv - peg - pass -smear- peg emph \\
`The weasel's mouth was smeared with blood.' (140518 xuezhe he huangshulang-zh)
0004032#S24
exe

exe

tɕʰeme nɯ kɯ [...] ɯ-rŋa taʁɟaz to-mar \\
girl dem erg 3sg. poss -face soot ifr -smear \\
`The lady smeared her face with soot.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

exe

ɯ-mtɕʰi ɯ-taʁ tɕe tɤ-se ra pjɤ-k-ɤ-mar-ci ʑo. \\
3sg. poss -mouth 3sg. poss -on loc indef. poss -blood pl ifr. ipfv - peg - pass -smear- peg emph \\
`Its mouth was smeared with blood.' (140518 xuezhe he huangshulang-zh) 0004032#S19
exe

The apparently puzzling optional use of the ergative in ( ex:tAse.kW.pjAkAmarci ) is in fact the same as that observed with the partitive argument of the verb mtsʰɤtbe full (§ sec:kW.mtshAt ), and has to be distinguished from either agent or instrument.

The agent can at best be expressed as a possessive prefix on the intransitive subject of the passive verb, as in ( ex:Wjandza ), though in this example the implication that the agent is 2sg is only contextual.

exe

nɤ-smɤn ɯ-j-á-ndza? \\
2sg. poss -medicine qu - peg - pass -eat: fact \\
`Has your medicine been eaten?' (elicited)
exe

The only case of a passive verb taking as argument an overt noun phrase corresponding to the transitive subject of the base verb is afskɤrbe surrounded from fskɤrturn around. As shown in ( ex:jAGAt.kofskAr ) and ( ex:tWji.afskAr ), an absolutive locative noun phrase referring to the surrounding entity (in square brackets) can appear with this verb after the intransitive subject (the surrounded entity/location).

exe

iʑɤra ji-kʰa nɯ [jɤɣɤt tɯ-tɤkʰrɤz nɯ] ku-o-fskɤr. \\
1pl 1pl. poss -house dem balcony one-row dem ipfv: east - pass -surround \\
`Our house is surrounded by one row of balcony.' (2011-11-kha2)
exe

exe
summary: The passage explains that Japhug passives demote the transitive subject and generally do not allow an overt agent in the same clause, though the agent may still be semantically recoverable from context or expressed only indirectly by a possessive prefix. It also contrasts passive and anticausative forms: passives are used when an implicit agent is recoverable or when no anticausative exists, while anticausatives are used for spontaneous or non-agentive events, and in some cases both forms are possible with different meanings or restrictions.

text:
a-kʰa ɯ-rkɯ nɯnɯ [tɯ-ji] a-fskɤr.\\
1sg. poss -house 3sg. poss -side dem indef. poss -field pass -surround: fact \\
`The sides of my house are surrounded by fields.' (elicited)
exe

However, the base verb fskɤrturn around in the meaning `surround' can be constructed with the surrounding entity as its transitive subject (in ex:praR.kW.kufskAr, praʁcliff). This ergatively-marked subject however is not a volitional agent and rather semantically corresponds to a locative argument, which may explain why it is not removed by passivization (though ergative marking is lost).

exe

kɯki sɤtɕʰa ki, ɯ-rkɯ tʰamtɕɤt [praʁ] kɯ ku-fskɤr ɲɯ-ɕti \\
dem. prox place dem. prox 3sg. poss -side all cliff erg ipfv: east -surround sens -be. aff \\
`The sides of this place are all surrounded by cliffs.' (elicited)
exe
summary: The passage explains that the verb **fskɤr** ‘turn around, surround’ can appear in passive constructions where the affected entity is the subject, as in “the sides of my house are surrounded by fields.” It also notes that when the surrounding entity is the ergative-marked transitive subject, this subject is not a volitional agent but functions more like a locative argument, which likely explains why it remains in the passive even though its ergative marking is lost.

text:
passive!ditransitive verb ditransitive verb!passive
Secundative verbs such as mbigive and jtsʰigive to drink (a lexicalized causative of tsʰidrink), which select as object the recipient rather than the theme (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ), can be subjected to the passive derivation. The resulting verbs ambibe given and ajtsʰibe given to drink however encode as subjects not the recipient, but the theme; in particular, they never take indexation affixes even when the recipient is a first or second person. The recipient can only be encoded as possessor of the subject ( ex:WsmAn.ambi ) or as left-dislocated focus constituent ( ex:tAlu.ajtshi ).

exe

tɤ-pɤtso ɯ-smɤn a-mbi \\
indef. poss -child 3sg. poss -medicine pass -give: fact \\
`The child has been given his medicine.' (elicited)
exe

exe

tɤ-pɤtso ra tɤ-lu a-jtsʰi \\
indef. poss -child pl indef. poss -milk pass -give.to.drink: fact \\
`The children have been given milk to drink.' (elicited)
exe

The causativization of these passive verbs yields the rogative derivation (§ sec:rogative.derivation ).
summary: Secundative verbs like *mbi* ‘give’ and *jtsʰi* ‘give to drink’ can undergo passive derivation, but the passive forms *ambi* ‘be given’ and *ajtsʰi* ‘be given to drink’ take the theme, not the recipient, as subject. Even when the recipient is first or second person, it is not indexed on the verb and can only appear as a possessor of the subject or as a left-dislocated focus constituent. The passage also notes that causativizing these passive verbs produces the rogative derivation.

text:
passive!reduplicated
The intransitive verb aβzdoʁβzdɯbe in good order derives from the transitive verb βzdɯcollect (itself borrowed from བསྡུ་bsducollect), and can be interpreted as a lexicalized passive derivation (`have been collected and put in order' `be in good order'). However, unlike other passive verbs, it presents reduplication with the rare -oʁ replicant (on this type of reduplication, see also § sec.distributed.action.oR ).

The verb aβdoʁβdibe in good health ( ex:koBdoRBdij ) apparently has the same morphological structure as aβzdoʁβzdɯbe in good order, but since its base verb βdibe well (from བདེ་bdebe well) is stative intransitive, this example cannot be analyzed as a passive.

exe

iʑora ɕɤxɕo ku-oβdoʁβdi-j \\
1pl these.days prs -be.in.good.health- 1pl \\
`These days we are in good health.' (elicited)
exe

Another interesting difference between aβzdoʁβzdɯbe in good order and aβdoʁβdibe in good health is that the former has a sigmatic causative sɤβzdoʁβzdɯput in order, while the latter has a velar causative ɣɤβdoʁβditidy up, put in order whose meaning is not derivable from that of aβdoʁβdibe in good health.
summary:
The intransitive verb **aβzdoʁβzdɯbe** ‘be in good order’ is a lexicalized passive derived from the transitive verb **βzdɯ** ‘collect,’ and it shows an unusual reduplication with the rare **-oʁ** replicant. By contrast, **aβdoʁβdibe** ‘be in good health’ has a similar form but cannot be treated as passive because its base verb is stative intransitive.  

The two verbs also differ in their causatives: **aβzdoʁβzdɯbe** has the predictable sigmatic causative **sɤβzdoʁβzdɯ** ‘put in order,’ whereas **aβdoʁβdibe** has a velar causative **ɣɤβdoʁβdi** ‘tidy up, put in order,’ whose meaning is not directly

text:
passive!compatibility
There are no examples in the corpus of passive derivations taking as input causative or applicative verbs, except for some lexicalized causatives such as jtsʰigive to drink (§ passive.ditransitive ). However, it is likely that the progressive prefix asɯ- originates from the combination of the passive and the sigmatic causative (§ sec:sig.caus.other.derivations, § sec:progressive.history ).

Passive verbs however can be subjected to sigmatic causative derivation. The fusion of the sigmatic causative sɯ- with the passive a- yield sɤ, a surface form identical to the antipassive (§ sec:antipassive.sA ) and the proprietive (§ sec:proprietive ) prefixes.

First, the causative-passive double derivations from secundative verbs (§ passive.ditransitive ) has become the rogative derivation (§ sec:rogative.derivation ). Second, the lexicalized passives apabecome and aβzubecome, grow (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ) have the causative forms sɤpa and sɤβzu, both of which predictably mean `cause to become, turn into, transform into'. These causative verbs are ditransitive, as in ( ex:sApaj ), taking as semi-object the entity in which the object is transformed.

exe

tɯ-ci tʰamtɕɤt tɤ-se sɯ-ɤpa-j \\
indef. poss -water all indef. poss -blood caus -become: fact - 1sg \\
`Let us turn all the water into blood.' (2003 smanmi)
exe

The object indexed on the verb is the entity that undergoes transformation, such as the 1pl in ( ex:nWwGsABzuj ), not the one that it is transformed into. Only the object is targeted by reflexivization (§ sec:refl.caus ).

exe

kɯki ji-βdaʁmu kɯ ki kɯ-fse, nɤki, sɯŋgɯ pɣa nɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-ɤβzu-j \\
dem. prox 1pl. poss -queen erg dem. prox sbj: pcp -be.like filler forest bird aor - inv - caus -become- 1pl \\
`Our queen has transformed us into bird from the forest.' (140520 ye tiane-zh)
0004044#S119
exe

The verbs sɤpa and sɤβzu `cause to become, turn into, transform' occur with a variety of semi-objects. In ( ex:tWmpCar.YWwGGsABzu ), the semi-object tɯ-mpɕar tɯ-mpɕar is a repeated counted noun (§ sec:CN.repetition ) expressing literally the meaning `turn (the rock) into sheets one by one'.

exe

cupa kɤ-tɕɤt tɕe ɲɯ-ɴqa ma praʁ ɕ-pjɯ́-wɣ-pʰɯt ɲɯ-ra […] tɕe nɯ tɯ-mpɕar tɯ-mpɕar ɲɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-ɤβzu ɲɯ-ra \\
stone.slab inf -take.out lnk sens -be.hard lnk cliff tral - ipfv - inv -take.off sens -be.needed
lnk dem one-sheet one-sheet ipfv - inv - caus -become sens -be.needed \\
`To extract stone slabs, one has to chop the rocks sheet by sheet (layer by layer).’ (14-siblings)
0003508#S155
exe

The semi-object of sɤpa and sɤβzu `cause to become' can also be an infinitival or participial clause. This combination is a common type of periphrastic causative construction (§ sec:sWpa.sABzu ), illustrated in example ( ex:kWmpCWmpCAr.nasABzu ) with the two relative clauses ɯ-ɕɣa kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi `who is young, whose age is small' and kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕɤr `who is beautiful' as semi objects. A more literal translation could be `he turned his mother into (someone) whose age was small and who was beautiful'.

exe

ɯ-mu [ɯ-ɕɣa kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi] [kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕɤr] ʑo na-sɯ-ɤβzu ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss -age sbj: pcp - emph be.small sbj: pcp - emph be.beautiful emph aor:3 - caus -become sens -be \\
`He made his mother become young and beautiful.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

This periphrastic construction is also possible with the reflexivized forms of sɤpatransform and sɤβzutransform (example ex:kWZo.YAZGAsApa, § sec:refl.caus )

The verb sɤrtsicount as (see ex:tutanWsArtsi, § sec:essive.abs ) is the sigmatic causative of artsibe counted as ( ex:mWYArtsi2 ), itself passive of the transitive rtsicount (from རྩི་rtsicount).

exe

xɕiri kɯ-fse nɯra kɯrŋi mɯ-ɲɯ-ɤ-rtsi lo. \\
weasel sbj: pcp -be.like dem: pl beast.of.prey neg - sens - pass -count sfp \\
`Weasel and the like do not count as beasts of prey (I think).' (150822 kWrNi) 0006260#S8
exe

Passive verbs can occur as second element of Noun-Verb nominal compounds, but in this case the a- prefix is absorbed by the previous nominal root, resulting in a surface form undistinguishable from that of the base verb. For instance, the compound ɕnɤstiperson with a stuffy nose can be parsed as ɕnɤ- (bound state of tɯ-ɕnanose) and -sti, a syllable ambiguous between the passive astibe blocked and the base verb stiblock ( ex:pjAkAstici, § sec:object.verb.compounds ).. The former is more probable, as this noun should be analyzed as meaning `(person) whose nose is blocked rather than as `blocking noses'.
summary: The passage explains that passive verbs can generally take sigmatic causative derivation, and the fusion of the causative prefix sɯ- with the passive a- yields the surface form sɤ, which is identical to some other prefixes. It gives examples such as sɤpa and sɤβzu ‘cause to become/transform,’ showing that these causatives are ditransitive and can take various semi-objects, including clauses; the passive form sɤrtsi ‘count as’ is also presented as a causative of a passive verb. It also notes that passives may appear in noun-verb compounds, where the passive prefix may be absorbed and thus not overtly visible.

text:
passive!rogative rogative
The rogative This term is from Latin rogo `I ask, I require'. sɤ- prefix is attested on the secundative verbs mbigive and jtsʰigive to drink, and produces intransitive verbs meaning `ask (someone) to $X$ (something) to oneself’ (where $X$ stands for the meaning of the base verb), sɤmbiask for and sɤjtsʰiask for something to drink, respectively.

The sɤ- prefix is homophonous to that of the antipassive (§ sec:antipassive.sA ) The rogative prefix on sɤmbiask for was mistakenly glossed as `antipassive’ in, example (32). The antipassive forms of mbigive and jtsʰigive to drink are rɤmbigive to someone and rɤjtsʰigive to someone to drink, respectively. These forms have the rɤ- antipassive prefix instead of sɤ- (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ). and of the proprietive (§ sec:proprietive ) derivations.

Rogative verbs are morphologically intransitive, as shown by ( ex:nWsAmbia ) (the past transitive suffix -t would be expected here if this verb were transitive, see § sec:transitivity.morphology ) and ( ex:nWsAmbinW ), where a type-C orientation prefix would be expected (§ sec:indexation.non.local, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ).

However, while the rogative derivation affects transitivity, it does not decrease valency: sɤmbi and sɤjtsʰi are trivalent like their base verb: they have two arguments in addition to the intransitive subject, a semi-object (the entity that is asked for) and a dative argument (§ sec:semi.transitive.dative ).

exe

aʑo a-pi ɯ-ɕki kɯmtɕʰɯ ci nɯ-sɤ-mbi-a \\
1sg 1sg. poss -elder.sibling 3sg. poss - dat toy indef aor - rog -give- 1sg \\
`I asked my elder brother/sister to give me a toy.' (elicited)
exe

The semi-object of sɤmbiask for can be a human (including a first or second person), in contexts like asking for someone in the context of arranged marriage ( ex:nWsAmbinW ) or asking for a child to become recognized as a reincarnated lama.

exe

tɕe a-ʁi nɯre ri, nɯ-sɤ-mbi-nɯ \\
lnk 1sg. poss -younger.sibling dem: loc loc aor - rog -give- pl \\
`They asked for my younger brother (to come to marry their daughter) there.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S188
exe

The dative argument is optional, and rarely expressed. Rogative verbs with non-overt dative can be used as a polite way to ask for something, as in ( ex:kAsAjtshi.WBrAtu ), where neither the person asking (the child) nor the addressee (the grandfather, that would take the dative) are expressed within the same clause.

exe

a-wɯ, tɯ-mgo kɤ-sɤ-mbi, tɯ-ci kɤ-sɤ-jtsʰi ɯβrɤ-tu \\
1sg. poss -grandfather indef. poss -food obj: pcp - rog -give indef. poss -water obj: pcp - rog -give.to.drink opt-exist: fact \\
`Grandfather, would there be food or water that [we could] ask for [you to give us]?' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

The rogative sɤ- is likely to have originated from the combination of the sigmatic causative sɯ- and passive a- prefixes (§ sec:passive.other.derivations ). The verbs mbigive and jtsʰigive to drink have the passive forms ambibe given and ajtsʰibe given to drink (§ passive.ditransitive ), which select as intransitive subject the theme. A causative derivation from these passive verbs `cause $X$ to be given' could yield the meaning of the rogative derivation (note the semantic similarity with the inversive and rogative functions of the causative discussed in § sec:sig.caus.inversive and § sec:sig.caus.rogative ). However, this analysis is not completely straightforward, as one would expect causative verbs to be transitive (not semi-transitive like the rogative verbs) and the dative marking of the addressee is also unexplained.
summary:
The rogative prefix sɤ- occurs on the verbs “give” and “give.to.drink,” forming intransitive verbs meaning ‘ask someone to give/drink something to oneself.’ Although these forms are morphologically intransitive, they do not reduce valency: they remain trivalent, with a subject, a semi-object, and an often optional dative addressee.  

The passage notes that sɤ- is homophonous with prefixes used in the antipassive and proprietive, but the rogative is distinct from the antipassive rɤ- forms. It may historically derive from a combination of causative and passive prefixes, though this account does not fully explain its semi-transitive behavior or dative marking.

text:
reflexive
While Japhug has a generic pronoun tɯʑoone (§ sec:genr.pro ) and an emphatic pronoun raŋoneself (§ sec:pronouns.emph ), it lacks any reflexive pronoun, and the only way to express reflexive meaning is by means of a dedicated prefix ʑɣɤ, different from the autive (§ sec:autobenefactive ), the reciprocal (§ sec:reciprocal ) and other valency-decreasing derivations.
summary: Japhug has a generic pronoun tɯʑo and an emphatic pronoun raŋ ‘oneself’, but it does not have a reflexive pronoun. Reflexive meaning is expressed only by the dedicated prefix ʑɣɤ, which is distinct from the autive, reciprocal, and other valency-decreasing derivations.

subsection: The reflexive prefix: form and basic function
text:
tab:ZGA.refl presents several examples of the reflexive prefix ʑɣɤ, deriving reflexive verbs from transitive ones.

The reflexive derivation turns the base verb into an intransitive verb whose subject acts upon itself, and corresponds to both the transitive subject and the object of the base verb. For instance, in ( ex:CpjWZGAGAlanW.kWZGAnWsmAn ), the subjects of the reflexive verbs ɕ-pjɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-la-nɯ `they bathe in it=they cause themselves to soak in it' and kɯ-ʑɣɤ-nɯsmɤn to heal themselves' are semantically both agents and patients. When the subject is non-singular, each member of the group corresponding to the subject is acting on himself, as opposed to the reciprocal derivation, where every member performs the same action to other members of the groups, and is agent and patient either simultaneously or in turn (§ sec:reciprocal ).

exe

tɕe nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ ri ɕ-pjɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-la-nɯ tɕe li kɯ-ʑɣɤ-nɯsmɤn ju-ɕe-nɯ tɕe, \\

lnk dem 3sg. poss -in loc tral - ipfv - refl - caus -soak- pl lnk again sbj: pcp - refl -heal ipfv -go- pl lnk \\
`People go and bathe in [warm springs], they go [there] to heal themselves.' (20-ldWGi, 52;56) 0003558#S52
exe

The prefix ʑɣɤ- is highly productive, but only targets objects. The only exceptions to this rule are a handful of intransitive verbs which take the ʑɣɤ- prefix (§ sec:refl.intr ). Other syntactic functions such as possessors of objects for instance cannot be reflexivized using ʑɣɤ-. The form $ $ ʑɣɤ-sɤɕɤt (intended meaning `comb oneself') found in one example in the corpus ( ex:pjAZGAsACAtndZi ) is a mistake, as pointed out by the consultant who told the story ( Tshendzin ) herself, since sɤɕɤtcomb can only take the noun tɯ-kuhead as object, not the person whose hair is combed. The only way to express the meaning `comb oneself' is by the autive prefix (§ sec:autoben.proper ) as in ( ex:pjAnWsACAtndZi ).

exe

xlist

$ $pjɤ-ʑɣɤ-sɤɕɤt-ndʑi to-rɤmpɕoʁ mpɕɤr-ndʑi, \\
ifr - refl -comb- du ifr - emph make.up- du \\
Intended meaning: `They combed themselves and made themselves beautiful.' (150830 baihe jiemei-zh)

ndʑi-ku pjɤ-nɯ-sɤɕɤt-ndʑi to-rɤmpɕoʁ mpɕɤr-ndʑi, \\
3du. poss -head ifr - auto -comb- du ifr - emph make.up- du \\
`They combed their hair and made themselves beautiful.' (correction of the previous example)
xlist
exe

Similarly, in the reflexive causative derivation ʑɣɤsɯntɕʰɤrcause oneself to appear from ntɕʰɤrappear (§ sec:refl.caus ), reflexivization by ʑɣɤ- only targets the intransitive subject of the base verb (the entity which appears in the dream, sɯŋgilion in ex:sWNgi.kontChAr ), not the experiencer, which is encoded as possessor of the noun tɯ-jmŋodream. Thus, example ( ex:koZGAsWntChAr ) cannot be interpreted as `he caused her to appear to himself'.

exe

xlist

ɯ-jmŋo ɯ-ŋgɯ sɯŋgi ko-ntɕʰɤr \\
3sg. poss -dream 3sg. poss -in lion ifr -appear \\
`He dreamt of a tiger / A tiger appeared to him in a dream.' (elicited)

ɯ-jmŋo ɯ-ŋgɯ ko-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-ntɕʰɤr \\
3sg. poss -dream 3sg. poss -in ifr - refl - caus -appear \\
`He made himself appear to her in a dream.' (2012 Norbzang) 0003768#S97
xlist
exe
summary:
The reflexive prefix **ʑɣɤ-** derives intransitive reflexive verbs from transitive bases, with the subject functioning as both agent and patient. In non-singular subjects, each member acts on himself, unlike reciprocal derivation, and the prefix is highly productive but normally only targets objects, not other roles such as possessors.

The passage also notes a few restrictions and exceptions: some intransitive verbs can take ʑɣɤ-, but forms like **ʑɣɤ-sɤɕɤt** intended to mean “comb oneself” are ungrammatical because the verb requires **tɯ-ku** “head” as its object. In reflexive causatives, ʑɣɤ- targets the intransitive subject of the base verb, not the experiencer, so it cannot mean “he caused her to appear to himself.”

subsection: The reflexive prefix: form and basic function
text:
All reflexive verbs are morphologically intransitive (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ). In terms of case marking however, they are not prototypical intransitive verbs. When their subject is overt, it is in absolutive form in most cases as in ( ex:kunWZGAfstWn ), but subjects of reflexive verbs in the ergative (§ sec:S.kW ) are also attested ( ex:tWZo.kW.tWZo, § sec:genr.pro ).

exe

ɯʑo ku-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-fstɯn cʰa \\
3sg ipfv - auto - refl -serve can: fact \\
`It [will] be able to take care of itself on its own.' (150822 laoye zuoshi zongshi duide-zh) 0006298#S146
exe

In particular, the semi-transitive lexicalized reflexive ʑɣɤpapretend (derived from pado, § sec:lexicalized.refl ) often occurs with subjects marked with the ergative, such as the right-dislocated constituent <tangseng> nɯ kɯ in ( ex:mAkWtso.toZGApa ) (see also example ex:kW.toZGApa, § sec:semi.transitive ).

exe

mɤ-kɯ-tso to-ʑɣɤpa, <tangseng> nɯ kɯ. \\
neg - sbj: pcp -understand ifr -pretend anthr dem erg \\
`He pretended not to have understood, Tangseng.' (180503 xiyouji 12-zh)
0006189#S43
exe
summary: Reflexive verbs are morphologically intransitive, but their case marking is not fully typical of intransitives. When the subject is overt, it is usually absolutive, though ergative subjects are also attested. In particular, the lexicalized semi-transitive reflexive ʑɣɤpa “pretend” often appears with ergative subjects.

subsection: The reflexive prefix: form and basic function
text:
reflexive!ditransitive verb ditransitive verb!reflexive
The reflexive is possible with indirective verbs of giving or speech, whose objects corresponds to the theme (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ): kʰogive and fɕɤttell yield the reflexive verbs ʑɣɤkʰogive oneself up and ʑɣɤfɕɤttell about oneself, as in ( ex:YWtWnWZGAkho ).

exe

nɤʑo ʁgra ɯ-jaʁ nɯtɕu ɲɯ-tɯ-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-kʰo ʑo ɯmɤ-kɯ-ɕti-ci? \\
2sg enemy 3sg. poss -hand dem: loc ipfv -2- auto - refl -give emph prob - peg -be. aff - peg \\
`(By doing that), aren't you handing yourself over to your own enemy?' (2014niulan li de lu-zh)
exe

The ʑɣɤ- prefix can only express reflexivization of the theme of indirective verbs, never the dative-marked recipient; for instance, it cannot be prefixed to an indirective verb such as tʰuask (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) to convey the meaning `ask oneself'. With the secundative verb mbigive, the reflexive prefix is not possible either, though for pragmatic rather than syntactic reasons.
summary: The reflexive prefix ʑɣɤ- can occur with indirective verbs of giving or speech, where it reflexivizes the theme argument, as in forms meaning “give oneself up” or “tell about oneself.” However, it cannot target the dative-marked recipient, so it cannot be used to mean “ask oneself” with verbs like *tʰu* ‘ask’; it is also unavailable with the secundative verb *mbi* ‘give,’ though this restriction is said to be pragmatic rather than syntactic.

subsection: The reflexive prefix: form and basic function
text:
The reflexive prefix can in some cases have the permissive function `let oneself be $X$', the most common case with the verb ʑɣɤnɯβlube fooled from the transitive denominal verb nɯβlucheat (`let oneself be cheated'). With most transitive verbs, this meaning is expressed by means of the reflexive+causative double derivation (§ sec:refl.caus ).

In ( ex:toZGAnWmbrApW ), an overt agent (corresponding to the causee of the causative construction) marked with the ergative kɯ appears with the verb ʑɣɤnɯmbrɤpɯlet oneself be mounted. Although taken from a text translated from Chinese, it is not considered incorrect after rechecking with Tshendzin.

exe

tɕendɤre mbro kɯ ``ɲɯ-pe" to-ti ɲɯ-ŋu. tɕendɤre tɯrme nɯ kɯ to-ʑɣɤ-nɯmbrɤpɯ ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe tɕe tɯrme nɯ mbro ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu to-ɕe ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
lnk horse erg sens -be.good ifr -say sens -be lnk man dem erg ifr - refl -ride sens -be lnk lnk man dem horse 3sg. poss -on dem: loc ifr: up -go sens -be lnk \\
`The horse said `good' and let himself be mounted by the man, and the man rode on him.' (ma he lu-zh)
exe
summary:
The reflexive prefix can sometimes express a permissive meaning, roughly ‘let oneself be X,’ most commonly with the verb ʑɣɤnɯβlu ‘be fooled,’ derived from the transitive verb nɯβlu ‘cheat.’ For most transitive verbs, however, this meaning is formed with a reflexive plus causative double derivation.  

The passage also notes an example with ʑɣɤnɯmbrɤpɯ ‘let oneself be mounted,’ where an overt ergative-marked agent appears; although the sentence comes from a translation, it was judged acceptable after checking with a speaker.

subsection: The reflexive prefix: form and basic function
text:
reflexive!intransitive verb
A handful of intransitive verbs can undergo reflexivization with the ʑɣɤ- prefix.

With intransitive deadverbial (§ sec:verbs.relative.location ) and denominal verbs of relative locations in mɤ, such as maŋlobe upstream and mɤpɤrtʰɤβbe in the middle, the reflexive prefix derives volitional motion verbs such as ʑɣɤmaŋloput oneself upstream ( ex:loZGAmaNlo ) and ʑɣɤmɤpɤrtʰɤβput oneself in between. It is possible that these forms come from the simplification of former reflexive+causative (§ sec:refl.caus ) by loss of the causative prefix.

exe

ɯ-lɤcu nɯtɕu jo-ɕe tɕe lo-ʑɣɤ-maŋlo. \\
3sg. poss -upstream dem: loc ifr -go lnk ifr: upstream - refl -be.upstream \\
`[The wolf] went to a place upstream [from the lamb], he placed himself upstream.' (2014 lang he yang-zh)
exe

The pair of intransitive verbs ɣɤtɕabe wrong and ɣɤŋgibe right have the reflexive forms ʑɣɤɣɤtɕarecognize one's mistake and ʑɣɤɣɤŋgiconsider oneself to be right, as shown by ( ex:pjWkWZGAGAtCa ). Note that the causative of these verbs has a tropative meaning, for instance the causative zɣɤtɕaconsider to be wrong in the second clause of ( ex:pjWkWZGAGAtCa ); the reflexive forms thus have the expected meaning of reflexive+causative double derivations (`consider oneself to be right/wrong').

exe

tɯʑo pjɯ-kɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤtɕa ra ma, tɯ-zda pjɯ́-wɣ-z-ɣɤtɕa, tɯʑo
(...) pɯ-kɯ-nɯ-ɣɤtɕa kɯnɤ pjɯ-kɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤŋgi tɕe, ɯ-mbrɤzɯ kɯ-tu me tu-kɯ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
genr ipfv - genr:S/O- refl -be.wrong be.needed: fact lnk genr. poss -companion ipfv - inv - caus -be.wrong genr ipfv - genr:S/O- refl -be.wrong also ipfv - genr:S/O- auto -be.right lnk 3sg. poss -result sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact ipfv - genr:S/O-say sens -be \\
`One has to recognize one's mistakes; if one considers one's companions to be wrong, and if one consider oneself to be always right even if one is wrong, there will be no [good] result.' (lWlu)
exe

The reflexive verb ʑɣɤsɤɕkeburn oneself appears to derive from the proprietive verb sɤɕkebe burning (from ɕkeget burned, § sec:proprietive ), though from its meaning it is tempting to wonder whether this prefix sɤ- here is not rather analyzable as an irregular causative (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular ).

exe

ma-pɯ-tɯ-ʑɣɤ-sɤ-ɕke \\
neg - imp -2- refl - prop?-burn \\
`Don't burn yourself!' (elicited)
exe

One reflexive verb seems to derived from an ideophone rather than from a verb root: ʑɣɤɕpʰɤβlay flat ( ex:pWZGACphaBa ) The vowel alternation in ( ex:pWZGACphaBa ) is regular, see § sec:intr.1. shares the same root ɕpʰɤβ as ɕpʰɤβɕpʰɤβlaying flat ( ex:CphABCphAB.Zo.YWrAZi ). It is possible that this verb originates from a deideophonic derivation (§ sec:voice.deideophonic ), with subsequent deletion of the denominal prefix.

exe

ɯ-tʰoʁ zɯ pɯ-ʑɣɤɕpʰaβ-a \\
3sg. poss -ground loc aor -lay.flat- 1sg \\
`I laid flat on the ground.' (elicited)
exe

exe

ɯ-tʰoʁ ɕpʰɤβɕpʰɤβ ʑo ɲɯ-rɤʑi, kɤ-nɯqambɯmbjom mɯ́j-cʰa \\
3sg. poss -ground idph (II):laying.flat emph sens -stay inf -fly neg: sens -can \\
`The bird is staying on the ground without moving, it cannot fly.' (elicited)
exe
summary:
A small number of intransitive verbs can take the ʑɣɤ- reflexive prefix. With deadverbial and denominal verbs of relative location, this prefix forms volitional motion meanings such as “place oneself upstream/in between,” and these forms may come from older reflexive+causative constructions after loss of the causative prefix.

The passage also notes reflexive forms of “wrong” and “right,” which mean “recognize one’s mistake” and “consider oneself to be right,” matching a reflexive+causative derivation. In addition, one reflexive verb appears to come from a proprietive verb (“burn oneself”), and another may derive from an ideophone rather than a verb root.

subsection: The reflexive prefix: form and basic function
text: The reflexive ʑɣɤ- is almost the only way to express reflexivity in Japhug. However, the antipassive verb ra-χtɕi (from the transitive verb χtɕiwash), has the meaning `wash one's face' or `have a shower' (§ sec:antipassive.reflexive ), almost like that of the regular reflexive ʑɣɤχtɕiwash oneself. Similarly, the prefix rɤ- in rɤmpɕɤrmake up from mpɕɤrbe beautiful is reflexive-like (`make oneself beautiful', see § sec:rA.non.apass ).
summary: In Japhug, the reflexive prefix ʑɣɤ- is the main way to express reflexivity. However, some antipassive or related forms can have reflexive-like meanings, such as ra-χtɕi ‘wash one’s face/have a shower’ from χtɕiwash and rɤ-mpɕɤr ‘make up, make oneself beautiful’ from mpɕɤr ‘be beautiful’.

text:
Transitive verbs such as tʂaβcause to fall/roll, kɤɣbend or xtʰomput horizontally which have a corresponding prenasalized anticausatives (§ sec:anticausative ) use the reflexive derivation to express the corresponding intransitive volitional action.

The action of the transitive verb itself can be either volitional ( ex:luxthomnW.kuCWrNgWnW ) or non-volitional (including involuntary actions of animate beings and actions of inanimate referents, as in ex:WthoR.pjAwGtsxaB ) depending on the context.

exe

tɤ-pɤtso nɯ ki kɯ-fse lu-xtʰom-nɯ ku-ɕɯ-rŋgɯ-nɯ pɯ-maʁ, \\
indef. poss -child dem dem. prox sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv: upstream -put.horizontally- pl ipfv - caus -lie.down- pl pst. ipfv -not.be \\
`People would not lie the babies down horizontally like this.' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR1)
exe

exe

rdɤstaʁ nɯ ɯ-tɯ-rʑi kɯ ɯ-tʰoʁ pjɤ́-wɣ-tʂaβ tɕe pjɤ́-wɣ-sat. \\
stone dem 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.heavy erg 3sg. poss -ground ifr: down - inv -cause.to.fall lnk ifr: down - inv -kill \\
`The stones [in the wolf's belly] were so heavy that they caused him to fall down and die.' (140428 xiaohongmao-zh)
0003884#S165
exe

The anticausative verbs are nearly always non-volitionally (see § sec:anticausative.volitionality ), as illustrated by ( ex:rNgW.nWni.pjAndzxaBndZi ) and ( ex:londom ).

exe

tɕe rŋgɯ nɯni (...) to-k-ɤmɯ-rpu-ndʑi tɕe pjɤ-ɴɢrɯ-ndʑi tɕe tʂɤndo pjɤ-ndʐaβ-ndʑi. \\
lnk boulder dem: du ifr - peg - recip -bump- du lnk ifr: down - acaus:shatter- du lnk side.of.the.road ifr: down - acaus:cause.to.roll- du \\
`The two boulders bumped into each other, shattered, and rolled down the side of the road.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S135
exe

In ( ex:londom ), the verb lo-ndom means `lie down horizontally after falling down (out of exhaustion)', as shown by ( ex:londom.explanation ), the gloss provided in Japhug for this verb form, which also involves the anticausative verb ndʐaβfall/roll.

exe

tɕendɤre ɯ-ʁi nɯ kɤ-ŋke mɯ-ɲɤ-cʰa tɕe tɕendɤre lo-ndom ɕti tɕe \\
lnk 3sg. poss -younger.sibling dem inf -walk neg - ifr -can lnk lnk ifr: upstream - acaus:put.horizontally be. aff: fact lnk \\
`His younger brother was not able to walk anymore, and lay down.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

exe

ɯ-ku lo lo-ru tɕe pjɤ-ndʐaβ, tɕe kɤ-nɯ-rɤru mɤ-kɯ-cʰa nɯ, tɕe lo-ndom tu-kɯ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -head upstream ifr: upstream -look lnk ifr: down - acaus:cause.to.fall lnk inf - auto -get.up neg - sbj: pcp -can dem lnk ifr: upstream - acaus:put.horizontally ipfv - genr:S/O-say sens -be \\
`He fell down, head looking upstream, not able to get up by himself, so one says lo-ndom.' (elicited, explanation of example ex:londom )
exe

On other hand, the combination of the transitive verb with the reflexive expresses a volitional meaning implying that the action was done on purposive by an animate agent. In ( ex:YAZGAxthom ), the subject of ɲɤ-ʑɣɤ-xtʰom `he put himself horizontally=he laid down horizontally' did not fall down (unlike that of example ex:londom ), but on the contrary lays down on the ground by himself voluntarily to pretend to have fallen down and have died.

exe

tʂu nɯtɕu ɲɤ-ʑɣɤ-xtʰom tɕe pɯ-kɯ-si to-ʑɣɤpa. \\
road dem: loc ifr: west - refl -put.horizontally lnk aor - sbj: pcp -die ifr -pretend \\
`He laid down on the road horizontally and pretended to be dead.' (140517 huli he lang-zh)
0004020#S11
exe

In ( ex:koZGAtsxaB ), the verb ʑɣɤtʂaβcause oneself to fall/roll expresses the same action as mtsaʁjump, a clearly volitional motion verb.

exe

tɯ-ci kɯ-wxtɯ wxti nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu ko-mtsaʁ. tɕe nɯtɕu ko-ʑɣɤ-tʂaβ qʰe \\
indef. poss -water sbj: pcp - emph be.big dem 3sg. poss -in dem: loc ifr: east -jump lnk dem: loc ifr: east - refl -cause.to.roll lnk \\
`He jumped into the river, he let himself roll into it.' (150830 baihe jiemei-zh) 0006368#S199
exe

When no prenasalized anticausative verb exists, the reflexive can still be used to insist on the volitional character of a usually non-volitional action in combination with a causative prefix (§ sec:refl.caus.volitional ).
summary:
The passage explains that for certain transitive verbs with corresponding prenasalized anticausatives, the reflexive derivation is used to express the matching intransitive action when it is done volitionally by an animate agent. By contrast, the anticausative forms are usually non-volitional, referring to events like falling or rolling that happen without deliberate control.

It also notes that the same transitive verb can be interpreted as volitional or non-volitional depending on context, and that reflexive forms can mark deliberate self-directed actions such as lying down or letting oneself roll. When no anticausative exists, the reflexive may still be used to emphasize that an otherwise non-volitional action is intentional.

text:
A few reflexive verbs have meanings that are unpredictable from their base verbs and have become highly lexicalized.

The semi-transitive verb ʑɣɤpapretend (§ sec:refl.erg, § sec:semi.transitive, § sec:subject.participle.complementation ) transparently comes from the reflexive of the light verb pado (§ sec:pa.lv ). This semantic evolution probably took place through a meaning such as `make oneself into $X$'. The lexicalized reflexive ʑɣɤpa is also attested as a stative verb meaning `be arrogant'.

The intransitive auxiliary ʑɣɤstu, which occurs as a light verb with ideophones (§ sec:stu.idph ) to express voluntary actions, is the reflexive of the similative verb studo like (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative, § sec:svc.similative.verb ).

The verb ʑɣɤɕtʰɯzreveal one's true nature ( ex:koZGACthWz ) derives from the orienting verb ɕtʰɯzturn towards (§ sec:orienting.verbs ).

exe

ɯʑo nɯstʰɯci pjɯ-sɯzdɯɣ-a mɯ́j-pe ɲɤ-sɯso tɕe ko-ʑɣɤɕtʰɯz. \\
3sg so.much ipfv -cause.to.worry- 1sg neg: sens -be.good ifr -think lnk ifr -reveal.oneself \\
`She thought: ``It is not good of me to cause him so much worries'', and she revealed her true identity to him.' (2003kAndzwsqhaj2)
exe
summary: Some reflexive verbs have meanings that are not predictable from their base forms and have become highly lexicalized. Examples include **ʑɣɤpa** ‘pretend,’ historically derived from the reflexive of the light verb **pado**, **ʑɣɤstu**, the reflexive of **studo** ‘like,’ and **ʑɣɤɕtʰɯz** ‘reveal one’s true nature,’ which comes from the orienting verb **ɕtʰɯz** ‘turn towards.’

text:
reflexive causative
Reflexive derivations from causativized verbs are extremely common in Japhug, and have a considerable diversity of uses.
summary: Reflexive derivations from causativized verbs are very common in Japhug and are used in a wide variety of ways. The passage emphasizes both their frequency and their considerable functional diversity.

text:
volitionality
The double causative+reflexive derivation also serves as a strategy to express volitional action, when applied to non-volitional intransitive verbs. For instance, a non-volitional verb like fkabe full is not attested in the Imperative (§ sec:imp.function ). The doubly derived ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-fka, which conveys the meaning `cause oneself to become full=eat to one's fill', can on the other hand occur in the Imperative, as in ( ex:tAZGACWfka ).

exe

tɤ-ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-fka \\
imp - refl - caus -be.full \\
`Eat to your fill!' (a common polite expression)
exe

Examples ( ex:tAZGACWfka ) and ( ex:atAtWGAZo.AtAZGAGAmbjom ), illustrate that the reflexive prefix is compatible with both the velar (§ sec:velar.caus.other ) and the sigmatic (§ sec:sig.causative ) causative prefixes.

Note that the meaning of ʑɣɤɣɤʑomake oneself light can also be expressed with a periphrastic construction as in ( ex:kWZo.YAZGAsApa ) below.

exe

nɤʑo nɯ, tɤ-muj stʰɯci a-tɤ-tɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-ʑo, nɤ-mbro nɯnɯ qale stʰɯci a-tɤ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-mbjom tɕe, \\
2sg dem indef. poss -feather so.much irr - pfv -2- refl - caus -be.light 2sg. poss -horse dem wind so.much irr - pfv - refl - caus -be.quick lnk \\
`[If] you make yourself as light as a feather, and your horse makes itself as quick as the wind, [you will succeed].' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

This use of the double causative+reflexive derivation is similar to the reflexivization of transitive verbs that have prenasalized anticausative counterparts to express the volitional intransitive (§ sec:refl.acaus).

When the meaning of the causative verb is not completely predictable from that of the base verb, the reflexivized verb always follows the meaning of the causative, rather than that of the base verb. For instance, ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-la `bathe into, immerse oneself into' (example ex:CpjWZGAGAlanW.kWZGAnWsmAn above), derives from the intransitive verb lasoak through the causative ɣɤ-laimmerse, dip in. However, even in this case the doubly derived verb ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-la is volitional and the base verb lasoak non-volitional (and essentially only takes inanimate subjects).

When the base verb is an intransitive verb that can be used volitionally, the doubly derived verb is used to put emphasis on the fact that the subject took active measures to perform the action. For instance the verb mbɣombe in a hurry (a verb whose Imperative form tɤ-mbɣom `hurry up!' exists) has the double derivation ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-mbɣom `hasten, hurry, strive to do $X$ as fast as possible', as in ( ex:toZGACWmbGom ).

exe

to-ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-mbɣom ʑo jo-nɯ-ɕe tɕe ɯ-jilco ra nɯ-ɕki to-ti. \\
ifr - refl - caus -be.in.a.hurry emph ifr - vert -go lnk 3sg. poss -villager pl 3pl. poss - dat ifr -say \\
`He hastened to go back [to the village], and told it to the other villagers.' (150902 hailibu-zh) 0006316#S104
exe

Some intransitive verbs have both volitional and non-volitional uses, with slightly different meanings. For instance, the intransitive ɴqoʁ has two meanings: `hang, be hanging' or `grab and cling onto' (see ex:WtaR.kANqoRnW in § sec:WtaR, and ex:jWfCWndzximWr in § sec:time.ordinals ). The doubly derived verb ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-ɴqoʁ `let oneself hang' (as in ex:pjWZGACWNqoR ) only reflects the first meaning of the base verb (the non-volitional `be hanging').

exe
