porɤt nɯ kɯnɤ tɕetu kʰɤrka nɯtɕu tɕe pjɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-ɴqoʁ ŋgrɤl. \\
small.spider dem also up.there ceiling dem: loc loc ipfv: down - refl - caus -hang be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`The small spider also lets itself hang down from the ceiling.' (26-mYaRmtsaR) 0003674#S94
exe
summary: The double causative+reflexive derivation can be used to express volitional action from a non-volitional intransitive verb, making such verbs acceptable in the imperative, as in “Eat to your fill!” It is compatible with both velar and sigmatic causative prefixes, and in cases where the causative meaning is not fully predictable, the reflexivized form follows the causative rather than the base verb; when a verb has both volitional and non-volitional uses, the doubly derived form typically targets only the non-volitional meaning, or adds emphasis that the subject acted intentionally and actively.

text: Some causative verbs have tropative (`consider $X$ to be $Y$', § sec:tropative ) or causative tropative (`cause people to consider $X$ to be $Y$'), for instance ɣɤkʰedepreciate, demean from kʰebe stupid (§ sec:tropative.other.construction ). Reflexive verbs deriving from this type of causative mean `(cause people to) consider oneself to be $Y$'; for example, ʑɣɤɣɤkʰedepreciate, demean is not used in meaning `cause oneself to become stupid'.
summary: Some causative verbs also have tropative or causative tropative meanings, such as “consider X to be Y” or “cause people to consider X to be Y,” as in forms derived from kʰebe ‘stupid.’ Reflexive forms built from this causative type mean “(cause people to) consider oneself to be Y,” and are not used with the meaning “cause oneself to become Y.”

text:
reflexive causative verb!motion
With the stative verbs of relative location armbatbe near and arqʰibe far, the reflexive+causative double derivations produce the motion verbs ʑɣɤsɤrmbatmove closer and ʑɣɤsɤrqʰimove further away, whose goal is marked in the dative, as in ( ex:WCki.koZGAsArmbat ) (see also ex:tWCki in § sec:indef.genr.poss ). Although zero conversion of these stative verbs into motion verbs is also attested (§ sec:convertion.orientable.verbs), the double derivation is by far the most common way of expressing these meanings.

exe

ɯʑo daltsɯtsa ʑo li, masɤrɯrju ʑo, srɯtpʰu nɯ ɯ-ɕki ko-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-ɤrmbat. \\
3sg slowly emph again in.secret emph ogre dem 3sg. poss - dat ifr: east - refl - caus -be.near \\
`He moved closer to the ogre slowly in secret.' (160706 poucet6)
0006109#S85
exe

When the base verb is a motion verb, the reflexive+causative double derivation also yields a motion verb, as in the case of ʑɣɤ-sɯ-ɤzɣɯt `manage to reach' from zɣɯtarrive (on the ɤ- prefixal element, see § sec:intr.person.irregular ). The verb ʑɣɤ-sɯ-ɤzɣɯt differs from its base verb in that it expresses that the subject had to strive hard to reach the goal, as example ( ex:nW.kWnA.joZGAsAzGWt ) illustrates.

exe

ɯ-tɯ-ɤrqʰi pjɤ-saχaʁ ʑo ri, nɯ kɯnɤ jo-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-ɤzɣɯt. \\
3sg. poss - nmlz:degree-be.far ifr. ipfv -be.extremely emph lnk dem also ifr - refl - caus -reach \\
`[China]$_i$ was very far, but even so he managed to reach it$_i$.' (140511 alading-zh) 0003953#S22
exe
summary:
The passage describes how reflexive+causative double derivation forms motion verbs from stative verbs of relative location, yielding meanings like “move closer” from “be near” and “move further away” from “be far.” These derived verbs take their goal in the dative, and this double derivation is said to be the most common way to express these motion meanings, though zero conversion is also possible.

It also notes that when the base verb is already a motion verb, the same derivation can produce a new motion verb with an added sense of effort or difficulty, as in “manage to reach,” which implies the subject had to strive to achieve the goal.

text:
When the base verb is transitive, the result of the reflexive+causative double derivation is still an intransitive verb.

The double derivation can have a plain compositional meaning, as in ʑɣɤ-sɯ-rtoʁ `have oneself examined' in ( ex:atAtWZGAsWrtoR ). The reflexivized argument corresponds to the causer and object of the base verb. The causee smɤnbadoctor does not received ergative marking, and is not indexed on the verb, as an inverse 3 2 configuration (§ sec:indexation.mixed ) would be nonsensical in ( ex:atAtWZGAsWrtoR ).

exe

smɤnba a-tɤ-tɯ-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-rtoʁ \\
doctor irr - pfv -2- refl - caus -see \\
`You should have yourself examined by a doctor.' (elicited)
exe

Doubly derived verbs can also express involuntary actions `get oneself $X$ed'. For instance, the reflexive+causative ʑɣɤ-sɯ-sat from satkill can have the meaning `get oneself killed', as in ( ex:pjWZGAsWsat ).

exe

ma βɣɯz ŋu tɕe, kʰɤrkɯ ra wuma ʑo ɣi. tɕe nɯnɯ pjɯ-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-sat ŋgrɤl. \\
lnk badger be: fact lnk side.of.the.house pl really emph come: fact lnk dem ipfv - refl - caus -kill be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`The badger often comes near houses, and gets itself killed. (The dogs chase it and kill it, and people also kill it).' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S114
exe

With some transitive verbs, the double derivation has the same meaning `take pains to $X$, strive to $X$' as with intransitive verbs above (examples ex:toZGACWmbGom and ex:nW.kWnA.joZGAsAzGWt ). For instance, the reflexive causative ʑɣɤ-sɯ-pjɤl of the transitive motion verb pjɤlgo around, cross, avoid (§ sec:motion.verbs ) means `strive to avoid $X$, take the necessary measures to avoid $X$' rather than `get oneself avoided': with this verb, the reflexivization targets the causee rather than the object (`cause oneself to avoid $X$' rather than `cause $X$ to avoid oneself').

exe

tɕendɤre nɯ tu-kɤ-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-pjɤl kowa ntsɯ tu-βzu-ndʑi pjɤ-ŋu. \\
lnk dem ipfv - inf - refl - caus -go.around manner always ipfv -make- du ifr. ipfv -be \\
`[The mouse and the sparrow] took every measure to avoid [the cat].' (lWlu)
0003361#S20
exe

The causative verbs sɤpatransform and sɤβzutransform (§ sec:passive.other.derivations ) derived from the lexicalized passive verbs apabecome and aβzubecome, grow (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ) are ditransitive, selecting as object the entity that undergoes transformation, and as semi-object the entity into which the change occurs. Reflexivization targets the object, and the corresponding reflexive forms ʑɣɤsɤpa and ʑɣɤsɤβzu mean `transform oneself into $X$' (rather than `transform $X$ into oneself'). They select as semi-object the entity into which the subject is transformed, for instance pjɤrgɤtvulture in ( ex:pjArgAt.nWnWZGAsABzu ).

exe

sloχpɯn nɯ ci nɯ-ʑɣɤ-sɤpʰɤr nɤ pjɤrgɤt ci nɯ-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-ɤβzu ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
teacher dem a.little aor - refl -shake add vulture indef aor - auto - refl - caus -become sens -be \\
`The teacher shook himself, and transformed himself into a vulture.' (2003kandZislama)
exe

Just like the causative verbs sɤpa and sɤβzu from which they are derived (example ex:kWmpCWmpCAr.nasABzu, § sec:passive.other.derivations, § sec:sig.caus.other.derivations ), ʑɣɤsɤpa and ʑɣɤsɤβzu can select as semi-object participial clauses, and be used as periphrastic causative constructions (§ sec:sWpa.sABzu ), as in ( ex:kWZo.YAZGAsApa ), where instead of the reflexive causative verb ʑɣɤɣɤʑomake oneself light (example ex:atAtWGAZo.AtAZGAGAmbjom above), the participle kɯ-ʑo `the one who is light' occurs as semi-object of ʑɣɤsɤpatransform oneself into.

exe

tɯrme ɯʑo nɯnɯ rcanɯ [tɤ-muj ʑo kɯ-fse kɯ-ʑo] ɲɤ-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-ɤpa, \\
man 3sg dem unexp: deg indef. poss -feather emph sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp -be.light ifr - refl - caus -become \\
`The man, him, made himself as light as a feather.' (04-smanmi)
exe
summary: When the base verb is transitive, the reflexive+causative double derivation still yields an intransitive verb, but the reflexivized argument may correspond to different roles depending on the lexical item. In some cases it has a compositional meaning like “have oneself examined,” in others it means “get oneself killed” or “strive to avoid X,” and with transformation verbs it means “transform oneself into X,” selecting the new state as a semi-object.

text:
reflexive autive
Reflexive and autive (§ sec:autobenefactive ) derivations have completely different semantics, and distinct morphosyntactic properties, since the latter does not change the verb transitivity. With a handful of verbs such as ʁmɯɣintend to, decide, the reflexive form has an autobenefactive meaning ( ʑɣɤʁmɯɣdecide for oneself), but the transitivity is changed.

The autive nɯ- (§ sec:autobenefactive ) is compatible with the reflexive ʑɣɤ-. It is the only derivational prefix that precedes the reflexive prefix in the prefixal chain (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain ). The autive+reflexive combination has four different meanings.

First, it can express and involuntary action that the subject both causes and suffers from (as in ex:YWtWnWZGAkho above).

Second, the nɯ- prefix can also be used to put emphasis on the fact that the subject perform the reflexive action by him/her/itself without external help, as in ( ex:kunWZGAfstWn2 ).

exe

tɕetʰa tɯ-ji ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯnɯra, iɕqʰa tɯ-rdoʁ kɯ-fse nɯra ɕɯ-ndze, tɕendɤre, ɯʑo ku-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-fstɯn cʰa \\
later indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -in dem: pl filler one-piece sbj: pcp -be.like dem: pl tral -eat[III]: fact lnk 3sg ipfv - auto - refl -take.care can: fact \\
`[This hen] will go and eat the grains in the fields, it will be able to take care of itself on its own.' (150822 laoye zuoshi zongshi duide-zh)
0006298#S145
exe

Third, the nɯ- prefix is also found with the autobenefactive meaning `for oneself' in these forms. In ( ex:tonWZGACWfkandZi ) for instance, the autive prefix occurs to insist on the fact that the parents (dual subject) ate to their full in the absence of their children.

exe

ndʑi-pɤri kɯ-pɯ pe to-βzu-ndʑi qʰe, ʑɤni to-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-fka-ndʑi. \\
3du. poss -diner sbj: pcp - emph be.good ifr -make- du lnk 3du ifr - auto - refl - caus -be.full- du \\
`They made a nice diner for themselves, and ate to their fill.' (160701 poucet2) 0006155#S16
exe

Fourth, it can occur to express an action taking place spontaneously without external agent, as in ( ex:chAnWZGAsAtsa ).

exe

kɯm cʰɤ-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-sɯ-ɤtsa \\
door ifr - auto - refl - caus -be.locked \\
`The dock locked itself.' (elicited; describes house doors with an automatic locking system)
exe

The autive is common on verbs with reflexive and causative prefixes (§ sec:refl.caus ), resulting in a triple derivation, as in ( ex:tonWZGACWfkandZi ) and ( ex:chAnWZGAsAtsa ) above.
summary:
The passage contrasts reflexive and autive derivations, noting that they have different meanings and morphosyntactic behavior: unlike the reflexive, the autive does not change verb transitivity. In a few verbs, the reflexive can take on an autobenefactive meaning, but the transitivity still changes.

It then explains that the autive prefix nɯ- can combine with the reflexive prefix ʑɣɤ-, and this combination has four meanings: involuntary self-affecting actions, emphasis that the subject acted without help, autobenefactive “for oneself,” and spontaneous actions without an external agent. The autive is also common in triple derivations with reflexive and causative prefixes.

text:
reflexive tropative applicative
Apart from the causative, the reflexive derivation can be added after other valency-increasing derivations such as the tropative and the applicative.

As an example of reflexivized tropative, nɤmpɕɤrfind beautiful (from mpɕɤrbe beautiful) can be reflexivized as ʑɣɤnɤmpɕɤrfind oneself beautiful (§ sec:tropative.other.derivations ).

The applicative verbs nɯɣmube afraid of and nɯrgalike, `love' (from mube afraid and rgalike) have reflexive form ʑɣɤ-nɯ-rga and ʑɣɤ-nɯɣ-mu which can either mean `like/be afraid of oneself' or have a reflexive+causative meaning `have people like/be afraid of oneself'. The latter meaning can also be expressed with a triple derivation such as ʑɣɤ-z-nɯɣ-mu with the causative z- between the reflexive and the applicative prefixes.

The applicative nɤstubelieve, which selects as object the person one believes in (example ex:WYWkWnAstua, § sec:applicative.promoted ), can also be reflexivized as ʑɣɤnɤstubelieve in oneself, as in ( ex:mWYAZGAnAstu ). This example is from a translated story, but the presence of a second object (the relative nɯ pa-mto nɯra ) is not due to calquing from the original (which has 不敢相信 bùgǎnxiāngxìnhe did not dare to believe it), and was not considered to be clumsy upon rechecking.

exe

nɯ pa-mto nɯra mɯ-ɲɤ-ʑɣɤ-nɤ-stu. \\
dem aor:3 -see dem: pl neg - ifr - refl - appl -believe \\
`He did not believe the things that he himself had [just] seen.' (150830 baihe jiemei-zh) 0006368#S104
exe
summary: The reflexive derivation can attach after other valency-increasing derivations besides the causative, including the tropative and applicative. Examples show reflexivized forms meaning ‘find oneself beautiful,’ ‘like/be afraid of oneself,’ or ‘believe in oneself,’ and in some cases a reflexive+causative interpretation is also possible, including with a triple derivation where the causative prefix intervenes between the reflexive and applicative prefixes.

text:
grammaticalization!reflexive reflexive!origin
The reflexive ʑɣɤ- is cognate to forms found in other Gyalrong languages, including Tshobdun oɟɐ-, Zbu vjɐ-  and Situ wjɐ-. Some dialects of Zbu however have a divergent reflexive prefix ɲɐ, which cannot be cognate to the forms discussed here. These prefixes go back to a proto-Gyalrong form *wjɐ- (with a variant *wəjɐ- for Tshobdun) with metathesis in Japhug. However, the cluster ʑɣ- is otherwise only attested in Japhug in ideophones such as ʑɣɤrʑɣɤrhaving some (pieces) coming out (out of a bundle) (§ sec:idph.onsets ).

This prefix itself is possibly the incorporated bound state form of the third singular pronoun *wəjaŋ (corresponding to Japhug ɯʑohe, § sec:pers.pronouns, whose irregular phonology is discussed in § sec:3sg.possessive.form ); typological parallels of the personal pronoun $ $ reflexive change proposed here also exist in Yukaghir (, ). For an alternative etymology, see.

The reflexive prefix is a core Gyalrong innovation, not shared even by Khroskyabs. The reflexive prefix ʁjæ̂- in Khroskyabs is not directly related to its core Gyalrong equivalent, as it is based on the denominal ʁ-, cognate of the Japhug stative denominal a- (§ sec:denom.contracting ). Both Khroskyabs ʁjæ̂- and proto-Gyalrong *wjɐ- reflexive prefixes share the bound state of the pronominal base *jaŋ- (Japhug -ʑo, § sec:pers.pronouns ), but result from independent grammaticalizations.
summary:
The Japhug reflexive prefix ʑɣɤ- is cognate with reflexive forms in other Gyalrong languages and is traced back to proto-Gyalrong *wjɐ- (with a Tshobdun variant *wəjɐ-), though Japhug shows metathesis and an unusual cluster otherwise found only in ideophones. It may derive from the incorporated bound form of the third singular pronoun *wəjaŋ, and similar pronoun-to-reflexive developments are typologically attested.

The reflexive prefix is a core Gyalrong innovation not shared even by Khroskyabs. Khroskyabs ʁjæ̂- is not directly related, since it comes from a different denominal source, although both forms ultimately involve the bound pronominal base *jaŋ- and arose through independent grammaticalization.

text:
reciprocal!reduplicated reduplication!reciprocal
The reduplicated reciprocal derivation is the productive way of expressing mutual action in Japhug. It combines the a- prefixal element found in the passive (§ sec:passive ) and several denominal derivations (§ sec:denom.contracting ) with the partially reduplicated stem of the base verb. If the verb has a polysyllabic stem (whether the non-final syllables are derivational prefixes or not), only the last syllable is reduplicated. For instance rqoʁhug, nɯpoʁkiss and nɯrɯtʂaenvy The verb nɯrɯtʂaenvy is denominal from rɯtʂaenvy (n). yield a-rqɯ rqoʁ `hug each other' ( ex:kokArqWrqoRnWci ), a-nɯpɯ poʁ `kiss each other' and a-nɯrɯtʂɯ tʂa `envy each other', respectively.

As in other cases of partial derivation, the reduplication disregards morpheme boundaries: when the reciprocal derivation is applied to verbs with the sɯɣ- and nɯɣ- allomorphs of the sigmative causative (§ sec:caus.sWG ) and applicative (§ sec:allomorphy.applicative ), the final ɣ- is reduplicated together with the monosyllabic verb root.

For instance, the reciprocal of the applicative nɯɣbɯɣmiss is anɯɣbɯ ɣbɯɣ `miss each other' (§ sec:reciprocal.other ), despite the fact that the verb root is bɯɣmiss home ( tab:applicative, § sec:applicative ) and that the preinitial ɣ- belongs to the applicative prefix.

Since reduplicated reciprocal has two exponents ( a- and reduplication), in the glosses only the a- prefix is glossed as recip, while the reduplication left unglossed to avoid unnecessary redundancy: thus a-rqɯ rqoʁ is glossed as recip -hug rather than as recip - recip hug.

The ɤ/a/o allomorphy of the a- element, and the presence of the peg k-...-ci (§ sec:peg.circumfix ) in the Inferential (as in ex:kokArqWrqoRnWci ) follows the same rules as other contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction, § sec:preverbs.contracting.verbs ).

Reciprocal verbs are morphologically intransitive, and their subject is necessarily non-singular except in the case of verbs expressing naturally collective action (as in ex:Wqa.YAndWndo below), in generic forms, where number is neutralized, or when the subject is a group of inanimate and poorly distinguishable entities.

When the plural or dual subject of the reciprocal verb is the combination of a previously mentioned entity or group with another group, the comitative cʰo (§ sec:comitative ) can be used to specify the second group.

For instance, in ( ex:kokArqWrqoRnWci ), the subject of the verb ko-k-ɤ-rqɯ rqoʁ-nɯ-ci `they hug each other' corresponds to the sum of referent of the subject of the first verb jo-nɯ-ɕe `he went back' with the group of people referred to by the postpositional phrase ɯ-ɣi ra cʰo `with his relatives' (see § sec:semi.transitive.dative for examples of the same phenomenon with non-reciprocal verbs).

exe

kʰa jo-nɯ-ɕe tɕendɤre [ɯ-ɣi ra cʰo] ko-k-ɤ-rqɯ rqoʁ-nɯ-ci ʑo ɲɤ-ɣɤwu-nɯ. \\
home ifr - vert -go lnk 3sg. poss -relative pl comit ifr - peg - recip -hug- pl - peg emph ifr -cry- pl \\
`He went home and he and his relatives hug each other and cried.' (140512 fushang he yaomo1)
0003969#S34
exe

Expectedly, the reciprocal of secundative verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ) targets the recipient object; for instance, mbigive yields ambɯmbigive to each other ( ex:YAmbWmbinW ).

exe

tɕe nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ srɯsmɤn ra pjɯ-lɤt-nɯ, tɕe nɯra pjɯ-nɯ-lɤt-nɯ tɕe nɯra ɲɯ-ɤmbɯ mbi-nɯ ra ŋu \\

`They put medicine [against sinus inflammation] into the [snuff tobacco]$_i$, and they give it$_i$ to each other.' (30-CnAto)
0003734#S17

The reduplicated reciprocal derivation can also express naturally collective events without clearly distinct agents and patients, such as awɯwumgather together ( ex:chAwWwumnW ) from wumgather.

exe

qartsɯ tɤ-mda qʰe tɕe cʰɯ-ɤ-wɯ wum-nɯ qʰe kɯ-dɯ dɤn ʑo tɯtɯrca ku-rɤʑi-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\

The meaning of this reciprocal form is also slightly different from that of the base verb, since wumgather has a wide range of extended meanings, such as `take as a X' (as in example ex:naslama.kukWwuma, § sec:essive.abs ) or `fold wings' (as in ex:YWqAt.nA.kuwum, § sec:centripetal.centrifugal ) which are completely absent from the reciprocal form. In addition, the verb wum typically takes non-human entities as objects when meaning `gather' as in ( ex:aCtAtWwum ).

exe

tɯrsa ɯ-rkɯ χpɯn-ŋga tʰamtɕɤt a-ɕ-tɤ-tɯ-wum tɕe \\
cemetery 3sg. poss -side monk-clothes all irr - tral - pfv -2-gather lnk \\
`Go and collect all the monk robes near the cemetery.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S157

The intransitive verb andɯndo derived from ndotake can have a prototypical reciprocal meaning `grab each other' (especially relative to fighting, see example ex:YWsAtWtea below, § sec:reciprocal.other ). It also occurs with the naturally collective event meaning `be clustered together' as in ( ex:Wqa.YAndWndo ) with a singular verb form, due to the fact that mushrooms are poorly differentiable inanimate referents (§ sec:optional.indexation ).

exe

tɕe tɕe ɯ-qa nɯ ɲɯ-ɤ-ndɯ ndo, ɯ-taʁ nɯ ki kɯ-fse kɯ-dɯ dɤn ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
lnk lnk 3sg. poss -foot dem sens - recip -take 3sg. poss -top dem dem. prox sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp - emph be.many sens -be lnk \\
`The base (of the mushroom 刷把菌 shuābǎjūnRamaria formosa) is all clustered together, but it has many top parts.' (23-tshAYCAnW)
0003616#S10
exe

A handful of intransitive verbs can derive reciprocal forms. The verb of speech rɯɕmispeak has the derived form a-rɯɕmɯ ɕmi `exchange words, talk to each other' (see example ex:YAmJAkhondZi, § sec:co.participation ), with reciprocalization of the dative-marked recipient (compare with ex:WCki.torWCmi, § sec:dative ).
summary:
The productive reciprocal in Japhug is formed with the prefix a- plus partial reduplication of the verb stem, typically repeating only the final syllable of a polysyllabic stem and ignoring morpheme boundaries. Reciprocal verbs are morphologically intransitive and normally require a non-singular subject, though they can also express collective actions or, in a few intransitive verbs, meanings like “gather together,” “be clustered together,” or “talk to each other.”  

The passage also notes that the reciprocal targets the recipient in secundative verbs and that the a- element follows the same allomorphy and contracting-verb patterns as elsewhere. In glossing, only a- is labeled as reciprocal because the reduplication is left unglossed to avoid redundancy.

text:
reciprocal!collocation
In some noun-verb collocations (§ sec:tr.light.verbs ), the verb can undergo the reduplicated reciprocal derivation, expressing mutual action between the subject and the possessor of the object of the base construction.

For instance, the collocation meaning `braid hair' ( ex:Wku.nWBzuta ) including the verb βzumake and the body part tɯ-kuhead (§ sec:body.part ) yields in ( ex:Wku.YABzWBzundZi ) a reciprocalized construction with the reduplicated verb aβzɯβzu and the noun tɯ-ku demoted as semi-object.

exe

a-pi ɯ-ku nɯ-βzu-t-a \\
1sg. poss -elder.sibling 3sg. poss -head aor -make- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I braided my sister's hair.' (elicited)
exe

exe

ɯ-pi cʰo ndʑi-ku ɲɯ-ɤ-βzɯ βzu-ndʑi ndɤre, \\
3sg. poss -elder.sibling comit 3du. poss -head ipfv - recip -make- du lnk \\
`She and her sister braided each other's hair.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

Example ( ex:nWBra.YABzWBzunW ) illustrates the same phenomenon with the collocation meaning `share with', combining the noun tɯ-βrashare with βzumake.

exe

nɤʑo kɯ ɯ-pɯ-tɯ-sat nɤ, nɤʑo kɯ aʑo a-βra ɲɯ-tɯ-βze, aʑo pɯ pɯ-sat-a nɤ, nɤj nɤ-βra ɲɯ-βze-a, nɯ kɯ-fse, nɯ-βra ɲɯ-ɤ-βzɯ βzu-nɯ pjɤ-ŋɡrɤl. \\
2sg erg qu - aor -2-kill add 2sg erg 1sg 1sg. poss -share ipfv -2-make[III] 1sg cond aor -kill- 1sg add 2sg 2sg. poss -share ipfv -make[III]- 1sg dem sbj: pcp -be.like 3pl. poss -share ipfv - recip -make- pl ifr. ipfv -be.usually.the.case- pl \\
`If it was you who had killed [game during a hunt], you would share some of it with me, if it was me who had killed [game], I would share some of it with you, this way, people used to share [their game meat] with each other.' (160714 XsWmsna)
exe
summary: In some noun-verb collocations, the verb can take a reduplicated reciprocal derivation to express mutual action between the subject and the possessor of the object in the base construction. In such cases, the original noun is demoted to a semi-object, as shown with collocations meaning ‘braid hair’ and ‘share with,’ where the reciprocalized form indicates that the participants act on each other’s possessed item.

text:
reciprocal!compatibility
The reciprocal derivation is highly productive, can be applied to verbs that have undergone a valency-increasing derivation such as causative (§ sec:sig.causative, § sec:velar.causative ), applicative (§ sec:applicative ) or tropative (§ sec:tropative ).

Reciprocalized causatives are found with both sigmatic and velar causative verbs. For instance, the velar causative ɣɤrlaʁdestroy (from the intransitive verb rlaʁdisappear, borrowed from བརླག་brlaglose) has a reciprocal form aɣɤrlɯrlaʁdestroy each other ( ex:chAGArlWrlaRnW ).

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe, tɤru ra tu-o-nɯsnɯɲɯ ɲaʁ-nɯ tɕe cʰɯ-ɤ-ɣɤ-rlɯ rlaʁ-nɯ pjɤ-ŋgrɤl \\
former.times lnk chieftain pl ipfv - recip -do.harm- pl lnk ipfv - recip - caus -disappear- pl ipfv. ifr -be.usually.the.case \\
`In former times, chieftains used to harm (murder) each other and destroy each other's families.' (elicited)
exe

Reciprocalization of sigmatic causatives is productive. Example ( ex:YAkAsWGYWGYaRnW ) illustrates two verbs with this double derivation: asɯɴqʰɯɴqʰimake each other dirty (from the causative sɯɴqʰimake dirty derived from ɴqʰibe dirty) and asɯɣɲɯɣɲaʁblacken each other (from the causative sɯɣɲaʁblacken from ɲaʁbe black). In the latter, note that partial reduplication targets the syllable ɣɲaʁ, disregarding morpheme boundaries (the ɣ is part of the causative prefix, § sec:caus.sWG ).

exe

ɲɤ-k-ɤ-sɯ-ɴqʰɯ ɴqʰi-ndʑi tɕe, ɲɤ-k-ɤ-sɯɣ-ɲɯ ɣɲaʁ-ndʑi-ci ʑo \\
ifr - peg - recip - caus -be.dirty- du lnk ifr - peg - recip - caus -be.black- du - peg emph \\
`They$_DU$ made each other dirty, they blackened each other.' (elicited, can be said of children playing in a dirty place)
exe

The lexicalized verb nɯsɯkʰorob, extort which etymologically derives from kʰogive with the causative and autive prefixes (§ sec:sig.caus.lexicalized ) can also undergo reciprocalization to anɯsɯkʰɯkʰoextort each other as in ( ex:pjAkAnWswkhWkhonWci ).

exe

nɯnɯ jɤ-kɤ-ɣɤrɤt nɯ pjɤ-k-ɤ-nɯsɯkʰɯ kʰo-nɯ-ci. \\
dem aor - obj: pcp -throw dem ifr. ipfv - peg - recip -rob- pl - peg \\
`The beasts fought with each other to get the [piece of cloth] that he had thrown [at them].' (150825 huluwa-zh) 0006346#S145
exe

Reciprocalized tropatives are not commonly found in the corpus, but potentially any tropative verb can undergo reciprocal derivation. For instance, the slightly lexicalized tropative verb nɤpeconsider to be good, like (from pebe good) yields anɤpɯpelike each other, as in ( ex:YAkAnApWpendZici ). The other verb anɤntsʰɯntsʰilove each other in ( ex:YAkAnApWpendZici ) derives from nɤntsʰilove, which is a lexicalized and synchronically non-analyzable tropative (§ sec:tropative.lexicalized ).

exe

ɲɤ-k-ɤ-nɤntsʰɯ ntsʰi-ndʑi-ci, ɲɤ-k-ɤ-nɤ-pɯ pe-ndʑi tɕe \\
ifr - peg - recip -love- du - peg ifr - peg - recip - trop -be.good- du lnk \\
`They fell in love with each other.' (150827 mengjiangnv-zh) 0006290#S103
exe

The reciprocal derivation is also completely productive with applicative verbs. For instance nɯɣbɯɣmiss, `long for' (from bɯɣmiss home), nɤkʰɤzŋgashout at (from akʰucall) and nɯrgalike (from rgalike) yield the reciprocal verbs anɯɣbɯɣbɯɣmiss each other, anɤkʰɤzŋgɯ zŋga `shout at each other' and anɯrgɯ rga `like each other', respectively. In the case of a-nɯɣ-bɯ ɣbɯɣ, partial reduplication disregards morpheme boundaries (the ɣ that belongs to the applicative prefixes is reduplicated together with the verb root), as in the case of the reciprocal of causative asɯɣɲɯɣɲaʁblacken each other discussed above (§ sec:reciprocal.other ).

A sigmatic causative derivation can be applied to a reciprocal verb. For instance, awɯwumgather together (see ex:chAwWwumnW in § sec:redp.reciprocal above) yields the verb sɤwɯwumgather, whose meaning is close to that of the base verb wumgather (see example ex:aCtAtWwum above and the related discussion), but lacking the extended meanings of this verb and more commonly used to express the meaning `gather' with human objects.

exe

srɯnmɯ ra cʰɤ-sɯ-ɤ-wɯ wum tɕe, \\
râkshasî pl ifr - caus - recip -gather lnk \\
`She gathered the râkhasîs together.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

Such double derivations are by no means rare. The causative+reciprocal sɤtɯtaseparate (of two persons that are fighting with each other, as in ex:YWsAtWtea ) is considerably more commonly used than the simple reciprocal atɯtarelease each other (from taput).

exe

ɲɯ-sɯ-ɤ-tɯ te-a ri tɕe mɤʑɯ ku-o-ndɯ ndo-ndʑi ɕti \\
ipfv - caus - recip -put- 1sg lnk lnk again ipfv: east - recip -take- du be. aff: fact \\
`I am (repeatedly) separating [two fighting ants], but they grab each other again [each time].' (conversation 14-05-01)
exe

The verb asɤmɯmtsʰɯmtsʰɤminform each other, which presents two instances of the reciprocal derivation, is treated in (§ sec:amW.reciprocal ).
summary: The reciprocal derivation is highly productive and can apply to verbs that have already undergone valency-increasing derivations such as causative, applicative, or tropative. The passage gives many examples showing that reciprocalization works with both simple and double derivations, including cases where partial reduplication crosses morpheme boundaries, and notes that some causative+reciprocal forms are more common than the simpler reciprocal forms.

text:
The meaning of reciprocal verbs is not always fully predictable from that of the base verb; some reciprocal verbs express naturally collective action (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ) and may have a meaning that is more restricted than that of the base verb.

In some cases, the meanings of the reciprocal form has changed to such an extent that the two verbs have become synchronically unrelated. The clearest example is the intransitive verb alɯlɤtfight, which requires a non-singular subject and can select a comitative phrase (§ sec:comitative ) as in ( ex:talalWlAtndZi ), like regular reciprocal verbs (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ).

exe

ʁdɯxpa kɤrpu ɣɯ ɯ-tɕɯ cʰo aʑo a-tɕɯ nɯ tɤ-alɯlɤt-ndʑi tɕe, tɕe a-tɕɯ ɣɯ-sat pjɤ-ŋu ri, \\
anthr anthr gen 3sg. poss -son comit 1sg 1sg. poss -son dem aor -fight- du lnk lnk 1sg. poss -son inv -kill: fact ifr. ipfv -be lnk \\
`Gdugpa dkarpo's son and my son fought with each other, and my son was about to be killed.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S237
exe

This verb originates from the transitive verb lɤtrelease, which is used as a light verb in several collocations related to fight. In these constructions, the syntactic object of lɤt is the instrument used to hit or shoot, such as weapons ( scapasword, tɯdiarrow, ɕɤmɯɣdɯgun etc) or body parts ( tɤŋkʰɯtfist etc) as objects ( ex:CAmWGdW.tulAtnW, ex:qachGa.WtaR.tWdi.tolAt and also ex:scoRqhu.tulAt in § sec:WtaR ), while the semantic patient (the entity that is hit or shot at) is marked by the relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:WtaR ).

exe

nɯnɯ ɕɤmɯɣdɯ tu-lɤt-nɯ tɕe pjɯ-sat-nɯ ɕti. \\
dem gun ipfv -release- pl lnk ipfv -kill- pl be. aff: kill \\
`They shoot at it with guns and kill it.' (28-qapar)
0003720#S20
exe

exe

qacʰɣa ɯ-taʁ ʑo li tɯdi nɯ ci to-lɤt. \\
fox 3sg. poss -on emph again arrow dem indef ifr -release \\
`He too shot an arrow at the fox.' (140507 jinniao-zh)
0003931#S80
exe

The reciprocal derivation here originally expressed mutual action between the subject and the oblique argument (marked by ɯ-taʁon, above) of the base verb; the original meaning may have been `shoot at/hit each other (with $X$)', and it can be surmised that the verb alɯlɤtfight used to require a semi-object corresponding to the instrument used for hitting/shooting at an earlier stage. The verb alɯlɤt became fully lexicalized when it ceased to co-occur with a semi-object, and when its meaning became narrowed to the meaning `fight', as opposed to all the other possible meanings of the light verb lɤt (§ sec:lAt.lv ).

In some cases, the base verb does not exist anymore but its possible form can be easily recovered. For instance, the reciprocal anɯrŋɤrɯrulook at each other's face (example ex:kanWrNArWrundZi ) is derived from a lost base verb $ $ nɯrŋɤru, an incorporating verb made from the intransitive rulook at (§ sec:orienting.verbs ) and the nominal root of tɯ-rŋaface, with the denominal prefix nɯ- (§ sec:incorp.other ).

exe

nɯnɯ cʰo ci kɤ-anɯrŋɤrɯru-ndʑi tɕe \\
dem comit a.little aor -look.at.each.other- du lnk \\
`They exchanged a look with each other'. (2010-07, pear story)
exe

Finally, we find a few intransitive verbs that resemble reciprocal verbs formally (presence of a- prefix and verb stem reduplication) and syntactically (non-singular subject, select comitative phrases), but whose verb root is not otherwise attested in Japhug: amɯmibe on good terms (§ sec:comitative ), aʑɯʑuwrestle and asɯsucopulate (the latter perhaps related to sɯsulive).

Reciprocal amɯ- prefix
reciprocal
In addition to the reduplicated reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ), a second reciprocal pattern is attested in Japhug: the prefix amɯ-. As shown by the examples in tab:amW.reciprocal, the amɯ- prefix can derive reciprocal verbs from ditransitive, transitive, semi-transitive and intransitive verbs. When prefixed to a- initial verbs such as atɯɣmeet, no vowel contraction takes place (the reciprocal is amɯtɯɣmeet each other rather than $ $ amɤtɯɣ as could have been expected).

The verbs that are compatible with amɯ- derivation can be divided into four groups: indirective, perception, semi-transitive and stative.

amɯ- reciprocalization of indirective verbs
Indirective verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) such as tisay become semi-transitive (§ sec:semi.transitive ) when subjected to the amɯ- reciprocal derivation.

The reciprocal verb amɯtisay to each other is compatible with a semi-object (noun phrase or reported speech complement clause as in ex:tokAmWtindZi and ex:amAtsa.tukAmWti ) corresponding to the object of the base verb. The reciprocal derivation here expresses mutual action between the subject and the dative recipient of tisay.

exe

`nɯtɕu tɯ-ci z-ɲɯ-kɯ-sɯ-ɤ-j-tsʰi ɲɯ-ntsʰi' to-k-ɤmɯ-ti-ndʑi \\
dem: loc indef. poss -water tral - ipfv - genr:S/O- caus - pass - caus -drink sens -be.better ifr - peg - recip -say- du \\
`They said to each other `we should go there and ask for water to drink.'' (Nyima wodzer 2002)
exe

Example ( ex:amAtsa.tukAmWti ) illustrates the use of this reciprocal verb with a generic person form, with neutralization of number marking (the verb otherwise always has non-singular number indexation in finite forms). Concerning the kinship rule described in ( ex:amAtsa.tukAmWti ), see § sec:ego.cousins.

exe

nɯnɯ kɤndʑi-sqʰaj ɯ-rɟit nɯ tɕe ``a-mɤtsa" tu-kɯ-ɤmɯ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
dem coll -sister 3sg. poss -offspring dem lnk 1sg. poss -MZCh ipfv - genr:S/O- recip -say sens -be \\
`Children of sisters call each other `my maternal parallel cousin'.' (140425 kWmdza4)
exe

The reciprocal amɯ- prefix expresses reciprocity between the subject and other oblique arguments, for instance those marked by the relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:WtaR ). For instance, the verb amɯstʰaβbe one against the other ( ex:kAmWsthWsthaB ) is derived from stʰaβput against, a ditransitive verb which selects a phrase in ɯ-taʁ ( ex:WtaR.kuwGsthaB ).

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ li bɤβbɤβ ʑo kɯ-pa tɕe, kɯ-ɤmɯ-stʰɯ stʰaβ ʑo kɯ-dɤn tu-ɬoʁ ŋu. \\
lnk dem again idph (II):growing.in.clumps emph sbj: pcp - aux lnk sbj: pcp - recip - emph put.against emph sbj: pcp -be.many ipfv -come.out be: fact \\
`[These mushrooms] grow in clumps, one against the other in great numbers.' (23-mbrAZim)
0003604#S9
exe

summary:
The passage explains that some reciprocal verbs in Japhug have meanings that are only partly predictable from the base verb, and in some cases the reciprocal form has become fully lexicalized and synchronically unrelated to the original verb. It gives examples such as *alɯlɤt* ‘fight,’ which developed from a verb meaning ‘release’ in weapon-use constructions, and notes other reciprocal-like intransitives whose base forms are lost or unattested.

It then introduces a second reciprocal pattern, the prefix *amɯ-*, which can derive reciprocal verbs from several verb types, including indirective, perception, semi-transitive, and stative verbs. This prefix marks reciprocity not only between subjects but also between subjects and certain oblique arguments, such as recipients or arguments marked by the relator noun *ɯ-taʁ*.

text:
ma nɯnɯ ɯʑo ʁɟa [tɯ-mdʑu ɯ-taʁ] kú-wɣ-stʰaβ tɕe mɤrtsaβ, \\
lnk dem 3sg completely genr. poss -tongue 3sg. poss -on ipfv - inv -put.against lnk be.spicy: fact \\
`If one puts it (this plant) on one's tongue (without anything else), it is spicy.' (13-tCamu)
0003498#S8
exe

The verb amɯrpubump against each other is a similar case (see example ex:rNgW.tokAmWrpundZici, § sec:pers.pronouns ), but its base verb rpubump into is labile (§ sec:goal.labile ).

amɯ- reciprocalization of perception verbs
The perception verbs mtosee, mtsʰɤmhear are also compatible with the amɯ- prefix. Unlike the indirective verbs discussed in § sec:recip.amW.indirective their reciprocal forms amɯmtosee each other and amɯmtsʰɤmhear each other (or `hear from each other') express reciprocal action between the subject (experiencer) and the object (stimulus) of the base verb. As shown by ( ex:pjAmWmtondZi ), these verbs also select the comitative like other reciprocal forms.

exe

<liangshanbo> cʰondɤre pjɯ-ɤmɯ-mto-ndʑi mɯ-pjɤ-jɤɣ tɕe \\
anthr comit ipfv - recip -see- du neg - ifr. ipfv -be.allowed lnk \\
`She and Liang Shanbo were not allowed to see each other.' (150826 liangshanbo zhuyingtai-zh) 0006244#S155
exe

amɯ- reciprocalization of semi-transitive verbs

In the case of the semi-transitive verbs tsoknow, understand and atɯɣmeet, the amɯ- derivation targets the semi-object.

The verb amɯtso can be used with the reciprocal meaning of `understand each other' as in ( ex:pjWkAmWtso.YWra ). It also has an additional meaning `be clear, be understandable (of speech)', which reflects the homophonous amɯ- distributed property derivation (§ sec:distributed.amW ). As discussed in § sec:distributed.amW, the reciprocal and distributed property amɯ- prefixes are historically related, and the verb amɯtso is one of the pivot forms between them.

exe

kupa-skɤt tú-wɣ-βzu tɕe nɯnɯ a-pɯ-ŋu, iʑo ɣɯ <guoyu> ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, nɯnɯ kɤsɯfse ɣɯ ji-rju ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, pjɯ-kɯ-ɤmɯ-tso ɲɯ-ra ri, li nɯ koŋla mɯ́j-tso-nɯ. \\
Chinese-language ipfv - inv -make lnk dem irr - ipfv -be 1sg gen national.language sens -be lnk dem all gen 1sg. poss -speech sens -be lnk ipfv - genr:S/O- recip -understand sens -be.needed lnk again dem completely neg. sens -understand- pl \\
`When we speak Chinese, since it is our national language, our common language, we should be able to understand each other, but [some people in Tshobdun] do not understand it completely either.' (150901 tshuBdWnskAt)
0006242#S14
exe

amɯ- reciprocalization of stative verbs
The amɯ- prefix occurs with a few stative verbs. The stative verbs of relative location armbatbe near and arqʰibe far have the reciprocal forms amɯrmbatbe close to each other and amɯrqʰibe far from each other. In ( ex:YAmWrmbat ), amɯrmbat appears in singular form due to the inanimate character of the stars and their poor differentiability from each other with a naked eye.

exe

ʑŋgri wuma kɯ-tʂot ɲɯ-maʁ ri, kɯ-ɤmɯ-rmbɯ rmbat ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, nɯ wuma ɲɯ-saχsɤl. [...] ɯ-tɯ-ɤʑirja ɯ-tsʰɯɣa nɯ, [...] ʁnɤmcʰi tsa ɲɯ-fse, [...] ri ɲɯ-ɤmɯ-rmbat. \\
star really sbj: pcp -be.bright sens -not.be lnk sbj: pcp - recip - emph be.near emph be: fact lnk dem really sens -be.clear 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.aligned 3sg. poss -shape dem gnam.khyi a.little be.like: fact lnk sens - recip -be.near \\
`(There six stars in the Pleiades.) They are not very bright stars, but they are close to each other, and for this reason they are quite visible. The way they are aligned is a bit similar to that of the constellation Gnam.khyi, but closer to each other.' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S15
exe

The verb amɯfseknow each other (example ex:kamWfsetCi.pamWmitCi ) historically originates from the amɯ- reciprocal form of a base -fse, which is not related to the intransitive stative verb fsebe like, but rather to a lost verb corresponding to the Tshobdun verb fsɛʔ `hear'. The isolated derivation nɯfseknow (a person) (possibly a lexicalized autive § sec:autoben.lexicalized ) is derived from the same base with the same meaning; it also has a Tshobdun cognate: nə́fsɛ `know well'.

exe

nɯre ri tɕe kɤ-amɯfse-tɕi tɕe, tɕendɤre wuma ʑo pɯ-amɯmi-tɕi \\
dem: loc loc loc aor -know.each.other- 1du lnk lnk really emph pst. ipfv -be.on.good.terms- 1du \\
`We got to know each other there, and we were in very good terms.' (12-BzaNsa) 0003484#S6
exe

Some reciprocal verbs derived either from dynamic transitive verbs ( amɯstʰaβbe one against the other in ex:kAmWsthWsthaB ) or from stative verbs ( amɯrmbatbe close to each other in ex:YAmWrmbat ) are stative, and often appear with emphatic reduplication. This reduplication is different from that of reduplicated reciprocal verbs (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ), which is one of the morphological exponents of that reciprocal formation.

Causativivization of amɯ- reciprocal verbs
reciprocal!causative causative!reciprocal
The sigmatic causative can be added to amɯ- reciprocal verbs. For instance, amɯmtosee each other discussed above yields the causative form sɤmɯmtocause to see each other, which also selects the comitative like its base verb, The Chinese original passage from which ( ex:cho.pjAsAmWmto ) is translated is 老翁便领着那两个少男女出来与耿去病见面 lǎowēng biàn lǐngzhe liǎngge shàonánnǚ chūlái yǔ Gěng Qùbìng jiànmiànThe old man then brought the girl and the boy to meet with Geng Qubing, and the presence of comitative could in principle be an effect of calquing of the preposition 与 yǔwith, but additional elicitation has confirmed that this construction is grammatically correct.
as shown by ( ex:cho.pjAsAmWmto ). The absence of plural indexation in ( ex:cho.pjAsAmWmto ) is expected since in direct 3 forms only the number of the subject is indexed on the verb (§ sec:indexation.non.local ).

exe

jo-sɯ-ɣe tɕe iɕqʰa <gengqubing> nɯ cʰo pjɤ-sɯ-ɤmɯ-mto. \\
ifr - caus -come lnk the.aforementioned anthr dem comit ifr - caus - recip -see \\
`The [old man] brought them in and had them meet Geng Qubing.' (150906 qingfeng-zh)
0006366#S53
exe
summary:
The passage describes how the prefix **amɯ-** forms reciprocal verbs with several verb classes, including perception verbs, semi-transitive verbs, and some stative verbs. In perception verbs like “see” and “hear,” the reciprocal meaning is between the experiencer and the stimulus, while in semi-transitive verbs the prefix targets the semi-object; some forms also have additional meanings, such as **amɯtso** meaning both “understand each other” and “be clear.”  

It also notes that some reciprocal verbs are stative and may show emphatic reduplication, and that reciprocal verbs can themselves take the sigmatic causative, yielding forms like “cause to see each other,” which still select a comitative.

text:
The verb asɤmɯmtsʰɯmtsʰɤminform each other underwent three derivations from the base verb mtsʰɤmhear: amɯ- reciprocal derivation ( amɯmtsʰɤmhear each other, `hear from each other'), sigmatic causative ( sɤmɯmtsʰɤm `cause to hear from each other') and then finally the reduplicated reciprocal derivation ( a-sɤmɯmtsʰɯ mtsʰɤm, § sec:reciprocal.other ). Unlike the non-volitional reciprocal verb amɯmtsʰɤmhear each other from which it is derived, asɤmɯmtsʰɯmtsʰɤm is a verb of speech, and expresses a volitional action (see ex:ZnasAmWmtshWmtshAmnW below and ex:Wzda.tWrdoR in § sec:possessive.prefix.obv.def ).

text:
co-participation
The compound verb amɟɤkʰogive and take, which derives from the transitive verbs mɟatake and kʰogive (§ sec:antipassive.t, § sec:ditransitive.indirective ) is not formally reciprocal but implies an action performed by more than one person. Contrary to a reciprocal or a reflexive, this collective action is not mutual or directed towards oneself: rather, it expresses that two distinct actions performed by different referents take place (near-)simultaneously and are linked with one another. Example ( ex:YAmJAkhondZi ) illustrates that one of the two people referred to by the third dual subject hands over the child (a semi-object, § sec:semi.object ) and that the other person takes the child from her hands. Note the non-iconic order in the compound, where the root mɟa occurs before kʰo, also the action of giving necessarily temporally precedes that of taking.

tɕeri tɤ-rɟit nɯ ɲɯ-ɤmɟɤkʰo-ndʑi qʰe koŋla tu-o-nɯ-rɯɕmɯ ɕmi-ndʑi kɯnɤ mɯ́j-tsu ma tɕe li tú-wɣ-nɯ-tsɯm ɲɯ-ɕti. \\
lnk indef. poss -child dem ipfv -give.and.take- du lnk really ipfv - recip -talk- du also neg: sens -have.time.to lnk lnk again ipfv: up - inv - vert -take.away sens -be: aff \\
`She$_i$ hands the child$_j$ to him$_k$ and he$_k$ takes him$_j$, but they$_i+k$ don't get the time to exchange any words and she$_i$ is taken back to heaven.' (150828 donglang)
0006312#S165
exe

Despite the presence of a reciprocal verb a-rɯɕmɯ ɕmi `talk to each other' (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ) in this passage, since there is no exchange of roles in the compound action described by the verb amɟɤkʰogive and take, it is preferrable to refer to this type of construction as `co-participation' (more precisely, `unspecified co-participation' in Creissels and Voisin's creissels08coparticipation terminology). This verb is isolated, as none of the other compound verbs recorded up to now have a meaning of this type.
summary: The compound verb **amɟɤkʰo** ‘give and take’ is not formally reciprocal, but it denotes a collective action involving more than one person, where two distinct acts by different participants occur nearly simultaneously and are linked together. In the example, one person hands over the child while the other takes the child, and although a reciprocal verb for “talk to each other” also appears, the compound itself does not involve an exchange of roles. For this reason, the construction is best described as **co-participation**, specifically **unspecified co-participation**.

text: anticausative
summary: An anticausative verb is an intransitive verb whose meaning corresponds to a transitive causative verb but does not express an external causer. The passage identifies this as a basic voice-type distinction, where the event happens without explicitly mentioning who or what caused it.

text:
alternation!prenasalization consonant!alternation
Voice derivations in Japhug are mainly concatenative and prefixal. An important exception is the alternation between unvoiced stops/affricates and their voiced prenasalized counterparts (which are to be analyzed as single phonemes, § sec:consonant.phonemes ), reflected in verb pairs whose unvoiced member is transitive, and whose voiced prenasalized member is intransitive.

There are 29 known examples of this alternation, involving both unvoiced unaspirated obstruents ( tab:anticausative.unaspirated ) and aspirated stops/affricates ( tab:anticausative.aspirated ).

In tab:anticausative.unaspirated, the verb nɯɴɢɤtpart ways has a lexicalized autive nɯ- integrated in the verb stem (§ sec:autoben.lexicalized ), but the bare stem ɴɢɤt is found in nominalized forms such as ɯ-sɤ-ɴɢɤtplace where X part ways (§ sec:determinative.n.n ). The verb pairs xtʰomput horizontally / ndomlie horizontally and ftʂimelt (vt) / ndʐimelt, which have a cluster in the transitive form but a single prenasalized stop in its intransitive counterpart, are discussed in § sec:anticausative.fx.

In the absence of a clearly identifiable derivational affix, the direction of the derivation is not completely obvious. It is conceivable in principle that the intransitive verbs in Tables tab:anticausative.unaspirated and tab:anticausative.aspirated are derived from their transitive counterparts, but the opposite direction is equally possible.

The latter direction could even seem more likely when looking at the meaning of some of the transitive verbs in these tables from a West European-cum-Chinese perspective: for instance, the meaning of kracause to fall has to be glossed in a way that makes it seem like it is derived from the intransitive verb ŋgrafall.

A cognate phenomenon is well-known in other branches of the Trans-Himalayan family such as Old Chinese, Tibetan and Lolo-Burmese, and several traditions of research analyse these cases as devoicing of the voiced initial by the sigmatic causative prefix (for instance ) while other scholars argue for the opposite direction (; see a summary of several opinions on this matter in ).
summary:
Japhug voice derivations are mainly prefixal, but one notable exception is an alternation between unvoiced stops/affricates and voiced prenasalized counterparts, with the unvoiced form typically transitive and the prenasalized form intransitive. The text reports 29 examples of this pattern, involving both unaspirated and aspirated obstruents, and notes that in some cases the derivational direction is unclear because no obvious affix is present.

The passage also points out that similar alternations are found in other Trans-Himalayan languages such as Old Chinese, Tibetan, and Lolo-Burmese. Different analyses either treat these as devoicing caused by a sigmatic causative prefix or as cases where the intransitive form is derived from the transitive one.

subsubsection: Evidence for the directionality of the anticausative derivation
text:
morphology!Trans-Himalayan comparison
In Japhug (and other Gyalrong languages), three independent pieces of evidence clearly indicate that the direction of derivation must be from the transitive verb to the intransitive one.

First, the transitive verbs in these pairs can have either unaspirated onset (see the examples in tab:anticausative.unaspirated ), an aspirated onset ( tab:anticausative.aspirated ) or even a fricative onset (the pair sarfilter out vs. ndzardrip dry). In the hypothesis that the intransitive verbs derive from their transitive counterpart, this observation can be trivially explained: the aspiration contrast is neutralized by the prenasalization, as illustrated in tab:prenasalization (some of the aspirated affricates are indicated in brackets in this table, as no examples are attested).

On the other hand, in the hypothesis that the intransitive verbs are primary, the origin of aspiration contrast on the transitive counterparts requires an additional set of explanations.

Second, the verb χtɤrscatter ( tab:anticausative.unaspirated ) is borrowed from Tibetan གཏོར་gtorscatter. The prenasalized form ʁndɤrbe scattered has no Tibetan equivalent, and its onset ʁnd- is incompatible with the phonotactics of Tibetan consonant clusters. Thus, this intransitive verb must be a Gyalrong-internal creation from a Tibetan base, Cognate pairs also exist in Zbu ( χtór / ʁⁿdór, ) and in Tshobdun ( χtor / ʁⁿdor, ), showing that this derivation goes back at least to the common ancestor of these three languages. and it follows that the direction of derivation should be from the transitive verb to the intransitive one.

Third, all scholars favouring the hypothesis that the intransitive verb is primary suppose that the onset of transitive verbs has been devoiced by the addition of a sigmatic causative. In Japhug, this hypothesis makes no sense, because the sigmatic causative (§ sec:sig.causative ) is not only attested but fully productive (§ sec:sig.caus.allomorphs ), with a considerable number of allomorphs but without ever devoicing either sonorant nor obstruents onsets. The same is incidentally true of various other languages of the Trans-Himalayan family, including Tibetan and Jinghpo, where anticausative derivation also exists. In addition, causativization of prenasalized verbs is attested in Japhug (§ sec:anticausative.other.derivations ) and other Gyalrong languages such as Tshobdun, for instance sɯɣ-ndʐi `melt (vt)' from ndʐimelt (vi) (compare with the transitive ftʂimelt vt).

Since the intransitive verbs in Tables tab:anticausative.unaspirated and tab:anticausative.aspirated have a non-volitional meaning (§ sec:anticausative.function ), it is likely that the prenasalization is a fossilized form of the autive nɯ- prefix (§ sec:autoben.historical ) in its `spontaneous event' function, like the isolated case of prenasalization in the verb pair sqlɯmcollapse vs. arɴɢlɯmbe caved in (§ sec:fossil.prenasalization ).

While traces of the voicing (prenasalization) alternation can be brought to light in most languages of the Trans-Himalayan family, Japhug and the other Gyalrong languages are the only branch of the family where the origin of this alternation is still visible. The study of the prenasalization derivation in Japhug is thus of considerable interest for comparative Trans-Himalayan. Independent evidence against the hypothesis that the voicing alternation originates from sigmatic prefixation is also found in Tibetan. Further evidence in Gyalrongic is provided by.
summary: The passage argues that in Japhug and other Gyalrong languages, the intransitive member of anticausative pairs is derived from the transitive one, based on three kinds of evidence: the phonological behavior of aspiration, borrowed forms that show an intransitive Gyalrong creation from a Tibetan transitive base, and the fact that productive sigmatic causative formation does not produce the devoicing pattern seen here. It also suggests that the prenasalization found in these intransitives is likely a fossilized form of an older prefix with spontaneous-event meaning, and notes that Gyalrong is the only Trans-Himalayan branch where the origin of this alternation remains visible.

subsubsection: Absence of clusters in the anticausative form
text:
Among the pairs in § sec:anticausative.pairs, two verbs stand out in having a preinitial consonant in the transitive form without equivalent in the intransitive one: ftʂimelt (vt), with a f- (phonologically w) prefixal element (the expected form of the intransitive ndʐimelt would be $ $ mdʐi ) and xtʰomput horizontally with a x- element (the expected form of ndomlie horizontally would be $ $ ɣndom ).

No decisive explanation can be provided to account for this idiosyncrasy, found in other Gyalrongic languages including Tangut. Two mutually incompatible hypotheses can be considered. First, it is possible that in these two pairs both the intransitive and the transitive verbs are derived from a common root with different fossil derivational prefixes. Second, the reconstructed nasal prefix responsible for the anticausative prenasalization might have caused cluster simplification ( *N-ptri $ $ *N-tri $ $ ndʐi ).

In the second hypothesis, the anticausative form ʁndɤrbe scattered from the Tibetan loanword χtɤrscatter would be phonetically irregular, possibly a clue of it being analogically created on the basis of other anticausative derivations.
summary: Among the anticausative pairs discussed, two verbs are unusual because the transitive form has a preinitial consonant not found in the intransitive form: *ftʂimelt* and *xtʰomput*. The passage says there is no decisive explanation, but offers two conflicting hypotheses: either both forms descend from a common root with different fossil prefixes, or a reconstructed nasal anticausative prefix caused cluster simplification. It also notes that the anticausative *ʁndɤrbe* from a Tibetan loanword is phonetically irregular and may have been created by analogy.

text:
anticausative
The discussion in the previous section has shown that the transitivity alternation exhibited by the verb pairs in Tables tab:anticausative.unaspirated and tab:anticausative.aspirated was a valency-decreasing derivation, turning a transitive verb with unvoiced obstruent onset into an intransitive verb with voiced prenasalized onset (following the rules in tab:prenasalization ).

Like the passive (§ sec:passive ), the only argument of the prenasalized intransitive verb corresponds to the object of the base verb. Unlike the passive derivation however, prenasalized intransitive verbs have a dynamic meaning (rather than expressing a resultative state) and also imply that the action took place spontaneously, semantically removing the agent. For instance, while the passive a-prɤt of the verb prɤtbreak (of a thread) implies the existence of an agent ( ex:pjAkAprAtci ), the prenasalized intransitive mbrɤt expresses a spontaneous action without external agent ( ex:nWmbrAt.pWmbrAt ). The anticausative meaning of the prenasalization derivation is a plot device in ( ex:nWmbrAt.pWmbrAt ). The context of this sentence is that the queen arrives in a room whose floor is tiled with turquoise and coral (see example ex:WBrAsqlWm, § sec:fossil.prenasalization ), and unsure whether it is safe to walk on it (worrying that it might yield under her weight), she willfully breaks her necklace, spreading the pearls on the floor. Her servants, unaware that she did it on purpose, enter the room first to pick up the pearls, and seeing that the floor does not collapse, she then follows them. For this reason, this derivation is henceforth referred to as `anticausative'.

While anticausativized verbs are not compatible with external volitional agents, they are however attested with an explicit expression of the cause and/or of an involuntary and indirect agent. For instance in ( ex:ndZimbrW.chAmbGAR ) the capsizing of the ship (expressed by the anticausative mbɣaʁturn over (vi) from pɣaʁturn over (vt)) is due to a storm mentioned in the previous clause, however without explicit marking of the causal relationship.

Instead of non-volitional action, what the anticausative ɴɢlɯt expresses in this case is the successful realization of the action: the subject of qlɯt controls his decision to attempt at breaking an object, but cannot control his success in performing this action.

summary: The passage explains that prenasalization creates an anticausative, a valency-decreasing derivation that turns a transitive verb into an intransitive one whose sole argument corresponds to the object of the base verb. Unlike the passive, anticausatives have a dynamic meaning and typically imply that the event happened spontaneously without an external agent, though they can also occur with an explicit cause or with a prior agent as an indirect, involuntary cause. In some contexts, the anticausative instead highlights the successful completion of an attempted action.

summary: The verb **tsʰoʁ** functions as a prototypical transitive verb meaning ‘attach,’ ‘plant,’ or ‘fix,’ but it can also appear in a dummy subject construction with the meaning ‘grow’ for fruits, leaves, and flowers. In this latter use, **ndzoʁbe** is the corresponding anticausative, occurring with the same ‘grow’ meaning and matching the object of **tsʰoʁ** with its intransitive subject. The passage also notes that **ndzoʁ** is unusual because it can be used with a volitional meaning.

text:
anticausative!collocation
Among the pairs in tab:anticausative.unaspirated, the verbs ɯ-ʁo+pʰibe disappointed by and ɯ-ʁo+mbibe discouraged are remarkable in that both are noun-verb collocations, taking the same inalienably possessed noun ɯ-ʁo (otherwise unattested) as object or intransitive subject, The noun and the verb are glossed with the same expression, but using the indices (1) and (2) (§ sec:orphan.verb ). Showing that the anticausative prenasalization, like several other derivations (§ sec:light.verb ), affects collocations as a whole despite being only morphologically expressed on the verb stem.

The intransitive mbi `be discouraged, feel frustrated, lose heart' is always in 3sg form (§ sec:intransitive.invariable ), and the possessor on ɯ-ʁo indicates the experiencer, as in ( ex:ndZi.Ro.amAnWmbi ) where the form ndʑi-ʁo takes a 2du possessive prefix coreferent with the subject of the previous verb (see also ex:nWRo.amAnWmbi in § sec:intransitive.invariable ). This collocation has an exact Tshobdun cognate o-ʁeʔ+ⁿbi `lose morale'.

The argument structure of the two verbs thus only differs by the loss of the subject (stimulus) in the intransitive form mbi meaning `be disappointed'.

In the intransitive form, mbi is always 3sg and the possessor on ɯ-ʁo marks the experiencer, while the transitive pʰi encodes the stimulus as subject and the experiencer as object possessor. The same construction can also express reflexive disappointment and serve as the base for further derivations such as facilitative and incorporating verbs meaning ‘be hopeless’ and ‘lose hope.’

text:
volitionality!anticausative
An important proportion of anticausative verbs are only compatible with inanimate subjects, for instance ɴɢrɯbreak (example ex:pjANWClWG.pjANGrW in § sec:anticausative.function ), ndʐimelt as in ( ex:tundzxi.YWcha ) or ndʑɣaʁbe squeezed out (example ex:WtWciste, § sec:body.part ), and therefore express non-volitional actions.

`There was a bit of snow, but it is not serious, it can still melt.' (conversation 15-12-17)

Even anticausative verbs that are compatible with human or animal subjects are poorly compatible with volitional meaning. For instance, ndʐaβfall/roll (from tʂaβcause to fall/roll) expresses involuntary fall as in ( ex:pWndzxaB.panWlwoR ), but cannot be used for voluntary rolling motion. The reflexive form of the base transitive verb ʑɣɤtʂaβcause oneself to fall/roll is required instead for this meaning (§ sec:refl.acaus ).

A few anticausatives can extend to voluntary actions to varying degrees, and two forms are singled out as exceptions: one that can indicate controllable turning over, and another that shows no restriction on volitionality and can mean ‘separate’ or ‘divorce,’ while one anticausative is also used with a clear volitional meaning like ‘cling onto’ or ‘grab.’

summary: The passage explains that anticausative verbs can combine with several other derivational processes in the language. Although the anticausative prenasalization probably comes from the autive prefix nɯ-, it is compatible with other derivations such as facilitative, proprietive, distributed action, and in a few cases causative forms, with meanings that may distinguish spontaneous action, repeated motion, or external causation.

text:
alternation!prenasalization consonant!alternation
The anticausative derivation is not the only type of voicing alternation in Japhug.

Among verbs, two cases of non-anticausative voicing alternations are found, the isolated pair treated in § sec:fossil.prenasalization and the irregular sigmatic causative ʑɴɢoʁhang (vt) from ɴqoʁhang (vi). The onset ʑɴɢ- in ʑɴɢoʁhang (containing the irregular ʑ- allomorph of the sigmatic causative prefix, § sec:caus.Z ) apparently results from the voicing of an earlier cluster like *ɕ-ɴq- due to phonotactic constraints (§ sec:shC.clusters ).

In ideophones, voicing alternations with or without prenasalization are also attested, as shown by the pair qɯqli and ɴɢɯɴɢli, both meaning `eyes wide open' (§ sec:idph.gradation ). In addition, at least one ideophone, dzoʁkneeling suddenly and respectfully, which appears in collocation with the transitive verb tsʰoʁ, originates from the anticausative verb ndzoʁbe attached (§ sec:genesis.idph ).
summary: The passage notes that, besides anticausative derivation, Japhug also has other voicing alternations in verbs and ideophones. In verbs, these include an isolated pair and an irregular sigmatic causative ʑɴɢoʁhang from ɴqoʁhang, where the initial cluster seems to reflect voicing of an earlier cluster under phonotactic constraints. In ideophones, alternations with or without prenasalization occur, such as qɯqli and ɴɢɯɴɢli, and at least one ideophone, dzoʁ, is said to derive from an anticausative verb.

text:
antipassive
The antipassive derivation converts a morphologically transitive verb into an intransitive one, removing the object and preserving the subject. As in the closely related Tshobdun language, two antipassive prefixes are found in Japhug: rɤ- and sɤ-.

rɤ- antipassive
antipassive!rhotic
The rɤ- antipassive prefix is productive, and it is thus impossible to provide a complete list of all examples. tab:antipassive1 provides a representative sample of this derivation, which includes a number of verbs of Tibetan origin (for instance fsoʁearn and βzjozlearn from བསོགས་bsogsaccumulate and སྦྱངས་sbʲaŋslearn, respectively). As in Tshobdun, this prefix is typically used when the suppressed argument is non-human (§ sec:antipassive.rA.sA ), though a few exceptions exist (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ).

This derivation takes as input mono- or ditransitive verbs (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ), and one labile verb ( sɯsothink, see § sec:lability.apass ).

The main morphosyntactic differences between transitive verbs and their corresponding antipassive forms are illustrated the following examples. In ( ex:tWsNaR.paBzjoz ), the base verb βzjozlearn is fully transitive, selecting the type-C preverbs in the non-local direct Aorist (§ sec:transitivity.morphology, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). The object is the topic studied (in ex:tWsNaR.paBzjoz, the nominalized verb tɯ-sŋaʁsorcery) and the transitive subject, the person learning, is taking the ergative case.

exe

aʑɯɣ a-me ci tu tɕe, nɯnɯ kɯ tɯ-sŋaʁ pa-βzjoz tɕe, \\
1sg. gen 1sg. poss -daughter indef exist: fact lnk dem erg nmlz: action -cast.spells aor:3 -learn lnk \\
`I have a daughter, and she has learned sorcery.' (140512 fushang he yaomo-zh)
0003967#S134
exe

The antipassive verb rɤβzjozlearn things in ( ex:Wme.pWrABzjoz ) is morphologically intransitive, selecting the type-A preverbs (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ) in the Aorist ( pɯ- instead of pa, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). It is used to avoid mentioning a specific topic of study, and it is often better to translate this verb as `go to school/university'. Like the transitive subject of βzjozlearn, the subject of rɤβzjozlearn things corresponds to the person(s) acquiring knowledge. However, when overt, its subject occurs in absolutive form as ɯ-me nɯ `her daughter' in ( ex:Wme.pWrABzjoz ).

`Her daughter went to school (studied things) but has no job now.' (17-lhazgron)

Although example ( ex:Wme.pWrABzjoz ) only illustrates one of the seven morphological criteria for transitivity (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ), all have been successfully tested with antipassive prefixes.

The non-orientable antipassive verbs select as lexicalized orientation the same one as that of their base verb. For instance, rɤmbigive to someone selects the eastwards preverbs like its base verb mbigive (§ sec:preverb.giving ).

The object affected by the rɤ- derivation is not only demoted morphologically but also removed syntactically, and verbs with the antipassive prefix cannot take an overt patient corresponding to the object of the base verb, even as semi-object or with an oblique case (the antipassive rɤfɕɤtreport is however an exception, see § sec:antipassive.lexicalized ).

The antipassive verbs are generally understood as having a generic/indefinite patient. In tab:antipassive1, their meaning is translated using the most usual patient associated with a particular activity, for instance `clothes' in the case of rɤ-tʂɯβ `sew' and rɤ-ɕpʰɤt `patch'. The patient that has been demoted from object status by the rɤ- prefix is nearly always an inanimate entity, but there are some examples of verbs (such as rɤntɕʰabutcher) with animal patient, and even demoted human recipient in the case of some secundative verbs (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ). The semantic contrast between the rɤ- and sɤ- antipassive derivations is described in (§ sec:antipassive.function ), and morphosyntactic constructions competing with antipassive derivations to express indefinite objects are discussed in § sec:non.antipassive.indef.patient.

Although the meaning of the derived verbs is not fully predictable in each case (§ sec:antipassive.lexicalized ), the formation of the rɤ- antipassive is almost perfectly regular. There are only three rɤ- antipassive verbs with irregular morphology. First, rɤnŋahave a debt from ŋabuy on credit, owe (a verb selecting as object the amount of money owed, ex:sqWmpCar.kANata ) has an additional -n element.

exe

sqɯ-mpɕar kɤ-ŋa-t-a \\
ten -money.unit aor -owe- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I bought [it] on credit and owe [him] ten renminbi.' (elicited)
exe

Second, rɤtsɣedo business from ntsɣesell lacks the n- preinitial found in the base verb. Third, rɯsɯsothink from sɯsothink (about) (§ sec:lability.apass ) has rɯ- instead of rɤ-. These cases are accounted for in § sec:antipassive.history.

Apart from these irregularities, the allomorphy of the rɤ- antipassive is limited to the variant ra- found with verb roots with an onset with uvular preinitial (§ sec:A.vs.a.prefixes ) as in raχtɯdo shopping. The antipassive rɤ- prefix is formally similar to the denominative rɤ- (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ), In addition, there is a residue of rɤ- prefixed verb that can neither be analyzed as antipassive nor as denominal derivations (§ sec:rA.non.apass ). to the extent that synchronic ambiguity exists between these two prefixes. In particular, the verb rɤzndemake a wall (vi) can be synchronically analysed either as a denominal form of zndestone wall or of the transitive verb zndemake a wall. Note that both options are equally likely, as the prefix rɤ- is attested with other denominal expressing the building of the base noun, for instance tɤ-loʁnest rɤloʁmake a nest (vi). The historical implications of this observation are explored in § sec:antipassive.history.

Not all transitive verbs with non-human patients can be antipassivized. In particular, when an intransitive verb having the meaning of the expected antipassive verb already exists, antipassivization is less likely. For instance, tisay lacks a rɤ- antipassive form, as the intransitive rɯɕmispeak (which can have an overt dative recipient, ex:WCki.turWCmia, § sec:intr.goal, but no reported speech complement clause) already serves as its `lexical antipassive'. The verbs of ingestion ndzaeat and tsʰidrink share the compound verb rɯndzɤtsʰihave a meal (§ sec:denom.intr.rA, § sec:denom.compound.verbs ) as their intransitive counterpart.
summary:
The passage explains that the antipassive in Japhug turns a transitive verb into an intransitive one by removing the object while preserving the subject, and that Japhug has two antipassive prefixes, rɤ- and sɤ-. It focuses on the productive rɤ- antipassive, which typically applies to mono- or ditransitive verbs, often with non-human patients, and shows regular morphosyntactic changes such as loss of overt object position and intransitive agreement/preverb behavior.  

It also notes that the derived verbs usually imply a generic or indefinite patient, though some meanings are lexicalized and a few forms are irregular or formally ambiguous with denominal derivations. Not all transitive verbs can form an antipassive, especially when an ordinary intransitive verb already exists with the needed meaning.

text:
sɤ- antipassive
antipassive!sigmatic
Like the rɤ- antipassive, the sɤ- antipassive is productive. tab:antipassive2 presents a list of representative examples, including Tibetan loanwords such as fstɤtpraise from བསྟོད་bstodpraise. Unlike the rɤ- antipassive, the sɤ- prefix is used when the demoted patient is human or equivalent (§ sec:antipassive.rA.sA, see on Tshobdun), except in the case of some secundative verbs (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ). The sɤ- antipassive derivation can also demote animal patients in specific contexts (§ sec:antipassive.rA.sA ).

The only cases of allomorphy with the antipassive sɤ- are the allomorph sa- occurring when the prefix is followed by a complex onset whose first element is a uvular fricative (§ sec:A.vs.a.prefixes ), and the allomorph sɤz- which appears with some polysyllabic stems whose first syllable has a sonorant initial sɤzɣɤmɯpraise people.

The sɤ- prefix is homophonous with the rogative (§ sec:rogative.derivation ), the proprietive (§ sec:proprietive ) and denominal derivations (§ sec:sigmatic.denominal ), as well as with the oblique participle sɤ(z)- (§ sec:oblique.participle ). Potential ambiguity exists with the proprietive derivation. For instance, the transitive nɯzdɯɣworry about has two homophonous intransitive derived verbs sɤ-nɯzdɯɣ, an antipassive meaning `worry about people', and a proprietive `causing worry to people'.

Most sɤ- antipassives derive from monotransitive verbs, but a handful of them are based on ditransitive verbs (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ). In addition, the labile verbs nɤrelaugh and sɤŋolisten are also compatible with the sɤ- prefix. The antipassive forms sɤsɤŋolisten to advice and sɤnɤrelaugh at people derive from the meanings `listen to' and `laugh at, mock' that these two verbs have when conjugates transitively (§ sec:lability.apass ).

Some of sɤ- antipassive verbs can either be dynamic verbs or stative verbs, in the latter case expressing a general tendency/propensity of the subject to do the action. For instance, sɤ-ndza from ndzaeat can mean `eat people, eat someone' (as in ex:kWsAndza.toGWGu, § sec:antipassive.indefinite.patient ), but also `be a man-eater', `prick' ( ex:mAsAndza ) or `be carnivorous' (animal eating other animals, ex:kWrNi1, § sec:antipassive.rA.sA ).

summary:
The sɤ- antipassive is a productive derivation, like rɤ-, but it is used especially when the demoted patient is human or equivalent, and sometimes for animal patients in certain contexts. It shows a few allomorphs (sa- and sɤz-), is homophonous with several other derivations, and mostly derives from monotransitive verbs, though some ditransitives and labile verbs also occur.

Some sɤ- antipassives can be either dynamic or stative, with the stative uses expressing a general propensity or tendency, such as ‘be a man-eater’ or ‘be carnivorous.’ These propensity antipassives are very close in meaning to constructions with generic human objects.

text:
Most antipassive verbs have meanings that are predictable from that of their base verbs. However, in some cases antipassivization not only demotes the patient from object status, but restricts the range of meanings of the verb root.

The meaning of the transitive verb pɣaʁturn over differs depending on the objects it occurs with; its possible meanings include `turning (clothes) inside out', `open (the cover of a box)', `cross (mountains, rivers)' ( ex:jannWpGaRndZi.jannWmGlandZi, § sec:motion.verbs ) or `plough (fields)' (see ex:nWji.lopGaRnW below and ex:lukWpGaR.nW.cinA in § sec:cinA ).

`They had ploughed many wide fields for them.' (2002 qajdoskAt)

By contrast, its antipassive rɤpɣaʁreclaim land The meaning of this verb corresponds to Chinese 开垦 kāikěnreclaim land, `clear a wild area for cultivation'. only preserves the last meaning of the base verb, with `land' or `field' as implicit patient as in ( ex:lurApGaR ). Note in addition that the antipassive selects the upstream preverbs ( lu- in ex:lurApGaR ) like the verb pɣaʁ in the meaning `plough' ( lo- in ex:nWji.lopGaRnW ).

Similarly, while the transitive verb tɕɤβburn can take various types of referents as objects (including humans, as in ex:Padma.katCABnW, § sec:obviation.saliency ), the antipassive rɤtɕɤβburn land The meaning of this verb is translated as 烧荒 shāohuāngclear land by fire in Chinese. is also restricted to its use in agriculture, with `land' as demoted patient.

The expected meaning of rɤpɣaʁreclaim land and rɤtɕɤβburn land if they had been regular antipassives would have been `turn things over' and `burn things', respectively. Despite the absence of an incorporated noun, these two verbs include information about the demoted patient. This semantic irregularity has implications for the study of the origin of the antipassive prefixes in Japhug, as discussed in § sec:antipassive.irr.semantic.

The verb rɤfɕɤtreport from fɕɤttell stands out among antipassive verbs from the point of view syntax. While rɤfɕɤt is morphologically intransitive, as is shown by the form kɯ-rɤfɕɤt in ( ex:kWrAfCAt.YWra ) with the intransitive subject generic prefix kɯ- (§ sec:intr.23 ), the patient of this verb can nevertheless be overt as a semi-object (in ex:kWrAfCAt.YWra, the demonstrative nɯnɯra, anaphorically referring to the previous complement clauses). The object of the base verb fɕɤttell is thus only demoted to semi-object status (§ sec:semi.object ), and not syntactically removed. The dative recipient is also preserved by the antipassive derivation.

exe

slama ra ɣɯ tʰɯtʰɤci kɯ-fse, nɯ kɤ-rɤ-βzjoz ra ɲɯ-stu mɯ́j-stu nɯ,
[...] nɯnɯra nɯ-pʰama ra nɯ-ɕki kɯ-rɤfɕɤt ɲɯ-ra. \\
student pl gen something sbj: pcp -be.like dem inf - apass -study pl sens -be.serious neg: sens -be.serious dem dem: pl 3pl. poss -parents pl 3pl. poss - dat genr:S/O-report: fact sens -be.needed \\
`(As a teacher), one has to tell the parents all kinds of things concerning the students, whether they try hard or not, whether they work seriously or not.' (150901 tshuBdWnskAt)
