summary: Most Japhug antipassive verbs are semantically predictable, but some are irregular in that they not only demote the patient from object status but also narrow the verb’s meaning. The passage gives examples where transitive verbs meaning broadly “turn over” and “burn” are antipassivized into forms used specifically for agricultural meanings like “clear land for cultivation” and “burn land,” with the demoted patient remaining implicit. It also notes an antipassive of “tell” that is syntactically unusual because the patient can still appear as a semi-object and the dative recipient is preserved.

text:
antipassive!ditransitive verb ditransitive verb!antipassive
Among ditransitive verbs, indirective verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) build their antipassive derivations the same way as monotransitive verbs. Note however the morphosynactic peculiarities of the lexicalized antipassive rɤfɕɤtreport from the indirective verb fɕɤttell (§ sec:antipassive.lexicalized ). For instance, tʰuask has the two antipassive forms rɤtʰuask questions and sɤtʰuask in marriage depending on whether the demoted patient is inanimate or human (see examples ex:korAthunW and ex:kWsAthu.Cea, § sec:antipassive.function ).

Three secundative verbs, mbigive, ɕtʂɯentrust with and jtsʰigive to drink, behave differently in this regard. Their object (semantically the recipient) is generally human, but the sɤ- antipassive prefix does not occur with these verbs: the corresponding forms (for instance sɤmbiask for) exist, but do not have antipassive meaning (they exemplify the rogative derivation, § sec:rogative.derivation ). Instead, their antipassive forms rɤmbigive to someone, rɤɕtʂɯentrust someone with and rɤjtsʰigive to someone to drink take the rɤ- prefix. These verbs are henceforth referred to as ` rɤ- antipassivized secundative verbs'.

The demoted recipient of rɤ- antipassivized secundative verbs can be indefinite and non-specific as in the case of most antipassive verbs (§ sec:antipassive.function ), as in ( ex:lonba.YWrAmbi ).

exe

ɯʑɤɣ ɯ-βra kɯ-rkɯ rkɯn ntsɯ ma mɯ-pjɤ-nɯ-ta. ɯ-ro ra lonba ɲɯ-rɤ-mbi pjɤ-ŋu. \\
3sg: gen 3sg. poss -share sbj: pcp - emph be.few always apart.from neg - ifr - auto -put 3sg. poss -rest pl all ipfv - apass -give ifr. ipfv -be \\
`He would only keep a little for himself, and give away the rest.' (150902 hailibu-zh) 0006316#S6
exe

However, often, as in ( ex:nWrAmbitCi ) and ( ex:CkArACtsxWa ), the identify of the recipient is known to the speaker, but the antipassive is chosen to leave it unspecified, either because the information is irrelevant (because the addressee does not know the people in question) or to hide information.

exe

kɯmŋu ma mɯ-nɯ-ʁaʁ ɯ-qʰu tɕe, tɕe χsɯm nɯ nɯ-rɤ-mbi-tɕi tɕe \\
five apart.from neg - aor -hatch 3sg. poss -after lnk lnk three dem aor - apass -give- du lnk \\
`Only five (of the twelve eggs) hatches, and we gave three [of the chicks] [to other people].' (22-kumpGa) 0003588#S76
exe

exe

a-kumpɣa ɯ-pɯ kɯ-sɤjndɯ jndɤt ʑo pɯ-ŋu ri, tɕeri <xingqitian> <fangjia> tɕe tu-nɯ-ɕe-a pɯ-ra tɕe ɕ-kɤ-rɤ-ɕtʂɯ-a. \\
1sg. poss -hen 3sg. poss -young sbj: pcp - emph be.cute emph pst. ipfv -be lnk lnk sunday holidays loc ipfv: up - vert -go- 1sg pst. ipfv -be.needed lnk tral - aor - apass -entrust.with- 1sg \\
`My chicks were very cute, but on sunday, I had to go back on holiday, and I went [to someone$_i$] and entrusted him/her/them$_i$ with them. (150819 kumpGa)
0006388#S43

In addition, antipassivization of secundative verbs does not removes the recipient: it can be demoted to oblique argument status, with dative marking, as in ( ex:YWrAjtshia.NgrAl ) and ( ex:aCki.kArACtsxW ).

exe

aʑo tɤ-tɕɯ ra nɯ-ɕki cʰa ɲɯ-rɤ-jtsʰi-a ŋgrɤl \\
1sg indef. poss -son pl 3pl. poss - dat alcohol ipfv - apass -give.to.drink be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`I (usually) give a drink to the guys.' (elicited)
exe

Although the three rɤ- antipassivized secundative verbs rɤmbigive to someone, rɤɕtʂɯentrust someone with and rɤjtsʰigive to someone to drink are morphologically intransitive like all other antipassives, as shown by the absence of past transitive -t- suffix in ( ex:CkArACtsxWa ), and of C-type orientation preverb in ( ex:aCki.kArACtsxW ), they do preserve more transitivity features than most antipassive verbs.

First, the three rɤ- antipassivized secundative verbs differ from other antipassive verbs in terms of case marking: their subject can receive ergative marking in some contexts.

With third person arguments and no overt recipient as in ( ex:akhWna.YArAmbindZi ), the subject a-mu a-wa ni is in absolutive form.

exe

a-mu a-wa ni a-kʰɯna ɲɤ-rɤ-mbi-ndʑi \\
1sg. poss -mother 1sg. poss -father du 1sg. poss -dog ifr - apass -give- du \\
`My parents gave my dog away.' (elicitation, 2019-11-30)
exe

However, ergative marking on the subject occurs in ( ex:aCki.kArACtsxW ) with a 1sg recipient, and in ( ex:nWwGrAmbia2 ) below with a 1sg semi-object (theme).
theme

exe

a-wa kɯ a-ʁi a-ɕki kɤ-rɤ-ɕtʂɯ. \\
1sg. poss -father erg 1sg. poss -younger.brother 1sg. poss - dat aor - apass -entrust.with \\
`My father entrusted me with my younger brother.' (elicited)
exe

Second, an even more unusual feature of the three rɤ- antipassivized secundative verbs is that the morphosyntactic status of the theme of the giving action. In all the examples above from ( ex:lonba.YWrAmbi ) to ( ex:YWrAjtshia.NgrAl ), the theme is a third person semi-object (§ sec:semi.object ), and its number cannot be indexed even with a 1sg subject (§ sec:double.number.indexation ).

However, in the very rare cases when the theme is first or second person, the verb rɤmbigive to someone exceptionally occurs with inverse wɣ- or local scenario indexation affixes ( ta- 1 2 and kɯ- 2 1, see § sec:indexation.local ) prefixes, as if the verb were morphologically transitive, and the theme were a direct object. No such example is found in the corpus, but forms such as ( ex:nWwGrAmbia2 ) can be elicited (§ sec:secundative.theme ).

exe

a-wa kɯ aʑo nɯ́-wɣ-rɤ-mbi-a \\
1sg. poss -father erg 1sg aor - inv - apass -give- 1sg \\
`My father gave me away.' (elicited)
exe

This puzzling construction is not only possible, but it is actually the only way to express a non-third person theme with the verb mbigive.

Not all secundative verbs however select the rɤ- antipassive like mbigive and jtsʰigive to drink. For instance, sɯxɕɤtteach, which encodes the recipient/addressee as object (the 2sg in ex:pjWtasWxCAt, as indicated by the ta- portmanteau prefix), is not compatible with rɤ- prefix: the only antipassive form of this verb is sɤsɯxɕɤtteach people, `work as a teacher', as in ( ex:pjWsAsWxCata ).

exe

tɤfsɤri kɤ-βzu ci pjɯ-ta-sɯxɕɤt. \\
thread inf -make a.little ipfv -1 2-teach \\
`Let me teach you how to make threads.' (vid-20140506043657)
exe

exe
summary:
Among ditransitive verbs, indirective verbs form antipassives like monotransitive verbs, though some lexicalized forms show special morphosyntactic behavior. In contrast, the secundative verbs *mbi* ‘give’, *ɕtʂɯ* ‘entrust with’, and *jtsʰi* ‘give to drink’ do not take the ordinary *sɤ-* antipassive; instead, their antipassive forms use *rɤ-*, and the demoted recipient may be indefinite, left unspecified, or marked as an oblique with dative case.

These *rɤ-* antipassivized secundative verbs are morphologically intransitive but retain unusual transitivity properties: their subject can sometimes be ergative, and the theme behaves in special ways, especially when it is non-third person. The text also notes that not all secundative verbs behave this way, since *sɯxɕ�

again teacher aor:3 -take- pst: tr - 1sg lnk dem: loc ipfv - apass -teach- 1sg pst. ipfv -be \\
`I too became a teacher, and I was teaching there.' (12-BzaNsa) 0003484#S17

Similarly, the secundative verb nɯsɯkʰorob, extort has the antipassive form sɤnɯsɯkʰorob people, also with the sɤ- prefix (example ex:zYAsAnWsWkhonW, § sec:antipassive.compatibility ).

text:
antipassive!reduplicated reduplication!antipassive
The intransitive verb rɤtʰutʰeinquire, `ask for information' derives from tʰuask like rɤtʰuask questions ( ex:korAthunW, § sec:antipassive.function, § sec:antipassive.ditransitive ), with the rare reduplication in -e in addition to the rɤ- prefix. This reduplicated antipassive form is isolated, but this type of reduplication is attested in a few other forms (§ sec.distributed.action.l ).

As shown by ( ex:aCki.GWnWrAthuthe ), rɤtʰutʰeinquire is an intransitive verb: the type A orientation preverb nɯ- is selected instead of type C if the verb were morphologically transitive (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). This verb also selects an oblique argument in the dative, like its base verb (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ).

exe

a-ɕki ɣɯ-nɯ-rɤtʰutʰe \\
1sg. poss - dat cisl - aor -ask.permission \\
`He came and asked me (for information).' (elicited)
exe

This verb is mainly attested as a negative infinitive converb mɤ-kɤ-rɤtʰutʰe `without asking (for permission)' (as in Chinese 问都没有问就 …… ) as in ( ex:mAkArAthuthe ). The ergative on the subject mbro nɯ kɯ `the horse' is due to the main verb pjɤ-qʰa `he hated that...'.

exe

mbro nɯ kɯ ɕkɤrɯ nɯnɯ [maka mɤ-kɤ-rɤtʰutʰe] kɯ nɯfse ju-kɤ-ɣi nɯ wuma ʑo pjɤ-qʰa ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
horse dem erg serow dem at.all neg - inf -ask.permission erg like.that ipfv - inf -come dem really emph ifr. ipfv -hate sens -be \\
`The horse hated that the serow came like that without asking [permission] at all.' (ma he lu-zh)
exe
summary: The passage describes the intransitive verb **rɤtʰutʰe** ‘inquire, ask for information,’ derived from **tʰu** ‘ask’ with the **rɤ-** prefix and a rare **-e** reduplication; this reduplicated antipassive form is isolated, though similar reduplication occurs in a few other forms. It behaves as an intransitive verb, taking the A-orientation preverb **nɯ-** rather than the transitive type, and it still selects a dative oblique argument like the base verb. The verb is most often attested in the negative infinitive converb **mɤ-kɤ-rɤtʰutʰe** meaning ‘without asking (for permission).’

text:
antipassive!Past Imperfective reduplication!Past Imperfective
Antipassive verbs, unlike most dynamic verbs (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ), are compatible with Past Imperfective pɯ- and Inferential Imperfective pjɤ-. This question is however difficult to study for three reasons.

First, many of the transitive base verbs in Tables tab:antipassive1 and tab:antipassive2, for instance βzjozlearn and ɕpʰɤtpatch, select the downwards preverbs as one of their lexicalized orientation (see for instance the perfective form pa-βzjoz `she learned it' in ex:tWsNaR.paBzjoz above). As a consequence, there is syncretism for these verbs between Aorist and Inferential on the one hand, and Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective on the other hand (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ). For instance, the form pɯ-rɤ-βzjoz `she went to school' in ( ex:Wme.pWrABzjoz ) above is Aorist, but in a different context the same form can be analyzed as a Past Imperfective `she was studying'.

Second, while simple Past and Inferential Imperfective are attested with antipassive verbs, they are also compatible with the Periphrastic Aorist and Inferential Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv ), combining the Imperfective verb form (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ) with a copula in Inferential Imperfective ( pjɤ-ŋu ) or in Past Imperfective ( pɯ-ŋu ) as illustrated by example ( ex:pjWrABzjoz.pWNu ). It is unclear whether any function difference exists between non-periphrastic and periphrastic tenses for these verbs, apart from the fact that the latter are unambiguously imperfective.

exe

tɕe ɯ-me nɯnɯ <xianzhong> nɯtɕu pjɯ-rɤ-βzjoz pɯ-ŋu ri, \\
lnk 3sg. poss -daughter dem district.school dem: loc ipfv - apass -learn ipfv -be lnk \\
`(At the time when) her daughter was going to school, (her father was drinking alcohol and neglected his parental duties).' (17-lhazgron)
exe

Third, since some of the sɤ- antipassives can be used as stative verbs (propensity antipassives, § sec:antipassive.sA ), they are thus compatible with Aorist and Inferential Imperfective anyway.

Despite these difficulties, unambiguous examples of non-periphrastic Aorist and Inferential Imperfective are not common in the corpus even with verbs selecting the downwards orientation. In ( ex:pjArABzjoz.ipfv ), it is clear from the context that pjɤ-rɤ-βzjoz is Inferential Imperfective rather than Inferential Perfective both due to the context, the presence of the adverb ntsɯ and the unambiguous Inferential Imperfective with Progressive pjɤ-k-ɤsɯ-ndɯn-ci `he was reading it' in the following clause.

exe

<caichen> nɯnɯ pjɤ-rɤ-βzjoz ntsɯ. jɯɣi ntsɯ pjɤ-k-ɤsɯ-ndɯn-ci. \\
anthr dem ifr. ipfv - apass -learn always book always ifr. ipfv - peg - prog -read- peg \\
`Caichen was always studying, always reading books.' (150907 niexiaoqian-zh) 0006262#S20
exe

In other contexts, there is genuine ambiguity: example ( ex:pjArAɕphAt ) can either mean `the wife was patching clothes' (the interpretation provided by Tshendzin ) or `the wife (had) patched clothes'.

exe

tɤ-rʑaβ nɯ pjɤ-rɤ-ɕpʰɤt, \\
indef. poss -wife dem ifr. ipfv - apass -patch \\
`The wife was patching clothes.' (qajdoskAt 2002) 0003366#S20
exe
summary:
Antipassive verbs are compatible with Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective forms, unlike most dynamic verbs, but this is difficult to analyze because many transitive bases show syncretism with Aorist and Inferential forms due to their lexicalized downwards preverbs. In addition, these verbs can also occur in periphrastic imperfective constructions, and some antipassives are stative enough to combine with Aorist and Inferential Imperfective anyway.  

Even so, clear non-periphrastic examples of Aorist and Inferential Imperfective are rare in the corpus, and some forms remain genuinely ambiguous between imperfective and perfective interpretations.

subsection: The uses of the antipassive derivations
text:
antipassive!indefinite object indefinite!antipassive
In Japhug, non-overt objects of (non-labile) transitive verb are always interpreted as transitive, even when a particular verb form happens to lack unambiguous markers of transitivity (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ). The minimal example ( ex:pWBzjoza ) with the 1sg 3 Aorist of βzjozlearn could in principle be an intransitive form (due to the fact that the past transitive -t suffix cannot surface with a close syllable stem, § sec:indexation.mixed ). Yet, this example cannot mean `I studied something' or `I went to school', but necessarily implies that the object has been previously mentioned in the discourse.

exe

χsɯ-sla pɯ-βzjoz-a \\
three-months aor -learn- 1sg \\
`I have learned [how to make ploughshares] for three months.' (2010-09)
exe

The antipassive derivations, which not only demote the object, but suppress it syntactically (except for ditransitive verbs, see § sec:antipassive.ditransitive ), are a way to express a non-referential indefinite patient, either a non-specific patient (translatable as `something'), or a whole range of possible patients. For instance in the case of rɤβzjozlearn things, the implicit patient can be a school curriculum (`go to school, study') as in ( ex:pWrABzjoza ) below and ( ex:Wme.pWrABzjoz ) above, or a non-specific topic `study something' as in ( ex:pjArABzjoz.ipfv ) in § sec:antipassive.pst.ipfv.

exe

nɯra nɯ-pʰe nɯtɕu, χsɯ-xpa nɯ pɯ-rɤ-βzjoz-a. \\
dem: pl 3pl. poss - dat dem: loc three-years dem pst - apass -learn- 1sg \\
`I have studied with them for three years.' (160721 XpWN) 0006181#S28
exe

Example ( ex:turAthu.mWnWjAG ) also illustrates the contrast between the transitive verb tʰuask Although tʰuask is ditransitive, since it has indirective alignment, it does not behave differently from monotransitive verbs regarding antipassivization (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ). with an overt object ɯʑɤɣ nɯ `his own (question)' and the corresponding antipassive verb rɤtʰuask questions with an non-specific patient (the prohibition against asking additional questions anymore is not limited to the one he forgot to ask).

exe

ɯʑɤɣ nɯ kɤ-nɯ-tʰu na-nɯ-jmɯt ɲɯ-ŋu, tɕeri nɯ ma tu-rɤ-tʰu mɯ-nɯ-jɤɣ ɲɯ-ŋu, \\
3sg: gen dem inf - auto -ask aor:3 - auto -forget sens -be lnk dem apart.from ipfv - apass -ask neg - aor -be.allowed sens -be \\
`He had forgotten to ask his own [question], but he was not allowed to ask questions anymore.' (divination, 2005)
exe

In rarer cases, the demoted patient is referential and semantically recoverable from the context. In ( ex:korAthunW ) for instance, by contrast with ( ex:turAthu.mWnWjAG ), the demoted patient of rɤtʰuask questions corresponds to the previous sentence ( ex:kWsi.torANgat ): taking the context into consideration the verb form ko-rɤ-tʰu-nɯ means `They consulted the lama (about the reason why the man was about to die and what to do about it)'.

exe

xlist

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ-si to-rɤŋgat. \\
indef. poss -son dem sbj: pcp -die ifr -be.about \\
`The man [had fallen ill] and was about to die.' (rkongrgyal2.2002)

βlama ɲɤ-ɕar-nɯ tɕe, ko-rɤ-tʰu-nɯ ri \\
lama ifr -search- pl lnk ifr - apass -ask- pl lnk \\
`They looked a lama and consulted him/ask for his advice.' (rkongrgyal2.2002)
xlist
exe

Similarly, in ( ex:kWsAndza.toGWGu ), the implicit patient of the verb sɤ-ndza `eat (someone)' is not `people' in general, but rather the group of characters present at the moment of the action with the demoness, and it is thus in fact partially referential.

exe

tɕe kɯ-sɤ-ndza tu-oɣɯɣu ri,\\
lnk sbj: pcp - apass -eat ipfv -prepare lnk \\
`[The râkshasî demoness] (revealed her true nature) and was about to eat someone (one of them), but...' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S378
exe

The contrast between rɤ- and sɤ- prefixes
The semantic difference between the rɤ- and sɤ- antipassive prefixes involves a contrast in humanity (following on Tshobdun) and animacity.

The rɤ- prefix is required for inanimate/abstract indefinite patients. In the case of verbs of speech, the removed object corresponds to a reported speech complement clause (as in ex:korAthunW above, § sec:reported.speech ). Some rɤ- antipassives however have animate non-human patients, in particular rɤftɕɤzcastrate and rɤntɕʰabutcher (from ftɕɤzcastrate and ntɕʰakill, butcher), which can only refer to animals.

The sɤ- prefix by contrast is mainly used to express generic human objects (with a meaning often close to that of the generic object indexation marker kɯ- § sec:non.antipassive.indef.patient ) or indefinite humans (sometimes even semantically recoverable from the context, as in ex:kWsAndza.toGWGu ). However, the sɤ- prefix when used as a propensity antipassive can demote animal patients, as in ( ex:YWsAsat ) where sɤ-sat is a stative verb meaning `have killing power, be lethal' (rather than `kill people').

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ ju-lɤt-nɯ tɕe tɕe nɯnɯ wuma ʑo ɲɯ-sɤ-sat [...] qro ri ɲɯ-xtɕi ɕti, tɕe nɯnɯ kɯ rcanɯ tɯ-kʰɤl tɕe ʁnɯz χsɯm jamar pjɯ-sat ɲɯ-ŋu \\
lnk dem ipfv -release- pl lnk lnk dem really emph sens - apass -kill pigeon also sens -be.small be. aff: fact lnk dem erg unexp: deg one-place loc two three about ipfv - kill sens -be \\
`They shoot with [scattering bullets], and it is very lethal, (...) the pigeons are small, [with scattering bullets] they kill two or three [pigeons] in one place.' (28-CAmWGdW) 0003712#S110, 0003712#S115
exe

In addition, when both agents and patients are (non-human) animals, the prefix sɤ- can also be used to demote the object, as in the case of the verb sɤmtsʰilead the way (from mtsʰilead) which can be applied to packs of animals. Note also that the antipassive sɤndza from ndzaeat, can both mean `eat someone' (as in ex:kWsAndza.toGWGu above) or `eat other animals' as in ( ex:kWrNi1 ) (a sentence which can be glossed by ex:kWrNi2 ).

exe

xlist

rɯdaʁ nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ kɯ-sɤ-ndza nɯ, kɯrŋi tu-kɯ-ti ŋu \\
wild.animals dem 3sg. poss -in sbj: pcp - apass -eat dem beast ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`Among the animals, the carnivorous ones are called `beasts'.' (elicited, explanation of example ex:kWsAndza.GW, § sec:subject.participle.subject.relative )
summary:
In Japhug, a non-overt object of a transitive verb is still interpreted as transitive and usually refers back to something already mentioned in discourse; it cannot normally mean an indefinite or new object. To express a non-referential or indefinite patient, Japhug uses antipassive forms, which suppress the object syntactically and can indicate meanings like “study something,” “ask questions,” or other context-dependent patients.

The two antipassive prefixes differ semantically: rɤ- is used mainly for inanimate or abstract indefinite patients and some non-human animate patients, while sɤ- is mainly used for generic or indefinite human patients, though it can also apply to animals in some cases.

subsection: The uses of the antipassive derivations
text:
nɯ-zda rɯdaʁ ɯ-kɯ-ndza tʰamtɕɤt nɯnɯra nɯ-rmi lonba kɯrŋi tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
3pl. poss -companion animal 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -eat all dem: pl 3pl. poss -name all beast ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`All those that eat the other animals, their name is `beasts'.' (150822 kWrNi)
0006260#S7
xlist
exe

The human vs. non-human contrast between the two prefixes can be observed on a handful of verbs that are compatible with both rɤ- and sɤ- antipassives. The indirective verb tʰuask takes the rɤ- prefix when the demoted patient is an action/state of affair (as in rɤtʰuask questions in ex:korAthunW above), but takes the sɤ- prefix when asking for someone in marriage (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ), as in ( ex:kWsAthu.Cea ).

exe

aʑo kɯ-sɤ-tʰu ɕe-a \\
1sg sbj: pcp - apass -ask go: fact - 1sg \\
`I am going to ask for (the girls) in marriage.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

A less lexicalized minimal pair is provided by ɕarsearch, which has the antipassive forms rɤɕarsearch things and sɤɕarsearch someone.
summary: The passage says that the choice between the rɤ- and sɤ- antipassive prefixes reflects a human vs. non-human contrast on some verbs. In particular, the verb tʰuask takes rɤ- when the object is an action or state of affairs, but sɤ- when the object is a person, such as someone being asked for in marriage. A similar minimal pair is noted for ɕarsearch, with rɤ- used for things and sɤ- for someone.

subsection: The uses of the antipassive derivations
text:
The sɤ- antipassive can be used as a strategy to avoid overtly referring to a particular entity. In ( ex:znArGAma ) for instance, despite the use of the antipassive sɤnɯrtɕatease people (from nɯrtɕatease), the implicit patient of this verb is not indefinite: it is a type of local deity called ʑɯβdaʁ (from གཞི་བདག་gʑi.bdaglocal deity). On the etymology of the placename znɤrɣɤma, see § sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle.

exe

tɯ-mɯ wuma ʑo tɤ-me tɕe, tɕendɤre tsʰitsuku ɕ-ku-sɤ-nɯrtɕa-nɯ tɕe, fsaŋ ra ɕ-pjɯ-ta-nɯ, ɕ-pjɯ-rɟaʁ-nɯ nɯra tɕe, tɕe tɯ-mɯ ku-sɯ-lɤt-nɯ pjɤ-ŋgrɤl. tɕe nɯ ɯ-sɤz-nɤma ɣɯ sɤtɕʰa nɯ znɤrɣɤma tu-ti-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
indef. poss -weather really emph aor -not.exist lnk lnk some.things tral - ipfv - apass -tease- pl lnk fumigation pl tral - ipfv -put- pl tral - ipfv -dance- pl dem: pl lnk lnk indef. poss -weather ipfv - caus -release- pl ifr. ipfv -be.usually.the.case lnk dem 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -make gen place dem placename ipfv -say- pl sens -be \\
`When there was no rain at all, people would go there and do teasing, make fumigations and dance, and cause rain to come. They call the place where these activities were performed znɤrɣɤma.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S237
exe

Tshendzin explicitly provided the sentence ( ex:ZWBdaR.CkuWwGnWrtCa ) as a gloss to the verb form ɕ-ku-sɤ-nɯrtɕa-nɯ in this context.

exe

ʑɯβdaʁ ɕ-kú-wɣ-nɯrtɕa \\
mountain.god tral - ipfv - inv -tease \\
`One teases the mountain gods.' (gloss of example ex:znArGAma ).
exe

The `teasing' in question refers to the belief that rain resulted from the wrath of mountain deities. The aim of this ceremony, rather than appeasing the gods, was to anger them. It has not been practiced for decades, and memory of this practice only survives in this toponym znɤrɣɤma, whose etymology is discussed in more detail in § sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle.
summary: The passage explains that the sɤ- antipassive can be used to avoid overtly naming an entity, but in this example the implicit patient is not indefinite: it refers to a specific local deity, ʑɯβdaʁ ‘mountain god.’ The cited ceremony involved teasing mountain gods to provoke rain, rather than appeasing them, and the practice has been forgotten except for its survival in the place name znɤrɣɤma.

subsection: The uses of the antipassive derivations
text:
The subject participle of antipassive verb is the preferred strategy to build nominals referring to persons with a particular activity of profession, as illustrated by the forms in tab:kWrAverb (see also § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ), or having a particular habit (see ex:qandzxe.thAlwACtsxat, § sec:object.verb.compounds ). These nominalized forms are frequently used but not lexicalized, and their meaning is predictable from that of the base verb.

Oblique participles (§ sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle) also need to undergo antipassivization to be used to derive nouns of instruments or of location without overt object. For instance, the antipassive participle ɯ-z-rɤ-rɤt ( 3sg. poss - obl: pcp - antip -write) is used to express the meaning `writing implement, pen' (§ sec:instrumental.participle.relatives).
summary: The passage says that subject participles of antipassive verbs are the preferred way to form nouns referring to people defined by a profession or habitual activity, and these forms are common but not lexicalized, since their meaning is predictable from the base verb. It also states that oblique participles must be antipassivized to derive nouns denoting instruments or locations without an overt object, such as the form meaning “writing implement, pen.”

subsection: The uses of the antipassive derivations
text:
reflexive!antipassive antipassive!reflexive
The indefinite patient interpretation is not the only meaning of the rɤ- antipassive derivation. For instance, the verb raχtɕiwash (vi) from χtɕiwash (vt) does not mean `wash things' as could have been expected, but has a reflexive meaning `wash one's face' or `have a shower/bath' (see example ex:pjAraXtCinW.torAmpCArnW, § sec:rA.non.apass ). A typologically similar irregularity is found with the antipassive-durative verb niza‑lā `wash oneself' in Bezhta. The regular reflexive form ʑɣɤχtɕiwash oneself is also attested with this verb (§ sec:refl.other ).
summary: The rɤ- antipassive derivation does not always yield the expected indefinite-patient meaning. In the example of raχtɕiwash from χtɕiwash, it instead has a reflexive sense, meaning ‘wash one’s face’ or ‘have a shower/bath,’ and a typologically similar irregular reflexive antipassive is also noted in Bezhta. The regular reflexive form is likewise attested for this verb.

subsection: Other strategies used to express indefinite patients
text: As a means of expressing indefinite patients, the antipassive derivations compete with five alternative constructions: indefinite object pronouns (§ sec:antipassive.vs.indef.pronouns ), generic object nouns (§ sec:antipassive.vs.generic ), light verb constructions with action nominal (§ sec:antipassive.vs.light.verbs ), incorporation (§ sec:antipassive.vs.incorporation ) and pairs of denominal verbs (§ sec:antipassive.vs.denominal.pairs ).
summary: The passage states that antipassive derivations are one way to express indefinite patients, but they compete with five other constructions. These alternatives are indefinite object pronouns, generic object nouns, light verb constructions with action nominal, incorporation, and pairs of denominal verbs.

subsection: Other strategies used to express indefinite patients
text:
indefinite!pronoun
Indefinite pronouns (§ sec:indef.pro ), in particular tʰɯcisomething (§ sec:thWci ) or tsʰitsukuwhatever (§ sec:tshitsuku ) as object functionally overlap to some extent with the rɤ- antipassive derivations. However, indefinite pronouns are preferred if the indefinite patient is referential, as in ( ex:tshitsuku.YAndWn ). Examples of antipassive verbs with referential implicit patient are however attested, as in ( ex:kWsAndza.toGWGu ) and ( ex:korAthunW ) above.

exe

ɯʑo kɯ tsʰitsuku ɲɤ-ndɯn tɕe kʰɤndɯn ra ɲɤ-βzu \\
3sg erg whatever ifr -read lnk recitation pl ifr -read \\
`He recited something, he recited a formula.' (140510 sanpian yumao-zh)
0003947#S95
exe
summary: Indefinite pronouns such as *tʰɯci* ‘something’ and *tsʰitsuku* ‘whatever’ overlap functionally with *rɤ-* antipassive constructions when used as objects. However, indefinite pronouns are preferred when the indefinite patient is referential, though examples show that antipassive verbs can also occur with referential implicit patients.

subsection: Other strategies used to express indefinite patients
text:
indefinite!generic
The generic noun tɯrmeperson (§ sec:tWrme.generic ) and generic person indexation of the object (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ) compete with the sɤ- antipassive. As shown by examples ( ex:mAsAmtsWG ) and ( ex:kW.kWmtsWG ) On the absence of dual indexation on kɯ-mtsɯɣ `they bite people', see § sec:indexation.generic.tr and § sec:agreement.mismatch. the meaning of the antipassive sɤmtsɯɣbite people (`be a biting/stinging entity') and that of the generic object kɯ-mtsɯɣ `$X$ bites people' in the Factual are very close semantically. The antipassive of propensity, being a stative verb, is however more often used in a comparative construction such as that in ( ex:mAsAmtsWG ) (§ sec:sthWci.equative ). Example ex:sAndza.kWndza above (§ sec:antipassive.sA ) presents a minimal pair of the same type.

exe

mtsʰalɤɣrum nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rme tu ri, [...] mtsʰalɤɲaʁ nɯ stʰɯci mɤ-sɤ-mtsɯɣ. \\
nettle.sp dem gen 3sg. poss -hair exist: fact lnk nettle.sp dem much neg - apass: prop -bite: fact \\
`Although the white nettle has hairs, it does not sting as much as the black nettle.' (19-mtshalu2) 0003544#S4
exe

exe

mtsʰalɤɲaʁ cʰo mtsʰalɤɣrum nɯ ʁnaʁna kɯ kɯ-mtsɯɣ \\
nettle.sp comit nettle.sp dem both erg genr:S/O-bite: fact \\
`Both black and white nettle sting.' (11-mtshalu)
0003472#S24
exe
summary: The generic noun *tɯrme* ‘person’ and generic object indexation can compete with the *sɤ-* antipassive. In meaning, the antipassive *sɤmtsɯɣ* ‘be a biting/stinging entity’ is very close to the generic object construction *kɯ-mtsɯɣ* ‘X bites people’ in the factual, though the antipassive of propensity is more often used in comparative constructions because it is stative.

subsection: Other strategies used to express indefinite patients
text:
Collocations involving transitive light verbs and their objects have a functional overlap with antipassive verbs, when their objects, either action nominals or nouns describing the product of the action, are generic and not referential. For instance, the collocation tɤ-ɕpʰɤt+ta `patch, make patches' (from the inalienable noun tɤ-ɕpʰɤtpatch (n) and the transitive verb taput) has a meaning close to that of the antipassive rɤɕpʰɤtpatch clothes (from ɕpʰɤtpatch, the verb from which the noun tɤ-ɕpʰɤt itself is derived, § sec:bare.action.nominals ) when the possessive prefix on tɤ-ɕpʰɤt is indefinite. As illustrated by example ( ex:tACphAt.kWta ), where the participial form of this collocation tɤ-ɕpʰɤt ɯ-kɯ-ta `(person) who makes patches' occurs in opposition to the participle of an antipassive verb kɯ-rɤ-tʂɯβ `(person) who sews clothes, taylor'.

exe

tɕʰeme [tɤ-ɕpʰɤt ɯ-kɯ-ta] kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi pjɤ-tu ma nɯ ma kɯ-rɤ-tʂɯβ pjɤ-me. \\
woman indef. poss -patch 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -put sbj: pcp - emph be.small ifr. ipfv -exist lnk dem apart.from sbj: pcp - apass -sew ifr. ipfv -not.exist \\
`There were a few women who made patches, but no (women) tailors.' (12-kAtsxWb) 0003486#S100
exe

The collocation tɤ-ɕpʰɤt+ta can however occur with a 3sg possessive prefix on the object ɯ-ɕpʰɤt+ta and refer to a definite patient, encoded as possessor of the object.

Other light verbs occurring in this type of collocation include βzumake, lɤtrelease and tɕɤttake out (see ex:tWpGaR.lotCAtndZi2, § sec:antipassive.history ).
summary: Collocations of transitive light verbs with nonreferential objects can function similarly to antipassive verbs, especially when the object is a generic action nominal or a noun for the product of the action. The passage illustrates this with *tɤ-ɕpʰɤt+ta* ‘patch, make patches,’ which is close in meaning to an antipassive form when the possessive prefix is indefinite, though it can also take a definite patient with a 3sg possessive prefix. Other light verbs used in this kind of collocation include verbs meaning ‘make,’ ‘release,’ and ‘take out.’

subsection: Other strategies used to express indefinite patients
text: Object-saturating incorporating verbs (§ sec:incorp.O ) are intransitive verbs derived from transitive bases whose intransitive subject corresponds to the subject of the base verb. The incorporated noun corresponds to the object of the base verb, and is indefinite and non-referential, and thus functionally close to an antipassive, in particular to lexicalized ones (§ sec:antipassive.lexicalized ). This closeness in function is also correlated with a closeness in origin, since both incorporating verbs and antipassive derivation come from denominal derivations (§ sec:incorp.denom ). For instance, the incorporating verb ɣɯ<piaozi>fsoʁearn money from 票子 piàoziticket, paper money and fsoʁearn has a meaning and usage identical to the antipassive rɤfsoʁearn money.
summary: Object-saturating incorporating verbs are intransitive verbs derived from transitive bases, with the intransitive subject corresponding to the subject of the base verb and an incorporated noun corresponding to the object. This incorporated noun is indefinite and non-referential, making these verbs functionally similar to lexicalized antipassives, and the two are also related in origin because both arise from denominal derivations. An example is ɣɯ<piaozi>fsoʁ, which means ‘earn money’ and uses the incorporated noun 票子 ‘ticket, paper money’; its meaning and usage are identical to the antipassive rɤfsoʁ ‘earn money.’

subsection: Other strategies used to express indefinite patients
text: Transitive denominal verbs with the nɯ- / nɤ- prefix can in some cases have sɤ- antipassives (§ sec:antipassive.sA ), but never rɤ- antipassives. Instead, intransitive rɯ- / rɤ- denominal verbs from the same noun occur as the functional equivalents of the antipassive. For instance, the transitive verb nɤmado (work) derived by the prefix nɤ- (§ sec:denom.tr.nW ) from the inalienably possessed noun ta-mawork (§ sec:inalienably.possessed.morpho ), does not have an antipassive form such as $ $ rɤ-nɤma. Rather, the intransitive rɤmawork from the same noun (see example § sec:autoben.permansive, § ex:nW.kWnA.pjAnWrAma and ex:mAkWmbrAt.YWrAma, § sec:inf.converb ) occurs to express the meaning that would have been expected from such an antipassive form (§ sec:denom.rA.pairing ). In addition to the semantic similarity with antipassive verbs, rɤmawork is compatible with non-periphrastic Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv ) like antipassive verbs (§ sec:antipassive.pst.ipfv ).
summary: Transitive denominal verbs with the nɯ- / nɤ- prefix may form sɤ- antipassives, but they never form rɤ- antipassives. Instead, the corresponding intransitive rɯ- / rɤ- denominal verb derived from the same noun serves as the functional equivalent of the antipassive, as shown by the pair based on the noun for ‘work.’ These intransitive forms also behave like antipassives in that they can combine with non-periphrastic Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective.

text:
The sɤ- antipassive derivation can be take as input applicative and tropative verbs. The most commonly attested examples of double derivations are however from verbs whose applicative or tropative prefix is synchronically unanalyzable, such as sɤnɤkʰuinvite people ( ex:YWsAnAkhunW ) and sɤnɤkʰebully people ( ex:nAtWsAnAkhe ) from nɤkʰuinvite (lexicalized applicative of akʰucall, § sec:applicative.lexicalized ) and nɤkʰebully (lexicalized tropative of kʰebe stupid, § sec:tropative.lexicalized ), respectively.

exe

nɯ-ʁjoʁ ra kɯ tɯ-ndza tu-βzu-nɯ nɯra, ɲɯ-sɤ-nɤkʰu-nɯ ra pjɤ-ɕti qʰe, \\
3pl. poss -servant pl erg nmlz: action -eat ipfv -make- pl dem: pl ipfv - apass -invite- pl pl ifr. ipfv -be. aff: fact lnk \\
`Their servants were making food, they were inviting people.' (28-qajdoskAt) 0003718#S131
exe

exe

nɤ-tɯ-sɤ-nɤkʰe nɯ mɤ-ra \\
2sg - nmlz: deg - apass -bully dem neg -be.needed: fact \\
`You are out of line.' (`you should not bully people like that.') (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S14
exe

Antipassive forms from non-lexicalized applicative and tropative verbs are not attested in the corpus, but can be elicited, for instance sɤ-nɯ-rga apass - appl -like `like people' from nɯrgalike (vt) (§ sec:applicative.semi.object ) and sɤ-nɤ-mpɕɤr apass - trop -be.beautiful `find people beautiful' from nɤmpɕɤrfind beautiful (§ sec:tropative ).

Only one causative verb takes the rɤ- antipassive: jtsʰigive to drink (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ), an irregular causative from tsʰidrink (§ sec:caus.j ), which competes with the regular one sɯ-tsʰi `make/let drink, drink with'.

Other causative verbs are only attested with the sɤ- antipassive, for instance sɤ-sɯ-rtoʁ apass - caus -look) `show to people'. The lexicalized causative nɯsɯkʰorob, extort, which historically derives from kʰogive by the combination of the sigmatic causative sɯ- and the autive nɯ- prefixes (see ex:YWkWnWsWkhoa, § sec:sig.caus.lexicalized ), has two sɤ- antipassive forms (§ sec:antipassive.ditransitive ): the sɤ- can be directly prefixed to the complex verb stem as in sɤnɯsɯkʰorob people ( ex:zYAsAnWsWkhonW ) (historically sɤ-nɯ-sɯ-kʰo apass - auto - caus -give), but the alternative form nɯ-sɤ-sɯ-kʰo ( auto - apass - caus -give) with the autive prefix nɯ- switching position with the antipassive is also possible (§ sec:autoben.lexicalized ).

exe

iɕqʰa tɕaχpa nɯra kɯ li, laχtɕʰa z-ɲɤ-sɤ-nɯsɯkʰo-nɯ \\
the.aforementioned robber dem: pl erg again thing tral - ifr - apass -rob- pl \\
`The robbers had gone and robbed some people from their things.' (140512 alibaba-zh) 0003965#S107
exe

Applicative verbs can serve as input for the sigmatic causative derivation. With the rɤ- antipassive, the z- allomorph of the causative is selected (§ sec:caus.z ) as in z-rɤ-rɤt ( ex:pjAwGzrArAt ) and z-rɤ-tʂɯβ ( ex:chWwGzrArtsxWB ) from rɤrɤtwrite/draw things and rɤtʂɯβsew things (antipassives of rɤtwrite, draw and tʂɯβsew, respectively, § sec:antipassive.rA ).

In combination with the antipassive, both the permissive/precative `make $X$, let $X$, ask to $X$' (as in ex:pjAwGzrArAt ) and the instrumental `$X$ with' ( ex:chWwGzrArtsxWB ) uses of the sigmatic causative are attested.

exe

Dai.Song ɣɯ, nɤkinɯ, ɯ-ɕaχpu nɯ kɯ ɲɤ́-wɣ-sqɤr tɕe, nɤkinɯ, pjɤ́-wɣ-z-rɤ-rɤt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
anthr gen filler 3sg. poss -friend dem erg ifr - inv -ask.to.do lnk filler ifr - inv - caus - appl -draw sens -be \\
`One of Dai Song's friend's asked him to draw something.' (2010-kewen-07)
exe

exe

tɕe nɯ tɤ-ri ɲɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-βzu tɕe cʰɯ́-wɣ-z-rɤ-tʂɯβ ŋu \\
lnk dem indef. poss -thread ipfv - inv - auto -make lnk ipfv - inv - caus - apass -sew be: fact \\
`One [can] then make the thread and use it to sew things.' (13-tAsAsqAri) 0003496#S30
exe
summary: The passage describes how the sɤ- antipassive can attach to applicative and tropative verbs, especially to lexicalized forms such as invite people and bully people; non-lexicalized applicative/tropative verbs are not attested in the corpus but can be elicited. It also notes that only one causative verb takes the rɤ- antipassive, while other causative verbs take sɤ-, including lexicalized causatives where the antipassive may either attach directly to the complex stem or appear with the autive prefix in a different position. Finally, applicative verbs can feed into the sigmatic causative, which selects the z- allomorph with rɤ- antipassive forms and is attested in both permissive/precative and instrumental uses.

text:
distributed property
The amɯ- prefix expressing a distributed property can be applied to a handful of transitive and semi-transitive verbs.

With the cognition verbs sɯzknow and tsoknow, understand (semi-transitive, see § sec:semi.transitive ), the meaning of this derivation is `be $X$ed by everybody, be $X$able', as shown by amɯtsobe clear (of speech) ( ex:mAZW.amWtso ) and amɯsɯzbe well-known.

exe

nɯ tu-kɯ-ti tɕe mɤʑɯ amɯ-tso. \\
dem ipfv - genr -say lnk even.more distr -understand: fact \\
`If one says this, it is clearer (easier to understand).' (heard several times during elicitation sessions)
exe

The verb amɯtso also has a reciprocal reading `understand each other', corresponding to the amɯ- reciprocal derivation (example ex:pjWkAmWtso.YWra, § sec:amW.reciprocal ). It is possible that amɯtso was the pivot form between the two derivations. A reanalysis from reciprocal to `distributed property' may have taken place through the causative of the reciprocal sɯ-ɤmɯ-tso `cause people to understand each other', which originally took as objects causee (see ex:kAsAmWtsotandZi ) and as optional semi-object the speech/words.

exe

a-pi cʰo a-ʁi ni kɤ-sɯ-ɤmɯ-tso-t-a-ndʑi \\
1sg. poss -elder.sibling comit 1sg. poss -younger.sibling du aor - caus - recip -understand- pst: tr - 1sg - du \\
`I helped my elder and younger brothers/sisters understanding each other.' (elicited)
exe

The semi-object was then reinterpreted as the object, and forms such as ta-sɯ-ɤmɯ-tso in ( ex:tasAmWtso ) were then reinterpreted as meaning `cause (words) to be understandable' rather than `cause people to understand (words)'. Note that the meanings of the causative sɯ-ɤmɯ-tso are correlated with different orientation prefixes: eastwards when meaning `cause to understand each other' and `up' when meaning `speak clearly'. The distributed property meaning of amɯ- was then created by back-formation from this causative form.

exe

tɯ-rju ta-sɯ-ɤmɯ-tso \\
indef. poss -word aor:3 - caus -???-understand \\
`He spoke clearly'. (Literally: `He made the words understandable'; elicited)
exe

When occurring on other verbs, however, the amɯ- prefix expresses that the action spreads everywhere (within a particular location), without external agent. The verb amɯ-rmbɯ (derived from rmbɯheap up) is specifically used to describe food piled up high in a container (bowl or pot) to the point of filling it up completely, as in ( ex:tAmWrmbW ), in particular as the result of cooking.

exe

fsosoz ndɤre, tɤ-amɯ-rmbɯ ʑo. \\
next.morning lnk aor - distr -pile.up emph \\
`The next morning, [the bowl] was completely filled [with food].' (2003kandZislama)
exe

The verb amɯ-zwɤr (from zwɤrburn) occurs to refer to the (non-controlled) spread of fire, as in ( ex:YAmWzwAr.mbat ).

exe

taŋi tɤ-ɣe tɕe ɣndʑɤβ a-mɤ-tɤ-lɯɣ ra ma ɲɯ-ɤmɯ-zwɤr mbat \\
drought aor -come[II] lnk fire.hazard irr - neg - pfv -come.off be.needed: fact lnk ipfv - distr -burn be.easy: fact \\
`When there is a drought, there should not be a fire as it can spread easily.' (elicited)
exe

reanalysis
It is also used metaphorically to describe the spread of information as in ( ex:YAkAmWzwArci.YAkAmWsWzci ). This example illustrates two verbs with distinct sub-functions of the distributed property amɯ- prefix occurring with a common subject, suggesting a path of reanalysis from the first sub-function (`be known by everybody' $ $ `be known to everybody') to the second one (`be $X$ed everywhere').

exe

kɯki ɣɯ ɯ-tɕʰa nɯnɯ, nɯɕimɯma ʑo rɟɤlkʰɤβ nɯtɕu ɲɤ-k-ɤmɯ-zwɤr-ci tɕe ɲɤ-k-ɤmɯ-sɯz-ci. \\
dem. prox gen 3sg. poss -news dem immediately emph kingdom dem: loc ifr - peg - distr -burn- peg lnk ifr - peg - distr -know- peg \\
`The news about this spread in the whole kingdom like fire and became known to everyone.' (150820 meili de meiguihua-zh) 0006286#S79
exe

The verb amɯzɣɯtbe evenly distributed, derived from the motion verb zɣɯtarrive, also illustrates the spatially distributed meaning of the prefix amɯ- (originally `reach everywhere'). Note that despite the fact that the root zɣɯt generally causes a ɯ ɤ vowel change on derivational and inflectional prefixes directly attached to it (§ sec:intr.person.irregular ), it is not the case with amɯ-.

This verb amɯzɣɯt mainly occurs in a serial verb construction (§ sec:svc.manner ). In ( ex:YAmWzGWt.YWlhoR ), it shares the same subject and TAME category as the following verb ɲɯ-ɬoʁ `(it) comes out'. It expresses the manner in which the action takes place, and has to be translated as the adverb `evenly'.

exe

tɤ-ndɤr nɯnɯ, [...] nɯ-βri rcanɯ, kɯ-so ɲɯ-me ʑo, ɲɯ-ɤmɯ-zɣɯt ʑo ɲɯ-ɬoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
indef. poss -pustule dem 3pl. poss -body unexp: deg sbj: pcp -be.empty ipfv -not.exist emph ipfv - distr -reach emph ipfv -come.out sens -be \\
`The pustules (...) come out evenly everywhere on their body, without any empty spot.' (27-kharwut) 0003698#S61
exe

When occurring with a transitive verb in this serial verb construction, the sigmatic causative form sɤmɯzɣɯtdo evenly is used instead, as in ( ex:YWsAmWzGWt.YWmar ) (§ sec:svc.manner.other ).

exe

tɕe tamar kɯnɤ, nɤki tɕʰorzi nɯ ɯ-mŋu me, ɯ-qa me nɯra ɲɯ-sɯ-ɤmɯ-zɣɯt ʑo ɲɯ-mar ɲɯ-ra \\
lnk butter also filler alcohol.jar dem 3sg. poss -opening whether 3sg. poss -bottom whether dem: pl ipfv - caus - distr -reach emph ipfv -smear sens -be.needed \\
`[The jar maker] also to apply butter evenly to the opening and the bottom of the alcohol jar.' (30-kWrAfcAr) 0003740#S58
exe

The distributed property amɯ- prefix is restricted to a handful of very lexicalized verbs. Hence, if the hypothesis of reanalysis from reciprocal presented above is valid, this process must have taken place in the remote past. The opposite hypothesis of reanalysis from the distributed property function to the reciprocal function also deserves to be taken into consideration.
summary:
The distributed-property prefix **amɯ-** applies only to a small set of transitive and semi-transitive verbs. With cognition verbs like **tso** ‘understand’ and **sɯz** ‘know’, it can mean ‘be understood by everyone’ or ‘be well-known’, while on other verbs it can indicate that an action spreads everywhere within a location, as in verbs for piling up, burning, or becoming evenly distributed.

The passage suggests that some of these meanings may have developed through reanalysis, possibly from a reciprocal form to a distributed-property form, or vice versa. Because the prefix is highly lexicalized, any such reanalysis must have occurred long ago.

text:
proprietive
The proprietive sɤ- prefix This category was previously referred to as `deexperiencer' in previous publications, such as. derives stative verbs from verbs of perception, feeling or some verbs of involuntary action. tab:proprietive presents representative examples of this derivation, which include some loanwords from Tibetan ( scitbe happy, rgalike and
βziget drunk from སྐྱིད་skʲidbe happy, དགའ་dgalike and བཟི་bzibe drunk, respectively), showing that the proprietive prefix is productive.

The base verbs are mainly intransitive (proprietive verbs derived from semi-transitive and transitive verbs are treated in § sec:proprietive.semi.tr and § sec:proprietive.tr ), and encode as subject the experiencer ( mube afraid, scitbe happy) or a patientive argument suffering from the action ( ɕkeget burned, ŋgioslip).

The proprietive derivation removes this experiencer or patientive argument from the argument structure and promotes instead the stimulus to subject status. Compare for instance the base verb mube afraid whose subject is the experiencer feeling fear ( ex:pjAmu ) with the proprietive sɤɣmube frightening ( ex:pjAsAGmu.pjAnWGmu ) whose subject is the entity causing fear to people.

exe

nɯ rgɤtpu nɯ pjɤ-mu tɕe, \\
dem old.man dem ifr. ipfv -be.afraid lnk \\
`The old man was afraid.' (140426 xiaohaizi he hua de shizi-zh)
0003832#S10
exe

Example ( ex:pjAsAGmu.pjAnWGmu ) also shows that the subject of the proprietive verb sɤɣ-mu is the same referent as the object of the applicative verb nɯɣ-mu `be afraid of' derived from the same verb root (§ sec:applicative.promoted ).

exe

sɯŋgi nɯnɯ pjɤ-sɤɣ-mu tɕe pjɤ-nɯɣ-mu ɲɯ-ŋu.\\
lion dem ifr. ipfv - prop -be.afraid lnk ifr. ipfv - appl -be.afraid sens -be \\
`The lion$_i$ was terrifying and [the old man] was afraid of it$_i$.' (shizi yu nongfu-zh)
exe

A minority of proprietive verbs allow the demoted experiencer to be encoded with the genitive, for instance sɤscitbe pleasant (from scitbe happy) in ( ex:aZWG.mAsAscit ), which takes as oblique experiencer aʑɯɣ 1sg: gen.

exe

nɯnɯ ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ fso tʰɯ-wxti tɕe tʰa aʑɯɣ mɤ-sɤ-scit \\
dem 3sg. poss -son dem in.the.future aor -be.big lnk later 1sg: gen neg - prop -be.happy: fact \\
`When his son has grown up, it will not be a pleasant situation for me.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S17
exe

In the case of the intransitive verbs mtsɯrbe hungry and ɕpaʁbe thirsty, the proprietive derivation removes the experiencer from the argument structure of the verb without adding a stimulus and the resulting proprietive verbs sɤmtsɯrbe a famine and sɤɕpaʁbe a lack of drink have dummy subjects, as in ( ex:pjAsAmtsWr ).

exe

tɯ-xpa tɕe, wuma pjɤ-sɤ-mtsɯr \\
one-year lnk really ipfv. ifr - prop -be.hungry \\
`One year, there was a famine.' (elicited)
exe
summary: The proprietive **sɤ-** prefix, formerly called *deexperiencer*, derives stative verbs from verbs of perception, feeling, and some involuntary actions, and it is productive, including in loanwords from Tibetan. In these derivations, the original experiencer or patientive subject is removed and the stimulus becomes the subject; in some cases a demoted experiencer may appear as a genitive oblique, while in others, such as derived from “hungry” and “thirsty,” the resulting verbs have dummy subjects and express states like famine or lack of drink.

text:
proprietive!allomorphy morphology!allomorphy allomorphy!proprietive
The main allomorph of the proprietive prefix is sɤ-. The variant sa- occurs when prefixed on a verb stem containing a cluster with a uvular preinitial (§ sec:A.vs.a.prefixes ).

The proprietive prefix, like other derivations (§ sec:caus.sWG )), had at an earlier stage the allomorph sɤɣ- with intrusive -ɣ, but it ceased to be productive and remains on only three verbs: sɤɣɲatbe exhausting, sɤɣmube frightening and sɤɣdɯɣbe unpleasant.
summary: The proprietive prefix normally appears as **sɤ-**, but it has the variant **sa-** when attached to a verb stem with a cluster containing a uvular preinitial. Earlier, it also had the productive allomorph **sɤɣ-** with intrusive **-ɣ**, but this form is no longer productive and survives only in three verbs: **sɤɣɲat** ‘be exhausting’, **sɤɣmu** ‘be frightening’, and **sɤɣdɯɣ** ‘be unpleasant’.

text:
generic
With verbs that can undergo proprietive derivation (see above), the generic intransitive subject kɯ- form and proprietive have overlapping uses.

In ( ex:kWNGio.YWsaRdAt ), the generic form kɯ-ŋgio `one will slip' expresses a potential consequence of the state described by the proprietive verb ɲɯ-sɤ-aʁdɤt `it is slippery'. A semantic commonality between generic and proprietive verb forms in this example is that both refer to an action to which all humans (including speaker and addressee) are potentially subjected.

exe

nɯnɯtɕu pjɯ́-wɣ-rɤtɕaʁ a-pɯ-ŋu tɕe, [...] ʑgrɯɣ ʑo kɯ-ŋgio ɕti ma, nɯnɯ ɲɯ-sɤ-aʁdɤt kɯ-fse. \\
dem: loc ipfv - inv -tread irr - ipfv -be lnk certainly emph genr:S/O- acaus:glide be. aff: fact lnk dem sens - prop -slip sbj: pcp -be.like \\
`If one walks on [the moss], one will certainly slip, as it is slippery.' (03-zhenzhuquan-zh) 0003386#S25
exe

With experiencer and modal verbs, the semantic closeness of generic and proprietive is even more obvious, if one compares for instance the generic of nɤzdare ( ex:kAndza.mWpWkWnAz ) with the proprietive sɤnɤzbe such that people dare to in ( ex:kAnAjaR.mAsAnAz ): the experiencer argument of the base verb that has been demoted by the proprietive derivation is by default interpreted as generic, unless it can be recovered from the context, or expressed by an oblique case as in ( ex:aZWG.mAsAscit ) above.

exe

[kɤ-ndza] mɯ-pɯ-kɯ-nɤz ma sɤndɤɣ tu-ti-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
inf -eat neg - pst. ipfv - genr:S/A-dare lnk be.poisonous: fact ipfv -say- pl sens -be \\
`We/people would not dare to eat it, because they say that it is poisonous.' (19-khWlu)
0003540#S79
exe

In ( ex:kAnAjaR.mAsAnAz ), note that generic reference is expressed by the proprietive derivation on mɤ-sɤ-nɤz `one does not dare to...' and by the generic possessor on tɯ-jaʁ `one's hand' in the immediately following clause.

exe

tɕe [kɤ-nɤjaʁ] mɤ-sɤ-nɤz ʑo ma tɯ-jaʁ ku-otsa ɕti tɕe mŋɤm. \\
lnk inf -touch neg - prop -dare: fact emph lnk genr. poss -hand ipfv -prick.into be. aff: fact lnk hurt: fact \\
`It is such that people do not dare to touch it, as it pricks in one's hand and it hurts.' (15-babW)
0003512#S52
exe

In addition, both the generic and the proprietive can serve as a indirect way to express first person (§ sec:1.genr ), as shown by examples ( ex:kArAZi.YWkWdWG ) and ( ex:aZosti.YWsAGdWG ), where the generic ɲɯ-kɯ-dɯɣ and proprietive ɲɯ-sɤɣ-dɯɣ have exactly the same meaning `be fed up with $X$, don't feel like $X$'. In both cases, the implicit experiencer is the 1sg referent mentioned in the previous clause.

exe

nɯfse kɯ-nɤ-ŋkɯ ŋke ɕe-a ma tɕe kʰa kɤ-rɤʑi ntsɯ ɲɯ-kɯ-dɯɣ \\
like.that sbj: pcp - distr:walk go: fact - 1sg lnk lnk house inf -stay always sens - genr:S/O-have.enough.of \\
`I go to walk (without a special reason), because I don't feel well staying at home all the time.' (conversation, 2013-12-24)
exe

exe

kutɕu aʑo-sti ɲɯ-ɕti-a tɕe ɲɯ-sɤɣ-dɯɣ \\
dem: prox: loc 1sg -alone sens -be. aff - 1sg lnk sens - prop -have.enough.of \\
`I am here alone, and I am fed up of [being alone].' (07-deluge) 0003426#S41
exe
summary:
The passage explains that the generic intransitive subject **kɯ-** and the **proprietive** form can overlap in meaning for verbs that allow proprietive derivation. In some cases both describe situations affecting people in general, as with verbs of slipping or daring, where the generic subject is interpreted as human in general unless the context specifies otherwise.  

It also notes that both forms can indirectly express a **first-person** meaning, especially when the implicit experiencer is the speaker; in the examples given, the generic and proprietive forms have the same meaning, such as ‘be fed up with X, don’t feel like X.’

text:
proprietive
The proprietive derivation takes some semi-transitive verbs such as dɯɣhave enough of, tsoknow, understand or rgalike (§ sec:semi.transitive ) as input. In such cases, the intransitive subject of the proprietive verb corresponds to the semi-object of the base verb. For instance, in ( ex:kArAZi.YWdWGa ), the infinitival complement clause nɯ kɯ-fse kɤ-rɤʑi `staying like that' is semi-object of dɯɣhave enough of, while in ( ex:kArAZi.pjAsAGdWG ) the complement clause is the intransitive subject of sɤɣ-dɯɣ (the experiencer being unexpressed in this clause).

exe

[nɯ kɯ-fse kɤ-rɤʑi] ɲɯ-dɯɣ-a. \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.like inf -stay sens -have.enough.of- 1sg \\
`I am fed up of living like that.' (140426 jiagou he lang-zh) 0003804#S31
exe

exe

[kɤ-rɤʑi] wuma ʑo pjɤ-sɤɣ-dɯɣ. \\
inf -stay really emph ifr. ipfv - prop -have.enough.of \\
`Living [there] was very difficult to endure.' (150827 taisui-zh) 0006390#S12
exe

The semi-transitive modal verbs cʰacan and nɤzdare also have proprietive forms sɤcʰabe such that people can and sɤnɤzbe such that people dare to which select the same types of complement clauses as those selected by their base verbs, as illustrated by ( ex:luwGtaR.YWsAcha ) (see also ex:kAndza.mWpWkWnAz ) and ( ex:kAnAjaR.mAsAnAz ) in § sec:proprietive.generic above). These complement clauses are the intransitive subject of the proprietive verbs.

exe

tɯ-sŋi [mɯntoʁ ʁnɯz χsɯm jamar lú-wɣ-taʁ] ɲɯ-sɤ-cʰa \\
one-day flower two three about ipfv: upstream - inv -weave sens - prop -can \\
`In one day, it is possible to weave two or three patterns (on the belt).' (2011-06-thaXtsa)
exe

However, the complement clauses can be elided, and the subject participle forms of the proprietive verbs can refer to an argument (generally object) of the (elided or overt) verb in the complement clause. For instance in ( ex:kWsAcha.mAkWsAcha ), the participle kɯ-sɤ-cʰa can be translated as `(the mice) that can be (caught)' (an elided infinitive form such as kɤ-ndo inf -grab is implicit in this example).

exe

βʑɯ [...], kɯ-sɤ-cʰa nɯra aʑo pjɯ-sat-a ŋu, mɤ-kɯ-sɤ-cʰa jɤ-kɯ-ɤ<nɯ>ri nɯra nɯʑora kɯ pɯ-sat-nɯ ra nɤ \\
mouse sbj: pcp - prop -can dem: pl 1sg ipfv -kill- 1sg be: fact neg - sbj: pcp - prop -can aor -< auto >go[II] dem: pl 2pl erg imp -kill- pl be.needed: fact sfp \\
`The mice, I will kill the ones that (I) can (get), but the one that [I] cannot [get] and have gone away, you will have to kill them.' (150831 BZW kAnArRaR)
0006378#S28
exe
summary: The proprietive derivation applies to semi-transitive verbs such as *dɯɣ* ‘have enough of’, *tso* ‘know, understand’, and *rga* ‘like’, and the intransitive subject of the derived verb corresponds to the semi-object of the base verb. It also forms proprietive versions of modal verbs like *cʰa* ‘can’ and *nɤz* ‘dare’, with the complement clause becoming the intransitive subject of the proprietive verb. In some cases the complement clause is omitted, and the subject participle of the proprietive verb can refer to an argument, usually the object, of the omitted or overt complement clause.

text:
The proprietive prefix occurs with some transitive verb stems, removing the transitive subject and converting the object argument to intransitive subject status, like the passive, anticausative and object-oriented facilitative (§ sec:facilitative.nWGW ) derivations. Proprietive verbs derived from transitive verbs are rare: the derivational sɤ- prefix on verbs is more often interpreted as an object-suppressing antipassive (§ sec:antipassive.sA ).

In the case of the labile perception verb mtosee, one could propose that the proprietive form sɤmtobe visible derives from the stative intransitive use of this verb (meaning `have sharp eyesight', § sec:labile.tr-intr ), but this is unlikely from a semantic point of view (the meaning of sɤmto is not `be such that people have sharp eyesight'). The other transitive verbs deriving proprietive forms in tab:proprietive are not labile, and no such ambiguity exists.

The transitive verbs that can be subjected to the proprietive derivation belong to four related semantic classes: verbs of perception ( mtosee, mtsʰɤmhear), of cognition ( sɯzknow, spabe able), of obtaining ( rnduobtain) and of evaluation ( nɯzdɯɣworry about, saχpaʁrespect). All of these verbs have experiencer or experiencer-like transitive subjects.

The proprietive of verbs of perception and obtaining such as sɤmtsʰɤmbe audible ( ex:tumbri.YWsAmtshAm ) and sɤrndube easy to find ( ex:tAjmAG.mWjsArndu ) express a potential state, semantically close to the object-oriented facilitative (§ sec:facilitative.nWGW ).

exe

tɕe sɯŋgɯ ku-rɤʑi ɕti tɤɣa kɤ-mto me. ri [tu-mbri] nɯ sɤ-mtsʰɤm.\\
lnk forest ipfv -stay be. aff: fact in.the.open obj: pcp -see not.exist: fact lnk ipfv -make.noise dem prop -hear: fact \\
`It stays in the forest and is never seen in the open, but it can be heard singing.' (23-scuz)
0003612#S109
exe

exe

tɯ-mɯ mɯ́j-lɤt tɕe tɤjmɤɣ mɯ́j-sɤ-rndu\\
indef. poss -sky neg: sens -release lnk mushroom neg: sens - prop -obtain\\
`It is not raining, and so it is not easy to find mushrooms.' (elicited)
exe

The proprietive of sɯzknow and spabe able both mean `be (widely) known', and mainly occur with the noun tɤ-rminame, as in ( ex:Wrmi.YWsAsWz ) and ( ex:Wrmi.mAkWsAspa ).

exe

ɯ-rmi ɲɯ-sɤ-sɯz \\
3sg. poss -name sens - prop -know \\
`His name is well-known.' (elicited)
exe

exe

mɤʑɯ ɯ-rmi mɤ-kɯ-sɤ-spa xcat ɕti \\
again 3sg. poss -name neg - sbj: pcp - prop -be.able be.many: fact be. aff: fact \\
`There are many other [plants] whose name is not known.' (08-tWrgi) 0003464#S51
exe

The case of the verb sɤnɯzdɯɣcausing people to worry, which is derived from applicative verb nɯzdɯɣworry about (§ sec:applicative ) is treated in § sec:proprietive.compatibility.
summary: The proprietive prefix can attach to some transitive verb stems, removing the transitive subject and making the object the intransitive subject, though such derivations are rare and the same prefix is often analyzed instead as an antipassive. The verbs that allow this derivation fall into four semantic classes—perception, cognition, obtaining, and evaluation—and they all take experiencer-like subjects. In perception and obtaining verbs, the proprietive forms express a potential state close to a facilitative meaning, while with know/able the forms mean “be widely known,” often with the noun “name.”

text:
The meaning of some proprietive verbs is not entirely predictable from their base verbs.

The verb ɕkeget burned encodes as subject the entity that suffers from burning, as in ( ex:pWCke ). The expected meaning of its proprietive sɤɕke would be `be burning'. While this meaning is indeed attested as in ( ex:pjAsACke ), sɤɕke can also simply mean `be hot', concerning for instance the weather as in ( ex:tukWNke.YWsACKe ), without the implication that people subjected to this weather suffer from burns.

exe

a-jaʁ pɯ-ɕke \\
1sg. poss -hand aor -burn \\
`My hand was burnt.' (elicited)
exe

exe

smi tʰa-βlɯ-nɯ ri, pjɤ-sɤ-ɕke qʰe, ʑakastaka jo-nɯ-rɤɕi-nɯ qʰe, \\
fire aor:3 -burn- pl lnk ifr. ipfv - prop -burn lnk each.their.own ifr - auto -pull- pl lnk \\
`They made a fire (and used their legs as tripods to make tea), but since it was burning, and each of them pulled [their legs] (and were not able to prepare food).' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

exe

<diandian> ʑo kɯ-rɤʑi ɲɯ-mɯɕtaʁ, tu-kɯ-ŋke tɕe ɲɯ-sɤ-ɕke \\
shop emph genr:S/O-stay sens -be.cold ipfv - genr:S/O-walk lnk sens - prop -burn \\
`Staying in the shop it is cold, but walking [on the street] it is hot.' (conversation, 14-05-10)
exe
summary: Some proprietive verbs have meanings that are not fully predictable from their base verbs. For example, the base verb ɕke means ‘burn (something/someone suffers burning),’ and its proprietive form sɤɕke can mean ‘be burning,’ but it can also mean simply ‘be hot,’ as with hot weather, without implying actual burning or injury.

text:
proprietive!compatibility
The proprietive derivation can take as input anticausative verbs (§ sec:anticausative.other.derivations ). For instance, sɤŋgiobe slippery comes from ŋgioslip, itself from kiocause to glide. The proprietive verb sɤŋgio expresses that the action of the base verb kio is possible due to the nature of the ground, as shown by ( ex:WthoR.YWsANgio ).

exe

ɯ-tʰoʁ ɲɯ-sɤ-ŋgio tɕe tɕoχtsi ɲɯ́-wɣ-kio ɲɯ-kʰɯ \\
3sg. poss -ground sens - prop - acaus:glide lnk table ipfv - inv -glide sens -be.possible \\
`The ground is slippery, and one can move the table by making it glide on it.' (elicited)
exe

The verb nɯzdɯɣworry about (which could be analyzed as a lexicalized applicative of zdɯɣsuffer, § sec:nWzdWG ) has the sɤ- proprietive sɤnɯzdɯɣcausing people to worry, as shown by example ( ex:YWsAnWzdWG ), homophonous with an antipassive verb meaning `worrying about people'.

exe

nɤ-wa nɯtʰamtɕɤt ʑo tʰɯ-wxti tɕe, nɯ kɯ-fse [...] ɕɯ-kɤ-ɤlɯlɤt [...] cʰa ɕi kɯma, ɲɯ-sɤ-nɯ-zdɯɣ\\
2sg. poss -father so.much emph aor -be.big lnk dem sbj: pcp -be.like tral - inf -fight can: fact qu sfp sens - prop -worry.about\\
`Your father has become so old, can he go to war like that? He is cause of worry [for all of us].' (150828 huamulan-zh) 0006396#S19
exe

Proprietive verbs cannot be subjected to (sigmatic sɯ- or velar ɣɤ- ) causative derivations. On the other hand, they can take the tropative nɤ- prefix, as shown by the common verbs nɤsɤscitfind pleasant and nɤsɤɣdɯɣfind unpleasant derived from sɤscitbe pleasant and sɤɣdɯɣbe unpleasant, respectively (§ sec:tropative.other.derivations ).
summary: The proprietive derivation can apply to anticausative verbs, yielding verbs that mean something is possible or causes a certain state because of the nature of the ground or other circumstances. The passage notes that proprietive verbs cannot undergo causative derivation, but they can take the tropative prefix nɤ-, as in forms meaning “find pleasant” or “find unpleasant.”

text:
The proprietive sɤ, like several other voice prefixes (§ sec:voice.denominal ), is related to the denominal sɤ- derivation (§ sec:sA.history ). It has a common origin with the antipassive sɤ- (§ sec:antipassive.sA; see in particular the propensitive function of the antipassive).

The proprietive and the sɤ- antipassive are however synchronically quite distinct. While only the former can have intransitive or semi-transitive verbs as input, both can occur on transitive verbs, in which case the former is object-oriented (§ sec:proprietive.tr ), while the latter is subject-oriented (§ sec:antipassive.sA ).
summary: The proprietive sɤ is historically related to the denominal sɤ- derivation and shares a common origin with the sɤ- antipassive, including its propensitive function. However, synchronically they are distinct: the proprietive can take intransitive or semi-transitive verbs as input, and on transitive verbs it is object-oriented, whereas the antipassive is subject-oriented.

text:
facilitative
Japhug has two productive facilitative derivations, the ɣɤ- and nɯɣɯ- prefixes, deriving stative verbs whose subjects correspond to the subject and the object (or goal) of the base verbs, respectively. Cognates of both prefixes are found in Tshobdun ( wɐ- and nwə- ), with an identical functional constrast

These prefixes are only valency-decreasing when prefixed to transitive verbs, and do not change transitivity when the base verb is intransitive.

The meaning of these prefixes is very similar to that of complement clauses headed by the stative verb mbatbe easy (§ sec:adjective.complement ). For instance, ( ex:kABzjoz.YWmbat ) was provided as a gloss for ( ex:YWnWGWBzjoz ) during an elicitation session.

exe

xlist

ɲɯ-nɯɣɯ-βzjoz \\
sens - facil -learn \\

kɤ-βzjoz ɲɯ-mbat \\
inf -learn sens -be.easy \\
xlist
`It is easy to learn.' (elicited)
exe

A third way of expressing facilitative meaning is by verb compounding; the only example of this type is apɤmbatbe easy to do from the transitive verb pado and the stative verb mbatbe easy (§ sec:denom.compound.verbs ).
summary: Japhug has two productive facilitative prefixes, ɣɤ- and nɯɣɯ-, which derive stative verbs and correspond to the subject and object or goal of the base verb, respectively; comparable prefixes with the same contrast also occur in Tshobdun. These prefixes reduce valency only when added to transitive verbs and do not affect intransitive verbs, and their meaning is similar to that of complement clauses with the stative verb *mbat* ‘be easy’. A third facilitative strategy is verb compounding, illustrated by a single example meaning ‘be easy to do’.

text:
facilitative!subject-oriented subject!facilitative
The prefix ɣɤ, homophonous with the velar causative ɣɤ- (§ sec:velar.causative ), generally derives stative verbs meaning `become/get X easily', `tend to become/get X'. For instance, from wxtibe big one can derive the stative verb ɣɤwxtibecome big easily, as illustrated by ( ex:wuma.Zo.YWGAwxti ).

exe

si kɯ-wxtɯ wxti ɲɯ-βze cʰa ma wuma ʑo ɲɯ-ɣɤ-wxti. \\
tree sbj: pcp - emph be.big ipfv -grow[III] can: fact lnk really emph sens - facil -be.big \\
`It can grow into a hug tree, as it easily becomes huge.' (07-Zmbri) 0003438#S9
exe

The facilitative prefix ɣɤ- is very productive on stative verbs, including on loanwords from Tibetan. For instance, rgɤzbe old (from རྒས་rgasget old) has a facilitative form ɣɤrgɤzage quickly, attested in ( ex:mAkWGArgAz ).

exe

tɯrme mɤ-kɯ-ɲɟɯr, nɯnɯ mɤ-kɯ-ɣɤ-rgɤz tɕe tɕe nɯnɯ tɤtʰo tu-sɤrmi-nɯ ŋu. \\
people neg - sbj: pcp -change dem neg - sbj: pcp - facil -be.old lnk lnk dem anthr ipfv -call- pl be: fact \\
`Persons who don't change, who don't age quickly, people call them `pines'.' (07-tAtho)
0003432#S23
exe

Some dynamic intransitive verbs are also attested with the ɣɤ- derivation, with meanings such as `X quickly/early/easily' or `X often'. For instance, mdabe the time derives the form ɣɤ-mda, which can mean `be the time (ripen) earlier', as in ( ex:YWGAmda ), and rɤruget up has the facilitative ɣɤrɤrugetting up early, `getting up easily' (as soon as one wakes him/her up).

exe

nɯra iʑo ji-ji pɯ-kɤ-z-mɤku nɯ iʑo ɯ-pʰɯt ku-z-mɤku-j ma ɲɯ-ɣɤ-mda \\
dem: pl 1pl 1pl. poss -field aor - obj: pcp - caus -be.first dem 1pl 3sg. poss - bare. inf:cut ipfv - caus -be.first- 1pl lnk sens - facil -be.the.time \\
`Our fields, that have been [sowed] first, we harvest they first, because the [crops] ripen earlier [than in other places, higher up in altitude].' (2010-09)
exe

It also occurs on some anticausative verbs (§ sec:anticausative ); for instance, the intransitive ɴɢrɯbreak has the facilitative form ɣɤ-ɴɢrɯ `easily break', which has the same meaning as the object-oriented facilitative nɯɣɯ-qrɯ of the transitive base verb qrɯbreak (§ sec:anticausative.other.derivations ). It is also attested with denominal verbs such as sɤmbrɯget angry (§ sec:denom.sA.proprietive ), whose facilitative is ɣɤsɤmbrɯget angry easily.

The ɣɤ- prefix is also found on intransitive verbs that only occur in collocation with a particular noun, for instance nmushake (of earthquakes) (on which see § sec:volitional.mW ) or the collocation ɯ-ʁo+mbibe discouraged (§ sec:anticausative, § sec:orphan.verb ), from which ɣɤ-nmu or ɯ-ʁo+ɣɤmbibe easily discouraged can be derived (examples ex:YWGAnmu and ex:nARo.WtWGAmbi ).

exe

iɕqʰa sɤtɕʰa nɯ waɟɯ ɲɯ-ɣɤ-nmu. \\
the.aforementioned place dem earthquake sens - facil -shake \\
`Earthquakes are frequent in this place.' (elicited)
exe

exe

nɤ-ʁo ɯ-tɯ-ɣɤ-mbi nɯ! \\
2sg. poss -discourage(1) 3sg - nmlz: deg - facil - acaus:discourage(2) sfp \\
`You are so easily discouraged!' (elicited)
exe

With the dynamic motion verb ɕego, the facilitative ɣɤ-ɕe only occurs in collocation with tɤ-rʑaʁtime in the meaning `pass quickly (of time)'), as in ( ex:WYWGACe ). In this example, the facilitative applied to the whole collocation tɤ-rʑaʁ+ɕe `spend (one's time)' (§ sec:intr.light.verbs )

exe

nɤ-tɤ-rʑaʁ ɯ-ɲɯ́-ɣɤ-ɕe \\
2sg. poss - indef. poss -time qu - sens - facil -go \\
`Is the time passing quickly for you?' (elicited)
exe

The facilitative ɣɤ- is also attested on a handful of transitive experiencer verbs, where it has an antipassive-like valency-decreasing function: ɕɯftaʁremember and jmɯtforget derive the stative verbs ɣɤɕɯftaʁto have a good memory and ɣɤjmɯtbe forgetful, respectively ( ex:YWGACWftaR ).

exe

ɲɯ-ɕqraʁ tɕe ɲɯ-ɣɤ-ɕɯftaʁ \\
sens -be.intelligent lnk sens - facil -memorize \\
`He is intelligent, he has a good memory.' (elicited)
exe

This derivation demotes the object, and the intransitive subject of the facilitative verbs ɣɤɕɯftaʁ and ɣɤjmɯt corresponds to the transitive subject of the base verb. In order to build a stative verb expressing a property of the stimulus/object `to be easy to remember/forget', the other facilitative prefix nɯɣɯ- is used instead (§ sec:facilitative.nWGW ). Hence, the prefix ɣɤ- can be described as a subject-oriented facilitative, following Sun's ( jackson14morpho) description of the cognate prefix wɐ- in Tshobdun.
summary: The prefix ɣɤ- is a highly productive subject-oriented facilitative that derives stative verbs meaning ‘become/get X easily,’ ‘tend to become/get X,’ or related senses. It appears on stative verbs, loanwords, some dynamic intransitives, some anticausatives, denominal verbs, and certain collocations, and in a few transitive experiencer verbs it reduces valency and assigns the intransitive subject the role corresponding to the transitive subject of the base verb. The text contrasts this with the object-oriented facilitative nɯɣɯ- for meanings like ‘easy to remember/forget.’

text:
facilitative!object-oriented object!facilitative
The facilitative nɯɣɯ- prefix is one of the rare disyllabic derivational prefix in Japhug. Like ɣɤ- (§ sec:facilitative.GA ), it is used to build stative verbs meaning `be easy to X'. It is most commonly prefixed to transitive action verbs: a typical example is for instance nɯɣɯ-krɤɣ `be easy to shear' from krɤɣshear, mow, as in ( ex:mWjnWGWkrAG ). Additional examples are found in tab:facilitative.nWGW.

exe

tɕe qaʑo kɯ-wxti nɯra ɣɯ qʰe, nɯ-rme ɲɯ-rɲɟi qʰe ɲɯ-nɯɣɯ-krɤɣ, kɯ-xtɕi nɯra ɣɯ, nɯ-rme ɲɯ-xtɯt qʰe, mɯ́j-nɯɣɯ-krɤɣ. \\
lnk sheep sbj: pcp -be.big dem: pl gen lnk 3pl. poss -hair sens -be.long lnk sens - facil -shear sbj: pcp -be.small dem: pl gen 3pl. poss -hair sens -be.short lnk neg: sens - facil -shear \\
`The big sheep, their wool is long and thus easy to shear, the small ones, their wool is short and difficult to shear.' (160712 smAG)
0006073#S25
exe

When the base verb is transitive, the nɯɣɯ- prefix is a valency-decreasing derivation, removing the transitive subject, and turning the object into an intransitive subject. In ( ex:mAnWGWmto ) for instance, nɯɣɯmtobe easy to see appears in the Factual third singular without stem III alternation, showing that it is an intransitive verb (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ).

exe

ci nɯ xɕaj ɯ-mdoʁ tsa ɯ-kɯ-ndo nɯ mɤ-nɯɣɯ-mto. tɕe wuma ʑo mɯ mɤ-pɯ-kɯ-tso nɤ mɤ́-wɣ-mto \\
indef dem grass 3sg. poss -colour a.little 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -take dem neg - facil -see: fact lnk really emph cond neg - pst. ipfv - genr:S/O-understand lnk neg - inv -see \\
`The other one, which has the colour of grass, is not easy to see; unless you know it very well, you won't see it.' (07-Cku) 0003424#S56
exe

Among the verbs in tab:facilitative.nWGW, the facilitative nɯɣɯjpabe convenient is particularly lexicalized, with both an irregular -j- element occurring between he prefix nɯɣɯ- and the root |pa|, and a non-predictable meaning derivation.

In the case of the verb tisay, the facilitative nɯɣɯti can either mean `be easy to pronounce' or `be easy to express', as in example ( ex:mWjnWGWti ), uttered by Tshendzin during an elicitation session.

exe

nɯ mɯ́j-nɯɣɯ-ti \\
dem neg: sens - facil -say \\
`This [meaning] is difficult to express (in Japhug).' (heard in context)
exe

Some intransitive verbs are attested with the nɯɣɯ- prefix. The only common one is nɯɣɯŋkebe easy to walk (on) (from ŋkewalk); the nɯɣɯ- derivation appears to be possible on a few other motion verbs and verbs of location (such as rɟɯɣrun or rɤʑistay), though their acceptability has to be rechecked. The subject of the facilitative verbs derived from such intransitive verbs corresponds to the locative adjunct ( ex:WmAtWnWGWNke ) or goal ( ex:YWnWGWCe ) of the base verb.

exe

tɕʰeme nɯnɯ tʰɤlwa ɲɯɣɲɯɣ zɯ to-ɕe qʰe, maka ɯ-mɤ-tɯ-nɯɣɯ-ŋke pjɤ-saχaʁ ʑo, \\
girl dem earth idph (II):soft loc ifr: up -go lnk at.all 3sg. poss - neg - nmlz: deg - facil -walk pst. ipfv -be.extremely emph \\
`The girl went up the [path made of] soft earth, and it was extremely difficult to walk on it.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

exe

tʂu ɯ-rkɯ ɲɯ-ɤrmbat tɕe, ɲɯ-nɯɣɯ-ɕe \\
path 3sg. poss -side sens -be.close lnk sens - facil -go \\
`[This place] is close to the road, it is easy to go there.' (elicited)
exe

The semi-transitive tsoknow, understand (§ sec:semi.transitive ) can also undergo the facilitative derivation to nɯɣɯtsoeasy to understand. Semi-transitive verbs in a, such as aʁehave to eat/drink or atɯɣmeet, are not compatible with nɯɣɯ, which appears to lack an allomorph with vowel fusion; a form $ $ nɯɣɤʁe for instance (intended meaning: `easy to get to eat') is utterly inacceptable.

goal locative
Since semi-objects, goals and some locative adjuncts do have partial objectal properties (§ sec:semi.object, § absolutive.goal, § sec:theme.ditransitive, § sec:semi.object.relativization, § sec:locative.relativization ), it is nevertheless appropriate to describe nɯɣɯ- as an object-oriented derivation, following. The contrast between nɯɣɯ- and subject-oriented ɣɤ- is clearest with the transitive verbs jmɯtforget and ɕɯftaʁremember, which can be subjected to both derivations: compare object-oriented nɯɣɯjmɯtbe easy to forget and subject-oriented ɣɤjmɯtbe forgetful (§ sec:facilitative.GA ).

It is possible to apply the facilitative derivation to an intransitive verb already derived by the sigmatic causative, for instance nɯɣɯ-sɯɣ-ɲaʁ ( facil - caus -be.black) `be easily blackened'. It is also possible to causativize a facilitative verb (with the z- allomorph of the sigmatic causative, § sec:caus.z ). For example, the causative of nɯɣɯntɕʰozbe easy to use is z-nɯɣɯ-ntɕʰoz ( caus - facil -use) `make easy to use'. The relative order of the facilitative and of the causative prefixes thus reflects their semantic scope (§ sec:sig.caus.other.derivations ).
summary:
The Japhug facilitative prefix nɯɣɯ- is a rare disyllabic derivational prefix that forms stative verbs meaning ‘be easy to X,’ most often from transitive action verbs. When added to transitive bases, it reduces valency by removing the original subject and promoting the object to intransitive subject, though it can also apply to some intransitive, semi-transitive, and motion/location verbs, with the derived subject corresponding to a goal or locative adjunct.  

The text treats nɯɣɯ- as object-oriented, contrasting it with the subject-oriented facilitative ɣɤ-, and notes that some forms are lexicalized or irregular. It also shows that facilitative verbs can combine with the sigmatic causative, with prefix order reflecting semantic scope.

text:
autive
The autobenefactive-spontaneous or autive I adopt the concise and elegant term ``autive'' from instead of ``autobenefactive-spontaneous'' used in previous publications. prefix nɯ- is one of the most productive voice prefixes in Japhug.

In this section, I first present the morphological properties of this prefix (allomorphy and position in the template), and then describe its three main functions: autobenefactive/self-affectedness, spontaneous and permansive (previously identified in ). Finally, I discuss cases of lexicalized autives and propose historical pathways between the autive and other derivations such as the vertitive and the anticausative.

The anticausative derivation in Japhug does not cause any stem alternation, unlike in other languages such as Bragbar.
summary: The passage introduces the prefix **nɯ-**, called the **autive**, as one of the most productive voice prefixes in Japhug. It outlines its morphological properties and three main functions: **autobenefactive/self-affectedness**, **spontaneous**, and **permansive**, and then discusses lexicalized autives and possible historical links to other derivations such as the vertitive and anticausative. It also notes that, unlike in some other languages, the **anticausative** in Japhug does **not** trigger stem alternation.

subsection: The autive prefix and verb transitivity
text:
autive!transitivity transitivity!autive
Unlike most voice markers, the autive prefix nɯ- neither increases nor decreases verb valency: whether the base verb is morphologically intransitive, transitive or labile, nɯ prefixation has no effect on any of the seven transitivity criteria (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ).

For instance, transitive verbs with nɯ still have stem III alternation (§ sec:stem3.form, for instance -ndo $ $ -ndɤm in ex:nAZo.tAnWndAm ) or the past tense -t suffix (§ sec:suffixes, see tɤ-nɯ-ndo-t-a in ex:aj.tAnWndota.me ).

exe
