laʁjɯɣ nɤʑo tɤ-nɯ-ndɤm je \\
staff 2sg imp - auto -take[III] sfp \\
`Take the staff.' (2005 khu)
exe

exe

nɤʑo nɤkinɯ, tɤ-tɯ-nɯrdoʁ, aj tɤ-nɯ-ndo-t-a me\\
2sg filler aor -2-pick.up 1sg aor - auto -take- tr: pst - 1sg not.exist: fact \\
`It is you who collected [the fruits], I did not take them.' (lWlu 2002)
exe

Conversely, intransitive verbs taking the autive prefix present neither stem III alternation nor the -t suffix. The autive derivation differs in this regard from the homophonous nɯ- applicative prefix (§ sec:applicative ).

The autive is compatible with valency-decreasing derivations, including passive (example ex:apAnWrku, § sec:autoben.position ), reflexive ( ex:tunWZGAraXtCAzi ) and antipassive ( ex:lunWrAjinW below and § sec:antipassive.compatibility ).

exe

lu-nɯ-rɤ-ji-nɯ tɕe, nɯ-kɤ-ndza nɯra ʑara pjɯ-nɯ-tɕɤt-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu \\
ipfv - auto - apass -plant- pl lnk 3pl. poss - obj: pcp -eat dem: pl 3pl ipfv - auto -take.out- pl ifr. ipfv -be \\
`(As they were receiving treatment), they were working in the fields, and earning their own food by themselves.' (25-khArWm)
0003644#S61
exe
summary: The autive prefix **nɯ-** does not change verb valency: it has no effect on whether a verb is morphologically intransitive, transitive, or labile, and it leaves the seven transitivity criteria unchanged. Transitive verbs with nɯ- still show features such as stem III alternation and the past tense **-t** suffix, while intransitive verbs with nɯ- show neither of these; this autive differs from the homophonous applicative **nɯ-**. The autive can also occur with valency-reducing derivations such as passive, reflexive, and antipassive.

subsection: Position in the verbal template and allomorphy
text:
autive!verbal template prefix!autive

The position of the autive prefix in the template depends on the structure of the verb form.

When occuring in combination with contracting derivational prefixes, the autive nɯ- is inserted after the contracting vowel, as in ( ex:apAnWrku ) with the passive -ɤ- (§ sec:passive ).

exe

ɕom kɯ scoʁ cʰɯ-kɤ-sɯ-βzu nɯ, tɯtsʰi ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯra a-pɯ-ɤ-nɯ-rku qʰe ɲɯ-ɲaʁ. \\
iron erg ladle ipfv - obj: pcp - caus -make dem rice.gruel 3sg. poss -in dem: pl irr - ipfv - pass - auto -put.in lnk ipfv -be.black \\
`Ladles that are made of iron (iron ladles), whenever they are put in rice gruel, they blacken.' (30-Com) 0003736#S77
exe

Even when the contracting vowel a/ɤ- is not a prefix but part of the verb root (§ sec:contraction ), the nɯ- prefix is inserted between the a- and the rest of the verb stem. There is only one counterexample where the nɯ- prefix is not infixed, but it concerns a highly lexicalized derivation (§ sec:autoben.lexicalized ).

For example in ( ex:pjAnWtAr.YWNu ) the nɯ- is actually infixed inside the verb stem of atɤrfall (see also in example ex:pannWri in § sec:autoben.spontaneous the infixation within the suppletive stem II ari of the verb ɕego). Although other homophonous prefixes exist in Japhug the autive is the only one that is infixable. All other nɯ- prefixes (the applicative § sec:applicative, the vertitive § sec:vertitive, the denominal nɯ- § sec:denom.nW, and inflectional morphemes like the 3pl possessive prefix § sec:possessive.paradigm and the type A westwards orientation prefix § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) occupy prefixal slots and undergo vowel contraction with the a- of the verb stem (for instance, the applicative yields nɤ- with contracting verb stems, § sec:allomorphy.applicative ).

exe

nɯnɯ ɯ-ʁrɯ nɯnɯ tʰɯ-rgɤz tɕe tɕe nɯ ɯʑo pjɯ-ɤ<nɯ>tɤr ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
dem 3sg. poss -horn dem aor -be.old lnk lnk dem 3sg ipfv: down -<auto>fall sens -be \\
`When its antlers age, they fall off by themselves.' (27-qartshAz)
0003702#S35
exe

The irregular existential verbs ɣɤʑuexist and maŋenot exist (§ sec:intr.person.irregular ) also take the spontaneous marker as an infix rather than as a prefix as in ( ex:GAnWZu ).

exe

pakuku ʑo ju-nɯɕe-nɯ tɕe nɯtɕu li ɣɤ<nɯ>ʑu ɕti. \\
every.year emph ipfv -come.back- pl lnk there again < auto >exist: sens be. aff: fact \\
`They come back every year, and it is still there.' (20 grWBgrWB)
0003554#S51
exe

In addition, like the inverse prefix (§ sec:allomorphy.inv ), the autive is obligatorily infixed within the progressive asɯ- (§ sec:inner.prefixal.chain, § sec:progressive.morphology ), as in example ( ex:panWsWfkur ).

exe

<gaoyucheng> kɯ ɯ-laχtɕʰa [...] pɯ-a<nɯ>sɯ-fkur ɣɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu ɯ-jaʁ cʰɤ-tsɯm ri,\\
anthr erg 3sg. poss -thing pst. ipfv -< auto > prog -carry dem 3sg. poss -inside dem: loc 3sg. poss -hand ifr: downstream -take.away lnk \\
`Gao Yucheng put his hand in the things (bag) that he was carrying on his back.' (150902 qixian-zh)
0006258#S130
exe

In all other cases (and excluding lexicalized autives, § sec:autoben.lexicalized ), the autive nɯ- occurs on the leftmost side of the verb stem, just before the reflexive (§ sec:reflexive ), but after inflectional prefixes (including orientational, participial, inverse and person indexation prefixes), as shown by the forms tu- nɯ -ʑɣɤ-raχtɕɤz-i `we treat ourselves' in ( ex:tunWZGAraXtCAzi ) and a-tɤ-tɯ́-wɣ- nɯ -ndza in ( ex:atAtWwGnWndza ).

exe

tɕe ji-kɤ-nɯ-raχtɕɤz ra jɤ-ɣe-nɯ, iʑora tu-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-raχtɕɤz-i, \\
lnk 1pl - obj: pcp - auto -cherish pl aor -come[II]- pl 1pl ipfv - auto - refl -cherish- 1pl \\
`When people we cherish come, or when we [wish] to treat ourselves,' (30 macha)
0003746#S74
exe

exe

tu-tɯ́-wɣ-ndza ɯ-ɲɯ-sɯsɤm qʰe a-tɤ-tɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-ndza ɲɯ-ntsʰi \\
ipfv -2- inv -eat qu - ipfv -think[III] lnk irr - pfv -2- inv - auto -eat sens -be.better \\
`If it wants to eat you, let it eat you!' (150901 dongguo xiansheng he lang-zh)
0006336#S94
exe

When occurring in this leftmost slot, forms bearing the autive prefix can be ambiguous: for instance the surface form nɯ-ɕe (from the verb ɕego) can either be parsed as 3sg Factual autive ( auto -go: fact ), 3sg Factual vertitive (§ sec:vertitive, ( vert -go: fact ) or 2sg westwards imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology, imp: west -go).

In addition to its infixability, the autive prefix has the particularity of being (optionally) realized as geminated -n- when it occurs before a verb stem or verb prefix in nɯ, as in ( ex:nWtCu.kWnA.pjAnnWrga ).

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯnɯ, kɯ, nɯnɯtɕu kɯnɤ pjɤ-n-nɯ-rga ɕti. \\
indef. poss -son dem erg dem: loc also ifr: ipfv - auto - appl -like be. aff: fact \\
`Even like that, the boy still loved her.' (140510 sanpian sheye-zh) 0003945#S117
exe
summary:
The autive prefix nɯ- has different positions depending on verb structure: with contracting derivational prefixes it follows the contracting vowel, and when the vowel a/ɤ- is part of the root it is inserted between that vowel and the rest of the stem. It is also obligatorily infixed in some contexts, including the progressive asɯ- and certain existential verbs, while in most other cases it appears in the leftmost slot after inflectional prefixes and before the reflexive.  

Unlike other homophonous nɯ- prefixes, the autive is the only one that can be infixed, and forms with it may sometimes be ambiguous with other prefixal meanings. It can also optionally surface as a geminated -n- when it occurs before a verb stem or prefix in nɯ.

text:
autive!autobenefactive autobenefactive
The autobenefactive function of the nɯ- prefix can be subdivided into four subcases: subject affectedness, beneficial, exclusive beneficial, and mild imperative.

First, the autive prefix frequently appears with transitive verbs when the object takes a possessive prefix coreferent with the transitive subject, especially in the case of body parts and other inalienably possessed nouns, to emphasize the fact that the agent is affected by his/her own action. For example, in ( ex:pWnWXtCi ), the 2sg possessive prefix on the body part nɤ-ku is coreferent with the subject of the 2 sg 3 imperative form pɯ-nɯ-χtɕi.

exe

nɤ-ku pɯ-nɯ-χtɕi \\
2sg. poss -head imp - auto -wash \\
`Wash your head.' (elicited)
exe

The autive is not restricted to body part objects, but also appears with more abstract possessed objects such as ɯ-sroʁ and ɯ-ʁrɯm in ( ex:konWri ) and ( ex:WRrWm.pjAnWmto ).

exe

ɯʑo kɯ ɯ-sroʁ ko-nɯ-ri ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg erg 3sg. poss -life ifr - auto -save sens -be \\
`He saved his own life.' (140512 yufu yu mogui-zh)
0003973#S126
exe

exe

tɯ-ci ɯ-ŋgɯ ɯ-ʁrɯm pjɯ-kɯ-ntɕʰɤr nɯ pjɤ-nɯ-mto tɕe, \\
indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -in 3sg. poss -shade ipfv - sbj: pcp -shine dem ifr - auto -see lnk \\
`She saw her [own] reflection in the water.' (140428 mu e guniang-zh)
0003880#S55
exe

Example ( ex:WjaR.Zo.tonWxtsWG ) presents a clear contrast between mɯ-to-xtsɯɣ (no nɯ- prefix) and to-nɯ-xtsɯɣ (presence of nɯ- prefix, coreference between possessor and transitive subject). It also illustrates that the subject affectedness expressed by the autive prefix is not necessarily beneficial, but can also be detrimental.

exe

tɯrpa ci to-lɤt ri, si nɯ ɯ-taʁ mɯ-to-xtsɯɣ kɯ ɯʑo ɣɯ ɯ-jaʁ ʑo to-nɯ-xtsɯɣ. \\
axe once ifr -release lnk tree dem 3sg. poss -on neg - ifr -hit erg 3sg gen 3sg. poss -hand emph ifr - auto -hit \\
`He swung the axe but did not hit the tree, and instead hit his own arm.' (140430 jin e-zh)
0003893#S38
exe

However, the nɯ- prefix prefix is optional in all four sentences: its presence is not required to express subject-object possessor coreference. In addition, non-coreference between subject and object possessor is possible on verbs taking the autive prefix.

Second, the autive prefix can also be found on both intransitive and transitive verbs to focus on the pleasant character of an action for the subject, as in ( ex:kunWrAZinW.pjANu ).

exe

kɤtsa ra χsɯm nɯ kɯ-scɯ scit ʑo ku-nɯ-rɤʑi-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu, \\
coll:family pl three dem sbj: pcp - emph be.happy emph ipfv - auto -stay- pl ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The three of them lived happily.' (Gesar 2003)
exe

Third, the autive nɯ- can be used to express that the action only benefits the subject, to the exclusion of other referents. In ( ex:tunWndzandZi ) for instance, the nɯ- prefix on the verbs tu-nɯ-ndza-ndʑi `they eat it' and ku-nɯ-tsʰi-ndʑi `they drink it' express that the 3du subject (the two elder sisters) performed these actions without sharing anything with the 1sg referent.

exe

nɤ-pi ni kɯ [...] qajɣi nɯra kɯ-mɯm ʑɤni tu-nɯ-ndza-ndʑi, ɯ-rkɯ kɤ-kɯ-ɕke ra aʑo ɲɯ́-wɣ-mbi-a-ndʑi, cʰa ra ʑɤni ku-nɯ-tsʰi-ndʑi, aʑo ɯ-ʁɟo ɲɯ́-wɣ-jtsʰi-a-ndʑi pɯ-ɕti \\

autive!spontaneous spontaneous
The spontaneous function of the autive prefix includes six subcases: actions without external cause, self-volitional actions, non-volitional actions, casual action, concessive clauses, and mocking imperatives.

First, the autive prefix expresses actions that are perceived by the speaker as occurring spontaneously by themselves, such as the growth of plants or animals ( ex:YWkWnWBze ) or action taking place due to an unseen force (example ex:WZo.tonWYJW, with an emphatic pronoun ɯʑo, § sec:pronouns.emph ).

In these constructions, the result described in the apodosis takes place regardless of whether the condition in the protasis is fulfilled or not. summary: The spontaneous function of the autive prefix has six main uses: actions without an external cause, self-volitional actions, non-volitional or mistaken actions, the meaning ‘casually/whatever,’ concessive conditional marking, and mocking imperatives. In its basic sense, it can describe events seen as happening by themselves or under an unseen force, and it can also mark actions done of one’s own free will or without help. In extended uses, it may signal that an action is independent of a condition, or be used in imperatives and irrealis forms to mock or defy the addressee, though it can also soften an imperative.

autive!permansive permansive
In addition to the two previous functions, which are relatively straightforward for a middle marker, the autive prefix also presents an aspectual function. It expresses the continuity of an action or a state, like the adverb `still' in English. Two subcases must be distinguished.

First, the autive can mean that the action of the verb goes on despite the occurrence of another action which could have been expected to stop it (as in ex:pjAnWGAwu and ex:anWmphWr ).

The permansive reading of the autive prefix is only possible in non-perfective verb forms, in particular Factual, Imperfective, Past Imperfective and Sensory.
permansive
The permansive use of the autive nɯ- is not without typological parallels. One of the clearest cases is the Russian pronominal element себе, originally the dative form of себя `oneself', and which alongside its autobenefactive value, is used in certain contexts with a permansive value (`continue to...'). I am indebted to Dmitry Nikolayev and Pavel Ozerov for pointing out this fact to me and suggesting the grammaticalization path proposed in this section, though I remain responsible for any error.

This construction is not fully grammaticalized in Russian, but it is nevertheless a good parallel to the permansive value of the autive in Japhug. Since it is clear in Russian that the original meaning of this marker can only have been autobenefactive, not permansive or spontaneous, this fact suggests that the directionality of grammaticalization is more likely to be from autobenefactive to permansive in Japhug too. The following pathway in four stages can be proposed to account for this evolution; note that all four stages represent attested uses of Japhug autive.

enumerate
`Do $X$ for/to oneself' ( autobenefactive, examples ex:pWnWXtCi, ex:konWri, ex:tunWndzandZi in § sec:autoben.proper ).
`Do $X$ on one's own' ( ex:zYWnWrua, § sec:autoben.spontaneous ).
`Do $X$ on one's own, disregarding external conditions' ( ex:pjWnWmtsaRa, § sec:autoben.spontaneous ).
`Continue to do $X$, despite (adverse) external factors.' ( permansive )
enumerate
summary:
The autive prefix has an aspectual, permansive function in addition to its other middle-marker uses: it can indicate that an action or state continues, like English *still*. This includes cases where an action persists despite an expected interruption, as well as cases where a state endures unchanged over time; the permansive reading is restricted to non-perfective forms such as Factual, Imperfective, Past Imperfective, and Sensory.

The passage also argues for a grammaticalization path from autobenefactive meanings to permansive ones, with the stages “do X for oneself,” “do X on one’s own,” “do X on one’s own disregarding external conditions,” and finally “continue to do X despite adverse external factors.” A Russian parallel with *sebe* is cited as typological support for this development.

text:
The autive nɯ- is lexicalized in a handful of verbs listed in tab:autive.lexicalized, whose meaning is not fully predictable from that of the base verb, and which present several morphological properties.

The clearest example of lexicalized autive is the verb nɤtɯɣhappen to be ( ex:YWnAtWG.pjANu ), which derives from atɯɣmeet. The autive nɯ- prefix, which undergoes here vowel contraction (§ sec:contraction ), occurs here in spontaneous action function (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ), but both the meaning of the verb and the position of the prefix are anomalous: the autive is normally infixed rather than prefixed in the case if verbs in a- (§ sec:autoben.position ).

The -t- element between -n- and the verb stem sɤndu is an effect of internal sandhi -ns- -nts- (a sound change reminiscent of Tibetan, ), as prenasalized fricatives do not exist in Japhug (§ sec:NC.clusters ).

summary:
The passage describes several lexicalized uses of the autive prefix nɯ-, in which the meaning is no longer fully predictable from the base verb and the morphology often departs from the regular pattern. Some verbs, such as nɤtɯɣ ‘happen to be,’ show unusual prefix position or irregular combinations with causative morphology, while others like nɯβde ‘lose,’ nɯte ‘take,’ nɯstʰoʁ ‘have sex,’ and nɯkro ‘share among themselves’ reflect spontaneous or autobenefactive functions.

It also discusses antsɤndu ‘be exchanged by mistake,’ analyzed as a double autive-plus-passive derivation with expected autive placement after the passive. This verb can be further causativized and may even take a second autive prefix, showing that these lexicalized forms participate in more complex and sometimes irregular derivational patterns.

text:
There are also examples of lexicalized autive nɯ- prefixes that are located in their expected locus in the template, further away from the stem than the causative. This is the case for instance with the verb nɯsɯkʰorob, extort (see example ex:YWkWnWsWkhoa, § sec:sig.caus.lexicalized ), from the causative sɯkʰocause to give of kʰogive. This verb has two sɤ- antipassive forms (§ sec:antipassive.sA ), the regular one sɤ-nɯ-sɯ-kʰo ( apass - auto - caus -give) `rob people', but also the variant nɯ-sɤ-sɯ-kʰo ( auto - apass - caus -give) with the autive prefix nɯ- moved further away from the stem than the antipassive sɤ- (§ sec:antipassive.sA ).

Additional possible examples of fossilized autive prefixes include nɯɴɢɤtpart ways (§ sec:anticausative.direction ) and mɟatake (§ sec:antipassive.t ).
summary: The passage notes that some lexicalized autive nɯ- prefixes occur in their expected position in the verbal template, farther from the stem than the causative. An example is *nɯsɯkʰorob* ‘extort,’ which has a variant antipassive form *nɯ-sɤ-sɯ-kʰo* where the autive prefix appears outside the antipassive prefix. It also mentions *nɯɴɢɤt* ‘part ways’ and *mɟa* ‘take’ as possible fossilized examples of autive prefixes.

text: Further semantic evolution of the autive prefix with some verbs has led to the development of distinct grammatical categories, the vertitive nɯ- (§ sec:vertitive ) which remained formally similar to the autive, and the anticausative (§ sec:anticausative ), which underwent phonological reduction to a non-concatenative alternation: the shift from unvoiced stops and affricatives to their corresponding prenasalized voiced counterparts.
summary: The autive prefix has undergone further semantic development with some verbs, giving rise to two distinct grammatical categories. One is the vertitive nɯ-, which remained formally similar to the autive, and the other is the anticausative, which was reduced phonologically to a non-concatenative alternation involving a shift from unvoiced stops and affricatives to their corresponding prenasalized voiced counterparts.

vertitive
The vertitive nɯ- is exclusively attested with a restricted set of motion (§ sec:motion.verbs ) and manipulation verbs (§ sec:manipulation.verbs ), indicated in tab:vertitive, expressing that the motion is directed back to the point of origin.

The vertitive meaning developed out of the autobenefactive function of the autive `take for oneself' $ $ `take to one's home' $ $ `take back home'. However, the two prefixes are synchronically distinct, and can be combined together, as in example ( ex:kunWnWGinW ); note that in this case the autive is generally realized as -n- (§ sec:autoben.position ).

abilitative
The abilitative sɯ-/z- prefix occurs on transitive verb bases. It is formally identical to the sigmatic causative, and possibly historically derived from it (§ sec:abilitative.origin ). As in the case of the causative, the allomorph z- is found on polysyllabic verb bases whose first syllable has a sonorant initial (§ sec:caus.z ). Since the abilitative only occurs on transitive verbs, there is no equivalent of the sɯɣ- allomorph (§ sec:caus.sWG ).

This prefix derives verbs expressing the ability of the transitive subject to perform the action of the base verb, as in sɯndzabe able to eat from ndzaeat (homophonous with the causative sɯndzamake/let eat, `eat with') in ( ex:mWnWsWndzaj ) and ( ex:nWmAkAsWndza ). It seems to be a productive derivation, but abilitative verbs are rare in the corpus, except for the highly frequent verb znɤɕqabe able to endure/resist from nɤɕqaendure, `resist'.

summary:
The abilitative prefix sɯ-/z- appears on transitive verb bases and is formally identical to the sigmatic causative, with z- occurring on polysyllabic bases beginning with a sonorant. It derives verbs meaning that the transitive subject is able to perform the action of the base verb, and it may also express intrinsic inability or inability caused by external circumstances beyond the subject’s control.  

Although seemingly productive, abilitative verbs are rare in the corpus and are attested only in negative form there; for some verbs, a negative prefix may be required, though non-negative forms can sometimes be elicited.

text:
There are a two lexicalized abilitative verbs with the reduced allomorph s-: spʰɯtcan cut In Chinese, this verb in negative form is translated as 切不动 qiēbúdòngcannot cut or 咬不动 yǎobúdòngcannot tear by chewing. from pʰɯttake out, cut, `take out' as in ( ex:mWjsphWt ) (see also ex:WndzrW.mWjsphWt, § sec:obligatory.negative ) and the complement-taking verb spabe able (§ sec:spa.verb ) from pado. In addition, the isolated verb jqube able to lift might also be a lexicalized abilitative with an irregular allomorph of the prefix (§ sec:j.abilitative ).

exe

mbrɯtɕɯ ki mɯ́j-mtɕoʁ tɕe mɯ́j-spʰɯt \\
knife dem. prox neg: sens -be.sharp lnk neg: sens -can.cut \\
`This knife is not sharp, it cannot cut.' (elicited)
exe

Both spabe able and its base verb pado have cognates in all Gyalrongic languages, including Tangut ( 𘘭0385.wjị2.60 `be able to' and 𘃡5113.wji1.10 `do', see ), Khroskyabs (Wobzi fsó `savoir faire', ) and Stau ( vzə with metathesis). Although West Gyalrongic languages lack an abilitative derivation, the existence of this cognate set demonstrates that this derivation goes back to at least proto-Gyalrongic, and has been lost in West Gyalrongic except in this lexicalized form.
summary:
The passage identifies two lexicalized abilitative verbs with the reduced prefix allomorph **s-**: **spʰɯt** ‘can cut’ and **spa** ‘be able,’ with **spʰɯt** traced to the verb meaning ‘take out, cut’ and **spa** to **pado**. It also notes that the isolated verb **jqu** ‘be able to lift’ may be another lexicalized abilitative with an irregular prefix form.  

Because **spa** and **pado** have cognates across all Gyalrongic languages and beyond, the abilitative derivation is argued to go back to at least Proto-Gyalrongic, although it has been lost in West Gyalrongic except in these lexicalized forms.

text:
abilitative!origin grammaticalization!abilitative
Although the abilitative derivation goes back at least to the common ancestor of Japhug and Tangut, it is nevertheless likely that it derives from the sigmatic causative.

reanalysis
Although abilitative and causative derivations share little semantic commonalities, there are nevertheless potentially ambiguous sentences, where a sɯ- prefix can be interpreted either as causative or as abilitative with very similar meaning, differing only in perspective. These ambiguous clauses may have been the pivot constructions allowing a reanalysis from causative to abilitative.

The main ambiguous construction between causative and abilitative occurs with the presentive meaning of the sigmatic causative in negative form (§ sec:sig.caus.negation ). For instance, in example ( ex:mAkAsWrqoR ), the verb sɯ-rqoʁ (from rqoʁhug) can be analyzed as an abilitative `be able to hug'.

exe

tɯrme laʁnɯlaχsɯm kɯnɤ mɤ-kɤ-sɯ-rqoʁ kɯ-fse kɯ-jpum ɲɯ-βze cʰa \\
people two.or.three also neg - inf - abil -hug sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp -be.thick ipfv -grow can:fact \\
`[The fir] can grow so thick that two or three people cannot hug [its trunk].' (08-tWrgi)
0003464#S6
exe

However, it is also possible to construe the meaning in a different way: `The fir can grow so thick that it prevents even two or three people from hugging (its trunk)', with a causative interpretation. This interpretation is possible due to the ambiguity of the scope of the negation of the causative, which generates the preventive meaning `prevent, hinder' in negative forms (§ sec:sig.caus.negation ), from which a modal meaning `not able to' can be derived, with the causee reanalyzed as the transitive subject of the sɯ- prefixed verb. The reanalysis of the causee as transitive subject is made possible in non-finite clauses by the fact that the causer can optionally take the ergative (§ sec:ditransitive.causative ) and that with the additive focus marker kɯnɤalso, even the ergative cannot surface anyway (§ sec:kWnA ), so that the surface ambiguity between causee and causer can only be resolved by person indexation.

This hypothesis is made more plausible by the fact that, as discussed above, abilitative verbs almost always occur in negative form.

Another potential pivot construction between causative and abilitative is found with the instrumental use of the sigmatic causative (§ sec:sig.caus.instrumental ). In ( ex:chWtWsWtsxWB ) for instance, the sɯ- prefix is an instrumental causative (`sew with') but the context also invites an abilitative interpretation (`be able to sew').

The crucial evidence is that some clauses with the sɯ- prefix are ambiguous between causative and abilitative readings, especially in negative presentive constructions where the causative can yield a preventive meaning, and in instrumental causatives where an abilitative interpretation is also possible.

text:
distributed action reduplication!distributed action
The distributed action derivation has a double morphological exponence, combining a prefix nɤ- with the partially reduplicated stem of the base verb. Partial reduplication applies to the last syllable of the stem if polysyllabic (§ sec:partial.redp ), and the replicant takes the vowel -ɯ by default, except in a few cases studied in § sec.distributed.action.l and § sec.distributed.action.oR. The distributed action derivation is not compatible with verbs that already have reduplicated forms or a nɤ- or nɯ- prefix. For instance, nɯqambɯmbjomfly lacks a distributed action form; to express this meaning, a serial verb construction (§ sec:svc.manner.other ) with the distributed action derivation nɤɕɯɕego around (from the motion verb ɕego) is used instead, as in ( ex:junWqambWmbjomndZi.junACWCendZi ).

exe

3sg. poss -wing pl ifr -attach- pl lnk lnk king dem comit everywhere ipfv -fly- du lnk ipfv - distr:go- du pl ifr -be.possible sens -be \\
`They attached wings on her back, and she became able to fly around everywhere with the king.' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh)

This derivation is found with both intransitive and transitive verbs, as shown by the examples in tab:distributed.action, and does not affect valency. It expresses a repeated action, often (with the base verb has a motional meaning) with aimless motion, distributed spatially and/or temporally. It is semantically very close to the Chinese construction X来X去 X lái X qù, and distributed action derivation can often be translated by this construction: for instance nɤrɟɯrɟɯɣrun around closely corresponds to Chinese 跑来跑去 pǎo lái pǎo qù.

The distributed action derivation preserves stem alternation (§ sec:stem2 ). The verb nɤtɯtitell around has the stem II -nɤtɯtɯt as expected from the base verb tisay (stem II -tɯt ), and nɤɕɯɕego around has the stem II anɤrɯri with a prefixed a- like the stem II -ari of the base verb ɕego.

The distributed action derivation can be semantically very close to the repetition of the verb with the additive linker nɤ, and both often occur in the same contexts. In the case of motion verbs, repetition with alternation between the eastwards and westwards orientations (§ sec:centripetal.centrifugal ) has the same `goal-less action' function as the distribution action derivation. For instance, the meaning of example ( ex:korJWG.nA.YArJWG ) could be expressed with the verb nɤrɟɯrɟɯɣrun around.

The former generally expresses the absence of a specific goal as in ( ex:junACWCe.mWpjAjAG ), and often co-occurs with the adverb aʁɤndɯndɤteverywhere (see ex:junWqambWmbjomndZi.junACWCendZi above). The distributed action verb nɤɕɯɕe is only compatible with the unspecified orientation prefixes, and cannot occur with any of the other six orientations (§ sec:tridimensional.preverb ).

summary:
The distributed action derivation is formed by a prefix nɤ- plus partial reduplication of the verb stem, usually with -ɯ in the reduplicant, and it is incompatible with verbs that already have reduplicated forms or nɤ-/nɯ- prefixes. It applies to both transitive and intransitive verbs without changing valency, and it typically conveys repeated, distributed, or aimless action in space and/or time, often especially with motion verbs.  

The derivation preserves stem alternations and is semantically close to verb repetition with the additive linker nɤ, though with motion verbs it usually indicates lack of a specific goal rather than continuous movement in one direction. With oriented verbs it expresses turning or directing oneself toward all directions, and with speech verbs it means repeated speaking to many people, often at different places.

text:
However, nɤtɯti can also have a temporally protracted action meaning `speak for an (overly) long time' without the implication of more than one recipient, as in ( ex:kAnWsWGndzita ), a sentence describing the plight of an informant assailed with questions by a linguist.

exe

kɤ-nɤtɯti kɯ a-rqo ʑo kɤ-nɯ-sɯɣ-ndzi-t-a \\
ifr - distr:say erg 1sg. poss -throat emph aor - auto - caus -be.hoarse- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`My voice has become hoarse (I have made my voiced become hoarse) because of speaking again and again.' (elicited)
exe

With the verb tsʰɤttry, the distributed action derivation nɤtsʰɯtsʰɤt `test/try again and again' expresses repetition, as in ( ex:CtonAtshWtshAt ) with first syllable reduplication indicating iterative coincidence (§ sec:iterative.coincidence ).

`He has gone and tested the girl again and again, and each time he tested her, she answered correctly with ease.' (2005 tAwa kWcqraR)

Stative verbs, including adjectives, are usually incompatible with the distributed action derivation. The resulting form would be formally identical to the tropative (§ sec:tropative ) with emphatic reduplication (§ sec:emph.redp ). The only adjective with such a derivation is sɲube mad (from སྨྱོ་smʲobe crazy), which yields nɤsɲɯɲu `be a little crazy, do crazy things (intermittently)', attested in ( ex:pjWnAsYWsYu ).
In this translated example, the form pjɯ-nɤsɲɯsɲu corresponds to Chinese 疯疯癫癫 fēngfēngdiāndiāna little mad in the original. However, it seems that the derivation turns the stative verb into a dynamic one.

exe

pjɯ-nɤsɲɯsɲu ntsɯ pjɤ-ɕti tɕe \\
ipfv - distr:be.mad always ifr. ipfv -be. aff: fact lnk \\
`He always did [all sorts of] crazy things.' (150829 jidian-zh) 0006338#S12
exe

The distributed action derivation also has the sense of `do $X$ in disorderly fashion': the form nɤfsɯfse (from the similative verb fsebe like) can be interpreted as `act foolishly', as in ( ex:YWtWnAfsWfse ). From this use, nɤfsɯfse has developed the extended meaning `be pretentious', like that of the auto-evaluative derivation (§ sec:autoevaluative ).

what sens -2-make[II] be: fact what sens -2- distr:be.like sens -be lnk filler imp -flee lnk \\

In addition to regular distributed action verbs, there is one example with the prefix rɤ-: rɤβʑɯβʑarcut into many pieces from βʑarcut.
summary: The distributed action derivation can express not only actions done to multiple recipients, but also temporally protracted repeated action, as in nɤtɯti meaning ‘speak for an (overly) long time,’ and iterative repetition, as in nɤtsʰɯtsʰɤt ‘test/try again and again.’ It is usually incompatible with stative verbs, but one adjective-derived example nɤsɲɯɲu ‘be a little crazy, do crazy things intermittently’ suggests that the derivation can make a stative verb dynamic. The derivation can also mean ‘do X in a disorderly fashion’ and develop the extended sense ‘be pretentious,’ and there is one example of a similar form with the prefix rɤ-, rɤβʑɯβʑar ‘cut into many pieces.’

text:
A certain number of verbs have a forms that is similar to a distributed action derivation, combining a nɤ- prefix with partial reduplication of the stem, but have no corresponding base verb with exactly the same stem. The intransitive nɤrɯralook around is a particularly good candidate to be analyzed as a fossilized derivation of this type, as its meaning exactly fits that of a distributed action form of a verb meaning `look'. It might be an irregular derivation from rulook at (§ sec:orienting.verbs ), with unexplained vowel alternation (note that the expected $ $ nɤrɯru does not exist). Khroskyabs and Western Gyalrongic in general have -a reduplication, but since proto-Gyalrong *-a is fronted in Khroskyabs, this Japhug pattern cannot be directly cognate.

The transitive verbs nɤkʰɯkʰrɯtdrag along, nɤɕɯɕidrag along and nɤmɯmastroke The verb nɤmɯmastroke is homophonous with the emphatic reduplicated form of the transitive verb nɤmado. are possible candidates for being analyzed as lexicalized distributed action verbs. The verb nɤɕɯɕi might be related to rɤɕipull, but for the other two no known root exist in the language, and if verbs such as *kʰrɯt and *ma did exist at an earlier stage, they have been lost at least in the Kamnyu dialect. Note however that nɤɕɯɕi and nɤkʰɯkʰrɯt `drag along' are orientable manipulation verbs (§ sec:manipulation.verbs ), and express an action occurring in one specific direction, as in ( ex:lunAkhWkhrWta ); if these verbs are indeed ancient distributed action derivations, this derivation possibly has the sense of `protracted action' (as in ex:kAnWsWGndzita above) rather than distributed action in the proper sense.

`I am going up there first, dragging this staff$_i$ [of mine] along, come after me and follow its$_i$ trace.' (2005 Kunbzang)

The intransitive verb nɤpʰɯpʰɯbeg could superficially seem to be a lexicalized distributed action verb, but it is better to analyze it as a denominal verb (§ sec:denom.nW ) from the inalienable noun ɯ-pʰɯpʰɯalms, which selects the person receiving the alms (rather than the one giving them) as possessor, as shown by ( ex:nAphWphW.kAGWt ) (see also § sec:biactantial.ipn ).

The verb nɤstɯstucause trouble to ( ex:nWkWnAstWstu ) is formally the distributed action derivation from the verb of similative studo like (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ), with a synchronically unpredictable meaning.

exe

ʑara-stɯsti tɕe nɯ-kɯ-nɤstɯstu maŋe, \\
3pl -alone lnk 3pl. poss - sbj: pcp -cause.trouble not.exist: sens \\
`When alone [without their young], [the wild yaks] have no [predators].' (20-RmbroN) 0003560#S47

summary: Several Japhug verbs have the shape of a distributed action derivation, with an nɤ- prefix and stem reduplication, even though no matching base verb is synchronically attested. The best candidate is intransitive nɤrɯralook around, which fits the meaning of a distributed action form of ‘look,’ while transitive nɤkʰɯkʰrɯt, nɤɕɯɕi, and nɤmɯma may be lexicalized distributed-action verbs, though some may instead reflect a sense of protracted action or have lost base forms. Other items discussed are nɤpʰɯpʰɯ, better analyzed as a denominal verb from ‘alms,’ and nɤstɯstu, which is formally a distributed-action derivative but has a synchronically unpredictable meaning ‘cause trouble to.’

text:
reduplication!irregular irregularity!reduplication
Partial reduplication with Cɯ- replicant (§ sec:partial.redp ) is not the only way of forming distributed action verbs. Suffixal reduplication in -lV (§ sec.distributed.action.l ) and prefixal reduplication in Coʁ- and Cɯm- (§ sec.distributed.action.oR ) are also attested.

Replicant in -lV
The verbs in tab:distributed.action.l take a suffixed syllable -le or -lu ( nɤmɲowatch nɤ-mɲo-l e ), or a syllable in lV whose rhyme replicates that of the verb stem ( mbɣaʁturn over nɤ-mbɣ aʁ -l aʁ ). This exceptional example of rhyme reduplication in Japhug has important consequences for phonological analysis (§ sec:W.i.closed.syllables ). A similar type of reduplication is observed in pattern IV ideophones (§ sec:ideo.IV ).

Apart from ɕarsearch, which has two alternative distributed action derivations nɤɕɯɕar and nɤɕarlar (both `search around, search in all directions'), the other verbs only occur with -lV replicant variant. The verb mtɕɯrturn has two variants nɤmtɕɯrlɯr and nɤmtɕɯrlu.

With the labile verb nɤmɲowatch, this derivation has an antipassivizing effect, since the derived verb nɤmɲolewatch the scenery is strictly intransitive.

This derivation can be applied to both the base verbs tʂaβcause to fall/rolland pɣaʁturn over and their anticausatives ndʐaβfall/roll and mbɣaʁturn over, respectively.

Replicant in Coʁ- or Cɯm-
A handful distributed action verbs take a replicant other than the regular -ɯ. The transitive verb mpʰɯrwrap yields nɤmpʰoʁmpʰɯr `preserve (something fragile) by wrapping under several layers' with -Coʁ- reduplicant (this rare type of reduplication is also attested in some passive forms, § passive.redp ).

The intransitive verb nɤʁaʁhave a good time has the derived form nɤʁɯmʁaʁ `play around' with -Cɯm- replicant, the only example of this type of reduplication in Japhug.
summary: Distributed action verbs in Japhug are formed not only by partial Cɯ- reduplication, but also by suffixal reduplication in -lV and by rarer prefixal patterns Coʁ- and Cɯm-. The -lV pattern usually appears as -le or -lu, or as an lV syllable whose rhyme copies the stem, and it can have an antipassivizing effect; it occurs with both base verbs and their anticausative counterparts. A few verbs show exceptional Coʁ- or Cɯm- replicants, including one example of each type.

text:
The distributed action derivation is not attested on verbs with prefixal derivations, including the sigmatic causative. However, the -lV variant (§ sec.distributed.action.l ) is found with a handful of anticausativized verbs (§ sec:anticausative.other.derivations ).

Further derivations on distributed action verbs are verb rare. The verb nɤmɲolewatch the scenery for instance can be causativized with the sigmatic prefix z, as in ( ex:chAznAmYole ).

exe

kɤntɕʰaʁ ra cʰɤ-z-nɤmɲole \\
street pl ifr - caus - distr:watch \\
`He [took] him to do sightseeing in the city.' (140511 alading-zh) 0003953#S53
exe
summary: Distributed action derivation is not attested on verbs that have prefixal derivations, including the sigmatic causative, though the -lV form does occur with a few anticausativized verbs. Additional derivation on distributed action verbs is very rare, but at least one example shows that the verb nɤmɲole ‘watch the scenery’ can still be causativized with the sigmatic prefix z.

text:
auto-evaluative reflexive!auto-evaluative tropative!auto-evaluative
Like the distributed action derivation (§ sec:distributed.action ), the auto-evaluative derivation has a double exponence: the prefix znɤ- and verb stem partial reduplication. It takes a stative intransitive verb as input, and derives an intransitive verb meaning `think of oneself as $X$, pretend to be $X$'(where $X$ stands for the meaning of the base verb, always expressing a positive characteristic), as in tab:autoevaluative. Although similar to reflexivized tropatives (§ sec:tropative ), auto-evaluative verbs have a derogatory meaning and imply pretentiousness and vanity or bragging.

When the base verb already has an auto-evaluative meaning ( χpabe proud), the auto-evaluative derivation only adds the derogatory nuance ( znɤχpɯχpabe arrogant).

The verb znɤjpɯjpebe full of oneself (from pebe good) has an irregular form with an inserted -j- element (the expected form would be $ $ znɤpɯpe ), and its meaning is slightly lexicalized `be full of oneself' (from `think of oneself as good').

exe

nɯ-rɟɤlpu nɯ kɯ nɯra, maka, ɯʑo tɤ-kɤ-fstɤt ɣɯ ɯ-rju nɯra pjɤ-mtsʰɤm tɕe, mɤʑɯ ʑo to-znɤjpɯjpe. \\
3pl. poss -king dem erg dem: pl at.all 3sg aor - obj: pcp -flatter gen 3sg. poss -word dem: pl ifr -hear lnk even.more emph ifr -be.full.of.oneself \\
`Hearing these words of praise, the king became even more full of himself than before.' (150830 afanti-zh) 0006380#S89
exe

Other examples of lexicalized auto-evaluative verbs include znɤlɯliplay the coquette (from libe spoiled) and znɤŋɯŋube arrogant, a verb built from the root of the copula ŋube, whose original meaning was `be right' (§ sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ).
summary:
The auto-evaluative derivation uses double exponence, with the prefix znɤ- and partial reduplication of the verb stem. It applies to stative intransitive verbs to form intransitives meaning ‘think of oneself as X’ or ‘pretend to be X,’ where X is a positive trait, but the derived verbs carry a derogatory sense of pretentiousness, vanity, or bragging.  

If the base already has an auto-evaluative meaning, the derivation only adds the derogatory nuance, and some forms are irregular or lexicalized, such as znɤjpɯjpebe ‘be full of oneself.’ Other lexicalized examples include znɤlɯliplay the coquette and znɤŋɯŋube ‘arrogant.’

text:
reduplication!attenuative
In verbal derivation, reduplication occurs to express reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ), distributed action (§ sec:distributed.action ) and emphasis (§ sec:emph.redp ). Combination of a- prefix with partial reduplication of the last syllable of the stem is also found with an attenuative meaning in a few stative verbs of colour ( tab:attenuative ). Note that the replicated syllables takes the vowel ɤ instead of ɯ in a-ɣɤ ɣrum `be whitish' and a-pɤ pɣi `be greyish', and the absence of w in a-ɣɤ ɣrum (on the cluster wxt, see § sec:wC.clusters ).

Since the base verbs in tab:attenuative can also be subjected to emphatic reduplication, we find minimal pairs like and a-ɣrɤ ɣrum `be whitish' and a-qarŋɯ rŋe `be yellowish' ( ex:aqarNWrNe ) vs. wɣrɯ wɣrum `be very white' ( ex:kWwGrWwGrum ) and qarŋɯ rŋe `be very yellow' ( ex:kWqarNWrNe ), respectively (§ sec:emph.redp ).

exe

ɯ-mɯntoʁ nɯra aɣrɤɣrum ɯ-ŋgɯz kɯnɤ aqarŋɯrŋe kɯ-fse \\
3sg. poss -flower dem: pl be.whitish: fact 3sg. poss -inside: loc also be.yellowish: fact sbj: pcp -be.like \\
`Its flower is whitish, with a taint of yellowish.' (`it is like yellowish inside the whitish colour') (16-CWrNgo) 0003518#S195
exe

exe

tɕeri qro nɯnɯ wuma ʑo wɣrum, kɯ-wɣrɯ wɣrum ʑo ŋu. \\
lnk pigeon dem really emph be.white: fact sbj: pcp - emph be.white emph be: fact \\
`The pigeon is very white.' (24-qro) 0003626#S3
exe

exe

ɯ-mɯntoʁ rca wuma ʑo mpɕɤr tɕe kɯ-qarŋɯ rŋe ʑo ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -flower unexp: deg really emph be.beautiful: fact lnk sbj: pcp - emph be.yellow emph be: fact \\
`Its flower is very beautiful, it is very yellow.' (15-babW) 0003512#S101
exe
summary: Reduplication in verbal derivation is used to express reciprocal, distributed action, and emphasis. In a few stative color verbs, the prefix **a-** combines with partial reduplication of the final syllable to give an attenuative meaning such as “whitish” or “greyish,” and these forms can contrast with emphatic reduplication forms meaning “very white” or “very yellow.”

text:
Volitional mɯ- prefix
volitionality!derivation
The intransitive dynamic verb mɯnmumove contains a prefix mɯ, as shown by the existence of the bare root nmu in the verb nmushake (of earthquakes), which is only found in collocation with the noun waɟɯearthquake ( ex:waJW.YAnmu ).

exe

waɟɯ ɲɤ-nmu \\
earthquake ifr -shake \\
`There was an earthquake.' (elicited)
exe

The Limbu labile verb |munt| `move' is probably cognate to the Japhug root (, see also § sec:historical.phono on the absence of coda in Japhug), and since mɯnmu means `move' in general (for both animate and inanimate beings), the restriction of the base verb nmu to earthquakes specifically cannot be an archaism. Rather, the ancestor of the base verb nmu must have had a more general meaning `move' when the proto-form from which mɯnmu originates was derived from it. The exact meaning of the ancestor of nmu, and the function of the mɯ- prefix in this verb are uncertain, but the following scenario can be proposed: the n- element in nmu could be a frozen allomorph of the autive (§ sec:autobenefactive ), and the original meaning of nmu could have been `move (spontaneously, without external agency)', and the derived form mɯnmu would thus have had the meaning `move (voluntarily)': in Japhug, this verb can refer to volitional actions, and it is used for instance with the imperative and prohibitive (for instance in ex:manWtWmWnmu ).

exe

ma-nɯ-tɯ-mɯnmu ma mɤ-pʰɤn \\
neg - imp -2-move lnk neg -be.efficient: fact \\
`Don't move, otherwise it won't work!' (2002 qala)
exe

In this interpretation, the original function of the mɯ- in this example would be deriving a volitional verb out of a non-volitional one (itself rendered non-volitional by the autobenefactive prefix).

In other Gyalrong languages, only cognates of the derived verb mɯnmu are attested. The Bragbar Situ form vərmô `bouger' suggests that mɯ- originates from *wə- with regressive nasalization from the last syllable. This invalidates a possible comparison with the volitional *m- prefix reconstructed by in Old Chinese.

Applicative -t suffix
applicative!suffix
Beside the productive prefixal nɯ- applicative (§ sec:applicative ), Japhug has vestigial traces of a -t applicative suffix, better attested in Kiranti and West Himalayish languages (see, and for comparative studies of this suffix). Only two examples of this derivation exist in Japhug: ɣɯtbring and mdɯtbe resolved to, be determined to. More examples of -t applicative are found in Situ, though all involving verbs of motion.

The verb of manipulation ɣɯtbring derives from the motion verb ɣicome; the vowel alternation is regular as pre-Japhug *i changes to ɯ in closed syllables. With a motion verb such as `come', the effect of the applicative ( ex:bring1 ) is similar to a causative ( ex:bring2 ).

exe

`come with X' $ $ `bring'

`cause X to come' $ $ `bring'
exe

The transitive verb mdɯtbe resolved to, be determined to is historically related to the verb mdɯlive up to, and constitutes another example of the -t applicative, though it is less immediately obvious than in the case of ɣɯtbring because each of the verbs has undergone semantic specialization after the derivation took place.

The verb mdɯ is semi-transitive (§ sec:semi.transitive ), and takes as its semi-object the lifespan; it can be applied to plants, animals and humans, as shown by examples ( ex:chWmdW ) and ( ex:chWmdWa ). It selects the downstream series of directional prefixes (§ sec:vertical.preverbs.time ).

exe

tɕe nɯŋa ɯʑo nɯnɯ, sqamŋu-xpa jamar cʰɯ-mdɯ ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl\\
lnk cow 3sg dem fifteen-year about ipfv -live.up.to sens -be.usually.the.case \\
`A cow can live up to fifteen years.' (05-qaZo)
0003404#S127
exe

exe

``nɤʑo nɯ kʰrɯtsu-xpa a-tʰɯ-tɯ-mdɯ ra nɤ" to-ti ɲɯ-ŋu. tɕe ``aʑo kɯnɤ kʰrɯtsu cʰondɤre tɯ-rʑaʁ nɯnɯ cʰɯ-mdɯ-a ra" to-ti \\
2sg dem ten.thousand-year irr - pfv -2-live.up.to be.needed: fact sfp ifr -say sens -be lnk 1sg also ten.thousand-year comit one-day dem ipfv -live.up.to- 1sg be.needed: fact ifr -say \\
`He said: `May you live ten thousand years! I want to live one thousand years and one more day.' (150830 afanti-zh)
0006380#S64
exe

The meaning `live until/up to' is however a semantic innovation in Japhug: its Situ cognate mdə́ means `reach' as a motion verb. Japhug has restricted the meaning of this verb to a very specific context.

The verb mdɯtbe resolved to, be determined to is morphologically transitive, and can take as its object an infinitive complement as in ( ex:chWmdWta ). It shares with mdɯlive up to the downstream directional prefixes ( cʰɯ- ).

exe

aʑo kɯrɯ-skɤt kɤ-βzjoz nɯ cʰɯ-mdɯt-a ʑo ɕti \\
1sg Tibetan-language inf -learn dem ipfv -be.determined emph be. aff: fact \\
`I am determined to learn Tibetan/Gyalrong.' (elicited)
exe

The precise meaning of mdɯt is to be determined to do something that one has confidence they can realize. If one accepts the idea that the original meaning of Japhug mdɯlive up to was `reach' as in Situ, the meaning `be determined to' of the verb mdɯt has the same relationship to that of the base verb as English `reach for' (`reach for the stars') to the verb `reach', with a conative interpretation `try/strive to reach'. The addition of the suffix -t turns the semi-transitive (morphologically intransitive) mdɯ into a transitive verb whose A corresponds to the S of the base verb. This applicative derivation from a semi-transitive verb is not unique in Japhug; the transitive verb nɯrgalike from the verb rgalike with the nɯ- applicative is another similar example (§ sec:applicative ).

Antipassive -t suffix
antipassive!suffix
The semi-transitive verb βɟɤtobtain,
as proposed by, is related to the orientable manipulation verb mɟa `take (from)', a meaning illustrated by example ( ex:tonWmJa ). The two verbs differ by vowel alternation, -t suffixation and preninital nasalization.

exe
summary:
The passage argues that Japhug **mɯnmu** ‘move’ likely contains a volitional prefix **mɯ-**, because the bare root **nmu** survives only in the restricted earthquake verb, suggesting the older root had a more general meaning ‘move’ and that **mɯ-** derived a volitional from a non-volitional verb. It also notes that the prefix’s exact origin is uncertain and that comparative evidence from other Gyalrong languages points to a different historical source, not a Proto-Old Chinese **\*m-** prefix.

The passage then describes vestigial traces of an applicative **-t** suffix in Japhug, seen in forms like **ɣɯt** ‘bring’ from ‘come’ and **mdɯt** ‘be determined to,’ with the suffix turning a semi-transitive verb into a transitive one. Finally, it mentions an antipassive **-t**

nɯnɯra ɣɯ nɯ-rte nɯ ci ɯ-qʰu ci ʑo to-nɯ-mɟa. to-nɯ-mɟa qʰe jo-tsɯm qʰe ɯ-pi ra tɯkaka nɯ-ku ɯ-taʁ pjɤ-ta. \\
dem. pl gen 3pl. poss -hat dem one 3sg. poss -after one emph ifr: up - auto -take ifr: up - auto -take lnk ifr -take.away lnk 3sg. poss -elder.sibling pl each 3pl. poss -head 3sg. poss -on ifr: down -put \\
`He took their crowns one after the other and put them on the heads of each of his brothers.' (160705 poucet5-v2)

The transitive verb mɟa can also mean `get, obtain' when used with the downwards orientation, as in ( ex:pjWGmJa.ma.mWpWkWcha ) (§ sec:preverb.gain ). Apart from Tshobdun mɟê, cognates in other Gyalrongic languages (such as Zbu vɟéʔ ) lack a nasal preinitial, suggesting that the Japhug and Tshobdun forms result from fusion with the autive prefix (§ sec:autobenefactive, ). This constitutes an interesting exclusive common innovation shared by Japhug and Tshobdun.

`Working a complete day, I could only get two cents of labour points, as I was young.' (2010-09)

The verb βɟɤt, meaning `obtain' (something that everyone is looking for) is semi-transitive (§ sec:semi.transitive ), optionally taking a semi-object or a complement clause as in ( ex:mWpjABJAt ) and ( ex:mWpWkABJAt ), but conjugated intransitively, as shown by the Aorist pɯ-βɟɤt ( aor -obtain) `he got (it)' (with a A-type preverb, § sec:transitivity.morphology ).

exe

kɤ-ndza maka mɯ-pjɤ-βɟɤt. \\
inf -eat at.all neg - ifr: down -obtain \\
`He did not obtain anything to eat.' (qajdoskAt 2002) 0003366#S104

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ stu kɯ-wxti nɯnɯ kɯ [nɯnɯ tɕʰeme nɯ mɯ-pɯ-kɤ-βɟɤt] nɯ wuma ʑo pjɤ-nɤ-sɤɣdɯɣ \\

`The elder boy was upset that he did not get the girl.' (140513 shenqi de feitan-zh) 0003981#S209

The verb βɟɤtobtain is not synchronically derived from mɟatake: both verbs come from an etymon reflected by Zbu vɟéʔ `prendre, obtenir, enlever' whose expected Japhug form would be * βɟa. Based on the comparative evidence in, this lost verb was transitive and had the same argument structure as Japhug mɟa.

Hence, the -t suffix in βɟɤtobtain used to remove morphological transitivity, turning the transitive subject into a intransitive subject, and the and the object into an (optional) semi-object. Given the fact that some -t codas in Japhug originate from earlier * -s (§ sec:suffixes ), it is possible that this -t suffix is related to the reflexive/middle suffix attested in Kiranti, Nungish and West-Himalayish (reflected for instance by Khaling -si, ), which has antipassive functions in many languages, including possibly Old Chinese.
summary: The passage explains that Japhug **mɟa** can mean “take” and, with downward orientation, also “get/obtain,” and it notes a cognate relationship with Tshobdun suggesting a shared innovation involving fusion with the autive prefix. It further describes **βɟɤt** as a semi-transitive verb meaning “obtain,” which is conjugated intransitively, and argues that it is not synchronically derived from **mɟa** but reflects an older transitive etymon whose transitivity was later reduced by a **-t** suffix.

The transitive verb tʰuask (with indirective alignment, § sec:ditransitive.indirective ), in addition to the regular antipassives rɤtʰuask questions and sɤtʰuask in marriage (§ sec:antipassive.function ), has two isolated intransitive derived forms: rɤmɯtʰuask around and ɕɯmtʰuask a lot of questions ( ex:nAtWCWmthu ), from which the compound ɕɯmtʰuspoʁchild who likes to ask a lot of question is derived (with spoʁhave a hole as second element).

`You really [like to] ask a lot of questions!' (elicited)
exe

It is possible that the -m(ɯ)- element in these complex prefixes is historically related to the amɯ- reciprocal and distributed property prefixes (§ sec:amW.reciprocal, § sec:distributed.amW ).

rɤ- prefix
Some verbs have rɤ- prefixes that can neither be analyzed as antipassive (§ sec:antipassive.rA ) nor as denominal (§ sec:denom.rA ) derivations, at least synchronically, and whose function is not clearly identifiable.

The verbs rɤwumtidy up and rɤtsʰɤttry are clearly derived from wumgather and tsʰɤttry, respectively. However, they cannot be analyzed as antipassives, since they are morphologically transitive like their base verbs.

The verb rɤwum can mean `tidy up' as in ( ex:nWkha.ra.turAwum ), taking as object a place (house or room) or `collect (and put in order)' as in ( ex:nWkAmbi.torAwum ).

exe

tɤɕime nɯ kɯ kʰa ku-rɤʑi tɕe, nɯ-ndzɤtsʰi ra tu-βze, nɯ-kʰa ra tu-rɤwum pjɤ-ŋu \\
girl dem erg house ipfv -stay lnk 3pl. poss -food pl ipfv -make[III] 3pl. poss -house pl ipfv -tidy.up ifr. ipfv -be \\
(140504 baixuegongzhu-zh)
0003907#S97

rgɤtpu nɯ kɯ nɯra rŋɯl nɯ-kɤ-mbi cʰo laχtɕʰa nɯ-kɤ-mbi nɯra to-rɤwum qʰe, \\
old.man dem erg dem: pl silver aor - obj: pcp -give comit thing aor - obj: pcp -give dem: pl ifr -collect lnk \\
The old man collected the money and the things that [the people] had given [them].' (150906 toutao-zh)

These meanings can also be conveyed by the base verb wumgather, as in ( ex:kAwum.taqurnW ). However, wum has a much wider range of meaning, including `fold, close' (of umbrellas, wings, see ex:YWqAt.nA.kuwum, § sec:centripetal.centrifugal ) and `take as (disciple)' ( ex:naslama.kukWwuma, § sec:essive.abs ). The derived verb rɤwum thus has a more specific and restricted use than its base verb.

dem erg 3sg. poss -apple pl inf -gather aor:3 -help- pl lnk \\

The meaning difference between rɤtsʰɤttry and tsʰɤttry is more difficult to ascertain, as both verbs can occur with a nominal object as in ( ex:tarAtshAt ). In the corpus, when the derived verb rɤtsʰɤt has an overt object, it is always however a complement clause, and it can have the sense of `compare' as in ( ex:CWrAtshAttCi ).

The intransitive verb rɤmpɕɤrmake up ( ex:pjAraXtCinW.torAmpCArnW ) is derived from the stative verb mpɕɤrbe beautiful.

It has the emphatic reduplicated form rɤmpɕoʁ mpɕɤr with a rare -oʁ replicated syllable, and often occurs in the causative form zrɤmpɕɤr `help $X$ making up' or `make up/dress up using', as in ( ex:tukWzrAmpCAr ).

This use of the rɤ- prefix could be analyzed as a quasi-reflexive `make oneself beautiful', reminiscent of the case of the antipassive raχtɕiwash (vi) (see ex:pjAraXtCinW.torAmpCArnW and § sec:antipassive.reflexive ), though it cannot be analyzed as an antipassive or a reflexive since the base verb is intransitive.

The transitive verb rɤɣrɯɣcherish comes from the intransitive rɯɣbe precious with a tropative meaning (`consider to be precious', § sec:tropative.other.construction ). The derivational prefix here rɤɣ, with an intrusive velar fricative (on which see § sec:caus.sWG and the references therein).

ɣɯ-/ɣɤ- prefix
A few verbs have ɣɯ- or ɣɤ- prefixes that can neither be analyzed as facilitative ɣɤ- (§ sec:facilitative.GA ), as causative (§ sec:velar.causative ), as denominal (§ sec:denom.tr.GA ) nor as deideophonic derivations (§ sec:voice.deideophonic ).

First, the transitive verb ɣɤtɕɤtselect from, more specifically `choose/select (someone) from a group of people' (in particular, as a leader), This verb has a Tshobdun cognate wɐtʃet $_II$ `select', and this derivation thus goes back at least to their common ancestor.
is derived from tɕɤttake out. It selects as object the person that is chosen, and also takes an essive adjunct (§ sec:essive.abs ) describing the office/position of the chosen person. In example ( ex:nWNgumdZWG.taGAtCAtnW ), the verb ɣɤtɕɤt occurs in a finite relative clause (§ sec:finite.relatives ) whose relativized element is the object. The noun nɯ-ŋgumdʑɯɣ `their leader' inside the relative is the essive adjunct.

exe
summary: The passage describes several irregular verb derivations in which prefixes create specialized meanings that are not synchronically analyzable as standard antipassives or denominal forms. It notes that tʰuask has isolated intransitive forms with rɤ- and ɕɯm- prefixes, while other rɤ- verbs such as rɤwum, rɤtsʰɤt, and rɤmpɕɤr show restricted or shifted meanings relative to their bases, sometimes with possible historical links to other prefix types. It also mentions a few verbs with ɣɯ-/ɣɤ- prefixes, including ɣɤtɕɤt ‘select from’, whose derivation appears to be older and historically related to a cognate verb in another language.

text:
tɕe nɯ <faliedong> nɯnɯ, [nɯnɯ nɯ-ŋgumdʑɯɣ ta-ɣɤtɕɤt-nɯ] kɯ <chake> nɯ ko-sɯ-βraʁ. \\
lnk dem anthr dem dem 3pl. poss -leader aor:3 3-choose- pl erg anthr dem ifr - caus -attach \\
`Feridun, the one they had chosen as their leader, had Zohak attached.' (140514 xiee de shewang-zh)
0003994#S99
exe

Its reflexive form ʑɣɤɣɤtɕɤtvolunteer (to go and go something) has a meaning that is not completely predictable from that of the base verb.

Second, ɣɤlɤtlock is related to lɤtrelease, which can mean `lock' when occurring in collocation with the noun sɤcɯkey ( ex:sAcW.malAt2, § sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle, § sec:passive ).

Third, the verb of perception ɣɯχsɤlrealize (§ sec:tso.sWXsAl ) originates from χsɤlbe clear (itself from གསལ་gsalclear), with a quasi-tropative meaning `clearly perceive that $X$'.

It is possible that these three transitive verbs originally were denominal verbs from deverbal nouns such as the bare action nominals (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ), but there is no evidence for the putative nouns from which these verbs could have been derived.

a- prefix
In addition to the passive a- prefix (§ sec:passive ), the reduplicated reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ) and the denominal stative a- (§ sec:denom.a ) derivations, we find examples of a- prefixes with unidentified function in the following examples.

The stative verb amtɕoʁbe pointy appears to be derived from mtɕoʁbe sharp. Both are stative verbs, and are obviously close semantically (both can take for instance mbrɯtɕɯknife as intransitive subject, as in ex:mWjsphWt, § sec:abilitative.lexicalized ).

The verb acʰɤtbe $X$ years apart is either plain intransitive, taking the number of years as subject ( ex:kWmNupArme.achAt ), or semi-transitive, selecting the years as semi-object ( ex:kWmNupArme.achAttCi ) (see also ex:RnWpArme.machAti, § sec:raNri ).

exe

xlist

tɕiʑo tɕi-pɤrtʰɤβ kɯmŋu-pɤrme acʰɤt \\
1du 1du. poss -between five-years differ.in.age: fact \\

tɕiʑo kɯmŋu-pɤrme acʰɤt-tɕi \\
1du five-years differ.in.age: fact - 1du \\
`We have a five year difference.' (elicited)
xlist

It could potentially be analyzed as a denominal verb in a- (§ sec:denom.a ) from a lost noun *cʰɤt borrowed from Tibetan ཁྱད་kʰʲɤtdifference. While the Tibetan origin of the root is beyond doubt, it is also possible that this verb is derived by the a- prefix from the semi-transitive cʰɤtdiffer by (itself from Tibetan), which selects as semi-object not a characteristic other than age, for example the quantity of fern eaten in ( ex:chAtnW ).

`They differ in that some [eat fern] a lot or fewer, but they search a lot [of fern] every year.' (conversation 140510)

The verb cʰacan, `be able', `be fine' has two derived forms in a-: acʰɯcʰabe capable (see ex:hundred.and.eight, § sec.hundred.plus ) with reduplication acʰɤlabe capable with suffixed trtlV replicated syllable (§ sec.distributed.action.l ). The meaning of this derivation is both emphatic and antipassive-like: unlike the base verb cʰacan, which can take a complement clause as semi-object (§ sec:inf.complementation, § sec:TAM.finite ), acʰɯcʰa and acʰɤla are strictly intransitive stative verbs.

Abilitative j- prefix
abilitative
The transitive verb jqube able to lift ( ex:mAjqu ) has an intrinsically abilitative meaning. This unusual property suggests that it may be the remnant of a lexicalized abilitative verb whose base *qu `lift' was lost, and that the j- preinitial was an abilitative prefix, possibly an irregular allomorph of the sɯ- abilitative (§ sec:abilitative ), reminiscent of the j- allomorph of the sigmatic causative (§ sec:caus.j ).

exe

pɤjkʰu ɯ-ku mɤ-jqe \\
yet 3sg. poss -head neg -be.able.to.lift[III]: fact \\
`[The baby] is not yet able to lift up his head.' (elicited)
exe
summary:
The passage discusses several Tibetan-derived or possibly denominal verbs whose meanings are partly unpredictable, including cases where a verb’s reflexive or stative form has a specialized meaning. It also notes that some verbs may originally have been formed with the a- prefix, though for several of them there is no direct evidence for the source noun, and the prefix may mark stative or antipassive-like derivations.

It further describes an abilitative j- prefix in the verb jqu ‘be able to lift,’ suggesting it may preserve an older abilitative construction after the base verb was lost. Overall, the text emphasizes that these verb forms show historical derivation, semantic shift, and uncertain morphological analysis.

text:
prenasalization
In addition to the anticausative derivation (§ sec:anticausative ), prenasalization alternation is found in an isolated pair of intransitive verbs: sqlɯmcollapse (of the ground) The verb sqlɯm can for instance express the collapse of the ground under the weight of an object or person, as in ( ex:WBrAsqlWm ) in §
sec:WBrA.functions. and arɴɢlɯmbe caved in ( ex:YArNGlWm ).

exe

ɯ-tʰoʁ ɲɯ-ɤrɴɢlɯm \\
3sg. poss -ground sens -be.caved.in \\
`The ground is caved in.' (elicited)
exe

The form arɴɢlɯm derives from sqlɯm by addition of a prefix a- and prenasalization of the uvular stop q to ɴɢ. In addition, the s was rhotacized to r as result of voicing: the combination zɴɢ is only attested across syllable boundaries in Japhug, as in the plant name razɴɢu, In this word, note also that a form such as $ $ rarɴɢu would violate another phonotactic constraint (§ sec:rhotic.dissimilation ). never in an onset, and this example suggest that a sound change *sɴɢ rɴɢ took place.

The combination of prenasalization with a- in arɴɢlɯm appears to have a resultative stative meaning, as opposed to the dynamic verb sqlɯm. It is possible that the prenasalization reflects a trace of the autive prefix (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ).
summary: The passage describes an isolated alternation between two intransitive verbs, **sqlɯm** ‘collapse (of the ground)’ and **arɴɢlɯm** ‘be caved in,’ where the latter is formed with the prefix **a-** and prenasalization of the stop, along with voicing that turns **s** into **r**. The derived form has a more **resultative stative** meaning than the dynamic base verb, and the prenasalization may preserve a trace of an older autive prefix.

text:
comparative
The pair of stative verbs snabe good, be worthy and mnabe better are possibly historically related, sharing a common root -na with different prefixes s- and m- (or *w, with nasalization, § sec:causative.m, § sec:NC.clusters ) prefixes. If genuine, this etymological relationship is not synchronically obvious, and a detailed description of the synchronic meanings of these verbs is necessary.

The verb sna can either mean `be kind, be generous' as in ( ex:ataR.kusna ) (see also ex:kW.toZGApa, § sec:semi.transitive ), `be pleasant' (example ex:tuwGnAkhAzNganW, § sec:applicative.lexicalized ) or `be worthy, be fit to', as in ( ex:WkWndza.mAtWsna ) and ( ex:kAndza.mAsna ) (also ex:kWnA.mAsna, § sec:kWnA ). In the third case, it selects a semi-object, which can either be a noun or participle ( ex:WkWndza.mAtWsna ), or an infinitival complement clause ( ex:kAndza.mAsna ).

exe

rɟɤlpu ri a-taʁ wuma ku-sna, \\
king also 1sg. poss -on really prs -be.kind \\
`The king is very kind with me.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

exe

lɤ-tɕɤt ma nɤʑo a-mtɕʰot ɯ-kɯ-ndza mɤ-tɯ-sna \\
imp: upstream -take.out lnk 2sg 1sg. poss -offering 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -eat neg -2-be.worthy: fact \\
`Spit it out, you are not worthy of being the one eating my offering.' (2014 kWlAG)
exe

exe

tɯrme kɤ-ndza mɤ-sna\\
person inf -eat neg -be.fit: fact \\
`It is unfit for people to eat.' (12-Zmbroko) 0003490#S93
exe

The range of meanings of mna only partially overlaps with that of sna. First, it can `feel better, heal', taking either the disease/wound ( ex:nACqhe.WYWmna ) (see also example ex:tAkAzbGaR, § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ), or the person (or body part) afflicted by it ( ex:WYWtWmna ) as subject. Note that in ( ex:nACqhe.WYWmna ), the verb is in the 3sg form, indexation as intransitive subject the noun nɤ-ɕqʰe `your cough' rather than the 2sg, showing that this noun cannot be analyzed as an essive adjunct (§ sec:essive.abs ).

exe

nɤ-ɕqʰe ɯ-ɲɯ́-mna? \\
2sg. poss -cough qu - sens -be.better \\
`Is your cough getting better?' (many attestations)
exe

exe

ɯ-ɲɯ́-tɯ-mna \\
qu - sens -2-be.better \\
`Are you feeling better?' (smAnmi 2003.2)
exe

Second, mna occurs in comparative constructions (§ sec:comparison ) with the standard marker sɤz(nɤ) (§ sec:comparative ) or the comparee marker kɯ (§ sec:comparee.kW ), as in ( ex:sAz.WYWmna ) (see also ex:tWZo.tWmtChi, § sec:indef.genr.poss ). By contrast, sna is not attested in comparative constructions in the whole corpus.

exe

nɯfse pjɯ-kɤ-fɕɤt sɤz ɯ-ɲɯ́-mna? \\
like.that ipfv - inf -tell comp qu - sens -be.better \\
`Is it better [to explain how to weave with video] than simply by telling it like that (without video)?' (vid-20140429090403) 0003776#S161
exe

The participle kɯ-mna is lexicalized in the sense of `leader, chief' (example ex:tCaXpa.ra.GW.nWkWmna, § sec:subject.participle.possessive ).

The data above suggest that mna originally was a lexicalized comparative (`be better') of sna (`be good'), and that these two verbs have undergone distinct semantic specialization (`be better' $ $ `feel better, heal' vs. `be good' $ $ `be worthy, be fit'). The morphological structure of these verbs is however elusive: the s- element in sna is possibly related to the proprietive sɤ- (§ sec:proprietive ), but the m- prefix in mna is isolated in Japhug. It could originate from *w- with regressive nasalization from the n- of the root.
summary: The passage argues that the stative verbs **sna** ‘be good, be worthy’ and **mna** ‘be better’ may be historically related through a common root *-na* with different prefixes, though this relationship is not synchronically transparent. It describes how **sna** has meanings such as ‘be kind,’ ‘be pleasant,’ and ‘be worthy, be fit to,’ while **mna** means ‘feel better, heal’ and also appears in comparative constructions, suggesting that **mna** may originally have been a lexicalized comparative of **sna**.

text:
reduplication!derivation
Reduplication occurs as a secondary exponent of several verbal derivations, including Distributed action (§ sec:distributed.action ), Reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ), and is also found sporadically with other derivations (for instance with the antipassive, § sec:antipassive.redp ).

In addition, reduplication is also attested by itself as the only marking of a valency-changing derivation in the case of rɯruguard, which derives from the intransitive verb rulook at. The base verb ru selects a goal in the dative or with locative marking (§ sec:intr.goal, § sec:orienting.verbs ), while rɯru is transitive (as shown by stem alternation in ex:paRtshi.YWnWre ) and the entity taken care of by the subject is encoded as object.

exe

tɕe paʁtsʰi ɲɯ-rɯre pjɤ-ŋu ri, \\
lnk hogwash ipfv -take.care[III]: fact ifr. ipfv -be lnk \\
`While he was taking care of the hogwash....' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

The compound noun βɣɤrumiller includes as second element the non-reduplicated variant of the same root -ru with the same meaning as that of rɯruguard (the first element is from the noun βɣamill, see § sec:object.verb.compounds ).
summary: Reduplication serves as a secondary exponent of several verbal derivations, including Distributed action and Reciprocal, and it also appears sporadically with other derivations such as the antipassive. It can also independently mark a valency-changing derivation: the intransitive verb *ru* ‘look at’ forms transitive *rɯru* ‘take care of,’ with the cared-for entity expressed as object. The same root appears in the compound noun *βɣɤru* ‘miller’ as a non-reduplicated variant.

text:
vowel!alternation

The rare verb rndeget into trouble is only attested in the expression in ( ex:pWrndeta ). The -t- suffix shows that this verb is morphologically transitive (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ), despite being unable to take an overt object.

exe

kɤ-rndu sɤznɤ pɯ-rnde-t-a \\
inf -obtain comit aor -get.into.trouble- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I not only did not obtain anything, but in addition I got into trouble.' (elicited)
exe

The co-occurrence of rnde with rnduobtain in the expression exemplified by ( ex:pWrndeta ) is probably not only a matter of euphony, but also of morphological relationship (a figura etymologica ). The verb rnde is invariable, but its stem is identical to the stem III (§ sec:stem3.form ) of rndu as in ( ex:kro.Zo.YWrnde ).

exe

ɯʑo stɯsti ʑo tu-ɕe qʰe, tɕe kʰro ʑo ɲɯ-rnde kʰi. \\
3sg alone emph ipfv: up -go lnk lnk a.lot emph sens -obtain[III] hearsay \\
`She goes [up there in the mountain], and found a lot of mushrooms (they say).' (conversation 14-05-10)
exe

It is possible to suppose that the verb rnde is a backformation from the stem III of rnduobtain. A hypothesis of this type is likely in the case of the defective intransitive verb βzegrow which originates from βzumake (§ sec:stem3.backformation ), due to the fact that the stem βze never occurs in tenses such as the Aorist and that the verb βzumake is also used with the meaning `grow' with a dummy subject (§ sec:transitive.dummy ).

In the case of rnde however, the fact that this rare verb is mainly attested in Aorist forms, where a Stem III is not possible makes the backformation hypothesis less likely. In addition, although the meaning of rndeget into trouble is relatable to that of rnduobtain (`obtain/get problems/trouble'), it is not a simple narrowing of the meaning of rndu, a verb all of whose attestations refer to positive events (see ex:kro.Zo.YWrnde above, as well as ex:CpWrndutCi in § sec:AM.volitionality ). For the backformation hypothesis to work, one would need to suppose that at an earlier stage, rnduobtain with a non-overt object had a negative overtone `get/obtain it' `get into trouble'.

Alternatively, one could consider that rndeget into trouble originates from rnduobtain by a valency-neutral derivation. The vowel alternation could be accounted for by hypothesizing the existence of a *-j suffix (as in the case of the Stem III, § sec:stem3.form ), whose exact function is difficult to describe in the absence of other examples.
summary: The passage discusses the rare verb **rnde** ‘get into trouble,’ which is only attested in a fixed expression and is marked as morphologically transitive by the **-t-** suffix even though it cannot take an overt object. Its co-occurrence with **rndu** ‘obtain’ may reflect a morphological relationship, perhaps a backformation from Stem III of **rndu** or a valency-neutral derivation, but the backformation analysis is considered less likely because **rnde** is mainly found in Aorist forms and its meaning is not a simple narrowing of **rndu**.

text:
derivation!noun to verb denominal derivation
Denominal verbalizing derivations turn nouns into verbs. Their source can either be an inalienably or an alienably possessed noun (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ), an isolated nominal root or a compound.

These derivations are referred to simply as ``denominal'' (without specifying ``verbalizing'') in this chapter and everywhere else in the grammar, since the only non-verbalizing denominal derivations, the denominal adverbs (§ sec:denominal.adverb ), are relatively marginal.

Japhug boasts a considerable number of denominal prefixes, most of which are highly productive (in particular, they can be applied to Tibetan and even Chinese loanwords). A consequence of the existence of these derivations is that conjugated verbs in Japhug are not a closed class, unlike in otherwise morphologically rich languages of the Trans-Himalayan family such as Kiranti, In the case of Khaling, provides an exhaustive list of all primary verbs, which only contains two borrowings from (Thulung and Nepali) and only one clearly denominal verb. where light verb constructions are the only productive way of forming predicates from nouns.

In the rest of the grammar, the denominal prefixes are not distinguished from the nominal root in the glosses (the prefixes and the nominal roots are treated as a single stem). By contrast, in this chapter, the denominal prefixes are segmented and glossed as denom.

This chapter provides a detailed account of all attested denominal prefixes (sections § sec:denom.contracting to § sec:denom.nW ). It also describes non-prefixal denominal derivations (§ sec:denom.other ) and deideophonic verbalizing prefixes (§ sec:voice.deideophonic ).

Some denominal prefixes are historically related to various valency-changing derivations, in particular the antipassive (§ sec:voice.denominal ). In addition to their basic function of deriving verbs from nouns, denominal prefixes also occur in compound verbs (§ sec:denom.compound.verbs ), incorporating verbs(§ sec:incorporation ), and in verbs recently loaned from Chinese (§ sec:zh.loanverbs ).

The following subsections present a general overview of the morphological alternations observed in denominal derivations (§ sec:denominal.prefixes.morph ) and on the functional correspondences between denominal derivations and light verb constructions (§ sec:denominal.vs.light.verb ), two topics which are treated in more detail in each of the sections in this chapter.
summary: Denominal verbalizing derivations in Japhug turn nouns into verbs, and their sources can be possessed nouns, nominal roots, or compounds. These derivations are numerous and highly productive, even with Tibetan and Chinese loanwords, which means Japhug conjugated verbs are not a closed class; the chapter treats these prefixes separately, surveys their attested forms and other related derivations, and notes that some are historically linked to valency-changing morphology and can also appear in compound, incorporating, and loan verbs.

text:
When a noun takes a denominal prefix, the root almost never exhibits any stem alternation. If the base noun is inalienably possessed, the possessive prefix is removed (including in many cases frozen indefinite possessor prefixes in tɯ-/tɤ, § sec:frozen.indef ). For instance, the ɣɤ- denominal verb (§ sec:denom.GW ) from the inalienably possessed noun tɤ-kʰɯsmoke is ɣɤkʰɯbe smoky (rather than $ $ ɣɤtɤkʰɯ ), and the same applies even to the noun tɤrʁaʁgame whose tɤ- prefixal element is not an indefinite possessor prefix, but whose denominal form is ɣɤrʁaʁhunt. Likewise, when the base noun is a counted noun (§ sec:counted.nouns ), the numeral prefix is also removed (§ sec:denom.tr.rA, § sec:denom.tr.GA ). Only action nominalization tɯ- prefixes can be preserved: for example, the lexicalized action nominal tɯsqawheat gruel (from sqacook, § sec:denominalization.action.nominal ) has the denominal form rɯtɯsqaeat wheat gruel (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ) rather than $ $ rɯsqa.

Some denominal prefixes, including sɯ-/sɤ- (§ sec:denom.sW.caus.instr ), rɯ-/rɤ- (§ sec:denom.rA ), ɣɯ-/ɣɤ- (§ sec:denom.tr.GA ), mɯ-/mɤ- (§ sec:denom.mA ) and nɯ-/nɤ- (§ sec:denom.nW ) have either ɯ or ɤ vocalism (with the variant a when the following syllables has a uvular preinitial, § sec:A.vs.a.prefixes ). This vowel contrast is partially based on that of the indefinite possessor prefix ( tɯ- vs. tɤ, § sec:inalienably.possessed.morpho ) when the base noun is inalienably possessed, but many exceptions exist.

A handful of denominal verbs have in addition an intrusive -ɣ-/-x- velar fricative element (like the sigmatic causative, § sec:caus.sWG ), for instance ɣɤxpradispatch from tɤpramessenger (§ sec:denom.tr.GA ).

Denominal prefixes are nearly always located closest to the root than any non-denominal derivational prefix. Only one exception is known: the causative sɤzmbrɯanger from the denominal verb sɤmbrɯget angry, whose causative prefix is irregularly inserted between the denominal prefix sɤ- and the nominal root -mbrɯ: sɤ-z-mbrɯ is to be parsed as denom - caus -anger (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ).
summary: Denominal prefixes usually attach directly to the root without stem alternation, and when the base noun is inalienably possessed or counted, the possessive or numeral prefix is typically removed; action nominalization tɯ- prefixes are the main exception and may be retained. Several denominal prefixes show ɯ/ɤ vocalism, sometimes reflecting the indefinite possessor prefix, and a few forms also include an intrusive velar fricative -ɣ-/-x-. Denominal prefixes are normally the closest prefixes to the root, with only one known exception where a causative prefix is irregularly inserted between the denominal prefix and the root.

subsection: Denominal derivations and light verb constructions
text:
denominal derivation light verb verb!light
Most denominal derivations described in this chapter are synonymous or near-synonymous with complex predicates involving light verbs such as βzumake, lɤtrelease or existential verbs like tuexist. Both types of construction serve to integrate a nominal root into a predicate.

For instance, the verb rɯqajɯget worms and rɤspɯfester, with the rɯ-/rɤ- denominal prefix (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ) have the same meaning as the collocation of their base noun qajɯworm and tɤ-spɯpus with the light verb βzumake, as illustrated by ( ex:tAspW.toBzu ) where both constructions appear. This example also shows that synonymous denominal and light verb constructions from the same nouns lexically select the same orientation preverbs: upwards in the case of rɤspɯ / tɤ-spɯ+βzu `fester, have pus', and westwards in that of rɯqajɯ / qajɯ+βzu `have worms, grow worms'.

exe

tɕe [tɤ-spɯ tɕe to-βzu] tɕe [qajɯ ɲo-βzu] ma kɤ-nɯqambɯmbjom ɯ-xɕɤt kɯ nɯnɯ ɯ-ʁar ɯ-ndzom ɣɯ ɯ-qa nɯra to-rɤ-spɯ qʰe ɲɤ-rɯ-qajɯ \\
