Tshobdun has cognate prefixes wɐ- and sɐ- with similar functions.

nɯ- deideophonic verbs
Deideophonic verbs in nɯ- are built on non-reduplicated ideophonic roots, but like the ɣɤ- and sɤ- prefixes (§ sec:GA.sA.deidph ), they have a meaning based on that of type III pattern `dynamic action' ideophones. The nɯ- derivation yields transitive verbs which differ from sɤ- deideophonic verbs in lacking a causative meaning. For instance, the verb nɯxɯrturn around ( ex:kAnWxWra ) from the root -xɯr `turn' expresses rotational motion of the subject (with a complex predicate involving the motion verb skɤrwa+ɕe `make circumambulations', § sec:motion.light.verbs
), like the type III ideophone xɯrnɤxɯr, which occurs with the corresponding denominal verb rɯ-skɤrwa `make circumambulations' (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ).

exe

skɤrwa kɤ-nɯ-xɯr-a ʑo kɤ-ari-a \\
circumambulation aor - denom -turn- 1sg emph aor -go[II]- 1sg \\
`I made circumambulations [again and again].' (elicited)

xɯrnɤxɯr ʑo kɤ-rɯ-skɤrwa-a \\
idph (III):turn emph aor - denom -circumambulation- 1sg \\
`I made circumambulations [again and again].' (elicited)
exe

By contrast, the corresponding transitive verb sɤxɯrxɯrcause to turn (again and again, quickly) expresses induced motion of the object.

In some cases the nɯ- and sɤ- deideophonic verbs are very close semantically, as illustrated by nɯ-bɤβ ( ex:panWbAB.paBde ) and sɤ-bɤbɤβ ( ex:pasAbAbAB.paBde ). Both of these express the action of repeatedly throwing down heavy objects which make a loud noise when reaching the ground, with no care for safety. The difference between the two verbs is subtle, sɤ-bɤbɤβ putting more focus on the speed and the quantity of objects.

exe

xlist

rdɤstaʁ pa-nɯ-bɤβ ʑo pa-βde \\
stone aor:3 3- deidph -heavy.object emph aor:3 3: down -throw \\

pa-sɤ-bɤbɤβ ʑo pa-βde \\
aor:3 3- deidph -heavy.object emph aor:3 3: down -throw \\

bɤβnɤbɤβ ʑo pa-βde \\
idph (III):heavy.object emph aor:3 3: down -throw \\
`He threw [stones] down, going `boom' [on the ground] again and again.' (elicited)
xlist
exe
summary:
The passage describes several deideophonic verbal prefixes in Tshobdun, especially the productive prefixes ɣɤ- and sɤ-, which derive verbs from ideophonic roots. Type I verbs use reduplicated roots and usually match the meaning of type III “dynamic action” ideophones, with ɣɤ- forming intransitives and sɤ- forming transitives with causative meaning, while type II verbs use partial l-reduplication and correspond to type IV ideophones expressing distributed action.  

It also notes that nɯ- forms transitive deideophonic verbs from non-reduplicated ideophonic roots and is semantically close to type III ideophones, but unlike sɤ- it lacks causative meaning. In some cases nɯ- and sɤ- verbs are very similar, though sɤ- tends to emphasize speed or quantity more strongly.

text:
a- and nɤ- deideophonc verbs
A few verbs in a- can be built from reduplicated ideophonic roots, with a meaning equivalent to the type II ideophonic pattern (§ sec:ideo.II ). For instance, the ideophone boʁboʁ `in a group, in a cluster' ( ex:boRboR.kundzoRnW ) is the source of the intransitive verb aboʁboʁcluster around, `huddle'.

exe

tɕe ɴɢoɕna me, porɤt me, ɯ-pɯ tɤ-tu tɕe, kɯki iɕqʰa, [...] ɯ-taʁ nɯnɯre boʁboʁ ʑo ku-ndzoʁ-nɯ tɕe \\
lnk big.spider whether small.spider whether 3sg. poss -young aor -exist lnk dem. prox the.aforementioned 3sg. poss -on dem: loc idph (II):in.group emph ipfv - acaus:attach- pl lnk \\
`When spiders$_i$, whether big ones or small ones, have offspring$_j$, those$_j$ attach in clusters on them$_j$.' (26-mYaRmtsaR)
0003674#S107
exe

exe

kʰɯzɤpɯ ra nɯ-mu ɯ-ɕki ko-k-ɤ-boʁboʁ-nɯ-ci ma ɲɯ-nɤ-ndʐo-nɯ \\
puppy pl 3pl. poss -mother 3sg. poss - dat ifr - peg - deidph -in.group- pl - peg lnk sens - denom -cold- pl \\
`The puppies huddled against their mother, as they feel cold.' (elicited)
exe

Intransitive deideophonic verbs in a- pair with transitive verbs in nɤ- such as nɤboʁboʁcluster around. The subject of transitive nɤboʁboʁ encodes the same semantic role as that of the intransitive subject of aboʁboʁ, while its direct object corresponds to the referent marked with the relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above in the intransitive equivalent.

exe

kɯ-mɤɕi ra ɣɯ, nɯ-tɕɯ nɯra kɯ tɕʰeme ci pjɤ-k-ɤz-nɤ-boʁboʁ-nɯ-ci \\
sbj: pcp -be.rich pl gen 3pl. poss -son dem: pl erg girl indef pst. ipfv - peg - prog - deidph -in.group- pl - peg \\
`Children from rich [families] were grouped around a girl.' (160630 abao-zh)
0006197#S84
exe

It is possible to analyze nɤ- deideophonic verbs as applicative derivations (§ sec:applicative ) from a- deideophonic verbs with regular vowel fusion nɯ-ɤ- $ $ nɤ- (§ sec:allomorphy.applicative ), promoting oblique arguments in ɯ-taʁon, above to object status.

In addition to ideophones expressing `grouping, clustering' like boʁboʁ, the a- derivation is also compatible with ideophones of shape like alɯljube cylindrical from ljulju `cylindrical'. Such verbs do not have a nɤ- counterpart.
summary: A few verbs with the prefix a- are formed from reduplicated ideophonic roots and have meanings corresponding to type II ideophonic patterns, such as aboʁboʁ ‘cluster around, huddle’ from boʁboʁ ‘in a group, in a cluster.’ These intransitive verbs pair with transitive nɤ- forms like nɤboʁboʁ, which may be analyzed as applicative derivatives that promote an oblique argument to object status. The a- derivation is also used with some ideophones of shape, such as alɯljube ‘cylindrical,’ and these do not have nɤ- counterparts.

section: The denominal origin of voice prefixes
text:
denominal derivation!voice
There is a remarkable similarity in Japhug between some valency-changing prefixes on the one hand, and denominal prefixes on the other hand, as illustrated by tab:voice.denom. These correspondences suggest that a historical relationship exists between these pairs of prefixes.

The resemblance between these two series of prefixes is not specific to Japhug, and found in all Gyalrongic languages, in particular Khroskyabs. The following sections (in particular § sec:antipassive.history ) provide evidence that these resemblances are due to the fact that the derivations in tab:voice.denom actually historically originate from the corresponding denominal derivations (see also,, ).

Not all valency-changing prefixes in Japhug are related to denominal derivations: the reflexive ʑɣɤ- in particular derives instead from the incorporation of the 3sg pronoun (§ sec:reflexive.origin and ), and some derivations such as the autive and anticausative are probably inherited from proto-Trans-Himalayan (§ sec:autoben.historical, § sec:anticausative,, ).

The origin of the rɤ- antipassive prefix
antipassive!origin
The resemblance between the rɤ- applicative (§ sec:antipassive.rA ) and the intransitive denominal rɤ- prefix (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ) suggests that a historical relationship between these prefixes is possible. In addition, the fact that the antipassive only has cognates in Tshobdun and Zbu (, ) makes it unlikely that this derivation is very ancient.

A few antipassive verbs have formal and semantic irregularities (§ sec:antipassive.rA ). In this section, I show that these irregularities are shared with corresponding action nominals (§ sec:antipassive.irr.form, § sec:antipassive.irr.semantic ), and that this observation is a crucial piece of evidence to propose that the antipassive prefix originates from the denominal derivation of action nominals from transitive verbs (§ sec:antipassive.pathway ).
summary:
The passage argues that several Japhug valency-changing prefixes resemble denominal prefixes, and that this similarity is found across Gyalrongic languages, suggesting that some of these derivations historically come from denominal formations. It also notes that not all valency-changing prefixes have this origin: the reflexive ʑɣɤ- comes from 3sg pronoun incorporation, and some forms such as the autive and anticausative are likely inherited from Proto-Trans-Himalayan.  

For the rɤ- antipassive, the resemblance to an intransitive denominal prefix and the limited cognate evidence suggest a relatively recent origin, and its formal and semantic irregularities match those of corresponding action nominals. This supports the claim that the antipassive prefix developed from a denominal derivation of action nominals from transitive verbs.

section: The denominal origin of voice prefixes
subsubsection: Formal commonalities between antipassive verbs and action nominals
text:
Two antipassive verbs have irregularities is stem formation: rɤnŋahave a debt, `owe money' from ŋabuy on credit, owe has an intrusive -n- element between the antipassive rɤ- prefix and the stem -ŋa, and rɤtsɣedo business presents the opposite situation: the corresponding transitive verb ntsɣesell has an extra prefixal n- element (§ sec:antipassive.rA ).

These morphological specificities are not isolated: the action nominals tɯ-nŋadebt (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ) and tɯtsɣecommerce (§ sec:action.nominals ) have the same stem as the corresponding antipassive verbs.

This commonality between action nominals and the corresponding antipassive verbs is explainable if one assumes that the latter derive from the former by a denominal rɤ, on the model of rɤkrɤzhave a discussion and rɤmawork from tɯkrɤzdiscussion or ta-mawork (n) (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ), rather than directly from the corresponding transitive verbs.

The n- element in tɯ-nŋadebt may be analyzable as a nasalized dental nominalization prefix ( *-t-ŋa $ $ -nŋa, § sec:bare.action.nominals ), and the relationship between rɤnŋa and the base verb ŋa is thus indirect, as shown in ( ex:rAnNa ).

exe

ŋa `owe' $ $ -nŋa `debt' $ $ rɤnŋahave a debt
exe

The verb rɤtsɣedo business is also directly derived from tɯtsɣecommerce rather than from the transitive ntsɣesell. The n- element on ntsɣe is explainable as a reduced allomorph of the transitive denominal nɯ- prefix (§ sec:denom.tr.nW ). Thus, while rɤtsɣedo business is synchronically perceived as deriving from ntsɣe, both verbs historically actually derive from the action nominal tɯtsɣe, as shown in fig:ntsGe.
summary: The passage notes two antipassive verbs with irregular stem formation: **rɤnŋa** ‘have a debt’ has an intrusive **-n-**, while **rɤtsɣe** ‘do business’ shows an extra prefixal **n-** in the corresponding transitive verb **ntsɣe** ‘sell’. These patterns are shared by the related action nominals **tɯ-nŋa** ‘debt’ and **tɯtsɣe** ‘commerce’, suggesting that the antipassive verbs are better analyzed as derived from action nominals rather than directly from the transitive verbs.

section: The denominal origin of voice prefixes
subsubsection: Semantic commonalities between antipassive verbs and action nominals
text:
Commonalities between antipassive verbs and action nominals are not restricted to stem formation as in § sec:antipassive.irr.form above.

The formally regular antipassive verb rɤpɣaʁreclaim land, `clear land for farming' has a restricted meaning in comparison with the corresponding transitive verb pɣaʁturn over: while the latter can occur with a wide range of objects, the former is exclusively used to refer to turning uncultivated land into fields (from the meaning `plough' of the base verb, § sec:antipassive.lexicalized ). The same semantic restriction is also observed with the action nominal tɯpɣaʁland clearing, used in collocation with tɕɤttake out with a meaning close to that of the antipassive rɤpɣaʁ.

exe

mɯ-lo-nɤ-tsoʁ-ndʑi kɯ tɯpɣaʁ lo-tɕɤt-ndʑi \\
neg - ifr - denom -silverweed- du erg field.clearing ifr: upstream -take.out- du \\
`They did not collect silverweed, and cleared fields for farming (instead).' (31-deluge)
0004077#S144
exe

This common semantic restriction suggests that the action nominal tɯpɣaʁ and rɤpɣaʁ are related, and can be accounted for by assuming that the latter is a denominal derivation from the former, rather than directly deriving from pɣaʁturn over, as shown in ( ex:rApGaR ).

exe

pɣaʁturn over, `plough fields' $ $ tɯpɣaʁ `land clearing' $ $ rɤpɣaʁ `clear land for farming'
exe
summary: The passage notes that the antipassive verb **rɤpɣaʁ** ‘clear land for farming’ has a more restricted meaning than its transitive base **pɣaʁ** ‘turn over,’ since it is used only for converting uncultivated land into fields. The same semantic restriction appears in the action nominal **tɯpɣaʁ** ‘land clearing,’ which suggests that **rɤpɣaʁ** is better analyzed as a denominal derivative from **tɯpɣaʁ** rather than as a direct derivation from **pɣaʁ**.

section: The denominal origin of voice prefixes
text: Another irregular antipassive involves the prefix rather than the stem: the verb rɯsɯsothink, `ponder' (§ sec:lability.apass ) from sɯsothink has rɯ- rather than the regular rɤ- prefix. This irregular form is easily accounted for by the hypothesis that antipassive verbs are denominal derivations from action nominals: rɯsɯso is the expected regular rhotic denominal from the bare action nominal tɯ-sɯsothought (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ).
summary: An irregular antipassive is found in the verb *rɯsɯso* ‘ponder’, which has the prefix *rɯ-* instead of the regular antipassive prefix *rɤ-*. The passage explains this form as regular under the idea that antipassive verbs are derived from action nominals: *rɯsɯso* is the expected rhotic denominal form from the bare action nominal *tɯ-sɯso* ‘thought’.

section: The denominal origin of voice prefixes
text:
reanalysis
Evidence from irregular antipassive verbs presented above in § sec:antipassive.irr.form, § sec:antipassive.irr.semantic and § sec:antipassive.irr.prefix suggest that the formal resemblance between the rɤ- antipassive prefix and the intransitive rhotic denominal rɯ-/rɤ- prefix is not simply a coincidence, but that the antipassive derivation came into being from the verbalization of an action nominal, following the pathway presented in fig:apass.

The transitive verb first undergoes nominalization into either an action nominal in tɯ- (§ sec:action.nominals ) or into a bare action nominal (taking either a definite or an indefinite possessive tɯ- or tɤ, § sec:bare.action.nominals ). This action nominal then takes the rhotic intransitive denominal prefix. The rhotic prefix removes the tɯ-/tɤ- prefix irrespective of whether it is an indefinite possessor prefix or a dental nominalization prefix, following a general property of denominal derivations in Japhug (§ sec:denominal.prefixes.morph, § sec:denominalization.action.nominal ).

With the exception of the few verbs studied in the section above, where a morphological or semantic irregularity in the action noun left a trace on the antipassive verb, the intermediate step leaves no traces. It is possible that once a sufficient number of verbalized denominal action nouns had been created by this process, the antipassive derivation became productive and that antipassive verbs were directly derived from the transitive base verbs.

Even if the antipassive prefix has become functionally separate from the intransitive denominal rɤ- in Japhug, many antipassive verbs remain synchronically ambiguous: for instance, the verb rɤɕpʰɤtpatch clothes can either be analyzed as the antipassive equivalent of ɕpʰɤtpatch or as a denominal from tɤ-ɕpʰɤtpatch (n) (§ sec:antipassive.vs.light.verbs ).

The pathway in fig:apass is not specific to Gyalrong languages; antipassive affixes from ancient light verb constructions with action nominals have been documented in Mande and elsewhere (, ), providing a parallel example of the functional overlap between denominal verbalization and light verb constructions in Japhug (§ sec:denominal.vs.light.verb ).

The same two-step mechanism can be used to account for the other resemblances between denominal prefixes and valency-changing derivations in tab:voice.denom. More generally, action nominalization neutralizes the transitivity of the verb stem, and the new argument structure of the derived verb is determined by the denominal prefix.

The proprietive and antipassive sɤ- prefixes and their tropative counterpart
antipassive!origin proprietive!origin
The form and meaning of the proprietive sɤ- derivation (§ sec:proprietive ) are close to that of the denominal proprietive sɤ- (§ sec:denom.sA.proprietive ). The sɤ- denominal verbs often occur in pairs with transitive or intransitive nɤ- denominal verbs from the same noun (§ sec:denom.nW.pairing ), as in sɤrebe ridiculous and nɤrelaugh, `laugh at' (from tɤ-relaugh (n), tab:sA.denom.proprietive, § sec:denom.sA.proprietive ).

Both the proprietive sɤ- (§ sec:proprietive ) and the tropative nɤ- (§ sec:tropative ) can be accounted for by assuming a pathway similar to that of the antipassive ( fig:apass ), by supposing sɤ- and nɤ- denominal derivations from abstract nouns (§ sec:tA.abstract.nouns ) or degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominals ). The intermediate abstract nouns are actually attested in many cases, as in ( ex:sAGmu.pathway ) and ( ex:nAmpCAr.pathway ).

exe

mube afraid $ $ tɯmufear $ $ sɤɣmube frightening

mpɕɤrbe beautiful $ $ tɤmpɕɤrbeauty $ $ nɤmpɕɤrfind beautiful
exe

In addition, the proprietive verb sɤɣɲatbe exhausting (from ɲatbe tired) with the allomorph sɤɣ- presents the same intrusive -ɣ- element as the abstract noun tɤɣɲattiredness, supporting the idea that this noun was indeed the intermediate step between the base verb and its proprietive form.

When the base verb undergoing action nominalization and proprietive verbalization is transitive, there is a potential ambiguity, since the proprietive derivation selects as intransitive subject a referent either possessing a particular property or having the tendency or propensity to perform a particular action. With action verbs such as mtsɯɣbite, the most natural interpretation will be `have the propensity to bite' rather than `tend to be bitten' ( ex:sAmtsWG ), yielding an antipassive derivation (§ sec:antipassive.sA ).

exe

mtsɯɣbite $ $ *tɯmtsɯɣ `action of biting' $ $ sɤmtsɯɣ `bite people'
exe

With verbs of cognition, an ambiguity is possible; for instance the sɤ- derivation from the transitive verb nɯzdɯɣworry about is interpretable either as proprietive sɤnɯzdɯɣcausing people to worry (§ sec:proprietive.tr ) or as the antipassive `worry about people' (§ sec:proprietive.compatibility ). Both of these meanings can be explained as proprietive denominal derivations from an abstract noun *tV-nɯzdɯɣ `worry'.
summary:
The passage argues that the Japhug antipassive prefix rɤ- likely originated through a two-step reanalysis: a transitive verb was first nominalized as an action nominal, then verbalized by the rhotic denominal prefix, with the original nominal morphology usually leaving no trace. Although the antipassive later became productive and distinct, some forms remain synchronically ambiguous between antipassive and denominal analyses.

It extends this explanation to the proprietive sɤ- and tropative nɤ- derivations, which can likewise be derived from abstract or degree nominals. In several cases, attested intermediate nouns and shared morphological material support this pathway, though some transitive bases create ambiguity between proprietive and antipassive interpretations.

section: The denominal origin of voice prefixes
text:
causative!origin passive!origin applicative!origin
Following the same type of pathways as for antipassive, proprietive and tropative derivations, the applicative nɯ(ɣ)- (§ sec:applicative ), the causative sɯ(ɣ)- (§ sec:sig.causative ) and the passive a- can be analyzed as having historically originated from the transitive nɯ- (§ sec:denom.tr.nW ), the causative/instrumental sɯ(ɣ)- (§ sec:denom.sW.caus.instr ) and the stative a- (§ sec:denom.a ) denominalizations from an action nominal, as illustrated in ( ex:pathways.denom ).

exe

xlist

mube afraid $ $ tɯmufear $ $ nɯɣmube afraid of

ɲatbe tired $ $ tɤɣɲattiredness $ $ sɯɣɲatexhaust, `cause to be tired'

tsʰoʁattach$ $ *tɯ-tsʰoʁ `attachment' This hypothesized action nominal is indirectly attested as the bare infinitive in ( ex:bare.inf.noun ) (§ sec:bare.inf.complement ). $ $ atsʰoʁbe attached
xlist
exe

The reduplicated reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ) originates from a stative denominal verb with reduplication expressing plural subject (as in Stau, where not only reduplication but even triplication is attested with this meaning, ), from which the reciprocal function was a pragmatic inference.

While the applicative, like the antipassive, is restricted to the Core Gyalrong languages and is certainly a recent innovation, the situation is more complex in the case of the passive and the causative.

The a- passive, which originates from *ŋa, is probably related to the valency-decreasing ŋV- prefix found in Kuki-Chin, which also expresses reciprocal, reflexive and even antipassive in some cases (,, ). The sigmatic causative, which has highly complex morphology across Gyalrongic languages, is also widespread in the Trans-Himalayan, and has been discussed in a considerable number of works, including,,, and.

The existence of the cognates of the valency-changing prefixes a- and sɯ(ɣ)- in other branches of Trans-Himalayan could been seen as contradicting the hypothesis that they originate from denominalization prefixes. However, two pieces of evidence suggest that the pathway of reanalysis developed to account for the origin of the antipassive is also applicable to these two prefixes.

First, the sigmatic prefix also has a denominal function in various Trans-Himalayan languages from Jinghpo (, ) to Old Chinese. There is consensus among scholars that this function is at least equally as old as the causative one.

Second, the irregular sɤ- allomorph of the causative in sɤrmigive a name (§ sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ) can be accounted for by analyzing this transitive verb as a causative denominal (§ sec:denom.sW.caus.instr ) from the noun tɤ-rminame rather than a direct causative derivation from the verb rmibe called.
reanalysis
It is therefore possible either that the postulated pathways in ( ex:sWGYat.pathway ) and ( ex:atshoR.pathway ) above have taken place independently in several branches, or that the reanalysis had already been completed in the ancestral language ancestral. These hypotheses do not imply that the reanalysis took place only once in each language. In all languages that have preserved the sigmatic denominal and that have some form of bare nominalization, pathways similar to ( ex:sWGYat.pathway ) can have occurred repeatedly even after the sigmatic causative had been fully grammaticalized.
summary: The passage argues that the applicative, causative, and passive prefixes in Gyalrong can historically be traced to older denominal prefixes built from action nominals, with the applicative nɯ(ɣ)-, causative sɯ(ɣ)-, and passive a- all reflecting earlier derivational pathways. It also proposes that the reduplicated reciprocal developed from a stative denominal verb with plural-subject reduplication, and notes that while the applicative is a recent Core Gyalrong innovation, the passive and causative have wider Trans-Himalayan cognates and may have undergone similar reanalysis in multiple branches or in the ancestral language.

text:
Tibetan!verb verb!loanwords Chinese!verb
While Tibetan verbs are generally borrowed directly, Chinese verbs and adjectives need to undergo denominal derivation to be compatible with verbal morphology.

Speakers born after 1990 profusely use verbs of Chinese origin. Due to the high variability of the pronunciation of Chinese loanwords in Japhug, I make no attempt here at representing them in phonological shape, and use pinyin except in highly lexicalized examples. Chinese adjectives can be borrowed almost freely with either the nɯ- (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ) or the rɯ- (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ) denominal prefixes, as illustrated by nɯ<yan> `be strict' (from 严 yánsevere, strict) in ( ex:WtWnWyan ) and rɯ<fuza> `be complicated' (from 复杂 fùzácomplicated) in ( ex:YWrWfuza ). The nɯ- and rɯ- prefixes are apparently freely interchangeable in this type of words.

exe

ɯʑo ɯ-tɯ-nɯ-<yan> ɯ-grɤl mu pɯ-me \\
3sg 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - denom -strict 3sg. poss -order at.all pst. ipfv -not.exist \\
`He was extremely strict.' (phurpa 2010)
exe

exe

ɲɯ-rɯ-<fuza> wo \\
sens - denom -complicated sfp \\
`It looks complicated!' (heard in context)
exe

For action verbs, the choice of the rɯ- and nɯ- prefixes is conditioned by transitivity (§ sec:denom.rA.pairing ): rɯ- denominal verbs are intransitive, for example rɯkʰɤjxwihave a meeting (from 开会 kāihuìhave a meeting), while their nɯ- counterparts are transitive ( nɯkʰɤjxwimeet about). In some cases a light verb construction with the Chinese verb borrowed as a noun also exists; for instance, in addition to rɯkʰɤjxwihave a meeting, it is possible to use kʰɤjxwi `meeting' in collocation with βzumake as in ( ex:kaihui ).

exe

kʰɤjxwi ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-βzu-nɯ \\
meeting sens - prog -make- pl \\
`They were having a meeting.' (17-lhazgron)
exe

Borrowed verbs, although they have undergone denominal derivation, sometimes preserve morphosyntactic peculiarities of the corresponding verb in Chinese. For instance, although the manipulation verb nɯtʰajcarry, like 抬 táilift, carry, specifically means `lift up and carry (something heavy, of more than one person)' with a constraint on the number of the subject (see example ex:WXcAl.Zo.natsWmnW, § sec:manipulation.verbs ).
summary: Tibetan verbs are usually borrowed directly, but Chinese verbs and adjectives must first be derived as nouns or denominal forms to fit Tibetan verbal morphology. Chinese adjectives can take either the nɯ- or rɯ- denominal prefix, which appear freely interchangeable, while action verbs are distinguished by transitivity: rɯ- forms are intransitive and nɯ- forms are transitive. Some borrowed verbs also preserve morphosyntactic properties from Chinese, and in some cases a Chinese verb may be used as a noun in a light verb construction instead of as a derived verb.

text:
compound!verb-verb

Compounds verbs combine two verb roots (henceforth referred to as `$V_1$' and `$V_2$' following the Kirantological tradition) within the same stem. Unlike bipartite verbs (§ sec:bipartite, ), the two verb roots are not separable and cannot take redundant person indexation affixes.

Most compound verbs have a denominal prefix ( tab:compound.verbs.denom ). In some cases, the $V_1$ preserves the form of the independent verb, but in other cases occurs in bound state (§ sec:status.constructus ), as in apɤmbatbe easy to do, where the root of the base verb pado undergoes -a $ $ -ɤ vowel alternation. Alternations in the $V_2$, as in the case of axtɕɯxtebe of uneven size (with xti $ $ xte alternation, § sec:denom.a ), are much rarer.

Some compound verbs clearly derive from a compound noun by denominal derivation. This is the case of stative verbs derived from compound nouns of dimension such as axtɕɯxtebe of uneven size ( tab:denom.dimension, § sec:denom.a, § sec.v.v.compounds.degree ), and also rɤjoʁβzɯrtidy up, whose corresponding compound action noun joʁβzɯrtidying up is used in collocation with the light verb βzumake (§ sec.v.v.compounds.action ).

The verb argɤlebe extremely happy does not derive from a compound noun *rgɤle, but rather from the bipartite verb rga=le, which only occurs in non-finite forms (§ sec:bipartite ).

The other verbs in tab:compound.verbs.denom lack a corresponding compound noun. For instance, although apɤmbatbe easy to do presumably derives from a noun *pɤmbat `easiness to do' rather than directly from pado and mbatbe easy, there is no such noun in Kamnyu Japhug. It is probable that such a noun used to exist, and that only its derived denominal verb was preserved.

A clue that denominal compounds do not directly derive from their base verbs is offered by raχtɯtsɣedo business. The $V_2$ -tsɣe has the same form as that found in the action noun tɯtsɣecommerce and the antipassive rɤtsɣedo business, `sell things' (§ sec:antipassive.rA ), while the corresponding transitive verb ntsɣesell has an additional n- prefix. The explanation for the absence of n- in raχtɯtsɣe is that this verb comes from a compound *χtɯtsɣe `commerce' directly built from the action noun tɯtsɣe rather than from the transitive verb ntsɣesell. Although *χtɯtsɣe is not in common usage, it is considered to be marginally acceptable by Tshendzin.

Some compound verbs lack denominal prefixes, as shown in tab:compound.verbs.n.denom. However, the fact that the $V_1$ occurs in bound state in the case of ngɤjtsʰifeed ( ŋgɤ- from ngufeed) and that all the $V_1$ of all of these verbs have a prenasalized onset may suggest a denominal origin: since the denominal nɯ- prefix has an irregular n- or homorganic N- allomorph (§ sec:denom.intr.nW, § sec:denom.tr.nW ), it is possible that the denominal prefix here was absorbed by the preexisting prenasalization of the $V_1$: *n-ŋgɤ-ɕtʰi $ $ *ŋgɤ-ɕtʰi $ $ ŋgɤjtsʰi.

The semantic relationship between the $V_1$ and the $V_2$ differs across compound verbs. In most cases, the compound has an additive meaning `do $V_1$ and $V_2$', as in nɤtsɯmɣɯttake away and bring back (in particular, all verbs in tab:compound.verbs.n.denom are of this type). Another possibility is a head-complement relationship, as that illustrated by apɤmbatbe easy to do, whose meaning is equivalent to a construction with mbatbe easy taking a complement clause containing the verb pado (§ sec:facilitative ).
summary: Compound verbs in Japhug consist of two verb roots within one stem, are inseparable, and cannot take redundant person-indexing affixes. Many are denominal in origin, with some showing a preserved or bound form of the first verb root and rarer alternations in the second; several appear to derive from compound nouns or action nouns, while some lack an overt denominal prefix but may still have such an origin. Semantically, most compound verbs have an additive meaning (“do V1 and V2”), though some show a head-complement relation, as in forms meaning ‘easy to do.’

text:
incorporation!noun
Japhug has few dozen complex verb stems comprising a nominal and a verbal root. Nearly all of these verbs contain a denominal prefix, and incorporation is thus analyzed in Japhug as a subtype of denominal derivation.

Although noun incorporation is not a frequent phenomenon in Japhug, its productivity is undeniable, as it applies to loanwords, as shown by the verb ɣɯ<piaozi>fsoʁ `earn money' ( ex:kWGWpiaozifsoR ), whose base noun 票子 piàoziticket, `paper money' is from Chinese and whose base verb fsoʁearn comes from Tibetan བསོགས་bsogsaccumulate.

exe

nɤ-mbro cʰo nɤ-rŋɯl tu-rke-a tɕe kɯ-ɣɯ-<piaozi>-fsoʁ jɤ-ɕe tɕe \\
2sg. poss -horse comit 2sg. poss -silver ipfv -put.in[III]- 1sg lnk sbj: pcp - denom -money-earn imp -go lnk \\
`I will give you a horse and some silver, go and earn some money.' (Lobzang 2005)
exe
summary: Japhug has a few dozen complex verb stems made from a nominal and a verbal root, and nearly all include a denominal prefix, so noun incorporation is treated as a type of denominal derivation. Although it is not frequent, the process is productive enough to apply to loanwords, as shown by a verb meaning ‘earn money’ formed from a Chinese noun and a Tibetan verb.

text:
denominal derivation!incorporation compound!noun-verb nominalization!compound
A considerable proportion of incorporating verbs in Japhug are denominal derivations from Noun-Verb action nominal compounds (§ sec:object.verb.compounds, § sec:adjunct.verb.compounds ) which are still synchronically attested. tabe:incorp.denom.compounds presents a sample of incorporating verbs with the corresponding action nouns, as well as the base nouns and base verbs. These action nominals also occur in collocation with light verbs, with meanings similar to those of the incorporating verbs (§ sec:denominal.vs.light.verb, § sec:incorp.vs.other ). Japhug (pseudo-)incorporating verbs are typologically similar to the type of οἰκοδομέω `build' in Greek.

When the incorporating verb is transitive, its direct object corresponds in some cases to an oblique argument in the light verb construction. For instance, the verb nɯzgrɯtɕʰɯgive a nudge encodes the patient (the person receiving the nudge) as object ( ex:tAwGnWwgrWtChWa ), while in the light verb construction with the compound zgrɯtɕʰɯnudge, the patient is marked by the relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above ( ex:zgrWtChW.matAtWlAt ) (§ sec:WtaR ).

exe

tɤ́-wɣ-nɯ-zgrɯ-tɕʰɯ-a \\
aor - inv - denom -elbow-stab- 1sg \\
`He gave me a nudge.' (elicited)

a-taʁ nɤ-zgrɯ-tɕʰɯ ma-tɤ-tɯ-lɤt ma ɲɯ-mŋɤm \\
1sg. poss -on 2sg. poss -elbow-stab neg - imp -2-release lnk sens -hurt \\
`Don't give me a nudge, it hurts.' (elicited)
exe

Alternatively, the patientive argument can be encoded as a possessive prefix on the base nominal compound. For instance, the object of the nɯsnɯɲaʁharm ( 2sg in ex:mAtnWsnWYAR ) refers to the person who is harmed, and corresponds to the prefix on the compound noun
snɯɲaʁharming people in the light verb construction ( 3pl in ex:nWsnWYaR ).

exe

ma-nɯ-tɯ-mu tɕe aʑo mɤ-ta-nɯ-snɯ-ɲaʁ \\
neg - imp -2-be.afraid lnk 1sg neg -1 2- denom -heart-black: fact \\
`Don't be afraid, I will not do any harm to you.' (140429 jiedi-zh)
exe

exe

tɯrme ra nɯ-snɯ-ɲaʁ ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-βzu tɕe \\
people pl 3pl. poss -heart-black sens - prog -make lnk \\
`It was harming people.' (150827 taisui)
0006390#S30
exe

tabe:incorp.denom.compounds only includes examples with the denominal prefixes ɣɯ- (§ sec:denom.GW ) and nɯ-/nɤ- (§ sec:denom.nW ), but other denominal prefixes are attested in this construction. In particular, the alternative forms rɯrɟɯfsoʁaccumulate a fortune (with the rhotic denominal, § sec:denom.rA ) and sɯzgrɯtɕʰɯgive a nudge (with the instrumental sigmatic denominal, § sec:denom.sW.caus.instr ) are attested alongside ɣɯrɟɯfsoʁaccumulate a fortune and nɯzgrɯtɕʰɯgive a nudge.

This use of the term ``incorporation'' to refer to this construction is debatable, since unlike prototypical incorporation, which originates from noun-verb coalescence, in the case of Japhug a two-step process has to be posited: (i) action nominal compounding followed by (ii) denominal derivation. However, this derivation process is not isolated cross-linguistically: similar constructions are found in Ancient Greek and may be posited for proto-Algonquian.

Not all incorporating verbs derive transparently from Noun+Verb compounds. In spite of the presence of a denominal prefix on the verb, the expected action nominal is not always attested. For instance, the intransitive verb nɯjlɤlɤɣherd hybrid yaks (from jlamale hybrid yak and lɤɣgraze ) might have been derived from a noun such as *jlɤ-lɤɣ, but no such noun exists anymore.

In some cases, denominal derivations are derived directly from a Noun+Verb collocation. tab:incorp.denom.collocation presents examples of denominal verbs in nɯ-/nɤ- and sɤ- coming from lexicalized complex collocations. In these constructions, the base verb is intransitive, and the base noun its subject (§ sec:incorp.S ). Some of the nouns and/or verbs are orphan lexemes (§ sec:orphan.noun, § sec:orphan.verb ), and are not attested as free elements.

Three types of denominal derivations are found in tab:incorp.denom.collocation, all independently attested with simple nouns. First, we find stative intransitive verbs in nɯ- (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ), whose intransitive subject corresponds to the possessor of the base noun as in the case of nɯɲɤmkʰebe skinny (compare ex:YWtWnWYAmkhe and ex:nAYAm.YWkhe ).

exe

xlist

ɲɯ-tɯ-nɯ-ɲɤm-kʰe \\
sens -2- denom -flesh-be.skinny \\
`You are skinny.' (heard in context)

nɤ-ɲɤm ɲɯ-kʰe \\
2sg. poss -flesh sens -be.skinny \\
`You are skinny.' (140517 mogui de jing zh)
0004022#S22
xlist
exe

Second, some verbs make use of the sɤ- proprietive denominal prefix (§ sec:denom.sA.proprietive ). The verb sɤʑiloʁbe disgusting is paired with the nɤ- denominal nɤʑiloʁhave nausea (other verb pairs of the same type are found in tab:sA.denom.proprietive ), while sɤmbrɯŋgɯbe detestable instead corresponds to the simple denominal sɤmbrɯget angry (§ sec:denom.sA.proprietive ).

Third, the transitive verbs nɤrɕɤmŋɤmcherish and nɤʁombilose hope have a tropative meaning (§ sec:denom.tr.nW ). Their transitive subjects corresponds to the possessor of the base noun, as shown by ( ex:YWnArCAmNama ) and ( ex:arCa.mNAm ).

exe

xlist

a-tɕɯ ɲɯ-nɤ-rɕɤ-mŋam-a \\
1sg. poss -son sens - denom -cherish(1)-cherish(2)- 1sg \\
`I cherish my son.' (elicited)

a-tɕɯ a-rɕa mŋɤm \\
1sg. poss -son 1sg. poss -cherish(1) cherish(2): fact \\
`I cherish my son.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

Other incorporating verbs probably originate from a Noun+Cerb collocation which does not exist anymore. From instance, amɲaχtsʰɯmbe petty ( ex:YWtAmYaXtshWm ) derives from tɯ-mɲaʁeye and xtsʰɯmbe thin with the denominal prefix a, but no collocation *tɯ-mɲaʁ+xtsʰɯm exists, though the etymological relationship with the base noun and verb is still synchronically transparent.

exe

ɲɯ-tɯ-ɤ-mɲaʁ-tsʰɯm \\
sens -2- denom -eye-be.thin \\
`You are petty-minded.' (elicited)
exe

There are also a handful of incorporating verbs without a dedicated denominal prefix, as illustrated by tabe:incorp.n.denom.

In the case of amɤʁuhave rickets and akɤmtɕoʁbe pointy-headed, the nominal stems mɤ, kɤ- and sɯ- in bound state appear to be infixed within the stem of the base verbs ajʁube bent and amtɕoʁbe pointy. The stem a<mɤ>ʁu in addition lacks the -j- preinitial found in ajʁu.
summary:
A large proportion of incorporating verbs in Japhug are denominal derivations from Noun+Verb action-nominal compounds that are still synchronically attested, and these action nominals also appear with light verbs in constructions similar in meaning to the incorporating verbs. The text notes that in transitive cases the direct object may correspond to an oblique argument in the light-verb construction, or alternatively to a possessive prefix on the base nominal compound.  

The author argues that calling this “incorporation” is debatable because it involves a two-step process: action-nominal compounding followed by denominal derivation, though comparable constructions are found in Ancient Greek and proto-Algonquian. Some incorporating verbs are no longer transparently related to attested compounds, and others derive from lexicalized noun+verb collocations or even lack a dedicated denominal prefix, with a few showing infixed nominal stems in the verbal base.

text:
Infixation is not the only possibility to account for these two verbs however, since the initial a- syllables themselves are probably frozen denominal prefixes (see also § sec:a.non.passive.denominal ). An alternative hypothesis is that both the apparent base verbs and the incorporating verbs are derived. The intransitive verb nɯsɯzʁetransport wood provides a possible model. This compound verb, which comes from the compounding of siwood (with vowel alternation sɯ, § sec:vowel.alternations.compounds ) and the root of nɯzʁetransport, at first glance seems to be a case of noun infixation within the stem nɯzʁe. However, the existence of the action nominal sɯzʁefirewood transportation shows that nɯsɯzʁetransport wood is a trivial example of denominal incorporation like the verbs in tabe:incorp.denom.compounds above. The anomaly here is the verb nɯzʁetransport, whose nɯ- prefix must be secondary -- a likely explanation for this prefix is that nɯzʁe is a denominal derivation from a lost action nominal *tɯ-zʁe `transportation'.

Hence, as illustrated in fig:nWsWzRe, nɯsɯzʁetransport wood is only indirectly related to nɯzʁetransport, and the infixation hypothesis is certainly wrong in this case. A scenario in the same lines is possible for amɤʁuhave rickets and akɤmtɕoʁbe pointy-headed.

The only example of nominal incorporation without a denominal prefix is the defective verb kɤtɯpatell (its conjugation is presented in tab:kAtWpa, § sec:irregular.transitive ), which comes from the compounding of the object participle kɤ-ti `the thing that is said' (§ sec:object.participle ) with pado. Non-denominal incorporating verbs are much more common in Khroskyabs  than in core Gyalrong languages.
summary: The passage argues that the apparent infixation in certain verbs is better explained as denominal prefixation and derivation, rather than true infixation. Using *nɯsɯzʁe* ‘transport wood’ as an example, it shows that the verb is indirectly related to *nɯzʁe* ‘transport’ through a denominal compound, with the initial *nɯ-* likely secondary and derived from a lost nominal base. It then notes that only one example of nominal incorporation without a denominal prefix is the defective verb *kɤtɯpat* ‘tell’, and that such non-denominal incorporating verbs are more common in Khroskyabs than in core Gyalrong languages.

text:
incorporation
Like other denominal verbs, incorporating verbs undergo productive voice derivations. In some cases, only the derived verb exists: for instance, the intransitive anɯrŋɤrɯrulook at each other's face has the form of a reduplicated reciprocal (§ sec:redp.reciprocal ) from a transitive verb *nɯ-rŋɤ-ru `look at $X$'s face' (from tɯ-rŋaface and rulook at, § sec:incorp.goal ), but no such base verb exists at least in the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug (§ sec:redp.lexicalized ).
summary: Incorporating verbs, like other denominal verbs, can undergo productive voice derivations. In some cases, only the derived form is attested: for example, the intransitive anɯrŋɤrɯru ‘look at each other’s face’ is a reduplicated reciprocal derived from a transitive verb *nɯ-rŋɤ-ru ‘look at X’s face’, but this base verb is not found, at least in the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug.

subsection: Syntactic function of the incorporated word
text: The incorporated nouns have four syntactic functions: intransitive subject, object/semi-object, goal/location adjunct and instrument. There are no examples of incorporated transitive subjects in Japhug.
summary: The passage states that incorporated nouns in Japhug can function as intransitive subjects, objects or semi-objects, goal/location adjuncts, and instruments. It also notes that incorporated transitive subjects are not attested in Japhug.

subsection: Syntactic function of the incorporated word
text:
subject!incorporation incorporation
Intransitive subject incorporation is found in verbs deriving from noun+intransitive verb collocations such as those listed in tab:incorp.denom.collocation above such as nɯsroʁmbrɤtbe in agony from tɯ-sroʁlife and mbrɤtbreak, `be cut'. None of these verbs has a dummy intransitive subject: the incorporated subject does not saturate the subject function. Rather, either the possessor of the base noun (see examples ex:YWtWnWYAmkhe and ex:nAYAm.YWkhe above in § sec:incorp.denom ) or an external referent is promoted to intransitive subject status (or to object status in the case of transitive verbs such as nɤrɕɤmŋɤmcherish).

There are no clear examples of subject incorporation among verbs deriving from noun+verb action nominals.
summary:
Intransitive subject incorporation is found in verbs derived from noun+intransitive verb collocations, such as forms meaning “be in agony” or “be cut.” In these cases, the incorporated subject does not fill the subject role; instead, the possessor of the noun or another external referent becomes the intransitive subject, or the object in the case of transitive verbs.  

The passage also notes that there are no clear cases of subject incorporation in verbs derived from noun+verb action nominals.

subsection: Syntactic function of the incorporated word
text:
object!incorporation incorporation
Object incorporation is found in some incorporating verbs that derive from noun+ verb action nominal compounds such as those presented in tabe:incorp.denom.compounds (§ sec:incorp.denom ) and others which probably originate from lost compounds. It is a saturating incorporation, which removes the object from the argument structure of the verb: incorporating verbs of this type are all intransitive, while their base verbs are all transitive. Typical examples include ɣɯcʰɤtsʰidrink alcohol (from cʰaalcohol and tsʰidrink) or nɤpʰɯxtsɯbreak clods of earth (from the stem of tɤ-pʰɯclod (of earth) with xtsɯpound) (§ sec:incorp.vs.other ).

Some lexicalized noun+verb collocations have an incorporating form. For instance, the transitive verb ru, which only This verb must (at least synchronically) be distinguished from two homophonous verbs: the intransitive rulook at (§ sec:orienting.verbs ) and the transitive rufetch, bring (which requires an associated motion prefix, § sec:ru.fetch ). occurs with the noun zrɯɣlouse with the meaning `pick lice off', can also incorporate the same noun to yield nɯzrɯɣrupick lice off.

The semi-transitive verb rgalike (§ sec:semi.transitive ) can incorporate a semi-object, as in nɯɕmɯrgabe talkative, `like to talk a lot' (with the bound state ɕmɯ- of the inalienably possessed noun tɯ-ɕmiword) and nɯcʰɤrgalike to drink alcohol (with cʰɤ- from cʰaalcohol).
summary:
Object incorporation occurs in some verbs derived from noun+verb compounds, and it is a saturating process that removes the object from the verb’s argument structure. As a result, incorporating verbs of this type are intransitive, while their base verbs are transitive; examples include forms meaning ‘drink alcohol’ and ‘break clods of earth.’

The passage also notes that some lexicalized noun+verb collocations have incorporating forms, such as a verb meaning ‘pick lice off’ that incorporates the noun ‘louse.’ In addition, the semi-transitive verb rga ‘like’ can incorporate a semi-object, as in expressions meaning ‘talkative’ and ‘like to drink alcohol.’

subsection: Syntactic function of the incorporated word
text:
goal!incorporation incorporation
Goals or locational adjuncts can also be incorporated. Unlike objects (§ sec:incorp.O ), they do not saturate the object function of the verb and the incorporating verb has the same transitivity as that of the base verb. For instance, the verb nɤqʰɤŋgaput on (of clothes worn on the shoulders on the top of other clothes) is transitive as is the base verb ŋgawear and selects as object the garment that is worn, typically a raincoat (see ex:mboR.maR.tWwWr, § sec:disjunction.nouns ). The incorporated noun ɯ-qʰuafter, behind (in bound state qʰɤ- ) here indicates the location where the piece of garment is worn (`wear on the back').

However, goal argument saturation occurs when the base verb requires a goal argument. For instance, rulook at selects a goal or dative arguments (§ sec:intr.goal ), but the incorporated verb nɤqʰarulook back, which contains the locational noun ɯ-qʰuafter, behind (with the bound form qʰa- rather than qʰɤ- ), is strictly intransitive.

The intransitive verb nɯkʰɤrŋgɯlie down to rest provides an example of locational adjunct incorporation. It derives from the noun kʰahouse ( kʰɤ- ) and the intransitive verb rŋgɯlie down, `sleep'. The original sense of this verb was probably `lie down (somewhere) in the house' or perhaps even more specifically `lie down in the dining room' (the term kʰɤjmudining room contains the bound state kʰɤ- as first element), but it has now lexicalized further, meaning `lie down to rest in a casual way' in a place unfit for this purpose and not necessarily within the house (as illustrated by ex:lonWkhArNgW ).

exe

smɤt tɯmda rɟɤlpu nɯra ɣɯ nɯ-sakaβ tʂu nɯtɕu ɕ-kɤ-rɤʑi ɲɯ-ŋu. lo-nɯ-kʰɤ-rŋgɯ kɯ-fse ndɤre \\
pl.n pl.n king dem: pl gen 3pl. poss -well path dem: loc tral - aor -stay sens -be aor - denom -house-lie.down sbj: pcp -be.like lnk \\
`He went to the water well of the king of Smad, and stayed there. He lay down on the ground in a casual way.' (2005-stod-kunbzang)
exe
summary: Goals or locational adjuncts can be incorporated without saturating the verb’s object function, so the resulting verb keeps the same transitivity as the base verb. When the base verb already requires a goal argument, however, incorporation can absorb that argument and yield a strictly intransitive form. The passage also notes an intransitive verb meaning ‘lie down to rest’ that originally incorporated the noun ‘house’ as a locational adjunct and has since lexicalized to mean casual resting in an unfit place.

subsection: Syntactic function of the incorporated word
text:
instrument!incorporation incorporation
Instrument incorporation, like object incorporation (§ sec:incorp.O ), is found in denominal verbs deriving from action nominal compounds ( tabe:incorp.denom.compounds ). Like goal and locational adjunct incorporation (§ sec:incorp.goal ), it does not saturate the object function: the verb nɯzgrɯtɕʰɯgive a nudge from tɯ-zgrɯelbow and tɕʰɯgore, stab is transitive like its base verb, as shown by example ( ex:tAwGnWwgrWtChWa ) (§ sec:incorp.denom above).

Some instrument incorporating verbs are lexicalized, for instance nɯ-rmbɯ-χtɕi from tɯ-rmbiurine (regular bound state rmbɯ- ) and χtɕiwash does not mean `wash with urine'; χtɕi is to be understood here as `drench' (as in `drenched in the rain' in ex:nAZo.rcanW, § sec:unexpected ), and although nɯ-rmbɯ-χtɕi probably originally meant `piss on', its present meaning is instead `spray a liquid on', in particular of a species of ants ( ex:tunWrmbWXtCi ).

exe

tɕe nɯtɕu tɕe qro nɯ ɯ-mɲaʁ ɯ-ŋgɯ ra ku-ɕe, ɯ-mɲaʁ nɯ ku-mtsɯɣ nɤ tu-nɯ-rmbɯ-χtɕi nɯra tɕe, \\
lnk dem: loc lnk ant dem 3sg. poss -eye 3sg. poss -in pl ipfv: east -go 3sg. poss -eye dem ipfv -bite add ipfv - denom -urine-wash dem: pl lnk \\
`(When the bear comes to eat them), the ants go into its eyes, bite its eyes and spray acid on them.' (26-qro)
0003682#S45
exe

Instruments other than body parts can be incorporated, for instance tɤ-jlɤβsteam in the verb nɤjlɤβsqastew from sqacook. However, this is also a lexicalized incorporating verb, which does not mean `cook with steam' as could have been expected, but rather `stew for a long time'.

Instrument incorporation is more common with transitive verbs, but examples also exists with intransitive verbs, for instance nɯmbrɯmtsaʁskip rope from tɯmbrirope ( mbrɯ- ) and mtsaʁjump.
summary: Instrument incorporation, like object incorporation, occurs in denominal verbs formed from action nominal compounds, and it does not saturate the object role: the verb remains transitive, as in the example meaning ‘give a nudge’ derived from ‘elbow’ and ‘gore/stab.’ Some incorporating verbs are lexicalized and their meanings have shifted, such as a form based on ‘urine’ that now means ‘spray a liquid on’ rather than ‘wash with urine,’ and another based on ‘steam’ that means ‘stew for a long time’ rather than ‘cook with steam.’ Instrument incorporation is more common with transitive verbs, but it can also occur with intransitive verbs, as shown by an example meaning ‘skip rope.’

text:
light verb
Incorporating verbs occur in the same contexts as the corresponding non-compounded syntactic constructions when these exist, both in the case of incorporating verbs from noun+verb collocations such as nɯɲɤmkʰebe skinny ( ex:qaZo.kWnWYAmkhe ) (see also ex:YWtWnWYAmkhe and ex:nAYAm.YWkhe above) and of those from action nominal compounds such as nɤpʰɯxtsɯbreak clods of earth ( ex:lukWnAphWxtsW ).

exe

iɕqʰa qaʑo nɯ-ɲɤm kɯ-sɯ nɯra qʰe ɲɯ-nɯɣɯ-krɤɣ, qaʑo kɯ-nɯ-ɲɤm-kʰe nɯra [...] mɯ́j-nɯɣɯ-krɤɣ. \\
the.aforementioned sheep 3pl. poss -flesh sbj: pcp -be.plump dem: pl lnk sens - facil -shear sheep sbj: pcp - denom -flesh-be.skinny dem: pl neg: sens - facil -shear \\
`Sheep that are plump are easy to shear, but sheep that are skinny are difficult to shear.' (160712 smAG)
0006073#S27

exe

maka lu-kɯ-nɤpʰɯxtsɯ tɕe tɕe rcanɯ, tɤ-pʰɯ lú-wɣ-xtsɯ tɕe, \\
at.all ipfv - genr:S/O- denom -clod-pound lnk lnk unexp: deg indef. poss -clod ipfv - inv -pound lnk \\
`When people break clods of earths,...' (26-mYaRmtsaR)
0003674#S82

Nevertheless, these constructions are not completely equivalent. The minimal triplet in ( ex:cWphWt ) can be used to illustrate some of the differences between them.

exe

xlist[(ii)]
(i)
cɯ-pʰɯt nɯ-βzu-t-a \\
stone-take.off aor -do- pst: tr - 1sg \\
(ii)
nɯ-ɣɯ-cɯ-pʰɯt-a \\
aor - denom -stone-take.off- 1sg \\
(iii)
cɯ nɯ-pʰɯt-t-a \\
stone aor -take.out- pst: tr - 1sg \\
xlist
`I cleared the stones [from the field].' (elicitation)
exe

The non-compounded construction (iii) is the only one that can occur if the argument is referential or takes a determiner (unlike languages like Hopi which allow determiners to have scope over an incorporated noun, see ). In the light verb construction with the action nominal compound cɯpʰɯttaking stones (out of the fields, before ploughing) (i) and the incorporating verb ɣɯcɯpʰɯttake out stones (ii), the bound nominal element cɯ- cannot be used to refer to specific stones that have been previously mentioned. A similar constraint is observed with other denominal verbs (§ sec:denominal.vs.light.verb ). The light verb construction (i) is used to highlight that an action takes a long time or effort, or occurs many times in this particular example.

The usage differences between (i)--(iii) in ( ex:cWphWt ) however are not generalizable to all incorporating verbs, in particular because the existence of an incorporating verb does not imply that the constructions in (i) and (iii) also exist, and because compounding is not always compositional. The triplet of constructions in ( ex:qharu2 ) with nɤqʰarulook back (§ sec:incorp.goal ), the compound qʰarulook back (§ sec:incorp.denom ) and the non-compounded construction with ɯ-qʰuafter, behind and rulook at, illustrate a different situation.

exe

(i)
ɯʑo nɯ, tatpa ta-ta ma qʰaru mucin ʑo mɯ-pa-lɤt nɤ tɤ-ari ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3sg dem faith aor:3 -put lnk look.back at.all emph neg - aor:3 -release add aor: up -go[II] sens -be \\
`He kept faith and did not look back at all and went up (did not fall down and reached the heavens).' (2005 Norbzang)
(ii)
tsʰoŋχpɯn nɤrɯβzaŋ ɯʑo mɯma ʑo pɯ-nɤ-qʰa-ru-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu, kɯ kɯ-tu ʑo pɯ-atɤr-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu, \\

`Apart from Tshong dpon Norbzang, they looked back, and all of them fell down.' (2005 Norbzang)
(iii.a)
ɯ-ʁrɯ nɯ ki tu-fse qʰe ɯ-qʰu ri lu-ru, \\
3sg. poss -horn dem dem. prox ipfv -be.like lnk 3sg. poss -behind loc ipfv: upstream -look \\
`Its horn is turned towards its back like that.' (20-RmbroN)
0003560#S99
(iii.b)
tɕʰeme nɯ lo-ɕe tɕe si ɯ-qʰu nɯtɕu lo-ru ri, \\
girl dem ifr: upstream -go lnk tree 3sg. poss -behind dem: loc ifr: upstream -look lnk \\
(150901 changfamei-zh)
`The girl went there and looked behind the tree.'(150901 changfamei-zh)
0006352#S207
(iii.c)
jo-ɕqʰlɤt-ndʑi tɕe, ndʑi-qʰu jo-ru ma nɯ ma ɯ-kɤpa pjɤ-me. \\
ifr -disappear- du lnk 3du. poss -behind ifr -look lnk dem apart.from 3sg. poss -manner ifr. ipfv -not.exist \\
`The two them disappeared, and the only thing she could do was looking at them from behind (at their back as they were going away).' (140506 shizi he huichang de bailingniao-zh)

The examples above show that the collocation of ɯ-qʰuafter, behind and rulook at is semantically quite different from the compound qʰarulook back and its corresponding denominal incorporating verb: its range of meanings includes `be turned behind, towards the back' (iii.a), `look behind $X$' (iii.b) or `look at $X$ from behind' (iii.c). The light verb construction (i) and the incorporating verb (ii) by contrast can only be used in the sense of `look back'. Unlike in ( ex:cWphWt ), the light verb construction (i) is not used to express either protracted or repeated action since qʰarulook back is semelfactive, but rather occurs in ( ex:qharu.mWpalAt ) to put more emphasis on the negation of the action (he did not look back in the slightest).

The contrast between the three constructions in ( ex:cWphWt ) and ( ex:qharu2 ) also has to do with the relative frequency of the verbal forms in which they appear. In particular, an important proportion of incorporating verbs in the corpus are subject participles (as in ex:qaZo.kWnWYAmkhe above) or generic forms (as in ex:lukWnAphWxtsW ).
summary:
Incorporating verbs can appear in the same contexts as the corresponding non-compounded constructions, both with noun+verb collocations and with action nominal compounds. However, the three related constructions are not fully equivalent: in some cases the non-compounded form is needed for referential or determiner-bearing nouns, while in others the light verb construction adds emphasis or highlights prolonged, repeated, or effortful action.  

The passage also shows that these differences are not uniform across all incorporating verbs, since some compounds are semantically noncompositional and the corresponding non-compounded construction may have a different meaning range. In addition, the distribution of these forms is affected by frequency, with many incorporating verbs in the corpus occurring as subject participles or generic forms.

text:
All finite verb forms in Japhug have one primary TAME (tense, aspect, modality, evidentiality) category, encoded by orientation preverbs (§ sec:preverb.TAME ), stem alternations (§ sec:stem.TAME ) and additional affixes in some cases (§ sec:other.TAME ). Primary TAME categories can be combined with secondary aspectual and modal prefixes (§ sec:second.aspect, § sec:second.modal ).

tab:primary.TAME summarizes the primary TAME categories in Japhug. Labels such as `Imperfective' or `Egophoric Present' are
conventional names for Japhug-specific morphological verbal categories, and therefore capitalized in this chapter and in the whole
grammar following the convention proposed by and others. The use of these terms makes no implication
that they have any crosslinguistic validity or that the Japhug categories are amenable to direct comparison with TAME categories in
other languages.

Apart from the Factual Non-Past, all primary TAME categories take one orientation preverb. Some categories, such as the Sensory, are marked by the same preverb on all verbs. Other categories select a preverb belonging to one of the four series (A, B, C or D, see tab:TAME.preverb below and sec:preverb.TAME, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), whose orientation is lexically specified by the verb (§ sec:lexicalized.orientation ).

Primary TAME categories in Japhug are divided into four groups: Non-Past (Factual, Egophoric Present, Sensory, § sec:TAME.npst ), Imperfective (which is mainly used in subordinate clauses or in periphrastic constructions, § sec:imperfective ), Past (Aorist, Inferential, § sec:TAME.pst ) and Modal (Imperative, Irrealis, Dubitative, § sec:TAME.modal ). This classification is based on both semantic and formal features, and is justified in each of the sections of this chapter.

In addition to the primary categories, periphrastic TAME categories are built by combining finite verbs with the copula ŋube. The main verb can be in the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ), § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic ), in the Factual Non-Past to express periphrastic Proximative (§ sec:proximative.periphrastic ) or in the Inferential (§ sec:ifr ). The use of the copula as postverbal TAME auxiliary should not be confused with its focalizing function (§ sec:focalization.final.copula ).
summary:
Japhug finite verbs have one primary TAME category, expressed through orientation preverbs, stem alternations, and sometimes additional affixes, and these primary categories can combine with secondary aspectual and modal prefixes. The primary TAME system is divided into four groups—Non-Past, Imperfective, Past, and Modal—and the labels used for categories such as “Imperfective” or “Egophoric Present” are language-specific morphological terms, not directly comparable crosslinguistically.  

Most primary categories take an orientation preverb, with some categories using a fixed preverb and others selecting one from lexically specified series, and periphrastic TAME forms are also built with the copula ŋube.

text: Some of the Primary TAME categories require the same preverb with all verbs (Egophoric Present, Sensory, Dubitative). The other categories (Imperfective, Aorist, Inferential, Irrealis, Imperative) only specify preverb type (§ sec:preverb.TAME.morphology ), while the orientation of the preverb is either lexically determined, or expresses spatial orientation (in the case of orientable verbs § sec:orientable.verbs ).
summary: Some Primary TAME categories use the same preverb with all verbs, specifically the Egophoric Present, Sensory, and Dubitative. By contrast, the Imperfective, Aorist, Inferential, Irrealis, and Imperative only determine the preverb type; its orientation is then either lexically fixed or, with orientable verbs, conveys spatial orientation.

text:
orientation!preverb
Orientation preverbs in Kamnyu Japhug come in four series, which contribute (in combination with other formatives and morphological devices) to mark TAME, transitivity and person. Each series comprises seven orientations, divided into Upper orientations (up, upstream, eastwards), Lower orientation (down, downstream, westwards) and unspecified orientation (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). Table tab:TAME.preverb lists the rules of preverb formation. The C- is the initial consonant of the preverb, which encodes the orientation: t- upwards, p- downwards, l- upstream, tʰ-/cʰ- downstream, k- eastwards, n-/ɲ- westwards and j- `unspecified'.

Upper vs. Lower orientation preverbs have a different vocalism (except for type C preverbs, whose vowel is neutralized to Ca- ), and type B and D lower orientation preverb have a palatalized onset, realized as cʰ- for downstream preverbs (rather than $ $ tʰj- ) and as ɲ- for westwards preverbs. A complete list of all preverbs in presented in tab:orientation.preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). Only types A and B are attested on non-finite forms (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes ).
summary: Kamnyu Japhug orientation preverbs are organized into four series and, together with other morphological devices, help mark TAME, transitivity, and person. Each series has seven orientations grouped into Upper, Lower, and unspecified, with consonantal and vocalic differences encoding direction; only types A and B occur on non-finite forms.

text:
ambiguity!orientation preverb
Type A preverbs occur with a wide range of TAME categories. In particular, Aorist and Imperative both select the type A preverb, without any additional prefix. A few ambiguous forms do exist in the case of intransitive verbs in particular: for instance, kɤ-rɤʑi with the type A eastwards preverb kɤ- and the verb rɤʑistay can either be analyzed as an 2sg imperative `stay!' or as a 3sg Aorist `he stayed'. However, four additional morphological marks can help disambiguate between the two categories in some contexts.

First, Aorist selects stem II (§ sec:stem2 ), and Imperative stem III (§ sec:stem3, § sec:stem.TAME ). Second, transitive verbs in Aorist take type C preverbs instead of type A. Third, the -t past tense suffix is found in the Aorist, but not in the Imperative (§ sec:other.TAME ). Fourth, the rules of vowel contraction (§ sec:contraction ) are different across TAME categories: the contracting vowel of the stem merges with the preverb as Ca- in the Aorist and Past Imperfective, and as Cɤ- in the Imperative and the Irrealis. For instance, a contrast can be observed between the 3sg Aorist kamdzɯ ( kɤ-amdzɯ, aor -sit) `s/he sat down' and the 2sg Imperative kɤmdzɯ ( kɤ-ɤmdzɯ, imp -sit) `sit!'.

Syncretism occurs in the cases of verbs whose lexical orientation is westwards and eastwards, the Imperfective of such verbs is identical to the Egophoric Present or Dubitative on the one hand, and the Sensory on the other hand (except in specific contexts, see § sec:neg.allomorphs, § sec:existential.basic ). For instance, the form ku-omdzɯ-a of the verb amdzɯsit, which takes the eastwards preverbs, can either be analyzed as Imperfective ( ipfv -sit- 1sg ) or Egophoric Present ( prs -sit- 1sg ) depending on the context.

Likewise, verbs selecting the downwards orientation have Aorist and Inferential forms that are identical to their Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective forms, respectively. Given the constraints on the occurrence of the non-periphrastic Past Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv ), however, such cases are much rarer.
summary: Type A preverbs occur with a wide range of TAME categories, including Aorist and Imperative, and some intransitive forms can be ambiguous between these two readings. This ambiguity can often be resolved by differences in stem choice, preverb type, the presence of the -t past tense suffix, and vowel-contraction patterns. The passage also notes syncretism in certain orientation classes: some verbs have Imperfective forms identical to Egophoric Present or Dubitative, and downwards-oriented verbs can show identical Aorist and Past Imperfective or Inferential and Inferential Imperfective forms.

text:
The Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective preverbs pɯ- and pjɤ- correspond to the downwards preverbs of series A and D, respectively. The grammaticalization process from `downward' orientation to imperfective has occurred (probably independently) in all core Gyalrong languages, and is discussed in detail in.

There are two additional less grammaticalized cases of orientations used with a specific aspectual meaning, and overriding the intrinsic orientation of the verb.

First, the downstream orientation occurs with stative verb to express progressive change of state occurring naturally, in particular to describe the growth of plants and animals (§ sec:preverb.adjectives.size ). This usage is common with the adverb ʑɯrɯʑɤriprogressively, and is observed across various TAME categories, including for instance the Inferential ( ex:chAmtshAt ), the Imperfective ( ex:chWwxti.YWCti, ex:chWGWrni ) and the Aorist ( ex:chWGWrni ). The verbs mtsʰɤtbe full, and wxtibe big normally select the upwards orientation (see example ex:Wkha.towxti, § sec:preverb.adjectives.size ), and ɣɯrnibe red the westwards orientation.

For instance, the negative existential verb menot exist (§ sec:preverb.loss ), whose intrinsic orientation is westwards, occurs with the upwards orientation as in ( ex:nWma.tAme ) in the meaning `when there is no...' without inchoative aspect `when... disappears' as is usually found in the Aorist (see also § sec:aor.temporal, ).

The passage also describes two less grammaticalized aspectual uses of orientation: downstream orientation with stative verbs can mark progressive change of state, especially for growth and gradual change, while upward orientation in the Aorist can override a verb’s lexical orientation to introduce a temporal reference in temporal clauses, as with “when there is no...” constructions.

text:
The Sensory ɲɯ- and Egophoric Present ku- markers correspond to the westwards and eastwards preverbs of series B, respectively. It is unlikely that a pair of preverbs encoding the solar dimension (§ sec:solar.dimension ) was directly grammaticalized to express an evidential contrast.

However, an extended function of the eastwards / westwards contrast is the expression of centripetal vs. centrifugal orientation (§ sec:centripetal.centrifugal ). The centripetal meaning of the eastwards orientation goes back at least to proto-Gyalrong, since it is attested in Situ, and the metaphorical use of centripetal/cislocative marker to express speaker affectedness could have been further grammaticalized as an egophoric marker.
summary: The Sensory ɲɯ- and Egophoric Present ku- markers are linked to the westwards and eastwards preverbs of series B, but it is unlikely that these preverbs were directly grammaticalized to mark an evidential contrast. Instead, the eastwards/westwards opposition also had an extended centripetal vs. centrifugal meaning, and the centripetal eastwards sense—attested as far back as proto-Gyalrong—may have been further developed into an egophoric marker through its association with speaker affectedness.

text:
stem alternation vowel!alternation
Stem alternation (§ sec:stem.alternation ) has a lower functional load than preverbs to encode TAME, since stem II is only attested on a handful of irregular verbs (§ sec:stem2 ) and stem III, although found on an important number of transitive verbs (§ sec:stem3.form ), is restricted to only a small subset of the paradigms, as it marks both TAME and person/number (§ sec:stem3.distribution ).

Three cases of systematic redundancy between stem alternation and orientation preverbs are observed. First, stem III alternation is redundant as a TAME marker (but not as a transitivity marker, § sec:transitivity.morphology ) with B type preverbs in the Imperfective, the Sensory and the Egophoric. Second, in 3 configurations, stem II and C type preverbs redundantly mark Aorist (§ sec:stem2 ). Third, stem III is redundant with the contrast between A and C type preverbs to distinguish between Imperfective and Aorist forms in the case of transitive verbs; taking ndzaeat as an example of an alternating transitive verb, its 2sg 3 Imperative tɤ-ndze `eat it!' (stem III, A preverb) differs from its 3sg Aorist ta-ndza `s/he ate it' (base stem, C preverb) by both the preverbs and the stems.

Since intransitive verbs lack the contrast between A and C type preverbs (and also stem III), stem II is the only clue to disambiguate between the third person Aorist and Imperative, which are both marked by A type preverbs: for instance, while non-alternating verbs such as rɤʑistay have ambiguity between these two forms (§ sec:ambiguity.preverb ), irregular alternating verbs such as ɕego make a clear distinction between Aorist 3sg ( jɤ-ari aor -go[II] `s/he went') and Imperative 2sg ( jɤ-ɕe imp -go `go!') and the corresponding dual and plural forms. It is the only case when stem alternation is critical for distinguishing between two TAME categories.
summary: Stem alternation has a lower functional load than preverbs in marking TAME, because stem II occurs only in a few irregular verbs and stem III is limited in distribution and also encodes person/number. The passage identifies three kinds of redundancy between stem alternation and orientation preverbs, but notes that for intransitive verbs stem II is crucial in one specific case: it is the only way to distinguish 3rd person Aorist from Imperative when both use A-type preverbs.

text:
Aside from preverbs and stem alternation, there are a few formatives used to mark primary TAME categories.

The negative prefixes (slot -5, § sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) have different forms depending on TAME categories, and one of them, the Sensory Negative mɯ́j- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ) is a portmanteau encoding both polarity and TAME.

The Past Transitive -t (slot +1, -z in some dialects of Japhug, § sec:suffixes ) is a secondary exponent of some TAME categories, only found in the 1/2sg 3 person configurations (§ sec:indexation.mixed ) of Aorist, Perfective and Imperfective Inferential, Past Imperfective (§ sec:TAME.pst ) and Apprehensive (§ sec:apprehensive.morphology ), unless the Progressive asɯ- is also present (§ sec:progressive.morphology ).

The prefix a- in slot -6 (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) is the main marker of the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.morphology ), together with type A preverbs and (when applicable) stem III.

Secondary TAME categories (§ sec:second.aspect, § sec:second.modal ) are encoded by several prefixes in slots -6 and one in -1 (the Progressive § sec:progressive ).
summary: Besides preverbs and stem alternation, several formatives mark primary TAME categories. Negative prefixes vary by TAME, and the Sensory Negative mɯ́j- is a portmanteau expressing both polarity and TAME; the Past Transitive suffix -t/-z is a secondary exponent used in certain person configurations of several TAME categories, with an exception when the Progressive is present. The prefix a- is the main marker of the Irrealis, and secondary TAME categories are expressed by several prefixes in slot -6 and one in -1.

text:
person!evidentiality
As in many languages with evidential systems, person and evidentiality present some degree of interaction in Japhug.

The Sensory (§ sec:sensory ) and Inferential (§ sec:ifr ) have restrictions on the use of first person in declarative clauses. First person subjects are not impossible, but have very specific meanings (see § sec:sensory.person and § sec:inf.1person ).

The Egophoric Present, on the other hand, is not compatible with second person in declarative clauses, and with first person in interrogative ones.

Like most languages of the Tibetosphere, interrogative sentences generally adopt the perspective of the addressee rather than that of the speaker, causing a phenomenon referred to as `anticipation rule'  or `flipping': the speaker anticipates the answer of the addressee and uses the form that he expect the addressee will choose to respond to the question. For instance, in example ( ex:WtWsWz ), the speaker uses the Factual because she expects and answer with the Factual such as sɯz-a (know: fact - 1sg ) `I know'.

exe

nɤj ɯ-tɯ́-sɯz? \\
2sg qu -2-know: fact \\
`Do you know it?' (19 GzW) 0003536#S8
exe

As a result of this change of perspective, compatibilities between evidential markers and first vs. second person are always reversed between declarative and interrogative sentences (§ sec:egophoric.interrogative ).

The addressee perspective however is not a syntactic rule. The addressee is free to adopt the evidential form suggested by the speaker who asked the question, or to choose another form if he sees fit: see for an account of this phenomenon in Tibetan. It is also possible to have in the same question two verbs referring to the addressee with the Egophoric Present in one case and the Sensory in the other, as in ( ex:WkutWpe ).

exe

wo, ɯ-kú-tɯ-pe, ɯ-ɲɯ́-tɯ-cʰa? \\
interj qu - egoph -2-be.good qu - sens -2-be.fine \\
`Are you feeling well, are you fine?' (140425 shizi huli he lu-zh)
exe
summary: In Japhug, person and evidentiality interact in specific ways: the Sensory and Inferential have restrictions on first-person subjects in declarative clauses, while the Egophoric Present is incompatible with second person in declaratives and with first person in interrogatives. In questions, Japhug generally follows the Tibetosphere “anticipation rule,” adopting the addressee’s perspective so that person–evidential compatibility is reversed between declarative and interrogative clauses, though this is not a strict syntactic rule and speakers may vary in the evidential forms they use.

text:
Imperfective
The Imperfective is one of the most common finite verb forms in Japhug, but rarely appears on its own without an auxiliary verb. It mainly occurs in periphrastic TAME constructions (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ) and subordinate clauses (§ sec:ipfv.temporal, § sec:ipfv.complement ). A specific hortative function (§ sec:ipfv.hortative ) has developed from its use in complement clauses with a modal auxiliary. In addition, verbs of perceptions are used in the Imperfective in specific contexts (§ sec:ipfv.perception ).
summary: The Imperfective is a very common finite verb form in Japhug, but it rarely appears by itself and usually occurs with an auxiliary. It is mainly found in periphrastic TAME constructions and subordinate clauses, and it has also developed a hortative use from complement clauses with a modal auxiliary. Verbs of perception can also appear in the Imperfective in certain contexts.

text:
The Imperfective selects type B preverbs (§ sec:preverb.TAME.morphology, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), and stem III (§ sec:stem3.form, § sec:stem.TAME ) when appropriate. The preverb orientation is not neutralized. tab:ipfv:example.33tr shows the Imperfective 3sg and 3pl forms of some transitive verbs, illustrating all six orientation preverbs and alternation between stem III (in 3sg ) and stem I (in 3pl ).

tab:ipfv.paradigms presents the Imperfective paradigms of the transitive verb ndzaeat ( upwards ) and of the intransitive contracting verb amdzɯsit ( eastwards ), with vowel contracting of the preverb and the vowel of the stem in the first and third person subject forms.

Verbs selecting the eastwards or westwards orientation (§ sec:solar.dimension, § sec:centripetal.centrifugal, § sec:lexicalized.orientation ) present syncretism between Imperfective on the one hand, and Egophoric Present or Sensory on the other hand. For instance, the 3sg form ɲɯ-sɯsɤm of the verb sɯsothink (which requires the westwards preverbs), can either be Imperfective or Sensory (§ sec:sensory.morphology, § sec:ipfv.inchoative ). Similarly, the 1sg forms ku-rɤʑi-a and ku-omdzɯ-a of the verbs rɤʑistay and amdzɯsit (whose lexical orientation is eastwards, see tab:ipfv.paradigms ), can be Imperfective or Egophoric Present (§ sec:egophoric.morphology ).

Verbs selecting other orientations do not have such ambiguity; for instance, the verb rɤmawork (selecting upwards orientation) has different Imperfective, Egophoric Present and Sensory forms: tu-rɤma, ku-rɤma and ɲɯ-rɤma, respectively.
summary:
The Imperfective uses type B preverbs and, when relevant, stem III; the preverb orientation remains distinct rather than being neutralized. In transitive verbs, the paradigms show all six orientation preverbs and alternation between stem III in 3sg and stem I in 3pl, while some intransitive contracting verbs show vowel contraction between the preverb and stem in first- and third-person forms.

Verbs with eastwards or westwards orientation show syncretism between the Imperfective and either the Egophoric Present or the Sensory, so the same form can have more than one interpretation. Verbs with other orientations do not show this ambiguity and instead have clearly distinct Imperfective, Egophoric Present, and Sensory forms.

text:
Imperfective!periphrastic
Periphrastic TAME categories with a main verb in the Imperfective are used to express habitual or ongoing actions. In these constructions, the main verb expresses person/number and aspect, while the copula encodes tense, modality and evidentiality.

The examples in ( ex:tundze.periphrastic ) (with the verb ndzaeat in the 3sg configuration) illustrate attested possibilities. With a copula in the Factual Non-Past ŋu ( ex:tundze.Nu ) or in the Sensory ɲɯ-ŋu ( ex:tundze.YWNu ), the periphrastic construction has a non-past meaning with an evidential contrast between non-Sensory and Sensory (there is no Periphrastic Egophoric). When the copula is in the Past Imperfective pɯ-ŋu or in the Inferential Imperfective pjɤ-ŋu, the interpretation is that of a past habitual `used to $X$' or a Past progressive (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic ). Additional periphrastic constructions are also attested with Secondary Modal prefixes on the copula (§ sec:second.modal ).

ipfv -eat[III] be: fact \\
`S/he/it eats/is eating it.' (Periphrastic Imperfective)

ipfv -eat[III] sens -be \\
`S/he/it eats/is eating it.' (Periphrastic Sensory)

tu-ndze pɯ-ŋu \\
ipfv -eat[III] pst. ipfv -be \\
`S/he/it used to eat/was eating it.' (Periphrastic Past Imperfective)

tu-ndze pjɤ-ŋu \\

`S/he/it used to eat/was eating it.' (Periphrastic Inferential Imperfective)

tu-ndze a-pɯ-ŋu \\
ipfv -eat[III] irr - ipfv -be \\
`If s/he eats it...' (Periphrastic Irrealis)
