summary: Periphrastic constructions with an Imperfective main verb are used to express habitual or ongoing actions, with the main verb marking person/number and aspect and the copula encoding tense, modality, and evidentiality. Depending on the copula, these forms can have non-past sensory or non-sensory meanings, past habitual or past progressive meanings, irrealis conditionals, and they may also express imminent future. The copula never takes person/number or associated motion marking; negation is formed with a suppletive negative copula, and multiple imperfective verbs can share one final copula in a verb chain.

The existence of Periphrastic TAME categories, in addition to the primary and secondary categories, makes the Japhug TAME system extremely complex. At the present stage of my knowledge of the language, the semantic differences between some categories still eludes me.

For instance, the (Primary) Sensory and the Periphrastic Sensory can both express habitual or generic actions, as in ( ex:YWndze.tundze ) where both forms appear redundantly (with tail-head linkage, § sec:tail.head.linkeage ).

It gives examples showing that primary and periphrastic Sensory forms can both express habitual or generic actions, and that postverbal copulas used in periphrastic TAME constructions can also function as focus markers.

Chains of verbs in the Imperfective without subordinating relation, but possibly sharing a tense-marking copula, can indicate a succession of events, as in ( ex:chain.pjANu ) above. The Imperfective also occurs in subordinate temporal clauses expressing precedence or simultaneous action.

Temporal clauses of temporal precedence headed by the postposition ɕɯŋgɯbefore (§ sec:temporal.postpositions, § sec:precedence.CWNgW, ) require the Imperfective, to the exclusion of all other finite and non-finite verb forms. In ( ex:lufsoR.CWNgW ) and ( ex:kulAt.CWNgW ) for instance, only lu-fsoʁ and ku-lɤt can occur with ɕɯŋgɯ, and neither infinitive (§ sec:inf ) or Aorist forms (§ sec:aor ) are possible, regardless of the TAME form of the verb of the main clause (Inferential in ex:lufsoR.CWNgW, Past Imperfective in ex:kulAt.CWNgW ).

`The next day, before the day broke, he went (there) and did like [she had said].' (28-smAnmi)

However, unlike ɕɯŋgɯ, ɯ-kʰɯkʰa does not select the Imperfective and other finite TAME forms are possible (§ sec:simultaneity ).

`I will teach you (how to weave) and weave at the same time.' (elicited)
exe

exe

qʰe ɯ-pɯ tɯ-nɯ ɲɯ-jtsʰi ɯ-kʰɯkʰa, ɯ-ku kɯra tu-ste tɕe zrɯɣ ra pjɯ-re ɲɯ-ŋu. tɕe zrɯɣ nɯra tu-ndze ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -young indef. poss -breast ipfv -give.to.drink 3sg. poss -while 3sg. poss -head dem. prox: pl ipfv -do.like[III] lnk louse pl ipfv -pick.off[III] sens -be lnk louse dem: pl ipfv -eat[III] sens -be \\
`While [the monkey mother] nurses her baby, she does this to its head at the same time and picks lice off. Then she eats the lice.' (19-GzW)
0003536#S36
exe
summary: Chains of Imperfective verbs without a subordinating relation can express a sequence of events, sometimes with a shared tense-marking copula. The Imperfective is also required in subordinate temporal clauses of precedence headed by ɕɯŋgɯ “before,” where no other finite or non-finite verb forms are allowed, whereas clauses with ɯ-kʰɯkʰa “while” use the Imperfective for simultaneous action but also permit other finite TAME forms.

text:
The Imperfective is common in complement clauses, in particular with modal verbs. In such clauses, no auxiliary copula is required.

Imperfective occurs in S-complement clauses with modal verbs such as rabe needed, `be necessary' ( ex:pjWwGsat.YWra, ex:pjWtWGi.mAra ), jɤɣbe allowed ( ex:tukWqura.WjAG ), ntsʰihave better and kʰɯbe possible.

exe

atu pɣɤtɕɯ nɯ pjɯ́-wɣ-sat ɲɯ-ra \\
up.there bird dem ipfv - inv -kill sens -be.needed \\
`We have to kill the bird upstairs.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

exe

pjɯ-tɯ-ɣi mɤ-ra \\
ipfv: down -2-come neg -be.needed: fact \\
`You don't have to come down (with us).' (heard in context)
exe

exe

tu-kɯ-qur-a ɯ́-jɤɣ \\
ipfv -2 1-help- 1sg qu -be.possible: fact \\
`Could you help me?' (150901 dongguo xiansheng he lang-zh)
0006336#S32
exe

The aspectual auxiliary ŋgrɤlbe usually the case (§ sec:NgrAl ) most often selects a complement in the Imperfective, expressing recurring actions or situations, as in ( ex:tuBze.pjANgrAl ).

exe

qala kɯ nɯra kɯ-fse βlaβlu tu-βze pjɤ-ŋgrɤl. \\
hare erg dem: pl sbj: pcp -be.like trick ipfv -do[ILI] ifr. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`The hare used to do tricks like that.' (31-qala)
0004081#S78
exe

The Imperfective is also found in object or semi-object complement clauses with modal verbs such as spabe able ( ex:YWkrAm.mWjspe ) or cʰacan (example ex:YWnWqambWmbjom.tocha, § sec:ifr.inchoative ).

exe

ɲɯ-krɤm mɯ́j-spe qhe, tɕendɤre nɯnɯ ɯ-pɯ tɯ-rdoʁ nɯ kɯ [...] tu-nɯ-ndɤm qʰe, ɯʑo stɯsti ʑo tu-nɯ-ndze ɲɯ-ŋu \\
ipfv -share[III] neg: sens -be.able[III] lnk lnk dem 3sg. poss -young one-piece dem erg ipfv - auto -take[III] lnk 3sg alone emph ipfv - auto -eat[III] sens -be \\
`[The mother cat] does not know how to share (the food she has brought for her kitten equally), one of the kitten takes [it all] and eats it alone (without giving anything to its mother or the other kittens).' (21-lWLU)
0003576#S76
exe

Imperfective complement clauses are found with main verbs in all primary TAME categories, including perfective ones like the Inferential ( ex:YWnWqambWmbjom.tocha, § sec:ifr.inchoative ) or the Aorist.
summary: The Imperfective is common in complement clauses, especially with modal verbs, and in these clauses no auxiliary copula is needed. It appears in S-complements with verbs meaning ‘be necessary,’ ‘be allowed,’ ‘have better,’ and ‘be possible,’ as well as in object or semi-object complements with verbs like ‘be able,’ and it also occurs with main verbs in all major TAME categories, including perfective forms such as the Inferential and Aorist.

text:
Imperfective!hortative
The Imperfective used without any copula or auxiliary can have a hortative meaning similar to the one it has when combined with a modal auxiliary such as rabe needed or ntsʰihave better (§ sec:ipfv.complement ).

The hortative function occurs in first person subject forms, with either transitive or intransitive verbs ( ex:kuZGACthWza ).

exe

ku-ʑɣɤɕtʰɯz-a ma zdɯxpa \\
ipfv -reveal.one's.true.nature- 1sg lnk poor \\
`Let me show him who I am, poor him.' (2003kandzwsqhaj)
exe

It is also found instead of the Imperative in the 2 1 configurations ( ex:kukWnAjoa, ex:jukWtsWma, ex:YWkWmbia.ma, ex:YWkWsWBzJWra ), since the Imperative only allows 2 3 forms (§ sec:imp.morphology ).

exe

ku-kɯ-nɤjo-a je \\
ipfv -2 1-wait- 1sg sfp \\
`Wait for me!' (heard in context)
exe

exe

ju-kɯ-tsɯm-a wo, a-wi \\
ipfv -2 1-take.away- 1sg sfp 1sg. poss -grandmother \\
`Take me away with you, grandmother!' (140519 mai huochai de xiao nvhai-zh) 0004036#S151
exe

exe

nɯ-me ɲɯ-kɯ-mbi-a-nɯ ma aʑo-sti kɤ-nɯ-ɕe mɤ-cʰa-a \\
3pl. poss -daughter ipfv -2 1-give- 1sg - pl lnk 1sg -alone inf - vert -go neg -can: fact - 1sg \\
`Give me your daughter, I cannot go back there alone.' (02-deluge2012)
0003376#S101
exe

exe

ɯ-ɲɯ-nɯkɯmaʁ-a nɤ ɲɯ-kɯ-sɯ-βzɟɯr-a \\
qu - ipfv -make.a.mistake- 1sg add ipfv -2 1- caus -correct- 1sg \\
`If I make a mistake (when speaking), correct me.' (elicited)
exe

The hortative meaning of the Imperfective occurs in three main contexts: (i) when the clause containing the verb in the Imperfective followed by a causal clause, with the linker ma in between, as in ( ex:kuZGACthWza ) and ( ex:YWkWmbia.ma ); (ii) when the verb is followed by the sentence final particle wo (§ sec:fsp.imp ), as in ( ex:jukWtsWma ); (iii) in the apodosis of conditional constructions ( ex:YWkWsWBzJWra ).
summary: The Imperfective can express a hortative meaning even without a copula or auxiliary, similar to its use with modal auxiliaries. This hortative function appears with first-person subjects and also in 2→1 forms where the Imperative is unavailable, and it occurs mainly in three contexts: before a causal clause with the linker *ma*, with the sentence-final particle *wo*, or in the apodosis of conditional constructions.

text:
Imperfective!inchoative
With stative verbs, like the Aorist (§ sec:aor ) and the Inferential (§ sec:ifr ) the Imperfective always expresses ongoing change, whether it appears in main clauses in a Periphrastic tense ( ex:chWwGrum.YWNu ), or in a complement clause ( ex:chWmACWndZi ).

exe

tʰɯ-tɯt ri tɕe cʰɯ-wɣrum ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
aor -be.ripe lnk lnk ipfv -be.white sens -be \\
`When it ripens, it becomes white.' (16-CWrNgo)
0003518#S156
exe

exe

nɯ kɯnɤ cʰɯ-mɤɕi-ndʑi mɯ-pjɤ-cʰa-ndʑi \\
dem also ipfv -be.rich- du neg - ifr. ipfv -can- du \\
`Despite [their hard work], they could not become rich. (divination 2003)
exe

This inchoative meaning often appears with initial reduplication of gradual increase (§ sec:redp.gradual.increase ), as in ( ex:tWtumpCAr.Zo.Nu ).

exe

ʑɯrɯʑɤri tɕe tɕendɤre ɯ-skɤt nɯ tɯ tu-mpɕɤr ʑo ŋu \\
progressively lnk lnk 3sg. poss -voice dem incr ipfv -be.beautiful emph be: fact \\
`(As the rooster grows bigger), its voice progressively becomes more and more beautiful.' (22-kumpGa)
0003588#S69
exe

Verbs selecting the westwards or eastwards preverbs as intrinsic orientations have syncretism between Imperfective on the one hand, and Sensory or Egophoric Present on the other hand (§ sec:ipfv.morphology ). For instance, the form ɲɯ-ɲaʁ is (inchoative) Imperfective in ( ex:YWYaR.Zo.Nu ), and (stative) Sensory in ( ex:kW.YWYaR ) (illustrating the comparative use of the Sensory, § sec:sensory.other ). The only formal difference between them is the presence of the auxiliary ŋu in ( ex:YWYaR.Zo.Nu ).

exe

pɯ-rom tɕe tɕe ɲɯ-ɲaʁ ʑo ŋu \\
aor -be.dry lnk lnk ipfv -be.black emph be: fact \\
`When [the puffball mushroom] dries, it becomes black.' (22-BlamajmAG)
0003584#S71
exe

exe

tɕe ɯ-jme nɯnɯ kɯ ɲɯ-ɲaʁ \\
lnk 3sg. poss -tail dem erg sens -be.black \\
`It tail is blacker.' (23-qapGAmtWmtW)
0003608#S58
exe
summary: With stative verbs, the Imperfective expresses an inchoative meaning, i.e. ongoing change, whether in main clauses or complement clauses. This meaning is often associated with initial reduplication marking gradual increase, and some verbs with westward or eastward preverbs show syncretism between Imperfective and Sensory/Egophoric Present forms, distinguished only by the auxiliary ŋu in the Imperfective.

text:
verb!perception
The verbs rtoʁlook and sɤŋolisten, which normally express volitional perception, occur in the Imperfective in an unusual construction which has three main characteristics.

First, the object or semi-object (§ sec:semi.tr.labile ) of the verb is non-overt, and cataphorically refers to the immediately following clause(s), which describe(s) the perceived event, as in ( ex:kurtoRnW.ipfv ). These clauses are in coordinating relationship with the clause of the perception verb, and are not subordinate complement clauses (§ sec:coordination.comp.str ).

exe

ɯ-zda ra kɯ ku-rtoʁ-nɯ tɕe, [nɯnɯ rdɤstaʁ ɲɤ-k-ɤβzu rcanɯ], wuma ʑo pjɤ-ɲɟɤt-nɯ. \\
3sg. poss -companion pl erg ipfv -look- pl lnk dem stone ifr - peg -become- peg unexp: deg really emph ifr -regret- pl \\
`His companion saw that he had been turned to stone, and regretted very much [not having trusted him].' (150902 hailibu-zh)
0006316#S145
exe

Second, despite having an Imperfective form, the verbs can express a semelfactive perception (note in particular the presence of the adverb ʁlɤwɯrsuddenly in ex:RlAwWr.kurtoR below), rather than an ongoing or recurrent perception when the following clause is in the Aorist or in the Inferential (as in ex:kurtoRnW.ipfv, ex:RlAwWr.kurtoR, ex:YWsANo.ipfv and ex:kurtoR.ipfv below)

exe

spjaŋkɯ kɯ ʁlɤwɯr ʑo ku-rtoʁ tɕe, kʰɯna ɣɯ ɯ-mke nɯtɕu ʁmazgrɯβ ci pjɤ-mto ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
wolf erg suddenly emph ipfv -look lnk dog gen 3sg. poss -neck dem: loc scar indef ifr -see sens -be \\
`The wolf suddenly saw [that there was] a scar on the dog's neck.' (140426 jiagou he lang-zh)
0003804#S37
exe

Third, the perception is non-volitional: the verbs in this construction can be translated as `notice' (of something unexpected), as shown by the fact that the verb of non-volitional perception mtosee occurs in the following clause in ( ex:RlAwWr.kurtoR ) to redundantly express the same perception event as ku-rtoʁ.

The clauses referring to the perceived event (shown in square brackets below) in the Inferential either express actions that had taken place before the perception event, and whose results only are perceptible (§ ex:kurtoRnW.ipfv, § ex:kurtoR.ipfv ), or actions that are immediately perceived as they occur (§ ex:YWsANo.ipfv ).

exe

a-wa kɯ-rɯjɤɣɤt ɲɤ-ɕe ri, ɲɯ-sɤŋo tɕe, [ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu tɯrme ci ɲɤ-ɣi] \\
1sg. poss -father sbj: pcp -go.to.toilets ifr: west -go lnk ipfv -listen lnk 3sg. poss -up dem: loc man indef ifr: west -come \\
`My father had gone to the bathroom, and heard someone coming upstairs.' (08-kWqhi)
0003454#S10
exe

The cataphoric object of the perception verb can comprise more than one clause, as shown by ( ex:kurtoR.ipfv ).

exe

iɕqʰa kɯ-nɯɕɤlɤmbɯmbjom nɯ cʰɤ-sta, [...] tɕendɤre ku-rtoʁ tɕe, [ɯ-tɯ-ci ri pjɤ-lwoʁ tɕe, tɕendɤre iɕqʰa nɯ, tɤɕime nɯ ri kɯ-ɤrqʰɯ rqʰi ʑo jo-nɯ-ɕe ɕti] tɕe, \\
the.aforementioned sbj: pcp -racing dem ifr -wake.up lnk ipfv -look lnk 3sg. poss - indef. poss -water also ifr -spill lnk lnk filler dem lady dem also sbj: pcp - emph be.far emph ifr - auto -go be. aff: fact lnk \\
`The racer woke up, and saw that his water had been spilled, and that the princess had already gone far away.' (140505 liuhaohan zoubian tianxia-zh)
0003913#S121
exe

In this construction, the Imperfective forms ku-rtoʁ and ɲɯ-sɤŋo can also refer to generic or recurrent events if the following clause is in the Imperfective too, as in example ( ex:chain.pjANu ) above (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ).

The Imperfective of perception should be distinguished from the regular uses of the perception verbs rtoʁlook and sɤŋolisten in the Imperfective. In ( ex:kuwGrtoR.tCe ) and ( ex:kurtoRa.YWnaXCtWGndZi ) for instance, the direct objects of the verb rtoʁ do not cataphorically refer to the following clause, but rather to concrete entities (the leopard's head in ex:kuwGrtoR.tCe, two birds in ex:kurtoRa.YWnaXCtWGndZi ), and there is no non-volitional perception interpretation.

exe

tɕe kɯrtsɤɣ nɯnɯ ɯ-ku nɯnɯ kú-wɣ-rtoʁ tɕe, lɯlu tsa ɯ-tsʰɯɣa fse, \\
lnk leopard dem 3sg. poss -head dem ipfv - inv -look lnk cat a.little 3sg. poss -shape be.like: fact \\
`Looking at the leopard's head, it seems a bit like that of the cat.' (27-qartshAz)
0003702#S159
exe

exe

aʑo ndɤre ku-rtoʁ-a ɲɯ-naχtɕɯɣ-ndʑi ɕti. \\
1sg lnk ipfv -look- 1sg sens -be.the.same- du be. aff: fact \\
`[When] I look at them (i.e. two species of birds), they look the same.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S5
exe

The verb rulook at occurs in construction similar to that described above for rtoʁlook and sɤŋolisten (§ sec:coordination.comp.str ) as in ( ex:kArqhi.jukWru ), but it keeps its volitional meaning and is not exclusively found in the Imperfective.

exe

ŋɤqa kɤ-ti ci tu tɕe, kɯ-ɤrqʰi ju-kɯ-ru tɕe, [salaboŋboŋ tsa fse]. \\
mushroom.sp obj: pcp -say indef exist: fact lnk sbj: pcp -be.far ipfv - genr:S/O-look.at lnk puffball a.little be.like: fact \\
`There is [a mushroom] called ŋɤqa (cow's foot), when one looks at it from far away, it is a bit like a puffball.' (22-BlamajmAG)
0003584#S79
exe
summary:
The Imperfective forms of the perception verbs rtoʁ ‘look’ and sɤŋo ‘listen’ can be used in a special construction where the verb has a non-overt object that cataphorically refers to following clause(s) describing the perceived event. In this construction, the following clauses are coordinated rather than subordinated, and the perception is non-volitional and often semelfactive, with the perceived event either preceding the perception or being noticed as it happens.

This use should be distinguished from ordinary Imperfective uses of these verbs, where the object refers to a concrete entity and no non-volitional “notice” interpretation is involved. A similar construction exists with rulook at, but that verb retains its volitional meaning and is not restricted to the Imperfective.

text:
tense!non-past
This section discusses Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ), Sensory (§ sec:sensory ) and Egophoric Present (§ sec:egophoric ), three TAME categories which have two commonalities. First, they almost always occur in sentences referring to Non-Past events (one exception is discussed in § sec:sensory.functions ). Second, they do not have an inchoative meaning when used with stative verbs, unlike the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.inchoative ). Like the Imperfective and the Modal categories, they select stem III in transitive direct configurations with singular subject and third person object (§ sec:stem3.distribution ).

Minimal pairs between these three categories can be found in specific contexts, and the tripartite evidential contrast between them is discussed in § sec:egophoric.tripartite.
summary: The passage discusses three TAME categories—Factual Non-Past, Sensory, and Egophoric Present—that are usually used for non-past events and do not take on an inchoative meaning with stative verbs, unlike the Imperfective. Like the Imperfective and Modal categories, they select stem III in transitive direct configurations with a singular subject and third-person object. Minimal pairs among the three appear in certain contexts, and their three-way evidential contrast is treated elsewhere.

text: Factual Non-Past
summary: The passage introduces the category “Factual Non-Past.” It does not provide further details beyond naming this grammatical category.

text:
The Factual is the only finite TAME category in Japhug without an orientation preverb and any other prefix in slot -3. The term Factual', taken from Oisel's ( oisel13aux) study of modern Lhasa Tibetan, corresponds to the category referred to as `assertive' in older publications on Tibetan languages (Lhasa Tibetan yod.pa.red ). In the case of verbs without stem III alternation (i.e. transitive verbs with a non-alternating rhyme and intransitive verbs), it is realized as the bare stem. It selects the negative prefix mɤ- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ).

Complete paradigms of transitive and intransitive verbs in the Factual Non-Past are presented in § sec:polypersonal, and need not be repeated here.

In spite of the absence of overt marking for most verbs, the gloss fact is nevertheless always specified on verbs in the Factual in this grammar, whether or not stem alternation occurs. This gloss is marked as a suffix (verb: fact ), rather than as a prefix, to avoid confusion with derivational prefixes, since suffixes (§ sec:suffixes are fewer than prefixes (§ sec:prefixal.chain ), and also because stem III, which occurs in Factual singular subject forms, is suffixal in origin (§ sec:stem3.form ).

The formation of the Factual is regular. However, the copula ŋube lacks an Egophoric Present form ($ $ ku-ŋu-a is not accepted, see § sec:egophoric ), and it thus appears that the preverbless forms of this verb are syncretic, analyzable either as Factual or Egophoric Present (however, no attempt will be made at distinguishing those two categories in the glosses).

A few verbs, such as kɤtɯpatell and mɤ-xsione does not know, cannot take orientation preverbs and are only attested in the Factual (§ sec:irregular.transitive ).

Due to the absence of orientation preverbs, vowel contraction with prefixes located before slot -3 (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) only occur in first or third person forms of the Factual (§ sec:contraction ). Otherwise, contracting verbs surface with initial a- in Factual Non-Past non-negative form.
summary: The Factual is the only finite TAME category in Japhug that lacks an orientation preverb and any other prefix in slot -3, and for verbs without stem III alternation it is realized as the bare stem. Although most Factual forms show no overt marking, the grammar always glosses them as fact, and the category is regularly formed with the negative prefix mɤ-; some verbs, such as the copula ŋube and a few others, show special or syncretic behavior. The lack of orientation preverbs also affects vowel contraction, which occurs only in first- or third-person Factual forms, while other contracting verbs appear with initial a- in the non-negative Factual Non-Past.

text:
The Factual has two main functions when used in an independent clause without an auxiliary verb.

First, in the case of stative verbs, the Factual occurs to describe facts considered to belong to everybody's common knowledge. Example ( ex:kumpGAtCW ) illustrates five verb forms in the Factual in this use (highlighted in bold), including copulas and adjectives.

exe

tɕe kumpɣɤtɕɯ nɯnɯ pɣɤtɕɯ nɯ-rca, kɯ-xtɕi ci zdoʁzdoʁ ŋu tɕe, ɯʑo xtɕi ri wuma ʑo ɕqraʁ tɕe ɯ-mɲaʁ ɯ-rkɯ nɯnɯ ra kɯ-ɲaʁ kɯ tú-wɣ-fskɤr, nɯ ɯ-taʁ ri, hanɯni, kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi kɯ-ɣɯrni kɯ-fse tu, ɯ-xtɤpa nɯ ra, ɯ-rqopa pjɯ-ʑe tɕe, nɯ ra, ɯ-jme mɯ-tʰɯ-nɯ-ɬoʁ mɤɕtʂa nɯ wɣrum \\
lnk sparrow dem bird 3pl -among sbj: pcp -be.small indef ideo: stat:small.and.cute be: fact lnk 3sg be.small: fact but really emph be.smart: fact lnk 3sg: poss -eye 3sg: poss -border dem pl sbj: pcp -be.black erg ipfv - inv -surround dem 3sg -on loc a.little sbj: pcp - emph be.small sbj: pcp -be.red sbj: pcp -be.like exist: fact 3sg: poss -belly dem pl 3sg: poss -throat ipfv -begin[III] lnk dem pl 3sg: poss -tail neg - aor - auto -come.out until dem be.white: fact \\
`Among the birds, the sparrow is tiny and cute. Although it is small it is very smart. Its eyes are surrounded by black [feathers], and above that there are some red [dots]. Its belly is white from the throat to the tail.' (22 kumpGatCW)
0003590#S3
exe

The Imperfective cannot occur in this function with stative verbs, since it has an inchoative meaning (§ sec:ipfv.inchoative ). With dynamic verbs however, the Imperfective does occur to express general knowledge, especially in generic forms (as in tú-wɣ-fskɤr ipfv - inv -surround `it surrounds it' above) or with a dummy subject (S/A) ( pjɯ-ʑe ipfv -begin[III] `it begins' above).

The Factual also is also found in this function with dynamic verbs, in particular when the subjects are overt and/or definite, as in ( ex:mAndze ). The Imperfective would also be possible here, however.

exe

ɯ-ku kɯ-mpɯ nɯ ɲɯ́-wɣ-pʰɯt tɕe, nɯŋa ra kɯ ndza-nɯ, paʁ kɯ mɤ-ndze \\
3sg. poss -head sbj: pcp -be.soft dem ipfv - inv -pluck lnk cow pl erg eat: fact - pl pig erg neg -eat: fact \\
` One plucks the [leaves] on the extremities, the soft ones, cows eat it, pigs don't.' (06 qaZmbri)
0003416#S19
exe

Second, with dynamic verbs, the Factual can express immediate future. In assertive sentences with first person subject ( ex:WqhWqhu.Gia ), or in interrogative sentences with second person subjects ( ex:tWGi ), the Factual can be interpreted as indicating the intention to perform an action.

exe

ŋotɕu tɯ-ɕe nɤ-qʰɯ qʰu ɣi-a, nɤ-ŋga nɤ-xtsa fkur-a \\
where 2-go: fact 2sg. poss - emph after come: fact - 1sg 2sg. poss -clothes 2sg. poss -shoes carry: fact - 1sg \\
`Wherever you go, I will go after you, I will carry your clothes and your shoes.' (26-kWlAGpopo)
exe

exe

mbarkʰom tʰɤjtɕu tɯ-ɣi? \\
Mbarkham when 2-come:: fact \\
`When are you coming to Mbarkham?' (Conversation 2014)
exe

The Factual can also be used to express non-intentional future events when the speaker has reasonable reasons for assuming that they will take place as in ( ex:GWsata ).

exe

si-a ɲɤ-sɯso, tʰa ɣɯ-sat-a ɲɤ-sɯso \\
die: fact - 1sg ifr -think in.a.moment inv -kill: fact - 1sg ifr -think \\
`He thought ``I will die", he thought ``It will kill me".' (Buxiejiang gaizuo yisheng-zh)
exe

Verbs in the Factual in this function can be combined with the affirmative copula ɕtibe ( ex:Gi.Cti ) to emphasize the certainty that the action will take place.

exe

tɕetʰa ɣi ɕti ma, sɲikuku ʑo ju-ɣi ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe nɯ ntsɯ tu-ti ɲɯ-ɕti \\
in.a.moment come: fact be: aff: fact lnk every.day emph ipfv -come sens -be: aff lnk dem always ipfv -say sens -be: aff \\
`It will come soon: it comes everyday and each times says this.' (qaCpa 2003)
exe

They are also compatible with sentence final particles of epistemic modality such as tʰaŋ `maybe, probably' ( ex:Gi.thaN ), which can be used to temper the degree of assertion.

exe

a-mu jɯɣmɯr tɕe tɕi-scawa ɣe ma kʰu ɣi tʰaŋ nɤ \\
1sg. poss -mother today.evening lnk 1du. poss -poor sfp lnk tiger come: fact sfp sfp \\
`Mother, poor us, this evening the tiger is probably coming (for us).' (The tiger)
exe
summary:
The Factual in independent clauses without an auxiliary has two main uses. With stative verbs, it marks facts treated as common knowledge, while with dynamic verbs it can express general knowledge, especially in generic contexts or with a dummy subject, and it may also appear with overt, definite subjects.  

It can further indicate immediate future, especially with first-person assertive or second-person interrogative subjects, and can also refer to non-intentional future events when the speaker has reason to expect them. In this future use, it may combine with an affirmative copula to emphasize certainty or with epistemic particles such as “maybe, probably” to soften the assertion.

text:
The Factual is found in the complement clause of modal auxiliaries such as rabe needed and jɤɣbe allowed, but occurrences are considerably fewer than those of the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.complement ). It is used to refer to actions just about happen at the time of utterance (as in ex:nWnaj.WjAG and ex:Cea.ra ), rather than generic statements.

exe

nɯna-j ɯ́-jɤɣ \\
rest: fact - 1sg qu -be.allowed: fact \\
`Could we rest?' (2003 qachGa) 0003372#S138
exe

exe

aʑo kɯ-kaβ ɕe-a ra \\
1sg sbj: pcp -scoop go: fact - 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`I have to go to scoop water.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe
summary: The Factual occurs in complement clauses of modal auxiliaries such as *rabe* ‘be needed’ and *jɤɣbe* ‘be allowed’, though much less often than the Imperfective. It is used for actions that are just about to happen at the time of speaking, rather than for generic statements.

text:
The Factual occurs in fewer Periphrastic TAME constructions than the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ).

With the Past Imperfective pɯ-ŋu and Inferential Imperfective pjɤ-ŋu forms of the copula ŋube, it is used to build the Periphrastic Proximative (§ sec:proximative.periphrastic ).

Some speakers (in particular Kunbzang Mtsho) combine the Factual with the Sensory ɲɯ-ŋu of the copula to express the same meaning as the Inferential in narratives, notably with the verb tisay, where the constructions in ( ex:ti.YWNu2 ) occurs instead of to-ti ( ifr -say) `s/he said' (§ sec:aor.narrative ).

exe

`....' ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
say: fact sens -be \\
`S/he said: `...'' (many examples)
exe

This form may however not be Factual in the proper sense, but rather the trace that tisay (a highly irregular verb, § sec:stem2.form ) used to have irregular preverbless forms (§ sec:verbs.no.preverbs ). The archaic form kʰɯ-ti `s/he said' provides additional support for this idea (§ sec:khWti ).
summary:
The Factual appears in fewer periphrastic TAME constructions than the Imperfective. It is used with the Past Imperfective pɯ-ŋu and Inferential Imperfective pjɤ-ŋu forms of the copula ŋube to form the Periphrastic Proximative.  

Some speakers, especially Kunbzang Mtsho, combine the Factual with the Sensory ɲɯ-ŋu of the copula to express a narrative meaning like the Inferential, especially with tisay “say”; this may reflect an older irregular form of the verb rather than a true Factual usage, as suggested by the archaic kʰɯ-ti “s/he said.”

text: Sensory
summary: The passage appears to be incomplete, consisting only of the word “Sensory.” As written, it does not provide enough information to summarize any linguistic facts or arguments.

text:
The assertive Sensory form of regular verbs is build by combining the B type westwards ɲɯ- preverb with stem I or stem III depending on person and transitivity (§ sec:stem3.distribution; stem II also occurs in one case, see ex:YAstWt below). It is thus potentially ambiguous with the Imperfective of verbs selecting westwards as their intrinsic orientation. Examples ( ex:YWYaR.Zo.Nu ) and ( ex:kW.YWYaR ) in § sec:ipfv.inchoative illustrate this syncretism between Sensory and Imperfective.

The negative Sensory is marked by the portmanteau prefix mɯ́j- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ), differing from the negative Imperfective form mɯ-ɲɯ- of verbs selecting the westwards preverbs. The mɯ́j- prefix is not compatible with contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction ) however: their negative Sensory form is mɯ-ɲɯ, as in ( ex:mWYArtsi ).

exe

ɣzɯtʰɯz ndɤre, sɯjno tɕi mɯ-ɲɯ-ɤ-rtsi, si tɕi mɯ-ɲɯ-ɤ-rtsi. \\
Selaginella lnk grass also neg - sens - pass -count tree also neg - sens - pass -count \\
`The Selaginella can be counted neither as a species of grass nor as a tree.' (16-RlWmsWsi)
0003520#S93
exe

The Sensory commonly appears in combination with the Progressive ɲɯ-ɤsɯ- / ɲɯ-ɤz- with transitive verbs. The negative form of the Sensory progressive is mɯ-ɲɯ- ( ex:mWYAsWlAt ), like that of a contracting verbs.

exe

tɯ-mɯ pɤjkʰu mɯ-ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-lɤt ri, qale ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-βzu.\\
indef. poss -sky yet neg - sens - prog -release lnk wind sens - prog -make\\
`It is not yet raining, but there is wind.' (conversation, 15-06-05)
exe

The Sensory form of the verb tisay has stem I ɲɯ-ti when occurring without the Progressive ( ex:YWtindZi ), but unexpectedly selects stem II ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-tɯt, ɲɯ-ɤs-tɯt with Progressive ( ex:YAstWt ), which also presents the irregular allomorph -ɤs- (§ sec:progressive.morphology ).

exe

nɯ kɯ-fse a-pa a-ma ni kɯ ɲɯ-ti-ndʑi tɕe \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.like 1sg. poss -father 1sg. poss -mother du erg sens -say- du lnk \\
`My parents are saying these things.' (2003nyima2)
exe

exe

a-ɬaʁ kɯ nɯ ɲɯ-ɤs-tɯt \\
1sg. poss -FZ erg dem sens - prog -say[II] \\
`My aunt is saying [those things].' (2003 smanmi2)
exe

The irregular existential verbs ɣɤʑuexist and maŋenot exist are the suppletive Sensory forms of tuexist and menot exist (§ sec:suppletive.negative, § sec:intr.person.irregular ). They are the only verbs whose Sensory forms is not marked by a prefix.
summary: Regular assertive Sensory forms are built with the westwards ɲɯ- preverb plus stem I or III, and can overlap with the Imperfective of verbs whose intrinsic orientation is westwards; the negative Sensory normally uses the portmanteau prefix mɯ́j-, though contracting verbs instead take mɯ-ɲɯ. The Sensory often combines with the Progressive in transitive verbs, where the negative form is mɯ-ɲɯ, and the verb *tisay* shows an irregular stem choice in this environment. The irregular existential verbs ɣɤʑu ‘exist’ and maŋe ‘not exist’ are suppletive Sensory forms and are the only verbs whose Sensory is not prefix-marked.

text:
The Sensory is used to express access to information through any of the senses, most commonly vision, but also hearing ( ex:tumbri ), touch ( ex:YWmpW ), smell ( ex:tunAmnAmnW ) and taste ( ex:YWmWm ). It implies the discovery of a previously unknown fact or confirmation of an uncertain fact.

exe

tu-mbri tɕe ɯ-skɤt wuma ʑo ɲɯ-mpɕɤr \\
ipfv -cry lnk 3sg. poss -voice really emph sens -be.beautiful \\
`When it cries, its voice is very beautiful.' (04-cuiniao-zh)
0003390#S25
exe

exe

ɲɯ́-wɣ-nɤmɤle tɕe ɲɯ-mpɯ. \\
ipfv - inv -touch lnk sens -be.soft \\
`It is soft to the touch.' (19-khWlu)
0003540#S23
exe

exe

tɕe nɯ tu-nɤmnɤm-nɯ tɕe, cɤmtsʰo ɯ-di, pɯ pɯ-ŋu nɤ, ɯ-di ɲɯ-mnɤm, tɕe nɯnɯ tɕu ɯ-fsa tu-ta-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl. \\
lnk dem ipfv -smell- pl lnk musk 3sg. poss -smell cond pst.ipfv-be lnk 3sg. poss -smell sens -be.smell lnk dem loc 3sg. poss -snare ipfv -put- pl sens -be.usually.the.case \\
`[The hunters] sniff [the places] (where they find deer hair). The smell of musk, it is very strong. They put the snare there.' (27-kikakCi)
0003700#S64
exe

exe

tú-wɣ-ndza tɕe wuma ʑo ɲɯ-mɯm ɲɯ-ti \\
ipfv - inv -eat lnk really emph sens -be.tasty sens -say \\
`She said: `[These ferns] (prepared this way) are very nice to eat'.' (said just after eating them; conversation 14.05.10)
exe

Although in the above examples there is no implication that the person producing the sound or the objects mentioned in the sentences are not visible to the speaker, in these contexts vision is largely irrelevant to determine the property in question, and there is no ambiguity as to which sensory channel was responsible for obtaining the information.
summary: The Sensory expresses access to information through the senses, especially sight, but also hearing, touch, smell, and taste. It often indicates the discovery of a new fact or the confirmation of an uncertain one. In these examples, although the source of the information is not necessarily hidden from view, the relevant sensory channel is clear and vision is largely irrelevant to identifying the property being described.

text:
Endopathic
As in other languages of the area, but unlike Lhasa Tibetan, the Sensory form is used for endopathic sensations (pain, itch, cold etc) relating to the speaker, as in example ( ex:YWmNAm ).

exe

tʰam tɕe mɯ́j-cʰa-a, a-mi ɲɯ-mŋɤm. \\
now lnk neg: sens -can- 1sg 1sg. poss -foot sens -hurt \\
`I can't now, my foot hurts.' (21-kuGrummAG)
0003574#S61
exe

In ( ex:tWCGa.YWmNAm ), the Sensory is used in a generic sentence, when the speaker has experienced himself the feeling and recounts his experience while presenting it as a generic fact (§ sec:1.genr ), and thus do not count as a real example of endopathic Sensory with an experiencer other than the speaker.

exe

kɯ-maqʰu qʰe tɯ-ɕɣa ɲɯ-mŋɤm \\
sbj: pcp -be.after lnk genr. poss -tooth sens -hurt \\
`Afterwards our teeth hurt.' (27-tApGi)
0003706#S66
exe

In ( ex:nWrqo.YWmNAm ), which describes the effects of foot and mouth disease on cattle, the speaker uses the Sensory to describe an inference about the endopathic feelings of the cattle suffering from the disease (they are in pain), based on information from vision and hearing (their whining and behaviour).

exe

nɯ-mci kɤ-rɤwum maka mɯ́j-cʰa-nɯ tɕe nɯ-mci tu-ɣɤrɯβrɯβ ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu. tɕe nɯ-rqo ɲɯ-mŋɤm rca, \\
3pl. poss -saliva inf -collect at.all neg: sens -can- pl lnk 3pl. poss -saliva ipfv -flow.continuously emph sens -be lnk 3pl. poss -throat sens -hurt sfp \\
`They cannot keep the saliva in their mouths, and it flows continuously. Their throats hurt.' (27-kharwut)
0003698#S6
exe

In ( ex:Wmi.YWmNAm ) likewise we have the Sensory used with mŋɤmfeel pain to describe an event visually witnessed by the speaker.

exe

kɯɕnɤsqi tʰɯ-azɣɯt ri, tɕe pɤjkʰu ɯ-mi ɲɯ-mŋɤm tɕe ri, nɯ kɯnɤ kʰa tsʰitsuku ɲɯ-nɤme ɕti. \\
seventy aor -reach but lnk already 3sg. poss -foot sens -hurt lnk but dem also house some.things sens -work[III] be. aff: fact \\
`He is seventy, his foot hurts already, but even so he does all sorts of work at home.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S48
exe

The Sensory is also possible in the case of extra-sensory perception obtained by divination. In ( ex:XsAr.tWtaNGoR.YArku ), it occurs on the verb ɲɯ-ɤ-rku which refers to a present situation (unknown to other people) and on ɲɯ-pʰɤn about a future event.

exe

``ɯ-qa nɯtɕu χsɤr tɯ-taɴɢoʁ ɲɯ-ɤ-rku tɕe, nɯ a-tɤ-sɯ-tɕɤt tɕe ɲɯ-pʰɤn'' ɲɯ-ti \\
3sg. poss -root dem: loc gold one-basket sens - pass -be.put.in lnk dem irr - pfv - caus -take.out lnk sens -be.efficient sens -say \\
`(After performing the divination), [the lama] said `There is one basketful of gold (buried) at the root [of the tree]$_i$, if [the tree]$_i$ asks someone to take it out, that will solve its$_i$ problems). ' (2003 divination)
exe
summary: The passage explains that, unlike Lhasa Tibetan, the Sensory form in this language is used for endopathic sensations such as pain, itch, and cold when they relate to the speaker. It also appears in some generic statements, in inferences about animals’ internal feelings based on observed behavior, and in cases of extra-sensory knowledge obtained through divination, including present and future situations.

text:
Mirative
Japhug has several interjections specifically used to express surprise (§ sec:interjections ), amaŋ and mtsʰɤrihow strange.

The Sensory often occurs in such contexts, as in ( ex:amang.YWmbro ), as expected for a direct visual perception (§ sec:sensory.evd ). This use of the Sensory evidential is what motivated its analysis as a mirative marker in some languages (,, ).

exe

amaŋ, nɯstʰɯci ɲɯ-mbro \\
interjection: surprise so.much sens -be.high \\
`It is so high!' (150826 liyu tiao longmen-zh) 0006266#S73
exe

When the predicate is a stative verb, the degree nominal construction (§ sec:degree.nominal.construction, § sec:non.verbal.predicates ), can alternatively be used to express the unexpected high degree of the observed property.

exe

amaŋ, nɯ ɯ-tɯ-sɤre, mtsʰɤri, ɯ-tɯ-sɤmtsʰɤr nɯ \\
interjection: surprise dem 3sg - nmlz: deg -be.funny how.strange 3sg - nmlz: deg -be.surprising sfp \\
`It is so funny, so surprising!' (150830 baihe jiemei-zh)
0006368#S111
exe
summary: Japhug has several interjections used to express surprise, including *amaŋ* and *mtsʰɤri*. In contexts of direct visual perception, the Sensory evidential often occurs and may function as a mirative marker, while stative predicates can also use a degree nominal construction to express unexpectedly high degree, as in “It is so funny, so surprising!”

text:
The Sensory is commonly used instead of the Factual for describing facts about animals that do not live in Tibetan areas. Compare for instance the forms of the stative verbs sɤɣmube frightening and mpɕɤrbe beautiful: they appear in the Factual when referring to spiders or flowers found in the area ( ex:sAGmu and ex:mpCAr ) and in the Sensory when referring to lions and gnus, which the speaker has only seen in zoos or in the television ( ex:YWsAGmu and ex:YWmpCAr ). The choice of the Sensory instead of the Factual in such context might be a way for the speaker to highlight the fact that this information comes from his/her own personal experience, because s/he may not take for granted that everybody shares this knowledge.

exe

ŋgoŋpu ɴɢoɕna kɤ-ti ci tu tɕe, nɯnɯ wxti nɯ stoʁ jamar tu. kú-wɣ-rtoʁ tɕe sɤɣ-mu. \\
disaster spider obj: pcp -say indef exist: fact lnk dem be.big: fact dem bean about exist: fact ipfv - inv -look.at lnk prop -be.afraid: fact \\
`There is one that is called `disaster spider', it is big, like the size of a bean. It is terrifying to look at it.' (26 mYaRmtsaR)
0003674#S35
exe

exe

nɯnɯ ɯ-mɯntoʁ nɯ mpɕɤr. \\
dem 3sg. poss -flower dem be.beautiful: fact \\
`It has a beautiful flower.' (15-babW) 0003512#S58
exe

exe

sɯŋgi nɯ ɲɯ-sɤɣ-mu. \\
lion dem sens - prop -be.afraid \\
`Lions are terrifying.' (20 sWNgi) 0003562#S64
exe

exe

<jiaoma> nɯ ɲɯ-mpɕɤr \\
gnu dem sens -be.beautiful \\
`Gnus are beautiful.' (20-RmbroN) 0003560#S126
exe

The Sensory is also common in all finite comparative constructions (§ sec:comparison ), whether the comparee is marked with the ergative ( ex:slAzWn.kW.YWdAn ) (§ sec:comparee.kW ) or the standard takes the comparative postposition ( ex:sAz.YWwxti ) (§ sec:comparative ). The presence of the Sensory in such constructions might be due to the fact that comparisons require an evaluation of the respective positions of the standard and the comparee on a scale, and that the result of this comparison is thus `freshly' obtained information.

exe

slɤzɯn kɯ ɲɯ-dɤn, tɕe tɯ-xpa tɕe ʁnɯ-ɣjɤn jamar ɣɤʑu, ʁmbɣɯzɯn ɲɯ-rkɯn ɕti. \\
lunar.eclipse erg sens -be.many lnk one-year loc two-times about exist: sens solar.eclipse sens -be.few be. aff: fact \\
`Lunar eclipses are more numerous, they occur about twice a year, while solar eclipses are rarer.' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S150
exe

exe

ɯ-rna nɯ mbro ɣɯ sɤz ɲɯ-wxti. \\
3sg. poss -ear dem horse gen comp sens -be.big \\
`Its ears are bigger than those of the horse.' (20-tArka)
0003566#S5
exe

The use of the Sensory is not obligatory in such constructions: the Factual is also possible.
summary: The passage says that the Sensory is commonly used in place of the Factual when describing animals outside Tibetan areas, especially when the speaker is drawing on personal experience rather than shared local knowledge. It also appears regularly in finite comparative constructions, possibly because comparisons yield newly obtained information, though the Factual is still possible there.

text:
With second person subjects, the Sensory is very commonly used to state a fact about the addressee that the speaker noticed (not something he knew previously). For instance, in contrast to ( ex:tWmkhAz ) in the Factual in which the addressee's (recent) actions are irrelevant, a sentence such as ( ex:YWtWmkhAz ) can be used if the speaker witnessed something revealing the proficiency of the addressee.

exe

ɲɯ-tɯ-mkʰɤz \\
sens -2-be.expert \\
`You are good.' (heard in several conversations)
exe

exe

nɤʑo stu ʑo tɯ-mkʰɤz tɕe, tɕe nɤʑo ɕ-tɤ-nɤme \\
2sg most emph 2-be.expert: fact lnk lnk 2sg tral - imp -do[III] \\
`You are the best, do it!' (150822 laoye zuoshi zongshi duide-zh)
0006298#S37
exe

With first person subjects, the Sensory is not rare. It is common with verbs such as rgabe happy whose intransitive subject is the experiencer, as in ( ex:YWrgaa ) (see § sec:egophoric.tripartite on the contrast between Sensory, Egophoric Present and Factual in such contexts).

exe

nɤ-tɕɯ tɤ-sci tɕe ɲɯ-pe tɕe papa, aʑo ɲɯ-rga-a\\
2sg. poss -child aor -born lnk sens -good lnk good 1sg sens -be.happy- 1sg \\
`It is nice that you now have a son, I am happy.' (conversation 2013)
exe

With non-experiencer adjectival stative verbs, it can occur if the speaker discovers something about oneself, for instance from the behaviour of others as in ( ex:YWsAjloRa ). This example is taken from the translation of Andersen's story `The Ugly Duckling', when a hunting dog appears before the eponymous character but does not bite him.

exe

aʑo ndɤre ɲɯ-sɤjloʁ-a tɕe, tɤrʁaʁkɕi kɯnɤ ʑo kú-wɣ-mtsɯɣ-a mɯ́j-sɯsɤm \\
1sg on.the.other.hand sens -be.ugly- 1sg lnk hunting.dog also emph ipfv - inv -bite- 1sg neg: sens -think[III] \\
`I am [so] ugly that even a hunting dog does not want to bite me.' (140519 chou xiaoya-zh)
0004034#S79
exe
summary: The passage explains that the Sensory is commonly used with second person subjects to report a fact about the addressee that the speaker has just noticed, especially when the speaker has witnessed evidence of it. It is also used with first person subjects, particularly with experiencer verbs like “be happy,” and can appear with stative adjectival verbs when the speaker discovers something about themself from others’ behavior.

text:
The Sensory never has an inchoative meaning with stative verbs, unlike the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.inchoative ). It can be used to describe both ongoing events or habitual/generic situations (§ sec:sensory.other ).
With transitive verbs, it often occurs with the progressive (§ sec:sensory.morphology ).

The Sensory is mainly found in non-past contexts. However, unlike the Factual and the Egophoric, the Sensory can refer to past events. In ( ex:aphe.YWtinW ), the verb ɲɯ-ti-nɯ `they say/said' concerns an event that had occurred decades before.

exe

aʑo a-pʰe ``nɤʑo ju-tɯ-ɕe ra" ɲɯ-ti-nɯ. \\
1sg 1sg. poss - dat 2sg ipfv -2-go be.needed: fact sens -say- pl \\
`They said to me: `You have to go.'' (2010-09)
exe

The Sensory ɲɯ-ti of the verb tisay is the normal way to report the words uttered by a third person, when the speaker has heard them directly (as is obviously the case in ex:aphe.YWtinW ). The Aorist ta-tɯt, which is used to describe past events directly witnessed by the speaker (§ sec:aor.main ), is never found in conversations to quote someone else's words (it occurs in temporal § sec:aor.temporal and relative § sec:aor.relative clauses).

The Sensory also occurs in future contexts in the apodosis of conditional clause to express the prediction of a likely outcome, as in ( ex:atAwxti.YWphAn ) (see also ex:XsAr.tWtaNGoR.YArku, § sec:sensory.endopathic ).

exe

nɯ tɤ-ŋu tɕe tɕe, si lú-wɣ-ɣɤjɯ, smi a-tɤ-wxti tɕe ɲɯ-pʰɤn \\
dem aor -be lnk lnk wood ipfv - inv -add fire irr - pfv -be.big lnk sens -be.efficient \\
`(He thought:) `In this case, if [I] add more firewood, and the fire gets bigger, it should work.' (150827 taisui-zh)
0006390#S62
exe

The Sensory is also found to express events that one has not yet perceived, but which one expects to be perceptible, as illustrated by the use of the verbs ɣɤʑu `exist' and ɯ-ɲɯ́-ŋu `isn't it' in ( ex:future.GAZu ).

exe

aki ɕ-pɯ-sɤŋo ma [...] ``ndzaʁlaŋ tɯrme jo-ɣi tɕe, tɯ-ci kɤ-kɯ-nɯχtɕɤn ɯ-ŋgɯ ɕ-pjɯ́-wɣ-βde ɲɯ-ra" ɯ-kɯ-ti ci ɣɤʑu tɕe, ɯ-ɲɯ́-ŋu kɯ? \\
down.there tral - imp: down -listen lnk Jambudvîpa man ifr -come lnk indef. poss -water aor - sbj: pcp -be.fierce 3sg. poss -inside tral - ipfv: down - inv -throw sens -be.needed 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -say indef exist: sens lnk qu - sens -be qu \\
`Go and listen down there to [see whether] there is someone saying `A man from Jambudvîpa has come, let us throw him into the fierce water.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S149
exe
summary: The Sensory does not have an inchoative meaning with stative verbs, but it can describe ongoing, habitual, or generic situations, and with transitive verbs it often appears with the progressive. Although it is mainly used in non-past contexts, it can also refer to past events, report directly heard speech, and occur in future or anticipated contexts, especially in conditional apodoses or when expressing events expected to be perceptible.

text: tense!present Egophoric Present
summary: The passage labels a tense category as **present** and identifies a subtype called **Egophoric Present**. It does not provide further explanation beyond this grammatical labeling.

text:
The Egophoric Present is built combining the B type eastwards ku- preverb with stem I or stem III depending on person and transitivity (§ sec:stem3.distribution ). Verbs selecting eastwards as their intrinsic orientation therefore have syncretism between Imperfective and Egophoric. For instance, the form ku-rɤʑi-a is in the Egophoric Present in ( ex:kurAZia.egoph ) and in the Imperfective in ( ex:kurAZia.ipfv ) (see § sec:ipfv.complement on this use of the Imperfective).

exe

kɯre ku-rɤʑi-a \\
dem. prox: loc prs -stay- 1sg \\
`I am here.' (heard in context)
exe

exe

kutɕu ku-rɤʑi-a ɲɯ-ɬoʁ \\
dem. prox: loc ipfv -stay- 1sg sens -be.needed \\
`I had better (have no choice but to) stay here.' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S75
exe

Unlike the Sensory (§ sec:sensory.morphology ), the Egophoric Present does not have a special negative form, and selects the mɯ- negative prefix, as in ( ex:mWkuchaa ).

exe

kɯ-ɤrqʰi kɤ-ɕe mɯ-ku-cʰa-a \\
sbj: pcp -be.far inf -go neg - prs -can- 1sg \\
`I cannot go very far.' (for now, due to an accident; conversation 17-09-21)
exe

The Egophoric Present form of the existential verbs tuexist and menot exist is regular: ku-tu and ku-me ( ex:kume ), respectively. The copulas ŋube and maʁnot be lack an Egophoric Present form.

exe

aʑo kɯre a-ʁa ku-me tɯ-mgo ku-osɯ-βzu-a ɕti \\
1sg here 1sg. poss -free.time prs -not.exist indef. poss -food prs - prog -make- 1sg be. aff: fact \\
`I don't have time, I am making food.' (Rkangrgyal) 0003943#S72
exe

Transitive verbs often combine the Egophoric Present with the Progressive asɯ- (§ sec:progressive.morphology ). The vowel of the preverb merges with that of the Progressive prefix as ku-osɯ- / ku-oz, as in ( ex:konWsWndzaj2 ).

exe

ɕa ʁɟa ʑo ku-o<nɯ>sɯ-ndza-j ma fsapaʁ ɯ-tɯ-si ɯ-grɤl maŋe. \\
meat completely emph prs - prog < auto >-eat- 1pl lnk animal 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -die 3sg. poss -order not.exist: sens \\
`(These days) we are eating only meat, as (farm) animals have been dying in great numbers (due to a disease).' (2003 kandZislama)
exe
summary:
The Egophoric Present is formed by combining the eastwards ku- preverb with stem I or stem III, depending on person and transitivity, and verbs with eastwards as their intrinsic orientation therefore show syncretism between the Imperfective and Egophoric. It uses the regular mɯ- negative prefix rather than a special negative form, and the existential verbs ku-tu and ku-me are regular in this construction, while the copulas ŋube and maʁ lack an Egophoric Present form.  

Transitive verbs often take the Egophoric Present together with the Progressive asɯ-, with the vowel of ku- merging with the progressive prefix.

subsubsection: Egophoric Present and first/second person indexation
text:
egophoric person!first
The Egophoric Present, while common in conversations, is nearly non-existent in narrative and procedural texts (outside of quotations) unlike the Factual and the Sensory.

In declarative sentences, Egophoric Present can occur with first person subject, whether intransitive subject as in ku-nɯna-j `we are resting' ( ex:kunWnaj ) or transitive subjects as in ku-taʁ-a `I am weaving it' ( ex:kutaRa ).

exe

kɯre ku-nɯna-j \\
here egop -rest- 1pl \\
`(Today, on the National Holiday), we are resting here.' (conversation, 16-10-01)
exe

exe

<kuabao> ɯ-spa ci ku-taʁ-a \\
satchel 3sg. poss -material indef prs -weave- 1sg \\
`I am weaving a satchel.' (conversation, 14-11-25)
exe

No example of Egophoric Present with second person subject in declarative sentences has been found in the corpus, nor could such example be elicited. However, second person objects are possible, as in ( ex:kutanAjo ).

exe

kɯre ku-ta-nɤjo \\
dem. prox: loc prs -1 2-wait \\
`I am right here waiting for you.' (heard in context)
exe

As a result of the anticipation rule
(§ sec:anticipation.person ), the person constraint on the Egophoric Present is reversed in interrogative sentences. As shown by ( ex:WkutWscitnW ) and ( ex:kutWrAZi ), the Egophoric Present appears with second person subjects, and is not attested with first person. These two questions expect answers such as ( ex:kusciti ) and ( ex:kurAZia.egoph ) (in § sec:egophoric.morphology ) with first person and Egophoric.

exe

ɯ-kú-tɯ-scit-nɯ? \\
qu - prs -2-be.happy- pl \\
`Are you (and your family) happy?' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

exe

ŋotɕu ku-tɯ-rɤʑi? \\
where prs -2-stay \\
`Where are you?' (heard in context)
exe

The person constraints described above are the reason for calling the TAME category discussed in this section ``egophoric'', designating a type of evidentiality specifically marking `information as known through conscious personal involvement'. Hill argues in favour of replacing ``egophoric'' with the term ``personal evidential''.
summary: The Egophoric Present is common in conversation but nearly absent from narrative and procedural texts except in quotations. In declarative sentences it occurs with first person subjects, while second person subjects are not attested; in interrogatives, this pattern reverses, with second person subjects attested and first person subjects not. These person constraints motivate the label “egophoric,” referring to evidential marking of information known through conscious personal involvement, though Hill prefers the term “personal evidential.”

text:
The Egophoric Present can occur with third person subjects. This use is particularly common in declarative sentences when the subject is a noun with a first person possessive prefix, whether an abstract inalienable noun as in the case of a-ʁa `my free time' in ( ex:kume ), or kinship terms as in ( ex:kunWsWmWzdWGndZi ).

exe

a-wi cʰo a-wa ni nɤʑo nɤ-ndʐa kɯ wuma ʑo ku-nɯsɯmɯzdɯɣ-ndʑi tɕe \\
1sg. poss -grandmother comit 1sg. poss -father du 2sg 2sg. poss -reason erg really emph prs -worry- du lnk \\
`Grandmother and Father are very worried because of you.' (150819 haidenver-zh)
0006314#S462
exe

Conversely, Egophoric is also frequent with second person possessors in interrogative sentences, such as nɤ-ma `your work' as in ( ex:nAma.WkudAn ).

exe

xlist

nɤ-ma ɯ-kú-dɤn? \\
2sg. poss -work qu - prs -be.many \\
`Do you have a lot of work?' (heard in context)

a-ma ku-dɤn \\
1sg. poss -work prs -be.many \\
`I have a lot of work.'
xlist
exe

With non-possessed subjects nouns, it also occurs when the first person is a beneficiary, marked either as a possessor ( ex:kW.koznAma ) or with oblique flagging as in the clause a-taʁ wuma ku-sna `he is nice to me' in ( ex:kusciti ) above.

exe

χpɤltɕin kɯ a-ma ra ku-oz-nɤma \\
anthr erg 1sg. poss -work pl prs - prog -do \\
`Dpalcan is doing my housework (in my stead).' (conversation, 16-04-12)
exe

exe

tɕʰeme nɯ kɯ `wuma ʑo ku-scit-i, rɟɤlpu ri a-taʁ wuma ku-sna, ʁjoʁ ra ri wuma ʑo ku-pe-nɯ' to-ti\\
girl dem erg really emph prs -be.happy- 1pl king also 1sg -on really prs -be.kind servant pl also really emph prs -be.good ifr -say\\
`The girl said: `We are very happy, the king is very kind to me, the servants are very nice.'' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

The use of Egophoric with third person subjects is an instance of what has been termed `broad egophoric' by. Japhug appears to allow a wider range of third person referents to occur with egophoric than most languages. There are examples of Egophoric Present with third person subjects in which the personal involvement of the speaker is not immediately obvious.

In ( ex:shangban.kosWBzu ), we find Egophoric Present on the main verb, even though the transitive subject and the speaker were not together at time of utterance. There is however a relationship between them, since the subject of ( ex:shangban.kosWBzu ) is the daughter of the speaker.

exe

alan nɤki, ʁdɯrɟɤt ri <shangban> ku-osɯ-βzu \\
anthr filler topo loc office.work prs - prog -do \\
`Alan, she is doing office work in Gdongbrgyad (these days).' (conversation, 2014-12-24)
exe

In ( ex:pAjkhu.kuWnme ), the use of the Egophoric Present is not straightforward. It is possible that the speaker selects this form because she describes a situation that directly concerns herself, since she is among the inhabitants of the district, who are not sick from the disease.

exe

kɯ-ngo wuma ʑo rkɯn, <abazhou> [...] pɯ-nɯ-mɯ me ɕti qʰe, pɤjkʰu ku-nɯ-me. \\
sbj: pcp -be.sick really emph be.few: fact Rngaba pst. ipfv - auto - emph not.exist be. aff: fact lnk still prs - auto -not.exist \\
\\
`There are few people sick (from Covid), (here) in Rngaba district there never was anyone, and even now there is not (a single) one.' (conversation 2020-07-31)
exe

Tshendzin explains the form ku-nɯ-me `there is not' here as ( ex:tham.kWnA.me ) with the Factual Non-Past.

exe

`tʰam kɯnɤ me' kɤ-ti ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
now also not.exist: fact inf -say sens -be \\
`It means `not even now'.'
exe
summary:
The passage explains that the Egophoric Present can appear with third person subjects in Japhug, especially in declarative sentences when the subject is a noun bearing a first person possessive prefix, including inalienable nouns and kinship terms. It is also common with second person possessors in questions and with non-possessed subjects when the first person is involved as a beneficiary, showing that this pattern extends beyond the narrowest notion of egophoric reference.

It further notes that this is an instance of “broad egophoric,” since Japhug allows third person referents to occur with egophoric marking more freely than many languages. Some examples suggest a direct relation to the speaker, while others are less straightforward and may reflect the speaker’s personal involvement in the situation.

text:
The Egophoric Present expresses ongoing events or repeated actions occurring during a short time range around the present time. Thus, the sentence ( ex:tChi.kutWnAme ) can either mean `What are you doing right now? ' or `What are you doing these days?'.

exe

tɕʰi ku-tɯ-nɤme? \\
what prs -2-do[III] \\
`What are you doing (now, these days)?' (heard in context)
exe

These two meanings are also possible when the Egophoric Present is combined with the Progressive, as shown by ( ex:jipAri.kosWBzu ) and ( ex:shangban.kosWBzu ).

exe

alan kɯ ji-pɤri ku-osɯ-βzu. \\
anthr erg 1pl. poss -dinner prs - prog -make \\
`Alan is preparing the dinner for us (right now).' (conversation, 15-01-02)
exe

The Egophoric Present marks actions or states that are temporary. For instance, mɯ-ku-cʰa-a `I cannot do it' in ( ex:pAjkhu.mWkuchaa ) (and ex:mWkuchaa in § sec:egophoric.morphology above) means that the speaker describes a non-permanent situation: she previously was able to do it, and will presumably be soon able to do it again when she has fully recovered.

exe

pɤjkʰu kɯnɤ ɯʑo kɯ ku-oz-nɤma ɕti ma pɤjkʰu mɯ-ku-cʰa-a wo. \\
still also 3sg erg prs - prog -do be. aff: fact lnk still neg - prs -can- 1sg sfp \\
`Even now, he is still doing [the housework], as I am still unable [to do it] (due to an accident).' (conversation, 17-09-01)
exe

The Factual ( ex:tundzea.maChaa ) or the Sensory are used instead when describing situations that have become permanent.

exe

tham a-pɯ-ŋu, tu-ndze-a maka mɤ-cʰa-a \\
now irr - ipfv -be ipfv -eat[III]- 1sg at.all neg -can: fact - 1sg \\
`Now, I cannot eat [the fruit of the Ribes stenocarpum ] at all (anymore, because it is too sour, unlike when the speaker was a child and did not mind about the sourness).' (18-NGolo)
0003530#S20
exe

The Egophoric Present is restricted to present tense. In ( ex:kutanAjo.future ), the form ku-ta-nɤjo `I (will) be waiting for you' referring to a future event is rather analyzable as an Imperfective, given the syncretism between these two in the case of this verb.

exe

a-jɤ-tɯ-ɣɯt tɕe, aʑo cʰo [...] tɤɕime nɯ kɯ nɯnɯ kɤntɕʰaʁ ɣɯ ɯ-pɕi nɯtɕu ku-ta-nɤjo. \\
irr - pfv -2-bring lnk 1sg comit princess dem erg dem town gen 3sg. poss -outside dem: loc ipfv -1 2-wait \\
`When you bring [the bird], the princess and I will be waiting for you outside of the town.' (140507 jinniao-zh)
0003931#S281
exe

The Egophoric Present can also occur in the case of periods of time including the present and the past. For instance, when asked whether she had seen a particular person, who was present at the time in Mbarkham, Tshendzin said the sentence ( ex:mWkotWGa.past.present ) with the Egophoric Present.

exe

mɯ-ku-otɯɣ-a \\
neg - prs -meet- 1sg \\
`I have not been meeting him (these days).' (conversation 16-03-10)
exe
summary: The Egophoric Present is used for ongoing or repeated events within a short period around the present, so it can mean both “right now” and “these days.” It also marks temporary actions or states, whereas the Factual or Sensory is used for situations that have become permanent. The form is restricted to present tense, though it may appear with periods that include both present and past when describing an extended current situation.

text:
Egophoric Present Sensory Factual Non-Past
The tripartite contrast between Egophoric Present ( ex:kusciti2 ), Sensory ( ex:YWscita, ex:YWscita2 ) and Factual ( ex:sciti ) with the experiencer stative verbs such as scitbe happy in declarative sentences with a first person subject can help understanding the semantics of these TAME categories in this context.

exe

ku-scit-i \\
prs -be.happy- 1pl \\
`We are happy.' (conversation, in a response to a new years' greeting)
exe

exe

nɯtɕu ɲɯ-scit-a ɕti li tɕe tɕe a-zda ri ɲɯ-pe-nɯ, \\
dem: loc sens -be.happy- 1sg be. aff: fact again lnk lnk 1sg -companion also sens -be.good- pl \\
`I am very happy there, the people with me are very nice.' (140501 jingli) 0003902#S149
exe

exe

nɯ tɤ-ŋu tɕe, aʑo ndɤre, ʁloŋbutɕʰi sɤz ndɤre ɲɯ-scit-a tɕe a-kʰi ɲɯ-ŋgɯ \\
dem aor -be lnk 1sg on.the.other.hand elephant comp on.the.other.hand sens -be.happy- 1sg lnk 1sg. poss -luck sens -be.lucky \\
`Things being as they are, I am happier than the elephant, I am luckier than him.' (140425 shizi puluomixiusi he daxiang-zh)
0003798#S40
exe

exe

χsɯ-xpa jɤ-tsu-j, nɯstʰɯci ʑo scit-i, amɯmi-j \\
three-year aor -pass- 1sg so.much emph be.happy: fact - 1pl be.on.good.terms: fact - 1pl \\
`We have been together for three years now, we are so happy together.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

In ( ex:sciti ), the speakers (humans stranded on an island) include the addressees (rākshasīs in human shape) in the first plural, and state their happiness together as an commonly agreed fact (the first step in a plan to cheat the rākshasīs), hence the use of the Factual.

In ( ex:YWscita2 ), the selection of the Sensory here may be due to the presence of a comparative construction (§ sec:sensory.other ). In ( ex:YWscita ) the choice of the Sensory rather than the Egophoric Present expresses that when thinking about it, the speaker feels that she is happy. The Egophoric Present in ( ex:kusciti2 ) entails the continuous conscience of being in a state of happiness, and that this state is temporary.
summary: The passage contrasts Egophoric Present, Sensory, and Factual forms with the stative verb *scit* “be happy” in first-person declarative contexts to clarify their meanings. The Factual is used when happiness is presented as an agreed-on fact, the Sensory can mark a speaker’s felt or observed happiness and may also appear in comparative contexts, and the Egophoric Present expresses a continuous, self-aware experience of being happy that is understood as temporary.

text: Irrealis
summary: The passage introduces **irrealis** as a category used for situations that are not presented as actual, including events that are hypothetical, desired, or otherwise unreal. It typically contrasts with **realis**, which refers to situations regarded as actual or factual.

text:
The Irrealis has three exponents: a dedicated prefix a- in slot -6 (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ), a type A preverb in slot -3, and stem III in appropriate forms (§ sec:stem3.form, § sec:stem.TAME ), as illustrated by ( ex:atAndze ). A cognate verb form with identical triple exponence in found in Tshobdun.

With dynamic verbs, the preverb follows the lexically selected orientation of the verb (for instance tɤ- upwards in ex:atAndze ). Stative verbs take the downwards pɯ- preverb like the Past Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ) when used with a stative meaning, as in ( ex:apWme ), and the intrinsic orientation ( westwards in ex:anWme ) when occurring with an inchoative meaning.

exe

xlist

a$^-6$-tɤ$^-3$-ndze \\
irr - pfv -eat[III] \\
`Let it/him/her eat/ if s/he/it eats'

a$^-6$-pɯ$^-3$-me \\
irr - ipfv -not.exist \\
`If it does not exist'

a$^-6$-nɯ$^-3$-me \\
irr - pfv -not.exist \\
`If it disappears'
xlist
exe

Unlike the Imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ), the Irrealis is compatible with all person configurations.
summary: The Irrealis is marked by three simultaneous exponents: the prefix **a-** in slot -6, a type A preverb in slot -3, and **stem III** in the appropriate forms. With dynamic verbs, the preverb follows the verb’s lexical orientation; with stative verbs, **pɯ-** appears in stative contexts, while the intrinsic orientation is used in inchoative contexts. Unlike the Imperative, the Irrealis can occur with all person combinations.

text:
In main clauses, the Irrealis has four main functions. The first three (wish, jussive and uncertainty) are treated in this section, and the fourth one (delayed imperative) in § sec:irrealis.delayed.imp.

First, it can express a wish, often in combination with the predicative noun smɯlɤmprayer (§ sec:smWlAm.TAME; see also in Tshobdun ), as in ( ex:apWtWtso.smWlAm2 ), or with the sentence final particle kɯ (§ sec:fsp.interrog ) as in ( ex:anApaa.kW ).

exe

pja mɯndʐamɯχtɕɯɣ nɯ-skɤt a-pɯ-tɯ-tso smɯlɤm\\
bird all.kinds 3pl. poss -speech irr - ipfv -2-understand prayer\\
`May you understand the speech of all species of birds!' (2003kandZislama)
exe

exe

tɯrme ci a-nɯ-ɤpa-a kɯ \\
human indef irr - pfv -become- 1sg sfp \\
`If only I could become a human!' (150819 haidenver-zh)
0006314#S229
exe

While in ( ex:anApaa.kW ) the wish is virtual, example ( ex:apWtWtso.smWlAm ) is a magical formula pronounced by a lama, and the Irrealis has a performative function, conveying to the addressee the ability it describes.

Second, the Irrealis can occur with third person referents with a jussive meaning (see also on Tshobdun), expressing either that the speaker allows the subject to perform the action ( ex:athWGi ), a request or an order. Jussive Irrealis clauses can be used in a purposive complementation strategy (§ sec:irrealis.purposive ).

exe

a-tʰɯ-ɣi, a-tʰɯ-ɣi \\
irr - pfv: downstream -come irr - pfv: downstream -come \\
`Let him come, let him come (as he wishes).' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

In combination with the Autive (§ sec:autobenefactive ), the jussive Irrealis expresses that the speaker does not care about the actions of the third person subject, as in ( ex:apWGnWsata ) (compare with the Autive Imperative, § sec:imp.autive ).

exe

ɯ-ɲɯ́-wɣ-sat-a nɤ a-pɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-sat-a ma mɤ-pʰɣo-tɕi \\
qu - sens - inv -kill- 1sg add irr - pfv - inv - auto -kill- 1sg lnk neg -flee- 1du \\
`If she is to kill me let her kill me, we will not flee.' (2002nyimavodzer)
exe

With second persons, the Irrealis is found instead of the Imperative to express non-controllable actions. In ( ex:atAtWmna.kArAZi ), compare for instance the non-controllable verb mnabe better in the Irrealis with the controllable one rɤʑistay in the Imperative.

exe

pɤjkʰu a-tɤ-tɯ-mna, mɤʑɯ kɤ-rɤʑi \\
still irr - pfv -2-be.better yet imp -stay \\
`[Wait till] you get better, stay a little more.' (said to a convalescent person who wants to leave the place where she is taken care of.' (12-BzaNsa) 0003484#S97
exe

The negative Irrealis is also more felicitous than the Prohibitive (§ sec:prohibitive ) with non-controllable verbs, such as nɯtɕʰombacatch a cold in ( ex:amAtAtWnWtChomba ).

exe

a-mɤ-tɤ-tɯ-nɯtɕʰomba ra ma tɕe nɤ-ɕqʰe ɲɯ-tʰɯ ɲɯ-ŋu wo \\
irr - neg - pfv -2-have.a.cold be.needed: fact lnk lnk 2sg. poss -cough sens -be.serious sens -be sfp \\
`Don't catch a cold, otherwise your cough will be become even more serious.' (conversation 17-09-01)
exe

Third, in interrogative clauses, the Irrealis can express the uncertainty of the speaker on his/her ability to realize the action, as in ( ex:tChi.atAstuj ).

exe

andi ki stʰɯci smar kɯ-wxti iʑo kɤ-sɯ-βzɯr tɕʰi a-tɤ-stu-j? \\
west dem. prox so.much river sbj: pcp -be.big 1pl inf - caus -move what irr - pfv -do.like- 1pl \\
`How can we move such a huge river? (2005 tAwakWcqraR)
exe
summary: In main clauses, the Irrealis has three functions discussed here: expressing wishes, jussive meanings, and uncertainty in questions, while a fourth function, the delayed imperative, is treated elsewhere. It can mark wishes, often with special particles or in magical formulas, can be used with third person subjects for permissions, requests, or orders, and with second persons it may replace the Imperative for non-controllable actions. In interrogative clauses, it can signal the speaker’s uncertainty about whether an action can be carried out.

text:
Imperative!delayed
The Irrealis can be used as a delayed or postponed imperative. This function indicates, according to Sun's ( jackson07irrealis) apt description of the same phenomenon in Tshobdun, `the speaker’s physical inaccessibility as an eyewitness, rather than simply delayed compliance.'

In ( ex:qhihihi.atAtWti ), the verb in the Irrealis a-tɤ-tɯ-ti refers to an action to be realized at a future moment expressed by the temporal clause in the Aorist jɤ-tɯ-azɣɯt `when you arrive...' (§ sec:aor.temporal ), when the speaker will not be present to remind the addressee to perform the action.

exe

[kʰa kɤ-mto jɤ-tɯ-azɣɯt] tɕe qʰihihi χsɯ-ŋka a-tɤ-tɯ-ti ra \\
house inf -see aor -2-arrive lnk interj three-word irr - pfv -2-say be.needed: fact \\
`When you arrive within seeing distance from the house, say qʰihihi three times.' (qachGa 2012) 0004087#S160
exe

The contrast between the Irrealis and the Imperative to express delayed command can be illustrated by the following pair of examples from two versions of the same story, referring to the same action (the method to pass a dangerous place where a pair of magical boulders crush all people coming between them) but from a different perspective.

In ( ex:atAtWZGAGAZo.delayed ), a nâga explains the method to the main character (Nyima 'Odzer). The nâga is not coming with him; only Nyima 'Odzer and his horse intend to cross the boulders. Therefore, the Irrealis verb forms a-kɤ-tɯ-βraʁ and a-tɤ-tɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-ʑo are selected, as the nâga will not be present when Nyima 'Odzer will have to realize these actions.

exe

nɯ-tɯ-armbat-ndʑi tɕe, nɤ-mbro ɯ-jme zɯ pʰuɲi a-kɤ-tɯ-βraʁ, nɤʑo tɤ-muj stʰɯci a-tɤ-tɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-ʑo, nɤ-mbro qale stʰɯci a-nɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-mbjom \\
aor: west -2-be.near- du lnk 2sg. poss -horse 3sg. poss -tail emph potentilla.fruticosa irr - pfv -2-attach 2sg indef. poss -feather so.much irr - pfv -2- refl - caus -be.light 2sg. poss -horse wind so.much irr - pfv - refl - caus -be.quick \\
`When you approach [the boulders], attach a branch of Potentilla fruticosa to the tail of your horse, make yourself as light as a feather, and may your horse be as quick as the wind.' (Smanmi2003.2)
exe

By contrast, in ( ex:tAZGAGAZo.delayed ), it is the horse Rtamchog Rinpoche who explains to Nyima 'Odzer how to cross the boulders. Since these two characters will do the crossing together, the horse uses the Imperative tɤ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-ʑo instead of the Irrealis (§ sec:imp.function ).

exe

aʑo nɯ, qale jamar ʑo tu-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-mbjom-a nɤʑo nɯ tɤ-muj jamar tɤ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-ʑo \\
1sg dem wind about emph ipfv - refl - caus -be.quick- 1sg 2sg dem indef. poss -feather about imp - refl - caus -be.light \\
`I will make myself as quick as the wind, make yourself as light as a feather.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S111
exe

In negative forms likewise, the Irrealis is better than the Prohibitive (§ sec:prohib.function ) if the addressee is to refrain from doing an action in the absence of the speaker who issued the order/request/suggestion not to do it, as in ( ex:WskAt.amAkAtWsANAm ), where both assertive and negative Irrealis verbs in delayed imperative function are found.

exe

[...] ntsɯ kɤtɯpe ri, maka ɯ-jaʁ a-kɤ-tɯ-ndɤm, a-kɤ-tɯ-sɤtɕitʂi ʑo a-lɤ-tɯ-ɣɯt ma ɯ-skɤt a-mɤ-kɤ-tɯ-sɤŋɤm \\
always tell: fact lnk completely 3sg. poss -hand irr - pfv -2-take[III] irr - pfv -2-continue emph irr - pfv: upstream -2-bring lnk 3sg. poss -word irr - neg -2-listen[III] \\
`She will not stop saying `...', but don't release your grasp on her hand, and directly bring her (here), and don't listen to her words.' (qachGa 2003)
0003372#S68
exe
summary: The passage explains that the Irrealis can express a delayed or postponed imperative, used when the speaker is not physically present to witness or enforce the action. This contrasts with the ordinary Imperative, which is used when speaker and addressee will carry out the action together, and with the Prohibitive, which is less suitable than the negative Irrealis for forbidding actions in the speaker’s absence.

text:
Irrealis!complement clauses complement clause!Irrealis
According to Sun's ( jackson07irrealis) description of Tshobdun, the Irrealis is required when occurring with matrix verbs expressing desire or intention. In particular, he points out that the verb səsiʔ means `think' when the complement clause is in realis mode, and `desire, want' with a complement clause in the Irrealis.

In Japhug, the cognate verb sɯsothink has the meaning `want' rather with Infinitive or Imperfective complement clauses (§ sec:sWso.complement ), such as ( ex:tundzea.YWsWsama ).

exe

[nɯ wuma ʑo tu-ndze-a] ɲɯ-sɯsam-a \\
dem really emph ipfv -eat[III]- 1sg sens -think[III]- 1sg \\
`I want to eat it very much.' (140506 woju guniang-zh)
0003929#S35
exe

Complement clauses in the Irrealis with sɯsothink as matrix verb are in all cases reported speech, reflecting functions such hypothetical protasis and apodosis (§ sec:irrealis.conditional ) in ( ex:apWsatnW.YWsWsama ) or jussive (§ sec:irrealis.main ) as in ( ex:atAndze.YAsWso ) and ( ex:atAmna.YWsWsama ).

exe

χawo ʑo kɯ-dɯ dɤn kɯ a-kɤ-nɯtsʰɤβ-nɯ tɕe a-tɤ-tɕʰɯ-nɯ tɕe, a-pɯ-sat-nɯ kɯ ɲɯ-sɯsam-a ri \\
interj emph sbj: pcp - emph erg irr - pfv -attack.in.pack- pl lnk irr - pfv -gore- pl lnk irr - pfv -kill- pl sfp sens -think[III]- 1sg lnk \\
`I am thinking that if only they attacked in a pack and gored [the lion], they would probably kill it.' (20-RmbroN) 0003560#S60
exe

exe

``nɯnɯ tɕe kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ci tu-tɕat-a tɕe nɯ a-tɤ-ndze" ɲɤ-sɯso \\
dem lnk sbj: pcp - emph be.small indef ipfv -take.out- 1sg lnk dem irr - pfv -eat[III] ifr -think \\
`He thought: `I will take a few (olives from the jar) so that she [can] eat some.' (140516 yiguan ganlan-zh)
0004014#S39
exe

The used of reported speech with sɯsothink in ( ex:atAmna.YWsWsama ) is a semi-grammaticalized purposive construction (§ sec:irrealis.purposive ), where the Irrealis is not obligatory: similar purposive clause with other TAME categories are also attested.

exe

``a-mi nɯnɯ a-tɤ-mna'' ɲɯ-sɯsam-a tɕe, nɯra ku-z-nɯsman-a ŋu. \\
1sg. poss -leg dem irr - pfv -be.better sens -think[III]- 1sg lnk dem prs - caus -treat- 1sg be: fact \\
`In order for my leg to get better, I am treating it (with footbaths).' (conversation 2013-11-12)
exe

The Irrealis in jussive function in a reported speech clause (`I am thinking `may my leg get better'') is semantically close to `want' (`I want my leg to get better'). This may explain how the Irrealis became required with the Tshobdun matrix verb səsiʔ in the meaning `want'.

Like the Imperative (§ sec:imp.compl ), the Irrealis occurs in subject complement clauses with modal auxiliary verbs such as rabe needed, ntsʰihave better and jɤɣbe allowed, with a jussive meaning as in ( ex:athWGindZi.ra ) and ( ex:athWGindZi.YWntshi ), or a delayed imperative, as in ( ex:qhihihi.atAtWti ) above (§ sec:irrealis.delayed.imp ).

exe

a-wɯ cʰo a-ʁi ni cʰɯ-ɣi-ndʑi ra ma ʑɤni-sti kɤ-rɤʑi mɤ-cʰa-ndʑi tɕe, [a-tʰɯ-ɣi-ndʑi] ra \\
1sg. poss -grandfather comit 1sg. poss -younger.sibling du ipfv: downstream -come- du be.needed: fact lnk 3du -alone inf -stay neg -can: fact - du lnk irr - pfv: downstream -come- du be.needed: fact \\
`My grandfather and younger brother have to come (with me), as they cannot stay on their own, let them come.' (2011-05-nyima 208-209)
exe

exe

ki ɲɯ-sɤ-ɕke tɕe, [a-nɯ-ɤfɕu] ɲɯ-ntsʰi \\
dem. prox sens - prop -burn lnk irr - pfv -cool.down sens -be.better \\
`This [tea] is too hot, let it cool down.' (elicited)
exe
summary: In Tshobdun, the Irrealis is required with matrix verbs of desire or intention, and Sun notes that the cognate verb səsiʔ changes meaning from “think” with a realis complement to “desire, want” with an Irrealis complement. In Japhug, the cognate sɯso ‘think’ instead takes Infinitive or Imperfective complements to mean “want,” while Irrealis complements with sɯso occur in reported speech, often in hypothetical, purposive, or jussive contexts. The passage suggests that the jussive use of Irrealis in reported speech is semantically close to “want,” which may explain its association with these matrix verbs.

text:
Irrealis!conditional clauses conditional clause!Irrealis counterfactual
In the protasis, the Irrealis competes with initial reduplication (§ sec:redp.protasis ), Prohibitive (§ sec:prohib.function ) and Interrogative (§ sec:interrogative.W.function ). When the apodosis is in the Factual Non-Past, the Irrealis protasis expresses a condition whose probability of being realized may not be high, but which, if it is verified, almost certainly brings the outcome expressed in the apodosis (at least in the speaker's opinion), as in ( ex:ajACe.tCetha ).

exe

nɯ a-jɤ-ɕe tɕe tɕetʰa kɤ-zɣɯt mɤ-cʰa tɕe si ɕti tɕe \\
dem irr - pfv -go lnk soon inf -arrive neg -can: fact lnk die: fact be. aff: fact lnk \\
`Should he go there, he would not be able to reach [his goal], and would die.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S55
exe

The combination of a protasis in the Irrealis and an apodosis in the Past Imperfective is used to express counterfactual meaning (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.apodosis, § sec:counterfactual ), as in ( ex:apWtu.mWpWnANkWNetCi ).

exe

tɕiʑɤɣ nɯ kɯ-fse ci a-pɯ-tu ndɤre, kɯra kɯ-fse mɯ-pɯ-nɤŋkɯŋke-tɕi wo \\
1du: gen dem sbj: pcp -be.like indef irr - ipfv -exist lnk dem. prox: pl sbj: pcp -be.like neg - pst. ipfv - distr:walk- 1du sfp \\
`If we had that (much cattle and fields), we would not be wandering around like this.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe
summary: Irrealis conditional clauses use an irrealis protasis, which competes with initial reduplication, prohibitive, and interrogative forms. With a factual non-past apodosis, they express a condition that is unlikely but, if fulfilled, is expected to bring about the stated result; with a past imperfective apodosis, they express counterfactual meaning.

text:
The Irrealis occurs in purposive complementation strategies. Two constructions are attested. First, as in ( ex:nAkArme.atAzbaR ), the Irrealis clauses expresse the purpose of an action referred to in another clause.

exe

kʰɤxtu ɕɯ-nɤʁaʁ-tɕi tɕe, [nɤ-kɤrme a-tɤ-zbaʁ] \\
rooftop tral -have.fun: fact - 1du lnk 2sg. poss -hair irr - pfv -be.dry \\
`Let us go to the rooftop platform to rest, so that your hair can dry (after bathing).' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

Second, with a similative verb such as fsebe like or studo like and interrogative pronoun as in ( ex:atAfse.YWphAn ), the Irrealis clause rather corresponds to the action needed to realize the purpose, which is indicated by a coordinated clause ɲɯ-pʰɤn `(so that) it is efficient/it works/it solves it'.

exe

[nɯ tɕʰi a-tɤ-fse] tɕe ɲɯ-pʰɤn \\
dem what irr - pfv -be.like lnk sens -be.efficient \\
`How [should he do] to solve [this problem]?' (Divination 2005)
exe
summary: The Irrealis is used in purposive complementation in two constructions. In one, the Irrealis clause directly expresses the purpose of an action in another clause, while in the other, it appears with a similative verb and interrogative pronoun to indicate the action needed to achieve a purpose, which is then stated by a coordinated clause meaning “so that it works/solves it.”

text:
Irrealis!prephrastic
The Periphrastic Irrealis combines the Irrealis copula a-pɯ-ŋu with one or a chain of several verbs in the Imperfective, as in ( ex:pjWwGnWXtCi.apWNu ) (see also § sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ).

exe

[ɯ-ŋgɯ pjɯ-kɯ-ɕe tɕe tɯ-ku ci pjɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-sɤɕɤt, pjɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-χtɕi] a-pɯ-ŋu ndɤre, wuma ʑo sɤ-scit tʰaŋ nɤ! \\
3sg. poss -inside ipfv: down - genr:S/O-go lnk genr. poss -head a.little ipfv - inv - auto -comb ipfv - inv - auto -wash irr - ipfv -be lnk really emph prop -be.happy: fact sfp sfp \\
`If one were to dive (in the water), comb and wash one's hair, it would be very nice!' (140515 congming de wusui xiaohai-zh)
0003998#S24
exe

It replaces the Imperfective Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.morphology ) in the case of telic verbs (see § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic ).
summary: The Periphrastic Irrealis is formed with the Irrealis copula *a-pɯ-ŋu* plus one verb or a chain of verbs in the Imperfective. It is used in place of the Imperfective Irrealis with telic verbs.

text: Imperative
summary: The passage is titled “Imperative” but does not provide any explanatory content beyond the heading. As given, it offers no linguistic facts or arguments to summarize.

text:
The Imperative is built by combining type A preverbs with stem I or stem III depending on transitivity and number (§ sec:stem.TAME ). It only has second person subject forms, which are however never marked with the second person tɯ- prefix, unlike in other TAME categories (§ sec:intr.23 ). In addition, transitive verbs can only take a third person object; 2 1 configurations cannot be expressed with the Imperative, and the Imperfective in hortative function is used instead (§ sec:ipfv.hortative ).

The Imperative can occur with an overt second person pronoun referring to the subject (see examples
