ex:tAnWndAm.je, § sec:imp.autive and ex:tAnWndAm.jAG, § sec:imp.compl ).

tab:imp.paradigms illustrates the Imperative paradigms of ndzaeat, a transitive verb with stem III alternation (§ sec:stem3 ), amdzɯsit, an intransitive contracting verb (§ sec:contraction ), and ɕego, a verb with stem II alternation (§ sec:stem2 )

For intransitive verbs which are neither contracting nor have stem II alternation, the Imperative forms are identical to the third person Aorist forms (§ sec:ambiguity.preverb ).

The Imperative lacks negative forms: the Prohibitive (§ sec:prohibitive ) or negative Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.main ) are used instead.
summary:
The Imperative is formed with type A preverbs plus stem I or stem III, depending on transitivity and number, and it has only second person subject forms without the usual second person tɯ- prefix. Transitive Imperatives allow only third person objects, so 2/1 configurations are not possible and the Imperfective in hortative function is used instead; the Imperative may also appear with an overt second person pronoun.  

For some intransitive verbs that are neither contracting nor show stem II alternation, Imperative forms are identical to the third person Aorist. The Imperative has no negative forms, so the Prohibitive or negative Irrealis is used instead.

text:
The Imperative expresses actions that the speaker wishes the addressee to realize. It is appropriate for blunt orders (§ ex:jACe ), requests ( ex:jAlAt.je ), and also polite invitations (§ ex:tAndzandZi ).

exe

jɤ-ɕe! \\
imp -go \\
`Go away!' (many examples)
exe

exe

toʁde tɕe jɤ-lɤt je ma a-<dianhua> ɯ-kɯ-lɤt ɣɤʑu \\
a.moment lnk imp -release sfp lnk 1sg. poss -phone 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -release exist: sens \\
`Call me in a moment, there is someone calling me on the phone!' (conversation, 22-08-2018)
exe

exe

<guazi> tɤ-ndza-ndʑi \\
melon.seed imp -eat- du \\
`Eat some melon seeds!' (conversation 14-05-10)
exe

The Imperative is not restricted to immediate commands/requests. In ( ex:thWsAtCAt.lArACi ), the actions referred to by the Imperative verbs lɤ-rɤɕi `pull it' and tʰɯ-sɤtɕɤt `add firewood' are to be realized (in the presence of the speaker) at two points of reference in the future indicated by temporal clauses in the Aorist (§ sec:aor.temporal ).

exe

``a-wi smi tʰɯ-sɤtɕɤt" tɤ-tɯt-a tɕe lɤ-rɤɕi, ``a-wi smi lɤ-rɤɕi" tɤ-tɯt-a tɕe tʰɯ-sɤtɕɤt ra \\
1sg. poss -grandmother fire imp -add.firewood aor -say[II]- 1sg lnk imp: upstream -pull 1sg. poss -grandmother fire imp: upstream -pull aor -say[II]- 1sg lnk imp -add.firewood be.needed: fact \\
`When I say `grandmother, add firewood', remove the firewood, and when I say `grandmother, remove the firewood', add firewood.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

As in Tshobdun, the Irrealis is found instead of the Imperative to express actions to be performed at a point in the future in the absence of the speaker (§ sec:irrealis.delayed.imp ).

The Imperative does not commonly occur for non-controllable verbs, especially stative verbs. However, this constraint is more pragmatic than morphosyntactic, and in some contexts, even a verb like mbrobe high can be used in the Imperative, as in ( ex:tWrtsAG.tAmbro ). In this type of example, the Imperative tɤ-mbro is identical to the 3sg Aorist. In principle, the quotation in ( ex:tWrtsAG.tAmbro ) could also mean `It grew by one node per day', but Tshendzin is positive that an Imperative was meant here.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ ɕɤr tɕe tu-mbri tɕe ``coʁcoʁcóʁcoʁcoʁ coʁcoʁcóʁcoʁcoʁ" tu-ti ŋu tɕe, ``tɯ-sŋi tɯ-rtsɤɣ tɤ-mbro, tɯ-sŋi tɯ-rtsɤɣ tɤ-mbro" tu-ti ŋu tu-ti-nɯ ŋgrɤl. \\
lnk dem night loc ipfv -sing lnk idph (X):cry idph (X):cry ipfv -say be: fact lnk one-day one -node imp -be.high one-day one -node imp -be.high ipfv -say be: fact ipfv -say- pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`(In June, when crops are about to grow), [the tacoʁcoʁ bird]$_i$ sings in the night, making the sound coʁcoʁcóʁcoʁcoʁ, people say that it$_i$ tells (the crops) `Grow by one node everyday!'.' (23-scuz)
0003612#S105
exe
summary: The imperative is used to express actions the speaker wants the addressee to carry out, including blunt orders, requests, and polite invitations. It can refer to actions not only immediate but also at future reference points, and in some contexts it may be replaced by the irrealis for delayed actions in the speaker’s absence. Although it is uncommon with non-controllable or stative verbs, such uses are possible in certain pragmatic contexts.

text:
Imperative!autive
With the Autive prefix (§ sec:autobenefactive ), the Imperative has two distinct and nearly opposite meanings.

First, it can indicate a mild suggestion or a request for a favour (§ sec:autoben.proper ), as in ( ex:tAnWndAm.je ).

exe

laʁjɯɣ nɤʑo tɤ-nɯ-ndɤm je tɕe, aʑo jɤɣɤt ci lu-ɕe-a nɤ \\
staff 2sg imp - auto -take[III] sfp lnk 1sg toilet indef ipfv: upstream -go- 1sg sfp \\
`Take the staff, I am going to the toilet.' (2005 khu)
exe

Second, it is also used in a mocking way to express defiance (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ), as in ( ex:nWnWnAre ) and ( ex:aqe.tAnWndze ).

exe

nɯ-nɯ-nɤre ma nɤʑo qaɕpa nɤ-rʑaβ nɤ-kɯ-mbi kɯ-tu me \\
imp - auto -laugh lnk 2sg frog 2sg. poss -wife 2sg. poss - sbj: pcp -give sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact \\
`Laugh as you wish, nobody will give you a wife, you frog.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

exe

kɤnɤβdi je a-wɯ tɯɟo, a-qe kɯ-sɤ-ɕkɯ ɕke ci tɤ-nɯ-ndze \\
farewell sfp 1sg. poss -grandfather demon 1sg. poss -shit sbj: pcp - prop - emph burn indef imp - auto -eat[III] \\
`Farewell, old demon, eat my hot shit!' (2005 tWJo)
exe
summary: With the Autive prefix, the Imperative can have two nearly opposite functions: it may soften into a mild suggestion or request for a favor, or it may be used mockingly to express defiance. The passage illustrates both uses with examples, showing that the same form can convey either polite prompting or sarcastic challenge.

text:
The Imperative is commonly used in complement clauses of modal verbs. The combination of the modal auxiliary jɤɣbe allowed with an Imperative complement clause expresses that the speaker politely allows the addressee to undertake an action that the addressee himself intends to do, as in ( ex:tAnWndAm.jAG ) and ( ex:tAthe.jAG ).

exe

[nɤʑo tɤ-nɯ-ndɤm] jɤɣ \\
2sg imp - auto -take[III] be.possible: fact \\
`Please take it.' (divination)
exe

exe

nɤ-kɤ-tʰu ɯ-ɣɤʑu nɤ, [tɤ-tʰe] jɤɣ \\
2sg. poss - obj: pcp -ask qu -exist: sens add imp -ask[III] be.possible: fact \\
`If you have a question, please ask.' (conversation, 14-11-08)
exe

The modal verb rabe needed with Imperative is used in requests ( ex:CtAthe ) and also blunt orders with death treats( ex:CtAre.ra.CWkAru ).

exe

ɕ-tɤ-tʰe ra \\
tral - imp -ask[III] be.needed: fact \\
`Go and ask him about it.' (divination)
exe

exe

ɕ-tɤ-re ra ma ɕɯ-kɤ-ru mɯ mɤ-pɯ-tɯ-cʰa ŋu nɤ nɤ-srɤm nɤ-sroʁ lɤt-i \\
tral - imp -bring[III] be.needed: fact lnk tral - inf -bring cond neg - aor -2-can be: fact lnk 1sg. poss -root 1sg. poss -life throw: fact - 1pl \\
`Go and bring it here; if you do not succeed in going and bringing it here, we will destroy your root and your life.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe
summary: Imperative complements commonly occur with modal verbs. With **jɤɣ** ‘be possible,’ the Imperative expresses a polite permission, allowing the addressee to do something they already intend to do. With **ra** ‘be needed,’ the Imperative is used in requests and also in blunt orders, including threats.

text:
Two verbs in the Imperative can be used in a Serial Verb Construction (§ sec:svc.manner ), the first verb conveying the manner in which the action is performed, as in ( ex:tAmbGom.tACe ).

exe

tɤ-mbɣom ʑo tɤ-ɕe ra\\
imp -be.in.a.hurry emph imp: up -go be.needed: fact \\
`Hurry up and go upstairs!' (160706 poucet6) 0006109#S5
exe

The first verb can be in the prohibitive (§ sec:prohibitive ), a construction meaning `do $V_2$ without doing $V_1$' ( ex:manWtWBde.tACe ).

exe

kɯki tʂu ki ma-nɯ-tɯ-βde ʑo jɤ-ɕe \\
dem. prox path dem. prox neg - imp -2-throw emph imp -go \\
`Go along this path without leaving it!' (140507 jinniao-zh)
0003931#S207
exe
summary: The passage says that two verbs can appear together in an Imperative serial verb construction, with the first verb expressing the manner of the action, as in “Hurry up and go upstairs!” It also notes that the first verb may instead be prohibitive, giving a meaning like “do V2 without doing V1,” as in “Go along this path without leaving it.”

text: Prohibitive
summary: The passage introduces the notion of **prohibitive**, a grammatical category used to express prohibition or the command not to do something. It indicates that this category is treated as a distinct type in the grammar description.

text:
The Prohibitive is built by combining the dedicated negative prefix ma- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ), a type A preverb and the stem III of the verb when appropriate (§ sec:stem3.form, § sec:stem.TAME ). In second person subject forms, unlike the Imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ), the second person prefix obligatorily occurs, as in ma-nɯ-tɯ-te `don't put him/her/it' ( ex:manWtWte ).

exe

nɯtɕu ma-nɯ-tɯ-te ma tɤ-pɤtso ra nɯ-sta ɕti \\
dem: loc neg - imp -2-put[III] lnk indef. poss -child pl 3pl. poss -place be. aff: fact \\
`Don't put her there, it is the place for the children.' (2003kAndzwsqhaj2)
exe

Unlike the Imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ), the prohibitive has no constraints on person. It can occurs in 2 1 configurations ( ex:matAkWndzaa ), but also with a first person intransitive ( ex:Za.matAnWnatCi ) or transitive subject ( ex:khramba.matABzea ) and also in very rare cases in the third person ( ex:manAtCaR.ra ).

exe

ma-tɤ-kɯ-ndza-a tɕetʰa nɤ-χpi pjɯ-fɕat-a \\
neg - imp -2 1-eat- 1sg later 2sg. poss -story ipfv -tell- 1sg \\
`Don't eat me, and I will tell you a story.' (tWJo 2012) 0004089#S60
exe

exe

ʑa ma-tɤ-nɯna-tɕi qʰe \\
soon neg - imp -rest- 1du lnk \\
`(In order to catch up with the wasted time), let us not stop (working) early (today).' (conversation 14-05-10)
exe

exe

nɯ kʰramba ma-tɤ-βze-a ra ma \\
dem lie neg - imp -make[III]- 1sg be.needed: fact sfp \\
`I musn't tell lies.' (27-kikakCi)
0003700#S208
exe

exe

tɕe tɯ-mdʑu ɯ-taʁ ma-nɯ-ɤtɕaʁ ra ma tɯ-mdʑu tu-sɤzoŋzoŋ ʑo qʰe cʰɯ-nɯɣmbɤβ ɕti. \\
lnk genr. poss -tongue 3sg. poss -on neg - imp -stain be.needed: fact lnk genr. poss -tongue ipfv -make.numb emph lnk ipfv -swell be. aff: fact \\
`[The Arisaema consanguineum ]$_i$ mustn't get on one's tongue$_j$, as it$_i$ makes it$_j$ numb and swell up.' (14-sWNgWJu)
0003506#S133
exe

The preverb is optional in second person prohibitive forms. For instance with tisay, ma-tɯ-ti ( neg: imp -2-say) and ma-tɤ-tɯ-ti ( neg - imp -2-say) both occur in free variation.

Despite the clear morphological differences between the Prohibitive and the Imperative, given the fact that these two categories are in complementary distribution and there is no risk of confusion, the type A preverb is glossed as imp and the negation as neg (to avoid a redundant gloss prohib on both prefixes). When the preverb is elided, the negative ma- is glossed as neg: imp.
summary:
The Prohibitive is formed with the negative prefix **ma-**, a type A preverb, and the verb’s stem III when appropriate. In second-person subject forms, the second-person prefix must appear, and unlike the Imperative, the Prohibitive is not restricted by person: it can be used with 2nd person, 1st person, and even rare 3rd person subjects.  

The preverb is optional in second-person prohibitives, with forms like **ma-tɯ-ti** and **ma-tɤ-tɯ-ti** occurring in free variation. Although the Prohibitive and Imperative are morphologically distinct, the type A preverb is glossed as **imp** and the negative prefix as **neg**, with **neg: imp** used when the preverb is omitted.

text:
The Prohibitive with a second person subject is essentially the negative counterpart of the Imperative, with exactly the same range of functions (§ sec:imp.function ), including orders, requests and polite suggestions, such as the polite expression ma-tɤ-tɯ-raʁle ( ex:matAtWrARle ), which corresponds to Chinese 不用客气 búyòngkèqìyou'r welcome.

exe

ma-tɤ-tɯ-raʁle, tɤ-ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-fka je\\
neg - imp -2-be.polite imp - refl - caus -be.full sfp \\
`Please eat your fill!' (heard in context)
exe

The prohibition can refer to an action to happen in the future, as in ( ex:taritCi.matWti ), where the moment when the action is to be avoided is indicated by the temporal clause in the Aorist (§ sec:aor.temporal ).

exe

tɕetu tɤ-ari-tɕi tɕe, ɯ-tɯ-ɣɤndʐo saχaʁ ʑo ri, ``ɯtɕʰɯtɕʰɯ" ma-tɯ-ti \\
up.there aor: up -go[II]- 1du lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.cold be.extremely: fact emph lnk interj neg: imp -2-say \\
`When we go up there (in the sky, near the moon), it will be extremely cold, but don't say `brrr'.' (07-deluge-64) 0003426#S62
exe

The negative Irrealis can also be used as a delayed prohibitive (§ sec:irrealis.delayed.imp ) as in ( ex:tatWt.amAtAtWti ), contrasting with the Prohibitive in the same way as the Irrealis in delayed imperative function contrasts with the Imperative (§ sec:imp.function ): the Prohibitive and Imperative imply that the speaker will be present when the action is to be realized or avoided (as in ex:taritCi.matWti ), while the Irrealis occurs when the speaker will not be present.

exe

iɕqʰa rɯdaʁ ra kɯ ta-tɯt nɯra, tɯrme ɯ-ɕki a-mɤ-tɤ-tɯ-ti ma \\
the.aforementioned animal pl erg aor:3 -say[II] dem: pl people 3sg. poss - dat irr - neg - pfv -2-say lnk \\
`You will have to avoid telling humans what the animals say.' (150902 hailibu-zh)
0006316#S80
exe

Like the Imperative (§ sec:imp.compl ), the prohibitive also occurs in subject complement clauses with auxiliaries such as rabe needed ( ex:khramba.matABzea, § sec:prohibitive.morpho ).

A construction with the same verb occurring in the Imperfective followed by its Prohibitive form in the first person, with the alternative interrogative particle ɕi (§ sec:fsp.interrog ) in between, is used to express hesitation between two possibilities ( ex:kuCea.makACea ).

exe

ku-ɕe-a ɕi ma-kɤ-ɕe-a kɯ \\
ipfv: east -go- 1sg sfp neg - imp -go- 1sg sfp \\
`[I wonder] whether to go or not.' (elicited)
exe

The Prohibitive is also used in manner clauses meaning `without doing $X$', sharing their subject (and also possibly object) with another verb in the Imperative or the Imperfective, as in ( ex:mapWwGsat ) (see also ex:manWtWBde.tACe, § sec:imp.SVC ).

exe

sɤtɕʰa kɯ-ɤrqʰi zɯ pjɯ́-wɣ-lɤt ma-pɯ́-wɣ-sat ra \\
place sbj: pcp -be.far loc ipfv: down - inv -release neg - imp - inv -kill be.needed: fact \\
`One has to take it far away (from the house) without killing it.' (2010-11)
exe

The Prohibitive is also found in the protasis of conditionals (§ sec:conditionals ), as in ( ex:matAwGnWBdaR ). This type of `warning' conditional construction expresses a possible undesirable result occurring if the subject fails to perform the action designated by the verb in the Prohibitive.

exe

tɤ-mtʰɯm kɯnɤ kɤ-kɤ-sqa nɯra ʑatsa ma-tɤ́-wɣ-nɯβdaʁ qʰe, ɯ-taʁ ri kɯ-wɣrum ku-te \\
indef. poss -meat also aor - obj: pcp -cook dem: pl soon neg - imp - inv -take.care lnk 3sg. poss -top loc sbj: pcp -be.white ipfv -put[III] \\
`In the case of meat also, if one fails to take care of cooked [meat] in time, white stuff will appear on it.' (20-sWrna,60)
0003564#S55
exe

Finally, it can also be used in a counterfactual construction as in ( ex:matAkWsWCqraRa ).

exe

nɯ sɤznɤ, nɤʑo kɯ ma-tɤ-kɯ-sɯ-ɕqraʁ-a kɯ pjɤ-mna! \\
dem comp 2sg erg neg - imp -2 1- caus -be.intelligent- 1sg erg pst. ifr -be.better \\
`It would have been better if you had not made me smart!' (160711 riquet8-v2) 0006201#S18
exe
summary: The Prohibitive with a second person subject is the negative counterpart of the Imperative and has the same functions, including orders, requests, and polite suggestions. It can also refer to future actions, serve as a delayed prohibitive with negative irrealis when the speaker will not be present, and appear in complement clauses, hesitation constructions, manner clauses meaning “without doing X,” conditional protases expressing warnings, and counterfactual constructions.

text:
Dubitative
The Dubitative ku- is formally identical to the B type eastwards preverbs, which also markes the Imperfective and the Egophoric Present (§ sec:egophoric ). It always occurs with the Autive -nɯ- prefix (§ sec:autobenefactive and with the polar question ɕi particule (§ sec:fsp.interrog, see example ex:kunWZru.Ci.kWma ), the interrogative kɯ (§ sec:fsp.interrog, ex:CW.ci.kunWNu.kW ) or the alternative polar question construction (combining a positive followed by the equivalent negative verb form as in ex:kunWphAn.mWkunWphAn ).

exe

tɕe lu-kɤ-nɯ-ji nɯ kɯ ʑru tu-ti-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe mɤ-xsi. ku-nnɯ-ʑru ɕi kɯma. \\
lnk ipfv - obj: pcp - auto -plant dem erg be.strong: fact ipfv -say- pl sens -be lnk neg - genr:know: fact dub - auto -be.strong qu sfp \\
`The cultivated [variety of Angelica] is better (than the wild one), they say, I don't know, maybe it is better.' (17-ndZWnW)
0003524#S33
exe

exe

ku-nɯ-pʰɤn mɯ-ku-nɯ-pʰɤn mɤ-xsi ma \\
dub - auto -be.efficient neg - dub - auto -be.efficient neg - genr:know: fact sfp \\
`I don't know whether it is efficient or not (as medicine).' (19-GzW) 0003536#S100
exe

In addition, dubitative verb forms are followed either by the sentence final particles kɯma or kɯɣe (§ sec:fsp.interrog ) as in ( ex:kunWZru.Ci.kWma ) or a verb form such as mɤ-xsione does not know (§ ex:kunWphAn.mWkunWphAn ).

The dubitative is mainly used to express doubts while reporting opinions from other people (as in ex:kunWZru.Ci.kWma and ex:kunWphAn.mWkunWphAn ), but with the interrogative kɯ as in ( ex:CW.ci.kunWNu.kW ), its meaning is rather that of emphasis on the fact that the speaker has no clue about the answer to the question (as in French donc...bien in ` Qui donc cela peut-il bien être? ').

exe

wo, nɯ ɕɯ ci ku-nɯ-ŋu kɯ? \\
interj dem who indef dub - auto -be qu \\
`Who on earth is it [who does all] that?' (2014-kWLAG)
exe
summary:
The dubitative prefix **ku-** is formally identical to the eastwards preverbs and always appears with the **Autive -nɯ-** prefix. It is also used with polar-question particles such as **ɕi**, **kɯ**, or the alternative polar question construction, and dubitative verb forms may be followed by **kɯma** or **kɯɣe**.

Its main function is to express doubt, especially when reporting other people’s opinions. With interrogative **kɯ**, however, it conveys emphasis that the speaker has no idea what the answer is.

text:
Tense!Past
The Aorist, Past Imperfective, Inferential Perfective and Inferential Imperfective all strictly express past tense events or states when occurring in main clauses. In addition, they all take the past transitive -t suffix (§ sec:other.TAME ) in 1sg 3 and 2sg 3 forms of open stem verbs (see § sec:aor.morphology, § sec:ifr.morphology and § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ). The only non-past TAME category that is compatible with the -t suffix is the Apprehensive (§ sec:apprehensive ).

This section describes the morphology of these TAME categories, their uses in main clauses and subordinate clauses, and also the semantic contrast between them in various contexts.
summary:
The Aorist, Past Imperfective, Inferential Perfective, and Inferential Imperfective all express past tense events or states in main clauses, and they all take the past transitive **-t** suffix in 1sg/3 forms and 2sg/3 forms of open stem verbs. Among non-past TAME categories, only the Apprehensive is compatible with this suffix.

The section goes on to describe the morphology and uses of these categories in main and subordinate clauses, as well as their semantic contrasts in different contexts.

text: Aorist
summary: The passage concerns the aorist, a grammatical category used to describe a form or tense in the language. However, no further details about its meaning, form, or use are provided in the excerpt.

text:
The Aorist is built by combining stem II (§ sec:stem2, or stem I for non-alternating verbs) with either A-type ( ex:tAGej ) or C-type preverbs ( ex:tatWt ) depending on person configuration and transitivity (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs, § sec:preverb.TAME.morphology ): the latter are restricted to transitive direct 3 configurations (§ sec:indexation.non.local ).

exe

tɤ-ɣe-j \\
aor: up -come[II]- 1pl \\
`We came up.' (many attestations)
exe

exe

ta-tɯt \\
aor:3 -say[II] \\
`S/he said it.' (many attestations)
exe

In addition, like the Inferential, the Aorist takes the 1/2 sg 3 Past transitive suffix -t (§ sec:suffixes, § sec:other.TAME ). Complete paradigms of transitive and intransitive verbs in the Aorist are presented in § sec:polypersonal, and need not be repeated here.

Some Aorist verb forms are ambiguous and could be interpreted as belonging to other TAME categories. The ambiguity with the Imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ) is discussed in detail in § sec:ambiguity.preverb. A more difficult case is that between Past Imperfective pɯ- (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv ) and the Aorist of stative verbs selecting downwards as their intrinsic orientation (§ sec:lexicalized.orientation ). The only way of differentiating between the two is the clear inchoative meaning of stative verbs in the Aorist (§ sec:aor.inchoative ), showing that pɯ-rom in ( ex:pWrom.kWnA ) can only be analyzed as an Aorist `(when) it has dried' rather than as a Past Imperfective `it was dry' (see also example § sec:ipfv.inchoative, § ex:YWYaR.Zo.Nu ).

exe

ɯ-jwaʁ rcanɯ pɯ-rom kɯnɤ ɯ-mdzu nɯ mɤʑɯ ʑo mtɕoʁ \\
3sg. poss -leaf unexp: deg aor -be.dry also 3sg. poss -thorn dem even.more emph be.sharp: fact \\
`When its leaves have dried, the thorns (on the leaves) are even sharper.' (18-NGolo)
0003530#S66
exe
summary:
The Aorist is formed from stem II, or stem I in non-alternating verbs, combined with either A-type or C-type preverbs, with C-type preverbs limited to transitive direct 3 configurations. Like the Inferential, it also takes the suffix -t in 1/2 singular and 3rd-person past transitive forms.  

Some Aorist forms are ambiguous with other TAM categories, especially the Imperative and the Past Imperfective. In particular, stative verbs in the Aorist have a clear inchoative meaning, which distinguishes them from Past Imperfective forms.

text:
The Aorist occurs in main clauses to express past perfective events that the speaker has witnessed him/herself. It is used to report actions that the speaker has performed himself, as in ( ex:tAXtWta.pWBzuta ) and ( ex:nACki.tAtWta ), unlike the Inferential, which is only compatible with first person in very specific contexts (§ sec:ifr ).

exe

nɯ kɯ-fse rcanɯ, <qibajin> ʑo tɤ-χtɯ-t-a. tɕe <dong> pɯ-βzu-t-a \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.like unexp: deg seven.or.eight.pounds emph aor -buy- pst: tr - 1sg lnk freeze aor -make- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`[Nettles] like that, I bought seven or eight pounds. Then I put them in the refrigerator.' (conversation, 14-05-10)
exe

In the absence of any adverb with a function comparable to English `already' in Japhug, the Aorist is used to express this meaning, in combination with a tense adverb as in ( ex:nACki.tAtWta ). Tshendzin said ( ex:nACki.tAtWta ) answering a question I had already asked a few days before.

exe

jɯfɕɯndʐi nɤ-ɕki tɤ-tɯt-a ma, wuma ʑo a-tsa ʑo ɲɯ-βze \\
a.few.days.ago 2sg. poss - dat aor -say[II]- 1sg lnk really emph 1sg. poss -adapted emph sens -make[III] \\
`I already told you a few days ago, [the shoes you have sent me] fit me really well.' (conversation, 2019-05-26)
exe

Actions that the speaker has witnessed as a passive participant are also expressed with the Aorist rather than the Inferential.

exe

a-kɯ-rtoʁ jɤ-ɣe tɕe ɣɯ-nɯ́-wɣ-mbi-a \\
1sg. poss - sbj: pcp -look aor -come[II] lnk cisl - aor - inv -give- 1sg \\
`He came to see me and gave it to me.' (conversation, 17-09-21)
exe

In ( ex:jWfCWCAr.tAjpa.kalAt ), the choice of the Aorist ka-lɤt and the Past Imperfective pɯ-wxti reflects the fact that the speaker has directly seen the snowfall (rather than deducing its occurrence from the presence of snow on the ground). By contrast, the Inferential to-ndʐi `it melted' (rather than the Aorist tɤ-ndʐi ) indicates that the speaker has not witnessed the melting, and only deduced that it has occurred due to the absence of snow, despite the snowfall in the previous night (§ sec:ifr.evd ).

exe

kutɕu hanɯni ɲɯ-ɣɤndʐo. jɯfɕɯɕɤr tɤjpa ka-lɤt. ka-lɤt ri mɯ-pɯ-wxti. jisŋi tɕe lonba to-ndʐi. \\
dem. prox: loc a.little sens -be.cold yesterday.night snow aor:3 -release aor:3 -release lnk neg - pst. ipfv -be.big today lnk all ifr - acaus:melt \\
`Here it is a bit cold. It snowed yesterday evening. There was snow but not much, and now it has melted completely.' (conversation, 17-11-23)
exe

The Aorist is also used to describe the events that the speaker has seen on a film, for instance the pear stories, as in ( ex:aor.pear ).

exe

tɤ-pɤtso kɯ-ɤ<nɯ>ɣro tsuku ɣɤʑu-nɯ jɤ-ɣe-nɯ tɕe, nɯra kɯ ɯ-paχɕi ra kɤ-wum ta-qur-nɯ tɕe, ta-sɯɣ-ndzur-nɯ \\
indef. poss -child sbj: pcp -< auto >play several exist: sens - pl aor -come[II]- pl lnk dem: pl erg inf -collect aor:3 -help- pl lnk aor:3 - caus -stand- pl \\
`There were some children playing (there), they came, helped him to collect the apples (that had been spilled) and helped him up.' (chen-pear)
exe

For events that have occurred in a more remote past, the requirement on direct (visual) perception may be less strict. For instance, in ( ex:tAngo.thWmdW ), the verbs in the Aorist express a series of events that have happened to a member of the speaker's extended family. They did not live in the same household, and did not meet very frequently, and the speaker did not witness all of the events, but is familiar enough with the situation to feel entitled to use the Aorist rather than the Inferential.

exe

nɯ-mu nɯ tɤ-ngo qʰe ci ci nɯ-si kɯ-fse ci ci tɤ-mna kɯ-fse qʰe kɯɕnɯ-xpa ʑo tʰɯ-mdɯ. \\
3pl. poss -mother dem aor -be.ill lnk one one aor -die sbj: pcp -be.like one one aor -be.better sbj: pcp -be.like lnk seven-year emph aor -live.up.to \\
`Their mother got ill, and survived seven years, sometimes looking like she had died, sometimes looking like she was getting better.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S31
exe
summary: The Aorist in main clauses marks past perfective events that the speaker has directly witnessed, including actions the speaker themselves performed, and it can also express the equivalent of “already” when used with a tense adverb. It is used for events the speaker observed as a participant or on a film, and in some more remote-past contexts it may still be chosen if the speaker feels familiar enough with the situation, whereas the Inferential is used when the event is only deduced rather than witnessed.

text:
Aorist!Temporal clauses
In main clauses, stative verbs (other than copulas, § sec:copula.basic ) in the Aorist always express a change of state, whether adjectival verbs such as dɤnbe many ( ex:tAdAnnW3 ) or existential verbs ( ex:nWme ).

exe

nɯre kɯmaʁ pɕoʁ <banqian> jɤ-kɯ-ɣe nɯra tu-nɯ tɕe, tɤ-dɤn-nɯ. \\
dem: loc other side move aor - sbj: pcp -come[II] dem: pl exist: fact - pl lnk aor -be.many- pl \\
`(Now) there are people who have come from other places (to settle in that village), [and the number of inhabitants] has increased.' (140522 tshupa)
0004053#S85
exe

exe

nɤ-<dian> nɯ-me \\
2sg. poss -electricity aor -not.exist \\
`Your [cellphone] is out of battery.' (you don't have any electricity anymore) (heard in context)
exe

The Aorist is however found on stative verbs in some temporal subordinate clauses (§ sec:aor.temporal ) without change of state meaning.

In addition to stative verbs, some modal verbs such as cʰacan select the upwards orientation with an inchoative meaning, as illustrated by example ( ex:tAnANkWNkea.tAchaa ) (§ sec:TAM.finite ) (see also § sec:ifr.inchoative ).
summary: In main clauses, stative verbs in the Aorist normally indicate a change of state, including adjectival and existential verbs. However, in some temporal subordinate clauses, stative verbs can appear in the Aorist without this change-of-state meaning. The passage also notes that some modal verbs, such as cʰacan, can take an upwards orientation with an inchoative meaning.

text:
The Aorist is used in subordinate clauses to mark a point of temporal reference. It occurs in generic statements to indicate the period when an event takes place. For instance in ( ex:ftCar.kAndzoR.tulhoR ), the temporal clause ftɕar kɤ-ndzoʁ `when summer arrives' must select the Aorist; no other TAME category would be possible here.

exe

ɯ-fsaqʰe, [ftɕar kɤ-ndzoʁ] qʰe li tu-ɬoʁ. \\
3sg. poss -next.year summer aor - acaus:attach lnk again ipfv -come.out \\
`The next year, when the warm season (spring) arrives, it comes out again.' (of a perennial plant, 18-qromJoR)
0003532#S134
exe

Direct visual perception is irrelevant in temporal clauses. In ( ex:tCaGi.tuti ), the Aorist jɤ-ɣe occurs even though the speaker is only reporting a story about a parrot that she has not witnessed personally, and only heard from someone else. Here the meaning of the Aorist is simply to state the temporal condition when the following actions (utterance of human speech) take place.

exe

tɯrme jɤ-ɣe tɕe <laikerenle> tu-ti, tɕe <nihao> tu-ti. \\
person aor -come[II] lnk a.guest.has.arrived ipfv -say lnk hello ipfv -say \\
`(Of a parrot which is able to say a few words) When someone comes, [the parrot] says `A guest has arrived', and says `hello'.' (24-qro) 0003626#S102
exe

With stative verbs, the Aorist can exceptionally be used without inchoative meaning (§ sec:aor.inchoative ) in temporal clauses, but always with the upwards tɤ- preverb. For instance in ( ex:tAjpum.tAxtshWm ), tɤ-jpum and tɤ-xtsʰɯm mean `when it is thick' and `when it is thin', not `when it becomes thick/thin', which would be expressed with the intrinsic westwards preverbs (see also ex:si.tAme, § sec:preverb.loss and ex:nWma.tAme, § sec:orientation.preverb.aspect ).

exe

tɤ-jpum tɕe tɕendɤre tɯ-sŋi kʰro lú-wɣ-taʁ ɲɯ-kɯ-cʰa ma tɤ-xtsʰɯm tɕe tɕe, koŋla lú-wɣ-taʁ mɯ́j-sɤ-cʰa \\
aor -be.thick lnk lnk one-day much ipfv - inv -weave sens - genr:S/O-can lnk aor -be.thin lnk lnk completely ipfv - inv -weave neg: sens - prop -can \\
`When [the threads] are thick, one can weave a lot in one day, when they are thin, it is not possible to weave.' (2011-06-thaXtsa)
exe

Apart from stative verbs, a similar use of the upwards orientation is found with the transitive verb sɯsothink, `want' in some contexts (§ sec:sWso.complement ).

While the Aorist is restricted to past events in main clauses, it is found in temporal clauses to express points of time reference in the future. In ( ex:pWtWnWGenW.nWtCu ) and ( ex:pWtari.nWtCu ), the Aorist forms pɯ-tɯ-nɯ-ɣe-nɯ `when you come back' and pɯ-tɯ-ari `when you go down' refer to events that have not yet taken place at the time of utterance. The use of the Aorist in future contexts is also observed in conditional clauses (§ sec:aor.cond ).

exe

nɯʑo pɯ-tɯ-nɯ-ɣe-nɯ nɯtɕu cuparkʰɤrkʰɤt a-pɯ-tɯ-ɬoʁ-nɯ tɕe aʑo tʰɤlwa ɲɯɣɲɯɣ pjɯ-ɬoʁ-a ŋu \\
2pl aor: down -2- vert -come[II] dem: loc stone.step irr - pfv: down -2-come.out- pl lnk 1sg earth idph (II):soft ipfv: down -come.out- 1sg be: fact \\
`When you come back, take the stone steps, I will come down on the soft earth.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

exe

tɕetʰa pɯ-tɯ-ari tɕe, ki a-kɤ-tɯ-ɕtʰɯz tɕe, tɕetʰa ju-nɯ-ɕe-nɯ ɕti \\
soon aor: down -2-go[II] lnk dem. prox irr - pfv: east -2-turn.towards lnk soon ipfv - vert -go- 1sg be. aff: fact \\
`When you go down there, turn [this magical object] in their direction (of the râkshasas), and they will go back (from where they are from).' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

In ( ex:tCetha.nWmbrAt ), both the temporal clause and the main clause contain a verb in the Aorist, but in the latter, that verb nɯ-me `it disappeared' is embedded in a complement clause headed by the noun ɯ-ndʐacause (§ sec:causal.clauses, § sec:nouns.cause.complement, with elided possessive prefix), while the main verb ŋube is in the Factual.

exe

a-ʁa tu ri, tɕetʰa nɯ-mbrɤt tɕe tɕe [a-<dian> nɯ-me] ndʐa ŋu \\
1sg. poss -free.time exist: fact lnk soon aor - acaus:break lnk lnk 1sg. poss -electricity aor -not.exist reason be: fact \\
`I have time (to talk with you), but in a moment when [the phone line] disconnects, it will be because [my cellphone] is out of battery.' (conversation)
exe

The Aorist in subordinate clauses is not always used to fix a point of temporal reference, however. It can also refer to an event preceding those of the following clauses, and which the speaker has witnessed (as in main clauses, § sec:aor.main ). In ( ex:nwWGmbia.plusquampft ), the clause tɤ-mtʰɯm nɯ́-wɣ-mbi-a is not to be translated as `when (s/he/someone) gave/gives meat' (a translation that is possible in other contexts), but rather as `(someone) had given me' with as pluperfect, as a background event that took place before the whole story begins.

exe

tɤ-mtʰɯm nɯ́-wɣ-mbi-a tɕe, tu-ndze-a pɯ-ŋu tɕe, kʰɤxtu ri pɯ-rɤʑi-a. \\
indef. poss -meat aor - inv -give- 1sg lnk ipfv -eat[III]- 1sg pst. ipfv -be lnk roof loc pst. ipfv -stay- 1sg \\
`[Someone] had given me [a piece of] meat, and I was eating it, I was staying on the roof platform (and then a kite flew down and robbed it). (150909 qandZGi)
0006358#S2
exe
summary:
The passage explains that the Aorist in subordinate temporal clauses marks a point of temporal reference, including events in generic statements and even future time, where no other TAME category is possible. It can also appear with stative verbs in temporal clauses, but then it requires the upward tɤ- preverb and has a non-inchoative meaning.  

Although the Aorist is limited to past events in main clauses, subordinate clauses may use it for future reference or, in some cases, for an earlier background event with pluperfect-like meaning.

text:
In the protasis of reduplicated conditional (§ sec:redp.protasis ), the Aorist has a purely aspectual function, and does not express absolute past tense, but past tense relative to the apodosis.

The Aorist occurs in the protasis in generic contexts, as in ( ex:mWmAthWwGndZWr ).

exe

tɤɕi, qaj, stoʁ staʁpɯ nɯra mɯ mɤ-tʰɯ́-wɣ-ɣndʑɯr nɤ kɤ-ndza mɤ-kʰɯ \\
barley wheat broad.bean peas dem: pl cond neg - aor - inv -grind add inf -eat neg -be.possible: fact \\
`If we don't grind barley, wheat, broad beans and peas, they cannot be eaten.' 06-BGa)
0003408#S5
exe

It is also found in conditional constructions referring to future events, as in ( ex:tWtAtWtWt ) and ( ex:pWpWnNo.nA ). This usage reminds of the use of the Aorist in future temporal clauses (such as ex:pWtWnWGenW.nWtCu, § sec:aor.temporal ).

exe

tɯ tɤ-tɯ-tɯt nɤ tɕe pjɯ-ta-sat ŋu \\
cond aor -2-say[II] add lnk ipfv -1 2-kill be: fact \\
`If you tell [people] about it, I will kill you.' (150901 changfamei-zh) 0006352#S48
exe

exe

pɯ pɯ-nŋo nɤ, ndʑiʑo ʁnɯz ɣɯ ndʑi-ku cʰɯ́-wɣ-pʰɯt ra \\
cond aor -be.defeated add 2du two gen 2du. poss -head ipfv - inv -take.off be.needed: fact \\
`If he fails, we will decapitate both of you.' (140505 liuhaohan zoubian tianxia-zh)
0003913#S103
exe

The Aorist is less felicitous in the protasis of counterfactuals (§ sec:counterfactual ), where the Irrealis is used instead (§ sec:irrealis.conditional ).
summary: In reduplicated conditionals, the Aorist in the protasis functions purely aspectually and indicates past time only relative to the apodosis, not absolute past tense. It appears in generic and future-oriented conditional clauses, but is less appropriate in counterfactual protases, where the Irrealis is used instead.

text:
relative clause!Aorist Aorist!relative clause
The Aorist commonly occurs in finite relative clauses (§ sec:finite.relatives ), as in the object head-internal relative in ( ex:nakho.nWnW.koCthWz ).

exe

iɕqʰa [srɯnloʁ-pɯ kɯ-fse na-kʰo] nɯnɯ ko-ɕtʰɯz \\
the.aforementioned ring- dim sbj: pcp -be.like aor:3 3-give dem ifr: east -turn.towards \\
`He$_i$ turned the little ring that [Smanmi Metog Koshana] had given him$_i$ in their direction (of the râkshasas). (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S161
exe

The verb in the relative can also undergo totalitative reduplication of the first syllable (§ sec:totalitative.redp ), as tɯ ta-stu `all (the ways) in which she had done it'. The object of the verb studo like refers to the manner in which the action is performed, not its patient (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ).

exe

[ɯ-pi kɯ tɯ ta-stu] nɯ to-stu qʰe \\
3sg. poss -elder.sibling erg total aor:3 -do.like dem ifr -do.like lnk \\
`She did everything like her elder sister.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

In relative clauses, the contrast between Aorist and Inferential is neutralized, as only the Aorist can appear. Thus, in both ( ex:nakho.nWnW.koCthWz ) and ( ex:tWtastu.tostu ) above, the verb of the relative clause in the Aorist, while that of the main clause is in the Inferential. The events referred to in the Aorist in these relative clauses occur in the Inferential earlier in the stories: compare for instance the Inferential ɲɤ-kʰo in the main clause in ( ex:kWfse.ci.YAkho ) with the Aorist na-kʰo in the relative in ( ex:nakho.nWnW.koCthWz ).

exe

srɯnloʁ-pɯ kɯ-fse ci ɲɤ-kʰo. \\
ring- dim sbj: pcp -be.like indef ifr -give \\
`[Smanmi Metog Koshana] gave him something like a little ring.' (28-smAnmi) 0004063#S150
exe
summary: The Aorist commonly appears in finite relative clauses, including head-internal relatives, and can also occur in relatives with totalitative reduplication of the verb. In these relative clauses, the contrast between Aorist and Inferential is neutralized because only the Aorist appears in the relative clause, even when the main clause uses the Inferential.

text:
complement clause!Aorist Aorist!complement clause
Some finite complement clauses take the Aorist when the main verb is also in the Aorist, as in ( ex:nWnAzreta.pWchaa ).

exe

aʑo [nɯ-z-nɤre-t-a] pɯ-cʰa-a \\
1sg aor - caus -laugh- pst: tr - 1sg aor -can- 1sg \\
`I succeeded in making her laugh.' (140430 jin e-zh) 0003893#S166
exe
summary: Some finite complement clauses appear in the Aorist when the main verb is also in the Aorist. The example given shows this pattern in a sentence meaning “I succeeded in making her laugh,” where both the causative main verb and the complement clause are marked Aorist.

text:
Some speakers (in particular Kunbzang Mtsho ) use the Periphrastic Narrative instead of the Inferential as the main TAME category of narration when telling traditional stories.

The Periphrastic Narrative combines a verb in the Aorist with the copula in the Sensory ɲɯ-ŋu. In ( ex:thWstanW.YWNu ), the periphrastic construction tʰɯ-sta-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu `they woke up' corresponds to an Inferential cʰɤ-sta-nɯ in a similar story told by another speaker ( ex:chAstanW ).

exe

nɯ ʁmaʁ kɯ kɯ-tu ʑo tʰɯ-sta-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
dem soldier total sbj: pcp -exist emph aor -wake- pl sens -be \\
`All the soldiers woke up.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S39
exe

exe

iɕqʰa kɯ-rɯru ʁmaʁmi nɯra cʰɤ-sta-nɯ. \\
the.aforementioned sbj: pcp -guard soldiers dem: pl ifr -wake- pl \\
`The guards woke up.' (140507 jinniao-zh)
0003931#S145
exe

As in the case of other periphrastic TAME constructions (see in particular ex:chain.pjANu, § sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME concerning the Periphrastic Imperfective), a chain of several verbs in the Aorist can share one copula. In ( ex:mWtAtWtndZi.YWNu ) for instance, the copula ɲɯ-ŋu has scope over two clauses, each containing a verb in the Aorist ( ta-tɯt and mɯ-ta-tɯt-ndʑi, respectively).

exe

tɕe [kɯ-wxti ni ndʑi-pʰe ta-tɯt] ri, [kɯ-wxti ni kɯ mɯ-ta-tɯt-ndʑi] ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk sbj: pcp -big du 3du. poss - dat aor:3 -say[II] lnk sbj: pcp -big du erg neg - aor:3 -say[II]- du sens -be \\
`He told it$_i$ to the two elder [sisters]$_j$, but they$_j$ did not tell it$_i$ [to their$_j$ parents].' (2005-stod-kunbzang)
exe

In the case of the verb tisay, while the regular Periphrastic Narrative is attested ( ex:mWtAtWtndZi.YWNu ), we also find a periphrastic form ti ɲɯ-ŋu ( ex:ti.YWNu ) with the Factual ti instead of the Aorist ta-tɯt.

exe

``a-pi ɲɯ-ɕpaʁ-a" ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
1sg. poss -elder.sibling sens -be.thirsty- 1sg say: fact sens -be \\
`She said: `Sister, I am thirsty.'' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

The verb tisay in the Factual can share a copula with verbs in the Aorist in Periphrastic Narrative chains. In ( ex:ti.nA.tatWt ), the Factual form ti belongs to the same chain as the following Aorist form ta-tɯt, and ɲɯ-ŋu has scope over both of them. This periphrastic construction is similar to that of ( ex:mWtAtWtndZi.YWNu ) above, but with a verb in the Factual instead of the Aorist in the first clause.

exe

[stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ ɯ-pʰe ti] nɤ, [nɯ kɯ li ta-tɯt] ɲɯ-ŋu \\
most sbj: pcp -be.small dem 3sg. poss - dat say: fact add dem erg again aor:3 -say[II] sens -be \\
`He told it$_i$ to the youngest [sister]$_j$, and she$_j$ told it$_i$ [to her parents].' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe
summary: Some speakers, especially Kunbzang Mtsho, use the Periphrastic Narrative rather than the Inferential as the main narrative TAME category in traditional stories. This construction consists of an Aorist verb plus the sensory copula ɲɯ-ŋu, and one copula can have scope over a chain of multiple Aorist clauses; in some cases, a Factual form of **tisay** can also appear in such chains.

text:
Inferential
In this section, the term ``Inferential'' is used as abbreviation for ``Inferential Perfective'', as opposed to the`Inferential Imperfective discussed in § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.
summary: “Inferential” here is used as a shortened term for “Inferential Perfective.” It is distinguished from the “Inferential Imperfective,” which is discussed elsewhere in the grammar.

text:
In the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug, the Inferential is built from the stem I of the verb with type D preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs, § sec:preverb.TAME.morphology ). For instance, the verb ɕego (whose stem II is -ari, § sec:stem2 ), has the Inferential 3sg form jo-ɕe ( ifr -say) `he said' with the indefinite orientation type D preverb jo- and the stem I -ɕe.

In the Xtokavian dialects of Japhug, there are only two series of preverbs (A and B), and the Inferential is marked by combining the B type preverbs with the Inferential prefix a-. The second person prefix tɯ- is inserted between the preverb and the Inferential a- (compare ex:YEtanWYAmkhe and ex:YAtWnWYAmkhe, § sec:xtokavian.preverbs ).

Transitive verbs with open syllable stem with first and second person singular subjects and third person object in addition select the -t past tense suffix (§ sec:suffixes, § sec:other.TAME, -z in some dialects of Japhug), as illustrated by ( ex:cha.kotshita ), ( ex:mWtotata ) and ( ex:WsroR.kotWrit ) (see also ex:mWtosAlata, § sec:inf.1person ).

exe

aʑo cʰa kʰro ko-tsʰi-t-a \\
1sg alcohol much ifr -drink- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I drank a lot of alcohol.' (aesop zuoke de gou-zh)
exe

exe

maka nɤ-βzaŋlɤn βze-a ra ma a-tɕɯ ɯ-sroʁ ko-tɯ-ri-t tɕe \\
completely 2sg. poss -payback make[III]: fact - 1sg be.needed: fact lnk 1sg. poss -son 3sg. poss -life ifr -2-save- pst: tr lnk \\
`I have to return the favour, as you have saved my son's life.' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

The verb tisay is irregular in lacking this suffix in the Inferential; the 1sg and 2sg Inferential of this verb are thus to-ti-a and to-tɯ-ti as in ( ex:tChi.totia ), not $ $ to-ti-t-a and $ $ to-tɯ-ti-t.

exe

tɕe nɯ ɯ-qʰu tɕe tɕʰi to-ti-a? \\
lnk dem 3sg. poss -after lnk what ifr -say- 1sg \\
`What did I say after that?' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S159
exe

The Inferential occurs with the negative prefix mɯ- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ), as in ( ex:mWtotata ).

exe

mɯ-to-ta-t-a \\
neg - ifr -put- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I did not put [the tea on the oven].' (Conversation, 28-04-2018, Dpalcan )
exe

In the Kamnyu dialect, the preverbs are prevented from merging with the initial a- of contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction ) by insertion of the peg circumfix (§ sec:peg.circumfix ), to avoid confusion with the Imperfective (since the result of the vowel merger of B type and D type preverbs with a- is identical). This insertion occurs in third ( ex:tWrme.YAkABzunWci ) and first person (see ex:WRjoR.YAkABzuaci, § sec:inf.1person ) forms.

exe

koŋla tɯrme ɲɤ-k-ɤβzu-nɯ-ci \\
really person ifr - peg -become- pl - peg \\
`[The puppets] became real people.' (150822 yan muouxi de ren-zh) 0006384#S42
exe

In the second person, the prefix tɯ- occurs in slot -2 (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain, like the prefixal element k(ɯ)- of the peg circumfix.) between the preverbs and the verb stem,

exe

nɤʑo pɣa ɲɤ-tɯ-ɤβzu ɕti tɕe \\
2sg bird ifr -2-become be. aff: fact lnk \\
`You have become (been transformed into) a bird.' (160630 abao-zh)
0006197#S143
exe

tab:ifr.paradigms presents the paradigms of a regular transitive verb ( tsʰidrink), the irregular tisay (both with a 3sg object) and an intransitive contracting verb ( aβzubecome, grow) in the Kamnyu dialect.

The contrast between upper A-type ( tɤ, lɤ, kɤ, jɤ- ) and D-type preverbs ( to, lo, ko, jo- ) is neutralized when followed by the inverse prefix (see tab:A.D.inv, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), so that transitive verbs without stem II alternation selecting the upper orientations have syncretism between Aorist and Inferential. For instance, the phonetic form kóɣndo is ambiguous between the Aorist 3$'$ 3 kɤ́-wɣ-ndo ( aor - inv -take) and the Inferential 3$'$ 3 kó-wɣ-ndo ( aor - inv -take), both translatable as `someone/it/s/he grabbed him/her'.
summary:
In the Kamnyu dialect of Japhug, the Inferential is formed with stem I plus type D preverbs, while in Xtokavian dialects it is formed by combining B-type preverbs with the Inferential prefix a-, with tɯ- inserted before a- in second person forms. In Kamnyu, transitive verbs with open-syllable stems and 1st/2nd singular subjects plus a 3rd object also take a -t past suffix, though the verb *tisay* is irregular and lacks it in the Inferential.  

The Inferential also co-occurs with the negative prefix mɯ-, and in contracting verbs Kamnyu inserts the peg circumfix to keep preverbs from merging with initial a-, especially to avoid confusion with the Imperfective. Upper A-type and D-type preverbs are neutralized after the inverse prefix, which can make Aorist and Inferential forms syncretic for some transitive

text:
In main clauses, the Inferential is used to express past perfective event, like the Aorist (§ sec:aor.main ). The contrast between these two categories is of an evidential nature: the Aorist is selected if the speaker had directly witnessed the event, while the Inferential occurs when only indirect clues allow him/her to deduce that the action has taken place.

For instance, ( ex:tAjpa.kalAt2 ) in the Aorist can be uttered if the speaker has seen the snowfall, while ( ex:tAjpa.kolAt ) in the Inferential is chosen if the speaker infers that a snowfall has taken place from the presence of snow on the ground.

exe

xlist

tɤjpa ka-lɤt \\
snow aor:3 3-release \\

tɤjpa ko-lɤt \\
snow ifr -release \\
xlist
`It snowed.' (elicited, see ex:jWfCWCAr.tAjpa.kalAt above)
exe

In the case of predicates involving a change of state, selecting the Aorist is only possible if the speaker has witnessed the whole process. For instance, to express the meaning `the water boiled', the Aorist in ( ex:tWci.tala ) is possible only if the speaker has observed the change of phase of water to ebullition, while the Inferential form ( ex:tWci.tokAlaci ) is used when the s/he notices that the water has already started boiling.

exe

xlist

tɯ-ci tɤ-ala \\
indef. poss -water aor -boil \\

tɯ-ci to-k-ɤla-ci \\
indef. poss -water ifr - peg -boil- peg \\
xlist
`The water boiled.' (elicited)
exe

In narratives concerning the speaker, the Aorist is used in the case of actions that s/he has directly seen, while the Inferential is chosen for events that s/he has not directly perceived. For instance, in ( ex:qandZGi.pjAGi ), the speaker selects the Inferential pjɤ-ɣi to describe the coming of the falcon, as she had not noticed the presence of that bird until the piece of meat in her hand was snatched away. Selecting the Aorist pɯ-ɣe ( aor: down -come[II]) `it came down' instead would mean that the speaker had seen the falcon approaching. The Aorist ta-nɯ-mɟa `it took it away' expresses that the speaker felt and saw the meat being taken away; choosing Inferential to-nɯ-mɟa instead would have implied that the speaker had not even noticed the snatching event, and had only realized the disappearance of the meat after it had been taken away.

exe

kʰɤxtu ri pɯ-rɤʑi-a tɕe tɤ-mtʰɯm tu-ndze-a pɯ-ŋu ri, toʁde tɕendɤre qandʑɣi pjɤ-ɣi tɕe, nɯra mɯ-pɯ-tso-a tɕe, ndɤre a-jaʁ tɤ-mtʰɯm nɯnɯ ta-nɯ-mɟa tɕe \\
terrace loc pst. ipfv -stay- 1sg lnk indef. poss -meat ipfv -eat[III]- 1sg pst. ipfv -be lnk suddenly lnk falcon ifr: down -come lnk dem: pl neg - aor -understand- 1sg lnk lnk 1sg. poss -hand indef -meat dem aor:3: up - auto -take lnk \\
`I was on the terrace eating meat, and suddenly a falcon came down without me noticing, and took away the [piece of] meat in my hand.' (150909 qandZGi) 0006358#S4
exe

The Inferential can occur to express events seen in dreams, as in ( ex:pWGAjmNota2 ).

exe

[aʑo [...] qartsʰi ɲɤ-k-ɤpa-a-ci] pɯ-ɣɤjmŋo-t-a \\
1sg cricket ifr - peg -become- 1sg - peg aor -dream- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I dreamed that I had become a cricket.' (150904 cuzhi-zh)
0006322#S178
exe

In retellings of narratives observed on film, such as the Pear stories, the Aorist is used for most events that have appeared in the video (§ sec:aor.main ). The Inferential is used when only the result of action is visible. For instance in ( ex:RnWkuxtCo.tosWmtshAt ), the Inferential to-sɯ-mtsʰɤt instead of the Aorist ta-sɯ-mtsʰɤt occurs because the filling process is already completed in the beginning of the pear story video.

exe

tɕendɤre ʁnɯ-kuxtɕo to-sɯ-mtsʰɤt tɕe \\
lnk two-basket ifr - caus -be.full lnk \\
`[The man] had filled two baskets (with the pears).' (chen-pear)
exe

The Inferential can also be used in a more subtle way: to express that one of the characters in the film has not witnessed an event, even though the narrator may have seen it. For instance, the stealing of the pears is described using the Aorist ja-nɯ-tsɯm `he took them away' in ( ex:tWkuxtCo.janWtsWm ) since it is visible on the video, but when describing the point of view of the old man discovering that the pears have disappeared when climbing down his ladder, the Inferential jo-nɯ-tsɯm `he took them away' occurs instead ( ex:jonWtsWm.Cti ).

exe

nɯnɯ kɯ ɯ-paχɕi tɯ-kuxtɕo nɯ ja-nɯ-tsɯm \\
dem erg 3sg. poss -apples one-basket dem aor:3 - auto -take.away \\
`[The boy] took away one basketful of pears.' (chen-pear)
exe

exe

rgɤtpu nɯ pɯ-ɬoʁ ri, tɕe pjɤ-sɯχsɤl ri jo-nɯ-tsɯm ɕti tɕe ɯ-kɤpa maŋe, \\
old.man dem aor: down -come.out lnk lnk ifr -realize lnk ifr - auto -take.away be. aff: fact lnk 3sg. poss -method not.exist: sens \\
`When the old man came down from the tree, he realized that [the pears] had been taken away, but could not do anything about it.' (chen-pear)
exe

The Inferential is the main TAME category to describe actions occurring in traditional stories, though some speakers rather prefer the Periphrastic Narrative construction (§ sec:aor.narrative ). Example ( ex:chArAGdWt.chAtsxWB ) illustrates this narrative function, where the succession of the verbs in the Inferential reflects the relative temporal order of the actions. The choice of the Inferential rather than the Aorist here is motivated by the fact that the fictional events described in these stories have not been witnessed by the speaker.

exe

ta-ʁi nɯ kɯ nɯŋa ɯ-ndʐi nɯnɯ cʰɤ-rɤɣdɯt qʰendɤre cʰɤ-tʂɯβ. tɕendɤre nɤki, ta-mar tɯ-tɯɣɟaβ nɯ to-ndo qʰe, ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu ko-ʑɣɤ-mpʰɯr. \\
indef. poss -younger.sibling dem erg cow 3sg. poss -skin dem ifr -peel.skin lnk ifr -sew lnk filler indef. poss -butter one- nmlz: action -churn dem ifr -take lnk 3sg. poss -inside dem. loc ifr - refl -wrap \\
`The younger brother skinned the hide of the cow and sewed it. He took one churnfull of butter, and wrapped himself inside [the hide].' (07-deluge)
0003426#S14
exe

The Inferential Imperfective occurs for imperfective events and states in narratives (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.main ).
summary: The passage explains that in main clauses the Inferential, like the Aorist, expresses past perfective events, but it is chosen when the speaker’s knowledge is indirect rather than based on direct witnessing. It illustrates this contrast with examples involving snowfall, change-of-state predicates, personal narratives, dream reports, film retellings, and traditional stories, showing that the Inferential is used when events are inferred, only partially observed, or not witnessed by the speaker or by a character in the narrative.

text: In narratives told in the Inferential, the Aorist is restricted to temporal (§ sec:aor.temporal ) and relative (§ sec:aor.relative ) subordinate clauses.
summary: In narratives told in the Inferential, the Aorist appears only in subordinate clauses. Specifically, its use is restricted to temporal and relative subordinate clauses.

text:
The Inferential is not rare with first person subjects in assertive clauses, but has specific meanings. With volitional verbs, this combination can be uttered when a speaker notices that s/he forgot to do or did not properly do an action. For instance, in ( ex:mWtosAlata ), the speaker ( Tshendzin ) selects the Inferential when realizing that she forgot to put the water to boil (see ex:mWtotata, § sec:ifr.morphology for a similar example).

exe

tɯ-ci mɯ-to-sɯ-ɤla-t-a \\
indef. poss -water neg - ifr - caus -be.boiling- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I did not put the water to boil.' (Conversation, 01-05-2018, Tshendzin )
exe

The Inferential with first person is also found when the speaker realizes a fact that s/he had failed to notice or not fully understood before.

For instance, in ( ex:koNla.YAkAtWGAci ), Inferential 1sg ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-a-ci `I have met' occurs in a sentence uttered when the speaker has ascertained that the person he has met is a Daoist master, after a long conversation.

exe

a-kʰi ma kɯki koŋla nɯ ɲɤ-k-ɤtɯɣ-a-ci \\
1sg. poss -luck lnk dem. prox real dem ifr - peg -meet- 1sg - peg \\
`I am lucky, I (finally) met a real [Daoist master].' (150907 laoshandaoshi-zh)
0006398#S33
exe

Similarly, in ( ex:WRjoR.YAkABzuaci ), the speaker (a horse) uses the Inferential ɲɤ-k-ɤβzu-a-ci `I have become' (as opposed to the Aorist nɯ-aβzu-a ) to express his sudden realization that it has been tricked into becoming a domesticated animal.

exe

tɯrme ɣɯ ɯ-ʁjoʁ ɲɤ-k-ɤβzu-a-ci \\
man gen 3sg. poss -servant ifr - peg -become- 1sg - peg \\
`I have become a slave of the men.' (aesop ma he lu-zh)
exe

Example ( ex:mWtozwara ) illustrates the contrast between Aorist and Inferential with first person subjects: the speaker did put the water on the oven, but forgot to open the oven, hence the use of the Inferential for the second verb.

exe

tɯ-ci kɤ-ta-t-a ri, <dian> mɯ-to-zwar-a \\
indef. poss -water aor -put- pst: tr - 1sg lnk electricity neg - ifr -burn- 1sg \\
`I put the water [on the oven], but did not open the electricity.' (Conversation, 04-05-2018, Tshendzin )
exe

The Inferential with first person can also be used when the speaker did the action he intended but on the wrong object.

For instance, in ( ex:koGAdZama.YWmaR ), a sentence said after Tshendzin realized (by looking into the pot) that she mistakenly warmed the wrong pot (not the one containing nettles). Here mtsʰalunettle is focalized using the copula ɲɯ-maʁ (§ sec:focalization.final.copula ).

exe

mtsʰalu ko-ɣɤ-ndʑam-a ɲɯ-maʁ \\
nettle ifr - caus -be.warm- 1sg sens -not.be \\
`It is not the nettles that I warmed.' (Conversation, 07-05-2018, Tshendzin )
exe

The Inferential with first person is particularly common with verbs expressing uncontrollable and non-volitional actions, such as ( ex:kAnWZWB.kordala ).

exe

kɤ-nɯʑɯβ ko-rdal-a \\
inf -sleep ifr -overshoot- 1sg \\
`I overslept.' (elicitation)
exe

The inferential does not however express by itself non-volitionality; the autive prefix -nɯ- (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ) is used in conjunction with the inferential to insist on the non-volitional character of a particular action, as in ( ex:YAnWjmWta ).

exe

ɲɤ-nɯ-jmɯt-a \\
ifr - auto -forget- 1sg \\
`I forgot.' (many attestations)
exe

With non-volitional perception verbs such as mtosee and mtsʰɤmhear, Inferential first person negative can be employed to express failure to perceive ( ex:jAtWlAt.mWpjAmtshama ) (see also example ex:khamu.pasWBzua, § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.main ), or alternatively to state that the speaker has not witnessed a fact of doubtful truthfulness ( ex:aNkhoR.mWpjAmtota ).

exe

jɯfɕɯr a-<dianhua> jɤ-tɯ-lɤt ri mɯ-pjɤ-mtsʰam-a, kʰa pɯ-a-ta tɕe \\
yesterday 1sg. poss -telephone ifr -2-release lnk neg - ifr -hear- 1sg house pst. ipfv - pass -put lnk \\
`Yesterday when you called [me] on the phone, I did not hear it, as [I was away and] had left the phone at home.' (conversation, 2015-06-18)
exe

exe

nɤʑo kɯ-fse a-ŋkʰor nɯ mɯ-pjɤ-mto-t-a \\
2sg sbj: pcp -be.like 1sg. poss -subject dem neg - ifr -see- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I have never seen anyone like you among my subjects.' (Smanmi 2003-2)
exe
summary: The passage explains that the Inferential with first person subjects is common in assertive clauses but has specialized uses, especially when the speaker later realizes a past oversight, misunderstanding, or mistaken action. It appears with volitional verbs for forgotten or incorrectly performed actions, with non-volitional verbs for events like oversleeping or forgetting, and with perception verbs to express not perceiving something or not having witnessed a doubtful fact.

text:
When used with stative verbs, the Inferential Perfective expresses change of state, like the Aorist (§ sec:aor.inchoative ) and the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.inchoative ). In ( ex:tompCAr ), mpɕɤrbe beautiful thus means `become beautiful' in the Inferential.

exe

mɤʑɯ ʑo to-mpɕɤr \\
even.more emph ifr -be.beautiful \\
`[The Phoenix] became even more beautiful than before.' (150901 bainiaochaofeng-zh) 0006296#S77
exe

The verb cʰacan, which normally selects the downwards preverbs (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ) to express both Imperfective Inferential/Past Imperfective (`was able to do $X$') and Inferential/Aorist (`succeeded in doing $X$'), has an inchoative meaning `became able to do $X$' when occurring with the upwards orientation, as shown by ( ex:YWnWqambWmbjom.tocha ) (see also ex:tAnANkWNkea.tAchaa, § sec:TAM.finite ).

exe

mɯrmɯmbju ɯ-pɯ nɯnɯ [...] ɯ-tɯɣmaz ra to-mna tɕe, ɲɯ-nɯqambɯmbjom to-cʰa. \\
swallow 3sg. poss -little.one dem 3sg. poss -wound pl ifr -be.better lnk ipfv -fly ifr -can \\
`The swallow's wounds healed, and it was able to fly [again].' (150825 huluwa-zh)
0006346#S43
