summary: With stative verbs, the Inferential Perfective can express a change of state, functioning like the Aorist and Imperfective in an inchoative sense. For example, a verb meaning “be beautiful” can mean “become beautiful,” and *cʰacan* with upward orientation means “became able to do X,” not its usual “was able to do X” or “succeeded in doing X” readings.

text:
The Inferential rarely appears in subordinate clauses, as in most contexts the contrast between Aorist and Inferential is neutralized, and only the former is attested. In particular, in finite relative clauses, the Inferential is not found (§ sec:aor.relative ).

In complement clauses, the Inferential is only found when the verb of the main clause is also in the Inferential, as in ( ex:CkonARdAn.pjAcha ).

exe

ɲimawozɤr nɯ kɯ, [srɯnmɯ nɯ pjɤ-ftɯl], [...] [rŋgɯ kɤ-kɯ-nɤχtɕɤn ra pjɤ-ftɯl],
tɕe iɕqʰa srɯnmɯ nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-kɯ-ra nɯra [smɤnmimitoʁkuɕana ri ɕ-ko-nɤʁdɤn] pjɤ-cʰa \\
anthr dem erg râkshasî dem ifr -subdue boulder aor - sbj: pcp -be.fierce pl ifr -subdue lnk filler râkshasî dem gen 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -be.needed dem: pl anthr also tral - ifr: east -invite ifr -can \\
`Nyima 'Odzer had subdued the râkshasî, subdued the magical boulders, and also succeeded in inviting Smanmi Metog Koshana to the east, as the râkshasî had requested. (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

In this sentence, the scope of the verb pjɤ-cʰa is ambiguous: it could be restricted to the last verb ɕ-ko-nɤʁdɤn, but could also be understood as encompassing the first two clauses (whose main verb is pjɤ-ftɯl ).

Examples of Inferential in the protasis of conditional constructions are presented in § sec:real.conditional (example ex:Wtope.nA ).
summary: The Inferential rarely occurs in subordinate clauses because the Aorist and Inferential are usually neutralized there, with only the Aorist attested in many such contexts. It does not appear in finite relative clauses, and in complement clauses it is found only when the main clause verb is also in the Inferential. The passage also notes that in one example the scope of the Inferential verb is ambiguous, and that Inferential forms in conditional protases are discussed elsewhere.

text: Past Imperfective
summary: The past imperfective is formed by combining the stem with the past tense marker **-de** plus the imperfective suffix **-ri**. It expresses an action or event that was ongoing or habitual in the past.

text:
The Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective are built exactly in the same way as Aorist (§ sec:aor.morphology ) and Inferential Perfective (§ sec:ifr.morphology ), but with the downwards preverbs pɯ- and pjɤ- instead of the preverb corresponding to the intrinsic lexicalized orientation, a peculiarity observed in most Gyalrong varieties. Thus, verbs selecting downwards as their intrinsic orientation present syncretism between Aorist and Past Imperfective, and between Inferential and Imperfective Inferential.

For instance, the form pɯ-rom of the verb rombe dry, which selects the downwards orientation, can either be interpreted as an Aorist `it became dry/when it becomes dry' (§ sec:aor.morphology ) or as a Past Imperfective `it was dry'.

Another case of syncretism is provided by the modal verb cʰacan which takes the downwards orientation to express the meaning `succeed in doing $X$' (where $X$ refer to the content of the complement clause), as the Inferential Perfective pjɤ-cʰa in ( ex:chAsWGjGAt.pjAcha ).

exe

[zdɯm kɯ-ɲaʁ nɯ cʰɤ-sɯ-jɣɤt] pjɤ-cʰa ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
cloud sbj: pcp -be.black dem ifr: downstream - cause -turn.back ifr -can sens -be \\
`He succeeded in making the black cloud retreat.' (25-kAmYW)
0003642#S61
exe

When the verb of the complement clause is in the Imperfective, the same form pjɤ-cʰa is rather an Inferential Imperfective, and means `s/he was able to do $X$' instead, as in ( ex:mWpjAchandZi ).

exe

cʰɯ-mɤɕi-ndʑi mɯ-pjɤ-cʰa-ndʑi \\
ipfv -be.rich- du neg - ifr. ipfv -can- du \\
`They were unable to become rich.' (Divination)
exe

In Japhug, not all verbs have Past and Inferential Imperfective forms. Only stative verbs (including adjectives, existential verbs, copulas and passive verbs, § sec:passive.stative ), some stative transitive verbs with (such as tropative verbs, § sec:tropative.pst.ipfv ) and some atelic intransitive dynamic verbs (such as rɤʑistay) are compatible with these two TAME categories in main clauses. tab:pfv.ipfv.ifr provides examples of these three categories of verbs, with minimal pairs taken from the text corpus.

Atelic dynamic intransitive verbs include the following: some verbs of location such as rɤʑistay, some modal verbs such rgalike and cʰacan, antipassive verbs (§ sec:antipassive.pst.ipfv ) and also some verbs expressing activities requiring a certain amount of time such as taʁweave or rɤmawork.

Like the Aorist and the Perfective Inferential, the Past and Inferential Imperfective require the past suffix -t in the 1/2 3 forms of open syllable stem transitive verbs (§ sec:suffixes, § sec:other.TAME ). However, since only very few transitive verbs are compatible with these two categories, relevant examples such as ( ex:pWnApeta ) are very rare (see also ex:apWNu.mWpWnWrputa, § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.apodosis ).

exe

pɯ-nɤ-pe-t-a \\
pst. ipfv - trop -be.good- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I used to like it.' (elicited)
exe

Most transitive verbs need to take the progressive asɯ- prefix (§ sec:progressive ) build Past and Inferential Imperfective forms. The peg circumfix k-...-ci is inserted between the pjɤ- preverb and the progressive prefix (§ sec:peg.circumfix ) in first and third person forms (§ sec:ifr.morphology ), as shown by ( ex:mWpjAkAsWtsxWBci ). The past transitive suffix -t does not occur with the progressive (§ sec:progressive ).

exe

rgɤnmɯ nɯ kɯ li iɕqʰa <yuwang> nɯ pjɤ-k-ɤsɯ-tʂɯβ-ci \\
old.woman dem erg again the.aforementioned net dem ifr. ipfv - peg - prog -sew- peg \\
`The old woman was sewing nets (like before).' (140430 yufu he tade qizi-zh)
0003900#S283
exe

One context however where all verbs appear to be found without restriction in the Past Imperfective is in the apodosis of counterfactual conditionals (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.apodosis ).

In other cases, the Periphrastic Past and Inferential Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic ) are used instead.
summary:
The Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective are formed like the Aorist and Inferential Perfective, but with the downwards preverbs pɯ- and pjɤ- replacing the preverb for the verb’s intrinsic orientation, which causes syncretism for verbs whose intrinsic orientation is downwards. The passage illustrates this with examples such as pɯ-rom, which can mean either Aorist or Past Imperfective, and pjɤ-cʰa, which is interpreted differently depending on whether the complement clause verb is perfective or imperfective.

It also states that only certain verbs, mainly stative verbs and some atelic intransitive dynamic verbs, can take Past and Inferential Imperfective forms in main clauses. Most transitive verbs require the progressive prefix asɯ-, with the peg circumfix in first and third person forms, while a special unrestricted use of the Past Imperfective appears in the apodosis of counter

text:
In main clauses, the Past and Inferential Imperfective indicate a previous state or habitual situation. For instance, in ( ex:pWtu.pWdAn ), the use of the Past Imperfective to refer to the presence of warts ( pɯ-tu `there used to be' and pɯ-dɤn `there were many') is necessary because of their subsequent disappearance, explicitly mentioned in the following clauses.

exe

a-jaʁ ri li kɯkɯra ntsɯ pɯ-tu tɕe pɯ-dɤn. tɕeri nɯ ɯ-qʰu li iɕqʰa stu kɯ-mɤku nɯ-kɯ-ɬoʁ nɯ-nɯ-me qʰe tɕe ɲɤ-nɯ-me \\
1sg. poss -hand loc again dem. prox: pl always pst. ipfv -exist lnk pst. ipfv -be.many lnk dem 3sg. poss -after again filler most sbj: pcp -be.first aor - sbj: pcp -come.out aor - auto -not.exist lnk lnk ifr - auto -not.exist \\
`I had [warts] on my hand there, and there were a lot. But later, the [wart] that had first come out disappeared by itself, and [the rest] disappeared.' (24-pGArtsAG)
0003624#S48
exe

The Past and Inferential Imperfective also express an ongoing process in the past, during which additional events have occurred, as in ( ex:khamu.pasWBzua ).

exe

jɯfɕɯr kʰɯ kʰro ʑo jo-tɯ-lɤt ri mɯ-pjɤ-mtsʰam-a ma kʰamu pɯ-asɯ-βzu-a \\
yesterday emph much emph ifr -2-release lnk neg - ifr -hear- 1sg lnk cooking pst. ipfv - prog -make- 1sg \\
`Yesterday you called [me] many times (on the phone), but I did not hear it, as I was cooking.' (conversation, 14-12-2018)
exe

In combination with the Autive, the Past Imperfective can convey permansive meaning (§ sec:autoben.permansive ), as in ( ex:pWnWGAwu ).

exe

tɕʰeme nɯ-nɯkʰɤda-t-a ri, mɯ́j-pʰɤn, tɕe pɯ-nɯ-ɣɤwu ɕti \\
girl aor -convince- pst: tr - 1sg lnk neg: sens -be.efficient lnk pst. ipfv - auto -cry be. aff: fact \\
`I comforted the girl, but to no avail, [as] she was still crying.' (2003 zrAntCW tWrme)
exe

The Inferential Imperfective is the standard TAME category used in traditional stories to describe states and ongoing actions, as illustrated by the chain of verbs marked in red in ( ex:pjAtu.pjAfsoR.pjAkArNici ). It is the counterpart of the Inferential Perfective in narrative function (§ sec:ifr.evd ).

exe

praʁkʰaŋ ci pjɤ-tu qʰe, praʁkʰaŋ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu pjɤ-fsoʁ. nɯ ɯ-rkɯ nɯra rcanɯ, li nɤkinɯ, si ra pjɤ-k-ɤrŋi-ci ʑo. nɤkinɯ, mɯntoʁ kɯnɤ wuma ʑo pjɤ-dɤn, tɕe pjɤ-sɤ-scit. [...] ɯ-ŋgɯ lo-ɕe ri, tɕe nɯnɯtɕu rgɤtpu χsɯm kɯ, nɤki, kumbrɤl pjɤ-k-ɤsɯ-lɤt-nɯ \\
cave indef ifr. ipfv -exist lnk cave 3sg. poss -inside dem: loc ifr. ipfv -be.bright dem 3sg. poss -side dem: loc unexp: deg again filler tree pl ifr. ipfv - peg -be.green- peg emph filler flower also really emph ifr. ipfv -be.many lnk ifr. ipfv - prop -be.happy 3sg. poss -inside ifr: upstream -go lnk lnk dem: loc old.man three erg filler chess ifr. ipfv - peg - prog -release- pl \\
`There was a cave. Inside the cave, there was light. Around it, the trees were green, and there were many flowers, it was a very nice [place]. (...) He entered [the cave], and in there there were three old men playing chess.' (150902 qixian-zh)
0006258#S114
exe
summary: In main clauses, the Past and Inferential Imperfective are used to describe previous states, habitual situations, and ongoing past processes, including cases where later events explain why the state no longer holds. The Past Imperfective can also combine with the Autive to express a permansive meaning, while the Inferential Imperfective is the standard form in traditional narratives for describing states and ongoing actions.

text:
The Past Imperfective, like the Aorist (§ sec:aor.temporal ), is used in temporal subordinate clauses. The clause in the Past Imperfective expresses an ongoing process in the middle of which the event referred to in the main clause (in the Aorist or in the Inferential Perfective) takes place, as illustrated by ( ex:pasWndzandZi.pWpe ).

exe

wuma ʑo pɯ-asɯ-ndza-ndʑi, pɯ-pe jamar ʑo tɕe tɕendɤre, nɯnɯ, nɤki, kʰa nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-kɯm to-ɲɟɯ\\
really emph pst. ipfv - prog -eat- du pst. ipfv -be.good about emph lnk lnk dem filler house dem gen 3sg. poss -door ifr - acaus:open\\
`While/Right at the moment when they were eating [the sweets] in big quantity and were [enjoying it], the door of the house opened.' (140507 tangguowu-zh)
0003933#S83
exe
summary: The Past Imperfective is used in temporal subordinate clauses, like the Aorist. It describes an ongoing process during which the event in the main clause, expressed in the Aorist or Inferential Perfective, occurs.

text:
The Past Imperfective is also used in the apodosis of counterfactual conditionals (with an Irrealis in the protasis, § sec:irrealis.conditional ), as shown by the form pɯ-pe in ( ex:apArAt.pWpe ).

exe

nɯnɯ mɯɣʑɯsapa nɯ tɕeki nɯ tɕe a-pɯ-ɤ-rɤt tɕe pɯ-pe ma \\
dem topo dem down dem loc irr - ipfv - pass -write lnk pst. ipfv -be.good lnk \\
`It would have been better if [the name] mɯɣʑɯsapa had been written down there (on a sheet of paper where many names of locations in the mountains had been written).' (140522 Kamnyu zgo) 0004059#S80
exe

In this very restricted context, all verbs can have a Past Imperfective form. For instance, rpubump into (§ sec:goal.labile ), which normally selects the eastwards orientation (the preverb kɤ- in ex:kAnWrputa ), takes the pɯ- Past Imperfective preverb in ( ex:apWNu.mWpWnWrputa ).

exe

nɤ-kʰa jɤ-ɣe-a ri, a-ku kɤ-nɯ-rpu-t-a \\
2sg. poss -house aor -come[II]- 1sg lnk 1sg. poss -head aor - auto -bump- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`When I came to your house, I bumped my head (on the door frame).' (elicited)
exe

exe

nɤ-kʰa jɤ-ɣe-a ri, a-ku pjɯ-pʰaβ-a a-pɯ-ŋu tɕe mɯ-pɯ-nɯ-rpu-t-a. \\
2sg. poss -house aor -come[II]- 1sg lnk 1sg. poss -head ipfv -lower- 1sg irr - ipfv -be lnk neg - pst. ipfv - auto -bump- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`When I came to your house, if I had lowered my head, I wouldn't have bumped it [into the door frame].' (elicited)
exe

The Inferential Imperfective is not attested in this construction.
summary: The Past Imperfective is used in the apodosis of counterfactual conditionals with an irrealis protasis. In this restricted context, even verbs that normally take other forms can appear with a Past Imperfective preverb, as shown by examples involving *rpu-* ‘bump into.’ The Inferential Imperfective is not attested in this construction.

text:
Only atelic verbs, in particular stative verbs, are compatible with Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ) in contexts other than the apodosis of counterfactuals (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.apodosis ).

To express the meanings otherwise conveyed by the Past Imperfective with telic verbs, two strategies are possible. First, the Progressive asɯ- makes all transitive verbs compatible with these two tenses (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology, § sec:progressive ). Second, the Periphrastic Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective, which combine the Imperfective form of the verb with the copula in the Past Imperfective pɯ-ŋu and the Inferential Imperfective pjɤ-ŋu, respectively (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ). For instance, instead of the incorrect form $ $ pjɤ-ndza (Inferential Imperfective of the telic transitive verb ndzaeat), the periphrastic construction in ( ex:tundze.pjANu2 ) is used.

exe

tu-ndze pjɤ-ŋu \\
ipfv -eat[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`S/he/it used to eat/was eating it.' (many examples)
exe

Just in the same way as the Aorist can be combined with the Sensory copula ɲɯ-ŋu to build the Periphrastic Narrative (§ sec:aor.narrative ), the Past Imperfective with ɲɯ-ŋu expresses an Periphrastic Imperfective Narrative, with the same meaning as the Inferential Imperfective. For instance, the construction in ( ex:pWtaR.YWNu ) is equivalent to the Inferential Imperfective pjɤ-taʁ ( ifr. ipfv -weave) `s/he was weaving'.

exe

tɕʰeme ci pɯ-taʁ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
girl indef pst. ipfv -weave sens -be \\
`A girl was weaving.' (2003 tWxtsa)
exe
summary: Only atelic verbs, especially stative verbs, can occur with the Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective outside the apodosis of counterfactuals. With telic verbs, the same meanings are expressed either by adding the Progressive asɯ-, which makes transitive verbs compatible with these tenses, or by using periphrastic constructions with the copula and the imperfective form of the verb. The passage also notes that Past Imperfective plus the sensory copula ɲɯ-ŋu yields a periphrastic imperfective narrative with the same meaning as the Inferential Imperfective.

text:
irregularity
The archaic 3sg kʰɯ-ti `s/he said' and 3pl kʰɯ-ti-nɯ `they said' forms with the isolated preverb kʰɯ, are attested in a few occurrences in stories told by Tshendzin 's mother. They are glossed by Tshendzin with the Inferential forms 3sg 3 to-ti and 3pl 3 to-ti-nɯ, respectively.

exe

``ɕɯ kɯ nɯ-tɯ́-wɣ-mbi tɤ-ti ma mɤ-jɤɣ" kʰɯ-ti-nɯ. \\
who erg aor -2- inv -give imp -say apart.from neg -be.possible: fact???-say- pl \\
`Who gave this to you, you must tell us.' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

These forms are not found in texts by younger speakers. No other trace of this preverb is found in Japhug. A possible origin for it would be the hearsay sentence final particle kʰi (§ sec:fsp.hearsay ), which sometimes occur in the reported speech complements (§ sec:reported.speech.sfp ) of the verb tisay, sometimes even in direct contact with the stem of this verb as in ( ex:khi.ti ), in its irregular preverbless inferential form (§ sec:fact.periphrastic ).

exe

``nɤ-kɤχcɤl nɤ-ʁrɯ nɯ pjɯ-tɯ-pʰɯt tɕe kɤ-nɯ-ɕe ɲɯ-kʰɯ kʰi" ti ɲɯ-ŋu\\
2sg. poss -top.of.head 2sg. poss -horn dem ipfv -2-take.off lnk inf - auto -go sens -be.possible sfp say: fact sens -be \\
`He said: ``If you remove the horn on the top of your head, it will be possible for you to go wherever you want.''.' (divination 2005,101)
exe

The preverb kʰɯ- would thus result from the procliticization and eventual absorption of a sentence final particle from a preceding clause into the verbal word, a scenario similar to that proposed for the Apprehensive ɕɯ- (§ sec:apprehensive.history ). If this hypothesis is correct, the form kʰɯ-ti may not be the residual form from an ancient paradigm, but rather an unsuccessful Japhug innovation that has eventually died out.
summary:
The passage describes archaic 3sg and 3pl forms kʰɯ-ti and kʰɯ-ti-nɯ, glossed as “said,” which Tshendzin interprets with the corresponding Inferential forms to-ti and to-ti-nɯ. These forms occur only a few times in stories told by his mother and are absent from younger speakers’ texts, with no other evidence for the preverb kʰɯ in Japhug.  

The author suggests that kʰɯ- may have arisen from a sentence-final hearsay particle kʰi that was procliticized and absorbed into the verb, making kʰɯ-ti not an ancient inherited form but possibly a short-lived innovation that later disappeared.

text: There are two secondary aspectual prefixes in Japhug, the Progressive (§ sec:progressive ) and the Proximative (§ sec:proximative ). They can be combined with several primary TAME categories, but cannot occur together in the same verb form.
summary: Japhug has two secondary aspectual prefixes: the Progressive and the Proximative. Each can combine with several primary TAME categories, but they cannot both appear in the same verb form.

text: Progressive
summary: The progressive is a complex aspect in Punjabi and is marked by the suffix **-dA**. It is distinct from the habitual aspect, which is marked by the suffix **-dA** in the masculine singular and **-dI** in all other forms, and from the perfective, which uses the suffixes **-IA**, **-yA**, and **-nA** depending on the phonological ending of the verb stem.

text:
Progressive!allomorphy allomorphy!Progressive
The Progressive prefix asɯ- is located in slot -1 of the outer prefixal template (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ). It is only compatible with transitive verbs, and does not appear with perfective TAME categories such as Aorist and Inferential Perfective. Its is almost only attested with finite verb forms; the only examples of non-finite Progressive forms are object participles (see example ex:pWkASWndo, § sec:object.participle.other.prefixes ).

The Progressive prefix has six regular allomorphs, as shown in tab:progressive.allomorphy. The monosyllabic variants az, -ɤz- and -oz- are found in the same context as the z- allomorph of the sigmatic causative (§ sec:caus.z ): in non-monosyllabic verb bases, when the first syllable has a sonorant initial ( mV, nV, ɣV- or rV- ). They are illustrated with the verb nɤjowait in tab:progressive.allomorphy. The disyllabic allomorphs asɯ, -ɤsɯ- and -osɯ- are found in all other contexts (illustrated with the monosyllabic ndzaeat in tab:progressive.allomorphy ).

The vocalism of this prefix follows the same alternations as the initial a- of contracting verbs (§ sec:contraction ).

The asɯ- / az- allomorphs are found in word-initial position, in first or third person Factual Non-Past (see for instance ex:WmdoR.asWndo ), following the Past Imperfective pɯ, with the negative mɤ- and the Rhetorical Interrogative ɯβrɤ- (§ sec:WBrA, ɯβrɤ-asɯ-ndo rh. q - prog -take: fact `it does not have (this colour), does it?').

The -osɯ- / -oz- allomorphs are restricted to Egophoric Present forms with the prefix ku- (§ sec:egophoric.morphology ).

The -ɤsɯ- / -ɤz- allomorphs are the most common, attested with the Sensory ɲɯ, with the peg circumfix (§ sec:peg.circumfix, in Inferential Imperfective form) and also in the Irrealis Imperfective with the preverb pɯ- (for instance a-pɯ-ɤsɯ-ndo irr - ipfv - prog -take `may it have (this colour)').

Like contracting verbs, the Progressive prefix selects the peg circumfix kɯ-...-ci (§ sec:peg.circumfix ) in the Inferential Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ), as shown by the form pjɤ-k-ɤsɯ-ɕar-ci `it was searching/looking for it' in ( ex:pjAtu.pjAkAsWCarci ).

exe

sɯŋgɯ nɯtɕu, nɤkinɯ, wuma ʑo spjaŋkɯ kɯ-mtsɯr ci pjɤ-tu. tɕendɤre nɯnɯtɕu ɯ-kɤ-ndza aʁɤndɯndɤt pjɤ-k-ɤsɯ-ɕar-ci. \\
forest dem: loc filler really emph wolf sbj: pcp -be.hungry indef ifr. ipfv -exist lnk dem: loc 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -eat everywhere ifr. ipfv - peg - prog -search- peg \\
`In the forest, there was a wolf, and he was looking for food everywhere.' (140428 xiaohongmao-zh)
0003884#S28
exe

The inverse (slot -1, § sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) and the autive (inner prefix, § sec:inner.prefixal.chain ) are infixed within the progressive, as shown by ( ex:YWtAwGznWkhramba ) and ( ex:YAnWsWNga ) (see also ex:pjAkAwGznAjoci in § sec:outer.prefixal.chain, ex:konWsWndzaj in § sec:inner.prefixal.chain and ex:panWsWfkur in § sec:autoben.position ).

exe

ɲɯ-tɯ-ɤ́<wɣ>z-nɯkʰramba \\
sens -2- prog < inv >-cheat \\
`S/he is cheating you.' (elicited)
exe

exe

ɯ-ŋga cʰɤ-ɴɢraʁ ldʐɤβldʐɤβ ʑo ri, ɲɯ-ɤ<nɯ>sɯ-ŋga \\
3sg. poss -clothes ifr - acaus:tear idph (II):in.shreds emph lnk sens - prog < auto >-wear \\
`His clothes are torn to shreds, but he is still wearing them.' (elicited)
exe

When both inverse and autive are combined with the Progressive, the -sɯ/z- element is removed, and only the first vowel of the Progressive remains, as in ( ex:YAwGnWnAjo ).

exe

ɯ-zda kɯ ɲɯ-ɤ́-wɣ-nɯ-nɤjo \\
3sg. poss -companion erg sens - prog - auto -wait \\
`His$_i$ companion is waiting for him$_i$.' (elicited)
exe

An irregular allomorph -ɤs- is found in the Sensory Progressive ɲɯ-ɤs-tɯt ( sens - prog -say[II]) `s/he is saying/said' of the verb tisay (§ sec:sensory.morphology ), a form also unusual by the presence of Stem II.

Transitive verbs with the Progressive prefix lack some of the morphological exponents of transitivity (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ).

First, in Sensory, Egophoric, Irrealis and Factual, Stem III alternation does not occur in sg 3 configurations of alternating verbs (§ sec:stem3.distribution ); for instance, the Progressive Sensory 3sg of ndzaeat is ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-ndza ( sens - prog -eat) `s/he/it is eating it' with Stem I, unlike the plain Sensory ɲɯ-ndze which selects Stem III (see example ex:YWndze.tundze, § sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ). Combining Stem III with the Progressive (something like $ $ ɲɯ-ɤsɯ-ndze ) is categorically rejected by native speakers.

Second, the past -t suffix (§ sec:other.TAME ) does not occur in 1/2 sg 3 forms of Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective of verbs with the Progressive prefix. For instance, the 1sg 3sg form pɯ-asɯ-βzu-a ( pst. ipfv - prog -make- 1sg ) `I was making it' (see for instance example ex:khamu.pasWBzua, § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.main ) lacks the -t suffix, and inserting it ($ $ pɯ-asɯ-βzu-t-a ) is not accepted by speakers.

Other exponents of transitivity, such as C-type preverbs (§ sec:indexation.non.local ), subject participles (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ) and bare infinitives (§ sec:bare.inf ) cannot be tested, due to the incompatibility of the Progressive with most non-Finite forms on the one hand, and the undetectability of the pɯ- / pa- contrast when followed by the vowel contracting asɯ-: the surface form pasɯβzu `s/he/it is making it' is equally analyzable as pɯ-asɯ-βzu ( pst. ipfv - prog -make) or as pa-asɯ-βzu ( pst. ipfv:3 - prog -make). The former analysis is adopted in this grammar.

The 1 2 ta- seems to be incompatible with the progressive. For instance, to express the meaning `I am waiting for you', only the simple Egophoric Present ku-ta-nɤjo ( prs -1 2-wait) is possible, the surface form kutaznɤjo can only be analyzed as a causative Imperfective ku-ta-z-nɤjo ( ipfv -1 2- caus -wait) `I will have you wait for him', not as an Egophoric Progressive $ $ ku-ta-ɤz-nɤjo.

Other person configurations, including inverse mixed scenarios 3 1/2 (§ sec:indexation.mixed ) and local scenario 2 1 (§ sec:indexation.local ) can be elicited with the Progressive, as in ( ex:YWtAwGznWkhramba ) and ( ex:YWkAsWzgroRa ), though no such examples have yet been found in the corpus.

ɲɯ-kɯ-ɤsɯ-zgroʁ-a \\
sens -2 1- prog -attach- 1sg \\
`You are tying me up.' (elicited)

summary:
The Progressive prefix asɯ- occupies slot -1, occurs mainly with finite transitive verbs, and is incompatible with perfective categories such as Aorist and Inferential Perfective. It has several regular allomorphs whose distribution depends on phonological context and TAME environment, with additional infixing behavior when combined with inverse or autive marking.

The passage also notes that Progressive forms often lack other transitivity exponents: Stem III alternation is blocked in certain singular configurations, the past -t suffix is absent in relevant past imperfective and inferential forms, and the 1 2 ta- marker appears incompatible with the Progressive. An irregular allomorph -ɤs- is attested in one sensory progressive verb form.

text:
The Progressive indicates the non-telicity of the verbal action. It occurs in the case of habitual ( ex:kosWBzjoz ) and ongoing actions (including events being protracted for a long time period, as in ex:kosWCari ) (see also ex:jipAri.kosWBzu and ex:shangban.kosWBzu in § sec:egophoric.tense ).

exe

east district.school loc junior.high.school prs - prog -learn \\
`She is in junior high school at the district school.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S329

`We are looking for the prince's wife, we had to walk for three years.' (2003 sras)

With the Factual and the Sensory, the Progressive precludes an imminent future interpretation (§ sec:fact.main.clauses ). For instance tɯ-mɯ asɯ-lɤt in ( ex:tWmW.asWlAt ) means `(when) it is raining' (as part of general knowledge), while the corresponding plain Factual tɯ-mɯ lɤt ( ex:qaprAnar.tWmW.lAt ) is to be understood as `it will rain'.

summary: The Progressive marks non-telic verbal action and is used with habitual and ongoing events, including actions extended over a long period. It also blocks imminent-future readings with Factual and Sensory forms, is required in the stative collocation “have the colour of,” and combines with Past Imperfective and Inferential Imperfective to express former habitual or past ongoing actions. In subordinate clauses, it can indicate simultaneity or the manner of the main clause action.

text:
The Japhug Progressive prefix asɯ- is obviously related to the Tshobdun ɐsɐ- and the Zbu ɐsɐ-/ɐsə- progressive prefixes, but no cognates are found in the rest of Gyalrongic, even in Situ. It is a possible northern Gyalrong common innovation.

As in Japhug, the Progressive ɐsɐ- in Zbu and Tshobdun is incompatible with Stem III and the past transitive -z suffix (cognate to Japhug -t, § sec:other.TAME ), but its distribution is considerably more restricted. Zbu ɐsɐ- is not compatible with orientation preverbs and the inverse prefix; the allomorph ɐsə- optionally occurs with verbs taking the sigmatic causative prefix.

The infixability of the inverse and the autive prefixes within the Progressive in Japhug (§ sec:progressive.morphology ) is a clue that asɯ- and its cognates are etymologically composite, comprising two elements a- and -sɯ-. Possible candidates for the former include the Passive (§ sec:passive ) and the Denominal a- (§ sec:denom.a ), and for the latter the oblique participle sɤ- (§ sec:oblique.participle ) or the sigmatic causative sɯ- (§ sec:sig.causative ).
summary:
The Japhug progressive prefix asɯ- is cognate with Tshobdun ɐsɐ- and Zbu ɐsɐ-/ɐsə-, but no cognates are found elsewhere in Gyalrongic, so it may be a northern Gyalrong innovation. In Zbu and Tshobdun, the progressive is also incompatible with certain stem forms and suffixes, though Zbu shows more restrictions than Japhug.  

The fact that inverse and autive prefixes can be infixed within the Japhug progressive suggests that asɯ- and its cognates are historically composite, made of two elements, a- and -sɯ-. The text proposes possible sources for these elements, including the Passive or Denominal a- and either the oblique participle sɤ- or the sigmatic causative sɯ-.

text:
Proximative
The Proximative jɯ, located in slot -6 of the outer prefixal chain (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ), corresponds to the Tshobdun jə- prefix (Prospective 前瞻体, ) and the Zbu jə- or wo- prefixes (depending on the dialect, ).

It mainly appears in the corpus in combination with the Aorist ( ex:zWmi.jWnWsi, ex:zWmi.jWpWwsata ) or the Inferential ( ex:Wlu.jipjAcW, ex:XsWtAxWr.jikoCe ) expressing that the action was almost realized, but not completed. The adverb zɯmialmost is commonly used together with the proximative, as in ( ex:zWmi.jWnWsi ) and ( ex:zWmi.jWpWwsata ).

`Her husband became sick a few years ago, and almost died.' (14-siblings)

The Proximative combined with the Factual Non-Past has the meaning `be about to do'. It is generally attested with a copula as in ( ex:jWnWZWB ), like the Periphrastic Proximative (§ sec:proximative.periphrastic ).

summary: The Proximative jɯ, in slot -6 of the outer prefixal chain, corresponds to related Tshobdun and Zbu prefixes and mainly appears with the Aorist or Inferential to indicate that an action almost happened but was not completed. It commonly co-occurs with zɯmi “almost,” can also express an intended but unrealized action, and with the Factual Non-Past means “be about to do,” including in copular and participial forms. In a more marginal subordinate-clause use, it can mean “as soon as” when the action is completed.

text:
Proximative!periphrastic
The Proximative is in competition with the Periphrastic Proximative constructions, which combines the Factual Non-Past with the 3sg copula in various TAME categories.

With the Past Imperfective copula pɯ-ŋu ( ex:sat.pjANu ) or the Inferential Imperfective pjɤ-ŋu ( ex:lAt.pjANu ), the periphrastic construction means `was about to do $X$, almost/nearly did $X$'.

`The son of Klu gdugpa nagpo was about to kill (almost killed) my son, but you separated them.' (28-smAnmi)

With the Past Imperfective or Inferential Imperfective copula, it means ‘was about to do X, almost/nearly did X’; in temporal clauses the Aorist form marks a point in time, and in the non-past the construction with the Sensory copula expresses imminent future ‘is about to X.’

text: Secondary Modal categories include the Probabilitative (§ sec:WmA ), Rhetorical Interrogative (§ sec:WBrA ) and Interrogative (§ sec:interrogative.W ) which can be combined with primary TAME categories, and the Apprehensive (§ sec:apprehensive ), which presents morphological commonalities with the Aorist (§ sec:aor.morphology ).
summary: Secondary modal categories include the probabilitative, rhetorical interrogative, and interrogative, all of which can combine with primary TAME categories. The apprehensive is also a secondary modal category, and it shows morphological commonalities with the aorist.

text: Apprehensive
summary: The passage introduces **apprehensive** as a grammatical category, though no further details are provided here. It therefore appears to function as a label for expressing fear or concern about a possible event.

text:
The Apprehensive prefix ɕɯ- presents a series of unique morphological properties in Japhug. It occupies the slot -3 of the outer prefixal chain (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ), the same as orientational preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ). It is the only finite TAME category apart from the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ) to lack orientation preverbs.

On transitive verbs, the 3 direct form of the Apprehensive is ɕa, with a vowel alternation identical to that found with type C preverbs in the Aorist (§ sec:indexation.non.local, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs, § sec:preverb.TAME.morphology ) as illustrated by the contrast between the intransitive (Anticausative, § sec:anticausative.morphology ) ɕɯ-ɴɢrɯ `(I am afraid that) it will break' and its counterpart transitive ɕa-nɯ-qrɯ `(I am afraid that) he will break it', with the same vocalism as that on the preverb ta- prefix on the Aorist ta-ndo `s/he took it'.

exe

tab:comparison.apprehensive summarizes the morphological commonalities between Apprehensive and Aorist (as opposed to Imperfective, § sec:ipfv.morphology ).

The Apprehensive is not only incompatible with all TAME markers, but also with associated motion prefixes (§ sec:am.prefixes ) and non-finite verb forms. On the other hand it appears with all person indexation markers ( 1sg in ex:CWmaqʰua, 2sg in ex:mWCWtWcha, and even 2 sg 1 sg in ex:CWkWmpCaa ) and the negative prefix mɯ- ( ex:mWCWtWcha and ex:mWCWkhW ).

exe

[nɤʑo stɤβtsʰɤt ci mɯ-ɕɯ-tɯ-cʰa] ɲɯ-sɯsam-a tɕe, nɯ ɲɯ-nɯzdɯɣ-a wo \\
2sg contest indef neg - apprehensive -2-can sens -think[III]- 1sg lnk dem sens -be.worried- 1sg sfp \\
`I fear that you will not win the contest, this is what I am worried about.' (2003 sras)
exe
summary:
The Apprehensive prefix ɕɯ- occupies the same prefixal slot as orientational preverbs and is unusual in that, unlike most finite TAME categories, it lacks such preverbs. In transitive forms it shows a 3 direct form ɕa with a vowel alternation like the Aorist, and this alternation is determined by morphological transitivity rather than meaning.  

It also patterns with the Aorist in taking the 1/2 sg 3 -t and in selecting Stem II where applicable. The prefix is incompatible with other TAME markers, associated motion prefixes, and non-finite forms, but it can cooccur with all person indexation markers and with the negative prefix mɯ-.

text:
The Apprehensive is used to indicate worry or even fear that the event referred to by the verb might happen. Several verbs with the meaning `fear' exist in the language (in particular the Applicative verb nɯɣmube afraid of, § sec:applicative ), but none is a complement taking verb meaning `be afraid that $X$'. The clause ɕɯ-maqʰu-a kɯ ʑo ɲɤ-sɯso-nɯ in ( ex:CWmaqʰua ) creatively translates the Chinese expression 争先恐后 zhēngxiānkǒnghòuvie with each other in order to. The Rhetorical Interrogative (§ sec:WBrA ) can have a meaning similar to that of the Apprehensive, but conveying a milder degree of concern.

exe

[ɕɯ-maqʰu-a kɯ ʑo] ɲɤ-sɯso-nɯ tɕe rcanɯ, pɕoʁʑi kɯβde ʑo jo-ɣi-nɯ. \\
appr -be.after- 1sg sfp emph ifr -think lnk unexpectedly corner four emph ifr -come- pl \\
`Afraid of being late (thinking `I am afraid that I will be late'), they came from the four corners of the world.' (150906 toutao)
0006326#S19
exe

The Apprehensive exclusively expresses the fear of the speaker, not that of the agent, though in the case of reported speech this may be a person different from the present speaker (as in ex:CWmaqʰua ).

Despite its Aorist-like morphological features (§ sec:apprehensive.morphology ), the Apprehensive is exclusively refers to fear for a future event at the time of utterance; for instance, ( ex:CanWri.kW ) above in cannot be interpreted as meaning `I am afraid that he may already be gone.' In complement clause with a matrix verb in the Aorist, it can however refer to an event which has already happened `(I) was afraid that it might $X$', as in ( ex:mWCWkhW ).

exe

mɯ-ɕɯ-kʰɯ kɯ nɯ-sɯso-t-a \\
neg - appr -be.possible sfp aor -think- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I thought it would not work.' (conversation, 02-05-2018; after opening a washing machine, expecting it would not open)
exe

The apprehensive prefix only occurs either in independent clauses with the exclamative sentence final particle kɯ ( ex:CWkWmpCaa ), and in reported speech with the verb sɯsothink ( ex:mWCWkhW, ex:mWCWtWcha, ex:CWmaqʰua ). It is strictly impossible in any other type of complement clause.

exe

ɕɯ-kɯ-mpɕa-a kɯ! \\
apprehensive -2 1-scold- 1sg sfp \\
`I am afraid that you will scold me.' (elicited)
exe

It is possible to use the Apprehensive in clauses with precautioning or preventive meanings (as in ex:NGrW.qrW and ex:CWmaqʰua ), but it is not the usual way of expressing these meanings in the language (§ sec:precautioning.clauses ).
summary: The Apprehensive expresses worry or fear that the event described by the verb may happen, and it is used only for the speaker’s own fear, not the agent’s, except in reported speech. It refers to a future event at the time of utterance, though in reported speech with an Aorist matrix verb it can mean fear about an event that already happened, and it occurs only in independent clauses with the final particle *kɯ* or in reported speech with *sɯso* “think.”

text:
Proximative!origin grammaticalization!Apprehensive
The Apprehensive ɕɯ- is superficially similar to the translocative associated motion prefix ɕɯ, which is grammaticalized from the verb ɕego (§ sec:translocative.morpho ), but the two prefixes do not occupy the same prefixal slot (-3 vs. -4, § sec:outer.prefixal.chain ) and do not share the same morphological alternations, and are not semantically close. It is unlikely that they are historical related.

A possible origin for the apprehensive ɕɯ- might be the alternative interrogative particle ɕi `whether... or' (§ sec:fsp.interrog ), which can coordinate two clauses (the second clause being the negative counterpart of the first one) to express hesitation or worry that an action might not take place, as in ( ex:chaa.Ci ) (see also ex:kuCea.makACea, § sec:prohib.function ).

exe

cʰa-a ɕi mɤ-cʰa-a mɤ-xsi, pɤjkʰu xtɕi-a ɕti \\
can: fact - 1sg qu neg -can: fact - 1sg neg - genr:know: fact still be.small: fact - 1sg be. aff: fact \\
`I don't know whether I will be able to do it, I am still young.' (2010-09)
exe

Although generally clause-final, the particle ɕi can be prosodically attached to the second clause, and could have been absorbed into the verbal template ( describes similar processes in Khroskyabs). In this hypothesis, the Apprehensive was first grammaticalized in negative forms, with reordering of the Apprehensive and of the Negative prefix ( ex:appr.grammaticalization ), and the non-negative Apprehensive forms were created by backformation.

exe

ɕi mɤ-cʰa $ $ *ɕɯ-mɤ-cʰa $ $ mɯ-ɕɯ-cʰa
`[I don't know] whether he [will be able to do it] or not be able to do it' $ $ `I worry that he might not be able to do it.'
exe

This idea should still be viewed as speculative, since it does not account for the Aorist-like morphological features of the Apprehensive.

The a vocalism of the Apprehensive prefix with 3 transitive forms is a clue that the C-type preverbs in Japhug originate from the fusion of A-type preverbs with an Aorist 3 *a prefix (§ sec:xtokavian.preverbs ). Given the ability of the Aorist to refer to future events in temporal clauses (§ sec:aor.temporal ), it is possible that in pre-Japhug or proto-Gyalrong, there was a TAME category without preverb but taking stem II and the 3 *a prefix expressing perfective future tense, and that the grammaticalization of ɕi as a prefix occurred on a form of this lost category.
summary: The Apprehensive prefix ɕɯ- is probably not historically related to the similar translocative prefix ɕɯ, because they occupy different prefixal slots, show different morphological alternations, and are not semantically close. A speculative etymology derives ɕɯ- from the interrogative particle ɕi ‘whether... or,’ which can express hesitation or worry and may have been absorbed into the verbal template, first in negative forms and then extended by backformation; however, this does not explain the Apprehensive’s Aorist-like morphology. Another possible clue is the 3rd-person transitive form’s a-vocalism, which may reflect fusion with an Aorist 3 *a prefix and suggest that ɕi grammaticalized on an older category expressing perfective future.

text:
Probabilitative
The Probabilitative prefix ɯmɤ, located in slot -6 of the outer prefixal template (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ), is transparently grammaticalized from the combination of the Interrogative ɯ- (§ sec:interrogative.W ) with the negative mɤ- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ). It is compatible with the Aorist ( ex:WmAjazGWt2 ), the Imperfective (§ sec:WmA.ipfv ) and the Factual Non-Past ( ex:tCitaR.WmApe ), and has the epistemic modality meaning `probably, presumably'.

exe

ɯmɤ-jɤ-azɣɯt \\
prob - aor -arrive \\
`He probably has already arrived.' (elicited)
exe

exe

tɕi-ɬaʁ nɯnɯ, tɕi-taʁ ɯmɤ-pe \\
1du. poss -MZ dem 1du. poss -on prob -be.good: fact \\
`(Now that we have money), maybe our stepmother will treat us better.' (140507 tangguowu-zh) 0003933#S151
exe

Although Probabilitative with Aorist ( ex:WmAjazGWt2 ) can be elicited, no such example is attested in the corpus. Instead, a periphrastic construction with the Factual Probabilitative form of the copula ɯmɤ-ŋu `maybe it is' combined with the Aorist is found, as in ( ex:mWtatWtndZi.WmANu ).

exe

nɤ-ja ndʑi-ɕki tɤ-tɯt-a ri, mɯ-ta-tɯt-ndʑi ɯmɤ-ŋu ma \\
2sg. poss -sister 3du. poss - dat aor:3 -say[II]- 1sg lnk neg - aor:3 -say[II]- du prob -be: fact sfp \\
`I have told your two elder sisters, but they presumably have not told [your parents] about it (since they have not given any answer).' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

When the speaker hesitates in his degree of confidence regarding a particular statement, s/he can alternate between the Factual copula ŋu and the Probabilitative form ɯmɤ-ŋu `maybe it is', as in ( ex:Nu.WmANu ).

exe

ɕɤr tɕe tu-mbri tɕe, ``qaqaqaqa" tu-ti ŋu tɕe nɯnɯ pɣɤɲaʁ ŋu. ``pɣɤɲaʁ ŋu" tu-ti-nɯ, ŋu tɕe ɯmɤ-ŋu ma mɤ-xsi matɕi ɕɤr ndɤre mɯ́j-sɤ-mto tɕe. \\
night loc ipfv -cry lnk interj ipfv -say be: fact lnk dem pheasant be: fact pheasant be: fact ipfv -say- pl be: fact lnk prob -be: fact lnk neg - genr:know: fact lnk night loc neg: sens - prop -see lnk \\
`It sings at night, it makes the sound qaqaqaqa, that is the pheasant Pucrasia macrolopha. They say it is the Pucrasia macrolopha, maybe it is, we don't know, at night it is not visible.' (23-pGAYaR)
0003606#S7
exe

The Probabilitative prefix is not compatible with negative prefixes or negative copulas: forms such as $ $ ɯmɤ-maʁ (intended meaning `maybe it is not') are incorrect. To express the meaning `maybe not $X$', the Rhetorical Interrogative ɯβrɤ- with peg circumfix occurs instead (§ sec:WBrA.kW.ci ).
summary: The Probabilitative prefix ɯmɤ- is a grammaticalized form of the interrogative ɯ- plus negative mɤ-, and it expresses epistemic meaning such as “probably” or “presumably.” It occurs with the Aorist, Imperfective, and Factual Non-Past, though corpus evidence for an Aorist combination is lacking and instead a periphrastic form with ɯmɤ-ŋu ‘maybe it is’ is attested. It cannot combine with negative prefixes or negative copulas; to mean “maybe not X,” the language uses the Rhetorical Interrogative ɯβrɤ- with the peg circumfix.

text:
The Probabilitative prefix can be combined with the peg circumfix (§ sec:peg.circumfix ), with an epistemic modality of substantial doubt `maybe', as in ( ex:WmAkWNuci ).

exe

pɣa ra kɯ tu-ndza-nɯ ɯmɤ-kɯ-ŋu-ci ma \\
bird pl erg ipfv -eat- pl prob - peg -be- peg lnk \\
`Maybe birds eat it.' (17-thowum) 0003526#S39
exe

This form is compatible with verbs in the Sensory, as in ( ex:GAZu.WmAkWNuci ); with the meaning `it seems, it looks like'.

exe

alo tɕu rgɯnba ci ɣɤʑu ɯmɤ-kɯ-ŋu-ci tɕe \\
upstream loc temple indef exist: sens prob - peg -be- peg lnk \\
`It looks like there is a temple up there.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe
summary: The Probabilitative prefix can combine with the peg circumfix to express epistemic modality of substantial doubt, meaning “maybe.” It is also compatible with Sensory verbs, where it conveys an evidential meaning such as “it seems” or “it looks like.”

text:
The combination of the Probabilitative prefix with the Imperfective form (§ sec:imperfective ) expresses optative modality `if only...', as in ( ex:WmAchWmACia ) and ( ex:WmApjWmtama ).

exe

ɯmɤ-cʰɯ-mɤɕi-a \\
prob - ipfv -be.rich- 1sg \\
`If only I could become rich!' (elicited)
exe

exe

``iɕqʰa rɟɤlpu ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ ɯmɤ-pjɯ-mtam-a" ntsɯ ɲɯ-sɯsɤm pjɤ-ŋu. \\
the.aforementioned king 3sg. poss -son dem prob - ipfv -see[III]- 1sg always ipfv -think[III] ifr. ipfv -be \\
`She was thinking all the time: `If only I could see the prince!'' (150819 haidenver-zh)
0006314#S147
exe

This type of compound form is also attested however with the expected compositional meaning `it will probably be', as in ( ex:WmApjWNu ).

exe

xlist

``nɯ-kʰi ɣe" ti qʰe, \\
3pl. poss -luck sfp say: fact lnk \\
`She said: `They are so lucky.' (to have so much cattle).'

``tɕiʑɤɣ ɯmɤ-pjɯ-ŋu nɤ lɤ-ɣi wo!" ntsɯ tu-ti pɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
1du: gen prob - ipfv -be add imp: upstream -come always sfp ipfv -say pst. ipfv -be sens -be \\
`He said each time: `Maybe [this cattle] will be ours, come.' (2005 Kunbzang)
xlist
exe
summary: The Probabilitative prefix combined with the Imperfective form expresses optative modality, meaning “if only…,” as shown in examples like “If only I could become rich!” and “If only I could see the prince!” However, the same compound form can also have its expected compositional meaning, “it will probably be,” as in a sentence interpreted as “Maybe [this cattle] will be ours.”

text: Rhetorical interrogative
summary: A rhetorical interrogative is a question form that does not seek information but serves a rhetorical purpose, often making a statement or implying an answer. The passage identifies this construction as a type of interrogative used for effect rather than for genuine inquiry.

text:
The Rhetorical Interrogative prefix ɯβrɤ, located in slot -6 of the outer prefixal template (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ), mainly occurs with verbs in the Factual Non-Past ( ex:WBrAsqlWm ) in the corpus, but forms with the Aorist ( ex:WBrACtAtWtWt ) or the Imperfective are also attested. It is not compatible with negative prefixes.

exe

rcanɯ mti pjɯrɯ ʁɟa ʑo tɤrɤmɕkʰo pɯ-ŋu ɲɯ-ŋu. `nɯ a-mi pjɯ-te-a ri ɯβrɤ-sqlɯm ma' na-sɯso ɲɯ-ŋu \\
unexp: deg turquoise coral completely emph floor pst. ipfv -be sens -be dem 1sg. poss -foot ipfv: down -put[III]- 1sg lnk rh. q -collapse: fact sfp aor:3 -think sens -be \\
`The floor was all tiled with and turquoise and coral. She thought `If I tread on it, it will not yield under my weight, will it?'' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

exe

tɯrmɯkʰa nɤ nɯ-βɣo jɤ-azɣɯt nɤ ``joβ ɯβrɤ-ɕ-tɤ-tɯ-tɯt-nɯ?" ti ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
evening add 3pl. poss -FB aor -arrive add interj rh. q - tral - aor -2-say[II]- pl say: fact sens -be \\
`In the evening, their lama arrived and said: `You did not go and say joβ (to the girl), did you?' (2003kandZislama)
exe
summary: The Rhetorical Interrogative prefix ɯβrɤ occurs in slot -6 of the outer prefixal template and is used mainly with verbs in the Factual Non-Past in the corpus, though Aorist and Imperfective forms also appear. It cannot combine with negative prefixes. The examples show it used in rhetorical questions, often expecting confirmation or a negative answer.

text:
The Rhetorical Interrogative has two main functions, both in the form of negative rhetorical questions.

First, it expresses concern on part of the speaker that the action described by the verb might happen ( ex:WBrAGWrBNgW ) or might have already happened ( ex:WBrACtAtWtWt above), depending on the TAME category of the verb. In this function, it is frequently combined with the sentence final particle ma (§ sec:fsp.epistemic ) as in ( ex:WBrAsqlWm ) and ( ex:WBrAGWrBNgW ).

exe

``a-taʁ nɯtɕu, loŋbutɕʰi nɯ ɯβrɤ-ɣɯ-rŋgɯ ma" ɲɯ-sɯsɤm tɕe, nɯ ntsɯ ɯ-kɤ-nɯzdɯɣ ɲɯ-ŋu kʰi \\
1sg. poss -on dem: loc elephant dem rh. q - cisl -lie.down: fact sfp ipfv -think[III] lnk dem always 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -worry/about sens -be hearsay \\
`[The marmot]$_i$ thinks: `The elephant$_j$ won't come and sleep on my [hole], will it$_j$?', this is what it$_i$ worried about.' (28-qapar)
0003720#S43
exe

In this use, ɯβrɤ- normally carries a negative presupposition `it will not $X$, will it?'. This negative meaning appears to be absent only in a handful of examples such as ( ex:WBrAGi.Ge ), where ɯβrɤ- is found with the final particle ɣe: in another version of the story from which this example is taken, the corresponding quotation has the verb ɣi `come' in affirmative form without the Rhetorical Interrogative, and instead the sentence final particle tʰaŋ (see ex:Gi.thaN, § sec:fact.main.clauses ).

exe

a-mu, jɯɣmɯr tɕe kʰu ɯβrɤ-ɣi ɣe! \\
1sg. poss -mother this.evening lnk tiger rh. q -come: fact sfp \\
`Mother, the tiger will come this evening (to eat us), won't it?' (X1-khu)
0004085#S3
exe

In this function, the prefix ɯβrɤ- has some overlap with the Apprehensive prefix ɕɯ- (§ sec:apprehensive.function ), though the latter conveys a higher degree of worry.

Second, the Rhetorical Interrogative occurs in interrogative clauses expressing polite requests, as in ( ex:WBrAkWznAmYoanW ).

exe

nɤki nɯ-tɤɲi ɯ-taʁ kɤ-rɤt nɯ ɯβrɤ-kɯ-z-nɤmɲo-a-nɯ? \\
dem: medial 2pl. poss -staff 3sg. poss -on obj: pcp -write dem rh. q -2 1- caus -watch- 1sg - pl \\
`You wouldn't show me what is written on that staff of yours, would you?' (2003 sras)
exe

This function is common in particular with the Rhetorical Interrogative form ɯβrɤ-jɤɣ of the modal verb jɤɣbe allowed selecting a complement clause in the Imperfective, as in ( ex:chWtWGinW.WBrAjAG ). The noun a-rʑaβ `my wives' in ( ex:chWtWGinW.WBrAjAG ) is an essive adjunct (§ sec:essive.abs ).

exe

nɯʑo ra χsɯm nɯ, [a-rʑaβ cʰɯ-tɯ-ɣi-nɯ] ɯβrɤ-jɤɣ? \\
2pl pl three dem 1sg. poss -wife ipfv: downstream -2-come- pl rh. q -be.possible: fact \\
`The three of you, would you come [to my palace and become] my wives?' (Norzang 2005)
exe

The prefix ɯβrɤ- also occurs in polite inquiries about a person's health, expressing sincere concern about a possible illness as in ( ex:nAkWmNAm.WBrAkutu ).

exe

nɤ-kɯ-mŋɤm ɯβrɤ-ku-tu, nɤ-ɕqʰe ɯβrɤ-ku-tʰɯ? \\
2sg. poss - sbj: pcp -hurt rh. q - prs -exist
2sg. poss -cough rh. q - prs -be.serious \\
`You don't have a disease (these days), do you? Your cough is not serious, is it?' (conversation, 2016-03-20)
exe

A more marginal use of ɯβrɤ- is found in ( ex:WBrApjWtua ), where it appears on two antonymic verbs linked by the adversative ri to express the meaning `if I don't $X$, at least I will not $Y$.' In another version of the story from which ( ex:WBrApjWtua ) is taken, the same meaning ( ex:mAphana.mARdWGa ) is expressed by verbs in the negative Factual Non-Past with the sentence final particle tʰaŋ (§ sec:fsp.epistemic ).

exe

pʰɤn ɯβrɤ-pjɯ-tu-a ri ʁdɯɣ nɯ ɯβrɤ-pjɯ-tu-a tɕe tɤ-rca cʰɯ-ɣi-a je \\
be.efficient: fact qu. r - ipfv -exist- 1sg lnk harm: fact dem qu. r - ipfv -exist- 1sg lnk indef. poss -together ipfv: downstream -come- 1sg sfp \\
`Even if I am of no use at least I will not do any harm, let me come along!' (X1-tWJo)
0004089#S36
exe

exe

aʑo cʰɯ-ɣi-a je ma mɤ-pʰan-a nɤ mɤ-ʁdɯɣ-a tʰaŋ nɤ \\
1sg ipfv: downstream -come- 1sg sfp lnk neg:be.efficient: fact - 1sg add neg -harm: fact - 1sg sfp sfp \\
`Let me come along, [even] if I am of no use, I will not do any harm.' (several occurrences)
0003368#S20
exe
summary: The Rhetorical Interrogative has two main uses, both as negative rhetorical questions. It can express the speaker’s concern that an action may happen or already have happened, often with the final particle *ma* and sometimes overlapping in meaning with the apprehensive prefix *ɕɯ-*; it is also used in polite requests and inquiries, including polite offers, questions for permission, and questions about someone’s health. A more marginal use occurs in clauses with adversative *ri* to mean roughly “if I don’t X, at least I will not Y.”

text:
The combination of the Rhetorical Interrogative with the peg circumfix (§ sec:peg.circumfix ) is not compositional. Despite the absence of any negative prefix (§ sec:negation ), it is the negative counterpart (in functional terms) of the Probabilitative prefix (§ sec:WmA ), expressing the meaning `it looks like/seems that $X$ is/does not', as in ( ex:khro.WBrAkWpeci ) In ( ex:khro.WBrAkWpeci ), ɯβrɤ-kɯ-pe-ci translates Chinese 这好像不太好吧 zhè hǎoxiàng bú tài hǎo baThis does not look good/nice. and ( ex:WBrAkWtuci ).

exe

kʰro ɯβrɤ-kɯ-pe-ci \\
much rh. q - peg -be.good: fact - peg \\
`[What you are proposing] does not look nice (fair).' (140506 nongfu he mogui-zh) 0003925#S69
exe

exe

ʁloŋbutɕʰi nɯ, ɯ-rme ra ɯβrɤ-kɯ-tu-ci \\
elephant dem 3sg. poss -hair pl rh. q - peg -exist: fact - peg \\
`The elephant, it seems that it does not have hair (on its body).' (19-RloNbutChi) 0003550#S8
exe
summary:
The Rhetorical Interrogative combined with the peg circumfix is a noncompositional construction. Although it lacks any negative prefix, it functions as the negative counterpart of the Probabilitative prefix, meaning roughly “it looks like/seems that X is/does not.”  

Examples show this pattern translating as “does not look good/nice” and “it seems that [the elephant] does not have hair,” illustrating its negative evidential-like interpretation.

text:
The prefix ɯβrɤ- is probably related to the Tshobdun interrogative prefix vré-, though the two prefixes are not entirely similar: Tshobdun vré- is monosyllabic, and the vowel -e (from ealier *a ) has not undergone reduction to ɐ as could have been expected in the view of its Japhug cognate. The fact that Japhug ɯβrɤ- contains two syllables, and that it occurs in the left-most (-6) slot of the verbal template suggests that it may been grammaticalized relatively recently in comparison with other elements of the prefixal chain. In view of the formal differences between the two languages, one cannot exclude at this stage the possibility of independent grammaticalization, though the source is unclear.

Possible sources (from a formal point of view) could include the noun ɯ-βrahis share (cognate to Tshobdun ó-vre ) or the adverbial noun ɯ-βrait is X's turn to... (§ sec.IPN.adverbs ). However, the semantic link between these meanings and that of the Rhetorical Interrogative is unclear.
summary: The Japhug prefix ɯβrɤ- is probably related to the Tshobdun interrogative prefix vré-, but the two forms differ in important ways: Tshobdun vré- is monosyllabic, while Japhug ɯβrɤ- is disyllabic and occupies the left-most position in the verbal template, suggesting a relatively recent grammaticalization. Because of these formal differences, independent grammaticalization cannot be ruled out, and the source of the prefix remains unclear. Possible formal sources include the noun ɯ-βrahis ‘share’ and the adverbial noun ɯ-βrait ‘it is X’s turn to…’, but their semantic connection to the Rhetorical Interrogative is uncertain.

text: Interrogative
summary: The passage introduces interrogative constructions, which are used to ask questions. It focuses on the main linguistic features that distinguish interrogatives from other clause types.

text:
The Interrogative ɯ, found in slot -6 of the outer prefixal template (§ sec:outer.prefixal.chain ), is a stress-attracting prefix (§ sec:stress.prefixal.chain ). When attached to a monosyllabic base, like the Factual Non-Past 3sg of monosyllabic stem verbs, the stress is on the Interrogative prefix itself, as in ɯ́-jɤɣ `it is possible to'( ex:YWtWkhAm.WjAG ) (see also ex:nWnaj.WjAG, § sec:fact.complement above).

exe

kɯki ɲɯ-tɯ-kʰɤm ɯ́-jɤɣ \\
dem. prox ipfv -2-give[III] qu -be.possible: fact \\
`Could you pass [me] this thing?' (2003, conversation taRrdo)
exe

If the base is polysyllabic, the stress is on the second syllable just following the Interrogative, whether this syllable is a prefix ( ex:WtWsWz2 ) or part of the verb stem ( ex:WGAZu ).

exe

nɤj ɯ-tɯ́-sɯz? \\
2sg qu -2-know: fact \\
`Do you know it?' (19-GzW) 0003536#S8
exe

exe

ki sakaβ ɯ-rkɯ nɯtɕu si ɯ-ɣɤ́ʑu? \\
dem. prox well 3sg. poss -side dem: loc tree qu -exist: sens \\
`Are there trees near this well?' (140517 mogui de jing-zh)
0004022#S95
exe

When occurring in direct contact with the stem of a contracting verb (§ sec:contraction ), the Interrogative ɯ- does not merge with the initial a-. Instead, an epenthetic -j- is inserted between the prefix and the verb stem (see examples ex:WjatsWtsu, § sec:contraction and ex:Wjandza, § sec:passive.agent ).
summary:
The interrogative prefix ɯ occurs in slot -6 of the outer prefixal template and attracts stress. With monosyllabic bases, stress falls on the interrogative prefix itself, while with polysyllabic bases it falls on the second syllable after the prefix, whether that syllable is a prefix or part of the verb stem.  

When ɯ- comes into direct contact with the stem of a contracting verb, it does not merge with initial a-; instead, an epenthetic -j- is inserted between the prefix and the stem.

text:
The Interrogative prefix ɯ- has two main functions. First, it expresses a polar question (as in ex:atAtWthe.WjAG for instance), expecting an answer with the same verb in affirmative or negative form ( ex:jAG.jAG ), a question studied in more detail in § sec:anticipation.person and § sec:egophoric.interrogative. An alternative way of marking polar questions is the sentence final particle ɕi (§ sec:fsp.interrog ).

exe

xlist

wortɕʰi ʑo a-tɤ-tɯ-tʰe ɯ́-jɤɣ? \\
please emph irr - pfv -2-ask[III] qu -be.possible: fact \\
`Can you ask [for me]?' (divination 2002)

jɤɣ, jɤɣ! \\
be.possible: fact be.possible: fact \\
`Yes, yes!' (divination 2002)
xlist
exe

Second, it occurs in the protasis of conditionals (§ sec:real.conditional ) in free variation with initial reduplication (§ sec:redp.protasis ). In this construction, the verb is generally followed by the additive marker nɤ, as in ( ex:WYWtWsWsAm ). The second person prefix nɤ- in ( ex:WYWtWsWsAm ) is a case of hybrid indirect speech (§ sec:hybrid indirect ).

exe

``nɤ-nmaʁ nɯ a-tɤ-sɯsu'' ɯ-ɲɯ́-tɯ-sɯsɤm nɤ, kɯki tɤ-ndze \\
2sg. poss -husband dem irr - pfv -live qu - sens -2-think[III] add dem. prox imp -eat[III] \\
`If you want your husband to live, eat this!' (150909 hua pi-zh) 0006278#S164
exe
summary: The interrogative prefix ɯ- has two main functions: it marks polar questions, which expect a yes/no answer, and it can also be replaced by the sentence-final particle ɕi. In addition, ɯ- appears in the protasis of conditionals, where it varies with initial reduplication; in this construction the verb is usually followed by the additive marker nɤ.

text: Many languages of the Trans-Himalayan family, including Chinese, Tibetan and Gyalrongic varieties, have vocalic prefixes marking polar interrogatives similar to Japhug ɯ-. However, it remains unclear whether these prefixes reflect genuine common inheritance: in particular, although some Tibetan languages do have an interrogative prefix e, it is not attested in Old Tibetan texts, and may therefore be an innovative feature. If this prefix is not an archaic feature in Tibetan, the Japhug Interrogative ɯ- and its equivalent in other Gyalrongic languages such as Khroskyabs ə̂-  may be better analyzed as borrowings from Amdo Tibetan.
summary: Many Trans-Himalayan languages, including Chinese, Tibetan, and Gyalrongic varieties, have vocalic prefixes used to mark polar questions, similar to Japhug ɯ-. However, it is uncertain whether these prefixes are inherited from a common source, since the Tibetan interrogative prefix e is not attested in Old Tibetan and may be innovative. If so, the Japhug ɯ- and comparable Gyalrongic forms such as Khroskyabs ə̂- may instead be borrowings from Amdo Tibetan.

text: There are two constructions involving a negative copula/existential verb and expressing specialized modal meaning.
summary: The passage states that there are two constructions that use a negative copula or existential verb. These constructions express specialized modal meanings.

text:
The negative existential verb menot exist (§ sec:existential.basic ) occurs in combination with the exceptive postposition maapart from (§ sec:exceptive ) and the indefinite ci (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ) following a verb in the Non-Past, in collocation with the verb sɯsothink, to express a wrong expectation `believe/be confident that... is true' Tshendzin translates it into Chinese as 满以为是 mǎnyǐwéishìbe confident that it is.... (whereas in fact it is not the case), as in ( ex:Nu.ci.ma.me ).

exe

ɯʑo kɯ nɯ ŋu ci ma me ɲɯ-sɯsɤm qʰe, \\
dem erg dem be: fact indef apart.from not.exist: fact sens -think[III] lnk \\
`It believed that it was like that.' (`The sparrow believed that making a nest in the chimney was safe, but in the end it was asphyxiated by the smoke and died.') (160707 kumpGAtCW)
exe

This construction can be used with a rectification clause in tɤ-mda `but in fact...' (§ sec:evd.rectification.clauses ), as in ( ex:ci.ma.me.tAmda ).

exe

ʑa zɣɯt-a ci ma me nɯ-sɯso-t-a ri, tɤ-mda tɕe pjɤ-k-ɤrqʰi-ci. \\
soon arrive: fact - 1sg indef apart.from not.exist: fact aor -think- pst: tr - 1sg lnk
aor -be.the.time lnk ifr. ipfv - peg -be.far- peg \\
`I thought that I would arrive quickly, but it turns out that it was very far.' (elicited)
exe
summary: The negative existential verb **menot exist** can combine with the exceptive postposition **ma** and the indefinite **ci** after a non-past verb, together with **sɯso** ‘think,’ to express a **wrong expectation** or belief that something is true when it is actually not. Tshendzin glosses this construction as meaning “be confident that it is...,” and it can also be followed by a rectification clause with **tɤ-mda** ‘but in fact...’.

text:
The negative copula maʁnot be is used with the restrictive focus marker cinɤ(not) even one (§ sec:cinA ) in a construction meaning `(anyway) it is not the case that...', semantically close to the apodosis of a universal concessive conditional (§ sec:universal.concessive.conditional ).

exe

qajdo kɯ tɕʰi mɤ-nɯ-ti ɕti nɤ, a-tɤ-nɯ-ti ma ŋu cinɤ maʁ kɯ, nɯ sɤznɤ kɯ-scɯ-scit rɤʑi-tɕi \\
crow erg what neg - auto -say: fact be. aff: fact lnk irr - pfv - auto -say lnk be: fact even not.be: fact sfp dem comp sbj: pcp - emph happy stay: fact - 1du \\
`What wouldn't a crow say (a crow tells only lies), let it say what it wants, in any case none of it is true, let us live [together] happily rather (than worrying about that).' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S24
exe

The copula maʁ in this construction is invariable: only the verb preceding the cinɤ maʁ kɯ sequence receives person indexation, as shown by ( ex:Nua.cinA.maR.kW ).

exe

kɯ-mɯrkɯ ŋu-a cinɤ maʁ kɯ \\
sbj: pcp -steal be: fact - 1sg even not.be sfp \\
`Anyway it is not I who am the thief.' (elicited)
exe

In addition to ŋube, a few other verbs such as fsebe like can occur in this construction.
summary: The negative copula **maʁ** ‘not be’ combines with the restrictive focus marker **cinɤ** ‘even one’ in a construction meaning roughly “anyway, it is not the case that…,” which is semantically close to the apodosis of a universal concessive conditional. In this construction, **maʁ** is invariable, and person marking appears only on the verb before the **cinɤ maʁ kɯ** sequence. Besides **ŋu** ‘be,’ a few other verbs such as **fsebe** ‘like’ can also occur in this construction.

text: Verbal morphology and periphrastic constructions are not the only ways to encode TAME in Japhug. Three other grammatical categories contribute to mark TAME.
summary: In Japhug, TAME is not expressed only through verbal morphology and periphrastic constructions. Three additional grammatical categories also contribute to marking TAME.

text: Tense, aspect and modality can be expressed by primary aspectual adverbs such as pɤjkʰustill, ʑɯrɯʑɤriprogressively or ntsɯalways (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ), time ordinals (§ sec:time.ordinals ), temporal counted nouns (§ sec:CN.time ), time adverbs derived from nouns (§ sec:time.adv ) and adverb of epistemic modality (§ sec:modality.adverbs ).
summary: Tense, aspect, and modality may be expressed through several kinds of adverbial forms. These include primary aspectual adverbs such as *pɤjkʰu* ‘still’, *ʑɯrɯʑɤri* ‘progressively’, and *ntsɯ* ‘always’, as well as time ordinals, temporal counted nouns, noun-derived time adverbs, and adverbs of epistemic modality.

text: Many sentence final particles contribute to the expression of modality and evidentiality. Some particles are dedicated markers: the hearsay particle kʰi (§ sec:fsp.hearsay ) is specifically encodes evidentiality, tʰaŋ indicates epistemic modality (§ sec:fsp.epistemic ) and je has a hortative/imperative meaning (§ sec:fsp.imp ). Other particles such as wo (§ sec:fsp.imp ) have meanings that are more difficult to describe exclusively in terms of modality or evidentiality. No sentence final particle expresses tense or aspect.
summary: Many sentence-final particles express modality and evidentiality. Some are dedicated markers: kʰi marks hearsay evidentiality, tʰaŋ marks epistemic modality, and je has hortative/imperative meaning, while others like wo are harder to classify strictly in those terms. No sentence-final particle expresses tense or aspect.

subsection: Nouns and the expression of modality
text:
noun!modality grammaticalization!modality
Two nouns of Tibetan origin, ɯ-mdoʁcolour and smɯlɤmprayer occur sentence-finally as modal markers. These sentence-final uses probably originate from complement-taking nouns (§ sec:complement.taking.IPN ) used predicatively (§ sec:non.verbal.predicates ).

The noun ɯ-mdoʁcolour
The noun ɯ-mdoʁcolour, borrowed from Tibetan མདོག་mdogcolour, occurs with the highly grammaticalized modal meaning `it looks like', as in ( ex:GAZu.WmdoR ) and ( ex:YWrtaR.WmdoR ).

exe

[ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ nɯ, [...] kɯrcɤ-ldʑa jamar ɣɤʑu] ɯ-mdoʁ \\
3sg. poss -limb dem eight-piece about exist: sens 3sg. poss -colour \\
`It looks like [the spider] has eight limbs.' (26-mYaRmtsaR-48) 0003672#S6
exe

exe

[iɕqʰa nɯ [kɤntɕʰɯ-sŋi ʑo tu-ndza-nɯ] ɲɯ-rtaʁ] ɯ-mdoʁ \\
the.aforementioned dem several-day emph ipfv -eat- pl sens -be.enough 3sg. poss -colour \\
`It looks like [the meat from one of those] is enough [for the lions] to eat for several days.' (20-sWNgi)
0003562#S55
exe

This construction occurs with the Sensory in the complement clause (§ sec:sensory ) as in the examples above, or with the Inferential to express a past event/situation (see ex:WmdoRo, § sec:verb.enclitics ). The combination of Inferential with ɯ-mdoʁ is semantically close to the Probabilitative with peg circumfix (§ sec:WmA.kW.ci, see also ex:WmAjakWzGWtci.gloss, § sec:peg.circumfix ).

The denominal verb nɯmdoʁlook like derived from this construction (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ) has the same meaning, but rather selects a subject participle in the complement clause as in ( ex:kWCe.mWpjAnWmdoR ), with subject coreference between the main clause and the complement (compare ex:kWCe.mWpjAnWmdoR and ex:kWCe.YWtWnWmdoR ).

exe

χpɯn kɯ-tsʰu nɯ maka mɯ-ɲɯ-mɯnmu tɕe ku-nɯ-rɤʑi pjɤ-ɕti ma [kɯ-ɕe] mɯ-pjɤ-nɯmdoʁ. \\
monk sbj: pcp -be.fat dem at.all neg - ipfv -move lnk ipfv - auto -stay ifr. ipfv -be. aff lnk sbj: pcp -go neg - ifr. ipfv -look.like \\
`The fat monk was not moving and remained there, and did not look like he was going [anywhere].' (150830 san ge heshang-zh)
0006416#S118
exe

exe

[kɯ-ɕe] ɲɯ-tɯ-nɯmdoʁ \\
sbj: pcp -go sens -2-look.like \\
`You look like you are going.' (elicited)
exe

The verb nɯmdoʁ can alternatively take a noun phrase as semi-object, as in ( ex:kWpe.YWnWmdoR ).

exe

[tɯrme kɯ-pe ci] ɲɯ-nɯmdoʁ \\
person sbj: pcp -be.good indef sens -look.like \\
`He looks like someone nice.' (elicited)
exe

The noun smɯlɤmprayer
The noun smɯlɤmprayer ( སྨོན་ལམ་smon.lamprayer, `wish') is grammaticalized as a quasi-sentence final particle, used in combination with the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.main ) to express a wish, as in ( ex:anWtABzu.smWlAm ). A similar construction has been documented in Tshobdun.

exe

tɕʰeme kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕɤr nɤ-ɕɣa kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ʑo, tɯrme ntsɯ tɯ-ndze mɤ-kɯ-ra ci a-nɯ-tɯ-ɤβzu smɯlɤm \\
girl sbj: pcp - emph be.beautiful 2sg. poss -tooth/age sbj: pcp - emph be.small emph people always 2-eat[III]: fact neg - sbj: pcp -be.needed indef irr - pfv -2-become prayer \\
`May you become a very beautiful, nice and young girl who does not have to eat humans.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S285
exe

It also occurs with the Factual Non-Past ( ex:tWmACi.smWlAm ), and can have scope over several clauses, comprising both verbs in the Factual Non-Past and the Irrealis, as in ( ex:tWscitnW.nWkWmNAm.smWlAm ).

exe

nɯ tɤ-nɯ-ndɤm tɕe tɯ-mɤɕi smɯlɤm \\
dem imp - auto -take[III] lnk 2-be.rich: fact prayer \\
`Take (this cattle and, and may you be rich!' (2003kAndzwsqhaj2)
exe

exe

nɯʑora kɯnɤ tɯ-scit-nɯ tɕe nɯ, nɯ-kɯ-mŋɤm ra a-pɯ-me smɯlɤm nɤ! \\
2pl also 2-be.happy: fact lnk dem 2pl. poss - sbj: pcp -hurt pl irr - ipfv -not.exist prayer sfp \\
`May you be happy and be free from any disease.' (conversation, 15-01-02)
exe

The basic meaning of smɯlɤm is still attested in Japhug, as in ( ex:smWlAm.smWlAm ), and its sentence-final function is performative, and particularly common in prayers and wishes.

exe

smɯlɤm nɯ na-ndɯn-nɯ ndɤre, ``ki ɯ-ʁɤri nɯ sɯstaʁ ʑo kɯ-ɤcʰɯcʰa, ki ɯ-ʁɤri nɯ sɯstaʁ ʑo kɯ-pe [...] a-nɯ-βze smɯlɤm" ta-tɯt-nɯ \\
prayer dem aor:3 -read- pl lnk dem. prox 3sg. poss -before dem comp emph sbj: pcp -be.capable dem. prox 3sg. poss -before dem comp emph sbj: pcp -be.good irr - pfv -make[III] prayer aor:3 -say[II]- pl \\
`They recited the prayer, and said `May you become even stronger and better than before.'' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

The noun smɯlɤm can be denominalized with the prefix nɯ- (§ sec:denom.tr.nW) as the transitive complement-taking verb nɯsmɯlɤmwish, which is compatible with either infinitival complements or complement clauses in the Irrealis as in ( ex:athWtWmACi.YWnWsmWlama ).

exe

nɤʑo a-tʰɯ-tɯ-mɤɕi ɲɯ-nɯ-smɯlam-a \\
2sg irr - pfv -2-be.rich sens - denom -prayer- 1sg \\
`I wish that you will become rich.' (elicited)
exe
summary: Two Tibetan-origin nouns, ɯ-mdoʁ ‘colour’ and smɯlɤm ‘prayer/wish’, are used sentence-finally as modal markers in Japhug, probably developing from predicative complement-taking nouns. The noun ɯ-mdoʁ expresses a highly grammaticalized meaning like ‘it looks like,’ while smɯlɤm functions as a quasi-sentence-final particle with the Irrealis to express wishes, though its basic noun meaning is still attested.

text:
This chapter focuses on the syntax of simple clauses, that is clauses which do not involve multiclausal constructions.

Five topics are discussed: word order within the clause (§ sec:word.order ), sentential adverbs (§ sec:sentential.adverbs ), verbless sentences (§ sec:non.verbal.predicates ), noun-verb collocations (§ sec:light.verb ) and copulas (§ sec:copula.existential ).
summary: This chapter examines the syntax of simple clauses, meaning clauses that do not involve multiclausal constructions. It discusses five topics: word order within the clause, sentential adverbs, verbless sentences, noun-verb collocations, and copulas.

text: With a few exceptions (§ sec:non.verbal.predicates ), Japhug sentences require a finite verb to be complete, while all other constituents are optional. The main verb is generally sentence-final: only a handful of words (§ sec:postverbal.adv ) and dislocated constituents (§ sec:right.dislocation ), can occur after it.
summary: Japhug sentences generally require a finite verb to be complete, while other constituents are optional except for a few exceptions. The main verb usually appears sentence-finally, with only a small number of postverbal words and dislocated constituents able to follow it.

text:
word order
This section describes the word order patterns involving verb and core arguments attested in the corpus (with the exception of right dislocation, § sec:right.dislocation ) when all arguments are overt. The question of non-overt arguments is treated in § sec:overt.non.overt, and the position of adverbials in § sec:sentential.adverbs.
summary: This section examines the word order patterns in the corpus involving verbs and core arguments when all arguments are overt, excluding right dislocation. It notes that cases with non-overt arguments are discussed elsewhere, as is the placement of adverbials.

text:
verb!intransitive
When overt, core arguments and adjuncts are located before the verb. In ( ex:RnaRna.YAsindZi ) for instance, the intransitive subject ɯ-mu ɯ-wa ni `his mother and his father' (§ sec:dyads ) in the dual is placed before the adverb ʁnaʁnaboth and the main verb ɲɤ-si-ndʑi `they$_du$ died'. The dual suffix on the verb here indexes the number of the intransitive subject (§ sec:intr.23 ).

exe

[ɯ-mu ɯ-wa ni] ʁnaʁna ɲɤ-si-ndʑi \\
3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss -father du both ifr -die- du \\
`His parents had both died.' (150828 donglang)
0006312#S8
exe

In the case of semi-transitive verbs (§ sec:semi.transitive ), which have two absolutive arguments, it is very rare to have both an overt intransitive subject and an overt semi-object (except if the semi-object is a complement clause, see § sec:complement.clause.case.marking ). The semi-object can be follow ( ex:kWkWra.YWrganW ) or precede ( ex:pGa.ra.mArganW ) the subject, but in the second case there is a pause, indicative of left dislocation.

exe

kɯkɯra <xuexiao> ɲɯ-rga-nɯ. \\
dem. prox: pl school sens -like- pl \\
`Those (the children) like school.' (conversation, 14-05-10)
exe

exe

tɤɕi nɯ, pɣa ra nɯstʰi mɤ-rga-nɯ. \\
barley dem bird pl that.much neg -like: fact - pl \\
`The barley, the birds don't like it so much.' (23-pGAYaR)
0003606#S23
exe

With intransitive verbs selecting a locative phrase (§ sec:intr.goal ), the locative phrase is generally located between the intransitive subject and the verb ( ex:SOblV ).

exe

[ɯ-pi ni] tʂu kɯ-wxti nɯtɕu jo-ɕe-ndʑi \\
3sg. poss -elder.sibling du road sbj: pcp -be.big dem: loc ifr -go- du \\
`His two elder brothers went [along] the big road.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S23
exe

However, it is possible to put the locative phrase before the subject, especially when it refers to the source of the motion (§ sec:motion.verbs ), as in ( ex:OblSV ) and ( ex:OblSV2 ).

exe

tɯmɯnɤmkʰa nɯtɕu [qro χsɯm] pjɯ-ɣi-nɯ \\
heaven dem: loc pigeon three ipfv: down -come- pl \\
`(Every day), three pigeon came down from heaven.' (02-deluge)
0003376#S48
exe

exe

mtsʰu ɣɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu [mtsʰoʁlaŋ] to-nɯ-ɬoʁ \\
lake gen 3sg. poss -in dem: loc water.monster ifr - auto -come.out \\
`A water monster came out of the lake.' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

Likewise, the standard of comparison (marked by the postposition sɤz, § sec:comparative ) can either precede or follow the intransitive subject (§ sec:sAz.kW ).

Oblique phrases with the relator noun ɯ-taʁon, above selected by the main verb (§ sec:WtaR ) are located between the intransitive subject and the verb, as in ( ex:tArAku.WtaR.wuma.pe ) and ( ex:ZmbrW.WtaR.karindZi ).
With the motion verb ɕego, in ( ex:ZmbrW.WtaR.karindZi ) in stem II ari, ɯ-taʁ specifically indicates the means of transportation (§ sec:WtaR ).

exe

[ɯ-ɣli nɯ] li tɤ-rɤku ɯ-taʁ wuma ʑo pe \\
3sg. poss -dung dem again indef. poss -crop 3sg. poss -on really emph be.good: fact \\
`Its dung is good (as fertilizer) for the crops.' (05-qaZo) 0003404#S89
exe

exe

tɕendɤre [ʑɤni pɣa ni] ʑmbrɯ ɯ-taʁ kɤ-ari-ndʑi ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk 3du bird du boat 3sg. poss -on aor: east -go[II] sens -be \\
`The two of them [including the bird] departed on the boat.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

essive
Unlike intransitive subjects, essive adjuncts (§ sec:essive.abs ) are closer to the verb than oblique arguments, as shown by tɯrmeperson in ( ex:ataR.tWrme.penW ), which is not an intransitive subject (`the people are nice to me') but an essive phrase `as people' (see also ex:tWGli.Wuma.Zo.pe, § sec:essive.abs ).

exe

tɕe <zhoujikong> tɕe mɤʑɯ li a-taʁ tɯrme pe-nɯ ma \\
lnk center.for.disease.control lnk even.more again 1sg. poss -on person be.good: fact - pl lnk \\
`At the district center for disease control, they are also very nice to me (as people).' (140501 tshering skyid)
0003902#S139
exe
summary: The passage describes the basic ordering of arguments and adjuncts with intransitive verbs: when overt, core arguments and adjuncts generally appear before the verb, and the subject may be separated from the verb by elements such as adverbs, locative phrases, standards of comparison, or oblique phrases. It also notes that with semi-transitive verbs, overt subject and semi-object cooccur rarely, that locative phrases usually come between subject and verb though they may precede the subject in source-of-motion contexts, and that essive adjuncts are placed closer to the verb than oblique arguments.

text:
verb!transitive
When the main verb is transitive, the transitive subject (with the ergative postposition, § sec:A.kW ) is found before the direct object (in absolutive form, § sec:absolutive.P ), as in ( ex:SOV.pjAmtonW ).

exe

kɯ-ɣɤrʁaʁ nɯra kɯ qartsʰaz ɯ-pɯ nɯ pjɤ-mto-nɯ \\
sbj: pcp -hunt dem: pl erg deer 3sg. poss -little dem ifr -see- pl \\
`The hunters saw the little deer.' (140429 jiedi-zh)
exe

The object of a transitive verb only rarely precedes the subject, except for object complement clauses (§ sec:complement.word.order ), and examples exhibiting this order are all analyzable as left-dislocated topicalized constituents, as in ( ex:OSV.thanWtsWm ).

exe

a-tɕɯ, ji-rɣa ra nɯ-mbala kɯ tʰa-nɯtsɯm tɕe nɯnɯ ɯ-kɯ-ɕar ɕe-tɕi \\
1sg. poss -son 1pl. poss -neighbour pl 3pl. poss -ox erg aor:3 3- auto -take.away lnk dem 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -search go: fact - 1du \\
`My son$_i$, the neighbour's ox has taken him$_i$ away, and we are looking for him$_i$.' (tWJo 2012)
0004089#S40
exe

In ( ex:OSV.pjAndo ), the object ɯ-mpʰɯz nɯnɯ is topicalized, and in addition the ergative phrase tɤjpɣom kɯ is not a real agent.

exe

ɯ-mpʰɯz nɯnɯ tɤjpɣom kɯ pjɤ-ndo \\
3sg. poss -buttocks dem ice erg ifr -take \\
`(The leopard's) buttocks had been caught in the ice.' (140427 qala)
0003852#S34
exe

The object-subject-verb order is however found to focalize the subject, together with a postverbal copula (§ sec:focalization.final.copula ) as in ( ex:OSV.janWtsWm ), where the transitive subject nɯnɯ kɯ follows the object (Chunjie).

exe

<chunjie> nɯnɯ kɯ ja-nɯ-tsɯm ŋu tʰaŋ \\
anthr dem erg aor:3 - vert -take.away be: fact sfp \\
`It is probably him who took away Chunjie.' (150825 huluwa-zh)
0006346#S115
exe

Note that without intonation, ( ex:OSV.janWtsWm ) is ambiguous, as [<chunjie> nɯnɯ kɯ ] could also be analyzed as a single constituent (since personal names can optionally take demonstrative determiners, § sec:personal.names.modifiers ), and in this case the translation of the sentence would be `Chunjie probably took him.' The above translation however is the correct one in the context of the story.
summary: In transitive clauses, the ergative subject normally precedes the absolutive object, yielding subject–object order. Object-before-subject orders are rare and usually reflect topicalization or left-dislocation, while object–subject order can be used to focus the subject, often with a postverbal copula; without intonation, such examples may be ambiguous in analysis.

text:
verb!secundative ditransitive verb
The recipient (direct object) generally precedes the theme (semi-object) of secundative verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ) as in ( ex:WRi.tWmgo.YAmbi ).
secundative

exe

ɯ-ʁi tɯmgo ɲɤ-mbi \\
3sg. poss -younger.sibling food ifr -give \\
