`He gave food to his younger brother.' (nyima 2003-2)
exe

In noun-verbs collocations where the verb is secundative such as tɯ-nɯ+jtsʰi `breastfeed' as in ( ex:WpW.tWnW.Yjtshi ), placing the recipient ( ɯ-pɯ ) after the them ( tɯ-nɯ ) is never attested.

exe

ɯ-pɯ tɯ-nɯ ɲɯ-jtsʰi kɯnɤ ʑo \\
3sg. poss -young indef. poss -breast ipfv -give.to.drink also emph \\
`Even when [the monkey mother] nurses her baby,...' (19-GzW)
0003536#S25
exe

However, with the verb mbigive there are examples of the opposite order as in ( ex:kWlAG.nW.nambi ), where the theme ( qajɣi kɤ-kɯ-ɕke nɯra `pieces of bread that had burnt') precedes the recipient ( kɯ-lɤɣ nɯ `the shepherd').

exe

tɕʰeme nɯ kɯ qajɣi kɤ-kɯ-ɕke nɯra kɯ-lɤɣ nɯ na-mbi \\
girl dem erg bread aor - sbj: pcp -burn dem:pl sbj: pcp -herd dem aor:3 -give \\
`The girl gave the shepherd pieces of bread that had burnt (to eat).' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe
summary: Secundative ditransitive verbs generally place the recipient/direct object before the theme/semi-object, as shown by examples with *give* and *breastfeed*. In noun-verb collocations this recipient-after-theme order is not attested, but with *mbi* ‘give’ there are examples where the theme precedes the recipient.

text:
causative!word order
Causative verbs (§ sec:sig.causative ) derived from plain intransitive verbs behave like monotransitive verbs (§ sec:monotransitive.word.order ), but those derived from transitive (§ sec:ditransitive.causative ) or semi-transitive (§ sec:semi.transitive.causative ) verbs are ditransitive.

Causative derivations from transitive verbs have a causee (§ sec:causee.kW ), whose syntactic status is intermediate between subject and object: it can be marked with the ergative, but is indexed as if it were an object if it is first or second person while the object is third person (§ sec:ditransitive.causative ). The causee in the ergative is normally placed before the object ( ex:Wmbro.kW.pjAzrAtCaR ), even when it serves as instrument (§ sec:sig.caus.instrumental ) as in ( ex:ZmbrWBJaj.kW.tuwGsWCmi ).

exe

ɯ-mbro kɯ qapri tɯ-rdoʁ nɯ pjɤ-z-rɤtɕaʁ \\
3sg. poss -horse erg snake one-piece dem ifr - caus -trample \\
`He made his horse trample one of the [two] snakes.' (smanmi 2003)
exe

exe

``ʑmbrɯ-βɟaj nɯnɯ kɯ cʰa nɯ tú-wɣ-sɯ-ɕmi tɕe cʰa mɯm" tu-ti-nɯ pɯ-ŋu ma \\
boat-oar dem erg alcohol dem ipfv - inv - caus -mix lnk alcohol be.tasty: fact ipfv -say- pl pst. ipfv -be lnk \\
`People used to say that if one mixes the alcohol [using] a boat oar, it is tasty.' (31-cha)
0003764#S41
exe

The object can be located before the causee, but it is always a left dislocated constituent, followed by a pause as ɯ-ɕnɤz nɯnɯ `its head/extremity' in ( ex:WmtChi.kW.kusWndAm ).

exe

qandʐe ɣɯ, (...) ɯ-ɕnɤz nɯnɯ, ɯ-mtɕʰi kɯ ku-sɯ-ndɤm tɕe \\
earthworm gen 3sg. poss -extremity dem 3sg. poss -mouth erg ipfv - caus -take[III] lnk \\
`[The earthworm's head] extremity, [the crow] takes it with its beak.' (140511 qajdo)
0003955#S11
exe

In the case of causative verbs from semi-transitive verbs (§ sec:semi.transitive.causative ), such as sɤrmigive a name (from rmibe called, § sec:sig.caus.irregular.other ), the direct object (the person to whom a name is given) is always located before the semi-object (the name given), as in ( ex:ndZitCW.tosArminW ).

exe

tɕe ndʑi-tɕɯ nɯ ɲimawozɤr to-sɤrmi-nɯ \\
lnk 3du. poss -son dem anthr ifr -give.a.name- pl \\
`They called their son Nyima 'Odzer.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe
summary: Causative verbs derived from plain intransitive verbs pattern like monotransitive verbs, whereas those derived from transitive or semi-transitive verbs are ditransitive. In causatives from transitive verbs, the causee has an intermediate status between subject and object: it may be ergative-marked, but is indexed like an object in certain person combinations, and it normally precedes the object even when functioning as an instrument. For causatives from semi-transitive verbs, the direct object always comes before the semi-object.

text:
verb!indirective ditransitive verb
Dative arguments (§ sec:dative ) of indirective verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) follow the transitive subject as in ( ex:kW.WCki.object ). For reason of place, the theme (the reported speech clause) is not reproduced here and simply indicated by (...), but corresponds to example ( ex:pWtWnWGenW.nWtCu in § sec:aor.temporal ).

exe

iɕqʰa nɯnɯ tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ [ɯ-mu nɯ ɯ-ɕki] (...) to-ti. \\
the.aforementioned dem indef. poss -son dem erg 3sg. poss -mother dem 3sg. poss - dat ifr -say \\
`The boy said to his mother (...).' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

Dative phrases can be located either after the theme or before it, as shown by examples ( ex:tAtsxu.WCki ) and ( ex:WCki.tAtsxu ) redundantly describing the same action in the same story.

exe

xlist

<alading> nɯ kɯ, nɤkinɯ, iɕqʰa tɤtʂu nɯ [ɯ-mu ɯ-ɕki] ɲɤ-kʰo tɕe, \\
anthr dem erg filler the.aforementioned lamp dem 3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss - dat ifr -give lnk \\
`Aladin gave the lamp to his mother.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S159

[ɯ-mu ɯ-ɕki] tɤtʂu nɯ ɲɤ-kʰo. \\
3sg. poss -mother 3sg. poss - dat lamp dem ifr -give \\
`He gave his mother the lamp.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S161
xlist
exe

The first pattern (object-dative) is rarer than the second one, but attested for all indirective verbs, including verbs of speech, as in ( ex:O.ndZiphe ), where the reported speech clause occurs before the dative phrase (compare with ex:kW.WCki.object above, the more common pattern).

exe

[nɯ-kɯ-lɤɣ lu-ɕe-a ɯ-ɲɯ́-pe a-tɤ-tɯ-ti ra] kɯ-wxti ni ndʑi-pʰe ti ɲɯ-ŋu\\
2du. poss - sbj: pcp -herd ipfv: upstream -go- 1sg qu - sens -be.good irr - pfv -2-say be.needed: fact sbj: pcp -be.big du 3du - dat say: fact sens -be\\
`He told the two elder [sisters] `Ask [your parents] whether it would be appropriate for me to go herding [cattle] for you'.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

Most oblique arguments also follow the subject and precede the object. It is the case of the goal argument marked by the relator ɯ-taʁ (§ sec:WtaR ) in ( ex:kW.WtaR.object ).

exe

kɯ-ɣɤrʁaʁ kɯ [pri ɯ-taʁ] tɯdi to-lɤt \\
sbj: pcp -hunt erg bear 3sg. poss -on arrow ifr -release \\
`The hunter shot an arrow at the bear.' (elicited)
exe
summary: Indirective ditransitive verbs take dative arguments after the transitive subject, and the dative phrase can appear either after the theme or before it. The first order, object-dative, is rarer than the second but is attested with all indirective verbs, including verbs of speech. Most oblique arguments similarly follow the subject and precede the object, as with goal arguments marked by the relator ɯ-taʁ.

text:
argument!overt
Sentences with two or three overt arguments such as those discussed in § sec:basic.word.order are a minority in Japhug. Most clauses comprise a verb with only one, or even without any overt arguments.
summary: In Japhug, sentences with two or three overt arguments are relatively rare. Most clauses contain a verb with only one overt argument, and many have no overt arguments at all.

text:
argument!core
Non-overt core arguments, including subjects and objects, are always definite, and anaphorically refer to a previously mentioned entity. For instance, example ( ex:tandza ) with a bare verb necessarily means `S/he/it ate it', and cannot be interpreted as `S/he/it ate/had a meal' with indefinite object or as `someone ate it' with indefinite subject.

exe

ta-ndza \\
aor:3 -eat \\
`S/he/it ate it.' (elicited)
exe

To express indefinite core arguments, non-overtness is an option only in the case of labile verbs (§ sec:labile.tr-intr ), but requires the conversion of the verb to the intransitive conjugation. Only a handful of verbs are labile (§ sec:lability.morphosyntax, § sec:lability.categories ), and for the rest of the verbs either an indefinite pronoun (§ sec:indef.pro ) or a valency-decreasing derivation such as antipassive (§ sec:antipassive ), passive (§ sec:passive ) or proprietive (§ sec:proprietive ) must be used instead.

Semi-objects (§ sec:semi.object ), like objects, are interpreted as definite where non-overt, as shown by ( ex:mWjpABJAt ) with the semi-transitive verb βɟɤtobtain (§ sec:semi.transitive, § sec:antipassive.t ).

exe

tɕʰemɤpɯ nɯ kɯ ɲɤ́-wɣ-nɯsɯkʰo tɕe mɯ-pjɤ-βɟɤt. \\
girl dem erg ifr - inv -rob lnk neg - ifr -obtain \\
`The girl had robbed him$_i$ of it$_j$, he$_i$ had not obtained it$_j$.' (150829 taishan zhi zhu-zh)
0006350#S131
exe
summary:
Non-overt core arguments, including subjects and objects, are interpreted as definite and anaphoric to a previously mentioned referent. Thus a bare verb like *ta-ndza* can only mean “S/he/it ate it,” not an indefinite subject or object interpretation.

Indefinite core arguments can be omitted only with labile verbs, and then the verb must appear in the intransitive conjugation. For most other verbs, an indefinite pronoun or a valency-reducing derivation such as antipassive, passive, or proprietive is required; semi-objects are also definite when omitted.

text:
argument!oblique
Unlike core arguments, oblique arguments can be interpreted as indefinite when non-overt. For instance, when motion verbs like ɕego and ɣicome (§ sec:motion.verbs ), lack both an overt goal and a purposive clause (§ sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ), two different meanings are possible. First, a previously mentioned goal can be understood as implicit as in ( ex:qapri.tuCe ).

exe

qapri tu-ɕe ri mɯ́j-cʰa tɕe \\
snake ipfv: up -go also neg: sens -can lnk \\
`Snakes cannot go up (there in the chimney) either.' (22-kumpGatCW)
0003590#S61
exe

Second, there is a minority However, when the motion verb takes a supine purposive clause, the goal is very frequently non-overt and indefinite, as can be observed in the majority of the examples in § sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs. of cases when no definite goal can be semantically recoverable, as in ( ex:kuCe.nA.YWGi2 ) where the two verbs ku-ɕe and ɲɯ-ɣi indicate back and forth distributed motion, without any clear direction.

exe

ɯ-zda ɲɯ-ɕar ɲɯ-sɯsɤm tɕe tɕendɤre, ki kɯ-fse ku-ɕe nɤ ɲɯ-ɣi \\
3sg. poss -companion ipfv -search sens -think lnk lnk dem inf: stat -be.like ipfv: east -go add ipfv:west-come \\
[That ant] wants to search for its companion, and goes here and fro like that.' (conversation 140501-01)
exe

Likewise, when the oblique argument of indirective verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective, § sec:indirective.word.order ) is non-overt, it can be interpreted as either definite or indefinite.

For instance, the indirective collocation tɯdi+lɤt `shoot an arrow', which selects an oblique argument (goal) in ɯ-taʁ (§ sec:WtaR, see ex:kW.WtaR.object above in § sec:indirective.word.order ), lacks an overt oblique in ( ex:non.overt.WtaR.kolAt ). In this example, it is clear that the subject must have aimed before shooting, and therefore that a covert definite oblique is implied, as confirmed by the choice of a specific orientation `towards east' rather than the indefinite orientation preverb.

exe

nɯnɯ χpɯn nɯ kɯ tɯdi ci ko-lɤt tɕendɤre iɕqʰa, qapri nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rpaʁ ʑo to-xtsɯɣ \\
dem monk dem erg arrow indef ifr: east -release lnk filler snake dem gen 3sg. poss -shoulder emph ifr -hit \\
`The monk shot an arrow, and it hit the snake in the shoulder.' (150820 qaprANar)
0006246#S22
exe

By contrast, in ( ex:tWdi.jAlAtnW ), also without overt goal, the command is to shoot arrows without aiming, simply to see whose arrows will reach the farthest, as confirmed by the choice of the indefinite orientation preverb. The absence of relator nominal clause in ɯ-taʁ in this example is to be interpreted here as absence of goal.

exe

tɯdi jɤ-lɤt-nɯ \\
arrow imp -release- pl \\
`Shoot arrows!' (elicited, based on a story)
exe

In ( ex:non.overt.dat.toti ), the verb of speech tisay lacks an overt dative argument (§ sec:dative ), and it is obvious in this context not only that there is no definite addressee, but that there is no addressee at all, since ti here means `utter (a sound)'.

exe

ɯ-tɯ-mɯɕtaʁ ʑo pjɤ-ŋu ri, ɲɤ-nɤɕqa qʰe, ``ɯtɕʰɯtɕʰɯ" mɯ-to-ti \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.cold emph ifr. ipfv -be lnk ifr -endure lnk interj neg - ifr -say \\
`Although it was very cold, he (successfully) endured it, and did not say `How cold!'.' (07-deluge)
0003426#S72
exe

To force a definite goal/addressee interpretation, the presence of an overt relator noun with a 3sg prefix is necessary, as in ( ex:overt.oblique ).

exe

xlist

ɯ-taʁ tɯdi to-lɤt \\
3sg. poss -on arrow ifr -release \\
`S/he shot at it.' (elicited)

ɯ-ɕki (...) to-ti \\
3sg. poss - dat reported.speech ifr -say \\
`S/he told (...) to him/her.' (many examples)
xlist
exe

The difference between core vs. oblique arguments is therefore distinct from the parameter of indexibility (§ sec:intr.indexation, § sec:tr.indexation ): core arguments are those with obligatory definite interpretation when non-overt, including (transitive and intransitive) subjects, objects and semi-objects, while oblique arguments lack this property.
subject
summary: Unlike core arguments, non-overt oblique arguments can be interpreted as either indefinite or definite. In motion verbs and indirective verbs, a missing oblique may be recoverable as a specific goal/addressee in some contexts, but in others it has an indefinite or even absent interpretation, and an overt relator noun is needed to force a definite reading. The passage concludes that the core/oblique distinction is separate from indexability: core arguments are obligatorily definite when omitted, whereas obliques are not.

text:
focalization
Focalized noun phrases are always overt, if limited to a demonstrative pronoun. They can be formally indistinguishable from non-focalized ones even by intonation, as the demonstrative nɯ in the last clause of example ( ex:nW.mAnWXtCWG ).

exe

mtʰɯmɤr ɣɯ ɯ-zbroŋ nɯnɯ, tu-nɯ-ɬoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu. tu-mɤmbɯr kɯ-fse ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe nɯ mɤ-naχtɕɯɣ. \\
seal gen 3sg. poss -pattern dem ipfv: up - auto -come.out sens -be ipfv -be.protuberant sbj: pcp -be.like sens -be lnk dem neg -be.the.same: fact \\
`The patterns on the seals (called mtʰɯmɤr ) are coming out, protuberant, that is how they differ [from the other types of seals].' (160706 thotsi)
0006133#S64
exe

Focalized first or second person referents require an overt pronoun to surface, as in ( ex:aZo.asni.mWjYaR ).

exe

nɤʑo nɤ-sni ɲɯ-ɲaʁ ma aʑo a-sni mɯ́j-ɲaʁ tɕe, ɬɤndʐi wuma nɯ nɤʑo ɲɯ-tɯ-ŋu ma aʑo ɬɤndʐi ɲɯ-maʁ-a \\
2sg 2sg. poss -heart sens -be.black lnk 1sg 1sg. poss -heart neg: sens -be.black lnk demon real dem 2sg sens -2-be lnk 1sg demon sens -not.be- 1sg \\
`You are evil, not me, you are the real demon, not me.' (2002 lhandzi)
exe

There is no dearth of strategies to explicitly indicate focus, including focus particles (§ sec:focus ), pseudo-clefts (§ sec:pseudo.cleft ) and postverbal copulas (§ sec:focalization.final.copula ).
summary: Focalized noun phrases are always overt, though they may be limited to demonstrative pronouns, and they can be formally indistinguishable from non-focalized noun phrases, even in intonation. When first- or second-person referents are focalized, an overt pronoun must appear. The language also has several explicit focus-marking strategies, including focus particles, pseudo-clefts, and postverbal copulas.

text:
right dislocation afterthought
While word order is rigid in Japhug, and the verb is normally located after all arguments and adjuncts (§ sec:basic.word.order ), left and right dislocation is attested, though accompanied with a specific intonation.
summary: Japhug normally has rigid word order, with the verb occurring after all arguments and adjuncts. However, both left and right dislocation are attested, and these constructions are marked by a specific intonation.

text:
All arguments and adjuncts can be right dislocated, including transitive subjects with ergative marking ( ex:A.right.disloc ), possessor with genitive (§ ex:possessor.right.disloc ), locative and time adjuncts (§ ex:time.adj.right.disloc ).

exe

sla tu-ngo ŋu tu-ti-nɯ ŋu, kɯrɯ ra kɯ. \\
moon ipfv -be.sick be: fact ipfv -say- pl be: fact Tibetan pl erg \\
`They say that moon is getting sick, the Tibetans.' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S135
exe

exe

nɯ ma ɯ-mɯntoʁ kɤ-mto maŋe, tɯrgi ɣɯ. \\
dem apart.from 3sg. poss -flower inf -see not.exist: sens fir gen \\
`Apart from that it has no flowers, the fir.' (08-tWrgi) 0003464#S68
0003464#S68
exe

Sentential adverbs (§ sec:sentential.adverbs ) also undergo dislocation, as shown by ( ex:time.adj.right.disloc ) and ( ex:adv.right.disloc ).

exe

paχɕi ndɤre pjɤ-tu, kɯɕɯŋgɯ \\
apples advers ifr. ipfv -exist former.times \\
`(Unlike other fruits,) apples did exist (in our area), in former times.' (07-paXCi)
0003430#S3
exe

exe

ɕlaʁ ʑo ɲɤ-me, li. \\
idph (I):immediately emph ifr -not.exist again \\
`She suddenly disappeared, again.' (150907 niexiaoqian-zh)
0006262#S108
exe

Subordinate clauses can also be right-dislocated, for instance infinite complement clauses (example ex:tutWste.kAsAfstWn, § sec:complement.morphosyntax ), supine participial clauses ( ex:purposive.right.disloc ) (§ sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ) or concessive conditionals ( ex:concessive.cond.right.disloc ) (§ sec:scalar.concessive.conditional ).

exe

tɕɯχtsi kɤ-ari-j, kɯ-nɤmɲo \\
Cogtse aor: east -go[II]- 1sg sbj: pcp -watch \\
`We went to Cogtse, to do some sightseeing.' (conversation)
exe

exe

tu-mbri ɯ-kʰɯkʰa ɯ-ʁar nɯ ki ntsɯ tu-ste ɲɯ-ŋu, lɤ-zo kɯnɤ. \\
ipfv -make.noise 3sg. poss -while 3sg. poss -wing dem dem. prox always ipfv -do.like[III] sens -be aor -land also \\
`It does this with its wings when it sings, even when it lands.' (23-RmWrcWftsa)
0003610#S106
exe

In ( ex:cause.right.disloc ), the consequence clause ʁmɯrtsɯ nɯ sɤre `The Berchemia yunnanensis is funny' is right-dislocated together with the linker ma (here meaning `because'), while the causal clause (§ sec:causal.clauses ) serves as the main clause. This example provides evidence that the linker ma can form a syntactic constituent with the preceding clause, even though it is most often prosodically linked to the causal clause following it.

exe

ɣɯjpa kɯ-fse nɯre ri tɕe ɯ-mɯntoʁ ɲɯ-lɤt, fsaqʰe tɕe tɕe ɯ-mat ɲɯ-βze ŋu, ʁmɯrtsɯ nɯ sɤre ma. \\
this.year sbj: pcp -be.like dem: loc loc lnk 3sg. poss -flower ipfv -release next.year loc lnk 3sg. poss -fruit ipfv -grow[III] be: fact Berchemia.yunnanensis dem be.funny: fact lnk \\
`The Berchemia yunnanensis is funny because it blooms this year, but its fruits grow the next year.' (11-qarGW)
0003480#S50
exe

The presence of a right dislocated constituent does not preclude an overt constituent with the same syntactic function in the main clause: for instance, in ( ex:A.in.situ.right.disloc ) the ergative phrase tɤ-wa nɯ kɯ `the father' and the right-dislocated constituent ɯ-nmaʁ nɯ kɯ `her husband' refer to the same person, transitive subject of the sentence.

exe

ɯʑo srɯnmɯ kɯ-ŋu nɯ tɤ-wa nɯ kɯ mɯ-pjɤ-sɯχsɤl, ɯ-nmaʁ nɯ kɯ. \\
3sg râkshasî sbj: pcp -be dem inf -father dem erg neg - ifr -realize 3sg. poss -husband dem erg \\
`The father$_i$ did not realize that she$_j$ was a râkshasî, her$_j$ husband$_i$.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S57
exe
summary: The passage states that many kinds of constituents can be right-dislocated, including transitive subjects with ergative marking, possessors, locative and time adjuncts, sentential adverbs, and even subordinate clauses such as infinitive complements, supine participial clauses, and concessive conditionals. It also notes that in causal constructions the consequence clause can be right-dislocated with the linker *ma*, showing that *ma* forms a syntactic constituent with the preceding clause. Finally, a right-dislocated constituent may cooccur with an overt constituent in the main clause that has the same syntactic role.

text:
Right dislocation in Japhug has three main functions, similar to those identified by in the Geshiza language.

The main function of right dislocation is that of afterthought, used to identify a referent that has no been mentioned previously ( ex:A.right.disloc ), provide additional side comments ( ex:adv.right.disloc, ex:cause.right.disloc ), complementary information ( ex:time.adj.right.disloc ) or even redundant information that can contribute to identify a referent ( ex:A.in.situ.right.disloc ).

Right dislocation is also used to reactivate a constituent in discourse, to avoid ambiguity with other referents. In ( ex:YWrko.Wkha ) for instance, the referent ɯ-kʰa `its house/shell' is found more than twenty clauses after its previous occurrence.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ ɲɯ-rko, ɯ-kʰa nɯ. \\
lnk dem sens -be.hard 3sg. poss -house dem \\
`It is hard, its house (i.e. the shell of the snail).' (26-tWcipaR)
0003694#S68
exe

Finally, right dislocation can serve to mark emphasis on a topical referent. In ( ex:WmAlAjaR2 ) for instance, the noun ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ is both left- and right-dislocated, showing that this instance is neither an afterthought nor a constituent reactivation.

exe

ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ nɯ, nɯnɯ, kɯrcɤ-ldʑa jamar ɣɤʑu rca, ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ nɯ. \\
3sg. poss -limb dem dem eight-piece about exist: sens unexp: deg 3sg. poss -limb dem \\
`Its limbs, it has eight ones, its limbs.' (26-mYaRmtsaR)
exe

In some cases, the exact function of right dislocation is ambiguous. In ( ex:purposive.right.disloc ) for instance, the purposive phrase could be emphasized by dislocation, but alternatively it is also possible to interpret it as an afterthought.
summary: Right dislocation in Japhug has three main functions: it can serve as an afterthought to introduce new or additional information, reactivate a previously mentioned constituent and avoid ambiguity, or mark emphasis on a topical referent. In some cases, its precise function is ambiguous because a right-dislocated phrase may be interpreted either as emphasis or as afterthought.

text: This section describes non-derived sentential adverbs, excluding those derived from nouns (§ sec:denominal.adverb ), lexicalized converbs (§ sec:converbs ) ideophones (§ sec:idph ), but including adverbs with non-synchronically transparent etymology and loanwords from Tibetan.
summary: The section treats non-derived sentential adverbs, while excluding denominal adverbs, lexicalized converbs, and ideophones. It does include adverbs whose etymology is not synchronically transparent, as well as loanwords from Tibetan.

text:
adverb!tense tense!adverb
Absolute tense is mainly expressed by time ordinals (§ sec:time.ordinals ) and other time adverbials derived from nouns (§ sec:time.adv ). There are in addition a few aspectual adverbs that are not transparently derived from nouns.

The adverb pɤjkʰu has a permansive meaning `still' when used with a positive verb form ( ex:pAjkhu.pjWnge.cha ).

exe

iʑo a-mu nɯ tʰamtʰam kɯrcɤsqaptɯɣ tʰɯ-azɣɯt ŋu. pɤjkʰu ji-paʁ pjɯ-nge cʰa. \\
1pl 1sg. poss -mother dem now eighty.one aor -arrive be: fact still 1pl. poss -pig ipfv -feed[III] can: fact \\
`Our mother is now eighty-one years old, she can still feed our pigs.' (2010, 9.2)
exe

Contrary to what could have been expected, pɤjkʰustill is only rarely used with a verb prefixed with the Autive in permansive function (§ sec:autoben.permansive ). Examples like ( ex:pAjkhu.pjAnnWZWB ) with redundant marking of permansive aspect are attested but uncommon.

exe

mtsʰoʁlaŋ nɯnɯ pɤjkʰu maka ʑo pjɤ-n-nɯʑɯβ ɕti ma \\
water.monster dem still completely emph ipfv. ifr - auto -sleep be. aff: fact lnk \\
`The aquatic monster was still asleep.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S184
exe

With a negative predicate, pɤjkʰu means `not...yet', as shown by ( ex:pAjkhu.mWpWtsua ) and ( ex:pAjkhu.mWnaCar ).

exe

aʑo pɤjkʰu tɯ-sla mɯ-pɯ-tsu-a \\
1sg still one-month neg - pst. ipfv -pass- 1sg \\
`It has not yet been a month since I have [come here].' (2003 tWxtsa)
exe

exe

ma ɯ-me kɯnɤ ɣnɤsqamnɯz-pɤrme tʰɯ-azɣɯt, tɕe nɯnɯ pɤjkʰu ɯ-χti ra mɯ-na-ɕar ma \\
lnk 3sg. poss -daughter also twenty.eight-years.old aor -arrive lnk dem yet 3sg. poss -companion pl neg - aor:3 -search lnk \\
`His daughter is twenty-two years old, but she does not yet have a companion (husband).' (14-siblings)
0003508#S284
exe

This adverb is generally located before the object (examples ex:pAjkhu.pjWnge.cha, ex:pAjkhu.mWnaCar ) but after the intransitive subject ( ex:pAjkhu.pjAnnWZWB, ex:pAjkhu.mWpWtsua ). It can also occur without a main verb, in combination with with the sentence final particle je (§ sec:fsp.imp ) as pɤjkʰu je `wait', hence the interjection pɤkʰijewait (§ sec:interjections ) with irregular fusion.

The reduplicated forms ʑɯrɯʑɤriprogressively and the rarer ʑɤrʑɯr, It is possible that these forms are borrowed from ཞོར་ʑorincidentally, though the semantics is unclear. are frequent with gradable stative verbs to express a progressive change of state as in ( ex:ZWrWZAri.ChWGWrni ), sometimes with incremental initial reduplication of the verb (§ sec:redp.gradual.increase ).

exe

ʑɯrɯʑɤri tɕe tɕe cʰɯ-ɣɯrni ŋu. \\
progressively lnk lnk ipfv -be.red be: fact \\
`It progressively becomes red.' (11-qarGW)
0003480#S55
exe

They are also found with dynamic verbs, in particular with temporal clauses in ɯ-jɯjaalong with (§ sec:simultaneity ) as in ( ex:ZWrWZAri.YWmbinW ).

exe

tɕe tʰɯ-wxti ɯ-jɯja nɤ, (...) kɯ-wxti ra kɯ nɯ-kɤ-ndza, tɕʰi tu-ndza-nɯ kɯ-ŋu nɯ ʑɯrɯʑɤri tɕe ɲɯ-mbi-nɯ. \\
lnk aor -be.big 3sg. poss -along add sbj: pcp -be.big pl erg 3pl. poss - obj: pcp -eat what ipfv -eat- pl sbj: pcp -be dem progressively lnk ipfv -give- pl \\
`As the child$_j$ grows older, the adults$_i$ progressively give [him/her]$_j$ their$_i$ food, whatever it is they$_i$ eat.' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR)
exe

The highly polyfunctional ci, whose functions range from the numeral `one' (§ sec:one.to.ten ) to various indefinite, partitive or non-identity markers (§ sec:ci.someone, § sec:other.pro, § sec:partitive.pronouns, § sec:indef.article, § sec:identity.modifier ), is used as an aspectual adverb `once' as in ( ex:qhihihi.ci ) (see also for instance ex:kWm.ci.thapa, § sec:pa.lv ). Semelfactive meaning is however more often expressed with a sentential counted noun (§ sec:CN.iterative ) with the `one' prefix (for instance tɯ-ɣjɤnone time). The attenuative adverb ci presumably derives from this meaning (§ sec:intensifier.adverbs ). Chinese 一下 yīxiàone time, a little has a similar range of meanings.

exe

``qʰihihi" ci ta-tɯt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
interj once aor:3 -say[II] sens -be \\
`He said qʰihihi.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S162
exe

Its reduplicated form ci ci has the meaning `sometimes, in some cases', often repeated in two or more clauses in parataxis `sometimes $X$, sometimes $Y$' as in ( ex:cici.pjWnWmtsWr ). See also ex:tAngo.thWmdW (§ sec:aor.main ) and ex:pjWsat.juGWt (§ sec:coordination ) for representative examples of this adverbial locution. In ( ex:cici.pjWnWmtsWr ), ci ci combines with the Autive prefix in spontaneous function (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ) to indicate the unpredictability of the alternative events.

exe

ɯ-me mɯ́j-nɯβdaʁ qʰe tɕendɤre ɯ-me nɯ, nɤkinɯ, ci ci pjɯ-nɯ-mtsɯr, ci ci pjɯ-nɯ-fka \\
3sg. poss -daughter neg: sens -take.care lnk lnk 3sg. poss -daughter dem filler one one ipfv - auto -be.hungry one one ipfv - auto -be.full \\
`He did not take care of his daughter, and his daughter would sometimes be hungry, sometimes have enough to eat.' (17-lhazgron)
exe

The adverb li means `again, like the previous time' as in ( ex:lici.tojGAt ). It can be optionally followed by the additive nɤ.

exe

tɕendɤre li to-jɣɤt tɕe, smɤnmimitoʁ kuɕana cʰo li pjɤ-rɯkʰɤcɤl-ndʑi. \\
lnk again ifr: up -turn.around lnk anthr anthr comit again ifr -discuss- du \\
`He returned again (up there), and had again a discussion with Smanmi Metog Koshana (as he had done previously).' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S183
exe

In combination with the adverbial ci, it can mean `one more, another one' as in ( ex:lici.pWfCAt ) (like Chinese 再 zàiagain). Alternatively however, ci in context can also be interpreted as an attenuative adverb (§ sec:intensifier.adverbs ).

exe

ama ɯ-tɯ-mpɕɤr nɯ! li ci pɯ-fɕɤt! \\
interj 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.beautiful sfp again once imp -tell \\
`Wow, what a beautiful [story]! Tell [me] another one.' (2005 tWJo)
0003368#S41
exe

The adverb ntsɯalways is used as a temporal universal quantifier `all the time' ( ex:ntsW.tuti ) or `every time' as in ( ex:Yikuku.ntsW.tuti ), a function from which it has become a distributive quantifier (§ sec:raNri ). It is one of the few adverbs that can be used postverbally (§ sec:postverbal.adv ).

exe

ɯ-skɤt mpɕɤr ma ``qusput qusput" ntsɯ tu-ti ŋu. \\
3sg. poss -voice be.beautiful: fact lnk onomatopoeia always ipfv -say sens -be \\
`[The cuckoo] has a beautiful song, it says qusput qusput all the time.' (24-qro)
0003626#S63
exe

exe
summary: Absolute tense is mainly expressed by time ordinals and other time adverbials derived from nouns, while a few non-nominal aspectual adverbs also occur. The passage describes several such adverbs: pɤjkʰu means “still” with positive predicates but “not yet” with negative ones; ʑɯrɯʑɤri and ʑɤrʑɯr express progressive change; ci can mean “once” and its reduplicated form ci ci means “sometimes”; li means “again”; and ntsɯ means “always” or “every time,” with some adverbs having restricted positional behavior in the clause.

text:
sɲikuku ʑo nɯ ntsɯ tu-ti ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
every.day emph dem always ipfv -say sens -be lnk \\
`[The bird comes] everyday and says this every time.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

In addition, ntsɯ can indicate a repeated action `again and again' as in ( ex:wojAr.ntsW.toti ), where the repetition is also marked by the additive nɤ (§ sec:additive.nA ).

exe

``wortɕʰi nɤ wojɤr, ma-tɤ-kɯ-ndza-a" ntsɯ to-ti ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
please add please neg - imp -2 1-eat- 1sg always ifr -say sens -be \\
`He said again and again `Please, don't eat me.'' (140427 bianfu yu huangshulang-zh)
0003838#S11
exe

Other temporal adverbs include ʁlɤwɯrsuddenly from Tibetan གློ་བུར་glo.bursudden, used with Aorist or Inferential verb forms to express an abrupt change of state ( ex:RlAwWr.Zo.tAmNAm ), toʁdea moment, which can also mean `suddenly' (example ex:qandZGi.pjAGi, § sec:ifr.evd ), and also `in a moment' referring to a future event ( ex:jAlAt.je, § sec:imp.function ) or `for a moment' ( ex:toRde.kunWnaa ), and iɕqʰajust now Its meaning is close to Chinese 刚才 gāngcáijust now, a moment ago. (on which see also § sec:iCqha ).

exe

maka pɯ-nɤʁaʁ-i, ʁlɤwɯr ʑo ɯ-xtu tɤ-mŋɤm tɕe pɯ-si ɕti \\
completely pst. ipfv -have.a.good.time- 1pl suddenly emph 3sg. poss -belly aor -hurt lnk aor -die be. aff: fact \\
`As we were having a party (in the mountain), his belly suddenly started to ache, and he died.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S318
exe

exe

kɯre ri toʁde ku-nɯna-a. \\
dem. prox: loc loc a.moment prs -rest- 1sg \\
`I am resting for a moment.' (conversation 2019-09-16)
exe
summary: The passage explains that **ntsɯ** marks repeated or habitual actions, meaning “always” or “again and again,” and can co-occur with the additive **nɤ** to emphasize repetition. It also introduces several temporal adverbs: **ʁlɤwɯr** ‘suddenly,’ used with Aorist or Inferential forms for abrupt changes of state; **toʁde** ‘a moment,’ which can mean ‘suddenly,’ ‘in a moment,’ or ‘for a moment’; and **iɕqa**, meaning ‘just now,’ similar to Chinese *gāngcái*.

text: This section presents adverbial quantifiers that are not temporal or aspectual markers, as those are treated in the previous section (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ).
summary: This section introduces adverbial quantifiers that do not function as temporal or aspectual markers. Those kinds of adverbs are discussed separately in the preceding section on tense and aspect.

text:
universal quantifier
The universal quantifiers kɤsɯfseall and lonbaall can have scope over a single noun phrase (§ sec:universal.quant ). When following an intransitive subject or object in preverbal position as in ( ex:XsWm.kAsWfse ), it is not clear whether the scope of the quantifier is on the preceding noun phrase or on the whole sentence.

exe

rgɤtpu rgɤnmɯ ni kɯ [kɯki tɤ-pɤtso χsɯm ki] kɤsɯfse ʑo cʰɤ-ɣɤ-wxti-ndʑi. \\
old.man old.woman du erg dem. prox indef. poss -child three dem. prox all emph ifr - caus -be.big- du \\
`The old man and the old woman raised all these three children.' (140514 huishuohua de niao-zh)
0003992#S58
exe

The postnominal mɯtɕʰimɯrɯzall kinds (§ sec:quantifiers.other ) appears in ( ex:rca.mWtChimWrWz ) stranded from the noun tɯ-ŋgaclothes by the unexpected degree marker rca (§ sec:unexpected ), suggesting that it could be analyzed here as a sentential adverb.

exe

tɯ-ŋga rca mɯtɕʰimɯrɯz cʰɯ́-wɣ-βzu kʰɯ \\
indef. poss -clothes unexp: deg all.kinds ipfv - inv -make be.possible: fact \\
`One can make all kinds of clothes (using it).' (05-qaZo)
0003404#S65
exe
summary: The passage notes that the universal quantifiers **kɤsɯfseall** and **lonbaall** can scope over a single noun phrase, though when they follow an intransitive subject or object in preverbal position it is unclear whether they modify that noun phrase or the whole sentence. It also suggests that **mɯtɕʰimɯrɯzall kinds** may function as a sentential adverb in one example, since it appears separated from the noun it modifies by an unexpected degree marker.

text:
The adverb aʁɤndɯndɤteverywhere can be used on its own, but also together with overt locative adjuncts (or goals); it can both precede ( ex:aRAndWndAt.Zo.loc ) or follow it ( ex:loc.aRAndWndAt.Zo, ex:aRAndWndAt.Zo.loc2 ).

exe

tɯ-ji ɯ-ŋgɯ aʁɤndɯndɤt ʑo tu-ɬoʁ ɕti. \\
indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -in everywhere emph ipfv -come.out be. aff: fact \\
`It grows everywhere in the fields.' (12-ndZiNgri)
0003488#S146
exe

Locative adjuncts used with aʁɤndɯndɤt often take the plural ra (§ sec:plural.determiners ) to mark approximate location as in ( ex:aRAndWndAt.Zo.loc ) and ( ex:aRAndWndAt.Zo.loc2 ).

exe

aʁɤndɯndɤt sɯŋgɯ ra kɯnɤ tu-ɬoʁ ɕti. \\
everywhere forest pl also ipfv -come.out be. aff: fact \\
`It also grows everywhere in the forest.' (14-sWNgWJu)
0003506#S159
exe

exe

aʁɤndɯndɤt ʑo kʰa ra cʰɯ-rɤpɯ. tɯ-ji ɯ-ngɯ ra cʰɯ-rɤpɯ \\
everywhere emph house pl ipfv -litter indef. poss -field 3sg -inside pl ipfv -litter \\
`[Mice] have litter everywhere in the house, in the fields.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S156
exe

There are a few examples where aʁɤndɯndɤt is followed by the locative postposition ri (§ sec:core.locative ) as ( ex:aRAndWndAt.ri ) like a locative noun phrase. However, no sentences with aʁɤndɯndɤteverywhere as core argument (like `everywhere is quiet') are found in the corpus, indicating that it would be clumsy to analyze it as a pronoun (§ sec:universal.pronouns ).

exe

nɯfse ʑo aʁɤndɯndɤt ri tu-nnɯ-ɬoʁ qʰe, ɯ-zrɤm nɯra kɯ-tu maŋe. \\
like.that emph everywhere loc ipfv - auto -come.out lnk 3sg. poss -root dem: pl sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: sens \\
`It grows simply like that everywhere, it has no roots.' (20-sWrna)
0003564#S68
exe

When aʁɤndɯndɤteverywhere occurs under the scope of negation, it never expresses the meaning `nowhere', as shown by ( ex:aRAndWndAt.me ) and ( ex:aRAndWndAt.juCenW ).

exe

stɤmku nɯra, tɯ-ci ɯ-rkɯ nɯra tu ma aʁɤndɯndɤt stʰɯci me \\
plain dem: pl indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -side dem: pl exist: fact lnk everywhere so.much not.exist: fact \\
`It is found in plains, or next to rivers, but it is not found everywhere.' (14-sWNgWJu)
0003506#S50
exe

exe

tɕe ɕɤr tɕe cʰɯ-nɯ-ɬoʁ-nɯ tɕe, aʁɤndɯndɤt ju-ɕe-nɯ mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ \\
lnk night lnk ipfv: downstream - auto -come.out- pl lnk everywhere ipfv -go- pl neg - sbj: pcp -be. possible \\
`[They make it] to prevent [animals] from coming out at night and going everywhere.' (150902 mkhoN)
0006300#S21
exe

The word ŋotɕuŋondɤteverywhere is semantically very close to aʁɤndɯndɤteverywhere but rarer; it may also be translated as `in all kinds of places'. It contains a partially reduplicated form of the interrogative pronoun ŋotɕuwhere (§ sec:NotCu ).

exe

ɕkrɤz ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕi ɲɯ-ɬoʁ, tɯrgi ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕi ɲɯ-ɬoʁ, ʑmbri ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕi ɲɯ-ɬoʁ, mbraj ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕi ɲɯ-ɬoʁ, tɕe sɤjku sɯŋgɯ nɯra tɕi ɲɯ-ɬoʁ, tɕe ŋotɕuŋondɤt ʑo ɣɤʑu ɕti ri, stɤmku me, sɯŋgɯ ʁɟa ʑo tu-ɬoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
oak 3sg. poss -inside also sens -come.out fir 3sg. poss -inside also sens -come.out willow 3sg. poss -inside also sens -come.out red.birch 3sg. poss -inside also sens -come.out lnk birch forest dem: pl also sens -come.out lnk everywhere emph exist: sens be: aff lnk plain whether forest completely emph ipfv -come.out sens -be \\
`[This mushroom] grows among oaks, among firs, among willows, among red or white birch forests, you find it everywhere, whether on plains or in forest.' (23-mbrAZim)
0003604#S224
exe
summary: The passage describes *aʁɤndɯndɤt* “everywhere” as an adverb that can occur alone or with overt locative adjuncts/goals, either before or after them, and these locative phrases often take the plural marker *ra* to indicate approximate location. It can also appear with the locative postposition *ri*, but there are no examples of it functioning as a core argument, so it should not be analyzed as a pronoun. Under negation it does not mean “nowhere,” and a rarer near-synonym *ŋotɕuŋondɤt* may mean “everywhere” or “in all kinds of places.”

text:
restrictive!adverb
The adverb ʁɟacompletely, which can be used to mark restrictive focus on a noun phrase (§ sec:restrictive.focus ), also occurs with scope over the whole sentence in the meaning `all, only, always' as in ( ex:kW.RJa.Zo ), where it follows the ergative kɯ (compare with ex:RJa.kW in § sec:restrictive.focus, where the ergative is located before ʁɟa ).

exe

tɯ-ŋga me, tɯ-xtsa me nɯ tɤ-tɕɯ ra kɯ ʁɟa ʑo cʰɯ-tʂɯβ-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu. \\
indef. poss -clothes whether indef. poss -shoe whether dem indef. poss -son pl erg completely emph ipfv -sew- pl ifr. ipfv -be \\
`Whether clothes or shoes, it was always the boys (not the ladies) who sewed them.' (12-kAtsxWb)
0003486#S99
exe

In copular sentences (§ sec:copula.basic ), when ʁɟa has scope over the nominal predicate, that nominal predicate can be preposed, as in ( ex:kW.RJa.Zo ) (see also example ex:WBrAsqlWm in § sec:WBrA.functions ). Example ex:CkrAz.RJa.Zo in § ex:attributive.prenominal is superficially similar, but the constituent [noun+ ʁɟa ʑo ] in that example is a prenominal modifier of the following noun, while in ( ex:tAtCW.RJa.Zo ) tɤ-tɕɯ ʁɟa ʑo cannot be a prenominal modifier of kɯ-rɤ-tʂɯβ `tailor', otherwise the existential verb pjɤ-tu rather than the copula pjɤ-ɕti would be expected.

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe [tɤ-tɕɯ ʁɟa ʑo] kɯ-rɤ-tʂɯβ pjɤ-ɕti ma tɕʰeme kɯ-rɤ-tʂɯβ pjɤ-me. \\
in.former.times lnk indef. poss -son completely emph sbj: pcp - apass -sew ifr. ipfv -be. aff lnk girl sbj: pcp - apass -sew ifr. ipfv -not.exist \\
`In former times, only boys were tailors (all tailors were boys), there were no women tailors.' (12-kAtsxWb)
0003486#S95
exe
summary: The adverb ʁɟa ‘completely’ can mark restrictive focus on a noun phrase, but it also has sentence-wide scope with meanings like ‘all, only, always.’ In copular sentences, when ʁɟa scopes over the nominal predicate, that predicate may be preposed; however, some similar-looking sequences are actually prenominal modifiers, not instances of this construction.

text:
restrictive!adverb
To express the meaning `alone', two constructions based on the root -sti `alone' are used.

The root -sti can be directly combined with personal pronouns in forms such as aʑo-sti with the 1sg aʑo 1sg or ɯʑo-sti with the 3sg ɯʑohe (§ sec:pronouns.possessive.markers ) as in ( ex:aZosti ).

exe

nɤ-rca tu-ɣi-a ra ma kutɕu aʑo-sti ku-rɤʑi-a mɯ́j-cʰa-a \\
1sg. poss -together ipfv: up -come- 1sg be.needed: fact lnk here 1sg -alone ipfv -stay- 1sg neg: sens -can- 1sg \\
`I am coming with you, I cannot stay here all alone.' (2-deluge2012)
0003376#S74
exe

Alternatively, the reduplicated form of the root stɯstialone occurs either on its own as in ( ex:stWsti ), or as a postnominal modifier as in ( ex:stWsti2 ).

exe

aʑo stɯsti ŋu-a \\
1sg alone be: fact - 1sg \\
`I am alone.' (conversation)
exe

exe

fsapaʁ kɤ-χsu mɯ́j-mbat ma maka aki prɤku rgali stɯsti kɯ ʑo, ji-tɯβɣi lonba ʑo, nɯ kɯ kɯ-jndʐɤz ʑo tʰa-ɕkɯt qʰe \\
cattle inf -raise neg: sens -easy lnk completely down anthr milk.cow alone erg emph 1pl. poss -chaff all emph dem total sbj: pcp -be.coarse emph aor:3 -eat.completely lnk \\
`Raising cattle is difficult, down there in Praku, the milk cow alone ate all our chaff, all the big ones.' (taRrdo2003)
exe

In a text translated from Chinese, we do find a calque of the Chinese construction ( 我一个人 wǒ yīgèrénI alone) with the pronoun aʑo 1sg followed by the counted noun tɯ-rdoʁone piece (§ sec:CN.restrictive ); this sentence is not idiomatic.

exe

aʑo tɯ-rdoʁ kɯ ntsɯ tɯ-ci ɕ-tu-re-a \\
1sg one-piece erg always indef. poss -water tral - ipfv: up -fetch[III]- 1sg \\
`It is always I alone who goes to fetch water.' (150830 san ge heshang)
0006416#S44
exe
summary:
The meaning ‘alone’ is expressed with two constructions based on the root -sti. This root may combine directly with personal pronouns (e.g., aʑo-sti ‘I alone’) or appear in the reduplicated form stɯsti, either standing alone or modifying a noun phrase.  

The passage also notes an idiomaticity issue: a calque from Chinese using a pronoun plus the counted noun tɯ-rdoʁ ‘one piece’ occurs, but this construction is said to be not idiomatic.

text:
identity!adverb
The adverb anamanaidentical is borrowed from the Amdo Tibetan form ཨ་ན་མ་ན་ʔa.na.ma.naidentical. It occur with the copula ŋu (§ sec:copula.basic ) as in ( ex:anamana.Zo ). It is similar in meaning to the reduplicated participle kɯ-naχtɕɯ χtɕɯɣ `completely identical' of naχtɕɯɣbe the same (§ sec:identity.modifier ) but does not occur as noun modifier.

exe

ɯ-βri rcanɯ, qaɕpa ɯ-βri nɯ anamana ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -body unexp: deg frog 3sg. poss -body dem identical emph sens -be \\
`The body of the [turtle] is identical to the body of a frog.'(140510 wugui)
0003951#S8
exe
summary: The adverb **anamana** ‘identical’ is borrowed from Amdo Tibetan and occurs with the copula **ŋu**. It is similar in meaning to the reduplicated participle **kɯ-naχtɕɯ χtɕɯɣ** ‘completely identical,’ but unlike that form, **anamana** does not function as a noun modifier.

text:
Intensifiers used to express high degree (`much') and quantity (`much, for a long time') are discussed in § sec:degree.adverbs. Negative intensifiers are discussed in § sec:negative.adverbs.

The attenuative ci is derived from the adverbial function `once' (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ) of the numeral `one' (§ sec:one.to.ten ). It conveys a milder and more polite tone to Imperative (§ sec:imperative ) and Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis ) verb forms, in particular with modal verbs in interrogative form (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ) as in ( ex:ci.apWmtama.WjAG ).

exe

wortɕʰi ʑo, aʑo a-ʁi ci a-pɯ-mtam-a ɯ́-jɤɣ \\
please emph 1sg 1sg. poss -younger.sibling a.little irr - pfv -see[III]- 1sg qu -be.allowed: fact \\
`Could I see my younger sister, please?' (140511 1001 yinzi-zh)
exe

Due to the high polyfunctionality of ci, in examples such as ( ex:li.ci.tAti ), the attenuative function is not always clearly distinguishably from its semelfactive one.

exe

li ci tɤ-ti \\
again a.little.once imp -say \\
`Say it again!' (many attestations)
exe

The intensifier koŋla, whose first syllable originates from the reduction of the lexicalized participle kɯ-ŋu `the one that/who is (really)' ( tab:lexicalized.S.nmlz, § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ), The non-reduced form of koŋla, kɯŋula, corresponds to Tshobdun kəŋólɐ `well'. originally means `really', a meaning still attested in ( ex:koNla.jazGWta ). In this meaning it can also serve as prenominal modifier (§ ex:attributive.prenominal ).

exe

wo a-mu, aʑo koŋla jɤ-azɣɯt-a \\
interj 1sg. poss -mother 1sg really aor -arrive- 1sg \\
`Mother, it is really me who arrived (i.e. not someone else pretending to be me).' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S187
exe

The secondary meanings `(doing) well, correctly' ( ex:koNla.mWkArtoR ) and `completely' ( ex:koNla.mWjtsonW) developed out the etymological sense of `really'.

exe

ma koŋla mɯ-kɤ-rtoʁ-a ri, ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ nɯra ɲɯ-dɤn, \\
lnk really neg - aor -look- 1sg lnk 3sg. poss -limb dem: pl sens -be.many \\
`I did not have a good look at [how many limbs it has], but it has many limbs.' (21-mdzadi)
0003578#S8
exe

exe

kupa ɯ-skɤt ri ɯ-qiɯ jamar ma mɯ́j-tso-nɯ. (...) li nɯ koŋla mɯ́j-tso-nɯ. \\
Chinese 3sg. poss -language also 3sg. poss -half about apart.from neg: sens -understand- pl again dem completely neg: sens -understand- pl \\
`Chinese$_i$ also, they only understand half, (...), they don't understand it$_i$ completely/well (so one has to learn to speak their language to be able to communicate).' (150901 tshuBdWnskAt)
0006242#S13
exe

Finally, in some negative contexts, koŋla acquired a meaning close to maka `(not)... at all', as in ( ex:jiatong.koNla.pWme ).

exe

tɕe kɤ-ɤmɯ-tɯɣ ri pɯ-me ma <jiaotong> koŋla pɯ-me tɕe (...) kɤ-ŋke ʁɟa ʑo ju-kɯ-ɕe pɯ-ra. \\
lnk inf - recip -meet also pst. ipfv -not.exist lnk completely transportation pst. ipfv -not.exist lnk inf -walk completely emph ipfv - genr:S/O-go pst. ipfv -be.needed \\
`We had no opportunity to meet, as there were no transportation means at all, (...) and we had no choice but to go on foot (whenever there was a meeting).' (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S19
exe
summary:
The passage first notes that intensifiers for high degree and quantity, as well as negative intensifiers, are treated elsewhere. It then explains that the attenuative **ci**, derived from the numeral *one* meaning “once,” softens Imperative and Irrealis forms and adds a milder, more polite tone, though its attenuative meaning is sometimes hard to separate from its semelfactive use.

The intensifier **koŋla** originally meant “really” and can also function as a prenominal modifier. From this meaning, it developed secondary senses such as “well/correctly” and “completely,” and in some negative contexts it came to mean something close to “not at all.”

text:
The adverbs cʰɤlɤnnɤmaybe and ʑgrɯɣcertainly can contribute to the expression of epistemic modality, together with verbal morphology (§ sec:TAME.modal, § sec:second.modal ) and sentence final particles (§ sec:sfp ).

The former cʰɤlɤnnɤmaybe, `perhaps' originates from an Inferential form of the verb lɤtrelease, followed by the additive nɤ, perhaps originally the protasis of a conditional construction (§ sec:real.conditional ). It is often combined with the sentence final particle tʰaŋ (§ sec:fsp.epistemic ) as in ( ex:chAlAnnA.GWlAti ), or with a verb in Probabilitative form (§ sec:WmA ).

exe

iʑora nɤki, cʰɤlɤnnɤ ɣɯ-znɯzdɯxpa-j tɕe ɣɯ-lɤt-i tʰaŋ wo \\
1pl filler maybe inv -have.mercy: fact - 1pl lnk inv -release: fact - 1pl sfp sfp \\
`Maybe [the ogre] will have mercy upon us and will let us go.' (160703 poucet3)
0006107#S38
exe

The latter ʑgrɯɣcertainly generally occurs with a main verb in the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ). It tends to be replaced by the Chinese adverb 肯定 kěndìngcertainly, even by the best speakers.

exe

nɤ-wi nɯ ʑgrɯɣ ʑo rga \\
2sg. poss -grand.mother dem certainly emph like: fact \\
`Your grandmother will certainly like it.' (140428 xiaohongmao-zh)
0003884#S50
exe
summary: The adverbs **cʰɤlɤnnɤ** ‘maybe’ and **ʑgrɯɣ** ‘certainly’ can express epistemic modality alongside verbal morphology and sentence-final particles. **cʰɤlɤnnɤ** is historically derived from an inferential form of *lɤ* ‘release’ plus additive **nɤ**, and it often co-occurs with the epistemic particle **tʰaŋ** or with a verb in Probabilitative form; **ʑgrɯɣ** usually appears with a main verb in the Factual Non-Past and is often replaced by Chinese **kěndìng** ‘certainly’ even among fluent speakers.

text:
orientation!adverb adverb!orientation
The tridimensional system found in orientation preverbs (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), egressive postpositions (§ sec:egressive, tab:egressive ) and locative relator nouns (§ sec:relator.nouns.3d ) is also reflect by locative adverbs ( tab:orientation.adverbs ). There is a one-to-one correspondence between these adverbs and the corresponds nouns and preverbs (§ sec:preverbs.adverbs ).

There are four series of adverbs shown in tab:orientation.adverbs. With the exception of the adverbs of the vertical dimension ( upwards and downwards ), the other series are trivially derived from the bare adverbs by prefixation of a, tɕe- (perhaps related to the postposition tɕe § sec:tCe.postposition ) and -cʰu (§ sec:approximate.locative ).

The bare adverbs are most often directly placed before an orientable verb (§ sec:orientable.verbs ) bearing a preverb encoding the same orientation, as in ( ex:thi.chWGi ) and ( ex:tCAlo.WndAcu ). The adverb kɯ, though homophonous with the ergative in isolation (§ sec:erg.kW ), is often pronounced ku as in the recording of ( ex:tCAlo.WndAcu ), due to regressive assimilation from the preverb ko-.

exe

tɤ-mpja tɕe tʰi cʰɯ-ɣi, tɤ-ɣɤndʐo tɕe lo lu-ɕe \\
aor -be.warm lnk downstream ipfv: downstream -come aor -be.cold lnk upstream ipfv: upstream -come \\
`(Contrary to expectations), when [the weather] becomes warm it comes downstream, and when it becomes cold it goes upstream.' (24-kWmu)
0003618#S25
exe

This is not the exclusive function of bare orientation adverbs however: they can also refer to a static location unrelated to the orientation of the verb, and non-adjacent to it ( ex:kW.ri.ndi.ri ). However, the basic and distal adverb are more often used in this function.

exe

kɯ ri ci (...) pjɯ-sɯ-ɤtsa-nɯ, ndi ri li ci pjɯ-sɯ-ɤtsa-nɯ \\
east loc one ipfv: down - caus -be.planted- pl
west loc again one ipfv: down - caus -be.planted- pl \\
`(In former times, when people installed the loom), [they] would plant one [sharpened peg] in the east (i.e. left), another one in the west (i.e. right) (to attach the upward extremity of the warp threads).' (vid-20140429090403)
0003776#S119
exe

All four series of orientation adverbs can be followed by the core locative postpositions (§ sec:core.locative ) as in ( ex:kW.ri.ndi.ri ), ( ex:akW.ri.kuru ) and ( ex:tCAlo.WndAcu ).

exe

qaliaʁ nɯtɕu lu-zo tɕe akɯ ri ku-ru, andi ri ɲɯ-ru \\
eagle dem: loc ipfv -land lnk east loc ipfv: east -look west loc ipfv: west -look \\
`Eagles land there and look around (to the east and the west, looking for food).' (140522 Kamnyu zgo)
0004059#S214
exe

Example ( ex:tCAlo.WndAcu ) shows that distal orientation adverbs can occur in the same context as locative relator nouns in -cu (§ sec:relator.nouns.3d ).

exe

ɯ-ndɤcu nɯtɕu, dɯxpakɤrpu ɣɯ ɯ-me nɯ kɯ kʰri pjɤ-ta tɕe kɯ ko-ru.
tɕe tɕelo nɯtɕu ɲimawozɤr ɣɯ ɯ-kʰri nɯ pjɤ-ta-nɯ tɕe, tʰi cʰo-ru-nɯ tɕe \\
3sg. poss -west dem: loc anthr gen 3sg. poss -daughter dem erg seat ifr: down -put lnk east ifr: east -look lnk upstream dem: loc anthr gen 3sg. poss -seat dem ifr: down -put- pl lnk downstream ifr: downstream -look- pl lnk \\
`On the west side, the daughter of Gdugpa Dkarpo placed her seat and turned it towards the east. On the downstream side, [the servants] placed Nyima 'Odzer's seat, and turned it towards the upstream direction.' (2011-04-smanmi)
0004063#S352
exe

The bare adverbial stems can be compounded to build nouns of dimension (§ sec.v.v.compounds.degree )

In addition to the adverbs in tab:orientation.adverbs, we also find tɤtonuphill, upwards and tɤʑɯndownhill, downwards specifically indicating orientation upwards and downwards a slope. They can be associated with both the vertical ( upwards, downwards ) and the fluvial ( upstream, downstream ) orientations, as shown by ( ex:tAton.tAZWn ), where the motion verb ɕego and the manipulation verb tsɯmtake away take the fluvial orientation upstream with tɤton, but the vertical orientation downwards with tɤʑɯn.

exe

tɕe tɤton lu-ɕe pɯpɯŋunɤ, snama tɤton tsa lú-wɣ-tsɯm pɯ pɯ-ra nɤ ɯ-koŋtaʁ tu-sɯ-ɤsɯɣ-nɯ tɕe nɯ kɯ lu-rɤɕi ɲɯ-ra. tɤʑɯn pjɯ-ɕe pɯpɯŋunɤ, ɯ-sɲɤt cʰɯ-sɯ-ɤsɯɣ-nɯ ɲɯ-ra. \\
lnk uphill ipfv: upstream -go top beast.of.burden uphill a.little ipfv: upstream - inv -take.away cond pst. ipfv -be.needed add 3sg. poss -front.strap ipfv - caus -be.tight- pl lnk dem erg ipfv: upstream -pull sens -be.needed downhill ipfv: down -go top 3sg. poss -crupper ipfv: downstream - caus -be.tight- pl sens -be.needed \\
`When it$_i$ goes uphill, [that is] if they need to lead the beast$_i$ of burden on an upward slope, they need to tighten the front strap of the saddle for it$_i$ to pull [the burden]. When it$_i$ goes downhill, they need to tighten the crupper.' (30-tAsno)
0003758#S92
exe

Despite their -n coda (§ sec:historical.phono ), these adverbs are native words, as shown by their Tshobdun cognates tɐ́təm `uphill' and tɐ́ɟət `downhill'. The expected Japhug forms would be $ $ tɤtom and $ $ tɤʑɯt, respectively. The coda -n probably results from the coalescence of the inherited adverb with the demonstrative nɯ. These adverbs probably originate from nominalizations of elevational motion verbs, which are lost in Northern Gyalrong but attested in Situ (for instance Bragbar tʰɐ̂ `move upwards' and
ɟə̂ `move downwards', respectively, see and ).
summary:
The passage explains that locative adverbs in Kamnyu reflect the same three-dimensional orientation system as preverbs, egressive postpositions, and locative relator nouns, with a one-to-one correspondence between the forms. Most of the adverbs are derived by prefixing a-, tɕe-, or -cʰu to bare stems, and they typically occur before an orientable verb with matching orientation, though they can also mark a static location and take core locative postpositions.

It also notes two special adverbs, tɤton ‘uphill, upwards’ and tɤʑɯn ‘downhill, downwards,’ which can express either vertical or fluvial orientation depending on context. These forms are native words with -n likely from coalescence with a demonstrative, and they may historically come from nominalized elevational motion verbs.

text:
postverbal position adverb!postverbal
The only part of speech that is always located after the main verb is the sentence final particles (§ sec:sfp, § sec:non.verb.TAME ). With the exception of right dislocated constituents (§ sec:right.dislocation ), only a handful of other words can occur post-verbally.

Some ideophones (mainly pattern II, § sec:ideophone.plus.lexical.verb ) can be put after the verb, optionally with the emphatic ʑo as in ( ex:V.prWNprWN.Zo ), even in some relative clauses (§ sec:relative.postverbal ).

exe

nɯre tu-rŋgɤβ-nɯ prɯŋprɯŋ ʑo \\
dem: loc ipfv -attach- pl idph (II):solidly emph \\
`They attach [the plough] there (on the hybrid yaks' horns) solidly.' (25-stuxsi)
0003660#S11
exe

Only three adverbs can occupy postverbal position. First, the emphatic marker ʑo (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ) commonly occurs after the main verb in constructions expressing high degree (§ sec:absolute.degree ), as in ( ex:WtWtCur.saXaR.Zo ).

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ tú-wɣ-ndza rca ɯ-tɯ-tɕur saχaʁ ʑo. \\
lnk dem ipfv - inv -eat unexp: deg 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.sour be.extremely: fact emph \\
`When one eats it, it is very sour.' (16-CWrNgo)
0003518#S219
exe

Second, the degree adverb tsaa little is postverbal when used in a comparative construction (§ sec:comparative.tsa ), as in ( ex:YWrYJi.tsa ).

exe

tɕʰitɕɯn paχɕi nɯ tɕe tɕe, ɯ-jwaʁ nɯra iʑora ji-paχɕi stʰɯci mɯ-ɲɯ-ɤrtɯm kɯ ɲɯ-rɲɟi tsa \\
topo apple dem lnk lnk 3sg. poss -leave dem: pl 1pl 1pl. poss -apple so.much neg - sens -be.round erg sens -be.long a.little \\
`Pears (Chuchen apples), their leaves are not as round as [those of] our apples, but a bit longer.' (07-paXCi)
0003430#S48
exe

Third, the temporal adverb and quantifier ntsɯalways has the same ranges of meaning as when in preverbal position (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ) when following the main verb: it can either indicate a constant state ( ex:anWrNi.ntsW ) or a recurrent action ( ex:postV.ntsW ).

exe

tɯxpalɤskɤr a<nɯ>rŋi ntsɯ. \\
whole.year < auto >be.green: fact always \\
`It remains always green the whole year.' (08-saCW)
0003462#S19
exe

exe

tɕʰeme ɯ-skɤt kɯ-snɯ sna ci kɯ ʑo tú-wɣ-nɯ-ɤkʰɤzŋga-nɯ ntsɯ. \\
girl 3sg. poss -voice sbj: pcp - emph be.nice indef erg emph ipfv - inv - appl -call- pl always \\
`A girl whose voice was very nice was calling them again and again.' (2003 kandZislama)
exe
summary:
The only part of speech that is always postverbal is the sentence-final particles, and apart from right-dislocated constituents, very few other words can appear after the main verb. These include some ideophones, usually pattern II, which may optionally take the emphatic marker ʑo.

Only three adverbs are found in postverbal position: ʑo in expressions of high degree, tsaa ‘a little’ in comparative constructions, and ntsɯ ‘always,’ which retains its usual meanings of constant state or recurrent action when placed after the verb.

text:
predicate!non-verbal noun!predicative
While a Japhug sentence generally requires a finite verb forms to be complete, there are nevertheless some constructions in which a noun or a nominalized verb form serves as predicate by itself.

First, zero copula predicate nominals are attested, in particular to name a referent (object or person) by showing it/him/her. For instance, in ( ex:kWki.sAndAr ), the subject is the demonstrative kɯkithis and the nominal predicate sɤndɤrthimble.

exe

kɯki sɤndɤr. kɯki sɤndɤr. iʑora kɯrɯ ra tɕe sɤndɤr tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
dem. prox thimble dem. prox thimble 1pl Tibetan pl lnk thimble ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`(Pointing to a thimble.) This is a thimble. This is a thimble. We Tibetans call it `thimble'.' (video-2014-04-29-09-5104)
exe

However, the zero copula construction is not restricted to such contexts, and is also found when the demonstrative pronouns are anaphoric, as in ( ex:tCheme.tWma ). The generic possessor prefix in ( ex:tCheme.tWma ) is due to the fact that tɕʰemegirl serves here as a generic noun, and also because the speaker includes herself in this group (§ sec:indef.genr.poss ).

exe

nɯnɯ tɕʰeme tɯ-ma. \\
dem girl genr. poss -work \\
 `This (the actions described in the previous sentences) is the work of women.' (12-kAtsxWb)
0003486#S97
exe

Absence of copula is also attested in multiclausal constructions, for instance in alternative concessive conditionals (§ sec:alt.concessive.conditional ) as in ( ex:tatChoNtChoN ).

exe

tɕe tɯ-ci nɯnɯ, pɯ-nɯ-xtɕi nɤ tatɕʰoŋtɕʰoŋ, pɯ-nɯ-wxti nɤ tatɕʰoŋtɕʰoŋ. \\
lnk indef. poss -water dem pst. ipfv - auto -be.small add waterfall pst. ipfv - auto -be.big add waterfall \\
Water [falling down from a cliff], whether it is big or small, [is called] a `waterfall'.' (hist 180428 tatChoNtChoN)
exe

The zero copula construction is however considerably rarer than the copular construction (§ sec:copula.basic ), even in the same context, when the speaker names a referent and points it/him with the finger as in ( ex:kWki.Cnat.Nu ).

exe

kɯki ɕnat ŋu \\
dem. prox heddle be: fact \\
`(Pointing to a heddle.) This is a heddle.' (vid-2014-04-29-09-0403)
0003776#S26
exe

Second, exclamative expressions with a degree nominal (§ sec:degree.nominal.predicates ), exclamative nouns (§ sec:exclamative.IPN ) can also be used as main predicate, followed by a sentence final particle such as nɯ, without any finite verb form.

Third, inflectionalized phatic expressions (§ sec:phatic.inflectionalization ) and interjections (§ sec:interjections ) such as mtsʰɤrihow strange as in ( ex:mtshAri.ataR.WtWpe ) can form complete utterances on their own without any verb.

exe

ki mtsʰɤri, kɯki a-βɣo ki a-taʁ ɯ-tɯ-pe nɯ \\
dem. prox how.strange dem: prox 1sg. poss -FB dem: prox 1sg. poss -on 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.good sfp \\
`How strange, this uncle of mine is so nice to me.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S54
exe

Fourth, the nouns ɯ-mdoʁcolour and smɯlɤmprayer have been grammaticalized as sentence-final modality markers (§ sec:nouns.TAME ).
summary: Although Japhug sentences generally require a finite verb, some constructions allow a noun or nominalized verb form to function as the predicate. These include zero-copula predicate nominals, which can name or identify a referent, as well as exclamative nominal predicates, inflectionalized phatic expressions and interjections, and grammaticalized nouns used as sentence-final modality markers.

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
light verb collocation!noun-verb
While Japhug has a very productive system of denominal verbalizer prefixes described in Chapter chap:denominal, it is also possible to build predicates out of nouns using noun-verb collocations, built in particular from a few highly frequent light verbs.

Apart from nouns, ideophones are also used with light verbs, but this question is studied in § sec:idph.syntax.
summary: Japhug not only has a productive system of denominal verbalizer prefixes, but also forms predicates through noun-verb collocations, especially with a small set of highly frequent light verbs. In addition to nouns, ideophones can also combine with light verbs, though that is discussed elsewhere.

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
verb!intransitive
In collocations involving intransitive verbs, the associated noun is the intransitive subject, so that the verb verb form is invariably 3sg (§ sec:intransitive.invariable ).
summary: In collocations with intransitive verbs, the noun associated with the verb functions as the intransitive subject. As a result, the verb form is always third-person singular (3sg).

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
The motion verbs ɣicome and ɕego (§ sec:motion.verbs ) are used with the nouns of cognition ɯ-sɯmmind and ɯ-ʁjizwish in the lexicalized collocations ɯ-sɯm+ɕe/ɣi `want' and ɯ-ʁjiz+ɣi `wish', which take complement clauses (§ sec:nouns.cognition.complement ).

They also occur with temporal nouns. The verb ɕego occurs with tɤ-rʑaʁtime and ta-ʁafree time to express the meaning `spend (one's time)', as in ( ex:aRa.ChWCe ), an excerpt from a conversation where Tshendzin describes her daily activities. In this function, the whole collocation can be subjected to the facilitative ɣɤ- derivation (§ sec:facilitative.GA ).

exe

nɯ kɯ-fse ntsɯ a-rʑaʁ ɲɯ-ɕe ŋu. tɤ-nɤpɤri-a qʰe li ci <sanbu> ju-ɕe-a qʰe, tɕe nɯ kɯ-fse ntsɯ sɲikuku a-ʁa cʰɯ-ɕe ŋu. \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.like always 1sg. poss -time ipfv: west -go be: fact aor -have.dinner- 1sg lnk again once walk ipfv -go- 1sg lnk lnk dem sbj: pcp -be.like always everyday 1sg. poss -free.time ipfv: downstream -go be: fact \\
`(...), this is how I spend my time. And after dinner, I go on a walk, this is how I spend my time every day.' (conversation 2015-12-05)
0006089#S2
exe

The verb ɣicome on the other hand is found with nouns referring to seasons ( ex:ftCar.jAGe ) or parts of the day ( ex:tWrmW.koGi ).

exe

ɯnɯnɯ ftɕar jɤ-ɣe qʰe, nɯ ɲɯ-ʁaʁ qʰe \\
dem summer aor -come[II] lnk dem ipfv -hatch lnk \\
`When the warm season (spring) comes, it hatches, and...' (25-akWzgumba)
0003632#S95
exe

exe

tɯrmɯ ko-ɣi \\
evening ifr -come \\
`The evening came.' (many examples)
exe

It also expresses the occurrence of specific events like catastrophes ( ex:taNi.toGi ).

exe

taŋi to-ɣi \\
drought ifr -come \\
`There was a drought.' (25-kAmYW)
0003642#S1
exe

The combination of ɕego with the locative noun ɯ-pabelow, under (§ sec:relator.nouns.3d ), in addition to the trivially predicatible meaning `go below $X$', is also used in the sense of `take all of $X$ for oneself (of things that do not exclusively belong to oneself)' ( ex:Wpa.YAnWCe ) when the verb has the Autive nɯ- (§ sec:autoben.proper ). In this construction, the agent (the person taking the things) is encoded as possessor of ɯ-pa, and the patient (the things taken) as the intransitive subject of nɯ-ɕe.

exe

ɯʑo ɯ-pa ɲɤ-nɯ-ɕe \\
3sg 3sg. poss -down ifr - auto -go \\
`S/he took all of it for him/herself.' (elicited)
exe

The verb ɕego also occurs in collocation with a few nouns designating places or objects to express the meaning `go and do', in particular with skɤrwacircumambulation and jɤɣɤtterrace, `toilet' In traditional houses in the Japhug-speaking area, toilets are built on a remote side of the covered terrace surrounding the house. The term as now been extended to modern flush toilets. as in ( ex:skArwa.koCe ) and ( ex:jAGAt.luCea ).

exe

skɤrwa ko-ɕe \\
circumambulation ifr -go \\
`He went to do circumbulations.' (elicited)
exe

exe

aʑo jɤɣɤt ci lu-ɕe-a nɤ \\
toilet indef ipfv: upstream -go- 1sg sfp \\
`I am going to the toilet.' (2005 khu)
exe

These collocations correspond to denominal verbs in rɯ- (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ).

The ablative motion verb ɬoʁcome out (§ sec:motion.verbs ) is commonly found in the meaning `grow' (of plants), but also occurs in a few more lexicalized collocations, with tɤ-relaugh (n) as in ( ex:Wre.pjAlhoR ) or with tɤ-rminame ( ex:Wrmi.tolhoR ). More of these collocations have corresponding transitive constructions with tɕɤttake out (§ sec:tCAt.lv ), such as tɤ-re+tɕɤt `mock' and tɤ-rmi+tɕɤt `give a name'.

exe

ɯ-re pjɤ-ɬoʁ \\
3sg. poss -laugh ifr -come.out \\
`S/he laughed.' (elicited; refers to an involuntary action)
exe

exe

ɯ-rmi to-ɬoʁ. \\
3sg. poss -name ifr: up -come.out \\
`He became famous.' (elicited)
exe

The anticausative verb ndzoʁbe attached
The anticausative ndzoʁbe attached (§ sec:anticausative.dummy ), in addition to its function as a quasi-existential verb (§ sec:existential.basic ) and also its dynamic meaning `cling onto, lean on, grab' (example ex:WtaR.kondzoR, § sec:anticausative.volitionality ) or `land' (with flying creatures), The meaning `land' is more commonly expressed with the verb zoland, probably borrowed from the Tshobdun cognate of ndzoʁbe attached. occurs in lexicalized collocations with a few nouns. With nouns referring to plant parts, it can mean `grow' (§ sec:anticausative.dummy ); with tɤ-rɟitchild or tɤ-pɯoffspring, young, its meaning is `become pregnant' (of humans or non-human animals), as in ( ex:WrJit.konzdoR ).

exe

iɕqʰa <sanshengmu> nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit ko-ndzoʁ \\
the.aforementioned anthr dem gen 3sg. poss -offspring ifr - acaus:attach \\
`Sanshengmu became pregnant with a child.' (150826 baoliandeng)
0006370#S53
exe

With time periods such as qartsɯwinter or ftɕarsummer, it is synonymous with the motion verb ɣicome above (§ sec:motion.light.verbs ) as shown by ( ex:ftCar.kANdzoR ).

exe

tɕe ɯ-fsaqʰe ftɕar kɤ-ndzoʁ qʰe li tu-ɬoʁ. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -next.year summer aor - acaus:attach lnk again ipfv -come.out \\
`The next year, when the warm season (spring) arrives, it comes out again.' (8-qromJoR)
0003532#S134
exe

It can also be used like the dummy transitive taput (§ sec:ta.lv ) with the noun sɣarust ( ex:sGa.koNdzoR ) in the meaning `become rusted, get rust', with a function similar to that of the nɯ- denominal prefix (compare nɯsɣaget rust, § sec:denom.intr.nW ).

exe

sɣa ko-ndzoʁ \\
rust ifr - acaus:attach \\
`It became rusted.' (elicited)
exe
summary:
The passage describes several lexicalized collocations involving motion and related verbs. Verbs such as ɕego and ɣicome combine with nouns of cognition, time, seasons, parts of the day, and events to express meanings like ‘want,’ ‘spend one’s time,’ ‘come,’ or the occurrence of something, while ɕego with locative nouns can mean ‘take all of X for oneself’ or ‘go and do’ certain activities.

It also notes that ɬoʁ ‘come out’ appears in collocations meaning ‘laugh’ or ‘become famous,’ and that ndzoʁbe attached occurs with nouns to mean ‘grow,’ ‘become pregnant,’ ‘arrive’ for time periods, or ‘become rusted.’ Several of these collocations correspond to denominal or related verbal constructions.

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
Existential verbs (§ sec:existential.basic ) commonly take inalienably possessed nouns as subjects. Some of these collocations can be analyzed as instances of the mihi est possessive construction (§ sec:possessive.constructions ). For instance, the combination of ta-ʁafree time with the existential verbs has the compositional meaning `have time' ( ex:kume, § sec:egophoric.evd, ex:tCetha.nWmbrAt, § sec:aor.temporal ), and apart from the fact that it can take complement clauses (§ sec:free.time.complement ), this collocation does not stand out as particularly lexicalized. The present section focuses on cases where the meaning of the collocation is not straightforwardly derivable from that of its constituent parts.

The noun tɯ-sɯmpamind (borrowed from སེམས་པ་sems.pamind), occurs with the existential verb tu with the meaning `keep/have in mind, remember', with the experiencer marked as possessor, for instance 1sg in ( ex:asWmpa.tu ).

exe

tɤjmɤɣ ɯ-sɤ-tu nɯ a-sɯmpa tu \\
mushroom 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -exist dem 1sg. poss -mind exist: fact \\
`I have in mind (I know, I did not forget) the places where there are mushrooms.' (elicited)
exe

The collocation of the noun ɯ-grɤlorder, rule (from Tibetan གྲལ་gralrow, a meaning still preserved in the intransitive denominal verb nɯgrɤlbe in a row) with the negative existential verbs me or maŋe is very commonly used to indicate high degree, in particular in the degree nominal construction (§ sec:degree.monoclausal ), as in ( ex:WtWsAGmu.WgrAl.maNe ).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-sɤɣ-mu ɯ-grɤl maŋe \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - prop -fear 3sg. poss -order not.exist: sens \\
`It is extremely frightening/fearsome.' (khu 2012)
0004085#S41
exe

It is also compatible with dynamic verbs, as in ( ex:tsxu.WtWmbWt.WgrAl.maNe ).

exe

tʂu ɯ-tɯ-mbɯt ɯ-grɤl maŋe \\
road 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - acaus:take.off 3sg. poss -order not.exist: sens \\
`The road had collapsed to a considerable extent.' (2010-1)
exe

This collocation has a second unrelated meaning: `be impudent, be shameless, act in an outrageous way' as in ( ex:nAGrAl.WtWme ), where the possessive prefix can be other than 3sg.

exe

tɯ-si tɤ-mda kɯnɤ nɯ kɯ-fse ɲɯ-tɯ-nɤre, nɯ nɤ-grɤl ɯ-tɯ-me nɯ! \\
2-die: fact aor -be.the.time also dem sbj: pcp -be.like sens -2-laugh dem 2sg. poss -order 3sg. poss -not.exist sfp \\
`Even as you are about to die, you are laughing like that, what impudence!' (140516 guowang halifa-zh)
0004008#S65
exe

This collocation can be causativized and reflexivized (§ sec:refl.caus ) as ɯ-grɤl+ʑɣɤɣɤme `cause oneself to act shamelessly' as in ( ex:WGrAl.YWZGAGAme ).

exe

ji-wa cʰo cʰa ku-tshi-ndʑi <shafa> ɯ-taʁ zɯ tu-nɯjmɤzdɤβ-ndʑi tɕe ku-rŋgɯ-ndʑi qʰe tɕe
ɯ-grɤl ʑo ɲɯ-ʑɣɤ-ɣɤ-me-ndʑi ɲɯ-ɕti \\
1pl. poss -father comit alcohol ipfv -drink- du sofa 3sg. poss -on loc ipfv -sleep.on.opposite.directions- du lnk ipfv -lie.down- du lnk lnk 3sg. poss -order emph ipfv - refl - caus -not.exist- du sens -be. aff: fact \\
`He and my father would drink alcohol, sleep on the sofa one over the other in opposite directions, presenting themselves in a poor light.' (17-lhazgron)
exe

While the constructions above do not have any equivalent denominal derivation, the collocation of existential verbs with nouns relating to meals such as tʂʰatea, breakfast, saχsɯlunch or tɤ-pɤridinner has the same meaning as the intransitive nɯ-/nɤ- denominal prefix (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ). For instance,( ex:tAnApArij ) with the denominal verb nɤpɤrihave dinner is a natural answer to ( ex:nApAri.WpWtu ) with the existential verb (see also ex:saXsW.WpWtu, § sec:denom.intr.nW ).

exe

nɤ-pɤri ɯ-pɯ́-tu? \\
2sg. poss -dinner qu - pst. ipfv -exist \\
`Did you have dinner?'

pɯ-tu, nɯ koʁmɯz tɤ-nɤ-pɤri-j \\
pst. ipfv -exist dem just.before aor - denom -dinner- 1pl \\
`We did, we just had dinner.' (conversation, 2016-04-12)
exe

The intransitive auxiliary pa
The transitive verb pado (§ sec:pa.lv ) has an intransitive counterpart pa (§ sec:lability.pass ), which is used as auxiliary for ideophones (§ sec:idph.pa ), and can also select a numeral as subject, meaning `pass $X$ years' ( ex:40.topa ) (see also ex:12.topa, § sec:CN.verbs ).

exe

tɕiʑo ni kɤ-amɯfse-tɕi nɯ jinde kɯβdɤsqi ɯ-ro to-pa \\
1du du aor -know.each.other- 1du dem nowadays forty 3sg. poss -excess ifr -pass.X.years \\
`We have known each other for more than forty years.' (`More than forty years passed', 12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S3
exe

It is not possible in this construction to replace the bare numeral by the counted noun tɯ-xpaone year. For a historical perspective on this construction, see § sec:num.prefix.paradigm.history and § sec:CN.verbs.
summary:
The passage describes several nontransparent collocations involving existential verbs and possessed nouns. Some combinations have straightforward meanings like “have time” or “have dinner,” but others are lexicalized, such as *mind + exist* meaning “keep/have in mind, remember” and *order/rule + negative existential* meaning both “be extremely” and “be impudent/shameless.”

It also notes that existential verbs can combine with meal nouns to function like the intransitive denominal prefix for eating, and that the intransitive auxiliary *pa* can take a numeral subject to mean “pass X years.” In this latter construction, a bare numeral is required and cannot be replaced by a counted noun like “one year.”

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
The categories listed above do not exhaust all lexicalized collocations involving intransitive verbs. tab:other.intr.collocations provides additional examples. In addition, there are also frozen collocations with nouns and/or verbs not otherwise attested (§ sec:frozen.collocations ).

Some of these collocations resemble Chinese constructions, and may have been calqued, for instance tɯ-ro+ŋgɤr `be petty-minded' (compare with 心胸狭窄 xīnxiōng xiázhǎibe petty-minded). In other case, the resemblance with Chinese may be a parallel development: the use ɴɢraʁbe torn, `break(vi)' (§ sec:anticausative.morphology ) in ɕɤrkʰa+ɴɢraʁ `break (of dawn)' reminds of 破晓 pòxiǎodaybreak, but this metaphor is not limited to Chinese.

The collocation meaning tɯ-skʰrɯ+ neg +βdi `be pregnant' ( ex:tWskhrW.mABdi ) requires a negative prefix (§ sec:obligatory.negative ) on the verb form. The denominal verb nɯskʰrɯbe pregnant with (§ sec:denom.tr.nW ) derived from this construction however is only based on the noun, and does not integrate the verbal root as could have been expected (§ sec:incorp.denom ).

exe

tɯ-skʰrɯ mɤ-βdi tɕe nɯnɯ qartsʰaz ɯ-se ɣɯ-tsʰi mɤ-βdi ma \\
genr. poss -body neg -be.well: fact lnk dem deer 3sg. poss -blood inv -drink: fact neg -be.well: fact lnk \\
`(People say that) when one is pregnant, it is not good to drink deer blood.' (27-qartshaz)
0003702#S106
exe
summary: The passage notes that lexicalized collocations with intransitive verbs are not limited to the categories already listed, and that additional frozen collocations also occur with nouns and verbs otherwise unattested. It adds that some of these collocations resemble Chinese and may be calques or parallel developments, while the expression for ‘be pregnant’ requires a negative prefix on the verb form and gives rise to a denominal verb that is based only on the noun, not the full verbal root.

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
verb!transitive
βzumake
The verb βzumake, borrowed from བཟོ་bzomake; manufacture, serves as a causative auxiliary (§ sec:sWpa.sABzu ), and occurs in a wide range of complex predicates, in particular with action nominals (§ sec:action.nominal.Bzu ), simultaneous action nominals (§ sec:simultaneous.action.nominal, § sec:simult.action.nominal.Bzu ) and compound action nouns (§ sec:compound.action.nominal.Bzu ). In this section, we focus on constructions with nouns that are not derived from verbs.

The verb βzu is found with noun meaning `method' or `manner' such as ftɕaka and kowa in complement-taking collocations meaning `try to $X$ by any means' or `prepare' (§ sec:nouns.manner.complement ).

It also occurs with nouns of speech activity (of Tibetan origin), as in kʰramba+ βzu `tell lies' ( ex:khramba.matABzea, § sec:prohibitive.morpho ), tɯ-skɤt+βzu `do/say something meaning $X$' (§ sec:nouns.speech.complement ) or tɯ-lɤn+βzu `give an answer' (with the addressee as possessor of the object, ex:alAN.naBzu ).

exe

a-lɤn na-βzu \\
1sg. poss -answer aor:3 -make \\
`He gave me an answer.' (elicited)
exe

With names of languages, βzu means `speak $X$' as in ( ex:mbroXpaskAt.kABzu ). It is also found with abstract nouns and also relator nouns in a variety of collocations ( tab:Bzu.abstract ).

exe

mbroχpa-skɤt kɤ-βzu ɲɯ-mkʰɤz-nɯ. \\
nomad-language inf -make sens -be.expert- pl \\
`They speak the nomad language (i.e. Amdo Tibetan) very well.' (140522 RdWrJAt)
0004061#S121
exe

The verb βzumake is attested in the dummy subject construction (§ sec:transitive.dummy ) with three types of nouns.

First, it occurs with nouns of natural phenomena ( tab:Bzu.dummy ), as illustrated by ( ex:qale.atABze ).

exe

nɯnɯ qale a-tɤ-βze qʰe, iɕqʰa nɯ ɣɯ-nɯ-tsɯm qʰe, \\
dem wind irr - pfv -make[III] lnk the.aforementioned dem inv - auto -take.away: fact lnk \\
`Whenever there is wind, it blows [this insect] away.' (28-kWpAz)
0003714#S150
exe

Second, it is found with parts of plants or animals in the meaning `grow' or `develop', as in tɤ-spɯ+βzu `fester, have pus' (§ sec:denominal.vs.light.verb ). A defective verb βze `grow' based on the third stem of βzu has been created by backformation from this function (§ sec:stem3.backformation ).

Third, the abstract nouns ɯ-tsʰɤt `with proper measure' (distinct from its use in tab:Bzu.abstract, see § sec:deputative ) and ɯ-tsa `with proper measure, fit, adapted' are found in a transitive but subjectless construction meaning `$X$ fit/be the right size/quantity/degree for $Y$' which encodes the referent $Y$ as possessor, and $X$ as an absolutive phrase: in ( ex:atsa.YWBze ), the head-internal relative clause (§ sec:object.causative.relativization ) in brackets does not receive ergative marking.

exe

(a-xtsa lɤ-tɯ-sɯ-ɣɯt-ndʑi nɯ) a-tsa wuma ɲɯ-βze \\
1sg. poss -shoe aor: upstream -2- caus -bring- du dem 1sg. poss -fit really sens -make[III] \\
`The shoes that you have sent me fit me very well.' (conversation, 2015-04-18)
exe

Many of the locutions in βzu have a semantics close to denominal derivations in rɯ-/rɤ- and nɯ- (§ sec:denominal.vs.light.verb ). In addition, βzu corresponds to the ɣɯ- prefix in the case of ɣɯlɤnanswer (§ sec:denom.tr.GA ), a verb similar in meaning to tɯ-lɤn+βzu ( ex:alAN.naBzu ) and also to sɯ- in sɯndzɯpesit without crossing legs (§ sec:denom.sW.caus.instr ).

lɤtrelease
The basic meaning of the verb lɤt is `throw' when employed with an inanimate object (like tɯdiarrow, see ex:kW.WtaR.object, § sec:indirective.word.order ), `pour' when applied to liquids or containers (§ ex:khru.chWftsxinW, § sec:anticausative.other.derivations ) and either `release, let go' ( ex:aZWG.nWkhAm, § sec:gen.beneficiary ) or `see $X$ off'
with a human object ( ex:akW.mACtsxa, § sec:terminative ). It is very productively used with noun-verb compounds with rpubump into or tɕʰɯgore, stab as second element (see examples ex:RzAnrpu and ex:RrWrpu, § sec:action.nominal.compounds ).

Like βzumake, lɤt is attested with tɯ- action nominals (§ sec:action.nominal.Bzu ), though this construction is less productive and limited to a few items such as tɯ-mɯrʁɯz+lɤt `make a scratch' (from mɯrʁɯzscratch) or tɯ-rkɤz+lɤt `make an engraving' (from rkɤzcarve). It also occurs with the inalienably possessed bare action nominal tɯ-sɯsothought (§ sec:bare.action.nominals ). From tɯ-sɯso+lɤt `think', the antipassive verb rɯsɯsothink, `ponder' (§ sec:antipassive.rA ) was derived by denominal derivation.

With iterative counted nouns (§ sec:CN.iterative ) as object, lɤt is highly common with the meaning `do $X$ times', where $X$ represents the numeral prefix on the counted noun ( ex:XsWtAxWr.talAt ).

exe

mbro nɯ kɯ rirɤβ raŋri χsɯ-tɤxɯr ta-lɤt \\
horse dem erg mountain each three-lap aor:3 -release \\
`The horse made three laps around each mountain.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe
