With the counted nouns tɯ-rzɯɣone section and tɯ-ɣdɤtone section, lɤt means `cut into $X$ pieces', as in ( ex:kWBderzWG.tolAt ).

exe

kɯβde-rzɯɣ ʑo tó-wɣ-lɤt pjɤ́-wɣ-sat \\
four-section emph ifr - inv -release ifr - inv -kill \\
`[The thief] killed him by cutting him into four pieces.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S109
exe

Example ( ex:kWBderzWG.tolAt ) shows that the counted noun is not the direct object: the inverse (§ sec:obviation.saliency ) on both verbs tó-wɣ-lɤt and pjɤ́-wɣ-sat (§ sec:svc.simultaneous ) shows that both share the same (obviative) object, and therefore that the object is the patient (the person that was killed), not the counted noun. This referent is also relativized like an object (§ sec:object.relativization ) using an object participial relative ( ex:kWBderzWG.tAkAlAt ).

exe

kʰa kɯ-qanɯ nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ zɯ, nɤkinɯ, tɯ-ɕpɤβ kɯβde-rzɯɣ tɤ-kɤ-lɤt nɯnɯ ku-sɯ-ɤlɤɣi-a cʰa-a ɕti nɤ! \\
house sbj: pcp - emph be.dark 3sg. poss -in loc filler indef. poss -corpse four-section aor - obj: pcp -release dem ipfv - caus -be.connected[III]- 1sg can: fact - 1sg be. aff: fact sfp \\
`(not only this, but) I am (even) able to put together a corpse that had been cut into four pieces in a dark house.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S152
exe

With tɯ- action nominals, lɤt also has an iterative meaning, but the number of occurrences of the action is indicated by a numeral after the noun as in ( ex:tWmWrtWG.XsWm.tolAt ).

exe

tɯ-mɯrtsɯɣ χsɯm to-lɤt \\
nmlz: action -pinch three ifr -release \\
`He pinched him three times.' (elicited)
exe
summary:
The passage describes **βzu** as a causative/light verb used with many kinds of nonverbal complements: nouns meaning “method/manner,” speech-related nouns, language names, abstract nouns, relator nouns, and in dummy-subject constructions with natural phenomena, plant/animal parts meaning “grow/develop,” and certain measure nouns meaning “fit” or “be the right size/degree.” It notes that many of these uses are semantically close to denominal derivations and sometimes correspond to related prefixal verb formations.  

It then describes **lɤt**, whose basic meanings include “throw,” “pour,” “release/let go,” and “see off,” depending on the object, but which is also productive in complex predicates. In addition to limited use with action nominals, it is very common with iterative counted nouns meaning “do X times,” and with some counted nouns it means “cut into X pieces,” where the counted noun is not the direct

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
Noun expressing hitting actions such as tɯqartsɯ `kicking' The tɯ- prefix on this noun synchronically neither an action nominal prefix nor a numeral prefix). in collocation with lɤt also indicate the number of hits by a free numeral ( ex:tWqartsW.RnWz.tolAt ). In this construction, the patient is not encoded as direct object, but as an oblique argument with the relator ɯ-taʁon, above (§ sec:WtaR ).

exe

ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu tɯqartsɯ ʁnɯz to-lɤt \\
3sg. poss -on dem: loc kicking two ifr -release \\
`He kicked two times on it.' (150824 kelaosi-zh)
0006276#S61
exe

A handful of action nominals such as tɯ-tʂɯβ `sewing' can however take numeral prefixes to indicate the number of iterations, as in ( ex:RnWtWtsxWB.ntsW ).

exe

ʁnɯ-tɯ-tʂɯβ ntsɯ cʰɯ́-wɣ-lɤt ra. \\
two- nmlz: action -sew always ipfv - inv -release be.needed: fact \\
`It has to be sewed two times.' (12-kAtsxWb)
0003486#S70
exe

Table ( tab:lAt.tr ) presents examples of collocations with lɤtrelease. From the meaning `throw, release' (an arrow), lɤt acquired the sense of `shoot' with shooting weapons, and then `hit' with body parts or other weapons. Additionally, it came to mean `use' with various types of instruments and implements.

The verb lɤt is the productive way to derive predicates from recent Chinese loanwords designating machines. Combined with 电话 diànhuàtelephone ( ex:jAlAt.je, § sec:imp.function, ex:jAtWlAt.mWpjAmtshama, § sec:inf.1person ) and 汽车 qìchēcar it means `phone' and `drive a car', respectively. It also occurs with nouns expressing actions derived from verbs such as 放假 fàngjiàhave a holiday, with a 3pl generic subject (§ sec:genr.3pl ) in ( ex:fangjia.lAtnW ).

exe

a-ɣe ra ɣɯ pɤjkʰu ʑatsa <fangjia> mɯ́j-lɤt-nɯ \\
1sg. poss -grandchild pl gen yet early vacation neg: sens -release- pl \\
`My grandchild [and the rest of his class] are not yet on vacations.' (conversation, 2014-12-24)
exe

Some nouns occurring with lɤt are also compatible with other light verbs, with slightly different semantics. For instance, from the noun rɤɣosong, the locution rɤɣo+βzu has the trivial meaning `sing, sing a song' ( ex:tWrJaʁ.pjWBzunW, § sec:action.nominal.Bzu ), synonymous with the denominal nɯrɤɣosing (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ), while rɤɣo+lɤt means `play a tune on an instrument', reminiscent of the use of lɤt with musical instruments.

The verb lɤt is also found with nouns referring to meteorological phenomena in the dummy subject construction (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), for instance with tɯ-mɯsky, weather ( ex:tWmW.kalAt ) and tɤjpasnow ( ex:tAjpa.kalAt ). In both examples, it takes the C-type eastwards preverb ka- ( tɯ-mɯ also occurs with the orientation downwards ).

exe

tɯ-mɯ ka-lɤt ɯ-mpʰru nɯ tu. \\
indef. poss -sky aor:3 -release 3sg. poss -after dem exist: fact \\
`It is found after it has rained.' (23-mbrAZim)
0003604#S72
exe

exe

qartsɯ tɕe tɕendɤre tɤjpa wuma ʑo ka-lɤt tɕe \\
winter lnk lnk snow really emph aor:3 -release lnk \\
`In winter, when a lot of snow has fallen,' (24-kWmu)
0003618#S20
exe

Collocation with lɤt correspond to various denominal derivations: rɯ- ( ɟuli+lɤt `play the flute' $ $ rɯɟuliplay the flute, § sec:denom.intr.rA ), nɯ- ( ɕɤmɯɣdɯ+lɤt `shoot with a gun' $ $ nɯɕɤmɯɣdɯshoot at, § sec:denom.tr.nW ) and sɯ- ( tɯqartsɯ+lɤt `kick' $ $ sɯqartsɯkick, § sec:denom.sW.caus.instr ).

tɕɤttake out
The manipulation verb tɕɤttake out (§ sec:manipulation.verbs ) has a wide range of derived meanings, including the relatively straightforward `remove' ( ex:wuma.YWnAmNAm, § sec:wuma ), `expel, banish' ( ex:tChi.kWNu, § sec:interrogative.pronouns ), `take off (clothes)' ( ex:tWNga.nWkAmbi, § sec:relative.possessor.neutralization ), but also `raise (a child)' ( ex:tChi.tAkWsci, § sec:tChi ) and `earn (food)' ( ex:pjWnWtCAtnW, § sec:pronouns.emph ). It occurs as auxiliary in a marginal causative construction ( ex:mAkWra.YAtWtCAt, § sec:sWpa.sABzu ).

Unlike βzu and lɤt, it almost never used with tɯ- action nominals, except with the lexicalized noun tɯpɣaʁland clearing (§ sec:lexicalized.action.nominals ), from which the irregular antipassive rɤpɣaʁreclaim land is derived by denominal derivation (§ sec:antipassive.lexicalized ).

tab:tCAt.tr collects the most common collocations with tɕɤt. Most of the nouns in this table are inalienably possessed. In the case of body parts, with the meaning `stick out', the possessive prefix is coreferent with the transitive subject ( 3sg in ex:Wku.totCAt ).

exe

tsʰɯtʰo-pɯ tɯ-rdoʁ kɯ ɯ-ku to-tɕɤt. \\
kid- dim one-piece erg 3sg. poss -head ifr -take.out \\
`One of the little kids stuck its head out of [the wolf's belly].' (140430 lang he qizhi xiaoshanyang-zh)
0003895#S131
exe

In the collocations whose gloss contains an $X$, the possessive prefix corresponds to this $X$ referent, for instance the recipient in ɯ-ftɕɤfkɤt+tɕɤt ( ex:aftCAfkAt.tAtCAt ).

exe

a-ftɕɤfkɤt ci tɤ-tɕɤt tɕe jisŋi tɕʰi ʑo ɲɯ-nɤme-a pe \\
1sg. poss -idea indef imp -take.out lnk today what emph ipfv -do[III]- 1sg be.good: fact \\
`Make me a suggestion, what should I do today?' (140515 jiesu de laoren-zh)
0004004#S119
exe

The nouns in the first section of tab:tCAt.tr are also compatible with ɬoʁcome out as light verb (§ sec:motion.light.verbs ). In most cases, the ɬoʁ collocations are functional anticausatives of the tɕɤt collocations, as in ɯ-tɕʰaʁ+ɬoʁ `have a handicap, be mutilated' vs. ɯ-tɕʰaʁ+tɕɤt `cause a handicap, mutilate' ( ex:atChaR.pjWtWtCAt ) (a noun borrowed from ཆག་tɕʰagdecrease, break) or tɯ-sroʁ+ɬoʁ `lose one's live' vs. tɯ-sroʁ+tɕɤt `cause to lose one's life'. The only exception is tɤ-rmi+ɬoʁ `become famous', whose semantics is not derivable from tɤ-rmi+tɕɤt `give a name'.

exe

xlist

a-mi ɯ-tɕʰaʁ pɯ-ɬoʁ \\
1sg. poss -leg 3sg. poss -handicap aor -come.out \\
`My leg became handicapped (as the result of an accident).' (elicited)

aʑo kɯnɤ, a-tɕʰaʁ pjɯ-tɯ-tɕɤt ɲɯ-ŋu \\
1sg also 1sg. poss -handicap ipfv -2-take.out sens -be \\
`(Not only did you do all these crimes), you also mutilate me.' (tou dongxi de xiaohai-zh)
xlist

The noun ɯ-βlutrick, `idea' forms its corresponding intransitive construction with the existential verb tu (example ex:aBlu.ci.tu, § sec:existential.basic ).
summary:
The passage describes how the verb **lɤt** functions as a light verb with a wide range of nouns, extending from its original sense ‘throw/release’ to meanings such as ‘shoot,’ ‘hit,’ and ‘use.’ With action nominals, lɤt can express repeated events, but the patient is marked obliquely rather than as a direct object; it also combines productively with recent Chinese loanwords and with some nouns under other light verbs, yielding related but slightly different meanings.  

It then contrasts **tɕɤt** ‘take out,’ which has many derived meanings but is only rarely used with action nominals, except for a lexicalized case. In these constructions, possessed nouns often have a coreferential possessor or another argument linked to the possessive prefix, and some tɕɤt collocations have corresponding intransitive **ɬoʁ** forms with anticausative meanings.

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
The collocation of tɕɤt with ɯ-qa `(its) root' can have the compositional meaning `uproot' ( ex:Wqa.tuwGtCAt ) like the denominal verb nɤqauproot(§ sec:denom.tr.nW ), but it also used in the sense of `do completely, until the end' as in ( ex:Wqa.chWtCAt ). This meaning is also found with the nouns rŋama (from རྔ་མ་rŋa.matail), tɤ-rmehair and the relator noun ɯ-ndoedge, border (§ sec:other.locative.relator ).

exe

tʂɤɕpʰɤt nɯnɯ ɯ-qa tú-wɣ-tɕɤt tɕe, pjɯ́-wɣ-ɣɤ-la tɕe tɯ-ɕɣa kɯ-mŋɤm pʰɤn tu-ti-nɯ \\
plaintain dem 3sg. poss -root ipfv: up - inv -take.out lnk ipfv - inv - caus -soak lnk genr. poss -tooth sbj: pcp -hurt be.efficient: fact ipfv -say- pl \\
`People say that, if one digs out the plantain's root and soak it in water, it is efficient against toothache.' (12-ndZiNgri)
0003488#S43
exe

exe

nɯ kɤ-ndɯn lonba ɯʑo pjɯ-sɤʑe tɕe ɯ-qa cʰɯ-tɕɤt \\
dem inf -read all 3sg ipfv -start[II] lnk 3sg. poss -root ipfv -take.out \\
`[This monk is in charge] of reading [the sûtras] from the beginning until the end.' (160721 XpWN)
0006181#S42
exe

Some of the collocations in tɕɤt correspond to denominal verbs in nɯ, for instance nɯqaɟyfish (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ) or nɤrelaugh, a labile verb meaning `mock' when transitive (§ sec:lability.apass ) like tɤ-re+tɕɤt. Alternatively, tɤ-rmi+tɕɤt `give a name'and tɯ-ɕtʂi+tɕɤt `cause to sweat' rather correspond to sigmatic causative denominal verbs (§ sec:denom.sW.caus.instr ).

ndotake
The basic meaning of ndo is `take' ( ex:nAZo.tAnWndAm, § sec:autoben.transitivity ) or `have in the hand' with the upwards orientation, `catch' ( ex:jWjAkWGe § sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes ), `grab' ( ex:Wku.kukWsWndo, § sec:indexation.generic.tr ), or `get attach to, stick on' ( ex:tWjaR.kundAm ) with the eastwards preverbs.

exe

ɲɯ́-wɣ-nɤmɤle tɯ-jaʁ ku-ndɤm ʑo ɕti ma, ɯ-taʁ, ɯ-ndʑɯɣ ʑo kɯ-fse tu. \\
ipfv - inv -touch genr. poss -hand ipfv -take[III] emph be. aff: fact lnk 3sg. poss -on 3sg. poss -resin emph sbj: pcp -be.like exist: fact \\
`When one touches it (a type of mushroom), it sticks on one's hand, as there is some kind of resin-like thing on it.' (21-kuGrummAG)
0003574#S25
exe

tab:ndo.tr presents a non-exhaustive list of lexicalized collocations with ndo. With the noun tɯ-jaʁhand, arm, it can predictably mean `grab by the hand' ( ex:WskAt.amAkAtWsANAm, § sec:irrealis.delayed.imp ) or `stick on the hand' ( ex:tWjaR.kundAm ), but in the imperative it can be interpreted as `don't interfere, don't meddle in it'.

The collocation of ndo with ɯ-kʰrɤtset, determined can take finite complement clauses as in ( ex:WkhrAt.kunwGnWndo ).

exe

tɕe kɯki χsɯ-ldʑa ra ɕi, kɯβde-ldʑa ra nɯnɯ, tɯʑo ɯ-kʰrɤt kú-wɣ-nɯ-ndo tɕe \\
lnk dem. prox three-long.object be.needed: fact qu four-long.object be.needed: fact dem genr 3sg. poss -determined ipfv - inv - auto -take lnk \\
`One has to control whether one needs three or four threads (for a given colour).' (vid-2014-04-29-092115)
exe

In addition to rɟɤlpuking in tab:ndo.tr, ndo can be used with all nouns referring to a status or a charge (such as χpɯnmonk) to mean `become $X$, assume the charge of $X$'. In this function, collocations in ndo correspond either to rɯ-/rɤ- (§ sec:denom.intr.rA ) or nɯ- (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ) denominal derivations.

With numerals, ndo indicates `be moving into one's $X$', without using the counted noun -pɤrme `$X$ years old', as shown by ( ex:42.kondo ).

exe

kɯβdesqaptɯɣ, kɯβdesqamnɯz ko-ndo ɲɯ-ŋu ma \\
forty.one forty.two ifr -take sens -be lnk \\
`She is moving into her forty-one, forty two years old.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S304
exe

In addition, ndo is used in the meaning `catch (a disease)' in the dummy subject construction, with tɤmtsʰɤzhyperostosis as only argument for instance.

Another dummy subject construction of ndo with the noun tɯ-pʰoŋbubody, is only found as the infinitive complement of either kʰɯbe possible or sɤcʰabe such that people can in negative form, the whole construction meaning `cannot help shivering' (due to cold), as in ( ex:tWphoNbu.kAndo ).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-mɯɕtaʁ kɤ-ti kɯ [tɯ-pʰoŋbu kɤ-ndo] ʑo mɯ-pɯ-sɤ-cʰa \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.cold inf -say erg genr. poss -body inf -take emph neg - pst. ipfv - prop -can \\
`It was so cold that one could not help shivering.' (29-RmGWzWn2)
0003730#S13
exe

pado
The native verb pado The root pa is cognate of Tibetan བྱེད་བྱས་bʲed;bʲasdo; the yod medial Tibetan is unexplained, but not shared by cognates in its closest relatives. has been largely superseded by the Tibetan borrowing βzumake (§ sec:Bzu.lv ) in the sense of `do, make'. It still means `do what' when used with the interrogative tɕʰiwhat ( ex:tChi.WkWpa, § sec:am.interrogative ), but as a complement-taking verb it rather means `discuss and decide' (§ sec:pa.complements ). It is one of the few verb with ergative lability (§ sec:lability.pass ), and its intransitive counterpart is a light verb used with numerals (§ sec:pa.intr.lv ) and ideophones (§ sec:idph.pa ).
alignment!ergative-absolutive

The causative sɯpa either has a tropative function `consider to be' (§ sec:sig.caus.tropative ), or serves in various periphrastic constructions (§ sec:sWpa.sABzu; § sec:bare.dental.inf.sWpa ). Its passive apabecome (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ) is used as inchoative copula (§ sec:copula.basic ), and its reflexive is the verb of pretense ʑɣɤpapretend (§ sec:refl.erg, § sec:constr.participial.clause; see ex:kWm.ci.thapa below).

As a transitive light verb, pa occurs in relatively fewer constructions than the previous verbs. It means `close' when used with kɯmdoor ( ex:kWm.ci.thapa ) or kʰɯɣɲɟɯwindow, but also with nouns meaning `light', `lamp' or electrical implements like phones, with either downstream or eastwards orientations.

exe

ju-kɯ-ɕe tɤ-ʑɣɤpa nɤ, kɯm nɯ ci la-cɯ, ci tʰa-pa nɤ, kɤ-anbaʁ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
ipfv - sbj: pcp -go aor -pretend add door dem once aor:3 -open once aor:3 -close add aor -hide sens -be \\
`She pretended to go [out], she opened the door, and then closed it, and hid [inside the house].' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

Although pa does occur with ci in its adverbial meaning `once' (§ sec:tense.aspect.adverbs ) as in ( ex:kWm.ci.thapa ), a lexicalized collocation ci+pa `get married' is also found ( ex:ci.kApatCi ).

exe
summary: The passage describes several lexicalized verb-plus-noun collocations. With **tɕɤt**, combinations can mean either the compositional sense ‘uproot’ or the extended sense ‘do completely, until the end,’ and some similar collocations correspond to denominal or causative verb formations; with **ndo**, the basic meaning is ‘take,’ but in different noun collocations it can mean ‘grab,’ ‘stick on,’ ‘become X,’ ‘move into one’s X years,’ or, in special constructions, ‘catch a disease’ or ‘cannot help shivering.’ It also notes that **pado** is a native verb largely replaced by a borrowing for ‘do/make,’ though it still appears in meanings such as ‘do what,’ ‘discuss and decide,’ ‘close,’ and in the lexicalized collocation **ci+pa** meaning ‘get married.’

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
amaŋ, βdaʁmu, ci kɤ-pa-tɕi nɯstʰɯci ʑo tɤ-nɤrʑaʁ nɤ ri \\
interj lady one aor -do- 1du so.much emph aor -pass(time) add lnk \\
`Oh, my lady, so much time has passed since we got married, but...' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

With the Autive prefix (§ sec:autoben.proper ), pa occurs with nouns such as βzaŋsafriend or ɣɯfsufriend in the meaning `become friend'. This construction is also possible with social relation collectives in kɤndʑi- (§ sec:social.collective ) as in ( ex:kAndZiGWfsu.nWpatCi ).

exe

a! jinde kɤndʑi-ɣɯfsu nɯ-pa-tɕi \\
interj now coll -friend auto -do: fact - 1du \\
`Let us be friends!' (smanmi 2003.1)
exe

taput
The manipulation verb taput also means `leave (vt)' ( ex:YotanW.Yota, § sec:mismatch.errors ) and `let go' like lɤtrelease (a polysemy reminiscent of Chinese 放过 fàngguòlet pass). Its lexicalized agentless passive atabe on (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ) is used as an existential verb (§ sec:existential.basic ).

Unlike βzu (§ sec:Bzu.lv ) and lɤt (§ sec:lAt.lv ), it is not used with tɯ- action nominals, except for the lexicalized nominalization tɯpumoxibustion (on which see § sec:lexicalized.action.nominals ).

tab:ta.tr presents a representative sample of collocation in which it occurs.

The collocations tʂʰa+ta `make tea' and kʰon+ta `steam' derive from `put $X$ on (the hearth tripod)', a meaning that is still obvious in examples such as ( ex:ndZitsxha.kanWtandZi ).

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ qapi χsɯm nɯ pa-ta ndɤre, nɯ ɯ-taʁ ndʑi-tʂʰa ka-nɯ-ta-ndʑi \\
indef. poss -boy dem erg white.stone three dem aor:3: down -put lnk dem 3sg. poss -on 3du. poss -tea aor:3 - auto -put- du \\
`The boy placed the three stones (on the ground), and they made their tea on it.' (2003 Kunbzang)
exe

With head covers or implements worn on one's body such as χɕɤlmɯɣglasses, the verb ta occurs with the autive in the meaning `put on, wear'.

In dummy subject construction (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), taput is also attested with nouns such as ʁjaverdigris or tɤ-rqʰuhull, skin to express spontaneous growth on a surface, as in ( ex:Rja.kute ) with the orientation `toward east' ku- and stem III.

exe

zaŋ cʰo raʁ ni ʁnaʁna ʑo ʁja ku-te ɲɯ-ŋu \\
copper comit brass du both emph verdigris ipfv -put[III] sens -be \\
`Both copper and brass get verdigris.' (30-Com)
0003736#S99
exe

rkuput in
The manipulation verb rkuput in occurs in considerably fewer collocations than the previous verbs. In addition to its basic meaning, it can be used in the sense of `pour (water, grain) into a container' (example ex:atWci.tArke, § sec:gen.beneficiary ), `give a parting present' ( ex:arkuz.tarku, § sec:z.nmlz ) and also `fix a joint dislocation'.

Prefixed with the Autive nɯ- (§ sec:autoben.proper ), it occurs with the relator noun ɯ-pabelow, under (§ sec:relator.nouns.3d ) and tɯ-kuhead in ɯ-pa+nɯrku `subjugate, vanquish' ( ex:apa.pjWnWrkea ), literally `put $X$ under oneself' and tɯ-ku+nɯrku `meddle into (other people's business)'. In both cases, the possessive prefix on the noun is coreferent with the subject.

exe

nɯ rɟɤlpu kɯ kɯ-tu nɯ pjɯ-ɕɯ-nŋam-a, nɯnɯ a-pa pjɯ-nɯ-rke-a ra \\
dem king total sbj: pcp -exist dem ipfv - caus -be.defeated[III]- 1sg dem 1sg. poss -under ipfv - auto -put.in[III]- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`I have to defeat all the kings (in the world), to subjugate them.' (150821 edu de wangzi-zh)
0006402#S8
exe

Without Autive prefix, rku is also found in oblique nominalized form with tɯ-ku and the negative existential me as in ( ex:nAku.sArku.kWme )

exe

nɤ-ku sɤ-rku kɯ-me \\
2sg. poss -head obl: pcp -put.in sbj: pcp -not.exist \\
`[Something] that is none of your business.' (elicited)
exe

In the dummy subject construction (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), rku is attested with tɕʰɯwɯrblister and cimbɤromblister ( ex:cimbArom.turke ) (see also ex:tCHWwWr.turke, § sec:dummy.subj.object.relativization ).

exe

tɤ-rʑaʁ kɯ-rɲɟi tu-kɯ-ŋke qʰe, tɯ-mɤpa ri cimbɤrom tu-rke ŋgrɤl. \\
indef. poss -time sbj: pcp -be.long ipfv - genr:S/O-walk lnk genr. poss -sole loc blister ipfv -put.in[III] be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`If one walks for a long time (with bad shoes), one gets blisters on one's soles.' (27-tWfCAl)
0003710#S131
exe

tsʰoʁattach
The verb tsʰoʁattach (§ sec:anticausative.dummy ) only occurs in a handful of collocations with non-dummy subject: tɯ-χpɯm+tsʰoʁ `knee' (§ sec:sig.caus.collocations ) and kʰɯna+tsʰoʁ `hunt with dogs'.

In the dummy subject construction (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), tsʰoʁ has the sense of `grow' with nouns referring to plant parts (§ sec:anticausative.dummy ),
in particular ɯ-mat+tsʰoʁ `bear fruits' (see examples ex:sqamNuxpa.koRmWz, § sec:temporal.postpositions or ex:Wmat.kukWtshoR, § sec:dummy.subj.object.relativization ). Its anticausative ndzoʁbe attached (§ sec:ndzoR.light.verbs) also occurs with the same meaning.
summary:
The passage describes several manipulation verbs and their specialized collocations. *pa* with the Autive prefix can mean “become friend” with friendship nouns or collectives, while *taput* means ‘leave’ or ‘let go’ and is also used in collocations like ‘make tea’ and ‘steam,’ as well as for ‘put on/wear’ with body-worn items and spontaneous growth on surfaces. 

It then notes that *rkuput* has fewer collocations, including ‘pour into,’ ‘give a parting present,’ and ‘fix a dislocation,’ and with the Autive prefix it forms expressions meaning ‘subjugate’ and ‘meddle in other people’s business.’ Finally, *tsʰoʁ* appears only in a few collocations, but in dummy subject constructions it means ‘grow,’ especially with plant parts such as ‘bear fruits.’

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
tab:other.tr.collocations presents a list of collocations with verbs other than those discussed above. The manipulation verb mɟatake, `pick up' (whose historical morphology is discussed in § sec:antipassive.t ) and cɯopen each occur in a few non-compositional expressions. Note that tɯtsoexperience is the lexicalized action nominal of tsoknow, understand (§ sec:semi.transitive ).

Although the noun tɤtsʰoʁnail probably derives from tsʰoʁattach (§ sec:tshoR.lv ), the two cannot be used as a collocation, and tɤtsʰoʁ rather selects nodrive or the causative verb sɤtsaprick, pierce with the downwards preverbs to express the meaning `hammer nails into'.
summary: The passage notes that several verbs besides those discussed earlier appear in a few non-compositional collocations, including manipulation verb **mɟatake** ‘pick up’ and **cɯopen**, and that **tɯtso** ‘experience’ is a lexicalized action nominal of **tsok** ‘know, understand’. It also says that although **tɤtsʰoʁ** ‘nail’ likely comes from **tsʰoʁ** ‘attach’, the two do not form a collocation; instead, **tɤtsʰoʁ** combines with **nod** ‘drive’ or causative **sɤtsa** ‘prick, pierce’ plus downward preverbs to mean ‘hammer nails into’.

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text: The noun-verbs collocations studied in the previous sections involve partially grammaticalized verbs that can be combined with a considerable variety of nouns. The following focuses on more opaque collocations, which comprise either nouns or verbs that are not otherwise attested (§ sec:orphan.noun, § sec:orphan.verb ) and/or which are borrowed from Tibetan (§ sec:borrowed.NV ).
summary: The noun-verb collocations discussed earlier involve partially grammaticalized verbs that can combine with a wide range of nouns. This section turns to more opaque collocations, including those with orphan nouns or verbs not otherwise attested, as well as collocations borrowed from Tibetan.

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
Orphan nouns do not exist in free form, and are only found in collocations, or as members of frozen compounds.

Some orphan nouns are found in collocations with (mainly transitive) light verbs (§ sec:tr.light.verbs ). A few items from this list originate from Tibetan verbs: ʂaʁ is from སྲེག་sregburn, ndaŋ from འདང་ⁿdaŋthink about, long for and mtʰoŋ from མཐོང་mtʰoŋsee, while ɯ-rtsa is from the noun རྩ་rtsaroot. Pure Tibetan collocations are treated in § sec:borrowed.NV.

The orphan noun ɯ-sɲɯrʑu is borrowed from སྙིང་བཞོས་sɲiŋ.bʑoscomfort; the variant ɯ-snɯrʑu is semi-nativized by reanalyzing the sɲɯ- from སྙིང་sɲiŋheart as the bound state snɯ- of its native cognate tɯ-sniheart.

The nouns tɤ-rtɕʰɣaʁ and ɯ-snɯrʑu are otherwise attested as the bases from which the denominal verbs sɤrtɕʰɣaʁquibble about and ɣɤrtɕʰɣaʁquibble on the one hand, and nɯsnɯrʑucomfort on the other, are derived.

orphan noun
Some of the orphan nouns in tab:orphan.nouns.lv are treated as direct object (for instance tɤlɟɣo, ʂaʁ, ɯ-snɯrʑu ), and other ones are semi-objects. The noun ndaŋ can have both grammatical functions; in ( ex:nAndaN.lata ) it is direct object (and the stimulus is encoded as its possessor), whereas in ( ex:ndaN.talAt ) it is semi-object (and the stimulus is encoded as direct object and is indexed on lɤt ).

exe

xlist

nɤ-ndaŋ lat-a ɕti \\
2sg. poss -think.about release: fact - 1sg be. aff: fact \\

ndaŋ ta-lɤt ɕti \\
think.about 1 2-release: fact be. aff: fact \\
xlist
`I will think about/be considerate of you.' (elicited)
exe

Other collocations with orphan nouns listed in tab:orphan.nouns.other involve verbs not otherwise used in light verb constructions.

Most of the verbs in tab:orphan.nouns.other are intransitive; the experiencer/main referent is encoded as the possessive prefix on the intransitive subject, as the 2sg in ( ex:nAtsW.YWrnaR ).

exe

nɤ-tsɯ ɲɯ-rnaʁ \\
2sg. poss -secret sens -be.deep \\
`You are keeping the secret very well.' (elicited)
exe

The collocation ɯ-lu+cɯ is a transitive dummy construction (§ sec:transitive.dummy ): the experiencer is marked as possessor of the object ɯ-lu ( ex:alu.pjAcW ), and no overt subject can appear. To express the meaning `cause to lose conscience', the causative sɯ-cɯ is needed.

exe

a-lu pjɤ-cɯ kʰi \\
1sg. poss -lose.conscience(1) ifr -lose.conscience(2) hearsay \\
`I lost conscience (people said).' (elicited)
exe

Some of the nouns in tab:orphan.nouns.other have etymologies. The noun ɯ-tsɯ, though not otherwise attested, presumably originally meant `secret', as it serves as the base of the denominal transitive verb nɤtsɯhide. The nominal root -lu is possibly related to the last syllable of nɯkɯlube lost, `lose one's way', a denominal verb (§ sec:denom.intr.nW ) from the kɯ- participle (§ sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ) of a verb *lu, from which ɯ-lu would be derived (§ sec:tA.abstract.nouns, § sec:bare.action.nominals ).

The noun ɯ-rɕa, though non-attested on its own, occur in several collocations, respectively ɯ-rɕa+mŋɤm `cherish' with mŋɤmfeel pain (example ex:arCa.mNAm,§ sec:incorp.denom ), This collocation can be denominalized as nɤrɕɤmŋɤmcherish ( tab:incorp.denom.collocation, § sec:incorp.denom ). ɯ-rɕa+χtɤt `concentrate, focus' with the transitive χtɤtlean on, and ɯ-rɕa+tsʰa `be thoughtful and considerate of the feelings of others' with the orphan verb tsʰa (§ sec:orphan.verb ).
summary: Orphan nouns have no free form and occur only in collocations or frozen compounds, often with light verbs or other verbs. Some are borrowed or semi-nativized from Tibetan, and several serve as bases for denominal verbs; in some constructions they function as direct objects, while others are semi-objects or are marked through possessive prefixes. The passage also notes that some orphan nouns have proposed etymologies and appear in fixed collocations whose meanings can be further derived or paraphrased by related verbal forms.

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
Orphan verbs are much fewer than orphan nouns. Among the verbs in tab:orphan.verbs, ri (example ex:asroR.kAtWrit,§ sec:lability.pass ) is the transitive labile counterpart of riremain, `be left' (§ sec:lability.pass ), and tsʰa and loʁ are borrowed from Tibetan ཚ་tsʰahot and ལོག་logbe upside down. The rest of the verbs are obscure.

The lower half of the Table includes collocations comprising both a orphan noun and an orphan verb. In such cases, the noun and the verb are given the same gloss, with the indices (1) on the former and (2) on the latter, as in ( ex:sala.YWtWzri ).

exe

nɯtɕu tɤ-rɤru ma sala ɲɯ-tɯ-zri ɲɯ-ŋu \\
dem: loc imp -get.up lnk be.a.hindrance(1) sens -2-be.a.hindrance(2) sens -be \\
`Get up from there, you are in the way.' (elicited)
exe

Several orphan verbs are denominalized together with their noun in an incorporating construction ( tab:incorp.denom.collocation, § sec:incorp.denom ).

Some orphan verbs can be subjected to voice derivations. For instance, ɯ-ʁo+pʰibe disappointed by has an anticausative form ɯ-ʁo+mbibe discouraged (§ sec:anticausative.collocation ), which can further receive the facilitative ɣɤ- prefix (§ sec:facilitative.GA ). The verb ŋgɯ selects the irregular ɕɯ- allomorph of the causative prefix (§ sec:caus.CW ).
summary: Orphan verbs are much fewer than orphan nouns; most of the verbs listed are obscure, though some are identifiable as the transitive labile counterpart of *ri* ‘remain’ or as Tibetan borrowings such as *tsʰa* and *loʁ*. The passage also notes that orphan nouns and verbs can appear together in collocations with matching glosses, sometimes in denominalized incorporating constructions, and that some orphan verbs still participate in voice derivations and causative morphology.

section: Noun-verb collocations and light verb constructions
text:
Several synchronically opaque noun-verb collocations (with orphan verbs and/or nouns) have been borrowed as a whole from Tibetan, unlike some constructions described in previous sections which combine a noun or a verb from Tibetan with a native word.

Among Tibetan collocations, tʰɯrʑi+ʑɯask for mercy comprises the noun tʰɯrʑimercy (from ཐུགས་རྗེ་ཞུ་tʰugs.rdʑecompassion), which has many functions in Japhug (§ sec:IPN.cause ), while the transitive verb form ʑɯ (from ཞུ་ʑuask) is not otherwise attested, Note however the verb ndʑɯaccuse, which is probably borrowed from a non-classical present from *ⁿdʑu of the verb ཞུ་ʑuask. with the meaning `ask for mercy' ( ex:thWrZi.toZWnW ).

exe

``wortɕʰi nɤ wojɤr" to-ti-nɯ tʰɯrʑi to-ʑɯ-nɯ. \\
please add please ifr -say- pl mercy ifr -ask- pl \\
`[The boys] asked for mercy, saying `please' one after the other.' (160704 poucet4-v2)
0006097#S25
exe

In other collocations, both the noun and the verb are orphan forms. For instance, tʰaʁ+tɕʰottake a decision was borrowed from the locution ཐག་ཆོད་tʰag.tɕʰodbe decided, built from the noun ཐག་པ་tʰag.parope and the intransitive verb ཆོད་tɕʰodbe cut off, neither of which are attested as independent words into Japhug. It does not take complement clause, and is better translated as `take a decision' rather than `decide'. The verbal element tɕʰot is transitive (unlike Tibetan ཆོད་tɕʰodbe cut off), and the person making the decision is indexed as subject ( ex:thaR.pWtChota ).

exe

tʰaʁ pɯ-tɕʰot-a \\
decide(1) aor -decide(2)- 1sg \\
`I took a decision.' (elicited)
exe

Similarly, the intransitive impersonal constructions tʰo+tʰɯɣmatch up, `be compatible', `be conform to each other' ( ex:tho.YWthWG ) from ཐོ་ཐུག་tʰo.tʰugmatch, and ɯ-ŋgu+tʰonbe well-off, `able to take care of oneself' ( ex:ndZiNgu.mAthon ) from འགོ་ཐོན་ⁿgo.tʰonable to take care of oneself are syncrhonically opaque from a Japhug-internal perspective.

exe

ɯʑo kɯ ta-tɯt cʰo nɤj tu-tɯ-ti nɯ tʰo ɲɯ-tʰɯɣ \\
3sg erg aor:3 -say[II] comit 2sg ipfv -2-say dem match.up(1) sens -match.up(2) \\
`What he said and what you are saying match up.' (elicited)
exe

exe

ci tʰɯ-kɯ-rgɯ rgɤz ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe, ci kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ɲɯ-ɕti tɕe, ndʑi-ŋgu mɤ-tʰon tɕe, aʑo mɤ-ɣi-a \\
one aor - sbj: pcp - emph be.old sens -be. aff lnk one sbj: pcp - emph be.small sens -be. aff lnk 3du. poss -be.well.off(1) neg -be.well.off(2): fact lnk 1sg neg -come: fact - 1sg \\
`One of them is very old, the other one is very young, they are not able to take care of themselves, I will not come (to the palace and leave them behind).' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

In addition, there are also partially compositional collocations, both of whose elements independently exist in Japhug. For instance, although tɯ-sɯm+βdibe relieved (§ sec:other.collocation.intr ) takes its specific meaning from Tibetan སེམས་བདེ་sems.bdebe relieved, both tɯ-sɯmmind (§ sec:nouns.cognition.complement ) and βdibe well are otherwise found, and also used in a variety of constructions not calqued from Tibetan.

There is at least one case of collocation from Situ: kʰɤli+rgi `be respected, have good reputation', from kʰalí `wind, reputation' (cognate of qalewind and ɯ-ʁlereputation, § sec:apn.to.ipn ), with a verb from དགེ་dgevirtuous.
summary:
The passage explains that Japhug has borrowed several noun-verb collocations from Tibetan as opaque units, including cases where one or both elements are no longer independently attested in Japhug. Some are fully borrowed compounds like *tʰaʁ+tɕʰot* ‘take a decision’ and others are only partly compositional, where both elements still exist in Japhug but the overall meaning comes from the Tibetan model.

It also notes examples such as *tʰrʑi+ʑɯ* ‘ask for mercy,’ *tʰo+tʰɯɣ* ‘match up,’ and *ɯ-ŋgu+tʰon* ‘be well-off,’ and mentions one collocation borrowed from Situ, *kʰɤli+rgi* ‘be respected, have good reputation.’

text: Copulas and existential verbs stand out not simply by their morphological specificities (suppletive negation § sec:suppletive.negative, infixed person index § sec:intr.person.irregular and other § sec:verb.doubling ), but also by their uses as auxiliaries in periphrastic tenses (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ), and various additional functions, including possessive constructions (§ sec:possessive.constructions ), emphasis (§ sec:affirmative.copula.function ), focalization (§ sec:pseudo.cleft, § sec:focalization.final.copula ), universal negation (§ sec:negation.existential ), superlative (§ sec:negative.existential.superlative ) and concessive conditionals (§ sec:bare.inf.negative ).
summary: Copulas and existential verbs are notable not only for special morphological properties such as suppletive negation, infixed person indexing, and verb doubling, but also for their use as auxiliaries in periphrastic tense-aspect-mood constructions. They additionally serve a range of other functions, including possessive constructions, emphasis, focalization, universal negation, superlative expressions, and concessive conditionals.

text:
copula
With the exception of a handful of predicative nouns (§ sec:non.verbal.predicates ), a copula is required to make a noun phrase or a pronoun predicative in Japhug.

The copulas are a distinct subclass of semi-transitive verbs (§ sec:semi.transitive ), whose semi-object is the nominal predicate. There are two assertive copulas, the neutral ŋube and the emphatic affirmative ɕtibe, and one suppletive negative copula maʁnot be (§ sec:suppletive.negative ). The emphatic affirmative copula occurs in particular to express contrast, as in ( ex:Ctia.ma.maRa ).

exe

aʑo βʑɯ ɕti-a ma, nɤki, pɣa maʁ-a \\
1sg mouse be. aff: fact lnk filler bird not.be: fact \\
`(The bat said:) I am a mouse, not a bird.' (140427 bianfu yu huangshulang-zh)
0003838#S7
exe

The copulas cannot be used with inchoative meanings (`become') in the Aorist (§ sec:aor.inchoative ) or the Inferential (§ sec:ifr.inchoative ) unlike other stative verbs. The Aorist of the copulas are only attested to fix a point of temporal reference (§ sec:temporal.reference ) and in periphrastic tenses (examples ex:tWwGCaB.tANu in § sec:proximative.periphrastic and ex:tAcha.tANu in § sec:prerequisite.clause ). The lexicalized passives apa and aβzu (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ) replace the copula to express inchoative meaning, as shown by ( ex:ki.kWfse.naBzua ).

exe

aʑo tɯmɯkɯmpɕi ra nɯ-tɕɯ pɯ-ŋu-a ri, [ki kɯ-fse] nɯ-aβzu-a \\
1sg heaven pl 3pl. poss -son pst. ipfv -be- 1sg lnk dem. prox sbj: pcp -be.like aor -become- 1sg \\
`I used to be a son of heaven, but I became like that.' (divination 2003)
exe

Person indexation on copula generally follows the subject, in particular when both subject and semi-object are non-third person as in ( ex:nAZo.maRa ).
subject

exe

aʑo nɤʑo maʁ-a kɯ, a-mu mɤ-nɤmqe-a. \\
1sg 2sg not.be: fact - 1sg erg 1sg. poss -mother neg -scold: fact - 1sg \\
`I am not you, I will not scold my mother.' (elicited)
exe

However, when the predicate is a first or second person pronoun and the subject third person, the copula indexes the non-third person argument. In the pseudo-cleft ( ex:pWkWcha.nW ) for instance, it would not be grammatical to replace aʑo ɕti-a with a third 3sg copula $ $ aʑo ɕti. (see also ex:akAnWrga.nW.nAZo in § sec:pseudo.cleft ).

exe

[pɯ-kɯ-cʰa] nɯ aʑo ɕti-a \\
aor - sbj: pcp -can dem 1sg be. aff: fact - 1sg \\
`The one who succeeded [in doing these things] was me.' (qachGa 2003)
exe

We also find examples of indexation with a (third person) predicative noun, as in ( ex:stAmku.nWra.NunW ), where the verb has plural indexation like the predicative noun phrase stɤmku nɯra, whereas the subject is in the singular. Note that the plural nɯra here cannot be interpreted as approximate location (§ sec:plural.determiners ), because in the next sentence the grasslands are analogically referred to by the plural demonstrative pronoun nɯra (§ sec:anaphoric.demonstrative.pro ).

exe

stu ɯ-sɤ-dɤn nɯ [stɤmku nɯra] ŋu-nɯ. tɕe nɯra nɯ-ŋgɯ tɕe tu-ɬoʁ ŋu tɕe \\
most 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -be.many dem grassland dem: pl be: fact - pl lnk dem: pl 3pl. poss -inside loc ipfv -come.out be: fact lnk \\
`The place where it is most numerous is the grasslands, and it grows there.' (19-qachGa mWntoR)
0003546#S23
exe
summary:
In Japhug, a copula is generally required to make a noun phrase or pronoun predicative, and the language has two assertive copulas—neutral ŋube and emphatic ɕtibe—as well as a suppletive negative copula maʁ. These copulas are a special class of semi-transitive verbs, but unlike other stative verbs they do not express inchoative meanings in the Aorist or Inferential; instead, lexicalized passives such as apa and aβzu are used for that function.

Person indexation on the copula normally follows the subject, especially when both subject and semi-object are non-third person, but it can instead index a non-third person predicative pronoun when the subject is third person. The passage also notes that copulas can show indexation with predicative nouns, including plural agreement with a plural noun phrase even when the subject is singular.

text:
verb!existential
Unlike other languages of the area such as Khroskyabs, Japhug is relatively poor in existential verbs. The verb tuexist and its suppletive forms (the Sensory ɣɤʑu § sec:intr.person.irregular, the negative menot exist and the Sensory negative maŋe, § sec:suppletive.negative ) have no selection restrictions on their subjects, and are compatible with abstract nouns ( ex:aBlu.ci.tu ), inanimate objects ( ex:khANqra.ci.pjAtu ) and humans ( ex:kWnApAri.aZo.ma.mea, ex:RzAmi.pjAtundZi ).

exe

aʑo a-βlu ci tu \\
1sg 1sg. poss -trick indef exist: fact \\
`I have an idea.' (150829 taishan zhi zhu-zh)
0006350#S196
exe

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ nɯnɯtɕu kʰɤɴqra ci pjɤ-tu. \\
in.former.times dem: loc house.in.ruin indef ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`In former times, there used to be a house in ruin there.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo)
0004059#S247
exe

The existential verbs index the person of the intransitive subject, as shown in ( ex:kWnApAri.aZo.ma.mea ) (see § sec:headless.relatives.quantification on this construction).

exe

[jɯɣmɯr kɯ-nɤpɤri] aʑo ma me-a. \\
this.evening sbj: pcp -have.dinner 1sg apart.from not.exist: fact - 1sg \\
`This evening nobody is having dinner (at home) apart from me.' (conversation, 16-04-28)
exe

With third person subjects, number indexation is possible as in ( ex:RzAmi.pjAtundZi ), but optional (§ sec:optional.indexation ), and never found in the possessive construction (§ sec:possessive.constructions ).

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ ʁzɤmi ci pjɤ-tu-ndʑi \\
in.former.times couple indef ifr. ipfv -exist- du \\
`In former times, there was a husband and his wife.' (rkangrgyal 2002.2)
exe

The assertive existential verbs can mean `be located', and take associated motion prefixes (§ sec:associated.motion ) as in ( ex:NotCu.CpWtWtunW ).

exe

ŋotɕu ɕ-pɯ-tɯ-tu-nɯ? \\
where tral - pst: ipfv -2-exist- pl \\
`Where (in which places) have you been?' (2003 sras)
exe

Other meanings include `be alive' as in ( ex:kutWtu ), and `be present' (especially in converbial form $X$ kɯ-tu ʑo `in $X$'s presence', see ex:Zara.kWtu.Zo, § sec:inf.converb ).

exe

nɤj ku-tɯ-tu ɯ́-ŋu \\
2sg prs -2-exist qu -be: fact \\
`Are you [still] alive?' (Nyima Wodzer 2003.2)
exe

The negative existential verb me is also employed in one of the comparative constructions (§ sec:existential.comparative ), and with infinitives in a construction expressing impossibility (§ sec:inf.exist, § sec:participial.complements.negative ).

Unlike copulas, existential verbs can be used in Aorist, Inferential and Imperfective with an inchoative meaning (see ex:ci.totu in § sec:preverb.gain and ex:mtshu.YAme in § sec:preverb.loss ).

The lexicalized agentless passives (§ sec:passive.lexicalized ) atabe on and arkube in, are nascent existential verbs. They do not have semantic restrictions on the subject as in Khroskyabs or Stau (they are attested with first or second person human subjects, as in ex:parkua, § sec:passive ), but indicate the location of the subject: on a surface or in a building in the case of ata ( ex:kha.ata ) and inside a closed and narrow space (or inside a compact matter) for arku ( ex:tArGe.ci.arku ).

exe

mɯ-to-ndo-t-a, kʰa a-ta ɕti tɕe \\
neg - ifr -take- pst: tr - 1sg house pass -put: fact be. aff: fact lnk \\
`I did not take it [with me], [I] left it at home.' (150830 afanti-zh)
0006380#S121
exe

exe

a-wa ɯ-kɯr ɯ-ŋgɯ zɯ, nɯtɕu tɤ-rɣe ci a-rku tɕe \\
1sg. poss -father 3sg. poss -mouth 3sg. poss -in loc dem: loc indef. poss -pearl indef pass -put.in: fact lnk \\
`In my father's mouth, there is a pearl.' (150902 hailibu-zh)
0006316#S35
exe

In addition, the anticausative verb ndzoʁbe attached (§ sec:anticausative.dummy, § sec:ndzoR.light.verbs can be used to describe the presence of limbs, appendices, excrescence, thorns, hairs and twigs on living organisms, as in ( ex:WmAlAjaR.kundzoR ) (see also ex:WmWntoR.kundzoR, § sec:passive.agent ).

exe

ɯ-ku ɯ-rkɯ ri ʁɟa ʑo ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ ra ku-ndzoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -head 3sg. poss -side loc completely emph 3sg. poss -limb pl ipfv - acaus:attach sens -be \\
`Its legs are located (i.e. attached) next to its head.' (26-mYaRmtsaR)
0003674#S44
exe
summary:
Japhug has relatively few existential verbs compared with languages like Khroskyabs. The main existential forms are unrestricted in the kinds of subjects they take, can index person and sometimes number, and can also express meanings such as location, being alive, and being present; the negative existential also appears in comparative and impossibility constructions.  

In addition, some lexicalized passive forms function as emerging existential verbs with location-specific meanings, and an anticausative verb is used to describe the presence of body parts or similar appendages on living beings.

text:
possessive construction possessor possessum
There are two main possessive constructions in Japhug. In the first one, illustrated by ( ex:amkWm.tu ), the possessum is the intransitive subject of an existential verb (§ sec:existential.basic ) and the possessor is indicated by a possessive prefix on the possessum (§ ex:prefix.expression.of.possession ) and (optionally) a genitive phrase (example ex:11.Zo.pjAtunW below, § sec:gen.possession ). In the second one ( ex:tamkWm.aroa ), involving the semi-transitive verb aroown (§ sec:semi.transitive ), the possessor is subject, and the possessum semi-object (§ sec:semi.object ); when the possessum is an inalienably possessed noun (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ), it selects the indefinite possessor prefix.

exe

xlist

a-mkɯm tu \\
1sg. poss -pillow exist: fact \\

tɤ-mkɯm aro-a \\
indef. poss -pillow have: fact - 1sg \\
`I have a pillow.' (elicited)
xlist
exe
summary: Japhug has two main possessive constructions. In one, the possessum functions as the subject of an existential verb and the possessor is marked by a possessive prefix on the noun, optionally with a genitive phrase; in the other, the semi-transitive verb *aroown* is used, with the possessor as subject and the possessum as semi-object. When the possessum is an inalienably possessed noun in this second construction, it takes the indefinite possessor prefix.

text:
possessive construction genitive prefix!possessive
The mihi est -type construction in ( ex:amkWm.tu ) is by far the most frequent one. It differs from the usual existential construction in that the number of the possessum (intransitive subject) is never indexed on the verb: in ( ex:11.Zo.pjAtunW ) for instance, the subject ɯ-tɕɯ takes the numeral sqaptɯɣeleven but the existential verb pjɤ-tu lacks plural indexation. Although number indexation in the existential construction is optional (§ sec:existential.basic, § sec:optional.indexation ), its presence is however more common than its absence. The non-indexation in ( ex:11.Zo.pjAtunW ) is thus indicative of a significant syntactic difference between the existential and the possessive constructions, despite superficial similarity.

exe

rɟɤlpu nɯnɯ ɣɯ ɯ-tɕɯ sqaptɯɣ ʑo pjɤ-tu. \\
king dem gen 3sg. poss -son eleven emph ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`The king had eleven sons.' (140520 ye tiane-zh)
0004044#S4
exe

Inalienably possessed possessums normally take a possessive prefix coreferent with the possessor, even when the possessor is overt and marked with the genitive. Possessor marked with the dative also exist, but only express temporary alienable possession (example ex:kWre.aCki, § sec:dative ).

In ( ex:tWtWpW.raNri.GW ), we observe a string of possessive clauses in parataxis, each sharing the same possessor with the genitive ( tɯ-tɯpɯ raŋri ɣɯ ). The possessums of all of these clauses are inalienably possessed nouns (farm animals). In the first three clauses, the expected 3pl possessor prefix is present. In the last two however the possessive prefix is absent; this is one of the very rare cases where the possessor is not marked on the possessum in this construction in the corpus.

exe

tɯ-tɯpɯ raŋri ɣɯ, nɤkinɯ, nɯ-mbro pjɤ-tu, nɯ-jla pjɤ-tu, nɯ-nɯŋa pjɤ-tu, qaʑo pjɤ-tu, tsʰɤt pjɤ-tu. \\
one-household each gen filler 3pl. poss -horse ifr. ipfv -exist
3pl. poss -hybrid.yak ifr. ipfv -exist 3pl. poss -cow ifr. ipfv -exist sheep ifr. ipfv -exist goat ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`Every household used to have horse(s), cow(s), hybrid yak(s), sheep and goat(s).' (150820 kAnWCkat)
0006256#S2
exe

The mihi est construction can be causativized by subjecting the existential tu to the ɣɤ- derivation (§ sec:velar.caus.modal ), yielding the verb ɣɤtucause to have, which marks the beneficiary (corresponding to the possessor of the intransitive construction) with the genitive case, as nɤʑɯɣ in ( ex:nAZWG.tAGAtuta ), or a as possessor of the object (as in ex:axCAt.Zo.tuGAte, § sec:velar.caus.modal ).

exe

tu-βze-a kɤ-cʰa nɯra lonba ʑo nɤʑɯɣ tɤ-ɣɤ-tu-t-a ɕti tɕe \\
ipfv -make[III]- 1sg inf -can dem: pl all emph 2sg: gen aor - caus -exist- pst: tr - 1sg be. aff: fact lnk \\
`I endowed you with all the things I could make.' (140425 shizi puluomixiusi he daxiang-zh)
0003798#S15
exe

possessum possessor
When the mihi est possessive construction undergoes relativization, there is ambiguity as to whether the relativized element is the possessum or the possessor, since both intransitive subjects (§ sec:S.possessor.relativization ) and possessors (§ sec:intr.subject.relativization ) are relativized by means of (mostly head-internal) subject participial relatives (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ). In ( ex:WlaXtCha.pWkWtu ), the relativized element is the possessum, and in ( ex:jla.nWRrW.kWtu ) its is the possessor, but these two relative clauses have exactly the same surface structure.

exe

[nɯɕɯŋgɯ ɣɯ ɯ- laχtɕʰa pɯ-kɯ-tu] nɯra ɕ-tú-wɣ-sɯ-rtoʁ tɕe, \\
before gen 3sg. poss -thing pst. ipfv - sbj: pcp -exist dem: pl tral - ipfv - inv - caus -look lnk \\
`They go (there) and show [the child$_i$ objects] that he$_i$ used to have before (in his$_i$ previous life, when he$_i$ was a lama).' (160722 skWBli)
0006227#S5
exe

exe

[ jla nɯ-ʁrɯ kɯ-tu] ra kɯnɤ, nɯ-rpaʁ kɯ ɲɯ-z-rɤɕi-nɯ pɯ-ŋu tɕe, \\
hybrid.yak 3pl. poss -horn sbj: pcp -exist dem: pl also 3pl. poss -shoulder erg ipfv - caus -pull- pl pst. ipfv -be lnk \\
`Even the hybrid yaks that had horns used to pull [the plough] with their shoulders (rather than with their horns).' (25-stuxsi)
0003660#S21
exe

Possessive constructions with the existential verb kɯ-tu in participial form can be combined with a negative existential verb kɯ-tu me/kɯ-tu maŋe to express the meaning `not have any' as in ( ex:Wmdzu.kWtu.me ).

exe

ɯ-ru nɯnɯ, kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕu ʑo ŋu, [ɯ-mdzu ri kɯ-tu] me \\
3sg. poss -stalk dem sbj: pcp - emph be.smooth emph be: fact 3sg. poss -thorn also sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact \\
`Its stalk, it is very smooth, and it does not have any thorns.' (11-qrontshom)
0003482#S40
exe

The mihi est possessive construction can be a gradable predicate and occur in a superlative construction (§ sec:negative.existential.superlative ) as in ( ex:WtshuxtoR.kWtu ) with the abstract noun tsʰuxtoʁloyalty.

exe

fsapaʁ nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ zɯ (...) kʰɯna kɯ-fse ʑo, nɤki, ɯ-tsʰuxtoʁ kɯ-tu me kʰi \\
animal dem 3sg. poss -in loc dog sbj: pcp -be.like emph filler 3sg. poss -loyalty sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact hearsay \\
`Among animals, the dog is the most loyal one.' (i.e. among animals, there isn't any one whose loyalty like that of a dog) (05-khWna)
0003398#S4
exe

Some possessive constructions, involving in particular abstract nouns, are lexicalized and are better described as noun-verb collocations (§ sec:existential.light.verbs ).
summary: The passage explains that the **mihi est** possessive construction is the most frequent possessive pattern, and that it differs syntactically from the ordinary existential construction because the possessum’s number is not indexed on the verb, unlike what is often found in existential clauses. It also notes that inalienably possessed nouns usually take a possessive prefix matching the possessor, though this prefix is very rarely absent, and that the construction can be causativized, relativized in an ambiguous way, combined with negation to mean ‘not have any,’ used in superlative-like expressions, or lexicalized with certain abstract nouns.

text:
There is in addition a third construction, intermediate between those illustrated in ( ex:have.pillow ), involving an existential verb, but in which the possessor is rather intransitive subject, indexed on the verb. It is only attested is double negative, with the negative existential verb menot exist and a negative verb participle such as mɤ-kɯ-pe `(something) that is not good' as possessum: compare the mihi est construction ( ex:mAkWpe.kume ) with this third construction ( ex:mAkWpe.kumea ), where the verb has 1sg indexation. Only one example is found in the whole corpus (identical to example ex:mAkWpe.kume, but with 1pl possessor).

exe

xlist

aʑɯɣ mɤ-kɯ-pe ku-me \\
1sg: gen neg - sbj: pcp -be.good prs -not.exist \\

aʑo mɤ-kɯ-pe ku-me-a \\
1sg neg - sbj: pcp -be.good prs -not.exist- 1sg \\
`I don't have any problem/anything bad.' (elicited, based on real examples)
xlist
exe
summary: The passage describes a third possessive construction, intermediate between the others, in which the possessor functions as an intransitive subject indexed on an existential verb. This construction is only attested with double negation, using the negative existential verb and a negative participial possessum meaning “something not good,” and only one corpus example is found.

text:
Copulas are commonly found in postverbal position, in periphrastic TAME constructions (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME, § sec:aor.narrative, § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic, § sec:proximative.periphrastic ) and in emphatic and focalization functions, as detailed below.

These constructions have in common that the copula remains in 3sg form, regardless of the core arguments of the preceding verb. In ( ex:nWtCu.Ce.Nu ) for instance, the copula ŋu lacks the 1sg suffix found on the verb ɕe-a, and using here the 1sg form ŋu-a would be agrammatical.

exe

nɯtɕu ɕe-a ŋu \\
dem: loc go: fact - 1sg be: fact \\
`(For all these reasons) I am going there.' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

A question concerning the syntactic structure of these constructions is whether part of the clause preceding the copula ( nɯtɕu ɕe-a ) is a subordinate clause, the copula being the main verb of the sentence. The fact that post-verbal adverbs such as ntsɯ (§ sec:postverbal.adv ) can located between the verb and the sentence-final copula, as in ( ex:pe.ntsW.Cti ), is a clue that the part of the sentence preceding the copula is a syntactic constituent.

exe

tɯ tɤ-tɯ-nɤma-t rcanɯ, pe ntsɯ ɕti\\
total aor -2-make- pst: tr unexp: deg be.good: fact always be. aff: fact \\
`Everything that you do is always good.' (150822 laoye zuoshi zongshi duide-zh)
0006298#S222
exe

The pre-copula constituents ( nɯtɕu ɕe-a and pe ntsɯ ) cannot be analyzed as finite relative clauses (§ sec:finite.relatives ), since this type of relatives are restricted to relativizing objects (§ sec:object.relativization ) and goals, and are thus not attested with most intransitive verbs, whereas the postverbal copula constructions are found with all intransitive verbs without restriction. Another possibility would be to analyze the pre-copula constituents as complement clauses (§ chap:complement.clauses ), whose function would be that of semi-object of the copula (§ sec:copula.basic ). In this hypothesis, example ( ex:nWtCu.Ce.Nu ) would literally be `it is (the fact that) I am going there', and ( ex:pe.ntsW.Cti ) `it is that it is always good'.
summary: Copulas commonly occur sentence-finally in periphrastic TAME constructions and in emphatic or focalizing uses, and in these cases the copula stays in 3sg form regardless of the person marking on the preceding verb. The passage asks whether the material before the copula is a subordinate clause, noting that postverbal adverbs can intervene between the verb and the copula, which suggests that the pre-copula material is a syntactic constituent. It also argues that these constituents cannot be finite relative clauses, and proposes instead that they may be complement clauses functioning as a semi-object of the copula.

text:
The postverbal copulas can have scope over the whole sentence. Copulas of opposite polarity ŋu / ɕti and maʁ can be used to mark an emphatic contrast between two predicates, as in ( ex:Nu.tuwGskAr.maR ) and ( ex:YWGAwua.maR2 ) (§ sec:periphrastic.negation ).

exe

tú-wɣ-ɕtʂo ŋu ma tú-wɣ-skɤr maʁ \\
ipfv - inv -measure be: fact lnk ipfv - inv -weigh not.be: fact \\
`One measures (the quantity to be used) by scooping, not by weighing.' (31-cha)
0003764#S12
exe

exe

ɲɯ-ɣɤkʰɯ ndʐa ɕti wo ma, tɕe a-mɲaʁ ɲɯ-ɕɯ-mŋɤm ndʐa ɕti ma, ɲɯ-ɣɤwu-a maʁ \\
sens -have.smoke reason be. aff: fact sfp lnk lnk 1sg. poss -eye sens - caus -hurt reason be. aff: fact lnk sens -cry- 1sg not.be: fact \\
`[The reason why I shed tears] is because it is smoky, and it hurts my eyes, it is not that I am crying.' (qaCpa 202)
exe

A postverbal assertive copula can put emphasis on the trustworthiness and reliability of a statement ( ex:tWsi.Cti ).

exe

tɕetʰa nɤʑo tɯ-si ɕti \\
later 2sg 2-die: fact be. aff: fact \\
`Otherwise you will (certainly) die.' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

The postverbal negation maʁ can be combined with the interrogative form of the assertive copula ɯ́-ŋu, as in ( ex:tAtWta.maR.WNu ), to express a rhetorical question concerning something that both the speaker and the addressee are supposed to know.

exe

`ɯ-kɤrme tɯ-ldʑa a-mɤ-jɤ-tɯ-ɣɯt ra' tɤ-tɯt-a maʁ ɯ́-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -hair one-long-object irr - neg - pfv -2-bring be.needed: fact aor -say[II]- 1sg not.be: fact qu -be: fact \\
`Didn't I say: `Do not bring back anything, not even a hair (from her head).'' (2014-kWlAG)
exe
summary: Postverbal copulas can take scope over an entire sentence, and opposite-polarity copulas ŋu/ɕti and maʁ may be used to create an emphatic contrast between two predicates. A postverbal assertive copula can also emphasize that a statement is trustworthy or reliable. In addition, maʁ can combine with the interrogative assertive copula ɯ́-ŋu to form a rhetorical question about something speaker and addressee are expected to know.

text:
focalization
The most common focalization construction in Japhug is not a pseudo-cleft construction (§ sec:pseudo.cleft ) or a focus marker (§ sec:focus ), but the combination of an overt noun phrase or pronoun (§ sec:focalization.overt ) with a postverbal copula, as in ( ex:CkAnWru ). These sentences are from a story where a child at school is bullied by another pupil, who forces him to bring water for him; the teacher (who guessed that the first child was being bullied) asks ( ex:CtAtWnWrut ) to have him tell the one who forced him to do it, but the bullied child replies ( ex:CtAtWnWrut ), as he fears reprisals. The focalized constituents are indicated in bold. In this construction, the copula is never adjacent to the focalized constituent, which is also marked by a specific intonation.

exe

xlist

nɤʑo nɤ-tɯ-ci ɕ-tɤ-tɯ-nɯ-ru-t ɯ́-ŋu? \\
2sg 2sg. poss - indef. poss -water tral - aor - auto -bring- pst: tr qu -be: fact \\
`Was it for yourself that you brought the water?'

aʑo ɕ-tɤ-nɯ-ru-t-a ŋu \\
1sg tral - aor - auto -bring- pst: tr - 1sg be: fact \\
`I brought it for myself.'
xlist
exe

Given the fact that many periphrastic TAME categories use copulas (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME, § sec:aor.narrative, § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic, § sec:proximative.periphrastic ), there are many cases where this focalizing function of the copula is ambiguous (for this reason, most of the examples presented below involve verbs in Aorist and Inferential form, which do not occur with the copulas in periphrastic tenses).

The postverbal copula construction is used to indicate focus on all core arguments, including intransitive subject ( ex:Wpi.mWpjArAzi ), transitive subject ( ex:pAnmawombAr.kW.Nu, ex:aZo.pWnWmtota, with optional ergative on the overt pronoun, § sec:absolutive.A ) and object ( ex:tutia.Cti, ex:nW.YWnArea ).

optional case marking
In (§ ex:CtAnWruta ), although the focalized argument is in transitive subject function, it is not focalized as subject (`it is I who brought it') but as beneficiary (`it is for myself that I brought it'), as this referent has both functions, the latter marked by the autive prefix nɯ- (§ sec:autoben.proper ).

All three copulas (§ sec:copula.basic ) are found in this construction, including the emphatic affirmative ɕti ( ex:Wpi.mWpjArAzi, ex:tutia.Cti ) and the negative maʁ ( ex:tutia.Cti, ex:nW.Wndzxa.kW.pWmaR ).

exe

tɕeri, ɯ-pi mɯ-pjɤ-rɤʑi qʰendɤre, ɯ-ɬaʁ nɯ pjɤ-rɤʑi ɕti qʰe \\
lnk 3sg. poss -elder.sibling neg - ifr. ipfv -stay lnk 3sg. poss -aunt dem neg - ifr. ipfv -stay be. aff: fact lnk \\
`But his elder brother was not there, it was his brother's wife who was there.' (140512 alibaba)
0003965#S57
exe

exe

pɤnmawombɤr kɯ [...] tɤ́-wɣ-sɯ-χtɯ-a ŋu \\
anthr erg aor - inv - caus -sell- 1sg be: fact \\
`It is Padma 'Od'bar who sold it to me.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S133
exe

Focalized first or second person core arguments, in addition to being marked by an overt pronoun, are also obligatorily indexed on the verb (§ sec:intr.indexation, § sec:tr.indexation ), as shown by 1sg and 2sg marking in ( ex:aZo.pWnWmtota ) and ( ex:tutia.Cti ) below and in ( ex:CkAnWru ) above.

exe

kɯki tɕʰeme ki ndɤre aʑɯɣ a-pɯ-ŋu tʂaŋ ma tɕe aʑo pɯ-nɯ-mto-t-a ɕti tɕe \\
dem. prox girl dem. prox lnk 1sg. gen irr - ipfv -be be.fair: fact lnk lnk 1sg aor - auto -see- pst: tr - 1sg be. aff: fact lnk \\
`This girl, it would be fair if she were mine, as it was I who found her.' (140517 buaishuohua)
0004018#S98
exe

exe

aʑo pɤnmawombɤr tu-ti-a ɕti ma, nɤj ɲɯ-ta-nɯ-ɤkʰɤzŋga maʁ \\
1sg anthr ipfv -say- 1sg be. aff: fact lnk 2sg ipfv -1 2- appl -call not.be: fact \\
`I am saying ``Padma 'Od 'bar", it is not you that I am calling.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S139
exe

exe

kʰɯɣɲɟɯ ri pɣɤtɕɯ ni ɲɯ-ɤnɯɣro-ndʑi tɕe, nɯ ɲɯ-nɤre-a ɕti wo \\
window loc bird du sens -play- du lnk dem ipfv -- 1sg be. aff: fact sfp \\
`On the window two birds were playing, this is what I was laughing about.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

This construction is also attested to focalize adjuncts, such as the causal phrase marked with the ergative (§ sec:manner.nominal.kW ) in ( ex:nW.Wndzxa.kW.pWmaR ).

exe

nɯ ɯ-ndʐa kɯ nɯ-si ʁo pɯ-maʁ. \\
dem 3sg. poss -reason erg aor -die advers pst. ipfv -not.be \\
`It was not because of this that shed died.' (150907 srWn)
0006360#S22
exe

The postverbal copula can be nominalized, and the whole sentence turned into a non-finite clause. This type of construction is also used for constituent focalization as in ( ex:qapri.bWxsi.pjAsat ). The form kɯ-ŋu is ambiguous between a stative infinitive and a subject participle (§ sec:infinitives.participles ), and therefore the non-finite clause is either analyzable as an infinitival complement clause (§ sec:inf.complementation ) or a participial clause in semi-object function (§ sec:relative.core.arg ).

exe

[ xɕiri nɯ kɯ qapri bɯxsi pjɤ-sat kɯ-ŋu] nɯnɯ ko-tso \\
weasel dem erg snake python ifr -kill sbj: pcp -be dem ifr -understand \\
`He realized that it was the weasel that had killed the python.' (140518 xuezhe he huangshulang-zh)
0004032#S34
exe
summary:
In Japhug, the most common focalization strategy is an overt noun phrase or pronoun followed by a postverbal copula, rather than a pseudo-cleft or special focus marker. This construction can focus core arguments and adjuncts, uses several copulas, and often relies on intonation and non-adjacent placement of the copula; first- and second-person focalized arguments are also obligatorily indexed on the verb.

Because many periphrastic TAM categories also use copulas, the focalizing use of the copula can be ambiguous, so examples often use Aorist or Inferential forms that do not occur in those periphrastic tenses. The postverbal copula can also be nominalized, yielding a non-finite clause that serves for constituent focalization.

text:
negation
Like the negative copula maʁ (§ sec:affirmative.copula.function ), the negative existential verbs me and maŋe occur postverbally as periphrastic negative construction (§ sec:periphrastic.negation ).

With transitive verbs, this construction can express universal negative object (`nothing'), in particular with the adverbial intensifier maka (§ sec:intensifier.adverbs ), which can be located either before the main verb ( ex:maka.V.me ) or directly before the negative existential verb ( ex:V.maka.me ).

exe

xlist

maka ʑo pɯ-mto-t-a me \\
at.all emph aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg not.exist: fact \\

pɯ-mto-t-a maka me \\
emph aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg at.all not.exist: fact \\
`I did not see anything/any of it at all.' 0006336#S58
xlist
exe

With secundative verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ), negative meaning can apply either to the object or to the theme (semi-object). In ( ex:rNWl.stea ), the object ( rŋɯlsilver) is definite, while the non-overt theme (the manner) is universal negative.

exe

aʑo rŋgɯ ɕti-a qhe, rŋɯl ste-a me qʰe, nɤʑo nɤ-ŋgra a-pɯ-ŋu tɕe tɤ-nɯ-ndɤm \\
1sg boulder be. aff: fact - 1sg lnk silver do.like: fact - 1sg not.exist: fact lnk 2sg 2sg. poss -salary irr - pfv -be lnk imp - auto -take[III] \\
`I am a boulder, I have no use of [this] silver, may this be your reward (for helping me), take it.' (divination)
0003364#S98
exe

The postverbal negative construction can also indicate a non-specific, but not completely indefinite entity (`not any $X$, none of the $X$' rather than `nothing'). In ( ex:pWmtota.me.nonspec ), the zero object anaphorically refers to qɯmdroŋcrane (§ sec:nonovert.core.arguments ), the main topic of the story from which this sentence is taken.

exe

tɕe jinde aj pɯ-mto-t-a me ri, pɯ-kɯ-xtɕi tɕe pɯ́-wɣ-mto \\
lnk nowadays 1sg aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg lnk not.exist: fact aor - genr:S/O-be.small lnk aor - inv -see \\
`I have not seen any [wild crane] recently, but when we were young, we did see (some).' (22-qomndroN)
0003598#S31
exe

The scope of the negation is however not necessarily restricted to the object. In ( ex:jinW.maNe ) for instance, the non-overt object anaphorically refers to jimamaize mentioned in the previous sentences, but the scope of negation is rather on the essive participial clause ʑara nɯ-kɤ-nɯ-ndza `as food for themselves/for themselves to eat' (§ sec:essive.abs ): the villagers do plant maize, but for a different purpose.

exe

tɕe ʑara nɯ-kɤ-nɯ-ndza tɕe koŋla ji-nɯ maŋe woma \\
lnk 3pl 2pl. poss - obj: pcp - auto -eat lnk completely plant: fact - pl not.exist: sens sfp \\
`They don't plant any [maize] for themselves to eat, (they plant it to feed their pigs).' (140522 kAmYW tWji)
0004055#S64
exe

With intransitive verbs, this construction is used to indicate the complete absence of the action `not... at all' ( ex:WNgW.ri.karia.me ).

exe

tɯ-ci ɯ-rkɯ zɯ ku-rɤʑi-a tɕe nɯre ri ku-nɯ-tsʰi-a ɕti ma ɯ-ŋgɯ ri kɤ-ari-a me, ɕ-tu-nɤŋkɯŋke-a ri me \\
indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -side loc ipfv -stay- 1sg lnk dem: loc loc ipfv - auto -drink- 1sg be. aff: fact lnk 3sg. poss -in also aor: east -go[II]- 1sg not.exist: fact tral - ipfv - distr:walk- 1sg also not.exist: fact \\
`I am staying near the water and drinking (water) there, I did not go into the water at all, I am not walking around in it.' (aesop lang he yang-zh)
exe

The intransitive stative verb snabe good, be worthy (§ sec:mna.sna ) is commonly used with negative existential verbs, with the meaning `not good for anything', as in ( ex:sna.me ). The scope of universal negation in this case is on the essive adjunct (for instance nɯŋa ɯ-ndza `cow fodder' in the first clause of ex:sna.me ).

exe

nɯŋa ɯ-ndza sna ma nɯ ma sna me \\
cow 3sg. poss -food be.good: fact lnk dem apart.from be.good: fact not.exist: fact \\
`[Oat] is good as fodder for cattle, but apart from that it is not good for anything.' (08-qaJAGi)
0003458#S8
exe

The clause preceding the negative existential verb can be embedded within a participial clause with the existential verb kɯ-tu, as in ( ex:CtAnWtWta.kWtu.me ). A similar use of kɯ-tu is also found in the possessive construction (example ex:Wmdzu.kWtu.me, § sec:possessive.constructions ).

exe

[[aʑo joβ tɕi ɕ-tɤ-nɯ-tɯt-a] kɯ-tu] me qʰe [aʑo ndɤre ɲɯ-ɤβzu-a ri kɯ-ra] me qʰe, nɤ-rcɯ rca ʑo ɣi-a ŋu ma nɯ ma [[aʑɯɣ kɯ-ra] kɯ-tu] me \\
1sg interj also tral - aor - auto -say[II]- 1sg sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact lnk 1sg advers ipfv -become- 1sg also sbj: pcp -be.needed not.exist: fact lnk 2sg. poss - emph together.with emph come: fact - 1sg be: fact lnk dem apart.from 1sg: gen sbj: pcp -be.needed sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact \\
`I did not go and heed [the girl who was calling us], and I don't need to become anything special, I don't need anything, apart from following you.' (2003 kandZislama)
exe

The postverbal negative existential verb can be combined with a verb taking the negative prefix, forming a double negation (§ sec:double.negation ) expressing universal quantification ( ex:mAnAmandZi.me ).

exe

kɯ-ŋɤn mɤ-nɤma-ndʑi maka me\\
sbj: pcp -be.evil neg -do: fact - du at.all not.exist: fact \\
`There is no evil thing that they do not do/They do all kinds of evil things.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh)
0003886#S162
exe

In addition, postverbal negative existential verbs are used in one of the superlative constructions (§ sec:negative.existential.superlative ).
(§ sec:bare.inf.negative )
summary:
The passage describes postverbal negative existential verbs me and maŋe as part of a periphrastic negation construction, parallel to the negative copula maʁ. With transitive verbs, this construction can express universal negation of the object or a non-specific object, while with intransitive verbs it indicates that an action does not occur at all.  

It also shows that the scope of negation is not always limited to the object: it can apply to a theme, an essive adjunct, or a participial clause, and the construction may combine with a negative prefix to express universal quantification. In addition, these negative existential verbs are used in certain superlative constructions.

text:
verb!repetition
Copulas are exceptional in being the only verbs that can be repeated to express emphasis. This usage is only found in the traditional story register, as in ( ex:tWNu.tWNu ). This construction differs from partial reduplication, which only targets one syllable (§ sec:partial.redp ).

exe

nɯ kɯ-fse ci tɯ-ŋu, nɯ mɤ-kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ ci tɯ-ŋu tɯ-ŋu \\
dem sbj: pcp -be.like indef 2-be: fact dem neg - sbj: pcp -be.the.same indef 2-be: fact 2-be: fact \\
`You are (someone) like that, you are different (from normal people).' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe
summary: Copulas are the only verbs that can be repeated to express emphasis, and this pattern occurs only in the traditional story register. It is distinct from partial reduplication, since it repeats the entire verb rather than just one syllable.

text:
Apart from the constructions discussed above, existential verbs are attested in an unusual type of alternative concessive conditional (§ sec:alt.concessive.conditional ), combined with the bare stem of the verb (§ sec:bare.inf.negative ), and in periphrastic modal constructions (§ sec:cimame.cinAmaRkW ).

Existential verbs can also occur with the adverb jamarabout to build an equative construction `as big as $X$' (§ sec:sthWci.equative ) as in ( ex:ajaR.ki.jamar.GAZu ).

exe

ki aʑo a-jaʁ ki jamar ɣɤʑu. \\
dem. prox 1sg 1sg. poss -hand dem. prox about exist: sens \\
`The wild yak horn is about as big as my hand here.' (20-RmbroN)
0003560#S26
exe
summary: Existential verbs are attested in several special constructions: an unusual type of alternative concessive conditional, with the bare stem of the verb in negative bare infinitive contexts, and in periphrastic modal constructions. They can also combine with the adverb *jamar* to form equative expressions meaning “as big as X,” as illustrated by the example meaning “about as big as my hand.”

text:
This chapter, building on previous work by on Tshobdun and Situ, and on on Japhug, presents an overview of relativizing constructions in Japhug.

Three different ways of classifying relative clauses are outlined, respectively based on the form of the verb and the structure of the clause (§ sec:relative.subtypes ), on the position of the relativized element (§ sec:position.head.relative ) and on its function in the relative clause (§ sec:function.relativization ).

Various morphosyntactic phenomena specific to relative clauses (including resumptive pronouns, case marking etc) are discussed in § sec:relative.morphosyntactic.specificities, and some potential ambiguities between relative and complement clauses are analyzed in § sec:relative.complement.ambiguities.

Two sections are devoted to the functions of relative clauses other than noun modification: focalization (using pseudo-clefts, § sec:pseudo.cleft ) and quantification (universal quantification and expression of indefiniteness, § sec:headless.relatives.quantification ).

Since an important proportion of relative clauses in Japhug are participial clauses, section § sec:participles in a previous chapter partially overlaps with some of the sections of this chapter.
summary:
The chapter gives an overview of relativizing constructions in Japhug, building on previous work on Tshobdun, Situ, and Japhug. It presents three ways of classifying relative clauses—by verb form and clause structure, by the position of the relativized element, and by its function—and also discusses relative-clause-specific morphosyntax and possible ambiguities with complement clauses.  

It further examines uses of relative clauses beyond noun modification, including focalization through pseudo-clefts and quantification, and notes that participial clauses overlap substantially with some of the material covered in this chapter.

text:
relative clause!participle
Participles (§ sec:participles ) are the main way of building relative clauses in Japhug. Three types of participles are found: subject kɯ- (§ sec:subject.participles ), object kɤ- (§ sec:object.participle ) and oblique sɤ-/z- (§ sec:oblique.participle ).

The subject participle (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ) is the only available strategy to relativize subjects (whether from intransitive § sec:intr.subject.relativization or transitive verbs § sec:tr.subject.relativization ) and possessor of subjects (§ sec:S.possessor.relativization ).

The object participle is used to relativize objects and semi-objects (§ sec:object.participle.relatives ). It competes in this function with finite relative clauses (§ sec:object.relativization, § sec:semi.object.relativization ). It can also marginally relativize locative arguments (§ sec:object.participle.other.relative, § sec:locative.relativization ) and possessor of objects (§ sec:O.possessor.relativization ). Unprefixed object participles in kɤ- are not easily distinguishable from subject participles of passive forms kɯ-ɤ, due to vowel contraction (§ sec:object.participle.ambiguity ).

The oblique participle can relativize many non-core functions, including locative adjuncts (§ sec:locative.participle.relatives ), instruments (§ sec:instrumental.participle.relatives ) and other adjuncts (§ sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ), and compete in these functions with prenominal finite relatives (§ sec:locative.relativization, § sec:time.relativization ).

Since participial relative clauses are described in detail in chapter chap:non-finite, the reader is referred to the relevant sections in that chapter for a focused discussion.
summary: In Japhug, participles are the main strategy for forming relative clauses, and three kinds are distinguished: subject participles with kɯ-, object participles with kɤ-, and oblique participles with sɤ-/z-. Subject participles are the only way to relativize subjects and subject possessors, while object participles relativize objects and semi-objects and oblique participles relativize various non-core functions such as locatives and instruments.

text:
relative clause!finite
Some relative clauses in Japhug have a verb in finite form, with person indexation and TAME marking. For instance, the verb pɯ-mto-t-a in 1sg 3 (§ sec:indexation.mixed ) Aorist form of the headless relative clause in ( ex:aj.pWmtota.nW ) could stand on its own as a complete sentence meaning `I saw/have seen it'. The only clue that this appositive clause is a relative is the presence of the determiner nɯ, whose status in this context is discussed in § sec:relative.determiners.complementizer.

exe

ma ɯʑo ɯ-mdoʁ nɯnɯ, [aj pɯ-mto-t-a] nɯ, \\
lnk 3sg 3sg. poss -colour dem 1sg aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg dem \\
`[The wolves] that I have seen, the colour [of their fur is brown]' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S21
exe

Finite relative clauses are not however completely identical to the corresponding independent clauses, even when the head is internal (§ sec:head-internal.relative ). Four main morphosyntactic differences can be observed.

First, the verb of finite relative clauses can be subjected to totalitative reduplication (§ sec:totalitative.relatives ), a morphological category that is restricted to relative clauses, and not found in main clauses or other types of complement clauses.

Second, possessor prefixes in finite relative clause can undergo possessor neutralization (§ sec:relative.possessor.neutralization ).

Third, some TAME categories are not allowed in relative clauses, including Modal categories such as Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis ) and Imperative (§ sec:imperative ) and Evidential categories such as Inferential (§ sec:ifr ), Sensory (§ sec:sensory ) and Egophoric Present (§ sec:egophoric ). The TAME categories attested in finite relatives are Imperfective (§ sec:imperfective ), Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ), Aorist (§ sec:aor, as in ex:aj.pWmtota.nW above) and Past Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv ).

Fourth, there are some restrictions on person indexation in finite relative clauses. Monotransitive verbs are not attested in the corpus in local forms, and in inverse non-local forms (§ sec:monotransitive.object.relativization ). Only ditransitive verbs allow inverse and local person forms in relatives.

Finite relative clauses are not compatible with subject relativization, but they can be used when relativizing objects (§ sec:object.relativization ), semi-objects (§ sec:semi.object.relativization ), possessors of objects (§ sec:O.possessor.relativization ), goals (§ sec:locative.relativization.finite ), objects embedded in object complement clauses (§ sec:out.complement.relativization.tr ) and some time adjuncts (§ sec:time.relativization ).
summary:
In Japhug, some relative clauses are finite, showing person indexation and TAME marking, and may look like independent clauses except for the determiner nɯ that marks them as relative. However, they differ from main clauses in several ways: they allow totalitative reduplication and possessor neutralization, restrict certain TAME categories and person forms, and do not permit subject relativization. 

These finite relative clauses are used for relativizing objects, semi-objects, possessors of objects, goals, embedded objects, and some time adjuncts.

text:
relative clause!genitive genitive!relative clause
Both participial and finite prenominal relatives (§ sec:prenominal.relative ) are attested with a genitive marker ɣɯ (§ sec:gen.other ) before the head noun, which generally does not take a possessive prefix in this construction. This type of construction is common in texts translated from Chinese, and is certainly due to calquing from Chinese in many cases, for instance in ( ex:kurAZi.GW.relative ).

exe

[ɯʑo ku-rɤʑi] ɣɯ si ɯ-pa nɯtɕu jɤ-azɣɯt-nɯ \\
3sg ipfv -stay gen tree 3sg. poss -down dem: loc aor -arrive- pl \\
`They arrived at the bottom of the tree where he was staying.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S22
exe

A similar tendency to calque Chinese relative constructions with the genitive is observed in other Gyalrongic languages. For this reason, examples of genitival relative clauses from translated stories will not be taken into account in this chapter.

In non-translated texts and in conversations, prenominal genitival clauses are also marginally attested to relativize core arguments, as in ( ex:WkWnWsmAn.GW.smAnba ), though this is uncommon. Finite prenominal genitival clauses are however often used for locative and temporal adjunct relativization (§ sec:locative.relativization.finite ).

exe

[tɯ-ɕɤrɯ ɣɯ sm..., ɯ-kɯ-nɯsmɤn] ɣɯ smɤnba ŋu. \\
