indef. poss -bone gen incomplete word 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -treat gen doctor be: fact \\
`It is a doctor who treats bone [fractures].' (140426 laXthAB)
0003810#S34
exe

This type of clause should not be confused with superficially similar constructions such as that of complement-taking nouns (§ sec:complement.taking.IPN ), and with true genitival constructions with a headless relative clause possessor, as in ( ex:WkWGAwu.GW.tWrNa ), where the noun following the genitive ( tɯ-rŋa `one's face') is not an argument of the relative clause.

exe

[ɲɯ-kɯ-ɣɤwu] ɣɯ tɯ-rŋa nɯ tsa ɲɯ-fse tɕe \\
ipfv - sbj: pcp -cry gen genr. poss -face dem a.little sens -be.like lnk \\
`It looks a bit like the face of someone crying.' (18-qromJoR)
0003532#S97
exe
summary: Both participial and finite prenominal relatives can take a genitive marker ɣɯ before the head noun, usually without a possessive prefix, but this construction is often a calque from Chinese and is common in translated texts. In non-translated material it is only marginally attested for core arguments, though finite prenominal genitival clauses are often used for locative and temporal relativization. The passage also warns not to confuse these with similar complement-taking nouns or with true genitive constructions involving a headless relative clause possessor.

text:
relative clause!relator noun relator noun!relativization
Three inalienably possessed nouns, ɯ-stuplace, ɯ-staplace and ɯ-spamaterial, are semantically bleached when used as head of prenominal relatives (§ sec:prenominal.relative ), and are in the process of becoming grammaticalized as relativizers.

These three nouns are fossilized oblique participles ( tab:spa.sta.stu, § sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle ). The former two are used to relativize locative adjuncts, more exceptionally goals (§ sec:Wstu.relativization.subject ), while ɯ-spamaterial serves to build instrument (§ sec:instrument.relativization ) and in some cases object relative clauses.

The noun ɯ-spa still preserves its original meaning in examples such as ( ex:kACphAt.Wspa ), from which its other uses derive.

exe

tɯ-jaʁ ʁe nɯ kɯ [kɤ-ɕpʰɤt] ɯ-spa nɯ pjɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-stʰoʁ ŋu \\
genr. poss -hand left dem erg obj: pcp -patch 3sg. poss -material dem ipfv - inv - caus -press be: fact \\
`One presses with the left hand on the piece of cloth that is to be patched.' (12-kAtsxWb)
0003486#S33
exe

From the purposive object relative meaning `(material) that is to be $X$ed' as in ( ex:kACphAt.Wspa ), an instrumental interpretation `(material) that is used to $X$' arose: example ( ex:paR.kAmbi.Wspa ) illustrates the semantic proximity between oblique instrumental relative clauses (§ sec:instrumental.participle.relatives ) and the ɯ-spa clauses. Purposive clauses in ɯ-spa (§ sec:purposive.clauses ) also derive from this type of constructions.

exe

[paʁ ɯ-sɤ-χsu] ŋu, [paʁ kɤ-mbi] ɯ-spa ŋu \\
pig 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -feed be: fact pig obj: pcp -give 3sg. poss -material be: fact \\
`It is pig fodder, it is [something that can] be given to pigs.' (150822 laoye zuoshi zongshi duide-zh)
0006298#S170
exe

The relator nouns differ from other nouns serving as heads of relative clause in that they can occur even when an overt non-generic head noun is present, such as kʰɯnadog in ( ex:kAtsWm.Wspa.khWna ) and kɯspoʁhole in ( ex:BZW.WsAGi.Wstu ).

exe

tɤrʁaʁkɕi nɯ iɕqʰa, kɯ-ɣɤrʁaʁ, [kɤ-tsɯm] ɯ-spa kʰɯna nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
hunting.dog dem filler sbj: pcp -hunt obj: pcp -take.away 3sg. poss -material dog dem sens -be \\
`Hunting dogs are dogs that are taken to hunt.' (140426 liegou he zhonggou-zh)
0003812#S1
exe

exe

[βʑɯ ɯ-sɤ-ɣi] ɯ-stu kɯspoʁ nɯtɕu, iɕqʰa nɯnɯ z-ɲɯ-rku-nɯ. \\
mouse 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -come 3sg. poss -place hole dem: loc the.aforementioned dem tral - ipfv -put.in- pl \\
`People put [the flower of the burdock] in the holes which mice come out from (as a trap).' (13-tCamu)
0003498#S67
exe

These examples are very rare, and not unproblematic It could be alternatively possible to analyze kɯ-spoʁ as a subject participle ( tab:lexicalized.S.nmlz, § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ), and argue that ɯ-stu kɯ-spoʁ is a participial relative `the place that has a hole'. but nevertheless suggest that ɯ-spa, ɯ-stu and ɯ-sta are advancing in the grammaticalization cline. In the closely related language Khroskyabs, the clitic =spi, exact cognate of ɯ-spa ( tab:spa.sta.stu, § sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle ), has become the main object relativizer. The clitic =spi has a function that is still close to that of ɯ-spa in examples such as ( ex:paR.kAmbi.Wspa ): explains that it refers to `un objet spécifiquement destiné à subir l’action.'
summary:
The passage says that three inalienably possessed nouns, ɯ-stu, ɯ-sta, and ɯ-spa, are semantically bleached when used as heads of prenominal relatives and are becoming grammaticalized as relativizers. ɯ-stu and ɯ-sta mainly relativize locative adjuncts (and sometimes goals), while ɯ-spa is used for instrument relatives and occasionally object relatives; its original purposive meaning “(material) that is to be X-ed” gives rise to the instrumental interpretation “(material) that is used to X.”

It also notes that these relator nouns can appear even when an overt non-generic head noun is present, though such examples are rare and somewhat problematic. Overall, the examples suggest that ɯ-spa, ɯ-stu, and ɯ-sta are progressing along a grammaticalization path, with the related Khroskyabs clitic =

text:
relative clause!correlative pronoun!interrogative
All interrogative pronouns, including tɕʰiwhat (§ sec:tChi ), ɕɯwho (§ sec:CW.pronoun ), ŋotɕuwhere (§ sec:NotCu ) and tʰɤjtɕuwhen (§ sec:thAstWG ), can be used in correlative relative constructions as free-choice indefinites `whoever/whatever/whenever' (§ sec:interrogative.indef ). The pronoun can occur on its own or in apposition with an overt head noun as in ( ex:cai.tChi.tandza ).

exe

ɯʑo kɯ [ <cai> tɕʰi ta-ndza] nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-mdoʁ nɯ ɲɯ-ndɤm ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3sg erg vegetable what aor:3 -eat dem gen 3sg. poss -colour dem ipfv -take[III] sens -be \\
`It takes the colour of whatever vegetable it has eaten.' (25-caiqajW)
0003634#S18
exe

When a postclausal relator noun head (§ sec:prenominal.relative, § sec:Wstu.relativization.subject ) is present as in ( ex:NotCu.jAkAri.Wstu ), the interrogative pronoun remains in situ.

exe

[ ŋotɕu jɤ-kɯ-ɤri] ɯ-stu nɯtɕu kɯ-mɤrʑaβ kɯ-ɕe ra tu-ti-nɯ ŋgrɤl. \\
where aor - sbj: pcp -go[II] 3sg. poss -place dem: loc sbj: pcp -marry genr:S/O-go: fact be.needed: fact ipfv -say- pl be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`People say that whatever place [the ladybug] flies to, is where one has to go to get married.' (26-kWlAGpopo)
0003670#S38
exe

Correlative relatives can be participial ( ex:NotCu.jAkAri.Wstu, ex:tChi.nWkWGe ) or finite ( ex:cai.tChi.tandza ), depending on the function of the relativized element (§ sec:function.relativization ).

exe

[ɯ-jaʁ tɕʰi nɯ-kɯ-ɣe ʑo] tu-ndze \\
3sg. poss -hand what aor: west - sbj: pcp -come[II] emph ipfv -eat[III] \\
`It eats whatever it can get its hands on.' (28-qapar)
0003700#S103
exe

In ( ex:CW.kW.kWmWrkW ), the fact that the interrogative pronoun ɕɯwho takes the ergative shows that it belongs to the same clause as the transitive verb lu-kɤ-tɕɤt, as the matrix verb cʰacan is intransitive (§ sec:semi.transitive ): it is therefore embedded within the complement clause.

exe

[[ ɕɯ kɯ [kɯ-mɯrkɯ kɯ-ŋu] lu-kɤ-tɕɤt] pɯ-kɯ-cʰa] nɯ, a-sci rɟɤlpu cʰɯ-ta-sɯ-ndo-nɯ ŋu \\
who erg sbj: pcp -steal sbj: pcp -be ipfv - inf -take.out aor - sbj: pcp -can dem 1sg. poss -instead king ipfv -1 2- caus -take- pl be: fact \\
`Whoever succeeds in catching (the one who) is the thief, I will make him king in my stead.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S5
exe

Possessors of subjects (§ sec:S.possessor.relativization ) can also undergo correlative maximalizing relativization, as in (§ sec:S.possessor.relativization ).

exe

[ ɕɯ ɯ -tɯ-ji kɯ-nɤtɯɣ] nɯnɯra kɯ tɤ-mtʰɯm ku-sqa-nɯ tɕe, \\
who 3sg. poss - indef. poss -field sbj: pcp -happen.to.be dem: pl erg indef. poss -meat ipfv -cook- pl lnk \\
`Whoever$_i$ [it is] whose$_i$ fields happen to be [the ones that are to be ploughed by the whole village$_j$], those people$_i$ cook meat (for the village$_j$).' (150909 kWnWjlAmtshi)
0006306#S17
exe

Correlative relatives have commonalities with universal concessive conditionals (§ sec:universal.concessive.conditional ), but in the latter the subordinate clause and the main clause do not necessarily share a common element.
summary:
All interrogative pronouns in the language can be used in correlative relative constructions as free-choice indefinites meaning ‘whoever/whatever/whenever,’ either alone or with an overt head noun. If a postclausal relator noun head is present, the interrogative remains in situ, and correlative relatives may be either participial or finite depending on the relativized function.  

The passage also notes that the ergative marking on an interrogative pronoun can show it belongs to the same clause as the transitive verb in an embedded complement, and that possessors of subjects may undergo this kind of correlative relativization. Correlative relatives resemble universal concessive conditionals, but unlike those conditionals, the subordinate and main clauses in correlative relatives share a common element.

text:
This section presents morphosyntactic phenomena distinguishing relative clauses from independent sentences or complement clauses, including resumptive pronouns (§ sec:resumptive ), case marking (§ sec:relative.genitive.possessor.subject ), possessive prefix neutralization (§ sec:relative.possessor.neutralization ), determiner replication (§ sec:relative.determiners ) and totalitative reduplication (§ sec:totalitative.relatives ).

It also shows that the demonstrative-like elements nɯ that follow the relatives
are not complementizers (§ sec:relative.determiners.complementizer ), and discusses word order within the relative, in particular the presence of postverbal elements in head-internal relative clauses (§ sec:relative.postverbal ).
summary: The section describes several morphosyntactic features that distinguish relative clauses from independent sentences and complement clauses, including resumptive pronouns, special case marking, possessive prefix neutralization, determiner replication, and totalitative reduplication. It also argues that the demonstrative-like element nɯ following relatives is not a complementizer, and it discusses word order in relatives, especially postverbal elements in head-internal relative clauses.

text:
pronoun!resumptive relative clause!resumptive pronoun
A resumptive third person pronoun ɯʑo occurs in conjoined relative clauses with the correlative additive focus marker ri (§ sec:ri.additive ). It is obligatory in this construction when the relativized element is the intransitive subject, as in the clause ɯʑo$_i$ ri kɯ-sna in ( ex:WZo.ri.kWsna ).

exe

nɯnɯ [ ɯ $_i$-pʰɯ ri kɯ-wxti] [ ɯʑo $_i$ ri kɯ-sna] ŋu \\
dem 3sg. poss -price also sbj: pcp -be.big 3sg also sbj: pcp -be.good be: fact \\
`[Silver] is (a metal that is) both expensive (whose price is big) and nice.' (30-Com)
0003736#S190
exe

This construction occurs in particular in texts from Chinese to translate the construction 又……又…… yòu X yòu Yboth X and Y, as in ( ex:WZo.ri.kWwxti ). The Chinese original has 这只癞蛤蟆又大又丑 zhè zhī làiháma yòu dà yòu chǒuthe toad was big and ugly.

exe

nɯnɯ qajɯ kɯ-sɤjlɯ jloʁ nɯ jo-ɣi tɕe, [ ɯʑo ri kɯ-wxti], [ ɯʑo ri kɯ-sɤjlɯ jloʁ] ci pjɤ-ŋu. \\
dem bug sbj: pcp - emph disgusting dem ifr -come lnk
3sg also sbj: pcp -be.big 3sg also sbj: pcp - emph be.disgusting indef ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The disgusting creature (the toad) came, it was big and disgusting.' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh)
0006334#S84
exe
summary: A resumptive third person pronoun ɯʑo appears in conjoined relative clauses with the additive focus marker ri, and it is obligatory when the relativized element is the intransitive subject. This construction is especially used in translations of Chinese **yòu X yòu Y** ‘both X and Y,’ as illustrated by examples meaning ‘both expensive and nice’ or ‘big and disgusting.’

text:
reduplication!totalitative totalitative!reduplication relative clause!totalitative reduplication
The main verb of relative clauses, whether in participial ( ex:kWkWngo.kWkAkWnAndza ) or in finite form ( ex:pWpaGWtndZi, ex:tWtAfsea ), can undergo reduplication of the first syllable (§ sec:verb.initial.redp ) to express universal quantification of the relativized element, whose syntactic function can be object ( ex:pWpaGWtndZi ), semi-object ( ex:tWtAfsea ) or intransitive subject ( ex:kWkWngo.kWkAkWnAndza ), and even transitive subject ( ex:qartshaz.pWpWkWmtshAm ) (however some transitive subject participle cannot undergo initial reduplication for morphological reasons, see § sec:totalitative.redp ).

exe

[ tɯ-rɣi pɯ pa-ɣɯt-ndʑi ʑo] nɯnɯ lo-ji-ndʑi. \\
indef. poss -seed total aor:3: down -bring- du emph dem ifr -plant- du \\
`They planted all the seeds that they had brought (down from heaven).' (31-deluge)
0004077#S145
exe

exe

[aʑo tɯ tɤ-fse-a] nɯ tɤ-fse tɕe \\
1sg total aor -be.like- 1sg dem imp -be.like lnk \\
`Do everything like I do.' (140426 jiagou he lang-zh,18)
0003804#S17
exe

exe

<zhengfu> kɯ [kɯ kɯ-ngo], nɯnɯ [kɯ kɤ-kɯ-nɤndza ʑo] nɯ, andi comuco tɕetu taʁ ri, nɤki tsʰupa ci tu tɕe, ɯnɯre to-sɯ-ɤwɯwum. \\
government erg total sbj: pcp -be.sick dem total aor - sbj: pcp -have.leprosy emph dem west topo up.there up loc filler village indef exist: fact lnk dem: loc ifr - caus -gather \\
`In the west up there in Kyomkyo there is a village. The government gathered all the sick people, all the lepers, up there.' (25-khArWm)
0003644#S58
exe

exe

tɕe nɯra qartsʰaz mu nɯra, [pɯ pɯ-kɯ-mtsʰɤm] nɯ ɯ-rkɯ nɯtɕu tu-owɯwum-nɯ ŋu \\
lnk dem: pl deer female dem: pl total aor - sbj: pcp -hear dem 3sg. poss -side dem: loc ipfv -gather- pl \\
`All the does that have heard [the buck] gather around it.' (27-qartshAz)
0003702#S131
exe

Although initial reduplication occurs with finite verb forms in main clauses with various meanings (§ sec:verb.initial.redp ), totalitative reduplication is exclusively attested in relative clauses. A more detailed discussion of this phenomenon is provided in § sec:totalitative.redp.

Totalitative reduplication is specificity to relative clauses, and does not occur in complement clauses. It can be used as a test to distinguish between the two types of clauses in ambiguous cases (§ sec:relative.complement.ambiguities ).
summary:
Totalitative reduplication is a relative-clause phenomenon in which the main verb may reduplicate its first syllable to express universal quantification over the relativized element. It can occur with relativized objects, semi-objects, intransitive subjects, and even transitive subjects, though some participial forms are excluded for morphological reasons.  

The text emphasizes that, unlike ordinary initial reduplication in finite main clauses, totalitative reduplication is attested only in relative clauses and not in complement clauses, so it can help distinguish ambiguous clause types.

text:
genitive
In object relative clauses (§ sec:object.relativization ), transitive subjects can sometimes be marked by the genitive instead of the ergative, in particular when the agent can be construed as a possessor of the object, as in the finite headless relative in ( ex:aZWG.nWnWBeta ).

exe

aʑɯɣ [nɯ-nɯ-βde-t-a] nɯ ɯ́-ŋu \\
1sg: gen aor - auto -throw- pst: tr - 1sg dem qu -be: fact \\
`Is it the one that I lost?' (140427 bianfu jingji he shuiniao-zh)
0003836#S28
exe

Example ( ex:GW.kW.nWkAkho ) illustrates the hesitation between the ergative in the first relative clause, and the genitive in the second one (where the agent is the former possessor of the object).

exe

tɕe [atu tɯmɯkɤrŋi kɯ ɯ-jaʁ nɯ-kɤ-kʰo] nɯ, smɤnmimitoʁ nɯnɯ ɣɯ [nɯ-kɤ-kʰo] nɯnɯ, ko-ɕtʰɯz\\
lnk up.there heavenly(god) erg 3sg. poss -hand aor - obj: pcp -give dem anthr dem gen aor - obj: pcp -give dem ifr: east -turn.towards\\
`He turned [the magical object] that the god from heaven had given him, that Smanmi Metog had given him, [in the direction of the râkshâsas].' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

In the case of participial object relatives with a possessive prefix, the transitive subject/possessor does not require genitive marking, just in the same way as possessive prefixes on the possessum (with optional genitive) are sufficient to mark possession between two nouns (§ ex:prefix.expression.of.possession, § sec:gen.possession ). In ( ex:WZo.WkAtshi ) for instance, the pronoun ɯʑo `it' (the camel) directly precedes the participle ɯ-kɤ-tsʰi `the (water) that it drinks' without either ergative or genitive marker.

exe

ɯ-zgo ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu ɯʑo [ɯ-kɤ-tsʰi] tu-nɯ-rke ɲɯ-kʰɯ \\
3sg. poss -mountain 3sg. poss -inside dem: loc 3sg 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -drink ipfv - auto -put.in[III] sens -be.possible \\
`[The camel] can store the [water] that it drinks in its hump.' (19-rNamoN)
0003552#S48
exe

The transitive subject in these constructions is formally a possessor, external to the relative clause. In ( ex:stu.WsAtCha.WkAnWrga ) in particular, the presence of the degree adverb stumost (§ sec:stu.superlative ) between the pronoun ɯʑo and the head noun ɯ-sɤtɕʰa `its place' is a clue that ɯʑo is not included in the relative clause.

exe

tɕeri ɯʑo [stu ɯ-sɤtɕʰa ɯ-kɤ-nɯ-rga] nɯ, \\
lnk 3sg most 3sg. poss -place 3sg. poss - obj: pcp - appl -like dem \\
`The place that it likes most...' (20-xsar 10)
0003568#S10
exe
summary:
In object relative clauses, transitive subjects can sometimes take genitive marking instead of ergative, especially when the agent can be interpreted as the possessor of the object. In participial object relatives with a possessive prefix, however, the subject/possessor need not be marked genitively, because the possessive prefix alone can express the possessive relation.  

These constructions show that the transitive subject is formally outside the relative clause and functions as a possessor; in one example, the placement of the adverb *stu* indicates that the pronoun is not inside the relative clause.

text:
prefix!possessive neutralization!possessive prefix
In relative clauses, the possessor of inalienably possessed nouns can be neutralized to the indefinite possessor prefix tɯ-/tɤ- (§ sec:indef.genr.poss ), even when the possessor is definite. In ( ex:tWNga.nWkAmbi ) for example, the possessor of -ŋga `clothes' is the transitive subject of both sentences (the main character of the story), and is marked with the 3sg prefix ɯ- in the first sentence. In the second sentence, the noun -ŋga is located in a head-internal relative clause (§ sec:semi.object.relativization ), and even though the possessor is the same as in the previous sentence, the indefinite prefix tɯ- appears.

exe

tɕendɤre ɯ-ŋga ra ɲɤ-tɕɤt tɕe iɕqʰa, [rgɤnmɯ kɯ tɯ-ŋga nɯ-kɤ-mbi] nɯra ɲɤ-tɕɤt tɕe \\
lnk 3sg. poss -clothes pl ifr -take.off lnk filler old.woman erg indef. poss -clothes aor - obj: pcp -give dem: pl ifr -take.off lnk \\
`He took off his clothes, he took off the (magical) clothes that the old woman had given him.' (140508 shier ge tiaowu de gongzhu-zh)
0003937#S165
exe

Some inalienably possessed nouns have constraints on the syntactic function of the referent indexed by the possessive prefix (§ sec:biactantial.ipn ). In particular, tɤ-pɤropresent indexes the agent (the person giving the present) as possessor, never the recipient, as shown by ( ex:apAro.YWtambi ), where a 2sg nɤ-pɤro or an indefinite possessor tɤ-pɤro would be agrammatical (see also examples ex:apAro and ex:nApAro in § sec:biactantial.ipn ).

exe

a-pɤro ɲɯ-ta-mbi ŋu \\
1sg. poss -present ipfv -1 2-give be: fact \\
`I am giving it to you as a present.' (elicited)
exe

In relative clauses (whether participial or finite ones), it is possible to index the agent like in main clauses ( ex:apAro.relative ), but possessor neutralization is also possible, as in ( ex:tApAro.relative ).

exe

[a-pɤro nɯ-mbi-t-a] nɯ a-rɟit ŋu \\
1sg. poss -present aor -give- pst: tr - 1sg dem 1sg. poss -child be: fact \\
`The one to whom I gave a present is my child.' (elicited)
exe

exe

[tɤ-pɤro nɯ-mbi-t-a] tɤ-rɟit nɯ a-tɕɯ ŋu \\
indef. poss -present aor -give- pst: tr - 1sg indef. poss -child dem 1sg. poss -son be: fact \\
`The child to whom I gave a present is my son.' (elicited)
exe

Relative clauses are not the only syntactic contexts where possessor neutralization is attested: it also occurs when inalienably possessed nouns take prenominal modifiers (§ sec:possessive.prefixes.prenominal ).
summary: The passage explains that in relative clauses, the possessor of inalienably possessed nouns can be neutralized to the indefinite possessive prefix tɯ-/tɤ-, even when the possessor is definite in the discourse. It also notes that some inalienably possessed nouns impose restrictions on which participant can be indexed as possessor, but in relative clauses the agent can still be indexed as in main clauses, and possessor neutralization may alternatively occur. This neutralization is not limited to relative clauses, since it also appears when such nouns take prenominal modifiers.

text: relative clause!determiner
summary: The passage labels the construction as “relative clause!determiner,” indicating a grammatical category or function involving a relative clause used in determiner position. It presents the phrase as a combined label rather than a full explanatory discussion.

text:
In head-internal and postnominal relatives, postnominal determiners such as the indefinte marker ci (§ sec:indef.article ) or the demonstrative nɯ (§ sec:nW.topic ) can appear both on the internal head noun and repeated following the relative clause. In ( ex:rJAlpu.ci.kWNAn.ci ) for instance, ci occurs after the noun rɟɤlpuking and at the end of the relative after the participle kɯ-ŋɤn `(the one) who is evil'.

exe

[wuma ʑo rɟɤlpu ci kɯ-ŋɤn] ci pjɤ-tu tɕe, \\
really emph king indef sbj: pcp -be.evil indef ifr. ipfv -exist lnk \\
`There was a very evil king.' (140511 1001 yinzi-zh)
0003963#S9
exe

In ( ex:tAkhW.sAZnWlhoR ), the indefinite ci is also repeated after the head noun kɯspoʁ `hole' (a lexicalized participle, § sec:lexicalized.subject.participle ) and following the participle sɤz-nɯ-ɬoʁ `which (the smoke) comes out from' (with locative § sec:locative.participle.relatives or instrumental § sec:instrument.relativization relativizing function). In this case the relative can be analyzed as either postnominal or head-internal.

exe

[ kɯ-spoʁ ci tɤ-kʰɯ sɤz-nɯ-ɬoʁ] ci ɲɯ-βze \\
sbj: pcp -have.a.hole indef indef. poss -smoke obl: pcp - auto -come.out indef ipfv -make[III] \\
`[The potter] makes a hole which the smoke comes out from.' (30-kWrAfcAr)
0003740#S27
exe

Determiner repetition is also found with relativized transitive subjects marked with the ergative (see ex:WkWnWmbrApW in § sec:head-internal.relative.postnominal ).

Examples like ( ex:rJAlpu.ci.kWNAn.ci ) and ( ex:tAkhW.sAZnWlhoR ) are however relatively rare, in most cases the determiner either follows the relative (see for example ex:mWNi.kAkWGe.XpWn in § sec:intr.subject.relativization ) or the head noun ( ex:pGAtCW.ci.kWmpCWmpCAr )

exe

[ pɣɤtɕɯ ci kɯ-mpɕɯ mpɕɤr ʑo] jɤ-ɣe \\
bird indef sbj: pcp - emph be.beautiful emph aor -come[II] \\
`A beautiful bird came.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S14
exe

In the case of prenominal relatives, the determiner ci can be found between the head noun and the relative clause, as in ( ex:nW.kWfse.ci.qajW ). This usage is not to be confused with that of prenominal ci (§ sec:identity.modifier ).

exe

tɕe [nɯ kɯ-fse] ci qajɯ ɣɤʑu. \\
lnk dem sbj: pcp -be.like indef bug exist: sens \\
`There is a bug (invertebrate animal) that is like that.' (hist180421 haixing)
0006113#S27
exe
summary:
In head-internal and postnominal relatives, postnominal determiners such as the indefinite marker **ci** and the demonstrative **nɯ** may appear on the internal head noun and then be repeated after the relative clause. These patterns are relatively rare; more commonly, the determiner appears either after the relative clause or directly after the head noun, and similar determiner repetition is also found with relativized transitive subjects marked ergatively.

In prenominal relatives, **ci** can occur between the head noun and the relative clause, but this should not be confused with prenominal **ci** used as an identity modifier.

text:
An important proportion of relative clauses are followed by the forms nɯ and nɯnɯ, whose functions in other contexts include distal demonstrative pronouns (§ sec:demonstrative.pronouns ), demonstrative determiners (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners ) or topic markers (§ sec:nW.topic, § sec:definiteness ), and ra (and nɯra ), a plural marker (§ sec:plural.determiners ). In the case of finite relative clauses (§ sec:finite.relatives ), whose main verb generally has the same form as that of the corresponding independent sentence (in ex:pWXsuj.nW for instance), the presence of these words may be the only clue that the clause is a relative.

exe

[iʑo ndɤre pɯ-χsu-j] nɯ, tɯ-rdoʁ tɕʰi mɯ-pɯ-nnɯ-pe mɤ-xsi ma nɯnɯ nɯfse pjɤ-si \\
1pl lnk aor -feed- 1pl dem one-piece what neg - pst. ipfv - auto -be.good neg - genr:know lnk dem like.that ifr -die \\
`Of the [tortoises] that we raised, one [of them] died just like that, I don't know what went wrong.' (140510 wugui)
0003951#S51
exe

Given the fact that many languages have complementizers, including relative pronouns, which are homophonous with (and historically related to) demonstratives (for instance `that' in English), it is legitimate to wonder whether such an analysis to possible for the nɯ or nɯra that follow relative clauses.

However, in prenominal relatives such as ( ex:akAsWz.Cku ), nɯ is located after the head noun, for instance ɕkuAllium in ( ex:akAsWz.Cku ), never before it. If it were a subordinator, one would expect nɯ to be located between the head noun and the relative.

exe

tɕe [aʑo a-kɤ-sɯz] ɕku nɯ nɯra ŋu \\
lnk 1sg 1sg. poss - obj: pcp -know Allium dem dem: pl be: fact \\
`These are the [plants belonging to the gender] Allium that I know about.' (07-Cku)
0003424#S160
exe

Another clue that nɯ, nɯnɯ and nɯra in this context are better analyzed as demonstrative determiners (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners, with or without topicalizing function, § sec:nW.topic, § sec:definiteness ) is that relative clauses can take circumposed demonstratives (exactly like circumnominal demonstratives, § sec:demonstrative.determiners ), as shown by the pre- and post-clausal nɯnɯ in ( ex:nWnW.pGArnoR.kAti.nWnW ).

exe

nɯnɯ [pɣɤrnoʁ kɤ-ti] nɯnɯ tɤjmɤɣ tɤrca ɲɯ-ŋu ɯmɤ-kɯ-ŋu-ci ma \\
dem fungus.sp obj: pcp -say dem mushroom together sens -be prob - peg -be- peg lnk \\
`That [thing that] is called pɣɤrnoʁ is probably [to be classified] among the fungi.' (22-BlamajmAG)
0003584#S130
exe
summary: The passage argues that the forms nɯ, nɯnɯ, and nɯra often follow relative clauses and may be the only overt marker that a clause is relative, especially in finite relatives whose verb form otherwise matches an independent clause. Although these forms could be thought of as complementizers or relative pronouns, their position after the head noun in prenominal relatives and their ability to occur as circumposed demonstratives support analyzing them instead as demonstrative determiners, sometimes with topicalizing or definiteness functions.

text:
relative clause!postverbal position
Although Japhug is a strict verb-final language, some words can appear post-verbally in independent sentences, including sentence-final particles (§ sec:interjections ), ideophones (§ sec:ideo:morpho ) and some adverbs (§ sec:postverbal.adv ).

Relative clauses never take sentence-final particles (unlike some complement clauses, § sec:reported.speech.sfp ), but some postverbal elements are nevertheless possible.

First, the adverb tsaa little can occur postverbally with a semantic scope clearly restricted to the relative clause, as in ( ex:nWlWz.thWkWGe.tsa )

exe

[nɯ-lɯz tʰɯ-kɯ-ɣe tsa] nɯra tɕe, ʁdɯrɟɤt ɯ-skɤt tu-βze-a ɲɯ-tso-nɯ, \\
3pl. poss -age aor - sbj: pcp -come[II] a.little dem: pl lnk topo 3sg. poss -language ipfv -make[II]- 1sg sens -understand- pl \\
`Those who are a little older understand when I speak the [Japhug] language of Gdongbrgyad. (150901 tshuBdWnskAt)
0006242#S11
exe

Ideophones are very commonly postverbal even in relative clauses, as in ( ex:kWwGrum.sWNsWN ), though mainly with stative verbs in subject participle form.

exe

tɕe nɯ ɯ-βri ɯ-taʁ nɯra qandʐi kɯ-fse, aɣrɤɣrum kɯ-fse ma [kɯ-wɣrɯ wɣrum ʑo sɯŋsɯŋ] maʁ \\
lnk 3sg. poss -body 3sg. poss - top dem: pl be.dark: fact sbj: pcp -be.like be.whitish: fact sbj: pcp -be.like lnk lnk sbj: pcp -emph be.white emph idph (II):pure.white not.be: fact \\
`The top part [of the mushroom called kuɣrummɤɣ `white mushroom'] is dark, whitish, it is not pure white.' (21-kuGrummAG)
0003574#S2
exe

The emphatic ʑo (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ) is also analyzable as a postverbal adverb especially when followed by a demonstrative determiner as in ( ex:stu.kWjaR.Zo ) (see also ex:pWpaGWtndZi and ex:kWkWngo.kWkAkWnAndza, § sec:totalitative.relatives ).

exe

[ skɤm-ndʐi kɯ-jɯ jaʁ], [stu kɯ-jaʁ ʑo] nɯ tu-qɤr-nɯ tɕe \\
ox-skin sbj: pcp - emph be.thick most sbj: pcp -be.thick emph dem ipfv -select- pl lnk \\
`People select very thick ox skin, the thickest.' (24-mbGo) 0003621
exe

However, the indefinite determiner ci is also attested before the emphatic ʑo as in ( ex:smar.kWwxtWxti.ci ), showing that it is external to the relative in this case, since ci itself must be external (otherwise it would be located just after the head noun smarriver, § sec:head-internal.relative.determiners ).

exe

[ smar kɯ-wxtɯ wxti] ci ʑo pɯ-tu ɲɯ-ŋu \\
river sbj: pcp - emph be.big indef emph pst. ipfv -exist sens -be \\
`There was a huge river.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

In the absence of determiner (as in ex:pWpaGWtndZi, § sec:totalitative.relatives ), it is unclear whether postverbal ʑo belongs to the relative or not.
summary: Although Japhug is generally verb-final, relative clauses can still contain certain postverbal elements. The adverb *tsaa* ‘a little’ and ideophones can appear after the verb with scope restricted to the relative clause, and the emphatic *ʑo* may also be postverbal, though in some cases it is unclear whether it belongs to the relative clause or outside it. Relative clauses do not take sentence-final particles.

text: Pre-, post-nominal and head-internal relative clauses are all attested in Japhug, though the position of the relativized element is not free and depends on various factors, in particular its function in the relative clause.
summary: Japhug attests pre-nominal, post-nominal, and head-internal relative clauses. However, the position of the relativized element is not freely chosen, since it depends on several factors, especially the role that element plays within the relative clause.

text:
relative clause!headless
An important proportion, if not a large majority of the relatives in the corpus lack an overt head. For instance, in ( ex:pWkWsi.WCa ), minimal relative clause pɯ-kɯ-si `(the one(s)) that has/have died' only contains a verb in participial form (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ). The noun ɯ-ɕa `its meat/flesh' in ( ex:pWkWsi.WCa ) is not the head of the relative, but the possessee of that head (§ sec:genitival.relatives ).

exe

[pɯ-kɯ-si] ɯ-ɕa nɯ tu-ndze ŋu ma. \\
aor - sbj: pcp -die 3sg. poss -flesh dem ipfv -eat[III] be: fact lnk \\
`[Crows] eat the flesh of [animals] that have died.' (22-qajdo)
0003596#S15
exe

Nominal heads are optional in relative clauses (as they are in the noun phrase in general, § sec:noun.phrases.word.order ). The only non-optional heads are the resumptive pronouns that occur in a very specific construction (§ sec:resumptive ) and the possessive prefixes on the possessee in relatives whose heads are possessor of subject or object (§ sec:possessor.relativization ).
summary: The passage explains that many relative clauses in the corpus are headless, meaning they do not contain an overt nominal head; an example is a clause consisting only of a participial verb meaning “that has/have died.” It notes that in such cases a nearby noun may be the possessee of the head rather than the head itself. More generally, nominal heads are optional in relative clauses, with only resumptive pronouns and certain possessive prefixes being obligatory in specific constructions.

text:
relative clause!prenominal
Three types of prenominal relatives must be distinguished, depending on the nature of the relationship between the head noun and the relative clause.

First, genitival prenominal relatives are those in which the genitive marker ɣɯ is inserted between the subordinate clause and the head noun (§ sec:genitival.relatives ).

Second, relator noun prenominal relatives take generic inalienably possessed noun such as ɯ-spamaterial (§ sec:instrument.relativization, § sec:Wspa.relative ), ɯ-stuplace (§ sec:Wstu.relativization.subject ) or ɯ-sŋi `the day when' (§ sec:time.relativization ). This type of prenominal clauses are common in the case of adjunct relativization.

Third, standard prenominal relative clauses have head nouns without possessive prefixes (unless the head noun is inalienably possessed, in which case possessor neutralization may take place, § sec:relative.possessor.neutralization ). They are the preferred relativization type in the case of transitive subjects (§ sec:tr.subject.relativization ), and are also available for other core arguments (§ sec:object.relativization, § sec:intr.subject.relativization ).
summary: The passage distinguishes three types of prenominal relative clauses, based on how the head noun relates to the relative clause: genitival relatives, relator noun relatives, and standard prenominal relatives. Genitival relatives use the genitive marker ɣɯ, relator noun relatives use generic inalienably possessed nouns such as ɯ-spa, ɯ-stu, or ɯ-sŋi, and standard prenominal relatives usually have head nouns without possessive prefixes and are the preferred type for transitive subjects.

text:
relative clause!head-internal
When the head noun of the relative is overt, it can occur within the relative at the position that would be expected in the corresponding independent sentence: for instance, the noun tɯ-ŋgaclothes is located between the instrumental adjunct and the verb both in the head-internal relative in ( ex:tWNga.thWkABzu ) and in the independent clause in ( ex:tWNga.chWBzunW ).

exe

[tɤ-rme kɯ tɯ-ŋga tʰɯ-kɤ-βzu] nɯra ʁɟa tu-ndze ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
indef. poss -hair erg indef. poss -clothes aor - obj: pcp -make dem: pl completely ipfv -eat[III] sens -be \\
`It eats all of the clothes that are made of [animal] hair.' (28-kWpAz)
0003714#S104
exe

exe

paʁ-ndʐi kɯ tɯ-ŋga cʰɯ-βzu-nɯ, paʁ-ndʐi kɯ tɯ-xtsa tu-βzu-nɯ ra ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl \\
pig-skin erg indef. poss -clothes ipfv -make- pl pig-skin erg indef. poss -shoes ipfv -make- pl pl sens -be.usually.the.case \\
`(Nowadays, unlike in former times), [people] make clothes and shoes from pig skin.' (05-paR)
0003400#S108
exe

The following subsections focus on the conditions where head-internal relatives are selected rather than prenominal ones (§ sec:head-internal.relative.prenominal ), and on the criteria that can be used to distinguish between head-internal and postnominal relatives (§ sec:head-internal.relative.postnominal ).
summary: When the head noun is overt in a head-internal relative clause, it appears inside the relative clause in the same position it would occupy in an independent sentence. The passage gives examples showing the noun for “clothes” occurring before the verb in both the relative clause and the corresponding main clause, and notes that later sections will discuss when head-internal relatives are used instead of prenominal ones and how to distinguish them from postnominal relatives.

text:
ambiguity!relative clause
Core argument relatives can be either head-internal or prenominal. When the relativized element is the transitive subject, prenominal position is more common (§ sec:tr.subject.relativization ), but for intransitive subject (§ sec:intr.subject.relativization ), direct object (§ sec:object.relativization ) and quasi-objects (§ sec:semi.object.relativization ), head-internal relatives are by far the most common type.

When the relativized element is a noun such as tɯ-tɕʰainformation, news or ftɕakamethod which can take adnominal complements (§ sec:complement.taking.nouns ), only head-internal relatives are possible, as prenominal clauses are interpreted as complements instead of relatives. For instance, the head noun tɯ-tɕʰa in ( ex:tWtCha.jAkAGWt ) cannot be moved after the participle: $ $ a-tɕɯ kɯ jɤ-kɤ-ɣɯt tɯ-tɕʰa nɯ is not accepted.

exe

[a-tɕɯ kɯ tɯ-tɕʰa jɤ-kɤ-ɣɯt] nɯ ɲɯ-pe \\
1sg. poss -son erg indef. poss -news aor - obj: pcp -bring dem sens -be.good \\
`The information that my son has brought is pleasing.' (elicited)
exe
summary: Core argument relatives may be either head-internal or prenominal. Prenominal relatives are more common when the relativized element is a transitive subject, but head-internal relatives are far more common for intransitive subjects, direct objects, and quasi-objects. When the relativized noun is one that can take adnominal complements, only head-internal relatives are possible, because a prenominal clause is interpreted as a complement rather than a relative clause.

text:
ambiguity!relative clause

Since Japhug has strict verb-final order (§ sec:basic.word.order ), in head-internal relative clauses the verb follows the head noun, as it would in a postnominal relative. In many cases it is indeed impossible to ascertain whether the head-noun belongs or not to the relative. For instance, in ( ex:khWtsa.pWkABRum ) kʰɯtsa pɯ-kɤ-βʁum `a bowl that has been turned upside down' there is no clear evidence for analyzing the head noun kʰɯtsabowl as internal or external to the relative.

exe

kʰɯtsa pɯ-kɤ-βʁum ʑo ɲɯ-fse. \\
bowl aor - obj: pcp -turn.upside.down emph sens -be.like \\
`It looks like a bowl that has been turned upside down.' (23-mbrAZim)
0003604#S195
exe

However, with other types of relative clauses there is sometimes positive evidence that the head noun is internal. When the function of the relativized element is that of transitive subject (§ sec:tr.subject.relativization ), the presence of ergative marking can be a criterion for analyzing it as relative-internal. In ( ex:WkWnWmbrApW ) for instance, the phrase tɤ-pɤtso ci kɯ is necessarily internal to the participial relative clause, since the main verb jɤ-ɣe is intransitive, and only the transitive verb ɯ-kɯ-nɯmbrɤpɯ in the relative clause can have triggered ergative marking. In addition, example ( ex:WkWnWmbrApW ) provides an interesting case of double determiner marking (§ sec:head-internal.relative.determiners ).

exe

[ tɤ-pɤtso ci kɯ <yangma> ɯ-kɯ-nɯmbrɤpɯ] ci jɤ-ɣe tɕe \\
indef. poss -child indef erg bicycle 3sg - sbj. pcp -ride indef aor -come[II] lnk \\
`A boy who was riding a bicycle arrived.' (Pear story, Tshendzin )
exe

In ( ex:tArJit.tAkWrqoR ) however, the transitive subject tɯrme owes its ergative to the main verb ɲɯ-jtsʰi rather than to the participle tɤ-kɯ-rqoʁ. The clause tɤ-rɟit tɤ-kɯ-rqoʁ `hugging the child' is analyzable either as an appositive postnominal relative clause, or as a participial clause.

exe

[tɯrme kɯ [tɤ-rɟit tɤ-kɯ-rqoʁ] tɯ-nɯ ɲɯ-jtsʰi] nɯ kɯ-fsɯ fse ʑo ɲɯ-jtsʰi ɲɯ-ŋu.\\
person erg indef. poss -child aor - sbj: pcp -hug indef. poss -breast ipfv -give.to.drink dem sbj: pcp - emph be.like emph ipfv -give.to.drink sens -be \\
`[The monkey mother] nurses [her baby] in the same way as a human breastfeeds, hugging her child.' (19-GzW)
0003536#S26
exe

In the case of object relatives, the presence of the transitive subject ( tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ `the boy' in ex:WtaYi.kathW ), of an adjunct (the instrumental phrase rŋɯl kɯ `from silver' in ex:qaR.thWkAsWBzu ) or of an adverb ( atʰi downstream in ex:kAntsGe.lukAGWt ) belonging to the relative before the head noun are sufficient criteria to show that the relative is head-internal, and cannot be analyzed as post-nominal.

exe

[tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ ɯ-tɤɲi nɯ ka-tʰɯ] nɯ ɯ-taʁ kɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ-ndʑi \\
indef. poss -son dem erg 3sg. poss -staff dem aor:3: east -spread dem 3sg. poss -on aor: east - auto -come.out- du \\
`They crossed [the river] on the staff that the boy had put across it as a bridge.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

exe

[rŋɯl kɯ qaʁ tʰɯ-kɤ-sɯ-βzu] nɯra ko-sɯ-ɤʑirja-nɯ. \\
silver erg hoe aor - obj: pcp - caus -make dem: pl ifr - caus -be.aligned- pl \\
`They lined up the hoes that had been made from silver.' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S97
exe

exe

kɯki [atʰi qaɕti kɤ-ntsɣe lu-kɤ-ɣɯt] nɯ cʰo naχtɕɯɣ \\
dem. prox downstream peach inf -sell ipfv: upstream - obj: pcp -bring dem comit be.the.same: fact \\
`[Wild peaches] are like those peaches that are brought from the areas downstream (i.e. the Sichuan plains) to be sold.' (08-qaCti)
0003456#S45
exe
summary: Because Japhug has strict verb-final order, head-internal relative clauses can be hard to distinguish from postnominal relatives, since the verb follows the head noun in both. The passage notes that ergative marking can sometimes prove that the head noun is internal in transitive-subject relatives, and that in object relatives the presence of a subject, adjunct, or adverb before the head noun shows the clause must be head-internal.

text:
relative clause!postnominal
There are only few unambiguous postnominal relative clauses in Japhug, since most relative clauses comprising a noun and a verb can be analyzed as minimal head-internal relatives. The only clear cases are provided by transitive subject (§ sec:tr.subject.relativization ) participial relative clauses in kɯ- (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ). In these cases, the head noun, being a transitive subject, must take the ergative kɯ (§ sec:A.kW ) if embedded in the clause. The presence or absence of ergative flagging can therefore be used as a criterion to distinguish between postnominal and head-internal clauses (§ sec:head-internal.relative.postnominal ). Examples are rather uncommon, since transitive subject relative clauses are most commonly prenominal (§ sec:tr.subject.relativization ).

Many examples of postnominal relatives are preceded by a pause, as in ( ex:tWsNaR.WkWspa ), and are appositive clauses, rather than truly subordinate clauses.

exe

tɤ - mu ci, [tɯ-sŋaʁ ra ɯ-kɯ-spa] ci pjɤ-tu tɕe \\
indef. poss -mother indef nmlz: action -cast.a.spell pl 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -be.able indef ifr. ipfv -exist lnk \\
`There was an old woman who knew spells.' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh)
0006334#S15
exe

Several examples of postnominal clauses are found with perception verbs with totalitative reduplication, such as ( ex:tWrme.pWpWkWmto2 ) below, ( ex:qartshaz.pWpWkWmtshAm ) in § sec:totalitative.relatives above and ( ex:tWrme.pWpWkWmto ) in § sec:tr.subject.relativization.

exe

[ tɯrme ra [pɯ pɯ-kɯ-mto]] kɯ ``wo, nɯ ɯ-tɯ-pe nɯ" ntsɯ to-ti-nɯ. \\
person pl total aor - sbj: pcp -see erg interj dem 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.good sfp always ifr -say- pl \\
`All the people who saw it said `It is so nice!'.' (150827 mengjiangnv-zh)
0006290#S24
exe

When the relativized element is the intransitive subject, head-internal and postnominal relatives can be distinguished by the relative position of head nouns and adjuncts. It is particularly clear in the case of the comparative construction (§ comparee.relativization ).
summary:
Japhug has only a few unambiguous postnominal relative clauses, because most noun–verb sequences can instead be analyzed as minimal head-internal relatives. The clearest postnominal cases are transitive-subject participial relatives in kɯ-, where ergative kɯ marking on the head noun helps distinguish them from head-internal clauses; however, such examples are uncommon and transitive-subject relatives are usually prenominal.

Many postnominal relatives are preceded by a pause and seem to function as appositive clauses rather than true subordinate clauses. Postnominal relatives also occur with perception verbs and totalitative reduplication, and for intransitive-subject relativization they can be identified by the relative ordering of head nouns and adjuncts, especially in comparative constructions.

text:
This section presents a classification of relative clauses based on the syntactic function of the relativized element inside the relative.

Core arguments, possessor of core arguments as well as a certain number of adjuncts can be relativized using participial or finite clauses. The syntactic functions that are not accessible to relativization are listed in § sec:accessibility.relativization.
summary: Relative clauses are classified according to the syntactic function of the element being relativized within the clause. Core arguments, possessors of core arguments, and some adjuncts can be relativized through participial or finite clauses, while other syntactic functions are not accessible to relativization.

text:
relative clause!intransitive subject subject!relativization
The only way to relativize intransitive subjects in Japhug is by a subject participial relative in kɯ- (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ).
summary: In Japhug, intransitive subjects can only be relativized through a subject participial relative construction. This construction uses the prefix **kɯ-**.

text:
When the head noun of an intransitive subject relative is overt, it is generally located before the participle as in ( ex:tArZaB.jAkWGe ). This example can be analyzed either as a postnominal relative (§ sec:postnominal.relative ) or as minimal head-internal relative (§ sec:head-internal.relative ).

exe

[ tɤ-rʑaβ jɤ-kɯ-ɣe] nɯnɯ kʰro mɯ-pɯ-sna ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
indef. poss -wife aor - sbj: pcp -come[II] dem much neg - pst. ipfv -be.good sens -be \\
`The wife who had come [to their house] (i.e. that they had married) was not nice.' (meimeidegushi)
exe

The presence of adjuncts, such as kɯ-mɤku `before' (§ sec:velar.inf.adverb ) before the head noun offers evidence that, in some cases, the head-internal relative analysis is preferable (§ sec:head-internal.relative ). Example ( ex:kWnArWra.jAkAri ) also illustrates that head-internal relatives with embedded purposive complements located between the head noun and the verb are possible.

exe

iɕqʰa [kɯ-mɤku tɕaχpa [kɯ-nɤrɯra] jɤ-kɯ-ɤri] nɯ ʁnɯz nɯ pjɤ-sat. \\
the.aforementioned inf: stat -be.before thief sbj: pcp -look.around aor - sbj: pcp -go[II] dem two dem ifr -kill \\
`He killed the two thieves who had gone scouting just before.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S188
exe

Prenominal clauses (§ sec:prenominal.relative ) are less common than head-internal or postnominal ones in the case of intransitive subject relativization, but still attested, especially in the case of multiple relative clauses sharing the same head noun, as in ( ex:mWNi.kAkWGe.XpWn ).

exe

[mɯŋi kɤ-kɯ-ɣe] χpɯn [tʰɯ-kɯ-rgɤz] ci pjɤ-tu tɕe \\
topo aor: east - sbj: pcp -come[II] monk aor - sbj: pcp -be.old indef ipfv. ifr -exist \\
`There was an old monk who had come from Mengi.' (08-kWqhi)
0003454#S18
exe

Participles of adjectival stative verbs in attributive function are one of the most common type of subject relative clauses (this construction is discussed in more detail in § ex:attributive.participles.stative.verbs ).
summary: For intransitive subject relatives, an overt head noun is usually placed before the participle, and such examples can be analyzed either as postnominal relatives or as minimal head-internal relatives. The text notes that adjuncts before the head noun and purposive complements between the noun and verb can support a head-internal analysis, while prenominal relatives are less common but do occur, especially when multiple relative clauses share the same head noun. Participles from adjectival stative verbs in attributive use are also described as one of the most common types of subject relative clauses.

text:
relative clause!comparee
The compared element of comparative constructions is relativized like a normal intransitive subjects, but with an overt standard. Head-internal ( ex:WZo.sAz.rWdaR.kWxtCi ), postnominal ( ex:rWdaR.WZo.sAz.kWxtCi ) and prenominal ( ex:WZo.sAz.kWxtCi.qajW ) relatives are all attested and equally common, and can be distinguished by the relative position of the head noun and the standard of comparison ɯʑo sɤz `than him/her/itself'.

exe

xlist

[ɯʑo sɤz rɯdaʁ kɯ-xtɕi] nɯra tu-ndze \\
3sg comp animal sbj: pcp -be.small dem: pl ipfv -eat[III] \\
`It eats the animals that are smaller than it is.'(20-sWNgi)
0003562#S22

rɯdaʁ [ɯʑo sɤz kɯ-xtɕi], pɣa [ɯʑo sɤz kɯ-xtɕi] nɯra tu-ndze ɲɯ-ɕti. \\
animal 3sg comp sbj: pcp -be.small bird 3sg comp sbj: pcp -be.smal dem: pl ipfv -eat[III] sens -be. aff \\
`It eats the animals and the birds that are smaller than it is.'(24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S87

[ɯʑo sɤz kɯ-xtɕi] qajɯ ra tu-ndze ŋgrɤl mɤ-ŋgrɤl mɤ-xsi ma \\
3sg comp sbj: pcp -be.small bug pl ipfv -eat[III] be.usually.the.case: fact neg -be.usually.the.case: fact neg - genr:know lnk \\
