summary: The passage states that the compared element in comparative constructions is relativized like a normal intransitive subject, but with an overt standard of comparison. It notes that head-internal, postnominal, and prenominal relatives are all attested and equally common, and that these types are distinguished by the relative position of the head noun and the standard marker *ɯʑo sɤz* ‘than him/her/itself’.

text:
relative clause!transitive subject subject!relativization
Transitive subjects are exclusively relativized using subject participial relative clauses in kɯ- (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative ) like intransitive subjects (§ sec:intr.subject.relativization ), but take a possessive prefix coreferent with the object (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ), unless another prefix is present (§ sec:subject.participle.other.prefixes ).

In a minority of cases, the transitive subject head noun can occur before the verb. In this position, it sometimes takes the ergative, as illustrated by the phrase tɤ-nmaʁ nɯ kɯ in ( ex:tAnmaR.nW.kW.YWkWnWCar ).

exe

[ tɤ-nmaʁ nɯ kɯ ɯ-rʑaβ kɯ-ɤntɕʰɯ ɲɯ-kɯ-nɯ-ɕar], [aʁɤndɯndɤt tɤndɤɣri tu-kɯ-βzu] pjɤ-tu. \\
indef. poss -husband dem erg 3sg. poss -wife sbj: pcp -be.several ipfv - sbj: pcp - auto -search everywhere illegitimate.child ipfv - sbj: pcp -make ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`There were men who had several female companions, and had illegitimate children everywhere.' (140427 tAndAGri)
0003858#S3
exe

The presence of the ergative here unambiguously indicates that the relative is head-internal and that the transitive subject is embedded inside it, since the main verb pjɤ-tu `there used to be' is intransitive (§ sec:head-internal.relative.prenominal ).

Alternatively, the transitive subject can occur in absolutive form (for example tɯrme `person' in ex:tWrme.pWpWkWmto ), In ( ex:tWrme.pWpWkWmto ), the ergative kɯ follows the relative clause, which has transitive subject function in the main clause. The head noun tɯrme itself is not assigned ergative case by the transitive participle pɯ pɯ-kɯ-mto. showing that the relative is postnominal (§ sec:postnominal.relative ).

exe

[ tɯrme [pɯ pɯ-kɯ-mto]] kɯ ɲɯ-nɤ-mpɕɤr-nɯ tɕe ``ɲɯ-pe" tu-ti-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu \\
person total aor - sbj: pcp -see erg sens - trop -be.beautiful- pl lnk sens -be.good ipfv -say- pl ifr. ipfv -be \\
`All the people who saw it found it beautiful and said it was nice.' (140510 sanpian yumao-zh)
0003947#S83
exe

There are no examples of double ergative marking, with a head-internal relative in transitive subject function in the main clause itself, taking the ergative both on the head noun and at the end of the clause, for instance as construction such as? [tɯrme kɯ pɯ pɯ-kɯ-mto] kɯ instead of [tɯrme [pɯ pɯ-kɯ-mto]] kɯ in ( ex:tWrme.pWpWkWmto ).
summary: Transitive subjects are relativized only by subject participial relative clauses in kɯ-, like intransitive subjects, and these clauses usually take a possessive prefix that is coreferent with the object unless another prefix is present. In a minority of cases the transitive subject head noun may appear before the verb and sometimes bears ergative case, which shows the relative is head-internal; alternatively, the head noun may appear in absolutive form with the ergative marking following the relative clause, indicating a postnominal relative. The text notes that there are no examples of double ergative marking on both the head noun and the clause.

text:
relative clause!object object!relativization
Relativization of direct objects allows for a greater variety of constructions than that of subjects: both finite and participial relative clauses are possible.

In object participial relatives, the participle can be prefixed with an orientation preverb as in ( ex:tCheme.pWkAsat ), or with a possessive prefix coreferent with transitive subject. In the first case (restricted to third person subjects), the relatives are most commonly head-internal (or postnominal) as in ( ex:tCheme.pWkAsat ), but other constructions are possible. Attested types of object participial relatives are described in § sec:object.participle.relatives.

exe

[ tɕʰeme pɯ-kɤ-sat] nɯ pɣɤtɕɯ ci to-sci qʰe, \\
girl aor - sbj: pcp -kill dem bird indef ifr: up -be.born lnk \\
`The girl who had been killed was reborn as a bird.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

Since object participles cannot take both possessive prefixes and orientation preverbs (§ sec:object.participle.possessive ), finite relativization is the only way to specify both TAME and person in an object relative, as in ( ex:qajW.tutia ) and ( ex:ndzrW.thWtWfset ).

exe

nɯ [ qajɯ kɯ-ɲaʁ tu-ti-a] nɯ nɯ kɯ-fse ɲɯ-βze ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
dem worm sbj: pcp -black ipfv -say- 1sg dem dem sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv -grow sens -be \\
`The black worm that I am talking about grows like that.' (28-kWpAz)
0003714#S30
exe

exe

nɤʑo [iɕqʰa ndzrɯ tʰɯ-tɯ-fse-t] nɯ ci tɤ-nɯ-tsʰɤt tɕe\\
2sg just.before chisel aor -2-whet- pst: tr dem a.little imp - auto -try lnk \\
`Try the chisel that you have just whetted.' (150902 luban-zh)
0006268#S116
exe

Object finite relatives with overt head noun are mainly head-internal, as ( ex:ndzrW.thWtWfset ) (see also § sec:head-internal.relative.postnominal ), or ambiguous between postnominal and head-internal as in ( ex:qajW.tutia ). Prenominal finite relatives are attested, but rarer. All four possibilities to relativize objects (finite vs? participial, head-internal vs. prenominal) are illustrated in ( ex:pGa.mto ).

exe

xlist

[a-tɕɯ kɯ pɣa pa-mto] nɯ \\
1sg. poss -son erg bird aor:3 -see dem \\

[a-tɕɯ kɯ pɣa pɯ-kɤ-mto] nɯ \\
1sg. poss -son erg bird aor - obj: pcp -see dem \\

[a-tɕɯ kɯ pa-mto] pɣa nɯ \\
1sg. poss -son erg aor:3 -see bird dem \\

[a-tɕɯ kɯ pɯ-kɤ-mto] pɣa nɯ \\
1sg. poss -son erg aor - obj: pcp -see bird dem \\
xlist
`The bird that my son saw' (elicited)
exe

There are some contexts where finite relatives have to be head-internal or postnominal and where the prenominal position is agrammatical (§ sec:head-internal.relative.prenominal ).
summary:
Object relativization permits more construction types than subject relativization, since both finite and participial relative clauses are possible. In participial object relatives, the participle may take either an orientation preverb or a possessive prefix coreferent with the transitive subject; because these cannot co-occur, finite relativization is needed when both TAM and person must be expressed.  

Finite object relatives with overt head nouns are mainly head-internal or ambiguous between head-internal and postnominal, while prenominal relatives are attested but rarer; all four combinations of finite vs. participial and head-internal vs. prenominal are shown. In some contexts, finite relatives must be head-internal or postnominal, and prenominal position is ungrammatical.

text:
When the object of monotransitive verbs are relativized using a finite relative, the verb must be in direct form, even when the transitive subject of the relative has a possessive prefix coreferent with the object. For instance, in ( ex:Wmu.kW.kanWpoR ), only the 3 form ka-nɯpoʁ is possible, the inverse 3$'$ 3 configuration kɤ́-wɣ-nɯpoʁ is not possible in the context.

exe

[ɯ$_i$-mu kɯ ka-nɯpoʁ] tɤ-pɤtso $_i$ nɯ \\
3sg. poss -mother erg aor:3 -kiss indef. poss -child dem \\
`The child whose mother kissed him' (elicited)
exe

In addition, only third person object forms (excluding inverse 3 1/2 and local configurations) of monotransitive verbs can be relativized. This constraint does not apply to triactantial causative (§ sec:object.causative.relativization ) or secundative verbs (§ sec:secundative.theme.relativization ).
summary: When the object of a monotransitive verb is relativized with a finite relative, the verb must appear in the direct form, even if the transitive subject has a possessive prefix referring to that object. Only third-person object forms of monotransitive verbs can be relativized; inverse 3–1/2 and local configurations are excluded. This restriction does not apply to triactantial causative or secundative verbs.

text:
relative clause!theme
The theme of indirective verbs such as kʰogive or tisay (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) has the same morphosyntactic status as the direct object of a monotransitive verb, both from the point of view of person indexation and of relativization: it is also relativizable by both finite clauses ( ex:tAkAtWt.tosWRjit ) and object participial clauses ( ex:mbala.kW.tatWt ).

exe

tɤtɕɯpɯ nɯ kɯ [iɕqʰa mbala-do nɯ kɯ tɤ-kɤ-tɯt] nɯ to-sɯʁjit. \\
boy dem erg just.before ox-old dem erg aor - obj: pcp -say[II] dem ifr -remember \\
`The boy remembered [what] the old ox had told him.' (150828 niulang-zh)
0006318#S56
exe

exe

tɕeri [mbala kɯ ta-tɯt] nɯ to-stu \\
lnk ox erg aor:3 -say[II] dem ifr -do.like \\
`He did it [the way that] the ox had said.' (150828 niulang-zh)
0006318#S133
exe
summary: The theme of indirective verbs like *kʰogive* or *tisay* has the same morphosyntactic status as the direct object of a monotransitive verb, especially in person indexing and relativization. It can be relativized by both finite clauses and object participial clauses, as shown in the examples.

text:
Causativized transitive verbs are triactantial (causer, causee and object, § sec:ditransitive.causative ) and differ from monotransitive verbs (§ sec:monotransitive.object.relativization ) in that their object can be relativized using finite relatives with a verb in inverse configuration ( ex:tAwGznAmYo.nWra ) or with a first or second person object (including local configurations, as in ex:jAkWsWCGaza.nW ).

exe

[tɤ́-wɣ-z-nɤmɲo] nɯra kɯ kɯ-fsɯ fse ʑo to-βzu pjɤ-cʰa. \\
aor - inv - caus -watch dem: pl total sbj: pcp - emph be.like emph ifr -make ifr -can \\
`[Luban]$_i$ succeeded in recreating all [the objects] that [his teacher]$_j$ had shown him$_i$ exactly as they were [before].' (150902 luban-zh)
0006268#S152
exe

exe

[ mbalɤ-pɯ jɤ-kɯ-sɯ-ɕɣaz-a] nɯ pa-mto tɕe \\
ox- dim aor -2 1- caus -take.back- 1sg dem aor:3 -see lnk \\
`She saw the calf that you had me take back home.' (140512 fushang he yaomo1-zh)
0003969#S128
exe

In examples ( ex:tAwGznAmYo.nWra ) and ( ex:jAkWsWCGaza.nW ), the person configuration indexes causer and causee, not the direct object.

The theme of secundative verbs can be relativized using the same type of constructions (§ sec:secundative.theme.relativization ).
summary: Causativized transitive verbs are triactantial, with causer, causee, and object, and their object can be relativized either by finite relatives with an inverse verb configuration or when the object is a first- or second-person participant, including local configurations. In these cases, the person configuration indexes the causer and causee rather than the direct object. The text also notes that secundative verbs relativize their theme with the same type of constructions.

subsubsection: Only argument of transitive verbs with dummy subjects
text:
The only argument of dummy transitive verbs (§ sec:transitive.dummy ), despite resembling a direct object, is relativized with subject participles, as tu-kɯ-rku in ( ex:tCHWwWr.turke ) (§ sec:rku.lv ) and ku-kɯ-tsʰoʁ in ( ex:Wmat.kukWtshoR ) (§ sec:tshoR.lv ).

exe

nɯre ri tɕʰɯwɯr tu-rke ŋu tɕe, tɕe [ tɕʰɯwɯr tu-kɯ-rku] nɯnɯ cimbɤrom ŋu \\
dem: loc loc blister ipfv -put.in[III] be: fact lnk lnk [ blister ipfv - sbj: pcp -put.in] dem phlycten be: fact \\
`(At the place where the skin is burnt), a blister forms there, the blister that forms is a phlycten.' (27-tWfCAl 122)
0003710#S115
exe

exe

tɕe iɕqʰa mbrɤz ɣɯ [ ɯ-mat ku-kɯ-tsʰoʁ] nɯ ɯ-tsʰɯɣa ɲɯ-fse \\
lnk the.aforementioned rice gen 3sg. poss -fruit ipfv - sbj: pcp -attach dem 3sg. poss -shape sens -be.like \\
`Its shape is a bit like that of grains of rice (growing on the stalk).' (19-khWlu)
0003540#S85
exe

Finite clauses and object participial clauses cannot be used to relativize these arguments. This is one of the clues (§ sec:dental.inf, § sec:transitive.dummy ) that the verbs in these constructions are only partially transitive.
summary: The passage says that the single argument of dummy transitive verbs behaves like a direct object, but it is actually relativized with subject participles, as shown by forms like *tu-kɯ-rku* and *ku-kɯ-tsʰoʁ*. Finite clauses and object participial clauses cannot relativize these arguments, which is presented as evidence that these verbs are only partially transitive.

text:
A certain number of absolutive arguments that are not indexed as direct objects on the verb (§ sec:polypersonal )) have objectal properties: the semi-objects of
semi-transitive verbs (§ sec:semi.transitive ) and the themes of secundative verbs (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ). They can be
relativized like direct objects of monotransitive verbs, both with finite and participial
relatives.
summary: Some absolutive arguments that are not indexed as direct objects on the verb still show object-like behavior, including the semi-objects of semi-transitive verbs and the themes of secundative verbs. These arguments can be relativized in the same way as direct objects of monotransitive verbs, using both finite and participial relative clauses.

text:
relative clause!semi-object semi-object!relativization
Semi transitive verbs like rgalike, βɟɤtobtain or aroown are morphologically intransitive and their subject is marked in the absolutive (§ sec:semi.transitive ), but they take in addition an absolutive semi-object (§ sec:semi.object ). The semi-object can be relativized with either object participial relatives ( ex:pGa.ra.nWkArga ) or finite relative clauses as in ( ex:pWBJata.nW ) and ( ex:aroa.nW ).

exe

[pɣa ra nɯ-kɤ-rga] nɯ qaj ntsɯ ŋu \\
bird pl 3pl - obj: pcp -like dem wheat always be: fact \\
`[The food] that birds like is always wheat (not barley).' (23 pGAYaR)
0003606#S24
exe

exe

[ laχtɕʰa pɯ-βɟat-a] nɯ kʰɯtsa pɯ-ŋu \\
thing aor -obtain- 1sg dem bowl pst. ipfv -be \\
`The thing that I obtained was a bowl.' (elicited)
exe

exe

[aʑo qaʑo aro-a] nɯ kɯki ŋu \\
1sg sheep own: fact - 1sg dem dem. prox be: fact \\
`The sheep that I own is this one.' (elicitation)
exe
summary: Semi-transitive verbs such as *rga* ‘like,’ *βɟɤt* ‘obtain,’ and *aro* ‘own’ are morphologically intransitive, with the subject marked absolutively, but they also take an absolutive semi-object. This semi-object can be relativized either by object participial relatives or by finite relative clauses, as shown in the examples.

text:
Secundative verbs such as mbigive or sɯxɕɤtteach index the recipient as direct object, but also take a non-indexed absolutive argument referring to the theme (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ). When both the subject and the direct object are third person, theme can be relativized either with a finite clause ( ex:sla.kW.nWwGmbi, ex:pWwGsWxCAt.pjAsWxCAt ) or an object participial clause (example ex:tWNga.nWkAmbi, § sec:relative.possessor.neutralization ). Head-internal clauses are most common ( ex:sla.kW.nWwGmbi ), but prenominal and even genitival ones (§ sec:genitival.relatives ) are also found, as in ( ex:pWwGsWxCAt.pjAsWxCAt ).

exe

[sla kɯ, nɤki, kumpɣɤ-ŋgɯm nɯ́-wɣ-mbi] nɯ pjɤ-qrɯ \\
moon erg filler hen-egg aor - inv -give dem ifr -break \\
`She broke the egg that the moon had given her.' (140506 shizi he huichang de bailingniao-zh)
0003927#S252
exe

exe

[tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ, saŋrɟɤz ra kɯ pɯ́-wɣ-sɯxɕɤt] ɣɯ kʰɤndɯn nɯ ɯ-rʑaβ χsɯm nɯ pjɤ-sɯxɕɤt \\
indef. poss -son dem erg buddha pl erg aor - inv -teach gen mantra dem 3sg. poss -wife three dem ifr -teach \\
`He taught his three wives the mantra that the Buddhas had taught him.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S311
exe

In finite relative clauses, the inverse 3$'$ 3 configuration is most often found when the transitive subject of the main clause corresponds to the direct object (recipient) of the relative clause, as in ( ex:sla.kW.nWwGmbi ) and ( ex:pWwGsWxCAt.pjAsWxCAt ), and the relativized element is the theme. Secundative verbs resemble in this regard causativized transitive verbs (§ sec:object.causative.relativization ) and differ from monotransitive verbs, whose objects cannot be relativized using a finite 3$'$ 3 configuration (§ sec:monotransitive.object.relativization ).

The themes of secundative verbs being relativized with the same constructions as their direct objects, ambiguity can arise especially in the case of short relatives. For instance, the participle a-kɤ-sɯxɕɤt of sɯxɕɤtteach can be understood as relativizing the direct object/recipient ( ex:akAsWxCAt.lhamo ) or the theme ( ex:akAsWxCAt.shuxue ). The antipassive can be used to disambiguate: since this derivation removes the object, the only interpretation left for the antipassive participle a-kɤ-sɤ-sɯxɕɤt is theme relativization `the (subject) that I taught' (see also example ex:nAkArAmbi, § sec:object.participle.relatives ).

exe

xlist

[a-kɤ-sɯxɕɤt] nɯ ɬamu pɯ-ŋu. \\
1sg - obj: pcp -teach dem anthr pst. ipfv -be \\
`The person whom I taught it to was Lhamo.' (elicited)

[a-kɤ-sɯxɕɤt] nɯ <shuxue> pɯ-ŋu. \\
2sg - obj: pcp -teach dem mathematics pst. ipfv -be \\
`The [subject] that I taught them/him/her was maths.' (elicited)

[a-kɤ-sɤ-sɯxɕɤt] <yuwen> pɯ-ŋu. \\
2sg - obj: pcp - antip -teach Chinese what pst. ipfv -be \\
`The [subject] that I taught them/him/her was Chinese.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

Finite relatives in direct form can also be used to relativize both the direct object ( ex:nWtWmbit.CW ) or the theme ( ex:nWmbita.kWmtChW ).

exe

xlist

[rŋɯl nɯ-tɯ-mbi-t] nɯ ɕɯ pɯ-ŋu? \\
silver aor -2-give- pst: tr dem who pst. ipfv -be \\
`To whom did you give money?' (elicited)

[a-tɕɯ tɤ-pɤro nɯ-mbi-t-a] nɯ kɯmtɕʰɯ pɯ-ŋu \\
1sg. poss -son indef. poss -present aor -give- pst: tr - 1sg dem toy pst. ipfv -be \\
`The present I gave my son was a toy.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

Finite clauses are needed to specify both TAME and a first or second person subject, as in ( ex:nWtWmbit.CW ) and ( ex:nWmbita.kWmtChW ), as object participles cannot index the subject ( ex:akAsWxCAt.lhamo ) while at the time taking an orientation preverb.

Finite relative clauses are also required to index a first or second person direct object (recipient), for instance in local configurations such as `the thing that I have (taught/given) you' in ( ex:pWtasWxCAt.nWndWn ). This type of clause is only interpretable as theme relativization.

exe

a-tɕɯ tɯ tɯ-ŋu nɤ, [pɯ-ta-sɯxɕɤt] nɯ ci nɯ-ndɯn ra \\
1sg. poss -son cond 2-be: fact add aor -1 2-teach dem a.little imp -recite be.needed: fact \\
`If you are my son, recite [the mantra] that I have taught you.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S188
exe
summary:
Secundative verbs like *mbigive* and *sɯxɕɤtteach* index the recipient as the direct object but also take an unindexed absolutive theme. When the subject and direct object are both third person, the theme can be relativized by finite clauses or object participial clauses, and ambiguity may arise because these same constructions can also relativize the recipient. 

Finite relatives are most common for relativizing themes and are required in certain configurations, especially when first- or second-person subjects or direct objects must be indexed; object participles cannot index the subject and therefore cannot be used in those cases. Antipassive morphology can disambiguate theme relativization by removing the object, leaving only the theme interpretation.

text:
relative clause!goal goal!relativization
relative clause!locative locative!relativization
Relativization of locative/goal adjuncts or arguments with oblique participial clauses is described in § sec:locative.participle.relatives. This section presents the relativization of locative phrases with finite clauses, object participles and relator nouns.
summary: The passage indicates that relativization of locative or goal adjuncts and arguments using oblique participial clauses is discussed elsewhere. Here, it focuses instead on how locative phrases are relativized with finite clauses, object participles, and relator nouns.

text:
Locative marking on goals and locative arguments and adjuncts is optional, and they can occur in absolutive form (§ absolutive.goal ), like semi-objects (§ sec:semi.object ). Another commonality between goal/locative arguments and semi-objects is the ability to be relativized using finite relative clauses (§ sec:semi.tr.relativization ).

Finite locative relative clauses are most often prenominal, in particular with a genitive marker (§ sec:genitival.relatives ), as in ( ex:YWCenW.GW.tsxu ).

exe

[ʑara kɯ-lɤɣ ɲɯ-ɕe-nɯ] ɣɯ tʂu ci tu tɕe \\
3pl sbj: pcp -herd ipfv: west -go- pl gen path indef exist: fact lnk \\
`(At that place), there is a path which they take to go herd [cattle].' (140522 Kamnyu zgo)
0004059#S292
exe

Headless ( ex:kurAZi.khu.Wsta ) and head-internal ( ex:kha.jAwGtsWmnW ) finite locative relatives are also attested. In the latter case, the head noun cannot receive locative case, and must be in absolutive form.

exe

[ku-rɤʑi] nɯ kʰu ɯ-sta ɕti ndɤre \\
ipfv -stay dem tiger 3sg. poss -place be. aff: fact lnk \\
`The place where he is [now] is a tiger's lair.' (2003kandZislama)
exe

exe

[ kʰa jɤ́-wɣ-tsɯm-nɯ] nɯnɯ, [lonba ɕom kɯ nɯ-kɤ-sɯ-βzu] kʰa pjɤ-ŋu \\
house ifr - inv -take.away- pl dem all iron erg aor - obj: pcp - caus -make house ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The house where [the king] had taken them, it was a house completely made of iron' (140505 liuhaohan zoubian tianxia-zh)
0003913#S149
exe

Non-permanent and non-specific location can be relativized with finite relative clauses, as in ( ex:kurAZi.khu.Wsta ) and ( ex:kha.jAwGtsWmnW ). Thus, the finite relative ku-rɤʑi nɯ in ( ex:kurAZi.khu.Wsta ) can be translated as `the place where he happens to be' while `the place where he stays (permanently), his staying place' is better expressed with an oblique participle ɯ-(sɤ)z-rɤʑi (§ sec:locative.participle.relatives ).
summary: Locative marking on goals and locative arguments or adjuncts is optional, and these elements can appear in absolutive form like semi-objects; both groups can also be relativized with finite relative clauses. Finite locative relatives are usually prenominal, often with a genitive marker, and both headless and head-internal forms are attested, though in head-internal relatives the head noun must remain absolutive rather than taking locative case. The passage also notes that finite relative clauses are used for non-permanent, non-specific locations, while permanent locative meanings are better expressed with oblique participial relatives.

text:
The negative object participle of the perception verbs mtosee and mtsʰɤmhear has a special use: in ( ex:WmAkAmto ) for instance, ɯ-mɤ-kɤ-mto means `(somewhere) s/he cannot see him/her', the relativized element being locative rather than object (see § sec:object.participle.other.relative for further discussion). This type of relative clauses are always headless.

exe

[iɕqʰa qaɕpa kɯ ɯ-mɤ-kɤ-mto ʑo] jo-ɕe \\
the.aforementioned frog erg 3sg. poss - neg - obj: pcp -see emph ifr -go \\
`She went to [a place] where the frog would not find her.' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh)
0006334#S143
exe
summary: The negative object participle of the perception verbs *mtosee* and *mtsʰɤmhear* can be used in a special way in which the relativized element is locative rather than an object, as in forms meaning ‘somewhere s/he cannot see him/her.’ These relative clauses are always headless.

text:
The two inalienably possessed nouns ɯ-stuplace and ɯ-staplace, both originating from lexicalized oblique participles ( tab:spa.sta.stu, § sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle ) can be used as relator nouns of prenominal locative relative clauses.

The noun ɯ-stuplace either selects subject participial clauses, as in ( ex:kWrAZi.Wstu ) and ( ex:tAntAm.lAkWZa.Wstu ), or oblique participial clauses ( ex:nWsAnbaR.Wstu ). The relativized element can be a static location, but also a goal (see ex:NotCu.jAkAri.Wstu, § sec:interrogative.relative ).

exe

[ɯʑo kɯ-rɤʑi] ɯ-stu ʑo nɯ kú-wɣ-sɯ-ɤsɯɣ. \\
3sg sbj: pcp -stay 3sg. poss -place emph dem ipfv - inv - caus -be.tight \\
`One presses the place (in the cow's hide) where [the bug] is.' (25-akWzgumba)
0003666#S11
exe

exe

[nɯnɯ tɯ-ɤntɤm lɤ-kɯ-ʑa] ɯ-stu nɯ ɯ-mpʰɯsku tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
dem inf:II-be.flat aor: upstream - sbj: pcp -start 3sg. poss -place dem 3sg. poss -rump ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`(When one goes upstream), the place where [the slope of the mountain] starts getting flatter (i.e. the point of inflection in the slope of the mountain) is called the `rump' (of the mountain).' (150908 Wmphsku)
0006302#S8
exe

exe

ʑara [nɯ-sɤ-ɤnbaʁ] ɯ-stu nɯtɕu jo-nɯ-ɬoʁ-nɯ tɕe, \\
3pl 3pl. poss - obl: pcp -hide 3sg. poss -place dem: loc ifr - auto -come.out- pl lnk \\
`They came out of their hiding place.' (140426 luozi he qiangdao-zh)
0003814#S23
exe

The noun ɯ-sta, though also compatible with subject participial clauses, is more often found with finite relative clauses, as illustrated by ( ex:pWnANkWNke.Wsta ) and ( ex:thWnAqharu.chAnAqharu ).

exe

[pɯ-nɤŋkɯŋke] ɯ-sta nɯra rcanɯ, tɯ-ɕnaβ pɯ-kɤ-βde ʑo fse \\
pst. ipfv - distr:walk 3sg. poss -place dem: loc unexp: deg indef. poss -snot aor - obj: pcp -throw emph be.like: fact \\
`The places where [the slug] has passed look like snot has been spilled [on them].' (26-qro)
0003682#S128
exe

While ɯ-stu and ɯ-sta have very close meanings, in the case of verbs taking a goal such as rulook at (§ sec:orienting.verbs ), a semantic difference can be observed: the former specifically indicates the goal ( ex:lAru.Wstu ), while the latter is used to indicate the place where the action takes place ( ex:lAru.Wsta ).

exe

xlist

lɤ-ru ɯ-stu nɯtɕu \\
aor: upstream -look 3sg. poss -place dem: loc \\
`The direction (upwards) he looked.' (elicited)

lɤ-ru ɯ-sta nɯtɕu \\
aor: upstream -look 3sg. poss -place dem: loc \\
`The place where/from which he looked upwards.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

For instance, in ( ex:thWnAqharu.chAnAqharu ), the clause tʰɯ-nɤqʰaru ɯ-sta cannot be understood as `the place where he had looked back (in whose direction he looked)'.

exe

lo-ɕe tɕe tɕelo [tʰɯ-nɤqʰaru] ɯ-sta lɤ-azɣɯt nɤ li cʰɤ-nɤqʰaru. \\
ifr: upstream -go lnk upstream aor: downstream -look.back 3sg. poss -place aor -reach add again ifr: downstream -look.back \\
`He went up there, and when he arrived at the place up there that he had looked back from, he looked back again.' (2003 kAndzwsqhaj.2)
exe
summary: The inalienably possessed nouns ɯ-stu and ɯ-sta, both derived from lexicalized oblique participles, can function as relator nouns introducing prenominal locative relative clauses. ɯ-stu may take subject or oblique participial clauses and can refer to a static location or a goal, while ɯ-sta is also compatible with subject participial clauses but is more often used with finite relative clauses and typically denotes the place where an action takes place.

text:
relative clause!instrument instrument!relativization
Instruments are most commonly relativized using oblique participial relatives (§ sec:instrumental.participle.relatives ). All instrument oblique relatives in the corpus are headless, and often limited to the participle itself. When the nominalized verb is transitive, the participial relative can contain an object as in ( ex:qandZi.chWsAGnda ). Antipassivization is required to demote the direct object even for participial verb forms (§ sec:antipassive.participle ).

exe

nɯnɯ [qandʑi cʰɯ-sɤ-ɣnda] nɯ tʰoŋtʰɤr ɲɯ-rmi \\
dem bullet ipf - obl: pcp -ram dem ramrod sens -be.called \\
`What is used to ram a bullet [into the muzzle of the gun] is called a ramrod.' (28-CAmWGdW)
0003712#S52
exe

Instrumental participial relative clauses can take the generic inalienably possessed noun ɯ-spamaterial as overt head, to disambiguate with other types of relatives, in particular locative ones, built with an oblique participle (§ sec:oblique.participle ). For instance, in ( ex:tusANke.Wspa ), the focus is on the use of the path (a path specially made in order to be able to walk inside the field), rather than simply on the location (`the place where one walks').

exe

tɕe tɯ-ji ɯ-χcɤl tu-kɯ-ŋke mɤ-kʰɯ ma tɤ-rɤku tu tɕe tɕe, nɯ ɣɯ [tu-sɤ-ŋke] ɯ-spa, ɯ-tʂu <zhuanmen> ɯ-rkoz ɲɯ́-wɣ-βzu ŋgrɤl tɕe ɯnɯnɯ tʂu nɯ ftɕɤru tu-kɯ-ti ŋu \\
lnk indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -middle ipfv - genr:S/O-walk neg -be.possible: fact lnk indef. poss -crops exist: fact lnk lnk dem gen ipfv - obl: pcp -walk 3sg. poss -material 3sg. poss -path specially 3sg. poss -special ipfv - inv -make be.usually.the.case: fact lnk dem path dem summer.path ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`One cannot walk in the middle of the fields, because there are crops. To walk into it, one specially makes a path, and that path is call `summer path'.' (definition, 15-06-05)
exe

Alternatively, in the case of verbs with a sigmatic causative prefix in instrumental function (§ sec:sig.caus.instrumental ), the instrument can be relativized as if it were a transitive subject using the kɯ- participle (§ sec:subject.participle.subject.relative, § sec:tr.subject.relativization ), for example ɯ-kɯ-sɯ-mpʰɯl `(the thing) that it reproduces with, (the thing) which makes it reproduce' in ( ex:WkWsWmphWl ).

exe

tɕeri nɯnɯ [ɯ-kɯ-sɯ-mpʰɯl] nɯ li ɯ-zrɤm ɲɯ-ɕti ma ɯ-rɣi ɲɯ-maʁ. \\
but dem 3sg - sbj: pcp - caus -reproduce dem again 3sg. poss -root seve -be. aff lnk 3sg. poss -seed seve -not.be \\
`What it reproduces with is its root, not its seeds.' (11-paRzwamWntoR)
0003476#S100
exe
summary:
Instruments are most often relativized by oblique participial relatives, which in the corpus are all headless and often consist only of the participle itself. If the nominalized verb is transitive, the participial relative may include an object, but antipassivization is required to demote the direct object even in these participial forms.

Instrumental participial relatives may also take the generic inalienably possessed noun ɯ-spa “material” as an overt head to distinguish them from locative relatives. Alternatively, with verbs that have a sigmatic causative prefix in instrumental function, the instrument can be relativized as a transitive subject using the kɯ- participle.

text:
relative clause!comitative comitative!relativization
Comitative arguments marked with the postposition cʰo (§ sec:comitative ) can be relativized with the oblique participle (§ sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ). Such relatives are generally headless, as in ( ex:WsAzrAkrAz ). The verb rɤkrɤzhave a discussion can select a comitative argument (see example ex:cho.torAkrAzndZi, § sec:comitative ).

exe

ɯʑo ɯ-χti ɲɤ-me tɕe, ɲɯ-sɤzdɯxpa tɕe ɯ-sɤz-rɤkrɤz ri maŋe, ɯ-kɯ-qur ri maŋe \\
3sg 3sg. poss -companion ifr -not.exist lnk sens -be.pitiful lnk 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -discuss also not.exist: sens 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -help also not.exist: sens \\
`Her husband passed away, poor her, she has nobody to talk with, and nobody to help her.' (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S111
exe

If overt, the head does not take the comitative postposition cʰo as in ( ex:asAmWmi ), showing that this type of relative cannot be head-internal and is rather postnominal (§ sec:postnominal.relative ).

exe

tɯrme [a-sɤ-ɤmɯmi] nɯ lɤβzaŋ ɲɯ-rmi. \\
person 1sg. poss - obl: pcp -be.on.good.terms dem anthr sens -be.called \\
`The person I am on good terms with is Lobzang.' (elicited)
exe
summary:
Comitative arguments marked with the postposition **cʰo** can be relativized using the **oblique participle**, and these relative clauses are generally **headless**. The verb **rɤkrɤz** ‘have a discussion’ can take a comitative argument, as shown by examples where the meaning is ‘someone to talk with.’  

When an overt head is present, it does **not** take the comitative postposition **cʰo**, which shows that these relatives are **not head-internal** but instead **postnominal**.

text:
relative clause!dative dative!relativization
Dative arguments (marked with the relator nouns ɯ-ɕki or ɯ-pʰe, § sec:dative ) can only be relativized with oblique participial clauses (§ sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ). For example, the recipient of the indirective verb tisay (§ sec:ditransitive.indirective ) is relativized with the participle sɤ-ti `(person) to whom one talks to', as in ( ex:aRi.sAti ). The relative clause tɕi-mu tɕi-wa kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ is analyzed in § sec:S.possessor.relativization.

exe

tɕeri [``a-ʁi" sɤ-ti] dɤn ma aʑo ɣɯ, nɤkinɯ, a-ʁi, [tɕi-mu tɕi-wa kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ] a-ʁi,
nɯnɯra nɯ-ɕki tɕe ``a-ʁi" tu-ti-a, a-wɤmɯ ɯ-rɟit tɕe ``a-ʁi" tu-ti-a. \\
lnk 1sg. poss -younger.sibling obl: pcp -say be.many: fact lnk 1sg gen filler 1sg. poss -younger.sibling 1du. poss -mother 1du. poss -father sbj: pcp -be.the.same 1sg. poss -younger.sibling dem: pl 3pl. poss - dat loc 1sg. poss -younger.sibling ipfv -say- 1sg 1sg. poss -brother 3sg. poss -children lnk 1sg. poss -younger.sibling ipfv -say- 1sg \\
`There are many [people] to whom one says `my younger sibling'; those of my ``younger siblings'' whose parents I share, I say `my younger sibling' to them, and I (also) say `my younger sibling' to my brothers' children.' (140425 kWmdza02) 0003786
exe

The subject can be optionally indexed as a possessive prefix on the oblique participle, as in ( ex:azrAthu ).

exe

[a-z-rɤ-tʰu] nɯ tsʰɯndzɯn <laoshi> ŋu \\
1sg. poss - obl: pcp dem anthr teacher be: fact \\
`The [person] I ask is teacher Tshendzin. (elicited)
exe

There are no examples of head-internal dative relative clauses, with the relativized element taking dative marking.
summary: Dative arguments marked with the relator nouns ɯ-ɕki or ɯ-pʰe can only be relativized by oblique participial clauses. The passage illustrates this with examples where the recipient is expressed by a participle meaning “(person) to whom one talks to,” and notes that the subject may optionally be indexed as a possessive prefix on the participle. It also states that there are no examples of head-internal dative relative clauses in which the relativized element itself carries dative marking.

text:
relative clause!adjuncts adjunct!relativization
Oblique participial clauses can have a temporal interpretation, both with transitive verbs ( ex:WsAphWt.WsNi ) and intransitive stative verbs ( ex:tAjmAG.WsAdAn ). This way of relativizing temporal adjuncts is however quite limited (§ sec:other.oblique.participle.relatives ).

exe

[ɯ-sɤ-pʰɯt] nɯ, ɯ-sŋi nɯ a-mɤ-pɯ-pe tɕe tɕe li tu-kɯ-ɕɯ-ngo ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl \\
3sg. poss - obl: pcp -cut dem 3sg. poss -day dem irr - neg - ipfv -be.good lnk lnk again ipfv - genr:S/O- caus -be.sick sens -be.usually.the.case \\
`If the day when [the tree] is cut is not auspicious, it makes people sick.' (24-kWqar)
0003620#S9
exe

exe

[tɤjmɤɣ ɯ-sɤ-dɤn] ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu, tʰamtʰam. \\
mushroom 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -be.many emph sens -be now \\
`Now is a [period] when mushrooms are abundant.' (conversation, 16-08-11)
exe

The more common way of relativizing temporal adjuncts is by using finite clauses followed by a temporal relator noun in 3sg possessive form such as ɯ-sŋi `the day when...' ( ex:RmbGWzWn.tu.WsNi ), ɯ-xpa `the year when...' ( ex:maozhuxi.nWme ), or ɯ-raŋ `the time when...' etc.

exe

[[slɤzɯn tu] cʰo] [ʁmbɣɯzɯn tu] ɯ-sŋi nɯnɯ, skɤrma mɤ-sna ra tu-ti-nɯ ŋu \\
lunar.eclipse exist: fact comit solar.eclipse exist: fact 3sg. poss -day dem time neg -be.good: fact pl ipfv -say- pl be: fact \\
`They said that the day of a lunar or a solar eclipse is not auspicious.' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S155
exe

When these prenominal relatives are used as temporal adjuncts in the main clause, with or without ( ex:maozhuxi.nWme ) locative marking, they serve to express temporal clause linking (§ sec:temporal.reference ).

exe

[iʑora <maozhuxi> nɯ-me] ɯ-xpa nɯnɯ, skɤrtɕin maŋe tu-ti-nɯ pɯ-ŋgrɤl. \\
1pl chairman.Mao aor -not.exist 3sg. poss -year dem Venus not.exist ipfv -say- pl pst. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`They say that the year when our Chairman Mao passed away, Venus did not appear.' (29-LAntshAm)
0003726#S75
exe
summary: Oblique participial clauses can relativize temporal adjuncts, with both transitive and intransitive stative verbs, but this strategy is quite limited. More commonly, temporal adjuncts are relativized by finite clauses followed by a temporal relator noun in 3sg possessive form, such as “the day when,” “the year when,” or “the time when,” and these prenominal relatives then function as temporal clause linkers in the main clause.

text:
relative clause!possessor possessor!relativization
Possessors of intransitive subjects and direct objects can be relativized using the same relative constructions as their possessees. It is unclear whether possessors of other arguments can be relativized (in particular possessors of transitive subjects).
summary: Possessors of intransitive subjects and direct objects can be relativized by using the same relative constructions that apply to the nouns they possess. The passage notes that it is not clear whether possessors of other kinds of arguments, especially possessors of transitive subjects, can also be relativized.

text:
possessor subject!intransitive relative clause!possessor
Possessors of intransitive subjects are relativized with subject participial clauses (§ sec:subject.participle.other.relative ). In this construction, the subject of the clause is overt and takes an obligatory possessive prefix, such as the 3pl nɯ- in ( ex:nWmtChi.kWdAn ). This expression may be a nativized calque from Chinese 多嘴 duōzuǐbig mouth.

exe

[ nɯ -mtɕʰi kɯ-dɤn] nɯra \\
3pl. poss -mouth sbj: pcp -be.many dem: pl \\
`Those who talk too much' (24-qro)
0003626#S112
exe

The head noun can be overt as in ( ex:qapri.WrW.kWtu ), with determiner repetition (§ sec:head-internal.relative.determiners ).

exe

akɯ zɯ [ qapri ci ɯ -kɤχcɤl ɯ -ʁrɯ kɯ-tu] ci ɣɤʑu tɕe \\
east loc snake indef 3sg. poss -top.of.head 3sg. poss -horn sbj: pcp -exist indef exist: sens lnk \\
`In the east, there is a snake with a horn on his head.' (2005, divinitation)
exe

Prenominal possessor relatives are also attested, but extremely rare, and the third person possessive prefix on the possessee is required as in ( ex:Wcu.kWtu.rJAGi ).

exe

[ ɯ -cu kɯ-tu] rɟɤɣi pjɤ-ɕti \\
3sg. poss -additive sbj: pcp -exist tsampa ifr. ipfv -be. aff \\
`It was tsampa mixed with broad beans.' (i.e. poor quality tsampa) (2003-kWBRa)
exe

Subject possessor relative can also occur in apposition with another relative clause, as in ( ex:Wmi.kWzWzri ).

exe

[ɯ-mi kɯ-zɯ zri ʑo] [rkaŋraŋ kɯ-rmi] ci pɯ-tu ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -leg sbj: pcp - emph be.long emph anthr sbj: pcp -be.called indef pst. ipfv -exist sens -be \\
`There was someone called Rkangring who had long legs.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

First or second person possessors can also be relativized, as in ( ex:aXti.kWtu ) and ( ex:nAmu.nAwa.kWtshoz ) (see also ex:amu.kWme, § sec:pers.pronouns ).

exe

aʑo [a-χti kɯ-tu] ɲɯ-ŋu-a \\
1sg 1sg. poss -companion sbj: pcp -exist sens -be- 1sg \\
`I am someone with a husband.' (i.e. whose husband is still alive, unlike hers) (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S110
exe

This type of relative can trigger either third person singular indexation, or index the relativized element: both options ( 3sg ŋu `s/he/it is' and 2sg tɯ-ŋu `you are') have been tested and are possible, as shown in example ( ex:nAmu.nAwa.kWtshoz ).

exe

[ nɤʑo nɤ -mu nɤ -wa kɯ-tsʰoz] ŋu/tɯ-ŋu \\
2sg 2sg. poss -mother 2sg. poss -father sbj: pcp -be.complete be: fact /2-be: fact \\
`You are someone both of whose parents are still alive.' (elicited)
exe

In example ( ex:tCimu.tCiwa.kWnaXtCWG ), The context of the relative clause ( ex:tCimu.tCiwa.kWnaXtCWG ) is found in example ( ex:aRi.sAti ) (§ sec:dative.relativization )., the relativized element corresponds to the third person component of the first dual (exclusive) possessive prefix tɕi- on the noun dyad tɕi-mu tɕi-wa `our parents' (§ sec:dyads ).

exe

[ tɕi -mu tɕi -wa kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ] \\
1du. poss -mother 1du. poss -father sbj: pcp -be.the.same \\
`Those whose parents are the same as mine.' (140425 kWmdza02) 0003786
exe

Although the verb naχtɕɯɣbe the same can select a comitative argument (§ sec:comitative ), ( ex:tCimu.tCiwa.kWnaXtCWG ) is not an example of comitative relativization (§ sec:comitative.relativization ). Rather, the construction from which ( ex:tCimu.tCiwa.kWnaXtCWG ) has been relativized is the one in ( ex:tCimYitChAz.YWnaXtCWG ), where the equality concerns the possessors of the intransitive subject.

exe

tɕi-mɲitɕʰɤz ra ɲɯ-naχtɕɯɣ \\
1du. poss -temper pl sens -be.the.same \\
`We have the same temperament = She has the same temperament as I.' (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S53
exe

In the participial relative taking mɤ-kɯ-sɤ-mto `the one that is not visible' as its main verb in ( ex:mAkWsAmto.schiz ), the head smarriver is not the possessor of the subject in the proper sense, but the possessor of a noun ( ɯ-βzɯrits side) subject of a clause embedded within another clause (headed by the participle kɯ-fse `that is like...') serving as the subject of mɤ-kɯ-sɤ-mto `the one that is not visible'.

exe

[maka tɕekɯ ku-kɯ-ru tɕe tɕendi smar [[ɯ-βzɯr tɕʰi kɯ-fse ŋu] kɯ-fse] mɤ-kɯ-sɤ-mto ʑo] scʰiz nɯ-azɣɯt ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
at.all east ipfv: east - genr:S/O-look lnk west river 3sg. poss -side what sbj: pcp -be.like be: fact sbj: pcp -be.like neg - sbj: pcp - prop -see emph approx. loc aor: west -reach sens -be \\
`He arrived at a river where if one looked from one bank to the other, what was on the other side was not at all visible.' (Divination 2005)
exe

This particularly convoluted example is however not representative of what is usually found in the corpus.

In ( ex:WkWXsu.kWme ), we find a prenominal relative containing another verb in subject participle form that can be interpreted a possessor relativization, as in ( ex:kWkWtu.head.internal ): ɯ-kɯ-χsu kɯ-me `having no feeder'.

exe

The head noun may be overt, prenominal possessor relatives are very rare, and first- and second-person possessors can also be relativized with either third-person singular or indexed agreement on the copula. The passage also notes a few more complex cases, but stresses that some apparent possessor relatives actually involve relativization of a subject in an embedded clause rather than a true possessor.

text: The clause tɯ-ɣjɤn cinɤ ʑo tɤ-kɯ-mbri kɯ-me here is in fact the nominalized version of the postverbal negative construction (§ sec:negation.existential ). In main clauses, this construction combines a negative existential verb in impersonal (third singular) form with a complement clause in finite form. In ( ex:tAkWmbri.kWme ), we see that when the intransitive subject of a postverbal negative construction is nominalized, both the matrix verb menot exist and the verb of the complement clause tɤ-kɯ-mbri occur in subject participle form (§ sec:relativization.complement.type ). This construction, though superficially similar to that in ( ex:WkWXsu.kWme ), is therefore different from it.
summary: The clause discussed is the nominalized form of a postverbal negative construction. In main clauses, this construction uses an impersonal third-singular negative existential verb plus a finite complement clause, but when the intransitive subject is nominalized, both the matrix verb and the complement verb appear in subject participle form. Although it looks similar to another construction, it is structurally different.

The contrast between pɯ-kɯ-rɲo in ( ex:kACe.pWkWrYo ) and pɯ-kɤ-rɲo ( ex:kAmtsWG.pWkArYo ) is not as straightforward as it might seem at first glance. With transitive complement-taking verbs like *rɲo* ‘experience’ and *spa* ‘be able,’ the subject participle is used when the relativized element is the subject of the complement clause, whether that subject is transitive or intransitive. To relativize the direct object of a transitive verb inside the complement clause, the complement-taking verb may appear either in finite form or in object participle form, as if that object were the direct object of the main relative clause.  

The passage notes, however, that the contrast between subject and object participles with *rɲo* is not entirely straightforward, because *rɲo* lacks non-generic inverse forms and treats both subjects and objects of its velar infinitive clauses like transitive subjects in the matrix clause.

The complements whose arguments or adjuncts are relativized can be either finite ( ex:tWthe.kWra, ex:tWnAjonW.kWra, ex:Cea.kWra, ex:YWnWpea.kWra, ex:tumbro.mAkWcha ) or infinitival clauses ( ex:kAnWtsW.kWra, ex:kArWCmi.kWspa, ex:kAmto.pWrYota ), just like when the complement-taking verbs are in finite form. In addition, the verb of the complement clause can also bear subject participle form if the relativized element is the subject of the complement clause, as in ( smAnkhaN.kWCe.kWra ) and ( WkukWndWn.kWcha ) (see also § sec:subject.participle.other.relative, § sec:subject.participle.complementation ).

Pairs of verbs in subject participle form should not necessarily be analyzed as complement clauses embedded in relatives. In ( ex:pWkWNGlWt.kWthW ), pɯ-kɯ-ɴɢlɯt `(bone) that has been broken, fracture' is not a (subject) complement of kɯ-tʰɯ `the one that is serious' (which is not a complement-taking stative verb). Rather, wuma ʑo pɯ-kɯ-ɴɢlɯt kɯ-tʰɯ is simply a head-internal relative clause (§ sec:head-internal.relative ) with the subject participle (itself a headless relative clause) pɯ-kɯ-ɴɢlɯt as its subject.

summary:
The passage says that complements whose arguments or adjuncts are relativized may be either finite or infinitival clauses, just as with complement-taking verbs in finite form. It also notes that the complement verb can take a subject participle form when the relativized element is the subject of the complement clause.

However, not every pair of verbs in subject participle form should be analyzed as a complement clause inside a relative clause. In some cases, the structure is instead a head-internal relative clause, with the subject participle itself functioning as the subject.

text:
relative clause!constraints
tab:relatives.japhug summarizes the syntactic functions accessible to relativization in main clauses in Japhug, indicating the clause types available for relativizing each function. The relatives can be headless in all cases, except that of possessor relativization, where a possessive prefix on the possessee is required (§ sec:possessor.relativization ). Intransitive subjects and object are preferentially relativized with head-internal clauses, while transitive subjects, goals and adjuncts are more often relativized by prenominal clauses.

Not all adjuncts are relativizable in Japhug: causees (§ sec:causee.kW ), standards of comparative constructions (marked by the postpositions sɤz or staʁ, § sec:comparative ) and exceptive phrases in maapart from (§ sec:exceptive ) apparently cannot be relativized, following a well-known cross-linguistic generalization.

In addition, relativization of the direct object of transitive verbs (in subject participle form) in the purposive clauses of motion verbs is not possible, as discussed in § sec:AM.mvc.relativizability. Many arguments or adjuncts from complement clauses can be relativized (§ sec:out.complement.relativization ), but the limits on relativizability in embedded clauses is a topic for further fine-grained research.
summary:
In Japhug, the functions that can be relativized vary by clause type: relatives may generally be headless, except in possessor relativization, which requires a possessive prefix on the possessee. Intransitive subjects and objects are typically relativized with head-internal clauses, while transitive subjects, goals, and adjuncts are more often relativized by prenominal clauses.  

However, some adjuncts are not relativizable, including causees, standards in comparative constructions, and exceptive phrases with *maapart from*. The direct object of transitive verbs in purposive clauses of motion verbs also cannot be relativized, although many arguments and adjuncts from complement clauses can be.

text: relative clause!focalization focalization!relativization
summary: The passage indicates a relationship between focalization and relativization in the treatment of relative clauses. It appears to point to a discussion of how these two grammatical processes are connected or contrasted.

text:
pseudo-cleft
Among the possible means of focalizing noun phrases, most if not all languages use an equative construction with a headless relative clause (or a relative clause with an overt head noun, if this head noun is different from the focalized noun phrase) in the topicalized position and the focalized noun phrase as the nominal predicate, as in English `[What matters] are his ideas ' or `[The thing that matters] is meaning '.

Such constructions are generally referred to as pseudo-clefts, by contrast with cleft sentences, a type of construction (such as English `It is his ideas [that matter]') where the focalized noun is the head of the clause defining it, that clause being built like a relative, but sometimes presenting language-specific differences with relative clauses of the same type. points out for instance that in French clefting of dative phrases ( C'est à Jean que tu as donné le livre) differs from the corresponding relativization ( La personne à laquelle tu as donné le livre).

Pseudo-cleft constructions in Japhug consist of a headless relative clause (generally with the determiner nɯ in topicalizing function, § sec:nW.topic ) followed by a nominal predicate with an affirmative ( ŋube, ɕtibe) or negative ( maʁnot be, § sec:suppletive.negative ) copula.

Pseudo-clefts in Japhug do occur in intransitive subject ( ex:jAkWGe.nW and ex:pWkWcha.nW ), direct object ( ex:WkAndza.nWnW and ex:akAnWrga.nW.nAZo ) or semi-objects ( ex:pGa.ra.nWkArga, § sec:semi.tr.relativization ) functions.

Most pseudo-clefts are participial relatives as in the examples above, but there are also finite object relatives (§ sec:object.relativization ) as in ( ex:tutWmtshi.nWnW ).

An alternative (and much rarer) type of pseudo-cleft has the headless relative as the nominal predicate, as in ( ex:stu.Zo.WkAnWzdWG ).

ɲɤ-ɣɤwu matɕi tɕendɤre nɯ [stu ʑo ɯ-kɤ-nɯzdɯɣ] nɯ pjɤ-ɕti tɕe \\

Although pseudo-cleft constructions are well-attested in the corpus, they are not the main morphosyntactic device to focalize constituents in Japhug. Other focalizing constructions include sentence-final copulas (§ sec:focalization.final.copula ) and focus particles (§ sec:focus ). Some focalized noun phrases are also devoid of any specific marking of focalization, even intonational ones (§ sec:focalization.overt ).
summary:
Pseudo-clefts are equative constructions with a headless relative clause in topicalized position and the focalized noun phrase as the nominal predicate; they are distinguished from cleft sentences, where the focalized noun is the head of the clause. In Japhug, pseudo-clefts typically use a headless relative clause followed by a nominal predicate with an affirmative or negative copula, and they can focalize intransitive subjects, direct objects, semi-objects, and locative adjuncts, though transitive subjects are rare.  

Most Japhug pseudo-clefts are participial relatives, but finite object relatives and a rarer alternative type with the headless relative as the nominal predicate also occur. The construction is well attested, but it is not the main way Japhug focalizes constituents, since sentence-final copulas, focus particles, and even unmarked focalization are also used.

text:
In addition, we find pseudo-cleft constructions whose second member is not a nominal predicate with a copula, but rather a clause which could stand as a complete sentence. The subject participle of pebe good is commonly used in these constructions in affirmative ( kɯ-pe `what is good is that...', `fortunately...') or negative form ( kɯ-pe `what is bad is that...', `unfortunately...') as in ( ex:mAkWpe.tCe ).
