In these constructions, the participle of *pebe* ‘good’ is commonly used in affirmative or negative form to mean ‘fortunately’ or ‘unfortunately,’ and the topicalized participial clause is followed by the linker *tɕe* in a topicalizing function instead of the determiner *nɯ*.

text:
relative clause!quantification quantification!relativization
Relative clauses are found in three quantificational constructions.

First, correlative relative clauses occur with interrogative pronouns used as free-choice indefinites (§ sec:interrogative.relative ). In ( ex:nAkAthu.tChi.kWtu ) for instance, the relative whose main verb is the participle kɯ-tu has the pronoun tɕʰiwhat in apposition with the object participle nɤ-kɤ-tʰu `(the things) that you ask' as head, with the meaning `any' or `whatever'.

exe

[[ nɤ-kɤ-tʰu ] tɕʰi kɯ-tu] tɤ-tʰe jɤɣ-o \\
2sg. poss - obj: pcp -ask what sbj: pcp -exist imp -ask[III] be.possible: fact - sfp \\
`Ask any/whatever question you [may] have.' (conversation, 17-09-06)
exe

Second, totalitative reduplication (§ sec:totalitative.redp ) indicates universal quantification of the relativized element (§ sec:totalitative.relatives ). In particular, the reduplicated form of the kɯ kɯ-tu `all those that/who exist' of the existential verb tuexist can follow nouns ( ex:azda.ra.kWkWtu ), with a meaning similar to the adverbial determiner tʰamtɕɤtall (§ sec:universal.quant ).

exe

a-zda ra kɯ kɯ-tu ʑo a-tɤ-bɯɣ-nɯ smɯlɤm \\
1sg. poss -companion pl total sbj: pcp -exist emph irr - pfv -miss.home- pl prayer \\
`May all of my companions miss home!' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

Constructions such as that in ( ex:azda.ra.kWkWtu ) originate from head-internal (or postnominal) participial relatives (`all my existing companions'). However, it is unclear whether this analysis is still valid synchronically, and even whether kɯ kɯ-tu is still a participle. It may have been reanalyzed as a postnominal quantifier, as suggested by the fact that it can occur with pronouns, as in ( ex:nWZora.kWkWtu ), where an interpretation in terms of a relative clause, whether restrictive (`all those of you who exist'?) or non-restrictive (`you, all the existing ones'?) is more difficult.

exe

nɯʑora kɯ kɯ-tu ʑo lɤ-nɯ-jɣɤt-nɯ \\
2pl total sbj: pcp -exist emph imp: upstream - vert -turn.back \\
`Turn back and go to your homes.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

Third, headless relative clauses (§ sec:headless.relative ) in existential constructions (§ sec:existential.basic ) are more often used than indefinite pronouns (§ sec:indef.pro ) to express non-specific indefinite entities, whether humans (`someone', ex:WkWlAT.GAZu ) or inanimate ones (`something', ex:WkAndza.GAZu1 ).

exe

[a-<dianhua> ɯ-kɯ-lɤt] ɣɤʑu \\
1sg. poss -phone 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -release exist: sens \\
`There is someone calling me on the phone!' (conversation, 22-08-2018)
exe

exe

sɯŋgɯ si ɯ-mat a-pɯ-dɤn tɕe, nɯ ɯ-xpa nɯ ɲɯ-rkɯn ma kʰro kɤ-mto mɯ́j-ɣi ma [ɯ-kɤ-ndza] ɣɤʑu. \\
forest tree 3sg. poss -fruit irr - ipfv -be.many lnk dem 3sg. poss -year dem sens -be.few lnk much obj: pcp -see neg: sens -come lnk 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -eat exist: sens \\
`In years when there are many fruits on the trees in the forest, there are fewer Garrulax sp. ( ʁmɯrcɯ ) because they do not come [where they can be] seen, as they have things to eat (in the forest).' (23-pGAYaR)
0003606#S77
exe

Head-internal relatives (§ sec:head-internal.relative ) can have a similar meaning if their head noun is a generic noun like tɯrmeperson (§ sec:tWrme.generic ), as in ( ex:tWrme.kWngo.GAZu ).

exe

iɕqʰa [ tɯrme kɯ-ngo] ɣɤʑu tɕe, ɯ-kɯ-rtoʁ jɤ-ari-a wo! \\
just.before person sbj: pcp -be.ill exist: sens lnk 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -see aor -go[II]- 1sg sfp \\
`There is someone who is sick, I went to see him/her.' (conversation)
exe

Headless relative clauses also occur with a partitive meaning (some individuals among a group), as in ( ex:WkAndza.GAZu2 ). Note the difference in interpretation of the proposition ɯ-kɤ-ndza ɣɤʑu in ( ex:WkAndza.GAZu1 ) `it has something to eat' and in ( ex:WkAndza.GAZu2 ) `there are some (fishes) that it eats'.

exe

qaɟy cʰo qajɯ ɯ-ŋgɯz kɯnɤ, [ɯ-kɤ-ndza] ɣɤʑu, [ɯ-mɤ-kɤ-ndza] ɣɤʑu. [ɯ-kɤ-nɤ-mɯm], [ɯ-mɤ-kɤ-nɤ-mɯm] ɣɤʑu. \\
fish comit bugs 3sg. poss -inside: loc also 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -eat exist: sens 3sg. poss - neg - obj: pcp -eat exist: sens 3sg. poss - obj: pcp - trop -be.tasty 3sg. poss - neg - obj: pcp - trop -be.tasty exist: sens \\
`Among fishes and other marine animals, there are some that [whales]$_i$ eat and some that they$_i$ don't eat, some that they$_i$ find tasty and some that they$_i$ don't find tasty.' (160703 jingyu)
0006169#S21
exe

Since Japhug lacks negative pronouns (§ sec:indef.pro ), the only way to express a meaning corresponding to negative pronouns in Japhug is by combining a headless relative clause with a negative existential verbs (§ sec:negative.pronoun ), as in ( ex:nAkWnWGmu.me ).

exe

nɤ-kɯ-nɯɣ-mu me \\
2sg. poss - sbj: pcp - appl -be.afraid not.exist: fact \\
` Nobody is afraid of you!' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

Headless relative clauses in negative constructions are often embedded in a participial relative with the positive existential verb tuexist, as in ( ex:WCWkWphWt.kWtu.me ).

exe

tɕeri [nɯra [ɯ-ɕɯ-kɯ-pʰɯt] ra kɯ-tu] me ma \\
lnk dem: pl 3sg. poss - tral - sbj: pcp -take.off pl sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: fact lnk \\
`But nobody goes and picks [wild strawberries].' (because nobody likes to eat them) (11-paRzwamWntoR)
0003476#S81
exe
summary: Relative clauses in this passage are shown to participate in three quantificational constructions: correlative relatives with interrogative pronouns function as free-choice indefinites meaning “any/whatever,” and totalitative reduplication expresses universal quantification, though this may have been reanalyzed synchronically as a postnominal quantifier. Headless relative clauses are used especially in existential constructions to express nonspecific indefinites, partitives, and, with negative existential verbs, the meanings corresponding to negative pronouns such as “nobody.”

text:
This section discusses constructions which present real or apparent ambiguity between relative and complement clauses, and proposes a few syntactic tests to disambiguate the two.

To the cases studied below, the adnominal complement clauses (§ sec:complement.taking.nouns ), which resemble prenominal relatives (§ sec:prenominal.relative ), must be added.
summary: The passage introduces constructions that may be ambiguous between relative clauses and complement clauses and says that syntactic tests will be used to distinguish them. It also notes that adnominal complement clauses, which resemble prenominal relative clauses, should be included among the cases considered.

text:
ambiguity!relative clause ambiguity!complement clause
Finite relative clauses (§ sec:finite.relatives ), when they occur as objects or semi-object of verbs of perception ( mtosee, mtsʰɤmhear etc) or cognition ( tsoknow, understand, `know' etc) may not be easily distinguishable from complement clauses, as this type of verb can take either nominal objects/semi-objects or complement clauses, and both finite relatives and finite complements are found with the same demonstrative determiners nɯ and nɯnɯ (§ sec:relative.determiners.complementizer, § sec:complement.determiner ).

For instance, in ( ex:mbrWtCW.latCAt.nW ), the clause mbrɯtɕɯ la-tɕɤt (§ sec:object.relativization ) can either be interpreted as a head-internal finite object relative clause (§ sec:head-internal.relative, § sec:object.relativization ) `the knife that (the butcher) had unsheathed' or as a complement clause (§ sec:finite.complement ) `that (the butcher) had unsheathed his knife'. Both interpretations would make sense in the context (§ sec:relative.core.arg ).

exe

spjaŋkɯ ʁnɯz ni kɯ nɯnɯ nɤki, [ mbrɯtɕɯ la-tɕɤt] nɯ pa-mto-ndʑi tɕe, wuma ʑo ɲɤ-mu-ndʑi. \\
wolf two du erg dem filler knife aor:3 -take.out dem aor:3 -see- du lnk really emph ifr -be.afraid- du \\
`The two wolves, seeing that he had unsheathed his knife (or: seeing the knife that he had unsheathed), were very afraid. (150902 liaozhai lang-zh)
0006340#S29
exe

Three criteria (already mentioned in § sec:finite.relatives ) can however help disambiguating between the two analyses in specific contexts.

First, the presence of totalitative reduplication (§ sec:totalitative.relatives ) indicates that the subordinate clause can only be analyzed as a relative, as in ( ex:tWtAmWtindZi.nW ). The relativized element of this headless clause is the semi-object, see § sec:recip.amW.indirective on the argument structure of amɯtisay to each other.

exe

stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ kɯ nɯra [tɯ tɤ-amɯ-ti-ndʑi] nɯ pjɤ-mtsʰɤm. \\
most sbj: pcp -be.small dem erg dem: pl t otal aor - recip -say- du dem ifr -hear \\
`The youngest [boy] heard all the things that they had said to each other.' (160630 poucet1)
0006065#S32
exe

Second, finite subordinate clauses whose verb is in the Inferential, Sensory, Egophoric, Irrealis or Imperative cannot be relative clauses. For instance mɯ-pjɤ-pe in Inferential Imperfective must be a complement clause.

exe

tɕe ɯʑo si tɤ-mda kóʁmɯz nɤ nɯ [mɯ-pjɤ-pe] nɯ ko-tso ri ɲɤ-maqʰu ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk 3sg die: fact aor -be.the.time only.then add dem neg - ifr. ipfv -be.good dem ifr -understand lnk ifr -be.late sens -be \\
`Just before dying, he understood that [what he had done] was not good, but it was too late.' (aesop nongfu yu she-zh)
0006268#S113
exe

Third, finite relative clauses cannot relativize subjects, and therefore `plain' intransitive verbs (excluding semi-transitive verbs § sec:semi.transitive and verbs with goals § sec:intr.goal ) cannot occur in finite relative clauses (except in the case of locative and time adjunct relativization, § sec:time.relativization ). Therefore, clauses such as mɯ-pjɤ-pe `it was not good' in ( ex:mWpjApe.nW.kotso ) and tu-ɣɤwu `it cries/howls' in ( ex:tuGAwu.nW.WmtshAm ) cannot be interpreted as subject relatives `(the thing) that was not good' or `(the wolf) that howls'.

exe

nɯ [tu-ɣɤwu] nɯ ɯ-mtsʰɤm pɯ-rɲo-t-a ma \\
dem ipfv -cry dem 3sg. poss - bare. inf:hear aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg lnk \\
`I did hear [wolves] howl.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S27
exe
summary: Finite relative clauses can be hard to distinguish from complement clauses when they occur as objects or semi-objects of verbs of perception or cognition, since both types can appear with the demonstrative determiners nɯ and nɯnɯ. The passage notes that context may allow either reading, but three diagnostics help: totalitative reduplication signals a relative clause, subordinate clauses in Inferential/Sensory/Egophoric/Irrealis/Imperative forms must be complements, and finite relative clauses cannot relativize subjects, so plain intransitive verbs in such clauses are not subject relatives.

text:
ambiguity!relative clause
Due to the resemblance between the velar infinitives kɯ- and kɤ- (§ sec:velar.inf ) on the one hand and the subject (§ sec:subject.participle.ambiguities ) and especially object participles (§ sec:infinitives.participles ), distinguishing between infinitival clauses and participial relatives is not always trivial.

In ( ex:yazi.tAkAmWrkW ), we find a series of non-finite verb forms in kɯ- and kɤ- in clauses that are object of the complement-taking verb fɕɤttell (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ). Given the meaning of this example, it could appear to be preferrable to analyze these examples as complement clauses, translating <yazi> tɤ-kɤ-mɯrkɯ, tɤ-kɤ-ndza as `(he told him) that he had stolen and eaten a duck' and ɯ-βri...nɯ-kɯ-ɬoʁ as `that his body started itching, and that feathers started growing on it'.

exe

tɕe nɯra [pɯ pɯ-kɯ-fse] nɯra, [< yazi > tɤ-kɤ-mɯrkɯ, tɤ-kɤ-ndza], qʰe ɕɤr tɕe [ ɯ-βri tɤ-kɯ-rɤʑa] qʰe, [ɯ-βri tɕe iɕqʰa, <yazi> ɣɯ ɯ-muj nɯ-kɯ-ɬoʁ], nɯra pjɤ-fɕɤt. \\
lnk dem: pl total pst. ipfv - sbj: pcp -be.like dem: pl duck aor - obj: pcp -steal aor - obj: pcp -eat lnk evening loc 3sg. poss -body aor - sbj: pcp -itch lnk 3sg. poss -body loc the.aforementioned duck gen 3sg. poss -feather aor - sbj: pcp -come.out dem: pl ifr -tell \\
`He told [the old man] everything that had happened, about the duck that he had stolen and eaten, and his body itching, and the duck feathers that had grown on it.' (150904 maya-zh)
0006364#S26
exe

However, the problem with analyzing these clauses as infinitival complement clauses is that the intransitive motion verb ɬoʁcome out, being dynamic, never takes a kɤ- infinitive, and that the form nɯ-kɯ-ɬoʁ can only be a subject participle `(something) that has come out'. For this reason, the non-finite clauses in ( ex:yazi.tAkAmWrkW ) have to be analyzed as head-internal and headless (object and subject) participial relative clauses.

An analysis of clauses in kɤ- as infinitive complement clauses is restricted to complement-taking verbs which unambiguously select kɤ- infinitives of plain intransitive verbs (§ sec:infinitives.participles, § sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ).
summary: Because velar infinitives in kɯ- and kɤ- resemble subject and especially object participles, it is not always easy to tell infinitival clauses from participial relatives. In the cited example, although the clauses could initially be read as complement clauses meaning “that he had stolen and eaten a duck” and “that feathers had grown on it,” the presence of ɬoʁ ‘come out,’ which cannot take a kɤ- infinitive and here must be a subject participle, shows that the forms are actually head-internal, headless participial relative clauses. The text adds that analyzing kɤ- clauses as infinitival complements is only justified with complement-taking verbs that clearly select kɤ- infinitives of plain intransitive verbs.

subsection: Participial clauses in core argument function
text:
Some verbs such as the verbs of pretence ʑɣɤpapretend and nɯɕpɯzpretend `dress up as', `imitate' select subject participle clauses as objects or semi-objects such as kɯ-ngo in ( ex:kWngo.toZGApa ), which could appear to be similar to the purposive complement of motion verbs (§ sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ).

exe

[kɯ-ngo] to-ʑɣɤpa tɕe \\
sbj: pcp -be.sick ifr -pretend lnk \\
`She pretended to be sick.' (Nyima Wodzer 2002)
exe

However, there is clear evidence that these clauses are in fact headless relatives: ( ex:kWngo.toZGApa ) can literally be translated as `she pretended to be a sick person'. The difference with purposive clauses can be shown by three tests.

First, unlike motion verbs, pretence verbs can take nouns as objects (as shown by ex:qaɕpa.tonWCpWz and ex:tAkWnWCpWz.pjAsWXsAl ) instead of clauses with subject participles.

exe

qaɕpa to-nɯɕpɯz, qaɕpa ɯ-rqʰu to-ŋga, \\
frog ifr -pretend frog 3sg. poss -skin ifr -wear \\
`He dressed up as a frog, he wore a frog's skin.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

Second, these verbs can occur with a participial clause whose subject is overt and different from the subject of the verb of the matrix clause, as in ( ex:tApAtso.kWGAwu.kAnWCpWz ) where tɤ-pɤtsochild is the subject of the verb ɣɤwucry in the participial clause, but not the subject of nɯɕpɯzpretend, `disguise as', `imitate' (§ sec:constr.participial.clause ). Such a subject mismatch would be completely ungrammatical with a purposive clause.

exe

[ tɤ-pɤtso kɯ-ɣɤwu] ʑo kɤ-nɯɕpɯz mɤ-spe-a ma nɯ mɯma spe-a \\
indef. poss -child sbj: pcp -cry emph inf -imitate neg -be.able[III]: fact - 1sg lnk dem apart.from be.able[III]: fact - 1sg \\
`I cannot imitate a child crying, but apart from that I can imitate [anything].' (27-kikakCi)
0003700#S134
exe

Third, we find examples like ( ex:Wmi.kWmNAm.tonWCpWznW ) where the subject of the verb in the main clause is not coreferent with the subject of the participial clause but with the possessor of the subject. These cases can be accounted for as possessor relative clauses (§ sec:subject.participle.other.relative, § sec:S.possessor.relativization ): ( ex:Wmi.kWmNAm.tonWCpWznW ) could thus be literally translated as `he pretended to be someone whose leg hurt'.

exe

tɕe [ ɯ -mi kɯ-mŋɤm] to-nɯɕpɯz \\
lnk 3sg. poss -leg sbj: pcp -hurt ifr -pretend \\
`He pretended to feel pain in his leg.' (140426 lang yisheng-zh)
0003808#S9
exe
summary: The passage argues that verbs of pretence such as ʑɣɤpa ‘pretend’ and nɯɕpɯz ‘dress up as, imitate’ take subject participle clauses that are not purposive complements, but rather headless relatives. This is shown by three differences from purposive clauses: these verbs can also take nouns as objects, they allow an overt subject in the participial clause that differs from the matrix subject, and some cases are better analyzed as possessor relative clauses.

text:
In ( ex:tWtatWt.tostu ), the clause sŋaʁspa kɯ tɯ ta-tɯt `all (the things that) the sorcerer had said' is a headless object finite relative (§ sec:object.relativization ); the presence of totalitative reduplication in particular, shows that it cannot be interpreted as a complement clause (§ sec:totalitative.relatives ).

exe

tɕeri [sŋaʁspa kɯ tɯ ta-tɯt] nɯ to-stu \\
lnk sorcerer erg total aor:3 -say[II] dem ifr -do.like \\
`He did it everything the way that the sorcerer had said.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S85
exe

The syntactic function of this relative clause in the main clause is semi-object of the secundative verb studo like, which encodes the manner of the action as semi-object, and the entity subjected to the action as the direct object (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ).

In view of ( ex:tWtatWt.tostu ), it is tempting to analyze the clause ``nɯ a-tɤ-fse ɲɯ-ra" tɤ-tɯ-tɯt `(that) you said ``it should be (done) like that'' in ( ex:YWra.tAtWtWt.nW ), which occurs in the same syntactic context, as a finite object relative clause too, differing from that of ( ex:tWtatWt.tostu ) by being head-internal (§ sec:head-internal.relative ) instead of headless.

exe

[[`` nɯ a-tɤ-fse ɲɯ-ra "] tɤ-tɯ-tɯt] nɯ tɤ-stu-t-a ŋu \\
dem irr - pfv -be.like sens -be.needed aor -2-say[II] dem aor -do.like- pst: tr - 1sg be: fact \\
`I did it [the way that] you said should be done.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S315
exe

What is remarkable about the construction in ( ex:YWra.tAtWtWt.nW ) is that the relativized element is not a noun, but the (object) complement clause nɯ a-tɤ-fse ɲɯ-ra `it should be (done) like that', embedded within the relative.

A common example of relativized complement clause is found when the transitive perception verb mtsʰɤmhear (§ sec:mto.mtshAm.complement ) occurs with the object participle kɤ-ti of the verb tisay as in ( ex:konWrNu.kAti ). In this example, tɯrme nɯ ko-nɯrŋu has a double status: it is the object complement clause of kɤ-ti within the relative, and at the same time, it constitutes the relativized element of the head-internal participial clause (§ sec:object.relativization ).

exe

`[[`tɯrme nɯ ko-nɯrŋu''] kɤ-ti] mɯ-pɯ-mtsʰam-a \\
person dem ifr -have.pig.disease sbj: pcp -say neg - aor -hear- 1sg \\
`I have never heard of people getting the pig disease.' (25-khArWm)
0003644#S77
exe

The literal meaning of this construction can be conveyed in English as `I have not heard ``a man got the pig disease'' being said'.
summary:
The passage explains that in one example, the clause meaning “all the things that the sorcerer had said” is a headless finite object relative clause, not a complement clause, as shown by totalitative reduplication. Its function in the main clause is as the semi-object of the verb meaning ‘do like,’ which expresses manner through a semi-object and the acted-upon entity through the direct object.

It then notes a similar construction in which the relativized element is not a noun but an embedded object complement clause, making the clause head-internal rather than headless. A further example with a perception verb shows a clause that is both the object complement of a participial verb and the relativized element of a head-internal participial clause.

text:
This chapter, based on Sun's ( sun12complementation) work on Tshobdun and on earlier research on Japhug, presents an account of complement clauses and complementation strategies On the notion of complementation strategy, see and § sec:strategies. in Japhug.

This chapter comprises six sections. The first section following the introduction § sec:complement.types provides a classification of complement clauses based on the form of the main verb in the clause. The second one, § sec:strategies presents an overview of complementation strategies (including ambiguous relative clauses). The third one, § sec:complement.morphosyntax analyses a certain number of morphosyntactic specificities of complement clauses (aside from verbal morphology) that distinguishes them from the corresponding independent clauses. The fourth section, § sec:complement.taking.verbs surveys complement-taking verbs and describes the complement clause types and complementation strategies that they are compatible with. The fifth one, § sec:complement.taking.nouns discusses complement-taking nouns and noun-verb collocations and how they differ from prenominal (§ sec:prenominal.relative ) and genitival (§ sec:genitival.relatives ) relative clauses. The sixth section, § sec:syntactic.errors briefly analyzes syntactic errors related to complementation in the corpus.

In this chapter, all complement clauses are systematically indicated between square brackets (with double embedding in some cases).

The sections on participles (§ sec:participles ) and infinitives (§ sec:inf ) in a previous chapter partially overlap with some of the topics covered in this chapter.
summary: This chapter, based on Sun’s work on Tshobdun and earlier research on Japhug, gives an account of complement clauses and complementation strategies in Japhug. It is organized into six sections covering the classification of complement clauses, an overview of complementation strategies, morphosyntactic properties of complement clauses, complement-taking verbs, complement-taking nouns and noun-verb collocations, and syntactic errors related to complementation. The chapter also notes that complement clauses are marked in square brackets, and that earlier sections on participles and infinitives overlap partly with this material.

text: This section illustrates the different categories of complements attested in Japhug. Five main types of complement clauses are distinguished: velar infinitival complements, bare infinitival complements, finite complements, multiclausal complements and reported speech. In addition, Japhug has many different complementation strategies, discussed in § sec:strategies.
summary: Japhug has five main types of complement clauses: velar infinitival complements, bare infinitival complements, finite complements, multiclausal complements, and reported speech. The section also notes that Japhug uses many different complementation strategies, which are discussed elsewhere.

text:
infinitive!velar complement clause!velar infinitive
Velar infinite clauses (§ sec:velar.inf ) are one of the most common types of complement clauses in Japhug (§ sec:inf.complementation ). Two velar infinitives are attested, kɯ- for stative verbs and impersonal intransitive verbs, and kɤ- for dynamic and/or morphologically transitive verbs.

A recurrent problem in the study of subordinate clauses in Japhug is the ambiguity between velar participles and infinitives (§ sec:infinitives.participles ), making participial clauses and infinitival clauses only distinguishable in specific contexts, and the ambiguity between complement clauses and relative clauses with some complement-taking verbs (§ sec:relative.complement.ambiguities, § sec:relative.core.arg ). As a result, participial (§ sec:participial.relatives ) and finite relative clauses (§ sec:finite.relatives ) are in some case difficult to differentiate from velar infinitival complement clauses (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ) and finite complement clauses (§ sec:finite.complement ), respectively.
summary: Velar infinitival clauses are one of the most common types of complement clause in Japhug, and there are two forms: kɯ- for stative verbs and impersonal intransitive verbs, and kɤ- for dynamic or morphologically transitive verbs. The passage also notes that subordinate clauses are often difficult to analyze because velar participles and infinitives, as well as complement clauses and relative clauses, can be ambiguous and only distinguished in certain contexts.

text:
While velar infinitives bear no person indexation markers, noun phrases receive the same case markers in infinitive clauses as in independent clauses, showing that infinitives have the same argument structures as finite verb forms.

When an argument is shared between the complement and the matrix clause, it does not necessarily have the same syntactic function in both clauses, as in ( ex:kW.nWra.kAstu ), where tɤɕimelady is transitive subject in the complement clause (see § sec:ditransitive.secundative on the argument structure of studo like) and intransitive subject in the matrix clause (§ sec:semi.transitive ).

exe

[tɤɕime nɯ kɯ nɯra kɤ-stu] pjɤ-cʰa \\
princess dem erg dem: pl inf -do.like.this ifr -can \\
`The princess succeeded in doing it.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S241
exe

In this sentence, the noun takes the ergative marker kɯ in accordance with the verb of the complement clause (§ sec:A.kW ), showing that it belongs to the complement clause rather than to the matrix clause directly. This is the most commonly observed pattern in Japhug texts: in infinitival clauses, the shared arguments more often take the case marking selected by the verb of the complement clause than that of the matrix clause.

However, when the complement-taking verb is a stative verb, there are cases where the ergative on the transitive subject is optional, as shown by ( ex:tWrme.kAndza.sna ) (without ergative on tɯrmeperson; Tshendzin has confirmed that this example is correct) and ( ex:tWrme.kW.kAndza.sna ) (with ergative). The precise conditions for this phenomenon still remain to be investigated.

exe

[ɯ-mat nɯ kɤ-ndza] sna, [tɯrme kɤ-ndza] sna \\
3sg. poss -fruit dem inf -eat be.good: fact people inf -eat be.good: fact \\
`Its fruit is nice to eat, it is nice for people to eat.' (09-stoR)
0003470#S45
exe

exe

[nɯnɯ tɯrme kɯ kɤ-ndza] sna \\
dem people erg inf -eat be.good: fact \\
`It is nice for people to eat.' (13-NanWkWmtsWG)
0003492#S157
exe
summary: Velar infinitives do not show person indexation, but noun phrases in infinitival clauses take the same case markers as in independent clauses, indicating that infinitives have the same argument structure as finite verbs. In shared-argument constructions, the shared noun typically bears the case required by the complement verb rather than the matrix verb, showing that it belongs syntactically to the complement clause. With stative complement-taking verbs, however, ergative marking on the transitive subject can be optional, and the conditions for this are not yet clear.

text:
Coreference restrictions between the arguments of complement clauses with kɤ- infinitives and their matrix clauses differ from verb to verb, and four cases can be distinguished.

First, in the case of impersonal verbs such as rabe needed, `be necessary' (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ), there is no argument coreference between the matrix clause and the complement clause. In this case, the arguments are neither indexed on the matrix verb nor on the verb in the complement clause.

Second, with a few transitive complement-taking verbs such as the transitive spabe able (§ sec:spa.verb ) and the intransitive nɤzdare (§ sec:nAz.verb ), coreference between the subject of the matrix clause and that of the complement clause is required.

Third, a handful of verbs, including sɯxcʰa (§ sec:sWxcha ), the causative of cʰacan (§ sec:sig.caus.modal ), have coreference between the subject of the complement clause and the object of the matrix clause.

Fourth, for most verbs taking infinitives (like the semi-transitive rgalike or the transitive rɲoexperience), the subject of the matrix clauses can be coreferential to either the subject of an intransitive verb ( ex:kAnWrAGo.rganW ), the subject of a transitive verb ( ex:kAnArtoXpjAt.pWrgaa ), the object ( ex:YWrganW ) and also possessors of core arguments (§ sec:rYo.complements ).

exe

tsuku tɕe [kɤ-nɯrɤɣo] wuma ʑo rga-nɯ tɕe \\
some lnk inf -sing really emph like: fact - pl lnk \\
`Some people like to sing.' (26-kWrNukWGndZWr) (S=S)
0003672#S102
exe

exe

aʑo [qajɯ nɯra kɤ-nɤrtoχpjɤt] pɯ-rga-a tɕe \\
1sg bugs dem: pl inf -observe pst. ipfv -like- 1sg lnk \\
`I liked to observe bugs.' (26-quspunmbro) (A=S)
0003684#S15
exe

exe

maka [tu-kɤ-nɤjoʁjoʁ], [tu-kɤ-fstɤt] nɯ ɲɯ-rga-nɯ \\
at.all ipfv - inf -flatter ipfv - inf -praise dem ipfv -like- pl \\
`They like to be flattered or praised.' (140427 yuanhou-zh) (P=S)
0003870#S53
exe

Other types of complement clauses differ from velar infinitive clauses by their constraints on coreference (see § sec:bare.inf.coreference ).
summary: Coreference restrictions between matrix clauses and kɤ- infinitive complement clauses vary by verb, and four patterns are identified. Some impersonal verbs like rabe ‘be necessary’ allow no argument coreference, while certain verbs require subject coreference between matrix and complement clauses; others link the complement subject to the matrix object. For most infinitive-taking verbs, the matrix subject may corefer with different roles in the complement clause, including the subject, object, or even a possessor of a core argument.

text:
infinitive!bare complement clause!bare infinitive
infinitive!dental complement clause!dental infinitive
Complement clauses with bare (§ sec:bare.inf ) and dental infinitives (§ sec:dental.inf ) are less widespread than those with velar infinitives. Only a limited number of complement-taking verbs select them: phasal verbs (including ʑabegin, sɤʑabegin, stʰɯtfinish, and jɤɣfinish), causative verbs derived from adjectives, the aspectual verb rɲoexperience and the causative sɯpa `cause to do' (§ sec:bare.dental.inf.sWpa ). With the exception of jɤɣfinish, these complement-taking verbs are all morphologically transitive.

In the Tshobdun corpus, the cognate verbs ɟeʔ `begin' and joɣʔ `finish' take velar infinitives, and there is no infinitival form comparable to the Japhug dental infinitive.
summary:
Complement clauses with bare and dental infinitives are less common than those with velar infinitives, and only a small set of verbs select them, mainly phasal verbs, some causatives derived from adjectives, the aspectual verb meaning ‘experience,’ and the causative ‘cause to do.’ Except for *jɤɣ* ‘finish,’ these verbs are morphologically transitive.  

The passage also notes that in the Tshobdun corpus, the cognate verbs for ‘begin’ and ‘finish’ take velar infinitives, and there is no infinitival form corresponding to the Japhug dental infinitive.

text:
Bare and dental infinitives are found in complementary distribution. Bare infinitives occur when the main verb of the complement clause is morphologically transitive (§ sec:transitivity.morphology ) as in ( ex:WCA.tuZanW.Cti ).

exe

pɤjkʰu pjɯ-si ɕɯŋgɯ ʑo [ɯ-ɕa ɯ-ndza] tu-ʑa-nɯ ɕti \\
still ipfv -die before emph 3sg. poss -flesh 3sg. poss - bare. inf:eat ipfv -start- pl be. aff: fact \\
`[The lions] start eating its flesh before it dies (i.e. while it is still alive).' (20-sWNgi)
0003562#S44
exe

Dental infinitives on the other hand are found when the verb of the complement clause is intransitive as in ( ex:tWmNAm.taZa ) (including labile verbs § sec:lability.morphosyntax ) or transitive with dummy subject ( ex:Wmat.tWBzu.naZa ) (§ sec:transitive.dummy ).

exe

[aʑo a-ku (a-mɤtsa), tɯ-mŋɤm] ta-ʑa \\
1sg 1sg. poss -head 1sg. poss -MZCh inf:II-hurt aor:3 -start \\
`My head$_i$, cousin, when it$_i$ starts hurting...' (TaRrdo 2003 conversation)
exe

exe

ɯ-mɯntoʁ nɯ pɯ-ŋgra tɕe [ɯ-ŋgɯ ɯ-mat tɯ-βzu] na-ʑa ri tɕe \\
3sg. poss -flower dem aor - acaus:cause.to.fall lnk 3sg. poss -inside 3sg. poss -fruit inf:II-make aor:3 -start loc lnk \\
`When its flower has fallen, and its fruit has started growing inside...' (12-ndZiNgri)
0003488#S109
exe

Since most complement-taking verbs selecting dental infinitives are transitive, case marking on the common subject can either be in the ergative or in the absolutive (§ sec:complement.clause.case.marking ).
summary: Bare and dental infinitives are in complementary distribution: bare infinitives appear when the complement verb is morphologically transitive, while dental infinitives appear with intransitive verbs, including labile verbs and transitive verbs with a dummy subject. Since most verbs that take dental infinitival complements are transitive, the shared subject may be marked either ergative or absolutive.

text:
Bare and dental infinitives strongly differ from velar infinitives as to their coreference restrictions. When the verb rɲoexperience occurs with velar infinitives, the subject of the matrix clause can be coreferential with either the subject, the object or even the possessor of the intransitive subject of the complement clause (§ sec:rYo.complements ).

The ambiguity between transitive subject or object coreference is particularly clear with the verb nɤkʰuinvite (to one's home as a guest, see examples ex:kAnAkhu1 and ex:kAnAkhu2 ), as with this verb both arguments are equal in terms of volition and control.

exe

[ɯʑo kɯ kɤ-nɤkʰu] pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
3sg erg inf -invite aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I have been to his house as a guest.' (= `He invited me to come to his house as a guest and I came.') (P=A)

[ɯʑo kɤ-nɤkʰu] pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
3sg inf -invite aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`He has been to my house as a guest.' (= `I have invited him to come to my house as a guest and he came.') (A=A)
exe

In the case of bare infinitives, on the other hand, the subjects of the matrix and complement clause must be coreferent, but the object of the matrix clause can, however, be neutralized to third person.

In example ( ex:nAkhu1 ), the shared subject (referring to the host) is 3sg. The verb of the matrix clause takes the complement clause as a 3sg object (hence the verb takes the 3 form without 1sg marking), while the verb of the complement clause takes a 1sg object (referring to the guest), marked by the possessive prefix a-. In the English translation, the 1sg is rendered as a subject, because translating a-nɤkʰu pa-rɲo as `He invited me' would be inexact, as this English sentence does not imply that the 1sg did attend the invitation.

exe

[a-nɤkʰu] pa-rɲo \\
1sg. poss - bare. inf: invite aor:3 -experience \\
`I have been to his house as a guest.' (= `He invited me to come to his house as a guest and I came.')

[ɯʑo ɯ-nɤkʰu] pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
3sg 3sg. poss - bare. inf:invite aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`He has been to my house as a guest.' (= `I invited him to come to my house as a guest and he came.')
exe

This generalization is observed for all transitive verbs taking bare infinitive complement clauses. However, the intransitive impersonal verb jɤɣfinish takes the bare infinitive clause as intransitive subject, and remains in third person singular regardless of the subject and object of the complement clause, as in ( ex:Wti.tojAG ), where although the subject of the complement clause is third person plural, no plural marker can appear on jɤɣ.

exe

[nɯra ɯ-ti] to-jɤɣ tɕe \\
dem: pl 3sg. poss - bare. inf:say ifr -finish lnk \\
`After saying that, (they went to the park)' (140515 congming de wusui xiaohai-zh)
0003998#S15
exe

With dental infinitives, subject coreference is the same, except in the case of transitive verb with dummy subject (example ex:Wmat.tWBzu.naZa, § sec:bare.inf.dental.complementary ), where the subject of the matrix verb is coreferent with the sole argument of the complement clauses, whose status is intermediate between that of a subject and an object (§ sec:absolutive.nature ).
summary: Bare and dental infinitives show stricter coreference patterns than velar infinitives. With velar infinitives, the matrix subject can refer to the complement’s subject, object, or even possessor, but with bare infinitives the matrix and complement subjects must be coreferent, while the matrix object may be neutralized to third person; this pattern holds for transitive verbs, though the impersonal verb jɤɣ ‘finish’ remains third singular regardless of the complement’s person/number. Dental infinitives behave like bare infinitives in coreference, except in cases with transitive verbs and dummy subjects, where the matrix subject corefers with the single argument of the complement clause.

text:
complement clause!finite
Complement clauses, like relative clauses (§ sec:finite.relatives ), can have a verb in finite, rather than infinitival form in Japhug and other Gyalrong languages. These constructions are called ``finite complement clauses'' in the present work, corresponding to Sun's ( sun12complementation) ``S-like (sentence-like) clauses''. I chose ``finite'' rather than ``S-like'' to avoid confusion with ``S'' as abbreviation for ``intransitive subject''. This category excludes reported speech complement, which present different characteristics (§ sec:reported.speech ).
summary: Japhug and other Gyalrong languages allow complement clauses with finite verbs rather than infinitival forms, a construction referred to here as “finite complement clauses.” The author uses this term instead of Sun’s “S-like clauses” to avoid confusion with the grammatical abbreviation “S” for intransitive subject. Reported speech complements are excluded because they show different properties.

text:
In finite clauses other than reported speech, TAME marking in the complement clause presents some restrictions. Of the 11 primary TAME categories (§ sec:tame.intro ), only the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.complement ) and the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:fact.complement ) are compatible with most if not all verbs selecting finite complement clauses, regardless of the TAME category of the matrix verb. In ( ex:junWCea.tAchaa ) for instance, the verb of the complement clause is the Imperfective while that of the matrix clause is in the Aorist.

exe

[aʑo a-ŋga ra tu-nɯ-ŋge-a, jɤɣɤt ju-nɯ-ɕe-a] ra tɤ-cʰa-a \\
1sg 1sg -clothes pl ipfv - auto -wear[III]- 1sg toilet ipfv - auto -go- 1sg pl aor -can- 1sg \\
`I am able now to get dressed by myself and use the bathroom by myself (again, after an accident).' (conversation, 17-08-21)
exe

The Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.complement.clauses ) and Imperative (§ sec:imp.compl ) are also found, but only with modal auxiliaries such as rabe needed as in ( ex:amApWwGnWClWG ). Unlike in Tshobdun, verbs of cognition such as sɯsothink do not select the Irrealis; although complement clauses in the Irrealis are found with these verbs, they are best analyzed in Japhug as reported speech (§ sec:irrealis.complement.clauses, § sec:reported.speech ).

exe

ndɤre [kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi a-mɤ-pɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-ɕlɯɣ] ɲɯ-ra ma rca nɯ ɲɯ-ndoʁ qʰe ɕlaʁ ʑo pjɯ-ɴɢrɯ ɲɯ-ɕti. \\
lnk inf: stat be.small irr - neg - pfv: down - inv - auto -drop sens -be.needed because unexp: deg dem sens -be.brittle lnk at.once emph ipfv - acaus:break sens -be: aff \\
`However, one should not let it drop at all, otherwise, as it is very brittle, it would break at once.' (30-Com)
0003736#S26
exe

Other TAME categories, such as Aorist (§ sec:aor.complement ) or Inferential ( ex:chAsWjGAt.pjAchaa ), are only attested in the complement clause if the matrix verb is also in the Aorist or in the Inferential, respectively. This constraint may not apply to complements of perception and cognition verbs such as mtosee (§ sec:mto.mtshAm.complement ). No semantic difference has yet been ascertained between Imperfective complements ( ex:junWCea.tAchaa ) and complements whose TAME category is copied from that of the matrix verb ( ex:tAnANkWNkea.tAchaa ); the latter are considerably rarer.

exe

[kɯ-xtɕɯ-xtɕi tɤ-nɤŋkɯŋke-a] tɤ-cʰa-a. \\
sbj: pcp - emph be.small aor -walk.around- 1sg aor -can- 1sg \\
`I am now able to walk around a little bit (again, after an accident).' (conversation, 17-08-21)
exe

exe

[zdɯm kɯ-ɲaʁ nɯ cʰɤ-sɯ-jɣɤt] pjɤ-cʰa ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
cloud sbj: pcp -be.black dem ifr: downstream - caus -turn.back ifr -can sens -be \\
`He succeeded in making the black cloud retreat.' (25-kAmYW-XpAltCin)
0003642#S61
exe

The TAME agreement between the matrix verb and the verb of the complement clause is not limited to Aorist and Inferential, and is also attested with Irrealis and Egophoric Present, as in ( ex:akAGWt.apWcha ) and ( ex:kutWndze.Wkura ), respectively.

exe

[nɯnɯ a-kɤ-ɣɯt] a-pɯ-cʰa tɕe nɯnɯ pʰɤn \\
dem irr - pfv: east -bring irr - pfv -can lnk dem be.efficient: fact \\
`If he succeeds in bringing him here, it will be efficient [to cure my disease].' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

exe

[nɤ-ɕqʰe smɤn ku-tɯ-ndze] ɯ-kú-ra? \\
2sg. poss -cough medicine prs -2-eat[III] qu - prs -be.needed \\
`Do you have to take medicine for your cough (now)?' (conversation 2019-08-16)
exe

Examples like ( ex:tAnANkWNkea.tAchaa ), ( ex:chAsWjGAt.pjAchaa ) and ( ex:akAGWt.apWcha ) are not analyzable as serial verb constructions, since subject coreference is not always observed, depending on the matrix verb (§ sec:svc.finite.agreement ).
summary: In finite complement clauses outside reported speech, Japhug shows strong restrictions on TAME marking: the Imperfective and Factual Non-Past are broadly compatible with many complement-taking verbs, while other categories are more limited. Irrealis and Imperative occur mainly with modal auxiliaries, and complements with Aorist or Inferential are typically possible only when the matrix verb has the same TAME, though this agreement pattern also occurs with Irrealis and Egophoric Present. The passage notes that these complement-clause patterns are not best analyzed as serial verb constructions because subject coreference is not consistently present.

text:
complement clause!coreference restriction
There are four different patterns of coreference restriction between the arguments of finite complement clauses and those of the matrix verb.

The first type includes verbs like spabe able (§ sec:spa.verb ), which require coreference between their subject and the (transitive or intransitive) subject of the complement clause. In ( ex:tulata.mWjspea ), both the verb of the complement clause and the matrix verb are in 1sg 3 form, with 1sg coreference. The same coreference restriction is observed when this verb takes a velar infinitive complement (§ sec:velar.inf.coreference ).

exe

[<weixin> tu-lat-a] nɯra mɯ́j-spe-a. \\
Wechat ipfv -release- 1sg dem: pl neg: sens -be.able[III]- 1sg \\
`I am not able to use Wechat.' (conversation, 17-03-27)
exe

The second type is represented by the semi-transitive complement-taking verb rgalike, which allows co-reference between its subject and either the (transitive or intransitive) subject ( ex:kunWtaj.rgaj ) or the object ( ex:tukWnAjoRjoRa.rgaa ) of the complement clause.

exe

[nɯ ku-nɯ-ta-j] wuma ʑo rga-j \\
dem ipfv - auto -put- 1pl really emph like: fact - 1sg \\
`We like to put it (in the tea kettle to make tea).' (30-macha)
0003746#S11
exe

exe

[nɤʑo kɯ tu-kɯ-nɤjoʁjoʁ-a] nɯra rga-a \\
2sg erg ipfv -2 1-flatter- 1sg dem: pl like: fact - 1sg \\
`I like it when you flatter me.' (elicited)
exe

The third type includes impersonal modal and aspectual verbs such as rabe needed, `be necessary' or ntsʰihave better, which take their complement clause as their intransitive subject (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb. For instance, in ( ex:pjWtWsi.ntshi ), the modal auxiliary ntsʰi can only occur in 3sg form, and cannot take the 2sg indexation of the verb in complement clause.

exe

[nɤʑo mɤlɤn ʑo pjɯ-tɯ-si] ntsʰi\\
2sg absolutely emph ipfv -2-die be.better: fact \\
`You must die!' (140512 fushang he yaomo1-zh)
0003969#S22
exe

Fourth, verbs of perception and cognition such as mtosee (§ sec:mto.mtshAm.complement ) have no constraints on person indexation and neither require nor prohibit any coreference between main and complement clause.
summary: The passage describes four patterns of coreference restriction between finite complement clauses and matrix verbs. Some verbs, like *spabe* “be able,” require subject coreference with the complement clause subject; others, like *rga* “like,” allow coreference with either the subject or object of the complement clause; impersonal modal/aspectual verbs such as *rabe* “be necessary” and *ntsʰi* “have better” take the complement clause as their intransitive subject and restrict person indexing; and perception/cognition verbs like *mto* “see” place no constraints on person indexation or coreference.

subsubsection: Finite complements vs. serial verb constructions
text:
ambiguity!finite complement clauses
Some complement-taking verbs such as cʰacan occur with clauses sharing the same subject and the same TAME category, as in ( ex:kotshi.pjAcha ). This could appear to be analyzable as a serial verb construction (§ sec:svc ) or pseudocoordination.

exe

qajdo nɯ kɯ [tɯ-ci ko-tsʰi] pjɤ-cʰa. \\
crow dem erg indef. poss -water ifr -drink ifr -can \\
`The crow succeeded in drinking water.' (aesop kouke de wuya-zh)
exe

However, I prefer to analyze these constructions as a particular type of finite complements with TAME agreement between the matrix verb and the complement verb (§ sec:TAM.finite ).

Subject coreference is not a specificity of this construction, but rather a property of the complement-taking verb (§ sec:finite.complement.coref ). With impersonal verbs such as rabe needed, which do not require subject coreference, TAME agreement is also attested, as in ( ex:totinW.pjAra ), where the verb to-ti-nɯ is in the Inferential (a category that does not normally occur in finite complement clauses, § sec:finite.complement.coref ) by agreeing with the matrix verb pjɤ-ra.

exe

[``ɣa" nɤ ``ɣa" nɯ to-ti-nɯ] pjɤ-ra. \\
yes add yes dem ifr -say- pl ifr. ipfv -be.needed \\
`They had no other choice but to say `yes'.' (140518 jinyin chengbao-zh)
0004028#S54
exe

Phasal verbs such as ʑabegin and stʰɯtfinish (§ sec:aspectual.complement ), which generally select bare/dental infinitives (§ sec:bare.dental.inf ), are marginally used in the construction, as in (§ ex:tAtWnAmat.tAtWZat ).

exe

[jɯxɕo tɕʰi tɤ-tɯ-nɤma-t tɤ-tɯ-ʑa-t] ʑo nɯ, ɕɤr mɤɕtʂa ɯʑo tɤ-nɤme ra \\
this.morning what aor -2-do- pst: tr aor -2-start- pst: tr emph dem night until 3sg imp -do[III] be.needed: fact \\
`That which you have started doing this morning, do it until night.' (140515 jiesu de laoren-zh)
0004004#S122
exe
summary: The passage argues that constructions with verbs like *cʰacan* should not be analyzed as serial verb constructions or pseudocoordination, but as finite complement clauses with TAME agreement between the matrix verb and the complement verb. Subject coreference is treated as a property of the complement-taking verb rather than of this construction itself, and the text notes that even impersonal verbs and some phasal verbs can occur in this pattern, though the latter only marginally.

text:
Complements are not always restricted to one single clause. Example ( ex:pjWsAtse.tuNke ) illustrates a finite biclausal complement: cʰacan (§ sec:cha.verb ) has two complement clauses, the first of which ɯ-mi pjɯ-sɯ-ɤtse specifies the manner of the second one (§ sec:svc.manner ).

exe

ma ju-mtsaʁ ʁɟa ʑo ma nɯ ma [[ɯ-mi pjɯ-sɯ-ɤtse] [tu-ŋke]] mɯ́j-cʰa\\
lnk ipfv -jump completely emph lnk dem apart.from 3sg. poss -foot ipfv - caus -be.inserted[III] ipfv -walk neg: sens -can \\
`It only jumps, as it is not able to walk with its feet (by taking steps).' (28-qaCpa2)
0003716#S4
exe

Multiclausal infinitive complements are also found, as in ( ex:kAnWrtsW.kANke.ra.tAcha ), though they are ambiguous with infinitive complements embedded within other infinitive complements, as in ( ex:kAndza.kAGAndWB ) (a manner causative complement, § sec:causative.manner.complement ) or complements containing converbial manner clauses (§ sec:inf.converb ).

exe

[kɤ-nɯrtsɯ] [kɤ-ŋke] ra tɤ-cʰa \\
inf -crawl inf -walk pl aor -can \\
`When [the baby] is able to crawl and walk,...' (140426 tApAtso kAnWBdaR1)
exe

exe

[[kɤ-ndza] kɤ-ɣɤ-ndɯβ] mɯ́j-kʰɯ tɕe lú-wɣ-sɯ-qioʁ ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe \\
inf -chew inf - caus -be.minute neg: sens -be.possible lnk ipfv - inv - caus -vomit sens -be lnk \\
`[Dogs]$_i$ cannot chew [ pɤŋɤxɕaj ]$_j$ (a type of grass) into fine parts, and it$_j$ makes them vomit.' (140505 panaxCAj)
0003915#S4
exe

Another type of biclausal complement, exemplified by ( ex:pe.mApe.arAtCha ) and ( ex:rtaR.mArtaR.zrAtCha ), comprises an affirmative verb form, followed by its negative counterpart, expressing a disjunction `whether $X$ or $ X$'.

exe

[[ɯ-ngra pe] [mɤ-pe]] nɯ, [[kɤ-nɤma pe] [mɤ-pe]] arɤtɕʰa \\
3sg. poss -salary good: fact neg -be.good: fact dem inf -work good: fact neg -be.good: fact be.determined.from: fact \\
`Whether his salary is good or not is determined by/depends on whether his work is good or not.' (elicited)
exe

exe

[[ɯ-spa rtaʁ] [mɤ-rtaʁ]] tɤ-z-rɤtɕʰe \\
3sg. poss -material be.enough: fact neg -be.enough: fact imp - caus -be.determined.from[III] \\
`Determine [the quantity of clothes that you are going to make] based on whether the [quantity of] cloth is sufficient.' (elicited)
exe

With bare and dental infinitives, multiclausal complements are only attested in the simultaneity construction (§ sec:bare.dental.inf.sWpa ).
summary:
The passage explains that complements can contain more than one clause. It gives examples of finite biclausal complements, where one complement clause specifies the manner of another, as well as multiclausal infinitive complements, though these can be ambiguous with other kinds of embedding.

It also describes biclausal complements formed by an affirmative verb followed by its negative counterpart, expressing a disjunctive meaning like “whether X or not.” With bare and dental infinitives, multiclausal complements are only attested in the simultaneity construction.

text:
reported speech
Verbs of speech (such as tisay or fɕɤttell) and cognition (in particular sɯsothink, `want') can take reported speech complements, in which the speaker either (exactly or partially) reproduces a sentence uttered by the person he is quoting, or verbalizes the words he assumes a person is thinking. These clauses have finite verb forms, and are thus a sub-category of finite complement clauses, but present some properties distinguishing them from the complements studied in § sec:finite.complement.
summary: Verbs of speech and cognition, such as “say,” “tell,” “think,” and “want,” can take reported speech complements that either reproduce someone’s words or express what a person is assumed to be thinking. These complements contain finite verb forms, so they are a subtype of finite complement clause, but they also show properties that distinguish them from the other finite complements discussed earlier.

text:
Reported speech clauses stand out among complement clauses in having no restriction on the verb form, in particular in terms of TAME (§ sec:TAM.finite ), and also in their ability to occur with sentence final particles, which are otherwise never found in subordinate clauses, including relatives, complements and other types of clauses.

For instance, the complement clause in ( ex:thWnWmblWmnW.je ) contains the imperative/hortative particle je (§ sec:fsp.imp ) as well as an interjection, and in ( ex:mAnAtsa.loB.toti ) we find the utterance mitigation particle loβ (§sec:fsp.attitude).

exe

``ja, tʰɯ-nɯmbjɯm-nɯ je" to-ti. \\
interj imp -warm.by.fire- pl sfp ifr -say \\
`She said: `Come, get warm by the fire!' (160703 poucet3-v2)
0006221#S27
exe

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ kɯ ``nɯ mɤ-nɤtsa loβ" to-ti, kʰro mɯ-to-kʰɯ. \\

The examples show reported speech containing particles such as the imperative/hortative je and the utterance mitigation particle loβ, as well as an interjection.

text:
indirect speech!hybrid
While Japhug allows direct speech quotation, the corpus reveals examples of mismatches between the viewpoint of the original speaker (the person whose speech or thoughts are quoted, subject of the complement-taking verb of speech/thought which selects the reported speech clause) and the current speaker (the person quoting the words of the original speaker).

In the present work, these phenomena are referred to as Hybrid Indirect Speech ( following ). also uses the term ``Semi-Indirect Speech''. In Hybrid Indirect Speech, the verb morphology (in particular person indexation) invariably presents the viewpoint of the original speaker, while pronouns and adverbs follow that of the current speaker.

Since grammatical relations are mainly marked by verb morphology and overt pronouns are not common (§ sec:pers.pronouns ), distinguishing between Direct Speech and Hybrid Indirect Speech is only possible in a minority of cases. Mismatch between pronouns and person indexation only occurs when a pronoun or possessive prefix is overt, and that pronoun or prefix indexes a referent that is assigned a different grammatical person by the original speaker and the current speaker.

Example ( ex:nWGi.kAsWso ) provides an example of this phenomenon. The verb nɯɣi `he comes/will come back (home)' in the complement clause of the verb kɤ-sɯso `think' is in the Factual Non-Past 3sg. In the same clause we find the 2sg pronoun nɤʑo; there is no pause between the pronoun and the verb, and no indication from the prosody that nɤʑo is left-dislocated.

exe

ma nɤ-wa kɯ [ nɤʑo nɯɣi] kɤ-sɯso kɯ kʰa ɯ-rkɯ tɕe ʁmaʁ χsɯ-tɤxɯr pa-sɯ-lɤt ɕti tɕe \\
lnk 2sg. poss -father erg 2sg come.back: fact inf -think erg house 3sg. poss -side lnk soldier three-circle aro:3 - caus -release be. aff: fact lnk \\
Direct: `Your father, thinking ` He is coming back', put three rings of soldiers around the house.'
Indirect: `Your father, thinking that you are coming back,'
Hybrid indirect: `Your father, thinking that ` you' is coming back,' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S155
exe

This type of mismatch between pronouns and indexation on the verb is anomalous and never found in independent sentences. Here the verb form corresponds to the point of view of the original speaker (indicated in blue in all following examples), whose original sentence would have been ɯʑo nɯɣi ( 3sg come.back: fact `he is coming back)'. The pronoun reflects the point of view of the current speaker (in red), for whom the equivalent sentence would be converted to nɤʑo tɯ-nɯɣi ( 2sg 2-come.back: fact `you are coming back'), since the addressee of the current situation corresponds to the subject of the original situation.

Examples ( ex:WtCW.anAtWGa ), ( ex:tunAmea ) and ( ex:WkWmtChW.juGWta ) illustrate that possessive prefixes on nouns undergo the same shift towards the point of the view of the current speaker, while the verb remains in the same form that was either thought or uttered by the original speaker.

In ( ex:WtCW.anAtWGa ) and ( ex:tunAmea ), the possessive forms ɯ-tɕɯ `his son' and ɯ-pi `her brother' underwent a shift to third person (representing the point of view of the current speaker). The original sentences corresponding to the complement clauses in ( ex:WtCW.anAtWGa ) and ( ex:tunAmea ) are presented in ( ex:WtCW.anAtWGa2 ) and ( ex:tunAmea2 ): the possessive pronoun is first person and coreferential with the subject of the main verb.

Example ( ex:WkWmtChW.juGWta ) illustrates the same phenomenon as in ( ex:WtCW.anAtWGa ) and ( ex:tunAmea ), but with the verb of speech tisay instead of sɯsothink. In this example, we know from the context that the girl is the addressee, so that if the sentence were in direct speech, a second person singular prefix form nɤ-kɯmtɕʰɯ ( 2sg. poss -toy) `your toy' would be expected instead.

exe

tɤɕime nɯ kɯ pjɯ-tɯ-mtsʰɤm tɕe, [nɯnɯ ɯ-kɯmtɕʰɯ nɯ ju-ɣɯt-a ŋu] ɯ-kɯ-ti pjɤ-tu ndɤre, \\

Direct: `As soon as the girl heard that there was someone saying `` I will bring your toy".'
Indirect: `As soon as the girl heard that there was someone saying that he would bring her toy.'
Hybrid indirect: `As soon as the girl$_i$ heard that there was someone saying `` I will bring her$_i$ toy".' (140429 qingwa wangzi-zh)

summary: Japhug allows direct speech quotation, but the corpus also shows Hybrid Indirect Speech, where the verb morphology keeps the original speaker’s viewpoint while pronouns and adverbs follow the current speaker’s viewpoint. Because grammatical relations are usually marked on verbs and overt pronouns are rare, direct speech and hybrid indirect speech are often difficult to distinguish except when overt pronouns or possessive prefixes conflict with verbal person marking. The passage illustrates this with examples where a pronoun or possessive prefix shifts to the current speaker’s perspective while the verb retains the original speaker’s person indexation.

text:
In ( ex:mWpWrAZia ), one could be tempted to analyze the pronoun ɯʑohe as exterior to the reported speech clause, as the subject of the matrix verb sɯsothink. However, since sɯso is transitive and requires its subject to be marked with the ergative (§ sec:A.kW ), this analysis is not possible. Instead, ɯʑohe belongs to the complement clause whose verb rɤʑistay is intransitive. The person mismatch, as in ( ex:nWGi.kAsWso ) above, is due to Hybrid Indirect Speech: the verb form mɯ-pɯ-rɤʑi-a with first singular marking reflects the viewpoint of the original speaker (the subject of the verb ɲɯ-nɯ-sɯsɤm ), while the pronoun ɯʑohe corresponds to that of the current speaker (the narrator of the story).

exe

`` ɯʑo χsɯ-sŋi χsɤ-rʑaʁ ma mɯ-pɯ-rɤʑi-a" ɲɯ-nɯ-sɯsɤm pjɤ-ŋu \\
3sg three-day three-night apart.from neg - pst. ipfv -stay- 1sg ipfv - auto -think[III] pst. ipfv -be \\
Direct: `He was thinking `` I have only stayed for three days and three nights".'
Indirect: `He was thinking that he had only stayed for three days and three nights.'
Hybrid Indirect: `He was thinking that he have only stayed for three days and three nights.'
0003376#S96
exe

A potentially even more confusing case occurs when the original speaker is the current speaker's addressee, and when both the original and the current speakers are referred to in the original utterance. This is the situation observed in ( ex:YWnWfsWGa ), a sentence pronounced by a fox who helped a prince to succeed in various tasks. Here, the first singular possessive prefix a- on the possessed noun ɯ-tʂɯnlɤnfavour and the first person singular suffix -a on the verb ɲɯ-nɯ-fsɯɣ-a do not correspond to the same referent. The verb form ɲɯ-nɯ-fsɯɣ-a `I will pay back' is the sentence that the fox attributes to his addressee (the prince), so that the first person here corresponds to the prince, while the possessive prefix on ɯ-tʂɯnlɤnfavour reflects the point of view of the fox and thus refers to himself.

exe

a-tʂɯnlɤn ɲɯ-nɯ-fsɯɣ-a ɯ-ɲɯ-tɯ-sɯsɤm nɤ, nɯ tɤ-ste ti ɲɯ-ŋu \\
1sg. poss -favour ipfv - auto -pay.back- 1sg q - ipfv -2-think[III] lnk dem imp -do.this.way[III] say: fact sens -be \\
Direct: `If you think `` I will return the favour (which I received from you)", do like that.'
Indirect: `If you want to return the favour (which you received from me), do like that.'
Hybrid Indirect: `If you think `` I will return the favour (which you received from me), do like that.'
0003372#S192
exe

In such a situation, the referents corresponding to first and second person are exactly reversed between the point of view of the current and the original speaker, and therefore between pronouns and possessive prefixes on the one hand and verbal indexation on the other hand.

The corresponding sentence in Direct speech would be ( ex:YWnWfsWGa2 ), with a second person singular possessive prefix on the noun ɯ-tʂɯnlɤnfavour instead.

exe

nɤ-tʂɯnlɤn ɲɯ-nɯ-fsɯɣ-a \\
2sg. poss -favour ipfv - auto -pay.back- 1sg \\
`I will return the favour (which I received from you).'
exe

Surprisingly, despite this complex shift of perspective between the original speaker and the current speaker, there is no logophoric pronoun in Japhug. A logophoric pronoun is, however, attested in the closely related Stau language, which appears to have a similar system of Hybrid Indirect Speech.

Hybrid indirect speech is not rare in Japhug, and this grammar contains additional examples, such as ( ex:mAwGndzaj.thaN ) in § sec:fsp.epistemic ).
summary: The passage explains that some apparent mismatches in person reference in reported speech are not due to the pronoun being outside the reported clause, but to Hybrid Indirect Speech, where different elements reflect different viewpoints. In one example, the verb marking follows the original speaker’s perspective while the pronoun follows the narrator’s, and in another, first- and second-person references are reversed between possessive prefixes and verbal indexation because the original speaker is the current speaker’s addressee. The text also notes that Japhug lacks a logophoric pronoun despite this complex system, though such a pronoun exists in related Stau.

text:
word order!complement clauses complement clause!word order
Complement clauses, are strictly preverbal in Japhug like other core arguments (§ sec:basic.word.order ), except in the case of right dislocated constituents (§ sec:right.dislocation ) such as the infinitive clause kɤ-sɤ-fstɯn `to serve' in ( ex:tutWste.kAsAfstWn ) (§ sec:similative.verb.complementation ).

exe

tɕʰi tu-tɯ-ste ŋu, [kɤ-sɤ-fstɯn]\\
what ipfv -2-do.like[III] be: fact inf - apass -serve \\
`How do you treat people?' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

While complement clauses are generally located directly before the verb, in examples such as ( ex:kACWnNo.mWYWchaa ) the subject of the matrix verb inserted after the complement clause.

exe

[nɤʑo kɤ-ɕɯ-nŋo] aʑo mɯ-ɲɯ-cʰa-a \\
2sg inf - caus -be.defeated 1sg neg - ipfv -can- 1sg \\
`I cannot defeat you anymore.' (140513 abide he mogui-zh)
0003975#S83
exe

Discontinuous complement clauses are rare in Japhug. The only clear example in the corpus is ( ex:lWlu.kW.aZo ). In this example, the 1sg pronoun aʑo is the subject of the matrix clause, and has no syntactic role in the complement clause, but it appears between the transitive subject lɯlu kɯ `the cat' and the object ʁnɯztwo of the complement clause. Despite the rarity of this construction, this sentence was not considered to be unusual by Tshendzin when listening again to the recording.

exe

[lɯlu kɯ aʑo ʁnɯz ʑo ka-ndo] pɯ-mto-t-a \\
cat erg 1sg two emph aor:3 -take aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I saw a cat catching two of them.' (22-kumpGatCW)
0003590#S53
exe
summary: In Japhug, complement clauses are generally strictly preverbal, like other core arguments, except when a complement clause is right-dislocated. In some cases the matrix subject may appear after the complement clause, and discontinuous complement clauses are rare but attested; in the single clear corpus example, a matrix-clause pronoun appears inside the complement clause without any syntactic role there.

text:
complement clause!case marking
When the verb of the matrix and the complement clauses sharing the same subject have different transitivity values, there is a conflict in case assignment on their common subject, which can either take absolutive (§ sec:absolutive.S ) or ergative marking (§ sec:erg.kW ).

Examples ( ex:no.erg.rga ) and ( ex:erg.rga ) provide a minimal pair illustrating this optional treatment. In both examples, the matrix verb rgalike is semi-transitive (and its subject cannot take ergative marking), while ndzaeat is transitive (and thus requires a subject with the ergative).

In ( ex:no.erg.rga ), the subject fsapaʁ ra `farm animals' has no ergative marking, showing that its case marking is assigned by the semi-transitive rgalike (§ sec:semi.transitive ), and therefore that the infinitival complement clause in this example is restricted to the sole infinitive verb form kɤ-ndza `to eat'.

exe

fsapaʁ ra [kɤ-ndza] wuma rga-nɯ \\
animals pl inf -eat very like: fact - pl \\
`Farm animals like to eat it.' (19-qachGa mWntoR)
0003546#S107
exe

By contrast, in example ( ex:erg.rga ), the common subject paʁ ra `pigs' takes the ergative kɯ selected by the transitive verb ndzaeat in the complement clause, suggesting that it should be analyzed as belonging to the complement clause.

exe

[paʁ ra kɯ kɤ-ndza] wuma ʑo rga-nɯ \\
pig pl erg inf -eat very emph like: fact - pl \\
`Pigs like to eat it.' (12 ndZiNgri)
0003488#S137
exe

In ( ex:erg.rga ) it is not possible to argue that the case marking on the subject is a case of long-distance ergative (§ sec:long.distance.kW ), since paʁ ra kɯ does not serve as subject for a transitive verb located a few clauses afterwards; in fact there is no mention of the pigs in the rest of the text.

Examples ( ex:tWNke ) and ( ex:tWnWrAGo ) with dental infinitive complements (§ sec:bare.dental.inf ) containing an intransitive verb (§ sec:dental.inf ) and the transitive matrix verb ʑabegin illustrate the opposite situation: the transitive verb requires the ergative on third person subjects (§ sec:erg.kW ), while the intransitive one precludes it. In ( ex:tWNke ), the common subject is in the absolutive, showing that it owes its case marking to the intransitive verb ŋkewalk, and therefore that it belongs to the complement clauses.

exe

[<xinbada> nɯ tɕe li tɯ-ŋke] to-ʑa \\
Sinbad dem lnk again inf -walk ifr -begin \\
`Sinbad started to walk again.' (140511 xinbada-zh)
0003961#S206
exe

In ( ex:tWnWrAGo ), the common subject is in the ergative following the transitive matrix verb ʑabegin (§ sec:phasal.complements ), and is thus located outside of the complement clause.

exe

pɣɤtɕɯ nɯ kɯ [nɯɕimɯma ʑo tɯ-nɯrɤɣo] cʰɤ-ʑa \\
bird dem erg immediately emph inf -sing ifr -begin \\
`The bird immediately started to sing.' (140514 huishuohua de niao-zh)
0003992#S208
exe

In the case of transitive matrix verbs such as rɲoexperience that allow coreference between the subject of the matrix clause and either the subject or object of the complement clause, the common argument receives ergative marking even when it is the object in the complement clause, as illustrated by example ( ex:kAmtsWG.pjArYo ) (§ sec:rYo.complements ).
summary: When a matrix verb and a complement clause share the same subject but differ in transitivity, the shared argument may receive either absolutive or ergative case, depending on which clause is taken to assign case. The passage uses minimal pairs to show that absolutive marking indicates the subject belongs to an intransitive or semi-transitive verb, while ergative marking indicates it belongs to a transitive complement or matrix verb; in one case, ergative on a shared argument can also appear when it is the object of the complement clause under a transitive matrix verb.

text:
determiner!complement clauses complement clause!determiner
Finite (§ sec:finite.complement ), reported speech (§ sec:reported.speech ) and infinitive (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ) complement clauses, like relative clauses (§ sec:relative.determiners.complementizer ), are often followed by nɯ and nɯnɯ ( ex:mAkACe.nW.mAkhW ) (which occur as demonstrative pronouns and determiners, § sec:demonstrative.pronouns, § sec:demonstrative.determiners, § sec:nW.topic, § sec:definiteness ) and/or by the plural marker ra ( ex:YWnWqambWmbjom.ra.mWjspe ) (§ sec:plural.determiners ), which adds the nuance that other activities may be implied. For instance, in ( ex:YWnWqambWmbjom.ra.mWjspe ), ɲɯ-nɯqambɯmbjom ra mɯ́j-spe can be glossed as `it is not able to fly (and do other related activities)'.

exe

[mɤ-kɤ-ɕe] nɯ mɤ-kʰɯ ri \\

`The [inchworm] moves as if it were measuring the ground span by span, it is not able fly.' (26-qambalWla)

These markers are analyzed in this grammar as determiners of the entire complement clause rather than as complementizers, the analysis proposed by concerning a similar construction in Tshobdun. As evidence for the analysis as determiners, note that the position of the markers nɯ and ra relative to complement clauses is exactly the same as that between demonstrative and plural determiners and nouns in a noun phrase (§ sec:demonstrative.determiners ). In particular, cirmcumposed determiners are attested with complement clauses as in ( ex:nWra.jAGWta.ra.mWtoti ), where the reported speech complement tɕʰeme jɤ-ɣɯt-a `I brought a girl' is both preceded and followed by plural markers. Examples like ( ex:nWra.jAGWta.ra.mWtoti ) directly refute my previous claim that determiners of complement clauses are strictly postclausal.

dem. pl girl aor -bring- 1sg pl neg - ifr -say \\

Bare and dental infinitival clauses (§ sec:bare.dental.inf ) rarely take the determiners nɯ and ra, but examples such as ( ex:tWmbri.ra.taZanW.pWtsu ) are attested in the corpus.

bird pl inf:II-cry pl aor:3 3-start- pl pst. ipfv -have.time.to \\

summary: Finite, reported-speech, and infinitival complement clauses are often followed by the markers nɯ/nɯnɯ and/or the plural marker ra, which can add the sense that other related activities are implied. The grammar analyzes these forms as determiners of the whole complement clause rather than as complementizers, because their distribution parallels that of demonstrative and plural determiners in noun phrases. It also notes that these markers can occur both before and after the clause, including circumposed patterns, though such determiners are rare with bare and dental infinitival clauses.

focus!restrictive focus!additive
Various focus markers are inserted between the complement clause and the matrix verb, including the additive/scalar focus marker kɯnɤalso, even (§ sec:kWnA ) in ( ex:kWnA.mAsna2 ).

text:
orientation!raising
With the exception of finite complements and some velar infinitives (§ sec:infinitives.other.prefixes ), verbs in complement clauses generally lack orientation preverbs, and only the matrix verb encodes orientation.

While some complement-taking verbs keep the same orientation regardless of the complement type and the lexical orientation of the verb in the complement clause (for instance, rɲoexperience always takes the downwards orientation, § sec:rYo.complements ), other matrix verbs, in particular causative verbs (§ sec:causative.manner.complement ) and phasal verbs such as ʑabegin (§ sec:phasal.complements ), select the orientation of the complement verb. This phenomenon is illustrated in tab:Za.complement.preverb and the following examples.

As shown in tab:Za.complement.preverb, the orientation preverb on ʑa in examples ( ex:tWmna.toZa ) to ( ex:tWmWnmu.YAZa ) (in all of these cases a D-type preverb marking the Inferential, § sec:kamnyu.preverbs ) is the same as that found when the verb in the complement clause is used as a main verb conjugated in the Inferential.
