pɣɤtɕɯ nɯ kɯ nɯɕimɯma ʑo tɯ-nɯrɤɣo cʰɤ-ʑa \\
bird dem erg immediately emph inf -sing ifr: downstream -start \\
`The bird immediately started to sing.' (140514 huishuohua de niao)
0003992#S208
exe

All phasal verbs (§ sec:phasal.complements ) and causative complement-taking verbs behave like ʑa. Additional examples of this phenomenon with stʰɯtfinish are presented in § sec:phasal.complements.
summary: Verbs in complement clauses generally lack orientation preverbs, so orientation is normally expressed only by the matrix verb, except with finite complements and some velar infinitives. However, certain complement-taking verbs—especially causatives and phasal verbs like ʑa ‘begin’—select the orientation of the complement verb, matching the orientation used when that verb appears as a main verb in the Inferential. When ʑa takes a nominal object, it can also pattern with the corresponding denominal verb, and all phasal and causative complement-taking verbs behave in this way.

text:
complementation strategy
introduces the term ``complementation strategy'' to refer to constructions with a meaning corresponding to that expressed by complement clauses in some languages, but which either are not core arguments or the verb of the main clause or are not clauses with a complete argument structure. Complementation strategies include nominalizations (when the verb sheds its argument structure as it becomes a noun), relative clauses (which are formally a modifier of a core argument), serial verb constructions and clause linking.
summary: A “complementation strategy” is a construction that expresses meanings like those of complement clauses, but it may either not be a core argument of the main verb or not be a full clause with complete argument structure. The text lists nominalizations, relative clauses, serial verb constructions, and clause linking as examples of complementation strategies.

subsection: Relative clauses in core argument function
text:
relative clause!complementation strategy
Some complement-taking verbs can alternatively select (semi-)objects instead of complement clauses. For instance cʰacan occurs with the noun 考试 kǎoshìexam (borrowed from Chinese) ( ex:kaoshi.pWcha ).

exe

<kaoshi> pɯ-cʰa \\
exam aor -can \\
`He passed the exam.' (12-BzaNsa)
0003484#S69
exe

In ( ex:tWtatWt.pjAcha ), the clause tɯ ta-tɯt superficially resembles a finite complement clause (§ sec:finite.complement ), but four pieces of evidence indicate that it should rather be analyzed as a headless relative clause in semi-object function like the noun <kaoshi> in ( ex:kaoshi.pWcha ).

exe

tɤ-pɤtso nɯ kɯ nɯra [tɯ ta-tɯt] nɯra pjɤ-cʰa \\
indef. poss -child dem erg dem: pl total aor:3 -say[II] dem: pl ifr -can \\
`The child had succeeded in doing everything that [the old king] had said.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh)
0003886#S240
exe

First, the subject of both clauses are not co-referential (this example cannot be interpreted as meaning `the boy succeeded in saying all these things'). If the subordinate clause in ( ex:tWtatWt.pjAcha ) were a complement, subject coreference would be expected (§ sec:finite.complement.coref ). Second, the verb of the relative clause has totalitative reduplication, a morphological device found in relative clauses (§ sec:totalitative.relatives ), but not in complement clauses. Third, the verb of the relative clause is in the Aorist while that of the main clause is in the Inferential; in finite complement clauses other than reported speech, the verb could be in the Aorist only if the matrix verb were in Aorist form too (see § sec:TAM.finite ). Fourth, it is possible to add an overt head noun in ( ex:tWtatWt.pjAcha ).

Correlative relative clauses (§ sec:interrogative.relative ) particularly commonly occur as objects or semi-objects. For instance, in ( ex:tAstuta.tustea ) the clause ɯ-wa tɕʰi tɤ-stu-t-a can be analyzed as the semi-object of the secundative verb studo like (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative, § sec:similative.verb.complementation ).

exe

[ɯ-wa tɕʰi tɤ-stu-t-a] nɯ tu-ste-a ɲɯ-ɬoʁ \\
3sg. poss -father what aor -do.like- pst: tr - 1sg dem ipfv -do.like[III]- 1sg sens -be.needed \\
`I have to deal with him in the same way as I dealt with his father. (=How I treated his father, I have to treat him like that)' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S135
exe

Ambiguity between finite or participial relative clauses on the one hand, and finite and infinitival complement clauses on the other hand, is pervasive in the case of verbs of cognition and perception such as mtosee (§ sec:finite.relative.complement.ambiguity, § sec:non-finite.relative.complement.ambiguity ) as in ( ex:WftaR.tAkAta ), where tɤ-kɤ-ta can be either analyzed as an object participle (§ sec:object.participle ) or a velar infinitive (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ). Disambiguization between the two analyses is possible when the verb is dynamic intransitive (§ sec:non-finite.relative.complement.ambiguity ).

exe

nɯɕimɯma ʑo iɕqʰa [kɯm nɯtɕu ɯ-ftaʁ tɤ-kɤ-ta] nɯ pjɤ-mto \\
immediately emph the.aforementioned door dem: loc 3sg. poss -mark pdv - inf / obj: pcp -put dem ifr -see \\
`She immediately saw the mark that had been put on the door / that someone had put a mark on the door.' (140512 alibaba-zh)
0003965#S177
exe
summary: Some complement-taking verbs can instead select semi-objects or headless relative clauses rather than complement clauses. The passage argues this for examples with *cʰa* and for correlative relative clauses used as objects, and it notes that verbs of cognition and perception often allow ambiguity between relative and complement-clause analyses.

text: Putting aside participial relative clauses used with verbs compatible with both nouns and complement clauses (§ sec:relative.core.arg, § sec:non-finite.relative.complement.ambiguity ), participial clauses are found in four types of complements and complementation strategies: purposive clauses, constructionalized object relative clauses, essive participial clauses and genuine participial complements.
summary: Excluding participial relative clauses that occur with verbs allowing both noun and complement-clause readings, participial clauses are attested in four complement or complementation types. These are purposive clauses, constructionalized object relative clauses, essive participial clauses, and genuine participial complements.

text:
purposive clause verb!motion
The motion verbs ɕego, ɣicome and ɬoʁcome out (§ sec:motion.verbs ) select purposive clauses whose verb is obligatorily in participle form (§ sec:am.vs.mvc ). This construction is reminiscent of the use of the future participle with motion verbs in Ancient Greek. The participles in this construction cannot take orientation, polarity and associated motion prefixes.

Both subject and object purposive clauses are found. Subject purposive clauses are subject participial clauses (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation ), as in ( ex:WkWCar.chACe ) and ( ex:WkWCar.jolhoR ). In this construction, there is obligatory coreference between the subject of the motion verb and that of the purposive clause, unlike other superficially similar constructions (§ sec:constr.participial.clause ).

exe

lo-fsoʁ tɕe tɕe tɤ-mu nɯ [ɯ-tɕɯ ɯ-kɯ-ɕar] cʰɤ-ɕe tɕe,\\
ifr -be.bright lnk lnk indef. poss -mother dem 3sg. poss -son 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -search ifr: downstream -go lnk \\
`When the sun came up (in the morning), the mother went to look for her son.' (tWJo 2012)
0004089#S31
exe

exe

pri nɯ [ɯ-zda ɯ-kɯ-ɕar] jo-ɬoʁ. \\
bear dem 3sg. poss -companion 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -search ifr -come.out \\
`The bear came out to look for its companion (another bear).' (elicited)
exe

To express coreference with the object of the purposive clause (in the case of a transitive verb), the object participle is normally used instead (§ sec:object.participles.complement ). Coreference between the object of the complement clause and the subject of the matrix clause is possible only if the object has control over the action as in ( ex:kAmto.mWjGi ); control of the subject of the purposive clause is not necessary in this case.

exe

[kʰro kɤ-mto] mɯ́j-ɣi ma ɯ-kɤ-ndza ɣɤʑu. \\
much obj: pcp -see neg: sens -come lnk 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -eat exist: sens \\
`(In the years when there are a lot of things to eat in the forest), it$_i$ does not come to [places where it$_i$ can] be seen, because it$_i$ has things to eat. (23-pGAYaR)
0003606#S77
exe

There is however at least one unexplained exception. The verb nɯβlɤmtɕʰɤtask to perform a task ( ex:tAnWBlAmtChata ) consistently occurs in subject participle form in the purposive construction in the meaning `go/come to perform a task (at someone's invitation)', where coreference is thus between the subject of the motion verb and the object of the transitive verb. The kɤ- participle is also acceptable with motion verbs, but this construction is not attested in texts. This problem deserves additional research. Another puzzling feature of this construction is the fact that there is no obligatory possessive prefix on the participle, and that when present, it indexes the subject rather than the object.

exe

aʑo βlama tɤ-nɯβlɤmtɕʰat-a \\
1sg lama aor -ask.to.perform.a.task- 1sg \\
`I asked a lama to perform a [ceremony] for me.' (elicited)
exe

exe

kɯ-nɯβlɤmtɕʰɤt ɕe-a ra \\
sbj: pcp -ask.to.perform.a.task go: fact - 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`(Their lama said:) `I have to go to perform [a ceremony at someone's invitation].' (160720 kandZislama)
0006147#S5
exe

When the verb in the subject purposive clause is transitive, the participle has a possessive prefix coreferent with the object as in the case of relative clauses (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ), and the subject can either take absolutive marking following the motion verb (which is morphologically intransitive), as in ( ex:WkWCar.chACe ), or ergative marking following the verb of the purposive clause as in ( ex:WkWCar.loCenW ). This difference in case marking can be analysed as reflecting clausal structure: in ( ex:WkWCar.loCenW ), the subject tɤ-rɟit ra `the children' belongs to the purposive clauses, whereas in ( ex:WkWCar.chACe ), the subject tɤ-mu nɯ lies outside of it.

exe

ɯ-fso-soz tɕe, [tɤ-rɟit ra kɯ nɯ ɯ-kɯ-ɕar] jo-ɕe-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe \\
3sg. poss -tomorrow-morning lnk indef. poss -child pl erg dem 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -search ifr: upstream -go sens -be lnk \\
`The next morning, the children went (there) to look for him.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S281
exe

The goal of the motion verb can, however, occur within the purposive clause, as in ( ex:khapa.WkWnnAjo ), where the subject in ergative form ɯ-wa nɯ kɯ `his father' is stranded from the transitive verb ɯ-kɯ-n-nɤjo by the goal kʰapa tɕe `downstairs'.

exe

[ɯ-wa nɯ kɯ kʰapa tɕe ɯ-kɯ-n-nɤjo] pjɤ-ɣi. \\
3sg. poss -father dem erg downstairs loc 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp - auto -wait ifr: down -come \\
`His father came downstairs to wait for him.' (140506 loBzi)
0003923#S5
exe

Motion verbs with purposive clauses have some semantic overlap with the corresponding associated motion prefixes (§ sec:am.prefixes ); the functional difference between the two constructions is discussed in § sec:am.vs.mvc.

Apart from the three motion verbs above, a few verbs expressing imminent aspect such as aɣɯɣube about to also selects participial clauses (§ sec:imminent.complements ), as shown by ( ex:kWsi.torANgat2 ).

exe

kɯ-maqʰu tɕe, tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ [kɯ-si] to-rɤŋgat \\
sbj: pcp -be.after lnk indef. poss -son dem sbj: pcp -die ifr -be.about.to \\
`The man was about to die.' (2002 rkongrgjal2)
exe

Although there is potential ambiguity between purposive clauses and headless participial relative clauses (§ sec:headless.relative ) used with motion verbs, ambiguous sentences are not common in the corpus. The presence of determiners such as the indefinite ci in ( ex:WkWmtshi.jAGe ) shows that the participial clause can only be a relative and is not interpretable as a purposive clause. However, ɯ-kɯ-mtsʰi jɤ-ɣe without the determiner could indeed be parsed as `s/he came to lead it'.

exe

[tsʰɤt ɯ-kɯ-mtsʰi] ci jɤ-ɣe tɕe \\
goat 3sg. poss -lead indef aor -come[II] lnk \\
`Someone came leading a goat.' (chen-pear)
exe
summary:
The motion verbs ɕego, ɣicome, and ɬoʁcome out select purposive clauses whose verb must appear in participle form, and these participles cannot take orientation, polarity, or associated motion prefixes. Subject purposive clauses require coreference between the motion verb’s subject and the purposive clause subject, while object purposive clauses normally use the object participle; one noted exception is nɯβlɤmtɕʰɤtask to perform a task, which appears in subject participle form with subject–object coreference.

When the purposive clause verb is transitive, the participle carries a possessive prefix coreferent with the object, and case marking may place the subject either outside the purposive clause or within it, depending on clausal structure. The passage also notes overlap with associated motion prefixes, that some imminent-aspect verbs also take participial clauses, and that ambiguity with headless

text:
Manipulation verbs such as tsɯmtake away or ɣɯtbring (§ sec:manipulation.verbs ) occur with non-finite purposive clauses in kɤ, as in ( ex:kAntsGe.jotsWm ), rather than subject participles like the motion verbs (§ sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ) despite obligatory subject coreference.

exe

ɯ-mbro ɯ-ndʐi nɯra [kɤ-ntsɣe] jo-tsɯm \\
3sg. poss -horse 3sg. poss -skin dem: pl obj: pcp -sell ifr -take.away \\
`He took the horses' skins to [the market] to sell them.' (150814 kelaosi-zh)
0006276#S82
exe

The non-finite verb form kɤ-ntsɣe could in principle be either analyzed as an infinitive or as an object participle (§ sec:infinitives.participles ). Unlike infinitival clauses, the kɤ- clauses in this construction can be optionally followed by quantifiers as in ( ex:kAntsGe.WkuxtCWxtCo ) and by the relator noun ɯ-spamaterial as in ( ex:kAsat.Wspa.jowGtsWm ) and ( ex:kAntsGe.Wspa.joGWt ).

In addition, all of these examples present coreference between the object of the transitive verb of the main clause and that of the participial clause, reminiscent of the use of object participles in the purposive clauses of motion verbs to express coreference between the intransitive subject of the motion verb and the object of the transitive verb of the purposive clause (see example ex:kAmto.mWjGi in § sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs above and § sec:object.participles.complement ).

exe

kutɕu rca [kɤ-ntsɣe] ɯ-kuxtɕɯ xtɕo ju-ɣɯt-nɯ ɕti. \\
dem. prox: loc unexp: deg obj: pcp -sell 3sg. poss - emph basket ipfv -bring- pl be. aff: fact \\
`[People] bring many basketfuls [of mushroom] to sell.' (23-mbrAZim)
0003604#S103
exe

exe

[kɤ-sat] ɯ-spa jó-wɣ-tsɯm ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
obj: pcp -kill 3sg. poss -material ifr - inv -take.away sens -be \\
`He was taken away to be executed.' (tou dongxi de xiaohai-zh)
exe

exe

tɯrme nɯ kɯ laχtɕʰa [kɤ-ntsɣe] (ɯ-spa) kɯ-dɯ dɤn jo-ɣɯt. \\
person dem erg thing obj: pcp -sell 3sg. poss -material sbj: pcp - emph be.many ifr -bring \\
`The man brought a lot of things to sell.' (elicited)
exe

These clauses are (at least historically) to be analyzed as participial clauses in essive function (§ sec:essive.abs ): kɤ-ntsɣe (ɯ-spa) and kɤ-sat (ɯ-spa) in the examples above literally mean `(bring/take away) as something to be sold/as someone to be killed', hence their use in purposive function. This construction is not specific to manipulation verbs: in ( ex:Ca.kAndza.Wspa ), the verb of the main clause χsuraise, `feed' is also found with the same type of participial clause. In ( ex:Ca.kAndza.Wspa ) however, the object of kɤ-ndza is not coreferent with that of the main verb, unlike what is found with the manipulation verbs.

exe

paʁ nɯra ʁo lɯski, [ɕa kɤ-ndza] ɯ-spa ku-χsu-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu ri \\
pig dem: pl advers of.course meat obj: pcp -eat 3sg. poss -material ipfv -feed- pl ifr. ipfv -be lnk \\
`As for the pigs, people of course raise them for their meat.' (150820 kAnWCkat)
0006256#S26
exe
summary: Manipulation verbs like *tsɯm* ‘take away’ and *ɣɯt* ‘bring’ occur with non-finite purposive clauses in *kɤ*, and these clauses are best analyzed historically as participial clauses in essive function rather than as simple infinitives. Although the object of the main verb and the participial clause is obligatorily coreferential in these examples, the construction is not limited to manipulation verbs: it also appears with verbs like *χsu* ‘feed*, though without such coreference in that case.

text:
The verbs of pretense select subject participial relative clauses as objects or semi-objects. Unlike the cases discussed in § sec:relative.core.arg, these verbs cannot take genuine complement clauses, and require participial relatives.

The status of the clauses with subject participles occurring with these verbs, though superficially similar to the purposive clause (§ sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ), is, however, entirely distinct. These clauses are not specific constructions, but simply headless relative clauses in object or semi-object function. This is shown by the fact that the same verbs are also found with participial head-internal clauses as in ( ex:pGatCW.kWGAwu.tunWCpWz ), where the three nouns pɣɤtɕɯbird, kʰɯnadog and lɯlucat are intransitive subjects of the participial clauses, and are not coreferent with the subject of their matrix verb tu-nɯɕpɯz. This example can be literally translated as `it is able to imitate a singing bird, a barking dog and a meowing cat.' (see also § sec:relative.pretence ).

exe

ɯ-zda nɯra, [[ pɣɤtɕɯ kɯ-ɣɤwu], [ kʰɯna kɯ-ɤndzɯt], [ lɯlu kɯ-ɣɤwu] kɯ-fse, nɯra tu-nɯɕpɯz] ɲɯ-spe \\
3sg. poss -companion dem: pl bird sbj: pcp -cry dog sbj: pcp -bark cat sbj: pcp -cry inf: stat -be.like dem: pl ipfv -imitate sens -be.able[III] \\
`It is able to imitate other animals, sing like a bird, bark like a dog, meow like a cat or call like a fox.' (27-kikakCi)
0003700#S132
exe
summary: Verbs of pretense take participial relative clauses as objects or semi-objects, and they cannot occur with genuine complement clauses. Although these clauses may resemble purposive clauses, they are instead headless relative clauses, as shown by examples where the participial clauses have their own subjects and are not coreferential with the matrix subject.

text:
In addition to the constructions studied above, subject participles also occur in a handful of syntactic contexts where an infinitival complement is normally expected; I call these clauses `participial complements.'

The velar infinitive + existential verb construction expressing impossibility (§ sec:inf.exist ) has a variant with Imperfective subject participles, as in ( ex:tukWGi.YAGAme ).

exe

tu-kɯ-ɣi ɲɤ-ɣɤ-me qʰe, \\
ipfv: up - sbj: pcp -come ifr - caus -not.exist lnk \\
`She made it impossible for her to come out (again).' (2003-kWBRa)
exe

In addition, when a complement-taking verb is itself in the subject participle form, it is possible for the complement either to be in the expected form (infinitive or finite), or to be in the subject participle form itself. For instance, in example ( ex:ndZikWsAndu ) the subject participle kɯ-cʰa `the one who can' takes a complement whose verb is a subject participle with a possessive prefix coreferent with the object ( ndʑi-kɯ-sɤndu ), instead of the expected kɤ- infinitive (or finite clause).

exe

[[rŋɯl kɯ ndʑi-kɯ-sɤndu] kɯ-cʰa] kɯ-fse pɯ pɯ-tu nɤ \\
silver erg 3du - sbj: pcp -exchange sbj: pcp -can sbj: pcp -be.like
cond pst. ipfv -exist if \\
`If there was someone who could redeem [the life of the two brothers] with money,...' (140507 jinniao-zh)
0003931#S327
exe
summary: Subject participles sometimes appear in contexts where an infinitival complement would normally be expected, and these are called “participial complements.” The passage gives two patterns: an impossibility construction that can take an imperfective subject participle, and cases where a complement-taking verb in subject participle form can itself take either the normal infinitival/finite complement or another subject participle complement.

text:
nominalization!action nominalization!complementation strategy
Some light verbs, in particular βzumake (§ sec:tr.light.verbs ) are combined with action nominals (§ sec:action.nominals ) in highly grammaticalized constructions.

tɯ- action nominals

The tɯ- action nominals (§ sec:tW.action.nominal ) can be combined with the verb βzumake to express habitual actions, especially actions taking a considerable amount of time. For instance tɯ-taʁ cʰɯ-βze `she was weaving' in ( ex:tWtAR.chWBze ) and tɯ-ɕkʰo pjɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-βzu `(when) we dry (grains in the field)' refer to actions taking place every day (and taking up most of the day) during a certain time period.

The main verb βzu takes over the orientation selected by the verb in action nominal form (§ sec:orientation.raising ): downstream in ( ex:tWtAR.chWBze ) (§ sec:orientation.loom ) and downwards in ( ex:tWCkho.chWBze ).

exe

tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ lu-rɤ-ji, tɕe tɕʰeme nɯ kɯ li tɯ-taʁ cʰɯ-βze tɕe, mɯntoʁ ra tu-tʂɯβ qʰe ku-nɯ-rɤʑi-ndʑi pjɤ-ŋu. \\
indef. poss -boy dem ipfv - apass -plant lnk girl dem erg again nmlz: action -weave ipfv: downstream -make[III] lnk flower pl ipfv -sew lnk ipfv - auto -stay- du ipfv. ifr -be \\
`The boy was working in the fields, the girl was weaving and doing embroidery, they were living like that.' (150828 donglang)
0006312#S133
exe

exe

tɕendɤre tɯ-ɕkʰo pjɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-βzu qʰe, nɯ kɤ-ɣndʑɯr ɯ-spa nɯ pjɯ́-wɣ-ɕkʰo tɕe nɯ-rom kóʁmɯz cʰɯ́-wɣ-ndʑɯr ra tɕe, ɯnɯnɯra ɣɯ-tu-mɯrki tu-ndze ŋu. \\
lnk nmlz: action -dry.in.the.sun ipfv: down - inv - auto -make lnk dem obj: pcp -grind 3sg. poss -material dem ipfv: down - inv -dry.in.the.sun lnk aor -be.dry only.after ipfv - inv -grind be.needed: fact lnk dem: pl cisl - ipfv -steal[III] ipfv -eat[III] be: fact \\
`When we dry things in the sun, when we dry the grains before grinding (one grinds them only after they have dried), it comes, steals them and eats them.' (22-CAGpGa)
0003586#S62
exe

This construction is found with both transitive ( ex:tWCkho.chWBze ) and intransitive verbs ( ex:tWrJaʁ.pjWBzunW ). In the former case, the object is not overt. Although βzu remains transitive, this construction shares with the antipassive derivations (§ sec:antipassive ) the function of demoting the object (§ sec:antipassive.vs.light.verbs ).

exe

rɤɣo ra cʰɯ-βzu-nɯ, tɯ-rɟaʁ ra pjɯ-βzu-nɯ pjɤ-ŋgrɤl ɲɯ-ŋu \\
song pl ipfv -make- pl nmlz: action -dance pl ipfv -make- pl indef. ipfv -be.usually.the.case sens -be \\
`(Every year, when the festival took place), [people] would sing and dance.' (150906 toutao-zh)
0006326#S13
exe

Action nominals either refer to the action itself or an object affected by the action (§ sec:tW.action.nominal ). While the collocation with βzumake probably derives from the first meaning of the action nominals, in some examples we have to take into consideration that the second meaning of the action nominal may intervene. For instance, in ( ex:tWCkho.chWBze ), tɯɕkʰo+βzu can be understood as `to do the action of drying in the sun', but also as `to do the action related to grains that are dried in the sun', since the grains in question are directly referred to in the next clause as kɤ-ɣndʑɯr ɯ-spa `(grains) to be ground'.

Action nominals can also occur with lɤtrelease, though this construction is considerably less productive. This collocation can be used to indicate a sudden semelfactive action as in ( ex:tWmWrRWz.chAlAt ), and the object can be overt.

exe

tɕe aʑo a-mtʰɯm ta-nɯ-tsɯm qʰe, a-jaʁ ra tɯ-mɯrʁɯz cʰɤ-lɤt qʰe, tɤ-se pa-tɕɤt. \\
lnk 1sg 1sg. poss -meat aor: up:3 - vert -take.away lnk 1sg. poss -hand pl nmlz: action -scratch ifr: downstream -release lnk indef. poss -blood aor:3 -take.out \\
`The kite took away the meat (that was in my hand), it scratched my hand, and made it bleed.' (150909 qandZGi)
0006358#S9
exe

Apart from βzu and lɤt, the transitive verb kʰɤtdo repeatedly, `do for a long time' also selects action nominals, but with ergative case marking (§ sec:oblique.kW ). The modal verb rabe needed (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ) can take degree nominals as subjects (§ sec:degree.nominal.complement ) instead of finite or infinitival complements.
summary:
Light verbs, especially **βzumake**, form highly grammaticalized constructions with **action nominals**, especially the **tɯ- action nominal**, to express habitual or long-lasting actions. In these constructions, βzu retains transitivity but often demotes the object, and it also takes over the orientation of the action nominal; action nominals may refer either to the action itself or to the affected object, and this ambiguity can matter in interpretation.  

The passage also notes that **lɤtrelease** can combine with action nominals to express sudden semelfactive actions, though this is less productive, and that **kʰɤtdo repeatedly** likewise selects action nominals with ergative marking. Finally, the modal **rabe needed** can take degree nominals as subjects rather than finite or infinitival complements.

text:
simultaneity
The simultaneous action nominals, prefixed in tɯ-tɯ- (§ sec:simultaneous.action.nominal ), are also used in collocation with βzumake. As in the previous construction, there is raising of the orientation preverb onto the main verb βzu (§ sec:orientation.raising ). For instance, in ( ex:tWtWnWmdar.pjABzundZi ) the downwards orientation preverb pjɤ- on βzu from the nominalized verb nɯmdarjump.

With an intransitive verb, the simultaneous constructions occur with a dual or plural subject, and means that several individuals referred do an action together at the same moment, as tɯ-tɯ-nɯmdar `jumping together' in ( ex:tWtWnWmdar.pjABzundZi ). The auxiliary βzu can even take the indefinite orientation prefixes jɤ- ja- as in ( ex:tWtWCe.jaBzundZi ) when occurring with a motion verb.

exe

mtsʰu ɯ-ŋgɯ tɯ-tɯ-nɯmdar pjɤ-βzu-ndʑi \\
lake 3sg. poss -inside simult - nmlz: action -jump ifr: down -make- du \\
`They (the two of them) had jumped into the lake together.' (nyima wodzer 2003)
exe

When used with transitive verbs, this construction is only found with dual or plural objects, and implies that several entities were subjected to the action together at the same time, as tɯ-tɯ-tʂaβ `causing to roll down together' in ( ex:tWtWtsxaB.Zo.pjABzu ), or that several object end up being tied together as result of the action as with tɯ-tɯ-tʂɯβ `sewing together' in ( ex:tWtWtsxWB.kABzuta ).

exe

pri cʰo jlɤkrɯ nɯra tɯ-tɯ-tʂaβ ʑo pjɤ-βzu \\
bear comit dem: pl basket simult - nmlz: action -cause.to.roll.down emph ifr: down -make \\
`He made the basket with the bear [in it] roll down (together).' (2011-13-qala)
exe

The comitative (§ sec:comitative ) can be used as in ( ex:tWtWtsxaB.Zo.pjABzu ) and example ( ex:tWtWrqoR.koBzu ) in (§ sec:simultaneous.action.nominal ) to link two nouns referring to the patients that undergo the action together.

exe

tɯ-ŋga tɯ-tɯ-tʂɯβ kɤ-βzu-t-a \\
indef. poss -clothes simult - nmlz: action -sew aor -make: pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I stiched the clothes together.' (elicited)
exe

In the case of transitive verbs, the verb βzumake takes the indexation of both subject and object, as in ( ex:tWtWtsxWB.tAtaBzunW ) where it takes the portmanteau ta- prefix, showing that the simultenous action nominal does not have object function.

exe

nɯʑora tɯ-tɯ-qur tɤ-ta-βzu-nɯ \\
2pl simult - nmlz: action -help aor -1 2-make- pl \\
`I helped you all at the same time.' (elicited)
exe
summary:
Simultaneous action nominals prefixed with tɯ-tɯ- are used with the auxiliary βzu ‘make,’ and the orientation preverb can raise onto βzu. With intransitive verbs, they require a dual or plural subject and express that several participants act together at the same moment; with transitive verbs, they occur with dual or plural objects and mean that several entities undergo the action together or end up jointly affected.  

The comitative can link the two nouns denoting patients undergoing the action together, and with transitive verbs βzu indexes both subject and object, showing that the simultaneous action nominal does not function as the object.

text:
compound!action nominal
The verb βzumake is also combined with noun-verb compound action nominals (§ sec:action.nominal.compounds ) as semi-object. Two such compound nominals have been identified. With kʰrambalie as first element, this construction means `pretend to do $X$' (where $X$ stands for the second element of the compound) as in ( ex:khrambaqur ) and ( ex:khrambanAre ).

exe

[kʰramba-qur] ma-tɤ-kɯ-βzu-a \\
lie-help neg - imp -2 1-make- 1sg \\
`Do not pretend to help me!' (elicited)
exe

exe

[kʰramba-nɤre] ɲɤ-βzu \\
lie-laugh ifr -make \\
`He pretended to laugh.' (elicited)
exe

With the lexicalized participle kɯzɣaa long time as first element of the compound, it means `do $X$ for a long time' as in ( ex:kWzGArAlaj ) (§ sec:action.nominal.compounds ).

exe

qajɣi pjɯ́-wɣ-rɤpɣi tɕe tɕe, li [kɯzɣɤ-rɤlaj] ʑo pjɯ́-wɣ-βzu. \\
bread inf - inv -mix.flour.and.water lnk lnk again long.time-knead emph ipfv - inv -make \\
`When one mixes flour and water to make bread, one has to knead [the dough] for a long time.' (160706 thotsi)
0006133#S34
exe

When the verbal component of the compound action nominal is transitive, both its subject and objects are indexed on the verb βzumake, as shown by the 2 1 configuration in ( ex:khrambaqur ). In addition, the orientation preverb on βzu reflects the lexicalized orientation of the verb in the compound (§ sec:orientation.raising ), for instance upwards in ( ex:khrambaqur ), westwards in ( ex:khrambanAre ) and downwards in ( ex:kWzGArAlaj ).

The verb lɤtrelease (§ sec:lAt.lv ) is also productively used with action nominal compounds (§ sec:action.nominal.compounds ) comprising a verb root such as rpubump into or tɕʰɯgore, stab as second element.
summary:
The verb βzu ‘make’ combines with compound action nominals as a semi-object in at least two attested patterns. With kʰramba- as the first element, it means ‘pretend to do X,’ and with the lexicalized participle kɯzɣa- as the first element, it means ‘do X for a long time’; when the verbal element is transitive, both subject and object are indexed on βzu, and its orientation preverb reflects the lexicalized orientation of the compound verb.

The verb lɤtrelease is also productively used with action nominal compounds, including compounds whose second element is a verb root such as rpu ‘bump into’ or tɕʰɯ ‘stab.’

text:
complementation strategy!coordination
Some verbs take post-verbal coordinated clauses instead of complement clauses. A clausal linker is inserted before that clause, showing its non-subordinated status. There are several constructions of this type.

First, some attitudinal verbs such as ʁnɯsuspect, nɯsɯmʁɲizhesitate, nɯʁlɯmbɯɣguess, estimate or nɯʁjɯβtsʰɤtguess, estimate occur in a coordinating construction strikingly similar to that described in Tshobdun by: the attitudinal verb is followed by the affirmative copula ɕtibe and a linker such as ri or ma, as in ( ex:tunWRlWmbWGa ) and ( ex:tuRnWa ).

exe

nɯ tu-nɯʁlɯmbɯɣ-a ɕti ri, ɯʑo kɯ kɤ-nɤma nɯ sɤpe \\
dem ipfv -guess- 1sg be. aff: fact lnk 3sg erg obj: pcp -work dem do.well: fact \\
`I suppose that he will perform this task well.'
exe

exe

tu-ʁnɯ-a ɕti ma ɯʑo kɯ ta-tɯt ŋu maʁ mɤ-xsi \\
ipfv -suspect- 1sg be. aff: fact lnk 3sg erg aor:3 -say be: fact not.be: fact neg - genr:know \\
`I am wondering whether what he said is true or not (suspecting that it is not true).' (elicited)
exe

Second, the verbs of perception rtoʁlook, rulook at and sɤŋolisten occur (exclusively in the Imperfective, § sec:ipfv.perception ) in narratives in a coordinating construction with the linkers tɕe or qʰe as in ( ex:kurtoR.tCe.pjAmpCAr ) and ( ex:luru.tCe ).

exe

ku-rtoʁ tɕe [tɕʰeme nɯ wuma ʑo pjɤ-mpɕɤr] \\
ipfv -look lnk girl dem really emph ifr. ipfv -be.beautiful \\
`He saw that that the girl was very beautiful.' (150909 xiaocui-zh)
0006386#S42
exe

exe

tɕe lu-ru tɕe [ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯtɕu ɯʑo lu-ntɕʰɤr ɲɯ-ŋu] \\
lnk ipfv: upstream -look.at lnk 3sg. poss -inside dem: loc himself ipfv: upstream -be.reflected sens -be \\
`[The rooster] looked at [a window] and [saw] its own reflection in it.' (150819 kumpGa)
0006388#S62
exe

The verb of speech fɕɤttell is often used in the Imperfective with a zero object cataphorically referring to reported speech clause(s) following it. The reported speech clause(s) can serve as complement of another verb of speech as in ( ex:pjWfCAtnW.tCe ) or be free-standing.

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ pjɯ-fɕɤt-nɯ tɕe, ``nɯtɕu tɕaχpa pjɤ-tu'' tu-ti-nɯ tɕe, \\
in.former.times ipfv -tell- pl lnk dem: loc bandit ifr. ipfv -exist ipfv -say- pl lnk \\
`In former times, people used to say that there were bandits there.' (17-lhazgron)
exe

These constructions are particularly common in texts translated from Chinese, where they might reflect calque from original language since in Chinese the perception verb precedes the complement, but it is also found in non-translated texts as in ( ex:YAsANo.tCe.nWme.pjAtu ) (see also ku-rtoʁ `he saw that...' in ex:chain.pjANu, § sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ) and there is no doubt that it is a native construction.

exe

ɲɯ-sɤŋo tɕe, smɤt kɯβʁa nɯra, wuma ʑo nɯ-me, nɯ-me χsɯm pjɤ-tu tɕe \\
ipfv -listen lnk topo noble dem: pl really emph 3pl. poss -daughter 3pl. poss -daughter three ifr. ipfv -exist lnk \\
`He had heard that nobles of Smad had three daughters.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

Third, some verbs optionally use a coordinating construction instead of complementation, without constructionalized semantic difference, in particular similative verbs (§ sec:similative.verb.complementation ).
summary: Some verbs take post-verbal coordinated clauses rather than complement clauses, introduced by a linker that marks the clause as non-subordinated. This includes attitudinal verbs like ‘suspect’ and ‘guess,’ perception verbs like ‘look’ and ‘listen’ (especially in the imperfective), and the speech verb ‘tell’ with a zero object referring to following reported speech. The construction is common in translations from Chinese but also occurs in native texts, and some verbs optionally alternate with coordination without any clear semantic difference.

text:
verb!complement-taking
An exhaustive survey of complement-taking verbs in Japhug would require a much larger corpus than the one available and a complete monograph of at least the size of the present grammar. For this reason, only a selection of the most frequent complement-taking verbs in the corpus is treated in this section. For each verb, the available complement types and complementation strategies are listed and exemplified.

Negative existential verbs can also take (subject) complements, but are discussed in § sec:negation.existential.
summary: The passage explains that a full survey of complement-taking verbs in Japhug would require a much larger corpus and a monograph longer than the present grammar, so only the most frequent such verbs in the corpus are discussed. For each verb, the section lists and illustrates the complement types and complementation strategies available. It also notes that negative existential verbs may take subject complements, but these are treated elsewhere.

text:
causative!complement clause complement clause!causative verbs
Some verbs derived with the causative prefixes (§ sec:sig.causative, § sec:velar.causative ) take complements or occur in complementation strategies. Three types of constructions are attested, expressing periphrastic causative, simultaneous events and manner.
summary: Some verbs formed with causative prefixes take complements or appear in complementation constructions. The passage identifies three attested construction types: periphrastic causative, simultaneous events, and manner.

text:
In addition to the sigmatic and velar causative derivations (§ sec:sig.causative, § sec:velar.causative ), a variety of periphrastic causative constructions are also attested. Four groups of verbs are used as causative auxiliaries, including both causative verbs and non-derived verbs.

First, βzumake can be combined with subject participles of adjectival stative verbs to express change of state or increase of degree, as in ( ex:kWndWndWB.chWBzunW ) and ( ex:matAtWGAwxti ).

exe

cʰɯ-ndɯl-nɯ tɕe [kɯ-ndɯ ndɯβ] ʑo cʰɯ-βzu-nɯ \\
ipfv -grind- pl lnk sbj: pcp - emph be.fine emph ipfv -make- pl \\
`They grind [tobacco] and make it very smooth.' (30-CnAto)
0003734#S8
exe

Example ( ex:matAtWGAwxti2 ) illustrates the fact that the velar causative ɣɤwxtimake bigger is semantically similar to the use of βzu with the participle kɯ-wxti.

exe

ɯ-pʰɯ ɲɯ-wxti tɕe, nɯra tʰamtɕɤt ma-tɤ-tɯ-ɣɤ-wxti, aʑo nɯ tu-nɯ-χti-a [nɯra stʰɯci kɯ-wxti] ɯ-pʰɯ ma-tɤ-tɯ-βze, [kɯ-tʂaŋ] ci tɤ-βze \\
3sg. poss -price sens -be.big lnk dem: pl all neg - imp -2- caus -be.big 1sg dem ipfv - auto -buy[III]- 1sg dem: pl as.much sbj: pcp -be.big 3sg. poss -price neg - imp -2-make[III] sbj: pcp -be.fair a.little imp -make[III] \\
`It is too expensive, don't make it that expensive, I will buy it, don't make its price that expensive, offer it for a fair price.' (Bargaining 12, 12)
exe

This construction is not restricted to stative verbs. It is attested with transitive verbs as in ( ex:pjWkWlAt.toBzu ) to express indirect causation.

exe

cɯβjiz kɯ-fse cʰɤ-ta tɕe, ɯ-kɯr ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕe, [tɯ-ci pjɯ-kɯ-lɤt] to-βzu \\
flat.stone sbj: pcp -be.like ifr: downstream -put lnk 3sg. poss -mouth 3sg. poss -in loc indef. poss -water ipfv - sbj: pcp -release ifr -make \\
`He positioned [the leaf of a rhododendron] like a flat stone [next to his younger brother's$_i$ mouth] in such a way that water could flow into his$_i$ mouth.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

With dynamic verbs however, the preferred construction is to use an impersonal modal verb such as kʰɯbe possible or rabe needed (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ) in participial form taking a complement verb, as in ( ex:mAkWkhW.tuBzunW ).

exe

la-rɤɕi-nɯ tɕe, [[lu-nɯ-ɬoʁ] mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ] tu-βzu-nɯ \\
aor:3 -pull- pl lnk ipfv: upstream - auto -come.out neg - sbj: pcp -be.possible ipfv -make- pl \\
`They pull [on the thread] (to close the opening) and prevent it from coming out.' (30-CnAto)
0003734#S38
exe

Second, the sigmatic causative forms sɯ-βzu, sɯ-pa, sɯ-ɤβzu and sɯ-ɤpa derived from the verbs βzumake, pado, aβzubecome, grow and apabecome (on the latter two verbs see § sec:passive.lexicalized ) are also commonly used as causative auxiliaries.

Like the base verb βzu, these causative verbs are also most often used with a modal impersonal auxiliary in subject participle form as in ( ex:CWkABde.mAkWra ), ( ex:mAkWkhW.YWtWsApe ) and ( ex:kWra.tAwGsWBzuanW ).

exe

[ɕɯ-kɤ-βde mɤ-kɯ-ra] nɯ ndʑiʑo kɯ nɯ-tɯ-sɯ-ɤβzu-ndʑi ŋu \\
tral - inf -throw neg - sbj: pcp -be.needed dem 2du erg aor -2- caus -become- du be: fact \\
`Thanks to both of you, there is no need to throw [people] (in the lake) anymore.' (2011-05-nyima)
exe

exe

a-tɯ-ci ɲɯ-tɯ-s-qarndɯm tɕe [[aʑo tɯ-ci kɯ-ɤmgri kɤ-tsʰi] mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ] ɲɯ-tɯ-sɯ-ɤpe ɲɯ-ŋu \\
1sg. poss - indef. poss -water ipfv - 2 - caus -be.muddy lnk 1sg indef. poss -water sbj: pcp -be.clear inf -drink neg - sbj: pcp -be.possible ipfv -2- caus -become[III] sens -be \\
`You have spoiled my water, you have made it so I am unable to drink clear water.' (lang he yang-zh)
exe

Other complement-taking stative verbs such as snabe good, be worthy, also occur in this causative construction, as in (§ ex:mAkWsna.YWsABze ).

exe

tɕe tɤ-mtʰɯm tʰamtɕɤt [kɤ-ndza mɤ-kɯ-sna] ɲɯ-sɯ-ɤβze ɲɯ-cʰa. \\
lnk indef. poss -meat all inf -eat neg - sbj: pcp -be.good ipfv - caus -become[III] sens -can \\
`[Maggots] can make all the meat improper for consumption (unfit to eat).' (25-akWzgumba)
0003632#S100
exe

The causee can be indexed as an object on the causative verb, as in ( ex:pjWkWlAt.Zo.YWtasABzu ) or ( ex:kWra.tAwGsWBzuanW ) (which have 2sg and 1sg causees, respectively), but this indexation is only optional, as shown by examples such as ( ex:mAkWkhW.YWtWsApe ) which rather select a 3sg object despite the 1sg causee.

exe

praʁ ɯ-pa nɯtɕu (...) ku-ta-z-rɤʑi tɕe, [tɯ-ci nɯnɯ sɲikuku ʑo tɕetu (...) nɤ-taʁ nɯtɕu pjɯ-kɯ-lɤt] ʑo tu-ta-sɯ-ɤβzu ŋu tɕe \\
cliff 3sg. poss -down dem: loc ipfv -1 2- caus -stay lnk indef. poss -water dem every.day emph up.there 3sg. poss -on dem: loc ipfv: down - sbj: pcp -release emph ipfv -1 2- caus -become be: fact lnk \\
`(I will not kill you), but I will keep you under the cliffs, so that the water flows down onto you.' (150901 changfamei-zh)
0006352#S153
exe

exe

[mɯ-tu-kɤ-nɤtɯti kɯ-ra] tɤ́-wɣ-sɯ-βzu-a-nɯ ndʐa ɕti ma \\
neg - ipfv - inf - distr:say sbj: pcp -be.needed aor - inv - caus -make- 1sg - pl reason be. aff: fact lnk \\
`It is because they made me [swear] not to tell anyone about it.' (tWxtsa 2003)
exe

Another verb that can be used with the modal verbs ra and kʰɯ in a periphrastic causative construction is tɕɤttake out. It is rarer and only compatible with negative participial forms to express the meaning `prevent from $X$'.

exe

[kɤ-ɤlɯlɤt mɤ-kɯ-ra] ɲɤ-tɯ-tɕɤt \\
inf -fight neg - sbj: pcp -be.needed ifr -2-take.out \\
`You stopped them from fighting.' (elicited)
exe

Fourth, the velar causatives ɣɤracause to have to and ɣɤkʰɯmake it possible to of the modal auxiliaries involved in the constructions above can take infinitive or finite complement clauses (§ sec:velar.caus.modal ) to express indirect causation as in ( ex:kAsci.mWnWtWGAkhWt ).

exe

[kɤ-sci] mɯ-nɯ-tɯ-ɣɤ-kʰɯ-t \\
inf -be.born neg - ipfv -2- caus -be.possible- pst: tr \\
`You made it impossible for me to be born.' (Gesar)
exe
summary:
The passage describes several periphrastic causative constructions in addition to sigmatic and velar causatives. It shows that verbs such as βzu and related causative forms can function as auxiliaries, often with subject participles or modal impersonal auxiliaries, to express change of state, indirect causation, or prevention; some constructions are especially preferred with stative verbs, while dynamic verbs more often use modal verbs like kʰɯ or ra.  

It also notes that the causee may be indexed as an object on the causative verb, but this is optional, and that certain velar causatives formed from modal auxiliaries can take infinitival or finite complements to express indirect causation.

text:
The causative verb sɯpacause to do (from pado, on which see
§ sec:pa.complements, § sec:pa.lv ), among other functions (for instance § sec:bare.dental.inf.sWpa ), has the meaning `consider $X$ to be $Y$'.

The parameter $Y$ can be a stative verb in participial form, such as kɯ-βdi in ( ex:kWBdi.tusWpanW ).

exe

tɤ-ɕpʰɤt nɯ a-pɯ-ɤndʑɤmstu tɕe, nɯ [kɯ-βdi] tu-sɯ-pa-nɯ ŋu \\
indef. poss -patch dem irr - ipfv -be.level lnk dem sbj: pcp -be.well ipfv - caus -do- pl be: fact \\
`If the patch is level (if it is neatly sewn), people consider it [to have been sewn] well.' (12-kAtsxWB-29)
0003486#S26
exe

The object $X$ can receive ergative case (§ sec:comparee.kW ) to express a comparative meaning `consider $X$ to be more $Y$ (§ sec:sAz.kW ), as in ( ex:kWmWm.tusWpanW ). Ergative marking in this construction can be ambiguous, since the subject (experiencer) of sɯpa also receives ergative case.

exe

nɯ ɯ-spa ra ɲɯ-naχtɕɯɣ ɕti, tɕe tʰoŋraʁ nɯ kɯ [kɯ-mɯm] tu-sɯ-pa-nɯ ŋu \\
dem 3sg. poss -material pl sens -be.the.same be. aff: fact lnk bucket.alcohol dem erg sbj: pcp -be.tasty ipfv - caus -do- pl be: fact \\
`Although its ingredients are the same (as those used to make other types of alcohol), [some people] consider alcohol in a bucket to be tastier.' (30-thoNraR)
0003762#S16
exe

The combination of sɯ-pa with participles is semantically similar to the tropative nɤ- derivation (§ sec:tropative ). For instance, the second clause in ( ex:kWmWm.tusWpanW ) can be glossed as ( ex:YWnAmWmnW ) with the tropative verb nɤmɯmfind tasty (in this example, the ergative on tʰoŋraʁalcohol in bucket is also a comparee marker, and does not mark transitive subject).

exe

tʰoŋraʁ nɯ kɯ ɲɯ-nɤ-mɯm-nɯ \\
bucket.alcohol dem erg sens - trop -be.tasty- pl \\
`They consider alcohol in bucket to be tastier.' (elicited)
exe

Unlike the nɤ- tropative derivation, The nɯ- denominal prefix can be sporadically used with a tropative meaning (§ sec:denom.tr.nW ), for instance nɯʁgratreat as an enemy from ʁgraenemy, but it synchronically different from the tropative nɤ, though these two prefixes are historically related (§ sec:sW.caus.history ). the sɯ-pa periphrastic tropative can be used with nouns as parameters, instead of stative verbs. As shown in ( ex:NgumdZWG.tutasWpa ), the direct object is the person/entity that the subject considers to have the property described by the parameter, while the parameter $Y$ (here the noun ŋgumdʑɯɣleader) is a semi-object, not indexed on the verb.

exe

nɤʑo ŋgumdʑɯɣ tu-ta-sɯ-pa ŋu \\
2sg leader ipfv -1 2- caus -do be: fact \\
`I consider you to be [my] leader.' (elicited)
exe

The participle clauses in the periphrastic tropative construction (such as in ex:kWBdi.tusWpanW and ex:kWmWm.tusWpanW above) can be analyzed as headless participial relative clauses (§ sec:constr.participial.clause ). The literal meaning of this construction is thus `consider $X$ to be something that is $Y$.'
summary:
The causative verb sɯpa, beyond its other uses, can mean “consider X to be Y,” with Y often expressed as a stative verb in participial form. In this construction, X may take ergative case to indicate a comparative meaning, though that marking can be ambiguous because the experiencer subject of sɯpa also receives ergative case.

The sɯ-pa construction is semantically similar to the tropative nɤ- derivation, but unlike nɤ-, it can also take nouns as the parameter Y, with the noun functioning as a semi-object rather than being indexed on the verb. The participial clauses in this construction can be analyzed as headless participial relative clauses, giving the literal meaning “consider X to be something that is Y.”

text:
In addition to its periphrastic causative and tropative functions discussed in the previous section, the causative verb sɯpacause to do also occurs in a construction expressing simultaneity between two actions.

This construction requires two complements, either two bare infinitives as in ( ex:Wti.cho.WnAma ) or a combination of a bare infinitive with a dental infinitive as in ( ex:Wti.cho.WtWCe ), connected by the comitative cʰo.

exe

tɕe ɯ-ti cʰo ɯ-nɤma ra ci ʑo to-sɯ-pa \\
lnk 3sg. poss - bare. inf:say comit 3sg. poss - bare. inf:work pl one emph ifr - caus -do \\
`As he said it, he did it at the same time.' (150826 liyu tiao longmen-zh)
0006266#S40
exe

exe

nɯɕimɯma ɯ-ti cʰondɤre ɯ-tɯ-ɕe ci to-sɯ-pa tɕe \\
immediately 3sg. poss - bare. inf:say comit 3sg. poss - inf: II -go one ifr - caus -do lnk \\
`As he said this, he immediately went [there].' (150830 baihe jiemei-zh)
0006368#S173
exe

Unlike other syntactic contexts (§ sec:bare.dental.inf ) where dental infinitives does not take possessive prefixes, in this construction they obligatorily take a possessive prefix coreferent with the intransitive subject, as shown by the forms ɯ-tɯ-ɕe vs. a-tɯ-ɕe in ( ex:Wti.cho.WtWCe ) and ( ex:Wti.cho.atWCe ), respectively.

exe

ɯ-ti cʰo a-tɯ-ɕe ci tɤ-sɯ-pa-t-a \\
3sg. poss - bare. inf:say comit 1sg. poss - inf: II -go one aor - caus -do- pst: tr - 1sg lnk \\
`I said it and went there [at the same time].' (elicited based on ex:Wti.cho.WtWCe )
exe
summary: The causative verb *sɯpa* ‘cause to do’ also functions in a construction that expresses simultaneity between two actions. This construction takes two complements linked by the comitative *cʰo*—either two bare infinitives or a bare infinitive plus a dental infinitive—and in the latter case the dental infinitive must carry a possessive prefix coreferent with the intransitive subject.

text:
Both sigmatic (§ sec:sig.causative ) and velar causative (§ sec:velar.causative ) causative derivations from adjectival verbs can be used as complement-taking verbs, expressing the manner in which the action described in the complement clause takes place.

This construction is found with dental/bare infinitival complements ( ex:WpW.Wpa.atAtWGABdi ) or velar infinitival complements ( ex:kArtoR.apWtWsWRzAB ). Additional example sentences are presented in § sec:sig.caus.complement and § sec:velar.caus.complement.

pado

The transitive verb pa, which occurs as a light verb (§ sec:pa.lv ) and presents ergative lability (§ sec:lability.pass ), selects imperfective infinitive complements when used in the meaning `discuss and agree/decide to do $X$' ( ex:kukAnAjWjo.topandZi ). All examples of this construction in the corpus occur with B-type orientation preverbs on the infinitive (§ sec:infinitives.other.prefixes ).

`The two of them agreed to meet there and wait for each other.' (150820 qaprANar)

The verb pa can take more than one infinitive complement. There is generally subject coreference between the clauses. However, in example ( ex:tukAqur.topandZi ) the singular subject of the infinitive clauses corresponds to only part of the dual subject of pa. This interesting sentence differs from the original Chinese text, which has 酋长...决定留下来帮助他 qiúzhǎng juédìng liúxiàlái bāngzhù tāThe chieftain... and decided to stay and help him. The dual to-pa-ndʑi is a translation error, but Tshendzin considered the resulting sentence to be grammatical and meaningful, though semantically different from the original text.

The verb of speech kɤtɯpatell, which selects reported speech complements, is derived from pa (§ sec:irregular.transitive, § sec:incorp.denom ).
summary:
The passage explains that both sigmatic and velar causative derivations from adjectival verbs can function as complement-taking verbs, indicating the manner in which the event in the complement clause is carried out. These constructions occur with either dental/bare or velar infinitival complements.

It also describes the transitive verb *pa*, which as a light verb with ergative lability can take imperfective infinitive complements meaning ‘discuss and agree/decide to do X,’ and may take more than one infinitive complement with generally matching subjects. Finally, it notes that the speech verb *kɤtɯpa* is derived from *pa* and selects reported-speech complements.

text:
verb!modal complement clause!modal verbs
Modality in Japhug is encoded by TAME categories (§ sec:TAME.modal ), derivations such as the abilitivative (§ sec:abilitative ), various sentence final particles (§ sec:fsp.epistemic ), and most importantly by complement-taking modal auxiliaries and noun-verb collocations (§ sec:nouns.cognition.complement ). This section provides a description of the use of some of the most common auxiliaries.

In addition to the verbs discussed in this section, some verbs of cognition such as sɯsothink also have modal functions (§ sec:sWso.complement ).
summary: In Japhug, modality is expressed through TAME categories, derivations such as the abilitative, sentence-final particles, and especially by complement-taking modal auxiliaries and noun-verb collocations. This section focuses on some of the most common auxiliaries used for modality. It also notes that certain cognition verbs, such as sɯso ‘think,’ can have modal uses as well.

text:
An important number of modal auxiliary verbs in Japhug are intransitive, and take a complement clause as their subject, and are therefore in 3sg invariable form (§ sec:intransitive.invariable ), regardless of the subject or object in the complement clause. The verbs rabe needed, `need', ɬoʁhave to, `have better', This modal verb is probably grammaticalized from the motion verb ɬoʁcome out(§ sec:motion.verbs ). and kʰɯbe possible are used with either finite complements (§ sec:finite.complement ) or velar infinitives (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ), as shown by ( ex:YWnWpea.kHW ) and ( ex:kurAZia.YWlhoR ) on the one hand, and ( ex:mAkABzu.mWjkHW ) on the other hand. In addition, ra is also attested with degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominal.complement ).

Despite being homophonous to the phasal verb jɤɣfinish (§ sec:aspectual.complement ), the modal verb jɤɣbe allowed differs from it both in meaning and in complement type: the modal jɤɣ takes finite complements ( ex:YWkhama.jAG2 ), while the phasal jɤɣ selects dental/bare infinitives (see example ex:Wti.tojAG, § sec:bare.inf.coreference ).

Impersonal modal verbs, in addition to finite complements in the Imperfective, are also found with Imperative (§ sec:imp.compl, § sec:prohib.function ) and Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.complement.clauses ) complements.

Verbs without alternation between stem I and stem III (§ sec:stem3; in particular intransitive verbs) that select the eastwards orientation take the kɤ- orientation preverb in the Imperative (§ sec:imp.morphology ), a form which can be superficially similar to a velar infinitive. For instance, the form kɤ-nɯ-rɤʑi in ( ex:kAnWrAZi.jAG ) could in principle either be parsed as an infinitive or an Imperative. However, the is the only possibility here, as demonstrated by the fact that the Imperative dual kɤ-nɯ-rɤʑi-ndʑi or plural kɤ-nɯ-rɤʑi-nɯ forms can occur in the same context, while the infinitive does not inflect for person and number.

summary:
Japhug has several impersonal modal auxiliaries that take a complement clause as their subject and therefore remain in an invariable 3sg form, regardless of the arguments inside the complement clause. Some of these verbs, such as rabe ‘need’, ɬoʁ ‘have to’, and kʰɯ ‘be possible’, can take either finite complements or velar infinitives, while others show more restricted patterns: ntsʰi ‘have better’, zgɤt ‘have to’, and jɤɣ ‘be allowed’ are mostly found with finite complements, whereas ŋgrɯ ‘succeed’ occurs only with velar infinitive complements.  

The passage also distinguishes modal jɤɣ ‘be allowed’ from the homophonous phasal verb jɤɣ ‘finish’: they differ in meaning and in the kind of complement they select. Finally, kʰɯ expresses possibility due to external

Among the verbs discussed in this section, only ra and kʰɯ are attested in forms other than 3sg. The verb kʰɯ, in addition to its function as modal auxiliary, can occur with any person when used in the meaning `agree, listen to, obey' (without complement clause) as in ( ex:mWjtWkhWnW ) with a 2pl subject.

exe

neg: sens -2-agree- pl lnk lnk lnk up.there 1sg. poss -mother indef exist: fact lnk dem 3sg. poss - dat loc cisl - imp - auto -ask- pl lnk \\
`(I am telling you that I am not the person you are looking for), you don't want to [listen to me],
my mother is up there, come (with me) and ask her (about it) as suits you.' (2003 sras)
exe

As for ra, in the meaning `need' it does not need to have a complement clause as subject, and can select a noun or even a first or second person referent as in ( ex:aZWG.mAtWra ) (see also ex:mAtWra, § sec:intransitive.invariable ).

The experiencer (the person/entity in need) is marked as a genitive oblique argument (§ sec:gen.beneficiary ), either as a genitive pronoun ( ex:aZWG.mAtWra ) or as a possessive prefix ( ex:nAkWqur.tAra ).

2sg 2sg. poss - sbj: pcp -help aor -need lnk \\
`When you need someone to help you...' (140506 shizi he huichang de bailingniao-zh)

The causative verbs ɣɤracause to have to and ɣɤkʰɯmake it possible to (derived by the velar causative prefix from rabe needed and kʰɯbe possible, respectively), are also complement-taking verbs, used in one of the periphrastic causative constructions (§ sec:velar.caus.modal, § sec:sWpa.sABzu ).

cʰacan

The verb cʰacan is morphologically intransitive, and can either be used as a plain intransitive (in the meaning `be fine', see for instance ex:WkutWpe, § sec:anticipation.person ) or as a semi-transitive verb (§ sec:semi.transitive ) selecting either a finite complement (§ sec:finite.complement ) or an infinitive one (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ), as shown by ( ex:tukWqura.mAtWcha ).

exe

[a-sroʁ kɤ-ri] ri mɤ-tɯ-cʰa, [tu-kɯ-qur-a] ri mɤ-tɯ-cʰa \\
1sg. poss -life inf -save also neg -2-can: fact ipfv -2 1-help- 1sg also neg -2-can: fact \\
`You can neither save my life nor help me.' (shizi he lare neithaoshu-zh)
exe

With finite complements, cʰacan can either have subject coference as in ( ex:tukWqura.mAtWcha, ex:chWtWmACi.tWcha, ex:YWkWCWGmua ) or be used as an impersonal verb as in ( ex:chWtWmACi.cha ), with slightly different meanings.

`You can become rich.' (elicited)

ipfv -2-be.rich can: fact \\
`It will be possible for you to become rich.' (140515 facaimeng-zh)

Since the 1sg form cʰa-a (can: fact - 1sg ) is phonetically identical to the 3sg cʰa (can: fact ), distinguishing between these two patterns is not possible when the subject is 1sg (or 3sg ). Clear examples of the cʰa in impersonal use (where it can be tested) are rare.

All examples in the corpus of cʰacan with a verb in 2sg 1sg form in the complement clause have 2sg indexation as in ( ex:tukWqura.mAtWcha ) above and ( ex:YWkWCWGmua ) below.

sɯxcʰacan
The verb sɯx-cʰa is the sigmatic causative derivation (§ sec:sig.causative ) of cʰacan (§ sec:cha.verb ). It is nearly always in negative form. It can occur with an overt nominal object in the meaning `cause to be (un)able to bear' (example ex:mWYWsWxche, § sec:sig.caus.modal ). As a complement-taking verb, it requires a velar infinitive complement (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ), and exclusively occurs in inverse form with a non-overt causer, and has the specific meaning of `make (physically) unable to $X$', with a non-overt implicit agent, the piglet or lamb in ( ex:mWYWwGsWxcha ) and the bee in ( ex:kAsat.mAwGsWxcha ).

The transitive subject of the infinitival clauses kɤ-tsɯm and ʑaʑa ʑo kɤ-sat in ( ex:mWYWwGsWxcha ) and ( ex:kAsat.mAwGsWxcha ) is here coreferent with the causee of sɯx-cʰa. Since cʰa is morphologically intransitive, this causee is syntactically equivalent to the direct object. spabe able
The transitive spabe able, `know how to' is historically a lexicalized abilitative of pado (§ sec:abilitative.lexicalized ). It indicates abiliy that was acquired through a learning process.

This verb can either select a noun or a noun phrase as object ( ex:kupaskAt.mWjspea, ex:kospa ).

summary:
The passage describes several verbs related to ability, necessity, and causation, noting which forms they can take and what kinds of complements they select. It says that only **ra** and **kʰɯ** are attested outside 3sg, with **kʰɯ** also meaning ‘agree, listen to, obey’ without a complement clause and **ra** meaning ‘need,’ where the experiencer is marked as a genitive oblique argument.

It also explains that **cʰacan** ‘can/be fine’ is morphologically intransitive but may take finite or infinitival complements, sometimes with subject coreference and sometimes impersonally, while its causative **sɯx-cʰa** is usually negative and takes a velar infinitival complement with an implicit causer. Finally, **spabe** ‘be able, know how to’ is a transitive abilitative verb meaning ability acquired through learning, and in infer

Alternatively, spabe able takes infinitival (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ) or finite complement clauses (§ sec:finite.complement ) as in ( ex:tuti.WYWspe ). Subject coreference between spa and the verb in the complement clause is required (§ sec:velar.inf.coreference, § sec:finite.complement.coref ).

nɤzdare, pʰotdare
The verbs nɤzdare and pʰotdare (the second is barely used in the Kamnyu dialect) can be used with both infinitival and finite complements. They require subject coreference.

In example ( ex:CWkAnAkhu.mAnaza ) with the verb nɤkʰuinvite (to one's home as a guest' (one of the few transitive verbs implying a volitional action of both subject and object, § sec:bare.inf.coreference ), the interpretation `I do not dare to go to his house as a guest' (with coreference of the object of the complement clause and the subject of the main clause) is not possible, and a different construction is needed to express this meaning ( ex:kAnAkhu.kACe.mAnaza, with an object participle as explained in § sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ).

The verb nɤzdare is attested in a double negation constructions `not dare not to $X$' (example ex:mAkAGi.mAnAzi, § sec:double.negation ).

It also notes that with **nɤkʰu** ‘invite,’ the intended meaning where the main-clause subject and complement-clause object corefer is not available, so a different construction must be used; additionally, **nɤzdare** can occur in a double-negation construction meaning roughly ‘not dare not to X.’

text:
sɯsothink, `want'
The verb sɯso describes either a cognitive process (`think that $X$') or volitional deontic modality (`want to $X$').

As a modal verb, it either takes infinitive complement clauses ( ex:kAtshi.tasWsonW, § sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ), or finite clauses ( ex:kuGWta.nWsWsota, ex:YWtWsANo.tAtWsot, § sec:finite.complement ), with subject coreference between the complement and the main clause.
