exe

[a-rɤɣo ɲɯ-tɯ-sɤŋo] tɤ-tɯ-sɯso-t tɕe, a-ɣɯ-jɤ-kɯ-sɯɣe-a qʰe nɯ ɕti \\
1sg. poss -song ipfv -2-listen aor -2-want- pst: tr lnk irr - cisl -invite- 1sg lnk dem be. aff: fact \\
`When you want to listen to my songs, send people to come and invite me and that's it.' (140519 yeying-zh)
0004040#S227
exe

The verb sɯso normally selects the westwards orientation as in ( ex:kuGWta.nWsWsota ) (or downwards when used in the Past or Inferential Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv ), but examples ( ex:kAtshi.tasWsonW ) and ( ex:YWtWsANo.tAtWsot ) also show that it sometimes occurs with the Aorist upwards orientation preverbs tɤ- or ta- in temporal clauses meaning ``when $X$ wants to $Y$'' (§ sec:aor.temporal ).

tsoknow, understand, `know', sɯχsɤlrecognize, `realize'

The semi-transitive verb tsoknow, understand, `realize', `know' can take nominal semi-objects (§ sec:semi.transitive ), and occur with three types of complement clauses or complementation strategy. First, it takes finite complete clauses (§ sec:finite.complement ) as in ( ex:GAZu.nW.kotsonW ).

exe

nɯnɯ [tɤ-tɕɯ nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-kʰa nɯtɕu tɕʰeme kɯ-mpɕɤr ci ɣɤʑu] nɯ ko-tso-nɯ. \\
dem indef. poss -son dem gen 3sg. poss -house dem: loc girl sbj: pcp -be.beautiful indef exist: sens dem ifr -understand- pl \\
`They realized that there was a beautiful girl in the boy's house.' (150828 donglang)
0006312#S89
exe

Second, subject participial clauses in kɯ- occur as semi-objects of this verb (§ sec:relative.core.arg ), as in ( ex:mWpWkWsi.kotso ).

exe

li [iɕqʰa tɤɕime nɯ mɯ-pɯ-kɯ-si] nɯ ko-tso \\
again the.aforementioned girl dem neg - aor - sbj: pcp -die dem ifr -understand \\
`She realized that the girl had not died.' (140504 baixuegongzhu-zh)
0003907#S174
exe

Third, tso also selects a (finite or participial) correlative clauses with an interrogative pronoun as in ( ex:thAstWG.nari.mWpjAtso ).

exe

[tɤ-rʑaʁ tʰɤstɯɣ nɯ-ari] mɯ-pjɤ-tso \\
indef. poss -time how.much aor -go[II] neg - ifr -understand \\
`He had not realized how much time had passed.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S246
exe

The transitive sɯχsɤlrecognize, `realize' also takes finite complement clauses (see ex:tari.CtatWt, § sec:redundant.AM ) or participial clauses as in ( ex:tAkWnWCpWz.pjAsWXsAl ).

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ kɯ [qaʑo tɤ-kɯ-nɯɕpɯz] nɯ pjɤ-sɯχsɤl. \\
lnk dem erg sheep aor - sbj: pcp -disguised dem ifr -recognize \\
`He (the shepherd boy) had noticed that the [nobleman] was disguised as a sheep.' (40513 mutong de disheng-zh)
0003977#S58
exe

However, despite being superficially identical to ( ex:mWpWkWsi.kotso ) above, in ( ex:kWNu.amApWwGsWXsala ) sɯχsɤl selects as direct object the 1sg intransitive subject of the participial clause. A possible way to explain this observation is to analyze the participial clause aʑo tɕʰeme kɯ-ŋu as a relative clause whose head is aʑo (`me who am a girl').

exe

<liangshanbo> nɯ kɯ [aʑo tɕʰeme kɯ-ŋu] nɯ a-mɤ-pɯ́-wɣ-sɯχsal-a \\
anthr dem erg 1sg girl sbj: pcp -be dem irr - neg - pfv - inv -realize- 1sg \\
`[I hope that] Liang Shanbo will not realize that I am a girl.' (150826 liangshanbo zhuyingtai-zh)
0006244#S73
exe

βzjozlearn and sɯxɕɤtteach
The verbs of learning βzjozlearn and sɯxɕɤtteach take infinitive complements, as shown by ( ex:kAlAt.kaBzjoz ) and ( ex:kAlAt.pjWtasWxCAt ).

exe

[<tuolaji> kɤ-lɤt] ra ka-βzjoz \\
tractor inf -release pl aor:3 -learn \\
`He learned to drive a tractor.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S208
exe

In the case of the secundative verb sɯxɕɤt (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ), the direct object is the person being taught, the 2sg in ( ex:kAlAt.pjWtasWxCAt ), while the infinitive clause is the theme.

exe

[tɤfsɤri kɤ-βzu] ci pjɯ-ta-sɯxɕɤt \\
thread inf -make a.little ipfv -1 2-teach \\
`Let me teach you how to make a thread.' (vid-20140506043657)
exe
summary: The verb **sɯso** means either ‘think that X’ or ‘want to X’; as a modal verb, it can take either infinitive or finite complement clauses, and the subject of the complement is coreferential with the main-clause subject. The verb **tso** ‘know, understand, realize’ can take finite complement clauses, kɯ- participial clauses, or correlative clauses with an interrogative pronoun, while **sɯχsɤl** ‘recognize, realize’ takes finite or participial clauses and may analyze a participial clause as a relative clause in some cases. The learning and teaching verbs **βzjoz** ‘learn’ and **sɯxɕɤt** ‘teach’ take infinitive complements, with **sɯxɕɤt** also taking a direct object for the person taught.

text:
verb!perception complement clause!perception verbs
The transitive perception verbs mtosee and mtsʰɤmhear, `smell', `feel (non-visually)' express non-volitional perception. The contrast between rulook at (§ sec:coordination.comp.str ) and mto can be illustrated by ( ex:schAru.mWpjAmto ), where the latter has a meaning close to `find'.

exe

kʰɯɣɲɟɯ ra s-cʰɤ-ru ri mɯ-pjɤ-mto \\
window pl tral - ifr: downstream -look lnk neg - ifr -see \\
`She went and looked from the window but did not see him.' (140505 xiaohaitu-zh)
0003921#S61
exe

These two verbs are compatible with finite complements (§ sec:finite.complement ), as in ( ex:YWGAwu.pjAmtshAm ), without any coreference restriction.

exe

[sɯŋgi nɯ ɲɯ-ɣɤwu] nɯ pjɤ-mtsʰɤm \\
lion dem ipfv -cry dem ifr -hear \\
`[The mouse] heard that the lion was crying.' (shizi he laoshu-zh)
exe

They are incompatible with infinitival complements, but often take participial or finite relative clauses as objects (§ sec:non-finite.relative.complement.ambiguity, § sec:relative.core.arg ).

Non-finite verb form in kɤ- such as kɤ-ntsɣe in ( ex:kAntsGe.mWpWmtota ) resemble velar infinitives, but since intransitive dynamic verbs do not occur with kɤ- in this context, these forms are analyzed as object participles (§ sec:infinitives.participles ).

exe

tɕe [ɯ-rdoʁ nɯ kɯ-fse kɤ-ntsɣe] nɯ mɯ-pɯ-mto-t-a \\
lnk 3sg. poss -grain dem sbj: pcp -be.like obj: pcp -sell dem neg - aor -see- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I have not seen its grains (of buckthorn) sold as is (it is always sold in processed form).' (09-mi)
0003466#S55
exe

The verb mtsʰɤm is often used in combination with the form kɤ-ti as in ( ex:YWsAmtsWG.kAti ). This form could be analyzed as a complementizer, but since positive evidence of its grammaticalized status is not obvious, I analyze kɤ-ti here as an object participle taking an object complement clause ( nɯ ɲɯ-sɤ-mtsɯɣ ). That complement clause itself is also the relativized element of the head-internal object participial clause [`` nɯ ɲɯ-sɤ-mtsɯɣ '' kɤ-ti] (§ sec:relativized.complement.clause ), a construction that can be glossed as `I have not heard `It bites people' being said'.

exe

[[nɯ ɲɯ-sɤ-mtsɯɣ] kɤ-ti] mɯ-pɯ́-wɣ-mtsʰɤm. \\
dem sens - apass -bite obj: pcp -say neg - aor - inv -hear \\
`I have not heard that it bites people.' (28-tshAwAre)
0003722#S69
exe

With intransitive verbs, the subject participle in kɯ- is always found in the clauses occurring as the object of mto and mtsʰɤm, as in ( ex:pWkWntChAr.pjAmto ). Such clauses are to be analyzed as participial relatives (§ sec:relative.core.arg ).

exe

pjɯ-ru qʰe [tɕeki tɯ-ci ɯ-ŋgɯ ɯʑo pɯ-kɯ-ntɕʰɤr] nɯ pjɤ-mto. \\
ipfv: down -look lnk down indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -in 3sg aor: down - sbj: pcp -appear dem ifr -see \\
`He looked down, and saw his own reflection in the water below (himself reflected in the water).' (140519 chou xiaoya-zh)
0004034#S164
exe

In ( ex:WkWti.pjAmtshAm ), mtsʰɤm even takes as object a head-internal relative clause in kɯ- (rather than kɤ- as in ex:YWsAmtsWG.kAti above), with the transitive subject as relativized element (§ sec:tr.subject.relativization ).

exe

ɲɯ-sɤŋo tɕe [iɕqʰa sŋaʁspa nɯ kɯ ``tɤtʂu ɣɯ-tɤ-sɤndu-nɯ" ɯ-kɯ-ti] nɯ pjɤ-mtsʰɤm tɕe \\
ipfv -listen lnk the.aforementioned sorcerer dem erg lamp cisl - imp -exchange- pl 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -say dem ifr -hear lnk \\
`She heard the sorcerer saying `Come and exchange [your] lamp'.' (140511 alading-zh)
0003953#S212
exe

Verbs of perception and cognition also occur with finite clauses containing interrogative pronouns which look like correlatives (§ sec:interrogative.relative ), such as ŋotɕu jɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ in ( ex:NotCu.jAnWlhoR.mWpWmtoj ).

exe

[ŋotɕu jɤ-nɯ-ɬoʁ] tɕi mɯ-pɯ-mto-j, [ŋotɕu jɤ-ɕqʰlɤt] tɕi kɤ-ɕɯftaʁ mɯ-pjɤ-cʰa-j \\
where ifr - auto -come.out also neg - aor -see- 1pl where ifr -disappear also inf -remember neg - ifr -can- 1pl \\
`We neither saw where she came from, nor can we remember which way she went.' (2003 sras)
exe

Although the volitional perception verbs sɤŋolisten (labile), rtoʁlook (transitive) and rulook at (§ sec:orienting.verbs ) can have nominal objects or semi-objects, they do not take complement clauses. However, they do occur in coordinating complementation strategies (§ sec:ipfv.perception, § sec:coordination.comp.str ).
summary:
The transitive perception verbs **mto** ‘see’ and **mtsʰɤm** ‘hear/smell/feel’ express **non-volitional perception** and can take **finite complement clauses** without any coreference restriction. They are **incompatible with infinitival complements**, but often take **participial** or **finite relative clauses** as objects, including object participles in **kɤ-** and subject participles in **kɯ-**, which are analyzed as relative-clause-like structures rather than true infinitives.  

These verbs can also appear with finite clauses containing interrogative pronouns that resemble correlatives, while **volitional perception verbs** like ‘listen’ and ‘look’ may take nominal objects or semi-objects but **do not take complement clauses**, instead occurring in coordinating complementation strategies.

subsection: Phasal verbs and other aspectual auxiliaries
text:
verb!phasal complement clause!phasal verbs
Aspectual and phasal complement-taking verbs present a much greater variety of constructions than modal verbs. tab:phasal summarizes the constructions attested with each verb, not all of which are equally common. The abbreviations are as follows: I. (velar infinitive, § sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ), BI (bare infinitive and tɯ- infinitive, § sec:bare.dental.inf ), F. (finite complement, § sec:finite.complement ), tr. (transitive), impers. (intransitive impersonal).

As shown in § sec:bare.inf.coreference, verbs in this group have different coreference restrictions depending on the complement type: when transitive verbs select bare/dental infinitive complements, coreference is required between the subject of the complement clause and that of the matrix verb.
summary: Aspectual and phasal complement-taking verbs allow a wider range of constructions than modal verbs, and the text notes several complement types and abbreviations used to describe them. It also states that these verbs differ in coreference requirements by complement type: when transitive verbs take bare or dental infinitive complements, the subject of the complement clause must corefer with the subject of the matrix verb.

subsection: Phasal verbs and other aspectual auxiliaries
text:
The transitive verb rɲo can be used with a nominal object in the meaning `try, taste' (of food), as shown in ( ex:tukWsWrYoa ) with the sigmatic causative sɯ-rɲo `let $X$ taste' (§ sec:sig.causative ).

exe

aʑo nɤ-paχɕi ci tu-kɯ-sɯ-rɲo-a \\
1sg 2sg. poss -apple a.little ipfv -2 1- caus -taste- 1sg \\
`Let me taste your apples.' (150904 zhongli-zh)
0006348#S15
exe

As a complement-taking verb, rɲo means `have already done...' (like Chinese 曾经……过 céngjīng...guò ), and commonly occurs with both bare/dental infinitival complements (§ sec:bare.dental.inf ) and velar infinitival complements (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ). These two complement types differ by their coreference restrictions: the former requires subject coreference (§ sec:bare.inf.coreference ), while the latter does not.

In example ( ex:kAmtsWG.P ), the first sentence aʑo kɤ-mtsɯɣ mɯ-pɯ-rɲo-t-a is ambiguous, and could be translated as either `I have never bitten it' (subject coreference) or `I have never been bitten by it' (object coreference), regardless of the fact that the 1sg is a transitive subject in both cases as shown by the absence of an inverse prefix and the presence of the -t- suffix (§ sec:indexation.mixed, § sec:other.TAME ). The verb rɲoexperience lacks inverse forms other than the generic subject (§ sec:indexation.generic.tr ), and the 3 1sg inverse form $ $ mɯ-pɯ́-wɣ-rɲo-a is rejected, and cannot be used to replace mɯ-pɯ-rɲo-t-a in ( ex:kAmtsWG.P ).

exe

aʑo [kɤ-mtsɯɣ] mɯ-pɯ-rɲo-t-a ri, χpɤltɕɯn kɯ pjɤ-rɲo \\
1sg inf -bite neg - aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg but p.n erg ifr -experience \\
`I have never been stung [by a wasp], but Dpalcan has.' (26-ndzWrnaR)
0003678#S19
exe

In the second sentence, the personal name χpɤltɕɯn predictably takes the ergative, being the transitive subject of rɲoexperience. However, it is at the same time object of (elided) infinitive kɤ-mtsɯɣ `to bite' present in the first clause, and the absolutive form would be expected if the verb in the complement clause had precedence over the matrix verb, as happens in some cases (§ sec:complement.clause.case.marking ). The complete clause without elision would χpɤltɕɯn kɯ kɤ-mtsɯɣ pjɤ-rɲo ` Dpalcan has been stung (by a wasp) before'.

exe

χpɤltɕɯn kɯ [kɤ-mtsɯɣ] pjɤ-rɲo \\
p.n erg inf -bite ifr -experience \\
` Dpalcan has been stung [by a wasp] before'. (elicitation based on ex:kAmtsWG.P )
exe

The sentence ( ex:kAmtsWG.pjArYo ) is also ambiguous, but can be interpreted as expressing coreference between the transitive subject of rɲoexperience with the object of the transitive verb mtsɯɣbite, with the ergative flagging of the matrix clause taking over the absolutive marking expected in the complement clause.

The subject of rɲoexperience can also be coreferential with the possessor of the intransitive subject in the complement clause, as in example ( ex:kAmNAm ), where the non-overt subject should be a-xtu `my belly', as in ( ex:kAmNAm.pWrYota ) (§ sec:other.collocation.intr ).

exe

aʑo pɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi-a ʑo ri tɯxtɤŋɤm nɯ-atɯɣ-a tɕe, [nɯ kɤ-mŋɤm] pɯ-rɲo-t-a \\
1sg pst. ipfv - emph be.small- 1sg emph loc dysentery aor -meet- 1sg lnk dem inf -hurt aor -experience- 1sg \\
`When I was very small, I had dysentery, [my belly] ached.' (24-pGArtsAG)
0003624#S116
exe

exe

[a-xtu kɤ-mŋɤm] pɯ-rɲo-t-a. \\
1sg. poss -belly inf -hurt aor -experience- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`I have had stomachache.' (elicited)
exe

However, despite the fact that rɲo indexes either the subject or the object of its complement clause without difference in the matrix clause as illustrated by ( ex:kAmtsWG.P ) and ( ex:kAmtsWG.pjArYo ) above, their relativization patterns are different. The subject of the infinitive clause is relativized by means of the subject participle pɯ-kɯ-rɲo, while the object is relativized by using either a finite relative clause or the object participle pɯ-kɤ-rɲo (§ sec:out.complement.relativization.tr ).
summary:
The transitive verb rɲo can mean ‘try, taste’ with a nominal object, but as a complement-taking verb it means ‘have already done…’ and occurs with both bare/dental and velar infinitival complements. The two complement types differ in coreference: bare/dental infinitives require subject coreference, while velar infinitives do not, allowing ambiguity between subject and object coreference in some examples. 

The passage also notes that rɲo lacks special inverse forms beyond the generic subject pattern, and that its coreferential relations are reflected differently in relativization: the infinitival subject is relativized with the subject participle pɯ-kɯ-rɲo, while the object is relativized with either a finite relative clause or the object participle pɯ-kɤ-rɲo.

subsection: Phasal verbs and other aspectual auxiliaries
text:
Phasal verbs such as ʑabegin and stʰɯtfinish are most often attested with dental or bare infinitives (§ sec:bare.inf.dental.complementary ) as in ( ex:tasthWt ). They can also take velar infinitives as in ( ex:nasthWt ).

exe

[nɯ ɯ-ti] ta-stʰɯt \\
dem 3sg. poss - bare. inf:say aor:3 -finish \\
`When she finished saying that...' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh)
0006334#S122
exe

exe

[tɯ-nɯ kɤ-jtsʰi] na-stʰɯt tɕe tɕe tɤ-pɤtso nɯ li ɯ-sta nɯtɕu ko-ɕɯ-rŋgɯ \\
indef. poss -breast inf -give.to.drink aor:3 -finish lnk lnk indef. poss -child dem again 3sg. poss -bed dem: loc ifr - caus -lay \\
`After she had finished breastfeeding, she put back the child on his bed.' (140429 jiedi-zh)
exe

In addition, some phasal verbs are also attested with finite complements sharing the same TAME and person indexation (§ sec:svc.finite.agreement ), though this construction is considerably rarer.

exe

[nɯra pa-βzjoz] pa-stʰɯt tɕe ɯ-sloχpɯn nɯ kɯ taqaβ tɯ-ldʑa ɲɤ́-wɣ-mbi \\
dem: pl aor:3 -learn aor:3 -finish lnk 3sg. poss -teacher dem erg needle one- cl ifr - inv -give \\
`When he finished learning this [craft], his teacher gave him a needle.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S95
exe

Unlike rɲoexperience (which selects the downwards orientation), phasal verbs take the lexical orientation of the verb in the complement clause (§ sec:orientation.raising ), upwards in ( ex:tasthWt ) (§ sec:preverb.speech ), eastwards in ( ex:nasthWt ) (§ sec:preverb.giving ) and downwards in ( ex:pasthWt ).
summary:
Phasal verbs such as *ʑabegin* and *stʰɯtfinish* most commonly occur with dental or bare infinitives, though they can also take velar infinitives. Less commonly, they may combine with finite complements that share the same TAME and person indexing.  

Unlike *rɲo* ‘experience,’ phasal verbs do not determine their own orientation; instead, they take the lexical orientation of the verb in the complement clause, which may be upward, eastward, or downward depending on the example.

subsection: Phasal verbs and other aspectual auxiliaries
text:
The intransitive verb rɤŋgat means `prepare to depart' when used on its own without a subordinate clause. It also selects participial clauses like motion verbs (§ sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ), with the meaning `be about to'. With subject participial clauses in kɯ- as in ( ex:kWsi.tArANgat ), there is coreference between the subject of rɤŋgat and that of its subordinate clause.

exe

[kɯ-si] tɤ-rɤŋgat, tu-rɤru mɯ-nɯ-cʰa ri, nɯ ɯ-ɕɣa ra pɯ-tsʰoz ʑo. \\
sbj: pcp -die aor -be.about ipfv -get.up neg - aor -can lnk dem 3sg. poss -tooth pl pst. ipfv -be.complete emph \\
`Even when she was about to die (from old age), when she was not able to get up anymore, (...) she still had all her teeth.' (27-tWCGArgu)
0003708#S24
exe

Like motion verb, rɤŋgatbe about to also takes object participial clauses in kɤ- with coreference with the object of the clause `be about to be $X$' as in ( ex:kAsat.tAkWrANgat ).

exe

jɤ-tɯ-ari tɕe, (...) tɯrme [kɤ-sat] tɤ-kɯ-rɤŋgat (...) ʁnɯz tɯ-mtɤm ri \\
aor -2-go[II] lnk person sbj: pcp -kill aor - sbj: pcp -be.about.to two 2-see[III]: fact lnk \\
`When you go there, you will see two people who are about to be killed.' (140507 jinniao-zh)
0003931#S305
exe

The intransitive contracting verb aɣɯɣube about to has the same meaning as rɤŋgat, and is used in the same constructions ( ex:akWRndW.tutAGWGu ), though it is slightly less frequent.

exe

[a-kɯ-ʁndɯ] tu-tɯ-ɤɣɯɣu ɲɯ-ŋu tɕe \\
1sg. poss - sbj: pcp -hit ipfv -2-be.about.to sens -be lnk \\
`You are about to hit me.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

The meaning of the imminent aspect auxiliaries overlaps with that of the Proximative (§ sec:proximative, § sec:proximative.periphrastic ), as shown by examples ( ex:GWCaBa.tANu ) and ( ex:akWCaB.tArANgat ) from the same passage of two versions of the same story, the former ( ex:GWCaBa.tANu ) with Periphrastic Proximative (§ sec:proximative.periphrastic ) and the latter with rɤŋgatbe about to.

exe

aʑo ɣɯ-ɕaβ-a tɤ-ŋu tɕe, nɤʑo χcʰa nɯ a-nɯ-tɯ-ɕtʰɯz \\
1sg inv -catch.up: fact - 1sg aor -be lnk 2sg right dem irr - pfv: west -2-turn.towards \\
`When they are about to catch up with me, turn the [thing in your] right [hand] in [their direction].' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

exe

[aʑo a-kɯ-ɕaβ] tɤ-rɤŋgat-nɯ tɕe, nɤʑo kɯ sŋaʁ kɯmtɕʰoχsɯm a-nɯ-tɯ-ɕtʰɯz \\
1sg 1sg. poss - sbj: pcp -catch.up aor -be.about.to- pl lnk 2sg erg sorcery triratna dem irr - pfv: west -2-turn.towards \\
`When they are about to catch up with me, turn the triratna in [their direction].' (2003 smanmi)
exe
summary:
The intransitive verb **rɤŋgat** means ‘prepare to depart’ when used alone, and in participial clause constructions it means ‘be about to.’ In these constructions, the subject or object of the participial clause is coreferential with the subject or object of **rɤŋgat**, respectively.  

A related intransitive contracting verb, **aɣɯɣu**, has the same meaning and occurs in the same constructions, though it is somewhat less frequent. The imminent-aspect auxiliaries overlap in meaning with the Proximative, as shown by parallel examples from the same story.

subsection: Phasal verbs and other aspectual auxiliaries
text:
The habitual aspect auxiliary ŋgrɤlbe usually the case is not compatible with infinitival complements. It only occurs with finite complements, as in ( ex:tu.NgrAl ).

exe

[ɕɤr tɕe tu] ŋgrɤl, [tu-mbri] ŋgrɤl \\
night loc exist: fact be.usually.the.case: fact ipfv -call be.usually.the.case: fact \\
`[Owls] appear, howl during the night.' (22-pGAkhW)
0003594#S19
exe

In the Past Perfective with an Imperfective complement, it expresses a former habit `use to $X$' ( ex:chWnWXsea.pWNgrAl ).

exe

[aʑo kumpɣa cʰɯ-nɯ-χse-a] pɯ-ŋgrɤl \\
1sg chicken ipfv - auto -feed[III]- 1sg pst. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`I used to raise chickens (for my own sake).' (150819 kumpGa)
0006388#S68
exe

The auxiliary ŋgrɤl, especially in negative form, can have overtones of epistemic ( ex:tWmaR.mANgrAl ) or deontic modality ( ex:tukWti.mANgrAl ).

exe

The habitual aspect auxiliary ŋgrɤl “usually the case” does not take infinitival complements; it occurs only with finite complements. In the Past Perfective with an Imperfective complement, it expresses a former habit meaning “used to X.”  

Especially in negative form, ŋgrɤl can also convey epistemic or deontic modality.

text:
similative!verb complement clause!similative verbs
The verbs fsebe like and studo like are semi-transitive (§ sec:semi.transitive ) and secundative (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ), respectively. Both select as semi-object the manner in which the action is performed.

These verbs are found with velar infinitive complements (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ), either with a demonstrative expressing the action (such as nɯ in ex:CAmWGdW.kAlAt.nW.tustunW ) or in questions with the interrogative pronoun tɕʰiwhat (§ sec:tChi ) as in ( ex:tChi.atAfsej ). The demonstrative or the interrogative pronoun are always located closer to the similative verb than the infinitive clause.

exe

tɕe [ɕɤmɯɣdɯ kɤ-lɤt] nɯ tu-stu-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
lnk gun inf -release dem ipfv -do.like- pl sens -be \\
`People shoot with guns like that.' (28-CAmWGdW)
0003712#S90
exe

exe

[kɤ-pʰɣo] tɕʰi a-tɤ-fse-j? \\
inf -flee what irr - pfv -be.like- 1pl \\
`How will we flee?' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S60
exe

The subject of the infinitival clause is always coreferent with that of fse or stu, but its object is never indexed on the matrix verb. For instance, although fsraŋprotect, `save' and bɯwacarry on the back are transitive verbs that can index first or second person objects (see for instance ex:aZo.tutafsraN, § sec:indexation.local ), in ( ex:kAfsraN.tChi.tustea ) and ( ex:kAbWwa.tChi.atAste ) the 2sg object is not indexed on the matrix verb stu, otherwise the forms tu-ta-stu ( ipfv -1 2-do.like) and a-tɤ-tɯ́-wɣ-stu ( irr - pfv -2- inv -do.like) would be expected. These examples show that the complement clause saturates the direct object of stu.

exe

[nɤʑo kɤ-fsraŋ] tɕʰi tu-ste-a? \\
2sg inf -protect what ipfv -do.like[III]- 1sg \\
`How [can] I save you?' (150901 dongguo xiansheng he lang-zh)
0006336#S39
exe

exe

pɣɤtɕɯ kɯ [nɤʑo kɤ-bɯwa] tɕʰi a-tɤ-ste ɕti? \\
bird erg 2sg inf -carry.on.the.back what irr - pfv -do.like[III] be. aff: fact \\
`How will the bird carry you on its back?' (2003 zrAntCW tWrme)
exe

Alternatively, stu can also index as object the object of the verb in the infinitival clause, as shown by ( ex:kAfsraN.tChi.tutastu ), a sentence whose meaning is the same as that of ( ex:kAfsraN.tChi.tustea ).

exe

[nɤʑo kɤ-fsraŋ] tɕʰi tu-ta-stu? \\
2sg inf -protect what ipfv -1 2-do.like[III] \\
`How [can] I save you?' (elicitation based on ex:kAfsraN.tChi.tustea )
exe

Deixis manner verbs are also often used in a variety of complementation strategies. First, they occur with a coordinated clause (generally in the Factual Non-Past) expressing the purpose of the action, as in( § sec:coordination.comp.str ). Second, they can take as semi-object a totalitative relative (§ sec:totalitative.relatives ) as object (§ sec:relative.core.arg ) as in ( ex:tWtastu.tostu2 ) in the meaning `do everything in the same way as $X$' (where $X$ is the transitive subject of the relative). Third, fse and stu are found in serial verb constructions (§ sec:svc.similative.verb ).

exe

tɕʰi ci ʑo tú-wɣ-stu tɕe pʰɤn \\
what indef emph ipfv - inv -do.like lnk be.efficient: fact \\
`What should [we] do to successfully [treat your disease]?' (2011-04-smanmi)
exe

exe

[tɤ-wɯ nɯ kɯ tɯ ta-stu] ʑo to-stu \\
indef. poss -grandfather dem erg total aor:3 -do.like emph ifr -do.like \\
`He did everything like the old man.' (140511 xinbada-zh)
0003961#S243
exe
summary:
The similative verbs **fsebe like** and **studo like** are semi-transitive and secundative, respectively, and both take a manner phrase as a semi-object. They commonly occur with **velar infinitive complements**, either accompanied by a demonstrative or with the interrogative **tɕʰi** ‘what/how,’ and the demonstrative/interrogative must appear closer to the similative verb than the infinitive clause.

In these constructions, the subject of the infinitival clause is always coreferential with the matrix verb’s subject, while the infinitival object is not indexed on the matrix verb, showing that the complement clause can saturate the direct object of **stu**. However, **stu** may also index the object of the infinitival verb, and similative manner verbs can additionally appear in coordinated purpose clauses, with totalitative relatives, and in serial verb constructions.

text:
adjective!complement-taking
Some adjectival stative verbs like mkʰɤzbe expert, `be knowledgeable' are semi-transitive (§ sec:semi.transitive ) and optionally take either a noun ( ex:CoNBzu.mkhAz ) or a complement clause ( ex:kAtaR.mkhAztCi ) as semi-object in addition to their subject. The complement clause can be either infinitival (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ) or finite (§ sec:finite.complement ).

exe

ɯ-nmaʁ jɤ-kɯ-ɣe nɯ ɕoŋβzu mkʰɤz tɕe \\
3sg. poss -husband aor - sbj: pcp -come[II] dem carpentry be.expert: fact lnk \\
`Her husband who came [to live in her family] is very good at carpentry.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S250
exe

exe

tɕiʑo rcanɯ, [kɤ-taʁ] wuma ʑo mkʰɤz-tɕi \\

Adjectives such as ɴqabe difficult, mbatbe easy, which unlike mkʰɤzbe expert do not have a semi-object, can take infinitival or finite complement clauses as their subject ( ex:YAjRu.YWmbat ). Note that this construction has a meaning close to that of the facilitative nɯɣɯ- derivation (§ sec:facilitative ).

Even in nominalized forms such as the degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominals ), these verbs retain the ability to take subject complements (§ sec:degree.nominal.arguments ), as in ( ex:chWwxti.WtWmbat2 ).

Some adjectival verb such as ʁzɤβbe careful select bare infinitive complements (§ sec:bare.inf ) like their causative form (§ sec:causative.manner.complement ).
summary: Some adjectival stative verbs, such as *mkʰɤzbe* ‘be expert,’ are semi-transitive and can optionally take either a noun or a complement clause as a semi-object; these complement clauses may be infinitival or finite. Other adjectival stative verbs, such as *ɴqabe* ‘difficult’ and *mbatbe* ‘easy,’ do not take a semi-object but can take infinitival or finite complement clauses as subjects, including in nominalized degree forms. The passage also notes that some adjectives, like *ʁzɤβbe* ‘careful,’ take bare infinitive complements.

text:
noun!complement-taking
Not all noun-modifying clauses should be analyzed as relative clauses: only subordinate clauses whose head noun (overt or covert) has a syntactic role in the clause (whether argument, adjunct or possessor) can be considered to be a relative.
summary: Not all noun-modifying clauses are relative clauses. Only subordinate clauses in which the head noun, whether overt or covert, has a syntactic role in the clause—such as argument, adjunct, or possessor—count as relatives.

text:
In examples ( ex:kongzhi ) and ( ex:kAtAB.ftCaka ), the head noun ftɕakamethod, `manner' is neither a core argument nor an adjunct. It is not possible to convert the infinitive subordinate clauses mɯ-tu-kɤ-mbro `not become too high' and qartsɤβ kɤ-kɤ-βzu ra kɤ-tɤβ `thresh the (grains) that have been harvested' into independent sentences that would include ftɕaka. These clauses should therefore be analyzed as adnominal complement clauses, rather than a prenominal relatives.

exe

a-<xuetang> ɯ-tɯ-mbro <kongzhi> tu-βze-a ŋu. [mɯ-tu-kɤ-mbro] ftɕaka tu-βze-a ŋu. \\
1sg. poss -blood.sugar 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.high control ipfv -do[III]- 1sg be: fact neg - ipfv - inf -be.high manner ipfv -do[III]- 1sg be: fact \\
`I control my blood sugar, I do what I can to prevent it from being too high'. (conversation, 15-12-05)
exe

exe

[qartsɤβ kɤ-kɤ-βzu ra kɤ-tɤβ] ftɕaka ɣɯ-βzu ra \\
harvest aor - obj: pcp -make pl inf -thresh manner inv -make be.needed: fact \\
`Then one has to prepare to thresh the [grains] that have been harvested.' (2010.10)
exe

The construction exemplified by ( ex:kongzhi ) and ( ex:kAtAB.ftCaka ) is a collocation combining the complement-taking noun ftɕaka with the verb βzumake, meaning either `do by any means possible' (as in ex:kongzhi ) or `prepare to $X$' ( ex:kAtAB.ftCaka ). In the latter meaning, the collocation is homonymous with the transitive denominal verb nɯftɕakaprepare (§ sec:denom.tr.nW ), which also selects velar infinitive complements, as shown by ( ex:kAtAB.kuwGnWftCaka ), uttered just before ( ex:kAtAB.ftCaka ) in the same recording.

exe

[kɤ-tɤβ] kú-wɣ-nɯftɕaka ra \\
inf -thresh ipfv - inv -prepare be.needed: fact \\
`One has to prepare the threshing.' (2010.10)
exe

The infinitive complement kɤ-tɤβ in ( ex:kAtAB.kuwGnWftCaka ) is exactly parallel to the adnominal complement clause in ( ex:kAtAB.ftCaka ). This parallelism between complement-taking noun and the complement-taking denominal verb derived from it is not found in all the cases (§ sec:complement.taking.noun.list ), but confirms the observation that the adnominal clause in ( ex:kAtAB.ftCaka ) is not a prenominal relative.
summary: The passage argues that in these examples, the noun *ftɕaka* ‘manner’ is not a core argument or adjunct, and the infinitival subordinate clauses should be analyzed as adnominal complement clauses rather than prenominal relative clauses. It also notes that the construction with *ftɕaka* forms a collocation with the verb *βzu* ‘do/make’, meaning either ‘do by any means possible’ or ‘prepare to X’. The parallel infinitival complement selected by the related denominal verb *nɯftɕaka* supports the claim that the clause in (ex:kAtAB.ftCaka) is not a relative clause.

text:
Among complement-taking nouns, some like ftɕakamethod, `manner' (§ sec:compl.taking.nouns.denominal, § sec:nouns.manner.complement ) and kowamanner (§ sec:nouns.manner.complement ) are alienably possessed nouns, but most (§ sec:complement.taking.noun.list ) are inalienably possessed (§ sec:complement.taking.IPN ).

Two categories must be distinguished among these inalienably possessed nouns. First, some nouns such as ɯ-skɤtlanguage, `sound' (§ sec:nouns.speech.complement ) always take a 3sg possessive prefix coreferent with the complement clause (treated as possessor of the noun), as in ( ex:amAjAtWGinW.WskAt ).

exe

ji-wɯ kɯ ``a-mɤ-jɤ-tɯ-ɣi-nɯ'' ɯ-skɤt to-βzu ɕti \\
1pl. poss -grandfather erg irr - neg - pfv -2-come- pl 3sg. poss -language ifr -make be. aff: fact \\
`(By these words) our father-in-law means that he does not want us to come back' (he means: `don't you come back') (2005 tAwakWcqraR)
exe

Other nouns like ɯ-sɯmmind (§ sec:nouns.cognition.complement ) on the other hand select as possessor the experiencer, which may not be 3sg, and the complement clause is not syntactically a possessor. For instance, in ( ex:tutWndAm.nAsWm.WCe ) the possessor of -sɯm is 2sg, not 3sg as would be expected if the finite clause nɯ-βdaʁmu nɯ tu-tɯ-ndɤm were the possessor of this noun.

exe

[nɯ-βdaʁmu nɯ tu-tɯ-ndɤm] nɤ-sɯm ɯ́-ɕe? \\
3pl. poss -queen dem ipfv -2-take[III] 2sg. poss -mind qu -go: fact \\
`Do you want to become their queen?' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh)
0006334#S472
exe
summary: Among complement-taking nouns, most are inalienably possessed, though a few like *ftɕaka* ‘manner’ and *kowa* ‘manner’ are alienably possessed. Within the inalienably possessed group, some nouns such as *ɯ-skɤt* ‘language, sound’ always take a 3sg possessive prefix coreferent with the complement clause, while others like *ɯ-sɯm* ‘mind’ take the experiencer as possessor, which can be non-3sg and is not syntactically the complement clause.

text: Complement-taking nouns selecting infinitive (§ sec:velar.infinitives.complement.clauses ), finite (§ sec:finite.complement ) or reported speech complements (§ sec:reported.speech ) can be divided into three semantic groups.
summary: Complement-taking nouns that select infinitive, finite, or reported speech complements can be classified into three semantic groups. The passage states that these nouns are organized according to the type of complement they take.

text:
noun!manner
The alienably possessed nouns ftɕakamethod, `manner' (§ sec:compl.taking.nouns.denominal ) and kowamanner, These nouns are both translated into Chinese as 办法 bànfǎmethod, `means', `manner'. both borrowed from Tibetan (from བཅའ་ཀbtɕa.kaimplement and བཀོད་པbkod.paarrangement, `method', respectively), occur in collocation with the verb βzumake (§ sec:Bzu.lv ) in the meanings `try to $X$ by any means' (in Chinese 想尽办法 xiǎng jìn bànfǎtry to do by any means) or `prepare'. They can select an infinitive clause with raising of the person indexation on the main verb, as shown by the 3 2sg form tɯ́-wɣ-βzu `they will $X$ you' in ( ex:kAndza.kowa.tuwGBzu ).

`My children are coming back home soon, and they will try to eat you, let me hide you.' (2012 Norbzang)

The complement-taking transitive denominal verbs nɯftɕakaprepare and nɯkowaprepare (§ sec:compl.taking.nouns.denominal ) can be derived from these two nouns.
summary: The alienably possessed nouns **ftɕaka** and **kowa**, both translated into Chinese as *bànfǎ* ‘means, manner’ and borrowed from Tibetan, occur with the verb **βzu** to mean ‘try to X by any means’ or ‘prepare.’ They can take an infinitival complement with person indexing raised onto the main verb, and the corresponding complement-taking transitive denominal verbs **nɯftɕaka** and **nɯkowa** ‘prepare’ are derived from these nouns.

The inalienably possessed nouns related to speech and noise ɯ-tiway of saying, `wording', `expression', ɯ-fɕɤtstory, ɯ-skɤtlanguage, `sound', tɤ-zgrasound, `noise' and tɯ-tɕʰainformation, news (about someone) (§ sec:biactantial.ipn ), and the alienably possessed kʰɤcɤldiscussion can occur with finite complement clauses ( ex:WfCAt.tu, ex:YWnWqambWmbjom.Wzgra ) (see also ex:rCWB4.pjWlAt, § sec:ideo.X ) or reported speech complements ( ex:ra.WskAt.ra.toBzu ).

`I don't want to go to sleep.' (elicited)
exe

The verb ɕego in this construction is never found in the Aorist or the Inferential. To express an inchoative meaning, the motion verb ɣicome occurs instead with tɯ-sɯm, as in ( ex:kAnWCe.WsWm.toGi ).

exe

daltsɯtsa tɕe tɕe kɤ-nɯ-ɕe tsa ɯ-sɯm to-ɣi. \\
slowly lnk lnk inf - vert -go a.little 3sg. poss -mind ifr -come \\
`He slowly started thinking of going home.' (150907 laoshandaoshi-zh)
0006398#S53
exe

Like tɯ-sɯm, the noun ɯ-ʁjizwish (a fossil -z nominalization, § sec:z.nmlz ) occurs in collocation with ɣicome (§ sec:motion.light.verbs ). This collocation, which means `feel like/want to $X$', has the same morphosyntactic properties as those described above: it is compatible with both infinitive complement clauses ( ex:kAnAma.tWRjiz ) and finite ones ( ex:Cture.WRjiz ).

exe

[kɤ-nɤma] tɯ-ʁjiz maka mɤ-ɣi. \\
inf -work genr. poss -wish at.all neg -come[III]: fact \\
`(When one is sick), one does not feel like working.' (27-tWfCAl)
0003710#S17
exe

exe

iɕqʰa [χpɯn kɯ-tsʰu nɯ kɯ tɯ-ci ɕ-tu-re] nɯ ɯ-ʁjiz mɯ-pjɤ-ɣi \\
the.aforementioned monk sbj: pcp -be.fat dem erg indef. poss -water tral - ipfv: up -bring[III] dem 3sg. poss -wish neg - ifr. ipfv -come \\
`The fat monk did not feel like (going down the river and) bringing the water [up to the monastery]. (150830 san ge heshang-zh)
0006416#S100
exe
summary:
The noun of cognition **tɯ-sɯm** ‘mind’ can combine with the motion verb **ɕe** to mean ‘want to X,’ taking either a finite or an infinitival complement clause. The possessive prefix on the noun marks the experiencer, and while infinitival complements must share their subject with this experiencer, finite complements may or may not do so; the verb **ɕe** is not used in Aorist or Inferential forms, and the inchoative meaning instead uses **ɣi** ‘come.’

A parallel construction exists with **ɯ-ʁjiz** ‘wish,’ which also combines with **ɣi** to mean ‘feel like/want to X.’ This construction shows the same morphosyntactic patterns as **tɯ-sɯm**, allowing both infinitival and finite complements.

text:
noun!time
The noun ta-ʁafree time can take infinitival complements, in particular when occurring in collocation with existential verbs (§ sec:existential.light.verbs ) as in ( ex:kACe.aRa.maNe ).

exe

[ʁdɯrɟɤt aʑo kɤ-ɕe] a-ʁa maŋe \\
topo 1sg inf -go 1sg. poss -free.time not.exist: sens \\
`I don't have time to go to Gdongbrgyad.' (conversation, 2016-03-20)
exe
summary: The noun **ta-ʁafree** ‘time’ can take infinitival complements, especially when it occurs with existential verbs. In the example, the phrase means ‘I don’t have time to go to Gdongbrgyad,’ showing that ‘time’ can be used with an infinitival clause in this construction.

text:
cause
The noun ɯ-ndʐacause, which is used as a relator noun to indicate the cause or the beneficiary (§ sec:IPN.cause ) with noun phrases, is also attested with finite and infinitive complement clauses, as in ( ex:mWYWkABzu.Wndzxa ). With ergative marking, they can either serve as causal (§ sec:causal.clauses ) or purposive (§ sec:purposive.clauses ) subordinate clauses.

exe

tɕe nɯ [rɟɤdɯm mɯ-ɲɯ-kɤ-βzu] ɯ-ndʐa kɯ tɯ-ci kɯ-mɯɕtaʁ nɯtɕu pjɯ́-wɣ-fkri tɕe tɕe rɟɤdɯm mɤ-βze \\
lnk dem lumps neg - ipfv - inf -make 3sg. poss -reason erg indef. poss -water sbj: pcp -be.cold dem: loc ipfv - inv -melt lnk lnk lumps neg -make[III] \\
`In order to prevent lumps from forming, one melts the flour in cold water [by mixing it] and lumps do not form.' (140428 rJAdWm)
0003882#S8
exe
summary: The noun **ɯ-ndʐa** ‘cause,’ which also functions as a relator noun for cause or beneficiary with noun phrases, is additionally used with finite and infinitive complement clauses. When marked with ergative, these clauses can function either as **causal** or **purposive** subordinate clauses.

subsection: Relative clauses as a complementation strategy
text:
Some inalienably possessed nouns can take subordinate clauses that look like complement clauses but are in fact relatives. A similar situation occurs with complement-taking verbs (§ sec:relative.core.arg, § sec:relative.pretence ).

For instance, in ( ex:tundze.GW.Wdi ), the clause tu-ndze `(the thing that) he eats' is formally a headless finite object relative clause (§ sec:object.relativization ). The head noun tɤ-dismell has no syntactic role in that clause and is not the relativized element. Otherwise, the construction would be nonsensical, its expected meaning being something like `the smell that he eats'. The relation between the prenominal clause and its head in ( ex:tundze.GW.Wdi ) is simply the same as that between a possessor and its possessee (§ sec:gen.possession ), and it is preferable not to analyze here tu-ndze as a complement clause, since its meaning is not `the smell of him eating' (on the ambiguity between finite relative and complement clauses, see § sec:finite.relative.complement.ambiguity ). The precise meaning of this sentence has been ascertained with Tshendzin. The corresponding passage in the Chinese text from which it has been translated is 果酱味招来了一群苍蝇 guǒjiàngwèi zhāolái le yīqún cāngyíngThe smell of the jam attracted a swarm of flies: the adnominal construction in ( ex:tundze.GW.Wdi ) is thus not due to calquing from the original.

exe

[tu-ndze] nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-di nɯ pjɤ-mtsʰɤm-nɯ tɕe tɕe jo-ɣi-nɯ. \\
ipfv -eat dem gen 3sg. poss -smell dem ifr -perceive- pl lnk lnk ifr -come- pl \\
`[The flies] smelled [the jam] that he was eating and came.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh)
0003886#S11
exe

Example ( ex:tumtshia.GW.WXpi ) provides a similar case with a head-internal finite relative. It is obvious here that ɯ-χpi cannot be the relativized element (since the head noun ɕkommuntjac is overt). At the same time, if aʑo ɕkom tu-mtsʰi-a were a complement clause, the expected meaning would be `a story about (why) I am leading this muntjac'.

exe

kɯki [aʑo ɕkom tu-mtsʰi-a] ki ɣɯ ɯ-χpi ci pjɯ-fɕat-a \\
dem. prox 1sg muntjac ipfv -lead- 1sg dem. prox gen 3sg. poss -story indef ipfv -tell- 1sg \\
`I will tell (you) a story about this muntjac that I am leading.' (140512 fushang he yaomo-zh)
0003967#S75
exe

The adnominal clauses in ( ex:tundze.GW.Wdi ) and ( ex:tumtshia.GW.WXpi ) are thus relative clauses used as possessors of inalienable nouns.

With non-finite clauses, given the similarity between participles and infinitives (§ sec:infinitives.participles ), there are cases where deciding whether a clause is a participial relative serving as possessor or an infinitival complement clause is not trivial (on ambiguity between participial clauses and infinitival complements, see § sec:non-finite.relative.complement.ambiguity ).

For instance, in ( ex:biaozhun ), the Chinese borrowing 标准 biāozhǔncriterion takes as possessor the clause(s) tɕʰeme kɯ-pe mɤ-kɯ-pe, whose status is ambiguous. If one analyses the form kɯ-pe as a subject participle (§ sec:subject.participles ), tɕʰeme [kɯ-pe] [mɤ-kɯ-pe] can be seen as two post-nominal participial relative clauses in apposition sharing the same head noun, implying a translation `the criterion (distinguishing between) good and bad women'. If on the other hand kɯ-pe is analyzed as a stative infinitive (§ sec:velar.inf ), the subordinative clauses are infinitival complements, and the translation would rather be `criterion (by which one judges whether) a woman is good or bad'. In this particular case, since both syntactic analyses are meaningful, the fact that the postclausal noun is a Chinese borrowing makes it difficult to reliably use elicitation to distinguish between the two possibilities (for instance, by testing whether a dynamic intransitive verb would rather have a kɤ- prefixed form in this context).

exe

[tɕʰeme kɯ-pe mɤ-kɯ-pe] nɯ ɣɯ koŋla ʑo ɯ-<biaozhun> ɲɯ-ŋu \\
woman?-be.good neg -?-be.good dem gen really emph 3sg. poss -criterion sens -be \\
`It is [one of the] criteria [by which one judges whether] a woman is good or bad.' (thaXtsa 2002)
exe

Tests can be applied to non-finite adnominal clauses occurring with tɯ-tɕʰainformation, news. This noun, in addition to finite complement clauses (§ sec:nouns.speech.complement ), is compatible with non-finite clauses in kɯ- or kɤ- as in ( ex:jAkWGe.WtCha ). The fact that non-stative intransitive verbs in this construction have kɯ- rather than kɤ- however ( jɤ-kɯ-ɣe instead of? jɤ-kɤ-ɣe ) shows that these clauses are participial clauses, and therefore that they should be analyzed as relative clauses like ( ex:tundze.GW.Wdi ) and ( ex:tumtshia.GW.WXpi ) above, despite what the meaning of this construction suggests. The constituent [a-tɕɯ tɤ-kɯ-ɣe] ɯ-tɕʰa in ( ex:jAkWGe.WtCha ) thus literally means `news about my son who came'.

exe

[a-tɕɯ jɤ-kɯ-ɣe] ɣɯ ɯ-tɕʰa ja-ɣɯt\\
1sg. poss -son aor - sbj: pcp -come[II] gen 3sg. poss -news aor:3 -bring\\
`S/he came to tell [me/you] that my son came.' (elicited)
exe
summary: The passage argues that some adnominal clauses with inalienably possessed nouns are not complement clauses but relative clauses functioning as possessors. In examples with finite and non-finite clauses, the head noun is not the relativized element; instead, the clause modifies the noun in a possessor-like relation, though in some non-finite cases the analysis is ambiguous because both a participial relative and an infinitival complement yield plausible meanings.

text:
speech error!complement clause complement clause!speech error
Example ( ex:turAt.kAsthWt.CWNgW ) presents an interesting case of incorrect exchange of prefix between the verb in the complement clause and the complement-taking verb.

Since the complement-taking verb stʰɯtfinish is embedded in a temporal clause in ɕɯŋgɯbefore, it would be expected to be in the Imperfective (§ sec:precedence.CWNgW ), while its complement verb should either be in the bare infinitive or the velar infinitive as in ( ex:kArAt.tusthWt.CWNgW ) (§ sec:phasal.complements ).

exe

$ $[ɯʑo kɯ [nɯra tu-rɤt] kɤ-stʰɯt] ɕɯŋgɯ tɕe \\
3sg erg dem: pl ipfv -draw inf -finish before lnk \\
`Before he had finished drawing it.' (160718 huashetianzu-zh)
0006123#S27
exe

exe

[ɯʑo kɯ [nɯra kɤ-rɤt] tu-stʰɯt] ɕɯŋgɯ tɕe \\
3sg erg dem: pl inf -draw ipfv -finish before lnk \\
Correction of ( ex:turAt.kAsthWt.CWNgW )
exe

In ( ex:turAt.kAsthWt.CWNgW ) however, the complement-taking verb is in Velar Infinitive form and the complement verb in the Imperfective, the opposite of the correct form ( ex:kArAt.tusthWt.CWNgW ).

Tshendzin has no hesitation to recognize ( ex:turAt.kAsthWt.CWNgW ) as a speech error, which is nevertheless unusual enough to deserve mention.
summary: The passage discusses an unusual speech error in which the prefixes of a complement-taking verb and its complement verb are exchanged. In the expected construction, the verb meaning “finish” in a temporal clause before “before” should be in the Imperfective, while the complement verb should appear in infinitival form; instead, the attested example reverses these forms. Tshendzin identifies the result as a speech error, noting that it is unusual enough to be worth mentioning.

text:
This chapter, based on, discusses multiclausal constructions other than (headless or noun modifying) relative clauses, complement clauses in core argument function and clauses involving the expression of degree (discussed in chapters chap:relatives, chap:complement.clauses and chap:degree, respectively). Some relative and complement clauses in essive function, or with oblique cases, are however discussed in this chapter (§ sec:marked.subordinate ).

The constructions treated in this chapter involve different degrees of subordination, from highly dependent (§ sec:marked.subordinate ) to loose parataxis (§ sec:coordination ). This section provides an overview of the criteria that can be used to classify subordination subtypes in Japhug.
summary: This chapter discusses multiclausal constructions other than relative clauses, core-argument complement clauses, and degree clauses, though some relative and complement clauses in essive or oblique function are included here. The constructions range in degree of subordination from highly dependent structures to loose parataxis, and the section gives an overview of criteria for classifying subordination subtypes in Japhug.

text:
Some subordinate clauses can be distinguished from main clauses by overt morphological marking. Four types of overt marks of subordination can be distinguished.

First, converbs (§ sec:inf.converb ), found in particular in temporal (§ sec:immediate.subsequence, § sec:simultaneity ) and manner (§ sec:manner.converbs ) clauses), being non-finite forms, cannot serve as the predicate of main clauses.

Second, verb-initial reduplication (§ sec:redp.protasis ) and the prefix ɯ- in non-interrogative clauses (§ sec:interrogative.W ) are non-ambiguous markers of the protasis of a conditional construction (§ sec:real.conditional ).

Third, relator nouns with prenominal complements (§ sec:complement.taking.nouns ) or prenominal relatives (§ sec:Wspa.relative ) in absolutive, locative or ergative form are used to build temporal (§ sec:subsequence.neutral, § sec:temporal.reference ) and causality (§ sec:causal.clauses, § sec:purposive.clauses ) clauses.

Fourth, postpositions can either contribute to subordination marking in combination with relator nouns (for instance, the ergative in causal clauses, § sec:causal.clauses ), or serve on their own as subordinating markers, as in the case of the locative position in temporal clauses ( ex:jari.nWtCu, see also § sec:temporal.clauses ).

exe

a-ʁi kɯ [jɤ-ari] nɯtɕu tɕe, nɤkinɯ, qapi jo-rɤmbɯmbri qʰe, tɕendɤre nɯ jo-nɯɴqʰu-j qʰe, tɕe kʰa jɤ-azɣɯt-i \\
1sg. poss -younger.sibling erg aor -go[II] dem: loc loc filler white.stone ifr -drop.while.going lnk lnk dem ifr -follow- 1pl lnk lnk house aor -reach- 1pl \\
` When he$_i$ went (to the forest), our younger brother$_i$ dropped white stones$_j$ one by one on the way as he was going, and we followed them$_j$ and found our way home.' (160701 poucet2)
0006155#S49
exe

Example ( ex:jari.nWtCu ) also illustrates that in addition to the markers listed above, word order and case marking are important additional clues of subordinating status. The subject a-ʁi `my younger brother' takes ergative case following the transitive verb jo-rɤmbɯmbri `he dropped them one by one on the way' (§ sec:long.distance.kW ), instead of absolutive case as would be expected if it belonged to the subordinate clause jɤ-ari nɯtɕu `when he went there' (since jɤ-ari is intransitive), showing that this clause is embedded within the main clause. In some cases the case marking mismatch is the only evidence that a clause is subordinate (§ sec:embedded.clause ).
summary: The passage explains that subordinate clauses can be identified by several overt morphological markers: converbs, which are non-finite forms and cannot function as main-clause predicates; verb-initial reduplication and the prefix ɯ- in non-interrogative clauses, which mark conditional protases; relator nouns with prenominal complements or relatives, used for temporal and causal clauses; and postpositions, which may either combine with relator nouns or independently mark subordination. It also notes that word order and case marking can provide additional evidence of subordination, as in an example where ergative case on the subject shows that a clause is embedded rather than main.

text:
Correlative constructions comprise two or more clauses with a parallel syntactic structure, each obligatorily marked by overt coordinating markers. With the exception of correlative relatives (§ sec:interrogative.relative ), correlative constructions are not very widespread in Japhug: usually only one of the two clauses has obligatory marking.

The correlative additive focus markers ri and tɕi (§ sec:ri.additive, § sec:addition.clauses ) are one of the clearest cases of correlative constructions. As shown by ( ex:pjWnWCWrNYJo.pjWNgra ), they follow the noun phrase on which they have scope, and the rest of the clause, including the verb, can be repeated as in ( ex:WmdoR.tCi.mAkWnaXtCWG ).

exe

ʑakastaka ɯ-mdoʁ tɕi mɤ-kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ ɣɤʑu, ɯ-tsʰɯɣa tɕi mɤ-kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ ɣɤʑu. \\
each.his.own 3sg. poss -colour also neg - sbj: pcp -be.the.same exist: sens 3sg. poss -shape also neg - sbj: pcp -be.the.same exist: sens \\
`Each of them (species of starfishes) has its own different colour and different shape.' (180421 haixing)
0006113#S15
exe

Other examples of correlative construction include the relator noun ɯ-jɯjaalong with with incremental initial reduplication (§ sec:redp.gradual.increase ) in the second clause (§ sec:simultaneity ).
summary: Correlative constructions in Japhug consist of two or more clauses with parallel syntactic structure, each marked by an overt coordinating marker, though they are not very common except in correlative relatives. One clear example is the additive focus markers **ri** and **tɕi**, which follow the noun phrase they scope over and can be accompanied by repetition of the rest of the clause, including the verb. The passage also notes other correlative constructions, such as those involving the relator noun **ɯ-jɯja** and incremental initial reduplication in the second clause.

text:
Japhug has quite a few periphrastic TAME categories, combining a verb in the Imperfective or the Factual with a copula (§ sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME, § sec:irrealis.periphrastic, § sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic, § sec:proximative.periphrastic ). It is common to observe chains of verbs in the Imperfective sharing a single copula. For instance, in ( ex:pjWnWCWrNYJo.pjWNgra ), the copula ɲɯ-ɕti in the Sensory has scope over two verbs, pjɯ-nɯɕɯrɲɟo and pjɯ-ŋgra. Such chains can be long, and comprise more than ten verbs in the Imperfective (example ex:chain.pjANu, § sec:ipfv.periphrastic.TAME ).

exe

tɕeri qartsɯ tɕe tɕe ɯ-jwaʁ nɯ pjɯ-nɯɕɯrɲɟo tɕe pjɯ-ŋgra ɲɯ-ɕti. \\
lnk winter loc lnk 3sg. poss -leaf dem ipfv -redden lnk ipfv - acaus:cause.to.fall sens -be. aff \\
`In winter, its leaves redden and fall.' (14-sWNgWJu)
0003506#S10
exe

In ( ex:CtunWrdoR.tundze ), the copula ɲɯ-ŋu occurs two times: the first occurrence has scope over one verb ( tu-nɯ-ɬoʁ ), and the second one over two verbs ( ɕ-tu-nɯrdoʁ and tu-ndze ).

exe

nɯnɯ la-ɕlu-nɯ cʰo la-lɣa-nɯ tɕe tɕe qandʐe tu-nɯ-ɬoʁ ɲɯ-ŋu. tɕe nɯ ɕ-tu-nɯrdoʁ tɕe tu-ndze ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
dem aor:3 -plough comit aor:3 -dig lnk lnk earthworm ipfv - auto -come.out sens -be lnk dem tral - ipfv -collect lnk ipfv -eat[III] sens -be \\
`When [people] plough and dig the earth, earthworms come out, and crows go (into the fields) and pick [the earthworms] and eat them (one by one).' (140511 qajdo kW qandzxe tundze)
0003955#S20
exe

Although all verbs in examples ( ex:pjWnWCWrNYJo.pjWNgra ) and ( ex:CtunWrdoR.tundze ) are finite, only the last verb of the chain can be considered to be fully conjugated, while the non-final verbs ( pjɯ-nɯɕɯrɲɟo in ex:pjWnWCWrNYJo.pjWNgra and ɕ-tu-nɯrdoʁ in ( ex:CtunWrdoR.tundze ) lack an element of their conjugation. For this reason, it is possible to consider that the last member of a periphrastic TAME chain is the main verb, and that all preceding clauses are subordinate.
summary: Japhug has several periphrastic TAME constructions in which an Imperfective or Factual verb combines with a copula, and these can extend across long chains of verbs sharing a single copula. In such chains, the copula may have scope over multiple verbs, but only the final verb is fully conjugated; earlier verbs lack part of their conjugation. This supports analyzing the last member of the chain as the main verb and the preceding clauses as subordinate.

text:
Embedded clauses such as tɕʰi a-tɤ-fse-a in ( ex:atAfsea.mAwGmtoa ) lack any formal subordinating morphology. However, their subordinating status is shown by the fact that they occur inside the main clause, located between two constituents: in ( ex:atAfsea.mAwGmtoa ), the embedded clause is preceded by the transitive subject tɤɕime kɯ (which is not an argument of that clause) and followed by the main verb.

exe

tɤɕime kɯ [tɕʰi a-tɤ-fse-a] tɕe mɤ́-wɣ-mto-a kɯ \\
princess erg what irr - pfv -be.like- 1sg lnk neg - inv -see: fact - 1sg sfp \\
`What should I do [in order] not to be seen by the princess?' (140505 xiaohaitu-zh)
0003921#S77
exe

In ( ex:tCe.WmYaR.YAznAmbju ), the clause ɯ-mɲaʁ ɲɤ-z-nɤmbju is inserted between the main verb pjɤ-mto and its transitive subject rɟɤlpu nɯ kɯ. This transitive subject is coreferent with the 3sg possessor of ɯ-mɲaʁ, object of the verb ɲɤ-z-nɤmbju `it dazzled it' in the embedded clause, and the presence of the ergative kɯ shows that it receives its case marking from the main verb rather than from the embedded subordinate clause.

exe

tɤ-wi nɯ kɯ tɤ-ri nɯ rɟɤlpu ɯ-tɕʰaʁla scʰiz pjɤ-k-ɤz-nɤndɯndo-ci tɕe, rɟɤlpu nɯ kɯ [ɯ-mɲaʁ ɲɤ-z-nɤmbju] ʑo pjɤ-mto tɕe, \\
indef. poss -grandmother dem erg indef. poss -thread dem king 3sg. poss -yard approx. loc ifr. ipfv - peg - prog -take.here.and.there- peg lnk king dem erg 3sg. poss -eye ifr - caus -be.bright emph ifr -see lnk \\
`The old woman was taking the (well-spun) thread$_i$ here and there in the yard of the king, and the king$_j$ saw it$_i$ as it$_i$ dazzled his$_j$ eyes (i.e. it$_i$ was so well spun that it was dazzling bright).' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S129
exe

Unmarked embedding is also found in serial verb constructions. In ( ex:ki.tuste.luznaRje ), the manner clause with studo like (§ sec:svc.similative.verb ) occurs between the instrument ɯ-jaʁ kɯ `with its paw' and lu-z-naʁje `it reaches into it'. The presence of the causative prefix z- indicates that the instrumental phrase is selected by lu-z-naʁje (§ sec:sig.caus.instrumental ), not by tu-ste.

exe

tɕe ɯ-jaʁ kɯ [ki tu-ste] lu-z-naʁje ɲɯ-ŋu \\
lnk 3sg. poss -hand erg dem: prox ipfv -do.like[III] ipfv -reach.into[III] sens -be \\
`[The cat] reaches with its paw [into the whole] like this.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S47
exe

The examples ( ex:atAfsea.mAwGmtoa ), ( ex:tCe.WmYaR.YAznAmbju ) and ( ex:ki.tuste.luznaRje ) above illustrate that unmarked embedded finite clauses have a considerable variety of semantic functions, including purposive clauses (§ sec:purposive.clauses ), temporal clauses of simultaneity (§ sec:simultaneity ) and manner clauses (§ sec:svc.manner ), respectively.
summary: The passage explains that some embedded finite clauses in the language lack overt subordinating morphology, but their subordinate status is shown by their position inside the main clause and by the fact that surrounding constituents are selected by the main verb rather than by the embedded clause. It gives examples showing that such unmarked embedding can express purposive, temporal, and manner relations, including in serial verb constructions.

text:
In Japhug, as in Tshobdun, we find serial verb constructions comprising two verbs sharing TAME category and subject (and often, but not in all cases, objects).

One of the verbs expresses the main action, and the other describes the manner in which the action is performed (§ sec:svc.manner ). Unlike Tshobdun, there is no constraint in Japhug against inserting a linker such as tɕe between the two verbs in the serial construction, as shown by example ( ex:ki.tuste.tuZmbri ). This construction cannot be considered monoclausal, and thus differs from what is usually understood as `serial verb constructions' in many languages, but I keep Sun's terminology for want of a better term.

exe

[ɯ-ʁar nɯ ki tu-ste] tɕe [tu-ʑ-mbri] ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -wing dem dem. prox ipfv -do.like[III] lnk ipfv - caus -make.noise sens -be \\
`[The grasshopper] makes noise by [moving] its wings like this.' (26-kWrNukWGndZWr)
0003672#S72
exe

In some cases, embedding of the first clause into the second one can occur (§ sec:embedded.clause ), suggesting that a syntactic hierarchy exists between them.

There are three main types of serial verb constructions in Japhug, involving deideophonic verbs (§ sec:svc.deideophonic ), similative verbs (§ sec:svc.deideophonic ) and bipartite verbs (treated in § sec:bipartite in another chapter). Constructions that are superficially similar to serial verb constructions but better analyzed as finite complement clauses are discussed in § sec:svc.finite.agreement.
summary:
Japhug has serial verb constructions in which two verbs share the same TAME category and subject, and often also the object; typically one verb expresses the main action and the other the manner of performing it. Unlike Tshobdun, Japhug allows a linker such as *tɕe* between the verbs, and some cases even show embedding of the first clause into the second, so these constructions are not fully monoclausal.

The text identifies three main types of such constructions: those involving deideophonic verbs, similative verbs, and bipartite verbs. It also notes that some superficially similar patterns are better analyzed as finite complement clauses.

text:
When none of the four set of criteria described above (§ sec:correlative.clauses, § sec:periphrastic.subordination, § sec:embedded.clause, § sec:svc ) are applicable, there remain a residue of clauses in parataxis or linked by tɕe (§ sec:tCe.postposition ) or qʰe, without a clear subordinating hierarchy.

In ( ex:pjWsat.juGWt ), all verbs are in the Imperfective, without correlative element (§ sec:correlative.clauses ), final copula (§ sec:periphrastic.subordination ) or embedding (§ sec:embedded.clause ). The verbs pjɯ-sat `it kills it' and ju-ɣɯt `it brings it' share the same subject and object, but unlike in serial constructions (§ sec:svc ) where both verbs express two aspects of the same action, pjɯ-sat and ju-ɣɯt refer to two actions occurring one after the other.

exe

tɕe ɯ-pɕi ju-ɕe tɕe, [ci ci pɣɤtɕɯ pjɯ-sat ju-ɣɯt], [ci ci βʑɯ pjɯ-sat ju-ɣɯt], [ci ci qaɲi ra pjɯ-sat tɕe ju-ɣɯt]. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -outside ipfv -go lnk one one bird ipfv -kill ipfv -bring one one mouse ipfv -kill ipfv -bring one one mole pl ipfv -kill lnk ipfv -bring \\
`(When her kittens are hungry), [the cat mother] goes out and sometimes kills a bird and brings it, sometimes kills a mouse and brings it, sometimes kills a mole or something and brings it [to them].' (21-lWLU)
0003576#S36
exe

Simple coordination and parataxis can both express temporal subsequence (§ sec:subsequence.neutral ) as in ( ex:pjWsat.juGWt ) between the first clause and all the following ones, and between pjɯ-sat and ju-ɣɯt in each of the three clauses. Parataxis can also indicate disjunction (§ sec:disjunction.clauses ), for instance between the three pairs of clauses (in squared brackets) in ( ex:pjWsat.juGWt ).

Coordination with tɕe and qʰe can in addition be used to indicate logical consequence (§ sec:consequence ) and neutral addition (§ sec:neutral.addition ).
summary: The passage says that when clauses do not fit criteria for correlative, periphrastic, embedded, or serial constructions, they may be left in parataxis or linked by tɕe or qʰe without a clear subordinating hierarchy. In the example, verbs in the imperfective share the same subject and object but denote successive actions rather than two aspects of one action, and the structure can express temporal sequence, disjunction, logical consequence, or neutral addition.

text:
tail-head linkage
Tail-head linkage is a type of linking strategy whereby an element (generally the verb) of one clause is repeated in the following clause (see for a typological overview). Such constructions are well-attested in languages of Western Sichuan (see for instance ). In Japhug, they occur predominantly with parataxis and loose temporal succession linking with finite clauses coordinated by linkers such as tɕe or qʰe. It is a very common strategy both for ensuring narrative coherence, and providing time for the storyteller to prepare the narration of the following events without hesitating and using speech fillers (§ sec:fillers ).

Tail-head linkage can involve an entire sentence, as in ( ex:YAmbinW.x2 ), but often leaves out a constituent: for instance in ( ex:sWNgW.zW.joCe2 ) the intransitive subject tɤ-pɤtso nɯnɯ is not repeated.

exe

[nɯ-me stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ ɲɤ-mbi-nɯ], tɕe [nɯ-me stu kɯ-xtɕi nɯ ɲɤ-mbi-nɯ tɕe], tɕe tɕʰeme nɯ to-nɯmbrɤpɯ, \\
3pl. poss -daughter most sbj: pcp -be.small dem ifr -give- pl lnk 3pl. poss -daughter most sbj: pcp -be.small dem ifr -give- pl lnk lnk girl dem ifr -ride \\
`They gave [him] their daughter (in marriage), and as they gave [him] their daughter (in marriage), the girl mounted [a horse].' (2002 qaCpa)

exe

tɕendɤre [tɤ-pɤtso nɯnɯ li sɯŋgɯ zɯ jo-ɕe]. [sɯŋgɯ zɯ jo-ɕe] tɕe tɕendɤre, pʰaʁrgot nɯ kɯ tɤ-pɤtso nɯ pa-mto tɕe \\

`The boy went again into the forest, and as he went into the forest, the boar saw the boy.' (140428 yonggan de xiaocaifeng-zh)
0003886#S218

In some cases, the verb form is slightly different in the repeated clause. For instance in ( ex:kowGsAmdzWnW.kasAmdzW ), the verb form in the first clause is in inverse configuration 3$'$ 3pl (the TAME is probably Inferential, though in this context the contrast between Inferential and Aorist is neutralized, § sec:allomorphy.inv ) while that in the second clause is in direct configuration 3sg. Aorist is used in the second clause of ( ex:kowGsAmdzWnW.kasAmdzW ) to mark a point of temporal reference, § sec:aor.temporal, § sec:temporal.reference.

summary: Tail-head linkage is a strategy in which an element, usually the verb, from one clause is repeated at the start of the next clause. In Japhug, it is common in paratactic and loosely sequential narration with finite clauses linked by particles such as *tɕe* or *qʰe*, and it helps maintain narrative coherence while giving the storyteller time to continue speaking. The repeated material may be a full clause or only part of it, and the repeated verb can sometimes appear in a slightly different form to mark temporal reference.

text: Conditional constructions are biclausal, comprising a subordinate clause (the protasis) and a main clause (the apodosis). The apodosis describes a result which takes place if the condition in the protasis is fulfilled. Depending on whether the protasis is a fact or a hypothetical situation, several types of conditionals can be distinguished: real, concessive, counterfactual and hypothetical. Some temporal clauses, such as iterative coincidence (§ sec:iterative.coincidence.clause ), can also be considered to be a subtype of conditionals, but are treated in § sec:temporal.clauses.
summary: Conditional constructions consist of two clauses: a subordinate protasis expressing the condition and a main apodosis expressing the result that follows if the condition is met. The passage distinguishes several types of conditionals based on whether the protasis refers to a real fact or a hypothetical situation, including real, concessive, counterfactual, and hypothetical conditionals. It also notes that some temporal clauses, such as iterative coincidence clauses, can be viewed as a subtype of conditionals, though they are treated separately.

text:
conditional clause
In real conditional constructions, the verb in the protasis has either initial reduplication (§ sec:redp.protasis ) or the Interrogative ɯ- prefix (§ sec:interrogative.W.function ) and is followed the additive postposition nɤ (§ sec:additive.nA ), as shown by ( ex:padma.tWtWNu.nA ) and ( ex:mWmAjAtWGWt.nA ) on the one hand, and ( ex:Wtope.nA ) on the other without semantic difference.

Non-past TAME categories, in particular the Factual Non-Past ( ex:padma.tWtWNu.nA ) or the Sensory ( ex:YWYWmaR.nA ) are used when the protasis concern a present state or an ongoing action whose truth value is known to the speaker, as in ( ex:padma.tWtWNu.nA ) and ( ex:YWYWmaR.nA ).

exe

[pɤnmawombɤr tɯ tɯ-ŋu] nɤ, pɯ-ta-sɯxɕɤt nɯ nɯ-ndɯn ra \\
anthr cond 2-be: fact add aor -1 2-teach dem imp -read be.needed: fact \\
`If you (really) are Padma 'Od'bar, recite [the mantra] that I have taught you.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

exe

[tɯrme ɲɯ ɲɯ-maʁ] nɤ, a-ku ɲɯ-sɤpʰar-a ŋu tɕe tɕe, jɤ-pʰɣo \\
person cond sens -not.be add 1sg. poss -head ipfv -shake- 1sg be: fact lnk lnk imp -flee \\
`If (the thing in the tree) is not a man, I will shake my head, and you (had better) flee.' (khu 2012)
0004085#S48

The Aorist in the protasis (§ sec:aor.cond ) can express potential future events ( ex:mWmAjAtWGWt.nA ), but also generic conditions ( ex:mWmAnWwGsWqhrWt.tCe ).

exe

[tɯrɟɯ laχtɕʰa cʰo rŋɯl ra mɯ mɤ-jɤ-tɯ-ɣɯt] nɤ, nɤkinɯ, pjɯ-ta-sat ŋu \\

`If you do not bring goods and money, we will kill you.' (160706 poucet6)
0006109#S101

The Inferential occurs in the two protases in ( ex:Wtope.nA ) in a generic context to specifically express a condition which only becomes testable after a special procedure (removing bandages) has been applied, when the action or change of state in the protasis cannot be directly observed.

kɯɕnɯ-rʑaʁ jamar tɤ-tsu tɕe tɕe pjɯ-rle tɕe tu-rtoʁ tɕe, tɕe ɯ-tó-pe nɤ tɕe nɯ ma mɤ-ra,
ɯ-mɯ́-to-pe nɤ tɕe li tu-xtɕɤr ŋu. \\

`After seven days, [the doctor] unties [the splint] and looks, if [the fracture] has healed, [the splint] is not needed anymore, if it has not improved, [the doctor] attaches [the splint] again.' (140426 laxthab)

Although the postposition coming after the verb in the protasis is almost always nɤ as in the examples above, this is not a requirement; for instance in ( ex:mWmAnWwGsWqhrWt.tCe ) the form mɯ mɤ-nɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-qʰrɯt `if one does not scrape it with it' in the protasis is rather followed by qʰe.

tɕe [tɯ-ndzrɯ kɯ mɯ mɤ-nɯ́-wɣ-sɯ-qʰrɯt] qʰe mɯ́j-ŋgra. \\
lnk genr. poss -nail erg cond neg - aor - inv - caus -scrape lnk neg: sens - acaus:cause.to.fall \\
`[Nits] (are firmly attached and) will not detach unless one scrapes them with one's nail.' (21-mdzadi)
0003578#S62

In reduplicated conditional forms, the negative prefix mɯ- has the special form mɯ mɤ- (§ sec:neg.allomorphs ), while no such vowel alternation occurs with negative prefixes in Interrogative forms ( ɯ-mɯ́-to-pe in ex:Wtope.nA ) or suppletive negative verbs ( ex:YWYWmaR.nA ).

Apart from reduplicated conditional and Interrogative, a third way of marking the protasis in a real conditional construction is the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.conditional ). While the Irrealis usually marks counterfactuals (§ sec:counterfactual ) conditionals, it also occurs in real conditionals as in ( ex:anWYatnW.tCe ) and ( ex:atAngo.tCe ), in particular in the case of possible but not highly frequent events. The Irrealis only very rarely followed by nɤ, and most commonly occurs with the linker tɕe.

exe

a-nɯ-ɲat-nɯ tɕe tɯ-tɕʰa nɤ tɯ-tɕʰa nɯ, nɤki <dianxian> ɯ-taʁ, qʰe sɯku ɯ-taʁ nɯtɕu tu-nɯna-nɯ tɕe \\
irr - pfv -be.tired- pl lnk one-pair lnk one-pair dem electric.wire 3sg. poss -on lnk treetop 3sg. poss -on dem loc ipfv -rest- pl lnk \\
`If/Whenever [the swallows] are tired (from flying), they rest in pairs on electrical wires or on trees.' (03-mWrmWmbjW-zh)
0003382#S50
exe

exe

kʰɯna nɯ a-tɤ-ngo tɕe tɕendɤre ɲɯ-sɲu kɯ-fse ɲɯ-ŋu \\
dog dem irr - pfv -be.ill lnk lnk ipfv -be.mad sbj: pcp -be sens -be \\
`If a dog gets ill (from rabbies), it will become like mad.' (29-chWsYu)

summary: Real conditional protases are marked either by initial reduplication or by the Interrogative ɯ- prefix, usually followed by the additive postposition nɤ, though this postposition is not obligatory. Non-past TAME forms are used when the protasis refers to a present state or ongoing action known to the speaker, while the Aorist can express future or generic conditions, and the Inferential is used when the condition is not directly observable and becomes testable only after a special procedure. A third marker, the Irrealis, can also appear in real conditionals, especially for possible but infrequent events, and it more commonly occurs with tɕe than with nɤ.

Necessary condition (`only if') can be expressed using the postposition kóʁmɯzonly after (§ sec:temporal.postpositions, § sec:immediate.subsequence ) as connecting element between the two clauses. The protasis selects the Irrealis, the apodosis is in the Imperfective and the whole construction is under the scope of the modal verb rabe needed as in ( ex:nWkoRmWznA.only.if ) and ( ex:nWkoRmWznA.only.if2 ).

`It is only if all [of the pigs] get to eat (hogwash) that they will all grow fat.' (i.e. a person has to be appointed to prevent the pigs from fighting, otherwise the weaker pigs would get nothing to eat).' (160708 paRtshi WkWrWru)

`Nanny goats can bear young and reproduce only if a male goat is present.' (05-qaZo)
0003404#S5

text:
concessive clause
There are three types of concessive conditional constructions: scalar (`even if'), alternative (`whether... or') and universal (`whatever, whenever, wherever etc') in Japhug. These conditional present two morphological commonalities concerning the verb in the protasis.

First, in the majority of cases, this verb takes the Autive prefix -nɯ- § sec:autoben.spontaneous, ), sometimes with emphatic gemination to -nnɯ-. Second, it never takes conditional initial reduplication (§ sec:redp.protasis ) or the Interrogative prefix (§ sec:interrogative.W.function ) unlike the verb in the protasis of real conditionals (§ sec:real.conditional ).
summary: Japhug has three kinds of concessive conditional constructions: scalar (“even if”), alternative (“whether... or”), and universal (“whatever, whenever, wherever,” etc.). In these constructions, the protasis verb usually takes the Autive prefix -nɯ- (sometimes geminated to -nnɯ-), and it never shows conditional initial reduplication or the Interrogative prefix, unlike real conditionals.

text:
scalar concessive conditional
In scalar concessive conditionals, the protasis is followed by the scalar focus marker kɯnɤalso, even (§ sec:kWnA ), and contains a verb in the Past Imperfective ( ex:nWkWGAdi.kWnA ) or the Imperfective ( ex:chWwGnWBlW.kWnA ) with the autive prefix (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ).

exe

tɤ-mtʰɯm ndɤre, [nɯ-kɯ-ɣɤdi pɯ-nɯ-ŋu] kɯnɤ tu-ndze ɕti. \\
indef. poss -meat lnk aor - sbj: pcp -be.smelly pst. ipfv - auto -be also ipfv -eat[III] be. aff: fact \\
`[Crows] eat meat even if it has become smelly.' (22-qajdo)
0003596#S20
exe

exe

[cʰɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-βlɯ] kɯnɤ, tu-nɯt ʁo ŋu ri, ɯ-ʁrɤt nɯ ɲaʁ ʑo qʰe, maka ɲɯ-ɣɤ-mpje mɤ-cʰa. \\
ipfv - inv -burn also ipfv -be.ignited advers be: fact lnk
3sg. poss -charcoal dem be.black: fact emph lnk at.all ipfv - caus -be.warm[III] neg -can: fact \\
Even when one burns it, although it does ignite, its charcoal is black and it does not warm anything. (17-thowum)
0003526#S9
exe
summary: Scalar concessive conditionals use the scalar focus marker **kɯnɤ** ‘also, even’ in the protasis, together with a verb in the **Past Imperfective** or **Imperfective** and the **autive prefix**. The examples show that this construction expresses “even if” meanings, as in cases where an action still occurs despite an unfavorable or unexpected condition.

text:
alternative concessive conditional
Alternative concessive conditional constructions express that the outcome in apodosis will occur irrespective of a list of alternative possibilities, indicated by several protases.

In ( ex:pWnnWNu4 ), each of the protases contains copula pɯ-nɯ-ŋu in Past Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ) Autive (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ) form, and share a single apodosis. In the clause qajɯ kɯ tu-ndze pɯ-nnɯ-ŋu, this copula is combined with the Imperfective verb tu-ndze `it eats it' to build a Periphrastic Past Imperfective construction (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.periphrastic ).

exe

[tɯ-ɕɣa pɯ-kɯ-ɴɢrɯ pɯ-nnɯ-ŋu], [pɯ-kɯ-ɣɤtsɯr pɯ-nnɯ-ŋu] qʰe, [qajɯ kɯ tu-ndze pɯ-nnɯ-ŋu], nɯfse tu-kɯ-mŋɤm pɯ-nnɯ-ŋu], nɯnɯ kɯ wuma ʑo nɯsmɤn. \\
indef. poss -tooth ipfv - sbj: pcp - acaus:break pst. ipfv - auto -be
aor - sbj: pcp -crack pst. ipfv - auto -be lnk
bug erg ipfv -eat[III] pst. ipfv - auto -be
like.that ipfv - sbj: pcp -hurt pst. ipfv - auto -be
dem erg very emph heal: fact \\
`Whether one's tooth is broken, cracked, decayed or whether it simply hurts, he (a particular dentist) treats it very well.' (27-tApGi)
0003706#S132
exe

The presence of a periphrastic TAME category with a copula is not required. In ( ex:kAnWrNgWnW.3 ), the protases contain an Aorist Autive verb form kɤ-nɯ-rŋgɯ-nɯ.

[stɤmku kɯ-fse kɤ-nɯ-rŋgɯ-nɯ], [sɯku ɯ-pa kɤ-nɯ-rŋgɯ-nɯ], [praʁ-pa kɤ-nɯ-rŋgɯ-nɯ], ɯnɯnɯ nɯ-ŋga ɯ-taʁ pjɯ-ta-nɯ. \\
pasture sbj: pcp -be.like aor - auto -lie.down- pl tree.top 3sg. poss -under aor - auto -lie.down- pl cliff-under sbj: pcp -be.like aor - auto -lie.down- pl dem 3pl. poss -clothes 3sg. poss -on ipfv -put- pl \\
`Whether [travelers] sleep in pastures, under trees or in caves, they put it on their blankets.' (30-mboR)

The alternative is often between the affirmative and negative versions of the same event (polar alternative concession), a meaning close to that of the scalar concessive conditional. In such cases, the conditional constructions has two protases, the first in affirmative form, and the second with the corresponding negative form as in ( ex:panWri.nA ). The same apodosis can be repeated after each protasis.

exe

[tɯ-sɯm pɯ-a<nɯ>ri] nɤ ju-kɯ-ɕe, [mɯ-pɯ-a<nɯ>ri] nɤ ju-kɯ-ɕe pɯ-ra \\

`One had to go whether one liked it or not.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S194
exe

The alternative concessive conditional is one of the few constructions where even transitive verbs such as nɤlaagree occur in the Past Imperfective (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.morphology ). The verb nɤlaagree selects the upwards orientation, as shown by the form to-nɤla `he agreed' in example ( ex:mAkArWsWso.kW.Zo ), § sec:inf.converb.

exe

[pa-n-nɤla] ɕe-a, [mɯ-pa-n-nɤla] nɤ ɕe-a ra \\
pst. ipfv:3 3- auto -agree lnk ipfv:go- 1sg
neg - pst. ipfv:3 - auto -agree lnk ipfv:go- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`I will go whether he agrees or not.' (elicited)
exe

A more concise type of alternative concessive construction shown in ( ex:tanAla.pWnWNu ) avoids repeating the content of the protasis and of the apodosis, and marks the alternative by combining the affirmative ( pɯ-nɯ-ŋu ) and negative ( pɯ-nɯ-maʁ ) copulas after the verb in the protasis.

[ta-nɤla pɯ-nɯ-ŋu pɯ-nɯ-maʁ] ɕe-a ra \\
aor:3 3-agree pst. ipfv - auto -be pst. ipfv - auto -not.be ipfv:go- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`I will go whether he agrees or not.' (elicited)
exe

Another way to indicate alternative concession is the interrogative particle ɕi (§ sec:fsp.interrog ) as in ( ex:pjWnAndAG ).

exe

[nɯŋa ŋu] ɕi, [mbro ŋu] ma, pjɯ-nɤndɤɣ ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl \\
cow be: fact sfp horse be: fact lnk ipfv -be.poisoned sens -be.usually.the.case \\
`Whether it is a cow or a horse, they end up poisoned.' (25-qarmWrwa)

In addition to these constructions, polar alternative concession `whether or not' can be expressed by a construction combining a negative existential verb with biclausal complements, comprising the same verb in bare root form followed by the bare root prefixed with the negative prefix mɤ, as in ( ex:Ce.mACe.tWme ). This unusual construction is discussed in more detail in § sec:bare.inf.negative.

exe

[[ɕe] [mɤ-ɕe] tɯ-me] ma kɤ-nɤma tɯ-cʰa me qʰe naχtɕɯɣ ɕti\\

`[It does not matter] whether you go or not, you are not able to do anything, it amounts to the same.' (elicited)
