summary:
Alternative concessive conditional constructions express that the apodosis holds regardless of a range of alternative protases, often corresponding to meanings like “whether X or Y.” The passage shows that these constructions may use repeated protases with a shared apodosis, can involve periphrastic Past Imperfective forms with a copula or simple verb forms, and often present polar alternatives such as affirmative vs. negative forms of the same event.  

More concise variants avoid repeating the full clauses by pairing affirmative and negative copulas after the protasis, and another strategy uses the interrogative particle ɕi. A special polar construction also expresses “whether or not” by combining a negative existential verb with biclausal complements.

text:
universal concessive conditional
Universal concessive conditional constructions comprise a protasis with an interrogative pronoun (in free-choice indefinite function, § sec:interrogative.indef, § sec:headless.relatives.quantification ) and a main verb in the Aorist or Past Imperfective. In addition, the autive (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ) occurs either in the protasis, with emphatic reduplication as ( ex:cai.tAwGnWBzWBzu ) or ( ex:tChi.pWnWfsAfse.Zo ) or in the main clause as in ( ex:thAjtCu.WRjiz.tAGe ). The emphatic marker ʑo (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ) often follows the subordinate clause.

garlic dem lnk 3sg. poss -fragrance really emph be.tasty: fact lnk what dish aor - inv - auto - emph make emph ipfv -exist be.needed: fact \\
`Garlic has a nice smell, (...), whatever dish one prepares, there has to be [garlic] (in it).' (07-kWmCku)

tɕʰomba tɕe [tʰɤjtɕu ɯ-ʁjiz tɤ-ɣe] qʰe ju-nnɯ-ɣi ɕti ma \\
cold lnk when 3sg. poss -wish aor -come[II] lnk ipfv - auto -come be. aff: fact lnk \\
`A cold (the disease) comes whenever it wants (i.e. it occurs spontaneously).' (22-tAmbrWm)
0003600#S7

Universal concessive conditionals are semantically close to correlative relative clauses with free-choice interrogative pronouns (§ sec:interrogative.relative ) such as ( ex:tChi.tWtAstuta ).

First, the verb tɯ tɤ-stu-t-a totalitative initial reduplication (§ sec:totalitative.relatives ), a specificity of relative clauses.

Second, the interrogative pronoun tɕʰi has a different syntactic function in these constructions. In the correlative relative ( ex:tChi.tWtAstuta ), tɕʰi is the relativized element, and serves as direct object of both the verb in the subordinate clause and that in the main clause. See § sec:ditransitive.secundative for an account of the argument structure of the similative verb studo like. In the universal concessive conditionals ( ex:cai.tAwGnWBzWBzu ) and ( ex:tChi.pWnWfsAfse.Zo ), tɕʰi in the subordinate clauses has no syntactic role in the main clause.
summary: Universal concessive conditionals use a protasis with an interrogative pronoun in free-choice indefinite function and a main verb in the Aorist or Past Imperfective; the autive prefix may appear either in the protasis or in the main clause, and the emphatic marker ʑo often follows the subordinate clause. Although they are semantically close to correlative relative clauses with free-choice interrogatives, they differ in that correlative relatives show totalitative initial reduplication and the interrogative pronoun functions as a shared syntactic argument, whereas in universal concessive conditionals it has no syntactic role in the main clause.

text:
counterfactual
In counterfactual constructions, the protasis describes a condition that is known to be false, and the apodosis indicates an outcome that would have occurred if the condition had been true. In Japhug, counterfactual conditionals have strict requirements on TAME marking in both the protasis and the apodosis. The verb in the protasis is in the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis.conditional ), and the Past Imperfective is required in the apodosis even for transitive dynamic verbs (§ sec:pst.ifr.ipfv.apodosis ), as illustrated by ( ex:GWtukWqura.apWNu.pWnApeta ) and ( ex:apWtu.apWNua.pWra ). In a previous publication, I claimed that there were counterfactual constructions with a verb in the Factual Non-Past in the apodosis (example 99), but this was an erroneous interpretation.

text: temporal clause
summary: The passage introduces the term **temporal clause**, which is a clause that expresses a time relation. It serves to locate an event or situation in time relative to another event or reference point.

text:
iterative coincidence
Iterative coincidence is a biclausal construction comprising a temporal subordinate clause ($A$) and a main clause ($B$), expressing that each time the event in $A$ takes place, that in $B$ necessarily follows, and that this has taken place several times in the past. It can be generally translated as `each time $A$ then $B$'. As shown by ( ex:jWjAGenW.Zo ) and ( ex:tWmW.kWkAlAt ), the temporal clause generally takes a verb in the Aorist with initial reduplication (§ sec:iterative.coincidence ) like the protasis of a conditional construction (§ sec:redp.protasis, § sec:real.conditional ), followed by the emphatic marker ʑo (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ).

summary: Iterative coincidence is a biclausal construction with a temporal subordinate clause and a main clause, meaning that whenever the event in the first clause occurs, the event in the second clause necessarily follows, repeated several times in the past. It is often translated as “each time A then B,” and the temporal clause typically uses an Aorist verb with initial reduplication plus the emphatic marker ʑo. In some cases, an unreduplicated Aorist can also express this meaning when the main clause verb is Imperfective.

text:
temporal clause!precedence
Three types of constructions are used to express temporal precedence between the event described in the main clause precedes that of the temporal subordinate clause: neutral precedence, immediate precedence and terminative.

These temporal clauses normally occur before the main clause, hence resulting in a non-iconic temporal relationship between the two clauses, since the first (subordinate) clause describes an event occurring after that in the second one (the main clause).
summary: The passage states that three construction types express temporal precedence between a main clause and a temporal subordinate clause: neutral precedence, immediate precedence, and terminative. These clauses normally appear before the main clause, creating a non-iconic order in which the subordinate clause is placed first even though it refers to a later event than the main clause.

text:
There is only one available construction in Japhug to express that the action of the main occurs before that of the temporal clause without further aspectual specifications: clauses with the postposition ɕɯŋgɯbefore (§ sec:temporal.postpositions ). The verb in ɕɯŋgɯ clauses is required to be in the Imperfective (§ sec:ipfv.temporal ). In ( ex:YWsi.CWNgW ) for instance, replacing the Imperfective form ɲɯ-si by the corresponding Aorist ( nɯ-si ), an infinitive ( kɤ-si or any other finite or non-finite form would result in a utterly agrammatical sentence.

A syntactic error involving a verb in a temporal clause in ɕɯŋgɯbefore is presented in § sec:syntactic.errors.
summary: Japhug has only one construction for expressing that one event happened before another without additional aspectual meaning: clauses with the postposition **ɕɯŋgɯ** ‘before’. In these clauses, the verb must be in the **Imperfective**; using the Aorist, an infinitive, or any other verbal form makes the sentence ungrammatical.

text:
temporal clause!subsequence
Temporal succession can be expressed by simple coordination, the order of the clauses mirroring the temporal sequence of the events they describe (§ sec:coordination ). The present section however focuses on subordinating construction devoted to encoding temporal subsequence between the subordinate clause and the main clause.
summary: Temporal succession can be expressed by simple coordination, with the order of clauses reflecting the order of events. This section, however, focuses on subordinating constructions that specifically encode temporal subsequence between a subordinate clause and a main clause.

text:
The most common way to specify temporal succession between two clauses is to use the locative/temporal relator noun ɯ-qʰuafter, behind (§ sec:other.locative.relator ). The temporal clauses are in finite form, in particular in the Aorist as in ( ex:pWsthWta.Wqhu ) and ( ex:smWntsxWG ).

Temporal succession between two clauses is most commonly expressed with the locative/temporal relator noun **ɯ-qʰu** ‘after, behind’. The temporal clause is finite, typically in the **Aorist**, and ɯ-qʰu may optionally take the linker **tɕe**, locative postpositions, or the adverb **tsa** ‘a little’.  

A rarer alternative is the relator noun **ɯ-mpʰru** ‘after, following’, which can also mark temporal subsequence.

Temporal clauses with the immediate converb (§ sec:immediate.converb ) describe an event immediately followed by the action referred to in the main clause ( ex:tutWlhoR.chWphWtnW ).

Another way to express immediate subsequence is a temporal clause with the temporal postposition ɕimɯmaimmediately after (§ sec:temporal.postpositions ) taking a clause with a verb in the Aorist. By contrast, kóʁmɯz ‘only after’ marks the subordinate-clause event as a prerequisite for the main-clause event, without restricting the tense-aspect-mood category of the subordinate verb.

text:
tense!reference point
Aside from indicating the temporal relation and ordering between the events in the subordinate and the main clauses, temporal clauses can also serve to specify a temporal reference point for the main clause. There are four constructions of this type.

First, one of the functions of the Aorist is precisely to fix a temporal reference, for both past and future events (§ sec:aor.temporal ).

Second, prenominal clauses with temporal relator nouns in 3sg possessive forms such as ɯ-sŋi `the day when...', ɯ-xpa `the year when...', ɯ-raŋ `the time when...' or other ones as in ( ex:pWnWmdarndZi.WGmWr ) can mark the time period when the action in the main clause takes place. These clauses can be formally as a subtype of finite prenominal relative clauses (§ sec:time.relativization ).

exe

[pɯ-nɯmdar-ndʑi] ɯ-ɣmɯr nɯtɕu tɕe mtsʰu nɯ cʰɯmcʰɯm ʑo, tɕe, tɯ-skɤm pjɤ-sɤʑa \\

`In the evening when they jumped [into the lake], the level of the lake started to drop slowly and the lake disappeared' (2003, Nyimawozer 2)
exe

Third, the locative postpositions ri, tɕu and zɯ (§ sec:core.locative ) can also occur with finite clauses, with a temporal meaning even without temporal relator noun as in ( ex:pWkWxtCi.ri ).

exe

ɯnɯnɯtɕu ʁo [tɯʑo pɯ-kɯ-xtɕi] ri rcanɯ, mtɕʰi kɯ-wxtɯ wxti ʑo pɯ-tu. \\

`There, when we were young, there was a huge sea buckthorn.' (140522 Kamnyu zgo)
0004059#S331
exe

Fourth, the temporal postposition jɤzwhen and its variant jɤznɤ (§ sec:temporal.postpositions ) can take finite clauses as in ( ex:pWxtCij.jAz ).

ma [iʑora pɯ-xtɕi-j] jɤz tu-ndza-j mɯ-pɯ-ŋgrɤl ma \\

`When we were little, we did not eat it.' (13-NanWkWmtsWG)

summary: Temporal clauses can do more than indicate the ordering of events: they may also establish a temporal reference point for the main clause. The passage identifies four ways this happens: through the Aorist, through prenominal clauses with temporal relator nouns in 3sg possessive form, through the locative postpositions ri, tɕu, and zɯ with finite clauses, and through the temporal postposition jɤz (and its variant jɤznɤ) with finite clauses.

text:
simultaneity
There are two types of subordinate clauses expressing an ongoing action or event taking place at the same time as that of the main verb without serving as a point of temporal reference, unlike the constructions discussed in § sec:temporal.reference above.

First, finite clauses with the relator nouns ɯ-kʰɯkʰawhile and ɯ-jɯjaalong with, `while' describe events that occur together with, and serve as background to the action of the main clause, as in ( ex:tunWsmAn.WkhWkha ) and ( ex:jurJWG.WkhWkha ). There are no coreference restrictions on the arguments of the subordinate and the main clauses.

exe

tɕendɤre [tu-nɯsmɤn] ɯ-kʰɯkʰa tu-rɤma-nɯ \\
lnk ipfv -treat 3sg -the.same.time ipfv -work- pl \\
[The lepers]$_i$ worked (there) while [the doctor] was treating them$_i$.' (25-khArWm)
0003644#S60

[nɯnɯ ju-rɟɯɣ] ɯ-kʰɯkʰa ɯ-se ku-tsʰi ɲɯ-ɕti. \\

`[The lion] drinks [its prey's]$_i$ blood while it$_i$ is (still) running.' (20-sWNgi)
0003562#S50

The relator ɯ-jɯjaalong with differs from ɯ-kʰɯkʰa in that it implies a simultaneous gradual change of degree in both the event or state of the subordinate clause and that of the main clause. The verb of the subordinate clause is generally in the Perfective (though a few Imperfective forms are also attested), while that of the main clause can be in any TAM form, in particular with incremental initial reduplication (§ sec:redp.gradual.increase ) indicating gradual increase as in ( ex:tAwxti.WjWja ).

exe

[ɯʑo tɤ-wxti] ɯ-jɯja tɕe ɯ-jwaʁ nɯnɯ ɲɯ ɲɯ-ndɯβ ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
3sg aor -be.big 3sg. poss -along lnk 3sg. poss -leaf dem incr ipfv-be.tiny emph sens -be \\
`As it grows big, its leaves become more and more tiny.' (09-mi)
0003466#S15
exe

The clause in ɯ-jɯja, rather than a gradual change of state across time, can indicate change across space, as in ( ex:tAmbro.WjWja ), where tɤ-mbro does not mean that the mountain becomes higher, but rather that the person observing the plants moves higher in the mountain.

exe

zgoku tɤ-mbro ɯ-jɯja nɯ ʑmbri tu-tɯ-ldʑɯz ʑo ŋu \\
mountain aor -be.high 3sg. poss -along dem willow incr - ipfv -be.flexible emph be: fact \\
`The higher [ones goes] in the mountain, the more the [wood] of the willows is flexible.' (07-Zmbri)
0003438#S39
exe
gerund
Second, gerundive clauses (§ sec:gerund.clauses ) are an alternative possibility to indicate a background event or state occurring concurrently with the event of the main clause, as in ( ex:sAznWGmWGmu.kuXse.YWra ), though in some cases gerunds express manner rather than temporal overlap (§ sec:manner.clauses ).

exe

nɯnɯ ɲɯ-nɯɣ-me rɯtɕi, nɯ kɯnɤ ku-χse ɲɯ-ra. tɕe [sɤz-nɯɣ-mɯ ɣmu] ʑo ku-χse ɲɯ-ra. \\
dem ipfv - appl -fear[III] lnk dem also ipfv -feed[III] sens -be.needed lnk ger - appl -fear emph ipfv -feed[III] sens -be.needed \\
`Even though it$_i$ is afraid of it$_j$, it$_i$ has to feed it$_i$, and it$_i$ has to feed it$_i$ while being afraid of it.$_i$ ' (24-ZmbrWpGa)

exe
summary:
The passage describes two kinds of subordinate clauses that express simultaneity without providing a temporal reference point. Finite clauses with the relator nouns ɯ-kʰɯkʰa ‘while’ and ɯ-jɯja ‘along with’ mark background events occurring at the same time as the main clause, with ɯ-jɯja additionally implying gradual simultaneous change in degree or even across space.  

Gerundive clauses are another way to indicate concurrent background events or states, though in some cases they instead express manner rather than temporal overlap.

opportunity

The transitive verb naχtʰɤβseize the opportunity can select as object a finite clause or a participial clause with a similar meaning: in ( ex:YWnWZWB.RaznA ), both constructions redundantly occur.

The postposition ʁazwhile... still, and its variant ʁaznɤ, means roughly ‘while ... still’ or ‘taking the opportunity of ...,’ similar to Chinese 趁着 chènzhe. It takes a finite clause, as in the example ‘They would sew the skin while it was still wet.’  

The transitive verb naχtʰɤβ ‘seize the opportunity’ can also take either a finite clause or a participial clause as its object, with similar meanings; in one example, both constructions appear together redundantly.

text:
serial verb construction
The main function of serial verb constructions (§ sec:svc ) in Japhug is to express manner. The most grammaticalized serial constructions involve deideophonic and similative verbs.

Serial verbs constructions can themselves occur as complements of a single complement-taking verb, resulting in a multiclausal complement (§ sec:multiclausal.complements ).
summary: In Japhug, serial verb constructions mainly serve to express manner. The most grammaticalized serial constructions use deideophonic and similative verbs. These serial verb constructions can also function as complements of a single complement-taking verb, producing a multiclausal complement.

text:
deideophonic derivation
Deideophonic verbs (§ sec:voice.deideophonic ) commonly occur in serial verb constructions. The transitive deideophonic verb nɯdrɯβgore again and again for instance, is only attested in serial construction with tɕʰɯgore, stab as in ( ex:totChW ). The ideophonic verb can either follow ( ex:totChW ) or precede the main verb ( ex:totChW2 ), the latter construction being by far more common.

exe

iɕqʰa srɯnmɯ nɯ to-tɕʰɯ to-nɯdrɯβ tɕe pjɤ-sat \\
the.aforementioned râkshasî dem ifr -gore ifr -repeatedly.gore lnk ifr -kill \\
`[The rhinoceros] gored the râkshasî repeatedly and killed her.' (28-smAnmi)
0004063#S381
exe

exe

srɯnmɯ nɯ to-nɯdrɯβ ʑo to-tɕʰɯ \\
râkshasî dem ifr -repeatedly.gore emph ifr -gore \\
`[The rhinoceros] gored the râkshasî repeatedly and killed her.' (elicited on the basis of ex:totChW )
exe
summary: Deideophonic verbs commonly occur in serial verb constructions. The transitive verb *nɯdrɯβgore* ‘again and again’ is only attested with *tɕʰɯgore* ‘stab’, and the ideophonic verb may either follow or precede the main verb, though the preverbal order is much more common.

text:
similative!verb
The similative verbs studo like and fsebe like I adopt the term ``similative verb'' rather than ``manner deixis verbs'' that I used in previous publications, since these verbs do not express deixis on their own, and require a demonstrative. commonly occur in a serial verb construction to indicate the way in which the action takes place. They are always the first verb of the series.

The ditransitive verb stu (§ sec:ditransitive.secundative ) is found with transitive verbs, and shares its subject and object with them, as shown by ( ex:ki.tuWGstu.pjWGqlWt ) (generic transitive subject) and ( ex:kuWGstuanW ) ( 3pl 1sg ).

exe

[ɯ-ru nɯ ki tú-wɣ-stu] [pjɯ́-wɣ-qlɯt] \\
3sg. poss -stalk dem dem: prox ipfv - inv -do.like ipfv - inv -break \\
`One breaks its stalk like this.' (14-tasa)
0003510#S76
exe

In addition, in some cases it takes the orientation of the other verb ( eastwards in ex:kuWGstuanW ), rather than its intrinsic orientation ( upwards as in ex:ki.tuWGstu.pjWGqlWt ).

exe

[aʑo kɯki ntsɯ kú-wɣ-stu-a-nɯ] tɕe, [kú-wɣ-znɯkʰrɯm-a-nɯ] \\
1sg dem: prox always ipfv - inv -do.like- 1sg - pl lnk ipfv - inv -punish- 1sg - pl \\
`They tortured me like this.' (Gesar)
exe

The demonstratives ki and kɯki in ( ex:ki.tuWGstu.pjWGqlWt ) and ( ex:kuWGstuanW ) are semi-objects that are not shared with the other verb.

With intransitive verbs, fsebe like is used instead of stu. It shares its intransitive subject with the other verb, as shown by ( ex:ki.fsea ) where both fse-a and ndzur-a have 1sg indexation.

exe

aʑo nɯ sŋiɕɤr ʑo kutɕu [ki fse-a] [ndzur-a] ntsɯ ɲɯ-ra tɕe \\
1sg dem night.and.day emph here dem: prox be.like: fact - 1sg stand: fact - 1sg always sens -be.needed like \\
`I have to stand like this night and day.' (The divination, 2002)
0003364#S44
exe

There are cases when fse rather than stu occurs with transitive verbs, and which could superficially appear to be cases of serial verb constructions with transitivity mismatch. In ( ex:chWwGnWchAmdaj ) the transitive verb nɯcʰɤmdadrink with a straw is preceded by fse, with 1pl coreference between the object of the former and the intransitive subject of the latter.

exe

tʰɯ-rgɤz-i, sna nɯ-me-j tɕe [ki tɤ-fse-j] tɕe [cʰɯ́-wɣ-nɯcʰɤmda-j] ɕti \\
aor -be.old- 1pl be.good aor -not.exist- 1pl lnk dem. prox aor -be.like- 1sg lnk ipfv: downstream - inv -drink.with.a.straw- 1sg be. aff: fact \\
`Now that we have become old and useless, we became like this, they drink our [blood] with straws (planted in our back).' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

However, note that although tɤ-fse-j and cʰɯ́-wɣ-nɯcʰɤmda-j share one argument, their TAME category is different, and the two clauses constitute a simple case of coordination rather than a serial verb construction: ki tɤ-fse-j means `we became like this' rather than `(they treated) us like this'. The corresponding genuine serial verb construction is shown by ( ex:ki.tWwGstu.tWGnWchAmda ), where nɯcʰɤmda occurs with stu as expected, and the two verbs have the same person-number configuration and TAME category (like ex:kuWGstuanW and ex:ki.tuWGstu.pjWGqlWt above).

exe

tʰɯ-tɯ-rgɤz tɕe [ki tɯ́-wɣ-stu] [tɯ́-wɣ-nɯcʰɤmda] ɕti tɕe, \\
aor -2-be.old lnk dem. prox 2- inv -do.like: fact 2- inv -drink.with.a.straw: fact be. aff: fact lnk \\
`When you become old, they will drink you (your blood) like this with a straw (planted on your back)' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S58
exe

Some non-deideophonic verbs expressing manner such as nɤxɕɤtdo with force (like its Tshobdun cognate nɐʃeʃet `exert oneself', ) can also be used in a serial verb construction.
summary:
The passage explains that **similative verbs** like *studo* ‘like’ and *fsebe* ‘like’ are used in serial verb constructions to indicate the manner of an action, and they always appear as the first verb in the series. *Studo* is used with transitive verbs and shares subject and object with them, while *fsebe* is used with intransitive verbs and shares the intransitive subject.

It also notes that some apparent mismatches with *fse* and transitive verbs are not true serial verb constructions but rather coordination, because the verbs differ in TAME category. In genuine serial verb constructions, the two verbs match in person-number and TAME, and some other manner verbs can also appear in such constructions.

text: Other verbs of manner can also occur in a serial construction, for instance the distributed action verb amɯzɣɯtbe evenly distributed (examples ex:YAmWzGWt.YWlhoR and ex:YWsAmWzGWt.YWmar, § sec:distributed.amW ) or atelic motion verbs like ŋkewalk ( ex:joNke.joCe, § sec:motion.verbs ) or nɯqambɯmbjomfly (example ex:junWqambWmbjomndZi.junACWCendZi, § sec:distributed.action ).
summary: Other verbs of manner can also appear in serial constructions, including the distributed-action verb **amɯzɣɯt** ‘evenly distributed’ and atelic motion verbs such as **ŋke** ‘walk’ and **nɯqambɯmbjo** ‘fly’. These examples show that serial constructions are not limited to a single verb type but can also involve verbs describing manner or motion.

text:
simultaneity
Serial verb constructions can be used to describe a secondary action simultaneous with the main action, optionally marked with the emphatic ʑo (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ) as pjɤ-sŋur `it was snoring' in ( ex:pjAsNur.Zo.pjAnWZWB ).

exe

pjɤ-sŋur ʑo pjɤ-nɯʑɯβ ɕti ma, maka ʑo mɯ-pjɤ-sɯχsɤl. \\
ifr. ipfv -snore emph ipfv. ifr -sleep be. aff: fact lnk at.all emph neg - ifr -realize \\
`[The aquatic monster] was snoring in its sleep, and did not notice anything.' (140508 benling gaoqiang de si xiongdi-zh)
0003935#S185
exe
summary: Serial verb constructions can express a secondary action that occurs simultaneously with the main action, and this is sometimes optionally marked with the emphatic particle ʑo. In the example, the monster is described as snoring while asleep, and it does not notice anything.

text:
degree
Serial constructions can also describe the degree, intensity or extent of an action (§ sec:degree.svc ), even for non-gradable predicates. In these constructions, the verb describing the main action or state is in the first position, and a stative verb of degree (such as arɕobe finished, tɕʰombe too much or rtaʁbe enough) occurs in second position, as in ( ex:nWsinW.narConW ).

exe

wuma ʑo kɯ-tso nɯra nɯ-si-nɯ nɯ-arɕo-nɯ ɕti \\
really emph sbj: pcp -understand dem: pl aor -die- pl aor -be.finished- pl be. aff: fact \\
`The [elders] who knew [traditional stories] really well have all died.' (conversation, 2016-03-20)
exe
summary: Serial constructions can express the degree, intensity, or extent of an action, including with non-gradable predicates. In these constructions, the main verb appears first, followed by a stative degree verb such as *arɕo* ‘be finished,’ *tɕʰo* ‘too much,’ or *rtaʁbe* ‘enough.’

text:
converb!manner
Infinitive converbial clauses (§ sec:inf.converb ) can indicate the manner of the action of the main clause, or a background event. The converb can be optionally followed by the ergative kɯ and/or the emphatic ʑo (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ), as in ( ex:kArJWG.kW.Zo2 ) and ( ex:kAfkur.RJa.kW ).

exe

[kɤ-rɟɯɣ] (kɯ) (ʑo) jo-ɕe \\
inf -run erg emph ifr -go \\
`He went running.' (elicited)
exe

exe

tɕe kɯɕɯŋgɯ ji-si nɯra [kɤ-fkur] ʁɟa kɯ jú-wɣ-sɯ-ɤzɣɯt-nɯ pɯ-ra. \\
lnk in.former.times 1pl. poss -wood dem: pl inf -carry.on.the.back completely erg ipfv - inv - caus -reach- pl pst. ipfv -be.needed \\
`In former times, one used to transport firewood exclusively by carrying it on one's back.' (140430 tWfkur)
0003898#S19
exe

The converb is often in negative form, meaning `without...ing' as in ( ex:WGi.ra.nWmAkAsWz ) and ( ex:mAkArWsWso.kW ).

exe

[ɯ-ɣi ra nɯ-mɤ-kɤ-sɯz] nɯ rŋɯl nɯ ɲɤ-mbi. \\
3sg. poss -relative pl 3pl. poss - neg - inf -know dem silver dem ifr -give \\
`She$_i$ gave him money without her$_i$ relatives knowing (about it).' (28-qajdoskAt)
0003718#S161
exe

exe

tɤ-mu nɯ kɯ rcanɯ, maka ʑo mɤ-kɤ-rɯsɯso kɯ to-nɤla \\
indef. poss -mother dem erg unexp: deg at.all emph neg - inf -think erg ifr -agree \\
`The woman accepted without thinking at all.' (150907 yingning-zh)
0006264#S113
exe

The manner infinitive clauses can express the degree of the state or action in the main clause, as in ( ex:kAcW.mAsAcha ) and ( ex:tChi.kAcha.Zo2 ).

exe

[tɯ-mɲaʁ kɤ-cɯ mɤ-kɤ-sɤ-cʰa] ʑo mŋɤm \\
genr. poss -eye inf -open neg - inf - prop -can emph hurt: fact \\
`[This disease] hurts so much that one cannot open one's eyes.' (25-kACAl)
0003640#S32
exe

exe

βʑɯ nɯ kɯ [tɕʰi kɤ-cʰa] ʑo to-nɯrdoʁ nɤ to-nɯrdoʁ \\
mouse dem erg what inf -can emph ifr -collect add ifr -collect \\
`The mouse collected as much [fruits] as it could.' (lWlu 2002)
0003361#S32
exe

The stative/impersonal infinitives in kɯ- are also used as converbs for some anticausative verbs, modal auxiliary and existential verbs (§ sec:inf.converb ) as in ( ex:kAlAt.mAkWra ), and some have become lexicalized as adverbs (§ sec:velar.inf.adverb ).

exe

nɯ [tɯ-jaʁ kɤ-lɤt mɤ-kɯ-ra] tɯ-ci kɯ cʰɯ-sɯ-mtɕɯr pɯ-ŋgrɤl \\
dem genr. poss -had inf -release neg - inf: stat -be.needed indef. poss -water erg ipfv: downstream - caus -turn pst. ipfv -be.usually.the.case \\
`The water would make the [toy waterwheel] turn without needing to use one's hand.' (08-kWmtChW)
0003452#S20
exe
gerund
In addition, gerundive clauses (§ sec:gerund.clauses ), which are used to describe actions that are simultaneous with that of the main clause (§ sec:simultaneity ), occur in clauses that express manner more than temporal overlap, as in ( ex:sAmtsMmtsWr.kurAZita ).

exe

[kutɕu sɤ-mtsɯ mtsɯr] ku-rɤʑit-a tɕe, jisŋi ndɤ tɯmɯkɯmpɕi kɯ pɯ́-wɣ-nɯ-mbi-a ɕti \\
dem. prox: loc ger -be.hungry ipfv -stay- 1sg lnk today advers heaven erg aor: down - inv - auto -give- 1sg be. aff: fact \\
`I am hungry while staying here, but today the heavens have sent me down [these humans to eat].' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S250
exe
summary: Infinitive converbial clauses can express the manner of the main clause action or serve as a background event, and they may optionally take the ergative *kɯ* and/or the emphatic *ʑo*. They are often used in negative form with the meaning “without ...ing,” and they can also indicate the degree of a state or action in the main clause. In addition, some stative/impersonal infinitives in *kɯ-* function as converbs for certain anticausative, modal auxiliary, and existential verbs, and some have become lexicalized as adverbs; gerundive clauses can also be used in contexts expressing manner rather than mere simultaneity.

text:
The only specific marker of consequence is the linker núndʐafor this reason ( ex:qapGAmtWmtW ).

exe

ɯ-mtɯ ɣɤʑu tɕe, tɕe núndʐa qapɣɤmtɯmtɯ tu-ti-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
3sg. poss -crest exist: sens lnk lnk for.this.reason hoopoe ipfv -say- pl sens -be \\
`It has a crest, and for this reason it is called `hoopoe'.' (23-qapGAmtWmtW)
0003608#S19
exe

This linker results from the fusion (§ sec:3sg.possessive.form ) of the noun ɯ-ndʐacause used in causal clauses (§ sec:causal.clauses ) with the distal demonstrative nɯ in anaphoric function `the reason of (the preceding sentence)' (§ sec:anaphoric.demonstrative.pro ). The phrase nɯnɯ ɯ-ndʐa without vowel fusion is also found in exactly the same context in the same text.

However, consequence is more generally simply indicated by the linkers tɕe and/or qʰe (§ sec:coordination ), as illustrated by ( ex:pWCtia.qhe.qhe ).

exe

tɕʰemɤ-pɯ pɯ-ɕti-a qʰe tɤ-tɕɯ ra nɯ-ɕki ku-rɤʑi-a mɯ́j-naz-a qʰe kɤ-ʑɣɤ-ɕɯ-fka mɯ-pɯ-naz-a \\
girl- dim pst. ipfv -be- 1sg lnk indef. poss -son pl 3pl. poss - dat ipfv -stay- 1sg neg: sens -dare- 1sg lnk inf - refl - caus -be.full neg - pst. ipfv -dare- 1sg \\
`As I was a little girl, I did not dare to stay at a boy's place, and thus did not dare to eat my fill.' (17-lhazgron)
exe
summary: The passage says that the only specific marker of consequence is the linker **nʊ́ndʐa** ‘for this reason,’ which is historically formed by fusion of the noun **ɯ-ndʐa** ‘cause’ with the distal demonstrative **nɯ** used anaphorically. It also notes that consequence is more commonly expressed simply by the coordinative linkers **tɕe** and/or **qʰe**.

text:
cause
The causal linker matɕibecause is the main way to indicate cause in Japhug. In this construction, it is not clear which clause is the main clause, since the linker can be prosodically linked to both the preceding, or the following one, even with a pause after matɕi as in ( ex:matCi.YWxtCi ). The clause preceding matɕi expresses the result/consequence (consequence clause), and the one following it the cause (causal clause).

exe

ma nɯnɯ kʰro mɤ-sɤ-mto. matɕi ɲɯ-xtɕi. \\
lnk dem much neg - prop -see: fact because sens -be.small \\
`That [species of ant] is barely visible, because it is [so] small.' (26-qro)
0003682#S79
exe

Example ( ex:matCi.mAndze.Zo.me ) cannot be analyzed as an attestation of a preposed matɕi causal clause, since the clause that follows qʰe ɯ-ɣli dɤn is a redundant consequence clause (§ sec:consequence ), repeating the real consequence clause paʁ ɣɯ ɯ-ɣli dɤn, which is located in the expected place before the linker matɕi.

exe

paʁ ɣɯ ɯ-ɣli dɤn [matɕi mɤ-ndze ʑo me] qʰe ɯ-ɣli dɤn \\
pig gen 3sg. poss -manure be.many: fact because neg -eat[III]: fact emph not.exist: fact lnk 3sg. poss -manure be.many: fact \\
`Pigs create a lot of manure because they eat anything, and so they create a lot of manure.' (05-paR)
0003400#S98
exe

The shorter form ma The two forms are historically related: matɕi is probably a combination of ma with the additive topic marker tɕi (§ sec:ri.additive ). can also mark cause as in ( ex:mAcha.ma.mpW ). However, ma has many additional functions, including marking precautioning (§ sec:precautioning.clauses ), adversative (§ sec:adversative.clauses ) and exceptive (§ sec:exceptive.clauses ) clauses.

exe

ɯ-jwaʁ nɯ (...) tu-ostɤko ʑo mɤ-cʰa ma mpɯ. \\
3sg. poss -leaf dem ipfv -be.straight emph neg -can lnk be.soft: fact \\
`Its leaves do not grow straight (i.e. they hang down), as they are soft.' (07-kWmCku)
0003428#S12
exe

Alternatively, the relator noun ɯ-ndʐacause (§ sec:IPN.cause, § sec:nouns.cause.complement ) with ergative (and/or locative) postpositions can serve to build causal clauses, as in ( ex:tAtWta.Wndzxa.zW.kW ). In some rare cases, ɯ-ndʐa -clauses can have a purposive meaning (example ex:mWYWkABzu.Wndzxa, § sec:nouns.cause.complement ).

exe

[``nɤʑo ɯ-rɯz ɣɤʑu" tɤ-tɯt-a ɯ-ndʐa] zɯ kɯ a-pa a-ma ni kɯ ``mtsʰukʰa ɯ-ŋgɯ tɕe (...) tɤrca pɯ-ɕe ma mɤ-jɤɣ'' \\
2sg 3sg. poss -supernatural.power exist: sens aor -say[II]- 1sg 3sg. poss -reason loc erg 1sg. poss -father. hon 1sg. poss -mother. hon du erg lake 3sg. poss -in loc together imp: down -go apart.from neg -be.allowed: fact \\
`Because I said that you had supernatural powers (§ sec:hybrid indirect ), my parents [said] `go together with him into the lake.'(Nyima wodzer 2003.2)
exe

Instead of being marked with the ergative, the causal clauses can also serve as predicate of a copular construction (example ex:tCetha.nWmbrAt, § sec:aor.temporal ). Predicative causal clauses occur often standalone as in ( ex:tutWtinW.ndzxa.Nu ), without any overt clause expressing the result.

exe

[``nɯ ma-tɤ-tɯ-ste, nɯ ma-tɤ-tɯ-fse" tu-tɯ-ti-nɯ] ndʐa ŋu wo \\
dem neg - imp -2-do.like[III] dem neg - imp -2-be.like ipfv -2-say- pl reason be: fact sfp \\
`(If your son wants so much to see his grandparents), this is because you (his parents always) tell him `Don't act like that, don't be like that.' (unlike grandparents, who are more lenient).' (conversation 16-08-11)
exe

Apart from ndʐa, the relator nouns ɯ-tʰɯrʑimercy and ɯ-xɕɤtstrength
can also be used to indicate cause on both noun phrases (§ sec:IPN.cause ) and subordinate clauses.

The noun ɯ-tʰɯrʑimercy is specifically used to indicate beneficial actions thanks to which a desirable result is obtained ( ex:tanWsmAn.WthWrZi ).

exe

[<guojia> kɯ ta-nɯsmɤn] ɯ-tʰɯrʑi tɕe tɕe (...) tʰam tɕe wuma ʑo tɤ-pe-nɯ. \\
country erg aor:3 -heal 3sg. poss -mercy lnk lnk now lnk really emph aor -be.good- pl \\
`Thanks to the fact that [our] country['s governement] has healed them, (...) now they are much better.' (140522 RdWrJAt)
0004061#S131
exe

The locution $X$ ɯ-xɕɤt kɯ $Y$ with the ergative specifically means `do $X$ so much/to the extent that $Y$', as in ( ex:khu.kW.tAwGndzanW.WxCAt ), specifying not only that $X$ is the cause of $Y$, but in addition that $X$ was performed to/with a sufficiently high degree/frequency/ to make the action/situation $Y$ possible. The locution $X$ ɯ-xɕɤt kɯ is reminds of French à force de $X$. More data on degree causal constructions is provided in § sec:degree.consequence.

exe

tsʰupa ci pjɤ-tu tɕe tɕendɤre, [kʰu kɯ tɤ́-wɣ-ndza-nɯ] ɯ-xɕɤt kɯ tɤ-mu kɤtsa ci pjɤ-ri-ndʑi tɕe \\
village indef ifr. ipfv -exist lnk lnk tiger erg aor - inv -eat- pl 3sg. poss -strength erg indef. poss -mother coll:family indef ifr. ipfv -remain- du lnk \\
`There was a village, but a tiger had eaten them (i.e. the villagers) so that only a mother and her daughter remained.' (khu 2012)
0004085#S2
exe
summary: Japhug mainly expresses cause with the linker *matɕi*, where the preceding clause states the result or consequence and the following clause states the cause; the linker may prosodically attach to either side, so the main clause is not always clear. The shorter form *ma* can also mark cause, but it has several other functions, and causal relations can additionally be expressed with the relator noun *ɯ-ndʐa* and, more specifically, with *ɯ-tʰɯrʑi* for beneficial causes and *ɯ-xɕɤt* for degree-based causal meaning.

text:
Prerequisite constructions do not express the direct cause of the action/situation in the main clause, but simply the basic conditions for that action or situation to be possible, like 既然 jìránsince in Chinese. This meaning is expressed by a clause in the Aorist as in ( ex:tAcha.tANu ), formally similar to a temporal clause (§ sec:aor.temporal, § sec:temporal.reference ).

exe

<huangdi> (...) tú-wɣ-sɯ-ndo-a tɤ-cʰa tɤ-ŋu tɕe (...) <jiaohuang> nɯ ʑgrɯɣ tú-wɣ-sɯ-ndo-a cʰa tɕe, ɕ-tɤ-ti ra \\
emperor ipfv - inv - caus -take- 1sg aor -can aor -be lnk pope dem certainly ipfv - inv - caus -take- 1sg can: fact lnk tral - imp -go be.needed: fact \\
`Since [the golden fish] has succeeded in making me emperor, he will certainly succeed in making me pope, go and tell him that.' (140430 yufu he tade qizi-zh)
0003900#S194
exe

The minimal clause nɯ tɤ-ŋu tɕe can have a prerequisite interpretation `given these circumstances, in this case' as in ( ex:nW.tANu.tCe ).

exe

nɯ tɤ-ŋu tɕe tɕe, si lú-wɣ-ɣɤjɯ, smi a-tɤ-wxti tɕe ɲɯ-pʰɤn \\
dem aor -be lnk lnk wood ipfv - inv -add fire irr - pfv -be.big lnk sens -be.efficient \\
`In this case, if one adds more wood, and the fire gets bigger, it should work.' (150827 taisui-zh)
0006390#S62
exe
summary: Prerequisite constructions do not state the direct cause of the main clause situation, but instead present the basic conditions that make it possible, similar to Chinese *jìrán* ‘since.’ This meaning is expressed by an Aorist clause, which is formally like a temporal clause. The minimal clause *nɯ tɤ-ŋu tɕe* can also be interpreted prerequisite-wise as meaning ‘given these circumstances, in this case.’

text:
Five main constructions are available in Japhug to express purpose. This section does not include the participial clauses (§ sec:subject.participle.complementation ) used as supine purposive clauses of motion verbs (§ sec:purposive.clause.motion.verbs ).

First, the purposive converb (§ sec:purposive.converb ) is a non-finite verb form dedicated to expressing the purpose of the action in the main clause. It is built by combining the prefix sɤ(z)- with a B-type preverb (§ sec:kamnyu.preverbs ), the reduplicated verb stem and a possessive prefix coreferent with one of the core arguments of the purposive clause (and almost always in negative form). Purposive converbs are productive: even denominal verbs of Tibetan origin such as nɯtɕʰombacatch a cold ( ex:WmAtusAznWtChombWmba ) can derive this type of converbs. However, they are barely attested in the Japhug corpus, and simpler constructions are preferred to express purpose.

exe

a-tɕɯ ɯ-mɤ-tu-sɤz-nɯtɕʰombɯ mba tɯ-ŋga kɯ-jaʁ tɤ-ʑ-ŋga-t-a \\
1sg. poss -son 3sg. poss - neg - ipfv - purp: conv indef. poss -clothes sbj: pcp -be.thick aor - caus -wear- pst: tr - 1sg \\
`In order to prevent my son from catching a cold, I made him wear heavy clothes.' (elicited)
exe

Second, the the verb nɯmgawant from can be combined with an infinitival clause to express purpose, as in ( ex:mWYWkABzu.kANWmga ) to express the aim of the action in the main clause.

exe

tɕe [kɯpɤz nɯ mɯ-ɲɯ-kɤ-βzu kɤ-nɯmga], iʑɤra, ji-mtʰɯm nɯra <binggui> tu-χtɯ-j tɕe nɯ ɯ-ŋgɯ ri pjɯ-nɯ-rku-j ɕti ma \\
lnk type.of.bug dem neg - ipfv - inf -grow inf -want.from 1pl 1pl. poss -meat dem: pl refrigerator ipfv -buy- 1pl lnk dem 3sg. poss -in loc ipfv -auto-put.in- 1pl be. aff: fact lnk \\
`In order to prevent kɯpɤz bugs from growing (in the meat), we buy refrigerators and put our meat in it.' (28-kWpAz)
0003714#S45
exe

The verb nɯmga in this function is generally a velar infinitive kɤ-nɯmga in converbial function (§ sec:inf.converb ) as in ( ex:mWYWkABzu.kANWmga ) and ( ex:kABzjoz.kAnWmga ), but a finite verb is also possible ( ex:kABzjoz.kAnWmgata ). The infinitival clause can be focalized, serving as the predicate of a copular construction in ŋu ( ex:kABzjoz.kAnWmga.Nu ).

exe

xlist

kɯrɯ-skɤt kɤ-βzjoz kɤ-nɯmga kɯ, mbarkʰom mɤɕtʂa jɤ-ɣe-a ŋu. \\
Gyalrong-language inf -learn in -want.from erg topo until aor -come[II]- 1sg be: fact \\

kɯrɯ-skɤt kɤ-βzjoz kɤ-nɯmga-t-a tɕe, mbarkʰom mɤɕtʂa jɤ-ɣe-a ŋu. \\
Gyalrong-language inf -learn aor -want.from- pst: tr - 1sg lnk topo until aor -come[II]- 1sg be: fact \\
`I came all the way up to Mbarkham to learn the Gyalrong language.' (elicited)

mbarkʰom ju-ɣi-a nɯ, kɯrɯ-skɤt kɤ-βzjoz kɤ-nɯmga ŋu \\
topo ipfv -come- 1sg dem Gyalrong-language inf -learn inf -want.from be: fact \\
`(The reason why) I come to Mbarkham is to learn the Gyalrong language.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

Third, the relator noun ɯ-spamaterial (§ sec:lexicalized.oblique.participle, § sec:Wspa.relative ) can take object ( ex:WkAnAmYo.Wspa ) and subject ( ex:WkWBzjoz.Wspa ) participial clauses with a purposive meaning. These constructions are to be analyzed as essive participial clauses (§ sec:participial.clause.essive ).

exe

tɯrme ra kɯ ɯ-<shipin> jo-lɤt-nɯ tɕe [nɯnɯ ɯ-kɤ-nɤmɲo] ɯ-spa jo-lɤt-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
people pl erg 3sg. poss -video ifr -release- pl lnk dem 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -watch 3sg. poss -material ifr -release- pl sens -be \\
`People send him this video for him to watch it.' (conversation 2019-02-26)
exe

exe

[kɯrɯ-skɤt ɯ-kɯ-βzjoz] ɯ-spa, mbarkʰom mɤɕtʂa jɤ-ɣe-a ŋu. \\
Gyalrong-language 3sg. poss - sbj: pcp -learn 3sg. poss -material topo until aor -come[II]- 1sg be: fact \\
`I came all the way up to Mbarkham to learn the Gyalrong language.' (elicited)
exe

Essive participial clauses without ɯ-spa can also have a purposive meaning, as in ( ex:nWkWqur.tundonW ).

exe

kɯ-ɣɤrʁaʁ ra kɯ tu-ndo-nɯ. [nɯ-kɯ-qur] tu-ndo-nɯ pjɤ-ŋgrɤl. \\
sbj: pcp -hunt pl erg ipfv -take- pl 3pl. poss - sbj: pcp -help ipfv -take- pl ipfv. ifr -be.usually.the.case \\
`(In former times), hunters would take [dogs] (on a hunt). They would take dogs to help them (i.e., as their helpers).' (05-khWna)
0003398#S33
exe

Fourth, a biclausal construction comprising a clause containing a similative verb ( fsebe like or studo like) in finite form with the interrogative pronoun (§ sec:tChi ), and another finite clause $Y$ linked by tɕe, specifically means `what should $X$ do in order to $Y$' as in ( ex:tufsej.jitWci.GAZu ) and ( ex:atAstunW.nWtWci.GAZu ).

exe

xlist

iʑora ɣɯ tɕʰi tu-fse-j tɕe ji-tɯ-ci ɣɤʑu (...) tu-tɯ-tʰe ɯ-tɯ́-cʰa \\
1pl gen what ipfv -be.like- 1pl lnk 1pl. poss - indef. poss -water exist: sens ipfv -2-ask[III] qu -2-can: fact \\
`Can you ask for us what we [need to] do in order to have water?' (said by villagers living in a desert where there is no water, divination 2005)

nɯnɯra kɯ tɕʰi a-tɤ-stu-nɯ tɕe nɯ-tɯ-ci ɣɤʑu? \\
dem erg what irr - pfv -do.like- pl lnk 3pl. poss - indef. poss -water exist: sens \\
`What should they do in order to have water?' (divination 2005)
xlist
exe

The clause in fse can be embedded within the clause $Y$, as shown by example ( ex:atAfsea.mAwGmtoa ) (§ sec:embedded.clause ).

Fifth, purposive meaning can be expressed by a clause in the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis with the adverb tɕetʰalater as in ( ex:tCetha.amAlAZGWt ). This type of construction resembles precautioning clauses (§ sec:precautioning.clauses ), but with opposite polarity.

exe

lu-zɣɯt ɕɯŋgɯ tɕe nɯtɕu ku-ɣɤrat-a tɕetʰa a-mɤ-lɤ-zɣɯt \\
ipfv: upstream -arrive before lnk dem: loc ipfv -throw- 1sg later irr - neg - pfv: upstream -arrive \\
`Before it arrives, I will throw [the enchanted white stone], so that it does not arrive.' (25-kAmYW-XpAltCin)
0003642#S57
exe

Finally, clauses with the relator ɯ-ndʐacause can also have a purposive interpretation (example ex:mWYWkABzu.Wndzxa, § sec:nouns.cause.complement, which resembles causal clauses § sec:causal.clauses ).
summary: Japhug has five main constructions for expressing purpose: a purposive converb, a clause with the verb nɯmga ‘want from’ plus an infinitival or finite clause, purposive uses of the relator noun ɯ-spa and related essive participial clauses, a biclausal construction with a similative verb and tɕe meaning ‘what should X do in order to Y,’ and an irrealis clause with tɕetʰa ‘later.’ The passage notes that purposive converbs are productive but rare in the corpus, and that the simpler constructions are often preferred. It also mentions that clauses with ɯ-ndʐa ‘cause’ can sometimes be interpreted purposively.

text:
justification clause
Justification clauses differ from strictly clausal clauses in that there is no direct causal relationship between the main clause and the justification clause. Rather, the truth value of the latter allows to make an inference concerning the truth value of the latter.

In Japhug, there is no dedicated construction to express such meaning, and as in many languages, the clausal linkers ma and matɕi (§ sec:causal.clauses ) can be used ( ex:matCi.justification ).

exe

cʰa tɕi ko-tsʰi matɕi lo-βzi ɕti ri \\
alcohol also ifr -drink lnk ifr -be.drunk be. aff: fact lnk \\
`He had also drunk alcohol, since he was drunk.' (140506 loBzi)
0003923#S13
exe

The justification meaning is clearest when the verb of the main clause takes the Probabilitative ɯmɤ- (§ sec:WmA.kW.ci ) or the Rhetorical Interrogative ɯβrɤ- (§ sec:WBrA.kW.ci ) prefixes with peg circumfix, and that in the clause following ma is in the Sensory, as in ( ex:WmAkWNuci.justification ) and ( ex:WBrApWtWnWZWBci.justification ).

exe

ɕɤxɕo pɤnmawombɤr jo-nɯ-ɣi ɯmɤ-kɯ-ŋu-ci ma, kʰa ɲɯ-ɣɤkʰɯ-nɯ \\
these.days anthr ifr - vert -come prob - peg -be- peg lnk house sens -have.smoke- pl \\
`Maybe Padma 'Od'bar came back in the last few days, since there is smoke coming out from their house.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S193
exe

exe

jɯfɕɯɕɤr ɯβrɤ-pɯ-tɯ-nɯʑɯβ-ci ma nɤ-mɲaʁ ɲɯ-ɣɯrni \\
last.night rh. q - pst. ipfv -2-sleep- peg lnk 2sg. poss -eye sens -be.red \\
`It seems that you did not sleep (well) last night, since your eyes are red.' (elicited)
exe

The use of ma as a sentence final particle with the modal tenses (§ sec:fsp.epistemic ) possibly originate from constructions as in ( ex:WmAkWNuci.justification ) and ( ex:WBrApWtWnWZWBci.justification ) with elided justification clauses.
summary: Japhug does not have a special construction for justification clauses, but instead uses the clausal linkers **ma** and **matɕi**, which express an inference from the truth of the justification clause rather than a direct causal relation. The meaning is especially clear when the main clause has the **Probabilitative** or **Rhetorical Interrogative** prefix and the following clause with **ma** is in the **Sensory** form. The text also suggests that sentence-final **ma** with modal tenses may have developed from such structures with omitted justification clauses.

text:
precautioning clause
Precautioning constructions comprise a clause describing an undesirable result, and another clause referring to a measure that can be taken to prevent this result. The precautioning meaning can be expressed with a negative purposive clause (§ sec:purposive.clauses ); in particular, purposive converbs, which are almost always in negative forms (§ sec:purposive.converb ), could be described as a type of precautioning clauses.

However, the most common way of expressing precautioning meaning in Japhug is by coordinating a clause in the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis ), the Imperative (§ sec:imperative ) or the Prohibitive (§ sec:prohibitive ) indicating the preventive measure, with a clause in the Factual Non-Past (§ sec:factual ) referring to the undesired event. The two clauses are coordinated by the linker ma ( ex:ma.tWndzxaB ) and/or the adverb tʰalater or tɕetʰa, as illustrated by ( ex:matABzea ) and ( ex:ma.tCetha.junWCe ), a crosslinguistically common strategy to express precautioning meaning.

exe

ma-jɤ-tɯ-ɕe ma tɯ-ndʐaβ \\
neg - imp -2-go lnk 2- acaus:cause.to.roll.down: fact \\
`Don't go (to the temple on the mountain to do circumambulations), you might fall down.' (conversation, conversation 15-12-05)
exe

exe

nɯ kʰramba ma-tɤ-βze-a ra ma tɕe <lishijizai> pjɯ-tɯ-βze ɕti tɕetʰa, nɯnɯ rcanɯ <zuzubeibei> kɯ ɣɯ-nɤmqe-a-nɯ. \\
dem lie neg - imp -make[III]- 1sg be.needed: fact lnk lnk history record ipfv -2-make[III] be: aff: fact lnk later generations erg inv -scold: fact - 1sg - pl \\
`I musn't tell lies, as you are making a historical record, and the past generations would scold me.' (27-kikakCi)
0003700#S208
exe

exe

a-mɤ-tʰɯ-sta ma tɕetʰa ju-nɯ-ɕe ɕti \\
irr - neg - pfv -wake lnk later ipfv - vert -go be. aff: fact \\
`May she not wake up (Don't wake her up), otherwise she will go away.' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh)
0006334#S103
exe

There is no categorical requirement for the first clause to contain a modal TAME category. In ( ex:kWxtshWm.mApe.ma ), we find instead the negative form mɤ-pe `it is not good' with a non-finite clause that can either be interpreted as a stative infinitive (`it is not good (if) they are thin') or a subject participle (`the thin ones are not good').

exe

roʁre nɯ kɯnɤ [wuma ʑo kɯ-xtsʰɯm] mɤ-pe ma tɕe pjɯ-qlɯt-nɯ. \\
fence.rail dem also really emph inf: stat -be.thin neg -be.good lnk lnk ipfv -break- pl \\
`As for fence rails also, it is not good [where they are] too thin, otherwise [the hybrid yaks in the cowshed] will break them.' (150902 mkhoN)
0006300#S38
exe
summary: Precautioning constructions consist of one clause describing an undesirable result and another clause expressing the preventive measure. In Japhug, this meaning is most commonly expressed by coordinating a clause in the Irrealis, Imperative, or Prohibitive with a clause in the Factual Non-Past, linked by *ma* and/or the adverb *tʰalater* or *tɕetʰa*. The passage also notes that the first clause does not have to contain a modal TAME category, since a negative form such as *mɤ-pe* can be used instead.

text: adversative
summary: The passage identifies **adversative** as a linguistic category, though it gives no further details in this excerpt. It appears to be a term used in grammar to describe a relation or construction expressing contrast or opposition.

text:
concessive clause
The most common way of expressing concession is the linker tɕeri `but, however', which can occur in sentence-initial position, after a pause as in ( ex:tCeri.WmAlAjaR.GAZu ).

exe

ɯ-βri nɯra qapri ɯ-βri wuma ʑo ɲɯ-fse, ɯ-rme ri kɯ-tu maŋe. tɕeri ɯ-mɤlɤjaʁ ɣɤʑu. \\
3sg. poss -body dem: pl snake 3sg. poss -body really emph sens -be.like 3sg. poss -hair also sbj: pcp -exist not.exist: sens lnk 3sg. poss -limb exist: sens \\
`[The gecko's] body looks a little bit like the body of a snake, and it too has no hair. However, it has limbs.' (28-tshAwAre)
0003722#S7
exe

The shorter variant ri The form tɕeri is a combination of the linker tɕe with ri; the concessive meaning of ri itself possibly derives from its function as a locative postposition, used with a finite clause as a temporal subordinator as in ( ex:pWkWxtCi.ri ) (§ sec:temporal.reference ). is also used to indicate concession ( ex:tu.ri.mAdAn ) when used between coordinated clauses. When ri follows noun phrases or complement clauses, it is a different marker, either that of additive focus `also' as in ( ex:tCeri.WmAlAjaR.GAZu ) above (§ sec:ri.additive, § sec:addition.clauses ) or a locative postposition (§ sec:core.locative ).

exe

kuwu nɯ iʑo kutɕu ji-ʑimkʰɤm tɕe tu ri mɤ-dɤn \\
bearded.vulture dem 1sg dem. prox: loc 1pl. poss -region loc exist: fact lnk neg -be.many: fact \\
`Bearded vultures are found here in our region, but not many.' (2011-08-kuwu)
exe

The linker ma also has a concessive meaning in some contexts, as in ( ex:toznWGmaz.ma.kAsat.mWpjAcha ). This function possibly derives from its use as an exceptive postposition meaning `apart from' (§ sec:exceptive, § sec:exceptive.clauses ).

exe

qaliaʁ nɯ to-z-nɯɣmaz ma kɤ-sat nɯ mɯ-pjɤ-cʰa\\
eagle dem ifr - caus -have.a.wound lnk inf -kill dem neg - ifr -can\\
`He wounded the eagle, but could not kill it.' (150902 hailibu-zh)
0006316#S19
exe

The topic marker ndɤre (§ sec:adversative.topic ) can also indicate adversative meaning, with scope overt one constituent of the sentence, in ( ex:ndAre.mAsna ) over an infinitival clause.

exe

paʁ kɯ tɕi ndze, nɯŋa kɯ tɕi ndze. tɕe [tɯrme kɤ-ndza] ndɤre mɤ-sna. \\
pig erg too eat[III]: fact cow erg too eat[III]: fact lnk people inf -eat contrast: foc neg -be.good: fact \\
`Pigs eat it, cows eat it, but it is not good for people to eat.' (17-ndZWnW)
0003524#S118
exe

In the register of traditional stories, the locution jinbala zɯ is also employed to mark adversative clauses as in ( ex:jinbala.zW ). The linker jinbala is borrowed from Tibetan ཡིན་པ་ལ་ jin.pa.la, a non-finite form of the copula ཡིན་jinbe which also has adversative meaning in the classical language.

exe

tɕe rɟɤlpu nɯ nɯ-rga jinbala zɯ ``e, a-tɕɯ ki stɤβtsʰɤt ci mɯ-ɕɯ-cʰa kɯ" ɲɤ-sɯso tɕe \\
lnk king dem aor -be.happy although loc interj 1sg. poss -son dem. prox contest indef neg - apprehensive -can sfp ifr -think lnk \\
`Although the king was happy (about that), he thought `I am worried that my son will not win the contest.' (2003 sras)
exe

Finally, velar infinitive converbs (§ sec:inf.converb ) with the ergative can have an adversative interpretation, as in ( ex:kWnA.mAkAti.kW ), where the converbial clause is better translated by `although...' than `without...'. In the Chinese original, …便主动要求嫁给国王 biàn zhǔdòng yāoqiú jiàgěi guówáng... and she asked to marry the king of her own initiative, what corresponds to the converbial clause is the adverb 主动 zhǔdòngof...'s own initiative. This construction cannot be a calque.

exe

``jɤ-ɣi" kɯnɤ mɤ-kɤ-ti kɯ, ``nɤ-rʑaβ ɣɯ-ku-βze-a" to-ti, rɟɤlpu nɯ ɯ-ɕki. \\
imp -come also neg - inf -say erg 2sg. poss -wife cisl - ipfv -make[III]- 1sg ifr -say king dem 3sg. poss - dat \\
`Although [the king had not] said `come' (i.e.  `without the king saying `come''), she told the king `I am coming to become your wife.' (140511 yinzi-zh)
0003963#S21
exe
summary: Concession is most commonly expressed by the linker **tɕeri** ‘but, however,’ which can appear sentence-initially or after a pause. A shorter form, **ri**, also marks concession between coordinated clauses, while **ma** can have a concessive meaning in some contexts and **ndɤre** can express adversative meaning with scope over one constituent. In traditional stories, **jinbala zɯ** is used for adversative clauses, and ergative velar infinitive converbs can also be interpreted adversatively, often best translated as ‘although...’.

text:
The negative copula maʁnot be followed by the ergative kɯ negates the first clause ($A$), and indicates that the events described by following clause(s) $B$ instead are true. The meaning of this construction can be glossed `not $A$, but rather $B$' as in ( ex:CkurAloR.YWmaR.kW ).

exe

kɯjka nɯnɯ sɯŋgɯ cʰiz ɕ-ku-rɤloʁ ɲɯ-maʁ kɯ, (...) kuxtɕo ɯ-mbe ɯ-ŋgɯ ri ku-rɤloʁ \\
chough dem forest approx: loc tral - ipfv -make.nest sens -not.be erg basket 3sg. poss -old.one 3sg. poss -in loc ipfv -make.nest \\
`The chough does not go in the forest and makes a nest there, but rather makes a nest (...) in old baskets, (...)' (22-CAGpGa)
0003586#S45
exe

The adversative additive adverb mɤ́ɣrɤzinstead, `on the contrary' (and its variant mɤ́ɣrɤz nɤ ), semantically similar to Chinese 反而 fǎn'érinstead, specifically indicates an undesirable result that occurs contrary to expectation instead of the intended result.

The clause expressing the intended result can take the comparative postposition (standard marker) sɤzcompared with (§ sec:comparative ), as in ( ex:ndAre.mAsna ).

exe

pjɤ-kɯ-nɯβlu-a tɕe, nɯnɯ kɯ-pʰɤn sɤznɤ, mɤ́ɣrɤz a-mpʰɯz ɯ-ntɕʰɯr pa-nɯ-pʰɯt \\
ifr -2 1-cheat- 1sg lnk dem sbj: pcp -be.efficient comp instead 1sg. poss -bottom 3sg. poss -piece aor:3 - auto -take.off \\
`You cheated me, not only was [your healing method] not efficient [to treat my illness], but it took off a chunk of my bottom. (140427 qala cho kWrtsAG)
0003852#S40
exe

In most cases however, mɤ́ɣrɤz occurs without any additional marker, as in ( ex:mAGrAz.YWmNAm ).

exe

ɕɤr tɕe ʑŋgri nɯ nɯ-mɤrʑaβ ʑo tɕe tɯ-kɤrme cʰɯ́-wɣ-rɤɕi ri, cʰɯ-kɯ-zri maŋe, mɤ́ɣrɤz ɲɯ-mŋɤm ma. \\
night loc star dem aor -marry emph lnk genr. poss -hair ipfv - inv -pull lnk ipfv - pcp: sbj -be.long not.exist: sens instead sens -hurt sfp \\
`In the night when there was a shooting star, we pulled our hair (thinking that our hair would grow longer), but not only did [our hair] not grow longer, [but the only thing that it did was] it hurt.' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S98
exe
summary: The negative copula maʁ followed by the ergative kɯ negates the first clause and presents the following clause(s) as the true event, with the meaning ‘not A, but rather B.’ The adversative additive adverb mɤ́ɣrɤz ‘instead, on the contrary’ expresses an undesirable result that happens contrary to expectation, often without an extra marker though the intended result may optionally take the comparative postposition sɤz.

text:
The Aorist tɤ-mda (§ sec:aor ) of the verb mdabe the time, without complement clause, and following a clause with the adversative linker ri, has the special meaning `actually', `it turns out that...', `but in fact...'. It is specifically used when a referent realizes that that the reality (the rectification clause) was different from his/her/its original belief or expectation.

This construction is common in stories translated from Chinese, as in ( ex:tAmda.pjACti ) and ( ex:tAmda.pjAtWNu ), where tɤ-mda corresponds to the Chinese linkers 结果 jiéguǒin the end or 原来 yuánláiit turns out that. For instance, the original of ( ex:tAmda.pjAtWNu ) is 原来是我的外甥来了 yuánlái shì wǒ de wàishēng láileit turns out that (the one who came, you) is my nephew.

exe

<huangshang> nɯ kɯ ko-mɟa tɕe to-rtoʁ ri, nɤkinɯ, tɤ-mda tɕe, nɯnɯ nɤki, ɕoʁɕoʁ kɯ-qarŋe kɯ tɤ-kɤ-βzu pjɤ-ɕti. \\
emperor dem erg ifr -catch lnk ifr -look lnk filler aor -be.the.time lnk dem filler paper sbj: pcp -be.yellow erg aor - obj: pcp -make ifr. ipfv -be. aff \\
\\
`[Wang Taichang$_i$ was accused of holding an imperial robe, a crime punishable by death] The emperor$_j$ [had] him$_i$ arrested, but when he$_j$ examined [the so-called imperial robe]$_k$ it turned out that it$_k$ was [just] made of yellow paper.' (150909 xiaocui-zh)
0006386#S86
exe

The rectification clause is always in the Inferential (§ sec:ifr ), not only in narration as in ( ex:tAmda.pjACti ), but also when reflecting the point of view of the speaker as in ( ex:tAmda.pjAtWNu ). It can be used with the mistaken expectation construction (§ sec:cimame ).

exe

aʑo ``nɯ ɕɯ tɯ-ŋu kɯ" nɯ-sɯso-t-a ri, tɤ-mda tɕe nɤkinɯ, a-ftsa pjɤ-tɯ-ŋu \\
1sg dem who 2-be: fact sfp aor -think- pst: tr - 1sg lnk aor -be.the.time lnk filler 1sg. poss -ZCh ifr. ipfv -2-be \\
`I was wondering who you were, but it turns out that you are my nephew!' (150907 yingning-zh)
0006264#S68
exe

The adverb təmdánə `actually' in Tshobdun is probably grammaticalized from a cognate construction.
summary: The Aorist form *tɤ-mda* of *mdabe the time*, used without a complement clause and after a clause linked by the adversative *ri*, expresses meanings like “actually,” “it turns out that,” or “but in fact,” especially when a referent discovers that reality differs from an earlier belief or expectation. This construction is common in translations from Chinese, corresponding to linkers such as *jiéguǒ* ‘in the end’ and *yuánlái* ‘it turns out that,’ and the rectification clause is always in the Inferential, whether in narration or from the speaker’s perspective.

text:
Neutral additive constructions describe events that are related but for which neither a temporal sequence, a causal nor a hierarchical relationship can be assumed. This type of meaning can be expressed by coordinated clauses (§ sec:coordination ) with the linkers tɕe or qʰe as in ( ex:pjAmenW.tCe ) or parataxis ( ex:YWwxti.YWtshu ).

exe

ʑara χsɯm ma pjɤ-me-nɯ tɕe tɕendɤre nɯ-nɯŋa ci pjɤ-tu. \\
they three apart.from ifr. ipfv -not.exist- pl lnk lnk 3pl. poss -cow indef ifr. ipfv -exist \\
`There were only the three of them, and they had a cow.' (07-deluge)
0003426#S3
exe

exe

ɯ-pʰoŋbu ra ɲɯ-wxti, ɲɯ-tsʰu ʑo. \\
3sg. poss -body pl sens -big sens -fat emph \\
`Its body is big and fat.' (26-GZo)
0003668#S12
exe

A more specific way to indicate neutral addition is the comitative cʰoand, with and its variants cʰondɤre and cʰonɤ (§ sec:comitative ), which are used as a clause linkers in addition to its function as noun phrase coordinator.

exe

mbro sɤznɤ ɲɯ-wxti. ɲɯ-mbro cʰo ɲɯ-wxti. \\
horse comp sens -be.big sens -be.high comit sens -be.big \\
`It is larger than a horse. Higher and larger.' (19-rNamoN)
0003552#S12
exe

The comitative cʰo can follow the linkers qʰe and tɕe when used to link clauses as in ( ex:Zo.qhe.cho ), but notice that the emphatic marker (§ sec:emphatic.Zo ) and the linker ʑo qʰe are repeated in both the clause preceding cʰo and the one following it.

exe

tɕe nɯ ɯ-rɣi a-mɤ-pɯ-ɕe ra ma pjɯ-tsɣi mɤ-cʰa tɕe tɕendɤre a-nɯ-ɤci ʑo qʰe cʰo ftɕar a-kɤ-ndzoʁ ʑo qʰe li tu-ɬoʁ ɕti \\
lnk dem 3sg. poss -grain irr - neg - pfv: down -go be.needed: fact lnk ipfv -be.rotten neg -can: fact lnk lnk irr - pfv -get.wet emph lnk comit summer irr - pfv - acaus:attach emph lnk again ipfv -come.out be. aff: fact \\
`One should not let its grains go into [the ground], because they cannot rot, and when they get wet and the spring comes, they grow again.' (08-qaJAGi)
0003458#S46
exe

The coordinated clauses do not need to have a completely parallel syntactic structure: in ( ex:YWmpCAr.cho.khatoR.GAZu ), the clause preceding cʰo has an adjectival stative predicate, while the second one contains an existential verb with the nominal kʰatoʁvariegated (§ sec:tibetan.colours ).

exe

ɯ-ku nɯra rcanɯ, wuma ʑo ɲɯ-mpɕɤr cʰo kʰatoʁ ʑo ɣɤʑu \\
3sg. poss -head dem: pl unexp: deg really emph sens -be.beautiful comit variegated emph exist: sens \\
`Its head, it is very beautiful, and variegated.' (24-qro)
0003626#S76
exe
summary: Neutral additive constructions express related events without implying sequence, causation, or hierarchy. In this language, they are marked by coordinated clauses with the linkers tɕe or qʰe, by parataxis, or more specifically by the comitative cʰo and its variants, which can also function as clause linkers. The clauses linked by cʰo do not need to be fully parallel in structure, and the emphatic marker and qʰe may be repeated in both clauses.

text:
correlative addition
The correlative (§ sec:correlative.clauses ) additive focus markers tɕi and ri (§ sec:ri.additive ) follow noun phrases in a series of two or more clauses in parataxis. The main verbs of these clauses are often identical and redundant, but are not always necessarily so, as in ( ex:tCi.YWtshi.tCi.YWndze ), where a clause with tsʰidrink is conjoined with clauses with ndzaeat as main verb.

exe

[ɕa] tɕi ɲɯ-ndze, [ɕɤci] tɕi ɲɯ-tsʰi, [tɤ-lu ta-mar] tɕi ɲɯ-ndze \\
meat also sens -eat[III] meat.stew also sens -drink indef. poss -milk indef. poss -butter also sens -eat[III] \\
`[Pigs] eat meat, slurp meat stew, and also eat butter and have milk.' (05-paR)
0003400#S29
exe

These markers can also have scope over verbs, in the existential construction as in ( ex:ri.kWmWm.ri ) or with a modal auxiliary verb as main predicate as ( ex:turWCmi.ri ). The meaning of this construction is `both $X$ and $Y$' when used with positive copulas or modal verbs, and `neither $X$ nor $Y$' with negative ones.

exe

kɯroz kɯ-mɯm ri maŋe, kɯroz mɤ-kɯ-ɣɤ-mɲɤt ri maŋe qʰe, \\
specially sbj: pcp -be.tasty also not.exist: sens specially neg - sbj: pcp - facil -be.spoiled also not.exist: sens lnk \\
` `[Scoring bread] neither [makes it] specially tasty nor really [prevents it from] spoiling.' (160706 thotsi)
0006133#S26
exe

exe

tɕendɤre tu-rɯɕmi ri mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ, cʰɯ-nɯrɤɣo ri mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ ci ɲɤ-k-ɤβzu-ci. \\
lnk ipfv -speak also neg - sbj: pcp -be.possible ipfv -sing also neg - sbj: pcp -be.possible indef ifr - peg -become- peg \\
`She became unable to speak and to sing.' (150819 haidenver-zh)
0006314#S285
exe
summary: The additive focus markers **tɕi** and **ri** follow noun phrases in a series of two or more paratactic clauses, often with repeated main verbs, though the verbs need not always be the same. They can also take scope over verbs in existential or modal constructions, where the meaning is **“both X and Y”** with positive copulas or modals and **“neither X nor Y”** with negative ones.

text:
incremental addition
Four constructions meaning `not only... but also...' (called in Chinese 递进复句 dìjìn fùjùincremental complex clause) are found in Japhug.

First, the locutions ʁo alala ri or ʁo alala ma, comprising the adversative topic marker ʁo (§ sec:adversative.topic ) and the adversative ri (§ sec:concessive.clauses ), can express incremental addition as in ( ex:pjAmpCAr.Roalalari ).

exe

ɯʑo [pjɤ-mpɕɤr] ʁo alala ri, rɤɣo ri pjɤ-mkʰɤz, tɯ-rɟaʁ ri pjɤ-mkʰɤz. \\
3sg ipfv. ifr -be.beautiful advers not.only lnk song also ifr. ipfv -be.expert nmlz: action -dance also ifr. ipfv -be.expert \\
`Not only was he good-looking, he was also very talented at singing and dancing.' (160702 luocha-zh)
0006135#S4
exe

Second, the relator noun ɯ-tɤjɯaddition, This form originates from an alienabilized abstract noun in tɤ- (§ sec:tA.abstract.nouns. from which the denominal verb ɣɤjɯadd was originally derived, has the grammaticalized meaning `in addition to $X$', `not only $X$, but also $Y$' when used as clausal linker as in ( ex:WtAjW.tCe.YWsAzoNzoN ).

exe

[ɕɯ-mŋɤm] ɯ-tɤjɯ tɕe ɲɯ-sɤzoŋzoŋ ʑo ŋu \\
caus -hurt: fact 3sg. poss -addition lnk sens -cause.numbing.sensation emph be: fact \\
`Not only does [nettle] hurt, it also causes a numbing sensation.' (140428 mtshalu)
0003878#S5
exe

The noun ɯ-tɤjɯ can also follow the demonstrative nɯ (§ sec:anaphoric.demonstrative.pro ), anaphorically referring to the preceding clause(s) ( ex:nW.WtAjW.tCe ).

exe

rɟɤlpu nɯ kɯ wuma ʑo (...) tó-wɣ-raχtɕɤz, ɲɤ́-wɣ-mgrɯn. tɕe nɯ ɯ-tɤjɯ tɕe tɕendɤre li iɕqʰa nɯ, ɯ-rʑaβ ra ɲɤ-ɕar. \\
king dem erg really emph ifr - inv -cherish ifr - inv -receive.as.guest lnk dem 3sg. poss -addition lnk lnk again filler dem 3sg. poss -wife pl ifr -search \\
`The king (...) treated him well as a guest, and in addition found a wife for him.' (140511 xinbada-zh)
0003961#S34
exe

Third, the locution mɤra ma, which is possibly grammaticalized form the negative form of the modal verb rabe needed, `be necessary' (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ) with the adversative linker ma (§ sec:concessive.clauses ), also has the same meaning as the constructions described above.

exe

tɯtsɣe ɯ-kɯ-βzu nɯ kɯ paχɕi mɯ-ɲɤ-mbi mɤra ma nɯ sɤznɤ to-nɤmqe tɕe jo-sɯx-ɕe. \\
commerce 3sg. poss -make dem erg apple neg - ifr -give not.only lnk dem comp ifr -scold lnk ifr - caus -go \\
`The merchant not only did not give him an apple, but scolded him and sent him away.' (150904 zhongli-zh)
0006348#S16
exe

Fourth, the form mɤkɯjɤɣ kɯ, from the negative participle or infinitive of either the modal auxiliary jɤɣbe allowed (§ sec:ra.khW.jAG.verb ) or the phasal verb jɤɣfinish (§ sec:phasal.complements ), also means `not only $X$, but' as in ( ex:mAkWjAG.kW ).

exe

tɤ-mtʰɯm nɯra tu-ndze mɤkɯjɤɣ kɯ, ɯ-di ɲɯ-ɕɯ-mnɤm \\
indef. poss -meat dem: pl ipfv -eat[III] not.only erg 3sg. poss -smell sens - caus -smell \\
`Not only does [the mouse] eat meat, it also stinks it up.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S187
exe

When the first clause is in negative form as in ( ex:mAra.ma.nW.sAznA ), the meaning of incremental additive construction is similar to the adversative additive construction with mɤ́ɣrɤzinstead `not only $ X$, but on the contrary $Y$' (§ sec:rectification.clauses ). The locution nɯ sɤz(nɤ) `rather than that, instead' can be added in the second clause.

These first three additive markers also found on noun phrases, instead of subordinate clauses (§ sec:incremental.add.np ).
summary:
Japhug has four constructions expressing incremental addition, meaning roughly “not only... but also...”. These include the locutions ʁo alala ri/ma, the relator noun ɯ-tɤjɯ, the form mɤra ma, and the form mɤkɯjɤɣ kɯ, each with slightly different grammatical origins but the same additive function.

The passage also notes that if the first clause is negative, the construction can resemble an adversative additive meaning “not only X, but on the contrary Y.” In addition, the first three additive markers can also be used with noun phrases rather than subordinate clauses.

text:
exceptive
laʁmaapart from the fact that
The postposition laʁmaapart from the fact that, which derives from the exceptive postposition maapart from (§ sec:exceptive ), cannot take a noun phrase, and requires a finite clause instead, as in ( ex:GWrni.laRma )

exe

tɕe [ɯ-rqʰu nɯ ɣɯrni] laʁma ɯ-ŋgɯ nɯ sɤjku cʰo ɲɯ-naχtɕɯɣ-ndʑi ri \\
lnk 3sg. poss -skin dem be.red: fact apart.from 3sg. poss -inside dem white.birch comit sens -be.the.same- du lnk \\
`Apart from the fact that its bark is red, its inside is the same as that of the white birch.' (06-mbrAj)
0003414#S11
exe

The semantic scope of laʁma can however be a noun phrase, if the verb in the exceptive clause is repeated in the main clause, as in ( ex:mAndze.laRma ).

exe

[kɤ-kɤ-pu kɤ-kɤ-sqa kɯ-fse nɯra mɤ-ndze] laʁma, nɯ ɯ-ro nɯ lonba tu-ndze ɕti. \\
aor - obj: pcp -bake aor - obj: pcp -cook sbj: pcp -be.like dem: pl neg -eat: fact apart.from dem 3sg. poss -rest dem all ipfv -eat be. aff: fact \\
`Apart from the fact that it does not eat food that has been baked or cooked, it eats everything else (=apart from cooked food, it eats everything else).' (19-GzW)
0003536#S11
exe

tɕʰimaʁnɤat least
The linker tɕʰimaʁnɤ or tɕʰimaʁ, optionally combined with tsaʁjust, only, occurs in imperative or hortative sentences with the meaning `at least'. As illustrated by ( ex:tChimaRnA.CWrAfCAttCi ) (where tsaʁ occurs in one version of the story, and does not occur in the other) and ( ex:tChimaR.tsaR ), tɕʰimaʁnɤ is placed at the beginning of the clause, while tsaʁ either follows the verb or a constituent overt which it has scope.

exe

wortɕʰi wojɤr ʑo tɕʰimaʁnɤ a-ɣi ra nɯ-pʰe ɕɯ-rɤfɕɤt-tɕi (tsaʁ) ma tɕetʰa ɣɯ-nɯzdɯɣ-a-nɯ \\
please please emph at.least 1sg. poss -relative pl 3pl. poss - dat tral -tell: fact - 1du just lnk later inv -worry.about: fact - 1sg - pl \\
`Please, at least let the two of us go and inform my relatives, otherwise they will be worried about me.' (qachGa 2012)
0004087#S74
exe

exe

tɕʰimaʁ ``pɯ-tɯ-χɕu" tsaʁ tu-ti-a ma \\
at.least pst. ipfv -2-be.strong just ipfv -say- 1sg lnk \\
`I [should] at least say `thank you'.' (2014-kWlAG)
exe

The linker tɕʰimaʁnɤ is built from the interrogative pronoun tɕʰiwhat (§ sec:tChi ), the negative copula maʁnot be (§ sec:suppletive.negative ) and the postposition nɤ (§ sec:additive.nA ). The original meaning of this locution was probably `whatever it is not', with the free-choice indefinite function of tɕʰi (§ sec:interrogative.indef ).
summary:
The exceptive postposition **laʁma** “apart from the fact that” is derived from **ma** “apart from” and cannot take a noun phrase directly; instead, it requires a finite clause. However, its semantic scope can extend to a noun phrase if the verb of the exceptive clause is repeated in the main clause.  

The linker **tɕʰimaʁnɤ** or **tɕʰimaʁ**, optionally with **tsaʁ** “just, only,” occurs in imperative or hortative clauses with the meaning “at least,” and **tɕʰimaʁnɤ** appears at the beginning of the clause. The form is historically analyzed as coming from an interrogative pronoun, the negative copula, and a postposition, with an original meaning roughly “whatever it is not.”

text:
disjunction
Exclusive disjunction is expressed by the linker nɯmaʁnɤ, either between the two alternative clauses as in ( ex:chWBdenW.YWmbinW ) or in a correlative construction (§ sec:correlative.clauses ), repeated before each clause ( ex:nWmaRnA.tuwGnWxsWr ).

exe

tɕe cʰɯ-βde-nɯ nɯmaʁnɤ fsapaʁ ɲɯ-mbi-nɯ ŋgrɤl ma \\
lnk ipfv -throw- pl otherwise animal ipfv -give- pl be.usually.the.case: fact lnk \\
`(People uproot it and) either they throw it away, or give it to the animals (to eat).' (12-Zmbroko)
0003490#S117
exe

exe

nɯmaʁnɤ tú-wɣ-nɯ-xsɯr, nɯmaʁnɤ <ban> tú-wɣ-βzu tɕe. \\
otherwise ipfv - inv - auto -fry otherwise mix ipfv - inv -make lnk \\
`People either fry it, or mix it in salad.' (conversation 14-05-10)
exe

The linker nɯmaʁnɤotherwise has stress on the second syllable ( nɯmáʁnɤ ), and transparently comes from the demonstrative nɯ (§ sec:anaphoric.demonstrative.pro ), the copula maʁnot be (§ sec:suppletive.negative ) and the adposition nɤ, probably from what originally was the protasis of a conditional construction `if it is not', with initial reduplication $ $ nɯ mɯ maʁ nɤ or Interrogative $ $ nɯ ɯ́-maʁ nɤ (§ sec:real.conditional, § sec:redp.protasis ).

In questions, disjunction between several clauses can be express by adding the interrogative particle ɕi after each clause except the last, as in ( ex:tWnWCe.Ci ).

exe

χsɤr rɟɤskɤt ɯ-taʁ tɯ-nɯ-ɕe ɕi, rŋɯl rɟɤskɤt ɯ-taʁ tɯ-nɯ-ɕe ɕi, ɕom rɟɤskɤt ɯ-taʁ tɯ-nɯ-ɕe ɕi,
si rɟɤskɤt ɯ-taʁ tɯ-nɯ-ɕe? \\
gold stairs 3sg. poss -on 2- auto -go: fact sfp silver stairs 3sg. poss -on 2- auto -go: fact sfp iron stairs 3sg. poss -on 2- auto -go: fact sfp wood stairs 3sg. poss -on 2- auto -go: fact \\
`Will you go on the golden stairs, the silver stairs, the iron stairs, or the wooden stairs? (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

Both nɯmaʁnɤotherwise and ɕi are only very rarely used with noun phrases instead of clauses (§ sec:disjunction.nouns ).
summary: Exclusive disjunction is expressed by the linker **nɯmaʁnɤ**, which can appear either between two alternative clauses or in a correlative construction before each clause. In questions, disjunction among several clauses can also be marked by adding the interrogative particle **ɕi** after each clause except the last. Both **nɯmaʁnɤ** and **ɕi** are only very rarely used with noun phrases rather than clauses.

text:
degree
This section describes the constructions available to express the absolute degree of a property of a referent, without standard of comparison.

All degree constructions can be used with the emphatic marker ʑo, either following a degree adverb, or in sentence-final position (§ sec:postverbal.adv ).
summary: The section describes constructions used to express the absolute degree of a property of a referent, without comparison to a standard. It also notes that all degree constructions can take the emphatic marker ʑo, which may appear after a degree adverb or in sentence-final position.

text:
adverb!degree
Degree adverbs in Japhug are intensifiers meaning `really, much, very, a lot'. There is also a comparative degree adverb mɤʑɯeven more (treated in § sec:mAZW below) and a superlative adverb stumost (§ sec:stu.superlative ). There are no adverbs indicating a degree above or under a limit such as `too much' or `not enough'; the degree nominal construction must be used instead to express this meaning (§ sec:degree.monoclausal ).

wumareal, really
The most common intensifier in Japhug is wuma `really', from Tibetan ངོ་མ་ŋo.mareal, true. While marginally attested as a postnominal attribute meaning `real' (§ ex:attributive.postnominal ), its most widespread function is to serve as clausal intensifier, with ( ex:wuma.Zo.YWNgWtCi ) or without ( ex:wuma.YWNgWtCi ) the emphatic marker ʑo.

exe

xlist

nɯra ɲɯ-fse tɕe wuma ʑo ɲɯ-ŋgɯ-tɕi \\
dem: pl sens -be.like lnk really emph sens -be.poor- 1du \\
`We are very poor like that.' (divination)

a-mu cʰo wuma ɲɯ-ŋgɯ-tɕi \\
1sg. poss -mother comit really sens -be.poor- 1du \\
`My mother and I are very poor.' (divination)
xlist
exe

The intensifier is not necessarily adjacent to the verb, and some constituents can be inserted, for instance absolutive nouns in essive function (§ sec:essive.abs ) such as tɯrme `as a person' in ( ex:wuma.Zo.tWrme.pe ).

exe

ɯ-χti nɯ wuma ʑo tɯrme pe ma \\
3sg. poss -companion dem really emph person be.good: fact lnk \\
`Her husband is a very nice person.' (`he is very nice as a person.') (14-siblings)
0003508#S315
exe

The flexibility in the position of wuma can be useful to distinguish head-internal relatives from postnominal ones (§ ex:attributive.participles.stative.verbs, § sec:head-internal.relative, § sec:intr.subj.head.noun.position ).

The intensifier wuma is not restricted to adjectival stative verbs. It can be used with tropative verbs (§ sec:tropative ) as in ( ex:wuma.YWnAmNAm ), but also modal verbs such as cʰacan (§ sec:cha.verb ) and action verbs that do not have an intrinsic degree parameter such as ndzaeat ( ex:wuma.Zo.ndze ).

exe

tɕe nɯ tɤ́-wɣ-tɕɤt tɕe nɯŋa nɯ kɯ wuma ɲɯ-nɤ-mŋɤm \\
lnk dem aor - inv -take.out lnk cow dem erg really sens - trop -hurt \\
`When one removes (the parasite by squeezing it out), the cow finds it very painful.' (25-zrW)
0003666#S26
exe

exe

maka tɤɕi qaj nɯra wuma ʑo ndze. \\
at.all barley wheat dem: pl really emph eat[III]: fact \\
`[The dove] eats wheat and barley a lot.' (22-CAGpGa)
0003586#S29
exe

When cʰacan takes an infinite complement, wuma generally follows the complement clause, as in ( ex:wuma.Zo.chaa ), whereas with finite complements it is generally located inside of the complement clause ( ex:wuma.tusApe.cha ).

exe

[si kɤ-pʰaʁ] wuma ʑo cʰa-a \\
tree inf -chop really emph can: fact - 1sg \\
`I am very good at felling trees.' (2011-10-qajdo)
exe

exe

tɯ-ji ɯ-ŋgɯ zɯ tsʰɤt ɯ-ɣli nɯ cʰɯ́-wɣ-lɤt tɕe, [tɤ-rɤku wuma ʑo tu-sɤpe] cʰa \\
indef. poss -field 3sg. poss -in loc goat 3sg. poss -manure dem ipfv - inv -release lnk indef. poss -crops really emph ipfv -do.well can: fact \\
`If one spreads goat manure on the fields, it can make the crops (grow) really well.' (05-qaZo)
0003404#S28

The intensifier wuma can be combined with stʰɯciso much (§ sec:denominal.adverb.s.prefix ).

exe

nɯ fsapaʁ ra kɯ ndza-nɯ ri, wuma stʰɯci mɤ-rga-nɯ. \\
dem animal pl erg eat: fact - pl lnk really so.much neg -like: fact - pl \\
`The animals eat it, but don't like it so much.' (12-Zmbroko)
0003490#S97

kʰromuch
The adverbs kʰromuch and ʑimkʰɤmmuch can serve as intensifiers of noun phrases (§ sec:nominal.intensifier ) but can also have scope over the whole clause, in pre-verbal position. Unlike wuma and nɯstʰɯci/kɯstʰɯci (§ sec:nWtshWci ), they are more often used with action verbs, and can both refer to the quantity and intensity of actions (`much', `a lot') or to the time taken by the action (`for a long time'), as in ( ex:khro.Zo.pjANke ) and ( ex:khro.Zo.YACar ), respectively.

exe

kʰro ʑo pjɤ-ŋke pjɤ-ra tɕendɤre, pjɤ-nɯʑɯβ. \\
much emph ifr. ipfv -walk ifr. ipfv -be.needed lnk ifr -sleep \\
`He had had to walk a lot (on that day, was very tired), and fell asleep.' (140430 yufu he tade qizi-zh)
0003900#S224
exe

exe

kʰro ʑo ɲɤ-ɕar ri mɯ-pjɤ-mto \\
much emph ifr -search lnk neg - ifr -see \\
`[The prince] looked for her for a long time, but could not find her.' (140504 huiguniang-zh)
0003909#S181
exe

Both intensifiers can be reduplicated as kʰɯ kʰro and ʑɯ ʑimkʰɤm as in ( ex:ZWZWmkhAm.Zo.YAnAthWthu ).

exe

ʑɯ ʑimkʰɤm ʑo aʁɤndɯndɤt ʑo ɲɤ-nɤtʰɯtʰu \\
emph much emph everywhere emph ifr - distr:ask \\
`[The bear] asked around [about the rabbit] everywhere for a long time.' (2011-13-qala)
exe

The adverb ʑimkʰɤm comes from ཞིང་ཁམས་ʑiŋ.kʰamscountry, universe (also borrowed as the noun ʑiŋkʰɤmcountry, realm, sometimes also pronounced ʑimkʰɤm ), and its grammaticalization as an intensifier perhaps went through a semantic change `universe' $ $ `in the whole universe, universally' $ $ `everywhere' $ $ `for a long time; much'.

Demonstrative+ stʰɯciso much
The combination of anaphoric demonstratives (§ sec:demonstrative.pronouns ) with the adverbs stʰɯciso much and stʰamtɕɤtso much (§ sec:denominal.adverb.s.prefix ) expresses the meaning `so (much)'.

The demonstratives can be in free form, but can also merge with stʰɯci and stʰamtɕɤt into the degree adverbs kɯstʰɯcithis much ( ex:ri.kWsthWci.WWmpCar ), nɯstʰɯcithat much, kɯstʰamtɕɤtthis much and nɯstʰamtɕɤtthat much ( ex:nWsthamtCAt.pjAmpCAr ).

exe

a-rʑaβ ri kɯstʰɯci ɲɯ-mpɕɤr, a-mbro ri kɯstʰɯci ɲɯ-ʑru, a-pɣɤtɕɯ ri kɯstʰɯci ɲɯ-mpɕɤr \\
1sg. poss -wife also so.much sens -be.beautiful 1sg. poss -horse also so.much sens -be.strong 1sg. poss -bird also so.much sens -be.beautiful \\
`My wife is so beautiful, my horse so strong, my bird so beautiful.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S119
exe

These degree adverbs can directly precede the verb as in ( ex:ri.kWsthWci.WWmpCar ), but can also occur before the subject as in ( ex:nWsthamtCAt.pjAmpCAr ).

exe
