summary: Japhug has several degree adverbs, including intensifiers meaning “really, much, very, a lot,” plus comparative and superlative forms, but it lacks adverbs meaning degrees beyond or below a limit such as “too much” or “not enough.” The most common intensifier is **wuma** “really,” which can function clause-wide with or without the emphatic marker ʑo, and it is flexible in position and can modify stative verbs, tropative verbs, modal verbs, and action verbs. Other intensifiers like **kʰro** and **ʑimkʰɤm** may scope over the clause and can refer either to quantity/intensity or to duration, while demonstratives combined with **stʰɯci** or **stʰamtɕɤt** express “so much” and can appear either as merged degree adverbs or in free combinations.

text:
tʰɯ-kɯ-ndʐaβ nɯ to-ndzur qʰe, li pjɤ-rɟaʁ. nɯstʰamtɕɤt ʑo iɕqʰa ɯ-ɟuli nɯ pjɤ-mpɕɤr. \\
aor - sbj: pcp - acaus:cause.to.roll dem ifr -stand lnk again ifr -dance that.much emph the.aforementioned 3sg. poss -flute dem ifr. ipfv -be.beautiful \\
`(The rich man$_i$ started dancing under the influence of the music and fell down). The one$_i$ who had fallen down stood up and danced again. This was the extent to which [the shepherd boy's] flute [music] was beautiful.' (`his flute music was that beautiful') (140513 mutong de disheng-zh)
0003977#S149
exe

The demonstrative can anaphorically refer to a previous entity or a previous clause, as in ( ex:nWsthamtCAt.pjAmpCAr ), where it is focalized. Although from a text translated from Chinese, this sentence was added by Tshendzin and is not in the original.
summary: The passage shows that the demonstrative can anaphorically refer either to a previous entity or to an entire preceding clause, and in this example it is focalized. The author notes that although the sentence comes from a text translated from Chinese, it was added by Tshendzin and does not occur in the original.

text:
The unexpected/high degree marker rcanɯ or rca indicates that the situation or action described by the predicate that follows is unexpected ( ex:nAZo.rcanW ), intensifies to a noticeable (and not foreseeable) extent ( ex:tokAnWmqajndZic.tCe.rcanW ) or occurs with a remarkably high degree or intensity, with ( ex:mbro.rcanW ) or without ( ex:apWme.rcanW ) surprise.

exe

wo nɤʑo rcanɯ tɕʰi ɲɯ-tɯ-nɤme ŋu ma, aʑo tɯ-mɯ kɯ pɯ-kɯ-sɯ-χtɕi-a, tɤndʐo nɯ! \\
interj 2sg unexp: deg what sens -2-do[III] be: fact lnk 1sg indef. poss -sky erg aor -2 1- caus -wash- 1sg cold sfp \\
`You, what are you doing, you caused me to be drenched by the rain.' (kWlAG 2014) \\
exe

exe

to-k-ɤnɯmqaj-ndʑi-ci tɕe rcanɯ, ʑɯrɯʑɤri tɕe ko-k-ɤndɯndo-ndʑi-ci, \\
ifr - peg - recip:scold- du - evd lnk unexp: deg progressively lnk ifr - peg - recip:take- du - peg \\
`They scolded each other and progressively started to fight, ' (lWlu2002)
exe

exe

mbro rcanɯ ɯ-xɕɤt kɯ-tɯ tu ʑo nɯ-ntsʰɤr ɲɯ-nu, \\
horse unexp: deg 3sg. poss -strength sbj: pcp - emph exist emph aor -neigh sens -be \\
`The horse neighed with all his strength.' (2003 qachGa)
0003372#S57
exe

The adverb rcanɯ is particularly common in the degree construction with a tɯ- degree nominal (§ sec:degree.nominals ), as in ( ex:apWme.rcanW ). In this particular construction, rcanɯ does not necessarily express unexpectedness.

exe

tɕe nɯnɯ lɯlu a-pɯ-me rcanɯ, βʑɯ ɯ-tɯ-ŋɤn saχaʁ. \\
lnk dem cat irr - ipfv -not.exist unexp: deg mouse
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.evil be.extremely: fact \\
`If there are no cats, the mice are extremely fierce (cause a lot of damages).' (21-lWlu)
0003576#S32
exe

In addition to its function as a degree adverb, rcanɯ also contributes to information structure: it marks the constituent preceding it as a topic, and the part of the sentence following it as a focus.
summary: The marker **rcanɯ/rca** indicates that the following situation or action is unexpected, or that it occurs with a noticeably high degree or intensity, sometimes with surprise and sometimes without. It is especially common in degree constructions with **tɯ-** degree nominals, where it may simply mark intensity rather than unexpectedness. In addition, **rcanɯ** has an information-structural function: it marks the preceding constituent as topic and the following part of the sentence as focus.

text:
The emphatic marker ʑo is one of the most common words in Japhug. It is never obligatory, but frequently occurs after all the intensifiers described above.

It is one of the few adverbs that can follow the main verb (§ sec:postverbal.adv, § sec:relative.postverbal ), in particular with the stative verb saχaʁbe extremely as in (§ ex:pjasaXaR.Zo ).

exe

tɤŋe ɯ-rkɯ tɤ-armbat qʰe ɯ-tɯ-sɤ-ɕke pjɤ-saχaʁ ʑo ri \\
sun 3sg. poss -side aor: up -be.near lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - prop -burn ifr. ipfv -be.extremely emph lnk \\
`When he approached the sun, it was extremely hot.' (31-deluge)
0004077#S110
exe

It also occurs after ideophones (§ sec:idph.syntax ) and deideophonic verbs (§ sec:voice.deideophonic ).

With personal pronouns, the emphatic ʑo can mean `by oneself', as in ( ex:aZo.Zo ) (§ sec:pronouns.emph ).

exe

aʑo ʑo nɯnɯ ɕ-pjɯ-sat-a ra \\
1sg emph dem tral - ipfv -kill- 1sg be.needed: fact \\
`I have to kill her myself.' (140504 baixuegongzhu)
0003907#S113
exe

It also appears on various types of subordinate clauses, in particular manner (including serial verb constructions § sec:svc.simultaneous and converbial clauses § sec:manner.converbs, § sec:gerund.clauses ), temporal (§ sec:immediate.converb, § sec:iterative.coincidence.clause ), conditional (§ sec:universal.concessive.conditional ) and neutral addition clauses (§ sec:neutral.addition ).

The emphatic marker may be historically related to the -ʑo stem of personal pronouns (§ sec:pers.pronouns ) or, alternatively, be a cognate to the Tibetan particle ཡང་jaŋalso, even.
summary:
The emphatic marker ʑo is a very common but non-obligatory word in Japhug, often appearing after intensifiers and functioning as one of the few adverbs that can follow the main verb. It also occurs after ideophones, deideophonic verbs, personal pronouns—where it can mean “by oneself”—and on several kinds of subordinate clauses, including manner, temporal, conditional, and neutral addition clauses.  

The passage notes that ʑo may be historically related either to the -ʑo stem of personal pronouns or to Tibetan ཡང་ jaŋ ‘also, even’.

text:
nominalization!degree
An alternative way to indicate the degree of a stative predicate is to use degree nominals (§ sec:degree.nominals, § sec:degree.nominal.construction ) as intransitive subjects of degree verbs like saχaʁbe extremely, sɤrebe ridiculous, `be extremely' ( ex:axtu.WtWmNAm ), tɕʰombe too much ( ex:natWxtCi.tChom ) or rtaʁbe enough ( ex:WtWrnaR.mWjrtaR ). The TAME is expressed on the degree verb, which is always in 3sg (§ sec:intransitive.invariable ). Degree nominals can also serve as possessors of the subject ɯ-grɤlorder, rule in the collocation ɯ-grɤl+me `be extremely' (example ex:WtWsAGmu.WgrAl.maNe in § sec:existential.light.verbs ).

exe

aʑo kɯnɤ a-xtu ɯ-tɯ-mŋɤm ɲɯ-sɤre ʑo \\
1sg also 1sg. poss -belly 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -hurt sens -be.extremely emph \\
`Me too, my belly hurts a lot.' (literally: `the degree of my hurting is ridiculously high') (qala 2002)
exe

exe

kɯki tɯ-ci ki ɯ-tɯ-rnaʁ mɯ́j-rtaʁ \\
dem. prox indef. poss -water dem. prox 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.deep neg: sens -be.enough \\
`This water is not deep enough.' (2010-03-zh)
exe

The use of sɤre as degree verbs illustrates a semantic change from `funny, ridiculous' to intensifier, similar to that of French drôlement ( drôlement difficile ) or of English ridiculously ( ridiculously difficult ).

The possessive prefix is coreferent with the entity whose property is referred to by the nominalized verb, for instance 2sg in ( ex:natWxtCi.tChom ).

exe

nɤʑo nɤ-tɯ-xtɕi tɕʰom-o \\
2sg 2sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.small be.too.much: fact - sfp \\
`You are too young.' (150828 huamulan-zh)
0006396#S28
exe

Causative forms of degree verbs (§ sec:sig.caus.stative ), for instance ɣɤtɕʰomcause to be too much, can also be occur with degree nominals, as in ( ex:WtWCqraR.tAGAtChoma ).

exe

kɯki maka ɯ-tɯ-ɕqraʁ tɤ-ɣɤ-tɕʰom-a ɯβrɤ-ŋu ɣe? \\
dem. prox at.all 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.intelligent aor - caus -be.too.much- 1sg rh. q -be: fact sfp \\
`I hope that I did not cause her to become too intelligent.' (hist160709 riquet6-v2)
0006159#S11
exe

With naχtɕɯɣbe the same as degree verb, the degree construction becomes an equative construction (§ sec:equative ), with the comitative postposition cʰoand, with (§ sec:comitative ).

exe

ʑmbri cʰo ɯ-tɯ-wxti naχtɕɯɣ \\
willow comit 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.big be.the.same: fact \\
`It is as big as a willow (its degree of ``bigness" is the same as that of a willow).' (08-qaCti)
0003456#S7
exe

The lexicalized infinitive form kɤ-ti of the verb tisay and the ergative can optionally follow the degree nominal ( ex:ndZitWNgW.kAti.kW ).

exe

kɤtsa ni ndʑi-tɯ-ŋgɯ kɤ-ti kɯ pɯ-saχaʁ ʑo \\
parent.and.child du 3du. poss - nmlz: deg -be.poor inf -say erg pst. ipfv -be.extremely emph \\
`The mother and her child were extremely poor.' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

Degree nouns are not the only type of nouns that can occur in this construction. Abstract nouns in tɤ- (§ sec:tA.abstract.nouns ) such as tɤɕpaʁthirst ( ex:tACpaR.kAti.kW ) or underived abstract nouns such as rɤŋomoutrage can also be used, though much less commonly. This construction however differs from the previous one in that the degree verb saχaʁ indexes the experiencer as intransitive subject ( 3pl in ex:tACpaR.kAti.kW ).

exe

tɤ-ɕpaʁ kɤ-ti kɯ pɯ-saχaʁ-nɯ ʑo pɯ-rɤʑi-nɯ ɲɯ-ŋu \\
nmlz: abstract -thirst inf -say erg pst. ipfv -be.extremely- pl emph pst. ipfv -stay- pl sens -be \\
`[The people there] live in extreme thirst.' (divination 2005)
exe

Example ( ex:tACpaR.kAti.kW ) is in addition a hybrid construction combining the abstract nominal and the degree verb with a serial verb construction of degree (§ sec:degree.svc ).

Without a degree verb, degree nominals and other abstract nouns can be used as predicates to express high degree in exclamation (§ sec:degree.nominal.predicates ), often with the sentence final particle nɯ, as in ( ex:nAtWsAjndAt ).

exe

nɤ-tɯ-sɤjndɤt nɯ! \\
2sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.cute sfp \\
`You are so cute!' (heard in context)
exe
summary:
Degree nominals can function as intransitive subjects of degree verbs to express the intensity of a stative predicate, with tense-aspect-mood marking on the degree verb itself, which is always in the 3sg form. The possessive prefix on the nominalized form refers to the entity whose property is being measured, and the construction can also occur with causative degree verbs, equative uses of naχtɕɯɣ, or optionally with an infinitive and ergative.  

The passage also notes that other abstract nouns may appear in similar constructions, though less commonly, and that without a degree verb these nominalized forms can serve as predicates in exclamations to express high degree. It further observes a semantic shift in sɤre from ‘funny, ridiculous’ to an intensifier.

text:
Degree nominals and abstract nouns can also occur with the ergative marker kɯ followed by a finite clause describing a consequence or a particular aspect of the high degree reached (`so $X$ that $Y$'; in the following, the clause $X$ is referred to as `degree clause', and $Y$ as `consequence clause'), as in ( ex:WtWnAmbju.kW ). This type of construction is a subtype of causality clause linking (§ sec:causality ).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-nɤmbju kɯ [rɟɤlpu kʰɤxtɤndo kɯ-nɯjaŋsa nɯ ɣɯ ɯ-mɲaʁ na-z-nɤmbju ʑo ɲɯ-ŋu]. \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.shiny erg king side.of.the.roof sbj: pcp -be.idle dem gen 3sg. poss -eye aor:3 - caus -be.shiny emph sens -be\\
`It was so shiny that it dazzled the eyes of the king, who was staying idle on the side of the roof (of the palace).' (2005 Norbzang)
exe

It is possible for several degree nominals to share a consequence clause. For instance, in ( ex:atAGWzrWG.kW ), the degree nouns nɯ-tɯ-ɤɣɯzrɯɣ and a-tɯ-ɤɣɯzrɯɣ are followed by only one marker kɯ and have a common consequence clause mɯ́j-cha-a. Here, the additional clause ci tu-pe tɕe `putting together' specifies that it is the conjoined quantity (of lice) referred by the two degree nominals that is the cause of the consequence clause, and therefore implies that the absence of a consequence clause just after the first degree noun nɯ-tɯ-ɤɣɯzrɯɣ is not due to ellipsis.

exe

paʁ ra ci nɯ-tɯ-ɤɣɯzrɯɣ, aʑo ci a-tɯ-ɤɣɯzrɯɣ kɯ [ci tu-pe tɕe mɯ́j-cʰa-a] \\
pig pl one 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -have.a.lot.of.lice 1sg one 1sg. poss - nmlz: deg -have.a.lot.of.lice erg one ipfv -do[III] lnk neg: sens -can- 1sg \\
`Pigs have so many lice and I have so many lice that all put together, I can't bear it.' (2005 Kunbzang)
exe

As in the monoclausal construction, the lexicalized infinitive form kɤ-ti of tisay can optionally be added before the ergative, as in ( ex:kAti.kW.WCtsxi.tolhoR ) (see also ex:tWphoNbu.kAndo, § sec:ndo.lv ).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-ɲat kɤ-ti kɯ [ɯ-ɕtʂi ra to-ɬoʁ.] \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.tired inf -say erg 3sg. poss -sweat pl ifr -come.out \\
`He was so tired that he started sweating (profusely).' (140513 mutong de disheng-zh)
0003977#S65
exe

The same meaning `... is so $X$ that...' can also be expressed by a finite clause $X$ followed by the relator noun ɯ-xɕɤtstrength with the ergative kɯ (§ sec:IPN.cause, § sec:causal.clauses ), as in ( ex:YWmaqhu.WxCAt.kW ).

exe

ɲɯ-maqʰu ɯ-xɕɤt kɯ, [kɯ-fsoʁ tɤ-rɤŋgat ri kóʁmɯz tu-ɬoʁ ŋu.] \\
ipfv -be.after 3sg. poss -strength erg sbj: pcp -be.light aor -be.about loc only.then ipfv -come.out be: fact \\
`[This star] is so late that it only comes out when the day is about to break.' (29-mWBZi)
0003728#S40
exe
summary:
Degree nominals and abstract nouns can take the ergative marker kɯ plus a finite consequence clause to express meanings like “so X that Y,” where X is the degree clause and Y the consequence clause. Several degree nominals may share one consequence clause, and an added clause can show that the shared consequence applies to the combined quantity rather than being omitted after the first noun.

The same meaning can also be expressed with a finite clause followed by the relator noun ɯ-xɕɤt ‘strength’ plus kɯ. An optional lexicalized infinitive kɤ-ti may appear before kɯ in this construction.

text:
serial verb construction
Some stative verbs of degree (in particular tɕʰombe too much and rtaʁbe enough) can occur in a serial verb construction (§ sec:svc.degree ) with the same meaning as the monoclausal degree construction (§ sec:degree.monoclausal ): examples ( ex:WtWxtCi.YWtChom ) and ( ex:YWxtCi.YWtChom ) are synonymous, though the former is more frequent.

exe

xlist

ɯ-tɯ-xtɕi ɲɯ-tɕʰom \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.small sens -be.too.much \\

ɲɯ-xtɕi ɲɯ-tɕʰom \\
sens -be.small sens -be.too.much \\
`It is too small.' (elicited)
xlist
exe

The serial verb construction as a whole can serve as a complement clause, as in ( ex:tudAn.tutChom ) where the constituent between square brackets is the subject of the verb mɯ́j-pe `it is not good' (§ sec:adjective.complement ).

exe

[nɯŋa ra nɯ-taʁ tu-dɤn tu-tɕʰom] mɯ́j-pe ma \\
cow pl 3pl. poss -on ipfv -be.many ipfv -be.too.much neg: sens -be.good lnk \\
`It is not good when there are too many (ticks) on cows.' (25-xCelwi)
0003664#S30
exe
summary: Some stative degree verbs, especially tɕʰombe ‘too much’ and rtaʁbe ‘enough’, can appear in a serial verb construction with the same meaning as the monoclausal degree construction, though the serial verb form is more frequent. The whole serial verb construction can also function as a complement clause, as in the example where the bracketed sequence serves as the subject of mɯ́j-pe ‘it is not good’.

text:
exceptive
A manner clause (§ sec:manner.clauses ) containing the exceptive phrase nɯ ma `apart from that' (§ sec:exceptive ) and a negative verb form can convey an extreme degree, as in ( ex:nW.mA.XXX.Zo.YWrgaa ). Example ( ex:nW.ma.mWjkhW.Zo ) is a rendering of Chinese 我表示十二分地满意 <wǒ biǎoshì shíèr fēn de mǎnyì>, a sentence that plays on the expression 十分满意 shífēn mǎnyì100% satisfied.

exe

xlist

nɯ ma aʑo maka, kɤ-nɯ-rga mɯ́j-kʰɯ ʑo ɲɯ-rga-a \\
dem apart.from 1sg at.all inf - appl -like neg: sens -be.possible emph sens -like- 1sg \\
`I like it a lot (to the extent that it is not possible to like it more than I do).' (140521 huangdi de xinzhuang-zh)
0004047#S126

nɯ ma kɤ-nɯ-rga mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ ʑo ɲɯ-rga-a \\
dem apart.from inf - appl -like neg - inf: stat -be.possible emph sens -like- 1sg \\
`I like it a lot.' (elicitation based on ex:nW.ma.mWjkhW.Zo )
xlist
exe
summary: The passage explains that a manner clause containing the exceptive phrase *nɯ ma* “apart from that” plus a negative verb form can express an extreme degree. This construction is illustrated with examples meaning “I like it a lot,” literally suggesting that it is not possible to like something more. It is also compared to a Chinese expression meaning “100% satisfied,” built on a similar “very satisfied” phrase.

text:
comparative
Adjectival stative verbs in Japhug do not have specific comparative or superlative forms, There is one potential example of a comparative derivation in Japhug between snabe good, be worthy and mnabe better (§ sec:mna.sna ), but in the additional examples, this remains speculative. and comparison is expressed by means of postpositions, adverbs or verbs marking relative degree.

The postpositions sɤz and kɯ
As illustrated in ( ex:comparative1 ), it is possible in Japhug to mark both the standard of comparison (by the postposition sɤz `than', § sec:comparative ), and the comparee (by the ergative kɯ (§ sec:comparee.kW ). In this section, the term ``standard marker'' ( std. mrk ) corresponds to Dixon's ( dixon08comparative) mark. The ``comparee marker'' ( cmp. mrk ) could be equated with Dixon's index.

exe

ɯ-ʁi sɤz ɯ-pi nɯ kɯ mpɕɤr \\
3sg. poss -younger.sibling comp 3sg. poss -elder.sibling dem erg be.beautiful: fact \\
standard std. mrk comparee cmp. mrk parameter \\
`The elder sibling is more beautiful than the younger sibling.' (elicited)
exe

The comparee marker is optional when the standard phrase is overt, as shown by ( ex:aZo.sAz.wxti ), where the comparee ɯ-rʑaβ `his wife' is in absolutive form.

exe

ɯ-rʑaβ aʑo sɤz wxti \\
3sg. poss -wife 1sg comp be.big: fact \\
`His wife is older than me.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S179
exe

This construction is exclusively used for comparisons of superiority. To express comparison of inferiority, one either has to select the antonym of the parameter, or to reformulate with another construction such as that with egressive postpositions (§ sec:egressive.comparative ).

The standard marker can follow a genitive postpositional phrase, when the entities being compared are possessees, and the second one is elided, as in ( ex:GW.sAz.YWwxti ). The genitive is however optional in this context, as shown by ( ex:mbro.sAz.YWwxti ), when we find mbro sɤz instead of expected mbro ɣɯ sɤz.

exe

ɯ-rna nɯ [mbro ɣɯ] sɤz ɲɯ-wxti. \\
3sg. poss -ear dem horse gen comp sens -be.big \\
`Its ears are bigger than those of the horse.' (20-tArka)
0003566#S5
exe

exe

tɕeri ɯ-pʰoŋbu nɯ mbro sɤz koŋla ʑo ɲɯ-wxti. \\
lnk 3sg. poss -body dem horse comp really emph sens -be.big \\
`Its body is bigger than [that of] a horse.' (19-rNamoN)
0003552#S34
exe

When the standard is not overt, the comparee markers kɯ (as in ex:qandzxe.kW.YWjpum ) or mɤʑɯ (§ sec:mAZW ). obligatory.

exe

tɯ-ɣli kɯ-dɤn ɯ-stu qandʐe nɯ kɯ ɲɯ-jpum. \\
indef. poss -dung sbj: pcp -be.many 3sg. poss -place earthworm dem erg sens -be.thick \\
`The earthworms that are in places where there is a lot of dung (fertilizer) are fatter.' (25-akWzgumba)
0003632#S117
exe

The comparee marker kɯ can occur on the possessor of the comparee rather than on the comparee itself, as in ( ex:aZo.kW.alaz ).

exe

aʑo kɯ a-laz ɲɯ-sna \\
1sg erg 1sg. poss -karma sens -be.good \\
`I am luckier [than you].' (140515 huli he yelv-zh)
0004002#S18
exe

The parameter indexes the comparee, never the standard, as shown in ( ex:sAz.YWtWrZi ), where the main verb has 2sg indexation. The comparee can be relativized like a normal intransitive subject (§ comparee.relativization ), but the standard cannot (§ sec:accessibility.relativization ).

exe

tɤru ɯ-tɕɯ nɯ sɤz ɲɯ-tɯ-rʑi! \\
chieftain 3sg. poss -son dem comp sens -2-be.heavy \\
`You are heavier than the prince!' (140506 woju guniang-zh)
0003929#S131
exe

The parameter can be combined with exceptive phrases
with maapart from (§ sec:exceptive ) containing counted nouns, to specify more precisely the difference in degree between the two referents as in ( ex:sAz.YWtWrZi ).

exe

waŋtɕin sɤznɤ ʁnɯ-pɤrme ma mɤ-xtɕi \\
anthr comp [two-years apart.from] neg -be.small: fact \\
`He is only two years younger than Dbangcan.' (14-siblings)
0003508#S219
exe

Comparees and standards are generally nouns, noun phrases or postpositional phrases as in the examples above, but can also be temporal adverbs ( ex:comparative2 ) or subordinate clauses, in the Irrealis (§ sec:irrealis ), or other modal categories as in ( ex:apWsi.kW ). The original Chinese is 还不如死了算了 háibùrú sǐ le suànleIt is better if he dies. The use of the ergative in rectification subordinate clauses (§ sec:rectification.clauses ) is historically related to this construction.

exe

jɯfɕɯr sɤz jɯsŋi kɯ ɲɯ-mpja \\
yesterday comp today erg sens -be.warm \\
`Today is warmer than yesterday.' (elicited)
exe

exe

nɯ sɤznɤ [a-pɯ-si] kɯ ɲɯ-mna \\
dem comp irr - pfv -die erg sens -be.better \\
`It is better that he dies.' (150909 xiaocui-zh)
0006386#S108
exe

Intensifier tsaa little
The degree adverb tsaa little, one of the very rare adverbs to occur postverbally (§ sec:postverbal.adv ), can by itself express comparison of superiority as in ( ex:YWtCur.tsa ).

exe

kɯ-mɤku cʰɯ-kɯ-tɯt nɯ ɲɯ-tɕur tsa \\
sbj: pcp -be.first ipfv - sbj: pcp -ripen dem sens -be.sour a.little\\
`The [variety of apple] that ripens earlier is a bit sourer.' (07-paXCi)
0003430#S42
exe

It can be combined with an overt standard marked by either sɤz `than' ( ex:sAz.YWwxti.tsa ) or stʰɯciso much (example ex:YWrYJi.tsa, § sec:postverbal.adv ).

exe

ʁmɯrcɯ sɤz ɲɯ-wxti tsa \\
Garrulax comp sens -be.big a.little \\
`It is a bit bigger than the Garrulax sp.' (23-qapGAmtWmtW)
0003608#S12
exe

The negative verb neg + ʑɯ `(not) just be'
comparative negative
The verb neg +ʑɯnot just be, which requires a negative prefix (§ sec:obligatory.negative ) serves to build another comparative construction. It takes as semi-object the standard, and can be followed by the adverb jamarabout and a verb in parataxis specifying the parameter of comparison as in ( ex:mWjZW.jamar ).

exe

tɤɕi ɯ-rdoʁ mɯ́j-ʑɯ jamar ɲɯ-wxti \\
barley 3sg. poss -grain neg: sens -just.be about sens -be.big \\
`It is a little bigger than a grain of barley.' (28-kWpAz,104)
0003714#S97
exe

The infinitive form mɤ-kɯ-ʑɯ of neg +ʑɯnot just be is attested in manner converb function (§ sec:inf.converb, § sec:manner.converbs ) as in ( ex:mAkWZW.Zo.YWjpum ).

exe
summary: Japhug adjectival stative verbs do not have dedicated comparative or superlative forms; instead, comparison is expressed through postpositions, adverbs, or verbs marking relative degree. The main comparative construction uses sɤz “than” for the standard and optionally kɯ for the comparee, and it is used only for superiority, while inferiority requires other strategies. Additional comparative expressions include the postverbal intensifier tsa “a little” and the negative verb mɯ́j-ʑɯ “not just be,” which can also form comparative meaning.

text:
ɯ-ru nɯra tɯ-jaʁndzu mɤ-kɯ-ʑɯ ʑo ɲɯ-jpum cʰa \\
3sg. poss -stalk dem: pl indef. poss -finger neg - inf: stat -just.be emph ipfv -be.thick can: fact \\
`Its stalk can grow thicker than a finger.' (12-ndZiNgri)
0003488#S5
exe

The stative verb expressing the parameter can be combined with modal verbs as in ( ex:mAkWZW.Zo.YWjpum ). Without an overt parameter, the default interpretation of the verb mɤ-ʑɯ means `not just like that' or `bigger than'. In ( ex:ndAre.mAZW ) for instance, mɤ-ʑɯ is redundantly followed by a comparative construction in sɤz (§ sec:sAz.kW ), and the two clauses βʑɯ ndɤre mɤ-ʑɯ and βʑɯ sɤz ndɤre wxti ŋu have the same meaning.

exe

nɯnɯ kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ci tɕe, βʑɯ ndɤre mɤ-ʑɯ. βʑɯ sɤz ndɤre wxti ŋu \\
dem sbj: pcp - emph be.small indef lnk mouse advers neg -just.be: fact mouse comp advers be.big: fact be: fact \\
`[The weasel] is a small [animal], but bigger than a mouse. It is bigger than a mouse.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S32
exe

In this construction, mɤ-ʑɯ indexes as subject the comparee, as in ( ex:mAZWa ).

exe

ki kɯm ki mɤ-ʑɯ-a \\
dem. prox door dem. prox neg -just.be: fact - 1sg \\
`I am bigger than this door.' (elicited)
exe

Alternatively, mɤ-ʑɯ can be combined with a degree nominal (§ sec:degree.monoclausal ) as in ( ex:atWmbro.mAZW ), in which case it only occurs in the 3sg.

exe

a-tɯ-mbro ki kɯm ki mɤ-ʑɯ. \\
1sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.high dem. prox door dem. prox neg -just.be: fact \\
`I am bigger than this door.' (elicited)
exe

The non-past form mɤ-ʑɯ has been further grammaticalized as a degree adverb mɤʑɯeven more, which can be combined with the standard marker sɤz, as in ( ex:ndAre.mAZW.Zo.amtCoR ). This construction indicates that the standard already has a very high degree relative to the parameter, and that the comparee's degree is even higher.

exe

qamtɕɯr nɯ ɯ-mtɕʰi nɯnɯ βʑɯ sɤznɤ mɤʑɯ ʑo amtɕoʁ \\
shrew dem 3sg. poss -mouth dem mouse comp even.more emph be.pointy: fact \\
`The shrew's mouth is even sharper than that of the mouse.' (27-spjaNkW)
0003704#S192
exe

The egressive postposition ɕaŋtaʁup from
comparative egressive
The egressive postpositions (§ sec:egressive ), in particular ɕaŋtaʁup from, can be combined with a verb (or a complex predicate) in negative form, meaning `no more than $X$', where the standard $X$ is the noun phrase preceding ɕaŋtaʁ as in ( ex:CaNtaR.mAzri ) and ( ex:CaNtaR.YWjpum.mAcha ).

exe

[tɯ-tɣa ɕaŋtaʁ] mɤ-zri. \\
one-span up.from neg -be.long: fact \\
`It is not longer than one handspan.' (28-tshAwAre)
0003722#S49
exe

exe

ɯ-ru ra (...), [tɯ-jaʁndzu ɕaŋtaʁ] ɲɯ-jpum mɤ-cʰa ma \\
3sg. poss -stalk pl genr. poss -finger up.from ipfv -be.thick neg -can: fact lnk \\
`Its stalk cannot grow/become thicker than a finger.' (15-babW)
0003512#S20
exe

The egressive ɕaŋtaʁup from also occurs in one of the superlative constructions (§ sec:negative.existential.superlative ).
summary:
The passage describes how the stative verb **mɤ-ʑɯ** ‘be bigger/just not like that’ is used in comparative constructions, either with an overt standard phrase or with a degree nominal, and can also combine with modal verbs to express meanings like “can grow thicker than a finger.” When no parameter is stated, **mɤ-ʑɯ** is interpreted as ‘not just like that’ or ‘bigger than,’ and it has further developed into the degree adverb **mɤʑɯ** meaning ‘even more.’  

It also explains that the egressive postposition **ɕaŋtaʁup** ‘from’ can combine with a negative verb or predicate to mean ‘no more than X,’ where the preceding noun phrase serves as the comparison standard.

text:
comparative negative
The negative existential verb me (§ sec:existential.basic ), combined with the scalar focus marker kɯnɤalso, even (§ sec:kWnA ), can have the meaning `not even as big as $X$', as in ( ex:kWnA.me ), where the noun
zrɯɣlouse is the standard of comparison.

exe

qajɯβlama kɤ-ti ci tu tɕe, nɯ rca kɯ-xtɕɯ xtɕi ci ʑo ɕti. zrɯɣ kɯnɤ me. \\
bug obj: pcp -say indef exist: fact lnk dem unexp: deg sbj: pcp - emph be.small indef emph be. aff: fact louse also not.exist: fact \\
`There is an [insect] called qajɯβlama, it is very small. It is not even as big as a louse.' (28-kWpAz)
0003714#S136
exe

Another example of this construction is found in ( ex:BZW.GW.WqiW ) in (§ sec:gen.possession ).
summary: The passage describes a comparative negative construction in which the negative existential verb *me* combines with the scalar focus marker *kɯnɤ* ‘also, even’ to mean ‘not even as big as X.’ In the example given, the size of an insect is compared against a louse, which serves as the standard of comparison. It also notes that another example of this construction appears elsewhere in the grammar.

text:
equative
This section discusses entity equative constructions, which express that two entities have a property in equal degree (`X is as Y as Z'; ). No less that five constructions are available to express this meaning.
summary: The passage explains that equative constructions express that two entities share a property to the same degree, as in “X is as Y as Z.” It also notes that the language has no fewer than five different constructions available to express this equative meaning.

text:
nominalization!degree equative
The nominalized entity equative construction is a particular case of the degree nominal construction (§ sec:degree.monoclausal ), with naχtɕɯɣbe the same as degree predicate. It has three subvariants.

In the first variant (corresponding to Haspelmath's ( haspelmath17equative) type 5 -- Primary reach equative unified), the comparee and the standard are included in a noun phrase, with the comitative marker cʰo (and its longer variant cʰondɤre, § sec:comitative ) serving as the standard marker, as in ( ex:chondAre.ndZitWwxti ).

exe

qalekɯtsʰi nɯnɯ cʰondɤre βʑar ni ndʑi-tɯ-wxti espace naχtɕɯɣ.\\
bird.sp dem comit buzzard du 3du. poss - nmlz: deg -be.big espace be.identical: fact \\
comparee std. mrk standard parameter espace param. mrk \\
`The qalekɯtsʰi bird is as big as the buzzard.' (literally: `The qalekɯtsʰi bird and the buzzard are identical in their degree of bigness.') (23-RmWrcWftsa)
0003610#S42
exe

The degree noun can be in dual/plural as in ( ex:chondAre.ndZitWwxti ) and ( ex:ndZitWwxti.naXtCWG ), corresponding to the sum of the numbers of the comparee and the standard, or in the singular as in ( ex:cho.WtWwxti.naXtCWG ): even though two referents are present here, the 3sg possessive ɯ- is used, coreferent with the comparee.

exe

qro nɯnɯ dɯdɯt cʰo ɯ-tɯ-wxti naχtɕɯɣ. \\
pigeon dem dove comit 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.big be.the.same: fact \\
`The pigeon is as big as a dove.' (24-qro)
0003626#S2
exe

These two possibilities are in free variation: example ( ex:ndZitWwxti.naXtCWG ), from the same text as ( ex:cho.WtWwxti.naXtCWG ) and referring to the same situation, has dual marking.

exe

tɕe dɯdɯt cʰo ndʑi-tɯ-wxti naχtɕɯɣ ʑo \\
lnk dove comit 3du. poss - nmlz: deg -be.big be.the.same: fact emph \\
`It is as big as a dove.' (24-qro)
0003626#S17
exe

In the second variant, the nominalized parameter takes a possessive prefix only coreferent with the comparee, and the standard together with the comitative (the standard marker) follows the parameter, as in ( ex:WtWwxti.cho.naXtCWG ).

exe

qaliaʁ nɯ ɯ-tɯ-wxti nɯ qandʑɣi cʰo naχtɕɯɣ tsa \\
eagle dem 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.big dem hawk comit espace be.identical: fact a.little \\
comparee parameter standard std. mrk espace param. mrk param. mrk \\
`The eagle is about as big as the hawk.' (19-qandZGi)
0003548#S36
exe

In the third variant, the parameter takes a third person singular possessive prefix, and the comparee and standard are marked by person indexation on the verb. In ( ex:WtWmWCtaR.YWnaXtCWGtCi ), the standard and the comparee are the speaker and the addressee; they are not expressed by overt pronouns, but are rather indexed on the verb by the 1du suffix -tɕi.

exe

tɕe ɯ-tɯ-mɯɕtaʁ ɲɯ-naχtɕɯɣ-tɕi tɕe, qʰe nɯ-tɤjpa ɲɯ-rkɯn ma\\
lnk 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.cold sens -be.identical- 1du lnk lnk 2pl. poss -snow sens -be.few sfr \\
parameter param. mrk - comparee+standard \\
`It is as cold here as it is in your place, you don't have a lot of snow.' (`You and I are identical as to coldness'; conversation, 2014/11)
exe
summary: The passage describes a nominalized entity equative construction, a type of degree nominal construction built with the degree predicate *naχtɕɯɣ* ‘be identical’. It has three variants: in the first, comparee and standard form one noun phrase with the comitative marking the standard; in the second, the nominalized parameter carries a possessive prefix coreferent with the comparee and the standard follows with the comitative; in the third, the parameter has a third-person singular possessive prefix and comparee plus standard are indexed on the verb. The text also notes variation in whether the degree noun appears in singular or dual/plural, with singular sometimes used even when two referents are involved.

text:
serial verb construction
Serial verb constructions with the similative verb fsebe like (§ sec:svc.similative.verb ), or more rarely naχtɕɯɣbe the same and afsujabe of the same size as first verb can also be used as an entity equative. These constructions correspond to Haspelmath's ( haspelmath17equative) type 1 (Only equative standard-marker).

The semi-transitive verb fsebe like (§ sec:semi.transitive ) takes the comparee as subject and the standard as semi-object. Since it is syntactically linked to the standard, it is analyzed here as the standard marker rather than as the parameter marker.

exe

nɯ li ɯ-wa fsɯfse ʑo pjɤ-fse pjɤ-sɤjloʁ \\
dem again 3sg. poss -father completely.like emph ifr. ipfv -be.like ifr. ipfv -be.ugly \\
comparee standard param. mrk std. mrk parameter \\
`[The frog son] was as ugly as his father. ' (150818 muzhi guniang-zh)
0006334#S98
exe

The reduplicated degree adverb fsɯfse `completely identical' which derives from fsebe like optionally occurs in this construction as a parameter marker.

exe

ɯ-qa nɯra li kɯmaʁ tɤjmɤɣ nɯra fsɯfse ʑo fse. \\
3sg. poss -root dem: pl again other mushroom dem: pl completely.identical emph be.like: fact \\
`Its root is completely identical to that of other mushrooms.' (23-mbrAZim)
0003604#S107
exe

Both fsebe like and the stative verb occurring with it in the serial construction (the parameter) are in participial form in ( ex:kWfse.kAchWcha ), forming a relative clause with the comparee as the relativized element. The superlative construction studied in § sec:negative.existential.superlative is essentially a particular use of such relativized equative sentences.

exe

aʑo kɯ-fse kɯ-ɤcʰɯcʰa ʑo ʁʑɯnɯ ɣurʑa kɯrcat ra\\
1sg sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp -be.capable emph young.man hundred eight be.needed: fact \\
standard std. mrk parameter comparee \\
`I need one hundred and eight able young men like me.' (2012 Norbzang)
0003768#S16
exe

The verb naχtɕɯɣbe the same requires in addition the comitative cʰo on the standard (as in the preceding construction, § sec:nmlz.equative ), as shown by ( ex:cho.naXtCWG.jamar.YWmWCtaR ).

exe

<bali> nɯ, kukutɕu iʑora cʰo naχtɕɯɣ jamar ɲɯ-mɯɕtaʁ ɲɯ-tɯ-ti\\
topo dem here 1pl comit be.the.same: fact about sens -be.cold sens -2-say\\
comparee standard std. mrk std. mrk param. mrk param. mrk parameter \\
`You said that it was as cold in Paris as here by us.' (conversation, 11-08-2016)
exe
summary: Serial verb constructions with the similative verb **fsebe** ‘like’, and more rarely **naχtɕɯɣbe** ‘the same’ or **afsujabe** ‘of the same size as’, can express entity equatives and correspond to Haspelmath’s type 1 equative construction with only an equative standard marker. In these constructions, **fsebe** takes the comparee as subject and the standard as semi-object, so it is analyzed as the standard marker; the reduplicated adverb **fsɯfse** may optionally mark the parameter, and both verbs can appear in participial form to form a relative clause. The superlative construction discussed elsewhere is described as a special case of these relativized equative sentences, while **naχtɕɯɣbe** additionally requires the comitative **cʰo** on the standard.

text:
noun!inalienably possessed equative
The inalienably possessed noun ɯ-fsuof the same size (§ sec:3sg.possessive.form, § sec:fsu.fse ) can be used as standard marker, as in ( ex:Wfsu.jamar ) and ( ex:Wfsu.jamar2 ). The possessive prefix is coreferent with the standard; when the standard is the generic noun tɯrmeperson, the prefix can either be in 3sg as in ( ex:Wfsu.jamar ), or with the generic possessor prefix (§ sec:tWrme.generic ).

exe

tu-mbro tɕe, tɯrme ɯ-fsu jamar tu-βze cʰa. \\
ipfv -be.high lnk man 3sg. poss -equal.in.size about ipfv -grow can: fact \\
`When it grows, it can grow about the size of a person.' (12-ndZiNgri)
0003488#S4
exe

exe

ɯ-tɯ-mbro nɯ tɯ-mtʰɤɣ ɯ-fsu jamar ma tu-mbro mɤ-cʰa \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.high dem genr. poss -waist 3sg. poss -equal.in.size about apart.from ipfv -be.high neg -can: fact \\
`As for its size, it can grow only about as high as a person's waist.' (18-NGolo)
0003530#S169
exe

The parameter is optional in this construction. It can be expressed either as a coordinated clause as in ( ex:Wfsu.jamar ), as a degree nominal or as the main predicate as in ( ex:Wfsu.jamar2 ). Only mbrobe high and wxtibe big are compatible with ɯ-fsu.

A similar construction is reported in Situ.

stʰɯciso much and jamarabout
The adverbs stʰɯciso much (on its etymology, see § sec:denominal.adverb.s.prefix ) and jamarabout (from Tibetan ཡར་མར་jar.marabout) are used as standard marker. The former one stʰɯci essentially occurs in a negative equative construction `not as $X$ as $Y$' (where $X$ is the parameter and $Y$ the standard) as in ( ex:sthWci.mArJum ).

exe

kɯmɕku ɯ-jwaʁ stʰɯci mɤ-rɟum \\
garlic 3sg. poss -leaf so.much neg -be.broad \\
`[Its leaves] are not as broad as garlic leaves.' (07-Cku)
0003424#S88
exe

The latter one jamarabout can be combined with either adjectival stative verbs such as wxtibe big ( ex:RnWz.jamar.wxti ), or with existential verbs (§ sec:existential.basic ) as in ( ex:ki.jamar.tu ).

exe

qajdo ʁnɯz jamar wxti \\
crow two about be.big: fact \\
`It is about as big as two crows.' (19-qandZGi)
0003548#S8
exe

exe

ɯ-mat ɣɯ ɯ-ru nɯ zri tɕe, tɕe tɯ-tɣa jamar, ki jamar tu tɕe \\
3sg. poss -fruit gen 3sg. poss -stalk dem be.long: fact lnk lnk one-span about dem. prox about exist: fact lnk \\
`The stalk of its fruit is long, about a handspan long, about this long.' (16-CWrNgo)
0003518#S210
exe
summary: The passage describes several ways to express equative or approximate comparison. The inalienably possessed noun ɯ-fsu ‘same size’ can mark the standard, with its possessive prefix coreferent with the standard, and it is optionally used in constructions involving parameters like height or size; only verbs meaning ‘be high’ and ‘be big’ are compatible with it. It also notes two adverbs used as standard markers: stʰɯci ‘much,’ which mainly appears in negative equative constructions, and jamar ‘about,’ which can combine with adjectival stative verbs or existential verbs.

text:
equative
In property equative constructions (`$X_i$ is as $Y$ as he/she/it$_i$ is $Z$'), two parameters (comparee parameter $Y$ and standard parameter $Z$), rather than two entities, are compared. No example of such constructions is found in the Japhug corpus. In, I used Perrault's fairy tale Riquet à la Houppe, whose whole plot is based on property equative sentences, as a way to conduct elicitation on this topic.

Property equatives, e.g. `$X_i$ is as stupid as s/he$_i$ is beautiful' (a sentence occurring several times in the story), can be expressed in Japhug in three different ways.

First, the standard parameter is in degree nominal form, followed by the possessed noun ɯ-fsuof the same size (§ sec:Wfsu.equative ), and the comparee parameter is the main predicate of the construction, in finite form ( ex:WtWmpCAr.GW.Wfsu.jamar ).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-mpɕɤr ɣɯ ɯ-fsu jamar ci ɲɯ-kʰe ɕti \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.beautiful gen 3sg. poss -equal.in.size about indef sens -be.stupid be. aff: fact \\
`S/he$_i$ is stupid to the extent of his/her$_i$ beauty.' (elicited)
exe

Second, the two verbs used as paramaters are in degree nominal form, linked by the comitative postposition cʰo, and serve as subject of the verb afsujabe of the same size ( ex:WtWmpCAr.cho.WtWkhe.YAfsuja ).

exe

ɯ-tɯ-mpɕɤr cʰo ɯ-tɯ-kʰe nɯ ɲɯ-ɤfsuja ɕti\\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.beautiful comit 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg -be.stupid dem sens -be.of.the.same.size be. aff: fact \\
`His/her beauty and his/her stupidity are equal.' (elicited)
exe

Third, it is possible to express the same meaning with a correlative construction, as in ( ex:correlative.parameter.equative ), though this may be a calque from Chinese.

exe

tɕʰi jamar kɯ-mpɕɤr nɯ, nɯ jamar ci ɲɯ-kʰe ɕti \\
what about sbj: pcp -be.beautiful dem dem about indef sens -be.stupid be. aff: fact \\
`A much as s/he is beautiful, s/he is stupid.' (elicited)
exe
summary: Property equative constructions compare two parameters rather than two entities, as in “X is as Y as he/she is Z,” but no natural example was found in the Japhug corpus. The author used a fairy tale with many such sentences to elicit Japhug equivalents, and found three ways to express them: with the standard parameter as a degree nominal plus a possessed “equal in size” noun, with both parameters as degree nominals linked by the comitative and functioning as the subject of “be of the same size,” or with a correlative construction, possibly influenced by Chinese.

text:
similative
Similative constructions express similarity in the manner in which an action is performed, rather than equal degree.
summary: Similative constructions express similarity in the manner of an action’s performance. They indicate resemblance in how something is done, rather than equality of degree.

text:
The main similative construction involves the similative verbs fsebe like or studo like in parataxis as in ( ex:tWrme.YWfse ).

exe

nɯnɯ pri nɯ kɯ, nɤki, tɯrme ɲɯ-fse tɕe, nɤkinɯ iɕqʰa nɯ, tɤ-rɤku tɕi tu-ndze, ɕa tɕi tu-ndze, (...) ɲɯ-ŋgrɤl. \\
dem bear dem erg filler man sens -be.like lnk filler filler dem indef. poss -crops also ipfv -eat meat also ipfv -eat sens -be.usually.the.case \\
`The bear, like a man, eats grains and meat.' (21-pri)
0003580#S17
exe

Alternatively, the infinitive kɯ-fse of fsebe like as a manner converb (§ sec:inf.converb, § sec:manner.converbs ) can convey similative meaning, either with a noun phrase or an infinitive clause ( ex:kAnWGro.kWfse ).

exe

[kɤ-ɤnɯɣro] kɯ-fse tú-wɣ-ndza ɕti ma \\
inf -play inf: stat -be.like ipfv - inv -eat be. aff: fact lnk \\
`People eat it for fun (as if to play, not as part of a real meal).' (08-rasti)
0003460#S53
exe
summary: The passage describes the main similative construction as using the similative verbs **fsebe** “like” or **studo** “like” in parataxis. It also notes that the infinitive **kɯ-fse** of **fsebe** can express similative meaning as a manner converb, either with a noun phrase or with an infinitive clause.

text:
The denominal prefix arɯ-/ɤrɯ- derives stative verbs meaning `be $X$-like' out of nouns (§ sec:denom.arW ), as in ( ex:arWsWjno ), an example in degree nominal form (§ sec:degree.nominal.predicates ) spontaneously produced by Tshendzin as a side comment on a story that we were transcribing.

exe

ɯ-tɯ-ɤrɯ-sɯjno nɯ! \\
3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - denom: similative -grass sfp \\
`[The princess cuts their head as easily/casually] as if it were grass.' (heard in context)
exe

The more elaborated sentence ( ex:YArWsWjno ) was given as an explanation for ( ex:arWsWjno ).

exe

kɤ-pʰɯt ɯ-tɯ-mbat kɯ ɲɯ-ɤrɯ-sɯjno ʑo \\
inf -cut 3sg. poss - nmlz: deg - denom: similative -easy erg sens -be.like.grass emph \\
`It is as easy to cut as if it were grass.' (elicited)
exe

In this construction, the standard is the verbalized noun, the comparee is the intransitive subject, and the denominal prefix arɯ-/ɤrɯ- is the standard marker. The parameter can be optionally indicated as a degree nominal as in ( ex:YArWsWjno ).

This unusual similative construction is productive, since it can be applied to nouns from Tibetan or Chinese. It does not fit in any of Haspelmath's ( haspelmath17equative) six types of equative constructions, but bears some resemblance to the ``similative adjective'' derivation in -lágan in Saami.
summary:
The denominal prefix arɯ-/ɤrɯ- forms stative verbs meaning “be X-like” from nouns, and in this similative construction the standard is the verbalized noun while the comparee is the intransitive subject. The standard marker is the prefix arɯ-/ɤrɯ-, and the parameter may optionally be expressed as a degree nominal.  

This construction is productive, including with nouns borrowed from Tibetan or Chinese, but it does not match any of Haspelmath’s six equative types. It is said to resemble the Saami similative adjective derivation in -lágan.

text: superlative
summary: The passage concerns the superlative, which is the form used to express the highest degree of a quality. It typically contrasts one entity with a larger set, indicating that it exceeds all others in the relevant comparison.

text:
The superlative adverb stumost is generally located before the verb, and optionally takes the emphatic ʑo. It most commonly expresses absolute superlative as in ( ex:tWmkhAz2 ).

exe

nɤʑo stu ʑo tɯ-mkʰɤz tɕe, tɕe nɤʑo ɕ-tɤ-nɤme \\
2sg most emph 2-be.expert: fact lnk lnk 2sg tral - imp -do[III] \\
`You are the best, do it!' (150822 laoye zuoshi zongshi duide-zh)
0006298#S37
exe

When the subject has a certain property in the highest degree only relative to a certain class (relative superlative), this class can be specified with the relator noun ɯ-ŋgɯzinside, among (§ sec:relator.postposition.location ), as in ( ex:nWNgWz.stu.xtCi ).

exe

nɯ pɣɤtɕɯ nɯ-ŋgɯz stu xtɕi low.\\
dem bird 3pl. poss -among most be.small: fact sfp \\
`It is the smallest of all birds.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S116
exe

Most examples of this construction appear with subject participle (§ sec:subject.participles ) of adjectival stative verbs as in ( ex:stu.kWNAn ), and object participles (§ sec:object.participle ) with transitive experiencer verbs as in ( ex:stu.WkAnWrga ).

exe

kɯɕɯŋgɯ tɕe <aizheng> kɤ-ti pɯ-me tɕe, kɤ-kɯ-nɤndza nɯ stu ʑo kɯ-ŋɤn kɤ-pa pɯ-ŋu. \\
long.ago lnk cancer obj: pcp -say pst. ipfv -not.exist lnk aor - sbj: pcp -have.leprosy dem most emph sbj: pcp -be.evil obj: pcp -consider pst. ipfv -be \\
`In former times, nobody talked about cancer, and leprosy was considered to be the most terrible [of all diseases].' (25-khArWm)
0003644#S32
exe

exe

tɕe tɯ-ci ɯ-rkɯ tu-ɬoʁ tɕe, nɯ stu ɯ-kɤ-nɯ-rga ŋu tɕe \\
lnk indef. poss -water 3sg. poss -side ipfv -come.out lnk dem most 3sg. poss - appl -like be: fact lnk \\
`It grows near the water, it is what it likes the most.' (09-mi)
0003466#S6
exe

The superlative adverb is also attested with transitive dynamic verbs of action, as in the pseudo-cleft construction (§ sec:pseudo.cleft ) in ( ex:stu.Zo.WkAndza ). The phrase tɤ-rme kɯ-fse `like hair' is incomplete; the correct way to express the meaning `clothes made of animal hair' is the head-internal relative clause tɤ-rme kɯ tɯ-ŋga tʰɯ-kɤ-βzu (see ex:tWNga.thWkABzu, § sec:head-internal.relative ).

exe

[stu ʑo ɯ-kɤ-ndza] nɯnɯ tɯ-ŋga, tɤ-rme kɯ-fse, tɯ-ŋga nɯra ŋu. \\
most emph 3sg. poss - obj: pcp -eat dem indef. poss -clothes indef. poss -hair sbj: pcp -be.like indef. poss -clothes dem: pl be: fact \\
`What it eats most is clothes, clothes (made of animal fur).' (28-kWpAz)
0003714#S74
exe

Oblique participles (§ sec:oblique.participle ) are also compatible with the superlative adverb, as shown in ( ex:stu.WsAdAn ).

exe

[stu ɯ-sɤ-dɤn] nɯ stɤmku nɯra ŋu-nɯ. \\
most 3sg. poss - obl: pcp -be.many dem grassland dem: pl be: fact - pl \\
`The place where it is most numerous is the grasslands.' (19-qachGa mWntoR)
0003546#S23
exe
summary:
The superlative adverb **stumost** usually appears before the verb and can optionally take the emphatic **ʑo**. It most often marks an absolute superlative, but it can also express a relative superlative when the relevant class is specified by the relator noun **ɯ-ŋgɯz** “inside, among.”

The construction is common with subject participles of adjectival stative verbs and object participles of transitive experiencer verbs, and it also occurs with transitive dynamic verbs in pseudo-cleft constructions. Oblique participles are likewise compatible with **stumost**.

text:
participle!subject
Another possibility to express superlative meaning is with a stative verb in subject participial form with a third plural possessive marker (§ sec:subject.participle.possessive ), as in ( ex:thamtCAt.GW.nWkWmpCAr ), where the headless participial relative in square brackets, literally meaning `the beautiful one (among/of) all birds' is to be understood as `the most beautiful of all birds.'

exe

tɕe [pɣa tʰamtɕɤt ɣɯ nɯ-kɯ-mpɕɤr] nɯ rmɤβja ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
lnk bird all gen 3pl. poss - sbj: pcp -be.beautiful dem peacock sens -be \\
`The peacock is the most beautiful of all birds.' (24-ZmbrWpGa)
0003628#S79
exe

This construction is only attested with mpɕɤrbe beautiful and mnabe better.
summary: The passage describes a superlative construction formed with a stative verb in subject participial form plus a third plural possessive marker. In examples like the one for “the most beautiful of all birds,” the headless participial relative literally means “the beautiful one among all birds,” but is interpreted as a superlative. This construction is only attested with the verbs meaning “be beautiful” and “better.”

text:
negation orientation!superlative
Another way of expressing superlative meaning in Japhug is by means of a negative existential verb (§ sec:suppletive.negative, § sec:negation.existential ) combined with a participial relative of fsebe like, as in ( ex:kWfse.me ). This construction is a particular use of the equative construction described in § sec:svc.equative.

exe

ama, a-pi kʰu nɯ tɕʰindʐa ku-tɯ-nɤpʰɯpʰɣo tɕe [nɤʑo kɯ-fse] kɯ-sɤɣ-mu me \\
surprise 1sg. poss -elder.sibling tiger dem why prs -2- distr:flee lnk 2sg sbj: pcp -be.like sbj: pcp - prop -fear not.exist: fact \\
`Brother tiger, why are you running away like that, you are the most dreadful [animal].' (literally: `There is no one dreadful like you.') (2005 khu)
exe

This construction is potentially ambiguous: the clause $X$ kɯ-fse kɯ-sɤɣ-mu me can be interpreted as meaning either `$X$ is the most dreadful thing' or `there is nothing dreadful that is like $X$'.

It is possible in some cases to use orientation preverbs to disambiguate between these two meanings. In example ( ex:tusWza ), Example ( ex:tusWza ) is translated from 夜莺，我再熟悉不过了 yèyīng, wǒ zài shúxī bùguòleThe nightingale, I am quite familiar with it, with the with the construction 再……不过 zài... bùguò involving a negated surpass comparative, and the negative existential verb here is possibly a case of calque. However, Chinese influence cannot be a factor in the use of orientation preverbs in ( ex:tusWza ) and ( ex:pjWsWza ). the verbs tsoknow, understand and sɯzknow in the superlative construction take the upwards prefix tu- instead of the expected eastwards ( ku-tso-a ipfv -understand- 1sg ) and downwards ( pjɯ-sɯz-a ipfv -know- 1sg ) prefixes that they normally select.

exe

aʑo [nɯ kɯ-fse] ʑo maka tu-tso-a me, tu-sɯz-a me \\
1sg dem sbj: pcp -be.like emph at.all ipfv: up -understand- 1sg not.exist: fact ipfv: up -know- 1sg not.exist: fact \\
`This is what I know best.' (literally: `There is nothing that I understand, that I know like that.' 140519 yeying-zh)
0004040#S59
exe

With the upwards prefix tu- as in ( ex:tusWza ), only the superlative interpretation is possible, while with the downwards prefix pjɯ- as in ( ex:pjWsWza ) the superlative interpretation is excluded, and only the negative existential one is found.

exe

aʑo [nɯ kɯ-fse pjɯ-sɯz-a] me \\
1sg dem sbj: pcp -be.like ipfv: down -know- 1sg not.exist: fact \\
`I know of no such thing.' (elicited)
exe

I interpret this difference as a matter of semantic scope. In ( ex:tusWza ), the clause nɯ kɯ-fse `like that' is outside of the scope of the negation, and the negation applies to the minimal relative clauses tu-tso-a `(that) I understand' (§ sec:semi.tr.relativization ) and tu-sɯz-a `(that) I know' (§ sec:monotransitive.object.relativization ) exclusively.

With the downwards prefix pjɯ- on sɯzknow as in ( ex:pjWsWza ), the scope of the negation is different: it applies to the whole constituent indicated between square brackets (`there is nothing like that that I know').

This contrast cannot however be generalized to all verbs; more research is necessary to ascertain the extent and the functional explanation for this puzzling phenomenon.

Instead of kɯ-fse, egressive postpositions such as ɕaŋtaʁup from (§ sec:egressive, § sec:egressive.comparative ) can also be used in a superlative construction as in ( ex:CaNtaR.kWcha.me ).

exe

aʑo ɕaŋtaʁ kɯ-cʰa kɯ-rkaŋ me \\
1sg up.from sbj: pcp -can sbj: pcp -robust not.exist: fact \\
`I am the most able one, the most robust one.' (literally: `There is no one that is more robust/able than me') (140425 shizi huli he lu-zh)
exe
summary:
The passage explains that Japhug can express superlative meaning with a negative existential verb plus a participial relative of *fse* “like,” forming a type of equative construction. This structure can be ambiguous between “X is the most ...” and “there is nothing ... like X,” but orientation preverbs such as *tu-* and *pjɯ-* can sometimes disambiguate the scope of negation.

It further notes that with *tu-* only the superlative interpretation is possible, while with *pjɯ-* only the negative existential reading remains, though this pattern may not apply to all verbs. The passage also mentions that egressive postpositions like *ɕaŋtaʁ* “up from” can serve in similar superlative constructions.

text:
kinship!abbreviation
Kinship terms (§ sec:kinship ) in Japhug are all inalienably possessed nouns (§ sec:inalienably.possessed ), and are presented in this section in their indefinite possessor form (§ sec:indef.genr.poss ), which generally also serves as the citation form.

This section is not concerned with the morphosyntactic properties of these nouns (which is treated in § sec:indef.genr.poss ), but rather with the semantic structure of the system.

The meanings of the terms are described using the abbreviations presented in tab:kinship.abb, which, combined with each other (for instance MB and eZ represent `mother's brother' and `elder sister', respectively), offer a concise way to represent the possible parameters relevant to the description of kinship terms.

The term ``male/female possessor'' corresponds to what calls `sex of the person through whom the relationship exists' or `sex of the connecting relative', encoded as inalienable possessor in Japhug. For instance, tɤ-snomsister ( ♂ Z) is only used with reference to the sister of a male (§ sec:siblings.gender ).

Kinship terms can be divided into self-reciprocal terms, in which both members of the relationship use the same term to refer to each other (from instance tɤ-mɤtsamother's sister's child MZCh, § sec:ego.parallel.cousins ), and non-self-reciprocal ones, which usually have to be described in reciprocal pairs.

To determine the reciprocal term, one applies to each symbol in the formula the equivalences in tab:kinship.reciprocal, starting from the end. Special care should be given to the sex of the connecting relative.

For instance, the reciprocal of MB is obtained by combining ( ♂ B| ♂ Z) with ( ♀ S| ♀ D): of the two options of ( ♂ B| ♂ Z), the second one ♂ Z is selected because the following element ♀ (S|D) has a female connecting relative, hence ♂ Z(S|D), equivalent to ♂ ZCh.

This procedure is useful to calculate the reciprocal of more complex configurations. For instance, the reciprocal of FFBDS can be obtained in the following way:

itemize
( ♂ F| ♂ M)+( ♀ F| ♀ M)+( ♂ B| ♂ Z)+( ♂ S| ♂ D)+( ♂ S| ♂ D)
♂ (F|M) ♀ +(F|M) ♂ +(B|Z) ♂ +(S|D) ♂ +(S|D)
♂ MFBS(S|D)
♂ MFBSCh
itemize

It makes it possible to easily recheck which configurations are intrinsically self-reciprocal, for instance maternal parallel cousins MZCh:

itemize
(F|M)+( ♀ B| ♀ Z)+( ♀ Ch)
(F|M) ♀ +(B|Z) ♀ +Ch
MZCh
itemize

Japhug lacks a specific vocative form of kinship terms (§ sec:vocative ), unlike Tshobdun, for instance, and there are only a few different terms of address and terms of reference.

Given the important changes in Gyalrong society since the 1950s, and in particular the fact that all speakers of Japhug are now bilingual in Chinese, it is not surprising that the kinship system is undergoing considerable reshaping. The aim of this chapter is to document use of the kinship terms both by contemporary younger speakers, and the system as it used to be in the traditional society, before massive Chinese influence.

The data in this chapter are mainly based on Tshendzin 's explanations of the use of the system in a text from the corpus (140425 kWmdza), but are also drawn from observations of the actual use of kinship terms in conversations.
summary: Kinship terms in Japhug are all inalienably possessed nouns, here presented in their indefinite possessor form, and the discussion focuses on the semantic structure of the kinship system rather than its morphosyntax. The passage explains the abbreviation system used to describe kinship relations, including how to determine reciprocal terms, with examples showing both reciprocal and self-reciprocal relationships. It also notes that Japhug lacks a special vocative form for kinship terms, and that the kinship system is changing under Chinese influence, so the chapter documents both contemporary use and the traditional system.

text: This section is an overview of the uses of all kinship terms, first ego 's parents, their siblings and their parents (§ sec:G+1 ), ego 's siblings (§ sec:siblings ), ego 's cousins (§ sec:ego.cousins ) and finally ego, ego 's siblings and ego 's cousins' children and grandchildren (§ sec:G-1 ). It also includes information on affines, though the terminology is considerably poorer than for consanguines.
summary: The section gives an overview of the uses of all kinship terms, covering ego’s parents, their siblings and parents, ego’s siblings, ego’s cousins, and ego’s own generation and descendants including siblings’ and cousins’ children and grandchildren. It also includes affinal terms, though these are much less extensive than the terminology for consanguineous relatives.

text:
ego 's parents
Two series of terms are in use for ego 's parents, the common terms tɤ-mumother and tɤ-wafather, and the honorific ones, borrowed from Tibetan tɤ-pafather and tɤ-mamother. The terms for `mother' and `father' can be combined without any linker with a collective meaning `parent', but the order is rigidly `mother' followed by `father' ( ex:nAmu.nAwa ) The opposite order $ $ nɤ-wa nɤ-mu is agrammatical. in the case of the native terms, and the opposite in the case of the honorific ones ( a-pa a-ma `my parents'), as is discussed in more detail in § sec:dyads.

exe

nɤ-mu nɤ-wa ni \\
2sg. poss -mother 2sg. poss -father du \\
`Your parents.' (many occurrences)
exe

The native terms tɤ-mu and tɤ-wa can be alienabilized (§ sec:alienabilization ) and become terms of reference for elder people as in ( ex:tAmu.nWra ).

exe

kʰa ɯ-ʁɤri kɯ-nɤʁaʁ tɤ-mu nɯra kɯ nɯ-sɤz-nɯmbjɯm smi cʰɯ-nɯ-βlɯ-nɯ pjɤ-ŋu \\
house 3sg. poss -before sbj: pcp -have.a.good.time indef. poss -mother dem: pl erg 3pl. poss - obl: pcp -warm.by.fire fire ipfv - auto -burn- pl ifr. ipfv -be \\
`The old women who were resting in front of the house were burning a fire to keep themselves warm.' (2002 qaCpa)
exe

ego 's parent's siblings
There are different terms for parallel and cross-uncles and aunts ( tab:uncle.aunt ), which are all native terms with cognates in Tangut except possibly for tɤ-ɲifather's sister, which is borrowed from Tibetan ཨ་ནེ་ʔa.nepaternal aunt.

The terms for parallel aunts and uncles also serve to designate parent's siblings's spouses, as described in ( ex:FZH.MZH.MBW.FBW ). Note in this excerpt the use of the autive nɯ- on tu-kɯ-nɯ-ti `one calls (them)' reflecting the `casual' spontaneous function (§ sec:autoben.spontaneous ), emphasizing the fact that no specific term exists (compare with ex:tunWtCAtnW in § sec:autoben.spontaneous ).

exe

tɯ-ɲi ɯ-nmaʁ cʰondɤre tɯ-ɬaʁ ɯ-nmaʁ ra nɯ-ɕki tɕe tɕe li ``a-βɣo" tu-kɯ-nɯ-ti ɕti ma nɯ ma ʑaka ɯ-rmi me. (...) tɯ-rpɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rʑaβ ɯ-ɕki tɕe ``a-ɬaʁ" tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. tɯ-βɣo ɣɯ ɯ-rʑaβ ɯ-ɕki li ``a-ɬaʁ" tu-kɯ-ti ɕti. \\
genr. poss -FZ 3sg. poss -husband comit genr. poss -MZ 3sg. poss -husband pl 3pl. poss - dat lnk lnk again 1sg. poss -FB ipfv - genr - auto -say be. aff: fact lnk dem apart.from each 3sg. poss -name not.exist: fact
genr. poss -MB gen 3sg. poss -wife 3sg. poss - dat lnk 1sg. poss -MZ ipfv - genr - auto -say be: fact genr. poss -FB gen 3sg. poss -wife 3sg. poss - dat again 1sg. poss -MZ ipfv - genr - auto -say be. aff: fact \\
`One calls one's father's sister's and one's mother's sister's husbands a-βɣo `my father's brother'. Apart from that they don't have their own term. One calls one's mother's brother's and one's father's brother's wives a-ɬaʁ `my mother's sister'.' (140425 kWmdza05) 0003789
exe

They can be used as polite address terms for elder people (§ sec:personal.name.APN ). In addition, tɤ-βɣo is also a term of address for lamas, expressing respect.

The mother's siblings term tɤ-rpɯmother's brother and tɤ-ɬaʁmother's sister can also designate their children (the maternal cross-cousins, § sec:ego.cross.cousins ) and their grandchildren (§ sec:omaha ).

Conversely, the reciprocal of tɤ-rpɯmother's brother, the term tɤ-ftsasister's child (§ sec:nephews ), can be applied to ego 's paternal grandfather's sisters' children (FFZCh), who belong to ego 's parent's generation, due to the same generational skewing rule (§ sec:omaha ).

G +2
The terms tɤ-wɯgrandfather and tɤ-wigrandmother are used to refer to ego 's grandparents and their siblings, and also as an affectionate for (unrelated) elders who are two generations above ego. This term is also applied to great-grandparents and all generations above.

As an effect of the Omaha skewing rules (§ sec:omaha ), the children of ego 's paternal great-grandfather's sisters (FFFZCh), who belong to ego 's grandparents' generation, are downgraded three generations, and called by the term tɤ-ftsasister's child (§ sec:nephews ) by ego, and they answer back using the G +1 terms tɤ-rpɯmother's brother and tɤ-ɬaʁmother's sister (§ sec:G-2 ).
summary:
The passage describes kinship terms for ego’s parents, noting both common native forms and honorific Tibetan borrowings, with a rigid compound order meaning “mother” followed by “father.” It also explains that terms for parents’ siblings distinguish parallel and cross relatives, can extend to spouses and some younger generations, and are sometimes used as polite address forms for elders or lamas.  

It further shows that grandparent terms cover grandparents, their siblings, and older unrelated elders, and that Omaha skewing affects how some relatives in more distant generations are labeled, shifting them into different kin terms.

text:
sibling
There are two competing systems for designating siblings in Japhug, one encoding the gender of the sibling and that of the possessor and the other relative age.
summary: Japhug has two competing systems for referring to siblings. One system encodes the gender of both the sibling and the possessor, while the other distinguishes siblings by relative age.

text:
gender!kinship
The gender-based sibling terminological system comprises four terms ( tab:sibling1 ), which all have cognates in Tangut with identical functions. The ♂ B and ♀ Z terms (in grey shading) are self-reciprocal: for instance, anyone ego addresses as a-xtɤɣ `my brother' replies back with the same word. The groups of same-sex siblings calling each other a-xtɤɣ `my brother' or a-sqʰaj `my sister' can be referred to by the social relation collective nouns kɤndʑixtɤɣbrothers and kɤndʑisqʰajsisters derived from tɤ-xtɤɣ and tɤ-sqʰaj, respectively (§ sec:social.collective ).

By contrast, tɤ-snom ♂ Z and tɤ-wɤmɯ ♀ B are non-self-reciprocal, and are used as reciprocal pairs of each other. If ego is male, he refers to his sister(s) as a-snom, and they/she refers to him as a-wɤmɯ, and reciprocally if ego is female. The compound collective noun kɤndʑiwɤmɯsnombrother and sisters built from these two nouns (§ sec:social.collective ) is used to designate groups of siblings of different sex.

In addition to siblings sharing the same parents, these terms can also be applied to paternal parallel cousins (FBCh, § sec:ego.parallel.cousins ) and siblings of spouses (WB, WZ, HB, HZ, § sec:spouses ).
summary:
The passage describes a four-term gender-based sibling terminology system, all of which have cognates in Tangut with the same functions. Two terms for same-sex siblings are self-reciprocal, while the terms for cross-sex siblings are non-self-reciprocal and used as reciprocal pairs; corresponding collective nouns are formed for groups of same-sex and mixed-sex siblings.

It also notes that these sibling terms extend beyond biological siblings to paternal parallel cousins and to siblings of spouses.

text:
The relative age-based system only comprises two terms, tɤ-pielder sibling and ta-ʁiyounger sibling. It distinguishes the relative age of the kin and his/her connecting relative (possessor).

Like the terms of the first system, tɤ-pi and ta-ʁi can be used for paternal parallel cousins (§ sec:ego.parallel.cousins ) and spouses of siblings (§ sec:spouses ), and also as affectionate address terms for non-kins of the same generation. The paternal cross-aunt (FZ) also uses ta-ʁi to call her cross-nephews ( ♀ BCh § sec:nephews ); the gender-based sibling terminology cannot be used to refer to cross-nephews.

Both systems are possible for address and reference, but the former ( tab:sibling1 ) is more frequently used for reference, and the latter for address.

In addition, it is possible to add tɕʰemegirl or tɤ-tɕɯson, `male' as postnominal modifiers ( ex:attributive.postnominal ) to tɤ-pielder sibling and ta-ʁiyounger sibling to specify the gender of the sibling, as in ( ex:aRi.tAtCW ).

exe

a-ʁi tɤ-tɕɯ kɯmŋu tu tɕe, \\
1sg. poss -younger.sibling indef. poss -son five exist: fact lnk \\
`I have five younger brothers.' (14-siblings) 0003508#S270
exe
summary:
The relative age-based kinship system has only two terms: one for an older sibling and one for a younger sibling, and it encodes the relative age of both the kin and the possessor. These forms can also be used for paternal parallel cousins, siblings’ spouses, and as affectionate terms for non-kin of the same generation, while a paternal cross-aunt uses the younger-sibling term for her cross-nephews.  

Both systems can be used for reference and address, though the age-based terms are more common in reference and the other system in address. Gender can be added with postnominal modifiers meaning “girl” or “male/son” to specify the sibling’s sex.

text: Parallel and cross-cousins (children of parent's siblings) are designated by different terms in Japhug.
summary: In Japhug, parallel cousins and cross-cousins are referred to with different kinship terms. The passage notes that children of a parent’s siblings are distinguished in this way.

text:
cousin!parallel
There is no dedicated term for paternal parallel cousins (FBCh). They are terminologically identified with siblings (§ sec:siblings ), and both the gender-based terms (§ sec:siblings.gender ) and the relative age-base terms (§ sec:siblings.age ) can be applied to them ( ex:FBCh ).

exe

tɯ-βɣo ɣɯ ɯ-tɕɯ cʰondɤre ɯ-me nɯra nɯ-ɕki tɕe, tɕe kɯ-wxti ra nɯ-ɕki ``a-pi" tu-kɯ-ti, kɯ-xtɕi ra nɯ-ɕki ``a-ʁi" tu-kɯ-ti ŋu. \\
genr. poss -FB gen 3sg. poss -son comit 3sg. poss -daughter dem: pl 3pl. poss - dat lnk lnk sbj: pcp -be.big pl 3pl. poss - dat 1sg. poss -elder.sibling ipfv - genr -say sbj: pcp -be.big pl 3pl. poss - dat 1sg. poss -elder.sibling ipfv - genr -say be: fact \\
`As for one's father's brother's sons and daughters, one calls the elder ones a-pi `my elder sibling' and the younger ones a-ʁi `my younger sibling'.' (140425 kWmdza01) 0003785
exe

Maternal parallel cousins have a dedicated term tɤ-mɤtsa, probably a lexicalized compound from tɤ-mumother (in bound state mɤ, § sec:vowel.alternations.compounds ) and tɤ-ftsasister's child, literally `mother's nephew'. A cognate compound is also found in Situ. This term is self-reciprocal, as shown in ( ex:MZCh ) (see also ex:amAtsa.tukAmWti § sec:recip.amW.indirective for a description of the same rule with a different wording).

exe

tɯ-ɬaʁ ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit nɯra tɕe tɤ-tɕɯ pɯ-nɯ-ŋu tɕʰeme pɯ-nɯ-ŋu tɯ-mɤtsa ŋu (...) tɯʑo kɯnɤ ``a-mɤtsa" tu-kɯ-ti, ɯʑo kɯnɤ ``a-mɤtsa" tu-ti \\
genr. poss -FZ gen 3sg. poss -offspring dem: pl lnk indef. poss -son pst. ipfv - auto -be girl pst. ipfv - auto -be genr. poss -MZCh be: fact genr also 1sg. poss -MZCh ipfv - genr -say 3sg also 1sg. poss -MZCh ipfv -say \\
`One's mother's sister's children, whether boy or girl, are one's maternal parallel cousins ( tɯ-mɤtsa ). (...) One calls [them] a-mɤtsa, and they also reply a-mɤtsa.' (140425 kWmdza04) 0003788
exe

However, some younger speakers also casually use the relative age sibling terms to refer to maternal parallel cousins ( ex:MZCh2 ).

exe

jinde tʰam tɕe ``a-pi a-ʁi" tu-nɯ-ti-nɯ ŋu ma \\
nowadays now lnk 1sg. poss -elder.sibling 1sg. poss -younger.sibling ipfv - auto -say- pl be: fact lnk \\
`Nowadays [maternal parallel cousins] call [each other] a-pi `my elder sibling' and a-ʁi `my younger sibling'(casually).' (140425 kWmdza01) 0003785
exe
summary: Paternal parallel cousins (father’s brother’s children) have no special term and are treated like siblings, using both gender-based and relative-age sibling terms to address them. Maternal parallel cousins, by contrast, have a dedicated reciprocal term, tɤ-mɤtsa, though some younger speakers also casually use the sibling age terms for them.

text:
cousin!cross Omaha skewing rule
By contrast, the cross-cousins are referred to by unequal terms. As explained in ( ex:MBCh.FZCh ), the paternal cross-cousins (father's sister's children FZCh) are called using the term tɤ-ftsa, the same as sister's children (§ sec:G-1 ), and they reply back by calling their maternal parallel cousins (mother's brother's children MBCh) with tɤ-rpɯ and tɤ-ɬaʁ, terms that also refer to the parallel cousins's parents (mother's brother MB and his wife MBW, § sec:G+1 ).

exe

tɯ-ɲi ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit nɯra kɯ tɯʑo tɯ-ɕki ``a-rpɯ", tɤ-tɕɯ pɯ-kɯ-ŋu nɤ ``a-rpɯ" tu-ti-nɯ, tɕʰeme pɯ-kɯ-ŋu nɤ ``a-ɬaʁ" tu-ti-nɯ kɯ-ra ŋu. tɕeri, nɤkinɯ, tɯʑo kɯ tɕe tɕe ʑara nɯ-ɕki li a-ftsa tu-kɯ-ti kɯ-ra ŋu. \\
genr. poss -FZ gen 3sg. poss -children dem: pl erg genr genr. poss - dat 1sg. poss -MB indef. poss -son pst. ipfv - genr -be add 1sg. poss -MB ipfv -say- pl girl pst. ipfv - genr -be add 1sg. poss -MZ ipfv -say- pl inf: stat -be.needed lnk filler genr erg lnk lnk 3pl 3pl. poss - dat again 1sg. poss -ZCh ipfv - genr -say inf: stat -be.needed be: fact \\
\\
`One's paternal aunt's children call one a-rpɯ `my maternal uncle'; if one is a man they say `my maternal uncle', if one is a woman they say a-ɬaʁ `my maternal aunt', but one calls them a-ftsa `my sister's son'.' (140425 kWmdza03) 0003787
exe

While parallel cross-cousins are given an equal status to siblings in terms of generation, cross-cousins are associated to either the lower generation (paternal cross-cousins) or the higher generation (maternal cross-cousins). This generational skewing rule is characteristic of Omaha kinship systems, and is discussed in more detail in § fig:omaha (see sec:omaha ).
summary: The passage explains that in this Omaha-type kinship system, cross-cousins are referred to asymmetrically: paternal cross-cousins are called by the same term as sister’s children, while maternal cross-cousins use terms that also refer to their parents, the mother’s brother and his wife. It also notes that although parallel cross-cousins are treated as siblings in generational terms, cross-cousins are skewed toward either the lower generation or the higher generation, which is a characteristic feature of Omaha kinship systems.

text:
ego 's children
The term for ego 's children tɤ-tɕɯson and tɯ-medaughter cannot be used for nephews and children of cousins, but can also designate one's children's spouses. The noun tɤ-tɕɯ is also alienabilized (§ sec:alienabilization ) in the sense of `boy, man, member of the male gender' (as opposed to tɕʰemegirl).

ego 's sibling's children
nephew
Sister's children are called tɤ-ftsa, regardless of whether ego is a man or a woman ( ex:MB.MZ.ZCh ). This term is also applied to one's paternal cross-cousins (§ sec:ego.cross.cousins ), and reflects an Omaha-type generational skewing rule (§ sec:omaha ).

exe

tɤ-rpɯ nɯ kɯnɤ ``a-ftsa" tu-ti, tɤ-ɬaʁ nɯ kɯnɤ ``a-ftsa" tu-ti \\
indef. poss -MB dem also 1sg. poss - ZCh ipfv -say indef. poss -MZ dem also 1sg. poss - ZCh ipfv -say \\
`Both the maternal uncle and the maternal aunt call [their sister's children] a-ftsa.' (140425 kWmdza04) 0003788
exe

The brothers' children are called differently depending on whether ego is male or female. If ego is female ( ex:ZCh.BCh.FP ), one calls one's cross-nephews with the term ta-ʁi used for younger siblings (§ sec:siblings.age ) and male parallel cousins (§ sec:ego.parallel.cousins ), though in this case they do not reply back with tɤ-pielder sibling as could have been expected, but with the dedicated term tɤ-ɲifather's sister (§ sec:G+1 ), infringing the reciprocity rule between ta-ʁi and tɤ-pi (§ sec:siblings.age ).

exe

aʑo tɕʰeme ɲɯ-ŋu-a tɕe a-sqʰaj ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit nɯ-ɕki tɕe "a-ftsa" tu-ti-a ŋu.... a-wɤmɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit ra nɯ-ɕki tɕe "a-ʁi" tu-ti-a kɯ-ra ŋu. ʑara kɯ a-ɕki "a-ɲi" tu-ti-nɯ tɕe, aʑo kɯ "a-ʁi" tu-ti-a ŋu. \\
1sg girl sens -be- 1sg lnk 1sg. poss -sister gen 3sg. poss -offspring 3pl. poss - dat loc 1sg. poss -FZCh ipfv -say- 1sg be: fact 1sg. poss -brother gen 3sg. poss -offspring pl 3pl. poss - dat loc 1sg. poss -younger.sibling ipfv -say- 1sg inf: stat -be.needed be: fact 3pl erg 1sg. poss - dat 1sg. poss -FZ ipfv -say- pl lnk 1sg erg 1sg. poss -younger.sibling ipfv -say- 1sg be: fact \\
`I am a woman, and so I call my sisters' children a-ftsa `my nephew', (...) and my brother's children$_i$ a-ʁi `my younger sibling'. They$_i$ call me a-ɲi `my father's sister' and I call them a-ʁi `my younger sibling' (140425 kWmdza02) 0003786
exe

If ego is male ( ex:BCh.MP ), one's parallel nephews and nieces (brother's children) are called by the dedicated term tɤ-mdɯ BCh ♂. This term cannot be used by women ( ex:BCh.MP.women ).

exe

aʑo tɤ-tɕɯ a-pɯ-ŋu-a qʰe tɕe, a-xtɤɣ ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit nɯnɯra nɯ-ɕki a-mdɯ ŋu. \\
1sg indef. poss -son irr - ipfv -be- 1sg lnk lnk 1sg. poss -brother gen 3sg. poss -offpsring dem: pl 3pl. poss - dat 1sg. poss -BCh be: fact \\
`If I were a man, I would call my brother's children a-mdɯ `my parallel nephew'.' (140425 kWmdza01) 0003785
exe

exe

tɕʰeme tɕe tɕe tɯ-mdɯ me. \\
girl lnk lnk genr. poss -BCh not.exist: fact \\
`Women do not have [any relative that can be called with the term] tɤ-mdɯ `parallel nephew'. (140425 kWmdza02) 0003786
exe

The reciprocal term of tɤ-mdɯ is tɤ-βɣofather's brother (§ sec:G+1 ).

ego 's parallel cousins's children
In the same way as paternal parallel cousins (FBCh) are terminologically identified with siblings (§ sec:ego.parallel.cousins ), their children (FBChCh) are identified with siblings' children: the children of one's male paternal cross-cousins (FBSCh) are called tɤ-mdɯ (§ sec:nephews ), and those of female paternal cross-cousins (FBDCh) are tɤ-ftsa ( ex:FBChCh ).

exe

nɯnɯtɕu tɕe tɕe li ``a-mdɯ" tu-tɯ-ti, woja, tɕʰeme ɯ-rɟit nɯ ``a-ftsa" tu-tɯ-ti, tɯ-mu tɯ-mu kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ cʰo kɯ-naχtɕɯɣ ŋu.\\
dem: loc loc lnk again 1sg. poss -BCh ipfv -2-say interj girl 3sg. poss -child dem 1sg. poss -ZCh ipfv -2-say genr. poss -mother genr. poss -father sbj: pcp -be.the.same comit sbj: pcp -be.the.same be: fact \\
`(Question: How do ♂ I address a-wa ɯ-xtɤɣ ɯ-ɣe ɯ-ɕki my father's brother's grandchildren? Response:) `In that case, ♂ you say a-mdɯ ` ♂ my brother's son'; in the case of a girl's child (FBDCh) you say a-ftsa `my sister's son', like [siblings sharing] the same parents.' (elicitation, 2019-11-30)
exe

The maternal parallel cousin are said by Tshendzin ( ex:MZChCh ) to be referred to using the same term as their parents tɤ-mɤtsa (§ sec:ego.parallel.cousins ).

exe

aʑo a-rɟit ra kɯ (...) aʑo a-sqʰaj ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit ra nɯ-ɕki tɕe ``a-mɤtsa" tu-ti-nɯ, nɯnɯra, ɣɯ nɯ-rɟit ra nɯ-ɕki qʰe li, ``a-mɤtsa" tu-nɯ-ti-nɯ \\
1sg 1sg. poss -offspring pl erg (...) 1sg 1sg. poss -sister gen 3sg. poss -offspring pl 3pl. poss - dat loc 1sg. poss -MFZ ipfv -say- pl dem: pl gen 3pl. poss -offspring pl 3pl. poss - dat lnk again 1sg. poss -MZCh ipfv - auto -say- pl \\
`My children (...) call my sister's children$_i$ a-mɤtsa, and also called their$_i$ children a-mɤtsa.' (140425 kWmdza01) 0003785
exe

There is some evidence that this rule was applied to all descending generations (§ sec:omaha ) in traditional society. However, Tshendzin also indicates that children of MZCh can be alternatively called tɤ-ftsa like sister's children (§ sec:nephews ), and reciprocate (to their MMZCh or FMZCh) using the term for MB (§ sec:uncle.aunt ). More data are necessary to confirm or disprove this possibility.

ego 's cross-cousins's children
The children of ego 's maternal cross-cousins ( ego 's mother's brother's granchildren, MBChCh) are referred to by the same terms as their father and grandfather, tɤ-rpɯ if male ( ex:MBChCh ) and tɤ-ɬaʁ if female: they are uplifted by two generations.

exe

tɯ-rpɯ ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit ɯ-ɕki tɕe ``a-rpɯ" tu-kɯ-ti, ɯ-ɣe ɯ-ɕki tɕe ``a-rpɯ" tu-kɯ-ti kɯ-ŋgrɤl ɲɯ-ŋu, iʑora kɯrɯ kɯ tɕe. \\
genr. poss -MB gen 3sg. poss -offspring 3sg. poss - dat loc 1sg. poss -MB ipfv - genr -say 3sg. poss -grandchild 3sg. poss - dat loc 1sg. poss -MB ipfv - genr -say inf: stat -be.usually.the.case sens -be 1pl Tibetan erg lnk \\
`One calls one's maternal uncle's children and his grandchildren a-rpɯ `my maternal uncle', among us Tibetans.' (140425 kWmdza07) 0003791
exe
summary:
The passage describes kinship terminology for ego’s children and various categories of siblings’ and cousins’ children. It shows that terms differ by ego’s sex and by the relative’s sex, with some relations treated as siblings or older/younger kin under Omaha-type generational skewing, and notes that some forms are restricted to men or women.

It also says that children of parallel and cross-cousins may be referred to with the same terms as their parents or grandparents, sometimes “uplifted” or extended across generations. The data suggest that these rules may have applied more broadly in traditional society, though the text notes that more evidence is needed for some cases.

text:
The children of ego 's paternal cross-cousins ( ego 's father's sister's grandchildren, FZChCh) and their descent are referred to with the term tɤ-ftsasister's child, like their parents ( ex:FZChCh ).

exe

nɤ-ɲi ɯ-rɟit ɣɯ ɯ-rɟit nɯ ɯ-ɕki tɕe tɕe ``a-ftsa" tu-tɯ-ti kɯ-ra. \\
2sg. poss -FZ 3sg. poss -offspring gen 3sg. poss -offspring dem 3sg. poss - dat lnk lnk 1sg. poss -FZ ipfv -2-say inf: stat -be.needed \\
`You have to say a-ftsa `my sister's child' to the child of the child of your paternal cross-aunt.' (elicitation, 2019-11-30)
exe

G -2
For the generation of ego 's grandchildren, the term tɤ-ɣegrandchild is used for ego 's own grandchildren as well of the grandchildren of ego 's siblings ( ex:ZChCh.BChCh ) and paternal parallel cousins.

exe

nɯ ɯ-pa pɯ-ari tɕe tɕe, a-wɤmɯ ɯ-ɣe pɯ-nɯ-ŋu, a-sqʰaj ɣɯ ɯ-ɣe pɯ-nɯ-ŋu tɕe aʑo tɤrcɯrca ``a-ɣe" tu-ti-a ɕti. \\
