dem 3sg. poss -down aor: down -go[II] lnk lnk 1sg. poss -brother 3sg. poss -grandchild pst. ipfv - auto -be 1sg. poss -sister gen 3sg. poss -grandchild pst. ipfv - auto -be lnk 1sg together 1sg. poss -grandchild ipfv -say- 1sg be. aff: fact \\
`To the [generation] below (that of one's nephews, see § sec:vertical.preverbs.time ), I say a-ɣe `my grandchild' [to all grandnephews], whether they are my brother's grandchildren or my sister's granchildren.' (140425 kWmdza02) 0003786
exe

In the case of the maternal cross-cousins however, the Omaha skewing rule still applies (§ sec:omaha ), and the term tɤ-rpɯmother's brother is used to refer to their grandchildren, who conversely call ego tɤ-ftsasister's child (§ sec:G+2 ).
summary: The passage explains that the term **tɤ-ftsa** ‘sister’s child’ is extended to the children and descendants of ego’s paternal cross-cousins, including the grandchildren of ego’s father’s sister’s grandchildren. It also states that **tɤ-ɣe** ‘grandchild’ is used not only for ego’s own grandchildren but also for the grandchildren of ego’s siblings and paternal parallel cousins. In contrast, for maternal cross-cousins the Omaha skewing rule applies: their grandchildren are called **tɤ-rpɯ** ‘mother’s brother,’ and they in turn call ego **tɤ-ftsa** ‘sister’s child.’

text:
kinship!affines
The terminology for affines in Japhug is poor. The only dedicated terms are tɤ-rʑaβwife and tɤ-nmaʁhusband; for all other affines, terms that also refer to consanguines are used.

Both ego 's spouse's parents and parent's sibling and spouses of ego 's parent's sibling are called using the terms for parallel aunts and uncles (§ sec:G+1 ).

Affines of ego 's generation, including those of ego 's siblings, are called using the age-based sibling terms ta-ʁiyounger sibling or tɤ-pielder sibling (§ sec:siblings.age ). In the case of ego 's spouse's siblings, both the age-based and the gender-based (§ sec:siblings.gender ) sibling terms can be used ( ex:HB.HZ.WB.WZ ).

exe

nɯnɯra tɕe tɯʑo sɤz a-pɯ-wxti-nɯ qʰe ``a-pi" tu-kɯ-ti, tɯʑo sɤz a-pɯ-xtɕi-nɯ qʰe ``a-ʁi" tu-kɯ-nɯ-ti ɕti. ``a-xtɤɣ" ra tu-o<nɯ>mɯ-ti-nɯ ɕti. \\
dem: pl lnk genr comp irr - ipfv -be.big- pl lnk 1sg. poss -elder.sibling ipfv - genr -say genr comp irr - ipfv -be.small- pl lnk 1sg. poss -younger.sibling ipfv - genr - auto -say be. aff: fact 1sg. poss -brother pl ipfv -< auto > recip -say- pl be. aff: fact \\
`Those (ego's husband's or wife's siblings), if they are elder than oneself, one calls them a-pi `my elder sibling'; if they are younger one calls them a-ʁi `my younger sibling'. They also call each other a-xtɤɣ `my brother' and the like.' (140425 kWmdza05) 0003789
exe
summary:
Japhug has a limited set of dedicated affinal terms: only wife and husband have special forms, while other affines are referred to with terms that also apply to consanguines. Ego’s spouse’s parents and the spouses of ego’s parent’s siblings are called by the same terms used for parallel aunts and uncles.  

Affines in ego’s generation, including siblings of ego’s spouse, are referred to with age-based sibling terms for younger or elder sibling, and in some cases with gender-based sibling terms as well. The example shows that these relatives are addressed according to relative age, using “my elder sibling” or “my younger sibling.”

text:
marriage
Marriage is prohibited between siblings and across generations between ego and ego 's parents siblings (whether parallel or cross-uncles and aunts).

Marriage is allowed between maternal parallel cousins ( ex:MZCh.marriage ), who call each other tɤ-mɤtsa (§ sec:ego.parallel.cousins ).

exe

kɤndʑi-mɤtsa nɯni tɕe ci ku-pa-ndʑi kɯ-kʰɯ ɲɯ-ŋu, kɯ-ŋgrɤl ɲɯ-ŋu, mɤ-kɯ-ʁdɯɣ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
coll -MZCh dem: du lnk one ipfv -make- du inf: stat -be.possible sens -be inf: stat -be.usually.the.case sens -be neg - inf: stat -be.harmful sens -be \\
`For two maternal parallel cousins, it is possible to get married, it is the custom, it is not wrong.' (140427 kWmdza stWnmW)
0003844#S3
exe

Cross-cousin marriage is tolerated ( ex:cross.cousin.marriage ), despite the fact they use cross-generational terms to refer to each other (§ sec:ego.cross.cousins, § sec:omaha ). There is here a contradiction between the terminology and the marriage rules.

exe

kɤndʑi-wɤmɯ-snom ɯ-rɟit nɯ pɯpɯŋunɤ, (...) ɯnɯni li ci ku-pa-ndʑi kɯ-kʰɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. tɕeri nɯnɯ ɲɯ-rkɯn. \\
coll -brother-sister 3sg. poss -offspring dem top dem: du again one ipfv -make- du inf: stat -be.possible sens -be lnk dem sens -be.rare \\
`Cross-cousins (the children of siblings of different gender) can also get married, but it is rare.' (140427 kWmdza stWnmW)
0003844#S4
exe

Marriage is prohibited between paternal parallel cousins ( ex:cross.cousin.marriage ), who refer to each other with the age-based sibling terms (§ sec:ego.parallel.cousins ).

exe

kɤndʑi-xtɤɣ ɯ-rɟit nɯ tɤ-ŋu tɕe tɕe, ci kú-wɣ-pa maka mɤ-kɯ-kʰɯ ɲɯ-ŋu. \\
coll -brother 3sg. poss -children dem aor -be lnk lnk one ipfv - inv -make at.all neg - inf: stat -be.possible sens -be \\
`As for brothers' children, it is completely impossible for them to marry each other.' (140427 kWmdza stWnmW)
0003844#S10
exe
summary: The passage states that marriage is prohibited between siblings and across generations, including between ego and ego’s parents’ siblings. It is allowed for maternal parallel cousins, and cross-cousin marriage is tolerated but rare, even though cross-cousins are addressed with cross-generational terms. In contrast, marriage between paternal parallel cousins is completely forbidden.

text:
lineage
Most speakers of Gyalrong languages lack a patrilineal family name in the Chinese fashion, unless they are of partial Chinese ancestry.

Family relatedness across generation can nevertheless by expressed by the term rɟitpalineage, borrowed from རྒྱུད་པ་rgʲud.palineage, which parents transfer to their children ( ex:praRwW.rJitpa ).

exe

aʑo nɯ praʁwɯ rɟitpa ŋu-a tɕe, a-rɟit ni praʁwɯ rɟitpa kɯnɤ kɯ-ɤ-rtsi ŋu-ndʑi, \\
1sg dem topo lineage be: fact - 1sg lnk 1sg. poss -offspring du topo lineage also sbj: pcp - pass -count be: fact - du \\
`I am ( Tshendzin ) from the lineage of Praqwu, and [therefore] my two children also count as being from the lineage of Praqwu.' (140426 rJitpa)
0003820#S4
exe

Lineage is transmitted by both father and mother ( ex:tWmu.tWwa.pCoR ), so that a given person can belong to several lineages.

exe

tɯ-mu pɕoʁ nɯ tɤ́-wɣ-rtsɯz tɕe, tɯ-mu pɕoʁ rɟitpa tu-kɯ-rtsi ŋu, tɯ-wa pɕoʁ pa-rtsɯz-nɯ tɕe, li tɯ-wa pɕoʁ rɟitpa nɯ pjɯ-rtsi-nɯ ɕti \\
genr. poss -mother side dem aor: up - inv -count lnk genr. poss -mother side lineage ipfv: up - genr:S/O-count be: fact genr. poss -father side dem aor: down -count- pl lnk genr. poss -mother side lineage dem ipfv: down -count- pl be. aff: fact \\
`When one counts from one's mother's side, one is counted as being from the lineage on one's mother's side, when people count from one's father's side (downwards), they count as being from one's father lineage.' (140426 rJitpa)
0003820#S2
exe

Lineage is preserved across many generations; even relatives who have moved to other places and become members of another household are still considered to belong to the same lineage ( ex:taRrdo.rJitpa ). There are no rules against marriage between two persons from the same lineage, if no other rule applies (§ sec:marriage.rules ).

summary: Most speakers of Gyalrong languages do not have Chinese-style patrilineal surnames, though they may use the term *rɟitpa* “lineage,” borrowed from Tibetan, to express family continuity across generations. Lineage is inherited from both father and mother, so a person can belong to multiple lineages, and it remains attached across many generations even if relatives move away or marry into other households. The passage also notes that there are no special rules prohibiting marriage between members of the same lineage, unless another rule applies.

Omaha skewing rule

Some uncertainty remains in parts of the system. In particular, the status of the MBDCh (and its reciprocal MFZCh) is unclear. In theory, given the MBD MZ rule ( ex:MMBS.MB ), one would expect that MBDCh = MZCh ( tɤ-mɤtsa ), and likewise that the MFZCh = MZCh (due to the reciprocal rule ex:FFFFZCh ). summary: The passage describes the Japhug kinship system as showing Omaha skewing, where certain kin terms are extended across generations: maternal cross-cousins and their descendants are identified with maternal uncles/aunts and their descendants, and several reciprocal equivalences are stated. It outlines three skewing rules, notes that some are recursive and that the system differs slightly from the classic Omaha type, while also mentioning a few unresolved cases where the expected equivalences have not yet been confirmed.

text: The Japhug system shows prototypical Omaha characteristics, in particular the basic skewing rules ( ex:FZS.ZS ) and ( ex:MBS.MB ), and the identification of paternal parallel cousins with siblings ( ex:FBS.B.FBD.Z ). It differs from prototypical Omaha systems described in the literature in lacking an Iroquois pattern identifying parallel uncles and aunts with parents (FB F, MZ M, ), maternal parallel cousins with siblings (MZS B, MZD Z), and the fact that preferred marriage is with maternal parallel cousins (§ sec:marriage.rules ) rather than with cross-cousins.
summary: The Japhug kinship system shows prototypical Omaha features, especially the basic skewing rules and the identification of paternal parallel cousins with siblings. However, it differs from typical Omaha systems because it lacks the Iroquois-like merger of parallel uncles and aunts with parents and of maternal parallel cousins with siblings, and because preferred marriage is with maternal parallel cousins rather than cross-cousins.

text:
Omaha skewing rule
A logical consequence of the recursivity of the skewing rule ( ex:kinship.recursive, § sec:skewing.merging ), as they are described by Tshendzin (§ sec:MBCh.FZCh.Ch ) is that a considerable divergence between biological age and age rank will occur in some cases. While a full investigation of genealogies is necessary to verify this implication (an endeavour that goes beyond the scope of this grammar), an anecdote reported by two witnesses suggests that this indeed used to be the case in the traditional society.

In ( ex:aftsa.beifen ), a man born in the 1950s reports his experience with the skewing rule: one of his great-grandmother (either MMM or MMMM, I could not ascertain) came from the village of Tshapa (with irregular orientation westwards, opposite of the geographical reality, § sec:local.toponyms.orientation ), where most inhabitants are from the lineage of her brother.

He thus had to call all the inhabitants of the village using the MB and MZ terms tɤ-rpɯ and tɤ-ɬaʁ, even young children. This report suggests that the recursivity of the rules as described in ( ex:kinship.recursive ) above is a reality: descendants of MMMB or MMMMB, even one or two generations below oneself, are still called MB and MZ. It also suggests that not only MBS*, but also MBDCh and their descendants might keep the privileged status (and thus not be equated with maternal parallel cousins MZCh as predicted in § sec:skewing.merging ), though this has to be tested with additional data.

Tshendzin reports the same anecdote ( ex:MMMMMBSSSSS ), and also indicates that the recursivity of the skewing rule is felt clumsy by younger speakers, who prefer to use terms for parallel uncles, aunts or siblings. This aspect of the Japhug languages is thus highly endangered.

summary: The passage argues that the recursive Omaha skewing rule can create large mismatches between biological age and kinship rank, so that even much younger people may be addressed with higher-rank terms such as MB and MZ. An anecdote from Tshapa supports this: a man reported having to call all villagers, including children, by these terms because they were considered relatives of elevated rank. The text also notes that younger speakers now find this usage awkward and increasingly replace it with parallel or sibling terms, suggesting that the system is endangered.

text:
The reliability of the skewing rule ( ex:MZChCh.skewing ) concerning maternal parallel cousins is confirmed by one particular case, in which a lady addressed her mother-in-law by the term tɤ-mɤtsa `MZCh' (who answered using the same term, § sec:ego.parallel.cousins ). When I asked her whether they were actual maternal parallel cousins (children of two sisters, MZCh), she answered that she used this term because her father himself called her mother-in-law (and her mother-in-law's mother) tɤ-mɤtsa, though they were not themselves true first cousins, the eventual consanguine relationship going back several generations. She also specified that she called her husband tɤ-mɤtsa before marrying him (§ sec:marriage.rules ).

This case suggests that the reciprocal tɤ-mɤtsa `maternal parallel cousin' relationship remains regardless of the number of generations in each lineages (as formalized in ex:MMMMMZChChChCh above).
summary: The passage confirms the skewing rule for maternal parallel cousins through a case in which a woman used the term *tɤ-mɤtsa* for her mother-in-law, even though they were not true first cousins. She explained that this term was used because her father had called the mother-in-law and her mother-in-law’s mother by the same term, showing that the reciprocal *tɤ-mɤtsa* relation can persist across several generations of lineage distance.

text:
As an illustration of the rules established in the previous sections, sec:cousin.once summarizes the theoretical possibilities for first and second cousins once removed, including the main points of uncertainty in grey shading. The equivalences are given below each term in brackets, referring to the equivalent focal kin ( tab:focal.kin ); for instance (=ZCh) should be read `called like the ZCh' ( tɤ-ftsa, § sec:nephews ).

The reciprocal terms can be rechecked using the inversion table tab:kinship.reciprocal above.

It is difficult to be fully certain of the reliability of these extrapolations without an in-depth study of genealogies. This Table provides a framework for future research on kinship systems in Japhug and Gyalrong-speaking areas.
summary: The passage explains that the table in the previous section lays out the theoretical forms for first and second cousins once removed, with uncertain cases marked in grey and equivalences shown in brackets to indicate the corresponding focal kin terms. It notes that reciprocal terms can be verified using the inversion table, but that the extrapolations remain uncertain without detailed genealogical research. The table is presented as a framework for future study of kinship systems in Japhug and other Gyalrong-speaking areas.
